## PREFACE TO THE READER.

I do not think I ought to fear greatly, Kind READER, that you will not graciously receive this present *System of Dieterich’s Biblical Antiquities*, since you so kindly received the specimen of the same which saw the light thirty years ago, divided into three distinct parts. The Author, <note>original: ὁ μακαρίτης — "the late" or "of blessed memory"</note> of blessed memory, undertook a Study <note>original: Meletema</note> primarily of profane antiquity as it existed among the heathens, and he considers the affinity and marriage, as it were, of the rites and customs among diverse nations in turn, and indeed in the order in which they appear in our Holy Bibles. Hence he gave and created for this book of his the title *Biblical Archaeology* <note>original: Ἀρχαιολογίας Βιβλικῆς</note>. Our Bibles, as we call them, are truly a tablet of all kinds of writings <note>original: πίναξ παντοδαπῶν συγγραμμάτων</note>, from which one may search, just as Erasmus aptly writes on Psalm 17, verse 4, page 243: "Such is the fertility of the Holy Scripture, like an inexhaustible vein, that something is always being dug out, nor is there ever a lack of what you may examine." From the deep ocean of archaeology <note>original: ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρχαιολογίας</note>—for many things from the outside are held in honor among many, both laws and other things—whatever is gathered from there certainly tends toward the praise of God <note>original: πρὸς ὕμνον τοῦ θεοῦ</note>. Holy Scripture is like some excellent panel which displays a painting drawn in various and ingenious ways; if you contemplate it longer, something new will always open itself up, which will be a joy to have seen. In Holy Scripture, traces of nearly all arts and sciences appear, to which fact I bring as a witness Charlemagne, who discourses thus in the *Capitulary on Images*, Book 2, Chapter 30, page 295, concerning the most profound treasure of all kinds of writings hidden in the Code: "Holy Scripture is a treasure, lacking no good thing, overflowing with all goods, to which whoever approaches with devotion, whatever he faithfully seeks, he rejoices to have happily acquired. Suppose the love of worldly wisdom and the secular school delights someone; let him approach the armories of the divine law, which precedes the wise of the world as much in the height of merits as in time; and let him rejoice to have known the depths of liberal studies which he knows, and to have found those which he knows not. There he will find the beauty of correct speech, the etymologies of names, varieties of figures, and tropical <note>In this context, "tropical" refers to tropes or figurative language.</note> complexities. He will find histories and meters," page 298. "There, in numbers through the art of Arithmetic, he will find the secrets of meanings and depths. There he will find Music, not only in the harmonies and instruments which most of the holy Fathers used, but he will even find its discoverer. He will also find the locations and dimensions of lands, which belong properly to the art of Geometry; and also the courses and positions of certain stars, and the variations of seasons, the cycles of months and years or hours; even the day and the cause of the creation of the stars, which belong properly to the art of Astronomy—there every studious person will recognize that he has found them."

<margin>Clement of Alexandria, 8th Miscellany <note>original: Stromata</note></margin>
When Moses, the Chancellor of God and the first teacher of letters among the Jews <note>original: πρῶτος ἐν ἸουDAÍΩΝ γραμματοδιδάσκαλος</note>, was commanded by divine order to build the Tabernacle for the better and more fitting performance of sacred rites, the whole multitude of the children of Israel offered from their goods what they could, with a ready and voluntary mind. One brought gold, silver, bronze, hyacinth, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine linen; another brought goats' hair and rams' skins dyed red, and Shittim wood. Each one strove to help and adorn the structure of the most polished and holy edifice they had undertaken, even if one contributed more splendid gifts than another. With the same readiness <note>original: προθυμίᾳ</note>, it is fitting for as many as have received any faculty from the Supreme Deity to contribute their token toward building the citadel of learned piety, lest we, the heirs of a far more ample and wealthy Tabernacle, be surpassed in promptness and liberality in so sacred a matter by those inhabitants of the Desert and the vast wilderness. We have the oracles of God <note>original: τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ</note>, written partly in the Hebrew and partly in the Greek tongue, by which alone we must stand and to which we must flee in unearthing the controversies of Holy Scripture. "In the Hebrew," says Driedo in Book 2 *On the Scriptures and Dogmas of the Church*, Chapter 3, folio 55, discussing the Code of the Old Testament, "we trust the Bibles of the Jews more than the Greek and Latin editions; and therefore, where a question concerning the true text turns among us, we consult their Codes, so that we may hold the true text of Holy Scripture from those from whom we received it." Erasmus acknowledges the necessity of the knowledge of the Hebrew and Greek languages, and commends it in every way in his *Method of True Theology*, page 65: "As far as those letters are concerned, by whose support we more conveniently reach Theological matters, without controversy the first care is owed to learning the three languages, Latin, Greek, and Hebrew, because it is certain that all mystic scripture was produced in these; although Augustine was skilled only in Latin, had touched lightly on Greek, and did not know Hebrew nor hope to, yet in his second book *On Christian Doctrine* he does not doubt that the knowledge of these is necessary for either understanding or restoring the sacred Codes..."

# PREFACE

->**PREFACE**<-

...to pronounce it necessary that, just as no one reads what is written if the shapes of the letters are unknown, so no one understands what he reads without a knowledge of languages. Later, having commended Busleyden <note>Hieronymus van Busleyden (c. 1470–1517), founder of the Collegium Trilingue at Leuven</note> and Poncher <note>Étienne Poncher (1446–1524), French bishop and diplomat</note>, who testified to their generosity in promoting languages, he proceeds: It is impossible by any reasoning to understand what is written if you are ignorant of the language in which it was written—unless perhaps we prefer to wait idly, like the Apostles, for whatever gift this is to come from the heavens. For I do not think we should listen to those certain people who, while they rot away in sophisticated trifles and unlettered letters until a decrepit age, are accustomed to say: "Jerome's translation is enough for me." For this is the primary response of those who do not even care to know Latin, so that for them, Jerome translated in vain. Furthermore, not to mention for now that it matters in many ways whether you drink something from its own springs or from any old puddles, what of the fact that certain things, due to the idioms of languages, cannot even be poured into a foreign tongue in such a way that they retain the same light, native grace, and equal emphasis? What of the fact that some things are too minute to be rendered at all? This is something Saint Jerome <note>original: "Divus Hieronymus"</note> complains of and cries out everywhere. What of the fact that many things restored by Jerome have perished through the injury of time—such as the New Testament corrected according to the Greek truth, or the marks of obelisks and asterisks, or the Prophets distinguished by commas, colons, and periods? What of the fact that the sacred Books were corrupted both long ago and are corrupted everywhere today, either by the error or the recklessness of scribes? What of the fact that Jerome alone did not restore everything, nor could he? What if he himself wrongly corrected or translated certain things? However pious a man, however learned, he was a human, and he could be deceived, and he could deceive. Many things escaped him; many things misled him. We have, I say, *the oracles of God* <note>original Greek: "τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ"</note>, which truly are, as they are called by the Leaders of the Rabbis, *the Sanctuary of the Lord* <note>original Hebrew: "מקדש יה" (Mikdash Yah)</note>. Here it is right for everyone to bring together all their counsels, to stretch every nerve of their intellect, and to strive with every work and resource, so that these things may be searched out and explained clearly. And indeed, the diligence of our fathers and ancestors brooded over this with care and heart, as so many monuments worthy of cedar <note>A metaphor for "immortal" or "long-lasting" works</note> left to us testify. One man *tracks down the hidden meaning in every word and every syllable* <note>original Greek: "τῇ ἐν ἑκάστῃ λέξει καὶ ἑκάστῃ συλλαβῇ κεκρυμμένον νοῦν ἐξχνεύει"</note>; these are called Grammarians or Philologists, that is, *those who skillfully account for the letters of the Scripture* <note>original Greek: "τὰ γράμματα τῆς γραφῆς ἐπισταμένως λογιζομένους"</note>. Justin Martyr teaches this in his *Dialogue with Trypho*; and the same opinion is held by Epiphanius against the Basilidians, when, regarding the interpretation of the word *kingdom* <note>original Hebrew: "ממלכה" (Mamlaka)</note> in the Prophet Isaiah, according to the sense of the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint (LXX)</note>, he adds an address to Students of Sacred Literature: *You might find, O LOVER OF LEARNING, even those things for your own benefit toward a love of knowledge and clarity for a pious composition and expression of the things lying in the divine scripture.* <note>original Greek: "Εὔροις ἂν, ὦ ΦΙΛΟΛΟΓΕ..."</note> For <term>Philology</term> <note>The study of language in historical sources; a combination of literary criticism, history, and linguistics</note> is like a common annual inheritance, and like a kind of generous workshop, from which grateful assistance is paid out to all disciplines, and foundations are granted to failing disciplines. Therefore, it spreads its use most widely into all sciences and contributes its labor everywhere—not so as to dominate by bringing laws to their subjects (which it neither establishes nor determines, nor approves nor defends). Regarding the old Philological freedom of treating Holy Scripture, Casaubon writes in *Exercise 14 on the Annals of Baronius*: In better ages past, in Philological questions of this kind—looking not at the heart and marrow of the Divine Word, but only at the husk—every learned man was free both to feel what he thought most right and to bring his opinion modestly into the open. In those Philological questions, no heresy is involved, no absolute necessity of feeling either this way or that. From the majesty of the divine utterances flashing with God-given names, and from various and manifold words and phrases, <term>Philology</term> and <term>Grammar</term> (which itself occupies the same benches) take their sacred origin—not to affect dominance, but to be in the service of the Clergy. Just as nothing befits a Merchant more than to understand the valuation of goods and the prices of coins so that he is not deceived, so to know the *specific powers* <note>original Greek: "ἰδυωναμίας" (idiodynamias)</note> of words and languages, lest he mix different accounts or substitute one for another, is the proper task of an Interpreter. Moreover, the path between words and things is mutual, says Strigelius in the *Wittenberg Colloquy*; the springs and foundations of things are learnedly shown in them, nor can they be unfolded without them, and their narration in the explanation of individual passages provides extraordinary utility, so that we cannot be guardians of the divinely purified doctrine unless we have learned and loved <term>Grammar</term> <note>In this context, "Grammar" refers to the systematic study of language and texts</note>, as Blessed Chemnitz says. Cicero himself, the Parent of eloquence, says in Book 3 of *On Duties*: Every treatment of any subject undertaken by right reason ought to proceed from a definition (of the name), so that it may be understood what it is that is being disputed. Deservedly, therefore, are those to be praised who, to adorn the tabernacle of God in the disciplines, *beginning first from the first things* <note>original Greek: "πρῶτον ἀπὸ τῶν πρώτων ἀρξάμενοι"</note> in a rightly observed order (without which one proceeding puts the reins on the horse's tail and places the light behind the lantern), investigate the force and meanings of words before they make the transition to the kernel of the matter itself. For the understanding of a thing, says Tremellius in his preface to the Bible, is to be sought not only from the series and continuation of arguments, but also from the nature of the words. In this kind of learning, the Scaligers and Casau-

It cites various authorities, from Church Fathers like Jerome and Justin Martyr to Reformation scholars like Chemnitz, to justify the critical study of original biblical languages.</summary>

# TO THE READER.

Casaubon, Vossius, and Camerarius, Glassius, and Fesselius, and those other masters of divine and human literature, whose footsteps I adore from afar and with reverence <note>original: "superstitione," here meaning religious awe or extreme scrupulousness</note>. One man uncovers the secrets of nature, their causes, and ancient philosophical matters from the Holy Scriptures, in which there is nothing that does not pertain to this subject. Another brings together the "overarching genus of theology, its proper causes and effects" <note>Greek: τῆς θεολογίας ἐπικείμενον γένος, αἴτια & παθήματα οἰκεῖα</note> from there for the "building up" <note>Greek: οἰκοδομὴν</note> of the tabernacle of God. Another brings forth certain things "from archaeology for the sake of God's justice" <note>Greek: ἐξ ἀρχαιολογίας... πρὸς δίκην τὰ θεοῦ</note>, by which a certain light can be kindled for various paragraphs of the Holy Scripture, especially those concerning common or specific matters. Indeed, it is the case with many ancient rites that nothing is more certain than uncertainty, since the customs and rites of men behave differently according to the position of places and regions. Thus, among one nation, it can happen that the same rite and custom varies as to places, times, and modes, according to the change of eras and governments. Look, I pray, even at the burial rites and wedding rites of Christians. In all of Germany, they vary in as many ways as the sky varies in April. I shall say nothing now of the author of "malice" <note>Greek: κακοηθειῶν</note> himself, the Devil, who indeed has remained one and the same in wickedness and fraud at all times since his first defection, but is "most multiform" <note>Greek: πολυμορφώτατος</note> in the diversity of worship, rites, superstitions, and ceremonies. By these means, he—the worst imitator of divine works—wickedly corrupted the sacred rites of the Jews, which were so often torn apart that one element hardly clung to another when they passed from the Jews to the Egyptians, from them to the Greeks and Latins, and thence to others. From this arose the variety of authors living in different centuries in describing the rites of nations and the monstrous worship of deities, which over the passing centuries became so confused and disrupted that, unless one is an Oedipus <note>A reference to the mythical figure who solved the riddle of the Sphinx; meaning a master of puzzles</note>, one can hardly discern the "emergence of the ancient god-makers" <note>Greek: τῶν πάλαι θεοποιῶν ἀνάδυσιν</note> among such a great discrepancy of writers' opinions. For, as error is variable, so also is the worship of the Gods, in which Satan played with various forms so that he might obscure in the common people the knowledge of the one Deity (which he could not snatch from the minds of the Wise), whom he harassed in wondrous ways, tossed about like storms by various delusions concerning their Gods and their foul worship.

<margin>* Question 114 in the Old and New Testament.</margin>
There were also, through the transmission of Antiquity—to speak with Augustine*—praiseworthy customs in common life, shared by Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins, all of which are dealt with here and there in this *Storehouse of Sacred-Profane Antiquities*. Nor is it permitted to wrap in a veil of silence that, while all histories fail and wander from the path of truth, the history of rites found in Holy Scripture is "complete and indifferent" <note>Greek: ἀδιάφορον; here meaning impartial or unbiased</note>. For the unique Biblical History preserves the law of truth most exactly and grants nothing to emotions, but treats far weightier and greater matters, the knowledge of which is wonderfully profitable for the happy administration of the Church and State, and for attaining eternal salvation. See where the Guide <note>Greek: Hodogeta</note> resigns his office and gives it up, since we must find rest in those things. Indeed, in obscure places where we cannot penetrate, nor have the Scripture going before us in a doubtful matter, even with any industry applied, let us feel with Johann Buxtorf*,

<margin>* 2. Defense of Hebrew Truth 13. p. 955.</margin>
who taxed the rashness and audacity of Cappel: "It is better," he says, "to hold back" <note>Greek: ἐπέχειν; a skeptical term for suspending judgment</note>, and in those things to admire the majesty and depth of the Style and the Divine Word, and to acknowledge the blindness and ignorance of our minds, especially in Histories and other things looking toward Sacred Antiquity, in which many things that are not recounted but kept silent can often provide the cause for an apparent "contradiction" <note>Greek: ἀντιφάσεως</note>, rather than to lay violent hands upon the Scripture. While indeed in both the Old and New Testament Codices of the Covenant innumerable places are found whose genuine interpretation and sense can in no way be tracked down unless they are illustrated from profane history. For it is evident to everyone that Holy Scripture has criticized the customs, rites, and superstitions of the Gentiles, and established prophecies against them, the fulfillments of which can nevertheless be known from the histories of the Gentiles, or their fables and "mythical" <note>Greek: μυθικοῖς</note> writings. Whence our Author, "a mind toward the holy" <note>Greek: ὁ νοῦς ἐς ἁγίους</note>, invested the talent of knowledge mercifully entrusted to him by God so that he might explain and illustrate those places of the Old Testament dealing with the affairs of the Gentiles, both sacred and profane, from the histories and fables of the Gentiles, from ancient common modes of speaking, as well as from the obsolete and long-antiquated customs of ancient men—the exposition of which in Sacred matters seems either certain, or doubtful, or even false and erroneous. It is truly to be lamented that, prevented by death, he could not add the final polish to this writing of his; for it is beyond doubt that this work would have seen the light much more polished and perfect had he survived. As for what concerns me, I have gladly taken upon myself whatever effort was spent in reviewing it, lest this labor, most useful to the Republic of Letters, should perish. But I have experienced in reality how difficult it is to be occupied with the labors of others, especially those which exceed the strength of the one undertaking them; whence I may preface with those words which Paschasius Ratbertus* uses,

<margin>* column 557.</margin>
when he comments on Matthew regarding a certain grave matter, saying: "Because we, thin and small, attempt great things, no one ought to despise us; and if we dare and presume more than we are able, I pray that no one should bar the gift of grace, at least the good which we desire"; looking perhaps to that saying of the Hebrews: "The thought of the desire is as the doing of the commandment" <note>Hebrew: מחשבת המאוה כעושה המצוה</note>—teaching that the intention and effort of a good work are to be held as the work itself. Or even among those who miss the final hand of the Author. Among them, I hope I shall easily obtain pardon for "slips" <note>Greek: Σφαλμάτων</note>, to whom the Blessed Author's method of excerpting is known—indeed, even his method of writing books, which consisted of mere slips of paper <note>original: "schedulis," small notes or scraps</note>, which he used to employ as faithful guardians of memory for assistance. Nothing was lacking in them, not the material (of which there was such a stupendous abundance of reading and diligence in the man, that if it had been necessary, he could have written a System much more often; whence little or nothing of my own, if you except the order and connection, was added by me, lest anything should be exhibited under his name which did not proceed from him), but only the order and the selection of the slips to be connected. Since it was otherwise customary for "the Blessed one" <note>Greek: τῷ Μακαρίτῃ</note> to mark the slips with a number and thereby indicate their order, posterity will not without cause grieve that his premature "dissolution" <note>Greek: ἀνάλυσιν; here meaning death</note> frustrated us in this certainly most useful and final labor. Therefore, that I have touched upon the same order everywhere, things being as they were, was "among the impossible" <note>Greek: σὺν τῷ ἀδυνάτῳ</note>, although greatly to be desired; but if at any time there were something for which I might congratulate myself, let the judgment be with the Kind Reader <note>Latin: B. L. - Benevolo Lectori</note>.

"Slips" <note>Greek: Σφάλματα</note>, if they occur anywhere in the cited authors, will also be "searched out" <note>Greek: ἐξητημένα</note> from the slips of paper; nor did I have so much leisure and library equipment left that I could investigate such a vast "medley" <note>Latin: farraginem</note> of cited authors, as well as not a few other "oversights" <note>Greek: παροράματα</note>, whether typographical or others which crept in due to haste, and the blemishes defiling this offspring—correct them according to your benevolence and humanity toward the "blessed" <note>Greek: μακαρίτην</note> Author. Warned of an error, I am an easy expiator, by the example of Cicero himself (than whom the Roman age saw no more perfect man), who did not fear to retract an opinion on a phrase, to "stay the oars," speaking thus to his friend Atticus: "That 'staying' of yours, which had greatly pleased me, now vehemently displeases me"; and when he had put Epolis by a "memory error" <note>Greek: μνημονικῷ ἁμαρτήματι</note> instead of Aristophanes, as also elsewhere Agamemnon for Ulysses, he immediately indicates this error of his to his Atticus and corrects it. I have come only to say these few things in preface, FRIENDLY READER, in the Author's name and my own; I shall conclude with the words of Augustine, which appear in Book 1 *On the Trinity*, Chapter 3: "Whoever reads this," he says, "where he is equally certain, let him proceed with me; where he equally hesitates, let him seek with me; where he acknowledges his error, let him return to me; where he acknowledges mine, let him recall me." Thus let us enter together the way of charity (and truth), tending toward Him of whom it is said: *Seek His face always.* It is useful that many books be made by many people in different styles, but not different faith, even concerning the same questions, so that the matter itself may reach as many as possible—to some in this way, to others in that. At Giessen, on the day before the Nones of April, in the Year of Christ 1671.

# FUNERAL ORATION
### Written and delivered on the 18th day of March, in the year 1669,
### In the solemn Auditorium,

-> ∽ <-

## By M. HEINRICH PHASIANUS,
### Professor Publicus <note>Public Professor</note>

### *Magnificent Lord Rector, etc. etc.*

<image-desc>A large square decorative woodcut initial 'V' adorned with vine and leaf patterns.</image-desc>

SCARCELY any medicine is as ready or as beneficial for the various calamities of men—with which they are tested by GOD—as patience. It is supremely necessary for mortals as the most certain anchor of the mind, toward which a very safe escape lies open when the most dangerous storms and waves arise in this hostile Ocean of human vicissitudes. Indeed, at the first appearance of evils, patience clings to the minds of the afflicted with greater difficulty the greater the misery that presses upon them; yet, with the passage of time and the nature of the evil having been perceived, it takes root in the breast. Having been admitted into a sort of companionship through long habituation, it begins to sprout, so that it is doubtful whether a greater power in enduring calamity should be ascribed to the aforementioned Virtue or to Time. And truly, one may perceive from various experiences that Time brings great momentum to affairs. For by time flints are worn away; by time the innate wildness leaves Lions; by the same, the ferocity of the noblest Horses is tamed, and the most savage Bulls bear the yoke, as that most ingenious of Poets, Naso <note>The Roman poet Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso)</note>, sets forth. Finally, it is well-acknowledged that if Time does not entirely remove grief and even the heaviest cares from the minds of the wretched, it nevertheless softens them.

Doubtless, it was for this reason that our Academy, weighing with silent sorrow the loss it suffered from the death of a Man who, while he lived, was the *Most Noble, Ample, and Excellent Lord Johann Conrad Dieterich, the most celebrated Professor of History and the Greek Language*, has until now deferred the duty of a pious Funeral Oration <note>original: "Parentationis," a speech honoring deceased parents or kin, here used for a beloved faculty member</note> owed to such great Virtues. To be sure, the Academy was waiting for grief and sorrow to be diminished by age so that minds might be rendered more calm, and that an oration might finally arise equal to the so many and so great merits of the Man—the kind of speech that cannot exist when a heart filled with mournful affections does not even allow those established in grief to keep a limit on their words. And this was indeed our prudent, and certainly pious, plan; but while we were hoping to carry it out by speaking the praises of the Blessed Man, behold! the slumbering pain has broken out afresh. The appearance of present cares renews the memory of a grief scarcely laid aside, and the Academy, which prayed against the deaths of its Fathers and hoped for itself to endure for a long time, is afflicted anew, with funeral following funeral. Hence there is such a void in the benches, as the Best of our Leaders migrate to the seats of the Blessed Souls—among whose number was also our Blessed Dieterich. He, indeed, has been made happy, nay immortal, by his departure, but he has provided us with the most ample material for mourning! Indeed, by the decree of Tully <note>The Roman orator Cicero (Marcus Tullius Cicero)</note>, it was not right to resort to antiquity and expect a medicine from time; rather, by the authority of the same Author, we ought to moderate our grief through reason and prudent counsel. But so many and such great evils, having delayed good counsel, have inhibited almost all use of calm reason. Therefore, let this oration degenerate into a lament...

# FUNERAL ORATION

...which was once intended to appear in a brighter and more joyful form; and mourn with me the fall of this Man. Mourn with the Republic of Letters <note>The "Republic of Letters" refers to the international community of scholars and intellectuals.</note> the fall of this Theologian, Physician, and Philosopher; mourn the fall of the Leader of the Academy; mourn the fall of a Man who was once a most faithful Father to his Family. And while I draw out the thread of my speech, showing why this grief is so justly stirred, favor me with your presence and tongues, and declare by your silence that he who has passed away is most worthy of this common sorrow. For while he lived, he aided the common good through his studies, counsels, and actions, and promoted its growth to the best of his strength.

MOURN, O Republic of Letters, the fall of this Man, Philosopher, Physician, and Theologian! And so that I may first draw the material for this public grief from his final days: how few are there who do not know that while this Man stood, a true Theologian stood? I say a Theologian, for as he was initiated into sacred study, so he blessedly died in the same. This will now become clear. He was born into this light at Butzbach <note>original: "Butisbaci"</note>, a well-known city of the Wetterauers, in the year 1612, on the nineteenth day of January, between the eleventh and twelfth hour of the day. He was born of a lineage fertile in great Theologians, such as his Father and Uncle, both Doctors of Sacred Theology. The latter, Conrad, after great service to his home University, became the most vigilant Pastor of the churches of Ulm; the former, Johannes, was first Pastor at Rodenau on the Eder, then at Kirchtorf, later at Butzbach, and finally both Pastor and Superintendent at Giessen. His mother was Barbara, from the most honorable Reichard family of Alsfeld. These parents took primary care to awaken the son's natural virtues. Therefore, having been washed in the fountain of Holy Baptism (from which, by the happy omen of his Father and Uncle, he took his name), and after he reached the years of boyhood, he progressed in primary literature and piety as much as his tender age allowed. Going further through schools both in his homeland and elsewhere, he was cultivated in the humanities to the satisfaction of his kin, and set his mind toward higher things. To this end, he attended the Universities of Marburg, Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentoratenſem"</note>, Jena, and others. How strenuously he bore himself in Sacred Study is shown by the many exercises in which he participated both publicly and privately. At Strasbourg, he heard Mr. Notter, Professor of Sacred Theology, as well as Dr. Schmidt, whom the Blessed Dieterich used to celebrate whenever his memory arose, as one who was to him "a good leader and first teacher toward the truth" <note>original: "πρὸς τὴν ἀλήθειαν κἀγαθὸν ἡγεμὼν, καὶ πρῶτος καθηγητής"</note>. Nor was he a lesser athlete in other Universities. For when he had gone to Jena for the sake of his studies in the year 1634, he held nothing more important than to approach the most celebrated Theologians of that place at that time, Dr. Johann Gerhard and Dr. Johann Himmel, and to enjoy their company and praised instruction in theological matters. And indeed, the business proceeded beautifully; for under the former he held a private *Syntagmatic College* <note>A "College" here refers to a private course of study or seminar</note> and a public *Galatinian* one; he heard the latter publicly interpreting the Second Epistle of Peter, and privately presiding over three Colleges: the *Aphoristic*, the *Isagogic*, and the *Anti-Wendelinian*, each a celebrated audience. And to show that he had not heard such great Theologians in vain, in the same year, on the twenty-seventh day of September, he gave a noble specimen of his theological knowledge from the public chair, defending theses on the Nature of God and Divine Attributes, which constitute the third Disputation in the *Isagogic College* of the Blessed Gerhard. There, Dr. Johannes Major, the Superintendent, examined and approved our subject's knowledge in sacred matters in a friendly discussion <note>original: "συζητήσει"</note>. Not content with having shown such a document of his industry, the following year, by his own effort, he held a publicly prepared *Anti-Wendelinian Disputation*, inscribed to the Theologians of Marburg; as he had written it learnedly, so he defended it against the tricks of adversaries, to the applause of all good men. Indeed, how highly he was regarded by orthodox Theologians living even in more remote places, such as Matthias and Brochmand (to say nothing of the rest), is clear from the various eulogies which the Blessed Dieterich left written to these teachers of his, to whom he professed himself a debtor even after death. How much Hieronymus Praetorius valued him for his Theological Study could be learned from his letters to a certain friend, if the nature of this undertaking permitted. In these, he calls him a Man of untiring Genius, for whom nothing is difficult, and whom he gladly sees and acknowledges as born for the highest things. From all of which I think it is established that our Blessed Dieterich was held in no mediocre place by the highest Theologians, and that the fame which had long placed him among the celebrated was not false. Indeed, for the weightiest reasons, he so applied himself to Theological Study that he nevertheless determined to give his life to others; throughout his whole life toward GOD, his Prince, colleagues, friends, and neighbors, he so conducted himself that you could see his soul was refined by true Theology. This shone forth from all his actions: in the sacred place, his Piety was observed; in conversation, his sincere Faith and...

# ORATION

Purity of heart, an untainted spirit toward all people of every condition and age, and such a character that knew He was with us—He who hears and sees all our thoughts, words, and deeds. Indeed, if we look deeply into all his actions, we will find that his life was spent in pure sighs directed toward GOD. Thus he spoke when pious thoughts about his Name entered his mind: *At my baptism I received the name Johann Conrad, with Dr. Conrad Dieterich <note>Conrad Dieterich (1575–1639) was a famous Lutheran theologian and Johann Conrad's uncle.</note>, then a Professor at Giessen and my father's only full brother, standing as my sponsor. The name Johann reminds me of GOD's grace, because in Hebrew it signifies the grace of GOD <note>original: "quod id DEI gratiam Hebræis notat"</note>; therefore I pray that GOD, the Greatest and Best, may kindly grant it to me always, both in this world and in the eternal life to come! And just as the first condition of his birth and the bestowing of his Name suggested most Christian meditations, so too did he very frequently think upon a happy departure from this life and a blessed entry into Heaven.* But why do I say he thought of it? He prayed for it most ardently, and these prayers are most elegantly recorded among his other writings as follows:

> O Lord JESUS! In the hour of my death, give me the efficacy of your comfort; grant that I may overcome whatever assaults there may be with a constant soul. Sustain my heart, lift up my mind against the weaknesses of the flesh and the temptations of the Devil; cherish the final palpitations of my heart through the bowels of your Mercy; extinguish the flickering sparks of failing warmth by the sprinkling of your Blood, and by the vehicle of the Divine Spirit, lead the breath of life to eternal rest. Amen! Amen! O JESUS! in whom are all things, Amen! Make it even so, Amen!

Indeed, how diligently he wished to be prepared for the struggle when his time finally came is more than apparent from the fact that he left these instructions to his family in his own hand: *As I am dying, let the words of CHRIST in John 5:28 <note>"Do not be amazed at this, for a time is coming when all who are in their graves will hear his voice..."</note> and Psalm 41 be set before me.* Since these passages deal with the Resurrection—the most effective argument against the fear of death and the fullest source of comfort—it is beyond doubt that our blessed Dieterich grasped this with true faith in CHRIST, and relying on it, resolved to fight against enemies of every kind with a great and undaunted spirit. What care he had for his small body even after death is gathered from this remaining writing of his: *If my bones can be placed in my father's tomb, this last and final duty of honor will be pleasing to me, so that as the bones of the son lie next to the bones of the father, they may together await the appearance of the Glory of our Savior in the universal Resurrection, which I hope will turn out as salvific and blessed for me as for my father. May the Supreme Deity grant that I hear that joyful voice: Enter into the joy of your Master.* To which he immediately subjoined: *Come, Lord JESUS! Come! That I may come to YOU, led to YOU through YOU.* As well as these little verses breathing pure piety:

->I give myself and have given myself, I shall give myself to YOU, O CHRIST,<-
->YOU shall be the Lord of my Life and of my Death.<-

And these things indeed sufficiently prove that our blessed Dieterich was a Theologian distinguished equally in doctrine and in life, whose intrepid soul not even death could break—death by which he passed to the Blessed, about to fulfill in every way what he had learned only in part while he lived on earth. MOURN the fall of this MAN, O literary Republic, as the fall of a perfected Philosopher! If I wished to begin here more deeply from his cradle, if I wished to describe more broadly the signs of genius that showed themselves in his childhood <note>original: "bullatâ ætate," referring to the 'bulla' worn by Roman children</note>, if I were to commemorate his youth and the sparks of spirit that radiated here; if I were to describe his most joyful youth, the applause of his teachers, the joys of his parents, the hope of his Fatherland, and the admiration of all; finally, if I presumed to narrate all the travels and various exercises undertaken by the blessed Dieterich for the sake of learning Philosophy, truly the material for this speech would expand too widely! Indeed, a day would scarcely, or not at all, suffice for the telling. It pleases me, therefore, to draw the curtain of silence over most things, content to touch only the highest peaks of his affairs, from which it may easily appear that the fame he carries through the world is far below the man's true merits. So that he might be led by the right path to Philosophy, in the first flower of his age he was educated in the school of his homeland until his fourteenth year under the city teachers, among whom the blessed Dieterich confesses he owes much to Georg Friedrich Kirchner of Thuringia, a strenuous instructor in more refined literature. The foundations having been happily laid, he was sent to Ulm at the request of his paternal uncle and successor—then the preacher and Superintendent of the church there—for the sake of acquiring richer erudition, under the then-Rector Johann Philipp Ebel and the Sub-Rector Johann Merck. His first six-month curriculum was in the Sixth Class, from which he was later promoted to the Seventh, which was the highest. However, he was not permitted to finish the course begun in this Gymnasium (which was then flourishing greatly), not indeed due to a lack of ability, but because of another impediment by which he was checked, so that he could not perform something worthy of his father's expectation and his own wish. Recalled from there, he was sent to Marburg, so that he might acquire firmer defenses for his letters in the Illustrious Pedagogy, from which he was finally released along with some <term>fellow students</term> <note>original Greek: συμφοιτητῶν</note> and <term>those educated together</term> <note>original Greek: συμπαιδευθέντων</note> and admitted to public lectures. Then indeed, with a high brow and contrary to the common custom of this age, he [resisted] the allurements of the body,

# FUNERAL ORATION

He began to look down upon those who constantly strive against the fortress of reason and lay snares for it, knowing that the cheaper slaves of the body are held fast by such things. He realized they cannot easily be raised from the lowest desires to taste that true and Highest Good which he himself strenuously pursued; that Good which, once conceived in the mind, invites one to honor—a truly Philosophical Pleasure, as Plato names it in his books *On the Republic*. He believed that this voluptuous life, overflowing with bodily delights, was brutal rather than human—a sheer night upon which no splendor of Virtue or Reason shines. He considered those bodily pleasures to be a Happiness shrouded in darkness, such as that described by Arrian in his *Libyan Voyage*, and which Hanno, the Athenian General <note>The text likely refers to Hanno the Carthaginian navigator; the attribution to an "Athenian" may be a contemporary error or specific historical reference</note>, happened to see. He believed that these allurements of bodily pleasure eventually turn savage against those who cultivate them, and that beneath their charms are hidden hooks and snares in which the wretched are finally entangled and perish miserably. He compared it to the Tarantula, which delights and tickles the senses while instilling a noxious poison into the body. Therefore, bidding farewell to these things, he resolved in his mind that true Blessedness—not of the body but of the soul—must be acquired through Virtue and industry. To this end, in the year 1630, he went to Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentoratum"</note>. Having presented his name to the Rector, Caspar Bitsch, Doctor and Professor of Both Laws <note>term: "J. U. Doctor" (Juris Utriusque Doctor) - a doctor of both Civil and Canon Law</note>, he promised loyalty to that Republic, obedience to the Rector, respect to the Professors, kindness to the citizens, and finally, a life conforming to the laws of the Academy. He stood by these promises as long as he remained there, and having finally been dismissed by his teachers with their blessing, he set out for Jena accompanied by the joyful prayers of those congratulating him. In this Academy, after various demonstrations of Theological learning mentioned above, he finally devoted himself entirely to Philosophical study, specifically to Languages and Antiquity. His fellow students who still survive know this, and it is declared by the scholarly Disputation of our late Dieterich *On the Use of Reading Profane Authors in Sacred Studies*, which was boldly defended under the Presidency of Master Dilherr on the third day of October in the year 1635. After this, by the common vote of all listeners, he obtained the reputation of a remarkably learned young man. Indeed, with what great industry he pursued his studies is manifest from this: not content with attending the schools nearest to his Fatherland, he also went to foreign lands—namely to the Dutch, the Danes, and the Prussians—and did not fear to draw learning from the entire choir of the literate, even at the cost of significant expense and the most certain danger to his life and health. For after his Father had passed away on December 27, 1635, he was called to Giessen by his brothers to settle private affairs. Having set out, he did indeed leave the College of Doctors at Jena, but so great was his desire to seek learning among foreigners that he could not be restrained from rushing out, even in the harsh winter, into the Netherlands through the very midst of the camps of most hostile enemies and the most dangerous places. Thus, having seen almost all the cities and towns on the banks of the Rhine, and having seen Cologne—that most ancient city—and its Academy, he was finally brought through Wesel, Emden, Arnhem, and Utrecht to Amsterdam. There, he stayed for eight days to greet the Professors of the Gymnasium, Gerard Johann Vossius, Caspar Barlaeus, and others. From there, after seeing Haarlem, he proceeded to Leiden, in which city the Academy then abounded with a wealth of most learned men in every branch of study. Those whom our late Dieterich chiefly consulted were Marcus Zuerius Boxhorn, Daniel Heinsius, and Constantinus L’Empereur. Furthermore, whenever access was open to the Library of this Academy—made famous by the manuscripts of Scaliger and Bonaventura Vulcanius, which happened every Wednesday and Saturday of the week—he unrolled the rarest monuments for his own use. Among these was the Eton edition of Chrysostom, upon which Henry Savile, the Provost of Eton College, is said to have spent twenty thousand florins. Here he publicly heard the celebrated Constantinus L’Empereur explaining clearly and in an easy manner, in the Hebrew tongue <note>original: "Ebræo ore"</note>, that golden "Alphabet of the Sons of God," the 119th and 110th Psalms; and privately, he heard him explaining the most learned of the Rabbis. Our late Dieterich very often confessed that he reaped the greatest fruit from this conversation, as well as from the mutual literary discussion <note>original: "συζητήσει" (syzetesei) - a seeking together or scholarly debate</note> with Johann Gronovius, who was then staying at The Hague; nor was this exchange of letters neglected when they lived further apart, one in Harderwijk and the other in Marburg. Having traveled through the Netherlands, a desire entered his mind to visit Denmark, so that he might go to Sorø and Copenhagen <note>original: "Haffnia"</note> and enjoy the libraries of this Kingdom and the meeting of learned men. While he spent a year in that Kingdom, he experienced such favor from the men of letters—especially Meursius, Stephanius, Burser, Lauremberg, and others—on account of his extraordinary gifts of mind, that he was recommended by Chancellor Reventlow to the King, and by the King to the Academy of Copenhagen for the office of Professor. That this matter is so, and not otherwise, can be made clear from the royal letters preserved in the Academic Archive.

# ORATION

...he visited for no other reason than to hear the Learned men, and to prove that he was not unworthy of their company. And indeed, at Königsberg <note>original: "Regiomontii"</note> he experienced the most pleasant kindness from the scholars who greeted and congratulated him. For he had scarcely entered the City with his guide, the most renowned Simon Dach <note>A famous German Baroque poet and professor at Königsberg.</note>, when the University congratulated itself on his arrival; received by individuals with the most generous welcome for several weeks, he entered the most well-stocked Library. He departed from there better equipped, as was his goal; for the Blessed Dieterich <note>The "B." stands for "Beatus," indicating he is deceased at the time of this writing.</note> frankly declared that while he had entered the City with great delight, he left it with far greater benefit. His mind, returning from such a distant "commerce" with the Learned, could not fail to be fertile; therefore, before he reached his paternal hearth, he deemed it worthwhile to seek the long-merited Master’s Honors at Jena. These he very easily obtained on February 19, 1639, under the Rectorship of the Magnificent Werner Rolfinck, a most celebrated Doctor of Philosophy and Medicine, with Master Daniel Stahl, Professor of Metaphysics and Physics, serving as his Promoter <note>The faculty member supervising the graduation.</note>. The Blessed Dieterich was not among those who, while still warm from the workshop of Erudition, imagine themselves to be deeply wise and ambitiously seek the highest honors in the faculties; rather, his first and greater care was to have a mind equipped with solid knowledge, and only then, as was the accepted custom, to receive titles. This is attested by an Epigram dedicated to the laurels of the Blessed Dieterich, inserted among other acclamations of friends by Master Johann Fabricius of Nuremberg:

->JOHANN DIETERICH, celebrated for your Father’s and Uncle’s virtue,<-
->*And for the riches of your own Genius;*<-
->*Whom Hesse brought forth, and whom friendly JENA held*<-
->*And cherished in her bosom for many years:*<-
->*You who have providently traveled the shores of the Belgians,*<-
->*And who are known to the Cimbrians <note>People of Denmark/Northern Germany.</note> by your speech;*<-
->*Why do you attain the highest honors of Virtue, long deserved,*<-
->*So late? If only it is permitted to ask.*<-
->*But if it is also permitted for me to answer, there is an old*<-
->*Proverb in chains: "Fast enough, if well enough."*<-
->*Since you have well deserved this honor of Philosophers,*<-
->*Let Jena now also bestow it quickly upon your return.*<-

Thus increased by these Honors, he was graciously called in the same year by the Most Serene Prince and Lord of glorious memory, Lord GEORGE II, Landgrave of Hesse, etc. etc., to profess the Greek Language in the illustrious University that was then at Marburg. He was to serve as an assistant to lighten the old age of Lord Victor, who had been granted an honorable discharge <note>original: "rude donatam," referring to the wooden sword given to retiring gladiators.</note> and was to enjoy leisure at home thereafter. With what skill and industry he performed his duty from the first moment of his calling, there is no need to seek witnesses from afar; I call upon you yourselves, Distinguished Listeners, who for the most part saw, heard, and approved of his laborious work. I produce as a sufficiently wealthy witness the said Blessed Prince, who ordered our friend to profess History along with the Greek Language. Truly, he never basely prostituted this professorial office of his; he did not exercise it for a paltry wage, nor for the sake of hunting his own praise, but he set before himself solely the glory of the Supreme Deity and, after that, the promotion of the good of his students. He always loathed the abjection and shame of Themistius and other Sophists, some of whom, out of a zeal for praise and fame, called listeners to their schools by providing grain everywhere, while others, like "merchants of knowledge," offered it for sale for a great deal of money. Tacitus and Athenaeus rightly and deservedly rebuke these men as slaves to glory and greed, catching either vanity or sordid rewards from their disciples. Our friend was not like this, nor was he from the choir of those who held back water so it would not flow to the public—men once fined by Themistocles so they might dedicate a statue of a Water-bearing Nymph. Indeed, he judged those of the Learned worthy of a greater fine who, with sordid stinginess, hold back knowledge—that great and free gift of GOD with which they are adorned. With Seneca, he desired to pour into others everything he knew, because the possession of no Good is pleasant without a companion. And from this it followed that, according to the innate will of a noble character to communicate himself, he so consecrated himself to the world that his heart and home were never closed to anyone. Instead, they always stood open like a venerable sanctuary of Erudition, to which, as to a perennial fountain of genius and learning, people flocked from all sides—not only youths, but Priests, and even the high priests of the Muses <note>i.e., great scholars or poets</note> placed in illustrious positions, whom the current purpose does not allow me to cite. Moreover, he persisted in teaching until his very last breath, believing that every dignity is adorned, not diminished, by a public Professorship; likewise mindful of teaching...

...the duty of teaching, which some have preferred even to the office of Praetor <note>A high-ranking Roman magistrate; the author is emphasizing the dignity of teaching.</note>, and that Isocrates, though ninety-eight years old, never ceased from his instruction. Furthermore, the pledges of his genius, labor, and industry are laid open to the world—monuments of manifold Erudition marked by the approval of the learned. The *Biblical Antiquities* deservedly lead the troop, followed in their own splendor by the *Historical and Geographical Breviary, the Breviary of Popes, Roman Antiquities, History of the Emperors, the Breviary of Electors, Counts, Doctors, Heretics, and Councils,* and the *Dissertation on the Use of Secular Writers in Sacred Matters.* These indeed are of historical subject matter. For the illustration of the Greek Language, the following late-night labors especially serve: the *Philological-Theological Lexicon* or *Illustrated New Testament, the Greek Etymological Lexicon, the Greek-Poetic Lexicon, the Harmony of the Greek and Latin Languages, likewise of the Greek and German Languages; the Greco-Talmudic Harmony, Commentary on Hesiod, the Aphorisms of Hippocrates Illustrated, the Hippocratic Medical Clinic, Greece in Exile from the Previous Century, Discourse of Travelers,* and the *Museum of the Entire Literary World.* Many of the leading men, admiring this fertile heart, labored earnestly to win him to themselves. We spoke above of King Christian IV of Denmark. When Breneccius, the Professor of the Greek Language at Helmstedt, had met his end, our Blessed Dieterich was nominated first by the Faculty of Philosophy, and afterwards by the public Council of the entire Academy to the Counselors of the Most Serene Dukes, to succeed in the place of the deceased Breneccius. It was even written down so that it might be clear what Dieterich’s mind was regarding the cultivation of this "Sparta" <note>A classical idiom meaning one's assigned sphere of duty or province.</note>; but since the letters were lost, and those at Helmstedt inferred the worse from his silence, the position went to another. Meanwhile, having discovered the matter, they grieved for this accident of their correspondence; therefore, a little later, lest they allow this man to slip away from them, they invited him to the Professorship of the Hebrew Language. Judging their inclination by this second vocation, he would have followed it, had he not considered it a matter of religious duty not to desert the Father of his Country, the Prince of most glorious memory mentioned above, who can never be praised enough. When the more serious disagreements arose in our Hesse between both Houses <note>Refers to the dynastic conflicts between Hesse-Kassel and Hesse-Darmstadt.</note>, he first withdrew to the court by order of the Prince to arrange the Archive; later, having obtained leave for a time, he betook himself to Hamburg in the year 1647, expecting a more tranquil state of affairs, but in truth seeking a greater apparatus for his Library while he was a little further removed from that constant din of arms. Scarcely had he lingered here for a few weeks in the company of illustrious men, when, beyond expectation, a very convenient opportunity was offered to him to serve the Reverend Chapter of Hamburg, in whose name he alone was sent to Osnabrück, while that most grave man, Dr. Johann Langermann, Counselor to the King of Denmark, was serving as Dean. And while Marburg was being afflicted by various fortunes, one business was born from another; while he held his mind occupied in the affairs of the Hamburg College, he became known to Salvius, the Ambassador of the Kingdom of Sweden, who showed him every benevolence, using his advice in Greek studies, with which he was captivated by love, spending whatever time he could steal from his chained labors. You see to whom and how dear our Blessed Dieterich was; you see how much labor, how many travels and difficulties it cost this man to finally present himself as a true Philosopher, and one who could promote the Republic of Letters. Since he did this so excellently, who is there who would dare to assert that his fall could be wept for with sufficient tears? How great his spirit was to be—upright, of course, and truly Philosophical—could formerly be guessed when, in an inn at Amsterdam, unfair hosts took away his entire travel allowance by a clandestine theft. For in this difficulty he took solace from Philosophy, uttering nothing but that saying of Cicero: *If fortune has taken money from someone, or the injustice of another has snatched it away, as long as one's reputation is intact, honesty easily consoles poverty.*

MOURN the fall, O Literary Republic, of your Dieterich, a Physician <note>Likely used metaphorically here as a "healer" of knowledge or a doctor of the church/academy.</note> of no mean rank. And indeed, I do not fear that I seem vain while I say these things, especially to those who know how he carried about a tireless spirit, most worthy of eternity, through all the monuments of the learned. Pliny, in the preface of his work, mentions a certain grammarian by the name of Apion [this is that enemy of the Jews, Apion, against whom Flavius Josephus wrote his apology, learned to the point of a miracle, in the opinion of Petrus Cunaeus in *The Hebrew Republic*, a work of wonderful Erudition and Charm]—Apion, I say, living with such celebrity of name, bearing himself with such a noise of doctrine and erudition, that he was called the *Cymbal of the World* by Tiberius Caesar, and was publicly held by all as the *Drum of Fame*. In our Blessed Dieterich there was no pride in his Erudition, no boasting or ostentation in public; he preferred to wait silently for the votes of the learned, rather than to be a seeker of public fame and a trumpeter of his own praise. And had it been otherwise, he would have acted the glutton by rushing with unextinguished passion through every kind of writing; but of books, but of Erudition...

# ORATION

...of [his] education. And to return to Medicine, from which I had digressed: how few are there who do not know that this man—whether you look at Theory or Practice—yielded to none of the most famous in this art? He held the writings and monuments of Galen and Hippocrates <note>Galen and Hippocrates were the foundational authorities of ancient Greek medicine.</note> as ready for use as his own fingers, to say nothing of other physicians, both ancient and modern. Those who have leafed through his *Hippocratic Physician* <note>original: "Jatreum Hippocraticum"</note> will easily grant me this; it is a work of inexhaustible learning, in which he does not merely strive to extract the meanings of the man of Cos <note>Hippocrates was born on the island of Cos.</note> hidden in the Greek language, but also discourses with a certain wonderful dexterity on medicine, diseases, the causes of illnesses, and various experiments and medicines. And who would have been able to illustrate the divine *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates with such vigorous brevity, unless he were a physician—and indeed no common one? The most excellent professors of that art have long testified to our blessed Dietericus being such a man with their most liberal praises. I remain silent on the fact that he led many privately in this study, as he does not deny in the preface to the *Hippocratic Physician*, where he expresses their names and explains how diligently they laid the foundations of their studies under his direction.

But, you say, what was said regarding his Practice is a fiction; for who ever saw our friend offering medicine to the sick, or visiting and helping the bedridden with his advice? But these objections are not so great as to make me change my opinion from its first proposal. I readily grant this: that he never visited any sick persons, that he did not prescribe medical potions to the faint, and administered no drugs to those failing; but who is there who will deny that he acted as a Practitioner while he gave, recorded in his writings, salutary remedies against every kind of disease? In this Practice he truly stood out as most successful, while he prescribed rules for himself, most useful throughout his life, which he spent almost entirely without disease by means of these, except for that fatal Fever which consumed the stubborn little flame of his life. These [rules] were Diet and Exercise—the former being the best medicine for the body without any violence, the latter rendering it vigorous—to which he was devoted to the point of amazement. 

Indeed, almost all who devote their labor to studies and keep watch for posterity are accustomed to consecrate themselves to the Muses <note>original: "Camænis"</note> in such a way that they sacrifice to no other profane gods, and with untiring effort they tend to and adorn the "Sparta" <note>A Latin idiom meaning "the lot or duty one has inherited."</note> they once obtained; but our blessed Dietericus so enslaved himself to his dead teachers that I do not know if many have had his equal in assiduity. He always hung upon their counsel; he was never outside their company. Never did the evening sky grow red but that our blessed Dietericus grieved that the torch for unrolling the monuments of the Doctors was being extinguished. Never did the Sun <note>original: "Phœbus"</note> bring back the light from the smoke in the morning but that he, with a watchful eye, waited for his library <note>original: "Musæum"</note> to be stained with the purple of the dawn, and for that which had been cut off by darkness to be opened again for his delights. And with this endurance of labors he lasted through the wintry sky, nor was the most biting cold able to wither his persistent ardor for reading, which remained even to his last breath of life; and as we find it was once decreed for *Vespasian* <note>Roman Emperor (r. 69–79 AD) who famously said an Emperor should die standing/working.</note> to lean and die upon imperial business, so it was for our friend upon the volumes of the learned. The Egyptians boast of some Mercury or other, called "Thrice-Greatest" <note>original: "Trismegisto"</note> on account of his knowledge of Philosophy, sacred rites, and justice. What need is there to turn to the Egyptians and follow the fictions of fables with vain inquiry? This man of ours was a true Hermes: namely, a most faithful interpreter of several languages, a Philosopher, a Physician, and moreover a supreme Theologian. But at last, if I look upon the face of our Academy, alas, with how much foul leanness it is marred! With how much deep filth it is filled!

**THE ACADEMY MOURNS** the fall of its leader; the Fathers mourn the loss of a most faithful colleague; the studious cohort and those whose heart's desire it was not lightly to touch but to imbue their minds with weightier studies, mourn the death of a most faithful Teacher. Here I again call to witness and adjure the consciences of all those who were once accustomed to flock to our blessed Dietericus for the sake of learning: did they ever return from him not instructed with more solid doctrine? Did they ever approach him without our blessed Dietericus shaking out his entire mind—stuffed with every kind of literature—for the benefit of his disciples? Asked about anything, he led the way; whatever he put his finger to, he showed what kind of things were to be drawn from which fountains of Erudition. And if it be permitted to attach my own example here, with what sad memory I recall him once speaking in profound dissertation at a private request concerning all antiquity, and opening with prudent counsel the method by which a solid mastery of all Greek Eloquence—both prose and verse—could be reached by a singular and brief method. He had outlined all these things to be published at last with most happy fruit, but death cut short this hope, so that I fear Greece must again go into exile, whom he had once happily restored from exile, and through this new daring he would have without doubt won her for us forever. But, you say, all these things, like many others, are in his notebooks. They are in his notebooks, I confess,

-># FUNERAL ORATION<-

But how few are there who can treat these matters with an artistry worthy of the subjects? For just as only Apelles might paint Alexander, Lysippus cast him in bronze, or Pyrgoteles engrave him, so it is scarcely permitted for any other to handle these sacred remains except for Him whom we now mourn as departed. There is an ancient dogma of Pythagoras that a wondrous Harmony is observed especially in the celestial bodies, a most sweet concert. And although Philosophers are accustomed to explain this regarding order, motion, and rules—and rightly so—I shall nonetheless, not without justice, turn this toward Academies and their Doctors, whom nothing suits so well as that Pythagorean concert attributed to the stars. These men, by the judgment of Holy Scripture, are likened to shining stars; and just as these stars adorn the ethereal orb with varied light and illuminate the vast globe of the earth cast beneath them, so do these men, with a harmonizing choir of virtues, wonderfully benefit and build up those below rather than merely delighting them.

In this regard, Dieterich <note>referring to Conrad Dieterich (1575–1639), a noted Lutheran theologian and educator</note> was conspicuous by his own light, equally skilled at illuminating his colleagues with his brilliance, scattering the rays of his virtues far and wide, and receiving those of others. However, just as when a mist arises and the splendor of the shining bodies is intercepted, much of their former beauty departs—indeed, the sharpness of the remaining lights appears dulled—so too, by the fog of death, darkness is brought upon the Choir of Doctors, the light of some being extinguished and obscured by the clouds of sorrow. And this is why the Academic Fathers and Leaders, established in mourning, have hitherto diminished their former splendor. They knew, furthermore, what a noble member of the Academy they have lost, and how he was both called and held by all by the true name of a Leader <note>original: "Antistitis," a high priest or overseer</note>. They knew with what great prudence his breast was fortified—prudence, I say, the soul of virtues, without which whatever remains of the others possesses only the shadow of virtue and holds no value.

If I were to presume to explain how great and how widespread this Governess of virtues stood out in Our friend, steering the helm for us all, it is amazing what vast material for a panegyric would be at hand! For there would encounter us no common prudence, not precocious, not superficial or tinged with dye, but a prudence to be called that of a true Nestor <note>The wise, long-lived counselor from Homer's Iliad</note>, drawn from the very springs of solid wisdom, by Nature, Experience, and the industry of Art. From the former were implanted his gifts: the sagacity of an erect mind and the dexterity of sublime judgment; from the latter, a long use of affairs conducted through the deep snows of his head <note>a poetic reference to his white hair/old age</note> to the fixed limit of mortality. From these stood a compendium for every kind of prudence: History, that *Witness of the times*, *Light of truth*, *Memory of Life*, *Mistress of life*, and *Messenger of antiquity* <note>A famous quote from Cicero's De Oratore</note>. These were his guides and familiars, just as Histories are the perpetual Dictators of prudence. And among these was Tacitus, that shaper of Heroes who hold the highest positions of state; he was held in such high esteem by the Emperor Tacitus (his namesake) that he was transcribed ten times every year and brought into the public Archives, preserved with solicitous care for the use of future centuries.

What other prudence, I ask, could emerge in Our friend but one that was choice and perfect in every part? In a man formed, as it were, by the hands of midwifing Nature as well as Art the Mistress, polished by living examples and the present use of affairs. What other Prudence could emerge from there but that which would snatch Magnates, Princes, and Kings into admiration of itself? But I am frustrated and vain while I attempt to adorn with words or narrate these and the remaining Virtues of the man—at the very least a farrago of so many distinguished things, illustrious by testimonies and greater than all praise. The Academy recognized these same qualities and often experienced them successfully in difficult matters. Many foreigners recognized the divine gifts of this Man—not men of the common count, nor idlers, but men of the most splendid and Illustrious status; what? I say Princes and others established in Majesty, who, after the setting of so many virtues, have put on mourning attire along with the Academy.

While I proceed through only the main headings of Dieterich’s praises, and narrate those things which excite the longing for the Man more and more within us, I fear, Gentlemen, lest I abuse your patience. Indeed, my mind is certain of this: that the remembrance of these things is most sweet to you, and that each of you is inclined to indulge in meditations mixed with joy and grief; yet it does not escape me that, however pleasant the memory of the most longed-for Man may be, my speech may not be such in your ears, which I confess is greatly elevated by the weight of the subject matter. Therefore, endure for a little while longer while I set forth the grief and its causes for the deserted Dieterich family, which being done, I shall conclude my speech.

*The illustrious Brother MOURNS the fall of his brother, under whose auspices the Dieterichian virtue was conspicuous to the world with its due rewards. He had turned aside to visit Our friend, if the gravity of business favored a fraternal greeting; and while they clung in mutual embraces, death tore them apart—it is doubtful whether there was greater brotherly faith and love among the living, or a longing to be recognized now that the other is deceased.*

*The Widow MOURNS the fall of this Man, she who gave help to her husband; the Sons mourn, who gave love and respect to their father; the household servants mourn, who had once religiously pledged to provide loyalty and obedience to their Master. And to speak first of the Widow, she rightly mourns her hus—*

<meta>This page continues the funeral oration for Johannes Conrad Dieterich, moving from his public academic achievements to his private life, specifically his marriage and his role as a stepfather.</meta>

->ORATION<-

...then undertaking such great care for him, cherishing, honoring, and looking up to him for his various virtues. He had married her with God as the matchmaker, friends as advisors, and an inner impulse of the soul as the driving force. To hear how happy this marriage was, it is pleasing to listen to the records set down on this matter by our Blessed Dieterich—records truly worthy of being unrolled as evidence of a most chaste conjugal love, in whose sight the ancient examples of love and loyalty usually passed around grow dull. They are of this sort: *I happened upon a wife according to my heart's desire: Pious, Prudent, and Provident. She was like a bee to me, going diligently to her work, laboring at home and abroad, bringing things into the house, storing them providently, bringing them out sparingly, shaping the whole family toward piety, training them for faithful service and ministry, maintaining order in household affairs, and seeing to it that each thing was performed in its proper order.* He continues: *In the year 1653, I celebrated my wedding with Barbara Bellin, daughter of Gerard Bell, a Senator of Butzbach <note>A town in Hesse, Germany</note>, whom I received as a widow from two previous husbands by the singular guidance of GOD; she blesses me with her charming veneration, her obedience, and her care for me, the children, and the home. She seemed to me to stand forth with the obedience of Sarah, the faith of Michal, the moderation of Abigail, the kindness of Esther, and the modesty of Susanna. With her, I sustained every turn of fortune, and by trusting in the presence of GOD, I overcame every inconvenience; I always found her to be the best of women, without any ostentation.* And lest it be suggested—as might be the trifles of the malevolent—that this love eventually grew old, behold the Epitaph which the most longing husband wished to be erected for his beloved spouse! *Here lies Barbara Bellin, the last of eight daughters of Gerard Bell, Senator and Juryman <term>Scabinus: a local judicial official or magistrate</term> of Butzbach, whom burning piety, German sincerity, unsullied chastity, and rare modesty fully recommended to Johannes Conrad Dieterich, so that he chose her as his faithful life partner in the year 1653. With her, he lived in a delightful marriage for many years, peacefully and quietly, without quarrel, without grudge, without trouble, happily and according to his desire. He found her to be fervent in prayers toward God, constant through various misfortunes and frequent labors, ready in spirit during uncertain times, strenuous in the care of the home, and solicitous in the education of the children accepted from her second marriage. Her husband wished this final Eulogy to stand in memory of their sweetest union, intimate harmony, sincere affection, mutual consensus, and incomparable loyalty, so that posterity may know, after the fated pause of our lives, that we loved one another.* V. These are the surest signs of a sincere and untainted love, the true effects of minds joined by God, which are not separated even after death. If that excellent widow, now established in grief, were asked about its end, she would reply the same as the noble matron Portia; who, when she had mourned her husband for a long time and was asked: *Which day would be the last of her mourning?* replied: *The same as the last day of my life.*

The household mourns the Man; the Sons accepted from the Mother’s second marriage mourn him—by nature a stepfather, but in care the Best of Fathers. A father's first care ought to be the forming of character in his children, namely so that wicked inclinations are rooted out, and then that they are instructed in proper discipline toward all honor. To procreate sons is a small thing unless they are well-instituted; nor would life be a benefit unless it were also a good life. Alexander of Macedon <note>Alexander the Great</note> acknowledged this well, doubting whether he owed more to his father or to Aristotle, the former of his mind; and even his father Philip, who gave great thanks to his gods because they willed his son to be born in the times of such a great Philosopher. Indeed, it is better for a son not to be born than to become evil through the neglect of a guardian or protector. Therefore, although our friend experienced a sterile bed with his excellent wife <note>meaning they had no biological children together</note>, nevertheless, while he transformed the nature of her sons—which, like all childhood, was prone to lesser things—and brought them back to good fruit by both precept and example, he must be said to have entirely fulfilled the role of the best Parent. Known is the law of Solon <note>An Athenian lawmaker</note>, which was always judged most wise among the ancients, by which it was ordained that a son did not owe the necessary supports of life to a father from whom he had received no trade. Indeed, it is also known from Dio that those sons were prohibited from the tombs of their ancestors who had neither learned doctrine nor practiced any art. Here, lest the Father or the sons commit any fault against the other, there was a struggle on both sides: he to prescribe, teach, and exhort; they to be obedient to their father’s word, to comply, and to make progress. By this very fact, it has come to pass that those who were once pupils worthy of paternal instruction have now come forth formed as an Example to others, from which posterity will learn how great a matter it is to have Parents to whom the education of children is a matter of care and heart. And so, I think it is established how mournful the death of our Blessed Dieterich has been for the entire Republic of Letters, the University, and finally his Family. But truly, such is not the condition of the most blessedly deceased. If our affairs are in a worse state since he migrated to the seats of the Blessed, it is not so for the great soul of Dieterich. We, indeed, almost waste away with longing for him, but his soul, triumphing in heaven, enjoys the perpetual company of Angels; a great soul, once a noble deposit among us, now received into heaven and carried above the falling things of earthly matters, exists blessed in the sight of God.

# FUNERAL TRIBUTE

<note>original: "PARENTALIS"</note>

...now exists. She <note>The soul of the deceased, referred to in the feminine Latin 'anima'</note>, now ignorant of our longings, enjoys a secure and deep peace. Established in the harbor of tranquility, she congratulates herself that after arduous study, after sweat and so many wicked labors—equal to those of Hercules—she has finally obtained the crown from the hand of the Supreme Judge <note>original: "Diribitor," a Roman official who distributed ballots or prizes</note>. These joys, if they do not entirely remove our sadness, nevertheless mitigate it; her gain compensates for our loss, and her triumphal grace consoles our solitude. To us, indeed, the Blessed Dietericus is dead, but he has begun to live for himself. He had lived long enough on earth; he had adorned his station <note>original: "ornarat spartam suam," a classical idiom meaning to do one's duty in the position one was born into</note> as much as was sufficient for his glory; nothing else remained but to live henceforth a heavenly and eternal life. **For that is not to be called life which is contained within the body and spirit, but that which flourishes in the memory of all ages, which posterity nourishes, and which eternity itself always gazes upon.** Although, his praise shall not die out among us on this earth either. And here is a prepared panacea <note>a universal remedy</note> against mortality: he shall live among us, and his memory will be present in the minds of all good men as long as the centuries are counted, and late-born grandsons will admire his virtue and his writings. His fame will flourish, which posterity will cherish as long as it values virtue. Nor shall any day be the last for the glory of his Name, except that which shall hasten the end of the world.
