Once the beam of wisdom for Giessen <note>original: "Gissiaciæ"</note> and its University,
DIETRICH, the splendor and love of our choir,
Not weary of the pen, having labored in sacred fields,
Gathers a harvest of praise in honor of his study.
Scraps of paper lay piled up in skillful heaps;
He knew how to build a great work from small beginnings.
Gifts shine from his writings, spread throughout the lands;
The Muse <note>original: "Cleio" (Clio), the Muse of History</note> would have wished for more streams from the man.
He honored the maxims of Hippocrates and the famous decrees
Of Themis <note>Goddess of Justice</note>, a greedy drinker of the Aonian water <note>The spring of the Muses</note>.
Whatever the order of ages brought forth from the Ancients,
He was a powerful user of that knowledge.
In historical series, the deeds of the Roman Monarchs
With the Pope, his charts are able to enumerate.
He was skilled in the Hebrew tongue, and taught the Greek;
He brought forth the riches of wealth from the fertile vein of his mind.
This work, printed at the expense of SEILER, shows
To the world, and distributes distinguished titles.
You see oracles taken from the inner shrines of the Word,
The sacred mysteries of the Mystic Way illustrated in new modes.
He is fervent for the diligent cultivators of the Muses; suitable
For theologians, the reader will grasp very great knowledge.
Let it not be a burden to pluck flowers from the flowering garden;
A joyful scent of things overflows from there.
With ever-watchful study, turn the volume cup by cup;
It will unlock the sacred senses of the mind of God.
Let his Honor live in books, and let the DIETRICH fame
Grow, and the honor of his merit not die.
The PISTORIAN Muse <note>Referring to the editor or collaborator Pistorius</note> applied no mean labors
To publishing this work; may he live in the citadel of Heaven!
The labor of DIETRICH and the arrangement of things by PISTORIUS!
After death, let these be the monuments of their fame!

### (o)
## With God’s Blessing! <note>original: "Q. D. B. V." (Quod Deus Bene Vertat), a common formula for success.</note>

The fame of Dieterich’s knowledge
Has left behind for the learned world,
Not without glory, polished monuments
Of his genius: his books.
Behold his *Biblical Antiquities*,
And you will clearly gather
The wide-ranging reading of the MAN,
Shining forth alongside his Piety.
Oh! Had he but reached—so I often said,
Grieving his passing—the days of Nestor <note>A legendary Greek hero known for his extreme old age and wisdom.</note>,
A man worthy, in the judgment of Apollo himself,
Of an Isocratic old age <note>Referring to the Greek orator Isocrates, who lived to be nearly 100.</note>.
While I was recently ruminating on these things
With curious sharpness, I seemed to perceive
The spirit of the excellent DIETERICH,
And thus he seemed to rebuke my prayer:
"Why do you, too harsh, envy the rest
Which your friend now enjoys?
Do you wish him to exchange life for death,
And eternal radiance for shadows?
Oh, cease to pray so, cease!
He who has once been made an inhabitant
Of eternity, scorns the distinguished
But heartless deceptions of this fleeting world.
One thing is necessary, if you desire to live.
After so many learned papers of mine,
What, I ask, would have remained at last,
Unless death had confirmed the final stroke

<column-break/>

Right here? Unless there had been a good
Conclusion to my life? Believe it, posterity:
To strive for fame is worthy of praise;
But for everyone, to die well is a necessity!"
Soon I stand like one awakened,
And was I perhaps playing with an image in my mind,
While I seemed to have seen his spirit?
Away with the shadows of superstition,
Which the beam of a purer faith
Has scattered all; away with the surviving
Anxieties of the gloomy Pagans.
(For I know better things). I was hardly finishing
This conversation within my own heart,
When I see brightest TRUTH
Standing near us with her companion PIETY.
"We," they said, "when we saw you
Oppressed by various anxieties,
Have come as Sisters to warn you,
Plucking at your ear with a whisper;
Behold, those whom you thought you saw
With these eyes were spirits! Give place to our warnings.
For if DIETERICH were to return,
He would say nothing else to the world."
I acknowledge, O pious people, the favor
Of your heart (I continue). No knowledge
Shall please me further, if TRUTH
Should be left destitute of PIETY.

Intent on things, DIETERICH proved with skill,
A wise **PHILOLOGIST**, what the holy letters of God
Signify; his care is for the symbols of sacred things,
And how much the value of gold differs from brass:
Nor does he linger merely on signs; he brings the mysteries
Of Light into the open, and drags them from the darkness.
With how much judgment and how much labor of mind
It is established to give mystical meanings to divine things,
He preferred to excel so greatly through labor,
And gradually break the threads of his own life,
Rather than leave the well-begun things of God raw after his fate,
Lest he should mark his entrusted gifts as exhausted.
He obtains his wish; he fell, and hardly sees the colophon <note>The finishing stroke or concluding statement of a book.</note>
Of such a precious work without it shining.
Lest the papers lie without order—divine pastures—
A skillful restorer of the dispersed work is then present,
Who, when he had overcome all that was prepared by sweating,
Sank down, oppressed by the weight of the stone <note>A metaphor for the burden of the work or perhaps a reference to a gravestone.</note>.
Each lived piously, each labored in the same task,
And the end of life and of the work was at the same time.

Thus, he venerates the work, and admires the singular labors, virtues, and merits of the piously deceased Author, his most longed-for Colleague, who deserved so well of our University and the whole Republic of Letters,

<summary>This page features two funeral elegies honoring Conrad Dieterich, praising his monumental scholarship in Biblical studies and philology while emphasizing that his intellectual pursuits were always guided by piety. The second poem notes that Dieterich died just as his work was reaching completion, and his successor in the task also passed away shortly after.</summary>

<meta>This page serves as the introductory front matter for Johann Conrad Dieterich’s work on Biblical Antiquities, featuring a dedicatory poem and several letters of recommendation (testimonia) from contemporary scholars dated between 1635 and 1671.</meta>

->( * )<-

The care of the Prince is for these very volumes,
->the Sacred ones,<-
The Biblical Antiquities
Which the Dietrichian Muse has brought forth for you
With watchful zeal, and now offers; cherish them.
The virtue of the descendants of Abraham, and the customs of the Eastern Nation
You shall learn—noted and most worthy things—
Which, if unknown, you can scarcely and skillfully
Comprehend many of the sacred oracles.

<column-break/>

You will not be able to cross the seas
And the wandering waters of the deep without a wooden horse <note>original: "durateo... caballo"; a poetic reference to a ship, likening it to the Trojan Horse</note>:
So, he who commits himself to the sacred Sea [of scripture],
Unless he has this boat and small skiff
Which the sharp genius of the great Dieterich
Has constructed,
Will scarcely ever reach the shores.
Come here then, use this work with success,
You will not regret it; farewell!

<column-break/>

->In honor of the Blessed Master Author, a Patron to be greatly respected while he lived; and in well-deserved praise of the Blessed Master Arranger, his most honored fellow-godfather, without whose help that distinguished Treasury of Antiquities would have lain in darkness, [the following] was written out of duty at Giessen, April 3, 1671.<-

### M. JOHANNES PETRUS RODAVG of Giessen
->Court Pastor and designated Inspector of Birkenfeld.<-

---

### There follow certain Testimonies and Poems of formerly most Distinguished Men concerning the first dissertation of the Author of Blessed Memory <note>original: "Μακαρίτου" (Makaritou)</note> regarding the use of Philology <note>term: Philology; here meaning the study of ancient languages and classical literature to better understand historical texts</note> in sacred and profane literature.

### From the letters of the Magnificent Lord Bernhard Bertram, Chancellor of Altenburg, to Doctor Gerhard.

The Philological Dissertation, which you sent to me in recent days, most Reverend and Excellent Gerhard, is entirely to our taste. I congratulate the Author, Dieterich, on the most praiseworthy gifts of genius which shine forth everywhere in this little work. What he undertakes is great and sublime. For "much-learning" <note>original: "Πολυμαθεία" (Polymathia)</note> and "love of language" <note>original: "φιλολογία" (philologia)</note>—what are they but a sea of sciences? Indeed, such are the beginnings that one may easily guess what the progress will be. That he thinks so honorably of the Son, "now among the saints" <note>original: "νῦν ἐν ἁγίοις" (nyn en hagiois)</note>, is not only pleasing to me but brings the greatest comfort. Truly, I have a few things which could be conveniently advised regarding one or two passages, but, lest I seem to rush into those sacred matters of the Academic Muses, I abstain. I suggest only this: that the Apostolic "fighting with beasts" (1 Corinthians 15:32) seems to be taken metaphorically, not literally. For it is not to be believed that the Blessed Paul would have wished to indicate such a notable history, if the matter were so, in only a single word. Rather, he perhaps looked to those things which the Apostle suffered at Ephesus; alluding at the same time to the ferocious and almost beast-like customs of the Ephesians, on account of which they are called "beasts" <note>original: "θηρία" (theria)</note> by their own citizen Heraclitus in that letter which he wrote to Hermodorus. I omit other things which most learned men have commented upon more fully on this matter.

### Johannes Saubertus to Dilherr
->November 14, Year 1635.<-

For the gift sent to me, dear as gold, I am a debtor; but in good faith, I shall think upon the payment. I salute the Author of such a worthwhile work, Master J. Conrad Dieterich, and ask that he continue.

### Hieronymus Reckleben, Professor of the Aristotelian Organon in the Academy of Leipzig, in a Letter to M. Gothofredus Schreiter, March 10, Year 1636.

I have examined the Philological [dissertation] held under Dilherr, in which many things please me. However, I think it is a "slip of memory" <note>original: "σφάλμα μνημονικὸν" (sphalma mnemonikon)</note> that in letter K. 1. b. it is said from Alciati that he refutes the opinion of those asserting that Christ was placed upon the pinnacle of the temple by the work of the Devil, and tempted there: for how can these things be refuted which are expressly held in Matthew 4? A distinction must be made between the leading into the desert and the temptation. Christ was led away into the desert by the Holy Spirit, but was tempted by the Devil, which the whole of Matthew chapter 4 clearly affirms.

The letters discuss specific theological interpretations, such as Paul's "fighting with beasts" and the details of Christ's temptation.</summary>

### To the Author: Words of Greeting <note>original: "προσφωνητικὰ" (prosphōnetika) - a Greek term for a welcoming or dedicatory address</note>

Take up the triumphal wreath which Apollo <note>The Greek god of music, poetry, and knowledge</note> gives to you,
**DIETERICH**; it has been earned by your studies.
All applaud; my Muse rejoices that the crown
is now bestowed upon you, offering these prayers:
*AS YOUR TITLE INCREASES, MAY YOUR HONOR GROW ALSO, AND FROM THENCE*
*MAY THE COMMONWEALTH RECEIVE A THOUSAND BENEFITS FOR ITSELF.*

->To the distinguished man<-
->**DIETERICH**<-
->For the erudition, learning, character, and reputation which he has acquired for himself<-
->By his genius, labors, studies, travels, and writings,<-
->*he congratulates him from the heart*<-
->**Werner Rolfinck, of Hamburg, Doctor of Philosophy and Medicine,**<-
->**Rector of the University of Jena.**<-

---

->TO<-
# JOHANN CONRAD DIETERICH.
->Teacher of Greek Literature, industrious Philologist,<-
->Colleague.<-

When that loud-sounding trumpet of GOD, **SAUBERT** <note>Johann Saubert (1592–1646), a prominent theologian and librarian at Nuremberg</note>, once
began to scatter his words in the manner of a Philologist <note>term: Philologist - here meaning a scholar of language and historical texts, especially one who applies these skills to the Bible</note>,
I, a Poet, sang along: "If this man penetrates to the depths
of Sacred things, he will nourish himself in the eternal book."
And no sooner said than done: now he ponders the innermost Sacred mysteries,
and now he has his dwelling place in the heavenly book.
You shall be the same: you scrutinize the hidden names of things,
and weigh them with silent lips.
But you are busy smearing those things upon paper with the nib of your pen,
and this ink shall carry you even to the bright heavens.
I scarcely believe there are some men—yet they seem to exist—
who, being foolish, love to "find a knot in a bulrush" <note>A Latin proverb (nodum in scirpo quaerere) meaning to find a difficulty where there is none</note>.
Senseless ones, whose heads are empty of brains,
they deny that intricate threads are woven through the Sacred Volumes.
Whoever you are, who seek such things in sacred arguments,
may you wish to keep yourself within the boundaries.
And remember to avoid "nothing in excess" <note>A famous Greek maxim (mēden agan) advising moderation</note>;
follow the lead and the path of **DIETERICH**.
It is a matter of genius to hand oneself over to books in such a way,
and to dig out nothing that is not useful from those books.
This is what it means to show oneself a Philologist: to reveal the languages
in sacred matters, and to reveal the worthy things themselves.

->**Conrad Bachmann wrote this with difficulty,**<-
->**at the age of 70.**<- <note>Bachmann was a professor of poetry and history at Giessen</note>

---

There is need of a Key of Wisdom: unlock what is hidden, Dieterich;
There is need of a Key again: Dieterich, hide away what is open;
But take care, lest a counterfeit key commit any fault against you.

->*At the walls of Bellona <note>The Roman goddess of war; likely a metaphorical reference to the turbulent times of the Thirty Years' War</note>, to his very dear and truly faithful friend,*<-
->**Johann Theil / Master of Arts and Poet Laureate.**<-

<meta>This page contains commendatory poems (laudatory verses) written by colleagues and friends of the author, Johann Conrad Dieterich, celebrating the publication of his work on antiquities. These verses serve as a formal preface to establish the author's scholarly authority.</meta>

# JOHANN CONRAD DIETERICH,
## RUN IN THE RACE, A GLORY IN THE STADIUM.

> *What the glory of the stadium was, and what that of the ancient Circus,*
> *is well known, and you, Dieterich, teach it in this book.*
> *But to have taught is too little, and to show with thin hands,*
> *how you yourself do not stretch toward the path, nor tread it before others.*
> *You have entered the stadium, but a sacred one, and of such a kind, dedicated*
> *to that which God wills to be His own and befits Heaven.*
> <note>The poet uses the metaphor of an ancient Greek athletic race to describe Dieterich's rigorous scholarly pursuit of sacred history.</note>
> *Run as you have begun, complete the race with a favorable foot,*
> *and seek the glory which honor has placed in this task.*
> *I shall honor the runner with applause, my friend, and for me*
> *I wish you to be Euryalus, and so I shall be Nisus to you.*
> <note>Nisus and Euryalus were famous inseparable friends and competitors in Virgil's Aeneid.</note>

->Johann Hirthenius, sends greetings.<-

---

## TO THE AUTHOR.
### An acclamation regarding the useful discussion of the Use and Abuse of profane rites in Sacred matters.

Great Friend, and my sweet glory,
And the primary part of my companions,
DIETERICH, a head destined 
Perpetually for the Muses: O heart consecrated
To eternity, and intimate
Searcher of antiquities which the Sacred records bring forth,
Beyond the genius and manner 
Of this over-swollen age!
For who has given so many antiquities of the Greeks,
And of the riches of India?
Who of the Syrians or of Latium <note>Ancient Rome</note>
So excellently applied to Sacred rites?
This great gift, which you have meditated upon,
DIETERICH, will prepare for you 
A perpetual laurel which shall rise with its leaf:
Nor shall a future age remain silent.
You, with a wise pen, have uncovered 
The cares of the wise and the secret 
Counsel of the Sacred mysteries 
To those who shrink from the paths 

<column-break/>

Of insolent idleness with effort; nor do you listen 
To what the lazy crowd snarls at you 
With an impudent mouth. For 
This unskilled and wretched race 
Is unable to go higher: Blessed 
And famous enough, if it knows how to explain 
From the professor's chair those light trifles 
Which the proud race of Scholastics 
Teaches its own with an arrogant mind.
O vain crowd, and playful Nation!
Glory is not in this wrestling-school, 
But it is a workshop of idleness, worthy of the Vulgar,
Who know not how to penetrate 
The secrets of Wisdom; they stand far off from those Sacred things
Which Apollo <note>The god of light and knowledge</note> brings. You, DIETERICH, 
Will repel this wicked cattle, born for the 
Victims of the Gods, with your excellent daring,
By pressing with the edge or more likely the point <note>original: "Casim, seu mage... Punctim" - terms from fencing/swordplay</note> 
As you wish, so that hereafter 
The profane man may never touch the Sacred things 
Which he neither understands, 
Nor will ever understand.

->Thus he congratulates his friend at Leiden in the Netherlands<-
->Georg Kirsten, Doctor of Medicine.<-

---

## To the most celebrated Man, most excellent philologist and Antiquarian,
# MR. JOHANN CONRAD DIETERICH,
### a friend to be honored,

While you, Dieterich, wear down the monuments of ancient sages,
As many as Latium <note>Rome</note> holds, as many as Greece holds.
You apply noble uses to better studies,
And report a famous name from varied art.
Just as the industrious bee visits the wedding flowers,
From which it may fashion honeycombs at a certain time:
Such a one are you, having ranged everywhere into books of every kind,
You produce from there the offspring of a good genius.

<column-break/>

He who blames this study is lazy, and that man 
Is a rustic Corydon <note>A stereotypical name for an uneducated shepherd</note>, to whom scarcely a grain of salt is left.
Let another go and refuse to handle the ancient sages;
He is hardly wise, who is wise without the ancient light.
But you are accustomed to join the ancient with the new,
And likewise the newest with the ancient, with a pleasing dexterity.
You labor at a work worthy of your genius and your name,
Which your own virtue, or that of your ancestors, gives to you.
Proceed, nor depart from the stadium, deterred by anything:
No one hates your work, unless he be a rustic.

->For the sake of friendship<-
->Frankfurt. In the Year 1649.<-
->M. LOTICHIUS.<-

<meta>This is the first page of the preface. The author is establishing the necessity of Philology (the study of language and history) for understanding Biblical antiquities.</meta>

# PREFACE
## To Biblical Antiquities.

In the name of the Lord <note>original Hebrew: בשם יהוה (B'shem Yahweh)</note>
PHILOLOGY can be called the Nurse of the sciences as truly as it is said. For she is the one who nourishes the study of the arts, inquires into the origins and rudiments of letters, examines the force of words, and opens and illuminates unknown meanings with her light; she serves the higher disciplines and dispels the darkness of decaying learning; she deserves great credit regarding all authors of human and divine wisdom, and she unearths the memory of ancient things. I call Philology a kind of provision where there is food *which the perfect man may eat, and which the infant may suckle*, and by whose juice the Republic of Letters grows, increases, and reaches maturity. Thus, she can be called a *certain Nursery*, by whose standing all those letters stand from which *Literati* <note>Learned men</note> find their name, and by whose fall, they fall. For what barbarism there would be when men (if it is right to call them men) were ignorant of Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, is idle and hateful to repeat here. The things we say are great, yet those who have the light of learning shining in their minds have said greater things; many of them have pursued the *Use of Philology in every kind of study* in all its parts with pious care; their Dissertations, established separately in this genre of writing, can be read.

What does PHILOLOGY, whether sacred or profane, embrace in its circuit other than a *sea of sciences*? What strait will you compare to this channel? Into whose abyss some lower themselves to gather shells and pearls, others to collect gems and precious stones, which neither the Hermus nor the Pactolus nor the Indus rivers carry in their riches.
->*swimming rare in the vast whirlpool.* <note>A quote from Virgil's Aeneid, referring to survivors of a shipwreck.</note><-

<margin>* 2. Tusculan Disputations.</margin>
Hesitantly indeed, I confess, and fearfully have I committed myself to this Ocean, partly moved by the difficulty of the waves, partly deterred by the weakness of my strength, and partly hindered by the force of the winds. For I am well aware of how unworthy I am to dive in that spacious and deepest sea, which sometimes rolls with the storms of envy. Yet I took courage more from the necessity of the demand than from my own will; and all the more so, because there were many Helpers ready, who by their aid and favor ensured that I, being engaged in maritime affairs, would not be overwhelmed by the waves, and—what was the greatest proof of love—gave me hope that it was impossible for me to fear when I was followed by Patrons who would direct the navigator. So that I might more willingly follow these guides, they bade me hope well from that old sentiment which among the Latins took the place of a proverb from Plautus: *He who knows not the way to the sea, let him follow the river.* Rather, one might affirm with Cicero* in a purified sense: *Cast yourself from the ship, there is one ready to receive you, either a Dolphin, like Arion of Methymna, or those horses of Neptune belonging to Pelops, which are said to have snatched away the suspended chariots through the waves.*

<column-break/>

<margin>* Psalm 72 v. 8.</margin>
In the name of GOD, therefore, who rules *from sea even unto sea*, carried in the skiff of the Muses, I have let down the net now here, now there; and not frustrated in my expectation, between the Scylla of rashness and the Charybdis of sluggishness, I have brought up—not indeed a noble pearl, but a *shell* <note>original: "testam"</note>, as the Hebrews say in a proverb—I, the last of all, the lowest of all, following the footsteps of others who were carried with full sails, and with a slow step having scraped the shore, I have fled to the harbor. What fruit of work and labor is to be expected, I entreat again and again that the Admirals of the Muses, to whom equity and perspicacity in judging are commended, do not hide from me. For that is the tribunal I approve. May the most kind Savior GOD, in whom is the only hope of our endeavors, lead us by His heavenly breeze* into that region which we seek with the ship itself.
<margin>* Psalm 107 verse 30.</margin>

It is my intention to range through the broad estate of those letters which we call, in a certain respect, profane; so that, while we experience their notable *uses*, we may at the same time detect the *abuses* often signally defiled by wicked and idle minds. In the higher discipline of Theology, no one is ignorant of how great the use of secular letters and Antiquity is. Indeed, in that field, without the previous light of profane writers and the knowledge of things and rituals drawn from them, we cannot progress in many matters; in a certain Exercise <note>term: Exercitatio - a formal academic essay or discourse</note> which stands in public, led from a humble beginning, I have shown by more than a hundred sacred testimonies, "according to the poverty of my understanding" <note>original Hebrew: לפי ענית דעתי (L'fi aniyat da'ati)</note>, as the Hebrews say. For there are very many places scattered in both the Books of the Old and New Covenant which, unless they are explained *from the histories of the gentiles, or from their fables and fictions, from ancient common modes of speaking, and from the customs of ancient men, long since obsolete and antiquated*, can in no way be understood, nor penetrated by any path. The divine Writers acted against the Pagans, they taxed their customs and superstition in manifold ways, and they set Prophecies against them; the fulfillments of which remain to be gathered from foreign writers, a study of such great value that Andreas Frankenberger, * Antonius Guevara, and Justus Lipsius exhort us toward it. In a Theologian, says Lipsius, * *if that accurate study of antiquity is absent, perhaps I shall not require it. If it is present, I shall embrace it vehemently. Not only as an ornament, but also, let it be permitted to say, as a help. For in sacred History there are many things whose deeper understanding depends on ancient customs and letters, as no one will deny.* Therefore, he who studies in Theology, the Queen of Disciplines,

> to reach the desired goal in his course
> must be a Philologist. For, in the opinion of the more learned, he who says he is ignorant of Philology confesses at the same time that he is ignorant of very many things.

# PREFACE

...they satisfy those inflamed with a desire for the waves. For they possess springs whose waters do not fail, and fertile fields which bring forth much more than they received; of which, to speak with the Poet <note>Likely Virgil, Georgics 2.201-202</note>:

*As much as the goats crop in the long summer light,*
*So much the fertile dew restores in the cool night.*

So too are the disadvantages [of learning] the fault of those who use them perversely. For many, cast down from the royal road by the weight of their own reckless infamy, are swept away into those floods of abuse. For as much benefit as accrues to the disciplines from Philology <note>The study of language and classical texts</note>, just as much is lost when we use it perversely, or when we do not use it at all. Alphius said shrewdly and truly: *Good debts become bad ones by not being called in.* We, in a different matter, say no less truly: *Profane literature <note>Non-religious classical texts</note>, if you cultivate it perversely, becomes evil.* Clearly, there are no things of such exquisite goodness or so harmless and holy that they cannot be harmful in some part, depending on how one uses them; and generally, the things that have the greatest use in human life are the same things in which the most abuses and corruptions are found. *For the virtuous man is able to use these things well, and the wicked man badly.* <note>original Greek: Τούτοις, γὰρ ὁ σπουδαῖος εὖ ἂν δύναται χρῆσθαι, καὶ ὁ φαῦλος κακῶς.</note> Regarding this sentiment, Augustine speaks excellently in his Epistles, as cited by Gratian in the Decree:

<margin>* Canon on killing, 23. q.5.</margin>

*Far be it from us that those things which we do for a good and lawful purpose should be imputed to us if any evil happens to anyone through them beyond our will. Otherwise, we should not have domestic or agricultural iron tools, lest someone kill himself or another with them; nor should there be a tree or a rope, lest someone hang himself therefrom; nor should a window be made, lest someone throw himself through it. And a little later: For what is there in good and lawful human use from which ruin cannot also be inflicted? Thus, all learning is like a sword to the insane.*

-> YOU GOOD CITIZENS, BEAR WITNESS TO THIS MATTER. <-

Sins are committed both within the walls of Troy and without. For you may find men who fail through omission—ignorant and at the same time quite morose—crying out that it is an unpardonable crime if anyone employs the *reading of Pagans* <note>original: "Ethnicorum lectionem"</note>, saying that their teaching contains the heavy burdens of useless labor. This was the view of some stubborn Cathars, Paracelsians, Weigelians, and other Fanatics of ancient times and our own, who, while avoiding vices, run into the opposite extremes. This began from the time of Gregory, who was the Bishop of Nazianzus. In that Oration in which he celebrates the life of Basil, he relates how many Christians rejected external erudition as insidious, dangerous, and turning one away from God (*as insidious and treacherous and casting one far from God*).

For the opinion settled in the minds of some in the age of that *Most Loud-Voiced* <note>original Greek: Μεγαλοφωνοτάτου</note> Father, that external disciplines, which the Gentiles accurately handed down, lead men away from God; which the great Doctor of the Church refutes in the Description of the life of Basil, which exists under the title *Monody*. Raphael Volaterranus <note>A 15th-century humanist scholar</note> translated his words into Latin in this manner:

<margin>page 59. b.</margin>

I think it is now confessed among all who are wise, that just as erudition or discipline is the first of all goods—not only Christian learning, which follows not the beauty of words but the sense and intelligence of things (*despising everything elegant and ambitious in speech, clinging only to salvation and the beauty of the things understood*); but also that

<column-break/>

which is outside the faith, which some Christians spit upon as if separated from God (*as insidious and treacherous and casting one far from God*), and have held in hatred, judging poorly indeed. For if they despise it for the reason that some have contracted harm from foreign Philosophy and fallen into various errors, in the same way they could hate the heaven and the earth and all things contained in them; since many are found who make these things Gods, or otherwise abuse them. Similarly, both fire and the other elements and food itself, which bring destruction and ruin to those who use them badly, would be avoided by all as evil. But on the contrary, we see that not only those things which are of the better sort, but even things entirely pestilential and to be avoided, are sometimes found to help when properly applied; and now from the flesh of the viper (*and there are some of the creeping beasts which we use as helpers in medicines for health*) a singular remedy for diseases has been found, which we call theriac <note>An ancient herbal "wonder-drug" or antidote</note>. Thus, therefore, from Greek teachings, whatever we build toward the knowledge of nature or the institution of morals (*the investigative and theoretical part*), we shall use; but whatever leads to error and superstition (*as much as leads to demons and wandering and the depth of destruction*), those things we shall avoid. With two similar examples, he aptly shows that profane letters are not to be despised by Christians; but their ornaments, and all philosophy which had been wrongly abused by the Gentiles, should be gathered for sacred uses. By this same artifice, Basil the Great (whom Saint Gregory had as a *companion* <note>original Greek: ὁμόσεχον</note>

<margin>* Nazianzen's funeral oration for Basil, p. 81</margin>

in the most celebrated Academy of the Athenians) prides himself in his *Oration to the Young on the Utility to be Drawn from Pagan Writings, so that they might be benefited by Greek words*. In this, he learnedly taught that the riches of a more liberal and elegant doctrine are to be sought from profane authors, and that gold of truth, worked from the mines of divine providence, should be transferred to happier uses. Whence it will not be a burden to bring here certain similar ideas, skillfully devised for that purpose, taken from the honey-making of bees, the dyeing of fullers, and the leaves of trees. *Just as in reading roses we avoid the thorns; so in profane authors, whatever is useful, we pluck; the harmful, we avoid. Having harvested what is useful, we shall guard against the harmful.* He illustrated this very thing by the example of little bees: which select the best (*whatever of them is suitable for the work*) from the flowers, leaving the rest. Furthermore, the same man says: *Just as for plants, whose proper virtue is to abound in beautiful fruit, the leaves joined to the branches nevertheless bring a certain ornament. So also the soul, whose excellent fruit is truth, is not without reason surrounded by external wisdom (the wisdom from without) as if by certain leaves providing shade for the fruit and a not unpleasant appearance.* And therefore he instructs the young that before the sacred [writings], they should converse with poets, and chroniclers, and orators, and all men: which very thing he declares more expressly by an immediately subjoined and very elegant comparison taken from Dyers: *Just as Fullers and dyers are accustomed to prepare the thing to be dyed with certain medicines before they induce the color they desire, whether purple or some other; so, he says, we also, if the glory of the good is to remain indelible for us, having been initiated first into these external things, then into the sacred...*

# ON BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>V. Caussin on Eloquence, book 15.</margin>
If we are to listen to <note>original: ἱερῶν & ἀποῤῥήτων ἐπακουσόμεθα παιδευμάτων</note> sacred and secret teachings, so that we may lay solid foundations of integrity upon solid ground, it is worthwhile to be steeped in the gentler studies <note>The "humanities" or classical liberal arts</note> from a tender age, before we approach the sacred and mysterious disciplines of Scripture. That truly Great Father <note>Saint Basil the Great</note>, after receiving baptism, practiced as a professor of Rhetoric for some time. He fulfilled this duty so magnificently that Libanius, a celebrated Sophist among the Pagans, submitted his own declamations to Basil’s critique; and at the request of that same Libanius, as Amphilochius writes <margin>* in the life of Basil</margin>, Basil taught the precepts of Christian living to students who were separated from him by religion <note>i.e., Pagan students</note>. And indeed, those venerable Fathers, Basil and Gregory, from the time they devoted themselves to letters in Athens, acquired such great erudition in every branch of learning that they were celebrated with illustrious fame not only among their teachers and peers (to use the words of Gregory as translated by Billius) but even throughout all of Greece, and especially among the most distinguished men of Greece. "Indeed," he says, "we progressed even beyond the borders of Greece, as has been discovered by the talk of many. For just as the fame of Athens extended as far as the fame of our teachers, so too did those same teachers come to know us; as soon as they heard of us, they spoke of us, and we were both considered and called a pair of no small renown among them." For they were, <note>original: διὰ τὴν ἐκ τῶν δογμάτων κοινωνίαν</note> through their fellowship in doctrines, both most eloquent men and most closely joined friends in Athens. As Petrus Crinitus long ago showed from Ruffinus (Book 7 on Honorable Discipline, chapter 1), Gregory himself mentions this mutual love between himself and Basil the Great in the Oration he gave at Basil’s funeral (page 81). Julian <note>The Emperor Julian "the Apostate"</note> had recognized their erudition and piety in Athens, as Gregory testifies elsewhere <margin>* Oration in praise of his brother Caesarius</margin> <margin>* Invective 2 against Julian</margin>, asserting that he had spent time with Julian in Athens and had noticed his wicked disposition from his face, dress, and gestures.

<margin>* Confessions, book 8, section 1.</margin> The Prophet’s prediction did not fail: for, to speak of the matter at hand, in his time a law was given prohibiting Christians from teaching literature and Oratory, according to Augustine. And it is recorded of him in Nicephorus (Book 10, chapter 25) that he provided by public law that the children of Christians should not be imbued with Greek disciplines, nor read the Poets, nor frequent public schools. "For he did not allow their children," as Sozomen writes <margin>* book 5, chapter 17</margin>, "to be taught the works of the Greek poets and writers, nor to attend their schools." For he thought nothing was less tolerable than for Pagan authors to be presented to Christian children. He knew, of course, <note>original: τοῖς νέοις τὰ μέγιστα ὠφελεῖν τὴν περὶ τῶν ἔξω λόγων παιδείαν</note> that education in external [secular] words is of the greatest benefit to the young, as they might eventually rely on it to undertake war against the Pagans. Indeed, Theodoret <margin>* book 3 of his history, chapter 7</margin> produced this reason from Julian's own mouth in these words: "For we are hit," he said, "by our own wings, according to the proverb; for being armed from our own writings, they take up the war against us." Nicephorus noted the reason for the same edict in the cited place: Lest, having their tongues polished by such sharpness, they might easily resist our arguments, and build up and amplify their own sacred rites while refuting our religion. For if they possess, as he says in Socrates <margin>* book 3, chapter 10</margin>, a tongue practiced in speaking, they will easily be able to meet the subtleties of the Dialecticians who are among the Gentiles. For this reason, Gregory inveighs against the man’s craftiness in Oration 1; and even <margin>* book 22, chapter 10</margin> Marcellinus, a pagan writer, when he recalled that this Apostate had barred and forbidden Christian teachers of rhetoric and grammar, judged this act of his to be so cruel that it ought to be buried in eternal silence <margin>* book 25, number 6</margin>. Thus, in Cyril (Book 7 against Julian), this "new Nebuchadnezzar" (as <margin>* Oration 1 to Julian</margin> Athanasius calls him) wonders why Christians would keep their people away from food sacrificed to idols, but not rather from the reading of Pagan books, since more danger looms from the latter, in his opinion. To which Cyril replied: Since it is sweet to know all things, for this reason and very prudently we also diligently discuss the opinions of the Greeks which they held on every matter, and especially concerning God; and from there we take the opportunity for mockery, because they wish to honor innumerable Gods and a multitude of unclean Demons. But let us leave Julian to his madness, and let us not put faith in the leaves of his fiction which he used as a pretext to veil his wickedness, as can be read among his Epistles published in Paris <margin>Page 300.</margin>. Let us follow the teaching of our Gregory. For even for this reason, God willed that the best of the pagan authors should exist: so that by comparison, Christians might understand how much difference there is between <note>original: ἐξουσίαν τοῦ σκότους</note> the power of darkness and the kingdom of the Son of God, between good and evil, and how much darkness differs from light. For <note>original: ἡ γὰρ ἐναντίων παράθεσις</note> the juxtaposition of opposites makes the nature of each more illustrious; and, if it be true, the Philosopher’s saying must hold: "everything appears more clearly through its opposite"; which those true fellow-students, Basil and Nazianzen, write. The former, in the Oration just praised, says: "If there is any agreement between our discourses and those of the pagans, the knowledge of them will be very profitable. If not, it will at least be pleasing to learn the difference by comparing them together, since comparison contributes not a little to the choice and selection of the better." The latter, in the same funeral oration, says: "We profit not a little from their dogmas for the worship of God <note>original: πρὸς θεοσέβειαν</note>, if we compare our things with theirs, and by comparison know that ours—as holy, pure, intact, and true—far excel those shameful, impure, and foolish things"; which is the sense Volaterranus expresses. Gregory of Nyssa, himself a most famous man and filled with all secular learning, was no less imbued with the study of Rhetoric and Eloquence than his brother Basil.

But leaving now that age in which lived those men of astonishing greatness, Gregory and Basil, let us look at the century of Jerome. The enemies of Jerome suborned a certain Great Roman Orator to inquire of the holy man (whose profound erudition in all antiquity and philosophy they envied): Why did he mix the literature of the Pagans with Ecclesiastical books, and sacred things with profane? To this, the eloquent man, about to give satisfaction, affirmed that in the writings of Moses and the Prophets there are also some things taken from the books of the Pagans. Solomon proposed many questions to the Philosophers of Tyre and solved those proposed by them. Paul the Apostle sometimes used verses from Epimenides, Callimachus, Menander, and Aratus. The Holy Father brings forward, to declare how absurd the opposing opinion is, examples of <note>original: θεοπνεύστων</note> divinely inspired writers <note>original: ἐν τοῖς τῶν ἔξωθεν μαθήμασι τὴν διάνοιαν γυμναζομένων</note> who exercised their minds in external [secular] studies; such as Moses, the first historian of the nascent world, who was nourished <margin>* Acts chapter 7, verse 22</margin> in all the wisdom of the Egyptians; who according to Origen, Basil, and Gregory...

# PROLEGOMENA

The eloquent opinion of Gregory is especially followed regarding that eloquence in which men flourish. For instance, from childhood, the first principles were liberally established in the royal court of Pharaoh, and polished by the cultivation of a nobler intellect, for him whom Pharaoh’s daughter adopted and, in a royal 
<margin>* Basil, on the beginning of the Hexaemeron.</margin>
manner, *educated and instructed by employing the wise men of the Egyptians as teachers* <note>Referring to Moses</note>. Nevertheless, he is 
<margin>* Sirach 45:1.</margin>
celebrated as *beloved by God*. But as for what Philo says in the *Life of Moses*—that he used Greek masters—the timeline refutes this; since Cadmus, who first brought letters into Greece (whence they are called Phoenician and Cadmean letters), lived several centuries after Moses. The same Philo, and from him Clement of Alexandria in *Stromata* Book 1, page 343, says: all the wisdom of the Egyptians which the Scripture affirms Moses learned, consisted of mathematics and geometry, rhythm and harmony, and furthermore medicine together with music; and additionally the philosophy conveyed through symbols, which they display in hieroglyphic writing. From Moses, the Bishop of Stridon <note>St. Jerome</note> passes to the Prophets, among whom Daniel was instructed *in all the wisdom of the Chaldeans*, <note>original Hebrew: בספר ולשון כשדים</note> *in the language and literature of the Chaldeans*, Daniel chapter 1, verse 4. Where, in his Commentary, Jerome says: *He who does not wish to eat from the King’s table or drink of his wine, lest he be polluted; surely if he knew that the very wisdom and teaching of the Babylonians were a sin, he would never have consented to learn what was not permitted.* Without a doubt, there were magical elements in the traditions of the Chaldeans; however, no one doubts that Daniel ignored those. 
<margin>Oration to Young Men.</margin>
*They say that the wise Daniel in Babylon, having learned the wisdom of the Chaldeans, then learned the divine teachings,* says Basil the Great. To the Prophets, the holy man joins Saint Paul of Tarsus, the herald of the Gentiles, whom they gather to have been most well-versed in the reading of profane authors, both from Strabo—who testifies of the Tarsians that they surpassed Alexandria and even Athens itself in the study of philosophy and other disciplines called "encyclical" <note>The "circle" of general education or liberal arts</note>—and from the sacred texts it becomes manifest. For he used a verse of Epimenides, the Cretan poet, concerning the fraudulent character of the Cretans, giving others the faculty to do the same: as Pacianus says in *Epistle 2 to Sympronia*. In another Epistle, he placed a six-foot line <note>a senarius</note> from the ancient poet Menander about avoiding the company of evil men. He used a half-line from Aratus, a most celebrated poet, for the glory of the Gospel in his sermon to the Athenians, whom he instructs in the Areopagus concerning the Best and Greatest God as being "most superstitious" <note>original Greek: δεισιδαιμονεστάτους</note>, and he twists a chance inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD, into an argument for the faith, as our Jerome speaks. *From which it is clear that even when using poetic verses, he nowhere approves of the things appearing in Aratus, but rather those things well-said among the Greeks,* as Clement of Alexandria says in *Stromata* Book 1, page 315, Paris edition. Which things, indeed, the divine man would not allege if he had wished to forbid the writings of "outsiders" <note>non-Christian authors</note> to the worshippers of Christ. These arguments brought forward by the Bishop of Stridon will suffice, unless I am greatly mistaken, for him who does not wish to be an altogether stubborn patron and defender of falsehood.

The holy, most learned, and above all most eloquent Doctor of the Church disputes more at length on this question in his *Epistle to Magnus, the Roman Orator*, proving by an induction from Quadratus, Bishop of Athens, who is said to have been a 

<column-break/>

disciple of the Apostles, down to his own times, that there have existed men wonderfully learned in both divine and human wisdom: *who all (as he says) so sprinkled their books with the doctrines and opinions of philosophers, that you do not know what you ought to admire first in them, whether their secular erudition or their knowledge of the Scriptures.* These are the Fathers whom he commemorates in order. Likewise, in his *Epistle to Titus*, he judges Grammar and Dialectic <note>Logic</note> to be useful to Christians for arguing well and distinguishing the false from the true, and that these, if applied to better uses, are of the greatest benefit. Therefore, he says, *if ever we are compelled to remember secular literature and learn some of those things which we once set aside, it is not of our will, but (so to speak) of the gravest necessity, so that we may prove that those things which were predicted by the holy Prophets many ages before are contained in the literature of both the Greeks and the Latins and other gentiles.* 

It is a trivial thing, however, which many—more like Rufinus than Jerome—object against those who cultivate human affairs: that Jerome was struck and warned by an Angel not to embrace human literature thereafter, which is seen to be affirmed as a fact in the *Decrees, Distinction 18*. We read concerning Blessed Jerome, that when he was reading the books of Cicero, he was rebuked by an Angel because a Christian man was intent upon the fictions of Pagans. Regarding this matter, the author himself does not deny it was a dream and a mockery of the night. Indeed, with his own hand he writes to Marcella, purging himself of the calumnies of *Rufinus*. 
<margin>* Volume 3, folio 95.</margin>
<margin>* Volume 1, folio 67a.</margin>
*You charge me,* he says, *with perjury mixed with sacrilege, because in the book (to Eustochium) where I speak for the instruction of a Virgin of Christ, I promised while sleeping before the Judge's tribunal that I would never give effort to secular literature: and nevertheless I remember that condemned erudition.* Surely this is that "Sallustian Calphurnius" (whom he frequently mentions, though it is not clear who he is) who moved a not-so-great question for us through Magnus the Orator; to which brief book we have given satisfaction. Now, as to what stands for the sacrilege and perjury of a dream, it must be answered. I said I would not read secular literature *henceforth*: the pledge is for the future, not an abolition of past memory, etc. Nor does he argue that faith should ever be placed in dreams of this kind, for he says he has sometimes seen himself in dreams flying, swimming the seas, or placed in a tomb, which could by no means have been true. *How many,* he continues, *are rich in dreams, but with eyes open are suddenly beggars? The thirsty drink rivers, and having woken up, they burn with dry throats. You demand from me the fulfillment of a dream.* You may read the dream in the same author's *Epistle on the Guarding of Virginity to Eustochium*, where the words of the Censor Erasmus are read: *This is that fable which even all those hold by heart who have never read a single word in the writings of Jerome. Jerome was beaten, they say, because he read Cicero. And with a certain strange religion they so abstain from all good literature that they do not even touch it, lest perhaps they inadvertently fall upon some word of Cicero and be beaten with Jerome: and then they seem to themselves closest to the Apostles, if they speak as filthily as possible.* But St. Jerome, when he responds to the one objecting to this passage, *calls it a dream, even if here he denies it was a dream.* Nor did Jerome ever feel that Cicero was not to be read; but only in this respect, that divine things [might be read] more rightly...

# ON BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

...that we may understand more rightly and handle them more conveniently. Otherwise, what does he mean by what he writes to the Great Orator? <note>Referring to Jerome’s Letter 70 to Magnus, defending the use of secular literature.</note> I cannot help but add the words of Jean Gerson, formerly Chancellor of the University of Paris (whose praise and holiness is proclaimed by Dauroltius \*) which are found in his sermon on the Angels. I do not want you to take this example to mean that you should think the books of Infidels <note>Non-Christian authors</note> are to be entirely cast aside, as some busily strive to argue falsely. Otherwise, Jerome himself, and Augustine, and Bernard, and to go back further, Paul, Cyprian, and Origen—indeed, to extend it more generally, all the prophets, all the lawyers, all the artists—would have erringly fallen into blame. To say such a thing is intolerable rashness, and so forth. Read more on this matter in the works of the same Erasmus, as well as Marianus Victorius of Rieti in his *Description of the Life of Jerome*, and Reinhard Lorich in his *Scholia on the Progymnasmata of Aphthonius, fol. 105, 106.*

<margin>\* in *Exempla Florum*, book 1, chapter 111, section 2.</margin>

What, then, was the view of Clement of Rome, who in *Book 1 of the Constitutions, chapter 7*, ordered that one should be frightened away from all books of the gentiles as things devised by the Devil? What was the opinion of Gregory the Great? Of whom Antoninus, Archbishop of Florence, reports that he *caused all the books of Titus Livy that he could find to be burned, because many things concerning the superstitions of idols are narrated there.* What nausea seized a certain Stoic Paracelsian? Who, not without stomach-ache, blurted out these words regarding a passage in Plautus found in the argument of *Amphitryon* concerning the adultery of Jupiter: *It is too impious to learn Latinity from those who do injury to God and to the good morals of men. It would be better for Plautus’s Amphitryon to be given to the fire than for the Deity and human virtues to be mocked by that most ruinous play.* So too regarding the Pope and many others, *Francesco Petrarch*, an Etruscan by nation, a most celebrated Philosopher, Rhetorician, and Poet, was firmly believed to be a Sorcerer \* because he had read *Virgil*, as Andreas Schröder testified in *his Life, page 30.* The same reputation befell the Frenchman Gerbert <note>Pope Sylvester II</note>, first Archbishop of Ravenna, because he had made public the abacus and the figures used by calculators, which were not understood in that illiterate age. *For at Rome then, there was scarcely anyone who had learned letters;* which was the statement of Arnulf of Orléans in the Council of Reims celebrated in A.D. 991. Were those who were once considered learned so unlearned and ignorant of good literature? In that unhappy century, anyone who devoted effort to Philosophy under that eclipse of letters was thought to be a Sorcerer. What kind of religiosity is this? If we think nothing should be read except what is in harmony with the Christian Religion, let us indeed cast away and omit all those ancient Greek and Latin authors. Let Homer be exiled from Christian sanctuaries, let Tully <note>Cicero</note> be exiled, let Livy depart, and in one word, all the ancient Poets, Historians, and Orators. For there is none among them who does not introduce a multitude of Gods; none who does not suggest examples of great and furious sins. *If anything contrary to Holy Scripture be found in the books of the gentiles* (which opinion of Augustine is cited among the rules \* for understanding the sacred scriptures by Francisco Ruiz, Abbot of the Order of St. Benedict), *if they be most false: either refute them from the sacred texts, or learn from the true David how to wrest the sword from the hands of the enemies, and to cut off the head of the most proud Goliath with his own blade.* For who would be so stupid, so insane, as to wish to bid a long farewell to these writers because of the admixture of examples of passions and lusts? This was indeed what Cornelius Agrippa, a disciple of Zoroaster \*, wanted; by which reasoning, one who was moved by it ought not even to use the books of Christians.

<margin>\* part 4, sum. tit. 11, c. 4, § 3 near the end.</margin>
<margin>\* See *Seniles*, book 1, Ep. 3.</margin>
<margin>\* page 182.</margin>
<margin>\* chapter 1, *On the Vanity of Science*.</margin>

> No one blames the fertile streams of the Nile
> Because it nourishes the Crocodile with its pestiferous offspring.

If many are intoxicated by wine, the vines are not to be cut down for that reason, as Lycurgus did. So, if many are offended by the writings of the Heathens, they are not immediately to be cast away, but rather, so that they may become healthy and useful, the cautious reading of an Interpreter must be applied, by whose care those redundant shoots of the Heathens may be pruned away, just as a skillful Vinedresser *performs the pruning by the guidance of the sickle, not by a blow; and does it narrowly, knowing when to prune against the grain, and which most sharp part of the sickle to use, lest the vineyards be devastated through his ignorance*, to speak with Columella *book 4, chapters 24 and 25.* In Canon Law, as if in a field growing wild, there are impious and superstitious things; even Civil Law has many things which do not seem to agree with the word of God, yet no one will cast away or entirely repudiate Civil and Canon Law for that reason. In the writings of the pagans, as if in an uncultivated and neglected vineyard, there are thistles and nettles of vices, and shoots of impiety. Through the field of Plato (<margin>\* Proverbs 24:30, 31, 32.</margin> *if it is lawful to imitate the words of Solomon \** ) *I passed, and through the vineyard of Plautus, and behold, nettles had filled the whole field, and thorns, briars, and brambles had covered its face, and the stone wall was destroyed. When I had seen this, I laid it up in my heart, and learned discipline by the example:* Whence the diligence of the Vinedresser must be imitated in this, who, finding a vineyard rough, unpruned, and accessible through a ruined wall, does not immediately abandon it, but restores it, prunes it, and takes away what must be removed. Rather, the reading of Profane authors is profitable, that we may learn how *fornication* ranged with impunity, and what Idolatry is compared to this in the sacred texts among them; how many outrages were brought in from there, and with full sails, what immodest and shameful things were accepted. To be sure, pious men see in these books, as in a mirror, the life and morals of men, and they receive the luxurious reproach of idleness and other vices with sober ears. For one must not approach reading unless with both minds and ears prepared, like divers who, descending into the depths <note>original: βαθη (bathe)</note> of the sea, carry oil in their ears and soak them with oil, lest the water burst through them: as Aristotle witnesses in *Problems, section 22, chapters 10 and 11*, whom it is fitting to imitate. For let us examine those writers in such a way that the oil of truth and divine Wisdom poured into our ears may be a panacea and, as it were, a faithful guardian, and it will not be necessary to fear any danger at all. Whence in this genre, the judgment of Joachim Camerarius, a man as most pious as he was most experienced in secular literature, greatly pleases me, which he left weightily regarding Plautus; and which ought deservedly to prevail over the preposterous judgment of that rigid Cato. Being about to commend the *Asinaria* of Plautus \*, he begins thus: *Let us contemplate, as if in a mirror, the supreme foulness of those times in this Comedy, and let us fear and venerate God, praying that He may kindly turn away from us such a great atrocity of punishment—that is, of blindness and worthlessness <note>original: ἀδοκιμιας (adokimias)</note>—and soften our souls, and move them through the Holy Spirit toward...*

<margin>\* p. 265, Leipzig Edition, Year 45.</margin>

# PROLEGOMENA

...repentance for sins, and lift them toward the hope of salvation in faith in Jesus Christ our Savior, Amen. Likewise in the *Bacchides* <note>A play by the Roman comedian Plautus</note>: This play is elegant, but it presents outrages and foul wickedness; at the knowledge of which the minds of the godly ought to be terrified by the consideration of horrible divine wrath, and what follows. Is not Petronius the most impure writer of the purest Latinity, treating the most impure subject in the purest speech? Yet we do not exterminate him on account of the ignorance of some; Goldastus, Pithoeus, and Barthius show that nothing is more unjust than such a judgment. What shall we say of Aristophanes? If Saint John Chrysostom had not thought that those "filthy" writers ought to be read, he certainly would not have kept that most witty, but also most obscene, writer of Old Comedy under his pillow, where he always had him.

<margin>
On Petronius, dissertation book 49. Adversaria chapter 11. Floridus 5. Lectures under chapter 7.
Preface to Petronius's Satyricon.
</margin>

*If you are well-born (to borrow the words of Théodore de Juges), imbued with the liberal arts and instructed in the decrees of true Philosophy (we add, of Theology), you will not suffer corruption, just as the murex is a fish of chastity. And as Socrates by his entry purified the prison, so if there is anything foreign to virtue or related to vice, your happy and good nature will purify it. Therefore, to conclude with Girolamo Vida:*

->Lay aside your cruel rages and the master's whips,<-
->Those foul duties, and cease from bitter threats.<-

Others, lest we should believe profane books, used to oppose us with the "holiness of teaching," though there is hardly any such thing; nothing is more meager than their exhortation. Let the ill-devoted monks, anchorites, and cenobites be an example, among whom the common saying was: *These things are profane, they cannot be read.* For those authors of more humane literature <note>The "humanities" or classical studies</note>—since they had either not read them, or had read them in such a way that it would have been better not to have read them—with what trifles, I ask, did they defame them? No better words could be given against that dregs of the monastic common-folk than those which Gregory gave in his *Monody* against the despisers of foreign learning. He says that learning is not to be held in low esteem just because it seems so to some, but it should be judged that those dull and unskilled men are so affected—those who, even in the century of our ancestors, where there was more of the barbarian than of the Muses, when it was most "hot in Armenia" <note>A proverbial expression for a time of great turmoil or ignorance</note>, while the republic of letters was collapsing. At that time, the "defenses" <note>original: ἀμυντήρια (amyntēria)</note> of the schools were turned into "bile" <note>original: χολὴν (cholēn)</note>, that is, into laziness. And those upon whom it had been incumbent to propagate piety joined with integrity of character through literate eloquence, instead offered ignorance to posterity, having eliminated good and approved authors by "praetorian authority" <note>i.e., by arbitrary decree</note>, under I know not what pretext of holiness and foolish severity. Johannes Dullardus used to instill in his students: *The better a grammarian you are, the worse a theologian you will be.* This was the "holy ignorance" (as it was called) and the excessively scrupulous religion of certain times past. It is hateful to go through examples; which Meisner, Finck, Clauder, Ebel, and others also bring forth in great number in their particular dissertations. So that I may deservedly exclaim regarding that age:

->O miserable minds of men, O blind hearts,<-
->In what darkness of life<-
->is passed whatever time this is!<-

It is indeed better to become better than to become more learned, if it is not permitted to attain both at once: It is better to be lame than blind, if

<column-break/>

one must be without one. But consider for yourself, did they compensate for their slowness of learning or their barbarism with the happiness of their morals? If it were permitted to pass over to their bad morals, we might perhaps prove with little effort that they had taken up dominion. But "do not judge before the harvest" <note>original: ἀλλ' οὐ πρὶν βαλανίζε (all' ou prin balanize) - a Greek proverb meaning don't judge too early</note>.

<margin>Book 1, preface of the Digest, on various and extraordinary knowledge.</margin>

They try indeed to cover the simplicity of their speech with the greatness of their sanctity; for they say it is better to fail in learning than to suffer the loss of morals. Truly, let them be masters of morals—far be it from us to forbid or envy it. But where there is no place for literature, which Ulpian calls the "liberal studies" <note>original: ἐλευθέρια μαθήματα (eleutheria mathēmata)</note>, a neighboring downfall in morals must also be present; for he who fails in letters and profits in morals, fails more than he profits, as Sophocles testifies. Let the same be said to each and every one of them. That fatal barbarism of the ages, what various changes, what paroxysms, what deaths of good authors did it not bring in? I shall go through examples. They bring forward the dictators of the Fourth Council of Carthage, who in chapter 16 published a decree: *A Bishop shall not read the books of the gentiles.* Which Gratian, the compiler of the Decretals, also inserted into his patchwork of laws. They add the Isidores, otherwise most highly commended for the praise of their genius; one indeed of Pelusium, who in Book 1, Epistle 63, seems to have altogether forbidden such study to a monk or anchorite, on account of the foulness and obscenity mixed into the subject matter. The other of Seville; to whom in Book 3 of his *Sentences on the Supreme Good*, chapter 13, the reading of secular authors is displeasing because of its wickedness. Therefore, he says in number 2, *A Christian is forbidden to read the fictions of the poets, because through the delights of empty fables they incite to the incentives of lusts. For one sacrifices to demons not only by offering incense, but also by too willingly receiving their words.* I know not how advisedly he writes; unless a kind interpretation be admitted, which you will perhaps have from paragraph 3, where he says, seized by the love of divine letters: *Therefore such books are to be guarded against, and avoided for the sake of the love of the sacred scriptures.* Since they wrote these things for the calamitous forum of their own age, in which it was not safe to permit the reading of the gentiles indiscriminately to anyone, and many things can be said in a comparative sense which cannot be said in an absolute one, I would judge that their words are to be interpreted kindly according to the reason of the time and the persons, as things said "leisurely" <note>original: εὐσχολικῶς (euscholikōs)</note> regarding the reading of Holy Scripture, which alone is the "basis of honor and the medicine of the soul" <note>original: βάσις τῆς τιμῆς καὶ φάρμακον ψυχῆς (basis tēs timēs kai pharmakon psychēs)</note>; in which way Cassiodorus rightly instructed the monks of his Monastery of Vivarium: to whom he even left secular literature of every kind, so that they might wear them out with constant reading, and the world having been exhausted, so to speak, by the geniuses of learned men, they might emerge from that reading as such men who would consult for the age with their own erudition.

<margin>
Distinction 37, chapter 1.
Trithemius in the History of the Monastery of Hirsau.
</margin>

Hence there was praise for Ruthard; who, a monk outstanding in the praise of sanctity and erudition, entered the Gymnasium of Hirsau, which was furnished with the best authors, and taught letters, having left behind the honors of the Bishopric which the Emperor Louis had decreed for him. With no less glory, the Emperor Charles <note>Charlemagne</note> and Boniface, Archbishop of Mainz, while blood was flowing through Germany from long-lasting war, established the monastery of Fulda under good auspices, vindicated the Muses driven into exile back into liberty, and enclosed four hundred monks in the College as if in a Trojan horse for the teacher Sturmius...

# ON BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES.

They record that men were handed over to be polished by Greek and Latin letters; many of whom, out of their great erudition, translated many things from the Greek tongue into Latin and ennobled the Gymnasiums <note>Schools or academies for higher learning</note> with distinguished libraries, not without benefit to all of Germany, as even the Spanish *Doctor* <note>Likely referring to a specific scholar like Juan Luis Vives or similar</note> bears witness. Indeed, even the Abbots in Monasteries
<margin>
Johannes Bonifacius, *Letters on the Fruitful Wise Man*, Book 5, pp. 641, 642.
</margin>
formerly required instructors to teach and educate the Monks, both in secular and in sacred letters, as attested by Evagrius in Book 4, Chapter 38, and Bede in Book 3 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. In the Council of Vienne under Clement V, it was decreed that in every Monastery there should be an enlightened Master and Doctor to educate the Monks and imbue them with the good arts <note>The liberal arts</note>. *Clement. r. d. pen. de Stat. Monach.* and *chapter 2. extr. de Magist.*—whether this institution always flourished, it is not permitted to dispute now. To discharge my own duty, it is fitting to bring forward *Cassiodorus*.
<margin>
*On Divine Learning*, chapter 28.
</margin>
*Nor did the most holy Fathers decree,* he says, *that the study of secular letters should be rejected; because from them our understanding is instructed in no small measure for understanding the sacred scriptures. If, however, by the aid of divine grace, the knowledge of those very things is sought soberly and rationally, not so that we place the hope of our progress in them, but passing through them, we desire that profitable and salutary wisdom be granted to us by the Father of Lights.* From the same mindset, Paulinus, Bishop of Nola, discoursing on the reading of pagan writers of that kind, says:
<margin>
*Letter to Lovius.*
</margin>
*It is permitted to take certain things, mostly from empty fables, as one might take common proverbs, for the use of true and serious speech.* Again, in the same letter: *Let it be enough for you to have taken from them a wealth of language and an ornament of speech, like certain spoils from the arms of enemies, so that, stripped of their errors and clothed in their eloquence, you may apply that veneer of eloquence—by which vain wisdom deceives—to substantial matters; so that, adorning not a vacuum of fictions but the marrowy body of truth, you may meditate on things that will please not only the ears, but will benefit the minds of men.* Hear now John of Salisbury, Bishop of Chartres four hundred and eighty years ago, in Book 7, Chapter 9: *Just as all living creatures were granted to man, except that he ought not to eat flesh with the blood, so all writings, both of Poets and of pagans, can be read for utility, provided the errors, which are understood by the blood, are excluded.* And in Book 3, Chapter 8: *But if this itself is patiently admitted, what prevents those things which were written by the philosophers of the nations for the sake of public utility from being heard? Whatever things were written, says the Apostle, were written for our instruction.* <note>original: "Quaecumque scripta sunt... ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt." A reference to Romans 15:4.</note> But indeed, he misuses the authority of the Apostle for his own purpose; just as some
<margin>
1 Timothy 4:13.
</margin>
write that by that saying, *attend to reading*, <note>original: "πρὸςεχε τῆ ἀναγνώσει" (proseche tē anagnōsei)</note> not only the unfolding of sacred books, but also human wisdom, both of Philosophers and even of Poets and Historians, was commended to Timothy. P. Stevartius notes in the same place that this is also affirmed according to the mind of the Fathers: which interpretations, being far-fetched, we leave in their own place.
<margin>
page 368. *Commentary on the book 'On the Dress of Women'.*

According to the opinion of Tertullian, *nothing can be directed and received by the wavering Holy Spirit for the present matter and not for every occasion of utility.* Hence so many allegorical senses, so many anagogical <note>Mystical or spiritual interpretations</note> ones, even where the argument is against the Pagans, are found among the Fathers, who transfer those things handed down in divine letters to the pagans in a far different sense, either allegorically or anagogically, nevertheless not rejecting

<column-break/>

the other literal sense of Scripture. Most well-known among them is that allegorical explanation of the Egyptian vessels and its application to the matter we are now treating. For they declare it with elegant allegories. Gregory of Nyssa writes that by the vessels borrowed from the Egyptians was prefigured *the riches of learning which the nations possess—moral and natural Philosophy, Geometry, Music, Dialectic, and the other
<margin>
*On the Life of Moses*, p. 506.

sciences in which those outside the Church flourish—we are commanded to receive from them, and to deprive those who misuse them, if possible, and transfer them to better uses.* He says that by the deed of the Hebrews, who by heavenly command carried away with them the wealth borrowed from the Egyptians and converted it to sacred uses, we are taught *to prepare the wealth of external education* <note>original: "τὸν ἔξωθεν τῆς παιδεύσεως πλοῦτον παρασκευάξωμεν"</note> and *to beautify the divine temple by devising a logical breadth.* <note>original: "τὸν θεῖον τῷ μηχανεῖν ναὸν διὰ τῷ λογικῷ πλάτῳ καλλωπίζειν"</note> And just as those who had acquired the wealth of the Egyptians brought it to Moses as he prepared the tabernacle for the sacred structure; so also it happens in the Church. With a similar allegory, that prince of Bishops and <gloss>among</gloss> the Latin Fathers, Saint Augustine, adapted that deed of the Hebrews to the same sense, *writing:

*On Christian Doctrine*, ch. 40, Vol. 4, f. 43.

Just as the Israelites took away the idols and the gold and silver vessels of the Egyptians and brought them to just uses pleasing to GOD, so Christian Philosophers ought not entirely to abandon the philosophy and liberal disciplines which exist in the writings of the Heathen because the Heathen used them impiously, but they ought to transfer them to the just use of preaching the Gospel.* That great Father commands us to use their writings rather than to enjoy them; and he urges that the whole method of studies be directed so that those things serve the higher ones for the use of truth. To that end, St. Augustine (what a great and significant
<margin>
See the Prefaces of Gesner and Calixtus in this place.
</margin>
man!) elaborated a most elegant book in which he instructs the Christian Teacher; and he spent himself entirely in it to teach how he who, having left behind the idol-mania of the nations, has given his name to God, ought after his conversion to use the Egyptian spoils, i.e., the doctrines of the nations: which we also very well adapt to our use; for the same thing remains, only the persons are changed; especially in chapters 20, 21, 22, 23, 28, 29, 31, and 37 of Book 2, he affirms that Astronomy, Physics, Geography, Dialectic, and Rhetoric have much importance for penetrating all kinds of questions and matters which are in the holy scriptures, even if they are learned as childish education outside the Church. For although secular sciences may be "fornicating" sciences, in which the ancient philosophers committed fornication; nevertheless, when by God's command the Christian Teacher enters into them, the children whom he receives are children of God and his seed, because he is free for them for His sake: as the interlinear Gloss has it on Hosea, chapter 1. He adds in chapter 40 that before him, men famous for holiness in the Church brought secular letters to sacred ones: *We see,* he says, *with how much gold and silver and clothing Cyprian, that most sweet Doctor and most blessed Martyr, went out of Egypt; how much Lactantius, how much Victorinus, Optatus, Hilary—to say nothing of the living: how many innumerable Greeks?* Of the Greeks, Basil especially, having opportunely purchased Egyptian wealth in the flower of his age, consecrated it to God and adorned the true tabernacle of the Church with it; Nyssa, in the place cited.
