<meta>This page continues the introductory arguments (Prolegomena) regarding the relationship between secular learning and Christian theology, specifically addressing how to handle the writings of non-Christian (pagan) authors.</meta>

# 8 PROLEGOMENA

which are practiced outside the Church of Christ, as if they *might dare to follow them securely in order to attain a blessed life, while seeking that blessed life*. He teaches in chapter 20 that superstition must be avoided, among which are *consultations with demons, the worship of idols, various omens, and thousands of other most vain observations, thousands of fables and falsehoods*. Superfluous things are to be cut away, and necessary things are to be used *for the righteous use of preaching the Gospel, for the use of worshipping the one God*; he advised in chapter 40 that they be used in obedience to Christ; so that those disciplines which they used to assist falsehood, we might use as a testimony to the truth. This very point was grandly encompassed by that greatest of the Fathers <note>Likely referring to St. Augustine</note> in that most learned work in which he builds the *City of God* against the pagans, assuming here and there other Philosophical and Philological matters after the knowledge of the true God, while also rejecting them here and there. Most sweet is the coupling of Theology and those arts which the Pagans have handed down to us in a refined state. Let there indeed be salutary and solid fruits from the sacred scriptures, yet the leaves of other arts communicated by outsiders also help wonderfully. For just as leaves do not only provide ornament, but also cover the fruit on the trees against the heat of the sun and the rains; so the liberal arts are both an ornament and a protection in the explanation and defense of heavenly doctrine.

Therefore, to say that everything said and written by the Heathens is *Heathenish*, or *devised by the Devil*, is too shameful a thing to say. Aristotle acknowledged **GOD** as *one, and called him life itself, unity, and goodness*. Aratus, as the Apostle <note>St. Paul in Acts 17:28</note> witnesses, established *the providence of God*; to pass over infinite other things in this note. Are such utterances therefore heathenish—that is, as they explain it, proceeding from Satan? Far be it from us to say so. Rather, we should say that where there is anything excessive, it must be pruned away with the sickle of truth. Nor can Charybdis and Scylla, or that fabled strait, deter us, for where does that mixture of good and bad things not occur? In this reading, we ought to imitate skilled sailors, who are accustomed to avoid the rocks of the sea by their nautical skill, which is said to be both great and cautious at the same time. Here too one must navigate with caution; *good and bad things are to be tested in all things in the land of foreigners*, to apply the words of the divine Writer; the filth of lies and other vanities must be wiped away, and
<margin>Deuteronomy 21:12</margin>
as the law speaks, *the nails of the captive woman must be trimmed* (which woman, as St. Jerome interprets,
<margin>Epistle to Pammachius on the death of Paulina.</margin>
is the reading of those writers who did not know Christ), *the hair must be shaved, and the garment in which she was captured must be put off*, that is, the superfluous, the impertinent, and if there be any impious things, must be cast away: *For if there is anything superfluous concerning idols, concerning love, concerning the care of worldly things, we shave these, we induce baldness upon them, we cut these away like nails with the sharpest iron*; says St. Jerome, explaining the
<margin>Volume 4, folio 52.</margin>
Gospel parable of the Prodigal Son; which same parable Herric of Auxerre, in his Homily for the Sabbath after the 11th Sunday in Lent, accommodates to secular doctrines which, as he says, *resound with a sterile sweetness*. St. Jerome best encompassed these same things in his Epistle to Pammachius: *If you have fallen in love with a captive woman, that is, secular knowledge, and her beauty, shave her head, and cut away the allurements of her hair and the ornaments of her words with tenacious nails, and resting with her, take her to wife.*

<column-break/>

And so there is no obstacle to entering into the best society, provided that this gentile and captive Philosophy and Philology—wherever it teaches things less than wholesome—is led to her husband, Holy Theology, with her hair shaved, her nails trimmed, and her garment cast aside; whom she may serve perpetually as one set free, so that she does not serve as a slave. In this, a remarkable passage on this matter by Gregory of Nyssa wonderfully captivates us, which in his *Mystical Narrative of the Life of Moses*, page 35, stands thus from the Latin translation: *Secular Philosophy and human discipline have a birth, a certain fleshly foreskin, which being circumcised, that which remains is found to be of Israelite nobility; as for example, the Philosophers maintain that the soul is immortal, and that is a pious thing*. They wish for souls to pass from bodies into bodies, and some assert they even pass from a rational nature into one devoid of reason. *These things must be circumcised like a foreskin, and cast far away altogether. They do not deny that God exists, the creator of all things, on whom all things depend, they truly assert, and demonstrate by reasons as much as possible; but they suppose matter for the creator as if for a needy craftsman, and many other such things are devised with true reasons, but stained by absurd and false oppositions, which if we remove, the Angel of God will become favorable to us*. This is surely to act as a scout in the enemy's camp: as Reuchlin cleverly said concerning his Kabbalah.
<margin>Book on the Mirific Word.</margin>
(Many of those ancient Fathers did this, especially Chrysostom, Gregory Nazianzen, Basil, Justin, Clement of Alexandria, Lactantius, and others, who, undertaking a particular struggle against the wisdom of the Heathens, had to survey all the dens and tents of heathendom, like diligent scouts in the camp of the Moabites; so that they might show the enemy drawn out from his hiding places to be laughed at, and judge the wicked servant out of his own mouth.
<margin>Luke 19:24</margin>
For since they were dealing with most learned enemies of the Truth, they had to contend for the overturning of their errors not so much from sacred as from profane authors; so that they might be able to more strongly and certainly repress the errors sometimes emanating into the Church from their raving opinions. And therefore, whatever poison they had sprinkled upon natural truth, good morals, and the decrees of the holy faith, had to be diligently investigated. For what do you think was the reason that those most holy and also most learned men wrote so many and such excellent writings against the Heathens? Surely necessity gave them that license of writing and reading: for they would have labored in vain unless the heralds of the sacred faith had thoroughly perceived their own writings. I have not shunned, says Lactantius, *this labor, so that I might fulfill the matter which Cyprian did not follow through in that Oration in which he endeavors to refute Demetrianus, who (as he says) was barking and clamoring against the truth: which matter he did not use as he ought. For he should have been refuted not by the testimonies of scripture, which he surely thought were vain, feigned, and fabricated, but by arguments and reason. For when he was acting against a man ignorant of the truth, having put aside divine readings for a little while, he ought to have formed him from the beginning as if he were unrefined, and shown him the principles of light little by little, lest he be blinded if the whole light were presented at once: for just as an infant cannot take the force of solid and strong food because of the tenderness of the stomach, but is nourished by the liquid of milk and softness, until with strengthened powers he can eat stronger—*
<margin>Book 5 on Justice, chapter 4.</margin>

it was possible for the more advanced: so also it was necessary for this person, because he could not yet grasp divine things, *first to be offered human testimonies, that is, those of the Philosophers and Historians, so that he might be refuted primarily by his own authors.* For adversaries could not be more powerfully attacked than with their own weapons. *“For the enemy is most thoroughly conquered when we use their own weapons against them,”* says Socrates <note>original: Σφόδρα γὰρ καταπολεμούμενοι οἱ πολέμιοι, ὅτι τοῖς αὐτῶν ὅπλοις χρώμεθα κατ' αὐτῶν. This refers to Socrates Scholasticus, the 5th-century church historian, not the Athenian philosopher.</note> *Book 3, Chapter 11,* where he had recounted the edict of Julian <note>Julian the Apostate, the Roman Emperor who forbade Christians from teaching classical literature.</note>, because he barred Christians from the study of literature. Origen supports this in Eusebius, responding to certain people who criticized secular studies, in this manner: *“When I had turned my studies to the words of GOD, and a more celebrated reputation was held concerning us, and because of this some of the Philosophers came together to meet us, either for the sake of questioning or resisting, and many of the heretics were also stirred up to attack us: it seemed to me necessary to examine more diligently the doctrines of either the Philosophers or the heretics, lest I be found less prepared to convict them if I were ignorant of what they hold.”* Moreover, we have done this following the example of our earlier *Apostolic* man *Pantaenus*, who *flourished greatly in Greek studies and the erudition of the Philosophers.* Moved by these things also was Didymus of Alexandria, who, though blind from boyhood, learned the <term>lessons</term> <note>original: μαθήματα (mathemata)</note> of Poetry, Rhetoric, Geometry, Astronomy, and the doctrine of Aristotle’s syllogisms and the eloquence of Plato, *not as teaching the truth, but as weapons of the truth, produced against falsehood,* according to Theodoret *History Book 4, Chapter 29.* For this end, they all searched through the books of the pagans. Now, since the times are adverse, the age is not the same, the lot of men is not the same, nor their talents, nor their customs, nor the condition of things and times; I would consider it a deed ill-done by those who abuse their sharpness of mind in this: that they hunt through every nook of pagan writers; whose license in this part has grown to an immense degree. For our reasoning is not the same as that of the Fathers of old. *We, by the grace of God, dwell having been born in the bosom of the Christian world: so that we might not even seem to be such; we write for Christians alone, we teach the poor and unrefined common people; they taught learned Philosophers and pagans. Therefore, it is not fitting to produce so many Patchworks <note>original: Centiones; poems made of fragments from other works.</note>, which prove a display of talent more than piety. Especially is this done faultily by those who transfer the time destined for sacred things to those Ethnic <note>i.e., Pagan/Gentile</note> writings.* The blessed held to a middle way: with which words Benedictus Aretius seals his learned Dissertation on the reading of the Pagans.

Very many sin *in excess* <note>original: ἐν ὑπεροχῇ</note>; who attribute more than is usual to the talents and studies of the Pagans; who with one mouth sound the praises of Christ alongside the praises of Jove;

<margin>distinction 86, chapter 5.</margin>
to use the words of Gregory the Great, with which he rebuked Bishop Desiderius: who devote themselves more freely to obscene fables, the commentaries of Philosophers, and the trifles of Poets, than to the scriptures promising us the immortality of the blessed life; who without any shame prefer the virtues and deeds of the Pagans (as the impiously-learned Machiavelli does, that stained fleece of Tuscany) to the Christian religion; who in the time destined for sacred things devote themselves to profane ones: which once happened in the time of Gregory, who rebuked a certain Bishop, not because he learned secular letters, but because contrary to his office, instead of the Gospel reading, he was explaining Gram-

<column-break/>

-mar to the people. And after the devastation of Italy brought about by the Goths and Vandals, there were more religious attentions in reading Comedies than in the Gospels: noble matrons heard the lyre of Flaccus <note>Horace</note> with greater applause than the precepts of Solomon; there were exercises in the arts of Naso <note>Ovid</note> rather than in the reading of Paul: Jerome complains of that to Pope Damasus; Victor of Marseilles to Abbot Salmon. Nor can this crime be so charged against Hypatia, that most learned virgin, who at Alexandria undeservedly endured the envy of foreign erudition under Bishop Cyril of Alexandria; of whom Synesius mentions in his *Letter to Herculianus* as *a genuine leader of the mysteries of philosophy.* <note>original: γνησίας καὶ ἡγεμόνος τῶν φιλοσοφίας ὀργίων</note> But I do not cease to marvel here at the <term>philosopher-craft-theologians</term> <note>original: φιλοσοφοτεχνοθεολόγους</note> of a later age, or rather the impiously theologizing Philosophers: who so deformed Theology and overwhelmed it with Pagan terms, that scarcely any image of it remains any longer: since they explain Scripture not through Scripture, but <term>the cart before the horse</term> <note>original: ὕστερον πρότερον (hysteron proteron)</note> narrating without judgment from Plato, Aristotle, and similar blind guides, whether from the chair or the pulpit.

I mean the Doctors whom they call Scholastics, whose age extended itself through three centuries, beginning around the year 1200 and ending around 1500. The Greek and Hebrew languages were then scarcely known by name. Latin was most foully defiled. *From the time of Peter Lombard, secular Philosophy began to defile sacred Theology with its useless curiosity, as Trithemius also witnesses in his book on writers.* From this source were born infinite disputes, consultations, sermons, and exhortations; with which they agitated the matter on both sides, and agitated the schools, from which it was called *Scholastic*. If I wished to enumerate these, there would never be an end. The Thomists, *most devoted to Aristotle* <note>original: δεισοτελικώτατοι</note>, mixed Aristotelian things with sacred ones and changed them, so that at last all flavor and sense failed. Upon this foundation, which was Christ, they ought to have built gold, silver,

<margin>1 Corinthians 3.</margin>
and precious stones; on the contrary, they built hay and stubble, the end of which was fire. Thomas Bradwardine, formerly Archbishop of Canterbury, in his preface *to the three books on the cause of God against Pelagius* (which the Author of the *Catalog of Witnesses of the Truth* pours into his own Work *in those very words*), after he had complained that in his age many fought with Pelagius for free will against gratuitous grace, and against Paul, the spiritual prize-fighter of grace, exclaims among other things: *“Just as the ancient Pelagians, puffed up by the windy name of secular sciences and despising the Theological Consistory, demanded the Philosophical one; so also do the moderns. Certainly that there was a great confusion of dogmas in past times will become known to the reader even from the reading of this book alone;”* which Henry Savile recently published in England from six manuscripts for the benefit of literature. They lost time in the Decrees and Decretals, in Thomas, Scotus, and other Masters of the Sentences, as they call them. Those speculations were let into the very heart of Theology, and occupied the pulpits and the rostrum.

The Holy Bible was scarcely read even in the Vulgate <note>The standard Latin translation of the Bible</note> translation; much less in the original languages <note>Hebrew and Greek</note>, which were unknown to them. An ear-witness, Thomas Freigius*, 
<margin>Oration on the Unity of GOD.</margin>

Concerning this barbarism, Luther complains thus in his *Table Talk*: **In our times, studying was a wretched business, when Theology and all good arts were despised, and clever minds were plagued with Sophistry. Aristotle the heathen was held in such honor that whoever denied him or contradicted him was held and condemned as the greatest heretic in Cologne—even though they did not rightly understand Aristotle, as was the case with the monk who spent two hours in a Passion-sermon on the question: Whether quantity is really distinct from substance?** After Luther, Vitus Winshemius* 
<margin>in the Funeral Oration for Philip Melanchthon.</margin>

To be sure, the importance of sermons has been largely removed, and the foolish and ridiculous method of adorning and persuading virtue (from Aristotle) has mostly become obsolete; therefore, those who remain from that ancient barbarism ought to appear all the more shameful—those who dress up a woman in a sermon, or make God, the parent of the Universe, play with papers or a ball, or set up a contest of arms, or lead dances, or philosophize slowly and fastidiously about human joints and limbs. They dreamed that writings composed with human skill, which were read most zealously by everyone, relied on demonstrations, but that the word of God relied only on probable reason. From this, the matter had proceeded to such perversity that Aristotle and the *Master of Sentences* <note>Peter Lombard, whose "Sentences" was the standard medieval theology textbook.</note> were held in higher regard than the very Codex of the Holy Bible itself. For a *Biblicus* <note>original: "Biblicus"; a lower-ranking student of the Bible.</note> (as they called them) in that squalor of the age, earned the name of *Bachelor* or one initiated with the first laurel and theological prerogative. Therefore, anyone who desired to return from the Latin alone to the Greek and Hebrew truth—which they knew not at all—was suspected of being a heretic, as the aforementioned Canus again confesses, as does Espence <margin>page 105.</margin> on the book of Titus.

Even to that point were certain Masters of the cloisters so unrefined that they did not even know how to speak Latin, and when they were about to celebrate Mass with a somewhat rustic sound of voice, lest they commit solecisms <note>grammatical errors</note> by robbing long and short syllables of their due sound, they governed their tongues with diacritical marks. For example: *Lord, hear my prayer* <note>original: "Domine exaudi orationem"</note> etc. They were moderately present for reading: but in the shorthand method of writing, as the times were, they sometimes stumbled. Here, if it had to be read in the hymns of the Church: *Jesus of Nazareth; Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the Prophets;* but *Barabbas* was a robber; *I am the Alpha and Omega* etc. These men, beyond any understanding or appreciation of the sense, would portentously say with halved and half-eaten sounds of words: *Jesum Nazum; Jarlim, Jarlim, who killed the profans; E, e, but he was a robber; I am the alphati-tout menga;* <note>The author is mocking the garbled, phonetic Latin of uneducated priests who could not pronounce the liturgical texts correctly.</note> so that you may know these things are so, read Étienne Tabourot, who recites the examples.

By God, I was more than 50 years old before I knew what the New Testament was.* When Robert Stephens <note>A famous Renaissance printer and scholar.</note> repeatedly asked them in what place in the New Testament something was written, they replied that they had read it in Jerome or in the Decrees, but what the New Testament actually was, they did not know. Truly remarkable praise! Gerard Listrius writes: I have known very many theologians, "Doctors" as they call them, who before their 50th year had not yet unrolled all the Epistles of Paul, as they confessed to me in familiarity. Whenever these men approach the interpretation of the sacred scriptures, good gods, how cold it is, how filthy everything is, how they bring nothing worthy of Christ. # PROLEGOMENA

...our sacred books, so that they do not blush to subject the language of the Holy Spirit to their own correction and childish rod; they themselves are worthy of the rod and the whip, being far more deserving of punishment than of discussion. I would believe that even today, amidst the thick darkness of the Papacy, there are so many of them that if they were to reveal themselves in our current age as they showed themselves in the previous century, there would scarcely be a more numerous sect. It is to be lamented that there are still those among them who, although they boast of being enclosed within the borders of the Church, peddle certain dogmas that attack Christianity itself under the splendor of Pagan Antiquity, being destitute of the forces of a fighting army. Certainly, they are carried with full sails toward this reef of atheism (for why should I use a milder word?).

The Parisian Doctors, who in the articles determined on matters of faith, Art. XII, attempt to establish the *Invocation of Saints* from the writings of the heathens, candidly admit in the meantime that we hold the unshakable foundation of our Religion, when they incautiously burst out into these words: *If this invincible shield were not for us (that the Church cannot err), we would have been defeated a hundred times already by the Lutherans, since they have the appearance of truth on their side and press us with strong arguments.* With the same <term>superstition</term> <note>original: δεισιδαιμονίᾳ (deisidaimonia) - often used to mean excessive fear of the gods or religious scrupulosity</note> Cornelius à Lapide brings forward the same reason for the worship of Saints: that they must be religiously honored lest the Church be surpassed in this regard by the heathens. For it is not fitting, he says, *that the pious religion of the faithful be conquered by the impious superstition of the heathens; the faithful should therefore exhibit and represent to themselves and others a constant memory and presence of God and the saints through crosses, images, and altars.* The Jesuit wishes that Christians should surpass the impious heathens not only in things unknown to scripture, but even in things plainly contrary to it. These heathens are also proposed in illicit matters to incite, rouse, and goad Christians by <margin>Book 2 on Discipline, ch. 3</margin> *Jacob Gretser*, a most impudent writer. Behold the parallelism of Paganism and "Papanism"! Through beads, these wretched men pay out prayers to male and female saints five, ten, or twenty times; often more intent on keeping the count than on conceiving the prayers, so that they might conquer God by number, rather than by the weight and heat of the soul; with a <term>babbling</term> <note>original: βαττολογίᾳ (battologia) - idle, repetitive speaking</note> almost identical to the heathens <margin>Matthew 6:7</margin> which Christ rebuked—these Babblers—

Our Fathers mumble their *Ave Marias.* How such prayers differ from the invocation of the false Divinities of the Greeks and other nations, except that the names are changed, I do not know, says <margin>Notes on Syrian in Augustine, book 8, last chapter</margin> *Ludovicus Vives*—a man beyond all suspicion of an irreligious mind (an elogy given to him by Claude d'Espence)—that no distinction can be found between Ethnic [Pagan] and Papistic worship toward statues, except that they have only changed the names and titles: where it is permitted to defeat the Papists with Papist blood, so that in this too, you may see one Midianite stabbed by another Midianite. <margin>Homily 91 on Matthew</margin> *For truth, when proclaimed against its opposite, shines more brightly*, says Chrysostom. For thus the most famous apostate Georgius Wicelius (whom Wilhelm Eisengrein writes <margin>in the Catalog of Witnesses of the Truth, folio 207. a.</margin> fought constantly against the phalanxes of heretics) fights against this invocation. *I confess (he says in the dedicatory Epistle to the Exercises of True Piety) that it displeases me that under the pretext or veil of I know not what "Dulia"* <note>Dulia: a theological term for the honor given to saints, distinguished from Latria, which is worship due to God alone</note>

Regarding Purgatory, chapter 11, he writes: "The third reason is taken from the common opinion of all nations." It is frivolous and improper that *Georgius Enjedinus* <note>A Unitarian theologian known for denying the Trinity.</note> in his book *Explanations of Passages of the Old and New Testament* compares that *Pauline* phrase concerning the eternal Deity of Christ in *Galatians 1:1*—*Paul an Apostle, not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ*—to that of *Aristophanes* in *Plutus*, Act 1, Scene 1: *O Zeus and gods, how troublesome a thing it is!* <note>original: Ὡς ἀργαλέον πρᾶγμ’ ἐστὶν, ὦ Ζεῦ καὶ Θεοὶ</note>. He says: *By the Apostolic opposition, Christ is not excluded from the number of men; but because of his excellence and singular privilege, which he has above other men, he is exempted from the rest of common men and named separately, and is opposed to all men living on earth, not indeed by nature, but at least by reason of his condition.* He claims it is a custom among both profane and sacred, Greek and Latin writers, *to exempt one person from the number and order of others of the same genus and species because of excellence and singular privilege.* He draws his first example from *Aristophanes*; the others from the sacred words of the Evangelists. It suffices for our purpose to deny that *Aristophanes* in the first verse of *Plutus* uses a similar expression; for he speaks conjunctively: *Zeus and the gods*. But the Apostle here does not speak conjunctively, "through men and through Jesus Christ"; but antithetically: *nor through man, but through Jesus Christ*. From which antithesis Christ is truly shown to be not merely a naked man, like those from whom and through whom the Apostle denies he was called, but much more than those who only deserve the name of man *elsewhere*; namely, the God-Man.

# ON BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

among Theologians, Philosophers, and other interpreters. Thus the word *Election* or *Predestination* is used one way among secular authors, and another way in scripture. The same judgment applies to many terms. I think it not at all out of place to bring forward here the excellent words of Joachim Camerarius <note>A 16th-century German classical scholar and reformer</note> regarding certain exceptional and singular expressions of Holy Scripture. *Other expressions are found that are exceptional and singular concerning those things which can neither be grasped by the capacity of the human mind, nor demonstrated by the faculty of speech; these are figures of speech commonly and, so to speak, naturally unused by all mortals in any place or nation. Nor do they signify anything anywhere, except in the assembly and congregation of those who, called by divine proclamation, have as their Master and teacher of truth the Holy Spirit, whom the only-begotten Son sends from his eternal Father to his Church, in which the Word of God is preached and heard with religious piety. Moreover, those exceptional and singular expressions are those by which dogma is understood—that is, the heads of the Christian faith—and by which the secret action of a revealed thing is established. These are called* <term>mysteries</term> <note>original: μυστήρια</note> *by the Greeks, and Sacraments by the Latins. For these ought in no way to be reduced to the investigation of human sagacity, nor should any aids of cleverness or cunning be employed in, as it were, shelling them out. And since they resist that understanding and perspective of men, one ought not to try to explain them by the benefit of figures in such a way that they no longer appear secret and sacred, but common and profane. But there is need only for faith and assent in this part, which indeed should be* <term>secure and unshakable</term> <note>original: ἀσφαλὴς καὶ ἀδιάσειστος</note>. Excepting these singular, exceptional, and unusual expressions (in which, nevertheless, it is necessary for one to understand the words and the speech if they are to give assent, as anyone can see), for all other matters, all sagacity of wit, skill of mind, industry of study, and finally the faculty and power of the mind may be applied so that what is said, and how it is said, can be clearly and transparently understood. Thus he writes in the preface to his *Notations on the Figures of Speech in the 4 Books of the Gospels*, pages 7 and 8. Compare the same author on Matthew chapter 26 regarding the words, <term>take, eat</term> <note>original: λάβετε, φάγετε</note>. # INTRODUCTION

<margin>
Cicero to Brutus.
</margin>
If eloquence is "wisdom speaking fluently" <note>original: *eloquentia est copiosè loquens sapientia*</note>, who could deny that the eloquence of Saint Paul was of the highest order? Which of the Latin Orators—to say nothing of the Greeks—can be compared to Paul alone in genius, erudition, diligence, or majesty of speech? He treats grand subjects with magnificence, moderate ones with restraint, and humble ones with simplicity so skillfully that those who find him lacking in that triple style of speaking described by the Roman Orator <note>Cicero</note> (*the humble, the middle, and the sublime*) must surely blush. Those who piously consider all his oratorical ornament, set within the circuit of both abstruse and admirable matters, cannot help but give the Apostle every point of credit. Furthermore, those who say that this supreme master of speaking violated the laws of oratory in his divine wisdom are altogether like those haughty Grammarians to whom Cicero, in his *Speech for Caelius*, seemed to speak with poor Latinity and to have strayed from the virtue of eloquence—as Gellius records *.

<margin>
Book 17, *Attic Nights*, chapter 1.
Seneca, *On Benefits*, book 1.
Ulrich Zasius in *Commentary on Cicero's Rhetoric to Herennius*.
</margin>
Vicious are the eyes that shrink from the light; blind are those who do not see *. One is blind if they think Paul lacks oratorical vigor or the "stings" of pointed thought. There is one * who finds fault with certain splendid elements in the speech of Stephen the Protomartyr as being "insufficiently Rhetorical"; he even demands an immoderate precision <note>Greek: *akribeian*</note> and a more-than-Laconic brevity in the sacred texts. For example, when it says in Saint Mark chapter 5, verse 26, regarding the sick woman: *She had suffered much from many physicians, and had not improved at all, but rather grew worse.* This last part, he says (*but rather grew worse*), would have been enough *.

<margin>
U. Z. *Commentary on Rhetoric to Herennius*, p. 92.
</margin>
The luxury of the interpreter has found something to fret over, contaminating it as if with the claws of Harpies. Who does not recognize in the holier retreat of Holy Scripture that lauded custom where, wishing to narrate an action or a thought to us, it is accustomed to amplify, exaggerate, and express the same meaning through diverse sentences? Doctor Luther excellently said that the scheme of Solomon’s speech consists of "painted words." It is a wonder how, in his writings, he confirms the same thoughts and the same precepts with new figures, coats them with new pigments, and frequently returns to the same ideas. This is surely so that through repeated turns, the doctrine of wisdom may be better and more deeply fixed in the mind. For it is solemn for Solomon, above others, to hammer home one and the same thought once and again in different places. Fastidious men praise things in Cicero and Plautus as grand and weighty, yet consider the same things in Scripture to be trivial. Those who follow Cicero’s precept take a passage containing some force and turn it through various sentences and modes; they praise, extol, and admire it. These things, I say, they admire in others but condemn in the sacred texts, where they have no reason to find fault. Caselius wrote to Galen that no one could attain the majesty of Plato’s elocution. Let us stand for Saint Paul. No one has ever imitated his power <note>Greek: *deinotēta*</note> and gravity of speech; his sweetness and great force in speaking were interpreted as *madness* by Festus (Acts ch. 26 v. 24) when he could not grasp them. And so that he might be heard more willingly by that enemy of truth, Paul most prudently avoided bitterness of speech; with that same facial eloquence, he defined King Agrippa. For in what was like a full theater, in order to narrate in decent order the eloquence shown to him from heaven, he first displays oratorical signs and decorous

<column-break/>

<margin>
Acts 12:17; ch. 13 v. 16; ch. 19:33.
Persius, Satire 1 v. 7.
Tacitus, book 16.
Ovid, *Metamorphoses* book 1.
Claudian, *On the War*, v. 133.
Gellius, book 9 ch. 15.
</margin>
gestures of the ancients, which those about to request silence would put forward. Therefore, before Festus, Agrippa, and the rest of the standing crowd, he began *to speak with hand extended* *. This was the customary ritual of those about to speak, who once prepared an audience with an outstretched hand, and demanded for themselves *the hot silence of the crowd by the majesty of the hand*, as Persius weightily says. This is what authors call "shaking the hand for silence" <note>Greek: *kataseiein tē cheiri sigan*</note>, venerating the assembly with the hand; suppressing murmurs with voice and hand, venerating the crowd with voice and hand, calming the tumult with the right hand, and signaling quiet with the hand. 2. With a modest delay intervening before he entered the course of the speech itself, to prepare goodwill, he says sweetly and artfully in verse 2: *I consider myself happy, KING AGRIPPA, that I am to defend myself before you today.* 3. He traces the origin of the unjustly instituted accusation back to its roots, and when he reaches the climax, he tempers his diction with interrogation, apostrophe, subjection, prayer, and other "little flowers" of figures. With such great gentleness and spirit (I know not which was greater), he breaks the mind of Agrippa, so that he confessed, almost groaning, that Paul with his most eloquent mouth had persuaded him—if not entirely, then at least to a great extent. Verse 28: *In a little you persuade me to become a Christian. You urge me, he says, you do not fully persuade.* What did Festus, a vehement man, say to this? That pagan man, who had not yet left Agrippa’s side, struck by that skill in speaking which the divine Orator had weightily discharged for the glory of God with great vehemence of spirit, unable to contain his own emotions, rushed by some impulse of nature to object in a loud voice before the whole multitude that Paul was insane—Paul, whose doctrine was gathering like rain and whose eloquence was flowing like dew *.

<margin>
Deuteronomy 32:2.
</margin>
*“You are mad, Paul; your great learning is turning you to madness.”* <note>Greek: *Mainē Paule, ta polla se grammata eis manian peritrei*</note> He prefers to interpret the divine will concerning the salvation of men, uttered by a human mouth, as madness—out of the envy of the gentiles, to whom Christ the bringer of salvation was foolishness—rather than give the glory of wisdom to God. He prefers to think Paul brought these things forth out of a boastfulness of his blossoming erudition or eloquence, rather than feeling them so from his heart. But what defense does Paul bring? *“I am not mad,”* he says, *“most excellent Festus, but I utter words of truth and soberness.”* <note>Greek: *Ou mainomai... kratiste Phēste, all’ alētheias kai sōphrosynēs rhēmata apophtheggomai*</note> Namely, setting aside the contention that was once common to certain Orators, he sustained the immoderate attack against him with a most gentle mind, and so calmly refuted it in a "common place" <term>commonplace: a general rhetorical argument applicable to many cases</term> that he seemed to gather new goodwill; for he calls him "Most Excellent." Soon, turning his speech to Agrippa, he says: *“I pray to GOD that not only you, but also all who hear me, might become such as I am, except for these chains.”*

<margin>
Acts ch. 7:2 etc.; ch. 22 v. 1.
</margin>
The same Apostle, accused of "novelty of doctrine" among the Greeks, handled the matter with an 
extraordinary speech before the Athenians, tempered with prudent gentleness. He begins his speech in Acts ch. 17 v. 22 with the customary preface: *“Men of Athens.”* <note>Greek: *Andres Athēnaioi*</note> For it was usual to employ this in an address; in the same way, Demosthenes addressed the Athenians at the start of his *Speech on the Crown*, as did Socrates in his *Apology*. To capture goodwill, he elsewhere * adds: *“Brothers.”* <note>Greek: *Adelphoi*</note> This appellation was also used in other languages; an example of which is found in Elmacinus, the Arab Historian, in that speech which he delivered to the people of Medina disputing about choosing a successor to Muhammad...

# ON BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
Book 1 of the History of the Saracens, chapter 2.
</margin>
Abu Bakr <note>original: "Abubecrus"; the first Caliph and successor to Muhammad</note>, who was later designated King, established this; the beginning of which was: *O Men of Medina*. Those, however, with whom Paul had to dispute in that tongue-gifted city <note>Athens</note> were the Epicureans and Stoics, the most contrary sects of all philosophers. For the one defined all things by chance, the other by necessity; one attributed too much to pleasure, the other too much to the lack of pleasure; one <term>clung to pleasures</term> <note>original Greek: ἔκεινε τῶν ἡδονῶν</note>, the other to <term>virtue</term> <note>original Greek: τὴν ἀρετὴν</note>. Regarding these and other such matters found in so many illustrious authors concerning their conflicts with Saint Paul, consult Augustine in his *Treatise on the Epicureans and Stoics*, in which he discusses the dissertation—which he calls a *Collation*—held between the Apostle and the philosophers. In that regard, the people of Lystra certainly seem worthy, if not of praise then of admiration, for they gave Paul the name of *Mercury*—whom superstitious antiquity believed to be the god of Eloquence—because he was the leader of the word; for which reason we shall treat that passage below. Why then should we not admire divine eloquence? No one else is worthy of God than he who admires the riches of the holy tongue. For the power of Divine Scripture is great above all others, and many riches of thought lie hidden in its words: as witnessed by Chrysostom, *Homily 36 on Genesis*; see there, with whom Augustine agrees, who in the *last book of Christian Doctrine, chapter 6, says: While I read the books of Holy Scripture, not only can nothing seem wiser than they, but also nothing more eloquent.* Even a small word weaves together almost an entire precept for us, which can scarcely be found in human learning: as the aforementioned Chrysostom and Augustine, and at greater length Sixtus of Siena in Book 4 of his *Library*, have demonstrated. We wish to record here the pious words of Michael Neander, which appear in his *Gnomologia*, page 46: *The speech of Scripture is sometimes too simple and unskillful, and they [the critics] require greater splendor and eloquence; yet in one little syllable, one tiny stroke, one single sentence, there is often more splendor of divine eloquence, doctrine, and heavenly wisdom—ineffable to us in this weak life—than you could find in the wisdom, doctrine, and eloquence of all the world's wise men if you gathered them into one. It is as if the Holy Spirit were an infant, and unless he, being stammering, sought the lights of oratory from Demosthenes, Plato, Isocrates, and Cicero, he could not have them from elsewhere.* Let us, following Neander's lead, begin a comparison of moral maxims. The Plautine sentiment concerning a bad conscience—*nothing is more wretched than a mind conscious of its own guilt*—when it is recited by teachers in the schools, the large lecture halls rustle with pens and the theaters ring with applause. Wretched Scripture! Which, though it be a banquet of wisdom, is nevertheless thought to have nothing similar; yet in all excesses, concerning all virtues, and finally concerning everything that happens in life, it has much better and clearer things, brought down from heaven and written by God himself in the Bibles (which are truly <term>The Books</term> <note>original Greek: βίβλοι</note>). To the impious, it is like a <term>boiling sea, which cannot rest</term>, says the Holy Spirit through Isaiah <term>the Holy Spirit followed</term> <note>original Greek: ἄγιον πνεῦμ’ ὄπυσευεν</term>. There is <term>no peace for the wicked</term>, says the Lord; the restlessness of a mind tossed by various tides is elegantly compared to a storm at sea. To use the words of Boethius here, from Book 1, Song 2 of *The Consolation of Philosophy*:

Moreover, we read a twin passage to this in the Proverbs of Solomon: *The way of the wicked is darkness*. Is this said for nothing? Is there no splendor of words here?

<column-break/>

What Apelles <note>a famous painter of antiquity</note> ever depicted a bad conscience in such a way? Who depicted a good one better and more succinctly than Solomon? *A good mind is like a continual feast.* And who among the rhetoricians or poets described it more graphically than the son of Sirach: *Substance is good, if there is no sin in the conscience.* Therefore, those people ride on "bad mules" <note>an idiom for being mistaken</note> who seek sweeter sentiments and more beautiful lights of figures in Plato, Pindar, Terence, Plautus, and other foreign writers, than in the Psalms of David, the writings of Paul, and other Biblical books. What shall we say of David alone? David certainly (to apply Quintilian’s encomium of Pindar to our David) stood out as far the prince in spirit, magnificence, sentiments, and figures, most blessed in the abundance of things and words and in the flood of eloquence. By which name Jerome also calls him his Simonides, Pindar and Alcaeus, and also Horace, Catullus, and Serenus, who sounded forth Christ upon the lyre. David was a distinguished lyric poet at the harp <note>original: "Nablium", a Phoenician stringed instrument</note>, since the Spirit of the Lord spoke through him.

<margin>
Book 10, Institutes, ch. 1, p. 447.
</margin>

<margin>
Epistle to Paulinus.
</margin>

-> Be silent, Orpheus; cast away your lyre, Hermes, <-
-> and you, Delphic ones, sink further into oblivion, <-
-> for David, ruling the lyre for us by the Spirit, <-
-> makes clear the hidden mysteries of God. <-

As in praise of King David and his Psalter, these are elegant <term>anonymous</term> <note>original Greek: ἄδηλα</note> Iambic verses, which Andreas Schottus presents in his work on Isidore, transcribed from the Menologium along with this one heroic line (<term>The honey-sweet songs of David’s holy harmony</term> <note>original Greek: Ἁρμονίης ἱερῆς μελιηδέα ἄσματα Δαυΐδ</note>). What shall we say of his poems? Especially if we remember they are older than the others; proceeding not from imitation, but from pure emotion. Do you seek triumphal chariots? You have them, but consecrated to the GOD of hosts. Do you want wedding songs? They are not lacking, but those which celebrate the chaste embraces of God and the pious. Do you want even Pastorals? Innumerable Eclogues occur, but with GOD as the shepherd and Israel as the flock. The art in them is so exquisite that whoever translates them seems to have achieved a great honor. The emotions are so vivid that they extinguish and suffocate all others. What, finally (tell me, whoever you are, admirer of the Pagans), does pagan antiquity have that can be compared with the utterances of David? What can be brought into comparison with the majesty of divine eloquence? The Pagans themselves, when they stumbled upon the sacred writings, could not help but admire their majesty. Dionysius Longinus, in his book <term>On the Sublime</term> <note>original Greek: περὶ ὕψους</note>, compares Moses and Homer; from the latter he brings forth Neptune, but from the former these words: *God said, let there be light. He adds that Moses was no ordinary man:* then he admires in him the wisdom of mind, <term>the strongest and most robust in conceptions</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ κρατιστον καὶ περὶ τὰς νοήσεις ἀroditeρον</note>: <term>In this excellence, he says, that lawgiver of the Jews surpassed others, being no ordinary man, since he recognized the divine power according to its worth.</term> <note>original Greek: ἡα̂κ... ἐγνώρισε</note> Amelius, a Greek Platonic writer, confesses that in the Hebrew language there is very great emphasis, brevity, and clarity—less variety, indeed, than in the Greek language, but less ambiguity. <term>The foreign tongue has words of great emphasis and great conciseness. It is subject to fewer ambiguities, and less of the variety and breadth of phrasing.</term> <note>original Greek: ἔχει δὲ ἡ βάρβαρος... λέξεων</note> O adamantine force of divine truth! Which so occupies the improvident minds of your adversaries that they voluntarily grant you the palm of victory. # PROLEGOMENA

he can be compared with Homer and other most illustrious poets, and that such things are proposed by him everywhere that not even Homer or Pindar ever spoke anything quite so poetically. With the same pious affection, Petrus Martinius *places David, the greatest of poets not only by the merit of his subject matter but also by the majesty and elegance of his song, before all Pindaric Odes and absolutely all Greek and Latin ones; and in comparison to David, he despises all others, even Pindar and Horace.* <margin>in the Preface to Technologia</margin> Similarly, Marcus Marinus, in the preface to *Noah’s Ark, or the Treasury of the Holy Tongue*, says that no orator, whether Latin or Greek, is more eloquent than Moses and Isaiah in the purity of their expressions; no poet is more acute in figures and tropes in verse than David and Job; no historiographer is more faithful than Samuel. Luther himself, when asserting the majesty of those writers, used to say that *Isaiah is grandiloquent and Ciceronian; David’s speech is similar to that of Sallust, that is, brief and pure; while Solomon’s is picturesque.* <margin>Preface to Luther's Genesis, folio 496.b.</margin> as Hieronymus Besoldus <note>A 16th-century jurist and scholar</note> reported from the mouth of Luther. Justus Lipsius (to whom G. Thomson writes that almost all matters of profane literature were more diligently sought, meditated upon, and labored over than sacred letters) says that the books of Solomon and Sirach are most full of divine and human wisdom, and he desires them to be uniquely commended to us. Regarding the speech of Paul, we are satisfied by the most skillful persuasion <note>original: πειθὼ (peitho) - persuasion/eloquence</note> of Theodore Beza, who is said to have studied all Greek authors, sacred and profane, before <margin>note on 1 Corinthians 11</margin> beginning his *Annotations on the New Testament*: *When I consider more closely,* he says, *the whole character and style <note>original: χαρακτῆρα (charaktēra)</note> of Paul’s speech, I confess I have found no similar grandiloquence in Plato himself whenever he chose to denote the mysteries of God; no equal power <note>original: δεινότητα (deinotēta) - forcefulness/intensity</note> in Demosthenes whenever he decided to terrify or warn minds with the fear of divine judgment, or to draw them to contemplate the goodness of God, or to exhort them to the duties of piety and mercy; finally, I find no more exact method in Aristotle and Galen themselves, otherwise the most outstanding masters of these matters.* Therefore, Angelus Bassus—whom we call Poliziano after his homeland—must have been vigorously unpolished (if what they say is true); his profane remark, common to many, regarding Pindar and David is circulated. For when he was asked what he judged of David’s Psalms, he said: *I see that those ancient poems are full of wisdom. There are precepts of all virtues, warnings about providence, threats of punishments for the wicked, and promises of rewards and protection for the just. Ancient histories of that nation are also inserted, and examples of both punishment and defense are visible. I value this wisdom highly, as it is useful for life and morals; and I think the figures of speech are elegant in their own language. But in Pindar, the same things are told more sweetly and illustrated more splendidly with examples.* <margin>in Letter to 47. Adv. S.</margin> To these things Poliziano [spoke], as Peucer reports; whose defense, however, Caspar Barth takes up. <margin>Selnecker on Corinthians, p. 496.</margin> Driven by the same gadfly of madness, Lazarus Bonamicus used to say with foolish pride that he preferred the Pindaric Odes to the Davidic Psalms. O insane man, who wants to [challenge] wisdom <note>original: σοφίαν (sophian)</note> itself! No one will even think that Pindar competes with equal elegance against the Lyre of David, or that there is as much in the Hebrew

<column-break/>

poems of both erudition and grace as there is in Pindar; yet Huldericus Geminius (or Zwingli) writes all of this *very hyperbolically* <note>original: μάλα ὑπερβολικῶς (mala hyperbolikōs)</note> in his learned preface to Pindar. Pindar, the prince of Lyricists, is called "most wise" <note>original: σοφώτατος (sophōtatos)</note> by Plato in the 3rd book of *Laws*, "divine" in *Meno*, and "most grand-voiced" <note>original: μεγαλοφωνότατος (megalophōnōtatos)</note> by Athenaeus in book 13, p. 564. Let us also transcribe those praises for David. The subject of meter in David is more illustrious and splendid. What the eloquence delivered by God provides over the eloquence that exists in human writing is declared by St. Bernard to the Bishops of Aquitaine, and by Isidore in the last book of the *Letters* edited by Andreas Schott, which I now leave aside. Compare Carlo Reggio in *The Christian Orator*, book 4, chapter 2.

Formerly, the haters and gnawers of divine eloquence used to object to some sort of rudeness of speech in the worshippers of Christ; and they held Christians in contempt, as we learn from Arnobius, Lactantius, and Clement of Alexandria. <margin>See Elmenhorst on Arnobius.</margin> *Some of them*, Theodoret writes, *because they have now become partakers of the Poets and Orators, and have even tasted the elegance of Plato, despise the monuments of sacred literature as things not adorned with the curling-irons of eloquence, and therefore think the fishermen unworthy to be the ones by whom truth is first taught.* Gregory Nazianzen (*Oration 26*) and Jerome (*preface to book 3 on the Epistle to the Galatians*) bore it very poorly that the eloquence of Plato, the artifice of Aristotle, and the ornaments of Cicero had crept into the Church of God like Egyptian plagues. It was certainly not the opinion of the Fathers to reject Cicero’s precepts of elocution, for they themselves, being instructed in the same abundance of speaking, achieved equal results in the brilliance of speech and words, as so many left-behind monuments show: for which reason Lactantius calls Cyprian the *Christian Cicero*, and others call Lactantius the *river of Tullian <note>i.e., Ciceronian</note> eloquence*; and Jerome calls Tertullian a *Ter-Tullius* <note>A pun on Tertullian's name and Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> who most perfectly imitated Cicero. Plutarch, intending to praise those three parents of Greek eloquence—Demosthenes, Isocrates, and Aeschines—ascribes the source of speech to the latter, assigns the stream to the second, and the river to the former; someone wished these similarities to apply also to the three Doctors of the Greek Church: that the eloquence of Nazianzen imitates the stream, Basil the ever-flowing source, and Chrysostom the river—to pass over the other encomiums of Ambrose and Augustine with a dry foot <note>i.e., briefly</note>. But the target in the eyes of the Ancient Theologians was the pride of certain triflers who, having abandoned the simplicity of Christianity for the allurements and charms attractively begged from Cicero and Plato, tried to lead away the simpler souls of Christians. Hence those tears of the Fathers! For in that age, having omitted the simplicity and purity of the words of the Apostles, they met as if at the Athenaeum <note>A school/theatre in Rome for literary activities</note> to excite the applause of the bystanders, *so that the Rhetorical Speech, painted with the lie of art, might go out into public like some little prostitute, not so much to instruct the people as to seek the favor of the people.* And in the *Letter to Paulinus*, chapter 6, <margin>Jerome, in that place.</margin> he attacks them with these words: *I say nothing of those like myself who, if by chance they come to the holy scriptures after secular literature, and soothe the ear of the people with composed speech, think whatever they say is the law of God; nor do they deign to know what the Prophets or the Apostles felt, but [they adapt] incongruous things to their own sense...*

It also critiques early scholars who prioritized pagan elegance over Christian simplicity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the dangers of prioritizing secular philosophy over Holy Scripture, specifically focusing on the influence of Plato and the Church Fathers' reactions to it.</meta>

# ON BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

They adapt testimonies as if it were a great thing—and not a most faulty way of teaching—to corrupt meanings and drag the resisting Scripture to their own will. It is as if we had not read the *Homerocentones* or *Virgilocentones* <note>Poems created by patching together lines from Homer or Virgil to tell new stories, such as Christian themes</note>; as if we could not likewise say that Virgil was a Christian without Christ because he wrote: *Now the Virgin returns, the kingdoms of Saturn return.* <note>A famous line from Virgil’s 4th Eclogue often misinterpreted by medieval Christians as a prophecy of the Virgin Mary</note> This was truly gathering leaves, not fruit—that is, words and not virtues; as St. Augustine excellently said in *The Mirror of the Sinner*, chapter 6, treatise 9. From this contempt for Scripture and lazy yawning over sacred matters, the beginning of "Heresiology" <note>The study or system of heresies</note> was born; from here the monsters of opinion, the divorces of sects, and the turbulent disagreements of heretics flowed. Just as the leaders of that ancient Church complain everywhere, the depravity in the commentaries of heretics took its beginnings from the reading of the gentiles, especially the Platonists. <margin>Book on the Resurrection of the Flesh, ch. 3</margin> *Heresies themselves,* says Tertullian, *are furnished by Philosophy (by accident): if those things which they hold in common with the Heathens were taken away from heretics, and they stood their ground on the Scriptures alone, they could not stand.* <margin>Letter to Ctesiphon against the Pelagians</margin> Therefore Jerome had also said elsewhere that *Philosophers are the Patriarchs of Heretics.* The reason was: because all their dogmas, since they are cold and cannot fly, find a seat and rest for themselves among the thorns of Aristotle and Chrysippus. Epiphanius (Book 2 against Heresies, vol. 2) observed that for the Secundians, their entire deception—both regarding eloquence and heresy—happened from the reading of Plato alone. Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 3, p. 414) observes that <term>Marcion</term> <note>An early heretic who rejected the Old Testament</note> drew <term>the starting points of his strange dogmas ungraciously and ignorantly</term> <note>original Greek: τὰς ἀφορμὰς τῶν ξένων δογμάτων ἀχαρείως τε καὶ ἀμαθῶς</term> from Plato. Thomas [Aquinas] (Part 1, Question 43) says the Arians were taught their heresy by Plato; indeed, even Origen himself, as the same author says in Opuscule 70. But what follows from that? Surely from such a great and impure engorgement, what can one hope for but vomit and filth. And therefore it was necessary to refute the writings of the Heathens and shatter their arguments, in which vein Tertullian (Book on the Soul, ch. 23) says: *Since arguments of this kind are introduced by Plato, which the heretics borrow, I shall sufficiently strike back at the heretics if I shatter the arguments of Plato.* St. Augustine, being very learned in Platonic Philosophy, everywhere admires and praises the Platonists, and affirms that their doctrine approaches the Christian one most closely; but not without error, which, having become more cautious, he retracts with laudable modesty in *Retractions*, Book 1, ch. 1, where he defines it in these words: *The praise also, by which I extolled Plato or the Platonic Philosophers so much, deservedly displeases me, especially since Christian doctrine must be defended against their great errors.* For that most pious man knew that in those allurements one is not even then rightly on guard when one is most on guard. Believe the experienced Augustine, for the same man (Confessions, Book 3, ch. 5) relates that he once fell upon Cicero’s *Hortensius*, which contains an encomium of wisdom: *By that speech,* he says, *I was stirred, inflamed, and I burned with an incredible heat of the heart to seek wisdom. I therefore set my mind to attend to the holy scripture, but it seemed to me unworthy to be compared to the dignity of Cicero.* He adds elsewhere that through that loathing of Scripture he fell into the Manichaean heresy, which held him for nine years. Therefore in *The Mirror of the Sinner*, ch. 6, he says: *The proud and unhappy sinner shall blush, and*

<column-break/>

*blinded by pride, inflamed by anger, and defiled by the vice of impatience, he shall fear—he to whom the art of Aristotle is more pleasing than the knowledge of the Apostles. More the Codex of Plato than the divine book; whom no reading gladdens, no knowledge builds up, no speech tastes sweet, unless it be grammatically conceived, dialectically imagined, and rhetorically clothed in purple.* Let the reader not be loath to read through the example of Augustine’s conversion in his books of *Confessions*; because it is suited to inform him usefully about many things. What shall I say of the "Deifiers" of Plato? Those who have consecrated themselves to Plato and his opinions as if to Oracles affirm that he taught the Trinity, and say that he skillfully wrapped the other heads of Christian doctrine in his fables. *We see,* says Giovanni Battista Crispo <margin>In the preface to the work on the cautious reading of Heathen Philosophers</margin>, *such a use of interpreting Plato's words and opinions, and it has been so religiously observed by some; that nothing was said by him (no matter how exorbitant) which is not brought to a right sense by the machinery of Allegories. And (if it please God) has not been dragged toward the meaning of the Gospel. But if he brought forth false things, and signally deceives, then his words so penetrate the minds of men, that there is nothing they do not devise by which they may interpret Plato's mysteries, not only with allegorical, but even with anagogical <note>spiritual or mystical</note> meanings. Finally, if they see Plato has slipped even inadvertently, do not think they would confess any such thing about their Teacher.* And would that most Christians did not venerate Plato as an *Attic Moses* <note>A common phrase in the Renaissance suggesting Plato was a Greek version of Moses</note>. He rightly accuses that monstrous interpretation of certain moderns, which deserves to be exploded by the hisses of all; as is discussed at length in the said book. Nor should it go unnoticed that the Holy Fathers sometimes exceeded moderation in citing Platonic passages, which they judged to be poorly imitated from the sacred Writers. Eusebius, in the book *Preparation for the Gospel*, referred almost everything of ours to Plato even unto satiety. Justin, in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*, is much occupied in scraping together examples from Homer, Plato, and others, so that he even affirmed Plato had received the true doctrine concerning GOD and His essence; indeed, that he even had some knowledge of the future crucifixion of our Savior; when he writes that *the power which is next to the primary God was placed crosswise in the universe in the form of the letter X.* Regarding this law, see the same author in *Exhortation to the Greeks*, page 14, and in *Apology 2 for the Christians*, page 72. To be sure, the authority of Plato was once great among the Pagans, therefore Christian Doctors thought it would be more successful and easier to pluck out ancient superstitions from the minds of men if they transferred or twisted Platonic things to a Christian sense; and from there Constantine in his *Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, Clement of Alexandria, Theodoret, and others collect similar things from Plato and Numenius; about whose pious curiosity others differ. The pious Ancients anxiously searched into the writings of outsiders so that they might build up the chief heads of Christian doctrine against the Pagans from there, although very often in vain; as the famous Marcus Boxhorn teaches in *Roman Questions*, page 62 and following. It is certain they did this <term>having been helped</term> <note>original Greek: ὠφελισθέντας</note>, to whom this alone seems to have been the purpose: to heap up many arguments against the gentiles; according to the saying:

-> *And things which do not help individually, help when many.* <-

I think the ravings of certain moderns are well known,

I consider those whose stubbornness has stirred up no small storms. Among their number is *Paul Skalich, Count of the Huns* (a title he bore with pride), who in his books on *Eternal Justice* and likewise on *Gradation*, labors to prove the dogma of the Trinity from Plato’s Epistle to three friends, and from *Proclus, Trismegistus, Orpheus*, and others. He says that among the higher theologians, by whom all Theology is encompassed, these names exist: *Son of God, Word, Mind, Maker, Cause*. Since these are found among the Ancient Theologians—*Plato, Aristotle, Anaxagoras, the Chaldeans, the Sibyls, Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>, Orpheus*, and the entire *Platonic school*—it appears that the whole Theology concerning the Son, which is now honored and celebrated, was known, adored, and preached before he himself became man.

<margin>Vol. 5 l. 4. p. 1311. a.</margin>
*Theodor Zwinger* in his *Theater of Human Life*, under the title of *Metaphysics*, writes that *Hermes* perceived this mystery more clearly than certain Jews: *Hermes Trismegistus, the greatest Egyptian Priest, greatest King, and greatest Philosopher, was the first to treat of the sacrosanct Trinity in divine matters, and asserted that there is one deity in a trinity <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐν τριάδι μίαν εἶναι θεότητα</note>, attaining by the light of intellect that which many of the Hebrews, even when invited by sacred testimonies, could not comprehend*. This great man erred significantly, since that *Trismegistus*—whether real or a forgery—holds monstrous ideas about the Gods and their worship;

<margin>Book 8 of City of God ch. 23, 24. Vol 2. book 16 ch. 4 p. 346.</margin>
which may be seen in the works of *Augustine*. For this reason, those words of *Zwinger* are purged in the Expurgatory Index of *Spanish Theology* found in *Possevino*. Supporting the same opinion are *Giovanni Pico della Mirandola* and *Agostino Steuco* in his *books on Perennial Philosophy. Antonio Majoragio* in his Reproof against *Nizolius*, book 2, chapter 15, page 197. Against these, *Leonard Lessius* pronounces harshly in book 2 of *On Justice and Law*, chapter 44, doubt 2, number 6, stating that all Platonists were either Mages or favored Magic; among whom it was a bold deed to include *Marsilio Ficino*. If Ficino had lived, he would have left an epitaph for *Lessius* equal to the one that once befell *George of Trebizond*:

<margin>Schovvert. in Delights of the World.</margin>
> In this urn rest the bones of *George*
> of Trebizond, a man little befriended by the Gods;
> Because with a sharp and too-insolent tongue
> He attacked *Plato*, the equal of the gods above.

We do grant this much to the two <note>likely referring to the two schools of thought</note>: that the Gentiles possessed the knowledge that *God was one* by the light of nature; a fact we are taught in Chapter 1 of the *Epistle to the Romans*. For among other things, the Apostle grants this praise to the Heathens: that they knew that which can be known of God. And the whole of Chapter 3 of the book *On the Truth of the Christian Religion* by *Philippe de Mornay*, a noble Frenchman, demonstrates this precisely. However, we deny that the relative consideration—that God is *THREEFOLD*—can be demonstrated by the light of reason. Even if they had certain glimmers of Truth, they merely emulated our opinions, as *Justin* writes.

<margin>Apology 2.</margin>
Among us, these things must be learned by those *who do not even know the shapes of the alphabet, unlearned in speech and barbaric, yet wise in mind*. For this reason, the Ethnic <note>Pagan</note> Philosophers are even called "Thieves of the Prophets and the Hebrews" by the Fathers. To this they drag the saying of *Numenius*, who calls *Plato* an *Attic* or *Greek Moses*. I would believe that *Plato* never saw the Holy Bible or the writings of *Moses*; or if he did read them, it would be more certain to say that because of the antipathy between the two peoples, he did so with a mind for mocking rather than approving.

<column-break/>

For they held the Jews in hatred as if they were some kind of "scum" <note>original: καθάρματα</note>, whence come those infinite Sceptical remarks: *Let the Jew Apella believe it* <note>A quote from Horace implying "I don't believe it, tell it to someone superstitious"</note>, and other things of that kind, which we shall deal with in their proper place. Regarding these Platonists, *Michael Neander* decided thus:

<margin>In the Dedicatory Epistle of the Catechism p. 40.</margin>
*Concerning God and His will, the Philosophers, however wise, eloquent, and admirable they may otherwise be, knew nothing for certain or explored. Although there are those who have tried to show the contrary with the greatest labor—having shaken out all the Ancient Writers, Fathers, Philosophers, Poets, and their Interpreters, Plotinus, Porphyry, Amelius—it was useless and superfluous. They are more worthy of pity than deserving of rebuke. They did not blush to assert impiously and rashly that what the Evangelist John writes concerning the divinity of the Son is found in Plato—things which Plato could not have even dreamed of, since they are a mystery kept silent for eternal ages.* There is no doubt that *Faustus Socinus* <note>Founder of Socinianism, which denied the Trinity</note>, with his mouth agape, snatched an opportunity for strife here. He saw the testimonies of Plato, Trismegistus, and the rest being admitted into the Church without any restraints, and being brought into such a great mystery of salvation with infinite esteem by the investigators of that time. This man from Siena <note>Socinus</note> attempted, under ill-fated auspices, to diminish the glory of that mystery in whatever way and occasion he could. For in that commentary in which he first scattered the seeds of error after the death of his uncle *Lelio Socini*,

<margin>On chapter 1 of John.</margin>
he did not hesitate to assert that the doctrine of the Holy Trinity *took its origin from the writings of Plato, Mercury Trismegistus, and Iamblichus*. He claimed the same consisted of certain strange fictions, slippery subtleties most unworthy of a Christian man, and portentous opinions—not only contrary to Holy Scripture, but even inconsistent with themselves, indeed largely ridiculous and utterly absurd, occupied solely with Plato’s dogmas and wonderful sophisms. Clearly, he seeks this, and wishes to achieve by this expansion of words, that the sacrosanct mystery of the Christian religion be rendered hated; yet we have the most certain defenses for it in the Holy Book. For those who agitate *Plato* with superfluous distress have achieved nothing here other than harming the Church at all times, and never helping it. But lest I wander sideways into another dispute, I return to the "pious frauds" of certain Christians (as I may call them). No one is ignorant that some, fired by a certain pious affection to hasten the conversion of the heathens, transcribed or forged volumes composed by themselves under the names of pagan authors to gain authority for their sacred rites. With this plan and end, there once went out under the name of *SENECA*, the most celebrated philosopher of Nero’s age, forged Epistles to *Paul*. With the same plan, to commend the "new offspring" of the newborn child Christ, they devised that the Poet *Virgil* sang of the Savior in those verses found in Eclogue 4, verse 5, to Pollio:

> The great order of the ages is born anew,
> Now the Virgin returns, the reign of Saturn returns,
> Now a new progeny is sent down from high heaven.
> Only favor the boy now being born, by whom the iron race
> Shall first cease, and a golden race rise over the whole world,
> O chaste Lucina; now your Apollo reigns.

Hence it is affirmed that *Virgil* was a Christian without Christ—

Whether Virgil, without knowing it, wrote a "Birth-Song" for Christ more poetically than prophetically, others may judge. In the same way, the same author introduces the *Sibyls* as prophetesses of Christ the Savior of the world in a charming poem, which its own sweetness commends. It appears that some of the Sibylline poems were "reminders" or "fictions" <note>original: "hypomnemata sive plasmata"</note> created by learned and pious men at the beginning of the New Testament era, which they commended to the Heathens under a pagan title, so that by the occasion of this "pious stratagem" they might win over the children of the Heathens. This is observed by the learned, among whom (if I may say so without offense) the most celebrated theologian of our age, Mr. Dr. Caspar Brochmand, stands out. He does not admit the fake Sibyls and Virgil as witnesses of Christ, regarding them as of "shaky credit" <note>original: "sublestae fidei"</note>; as he solidly showed in the first section of his *Exercises*, which he began to establish with a most useful "hand-guide" <note>original: "cheiragogia"</note> into Ecclesiastical writers. I heartily pray that he may finish <note>original: "telessein"</note> this labor with God's blessing. It must also be confessed that the holy Fathers were sometimes excessive in seeking allegories in the fables of the nations to commend Christian rites to barbarians; they pursued allegorical meanings everywhere in external writings, often against the will of the pagan texts themselves. Many such things exist in the commentaries of ancients and moderns, where they believe images of mystical and divine things lie beneath the surface. Justin, in his *Second Apology for the Christians*, tries to teach that the fables of Bacchus, likewise of Bellerophon, Hercules, and Aesculapius—indeed almost the entire theology of the nations—were elicited from a corrupted sense of the Holy Scriptures and thrust upon the common people. They say the fable of Prometheus, fashioning man from clay, was transformed from the creation of man. They say the Gardens of Alcinous, the Golden Age, and the Elysian Fields were colored by the Devil's wickedness and frauds from the description of Paradise. Janus seems to them to be Noah; Jupiter Ammon is Ham, the son of Noah. Proserpina ravished by Jove is Eve deceived by Satan. They compare Bacchus with Moses. They say the sacrifice of Isaac relates the fable of Iphigenia. They derive the War of the Giants from the building of the Tower of Babel. They draw the fable of Deucalion from the history of the flood under Noah. They twist the fiery chariots of Elijah carried into heaven into the horses of the Sun. The dove sent from the ark of Deucalion from the history of the raven sent by Noah. "Egyptian Days" from the plagues of Egypt. The fable of Ixion from the cohabitation of the sons of God with the daughters of men. The religious anointing of stones from the anointing of the stone at Bethel. The fire of Phaethon from those burned by celestial fires...
