Sodom and Gomorrah; they assert that the fable of Serapis, worshipped by the Egyptians, was transformed from the history of *Joseph*; that Phyllis being changed into a tree was taken from the history of *Lot's wife being transformed into a pillar of salt*; that the twelve labors of Hercules came from the *deeds of Samson*, and infinite other things were born from a foul concealment of divine truth. Concerning these examples of <term>perverse affectation<note>original: "kakozēlia" (Greek: κακοζηλία). A rhetorical term for a faulty or distasteful imitation of style.</note></term>, read, if you wish, Annius of Viterbo on the fictitious Berosus and other worthless authors whom John Annius ineptly stuffed together and published with a self-contradictory commentary; as learned men such as *Joseph Scaliger*, *Rhenanus*, *Canus*, *Possevinus*, *Pererius*, *Ant. Augustinus*, *Ribera*, *Rainoldus*, *Gerh. Vossius*, *G. Gualterius*, *G. Varrerius*, *Tilemannus*, *Calvisius*, *Cassannus*, and others have observed. Add *Alsted in his Historical Encyclopedia, book 20, chapter 11, section 8, etc.* and *Lambert Daneau in his Antiquities of the First Age of the World*. Also Caspar Peucer *On the Kinds of Divinations*, where you will find many things noted. Indeed, no one even moderately skilled in ancient memory can be ignorant of the fact that the Devil’s greatest care was to keep the Gentiles in superstitious worship by working in them an imitation of divine truth. For Superstition discovered this: that it could make itself an imitator of true religion by the authorship of the evil Demon, the enemy of God, who learned to craftily mix the clinging burrs of superstition with fragrant roses; for this reason *Tertullian* calls him the "adulterer of salutary discipline." *Yet to wish to reduce everything to this through ingenious curiosity is nothing other than to act out great trifles with great effort*, says Boxhorn *in the cited place, page 65.* But why do I mention the Ancients, whom we know were refined in letters, learning, and piety? Ridiculous are the writers of a later age who, following a different path from those ancients, have very preposterously mixed fables with sacred things through a loose "profane-sacred" glossography, so as to deform the sacred; and they mixed the sacred to illustrate the profane, under I know not what pretext of investigating some "hieroglyphic antiquity." There were, as Neander noted, appointed teachers who, with such a <term>malicious habit<note>original: "cacoëthe" (Greek: κακόηθες). A medical term used metaphorically for an incurable itch or bad habit.</note></term>, *adapted Ovidian fables and the maxims of Aristotle, Theophrastus, and Hippocrates to Christ, Mary, and the disciples of Christ; comparing Perseus with Christ, Danaë with Mary*, and I know not what *shoe of Pandora with eternal beatitude*. What a hodgepodge they left us! If a peasant were to gather barley, wheat, vetch, and legumes into one heap, I would not think his heap more disordered than the commentaries of these men. Theodolus once, in the *Eclogue of Pseustis*, introduced Alethia and Phronesis debating in such a way that he anxiously and superstitiously composed sacred history and the equal fables of the nations born from it. Upon that author, who is said to have lived around 480 A.D., a certain anonymous interpreter wrote a childish commentary in which he piles allegories upon allegories with a "most holy" explanation (as he calls it), which can neither be read without nausea nor called holy; unless you wish to pronounce equally "holy" the tasteless, crude, and ridiculous concordances between Holy Scripture and poetic fables which Thomas de Waleys, an Englishman, once engineered with "pious moralization" (to use the words of the past) upon Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*. What madness is this: to derive allegories from Holy Scripture for Diana, Cadmus seeking his sister,

<column-break/>

the twice-born Bacchus, Semele, the serpent Python, Saturn eating his sons, Jupiter deflowering the virgin Callisto, Aglauros turned to stone, Jupiter committing adultery with the virgin Europa, Actaeon watching Diana naked, Pyramus and Thisbe, or Vulcan cast out of heaven and made lame? These are surely so wretched that one might seek a cure for <term>strangury<note>A condition characterized by painful, frequent urination; here used metaphorically for a painful or difficult experience.</note></term> from reading them; just as the author of the *Letters of Obscure Men* and Francis Rabelais in the *Mythology of Pantagruel* exhibit them for derision. With the same subtlety, Matthias Farinator treats Holy Scripture just as cobblers treat leather. He wrote a book to "unburden consciences" titled *THE LIGHT OF THE SOUL*, where he accommodates the disputations of Galen, Aristotle, and Plato to Christ; which, however, cohere in argument just as "a horse's neck with a human head," as Horace said. If Hercules had stumbled upon such monsters, he would have thought a thirteenth labor remained for him. Luther, in his *Commentary on Genesis, folio 417a*, taxes this luxury of allegorical interpretations as a sufficiently evident error of idle men, in these words:
> *Allegory is like a beautiful harlot, who so flatters men that she cannot help but be loved, especially by idle men who are without temptation. Such men think they are in the midst of Paradise and the lap of God whenever they indulge in those speculations. At first they arose from stupid and idle monks, and at last they crept so far that some turned Ovid’s Metamorphoses into allegories; they made Mary the Laurel and Christ Apollo. However absurd these things may be, when they are proposed to unskilled youths who are lovers of letters, they are very pleasing at first, so that they give themselves entirely to those interpretations.*
Regarding this matter, the opinion of Epiphanius is also memorable. May God mercifully turn away from us all abuse and profanation of His word, and keep us in His rectitude and piety with a simple and sincere heart and faith unfeigned; may He remove from the choir of Christians those pernicious customs of interpreting the sacred, and those foul abuses which offend the eyes and impose a heavy wound on souls. Let it be so! Let it be so!

I return from this "foreign house" to the most ample dwelling of Holy Scripture, to show—compensating for the delay with brevity—<term>as in a sketch<note>original: "hōs en typō" (Greek: ὡς ἐν τύπῳ).</note></term> the treasures of human rituals and antiquity deposited in the ark of divine wisdom, with a simple economy of words. Holy Scripture lies open wide to the one who reads well. If you wish to contemplate the *Antiquities of the Palestinians, Babylonians, Egyptians, Persians, Syrians, Romans, Greeks*, and other nations, there is an abundance of everything there; as well as <term>the things of the present<note>original: "ta nyn ta" (Greek: τὰ νῦν τὰ).</note></term>, to use a Pindaric expression: in which one can estimate how much the use of secular letters is worth. For without the reading of secular writers, who would there be who could understand the many testimonies existing in the sacred texts?

The Egyptians hold the first place among all nations in Superstition, which among them was both most absurd and most fertile. We see that the very principles of their idolatry were in the worship of certain animals; for
<margin>* Lucan, book 10.</margin>
> *Many birds and beasts*

This is confirmed by Onkelos, Rabbi Solomon Jarchi, and Rabbi Aben Ezra; so that the Hebrew nation

<margin>Rhodius of Alexandria</margin>
could reproach the Egyptians with the same words as the Comic Poet:

->You worship the ox, but I sacrifice it to God.<-
<note>original Greek: Βοῦν προσκυνεῖς, ἐγὼ δὲ θύω τῷ Θεῷ.</note>

The EGYPTIANS, in preparing the bodies of the dead, filled them with spices, myrrh, cassia, aloe, salt, wax, bitumen, and other scents, so that they might preserve the deceased bodies from decay for a long time, as Herodotus in *Euterpe* and Diodorus Siculus (Book 2, ch. 5) teach more fully:

<margin>Pliny, Book 16, ch. 11.</margin>
<margin>Statius, On the Funeral of Priscilla.</margin>
> * There, all the spring of the Arabs flows, packed in a long train,
> And the flowers of Sheba, and the harvest of the Indians about to be burned;
> And frankincense snatched from Palestinian temples, together with Hebrew liquids.
<note>original: "omne illic stipatum examine longo Ver Arabum circūq; fluit..."</note>

Josephus, soberly following this regional custom, wished to show this honor—usually reserved for Great Men—to his father Jacob out of a sense of piety, regarding him as a Prophet and distinguished man.

<margin>Genesis 50:3.</margin>
For he immediately took care that the lifeless body of his father be handed over to the servant-physicians (Genesis 50:3), so that it might be preserved longer against rot during the journey, and that they might embalm it with the spices in which the Orientals usually abound, according to the customary manner of the Egyptians; for

<margin>Silius Italicus, Book 12.</margin>
> * The Egyptian land
> Encloses bodies standing in scented stone after death.

We have given at least a taste of those Antiquities, the understanding of which in sacred matters depends on ancient customs and ceremonies, reserving a more prolific treatment of them for the work itself. Leaving that now, we are about to attempt a rocky sea, treacherous and infested with the robberies of pirates, so that we may finally return safely to where we set sail, with the Muses favoring us. You, therefore, I first invoke to this day: O RABBIS, is this how you shall open the seas? Rather, you stand in the way.

<margin>The cold sentiments of the Rabbis regarding the sacred and historical matters of the Gentiles.</margin>
There is no one who does not know that almost all the RABBIS were ignorant of foreign histories. Indeed, with such severity as they possess, they regard the Pagans as of no account, just as that Niobe of the Poets regarded the children of others.

<margin>II. Loc. 6.</margin>
Hence, since these sons of darkness knew neither Latin nor Greek, they—as the most bitter enemies of the Pagans—often fabricated pure and simple lies about the affairs of the Gentiles and added fables upon fables. Wherefore Melchior Canus rightly writes that the Hebrews are utterly ignorant of human history, since they have no monuments of foreign kingdoms in their own language, nor do they recognize any Kings of the Persians or Greeks except those whom the Scripture mentions. In advance, we shall give

<column-break/>

a few examples out of many of this <term>unhistoricalness<gloss>original Greek: ἀνιστορησίας</gloss></term>, by which they make themselves ridiculous; for they babble things which no authority of a good writer supports. Rabbi SEADIAS, a man of great authority among the Rabbis and skilled in the Talmudic books (for he is one of those they specifically call the *Hagajonim* <note>The Geonim, or heads of the Babylonian academies</note>, whence he is also called *The Gaon* by Aben Ezra and others by way of excellence), says, regarding the words of Daniel chapter 8, verses 5 and 8: when the Prophet speaks of the kingdom of Alexander the Great in verse 5, saying a conspicuous horn was situated between his eyes; and in verse 8, that when he had grown strong, that great horn was broken, and four conspicuous horns rose up in its place toward the four winds of heaven. These four winds, he says, are the four Kings whom Alexander appointed while he was still alive, and among whom he divided his kingdom. The names of the successors are added: *Romanus, Alexander, Arudus, and Antiochus*, who reigned in *Rome, Alexandria, Ptolemais, and Antioch*.

You will find these to be wonderful trifles if you consult approved writers concerning Syria, Egypt, Macedonia, and Asia Minor, which fell under the dominion of Seleucus, Ptolemy, Cassander, and Antigonus. These are the ones shadowed here by the four horns, which the Angel calls "illustrious" because all other principalities vanished. Those even moderately versed in Greek Antiquities know it is not true, as Seadias here relates, that Alexander himself divided his kingdom while he was still among the living. All the historians of the *Journals*, Arrian, Diodorus Siculus, Pompeius Trogus, and Quintus Curtius, profess with one voice that Alexander (who died in the 114th Olympiad) did not divide his kingdom among successors while still alive as his illness grew worse; but when he had despaired of life, he took the ring from his finger and handed it to Perdiccas. When his friends asked to whom he left the kingdom, he replied: "To the best." There was also a great contention between the most distinguished cavalry and infantry about designating an heir. Some of the successors divided the kingdom for themselves after his death; almost as many Kings emerged as there were Generals, and they all ruled so insultingly and violently that they brought great disgrace upon his empire. John Rainolds follows this in more detail, having spared everyone the labor here in his first volume of lectures. And let this be the first <term>error<gloss>original Greek: παράπτωμα</gloss></term> born from ignorance of Greek history.

But if we further seek Hebrew authors in their "Greater Chronology of the World," which is inscribed *Seder Olam Rabbah* <note>original Hebrew: עולם רבא</note>, they invent eight Kings of the Greeks, of whom you might truly say:

->The names are to be feared by their very sound.<-

The first is called Alexander the Macedonian, 2. Phirton, 3. Selymon, 4. Seleucus, 5. Sentroc, 6. Antiochus, 7. Antiochus, 8. Gaselanas. We are ignorant of the greater part of these names; and because it is a second folly to laboriously refute foolish things, we shall move on. With the same rudeness, they assign only three years of empire to CYRUS, the first King of the Persians, because in Daniel chapter 10, the third year is assigned to that King; whereas it is established from historians that Cyrus died in the thirtieth year of his reign. In the same way, they hand down 12 years of reign for Ahasuerus (whom they count as ruling immediately after Cyrus), which are mentioned in Scripture. So to DARIUS—whom the *Zemach David* trifles succeeded his father in the seventh year of his age—they attribute six years of reign;

# PROLEGOMENA

They also imagine three Kings of the Persians, with a great confusion of times and persons, based on *Daniel* chapter 11, verse 2. yet it is certain that there were eight other Kings of the Persians, of whom no mention is made in that place. Indeed, they often confuse the Kings of Asia and Syria with the leaders of Greece. With a great ignorance of time and history, Benjamin of Tudela <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler</note> in his **Travels** (page 15) makes King David of the Jews and Romulus of the Romans <term>contemporaries</term> <note>original: "συγχρόνους"</note>; whereas David began his reign about three hundred years before Romulus. And there are other trifles by which they display their ignorance in history to the more enlightened world. Who, then, would dare to deny that secular writers must be consulted in matters of Chronology? For if these are ignored, a great darkness will present itself to us. Indeed, Holy Scripture does not treat profane history and Chronology <term>plainly</term> <note>original: "ἁπλῶς"</note> at all; but, as much as is sufficient for the sacred histories, it briefly indicates what the monuments of foreign histories explain more at length and more clearly.

*The purpose of Holy Scripture is not to weave an external history without the Jews, but that which is joined to the people of Israel.*
<margin>Jerome on Daniel chapter 11.</margin>
Thus it happens that it delivers the histories of nations neither fully nor in order; for it was not the concern of the Prophetic Spirit to follow the order of history, but to touch upon the most excellent things. However, just as the Jews possess nothing for exquisite knowledge in Chronology, so too are they far off when they come to explanations of the gods of the heathens and their rites, which they defile with fables and empty commentaries, turning their vain fables into even vainer ones. Hear three or four examples of these trifles. For who could recount them all?

Genesis chapter 11, verses 28 and 31. **Ur of the Chaldeans**, the Jews take the name of the city for the "Fire-God" of the Chaldeans; here they make Abraham's journey from Ur of the Chaldeans—which our geographers leave to us as a very well-known place—into a wandering tale. They write that when Abraham, having left Haran his fatherland, had come into Ur of the Chaldeans, he found that everyone had consecrated divine honors to the Sun; and Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel reported that Rabbi Moses <note>Maimonides</note> found this recorded in the histories and books of the nations.
<margin>Question 40 in Genesis, pages 55, 56.</margin>
Mercerus refutes the opinion of Rabbi Moses. Furthermore, they devised a story that Haran, the brother of Abraham, because he refused to follow the ancestral rites in the same way (since the Sun was usually worshiped as a Deity by the Chaldeans), was cast into the fire by the Chaldeans while his father Terah looked on. Similarly, they say that Abraham, having denied religious worship, was delivered from the flame of the fire by divine power and paid <term>thanksgivings</term> <note>original: "χαριστήρια"</note> to the God of Israel.
<margin>In Genesis, dispute 15, page 447 following; and Johannes Annius, otherwise a fabulous writer, in his Commentary on the spurious Berosus, page 30.</margin>
<margin>Questions on Genesis, Drusius to Sulpitius, page 43.</margin>
Yet Moses, who recorded many things to the praise of Abrahamic constancy, produced nothing concerning that casting of Abraham into the fire. Therefore, Pererius and others consider that tradition among the fables; on which see also Jerome’s Questions on Genesis. Ur, a city of the Babylonian region, received its name from light or fire. Fire-worship belonged to the Persians and Chaldeans, from which comes the God Oromasdes <note>Ahura Mazda</note>.

Exodus chapter 14, verse 1. *Speak to the children of Israel, that they turn and remain before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, and over against Baal-zephon.* This Baal-zephon was likewise a town, as is clear from Numbers chapter 33, verse 7. But Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> and the others dream, as if

<column-break/>

seized by some fever, that Baal-zephon was a bronze dog fabricated by Pharaoh's Magicians according to the positions of the celestial bodies by Magical power, so that it might turn the Israelites away from their destined journey by its horrid barking and stop their flight. A commentary worthy of the Rabbis! Just as that one will be concerning the golden image of Nebuchadnezzar, which the Marrucini <note>likely a reference to a specific group or error in source</note>, bold as they are in inventing things, think was erected as a propitiation so that the effect of the dream might be repelled by that amulet. This divination is too frivolous and ascribes power to it in vain.

Deuteronomy chapter 3, verse 11. *Only OG, King of Bashan, remained of the race of Giants.* Scarcely had the cock crowed and ordered one to wake from the dream of Baal-zephon, when behold, another dream from the "ivory gate" <note>A classical reference to false dreams</note> concerning King OG. They say he placed a huge mountain on his head to overwhelm the entire multitude of the Israelites with one throw; and it was nearly successful, had not a divinely sent hoopoe bird perforated such a great mass by continuous gnawing. They add that his teeth then grew out ten cubits through his head, and thus, weighed down by such a mass, he yielded to fate. Lyranus and Abulensis relate this "foot-and-a-half long" fable, and from them Vossius in his book on Idolatry (page 190). Of the same sort is that thick and greasy commentary on the words of the Psalmist: *The cattle on a thousand hills:*
<margin>Psalms.</margin>
in which they tell that one most vast beast was designated by the plural number, to whom the grass of a thousand mountains was assigned by GOD for daily fodder. This is as true as the stories about Eleazar and Ishmael, whose bellies were so large and abdomens so fat that they protruded a foot and a half; so that, when they stood with faces and bodies joined, two strong oxen could have passed between them without touching either one. Who is so <term>unlaughing</term> <note>original: "ἀγέλαστος"</note> as Crassus, or as the Poet says:

-> so iron-willed, that he can restrain himself <-
-> from laughing. <-

For these things are <term>nonsense and long-winded</term> <note>original: "λῆρος & μακρὸς ταῦτα"</note>, and as that man says, *Pure trifles and fiddle-faddle.* O, if only the servants had carried that fat man to some hungry Abbot or to that noble physician who, in a deep and dark prison, would have dispersed this portentous burden of the belly!
<margin>Plautus, The Little Carthaginian.</margin>
<margin>See Vir. Hagstr. on the French Disease, chapter 18.</margin>
That saying of the Rabbis is indeed well-known: *There is nothing in the Torah from which a thousand mountains of doctrines do not hang.* But those sellers of trifles abuse it so much that they build mountains of fables upon a single "Jod" <note>the smallest Hebrew letter</note> of Scripture. For this reason, Christian interpreters bring a charge against the Talmudists, examining in proper order those portents and monsters of things and words which their Talmud has brought forth; among whom I name D. Christoph Helvicus in his Treatise on Talmudic Legends, and Peter Costus in the Type of the Messiah. How few Christians are there whom these things have not moved? So that even Conrad Graser, who was long and much versed in the Rabbis, replied to someone asking what he thought of the Rabbis: *that in the whole class of interpreters he knew no more inept and foolish fools than the Rabbis themselves.* As can be read in his most learned preface to the Exercises on Daniel chapter 9. In reading the books of the Jews, such a moderation must be applied that each person rejects those things which either their superstition or their fragrant envy toward other nations has invented. I have recounted the good fable about Og, to which six hundred others could be added.

# ON BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

PSALM 22, verse 17: *They pierced my hands and my feet.* <note>original: "Foderunt manus meas & pedes meos."</note> The "hardening of heart" <note>Greek: τῆς πώρωσις (tēs pōrōsis)</note> of the Rabbis is to be deplored, because in all the places of Scripture upon which our faith in Christ rests, they either change the words, or remove and erase them from the midst, or strive to corrupt the true sense with a false one—not so much out of ignorance as by a perversity of will. Those things which are read widely and explicitly throughout the body of the Old Testament concerning the Messiah, they entangle; in a clear matter, they are almost in a fog, or entirely blind. That ancient architect of obscurities, Beelzebub, is accustomed in his usual way to dictate old wives' interpretations to his scribes, so that he may sweetly drive them mad, lest they open their eyes to the light. Among others, the author of the book *Nizahon* <note>A famous medieval Jewish polemical work against Christianity</note> did this when he falsely wrote: <margin>in their books</margin> *It is written in their books, "They pierced my hands and my feet," where they say these are the nails with which he was fastened by his hands and feet to the cross after he was hung up.* To which I say, it was not the custom in Israel for nails to be driven into the hands and feet of men who were stoned and hung. Do you not know, you Jewish mocker, that the power of capital judgment was taken away from the Sanhedrin by the Romans? Has it escaped you that capital punishments ceased to be carried out according to the prescription of the Mosaic law, and began to be done according to the consensus and judgment of the Roman tribunal? Scourging, crucifixion, the breaking of legs, and the piercing of the chest are not from your law, but from a foreign one; you are foolish if you insult the manner of death accepted then, which forces you to conclude that in the history of the Passion of our LORD, many things were administered according to Roman custom. This surely ought not to be a doubt to any of you. If you doubt it, read the writings of the heathens, which are most hostile to our religion, and take from our adversaries that in which you oppose us. Tacitus, a friend to you no more than to me, says openly: *The punishment of the cross was introduced to the Jews by the Romans.* This is taught by Lipsius <margin>Book 1 on the Cross, 14</margin> and Bartholinus in his *Dissertation on the Side of Christ, chapter 8, pages 54, 55.* Therefore, it must be established once and for all by anyone dealing with the books of the Rabbis that they must beware of most of their interpretations regarding the affairs of the heathens; one should rather examine the original authors themselves; <margin>for the Jews, out of hatred for the nations, are most audacious in inventing crimes with which to sprinkle some stain upon them.</margin> as Luther long ago warned in his *Commentary on Genesis, folio 493, a.*, so that in this place you might more rightly say, *An animal without intellect*, as Luther has it elsewhere; indeed, *an animal without common sense*. To be sure, they have at other times successfully discovered many things in which they excel in noting the ancient rites of Judea, which the industry of others would never have attained. Among these, Rabbi *Moses Ben-Maimon* <note>Maimonides</note> is commended, whose writings contain *many things both pleasing and useful* <note>Greek: πολλὰ κεχαρισμένα τε καὶ χρήσιμα</note>, according to Scaliger's testimony to Casaubon: *I value not only that book (The Guide for the Perplexed) but all the works of that Master so highly, that I would say he alone among the Jews ceased to trifle.* Casaubon, in *Exercise 16, number 77*, says: *Moses Maimonides (who is also called Moses the Egyptian), a man of solid and immense learning, of whom I think I can truly say what Pliny said of Diodorus Siculus: he was the first among his own people to cease trifling.* Likewise, *Abarbanel*, whose commentaries on the Pentateuch and the Minor Prophets exist printed in Venice, is praised by Master L’Empereur <margin>Commentary on Middoth, p. 174</margin> above all other Hebrew Doctors. Even the Masters of the Jews themselves greatly com-

<column-break/>

mend him, and consider him a plainly divine author (as I remember hearing from a certain Spanish Jew). He occasionally cites *Aristotle*; by which very act he shows that the reading of secular authors was a care to him. *Rabbi Menasseh Ben-Israel* follows in his footsteps, who now flourishes in Amsterdam, a distinguished and learned man of his order, so greatly praised by *C. Barlaeus* that for that reason certain idle minds even brought a public lawsuit against that most famous man. Nor today are they lacking men of singular learning and genius, such as I have known from conversation with *Dionysius Musaphia*, the unique glory of his order in Hamburg. There are in their writings, to summarize in a brief handful,
> *Many drugs, some good when mixed, and many baneful.* <margin>Homer, Odyssey, book 4</margin>

In reading harmful things, everyone takes care how they use them, because <margin>1. Anth. 39. d. & 4. v. 1.</margin> they are harmful. But one uses good things to enjoy them, even if the fruit is unequal: *for the first step of wisdom,* as Lactantius says, <margin>1. Institutes 23. chapter 20.</margin> *is to understand what is false; the second is to know what is true.* And just as that Cicero of the Latins said the Greeks would answer, *that they worship some Gods so that they may help, and others lest they do harm;* so we shall say that we read the Rabbis not so much that they may help, as that they may not harm. Just as it is permitted to freely rebuke whatever "bad coins" <note>Greek: τὰ πονηρὰ κόμματα (the base/wicked elements)</note> are in Jewish traditions; so it is fitting to imitate and transfer to our own uses whatever things lead to piety and integrity. Truly, if we wish to judge sanely, there are sometimes, at rare intervals, men of good character among the enemies of the New Testament. I judge men politically from no specific polity of their own. If they were as strong in the knowledge of the true as they are in the honorable, the flesh of the foreskin would have been the flesh of the Spirit. *Ambrose* professed that he had read everything, *most things lest he neglect them, or be ignorant of others; some things, not to hold them, but to rebuke them.* For there is no less danger in approving nothing that you read than in approving everything. *I hate the profane crowd and keep them away.* <note>A quote from Horace</note> In their number is *Pfefferkorn*, that mockery of Germany (as that famous inhabitant of the tub, Diogenes, was of all Greece), who agitated this question with *stretching of heads* <note>Greek: κεφάλοις ἐκτάσεις (strenuous effort)</note> against Reuchlin: *Whether it is for the use of our Religion that, with the exception of the Bibles, all the books of the Jews should be burned?* concerning which see Sleidanus. <margin>Book 2, Commentaries</margin> What is this cruelty against the miserable Rabbis? They usurp the same right against the *Koran*, because in it also not a few things are read from the comments of the Rabbis. Therefore, the Koran printed in Arabic was once <margin>Venice, Year 1530</margin> punished by fire; although it is greatly conducive to refuting the *superstition* <note>Greek: δεισιδαιμονίαν (deisidaimonian)</note> of Muhammad to have copies, and to have them bound together. For a Christian man is no more moved by the fables of the Rabbis and Muhammadans than by the fictions of Ovid or Apuleius; on which matter one can read the Apologetic discourse of Bibliander for the edition of the Koran, reprinted at Rostock by the care of the most learned Fabricius. The same error is evident in the Enthusiasts <note>Radical reformers who claimed direct divine inspiration</note>, who agitate the question: *Whether it is for the use of Christianity that, with the exception of the Bibles, all the volumes of the Philosophers and Philologists should be exterminated?* It is monstrous how much those who breathe "enthusiasm" rave here; their solemn asylum of ignorance is the *contempt of Philosophy and good authors*, as can be seen in all the books of those men. If they were to gain power in the Literary Republic of Christians, immediately with... <meta>catchword: Julian</meta>

...that like Julian the Apostate <note>The Roman Emperor (r. 361–363 AD) who attempted to revive paganism and forbade Christians from teaching classical literature.</note>, they would strip away all secular writers, punish them with exile, and issue a mandate that the writings of the Philosophers should not be read in Christian schools. Where the itch of this erratic and wandering Politician tends—boasting of a triple erudition—a word is enough for the wise; he is not moved by the quips with which they mock right reason and accuse nature itself. For we do not judge that to be true Philosophy which exists only in the books of the Chaldeans, Egyptians, or Greeks; rather, that is finally Philosophy which is inscribed by the hand of God Himself upon nature, proposed for all to contemplate. We believe Aristotle and Plato not because they said it, but because what they said, nature says; otherwise, where they departed from nature, there also Christian Philosophers depart from them; concerning which

Elegantly, Bertharius of Monte Cassino in his <term>Oppositions</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀντικειμ.</note> Book I, *Question 31: Human doctrine is the art of Grammar, or Rhetoric, or even Dialectic; from which doctrine nothing is to be taken up for the sacrifice—that is, in those things which are to be felt concerning God. Meanwhile, to deny to illuminated reason a certain *ministry* of *Logic and Metaphysics* in divine matters is the mark of "Enthusiasts" <note>Radical reformers who claimed direct divine inspiration over academic study.</note>, who do not know the distinction of better studies, much less do they *possess even a shadow of the true and solid wisdom which they boast of in Christ*. This is demonstrated most extensively by the book written solidly and learnedly against the *New Prophets* in the name of the Ministers of Lübeck, Hamburg, and Lüneburg in the *Year 1634*, which ought to be most highly recommended to all good men and lovers of truth, so that they may know how to guard themselves entirely against Evangelical Pseudo-prophets; specifically to "come out of Babylon" <note>A call to separate from false religious systems.</note> from our Apocalyptic Politician, who judges enthusiastic darkness to be the image of light, boasts of a "fifth essence" of Christianity, and under a sheep’s skin (as fanatics are wont to do) insults all Philosophers and Theologians. The poison of his mind, hidden for a long time, he finally vomited out under the assumed name of *Angelus Marianus* in a recently published book, from which one may recognize the inverted and preposterous *Silenus* <note>A reference to Alcibiades' description of Socrates: an ugly exterior (Silenus statue) hiding a divine interior; here, the author suggests the opposite.</note> he has long and craftily carried about—bearing the title of a shepherd of Angelic purity in word, while in reality being a masked wolf and a predator of Christ’s sheep, whom this schismatic gatekeeper casts into miserable slaughter under the appearance of righteousness. But there is no reason for us to linger in refuting such things; therefore, not a word more. We shall proceed to follow our discourse concerning some of the older and obsolete expressions and less common words of the *Vulgate Translator*, attempting to see what the reading of secular authors can provide.

# ON BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES.

If we speak of style, we freely admit that there is much of good value and of the ancient stamp within it, which should not be despised by students of Antiquity; for if you were to offer these things to others to be laughed at—as sometimes happens too undeservedly—you yourself would be the ridiculous one. Furthermore, the learned detect in these very modes of speaking <term>many things I have refuted</term> <note>original Greek: πολλὰ ἠλέγχησα</note> and <term>many things you achieve</term> <note>original Greek: πολλὰ κατεργᾷ</note>. We are not about to fight <term>with tooth and nail</term> <note>original Greek: πῶς καὶ λὰξ; literally "with fist and heel"</note> merely for the sake of the matter.

Jeremiah chapter 18:23. <term>In the time of your anger, deal with them</term> <note>original Hebrew: בְּעֵת אַפְּךָ עֲשֵׂה בָהֶם; Greek: ἐν καιρῷ θυμοῦ ποίησον ἐν αὐτοῖς</note>. In the time of your fury, use them. The ancients used <term>to abuse</term> <note>Latin: abuti</note> to mean <term>to consume</term> or <term>to be consumed</term>; as the illustrious Mr. Johann Laurenberg recorded in his *Antiquarius*, folio 3, citing Plautus, Hortensius, and Varro. Hence Cornelius à Lapide on this passage maintains that his Translator [the Vulgate] translated elegantly and learnedly: <term>Abuse them</term>, that is, consume or destroy them. He brings forward Cato as a witness <term>On Agriculture, chapter 76</term>, where he writes: <term>Until you have abused all the cheese with honey</term>. This is the true reading over that of <term>Zwinger</term>; in the <margin>Basel Edition</margin> which <term>Cato</term> reads: <term>Until you have used up all the cheese with honey</term>. Thus, "to abuse" in the Ancient Translator is not that Greek word <term>to misuse</term> <note>original Greek: καταχρήσασθαι</note>.

Psalm 50:7. <term>Hear, my people</term>. They wish to justify this mode of speaking because <term>my</term> <note>Latin: meus (nominative)</note> is found instead of <term>O my</term> <note>Latin: mi (vocative)</note> among the Ancients. This matter so disturbed <term>Scaurus the Grammarian</term>, as reported by <term>Charisius</term>, that he asserted the vocative singular masculine of "my" produced many doubters... on which <term>Valla, Elegances book 3, 22; Gerard Vossius, book 6 of Commentaries on the Art of Grammar, chapter 7; and Johann Pincier in his Parerga of Marburg, book 2, chapter 2</term> may be consulted.

Matthew 2:18. <term>And she would not be comforted</term> <note>original Greek: Καὶ οὐκ ἤθελε παρακληθῆναι</note>. And <term>she was unwilling to be consoled</term>. In this place, the Vulgate takes "to be consoled" to mean <term>to receive consolation</term> or <term>to admit it</term>. In this sense, it appears in <term>Genesis 37:35</term> regarding <term>Jacob</term> grieving for <term>Joseph</term>: <term>He would not receive consolation</term>, as the Vulgate version has it there. This is said passively in <term>Jeremiah 31:15: A voice was heard on high of lamentation, mourning, and weeping, of Rachel weeping for her children: and refusing to be consoled over them.</term> They prove these things with testimonies from writers. <term>Aulus Gellius</term> produces that letter of <term>Q. Metellus</term> which he had given to <term>Cn. and L. Domitius</term> while in exile: <term>But when I see your spirit toward me, I am greatly consoled, and the faith of both of you dwells before my eyes</term>. Priscian brings forward that line of <term>Asinius Pollio</term>: <term>But while I grieved over those things I had hoped for, I was consoled over those things I feared</term>. <term>Boethius, book 3 of the Consolation of Philosophy, chapter 3</term>, spoke in the same sense; as Mr. Vossius has observed again.

Matthew 20:25. <term>The princes of the nations lord it over them</term>. They write that the Translator used a Greek idiom: and to prove this they bring forward those lines of <term>Horace*</term> <margin>Odes 3.30, 2.9, 3.21</margin>: <term>He ruled of the peoples, Cease from soft complaints, Abstain from angers and hot strife</term>; and others by the same poet of Venusia. For among Latins, especially in the Odes, <term>to Hellenize</term> <note>to use Greek-style syntax</note> is almost peculiar to him. Unless one easily rejects the authority of Horace; both because he <term>Atticizes</term> <note>imitates the dialect of Athens</note> and because poets speak in another <margin>On the Orator, book 2</margin> language, as <term>Tully [Cicero]*</term> says. For what if it is a religious scruple for a great part of writers to import new and harshly Greek-sounding formulas of speech from foreign languages into Latin discourse? Compare <term>Vossius, book 7 on the Art of Grammar, chapter 33, pages 119–120; Goldast in his notes on the sermon of Valerian on the good of discipline, page 36</term>, where he decides against <term>Beza</term>.

<column-break/>

John 5:8. <term>Take up your bed</term> <note>original Greek: Ἆρον τὸν κράββατόν σου</note>. Take up <term>your</term> cot. In the New Testament, where mention is made of the sick, the word <term>grabatus</term> <note>a low, humble cot</note> is read several times. Four times in this very chapter, and <term>Matthew 2:4, 9, 11, 12; chapter 6:55; Acts 5:15; chapter 9:33.</term> Also in <term>Amos 3:12</term> is "grabatum," which in Hebrew is <term>eres</term> <note>original Hebrew: ערשׂ</note>. It is found more than once among approved Latin authors. <term>Seneca, Letter 18</term>: <term>Let that cot be real, and the cloak, and the bread hard and filthy</term>. <term>Martial, book 1, 93: There is no hearth, nor the frame of a bare cot</term>. The same in <term>book 12, 32</term>, concerning the furniture of the poor: <term>A three-legged cot went along</term>. The commentator on Aristophanes: <term>The Attics call the cot 'sympodia'</term>. The Glosses of the Basilicas: <term>A secondary bench, a cot</term>, in Meursius's Glossary. The use of litters was almost exclusively for the sick: on which one should consult <term>Lipsius on Tacitus's Annals 2, note 48; Donatus on Suetonius's Augustus, chapter 78; Pignorius on Slaves, page 139; Robierzyck 2 on Roman Luxury; and on the cot, Barthius, Adversaria 35, 8, page 1600 and 44, 19, page 2003.</term> But to what end is this? Because a certain know-it-all <term>Triphyllius</term>, Bishop of Ledra, had rejected the word <term>grabatus</term>—which the Holy Spirit nevertheless uses—as being insufficiently Greek, changing it to the Attic word <term>skimpodion</term>. <term>Spiridion</term>, Bishop of Tremithus in Cyprus, restrained his arrogant mouth in a meeting of Bishops, adding that he was no better than the one who had said "grabatus": as <term>Joachim Camerarius</term> relates this history from <term>Sozomen*</term> in his <term>notes on the history of Mark 2, folio 112</term> and <term>Caussin, book 15 on Eloquence, chapter 1, page 946 of the Church history</term>.

Luke 4:35. <term>The Demon went out from him, and did not hurt him</term>. They defend this construction from Plautus's *The Braggart Warrior*: <term>Swear that you will hurt no man regarding this matter</term>. <term>Salmasius on the Augustan History, page 54, and Vossius, book 7, chapter 21, page 86 of the Art of Grammar</term>, saw that people spoke this way. Let the speech be more for you to abstain from than to imitate, for "he will lie" <note>Latin: mentibitur</note> will not immediately become common for us as the future of "to lie" <note>Latin: mentior</note>, even if we have the <margin>Willich on Horace's Art of Poetry, page 55</margin> reason, analogy, and authority of <term>Terence</term>. Therefore, let us leave this kind of speaking entirely to antiquity: as also many other things of that kind which <term>Alberico Gentili</term> recorded in his *Dissertation on the Latinity of the Old Interpreter of the Bible* which was wrongly accused; in which he labors with all zeal to cover the unusual expressions of the Old Translator with "fig leaves" <note>metaphor for excuses</note>. For this curiosity is not unlearned, and we do not reject it entirely; except that <term>Philippus Carolus</term>—formerly a Professor at Altdorf, but an Apostate—rejoices that it was instituted against a great Man [Johann Gerhard] with a critical brow. Those who have visited the people of Nuremberg know that he approached the knowledge of divine and heavenly things with a fleeting eye in his spare hours. Unprepared in Hebrew letters, with a boastful display of some knowledge in secular letters (whose authors he carried in his eyes), he broke into the sacred volumes <term>with unwashed hands</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνίπτοις χερσὶν; meaning without proper reverence or preparation</note>. He displays a glorious specimen of his erudition, like that soldier of Plautus, in a book or certain <term>denunciatory</term> <note>original Greek: στηλιτευτικῇ</note> paper to which he gave the title *Triumph*; and he issued that "abortion of a triumph" for the sake of the Enemies of Truth, as well as to the envy of the most well-deserving Theologian <term>Dr. Johann Gerhard</term>, whose countenance and gravity he could not have even endured. Against the bites of that <term>enemy of the Muses</term> <note>original Greek: φιλομόσου</note> apostate, the illustrious Mr. Dilherr, our respected patron, in his Inaugural Disputation as Professor (which exists in print), excellently [defended] that man of blessed memory, <term>the most excellent</term> <note>original Greek: πανáειστον</note>...

<margin>Jeremiah chapter 31, verse 24.</margin> *The farmer and those driving <note>original: "minantes"</note> the flocks.* "To threaten" <note>original: "minare"</note> is an unusual word to Latin ears. For this word is frequent, especially in the ancient Laws of the Lombards, Burgundians, Alemanni, and in the Salic law. From which also, word for word from *minare*, the French made *mener* <note>to lead</note> and *promener* <note>to walk/lead</note>.

Whatever may be said of the Latinity of the Vulgate Translator, those who, fired by the appearance of Antiquity, come to his aid with a healing ointment <note>original: "malagmate"</note> do not seem to do badly; or even when the disease is pressing, which the weakness of the age gave him, they offer medical hands to cure him with the integrity and propriety of words.

<margin>Observations on the New Testament.</margin>
*When one is sick within, he needs wise medicines,* to speak from Euripides' *Phoenician Women*, verse 429. # INTRODUCTION

### Page 30

It protects against the diseases of the shadowy **Aristarchuses** <note>Aristarchus was a rigorous critic of Homer; here used to mean overly pedantic or harsh critics.</note>: "If ever," he says among other things, "you must handle divine matters, you are so far from being content with a moderate faculty of speech that you are accustomed to examine every little word with a brush; you count the tips of the letters, you take care lest anything gaping or worn-out should fall out, you smooth stubborn syllables with constant pumice-stone; finally, you have fallen into such eloquence with your trappings that you are ashamed to call the Lord JESUS 'Savior' [*Salvator*]." In the Church, we call JESUS 'Savior' [*Salvator*], even if this displeases the **Logodaedali** <note>Literally "word-craftsmen" or those who play with words artfully but deceptively.</note>. For those who kiss **Livy**, **Ovid**, and **Cicero** prefer to say 'Preserver' [*Servator*] rather than 'Savior' [*Salvator*]. 

<margin>Commentary on Verse 1. 2.</margin>
Against these, the words of **Manutius** are observed: *Soter* is a Greek name, and that it signifies one who gave salvation is established by the interpreter **Cicero** himself; from which the common error of those who call Jesus Christ 'Preserver' [*Servator*] is evident—whose immortal merits can be expressed by no single Latin word sufficiently. For it is one thing to preserve [*servare*], and another to give salvation [*salutem dare*]. He preserves who, by some means, ensures that safety is not lost; he gives salvation who restores it when lost. Because if 'Preserver' is not *Soter* (because it carries less weight), and **Cicero** avoided 'Savior' [*Salvator*] as unusual, he preferred to say: "He who gave salvation." Surely if we speak of Him who did not merely preserve the afflicted human race in the same state, but led them from eternal destruction to the goods of perpetual life—which the Son of the supreme God both did and alone was able to do—it is necessary either to call Him 'Savior' [*Salvator*] (which is called *Soter* in Greek), using a new word for a new thing (which the Ancients also approved), or to use Cicero's example of circumlocution and say: "He who gave salvation." 

**Abraham Scultetus** in *Delights of Prague*, book 1, p. 17: "Whether you should more rightly call JESUS 'Preserver' or 'Savior,' the learned doubt. Those who know from **Livy**, **Ovid**, and others of the ancients that the terms 'Preserver' and 'Liberator' were made common, if they shrink from the name 'Savior'..." and after a few words, when he had explained the mind of **Cicero**, **Polybius**, and others, he concludes with these 

<margin>Against book 12, page of Clement.</margin>
words: "Therefore I do not think (whatever **Gentianus Hervetus*** says) that the immortal merits of Christ toward us are sufficiently aptly signified when He is called 'Preserver' [*Servator*]." Nor is it unknown that the word 'Savior' [*Salvator*] was used by **Lactantius**; indeed, neither by **Alfonso** nor **Porphyry**. To me, Christ Jesus is Savior and Preserver and everything. Although I have a singular reason why I prefer 'Savior' to 'Preserver.' Compare **Salmeron**, Vol. 3, *History of the Gospel*, page 327 ff.; **Masius**, *Academic Exercises*, Vol. 1, Comm. 10, page 370 ff.; **Angelo de Rocca** in the *Vatican Library*, p. 134; **Danqueus** in *Notes on Basil of Seleucia*, page 84. 

And even if the title of 'Savior' were most worthy of eternity, nevertheless certain religious of the **Canonical Order**, granted the title of **St. Savior*** by Pope **Gregory XII**, 

<margin>Year 1408, April 3rd.</margin>
being certainly too studious of Latinity, preferred the title of 'Preserver' rather than 'Savior.' Against them disputes the "Grammarian," as he calls him, **Johann Baptista Signius**, Regular Canon of St. Savior, in the *Treatise on the Canonical Order and State*, published at Bologna in the year 1600, book 2, chapter 7, p. 156 ff. 

But there are also other **Aristarchuses** of the Bible, whose delicate ears are immediately wounded when the manifold variety of divine things is set forth in simplicity of speech, and by whom all things are thought filthy unless they are wrapped in **Ciceronian** allurements. 

<margin>Preface to the Old Psalter.</margin>
For that reason, **Dr. Luther*** formerly railed against those who ambitiously recalled sublime things under the anvil of **Tully** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> with decorated words and formulas of speaking. 

<column-break/>

He hoped (I will give this logically, as **Matthesius*** conceived it) that the young Hebraists would bring forth something special and precious; but it went for him like King Solomon, who hoped for something precious from India, yet they brought him apes and peacocks. The greater part use "monkey-work" and either imitate the Rabbis or previous versions, or clothe their work with "peacock-mirrors," crumbling in Hebrew and burning their work with **Cicero's** words and formulas, and tying it up with Greek words. 

The **Tigurini** <note>The Zurich theologians/translators.</note> chastise this insolence in the *Preface to the Bible*, when they write among other things: "Certain people seem to us to be too fastidious, who, while they permit certain peculiar words to all Professions or Faculties, do not grant it to divine literature alone, and strangely mock those using them. What of the fact that there are certain expressions in the scriptures which can hardly be turned into a foreign language cleanly without a good part of the grace and even the mystery perishing at the same time, which otherwise is more rightly and easily recognized from the retained property of the language?" 

Indeed, if in the philosophical forum, words and terms are not to be rigorously examined at the tribunal of the critical forum by the judgment of the learned world, much more will that be foreign to the purity of Theology, the idea of which **Cicero**, **Plautus**, **Terence**, and all Latin Orators did not have in mind; and therefore they could not bestow terms, as they are called, and weight of words upon it. 

<margin>Vagetius, Disquisition on Latin Style, 4, Section 3, p. 32.</margin>
Divine matters will have their own Graces and their own Venuses, even if everything does not perhaps seem sufficiently turned and polished to everyone according to the "lamp of **Aristophanes**," as it is said, or the "wick of **Cicero**," when they have been translated into another language. For (as that **Quintilian** of the Christians, **Jerome**, excellently says somewhere): "For one disputing about the Scriptures, it is not fitting for **Aristotle** to seek out arguments; nor is a streamlet to be drawn from the river of **Tullian** eloquence; nor are the ears of **Quintilian** to be soothed with little flowers and scholarly declamation; but a pedestrian and simple speech is necessary, which explains the matter, sets forth the sense, and makes manifest the obscure." 

Those who, in difficult and grand matters—namely Theological ones—luxuriate in style and encrust them with trappings of words or a kind of plaster, using curling irons and dyed medicines of white and red, do not seem unlike those who, when they ought to walk through the streets, dance; or even those who, about to address someone they meet, attack them with shouting and song. 

Meanwhile, it nevertheless follows from this that it is not permitted to defile Theology with words and sentiments that are cold or even filthy. Simplicity of speech properly becomes a Theologian; filthiness just as little as that pride and barbarous arrogance in words of certain men. 

All the more will those arrogant emenders of the Bible be flogged in the Theological forum by fair censors—interpreters whom you might call semi-pagans—who, with **Sebastian Castalio**, in order to exhibit a **Ciceronian** Gospel to us, 

<margin>Sohnius, book 2, On the Word of God.</margin>
translate 'Angels' as 'Genies,' call 'God' 'Jupiter,' the 'Prophets' of the Israelites 'soothsayers,' 'shrine' [*fanum*] for 'temple,' 'John washed' for 'baptized,' 'Fate' for 'providence,' along with 'under good birds' [*bonis avibus*]—an expression taken from the observation of augurs—and other things fashioned from Transalpine antiquity with a perverse zeal for elegance, which they obtrude...

They even honor the Roman Pope with the title of Jove; who, notwithstanding Apostolic constitutions and ordinances and other contrary things, says in words that he is the "Servant of Servants," but in fact allows himself to be adored as a Jovian Divinity. In title he feigns to be a parent, but in deeds he displays JUPITER: such are the words of Gunther, Bishop of Cologne, and Thergand, Bishop of Trier, to Pope Nicholas, as witnessed by Aventinus. Certainly, it is to be lamented that many words of no or little fruit occur everywhere among Christians. Tertullian rebuked the Christians of his time who, either through ignorance or the vice of habit, would say "By Hercules!" and "By the god of faith!" <note>original: "Mehercule & Medius-fidius"</note>: which Jerome also did after him. They think nothing is said elegantly unless they call upon all the Gods and Goddesses; unless they invoke Juno the bridesmaid, Diana the helper, Mars the favorer, Ceres the aspirer, Mercury the assistant, Lucina the helper, and Hercules the Savior; mixing things up and down; unless they use "By Pollux," "By the temple of Pollux," "By Hercules," "O the faith of the Gods," "O Jupiter," in their oaths; unless even

> Phoebus from Ortygia, Evan the son of Semele from Nysa,
> Juno from Samos, Vulcan from Lemnos, and nourishing Cytheris
> Of Cyprus, and the Muses from Boeotian Helicon are present:
> Let Neptune and Amphitrite come from the Ocean,
> And Doris, Panope, Eudora, and Cymothoe,
> Proto, Eucrate, Sao, and beautiful Galene,
> Spio, Glauce, Thalia, and Cymodoce.

Why these labyrinths of so many words? To what end so many gestures, to what end so many empty words? Lest we seem to be wise only from our own brain, let us interpose the authority of Dr. Rungius on Exodus chapter 23, page 868; Dr. Frantzius on the *Interpretation of Holy Scripture*, pages 95 and 941; Dr. Rivetus on Psalm 16, page 57; Eobanus Hessus in the dedicatory letter of his *Christian Heroines*; Pasor in the preface of his *Lexicon*; Dr. Finckius in his *Syllabus of Illustrious Questions*, section 1, question 22, page 180 and following; and Becmannus in his *Manual to the Latin Language*, chapter 10.

To finally fold our sails: the reading of so many authors and historians can do much for the use of truth and honor, for refutation, for exhortation, and sometimes for consolation—if we convert their sayings and precepts to our use and the ornament of our religion; if we reject the "unhappy darnel and sterile oats" <note>A quote from Virgil's *Georgics*, referring to weeds in a field.</note> from the writings of the Ancient Poets and Orators, and cut away what seems adverse to Christian purity; if we learn from their errors and calamities to better compose our lives and morals. For although Holy Scripture is *self-sufficient and in need of nothing*, as Clement of Alexandria writes in the 1st *Stromata* after the middle: *But Greek philosophy, while it does not make the truth more powerful, yet by rendering the sophistical attack against it powerless, and by parrying the treacherous plots against the truth, has been called its proper fence...*

# PROLEGOMENA

...and to be a fence for the vineyards. <note>original: καὶ θριγκός εἶναι τῶν ἀμπελῶν</note> We have everywhere examples to imitate: the testimonies of the wisest men, either sprinkled with moral precepts or filled with the most polished sayings. Augustus used to seek these out when unrolling the authors of both languages <note>Latin and Greek</note>, as Suetonius wrote in his *Life*. That Emperor of blessed memory, as Aurelius Victor reports, had been so intent upon liberal studies—especially eloquence—that no day passed, not even in the heat of battle, in which he did not read, write, or practice oratory. Who would not admire Aristotle when he discourses on morals? From his *Ethics*, certainly, the Theologian perceives how far the human mind can proceed by natural discourse after the Fall, without the renewal of the Holy Spirit, in the knowledge of virtues and happiness, and how much human industry can achieve in action; <term>not inaction</term> <note>original: οὐκ ἀπραξί</note>. Yet, because of the frequent battle between appetite and reason, the mind is likewise found to be languid in its natural state of strength; as the sacred scriptures dictate and nature itself proves. Here, there are some who, in contempt of Aristotle, will cry out that much was said by Luther, asserting the words which appear in Volume I of the Jena German edition: *“The book of Ethics is worse than any book, directly contrary to the grace of God and Christian virtues, yet it is accounted as one of the best. O, far away with such books from all Christians!”* By this hyperbole of words, that great man <note>Luther</note> was inveighing against those who had introduced that noble system of ten books written by Aristotle to Nicomachus into the chairs of the Schools—and indeed the Churches—as if it were the North Star of Christian virtues. Against these people, he disputes sharply and harshly in many places. Because of this <term>contrary presentation</term> <note>original: ἀντεκπαρεξαγῶς; a rhetorical term for counter-argument</note>, he gravely warned in the Jena edition, Vol. I, f. 343, *“that the Universities stand in need of a strong reformation.”* Yet he adorns that same writing with distinguished praise when he was in a more settled spirit, saying in his *Table Talk*: **“Aristotle was one of the best teachers in moral philosophy, regarding how one ought to lead a fine and capable outward life.”** A testimony which can stand for all is provided by the *Apology of the Augsburg Confession*, which is as follows: *“Aristotle wrote so learnedly concerning civil morals that nothing more needs to be required from his words.”* Who is sharper in exhortations than Seneca, the sharpest of all the Stoics? Who is greater than Virgil in moving the emotions? As Augustine testifies, he could not read the tragic fall of Dido in Virgil without tears. Who would not praise the maxims of Pythagoras, Phocylides, Plutarch, Cicero, and others, who exercised themselves entirely in delivering precepts for living well and composing the morals of men? Their maxims were collected with extraordinary labor by *Masters Nanus, Erasmus, Neander, Mirandulanus, Langerius, Langius, Gruterus, and others.* No one should doubt 
<margin>Psalm 94:10</margin>
that God, who teaches even the Heathens to seek what is right, dictated by His admirable counsel those things which we read today, so that they might be witnesses to us of the truth <term>of the knowledge of God</term> <note>original: τῆς γνώσεως Θεοῦ</note>. And truly, if the Pagans provided us with nothing else, this would certainly be by far the greatest and most ample thing: that, by God’s disposition, they described virtues and vices with great firmness. From their <term>ancient records</term> <note>original: ἀρχείως</note> we are able to adopt many ornaments for Christian Ethics, just as if we were bringing the precious vessels of the Egyptians to adorn the Tabernacle of the Lord. Certain maxims 

<column-break/>

<margin>to Treterus in the Index of Horace</margin>
drawn from secular writers, and the arguments of Theologians adapted within certain boundaries, do not lack their own beauty and are highly conducive to stirring men up. While something is either praised or blamed by the Heathens, it is all the more fitting for those who have given their names to Christ to either follow or flee those things (in matters not contrary to religion), inasmuch as the pure and holy religion of Christians is more powerful and excellent than Heathen superstition. For although Athens has no commerce with Jerusalem in the matter of saving faith, nevertheless, it will be of great use to read them insofar as they concern external discipline and those exercises which contribute greatly to virtue. One sees how far the Pagans reached by the light of human genius, though inspired by no higher spirit nor instructed by revealed truth. From this, Christians may correct their own sleepiness, and at the same time prove their labor for the Church with greater industry of praise. They should think to themselves how foul, how full of disgrace it would be, if a Christian man—dependent on his God and for whom the hope of eternal life is certain—should be loath to apply himself to virtue, to liberality toward the needy and the pious ministers of God’s mysteries, and to continence; especially when he finds that Gentile men, far removed from the true worship of God and religion, studied integrity, modesty, frugality, and other such ornaments of the human soul so intensely. It is a thing to be greatly ashamed of if the Philosopher of Christ exhibits less than the Philosopher of the world, and if the love of empty glory can do more in a Gentile heart than the affection of religious piety in a Christian soul. No one will be more wretched than the Atheists and their fellow-initiates. It is certain that on that day of judgment they will be put to shame by Seneca, Aristotle, Cicero, Pythagoras, Socrates, and others, who hated to sin even out of the love of virtue alone, while the former could not be kept within the bounds of piety even by the fear of punishment. The Holy Fathers observed this and drew many of the precepts and noble maxims of the Heathens into their own writings, so that by the example of the Pagans a greater fervor might be excited in the souls of their own people, and from this antithesis of opposites, <term>benefits for life</term> <note>original: κατὰ τὸν βίον ὠφελήματα</note> might be more strongly instilled. Hence St. Basil, in his small work on reading the books of the Heathens, gave most beautiful warnings for nourishing and increasing virtue from the rich—yet not "heathenish"—doctrine of the Gentiles (since some spark of divine light shone even upon them) concerning virtues and examples. Yet he advises that all this be done in moderation, by tasting rather than by drinking deep. Basil, the Emperor of Constantinople, in his *Exhortation to his son Leo* (surnamed the Philosopher), chapter 66, commends <term>the opinions of the ancients, and more than all, those of Solomon and Isocrates</term>. For that wise man thought the writings of Isocrates were wonderfully suited for educating royal youths and kindling them to cultivate virtue, especially if they were joined to the golden books of Solomon and Sirach. This is also evidenced in chapter 23 of his *Exhortations*, which he took from Isocrates concerning friends. St. Nazianzen writes in a certain sacred poem that he finally cast all human learning at the feet of Christ. For that most holy Father judged that all studies of doctrine and actions of life, <unclear>and the honors of the Muses and of those things</unclear> <unclear>to whatever extent</unclear>, must be referred to the fountain <term>of all true wisdom and goodness</term> <note>original: πάσης ἀληθοῦς σοφίας καὶ χρηστότη</note> for the worship and glory of this One alone. # ON BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

Chrysostom, in his 66th Homily, uses that generosity of Pharaoh and the Egyptians toward their priests (Genesis 47:22, 26) to commend Christian liberality toward the ecclesiastical ministry with weighty words; for Juan Azorius* <note>original: "Joh. Azorius"; a Spanish Jesuit moral theologian (1533–1603)</note> proves at length that the gentiles paid tithes to their priests with a liberal hand.
<margin>Book 7, Moral Institutes, ch. 23, question 22.</margin>
Dr. Luther did not neglect to mention this repeatedly in his writings. Thus, in his Commentary on Genesis chapter 47, he praised that elegant and true sentiment of Aristotle (*It is better to be a patron of the truth than to be too devoted to those who are familiar to us*). If a pagan man, he adds, thinks this should be done in civil disputes, how much more should it be done in those matters which have manifest testimony in the Scriptures. And so that we may illustrate our sacred matters to some by means of their opposites <note>original: "ἐκ τῶν ἐναντίων αὐθῆρες" (from opposing things themselves)</note>, let it be permitted for Christians to read gentile books for this reason alone: so that they may discern from them how much light and darkness, truth and error, stand apart; a point once made by Willeram,
<margin>Preface to the Song of Solomon.</margin>
Abbot of Ebersberg. Wilhelm Fabritius, the Apostolic and Archducal Censor of books, saw the same reasoning when, in his Censure of Pierre Castellanus's book on the *Festivals of the Greeks*, he permitted those ancient rites of heathendom to be printed for this very purpose: so that the pious man might recognize his own happiness even out of the darkness of such superstitions, because having been snatched from the power of darkness, he has been translated into the light of God. Thus, by perceiving this mental gloom and the foulness of superstitions, the minds of the godly might be stirred to value the light of the divine word more and more, and recognize with a grateful heart how much more fortunate they are than those who are outside the Church. Theodorus Pulmannus advised the same to Fleming in a letter: *God willed such testimonies to exist among the pagan Seers so that mortals might recognize in what great darkness they were living, and, being deterred by the very depravity of the soul, might finally be enticed and led by a driving conscience toward a virtuous and blessed life.* Barthius (42 Adv. 11) says: Without doubt, by the singular permission and indulgence of Almighty God, such writings were brought to light in this final age—not having been extinguished through the calamities of so many centuries—so that posterity might learn in what a great night mortality once lived while despising the fear of God. Hence Chemnitz <note>Martin Chemnitz (1522–1586), a leading Lutheran theologian</note> exhorts us in some places to take up Cicero’s three books *On the Nature of the Gods*; for then, from a comparison of those books with our own doctrine, we may most evidently recognize how great the darkness of the gentiles (even the wisest among them) was concerning God, and how great the light of divine grace communicated to us through the revealed word is, and how great the thanks we owe to God. Regarding the same book, Luther says in Genesis ch. 12, fol. 153a: *When you read Cicero’s discussions on the nature of the Gods, and on the ends of good and evil, you see that nothing was omitted by him which can be achieved by human reason and all a man's strength; and yet, what GOD wills, or what His opinion of us is, he does not know. The reason for this ignorance is that reason was not born to see God, but the Spirit of God, illuminating our minds through the word. Since Cicero was destitute of this, he necessarily labored under invincible ignorance.* These things were truly said by Luther. For where, I ask, does the wretched Cicero rush? In place of the true GOD, he worships Roman idols, and the most ancient and therefore truest religion of all—in which God had revealed His wisdom to the Jewish nation—he calls "barbarous superstition" with a clearly poisonous mind.

<column-break/>

Thus you may see from this how far the greatest Philosopher was able to ascend by his own wisdom; he measured true religion by the splendor of the empire, the gravity of the Roman name, the institutions of the ancestors, and the success of fortune. Likewise, that long narrative of Herodian concerning the consecration of a Roman Emperor—what else does it prove but the superstition, folly, and proud vanity of the heathens? So too the saying of Cornelius Tacitus on the customs of the Germans: *No one there laughs at vices* etc., convicts us of our own hardness of heart <note>original: "σκληροκαρδίας" (sklerokardias)</note>. Whereupon Beatus Rhenanus notes there on p. 106: *How much holier were the heathens than we; for how many today either do not laugh at vices, or do not cloak even the most enormous vices with that excuse, "Such is the age." If anyone condemns one who defiles another's marriage or mocks young girls, he immediately adds: "Such is the age."* That Caesar, who received the surname Augustus from his deeds and his increasing the state, lest the Roman Republic suffer great harm from Ovid’s books written about love, publicly proscribed them; and he condemned the author to exile in the fifty-second year of his reign because he had written three small books on the art of love.
<margin>Aurelius Victor in the Epitome.</margin>
Naso <note>Ovid's family name</note> himself mentions this in the second book of *Tristia*:

> Since two crimes have ruined me: a poem and an error,
> The fault of the second deed must be kept silent by me.

Attentively considering this act of Augustus, Johannes
<margin>Against the Romance of the Rose, 70th edition, Year 1513.</margin>
Gerson <note>Chancellor of the University of Paris (1363–1429)</note> exclaims: *O God, O holy men and women, O devoted court of the Christian religion, O morals of the present time! Among Pagans, a pagan and unbelieving Judge condemns a pagan who writes doctrine that enticed love toward crime; and among Christians and by Christians, such or worse work is sustained, praised, and defended. Lay this up in your deepest senses (it is no small matter).* Nor can that practice of the Jesuits be entirely disapproved, who sometimes chastise—or as they say, "castrate"—the Poets who are to be placed before the Schools, lest license be given to the lusts in the tender minds of youth, which is already great in itself. Ignatius Loyola specifically forbade Terence, the best author of Latinity, from being explained in the Schools because he judged him to be insufficiently modest and insufficiently chaste, as Pietro Maffei recorded in Book 3 of the *Life of Ignatius*, ch. 8. For the lust for sinning can easily be kindled by the reading of lustful books. For this must be striven for in life: that not only wicked company be avoided, but moreover the lascivious books of wicked companies—especially the obscene, scurrilous, futile, and finally useless ones—should be abolished by the laws of the empire and the decrees of councils; lest the minds of boys (of whom we are chiefly speaking), having drunk the poison, be carried headlong. In this matter, one is hardly on guard even when he is on guard; even when deeply cautious, that cautious man is often caught.
If Poetry delights you, that which exhibits the evidence of a better faith from the use of chaste antiquity is better, and which applies itself to celebrating GOD and the mysteries of religion after the example of Prudentius, Juvencus, Vida, Buchanan, Flaminius, Lauterbach, Huygens, and other Christian Poets. Better also is that poetry which, lest the vein of talent grow sluggish through idleness,
<margin>Oration on the dignity of Ethics, p. 44.</margin>
treats the doctrine of morals in decent verse—as P. Bertius* advises—than that which, in idleness, drains the sewers of profane poets and the cesspools of gentile fables to the detriment of the soul, or which departs into lascivious and less modest numbers and feet after the example of Naso.
