# PROLEGOMENA

<margin>
Lord Nanus in the *Polyanth.*
<note>Referring to Dominicus Nanus Mirabellius, author of the *Polyanthea*, a famous Renaissance encyclopedia.</note>
</margin>
> Let no Venus be sung by us, nor any Loves here,
> Nor shall the adulteries of Jove or the thefts of Mars be found here.
> Who would believe it honorable to speak of what is shameful to do?
> For such things drive the seeds of death into the very fibers of the soul.

Away with those ridiculous teachers of fables and the fools of the Poetic deities, whose harvest has come forth most abundantly in this age; whom, if they were alive today, the Pagans themselves would condemn, and they would accuse them of immodest play in their most deceitful love-poems <note>original: *erotopepniis*</note> for soft young girls. For in such great light of the divine word—compared to which all human wisdom is mere darkness—they have loved the darkness more than the light itself; following the blind and the leaders of the blind more than the Savior, the Leader of truth himself. What else is this, I ask, than wanting to bring darkness upon the Sun? For do you not think those great Poets, Virgil, Ovid, Horace, and many others, would have written about God without false Gods, and about love without obscenity, if they had possessed knowledge of the divine scriptures which exhort us to holiness? Indeed, we think so.

<margin>
Boniface, book 1 on Wisdom, p. 70.
</margin>
Should a Christian Poet not avoid what those pagans would have shunned? *Serious and ample subject matter cannot be lacking for Christians, which we see was lacking for the ancient writers: therefore their art is admirable to us, not their subject matter. If we wish to be fruitful Poets, we must take care that our argument is our own, but the art is that of the ancient Poets.* Thus we wonder all the more at the dreams of Johannes Major against Georgius Fabricius, a learnedly-pious Poet known by fame above the heavens, <margin>Leuting. on the March of Brandenburg, book 3, part 6, page 71.</margin> to speak poetically of so great a Poet. For when he revised his poems and rooted out the profane from them, like nettles and ferns from a field about to be cultivated, moved by the most grave voice of Jerome: *Far be it that "Almighty Jupiter" should sound from a Christian mouth, or "by Hercules" be heard,* he was noted by that sharp couplet:
> Fabricius removes all Venuses from his song,
> I wonder how he could remove them, for there were none.

It should be characteristic of Christians, when they are censors of vices or are engaged in describing <term>the poetic grace</term> <note>original: τὴν χάριν ποιητικὴν</note> in the love of the more pleasant Graces, to assign words most suited to nature and morals from a sense of decorum and a modest style, so that they deter others from the reproach of fornication and other crimes, rather than alluring them with a lustful diligence of words; for the greatest reverence befits a Christian Poet. He who wishes to be a chaste Poet must love chaste rhythms. Those excuses are most vain:
<margin>Catullus.</margin>
> It befits a pious Poet to be chaste
> Himself, but there is no necessity for his verses to be so,
> Even if they are soft and little modest.

->Again, that other one:<-
<margin>Ovid.</margin>
> Believe me, my morals differ from my song:
> My life is modest, but my Muse is playful.

For we do not listen to those making excuses, whom their own impiety and impurity of both mind and body accuse, so that it is beyond doubt that while they wrote such things, they burned inwardly.

<margin>
Palingenius in *Zodiac of Life*.
</margin>
> *For who would not judge them
> To be imbued with every disgrace, and to have been such
> As the things they committed to their wicked papers?
> Speech is the index of the soul.*

<margin>
In *Theotimus*, book 1, Paris Edition, Year 1549.
</margin>
Can you hold back laughter, says Gabriel Putherbeus, when you hear from Catullus that a Poet ought to be chaste,

<column-break/>

while at the same time Catullus is so little chaste that he is called "lewd" by the most lewd Poet; and not content with one, he chased many loves, in which he himself confessed to adultery. Truly, no good man ought to name foul things, let alone commit them to writing, from which those who read them <margin>Lace- 3. Poet. c. 97. p. 343.</margin> turn out worse, as Scaliger warns. We read that the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note> expelled the books of Archilochus from their city solely because of the obscenity of the words. Let those Masters of Wickedness consider this said to themselves, whose pages are lewd and whose lives are wicked. Excellent is the warning of Cicero in *Pro Caelio*: *As much as you separate yourself from the baseness of things, so much should you separate yourself from the liberty of words.* For that reason, the Orator taught that <term>foul language</term> <note>original: αἰσχρολογίαν</note> should not be used even in metaphorical expressions. Who can read without passion what Propertius did with his Cynthia, Catullus with Lesbia, or Ovid with Corinna? Fearing something of the sort, Plato, when he was of mature age, <margin>Laertius in his *Life*.</margin> delivered his poems about love to Vulcan <note>i.e., to the fire</note> to expiate them. Another gave ten thousand lines of poetry elaborated on amatory matters to be burned by the flames, promising that he would spend the rest of his life on pious songs: <margin>Boniface, book 1 on Wisdom, p. 83.</margin> *I realize, he said, what that means: it is better for him who provides a scandal to be drowned in the depths of the sea than to set snares in which his brothers are entangled. But what shall I do? Following the custom of the world, those things slipped out; now hearing the voice of Christ the Lord, I come to my senses.* With equal zeal, Frederick II, Elector Palatine, when he observed demonic adjurations in the *Steganographia* of Trithemius given to the Elector Philip, took care that the <term>original manuscript</term> <note>original: αὐτόγραφον</note> be handed to the flames, lest anyone abuse Trithemius's narrative, or the excellent Prince seem to encourage incantatory arts. Gustavus Selenus <note>Pseudonym for Augustus the Younger, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg.</note> cannot stomach this, and on that account brings a charge against Franciscus Junius, whose advice the Elector had used; thinking that the man from Spanheim <note>Trithemius</note> had taught a secret method of writing pure from the delusions of demons in covered words; which even Sigismund, Abbot of the Monastery of Seon in Bavaria, proved in 1616 in his *Apology for Steganography*, and Johannes Caramuel continued at Cologne in 1635. By the same fate, to use a similar example, Gerbert was once received on account of his remarkable knowledge of Mathematics—who later obtained the name Sylvester II in the Papacy—because he was the first to teach in Europe with "barbaric" terms and figures (for he had received them from a Saracen Philosopher), he was held to be a MAGICIAN by the common voice of that unlearned age, as Baronius noted at the year 991 AD. However, anyone who reads what Cardinal Benno has to say about the lives of the Popes of his time will not undeservedly hold him suspected of that crime. Nor does the famous Gerard Vossius entirely excuse Trithemius. But we do not make that little dispute our own. A shameful thing, as we have said, is not to be increased by a multitude of impurities. In this matter, many (whose names we spare) have erred greatly. In order to restore authors, <margin>V. Campes. Admonition to Critics.</margin> they do not so much wipe away as uncover the most foul passages in writers with idle effort; and they turn themselves toward every brothel, harlot's cell, and chamber-pot. Explaining at length the lying-together of Jove with Alcmena and his innumerable bastards; and in what way Danae received the golden shower in her lap; and what the hollow hand of Baubo, <term>to wag the tail</term>, <term>to suck</term>, <term>the three-legged night</term>, <term>to pelt with apples</term> <note>Greek terms for various obscene or ritual acts</note> might mean. I say nothing of the jealousy of Vulcan, or the abduction of the Phrygian Ganymede,

# ON BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES. 35

*Neptune’s Melanippe, Venus’s* adulterous affairs, *Laius’s* pederasty <note>homosexual relations with boys</note>, *Galathea’s* evil, and other things foul, filthy, and shameful to speak of. It should grieve a Christian to speak of these at length here; for much study and effort is not spent on these grim trifles without a loss of piety and damage to better studies, where it befits us to be Cryptics <note>those who hide or guard mysteries</note>, not Critics. In *Owen* <note>John Owen, the Welsh epigrammatist</note>, that second *Martial* of our century, we desire modesty more than wit. Was it for this reason God willed us to be Christians—so that we might bring shameful loves out of a stinking sewer into the light so profusely and petulantly! So that, following the example of that lazy and wicked servant, we might bury our talent in the filthy dust, and, no differently than the *Jews*, melt down precious earrings and bracelets—that is, the gifts of intellect—for the Idol of the golden calf? That is, to consecrate them to vain and obscene things in such a great light of letters? *Be confounded and blush over your ways, O house of Israel.*

<margin>
Ezekiel 36.
See Gambara, "On the Method of Perfect Poetry."
</margin>

To know vices and to recognize the foulness of crimes in a common accusation is not a crime; nor can it be attributed to vice to express vices and call vices "vices" so that they may be exploded <note>rejected or driven off the stage</note>, following the example of Holy Scripture, which sometimes names *shameful things* cautiously <note>original Greek: εὐλαβουμένως</note> *for the sake of utility*, and sometimes *does not name them out of modesty*. But to be vicious, and to commit those things which you have learned, to dissect curiously and to the life those things which the most lecherous villains have committed; to also describe what you yourself have committed—that is a crime. Just as there exists, to the eternal ignominy of the Roman See, that monstrous little book—the likes of which never existed among the most impure Heathens since men were born—written by GIOVANNI DELLA CASA, Secretary to the Pope, Dean of the Apostolic Chamber, Archbishop of Benevento, and Legate in the Venetian territory, *In Praise of Sodomy*, written in verse, which *Erhard Schnepf* saw with his own eyes. *Scaliger* said truly:

<margin>Sedulius on Ephesians, chapter 5.</margin>
->*ROME, because she delighted in love written backward,*<-
->*Took her name from the inverted name of LOVE.*<-
<note>A play on the word ROMA, which spelled backward is AMOR (Latin for Love).</note>

Look, I ask you, at the remarkable lewdness of *Juan Bautista Poza*, who indulged himself so much that he celebrated the immaculate conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary with the soft delights of words with which *Venus, Medea, Helen, Phryne, and Thais* were distinguished among the ancients; *Vargas* rightly notes these things. *Isaac Wake*, in *The King’s Plato*, condemned a similar profanity by a certain poet (*Gaguin*, if I am not mistaken). Let them purge their minds as much as they purge *Juvenal, Persius, Martial*, and certain *Eclogues of Virgil*: concerning which authors we rightly advise that what is to be imitated should be taken from them, but what is foul in its beginning and foul in its end should be avoided. For whether they teach good or evil, the Christian Interpreter always has work to do: to detest, attack, and refute the latter; to praise, illustrate, and instill the former. For to this end, one may know evil things alongside the good, *not so that we may do both (for I say one must not do base things), but so that it may not be hidden how they are, and so that we may be able to justly refute others who use those very words*, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> discusses, clearly in agreement with St. Paul’s precept: *Test all things; hold fast to that which is good.* Good things for imitating, but evil things for avoiding. Now, as for what remains to be said, it is fitting for us—who have dismissed secular wisdom and despised the *Egyptian* meat-pots—to reclaim whatever utility we find in profane works for the praise of the ONE GOD, Best and Greatest, and to give sacred things bound in profane meters with praise.

<margin>On Jesuit Stratagems, ch. 16.</margin>

<column-break/>

With that purpose, many centuries before us, *Eudoxia* composed elegant Centos <note>poems made of borrowed verses</note> from *Homer* in praise of Christ the Lord. *Proba Falconia*, wife of the Roman Proconsul Adelphius, celebrated the wondrous works of Christ in Virgilian verses in an elegant work called the *Centometrum* <note>The "Hundred-Measure" or "Cento"</note>, mentioned by *Burchard*, Bishop of Worms, <margin>book 3, ch. 22.</margin> and *Ivo*, Bishop of Chartres in Gaul, as an *apocryphal* work about Christ composed of Virgilian verses. <margin>part 4, ch. 65.</margin> *Ephrem the Syrian*, the Hermit, and *Apollinaris the Syrian* established this laudable practice of driving out pagan poets; they introduced their own poems into the schools in place of Homer, Menander, and Euripides, as witnessed by *Sozomen*. His words concerning Apollinaris in Book 5, Chapter 17 are: *Apollinaris, employing his great learning and natural talent, composed the Hebrew antiquities in heroic verse in place of Homer's poetry, down to the reign of Saul, and divided the whole work into twenty-four parts, giving each volume a name corresponding to the Greek letters, etc.* <unclear>and</unclear> <unclear>their</unclear> number and order. *Isidore* adds a certain Pomponius, who *in his leisure wrote a "Tuvrum" in honor of Christ, and likewise an "Aeneid."* <margin>See Goldast on Columbanus, p. 73, 75.</margin> The Magnificent Lord Georg Volckamer, Magistrate of Nuremberg, surpassing all praise, commended this study in an elegant letter to the Reverend Lord Saubert: *"I am of the opinion that those (pagan poets) should be read with chaste eyes and minds, and their phraseology, as far as possible, should be transferred to the sacred explanations of the true Religion. For in this way alone can the spoils of Greece and ancient Latium <note>Rome</note> be most rightly put to use."* The famous Saubert obeyed this advice and composed a beautiful Cento from Homer concerning the Victory of our Savior, which you may see in the funeral rites of the great man Volckamer. With equal success, the famous *Conrad Rittershusius*, a Nuremberg jurist, once adapted an elegant and witty epigram (which appears in the *Greek Anthology* regarding Tantalus) by way of parody to the *Rich Man Dives* <note>from the parable of Lazarus</note>, and recorded it in his notes on Salvian, p. 510. Others have done the same; for with the same thread Paurmeister rendered a *Christian Martial*, Sagittarius a *Christian Horace*, and Cornelis Schonaeus a *Christian Terence* in thoroughly purged verses. Following their example, let us prune external knowledge for the illustration of Christianity rather than for those external things in which there is empty delight; as those have confessed who finally condemned their own impure papers: *Nonnus, Aeneas Sylvius, Giovanni Pico, Pietro Bembo, Torquato Tasso, Theodore Beza, Pierre de Ronsard, Lazzaro Gambara*—a worthy and laudable deed; so that the profane things we once saw as pleasing might be surpassed by the greater pleasure of sacred things.

> Let the profane wrongly plow the profane,
> Devoted to fables,
> And hunt for a new name therefrom: but the mind
> Destined for holy days
> Should elegantly frequent sacred hymns.
<margin>Melissus, book 3, Ode 13.</margin>

However, I would not wish what I have said to be taken as if no Heathen Poets should be taught in the Schools; as will be clear of its own accord from what has been said: since they are of so many and such great uses, and have been received and approved by Christians for many centuries. For the books of the Poets will not infect the minds of boys with depraved opinions and sentiments, provided the teacher's interpretation and proper instruction are added; yet not every reading should be employed, but *students, so that*

# PREFACE

<margin>Book 1, chapter 13.</margin> To use the *words of Quintilian* <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, a famous Roman rhetorician</note>, young minds stand in great need of warning; primarily because, as they are about to be shaped, whatever settles deep within those who are unrefined and ignorant of all things should be not only eloquent, but even more so, morally upright. It is a lamentable state of perversity that human affairs, both in ancient times and our own, have reached such a point that the better things—which can and should be more profitable for true piety, the kingdom of Christ, the glory of God, and the salvation of men—are commonly cast aside. Meanwhile, the worse things are frequently chosen, to the extent that thorns are not seldom preferred to ears of grain, and briars to the harvest. This is what our ancestors complained of, what we complain of, and what our descendants will complain of: that education is sliding into decay. So far are many from seeking a selection of Christian words, that they studiously seek to stain their writings with the rust of paganism, believing nothing is well-written unless you place Jupiter and the other gods before you in the manner of Cato, as if there were no God in Israel. The Holy Fathers in the Church of old could not bear to hear the terms *Nature, Fate, and Fortune*. Yet we hear of nothing but the Muses, Apollo, the Fates, Fauns and Satyrs, Olympus and the Elysian Fields, Jupiter born of Saturn and the "All-Voiced," Apollo of Thymbra and the "Lord of the Bow," Minerva the "Bringer of Spoils," and the Muses of Pegasus and Helicon. No poem seems poetic or magnificent unless it is stuffed with these sorts of loud-sounding names of the Gentile gods. Although they may take for themselves the power of "daring anything" by poetic right, let them know that this power, full of unbridled license, is denied them by Divine right. Judge for yourself, Pious Reader, and sharpen your intellect toward the <term>worthy</term> <note>original: ἀξιόλογα (axiologa)</note> words of Eobanus Hessus, a pious poet, under whose leadership the Muse <note>original: Pieris</note> raised her chaste head on high. *I am not accustomed to approve of those*, he says in that place, *who are so studious of antiquity that they think they can express its image more clearly the further they are removed from our Religion. Those who, in all their poems, even sometimes in light and trivial ones, are accustomed to invoke Pagan Deities: and so, by those most filthy allurements of ancient names, they are baited like the bones of Cerberus and most badly affected, so that they seem more like followers of Jove than Christians. Furthermore, if any good man should force Christ or some other inhabitant of Heaven into a poem instead of Jove or Phoebus, these most filthy carpers immediately pursue him with slanders as if he were guilty of insulting poetic majesty—as if the divine name of Poetry were shut up and confined within those profane and sometimes most immodest trifles, as if by certain boundaries which it is not permitted to cross... There are also those who devote their entire talent to profane Gods, and while they sing natural hymns, they seem to be making a sacrifice. I would not deny that some have expressed the image of our common nature in all its features, as they say, but in such a way that they seem to have sown a certain plague in Religion, while they worship and adore nature itself only by the names of the ancient Gods—as if Earth, Water, Air, Fire, and the things existing through and beyond these could not be described unless they are called Gods. For what did Marullus, a most noble lyric poet of our age, lack for the highest success of talent, except the fervor of the Christian Religion alone?* Thus far the immortal poet of Hesse, <term>a great star for his fatherland</term> <note>original: μέγας πατρίδ’ & ἀστήρ (megas patrid' kai aster)</note>, both religiously wrote and practiced himself.

> In the most vain affairs, enough and more (but thus far
> Alas, you individuals were vacant in so many errors and disputes.
> To speculation and futility, I ask you, flee these dreams,
> Which have no power to be of use.

Wherefore Victor Giffelinus also warned quite skillfully and gracefully how much those things are to be avoided—things which it would be worth the effort to hold in heart and memory—when among other things he sang:

> Let the Muses of Helicon be Christ's, let Christ be Apollo,
> And let his laurel go upon your temples.
> Let not the fountain of Pegasus or the waters of Libethra,
> But the living water of Christ extinguish your thirst.

But lest we wander too far, with the HELP OF GOD we direct our course to the shore, to say at last: <term>when all things, when at all times, when by all people</term> <note>original: ὅτε πάντα, ὅτε πάντοτε, ὅτε παρὰ πάντων</note> secular writings are to be read, and that in that reading and study neither nothing nor too much effort ought to be spent. But let that saying of Augustine remain, which he says in 

<margin>Book 2 of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 39.</margin> it is not necessary to labor over many things for the sake of a few, since neither the age nor the talent of a man is sufficient for all things. Properly considering these things, I made the first trials of my talent when I was giving effort to literature at the University of Jena, in Biblical Antiquities, so that I might illustrate them from pagan antiquity. Let the doctrine handed down in the Word of God be the rule of judgment in the reading of all those authors. For the salt of the divine word is lacking in Pagan writings, without which all things are tasteless.

> We do not forbid you to wander through the fields
> Of all the arts, provided they prepare your mind
> For brighter things, and do not occupy it.
> But one science must be caught by you,
> The mistress of life, the rule of truth;
> He who knows it not, knows the others wrongly.

To which aphorisms we shout a great "Bravo!" For the School of Christ is not one of Logic, Rhetoric, or Grammar, but of Ethics—that is, of life and good works; and all doctrine, if piety is removed, is poison. Therefore let us dwell entirely in the divine scriptures, of which we shall find every single word to be a single axiom and a kind of medicine for a languishing soul. Golden are the words of Pope Gregory XIII in a letter to King Philip II of Spain, which appear in the Royal Bibles: *As far as Theology is concerned, the mysteries of our Religion and divinity are explained in these books; as far as that part which is called moral is concerned, from here also are gathered all the precepts of virtue, in which parts the whole account of our salvation and happiness is contained.* The Pope could not have said anything more weighty; and the sentiment will be all the weightier for being so rare. For Holy Scripture is the most fertile fountain of heavenly wisdom, a storehouse of erudition and science, from which sweet instructions for a piously and justly ordered life can be drawn. This points a finger, as it were, at the wandering wisdom of the Pagans and restrains it within the orbit of right reason. This allows no one to slip or err; it establishes the boundaries of good and evil; it marks what is deadly and what is vital; it defines what is to be done and what is to be avoided, so that it forms character excellently. Whatever a man teaches outside of this, to use the opinion of Blessed Augustine, is harmful; there it is condemned; if it is useful, it is found there. Here a man says things which the most learned Plato did not know, the most acute Seneca was ignorant of, Homer (the parent of pagan doctrines and antiquity) did not understand, and Hegesias—who because of his astounding eloquence was called <term>the persuader of death</term> <note>original: πεισι θάνατος (peisithanatos)</note>—never heard. Demosthenes the most eloquent never reached it; Aristotle the wisest never tracked it down. Anastasius of Nicaea, from the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book 7: *Whatever things can be desired in the books of the Gentiles are found far better in Holy Scripture.* Luther in Genesis chapter 12: *Holy letters teach Ethics or the account of Duties far better than any Ciceros or Aristotelians.*

<margin>Theodulph of Orléans in *Instruction on the Old and New Testament*.</margin>
> Whatever is learned in the noble arts by worldly
> Skill, here runs in a freer path.

<margin>Plutarch in *Marius*.</margin> Moreover, just as they record that Plato deservedly gave thanks to the Gods on three main counts: that he was born a MAN, not a beast; that he was a Greek, not a barbarian; and that he had fallen into the times of the most upright teacher, Socrates; so let us Christians, in every remembrance of divine beneficence, celebrate God with a grateful memory and our whole heart: because he did not leave us in the pit of errors with which <margin>Ephesians 1:12</margin> Plato, Socrates, and all the gentiles struggled; because with rich mercy he willed that even we gentiles, who were once <term>without Christ</term> <note>original: χωρὶς χριστοῦ (choris Christou)</note>, should come to the Church and the fellowship of the heavenly kingdom, and entrusted to us the use of his benefits <margin>verse 19</margin>, so that we are now <term>fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God</term> <note>original: συμπολῖται τῶν ἁγίων καὶ οἰκεῖοι τοῦ Θεοῦ (sympolitai ton hagion kai oikeioi tou Theou)</note>; because at this very time the Best and Greatest God willed us to be born and to live in those places where the living and inviolate voice of the Gospel still sounds, while so many kingdoms and provinces here lack the light of the divine word and are most miserably in darkness. TO THAT TRIUNE GOD, GOD THE FATHER, GOD THE SON, GOD THE HOLY SPIRIT, BE PRAISE AND HONOR.
-> AMEN. <-

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES.
## From Genesis Chap. I. verse 1.

-> קקק צמחתן <- <note>Hebrew decorative or mystical characters, likely a printer's mark or symbolic heading.</note>

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
The Most Holy Majesty speaks with mortals in a brief but brilliant discourse, and reveals Himself in many ways. We shall begin these BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES from the wonderful work of Creation, by which He first revealed Himself; here, certainly, the first words of the Bible encompass the entire business of Creation in a marvelous compendium, as if in a single bundle, so that every single word carries its own weight.

The words, then, are immediately at the very entrance concerning the <term>Megalourgia</term> <note>Greek: "Great Work" or "Magnificent Creation"</note> of the world.

<margin>Gen. 1. 1.</margin>
> In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. <note>original Hebrew: בראשית ברא אלהים את השמים ואת הארץ.</note>
> In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth. <note>original Greek: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν.</note>
> In the Beginning God created heaven & earth. <note>original Latin: In Principio creavit DEUS caelum & terram.</note>

In this manner Moses—the standard of all antiquarian knowledge and the rule of all history—begins his work. According to Justin in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 7, Moses stood as much more ancient than all others, whether sages, poets, historians, philosophers, or legislators. His work is called *Bereshit* from its first initial word, or the <term>Book of Formation</term> <note>original Hebrew: ספר יצירה, Sefer Yetzirah</note>, <term>Genesis by the Greeks</term>, and the <term>Book of Creation by the Rabbis</term>, a name derived from its subject matter.
<margin>Book 12, Commentary on Isaiah & ch. 28 Ezekiel.</margin>
<margin>According to Jerome*, <term>Yashar</term>, <term>Indus</term>, or <term>Entheon</term> <note>Greek: "of the inspired"</note>, meaning "of the upright," because it describes the history of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whom the Cabbalists call the <term>Upright</term>; concerning what should be thought of this matter, consult Blessed Gerhard, *Exegesis on Scripture*, sections 16 & 119.</margin>

The matter itself speaks to how much an accurate and diligent reading of the first chapter of Genesis profits both theologians and philosophers, and how much its neglect causes harm. For who will deny that the <italic>First Origins of things</italic> are recounted by Moses in the first three chapters? The <italic>first and second</italic> chapters contain the work of creation accomplished in the space of six days, which is usually called the <term>Hexaëmeron</term> <note>Greek: "Six Days"</note>. The <italic>third</italic> contains the origin of the Fall and of sin.

Since the Pagans were ignorant of those three chapters regarding the original creation and constitution of all things, it is no wonder that they fell into marvelous errors in their Archaeology. Plentiful witnesses are the books of Plato alone, <italic>concerning the eternal matter of the world and the infinite ages running back and forth of their own accord, before God brought the same into order out of that shapeless confusion</italic>. The occasion for this error seems taken from the words of Moses in Gen. 1:2, as Basil the Great* teaches; nor is it obscure from a comparison of the opinion of Plato's disciple brought forward by Basil, though for this turn we shall pass over it with a "dry foot," as they say,
<margin>Book 11, Hexaëmeron.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
lest we dwell on Aristotle's opinion concerning the eternity of the world, which he maintained against the more ancient philosophers, as he himself confessed* <margin>Book 1, On the Heavens, ch. 10.</margin> <italic>"all say that it [the world] was indeed created,"</italic> although others demonstrate the contrary from Aristotle himself, as we shall see below.

Therefore, that holy and majestic act of Creation—which can be worthily recounted by no abundance of speaking or writing, let alone adorned—must have its order and <term>taxis</term> <note>Greek: "arrangement"</note> taken more accurately, indeed more fully (though in a compendium), from this one chapter of Genesis than from the volumes of anyone else, whether Aristotle or Plato, however lengthy they may be. Thus, it can rightly be said with Juan Nieremberg*: <margin>*On the Origin of Holy Scripture, Book 2, ch. 7, p. 39.</margin> <italic>"I think Moses taught more in just the first chapter of Genesis than all other philosophers and interpreters of Nature."</italic>

Plato does not seem to wander far from this in the *Timaeus* when he says: <italic>"Those things which pertain to divine matters must be learned from those who were closest to the ancient ones taught by God,"</italic> which must also be admitted here. Let us therefore seek the Origins of things from Moses, whom we believe (along with Augustine* recounting past events) better than one who even predicted future things which we now see as present.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
The word <term>Bara</term> <note>Hebrew: ברא</note> properly denotes production out of nothing, or from matter entirely undisposed, which is to be regarded as nothing in respect to the thing to be produced. As Rabbi David Kimchi teaches in his Dictionary, creation is spoken of *when a thing is brought forth from nothing*, which Rabbi Aben Ezra admits is the common opinion of the Hebrews. Regarding the verb <term>Bara</term>, they elsewhere note that in the history of creation, before the rest of God is discussed, it is found thirty-two times; the Hebrews mystically refer this to signify the thirty-two ways of wisdom. Among Christians, those who agree with the older Rabbis feel that the mystery of the Holy Trinity exists in the word <term>Bara</term>, such that the <term>B</term> <note>Beth</note> denotes the Father, <term>R</term> <note>Resh</note> the Son, and <term>A</term> <note>Aleph</note> the Holy Spirit, united in one individual and indivisible essence in the word <term>Bara</term>. This Cabbalistic interpretation—pious in itself even if less than accurate—is exploded with heretical laughter as "childish" by Georgius Enjedinus, a Photinian <note>A follower of Photinus, denying the Trinity</note>, who even added another sarcasm: that <term>ABA</term> denotes "Father," and <term>AB</term> designates "Father," and <term>A</term> is the beginning of the phrase <term>lo yitzlach</term> <note>Hebrew: לא יצלח</note>, in this sense: *You are the Prince of the wicked*. On this matter, see more in *Galatinus book 2, ch. 10; also in Galakazia by Rabbi Julius on the detection of hidden things, ch. 5, 6, 7; Conrad Aslac, Mosaic Physics, p. 120; Hackspan, Jewish Cabbala, p. 285.*

Turning to the synonyms of this word, it is not unknown to students of the Holy Language that this immense work of primordial Creation is described with a manifold phraseology joined with singular emphasis. However, we think the distinction between <term>Bara</term> (*to create*), <term>Yatzar</term> (*to form*), and <term>Asah</term> (*to make*) should be set forth first, though they are sometimes used interchangeably. Of these: 1. denotes *production from nothing*. 2. *The distinction and polishing of the created things*. 3. *The adornment and completion of the Divine work*. As Rabbi David Kimchi notes in his Book of Roots, where he explains that passage in *Isaiah 43:7*, in which these three are found joined together: <term>I have created him, I have formed him, even I have made him</term>. In the history of creation there occurs (1.) the verb <term>Bara</term> in *Genesis 1:1, 21, 25, 26*; then (2.) *He formed, He fashioned*, which is read concerning the formation of man in *Genesis 2:7, 8. Compare Psalm 94:4, Zechariah 12:1, Jeremiah 10:16, ch. 51:19.* (3.) <term>Yasad</term>, which the Greeks render as <term>themeliōn</term> (*to found*), and is used specifically of the creation of the earth in *Psalm 102:26, Proverbs 3:19*, and elsewhere. To this are also rightly referred <term>Kun</term>, which is used not only of the formation or creation of the earth in *Psalm 24:2* but also of heaven in *Proverbs 3:19*; as well as <term>Natah</term>, which is read as specifically applied to the creation of heaven, which God extends like a skin or a tent in which we dwell; compare *Isaiah 40:22, ch. 44:24, Jeremiah 10:12.* Although all those words, and others that could still be attached from the authentic text, are considered <term>toward the same end</term> <note>Greek: πρὸς ταυτὸ</note> and abound in their own peculiar emphasis—and for that reason seem to suit certain creatures specifically, such as "extension" for the heaven, "foundation" for the earth, "formation" for man, etc.—they are nevertheless exchanged among themselves in a singular way. Thus, any of them may be used to describe creation from nothing: <term>Bara</term> for the origin from nothing; <term>Asah</term> to denote the end, that all things were finished and fitted for their uses; <term>Yatzar</term> for the *glory* and *beauty of the creatures*, because clearly all things were formed beautifully and most fairly; <term>Natah</term>, to which from *Psalm 42:5* add <term>Raka</term> for 

<column-break/>

solidity and firmness, because they were most firmly founded and consolidated; <term>Kun</term> for *proportion* and *amplitude*, because all things were joined and ordered in a fitting and decent manner; finally <term>Neshamah</term> <note>Usually "breath," here used for the harmony of life</note> for the *suitability* and *community of creatures* that carry us away into admiration of them from every side, because each thing is most suitably expanded, extended, and exposed to the eyes of all.

Of all temporal things, therefore—with not even the smallest exception—the Creator without time, the invisible and eternal Performer <margin>*preface 2, prepared for admission*</margin> of things visible and invisible, is read with this eulogy in Ambrose: *The HOLY TRINITY, which in the creation and production of all things, manifested its person chiefly by speaking and producing*. Hence in the Apostles' Creed, the first person of the Divinity is called <term>Father Almighty, maker of heaven and earth</term> <note>Greek: πατὴρ παντοκράτωρ, ποιητὴς ὀυρανῶ καὶ γῆς</note>, not excluding the Son and the Holy Spirit. For that reason, Moses uses a phrase noting God as one in essence through a singular verb, but consisting of distinct persons through the plural name <term>Elohim</term>. For the name *Elohim* implies not one but several persons, as is proved most extensively from Holy Scripture and the consensus of almost all antiquity by Dr. Haberkorn in *Syntagma 1, p. 114 ff.* Furthermore, <term>the making of things material and things immaterial</term> <note>Greek: ἡ τῶν μὲν ἐνύλων, τῶν δὲ ἀΰλων ποίησις</note> is peculiarly attributed to God the Father in the Holy Scriptures; however, no <term>superiority</term> <note>Greek: ἐξοχὴ</note> is to be imagined there, no disparity, no partiality or lack of shared cause, *but that which He does, is the one Deity common to the three*, as we rightly confess with Nazianzen in *Oration 11 on Theology*.

<margin>Lecture 18, p. 220.</margin>
The Pagans indeed handed down many things aptly concerning the origin of things, but in the sequence of created things—how and at what time they were produced—they knew nothing, since they were destitute of the Biblical record. In this record, as Hieronymus Vielmius holds, *Moses narrated with deliberate counsel how and at what time all things were created, namely that God both commanded and acted, and therefore he commemorated the command everywhere to warn readers that God did not do this work by an impulse of nature or blindly, but after he had previously weighed and consulted the matter well—that is, he deliberated with wonderful providence and thus with the highest freedom and wisdom*. Moses places the word <term>Bara</term>, *He made*, so that the Creator might demonstrate to us both his power and his efficiency, and exclude all co-workers and ministers; and then the word <term>Vayomer</term> <note>Hebrew: ויאמר</note>, *He commanded, or He said*, to set forth in this way His providence and, as it were, His consultation, judgment, and freedom in acting.

For who is so senseless of heart, and so "big-nosed" <note>arrogant or critical</note> with Epicurus, as to find fault with the <term>all-wise</term> <note>Greek: πανσοφώτατον</note> Creator, at least in this earthly globe, for having established too many mountains and in them so many wild beasts? Alas! men rash beyond measure, do you dare to measure the Providence of God by your own small scale (that tiny capacity, which is like a vessel with a very narrow mouth, into which if you wish to pour anything, it must be distilled drop by drop and at intervals), and pass judgment on His works, concerning which it is written seven or eight times <term>all things are very good</term> <note>Hebrew: כל-טוב מאד</note>? Hence we cannot but marvel with Erasmus <margin>*Sermon on the Mercy of the Lord, p. 469.*</margin> at *three things in God the Almighty <note>Greek: παντοκράτορι</note> himself: namely, the highest power, the highest wisdom, and the highest goodness. The first He declared by a mere nod, having founded this wonderful work, of which no part is not*

# From Genesis Chapter I, verse 1.

is full of miracles; even the gnats and spiders themselves cry out the immense power of the Creator: *that power which, while it established all things by ineffable might, a portion of wisdom preserves and governs, and by that very fact demonstrates itself to be no less wise than it is omnipotent.* This is found in contemplating the works of the **Hexaemeron** <note>The "Six Days" of Creation described in Genesis.</note>; when considered more intimately, one cannot help but exclaim with the Church: *Heaven and earth are full of your glory*, nor will one restrain oneself from breaking out into the hymn of the three youths: *Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord; praise him and highly exalt him forever.* Hence in *Psalm 104*, God's wisdom, power, goodness, and providence are preached and celebrated as conspicuous in the making of the whole world and its individual parts; for which reason the Greek translator prefixed this title to it (though it is untitled among the Hebrews): *A Psalm of David concerning the constitution of the world.* <note>original: Ψαλμὸς τῷ Δαυῒδ ὑπὲρ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου συστάσεως</note> As he begins the consideration of these things with a mouth full of Thanksgiving, so he ended with the same, saying: *Bless the Lord, O my soul* <note>original Hebrew: בָּרְכִי נַפְשִׁי אֶת־יְהוָֹה</note>; and in the middle of his course he exclaims: *How magnificent are your works, O Jehovah: You have made them all with wisdom.* <note>original Hebrew: מָה־רַבּוּ מַעֲשֶׂיךָ יְהוָֹה כֻּלָּם בְּחָכְמָה עָשִׂיתָ</note> Without the supreme Deity, therefore, nothing is constant in its order. Wonderful things were done, therefore, when God spoke, and all things were made. Wonderful are the things which God does daily. God makes the *earth* remain stable, as if resting on bases. He daily imposes a law upon the sea and the waters, lest they cross their boundaries. He so connects contrary qualities in the Elements that they preserve God's statutes by a perpetual harmony and a wonderful consensus. What foolishness is it, I ask, to still murmur against one's benefactor even out of plenty; and whereas before, when there was no supply, the soul was immediately complaining, now when some things abound, it is ungrateful. For it is God who placed the order of nature, and gave a law and a certain measure of acting: *He commanded and they were created*, says the *Psalmist in 148:5.* <note>original Hebrew: הוּא צִוָּה וְנִבְרָאוּ</note> He set a decree, and it shall not pass away. he says: *Fire, hail, snow, vapor, stormy wind, fulfilling his word:* Where Prosper of Aquitaine in his exposition (p. 851) says: *Nothing is subject to stronger motions, yet each individual thing serves His laws; He who, as He wills, works concerning all things and in all things according to the causes of hidden reason.* To this also aim the words of Diodorus Siculus, who, while others attribute various events and adverse accidents to fortune, himself ascribes them to Divine Providence, saying: <margin>Book 5, p. 240.</margin> *Thinking that Tennes was saved by the providence of some of the gods, he ruled the island, and becoming famous for his justice and other virtues, he obtained immortal honors.* He relates that Tennes, beyond the hope of all, was saved by the providence of some God and gained the kingdom of the Island: and being illustrious for justice and other virtues, he attained the honors of the immortals. that Power and providence, which sits in the heavens, reaches to all things.* In his *Ethics*, both to Nicomachus and to Eudemus, he asserted the same; where among other things he says: *It is agreeable to reason, it is evident, that the Gods care for human affairs, love the upright and wise, and bestow benefits upon them.* In the same manner, the most ancient interpreters and his disciples Theophrastus and Alexander of Aphrodisias explain the mind of the Philosopher, who in Book 2 *On Providence* says: *For Aristotle is the author that the preservation of those things which happen here, and their permanence in their own species, does not exist without divine Providence; for that power which emanates from the Sun and those other stars is, in his opinion, the cause for all things which consist by the nature of birth and safety.* Since these things are so, they are a clear testimony—

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
By testimony: The wiser among the Pagans recognized Divine Providence as creator and preserver by the light of nature, even if they were ignorant of how far it extends due to a lack of the light of Scripture. Hence they dispute the causes of calamities and where they come from, but they remain ignorant of the source, clinging to murky streams. For the ancients who did not read *Moses*, since they were ignorant of the **BEGINNING**, could not help but wander—by a whole heaven's distance, as they say—from the Beginning that has no beginning <note>original: ἀνάρχῳ (anarchō) - without beginning</note>. Therefore, lest we also deflect from it and slip into error, that Mosaic *Hexaëmeron* <note>The "Six Days" of Creation</note>, of which the gentile philosophers were ignorant, becomes for us like a ladder by which we ascend to the knowledge of God. Let us make six steps of this ladder according to the six days, so that by this ladder of creation we may ascend to the eternal Lord. "Come then," as we rouse ourselves with the words of *Basil* <margin>Oration I, p. 2.</margin>, "let us also contemplate divine things with a willing heart, and let us ascend to the Master of creation through creation itself. For God, having fashioned creation like a ladder, engineered through it an ascent to Himself for those who love God."

The beginning of the Bible is: *In the beginning **GOD** created the heaven and the earth.* By this we are warned that the creation of things was not done from eternity, but in that beginning in which all time began to flow. Therefore, creation did not begin in "time" properly so-called, but in the first instant and beginning of time, which is called the *beginning of the ways of the Lord* <margin>Proverbs 8:22.</margin>. Before this, just as there was no way, no external action, and no work, so there was no time, no age, and no era, but nothing except pure eternity; likewise, there was no matter.

->Do not seek for Matter; there was none.<-

Hence one must speak with the Scripture: *He made heaven and earth out of things that were not* <margin>2 Maccabees 7:28.</margin>. He calls *things that are not as though they were* <margin>Romans 4:17.</margin>. Out of darkness He commanded light to shine (2 Corinthians 4:6). By the word of God the ages were prepared, *so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear* <margin>Hebrews 11:3.</margin>. And in sum, God created all things *out of nothing*; *out of nothing*, I say, by which not a "material" is implied, but a starting point, and at the same time every relation to a material cause is denied. "Out of nothing," that is, <margin>part 1, q. 45, art. 1; l. 2. O. F. c. 5.</margin> "not out of something," says *Thomas [Aquinas]*. Add *Damascene*: *"GOD made all things out of nothing, some indeed immediately, others mediately."* <margin>Augustine, Book on Genesis against the Manicheans, ch. 6.</margin> *Augustine* says: *"Even if all things were formed from that unformed matter (created on the first day), nevertheless this matter itself was made out of absolutely nothing, whence it is most rightly believed that God made all things out of nothing."*

Since God is the Parent and effector of all things, He most wisely created this magnificent machine of the most beautiful universe right **FROM THE BEGINNING**, not from the forms of things (which Plato dreams of and calls "ideas"), nor from any pre-existing matter, but by the living word of His mouth alone within the Six Days. He adorned the heaven with the most bright lights of the Sun, Moon, and Stars, and the earth with greening shrubs, fragrant herbs, and various living creatures, according to these verses:

->The first day brought forth light, the second heaven, the third earth,<-
->The fourth the stars, the following has fish and fowl,<-
->The sixth every animal and man from the dust of the earth,<-
->But the seventh light honored the Sabbath.<-
->Or more briefly:<-

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
->Before the Day, God created Heaven and Earth,<-
->Plants, Stars, Birds, Quadrupeds, and Man.<-

The *creations* <note>original: δημιουργήματα (dēmiourgēmata)</note> of the first day are therefore heaven and earth, which in the original sources are named *Shamaim* <note>Hebrew: שמים</note>, "heavens," from their height; since the root of the word, though now unused in Hebrew, signifies "to be high" (*shama*) in the related Arabic language; and *Eretz* <note>Hebrew: ארץ</note>, "earth," which word descends not from "running" (*rutz*) nor from "crushing" (*ratzatz*), but from *ara*, which in the Arabic language signifies "to be humble or depressed," whence the earth is also called *Araa* by the Chaldeans, i.e., the lowest thing. Furthermore, as to what should properly be understood by these words, there are found almost as many different opinions of the Doctors as there are letters in them. We, setting aside the recitation of contrary opinions (which the Blessed Reader will find at length in *B. Walther, Harm. p. 55; Calovius, Vol. 3 System of Theology, p. 931; Conrad Aslac, Mosaic Physics, p. 123*), approve for the present "step by step" <note>original: κατὰ πόδα (kata poda)</note> the common opinion of the Fathers, Luther, and other theologians of our own, who judge that by the words "heaven and earth" proposed here, the Hebrew writers designated a "place and a container" <note>original: מקום ומחזור (makom u-machzor)</note>—namely, the matter from which the heaven and earth and the bodily creatures in them were produced. This was a rude and undigested mass, which is called by Moses in verse 2 *Tohu va-Bohu* <note>Hebrew: תהו ובהו</note>, by which terms the Scripture signifies a vastness and horrible confusion (Isaiah 34:11; Jeremiah 4:23). Thus, in that undigested matter, it is suggested that not only heaven and earth, but also the waters and their abyss, existed as a purely dark, unarranged, and confused state. Hence, specifically by the word *Tohu*, not only is the "privation" <note>original: στέρησις (sterēsis)</note> of accidental form and figure indicated (because the earth was empty and undigested), but also that the earthly mass lay in *Tehom*, that is, the abyss or immense depth of waters; for this reason it is immediately added, *"Darkness was upon the face of the abyss."* And by the word *Bohu*, the earth is meant as empty or uncultivated and plainly sterile, *because where there was no distinction, there was no separation*. Therefore, these words are rendered by the Septuagint as "the earth was invisible and unfinished," *invisible* because covered by waters (as Epiphanius and Basil after him explain, as well as Augustine), and *unarranged or unworked*, because there was mere confusion, a rude and undigested mass. *Symmachus* renders it "idle and indistinguishable," *something empty and disordered*; the *Targum Onkelos* explains it as "desolate and empty." The *Author of the Book of Jezirah* explains *Tohu* as "recent stones" (*others say hidden or concealed*) submerged in the abyss from which the waters go forth; and *Bohu* as a "green line" surrounding the whole world (compare the book *Cosri* by Johannes Buxtorf, p. 312). Rabbi Solomon explains the word *Tohu* as "astonishment" and *Bohu* as "emptiness," because the face of the earth was such that it could not be seen without astonishment and a sense of vastness—though these do not fully exhaust the force of the words, since they imply not only vastness but also a stupendous confusion. To this belongs the testimony of the wise man, who says to God in *Wisdom 11:18*: *"Thy hand created the world out of unformed matter"* <note>original: ὕλης ἀμόρφου (hylēs amorphou)</note>; and of Augustine, <margin>Book 1 on Genesis against the Manicheans, ch. 7, ch. 5.</margin> who not incongruously calls the undigested mass "prime matter" because of the origin of heaven and earth and other things arising from this matter; and "Chaos" because of the confusion of forms which it contained, even if from...

# From Genesis Chapter I, verse 1.

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
The first matter <note>original: *materia prima*</note> of Aristotle differs greatly: For that original mass was not entirely destitute of all form, since mention is made of *the earth and the deep and the waters*, and the *earth is said to have been founded from the beginning*, in *Psalm 102:25: You, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth*, but rather it was only destitute of a complete and perfect form. Nor is it the same as the Chaos of the Poets and other Pagans, which they invented. For they make a wonderful <term>mixture <note>original: *κυκεῶνα* (kykeona); a thick potion or jumble</note></term> of things, so that they are deservedly to be left with their *stupid Chaos*. Yet they show in a single word how far they have strayed from the truth, although they may have glimpsed something through a long lattice-window; hence *Hesiod* (whom *Lactantius* nevertheless reproves because, taking his beginning from Chaos, he did not first explain whence that very thing began to be or consist, or when or how), in the *Theogony* line 115 of the poets:

->Verily, first of all Chaos came into being, and then<-
->The broad-breasted Earth &c.<-

*Chaos existed first, after these the very wide earth.*
*And Ovid in Book 1 of the Metamorphoses:*
> Before the sea and lands, and the sky which covers all,
> There was one face of nature in the whole orb,
> Which they called Chaos, a rude and undigested mass,
> Nor anything but sluggish weight, and heaped in the same place
> The discordant seeds of things not well joined.
> No Titan <note>The Sun</note> as yet provided light to the world.

->And presently:<-

> And where there was Earth, there also was Sea and Air,
> Thus the earth was unstable, the wave unswimmable,
> The air lacking light, to no thing did its own form remain.

<margin>See Walther, Biblical Office of the Royal Physician p. 515 and others cited above.</margin>
Hence concerning the primordial matter, from which all things were born and produced, the opinions of the Philosophers are ambiguous; nor is it a wonder in those who, illuminated by no light of Sacred <term>Archaeology <note>original: *ἀρχαιολογίας*; here meaning the study of origins or ancient history</note></term>, lay hidden in the darkness of Greece and Rome. Those who believed all things were born from the Ocean do not know the Ocean; for it is not the <term>progenitor of all <note>original: *αρχέγονος πάντων*</note></term>. For a dense fog obscured the minds of the pagan Philosophers in handing down the beginnings of things. There are, however, some among the Christians who do not fear not only to excuse the decrees of the Philosophers concerning primordial matter, but even to show their harmony with Moses in handing down the beginnings of things. Let us hear one, <margin>I. S. Gall. p. 126.</margin> *Goropius Becanus*, who proceeds thus: *In the generation of the whole Universe, all the ancients placed unformed matter prior to form, and some called it night, others chaos, others the abyss, others darkness, others by another name. Hesiod procreates night from chaos, and soon from night the ether and the day; in whose work I seem to hear that which we have handed down from Moses concerning the same matter: And darkness was upon the face of the deep. Aristotle subjects matter, like a certain chaos, to generation, to which he pronounces privation to be present, like a certain night.* And after a few lines interspersed he writes further: *When he calls night the mother of all with Orpheus, he says nothing else than that darkness was before all things. In the same way Hesiod is to be heard, both of whom received the same from their ancestors as is handed down by Moses, namely that the world was created out of nothing, so that by the name of Night, "Nothing" is understood. Thus he says.*

<column-break/>

We determine, therefore, that this is the right way of philosophizing: that we should not value the authority of Philosophers, however illustrious, so highly that we snatch up whatever Physics they have written without judgment or selection, but rather, applying the ruler of philosophical truth, we should discern the true from the false, the use from the abuse. For even the leaders of the Philosophers are so constituted that they have brought great errors into their Schools. To *establish that the World is co-eternal with God*—is that part of Philosophy? It is a vain error and an insane wisdom, a rock upon which the most acute Aristotle nevertheless struck. But we, acknowledging him to have been a man, should not excuse his blemishes. Let us commend in him his great <term>shrewdness <note>original: *ἀγχίνοιαν* (anchinoian)</note></term> in finding the weight of reasons, his prudent <term>arrangement <note>original: *διάθεσιν* (diathesin)</note></term> of philosophical matters into their classes, his wonderful skill in disputing, his distinguished sagacity in logical precepts, his express subtlety in physical matters, and his greatest clarity in ethical and political matters. Thus we shall philosophize soberly, that is, we will neither rashly embrace everything, nor reject everything, but we will apply that moderation, so that having separated vain error and abuse from true and genuine Philosophy, we may approve the former and reject the latter, imitating in this the bees, which although they sit upon various flowers, nevertheless pluck only those things which will be of use to them for making honey, and let the rest be passed over. That the most ancient Philosophy is most to be approved is testified by the words of Cicero in the first *Tusculan Disputation*: *For that opinion which we wish to obtain,* he says, *we can use all antiquity, which, the closer it was to the origin and divine progeny, the better it discerned those things which were true.* Since there is no antiquity older than that of Moses, the volumes of Moses should deservedly be the measure of all other books. For just as in singing there is as much sweetness of voices as there is harmony of the rest with the instrument or the lowest voice: in the same way, other writings outside the Church are true or false as they agree more with the Mosaic account or depart further from it. These things are not placed by us to the end as if Philosophy offers no use to the student of Holy Scripture: for it is well known—to speak briefly of the discipline of physics alone and its use—how much weight the knowledge of that discipline which is usually called *Physics* contributes to the proper understanding of the Holy Book. This can be demonstrated by no other chapter better than the *first of the whole Holy Bible*, in which Physics has an ample theater, not only of earthly things, but also in some way of heavenly things. For the physical investigator lifts his eyes across the sky, and beyond the depth of the earth and the abyss, he is immersed into a certain void, as Jerome testifies in chapter *nonne* 3. dist. 37, concerning which Seneca in Epistle 95 recites the verses of Lucretius:

> For I shall begin to discourse to you concerning the supreme
> logic of the sky and the Gods, and I shall reveal the first beginnings of things.

Therefore, the Theologian who is a stranger to the Book of Nature fares poorly in interpreting the Book of Scripture; for he who does not bring a knowledge of Physics to the reading of the Old Testament will not taste the sweet kernel of many of the Holy Spirit's oracles, but, being unrefined, will be forced to bite the rough bark. For there are so many fragrant flowers plucked from the field of Physics and propagated into the Sacred Paradise of Theology. Hence Bullinger truly says: <margin>Book 2 against the <br/> Anabaptists tr. 7 p. 97.</margin> *I know he will grant that Physics is necessary for Holy Letters...*

The author advocates for a "sober philosophy" that uses the Bible as the ultimate measure of truth while still utilizing the useful tools of natural science (Physics) to better understand scripture.</summary>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Physics <note>original: "Physica Sacra"</note></margin>
...you have been too little practiced in them. For there, mention is made of various trees, herbs, roots, animals, birds, stones, metals, and similar things, which you will never understand unless you learn their nature from the Natural Philosophers. Witnesses to this are Job, David in the Psalms, and the books of the Prophets, in which these things can be seen abundantly; without natural science in these matters, you will grope as if without light in the darkness. Regarding Adam and his knowledge in natural philosophy, the thoughts of Victorinus Strigelius <note>A 16th-century Lutheran theologian</note> are not to be despised: that after the murder of Abel and the rejection of Cain, Adam delighted himself chiefly in the study of Physics and Astronomy.

<margin>Oration on Physics, Jena, p. 121.</margin>
Thus he says: *Adam, since he had no family until the birth of Seth, devoted all his time after the Gospel <note>referring here to the first promise of redemption in Genesis</note> to the observation of nature. Nor is there any doubt that he laid the foundations of the greatest arts—Astronomy, Physics, and Medicine—having noted the motions of the wandering and non-wandering stars <note>planets and fixed stars</note>, and having observed, especially in such a long span of life, the qualities and actions of lower things, some of which are beneficial to human life, while others bring certain plague and destruction to bodies. Often he spoke with Eve about Spleenwort <note>original: "Aspleno"</note>, which diminishes black bile. He discoursed on saffron, and finally handed down other easily-obtained <note>original Greek: "εὐπόριστα"</note> remedies to the memory of posterity.*

<margin>Vol. 4, p. 417, ch. 1.</margin>
Regarding the same First-Formed Man <note>Adam</note>, he mentions that he taught Physics to his children (p. 605). Nor should we pass over Solomon, the wisest of Kings and most skilled in natural things, about whom and his science in natural matters and universal wisdom <note>original Greek: "πανσοφίᾳ"</note> Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose of Milan</note> discourses excellently. The book of Job is of such manifold and rare learning that he who would perceive even its literal sense must be skilled in all philosophy; for other examples drawn from Holy Scripture, consult Simon Gronenberg in his *Oration on Physical Studies and their Use in the Doctrine of the Church*, published at Wittenberg, 1588.

<margin>Lecture 18, p. 221.</margin>
Furthermore, as Vielmius teaches: *The Theologian demands auxiliary reinforcements from Philosophy when treating the Creation; let him, however, propose the constitution of heaven and earth chiefly from the Word of God. For in the Holy Bible, there are scattered here and there things regarding heaven and earth and its works, and the sources of these things are to be drawn from there; but since the Bible does not treat these subjects professionally, the diligence of the Pagans is not to be despised here, and the chaff in the husks of Hippocrates, Aristotle, and Plato must be separated from the grain.*

<margin>Bacon, On the Advancement of Learning, Book 9, p. 293.</margin>
To those, however, who wish to pluck all philosophy from Holy Scripture, Bacon <note>Francis Bacon</note> responds: *In this way, they do not defer honor to the Scriptures, but rashly pursue transitory things among divine ones; to seek Theology in Philosophy is like seeking the living among the dead; to seek Philosophy in Theology is nothing else than seeking the dead among the living.*

Nor should it be omitted here that in the Holy Bible, the natural and supernatural revelations of God are mixed; though their principal scope was to reveal the principles of Theology (for its principles can only be had from divine revelation), nevertheless, in the same most holy book, precepts and examples of Philosophy occur in great number.

<margin>Logic, Book 2, p. 213.</margin>
Regarding this dual use, Amandus Polanus says: *Holy Scripture is the sole principle of Theology and of all Theological treatises and disputations, being simply indemonstrable <note>original Greek: "ἀναπόδεικτον"</note> and self-evident <note>original Greek: "αὐτόπιϛον"</note>. According to this*

<column-break/>

standard, whatever is prescribed and taught in Physical Theology is judged to be true if it agrees with it. According to this Sacred standard, the precepts of sound Philosophy—especially Physics, Ethics, Economics, and Politics—are deemed true if they harmonize with it. For there is an admirable harmony and consensus between the natural and supernatural revelations of God; since both Reason and Scripture are from God, and the Holy Spirit, through Scripture, again illuminates Reason (which was obscured by sin and corrupted by foul errors) and renders it free from error. Therefore, whatever agrees with this standard is true, whether in Theology, Philosophy, or any other discipline; and whatever fights against this standard is false, in whatever discipline it is taught; for Holy Scripture is the standard of truth according to which the errors of other disciplines that conflict with it must be corrected.

Indeed, as widely as the universe of all things extends, so widely does the true and most ancient Natural Philosophy extend—in the beginning, middle, and end of the universe; in the height of heaven, the depth of the earth, and the middle of the air. Hence, since it is shameful and unworthy of a human inhabitant of the world to be ignorant of the world's origin, constitution, and nature, we shall repeat the Mosaic Philosophy in the contemplation of heaven and earth, and whatever meets us regarding the consideration of nature in the Sacred tablets of the Old Testament, as briefly as is permitted, for the glory and veneration of God the Creator alone. Let us therefore hear Moses, the Chancellor of the nascent world:

> In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.

That heaven and that earth come under the single name of *Cosmos* <note>original Greek: "κόσμος"</note>; just as the word "World" <note>Latin: "mundus"</note> takes its name from adornment and beauty.

-> By no other name should the World be called, <-
-> It takes its name fittingly from its adornment. <-

Because next after God the Creator of the world and the Spirit, there is nothing more beautiful or more adorned than the World itself. This World is completed by Heaven and Earth, which together constitute "The All" <note>original Greek: "τὸ Πᾶν"</note>, or the university of all the creatures of God the Creator, and contains all universal bodies, whether simple or mixed. This amphitheater of Heaven and Earth was founded by God *in the Beginning*, lest it be believed to be from eternity, and so that it might be believed that all things which belong to the world began, and that nothing is from eternity except God the Creator of the World. From this it is clear that this universe does not owe its origin to Angels, as Menander and his disciples taught; it did not draw its origin from certain "Powers" of the Carpocratians; nor from the "Princes" of the Archontics; nor from the seven Angels alone without the knowledge of God the Father, as the Saturnians held; nor from the 365th heaven of Basilides; nor before the infinite fabulous ages of the heretic Valentinus. The Pagans, contemplating this most elegant theater of the World, fell into various praises: they recognize God as the Architect, but they do not *know* Him, for they could not investigate the efficient cause of such varied and wonderful creatures by the sagacity of their own wits. Hence Ovid, stammering somewhat about these things, says:

> Whichever of the Gods it was?

Neither did they know the matter from which the creatures were produced and built, nor how they were founded in the beginning...

# From Genesis Chapter I, verse 1.

->**Sacred Physics**<- <margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
creatures were [uncertain]; indeed, they did not even perceive the principal end of Creation. Hence, some denied the origin of the World, *others affirmed it, and others fell into the most absurd opinions concerning its origin.* Hilary <note>St. Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), a Bishop and theologian who wrote extensively on the Trinity and Genesis.</note> notes the same <margin>on Psalm 148, p. 647.</margin> regarding them when he says: *The first error of human ignorance (concerning the nature of the world) is that some have dared to imagine that this state of the WORLD came together by fortuitous encounters, and thus order consisted out of disorder. Then, that others think this World itself is GOD, which stirs and moves itself, and moderates its inanimate temperament by the measured reason of its course. Finally, that each one chooses for himself from these very elements—either Heaven, or the Sun, or Water, or Air—to which he might defer the honor of God in a vain and impious religion.* Nor should the impudent statement of Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist.</note>—otherwise most sagacious in natural matters—be hidden here, as he forges a Deity out of the World, saying in Book 2 of his Natural History, Chapter 1: *It is right to believe that the World, and this which by another name it has pleased us to call heaven, by whose circumference all things are covered, is a Deity: eternal, immense, neither begotten, nor ever to perish.* <note>original: "Mundum, & hoc quod nomine alio cœlum appellare libuit... Numen eſſe credi par eſt..."</note> But who does not see how these things contradict one another? Homer, Hesiod, Pythagoras, and others were not so insane. Hence Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a syncretism of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth.</note> says: *Man was made a spectator of the works of God, and he admired them and recognized the CREATOR.* <note>original: "Θεατὴς ἐγένετο τῶν ἔργων τοῦ Θεοῦ ὁ ἄνθρωπος..."</note> And famous is the sentiment of the most ancient poet Orpheus: *There is one, who is of himself, and from that one all things have been made.* <note>original: "εἷς ἐστ’ αὐτογενὴς..."</note> To which that of Sophocles conforms: *There is one, truly one God, who established the heaven and the wide earth.* Plato and Aristotle were not so insane, even if to this day it is not agreed upon among his followers, nor among the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note>, concerning the creation of the world. For many assert, according to the mind of Plato and especially Aristotle, that no creation is given, whom Suarez and the Conimbricenses <margin>Disputation 20, section 1, n. 24. Book 8 of Physics, ch. 2, q. 2, a. 2. Book 5, ch. 7, p. 291.</margin> cite copiously. Among whom is Pererius <note>Benito Pereira (1535–1610), a Jesuit theologian.</note>, who says: *Nothing can be found or imagined that is more contrary to the doctrine of Aristotle, and which more violently strikes at all his joints and sinews, than to admit Creation in him.* Others, however, feel the opposite: that Plato and Aristotle knew the Creator of the World and the creation. So felt Scaliger (Exercise 61, section 3), Suarez, the Conimbricenses in the cited places, Toletus (Book 8 of Physics, ch. 2, q. 6), and Zanardus (Book 2 of Metaphysics, lecture 4, q. 4). And it is evident: for most truly Plato in the *Timaeus* professes that God created, formed, and established this World, and affirms that God is the *Eternal Mind and the cause of Good* in nature. Hence, concerning Plato, Johannes Ferrariensis <margin>Book 1 on the Nature of the Soul, section 5.</note> testifies: *Most constantly in the Timaeus, Plato professes that the most beautiful mass of the World was wrought by the supreme Artisan of all things.* When they inquired of him the cause for founding the World, we have received that he concluded the matter thus: *that good works might be founded by a good GOD.* I truly do not know what more holy answer could have been given by a man, whether he read these things (as some suspect), or perhaps learned them from those who had read them; or whether by his own most sharp genius—which I think more likely—he perceived the invisible things of GOD through the understanding of those things which were made. Yet he assigned this cause, i.e., the Goodness of God, as so just and so suitable that it might most easily terminate all the controversies of those seeking the origin of the world. Thus he spoke.

<column-break/>

Regarding Aristotle, the matter is clearer, and illustrious testimonies can be brought from him for this purpose. For he says in Book 2 of *On Generation and Corruption*, ch. 10, text 59: *God completed the Universe.* <note>original: "συμπλήρωσε ὁ Θεὸς τὸ ὅλον"</note> And <margin>Book 2 of Gen. & Corr. ch. 10, text 59. Book 12 of Metaphysics, 8. Book 8, Book 2 of Rhetoric, ch. 23. Book on the World to Alexander, ch. 6.</margin> *he calls God absolutely the cause and principle*, and in chapter 7: *The Principle, which does not happen to be otherwise, but simply is: from such a Principle (God), then, both the world and nature depend.* <note>original: "Ἐκ τοιαύτης ἄρα ἀρχῆς ἤρτηται ὁ κόσμος..."</note> And in Book 2 of *Rhetoric*, ch. 23: *The divine is nothing if not either God, or the work of God: But whoever thinks it is the work of God, it is necessary for him to think that there are also Gods.* Finally, he asserts the same most clearly and beautifully: *There is an ancient saying, handed down from our ancestors among all men, that all things were established and joined together both from GOD and through GOD, and no nature is sufficiently equipped for its own safety which, deprived of the protection of GOD, is left at last to its own defense.* <note>original: "Ἀρχαῖος μὲν οὖν τις λόγος... ὡς ἐκ Θεοῦ τὰ πάντα..."</note> From which places it is surely perceived that the Creation of things was not hidden from Aristotle, and that God is the efficient cause of the World. But when the World is called by him *eternal and unbegotten*, <note>original: "ἀίδιος καὶ ἀγέννητος"</note> and it is said everywhere by Aristotle that the World has *neither beginning nor end*, a grave controversy has arisen among the Peripatetics concerning the mind of Aristotle, and it has not yet been decided by them. *For some establish* that Aristotle proposed this opinion *only as probable*, but did not *persuade himself of it as demonstrable*; to that end they bring up that in Book 1 of the *Topics*, ch. 9, *he called it a dialectical problem, whether the world is eternal or not.* *Others, however*, assert that Aristotle said it *for the sake of example*, and in examples *truth is not required according to Aristotle.* <margin>Book 1 of Prior Analytics, ch. 39.</margin> *Some* say that he established the World as eternal by reason of its end, not its beginning. Certain others absolutely ascribe the opinion of the eternity of the World to Aristotle. From these points, even lightly brought forward, the internecine and domestic war of the Peripatetics concerning the mind of Aristotle is established. There are, however, also those who wish that no indictment should be written on account of the word *eternal*, as the Philosopher [Aristotle] does not take it in a metaphysical rigor, but in a physical manner and way, while he himself says: <margin>Book 6 to Nicomachus, ch. 3. Book 1 on the Parts of Animals, ch. 1.</margin> *eternal things are those which are incorruptible and ingenerable*, and again *he opposes "eternal" to falling things; by which they try to hint that the Philosopher, when he said the world was eternal, said nothing other than that it did not begin through the principles of nature, nor fail through the principles of nature, by which reasoning the Philosopher's problem—that the world has neither beginning nor end—would be conforming to our faith and Holy Scripture, and would contain nothing discordant with Holy Writ. But lest we seem to have put our sickle into another's harvest; returning to the proposal, it pleased us to annex a few things concerning the time of creation before we come to the study of the remaining theorems of the first day. For it is certain, as Dr. Hottinger <note>Johann Heinrich Hottinger (1620–1667), a Swiss philologist and theologian.</note> hands down, <margin>Dissertation 1 on Genesis, p. 9, 10.</margin> that the world began at a certain time.
