# SACRED PHYSICS
<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>

It is uncertain, however, in which quarter of the year the world began. God has not revealed this, and it is a matter of human curiosity that men take upon themselves the labor of inquiry to place the exact point of time more specifically before our eyes—whether it began in autumn or spring, summer or winter. It does no harm to be ignorant of the exact moment, nor does it do harm to inquire, though one must rely on conjecture. The Jews invite us to their Kabbalah <note>Jewish mystical tradition</note>, and from there they derive the month of *Tishrei* <note>roughly September/October</note>, which partly corresponds to our September and partly to October; in this, they show from the word *Bereshit* <note>Hebrew: "In the beginning"</note> that the world was created in autumn, and indeed through the letter <term>א</term> (Aleph) rather than <term>ב</term> (Bet) <note>The author refers to complex mystical debates about the first letters of the Bible</note>, concerning which you may see, if you wish, the illustrious **Hackspan** in *Jewish Kabbalah*, pages 314, 420, and **B. Walther** in *Biblical Office*, page 560 and following. Regarding its creation in time, the pagans knew nothing, except this: that God was the Author of this entire Machine of the World, since nothing besides GOD has existence from itself, but all things depend on God. For the Creation of the World is a "work of God directed outward" <note>Latin: *opus DEI ad extra*; a theological term for God's actions affecting the universe rather than His internal nature</note>; moreover, those outward works are subject to Divine liberty and will, which is the sole and unique cause of creation. However, the will and act of God are known to us only from the Holy Book, which the pagans lacked. Hence it is well to note what the Blessed **Dr. Meisner** says: <margin>part 1. *Sober Philosophy* section 3. ch. 3. q. 1.</margin> The creation of the world (namely, in time) is a <term>subject of faith</term> <note>Greek: *hypokeimenon pisteos*</note> or something believable, not a <term>subject of science</term> <note>Greek: *episteton*</note> or something knowable; it is an article of faith, not a principle of reason; it is revealed in Scripture, not demonstrated from nature; and thus it is not understood in order to be believed, but believed in order to be understood. For that reason, the Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews (11:3) clearly refers the knowledge of the completed Creation to faith, saying: <term>By faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God.</term> <note>Greek: *Pistei nooumen katertisthai tous aionas rhemati Theou*</note>. And so the <term>divine mode of production</term> out of nothing, as far as the distinct six days of creation are concerned, belongs to <term>faith</term> <note>Greek: *pistin*</note>, although both the act and effect of creation can be known, albeit confusedly, from the light of nature, as is well established.

Hitherto we have been occupied in describing the first work of the first day; it follows that we descend to the second work of the first day, namely **Light**, which is the first principle of celestial things; Moses deals with this in verses 3, 4, and 5.

->VERSE 3.<-
> And God said, Let there be light: and there was light. <note>Original: Hebrew *Wayyomer Elohim yehi-or wayyehi-or*</note>
> And God said, Let light be made, and light was made. <note>Original: Greek *Kai eipen ho Theos, Genetheto phos, kai egeneto phos*</note>
> And God said, let there be Light: and there was Light. <note>Original: Latin *Et dixit Deus, esto Lux: & fuit Lux*</note>

->VERSES 4 & 5.<-
> And God saw the light, that it was good: and God divided the light from the darkness. And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And the evening and the morning were the first day. <note>Original: Hebrew text provided</note>
> And God saw the light, that it was good, and God separated between the light and between the darkness. And God called the light day, and the darkness he called night. And there was evening, and there was morning, one day. <note>Original: Greek text provided</note>
> And God saw the light, that it was good, and divided the light from the darkness. And he called the light day, and the darkness night: and the evening and morning became one day. <note>Original: Latin text provided</note>

The first outlines of the Divine works lay in darkness—Water, Earth, Air, Fires—but the Divine Power, having immediately struck away the night, introduced Light, illuminating the cloudy depths with a shining face, **And He said**...

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
...and He said. "Then you spoke," says the Author of the fourth book <term>under the title of Ezra, chapter 6:40</term>, "that a luminous Light should be brought forth from your treasures, so that your work might appear." With this coincides what is read in **Basil of Seleucia** <margin>Oration 1. p. 3.</margin>: <term>The first voice was sent from God, and light was brought forth; the voice heard, and nature was produced; the calling happened, and creation was formed.</term> <note>Greek: *Prote phone theothen epempetho...*</note> Furthermore, Interpreters contend among themselves as to what should be understood by the word **And He said** <note>Hebrew: *Wayyomer*</note>. There have been those, both among the Ancients and the moderns, as **Conrad Aslacus*** mentions, who <margin>*Mosaic Physics ch. 168.</margin> judged that the substantial generation of the Son of God was to be understood from this place. But by no means is the eternal Generation of the Son described here, but only an external operation or external work in the creation of **Light**.

Therefore, the ambiguity and various meanings of the word **said** <note>Hebrew: *amar*</note> must be observed. For 1. it is used for that which is to speak the conceived or thought words of the mind with the organs of the mouth, or even of a thought formed in the intellect but not brought forth by the mouth or will. In this sense **Maimonides*** shows <margin>in *Guide for the Perplexed* p. 1. ch. 65.</margin> that in this place it does not signify speech, but will; **Saadias** (who explains *said* through *willed*) and **Rabbi Isaac Karo** (ch. 65), who brings forward a similar passage from 1 Samuel 20:4, agree; compare **Hackspan**, *Philological Notes on ch. 1. v. 3, p. 37*. But God does not speak in that [human] manner, for He is an infinite Spirit, destitute of all bodily instruments. Secondly, **And He said** sometimes denotes a mandate or command, in which sense **Rabbi Abenezra**, appealing to Psalm 33, interprets it as *commanded* <note>Hebrew: *tzivvah*</note>, and considers it to note <term>existence without the weariness of labor</term> <note>Hebrew: *hawayah bi-yegiah maaseh*</note> and to allude to a King, commanding his servants with a single word, so that the thing is ready sooner than said and as quickly as possible; compare Psalm 33:6. Nor are **Flacius** and others foreign to this opinion, who therefore call this "saying" a **creative** saying. This opinion is confirmed partly by **St. Paul in 2 Corinthians 4:6**, when he says: <term>God commanded the light to shine out of darkness</term>, and partly by the words immediately following, **and there was light**, as being brought forth in time; thus "to say" is taken for "to command" or "to order." **Psalm 33:9: For he spoke, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast** <note>Hebrew: *ki hu amar wayyehi...*</note>, and **Matthew 8:8: but only speak the word, and my servant shall be healed** <note>Greek: *alla monon eipe logon...*</note>. Compare Mark 4:39, 5:8, 41; Luke 7:14; 2 Corinthians 4:6, where the Latin Interpreter and with him **Erasmus** express the Greek *to eipein* (to say) through *to jussit* (he commanded). In this way, here GOD SAID, i.e., he commanded by his immense power and wisdom, which is the Son of God himself, the second Person of the Holy Trinity. Hence, with the **Blessed Gerhard** in *Exegesis of the Holy Trinity § 122, p. 1049*, we establish that **"He said" in this place** <note>Latin: *to amar h. l.*</note> not only notes the efficacious will and mandate of God commanding and effectively willing that the world be made, but also that by the same word of SPEAKING is expressed and denoted the **hypostatic** <note>personally distinct</note> and substantial Word, namely, the Son of GOD. This is both because of the comparison with **John 1:1-3: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made** <note>Greek: *en arche en ho logos...*</note>, with which compare that classic passage of St. Paul in Colossians 1:16 and Proverbs 8:22 following, where the same things are attributed to the Wisdom of God which Moses here attributes to the Word of God; and because of the agreement of the Chaldean paraphrase <note>The Targum</note>, in which it is most common...

# From Genesis Chapter I. v. 3. 4. & 5.

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
it is, that the Son of God is called the promised Messiah, the <term>Memra</term> <note>Hebrew: "Word"</note> or the <term>Memra Da-Yeya</term> <note>Aramaic: "The Word of the Lord"</note>.

Moses records first, however, that Darkness was upon the face of the Deep; this was not something positive <note>meaning a physical substance with its own existence</note>, as the Manichaeans <note>followers of a dualistic religion that saw good and evil as equal physical forces</note> deliriously claimed, asserting that darkness was a *principle co-eternal with GOD, or a certain uncreated evil substance* from which all evils originate. Rather, it was a privation or negation of light not yet existing, a gloom naturally clinging to the earth and water. Hence Augustine in *Book on Genesis against the Manichaeans, ch. 4* says: *Where light is not, there is darkness; not because darkness is anything, but the very absence of light is called darkness, just as silence is not a thing, but where there is no sound, it is called silence.* Therefore, that primordial Darkness was not a "privation" properly speaking—since a habit <note>a state of being</note> must necessarily precede a privation—and Light did not precede it. Instead, in terms of reality, that darkness was nothing other than the primeval mass itself, confused and indistinct; and in terms of its form, it was a mere negation of light or brightness. Nor does that phrase in St. Paul, *2 Corinthians 4:6*, <term>the one who commanded light to shine out of darkness</term> <note>original Greek: ho eipōn ek skotous phōs lampsai</note> imply that darkness was like a storehouse for God, in which that <term>first-born</term> <note>Greek: protogonos</note> light was previously hidden and from which God produced Light and Splendor. Rather, the Supreme Architect of the World commanded *light to shine forth out of darkness*—out of darkness, not as if from a material, but as if from a starting point. Hence Danaeus speaks well in *Christian Physics*: *Just as God is said to have created all things out of nothing, not because Nothingness itself was the material of created things, but because when all things were previously nothing, God willed them to Be and to be Something.* For that darkness, which preceded the cradle of the world, was a *negative Nothing*. Rightly, therefore, the Blessed Chemnitz says:

<margin>Commonplaces, Article on Creation, p. 120.</margin>
> God commanded light to shine out of darkness, that is, while there was darkness, at God’s speaking and commanding, Light suddenly existed; Therefore it seems Light was also created immediately out of nothing.

Otherwise, as to what <term>Or</term> <note>Hebrew: "Light"</note> designates in this place, authors vary. Blessed Augustine, Bede, Eucherius, Rupert, and others, as cited by Blessed Dr. Gerhard in *Isagogic Disputation XI*, understand this word to mean the Angels; many of the Rabbis were also of this opinion, who wish it to mean the <term>world of angels</term> <note>Hebrew: olam ha-malakhim</note>, that is, the *world of spirits* or the Angels expressed. But since the Creation of corporeal <note>physical</note> things is described in this place, we cannot agree with those who foster this opinion. Even if it must be maintained with the Doctors that it is probable the Angels were also created on the first day of Creation—as gathered from *Job 38:6* (compare Blessed Gerhard, *Isagogic Disputation 12 on Angels, ch. 4, § 5*; Dr. Calov, *System of Theology Vol. 3, p. 991*; Conrad Aslac, *Christian Physics, p. 132*). Nor are we moved by the authority of certain Greek and Latin Fathers who thought Angels were founded before the beginning of the world, such as Hilary in *Book 12 on the Trinity*; Isidore, *Book 1, ch. 12*; Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith, Book 2, ch. 3*; Bede, *Separate Questions, q. 9*; Theodoret, *Question 3 on Genesis*; Jerome on the *Epistle to Titus*. For Scripture testifies that within the <term>six days</term> <note>Greek: hexaemeron</note> God made *heaven and earth and the sea, AND ALL THAT IS IN THEM, Exodus 20:11*; the heavens and earth were finished, and ALL THE HOST OF THEM, *Genesis 2:1*, in which number the Angels are certainly included. Nor do those deserve credit who suspect that by the <term>first-born</term> light is meant <term>α.</term> <note>Alpha/First</note> either Ele-

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
mentary fire, as Damascene suggests in *Book 2, ch. 7* and partly Danaeus in *Christian Physics, Book 2, ch. 8*. For the function of fire is not to establish the day, which was the task assigned to the primeval light in *Genesis 1:5*; nor is it always true that where there is light, there is fire. For the twinkling stars shine, yet they are not fiery; the scales of fish shine; rotten wood shines in the darkest night; glow-worms shine; the eyes of cats shine in dark places—certainly with no fire present there at all, as experience testifies. <term>β.</term> <note>Beta/Second</note> or the Sun: as Valencia and Ambrose Catharinus suggest. But this does not fit the Mosaic description, which asserts that the luminaries, the Sun and Moon, with the rest of the host of Stars, were produced by God only on the fourth day (compare verses 15, 16, 17). If these luminaries had been produced immediately on the first day, then in the work of the 4th day it would rightly have been said <term>Let there be lights</term> <note>Hebrew: Yehi me'orot</note>, namely, those previously founded in the heaven to bring forth Light, as Mercer notes. <term>γ.</term> <note>Gamma/Third</note> or an accident <note>a philosophical property</note> and specifically a quality, as Thomas Aquinas suggests in *Part 1, q. 67, art. 3*; whether that accident be <term>subsisting</term> <note>Greek: enypostaton</note> inherent in a subject, or <term>non-subsisting</term> <note>Greek: anypostaton</note> or <term>self-subsisting</term> <note>Greek: idiosystaton</note>, that is, existing through itself and absolutely without a supporting subject, as Molina, Tanner, and Giovanni Battista Riccioli (*recent founder of the New Almagest, Book 9, sec. 1, q. 7, p. 210*) believe. The more common and likely opinion is: that the <term>first-born</term> Light was a corporeal substance (or Mass) of light, produced by God immediately out of nothing after the undigested mass of Heaven and earth, to be the material of the stars, from which on the fourth day the Sun, Moon, and remaining stars were produced through a certain condensation and display. It was *different from our light in respect to its accidents:* for just as the primeval earth and primeval water were rough and unformed bodies, more shaped, polished, and adorned in the following days; so also this Light, this work of the first day, was a certain rough and imperfect work, and thus different in its properties from the splendid body of the Sun. Yet it was not different from our Light in terms of its Substance, for the light produced on the first day was then collected into the solar orb on the fourth day, more polished and endowed with a more illustrious power. Therefore, it is not without merit to establish that before the Creation of the Sun, the distinction between days and nights was made, *not by the emission and contraction of rays* (which is the opinion of Basil and Damascene), but by the circular motion of the luminous body or mass of primeval Light. This moved around the raw mass in such a way that by its approach it brought day, and by its departure, night, returning to the same point in a 24-hour space. Thus the *first natural day* was made of darkness lasting 12 hours before the light was founded (which was the first night); but when light was created by God, morning first arose, and through the remaining hours of the <term>day-night</term> <note>Greek: nychthēmerinou</note> span, with light and motion diffused until darkness returned from the completed circuit, the *first day was made*. Hence the sacred Scribe says, *and there was evening and there was morning, one day*, that is, the first, using a cardinal number for an ordinal according to custom (*Gen. 3:1, Haggai 1:1*). Here, however, the observation of Ambrose deserves notice: *that it was called "one day" rather than "first" because this was the general measure of all days, as if to say, the time of one day.* Compare Blessed Hunnius.

This question has given some cause to seek a hidden meaning in it, etc. However, if anyone desires to know what seems to me closest and most similar to the truth, I hold that this light was in motion, such that it made a natural day from rising to setting.”* <note>Luther suggests the light moved like the sun before the sun existed.</note> Regarding the excellence and utility of this Light, since it is our duty <term>to be brief</term> <note>original: λακωνίζειν (lakonizein) - to speak like a Spartan</note>, we refer the Benevolent Reader to the most learnedly elaborated Dissertation on the Primordial Light by Dr. Johann Tackius. > Thus He was able to extend the light, having driven out the darkness,

In the body of the World, all things are contained and arranged in the most beautiful order; for the World, like <term>the storehouse of Nature</term> <note>original: τῆς Φύσεως ταμιεῖον</note>, is nothing other than the framework and arrangement of all bodies created by God first, and preserved for God’s sake. For after the most omnipotent and wisest <term>Almighty Ruler</term> <note>original: Παντοκράτωρ (Pantokrator)</note> created the World on the first day according to its substance—which, due to the confusion of forms it still contained within itself, <margin>Book 1 on Genesis against the Manichaeans, ch. 5.</margin> could be considered a certain "chaos" according to Augustine*—He now proceeds on the second day to distinguish it, or to restore its various parts to their proper places. Indeed, as Dr. Calixtus learnedly discusses in *On Genesis* p. 13, the Earth for the most part cleaved the waters by its own native weight and penetrated to the bottom, and thus had either already occupied or was about to occupy the lowest place. The air and water, mixed and joined together, were as if struggling, occupying the space from the earth all the way to the ethereal region. Therefore, so that the Wisest Architect of the World might perfect His work and remove the confusion, He said:

It is a magnificent thing that God created HEAVEN, a work so divine, so noble and magnificent, that even a crude and imperfect knowledge of it is more desirable than an exquisite and perfect knowledge of other more ignoble things, as Zabarella says in *On the Nature of the Heavens*, ch. 4. However, so that the nature of the WORLD and those things contained in the world may be better understood, HEAVEN comes chiefly into consideration—the first work of the second day, and that supreme part of the World which is distinguished by a double name by the Sacred Scribe <note>Moses</note>. For first it is called <term>Rakia</term>, an <term>expanse</term> from <term>raka</term> <term>he stretched out</term>; though others derive it from <term>rakak</term> <term>it was thin</term>. Secondly, it is distinguished by the name <term>Shamayim</term> <note>Heaven</note> from <term>shamah</term> <term>to be high</term>, a root which has fallen into disuse, though a trace of it exists among the Arabs and its derivatives are in use. It is frivolously derived by the Talmudists from <term>esh</term> <term>there</term> and <term>mayim</term> <term>water</term>. For why it is expressed in the dual number in Hebrew and Chaldean, see Schindler’s Lexicon under the part <term>shem</term>. As Radack says in his Lexicon and the Talmud according to Rabbi Jose Chaninides: it is from <term>esh</term> <term>fire</term> and <term>mayim</term> <term>water</term>, because, according to the interpretation of Rabbi Abba, <term>The Holy One (Blessed be He) took fire and water and mixed them together, and from them the heavens were made</term> <note>original Hebrew: נעשו שמים נטל הקבה אש ומים...</note>. See *Bereshit Rabbah* sec. 4, fol. 6, col. 4; also the tractate *Chagigah* ch. 2, fol. 12. Or from <term>shamah</term> <term>he was amazed</term>: <term>because creatures (men) are amazed by them</term> <note>original Hebrew: משתוממים על ידו...</note> according to Rabbi Levi fol. 10 from *Bereshit Rabbah*. We shall now intentionally wrap other names in the veil of silence, such as when it is called <term>shechakim</term> from <term>shachak</term>, because it is most thin and subtle; or <term>zebul</term> <term>he dwelt</term>, because it is the proper dwelling place of GOD (Isaiah 63:15) and of the stars (Habakkuk 3:11); or <term>ma'on</term> from <term>anah</term> or <term>on</term> <term>time</term>, or <term>kun</term> from <term>kin</term> <term>he prepared, arranged</term>; or <term>arabot</term> from <term>arab</term> <term>he mixed</term>, also <term>to be pleasant, delightful</term>, because God’s seat is there, as is the most perfect pleasantness and sweetness; see Maimonides in *Moreh Nevukhim* part 1, ch. 70 and Rabbi David Kimchi in his Commentary. # From Genesis Chapter I. v. 6. 7. 8.

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
As we noted above, the word *Raqiya* <note>Hebrew: רקיע, usually translated as "firmament" or "expanse"</note> denotes the extending or expanding of something. This is understood either as a thin and rare expansion—from which Opticians observe that the heaven is a subtle and permeable celestial body (proven by refraction, which would otherwise be seen as double if vision occurred through a twin medium of dense and rare)—or as Astronomers prove from the motion of comets observed in the sky and other evidence. To this point aim Isaiah 40:22 and the Psalmist in chapter 104:2, describing how the heaven was expanded in the first creation like a tapestry, a curtain, a web, or a thin plate.

<margin>On Psalm 103, column 1174.</margin>
Hence Augustine * says: *“As easy as it is for you to stretch out a single skin, so easy was it for God to stretch out so great a heaven.”* It is also understood as a firm and solid extension (Isaiah 42:5); hence the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament</note> render *Raqiya* as *stereoma* <note>Greek: στερέωμα, something solid</note>, and the Latin as *firmamentum* [firmament], not by reason of a hard and rigid material, but by reason of its form and purpose, owing to its perfection, distinctness, and firmness or perpetuity. Luther uses the word *Feste* [Firmament]; the Germans *Himmel* [Heaven]; because it appears *homalon* <note>Greek: ὁμαλὸν</note>, equal and evenly arched, according to Martinius in his *Lexicon*. Hence *Job*, speaking of the heaven in chapter 37:18, used this word: *“Hast thou with him spread out the sky, which is strong, and as a molten looking glass?”* This implies nothing other than the solidity of existence, the firmness, and the transparency of the heaven; and as the Latin Interpreter has it, "you have fabricated the heavens," while the Seventy said *stereoseis* <note>Greek: στερεώσεις, "you shall make firm"</note>.

<margin>On Psalm 22, page 536.</margin>
Hence Hilary * says: *“The heaven, which lies beneath our use through its own matter, which was solidified like smoke, received both the nature and the name of a firmament.”* Therefore, both qualities are rightly attributed to the heaven. Glass and crystal are solidified from fluid matter but are easily broken; yet God, by His almighty word, was able to make a most firm and solid body out of fluid matter. Wherefore the words of Basil in his *3rd Homily on the Hexaemeron* <note>A treatise on the six days of creation</note> are most worthy of note: *“It is familiar to Scripture to call a robust and unyielding thing a firmament.”* Compare Gerhard, *Commentary on Genesis, p. 21.*

Regarding the "expanse," however, there are various opinions. To review the more prominent ones: some take it to mean the air alone; some the ethereal heaven; some the air and heaven together as one continuous body. Among these, the middle view pleases many of the Fathers and our own theologians. The first view enjoys the patronage of the Calvinists and all those who interpret the "waters above the heavens" as clouds. The last view, like the first, is not without support in the text of Moses, since in the Hebrew Codex no word is found that applies equally to the air as *Raqiya* and *Shamayim* <note>Hebrew: שמים, heavens</note>, in which the air is found to be more included and encompassed. Hence *“birds fly above the expanse of the heavens”* (Gen 1:20), also the *“stork in the heaven”* (Jer 8:7), and *“bread from heaven”* (Exod 16:4). *“Rain and thunder are said to be from heaven,”* etc. (Jer 10:13). In such a divergence of opinions and reasons, we, with the Blessed Dr. Gerhard (*Commentary on Genesis, p. 19*), determine most simply that by "firmament" is understood the entire system of celestial bodies, all the orbs and spheres from the *primum mobile* <note>The outermost moving sphere in classical astronomy</note> down to the sphere of the Moon, because in that firmament, on the fourth day, the Lights of heaven—the Sun, Moon, and Stars—are said to have been placed.

Reason suggests, and Scripture and the very nature of heaven command, that substance or matter belongs to the heaven. Hence we cannot help but wonder at, on one hand, Durandus, Gabriel, Bassolis, and other philosophers of no low rank (whose individual

<column-break/>

names and citations can be seen in Conimbricenses, book 1, *On the Heavens*, question 4, article 1), who teach that the Heaven is devoid of essential composition; and on the other hand, Zabarella, who in his book *On the Nature of the Heavens*, chapter 2, following Averroes, Theophrastus, Alexander, Olympiodorus, and other writers of good reputation, pronounces that the heaven is indeed a simple body, but does not consist of matter and form. Compare Compton, *Disputation 3 on the Heavens, section 3, number 3, folio 406.* Also Keckermann, who in his *2nd System of Physics, chapter 1, page 89*, asserts that *“the matter of heaven cannot be expressed by a certain and proper name.”* But as Sperling admits in *Physics, book 3, question 1, page 440*: *“As the heaven has a peculiar form, so it also has a peculiar matter, because a proportion must be granted between matter and form.”*

But what kind of matter is it? Is it airy, as Ambrose suggests (*Hexaemeron, book 1, chapter 6*)? Or fiery, because of the splendor shining out from the parts of heaven, as Zanchius suggests (*On the Works of the Six Days, part 2, book 2, chapter 3, section 4, page 369*)? Or watery, as Josephus (*Antiquities, book 1, chapter 2*), Lombard (*book 2, distinction 4, letter A*), and Theodoret (*Question 11 on Genesis*) suggest? To these add the Blessed Hunnius (*Questions on Genesis, page 30*) on the word *Shamayim* from Moses (*Gen 1:6*), where God commanded the firmament to come forth from the midst of the waters, and they appeal to 2 Peter 3:5: *“For this they willingly are ignorant of, that by the word of God the heavens were of old, and the earth standing out of the water and in the water.”* Regarding this passage, Beza says: *“The waters clearly have nothing to do with the heavens, because the feminine participle 'standing' [sunestosa]* <note>Greek: συνεσῶσα</note> *is present, which refers only to the earth [ge].”*

How these divergences of opinion can be reconciled is reviewed by the Blessed Meisner in *Sober Philosophy, part 1, section 3, chapter 4, question 2, page 434.* Therefore, although the heaven consists of a peculiar matter, it is of such a kind that it is not held by a desire for other forms; for this matter has a certain prerogative, being free from the admixture of foreign things. This celestial body was so formed by God that it shall not be transmuted or altered before the last day. However, Scripture clearly testifies that in the final times it will totally perish, whether in its essence or by a change <note>Greek: κατ’ οὐσίαν, ἢ κατ’ ἀλλοίωσιν</note> through the addition of new light and form. To this end tend the words of David, who, to commend the eternity of God, supposes the destruction of the heavens, comparing the heavens to a garment eaten by moths and a cushion torn by old age, which go to refuse or are turned to ashes. *“In the beginning,”* he says, *“thou hast laid the foundation of the earth: and the heavens are the work of thy hands.”* (Psalm 102:25-26). *“They shall perish”* <note>Hebrew: המה יאבדו</note> *“but thou shalt endure: and all of them”* <note>Hebrew: וכלם כבגד יבלו</note> *“shall wax old like a garment; as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed”* <note>Hebrew: וחלפו</note>. The Greek says: *“All shall wax old as a garment, and as a cloak shalt thou fold them up, and they shall be changed.”* He says the heavens are rolled up and folded like a toga, which, being cast around other clothes, involves the whole body. Although the whole heaven is not corruptible due to the nobility of its form, it is nevertheless certain that the generation and corruption of stars—which acknowledges natural causes—must be conceded. This is sufficiently and abundantly testified by the more excellent Mathematicians equipped with certain instruments, by which they have detected such new stars. Thus we read from the writings of Marcus Varro and St. Augustine (*City of God, book 21, chapter 8*) that at one time the star of Venus changed its size, shape, course, and color; though it is quite probable that this should rather be understood as another new star...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
...clearly, they were removed no differently than many in our own time who for a long while mistook the star of 1604 <note>A reference to Kepler's Supernova</note> for Hesperus <note>The Evening Star/Venus</note>; but we leave these matters to the Mathematicians. Regarding the figure or form and the motion of the heavens, those things which Isaiah brought forth in narrating the glory of God might suffice, saying: *He who established the heaven like a vault, i.e., round and circular,* unless more necessary points of knowledge occurred here in the subject matter. The Gentiles and some of the Church Fathers made the Heaven a living being <note>original: "animatum"</note>, but to have recited this erroneous opinion is to have refuted it. It must therefore be established that the Heaven is indeed not destitute of an intrinsic substantial form; however, what that form properly is, we are unable to determine in this weakness of life. This much only we know: that form is most perfect and most noble, since we perceive many noble operations of the heaven which anyone will easily concede proceed not from matter but from form. As for what pertains to the figure of the heaven, it is round and circular; for since the heaven is the simplest and most perfect body, it deservedly enjoys the simplest and most perfect figure, which is the circular one. Hence Philip the Presbyter <note>A 5th-century commentator on Job</note> says:
<margin>on Job 38, p. 168.</margin>
> *The roundness of the circle is a figure more beautiful than all other figures; for a circle is consistent with itself in every part and entirely equal, which through itself becomes solid and whole, and leads the sharp sight of the eyes through its infinite circuit, by which it runs over itself without any end and is inexplicably guided. For this lacks a beginning and an end, and because of that, it cherishes a great similarity with God; moreover, it is most simple, since it exists similar to itself through all things.*

To this is added that almost all parts of the entire Universe approach this circular figure. Thus, in the class of simple bodies, the Stars are spherical and round, as is especially to be seen in the Sun and Moon, even if sometimes they appear flat due to the excessive distance and the weakness of our sight. To now briefly touch upon mixed bodies in general, whose roundness seems to prevail everywhere: let us contemplate man and the rest of the brute animals, both terrestrial, aquatic, and volatile; everywhere roundness offers itself, though not always so exact. Do not their whole bodies, do not almost all parts—heads, eyes, ears, necks, arms, fingers, feet, hearts, and intestines, and other parts—seem to reflect a certain roundness? So further, all trees and their fruits, such as apples, pears, cherries, nuts, etc.; likewise all other plants and herbs, and all legumes similarly seem to participate somewhat in this circular figure. Indeed, we add this: that the observable appearances in the heaven, such as the motions and progressions of the heavens, stars, etc., and the organs or instruments suitable for capturing motions from the sky—such as Astrolabes, Armillary Spheres, Globes, Octants, Sextants, Quadrants, etc.—either being actually round or merely emulating roundness, require the same; and any other figures, whether simple or mixed, would be plainly absurd in the Heaven. That motion also belongs to the Heaven, and that it was instilled into it by GOD, the Best and Greatest, in the first creation, who will deny? For from where else comes the distinction of times, years, and days, if not from the motion of the heaven? Nor does it stand in the way what is said in *Psalm* 136:5: *Who made the heavens*
<margin>with understanding <note>original Hebrew: "B'tevunah"; Greek: "en synesei"</note></margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
...speaks of the ingenious creation and disposition of the heavens, and extols it; namely, that God so founded the celestial bodies, and instilled such a fixed order, such constancy and proportion in their motions, as if He had made them *endowed with intellect.* Nor is anything else hinted at in *Proverbs* 3:19: *God established the heavens by prudence or intelligence.* For just as nothing is gathered from this saying in favor of "assisting intelligences" <note>The medieval idea that angels or spirits physically pushed the spheres</note>, so the natural motion of the heaven cannot be denied from it. For the wisest of Kings <note>Solomon</note>, asserting the consistency and perpetuity of the heavens with these words, does not, as one most skilled in physical things, deny motion to the heaven. For celestial bodies were founded for this purpose, according to the testimony of Moses; thus the Sun, progressing through the Northern signs, brings about summer, and through the Southern signs, winter. Thus the Ascent of the Sun with certain Planets and fixed stars above our Horizon brings us day; while the descent below the Horizon brings us night. The same was also acknowledged by *Aristotle*, who, considering the heaven concretely as it also encompasses the stars, attributed to it a circular motion, which according to Aristotle (*On the Heavens*, book 2, text 14) exists in no other simple body <term>by nature <note>Greek: "physei"</note></term>. This motion is prior to all other motions <term>in nature, in reason, and in time <note>Greek: "tē physei, tō logō kai tō chronō"</note></term> (*Physics*, book 8, text 56); it is perfect (*On the Heavens*, book 1, text 12); continuous (*Physics*, book 8, text 46 ff.); most natural (*On the Heavens*, book 1); most regular (*Physics*, book 8); most uniform (*On the Heavens*, book 2); the measure of all others (*Physics*, book 4); and admitting no reflection (*Physics*, book 8).

### The second work of the second day is the waters above the heavens.

---

> And God made the expanse, and divided the waters which were under the expanse from the waters which were above the expanse. <note>Genesis 1:7 in Hebrew</note>
>
> And God made the firmament, and God divided between the water that was under the firmament and between the water that was above the firmament. <note>Genesis 1:7 in Greek Septuagint</note>
>
> *And God made the firmament, and divided the waters which are under the firmament from those which were above the firmament.* <note>Genesis 1:7 in Latin Vulgate</note>

It is indeed argued by some that there are no waters above the heavens; those who defend that "air" is meant move every stone to destroy the waters <term>above <note>Greek: "hyperanō"</note></term>; compare Conrad Aslac in *Mosaic Physics*, p. 200. But it is more probable that such waters exist, and indeed that they were elevated to the extremes of heaven on the second day is very easy to prove from the sacred book. As to what the condition of those Waters is, there are diverse opinions; some understanding them as *Clouds*, some as a *crystalline heaven*, others maintaining they are *waters of the same substance and species as the lower waters.* The Orthodox, even if they confess with Augustine:
<margin>Book 2 on Genesis according to the letter, ch. 5.</margin>
that they are ignorant of how and what kind of waters are there, they prove their existence from the historical letter of creation in *Genesis 1:7*, where the words of the text clearly confirm waters above the firmament; since the Hebrew <note>original: "Me-al l'raquia"</note> cannot be explained here otherwise than ABOVE the *firmament*. Nor is it an obstacle to this opinion if someone should object that it does not say "upon" <note>Hebrew: "al"</note>, but "from above" <note>Hebrew: "me-al"</note> the expanse, implying they descend to us from a higher place of the expanse. For it is well known that "me-al" is the same as ABOVE and UPON in *Genesis 22:9*; therefore it is rendered in Greek as "epano" <note>above</note>, and it is clearly opposed to "me-al" (above) and "mitachat" (below). If therefore by the firmament nothing else than the heaven...

# From Genesis Chapter I. v. 6. 7. 8.

If this is understood, what prevents us, I ask, from establishing that there are "supra-celestial" waters? Hence, in the Davidic natural theology <margin>Sacred Physics.</margin> *Psalm 104:3*, God is said to dwell in inaccessible light <note>original: "lumen...inaccessibile"</note>, but externally and visibly to have clothed Himself in the most pleasant light of the Sun; to have stretched out the heaven like a tent supported by no bases, and to have covered the heaven itself above with waters, as if with a floor, and to be carried by the clouds as if by a chariot. Concerning those divine waters: *He who lays the beams of his upper chambers in the waters.* <note>Hebrew: הַמְּקָרֶה בַמַּיִם עֲלִיּוֹתָיו</note> The Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> says: *He who covers his upper chambers with waters.* <note>Greek: ὁ στέγαζων ἐν ὕδασι τὰ ὑπερῷα αὐτοῦ</note> What are these *upper chambers* or higher places? They attribute to Him, as it were, certain dining rooms or private chambers. Heaven is compared to a Palace, which God does not build from stones, or upon the stone masses of men, but places His beams in the waters. Gregory Nazianzen, alluding to this, says: <margin>Orations on Pentecost, p. 266.</margin> *...and certain upper chambers are covered by divine waters.* *Compare Psalm 148:4.* Hence Augustine in *Psalm 103, column 1176: Let the superior waters be removed from human passions, yet entrusted to faith.* And Hilary in *Psalm 135, p. 588: God made the heavens in understanding, not irrational, nor formless, nor confused and disordered; but when He, who is infinite, established the region of His own knowledge, having placed the superior and first heaven in a circle, He included a certain limit for the Virtues <note>A rank of angels</note> which were first produced to know Him; for the produced virtues of creation could not have borne the power of the invisible God, unless they inhabited this seat of a moderate dwelling, tempered by the nature of a milder object. For by the elevated waters He tempered that very nature of the first heaven, which, ignited by the power of the God above, was by no means to be endured by inferior natures. But the lower heaven He stretched out, not uniform but manifold, calling the whole the Firmament, and He solidified it with the firmness of our air, making it strong for the support of the tempering of the superior waters.*

Even if their use is hidden from us, the thing itself is by no means to be denied because of our ignorance, but rather it must be confessed with St. Augustine: *The authority of this Scripture is greater than the capacity of our mind.* Nor is any other use certain to us, than that they serve for the adornment of the universe and the praise of God the Creator of all, rightly weighing that man—according to Aristotle *On the Parts of Animals, Book 3, ch. 6*—was created upright for the contemplation of heaven, so that he might consider the forces and power of the heaven. Hence, concerning the contemplation of heaven, the Author under the name of <margin>Sermons to the Brothers in the Desert.</margin> Augustine says: *Man was made on earth, not for the earth, but for heaven; and made from earth, not because of the earth, but because of heaven.* He brings forward the example of a certain man, of whom a Tyrant had asked, "Why did God make you?" To whom he replied: "That I may contemplate the heaven and the lights of the heavens." This agrees with what they write of Anaxagoras, who replied to one asking why he spent the night under the open sky: *To behold the world* <note>Greek: τὸ κόσμον θεάσασθαι</note>; then to another, why he was born: *To contemplate the heaven and the order concerning the world* <note>Greek: τὸ θεωρῆσαι τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν περὶ τὸν κόσμον τάξιν</note>, Aristotle *Eudemian Ethics, Book 1, ch. 5.* And this indeed not without merit: for the heaven is a distinguished mirror of Divine wisdom, and there is nothing in the order of inanimate things that shows God more than the heaven. Hence to the wiser of the Heathens, the heaven is like the temple of God or a building sacred to God, just as Lucretius, *Book V, 1435*, who elegantly calls the heaven,

<column-break/>

—— *the great and versatile temple of the World.*
*and Book II, 1037: and Book I, 1096, he praises:* <margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
—— *the bright temples of heaven.*
—— *and the thundering temples of heaven.*

From this arose the reverence of the Romans toward the Gods, who, according to the prescription of their ancestors, deemed it a sin for the assemblies of the people to be held when the heaven was thundering and Jove was flashing, as witnessed by Cicero *Philippics V and On Divination, Book 2.* For the stable order of the heavens and the admirable distinction in the stars led the Heathens of better character into admiration, so that they recognized the divine goodness therefrom; hence their praises are derived, as Euripides testifies: Heaven is *the beautiful embroidery of a wise craftsman.* <note>Greek: καλὸν ποίκιλμα τέκτονος σοφοῦ</note> Everywhere Homer discusses the order of the heavens in his poetry, naming the two most conspicuous stars. He places the Bear at the summit, because he says it does not sink into the Ocean; and since he had assigned to it the Northern part, he places Orion in the opposite region, wishing no doubt that both the axis of heaven and these stars be most well-known to all. Hence Orpheus:

-> You indeed among the stars <-
-> Contain the order by unchangeable commands. <-
<note>Greek: Σὺ μὲν ἐν ἄστροις / Τάξις ἀναλλάκτοισιν ἐφημοσύνῃσι περιέχεις.</note>

Thence the skill of the Chaldeans in celestial matters is most famous among all: for the *Chaldeans* were carried with great impetus to the contemplation of sublime and celestial bodies, and they perfected this noble doctrine in the succession of time with many labors of observation, yet in such a way that they occasionally devoted themselves to vain speculations. Their remarkable discoveries prove the sharpness of their genius and the keenness of their judgment; and while they surveyed and illustrated every innermost part of the celestial theater situated at such a distance from the earth, it must be judged that this did not happen without divine illumination. For it is not likely that without some ray of the divine Deity, the sharpness of the human mind could have penetrated so far into deep darkness as to bring forth for us such evident science of celestial motions hidden in the most secret recesses of nature, even if they did not follow the primary cause from which they had this knowledge with due worship, attributing this honor and reverence to their Belus <note>The Babylonian god Bel/Marduk</note>, of whom Achilles Tatius says, *Introduction to Aratus, p. 121: The story goes that the Egyptians were the first to measure the heaven and the lands, and recorded their experience for posterity on pillars. But the Chaldeans claim the discovery for themselves, attributing it to Belus.* <note>Greek: Αἰγυπτίους λόγος ἔχει πρώτους... Χαλδαῖοι δὲ εἰς ἑαυτοὺς μετάγουσι βήλῳ τὴν εὕρεσιν ἀναθέντες.</note>

And thus far concerning the expansion and the supra-celestial waters; it remains now that we attentively hear that Divine describer of created things, Moses, discussing the workmanship of the other days, who in verses 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 describes the works of God the *Wonder-worker* <note>Greek: Θαυματέργου</note> performed on the third day of Creation.

From the depths of the waters, we are brought down from heavenly meditations to those of <term>earthly things</term> <note>original: ἐπιγείων (epigeiōn)</note>: Since in the creation of the world the Waters covered all the earth, and darkness was upon the face of the deep, then God, **Who by His word created all things, both heaven and sea**, <note>original: Ὅς λόγῳ ἔκτισε πάντα καὶ οὐρανὸν ἠδὲ θάλασσαν</note> according to the faith of the book of Genesis, commanded on the third day that all the waters be gathered into one place. For although the earth was relieved of the great mass of the waters of the Deep, which were carried up above this Expansion of the heaven on the second day, a huge portion of water still covered the earth everywhere under the heaven; Hence the Best and Greatest God, **the parent of all and the distributor of nature**, <note>original: D.T.O. πάντων γενέτης νομεύς τε φύσεως</note> in separating the water from the earth—the receptacle for all living creatures—said: *let the waters flow together, i.e.* let them be gathered, let them be thickened, and let the waters be collected into one heap, as it were, which until now remained motionless, as 
<margin>Ambrose, Hexaëmeron, book 3, chapter 2.</margin>
Ambrose feels, brooding over the orb of the lands; indeed, according to *Augustine in book 1 of "On Genesis against the Manichaeans,"* they were like vapor and thin mists, but now by this word of command <term>they were congealed</term> <note>original: קָפְאוּ (qaph'u)</note>, they became heavy, thick, and stable. Wherefore Blessed Augustine says in *book 1 of "On Genesis according to the Letter," chapter 2*: *Since the unformed matter covered the whole earth entirely, where would it withdraw to, so as to lay bare some parts? Or perhaps the water, thinner like a mist, held the lands, and was thickened by the gathering, so that it might uncover those parts from many places in which the dry land could appear.* Moreover, the Secretary of the Holy Spirit <note>A poetic reference to Moses as the divinely inspired author.</note> proceeds to describe the place into which the waters covering the whole earth were to be gathered, saying, *let them be gathered into one place:* for <term>place</term> <note>original: מָקוֹם (maqom)</note> the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> seems to have read <term>gathering</term> <note>original: מִקְוֶה (miqveh)</note>, while they read it thus: let them be gathered *into one congregation* <note>original: εἰς συναγωγὴν μίαν</note>. This is not to be understood collectively, but distributively, i.e., each into its own place, so that, even if there are many collections—so many seas, so many rivers, springs, streams, and lakes—all water nevertheless stands in a certain and predefined place for itself; hence our "Great Hero" Luther translates: <insert>The water should gather itself into special places.</insert> The place

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
of the gathered waters is therefore called <term>Sea</term> <note>original: יַם (Yam)</note> from <term>Waters</term> <note>original: מַיִם (Mayim)</note>, with the letters merely transposed, because they themselves, being transposed by God, form the sea, for which God set a law, that it should not pass its boundaries, *Proverbs* 8:29. This is a distinguished <term>proof</term> <note>original: τεκμήριον (tekmerion)</note> of divine mercy and wisdom; whence the Poet says,

Hence the Sacred Writers admire not so much the creation of the waters as their restraint in channels and the Ocean. Agur in *Proverbs* 30:4 is carried into admiration in his confession when he weighs these things with himself, saying: **Who has gathered the waters in a garment?** <note>original: מִי צָרַר־מַיִם בַּשִׂמְלָה</note> with which compare *Psalm* 104:6, 8. This binding of the waters in one bundle, as it were, encompasses the creation of the waters, their arrangement and digestion into lower and upper parts, their sustenance and conservation, and their restraint either by means of the clouds or by the determination of the sea shore, the deep abyss, and the channels; Hence Moses says of the Red Sea in *Exodus* 15:8, **the flowing waters stood up like a heap** <note>original: נִצְּבוּ כְמוֹ־נֵד נֹζְלִים</note>, as if by masses of earth placed in the way. The waters were made into <term>heaps</term> <note>original: עֲרֵמָה (aremah)</note>, heaps, a <term>Mound</term> <note>original: נֵד (ned)</note>, by which the waters are restrained. For Job himself also meditated upon this all-wise disposition: *By the breath of God*, he says, *frost is produced, and again the waters are poured out most widely* (chapter 37:10). *Who gave a course to the most violent rain?* (chapter 38:8). *Who shut up the sea with doors, when it broke forth as if proceeding from the womb* (as the Old Translator renders it); Whence Philip 
<margin>book 3 on Job, chapter 33, page 169.</margin>
the Priest understands *by the womb, from which the sea proceeded*, the underlying earth itself <note>original: κατασκηνῶσ’ (kataskenos)</note>. *I surrounded it*, Job continues in *chapter 38:8, 10, 11, with my boundaries and set a bar*, i.e., the weak and wandering sand. Though it be like a spider's web, and doors, and I said: *Hitherto shalt thou come, and shalt go no further, and here shalt thou break thy swelling waves.* Whence Chrysostom says in *Homily 9 to the people of Antioch*: *The boundary set by God for the sea is the sand, by which it is denoted that it is not mountains, but small sand, so that the power of GOD might be shown. Behold, against the wild sea is opposed not a rock, but weak sand.*
Therefore, although the Water, contracted within its bays, is girded by its valleys and mounds as if by walls, and being fixed does not leap over its limits, yet at the rebuke of Jehovah and His breathing, the Channels through which the most rapid rivers are accustomed to run become visible, and the fierce sea—upon which God has cast a bridle, namely the easily sliding and dissipatable Sand—at God's command suffocates and sinks the earth everywhere, following the example of the Universal Deluge, of which the Psalmist says in *chapter 18:15: The effusions of waters appeared, and the foundations of the earth were laid bare at thy rebuke, O Lord; at the blast of the breath of thy nostrils.* He calls the channels and gulfs, the whirlpools and abysses of the waters **the foundations of the world** <note>original: מוֹסְדוֹת תֵּבֵל</note>, <term>the foundations of the inhabited world</term> <note>original: θεμέλια τῆς οἰκουμένης</note>, as the Septuagint has it, because of their depth. # Sacred Physics
### From Genesis Chapter I, verses 9, 10, 11, 12, 13.

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
...abysses and chasms, which can be penetrated by no means or inventions of human wisdom; for it belongs to God alone to know the depths of the Ocean, its spans, and whatever the sea, the ether, and the earth contain; He alone can rule them at His nod and use them in His service as He pleases. *Jehovah alone is He, as Isaiah witnesses in chapter 40:12, who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and marked off the heavens with a span, and enclosed the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales.* To wrap other plays of the waters in a veil of silence: we experience daily how, by the violence and force of waters, lands are sometimes swallowed up and at other times those very lands are overwhelmed by earth, so that now there is dry land in these places, and in those same places at another time lakes burst forth. We speak of natural change, for what human diligence has done, whether in the region of the Venetians, or in East Friesland, Holstein, and elsewhere, is not our concern now. To speak of Islands, others and still others are accustomed to emerge. *Ptolemy* <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Roman geographer.</note> had diligently searched the *Adriatic* and *Aegean* seas, yet far more islands are seen in both than he himself or *Pliny* <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist.</note> wrote from *Strabo*. *Guillaume Postel* <note>A 16th-century French linguist and cosmographer.</note> gave examples of changed and diminished seas and rivers in the Peloponnese, on the furthest coasts of Gaul and Germany, as well as elsewhere on earth.
<margin>I. on the Concordance of the Globe, p. 38.</margin>
All of Holland and the whole of Zeeland were carried and built up by the Rhine and Meuse rivers, according to *Scaliger, Exercise 49, p. 172.*

Therefore, the water withdraws and contains itself within the receptacle of the earth; it flows between the lands, yet does not cover them; so many streams, so many springs, so many rivers flow through the earth; dew irrigates the earth, the shower floods it, and the right amount of rain promotes the sowing of the earth—which, if it falls beyond measure, places a barrier to fertility. Hence, what *Hilary* <note>St. Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century theologian.</note> says is worthy of note:
<margin>on Psalm 142, p. 625.</margin>
*The earth without water is arid and unfruitful, and always waits to be irrigated by the shower of heavenly rain.* Nor is it without emphasis that the Holy Spirit uses the name $מים$ <note>Hebrew: *Mayim*, meaning "waters."</note> rather than another, since by this very word He seems to indicate an all-encompassing abundance and fertile plenty. This is what *Balaam* refers to when he said he saw that a great increase of seed and posterity was to be given to the Israelite people, while he wove into his prophecy: *Water shall flow from his buckets, and his seed shall be in many waters, Numbers 24:7.* For that provident Author of things instilled this into the streams and springs of waters, so that by its irrigation the earth might grow moist, and the fields, lands, and meadows might be made fruitful—to mention briefly on this occasion, in praise of the Giver of all good things, the virtues and protections which God has placed especially in waters for the recovery and preservation of human health. For we see and have found by experience a most manifest specimen of Divine Goodness in mineral springs, thermal baths, and others, through which we preserve our health when prosperous and drive it away when adverse. No place, no land or region is destitute of such heavenly munificence and the bountiful cornucopias of God the Giver. To this may be conveniently referred the word $חמים$ <note>Hebrew: *Chamim*, often translated as "hot springs."</note> mentioned in *Genesis 36:24*, which was retained by the Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament.</note> and explained by the *Vulgate* as *Thermal Baths*, with which *Blessed Luther* agrees in his *Commentary*; compare also *Blessed Gesner, Commentary on this place, question 4, p. 600* and *Blessed Gerhard, Commentary on this place, question 9.* Some interpret them as "hot waters" according to the proximity of the Punic language, which is bordering on Hebrew. From this, *Cornelius à Lapide* <note>A prominent Jesuit exegete.</note> suspects

<column-break/>

that it should be read as $חמים$, which is composed of $חם$ (*hot*) and $מים$ (*water*), instead of $המים$. But
<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
since this word $חמים$ is found nowhere else in Holy Scripture, we rightly wish to leave the task of eliciting its genuine meaning to the more learned. Nor are the words in *Joshua 11:8* foreign to our purpose. For there are the $משרפות מים$ <note>Hebrew: *Misrephoth-maim*.</note>, which the Septuagint and Vulgate retain as a proper name, but others translate as *hot waters*. Others say *burnings of waters*; Junius says *glass furnaces*; others *salt pans*; those of Tübingen say *glowings of waters*; others explain them as *thermal baths*, which burn with either high or low heat, from which it seems to follow that $שרף$ means *to burn, to consume with fire, to kindle, to cremate*. This word recurs in *chapter 13:6* and *Isaiah 33:12*, where most translate it as *burnings of lime*.

We must now go out with our rafts from the streams, springs, and rivers into the *Sea*, which is infested by winds and stormy with tempests and gales; into the *great and wide sea*, filled with fish without number, *Psalm 104:25*; into the *sea which has fixed its dwelling as if in the middle of the world*, which is unfolded into many bays and many colonies like the marketplace of a great city, serving for trade and the importation and exportation of necessary things. By the benefit of the wind, the most remote nations can meet more quickly by navigation in a short space of time—since journeys across land are too long—and can share necessities with one another through trade. Regarding this, *Theodoret* <note>Theodoret of Cyrus, 5th-century bishop and theologian.</note> in *On Providence, Book 2*, says: <note>original Greek: Πρόκειται ἡ Θάλασσα μέση τῆς οἰκουμένης... </note> *The Sea lies in the midst of the inhabited world, divided into myriad bays, like the marketplace of a very great city, providing an abundance of necessities to all; receiving many merchants and buyers, sending some away from there, and bringing others here.* Into the *Sea*, which is the Parent and host of all rivers and all water; for the origin and derivation of rivers and springs are the same, whose waters are led from the sea through certain channels, whence the sea, surging and waving, flows in and out. This reciprocity of the waves receives special names among the Greeks: it is called *ampotis* <note>original: ἄμπωτις</note> when it flows back, and at other times *pleme* <note>original: πλήμη</note> and *plemmyra* <note>original: πλήμμυρα</note>, as *Stephanus* shows from *Plutarch*. *Hesiod* sings of this opinion in his *Theogony, line 338*:

> Tethys bore to Ocean the eddying rivers,
> The Nile, and the Alpheus, etc.

Where *Tethys*, that is the *Earth*, is established as the mother of rivers and springs, indeed of all water, but *Ocean* as the Father, because from the sea through subterranean veins all springs and rivers are accustomed to arise, which afterwards flow back into the sea. If I attend to Moses as a Natural Philosopher, he separated the lands from the waters by his word, and gathered them all into one place. This gathering of waters Moses says was named by God $ימים$ <note>Hebrew: *Yamim*</note>, that is, *Seas*. If you interpret this, it sounds like the bottom or floor of the waters, so that the *Seas* are the proper place and natural home <note>original Greek: οἰκεῖον domicilium</note> of water. From this source, whatever waters occur anywhere pour themselves out; into this, as if to their origin, they also return, *Ecclesiastes 1:7*. Whence *Junilius*, the African Bishop, says: *Although it is well established that there are many seas, they are nevertheless gathered into one place...*
<margin>Commentary on Genesis I.</margin>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES.

<margin>
Sacred
Physics.
</margin>
The scripture speaks of "waters" because all things are joined to the Great Sea and the Ocean by this continuous wave. But even if some lakes appear to be self-contained, they say that these also discharge their paths into the sea through certain hidden, perforated caverns. How this gathering of waters occurs is indicated by Holy Scripture; it happens not by the power of the sun, nor by any wind, but by the almighty word of God, by which the waters are still held back so they do not overwhelm the earth. *Job* is a witness to this in *chapter 28:8*, and especially the *Psalmist in chapter 104:6, 8: "The abyss is like a garment of his covering; you set a boundary which they shall not pass, nor turn back to cover the earth,"* <note>original Latin: *Abyssus sicut vestimentum amictus ejus...*</note> namely, as they covered it before. And *Jeremiah chapter 5:22: "I have placed the sand as a bound for the sea, an everlasting decree, which it shall not pass: and though they toss themselves, they cannot prevail; though its waves roar, yet they cannot pass over it."* By these words, if weighed accurately, it is clearly hinted that the sea is higher than the earth and is held by the divine hand, lest in turn—as before the separation—they cover and overwhelm the land. Indeed, GOD, the great Arbiter of the Universe, does not measure the stability of things by their own strength, but His power alone is sufficient for Him. Therefore, He joins the strong to the weak, and opposes the manageable and clearly fluid to the robust and dense. What, I ask, restrains the swelling floods of the sea and the horrible whirlpools of water, except the slender sand on the shore, which even gives way under the feet of those walking? Whence Blessed Luther says: *"The Philosophers," he says, "do not know that all that stability is from the force of the word of God. Therefore, although the water is higher, it cannot go out of its bounds and cover the earth; we live and hope just like the children of Israel in the midst of the Red Sea."* This sea, however, in *Exodus 23:31*, is called *Suph* <note>Hebrew: סוּף</note>, which Luther translates as *the Reed-sea* <note>German: *das Schilff-meer*</note>; the Septuagint and the Vulgate call it the *Red Sea* or *Erythraean Sea*. Regarding what the word *Suph* properly denotes, not everyone holds the same opinion; for to some, this word denotes *a rush, seaweed, sedge, or a reed-bed,* because this sea is said to abound in reeds, so much so that Herodotus (Book 2) records that the Egyptian neighbors once made their boats from this reed. To others, *Suph* denotes *red*, an opinion also held by Jerome, as witnessed by Drusius.
<margin>2. Obs. 13.</margin>
As to why it is called "Erythraean" <note>from the Greek *erythros*, meaning red</note>, others usually attribute it either to the sand and the bottom, which they say is red; or to the neighboring mountains, which are reddish, from whose reflection these waters take on a red appearance; or to the seaweed growing there. Fuller (Book 4, *Miscellanies*, chapter 20) is entirely devoted to proving that King Erythras—who was none other than Edom or Esau himself—gave his name to this sea.

Furthermore, it is not infrequent in Holy Scripture for the words for waters, rivers, fountains, and the sea to imply abundance, wisdom, grace, or even calamity and misery. Indeed, as Innocent witnesses:
<margin>
on Psalm 2.
penit. p 241.
</margin>
*"Water is taken in many ways in the divine Scriptures, for there is the water of nature, of doctrine, of wisdom, of grace, of guilt, of punishment, and of misery."* Hence, water in divine discourse is a hieroglyph <note>a symbolic representation</note> of abundance, plenty, and affluence. God amplified the greatness of His wrath and its most abundant plenty in *Hosea 5:10* by the likeness of water: *"I will pour out my wrath upon them like water."* In the same way, water is a hieroglyph of vexation, trouble, and calamities. Hence the most troubled King David, considering the rolling rivers and overflowing seas, and how easily destruction falls

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred
Physics.
</margin>
upon a man if he is enveloped by waves, is accustomed to use somber expressions regarding calamities. *"Save me, O God,"* he says in *Psalm 69:1, "for the waters have come in even unto my soul."* This is a metaphor taken from one whose soul (that is, life) is endangered in the waters, in which he dwells until verse 4, to exaggerate the narrowness, tribulation, and vehemence of his sorrows. For thus he continues: *"I have sunk in deep mire,"* <note>Hebrew: טָבַעְתִּי בִּיוֵן מְצוּלָה</note> *"and there is no standing: I have come into deep waters, and the force of the flood overwhelms me."* The Septuagint learnedly translates: *I was stuck in the mud of the abyss, and there is no foothold. I came into the depths of the sea and a storm-wind drowned me.* <note>original Greek: Ἐνέπαγην εἰς ὕλην βυθοῦ...</note> The Latin translator, whoever he may be, as he usually follows the Greek, does so here as well, but fails to capture the meaning. He translates it as *"I am fixed in deep mire, and there is no substance."* He should have said *"subsistence"* <note>meaning a place to stand</note>, for here the Greek *hypostasis* implies *stability, a place of standing*, a spot where one can stand with a firm foot. So also, by the likeness of swelling waters and the shaken earth, the tumults of empires and the plots of the wicked against the kingdom of God are depicted. With God present as a Helper in tribulations (*Psalm 46:1, 2, 3*), there is nothing for us to fear, *"though the earth be troubled, and though the mountains be cast into the heart of the sea,"* <note>original Greek: ταράττεσθαι τὴν γῆν...</note> though the waters of the sea roar and swell, and though the mountains shake with its tempest. This is a metaphor taken from the dangers of those sailing on the sea, and the divine protection of the same among the waves of great waters, of which the Psalmist says:
<margin>Ps. 107. 23.</margin>
*"Those who go down to the sea in ships,"* <note>Hebrew: עֹשֵׂי מְלָאכָה בְּמַיִם רַבִּים</note> *doing business in great waters (v. 24), these see the works of Jehovah and his wonders in the deep; (v. 25) for he commands and raises the stormy wind, which lifts up its waves. (v. 26) They mount up to the heaven, they go down again to the depths, so that their soul melts because of trouble."* For indeed, in the sea more than in many other places, one may behold the wonderful works of Jehovah and His most present help to those who commit themselves to the merciless waves in fragile rafts, and who trust in the "surges of the sea," as the Greek aptly has it in *Psalm 93:3*. We see the winds rise and storms be stirred up, so that now the ship is lifted up as if to heaven, now depressed to the lowest whirlpools, with souls melting for fear, according to the words of the Poet:

---

<margin>
Virgil.
Aeneid. Bk. 3.
p. m. 143.
</margin>
> Together the East and South winds rush, and the South-west
> thick with storms, and roll vast waves to the shores.
> There follows the cries of men and the creaking of cables. <note>Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book 1, p. 95</note>

Then they cry (v. 28) to Jehovah in their trouble, and He brings them out of their distresses. <note>Hebrew: וּמִמְּצוּקוֹתֵיהֶם יוֹצִיאֵם</note> He makes (v. 29) the storm a calm, and its waves are still. (v. 30) Then they are glad because they are quiet, and He brings them to the haven of their desire. So also the Church of God actually feels and experiences His help: the Church of GOD shall remain, even if the shaken earth and the roaring, boiling sea are confounded together into one Chaos; even if all the empires of the whole world are dashed against each other in horrible tumults, turned and overturned, yet the seat of GOD and the [streams] of the river shall be firm.

<meta>This page continues the theological and natural philosophical examination of the Creation, specifically focusing on the element of Earth as described in Genesis 1:9-13. The author bridges biblical exegesis with classical philosophy.</meta>

# From Genesis Chapter I. v. 9. 10. 11. 12. 13.

<margin>Psalm 46:4 <note>Original cites v. 5 in some versions.</note></margin>
The streams shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the Most High.

<margin>Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book 1, p. 137.</margin>
From the Heavens to the Soil our meditation now turns; for it is a shameful thing for a man to be ignorant of the nature and properties of his Mother, that is, the Earth, from which he was taken, and in which he has been placed as if in a beautiful city. According to Tertullian, the Earth is the "matrix" <note>womb or source</note> of our flesh. For she receives us at birth, nourishes us once born, sustains us in old age, and finally, embracing us in her bosom when we are rejected by the rest of nature, she then most especially receives us as a mother, as Pliny says in Book 2, Chapter 3. It is right, therefore, that we who are from the Earth, live on the Earth, and are finally covered by the Earth, should speak gratefully of the Earth. However, we shall speak only of what the Holy Books provide; hence the beginning of our discourse on the Earth comes from the beginning of the words of the Old Testament, where the Hebrew Lawgiver <note>Moses</note> thus begins the books of Origins: *In the Beginning God created the HEAVEN and the EARTH:* By which we understand the WORLD, the simplest division of which—found in the book of Origins and other places of Holy Scripture—consists of EARTH, WATER, AIR, and HEAVEN. In treating the Earth, let us observe the simplicity and Truth of the Holy Codex, in which it is divinely revealed and recorded that the earth was indeed created in the beginning, but because it was still covered by waters, it was only on the third day of Creation uncovered from the waters and dried by the power of Almighty God (and not by the sun, which did not yet exist), the waters being partly distributed into caverns and partly gathered into the great Ocean, so that it could not only be seen, but also provide an origin for plants and a dwelling for living creatures. This is called *Eretz* <note>Hebrew: ארץ</note> by the Hebrews, with which the German *Erdt* and *Erth* (that which is dug from the earth) seem to have no small agreement. This name is derived either from *ruts* <note>רוץ</note>, *to run*, because all things move around it while it remains immobile; or from *ratsats* <note>רצץ</note>, *to crush*, because it is crushed by the feet of those walking on it like a pavement (whence Varro thinks *terra* is named from *terendo*, "rubbing/wearing down"); or from *ratsah* <note>רצה</note>, *to desire*, because for the use and convenience of animals and things growing on the earth, it always seeks celestial fertility and greedily desires to bring forth its offspring; or even from *eretz* <note>ארץ</note> meaning *not* and *ruts* <note>רוץ</note> *running*, because it least runs or moves. It is also distinguished by another name by the Holy Cosmographer Moses, namely, *Yabashah* <note>יבשה</note>, *the dry land*, from *yabash* <note>יבש</note>, *it dried or parched itself*. This corresponds nearly with the Greek name *Oikoumene* <note>τῆς Οἰκουμένης</note>, which denotes the habitable earth, and which is also usually called *Tebel* <note>תבל</note> in Hebrew.

<margin>Job 38:4, 5, 6.</margin>
It is surely a great eulogy for the Earth that it was established by the very hand of God, for God himself "formed the earth and made it" (*Isaiah 40:28*). Moreover, He established the earth in the very center of the Universe so wonderfully and so skillfully that holy Job marveled that such an immense mass stands without any support. Where Job recounts that God laid the foundations of the earth and gave it measure—that is, a certain length, breadth, depth, and height—He rectified it according to a plumb line. "Who stretched the line upon it?" Hence, various figures are usually assigned to the terrestrial globe by Philosophers: by Empedocles and Anaximenes it was flat; by Plato cubic and four-sided; by Leucippus like a drum; by Heraclitus like a skiff; by Anaximander like a cylinder;

<margin>Compare Cleomedes, *On the Circular Motions of the Celestial Bodies*, book 1, p. 376.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Isidore, Epistle 273, p. 245.</margin>
with whom Isidore agrees. It was called hollow and round by Democritus; oval by Helmont. The earth is said to bear the shape of a sling-stone by Dionysius of Alexandria at the beginning of his *Description of the World*:

> *Yet it is not entirely circular all around, but on both sides*
> *It goes wider toward the paths of the sun,*
> *Resembling a sling.*

Which Rhemnius Faunius interprets thus:
> *Yet it is not closed with a smooth margin everywhere around,*
> *But spreading its arms with a two-part shore,*
> *It is narrowed toward both rapid courses of the sun,*
> *Like unto a sling.*

This implies that the earth is widened on each side, but on the other sides, in the likeness of a stone-throwing sling, it is drawn together into a sharper point, as Eustathius explains in the same place.

<margin>Job 38:6.</margin>
It suffices for us to know that God, the Great and Best Creator of the Universe, reduced the Earth and Sea into one body of spherical shape, which by its own weight rests upon the center of the universe and is firmly established; hence: "Upon what are its bases sunk?" The Septuagint <note>Greek Old Testament</note> reads: "Upon what are its rings fixed?" where Aben Ezra interprets "bases" as mountains. Rabbi Levi, however, interprets them as columns. *Adon* <note>אדן</note> means a base or pedestal. Hence the Vulgate: *Upon what are its bases grounded? Or who laid its cornerstone?*

<margin>Psalm 119:90, 91. <note>Original cites 91, 92.</note></margin>
Hence the Psalmist sings thus of the earth's stability: *Thy truth is from generation to generation: Thou hast founded the earth and it persists: according to Thy decrees they persist unto this day, for all things serve Thee.* The Hebrew words are *Le-dor va-dor emunatecha konanta eretz va-taamod*, which I remember Constantinus L'Empereur once explained to us in a public lecture: *From generation to generation, by Thy constancy, Thou hast disposed the earth so that it stands.* He preferred to interpret *Emunah* <note>אמונה</note> not as "truth" but as "firmness" and "constancy," with the preposition "by" understood, just as the same word recurs regarding the performance of constancy in verse 138. Thus the sense is: *That the work of the earth remains through every generation and for all ages, this is from Thy constancy; as Thou art constant, so also Thou makest constant works.* Furthermore, the phrase *to Thy judgments* means "to execute Thy judgments and decrees," as Kimchi observes on this passage; for creatures are ready at the nod of their Creator.

<margin>Job 26:7.</margin>
Moreover, we recognize a great miracle of God, that He "suspended the earth upon nothing," to speak with Job. It is suspended in the middle of the whole universe; it moves neither around the center nor in the center around its own axis, but as the Psalmist thunders: *Thou hast founded the earth upon its stability; it shall not be moved forever and ever.*

<margin>Psalm 104:5.</margin>
Hence the Ancients disputed whether the earth was sustained by the air; indeed, some said it was compressed by the external air as if held in its station, concerning which see the old *Introduction to Aratus's Phenomena*. Anaximenes said it was carried by the air, according to Plutarch in *Opinions of the Philosophers*, book 3, ch. 15. Others said it was carried by internal air, as Seneca witnesses in *Natural Questions*, book 6, ch. 16. Whence Marcellinus also says: *the earth is suspended by the motion of a certain internal spirit*; compare Macrobius and Valesius.

<margin>Ammianus Marcellinus, book 20, p. 176; Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book 1, ch. 21.</margin>
From Holy Scripture it is known to us that the earth is founded upon its bases and hung upon nothing; whether it is now fixed in itself, or in the air, or in the waters, or in nothing, it becomes us to confess that all things are simultaneously contained, supported, and bound together by the power of Him who created all things, so that what Nazianzen says must be true: To Reason...

<margin>Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 34.</margin>

Cc
