<meta>This page continues the discussion of "Sacred Physics," specifically addressing the stability of the Earth and the creation of plant life on the third day. It maintains the theological defense of a stationary Earth against Copernican theories.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
"Nothing," he says, "is found in creation upon which the earth rests, if you except the divine will." <note>The author is likely quoting a contemporary commentator on Job or the Psalms.</note> Moreover, the earth is situated not to be moved—whether in a circle or by any other means—much less to define the seasons by its own motion (a duty given to the Luminaries), but to stand stable and unmoved, *Psalm 104:5*. Although the earth was drawn out from the waters and is washed on all sides by waves of water rising above the land, it was nevertheless so founded by divine power that at no time, until the final day, can it be moved entirely from its place; compare *Job 26:7, 38:6-7, Ecclesiastes 1:11*. Nor does it oppose our opinion that the earth is moved by violent and extraordinary motion; for it is in the sense of the shaking of the pillars of the earth and the commotion of the mountains and the lowest parts of the earth itself that we must understand *Job 9:5 and following*, who also speaks of the heavens, saying their pillars tremble, *chapter 26:11*. Indeed, God can miraculously move the earth from its natural place, transpose mountains, and thus show Himself the Lord of the nature He established. Hence we experience almost every year that such extraordinary earthquakes happen, such as Ragusa <note>Modern-day Dubrovnik, Croatia; likely referring to the Great Earthquake of 1667.</note> suffered this year; nor are earthquakes infrequent in China, so much so that they swallow entire cities, render regions desert, bury old rivers and reveal new ones, level mountains to the ground, and cause a piteous slaughter of that people, as reported by *Botero in his Account of the Kingdom of China, page 162.* Nor does it alienate us from the truth, whichever opinion appears more probable by physical and mathematical reasons: for since that question is largely aired with arguments of that sort, it is not our place to weigh their gravity and momentum—which we leave to the Philosophers—but rather which opinion agrees more with the Word of God. For however great the appearance of probability with which the motion of the earth is asserted over the motion of the Sun or the Firmament, if it is certain from Holy Scripture that the earth is immobile and the Sun truly moves, no one will be so estranged from piety as to prefer to trust his own subtleties (by which he has persuaded his mind of a greater likelihood) rather than the word of God, or wish to resist the manifest sense of Scripture under this pretext <note>original: πρόφασι (prophasi)</note>: that Holy Scripture speaks only in a popular way and accommodates itself to common opinions, and therefore should not be held as a demonstrative principle <note>term: apodictic (conclusive proof)</note> but only a topical one in such matters concerning Physics or Mathematics, nor provide an infallible argument. How shameful these taunts are against the Word of God is vigorously shown by *Dr. Calovius, System of Theology, Vol. 1, p. 606 and Vol. 3, p. 1037.* Johannes Herbinius also complains of these distortions in a booklet published for the defense of passages of Holy Scripture against the motion of the Earth,

<margin>In the Letter to Maria Cunitia, p. 317.</margin>
where he writes: *“When the defense of a hypothesis must be reconciled with the holy oracles of God, I find that everything there is explained, judged, and rejected according to erroneous appearance and the opinion of the common people. Indeed, I have noticed that the Copernicans respond to all sacred matters falsely, incidentally, and in a leaping manner. To address such an inhuman tearing apart of the Holy Book: I first unroll the commentaries of Mr. Lansbergius on the daily motion of the Earth, in which I saw the distress of Holy Scripture, heard the groan of the dove with pain, and condemned the forced and impious distortion of Holy Scripture to a hypothesis and*

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
*irreverence.”* Thus he spoke.
We conclude with these excellent verses by Stigelius:

> The Earth, like a ball supported by no prop,
> Hangs as a heavy burden in the balanced air.
> When you consider that you stand upon a hanging earth,
> Do you not clearly see from this that there is a God?

When we look upon the Earth, we truly see the Womb of the World, which can be proud of the various gifts granted to it by God. Nothing is empty in the womb; the ancient and poetic part is fertile. In this part gems are born, in that spices; here plants are made, there herbs; whether you look up or down, you will find a diverse variety, with nature administering all things in various ways. From the earthly larder comes the best provision. From the earth—which indeed is not taken as a partner in procreation, as *Cajetan and Daneau* wish, but behaved purely passively in the production of herbs, since not even on this day does it actively concur to procreate herbs, nor is a plastic power <note>term: vis plastica (the formative power believed to shape living things)</note> found in the earth, but in the seed—by the command and mandate of God alone on the third day of Creation, herbs, trees, and fruits are immediately procreated: *"Let the earth bring forth green herb, and yielding seed and wood etc."* and it concludes: *in which is its seed*, that is, in which its seed is made, according to the Hebrew idiom. A double relative is placed here, though one would suffice. Hence the Chaldean <note>The Aramaic Targum.</note> brings forth these words thus: *"Let the earth germinate the germination of the earth, whose son of sowing is sown, and the fruit-tree making fruit according to its kind, whose son of sowing is in itself upon the earth."* Now Moses, the Divine Botanist, enumerates here three kinds of plants, which are *Deshe* <note>original: דשא</note>, from the root *desha* which is to germinate or become green; the Septuagint has *blastanein* <note>original: βλαστάνειν</note>, as if you would say a sprout or a plant, *a growth* <note>original: ein Gewächs</note>; which is born from the earth, *Joel 2:22*. It denotes in this place the tender herb, unsown or voluntary, which having recently arisen is not yet indeed a stalk, yet adorns the earth exceedingly with its greenness. Nor does the Vulgate seem to have understood it otherwise: *"Let the earth bring forth the green herb, namely the herb yielding seed,"* or Blessed Luther, who translates this as *Grass* <note>original: Graß</note>. The name seems to be general, signifying any herb according to Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note>, whence it is also called the fodder of wild asses, *Job 6:5*; of hinds, *Jeremiah 14:5*; of heifers, *a heifer of grass* <note>original: עגלה דשא (eglah desha)</note>, *Jeremiah 50:11*, according to

<margin>In the Commentary of Rabbi Solomon.</margin>
Kimchi, *a heifer of the grass* <note>original: βοίδια ἐν βοτάνῃ</note>, which Blessed Luther rendered as *frisky calves* <note>original: geile Kälber</note> from the effect; for they are accustomed to frolic from the abundance of fodder, whence the Proverb: *"he carries hay on his horn"* <note>A Latin idiom for a dangerous person, here linked to overfed livestock.</note>; *"Satiety brings forth insolence,"* <note>original: τίθει γὰρ κέρας ὕβριν</note> as the sentiment of Solon has it. In the same sense others translate, *"threshing heifers,"* who were allowed to eat as much as they wanted from the grain beneath them, from the root *dush* <note>original: דוש</note>, which is to thresh <note>original: ἀλοᾶν</note>; compare Boetius <note>likely Bochart, the naturalist</note> and others. Strictly and specifically <note>original: εἰδικῶς</note>, however, it is taken for the sprout first budding from the earth, *Proverbs 24:27*, which is properly called *the coming forth of the sprout* <note>original: דשא מוצא (motsa desha)</note>, in Greek otherwise *chloe* or *chloē* <note>original: χλόη</note>.

<margin>Sacred Observations, book 3, ch. 4, n. 4.</margin>
To this is added *Esebh* <note>original: עשב</note>, not as a synonym, as in *Deuteronomy 32:2*, but specifically; as if Moses were saying the earth did not germinate and bring forth just any herb in any way, but perfect and already seeding: or both kinds at once, the herb fit for fodder to which *Deshe* is joined, *Job 6:5, Proverbs 27:25*, and to it is attributed as a fruit *Yereq* <note>original: ירק</note>, *a potherb, a green sprout*, properly sown and edible.

# From Genesis Chapter I. v. 14. 15. 16. 17. 18. 19.

pasture, upon which beasts and birds feed, Genesis 1:30.
<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin> Exodus 10:15. 2 Kings 19:26. Psalm 37:2. Isaiah 37:27. and the herb already producing seed for the propagation of its kind: Hence, as Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf, a celebrated 17th-century Hebraist</note> notes, it signifies a larger herb, sown and arising from cultivation, which rises into stalks and stems, and produces seed for making bread for the use of man: For as the proper food of cattle is <term>חציר</term> (*chatsir*) *hay*, from <term>חצר</term> (*chatsar*) *to be cut short, to reap*, which the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated as *green grass* in Genesis 1:29, *all-nourishing* in Job 5:25, and that which grows in the mountains as *mountain grass* in Proverbs 27:25; so the proper food of men is <term>עשב</term> (*eseb*) <note>herb or vegetation</note>.

The third Mosaic species is <term>עץ</term> (*ets*), *wood*, which is called the second genus of plants, and signifies fruit-bearing trees; yet it is so general that, as noted by Buxtorf in his Lexicon and J. Ursinus in <margin>Phytology, book 1, ch. 2, p. 16.</margin> it is transferred to shrubs, bushes, and dwarf-shrubs. These, however, are usually sub-distinguished among the Greeks so that a Tree is *a plant with a single trunk*; a Shrub is *a woody plant smaller than a tree*; a dwarf-shrub is *a small woody plant* branching out *with many stems and many branches* immediately from the roots. To the Hebrews, however, a Shrub or rather a dwarf-shrub seems to be called by the proper name <term>שיח</term> (*siach*) *stock, sprout*, from the root <term>שוח</term> (*suach*) *to meditate* <note>or to grow/spring up</note>. Genesis 2:5. Job 12:8. ch. 30:4, 7. <insert>a thicket / shrubbery.</insert> Thus Hagar is said to have cast Ishmael <term>תחת אחד השיחים</term> *under one of the trees*, or as the Septuagint has it, *under a fir tree*, <insert>under a tree</insert> / Genesis 21:15. or as Pagninus has it, *under a certain shrub*, and Junius translates it, *under one of the bushes*, by whose shade she might defend his tender head from the heat.

Under these species of plants are also comprised *thorns, thistles* and *poisonous herbs*, because it is expressly said in Genesis 2:2 that *God rested from all His work which He had made*. For they existed according to their *nature*, but not according to a *noxious quality*; they degenerated in use and qualities because of sin. They were therefore indeed present from the beginning, but they were not *for punishment*, because every shrub was from the beginning, Genesis 2:5. Nor is it unknown that many things after the Fall are deemed poisonous, harmful, and useless due to human error and ignorance, which nevertheless, if their nature and qualities were open to us, would be of great profit and convenience to all. Although not all things serve for the nourishment of man, it suffices if they serve for the nourishment of other living creatures; and those which are not valid for food can be conducive to medicine or other uses. Whence even after sin, Basil and Ambrose learnedly dispute that nothing is plainly useless.

In this manner, the *Water and Earth* established by God the Best and Greatest, and distinguished from each other in a certain order, with those things added and created at the same time which seemed to God, the Architect of things, to serve as the beauty and ornaments of the earth, closed the third day, so that there was evening and morning, the third day. This being finished, he proceeds to the works of the 4th day, which are recounted by Moses in verses 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, and 19.

That the stars, and among them especially the Sun and Moon, were established by God on the fourth day is taught so evidently by Moses, the Scribe of the Holy Spirit, that those who assert the contrary must be most perverse. For hitherto Moses was occupied in recounting the dwellings and common principles of things, while he had taken up the description of the Expanse and the heavenly waters within it, also commemorating the earth beautifully adorned and decorated with herbs and plants of every kind; now he proceeds to the most ample adornment of heaven, which God the Best and Greatest produced on the 4th day in the heavenly palace, while the heaven, which for three whole days was <term>starless</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνάςρον</note> and illustrated only by the first-created light, He now produces most elegantly adorned with new light-bearers. Moreover, He produces these ornaments of heaven, not *from the heaven*, for we do not read, *Let the heaven bring forth lights*, as we read: *Let the earth bring forth grass; nor from water*, in which *Episcopius* <note>Simon Episcopius, a Remonstrant theologian</note> is dreaming, perhaps borrowing that opinion from the Stoics, who said the Sun *was something kindled from the sea waters* <margin>Clement of Alexandria, Miscellanies, book 3, p. 770.</margin> *endowed with intellect*, or, to use the words of Clement, *an intellectual flame from the marine waters*. But by SPEAKING: *Let there be Lights, and it was so*. For the most wise Founder of things foreknew how much this creation of Luminaries from the first-created light would benefit the whole Universe. What would the world be, if the sun with the rest of the stars were not? A dark prison: Therefore, to have seen the Sun by day, and the Moon and Stars by night, what else is it than to have been stunned, indeed, to be struck senseless at the works of God in their sublime pre-eminence! The spectacle itself in that glory of loftiness makes the mind grow numb, so that the eyes are more stunned by contemplating than the mind is by considering such sublime depth, or the tongue by narrating, so much so that with the son of Sirach <note>Author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus</note>...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
## Page 56

<margin>Sacred Physics <note>original: *Physica Sacra*</note> ch. 43. 1.</margin>
...we are compelled to confess with the son of Sirach <note>The author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus</note>: *The beauty of the height is the firmament, the appearance of heaven in a glorious vision.* Moses seems to hint not obscurely at the origin of these lights when he says, *Let there be lights* <note>original Hebrew: יהי מאורות (*yehi me'orot*)</note>; namely, let that primordial light, which for three days had distinguished night from day, now become *lights* <note>original: *me'orot* or *le-me'orot*</note>, or let the lights be made from it. This is shown clearly enough by the relationship of the words *light* <note>original: *or*</note> and *luminary* <note>original: *ma'or*</note>; and hence it is that Basil calls the luminaries the *first-born vehicles of light* <note>original Greek: ὀχήματα πρῶτογονα τοῦ φωτὸς</note>. For Holy Scripture shows us no other material from which the Sun, Moon, and other stars were produced than that primordial light. They were not produced from the material of the Expansion <note>The firmament or atmosphere</note>; for since the stars are denser than the ether or Expansion, and the Expansion received its boundaries and limits on the second day—namely, the Waters above and below—it cannot be admitted that the Sun or stars were produced from the Expansion, unless we wish to admit a vacuum within it (by condensing certain parts into such huge bodies) or a massive change in a body already established in its natural order on the second day. Nor can it be said that some new matter was produced for the stars within the Expansion: for if this were admitted, it would follow that parts of the Expansion must have been annihilated to make room for that stellar matter, or the whole Expansion must have been condensed against the nature it originally received at creation. Therefore, the matter of the Sun can be nothing other than the primordial light, which is also evident from the identity of their function: because the division of light and darkness, and the alternation of night and day, is ascribed to the Sun and Moon in Genesis 1:14–19, which the primordial light previously distinguished. Regarding the nature of the Sun, Moon, and Stars, there were various opinions among the pagan philosophers, all of which it is not our purpose to review—to say nothing of the hypothesis of others who assert that the nature of the Moon and the other planets is entirely distinct from that of the Sun, being in themselves completely opaque bodies that borrow all their light from the Sun. But the opinion of Holy Scripture regarding the light of the Moon and other planets is placed in what is called the "disk" of the Sun. Moses calls the Moon a *great light*, a title that would in no way fit the Moon if it enjoyed no light of its own and were an opaque body—indeed, the most opaque of all. All stars, both wandering <note>planets</note> and fixed, are named and celebrated for their Light. God said: *Let there be lights in the heaven, to shine in the heaven*: now in the Hebrew Codex, "star" is called by the common name "luminary," and finally in verse 17 it is said of all the heavenly bodies, *and God set them in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth.* From which it appears clearer than the Sun that all stars are hitherto of the same nature, even if they differ by reason of quality, so that there is one glory of the Sun, another of the Moon, and another of the stars, as Paul witnesses in 1 Corinthians 15:41.

As for the stars, their multitude is so great that *to us* <note>original Greek: καθ' ἡμᾶς</note> they are innumerable, as Holy Scripture witnesses in Gen. 15:5, 22:17, 26:4, and Jer. 33:22; they can be numbered by God alone, Psalm 147:4. Ovid seems to aim at this when he says:
> You count the stars, whose names alone you know,
> Their signs, their powers, courses, places, times.

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
And to mention just one path, which they call the Milky Way, in which many stars are seen that have been observed by the benefit of the optical tube <note>The telescope</note>—but who is skilled enough to express the exact and adequate number of them all? Certainly no mortal. The observations of astronomers in counting the notable stars indeed deserve praise, but who will say that all have been noted, and that no more are found in heaven than have been noted so far, except one who would basely and maliciously presume to deny the truth of Holy Scripture?
<margin>Jeremiah 31:37.</margin>
For as the heaven is immeasurable, Jeremiah 31:37 (saving, however, Uranometry <note>The measurement of the heavens</note>, which is sufficient for observations, measuring only the visible sky and stars), so also the stars are *to us* <note>original Greek: καθ' ἡμᾶς</note> innumerable. To Abraham the promise of offspring was made according to the multitude of the stars; when, anxious about his posterity, he said that a certain Eliezer, his house-born slave, would be his heir, he immediately heard the promise of a multitude: *Look now toward heaven, and count the stars, if thou be able to number them: so shall thy seed be.*
<margin>Genesis 15:5. Book on the City of God p. 903.</margin>
On this promise, Saint Augustine* comments thus: *Immediately an heir was promised, not that house-born slave, but one who was to come from Abraham himself; and again an innumerable seed, not like the sand of the earth, but like the stars of heaven, where it seems to me a posterity sublime in heavenly happiness was promised; for as far as multitude is concerned, what are the stars of heaven to the sand of the earth, unless one says this comparison is similar only insofar as the stars cannot be counted.* Because it is not to be believed that all of them can be seen; for the more sharply anyone gazes, the more he sees. Whence it is rightly thought that some are hidden even to those with the keenest sight. Whoever boasts of having comprehended and recorded the entire number of stars, such as Aratus or Eudoxus, or any others, the authority of this book <note>The Bible</note> despises them. Indeed, the Planets were defined by the ancients as seven in number, whence the Hebrews were accustomed to note them by these initial letters: כבש נלצח <note>K-B-Sh N-L-Ts-Ch</note>. Where the first, כ <note>K</note>, is *Kokhav* (Mercury), indicated by the general name for a star by synecdoche; ב <note>B</note> is *Levanah* (the Moon), named for its whiteness; ש <note>Sh</note> is *Shabbatai* (Saturn), which they call the Sabbatical one, as if he were the Presider over the Sabbath; צ <note>Ts</note> is *Tzedek* (Jupiter), from justice; ל <note>L</note> is *Ma'adim* (Mars), from redness, because it is blood-colored; ח <note>Ch</note> is *Chamah* (the Sun), from heat; נ <note>N</note> is *Nogah* (Venus), from light, because it is the light-bringer; but the skill of modern astronomers demonstrates that there are even more wandering stars. Holy Scripture also mentions the Pleiades and Orion. The Greeks gave the former their name from their very multitude, because many are together: for *Pleiades* <note>original Greek: Πλειάδες</note> means a multitude, and it is derived from that. Concerning these, the Lord said to Job out of the whirlwind in ch. 38:31: *Canst thou bind the sweet influences of the Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion? Wilt thou restrain the Pleiades, lest they bloom and bring forth their delights? Wilt thou loose the course of Orion, bringing with him rains, storms, and cold?* Where, for the Pleiades, as Brentius notes on Job f. 291. b., the Hebrew has *Kimah* <note>original Hebrew: כימה</note>. Some write that it is a congregation of seven stars at the end of the sign of Aries, whence in this place they are called the "bindings of the Pleiades"; for those seven stars, which they call "the hens," are so arranged that they are not separated from each other, just as a hen is not from her chicks. # From Genesis Chapter I. v. 14. 15. 16. 17. 18. 19.

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
The Hebrew has <term>Kimah</term> <note>original: כימה; usually identified as the Pleiades</note>, which they write is a constellation of fixed stars; hence perhaps, because it is a fixed constellation, it is said in this place, **that no one can loosen its bonds so that it becomes a wanderer.** <note>A reference to Job 38:31 regarding the "bands of Orion" or "chains of the Pleiades."</note>

Hastening toward the end of the Lights, it must first be observed that God wills the most beautiful lights, the Sun and Moon, to be gazed upon, and their circuits and laws to be considered. For thus He says: *They shall be to you for signs, months, days, and years*. These were the first and sacred cradles of Calculation; here was the origin of Time-keeping, so that it is no wonder that nations, out of a certain innate care and solicitude, labored chiefly on this: to divide time according to the pattern of celestial motions. Hence the custom prevailed that almost all nations calculated the passing year within the observation of these two stars. From this, Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a famous 16th-century scholar of chronology</note> clearly teaches that the Jews, before and around the flood, used what they call solar years of **XII.** months <term>of thirty days</term> <note>original Greek: τριακονθημέρων</note>, that is, **30** days, with **5** <term>intercalary</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπαγομένοις; extra days added to align the calendar</note> days added at the end <margin>On the Emendation of Time, book 3, p. 151; book 1, title 2, ch. 3, p. 10.</margin>—with whom Dr. Behm agrees in his *Chronology*—and whom the <margin>cited place, p. 20.</margin> *Chaldeans and Egyptians* followed, as Herodotus testifies in *Euterpe*. For whatever good arts the Egyptians possessed, they drew all of them from Joseph, the son of Jacob, and he from his grandfather Abraham the Chaldean. After the departure of the Jews from Egypt, *Luni-solar* years began to be in use. For the aforementioned Dr. Behm establishes by four reasons that they took the beginning of the year from the new moon which most closely precedes the vernal equinox. Among the Greeks, however, the system of the year was not always one and the same; eventually, the *Olympiad*, otherwise called the *Tetracteris* <note>a four-year period</note>, prevailed among them, named after Olympia, a town of Elis near the Isthmus, in honor of Olympian Jupiter, with Hercules being the first inventor and institutor of those games. For the assemblies of all Greece were celebrated there, as well as contests and spectacles of all kinds with prizes proposed, and at the same time, they deliberated on the form and rule of the year. Whence he who prevailed in the struggles of wrestling, boxing, jumping, running, and the discus, and was made a <term>pentathlete</term> <note>original Greek: πένταθλος; a winner of five events</note>, that is, a *Master of Five Exercises*, earned this dignity: that the Olympiad would be called by his name, written in golden letters on parchment for eternal memory. Furthermore, it is clear from this that in this Greek calculation, the *Luni-solar* years were observed annually, especially by noting the moments of the Equinoxes. For when the Greeks consulted how to rightly perform their sacred rites, the oracle replied that they must sacrifice <term>according to ancestral customs</term> <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὰ πατρια</note>; when they further inquired about the manner of sacrificing according to ancestral rites and customs, the answer was given again: <term>according to three</term> <note>original Greek: κατὰ τρία</note>. Because they found this latter part equally obscure, the skilled Priests, whom they call <term>Kings</term> <note>original Greek: Βασίλας</note>, interpreted this to mean sacrificing <term>by years, by months, and by days</term> <note>original Greek: κατ’ ἐνιαυτὸς, κατὰ μῆνας & καθ’ ἡμέρας</note>. By this oracular response, a form of the year is proposed which carefully observes the motions of both stars. Among the Romans before Julius Caesar, by the institution of Romulus and his successor Numa, the lunar year prevailed, which Julius Caesar later changed into a Solar one—using the labor and industry of Sosigenes, an Alexandrian Mathematician—on account of the inconsistency of the seasons, and reduced it to a fixed definition, as Macrobius testifies in *Saturnalia, book 1, ch. 14, p. 218* and Suetonius in *Life of Caesar, p. 28.* Nor could the ancient Germans, our

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
Ancestors, have been ignorant of this divine institution of the Lights, even if we easily grant that they were not so devoted to the more subtle speculations of the stars (in the knowledge of which the Chaldeans and Egyptians excelled above others); yet such ignorance, which savors of the character of the people and the age, easily deserves excuse. For if Romulus, instituting a ten-month year entirely against the will of Urania <note>the Muse of Astronomy</note>, is to be excused, why should the Germans not be excused, who are not guilty of so great a fault? Indeed, they, like other nations, ordained months and years not according to their own whim, but according to the laws of the stars, and observed the motion of both Lights in ordering time, whether they were led to it by natural instinct or by <term>tradition</term> <note>original Greek: παραδόσει</note> is not certain. However, that the form of the year for the ancient Germans was *Luni-solar*—which, being the most ancient, is coeval with the world—Philipp Clüver deduces from Pliny <margin>Ancient Germany, book 1, ch. 32, p. 224.</margin> in *Natural History, book 16, ch. 45*: *The sixth moon made for them the beginnings of months and years; of which matter,* he says, *I see no reason, except that the race of mortals took its origin only on the sixth day after the beginning of the world.* Thus he says. But by what method the Germans ordered their Luni-solar calculation is very difficult to define, since little or nothing can be found in the writings of the Ancients on that matter; yet it is likely that they chiefly took account of the Moon, though not excluding all reasoning of the Sun, in ordering the months. <margin>Julian the Apostate</margin> *Julian* the Apostate indicates the custom of the ancient Gauls and Germans in this matter in his hymn dedicated to the Sun, King of all things: <term>Months for all other men, so to speak, are numbered from the moon, but we alone, and the Egyptians, measure the days of each year according to the motions of the Sun.</term> <note>original Greek: οὐ μῆνες ἅπασι μὲν τοῖς ἄλλοις... τὰς ἡμέρας</note>

Since, however, various spectacles occur in the theater of this whole Universe, and various stars in heaven, let us be more advised by that word which, setting others aside, especially commends the effect of those two Lights, which is primarily threefold (see B. Walther, *Biblical Offices, p. 571*): (1) <term>physical</term> <note>original Greek: φυσικὸς</note>, that they may shine upon the earth: for that purpose they are also called lights <term>Maor</term> and <term>Maorot</term> <note>Hebrew: מאור & מאורות</note> in the singular, which comes from <term>Or</term> *light*, because they act <term>to give light</term> <note>Hebrew: להאיר</note> *upon the earth*. (2) <term>distinguishing</term> <note>original Greek: διαχωρητικός</term>, that they may be for the earth, days and years. By <term>Moadim</term> <note>Hebrew: מועדים</note> are understood not the Jewish festivals, instituted much later, but the **IV.** seasons of the year: Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter. By *Day* is meant the so-called artificial day; by years, those we call Solar years. These times are therefore not produced by the earth through a universal or diurnal motion, but by the Sun, which is called by the *Hebrews* <term>Shemesh</term> <note>Hebrew: שמש</note> from "administering," and by the Greeks <term>Helios</term> <margin>4th Hexaemeron</margin> and <term>Halios</term> <term>according to the gathering of life</term> <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὸ ἀλί ζῆν</note>, as *Plato* says, because it calls men together into one after it has risen, or <term>from always revolving</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀεὶ εἱλεῖν</note> from its perpetual revolution; in Latin it is called as if *Solus* <note>meaning "Alone" or "Unique"</note>. By *Homer*, on account of its remarkable brightness, it is called <term>the shining sun</term> <note>original Greek: ἠέλιος φαέθων</note>, <term>from light</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ φάος</note> and <term>I burn</term> <note>original Greek: αἴθω</note>. The Sun, I say, was created by God for this: that by traversing the Zodiac it might make the distinct seasons of the year, and by its diurnal and nocturnal course pervade the whole world; hence Ambrose says: *It is so swift...*

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
Sacred
Physics.
<note>Latin: *Physica Sacra*. A 17th-century discipline that sought to explain natural science through the lens of Scripture.</note>
</margin>
The Sun is such that it illuminates all things with its rapid courses by day and by night. Augustine, in his *Preface to Psalm 93*, column 1040, says: *The lights in the heaven proceed through the day and through the night, they complete their journeys, they have fixed courses; nor do the fixed stars in the heaven deviate from above, acting through the celestial tracts where their Creator provided and established for them.* And Prudentius in 
<margin>The Origin of Sin, line 70. <note>Latin: *Hamartigenia*.</note></margin> 
*One flame provides the days revolved through the immense hollow of heaven; a single Sun weaves the year.* 
To this also refer what is read in Dio’s *Third Oration on Kingship*, page 49: <note>Original Greek translated here</note> *The Sun creates and distinguishes the seasons; it increases and nourishes all animals and all plants. Apart from it, the most beautiful and pleasant of things seen is light, without which there is no benefit from other beautiful things, whether heavenly or earthly, nor even from life itself.* Likewise, the Moon, by completing its circuit twelve times, makes as many months in a year. Therefore the Sun, which distinguishes day from night, is called the ruler of the day, and the Moon the ruler of the night; hence the Sun is said by Moses to be created <note>Hebrew: *le-memshelet ba-yom*</note> **for dominion over the day**, and the Moon 
<margin>Psalm 136:8, 9.</margin> 
<note>Hebrew: *le-memshelot ba-lelot*</note> **for dominion over the nights**, which the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translate as <note>Greek: *eis archas tēs hēmeras kai tēs nyktos*</note> *for the beginnings of the day and the night*, where they do not mean the "start" but the "sovereignty," according to the Hebrew truth. Yet, by the very fact that we attribute proper motion to the heaven and its stars, we do not declare them to be living beings, since the heaven has within itself a principle of motion divinely instilled into it: 
<margin>Psalm 104:19.</margin> 
**The sun knows its going down** <note>Hebrew: *shemesh yada mevo’o*</note>, which the Seventy translate as <note>Greek: *ho hēlios egnō tēn dysin autou*</note> *the sun knew its setting*. The Hebrew word denotes a "return," and it is noted that the Sun moves by a law prescribed for it by God. For just as God engraved upon other things created by Him their own peculiar virtues or <note>Greek: *dynameis*</note> powers, fitting for the nature of each thing, so he did especially for the Sun, which always moves in the same way without fatigue or labor; as Claudianus speaks well on this matter 
<margin>Against Rufinus, book 1.</margin> 
in his poem:
> *Then all things were*
> *Strengthened by the counsel of God, who commanded the stars*
> *To move by law, the fruits to be born at different times,*
> *And the changing Moon to be filled with*
> *A borrowed fire.*
<margin>On Psalm 118, sermon 12, p. 682.</margin>
And Ambrose says: *Is there any transgression in the Sun? Does it not keep its daily courses? Does the Moon not know its continuous wanings, and does it ever desert the duty of the ministry committed to it? Indeed, the Year returns by these same turns, the seasons are restored in the same state, and reformed by these same services. The Sun illuminates the day, guarding the appointed times. The Moon shines with nightly splendors, and its light gleams in the darkness. The globe of shining stars glows red, and they perform their solemn station, conversion, and change. There is one law for diverse things: to guard the turns of their courses once established, and not to cross the prescribed boundaries. The very change remains immutable, and the turning of spring, with distinct duties, holds the harmony prescribed by the constitution.*
Therefore, a law was imposed on the Sun to be moved in a perpetual course, and to be carried around by the motion of the "prime mover" in the space of 24 hours, but to complete its own period in the space of a year. God concurs in these motions as a Universal Cause, and as long as He so concurs that the Sun moves in that manner, it is said to happen by His "ordered power." But if in that course of the heavens, beyond the common order, the Sun

<column-break/>

stands still or moves backward, God is not acting according to the prefixed law, but by His "absolute power." Hence, 
<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin> 
<margin>Habakkuk 3:11.</margin> 
not without merit, Habakkuk enumerates among other Divine miracles that the Sun and Moon stood still. For thus the Author of Nature, at the petition of Joshua, brought it about that the Sun did not proceed, but stood in the middle of the heaven until the end of the battle (*Joshua 10:12, 13, 14*). So also the Sun moved back ten lines on the sundial of Ahaz as a sign of the most certain liberation from sickness (*2 Kings 20:11*); and God made the hours of that day increase, so that instead of 12 daytime hours, there were 22. Since this was hitherto unusual, and the Chaldeans—most famous for their observation of the stars—could not give natural reasons for this miracle, the fame of it flew through all nations. They learned that the course of the Sun had been changed on account of the illness of the King of Judah, about which Paul Sherlog 
<margin>Antiquities of the Hebrews, book 1, section 7, num. 61, p. 249.</margin> 
says: *We must hold for certain that not only was the shadow turned back, but the Sun itself: for certainly Berodach (or Merodach), the Monarch of the Babylonians, sent messengers with gifts to greet King Hezekiah after he knew he was freed from sickness. Among the memorable causes of this embassy was that which the second book of Chronicles indicates: to inquire about the portent that had happened upon the earth. For the Chaldeans, accustomed to investigations of the stars, when they noticed the shadows of the sundials changing, the day being prolonged, and the Sun being carried differently than was its custom, and being unable to draw foundations from natural principles according to their discipline, and the fame of Hezekiah’s recovery having reached them, it is likely that the notice of the prodigy was spread with the same rumor; to ensure a certain report of this, the Ambassadors were commanded to explore the truth. Unless the Sun itself moved and repeated its previous path, no occasion for such amazement would be given to mortals of other provinces from the retreat of the shadow alone; for the reversal of the shadow could have happened on Hezekiah’s sundial alone. But with the Sun itself stepping backward, wherever the arrangement of light allowed the Sun’s backward walk to be seen, there the shadows of the sundials rolled back, and a huge wonder struck the Mathematicians.* However, the Chaldeans pass over this miracle in silence, nor do they record it among the eclipses that happened around these times, as can be seen in Ptolemy; the Greeks, however, clearly turn it into a fable, pretending that the Sun prolonged the night on account of the birth of Hercules, as Hugh Broughton warns in his *Concent of Scripture, p. 105.*

The third purpose of the Lights is <note>Greek: *sēmantikos*</note> **signifying**, so that they may be for signs, namely predicting future storms and certain other things—specifically those effects which depend on the natural motion of the stars, conjunctions, oppositions, aspects, etc. Hence come the foreknowledges of a future eclipse of the Sun and Moon. Likewise, signs of a cloudy or rainy sky, or of dry sterility, heat, cold, and many other things are generally drawn from signs probably observed through long experience. To this 
<margin>Matthew 16:2.</margin> 
Christ himself looked: *That the red sky of the evening is a sign of future fair weather, and the morning red a sign of a storm.* To this also can be referred, in its own way, when in a figurative sense the darkening of the Sun, Moon, or stars is used as a sign to describe great changes, supreme calamities, and miseries; all things unhappy and sad are depicted. Prophetic—

The end of the twenty-fourth chapter is as follows: <term>וְחָפְרָה הַלְּבָנָה וּבֹוֹשָׁה הַחַמָּה</term> <note>Hebrew: ve-chafrah ha-levanah u-voshah ha-chammah</note>: <term>ἐντραπήσεται ἡ σελήνη, καὶ αἰσχυνθήσεται ὁ ἥλιος</term> <note>Greek: entrapēsetai hē selēnē, kai aischunthēsetai ho hēlios</note>. *The Moon shall blush, and the Sun shall be affected with shame.* Regarding the Sun, both words appear in Jeremiah <margin>c. 15. 9.</margin> <term>בּוֹשָׁה וְחָפְרָה</term> <note>Hebrew: boshah ve-chafrah</note> <term>κατησχύνθη καὶ ὠνειδίσθη</term> <note>Greek: katēschunthē kai ōneidisthē</note>. Likewise figuratively, where it treats the destruction of the King of the Egyptians in Ezekiel: c. 32. 7. <term>שֶׁמֶשׁ בֶּעָנָן אֲכַסֶּנּוּ וְיָרֵחַ לֹא־יָאִיר אוֹרוֹ</term> <note>Hebrew: shemesh be-anan akassennu ve-yareach lo-yair oro</note> <term>ἥλιον ἐν νεφέλῃ καλύψω, καὶ σελήνη οὐ μὴ φάνῃ τὸ φῶς αὐτῆς</term> <note>Greek: hēlion en nephelē kalupsō...</note>. *I will cover the Sun with a cloud, and the Moon shall not make her light to shine.* <term>Parallelly</term> <note>In a parallel manner</note> in Joel twice, c. 2, 10. and c. 3, 15. <term>שֶׁמֶשׁ וְיָרֵחַ קָדְרוּ וְכוֹכָבִים אָסְפוּ נָגְהָם</term> <note>Hebrew: shemesh ve-yareach qadru...</note> <term>ὁ ἥλιος καὶ ἡ σελήνη συσκοτάσουσι, καὶ τὰ ἄστρα δύσουσιν φέγγος αὐτῶν</term> <note>Greek: ho hēlios kai hē selēnē suskotasousi...</note>. *The Sun and Moon shall be darkened and the stars shall withdraw their splendor.* <term>הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ יֵהָפֵךְ לְחֹשֶךְ וְהַיָּרֵחַ לְדָם</term> <note>Hebrew: ha-shemesh yehafek le-choshek...</note>. <margin>c. 2. 31.</margin> <term>ὁ ἥλιος μεταστραφήσεται εἰς σκότος, καὶ ἡ σελήνη εἰς αἷμα</term> <note>Greek: ho hēlios metastraphēsetai eis skotos...</note>. *The Sun itself shall be turned into darkness, and the Moon into blood.* In these places indeed the Sun and Moon are joined; yet there are times where the Sun is placed without the Moon by the same mode of speaking, as in *Amos*: c. 8. 9. <term>הֵבֵאתִי הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ בַּצָּהֳרַיִם וְהַחֲשַׁכְתִּי לָאָרֶץ בְּיֹום אוֹר</term> <note>Hebrew: heveti ha-shemesh ba-tzohorayim...</note> <term>δύσεται ὁ ἥλιος μεσημβρίας, καὶ συσκοτάσει ἐν ἡμέρᾳ φωτός</term> <note>Greek: dusetai ho hēlios mesēmbrias...</note>. *I will cause the Sun to go down at noon, and I will overwhelm the earth with darkness in the day of light;* where Vatablus <note>François Vatable, a 16th-century French humanist and Hebraist</note> says: *A Hebrew way of speaking, <margin>page 600.</margin> by which, when you are at the highest degree of happiness, then I will cast you down from there, and render you most unhappy. By light he understands prosperity, by darkness misfortune.* So also Moses, about to die in Deut. 33, 13. blessed the tribe of Joseph with these words: *Blessed of the Lord be his land for the precious things of heaven, for the dew, and for the deep that couches beneath. And for the precious fruits brought forth by the Sun, and for the precious things put forth by the Moon. And for the precious things of the top of the ancient mountains, and for the precious things of the everlasting hills. And for the precious things of the earth, and the fullness thereof.* Joseph is proclaimed happy by the produce of heaven, earth, the abyss, and the mountains, and by the gifts of the Sun and Moon as signs. The Hebrew word, <term>מֶגֶד</term> <note>Hebrew: meged, meaning "precious thing" or "excellence"</note> repeated several times, signifies *delights and delicate fruits*, and they are called the delicate things of the heavens in respect to the earth, which the mercy of heaven favors, and which the propitious solar rays look upon, so that it may bring forth the best fruits. *Delicate Moon* on account of the monthly influences on the things growing on the earth. While these things are not obscure to him who weighs the Hebrew text, they are so to him who, setting this aside, gets stuck in the Greek Codex, in which <term>ἀπὸ ὀרῶν</term> <note>A mix of Greek "from" and Hebrew "mountains"</note> <term>ἐρῶν</term> is read, or even <term>ἀπὸ τῶν ὁρῶν</term> <note>Greek: from the mountains</note>, both of which joined readings you would seek in vain in the original Codex, even if all pertain to the sense of the word. By a slight change, read <term>ἀπὸ τῶν ὡρῶν</term> <note>Greek: from the seasons/hours</note>, from the fruits, and you will have a most praiseworthy sense; and from this, correct the Concordances of Kircher.

By these examples, divinatory Astrology is in no way supported, insofar as it presumes to predict for lands, kingdoms, empires, and men, future events that are merely contingent or dependent on free causes through Physics. A supernatural and extraordinary sign of a case of joy <note>likely a typo for "sorrow" or "judgment" in the original Latin context</note> is the darkening of the Sun etc., and its prediction, since it is divine and has God as its author, argues from itself an effect which, given the hypothesis of the impenitence of men, must necessarily follow. Nor is the matter otherwise in the other example we brought forward: for just as the power of the Sun, Moon, and the rest of the stars is great upon these lower things, by nourishing, vegetating, and preserving them. So Moses prays for these gifts of the Sun and Moon abundantly and a hundredfold as it were for the tribe of Joseph, imitating the vow of the Patriarch given to Joseph in Gen. 49. 25. in which the aforementioned Patriarch predicts that Joseph's descendants would obtain not only a most fertile region by the fecundity of the Sun, the abundance of dew and rain, and the mildness of the air. compare B. Gerhard *Commentary on Genesis 49. p. 854.*

The adornment of the Heaven being thus finished, as the work of the 4th day, and brought to the highest perfection, God <term>ὁ παντεργάτης</term> <note>Greek: ho pantergatēs, "the all-worker" or "creator of all"</note> destines for the Soil and Air their own inhabitants, whose Creation Moses, the <term>most certain</term> <note>Greek: asphalestatos</note> interpreter of the first and most ancient things, enumerates in verses 20. 21. 22. & 23.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
## Page 60

<margin>Sacred Physics. tract 3 Hist. ch. 1. p. 585.</margin> That there is a relationship and suitability or kinship between fish and birds, even if the types of fish and birds seem most diverse in terms of external form, is shown in many ways by *B. Frantzius* <note>Wolfgang Franz (1564–1628), a Lutheran theologian known for his work on "Sacred Zoology."</note> regarding the phrase *Yishretzu Ha-mayim* [Let the waters bring forth]. Here, one must note the genuine meaning of the verb *sharatz* <note>Hebrew: שרץ</note>, which does not simply denote "to produce," but as Commentators commonly explain these words: "Let the waters produce or bubble up in great abundance." (For they prefer the Hebrew verb *sharatz* to be translated as "to bubble up" rather than "to creep," as they establish the same matter for both fish and birds.) These are animals which, because of their great multitude, swarm as if from massed tiny bodies being born out of the water. Compare *Psalm 104:25* and *105:30*. So say *B. Gerhard* and *Friedl.* Furthermore, an elegant paronomasia <note>A play on words or pun</note> occurs in this place: *sharetzu sheretz* [let the waters swarm with swarming things] <margin>Commentary on this place.</margin> and *let the winged creature fly*. By the former word, any creeping things are designated, in whatever element they may live (for according to Buxtorf, *remesh ha-mayim* [creeping things of the waters] includes terrestrial, aquatic, amphibious, swimming, and flying creatures). Hence some wish for fish to be called *sharatz* as if from *she* and *ratz*, namely because they "run" or "creep" swiftly. Hence also Aristotle says, *apodes ichthyes pantes*, "all fish are without feet." From this they took the opportunity, as advised above, that *sharatz* could better be translated as "to bubble up" than "to creep." This is because, speaking properly and accurately, fish cannot be said to "creep" out of the waters; nor do they say the emphasis of this word is sufficiently explained in this way—as if they only began to move themselves out of and in the waters—but rather that by "bubbling up" they drew their nature and bodily substance from the waters. For it is evident that the waters concurred in the production of fish and birds not merely as an efficient cause, nor as a supporting place, but as the *matter* produced for this specific purpose by omnipotent power. Regarding the production of fish from water as matter, Pareus <note>David Pareus (1548–1622), a Reformed theologian.</note> raises a dispute among the Calvinists, defending that they were produced from water as a *place*, but properly from nothing. But since Pareus attributes their production to all elements, he does not exclude but includes water; for it is well known that every mixture is judged according to the predominance of an element. Since water is never without the remaining elements, being spread through mixed bodies, and moreover water predominates in fish, it can truly be gathered from that predominance that they were principally created from water, and from the other elements less principally, as if from mixed seeds diffused everywhere in the water. For just as it does not imply a contradiction that four-legged brute animals were produced from the earth, even though the remaining elements concurred, so it does not happen otherwise in this place in the production of fish from water. Regarding the production of birds from water, there is greater difficulty: those who defend the negative position place the strongest support for their opinion on the *Atnach* accent <note>A Hebrew grammatical mark indicating a major pause in a verse</note>, which they say never joins sentences but always disjoins them. Moreover, they appeal <margin>In his Corrections. In the Antibarbarus Biblicus.</margin> with *Francis Raphelengius* and *Sixtinus Amama* in this place to the Venice Codices, considering them more corrected and emended than the others. We are about to set forth our opinion on this controversy in the words of *Dr. Johann Adam Osiander, Professor*

<column-break/>

of Theology at Tübingen, in his *Physico-Theological College on the Works of the Hexaemeron* <note>The Six Days of Creation</note>, and specifically his words because they are in the hands of few. (1.) The office of the *Atnach* accent is not always to distinguish [separate], as we demonstrate from this very chapter, specifically from verse 1: where the same accent occurs under the word *Elohim* [God]. But who would be so absurd as to say that the statement "In the beginning *Elohim* created" completes the entire sentence and period of Moses, and that the remaining words "the heaven and the earth" are not connected? (2.) Even if it does distinguish, when will it be proved that the distinction is made by the exclusion of the original matter, and not by the exclusion of flight (which is remote from fish) and attributed to birds by their own motion? (3.) In favor of the [watery] matter of birds stand the structure of the words, the elegance of the comparison, and the true and genuine reason of the sense. The structure, because it can be conveniently translated thus: *Let the waters abundantly bring forth the creeping thing of a living soul and the winged creature, which shall fly above the earth*, so that the words "fly" and "creep" are not joined, but the nouns "creeping thing of a living soul" and "winged creature" are, and indeed in the Accusative case, with the future verb "shall fly" taken as a participle, in the manner used by the Orientals. Nothing is distorted here, for to take "shall fly" for "flying" is familiar to the Sacred Writers; nothing is violently mixed in except the relative pronoun "which," which is quite often omitted through ellipsis in the Scriptures and must be filled in, according to *Mersenne of Paris*. As for the comparison, Moses is dealing with the creation of birds; however, his speech is not precisely about creation itself, but about *production*, which is clear from a comparison of all the phrases used for the things to be produced on the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and following days. For just as in all of those either creation is intimated or, being intimated, is presupposed, so this too must be accepted. Here, however, one must distinguish between the "womb" and the "home" of birds; since birds ought not to live in the water like fish, Moses did not say: "let the waters produce fish and the winged creature," but "let the waters produce fish, and let the winged creature fly above the earth": hinting at the womb [origin] with the first words, and the home with the subsequent words. But a home cannot be assigned, nor can it even be commanded to fly, unless it is presupposed to have been produced. Therefore, by the word "bubbling up," the production of birds must also necessarily be understood. (4.) Against the Venice versions, we oppose the Chaldean version of the Royal work and the Buxtorf edition, as well as the Septuagint and the Arabic version, which, according to the most learned Philosopher of the Belgians, openly says the winged creature is from the water. These are his words. Compare *B. Walther, Harmony on this place.*

But to return again to that from which we departed on account of the primeval production of birds, *Moses makes special mention of the whales*; because in no genus of animals are such large things found as in the genus of fish. *Vayivra Elohim et-ha-tanninim ha-gedolim* [And God created great whales]. It should be noted that the verb *bara* [created] is not used here in the same sense as above in verse 1, for it is established from the above that fish were produced from water as matter. By *tanninim*, or the contracted *tannim* which is read in *Jeremiah 9:11* and *14:6*, they wish to be understood whatever are endowed with a serpentine form, such as dragons among the winged creatures, and whales in the waters, and likewise terrestrial serpents; hence *Psalm 91:13*...

> Horses are the origin of wasps, and bulls of bees. <note>original: "ἵπποι μὲν σφηκῶν γένεσις, ταῦροι δὲ μελισσῶν." This reflects the ancient belief in spontaneous generation, where insects were thought to emerge from decaying carcasses.</note>

Where the scholiast <note>An ancient commentator</note> on page 49 says: *They are born from the dying and rotting bodies of horses and bulls; wasps from horses, and bees from bulls.* Suidas cites the same verse under "horses" and "ox-faces," and it appears in the Anthology book 1. 60. 8. p. 179. *From the putrefied carcasses of horses, fierce wasps are born, but bulls are the producers of mild bees.* And Plutarch relates the same in his life of Cleomenes with these words: *Bees flower forth from oxen, and wasps from horses when they have rotted; and beetles are brought to life from donkeys suffering the same fate.* <margin>4. against Celsus p. 209.</margin> Similarly to Plutarch, Origen says: *A serpent is transformed from a dead man (as many say), and a bee from an ox, and a wasp from a horse, and a beetle from a donkey, and simply worms from most things.* Regarding the generation of a wasp from a horse, Horapollo in Hieroglyphics 2. 44. p. 141 says: *From a dead horse many wasps are produced,* which is why the Egyptians, when they wished to designate wasps, would paint the carcass of a horse.

In this manner, God the <term>κοσμοποιὸς</term> <note>World-maker</note>, blessing the waters and those things which owe their origin to the waters, thereafter filled the earth—which until that day was uninhabitable and destitute of inhabitants—with terrestrial animals. Of the terrestrial animals, some of which are <term>ἄλογα</term> <note>aloga</note>, lacking reason, while others are endowed with it, Moses constructs a catalog, and says the matter from which they were produced is the earth: <term>תוצא הארץ נפש חיה</term> *Let the earth produce the living soul*: <term>תוצא</term> <note>totsa</note> is the Hiphil future from the verb <term>יצא</term> <note>yatsa</note> *to go out, to proceed*, whence * <term>השמש יצא</term>, the sun is said to have "gone out" over the earth: <margin>Gen. 1. 9. 21. However, <term>נפש</term> is used for both the soul of man and of brutes, without regard for that great difference or distinction between the human and animal soul. In this place, it should be well noted that by the phrase *living soul*, the whole animal is named from its more noble part, which is also hinted at in verse 20, where Moses says, *Let the waters bring forth the reptile of the living soul*. Verse 24 agrees with this, so that it is established that the forms of terrestrial living things (for we speak of the soul of any brute, whether fish, bird, or beast) were not produced from the power of matter, but were created, as is clear from the context. For Moses says all living things were produced <term>למינהם</term> <note>le-minehem</note>, which for some is singular, as if from <term>מנה</term>, and therefore they render it *according to its species*; but for others it is plural, *according to their species*, with the omission of the letter *yod* as a plural marker, from the singular <term>מין</term> <note>min</note>. The Chaldean <note>Aramaic Targum</note> follows this with <term>לזניהון</term> and the Greek with <term>κατὰ γένη αὐτῶν</term>, *according to their kinds*. I say they were created and produced regarding the soul—by which we understand the substantial form—immediately out of nothing. Nor does it oppose this opinion that Holy Scripture calls the soul of brutes "blood" in *Gen. 9:5*, since the soul is not called blood formally and considered in itself in that passage, but figuratively and relatively, because blood is the proper instrument of the soul, in which the soul exists, not indeed by informing it, but by operation. For the rest, it is established that all species of brutes were produced from the earth as if from matter; whence all conclude with great consensus that animals, as we just said, were all produced from the earth. In this matter, we include Pareus <note>David Pareus, a Reformed theologian</note> as unique among the rest regarding the works of the 5th day, who contends that animals were created immediately out of nothing, and through the earth only...

# Sacred Physics
### From Genesis Chapter 1, verse 24 to the end of Chapter 1.

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
...only the place, not the material from which they were designated, as he presumes to prove with many arguments. However, since Moses speaks of the other living creatures in no other way than he speaks of man, proposing the earth as the material from which both were formed, we likewise see that Pareus <note>David Pareus (1548–1622), a Reformed Protestant theologian.</note> challenges Moses; we do not envy him if he can contend with him. Three species of terrestrial animals are recounted by Moses, the first of which comes under the name **Behemah** <note>Hebrew: בְּהֵמָה</note>, "beasts of burden," which seems to be derived from "helping" [*juvando*]. Taken collectively, it denotes not only domestic cattle of both sexes or tamed animals under human power (Gen. 7:2), but also, when used in the singular, it is taken for the Elephant because of its vast size, by which it is like many animals combined (Job 40:10); for this usage, see Dr. Franz.

<margin>Sacred History of Animals, book 1, ch. 4, p. 32.</margin>
Otherwise, the rule held by the Hebrews is not inconvenient: when **Chayyah** and **Behemah** <note>Hebrew: חַיָּה and בְּהֵמָה</note> (living creature and beast) are joined, the former signifies a domestic and tame animal, while the latter signifies a wild and savage one. Because deer, hares, etc., are comprised under none of these three, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> added the general term "four-footed animals" [*tetrapoda*]; compare Blessed Gerhard, *Isagogical Disputations*, p. 471. The second is called **Remes** <note>Hebrew: רֶמֶשׂ</note>, "creeping thing," from the root *ramas*, "to tread," such as various kinds of serpents and worms; from this we probably gather that even those beasts that are feared, but are good by their own nature, were created on the sixth day. Three kinds of creeping things are enumerated: 1. Those that drag themselves, like worms, which pull themselves along with their mouths fixed to the earth. 2. Serpents, like snakes, which move themselves by the force of their ribs. 3. Creeping things with feet, like lizards, concerning which see Pliny, Aristotle, Aelian, and others. Finally, the third genus is **Chayto-Eretz** <note>Hebrew: חַיְתוֹ־אֶרֶץ</note>, "beasts of the field," in which the "v" is redundant and does not belong to the word itself, which is **Chayyah**, "wild beast," from the root *chayah*, "to live" or "to recover." The Jews are accustomed to use this word in their letters from Deuteronomy 30:16: <margin>Gen. 7:21.</margin> "Live and be well" [*Chayyat ve-zavit*], for what we say as "live and be healthy." It signifies wild beasts, such as wolves, lions, bears, leopards, etc., which are never or only with difficulty tamed, and according to others, are carnivores. But were they such from the beginning and in Paradise? Not a few deny it. Indeed, it is clear from Genesis 1:29 that a food other than flesh was destined for all the beasts of the earth. Hence there is a very ancient tradition that all animals were gentle, to which Isaiah 11:4 and the Sibylline oracles allude:
> — nor shall the herds fear the great lions.

To these join Martial, book 9, Epigram 71, and book 1, Epigrams 7 and 15. Otherwise, brute animals do not go by only one name in the Sacred Scriptures; for they are called **Chayyah**, not only because they live, but because they live in a more excellent degree than plants, to which a "vegetative soul and life" is usually attributed by Philosophers, whence they are also said to "live and die" (Seneca, Epistle 58). They are likewise called **Basar**, "flesh," which by synecdoche <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole.</note> denotes sometimes men and sometimes brutes, by which the perfection relative to plants is signified, according to Daneau, *Christian Physics*, part 2, tr. 5, ch. 9. Hence "moving flesh" [*basar ha-romes*] is named from the faculty of moving, just as it is called by Clement of Alexandria (8th *Stromata*) "animated and sensitive" [*empsychos aisthetikē*] from the faculty of feeling. So also "living soul" [*nephesh chayyah*], from *nephesh*, "soul," which according to Ibn Ezra is said only of the human soul, but Buxtorf proves in his *Hebrew Lexicon* that it is taken more broadly by many. Also "beast of the earth" with the epithet "of the field" [*shaddai*], a wild beast which,

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
having neither master nor home, wanders for the sake of food; about which Rabbi Judah <margin>On Psalm 50:11.</margin> fables that there is a bird of such great size that if it extends its wings, it makes the whole world dark; compare Buxtorf, *Jewish Synagogue*, ch. 36, p. 73. Also very celebrated in the Sacred Scriptures is the division into clean and unclean, which is first read in Genesis 7:2; not that any are unclean by nature in themselves, but by decree and the will of the Lawgiver. For there is no doubt that immediately after the Fall, God taught the First Parents with what sacrifices He wished to be worshipped, and from this Noah could easily know the distinction between clean and unclean animals, or we may suppose he had it from divine revelation. From there, this distinction passed to the Gentiles through the "evil imitation" [*kakozēlia*] of the Devil, but greatly corrupted. Thus, it was religiously observed which victims should be sacrificed to which God: to whom the larger? to whom the sucklings? to whom the males? to whom the females? (Cicero). <margin>2. On the Laws.</margin> And not only this, but sacrifices and offerings were also estimated by the intention and mind of the offerer, as is clear from Seneca: <margin>Book 1, On Benefits, ch. 6.</margin> "For the honor of the Gods does not consist in victims, though they be the best and shine with gold, but in the pious and upright will of the worshippers." Hence that famous "Altar of the Elders" among the Delians, which Pythagoras is read to have adored because it was stained with no blood (Cyril, *Against Julian*, book 9). Regarding the eating of meat, as to when it began, to say little, Pythagoras concluded it was a crime for "entrails to be buried in entrails," because according to Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 15:
> — — That ancient age did not pollute its mouth with blood.

And Plutarch teaches that "meat-eating" [*sarkophagia*] is "against nature" [*para physin*]; but that superstitious abstinence is condemned by Paul, 1 Timothy 4:3. Hence, by the common consensus of the Doctors, it is taught that the eating of meat was practiced immediately after the Fall, so that they used the same animals for food as they did for sacrifices (Blessed Gerhard, *Commentary* on this place; Pererius, *Commentary* on this place; Salianus at Year of the World 1657). Thus also necessity compelled some, and ferocity others, to take those foods from which others rightly shrink by a certain common sense; hence the Phrygians and those in Pontus ate worms that are born in the decay of wood; Syrians ate land crocodiles; Africans, green lizards; in the West Indies, human flesh, as historians testify here and there. Solinus (ch. 33) mentions that there were once cannibals among the Ethiopians, and Mela (book 2, ch. 2) among the Scythians. And according to Jerome, <margin>Witnessed by Jerome against Jovinian.</margin> the British race used to eat human flesh, and when they find herds of pigs and cattle in the forests, they are accustomed to cut off the buttocks of the shepherds (perhaps better, the boys) and the breasts of the women, and consider these the only delicacies of food; see Ursinus, *Sacred Analects*, pp. 55, 150. But to the point: it is not our purpose here to deal with brute animals in detail, as we reserve a special meditation for them in their own place and title; however, I have chosen to add a few more things about the wonders of living creatures, about which much can be read in Francesco Giorgio Veneto in *Sacred Problems*, vol. 6, Nieremberg, Jonston, Franz, and others. There are those who ascribe religion to brutes—namely the Stork and the Elephant—and commonly a language by which they understand each other; compare Porphyry, book 3, *On Abstinence from Animal Food*; Angelo Rocca, *Vatican Library*, pp. 304, 305. Hence Plato, in Eusebius, book 12, *On the Preparation*, ch. 9, says: "The men of the golden age, under the rule of Saturn, [possessed] such great virtue..."

Just as nature proceeds from the more imperfect to the more perfect, so God, the <term>world-maker</term> <note>original: κοσμοποιος</note>, left for the last place the creation of the most perfect of all, which is man—who exists as a <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: μικρόκόσμος</note> and a type and image of the greater world, for whose sake this entire amphitheater with all things in it was produced. He is called <term>thistle and thorn</term> <note>original: קוֹץ וְשָׁמִיר (Kotz ve-Shamir); likely a reference to man's lowly material but sharp intellect</note> by Kimchi *on Zechariah 2.* He is a <term>small-born</term> <note>original: μικρόγονος</note> *Physics 8, text 17*, a compendium of all things. In his formation, God used a manner hitherto new and unusual: He instituted a certain and peculiar deliberation concerning the creation of man, both to indicate the dignity of the work He had at hand, and to demonstrate by such a solemn consultation the excellence of the image according to which man was to be created—to produce which required the more sacred counsel of the Holy Trinity. Furthermore, it was to attest to the end for which man was created; for while the remaining creatures were for the habitation of this world alone, man was to be the <term>one called</term> <note>original: ὁ κλήτης</note>, and thus a <term>dweller-with</term> <note>original: σύννοικος</note> and heir of eternal life, not only of this world, but especially of the world to come. Hence, in forming man, God the Builder of the world does not repeat His <insert>Let it be</insert>, through which He produced the whole host of heaven from nothing; nor did He employ here His <term>let the earth bring forth</term> <note>original: תדשא הארץ (Tadshe ha-aretz)</note>

<margin>

</margin>
earth: but He uses a new and singular phraseology to suggest the elegance, dignity, and excellence of the thing to be created: <term>Let us make man</term> <note>original: נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם (Na’aseh Adam)</note>, from the root <term>to make</term> <note>original: עשה (Asah)</note>, which means to do something ornately, elegantly, and becomingly. To this may be rightly referred what Basil says in *Homily 10 on the Hexaemeron*: *Concerning none of the works which God had built up to that point was this voice, "let us make," committed to letters; rather, all things were created by the simple Word and command of God. And Blessed Luther says in Genesis chapter 1: "Today man grows and multiplies in the same way as the rest of the beasts, but in the first condition Moses shows there was the greatest dissimilarity, since human nature was established by singular counsel and wisdom, and formed by the finger of God."* "Let us make," says <term>Elohim</term> <note>original: אֱלֹהִים; a plural name for God</note>, that is, one of the Elohim, God the Father to Elohim the Son and the Holy Spirit; or the Elohim, the Holy Trinity, said it to themselves; the persons of the Holy Trinity spoke to one another. Nor do we care for the <term>nonsense</term> <note>original: φλυαρίας</note> and evasions of Apelles and the Photinians <note>followers of Photinus, who denied the Trinity</note> who follow their camp, which they invent and paint to destroy the Mystery of the Holy Trinity. 

That <term>Na’aseh</term> <note>Let us make</note> should be read as <term>Na’asah</term> <note>He was made</note> with a Kametz vowel is a dream of the Jews against the testimony of the Masoretes <note>Jewish scholars who preserved the Hebrew text</note>, whose authority is by no means to be lightly esteemed, and who mention no other reading. Moreover, the Talmudic tradition proves this to be the genuine and native reading, testifying that it was once read as <term>Na’aseh</term> when it relates that Moses, having reached this verse while writing, said to God: <term>"You give an opening of the mouth to the Heretics"</term> <note>original: אתה נותן פתחון פה למינים; meaning "You give them an excuse to argue against monotheism"</note>. But God replied: <term>"Write, and he who wishes to err, let him err."</term> <note>original: כתוב ותרוצה לשונות שעלה</note>. If it ought to have been or could have been read as "He was made," no such thing would have been feared. Furthermore, if it were read with a Kametz, the execution of the decree and the decree itself would necessarily be confused; see *Slevogt, Academic Dissertation 21, page 477 and following.* Nor did he <term>seek the golden fleece</term> <note>original: χρυσόμαλον ἔψας; a metaphor for a futile or overly ambitious task</note> when they fable that God spoke of Himself in the plural in the manner of Great Lords, or that He addressed the Angels. For the Holy Spirit does not imitate this "Chancery style," so to speak, nor does Holy Scripture recognize this mode of speaking; these are the words of our Great Man *Luther, Commentary on Genesis, folio 17; see also Blessed Glassius, Grammar, treatise 3, canon 51, page 393; Francis Junius, vol. 2 of works, column 70 and following; Slevogt, in the place cited.* Indeed, Great Lords in the Orient did not formerly use that formula of speaking of themselves in the plural as they do now, as is clear from *Daniel 4:1 and Isaiah 2:1-2; compare chapter 4:12.* In these places, the clarity will be plain to anyone that the formulas of speaking used by Great Lords and their officials <term>differed completely</term> <note>original: δὶς διὰ πασῶν; literally "twice through all [notes]," meaning a total difference</note> from modern ones; see on this argument *Michael Havemann in the treatise entitled "The Way-Light against Jewish Darkness," page 500.* For just as no one other than God alone concurs in the production of any creature, so also God used the counsel or partnership of no one in creating man. Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] noticed this, and hence said that God indeed spoke to the Angels, "let us make man," etc., even if they did not help Him in His work of creation. But this is <term>beating the air</term> <note>original: κλαδῶν τὰ δ’ οὐχ ηλοα; a Greek idiom for futile effort</note>. For either God spoke falsely to the Angels in the plural, saying "let us make," which denotes help and partnership in work, or that voice of consultation and exhortation does not pertain to the Angels, as *Dr. Glassius learnedly argues in Mosaic Christology, Dissertation 1, thesis 39, page 20.*

<summary>This page discusses the transition from animal instinct to human reason, arguing that man's creation was a unique, deliberative act of the Holy Trinity. It refutes Jewish and heretical interpretations of the plural "Let us make" in Genesis, asserting it as proof of the Trinity rather than a royal plural or address to angels.</summary>
