# From Genesis Chapter I, verse 24 to the end of this chapter.

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin> Concerning the material from which man was established, it is the earth, which is called *Adamah* <note>Hebrew: אדמה</note>, from which the first man received his name *Adam* <note>Hebrew: אדם</note>, either because he was ruddy <note>reddish in complexion</note>, or because he was made from red earth, such as is found everywhere in the East, and especially in the Babylonian region. In this place, it is the name of the species, not an individual, connoting male and female; thus it is understood as referring to both sexes if taken as a common noun, which is why it is commonly found in the Sacred Scriptures with the demonstrative *He* <note>The Hebrew definite article 'the'</note> when used for both human beings. For just as God used a singular way of speaking in forming man, so also the name God gave to man enjoys a singular emphasis and mystery; *Adam* (man) and *Dam* (blood) <note>Hebrew: דם</note> seem to descend from one stem and agree in quality, while both names derive from redness and color, to suggest that great "unknowable mystery" <note>Greek: ἀγνώστως</note> that without blood the God-Man <note>Greek: Θεάνθρωπος - referring to Christ</note> could not be reconciled with God. In Genesis 2:19, the man <note>Hebrew: האדם</note> is said to be formed as "dust from the earth" <note>Hebrew: עפר מן-האדמה</note>; hence comes Callimachus’s "clay" and Hesiod’s "to mix earth with water." For in the work of creation, God used two words, *Bara* <note>to create from nothing</note> and *Asah* <note>to make/fashion</note>, but now he adds a third, *Yatzar* <note>Hebrew: יצר</note>, which properly means to mold or fashion, in the way a potter fashions something from clay, or a sculptor brings a trunk to a most becoming form so that it becomes a vessel of honor. Hence the Holy Spirit, speaking of the formation of man, leads us to the potter’s workshop (Job 10:8, Isaiah 64:8, Jeremiah 18:6, Romans 9:21). Accordingly, God himself, addressing man after the Fall in Genesis 3:19, says: *You are dust!*—namely, by origin, not by substance. *I now hold flesh, not earth: though the flesh may hear: "Earth you are, and to earth you shall go": the origin is recounted, the substance is not revoked,* says Tertullian in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh, ch. 6.* Indeed, students of the Holy Language observe that in the word *Vayyietzer* <note>Hebrew: וייצר - "and He formed"</note> a double *Yod* <note>the letter י</note> is placed, whereas regularly there should be one *Jod* and a double *Tzere* <note>a vowel mark</note>, just as in the creation of the beasts it is read with a single *Jod*. This is to suggest the double creation of man: the earthly of the body and the heavenly of the soul. Hence Rabbi Solomon says: "Two *yods* denote two ages, the present and the future: Man was established for both ages; the beast for the present only." Moreover, God formed man as "dust from the earth," that is, from the dust of the earth (by a transposition of the preposition), from dust already moistened and tempered by the rain that had fallen in *Gen. 2:6*; as if to say, from a certain mass of moistened earth, or from earth coagulated into mud and clay by the pouring of a rich liquid. Nor does it oppose this exposition that *Aphar* <note>Hebrew: עפר</note> signifies thin and minute dust (Gen. 13:16, 1 Kings 23:6). For by that phrase it is not only indicated that man, being made from the dust of the earth, is dusty and destined to return to dust (Gen. 3:17), but the highest Wisdom of God is suggested: that from the most minute dust of the earth He formed the most noble creature along with the other living things. And indeed from dust, <margin>Hexaemeron v. 220.</margin> according to those lines of Dracontius:

> *He smoothed the man into limbs made from dust,*
> *The clay was yet shapeless; it is jointed into bodily*
> *Members, the appearance of man, the heavenly image.*
> *The new form of the man is beheld, for a little while without a mind,*
> *Until the infused Spirit suddenly ran through the limbs.*

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin> Which dust He so skillfully polished and adorned for the nature of the man to be formed, that man seems as if circumscribed by a compass, or expressed and carved out by a lathe, according to the mind of Basil, Bishop of Seleucia, in his *Homily on Cain and Abel, p. 33*, whose words are these: "Adam was molded from the soil, and the earth was turned on a lathe into the nature of men; a rib brought forth a rib, and He united them by the law of nature, but by the authority of a command." <note>Original Greek: Ὁ Ἀδὰμ ἐκ χοὸς διεπλάσθη...</note> This sentiment is founded on those words concerning the formation of both humans: *male and female He created them*. God formed two humans distinct in sex: the body of the *Male* He fashioned from the soil, whence He named him *Adam*; but the body of the *Female* was built from a living rib of Adam, who had been cast into a deep sleep. And because she was to be the Mother of the living, the name *Eve* was given to her by Adam, the reason for which the First-Formed himself seems to give: because she was taken from man—that is, formed as a part of man or for the sake of man. Hence Basil, in *On Virginity p. 268*, calls woman a "segment and particle of the man." Thus, by God the Creator, the female is called *Ezer* <note>Hebrew: עזר</note>, a help or aid, which the Targum renders as *Adiq* (a support), and the Septuagint as *Boethon* (a helper). *Tobit 8:5.* *Negdo* <note>Hebrew: נגדו</note>, meaning she is "before him," or "another self." The Chaldean version says *Kekableh*, "in front of him" or "alongside him," so that the two parts are joined, because she is always ready for him and serves him; this alludes to those who, in lifting burdens, offer mutual work to each other and join helping hands.

Furthermore, into this body formed from clay, God breathed a soul, *Gen. 2:7.* "And He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life." <note>Hebrew: ויפח באפיו נשמת חיים</note> Just as "molding" <note>Greek: πλάσις</note> is attributed to the body, so "breathing into" <note>Greek: ἐμπνευσις</note> is attributed to the soul. *Naphach* <note>Hebrew: נפח</note> properly means "he blew or breathed upon" (Isaiah 54:16); hence the creation of the soul is rightly called an "insufflation" <note>a breathing-into</note>. This is not by reason of the *manner* of creation—as if God, clothed in human form, fashioned man's body with His own hands and breathed a soul from His own lungs, as Eugubinus and Oleaster <margin>In the Cosmopolite on Genesis</margin> would have it—nor by reason of *substance*, as if God breathed a soul into man from His own substance (as the Stoics, Epictetus, Seneca, and Cicero called the soul a "particle of the divine breath"). Rather, it is by reason of the *effect*: because He brought about the building of the body by His own power and wisdom, and placed within it a vital breath. Thus the nature of the soul is indicated, which is Spirit, and is called the "breath of life" <note>Hebrew: נשמת חיים - Nishmat Chayyim</note>, because it is immortal and proceeded from heaven. Hence some wish to derive the word *Nishmat* from *Shamayim* <note>Heaven</note>. It also designates the faculty of creation: that by this inspiration, the soul was produced at the same time it was breathed into the body, and was not created on the first day (as it seemed to Augustine in *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 7, ch. 7*, though elsewhere he acknowledges with Gregory of Nyssa that it was established only on the sixth day). Thus man was made into a "living soul," or a living creature, a participant in the soul which is the principle of life: "so that the body might have a soul governed by its powers," as interpreted by Theophylact (cf. 1 Cor. 15:46). For that reason, <margin>Book 13 of City of God, ch. 23.</margin> <margin>On the Origin of the World, v. 123.</margin> Alcimus Avitus sings excellently:

> *Then, when the whole man is accustomed to live in perfected limbs,*
> *And the warmed vitals smoke and wait for the soul alone,*
> *Which the Creator brings forth from a pure fountain,*
> *And sends to rule the upright joints;*
> *For He pours a gentle breath from His sweet mouth,*

<sig>Dd 3</sig> <meta>Catchword: Inspi- (Inspiration)</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
->*Inspired into man, who straightway draws it in,*<-
->*And learns the breaths of frequent respiration.*<-
<note>Original Latin: "Inspirata homini, quem protinus ille receptum / Attrahit, & crebri discit spiraminis auras."</note>
With the breathing in of the soul, the image of God was simultaneously communicated, according to which, as Moses witnesses, man was created. How excellent a gift the Image of God in man was, Moses wished to indicate when he repeats the words by which the Creation of man in the Image <margin>v. 26.</margin> of God is described, saying: <term>נעשה אדם בצלמנו כדמותנו</term> <note>Hebrew: "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness"</note> *Let us make man in his own image according to his own likeness; in the image of GOD he created him*: by which emphatic repetition he wished to indicate the excellence of the Divine Image, as if to say: "Pay attention to what I say." In the Image of God—to a thing so excellent—God created man; in the image of God, not of Angels (notwithstanding some degree of suitability and similarity between man and Angel) he created him. However, he did not intend to imply the difference that the Papists <note>A common 17th-century term for Roman Catholics</note> imagine between <term>צלם</term> <note>Tzelem: Image</note> and <term>דמות</term> <note>Demut: Likeness</note>, the former of which they refer to the substance, and the latter to the qualities; while they refer that to the soul, they refer this to the virtues. Hence they add that the *likeness* perished after the fall, but the *image* <margin>Book 2 on the grace of the first man.</margin> remains; see Bellarmine, from whom however Pererius, Cornelius à Lapide, and others depart. <term>Commentary on this place.</term> Truly, there is no difference between these, even if those words are distinguished in the Hebrew text. For just as *eikon* and *homoiosis* <note>Greek: "image" and "likeness"</note> are used interchangeably in the New Testament, so also are these in the Old Testament; indeed, in the *following verse* where the execution of the decree is read, at least one particle, namely *image*, is repeated, while the other is omitted. Rightly, therefore, with Blessed Meisner in *Anthropology* <term>dec. 1. Disp. 1. qu. 4. §. 4.</term> we recognize a <term>Hendiadyn</term> <note>A figure of speech where two words express a single complex idea</note> in this place, since it is frequent among the Hebrews for two substantives of either the same or different meaning to be joined, one of which sustains the force of an Adjective. For example, <term>Jer. 29:11</term> *I will give you an end and an expectation*, that is, an *expected end*. <term>Gen. 19:24</term> *The Lord rained sulfur and fire*, that is, *sulfurous fire*. So in this place, *in the image and likeness* means the same as a *most similar image*, or *in an image very much like*, as Emanuel Sa explains in his <term>notes on this place</term>, or *in an image <margin>in Commentary on Eph. 4.</margin> exceedingly like us, as Cornelius à Lapide* says. *Image*, he says here, *and likeness many distinguish, but I say it is a hendiadyn, as if he said, let us make man in the image of our likeness*, as the wise man speaks in <term>ch. 2:24</term>, that is, *in an image very similar or most like us*. From these and other sayings of Scripture, <term>Gen. 5:1, Col. 3:10</term>, it is gathered that the Image is not distinguished from the likeness. Thus he says. Compare on this matter Flacius <term>part 2, Clavis, tract 3, on the construction of nouns, rule 23, p. 153</term>; Blessed Glassius <term>Sacred Grammar, book 3, canon 6, p. 23</term>; the Famous Hackspan <term>in Philological Notes on this place.</term>

It is therefore a very great <term>proof</term> of nobility and an illustrious testimony <term>of the world</term> that man was made by the certain counsel and decree of the entire Holy Trinity; that his body was formed by the hand and fingers of God himself; that the Breath of life, the rational soul, was inspired into the body by God himself. We read nothing of the kind regarding the other parts of the world, indeed, not even regarding the world itself. The highest and ineffable majesty of man is commended by those words which testify that man was founded in the Image of God. For that he might be a man, he was gifted with body and soul; that he might *be well*, he was founded in the image of God. A certain obscure rumor of this so wonderful <term>first-formation</term> even—

<column-break/>

—reached the gentiles, whence man to Plato in book 5 <term>of the Laws</term> is the <term>most divine animal</term>; and Justin <term>Exhortation 1 <margin>Sacred Physics.</margin> to the Greeks p. 28</term> records an Ethnic oracle by someone who, being asked to produce a hymn and praise of the Almighty, sang thus in the middle of the hymn:
> <term>First, because having formed the mortal, he called him Adam.</term>
> <note>Original Greek: Πρῶτον ὅτι πλάσας μερόπων Ἀδὰμ δὲ καλέσας.</note>
And on <term>p. 23</term> he notes that Homer calls the body of the dead Hector <term>mute earth</term>, <term>Iliad book 24, v. 54</term>:
> <term>For in his fury he insults the mute earth.</term>
> <note>Original Greek: κωφὴν γὰρ δὴ γαῖαν ἀεικίζει μενεαίνων.</note>
To this also can be referred the verses of Lucretius <term>book 2, v. 997</term>:
> *Likewise, what was from the earth before goes back*
> *Into the earth; and what was sent from the borders of the ether,*
> *That, being returned, the temples of Heaven receive again.*
> *Which is also found in Euripides in The Suppliants, Act 2:*
> *For the body, from whence anything proceeds,*
> *Thither it returns: the Spirit seeks heaven,*
> *And the body the earth.*
And on the Quirinal hill in Rome, an old inscription has:
> *Life enters heaven, the body is held by the earth;*
> *Thus all things seek again their own rights and places.*
These and other things are read everywhere among Ethnic writers, so that it may be clear even from this that they have stealthily pilfered their own ideas from the Sacred letters, and that many fables of the gentiles drew their origin from the context of Sacred history—which, because of its sublimity, they either did not understand, or if they did understand, they veiled with their allegorical fictions or applied to mortal things. The history of the primeval creation of man suffered the same fate, as the fable of *Cura* <note>Care or Concern</note> is brought forward by Hyginus <term>Augustus's Freedman, fable 120, book 1</term>, who is said to have fashioned man, while Jove gave the Spirit. *Cura*, he says, *when she was crossing a certain river, saw clayey mud; she picked it up thoughtfully and began to fashion a man. While she deliberates with herself what she had made, Jove intervenes; Cura asks him to give it Spirit, which she easily obtained from Jove. When Cura wanted to impose her own name, Jove forbade it, and said his name must be given. While Cura and Jove were disputing about the name, Earth also arose, and said her name ought to be imposed, since she had provided her body. They took Saturn as judge, to whom Saturn seemed to judge otherwise: You, Jove, because you gave the Spirit, shall receive the body; Cura, because she first fashioned him, let care possess him as long as he lives; but because there is a controversy about his name, let him be called Man [Homo], because he seems to have been made from the ground [humo].* To this also belongs the fable of the people of Ceylon <note>Sri Lanka</note> concerning the origin of Adam, which Ursinus recites in <term>book 4 of Sacred Analects 1, p. 207</term>. The people of Ceylon boast that Adam originated among them. Now, Ceylon is an island of the East Indies, situated opposite the Cape of Comorin, which closes the kingdom of Calicut, and is not separated by a wide sea. In it, a very high mountain raises its head far among the other adjacent ones; they call it Adam's Peak. From the highest summit of this, a hill rises, pouring forth sweet and perennial waters as if from a navel. Nearby a flintstone is seen, with the footprint of a man impressed, two spans in length. They say this monument was left to posterity by Adam when he ascended into heaven from there. But also a cave is shown nearby, in which he long bewailed his fall. This opinion is so spread through the East—

# From Genesis Chapter 1, verse 24 to the end of this chapter.

## Sacred Physics
<margin>Sacred Physics</margin>
The East has so occupied the minds of all that even Saracens <note>A medieval term for Muslims</note> and Pagans frequent the place with sacred pilgrimages. And since there is no access by foot, nor is it permitted to crawl with hands—so steeply does that hill threaten the very Heavens—they ascend aided by ladders and chains, each intending to lament their own sins in that sacred cave. The Arabs call the island *Tenarizim*, as if to say, *a storehouse of every pleasure* <note>original Greek: πάσης ἡδονῆς ταμεῖον</note>, just as Damascene calls Paradise, or literally, the *Land of Delights*. You will find many fables of this sort among the Arabs, Greeks, and Indians concerning the first Author of our race, which the Hebrew skill for invention <note>original Greek: ἐπιπέρεια</note> brought forth. Among these, two are especially famous: one concerning the first man as *androgynous* <note>original Greek: ἀνδρογύνῳ</note>, or *male-female* <note>original Greek: ἀῤῥενοθήλει</note>; the other concerning him as *fish-like* <note>original Greek: ἰχϑυώνῳ</note> or in the form of a fish, which has even found some patrons among Christians; 
> *That he was a Giant, who traversed the vast Ocean on foot, and passed from some island Paradise into our world.*

<margin>Codex 279. Gen. ch. 2 v. 7.</margin>
Compare *Pererius on Genesis ch. 2 v. 7. Photius recites a fable from Helladius Besantinus, Book 4 of the Chrestomathy* in this manner: He tells of a certain man named *Oën* seen in the Red Sea, *having the other members of a fish, but the head, feet, and hands of a man, and that he taught Astronomy and letters*. Some say, he says, *that he was born from the first parent named Oi, which name testifies that he was truly a man, but appeared fish-like because he was clothed in the skin of a fish*. This seems to have taken its origin from Josephus, who in *Antiquities Book 1, ch. 4* records that *Adam and Seth discovered Astronomy and letters, but were clothed in the skin of a fish*. The other story about the first man being androgynous, which is commonly attributed to Plato in the *Symposium*, also owes its origin to the Hebrews; for when they could not grasp how God, who had set out to create one man for Himself, afterwards created two, they fell into the opinion that man was originally made such that he was one in substance, but double in face. For they believe the woman was joined to Adam's shoulder-blades, so that from the front he was *Adam*, but from the back he was *Eve*, as *Rabbi Samuel Ben Nachman* explains. So also in *Bereshit Rabbah section 8* <note>A collection of ancient Jewish interpretations of Genesis</note> we read: *Rabbi Jeremiah, son of Eliezer, said: at that hour in which God created the first man, He created him Androgynous, and this is exactly what is said: Male and Female He created them*. In the same way in *Midrash Tehillim*.

<margin>on Psalm 139.</margin>
*Rabbi Eliezer said, that man was created Androgynous, because it is written, Male and Female He created them;* where they do not understand "Androgynous" as Augustine does in *City of God Book 16, ch. 8* or Bausinus on Hermaphrodites *Book 1, ch. 30*, of which matter Torquemada collected more examples in *Hexameron Colloquy 1, page 28*. See also Harsdörffer’s *Great Stage of Joyful and Instructive Stories, part 6, example 141, regarding the "Zwiedorn" <note>A German term for a double-thorn or hybrid creature</note> page 152.* This opinion of a two-bodied Androgynous being, Male from the front part and Female from the back, has been adopted today by *Menasseh Ben Israel* in *The Conciliator on Genesis, question 8*. Nor are there lacking among Christians some who follow this opinion of the visionaries <note>original Greek: φανταστικῶν</note>, among whom Franciscus Georgius is to be numbered in *Sixtus of Siena, Library of the Saints, book 5, annotation 45*. Likewise *Cornelius à Lapide* mentions a certain person in France who fell into the same error. But against the Jews we oppose Moses, who does not say, *male and female* <note>original Hebrew: ברא אותו</note> *He created him, namely Adam,*

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Physics</margin>
but <note>original Hebrew: ברא אותם</note> *He created them*, implying distinct substances or distinct persons. We also oppose them with other Rabbis, especially *Rabbi Moses Maimonides, Isaac Abarbanel, and Rabbi Solomon Jarchi* in the *Portion of Bereshit*, who loathe those trifles and all affirm with one voice that *Eve* was created with *Adam* in no other way than potentially—insofar as the rib was created, from which God later formed *Eve*. To the Christians, however, we reply with what *Saint Paul* says in *1 Corinthians 11:8: For the man is not from the woman, but the woman from the man; and 1 Timothy 2:13: Adam was formed first, then Eve.* For if Adam had been created a Hermaphrodite, one could no less rightly say the man was produced from the woman as that she was born from him; or rather, neither was produced from the other: for it would not have been a new production, but a separation of different sexes existing in one body. And how could *Adam* be said to be formed first, and then *Eve*, if he were created androgynous at the same moment? It remains, therefore, that Eve was made from Adam's rib in such a way that before and after they were *both together* <note>original Greek: συναμφοτέρω</note> one body—not physically or in a natural sense through a natural union (such as exists between essential parts in a human or integral parts in a body), but politically and in a moral sense, such as exists among people in one family, where the Father of the family and the household constitute one body, yet in such a way that he is the head and principal part of the family. So also Husband and Wife are one body chiefly through the affection of love, or through mutual power of one over the body of the other, or through the mingling of bodies, or because by cohabitation and love they ought to hold themselves toward each other as if they were one person, and one ought to regard the other as something of oneself, and thus, not be torn away from the other any more than one and the same person is torn from himself or a part of himself. Hence, since love also united Adam and Eve so that, in respect to the union proceeding from mutual love, they were no longer two, but one flesh, the Scripture also says of them, *and they shall be one flesh* <note>original Hebrew: וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד</note>,

<margin>Gen. 2:24.</margin>
which by a Hebraism is nothing other than "one flesh." For more on this argument, please see *P. Slevogt, Academic Disputation 21, page 488 and following; Hackspan in Philological Notes on Genesis ch. 2.* It is also pleasing to touch upon, in at least a word or two, the fiction of the Pre-Adamites, of which monster the author in the previous year, 1656, was a certain Frenchman, *Isaac Peyrerius*, whom *Johann Mesfrezotius* reports lived in the external communion of the Reformers, but *Maresius* testifies was brought to a recantation by the *Leaders of the Spanish Netherlands*. The sum of his paradox comes to this:
> *That the Gentiles are different in race and origin from the Jews; that the latter were formed by God in Adam; but the Gentiles were created before then, on the same day as the other living creatures. The origin of the latter is described in Genesis chapter 1; but that of the former in chapter 2.*

But since this knot has been most sufficiently untied from the Holy Scriptures by both our own scholars and the Reformers, it suffices for us to bring forward at least some testimonies from antiquity; *Diodorus Siculus* testifies concerning the Egyptians in *Book 1* that it is read in their writings that *the first humans lived clothed in no garment*, which the Scripture testifies of Adam and Eve in *Genesis 2:25*. *Scaliger* writes concerning Eusebius in *Observations on his Chronicle, page 4*: *Just as Eusebius in the Divine Commentaries* ... as the Jewish law.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
And from there, in order to assert Christian truth, he threw open all the libraries of the ancient philosophers, historians, theologians, *Egyptians, Phoenicians, and Greeks*, either to prove their vanity by the law of God, or to show that the most ancient Egyptians, Chaldeans, Phoenicians, and Greeks had drunk from the fountain of the Prophets and the Hebrews, and had watered the thirst of their own genius from that source. Thus, some years earlier, to prove the antiquity of Mosaic doctrine, he had established a most excellent work of Chronicles and a universal history of all times; in proof of which, he had to travel through the spacious world of all literature and the histories of foreign nations. And on page 242: The heroic labor of Eusebius alone surpassed the works of all others combined; from their writings, gathered into one body and organized into parts, he wove together brilliant volumes greater than any praise, in which he established a defense of Christian worship—twenty books of *Demonstrations* <note>original: "ἀποδείξεων" (Apodeixeon)</note> against the Jews, and fifteen volumes of *Preparations* <note>original: "προπαρασκευῆς" (Proparaskeues)</note> for the doctrine against the Gentiles; and for its antiquity, the work of *Chronological Canons of Universal History*. In the first book of this work, having discussed the beginnings of all kingdoms, dynasties, nations, and republics, he showed that the Mosaic origins were far older than the births of all the fabled Gods. Let us end this fable with the Epitaph of Blessed Danhavver, with which he finishes his *Pre-Adamite*.

> Stop, Traveler, your step and ask here! Do you ask who lies buried here? NOBODY <note>original: "UTIS" (Greek for 'nobody')</note>. By what father? Fantasy. By what mother? Folly <note>original: "Moria"</note>. Where born? In the brain, not like Minerva from Jove, but like Morpheus from sleep. By what nurse? Vanity. How great in time? Eternal in opinion, but in truth having scarcely passed twenty-five years. What did he do in the world? He rested, he mocked, he stood away from errors, he fashioned gourds <note>a metaphor for empty-headed follies</note>, he hunted the winds. What did he endure? Wonderfully wondrous fictions, imputations, and back-dated claims.
> If you, Scavengers <note>original: "Offilega"</note>, should ever find NOTHING here, do not wonder, because here is buried

### THE PRE-ADAMITE NOBODY.

Many other things could be introduced and brought forward here concerning Moon-dwellers <note>original: "Selenitis"</note>, (for *Paracelsus*, besides the descendants of Adam, devised four kinds of men and placed them in each of the Elements,) sea-people of both sexes, Nereids, Centaurs, Wood-spirits, Satyrs, Fauns, Goblins or mountain-dwarfs, Kobolds, and others of that kind; but since they are mere fables, even if they smack of antiquity, we rightly pass them by. Meanwhile, one may read about them in Voëtius, *Select Disputations, Vol. 1, p. 878 and p. 738 ff.*, M. Johann Praetorius’s *Plutonic Sociology*, as well as Henry Kornmann’s *The Mountain of Venus*.

To this meditation of ours on the works of the Six Days <note>term: Hexaëmeron; the six days of creation</note>, which is presented as if in a summary, there follows an inseparable connection—and so it is said of the whole creation, and immediately annexed to the creation of man is the eulogy of created things: *And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good* <note>original Hebrew: וירא אלהים את-כל-אשר עשה והנה-טוב מאד</note>. *God inspected all things which he had made, and they were very good, that is, the best*. (The masculine word *good* [Tob] is placed by a grammatical shift <note>term: enallage; a substitution of one grammatical form for another</note> for the neuter "a good thing," which the Hebrews lack.) It signifies not only each thing individually, but *all things together* were in such beautiful symmetry <note>original: "εὐσυμμετρία"</note> and perfection that a more perfect state could not be imagined. For it belongs to the formal reason of creation that the production was made out of goodness, as far as

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Physics.</margin>
perfection is concerned; for the word "finished" <note>original Hebrew: כלה (Kalah)</note> denotes a perfect consummation, and indeed such a one in this place, "very good," which is in the superlative degree, as indicated by the intensifying particle "very" <note>original Hebrew: מאד (Me'od)</note>. For the Hebrews, to express the superlative which they lack, are accustomed simply to join "very" to a noun, according to Kimchi. This perfection is attributed both passively to the world and actively to God. If actively, this is not to be taken so absolutely as if God, through His Divine omnipotence, could not have produced something more perfect, but determinately according to His will through a directing principle—namely, Wisdom—so bounded outside Himself that God did not *wish* to act more perfectly. If passively, perfection is to be taken absolutely, meaning that nothing is lacking to the world for its own perfection, and that the World is not capable of a greater perfection. For so great is the perfection of things created by God, and such is their elegance and goodness, that whether you look above, below, or beside you, or indeed wherever you turn your eyes, you cannot sufficiently contemplate God's goodness in created things. *The whole world of creation,* says Basil, *is an image of divine love for mankind, first educating the creation through the eyes themselves regarding the Good. For this very first thing—to come to the act of creation and to give the passage into being to those things that were not—is a hallmark of His kindness.* <margin>Sermon 12 on Jonah, p. 99.</margin> While God, the best distributor of things, granted His own being to all those things which were deprived of their own being, while He called those things which were not, not so much that they might exist, but that they might exist *well*, so that they might work and act according to their condition—in that is shown the *overflowing wealth of His kindness*, and by that very act He made the creature *a good thing from His own goodness*, which Basil elegantly demonstrates in the cited place. Hence Moses himself begins the fruitful chapter of his Cosmography from perfection: *Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them* <note>original Hebrew: ויכלו השמים והארץ וכל-צבאם</note>. The word "were finished" <note>original Hebrew: ויכלו (Vaykhulu)</note> is placed here for "therefore"; it literally means "they were made complete," "they were perfected," from the root "to finish." It is as if to say: all things pertaining to the integrity, perfection, and ornament of heaven and earth are completed. But what is that ornament? What is that beauty? The nature of the beautiful, and beauty itself, consists in the various adornment of things; nor was there anything in the whole nature of things that was not clothed and adorned in wondrous ways for the sake of grace and decorum. Just as each individual thing was good, and all were very good, so also each was beautiful, so that nothing more beautiful or more adorned could be imagined. The heavens were adorned and illustrated by ranks of stars, each star by its rays, the rays by splendor, and the splendor by heat. The *Air* was filled with so many and such great kinds of birds; various and wonderful kinds of fish adorned the sea; God's kindness clothed the *Earth* with fields, trees, and animals; the fields with herbs; the trees with flowers; the animals with senses. He decorated all matter itself with various figures, filled forms with virtues, and marked virtues with operations. This work of creation was therefore completed on the sixth day, or to speak with the text: *And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made* <note>original Hebrew: ויכל אלהים ביום השביעי מלאכתו אשר עשה</note>, as Pagninus translates. But since a certain apparent contradiction <note>original: "ἀντιλογία"</note> occurs here, commentators untie this knot in more than one way: Jerome in his *Hebrew Traditions on Genesis*, whom Galatinus and Weidner followed, in Jacob Martini, book 3, *On the Three*...

# From Genesis Chapter I, verse 24 to the end of this chapter.

<margin><term>Sacred Physics</term><note>A branch of early modern study that sought to explain natural phenomena through the lens of Biblical scripture.</note></margin> Elohim <note>original: "Elohim" - the Hebrew name for God</note> p. 169 and others have divided the hours of the seventh day in such a way that they repeatedly claim God perfected the remaining work in some hours, and ceased from work in others; hence some think the Jews can be refuted in their observation of the seventh day as being too religious or superstitious, since even God did not plainly desist from all work on the 7th day. But this is less solid, whatever Mersenne, Cajetan, Lyranus on this passage, Thomas and Bannes in their *Commentary on Part 2 of Thomas* p. 86, or Lombard in *Book 2, distinction 15* might devise to save the Vulgate <note>The Latin Bible translation used by the Catholic Church</note> reading. 2. Spanheim in *Evangelical Doubts p. 29* considers the prefix "in" <note>original: "ב" (Beth)</note> to be placed in the sense of "at" or "upon" and elicits this sense: *God perfected His work around the seventh day*, that is, at the end of the sixth and the beginning of the seventh. He also supports this exposition with several examples, among others he cites:

<margin>Exodus 12:15</margin> *Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, nevertheless* <note>original: "ביום" (bayom)</note> *on the first day*, that is, around the first, you shall cause leaven to cease. In the same manner he explains that passage in *Matthew 1:2* "at the time of the Babylonian deportation" <note>original: "ἐν τῆς μετοικεσίας Βαβυλῶνος"</note>, meaning around that time when the migration occurred. To these, Hackspan adds in his *Philological Notes on this passage* (from which we have taken these points) that the Hebrews have a custom of saying a time is "completed" when it has not yet elapsed, but is already imminent.

<margin>Acts 2:11</margin> Thus* the *days of Pentecost* are said to be *completed*, since the sending of the Holy Spirit, which is dealt with there, occurred as the days of Pentecost were approaching. And what is more, "after" <note>original: "μετὰ"</note> in *Matthew 27:63* is used for "around" or "within." 3. There are those who think the Future tense <note>original: "יויכל" (way-yekhal)</note>, which by a "conversive" <note>A Hebrew grammatical feature where a prefix changes a future verb to a past tense</note> is changed into a preterite, should be explained as a pluperfect *He had completed*, so that the sense is: *when God had completed His works, He rested on the seventh day*. Thus the verbs in verses 3, 7, and 22 are understood. We also agree with this exposition: For when God had perfected (namely, already before) on the seventh day His work which He had made, on the seventh day itself He rested from all His work which (before the seventh day) He had made. Nor yet should the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, when they read: "God finished His works on the sixth day" <note>original: "συνετελεσεν ὁ Θεὸς ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἕκτῃ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ"</note>, be said to have strayed from the simplicity of the Hebrew speech. They do not everywhere observe the exact logic of the Hebrew words so as to remain chained to them. They sometimes assume other words, the sense so requiring, as Holy Scripture testifies here and there regarding this matter; and they make a change here which should not immediately lead us to say the Hebrew text was altered, or that the good Greeks should be accused of sacrilege.

<margin>Compare the Vulgate version.</margin> *They seem to me to have seen*, says Sixtus Amama*, *what escaped so many eyes. For who does not see that these two propositions sound the same in sense: "God had completed all His work by the seventh day" and "God completed all His work on the sixth day." For if He had completed it by the seventh day, when did He complete it, I ask you, if not on the sixth day? Therefore, what does it matter whether you say the former or the latter, if it falls back into the same sense? God therefore completed all the work of creation on the seventh day understood exclusively, not inclusively, so that on the seventh day nothing further was created, not even Eve the first mother, who was created on the same day as Adam, namely the sixth; but that He then ceased to create anything further, and on the seventh day He rested. In rest, indeed, two things occur: 1. cessation from work (Joshua 5:12, Revelation 4:8) and 2. the restoration of weary strength: according to the first meaning, rest is attributed to God, but not according to the latter.*

<column-break/>

Augustine in *Book 4 on the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chapter 14* says: *Neither when He created was He exhausted, nor when He rested was He refreshed.* And in the same work, chapter 10, he explains that rest thus: that God made us rest on that day, i.e., that He destined that 7th day for the Sabbath. So also Aristobulus in *Eusebius, Book 13 on the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 6*: that GOD instilled rest into the things established by Him, i.e., stability, permanence, and a fixed and settled order. But we are compelled by no necessity to depart from the literal meaning, says Dr. Gerhard in his *Commentary on Genesis, chapter 2, page 35.*

This study of the six-day <term>divine masterpiece</term> <note>original: "θεαγνήματος μελέτημα" (theagnēmatos meletēma)</note> is therefore a most ample field, in which and from which the justice and goodness of God, the Creator of all, shines forth above other attributes, as Tertullian says: <margin>2. Against Marcion p. 155.</margin> *From the beginning the Creator was as good as He was just; both proceeded equally. His goodness worked the world; His justice modulated it, by which He judged that the world should be made of good things, because He judged with the counsel of goodness. It is the work of justice that a separation was pronounced between light and darkness, between day and night, between heaven and earth, between the upper and lower water, between the whale of the sea and the dry mass, between the greater and lesser lights of day and night, between male and female, and between the tree of the knowledge of death and of life, between the world and paradise, between water-born and earth-born animals. All things, as goodness conceived them, so justice distinguished them. All this was disposed and ordered by judgment. Every site, the condition of the elements, the effect, motion, state, rising, and setting of each thing, are the judgments of the Creator.* This hour is most ample and wide, in which there are as many Teachers and Masters as there are works of God, in which all Doctors, however much they may excel in erudition and science, can continually become more learned. For the wisdom of God shines from there, because He established all things in a certain order, degree, and measure; then the power of GOD, because He created this most beautiful amphitheater of heaven and earth within six days, so polished and skillfully out of nothing. It will not be unpleasant to relate what Johannes Goropius Becanus has in his *Chronicles on sacred or mystical numbers*, specifically these four: 1, 2, 3, 6. For by the **first** number he says the Unity of the Divine Essence was denoted; by the **second** (binary) the mystery of the two Natures in the person of Christ; by the **third** (ternary) the Holy Trinity; and by the **sixth** (senary) that the workmanship of the world was finished in six days, and this same world is destined to perish through the course of six thousand years. Whenever the Ancients wrote the years of the world, such as the year of the flood 1656, they would place that other mystical 1, 2, 3, 6 beneath it in this manner { 1656 / 1. 2. 3. 6. } and indeed above it, so that they might add a confession of their faith. Since we are living at the end of the world through the fall of the unclean, as we ruminate on these thoughts of the ancients, let us always be mindful of both our origin and our end, and of God the Founder of all, to whom, because He willed us to be men, let us give deserved and immortal thanks; and thus let these be the boundaries of Sacred Physics.

->Blessed be GOD, who created heaven and earth.<-

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

->Genesis 1, verse 2.<-
->*And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.* <note>Hebrew: Ve-ruach Elohim merachephet al-pene ha-mayim</note><-
->*And the Spirit of God was borne over the water.* <note>Greek: kai pneuma Theou epephereto epano tou hydatos</note><-
->*The Spirit agitated itself upon the surface of the waters.* <note>Latin: Spiritus agitabat se in superficie aquarum</note><-

<margin>The Maker and Ruler of the World.</margin>
**I**t is helpful here to contemplate the opinion of the initiates of Nature regarding what they philosophized concerning the <term>nous</term> <note>Greek: Mind or Intellect</note>, and whether they approach in some way the Spirit of whom Moses speaks. Anaxagoras, the Athenian philosopher, once said (according to Laërtius): *All things were together, then Mind came and set them in order.* <note>Greek: Panta chremata en homou, eita nous elthon auta diekosmese</note> Plutarch handed this down more explicitly <margin>in the Life of Pericles</margin>, saying of him: *He was the first to appoint over the universe not Chance, nor Necessity, as the principle of arrangement, but a Mind, pure and unmixed, pervading all other things.* <note>Greek: Protos tois olois ou tychen... alla noun epestese...</note> The supreme dictator of philosophy, Aristotle, was of this same opinion, recording <margin>Physics, Book 8</margin> that *the Mind produced motion and separation* <note>Greek: ton noun... kinesin poiesai, kai diakrinai</note> within infinite matter. Thales of Miletus also recognized this <term>world-making</term> <note>Greek: kosmopoion</note> Mind even before Anaxagoras; he said that water was the beginning of things, but God was that Mind which formed all things from water, according to Cicero <margin>On the Nature of the Gods, Book 1</margin>. It was also the opinion of that same Orator [Cicero] in his *Tusculan Disputations* (Book 4) that the particles of infinite matter, similar to one another and minute, were first confused and afterwards brought into order by the divine mind. Thus the Pagans established an infinite Mind which, in an infinite and confused mass, secreted similar parts from others, and by composing and segregating them, produced new things. This opinion concerning the Mind as the ruler of the world was once widespread, especially after the time of Socrates. Aristotle noted this opinion regarding the Mind or intellect—which Anaxagoras interpreted as the Maker of the world—with an asterisk in his *Metaphysics* (Book 1, Chapter 3); when proposing the opinions of his ancestors regarding the principles of things, he finally introduced this: *Wherefore,* he says, *he who said that an intellect or mind exists in nature, just as in animals, as the cause of the whole world and its order, appeared like a sober man compared to the ancients who spoke vanities.* We know it was Anaxagoras who openly touched upon these reasons, yet Hermotimus of Clazomenae is said to have mentioned the cause earlier. This is from the version by Bessarion. Julius Firmicus also aims at this in his *Mathesis* (Book 1, Chapter 3): *That Divine Mind,* he says, *and celestial spirit, situated throughout the whole body of the world in the manner of a circle, and placed now inwardly, now outwardly, rules and composes all things; conceived by its own generation of origin, it perpetuates itself for the procreation and preservation of all things by a fiery and eternal agitation, nor does it set aside this duty through any fatigue, so that it sustains itself, the world, and all things within the world by its perpetual and indefatigable mobility.* Nor is Plato’s opinion in the *Timaeus* concerning the "Soul of the World" foreign to our purpose; Plato received this from Pythagoras, Pythagoras from Aglaophemus, and Aglaophemus from Orpheus, who (as Eusebius testifies in *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 3) most clearly perceived it; and Orpheus received it from Trismegistus. Regarding Plato, he speaks thus in the *Timaeus*: *GOD generated the soul of the universe older than the world, and he fashioned it in such a way: from the substance which is indivisible and always remains the same, and from the divisible which is produced around bodies, he mixed a third kind of nature, etc.* In which matter he philosophized so abstrusely and occultly,

<column-break/>

<margin>The Maker and Ruler of the World.</margin>
this most divine of philosophers, that he stands in need of a "Delian diver" <note>A proverbial expression meaning a very skillful interpreter to plumb the depths of a difficult text.</note>. Indeed, the Platonists explain him in various ways and yet do not hit the mark. Hermes Trismegistus, from whose fountains Plato drew his entire philosophy, begins thus in the *Poimandres* (Part 2, Discourse 4) concerning the Spirit, of which all things are full, and which, mixed with all things, gives life to all:
> O life, save all that is in me. O light, illuminate the whole; the Spirit is GOD. Your Word is the spirit-bearing, world-making mind. You alone are God. All things stand in need of this Spirit, for it carries all things according to their dignity, gives life and nourishment to all, and from this holy fountain all things depend; it is always the helper to all spirits and living things. This is the ruler of the other spirits, etc.

If Trismegistus and the Platonists who follow him in this regard understand it such that they call the divine power penetrating the universe and governing and sustaining the whole world the "Soul of the World," hardly anything better could have been said by a Heathen man that would be more conformable to Holy Scripture. See Sperling, *Institutes of Physics*, Book 9; compare Dorsch, *Theology of Zechariah*. It is also worth mentioning what Plotinus discusses concerning the Soul of the World, and thus the whole Deity: In the first place, he says, is the Good; in the second, the Intellect, the Son of the Good; and in the third, the Soul of the World. Through this, Chalcidius the Platonist, in his commentary on the *Timaeus*, most openly thinks that what Christians call the Holy Spirit should be understood. Hence Cyril of Alexandria <margin>Against Julian, Book 1</margin> asserts that the Holy Spirit was called the "Soul of the World" by Plato. For he has it thus: *There is one GOD of the universe, but He is extended, as far as is known of Him, into a holy and consubstantial Trinity: into the Father, I say, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, whom Plato also calls the soul of the world.* Thus he says. Hence it is that in the Ancient Theology of the Heathens, the Father is called the Supreme Good, the Son the Mind and Maker, and the Spirit the Soul of the World, as Mutius Pansa deduces at length from Ancient Heathen Theology in the treatise titled *The Kiss, or the Consensus of Heathen and Christian Philosophy*. In that same manner, many from the families of the Hebrews, Arabs, and Chaldeans said the world was animated, especially Philo the Jew and Rabbi Moses [Maimonides], who made the world endowed with reason and intellect—with a futile reason, clearly, and an entirely empty intellect. This opinion, however, being sufficiently refuted by itself, requires no further refutation; for it is well known that there is no matter found in the world capable of receiving a soul, whether rational, sensitive, or even vegetative. The new Hermeticists, to be sure, try by every reason and method to excuse the opinion of the ancient philosophers who taught that this world was animated, and to change their sentiment concerning the Soul of the World into a better meaning than it seems to possess in itself. Let us hear Pierre Jean Fabre, in the first volume of his *Panchymical Work*, regarding the opinion of the ancients about the animation of the world...

# From Genesis 1:2

<margin>The Maker and Ruler of the World.</margin>
...differing in opinion. *Thus are the ancient Philosophers to be interpreted when they assert that this world is animate—that is, full and swelling with vital light and heat. Since this vital light and heat is the actuating and informing form of this world, it can therefore be called simply the actuating and informing soul, and from it the world can be called "animate"—that is, informed and simply actuated.* These are his words. Let us now draw the curtain of silence over the things the Chemists <note>Alchemists</note> devise concerning the essential parts of the world—namely, Spirit, soul, and body—while they busy themselves trying to hide I know not how many Divine mysteries within the "Spirit of the World." Certainly, they think they can search out the mystery of the Holy Trinity in this Spirit of the world (as they call it). However, this is not the case, since Divine mysteries are above nature and so great that no creature could conceive even the slightest bit of them outside of Holy Scripture. For just as the Father in Divine matters is the first, the fountain and origin of Divinity from whom alone the first Divine essence springs; and the Son is the second, begotten of the Father from eternity; and the Holy Spirit is the third, proceeding as if from both; so in the "salt of the world," which the chemists call Mercury, they call the *innate heat* first—not in time, but only in origin, because it is the fountain and source of life, granting and communicating life to all. They call the *primordial moisture* second—not as being later in time than the innate heat, but as something drawn out from that innate heat at the very moment of creation and receiving life. The *dryness* found in the same salt they call third, as something proceeding from both. Let these things be said regarding the opinions of the Ancients on the Mind. Furthermore, let us relate what Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage, 3rd-century bishop</note> thought of the opinion of the Ancients on this matter; for he says in his *Sermon on the Holy Spirit*, page 436: *Since the power and divinity of the Holy Spirit could not be properly investigated in its own nature by the ancient Philosophers, the searchers of the world, they nevertheless perceived by very subtle conjectures in the composition of the world—through the combined and distinct qualities of the Elements—that a present soul was near to all things, which provided life and motion according to the kind and order of each, fixed boundaries that could not be crossed, and assigned stability and use. This life, this motion, this essence of things the Philosophers called the Soul of the World, thinking that the celestial bodies—I mean the Sun, Moon, and stars—and the firmament itself were moved and ruled by the power of this soul; and that the Waters, Earth, and Air were impregnated by its seed. If these men had believed him to be the Spirit, Lord, Creator, and Giver of Life and nourisher of all things under him, they would have had a suitable approach to the faith.* Therefore, what the Philosophers attribute to the Soul of the World, Cyprian asserts of the Holy Spirit, writing later: *This Holy Spirit, the soul of all living things, so abundantly pours himself into all by his generosity that all rational and irrational creatures have from him, according to their kind, that which they are and the fact that they act in ways fitting to the order of their nature; not that he himself is a substantial soul to each individual, but remaining singularly in himself, a magnificent distributor from his own fullness, he divides and bestows specific powers to each. Like the Sun warming all things subject to it, he nourishes all, and without any diminishing of himself, from his inexhaustible*

<column-break/>

*abundance, he lends and imparts what is enough and sufficient for all.* Gregory Nazianzen <note>4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople</note> agrees with this in Oration 37 (the fifth on Theology), who calls the world <term>the mind of the universe and the mind from without or arriving from the outside <note>original Greek: τὸν τοῦ παντὸς καὶ τὸν θύραθεν νοῦν</note></term>.

<margin>The Maker and Ruler of the World.</margin>
But to the matter at hand: what is understood in this place by the *Spirit of God* has been questioned and debated among the learned both in the past and in our own age. Setting aside the opinions of the Ancients in the Church, let us at least review those of the more recent scholars. One group maintains that *air* or *wind* is meant by these Mosaic words; another the *Holy Spirit*; and a third the *third person of the Holy Trinity*. The Photinians <note>A group denying the pre-existence of Christ and the personality of the Holy Spirit</note> still undertake the defense of the former view today. Among them, Enjedinus considers not only this but whatever probable arguments have been brought by anyone to this passage—even the opinion of Franciscus Valesius in his *Sacred Physiology, chapter 1, page 28* regarding Elementary fire—for the purpose of evading the orthodoxy of the Faithful concerning that Spirit of God, whom they worship and venerate with the Father and the Son as the true and eternal GOD. The modern Jews side with the Photinians, but against Scripture and their own older associates. Psalm 33:6 explains the *Spirit of the mouth* hovering as <term>the Spirit of the mouth of GOD <note>original Hebrew: רוח פיו</note></term>, by which he testifies that all the host of heaven was prepared. Who, therefore, would be of such hardened brow <note>so bold/shameless</note> as to dare oppose himself to the Holy Spirit so clearly and openly explaining the Mosaic passage, and attempt to explain it as a natural wind, which at that time was not yet in the nature of things? The Jerusalem Targum <note>An Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible</note> also points to this when it says: <term>The Spirit of mercies from before the face of the Lord was breathing upon the face of the waters <note>original Aramaic: ורוח רחמין וגו׳</note></term>. So too *Baal Hatturim* <note>Jacob ben Asher, Jewish scholar</note> explains that <insert>hovering</insert> Spirit through Gematria <note>Jewish numerology</note> as the Spirit of the Messiah, saying from the ancient book *Bereshit Rabbah*: <term>this is the Spirit of the King Messiah <note>original Hebrew: זה רוחו של מלך המשיח</note></term>; namely, that of which Isaiah 11:1 prophesied, that *the Spirit of Jehovah shall rest upon the Messiah*. To this is added what is read in the same manner in *Rabbi Solomon Jarchi* <note>Rashi</note>: <term>The throne of glory stood in the air and hovered over the face of the waters by the Spirit of the mouth of the Holy and Blessed God, and by his word, just as a dove hovers over the nest <note>original Hebrew provided in text</note></term>. Compare Galatinus, book 2 on the *Secrets of Catholic Truth*, chapter 6; and Volume 4 of Glassius, page 224; D. Glassius, *Sacred Christology*, page 34 and following; book 3 of *Sacred Grammar*, chapter 26, page 314; D. Haberkorn, *Syntagma 2*, page 538; Hackspan, *Philological Notes* on this place; Haveman, *Way-Light*, page 490. Nor does it help them that they object regarding the <term>multiple meanings <note>original Greek: πολυσημία</note></term> of the words *Spirit* <note>Ruach</note> and *hovering* <note>Merachephet</note>, and the passive signification, as well as the placement in the feminine gender. For we do not deny that the word *Spirit* in the Sacred writings has <term>many meanings</term>. However, in this place, we do not argue for the Deity of the Holy Spirit from the bare word *Spirit* alone, but from the very heart and circumstances of the text itself; for it is established that it is not simply said that a "spirit" hovered over the waters, but the *Spirit of Elohim* or *of GOD*. Although the addition of the name *Elohim* in Holy Scripture sometimes denotes <term>increase</term> or the *excellence of a thing*, nevertheless, from the perpetual use and custom of Holy Scripture, it is established that by the name "Spirit of the Lord," the Spirit of God is indicated, not...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<page-num>72</page-num>

<margin>The Maker and Ruler of the World.</margin> ...not a created wind or an elementary fire; wherefore Octavius Brancifortius in book 2 *On the Disturbances of Souls*, page 3, says: *I marvel greatly that by some in this passage of Scripture "Spirit" is taken for Wind or air, which God had not yet created; but I marvel more at those who deny that by "Spirit" the Holy Spirit can be understood. Certainly the Divine Spirit, that is, uncreated love proceeding from the divine will, offers life to all things, cherishes all things with a vital breath, comforts, animates, and nourishes them, and adorns and distinguishes animated things with its own gifts.* Nor does the word <term>merachephet</term> <note>Hebrew: מרחפת, usually translated as "hovering" or "moving"</note> denote a mere motion or a passive lying-upon, for this exposition of the text is more a distortion than an explanation. It contradicts the nature of the Hebrew conjugation, which here is the *Piel* <note>An intensive or causative verb form in Hebrew</note>, by its nature impressing an active or transitive notion upon the verbs; therefore, let us not seem to set a <term>hypogrammon</term> <note>Greek: ὑπογραμμὸν, a model for imitation or a rule</note> for the Holy Spirit, or prescribe a way of speaking to Him. Let us rest in the <term>divinely inspired</term> <note>Greek: Θεοπνεύστῳ</note> word of Moses, than which nothing more <term>emphatic</term> <note>Greek: ἐμφατικώτερον</note> can be given. He uses this word, which some translate as "to move" or "to flutter," yet it is more rightly translated as *to brood* <note>Latin: incubare</note>, which indeed seems neutral, but in itself—by reason of its end and use—truly expresses the natural <term>energy</term> <note>Greek: ἐνέργειαν</note> of a bird brooding over its nest, eggs, and chicks. Thus is noted emphatically the action of that divine providence and goodness, by which He so cherishes, defends, leads, and preserves His own, just as a bird broods over its eggs and later its chicks, and cherishes them with its heat, and gradually leads them forth to maturity and flight. So the Holy Spirit was carried over the waters, that in His own time He might animate them. From this it is clear that the Holy Spirit in this place uses a Metaphor taken from birds, which animate eggs by their brooding and offspring. The Hebrew expression itself, says Diodorus of Tarsus in the *Catena*, seems of itself to signify *what we are taught by a Hen while she cherishes her eggs, who with suspended wings, lightly touching them, renders them [alive] with a vital breath: so the Holy Spirit was carried over the waters, that in His own time (it should be read "warmth") He might animate them.* Photius cites the books of this Diodorus.

<margin>On the Holy Spirit and Fate.</margin>
> When black Chaos covered all things, and for the world
> There was neither appearance nor form, God acted within,
> Mingled with the hidden bodies, a secret power,
> Even then arranging the rising walls of the world
> And the various faces of things, and future souls.

From this divine warming came the first motion and the first division of created matter, concerning which Louis de Beaufort says in his *Divine Cosmogony*, book 1, page 18: *Just as birds brood on eggs to form the offspring, flying over and beating with wings to hatch the chick; so the Spirit of God was carried over the abyss—the waters, I say, which like a dead glacial sea were hitherto frozen and would have remained in the same state forever, unless the warmth of the brooding Spirit of God had gradually loosened them as if from frost.* The Spirit, I say, not an Angel, as some wish, nor a wind or a blast stirred up by God, but the Holy Spirit Himself proceeding from the Father and the Son, and by His own force, power, and presence breathing a warm aura into the waters, by whose benefit they might be stirred to motion. From this Mosaic Metaphor seems to have arisen the very ancient and common opinion of the oval form of the World—namely, that the World not only <term>resembles the shape of an egg</term> <note>Greek: ὁμοῖος τῷ τοῦ ὠοῦ σχήματι</note> and enjoys an oval form, as Sanchoniathon of Berytus, the most ancient historian of the Phoenicians, writes, but also that it is an egg and came forth from an egg. Whence also was born the Egyptian—

<column-break/>

<margin>The Maker and Ruler of the World.</margin> —painting of their God, whom they called *Kneph*, whom they were accustomed to paint in such a way *that he produced an Egg from his Mouth*, even if otherwise they represented his image in the form of a man of blue color, holding a belt and a scepter, and on his head a feather, as witnessed by Eusebius in book 3, chapter 3 of *Preparation for the Gospel*. The same is to be determined concerning the Theology of Zoroaster, though most corrupt, who devised that there are Two Gods, the principles of things: one Good, *Oromazon*, born from the purest light; the other Evil, *Arimanium*, from darkness. That the former created twenty-four other Good Gods and enclosed them in an Egg; that the latter produced as many Evil ones, who pierced that Egg, and from there Good things were mixed with evil; compare Plutarch *On Isis and Osiris*. The *Orphic Egg*, arising from the same opinion, is recorded by Athenagoras in his *Embassy for the Christians*, *which, when it was cherished by Hercules (who is also Chronus), burst into two equal parts, of which one, which tended upward, became heaven, and the other lower part became earth.* For that reason those initiated into the Rites of Liber <note>Bacchus/Dionysus</note>, as witnessed by Macrobius in book 7 of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 15, *worshipped the Egg with such veneration that, because of its smooth and nearly spherical form, closed on all sides and enclosing life within itself, they called it a likeness of the World.*

<margin>Symposiac Questions, 3.</margin> So Plutarch witnesses: *The Egg was consecrated in the Bacchic Orgies as an example of that which generates all things and contains all in itself.* So Aphrodisiensis in his *Problems* *said that the appearance of this Universal Orb is demonstrated in the Egg; for it both consists of four elements, and is so gathered into a sphere, and contains a vital power within itself.* Hence Eggs, being cleansing and lustral, were used for expiations. Hence in the Cereal procession <note>Procession for Ceres, goddess of agriculture</note> an Egg used to be made first, as Varro reports.

<margin>On Agriculture.</margin> Also in the dinner of the Ancients, the first food was an Egg, from which the proverb *from the egg to the apples* <note>Latin: ab ovo ad mala; meaning from the beginning to the end of a meal</note> seems to have been born, which Porphyry explains: *from the beginning of the Dinner to the end*; compare Ursinus, *Sacred Analects*, book 5, page 243. Therefore, the word <term>merachephet</term> notes the strongest <term>energy</term> <note>Greek: ἐνέργειαν</note> and action of the Holy Spirit—namely, communicating life, motion, and essence to all things in creation. Whence Basil says in *Homily 2 on the Hexaemeron*: *He warmed and gave life to the nature of the waters according to the image of a brooding bird, and introduced a certain vital power to the things being warmed.* And Augustine in book 1, chapter 18 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis* (who however is not consistent with himself, since in chapter 4 of the *Unfinished Literal Meaning of Genesis* he records three opinions on these words): *That which was said through the Greek and Latin languages concerning the Spirit of God, that it was carried over the water, according to the understanding of the Syrian language, which is close to Hebrew (for this is said to have been explained by a certain Syrian Christian Doctor), it was not carried over, but rather CHERISHED, as eggs are cherished by birds, where that heat of the mother's body also assists in some way in forming the chicks, through a certain affection of love in its kind.* This, as Dr. Glassius rightly notes in book 3 of his *Grammar*, canon 26, page 314, which Augustine interjects concerning the language of the Syrians (which Basil also has, who relates that he received this meaning from a certain Syrian), must be understood concerning the meaning of the word <term>rachaph</term> in that Syrian language; for in it, it expresses an affection of pity, corresponding to the Greek <term>viscera</term> <note>Greek: σπλάγχνα, literally "bowels" or "inward parts," used for deep compassion</note> of mercy in Philippians 2:1 and Colossians 3:12. And this is indeed conformable to the meaning placed by Augustine and Basil, but not to the native meaning of this word among the Hebrews,

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
Paradise, the dwelling of Adam and Eve.
</margin>

Regarding Paradise, see Zosimus, *History*, book 3, p. 725; Xenophon, *Oeconomicus*, ch. 8, p. 484; Philostratus in *Life of Apollonius*; Cicero, *On Old Age*, vol. 4, col. 553; Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book 2, ch. 20, p. 91.

Suidas maintains that the word is of Greek origin, deriving it from <term>para</term> <note>original: "παρὰ"</note> meaning "beside" and <term>deuo</term> <note>original: "δεύω"</note> meaning "to water," so that it denotes a well-watered and fruitful garden; hence it is called by Nonnus an <term>endeudios paradeisos</term> <note>original: "ἐνδεύδιος παράδεισος"; a "well-watered paradise"</note>. From this comes the verbal noun <term>deusos</term> <note>original: "δεῦσος"</note> by changing the 'u' to 'i', on which consult Gualtperius on *Genesis ch. 2* and Pererius's *Commentary on this passage*. Others contend it is named from <term>para ten deisan pyein</term> <note>original: "παρὰ τὴν δέισαν πύειν"</note>, that is, from a "collection of herbs," as noted by Cornelius à Lapide.

<margin>
Commentary on Genesis ch. 2, p. 66.
</margin>

Furthermore, Franciscus Junius and Tremellius prefer to write this word in Greek with an *eta* (η) rather than an *epsilon* (ε). However, "I see no reason for this spelling," says Otto Gualtperius in *Genesis 2:8, p. 111*. For the common spelling with *epsilon* (ε) relies on the authority of both Sacred and Profane writers: the Evangelist Luke, Paul, the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, and elsewhere; among the Fathers, Ambrose in *On Paradise ch. 5* and others; and among profane authors, Xenophon, Plutarch, Pollux, Gellius, and others throughout.

<margin>
Luke 23:43; 2 Cor. 12:4; Gen. 2:15 / ch. 13:10.
</margin>

But whatever the case regarding the first origins of this word, it is known from the sacred texts that <term>paradeison</term> <note>paradise</note> occurs chiefly in a threefold meaning. First, it denotes any most pleasant place, most delightful for a man's enjoyment. Whence it is said in *Genesis 13:10* that Lot lifted up his eyes and saw the whole plain of Jordan, that it was entirely well-watered, before the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, <term>kegan-yehovah</term> <note>original Hebrew: "כגן־יהוה"</note> "like the garden of Jehovah"; the LXX translates <term>as paradeisos tou theou</term> <note>original: "ὡς παράδεισος τοῦ θεοῦ"</note>, and hence the Latin, "like the paradise of the Lord." Secondly, it denotes heaven, the place of the blessed, due to a spiritual pleasantness which is metaphorically similar to physical pleasure, according to D. Glassius, *Sacred Rhetoric, tr. 1, ch. 11, p. 292*. Thirdly, by this word is understood the garden planted in Eden, in which Adam and Eve were placed, which is the meaning that now concerns our pen. Therefore, this garden is distinguished by this most excellent name. While in *Gen. 2:15 and 3:24* it is called the "Garden in Eden," the society of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint translators</note> substituted the word <term>paradeisos</term> <term>kat' exochen</term> <note>original: "κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν"; meaning "pre-eminently"</note> to imply that this garden was planted by God in a most pleasant place, adorned with the most fertile trees and their sweetest fruits, and watered by most abundant rivers. Yet this garden is said to be planted <term>be-eden</term> <note>original Hebrew: "בעדן"</note> "in Eden"; a word which admits various meanings. In part it signifies "pleasure," from which some derive the Greek <term>hedone</term> <note>original: "ἡδονὴ"; pleasure</note>, almost agreeing with the Hebrew <term>ednah</term> <note>original: "עדנה"</note> or "pleasure," with which our word *Wollust* <note>German: "delight" or "lust"</note> almost coincides in Latin. With the Hebrew <term>eden</term> <note>original: "עדן"</note> our word *Heide* <note>German: "heath" or "meadow"</note> agrees; hence we say "a beautiful green heath" <note>original: "ein schöne grüne Heide"</note>. In part, it signifies a place named after pleasure; which is the sense of the word in this passage. For <term>eden</term> <note>original: "עדן"</note> denotes any garden, to which "in Eden" is added for the sake of difference and distinction, to denote both the place and the quality of the place as distinct and pre-eminent from others. Therefore, it is inconveniently translated in this passage as "garden of pleasure," although we do not deny it is used for pleasure elsewhere, namely in *Ezekiel 28:13*; since the prefix *beth* (ב) <note>The Hebrew preposition "in"</note> sufficiently implies that in this passage it is not only a proper name, but also marks a place named for its pleasantness or pleasure and delights. This also seems to be indicated by so many descriptions later added to this little word, which truly apply to a place; for it is said to have been a Para-

<column-break/>

<margin>
Paradise, the dwelling of Adam and Eve.
</margin>

-dise in the region of Eden toward its Eastern side, watered by a certain great spring, which was afterwards divided into four great and most famous rivers, and that this river went out from Eden to water paradise. All these things signify a description of a place more than sufficiently. Whence Pererius, in his commentary on this passage, openly contradicts the Vulgate: "To me," he says, "it seems most likely that by this word Moses designates a certain place in which Paradise was located." Whence also Hopkinson says: "That place in which Paradise was, is called by the name <term>Eden</term> <note>original: "עדן"</note> from its abundance and delights, as it truly was such." For the Hebrews are most significant in the imposition of names, and finally in their work: so that they agree as closely as possible with the things themselves. It is, therefore, as if you were to say: The Lord planted a Paradise <term>en tryphero topo kai kalo</term> <note>original: "ἐν τρυφερῷ τόπῳ καὶ καλῷ"</note>, that is, in a delicate and pleasant place. According to Dracontius:

->A garden in God's world more happy than all gardens.<-

<margin>
Malachi 3:12.
</margin>

So that Paradise is truly a <term>eretz chefetz</term> <note>original Hebrew: "ארץ חפץ"</note> "a land of desire, a land of pleasure." Which we say was created on the third day, like every tree desirable to the sight and good for food; contrary to Jerome, who in vol. 4 of *Hebrew Traditions on Genesis*, gathers from the word <term>mi-kedem</term> <note>original: "מקום" (likely a typo for מקדם in the source)</note> that Paradise was founded before heaven and earth. But this is against the genuine meaning of the word, since for <term>mi-kedem</term>, Aquila put <term>apo arches</term> <note>original: "ἀπὸ ἀρχῆς"; from the beginning</note>; Symmachus indeed <term>ek protes</term> <note>original: "ἐκ πρώτης"; from the first</note>; and Theodotio <term>en protois</term> <note>original: "ἐν πρώτοις"; among the first things</note>. Compare *Proverbs 8:22*, where <term>kedem</term> <note>original: "קדם"</note> denotes "the beginning" <note>original: "ἀρχὴν"</note>; yet in this place it refers rather to the description of the place than the time, as the words of *Genesis 3:24* sufficiently prove, which are used in the same sense regarding the garden of Eden; compare a similar passage in *Genesis 11:1*. Hence the LXX also translated it "toward the East" <note>original: "κατὰ τὰς ἀνατολὰς"</note>, because in respect to Judea, that garden was situated in the Eastern region of the world.

Furthermore, setting aside (though not entirely omitting) the opinions of others built upon a "spiritual Paradise" in this passage, let us state the truth: that Paradise was a physical place, which also, when all things were devastated, was lost through the flood as far as its elegance and the peculiar <term>kosmoteta</term> <note>original: "κοσμότητα"; order/beauty</note> of the place are concerned. Let us hear Hopkinson while he writes:

<margin>
On Paradise, p. 9, 10.
</margin>

> Others have believed that Paradise was on the earth, but has now been taken away by the judgment of God. *Whether that is plainly to be admitted, I doubt.* The Fathers decide quite otherwise and go against that opinion. Its appearance could indeed be changed by various accidents, but who would dare to say that its place and seat no longer exist? And Paradise was subject to accidents, just like all other mortal things. For such is the nature of gardens, that they can easily become neglected. And this is perhaps the reason why that garden, which now lies uncultivated and shapeless, is found by the men of our age not without great difficulty. Nor should this seem strange to anyone. Jerusalem, the most flourishing city of God, is now overturned; and Zion, the mountain of God, and the sacrosanct Ark of God have long since wasted away with age.

Others rightly include Eden within Babylonia, but they claim its appearance was made different by the flood; however, I do not see the reason for this. For Moses, who wrote after the flood, presents the region of Eden as known to his own age. Furthermore, if it was known in the times of Isaiah and Ezekiel, it certainly could have been better known in the times of Moses, in which such great ruins and changes of nations had not yet occurred as followed afterward. Therefore, even if...
