# From Genesis I. II v. 8.

<margin>
Paradise of Adam and Eve.
</margin>
Regarding Paradise, let us say that although its beauty and elegance were removed by time or the Flood, we must not think that the land of Adam, the rivers, and the locations—which are expressly described by Moses—perished along with them. These are his words. However, opinions are so divided concerning the site of Paradise, as well as its length and breadth, that some err in excess and others in deficiency; some extend it too far, while others contract it too much. We do not know what came into the mind of Augustine, who wrote thus to Orosius: *Paradise is situated in the East, with the Ocean cast between, and far removed from our world, established in the highest place, reaching even to the lunar circle, whence it is said the waters of the flood could not reach it at all.* <note>original: "Paradisus in Oriente situs est... ad lunarem circulum"</note> But what is more similar to Jewish fables than a Paradise still existing? Those who feel this way do not know the Scripture, which first asserts that the garden was situated in the region of Eden; and says it was leased to Adam to cultivate, mentioning trees and rivers—circumstances which certainly find no place outside this earthly globe. Others have spread Eden and the garden itself most widely in the East through Syria, Arabia, Mesopotamia, Damascus, and Egypt. Truly, while these men assign vast estates to Adam to be guarded and cultivated, they do not see that they are uprooting both the nature of things and the convenience of our common Parent, by whose example the Lord of nature taught us that nature ought to be content with little. And who inspired them with such great length and breadth for Paradise? We rather count these among the "curious questions"—uncertain and unnecessary to know—along with Augustine in Book 2 *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins* against Pelagius and Caelestius: *when it is asked what kind of place and where Paradise is, where God placed man made from dust, since nevertheless Christian faith does not doubt that Paradise exists.* <note>original: "cum quæritur, qualis & ubi sit Paradisus..."</note> However, those feel more appropriately who—along with Agostino Steuco, Oleaster, Estius, Bonfrère, Beroaldo, Genebrard, Pereira, Tornielli, Spondano, Marius, Salian, Granado, and Malvenda, whom <margin>2. Hebrew Antiquities 3. sect. 3. p. 325. 326.</margin> Paul Sherlock cites in great number—place that region of Eden in the East, in Mesopotamia, or on the borders of Arabia and Mesopotamia. For Edenna or Edessa is celebrated in Mesopotamia, also called a holy city, perhaps because of the ancient memory of Paradise, which the deluge of the flood surely washed away. And in *Ezekiel* 27:23, as well as *Isaiah* 37:12, mention is made of the place Eden. Nor is it unknown that Mesopotamia was the most fertile of the whole world (see Pliny). <margin>Book 18 Natural History 6. 17.</margin> In this region, therefore, if one may guess, Paradise was situated as a part; but concerning its space and manner and other circumstances, since neither Moses nor other certain writers have written anything, there is finally room for conjectures. For who revealed to *Tostatus* that the length of Paradise was about twelve miles, and its circuit thirty-six or forty? We should be deservedly content with at least that revelation from Holy Scripture: that Paradise was situated in the East. From this eastern position, not only some Fathers but also historians testify that the custom of Christians looking toward the sunrise in prayers flowed forth. Basil, in his book *On the Holy Spirit* to Amphilochius, ch. 27, p. 376, thinks that for this reason the ancients stood toward the sunrise in prayers: because Paradise was situated in the East, and because the ancients, accustomed to praying toward the East,

<column-break/>

wished by that rite to testify to their desire to return to Paradise. Thus the Author of the *Questions*, who exists under the name of Athanasius, felt <margin>Paradise, the home of Adam and Eve.</margin> that they prayed to the East so that, looking back toward Paradise, the suppliants might seek from God the restoration of the ancient Paradise. Mention of this rite is also made by Tertullian in his *Apology* ch. 16 and 30, and in his book *Against the Valentinians* not far from the beginning; Justin in *Questions and Answers to the Orthodox* q. 118; Clement of Rome in *Apostolic Constitutions* book 2, ch. 61; Epiphanius in *Heresy 19, which is that of the Essenes*; Origen in *Homily 5 on Numbers*; Athanasius in *Question 37*; Nazianzen in *Epistle 60 to Philagrius*; Gregory of Nyssa in *Homily 5 on the Lord's Prayer*. Yet the reasons of these men consist in mere conjecture. For what shall be said of Christians for whom Paradise is situated to the West? Should they then have looked to the West for that reason? What of the Pagans, for whom Polydore Vergil <margin>On the Discovery of Things book 5, ch. 9, p. 372.</margin> proves the same custom of praying from Apuleius: that praying facing the East, one silently prays for the increases of the Sun? Which, however, he hands down to be explained by Christians as referring to Christ, the Sun of Justice. Alexander ab Alexandro in book 4 of *Genial Days* p. 224, testifies the same: that it was the custom of the Magi and Persians always to sing to the Gods at first dawn, to give hymns and praises, and to worship the rising Sun. It suffices that Moses indicated it is a terrestrial place, situated in the Eastern region, in which trees were produced from the earth, with rivers and regions which they flow through, near which also Adam is said to have lived after his banishment from Paradise, as well as Cain himself. Therefore, as a finishing touch for a terrestrial Paradise, I am pleased to bring forward the words of Epiphanius: *If therefore there is no sensible Paradise, there is no fountain. If there is no fountain, there is no river. If there is no river, there are no four headwaters; there is no Pishon, and Gihon, and Tigris, and Euphrates. There is no fig tree, there are no leaves, Eve did not eat from the tree, there is no Adam, there are no men, but the truth is henceforth a myth and everything is allegorized.* <note>original Greek: "Εἰ τοίνυν μὴ ἔνι παράδεισος αἰσθητός..."</note>

It remains, therefore, that Paradise was the most fortunate land of all lands, situated under the best region of heaven, which that supreme Fabricator of things indulged more lavishly than other regions to be cultivated and enriched; which was neither liable to southern heats nor subject to northern chills, but was cherished by the best temperament of both poles. It was the *portal and vestibule* or the *preeminence of the age*, indeed of heaven itself, not indeed situated in the spaces of the air and heavens, nor *higher than all the earth*, as Basil, Damascene, and others of the Greek Fathers felt out of an excessive love and zeal for allegory. <margin>Vol. 4 p. 92.</margin> Ambrose fell into nearly the same Scylla <note>A metaphor for a difficult danger or error.</note>, who says by way of a pretext: *A discourse to be undertaken concerning Paradise seems to strike no small heat in us, desiring to investigate and explain what Paradise is, and where it is, or what kind it is.* In the progress of his discourse, he slides down to a mystical interpretation in his usual manner; if we wish to give a taste of this, we first place those words from p. 93: *If Paradise is that in which twigs had sprung up, Paradise seems to be the soul, which multiplies the seed received, in which every virtue is planted, in which there was also the tree of life, that is, wisdom.* Thus Ambrose—to say nothing of others—frequently turns away from the true and proper sense of the letter to forced allegories, so that, having dismissed the historical sense, the history...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES.

Paradise, <margin>The home of Adam and Eve.</margin> turned the story of Paradise into an allegorical sense; in which he followed the lead of Origen, who, to use the words of Blessed Luther, <margin>in Genesis, folio 26.</margin> *was offended by the distance* of the rivers. For he imagined the space of the garden to be like those commonly found among us; therefore he turned to Allegory. He feigns Paradise to be heaven, the trees to be Angels, and the Rivers to be Wisdom. But such trifles are unworthy of a Theologian. Perhaps they would not misbecome a playful Poet. Origen did not see that Moses was writing history, and that concerning things of the past. And condemning the *zeal for allegories* <margin>in chapter IV, folio 67, column 6</margin> in Origen, [Luther] again repeats Origen's fiction concerning Paradise, because it involves and disturbs the history. Origen and Jerome sometimes indulged their own wits. And Augustine also often neglects the historical meaning, especially in the Psalms. For they were persuaded that, especially in the histories of the Old Testament, allegories were the spiritual understanding. History, however, or literal knowledge, was considered the carnal understanding. Origen makes heaven out of Paradise, and Angels out of the trees. If this is so, where will the article of Creation remain? There is need, therefore, especially for beginners <term>tyronibus: novices or students</term> of Holy Scripture, when they approach the reading of the ancient Doctors, to read them with judgment, or rather with a firm resolve to reject those things which are less probable, lest they be deceived by the authority of the name of the Fathers and Doctors of the Church. Let us hear Origen himself, for how willingly he was accustomed to leave the literal sense, indeed to entirely remove and deny it, the present testimony from him will demonstrate; for he says thus of the history of Paradise itself: <margin>Philocal. ch. 1, p. 33.</margin>

> "Who is so foolish as to think that God, after the manner of a husbandman, planted a paradise in Eden towards the east, and placed in it a tree of life, visible and palpable? So that by tasting the fruit with bodily teeth, one would receive life. And again, that one participates in good and evil by eating what is taken from a physical tree. And if God is said to walk in the paradise in the evening, and Adam to hide under the tree, I do not think anyone doubts that these things indicate certain mysteries through a seeming history, and not things that happened physically." <note>original Greek: Τίς ἔχων πλύτιος... This passage from Origen's Philocalia argues that the Genesis account is a spiritual metaphor rather than a literal event.</note>

In this matter, Origen has a most faithful supporter among the more recent writers, Francesco Giorgio of Venice, a man otherwise learned, whom Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a prominent Jesuit cardinal and theologian.</note> wonders could depart from the common opinion of the whole Church for such very slight and weak reasons (*On Grace, book 1, ch. 10*). He published the *Harmony of the World*, and likewise *Problems*, and after he had asked problematically: *Where and how the garden of delights was planted*, he responds: *Was it perhaps on earth, as is the common opinion? Whence also it is falsely called the terrestrial Paradise.* Having explained some dreams, he concludes by dragging out the "new-old" metaphor condemned in Origen by the Fathers: *Thus the garden was planted in the land of the living, of which the Prophet sings: I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. For where could the Tree of Life be better planted than in the land of the living?* Even if, while we tax the excessive zeal for Allegories in Origen and his followers, allegories are not to be entirely sent away, provided they are suitable and the existence of the things themselves is not denied; which happens when, while retaining the literal sense, we say that in them is contained an allusion to more excellent and heavenly things, just as the work of the Tabernacle both exists in the nature of things and is an allusion to things

<column-break/>

<margin>Paradise, the home of Adam and Eve.</margin> heavenly and excellent, as Josephus writes <note>original: *Albo 3. l. c. 21. fol. 161.* likely referring to Joseph Albo, a Jewish philosopher.</note>. Yet in Origen, an immoderate admirer of figurative speech, we find fault that he transfers Paradise from the earth to heaven by the pulley of figures—indeed, by the adultery of figures, to speak with Jerome in his *Letter to Pammachius*—he so allegorizes Paradise that the History loses its truth, understanding Angels for trees, heavenly virtues for Rivers, and subverting the entire content of Paradise with a tropological <term>tropological: a method of interpretation that finds moral or spiritual meanings</term> interpretation. Moreover, Origen drew this comment about a Spiritual Paradise from the allegories of Philo and other Jews. The same also happened to Jerome, who, while applying himself to Hebrew letters among the Jews (as he specifically names a certain teacher of his), sometimes drew something from the turbid decrees of the Rabbis. Among these is what he asserts in *Hebrew Traditions on Genesis ch. 2, v. 8*: that God planted Paradise before He created heaven and earth, namely *Mi-kedem* <note>Hebrew: מקדם, meaning "from the beginning" or "in the east."</note>, which was a tradition of the Jews, who taught that seven things were created before the world was founded, namely: <insert>The Garden of Eden or Paradise, the Law, the righteous, the Messiah, Israel, the throne of glory, and Jerusalem.</insert> <note>original Hebrew: גן עדן תורה צדיקים ומשיח ישׂראל וכסα הכבוד וירושלם</note> Concerning this, see the *Preface* to *Ein Yisrael* on the passage of Genesis 2, and page 3 of *Beit Yisrael*, page 20, and Münster on Genesis chapter 1. Of the same sort is the other dream concerning the continued existence of Paradise. For the Jews dream that Paradise still exists, about which they devise wonders in their own fashion. They say that only four Doctors visited it, who are mentioned by the Talmudists in the *Tractate Chagigah, or on the Festival, chapter two.* Namely, the son of Azzai, the son of Zoma, another certain one, and Rabbi Akiba; of whom the first three are said to have paid the penalty for their rashness, but Akiba alone returned unharmed, more fortunate than the rest; concerning which see Johannes Crojus, *Specimen of Conjectures, page 29.* This Jewish fable is canonized in the Popish Church by Bellarmine among the more recent writers (*On Grace, book 1, ch. 14, § 2*), and that for this reason: *Because truly, he says, I have never read any of the ancients who wrote that the terrestrial Paradise perished either by the waters of the deluge or for any other cause; and on the contrary, I have read many who affirm that it exists*, as do almost all the Scholastics in the *Second Book of Sentences, distinction 17*, and Thomas [Aquinas] in the *First Part, question 102, article 1*; and besides the ancient Fathers Irenaeus, Jerome, Augustine, Theodoret, Bede, Almus, Avitus, etc. *I would not easily dare to depart from such a common and celebrated opinion.* But in truth, a multitude of those in error does not provide a defense for the error. We oppose Bellarmine with his "Cadmean brothers" <note>A reference to brothers who destroy one another; here, fellow Catholic theologians who disagree.</note> who affirm their thesis with too much doubt: Gregory de Valentia, Caspar Sanctius, Barradius, Tirinus, Viegas. Thus that ancient serpent, in whatever way he can, spreads his poison from the pools of the Rabbis—whom you might better call "rabid dogs" than Rabbis.

<margin>Paradise, the dwelling of Adam and Eve.</margin>
...and many other things are read to have been seen there, or transported from there, concerning which Bernardo Aldrete writes in *Antiquities of Spain and Africa, Book 4, Chapters 6 and 7, page 509 and following.* The poets write that in the Golden Age, the gods mingled with men and lived <term>like a god</term> <note>original Greek: ὡς θεὸς</note>. Catullus especially writes of this fellowship of the gods in the *Marriage of Peleus* (Argonautica, page 63, verse 23 and following):

> For the heavenly beings used to visit the chaste homes 
> of heroes in person, and show themselves to the assembly 
> of mortals, before piety was despised.

The poets describe the Golden Age of Saturn in such a way that they seem to have heard rumors of the happiness of Paradise and the full tranquility of all things. Since Hesiod takes the prize among those who support this view, we shall examine his verses, studiously composed <term>concerning the prosperity under Saturn</term> <note>original Greek: εἰς τὴν ἐπὶ τοῦ Κρόνου εὐδαιμονίαν</note>. (*Works and Days, verse 108*):

> When gods and mortal men were born together, 
> first of all the Immortals who hold Olympian homes 
> made a golden race of speaking men. 
> These lived in the time of Saturn, when he reigned in heaven. 
> And they lived like gods, having a heart free from care, 
> apart and far from labors and grief; nor did miserable 
> old age come upon them. Always the same in feet and hands, 
> they delighted in festivities, far from all evils. 
> And they died as if overcome by sleep; all good things 
> were theirs. The grain-giving earth bore fruit 
> of its own accord, much and without stint; and they, willing 
> and peaceful, tended their works amid many good things.

Lucian also mentions this Golden Age while Saturn was reigning (*Saturnalian Letters, page 955*). For those who are ignorant of the knowledge of Divine truth revealed in Moses and the Gospel write about the first age in this way; they move <term>up and down</term> <note>original Greek: ἄνω καὶ κάτω</note>, clinging neither to heaven nor to earth, and hand down the origin of things with a disguised commentary. Regarding the Elysian fields, Quintus Smyrnaeus notes that Pallas [Athena] traveled there, and that there are the ascents and descents of the gods:

> Swiftly she went to the Elysian plain, where is 
> the descent from heaven, and the path back up 
> for the blessed Immortals.

Truly, above all others, to those looking at the ancient poet Hesiod, it seems that the wise man intended nothing else under the cloak of the Golden Age and the covering of Pandora than to place before the eyes of his students this very thing which he had heard—either by the fame of tradition or some other way—concerning Paradise, and the evil which we still experience today due to the Fall of our Paradisiacal Parents. However, when he writes that the first men under Saturn lived <term>apart and far from labors and grief</term> <note>original Greek: νόσφιν ἄτερ τε πόνων καὶ ὀϊζύος</note>, the cultivation of the Garden of Paradise does not seem to admit this; for God gave the fields and the earth to the first men <term>for the purpose of planting</term> <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὸ φυτεῦσαι</note> (*Genesis 2:8, 15*). But was that plantation, <term>both the planting and the husbandry</term> <note>original Greek: καὶ φύτευσις, καὶ γεωργία</note>, truly <term>without labors</term> <note>original Greek: ἄτερ πόνων</note>? Was man in Paradise without work? To Augustine, the matter seemed easy to solve, because after the Fall he noticed that some people farm with such pleasure of the mind (*Book 8 on the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chapter 8, Volume 3, folio 613*) that it is a great punishment for them to be called away from it to something else. From this he concludes that whatever delights agriculture has now, it had far more then,

<column-break/>

<margin>Paradise, the dwelling of Adam and Eve.</margin>
when nothing adverse happened either from the earth or the sky. And then he concludes under the heading of the chapter: *What is so far from the truth if we believe that man was so established in Paradise that he worked not with servile labor, but with an honest pleasure of the mind? For what is more innocent than this to those who call upon it, and what is fuller of great contemplation for the prudent?* That agriculture had no toils and no <term>miseries</term> <note>original Greek: ὀϊζύας</note>; <term>it was neither laborious and wretched, nor difficult and burdensome</term> <note>original Greek: οὐδ᾽ ἦν ἐπίπονος καὶ ταλαίπωρος, οὐδ᾽ χαλεπὸς καὶ ἀχθίς</note>, as Chrysostom also affirms (*Oration 19 to the People of Antioch, at the beginning; and Homily 14 on Genesis chapter 2*). So also Eusebius seeks out traces of the Paradisiacal life and the misery following the Fall from Plato’s *Statesman* (*Preparation for the Gospel, Book 2, 13, page 256 and Book 1, chapter 7*), from the *Library* of Diodorus Siculus, and from Plato’s *Symposium* (*Book 12, chapter 11, page 25*), when they describe the first life of man as naked and without political organization, and the fruitfulness of the earth as <term>unworked</term> <note>original Greek: ἀέργατον</note>. Many testimonies could be piled up here which those who deserted the Church undoubtedly received from the fame of the primeval life and uncertain, doubtful tradition. These people usually betray by various signs—though not manifest, yet not obscure—that they have departed from the signs of the Church and left its solemn Sacraments and public preaching. But content with a parsimony of words, we leave this field to be trodden by others who find pleasure in idling in matters that leave great obscurity behind them. The painstaking labor of the Church Fathers in this deserves praise, since their business was with the Pagans, who had to be met with every kind of weapon. Today no necessity drives us, as Paganism has already fallen. Yet, if any fragment can be known in this internal shipwreck of truth, it should be collected as the occasion allows. For the remains of a shipwreck are also suited for fitting a course toward truth, even if one must sometimes sail with a torn sail. We see at least from these and the examples to follow, that once the foundation of truth is lost, nothing remains but scattered ruins and the vanishing outlines of a solid work. For so they are accustomed to do—those who do not hold a certain foundation for their traditions—to mock most profanely and play with conjectures, than which often nothing more foul or absurd can be devised. Because they had abandoned Moses, the first steward of the histories of the primeval age, nothing remained but for them to wander—and how immensely!—concerning the cradle of the created world, the Paradise of God, and the Adamic Fall. And so the rest raved along with Plato, so that we may not undeservedly say with Scaliger <margin>* Exercise 307, section 11, page 936.</margin>: *Those most pleasant Elysian fields of the Platonists—which of those little Greeks did they not make mad, and drive them to dreams?* From this also arose the fiction that in the Golden Age, rivers of wine flowed everywhere, as in Ovid:

> Now rivers of milk, now rivers of Nectar flowed, 
> and yellow honey dripped from the green oak tree.

And the Author of *Aetna*:

> Who does not know the Golden Age of the carefree King? 
> When no one boasted of grain with conquered arms, 
> and the one to come prohibited bad weeds from the crops, 
> but the annual harvests filled the sated granaries.

# From Genesis II. v. 8. 9.

<margin>Paradise, the dwelling of Adam and Eve.</margin>
The same accounts are read among others, for instance Virgil in *Georgics 1. 125*, Ovid in *Metamorphoses 1. fable 3*, and Tibullus in *Book 1. Elegy 3*. By these, without a doubt, the state of humans living in Paradise is signified. Justin Martyr also thinks this state was sketched by Homer in *Odyssey 7. 114* in the description of the garden of Alcinous <note>Justin Martyr, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, page 21; compare Seber’s *Florilegium*, page 323</note>.

Certainly the *Golden Ages*, of which there are so many memoirs <note>original: ὑπομνήματα (hypomnemata)</note> by poets and others, are rightly understood as referring to the state of innocence; once this was lost, the whole nature of man and of things themselves degenerated from their integrity and perfection. *That ruinous day of the Fall*, to use the word of Horace in *Odes 1. 6*:

->*---- what has it not diminished?*<-

The first of mortals, to imitate the words of Seneca in *Epistle 90*, had God as both Leader and Law, committed to the judgment of a better being. Would that they had followed Him in that incorruption! At the first birth of the human race, there was a *Golden Age* in Paradise, which shone forth among metals just as glittering gold. It was truly a *Golden* age, when for the naked first inhabitants of Paradise, as Silius speaks in *Book 4*:

->*The milky necks of men did not yet shine with yellow collars,*<-
->*Nor were their garments striped with gold, or their sleeves stiff.*<-

The excellence and distinction of Paradise consisted chiefly in three things: namely, in the supreme healthfulness and clarity of the sky and air; in the great abundance of waters watering the garden, with their wonderful transparency and sweetness for drinking; and finally, in the rich fertility of the Paradisiacal soil everywhere. For nothing was lacking of those things which could fill all the senses of man with the sweetest delight and pleasure. God, the most munificent Creator, bestowed taste with the sweetest flavors; smell with the most fragrant herbs and flowers; sight with a variety of colors and beauty of forms; and hearing with the gentlest sound of breathing breezes and the sweet harmony of birds. Finally, the sum of nourishment from the fruits of so many flourishing herbs and trees provided healthfulness and joy in as great an abundance as could be desired, with the ease of preparation without any labor or human trouble. For among the trees, the *Tree of Life* stood out. No greater tree grew in the world than the *Tree of Life*, and indeed in that most blessed habitation; nor one more considered than the *Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil* in the same place. Each, among the delights of that most blessed dwelling, contained a sacrament within itself: *One of Life*, if man should eat from it; the other *of Death*, if the inhabitant dared to eat, or, what is the same, to neglect God’s command and pollute himself by eating what was forbidden. Concerning both, Moses writes thus in *verse 9*, with which compare *verse 16, 17 and chapter 3, verse 22, 24*:

> And out of the ground the Lord God made every tree grow that is pleasant to the sight and good for food; the tree of life was also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. <note>original: Hebrew text provided in source</note>
>
> And God made to spring up yet out of the earth every tree beautiful to the eye and good for food, and the tree of life in the midst of Paradise, and the tree to know the knowledge of good and evil. <note>original: Greek Septuagint text provided in source</note>
>
> And the Lord God produced from the ground every tree beautiful to the sight, and sweet for eating. The tree—

<column-break/>

—also of life in the midst of Paradise; and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

<margin>Paradise, the dwelling of Adam and Eve.</margin>
Paradise was planted with various trees like an orchard, among which the *Tree of Life* stood out <note>original: עֵץ הַחַיִּים (*Etz HaChayim*)</note>, *THE TREE OF LIVES*, where a double Hebraism occurs; for both *of Lives* is said for *life*, and again *tree of life*, according to the custom of the Holy Language <note>Hebrew</note> which lacks adjectives, is placed for "vital" or "life-giving tree." <note>Compare Giovanni Stefano Menochio in *Brief Explanation of the Bible* on Gen 2:9; Jacques Bonfrère in *Pentateuch Illustrated*; Willem Estius in *Annotations on Difficult Passages of Holy Scripture*, p. 4; Leonardus Marius on the *Pentateuch*, p. 28.</note> Chrysostom, and Flacius who follows him in this matter, seem to establish nothing certain when intending to give the reason for the naming of this tree. For the former says: *If some curious person asks why it was called the tree of life: let him know that if we rely on our own reasons, man cannot behold all the works of God. For it seemed good to the Lord that the man made by Him and living in Paradise should have a certain meditation on obedience and disobedience.* However, Augustine is bolder in giving the reason for this name, saying the TREE OF LIFE was so called and named FROM ITS EFFECT. He claims the power of this tree was so great that eating it could confer immortality on man forever and preserve him immune from corruption. <note>Augustine, *The City of God*, book 14, chapters 20 and 23.</note> And Blessed Luther in his *Commentary on Genesis, p. 20* describes it: *Moses describes Paradise so as to make God a gardener, who planted that garden according to His will with great diligence, choosing one or two trees which He tends and loves above the rest. One of these was the tree of life, created for this purpose: that man, eating from it, might be preserved with an intact body, without diseases, and without fatigue.* Dr. Gerhard also writes in his *Commentary on Genesis, p. 51*, that the reason for the name depends on the effect of this tree—namely, on bodily life, not spiritual—which is evident to the eye. He says it is called the tree of lives: *1. because it would have granted the longest life to man. 2. it would have given man not only to live, but to live well, i.e., to live in tranquility and pleasure. 3. it would not only have restored consumed natural moisture, but also renewed what was lost.* Most of the Roman Catholic scholars agree with this opinion, namely Tostatus, Cornelius à Lapide, Menochio, Bonfrère, Estius, Marius, and others. From all of whom it is clearer than the midday light that the Tree of Life was produced by GOD for the sake of the first man, to supply life to both Adam and his descendants, and to make it for them most long and sweet. Which good he could have enjoyed, had Adam not lost it through sin. The same is also gathered from *Genesis 3:22*: namely, that it was so called from an intrinsic and natural, not supernatural, faculty of preserving the life of man from old age, disease, and death until the natural term, at which point he would have been translated without pain or death into spiritual and heavenly life. <note>Compare Dr. Gerhard, *Isagoge*, Dissertation 22, chapter 9, § 20.</note> However, as to how far that Virtue extended:

# On Genesis Chapter II. verse 9.

<margin>Paradise, the dwelling of Adam and Eve.</margin>
It seems that their opinion is approved by what we read in chapter 3, verse 7: *And the eyes of both were opened, etc.* From this, some have thought that the First-Created <note>original: "Protoplastos," referring to Adam and Eve</note> were created blind by God; and the Ophites <note>A Gnostic sect that revered the serpent</note> according to Epiphanius in *Heresies 31*, worshipped the serpent in place of CHRIST, because he was the author who helped men acquire knowledge when he persuaded them to eat of the forbidden tree. But in truth, the voice of God teaches that all things were lost through the eating of the forbidden tree, when, pitying the First-Created in chapter 3, verse 22, He said: *Behold Adam, he has become as one of us.* Therefore, Lyra, intending to refute their error, uses this argument above all: *A physical thing does not have power over an incorporeal thing.* This is more broadly deduced by Mercerus the Reformer, the Royal Professor of the Hebrew language at Paris <margin>in his lectures on Genesis, p. 50.</margin> It does not seem consistent, he says, *since the Tree is material and physical, that it should provide this power of understanding to an incorporeal thing.* And he adds: *Furthermore, the event shows that the eating of this brought something else to man, since instead of making him the most knowledgeable of all, it rendered him the most ignorant.*

Nor, secondly, does the reason for the name depend on the false persuasion and deception of Satan practiced upon Adam and Eve, when he said to them: *You shall be as Gods, knowing good and evil.* For that ancient and masked serpent who in chapter 3, verse 5 seduced Eve, and through her later Adam, had promised the woman "golden mountains" <note>An idiom meaning extravagant, impossible promises</note>, saying among other things: *For God knows that on whatever day you eat of it, your eyes shall be opened, etc.* But the human race even now deplores and experiences how sad an outcome followed this false promise, which the Father of Lies had brought forth. Of no nobler coinage is the opinion of a certain man regarding the Tree of Life, whose naming some have tried to assert arose or was taken from a specific dispute with the Devil; Hakspan <margin>Philological notes on this passage, p. 62.</margin> refutes his arguments at length, where among other things he urges that this new opinion about the tree of life opposes both Holy Scripture and all the best interpreters. For it would be absurd for a formula of speaking devised and instilled by Satan to have persisted and been used by those <term>inspired by the Holy Spirit</term> <note>original Greek: ϑεοπνεύματος ἁγίος φερόμενος</note>. Think of David in *Psalm 69:29*, Solomon in *Proverbs 3:18*, and He who must be placed in the first rank, the mouth of truth, Christ the Savior, who in *John 6:48* <note>The text cites Jos. 6:48, likely a typo for John</note> calls himself the bread of life, alluding without doubt by the word "bread" to the Hebrew <term>bread/food</term> <note>original Hebrew: לחם (Lechem)</note> which signifies *any kind of food*; whence also the tree of life is allegorically a symbol of Christ in *Luke 23:31, Revelation 2:7, and 22:2.* Truly, this tree received its name, and indeed before the fall, <term>from God</term> <note>original Greek: ϑειόϑεν</note>, that is, from the purpose and use of the tree divinely established. For God led the recently created man to that tree as if to an altar and a temple, where He explained the sum of His Divine will to him in a command both very brief and very easy: *You shall not eat,* He said, *of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil: For on whatever day you eat, you shall die the death.* This is the same as if we were to say that the reason for the naming of this tree is sought from its end [purpose]. *For this tree was,* to use the words of Blessed Gerhard, *like a certain altar and temple, in which he might learn* <margin>Commentary on Genesis p. 49. Isagogical Disputation 22. c. 9. §. 20.</margin> *how great a good it is to persist in created integrity, and how great an evil it is to fall away from it.* However, with Augustine in book 8 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis, ch. 15 and book 14 of The City of God, ch. 17*, whom Theodoret also follows in *Question 26 on Genesis*, Blessed Luther in *Commentary on Genesis p. 21*, Hugo the

<column-break/>

Cardinal in *Genesis ch. 2*, Dionysius the Carthusian in *Expositions on Genesis ch. 2, folio 23*, Torniellus in the *Annals, first part, p. 50*, Rivetus in *Exercise 18 on Genesis p. 74*, and Mercerus on *this passage*: We say that this Tree is so named by prolepsis or a certain anticipation of a future event and *experience*, because after Adam erred regarding the fruit, he not only saw and experienced how many goods he lost, but also how much misery he brought upon himself and all his posterity. Hence, after the fall, it is no longer the *tree of knowledge of good and evil* in terms of experience regarding us, but now we experience only *evil*; therefore, after the fall, it can be called the *Tree of the knowledge of evil*. Of what species this tree was, however, is most uncertain. Theodoret in *Question 37 on Genesis p. 9*, Moses Bar-Cepha in *chapter 19 on Paradise*, and others defend that it was a Fig tree, from which the first Parents made themselves loincloths. But it will not be easily proved whether those leaves, from which the first parents prepared loincloths for themselves, were taken from the tree of knowledge of Good and Evil. For the contrary is far more probable: that the parents, both out of hatred and also fear lest by that very act their transgression be betrayed and made manifest, did not make loincloths for themselves from it. To this is also added that Eve, after eating from the forbidden tree, did not linger long around it, but immediately, as is believable, hurried to her absent husband, explaining the deed so that he too might eat, persuading him; which the Mosaic words seem to hint at: *For she took of its fruit and ate, and gave to her husband, who ate.* By which very thing it is gathered by no small conjecture that Adam was absent, and Satan spoke with Eve alone at this tree while Adam was away, and persuaded her to pluck and eat of the forbidden fruit. Goropius Becanus in *book 5 of Indo-Scythica* and Beccefel p. 485 and following, tries to prove that the wood of the knowledge of good and evil was the Indian fig, about which Pliny tells many wonders. <margin>* Book 12 ch. 5. Book 13 ch. 7. 53.</margin> And regarding the Egyptian fig, Solinus says: *The orchards of the Indians* <margin>* ch. 52.</margin> *have figs whose trunks swell to a space of sixty paces in a circle, the shade of the branches consumes two stadia in circumference, the width of the leaves is compared to the shape of an Amazonian shield, and the fruit is of extraordinary sweetness.* Those who have traveled the world in our age report that on the Island of Zamal, which with others is called the *Isle of Thieves* <note>The Ladrones or Mariana Islands</note>, figs of admirable vastness are found, which have oblong fruits to the measure of a palm, and their leaves spread to the width of an arm. The Egyptian fig, with leaves to be compared to a mulberry, bears fruit not only on the branches but on the trunk; it is so majestic in its fertility that it produces fruit seven times in one year—where you pluck a fruit, another swells out without delay. Hence Balthasar Nugnez, from the *Kingdom of Travancore in 1548*, concludes it is no wonder that Eve, moved by the elegance of the tree, ate its fruit, and afterwards with her husband sewed loincloths for themselves from it because of the size of the leaves. But while the Sacred Codex testifies that the first parents made coverings from a fig, it is not thereby proven that the tree of knowledge of good and evil was a fig, especially because of the description we read attributed to this tree by Moses: it is called <term>a delight to the eyes</term> <note>original Hebrew: תאוה לעינים (Ta'avah la-einayim)</note>, which in Hebrew is emphatically *desire itself to the eyes*, that is, so desirable that it was desire itself to the eye—

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
## Page 82

<margin>The dwelling of Adam and Eve.</margin>
**Paradise** would seem to be a place of colors. Thus, the abstract term for the dwelling is emphatically used for the concrete. The *Targum Onkelos* <note>An ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Torah</note> translates it as the dwelling of **Adam and Eve**, and adds that it was *health to the eyes*. This does not mean it possessed a medicinal power to heal eyes, but that it fed the eyes sweetly with its appearance—something that does not apply to a mere fig tree. Others, therefore, letting the fig tree pass, turn to other trees. There are those who think it was an **apple**;
<margin>From Song of Solomon 8:5 and Matthew 26:27.</margin>
this comes as a theory, for in the *Song of Solomon* almost everything is parabolic, and for that reason, such things produce no firm argument. Mention was made of a certain tree by **John Mandeville** <note>original: "Johannes de Montevilla"</note>, an Englishman; **Fr. Felix Faber** of the Dominican Order; **Melchior von Seidlitz**; and others in their *Eastern Travels*. It is called the **Musa** <note>The banana tree</note> by the Egyptians, the **Adam’s Apple** <note>original: "Pomo d' al Adamo"</note> by the Italians, and is called *Maus* or *Musa* by **Simone Maiolo**
<margin>Hieronymus Canini, Vol. 1, colloquy 21, on plants.</margin>
following Leo Africanus. The Turks believe this to be the tree we are now discussing: the **Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil**. Furthermore, *Mandeville* reports that the aforementioned fruit has a bite-mark not unlike a human bite. However, *Leo* is contrary to the rest here, writing that the leaves of this tree occupy the measure of one arm's length in every direction. See regarding these matters **Andreas Rivetus** in his *Cosmography of the East*, which **Gregor Horst**, Doctor of Medicine and Professor at Giessen, translated into German and published in an expanded edition; there you will also find a figure of this tree quite elegantly depicted in copperplate. But why do we desire more uncertainty in an uncertain matter? It will therefore be safest to say: *it is not clear what kind of tree this was*. This, alas, is clear to us: that our First Parents, by the transgression of this Divine precept, fell into the deepest misery along with all their posterity. For the first parents delighted in Paradise; Eve walked before Adam at his side, deferring honor to him with love and kisses. Various fruits delighted the eyes, there was an abundance of all things, and Paradise was the heaven of the earth—a microcosm of the macrocosm. Everything was given for their use except this one single tree, which was called the **Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil**. And a single law was given: not against theft, for all things belonged to Adam; not against adultery, for there was only one wife; but against unlawful desire and wicked craving, or *unlawful appetite* <note>original Greek: παράνομον ὄρεξιν</note>. God said to him,
<margin>Oration 3, p. 22.</margin>
as **Basil** says: *“The abundance of my provision overcomes your need; Paradise is a wide space for your desires. Where you see the Word written, there restrain your longing. Flee the sight of that food, as it is the poison of life. Turn away your gaze which leads the way toward transgression. Flee the sight so that you may be saved.”* <note>Translated from Basil's original Greek</note> For this law is, as it were, the matrix of all precepts, from which all things later given through Moses sprouted, as the Doctors try to prove emphatically from the Hebrew word *mimenu* <note>original: ממנו, meaning "from it"</note>. Therefore, by the command of one thing, God wished to rouse Adam so that his pleasure and desire for lawful things might be greater, and that a remembrance of God might enter his mind—the God who had granted all things on this condition: that he abstain from only one. **Basil of Seleucia** says even more elegantly in *Oration 3, p. 19*: *“The first decree of the King, granting food and establishing a good law. ‘Have,’ He says, ‘authority over all things, but stay away from only one. Let the hand be extended toward everything, but let it be drawn back from one. Let the setting aside of that which is outside be a reminder to you of Him who gave all things, lest luxury flowing from every side bring forgetfulness of the memory*

<column-break/>

<margin>Of Adam and Eve.</margin>
*of grace, and lest by the greed of eating you slip into ignorance.’”* And later on p. 21: *“Have immeasurable enjoyment; only stay your hand from a meal judged to be improper. Show, by the guarding of the law, honor to the Lawgiver. Let me see your intent, so that I may marvel at your love. Give me thanks by drawing back your hand—I who gave the whole of Paradise, yet set apart only one tree. Repay your Benefactor with temperance in tasting.”* <note>Translated from Basil of Seleucia's original Greek</note> The Giver of all Paradise was to be preferred; every tree was to be preferred over the single tree. The Law was given for the exercise of free will and power in choice; and that Law was set forth on the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil like a tablet or a notice-board, so that the edict hung before their eyes on the Tree, showing what was to be done and what was to be avoided. *“Having clothed man with the gift of free reason, He gave him a law, exercising his choice; and as if sketching the commandment on the plant as on a writing tablet, He examined the hidden judgment within, attaching the difference between obedience and disobedience to the tree. From this, the tree is named the knowledge of good and evil. For from the things that were taught, the tree was named, and the teaching of that time became the name of the plant.”* <note>Translated from the Greek</note>

<margin>In Genesis, Homily 15.</margin>
With this, **Chrysostom** agrees excellently, writing in almost identical words: *“I do not ask anything troublesome or heavy of you: for I permit you to enjoy all things. One thing I command: do not touch. And I decree a great penalty, so that even restrained by fear, you might keep the mandate given by me.”* He did this like a liberal master, granting a large house to someone, and so that his Lordship might remain secure for himself, he prescribes that only a small sum of money be given by the tenant. So indeed our merciful Lord, having granted the fruit of all things in Paradise, commanded him to abstain from only one tree, so that he might know he is under a Lord, whom he ought to obey and serve if He should command anything. From these things it is clear that it was very easy for our first Parents to obey the mandate they received, and that they could have served God with the greatest pleasure of mind. Hence,
<margin>Blessed Luther, Commentary on Genesis, p. 23, folio 6.</margin>
**Blessed Luther** calls this Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil the **Church**, *“to which Adam with his posterity would have gathered on the Sabbath day, and after refreshment from the Tree of Life, he would have preached God and praised Him for the dominion handed over of all creatures upon the earth. He would have exhorted his descendants to live holily and without sin, to work faithfully in the garden and guard it diligently, and to beware with the greatest zeal of the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. Man would have had this external place, rite, and worship; afterward he would have returned to his work and guarding, until the preordained time was fulfilled, when he would have been translated into heaven with the greatest sweetness.”* These are his words. But truly, even if this precept of religion (as it is called by **Blessed Rungius** in his commentary on this passage) was not heavy, it was unique and particular, by which the abstinence from the fruit of a certain tree was forbidden to Adam, with a majestic and severe threat of eternal death; for God says, *“Of the tree of knowledge of good and evil”* (original Hebrew: ומעץ הדעת טוב ורע) *“you shall not eat; for in the day that you eat of it,* **dying you shall die** <note>original Hebrew: מות תמות, *mot tamut*</note>.”
<margin>Chapter 2, verse 17.</margin>
This phrase contains an emphasis, and notes the certainty, perfection, and *increase* of the matter. For this doubling among the Hebrews increases and intensifies the sense, or denotes certainty. *“By death you shall die.”*

# From Genesis II. v. 9. 10.

<margin>Paradise, the home of Adam and Eve.</margin>
Paradise, therefore, is: "you shall surely die" <note>original: *omninò vel certissimè morieris*</note>. Just as in *Genesis 37:33* it is said of Joseph, "torn in pieces," that is, "surely or certainly torn." Facius <margin>in *The Key to Scripture* col. 673. Glassius *Sacred Philology* book 3. canon 37. p. 350.</margin> *in The Key to Scripture col. 673. Glassius Sacred Philology book 3. canon 37. p. 350.* Yet Adam, for the sake of his wife—who was seduced by Satan and deceived by false persuasions—immediately violated this law by a spontaneous and most free will; *for he was not driven by any violent external impulse,* as Episcopius writes in *Theological College p. 50. nor was he led to that violence by any secret or hidden determination from God; nor did he fall into this sin through the removal, omission, or denial of some action necessary to avoid sin; nor finally was he enticed by God to transgress through any command, order, or hidden instinct. Rather, he fell into sin by the pure and simple freedom of his choice, immune from any internal necessity of external things, with only the persuasion of the Devil leading the way (which can bring no necessity), and the desirable fruit alluring him without any force properly so called.* It can be said in its own way that there was some objective enticement of the illicit fruit in the Fall, for the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was <margin>Genesis 3:6</margin> *desirable to the eyes* <note>original Hebrew: *תאוה הוא לעינים*</note>, and *a tree to be desired to make one wise* <note>original Hebrew: *ונחמד העץ*</note>, *and she took of its fruit and ate. And she gave also to her husband with her, and he ate.* But oh, most unhappy hand, which against the prohibition offered the husband a taste of death from the unhappy tree! This apple of Paradise bitten by Eve had no poison in itself, but the fountain of evil poison was instilled into the soul by the Serpent; who, moved by envy, crept in, laid snares, attacked Eve, and through a light temptation achieved her immediate assent to the deceiver, neglecting the command of the Creator. She soon dragged her husband with her, and together they drew into evil not just one Adam, but all those born of Adam <term>Adamigenas: descendants of Adam</term>. What then have you done, O man, what have you wrought? By transgression you have undermined the covenant—what a great covenant, what a blessed covenant! By the violation of the law you have alienated your Maker—what a great Lord, what a benevolent Creator, from whom you had received both life and the possession of such a most blessed and pleasant garden, and the full power to enjoy it! To your fall, alas! to your fall, O Adam, we attribute the wretched condition of human life, which is now common to us in the whole race of mortals. To the Fall we attribute whatever troubles there are, whatever calamities, whatever vanities. From this comes the brevity of human life, from this comes death, from this the many images of death, from this so many forms of misery that they are innumerable to everyone. From this comes such darkness of human minds, from this such depravity of the will, that we may rightly repeat with Theodotus:

> <margin>Eclogue 1. 41.</margin>
> *The first man was an inhabitant in green Paradise,*
> *Until, by the persuasion of his spouse, he drank*
> *The viper’s poison; by mixing that cup of death for all,*
> *His offspring still feel what the Parents committed.*
> *The First-Formed <term>Protoplastus: a term for Adam as the first created being</term> wails, cast out from the holy seat,*
> *And the honor of nature changes, ashes to ashes.*
> *Lest he should return forever because of the tree's fruit,*
> *A flaming sword before the gates forbids those wishing to enter.*

Thus far was the first ornament of Paradise, namely trees of every kind, and especially the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

<column-break/>

Now follows the second glory and ornament of the same, namely the rivers, by which the region of Eden was most pleasantly and fruitfully watered, concerning which and their source Moses continues in the description of Paradise *v. 10. seqq.*

->And a river went out of Eden to water the garden; and from thence it was parted, and became into four heads.<-

->And a river goes out of Eden to water the paradise; from there it is divided into four beginnings.<-

->*A stream went out from the place of pleasure to water Paradise, which from there is divided into four heads.*<-

FOR the right investigation of Paradise, the knowledge of the rivers by which it is usually described will have the greatest weight; yet in the knowledge of these the path is not so easy, although some have spent their studies on this "aqueduct" and seemed to have placed all their contemplation there. Truly the difficulty depends, as Beyerlingius rightly judges, on two rivers, namely *Phison* and *Geon*, for whoever knew these would easily track down Paradise from them. <margin>Thomas 6. Theater book 14 page 11.</margin> Before we descend to the specific meditation on the rivers, however, we must put forward the source or river from which the other four emerged. *And a river, "went out" <note>original Hebrew: *יצא*</note>.* It is well known that the Euphrates is sometimes called in the Sacred Book by the name "The River" <note>original Hebrew: *נהר*</note> on account of its greatness, namely in *Joshua 24:2, Psalm 72:8, Micah 7:12* and elsewhere, whence some conclude that by this river, which was later divided into four channels, the Euphrates is understood; but these people confuse what Moses distinguishes. There are also those who think the singular was put for the plural in this place. But from the history of the narrative it appears that this opinion is forced. *I for my part would feel,* says Hobkinson in *On Paradise p. 11. 12. that one should not rashly depart from the simplicity of the words which the Spirit of God dictated; nor should anything be changed without a most evident reason, which I do not notice here.* Therefore I do not agree with their opinion, and all the more because I see that not even one of the classic writers felt this way. Concerning this river or source Moses says *it went out* <note>original Hebrew: *יצא*</note>, from the root meaning to go out, to exit, to come forth, or to arise; which last meaning Pererius disapproves of, for this reason: *It is not necessary, he says, for that word to signify the first birth and the first origin of that river, but only to indicate that the river flowing from the region of Eden flowed into Paradise in a direct path and course;* with whom Junius agrees in *The History of Creation p. 103.* to obtain what he intends, namely that by this river the Euphrates is understood. But we side with Bonfrerio in this matter, who explains this word as referring to the first origin. For if this word were to be explained as progression, the phrasing of Moses would be absurd, who rather should have said "it entered" and afterwards writes "into four heads," which the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated as *four beginnings* <note>original Greek: *τέσσαρας ἀρχάς*</note>. If, however, they are beginnings and heads, certainly they will not be rivers moving forward, but drawing their origin from here, as Dr. Christiani learnedly observes in his *Disputation on Paradise p. 27.* Moses therefore defined the spring, even if he did not name it; he gave the thing, but kept the name silent. Concerning this river Moses further says, that it went out to water and was divided into four other rivers—

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Paradise, the dwelling of Adam and Eve.</margin>
Paradise, the rivers; *rashim* <note>original: ראשים</note>, heads, which is indeed *lysimon* <note>Greek: λύσιμον, meaning "loosenable" or "dissolvable"</note>, yet in this place it is taken for the flowing forth, the beginning, the entrance, or the source. See Scherræus in *Itinerarium Psalt. root 992. p. 781.* Schindler, and Buxtorf in their *Lexicons*. Therefore, even if Paradise is held to be blessed by many and various proclamations, it is especially blessed by this benefit of nature: that it was watered by four most famous rivers flowing forth into various parts of the world. The first of these is called by Moses, the Divine River-Describer, *Pishon* <note>original: פישון</note>, which the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> rendered as *Phison*, from the root *push* or *pashash* <note>original: פוש / פשש</note>, which signifies *to grow and multiply*, as if an overflowing, a flood, or a breaking forth. From this, others have come to the opinion that the abundance of fish gave this river its name, because it abounds in fish, and indeed very large ones, namely eels of thirty feet in length, as Pliny reports in *book 9, chapter 3*. Others seek another naming for this river, as is usual in obscure matters. I, says Hopkinson in *Synopsis of Paradise p. 13*, would think it came from *pash* and *nush* <note>original: פש & נוש</note>, as if to say *changing face*, because it is often unlike itself in its course or in its quantity—sometimes spread very wide, but sometimes narrowed into a tight space; or in color, flowing clear in one place and turbid in another; or in quality, cold in one place and hot in another. This opinion is also favored by Isidore, Rabanus, Rupert, and the Master of the Scholastic History. The second river flowing forth from Paradise is *Gihon* <note>original: גיחון</note> from *guach* <note>original: גוח</note>, which is to be carried with great force, or from *guach*, to go out, to lead forth from the belly, to break out, to groan; from whose Hiphil form *hagiah* <note>original: הגיה</note> comes *Gihon*, from the continuous breaking forth of waters. Compare Blessed Gerhard in *Commentary on Genesis p. 49*, Scherræus in *Itinerarium Psalt. root 161. p. 137*, and Gregor. Franc. in *Sacred Lexicon p. 244. num. 194*, who observes that in certain places of Scripture this word is used and alludes to that flow which breaks out from a woman's womb during birth along with the fetus, or a little before its exit. See especially *Job 38:8*. *mibbeten* <note>original: מבטן</note> "from the belly" and *Leviticus 11:42*, where the Masoretes note that the letter *Vau* is the middle of the entire Law: as Buxtorf advises.

<margin>i.e. Key to the Masorah 52.</margin>
The third river is *Hiddekel* <note>original: חדקל</note>, which the inhabitants of the region call by the corrupted name *Diglito*, according to Pliny *book 6, chapter 27*. Josephus, however, names it by the word of his time, *Diglah* and *Tigris*. The Seventy also retained this as *Tigris*, which to the Persians is like *chets* <note>original: חץ</note> an Arrow, whence the Greek *thego* <note>Greek: θήγω</note> "I sharpen." In *Daniel 10*, the same word occurs, which the Seventy translated as *Eddekel*, not as *Tigris* as before. However, the Mosaic word descends from *chadad* <note>original: חדד</note> "he sharpened" and, according to Bonfrerius, from *qal* <note>original: קל</note> "to be swift," for an arrow is swift and sharp. Hence Jerome says: It is called *Tigris* because of its speed, like a beast running excessively, namely because its waters are *chaddim* <note>original: חדים</note> "sharp" and *qallim* <note>original: קלים</note> "swift," from which arose the corrupted word of the Chaldeans, *Diglat* or *Dikel* <note>original: דגלת / דקל</note>, by which word Josephus says in *Antiquities book 1, chapter 2* that it is signified to be simultaneously narrow, tight, and swift. The Seventy seem to have taken their naming either from the speed of its course, and indeed from the Tiger, the swiftest of animals, whose wonderful speed and agility in running Pliny describes in *book 8, chapter 18*, as do Aelian and Oppian in *On Hunting book 3*. Blessed Frantzius in *chapter 9 of Sacred History of Animals page 103* also notes this; or, as advised above, from the speed of an arrow, since according to Curtius *book 4* and Strabo *book 11*, "tigris" in the language of the Medes denotes an arrow. Whatever the case may be regarding its notation, experience itself proves to those who have genuine knowledge of this river,

<column-break/>

<margin>Paradise, the dwelling of Eve.</margin>
that it was not without cause that this name was given to this river. Schindler in *Pentaglot Lexicon p. 649* notes: *In only one day, this river covers as much distance as a strong and swift traveler does in seven days.* It penetrates Lake *Arethusa* in such a way that, because of its speed, it does not mix with its waters. Solinus testifies to the same in *chapter 38*. On the occasion of the root *qalal* <note>original: קלל</note> from which *qol* <note>original: קול</note> "voice" or "sound" seems to have arisen, we note from Gregor. Francus's *Sacred Lexicon n. 195. p. 245* that the words *calare* and *kalein* <note>Greek: καλεῖν</note>, "to call," have no small kinship; a *Calator* among the Latins is one who calls together, and *procalare* is to provoke; *Clarus* is as if *calarus*, he who was "called" by a herald, i.e., pronounced a victor; hence the *comitia calata* <note>A type of Roman assembly</note>, which according to Fenestella <margin>book 2, chapter 7</margin> were accustomed to be *called* by a lictor. Compare *Funger's Etymological Lexicon p. 149*. Finally, the last river flowing out of Paradise is *Perath* <note>original: פרת</note> from the root *parah* <note>original: פרה</note> "he grew, was fertile, fruitful, or productive"; with an accusative, however, it meant "he bore fruit" or "brought forth," whence Isidore in *book 13, chapter 21* says: *The Euphrates received its name from fruits (frugibus) or abundance: hence the Greek phero, phoryo* <note>Greek: φέρω, φορύω, meaning "to bear" or "to produce"</note>. It agrees most closely with the word for Paradise, which is *Gan-Eden* <note>original: גן-עדן</note>. Also from this word comes *Ephraim* <note>original: אפרים</note> in *Genesis 41:52* and *Ephrata* <note>original: אפרתא</note> "fruitful" in *Genesis 35:19*, as well as *parnaim* <note>original: פרנים</note>. Peru, the island of the New World, as Arias Montanus observed. There is also another root, *para* <note>original: פרע</note>, "to make free" or "to loosen a bond," from which comes the name of the Kings of Egypt, *Pharaoh* <note>original: פרעה</note>, which means *free*: from which the word *Baron* or *Barones* seems to be derived, to whom the German name for the same is certainly appropriate, as they are called *Freyherrn*: as Vultejus notes <margin>* On Fiefs, ch. 4, p. 62.</margin> *Barons are called in our language Freyherren: as if free Lords, because it is free for them to become part of the Community whenever they please; just as those with a license are allowed to become Doctors whenever they wish.* As to why it is called Euphrates, some assign a probable reason, namely, because in this place in the Hebrew it is written *Hu Perath* <note>original: הוא פרת, meaning "It is Perath"</note>, from which later came *Euphrates*, which the Greeks, out of ignorance of the Holy Language, derive from *to euphrainein* <note>Greek: τὸ εὐφραίνειν</note>, i.e., from "gladdening," as in Ambrose's *book on Paradise, ch. 3*. Hence Hopkinson says on *page 17*: *Regarding Perath, the etymology is ready,*

those who bring forward another from *phrazein* <note>Greek: φράζειν, "to declare"</note> are ignorant of the hidden things of primeval origins, and they should go to those who clearly know how to reveal the causes of names from the furthest antiquity—in which, while most Greeks are like children, they are accustomed to judge exotic things from their own language. It would not be out of place to warn the Greeks that when they form words on their own anvil, they fashion them to their own shape, and when they receive names from Barbarians, they terminate them as their own language is capable of. Posterity, the origin of the word being unknown, estimates it from its own position, and etymologists invent strange, sometimes monstrous reasons, with some calling to others, those more peculiar to their own nation attributing and arrogating to themselves what nevertheless came to them from elsewhere. Arrogant above others, they do not want to submit to others, as if something of their esteem and worth would be lost. Magnifying themselves, they do not want to confess through whom they have progressed, and from where that which they boast of was communicated. The Egyptians esteemed themselves more highly for this reason, as they had more prerogatives of antiquity than others, and hence they judged the Greeks as children.

Thus he spoke. Nevertheless, Genebrard—who by the judgment of Pererius is heard to be most skilled in languages and most praised for his exquisite knowledge of the best doctrines—feels in his *Introduction to Rabbinic Doctrine, following Jerome*

# From Genesis II. v. 10.

<margin>
Paradise, the home of Adam and Eve.
</margin>
<margin>
Jerome, in his *Commentary on Chapter 11 of Daniel*, notes that among the Hebrews the letter *He* [η] sounds like the Greek *Theta* [θ], so that it is pronounced *Phrath*; and because the vowel E (the simple *sheva*) is not to be uttered clearly but rather whispered, it is expressed as *Phrath*. In Greek it ought to be called *Phrathes*. See on this Schindler’s *Lexicon Pentaglotton* p. 1494; Schereus’s *Lexicon of the Psalms* root 881, p. 704; and Bonfrère’s *Commentary* on this passage.
</margin>
Having looked at the names, we now approach the controversies. While submitting our own opinion in a matter so obscure and uncertain, we nevertheless presuppose as a universal truth that the origins and courses of these rivers were so changed by the Flood <note>original: "diluvium"</note> that it is entirely futile to judge their ancient state by their modern courses. For since Scripture testifies that in the universal cataclysm the waters rose to such a height that they surpassed even the highest mountains by fifteen cubits, there is no doubt that the water ran miserably to and fro across the earth and tore it apart—turning valleys into hills and vice versa, uncovering lands never before seen and hitherto covered by water, and conversely inundating lands and cities and casting them down into the abyss of the sea, just as the unexpected floods of rivers testify every year. For if a particular cataclysm of one or two rivers possesses such power and strength, how much more must we believe and establish that this happened in that universal cataclysm of the whole world, when all the fountains of the great deep were broken and the windows of heaven were opened? What wonder is it then, with those fountains opened, that the rivers changed their original paths and forged other channels and ways for themselves under the earth? There is no doubt, therefore, since God wished Paradise to be unknown, that He utterly annihilated the signs and other <term>evidence</term> <note>original: "τεκμήρια" (tekmēria) - sure signs or proofs</note> by which the location of Paradise could have been recognized, the chief of which was the river rising in the Garden of Eden and afterwards divided into four principal rivers. Therefore, although we suppose that the Garden of Eden was established by God in Mesopotamia, even if the Pishon and Gihon do not wash those lands today, but rather the former runs through India and the latter through Egypt according to the common opinion regarding these rivers—and even if the sources of *the former* are distant from the Euphrates by more than 700 miles, and those of *the latter* are even more remote—our judgment must be captivated by a matter so abstruse and hidden, rather than babbling anything against or beyond the will of God. Nor do we see what can stand in our way when we assert that these Paradisiacal rivers, by the command and guidance of God, hold their course for so many thousands of miles under the earth and even through the Ocean itself. Take the example of the river Alpheus in Achaia, which falls into a certain pit in the earth and emerges again at the fountain of Arethusa in Syracuse, Sicily; this was proven by objects from its birthplace being thrown into the river and exiting at the fountain of Arethusa. Thus they may emerge in another place on earth where their origin has been hitherto unknown, for the sole purpose that the traces of the terrestrial Paradise should not be known to those living near or far. For if, as we warned before, the place where the terrestrial Paradise was established by God cannot be certainly defined, what prevents the same being said of the rivers once flowing out of it? We leave it undecided, therefore, whether one wishes to follow the common opinion (in which almost all the Fathers agree) who understand the Pishon to be the Ganges,

<column-break/>

the river of India, and Havilah to be India, and the Gihon to be the Nile, the most celebrated river of Egypt; or whether one prefers the view of Pererius, Junius, and those among the more recent scholars who support them, for whom the river watering the garden in Eden is the Euphrates, and the Pishon and Gihon are channels of the Euphrates and Tigris, as Pererius discusses at length in his *Commentary* on this passage; likewise Franciscus Junius in his *Notes on Genesis* and in his special treatise on the first three chapters of Genesis, p. 101 ff.; and Wendelin in *On the Wonders of the Nile*, ch. 3, p. 27 ff. We shall not be <term>dissenters</term> <note>original: "ἀντιλέγοντας" (antilegontas) - those speaking against or contradicting</note> against them. But let us finish this meditation on those streams watering Paradise with those four streams of interpretation which many writers derive from these four rivers: namely, the historical, allegorical, moral, and anagogical. Innocent III discusses this in his *Homily on the Feast of Pope Gregory*, p. 112-113, and in his *Sermon on the Evangelists*, p. 166-168. In the first place he writes: *Just as that river was divided into four heads—Pishon and Gihon, Tigris and Euphrates—so Holy Scripture is divided into four species: history and allegory, anagoge and tropology.* The Gihon is interpreted as an "opening of the earth," designating history, because according to the ancients they gaped for earthly things, since according to history earthly things were promised. The Pishon is interpreted as a "change of the mouth," signifying allegory, according to which the letter is changed into the Spirit, and one thing sounds in the letter while another is contained in the spirit. The Tigris is interpreted as "swift," designating anagoge <note>Anagoge is a method of spiritual interpretation that finds hidden meanings regarding heaven or the future life.</note>, for the understanding of which a swift wit and easy intelligence are declared, because it deals chiefly with super-celestial things, i.e., the Trinity of persons and the orders of Angels. The Euphrates is interpreted as "fruitful," signifying tropology <note>Tropology is the moral or ethical interpretation of scripture.</note>, through which the soul is planted in morals, sprouts in virtues, and bears fruit in works.

<margin>
book 25, ch. 4.
</margin>
<margin>
book 2, on the Orthodox Faith.
</margin>
<margin>
4. Heroics, p. 560, 563.
</margin>
And so, thus far concerning the rivers and the principal trees of Paradise. No one fails to see that the knowledge of these even reached the Pagans; for while Moses testifies that the Tree of Life preserved immortality, Hesiod celebrates his Nectar and Ambrosia, which is said to be "without death." By other poets it is called Nepenthe, which takes away all pain and grief. Homer favors Moly, which restores men to youth, the powers of which Pliny describes in many words. Likewise concerning Paradise itself, which Damascenus calls <term>a storehouse of all joy and gladness</term>; and he adds: <term>since God was about to fashion man from visible and invisible creation, as a kind of king and ruler of all the earth and those things in it, He prepared for him a kind of palace, in which dwelling he might have a blessed and all-happy life</term>. With which Barlæus is not <term>in disagreement</term>:

->Here the floor of the world<-
>A beautiful expanse lies open, the labor of the gods, and secret pleasure,
>The delight of the human race, the hospitable home of the Fathers,
>The love of the world, such as Thessalian Tempe never saw,
>Nor the region of Baiae, nor the flowery land
>Of the Phaeacians, or the fields of the Hesperides cultivated
>By the African sisters; or the heights of Babylon which
>Suspended its fruits in the air, with the rare daring of Semiramis.
>Here purple Spring thrusts forth her head, inviolable by clouds,
>And of its own accord pushes out sun-drenched flowers.
>Far off is wicked, cloud-bearing Winter with its inconstancy,
>And sinful Autumn is absent; Summer withdraws itself further...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Paradise, the dwelling of Adam and Eve.</margin>
> *It unfolds, and swelling with stalks of grain*
> *It luxuriates, and the whole year was beneath the harvests, etc.*
> *Here is the Elysian Grove, the most pleasant station of life,*
> *A home full of delights, a royal palace suited for*
> *All good things, a safe rest, no fear, the best face of things*
> *And of the world, and abundance from a full horn.*
> *Neither envy, nor fierce anger, nor base poverty*
> *Has a way to prowl; the favor and mercy of heaven rule,*
> *And God stands as the summit of every prayer.*
<note>The author uses classical imagery (Elysian Grove, Horn of Plenty) to describe the biblical Eden.</note>

Truly, all things were great and excellent to behold in Paradise; all was splendid and magnificent, all was noble and miraculous. But Adam lost everything, Eve lost everything, and their descendants lost everything. All things were "very good," whether for the use of life, for the contemplation of divine goodness, or useful and excellent for some other cause. All those things were lost and turned into their opposite: immortality into mortality, health into disease, laughter into weeping, the perpetual into the temporary. Yet one thing remains in which we can find solace for our loss and repair everything infinitely. The earthly Paradise was most splendid, but compared to the celestial one, it is most cheap. In vain, therefore, do we now seek the Garden of Delights, which God had placed as a location of joy, a field of pure and sincere pleasure. And why is it that we search for Paradise and examine the space in the land of Eden, when that place is now most polluted by vices and defiled by the malice of its inhabitants? Though in Adam we lost the garden pleasant with springing water, Christ, the second Adam, restored another springing with the water of salvation, as George Olaus sings:

<margin>Poem on the Nativity of Christ, verse 138.</margin>
> *He restores all things that once collapsed into something better;*
> *For God himself has arranged a garden with new cultivation,*
> *Where Christ, the Tree of Life, spreads out his branches:*
> *From which we pluck the celestial gifts of perpetual salvation,*
> *And in faith, we eat the life-giving food.*

Now, since we have lost the earthly Paradise, let us hasten to the celestial one, in which a river better than those four of Eden shall flow—a river of the water of life gushing from the Lebanon of holiness. Here is that true Tree of Life in the midst of Paradise, putting forth leaves for a health that shall never fail, and fruit to nourish all who stand before the throne of God. Here we have the earthly, there the super-celestial, which I would make lesser by speaking of it, since no eye has seen it, nor ear heard its joys, nor can any tongue sufficiently pronounce them. Let us hear Saint Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a highly influential mystic and abbot.</note> discussing the celestial Paradise in this way *on the feast of St. Nicholas, column 436:*

> *The super-celestial Paradise is a blessed and glorious region of pleasure and grace, of sweetness and gladness, of kindness and glory. There is rest from labor, joy from novelty, and security from eternity. There all live, no one dies, and all exult in the voice of exultation.*

<margin>In the sermon on the Five Negotiations, column 440.</margin>
The same author says of the same: *O blessed region of heavenly virtues, where the blessed Trinity is seen face to face by the blessed, where those sublime ranks with the sublime applause of their wings do not cease to cry: Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord of Sabaoth. It is a place of pleasure, where the righteous are given to drink from the torrent of pleasure. It is a place of splendor, where the righteous shine like the brightness of the firmament. A place of gladness, where everlasting joy is upon their heads. A place of abundance, where nothing is lacking to those who see Him. A place of sweet-*

<column-break/>

ness, where God appears sweet to all. A place of peace, where His place has been made in peace. A place of wonder, where His works are marvelous. A place of satiety, where we shall be satisfied when His glory appears. A place of vision, where a great vision shall be seen—O sublime palace, full of riches! Meanwhile, as we are still clothed in this "little body" <note>original Greek: σωμάτιον (somation)</note> in these lands of mortality, let our Paradise be the Temples and Oratories where we may sincerely worship God, meditate on His memory and our own misery, until we are eventually transferred from the garden and Paradise of the Church Militant <note>The Church on earth struggling against sin.</note> into the Paradise of the Church Triumphant above, so that we may become **trees of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, that he might be glorified** <note>original Hebrew: אֵילֵי הַצֶּדֶק מַטַּע יְהֹוָה לְהִתְפָּאֵר (Isaiah 61:3)</note>, where **THE LORD GOD, OUR MESSIAH**, the Tree of Life, shall eternally satisfy His chosen ones—**a planting unto glory** <note>original Greek: φύτευμα εἰς δόξαν</note>—with the fruits of life, joy, and sweetness. To Him be honor and glory forever and ever.

<margin>Paradise, the dwelling of Adam and Eve.</margin>
<margin>Isaiah 61:3</margin>

->Genesis 3, verse 12.<-

->**And the man said: The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.**<-
