<margin>The Fall of Adam.</margin>
The beginning of Genesis—indeed, of the entire Holy Book—is a joyful description of that most happy state of man in which he was created by God, a most joyful and blessed cultivator of God his Creator in Paradise. For the First-Created <term>Protoplasts; the first formed humans, Adam and Eve</term> were endowed with the highest innocence, free from every foulness of sin; adorned with justice and every kind of virtue. God loved them as children and made them masters of the world, of which Paradise was a sort of compendium, cheering them with its pleasantness and granting them a perpetual "good habit of body" <note>original Greek: εὐεξία (euexia)</note> and immortality. The most choice gifts of God were heaped upon Adam, riches of the mind that surpass all treasures, so that it may be said with Lucian:

<margin>Anthology, book 6, section 3, verse 11.</margin>
> *The wealth of the soul is the only true wealth.*

Namely: uprightness, innocence, justice, holiness, and an excellent conformity with God the **Original Pattern** <note>original Greek: πρωτοτύπῳ (prototypo)</note>, in which the condition of his soul was wise and holy, his body beautiful and immortal; his state of life happy and free from all pain, his dwelling most pleasant, and his clothing most precious, in which he walked in Paradise like an earthly God, clothed in the purple of innocence and the robe of glory. In this most noble ornament, Mother Eve saw herself happy in the highest eminence, exalted and glorified, pleasing God, the Angels, and Adam in that same most precious robe. The covenant that God entered into with man was simple and pure. The condition of the covenant was perfect obedience, even regarding an external object like the forbidden tree. A promise was added of reward through life without death, and a threat of eternal death.

<meta>This page continues the theological commentary on the Fall of Man, specifically focusing on the serpent's deception of Eve as recorded in Genesis 3.</meta>

# From Genesis III, v. 12.

<margin>The Fall of Adam.</margin> They could have observed this precept, this law, with the greatest happiness and preserved themselves in glory <note>original: *κόπασοι* (perhaps a transcription error for *κόποις*, "without labors")</note>; for what God had commanded was very easy—namely, that they should not eat from one tree. God did not wish to demand a greater or more difficult precept, but in exchange for sublime grace and glory, He imposed a small labor: that they avoid a single tree. Therefore, the fact that man did not fulfill such a small thing renders him all the more inexcusable. If God had imposed a great and laborious task, man ought to have performed it to retain such a treasure, and he should have done so for no one else but his Creator, from whom he had received both life and such excellent gifts, as well as the possession of a most blessed and pleasant garden, and the full power of enjoying it—with only that one fruit excepted, as we have said. But, persuaded by the enemy and neglecting God's command, they suffer the loss of all goods and ornaments; cast down into every kind of sin and lust, they lose the praise of innocence, and that fall inflicted a change of health into disease, of life into death; the loss of Paradise and heaven into infernal torments follows. Satan, the contriver of all evils and the head of crimes, did not rest for the space of an hour after his own fall and destruction; envying such great happiness in the first man, he turns and examines everything in Paradise that might harm Adam and Eve while they lived in a flourishing state with God—whether by himself, or through inanimate creatures, through food or drink, through water or air. Finally, because of his infinite *craftiness* <note>original: *πανουργίᾳ* (Greek: panourgia)</note> and cunning, he turns to Eve, the charming wife of the man, to suggest an occasion for sinning, and to bind and ensnare them in sin so that no way out might lie open. Basil <note>St. Basil the Great, 4th-century Church Father</note> introduces him, masked in the form of a serpent, haranguing and addressing our First Parents thus:
<margin>Oration 3, p. 23.</margin>
> *I saw you in such an abundance of goods not daring to enjoy them, and I came out of pity. I saw you hungry in the middle of Paradise, and I came to share your sadness; for tell me, by what counsel did God forbid food? Why, having shown you a beautiful thing, did He deprive you of its use? For whom does He store up this delight? For whom does He reserve the gifts taken from you? It were better not to have given them than to have forbidden them once given. He gave Paradise, but did not grant food. It was not through love but through envy that He forbade the tree; He deprived you of eating so that He might block the way to divinity.* (cf. B. Brenz, Commentary on Genesis, p. 42, 43.)

Observe, I pray, with what art that old serpent, who is called the Devil and Satan (*Revelation 12 & 20*), approaches Eve, as if he cared for her affairs and followed her with benevolence. The *crafty one* <note>original: *πανουργος*</note> knows that we desire nothing except under the appearance of good; therefore, he presents a false color of good. Having entered the serpent, which he knew was more familiar to the first man in the state of innocence than all the beasts of the field, he acts so that man, by transgressing God's precept and command, might become like himself rather than like God. *Why*, he said to the woman, *did God command you not to eat of every tree of Paradise?* But she said: *Lest perhaps we die.* And he: *You shall by no means die the death.* But, O most lying spirit, with what appearance of truth do you promise life, when God has decreed death for transgressors? This was a great, indeed the greatest, trick of Diabolical lying, by which Satan intended to attack the goodness and truth of God—

<column-break/>

<margin>The Fall of Adam.</margin> —while he says, "Not at all," when God had said, "Most certainly." But this was scarcely the beginning of the Diabolical temptation: for he sprinkles that impudent and poisonous speech with treacherous eloquence to disparage God and procure exile from Paradise all the sooner. "But why did He command it? Do you wish to know why He so commanded? Behold, I tell you. For God knows that on whatever day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like Gods, knowing good and evil." All the words which the most lying one thrust out of his most lying mouth were adapted for corruption. Each and every thing was fashioned and done in such a way that he might deceive man and plunge him with himself into the eternal pit of everlasting damnation. First, he did not come in his own form, but to accomplish the design of his malice, he misuses the serpent (which is numbered among living things and called *arum* <note>Hebrew: ערום (transliterated), meaning "shrewd" or "crafty"</note>, *shrewd, cunning*, by which is understood that natural cunning implanted in certain animals, such as is noticed today in the little fox; cf. *Psalm 58:2, Matthew 10:16, Pliny book 8, ch. 23*). He used it as a naked and brute organ, speaking through the serpent as a little beast familiar to man before the fall, and utterly ignorant of the things being said by Satan. Hence the serpent is rightly and truly described by the appearance and pretext of humility, because like a serpent it crawls humbly until it infects and wounds everything with poison. Then he says, *You shall by no means die*, abusing the ambiguity of "death"; furthermore, he announces that their eyes are to be opened, with a similar illusion of speech; for they opened them to their own confusion. He also promised *to be like Gods, knowing good and evil*, but they came to know their loss with pain and without remedy. How great, O good God, is the distance between the meaning of the Demon speaking and Eve hearing! Eve understood some great good; but the Demon, the Father of Sophists, meant nothing but destruction. The serpent creates a hope of divinity in our ancient Parents in Paradise, saying: *as Elohim* <note>Hebrew: כאלהים</note> *and you shall be as gods* <note>Greek: καὶ ἔσεσθε ὡς θεοὶ</note>, *you shall be, as it were, like Gods.* Nor should it be overlooked in this place that an absolute equality is not meant, but such an *excellence* <note>original: *ἐξοχὴν*</note> which exceeded the state of a human creature and was suitable and fitting only to the Divine nature. Georgius Hornius <note>17th-century historian and geographer</note>
<margin>Book 1, History of Philosophy 2, p. 13</margin>
indeed thinks that *as Elohim* should be translated: *like angels*, in which matter he followed *Munster, Junius, and Pagninus.* Yet it is a marvelous speech to equate them to Gods, coming from one who had himself been stripped by God of all honor because of ambition, while he contended to make himself equal to God. Our first Parents do not smell the deceitful words and the envious atrocity of the speech; they who were already flourishing in both honor and grace, who already held solid and true glory in full possession, allow themselves to be deceived and deprived of glory. Regarding this lost and overturned glory, no speech occurs now more fit than this of Homer, when it is said in *Iliad 5*:
<margin>v. 440.</margin>
> *Of the immortal gods and of men who walk upon the ground...*
> *Think, son of Tydeus, and give way, nor to the gods*
> *wish to be equal in spirit, since the race is never similar.* <note>original: Greek text from Homer's Iliad, warning mortals not to strive for equality with the gods.</note>

What does this mean? Except that such great spirits should not be carried by anyone that he thinks himself equal to the Gods; let no one think so magnificently of himself as if he were of the number of the Gods; let no one presume to carry spirits as great as if he were one...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Fall of Adam.</margin>
...as if he were one of the Gods. These are the words of Apollo used to restrain Diomedes, which Eobanus rendered into Latin meter on page 122 as follows:
> *But come now, son of Tydeus, see where you advance,*
> *Step back, nor wish to be equal to the immortal Gods,*
> *For never could you make this mortal race of men*
> *Equal to the Gods who are free from all care.*
<note>The author quotes Eobanus Hessus’s Latin translation of Homer's Iliad to illustrate the danger of human pride.</note>

Adam ought to have said to the infernal Apollo <note>The Serpent/Satan</note>: "Step back. I keep what I have. I do not seek that by which I perish. Perish with your Gods." But alas, the woman believed the Devil more than God, and the serpent creature more than God the Creator. The conversation of the serpent, which he joined with Eve, contained a suggestion: from there proceeded delight, consent, and the deed. Would that she had repelled that first assault of the infernal enemy and foe, which could have been easily repelled. For in the beginning, the Devil is a gnat and a water-strider <note>original: "cynips et tipulus" — meaning small, insignificant pests</note>, but having become the victor, he puts on the mask of a Giant. Would that Mother Eve had resisted at the start and judged the tempter as a mere chirp; then she would have easily overcome this infernal water-strider. But while she believes the serpent offering a lie, she falls into the most grievous sin of all, the whole process of which we shall give in brief. Indeed, Satan attacks man in Paradise both within and without, and infects his mind and body with his poison. The internal poisoned arrows are three:

1. Doubt concerning the certainty of the *literal word* <note>original Greek: τῷ ῥητῷ (to rheto)</note> of the Lord, to which he attaches a diabolical *interpretation* <note>original Greek: διάνοιαν (dianoian)</note>, and thus robs the mind in Eve of the light of Divine recognition, and in place of the certain *decree* <note>original Greek: ἀπόφασιν (apophasin)</note> of divine threat, he introduces to her a doubtful *suspension of judgment* <note>original Greek: ἐποχὴν (epochen)</note>, by which he says, "Perhaps."

2. Hatred of God, by which he persuades Eve to decide that God is envious and a deceitful enemy of men. This wound was inflicted upon the will, specifically the *practical or reasoning faculty* <note>original Greek: τῷ πρακτικῷ ἢ λογισικῷ (to praktiko e logistiko)</note>.

3. Vain pride and elation against and above God, by which the *struggle* <note>original Greek: ἀγωνία (agonia)</note> of mind and will in Eve is dissolved. These are the *logical or intellectual* <note>original Greek: λογικὰ ἢ διανοητικὰ (logika e dianoetika)</note> arrows.

To these, that most crafty enemy adds external or *sensory* <note>original Greek: αἰσθητὰ (aistheta)</note> things, of which there are four steps:
1. He attacks and captures the eyes with the beauty of the forbidden fruit.
2. The common sense and fantasy with the imagination of a pleasing and acceptable taste.
3. The *appetite* <note>original Greek: Oρεξιν (orexin)</note> for the *apparent* <note>original Greek: φαινομένοις (phainomenois)</note> goods of mind and body. This was already a bad *choice and impulse* <note>original Greek: προαίρεσις & ὁρμὴ (proairesis & horme)</note> in Eve; from which finally,
4. He overcomes the *motive power* <note>original Greek: ἰσχὺν κινητικὴν (ischyn kinetiken)</note>, so that the wretched woman extends her hand. Unhappy hand, therefore, which plucks from the unhappy tree the fruit against the prohibition! How many misfortunes, I ask, and how many miseries entered through sight? The first woman lifted her eyes to see the forbidden fruit, which appeared to her beautiful to see and delightful to the aspect, and pleasing to the eyes, and so she is led to believe, to pluck, and to eat the fruit of human perdition. The perverse eye of Eve attributed to itself all the acts of the senses. She gazed at the tree, she saw that the wood was good for eating and that it was a most desirable *longing* <note>original Hebrew: תאוה (ta'avah)</note>. The objects of the senses are changed; sight hungers for what belongs to taste. If the palate did not pre-taste it, who taught the eyes that the fruit was sweet to the taste? The eye looks, and there the whole soul sees as if through a window, and all the senses lie in wait at the door of sight. Taste was present there when the eyelids moved, and from one sense the whole mind, disturbed, collapsed. Unhappy sight, which though it belongs to a single and corporeal sense, subjugated the whole

<column-break/>

<margin>The Fall of Adam.</margin>
soul unto death; it perishes while it sees, and tastes before it had experienced. The fruit, therefore, is the enticement, the serpent the instigator, abusing the free will of man and promising impunity. Behold the genius of the Demon in this temptation. He offers only a fruit, a small thing, but by which he deceived the woman with the man, and our whole race at once. How easy it was for Eve to eat the fruit, but into what straits was she then cast? Impudent Spirit, why did you not show all the kingdoms of the world along with the fruit, saying: "All these I will give to you"? But this is also his genius: if he can conquer with a small thing, he does not offer the greatest; if indeed he cannot with a small thing, then finally he shows greater things. He recognized that Eve was a delicate little woman, therefore he showed the delights of the fruit to her, who was ignorant of the Devil the deceiver. Behold, how small a thing and of no price the fruit seems to be, and yet under its delight a transgression of the law is committed; the sin therefrom was made the greatest, it offended God the lawmaker, it brought the deprivation of grace and the wrath of the Divine Power, it brought in death, and attracted for herself and the descendants of Eve every kind of death and punishment by that eating. For the offense and merit ought not to be estimated from the worthlessness of the fruit, but from the greatness of the Lawmaker, forbidding the offense against Himself, as much in small things as in great. Thus the fruit of death snatches away the gift of immortality. Paradise was snatched away when the food was held out; from the tree the woman ate, she who was to perish, she who was to give birth to those who would perish. From the fruit, therefore, let us learn to recognize our misery, and to deplore its propagation according to the Poet:

> *With this the parents dwelling in Paradise infected themselves,*
> *To defile the warnings of God, and by a wicked theft*
> *To pluck the ill-fated fruit from the forbidden apple tree,*
> *And having plucked it, dared to devour it; now the late*
> *Offspring drawing from there a long, uninterrupted chain,*
> *Retains the traces of the ancient fault,*
> *Fixed in the very marrow by that contempt.*

Our stepmother Eve effected this lot for us, and stood forth, alas, as the mediatrix of death, and evil was brought from there upon all men according to that couplet:

> *Because a woman plucked the apple from the forbidden tree,*
> *Through an apple [malum] she brought upon us every evil [malum].*
<note>A wordplay on the Latin word 'malum', which means both 'apple' and 'evil'.</note>

Hence Tertullian, inveighing greatly against Eve, deceived by that ancient serpent the Devil, says: *“You are the devil’s gateway: you are the unsealer of that tree: you are the first deserter of the divine law: you are she who persuaded him whom the devil was not valiant enough to attack.”* To which Ambrose assents in his *Sermon on Double Baptism, column 488*, when he says: *“The woman gave to you, O Adam, from the tree, but certainly by offering it, not by bringing violence. For it was done not by her power, but by your will, that you obeyed her voice more than the divine voice.”* Thus Adam fell, whom the Serpent did not dare to tempt, by the food of the mouth and the power of Eve's love, whose enticement was greater than the pleasure of Paradise itself, indeed of the whole world with all its adornment; for him whom the magnitude of the whole world could not conquer, the lust for a woman crushed. Strong Adam fell, whom all nature could not conquer, following weak Eve; and he fell because he had Eve. Eve stands for the temptation, Adam consents to the tempter, and while they think they stand, they fall. Eve persuades and prevails, the helper of the Serpent, not his despiser.

# From Genesis III. v. 12.
## Gg 3

<margin>The Fall of Adam.</margin>
Adam would have remained steadfast if Eve had not been present, and perhaps would not have fallen if he had not had Eve. But while the serpent persuades and deceives, Eve extends her hand and plucks; Adam adds his consent. Both, with a perverse mind, seize what was forbidden. Neither reflects in their heart upon those things which God had spoken. <margin>On Psalm 38, page 521.</margin> *Would that either Adam had been deaf or Eve had been struck mute*, to speak with Ambrose; *the former, so that he might not hear the voice of his wife; the latter, so that she might not speak to her husband and, by the service of a slippery voice, pour the serpent's poisons into the man.* Truly they vanished in their own thoughts, thinking they could be Gods. But they who desired to be <term>isotheoi</term> <note>original: ισόθεοι; "equal to God"</note> turned out to be, along with their descendants, <term>misotheoi</term> <note>original: μισόθεοι; "haters of God"</note>. For by the sin of [dis]obedience it came to pass that, whereas before the fall it was true that *I said: Ye are Gods and all sons of the Most High*; that which the lying mouth of hell imitates—*Ye shall be like unto Gods*—resulted in nothing less than their becoming children of wrath. How well Satan stood by his promises, therefore, the outcome has taught. God considers man as one who sees, endowed with the best eyes, by which he might best perceive all natural things, clearly know all things, and acutely investigate them; <margin>Question 33 on Genesis, p. 10.</margin> Hence Theodoret *says: That even before the eating they did not have their eyes closed is sufficiently clear to those who wish to pay attention. For how would the woman have seen the tree, both beautiful for food and pleasing and fair to the eyes (for so it may be understood), if they had not had their eyes open:* with whom agree the writings of Chrysostom *Volume 1, Homily 15 on Genesis, p. 93.* Augustine *Volume 3, Book 11 on the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chapter 31, page 291.* Moreover, he could see GOD himself clearly with his eyes. Man delighted his eyes with the most excellent works of nature, with which he could not satisfy the greed of his eyes; and while he considers all things with curious eyes, behold, the Devil, moved by envy toward him, looks back with squinting eyes, envies man his fortune, and quickly deceives him. The Devil is "eyed" <note>sharp-sighted</note> in evil, persuading Adam and Eve that there was a film and bleariness in their eyes by which they could not discern what was for their use; and he said that if they wished to obtain something with their eyes, they would be more clear-sighted by eating of the forbidden tree: *In the day,* he said, *that you eat of it, your eyes shall be opened.* The pleasantness of the tree delights the eyes; they look with unrestrained eyes, they apply their hands, they pluck and eat. But what gain came from it? As the divine light of the Spirit departed, a prudence of earthly things succeeded that heavenly wisdom of blessedness; indeed, the knowledge of the flesh begins, in which <term>tipaqachnah</term> <note>Hebrew: תפקחנה; "were opened"</note> *the eyes of both were opened, and they knew evil.* What then did they know? What did they see? They knew themselves to have been made liable to the death of the body and soul and other evils. They knew then at last that their eyes were altogether wicked, then at last truly bleary. They knew the malice and immodesty of their flesh, and they saw <term>ki erummim hem</term> <note>Hebrew: כי עירומם הם</note>, *that they themselves were naked.* They saw nakedness with carnal eyes and were ashamed, *and the man and his wife hid themselves from the face of Jehovah God in the midst of the trees of the garden.* They saw, therefore, how gravely they had sinned, how much good they had lost through disobedience, and how many evils they had drawn upon themselves, from which inexplicable anguishes arose in their hearts. For let anyone consider—these are the words of Blessed Gerhard *Commentary on Genesis, page 90*—what the state of mind was and could have been for our first Parents after the

<column-break/>

<margin>The Fall of Adam.</margin>
fall? No promise of reconciliation and pardon then existed, no example of those received back into grace; on the contrary, they knew that the Devils had been rejected by God without hope of pardon; they knew that God's justice and truth were immutable. They saw nothing else, therefore, but a living hell, and unless God had sustained them by grace, they would have fallen into despair. Behold the "opening of the eyes" promised by the Devil! Where are you now, most lying Devil? Where are your most lying promises? The sin having been committed, you depart as if the matter were well done, leaving the First-Created in the greatest sadness and calamity. These, truly, hide the members of their lust, and having covered their shameful parts, they were ashamed of their nakedness, and *they sewed fig leaves together and made for themselves aprons.* They blush because of the immodesty committed, and with revealed eyes they recognize the fruit of the *tree of knowledge of good and evil* to be the fruit of corruption and death. With aprons they cover what was not necessary to be covered in the state of innocence. They cover the members of generation; the internal concupiscence of the flesh they cannot cover. They cover the shameful parts, not the desire for shameful things, which they were unable to cover because of the eating of the forbidden tree. And so they wove loincloths from the leaves of figs, so that they might at least cover the nakedness of the flesh, since they could not cover its rebellion. These aprons, led by I know not what reasoning, Augustine calls <term>campestria</term> <note>field-garments or loincloths</note>, <margin>City of God, 14, c. 17.</margin> which name is taken from the wrestlers and gymnasts who, in those naked contests usually held in the Campus Martius at Rome, covered the middle part of the body. For thus he says: *They sewed fig leaves and made for themselves "campestria," that is, belts for the genitals; for some translators have put "girdles." Furthermore, "campestria" is indeed a Latin word, but so called because the youths who exercised naked in the field [campus] covered their shameful parts; whence the common people call those so girded "campestratos."* The *campestre* was a girdle which wrestlers, stripped in their fashion, used in the fields and public gymnasia. Horace in his Epistles: <margin>Book 1, Epistle 11, v. 18.</margin>
> A heavy cloak in the midsummer sun, a loincloth in snowy breezes.

where on page 551 the Old Commentator says: *The campestre is a thin linen garment, useless in winter, because it covers nothing of the whole body except the loins; it is called "campestre" because youths used them in field exercise, that is, in the Campus Martius.* To recall Bullatius, the Poet indicates that happiness does not consist in a place, but in the mind, and that places—whether it be Lebedus, Rhodes, Mitylene, or Rome—contribute no more to a wise man for living well than a thick cloak does to cooling one in the summer solstice, or a loincloth to driving away the cold in midwinter. Acron: p. 725. *A cloak brings no coldness in summer because it is thick and heavy. A loincloth brings no warmth in winter because it is thin, and rules nothing of the whole body except the loins; just as a fireplace is of no use in the month of August, nor the Tiber in midwinter; so places contribute nothing to the wise man.* The apron was of no use to good Adam <term>synion</term> <note>Greek: συνιὼν; "understanding/perceiving"</note> for covering the vice of the soul; for if he had lived rightly, he could easily have done without it, nor did that loincloth provide anything else than what (to say it again with Horace):
> A heavy cloak in the midsummer sun, a loincloth in snowy breezes.
> The Tiber in midwinter, a fireplace in the month of August.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES.

<margin>The Fall of Adam.</margin> That loincloth indicates how poorly he fared in the struggle within the fields of Paradise, and it bears witness to his disobedience. They had lost the good and fallen into evil; therefore, confounded by the disobedience of their own flesh—as if by a witness to the punishment of their disobedience—they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths, to speak again with Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a central figure in Western Christian theology.</note>. They cover their genitals, which they had not previously covered in their state of integrity, nor was there a necessity to cover them since they were without fault. For that movement of the genitals, without which the union of spouses cannot occur, was so ordered that it held nothing shameful or indecent before sin; for then those members destined for generation were moved not by the flesh lusting against the Spirit, but by the command of the will. Whence <margin>Book on Marriage.</margin> Augustine says: *Under the state of innocence there would indeed have been a movement of the genital member, without which spouses cannot couple and procreate, but it would have served the rational will, and not lust, but rather the generation of offspring; through sin, however, there succeeded a disobedience of the members and movements toward inordinate impulses.* Lust and the disobedience of the flesh are the punishment for sin, before which that sense of pleasure was moved neither against the law of the mind nor against the command of reason; see Mercerus <note>Jean Mercier (d. 1570), a French Hebraist and commentator.</note> on this passage, page 50.

The apple was the lure, the serpent the instigator, abusing man's free will and promising impunity. Sin is immediately accompanied by a disturbed conscience, which was previously secure. Adam and Eve blush, fearing great punishments; most sorrowful since the fall, they could scarcely lift their faces to the stars; they wander with trembling step, seeking hiding places, fleeing from Him whom they could not escape. For what foolishness is it to flee from God? To flee from Him who fills heaven and earth? The first Parents flee because fear had struck their minds regarding the account of their deed to be rendered to God; but while they persuade themselves they will be freed through flight, they create a great presumption of the crime committed, according to the legal authority *if indeed* book 1, title 49, Code *that all judges* <note>A reference to the Corpus Juris Civilis, the Roman law code.</note>. <margin>As Ambrose speaks in the Apology of David, chapter 9, page 386: When they heard the voice of the Lord walking in Paradise, they desired to hide themselves, though no one was seeking them.</margin> For when, as Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose (c. 340–397 AD), Bishop of Milan.</note> speaks in the *Apology of David*, chapter 9, page 386, *they heard the voice of the Lord walking in Paradise, they desired to hide themselves, though no one was seeking them.* Therefore, after the violation of the Divine Power's decree, God is nonetheless present, even though He had been held in contempt; when the First-Created <note>original: "Protoplasti," a common theological term for Adam and Eve.</note> heard His voice, they hid themselves. Now the voice of God, the herald of His arrival, can be established as twofold: heavy and formidable, joined with a great and strong Spirit, by which mountains are overturned and rocks crushed before the face of the Lord; or gentle and peaceful, with the whistling of a thin breeze. God is accustomed to use the former way when He proceeds to judgment. Thus the ancient Hebrews said: *God goes out from His place and descends when He passes from the throne of mercy to the throne of justice,* Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the famous Jewish commentator.</note> on Micah chapter 1:3, and Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), translator of the Vulgate.</note> in the same place, where the Prophet says: *Behold, the Lord shall come forth, etc., and shall tread upon the high places of the earth, and the mountains shall be consumed under Him, and the valleys shall be split like wax before the face of fire.* David paints the same terrible majesty of the coming Lord in Psalm 18:10, 15; Ezekiel chapter 38:18, 20; Nahum 1:3. The poets have imitated these passages everywhere, so that it is clear they have stealthily pilfered their own material from the Sacred Scriptures. Thus Quintus Calaber <note>Quintus Smyrnaeus, a 4th-century Greek epic poet.</note> describes the descent of Pallas Athena to sink the ships of the Greeks in book 14 of the *Posthomerica*, verse 459:

<column-break/>

<margin>The Fall of Adam.</margin>> She seizes the weapons of her Father, and no one except the Great
> Thunderer dared to handle them among the gods. And shaking
> the heights of Olympus, she confounds the clouds and the peaks
> of the mountains; black night broods over the land and sea.

And soon he adds:

> — — — the goddesses trembled beneath the raging one,
> bound under her feet, and the ether bellows all around.

as it seemed fit to translate in passing. And Virgil in book 3 of the *Aeneid*:

> — — — Suddenly all things seemed to tremble,
> both the thresholds and the laurels of the God, and the whole
> mountain moved around — — —

*Now the shrines seem to me to move in their trembling seats, and to scatter bright light, witnessing the arrival of the God: now a great rumbling is heard from the depths of the earth, and the temple of the Athenians bellows back, etc.* Claudian <note>Latin poet (c. 370–404 AD).</note> in *The Rape of Proserpine*, from the beginning. Barthius collected many such things for this passage of Claudian, and Ramirez gave certain others in *Sacred Gleanings*, chapter 35. Yet the poets sound nothing so grand, despite their great gaping mouths, that could in any way approach the <term>majesty and greatness <note>original: "σεμνότητα καὶ μέγεθος"</note></term> of the Prophetic speech. Nor is there any doubt that the Devil, as he is the "ape of God," wished to emulate the Majesty of God in this matter also, and to witness his own arrival sometimes with such preceding terror. Thus they were also accustomed to pray to their own Gods that they might come peaceful and serene. As Lucretius said of Venus in book 1, verse 6:

> From you, Goddess, from you the winds flee, from you the clouds of Heaven
> and your arrival; for you the Daedal earth puts forth
> sweet flowers, for you the levels of the Sea laugh,
> and the peaceful sky shines with diffused light.

Regarding the same, the Prince of Poets <note>Virgil.</note> says she was peaceful:

> — — — turning away, she shone with her rosy neck,
> and her ambrosial hair breathed a divine fragrance from her head.
> Book 1 of the *Aeneid*. And regarding Aesculapius, Serenus Sammonicus in the Prologue:

> You who once, covered under the peaceful skin of a Dragon,
> sought the Tarpeian heights and the famous temples,
> driving away foul diseases with your present power.

These things are from Ursinus's *Sacred Analects*, book 4, section 8, page 339, on the occasion of the voice of God walking in the garden. Regarding His arrival, whether it was peaceful or formidable? It can be disputed on either side. Moses seems to indicate that the arrival of God was gentle and peaceful when he said: God came <term>in the breeze of the day <note>original Hebrew: "לרוח היום" (le-ruach ha-yom)</note></term>, that is, after midday, toward evening. Theodotio <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Old Testament into Greek.</note> translates: <term>in the spirit toward the cooling of the day <note>original Greek: "ἐν τῷ πνεύματι πρὸς κατάψυξιν τῆς ἡμέρας"</note></term>. The Chaldean <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase.</note>: <term>at the rest of the day <note>original Aramaic: "למנוח יומא"</note></term>, namely when the day was inclining toward rest and its end. For "breeze" <note>Hebrew: "ruach"</note> the Septuagint reads "scent" <note>Hebrew: "reyach"</note> or <term>at the afternoon time <note>original Greek: "τὸ δείλινον"</note></term>, or as others interpret, *at the evening twilight*. Luther: *When the day had become cool*: where he notes, *that was around evening, when the heat has passed*. Yet the same Luther, in a slightly different place <margin>* in the Commentary on Genesis.</margin> in his *Commentary on Genesis*, embraces this opinion: *“In the breeze of the day,” as if to say, the voice was like the wind of the day: so that the emphasis is on the word "day." For he does not speak of winds in the night, so that he might exaggerate the immense dread that followed sin; as if to say, they were so fearful that in clear light they were afraid at the sound of a leaf; what would have happened if GOD had come in the darkness and night? For there the terror is far greater. For just as light makes men bold, so darkness...*

# On Genesis III. v. 12.

<margin>The Fall of Adam.</margin>
...the shadows increase the dread, etc. But the former explanation is the most fitting of all: to which Fuller (Book 3, Chapter 5) adds this note from Robert Estienne’s edition: *At the breeze of the day*, that is, toward evening, at which time the wind usually rises and the Zephyr <note>The West Wind</note> breathes. And indeed quite appropriately (says Fuller), for Aristotle observes in his *Problems* that <term>the zephyr blows toward evening</term> <note>original Greek: τὸv ζέφυρον πρὸς τὴν δείλην πνεῖν</note>. The Zephyr or Favonius (called "Fruitful" by Virgil and "Bright" by Horace, and therefore most suitable for those blessed seats of Paradise) breathes at evening time. See regarding this same phrase Drusius (Book 16, Observation 25), Johann Gerhard’s *Commentary on Genesis* (p. 49), and Salomo Glassius’s *Sacred Grammar* (Book 4, Tract 2, Observation 6, p. 676). By this phrase, therefore, the time is noted—namely, when the setting sun

->Now with night approaching, it had sent forth light breezes<-

as Alcimus has it: then the means by which the voice of God was carried to the ears of the First-Created. The first thing we read that was said to Adam after the fall is that: *Where are you, Adam? What have you done?* It must be held in memory, that "Where" and that "done," so that we may know what Adam and Eve did. Before man sinned, God did not cry out, but spoke, saying: *Let there be light.* But after sin He cries out, and the peaceful voice of God becomes, because of sin, the voice of one crying out, because He knew man was lost; and Adam is the first called to examination by God, though he had been later in the fall. Eve, who had taken the evils first, stands after him, as God observes the order not of the sinning, but of dignity and nature. <term>Where are you?</term> <note>original Hebrew: איכה; Greek: πῦ εἶ</note>, where are you, Adam? Thus Jehovah Elohim—whom the pious ancients by unanimous consent say was the Son of God himself (Justin in *Dialogue with Trypho*, Irenaeus Book 5 Chapter 14, Tertullian *Against Praxeas*, Clement of Alexandria in the *Miscellanies*, Hilary Book 12 *On the Trinity*)—cries out as He approached in an assumed human form, not as if He were ignorant of where Adam and Eve lay hidden. For the voice of God in this place is not that of one questioning—for among the Hebrews some questions imply one thing, some another: sometimes difficulty, sometimes total negation, sometimes even ignorance, none of which apply to God—but it is the voice of a judge summoning a sinful man to judgment. For Adam the sinner is sought by God so that he might confess his sin and receive indulgence; for God wished to call Adam first and discuss his case, lest He seem to condemn him without a hearing. Legal scholars are accustomed to imitate this judicial process of God, as they wish no one to be condemned in their absence without their case being heard (Book 48, Title 16 in the <term>Digest</term> <note>abbreviated as 'ff'</note> *on searching for or condemning the absent*; Code, same book, Title 19, Law 5; <term>Digest</term> <note>marked with π</note> *on punishment*; and Law 9, Title 2, Law 6 of the Code *on accusations*), not only in criminal matters, but in every business where all whom the case affects are present (Book 42, Title 1, Law 47 of the <term>Digest</term> *on judged matters*). It was also the voice of a Father rebuking a son. For God reproaches Adam because he lost his created happiness and fell into the foulness of sin—indeed, that he sought hiding places, even though nothing is covered or secret to God.

<margin>Book on Paradise, Chapter 14.</margin>
He does not seek the location, says Ambrose, who knows the secret; for He did not have His eyes closed. It is therefore not a question, but a rebuke. From what goods, from what blessedness, from what grace, into what misery have you fallen? Where is your confidence, born of a good conscience? This fear confesses guilt; the hiding place confesses the transgression. Where are you then? I do not ask in what place, but in what state—to what point have your sins led you, that you flee

<column-break/>

<margin>The Fall of Adam.</margin>
your God, whom you previously sought. Tertullian agrees with this in *Against Marcion*, Book 2, p. 162: God cries out, "Adam, where are you?"—as if ignorant of where he was; and having the shame of nakedness as a pretext, He asks if he had tasted of the tree, as if uncertain. Nay, He was neither uncertain of the deed, nor ignorant of the place. Truly, it was necessary for one hiding with a conscience of sin to come forth into the sight of the Lord when called, not by a simple calling of the name, but with a stinging rebuke for the deed already admitted. For it is not to be read in a simple way, i.e., with a questioning tone, "Where are you, Adam?" but with an impressed, striking, and imputative tone: "Adam, where are you?"—that is, you are in perdition; that is, you are no longer here. Thus it is a voice both of rebuking and of grieving over the outcome. Thus says he. Adam, having been thus sought and found, says: *I heard your voice in the garden and I was afraid,* <term>because I was naked</term> <note>original Hebrew: כי־עירם אנכי</note>, that is, I am naked. For demonstratives joined to nouns are placed in the stead of the substantive verb <note>the verb "to be"</note>, or as others prefer, they induce an ellipsis of it, with singular elegance (compare Glassius, *Sacred Grammar*, Book 3, Tract 2, Canon 7, p. 186). By this very act, Adam withholds the legitimate cause of his flight and excuses it on a double account: first, that he heard the voice of God (which he had nevertheless heard even before the fall), and second, that he is naked (whereas even before the fall he was naked and had neither fled the sight of God nor hidden himself under the trees). There was, therefore, another underlying cause, which he finally confessed when God inquired further into the crime; and he cast the fault or crime of the transgression upon Eve, saying: *The woman, whom you gave to be with me,* <term>with me</term> <note>original Greek: μετ᾽ ἐμῶ</note>, namely in the partnership of all life (Book 23, Title 2, Law 1 of the <term>Digest</term> *on the rite of marriage*), so that she is a partner in all actions of life (Book 24, Title 3, Law 22, Section 7 of the <term>Digest</term> *on the dissolution of marriage*; Book 9, Title 32, Law 4 of the Code *on the crime of plundering an inheritance*); *she gave to me from the tree and I ate.* He thus casts all the blame upon Eve, the woman given to him by God; for when God asked what he meant by violating a law so holily given, he did not wish to confess that he himself had sinned, but that the wife given by God had turned and alienated his mind with all her charms, and did not rest until he took the fruit with his own hands. This very excuse, by which he indeed confesses the sin, is guilty of blasphemy, while he does not fear to derive some part of the fault onto God Himself, who gave the seductive wife. Hence Salvian exclaims heavily, saying: *O blind impudence!* <margin>Book 4 on Providence.</margin> *O sacrilegious rashness! It is not enough for us that, involved in innumerable sins, we are guilty before God in all things, unless we are also accusers of God. What hope, I ask, will there be for a man who accuses the very Judge he must answer to?* Eve the seductress, called into judgment, having admitted the sin, also attempts to remove the cause of the transgression from herself following the example of her husband, and tries to derive the fault partly onto God and partly onto the serpent, who deceived her with his craftiness, saying: *The serpent beguiled me and I ate*; as if to say, the serpent, whom you perhaps created for that purpose, that he might seduce me, seduced me. And while Eve thus blames the serpent and Adam blames Eve, and each strives to push their crime away from themselves, we see by this oldest and first of all examples that the nature of men is so constituted that no one willingly acknowledges his own fault, but casts it upon another. By these signs, therefore, they betray a bad case: which are flight, hiding, fear, blushing, and aprons. They confess the crime, but...

It highlights the human tendency to shift blame—Adam to Eve and God, and Eve to the serpent—establishing this as the first historical example of avoiding moral responsibility.</summary>

# From Genesis III. v. 12.

The Fall of Adam.
*Book on the Holy Trinity, last chapter.*
</margin>
Indeed, the condition of man was "not to die," but because of the punishment for sin, it happened that he "could not not die"; there remains in that future state of happiness a third state: "not to be able to die," as Alcuin writes <note>Alcuin of York (c. 735–804), a Carolingian scholar and theologian.</note>. There was, therefore, in the First-Created <note>original: *Protoplaſtis*, referring to Adam and Eve as the first formed beings.</note> a power of not dying, and this was natural—that is, created together with them by the will and arrangement of the Creator. Once this was taken away after the Fall, the pronouncement of God remains true: *You are dust, and to dust you shall return.* From these things it is clear how gravely God was offended by the disobedience of our first parents, since he condemned Eve to endure the hardships of childbirth and the dominion of her husband; while Adam he destined to sustain labor with sweat in obtaining food. Then truly that saying of Homer held true:

> For truly there is nothing more miserable than man
> Of all things that breathe and creep upon the earth. <note>original Greek: Οὐ μὲν γάρ τί πώ ἐστιν οἰζυρώτερον ἀνδρὸς / Πάντων ὅσσα τε γαῖαν ἐπιπνείει τε καὶ ἕρπει. From the Iliad, 17.446-447.</note>

and that of Euripides in *The Phoenician Women, line 1683*:

> In one day he made me blessed, and in one day he destroyed me. <note>original Greek: Ἐν ἤματι μ̓ ὤλβισεν, ἐν δ̓ ἀπώλεσεν.</note>

To the Fall—ah, to your Fall, O Adam!—we attribute the wretched condition of human life, which is now common to us with the whole race of mortals. To the Fall we attribute whatever hardships there are, whatever calamities, whatever vanities. From this comes the brevity of human life, from this comes death, from this the many images of death, from this so many forms of calamity that they are beyond counting for anyone. From this comes such darkness of the human mind, such depravity of the will. From this we certainly gather that you did not so much deplore your own fate alone, as the fate of us all. Even the most accurate Philosophers did not know how to speak of the first man; as far as they were from the knowledge of him, so far were they from the knowledge of themselves. Nevertheless, Homer described the Fall of Adam in a way quite consistent with Holy Scripture, concerning which Budé <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a French humanist scholar.</note> writes. So too Hesiod’s Pandora, upon whom all the Gods bestowed their power, and who, by pouring out her jar, sent every kind of evil upon men, with only hope left in the jar—who else is she but Eve, the first mother? In whose habituation and deception Satan and all his supporters contributed all their snares, cunning, arts, and indeed all Satanic power. Meanwhile, while they meditated on why men were subject to so many miseries, and seeking the causes of miseries, they failed in the investigation itself. They referred it chiefly to three causes: *to matter, to error of the mind, and to depravity of the will.* They could not proceed further, and therefore, when they did not find firm reasons, they dissolved into complaints, saying: *It is best for a man not to be born, or if born, to die quickly.* From the Sacred Pandects <note>A term here used for the Holy Scriptures.</note> it is known to us that there was no sadder day on this earth than that on which Adam fell, and an evening more cruel than any other; DEATH followed this transgression according to the divine threat, from which Adam would otherwise have been immune, as well as all the evils which gradually dispose a man toward death. This was signified by the ejection of man from the garden of God and separation from the tree of life, by the use of which he could have been preserved from death. For it is said by God: *Behold, this man has become as one of us <margin>in the Pandects, page 63.</margin> knowing good and evil <gloss>original Hebrew: לדעת טוב ורע</gloss>: now therefore, lest perhaps he put forth his hand and take also from the tree of life <gloss>original Hebrew: מעץ החיים</gloss> and eat, and live forever, Jehovah sent him out to till the ground from which he had been taken, and he drove out the man <gloss>original Hebrew: ויגרש</gloss>, and placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubim and a flaming sword turning every way, to guard the way to the tree of life.*

<column-break/>

<margin>The Fall of Adam.</margin>
The first inhabitants, thus expelled from Paradise, had among the first experiences of their sorrow the unhappiness of the earth. While they tilled it, mindful of their first happiness, they looked back with sad faces at those blessed seats; they walked mournfully outside Paradise. Now Adam alone, now with his companion, experiences hard labors amid tears and sighs. But while he spends his life outside Paradise in a valley of exile and tears, devoid of Paradisiacal joy, the First-Created ones raise themselves up by the promise of the Messiah: *The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent.* Order and the necessity of continuity <note>original Greek: συνεχειας</note> demand that we immediately illustrate this promise and the first Gospel sermon of Paradise, which is repeatedly echoed and clarified.

### Genesis III. v. 15.

-> And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed; <-
-> he shall crush your head, and you shall crush his heel. <-

> *I will put enmity between YOU and the woman, and between your seed and her seed; HE shall crush your head, and you shall crush his heel.*

<margin>The First Gospel.</margin>
Thus we had man: stubborn toward God the Parent, injurious toward all creatures, cruel toward himself, eager to taste forbidden things, and a transgressor in the tasting; falling from the empire of the universe and exchanging life for death. For before Man sinned and separated himself from God through sin, God and Man were as if joined and contiguous; nothing here was divided, nothing disjointed. But when miserable man sinned, God receded far from him, and he fled from the Lord, hiding among the thickets of Paradise. There was a long space here, and a huge Chaos between God and Man, and iniquities divided the first humans from God. But God seeks the Creature separated from Him, and, out of His ineffable mercy, found a medium for man’s remedy; and what was the greatest of all means, He made Himself the medium and Mediator. A medium usually participates in both extremes; behold the extremes: **GOD and MAN**. They become total extremes by means of the Fall. But behold the medium participating in the extremes: **the God-Man, MESSIAH**, through which medium and Mediator all good has returned to us. Oh, wondrous and unheard-of benefit, where the most innocent becomes the most beneficent, to free man from eternal punishment and snatch him from the power of darkness! God proposed the benefit of the Mediator and the mystery of Redemption in those words, filled with the nectar of Divine goodness: *The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the Serpent.* Behold the divine condescension toward us! Let us weigh the individual words: *and I will put enmity* <gloss>original Hebrew: ואיבה אשית</gloss>. The conjunction "and" (ו) is placed first, which was omitted by the Vulgate translator, though it is not lacking in emphasis; it indicates that this verse is to be joined with the preceding one, and that GOD, having begun the judicial act or process in verse 14 against the natural serpent, now in verse 15 continues it against the infernal serpent, and dictates to him also his well-deserved punishment. 2. *Enmity* (איבה) properly signifies hostile and implacable hatreds.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The First Gospel.</margin> *Oyeb* <note>Hebrew: אויב</note> from which comes *Ayab* <note>Hebrew: איב</note> means **enemy**: whereas *Sane* <note>Hebrew: שׂנא</note> and *Sin’ah* <note>Hebrew: שׂנאה</note> signify hatred or any kind of aversion, as in *Psalm 7:6: "Let the enemy pursue my soul,"* etc. and *Deuteronomy 28:57: "Your enemy* <note>Hebrew: אויבך</note> *shall distress you in your gates,"* etc. Thus, what is noted here is an extreme or, as they say, "Vatinian" hatred <note>A classical reference to an irreconcilable, proverbial hatred</note> and an "implacable war" <note>Greek: πολέμῳ ἄσπονδῳ</note> between the Devil with his gang, and Christ with his company. And this enmity is said to be *set*, that is, established, ordained, eternal, and never to die away; so explain the Blessed Helvicus in *The Longing of Mother Eve, page 60*, and the Blessed Gerhard in his *Commentary on Genesis, page 102*. However, the Blessed Glassius in *Mosaic Christology, Dissertation 2, thesis 24, page 69*, advises—following Rabbi Mordecai Nathan in the Hebrew Concordances—that these words *Oyeb* and *Sane* possess entirely the same meaning, which is also consistent with the scriptural passages cited for each word. But if one were permitted to judge the meanings of words by conjecture beyond scriptural usage, a certain prerogative of emphasis should rather be granted to the word *Oyeb*, insofar as it has fallen as a title to the Devil, the author of all hatred and enmity, and the most exquisite adversary of God and men, so that he is called Satan *by excellence* <note>Greek: κατ' ἐξοχὴν</note> in *1 Chronicles 21:1, Job 1 and 2 repeatedly, Psalm 109:6, Zechariah 3:1, 3, Matthew 4:10, chapter 12:26, John 13:27,* etc. Thus far his view. **Between you and the woman.** <note>Hebrew: בינך ובין האשה</note> The masculine pronoun of the second person singular with the preposition, which the Greeks translate as *in the midst* <note>Greek: ἀνὰ μέσον</note>, as if "through the middle," refers to that whole complex: either to the masked serpent, or what is the same, to the Devil "enserpented," and both parts of this complex are struck by the lightning of God's judicial voice: the visible part, or the natural Serpent itself in verse 14; the invisible part, however, or the infernal Serpent and Satan, the chief cause of the seduction, in this very verse 15. That by **the woman** <note>Hebrew: האשה</note> is understood Eve, our first mother, is sufficiently indicated by the demonstrative "the" <note>The Hebrew letter He (ה)</note>, as she was the one first seduced by the Devil through the serpent, and called *Ishah* from *Ish* (man), because she was taken out of man (*Genesis 2:23*). Yet by *synecdoche* <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note> this includes Adam and all his posterity, whom they represented. Why God names Eve alone, the Blessed Glassius (in the place cited, page 104) adds this reason among others: he says there is a proverb of the Hebrews, **measure for measure** <note>Hebrew: מִדָּה כְּנֶגֶד מִדָּה</note>, that is, by the things through which one sins, by those he is also punished. The serpent seduced through the woman; through the woman he is in turn destroyed and devastated, namely by the power of the Blessed Seed, according to those lines of Melchior Lauban:

<margin>The Birth of God: Fathers of the O.T. part I.</margin>
> The Seed which the Woman shall bring forth in virginal birth,
> Shall crush the neck and head of the fierce Serpent.
> But he shall press back his arrows into the victorious heel;
> Hence this strike still stings the Saints today.

<margin>Lectures on this passage, column 83.</margin> Therefore, to the contempt and grief of Satan, God opposes the woman to him, so that he might be destroyed by the weaker sex, upon whom he first exercised the lust of his tyranny and pride. Hence Francis Junius says: Since the woman is the more tender and weaker vessel, and Satan first attacked her with his *cunning* <note>Greek: πανουργίᾳ</note>, and still attacks her most. Thus, by a certain law of nature, God brings it about that in the woman a certain more tender zeal for this enmity remains. This zeal, however, out of the ignorance and weakness of the woman—Satan blurring her eyes—turned into wretched superstition, by which name Luke in *Acts 13:50* calls women *devout* <note>Greek: δεισιδαίμονας</note> and superstitious. And a little further on: Compared in this

<column-break/>

<margin>The First Gospel.</margin> way, the words are to be understood, namely that while enmity is indeed set between man and Satan, it indicates something more vehement in the enmities between Satan and the female sex; which sex, being more weak, fears more for itself, and as it abounds in suspicions, more easily conceives hatreds and enmities and nourishes them more uncontrollably. Thus far his view. **And between your seed and her seed.** <note>Hebrew: ובין זרעך ובין זרעה</note> The word **Seed** is otherwise ambiguous, for it is taken either literally or metaphorically. Literally and in its genuine and native meaning, Seed is, partly in herbs, trees, flowers, and things growing from the earth, the kernel and grain which, committed to the earth, is the material principle for producing another individual of its own kind; partly in animals, both brute and rational (namely man), that generation <note>Greek: σπέρμα</note> from which each procreates its like. Metaphorically, seed denotes either *metonymically* the thing made for the material, the subject for the adjunct, etc.; or *synecdochically* and collectively, posterity, which meaning is found everywhere; or *eponymously* and *personally* for only a single subject, and that one singular and individual, just as *Seth* in *Genesis 4:25* is called "seed"; or finally, *consequently* and by a certain accommodation or allusion, in which respect the pious and faithful are called the Seed of the Messiah (*Psalm 53:11, Psalm 22:31*) and the impious the seed of the Devil. In this place, by the name of Seed—specifically that which comes first—is understood the *evil demon* <note>Greek: κακοδαίμων</note> himself, the primary and most crafty of the evil angels, with the whole dregs of infernal spirits, not excluding but including (as just said) their Leader and Prince, who undertook the perverse work of deceiving Eve (created in the image of God) as the captain and Prince of the rest, while the whole troop of damned spirits stood by and most greedily awaited the *outcome* <note>Greek: ἔκβασιν</note> of this work, and when they found the whole matter had gone according to their wish, they triumphed *congratulatory-wise* <note>Greek: συγχαιρητικῶς</note> over this victory obtained over man. Therefore, Jehovah Elohim addresses that individual Devil directly with these words: *I will put enmities between you (O Leader and Prince of the Devils and of the whole infernal kingdom, who stood as the author and chief of the seduction!)* Concerning this Prince and Author, then, not excluding the rest of the army of infernal spirits, the word Seed placed in the first position in this First Gospel is to be understood in its proper and literal sense. However, this exposition does not prevent us from understanding—by a certain accommodation or analogy, or what is the same, an allusion to that place—all the instruments of Satan among men as well: namely, impious tyrants, persecutors, heretics, members of the Anti-Christ, who are all themselves called the offspring of vipers, serpents, and children of the Devil, because they imitate him and express his character by their pursuits, following the example of the Jews in *John 8:44*. Whence Augustine says: <margin>*Tract 42 on John*</margin> "Whence are the Jews children of the Devil? By imitating, not by being born. Hear the custom of Scripture. The Prophet says to the Jews themselves: 'Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite.' The Amorites were a certain nation from which the Jews did not draw their origin. The Hittites also had their own nation, entirely foreign to the race of the Jews. But because the Amorites and Hittites were impious, and the Jews imitated their impieties, they found parents for themselves—not those from whom they were born, but those whose morals they followed so as to be damned likewise." In this sense also, Jonathan is called by his father Saul a **son of death** <note>Hebrew: בן מות</note>...

It argues that while the text literally refers to the Devil, it metaphorically includes all who imitate his wickedness, such as tyrants and heretics.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological analysis of Genesis 3:15, specifically focusing on the identity of the "Seed of the Serpent" and the "Seed of the Woman."</meta>

# From Genesis III. v. 15.

<margin>The First Gospel.</margin>
of death, 1 Samuel 20:31, that is, one guilty of death. So Deuteronomy 25:2; <note>Hebrew: *ben belial*</note> a son of Belial or of iniquity, that is, one devoted to iniquity; and Matthew 3:7, chapter 23:15, 33, where the Pharisees are called <note>Greek: *gennemata echidnon*</note> the offspring of vipers. From these examples it is clearer than the midday sun that **primarily and properly** <note>Latin: *prōtōs kai kyriōs*</note> this passage does not deal with the application of redemption, but at least with the work of redemption itself. For whatever pertains to that opposing subject, from which and by whom we are redeemed through Christ, that cannot be denoted by the serpent and its seed in the immediate literal sense. Now, since the ungodly also belong to the company and assembly of those redeemed by Christ, they do not belong to the opposing subject of redemption, as the Blessed Glassius <note>Salomon Glassius (1593–1656), a prominent Lutheran theologian and philologist.</note> learnedly concludes in his *Sacred Christology, disputation 4, thesis 5, page 114.*

These things concern the first part of the Mosaic phrase; now order requires that we come to the second part, thoroughly examining what is understood by the name **Seed of the woman**. There are those who understand by the *Seed of the woman* all humans naturally descended from Eve, between whom and the serpent a natural hatred flourishes. But this opinion fails by this very fact: it rests on a false principle, as if this passage were speaking of the serpent as a mere brute animal. This opinion is absurd in itself because, if we accept this hypothesis they pretend, no punishment would have been imposed in this judicial act upon Satan, who was the principal and primary cause of the Fall of Adam. It remains, therefore, that just as that enmity is not understood as the natural hatred between snakes and humans, so the "seed of the woman" is not to be understood as all humans naturally born of Eve. Above all, it must be well noted that in this place the **First Gospel** <note>Latin: *Protevangelium*; the first announcement of a Savior.</note> and the first of all promises is set forth, from which all the rest of Scripture, regarding the Gospel promises, flows as if from a certain fountain and spring—indeed, from a great spiritual Ocean. Its sole scope and unique, singular foundation is the Messiah, who alone could provide the most effective comfort to our First Parents against the power of Satan and death. Now, it was necessary that some title for the Messiah appear in the text; for how else could the First Parents and their descendants have known in whom they should place their trust against sins and the stings of conscience, unless the Messiah were expressed by some specific nomenclature? Since no other name exists in this very first promise of the Gospel except the *Seed of the woman*, we rightly conclude that the Messiah is understood by this very term. Hence, we understand this **as referring to one person** <note>Greek: *monoprosōpōs*</note> and **by way of excellence** <note>Greek: *kat’ exochēn*</note> of no one else but the Messiah, inasmuch as he alone is opposed to the whole troop of Devils—thus one is opposed to many. In this opposition, we must look not strictly at the dictionary meaning of the words, but at the reality itself, which is properly and principally the destruction of the power of the Devils over the human race—a work, certainly, that surpasses all the powers of a mere human.

<margin>Disputation on the desire of Eve and the First Gospel, thesis 32, 33, page 37, 38.</margin>
Therefore, the words of the Blessed Helvicus <note>Christoph Helwig (1581–1617), a German chronologist and theologian.</note> are worthy, indeed most worthy, of note:
> If this context is not understood as being about the Messiah, who would overthrow the power of Satan and deliver humans from it, it follows that no comfort or remedy was left to Adam and Eve against the wrath of God on account of the sin committed; nor would their posterity, whose cause was at stake in Adam, have had such comfort, unless this promise had been publicly proclaimed in the Scriptures.

<column-break/>

<margin>The First Gospel.</margin>
But this is plainly absurd; therefore, the prior point stands. The consequence is certain. For that which was necessary for Adam's descendants to know before Moses, Moses himself, by the command of God, committed to writing for his own posterity. If, therefore, such comfort was not noted in Moses' text, then those who lived before him could not have had it. Indeed, since Moses, by divine instinct, had to describe the **first origin** of sin, of all evils, and of death itself, it would be entirely **paradoxical** <note>Greek: *paradoxon*</note> for the **remedy** of all evils, which is the chief thing (and certainly the goal of this promise), to be omitted by him. For that remedy was not first shown in the time of Moses, but it was necessary to show it to the human race immediately after sin was introduced; otherwise, there would be no reason for the distinction as to why some humans were damned while others were saved and made partakers of the remedy. Thus he says. From what has been said, it is clear that by the term *Seed of the woman*, in the literal and immediate sense, only the Messiah is understood, and thus Jesus Christ born of the Virgin Mary in the fullness of time. However, we do not deny that secondarily and **consequently** <note>Greek: *epomenōs*</note>, or through a certain accommodation, the godly and those truly believing in Christ can also be understood by this word, as they are also said to *crush Satan under their feet* by the power of the Holy Spirit (Romans 16:20). Thus they belong to that *holy seed* on account of their Head; nevertheless, that is not what is understood **primarily and properly** in the words of our oracle, but it only flows and follows from it. For it is one thing for something to be contained and understood in the words of Holy Scripture in the **literal sense**; it is another thing for it to be drawn from there by a certain and immediate consequence. We call the **former** the Grammatical way of explaining scriptures; the **latter** the Logical way. These two must be accurately distinguished so that confusion does not arise. For not everything that is proved and deduced from a saying of Scripture by an unshakeable sequence is immediately of the same literal sense, as the Blessed Glassius learnedly warns in his *Sacred Grammatical Disputations, section 25, page 1028.* It is not our task here to review all the arguments in detail by which theologians are accustomed to support our orthodox thesis, but we refer the Kind Reader to the Blessed Helvicus (cited above), Blessed Gerhard <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a leading Lutheran scholastic theologian.</note>, Blessed König, Blessed Glassius, Blessed Walther, and Doctor Haberkorn.

Therefore, the opinion of the followers of Calvin <note>Latin: *Calvinisequarum*; a polemical term for Calvinists.</note> must be rejected. They, when the seed of the woman is opposed to the seed of the serpent, take the former **plurally** <note>Greek: *plēthyntikōs*</note> and collectively—that is, regarding the whole human race and all its individuals, or certainly regarding all the faithful. Even if we freely grant that the word *seed* is sometimes taken collectively in Holy Scripture, it is nevertheless also taken **singularly, uniquely, or as one person** <note>Greek: *henikōs, monadikōs ē monoprosōpōs*</note> regarding one individual quite often in the Sacred Books. Thus Seth (Genesis 4:25) is called *Seed*; and Ishmael (Genesis 21:13); and Isaac (Genesis 15:3). Thus the Son of David is called *Seed* as an individual in 2 Samuel 7:12 and 1 Chronicles 17:13. To this is added Paul's interpretation of the promise in Genesis 22:18 and 26:4: "In your seed shall all nations be blessed." This citation alone ought to restrain **those who speak against us** <note>Greek: *tous antilegontas*</note>, so that we might pass over in silence and indeed **before our eyes** <note>Greek: *en ophthalmois*</note> other sayings of Holy Scripture in which the Holy Spirit provides us with the same **excellence** <note>Greek: *exochēn*</note>. To these are added the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, who use the pronoun "he" <note>Greek: *autos*</note> as a mark of an individual, even though the neuter word "seed" <note>Greek: *sperma*</note> preceded it, which is no small indication...

The Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> took the same to be singular; then the Targum Onkelos <note>An ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Torah.</note>, which rendered it: *I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your son and her son; he shall be mindful of that which you did to him of old, and you shall observe him until the end.* And the Jerusalem Targum: *Nevertheless, there shall be a remedy for the sons of the woman, but for you, the serpent, there shall be no remedy, since it is to be that they shall remove the bite which was made in the heel at the end of days, specifically in the days of the King Messiah.* See Blessed Helvicus in the cited place, page 41 and following; Blessed Gerhard in the cited place, page 107. **He shall crush your head.** <note>Hebrew: *Hu yishuphekha rosh*</note> That the Vulgate <note>The Latin Bible used by the Catholic Church.</note> deserves a dagger <note>A critical mark indicating a suspected or corrupt reading.</note> in this place is something those who have sworn a faithful oath to the banner of the Roman Pontiff by no means concede; yet anyone who is not entirely a fungus or a blockhead <note>Literally "hay," meaning someone dull-witted.</note> can see at first glance that it has strayed from the golden path of golden truth. For even to one looking at the original text through a lattice <note>i.e., even a cursory glance</note>, it is clearer than the midday light that the Vulgate translator, whoever he may have been, certainly against all reason, committed a "change from one genus to another" <note>Greek: *metallaxen ek genous eis allo genos* — a grammatical gender swap.</note>, eliminating the masculine and substituting the feminine in its place. For in the Hebrew text, the pronoun *hi* (היא), which is of the feminine gender, is not found, but rather the masculine *hu* (הוא), which for the Latins is "properly and primarily" <note>Greek: *kyriōs kai prōtōs*</note> the same as *ipse* [he himself]. Neither can the preceding noun *zera* [seed/offspring] admit any other gender, nor the following verb *yishuph* [shall crush], neither of which is read in the feminine, but both in the masculine gender. Nor does it help the patrons of the Vulgate to cite the "enallage" <note>A grammatical substitution of one form for another.</note> very common in the Scriptures, which they insist has a place here under the threat of a thunderous anathema. But truly, let them show us a genuine cause, if they have any, why we should change the masculine *hu* into the feminine *hi*, and again through a new Enallage transform the masculine *yishuph* into the feminine *teshuphennu*, and yet again through another new enallage for a third time change the masculine pronoun into the feminine. Since they have not yet been able to show a genuine cause for this change, we do not value their decrees so highly as to leave the clearest fountain and seat of truth to follow their opinion, which is most contrary to the text and the analogy of faith. Three Chaldean Paraphrases agree with us regarding the masculine pronoun: Onkelos: *He shall observe for you.* The Jerusalem, which expressly refers it to the Messiah; Jonathan: *And they shall be such as to have a healing in the days of the King Messiah.* Add to these the Masoretes <note>Jewish scholars who preserved the Hebrew text.</note>, who note no variant reading, and the Rabbis: Rashi, Aben Ezra, Radak, Bechai, Rambam, and others. Seeing this, the Seventy and the other Greeks constantly read *autos* [he], although the neuter *sperma* [seed] preceded it—a variation <note>Greek: *heterōsin*</note> which Saint Paul also employs in Galatians 3:16. Compare other examples in Exodus 1:21, 29:14, Isaiah 5:14, Ezekiel 17:7, Matthew 28:19, John 14:26, 15:26, Acts 1:4, 48, Romans 2:14, 1 John 1:1. For it is frequent and customary in Holy Scripture to vary the speech by such a change of genders in the relative and antecedent when mention is made of persons; these are the words of Blessed

Finally, the very condition of the matter requires that we interpret this as being about the Messiah; for to destroy the kingdom of Satan is not within the power of Mary, or any creature. God speaks expressly of this destruction in this place: **He shall crush your head.** The word *yishuph* [crush/bruise] is read four times in the Holy Bible: twice in this place and in Job 9:17, where Rashi and Rabbi Levi ben Gershom explain it by *karach* [to break in pieces, to crush]; the Greeks rendered it *thrypsei* [he will break, he will strike out]. But the condition of the subject shows that the meaning should rather be taken from *chashaph* [darkness] (as if to say, "darkness shall obscure me"), with verbs of different orders, otherwise not dissimilar, being swapped for one another, which is not unusual elsewhere; and thus this latter passage has nothing to do with our business.
