<meta>This page continues the theological analysis of Genesis 3:15, focusing on the linguistic roots of the "First Gospel" (Protevangelium) and its role in comforting Adam and Eve after the Fall.</meta>

# From Genesis III. v. 15.

<margin>The First Gospel <note>Latin: Protevangelium; the first announcement of the Gospel in the Bible.</note></margin>
Furthermore, this crushing must be of the *head*; the Hebrew word *Rosh* (ראשׁ) signifies "head," and metaphorically represents supreme power and excellence, for the head is the chief member of the body, and in it resides the leadership and dignity of the senses. In this entire phrase, two accusatives are joined by ellipsis <note>A grammatical omission where words are understood from context.</note>, in this sense: *he shall crush* (ראשׁ) *the head*, that is, "with respect to the head" (Greek: *tēn kephalēn*), a construction very familiar and common to the Greeks. It is also used in the Hebrew of *Habakkuk 3:9*, where it says of God: *you split the earth with rivers*, meaning you split the earth with respect to rivers. Rabbi Abenezra and Kimchi <note>Famous medieval Jewish biblical commentators.</note> say there is an ellipsis of the letter *Bet* (ב) for *be-rosh*, "in the head," examples of which are found in *Exodus 6:3, 2 Chronicles 34:30, Psalm 109:4, Proverbs 8:22, Isaiah 20:5, 12:13, and 2:2*. Onkelos <note>Author of the standard Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note> takes the word "head" in another metaphor, namely for the *beginning of the world*, just as he takes "heel" for the *last times of the world*. For he translates *mi-kadmin* as "from the beginning, from of old," as if to say: he will be mindful of what you did to him, right from the start, from of old, long ago and many centuries past. Time, the devourer of things, will not age or erase this evil, which Paul Fagius <note>A 16th-century Renaissance scholar of Hebrew.</note> calls the "slaughtering corruption" (Greek: *phthoran sphageus*). For this reason, the power of the Devil, which consists in sin and death, is understood above by the "head," since the Messiah—the promised seed of the woman—powerfully liberated us, who were all subject to death (*Romans 6:23*) and lived in perpetual slavery to the Devil and the fear of death (*Hebrews 2:15*). Because of this deed, the Devil shall crush the *heel* (*Eqeb*, עקב) and *you shall crush him in the heel* (וחשׁופנו). The same verb is used for Satan that is attributed to the Messiah who is about to attack and conquer Satan. Without a doubt, we firmly gather from this comparison that it is not a light strike or a mere prick of the infernal serpent being suggested here, but the most bitter passion and most ignominious death of Christ is silently hinted at. Yet, in respect to the destruction of the Devil, this shall hold no comparison of damage, no different than if someone were only injured in the heel while the rest of him remained unharmed. Hence the Holy Spirit uses *Eqeb* (עקב), "heel," to indicate how the ancient serpent will have no strength against the Seed of the woman, and that most wicked enemy, with all his power, all his arts, and his lethal poison, could do nothing against the Messiah. He struck not the *head*, but the *heel*. As a concluding note, it should be observed that the Vulgate <note>The standard 4th-century Latin Bible translation.</note> renders these last words as: *and you shall lie in wait for his heel*, which does not agree with the Hebrew text. Gordon the Jesuit indeed wished to excuse the Vulgate, as if the meaning were: *By lying in wait and not by open warfare you shall crush his heel*. He argued the translator looked to the Hebrew word *Eqeb*, which properly signifies "to lie in wait" or to attack from ambush, and thus the emphasis of the Hebrew word *Eqeb* was captured by that version. But if the translator looked to this meaning, why then did he clearly render it as "heel"? For these are two very different meanings which cannot possibly apply to one and the same word placed once in the text. Furthermore, when *Eqeb* is a noun, it means "heel"; when it is a verb, it means "he deceived, he lay in wait, he cheated" (*Genesis 27:30, Jeremiah 9:4*). The translator, however, did not wish to give a verbal meaning, but a nominal one, hence he expressly puts "heel." Finally, the translator 

<column-break/>

<margin>The First Gospel.</margin>
[did not translate "you shall lie in wait" from the Hebrew *Eqeb*, but from *ve-hushuphenu*, which is placed in the preceding clause and means "to crush, to shatter." See, if you please, B. Walther, *Biblical Offices, p. 589*, and B. Glassius in the cited locations.]

By this First Gospel—which indeed is not found *explicitly* (Greek: *rhētōs*) by that name in Holy Scripture, but is most sufficiently revealed in it as a matter of fact, not only in the order of revelation and writing but also by reason of its account—by this good news, I say, and by this joyful hope, God comforted the world for many years, lest it fall into despair. He revealed this first Gospel to Adam, lest he despair entirely. For since Adam was endowed with divine intellect and considered the good things he had lost, the evils he had committed, and what he had brought upon the whole human race, would he not lose heart? But God, in His immense mercy, while He had scarcely shown the face of His anger and delivered the sentence, simultaneously reveals the remedy for the evil. He instills this First Gospel into Adam's trembling and anxious soul, from which, as if from a fountain and spring, all other Prophetic sayings that speak of the Messiah, and all the oracles of Holy Scripture that preach the victory over sin, death, the Devil, and hell won through the Messiah, look back to this oracle as their common mother. What could happen more desirable and sweet to the afflicted minds of our first Parents than to hear this voice sounding through the mouth of God:

-> THE SEED OF THE WOMAN SHALL CRUSH <-
-> THE HEAD OF THE SERPENT. <-

Certainly, these words contain such great consolation that we can neither express it in words, nor follow it in thought, nor finally can the narrowness of the human breast contain it. They excited such gladness and joy in the hearts of the first-created ones that they not only received this promise with open ears and a contrite heart, but also comforted one another in their most sad exile. Hence the grave and wise theologian Dr. Johann Bugenhagen <note>A primary reformer and associate of Martin Luther.</note> introduces Adam preaching thus:
<margin>Commentary on Jeremiah ch. 31, fol. 340, 341.</margin>
> "You see, dearest Eve, into what misery and death the human race has fallen through our sin, and how shameful this will be among our posterity, that man was deceived and fell by the persuasion of a woman; but the Lord God has comforted us by this Gospel of His: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent, that is, the Kingdom of the Devil, sin, and death. There God will then honor the woman again, when a woman shall bring forth for us a Savior, she who had brought destruction to the world. If he is the seed of the woman, he is a true man like us. If he will abolish sin and death, that seed itself will not be subject to sin and death as we are. Therefore he will not be conceived from the seed of sin, nor be born in sins like our posterity, but God will create that seed in a singular and new way—that man, the crusher of the Serpent's head and the triumpher over death, the eternal King and Priest. O good Eve, when I diligently consider in this Evangelical promise of God the crushing of the Kingdom of the Devil—that is, of sin and death, under which the human race is oppressed and from which no one can snatch himself—who, I ask, can crush sin and death, and take away from us the wrath of God and triumph over God, except the **Lord God alone? Therefore Jehovah God him-**

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "First Gospel" (Protevangelium) and the lineage of the promised Seed, tracing the theological expectations from Adam and Eve through the Patriarchs to the promise given to Abraham and Judah.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The First Gospel.</margin>
He himself in his very anger, when he cast us out of Paradise, remembered his infinite mercy, when God the Word—that is, the Son of God—said: *The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the Serpent.* <note>Genesis 3:15. This is the "Protevangelium" or first gospel message in the Bible.</note> It is as if he said: I myself will be in that seed of the woman; for he who shall crush the head of the Serpent—that is, sin and death—must necessarily be God. If, therefore, he will be the seed of the woman, he will be true man. This divine Man will restore to us all things that we have lost; we can do nothing. I wait for him as Redeemer, in him I hope and trust. In these miseries, our sins and death, we are received back into grace by God through him, having received the remission of sins. I believe the Gospel and God’s promise: *The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent.* Believe also, my Eve, and receive the consolation of God in this Gospel, hoping well in the mercy of God promised to us in the seed of the woman; and indeed, you should hope all the more and love this Gospel, because you not only hear of liberation, but also the greatest glory for the Woman, you who fell into the greatest ignominy. The seed of the woman, not the seed of the Man, shall be that crusher of the serpent's head.
What else is "crushing the head of the serpent" than that all the families of the earth shall be blessed through that seed of the woman? Thanks be to God for his ineffable Grace, which he offered to us in this Gospel and promise.

Thus this First Gospel had placed such firm roots in the minds of the First-Created <note>Adam and Eve</note> that they believed without any hesitation that whatever God had delivered in the new promise of the blessed Seed was most certain. But since that promise of the Messiah extended itself to a future time, and not immediately to the present while the First-Created were still living, they had, by poor reasoning, concluded that the blessing of the promise would be in the future Firstborn. For truly memorable is the congratulation *on the occasion of birth* <note>original: γενεθλιακὴ</note> with which the Mother received Cain. It was a premature vow of Eve’s, with a shout and a dance of joy; and as joy is usually eloquent, suddenly, when no one expected it, these words came forth from her: *I have acquired a man, the Lord.* <note>Genesis 4:1. Eve likely believed her first son was the promised Savior.</note>

<margin>Oration on Abel, p. 33.</margin>
Basil of Seleucia <note>A 5th-century bishop and theologian.</note> referred these words of Eve to the wonder of the Parents when they saw the infant *truly worthy of God* <note>original: ὡς ἀληθῶς Θεᾶς ἄξιον</note>, fashioned with such skillful features and limbs by divine goodness: "This," he says, "he brought forth to the astonishment of her who bore him. Eve saw a marvelous sight: nature wandering in number, and bodies being divided, and the miracle proclaims the Creator and bears witness to his works. *I have acquired a man through God.* She confesses the Maker, that the work is offered to God. Well said, 'through God'; she proclaims the Maker as the Creator, not as an assistant." The old translator, following him, rendered it: *I have possessed a man through God;* but it is translated thus in vain. Properly, as Blessed Bugenhagen <note>Johannes Bugenhagen, a major figure in the Protestant Reformation and associate of Luther.</note> 

<margin>In the same place, folio 341. b.</margin>
introduces Eve speaking: > I have possessed, that is, I have here now the Man-Lord, that is, the Man who is the Lord God. It is as if she said: "Behold Adam, here I have the Seed of the woman promised to us by God, which shall crush the head of the serpent, deliver us from this death of ours, and restore to us the life we lost."
There is no doubt but that the most wise Adam then replied: > Dearest Eve; I do not think that seed of the woman, mercifully promised to us by the Lord God, will come so very quickly. This seed which you have now brought forth cannot be that promised seed; for that Seed will be the seed of the woman

<column-break/>

and not of the Man. But this seed which you have now brought forth is the son of a Man and my son, as you know. Therefore, 

<margin>The First Gospel.</margin>
this Seed which you have now brought forth cannot be that Seed of the woman promised by God. You have not possessed—that is, you do not have—the Man-Lord who will crush the head of the Serpent. > But miserable Eve, while she expects salvation in her son Cain, Cain himself becomes an unfaithful hypocrite and a legalistic idolater, trusting in his own works and sacrifices (which he had learned from his father Adam were to be performed) and not trusting in the seed promised by God, according to the Gospel he had heard from his Father.

The long-lived Patriarchs before the flood, being closest to the First-Created, propagated this First Gospel down to Noah, who, after that most severe example of God's wrath upon the whole world, very diligently instilled this doctrine of salvation into his sons and grandsons—that doctrine of the first Gospel concerning the Seed of the woman—so that they might guard and propagate it to all posterity, and be preserved through it. Moreover, that Herald of Righteousness <note>Noah</note> lived three hundred and fifty years after the flood, until the 58th year of the age of the Patriarch Abraham. To him also this promise of the Seed of the woman was made by word of mouth, than which no weightier, nor more burning, nor more salutary voice was ever heard on earth, when the Lord said: *Genesis 26: In your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed.* <note>original Hebrew: וְהִתְבָּרְכוּ בְזַרְעֲךָ כֹּל גּוֹיֵי הָאָרֶץ</note> He said *in seed* and not *in seeds*, so that *by way of excellence* <note>original: κατ᾿ τὴν ἐξοχὴν</note> that Seed might be understood through which fallen human affairs were restored. For thus the Apostle in Galatians interprets this passage: *The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed,* 

<margin>Galatians 3:16. He does not say "and to seeds," as of many, but as of one, "and to your seed," which is Christ.</margin>
In this single promise were pronounced all things which after many centuries were exhibited in the Messiah the Lord: concerning righteousness, sanctification and redemption, the sacrifice, the priesthood, satisfaction, the kingdom and eternal life, the calling of all nations, spiritual blessing, the abrogation of the law, and the glory of the Church gathered from Gentiles and Jews. To this promise God added the Sacrament of Circumcision, for the purpose that it might be a *seal* <note>original: σφραγὶς</note> of the righteousness of faith. Later, when the descendants of Abraham were led out from Egyptian servitude, God instituted the Paschal Lamb, which would not only recall to their memory the wonderful liberation already achieved from Pharaoh, but also—and much more so—foreshadow in a type the most extensive vindication from the devil to be performed by the Lamb of God in assumed flesh, and would even then confer its fruit upon the Faithful, concerning which we shall speak in its proper place. God continues this promise further, repeating it not to the descendants of Esau, but to Jacob, and from Jacob to his son Judah; which the Patriarch Jacob carries out in the name of God, saying: *The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, until Shiloh comes, Gen. 49:10.* That is, to use the words of Blessed Bugenhagen, *the blessed* 

<margin>On Jeremiah, ch. 31, fol. 343.</margin>
*womb from Judah (the container is taken for the thing contained), that is, the promised Seed of the woman. For "Shiloh,"* the Chaldean <note>The Aramaic Targum or translation.</note> reads: *until the Messiah comes.* It is known from Deuteronomy what *his afterbirth* <note>original Hebrew: שִׁלְיָתָהּ</note> signifies, namely the *Secundines* <note>The placenta/afterbirth</note>, where also the container is said for the thing contained, and it signifies a recently born infant. Thus Jacob, looking back to the seed of the woman promised by God, from the afterbirth of Judah...

# From Genesis III. v. 15.

<margin>The First Gospel <note>original: "Protevangelium." The first messianic prophecy in the Bible.</note></margin>
...destined to arise according to the flesh, he said: *The scepter shall not be taken away, until Shiloh comes, that is, the one promised from the woman.* <note>Genesis 49:10</note> Finally, the promise was restricted to the posterity and family of David. For this reason, Paul says that Christ was born from the seed of Abraham according to the flesh; and Matthew begins the genealogy of Christ: *The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of Abraham, the son of David.* These two are named above all others because the promise of the coming Liberator, through whom all nations were to be blessed, was bound to their lineage and posterity. It can hardly be expressed with how many praises the Prophets enriched and adorned this promise of the woman's seed; for, exulting with exceeding joy, they preach about the coming Messiah no differently than if he had already been presented. They do this out of the certainty and full assurance <note>original: "πληροϕορίᾳ" (plerophoria)</note> of faith, which is accustomed to look upon the benefits promised by God as if they were already before one's eyes and placed in the sight of all. A very distinguished and illustrious prophecy concerning the Incarnation of the Son of God was published by Isaiah, chapter 7:14.

<margin>Preface to Isaiah.</margin>
(Whom Jerome honors with an excellent eulogy for his pleasantness of speech, saying: *Isaiah, a noble man of urban eloquence, having nothing of rusticity mixed into his speech.*) seven hundred and sixty years before the Savior's coming in the flesh: *Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.* This noble oracle seems to have been brought forth more by an Evangelist than a Prophet, as was said by Jerome in his *Prologue on Isaiah*, that *he should not so much be called a Prophet as an Evangelist.* The occasion for this was the alliance entered into between the most powerful kings of Israel and Syria against the kingdom of Judah, intended to root it out entirely. Thus, while the saving mystery was not yet fulfilled, even during the encroaching Babylonian captivity, the truth of the promises did not cease. For Habakkuk, in his second chapter, consoles the Jewish people with promises of the coming of the Messiah and his kingdom; that he will surely come, even if the matter is delayed for a little while, though the face of things appears strange, and the people are led away into Babylonian captivity because of their sins. Despite all these things, the coming of Christ and his kingdom cannot be hindered or overturned, but he will certainly come, and for this mystical matter, faith is needed; *for the just shall live by his faith,* says the Prophet there. And so the promise of the blessed seed is scattered through the entire book of the Old Testament, of which the Blessed Chemnitius <note>Martin Chemnitz (1522–1586), a preeminent Lutheran theologian.</note> enumerates a fourfold series: I. From the fall of Adam to the flood (Gen. 3:15, 4:1, 5:29). II. From the flood to Moses (Gen. 8:21, 9:26, 12:1-4, 26:3-4, 27:27-29, 28:13-15, 32:10, 35:2, 49:10). III. From Moses to the Prophets (Exod. 25:17). IV. From the Prophets to Christ (2 Sam. 7:12, 1 Chron. 22:9-10, Isa. 5:1, 43:3, Hos. 1:2, Amos 9:11). We cite only a few from such a great number of prophecies and Gospel promises. When all these have been thoroughly weighed by those who do not have a "fungus" <note>A metaphor for dullness or spiritual blindness.</note> before their eyes, it becomes clear that one and the same Gospel was always proposed to the whole world in the "First Gospel." It is plainly the same both in substance with the Gospel fulfilled in the New Testament, and in regard to God's favor and grace, except that in the New it was given and revealed more clearly. For the prophecies of God

<column-break/>

<margin>The First Gospel.</margin>
concerning the rising Messiah were at first more hidden, but the passage of the centuries rendered them more uncovered and shining, with greater rays day by day, until the Messiah—the shadows and images now removed—came and shone with full light, like a living and life-giving body, and like the sun in the midst of the heaven's light. For at first, by a general promise, God gave a more hidden prophecy about the seed to be born of the woman who would crush the serpent's head; this became more uncovered day by day when later the family of *Abraham* and the tribe of *Judah* were noted, and the lineage of *David* was added. The *Virgin Mother* was described by *Isaiah*; the *place of Birth* was determined by *Micah*; the *Time* was calculated by *Daniel*; the *Forerunner and Herald* <note>original: "Metator" - one who prepares the way.</note> was designated by *Malachi*. All these were preludes, foretelling the mystery of faith and salvation. The times that followed are pure dances of joy; the ancient and figurative time having passed, Christians are glad, leaping for joy, exulting, giving thanks, and celebrating triumphs because the blessed Messiah has arrived—the apex, summit, and crown of all religion, than whom nothing worthier, holier, or more honorable can be imagined. Hence that Gospel which was heard in Paradise, which once sounded among the Patriarchs, sounds no different this very day, at this very hour, because *Christ is the same YESTERDAY and TODAY (Hebrews 13:8).* The time is new in the proclamation of him being given and seen, *and what is new in time is not new to Him who created the times,* as Augustine says:

<margin>Against the Manichaeans, Vol. 6, Book 32, Ch. 9.</margin>
*The grace which was given to us in Christ was given before the secular ages (2 Tim. 1:9).* And that first promise of the blessed Seed is the first and perpetual Gospel, given without time, the explanation of which is its confirmation, the prophecy of which is the perpetual Gospel. The Prophets themselves in this reasoning are Evangelists; *and indeed, whatever promises our remission, justification before God, illumination, and regeneration, all this also properly belongs to the Gospel of Christ,* as witnessed by *Augustine in the Enchiridion, ch. 46.* In this sense, as *Justin [Martyr] says to the Orthodox: "The law is the Gospel foretold, and the Gospel is the law fulfilled."* Concluding our "First Gospel" on account of the benefits of liberation, salvation, and glory, we rightly celebrate our REDEEMER <note>original: "GOELEM" - from the Hebrew 'Goel', a kinsman-redeemer.</note> with the words of David in *Psalm 124:6: Blessed be Jehovah, who has not given us as a prey to their teeth,* namely, the infernal enemies; *and v. 7: Our soul has escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we have escaped. and v. 8: Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.* Therefore, just as the first Parents, having heard the promise of the seed that would crush the serpent's head; just as the pious Patriarchs and faithful Israelites in dangers and disturbances consoled and uplifted themselves with this First Gospel of the coming Messiah; so let us worship the Messiah now exhibited, born and given to us, as our protector. And as they were carried with all the desire of their soul toward him who was to be born, so let us be toward him who is born, looking into whose birthday let us sing with voice and pen with the heavenly choristers:

->**GLORY TO GOD IN THE HIGHEST.**<-

This is the day the Lord has made for joy; let us exult and be glad in it, shouting for joy with...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

With the heavenly spirits thundering again and again:
->GLORY TO GOD IN THE HIGHEST.<- <note>original Greek: ΔΟΞΑ ΕΝ ΥΨΙΣΤΟΙΣ ΤΩ ΘΕΩ.</note>

### Genesis VII. v. 1.

And the Lord said unto Noah, Come thou and all thy house into the ark; for thee have I seen righteous before me in this generation. <note>The text provides this verse in the original Hebrew, then the Greek Septuagint, and finally the Latin Vulgate.</note>

<margin>Noah's Ark. Ambrose * treatise on Noah & the Ark ch. 13. System of Theology Book IV. ch. 7. p. 217.</margin>
In the first age of the rising world, the race of men, overflowing with malice, called down upon themselves an overflowing deluge; for an angry God said in *Genesis 6:7: I will destroy man, whom I have created, from the face of the earth.* When He says he is to be destroyed "from the face of the earth" and not simply "from the earth," Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose (c. 340–397), an influential Bishop of Milan.</note> weighs the matter more deeply, writing: He strikes off the flower, but preserves the root; so that in the depths of the substance, human *virtue* might remain, which may labor on the surface, but remains *capable of feeling* within. Indeed, He strikes off the leafy luxury blooming wickedly, and the wanton progeny of men—like withered and dry flowers on a deformed plant—with the water of the flood. For the nefarious crimes of men required an inundation as a most just punishment for their sins. Indeed, Moses recounts the wickedness of the Antediluvians in two ways: one in general, that such was the corruption of morals that it contaminated the very earth they inhabited; the other in specific, by recording two of their vices: *lust* and *injustice*. He reports the madness of *lust* was so great that, having disregarded piety and honesty, they chose for themselves only those wives who seemed preferable for the beauty of their form, even if they were entirely foreign to the truth of religion. Truly, he says *injustice* toward one's neighbor increased so much that it filled the earth. Yet the most just God did not wish to destroy the ancient world immediately, but rather wished to spare it; for God punishes no one unless He first warns them, lest they be punished. He first warns the world and grants it 120 years to perform repentance; but the Antediluvians held these warnings of the kind Father God in total disregard. Indeed, the "Sons of God" <note>Hebrew: בני האלהים</note>—by whom we are by no means to understand Angels, as if they, captured by the beauty of virgins and scorning their heavenly seat, descended to these lands and desired illicit loves and mingled with them—which was an opinion held among the Ancients by Philo, Josephus, Justin Martyr, Cardanus, Cajetanus, and others. Not foreign to this opinion is Isaac Peyrerus, the creator of the *Pre-Adamites* <note>A controversial 17th-century theory that humans existed before Adam.</note>; hence also the ancient Septuagint reads "Angels of God" <note>Greek: ἀγγέλους τοῦ θεοῦ</note> where we now read "Sons of God" <note>Greek: οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ</note>, and indeed most correctly. For this nefarious crime does not fall upon good Angels, nor do Devils go by the name of "Sons of God" in the sacred Books. It remains, therefore, to understand them as the sons of men, and indeed of the pious, to whom are opposed

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary on this place. * Gen. 24:16.</margin>
the "daughters of men" <note>Hebrew: בנות האדם</note>, that is, of the impious, namely the lineage of Cain. This exposition is also held by *Aben Ezra* <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a 12th-century Jewish scholar.</note>, who understands the Sons of God as men acknowledging the true God; and *Augustine*, who in Book 15 of *The City of God*, ch. 23, says: *They are called Sons of God, either because they had formerly been such, or because their ancestors had obtained this title; and Theodoret, who in Question 47 on Genesis says: They were named Sons of God, just as we are called Christians from Christ.* The Chaldean also subscribes to this view when he calls them "sons of nobles" <note>Aramaic: בני רברביא</note>, and the Jerusalem Targum explains it as "sons of Princes," with whom *Pagninus* agrees. Therefore, the explanation of *Blessed Brentius* in his commentary on this place is fitting: The principal descendants of the *Patriarchs* and heroes are understood, who possessed the highest authority due to birthright and other gifts of God, and who ought to have led others by both doctrine and example—the *Princes and heads of the rest of the people;* just as elsewhere in Scripture *judges and Princes* are called *Gods*. The daughters of men, however, are either girls from the families of the Cainites, or indiscriminately any girls from the common folk; so you may understand that the Princes, who should have been an honorable example to the rest, took for themselves at their own will any girls they encountered, of whatever sort, whether relatives, or kin, whether honorable or dishonorable. *Blessed Gerhard* amplifies this thus: The Sons of God therefore saw those daughters of men, that they were beautiful <note>Hebrew: טובות, "good"</note>, where "to the sight" is understood. * And they took for themselves wives from all whom they had chosen. In this, Augustine (City of God, Book 15) especially urges the emphasis of the pronoun "For Themselves"; for they ought to have procreated for God first, not for themselves—that is, not a family for their own pride, but citizens for the City of God; not with the lust of copulation dominating, but with the duty of propagation burning. The sense, therefore, is that they sinned against matrimonial laws in many ways: 1. By contracting marriage against the will of parents, as is gathered from the word "chosen." The word "took" <note>Hebrew: לקח</note> sometimes signifies to seize or ravish, as *Drusius* notes on this passage (Gen 34:2, Job 5:5). 2. By seeking only beauty in future spouses without any respect for piety, as gathered from the phrase "they saw that they were beautiful." 3. By contracting affinities with the apostate Cainites. 4. By marrying within prohibited degrees, both of which are gathered from the word "from all," meaning from the daughters of any parents whatsoever, whether those parents were devoted to true religion or foreign to it, whether pious or impious, or joined to the contractors in a remote or near degree of blood or affinity. 5. Perhaps also following the example of Lamech, they had many wives at once, because they took "whomever they chose," and the name "wives" <note>Hebrew: נשים</note> is accepted not only for legitimate wives but also for concubines. The shameful and detestable fruit of these shameful marriages were the *Nephilim* <note>Hebrew: נפילים</note>, strenuous assertors of cruelty, an insolent progeny who, in the confidence of their strength, despised all law and right. *Aquila* rendered this as "those who fall upon" <note>Greek: ἐπιπίπτοντας</note>, i.e., attackers. And *Symmachus* as "the violent" <note>Greek: τοὺς βιαίους</note>; but our *Luther* translates it as "Tyrants" and *Piscator of Herborn* as "Giants." From this variety of versions, a variety of opinions clearly appears. There are those who by *Nephilim* understand the evil Angels cast down from heaven, who were previously the sons of God. But from the context of the text, it appears others are meant by the sons of God.

# On Genesis VII. v. 1. 101

<margin>
Noah’s Ark.
</margin>
...of God, and others by the <term>Nephilim</term> <note>original: "נפילים"</note>, for it is derived from <term>naphal</term> <note>original: "נפל"</note>, meaning he fell, he rushed down, or he attacked. They are called this either because by their immense height and stature they caused men to fall; or because through impiety they fell away and defected from God; or because they violently rushed upon men and oppressed them. Hence they are later called <term>mighty men of old, men of renown</term> <note>original: "גבורי אנשי השם"</note>, that is, famous and named men, who labored to acquire for themselves the glory of their name and the increase of their power through the oppression of others. We judge this latter meaning, combined with the middle one, to be more probable and prefer it to the first. We understand by the word <term>Nephilim</term> cyclopean men—savage, monstrous, impious, oppressors, and bandits—with whom the Holy Spirit had to <term>contend or strive</term> <note>original: "דין"</note>, and who possessed, as Hesiod describes them, <term>might in their hands</term> <note>original: "βίη ἐν χερσί"</note>, or as the proverb says, *justice in a scabbard*. From this, Blessed Luther most correctly translates it as <term>Tyrants</term> <note>original: "Tyrannen"</note>; see Blessed Walther. Whether indeed, as the first exposition claims, they exceeded other men in stature, as Drusius, Pererius, Junius, and Tremellius feel in this passage, is not clear but remains in doubt. Nor does it please us what is usually cited by some in this place: namely, that the women bore to the sons of God certain wonderful, prodigious, and portentous offspring; that God, on account of their unbridled lust, deformed the very beauty of human bodies; and further, that the heat and vehemence of lust arising from incontinent love led to a multitude and activity of seed beyond the common vigor of nature at that time. While this opinion is not without its probability, it cannot be proven from the word <term>Nephilim</term> alone.

<margin>
Biblical Office §. 697.
</margin>

Noah alone, and no other with him, a preacher of righteousness, a just and upright man, rebuked the whole world as it rushed headlong into ruin with the greatest security, having disregarded the serious exhortations of God. He found grace before God so that, with his children, he might be preserved in a marvelous way, unheard of until then and never to be heard of again. The decree of the most glorious Holy Trinity was first revealed; for by a voice sent down from heaven, God warned Noah that it would soon happen that an immense force of a cataclysm <note>a great flood</note> would overwhelm the whole earth with an inundation. To escape this with his family, He exhorted him to the construction of an ARK with these words: <term>Make for yourself an ark</term> <note>original: "עשה לך תבה"</note>. MAKE FOR YOURSELF AN ARK, namely, for preserving the remnants of the human race. Noah did what the Divinity commanded; he built the ark as an architect of admirable genius, and that <italic>one hundred years before the flood</italic>, the sad epoch of which fell in the year of the world **1656**. Nor was the structure difficult for Noah, since God prescribed both the material and designated the entire form. Let us look at both. It will be for the fair reader not to demand from me an accurate explanation of all things. Let us admire the supreme craftsmanship of the ark because of its divine origin, of which God Himself provided the ground plan and drew the first outlines. Therefore, this Ark is not a human invention, but a work of Divine art. GOD was the Architect, Noah the Builder, in whom the Holy Spirit <term>wrought</term> <note>original: "ἔκτισε"</note>, instructing his mind concerning the Divine command and the use of the Ark, and impelling his will to act according to the Lord's prescription.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Noah’s Ark.
</margin>
The <term>co-causes</term> <note>original: "Συναίτια"</note> were a Mind reverently weighing the Lord's command, and a Will obeying the Holy Spirit. For Noah did all things with a prompt and faithful soul which had come to him by the admonition and command of God, nor is it ever read that he disputed them. He preferred not to know what God had determined rather than to be made more certain with any danger. He refused nothing, but took care and labored to perfect all things; and because he dispatched everything so willingly and so quickly, God commended that liberality of most prompt obedience again and again, twice testifying how pleasing that compliance was to Him. For when Noah had so conducted, handled, and finished the whole business demanded and committed to him that he could not have acted with greater zeal or more to the divine pleasure, he brought back a most honorable testimony of his diligence, as the Secretary of God wrote of him: <term>And Noah DID according to all that God had commanded him, so he DID.</term> <note>original: "ויעש נח ככל אשר צוה אותו אלהים כן עשה"</note> This emphatic repetition of the verb <term>did</term> should not have been neglected by the Old Interpreter; because the Greek Interpreters saw it was more penetrating and served to increase the praise of Noah, they expressed the holy words with dignity: <term>And Noah did all things, whatever God commanded him, so he did.</term> <note>original: "Καὶ ἐποίησε Νῶε πάντα, ὅσα ἐνετείλατο αὐτῷ ὁ Θεός, οὕτως ἐποίησε."</note> The words of the Holy Spirit are deliberate... Because he proved himself a son in obedience, these words of almost the same sound are read again in <italic>chapter 7, verse 5</italic>: <term>And Noah did according to all that Jehovah commanded him.</term> <note>original: "ויעש נח ככל אשר-צוהו יהוה"</note> For God did not want those matters concerning the singular structure, composition, and perfection of the Ark to be read or perceived here negligently, as if the affairs of Noah were so obscure that they did not require testimony and praise. Since, however, the Holy Spirit depicted the Ark with such wonderful and admirable art and placed it before the eyes of all as a memorial of the event, let us weigh the structure built. The first ship, a work of wonderful labor and stupendous magnitude, a machine salutary to the human race and full of mysteries, built by Noah at the warning and counsel of God, the <italic>Hebrews</italic> called <term>tebah</term> <note>original: "תבה"</note>, a name placed in the construct state, which is read at least twice in the Sacred Books: namely in this place, and in <italic>Exodus 2:3</italic>, where it is used for the basket of bulrushes in which Moses was preserved. From which word Marius gathers that it was so called because it was destined only for saving men from water, so that both rightly bore the figure of a man. Another name for the ark also occurs among the Hebrews, namely <term>aron</term> <note>original: "ארון"</note>, perhaps from <term>oren</term> <note>ash tree, Exodus 25:14</note>, where it refers to the famous Ark of the Covenant; in <italic>Genesis 50:26</italic> for the coffin in which Joseph was buried; and in <italic>2 Chronicles 14:8</italic> for the chest made by King Joash for collecting money for the preservation and repair of the Temple in Jerusalem. The Greeks call it <term>kibotos</term> <note>original: "κιβωτόν"</note>. The Latins call it an <italic>Arca</italic> (Ark), not a ship. For like an Ark, it was fortified on all sides and covered from above, to ward off the waters that were about to fall from heaven with great force. It was governed by no sail, no rudder, but was carried solely by the rowing of divine providence. Nor is it inconvenient for this Ark...

**I**n the first age of the rising World, the race of men, overflowing with malice, called down upon themselves an overflowing deluge; for in His anger, God says in Genesis 6:7: *I will wipe out man, whom I created, from the face of the earth.* While He says man is to be wiped out "from the face of the earth" and not simply "from the earth," Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397), an influential Bishop of Milan.</note> weighs this more deeply, writing: *He says He will destroy all flesh not from the earth, but from the face of the earth. He strikes off the flower but preserves the root; so that in the depths, the substance of human virtue remains, while that which labored on the surface is removed, yet remains capable of feeling within.* Indeed, like withered and dry flowers on a deformed plant, He strikes off the leafy luxury of evil growth and the lustful progeny of men with the water of the flood. For the wicked crimes of men demanded an inundation as the most just punishment for their sins. Moses relates the wicked deeds of the Antediluvians <note><term>Antediluvians</term>: People living before the Biblical Flood.</note> in two ways: one in general, that there was such a corruption of morals that it contaminated the very earth they inhabited; the other specifically, by recording two of their vices: lust and injustice. He reports the madness of lust was so great that, having cast aside piety and honesty, they chose wives for themselves solely because they seemed superior in beauty of form, even if they were entirely foreign to the truth of religion. He says injustice toward neighbors grew so much that it filled the earth. Yet the most just God did not wish to destroy the ancient world immediately, but rather wished to spare it; for God punishes no one unless He first warns them, so that they might not be punished. He first warns the world and grants it 120 years to perform penance; but the Antediluvians held these warnings of the kind Father God in total disregard. Indeed, the "Sons of God" <note>original Hebrew: בני האלהים</note>—by whom we should by no means understand Angels, as if they, captured by the beauty of virgins and despising their heavenly seat, descended to these lands to seek illicit loves and mingled with them—which was an opinion held among the Ancients by Philo, Josephus, Justin Martyr, Cardanus, Cajetan, and others. Isaac La Peyrère, the fashioner of the "Pre-Adamites" theory, is not far from this view.
<margin>Theological System, Book IV, ch. 7, p. 217.</margin>
Hence, in ancient times, the Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament.</note> read "Angels of God" <note>original Greek: ἄγγελοι τοῦ Θεοῦ</note>, where we now read: "the sons of God" <note>original Greek: οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ</note>, and quite rightly so. For this wicked disgrace does not apply to good Angels, nor are Devils referred to by the name "sons of God" in the sacred records. It remains, therefore, to understand them as the sons of men, and indeed of pious men, who are opposed to

<column-break/>

the "daughters of men" <note>original Hebrew: בנות האדם</note>, that is, of the impious—namely, the lineage of the Cainites. This is also the exposition of Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a 12th-century biblical commentator.</note> regarding Noah, who understands the "sons of God" to be men acknowledging the true God. Augustine also says in *The City of God*, Book 15, ch. 23: *They are called sons of God either because they had been such, or because their ancestors had obtained this title.* Theodoret likewise says in his 47th question on Genesis: *They were named sons of God, just as we are called Christians after Christ.* The Chaldean translation also subscribes to this view when it calls them "sons of the great" <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: בני רברביא</note>, and the Jerusalem Targum explains it as "sons of Princes," with which Pagninus agrees. Thus, the explanation of Blessed Brentius in his commentary on this passage is fitting: *They are understood to be the chief descendants of the Patriarchs and heroes, who held the highest authority due to birthright and other gifts of God, and who ought to have led others by both doctrine and example as Princes and heads of the remaining people; just as elsewhere in Scripture, judges and Princes are called "Gods."* The "daughters of men," however, are either girls from the families of the Cainites, or indiscriminately any girls from the common people. You are to understand that the Princes, who should have been an honest example to the rest, took for themselves, according to their own whim, any girls they encountered, whoever they were—whether relatives, kin, honest, or dishonest. Blessed Gerhard <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a Lutheran scholastic theologian.</note> expands on this: *The Sons of God saw those daughters of men, that they were beautiful*
<margin>Commentary on this passage, Gen. 24:16.</margin>
*that they were good* <note>original Hebrew: כי טובת</note>, where "in appearance" is to be understood. *And they took wives for themselves from all whom they chose.* In this, Augustine (City of God, Book 15) especially emphasizes the pronoun *For themselves*; for they ought to have procreated for God first, not for themselves—that is, not for the family of their own pride, but as citizens of the City of God; not with lust dominating the union, but with duty serving propagation. The sense, therefore, is that they sinned against the laws of marriage in many ways: 1. By contracting marriage against the will of parents, as gathered from the word "chose." The word "took" <note>original Hebrew: לקח</note> sometimes means to seize or snatch, as Drusius notes on this passage. 2. By seeking only beauty in future spouses without any regard for piety, as gathered from the phrase "they saw that they were beautiful." 3. By contracting affinities with the apostate Cainites. 4. By marrying within prohibited degrees, both of which are gathered from the word "from all" <note>original Hebrew: מכל</note>, meaning from the daughters of any parents whatsoever—whether those parents were devoted to true religion or foreign to it, pious or impious, or joined to the contractors by a remote or near degree of blood or marriage. 5. Perhaps also following the example of Lamech, they had several wives at once, because they took "whomever they chose," and the name "wives" <note>original Hebrew: נשים</note> is taken not only for legitimate wives but also for concubines. The shameful and detestable fruit of these shameful marriages were the *Nephilim* <note><term>Nephilim</term>: Often translated as giants; here described as violent men.</note>, vigorous enforcers of cruelty, an insolent progeny who, trusting in their own strength, despised all law and right. Aquila rendered this as "those who fall upon" or "attackers" <note>original Greek: ἐπιπίπτοντας</note>. And Symmachus as "the violent" <note>original Greek: τοὺς βιαίους</note>; our own Luther translates it as *Tyrants*, and Piscator of Herborn as *Giants*. From this variety of versions, a variety of opinions clearly appears. There are those who by *nephilim* understand evil Angels cast down from heaven, who were previously the sons of God. But from the context of the text, it appears others are meant by the sons of God.

# From Genesis VII. v. 1, 1.

<margin>Noah’s Ark.</margin>
[The author] and others [interpret] the *Nephilim* <note>original: "Nephilim"</note> through the root *naphal* <note>original: "נפל"</note>, for it comes from *naphal*, meaning *he fell, he rushed down, or he fell upon.* Thus they are so called either because by their immense height and stature they made other men fall; or because through impiety they fell away and defected from GOD; or because they violently rushed upon men and oppressed them. Hence they are afterwards called *the giants* <note>original: "הגבּורים" (ha-gibborim)</note>, *those most powerful robust ones* and *men of name*, i.e., famous and renowned, who labored to acquire for themselves the glory of their name and the increase of their power from the oppression of others. Joining this latter interpretation with the middle one, we judge it more probable and prefer it to the first. By the word *Nephilim* we understand cyclopean men—wild, monstrous, impious, oppressors, and bandits—with whom the Holy Spirit had to *contend* <note>original: "לדון" (ladun)</note> or strive. As Hesiod describes them, they had <term>justice in their hands</term> <note>original: "δίκη ἐν χερσὶ"</note>, or as the proverb says, *justice in the scabbard*. Whence Blessed Luther most correctly translates it as *Tyrants* <note>original: "Tyrannen"</note>; see Blessed Walther. Whether indeed, as the first exposition claims, they exceeded other men in stature, as Drusius feels in his *Commentary on Difficult Passages of Genesis* page 34, and as Pererius, Junius, and Tremellius hold on this passage, is not clear but is left in doubt. Nor does it please us what is usually brought forward by some in this place: namely, that the wives of the sons of God gave birth to certain strange, prodigious monsters; that GOD, on account of their unbridled lust, deformed the very beauty of human bodies; and further, that the heat and vehemence of lust arising from incontinent love led to a multitude and activity in the women beyond the common vigor of nature at that time. While this opinion is not devoid of probability, it cannot be proven from the word *Nephilim* alone.

<margin>Biblical Office § 697.</margin>
Noah alone, and no other with him, a preacher of justice, a just and upright man, rebuked the whole world when it rushed headlong into utter carelessness, having disregarded God’s solemn exhortations. He found grace before GOD so that he might be saved with his children in a miraculous way, unheard of until then and never to be heard of again. The decree of the most glorious Holy Trinity is first revealed; for by a voice sent down from heaven, God warns Noah that it would soon happen that an immense force of cataclysm would overwhelm the whole earth with a flood. To escape this together with his family, He exhorts him to the building of an ARK with these words: <insert>MAKE FOR YOURSELF AN ARK</insert> <note>original: "עשׂה לך תבת" (Aseh lecha tebat)</note>, namely, for preserving the remnants of the human race. Noah does what the Divinity commands; he builds the ark as an Architect of admirable genius, and that one hundred years *before the flood*, the sad epoch of which fell in the year of the world 1656. Nor was the structure difficult for Noah, since God prescribed both the material and designated the entire form. Let us look at both. It will be for the fair reader not to demand from me an accurate explanation of all things. Let us admire the supreme craftsmanship of the ark because of its divine Origin, of which God Himself bears the floor plan and of which He drew the first outlines. Therefore, this Ark is not a human invention, but a work of Divine art. GOD was the Architect, Noah the Builder, in whom the Holy Spirit <term>breathed</term> <note>original: "ἔπνει"</note>, instructing his mind concerning the Divine command and the use of the Ark, and impelling his will to act according to the Lord’s prescription.

<column-break/>

<margin>Noah’s Ark.</margin>
The <term>contributing causes</term> <note>original: "Συναιτία"</note> were a Mind reverently weighing the Lord’s command, and a will obeying the Holy Spirit. For Noah did all things with a prompt and faithful soul which had come to him by the admonition and command of God, nor is he ever read to have argued. He prefers not to know what GOD has determined rather than to be informed with any danger. He refuses nothing; he cares for and labors to perfect all things. Because he dispatched everything so willingly and so quickly, GOD commended that liberality of most prompt obedience again and again, twice testifying how pleasing that compliance was to Him. For when Noah had so shaped, handled, and finished the whole business demanded and committed to him—such that he could not have acted with greater zeal or more according to the divine pleasure—he brought back a most honorable testimony of his diligence, so that the Secretary of God wrote of him: <insert>And Noah DID according to all that God had commanded him, so he DID.</insert> <note>original: "ויעשׂ נח בכל אשר צוה אתו אלהים כן עשׂה"</note> This emphatic repetition of the verb *did* <note>original: "עשׂה" (asah)</note> should not have been neglected by the Old Interpreter. Because the Greek Interpreters saw it was more penetrating and was not present in vain for increasing the praise of Noah, they expressed the holy words with dignity: <term>And Noah did all things, as many as God commanded him, so he did.</term> <note>original: "Καὶ ἐποίησε Νῶε πάντα, ὅσα ἐνετείλατο αὐτῷ ὁ Θεός, οὕτως ἐποίησε"</note> The words of the Holy Spirit are deliberate; where He places a word in the word-order, and in a word often neglected (at least appearing so to us), there is <term>something mindful of the past</term> <note>original: "μνησικακῶς τι"</note>. Because he proved himself a son in obedience, these words of almost the same sound are read again: <insert>And Noah did according to all that Jehovah had commanded him.</insert> <note>original: "ויעשׂ נח בכל אשר־צוהו יהוה"</note> For God did not want those matters concerning the singular structure, composition, and perfection of the Ark to be read or perceived here negligently, or as if Noah’s business were so obscure that it did not require testimony and praise. Since, however, the Holy Spirit depicted the Ark with such wonderful and admirable art and placed it before the eyes of all as a memorial of the event, let us weigh the constructed structure. The *Hebrews* call this first ship—a machine of truly admirable work and stupendous magnitude, yet salutary to the human race and full of mysteries, built by Noah at the warning and counsel of God—*Tebah* <note>original: "תבה"</note>, a name placed in the construct state, which is read at least twice in the Sacred Books: namely in this place, and in Exodus 2:3, where it is used for the wicker basket in which Moses was preserved. From which word Marius <margin>Commentary on Genesis p. 86.</margin> concludes that it was so called because it was destined solely for saving men, and specifically from water, so that therefore both [vessels] deservedly bore the figure of a man. Another name for the ark occurs among the Hebrews, namely *Aron* <note>original: "ארון"</note>, perhaps from *oren* (*ash tree*), in Exodus 25:14 where it is used for the famous Ark of the Covenant; in Genesis 50:26 for the coffin in which Joseph was buried; and in 2 Chronicles 24:8 for the chest made by King Joash for collecting money for the preservation and repair of the Temple of Jerusalem. The Greeks call it <term>kiboton</term> <note>original: "κιβωτόν"</note>, and the Latins call it *Arca* (Ark), not *navis* (ship). For like an Ark, it was fortified on all sides and covered from above, so that it might ward off the waters that were about to fall from heaven with great force. It was governed by no sail, no rudder, but was carried solely by the rowing of divine providence. Nor is it inconvenient for this Ark if such...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Noah's Ark.</margin>
If it were to be given another name than that used by the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, it might be called by a name not uncommon among the Greeks, which is <term>larnax</term> <note>original: "λάρναξ" - a chest, coffer, or ark</note>, of which it is said in the *Iliad*, Book 6:

> All the tools,
> he collected into the silver **larnax** with which he worked.

Now, Noah's Ark can be called a <term>larnax</term>, and quite excellently so; for in ancient times there were ships vaulted into a certain shape which they called <term>larnakes</term>, which you might call arks or chests. There was, under a petty king of Pontus named Anicetus, a leader who in the time of Vespasian devised a new kind of vessel in which there was no use of iron or steel, but it consisted only of wooden pegs and pins; and from their new shape these ships were also called <term>Chambers</term> <note>original: "Cameræ"</note>. Their sides were narrow at the top but supported by a wide hull, and rising from the water itself not straight up, but slightly inclined. And since the waves, rising higher when the wind lifted them, used to overcome the edges of the sides and thus invade the decks themselves, he had prepared a certain new instrument to exclude the waves: namely, movable planks which, according to the measure of the storms, he added one above the other, rising and gently sloping, until at the last, if the nature of the storm required it, they met at the top in the manner of a roof. From this curvature and vaulting of the planks, <term>Tacitus</term> calls them <term>Chambers</term> in *Histories* Book 3, Chapter 47. The inhabitants of the Pontic coast retained these "Chambers" over a long stretch of time, but as the sound was gradually corrupted, they called them first <term>Cumbras</term>, then <term>Cumbarias</term>, and finally <term>Gumbaria</term>, as <term>Rivius</term> teaches in *History of Medieval Navigation*, Book 1, Chapter 24, page 62. The words of Tacitus are: *The barbarians wandered about with more contempt, having suddenly built ships which he calls Chambers, with narrow sides and wide bellies, fastened together without bonds of brass or iron; and when the sea is swollen, as the wave is raised, they increase the height of the ships with planks until they are closed in the manner of a roof.* Thus they are tossed among the waves, with an equal prow on both sides and changeable rowing, so that to put in here or there is indifferent and harmless. Altogether great is God's care for Noah, because while He commands the ark to be constructed, He outlines and prescribes its every measure; he who denies that this was a great act of grace, I know not what could be proven great to him. Is it not very great that God Himself took on the persona of the Architect, and teaches Noah like a Master how to form the greatest ship? Truly it must have been a great work which the Creator of the entire created Machine Himself prescribed, showing Noah a singular benefit against the coming waves of the cataclysm. Waves never heard of, and never to be heard of again, required a ship; it had to be equipped with new diligence in all necessary things, and especially a peculiar wood had to be selected which would endure among constant winds and thick storms. For this wood for the Ark required a hard strength that could bear the violence of the water and sudden tempests. Nor should it be thought that God, the Best and Greatest, gave so many and various kinds of trees in vain—some fit for this thing, others for another—which we shall demonstrate by a humble example. In making a plow, since it is the principal instrument for agriculture, the farmer applies altogether diligent care. He makes the plow-tail from elm, which by its nature can be more easily bent and tamed; he fashions the pole and the two "ears" and

<column-break/>

the share-beam from beech, and the yoke and handle from lime-wood. For not all parts of the plow can be conveniently made from the same material, but some from one and some from another. Hence among the rustic precepts, <term>Virgil</term> in the *Georgics*, Book 1, line 10, places first the making of instruments suitable for plowing, sowing, and reaping, and the appropriate material.

<margin>Noah's Ark.</margin>
> Immediately in the woods the elm is tamed with great force,
> Bent into a plow-tail, and receives the form of the curved plow.
> To this, from the base, a pole is extended eight feet in length.
> Two ears, and share-beams are fitted to the double back.
> The lime-tree is also cut beforehand, light for the yoke, and the tall beech.
> And the handle, which may turn the bottom of the carriage from behind,
> And the smoke explores the timber hung above the hearth.

The same precepts are read in <term>Hesiod</term>, so much so that there is no doubt that <term>Maro</term> <note>Virgil's cognomen</note> borrowed all these things from Hesiod. But these things are mentioned <term>in passing</term> <note>original: "ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ"</note>. Let us admire the material which God Himself prescribed, saying: **Make for yourself an ark of Gopher wood** <note>original Hebrew: "עצי-גפרי"</note>. As to what kind of wood these are, interpreters go off into side-paths of opinion. The woods from which, as from raw material, the whole structure was made, are <term>difficult to interpret</term> <note>original: "δυσέρμηνευτα"</note>, nor can we be led to a knowledge of them by any certain plumb-line. Thus it happens that the Greeks make the material of that most orderly structure <term>quadrangular wood</term> <note>original: "ξύλα τετράγωνα"</note>, or squared wood, whence they think a greater firmness would come to the ship, because things of that shape could be fitted together most conveniently. I have seen no one, says <term>Buxtorf</term>, <margin>Vindication of the Hebrew points, part 2, ch. 11, p. 771.</margin> who gives a reason for this. What did those who saw it thus read? For "Gopher" <note>original: "גפרית"</note> does not mean that. If one might conjecture, I would think that interpretation was born from the Targumists or Talmudists, who have for it <term>cedrina</term> <note>original: "קדרנוס" or "קדרנית" - cedar-like</note>. That interpreter, not rightly grasping the force of this word, understood it as <term>Quadra</term> or <term>Squared wood</term>, just as elsewhere <term>kadrinos</term> is read for <term>Quadrans</term> <note>A Roman coin/measurement</note>. This conjecture would be more persuasive if he were speaking of a Latin interpreter, but since that Talmudic word departs far from the Greek <term>tetragona</term> (squared), I fear to derive the reason for the version from here. Therefore, I am easily led away from the opinion that the cause of the name came to the Greek interpreters from the Talmudic language. If they had used that aid, I would believe that not "squared" but "cedar-like" <note>original: "κέδρινα"</note> came to them from that language, for the Greeks would have easily accommodated that <term>kadrinos</term> to their own rule. Indeed, I would easily believe this was a refuge for the Greeks in the Targumists if they had interpreted it as <term>cedar wood</term>. For who would not believe, if they had consulted those Hebrew Codices, that they would have preferred to speak of Cedar rather than Squared wood? Jerome, seeing the novelty of this opinion used here by the Seventy, does not explain its origin—he who otherwise is accustomed to descend to the very depths—but having rejected "squared," he sticks in "bituminized," like a mouse in pitch or bitumen. *Instead of squared wood,* he says, *we read bituminized in the Hebrew.* But how is that drawn from the Hebrew? Other opinions of others are recorded, the authority of which we do not diminish. If it must be taken in that sense, it must be said either that Jerome looked to <term>Kopher</term> <note>pitch/bitumen</note> and believed it to be the same as <term>Gopher</term>; or he was taught by the Hebrews that this "Gopher" signifies some bituminous tree, either pine, or fir, or terebinth, or something similar, which drips bitumen and resin. While we consider these things in Jerome, and in the tradi-
<meta>The catchword "tioni-" indicates the next page begins with "traditionibus" (traditions).</meta>

# From Genesis VII. v. i.

<margin>Noah's Ark.</margin>
...we behold it covered in bitumen in its layers, I do not know what should be thought of the common tradition from which that famous Translator of the book of Genesis is handed down.

Indeed, he does not act or determine in this or any other place what the Author of the so-called Vulgate version <note>The standard Latin Bible translation</note> hands down. For while that author speaks of *polished wood*, our Jerome speaks of *bituminized* wood. We could present a shining abundance of many disagreeing examples, by whose multitude and density the battle line of those thinking otherwise could be broken through as if by a certain Macedonian phalanx, if this were a convenient place to set up a battle line. The Chaldean <note>The Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase</note> translates it as *cedar wood*, that is, *incorruptible, which does not feel decay*, which is supported by Symmachus, who rendered it as <term>unrotting wood</term> <note>original Greek: ἄσηπτα ξύλα</note>. Most agree with these, because cedar does not feel decay, nor age, nor moths; added to this is what is read in Theophrastus, that Cedars in the Island of Cyprus were of such great multitude that there was enough from which the *undeciremes* <note>Ships with eleven banks of oars</note> of Demetrius were built, being one hundred and thirty feet in length, and in thickness requiring the embrace of three men.

<margin>16. Natural History ch. 33.</margin>
Others believe it was Cypress, a rare material, with Pliny * commending it for its excellence in duration; some say *Pine*; others *terebinth*, a resinous wood bearing sulfurous berries, which they say grows tall in Syria, and they derive some reasoning from the word, upon whose examination Sebastian Castellio applies himself. Jerome, as we mentioned above, seems to have come closer to the Original text, translating it as: *a species*; for from there comes <term>gopher</term> <note>Hebrew: גפר</note> pitch or sulfur. And in this way it must be said that <term>gopher</term> is a certain species of firs or trees that sweat resin. From this, Blessed Luther rendered it <term>from Fir-wood</term> <note>original German: von Tannenholz</note>; by which he expressed the genus, and perhaps intended the species to be <term>Pine</term> <note>original German: Kiefern</note> / which has a close agreement with the Hebrew <term>gopher</term>. The Historian himself confirms us in this opinion when he subjoins the name with a single letter changed, <term>kopher</term> <note>Hebrew: כפר</note>, so that it might be covered with bitumen etc.

Added to this is the fact that fir planks are most suitable for ships because of their lightness and viscous, gluey toughness. See Blessed Gesner *Commentary on Genesis page 167.* who also determines it as very probable that the planks were joined together with nails, handles, rings, buckles, hooks, and other ligaments of that kind—and those of iron rather than wood, because of the force of the waves and the duration of the cataclysm—and that those iron tools were sought from the workshop of Tubal-cain, who is said to have invented the art of making weapons from iron.

However, whatever doubt there may be concerning *Gopher*, it is nevertheless certain that Noah, according to the divine command, used solid wood, not at all decayed or porous, incorruptible wood, squared wood, which could be fitted together neatly and which could withstand the whirlpools and assaults of the waters. Its three dimensions are accurately prescribed to Noah by GOD; its length 300 cubits, its width 50, and its height 30 cubits. Where, as others observe, it should be noted that if the length is divided by the height, 10 will result, which corresponds to the letter <term>Yod</term> <note>י</note>, let the length be added, to which the letter <term>Shin</term> <note>ש</note> fits, now let it be divided by the width, and 6 emerges, which is noted by the letter <term>Vav</term> <note>ו</note>, from which comes <term>SH-Y-V</term> <note>שיו</note>, JESUS. <note>This is an example of Gematria, finding mystical numerical meanings in text</note> Concerning the length of these cubits, however, Interpreters greatly disagree; some understand Geometric cubits, others truly

<column-break/>

<margin>Noah's Ark.</margin>
understand common ones. Origen *Adamantius* asserts that they were Geometric cubits, each of which encompasses six common cubits. But according to this calculation of Origen, the ark, by the benefit of multiplication, would have grown to a vast and almost <term>impossible</term> <note>original Greek: ἀδύνατον</note> magnitude. Indeed, as for *length* it would have been 1800 cubits; as for *width* 300, and as for *height* 180 cubits, and so if the ark had risen equally from its base, its total capacity would have been 97,200,000. Since, therefore, it is likely that Moses accommodated himself to the grasp of the common people, and just as elsewhere he understands vulgar or usual or common cubits, so also in this place it must be determined that he understood no others than those same ones, especially since this very common calculation and dimension prescribed by God is thought to have sufficed for the fullest capacity of all things that were in the ark. Which *Marius* demonstrates thus: just as 30 multiplied by 5 makes 150; so 300 cubits of the ark's length multiplied by 50 of width makes 15,000, which was the size of the floor of the ark, which we have named in that manner. But if these cubits are again multiplied by the other 30 cubits of height, we will find the total capacity of the ark was 450,000 cubits. Moreover, those things which the ark had to contain were 8 humans, then species of land animals, of reptiles indeed at least 25, and of those walking on the earth 150, which computed together with the reptiles, can refer to 175 species, of which only 6 are larger than a horse, a few equal, many smaller than sheep: Let us take therefore, he continues, from each species either two or seven and give as much space as 350 oxen would take; how much is this for the ark, or an ark of 15,000 cubits? 3. Species of birds 150, and almost all smaller than a swan. 4. food. These are his words. Johann Hartman has the same in *Theological Illumination against Treutler*. See also *Johannes Buteo* in his *book on Noah's Ark* arguing subtly on this matter; Goropius Becanus in *Beccefelana*; Tremellius on *Genesis 9, 15.*

Coming to the shape of the ark, which is depicted variously by various people, without doubt it was quadrangular, the bottom flat, not curved into a prow and stern, from which *Leonhardus Marius* concludes that this Noahic ark was not made in the form of a ship, whence it was not necessary for the extremities of the same length to end in a point, as it was not to undertake a journey through the waters like long ships, but only that floating on the waters it might preserve those within it from the water. <margin>Noah's Ark page 26.</margin> Georgius Hornius * mentions a certain ship built in the fourth year of this century according to the proportions of Noah's *Ark*, the use of which was not small in time of *Peace* for exercising commerce without <margin>book 15 of City of God.</margin> any apparatus of war engines. But by no effort of man, as Augustine * says, was there a need for it to be launched into the sea, but the approaching wave lifted it by the natural order of weights. It was also closed on all sides, the sides were straight, the roof curved in the form of an arch, so that from every part the rain water might flow off more quickly. The door was in the middle of the ark, a window stood out from a higher place, so that light might be conveniently let in. But what its figure finally was, cannot be certainly known nor described, for just as the building of the Ark was ingenious, made not by human industry but by the guidance of God alone, so hitherto human wits...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Noah's Ark.</margin>
The abundance of words would fail an army of craftsmen sooner than they could explore and examine all the walls and compartments of this most skillful and utterly divine structure. Concerning the arrangement of the interior parts, it is known from *Genesis 6:16* that the ark was divided into three stories: the *lowest, middle, and uppermost*, just as the human body is usually divided into three cavities <note>original: "ventres" - referring to the head, chest, and abdomen in early anatomy</note>. It is very probable that these were again divided into various small cells for each pair of birds and wild beasts. The *lowest* deck was accordingly divided by several partitions into various small chambers to receive quadrupeds of different kinds separately, with their own walkways through which one could conveniently reach each chamber. There were, moreover, little hatches, doubtless descending directly over the mangers from the upper story like long boxes or channels—some wider, through which straw, hay, and other fodder for the beasts could be sent down for several days; others narrower, from which water for drinking in vessels prepared for this purpose could be conveniently lowered from the upper dining-room <note>original: "cœnaculo" - used here to mean an upper living story</note> at fixed times. There were besides certain vents, like chimneys, which extended all the way to the top of the ark, so that through certain small open doors—aptly constructed on both sides under the projecting drip-edge of the roof so they would be safe from the rains and further removed from the waves—the stenches could exhale and the trapped air could circulate in some way, lest the animals themselves be killed by being infected with the foul filth. In the *middle story*, which was likewise divided in various ways by many partitions into different storehouses, were the repositories for every kind of provision and grain. There were large straw-lofts, hay-lofts, and granaries for barley, oats, millet, and other crops usually given to beasts and birds. There were separate and well-arranged cells for all fruits, such as apples, nuts, chestnuts, grain, oil, and legumes for the sustenance of the humans, with their own walkways through which each place could be easily accessed whenever necessary. These two lower stories had no window, because they required no light. *Not the second*, because it was like the pantry of the house. *Not the first*, because irrational creatures are believed to see somewhat in the dark and are naturally delighted by shadows in a certain way. However, the use of lamps could assist whenever it was necessary to descend to those stories via aptly attached ladders, either for retrieving victuals or for feeding the animals and clearing away the filth. The *third and uppermost story* is thought to have been divided again into three equal parts. The *middle* part, destined for human habitation, had a large window on the side of the ark, perhaps protected on the inside by glass lookouts <note>original: "speculatoribus" - likely meaning panes or shutters</note> which could be closed and opened during the day, but from the outside by wooden folding-doors which could be pulled inward, shut, and firmly barred with iron bolts during the night and when storms were threatening. At the sides of the said hall, they believe many small houses were built: some indeed for the beds of Noah himself, his sons, and their wives; others for a kitchen, for a woodpile, and for cells and food necessary for sustenance. The remaining two spaces on the top story were designated for birds—domestic on one side, wild on the other—with nests

<column-break/>

<margin>Noah's Ark.</margin>
suitably fashioned for them on both sides, and separated from one another as seemed necessary. Therefore, the Ark had the right measure in all things: the right length, height, and width, and a window, as said above, very well-suited for bringing in light. Of what material this window was made, we (along with the Scripture) are ignorant; according to the Rabbis, as witnessed by the Blessed Gerhard in his <gloss>Commentary on this passage</gloss>, it was some precious stone and a most shining one, like a carbuncle <note>a glowing red gemstone</note>, illuminating the whole ark with its brilliance. Concerning this, *Jonathan Ben Uziel* mentions that GOD, as it were, sent Noah away to the river *Pison*, which is fertile in gems, to gather from there the *foreda* <note>a transliterated Hebrew/Aramaic term for a specific gem</note>, and to build it into the ark for illumination to provide light, and commanded him to finish it to a cubit. What *foreda* properly is, is not certain; yet if you consider the circumstances, it could be said to mean Crystal, or a carbuncle, or some other transparent gem. This Noahic Ark also had a proper door, and one high and wide enough even for the larger animals—for instance, *Elephants*, *Camels*, etc.—and placed in the middle story, which had to be ascended by ladders or a small bridge. The Ark was completed in the space of 52 years, as *Eliezer* reported in *Pirke chapter 23, page 51, from Tanchuma*; however, *Rabbi Solomon Jarchi* <note>Rashi</note> cherishes a contrary opinion in *Genesis 6:15*, who established that Noah was occupied for 120 years in building it. We do not define a certain time for the construction: we know this Ark was built by Noah and his three sons, as well as with the help of others who held Noah's undertaking in contempt. We shall now survey the animals entering over seven days—not captured by hunting, nor forced, nor gathered into the ark by the ministry of Angels as the Rabbis dream, but occupying their year-long prison of their own accord; not indeed every individual of the kinds, but the kinds of every individual. Let us contemplate Noah distributing to each their distinct places, bringing in food, and arranging everything necessary for such a great expedition, in which Noah showed his knowledge in natural study, while he fed all the animals gathered in the Ark for a whole year. With all these things thus prepared and arranged, Noah, when he was now a son of 600 years <note>i.e., 600 years old</note>, and his sons, and his wife, and the wives of his sons, entered with him into the ark because of the imminent waters of the Flood. In matters of greatest necessity, he holds that what began by God's authorship is brought to completion by His help for the salvation of himself and his family. For eight souls obtain the mercy of God and enter the ark fabricated by Noah. Some call this number of eight into doubt, being persuaded that more than eight persons were saved within the ark itself, among whom is *Constantinus Manasses*:
> With Noah there sailed sons and daughters,
> His wife, and the wives of his sons, and the bridegrooms of the daughters.
<note>original: Greek verse</note>
The Gnostics also tell fables about the wife of Noah, to whom they give the name *Noria* (that is, *splendid* or *of the stars*), who, when she was not received into the Ark, set it on fire several times because she perceived herself excluded; which was also the cause that delayed the construction of the ark for 120 years.
