# From Genesis VII. v. 1.

<margin>Noah’s Ark.</margin>
Setting aside these fables, we adhere to the literal text, which expressly says that eight souls—and among these the wife of Noah—entered into the ark, while eight times eighteen myriads <note>A myriad is 10,000; the author is estimating a massive death toll of 1.44 million.</note> perished in the waters of the flood. Solon was one wise man among the seven sages of Greece, and the only lawgiver among the seven. Noah was one among eight, and the sole President of the human race, and the only guardian of the Holy Laws of God among the eight. The only safety in the salt sea belonged to Solon alone, the unique teacher of wisdom. He alone enters with a single wife; he alone with three sons, and each of the three with a single wife. Eight souls are preserved for the preservation of the human race, so that three men with three women in that group of eight might benefit the human race through lawful propagation—not three with six, nor three with ten, but three with three. This was not only so they might exist as three couples, but so that in each of the three, one man should depend solely on one woman and find rest in her; that there should be one husband for one wife, and one wife for one husband. It was also so that the whole of humanity might be preserved in an indissoluble bond of unity, and that fertility, which had already ceased in the one <note>Noah</note> due to old age, might pass to the others. What we all are now, we certainly owe to those three from whom we received life. No house was ever governed with such great counsel, such discipline, and such chastity as the House in the Ark.

The voice of Noah was full of gravity, full of authority, and finally, full of salvation. Here are the most proven spectacles of economic life and domestic frugality; genuine examples of a more holy and pleasant conjugal society, when each of those eight is the same as the other, and each of those four <note>the couples</note> is the same as the other: two bodies in one conforming mind, and one mind and one consensus in two bodies. That unity breathes the image of that first unity between Adam and Eve, when at the very beginning of things marriage was first instituted by God; so that they might be two in one flesh, in one mind, and in one concord. This does not consist in plurality, for where there is a plurality of spouses, the unity of marriage ends. God did not say to Noah, nor did He say to Noah’s sons: "Take as many wives as you wish; take two, three, or four, and enter the Ark." What God established in the first man of the first world, the same God confirms in the first man of the second world; and in Noah’s Ark, He commanded that no more women than men be preserved, so that one man should have only one spouse. This beautiful paradigm of unity is recognized even in the animals themselves, while wild and tame creatures dwell together, pairs with pairs, though differing in species. One male and one female of each species enters; not two females, nor two males. Each bird with its mate, and each animal with its partner enters the ship, so that a new genesis might begin. A pair was destined for propagation: male and female. But why was such a strict law placed on irrational creatures? Concerning this "twoness" as an emblem of the marriage bed,

<margin>On Monogamy, ch. 4, p. 467.</margin>
*Tertullian* <note>An early Christian author from Carthage, c. 155–220 AD.</note> discusses it thus: *“The reformation of the second human race is judged with Monogamy as its mother. Again, two undertake to grow and abound in one flesh. Even in the animals themselves monogamy is recognized, lest even beasts be known for adultery. From all the beasts, he says, from all flesh, you shall bring two into the ark, so that they may live with you, male and female; they shall be of the winged animals*

<column-break/>

*according to their kind, and of all the serpents of the earth, according to their kind, two of all shall enter with you, male and female. By the same form, seven pairs are commanded to be chosen from the clean animals, male and female, one and one.”* What more shall I say? Even for the unclean birds, it is not permitted to enter with two females: thus he says. For concerning the number of living things that entered the ark, Moses himself expresses it. For of the clean, seven—that is, 4 males and 3 females <note>The author interprets "seven" as individuals, though others interpret it as seven pairs.</note>—so that the three males would correspond to the three females preserved for the conservation of the species, while the fourth <note>male</note> would be offered as a Thanksgiving sacrifice to a reconciled God. Of the unclean, however, only two entered, where we perceive that the distinction between clean and unclean animals was known even at that time. Therefore, the words of <margin>Gen. 7:3.</margin> *“that seed may be saved upon the face of the whole earth,”* seem to confirm that God intended the conservation of species by this number. However, in the number of these animals, fish are not included, for whom no danger threatened from the waters of the flood; nor amphibians, for which some people—contrary to reason—fabricate cavities or nests on the outside of the ark's wall; nor those which lack sex but are generated from the mixing of different species or born from rot <note>A reference to the historical belief in "spontaneous generation" from decaying matter.</note>.

The ark was now shut <note>original: "ויסגר" (and he shut)</note> for him, that is, for his benefit; for undoubtedly God smeared the door with pitch on the outside either by His own power or by the ministry of Angels, which Noah himself could not do. This being done, the fountains of the great deep were broken; the flood did not come in one day and swallow men, but for forty continuous days and nights, without any delay or intermission, the rains fell. The drops did not drip bit by bit, but the flows of the clouds were torn open. Water overwhelmed all the ground, covered the highest mountains; the straits, seas, and rivers merged in one inundation. No walls protected anyone, no towers. Temples did not profit the suppliants, nor did altars help. Nor did the destroying wave cease until the evil progeny and the wicked race of men had perished. Rare wickedness found an evil end in a horrendous kind of punishment; wicked lust demanded public destruction. Fearing death and the waves of water, they run here and there; now mothers run about the houses trembling with their little ones, not knowing where to go. Now the fearful rise from the table, and the bridegroom and bride from their bed. Now they climb the upper parts of the house, cling to the roofs, and scale the high branches of trees. Now they swim to the hills and flee to the mountain ridges. But, alas, there is safety nowhere, no harbor in any place or land. Indeed, God sends forth waters from above and below by a just judgment, so that they might be submerged in the immense waves—yet not all who despised God's kindness when provoked to repentance would be eternally damned. <margin>Oration 5 on Noah, 45.</margin> Basil <note>Saint Basil the Great, 4th-century Bishop.</note> graphically describes this inundation of the horrendous flood *in these words: “From above the heaven hurled down torrents, from below the earth sent up abysses, and creation was reduced to the nature of water. There was no longer a distinction between dry land and sea; everything was held together in one stream. No longer did springs, lakes, and fountains flow with grace, but they were plunged into wild seas—”*

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
->Page 106<-

<margin>Noah's Ark.</margin>...all things were being destroyed: the beauty of the sprouts and the flowers of the trees, the city, the Pleiades; not even the mountain peaks remained, but everything shone back from the waves, covered in a common grave. <note>The author is quoting a Greek passage describing the total submergence of the world.</note> Again the abyss of waters covered the earth; the sky seemed to fall into the waters, and it inclined as if into the ancient confusion of <term>chaos</term> <note>original Greek: κεχάουσμίαν (kechaousmian), referring to the primordial state of the universe before order.</note>, when, as Basil says in his 6th Oration, page 49: the sun was walled off by clouds, when the light completed its course stripped of its glow, and when there was no moon, no sight of stars, but night followed night, and the creation of the day was widowed, and the boundaries of nature were confounded. By the wrath of God the world "melted into water," to use the word of Censorinus <note>A 3rd-century Roman grammarian.</note>, and the earth was as if converted into the form of a sea, which Basil elegantly describes: *Creation was reduced to the elemental nature of water.* For, as Dausqueius explains on page 40, he describes *a universe so horrible, so foul and deformed, that with all buildings prostrated, all trees torn up, and all living things killed, with heaven and earth snatched from sight (for crowded waves burst forth from both), seas appeared everywhere, and water was everywhere, from which elements all things were first forged in the first part of Genesis.*

Regarding the horrendous slaughter of men in that cataclysm, let us hear Leonard Lessius <margin>On the perfection of divine manners, p. 371.</margin> <note>A Flemish Jesuit theologian (1554–1623).</note>: *A vengeance seems great when some wealthy city is utterly overturned with its houses burned and all who inhabited it deleted by slaughter. But there, it was not some city or kingdom, but the whole world with all its inhabitants, wealth, and ornaments that was deleted.* The men of that age were most adorned with all gifts of nature: of tall stature, with best-formed bodies, immense strength, the greatest boldness, most skilled in warfare, of the firmest temperament, prolonging a flourishing life and age for many centuries. There was also a greatest and innumerable multitude of them, and they occupied almost the whole world; so much so that it is very credible that far more men existed then than exist in this our century. For since they lived so very long, were of the firmest body, and all were intent on propagation—and many took several wives—it happened that within three hundred or four hundred years they spread into many myriads, and individuals could fill great kingdoms, with new ones constantly being born and the old ones not dying off, but persisting together for seven hundred, eight hundred, or nine hundred years. Thus many of the ancestors saw the largest provinces occupied by their own lineage, and two or three hundred myriads of men procreated from themselves. For if from one Jacob within three hundred years so many were procreated that they made up an army of six hundred thousand men from twenty years of age, besides women and little ones (whose number was easily twice as large), even though men then reached scarcely a seventh part of the former lifespan: how great a multitude shall we estimate was procreated in that primeval age through 1656 years, when men were of such long life, and as others were born, the earlier ones did not fail except after many centuries? Yet God made nothing of that infinite multitude and all their ornaments, which are so great among men, and removed them all by slaughter through the immense force of waters sent down from above.

However, in what year of the world, month, and day the flood happened, there are as many opinions as there are authors, some placing

<column-break/>

its beginning in the year of the world 1655, others in the year 1656. That the flood happened in the month of November in the year 1656, Scaliger (5. *On the Emendation of Time*, p. 371, 372), Emmius (2. *Chronological Matters*, p. 41), Petavius (2. *Account of Time*, 2. c. 1. p. 83), Pererius (*Commentary on Genesis*, Vol. 1, book 7, p. 251, 252), Calvisius (*Chronological Introduction*, c. 35, p. 136) and others agree; but they disagree on the day, some embracing the 17th of November, others the 25th and 28th. <margin>Ger. Chron. book 1, p. 64.</margin> Wichmann thinks it is more consistent with the Mosaic words if it is established that from the beginning of the world to the flood 1655 years elapsed, and furthermore one month and 16 days from the year 1656. He establishes this by two arguments: 1. He takes it from the fact that in Genesis 8:13 it is said in the 601st year of Noah, and in the first month and first day, the waters of the flood <term>were dried up</term> <note>original Hebrew: חרבו (charvu)</note> from the surface of the earth, and Noah removed the covering of the ark, etc. From this he gathers that from the beginning of the world to the start of the flood, 1656 years and 46 days did not pass (as Calvisius conjectures), but at least 1655 years and furthermore one month and 16 days. 2. Because in chapter 9:28-29, Noah is said to have lived 350 years after the flood, so that the days of his life were 950 years. If, therefore, at the coming of the flood Noah had completed his 600th year, it follows the days of his life would have been not 950 but 951, which is against the express letter of Holy Scripture, since the cataclysm lasted a whole year, and Noah stayed in the ark for a whole year, which year joined to the rest makes 951 years. So says he. But in book 2, p. 264, he places the beginning of the flood in the Year of the World 1656 and its end in 1657, which he also repeats in the appended *Outline of his Sacred Chronology*.

However, by what computation one should proceed—since the flood is said to have begun in the second month of the year—whether by the sacred year or the profane year, not everyone feels the same. Torniellus understands it as January, which he claims the Gentiles afterwards consecrated to Noah, and from him (as he was otherwise called the two-faced Janus) they named it January. <margin>book 1. antiq. c. 4.</margin> But no reason appears why Moses would call this month the second. Josephus (c. 4) refers the beginning of the flood to the month of *Marcheshvan* <note>The second month of the Jewish civil year, occurring in autumn.</note>, which corresponds to our October; he therefore established that the civil computation of the year, in which the beginning of the year is in autumn, should be the starting point for the flood beginning in the second month. But it is more likely that according to the Ecclesiastical or sacred computation, in which the beginning of the year is established at the vernal equinox, Moses is to be understood; so that the flood occurred in the month of *Iyar* <note>The second month of the Jewish religious year, occurring in spring.</note>, which corresponds partly to our April and partly to May. This is because this method of counting the year from the vernal equinox was established by God himself in Exodus 12:2, and in the description of the Israelites' crossing of the Jordan, the account of time is likewise referred to the sacred year in Joshua 3:19 and 5:9. Nor does it stand against this computation that at the time of the flood the sacred year was not yet in use. For it is not unfamiliar for Moses to use a historical <term>prolepsis</term> <note>A rhetorical device where a future name or concept is applied to a past event.</note> to describe things done long ago with terms used in his own time; an example among others is the word *Cherubim*, to omit others for now. It was said above that Noah remained in the Ark for a full year, the calculation of which (without prejudice to anyone else's view) we establish thus: Noah was in the ark for a full year and ten days, since a year has 12 months, each of 30...

Noah entered into the ark on the 17th day of the second month, or May 2nd according to some; according to Calvisius <note>Sethus Calvisius (1556–1615), a German astronomer and chronologer.</note> it was April 26th. On the 17th day of the fifth month, the waters decreased. From the beginning of the flood, therefore, until the day on which the ark rested on the mountains of Ararat, there are 150 days. From then until the first day of the tenth month (which Calvisius places on July 8th), when the tops of the mountains were seen, there are 73 days. From then further until the opening of the window and the sending out of the raven, there are 40 days. Afterward, since Noah waited seven days from the sending of one dove to the sending of another, it is inferred that he also waited 7 days from the sending of the raven until the sending of the first dove. From the sending of the first dove to the sending of the second is 7 days. From the sending of the second to the third, 7 days. From the sending of the last dove until the removal of the covering, there are 29 days. For it is necessary that these days intervened entirely, which becomes manifest from the fact that on the first day of the tenth month the tops of the mountains were seen; but on the first day of the first month, Moses says Noah removed the covering of the ark. These days therefore end on the first day of the first month, from which until the 27th day of the second month there are 57 days. All of these collected into one number make 370 days, that is, a full solar year and ten days. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Noah’s Ark.</margin>
...peoples, whom Stephanus [of Byzantium] calls the *Gordyaeans* in his entry on the city of *Gordyos*, but Xenophon, according to Pliny (*Natural History, Book 6, Chapter 15*), calls the *Carduchi*, now known as the *Cordueni*. Regarding the name *Lubar* <note>A mountain name found in the Book of Jubilees and other apocryphal texts</note>, there is no small controversy among scholars, which we do not wish to make our own in this place, but we refer the Benevolent Reader to Fuller (*Sacred Miscellany, Book 2, Chapter 1, page 134*) and Allacci (*Observations on Antonius the Etruscan, note 87, page 196*). There are others, however, who think that Ararat is *Imasus* or the highest peak of the Caucasus, which divides India and Scythia; see Gesner on this passage. In weighing the location of this mountain, Goropius Becanus (*Hispanic Origins, page 7 and elsewhere*) proceeds so confidently—a fault truly peculiar to him—as if he himself had exited the ark with Noah and led the first ranks in the company of Japheth. He judges it more likely that the ark settled on Mount Taurus, and that Noah fixed his seat in Margiana, founded Nysa, reigned there as High Priest and King, and sent out colonies from his large number of family members. Whatever the case may be regarding the ridge of the mountain on which the ark rested, it is the opinion of almost everyone that the Ark settled on Mount Ararat, located in Greater Armenia (which is assigned various names in different places), than which there is no higher mountain in the whole world. Of this mountain, Hayton [of Corycus] records: *Mount Ararat, because of the abundance of snow which is always found on it in both winter and summer, can be climbed by no one; yet on its summit there always appears something black, which is said by men to be the Ark.*

Established on that ridge of the highest mountain, Noah—the Father of all mortals after the flood, to whom all posterity owes as much as it owes to him through whom it received seed, the breath of life, and the use of this light—as Goropius Vertumnus says on page 93, sends out a raven to explore whether the water had diminished even in the valleys. It is often said of a tamed raven that it does not easily forget its home. Whether this raven actually returned is a matter on which not everyone holds the same opinion. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translates it as: *and having gone out, it did not return*, which the Vulgate translator followed, rendering it: *The raven went out and did not return.* Some imagine this cause for its absence: that the raven, being an unclean bird, fell upon the carcasses of men and beasts as the waters receded, and having found suitable food for itself, it settled there. The Hebrew text provides us with this sense: that the raven returned to the ark, sat upon it and flew around it, and from there flew down again to the floating carcasses; for we read *yatsô vashôv* <note>original: יצוא ושוב</note>, i.e., it flew around the ark until the waters were dried up. Hence Blessed Luther expressed it most aptly: **It flew ever back and forth / until the waters dried up on the earth.** Whether it finally returned to the interior of the ark is doubtful, nor can this be determined from the particle "until," which is not always a marker of time but often signifies continuation. Let it suffice for us that there is no error in the authentic text, while even the Papists themselves depart from the Vulgate in this place, among whom is Bellarmine (*On the Word of God, Book 2, Chapter 2*). See also the Douay theologians in their *Notes on the Latin Bible, Volume 1, page 1715*, and among our own scholars, Blessed Gerhard (*Commentary on Genesis, page 215*), Blessed Glassius (*Sacred Philology, Book 1, page 48*), and Blessed Walther (*Biblical Harmony, page 91*). While the raven was thus flying around,

<column-break/>

he sent out a dove three times—a bird that frequents meadows and fields and gathers seeds. Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, Zonaras, Eusebius, Bede, and others maintain that there was only one dove that performed a three-fold mission; they perhaps find the Hebrew text favoring them, where the letter *He* (the definite article) is placed before the word *Yonah* (dove), as if to say: "that very dove." Others, however, feel differently. For the first dove, sent out to explore whether the flood waters had ceased, returned within the same day as a bird of no good news; for since its foot found no place to rest, it returned to the ark, of which Josephus says that it returned muddy, namely on its wings and feet. The second one, having been sent out and its mission accomplished, returned toward evening, carrying a small olive branch with green leaves in its mouth, by which very thing it announced that the flood had departed from the world. Regarding this second sending of the dove, Chrysostom writes (*Homily 10 on Matthew*): *When the common shipwreck flooded the entire inhabited world, and our race was in danger of being wiped out, the dove appeared and showed the end of the storm; and bearing an olive branch, it brought the good news of common peace to the world.* And Tertullian (*On Baptism, Chapter 8*): *God, after the waters of the flood by which ancient iniquity was purged—after the baptism of the world, so to speak—announced the peace of heavenly wrath being dismissed to the lands through the dove sent from the ark, which returned with an olive branch, a sign which even among the nations is held out for peace.* By this very act, it stood as a type <note>A prophetic symbol or foreshadowing</note> of the peace that usually shines upon the Church after the waves of storms have been calmed. Furthermore, that leaf in the authentic text is called *aleh zayit taraf* <note>original: עלה זית טרף</note>, *a leaf of olives*; the Septuagint says *a leaf of olive, a dry twig*, i.e., not just a leaf, but a small branch. Josephus calls it a *shoot of olive*, which seems properly to suit a branch sprouting with leaves. The Jews fabulate that this leaf was snatched from Paradise, and Bellarmine agrees with them to preserve the beauty of Paradise; but he is left alone with his little fable by the defenders of his own faith. For if, as Moses testifies, the water rose above the highest peaks of the tallest mountains, let him explain—if he is a man!—how a terrestrial Paradise built on a plain could remain unharmed by it. Finally, he sent a third dove, which, since it found food on the surface of the earth, did not return. From this, Noah concluded that the surface of the earth was relieved of the waters; hence, having removed the roof, he saw the surface of the earth stripped of the waters.

We have sailed enough now with Noah. Let us consider finally with what studious labors he, enclosed in the ark, warded off the boredom of the time, which we shall present in the words of Victorinus Strigelius from his *Oration on Physical Doctrine, page 70*: *What works must we think this old man performed when, enclosed in the ark for thirteen lunar months, he was carried along amidst the horrible sounds of the waters? Surely he could not practice agriculture or rule a Republic with counsel. He therefore performed the duty and office of both a Philosopher and a Preacher; he not only taught his listeners about God, the coming Liberator, and eternal life, but he also discoursed on the nature of things, and wisely advised how many most sweet images of God are impressed upon it. The raven sent from the ark, not returning because it was occupied with tearing at carcasses, he compared to a greedy Teacher, who so guards his own utility that whatever he does, he refers back to it, forgetful of the benefits of the Church. But the dove re-*

...going forth with the olive branch, he said it was the image of a good and wholesome Teacher, who is more distressed by the salvation and preservation of the Church than by his own safety and that of his children. Nor is there any doubt that this most excellent Philosopher <note>Referring to Noah as a "philosopher" or lover of wisdom</note> accurately described the layout of the places, so that he might know, upon exiting the ark, in what part of the world he was and how far he was from his Fatherland. For he gathered the history of the first Church, which flourished in wisdom and virtue before the flood, and diligently noted the series of times. By these scholarly works, this best of Old Men undoubtedly lightened the losses of the flood. *Compare Torniellus under the Year of the World 1657.*

Nowhere does there exist a more illustrious example of Wrath, nor of mercy, than in the history of Noah’s Ark, in which, if we attend to the judgment upon the impious, we tremble at the magnitude of the wrath. We are stunned by the mercy, seeing a few from the world preserved within the Ark in a miraculous way, so that hereafter the whole world might be saved from destruction. As just as GOD was toward the wicked, so was He merciful toward Noah and his family; who, after that famous disaster of the waters, having seen the Bow of God in the clouds, acted as the Parent of the then-rebirthing world. To give thanks to God for all men who were in him (as if in a seed), he built an altar, upon which he offered a sacrifice of clean animals—which he himself, as a High Priest taught by divine instinct, had preserved in the Ark. This sacrifice, as *Moses* testifies, was so sweet and pleasing that God not only received it with favor, but even promised that He would not further destroy the world as He had done in the flood.

We have hitherto seen and surveyed Noah’s Ark together with the Universal Flood as a well-equipped Citadel; but as nothing can be so well-equipped that it is not sometimes infested by the injuries of the air or the snares of some thief, so also that most wicked Thief *Muhammad* infested this most noble work. He attached many fables to the Ark of Noah, as *Guillaume Postel*, that excellent writer on Mahometan affairs, taught us in *Book 2 on the Concord of the Globe, ch. 12, p. 196.* He seems to have touched upon the history of Noah in his "dung-like" Koran to instill terror, introducing a thousand fables of Noah's ark regarding dung, the mouse, the pig, the elephant, adding various fabrications and weaving six hundred trifles. But leaving these fabrications to their own storyteller, we shall finally subjoin the profane <note>secular or non-biblical</note> history regarding what has been said: for it is certain that the history of the flood reached the Heathens as well. However, the Devil, the "Ape of God," because he could not delete and obliterate it, nevertheless obscured it with various fables. For that flood of *Deucalion*, which *Alsted* says happened in the *Year of the World 2437*, by which Greece and Italy were devastated, they either confuse with the flood of Noah or corrupt its circumstances, so that they exist today like the planks and fragments of a most sad shipwreck after so much darkness and alterations of the truth. Meanwhile, *Berosus, Hieronymus the Egyptian, Mnaseas, Phoenix, and Nicolaus of Damascus* make mention of the universal inundation that occurred in the time of Noah, as we previously perceived from *Josephus*. The memory of the dove sent out also remained in

<column-break/>

<margin>
Noah’s

</margin>

*Plutarch’s* little book, which he titled, <term>Whether land or water animals are more intelligent</term> <note>original Greek: pōtera tōn zōōn phronimōtera...</note>, that is, <term>which of the living creatures have more reason, the terrestrial or the aquatic?</term> <term>The mythologists say that a dove sent out from the chest was a sign to Deucalion; retreating inside when it was stormy, but flying away when it was clear.</term> <note>original Greek: hoi men oun mythologoi...</note> That is: The poets write that a dove was sent out from the ark by Deucalion, so that as long as it returned, it betook itself to the same place immediately, giving an argument for a storm; but after it flew away, an argument for serenity. Thus, for Noah he substituted the name of Deucalion, in whose time they write that among men there was no religion of the Gods, no majesty of laws, and no authority of Princes. But *Deucalion*, a good and pious man, built temples to the Gods and founded cities, and thus with his wife *Pyrrha* stood before other men in reverence toward the Gods. Warned therefore by *Prometheus*, he entered an Ark—which *Lucian* calls a <term>small box</term> <note>kibōtion</note> and *Andrus of Teos* calls a <term>chest</term> <note>larnaka</note>, from which later came *Larnassus* or *Parnassus*, because that Skiff landed there—and he alone was saved with her while the mountains were covered by that inundation. Furthermore, *Ovid* in the *Metamorphoses* and *Lucian* in *The Syrian Goddess*, even if they erred in Chronology and confused the Thessalian flood with the universal one, nevertheless borrowed the seeds of truth from *Moses*. Indeed, *Lucian*, in imitation of Holy Scripture, recounts the causes of the inundation: <term>because being very insolent, they committed lawless deeds; they neither kept oaths, nor received guests, nor pitied suppliants, etc.</term> <note>original Greek: hoti hybreis au karta eontes...</note> He adds also the form of the calamity, and how Noah, whom he calls Deucalion, embarked upon the ark with his family, and the animals, whichever were fed by the earth, entered the ark in pairs of every kind. So *Alexander Polyhistor* and *Abydenus*, in *Cyril's 1st book against Julian*, report: *that Saturn predicted to Xisuthrus the coming flood, and commanded him to build an ark for himself, in which he could receive every kind of animal; and that in Egypt, in the city of Heliopolis, monuments of this were preserved in certain sculptures, and that he was finally carried in that Ark toward Armenia.* After some days, he sent out some birds, which found nothing dry, and then others and others, until, having sighted land, he descended into Armenia; in which place they assert the remains of the Ark are studiously guarded by the inhabitants, who use them against various diseases. What these men say concerning Saturn flowed from the opinion of the Greeks, who, because the seventh day is sacred, thought Saturn was worshiped by the Jews. And Xisuthrus in the Syrian language is perhaps the same as Noah, who in different places, as we read, obtained different surnames. From these sayings it is clear how the Devil perverts the truth, confuses men left to themselves when God is neglected, and utterly veils true things with the coverings of fables, drawing men away from the truth, so that according to *St. Paul*, exchanging the truth for a lie, they venerated and worshiped those things which were created above Him who created them, who is to be praised forever, Amen.

### Genesis IX. v. 27.

->May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant. <note>original Hebrew: יפת אלהים ליפת וישכן באהלי־שם ויהי כנען עבד למו</note><-
->May God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the houses of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant. <note>original Greek: Πλατύναι ὁ Θεὸς τῷ Ἰάφεθ, καὶ κατοικησάτω ἐν τοῖς οἴκοις τοῦ Σὴμ, καὶ ἔστω Χαναὰν παῖς αὐτοῦ.</note><-
->*May God enlarge JAPHETH, and may he dwell in the tents of SHEM, and let CANAAN be his servant.*<-

<margin>The migration and division of nations.</margin>
Nothing under the sun is so difficult to explain as the migration of nations, and the mixing of peoples into other peoples—whether neighboring or far distant—and the changes that followed throughout the inhabited world from that <term>metoikesia</term> <note>migration or change of abode</note> and <term>epimixia</term> <note>intermingling or social intercourse</note>. And this is the reason why, out of so great a number of writers, scarcely one survives who has described the lineage of nations <term>haplosphalos</term> <note>without error or simply and securely</note>. Therefore, if in this part I do not satisfy your expectation, Blessed Reader, you will not wonder at all. For who could divide that vast multitude of men scattered across the whole world into various provinces and various generations, so that from that innumerable number which has inhabited the globe from Noah down to our own memory, he could determine with certainty that this nation belongs to the tent of Japheth, that one to Shem, and that other to Ham? It would be the same as if one wished to determine, regarding this or that pile in a royal granary, that it came from this or that field. We know that in the beginning all flowed from one source, and were born of one parent, Noah, after the flood, and gradually passed into various regions of the world. But if we can make progress in the first millennium, in the second we are blind, in the third we stumble, and in the fourth we are utterly uncertain. For to seek the original seats of nations is a matter agitated by the various controversies of many, mixed with many conjectures, which even today—indeed, for all eternity—cannot be freed from dispute. Pagan writers, thinking it a disgrace to pass the matter over in silence, yet unable to give true and authentic interpretations, resorted to all sorts of things; and so that they might win some veneration for these or those regions, or these or those inhabitants, they traced the beginnings of their dwellings back to certain Gods; they were more prudent than those who recounted the peoples presented to them as being without any origin. Callimachus, being curious in this area regarding the migration of nations and the various <term>paradosis</term> <note>tradition or handing down</note> of customs, wrote a book *on the origins of cities and nations and the changes of names, and on the changed seats of nations*, aided no doubt by the Alexandrian Library, for he lived in the household of Ptolemy Philadelphus, and later Euergetes. If this book were extant, the beginning and the more certain end of our labor would be easier. However, ignorance of Jewish antiquity prevented the gentiles from being able to leave anything certain to the memory of posterity. The Greeks write about the origin of things in such a way that you do not miss their diligence, but rather their lack of knowledge; hence, being ignorant of foreign affairs as well as of places and lands, they very frequently <margin>Censure of Berosus p. 34, 35.</margin> hallucinate, as Caspar Varrerius demonstrates with many examples and by the authority of Polybius. Nor are they alone, but with them also the Latin writers, all of whom, even if they received some memory of the first nations and the first seats of this or that nation through the tradition of their ancestors, yet it is so obscured and involved in such fictions, as they say, that nothing solid

<column-break/>

can be perceived from it; for they often so pervert kinship that they make him who was the father the son, and him who was the grandson the grandfather. Great diligence is found in Ptolemy, Strabo, Pausanias, and others <margin>The migration and division of nations.</margin> in describing the world and in investigating the beginnings and progress of peoples, from which we can gather much. Whatever the case may be regarding the seats of peoples, they are often made doubtful by the <term>fortune of war</term>, or the <term>frequent change of jurisdictions</term>, or the <term>desire for new settlements</term>, or the <term>mixing of different peoples in one seat</term>. All these things do not disentangle but rather entangle the migrations of nations, their seats, boundaries, and borders. The Phrygians and Mysians lived so mixed together that their boundaries passed into a proverb to designate doubtful and intricate matters, as Strabo testifies, teaching moreover that the Mysians led colonies into Europe, while another geographer errs when he writes that the Mysians came from Europe into Asia. These things being so, that immense crop of fables is immediately torn up and rooted out. He must be insane who would dare to attribute the origin of nations to any other, whether he seeks it in the heavens or on the earth, than to Adam, who is the first sower of men, or Noah, who is the second after the flood. But so that we may more easily arrive at an understanding of universal history and the true origin and seat of the first inhabitants, the heads and migrations of nations must be considered: The heads of the families of Noah, through three branches in a three-forked path, rightly claim for themselves the <term>proteia</term> <note>pre-eminence or first place</note>, which are the foundations and roots of all narrations. Moses describes them so accurately in chapter IX and especially chapter X of Genesis, that the use of this chapter is immense throughout the entire body of Scripture and through all the monuments of all writers. For if we lack this beginning of narrations, although it be a summary beginning, everything would be in narrowness and obscurity. Therefore, since Moses alone describes the first parents of the world and the first cities most certainly—so much so that where that first writer of the first age ends, more is conjectured than known about the rest—we should rightly and faithfully submit ourselves to his faithful information. For here, while he sets down the first beginnings and origins of nations after the cataclysm, he introduces Noah, the father of all, thus blessing his son Japheth: >May GOD enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant.< This is indeed a most ample consecration, which promises this: that his descendants would reign so widely that they would not contain themselves only in their hereditary part of the world, but would extend their empire even to the regions of others, and dwell in Asia and Africa, the former of which fell to Shem and the latter to Ham in the division of the fatherland. For Noah, after he noticed the numerous progeny of his sons, believed that his only task was to assign seats to the family growing from him in a timely manner. Therefore, however many changes of kingdoms, states, nations, and things there have been in the whole world, it is necessary that the inhabitants of the entire earth proceeded from the house of the one Noah, so that they are the sons of one of his three sons; nor can it be otherwise than that through whichever of his sons they are descended, as many as inhabit the face of the earth everywhere. Since, therefore, the first origins of nations can be known from the sacred Tablets, but their migrations cannot be known from the same, as concerning...

# From Genesis IX. v. 27.

<margin>The migration and division of nations.</margin>
...how they passed from nation to nation and changed locations. For it is such an intricate burden to show the distinctions of nations, to show which seats they occupied and which they changed. Indeed, no nation could ever promise itself a stable and fixed seat, nor dare to say, *I am immovable.* So wonderful a turning of seats presents itself, and even more wonderful a turning of Republics. No city could promise itself a tomorrow, no village, no castle. If we consider the incursions of nations into nations—how either poverty or greed and ambition drew each to occupy neighboring or distant seats—we do not know what should be said first or last. Now the East has mixed itself with the West, now Hesperia <note>The western lands, usually Italy or Spain</note> with Iberia, now Asia with Africa. Change and exchange occurred through various inversions, no less of men than of customs, and contagion drew contagion, for some evil always clung from a neighboring evil. It would be a matter for a book and a thick volume to comment upon and describe everything; we will endeavor to review certain things here, as far as the space allows, on the occasion of the passage proposed from the Sacred Pandects <note>A term for the Bible, likening it to a complete body of law</note>, bringing to its aid at the same time Chapter X of Genesis, which is like a Hermes <note>A guide or signpost</note>, especially since what Moses reported here precedes all memory of writers, and by whose ruler everything that others have most abundantly produced must be corrected. Hence, no one can be an Antiquarian, nor any Politician, unless he has known and read the tenth chapter of Genesis, which, although it seems sterile in appearance and to linger on bare names, we nevertheless have here an excellent fragment of the History of the world: how the whole earth was filled with men by the three sons of Noah, and how the nations were divided throughout the entire earth. If this second origin of the human race had been known to profane <note>Secular or non-biblical</note> historical writers, their history would not have been contaminated with so many fictions, from which, however, some can be taken for true use, such as those concerning floods, Janus, and Saturn. The whole world is now the offspring of three men, by a propagation so admirable, known only to God alone, and proceeding only from the inestimable power of God. First, therefore, we shall take up the *Division of the Earth*, which was made first of all after the Flood among the sons of Noah. In the first partition of lands, which Noah ordained in the family-division of the whole world, *Asia* fell to Shem beyond the Taurus mountains, *Africa* to Ham, and the Northern part of Europe and Asia, comprised by the ridges of the Taurus and Caucasus, fell—according to <margin>Goropius Becanus, *Gallicorum*, Book I, p. 27.</margin> Becanus—to Japheth and his sons and grandsons. Each occupied his own seat, though the brotherly bond in the heart was uncertain. Concerning this threefold division of the world, Laurentius Rhodomannus in *Palæstina*, p. 23, writes thus:

> Shem obtained the greater Asia, while noble
> Japheth received the lesser, and the well-grazed Europe
> By the casting of lots. Ham obtained the Libyan and Ammonian plains.
> <note>Original Greek: Μείζονα μὲν Ἀσίην Σῆμ’ ἔλαχεν... This verse describes the traditional division of the three known continents among Noah's sons.</note>

Let us migrate, therefore, with Noah and his sons, the men of the first migration, first to the neighbors, and from these to those, and from those to others, as much as we can, through a rugged path. However, no one will ever find a certain method of migrations, with some withdrawing here and others there, wherever the convenience of dwelling invited, or the force of enemies drove, or their own rashness impelled.

<column-break/>

Who shall relate the migrations of Japheth and Shem and Ham into the whole world? <margin>The migration and division of nations.</margin> *Goropius Becanus* is anxious in these migrations of the Hamites, Shemites, and Japhethites, and he migrates now here, now there, not knowing where to stop. There is no book he published in which he does not narrate or conjecture; from there to Illyricum, and soon to the shores of the Adria, he crosses the Tanais <note>The Don River</note>; now he crosses from Phrygia into Thrace, then to Illyricum, and soon to the shores of the Adria; he leads Noah holding a course to the mouths of the Tiber. With Japheth he hastens into Japygia <note>Apulia, Italy</note>, and shows the nation propagated from him by wondrous windings. These and other things he dreams, intoxicated by a jar of Falernian mountain wine; see his *Gallica, Francica, Hispanica, Vertumnus, Hermathena* and others. But who would believe that Noah, at 870 years old, went out from the East into a colony? To this we easily agree, which Epiphanius has in the *Ancoratus*: that Noah, having made the division of the world among his sons, exacted an oath from them that they should keep themselves in the worship of God and maintain harmony among themselves: *“He divided,” he says, “the whole world among his three sons by lot, and assigned to each a portion according to the lot.”* <note>Original Greek: διαιρείζει μῷ, αἰτ, τοῖς τρισὶν υἱοῖς... Epiphanius describes the division as a formal legal act.</note> He says he *divided the world by lot*, as if it were some hereditary possession, so that each might undertake to inhabit and cultivate that part of the earth which had fallen to him by lot. Josephus goes further, saying that when the posterity of Noah had increased, God himself first commanded the migration, so that colonies might be led out to propagate the human race without internal dissensions; but men, though the command was given twice, were disobedient, and on the contrary contended that they should not be separated from one another, at the instigation of Nimrod. His words are these: *“When God commanded them to send out colonies for the sake of a multitude of people, so that they might not riot against one another, but by farming much land might enjoy an abundance of fruits, through ignorance they disobeyed God, and having fallen into calamities because of this, they perceived their sin. For when the youth were in great number, God again advised them to make the colony.”* <note>Original Greek: Τῷ Θεῷ κελεύσαντι αὐτοὺς... Josephus argues that the dispersal was a divine command for human prosperity, not just a punishment.</note> Following these things, he goes on to say that the inconveniences themselves were seen by God, and they interpreted the counsel about leading colonies not as a favor of the Deity, but as a snare, namely, *“so that being divided they might be more easily attacked.”* Therefore, they resolved to stay together in one place, and from this flowed those words: *“Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower, whose top may reach to heaven, and let us make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered over the face of the whole earth.”* Thus, unwillingly, they were carried away from each other and dispersed into diverse and distant places of the earth, and thus the inhabitation of diverse and far-flung regions first began. Therefore, those who wished to be more blessed than miserable went where they could, and those who were of the same speech went together and sought another place of the earth. Moreover, the height of this most vast structure is not certain from the Holy Bible; Jerome indeed, on Isaiah 14, reports that he understood from others who had carefully inspected that tower, that it had already been raised to 4,000 paces <note>About 4 miles</note> when they stopped the work. Herodotus attributes to it a wall of 50 cubits in thickness, 200 in height, bronze gates, a square shape, and a size of 480 stadia, that is, 15 German miles. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
The migration and division of nations.
</margin>
That Nimrod was the author and leader of this plan is suggested by those words where he is called a "mighty hunter," as well as the word *Hevah* <note>Hebrew: הבה "Come" or "Let us"</note> which in this passage is the cry of one inciting others, having the same force and elegance as the Latin *eja* or *age* or *agite* <note>Come now! / Get to work!</note>, which are used for exhortation; compare B. Glassius, *Sacred Grammar*, book 3, and Pererius's *Commentary* on this passage. Besides him, the descendants of Ham—and perhaps even the descendants of Japheth, as is likely, being forced by the tyrant Nimrod—participated in this building. Nor is it probable, as Abulensis, Myricæus, Cornelius à Lapide, and others maintain, that Noah and Eber also took up work as equals in building this tower. Rather, it must be held that the Patriarchs did not participate in this work, which was built against the will of God and in contempt of Him. We shall set forth our opinion in the words of Mayer’s *Sacred Philology*, Part 2, page 338 and following.

<margin>
Genesis 11:2.
</margin>
> We read indeed, he says*, that when after the flood the whole earth used one language and the same words, it happened that they set out from the East and settled in the land of Shinar; that is, leaving the mountains of Ararat where the Ark had rested, they betook themselves into Adiabene in Assyria, and from there into Mesopotamia, of which Babylonia was a part. But a great doubt arises here: should that departure be attributed to the entire family of Noah, or truly only to a certain part of it? The common opinion, which I followed in the first book of *Sacred Philology*, is that Noah, who had settled by the mountains of Armenia for a full hundred years, sought new seats in Assyria as his family grew, and chose the open plains of Babylon above other places. Conversely, others, moved by no small reasons, determine that this journey into Shinar was neither the first nor involving the whole Noahic family, but was some later movement, and chiefly of the family of Ham. For it is clear from Holy Scripture that these new inhabitants of Shinar were the architects of the Tower of Babel and the authors of the most sorrowful confusion of languages. But who would believe that the most Holy Fathers—Noah, Shem, Arphaxad, Shelah, and Eber—approved of the impious and accursed undertakings of the Nimrodic crowd, and built a tower together with that most ambitious race? Nor can it be proven that those pious Patriarchs were present but merely discouraged the architects from that insane work. It is indeed true, and placed beyond the risk of doubt, that the Holy Patriarchs never approved the madness of that most foolish race; but whether they did so while present in person is doubtful and uncertain. Indeed, since Moses teaches that the building of that tower began with the full consent of all (which Myricæus himself gathers from this phrase, "each said to the other," Genesis 11:3), and God Himself confirms regarding the builders that they are "one people" <note>Latin: *populus unus*; Hebrew: *am echad*</note>, it is clearly evident from this that the Holy Patriarchs were not among the number of those architects. Rather, they remained in Armenia while the Hamitic family and race emigrated, and they fruitlessly dissuaded the Nimrodites, the descendants of the impious Ham, from that foolish work.

<margin>
Commentary on Genesis 11.
</margin>
Thus far his words. From what has been said, it is clear that Noah and the rest of the Patriarchs—although he was a contemporary <note>Greek: σύζζων (syzzon)</note> of these tower-builders <note>Greek: πυργοποιῶν (pyrgopoion)</note> (for he lived 350 years after the flood, and the building of this tower and the subsequent confusion of languages is, according to B. Gerhard*, to be referred to the year 171 after the flood)—notwithstanding the fact that Eber's family later inhabited this region, they did not conspire with the impious dregs of the Hamites. Consequently, the 

<column-break/>

very first language, the one proper to the first-created Adam and Eve—namely Hebrew—remained uncorrupted in the family of Eber. See on this Buxtorf in his *Dissertation on the Making of Languages* <note>Greek: γλωττουργίᾳ (glottourgia)</note>, section 65; Mayer, *Sacred Philology* Part 2, page 329; and Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*, chapter 1.

<margin>
The migration and division of nations.
</margin>
God—and not the Angels—punished this stubborn impiety and audacity of the Hamites by the destruction or total obliteration of the original language, which was common and previously used by all the tower-builders <note>Greek: πυργοποιοίς (pyrgopoiois)</note>, and by a new infusion of languages. This was a unique gift instilled into the mind of each person, with a perfect habit ready and permanent for use, so that no one could understand the desire of another's mind, even if they heard the sounds of the words. This is what the word *shama* <note>Hebrew: שמע "to hear/understand"</note> implies, which also denotes the internal understanding of the mind; compare B. Glassius in *Sacred Philology*, treatise 1; B. Dorsch in *The Wonders of the Lord's Gift of Tongues*, page 630; Buxtorf in the work cited above, section 26; and Zehner in *Adages*, century 5, proverb 12. Hence Scaliger* rightly says:
> It was brought about by God, the Best and Greatest, that when one asked for a stone, another brought lime, another sand, another mortar, another bitumen, and another water. I also think it likely that there were those who thought an insult had been spoken to them, and therefore they came to blows.

Thus it happened that those who were previously taught one language had the habit of different languages impressed upon them individually, by which they could not only pronounce and understand individual words, but also arrange phrases and formulas of speech, and use them most readily wherever necessary. Although the variety of languages was not given by God as a punishment when the Apostles spoke the great works of God in various tongues:

<margin>
Collected notes on the Epistle to the Romans, ch. 14.
</margin>
Hence Sedulius Scotus*, when speaking of the seventy-two languages in the world, explains the Apostle's words, *And every tongue shall confess to God*, as follows: *every tongue*, that is, the three kinds of the sons of Noah; for from Shem 27 languages were born, from Ham 22, and from Japheth 23. Nevertheless, the confusion of languages without mutual understanding was a just and worthy punishment for pride. For from this confusion of languages or "other-tonguedness" <note>Greek: ἀλλογλωσσίᾳ (alloglossia)</note> not only did this evil arise, that man is a stranger to man,

<margin>
Book 19 of *The City of God*, ch. 7.
</margin>
for as Augustine* says, *if two people meet each other, neither of whom knows the other's language, dumb animals are more easily associated with one another than they are, even though they are human. For when they cannot communicate their thoughts to each other, solely because of the diversity of languages, such a great similarity of nature is of no use in uniting men; so much so that a man would rather be with his dog than with a foreign man.* Truly also from such "foreign-tonguedness" <note>Greek: ἀλλογλωττίᾳ (alloglottia)</note>, as Josephus calls it,

<margin>
Book 1 of *Jewish Antiquities*, ch. 5.
</margin>
"they were scattered thereafter, making colonies everywhere, and each occupied the land they happened upon and into which God led them, so that every continent, both inland and coastal, was filled by them," the beginning of migrating into other regions of the world was made. For those who with wicked daring opposed the Divine command and blessing, *increase and multiply, bring forth on the earth, and fill it* (Genesis 9:7), were dispersed into various regions of the globe. The bond of concord and friendly familiarity—namely, "same-tonguedness" <note>Greek: ὁμογλωττίᾳ (homoglottia)</note>—was removed, and in its place a horrid confusion of languages was introduced in a single moment. By this, not only was the unity of religion and the consensus of piety extinguished, but also the mutual understanding between them was taken away. Once this happened, those tower-builders <note>Greek: πυργοποιοί (pyrgopoioi)</note> were thrown into disorder and each sought his own; from which this cry seems to have penetrated to almost all peoples, and to each their own manif—

# From Genesis Chapter 9, Verse 27

<margin>The migration and division of the nations.</margin> ...to have remained. With these things premised, we wish it to be well noted that just as we establish a twofold division of the earth, so too do we establish a twofold migration of the nations. The first was instituted by the casting of lots and by Noah through <term>divine oracle <note>original Greek: τῇ θείᾳ χρησμῷ</note></term>, as the ancients say, among his sons, which we also mentioned above. The second, however, occurred after the confusion of languages was made. This prior division of the world among the sons of Noah, even if it is not openly established from Scripture, is nevertheless asserted to be highly probable—indeed certain—from the unanimous consensus of so many trustworthy authors. For who would deny that Noah, as the lord of the whole world before he died, divided the earth among his sons and assigned to each his own portion? In support of this matter, we have previously cited Epiphanius and Josephus, to whom are added Jerome in his *Hebrew Traditions on Genesis Chapter 10*, Philastrius on *Heresies* (Heresy 70 from the time of the Apostles), Arnobius on *Psalm 104*, Cedrenus in his *Compendium of Histories*, Zonaras in *Annals Volume 1*, Lyra and Abulensis on *Genesis Chapter 12*, Cornelius a Lapide, Bonfrère, Pererius, Ribera, Serarius, and Bartholomäus Mayer. <margin>Part 1, Sacred Philosophy, page 27.</margin> After this division was made, they migrated from the East into Shinar. For up to that point, men had inhabited those mountainous places of Greater Armenia where the ark had come to rest for some interval of time out of fear of the flood. But after some time had elapsed since the flood, with their fear decreasing day by day, they set out for Babylonia, where the plain of Shinar was located—according to the testimony of Josephus in *Antiquities of the Jews, Book 1, Chapter 4* (which also agrees with *Zechariah 5:11*)—partly because of the pleasantness of the place, and partly out of a desire for more agreeable locations. Moses mentions this departure in the words of *Genesis 11:2*: <insert>And it came to pass, as they journeyed from the east, that they found a plain in the land of Shinar; and they dwelt there.</insert> <note>The author provides the quote in Hebrew and Greek: ויהי בנסעם מקדם... and καὶ ἐγένετο ἐν τῷ κινῆσαι αὐτοὺς...</note> In these words, briefly yet powerfully, Moses—the first historian of the first migration—describes the journey from the east into Shinar. There are those who interpret the word <term>from the east <note>Hebrew: מקדם (mi-kedem)</note></term> in this text as *toward* or *versus*, while others interpret it as *from* or *out of*. Since this latter interpretation is supported both by the very frequent usage of Holy Scripture and by the common opinion of commentators, we rightly give our vote to the latter explanation. Nor is it an obstacle, as is commonly objected, that if this hypothesis is accepted, it might be more correctly said that the first <term>migrants <note>Greek: μετοικέτας</note></term> in this first migration should be judged to have set out from the mountainous places of Armenia <term>from the North <note>Hebrew: מצפון (mi-tzafon)</note></term> rather than <term>from the East</term>, since the place where Noah’s Ark rested is said to have been in the mountains of the Kurds. But in truth, since Armenia is east of Babylon, there is no doubt that the word denotes the starting point, and thus should be explained as *Out of* or *From*. Fuller seems to confirm this opinion to some extent in *Book 1, Chapter 4, page 43*, and <margin>on this passage</margin> Rivet, writing after him: *Namely, since almost all the surrounding areas in the mountains of Armenia were mountainous and rugged, it was easier for those ancient mortals to descend from the mountains of Ararat or the Ardennes into the nearby parts of Media. From there, when they had gradually progressed as wanderers to the borders of Media and Assyria, and were later collected into one body, they began an organized and composed departure through the wide-stretching plains of Assyria to the bank of the Tigris; it is probable they all extended their reach together.* In this

<column-break/>

way, that journey, for its greater and most significant part, is most truly judged to have been made <term>from the East</term>. Thus also Junius, in his later editions, cleared up the difficulty <margin>The migration and division of the nations.</margin> as follows: *When they had first sought Adiabene in Assyria from the mountains of Ararat, there was a return from there toward the West into Babylonia.* Thus the difficulty is removed, unless the crossing of the Tigris—a very large, deep, and rapid river in that place—still stands in the way. But those who did not lack the industry to build towering structures could also prepare for themselves vessels to cross rivers, which was certainly necessary above all in the dispersion of men. Moreover, the material can be prepared not only from wood, but also from other materials: wicker, rushes, papyrus, leather, etc. That barbarian men did not lack such industry is sufficiently proven by the voyages of former times. Thus far his argument. Having thus entered into a coalition of all into one, they entered into a plan to build a tower <term>unto heaven <note>Hebrew: עד השמים (ad ha-shamayim)</note></term>, by which figure of speech—used as a hyperbole in the Sacred Books (compare Blessed Glassius in *Sacred Rhetoric, Book 1, Chapter 19, page 469* and Vossius in *Oratorical Partitions, Book 4, Chapter 9, page 325*)—the greatest height is implied. <term>Lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth</term>, they said; in which phrase the word <term>lest <note>Hebrew: פן (pen)</note></term> is noted for its various meanings. While some explain this word as *lest*, others explain it as *perhaps* (perchance) so that it is a term of doubt, just as Blessed Luther has it: <note>German: "Wir werden vielleicht zerstreuet."</note> *We will perhaps be scattered.* To us, however, the opinion of those who translate it as *Before* or *Ere* is more pleasing, following the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX) Greek translators</note> who rendered it <term>before being scattered <note>Greek: πρὸ τοῦ διασπαρῆναι</note></term>. In this way, that twofold division and migration is indicated: namely, the Noahic division and the migration from Armenia into the land of Shinar (of which we have spoken so far), as well as the future division and migration into all regions of the entire world, which they feared. Enticed by the pleasantness of the land of Shinar, contrary to the Divine will and Father Noah’s partition of the lands, they intended to inhabit the land of Shinar all together. But while they were occupied in building the tower, God admitted a flood of new languages into their minds, so that they were forcefully called away from their bold purpose of that abominable structure. Without any interpretations being provided, they were unable to penetrate their former shared counsel; instead, through troops and companies, amid the emptiness of their speech to one another—yet in such a way that no distraction was made of the families themselves, but those whom the condition and sequence of birth had bound to the same family were gifted with the same language—they were forced to separate themselves, not without an incredible shaking of their minds. Thus began the second migration, which they call the "real" migration, the beginning of which is easier to find than its progress. Indeed, the primeval antiquity of all ages is handed down in Moses, than whose writing nothing older exists, in which the series of the years of the world, the origins of nations, as well as their propagations and changes, and the beginnings and progress of religions are described in a certain order. Here that saying of Tertullian applies: *Whatever is first is truest; whatever is later is adulterated.* Moses therefore provides us with the first excursion of the nations, as each tended toward that part of the earth which Noah had assigned to his sons. Concerning Shem and his descendants, since they did not participate in the counsel of the <term>tower-builders <note>Greek: πυργοποιῶν</note></term>, they were also not dispersed into another part of the world...

The author uses linguistic analysis of Hebrew and Greek terms to argue that the migrants moved from the mountains of Armenia toward the plains of Shinar.</summary>

From the remnants, however, as if by a silent instinct, each descended into his assigned portion; that impious Ham proceeded with his own into Africa, and, as Sabellicus notes in *Enneads* 1, book 1, column 4, he settled as a fugitive with his wife and children in that part of Arabia which afterwards obtained its name from his own. From his son Canaan, the families of the Canaanites were later scattered. From Ham, besides his sons Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan, there also arose all idolatry and superstition. Let us look at both of these with Moses as our guide <note>original Greek: ὅσον σθένος — "with all our might"</note> and as far as the reasoning of our undertaking allows. Cush is the Father of the Arabs and Ethiopians, for the regions of these peoples come under one designation, so that both are called the Land of Cush; hence Josephus says: *The Ethiopians, over whom he ruled, are even now called Cushites by themselves and by all those in Asia.*
<margin>1. Jewish Antiquities 7. p. 13.</margin>
Mizraim is the Father of the Egyptians, whose region is named the land of Mizraim in Genesis 12:10 and elsewhere, whence even today the Indians call them *Meseri* and *Misri*, according to Bontius in his *Observations on Garcia de Orta*, folio 9. Whence Stephanus of Byzantium says: *Ammonia is the interior of Libya, and Libya itself was anciently so called from Ammon.* Canaan is the Father of the Canaanites, whose border extends from Sidon as you go toward Gerar as far as Gaza, until you enter Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha, according to Moses in Genesis 10:19. All this posterity of Ham, in those lands which they possessed, worshipped their own Gods, receiving names according to the dialect of each nation, fabricating for themselves <note>original Greek: τρόπες παντοίας θρησκευτικῆς — "all sorts of religious modes"</note> and <unclear>cities</unclear> and nations <unclear>opinions</unclear> concerning the gods. But since it is not our purpose at this time to describe the religions of all nations and the sacred rites concerning their gods—as we wish that to be reserved for a special <term>study</term> <note>original Greek: μελέτηματι — "meletemati," a focused exercise or treatise</note>—we migrate with the descendants of Canaan into Palestine itself. God himself seems to have given this region to the Canaanites, a people destined for destruction; those words mean: *When the Most High distributed inheritances to the Nations* <note>original Hebrew: בְּהַנְחֵל עֶלְיוֹן גּוֹיִם</note> <note>original Greek: ὅτε διεμέριζεν ὁ ὕψισος ἔθνη</note>, *when he separated the sons of men, he set the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel. For the Lord's portion is his people, Jacob is the lot of his inheritance.*
<margin>Deuteronomy 32:8, 9.</margin>
The sense of which is this: When God dispersed the nations at Babel, he established the boundaries of regions and lands for all of them, and this for the purpose that he might set apart and exempt for the children of Israel—not yet born, but to be born—as much space of land for dwelling as he knew would be required and suffice for their number and the convenient habitation of each. As if to say: From that very time, God designated and bounded the land of Canaan, lest it be occupied by others

In this way, the word <note>original Hebrew: לְמִסְפַּר — "according to the number"</note> is not to be translated as "according to," but as "into," or "for," or "on behalf of"; he established the boundaries *for* the children of Israel, as Tremellius reads. Thus, therefore, while the Israelites were not yet born, and later while they stayed first in their ancestors for 430 years in Palestine itself and in Egypt, and migrated for a space of 40 years in the desert, the Canaanites inhabited the land promised to Abraham and his seed for all of seven hundred years and more, until the preordained limit of their expulsion. When that was completed, shortly after the age of Moses, they were driven from their ancestral soil by Joshua and the Israelites, first to the shores of Phoenicia, and soon they began to spread themselves through the whole Mediterranean Sea and to sow colonies in many places of Europe, Asia, and Africa. # From Genesis IX. v. 27.

## The Migration and Division of Nations
<margin>The migration and division of nations.</margin>
The fugitives did not confine themselves to a single province, but mingled with the Greeks, Egyptians, and other nations. Having gone out to the Greeks, they introduced various rites and customs, as is wont to happen in such <term>metoikisiai</term> <note>original: μετοικισίαις; migrations or changes of abode</note>. The origin of the Inachidae among the Greeks is owed to the sons of Anak <note>A race of giants mentioned in the Bible</note> among these Phoenician refugees; for Inachus, the most ancient of the Kings of Greece, is said to have built the first of the cities, Argos. It is probable that these people also narrated the formidable deeds of Moses and Joshua to the natives among whom they arrived, though not without reproach and the admixture of fables. From this arose the origin of the most subtle Greek <term>leron</term> <note>original: λήρων λεπτοτάτων; "trifles" or "silly stories"</note> concerning Giants and their <term>theomachic</term> battles <note>original: θεομαχικοῖς; battles against the gods</note>, concerning Bacchus and the Dionysian rites, and Hercules and his club—all of which we shall indicate elsewhere represent the history of Moses and Joshua. Cadmus, born in Phoenicia, was of great fame; without considering his migrations, we would not know the meaning of <term>Kedem</term> <note>original: קדמה; Hebrew for "East" or "Ancient times"</note>. It is common knowledge among the learned that Cadmus came from the East, out of Phoenicia into Boeotia. Camerarius records that this name was given to him because he is said to have had an ox as a leader while changing his settlements, and there he led a colony and founded Thebes, where he established the seat of his affairs and fortunes. Herodotus ascribes to him that he and the Phoenician newcomers in Greece, <note>original: χρόνῳ προβαίνοντες ἅμα τῇ φωνῇ μετέβαλον καὶ τὸν ῥυθμὸν τῶν γραμμάτων</note> "as time went on, changed the rhythm of the letters along with their language," hence the Epigram of Zeno regarding him in Suidas:

<margin>Sophocles p. 385.</margin>
> If my fatherland is Phoenicia, why the envy? I am that
> Cadmus, from whom Greece holds her written page.
> ->I am a Phoenician by fatherland. Why the malice? Yet I am that<-
> ->Cadmus, to whom all Greece owes her books.<-

The same is testified by the Author of the *Thebaica*, first brought to light by Neander:

<margin>v. 27.</margin>
> Ruling there among the earth-born men,
> He accomplished many glorious things, and opened for noble Athens
> A gymnasium for all of lovely Greece,
> Raising a light for all the inhabitants,
> He showed them letters and the secrets of wise myths,
> Thus the ancient Achaean came from a distant land
> By skill, and the Phoenician Cadmus bestowed him upon Greece,
> Having been nourished in the learned borders of old.

Order requires that our meditation approach Japheth and his descendants. The region assigned to him by his Father cannot be handed down so precisely, but is shrouded in the greatest difficulties. However, it is highly probable that Japheth, when he sailed from Asia, came first into Greece and from there into Europe. The illustrious Greek nation descended from Javan, the son of Japheth (whom others call Ion), by whose descendants the regions of Greece were occupied. Their migration was easy, established by a crossing through the Hellespont or the Thracian Bosphorus. To speak of the ancient affairs of the Greeks is not without its own difficulty, a fact noticed long ago by Thucydides, the most skillful observer of Greek history; for when that nation was in its infancy, it had no fixed settlements, nor did it flourish in wealth, power, or numbers, but was compelled to change its soil by frequent migrations due to more powerful groups. The praised Historian describes these causes of migration and the unsettled seat in these words: "It appears that what is now called Hellas

<column-break/>

<margin>The migration and division of nations.</margin>
was not anciently inhabited in a settled way, but there were migrations in earlier times, and each group easily left their own land, being forced by those who were always more numerous. For as there was no commerce and they did not mingle fearlessly with one another, either by land or sea, each farmed their own land just enough to live on, having no surplus of wealth, nor planting the earth (since it was uncertain when someone might invade and take it away, especially as they were un-walled); and thinking they could obtain their daily necessary food anywhere, they moved without difficulty. Because of this, they were strong neither in the size of their cities nor in other resources, and especially the best of the land always underwent changes of inhabitants." He calls these migrations <term>metanastaseis</term> <note>original: μεταναστάσεις</note>, just as he uses the term <term>apanistasthai</term> <note>original: ἀπανίστασθαι</note> for the Greeks migrating from their original seat. So that the <term>metabole</term> <note>change</note> of inhabitants might be easy due to the incursions of neighbors and foreigners, they were not much occupied with building cities and lands. Being poor, and unable to trade safely by sea or land, they hoped they would easily find a living elsewhere outside their borders. They went, therefore, wherever they could when suffering violence, and from these frequent migrations it happened that the strength and wealth of Greece did not grow in the beginning. These things and more the aforementioned Thucydides wrote concerning the ancient affairs of the Greeks. From this it happened, as Beurerus shrewdly observed, that the Greek tribes were variously mixed among themselves and with others by those perpetual migrations of nations.

Vain, therefore, are the Athenians who boasted with great ostentation that they were <term>autochthones</term> <note>original: αὐτόχθονες; sprung from the earth itself</note>. Vain are the Thessalians, who dreamed they were born from stones; vain the Arcadians, who asserted they were brought forth before the Moon. Therefore, whatever the Greeks write about themselves—whose opinion is varied and inconsistent—it is not such that it should move us from our view, we who have knowledge of a better antiquity from the sacred scriptures. Indeed, even that fable of Jupiter, who is said to have had a wife named Asia, leads us to the conclusion that the descendants of Japheth set out from Asia to other places. Thus, without doubt, the first crossing of the peoples of the East descending into Europe occurred here. Nor is it trivial that Osiris, according to the traditions of Diodorus, traveled through the other regions of Asia, and crossing into Europe through the Hellespont, established his own people in Thrace, Macedonia, and Attica.
