# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The migration and division of nations.</margin>
<margin>5th Letter, book 1, page 862.</margin>
Cornelius Tacitus, that eyewitness describer of Germany, enumerates among the ancestors of our ancestors Tuisto, his son Mannus, and Mannus's three sons: Ingve, Hermin, and Istvae. The Germans are therefore indigenous peoples; they by no means draw their origins from the fugitive remnants of Trojans or Greeks, as many fabulists claim. This is the true opinion of Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa <note>A famous 16th-century polymath and occult writer.</note>, who rightly observed that the names of the German peoples and their borders have often changed due to various events. He justly criticized those who, led by a certain desire for glory to extend their origin back to the most ancient leaders, resort to foreign origins and fables. They invent all sorts of stories to bolster the nobility of their lineage, not understanding that it is far more distinguished to derive one's origin from a most ancient nation that remained unconquered in its own seats than to have proceeded from foreign exiles and fugitive bandits. Hence, Cluverius <note>Philipp Clüver, a founder of historical geography.</note>, the defender of German nobility, not undeservedly attacks those who derive the Germans now from Maeotis (a very swampy place where Herodotus located the free Scythians), and now derive their migrations from I-know-not-what little worlds. <margin>Book 3, Ancient Germany, 26, page 603.</margin> *“I see this is a common thing,”* he complains, *“for all writers of that age to derive nations unknown to them from the farthest North, and to fashion marvelous fables about their migrations, of which the books of the Deacon regarding the Lombards and Jordanes regarding the Goths are full.”* The men of our own age have approved such trifles and the dreams of delirious men to such an extent that, following their example, they have not hesitated to derive the Alemanni, Franks, and Saxons from the same source. Else-<margin>Book 1, chapter 3, page 29.</margin>where in the same volume: *“It is a common vice among historians—one that did not arise ‘only yesterday or the day before’ <note>original Greek: πρώην τὲ καὶ χθὲς (proen te kai chthes)</note>, as the saying goes, but has been practiced since the earliest ages—to construct the beginnings of nations out of ridiculous, trifling fables and monstrous lies, so that they might appear more ancient and august.”* This so pleased our Germans even in a later century that these wretched men, while they studied to acquire some sort of honor for themselves from elsewhere, did not notice that they were losing their genuine, home-grown glory—glory granted even by their fiercest enemies and celebrated with the highest praise. You, O unhappy German seeker of foreign glory, derive your Saxons from the Sasons or Sacae, the Cimbri from the Cimmerians, the Misnians from the Mysians, the Thuringians from the Tyrigetae, the Chauci from the Caucones, the Frisians from the Phrygians, and other peoples from I-know-not-where; led by no other evidence than a bare allusion of words, while all ancient monuments of both sacred and profane history cry out against it. Germany is therefore the inheritance of Japheth, whose colonists we "Japheth-born" are. We received our fields, as it were, for our use from the first giver, Japheth, the first author of our nations. To him was given such a prerogative by his father Noah above his brothers that he assigned him a double portion—that is, by far the largest region of the world—in the formula of blessing which stands in the text: *“May God enlarge Japheth”* <margin>Genesis 9:27.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: יפת אלהים ליפת (Yapht Elohim le-Yephet)</note>. Indeed, the meaning of "enlarging" is to be preferred here over the meaning of "alluring" or "persuading," which the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> also observed, translating it thus: *“May God enlarge Japheth”* <note>original Greek: πλατύναι ὁ Θεὸς τῷ Ἰάφεθ (platunai ho Theos to Iapheth)</note>. Therefore, those things which Noah, driven by a Prophetic Spirit, foretold so long ago,

Once the descent was made and the building project examined, the matter was brought to judgment: a sentence was passed, an example was set, and the things begun and attempted were reduced to nothing, *as Jehovah scattered them from there over the face of the whole earth, and they ceased building that city.* By dispersion they were scattered; by a miraculous divorce of languages they were divided. With their work destroyed, the builders constructed another kind of solitude for themselves; they traversed other lands and made various journeys, so that men of a single tongue might build dwellings for themselves amidst that variety. A great multitude had drawn together into the valley, settled themselves in a certain place, and taken counsel to establish a glorious seat. *In the manner of human nature*, as Sulpitius says in Book 1 of his *Sacred History, page 7*, *to seek fame through speech and some remarkable work before they were led away from one another. From Josephus, Book 1 of *Jewish Antiquities*, it is clear from Nimrod's speech—in which he exhorted his countrymen—that they intended to raise a tower higher than the floodwaters reached; but the Mosaic history in *Genesis 7, verse 20* records that the flood surpassed the highest mountains of the earth by fifteen cubits. Since some mountains, according to the observations of Mathematicians, exceed four miles if you take the perpendicular height, it is easily gathered from this that they wished to raise the tower to a height of nearly five miles. Added to this, as Josephus reports, due to the immense number of workers, the work grew beyond what they had hoped, so that its thickness exceeded its height. Jerome, in Book 5 on Isaiah at chapter 14, reports that he learned from those who had carefully inspected that tower, that even then, when the work was interrupted, it had been raised to four thousand paces <note>about 4 miles</note>, and several other things which he asserts seem almost incredible to him. And because the lineage of Nimrod was distinguished by the name of tyranny, the Prophet hints that such a nation would be brought against the Jews as would treat them tyrannically, and whose language they would not know. For the Jews used that pure language which, named after Eber <note>The ancestor of the Hebrews</note>, remained in his family; but the Babylonians used that impure tongue which, though originally born from Hebrew, at first differed only by certain dialects, but in the course of time degenerated into its own peculiar language. The Jews were no longer able to understand it, as is evident from the history of Hezekiah; just as the ancient German language (of which Goldast gave several illustrious examples in his advisory writings) gave birth to modern German, yet very few modern students of the language can understand that primeval version. Moreover, God threatens that he will bring against the Jews the Babylonians, who are a nation from an ancient age <term>me-olam <note>original Hebrew: מעולם, meaning "from eternity" or "from of old"</note></term>, most ancient and venerable, but also in power and tyranny, following in the footsteps of their progenitor Nimrod. This is noted on the occasion of the word "Babylon." Alexander and Abydenus, quoted in Cyril, report:
> It is a common opinion and rumor that men, born from the earth and relying on their own strength, wished to raise a tower as high as the sun against the will of the Gods, in the place where Babylon is situated.

Hestiaeus and Eupolemus, as witnessed by Eusebius in book 9 of *Preparation for the Gospel*, hand down the tradition that the Priests who survived the ruin, having snatched up the sacred mysteries of their Jupiter (who was Nimrod, or Jupiter Belus), betook themselves to the plain of Shinar. Hence Kornmann, in *The Temple of Nature, page 289*, reports: In the East there is a city, a noble trading center of the Chaldeans near the Euphrates called Baghdad; the inhabitants there say that not far from the city a great heap of stones and devastation can be seen. And because of the rocks and venomous animals, access is not open; they believe it was there, and that every single thing was moved from there to their city from Babylonia. Whatever the truth may be regarding the place of the struggle, we judge with Vossius, Petau, and others, that Belus—whom the Gentiles call the founder of Babylon, including the ancient poet Dorotheus of Sidon:
> *Ancient city of Babylon, founded by the Tyrian Belus.*

—was the same person whom the Scripture calls Nimrod. Because he invaded his father's rule and turned it into lordship and tyranny, he was called <term>Nimrod <note>original Hebrew: נמרד, meaning "rebel"</note></term>, that is, "the rebellious one," whereas before he held the name of Belus (compare Wichman, *Sacred Chronology*, book 2, page 266; Rivet, *Exercise 65*). The beginning of his kingdom was Babylon in the land of Shinar, Genesis 10:10. He began to build the city of Babylon, but being prevented by death, he could not finish it; finally, Ninus, the son of Belus or Nimrod, put the finishing touches to it. Berosus in book 4 seems to indicate this when he mentions that Nimrod indeed built the tower, but did not

<column-break/>

complete it, nor did he found the designated city, because after 56 years he suddenly disappeared, having been "translated" by the Gods.

### Genesis Chapter 30, Verse 11

-> And Leah said: With luck. <-
-> And Leah said: In fortune. <note>Greek: Καὶ εἶπε Λεία. ἐν τύχῃ.</note> <-
-> And Leah said: HAPPILY. <note>Latin: FELICITER.</note> <-
-> Then Leah said: Joyfully. <note>German: Lustig.</note> <-

<margin>
The law of youth. <note>The marginal note "Lex iutenia" appears to be a truncated reference to youth or tribal law.</note>
</margin>
To the Patriarch Jacob, by the handmaid Zilpah (whom he had taken as a partner of his bed for the sake of procreating offspring at the urging and persuasion of his wife Leah), a son was born. From the present state of affairs and the future outcome, he was named GAD; for when Gad was born to Zilpah, Leah, omening well for herself, said with this auspicious shout: <term>Ba-Gad <note>original Hebrew: בגד, "with luck" or "a troop comes"</note></term>; and she called his name Gad. We know there is doubt as to what this means. Those who place the birth of a man under the fate of the stars (an art which Juvenal says the Mathematicians practice), want this to be the name of a fictitious Deity: Fortune, or the <term>natal spirit, the guide of life <note>Greek: δαίμονα γενέθλιον, μυσαγωγὼν βίου</note></term>, as it is called by Menander in Eusebius. They suggest it was invoked by Leah, as if she had omened well for the birth of the handmaid out of the superstition of her ancestors, by which offspring and other favorable things were attributed to the stars in this sense: <term>A good fortune has come <note>Aramaic: אתא מזלא טבא</note></term>, as Jonathan translates it, <term>Good luck has come <note>Hebrew: בא מזל טוב</note></term>, that is, a good fortune came, or a more benign star, a favorable constellation, a good Spirit <term>agathos daimon <note>Greek: ἀγαθὸς δαίμων</note></term>, which is opposed by an <term>evil fortune <note>Hebrew: מזל ביש</note></term>. Indeed, the ancient Chaldeans taught that fates, whether good or evil, depend on the stars. By the happiness or unhappiness of those below, they held that the Moon disposes one to chastity and the practice of marriage; Mars inclines one toward bravery; Mercury gives eloquence; Jupiter gives magnanimity and certain sublime spirits; while Venus pours love into the souls subject to her fertile power. Likewise, they established the "fortes" <note>strengths or lots</note> of the Planets such that they called the part of the Sun the <term>good spirit <note>Greek: ἀγαθὸν δαίμονα</note></term>, that of Jupiter <term>victory <note>Greek: νίκην</note></term>, that of Mercury <term>necessity <note>Greek: ἀνάγκην</note></term>, that of Venus <term>love <note>Greek: ἔρωτα</note></term>, that of Mars <term>daring <note>Greek: τόλμαν</note></term>, and that of Saturn <term>nemesis <note>Greek: νέμεσιν</note></term>. The distance of the Sun from the Moon in any birth they called the <term>lot of fortune <note>Greek: κλῆρον τύχης</note></term>. Moreover, it was believed that to everyone from their first birth a certain genius is attributed, whom they invoked, who is the perpetual and inseparable companion of the offspring and presides over the man until his last breath. They called such a genius or Angel <term>natal, averting evil, warding off ill, natural, or liberating <note>Greek: γενέθλιον, δαίμονα ἀποτρόπαιον, ἀλεξίκακον, φύσειν, λύσιον</note></term>; his antagonist is the <term>Angel of destruction <note>Hebrew: מלאך החבלה</note></term>, whom the Latins called the "adverse Genius." For they assigned two genii to everyone, from one of whom comes happiness, and from the other calamity. Censorinus, in *On the Birthday*, chapter 3, page 18: "The Genius is the God under whose protection everyone lives once born... *The Genius is placed by us as such a constant observer that he does not depart for even a moment; but having received us from the mother's womb, he accompanies us to the last day of life.*" Apuleius, in his book *On the God of Socrates*: "Plato maintains that for individual men in the conduct of life, individual witnesses and guardians are added, who are always present though visible to no one... *This very guardian, singular prefect, domestic scout, individual judge, inseparable witness, disapprover of bad things, approver of good things...*" who to you...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
The law of the way.
</margin>
...be able, whether through dreams, signs, or perhaps even in person when need demands, to avert evils and make good things prosper, as noted by Ammianus Marcellinus in Book 21. This "Genius" <note>A guardian spirit assigned to a person at birth</note> is the same as the "protector of safety" mentioned by Horace in his second Epistle:
> The Genius, the companion who governs our natal star.

Servius, commenting on the first book of the *Georgics*, says: *The ancients called the "Genius" the natural God of every place, thing, or man.* Macrobius, in the first book of the *Saturnalia*, records that *four gods are present at a human's birth: the Daemon, Fortune, Love, and Necessity.* Thus, in the opinion of some, the text of the Law <note>The Torah/Pentateuch</note> refers to the pagan customs of that nation, which, being accustomed to Chaldean superstitions, still retained the habits of Gentilism (as Augustine speaks in *Questions on Genesis*). This consisted of the belief that a "Strong One of Fortune" or "Good Fortune" presided over one coming into the light—like a Guardian or *Overseer*—and that the newborn was not *born to adverse gods and a sinister fate*, as Juvenal puts it. Rather, at his birth,
<margin>
Horace, Book 4, Ode 3.
</margin>
*fair Jupiter* looked upon him with a peaceful light, whom Homer would call *blessed by the gods* (Iliad 3) and *born to a happy fate*. It is well known that writers often attribute the best and worst things of this lower world to celestial secrets; it was believed that everyone draws their fate from heaven. The Rabbis themselves dispute this here, and as they usually do with an obscure word, they flee to the Arabic language, in which they say that the beneficent star of Jupiter is called *Mazal* <note>original: <span style="font-family: 'SBL Hebrew';">מזל טוב</span> - Mazal Tov, literally "good constellation"</note>. So say Aben Ezra and others. Certainly, *Gad* <span style="font-family: 'SBL Hebrew';">גד</span> is "good and beneficent" to the Arabs, and thus denotes the star of Jupiter, as noted by Fuller, Drusius, and Selden in *On the Syrian Gods*. That star of Jupiter is also called the *Star of Justice* <span style="font-family: 'SBL Hebrew';">כוכב צדק</span>, or simply *Justice* <span style="font-family: 'SBL Hebrew';">צדק</span>, named for equity because it indicates all things favorable. For, as Cicero says, *that brightness called Jupiter is prosperous and salutary to the human race*, while the brightness of Saturn and Mars is harmful, according to the saying: *Saturn and Mars are the damaging stars* <note>original: <span style="font-family: 'SBL Hebrew';">כוכבים המזיקים שבחאו ומאדים</span></note>. Juvenal says the same in Satire 6. I should not omit that Josephus, in Greek, explained the Hebrew name as *Fortuitous* or *by chance*. His words are: *Leah, countering her sister's work, gave her own handmaid to Jacob. The son of Zilpah was born, whom she called Gad, which one might translate as "Fortuitous."* Following the same notation, Theodoret says: *The word for "good fortune" was not Jacob's, but Leah's, who had been raised in impiety and was only slowly being educated in divine matters.* He adds: *Leah, being imperfect in piety, said "I have had good luck."* However, the exposition they give is not suitable; for the 
<margin>
Commentary on Genesis, p. 629.
</margin>
piety of Leah was greater (in the words of Wolfgang Musculus) than to attribute a divine power to "Fortune" after the manner of the Gentiles, or to credit a daughter's birth to her and consecrate it with a name. For how could she attribute the gift of fertility in a handmaid to Fortune, when she had previously accepted it in herself as the grace of God? Since she was with Jacob, she so honorably remembered God's providence in her first four sons that it is nowhere read that this pious woman attributed offspring to *Good Fortune*, *Good Fate*, or blind chance, rather than to God, whom she deemed the sole giver of all fortune. Therefore, we must understand *Gad* in another sense. It is a truly elegant *paronomasia* <note>a play on words</note> and 

<column-break/>

<margin>
The law of the way.
</margin>
parallelism, which the Hebrews call the "polish of the language." For *Gad* is reduced to a "troop," "army," or "preparation for battle" from the root *G-D-D* <span style="font-family: 'SBL Hebrew';">גדד</span>, which means to gather an army or to rush together in troops. This reasoning is deduced from Genesis 49:19, where the last words of the dying Jacob are: *Gad, a troop shall overcome him, but he shall overcome at the last.* <note>original: <span style="font-family: 'SBL Hebrew';">גד גדוד יגודנו והוא יגד עקב</span></note> Who does not know that most Hebrew *namings* were ominous and allusive? Examples of this abound in the majestic style of the Canon. Hence in Numbers 33:32, *Gidgad* is a place where the Israelites camped; and in 2 Kings 5:2, the Syrians are called *troops* <span style="font-family: 'SBL Hebrew';">גדודיס</span>, which the Genevans render as *les Bandes* (bands of soldiers), and the Vulgate usually calls *latrunculos* (little robbers/mercenaries). Philo (or Jerome his translator) explained it thus: *Gad means temptation, or a little robber, or fortune.* The Vulgate uses "robbers" for soldiers. For in their primary meaning, *latrones* were soldiers, named from *serving* (latreuein), as if they were "siders" because they protected the *side* of their masters. Plautus uses this ancient sense in *The Braggart Warrior*:
> For King Seleucus begged me with great effort,
> That I might collect and enroll "latrones" (soldiers) for him.

In German we say: *Streiffende Rotten* <note>prowling companies/bands</note>. The sense, therefore, would be that Leah, as if exulting, congratulated herself on the son recently born to Zilpah, who, joined to the others she had previously borne, ought to make a "troop." By his birth, she would have a *troop* or army of sons; *as the name itself shows when etymologized*. From this, the sense is excellent and the derivation easy; there is no need to flee to the unknown land of Arabia when we have Palestine right before our feet. To us, the opinion that adapts *Gad* to an *army*, *abundance*, or *troop* seems more convenient, truer, and more fitting to this place. *The very name proves the same*, so that she wished to name this son from the hoped-for multitude of children, or from the gathering of forces, military valor, or a military expedition. This view is more genuine and approaches the history of this tribe most closely, if you look at the military order of the Gadites, who were well-equipped and placed before their brothers in Joshua chapters 1 and 4. Whence Aquila also translates: *the equipment comes*, as Jerome witnesses in *Questions on Genesis*: <margin>Volume 3, p. 217.</margin> *Leah said, "in fortune," and called his name Gad. Where we put "in fortune," the Greek says "in luck" (en tyche). In Hebrew it has "Bagad," which Aquila interprets as "the equipment comes"; we can say "in readiness." For "Ba" can sound like the preposition "in" and "comes." Therefore, he is called Gad from the event or the readiness.* Jerome sins against Grammar here, which teaches that the letter *Beth* <span style="font-family: 'SBL Hebrew';">ב</span> with a certain vowel is a preposition. The Septuagint also thought it was a preposition, rendering it *in luck*. Luther, in his *Commentary on Genesis*, explained it as *equipped, armed, prepared for war, who conquers and propagates the family*; and in the marginal notes of his German version he adds: *Gad means ready for the fight / as if Leah said, "bravely at it" / in this way I shall have many sons.* Piscator rendered it, *A squadron*...

<summary>This page analyzes the etymology of the name "Gad," debating whether it refers to the pagan concept of "Fortune" (associated with the planet Jupiter) or a "troop/army" of children and soldiers. The author favors the military "troop" interpretation, citing Hebrew grammar and the tribe's later history as warriors.</summary>

...or a troop of horsemen. Nor did the senses of Junius, the Genevans, the English, or the Belgians <note>Refers to various Reformation-era Bible translations</note> differ in their versions. Let it be settled, therefore, that the woman <note>Leah</note> had in mind a <term>full return for heavenly favor and kindness</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπάντησιν τῆς ἄνωθεν εὐεργεσίας καὶ εὐποιΐας πλήρη</note> when she spoke, omening a numerous progeny: **"Good fortune comes"**, **"Good fortune comes"**: **"Breasts"** <note>original Hebrew: בא גד, בא גד: שדים</note>, after a birth most happily completed three and four times over. "Happy and fortunate am I," she exclaims, by the singular benefit of God, by whose help the <term>success</term> <note>original Greek: εὐτύχημα</note> of sons proceeds prosperously; "now, however, with Gad born, no one shall be lacking from my family, nor shall strong men be lacking from the house of Gad, etc., who shall be born from him, the renowned of the earth." Indeed, an Ammonite troop shall invade Gad in troops, but he himself shall invade in turn in troops, and at last with an armed hand shall restrain the wild crowd of robbers. The Gadites were badly vexed by the incursions of their neighbors; for the region of the Ammonites was nearby, with whom there was perpetual war, so that it can almost be said of the Gadite territory what Cicero once said of Macedonia: *Macedonia is touched by such great barbarian nations that the same boundaries of the province have always been for the Macedonian Commanders* (the Princes of the Gadites) *which were the boundaries of their swords and spears.* Or, what gave place to the proverb: "Syrians against Phoenicians," concerning those who agree poorly; for those neighboring nations were in the greatest enmity, because of which they very rarely entered into treaties or friendships.

I think it is now clear to anyone that the marriage of Jacob with Zilpah was auspicious; and from there it was alluded to by Leah and Jacob in the name Gad, by which she wished to intimate that her own sterility was compensated by the most copious reward of the insuperable goodness of God, through the help of her handmaid—from whom, as if from a most fertile spring and a kind of horn of plenty, she had received a son. Nor would an allusion founded on the true etymology of the name fit here, which Jacob placed in the cited chapter: *a troop shall invade him*, unless the intention had been to congratulate herself on the crowd of sons and at the same time the numerous offspring and posterity, which she surely promised herself from faith to faith. See a similar example in *Genesis 51:42* <note>likely a citation error for Gen 41:52</note> regarding the name Ephraim, with the reason for the name added immediately: *because God has made me to grow:* as if Joseph were already abundantly heaped with sons; so also here Leah celebrates an <term>unimaginable happiness regarding the procreation of children</term> <note>original Greek: ἀμήχανον εὐδαιμονίαν περὶ τεκνοποιΐας</note> in her son Gad. Thus 
<margin>Gen. 29 v. 32.</margin>
Leah also engraved a <term>memorial</term> <note>original Greek: μνημόσυνον</note> in the person of her son Reuben, by which she might incite herself to the praise of God. And so the pious woman expresses and acknowledges by the names of her sons that this fertility is the gift of Jehovah, and at the same time gives thanks. Thus it would be impious to seek vanities from pagan superstition and the vanity of the nations, which is a most common fault of certain critical interpreters today. For what, I ask, is the point of burdening Leah—who for so many years had Jacob not only as a most wise husband but undoubtedly as a teacher—with the utterances of heathens without necessity? <term>In a happy state, all things are happy</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν ὀλβίῳ ὄλビア πάντα</note>, I conclude from Theocritus *Idyll 15, v. 24.*

### From Genesis Chapter XXXVII, v. 36.

->And the Midianites sold him into Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard.<-

> Septuagint: The Midianites sold Joseph into Egypt to Petephres, the eunuch of Pharaoh, the chief cook.
> Vulgate: The Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, a Eunuch of Pharaoh, Master of the soldiers.

<column-break/>

<margin>The Egyptian Praetorium.</margin>
**A**nciently in the East, the *Prefecture of the prison* was a great and honored office; for there were Praetoria <note>Headquarters or official residences</note> to which the <term>oversight</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπισκοπὴ</note> of those to be captured and punished was entrusted—great men, and especially *Prefects of the soldiers*, which can be seen from various places in Scripture and Antiquity. In the first book of the Pentateuch, Potiphar, who had great authority in the court of Pharaoh, is read named as <term>Sar Hattabachim</term> <note>Hebrew: שר הטבחים</note>, which is, if you *translate* <term>word for word</term> <note>original Greek: κατὰ πόδα</note>, *Prince of the slaughtered*, since for the Hebrews <term>Tabach</term> <note>Hebrew: טבח</note> is *to slaughter, to kill, to sacrifice* <note>original Greek: σφάττειν</note>, *1 Sam. 25:11, Jer. 11, Exod. 22:1, Deut. 28:31.* <term>To sacrifice</term> <note>original Greek: θύειν</note> *1 Sam. 25:11, Jer. 11:19*; and this is said in a double respect, by reason of the different objects around which the slaughter is occupied. Said of criminals, it is certain that it denotes among the Arabs no less than the Hebrews *beheading* <term>apokephalismon</term> <note>original Greek: ἀποκεφαλισμόν</note>; just as among the *Greeks* metaphorically <term>to cook/butcher</term> <note>original Greek: μαγειρεύειν</note> denotes *to kill*, *Lamentations 2:21* concerning the vengeance of God, when, angry at the most grave crimes of the people of Judah, He is said to kill and slaughter, <term>to kill and to butcher</term> <note>original Greek: ἀποκτείνειν καὶ μαγειρεύειν</note>. From that meaning in which it denotes *to kill*, it is that the Septuagint said <term>chief cook</term> <note>original Greek: ἀρχιμάγειρος</note> concerning the Prefect of the forces, whose work it is to slay and kill his soldiers in wars. And to this belongs the derivative <term>Matbach</term> <note>Hebrew: מטבח</note> which is said of the future slaughter of men in *Isaiah 14:21*; but *on the contrary, said of beasts*, the name <term>Tabach</term> will be <term>cook</term> <note>original Greek: μάγειρος</note>, a butcher, or even a cook *1 Sam. 9:22, 24*, because butchers and cooks kill the cattle to be cooked, from which the Arabs took the <term>culinary verb</term> <note>original Greek: ῥῆμα μαγειρικόν</note>, as also Aben Ezra <margin>on Prov. 9:2.</margin> teaches, which signifies to cook; from which meaning some take <term>Sar Hattabachim</term> as Master of the cooks, *Küchenmeister*. <term>Cooks</term> <note>original Greek: Μάγειροι</note> come in a double sense to the Greeks. 1. *Meat-sellers*, <term>cooks in the market, those who cut up and sell meat</term>. 2. *Cooks*, <term>cooks in the home</term>. *The former had raw meats; the latter had cooked.*

> <term>Adorning</term> <term>pots</term> <term>with seasonings</term> <term>of all kinds</term>,
<margin>Batrachomyomachia v. 41.</margin>
> as the Homeric *Psicharpax* <note>A character in the "Battle of Frogs and Mice"</note> speaks of his cook, who served the delicate palate of his Master, and knew how to prepare and season foods best; by which name also a certain cook is praised in Athenaeus *9. Deipnosophistae 16*, where also a <term>cook</term> <note>original Greek: μάγειρος</note> exalts himself against Aemilianus the Grammarian, because he served Seleucus, King of Syria, and Agathocles, the Sicilian Tyrant; and in the same place a <term>well-cooked</term> <term>smoky</term> <term>tyranny</term> <note>original Greek: εὐμαγειρεῖν καπνιζομένη τυραννίς</note> is described by the poet Demetrius, *a dominion subject to smoke*; since the cooks held their empire and tyranny in the smoke-filled kitchen. The Greek Interpreters, therefore, thought that Potiphar (who is named by them <term>Petephres</term>, but by Aquila and Symmachus <term>eater of delicacies</term> <note>original Greek: ὀψοφάγος</note>) was either *Prefect of the Cooks*, or, if you prefer, *Prefect of the Butchers*, such as the Inspector also was to the Romans in *Law 1, § 11, on the office of the Prefect of the city*, where we read these things: *The care of all meat, that it be provided at a fair price, belongs to the care of the Prefecture, and therefore the swine market is under his care, but also the rest of the cattle or herds, which look to this kind of provision, belong to his care.* But we judge that opinion should be rejected, since it shrinks from the history, from which I think it will be clear to the reader that Potiphar was a Prince in the royal court, whom we name *Marshal* or rather *Captain of the Royal Guard*, from whom authority for conducting affairs was sought; for he was the arbiter of the causes of the whole court, so that he also presided over the prisons and capital—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of biblical offices and titles, specifically focusing on the role of Potiphar in Egypt and comparing his title to Roman and military legal structures.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
The Egyptian Praetorium.
</margin>
The Prefect of capital punishments held the custody of the prison in his power, as is clearly evident from chapter 40, verse 3, where two court officials imprisoned there expected all necessities for food from Joseph. From this, the Chaldean <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> translated more correctly as *Rab Qatulaya* <note>original: רב קטוליא</note>, "Prince of the Slain," from *qatal*, which among the Chaldeans and Syrians means to kill or slay. Jonathan and the author of the Jerusalem edition have: *Rab Spuqitula* <note>original: רב ספוקיטולא</note>, "Prefect of the Scouts" <note>Speculatores</note>; for this is a word distorted from the Latin, as we shall soon declare. Without doubt, however, it is understood as the Prince or Prefect of the Bodyguards, or the prefect of capital matters. Hence the Zurich translators rendered it: *An Officer of Criminal Matters* <note>original German: *Ein Obrister der Criminal Sachen*</note>. Theodoti’s Italian version has *Captain of the Guards* <note>original: *Capitano delle Guardie*</note>, and similarly the English: *Capitaine of the guard*. The Genevans: *Provost of the Household, Prefect of the Palace*. Junius and Tremellius: *Prefect of the Bodyguards*, where they add in the notes: *The Hebrew word is common to butchers, cooks, and bodyguards; it signifies "slaughterers," because the former slaughtered animals for food, while the latter slaughtered the guilty for punishment.* Hence those two court officials of Pharaoh were handed over to this guardian for custody, whose duty it was to punish the condemned; and the King of Babylon, after Jerusalem was captured and the King led away, sent his "slaughterer" or Prefect of the Bodyguards there to execute his capital sentence upon the remnants of the people and the city itself. In Latin, these could be called *Quaestors of capital matters*, but not *archimageiroi* <note>original Greek: ἀρχιμάγειροι, meaning "chief cooks"</note>, as the Greeks translated. In this place, the Vulgate translator snatches the prize from the Greeks, explaining it as *Master of the Soldiers*; but he provided an occasion for error in that he translated *Rab Saris* as "Eunuch." Sebastian Castellio did not render it badly as *Master of the Horse*, 
<margin>
in Notes p. 54.
</margin>
where he adds: *Usage prevailed that prefects were called Eunuchs, even if not castrated; just as among the Latins they are called Senators, even if not old men [Senes]. For if Potiphar was castrated, why did he have a wife? As for my translating it "Master of the Horse" rather than "Master of the Butchers or Cooks" like others, the reason is that in 2 Kings 24, Nebuzaradan is called by this same name, to whom the burning of Jerusalem was commanded; which task is certainly not that of a Master of Butchers. He is named by the Hebrews from "slaughtering," perhaps because he imposed punishments on the guilty.* Among the Orientals, it is customary to distinguish Satraps and Princes of the courts, as well as any court ministers, by the name *Taphsar* <note>original: טפסר</note>; so that I judge Marcus Marinus to be entirely in error, writing in *Noah's Ark* (as the title of his Lexicon goes) that Potiphar was truly castrated; and that he married either because he had only his testicles removed, or certainly for the sake of fulfilling lust through touch, kissing, and the like. This explanation is colder than any Eunuch, and we leave it behind. Let us instead interpret Potiphar here as the Master of the Palace, Prefect of the Bodyguards, or, to speak with the Romans, the *Praetorian Prefect*, to whom among other duties belonged the care of those punished and those to be punished. We are taught everywhere that capital punishments were imposed by soldiers and bodyguards; indeed, often those who were in command of the military killed the condemned with their own hand. Thus it is no wonder if our Vulgate translator expressed *Sar Hattabachim* as "Master of the Militia," for if the places in which *Sar* and *Tabbachim* appear are weighed, most are observed to pertain to war and to men set over military matters. In the Roman custom of speaking, they were called *Lictors* and *Apparitors* when they attended the magistrates and offered themselves ready and prompt to carry out their orders; which very service is called *Apparitura* by Suetonius and *Apparitio* in the last law, section 3, "because of fear, from *apparere*," which is to be present for obedience.

Lictors bound the hands of the accused and performed the office of the executioner, whence that saying: *"Go, lictor, bind his hands,"* and the flogging. These things serve to explain the Vulgate translator; for he used this liberty of inserting expressions taken from the rituals of the Roman forum throughout. In the first book of Kings, chapter 22:26, when Micaiah the Prophet was to be shut in prison, he was delivered into the power of the King’s Son: for the King of Israel said: *"Take Micaiah and return him to Amon the Prefect of the city,"* *Sar ha-Ir* <note>original: שר-העיר</note>, the "ruler of the city" <note>original Greek: ἄρχοντα τῆς πόλεως</note>, "and to Joash the King’s Son, and say: *Thus says the King: Cast this man into prison*, and give him the bread of affliction and the water of anguish." Thus the King’s Son was the highest overseer of the prison and the captives, the dispenser of life and death: such as Potiphar was among the Egyptians during the reign of Pharaoh. Common laws prescribed these duties to him, and they had Prefects under them, which is worthy of observation, so that you may know these Overseers were in great honor, in whose hands was the supreme province of capital matters over all criminals and accomplices in crime. Capital matters in this kind of judgment are those which take away the natural head, or even the civil head, of the delinquent. *"For there are penalties which either take away life, or impose slavery, or take away citizenship,"* Law 6, final section, on penalties. Let us here compare the Romans, among whom the Praetors and Quaestors of capital matters presided over the judgments and the judges. *"To be made a defendant,"* says Asconius, *"is to be interrogated according to the laws before the Praetor;"* which jurisdiction also belonged to the Praetor by the Law of the XII Tables. 
<margin>
3. On the Laws.
</margin>
At Rome, the Praetors first administered justice, yet in such a way that they did not have the authority to establish law, but were only the deciders of disputes and guardians of civil law, and judges of the inquiry <note>quaestio</note> for a capital cause. G. Budé affirms that the Praetor is called the *Judge of the Inquiry* by the jurist Marcian; and some say he was different from the *Quaesitor*. We know they are sometimes exchanged, and the *Quaesitor* himself is called the Judge of the Inquiry, and vice versa. In our military service, the general investigator of military causes is called the *Auditor General*. The same method and order of punishment seems to have existed formerly in the East. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

## The Egyptian Prefecture.
The office of the Prefect <note>original: *Præfectura*</note> was held in honor of God. O Prophetic Prayer! In former times, even the Magistrates of capital matters took special care of those condemned to prison. Regarding the "Eleven" of the Athenians <note>The *Hendeka*, a board of officials in charge of prisons and executions</note>, Suidas (under the word *endeka*), Aristotle in *Politics* Book 6, Chapter 8, and Plato in the *Phaedo* bear witness. Their function was almost the same as that of the *Triumviri Capitales* at Rome, who held custody of the prison; so that when it was necessary to carry out a sentence, it was done through their intervention. Examples of this are noted by Budé in *Annotations on the Pandects* page 215, and Muretus in *On the Origin and Progress of Roman Law* page 47. Assisting these were the guards of the bound, the attendants, the registrars, and the *desmophylakes* <note>Greek: *δεσμοφύλακες*, "jailers"</note>. Julius Firmicus, in *On the Error of Profane Religions*, notes there were those appointed over public homicides, and the recorders of those sentences pronounced regarding the heads of men; either the *cornicularii* <note>military administrative officers</note>, or the *Commentarienses* <note>registrars</note>, to whom the care of the damned is committed: or the *clavicularii* <note>key-bearers</note>, or prison guards, and those to whom the care of the public chains is entrusted, such as the overseers of the executioners, or the executioners themselves, or those accustomed to tear the condemned men with whips. Joseph was a *desmophylax* <note>jailer</note> in Egypt. There were ministers who provided Micaiah with his daily food and drink, namely bread and pure water; that this was the way to "live through the prison" <note>Greek: *δεσμωτηρίῳ διαζῆν*</note> is also found recorded among the *Gnomica* of Alexis. In the history of the Apostles, chapter 16:27, the *desmophylax* of the Philippians is named, when Paul and Silas—zealots for the glory of the Savior—were sent into prison by order of the Magistrate (verse 22): *And the crowd rose up together against them, and the magistrates tore off their clothes and commanded them to be beaten with rods.* Verse 23: *And when they had laid many stripes upon them, they cast them into prison, charging the jailer to keep them safely.* The Arabic Interpreter explains the "magistrates" <note>Greek: *στρατηγοὺς*</note> as the Prefects of the Satellites or lictors, who preside over the punishment of criminals. Those lictors are called *rhabdouchoi* <note>Greek: *ῥαβδοῦχοι*, "rod-bearers"</note>, whom our Interpreter renders as "Travelers" <note>Latin: *Viatores*</note>, whose principal duties were three: Removal, Punishment, and Preceding; about which see B. Brisson, *Antiquities of Law* Book 3; Gualtherius in *Observations on Ancient Tablets* page 178; and much more extensively Lipsius, *Electa* Book 1, Chapter 23. Romulus, the first King of the Romans, established laws and asserted their authority not without force, and especially by the threats of the twelve lictors by whom he was surrounded. St. Mark, narrating the beheading of the imprisoned John the Baptist—requested by the vow of the dancing girl—says he was beheaded by a *speculatore* <note>Latin/Greek: *σπεκουλάτορι*, a scout or executioner</note> of Herod (Chapter 6:27). Such men—to use a more recent and previously unusual example—were the forty-five assassins called *Couppe jarrets* <note>French: "hamstringers"</note> whom King Henry III of France enrolled in his bodyguard, concerning whom see Bronchorst on *Political Aphorisms* page 306. You might call them "ministers of punishment" with Manilius, Book 5, line 635:
> — the pitiless one will come, the minister of punishment,
> The guard of the prison and the harsh keeper, by whom standing,
> The proud mothers of the wretched lie prostrate on the threshold.
Indeed, the matter was so handled in the Roman forum that the sentence of the Judge was executed upon the defendants by the hands of Tribunes, Centurions, and Soldiers; of which there are manifest signs in various monuments of history. Christ the most innocent Savior himself experienced whips, chains, and the cross. *All were scourged from without* <note>Greek: *μαστιγωθέντες πάντες ἔξωθεν*</note>; this was the duty of the soldiers. Whence he is also said to be scourged, humbled, and struck by God <margin>Isaiah 53:4</margin>. St. Paul, led by the Tribune into the

<column-break/>

## The Egyptian Prefecture.
camp, is examined with whips (Acts 22:24). In the Arabic copy, the word is *Alamiron*, which comes from *amara* <note>Hebrew: אמרן</note>, meaning he commanded or ordered, and from there *paqad* <note>Hebrew: פקד</note>: Leader, Captain, Prefect, Tribune. Today in Turkey the word is frequent, and passed from there to the Europeans, by whom the Prefect of the sea is called an "Admiral." The Greeks of a later age sometimes call them *amphainas* and *amphallas*, as Meursius notes in his *Greco-Barbarian* lexicon; that they are wonderfully varied by Latin writers is shown by Gretser, Volume 3, *On the Holy Cross* chapter 12, and Henry Spelman in *Archaeologus* pages 12, 13, and 14. It is nothing new for words to migrate from nation to nation. Thus I would think the word *Sar* <note>Hebrew: שר</note> or *Sarim* passed to the Muscovites, who are accustomed to call their Emperor "Czar." Paul is handed over by the Tribune so that he might be questioned by whips, for in antiquity they used whips (otherwise fire, the wheel, the rack, and the goad) to express the truth. And when they had bound him with thongs and readied the scourges, the shrewd Paul said to the Centurion standing by him: *Is it lawful for you to scourge a man who is a Roman and uncondemned?* It was a crime for a free man to be beaten with thongs; for free men or Roman citizens could not be afflicted with this punishment of scourging, which was servile and plainly unworthy of a free man, unless they had first been made subject to the punishment of slaves. "It is a misdeed to bind a Roman citizen, a crime to strike him," says Cicero <margin>Action against Verres</margin>. Regarding whips applied to the guilty according to Roman custom, one may see the notes of Petrus Faber, *Semestria* 2, 10. Because the Romans used military men to impose punishments, it follows that Matthew (Chapter 27) reports that after the sentence was delivered by Pilate in the praetorium concerning the death of Christ, the soldiers and attendants took the now-condemned Christ and gathered the whole cohort <note>Greek: *ὅλην τὴν σπεῖραν*</note> (verse 27). Four soldiers took the clothes of the crucified Christ; a Centurion guarded Christ and the thieves, for it was the custom that those driven onto a cross were guarded by the hands of soldiers, as Petronius testifies. "A soldier," he says, "watched the crosses, lest anyone pull down the bodies for burial." Hence, when the Jews requested of Pilate that he order the tomb of the buried Christ to be guarded or fortified, Pilate responded: *You have a guard; go, make it as secure as you know how* <note>Greek: *ἔχετε καστωδίαν, ὑπάγετε, ἀσφαλίσασθε, ὡς οἴδατε*</note> (verse 65). Once placed in the sepulcher, the lictors and investigating attendants surrounded it with a diligent guard, even by military hand; for Fuller (in *Miscellanea* 4, 17) observes from the Syriac that those men who were called *quaestionarii* <note>investigators/torturers</note> by the Romans were the guards of the Holy Sepulcher. This is contrary to Theodore Beza, who notes they were garrison soldiers designated for the custody of the temple; Barth. Mayer and Ludovicus de Dieu agree with Fuller that Beza's opinion should be given no weight. For that cohort in verse 27 was different from the one assigned to the temple and the Priests. That Centurion employed in the custody of the Savior is called "Centgrave" in an ancient voice by the author of a stage play on the death of Christ, which I saw in a very old parchment codex belonging to Bachmann, formerly my most close colleague. The *Centgravii*, whom Cornelius Tacitus describes to us, were Prefects or Judges of a hundred soldiers, whom the warlike Teutons once chose from the villages; they held the same honor and name as those at Rome—

# From Genesis XXXVII. v. 26. 125

<margin>The Egyptian Praetorian Prefecture.</margin>
Among the Romans, these were the Centurions. Even today, the fame of these names has not died out in the titles *Landgrave*, *Margrave*, and *Palsgrave* <note>German noble titles: Landgraf, Markgraf, Pfalzgraf</note>; these are august titles, greatly increased by long-standing custom and differing in innumerable ways from the *Centgravius* <note>Centenarius or Hundred-man, a local judge</note>, of which some obscure traces remain even now in those same regions of Germany. Indeed, to this day, the word has not ceased to be used in my homeland for one who is in charge of prisoners. It is now a shadow of a name, without much honor, which lost its force and value when the old Republic changed; it signifies one thing now, but meant another before. For nothing is stable; the offices and titles of men shift no less than the fate of cities. It is well known that this was once a noble rank among the Germans, for the *Centgravius* was supreme in both war and peace, as that sagacious steward of antiquity, Henry Spelman, has learnedly shown. The secret judges called *Scabini* <note>Lay judges or assessors</note> are also witnesses to this change; they once had the right to punish perjurers or those convicted of crimes, for they took upon themselves the faculty of responding to the law in both criminal and civil matters, as legal scholars clearly teach. In our vernacular, they are called *Schöffen*. Some believe that Charlemagne gave them the power to execute and remove those who defected from the Christian faith which they had recently accepted; and from this, Adrianus Junius noted in his *Nomenclator* that they were called *q. Schaf.* <note>A play on the German "Schaf" (sheep) or "Schaffot" (scaffold)</note>. I shall not be troubled by such a bold etymology; it is a mere allusion, like that of a certain Rabbi who twisted the word *Sheret* (service) to refer to his wife, saying "It must be so" <note>original: "Sic muss."</note>. But I leave these things aside; if they are not unwelcome, they are perhaps ill-timed. However, I think it will not be an ill-timed inquiry to ask whether the Oriental *Sar Hattabachim* <note>Hebrew: Chief of the Slaughterers/Guard</note> can be compared to the Roman *Tribune*, or even the *Praetorian Prefect*. To these men was once given the license to correct public discipline, and for them, soldiers performed the role of the executioner—a name which among us today is most vile and joined with the hatred of men, as Magius shows in his *Miscellanea, book 4, chapter 16*.

<margin>Loff. 12. §. 2 ff. on military affairs</margin>
*The duty of the Tribunes*, says Macer, *or of those who lead the army, is to keep the soldiers in camp, to lead them out for exercise, to inspect the bars of the gates, to go around the watches occasionally, to be present at the grain distributions of their fellow soldiers, to test the grain, to restrain fraud in measures, to punish offenses according to the limit of their authority, to be frequently present with the commanders, to hear the complaints of fellow soldiers, and to inspect the sick.* The Praetorian Prefect was in charge of those soldiers whom the Emperor had chosen for his own protection, and his insignia was a sword, given to him by the Prince as a sign of office; concerning which I think the things Peter Faber noted in *Semestria, book 1, chapter 3* are worthy of reading. We know that this was a most excellent and honorable office, just as it was for Potiphar in the Egyptian court; his office cannot exist or be understood without the power of carrying a sword and the attendance of bodyguards <note>original Greek: δορυφόρων (doryphoron) - spear-bearers</note>. Therefore, Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum <note>Aramaic translations/commentaries on the Hebrew Bible</note> rightly call Potiphar the *Prefect of the Scouts* <note>Aramaic: רב ספוקלטוריא (Rab Spiculatore)</note>. By "Scouts," they clearly understand bodyguards, to whom the guilty were also delivered to be killed. Hence Onkelos has: *Prefect of the slain* <note>Aramaic: רב קטולא (Rab Katola)</note>. Therefore, the *Tabachim* are not "cooks" or "butchers" in that context, as the Greek translator dared to interpret, and among the Latins, Prosper of Aquitaine, who

<margin>part 1. on promises and predictions</margin>
called Potiphar the *Provost of the Cooks*, when he writes: *The Ishmaelites sold Joseph*

<column-break/>

<margin>The Egyptian Praetorian Prefecture.</margin>
in Egypt to a certain provost of Pharaoh's cooks. Not even this is without meaning, that he is called "Provost of the cooks." For by that "scarlet" <note>A pun on the Latin 'coquus' (cook) and 'coccus' (scarlet dye)</note> the shadow of the garment of Christ's passion is signified. Away with such a silly comparison of a cook and scarlet! From the work of slaughtering, such a sword-bearer was called *Tabach* or *for slaughter and killing* <note>Hebrew/Aramaic: לטבח וקטול</note>, whose duty it was (to use the words of Nathan the Just in the *Aruch* under the letter *V*) to scatter and give over to slaughter, or, to use a Ciceronian phrase, *to sacrifice with death*. Hence the "butcher's table" in the instrument of the executioner mentioned in Suetonius' *Life of Claudius, ch. 15*, where it is read that the executioner carried a sword, summoned to cut off the hands of a certain forger. The words of the historian are: *When someone cried out that the hands of a forger ought to be cut off, he immediately demanded an executioner be summoned with a sword and a butcher's table.* They used the labor of bodyguards and soldiers to maintain custody not only in Egypt, but also in Latium <note>Rome</note>, over whom *Tribunes* and *Centurions* presided. Furthermore, we shall clarify the matter with examples. Christ was delivered to the soldiers, who led him from the place of the Praetorium to the place of punishment, *Matthew XXVII:31, John XIX:17*, as we have heard. The Apostle Paul was led to Rome by the Centurion Julius, *Acts 27:1*, so that he might stand before Caesar to assert the cause of the Christians; he was even permitted to remain with a soldier guarding him <note>original Greek: σὺν τῷ φυλάσσοντι αὐτὸν στρατιώτῃ</note>, *chapter 28, v. 16*. The Apostle Peter is read to have been bound with two chains *between two soldiers* by the command of Herod, *Acts ch. 12, v. 6*. For that impious King, seeing *that it pleased the Jews, having seen Peter, delivered him into prison to four squads of soldiers to guard him* <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἀρεστόν ἐστι τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις... κ.τ.λ.</note>, *verse 4*. He names four quaternions <note>groups of four</note> because it was a more diligent watch; for the sake of guarding, usually one maniple—namely, ten soldiers—was accustomed to be added. But for Peter, whom the Tyrant knew had performed many miracles, he gave a more certain guard by adding six soldiers. The Keeper threw Paul and Silas, bound in wooden stocks, into the inner prison, *Acts XVI:24*. Here the custom of binding must be observed, which that most sharp investigator of Roman antiquity, Justus Lipsius, handed down in these words:

<margin>Commentary on Tacitus' Annals, book 3.</margin>
*There is a threefold method of keeping prisoners: either they were held in a prison and a closed place without any soldier, as is usually the case for slaves and cheaper persons; or 2. in military custody; or 3. in the houses of Magistrates.* Military custody was very frequent both in Rome and in the provinces, and its method was *that he who was in guilt had a chain bound to his right hand, which same chain also bound the left hand of the soldier, under the prefecture of his guard.* Lipsius confirms this with several examples, to which I add this from an Ancient Author's Letter on the exile of St. Martin: *The Master of the guard was joined to the same Blessed man, since it was the custom that he who was to suffer by the sword should be bound to the Master of the guard.* Manilius in his *Astronomica* elegantly calls this a "Partner of the chain":

<margin>book 5. v. 644.</margin>
*The Lord of the bound, and a partner in part of the chain.*
For by the same chain both the guard and the soldier were bound, and it is not to be understood otherwise regarding the Apostle Paul and the soldier given to him. Nor were only soldiers employed to keep watch, but they were also sent for that purpose by the Praetorian Prefects, Centurions, and Tribunes of the Praetorian cohort. Concerning the care of the Praetorian Prefects in judging the crime of majesty <note>treason</note>, I cite a passage from Statius, *Thebaid book 3*, elegantly alluding to this, where when Maeon had offended King Eteocles with very free speech, v. 80...

### Genesis XLI. v. 8.

<margin>The Magi and Diviners of Egypt.</margin>
<note>Hebrew: "And it came to pass in the morning that his spirit was troubled; and he sent and called for all the magicians of Egypt, and all the wise men thereof: and Pharaoh told them his dream."</note>
*His soul was troubled, and sending out he called all the interpreters of Egypt, and all its wise men, and Pharaoh narrated his dream to them.* <note>Greek: "Ἐταράχθη ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτοῦ..." from the Septuagint.</note>

Terrified by fear, he sent for all the **diviners** <term>conjectores: those who interpret signs or dreams</term> of Egypt and all the wise men, and having summoned them, he told his dream.

This was a great proof of divine goodness: that God would sometimes send dreams to Kings, the interpretation of which they could receive not from their own Magi and Diviners, but from holy men in Israel. Thus Pharaoh was instructed by Joseph, and Nebuchadnezzar by Daniel. Pharaoh was dismayed by a dream; and having consulted the Priests, Diviners, and Magi—as many as Egypt nourished—concerning its interpretation, he received no answers, or only uncertain ones amidst a great confusion of opinions. They went to Joseph, who was brought out of the squalid prison and, dressed in cleaner clothes, appeared before the King, who addressed him saying: <margin>v. 14.</margin> <margin>v. 15.</margin> *I have dreamed a dream, and there is no one who can interpret it. But I have heard it said of you, that you hear a dream to solve it.* To whom Joseph replied: *Not I, but God shall answer peace to Pharaoh.* <margin>Chaldean</margin> Not from my own wisdom, but from the face of the Lord shall peace be answered to Pharaoh. The King had thought that Joseph could interpret dreams by some natural sagacity, an opinion which Joseph modestly puts away from himself, teaching that the investigation of hidden dreams must be expected from God alone; just as in chapter 40:8, he had prefaced his explanation of the dreams to the cupbearer and the baker: <note>Hebrew: "Do not interpretations belong to God?"</note> *Does not interpretation belong to GOD?* as our version has it. Interpretations are from the Lord, without whom no one can truly interpret dreams. Dreams were occasionally sent by God to the pious: to Abraham (*Gen. 15:12*), to Joseph (*Gen. 37:5*), to Solomon (*1 Kings 3:15*), and others; and sometimes to the impious and Heathens: to Laban (*Gen. 31:24*), to Nebuchadnezzar (*Dan. 2:1, 4:2*), and here to Pharaoh. And as they were **sent by God** <note>Greek: θεόπεμπτα (theopempta)</note>, so their interpretation came only from a supernatural light and irradiation. This was the reason why the Egyptian Magi, with all their wisdom, could not interpret Pharaoh's dream. "I have heard that you conjecture most wisely" (so our translator rendered it) says Pharaoh; and the Heathens heard of this peculiar gift of interpreting dreams, of whom the historian Justin says: <margin>Book 36, ch. 2.</margin> *Joseph was the youngest among his brothers in age; his brothers, fearing his excellent genius, secretly intercepted him and sold him to foreign merchants; by whom he was carried into Egypt, where, when he had perceived the magic arts with his shrewd genius, he soon became very dear to the King himself; for he was most sagacious in portents, and of dreams...*

Foreigners were persuaded that whatever Moses and Joseph performed in Egypt beyond the usual course of divine and human affairs proceeded from Magic, from which they gave accounts of secrets, and by which they were performers of miraculous things. For Pliny does not hesitate to assert that Moses was a Magician in Book 30, Chapter 1, when he makes Magic the genus of all such incantations, however they are performed. Berosus was delighted by the same lie—whom we have as a forgery from Annius—whose <term>knowledge<note>original: γνῶσιν (gnōsin)</note></term> is nevertheless defended with great effort by Baronius and <margin>on Habakkuk ch. 3 p. 385.</margin> Antonio de Guevara. And Strabo in Book 16, page 524, makes the same man an Egyptian Priest, and casts him into the order of Astrologers, and says he was a diviner, such as Orpheus, Zamolxes, the Magi of the Persians, and the Chaldeans of the Assyrians were. Furthermore, he mentions that he departed from the Egyptians for the sake of worshipping God. *Moses (he says), one of the Egyptian priests, holding a certain part of the region called... having become dissatisfied with the established institutions there, emigrated from there, and those who honored the divine went out with him.* Egypt was most devoted to the study of magic, so much so that guests of that region fell under suspicion of magic. Certainly, from the time Egypt became famous for the reputation of its teaching and erudition, Orpheus, Plato, Pythagoras, and many others moved there, stirred by the desire for wisdom, by whom, as if from Teachers, superstition was propagated to others. The Pagans heard rumors, as we have already shown, concerning Moses's contention with the Magicians in Egypt, and from this they fabled that he had pursued Magic. Pliny makes Zoroaster the first inventor of Magic, after whom Moses lived many thousands of years later, though it is certain that Moses lived several centuries before absolutely all the wise men of Greece. The Egyptian priests themselves thought much more laudably of Moses, from whom <margin>Book 2 ch. 5.</margin> Diodorus Siculus writes that he understood him to be the first legislator of all, a man otherwise great-souled, *a man great in soul and most capable in life*, and who received the law brought to the Jewish people from the God *Iao*. He derives the origin of the Jewish laws from the God *Iao*, in which see a trace of the <term>tetragrammaton<note>The four-letter holy name of God (YHWH)</note></term> יהוה, which was written by the Greeks as *Iao* and *Iau*; and the oracle of Apollo at Claros in Macrobius produced that name, in which the highest of the Gods is called *Iao*. The name of the true God, Jehovah, passed from the Jews to the neighboring Tyrians, and from these to the Greeks through commerce, who from that most holy name, by a slight distortion and contraction, made the name of Jove (Jupiter), which was turned into various fables by the Greeks, the rivals of the Orientals. I do not know, however, from what archive Justin produced the lying

secret concerning the sacred objects of the *Egyptians* stolen by Moses, which he, as a fugitive, perhaps while the Gods were snoring, carried back through unknown ways into a seat ungrateful to the Gods. Thus the deeds of that most noble Leader of the Hebrews are accustomed to be contaminated and profaned by those profane Writers. The Egyptians had moved a harsh persecution against the Hebrews, they had enrolled them as slaves, *and God knew the children of Israel and looked upon them*, <margin>Exodus 2:15.</margin> so that at last they cast off this servitude, and with Moses as leader they went out *not empty-handed*, <margin>ch. 3:21-22 & ch. 12:35.</margin> carrying away with a full hand *vessels of gold and silver and garments*, in compensation for the servitude and labors which they endured for so many years. But let us see by what argument Magic and other forbidden arts introduced themselves into the land of Mizraim <note>The Hebrew name for Egypt</note>, the most superstitious of all lands as many as the Sun has seen. The Egyptians, the chief masters of all superstition, were in this persuasion: that nothing was to be done, nothing was to be held for certain, unless it had first been confirmed from the mouth of some Magician and by a prophetic saying. For foolishly curious and insanely credulous Egypt itself always nourished some monster (which has been said elsewhere of Africa) and always produced pupils of the more secret magical art of various kinds and wonderful genius, the first certainty of which thing can be drawn from nowhere else than from our sacred Pentateuch. For it is known as much as possible from that history, which copiously relates the affairs of King Pharaoh, that the first of the Kings who were of Egypt used Magicians in matters of great importance.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
**Page 128**

<margin>The Magi and Soothsayers of Egypt.</margin> In the time of Joseph, Pharaoh summoned all the Magicians and Wise Men of Egypt so that he might learn from them a precise interpretation of a certain dream by which he felt himself disturbed. Without doubt, he had first proposed this dream of his to his own court Magicians; when they found themselves unequal to the task of explaining the dream, they advised the King to convoke a Synod of all the Magicians of his empire. But the practitioners of that secret art frustrated the King, who expected in vain something worthy of his dream from those impostors. With incantations, prayers, chants, and other magical ceremonies, they raised the astonished King’s hopes, but these "Professors of Vanities" brought nothing worthy of such a great King. While they turned themselves in every direction, they finally reached the point where they confessed themselves abandoned by all their art. Joseph lay in a dark prison, whom God wished on this occasion—by His incomprehensible kindness—to deliver from his foul dwelling and to elevate eminently, for the great benefit of His people. God gave him the interpretation of the dream, and brought it about that he was proclaimed next to the King by public edict, through the incredible and inestimable providence of God. Where then were the Magicians and petty sorcerers? Where were the *Charthymim* <note>original: "Charthymim," a Hebrew term for soothsayer-priests</note> with their curled and adorned Magic? They were mocked by their own nation, which was swept up in admiration for the Hebrew youth, and by a sort of mutual consent declared him the *Father of the Country*. I do not doubt that in this acclamation there were those who detested the vain arts of the Magicians. But let us consider for a moment these magical trifles! This was an old device of Satan, and Magic was by no means the least of the evil arts. The domestic writer Apollonides is said to have handed down its origin, as well as its study among the Egyptians, in the second book <margin>Book 2.</margin> of the *Semenuthi* <note>A lost work on Egyptian history</note>, which is mentioned by Theophilus of Antioch, as well as by Pliny in Book 30, Chapter 1. Where Pliny deals with Magic, he says that Moses was a practitioner of it—a passage that cannot be passed over at this time. *There is,* he says, *another faction of Magic, depending on Moses and Jannes and Jotape, who were Jews, but many thousands of years after Zoroaster.* One may observe this same false accusation in Apuleius’s *Apology*, where on page 156 he says: *Let me be that Carinonnas, or Damigeron, or that Moses, or Jannes, or Apollonius, or Dardanus himself, or whoever else after Zoroaster and Hostanes has been celebrated among the Magicians.* These are lies worthy of pagan authors; nevertheless, we have this "memorable fact" <note>original: ἀπομνημόνευτον</note> from them: that the fame of that noble history concerning the Pharaoh who persecuted the Israelites reached the Gentiles, albeit through false rumor. At that time, the strenuous antagonists against the wonder-working of Moses <margin>2 Timothy 3:8.</margin> were Jannes and Jambres, whom Pliny understood here, but wrongly reckoned among the Jews. Mention of them is made in the Hebrew Talmudic writings under the names *Mamre* and *Jochanna*, whom the Targumists <note>Translators/commentators of the Aramaic Bible</note> are accustomed to call concisely *Janis* and *Jannes*, and *Iambres*. For so we read in the Targum of Jonathan: *And <margin>Exodus 7:11.</margin> Pharaoh called the Wise Men and the Sorcerers, and they also did the same—namely Jannes and Jambres, the Magicians of Egypt—by the incantations of their sorceries.* In the same Jonathan, in Chapter 1 of Exodus, they are called "Princes of the head of the Magicians or enchanters." Moses says in the cited Chapter 7 that Pharaoh ordered

<column-break/>

the wise men and evildoers to be summoned (so the old interpreter Vatablus translates <margin>The Magi and Soothsayers of Egypt.</margin> the Hebrew *Lachakamim u-lemakasephim*), who, in order to overturn the Jewish religion and bring ignominy upon the true God of the Jews, resisted the power of God—which was working through Moses—with a fictitious rivalry of their magical arts. <margin>And the magicians of Egypt also did the same with their secret arts.</margin> The Septuagint <note>Greek Old Testament</note> says: *And the enchanters of the Egyptians did likewise with their sorceries.* The Vulgate: *And they also did in like manner by Egyptian incantations and certain secrets.* Moses and Aaron used a rod, which is here called *Matteh*, in the presence of Pharaoh as an instrument to prepare signs and wonders. The *sorcerers of Pharaoh*, among whom Jannes and Jambres were prominent, <margin>v. 9, 10.</margin> did similarly, *and they each threw down their rod, and they were turned into serpents.* <margin>v. 11, 12.</margin> And indeed these Magicians, through certain secret magic words and gesturing fantasies, used the Rod to perform deceptive and illusory transformations; exactly as in Homer, where Circe is said to have transformed the companions of Ulysses into swine <margin>Odyssey, Book 10, v. 238.</margin> when touched by her small rod (*rhabdos*) along with certain magic words. The Magicians, infamous for their magical art, were able by divine permission to produce in appearance some of the things that Moses himself did; but God willed this to happen *so that the difference might be proven* <note>original: ἵνα ἐλεγχθῆ τὸ διάφορον</note>, as Theodoret well says in *Question 18 on Exodus, page 79.* For they also changed their rods into serpents; but the rod of Moses devoured <margin>v. 12.</margin> their rods. *The bodies of the dragons of the magical rods appeared to Pharaoh and the Egyptians (as Tertullian says in "On the Soul," chapter 57, page 361), but the truth of Moses devoured the lie.* They also changed water into blood <margin>v. 22.</margin> with their incantations; but they were not able to lead the water back *to its former nature*. They also produced <margin>c. 8, v. 7, 8.</margin> frogs, from which, however, they could not deliver the land of Egypt. And thus, by the wonderful "divine economy" <note>original: ἐπὶ τῆς θείας οἰκονομίας</note> of God, Pharaoh—who had sent them against Moses—was punished and hardened by the work of his own Magicians. Moreover, God wished to show how vain and ridiculous their power was from this: that although they had previously produced larger animals upon the land of Egypt, they could not produce a *tiny louse*, <margin>v. 18, 19.</margin> but had to acknowledge that "the finger of God is here," and that they could do nothing with their sorceries against divine power. Thus, magical wisdom was deluded by the finger of God, by which He worked admirable effects, and the glory of the wisdom of those impostors was corrected with disgrace. <margin>Wisdom 17:7.</margin> It was elegantly called "the mockeries of the magical art," for they were delusions of the eyes, and certain empty likenesses of serpents and frogs. ->*The jugglery of the black art lay prostrate / and the boasting of their art became a mockery*<- <note>original German: "Das Gauckelwerck der schwarzen Kunst lag darnieder / und das Rühmen von ihrer Kunst ward zum Spott"</note> as our version emphatically expressed it; concerning which see the homilies of D.
