# From Genesis Chapter XLI. v. 8.

<margin>The Magi and Diviners of Egypt.</margin>
<margin>v. 45. D. C.</margin>
The Hebrew <note>Joseph</note> carried all the votes, and by the unanimous opinion of all, he was pronounced by Pharaoh as *Zophnath-paaneah*, that is, *the great Master of secrets*; or rather *Abrech*, that is, the *Vice-regent of Egypt*. He is designated to the world as one who carried out this office of Plenipotentiary with singular prudence, which alone imparts both weight and esteem to great titles. The followers of a pernicious discipline also bore a splendid name and went about desiring to be called חכמים <note>Chakhamim</note>, *wise men*. Thus the Babylonian scholars sought recommendation for their name among their own people from this very title, who are called by Daniel חכימי בבל <note>Chakime Bavel</note> *the Wise Men of Babylon*. One who studies the Law is usually called by the Jews תלמיד חכם <note>Talmid Chakham</note>, *a disciple of a wise man*, a name which even the Doctor of the Law calls himself for the sake of modesty. Plainly, just as the followers of various sciences in Greece first called themselves *sophoi* <note>Greek: σοφούς, wise men</note>, a splendid name which Pythagoras later fled from, preferring to be called a *philosopher* <note>Greek: φιλόσοφος, a lover of wisdom</note>. However, the philosophy of the Egyptians consisted of "bad wisdom"; for they were חרטמים <note>Chartummim</note>, *enchanters*, *Soothsayers* / *Sorcerers* / Exodus 7:11, who simultaneously scrutinized the secrets of nature and the understanding of dreams; hence our Latin translator calls them *conjectores* <note>interpreters/diviners</note>, just as Plautus in *Amphitryon 1.1.76* calls an interpreter of dreams a *conjector*. Pharaoh summons experts of this kind and demands an interpretation of his dream. But the perceptive *Chartom* <note>magician</note> can divine nothing of the future if he is destitute of the secret suggestion of his own Genius <note>a guardian spirit</note>. This is the intent of the word: that it suggests a forbidden art and supposes a pact with an evil Spirit; for it is joined everywhere with other names of forbidden arts, as in *Exodus 7:11*, where there are coupled with it מכשפים <note>Mekhashephim</note> *sorcerers*, who used prestigiatory and malicious means so that there might come forth <margin>On the Law, fol. 95.</margin> something admirable and strange; according to Rabbi Bechai, the old Latin translator of the Bible everywhere renders this as *maleficos* <note>evildoers/sorcerers</note>. The Septuagint <note>Greek Old Testament</note> usually uses *pharmakeis* <note>Greek: φαρμακεῖς</note>, poisoners, from which the Hebrews made their own term from the same nation, *parmakos* <note>Hebrew: פרמקוס</note> in *Bereshit Rabba section 77*; just as from *magos* <note>Greek: μάγῳ, magician</note> they made *moni* <note>Hebrew: מוני</note> in the *Targum of Jonathan, Exodus 7:11, 8:16*. *Pharmakon* <note>Greek: φάρμακον</note> occasionally denotes *poison*; hence *veneficus* <note>sorcerer</note>, as if "poison-maker"; in this way they explain the *Chartummim*, whom they call sometimes *interpreters* and sometimes *enchanters*. He expressly hints at the interpretation of dreams; and the interpreters of dreams were famous among the Egyptians, among whom the Alexandrians were said to "dream with natural talent and good fortune," according to the testimony of Damascius in the *Life of Isidore* found in Photius, Code 242, p. 546. How studious they were of Magic was explained by Petrus Crinitus in *De honesta disciplina, book 9, ch. 5*, who also took occasion from the sacred rites of the Jews to devise magical ceremonies with the worst sort of perverse imitation <note>Latin: Cacozelia</note>. Well known to them was the slaughter of the firstborn, from which the Israelites—whose <margin>Exodus 12:12-13.</margin> houses the Angel had marked with blood—were delivered. Mindful of this mournful night, they used to take red earth at the start of the spring equinox, which the Greeks call *miltos* <note>Greek: μίλτον, red ochre</note>, and mark their flocks, plants, and all other things from which they desired to avert a plague. Epiphanius, in his work on the Nazarene heresy, records this "rubricism" <note>marking in red</note> for the deprecation of evils, and it is referred back to the slaughter by the Angel in Egypt. They pronounced those days to be ill-omened and unlucky on which they were struck by so many plagues by Moses, and on which Pharaoh perished in the sea with his army; hence the origin of the "Egyptian Days," which were held to be *most unlucky*

<column-break/>

according to the conjecture of Delrio in *Magical Disquisitions, book 3, p. 93*. The Magi also saw that Moses had struck the Earth with a rod; from this, I easily imagine that in imitation the Egyptians placed and worshipped a rod in the temples of Isis, as witnessed by Artapanus in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel, book 9*. The bronze serpent erected in the desert migrated into the impious cult of serpents. The masters of magic transferred these things to their own vanities with most [foolish] fictions, which the superstitious nation admired as if they were divine. They attributed too much to *monomeria* and *dodecathemoria* <note>astrological divisions of time/degrees</note> in all divination and prediction; hence Ptolemy, obliquely criticizing them, says he will deliver his dogmas "not to be read through lots and numbers," which are all "randomly babbled by the many and possess no persuasive reason." They clung greedily and expensively to this divinatory Astrology, and from it they anxiously predicted the occurrences of life, as noted by Diodorus Siculus. Hence the Rabbis write of the חכמי התולדות <note>Chakhamim ha-Toledot</note> *Wise men of nativities*, whom the Greeks call *genethliakoi* <note>Greek: γενεθλιακοί, casters of nativities</note>. Sometimes they used the help of Demons, whom they called upon familiarly, using certain ceremonies for that purpose. Thus did those famous Magi in the presence of Moses בלטיהם <note>be-latehem</note>, <margin>Exodus 7:11.</margin> *which the Old translator rendered: through incantations and certain secrets*, doubtless hinting at gesticulations and other types of apparitions <note>Greek: φαντασμάτων</note>, by which the enchanters showed themselves to the common people with a certain sacred horror. Bonfrerius <margin>at this place, p. 373.</margin> notes that the Hebrew word *lehat* <note>להט</note> properly signifies a flame; and subsequently the glitter of a spear or sword, *which emulates a flame; some wish that this was used for these incantations; for not only words, but also gesticulations and some wonders are usually employed in incantations.* Our translator seems to have understood "through incantations and secrets" as magic words, which are generally used by magicians; as does the Chaldean <note>Targum</note>, who uses the word *lat* <note>לט</note>, which sounds like a muttering or whispering. For he uses a root here that has the meaning of low speech; for *lachash* <note>לחש</note> to the Hebrews and Chaldeans denotes *to mutter, to whisper, to say something secretly and silently*; hence it is said of incantation in *Jeremiah 8:17*, where God threatens that he will send among the Jews "cockatrices or basilisks," which are said to put other serpents to flight by their hiss alone, אשר אין-להם לחש <note>asher ein-lahem lachash</note>, *for which there is no incantation*, i.e., against which no incantation or magical consecration has any effect. Luther translates: *which are not charmed.* This is aptly suited to the Chaldeans, of whom there is speech there, among whom were enchanters and *Chartummim*, who knew how to enchant serpents with sacred words, which was done by muttering. An enchanter associates evil Spirits to himself by chanting and muttering, hence from that association he is called by the paraphrase חבר חבר <note>chover chover</note>, which Arias translates as *joining a joining*, so called from the society of an evil Spirit, with whom he joins himself in an evil fellowship. *Chavar* <note>חבר</note> means *to associate, to join*. An enchanter, moreover, is one who effects certain wonders by certain whispers and mutterings. That muttering was sometimes done through apertures; hence some etymologists derived *Chartum* <note>חרטום</note> from *char* <note>חר</note>, *a hole*, which is an allusion rather than an etymology, concerning which Hottinger may be consulted in *Thesaurus Philologicus, book 1, section 8, p. 57*. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Magicians and Soothsayers of Egypt.</margin>
...with the voice. They performed their magical rites in a fixed position, in specific places, with a certain posture of their bodies, with specific instruments, and with specific vocalizations. Hence, when the Prophet *Isaiah (chapter 29, verse 4)* speaks of a spirit of divination or a necromancer, he aptly uses two words: *shachach*, **to bow down or cast oneself down**, and *tsaphaph*, **to chirp or mutter**. Luther translates it thus:
> Then you shall be brought low, and shall speak out of the ground, and your speech shall mutter out of the dust; your voice shall be like that of a magician out of the ground, and your speech shall whisper out of the dust. <note>original: "Alsdann soltu genidrigt werden..." This German quote is Luther's translation of Isaiah 29:4.</note>

Thus Arnuphis, a most celebrated and powerful Magician of Egypt, used certain **sorceries** <note>original Greek: μαγγανείας (manganeias)</note> to invoke Mercury and other Demons to make it rain, as witnessed by Xiphilinus in the *Life of Antoninus, page 270*. A rude antiquity believed that *rains could be both drawn down and driven away by chants; however, Seneca affirms in Natural Questions, Book 4, Chapter 7, that it is obvious none of these things can actually happen.* They ascribed the greatest power to certain words and certain songs, by which they carried out consecrations and incantations. *To chant an evil song, and to charm the crops away from a field,* is mentioned in the **Laws of the Twelve Tables**. <margin>Title 11.</margin> Regarding these incantations of songs, Pliny treated them in *Book 28, Chapter 2, based on the teaching of the Ancients*, and concludes his discourse: *Certain songs exist against hailstorms, against types of diseases, and against burns. Some have even been tested. But a great shame prevents me from publishing them, given such a variety of opinions.* Therefore, let everyone think of these things as they please. But for us Christians, it is not permitted to think as we please, for we detest them in our hearts. Origen, in *Book 1 Against Celsus*, maintains that there were certain names used in the **incantations** <note>original Greek: ἐπῳδῇ (epōdē)</note> of the Egyptian sages, just as there were among the Magi of the Persians and the Brahmans of the Indians. The Priests were skilled in this matter, as Artapanus records in Eusebius, <margin>Book 9, Preparation for the Gospel</margin> where he identifies those Magicians as *Memphite priests of Moses*. What madness of **sorceries**, to try to contend in shameful Magic against the *finger of God*? These foolish men had promised they would bring help to Pharaoh against Moses by some more powerful magic. Here it became apparent how vain was that which Charicles used to boast elsewhere concerning the Egyptian Priests and <margin>Heliodorus, Book 3</margin> Prophets: *that it is not impossible for prophets to achieve even the greatest things.* Indeed, they could not even produce the smallest lice (which the Latin translator calls *ciniphes*). The guardians of that most wicked art sold their trifles under the name of religion, just as Ammianus Marcellinus seemed to speak of Magic under that name in *Book 22, Chapter 43 (or the last)*: *First, these men reached the cradles of various religions long before others, and they cautiously guard the first beginnings of sacred rites, preserved in secret writings.* Pythagoras, instructed in this wisdom and worshiping the Gods more secretly, established that whatever he said or wanted was to be considered authoritative; he often showed his "golden thigh" at Olympia and was seen from time to time conversing with an eagle. It is very likely that the first school for the exercise of Magic was established by the Egyptians. Some make Zoroaster the first fabricator of Magic, whom Clement conjectures was Mizraim, the son of Ham, tracing the first origin of Magic from Egypt in the books of the *Recognitions*. *Ham (he says in Book 4) handed down a poorly understood discipline to one of his sons named Mizraim, from whom the race of the Egyptians, Babylonians, and Persians is derived.*

<column-break/>

<margin>The Magicians and Soothsayers of Egypt.</margin>
[...discipline:] *The nations that existed then called him Zoroaster, admiring him as the first author of the magical art, in whose name many books on this subject are also held.* In truth, Magic is nothing other than a mask of the Devil and harmful Spirits, fashioned to introduce demon-worship into the Theater of the world and to play with miserable people. This mask was stripped away by the presence of the Good Spirit in the time of Pharaoh, and it harmed the worshiper himself. But the Devil later, in his descendants who did not remember the things gloriously done under the leadership of Moses, raised up other Magicians famous for no less ill-repute, of whom mention is made here and there in the monuments of the Ancients. Lucian mentions the Memphite Magician Pancrates in *The Lover of Lies*; and Apuleius recounts the magic of Zachlas, an Egyptian Magician, in his *Milesian Tales*. *Plotinus* and <margin>Porphyry, Life of Plotinus.</margin> Olympius, two Egyptians, contended with each other in magical arts. There were various kinds of divinations, which Caspar Peucer treated in an entire book, and later Martin Delrio followed up on the same more laboriously. God forbade the Jews to follow diviners and soothsayers to fish for information about fortuitous events and other happenings. For there was no necessity to consult these vain men when true Prophets were not lacking, who could be consulted in times of urgent need. Our discourse here is not about divinations that rely on their own causes, signs, and natural effects gathered through reasoning, but about divinations that exceed the limits of nature and are usually made from superstitious signs or conjectures about future things, and where the suitability of actions is sought through superstitious observations of the dispositions of the sky, air, clouds, and winds. A physician may take a conjecture from natural dreams about the balance or imbalance of the body. It is not permitted for a man to conjecture vainly and superstitiously about future events from chance dreams. On this, see Delrio, *Magical Disquisitions*, Book 4, Question 6. **Dream interpretation** <note>original Greek: ὀνειρολογία (oneirologia)</note> supported by divine revelation does not belong here. The Heathens used to seek divination: 1. *From oracles*. Just as God built Churches through His Prophets, so the Devil, the "ape of God," built the citadels of his blasphemies in which he might vomit out his responses and oracles. The most famous oracles are said to be those of Hammon and Dodona; it can be likely gathered that the former occupied the principal school of Ham or his descendants, while the latter was a **dwelling place** <note>original Greek: κατοικητήριον (katoikētērion)</note> of the family of Dodanim, the grandson of Noah through Javan. 2. *From the stars*, about which we shall speak extensively in another place. 3. *From auguries*, which were accepted from any source, as happened in auspices, the inspection of entrails, in **water-divination** <note>hydromancy</note>, **sieve-divination** <note>coscinomancy</note>, **fire-divination** <note>pyromancy</note>, **smoke-divination** <note>capnomancy</note>, **name-divination** <note>onomancy</note>, **omen-watching** <note>teratoscopy</note>, and other such vain and superstitious divinations, hardly worth remembering. Often someone leaving his house saw a blind man, or a Eunuch, or a lame man, and took it as an omen. Another was deterred on a journey by the encounter of a hare or the flight of a bird on the left. Augustus Caesar observed certain auspices and omens as most certain. <margin>Suetonius, Life of Augustus, chapter 96.</margin> It happened to him, when he was going down into battle at Actium, that he met a little donkey with a donkey-driver named Eutychus (which means "Fortunate"), and the beast's name was Nicon (which means "Victor"). From this, the omen of victory was accepted, and the city was later called Nicopolis ("City of Victory"), and in its temple, a statue of the donkey and the driver was placed...

# From Genesis Chapter XLI. v. 8.

### The Magi and Diviners of Egypt.
<margin>Magi and Diviners of Egypt.</margin>
The same is recorded of Augustus (Chapter 92): if in the morning his shoe was put on incorrectly—the left for the right—he held it as a dire omen. Cicero laughs at such things in the second book of *On Divination*, adding that if we accept these, we would also have to observe the tripping of a foot or the *breaking of a shoe-lace* <note>original: "corrigia quoque abruptionem"</note> as omens. 4. Regarding fortune-telling: To this I refer "belomancy" <note>divination by drawing arrows</note>, which Nebuchadnezzar used before moving his army against Jerusalem. At a crossroads (which is noteworthy), he took a divination according to the rite of his nation, as seen in *Ezekiel 21:21*. For he mixed various arrows in one quiver as if in an urn, inscribed or marked with the names of each place in question; whichever arrow came out first determined the lot. Jerome says on this passage: *By the rite of his nation he consults the oracle, putting his arrows into a quiver and mixing them inscribed with names, to see whose arrow comes out and which city he should attack first.* The same King divined the future outcome of the war from the entrails of carcasses. Luther: *Look at the liver.* The Vulgate: *he consulted the entrails.* The Septuagint: *looking into the liver* <note>Greek: ἠπατοσκοπήσας / hepatoscopy</note>. In Hebrew: *he inspected the liver.* Those who inspect entrails are called by the fitting name *sectores* <note>cutters</note> in *Daniel 2:11 and 4:7*, from the cutting out of victims to predict the future. To this they also relate "rhabdomancy" <note>divination by rods or sticks</note>, which they claim Hosea speaks of in chapter 4:12 when he says: *My people consult a piece of wood, and their staff* <note>Hebrew: מקלו / maqlo</note> *reports to them.* The Septuagint: *and by his rods they declared to him*, which Jerome interprets as a divining rod, where they gave credit to the accidental throwing and falling of little sticks as if to an oracle. So the Romans used to *perform auguries by letters or rods*, as Livy testifies in Book 1. This whole filth of oracles, seers, spirits, augurs, and enchanters, which Satan introduced to drive the Egyptians and other peoples mad,
<margin>Deut. 18. v. 10. 11. 14.</margin>
God condemns, *saying to his people: There shall not be found among you anyone who uses divination, a practitioner of magic, or an augur, nor a sorcerer, nor an enchanter, nor one who consults a spirit, nor a wizard, nor one who seeks the dead.* The Septuagint: *there shall not be found in thee one divining a divination, and one using omens, and one practicing augury, a sorcerer...* (v. 11) *one chanting an incantation, a ventriloquist <note>one possessed by a spirit</note>, and a watcher of wonders, one questioning the dead.* Regarding the interpretation of the Hebrew words, the translators do not entirely agree. Luther renders it: *That there be not found among you a soothsayer, or a chooser of days* <note>Hebrew: מעונן / me'onen</note>, *or one who pays heed to the cry of birds* <note>Hebrew: מנחש / menaches</note>, *or a sorcerer, or a charmer* <note>Hebrew: חובר חבר / chober chober</note>, *or a fortune-teller* <note>Hebrew: שאל אוב / shoel ob</note>, *or an interpreter of signs* <note>Hebrew: ידעני / yide'oni</note>, *or one who
<margin>Levit. 19. 31.</margin>
asks the dead.* The same was forbidden: *Do not turn yourselves to spirits, nor seek anything from soothsayers.* The Septuagint: *You shall not follow those with spirits in their bellies, nor join yourselves to enchanters.* Luther: *You shall not turn to the fortune-tellers* <note>Hebrew: אל־האבת / el-ha'obot</note> *and do not search from the interpreters of signs.* And among the praises given to the Jews by the Gentile Balaam was that there is no augury <note>Hebrew: נחש / nachash</note> in Jacob, nor divination <note>Hebrew: קסם / qesem</note> in Israel (*Num. 23:23*). Would that they had remained pure from this crime! Saul, through a medium who had a familiar spirit, ordered Samuel to be raised (*1 Sam. 28:7*), even though at the beginning of his reign, in a most illustrious act according to the law of *Exod. 22:18*, he had removed the
<margin>1. Sam. 28. 7.</margin>
*mediums and wizards* <note>Hebrew: את־האבות ואת־הידענים</note>.

(v. 3) Balaam was a soothsayer and an impious prophet,
<margin>Magi and Diviners of Egypt. Num. 22. 7. 11.</margin>
whom the *elders of Moab and the elders of Midian* had hired with money to curse the Israelites, and to whom King Balak sent messengers to consult him in desperate matters. There are those who say he was a Magician and had fellowship with a Demon, who, in order to *seek an augury*, used certain superstitious rites, erecting seven altars

In Chaldean Babylon, Satan carried out his various deceptions through the work of the Magi, who are called *Wise Men* in *Isaiah 44:25*, whom God threatens with infatuation and the annihilation of their foolish divinations. Thus said the Lord Jehovah: *I am Jehovah, making all things, frustrating the signs of the diviners* <note>Hebrew: בדים / baddim - lies</note> *and making the soothsayers mad, turning the wise men backward and making their knowledge foolish (v. 24, 25).* Luther: *Who brings the signs of the soothsayers to nothing and makes the diviners mad. Who turns the wise back and makes their art into folly.* Musculus on this passage (p. 636): Babylon had the most famous diviners, *soothsayers and wise men, whom they call Magi.* To their divinations, soothsayings, auguries, and presages they securely entrusted all their fortunes and the entire state of the kingdom. *They judged that nothing adverse would happen that those men had not foreseen; then, they believed that what they predicted would certainly come to pass. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES. Genesis XLI. v. 43.

<margin>The Magi and Soothsayers of Egypt.</margin> ...so that they might be deceived, led astray, and thus, contrary to hope, be overthrown; he says that the signs of the diviners would be scattered, the soothsayers driven to madness, and the knowledge of the wise made foolish—that is, he would bring it about that, having become mindless, they would divine falsely. Here the deceit of trickery and prophesying was uncovered, and, to speak with Plautus in *The Captives*:

> What was hidden has been opened; the tricks lie exposed.

The Babylonians depended on a foolish trust in divinations and incantations, even from the first origin of the city of Babel, in a very long-established manner, as the same Prophet <note>Isaiah</note> objects in chapter 47, verse 12: *Stand now with your incantations* <note>Hebrew: *be-chavrayich*</note> *and with the multitude of your sorceries* <note>Hebrew: *u-ve-rov keshaphayich*</note> *in which you have labored from your youth.* **So step forth now with your conjurers and with the multitude of your sorcerers, among whom you have labored from your youth.** He likens these sorcerers <note>Hebrew: *keshaphim*</note> to stubble in verse 14, which cannot protect itself against the power of fire, and he censures their deceptive wisdom in verse 10. The Magi of the Egyptians were "Sophi" <note>Wise men</note>, who used to devise the hieroglyphic letters of the Egyptians and through them hand down wisdom. Thus understand the "magical tongues" in Lucan, Book 3, by which the Magi presented the precepts of their philosophy and the mysteries of their theology in a more sacred type of figures. Papyrus was not yet in use when these things were done, whence the Poet says in that place:

> Not yet did river-side Memphis know how to weave
> Books of papyrus; and only on stones did birds and beasts
> And carved animals preserve the magical tongues.

Whatever was in the secrets, and in which they thought some mystery lay hidden, they interpreted for those whose interest it was to know. If prodigies and portents were seen, or dreams, they were brought to these men as solemn interpreters appointed by the Magistrate, namely so that by certain solemn observations and ceremonies they might avert future destruction, or, if good things were portended, thanks might be given to the Gods.

In our own time, there exists a book under the name *Zebel*, first edited by Dr. Heinrich Khunrath, under the praise of being "useful doctrine for the benefit of one's neighbor," though it contains old wives' tales and wonderfully superstitious nonsense. It promises future events according to the motion of the moon through the 12 signs of the celestial Zodiac. I have not seen a more foolish book, nor do I think the Author was an Arab. Many things are hawked by triflers under the name of an ancient author, so that the trifles might become more saleable. If the Editor had kept this useless book to himself, much vanity would have perished. Nevertheless, he dares to call them *most accurate observations*. Listen, I pray, <margin>Num. 111.</margin> to a few: *If the Moon is in Aries, and an old woman meets you, you will lose either money or another thing dear to you. Do not play.* And again: *If the Moon is in Taurus, and an old woman meets you, you will find a foul and hungry lodging on your journey.* The braying of a donkey denotes <margin>Num. 108.</margin> temptation or sadness or necessity. It is shameful to bring forth other similar things, and yet that "distinguished labor" was produced in a German dress so that it could be read by old women, and to gain authority for the trifles, the name of Emperor Rudolf was prefixed. Would that what is written as having been done at Ephesus in *Acts 19:19* were done today—that Christians who enjoy the name but have followed curious arts would bring together such forbidden books and burn them before everyone!

-> And a herald proclaimed before him. <note>Greek: Kai ekeryxen emprosthen autou keryx.</note> <-
-> *The Herald crying out, that all should bow the knee before him.* <-

<margin>The Inauguration of Joseph.</margin> IN that inauguration of Joseph, son of Israel, as a certain eulogy of honor and most ample dignity, the Egyptians vied with one another crying, *Abrech, Abrech, Abrech*, and Joseph, as is the custom at the arrival and auspices of a new Prince, was saluted:

-> *They called out "Parent" with a loud voice.* <-

The name *Abrech* is august, and without doubt was used in the auspicious acclamations of the natives of that land, so that both he who was being raised to dignity might be greater, and his dignity and majesty might be more ample before the people. Just as we read that in the land of Canaan there was an acclamation of this kind in the creation of Kings, or a "proclamation" <note>Greek: ekphonema</note>, when, after King Joash was created, <margin>2 Kings 11:v. 12.</margin> *they spoke with one wish of all and acclaimed with equal applause on every side:* **Long live the King!** <note>Hebrew: *Yechi ha-Melech*; Greek: *Zeto ho basileus*.</note> And in this sense the Jerusalem Targum explained *Abrech* when it rendered it: *Long live the Father of the King!* <note>Aramaic: *Yechi avui le-malka*</note> just as if the Egyptians had undertaken the same vows for safety which the Hebrews otherwise employ. That this was the voice of those "offering cheers" <note>Greek: ton epheuphomounton</note> is clear from Daniel 11:4, 3:9, 5:10, 4:21, and Judith 11:5, so that there is scarcely any doubt about the proper and native sense of the word *Abrech*. Rabbi Jonah conjectures that it was proclaimed before the chariot by Royal heralds that Pharaoh, King of Egypt, had appointed Joseph as Prefect of his whole Kingdom, as one most worthy of that honor, and therefore knees should be bowed before him; *Habrech* <note>Hebrew: הברך</note> would be the same by "letter exchange" <note>Greek: antistoichon</note> as <margin>Gen. 9 v. 3.</margin> *Habrech*, that is, *bow the knee*; just as Rabbi David wishes it to be the Hiphil imperative, with the letter *Aleph* placed in the spot of the characteristic *He*. Luther already knew this exposition of the Rabbis, for in the first version of the Bible which appeared in the year 1524, he had approved it, rendering it: **And he had it cried out before him, that one should bow the knee before him.** And he remembered <margin>In the commentary on Genesis, p. 560.</margin> where he writes: *Others derive Abrech from the verb barach, that is, to bless or to bow the knee.* But since the letter *Aleph* seems to conflict, because it is a "Heemantic" letter <note>a prefix letter</note>, they say the *Aleph* is placed instead of *He*, which permutation of letters is common for the Hebrews. Others want *Abrech* to be an infinitive with the same anomaly, followed at the same time by *and he placed him* <note>Hebrew: *ve-naton*</note>, that is, "having been given or placed," since the permutation of the active infinitive for the passive is not infrequent. With this acceptance the Old Interpreter <note>the Vulgate</note>, Junius, the Genevans, the Italians, and the Swiss translated it, and Castalio expressed it the same way: *Bow the knees*; Piscator: **Bend the knees**; the English: **Bow the Knee.** Thus most Interpreters explain it as genuflection, as if Pharaoh commanded everyone to bow their knees before the approaching Prince, in whom all the hope and safety of Egypt was placed. Hence also Aben Ezra explains it by two words of submission, *shachu* and *barech*, which appear together with *barach* in Psalm 95:6, so that the Rabbi seems to have looked to that; his words are: *Every man cried before him: I will fall on my knees and I will worship.* Among the Orientals, genuflection and the bending of the whole body was a symbol of civil adoration...

And all the king's servants who were at the king's gate bowed and prostrated themselves before Haman.* So too Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon, magnified Daniel, and having bestowed many great gifts upon him, appointed him ruler over the whole province of Babylon and chief of all the wise men of Babylon. In the same way, Pharaoh, King of Egypt, magnified *Joseph*, giving to him—as the Chancellor of the kingdom and as an <note>original: "εἰς ἀναγέλαστον δείγμα πίσεως"</note> <gloss>unshakable proof of trust</gloss>—his own signet ring with which he might seal royal letters; he clothed him in garments of fine linen, placed a gold chain around his neck, and appointed him over the entire land of Egypt. *You shall be over my house,* he says in <margin>v. 40</margin>, *and all my people shall be ruled according to your word <note>literally: "shall kiss your mouth"</note>. Only in regard to the throne will I be greater than you.* Among these honors was the "kiss," which was a symbol of subjection, whence the Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> aptly translates: <gloss>at your mouth all my people shall be obedient.</gloss> And the Latin: <gloss>At the command of his mouth the whole people shall obey.</gloss> Bowing was also a sign of subjection, which is why Joseph's brothers, when they first came into Egypt for the sake of buying grain, honored *Joseph* with their faces bowed to the ground, surely thinking him to be that Egyptian Prince; those who approached him would lower themselves to the earth and, full of reverence, bow their bodies once and again. Therefore the brothers <margin>v. 43. v. 26.</margin> <gloss>prostrated themselves before him with their faces to the earth</gloss>, by which very act the prophecy was fulfilled concerning the brothers' sheaves falling prostrate and worshipping Joseph's upright sheaf. For we read that those brothers, with heads bowed, <margin>v. 37. 7.</margin> prayed toward the earth. <margin>v. 42. 6. Philo on Joseph p. 373.</margin> <gloss>The brothers, having come into Egypt, encountered their brother as a stranger, and being struck with awe at his dignity, they prostrated themselves according to ancient custom.</gloss> Therefore, those who examine the word *Abrech* in relation to the root *Barak* <note>Hebrew: בורך</note> maintain that Pharaoh commanded that Joseph be honored with fitting rites, namely the bending of the knee and prostration of the body; for in Hebrew *Barak* also means to kneel; <margin>2 Chronicles 6:13</margin> <gloss>he set himself upon his knees</gloss>, <margin>Daniel 6:10</margin> <gloss>and kneeling upon his knees</gloss>, and it occurs in the same sense in <margin>Psalm 95:6</margin> in a vehement exhortation to reverence and total subjection toward God, where the Septuagint awkwardly has <gloss>to weep</gloss> <note>original: "κλαίειν"</note>, though there is no talk of lamentation there. *Come,* says the assembly of the faithful, *let us worship and fall down, and let us kneel before the face of Jehovah our Maker.*

Thus <margin>The Inauguration of Joseph.</margin> must we understand that mockery which the soldiers did to Christ <margin>Matthew 27:29</margin> <gloss>kneeling before him</gloss>, for that genuflection was a symbol of civil worship performed with a mocking spirit, by which those colorful scoundrels pretended to congratulate our Savior as if he were a new King. Therefore, the learned translator Aquila of *Pontus* thought this meaning should be observed in our much-debated word *Abrech*, which he translated as <gloss>kneeling</gloss> or <gloss>genuflection</gloss>, as we shall soon confirm by the testimony of Jerome. So too for Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> it signifies nothing other than kneeling; since <margin>ברכים</margin> "knees" are said to be what were bent before Joseph, under whose command and power all entered and exited. Although Luther accepted this opinion regarding kneeling, he preferred, <gloss>upon second thoughts</gloss>, to render it: *This is the Father of the Land*; for the administration of Egyptian affairs was granted to him as if to a Father, so that it could be called a <gloss>fatherly rule of Egypt</gloss>. They were preceded, without doubt, by the Chaldean Paraphrasts <note>The Targums</note>, who believe the acclamation was: <margin>דין אבא למלכא</margin> *This is the Father of the kingdom.* In this, Onkelos and Jonathan agree. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Inauguration of Joseph.</margin>
To Augustus and Trajan, who were called "Fathers of the Fatherland" by the judgment of the Senate, the Republic was committed under the name of the most lauded Princes. I would wish the same to be understood regarding Joseph, the Prince of Egypt, <margin>1 Clement 14.</margin> using the words of Seneca slightly altered: *We have called the Prince Joseph "Abrech," that is, Father of the Fatherland, not led by vain flattery. Other surnames like Zaphnath-Paaneah were given for honor. We called him Father of the Fatherland so he would know that a fatherly power was given to him, which is most temperate, consulting the interests of his subjects and placing them before his own.* We said "Zaphnath-Paaneah" <note>original: "Zophnath Paaneach"</note> so he would know the task given to him was to deliberate on what is best to do in arduous times. Thus, to such a great Savior—the likes of whom Egypt had never seen nor would ever see again—it could deservedly be acclaimed, <margin>Ovid, Fasti, Book 2, line 128.</margin>

> Holy Father of the Fatherland. To thee the common people, to thee the Senate
> gave this name. We, the Knights, gave this name to thee.

It will be useful to compare other translations as well, so that from their very collision, if not the light of truth, then at least the "cross of difficulty" <note>A scholarly metaphor for a particularly thorny problem.</note> might shine forth. Interpreters who admit this is an Egyptian word use this device: that it should correspond to the Hebrew language, of which Egypt professes itself a vassal. Since it is no less helpful than safe to follow the more favorable interpretation in a doubtful matter, the zeal of the Paraphrasts, Chaldeans, Rabbis, and Christians should not be displeased. They have traced the word back to either the Hebrew or Aramaic language, and with not-to-be-rejected labor, they sought learned allusive derivations in foreign terms, <margin>2 Grammar 8.</margin> concerning which Francis Junius handed down this rule: *Many things are read in Holy Scripture which, by the nature of those who speak or those spoken of, are foreign and not Hebrew. Therefore, it is proper to skillfully refer them back to their own dialects, such as* אברך [Abrech], *bend the knee, to the Egyptians, or* אב-יט [Ab-it], *he departed, to the Syrians, and six hundred other things which the prudent reader can easily notice are uttered imitatively.* <note>original: "μιμητικῶς" (mimetikos)</note> Thus, the force of the word *Abrech* is not to be drawn from any language other than Egyptian, from whence it came. But since knowledge of that language escapes us, those who bring forth their conjectures from a mutual comparison of Hebrew and Egyptian should not be mocked, so that wherever difficulty and obscurity occur, they may be removed and illustrated. Indeed, the language of the Egyptians and Hebrews was different, which is confirmed by Joseph’s conversation with his brothers, where business is conducted through an interpreter; but nevertheless, they touch upon each other in some proximity, as others teach. Wherefore, men most learned in languages—Mercer, Drusius, and Forster—attempt something similar here, comparing that foreign name with the verb *Barak* [to bless], especially when in the second conjugation it signifies "to bless," so that *Abrech* is the same as *Baruch*, *blessed*, as if it were shouted by a Herald or even by the whole people: *BLESSED.* In this respect, Drusius explained it from the imperative <margin>2 Questions 71.</margin> "Bless," observing the custom of the Orientals, who desired to be blessed by men great in age and wisdom. An example exists in Jerome regarding Hilarion, from whom the Saracens sought a blessing. <margin>Volume 1, Life of Hilarion, p. 247.</margin> His words: *The nation of the Saracens is devoted to the cult of Venus. But even the town itself (Elusa) is largely semi-barbarian due to its location. Therefore, hearing that Saint Hilarion was passing by, they went out to meet him in crowds with wives and children, bowing their necks and shouting in the Syrian tongue, "Barach," that is, "Bless."* <margin>Dictionary p. 117.</margin> To this explanation I bring John Forster, who writes: *Barak signifies either the knee or*

<column-break/>

<margin>The Inauguration of Joseph.</margin>
to bend one's speech toward someone, to peacefully and kindly bend the knees or the speech, to address with genuflection, *as happens in salutations, congratulations, prayers, departures, and farewells.* The past participle *Baruch* means blessed, praised, worthy of praise and honor, auspicious, fortunate, august. In the second conjugation, it means to bless. *Berakah* is a blessing, either verbal or real, which is brought to someone with a salutation and genuflection. Although *Abrech* is a foreign word, and therefore variously explained by interpreters, it nevertheless seems to signify to the Egyptians the same as *Baruch* does to the Hebrews, and to be a congratulatory acclamation of those wishing well. Pharaoh saw to it that Joseph was carried in the second chariot which he had, and they called him *Abrech*, that is, blessed or to be praised or praiseworthy. Mercer does not depart from this explanation in his commentary on Genesis, p. 657. I lean no more toward this opinion than that one, and as the Skeptics say, "nothing more." <note>original: "οὐδὲν μᾶλλον" (ouden mallon)</note> If you contend it was an ancient custom of bowing with genuflection, <note>original: "παλαιισμὸν σὺν γονατισμῷ" (palaismon syn gonatismo)</note> I would not reject it. Nor would I contend if you said the Hebrew word passed, like many others, to the Egyptians, in whose language it was undoubtedly the voice of those praying well for Joseph regarding his new and unexpected prefecture. Nor is the custom of acclamation obscure. Nations everywhere, to increase the veneration of their Great Men, mixed certain formulas of acclamation among their vows. Common was that cry: *MAY HE LIVE.* This is clear enough from various places in Holy Scripture, so much so that the Targumist sought light from it for the obscurity of the word *Abrech*, as we noted above. Therefore, because it contributes somewhat to our purpose, it might perhaps be neither useless nor unpleasant if I insert those formulas here. It was a solemn custom of saluting that those who approached Kings and Princes prayed for eternal life and empire for them. The Chaldean men brought before the King of Babylon addressed him in these words, <margin>Daniel 2:4.</margin> *O King, live forever,* <note>original: "מלכא לעלמין חיי" (Malka l'almin chayi)</note> that is, they speak in the Babylonian tongue: *King, live into eternity.* <note>original: "ζῆ συ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας ἄναξ" (Ze sy eis tous aionas anax)</note> *May the God Bel grant you long life.* The Chaldeans accusing the Jews say to Nebuchadnezzar in the same words: *O King, live forever.* <margin>chapter 3, verse 9.</margin> The Queen speaking to King Belshazzar says: *O King, live forever.* <margin>chapter 5:10.</margin> The Satraps coming into the sight of Darius <margin>chapter 6:6.</margin> salute him thus: *King Darius, live forever.* <margin>verse 21.</margin> Daniel follows the King with this very vow: *O King, live forever.* Judith addresses Holofernes thus: *May King Nebuchadnezzar of all the earth live, and may his power live.* <note>original: "ζῆ ὁ βασιλεὺς Ναβουχοδονόσορ πάσης τῆς γῆς, καὶ ζῆ τὸ κράτος αὐτοῦ"</note> Which the Old Interpreter rendered: *Nebuchadnezzar King of the earth lives,* <margin>chapter 11:5.</margin> *and his virtue lives.* Our version: *God give Nebuchadnezzar luck and salvation, the King of the whole land.* If she said: *May the King of the whole world live* and may his power endure happily, the Jewish woman did not speak from her heart's true sentiment, for she was revolving destruction in her heart and was attempting to win favor by a clever circumlocution of words. But if she wished to testify to the life of the King and his power, it was not a wish; <note>original: "εὐτικὸν" (eutikon - optative/wish)</note> hence the Herborn version: *As truly as Nebuchadnezzar the King of the whole earth lives / and as truly as his power lives.* Thus it was customary to confirm one's words by the life of Great Men, just as Joseph also said: *By the life of Pharaoh.* <margin>Genesis 42:15, 16.</margin> The Septuagint: *By the health of Pharaoh.* <note>original: "μὰ τὴν ὑγíειαν Φαραώ"</note> It is the same as if he said: *As Pharaoh lives, so shall this happen to you.* Just as that is true, so is this. And there is nothing else in that locution than a confirmation of a statement by comparison to a most certain thing. Properly it is not an oath, but only a more rare...

# From Genesis Chapter XLI. v. 43.

## The Inauguration of Joseph

<margin>The inauguration of Joseph.</margin>
The King includes a certain prior affirmation in that formula based on the affirmation of another's status. He who embraces this simple sense does not find it necessary to dispute with Augustine and others about I know not what regarding oaths and perjury, nor to charge Joseph with impiety, as the Dutch Bibles published with notes do. Joseph, when dealing with his brothers, pretends one thing while doing another; he feigns to be an Egyptian to his brothers (by whom he did not yet wish to be recognized), and thus he uses an Egyptian formula of assertion rather than the custom of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Yet, this was not foreign to the piety of his ancestors, despite the objection of Musculus, to whom the oath seemed entirely pagan.

<margin>See page 752.</margin>

<margin>1 Samuel 17:55.</margin>

It was a solemn formula that those approaching the Kings of the East should pray for eternal life and empire for them.

<margin>Aelian, Various History, 32.</margin>
A sweet little story is told of Sinaeta the Persian, who, having met Artaxerxes far from his cottage and having no gift to offer the King according to custom, ran to a nearby flowing river. Scooping up the waves with both hands, he addressed the King: <note>Greek: "O King Artaxerxes, may you reign forever."</note> Mindful of the very common formula, he prayed for perennial happiness of life for his King; and the peasant, offering a common gift in his rustic and lowly speech, said something uncommon. No one explains the cited formula <note>Hebrew: "Live forever."</note> better than that courteous rustic, by praying for the King <note>Greek: "to endure through the ages."</note>.

<margin>Curtius, History, Book 6.</margin>
With such courtly refinement Artabazus received Alexander, saying: *You indeed, O KING, may flourish in perpetual happiness. I, happy in all other things, am tortured by this one: that in my headlong old age I cannot long enjoy your goodness.* Nothing was more ancient than that he should be acclaimed with a solemn vow: <note>Hebrew: "Let him live."</note> Thus it seemed fit to the Jews to begin when their first King, SAUL, was chosen by a huge gathering of people, where everyone, to testify to their sudden joy, mingled this blessing amidst the grateful wandering of voices:

<margin>1 Samuel 10:24.</margin>
<margin>Hebrew: "Long live the King." Greek: "Let the King live."</note> LONG LIVE THE KING. *Good luck to the King.* Among the Hebrews and Chaldeans, the <term>optative verb</term> <note>expressing a wish</note> was *hayah* <note>to be/live</note>, which other peoples used to express in various ways. The Greeks would happily say this same thing with three words: *to rejoice*, *to be healthy*, and *to fare well*; the first properly pertains to the *soul*, the second to the *body*, and the third to external affairs, so that with that "well-rounded" trio they pray for the good things of soul, body, and fortune for someone. I will provide a very suitable witness here—if the comparison of like with like has any value in illustrating this matter—Antipater; hear his verses on Meleager of Tyre.

<margin>3 Anthology 26. n. 79. v. 7. p 583.</margin>

"Audonis." If a Greek, "Chaire" <note>Greetings/Rejoice</note>. Say the same thing.

The voice of one greeting or bidding farewell in Punic is *Audonis* (for which *vaidis* was poorly read), and it is from the Hebrew *Adonai* <note>My Lord</note>, from which comes that *donis*, as if to say: "Hail" or "Farewell my Lord, LIVE." This word makes us remember the Punic speech extant in Plautus, into which

<margin>Plautus, The Little Carthaginian, Act 5, Scene 2.</margin>
<margin>Miscellany.</margin>
many interpreters inquire, especially Samuel Petit, who seems to have elegantly translated the Punic verses with much grace, more than if they had corrupted them in the Punic manner. Moreover, the Plautine *Havdonni* or *Havedoni* corresponds to our *Audonis*, that is, "Hail Lord." But that first word of the Epigrammatist, SALOM, is from the native language, whether Hebrew *Shalom* or *Shelem*, "Peace," by which word health and prosperity are vowed to someone, as in <note>Hebrew: "Peace to you"</note> *Peace be to you*, Gen. 43:22; <note>Hebrew: "Peace with you"</note> <note>Greek: "Peace to you"</note> *Peace be with you*, Judges 6:23; for which <note>Hebrew: "To you be peace"</note> is used in chapter 19:20; and without the pronoun in 2 Samuel 18:28, where Ahimaaz said to King David: *Peace.* Nothing was more common than that salutation, which is expanded into a formula in 1 Samuel 25:6. They gave and returned greetings by that name, and used it when about to inquire concerning someone's comfortable life and health.

<margin>Genesis 29:6.</margin>

### Genesis 46:34

->Every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians.<-
->For every shepherd of sheep is an abomination to the Egyptians.<-
->*The Egyptians detest all shepherds of sheep.*<-

<margin>The abominable <term>theolatry</term> <note>The worship of animals as gods.</note> of the Egyptians.</margin>
To bring forth Antiquities from their ultimate origin is a laborious task, and to assert them is highly uncertain where rituals change repeatedly over the centuries and ancient testimonies of books are absent—especially regarding such an ancient nation. It is investigated in this place what the cause was for the Egyptians, on account of which they loathed the Hebrew nation with an abominable disdain. There are those who flee to the pride of the nation and their dominant status; from this view, they suggest that because of a certain regard for the common life in that Jewish and pastoral nation, the Egyptians impatiently bore a certain "dregs of the people" being brought to them, whom they deemed unworthy of their conversation. Since they were accustomed to national pride, they conceived of nothing more in their minds than what seemed to contribute to the majesty of their empire and the glory of their wisdom; when they saw this in that pious nation beloved by God, they laughed and detested it. For the pastoral life was filthy to that conceited nation, and for that reason, they left it to the Jews as a filthy and ignoble people. Furthermore, they neglected them as people indifferent to and ignorant of the disciplines and wisdom of the Egyptians (which Moses later learned), as if they were men of slow wit whom the Muses and Graces had not, so to speak, nursed in their cradles, and who could not boast of great ancestors and famous names. Peter Cunaeus <note>A 17th-century Dutch scholar known for his work on the Hebrew Republic.</note> inclines toward this opinion, whose very words I shall produce: <margin>Hebrew G.)</margin> *When you have surveyed everything with reason and spirit (he writes, concerning the Hebrew Republic), this one thing made the Egyptians hostile to shepherds from every age: that sedentary men and craftsmen could not bear their vigorous strength and sharp spirits. Nor, by Hercules, do I agree with those who fetch the cause of public hatred <margin>from superstition, as if that nation could not bear the Hebrew men as shepherds of herds and flocks because one part feared to slaughter sheep, another goats, and another other quadrupeds, in which something divine was believed to reside.</margin>* To us, it becomes clearer that the cause of this hatred and aversion was primarily the wondrous superstition of the Egyptians, for whom cattle were either in the place of Deities or held the symbolism of a Deity; so much so that they abstained from certain animals, if not as Gods, certainly as things that were sacred to the Gods. It is no wonder if the Egyptian commoners proceeded to such madness that they worshiped the symbols as the deity itself. If the wiser ones felt and understood otherwise, they still worshiped that which, if the cattle were handled irreverently against the prescription of their custom, would seem to be done not without a ritual crime. Hence they use the word "abomination" or <term>bdelugma</term> <note>Greek for "abomination" or "loathsome thing."</note>—a vehemently emphatic voice—<margin>ch. 8 v. 26.</margin> which is also read in Exodus concerning the same matter; this term is used everywhere in the sacred texts specifically regarding idolatry,

<column-break/>

<margin>The abominable theolatry of the Egyptians.</margin>
and at the same time, it proves the extreme and brutal superstition of that name, which attributed divinity and hence divine worship to those things which God had granted to man for food, never for worship. However, this which seemed abominable to them—whether the one bringing it for food was an abomination, or the things to be abominated—did not even fall to the Israelites for kitchen use. This was surely the cause from which the loathing of <note>original: "רעות צאן"</note> *shepherding flocks* arose, which the Old Translator <note>Referring to the Vulgate or an early Latin version.</note> and others of the ancients understood not very accurately as being only about sheep. For thus Gregory the Great says on Job ch. 12:4: *The Egyptians disdain to eat sheep, but what they abominate, the Israelite offers to God.* He mentions at least sheep, relying on the old Latin interpretation; but that Hebrew phrase *shepherding flocks* is broader than can be attributed solely to sheep; for it is not said of one animal, but of everything that acts under the command of man and feeds on pasture for the food of man. They shrank away mostly from the common pastoral life; for not every shepherd was an "abomination" to them; this is manifest from ch. 47 v. 6, where Pharaoh says to Joseph: *If you know there are industrious men among them, appoint them* <note>original: "שרי מקנה"</note> *i.e., masters of my livestock*, from which it is clear that it was not illicit for them to care for flocks or pastures for wool and milk, for pleasure, or for the manuring of fields. But they bore it most grievously when people ate, without distinction, oxen or other animals consecrated in their custom, or sacrificed them. The Egyptians, *having become the most superstitious of all*, had receded so far from religion that they did not even abstain from the worship of brute animals, and hence they prohibited their sacred slaughter or domestic consumption. As far as sacrifice is concerned, this is evident from Exodus ch. 8:26, where Onkelos <note>The author of the famous Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Torah.</note> paraphrases: *It is not fitting to do so, because we would take the animal that the Egyptians worship to sacrifice before our God. Behold, if we sacrifice the livestock of the Egyptians, which they worship, before their eyes, will they not command us to be stoned?* Behold, says Moses, *we are about to sacrifice, and will they not stone us?* Which formula of speaking through a negative interrogation implies nothing other than this: *They will certainly stone us.* The Latin and Greek translators best captured this explanation in their versions, rendering it: *They will overwhelm us with stones.* <note>original: "λιθοβοληθήσεται"</note> It is represented by a negation, as you see, and this itself must be held as a kind of madness. Whatever the case, the superstitious and absurd worshipers used to <term>theoplasize</term> <note>To make into a god.</note> certain animals, which Diodorus Siculus calls *consecrated animals* or *honored things* <margin>Library book 1, p. 57, 63.</margin> p. 54. Artapanus, in his book on the Jews (from whom Eusebius noted in *Preparation for the Gospel* 9.27), says the King of Egypt pursued the fleeing Jews with a huge army, and had with him for a more successful expedition "consecrated animals," as Francis Viger translates it. Those sacred animals, as error is prolific, were various and monstrous, which they perhaps led out with them in the expedition for the sake of piety and religion; just as the Jews carried the Ark of the Covenant. Thus it must be established that this wicked worship anticipated the times of the Pharaonic drowning in the Red Sea. For the opinion of Vincentius Omnibonus in his notes on Lucan, who thinks the beginnings of idolatry in the worship of these animals fell immediately afterward, is foul. For he says:

# From Genesis XLVI. v. 34.

<margin>
The abominable idolatry <note>original: *ειδωλατρεια*</note> of the Egyptians.
</margin>
He says: When Pharaoh pursued Moses and the people of God with a great army and reached the Red Sea, the divine power immediately caused the sea to give way for the fleeing Hebrews. When Pharaoh and his men entered the sea, which had been raised up on both sides, it returned all at once and overwhelmed them all. However, those who were not forced to set out, being hindered by some necessity—some while feeding horses, others while tending swine, some while cultivating their gardens—worshipped at home as Gods those same animals and things with which they had been detained. Isocrates, in his praise of *Busiris* (p. 537), gives a clever reason for these superstitions, and John Rainolds, in his *Lectures* (vol. 2, p. 1320), shows from Plutarch and Diodorus that there was great disagreement among the ancients regarding the reasons that moved them to bestow divine honors upon animals. After those first true notions of God had been erased by evil customs and institutions, divine matters proceeded to such a point that even living creatures were brought into worship well before that most famous slaughter of Pharaoh; so much so, that the principles of that idolatry consisted in the veneration of certain animals. For that reason, that nation, out of a singular superstition <note>original: *δεισιδαιμονιᾳ*</note>, most religiously abstained from eating or slaughtering certain animals which it had selected for worship; and thus it detested or abominated the Hebrew men. For "every shepherd is an abomination" <note>original: *βδελυγμα γαρ πας ποιμην*</note> to that most superstitious nation, which worshipped certain kinds of quadrupeds and birds as if they were images of the Gods, pregnant with significance. Thus it is entirely likely that they recoiled from the Jews, who ate oxen or other animals indiscriminately, or had it in their custom to offer them as a burnt offering, or to sacrifice them in any other way. They bore this promiscuous slaughter of brutes most bitterly in these newcomers, who were so different in language and sacred rites, and who prostituted the secrets of religion (as it seemed to them). And so, with the question turned into a simple affirmation, Pharaoh responds in verse 28. Considering these things, I would hardly hesitate to affirm that the practice of sacrificing was not permitted to Israel while they stayed in Egypt. Although Joseph used what authority and favor he had to obtain a rich land and pasture, he perhaps did not obtain the free power of sacrificing. This may be further strengthened by the fact that, at the Lord's command, Moses came to Pharaoh with this mandate: "Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me." This embassy so exasperated Pharaoh, who was rabid with superstition, that he gave no place for sacrificing either in his own land or elsewhere. Unless this superstition had settled in his mind, he would never have composed his soul to such anger. The Egyptians were exceedingly diligent in enriching their superstition, and they consecrated certain kinds of animals for worship, which they spared for that reason; hence Rabbi Solomon Jarchi notes the cause of the hatred: that cattle were Gods to them. Moreover, it was not permitted to attack the Gods, or what was consecrated to the Gods, with impunity, as we shall soon hear. Therefore, God also commanded His worshippers to sacrifice what were worshipped as deities by the Egyptians—namely the calf, the goat, and others—lest they should think them Gods. Thus, it was a precaution to turn them away from idolatry, as Theodoret excellently conjectures in *Question 1 on Leviticus* (p. 105); and Nicholas of Lyra touches on the same matter with the same conjecture, teaching on Exodus chapter 12, verse 7, that the lamb was sacrificed among the Jews primarily for the

Indeed, these most learned interpreters think that the ceremonies of sacrifices, most common according to the prescription of the law in Exodus 29:38-39, were ordained by God for the Jews so that idolatry and the "worship of beasts" <note>original: *Θειολατρεια*</note> might be torn from the minds of the Israelites. But Rabbi Moses Maimonides understood it in the same way in *The Guide for the Perplexed* (part 3, ch. 46), which you may consult. That learned man Aben Ezra, commenting on our passage, affirms that the Egyptians in those times neither ate meat nor sacrificed. His words are: <note>Hebrew: "A sign that in those days the Egyptians did not eat meat, nor would a man allow anyone to sacrifice sheep."</note> Macrobius related this many centuries later in *Saturnalia* (Book 1, ch. 7), saying: *It was never lawful for the Egyptians to appease the Gods with cattle or blood, but with prayers and incense alone.* I know there are among the Pagan writers those who hand down the contrary, but if we consult our sacred texts, we read that a different practice obtained at that time. We are sometimes forced to withdraw faith and authority from the Greek writers, who, when they write about foreign nations, are sometimes prone to stumble; there they find so few who agree with them that most people think their traditions should be followed. Just as the whole life of the Israelites was pastoral, so they sustained the same from the slaughter of cattle, which they ate indiscriminately. The Egyptians, on the contrary—as many as wished to excel others in superstitious worship or the praise of self-restraint—abstained entirely from the eating of meat, or kept certain parts of them untouched and holy. Sextus Empiricus <note>original: *Sextus Pyrrhonius*</note> in *Outlines of Pyrrhonism* (Book 3): *Now indeed, even among the Egyptians who were considered wise, some think it profane to eat the head of an animal, others the shoulder-blade, others the foot, others something else. But none of those who are initiated into the rites of Casian Jupiter at Pelusium ever eat onions.* The people of Coptos were accustomed to eat the goat <note>original: *εσθίειν*</note>, and to abstain from eating the female, but not the male. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The abominable animal-worship <note>original: θηριολατρεία (theriolatreia)</note> of the Egyptians.</margin>
...separately for Joseph, and separately for his brothers. <insert>Also for the Egyptians, who ate at the same time, but separately. For it is unlawful for Egyptians to eat with Hebrews, and they consider a banquet of this kind profane.</insert> Onkelos <note>A famous 2nd-century convert and author of a standard Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note> adds the reason there: because the Hebrews eat the cattle which the Egyptians worship. Joseph thought it would go far more happily for his people if they practiced animal husbandry separately in the land of Goshen, so that they might live there quietly; and, what is the heart of the matter, he judged it would be more conducive to preserving the purity of their religion if, gathered into one place apart from the Egyptians, they could practice their own religion freely and sincerely. For the stain of superstition is easily spread, and those who are mingled with idolaters are often moved and swayed in their manner of worship. Therefore, those words: **A shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians**, and: **It is unlawful to eat bread with the Hebrews**, explain the idolatry of the people of Mizraim <note>The Hebrew name for Egypt.</note>, who held the Hebrews as abominable for this reason—in the words of Mercerus <note>Jean Mercier, a 16th-century French Hebraist.</note>—*because they often slaughtered cattle which the Egyptians held as Gods; since they did not eat meat then, whoever slaughtered it was hateful to them, such as the Hebrews, who often sacrificed those animals to the Lord, while the Egyptians worshiped them in the form of Apis and the figure of an ox. The Egyptians did have shepherds, but that class of men was weak and most abject among them, because the Egyptians were exceedingly haughty and arrogant. Therefore they easily despised shepherds, whether of their own nation or a foreign one, both because of their occupation and because of the superstition by which they held cattle among the Gods.* He says it was due to pride. <margin>at this place, p. 708.</margin> Luther, Scaliger, and Cunaeus <note>Prominent Reformation-era scholars and theologians.</note> agree with this; nor do we object, provided the note of superstition is added, by which they used to spare certain kinds of animals. For the Gentiles everywhere were held bound by this error: that they would abstain, moved by religion, from those things upon which they bestowed the character of divinity and worship <note>original: θρησκείας (threskeias)</note>, and which they consecrated to their Gods. No nation has been found under the sun that has been so monstrously insane as the Egyptian race, and which has more fascinated and, as it were, provoked neighboring peoples with the heat and frenzy of superstition—peoples who mostly took their idolatrous rites from them. Truly, they were, beyond other nations, *truly abominable in their error, and more abominable in the worthlessness of the things they worshipped and venerated.* Yet they did not shrink from regarding the Jews—whom they had received as strangers and worshippers of the one Deity—as an abomination <note>original: ὡς βδέλγμα (hos bdelgma)</note>, and abstaining from their company. Procopius says on Isaiah, p. 123: *In Egypt every kind of irrational animal is deified.* Lucanus <margin>ibid. book 10, v. 159</margin> says: *The Egyptians established many birds and wild beasts as Gods.* Strabo specifically testifies to this in Book XVII: *Some animals all Egyptians honor in common, such as three among the land animals: the ox, the dog, and the cat. Among the birds, two: the hawk and the ibis. Among the aquatic creatures, two: the lepidotus fish and the oxyrhynchus.* But there were also other irrational animals <note>original: ζῶα ἄλογα (zoa aloga)</note> which were in their worship, and from which they abstained as if from sacred things. We shall give examples. The *worship of the Asp* flourished among them; and <margin>Tusculan Disputations</margin> from this proceeded that vanity mentioned by Marcus Tullius [Cicero], that they would undergo any execution sooner than violate an asp or an ibis. Regarding the worship of the cat, Nectanebo, King of Egypt, said to Aesop, who had ordered an animal to be beaten: *Did you not know, Aesop, that the cat is worshipped as a god among us? Why then have you done this?*—found in Planudes' *Life of Aesop*, page 86. The cat was being beaten, and the King bore the insult of the blows with an indignant mind. Among the garden plants

<column-break/>

regarded as divine <note>original: ἐνθεαζομένα (entheazomena)</note>, the Onion held the primacy, which the people of Pelusium felt should not be eaten; concerning this, according to the Satirist [Juvenal]:
<margin>The abominable animal-worship of the Egyptians.</margin>
> *O holy nations, for whom these divinities*
> *grow in the gardens.*

I would add more concerning the worship of the crocodile, the scarab, and other small animals deified by the Egyptians <note>original: παρ᾽ Αἰγυπτίων θεοποιουμένοις</note>, if I did not fear to cause loathing in the reader; wherefore I say with Lucian <margin>In the Council of the Gods.</margin>: *I am ashamed to mention ibises and apes and goats, and other things far more ridiculous, which I know not how were thrust out of Egypt into heaven.* But I also do not know how that crafty superstition passed from Egypt into the world, for the Greeks, who were later the providers of religion to the Latins, brought back from the land of Egypt not so much the names of the Gods as their temples, altars, images, and sacred rites, as Herodotus testifies in *Euterpe*. The Athenians are said to have been colonists of the Egyptians, led from the city of Sais under the leadership of Cecrops, who is said to have been the first to bring in Greek letters. Nazianzen is a witness in his *Monody on Basil*. He was the first of all to establish an altar to Isis, set up images, and immolate victims, as Justin (Book 2) and Eusebius (in the Preface to the *Chronicle*) believe. Yet there were those among the Greeks who laughed at this insanity of the Egyptians, just as the Jews (except for the single case of the pig) could have reproached them, as the Comic Poet Anaxandrides of Rhodes does, as found in Athenaeus <margin>Book 7</margin>:
> You worship the ox, but I sacrifice it to the gods (to God).
> You consider the eel a very great deity,
> but we consider it the greatest of delicacies.
> You do not eat pork, but I enjoy it
> very much. You venerate the dog, but I beat it.

The same superstition held other nations as well. *Fire* was worshipped by the Persians; hence they judged it a crime to cremate human bodies; *for it is a divine and just thing to assign the corpse of a man [to the earth]*, as Herodotus says in his 3rd Muse. We have an example of this in Euphrates the Persian in Dioscorides (3rd Anthology, 13, p. 490), who forbids his body to be cremated, lest the fire be violated:
> Do not defile the fire
> for us, which is more bitter than a harsh death.

The greatest of the deified things <note>original: Τῶν θεοποιουμένων (Ton theopoioumenon)</note> was the SUN. Hence Datis, a fleet commander under Xerxes, spared the island of Delos, dedicated to the Sun, a fact which Cicero recounted from Herodotus in the *First Action against Verres*. The Syrians abstained from eating fish out of reverence for the deity Derceto, according to Hyginus in *Poetic Astronomy* (fable 196), because Derceto—who is also Atargatis—was worshipped in Syria as half-woman and half-fish, *whom they honor because of their piety and by abstaining from fish*, as Phurnutus says *Concerning the Gods*. *Purity consists in part of abstaining from fish*, says Plutarch <margin>Thus in 8th Symposiacs, question 8.</margin>. Xenophon says in the first book of the *Anabasis*: *He marches to the river Chalus, which is a plethrum in width, full of large and tame fish, which the Syrians considered gods, and they did not allow them to be harmed, nor the doves.* We find that doves were left untouched by ancestral superstition, a fact so widespread that among the Latins, Tibullus (Book 1, Elegy 7) recorded:
> *Why should I tell how the white dove, sacred to the Palestinian Syrian,*
> *flies untouched through the crowded cities.*

It seems to be from this also that Ethnic [Pagan] writers calumniously write of the Jews, that they [worship] a swinish <margin>Petronius, in the Satyricon.</margin> [deity]...

# From Genesis 46:34 and Genesis 49:10

<margin>
The abominable animal-worship of the Egyptians.
<note>original: "θειο-λατρεία" (theiolatreia) - divine worship/animal deification.</note>
</margin>

...to worship a deity, because it was known among the nations that the Jews abstained from swine's flesh. Hence, judging others by their own nature, they invented such stories as they had seen prevail among the Egyptians, who would not eat those animals which they venerated; and thus they detested and abominated the Hebrew men—who were shepherds of flocks and herds and indiscriminate slaughterers—as profane and impure. For it was an abomination <note>original: "βδέλυγμα" (bdelygma) - a foul thing or detestable object.</note> to all the Egyptians, that nation which cherished every genus of animal and bird as if they were images of the Gods. Consequently, they recoiled from commerce with the Jews, who ate oxen and other living creatures indiscriminately, and did not fear to sacrifice cattle if they were allowed to follow their ancient and received custom. For it seems they were altogether forbidden, especially under the tyranny of Pharaoh, to administer sacrifices; and although it might be conceded that it was permitted under Joseph (which, however, I believe can be confirmed by no testimony of Holy Scripture), I would not easily concede that it was permitted under the Pharaoh who *knew not Joseph*, and who was a most bitter enemy to the Hebrew race no less than to their solemnities and sacred rites. Nor did that supreme rancor of mind depart, although he had been warned by many miracles from heaven

<margin>
Artemidorus, Book 1, Chapter 9.
</margin>

<margin>
Exodus 1:8.
Acts 7:4.
</margin>

to *let the people go, that they might sacrifice*; for he could not be induced, even by a hundred or more miraculous acts, to send away the nation that was famous for its pious sacrifices and ceremonies from of old, before it had descended into Egypt. It happened not without the singular

<margin>
Exodus 8:2; 9:2, 13; 10:27.
</margin>

providence of God that Moses *was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians*, with a mind immune to all idolatry; for those words are not to be understood as referring to the "vain talk" <note>original: "matæologia" - empty or foolish discourse.</note> of that most profane nation, but to the letters of the Egyptians and to those disciplines which are liberal and do not conflict with true piety and religious worship. For when that school, which Joseph had founded in that land many years before, had fallen into disuse, God raised up Moses there, instructed in letters, so that he might oppose their superstitions using their own books. Glycas taught this best in the first book of his *Annals*; and in this matter, it is especially notable what the Gentile writer Strabo recorded concerning Moses: that he taught that the Egyptians did not act rightly by "likening the divine to wild beasts and cattle." <note>original: "θηρίοις εἰκάζοντας καὶ βοσκήμασι τὸ θεῖον"</note> Moreover, Moses flourished during that time of the Egyptian captivity, distinguished in age as well as in that piety by which he remained most observant of his ancestral law; so that the most miserable condition of religion and the face of the Church as it then was did not hinder him, as can be clearly read in the History which he himself wrote. Moses consoled himself and his people with the hope of better times, which did not frustrate him or them for long, Pharaoh being at last extinguished in a horrendous manner in the Red Sea. So that then, finally, for Moses and all the pious who had been more than enough oppressed in Egypt, there was free exercise of sacrificing and praying—more out of weariness for that deformed and foul religion than offended by the long journey in the desert. Then the Holy One of Zebeoth truly sanctified His sanctuary, taking away the reproach of Egypt, and the Giver of all goodness and mercy largely granted "halcyon days" <note>A period of peace and calm.</note> to His Church, which had suffered a certain interruption in Egypt.

> The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a Leader from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.

**M**agnificent and most illustrious is the prophecy of the Sceptre by the holiness of the famous Patriarch JACOB regarding Judah. When near death, having called his son Judah to him, he imparted his final blessing and, from a Prophetic Spirit, indicated future events; and indeed primarily how, from his line and lineage, the Anointed of the Lord, the Lord MESSIAH, was to arise in the fullness of time: *The Sceptre shall not be taken away*, he says, *from Judah*, etc. When he brought these things forth, how his most holy breast burned! Like a celestial Eagle carried on the wings of faith into the Sanctuary of God, he discourses—briefly indeed, but very clearly—under an admirable compendium of words concerning the times of the future Messiah, His chief benefits, and His assumption of Human nature. This promise, given to himself, his Father, and his Grandfather concerning the blessed seed, he hands over to the son Judah alone, saying: *The Sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah*.

<margin>
B. Gerhard, Commentary on this place, p. 838.
</margin>

Various things are strongly signified in the Sacred Books <note>original: "Pandectis" - a reference to the whole body of scripture.</note>; compare them. Properly, it signifies a rod or staff, which is the proper meaning and acceptance of the word in this place; thus by this very word is denoted the royal sceptre, or the princedom and power of governing, taken away from Jacob's firstborn son Reuben and conferred upon Judah, the fourth-born. Since Jacob, in his "swan song"—which is as it were a testament by which he predicted the fates of his twelve sons and their posterity—prophesies in a summary way <note>original: "κατ' ἐπιτομὴν"</note> and quite majestically concerning the royal power of Judah and its end. For this purpose, he uses this symbolic name *Shebet* <note>Hebrew: שבט</note> to designate the majesty and royal power proper to the tribe of Judah. The Jews indeed seek subterfuges when they explain *Shebet* not as a sceptre, but as a rod (which they call a rod of chastisement) or as a tribe. By the one reasoning, they do violence to the text; by the other, they achieve nothing, even though they have Fathers of great name agreeing with them. If the discourse is not about the sceptre of dominion, how, I ask, does that fit which is immediately added concerning the Lawgiver? And how does this pertain specially to the posterity of Judah if the *Shebet* denotes chastisement or striking (which is done with a rod and staff), since the rest of the descendants of the Patriarchs were also subject to similar, even greater, chastisements? Not to omit that if this were the case, there would be continuous tribulation for the Jewish people until the coming of the Messiah, which is against the open history of the tranquil state under David, Solomon, and several other Kings. If the word *Shebet* denotes "tribe" to you, you will still be stuck, since it nonetheless follows from this that the tribe of Judah was to remain distinct from the other tribes until the coming of the Messiah; but this distinction expired long ago, whatever they may prattle and dream even to this day about two families arisen from the house of David, namely the sons of David and the sons of Abravanel...
