# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
### Page 140

<margin>The Scepter of Judah.</margin>
...the devastation of Jerusalem brought into these western regions. See *Michael Havemann’s Way-Lamp, p. 143.* With these things having been premised, our meaning of the word *Shevet* <note>original: שׁבט; the Hebrew word for scepter or staff</note> stands on its firmest footing: namely, that it is understood as *royal power*, signified by the *Scepter* through metonymy <note>a figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it</note>, which is not to be entirely taken away from this tribe until the Messiah comes. This interpretation *partly* agrees with the context itself and the goal of the prophecy, while the Patriarch Jacob, predicting nothing but happy and prosperous things for his son Judah, addresses him with such an emphatic exclamation: *Judah, you are he, your brothers shall praise you*, with which compare the Mosaic prophecy concerning the victory and preeminence of Judah in *Deuteronomy 33:7*; *partly* with the outcome, which is the best interpreter of prophecies; and *partly* with the Chaldean Paraphrasts. For thus Onkelos <note>author of a famous Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> explains our text: *There shall not fail,* he says, *one exercising dominion.* So says Jonathan: *Kings and a Prince shall not cease.* So says the Jerusalem Targum: *Kings shall not cease.* So the Talmud: *The Scepter shall not be taken away from Judah: these are the Princes of the exiles in Babylonia, who govern Israel with a scepter; Nor the lawgiver from between his feet: these are the descendants of Hillel, who teach the law.* To these, on account of the blinded Jews, we add from an abundance of evidence the glosses of the Rabbis. *Rashi: The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah: from David and onwards; however, the princes of the exile in Babylonia are understood, etc.* The same author in the Talmudic Glosses on this passage says that *Shevet* is a *term for authority* <note>original: לשון שררה</note>, that is, it signifies leadership. *Rabba: The scepter shall not depart from Judah: i.e., the Sanhedrin <note>the supreme council of the Jews</note> which strikes and dominates; and the Lawgiver from his feet: these are the two scribes of the judges, who stand before them, one on the right, the other on the left.* Rabbi Abraham, Bechai, Rabbi Solomon Urbinas, Isaac Abravanel, and others among the more recent scholars feel the same. Hence also Rabbi Kimchi in his Lexicon under the root *sh-b-t* writes: *It is customary for Kings to carry a scepter in their hand.* Hence the Greek translators of the Septuagint use the word *archon* <note>ruler</note>, and elsewhere *skeptron* <note>scepter</note>, which fits perfectly. For just as *Shevet* is properly a rod, so is *skeptron*; first it denotes a rod or a staff, from the Greek *skeptien*, that is, to lean upon, <margin>Fragment 124.</margin> then a kingdom, see Drusius; whence Pindar joins the *monarchic scepter to the throne* in *Ode 4, p. 250.* Compare Euripides, *The Phoenician Women, lines 594, 604.* From this, the staff is the ancient form of the scepter, about which Pontanus writes in *3. Progymn. p. 88.* To this also belongs the epithet of the Poets, who call Kings <margin>Iliad, book 1, line 279.</margin> *skeptouchos*, or *scepter-bearers*. Just as Homer calls *Agamemnon* a *scepter-bearing king, to whom Zeus gave glory.* From the Greeks, the Latins and Germans received the idea that it is accepted for a royal scepter, if you look at modern Kings, whose scepters are made of gold and silver. For in ancient times they carried a wooden scepter, of which thing traces still exist in ancient writers. For Achilles' scepter was wooden, *Iliad, book 1, lines 234-237.* But *pierced with golden nails*, that is, distinguished by golden studs, *Iliad, book 1, line 246*, whom Virgil imitates in *Aeneid, book 12, lines 206 to 212.* So also among the insignia of the Consuls is listed the *ivory staff*, upon which an eagle sat, as Juvenal teaches in *Satire 10.* In the *Dialogues, p. 526*, Plato interprets the scepter attributed to Minos by Jove as *paideia*, that is, discipline and the laws by which he governed Crete. And just as the Patriarch...

<column-break/>

...joins the *Shevet* <note>scepter</note> with the *Mechokek* <note>lawgiver</note>, so also <margin>The Scepter of Judah.</margin> Homer elegantly observes the same, joining laws with the scepter, in clearly the same sense: <margin>Iliad, book 2, line 205.</margin>

-> Let there be one ruler <-

> One King, to whom the son of crooked-counseled Cronus gave
> Both the scepter and the laws, so that he might rule over them.

For laws are the foundation for preserving human society, without which no empire can subsist, and the scepter is nothing other than a *symbol of justice and dignity*, whence Achilles swears by the *scepter*, and such an oath was held to be great, and as if *divine*, and therefore it is even twice called a *great oath*:

---
<margin>Iliad, book 1, lines 233 & 239.</margin>
> But I will tell you, and I will swear a great oath upon it,
> — — — and this shall be a great oath to you.

From these things it is established that the *skeptron* was always a sign of the highest power, and the scepter-holder was nothing but the highest leader, than whom no one higher existed, according to: <margin>Iliad, book 14, line 93.</margin>

-> He would be a scepter-bearer, and the people would obey him. <-

Hence to King Ptolemy of Egypt, when he had dared to rebuke a certain musician named Stratonicus, as if he had not sung correctly according to the laws of his art, the musician replied: *Lord King, a Scepter is one thing, a plectrum <note>a pick for a stringed instrument</note> is another*, as Athenaeus reports in *book 8.* *He said, O King, the scepter is different from the plectrum.* By the scepter he hinted at the government of the kingdom and the state; by the plectrum, the exercise of the musical instrument or the lyre, for he was a lyre-player. Nor did the Patriarch wish to hint at anything else in the following phrase, when he says *and a lawgiver from his feet* <note>original: וּמְחֹקֵק מִבֵּין רַגְלָיו</note>, where with Blessed Gerhard we first observe that the particle *lo* <note>not</note> is to be taken here in the negative sense "nor," because the negative particle *lo* in the Hebrew manner is to be repeated from the preceding member, just as the verb *yasur* (shall depart) is. Otherwise, *Mechokek* is derived from the root *chakak*: he established, commanded, inscribed, or engraved. Therefore, by this word is signified a Ruler or Prince, who gives to the people *chukim* (statutes and decrees), whose role it is to establish laws and prescribe to the people what must be done, etc. There are indeed not a few among the Rabbis who by *Mechokek* understand scribes sitting at the feet of princes, who in this matter follow the Targum of Onkelos and Jonathan. But the former exposition is more suitable to the prophecy, which even Rabbi Solomon and Rabbi David Kimchi prefer to the latter <margin>in his Lexicon</margin> under the root *ch-k-k*, where he says: *Mechokek in this place is one who dominates, and he is called so because he himself enacts laws in his land.* In which sense it is very often used in Holy Scripture; in *Judges 5:14* it is read: *From Machir descended the Mechokekim*, where the Targum expresses it thus: *From the house of Ephraim arose Joshua, who joined battle with the house of Amalek; after him arose King Saul.* With these the Septuagint agrees: *behold, a leader from his thighs.* From which it is clearer than the midday sun that the *Mechokekim* have the power of decreeing and judging, and such a power that is joined with command; and from this emerges the sense of such a prophecy: that there would always remain in the family of Judah some *dignity* or leadership, whether it be more ample, as in the time of the Kings, or diminished, as in the time of the Leaders and the Sanhedrin after the Babylonian captivity. Nor should it be thought that the Patriarch added *Mechokekim* to the royal scepter without cause, since without these, government is unstable; hence the Patriarch added laws and statutes as the supports of the republic and of all...

# From Genesis Chapter 49, verse 10.

<margin>The Scepter of Judah.</margin> He connects all forms of government [to this tribe]. Therefore, although the scepter often seemed entirely removed from the tribe of Judah, as in the Babylonian captivity and after it, there nevertheless always remained *Mechokekim* <note>Hebrew: "Lawgivers" or "Leaders"</note> among the Jews from the tribe of Judah. This is why even in the Babylonian captivity itself, they are proved to have had their own *Resh Galuta*, that is, a "Prince of the Exiles" from the tribe of Judah and from the very lineage of David; this is shown by the elevation of King Jehoiachin from prison and his preference over other kings (*Jeremiah 52:31-34*). Nor should it be overlooked that Daniel, born of the royal family, was appointed prefect over the entire Babylonian empire (*Daniel 2:48*). To touch on this briefly: although the kingdom was overturned by Nebuchadnezzar, the lawgiver remained not only in captivity (whence the *Jerusalem Targum* on *Song of Solomon 6:1* says: *The Sanhedrin migrated to Babylon, and God governed His people through it;* a point repeated by Rabbi Solomon <margin>Commentary on this place.</margin>) but also after that Captivity. Indeed, the Sanhedrin, or that venerable College of Senators, represented the *Mechokekim* predicted here by the Patriarch. To this Sanhedrin, a royal throne is attributed in *Psalm 122:5*, and in *2 Chronicles 19:8*, its President is called *Nagid* <note>Leader/Prince</note> and commonly by the Jews *Nasi* <note>Prince/Patriarch</note>. For even after the Babylonian captivity, there remained in Judea a *triple order of Senators*, established after the return from captivity from the descendants of David. The *first court* was *Triumviral* <note>Three-man</note>, presided over by three primary Judges, called the *Lesser Sanhedrin*. The second consisted of twenty-three Judges and was called the *Small Sanhedrin*. The third was the *Supreme Senate*, consisting of 72 Elders, called the *Sanhedrin or Great Sanhedrin*, whose president or leader was always elected from the family of David, as Jewish chronology testifies. This entire Sanhedrin, which held supreme power and authority, was—according to the calculation of some—totally <margin>Book 14, Jewish Antiquities, ch. 18.</margin> subverted and utterly extinguished by Herod in the thirtieth year of his reign, *the very year in which Christ was born*. Compare Josephus, who places this crime in the thirty-sixth year of his reign, according to Michael Havemann in *Lamp of Jewish Darkness, p. 277*. How great the authority of the Great Sanhedrin was is clear from the fact that Herod himself, while still Prefect of Galilee and accused of tyranny, was forced to present himself before this Senate and barely escaped the danger of death. Whereupon, as Josephus reports in *Jewish Antiquities, Book 14, ch. 17*, Sameas delivered this speech regarding Herod in the full senate: *Men of the Sanhedrin and King, etc. But whoever comes before this Sanhedrin to be judged presents himself humble, in the appearance of one who is afraid and seeking mercy from us, with his hair let down and dressed in black clothing.* In this speech, it is worth noting, first, that he places the Senators before the king (who was then Hyrcanus). **Secondly**, that he describes the dress and gesture of the accused, which ought to be composed for humility and mercy. **Then**, for that reason, he severely rebukes the audacity of Herod, who had come armed, clothed in purple, and with his hair elegantly arranged and composed. These things being thus well compared with one another, it becomes clear that the *Shevet* <note>Scepter/Staff</note> and *Mechokek* <note>Lawgiver</note> were not removed from Judah until Shiloh came, to whom all nations shall cling. However, they labor much over the interpretation of these words—

<column-break/>

<margin>The Scepter of Judah.</margin> —especially the Jews, who have applied whatever art and wit they possess to overturning this testimony concerning the Messiah. Nor was there any word in this prophecy of Jacob so fortunate that they did not lay violent hands upon it. They separate the little word *Ad* <note>Until</note> from the following particle *Ki* <note>That/When</note> and join it with the preceding words in this sense: "The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor a lawgiver from his feet forever, *when* Shiloh comes," as if only in the time of the Messiah an eternal kingdom is to be expected by the Jews in this life; for so Rabbi Bachai (folio 73) pretends to have learned from his teacher, Rabbi Solomon. But the particle *Ad* signifies "eternity" only when it is placed absolutely, outside of a construction. But here it is not placed absolutely, but is joined with *Ki*; nor, as should be well noted, is it ever found in an absolute sense before the particle *Ki*. Rather, both together signify *until* or *up to the time that* (*Genesis 26:13, 41:46*). Nor does the accent *Jethib* placed under the word *Ad* help them, though they say it indicates a reference to the preceding words. For this accent cannot look back to the preceding words because the previous word, *Raglav* <note>"his feet"</note>, already has its own great accent, the *Atnach*, which according to Buxtorf <margin>in his Grammar, page 552.</margin> is the distinction of a completed sentence. Furthermore, *Jethib* does not constitute a major pause like the preceding *Atnach*, but is only a minor accent, a "sub-distinguishing comma" or a minor incision. Therefore, when the Jews allege the *Jethib* accent, they betray their own notable ignorance in grammatical matters, since the *Jethib* accent is not a pausing one, whereas the *Atnach* is the principal pause, more powerful than all accents except the *Silluck* (*Exodus 32:35*). Since, therefore, the *Atnach* (the pause constituting the middle of a verse and dividing the preceding from the following) is placed immediately before the word *Ad*, how could this particle, cut off by the *Atnach*, be joined to the preceding words? It remains, therefore, that *Ad* with the *Jethib* accent, following the *Atnach* as a "royal" accent, pertains not to the preceding but to the following member, and signifies *until*. Compare parallel passages (*Exodus 23:9, 32:33, Judges 4:44, 1 Samuel 22:3, Ruth 1:13*). Thus falls the first false interpretation of the Jews; having relegated that to hell, they seek another escape in the word *Shiloh*, which to them signifies "to be devastated or overturned." This is the corruption of Rabbi Bachai, Rabbi Joseph, and Rabbi Abraham: "until Shiloh comes," that is, until the tabernacle in Shiloh is destroyed. But this exception contradicts the finding of the Patriarch, as well as the scope and context, and also the **Chaldean Paraphrase** <note>The Targum</note>; for all read it thus: *Until the Messiah comes.* It also contradicts the word itself, which is nowhere found in that meaning except where it deals with the setting of the sun. For the Patriarch here promises some distinguished benefit to the tribe of Judah. From the preceding verses, it is clear that Jacob had complained of the malice of his sons Reuben, Simeon, and Levi; as sad as it was for the pious old man not to be able to bless them and their posterity, it was just as pleasing and acceptable to him to enter into a sweeter conversation with his son Judah. Therefore, with a singular exclamation and a joyful exultation of voice and soul, he breaks out into these words: *Judah, you are—namely, to me—a pleasing son; you shall be to me*

<sig>Oo</sig>
<meta>catchword: mihi (to me)</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

to me the firstborn, the prince, the father and the head;
<margin>The Scepter of Judah.</margin> from you the Messiah shall go forth, from you the kingdom and the law-giving majesty shall not depart, until the longed-for and desired **Shiloh** comes. This is that voice which has fixed so many crosses for the Rabbis <note>A metaphor for causing great intellectual distress or difficulty</note>; hence they have joined all their forces in corrupting it. For this reason, to some this Jacobite **Shiloh** is either *Moses* or *Saul*; to others *David* or *Jeroboam*; to these *Nebuchadnezzar* or *Ahijah the Shilonite*; to others *Herod* or *Vespasian*. But we shall prove with little difficulty that the name **Shiloh** can be applied to none of these—indeed, to no man—except Christ, the Messiah of the world. For if we weigh the etymology of the word, a *fourfold variety* of meaning occurs. For some derive it from *shalah* <note>original: שלח</note>, *he sent*, whom the Vulgate interpreter follows, rendering these words as *he who is to be sent*; others from *she* <note>original: ש</note>, *who*, and *lo* <note>original: לו</note>, *to him* or *for himself*, so that this elliptical speech emerges: *he who is his, namely, his son*, or *he who is for himself, namely, is sufficient for himself*. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> seems to allude to this, rendering it *the things laid up for him*, until they come, that is, until those things which are stored up for him are fulfilled; or as others of the ancient Greeks read, *until he comes for whom it is laid up*, namely the Scepter or the kingdom; or until he comes for whom it is laid up, so that he is *desired, chosen*, and to be valued at no price; for such are usually *laid up things* <note>original: ἀποκείμεנה</note>, heirlooms and precious items. Some translate it as **Hero** <term>Held: German for "Hero" or "Champion"</term> from *shalah* <note>original: שלה</note>, which is the same as being *peaceful, happy, fortunate*, and *acting prosperously*. Finally, some derive it from *shilyah* <note>original: שליה</note>, which denotes the *afterbirth* and by synecdoche <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note> the offspring, which opinion is also among the primary ones. However this word may be explained in this place, it always designates our Messiah; for if it signifies *to be sent*, Christ is truly he who was to be sent; if it is he for whom it is *deposited*, certainly the Messiah is thus the best treasure of all; if it denotes the *fortunate one*, who had more saving successes than Christ? For all things turned out prosperously for him against the Devil, hell, death, and the world. Finally, in the last interpretation, if "offspring" is taken for his son, who shall be born *from the afterbirth of a woman* <note>original: משיח אשה</note>, after the manner of all who are born, to whom can it be more deservedly attributed than to Christ? Who, because of the *new mystery of conception and generation*, is truly the *son of the womb and the afterbirth*, from the Virgin Mary *alone*, without male seed, conceived by the power of the Most High.
<margin>Matthew 1:20.</margin> * This etymology was wonderfully pleasing to Blessed Luther, who from it—as he was a man of great eloquence—wove a long sermon full of the greatest consolation. Since, therefore, this exposition leads us back to the first promise made to the First-Created in Paradise in Genesis 3:15, and places the whole mystery of the *incarnation* <note>original: ἐνσαרקώσεως</note> before our eyes, we gladly receive it with Blessed Luther. Although the reasoning of those who derive it from *shalah*, to be *happy*, does not displease us either, in favor of which is Luther's German version: *until the **Hero** comes* <note>original: biß daß der Held komme</note>. For this exposition supplies us with pious thoughts concerning the prosperous success of Christ's kingdom in destroying the power of Satan, death, sin, and hell, and concerning the merciful and powerful preservation and protection of the Church against all the insults and machinations of all enemies. Furthermore, the Chaldean Paraphrases, which are authentic to the Jews, explain this with us as referring to the Messiah. The Targum Onkelos says, *until the Messiah comes* <note>original: משיחא</note> and adds, *whose is the kingdom* <note>original: דליה היא מלכותא</note>. He took it for

<column-break/>

**Shiloh**, which to the Rabbis means *whose*, and understood "the kingdom." The Targum of Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum say, until the *King Messiah* <note>original: מלכא משיחא</note> comes; so also many of the ancient Rabbis: In *Bereshit Rabbah*, "until Shiloh comes," *this is the King Messiah* <note>original: זה מלך המשיח</note>. In *Echa Rabbathi*, a very ancient book, page 68, the name of the *Messiah* is said to be Shiloh. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> on this passage: *Shiloh* is the *Messiah*, whose is the kingdom. # From Genesis 49, verse 10.

<margin>The Scepter of Judah.</margin>
The terms *peoples* <note>Hebrew: *ammim*</note> and *nations* <note>Hebrew: *goyim*</note> are used; the rest are either specific or derived from elsewhere. First, the word *am* <note>people</note> signifies generally any congregation or assembly; hence it is used even for locusts in Joel 2:25 and for ants and rock-badgers in Proverbs 30:25-26. Although in Holy Scripture the second word, *goy* <note>nation</note>, also applies to the Jews, it is used more sparingly in that way. From this, a custom has developed where today the Jews use that name to call and distinguish all those who are not of the lineage of Jacob according to the flesh. The third word, *leummim* <note>peoples/tribes</note>, is traced back to the root *ummah*, which signifies "mother," and properly denotes a uterine people—those drawing their origin from the same mother. By this word, the Jews commonly refer to the "unbelieving" nations (as they themselves think) who do not hold to their own superstitions; hence the frequent mention in their books of the *ummot olam*, the "peoples of the world" or of "this age." From these points it is clear, according to the Rabbis themselves, that the word *ammim* <note>peoples</note> is the most general of all, and therefore in this passage it should be expanded to include any nations whatsoever, and not restricted solely to the Israelite people, as the Jews do out of their most bitter hatred toward Christians. With these premises, one can easily respond to the trifles of the Jews: for while Moses uses the plural number *ammim* (peoples), and the Israelites are not "peoples" but "one people," it is an evident sign that all nations are understood. # From Genesis Chapter 50, Verses 2 and 3.

<margin>
Egyptian
funeral
rites.
</margin>
We have learned that they took care to treat [bodies] with spices so that, in their monuments and coffins, they might be preserved whole and least subject to putrefaction for a long time. For the dead bodies were filled with aromatics, myrrh, cassia, salt, bitumen, and whatever other kinds of seasonings there were. Joseph, soberly following the custom of that region—a civil honor usually paid to great men—wished it to be granted also to his father Jacob, as a Prophet and an eminent man. For when he [Jacob] had been piously gathered to his people in the true recognition of the promised seed, the son ordered a public mourning out of a sense of piety, and commanded the lifeless body to be delivered to the embalmers <note>original: "pollinctoribus" — those who prepared bodies for funeral rites</note> so that they might season it with spices and anoint it with balsam; and he took care that it be carried, escorted by a great crowd of nobles and priests, to that place which the piously deceased had chosen for himself, so that in that very place where the promise of the coming deliverer had been issued, the body might await the restoration of life. Among the things of the Egyptian nation especially worth mentioning, the preservation of medicated and, if I may say so, embalmed bodies is usually recounted. Those who were in charge of this duty are called by Moses <term>רפאים</term>, *Rophæim*, that is, Physicians, from <term>רפא</term>, which is the participial noun of the verb <term>רפא</term>, *to medicate, to heal, to cure*. Now, they are called Physicians here because they were in charge of caring for and medicating the funerals. This was a singular office among that nation, and not unsuitable for Physicians, because they were not ignorant of the power and nature of spices, and they appropriately understood the dissection of the body. Just as the Egyptians were curious about all things, so they were especially so regarding the bodies of the dead; for they wanted the embalming to be administered by Physicians, as those who had knowledge of the method of both cutting and seasoning, and who had the necessary material for the preparation ready at hand. For if that province had been offered to the unaccustomed and unskilled, they would have seasoned it in such a way that the corpse would have rotted within a short space of time, with disgrace and ignominy, with the waste of precious material, and with loss to the heirs and blood relatives. For which reason Joseph, with the greatest foresight, took care that the seasoning be done by Physicians, lest the body, which had to be carried a long distance, should exhale a rotten and foul odor. 
<margin>Book 1, chapter 1, page 740.</margin>
Mercerus* <note>Jean Mercier, a 16th-century Hebrew scholar</note> wishes this duty to have been given to the Physicians for the sake of honor, because they knew the ratio of spices which were adapted to seasoning the body and protecting it from rot. And Musculus <note>Wolfgang Musculus, a Reformer and commentator</note> says: Those who are called Physicians here were properly called embalmers and undertakers <note>original: "pollinctores et Libitinarii"</note>, just as the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> also translated it. This much is certainly clear: there were among the Gentiles certain designated men who seasoned the corpses of the dead, and these are called *libitinarii* and *pollinctores*, which latter word some think is the same as "washers of the polluted." However, the Hebrew word which Moses uses in this place sounds like "Physicians." What <term>רפא</term> signifies is well enough known, and the Chaldean <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> uses the same interpretation, which has: <term>ית עבדוהי אסיא</term> <note>original Aramaic: "his servants the physicians"</note>. To the Chaldeans, <term>אסיא</term> is the same as <term>רפא</term>, hence <term>אסיא</term> means Physician. Understand "Physicians" as those who were in charge of caring for funerals so that they might be preserved from putrefaction. By what name they were called by the Egyptians is unknown. Although the name is unknown to us, having slipped away through the antiquity of time, the reason for the Hebrew word is not obscured, though it seems to Pererius <note>Benito Pereira, a Jesuit commentator</note> not to be 

<column-break/>

<margin>
Egyptian

</margin>
properly placed, since the office of a Physician is to make a *living* body healthy from sickness, or to protect a *healthy* one; *not, however, to deliver the seasonings or burials of dead bodies*. But truly, one must not measure ancient things by the present state of Physicians. At that time, they were perhaps among the servants; today they are not. The sad ministry of funeral Physicians was in servile obedience, whence Joseph is even said to have *commanded* <term>את עבדיו את רפאים</term> *his servants the Physicians*. If you were to give the name "display-servants" <note>original Greek: ἐπιδεικτικοὺς</note> today, you would be soundly beaten. But one must not cling to the name as if it were ill-omened. It was an honor to be a servant of Joseph, just as today it is to be called the servant of some Great Man. Nor are we moved by the authority of Diodorus Siculus, who noted in Book 1, page 57: <note>original Greek: "The Embalmers are deemed worthy of every honor and great care, associating with the Priests, and they make their entrances into the temple without hindrance, as being holy."</note> For <term>עבד</term>, *Servant*, always shares in some common or plebeian mark, the face of which is not to be judged from the first glance as if marked and branded with some stigma. It is often a name of dignity, such as when it is mentioned that <term>עבדי פרעה</term> <note>servants of Pharaoh</note> were companions present at the funeral of Jacob in verse 7, who were more honorable court ministers, like Nobles and Barons. They were formerly held in a servile condition by the Egyptians, and later by the Romans, among whom medicine began to be practiced late and to be held in some value. If I show this by a few examples, it will not be out of place.

For if we look at our Hebrew word <note>original: *Ebræam*</note>, it is a general term. The Egyptian *Taricheutae* <note>Embalmers or "curers" of meat/bodies</note> obtained the name of "Physicians," and among others it was used loosely, so much so that *we read in the law (Digest 1.1 on various and extraordinary cognitions) that nurses and all those who promised to provide health to any limb—such as those who professed to heal teeth or ears—were added to the number of physicians,* as were pharmacists, surgeons, and any cutters of the body. Clearly, among the Latins, the name *Physician* <note>original: *Medici*</note> was formerly extended to those who today are not placed on the official roll of doctors. Among the Egyptians, Herodotus asserts there were individual physicians for individual diseases, and no one could be a physician for all ailments. Their art and industry were occupied with specific parts of the body: while one treated eyes, another the head, another the feet, and another some other part. *Medicine* (he says in the said book, page 134) *is distributed so that each physician is for one disease and no more, and everything is full of physicians. For some are established as physicians of the eyes, others of the head, others of the teeth, others of the belly, and others of hidden diseases.* The physicians themselves rendered this name more ignoble after they began to profess a noble art, which resulted in the profession eventually becoming the property of slaves. For did it not lead to contempt that they applied enemas and unskillfully took upon themselves the roles of surgeons? Piso commanded a physician to cut the vein of Plator so that he might die. This is reproached against Piso by Cicero <margin>Speech against Piso, n. 83.</margin> *in these words: You did not even punish Plator in the manner of our ancestors, but you commanded that physician, whom you had brought out with you, to cut the man's veins.* By the name "Physician," he means a *Surgeon*; and by the same witness <margin>On the Orator, book 3.</margin>, the duties were indistinct even in the time of Hippocrates, where there were not some who treated eyes and others who treated ears. Hence, in the physician's kit, eye-salves, plasters, and iron tools are placed by Paulus <margin>Sentences, book 3, 9.</margin>; and for that reason, Diaulus is called by Martial sometimes a *surgeon* and sometimes a *Physician*, and that in the first book:

> Diaulus had been a surgeon, now he is a corpse-bearer.
> He began to be a clinicist in the only way he could.

And after a few lines, it follows:

> He who had been a Physician, now is a corpse-bearer, Diaulus.
> What the corpse-bearer does, the Physician had also done.

Regarding Commodus, Lampridius says: *He also imitated a Physician, so as to draw blood from men with deadly scalpels.* Suetonius says in Nero, chapter 37: *To those ordered to die, he gave no more than an hour's space. And lest any delay intervene, he applied Physicians, who would immediately "cure" those who hesitated.* For that was what he called *cutting the veins for the sake of death.* Regarding Vesticulus, the Physician is ready, the veins are cut, and while still vigorous he is carried into a bath and submerged in hot water. Gellius writes of a gladiator in *Attic Nights* 12.5: *who, when his wounds were being dried by Physicians, was accustomed to laugh.* The first physician in Rome, Archagathus, in the year 535 of the city, was called a *butcher* <note>original: *carnifex*</note> and a *wound-maker* because of the cruelty of his cutting and searing, as Pliny witnesses. <margin>Book 29, chapter 1.</margin> Regarding Iapyx, healing the wound of Aeneas, Virgil says: <margin>Aeneid, book 12, v. 342.</margin>

> Much with the medical hand and the powerful herbs of Phoebus

<column-break/>

<margin>Egyptian funerals.</margin>
> He trembles in vain; in vain with his right hand he
> Worries the arrow-head, and grips the iron with tenacious forceps.

I doubt whether such things should be said of Joseph's "Physicians," to whom the title *Rophe* <note>Hebrew: healer/physician</note> is attributed, since they were actually *pollinctores* <note>Roman officials who prepared the dead</note> who embalmed the bodies of the dead; indeed, as Menochius <margin>Commentary, page 74.</margin> prefers, they were "undertakers" who wrapped and buried the bodies. Hence, by the Seventy Translators <note>The Septuagint</note>, they are called *entaphiastai* <note>Greek: those who prepare a body for burial</note>, a word which denotes arranging a body for burial, and, to express the present matter more precisely, seasoning the body of the deceased with spices and placing the seasoned body in a tomb. Agostino Steuco, folio 145b, says: *It differs nothing from the Hebrew, "his servants the physicians." But the Seventy are far more diverse with "entaphiastais," which word, as I judge, signifies those who bury corpses.* If we look to the proper meaning, an *entaphiastes* is the same as an undertaker; just as *entaphiasai* means to perform funeral rites, to bury, or to place in tombs. The Glosses say: <margin>Ev- page 458.</margin> *taphistes*, a *pollinctor.* *entaphion*, the *goddess of funerals.* *entaphiastes*, an *undertaker*, *entaphiazo*, I perform a funeral. The Glosses of Philoxenus: *Pollingo* <note>I prepare for burial</note>, I shall place the dead, I weave a coffin, I prepare for burial, I embalm. Just as the *pollinctor* was the one among the Romans who anointed the body of the dead and prepared it for burial; so the *entaphiastes* was the one who performed the duty of anointing and burying bodies. Often synecdochic expressions occur <note>where a part represents the whole</note>, and related duties are not excluded. Thus, it is not so far-fetched that they are called *entaphiastai* here, who performed the service of disemboweling, seasoning, and burying bodies. In the same way, the word *thapto* <note>Greek: I bury</note> must be expanded where they used it for the embalming of Joseph in verse 26, to correspond to the Hebrew word *chanat* <note>to spice/embalm</note>, unless you prefer to say the Hebrew word was not fully known to them. What Drusius <margin>Difficult passages in Genesis, p. 156.</margin> brought up here regarding the Hellenistic language as "a certain medicine," I fear is an insipid seasoning. The Royal translator of the Greek Bible takes it as the word regularly sounds to the Greeks, for *to bury*, in which he was preceded by the Basel editor. But let us set aside the Hellenistic funeral. Joseph managed the funeral rites <note>original: *ta dei tas taphas*</note> excellently. Nothing was idle or neglected. First, removing all superstition that the Egyptians had, he orders those to be present who would treat the body with spices. The funeral servants are present, *preparing the corpse for burial with fitting Egyptian songs.* Diodorus Siculus said this well, <margin>Library, book 1, p. 57.</margin> *to care for the bodies*, noting this *care* for the deceased in these words: *Those who care for the bodies are craftsmen who have received this science by family tradition.* To the Romans, they are *pollinctores* who care for the dead, who attend to funerals, who prepare the spices and wash and anoint the body of the cold one. <margin>Virgil, Aeneid book 6, v. 219.</margin> The Old Translator uses it in *Ezekiel chapter 39, verse 15:* They shall go through the land, and when they see a man's bone, *they shall set up a sign beside it*, (a sign, a peg, a *marker*) until the *pollinctores* bury it in the valley of the multitude of Gog. The subject there is the ordinary caretakers of burial, who, lest the land remain defiled by corpses, searched with exquisite care for the bones of men so they might be hidden in graves. He calls them *kevarim* <note>Hebrew: buriers</note>, and understands them as "corpse-buriers"; for *kavar* means "he buried." Junius renders it as *vespillones* <note>corpse-bearers for the poor</note>. The Septuagint: *those who bury*. Martin Luther: *Grave-diggers*. Certain men were designated, who trans-

# On Genesis Chapter 50, verses 2 & 3

<margin>Egyptian funerals. *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 27, page 414.</margin>
...they passed through the land, so that they might commit the corpses to the earth (verse 14). There were men designated among the Egyptians to take care of funerals and—to speak with **Tertullian**—to sequester the bodies in mausoleums and monuments by means of a medicated embalming burial. It was their duty, indeed, to involve the bodies in linens once they were properly disemboweled, washed with wine, and filled with balsam and other spices, so that they might be preserved immune from decay for a long time. This follows the custom noted by **Herodotus**, who accurately describes the Egyptian *taricheuein* <note>original: ταριχεύειν — to preserve or mummify</note>. It is worth adding his words, as they agree well with the present Mosaic description, in *Euterpe*, page 135: <note>Herodotus, Histories, Book II (Euterpe)</note> "Having made an incision along the flank with a sharp Ethiopian stone, they take out all the intestines. Having cleaned the cavity and rinsed it with palm wine, they rinse it again with pounded incense. Then, having filled the belly with pure pounded myrrh, cassia, and other spices—except frankincense—they sew it back up." That operation is called *taricheia* by the Greeks, from *taricheuein*, which in this context is the same as seasoning the rest of the body after the parts have been disemboweled. For we see this applied by Herodotus to bodies preserved by aromatic seasoning. Likewise by **Lucian**,
<margin>*On Mourning*, page 794.</margin>
who, reviewing the various burial customs of nations, says that the Egyptians *mummify* <note>original: ταριχεύειν</note> while the Greeks burn <note>cremate</note>. Its common use in the salting of meat and fish is evident everywhere; but that kind of "pickling" no more resembles human mummification than a service-berry resembles a fig. It differs greatly, and in a broad sense includes the washing, soaking, stuffing, and anointing of corpses; just as *splanchneuein* <note>original: τὸ σπλαγχνεύειν</note> encompasses every rite by which the entrails are inspected, selected, placed on the altar, or set aside for food. There were "mummified bodies" <note>original: ταριχηρὰ σώματα</note> which were filled with opobalsam, myrrh, aloe, cassia, cinnamon, asphalt, and salt. And thus "the durability of mummification" <note>original: τὸ πολυαρκὲς τῆς ταριχείας</note> in Lucian’s *Menippus*, page 232, is to be understood. **Diodorus Siculus** specifically handed down the particulars: first, the funeral directors would approach and ask how the funeral rites were to be celebrated. "Then, having presented to the relatives of the deceased a written list of the expenses for each type of burial, they ask in what manner they wish the body to be treated." When all had been agreed upon, the body was received, properly placed, skillfully cut, and the aromatic materials were brought and thickly applied, so that they might preserve the body no less than provide a pleasant odor. Various ministers were present, and their duties were varied. One washed, another soaked. This one cut, that one stuffed, another wrapped. "Those appointed to the prescribed care received the dead," performing an *anatomy* <note>original: ἀνατομὴν — dissection</note> according to certain ceremonies and laws, which determined which parts were to be kept, which removed, which taken out, and which replaced. The *Taricheutes* <note>the embalmer</note> did not undertake the cutting of the corpse himself, but left it to the *Paraschistes* <note>the slitter/cutter</note> who professed that skill. Nor could the cutting begin unless the *Grammateus* <note>the scribe</note> (as he is called by Diodorus) had first circumscribed how much was to be cut away. The *Paraschistes*, or incisor, awaited his judgment. Nothing was attempted by the cutter with the Ethiopian stone (which they used in place of a knife) unless he had first heard the one they called the scribe speaking. Let us hear the words of the historian: "First, the one called the scribe, the body having been placed on the ground,

<column-break/>

marks out upon the left flank how much must be cut." The beginning of the cutting was made at the looser cavity of the side, which is seen between the hips and the hip-bone, and that on the left side. Once this cavity was opened, the *Paraschistes* would flee as if he had committed some crime, and as many as were present would pursue him with the throwing of stones and with curses. They cursed him as if he had done an injury to nature; they attacked him with stones as if they could avert future misfortunes by "stone-throwing" <note>original: λιθοβολίᾳ</note>. Regarding this silly custom, Siculus says again: "The one called the *Paraschistes*, having an Ethiopian stone and cutting the flesh as the law commands, immediately flees at a run, while those present pursue and throw stones, and further, turning the curse upon him, they heap abuse; for they suppose that anyone who brings violence to a body of the same race, or inflicts wounds, or works any evil at all, is hateful." After his departure, the *Taricheutae* <note>embalmers</note> succeeded him; one of them, inserting his hand into the viscera, extracted the parts contained in the middle of the belly, which go by the name of *splanchne* and *entera* <note>inwards and intestines</note>, though leaving the heart and kidneys untouched; another washed the belly with palm wine, mixed the scents, and performed the other "treatments" <note>original: θεραπεύματα</note>, about which Diodorus says:
<margin>page 58.</margin>
"When they have gathered for the treatment of the opened body, one lets his hand down through the incision of the dead man into the chest and takes everything out, except the kidneys and the heart; another cleanses each of the entrails, rinsing them with palm wine and incense. Generally, they treat the whole body first with cedar oil and other things they deem worthy of care for more than thirty days. Then, they treat it with myrrh and cinnamon and those things which are able not only to preserve it for a long time but also to provide a sweet fragrance." The actual *enchiresis* <note>manual method</note> and administration of the act seems to have been thus: They cut the belly transversely on the left side. They removed all the internal organs except the heart and kidneys; and they replaced them according to a certain peculiar rite, as **Porphyry** handed down from the testimony of Euphantus.
<margin>4 *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, page 379.</margin>
They separated the sternum from the ribs. They washed the cavities and "the hollow of the belly" with palm wine and aromatic waters, and wiped them with sponges. They rubbed in the spices prepared for the seasoning, and having filled the cavity of the belly and chest, they sewed the skin back up. They also filled the head with medicines after the brain had been extracted through the nostrils, "taking out the brain through the nostrils with a hooked iron tool, thus removing part of it, and pouring in drugs for the rest." After the seasoning of these parts, they anointed the whole body, sprinkled it with aromatic powders, and soaked it in nitre. When they had done these things, they wrapped it in fine linen, surrounded it with waxed cloths, and placed the corpse in a chest or coffin. **Herodotus**: "Having done these things, they mummify it with nitre, hiding it for seventy days. When the seventy days have passed, having washed the corpse, they wrap its whole body in bandages of fine linen cloth, smearing it with gum, which they mostly use instead of glue. Then the relatives, receiving him, make a wooden case in the shape of a human. Having made it, they enclose the dead man." Thus all things were cared for step by step, and everything was arranged with particular zeal and not without elegance, yet with consideration for the means of those who gave the dead over for burial. Hence there was one simpler mode of seasoning, another more profuse and expensive, and again another cheaper. Three-

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

There were, of course, three conditions of burial: the sumptuous, the mediocre, and the very cheap. Diodorus says again:
<margin>Egyptian funerals</margin>
"There are three ranks of burials: the most expensive, the middling, and the most humble." <note>original Greek: τῶν δὲ ταφῶν τρεῖς ὑπάρχουσι τάξεις, ἥ τε πολυτελεστάτη καὶ ταπεινοτάτη</note> The corpses of the great were sumptuously preserved with the application of the most precious perfumes. Men of thinner and commoner lot were placed by the "Sandapilarius" <note>A person who carried the sandapila, a cheap coffin for the poor</note>—to use the terms of Horace and Lucan—without rich preparation in a cheap chest, after they had been filled only with bitumen. Thus, the method of preservation varied according to the varying condition and fortune of the men. Precious balsam was given to the more worthy, but unpleasant asphalt to the thinner [poorer] ones.

Let us look at a handful of the materials gathered for funerals. In the first and principal place was *Balsam*, which is the noblest of plants, and its "tear" [resin] is more famous than all others for its virtue; hence it rightly earned a "splendid naming" among the Hebrews, because it is *Baal Shemen*, that is, the Lord of Oil, for from it the chief oil is made, so that it can be called in the words of the Prophet <margin>Amos 6:6</margin> *reshit shemanim*, the *head or first of ointments*, or, as I might say in French, *maistre huile* <note>Master oil</note>. It happened from this that it held the mastery among the oils of preservation, so that the preservation of human corpses is commonly called *Balsamation*, a word of later Latinity, as is *to embalm*. Guitherimus in his *Postils on Easter* says: *The body of Christ is embalmed by the Deity.* This has remained among the Italians, Spaniards, and French, which peoples have used this word in their Biblical versions regarding the "balsamation," so to speak, of Jacob. For thus the Spanish Bibles have it: *And Joseph commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father; and the physicians embalmed Israel.* <note>original Spanish: Y mandò Ioseph a sus siervos medicos, que embalsamaſſen à su Padre; y los medicos embalſamaron à Israel.</note> The Italian: *Joseph then commanded his servant physicians to embalm his father; and the physicians embalmed Israel.* <note>original Italian: Commando dunque Ioſeph à i medici ſuoi ſervitori, che imbalſamaſſero ſuo padre; & i medici imbalſamarono Israel.</note> The French: *Joseph commanded his servant physicians to embalm his father; and the physicians embalmed Israel.* <note>original French: Ioſeph commanda à ſes ſerviteurs medecins d' embaumer ſon pere; & les medecins embaumerent Israel.</note> A note is added: *According to the custom of the ancient Orientals, who willingly had the dead bodies of Kings and other great Lords embalmed.* The Belgian [Dutch] versions harmonize: *And Joseph commanded his servants, the master-medics, that they should balsam his father; and the master-medics balsamed Israel.* The juice that flows from the balsam goes by the name of *opobalsamum*. Dioscorides in his *Medical History* (1.18): *The so-called opobalsamum is extracted during the heat of the Dog Days by cutting into the bark with iron nails.* <margin>Natural History 12.25</margin> Pliny says: *The juice flows from the wound, which they call opobalsamum, of extraordinary sweetness, but in thin drops.* <margin>On Virgil's Georgics p. 105</margin> Servius says: *Balsam is the tree itself. Opobalsamum is the juice collected from the tree, for "opos" means juice.* The juice flows from the incision; concerning the collection and virtue of this balsamic resin, Veslingius is worth reading in his *Vindication of Opobalsamum*, pages 15, 16, 17, and others. Its odor is most fragrant, and for that reason balsam oil is useful for treating a corpse. This was undoubtedly applied to the bodies of Jacob and Joseph, for the more honorable and wealthy used perfumes of the greatest price and ointments prepared at great expense, especially the "tear" of balsam; and with similar juices of odorous plants mixed together, they preserved bodies from the injury of rot. Other things also completed the preservation. Writers report that bodies were anointed with "cedria" liquor. The Cedar grows in great abundance in Syria, especially on Mount Lebanon.

<column-break/>

It is a tall tree, whence the Royal Psalmist [David], when he wished to designate something proud, took a comparison from it. Its wood is of a pleasant odor, impervious to moths, and durable, which is why its material seemed worthy to Solomon for building the temple and the Royal palace. That tree gives a resin which is called *cedria*, and the oil made from it is called *kedrelaion* by the Greeks. Pliny mentions the juice of the cedar: <margin>Book 16, ch. 11</margin> *which has such great power that in Egypt the bodies of deceased men, when drenched in it, are preserved.* And elsewhere: <margin>Book 24, ch. 5</margin> *The great cedar, which they call cedrelaten, gives a pitch called cedria. We have said how the juice of the cedar is made from it. It is of great use for lights, unless it brings pain to the head. It keeps dead bodies incorrupt, but it destroys living ones. A wonderful difference, since it takes life from those breathing, yet stands in place of life for the dead.* The great cedar was called *kedros ate*, equaling the fir tree in its size. *Kedria* is the same as *cedar pitch*. Nicander calls that cedar pitch *kedrinen pissen*. <margin>Alexipharmaca v. 488</margin> Balenus commends *cedria* because *it dries and keeps dead bodies free from rot.* For which reason the Scholiast of Nicander teaches us that the cedar was called the *life of the dead* <note>original Greek: νεκρῶν ζωήν</note> in these words: *it makes the dead free from rot, it dries up the moisture and the flux, whence some have called it the life of the dead.* By "moisture" he notes the "tear" of the cedria, sweating translucently from the bark of the cedar tree, by which dead bodies are preserved. Dioscorides teaches the same: <margin>Book 1, ch. 89</margin> *concerning the cedar, it is a great tree,* and from it is gathered what is called *cedria*, namely a liquor or resin, and the best is that which is thick, transparent, of a strong odor, and which, when poured out in concentrated drops, holds itself together and does not flow away. He says its power and nature is *to be a drawer of living things, but a preserver of dead bodies* (which words Pliny rendered just as was said from him); and because by drying it preserves from rot and gives permanence to the dead, it was therefore nicknamed by some the *life of the corpse*. In olden times, the Gauls used it to embalm the heads of illustrious men. Strabo (Book 4): *They used to show the cedar-treated heads of famous men to strangers, and would not deign to give them up even for an equal weight of gold.* That resin of the cedar, which is properly called *cedria*, and the oil of cedar, which they call *cedrium*, also preserved other things from corruption. By cedar oil (says Pliny) <margin>Book 16, ch. 39</margin> *wood that has been anointed feels neither decay nor the moth.* For the same benefit Vitruvius commends *cedrium*: <margin>Architecture 2.11</margin> *The cedar and the juniper have the same virtues and utilities. But from the cedar comes the oil called cedrium, with which other things, such as books, when anointed, are not harmed by moths or decay.* And Servius: <margin>Aeneid 7</margin> *The wood of the cedar in Virgil is not easily consumed by age. The moth does not know this kind of wood, and it does not feel corruption from antiquity. Whence comes cedria, which preserves paper.* Hence comes that saying: *Words worthy of the cedar.* Or, *anointed with cedria*, since it preserves the wood-guards [bindings]. In this way, for five hundred years and more, the books of Numa, anointed with *cedrium*, had been preserved without blemish. Cassius Hemina says in Pliny: <margin>Book 13, ch. 13</margin> *Others wondered how those books could have lasted. That reason gave the explanation: the books had been treated with cedar, and therefore I would think the moths had not touched the lines.* Books were accustomed to be "cedar-treated" and smeared with oil, lest moths and beetles should destroy them.

<summary>This page details the various grades of ancient embalming, focusing on the use of balsam and cedar resin (cedria) to preserve both human remains and important documents like the books of Numa.</summary>
<keywords>embalming, balsam, cedar oil, cedria, opobalsamum, Egyptian burial, ancient medicine, preservation of books, Pliny, Dioscorides</keywords>

"fat toga," which was of a thick or doubled texture.
So "thick" and "fat" amomum was that which was spent largely
and doubly upon a funeral. Assyrian amomum was praised most highly

From this, perhaps, comes the name **Mummy**, from which

in section 1 on antidotes, chapter 13, and attributes this name to the Italians.
Mummy is defined by Joachim Struppius * as the moist juice and essence of a human,
anointed, smeared, and filled internally with aloe, myrrh, bitumen <note>original: "pissasphalto"</note>,
likewise with the best saffron and the noblest balsam, or anointed in its
stead with cedar oil. They are still dug up in Egypt around the pyramids, and
carried to far distant regions for the sake of

<column-break/>

<margin>Egyptian burial rites.</margin>
medicine. Concerning its use in medicine, different doctors
hold different opinions. One says it wonderfully benefits the wounded, ruptured, and
bruised. Another holds it in low regard, nor thinks it worth so much
that it should be bought at a high price, especially because of deception and adulteration.
It is not consistent with reason, as Sebizius teaches *, that
<margin>Dissertation on the balsam of human corpses, no. 46, 45.</margin>
sepulchral mummy can produce many great effects, because many of those
who were embalmed died either of the plague, or a malignant fever, or consumption,
or dropsy, or putrid fever, or leprosy, or some other abominable
disease. The preservation might also easily contract something
evil from the vaults and subterranean caverns in which they are kept,
on account of the sluggishness and torpor of the air and the cadaverous conditions.
Add to this that the mummy which is brought to us is of the common sort,
and a pure liquid of bitumen. Aromatized mummy, which is more expensive,
can hardly—if ever—be obtained from the Great Lords, and even if it were,
their small number would not suffice for the pharmacies of all
Europe. Therefore, in the judgment of Scaliger *,
<margin>Exercise 104, ch. 9.</margin>
the mummy brought to us from Egypt is not a seasoning of
aloe and myrrh, but of asphalt. For the nobles use those [spices], and to dig up
their bodies is a capital crime. Certainly, the mummies that are brought,
we see are preserved with asphalt; Paré * abhors these no
<margin>Book 11, ch. 7, on confusion and gangrene.</margin>
less than the aromatized ones, not only because it is unknown what Mummy actually is,
and because men driven by base greed have been caught snatching the
corpses of hanged men by night, seasoning them with salt and spices,
drying them in an oven, and selling them dearly as exotic mummy;
but also for this reason: because he experienced a hundred times that Mummy
brought no help in such conditions. He considered it a "barbarous" thing
to devour the dissected and rotting portions of the corpses of the vilest Egyptian
commoners or criminals, as if the art of rescuing a man who had fallen from a height
and was bruised from the underworld was nothing other than if he should
bury a man within his own—that is, human—entrails by a truly
horrendous grafting. That common mummy, as it is brought to us,
shows the black color of asphalt. Now, asphalt is a fat and oily
juice, floating on waters, especially in the Dead Sea, which is therefore
called the *Asphaltite Lake* by the Greeks; they call it *pissasphaltos* <note>pitch-asphalt</note>.
With this, they filled the bodies of the poor so they would remain unrotted.
A simple funeral for a commoner, a simple bier without an undertaker's preparation.
No balsam here, no myrrh. They poured liquefied bitumen, especially
Jewish and Babylonian, into the corpse. These bituminized bodies
are carried to us, and an infinite number of such are preserved. We (says
Belon *) have entered many tombs,
<margin>2 Observations 47, p. 118.</margin>
some of which are vaulted; others built in the form of a chamber;
for their number is infinite throughout those sandy places among the Pyramids.
The frequency of flies at the Pyramids is so great that the air
resounded with their humming as they flew away when we passed.
Brought to the same places, Christophorus Fuernus * saw individual tombs
<margin>In his Travels, p. 25.</margin>
constructed with stones like a well with a square hole,
reaching a depth equal to the length of a spear; he saw
caverns full of corpses and arranged in such an order that a passage
was given from one to another. These corpses are sought out and sold
to foreigners, who, to make the merchandise more saleable, [prepare them]...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Egyptian funerary rites</margin>
...they attribute such great medicinal power. A corpse of this kind, filled with bituminous juice, was once brought from Egypt by a merchant from Nuremberg; Camerarius saw it and, taking the opportunity of this mummy, inserted an entire chapter on non-decaying corpses into his *Hours* (Book 2, chapter 70, page 404). I myself saw mummies of this kind in the anatomical theater at Leiden, brought there through the efforts of David de Willem, Counselor to the Prince of Orange, who had carried it back with him from the ruins of the Pyramids while traveling through Egypt. There also lies near the left side of a certain mummy a small clay figure of Isis, fixed into the very material of the preservation. For it was a solemn custom for the Egyptians to place small figures in the worship of such corpses. Camerarius saw such a small bronze image in Venice and discussed its use.

<margin>1. hor. subc. 14. p. 59.</margin>
* Augustine provides the Egyptian name by which a preserved corpse was called.

<margin>Sermon on various subjects 120. tr. 1. c. 12.</margin>
* The Egyptians (he says *) alone believe in the resurrection, because they diligently care for the bodies of the dead; for they had a custom of drying the bodies and making them almost like bronze. They call them <term>Gabbaras</term> <note>original: "Gabbaras"; a term used by Augustine for mummies, possibly of Coptic or Aramaic origin</note>. I have read nothing of this word elsewhere, and Athanasius Kircher, the modern steward of the Egyptian language, will lend his assistance here. So that bodies cared for through <term>perieikai</term> <note>original: "περιεικαὶ"; likely a Greek term for wrapping or surrounding the body</note> may become clearer, we shall proceed. So that the <term>periechein</term> <note>original: "περιέχειν"; to encompass or enclose</note> might be more effective, they also applied aloes, which, just as it protects the humors from rot in living bodies, so it protects corpses from corruption. Likewise, myrrh wards off rot and especially preserves and protects the solid parts. Anshelmus on *Matthew* fol. 28. b.: *The bodies of the dead are preserved with myrrh because, through its extreme bitterness, worms are extinguished by it.*

<margin>book 27. c. 4. p. 552.</margin>
Aloe, with its heavy scent, thickened and condensed the flesh, as Pliny records. * Myrrh spread a pleasing and fragrant odor, and with it the body was anointed against <term>dysodian</term> <note>original: "δυσωδίαν"; a foul smell or stench</note>. For from myrrh was made a most fragrant ointment, the nature of which was recognized as suitable for embalming Christ by Nicodemus, who honored the body of our deceased Savior (*John 19:39*) with a <term>mixture of aloes and myrrh</term> <note>original: "μίγματι ἀλόης καὶ μύῤῥας"</note>. This good man had come thinking of the human reality of decay, from which there was no danger to the body of the Lord. He brought to the burial of Christ a mixture of myrrh and aloes weighing about a hundred pounds. That this type of spice was the legitimate standard for the Jews is shown by the words: *

<margin>v. 40.</margin>

<margin>Dioscorides l. 1. c. 67.</margin>

Therefore, the bodies of the dead, after the intestines were removed, were usually filled with myrrh and cassia by the Egyptians. They also used salt and nitre against rot.

<margin>Mantuanus 1. Parth. 3 v. 891.</margin>

# From Genesis Chapter 50, verses 2 & 3.

<margin>Egyptian funerals. Toward the Gods, and [men].</margin>
...opinions concerning what is shameful and what is not, concerning things illicit and licit, concerning laws and customs, and concerning piety toward the Gods, and concerning sanctity toward the dead, and similar matters. For in this way, we shall find a great discrepancy regarding things to be done or not to be done.
After he had reviewed several particular <margin>page 532.</margin> <term>customs</term> <note>original: νόμιμα (nomima)</note> of the Egyptians, he adds their funeral rites, proceeding: *But also concerning piety toward the dead, things not dissimilar to these can be said. For some, composing the entire <margin>page 533.</margin> bodies of the dead, cover them with earth, deeming it impious to show them to the sun. But the Egyptians, extracting the intestines, preserve the deceased and keep them with themselves above the ground. Among the Ethiopians, however, those who are <term>fish-eaters</term> <note>original: ἰχθυοφάγοι (ichthyophagoi)</note> cast them into marshes to be food for fishes. The Hyrcanians truly expose them to be devoured by dogs; some of the Indians even to vultures. Moreover, they say it is the custom of the Troglodytes to lead the deceased to a certain hill, then, having bound his head to his feet, they pelt him with stones, not without laughter; when they have covered him with a mound of thrown stones, they depart. There are furthermore some Barbarians who sacrifice and eat those who have exceeded sixty years of age; but those who die young, they bury in the earth. Some also burn the dead, of whom some, taking their bones, keep them stored away; others leave them cast away at random.* Furthermore, they say the Persians suspend the dead and preserve them with <term>natron</term> <note>A natural salt used in mummification; original: nitro</note>, and only then wrap them in bandages. To Gellius, inquiring <margin>10. Attic Notes 10. p. 313.</margin> into Egyptian matters, the Egyptian books of Apion were brought, which taught him the [preservation] of human bodies, as was the custom in Egypt. Many things of that kind, which were practiced by <term>dissection</term> <note>original: ἀνατομῇ (anatomē)</note>, those books could teach us if they were extant; just as <margin>Gellius book 6. 6. 17. p. 229.</margin> many more volumes would be extant if, during the former Alexandrian war while that city was being plundered, they had not perished, burned not by design <margin>page 60. e.</margin> nor by deliberate effort, but by chance by the auxiliary soldiers. This custom was celebrated by Plato in the *Phaedo*, showing that a corpse necessarily dissolves, falls apart, and flows away, unless it is dried out and preserved, just as they do in Egypt: <note>original Greek: Ἐννοεῖς, ὅτι ἐπειδὰν ἀποθάνῃ ὁ ἄνθρωπος... (Ennoeis, hoti epeidan apothanē ho anthrōpos...)</note> <note>Plato, Phaedo 80c: "You notice that when a man dies, the visible part of him, the body, which lies in the visible world and which we call the corpse—to which it belongs to dissolve and fall away and be blown away—does not suffer any of these things immediately, but remains for a fairly long time. If someone dies with his body in a graceful state and at such an age, it remains very much so. For the body, collapsed and embalmed, as those embalmed in Egypt, remains almost whole for an incredible amount of time. And some parts of the body, even if it decays, such as the bones and sinews and all such things, are still (so to speak) immortal."</note> Augustus noted the same in that speech with which he exhorted his men before the Battle of Actium in Dio: <note>original Greek: Ἀλεξανδρεῖς τε καὶ Αἰγύπτιοι ὄντες... (Alexandreis te kai Aigyptioi ontes...)</note> <note>Dio Cassius 50.24: "Being Alexandrians and Egyptians (for what else could one say more foully or more truly?), worshipping reptiles and other beasts as if they were gods, and embalming their own bodies for a reputation of immortality."</note> Caesar speaks contemptuously of the Egyptians, who were ill-reputed by their very name, yet meanwhile looked toward the glory of immortality through the preservation of bodies; which Augustine also writes of mockingly: *The Egyptians alone rightly believe in the resurrection of their dead, but the hope of other Christians is in a narrow place.* For they thought this contributed to future reputation and to the

<column-break/>

perpetual glory of bodies, so that <margin>Egyptian funerals.</margin> they might thus be simultaneously incited to the virtue of their ancestors, and so that they might wish to have contended with their ancestors by this funeral spectacle, sanctioned as if by perpetual law. This is proved by the carrying [of the mummy] around during banquets and the standing of it against the walls. They wished anyone who had acted rightly to be carried out with joy, and in their desire for praise, they introduced them into the intervals of the table, so that they might gaze upon the image of the deceased as a model of virtue. While some rightly recognized this use, others wrongly took it as an argument for luxury. It is an altogether strange custom, which Lucian in *On Mourning* p. 794—who narrates that he himself was present at banquets and drinking parties of this kind—ridicules; which also Saint Anthony forbade to be observed after his death, as Athanasius notes in <margin>page 117.</margin> his <term>biography</term> <note>original: βιογραφίᾳ (biographia)</note> *in these words: <note>original Greek: Εἰ μέλει ὑμῖν ἐμοῦ ἐμὲ... # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Egyptian funeral rites. page 148.</margin>
...to do, the corpses are opened and exposed to the Sun in some sunny place, the intestines are cast into a flowing stream, and the rest of the cleansed body is preserved. Concerning these same people, he had previously noted the custom of bringing a skeleton into their banquets, by which they might indicate that they themselves would be similar not much later. <note>original Greek: Οἱ Αἰγύπτιοι σκελετὸν ἐπιεικῶς εἰσφέρουτες εἰς τὰ συμπόσια προτίθενται, καὶ παρακαλοῦσι μεμνῆσθαι τάχα δὲ τοιάυταις ἐσομένους.</note> <note>Translation: "The Egyptians bring a skeleton into their symposia and set it out, and they exhort [the guests] to remember that they will soon be such as this."</note> Herodotus teaches that they did these same things with a wooden image of a man,
<margin>page 133</margin>
writing: <note>original Greek: Ἐν τῇσι συνεσίῃσι τοῖσι εὐδαίμοσι αὐτέων...</note> <note>Translation: "In the social gatherings of their wealthy, when they have finished dinner, a man carries around a wooden corpse in a coffin, made to look as much like the real thing as possible by painting and carving, about a cubit or two in size. Showing it to each of the guests, he says: 'Look upon this, then drink and be merry; for when you are dead, you shall be such as this.'"</note> If this was their custom, to invite one to drink by carrying around the likeness of a dead man, they would have been "pigs from Epicurus's herd" <note>A common Latin idiom for those who pursue only physical pleasure.</note>. The origin of the matter seems to lie deeper, and rather has this significance: that by presenting this image of death, they might incite themselves and their guests to a moderate consumption of food and drink, to weigh the approaching goal of fleeting time, and to hasten toward a better life to come. The reason of their frugal diet stands in favor of this opinion, which is commended by Diodorus, who writes:
<margin>page 64.</margin>
<note>original Greek: τροφαῖς οἱ ἔϑη ἦν αὐτοῖς ἁπλαῖς χρῆσθαι...</note> <note>Translation: "Their custom was to use simple foods, partaking only of veal and geese, and drinking a certain fixed measure of wine, which was not able to produce untimely fullness or drunkenness; and in general, their whole diet was so proportionately arranged that it seemed not a legislator, but the best of physicians had arranged it, aiming at health."</note> A grander eulogy could not be given regarding the moderate system of diet which they established for sound health, so much so that not a lawmaker, but the best of Physicians seems to have established it. That inspection of skeletons, as well as familiar admonition, persuaded them toward this <term>self-sufficiency</term> <note>original: αὐτάρκειαν (autarkeian) - the virtue of being content with little.</note> of living. That spectacle of a shapeless skeleton would have produced a nausea for drinking rather than, as some wish, exciting it. But we need not labor over this for now. It is peculiar what Servius notes: that the embalming of the body was done by the Egyptians so that the soul might be satisfied and the "dwelling place" of the body might be pleasing.
<margin>on the 3rd Aeneid, page 274.</margin>
For he writes thus: *When the tombs have been duly rendered according to law, the soul returns to the quiet of the tomb; which the Stoics, following a middle path, say lasts as long as the body lasts.* Whence the Egyptians, skilled in wisdom, preserve the embalmed corpses for a longer time, namely so that the soul may endure for a long time and remain subject to the body, and not quickly pass over to others. The Romans, by contrast, used to burn the corpses, so that the soul might immediately return to "generality," that is, into its own nature. Let us allow the Grammarian to enjoy his "generality," who, while subjecting the soul to a prison and a sentence, harms himself incautiously. It does not matter much how they felt about the body and the soul. ...to call it [immortality] vanity, madness, and a childish delusion. Whatever it is that is spewed out in that speech of yours, it is said <note>original: "μάλα αἰσχρῶς" (very shamefully)</note> very shamefully against

Unless the immortality of the soul is established, neither religion nor sacred rites could be maintained, nor could discipline and good morals flourish among mortals. Truly, the doctrine of the soul's destruction carries with it a sink-hole of innumerable evils, while the doctrine of its immortality is a limpid fountain of all good. From this fountain flow those channels, whether of the origin of this perishing life, or of the celestial life that shall endure eternally. This truth concerning the soul remaining forever was recognized by Plato, the pinnacle of the philosophers of his age, and he proved it by many reasons both elsewhere and especially in the *Phaedrus* and the *Phaedo*. Concerning this, 
<margin>On the Resurrection of the Flesh, ch. 1.</margin>

That there is nothing after death is the School of Epicurus. Seneca also says, *all things end after death, even death itself.* But the Platonists, on the contrary, cry out that the soul is immortal; indeed, they even affirm it is capable of returning into bodies. Cicero, the Orator of Orators,

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Egyptian funerals.</margin> They deliver (he says on page 58) <note>original: "Παραδιδόασι..." quoting Diodorus Siculus</note> the bodies of the deceased to the relatives; thus each part of the body is preserved so intact that even the hair on the eyelids and eyebrows remains, and the entire appearance of the body is unchanged, and the form of its shape is recognized. --- so that the size and physical features of each body, and even the characters of the face being seen, provide a marvelous psychological comfort, as if they were living together with those being beheld. A proof of this is King Alexander, whose seen countenance and recognized features of the face Augustus felt himself affected by with wonderful pleasure, marveling at the uniqueness of the deceased <note>original: "θαυμάζων τὴν ἰδιότητα τοῦ τετελευτηκότος"</note>, whom he venerated with a golden crown and scattered flowers. This <margin>History p. 52. Epitome p. 64.</margin> was left recorded by Dio and his Epitomizer Xiphilinus, who report concerning Augustus that he touched the nose of the cadaver which was still intact, and when it was handled a little, a small piece fell off, so that a bit of the nose, as they say, was broken <note>original: "ὥς τέ τι καὶ τῆς ῥινὸς... θραυσθῆναι"</note>. To the same Emperor the Alexandrians wanted to show the still intact bodies of their Ptolemies, which he did not wish to see, saying wittily: *I desired to see a King, but not dead men.* With this brief response he touched upon which of the dead was more worthy of expectation and royal eyes. A certain image of emulous struggle remained in Alexander, but in the Ptolemies, nothing. It is probable that Gaius Caligula saw that Mausoleum, who took from there a breastplate, concerning which Suetonius says in chapter 52: *He constantly wore triumphal dress even before his expedition. Sometimes also the breastplate of Alexander the Great, taken from his tomb.* The Emperor Severus was also a curious spectator of the same royal monument and body, who, having set out for Egypt <margin>Xiphilinus page 328.</margin> investigated everything, even the most hidden things <note>original: "ἐπολυπραγμόνησε πάντα καὶ τὰ πάνυ κεκρυμμένα"</note>. Having also seen the site of Alexander's monument, by I know not what more severe presumption, he wished it to be closed, so that no one in the future might see it, nor read those things which were written upon it. The words of the Historian themselves have it: *He closed up the monument of Alexander, so that no one might any longer see his body, nor read the things written in those places.* And he indeed did these things. By what occasion the body of Alexander was brought to Alexandria by Ptolemy son of Lagus <margin>book 17. p. 546</margin> (who had snatched it from Perdiccas), Strabo teaches. We judge that the beginning of funeral embalming started with the Egyptians, and spread to the Chaldeans, Jews, Ethiopians, and others, though they may differ in material and method. Egypt had many things both peculiar and proper above others, difficult for others to imitate, both due to a lack of perfumes and due to the mark of superstition. Egypt is celebrated by Pliny (XIII. 3) as the most suitable of all lands for ointments, and glorious for herbs (XXIV. 1), whence a collection of materials with which cadavers were adorned could easily be made. There was a great apparatus of medicines there, a great heap for various parts of the body. Also a great space of time was required, so that the force of the embalming might penetrate more strongly into all parts of the body. Daily new spices, now these, now those, the Egyptians were accustomed to apply for the seasoning of bodies with certain rites. Which time is expressed in our text, namely that they were filled with aromatic embalming for forty <margin>verse 3 of said chapter.</margin> days. <gloss>וימלאו-לו ארבעים יום</gloss> And forty days were completed for him. <insert>The physicians anointed Israel until forty days were over. i.e. Forty</insert>

By which reasoning they defined thirty and more days for themselves, in which course of time it was fitting for the body first to be washed with Phoenician wine made from fragrant things, then the whole first anointed with cedar and other precious ointments, and next smeared with myrrh and cinnamon and others. So much so that the work grew beyond thirty days. Scripture does not disdain to mention the days of embalming, so that even from this it might be established how magnificently Jacob was buried, and indeed in such a land which disdained the Jews. That which will appear more fully from the final ceremonies and the solemn company of the funeral. From that day on which he died, as if in a common sorrow, the consensus of all conspired; the care of the funeral was demanded of the servant-physicians, continued carefully through 40 days, successfully completed, and with some delay of time still added through public mourning, which among the Egyptians was like a cessation of public business. This greatly increases the glory of Jacob, that they honored the one who met his fate with a mourning otherwise solemn and public.
