# From Genesis Chapter 50, Verses 2 & 3

<margin>Egyptian funeral rites.</margin>
The words of the text leave it uncertain whether they only began to weep for the dead according to their custom after the 40 days of embalming, or whether the mourning began immediately after death and thus lasted until the 70th day. If the words imply the former, there would be a total of 110 days spent in public mourning. The second opinion seems more probable to the Hebrews: that the 40 days of <insert>embalming</insert> and the 30 days of <insert>weeping</insert> are counted together as the seventy days of mourning. Lyra follows this opinion based on Hebrew guidance, noting: *Egypt wept for him 70 days; namely, 40 days of spicing <note>original: "condimenti," referring to the mummification process</note> and 30 of weeping.* Thus, the days of preparation and mourning combined would constitute seventy. This pleases Menochius, Mercerus, Calixtus, and others. This number of seventy days seems to contain something <term>worthy of evidence</term> <note>original Greek: ἀξιοτέκμαρτον</note>. It is well known how sacred that seven-fold number has always been considered. Whether there is some religious significance here, I cannot determine. Twelve weeks pass while the embalming, the mourning garments, and other <term>things pertaining to burial</term> <note>original Greek: τὰ ἐνταφιασμῷ</note> are performed. In Egypt, the days of public mourning lasted seventy-two after the passing of any King, as Diodorus exquisitely notes in Book 1, page 46. At such times, the sacred temples were closed, sacrifices were forbidden, no festivals were celebrated, and neither baths nor other places of pleasure were frequented. It seems likely something of this sort was done upon the death of Jacob, out of favor for Joseph, who was next to the King; and thus that single word <insert>wept</insert> encompasses everything usually exhibited regarding a funeral. It is not to be understood that the Egyptians shed continuous tears for seventy days, for not even Heraclitus himself, even if he dissolved entirely into tears, could endure mourning for so long. *That solemn lamentation does not command long tears from the Egyptians, but rather demonstrates the adornment of the funeral,* says Jerome. <margin>1st Epistle 25 to Paula.</margin> For so many days, they testified to their grief not with continuous and disordered wailing, but through specific dress and rituals. Otherwise, the Egyptians were accustomed to walk about covered in mud and filth during mourning, pouring out into the streets with lamentation. Herodotus <margin>page 135</margin> says: > Their dirges are as follows. When a man of any account dies in a house, all the female kin of that house plaster their heads or even their faces with mud. Then, leaving the corpse in the house, they wander through the city, beating themselves with their clothes girt up and exposing their breasts, and with them all their relations. On the other side, the men beat themselves, they too having their clothes girt. In the same way, Diodorus <margin>page 57</margin> says: > Whenever anyone dies among them, all the relatives and friends, having sprinkled their heads with mud, go around the city lamenting until the body receives burial. The ceremonial mourning of the Egyptians was unusual, where one could see the common people running to and fro, sprinkling their heads with dust and making other signs of grief until the corpse was buried. Meanwhile, they abstained from all luxuries. <note>original Greek: οὐ μίω᾿ ἔτε λυτρῶν...</note> They partake of neither baths, nor wine, nor any other noteworthy food, nor do they put on bright clothing. If the Egyptians used such a mournful appearance regarding the death of Jacob, the affection of the people toward the deceased was altogether great and singular. Or at least it can be presumed from this with what faith and zeal they honored Joseph, for whose sake they followed his Father with communal mourning for seventy days. They knew that whatever honor was deferred to the Fa-

<column-break/>

-ther would redound to the Son, who was second only to the King of the Egyptians. The Hebrews say this was done in consideration of the benefit that, since he descended into Egypt, he had saved them from famine, so that it did not rage beyond two years. Mercerus explains this on page 740, commenting here: <gloss>Why do the Egyptians weep for him? Regarding the sons, grandsons, and the whole family, it would be no wonder. He must have been very dear even to the Egyptians, whom they regarded as a great Man and a Prophet. They did this also for the sake of Joseph; but mostly moved by his singular virtue and holiness.</gloss> Luther says: *It is truly a great thing that this stranger was in such honor and favor with King Pharaoh and the Princes of Egypt, that they mourned him for so long, and performed the final duties of piety for the deceased with the greatest goodwill and reverence.* Let us see how he later set out with the sarcophagus for the journey. When the time of lamentation was finished, he addresses the household of Pharaoh <margin>v. 4, 5</margin> so they might obtain for him departure and passage from the King. He conducts his business through interpreters and intermediaries because in mourning it was not permitted to approach the King. Tremellius <margin>page 77</margin> notes: <gloss>He addressed the family of Pharaoh, not because he had fallen out of the King's favor, but because he was dressed in mourning <note>original: "pullatus," wearing dark funeral clothes</note>, and was himself in mourning with his whole kindred. Therefore he uses Egyptians as intercessors. For those in mourning were not accustomed to appear before the King (Esther 4:2). No one unkempt, shivering, or sorrowful appeared before the King, as was provided for by law and custom.</gloss> Having obtained permission from the King, he departed accompanied by a great retinue. <margin>Gen. 41:14</margin> To the funeral rites come <insert>all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his house, and all the elders of the land of Egypt.</insert> <margin>v. 7</margin> This <term>Jew</term> <note>Jacob</note> was carried out with a greater funeral pomp than any Egyptian in all memory, and with a greater span of both time and distance. Who would not be stunned by such a <term>wholly marvelous funeral procession</term> <note>original Greek: πάνυ θαυμασίω ἐκφορᾶν</note>, and who would not admire the <term>procession of the greatest men of Egypt present and wisely leading the way</term> <note>original Greek: μεγίϛων τῆς Αἰγύπτου...</note>? For the sake of honoring and escorting the funeral, so many Princes, so many Satraps, so many Prelates, so many Senators of the Kingdom, and so many Nobles were present. He was so favored by all that each and every one rejoiced to grace the funeral with their company. So favorable was the name of Joseph that even the Princes, Nobles, Prefects, and those who shone with the fame of their name in the court and the whole region, illustrated the pomp of the most splendid apparatus such as had scarcely ever been seen in Egypt. Moreover, as many were present as could be absent from the affairs of the kingdom for a little while, and as many took part as the King permitted. The most honored of all ranks were present, nor is there any other sense to the word "all" <note>Hebrew: כל</note>, which is used in the same way as it is said at the funeral of Samuel <margin>1 Sam. 25:1</margin> that <insert>all Israel</insert> was gathered, meaning at least some from every city appeared in Ramah in a public capacity to pay their respects. That universal word often implies a multitude and frequency, and is used "for the types of individuals," as they like to say in the schools, so that it denotes not every single person, but some from every group. Thus it is written in Genesis 41:57 that as the famine grew strong, <insert>all the earth came into Egypt</insert>, meaning they arrived in great numbers from all provinces. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

### On Egyptian Honors
The funeral was attended by many nobles and other honored men. To pay their final respects to the deceased, and having obtained permission and passage from the King through intermediaries, Joseph—along with his entire kinship, many courtiers and royal counselors, and many honored men from all of Egypt—carried the funeral procession out of Egypt. A wise man begins nothing rashly but proceeds with caution; he took with him <margin>verse 9</margin> **both chariots and horsemen** <note>original Hebrew: *gam-rekhv gam-parashim*</note> so that he might be safer against robbers, who were accustomed to commit banditry in those places either secretly or openly. And so, with a glittering assembly and a very grave company <note>original Hebrew: *kaved me’od*</note>, he proceeded and came **as far as the threshing floor of Atad**, where <margin>verse 10</margin> they mourned again with a **great and very sore lamentation**.

They remained at that threshing floor for seven days to perform the funeral rites, which otherwise would have been spent at the site of the sepulcher. The Egyptians, with great shouting and lamentation, turned their dirges into praises for the dead according to their custom. Joseph and his brothers followed their father, the grandsons their grandfather, and the others their Patriarch and the parent of their origin, with the warmest tears, offering a final eulogy through all the stages of his life. Seeing such a funeral pomp and such great mourning, the inhabitants of the land, <margin>verse 11</margin> the Canaanites, said: **This is a grievous mourning for the Egyptians** <note>original Hebrew: *avel-kaved zeh l’mitsrayim*</note>. The Egyptians are holding a great lamentation there; they must certainly have lost a distinguished man. From this, they named that place **Abel Misraim**, that is, the mourning of the Egyptians. The mourning was honorably renewed with a seven-day lamentation by Joseph and his brothers—affectionately, so to speak—and by the Egyptians, tumultuously. The Egyptians, ignorant of what they were mourning, undoubtedly sounded something unrefined and disordered with a lamentable voice and wailing through funeral singers. Weighing this ill-conceived custom, <margin>9. Comm. 41.</margin> Rupertus thinks they uttered many things contrary to their true feelings, confirming this with the verse of the Poet [Horace], who said:

<margin>Horace, Art of Poetry</margin>
> But those who are hired to wail at a funeral, say
> and do almost more than those who grieve from the heart.

When the seven-day mourning was finished, the sons moved from the threshing floor of Atad toward Hebron, **and they did for him just as he had commanded them (v. 12); namely, they carried him and buried him** <margin>v. 13</margin> **in the cave of the field of Machpelah, which Abraham had bought with the field for a possession of a burial place.** The Patriarch wished to be transported to that place, of which he was the King and hereditary possessor appointed by God. <margin>Theodoret, Question 107, p. 63</margin> <note>original Greek: "Not caring for a tomb, as some have supposed, but encouraging and teaching his race that this Master God will lead you out of Egypt after this, and give back to them the promised land."</note> He wanted his body brought into the land of Canaan, not as if he were anxious about some holier location or about the future votes and prayers of posterity, but so that by this pledge, the faith in the divine promise might be confirmed, and posterity might be warned that they would one day depart from Egypt to enter that most desired inheritance. When the final process of the burial was completed, <margin>verse 14</margin> **Joseph returned to Egypt, he and his brothers and all who had gone up with him**, out of the loyalty owed to the King for his promise; and there he finished his life, heavy with old age, in his 110th year. <margin>verse 15</margin> But before dying, he made a pact with his brothers about carrying his bones with them into the <margin>v. 25</margin>

<column-break/>

promised land, whenever the Lord should lead them back and, as he says, "surely visit" them. Both father and son wished to be transferred out of Egypt; for those who in life flee the company of the impious do not wish to be mixed with them in death. They do not want themselves or their own to be mingled with those who hate the Lord, and whom the Lord hates. They do not wish to be buried in a land of contamination, but in the land of promise and holy inheritance, so that they might turn the minds of their children away from Egypt and lead them straight to the land where the tombs of their ancestors were. Therefore, Joseph so solicitously commanded **his bones** to be transferred to the land of Canaan—indeed, he bound them by oath—so that he might more vehemently strengthen the hope and faith in God's promises, and that in their exile, future and present, he might kindle the hope of his people, being secure in the promise made to the Fathers, and (to rise higher) certain of the Savior Messiah who would come to that land. Thus the holy man did not look so much to a natural affection for his native soil as he did to testify to his confidence in the dwelling and hospitality of the Church. When these pious thoughts came to the mind of *Lyra* <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a 14th-century theologian</note>, he almost exults in the Spirit with Joseph, writing: *The reason why Joseph was so solicitous to adjure the children of Israel concerning the burial of his bones in the promised land seems to have been that he had a prophetic spirit, as was clear from the foregoing; and it is now piously believed that through the Holy Spirit he foresaw that Christ would die and rise again in that land, and... that many bodies of the saints would rise, as is held in Matthew 27; and it is now likely that he hoped to rise with Christ, to whom is honor forever and ever, Amen.* Lyra is not raving here, as he sometimes raved elsewhere with the Jews, for the Apostle testifies to this full assurance of faith, <margin>Hebrews 11:22</margin> saying: **By faith Joseph, when he was dying, made mention of the departure of the children of Israel and gave instructions concerning his bones.** Therefore, as Luther observes <margin>Commentary on Genesis</margin>, Joseph declares his faith in this: *that he wanted his bones carried to the land of Canaan, since he was not permitted to live in it. To a carnal man, a concern of this kind would be held as foolishness; but by the example of these Fathers—Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph—we see expressed in this matter the character of faith, which is so fashioned that it extends itself beyond the advantages and delights of the present life to future things, and adheres to the promises of God, even those which it is not granted to enjoy in this life.* Therefore, to testify to his faith in Christ, Joseph orders his bones to be carried to the land of Canaan. Thus, to fulfill their faith and mindful of the oath, the Israelites—after they had preserved him with spices—placed the dead Joseph <margin>v. 26</margin> **in a coffin in Egypt.** He was preserved with spices like his father, whence Tremellius renders the Hebrew words <note>original: *vayiḥantu oto*</note>: *After the physicians had preserved him with spices.* Arias: *And they embalmed him.* The Spaniard, Italian, and Frenchman here again used their words *embalsamar, imbalsimare, embausmer*, just as the Belgians [Dutch] use *balsemen*. The body was not immediately carried to the land of Canaan, but only 155 years after his death, when they migrated from Egypt. Joseph died in the year of the world 2360, and the first book of the World and of Moses [Genesis] contains the history of so many years. Nor was he placed in a tomb like the body of his parent, but was put in a certain chest as a deposit, to be kept until...

# From Genesis Chapter 50, verses 2 & 3.

<margin>Egyptian funeral rites.</margin>
...the time of the return to Canaan. Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a medieval Franciscan theologian</note> says: *He was placed in a coffin.* It does not say he was buried; but his bones are said to be buried in Sichem, where he had chosen to be interred.

From this it is clear that such a placing of a corpse in a location until the time it is transferred elsewhere to remain permanently is not called, nor is it, a burial. Pererius <note>Benito Pereira, a Jesuit commentator</note> on page 1401 of this passage: *Joseph was not brought into a sepulcher, but was enclosed in a coffin like a deposit, so that in time he could be carried out without any trouble.* That he was not buried in the earth is testified by the two Targumists <note>Translators of the Hebrew Bible into Aramaic</note>, Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum; they seem to use no other word than that which denotes an ark, a chest, or a certain shrine, and from the Greek *glossokomon* <note>original: γλωσσόκομον</note> or *glossokomeion* <note>original: γλωσσοκομεῖον</note>. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> on page 612: *glossokomon, a wooden chest for remains.* In the books of the Hebrews, it is held that there was a bronze ark in which the body was placed, and about which they dream many other great things. If it was wooden, it was more portable. The Old Interpreter <note>The Vulgate</note> called it a *loculus* <note>a small compartment or coffin</note>, which is said of the ark in which a corpse is usually placed. This is fitting, for Pliny <margin>Book 7, ch. 2, p. 111.</margin> says of the bier of Pyrrhus: *They say his thumb could not be burned with the rest of the body, and it was stored in a loculus in the temple.* The Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> also does well with *en soro* <note>original: ἐν σορῷ, "in a coffin"</note>, although it does not seem right to Steucho on page 145. *Soros* is the same as *loculus*, whence comes *soropegos*, a maker of coffins. Luther uses *Lade* <note>Chest/Ark</note>. The Belgians *kistse*. The Italians *Cassa*. The Spanish *Arca*. *Capsa* is named from "containing" (*capiendo*), as is *Capulum*, which was the chest in which the dead were carried out, a *Todtenkist* <note>German: Coffin</note>. Hence the "capular old man," who is near death and worthy of the *capulum*. Finally, he was to be carried out in the *capulum* at the departure of the Israelites from Egypt; nor did they do so before that time for the sake of the *ekphoras* <note>original: ἐκφοράς, "carrying out/funeral procession"</note>, lest they incur ill will or fall into bad suspicions. It did not help <margin>page d.</margin> the Brothers (these are the words of Lyra*) to carry his body there immediately after his death, as they carried the body of their Father; so that by this, because the body of Joseph remained in Egypt, the memory of his benefits would remain longer among the Egyptians, and thus they would treat the children of Israel staying among them more gently.

The pious bones of Joseph are treated playfully by Pseudo-Jonathan, who adds in his Paraphrase that the corpse was toasted and fumigated. *And they made for him tithes and incense* <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: ועשו לו עשורין וקירין</note>, which is ambiguous, for it denotes both crowning and fumigating. Then, he says in the same place: *and they submerged him in the midst of the Nile* <note>original: ושקעו יתיה בגו נילוס</note>. The same is believed by modern Jews, who, relying on that tradition, fable that his bones were secretly cast into the Nilotic river of Egypt, lest the Egyptians find out where they placed them; and, lest they stop raining lies upon lies, they interpose another strange invention like an internal wall: that it happened once that <margin>Peter Comestor, Hist. Scholastica</margin> the Nile, rising more than usual, flooded the land where that coffin of Joseph was, and overwhelmed that whole place with water. The Hebrews, bound by an oath, were to carry his bones away with them when they departed from Egypt. Then Moses cast into the waters the Tetragrammaton (the name of God) written on a golden plate, and the plate, floating on the waters, was carried until it stood over the place where Joseph’s coffin was; and from there the Hebrews lifted his bones, which are said to have prophesied the difficulty of the future journey. These inventions would not suffice unless they also added the bleating of a sheep, by which they were led to the traces of the coffin, and because of this benefit they led with them that *divining* <note>original: μαντικήν</note> sheep, calling it the "Sheep of Joseph," about <margin>Psalm 79</margin> which they want it understood what is written*: *You lead Joseph like a sheep.* They add also another invention...

<column-break/>

...by which they conclude the transportation of Joseph's bones as if with a corollary: namely, even today they hope for a return to the land of Canaan, and believe that the bones of the deceased will all eventually be carried there according to that verse: <margin>Joel 3:2</margin> *I will gather all nations into the valley of Jehoshaphat.* Hence, as much as they can (says <margin>Against the Jews, ch. 33</margin> Victor von Carben*), they hasten to travel there during their life. But if they cannot because of life's necessity, they do not despair of salvation, provided their bones are carried to that land by their descendants, led by the example of Joseph, who ordered his own bones and those of his father Jacob to be transferred from Egypt to the land of Canaan. There is a great harvest of fables, and a good crop of them everywhere; to keep them from smelling, it is necessary to season them with aloe and myrrh, not with a frugal and sparing hand, but a generous one, like the Egyptians. Let them delight in their trifles and dirges, and overshadow the *carrying of the bones* <note>original: σκελοφορίαν</note> with their mystical veil.

But if they set the deportation of Joseph as an example for their own future deportation into the valley of Jehoshaphat, let them also set the eternal covenant of God concerning the eternal and spiritual kingdom of the Messiah, in which Joseph bids his descendants to rest safely; and they will certainly be carried into the certain and eternally lasting seats of the mansions. Let them emigrate with Joseph in that faith by which he migrated, and they will migrate into the true land of rest. For a ready transport, let them not immerse the little ark in the muddy marsh of the Nile, but bringing it into the sanctuary of the heart, let them show it as a certain monument of faith, so that they remember both Joseph and the Ancestors, and by their example, sleep in the same faith and promise in which they fell asleep.

Furthermore, let us survey the journey by which Joseph was led to the land of desire. The most holy man had predicted shortly before his death that it would happen someday that they would enter upon the most desired journey after liberation from the Egyptian yoke, and he beautifully testified with the word *Pakad* <note>original: פקד</note>, the certain care and benevolence of God testifying doubly, saying in verse 24: *I die, and God visiting will visit you* <note>original: אנכי מת ואלהים פקד יפקד אתכם</note>. Moses repeats these words when, in Exodus 13:19, he carried *the bones of Joseph with him* <note>original: את עצמות יוסף עמו</note>. These bones of the holy man are read to have been committed to the earth <margin>Joshua 24:23</margin> in that place of the promised land which his Father had given as a special possession. It was the public field of the city <margin>Genesis 48:22</margin> of Sichem, just as Blessed John made mention of that Sichem field in chapter 4:5, but under the name of Sychar, as the place was later named.

I will not now recount how it happened that Moses finished the embalming and burial of Joseph in so few words, mentioning nothing at all of those things that had happened around it, as he had done in the case of Jacob. We have seen enough so far of the magnificently performed funeral, as well as the transportation of Jacob magnificently cared for by Joseph, in which I cannot yet be brought to rebuke certain things along with Calvin <note>John Calvin, the Reformer</note> in his Commentary, page 316. That learned man says that Joseph did not behave himself prudently enough in some matters, and sometimes sinned in excess; that he conformed to foreign customs out of fear rather than judgment. Our Joseph, in the use of external things, had the mind of Paul: to the Jew he is a Jew, to the Egyptians an Egyptian, so that in both places he might gain some. In those rites which were consistent with the custom of religion, he wished to find no fault peevishly, lest he or his people among a nation so proud and tenacious of ancient purpose...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

...lest it should bring about either loss or destruction. He knew he was dealing with a people of a stiff neck, who could not be easily restrained or led toward things that were new and unusual. Here, his political wisdom is recognized, by which he occasionally indulges the customs of a nation when he cannot stop them. He prepares himself for civil customs; he prepares himself for the public square. When he was at Memphis, he lived according to the Memphite custom. It is no small part of wisdom to be able to accommodate oneself to the time, and from there to take opportunities for doing or omitting those things which are expedient. A wise man, through his work and charming speech, either fosters acceptance or softens matters with sweet eloquence. Local custom—and it was not unpraiseworthy—was to embalm the deceased with spices. Joseph was entirely able to observe this, and indeed wished to, giving orders to his <term>pollinctores</term> <note>undertakers or embalmers who prepared the body</note> that they should perform the embalming according to their established rules. He employs his own embalmers, whom he could command to carry out his orders without any mark of superstition. The interpreter Mercerus (p. 740), a man of excellent judgment, affirms that Joseph did this for the sake of honoring his father and preserving the body longer, without the *superstition* of the Egyptians. Jacob was King of the land of Canaan in promise, and therefore he is embalmed in a royal manner, so that he might be buried with royal pomp. He had to be carried a long distance, and it was necessary to be preserved against <term>sepsis</term> <note>original Greek: σήψιν; decay or putrefaction</note>. Humanity, the dignity of Jacob, and moreover necessity demanded this rite. Thus, we wonder less at the manner of <term>the burial preparation and the lamentations</term> <note>original Greek: ἐνταφιασμῷ καὶ θρήνων</note>. If the inhabitants showed no moderation in their manner, we wonder less. But we wonder most of all that, hindered by no prejudice, they were of such a profuse spirit toward those whom they usually loathed as "men who are shepherds." That they followed Jacob, the foster-son and parent of shepherds, with such great honors. Diverse in spirit, diverse in dress, diverse in religion, they here turn aside into one threshing floor, wailing, mourning, and weeping. The more I think on it, the more I marvel at this astounding deed, while I see the eyes of so many leaders, so many prophets, and so many nobles conspiring in the same tears. Whatever the custom may have been, whether it had more ostentation than true grief, it suffices that it was given to the honor of Jacob. That ample, frequent, and clearly royal pomp indicates and testifies to the favor which both Jacob and Joseph possessed with the King and all the Egyptians. That very large company shows that Joseph’s integrity was so accepted by the King and all the Egyptians that he obtained much more than he asked of them. Meanwhile, let it be that different people did the same thing in different ways and signs, and with different intent. It is pleasing to speak with Augustine*, that those things which are enjoined neither against good faith nor against good morals are to be held as indifferent, and should be observed for the sake of the society of those among whom one lives. If at that time that nation had <term>malice</term> <note>original Greek: κακοήθειαν; or "bad character/customs"</note>, far be it from us to say that a man so pleasing to God and men approved of it or observed it with his own people. Just as the Egyptians did not impose their customs upon Joseph, though he was a foreigner, so Joseph did not impose his upon the Egyptians. Nor is it presumed that he was feared, by whom the whole land feared for itself, and at whose command the nobles and the whole people...

Letter to Casulanus and Januarius.
</margin>

<margin>
Egyptian funeral rites.
</margin>

...rose up. Just as the Jews learned certain customs from the Egyptians, such as performing the most grand funerals for Jacob and Joseph, so along with the transportation of their bones, they carried certain "small baskets" <note>metaphorical for small customs or traditions</note> out of Egypt into the land of Canaan. It will not be out of order to subjoin the burial institutions of the Jews to the Egyptian ones; for, since we have seen the funerals of Jacob and Joseph celebrated in Egypt conspicuously and splendidly according to the custom of a foreign nation, we shall see how they carried away from here certain fragments <note>original Greek: ἀποσπασμάτια</note> from a foreign rite, venerable by its very antiquity. Therefore, having left Egypt, so that this may appear in some way, we will now approach closer to the land of Canaan. However, so that this may be done rightly and in some order, we shall consider *mourning and the care of the funeral*. You may read everywhere that the whole people followed the deaths and funerals of Moses, Aaron, Joshua, and others with mourning and long weeping. Examples closer to the departure of the Israelites from Egypt are those of Moses and Aaron. The Israelites wept for Moses thirty days <margin>Deut. 34 v. 8</margin>, and for Aaron just as many <margin>Numbers 20 v. [29]</margin>. Truly, their custom brought this about: that they should spend certain days in public mourning, which they had seen done in Egypt; these days are called <margin>ימי בכי</margin> *days of weeping, i.e., Deut. 34 v. 8*. Rupertus says on this passage: *That the children of Israel are said to have wept for Moses and Aaron for thirty (wrongly written as three hundred) days, this remained with the people not yet fully instructed from the Egyptian custom; for thereafter, having gradually become accustomed to better things, they departed from that superstition, as Scripture says: Weep a little over the dead. But the mourning for the dead is seven days.* According to the institution of this or that region, the account of the funeral rites was established. Just as the rites of mourning were various among various nations, so likewise were the days. Sometimes the number seven was pleasing, sometimes nine, sometimes another. *For mourning is seven days* says the son of Sirach <note>Ecclesiasticus 22:12</note>, which number was observed by Joseph, when at the funeral of his father <margin>ch. 22:13</margin> *he made a mourning of seven days. And the inhabitants of the land of Canaan saw the mourning and said:* <margin>Gen. 50:10</margin> *This is a great mourning for the Egyptians.* From this it appears that the mourning of seven days remained for the Jews from this ancient custom, and that number seven has the significance of rest because of the memory of the Sabbath. Augustine says: *I do not know whether it is found in the scriptures that a mourning of nine days was celebrated for any of the Saints, which among the Latins they call the Novendiale. Whence it seems to me that any Christians who observe this number for their dead should be prohibited from this custom, which belongs more to the custom of the gentiles. But the seventh day has authority in the Scriptures, whence it is written in another place: The mourning of the dead is seven days. Moreover, the number seven is especially a sign of rest because of the Sacrament of the Sabbath, whence it is deservedly shown to the dead as to those who are resting. However, the Egyptians decupled <note>multiplied by ten</note> this number in the mourning for Jacob, for they mourned him seventy days.* For some pagans, the funeral solemnities were concluded on the ninth day, on which the man was buried and a sacrifice was offered, whence the custom of the <term>novendial</term> <note>nine-day</note> sacrifices; the institution of nine-day holidays and games; and the scattering of the nine-day ashes.

Questions on Genesis 172, p. 88, Vol. 4.
</margin>

Servius <margin>on the 5th Aeneid, page 378.</margin> says: *It should be known among the ancestors that where someone had died, he was carried back to his house, and remained there for seven days; on the eighth he was burned, and on the ninth he was buried,* hence Horace: *To scatter the nine-day ashes.* <term>Ennata epi nekro agomena</term> <note>Greek: Εννατα ἐπὶ νεκρῷ ἀγόμενα — rites performed on the ninth day for the dead</note> Philoxenus explains <gloss>Glossary page 143.</gloss> as "Nine-day rites." A nine-day period pleased the Romans; a seven-day period (if I may be allowed to <term>coin a term</term> <note>Latin: *onomatologein*</note>) pleased the Jews, and that in honor of the Sabbath. But neither was this unique to the Jews. Ammianus Marcellinus mentions the son of Grumbates, a royal youth, whom they mourned for seven days <margin>Book 19, page 242</margin> in these words worthy of memory: *Grumbates, King of the Chionitae, was advancing toward the walls with a very ready band of attendants; when a most skilled observer noticed him coming within range of a missile, he discharged a ballista and pierced through the breastplate and chest of his son, a youth in the first flower of manhood, who was clinging to his father's side... At which death the Royal court was saddened, and all the nobles along with the parent were struck by the sudden disaster; a public mourning being declared, the youth, commendable for his nobility and beloved, was mourned according to the ritual of his own nation. Therefore, just as he was accustomed to be armed, he was carried out and placed on a certain large and high platform, around which ten couches were spread, carrying effigies of dead men, so carefully prepared by the undertakers <margin>page 243.</margin> that they were images similar to bodies already buried; and for the space of seven days all the men indeed, throughout their quarters and companies, indulged in feasts, dancing and singing certain sad kinds of dirges, lamenting the royal youth. But the women, with miserable wailing, cried out in their accustomed weeping for the hope of the nation, cut down in the first flower of age.* There was a mourning of seven days when Severus departed from the living, of which Herodian says <margin>Book 4, 2.</margin>: <term>For it is the custom of the Romans to deify those emperors who die leaving children as successors; and such a ceremony they call "apotheosis" <note>Greek: ἀποθέωσιν — becoming a god</note>. A mixture of mourning with festival and religious rite is displayed throughout the whole city. For they bury the body of the deceased with a costly funeral, according to the law of men. But having fashioned a wax image in every way like the deceased, they place it on a very large ivory couch raised up high at the entrance of the palace, spreading gold-woven covers beneath it. And that image lies there in the guise of a sick man, looking pale. On either side of the couch they sit for most of the day: on the left side the whole Senate, wearing black cloaks; on the right, all the women to whom the dignity of husbands or fathers grants distinguished honor. None of them is seen wearing gold or adorned with necklaces, but clothed in plain white garments, they present the appearance of mourners. These aforementioned things are performed for seven days.</term> Herodian looks back to the origin of this rite and the examples, since from the beginning Augustus consecrated Julius, Tiberius consecrated Augustus, Nero Claudius, Titus Vespasian, Domitian Titus, Trajan Nerva, Hadrian Trajan, Pius Hadrian, Marcus Pius, and Commodus Marcus; all were sons or at least designated successors in the Empire, which is why Herodian speaks only of the consecration of Emperors, not excluding meanwhile

<column-break/>

other consecrations, performed for singular causes and by various counsel and judgment. For no one, as far as I remember, has described the rite of consecration used among the Ancients as extensively as Herodian in this place, with whom those things which are read more briefly in Dio regarding Severus are entirely to be compared. Lycurgus defined mourning as eleven days, according to Plutarch: <term>He prescribed a short time for mourning, eleven days. On the twelfth day, after sacrificing, it was necessary to end the mourning.</term> <margin>Plutarch, Numa page 67.</margin> The Lawgiver Numa <gloss>the same, Volume 1, section 6.</gloss> limited mourning to certain ages and times; he determined the longest to be ten months. The same Plutarch in *Numa* page 67: <term>He arranged mourning according to age and time. For example, that one should not mourn a child younger than three years, nor one older for more months than the years he lived, up to twelve. And for no age beyond that. But the longest time of mourning should be a ten-month period, during which also the wives of the deceased remain widows.</term> Seneca says: *The Ancestors established a year for women to mourn,* <margin>Epistle 62, page 637.</margin> *not so that they should mourn that long, but that they should not mourn longer: which he repeats elsewhere.* *The Ancestors gave a space of ten <margin>Consolation to Helvia, chapter 15, page 640.</margin> months to those mourning husbands, so that they might settle the persistence of female grief by public decree. They did not forbid mourning, but limited it.* The prescribed time of ten months, of which the year consisted in the age of Romulus, as Macrobius teaches: *The Romans once, by the authority of Romulus, had their year organized into ten months,* <margin>1. Saturnalia 12, page 201.</margin> *which year began from March, and was completed in three hundred and four days, so that six months indeed—that is, April, June, Sextilis (August), September, November, December—were of thirty days. But four—March, May, Quintilis (July), October—were dispatched with thirty-one each.* Numa increased the year by two months, but did not increase the spans of mourning. The severity of mourning was enjoined upon women for those ten months, hence Ovid:
> Therefore he kept the accustomed numbers in the year; <margin>3. Fasti</margin>
> For this space of time the sad woman mourns her husband.
When Poplicola died, the matrons, having held a separate council, <term>mourned a whole year for a man so very honorable and worthy of emulation.</term> <margin>Plutarch, Poplicola page 109.</margin> When Livia, the wife of Tiberius Caesar, died, the Senate decreed mourning for the women <term>for a whole year,</term> as Dio witnesses. <margin>Book 58, page 712.</margin> These few things prove how unequal the days and months of funeral mournings were, nor is that surprising given the variety of nations. They were shorter or longer, according to the dignity of the dead. Students of wisdom, according to Maimonides, <margin>Laws of Mourning, chapter 13.</margin> are to be wailed for according to the measure of their learning, yet never to be wept for beyond a month, nor mourned beyond a year. He cites the examples of Moses and Rabbi Judah.
From the example of Moses and Aaron, the Jews calculated the number of mourning days, and regarded the matter as settled from then on. The example of foreign female captives also persuaded them, who were to mourn their parents killed in war for a <term>month of days</term> <note>Hebrew: ירח ימים — Yerach Yamim</note> <margin>Deuteronomy 21:13.</margin> i.e., for as many days as the moon completes in its circuit, until the moon returns in its orbit to the same state in which it had started. Thus a *whole month* is circumscribed, because the Hebrews had lunar months, and measured months by the lunar circuit and revolution. Thus the time of mourning is assigned by God as a lunar month, which has 29 and a half days.

Egyptian funeral rites.

When this period of mourning was completed, the captive Israelite woman could be joined in marriage to the one who had been persuaded by her beauty. Treating this example, Josephus derives from here a general rule for mourning, writing: <margin>Antiquities of the Jews, Book 4, Chapter 8, page 126.</margin> *Thirty days of tears for a beloved one are sufficient for the wise.* To which words <note>original: "Αὐτάρκεις ἐπὶ τοῖς δακρύοις τριάκοντα ἡμέρας τῷ φιλτάτῳ τοῖς φρονίμοις."</note> <margin>Oration on the death of Theodosius.</margin> [Ambrose adds] *Josephus records that the period of thirty days was a suitable time among the Jews according to the Mosaic laws.* It was not permitted to touch the marriage bed until she had been shaved, put on mourning attire, and lamented her kinsmen and friends. *When, however, she had completed thirty days in this mourning* (for those thirty days were sufficient for the well-instructed to weep and mourn for their dearest ones) *then they could proceed to nuptials and marriage.* The Jews did not cross these limits even during the final siege of the City [Jerusalem]. When the death of the leader Josephus, son of Matthias, was announced, there was public mourning in Jerusalem for thirty days, concerning which lamentation Josephus writes in *The Jewish War, Book 3, Chapter 15, page 856*: <margin>p. 856.</margin> *The mourning over the disaster was made public. And some lamented guests, others relatives, others friends, others brothers. But everyone lamented Josephus, so that for thirty-one days the wailing in the city did not cease. And many hired flute-players, who led the dirges for them.* <note>original Greek: "Τὸ ἐπὶ τῷ σφάλματι πένθος ἐδημοσιεύθη... Πλείστους δὲ μισθοῦσθαι τοὺς αὐλητὰς, οἳ θρήνων ἐξῆρχον αὐτοῖς."</note> Here, in the circumstance of time, the custom of hiring flute-players who would play a mournful melody is revealed. He relates that in that celebration of the final day, <term>leaders of the dirges</term> <note>Greek: θρήνων ἐξάρχους (threnon exarchous)</note> were interspersed. The music of flutes was in use for a long time in funeral preparations. Among the Jews, indeed, a custom of this kind can hardly be traced from the most ancient times, since no certain trace of it appears in the histories of the Old Testament. If we search the ancient heroic times of which Homer writes, there are some recent examples of these ceremonies; regarding Hector: <margin>Iliad, Book 24, line 720.</margin> *Then they laid him on a carved bed, and beside him they seated singers, leaders of the dirges, who wailed a mournful song; they lamented, and the women groaned in response.* <note>original Greek: "ἔπειτα Τρητοῖς ἐν λεχέεσσι θέσαν..."</note>

### Exodus Chapter 1, verse 8.

> Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.
> <note>Hebrew: ויקם מלך חדש על-מצרים אשר לא-ידע את-יוסף</note>
> <note>Greek: Ἀνέστη δὲ βασιλεὺς ἕτερος ἐπ' Αἴγυπτον, ὃς οὐκ ᾔδει τὸν Ἰωσήφ.</note>
> *A new King meanwhile rose over Egypt, who was ignorant of Joseph.*

<margin>A new King.</margin>
**W**ho this NEW KING is in this passage, who is said to have been ignorant of Joseph, is a matter of controversy; nor is this surprising in such an ancient matter. It is probable that it was Memnophis II, who is called Memnon by others, who was the afflicter of the Jewish race; he is called a <term>new</term> or <term>different king</term> <note>Greek: ἕτερος βασιλεύς (heteros basileus)</note> in *Acts 7:18*, because he was of a new and different character, habit, manner, and government from the preceding Kings, who "knew" Joseph and the Hebrews—that is, they had treated them kindly. Just as by the same phrase the Savior said to the impious, <margin>Matthew 25:12.</margin> whose lives he does not approve: *I do not know you*; but of the pious, whose actions he approves, it is said *the LORD knows the way of the righteous*, *Psalm 1:6.* To be known by God is eternal happiness; not to be known is eternal misery. One hundred years after the death of Joseph, a new King was elevated to the throne of Egypt, who did not acknowledge Joseph, and whose descendants—lest they should plot against his throne—

<column-break/>

<margin>A new King.</margin>
he had determined to diminish by force and fraud. But the victorious hand of God frustrates the new plans of the new King. The Seventy [the Septuagint] translated it as <term>another king</term> <note>Greek: βασιλεὺς ἕτερος</note>, for which Aquila and Theodotion used <term>a new king</term> <note>Greek: βασιλεὺς καινός</note>; this substitution is not new, for in the New Testament, what *Mark 6:17* calls <term>another</term> [shows the terms are interchangeable]. From this, the hallucination of Cajetan is evident, who—because Joseph is said to be unknown to the new King by a peculiar idiom, and based on a misunderstood passage in *Isaiah 52:4*—judged that this King was an <term>Assyrian</term> by race, not an Egyptian. As we have said, the word *knowledge* is taken, according to Hebrew custom, for the affections and effects following knowledge: <term>to know</term> <note>Hebrew: ידע (yada)</note> means *to pay attention to and care for*, just as <term>to hear</term> <note>Hebrew: שמע (shama)</note> means *to obey and be compliant.* Not dissimilar is the use of <term>to not know</term> for <term>to not use</term> in Juvenal: <margin>Satire 7, line 97.</margin> *To not know wine for the whole of December.* To be known is a matter of gratitude and benefit; just as, on the contrary, to not be known is a matter of ingratitude. However, not only malice, but also the imprudence and ingratitude of the King is rebuked. <margin>Pindar, Isthmian 7, line 23.</margin> Cinglius [says]: <term>For old favor sleeps, and mortals are unmindful.</term> <note>Greek: υπ. καὶ παλαιὰ γὰρ εὕδει χάρις, ἀμνάμονες δὲ βροτοί.</note> The gratitude for the old deed had ceased, and a barbaric confusion of opinions, cults, and manners had taken hold after the death of this blessed man, Joseph. Do men receive incoming grace so kindly, let alone remain sufficiently mindful of the past? Livy [says the same]. Thus, among few does gratitude remain at the last, says Seneca in *On Benefits, Book 1, Chapter 12*: <term>Every benefactor is unrequited</term> <note>Greek: Πᾶς ἀχάρις ἐστὶν εὐεργετὴς</note>, [and] Philo in *On Joseph, page 567.* Therefore, the text argues the ingratitude of the Egyptian King, which is why the Chaldean [Targum] says best, according to the translation of Cardinal Toletus: *He did not confirm the decrees of Joseph*, i.e., out of hatred for him and his race, he changed the things piously and wisely established by him in religion and politics. Elated by the success of affairs, he began to disdain the pacts which had once been struck between the King of Egypt and the family of Jacob by the law of hospitality while they were sojourning in Egypt. With the noble merits of Joseph obliterated by the injury of time, he harassed those born of Jewish blood with the harshest labors, using the idleness of the people as a pretext for his envy. For, as Josephus says, they were ordered to divide the river into many trenches, <term>to build walls for the cities, and to heap up mounds.</term> <margin>v. 12, 13, 14, 22.</margin> <margin>Antiquities, Book 2, Chapter 5, page 54.</margin> <note>Greek: τείχη τε οἰκοδομεῖν... ἐπεμβαίνειν</note> Nor did he omit plans for the destruction of their whole race, <term>dealing craftily</term> <note>Greek: κατασοφισάμενα</note> (*v. 10*) so that the descendants of those for whose sake God had once blessed them might be oppressed. And that new King began to build store-cities. Finally, he turned his cruel mind toward the universal slaughter of the male offspring, to satisfy his grim soul; <term>this man</term>, says Saint Stephen, <margin>Acts 7:19.</margin> *dealt craftily with our race, forcing them to expose their infants, so that they might not be kept alive.* <note>Greek: κατασοφισάμενον τὸ γένος ἡμῶν...</note> The tyranny begun under Memnophis continued through four successors—Orus (or Busiris), Cecrops, Thermutis, and Rathoris—for 64 years. In Cenchres, whom Tacitus calls Bocchoris, it saw a tragic end, as befits tyrants; for, submerged in the sea, he suffered a just destruction for the crime of injured divine majesty along with his whole army. *And the indignant life fled with a groan to the shadows below.* For what will you say? Is not this new King called Pharaoh in *verse 11*? We know that the name Pharaoh was a common name for Kings in Egypt, as Josephus also testifies...

# Exodus Chapter 1, Verse 8

<margin>A new King. Book 16 of *The City of God*, chapter 43.</margin> even according to Augustine. * For it was a solemn custom among most peoples to address Kings and Magistrates by a certain common name of dignity, or even by the proper name of some distinguished Prince; just as among the Romans there were the "Augusti"; so among the Egyptians, the "Pharaohs." *Servius on the 12th book of the *Aeneid*, page 759: "We know it often happens that the rest possess the name of the first King: as among the Romans they are called Augusti, among the Albans Sylvii, among the Persians Arsacidae, among the Egyptians Ptolemies, and among the Athenians Cecropidae."* This very point is read among the fragments of Manetho <note>An ancient Egyptian priest and historian</note> in Eusebius, as cited by Annius of Viterbo. *“All the Kings of the Egyptians were then called Pharaohs, not having this as a proper name, but they used this name for their dignity as Kings, just as among us the Emperors are called Augusti. Therefore, each Pharaoh had his own proper name.”* There is also another Manetho circulated, which Annius published, but who should be considered anyone else rather than Manetho, in which on folio 94b, Pharaohs were so called for their dignity. Therefore, in this place, Pharaoh will be a name not of a man, but of an honor, to speak with Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville</note> in Book 7, chapter 1; in which sense mention is made of a certain Pharaoh in the time of Abraham (*Genesis 12:15*) who commanded Sarah, Abraham's wife, to be brought to him; in the time of Joseph (*Genesis 41:1*); in the age of Moses, throughout this book; and finally in almost the latest times, where Pharaoh Necho (*2 Kings 23:29 and Jeremiah 46:2*) is named; and lastly Pharaoh Hophra (*Jeremiah 44:30*). From this it is clearly established that it was a title of dignity, so that there was a need for a proper name to distinguish who the King was. Later, after Alexander, they were called Ptolemies after the first King of Egypt of that name, Ptolemy son of Lagus, such as Ptolemy Philadelphus, Ptolemy Euergetes, Ptolemy Philopator, Ptolemy Epiphanes, Ptolemy Philometor, Ptolemy Euergetes II, Ptolemy Lathurus (or Lamyros), and Ptolemy Auletes. This was also customary among other Kings. The Kings of the Philistines were called Abimelech (*Genesis 20:2, 26:1, 4, 34:1*); of the Amalekites, Agag (*Numbers 24:7, 1 Samuel 15:8*); of the Persians, Artaxerxes (*Ezra 4:7, 7:1, Nehemiah 13:6*). Not otherwise than the Parthians had their Arsacids, the Indians their Palimbothi, the Romans their Augusti, the Edessenes their Agbari, the Damascenes their Adadi, the Turks their Sultans, the Persians their Khosraus or Chosroes, the Syrians their Antiochi, and the Cilicians their Teucers or Ajaxes.

Indeed, the common pronunciation of the Tetragrammaton <note>original: יהוה</note> now resounds in the Chairs of the Doctors and the benches of the learners, but care must be taken lest it be pronounced in any company except with great reverence, and though it be common, let it not become

<margin>Jehovah is the essential name of God.</margin> worn out or cheapened by the common rabble or by light minds, who have no regard for where or by whom it is pronounced. Nor should those things be despised which Fuller <note>Nicholas Fuller, a 17th-century philologist</note> (*Book 4, chapter 13*) brought forth with what seems to be fair judgment: that it is expedient for the unrefined and unskilled, *of whom there is the greatest number, that "Lord" be more frequently set forth, but for the learned, "Jehovah" should more often be enunciated, and then especially where some hidden force of emphasis lies beneath.* By a great consensus of all, whether those initiated into the mysteries or those to be initiated, it is fitting that we hear and follow the voice of Moses in fear (*Deuteronomy 28:58*): *Fear this most glorious and supremely reverend name, namely Jehovah, your God.* For the name JEHOVAH is of such virtue and magnificence that to extol its dignity and reverence in a due manner, neither the uncovering of the head nor the bowing of the knees suffices. Isis had such honor among the Egyptians that on the pavement of the Isiac temple, as Plutarch reports, it was inscribed: *I am all that was, is, and shall be, and no mortal has ever lifted my veil.* This eulogy fits none but our JEHOVAH, the veil of whose wisdom and essence no mortal has ever revealed by speaking. For here all the speech of Rhetoricians is conquered; all the voices of the Sophists, I say, are surpassed by the magnitude of the voice of JEHOVAH, and everything we say is less than the truth. Yet let us speak while we live, while we write, and while we cannot speak of Him worthily, let us never cease to speak of Him. Hence, if we had the sweetness and power of speaking of an Augustine, a Jerome, a Chrysostom, or a Lactantius, we could still find no words significant enough to thunder out the discourses, hymns, and praises of our JEHOVAH. Indeed, if we were to fly up with St. Paul into the third heaven, we would see nothing but the "back parts" of God. In this fragility of life, therefore, all our knowledge of the name JEHOVAH is fragile, a fact which Gregory Nazianzen weighed well while acknowledging our weakness in grasping the name Jehovah or "The Lord over all, most venerable" <note>original Greek: Κύριος ἐπὶ πάντων σεβασμιώτατον</note>, distinguishing between "the things around God" and "the things concerning God," saying: *“Neither did He allow the essence of God to be taught, nor has any voice encompassed it; but being sketched from the things around God, we gather a certain dim phantom of the things according to Him.”* Explaining this, he adds: *“Lord is His name, but we seek after His nature, or His being in itself, and that which is bound together.”* Cyprian also aims at this (*Epistle 57*): *“There is need,” he says, “of those words where a multitude must be distinguished by the proper marks of names. For God, who is alone, the whole word is His. God has no name, and everything that has a name is His, and all names which are of goodness and eminence are God's.”* If you seek a name, it is beyond all names. It is the confession of the Heathens themselves, fortified by the oracle of Apollo of Clazomenae, that He is:
->*Self-begotten, untaught, motherless, unshakable,*<-

->*This is God.*<-

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES.

**Column 1**

<margin>Jehovah is the essential name of God.</margin>
...it can never be said enough. In the mysteries of the Pagans, the High Priests used to command the "profane" to depart, though the priest himself was often the most profane and sometimes the most wicked of all. Here, we invite even the profane themselves, so that by approaching they may search out the sublimity of our Jehovah, and at the sight of this admirable name, cease to be profane. If you are profane, go out from yourself, strip off your old self, and enter here; for here is God, here is Jehovah, who repels no one from the consideration of his name, but admits all. Strip off the profane man, strip off the sorcerer, strip off the superstitious heart, and enter with a humble spirit to behold that adorable and admirable name יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton: YHWH</note>, the adored holy and sanctifying name; let us hear the Holy of Holies and the Sanctifier. Truly! Just as Abraham, when about to speak before Jehovah, sought permission to speak from Him and acknowledged himself to be but dust and ashes, *Genesis 18:27*; so we also, about to speak of *Jehovah*, standing before Him with humility of mind, pray for His countenance, that He might deign to be the guide of our writing and speaking, and rule our tongue with His celestial light. Come then, Jehovah, act according to Your clemency, *O Lord, save us; O Lord, grant us success* <note>original Hebrew: אנה יהוה הושיעה נא אנה יהוה הצליחה נא; original Greek: σῶζον δὴ εὐοδωθὴν δή</note>; so that we may celebrate Your most sacred name with mouth and heart, *Psalm 118:25.* *Act for the sake of Your name,* *Jeremiah 14:7.*

In this *study* <note>Greek: μελετήσει</note> concerning the four-lettered name, the first thing to be considered is the variety of its writing. For this name is found written in various ways among the Hebrews: In the Canon <note>The Bible</note> with four letters, or with two (if the *Yod-He* is not considered a single letter), and it is written with three vowel points, which belong to the names either *Adonai* or *Elohim*. Hence this name is called by the Hebrews the "Name of Four Letters" <note>Hebrew: שם ארבע אותיות</note>, by the Greeks the *Tetragrammaton*, and by *Rabbi Maimonides in Moreh Nevukhim, chapter 61* as "the name Yod He Vav He" <note>Hebrew: שם יוד הא ווו הא</note>. The Jews, for the sake of superstitious piety, or even out of hatred for Christians, are accustomed to almost obliterate this complete writing of the Tetragrammaton by changing the second *He* into a *Dalet*, as is commonly found in the *Jerusalem Targum* as *Al-dom* or *Al-dim*!

<insert>Photius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, notes in Epistle 162 (p. 218) that the name Jehovah was "ineffable" <note>unutterable</note> to the Jews, and was not written in common letters; he claims that among the Jews, to name it or to curse it were held in equal regard.</insert>

*Regarding this,* he says, *the phrase "Naming the name of the Lord God" refers to the fact that the name of God was forbidden to the Jews. Rather, they thought that by some glory, the word GOD was the only sound to be brought forth through the lips. It was altogether unutterable and unspoken, except for what was preserved for the High Priests alone, for the honor and veneration of the Divine. Therefore, it was not even written in their own letters, but they characterized it with certain strange and altered forms of letters, representing it with more mystical symbols. There were four letters, from which it was called the Tetragrammaton by them. Thus, they say, it was the same among the Jews to curse God as to name Him; that is, to bring His unutterable name through the lips, and especially to utter it to common ears.* <note>Translated from the Greek quote of Photius</note>. It is indeed probable that the Jews initially abstained from the native reading and pronunciation of the Tetragrammaton out of a certain religious feeling, namely, lest it become cheapened by daily use; for so says <margin>Maimonides in the chapter cited above.</margin> Maimonides in the chapter cited above. But this religion of theirs eventually degenerated into a most foul superstition, so that as if by divine command, they forbade the reading of this name to everyone

**Column 2**

<margin>Jehovah is the essential name of God.</margin>
except for the High Priest when publicly reciting the Ecclesiastical blessing described in *Numbers 6*. Not only did they forbid it, but they even established capital punishment for those who dared to utter it and made them exiles from the world to come, according to the pronouncement of *Abba Saul*, who also excludes from eternal *salvation* the one who pronounces the name יהוה according to its letters. Hence we find a tragic story in the Talmudic work *title: Avodah Zarah.* When Rabbi Chanina son of Teradion was brought forth, they said: "By what reason have you acted thus regarding the Law?" And when he replied: "*As Jehovah my God commanded me*, so I acted," they immediately condemned him to burning, his wife to death, and finally his daughter to a brothel. The Benevolent Reader will find more on this matter in *M. Amama*, Drusius, Galatinus, and others. From this, the religion of those who do not dare to pronounce this name according to its characters and points was evident. While we attribute all excellence and uniqueness to this word, we assert that there is nothing singular here that can be brought forward without a sense of duty. Nor is there reason for us to revere the Jews, who, as they have failed to achieve a correct understanding of names in many things, are also unreliable witnesses here regarding the claim of truth. Therefore, the truth must be investigated by another path, which will be clearer if we follow guides closer to God than the Jews. It is clear (writes Gregor Franck*) from the names *Ieuo, Iao, and Io* <margin>Lexicon Sanctum n. 60. p. 67.</margin> (*for so the ancients used to say for Jupiter*) that the word *Jehovah* was so frequent among the ancient Jews that the knowledge and use of it spread to other nations, especially the Greeks, the rivals of the Easterners. To whom, then, would it seem likely that the ancient Israelites religiously abstained from its pronunciation? *Therefore, I do not understand who incited Drusius against the English when he wrote that they sin gravely because they read this name.* But it was enough that he was countered by <margin>chapter 6, Mishnah book 2.</margin> Fuller*, and his vain mockery is refuted by six hundred instances of our *naming conventions* <note>Greek: ὀνοματοθεσίας</note>, in which there repeatedly occur proper names that embrace almost the entire Tetragrammaton (or Trigrammaton according to the Chaldeans) within themselves, such as *Jehonathan, Jehoram, Jeho-chavath, Jehotzadak*, etc. These were commonly pronounced in such a way that they leave no room for doubt. Furthermore, the abbreviated writing of this name in the Targums is not infrequent among Jewish commentators, and it is established by them in various ways. In the Chaldean Targums, this Tetragrammaton is written sometimes in this way '', sometimes with this character ויי, and also in this form ייי, as in the Genoese edition of the Octapla Psalter. In the most ancient Targum, according to Elias Levita in his *Meturgeman*, it has a figure made of three *Yods* and a circle that passes through the upper two and rests upon them, partly without points, partly with points placed beneath ⸬; this figure is not unlike the figure in the *Pirke Avot of Rabbi Nathan the Babylonian*. Hebrew commentators, however, use this form יי, or י'י, or likewise two ייי, or even just י. See *Rabbi David Kimhi on Amos; Aloysius 2. Sacr. elect. 27. Vol. 1; Kircher, Prodromus Coptus ch. 8; Galatinus book 2 on the Secrets of Catholic Truth ch. 10*, who in that same place shows us this figure, י, which he says is found in the manuscripts of the ancient Hebrews to express the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity. # Exodus VI. v. 6. 7.

<margin>
Jehovah, the
essential
name of
God.
</margin>
...is found among the Jews and their commentators in various forms; indeed, even today it is read by some Christians with the vowel points of *Adonai* <note>Hebrew: "Lord"</note> and *Elohim* <note>Hebrew: "God"</note> added to the letters יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH</note>. Yet this is done without the superstition of the Jews, which they still constantly observe today, as is evident from the writings of Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel <note>A famous 17th-century Portuguese rabbi and founder of the first Hebrew printing press in Amsterdam</note>.
<margin>
The Conciliator
on Exodus,
question 3.
</margin>
Nevertheless, the word is by no means destitute of its own proper punctuation <note>vowel points</note>, a fact which has been proven by many learned doctors until now. In this nomenclature, therefore, we worship God, inasmuch as He consecrated this name for Himself, revealed it to us, and exhibited it in letters. Why then should we shudder at its pronunciation, as Beza does in his commentary on *Psalm 70:7*? For by this name, the *Tetragrammaton* <note>Greek: "four-lettered name"</note>, God manifested Himself of old, not only to Moses and the Jews, but also to the Patriarchs before and after the Flood. Nor do we allow ourselves to be persuaded that this most august name was not manifested by God to the Patriarchs living before Moses, and that Moses—who frequently insists on the use of the name יהוה in Genesis—used it by "historical anticipation," describing the events of earlier times with words common to his own age. For truly, even if this reasoning holds weight in other matters, yet when it comes to the specific words of the Deity or the Patriarchs, we do not see it as likely that Moses exchanged their words for the vocabulary of his own century. For upon these words rested either the authority of God or the faith of the Patriarchs, neither of which ought to or could be removed. Nor are we moved from this opinion by that Mosaic testimony in *Exodus 6:3*, where we read it written: *I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as El Shaddai <note>God Almighty</note>, but by my name יהוה I was not known to them.* For since, besides the "self-existence" <note>original: αὐτουσίαν</note> of God, that name also denotes eternity, independence, efficacy (by which all creatures have their being from God), and truth, God regarded this last aspect most especially in *verse 2*. Thus, the sense of those words emerges as follows: *I indeed appeared to Abraham in the name El Shaddai, that is, God Almighty, and so I taught that I was able to fulfill for them the promise of the land of Canaan; but in the name יהוה I did not become known to them, that is, I had not yet performed for them what I promised. Now, however, at last you shall know the power of this name; namely, you shall know that I am not only "the one who is" <note>original: ὄντα</note> but also "the one who will be" <note>original: ἐσόμενον</note>.* What I promised, what I declared to Abraham was possible for me to do, I will now finally cause to exist; I will now perform it. These are the words of Sixtus Amama in his treatise on the name יהוה inserted in his *Antibarbara Biblica, p. 477*, whom the Blessed Glassius cites in this manner in *Sacred Philology, book 4, tract 2, p. 674*; compare also Blessed Walther in *Spicilegium of Controversies, p. 98 and following*. Conformable to this exposition are the things read in the Chaldean Paraphrase <note>The Targum</note> interpreted by Fagius: *I promised them promises, and in all of them I said to them, I am God Almighty. And in the name יהוה I was not made known to them—it is not written "I did not make known," but "I was not made known," that is, I was not made known in the property of my truth, for which my name is called יהוה, that is, truthful and constant, because of the truth of my words, since behold, I promised them and have not yet performed or confirmed it.* Thus Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note>, whose words are in the Chaldean Paraphrase, accurately observes that in the Mosaic text, it is not the active verb *hoda'ti* <note>I made known</note> that is placed—by which those of the contrary opinion might

<column-break/>

establish their view—but the passive *noda'ti* <note>I was known</note>. This is also what Rabbi Ezra <note>Ibn Ezra</note> maintains in his commentary on the name יהוה against a certain Menahem <note>Menahem ben Saruq</note>, about whom he writes: *Menahem says the word "noda'ti" is of the Niphal <note>passive</note> form and is not like the name יהוה.* And from this he reads the passive verb. Some establish that *shemi* <note>my name</note> is put for *bi-shemi* <note>in my name</note>, so that the sense is: "in my name," or as Tremellius reads, "by my name יהוה I was not known to them." And thus, from what has been said so far, it clearly appears that this Tetragrammaton name was by no means unknown to the Fathers before Moses; see, if you please, Weidner in his *Places of Faith, p. 126 B*; Rungius, *Commentary on Exodus, p. 222 B*; Gerhard, *Theological Commonplaces, Vol. 1, on the Nature of God, p. 23 B*; Dorscheus, *Disputation on the Name Jehovah, p. 8 D*; Calovius, *System of Theology, Vol. 2, p. 118*. After the reading of the Tetragrammaton, order requires that we inquire briefly into the origin of this most glorious name. Blessed Luther, in *Vol. 2 of the Latin Jena edition, p. 62*, and some others with him, count this name among the "unoriginated" <note>original: ἀγένητα</note> words, as being of no etymology, but consisting of Hebrew letters by divine counsel to foreshadow some mystery. More correctly, however, according to the common opinion, it is derived from the verb of "essence" <note>to be</note>, which derivation Blessed Luther himself approves in *Vol. 8 of the German Jena edition, p. 118*. This derivation, as it is most true, so it is most certain and indubitable; it immediately elevates our mind to the contemplation of the Being who is most true, best, most perfect, Independent, supreme, the first cause and ultimate end of all other things. It is derived, moreover, from *hayah*, "he was," not, as Jerome ab Oleastro began to suggest, from *havah*, "destruction" or "ruin." This etymology is also hinted at by Hiscupus, whom Amama cites in *Antibarbara Biblica*, writing: *Vau* in *matzpitz* <note>A cryptogram for the divine name</note> is put for *Yod*, as in יהוה for *hayah*. Lest, however, they pour darkness over such light, it should be noted that by the *Atbash* <note>A substitution cipher where the first letter of the alphabet is replaced by the last, etc.</note> permutation of letters, that *matzpitz* [מצפץ] is put for יהוה. For the Hebrews are sometimes accustomed to invert their alphabet, so that they put *Aleph* in place of *Tav* and vice versa, *Beth* in place of *Shin* and vice versa; and thus, consequently, from that conversion of letters, that *matzpitz* arises from יהוה; compare Münster in his *Biur Happershim annexed to the Chaldean Grammar*. The Socinians, and among them Smalcius in his *Response to Ravensperger, p. 17*, and Crellius in his *Book on God and Divine Attributes, ch. 11, p. 77*, partly embrace Oleastro's opinion with "both hands" (as they say), and partly devise a new origin for this. Both, in order to remove all significance of "Essence," say that by this name at least the *real fulfillment of promises* is noted. But "it is greater than what anyone could say in words" <note>original Greek: μεῖζον γάρ ἐστιν, ἢ ὡς ἂν λόγῳ τις εἴποι</note>. For there is such power of speech in the name JEHOVAH, by reason of the identity of Essence, that whatever God is, all of that resides and shines forth in that name; so much so that if anyone could comprehend that name, he would think he had comprehended God Himself—that is, the whole of what God is—in himself. For Jehovah is the source of sources; He is the Source who opened the fountain and liquid of letters from the first age; He embraces all essence, breathes essence into things, and gives Spirit to the world. All this very thing that is, is in Him, and outside of Him there is nothing; and it depends on Him, moves in Him, and through Him proceeds everything that is. He is the Being of Beings <note>Ens Entium</note>, from whom is the being of all things, and without whom there is no being. Whence not only the firmness of promises and threats and con—

But since such a form is not unusual in proper names, Critics rightly observe that *Jehovah* is a name derived from the root *havah* <note>to be</note> and the initial *yod* is a prefix of the name, as can be seen in other proper names like *Isaac*.
<margin>Jehovah is the essential name of God.</margin>

->Furthermore, we are not merely concerned with the reading and origin alone when we call this most august name into the meditation of our mind and pen; rather, we must inquire as much as possible: what is the genuine meaning of this word, and is it the proper and incommunicable name of God alone? Many *Socinians* <note>A sect that denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ</note> within the bosom of the Church deny this, following the footsteps of the Jews; but it is certain to us, and ought to be to all, that this name is proper and incommunicable to the one and only God. For as it is the most proper name of the Divine Essence and nature—which Divine essence is so simple that it lacks all composition, in which essence the absolute perfection of God resides, through which essence God is present to all created things and knows all things, and through which essence He is immutable—so also this name *Jehovah* is most proper to God alone. it is common to none of the creatures with Him, but is such that it distinguishes God from the rest of creatures truly and most really. For since "names are imposed on things for the sake of manifestation and distinction," as *Justin Martyr* says in his *Admonition to the Greeks*, the same will be true of the name proper to God alone. *For what is a name,* says *Ambrose*
<margin>On Psalm 43, p. 333.</margin>
*except that by which each one is properly signified, so that it is not common to him with others.* Therefore, a name is the property of each individual, by which he can be understood. Whence the Hebrews say, "He is His name, and His name is He" <note>original: הוא שמו ושמו הוא</note>; hence, when they are about to call upon God, they very often call Him *The Name* <note>original: השם / HaShem</note>, understanding the name *Jehovah*, but they do not express it according to its letters and native notation out of a certain superstition which was discussed above. *Erasmus*, in his *Catechism VI on the Creed*, suggests that something should be conceded to their dullness. *Among the Jews,* he says, *there was such veneration of the divine name that they wrote that mystical name, which they call the Tetragrammaton, in letters not to be spoken aloud.* But let this be granted to the dull minds of the Jews; for God is as unnamable as...
<margin>T. V. works p. 990.</margin>
