# Exodus VI. v. 6. 7.

<margin>
Jehovah is the essential name of God.
</margin>
...is unimaginable and invisible. Indeed, God is altogether unnamable, just as he is indefinable, if we wish to speak with the utmost precision; for we are not those who are fit even to discourse upon the name of God. However, since we read it said in the Holy Books <note>original: "S. Pandectis," a term for the Bible</note>: *You shall not take the name of God in vain*, we rightly abstain from all irreverence toward this name; yet nowhere is it said: *You shall not name God*. That point is made by the Scholiast on Theodotus’s *Eclogue v. 213*:

> Say where the earth towers above the light axis of heaven,
> And I grant that you can speak the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter name of God: YHWH</note> of God.

We confess it is ineffable, not because no one is able to utter or say it, but because no one can fully explain it on account of the depth of the divine name, because *it is the name which is above every name*. But to the matter at hand. Theologians prove by many arguments that God claims this name for himself alone and uniquely, so much so that we can easily dispense with the proof of it. We shall bring forward at least one classic testimony, lest we seem <term>empty</term> <note>Greek: κενὸν (kenon)</note>, by which it may be clear to all that this name is proper, essential, and incommunicable to God alone: *Psalm 83:18*. Expressly this <term>name יהוה (Jehovah)</term> is said to be proper to God alone — *That they may know that you, whose name is Jehovah, you alone are the Most High over all the earth*. However, so that the sense of these words (by which the exclusive proposition is fully completed) may be clearer, we determine the subject of this proposition, which the word *alone* <note>Hebrew: לבדך (levadcha)</note> expresses, and the predicate, which the remaining words describe. Thus, whether the Blessed Luther refers the particle ALONE to the predicate, or wishes it to be added to the subject, we do not object, since we intend at least this: namely, that in this exclusive proposition, this particle excludes all other subjects—except that which is noted by the pronoun *You* (and according to the text, is that Most High over all the earth)—from participation in the Predicate, which is Jehovah. Moreover, the repetition of the pronoun adds greater emphasis, by which Rabbi Kimchi also testifies *on Hosea chapter 5 verse 14* that an increase of meaning is introduced, so that the significance is strengthened and increased. Compare Buxtorf <margin>Thesaurus book 2, section 8.</margin> Ambrose departs from our opinion in *book 3 on Faith to Gratian, chapter 2*, who refers the exclusion not to the words *the name Jehovah* but to what follows: namely, that God alone is the most high. Thus also the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> determine: <term>the only most high</term> <note>Greek: ὁ μόνος ὕψιστος</note>, whom Blessed Luther follows in his first version: *That you alone are the All-Highest*; but in his last version he approaches our interpretation: *that you with the name are called LORD alone / and the highest in all the world*. Whence some explain these words of the Psalmist as: that you, O Jehovah, are alone and your name alone is, and that you alone are the most high. *Others*: That you, whose name alone is Jehovah, are the most high. *That is*: that you, to whom alone the name יהוה (Jehovah) belongs, are the most high. *Others*: that you alone are, your name is Jehovah, and that you are the most high, *that is*: you alone are what you are called, the only true God Jehovah, who presides over the whole earth, not just one region. Compare Rauppius, Friedlibius, Prückner and others. <margin>Commentaries on this place.</margin> And since among other names Jehovah is also called MOST HIGH in this place, we cannot fail to bring up Melchizedek here, while he was blessing Abraham <margin>Jehovah is the essential name of God.</margin> *Genesis 14:19, 20, 22*. In the hearing of the army, he invoked God <term>Elyon</term> <note>Hebrew: עליון (Most High)</note>, by whose blessing that great Father of believers, lifting his hand to heaven in a new rite, introduced this *new* name of the Lord—whereas previously only those two were in use, יהוה (Jehovah) and אלהים (Elohim)—saying under oath: *I have lifted my hand to Jehovah, the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth*. When Cornelius Musso, Bishop of Bitonto, had noted this <margin>Synod of Bitonto p. 264.</margin> he adds concerning Moses, when he had said: *He is, and the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob*, that by the first name it was declared that God alone exists, and others do not exist [of themselves] but are made, and therefore depend continually upon Him; by the others it is noted that the souls of men do not perish with their bodies, but live an eternal life set free. *So says he.* But we proceed to the other Essential names of God expressing the Divine: for <term>I AM</term> <note>Hebrew: אהיה (Ehyeh)</note> <term>and</term> יה (Jah), which we judge to be primitive from the conjunction of these two names in *Isaiah 12:2 and 26:4*, not contracted or shortened from the name Jehovah, are names proper to God alone, so much so that the name Jah nowhere occurs in Holy Scripture concerning anyone else but God, especially in hymns consecrated to God, *Exodus 15:2, Isaiah 2:2, 25:4, 38:4, Psalm 68:5, 89:9* and elsewhere. Concerning the name *Ehyeh* (I AM), that this is an essential name of God, and thus truly a <term>synonym</term> <note>Greek: συνώνυμος</note> of the Tetragrammaton, is clear from this: because it has the same root as the Tetragrammaton, and also because this *Ehyeh* is rendered by this very Tetragrammaton in the immediately following verse; for where in *verse 14* God had said *I AM sent me to you*, immediately in the following verse he adds *Jehovah sent me to you*. Hence it happened that Blessed Calixtus, in his *Disputations on the chief heads of the Christian religion*, where he treats of the Triune and One God, well weighed the word *Ehyeh*, and distinguishing it from other divine words says <margin>page 8.</margin> *The essence of God is best enunciated because He himself is the most simple Being, supremely necessary, in whom you cannot distinguish even by reason between Being and Essence, or between Being itself and the possibility of Being; and because He is a Being of this kind, He wished to be called by a name proper and peculiar to Himself, Jehovah, which descends from the root "to be" (hayah or havah), to signify that He is such a Being that is His own Entity, and does not have it from elsewhere, but all other things have it from Him. And hence to Moses asking what His name was, He answered "I am who I am" (Ehyeh asher Ehyeh), or as the Seventy interpreted it: <term>I am the One who Is</term> <note>Greek: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν</note>. See on this matter Rupert in his exposition of Psalm 44, Jerome to Damasus, the Fathers of the Synod of Frankfurt in the Capitularies of Charlemagne, Gregory the Great, and Rudolph Ardens.* Nor does the name *El* (God), which others wrongly wish to be a shortening of *Eloah*, receive a different meaning in the singular, since it is a proper name of God not so much by reason of Etymology as by *biblical usage*. Whence even if in the plural it is used either of strong men or of the gods of the nations, in the singular it denotes either *power and strength* in respect to its origin, or *the very essence of God* from Biblical usage; for that reason it is commonly rendered by the Seventy by the word <term>God</term> <note>Greek: θεὸς (Theos)</note>, and almost only by the word <term>Strong One</term> <note>Greek: ἰσχυρὸς (Ischyros)</note>, very rarely by "strong" as an epithet, attributed to God alone in those places of Scripture, namely *2 Samuel 22:31, Nehemiah 1:5, Job 22.*

</margin>

17. 6. 33. 29. chapter 34. 31. chapter 35. 22. chapter 37. 5. 10. Psalm 7. 12. chapter 42. 3. In the New Testament, however, it is expressed by the Syrian idiom *Eli* <note>original: אלי</note>, Matthew 27:46, and in the Jerusalem dialect *Eli, Eli* <note>original: ηλι ηλι</note>, Matthew 15:34. Finally, we come to the words *Elohim* <note>original: אלהים</note> and *Adonai* <note>original: אדני</note> signifying the Divine persons; before we speak of them, we speak with Daniel in chapter 9:19, with the sacred opening: *Adonai shemaah*, "O Lord, hear." In this place, we first note that *Adonai* with the *Kametz* <note>A Hebrew vowel mark indicating a long 'a' sound</note> at the end is a name proper to God alone, which denotes such a Lord who is the absolute Lord of all things, <term>Lord of lords and King of kings</term> <note>original Greek: κύριος κυριευόντων, καὶ βασιλεὺς βασιλευόντων</note>; one who is the *Adon* <note>original: אדן</note>—the basis, support, and pillar upon which all things in this entire universe rest as their principle. By His quickening power they consist and live; if He withdraws His strength, they vanish into vanity, indeed, into purest nothingness. He is the one in whom, as our basis, "we live, move, and have our being," Acts 17:28. He is the one who, to the pious and faithful in whatever adversities and storms of tribulation—and to whom Daniel looks in this prayer—provides *Adonai*: a pillar, support, and fortification, lest they fall, broken in spirit, swallowed by temptations, or conquered by Satan, and thus lose their salvation. Moreover, since both names are plural in number, they always imply a plurality of persons; thus, it is plural not only by reason of its grammatical ending but also by reason of its meaning. However, the latter name, *Elohim*, when accepted <term>metonymically</term> <note>Using one word to stand in for a related concept</note>, is also attributed to creatures as instruments of God, who in a certain way and manner act in His stead on this earth, Psalm 103:20, Exodus 21:6, chapter 22:7, 1 Samuel 2:25. But what we have written so far concerning the names of God, especially the name JEHOVAH, we confess is like the stammering of a child; for the depth of riches in this one name hides such mysteries that all flesh cannot grasp them. Human intellect grows dull before it, and the senses recoil. Nothing earthly, nothing human, nothing accessible to our senses is proposed here; rather, this name remains utterly incomprehensible in the sterility of human genius. Not only this, but His other names and attributes are also impassable to human wit, so that one may rightly confess with the wise Agur and say with wonder: *Mah shemo?* "What is His name?" <note>Proverbs 30:4</note> where the particle *Mah* <note>original: מה</note> is the voice of one wondering to extol the matter, as Rabbi Joseph Albo* advises.

<margin>4. Iccar. 10.</margin>

Therefore, since the name *Jehovah* <note>original: יהוה</note> surpasses all grasp of the human mind by so many leagues, and is so perfect and sublime that when it is spoken, it cannot truly be spoken; when it is estimated, it cannot be estimated; when it is defined, it escapes definition and far exceeds its boundaries—it is fitting to venerate this name and not use it in vain. As for the impieties and profanations practiced with this name, we rightly refrain from listing them, lest we seem to be teaching them. Casters of metal plates for amulets abuse it, an example of which is shown by Wierus*, who acted as a Christian by refusing to explain the details too openly, for fear of curious imitators of such impieties, thus blocking every path to error. Those who manufacture amulets from the name *Jehovah* intend to procure safety for both soul and body. The superstitious transfer such a sacrosanct name to that which it should by no means be extended. Let the sign be signed for you, not on the neck but in the heart; not

<margin>5. De Praestigiis Daemonum, book 10, p. 541.</margin>

<column-break/>

upon the chest, but *within* the breast. The most faithful amulet is in the name of Jehovah, if you adore Jehovah with your whole heart and grasp Him with your whole soul. There is no safer, no more secure amulet for you than if one invokes Jehovah in truth; if you carry Him in your breast, you have nothing to fear, even if the power of the heavens should break or your body be exposed to fire.

<margin>* 4. Hieroglyphics p. 51.</margin>

He who lacks this phylactery <note>A protective charm or prayer-case</note>, says Goropius Becanus*, will find no profit in having six hundred charms hanging from his neck, or bound to his arms, or sewn into his clothes, or carried for protection in any other way. I would indeed wish that nothing similar were found among Christians, and that no one would trust so much in the phylacteries hung upon them that the signs are taken for the things signified. What ought to be referred to the memory of past things, or the expectation of future ones, or some useful admonition, is instead worshipped superstitiously with divine honors and believed to have some divine power to guard the body, the soul, or both. Compare Jacobus de Valentia, Bishop of Christopolis, in his Commentary on Psalm 148, p. 1012. Away, then, with those "character-bearers" with their characters and superstitious amulets! No faith should be shown to them as if they were "Pseudo-Jehovists," and no virtue or efficacy should be ascribed to them, regardless of their chatter to the contrary—that the word they use is sacrosanct, or that there is no blessing except in the name of the Most Holy Jehovah, in whom all things are blessed. But this is a malicious and blasphemous abuse, not a pious use of the best name, which belongs to God alone, not to the Devil, who seeks his own advantage, honor, and glory under such amulets and superstitious characters. The same thing happens to this Most Holy name as happened of old: for how many names of the Heathen gods, I ask, were born from it? We see no reason to conclude otherwise than that this name was spread far and wide among the Gentiles. For the neighboring nations to the Jews were not ignorant of this Most Holy name, whether you look at the Canaanites or the Assyrians, who (the Devil driving them) inverted it and transferred it to foul Orgies, calling it *Jao* or *Jove* more openly. Hence arose the word <term>Iao</term> <note>original Greek: ιαω</note> in Orpheus, just as Diodorus Siculus reports*; Irenaeus* reads it as *Laoth*; Tertullian as *Jaa*; Epiphanius and Origen as *Iaoth*; Clement of Alexandria as <term>Iau</term> <note>original Greek: ιαυ</note>; and Theodoret, from the opinion of the Samaritans, as <term>Iabai</term> or <term>Iabe</term> <note>original Greek: ιαβαὶ / ιαβὲ</term>.

<margin>book 1, ch. 2, sec. 66.</margin>

Furthermore, they uttered the name of JEHOVAH as <term>Ido</term> <note>original Greek: ιδω</note>, by which name the Supreme God is read to be called in Macrobius*: <term>"Declare that Iao is the highest god of all."</term> <note>original Greek: Φράζεο τῶν πάντων ὕπατον θεὸν ἔμμεν Ἰάω</note>. Concerning this remarkable mutation of this most glorious and holy name *Jehovah* <note>original: יהוה</note>, besides Johannes Crojus in his *Sacred and Historical Observations*, part 1, ch. 12; Gerhard Vossius in his *Addenda to Book 1 on Idolatry*, p. 15, and *Book 2 on Idolatry*, 14, p. 378; and Selden in *Syntagma* 2, ch. 1, *On the Syrian Gods*, p. 202 ff.; Bochart in *Geography*, book 2, ch. 18, p. 479, says: When the Amalekites were conquered by Israel while Moses, prostrate before God on the mountain, lifted his hands to heaven, an altar was erected as a monument of victory with this inscription: *JEHOVAH NISI* <note>original: יהוה נסי - The Lord is my Banner</note>. Posterity, interpreting this as the "Nysaean" or "Nissean" God, thought that *Nysa* was there, and they called Bacchus <term>Dionysus</term> <note>original Greek: Διόνυσον</note> instead of *Jehovah Nysaeus*, substituting *Jova* for *Jehovah*. Although the name *Iao* itself (how the Greeks pronounced *Jehovah* <note>original: יהוה</note>) is referred to Bacchus in the Oracle of Clarian Apollo. So...

# Exodus VI, v. 6, 7. Exodus IX. v. 18.

<margin>Jehovah is the essential name of God.</margin>
From the name **Jehovah**, as some would have it, was made *Jo-Bacchus*; from **Adonai**, *Adoneus*; from **El**, **Eloah**, or **Eleloe**, came *Eleleus*. Thus, the most holy names of God were, through remarkable blasphemy, transferred to the most impure idols. So says that author.

<margin>1. Preparation for the Gospel, book 1, ch. 7.</margin>
From this it also happened that the Hebrew name of God, **El**, was *El* to the Phoenicians. Sanchoniathon is the authority (cited in Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian</note>) that they called Saturn by this name, where it stands thus: *“But Kronos <note>Saturn</note>, taking over the rule of his father, took the Earth in marriage, and fathered from her four children: Ilus (who is also called Kronos), Betylus, Dagon (who is the god of grain), and Atlas. The allies of Ilus-Kronos were called Elohim, as if they were the 'Kronians' or those associated with Kronos.”* Here, *Il* is none other than **El**, and *Elohim* is nothing other than the Hebrew **Elohim** <note>original: אלהים</note>. It is well known even to schoolboys that this name is used throughout the Scriptures for Angels, judges, false gods, and indeed for the supreme and only God. Thus, a passage of Porphyry cited by Eusebius in the same book concerning "Israel, otherwise Saturn" seems in need of correction: *“Kronos, whom the Phoenicians call Israel.”* It is hardly credible that the Phoenicians would regard Israel—the father of a neighboring and most hated nation—as their supreme God (that is, Molech or Saturn). Therefore, the passage seems corrupt; instead of *Israel*, one should read *Il*. The error likely arose because those who used abbreviations often wrote *Is* for *Israel* with a line drawn above it. These points are from Vossius, *On Idolatry*, book 18, p. 143.

<margin>On Magistrates, p. 10.</margin>
In almost the same way, Postellus, Goropius, and others think the name *Jove* <note>Jupiter</note> comes from **Jehovah**. Truly, although the name of Jove alludes to the ineffable name of God, and one might suspect (as Camerarius says) that this sound, heard from the Patriarchs, reached the posterity of various nations in this way; nevertheless, one must speak of these things cautiously, distinctly, and religiously, lest divine and heavenly truth be profaned in any part. For cultivated fields are not more foully wasted by wild boars than the sanctity of religion and the truth of God's wisdom are by the arguments and conclusions of human reason.

<margin>On Sirach, p. 142.</margin>
But we, having removed and extinguished those superstitions and profanations of the Divine name, enter into the praises of our **Jehovah**. Singing to **Jehovah**, we say with a redoubled voice with David from Psalm 3:9: *“Salvation is from JEHOVAH”* <note>original: ליהוה הישועה</note>; and from Psalm 18:3: *“JEHOVAH is the horn of my salvation”* <note>original: יהוה קרן ישעי</note>. For the more we intend to describe the name of **JEHOVAH**, the less we comprehend it; therefore, we bring our words to an end with the saying of the Royal Prophet: *“Great is JEHOVAH and greatly to be praised”* <note>original: גדול יי’ ומהלל מאוד</note>, *“and of his greatness there is no searching out”* <note>original: ולגדלתו אין חקר</note>. Psalm 145:3. We have tasted, sipped, and sought the name that is mysteriously immense, yet once sought it is not immediately found, because the greatness of the name is beyond all comprehension. <margin>Isaiah 26:4.</margin> Meanwhile, regarding what we have written about your most sacred, holy, and merciful name, **Jehovah**, in such poverty of mind and intellect, may you look upon it with favor—this small sign of Christian affection and pledge of most humble observance. Grant that my final word may be **JEHOVAH**. Thus I pray.

<column-break/>

<margin>The Egyptian Plagues.</margin>
->“For this cause have I raised thee up, to show in thee<-
->my power; and that my name may be declared<-
->throughout all the earth.”<-
<note>Exodus 9:16. The text provides the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin versions of this verse.</note>

As we begin the narration of the things done in Egypt by the powerful hand of God, we set forth **PHARAOH**, the father of all evil kings, as an example. God made him stand, or appointed him, so that He might show and demonstrate in him the force of His power and the honor of His glory, so that these omnipotent deeds might be proclaimed by the shared remembrance of all throughout the whole world. In squalor, grief, and thick clouds of calamity, the people of Israel had grown numb under the Egyptian blows; and it was fitting that "blow-striking" Egypt should feel the blows herself and pay the penalties due. The first voice of God, indignant at the Egyptian Tyrant, was to Moses: <margin>ch. 3 v. 6, 7.</margin> *“I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.”* *“I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt <note>original: Misraim</note>, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows.”* <margin>v. 8.</margin> *“And I am come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians, and to bring them up out of that land unto a good land and a large, unto a land flowing with milk and honey; unto the place of the Canaanites, and the Hittites, and the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites.”* <margin>v. 9.</margin> *“Now therefore, behold, the cry of the children of Israel is come unto me: and I have also seen the oppression wherewith the Egyptians oppress them.”* <margin>v. 10.</margin> *“Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt.”* **Jehovah** speaks His sentence and judges the cause of His people; He weighs and estimates the afflictions of the children of Israel. He frequently uses the phrase that He is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; by the doubling of words—that He has "surely seen" <note>literally "seeing I have seen"</note>—He places before their eyes with that <term>anadiplosis</term> <note>the repetition of a word at the end of one clause and the beginning of the next</note> the speed and certainty of help against the "inclement taskmasters," as He calls them. It is something immense that God promises when He says He will "come down." God descends when He hears, when He helps. God descends from heaven when the cry of the oppressed ascends. <margin>ch. 2 v. 23.</margin> For the children of Israel sighed by reason of the work, and they cried out, and their cry came up unto God by reason of the work: *“And their cry for help rose up to God from the service.”* <note>original: ותעל שועתם אל-האלהים מן-העבודה</note> That most harsh servitude of the Israelites is expressed by the word *Avodah* <note>original: העבודה</note>, which the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament</note> express elsewhere as "enslavement" and here as "tyrannical oppression." That <term>Hiphil</term> <note>a Hebrew verb form indicating causative action</note> verb is used not so much for this oppression as for that with which the Babylonians tortured their captives (Jer. 17:14). Certainly, a severe servitude is described, which was without any relief of spirit or mercy, whereby the souls of the servants were broken; for that exaction was "to tyrannize over life with hard works," utterly wearing them out with sorrows (which is the emphasis of the Greek verb), performing extremely hard tasks which exhausted the Jews into a state of faintness. **Eloah** God descended to destroy and cast down the impious King with his impious subjects, who wished to keep the people chosen by God cast down, so that they might enter the land...

# 168 BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Plagues of Egypt.</margin> *a land flowing with milk and honey*, that is, with an abundance and plenty of all things, a richness of crops, and a multitude of goods at low cost. Moreover, God had selected Moses for this work of liberation, which was not to be accomplished by an army or weapons; Moses, who, upon hearing that he would not be recalling his people by means of an army or weapons, did not merely ask, but actually pleaded to be relieved of the burden of this embassy, saying: *Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh, and that I should lead the children of Israel out of Egypt?* <note>Exodus 3:11</note> He speaks as one struck down and prostrated, feeling within himself no ornaments of dignity or protections of authority; but God raises up the man of a different opinion and a hesitant will, marks and designates him as the minister of His will, and declares him sufficient, saying: I WILL BE WITH THEE. How much is contained in those four words <note>original Latin: "duobus verbis" (two words: *Ero tecum*)</note> spoken by Jehovah! He makes Himself a partner and companion. Truly, this is a remarkable speech of God, comforting and strengthening, and necessary for the present embassy. He who had been of a stricken and dejected spirit, now with an upright <margin>v. 13 & following</margin> and ready mind, asks and says: *Behold, I will go to the children of Israel, and I will say to them, "The God of your fathers has sent me to you," and they will say to me, "What is his name?" What then shall I answer them?* He inquires about the divine name so that the embassy might exult and triumph. Here, the Deity does not show Himself harsh or violent toward one ignorant of the divine Name, but rather, providing instruction amidst the Egyptian mist and darkness, He answers: אהיה אשר אהיה <note>Hebrew: *Ehyeh asher Ehyeh*</note>: I AM WHO I AM <note>original: "ERO, qui ERO" (I will be who I will be)</note>. What God says to His attendant and Minister is immense and infinite. The speech of God exults and triumphs in that *Ehyeh* (I AM), and so that he might lean more upon that *Ehyeh* and trust more and more in the power of the most mighty GOD, God added <margin>v. 15.</margin>: *Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: Jehovah, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, hath sent me unto you. This is my name forever, and this is my memorial unto <margin>v. 16.</margin> generation and generation.* *Go and gather the elders of Israel together, and say to them: Jehovah, the God of your fathers, appeared to me—the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—saying: "In remembering, I have remembered you <note>A literal translation of the Hebrew idiom *paqod paqadti*, meaning "I have surely visited/remembered you."</note>, and that which has been done to you in Egypt <margin>v. 17.</margin>;" therefore I said: "I will lead you out of the affliction of Egypt, to the land of the Canaanite, and the Hittite, and the Amorite, and the Perizzite, and the Hivite, and the Jebusite, to a land flowing with milk and honey."* With ready words, He provides ready aid and assistance, such as He furnished to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; hidden in those words, *paqod paqadti*, is the firmest promise of protection and defense, making and confirming the pledge for certain that He would snatch away the Jewish people and transfer them from the seat and region of the wicked into a seat where there is no want, no beggary, nor a miserable or pitiable condition of living. Moreover, Moses exults with happiness and triumphs with joy while he further hears God saying: <margin>v. 18.</margin> *They shall obey thy voice, and thou shalt go, thou and the elders of Israel, unto the King of Egypt, and ye shall say to him: "Jehovah, the God of the Hebrews, hath met with us. Now therefore let us go, we pray thee, three days' journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to Jehovah our God."* Moses hears the beginning and foundation of his defense, and lest he doubt any longer, God meets his doubt, saying: ושמעו לקלך <note>Hebrew: "And they shall listen to your voice"</note>: and to instruct him with greater certainty, He handed over the outcome of the embassy to be thoroughly perceived, speaking of that monster

<column-break/>

and prodigy of a man <note>Referring to Pharaoh</note>: *But I know that the King of Egypt will not permit you to go, except <margin>The Plagues of Egypt.</margin> by a strong hand.* <margin>v. 19.</margin> *I will therefore stretch out my hand and <margin>v. 20.</margin> strike Egypt with all my wonders (בכל נפלאתי <note>Hebrew: "with all my wonders"</note>) which I shall do in the midst thereof, and after that he will let you go;* <margin>v. 21.</margin> *and I will give this people favor in the eyes of the Egyptians, and it shall be, when ye go, ye shall not go empty;* <margin>v. 22.</margin> *but every woman shall ask of her neighbor and of her that sojourneth in her house, vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, and raiment, which ye shall put upon your sons and upon your daughters, and ye shall spoil Egypt.* This indicates the mind of the obstinate King: that he would not send the people away until they were plainly extorted by a strong hand, that is, in a violent manner, through various prodigies, through various plagues, with no small struggle, and no minor fight. He predicts that there will be resistance and opposition, lest the Israelites, broken by calamities and the fury of the King, should cast away hope. But when the people are finally expelled and cast out, they will not depart without rich spoils, nor leave the land without gold, silver, and other precious things. Yet Moses, the leader and standard-bearer, though left with the strength and firmness of the embassy, hesitates again, questioning because of the unbelief of the people and the power of the Tyrant, saying: <margin>ch. 4 v. 1.</margin> *Behold, they will not believe me, nor obey my voice, for they will say: "Jehovah hath not appeared to thee."* The Lord had just said: *They shall hear thy voice.* Having heard this voice of divine counsel and singular power, why does he tremble? Why does he call into doubt the sentence passed? Why does he suddenly change his excited and inflamed mind? <margin>Borrhäus col. 443.</margin> <note>Martin Borrhäus (1499–1564), a Protestant theologian and commentator.</note> *No light struggle with the word of God is indicated here, by which the calling of Moses was tossed about. But it was not without progress and increase of his contending faith.* God restrains his doubting mind; He leads him by the eyes and hands into the present matter, commanding him to gaze with intent eyes upon the future reality itself, saying to him: *What is that in thy hand?* Now, he was holding a rod in his hand. A lesson is given from the rod; he is commanded to cast it down. The rod is cast down, and it turns <margin>v. 3.</margin> *into a serpent*. Moses sees the snake moving itself and flees in terror, but Jehovah said: <margin>v. 4.</margin> *Stretch out thy hand and take it by the tail.* Strengthened, he took the serpent in his hand, and the rod returned to its former shape. The power of performing portents is granted to Moses's hand, by which he might prove his calling to the Israelites, and <margin>v. 5.</margin> *that the Israelites might believe that Jehovah, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, had appeared to Moses.* Not content with this prodigy alone, so that He might further declare His power and divinity, and His present help in the most difficult matters, the Lord said again: *Put thy hand into <margin>v. 6.</margin> thy bosom. And when he had put it into his bosom, behold, his hand was leprous as snow.* Moses's eyes are struck with amazement; they are aroused by the new portent, and it remains fixed in his mind and sense that these things, through which God speaks, pertain to the salvation of the Israelites and the life of the Jewish citizens; and providing the meaning Himself, He says: <margin>v. 8.</margin> *It shall be, if they will not believe thee, nor obey <margin>v. 9.</margin> the voice of the first sign, they will believe the voice of the latter sign.* *It shall come to pass, moreover, if they will not believe even these two signs, nor obey thy voice, then thou shalt take of the water of the river and pour it upon the land, and the waters which thou takest from the river shall be turned into blood upon the land.* With these things thus presented to strengthen his faith, Moses becomes a suppliant, and thinking humbly of himself, he says, after—

I do not know Jehovah, and I will not let Israel go.* The mind and speech of an impious man are expressed by this Cyclopean sentiment. <note>The author compares Pharaoh's arrogance to the lawless Cyclopes of Greek mythology.</note> I worship the Gods of my fathers, I observe ancient institutions, and since the power of the immortal Gods has either been transferred to me, or certainly shared with me, I plainly ignore this new Israelite God. So I think, so I persuade myself, that I am King in my own kingdom. I do what I want, and I acknowledge no superior. May the Gods destroy you with your petitions. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Egyptian Plagues.</margin>
When an account of the work was demanded, they approached Pharaoh and protested against the injustice: that no straw was provided for them, yet the full production of bricks was still required. Thus, they and the people were being harshly punished and unworthily penalized—or, as the Hebrew idiom uniquely puts it, <gloss>והטאת עמך</gloss>, which Pagninus translates as: *And your people sin.* The ancient interpreter: *And it is acted unjustly against your people.* The Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>: <gloss>you will wrong your people</gloss>. Junius: *The fault is with your people,* that is, as he explains, with the Egyptians, who do not supply the straw and yet daily demand from us the former number of bricks. The Genevans: *And the fault is in your people.* The Hebrew <gloss>חטאת</gloss> <note>chata't</note> is not a noun there; for if it were, the punctuation would be <gloss>חַטַּאת</gloss> or <gloss>חַטָּאת</gloss>, but it is a past tense verb in the 3rd person feminine singular, which is placed as <gloss>חָטְאת</gloss> just as <gloss>קָרָאת</gloss> is used for <gloss>קָרָאתָ</gloss> in Deuteronomy 31:29. Therefore, they cast the blame upon the Egyptians and remove it from themselves. But the King, being more vehemently moved by these things, said:

<margin>verse 16.</margin>
*<gloss>נרפים אתם נרפים</gloss>: You are idle, you are idle.* The stiff-necked and hard-hearted Tyrant says that those whom he knew to be most occupied are loitering; he alleges laziness, for which they use the worship of God as a pretext. And he repeats the command, lest anything be lacking in his tyranny, saying:

<margin>verse 18.</margin>
*Go and work. Straw shall not be given to you, and you shall deliver the full sum of bricks.* The foremen of the children of Israel depart without any remedy or relief; they grieve and are vehemently distressed, seeing

<margin>verse 19.</margin>
*<gloss>ברע אתם</gloss> that they were in a bad state*, that affliction and misery were continuing, and that things were going very poorly for themselves and their countrymen. They object and oppose Moses and Aaron, after they had reported the failure of their mission:

<margin>verse 21.</margin>
*<gloss>ירא יהוה עליכם וישפט</gloss>, May Jehovah look upon you and judge, because you have made our odor to stink in the eyes of Pharaoh and in the eyes of his servants, so as to put a sword in their hand to kill us.* A truly heavy protest, by which they call upon Jehovah as an avenger, and by which they claim these innocent men are the authors of Pharaoh's hatred toward the people. "You," they say, "hand the sword to Pharaoh with which we are to be finished; you are our murderers. You, you are at fault, causing Pharaoh to turn his eyes away and avert himself entirely from us. Because we have fallen from all the King's favor, because we are perishing, the blame sticks to you." Moses, the author and leader of these counsels, hastens to Jehovah with a dismayed mind, and as if protesting why He had imposed this burden and business upon him, he says:

<margin>verse 22. verse 23.</margin>
*Lord, why have you afflicted this people? Why have you sent me? From the time I entered to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has afflicted this people, and you have not delivered your people by delivering them.* God incites, inflames, and raises up the fainting and softened Moses, and asserting a new hope, He says:

<margin>chapter 6 verse 1.</margin>
*Now you shall see what I am going to do to Pharaoh; for with a strong hand he will let them go, and with a strong hand he will drive them out of his land.* He explains the whole cause, sets the outcome before his eyes as if present, and opposes Pharaoh with the majesty of His name:

<margin>verse 3.</margin>
*I am JEHOVAH; I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty. By my name Jehovah I was not known to them.* He declares and wages war with immortal glory and the stupendous power of His name; He emphasizes the promises made to the Fathers of the Israelites. Indeed, no protections appear against the power of Pharaoh, but God promises the greatest protection and a strong hand, saying:

<margin>verse 6. 7.</margin>
*Say to the children of Israel: I am JEHOVAH, and*

<column-break/>

I will lead you out from the burdens of *Egypt* <note>original: Misraim</note>, I will rescue you from their servitude, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great judgments.

<margin>The Egyptian Plagues.</margin>
I will take you to myself as a people, and I will be to you as a GOD, and you shall know that I am JEHOVAH your God, who leads you out from the burdens of *Egypt*. In this consoling speech, the weight of the words must be observed. He gives the matter itself as proven by three distinct verbs: <gloss>הוצאתי, הצלתי, גאלתי</gloss>, I will lead out, I will deliver, I will redeem. He orders the badge of victory and the monument of liberation to be inscribed on His banner: <gloss>אני יהוה</gloss>, I AM JEHOVAH, so that by seeing and hearing this name they might raise themselves to the hope of a liberty certainly to come, relying on the omnipotence and all-sufficiency of the divine majesty. He says the liberation will be powerful

<margin>verse 3.</margin>
<gloss>באל שדי</gloss>, in the name *El Shaddai*, which denotes the abundance and sufficiency of God, the strength and power of God. "You shall remember that I am *El Shaddai*, and the insolent and arrogant speech of Pharaoh shall not disturb you":

<margin>chapter 5 verse 2.</margin>
*<gloss>מי יהוה</gloss>, Who is Jehovah? <gloss>לא ידעתי את-יהוה</gloss> I do not know Jehovah.* Pharaoh had blasphemed the divine name, etc., just as the notorious Nicanor <note>A Syrian general who oppressed the Jews in the Maccabean period.</note>,

<margin>2 Maccabees 15 verse 5. 6.</margin>
<gloss>not ceasing from all arrogance and being high-necked, he had determined to set up a common trophy over the Jews. I am a sovereign on the earth, who commands to take up arms and perform the royal duties.</gloss> His achievements had excessively exalted Nicanor the Egyptian <note>The author likely refers to Nicanor's pride as being like that of the Egyptians.</note>, and he had brought some sort of spirits of the Gods; against those Gods from whom they hoped for help and safety, Jehovah-God opposes the majesty of His own name. He explains the manner of liberation as being by an outstretched arm and great judgments, <gloss>in a high arm and great judgment</gloss>, that is, with the greatest force and power, by memorable signs and deeds, by hand and virtue, as Cicero joins in these words:

<margin>For Balbus.</margin>
*Could the approach to the city be opened by tongue and command, but could not be by hand and virtue?* What the supplicating tongue of the Ambassadors and the one common voice of the whole afflicted people could not obtain—the departure to the desert—the *hand and virtue of Jehovah*, which the King despised, could. Those to whom the entrance to the royal dwelling and seat is closed, nevertheless go out with the common spirit and will of their enemies. To those whom Egypt denies a dwelling and a quiet seat, Canaan offers one. The people are led out <gloss>with great judgments</gloss>, not by flame and sword with the Egyptians destroyed, but by plague and water. The nation beloved by God is not led out in the dissension and discord of the Egyptian citizens, but in the greatest consensus and incredible concord. Are these not the great judgments of a great God? Pharaoh now felt that the most august name <gloss>יהוה</gloss> <note>Jehovah</note> has sinews and strength, the force of which he felt anew, as much as it could strive and achieve. Finally, he obeys and is attentive to the word; he releases and relaxes, and he whose mind could be moved by no supplication is moved by great judgments, various penalties, and punishments, so that at once the mind and voice of the King and the common people were in agreement. Thus, by deed and fact, it is declared what it means: I AM JEHOVAH. I am EL SHADDAI. I am that God who declares by reality and decrees what He signifies by countenance and words. I am God Almighty, who can make things out of words, and fulfill what was promised long ago; and in this name I will now most greatly appear, by which I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, about to testify by evident proofs of judgments that I am still that powerful GOD.

# From Exodus IX. v. 18.

<margin>v. 9.</margin> The Egyptian Plagues. Moses went forth exulting in spirit, having spoken all the promises of God to the children of Israel; but because of their anguish of soul and <note>original: ἀπορία (aporia)</note> confusion of mind, they did not listen to Moses on account of their broken spirit and harsh servitude, <margin>from shortness of spirit and from hard work</margin>, <note>original Hebrew: מקוצר רוח ומעבודה קשה</note> from faint-heartedness and from cruel labors. Pharaoh had become hardened and callous; the soul of the Israelites had become hardened by the most difficult labor. The order of the Israelites was in a ferment of sorrow; the Pharaonic order in a ferment of wrath. Israel was to be refreshed and restored; Pharaoh, already ruined and lost, was to be further destroyed and blinded. The cry of the Israelites goes up to heaven; Moses cries out to the Lord of heaven: <margin>v. 12. 30.</margin> *Behold, the children of Israel have not listened to me; how then shall Pharaoh listen to me, seeing I am of uncircumcised lips?* <margin>I am of uncircumcised lips</margin> <note>original Hebrew: אני ערל שפתים</note>. Moses retains his old character, returning to his natural disposition; he refuses to perform the duty of an ambassador, claiming he is unequipped and unprepared with gifts, forgetting that which the Lord had promised: *I will be in your mouth*. By consolation Moses is again raised up, and shows himself obedient. He goes again by God's command to the King and to the children of Israel, Moses with his Aaron; and they did this not only with courage and strength, but also considerately and wisely. By the grace and gift <margin>2 Cor. 4:7</margin> of God, a great spirit was given to Moses, *so that*, to use the words of St. Paul, *the excellence of the power may be of God, and not of us*. He is appointed the executor of divine judgments, <margin>Wisdom VII. v. 1. 2.</margin> as the Lord said: *Behold, I have made you as a God to Pharaoh himself. And Aaron your brother shall be your prophet. You shall speak all that I command you. And Aaron your brother shall speak to <margin>v. 3.</margin> Pharaoh, that he let the children of Israel go out of his land.* <margin>v. 4.</margin> *But I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt. And Pharaoh will not listen to you, and I will lay my hand upon Egypt, and bring forth my armies, my people, the children <margin>v. 5.</margin> of Israel, out of the land of Egypt by great judgments; and the Egyptians shall know that I AM JEHOVAH, when I stretch forth my hand over Egypt, and bring out the children of Israel from among them.* The embassy is commended, and the divine name is granted to Moses, <margin>I have made you a god to Pharaoh</margin> <note>original Hebrew: נתתיך אלהים לפרעה</note>, which the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> and the Latin translator render: *I have given you as a god to Pharaoh*. God increases and adorns Moses, bestowing the sublime name *Elohim* <note>A Hebrew name for God, also used for judges or rulers</note>, because he performs a sublime embassy, because he is the Judge of all Israel, just as God is accustomed to grant his own name to Judges and Princes as a great title of honor, saying: <margin>ch. 22 v. 28.</margin> *You shall not revile the gods.* <note>original Hebrew: אלהים לא תקלל</note> <margin>In defense of Murena</margin> In this sense Cicero says: *Since all the power of the immortal Gods has either been transferred to you, or certainly shared with you.* God had shared power with Moses, had girded him with power and authority from on high, whom Pharaoh ought to have feared, not one who should dread Pharaoh; and so that the Egyptians might know that the God of Israel is the true God, who is to be feared and worshipped. By this new oracle of God, Moses is confirmed, endowed with a divine mind and purpose, released and free from all care; driven by the reason of his high office, he strenuously prepares himself for the duty of the embassy together with <margin>ch. 7 v. 6.</margin> his brother, and all unbelief being set aside, Moses and Aaron did just as Jehovah had commanded them, so they did. With a ready mind both approach Pharaoh; Aaron announces God's serious mandate concerning the dismissal of the people, who had been vexed and devastated long enough.

<column-break/>

The elders, with their venerable gray hair (for Moses was <margin>v. 7.</margin> eighty years old and Aaron eighty-three), standing with intrepid spirit before Pharaoh, are ordered to attest to the duty of their embassy with signs, so that from there he might find a reason and a way to elude the mandate and authority of the Ambassadors. To repel all suspicion from themselves and to rescue themselves from the mark of infamy, Aaron threw down his staff, <margin>his staff</margin> <note>original Hebrew: את - מטהו</note>, before Pharaoh and before his servants, <margin>and it became a serpent</margin> <note>original Hebrew: ויהי לתנין</note>, and it was turned into a snake, as the Old Translator renders it. He ought to have estimated this omen of a portent from the very entrance as an omen of a great matter, a dire and fatal omen, an omen of imminent slaughters. He ought to have turned away and detested this sad omen, for the Dragon <note>The Latin 'draco' can mean dragon, large serpent, or sea monster</note> could signify nothing but sad things; but that Egyptian Dragon, and those who were subject to the power of the snake, are not improved by this, nor corrected, but they trust in their own staff; they presume to elude signs with signs—those which were done without magic art through the power of God, they attempt to match with their own magic art. Therefore, <margin>v. 11.</margin> the *wise men and sorcerers* are summoned; *they also did in like manner with their enchantments.* The jugglers and Egyptian Magi, among whom Jannes and Jambres excelled, <margin>2 Tim. 3:8</margin> by their songs, or, as the Old Translator has it, *by their secret enchantments*, did the same in appearance, though not in reality; with a very great difference, for it was done by the artifice and work of the Devil, so that in the place of the thrown-down staffs, serpents were substituted from elsewhere in an invisible manner, as Cyril explains. The <margin>book 7 on John ch. 8</margin> serpents produced by the Magi through trickery are conquered, and they vanish as if devoured. The true Dragon conquered and devoured the phantasmal dragons. Philo relates that when each had thrown down their staffs, a great multitude of Dragons was made, but all turned themselves around that first one, which was Aaron's; Aaron's Dragon, however, after waiting a little, soon raised its chest and its whole body, and with open mouth and violent breath drawn in, dragged them all to itself like fish into a net, and having devoured them, returned to its former nature, which had been a staff. The Egyptian Magi imitate Moses and Aaron in performing wonders, but there is another cause, another use, and another outcome for the miracles which the holy perform; and another cause, use, and outcome for those which the impious perform. Aaron's staff devours, but the staffs of the Magi are devoured, by which sign it was declared that it would come to pass that Israel, the people of God, would conquer the power of Pharaoh; whence Augustine says: <margin>10. City of God 8. col. 548.</margin>
> Those things, great and many as they are, which were wonderfully done through Moses in Egypt for the purpose of rescuing the people of God from the yoke of servitude—where the Magi of Pharaoh, that is, of the King of Egypt, who was oppressing that people with his dominion, were permitted to do certain wonders to this end: that they might be more wonderfully conquered. For they did these things by sorceries and magic incantations, to which the evil Angels, that is, the Demons, are devoted; but Moses, as much more powerfully as more justly, easily overcame them in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth, with the Angels serving him.

Egypt abounded in learned and skilled men, but because they so mixed impious and illicit arts with good disciplines, the noble sciences among them were impregnated with poison; we shall soon deal with these magic and illicit arts. Pharaoh was delighted by this first wonder...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Egyptian Plagues.</margin>
...so much so that he hardened his heart, and would not obey even after seeing this contest; and he who was previously difficult regarding the release of the people now becomes even more stubborn, as Jehovah himself said to Moses: * <note>original Hebrew: כבד לב פרעה מאן לשלח העם</note>

<margin>verse 14.</margin>
*Pharaoh's heart is hardened; he refuses to let this people go.* He does not yield to the first sign, seizing upon this one fact: that the Magicians had performed something seemingly similar. A close-quarters struggle ensued; the Magicians placed their hope in magic power, but Aaron’s staff rushed upon the magic staffs, and the Magicians were overcome by a wondrous kind of combat. This deed should have been enough, but room is given for hesitation, and the ambassadors are dismissed without having achieved their goal. This was not without the arrangement of the Divine Will, which, through a sharp contest of faith and a vehement struggle, strove toward the greater glory of the liberation and a more joyful resolution to the calamities. As Augustine says*, power is given to Magicians to perform certain miracles, either to deceive the deceivers (both the Egyptians and the Magicians); or to warn the faithful not to greatly desire to do such things; or to exercise and make manifest the patience of the righteous. Pharaoh had deliberated and determined <note>original Greek: μὴ ἐξαφιέναι τὸν λαόν</note> *not to let the people go*, but God had determined to exercise more severe judgments upon him, to mark him with true and notable shame, and to provide other portents—hidden things revealed through the reality and the infamy of the royal name.
<margin>Augustine, On the Trinity, Book 3, Chapter 7.</margin>
<margin>verse 15.</margin>
"Go," says Jehovah, *"to Pharaoh in the morning; behold, he will go out to the waters, and you shall stand to meet him by the bank of the river; and the staff which was turned into a serpent you shall take in your hand;"* and you shall say to him,
<margin>verse 16.</margin>
*"JEHOVAH, THE GOD OF THE HEBREWS, has sent me to you with these commands: Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness; and behold, you have not listened until now."* Since Pharaoh neither recalls nor redirects his mind once it is incited, but proceeds with his mind fully set, Moses, in the name of God, indicates his full duty:
<margin>verse 17.</margin>
*"By this you shall know that I am Jehovah. Behold, I am about to strike with the staff that is in my hand the waters that are in the river, and they shall be turned into blood;"*
<margin>verse 18.</margin>
*"and the fish that are in the river shall die, and the river shall stink, and the Egyptians shall be weary of drinking the waters from the river."* Truly a horrific example of a wondrous transformation, both of substance and color in the waters, when, after the river Nile was struck by the staff of Moses, all the waters of Egypt in the riverbeds, streams, marshes, lakes, and in vessels of wood and stone turned into blood, undergoing a change even unto putrefaction, with the fish also dying. For Jehovah said to Moses: (chapter 7, verse 19) *"Say to Aaron: Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt <note>original: Misraim</note>, over their rivers, over their streams, and over their marshes, and over every gathering of their waters, and they shall become blood; and there shall be blood in all the land of Egypt, both in vessels of wood and in vessels of stone."* No sooner said than done, and it was done upon the striking,
<margin>verses 20, 21.</margin>
*so that all the waters that were in the river were turned into blood.* The Magicians exhibited a sophisticated or deceptive appearance of this miracle to Pharaoh through their incantations; but it was a form of wicked Magic, a deception of the sight and a fraudulent substitution. With Pharaoh not turning back and still refusing, the waters throughout all Egypt are converted into blood; and since words and signs were empty to Pharaoh, blows and plagues are foretold, so that the "Phrygian might be improved by lashes" <note>A Latin proverb meaning some only learn through suffering.</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>The Egyptian Plagues.</margin>
However, neither this first plague nor the other nine could entirely correct Pharaoh's hardened character, except that at times he seemed to slightly improve and conform. He acts and sets everything in motion to the contrary; for a hatred against the Israelites had once settled and grown old within him, and a mind once corrupted and depraved could not be drawn in a different direction except by ten notable plagues, concerning which St. Augustine says:*
<margin>City of God, Book 16, Chapter 43, column 931.</margin>
> Moses, sent by divine authority in the power of the Spirit of God, overcame the resisting Magicians of Pharaoh. Then, through him, ten memorable plagues were brought upon the Egyptians when they would not let the people of God go: the water turned into blood, frogs and gnats, the dog-fly, the death of livestock, boils, hail, locusts, darkness, and the death of the firstborn. At last, the Egyptians, who had finally let the Israelites go after being broken by so many and such great plagues, were destroyed in the Red Sea while they were pursuing them.

The first plague was the change of the waters into blood, universally affecting everyone in the whole kingdom, in all rivers, springs, wells, and vessels which the Egyptians used for drinking, cooking, and washing. The water of the river is turned into blood—the same river to which they had delivered the Hebrew infants to be killed—so that a cup of blood might be returned to the authors of the crime, and they might feel the gore of the polluted whirlpool, which they had stained with parricidal slaughter, by drinking it.
<margin>Pelicannus on this passage, page 75.</margin>
Like was returned for like, and they were not dismissed unavenged or unpunished by the blood of the water; the blood signified and thus openly showed that they had sinned in blood. But not even thus is Pharaoh brought back to his duty and sanity of mind, nor does he rescind or void the decree of not letting them go. For when he had seen that the Magicians by their incantations had presented to him a similar spectacle of waters changed into blood—although the entire change consisted of fabricated and invented things and deserved deceptions—Pharaoh's heart was strengthened,

The conscience of his crime would have been felt in Pharaoh, and a fury conceived from his evil deeds would have been stirred up to destroy and extinguish the people dwelling with him, or to spoil and plunder them—those who were themselves finally plundered. Therefore, a second plague is announced to Pharaoh, who was stubbornly detaining the people of God, through Moses, saying*: *Let my people go, that they may serve me. But if you refuse to let them go, behold, I will strike all your borders with FROGS, and the river shall bring forth frogs, and they shall go up and come into your house, and into your bedchamber, and upon your bed, and into the house of your servants, and upon your people, and into your ovens, and into your kneading bowls. And the frogs shall come up both upon you and upon your people, and upon all your servants.* God warns with words, and warns with the signs themselves; He calls Pharaoh to repentance, but Pharaoh trusts again in the Magicians, who themselves—after Aaron* extended his hand over the waters of Egypt <note>original: "Misraim"</note> to summon the frogs—did likewise with their incantations, and caused frogs to come up upon the lands of Egypt. Produced in great numbers, the frogs crawled over everything, huts and palaces, kneading troughs and ovens, except for the dwellings of the Israelites; and it is noted that <term>sharats</term> <note>Hebrew: שרץ</note> means to produce in great abundance in the manner of fish and reptiles, as noted by Vatablus*. Pharaoh is moved by this plague; he asks to be snatched and delivered from the midst of the plague, urging Moses and Aaron to entreat Jehovah to drive away the frogs from him and his people, promising that he would let the people go to perform sacred rites to Jehovah. *Entreat Jehovah, he says, and let him let the people go and they will sacrifice to Jehovah. <term>Ha’atiru el-Yehovah</term> <note>Hebrew: הַעְתִּירוּ אֶל-יְהוָה</note> so that he may take away the frogs from me and from my people.* By the miracle of the frogs, God shows His power, He who so conquers and tames this King with the vilest of animals that He forces him to beg and pray for Moses's intercession. To the one asking for intercession, Moses responds: *Assume glory over me, <term>hitpa’er alay</term> <note>Hebrew: הִתְפָּאֵר עָלַי</note> and say when I should pray for you, and for your servants, and for your people, that I may cause the frogs to be cut off from you and from your houses, and they shall remain only in the river.* Where Tremellius* says: *Even if this glory is not owed to you, that you should prescribe to me the time in which you wish the frogs to be taken from you, nevertheless you may assume it through me.* He speaks thus not presiding over himself, but confirmed in faith by the certain testimony of God, and at the same time he pricks Pharaoh in passing, who had boasted in vain of his Magicians. Furthermore, this expression is read in two other places in this sense, Judges 7:2 and Isaiah 10:14. And Conrad Pellican*: *Tell me clearly and signify openly when you wish prayer to be made for you.* He says this lest the enchanters and Astrologers should claim a "moment of time," which they used to hunt for from their horoscopes—namely, a certain time for applying Astrology or Necromancy. Moses, relying on that promise, "I have made you a God to Pharaoh," thought no matter so difficult that he could not accomplish it by divine power. However, there is an example of false repentance in the King, which not faith but present punishment extorted from him. The impious King begins to fear God, but servilely. He becomes a suppliant simulator of repentance, which he immediately casts away as soon as he is delivered from the evil, the frogs having been expelled and exterminated from every side; and he enjoys again a life of luxury and convenience. For how slippery and uncertain his repentance was, the ungrateful man immediately provides an example of wickedness for such a great benefit; for seeing that there was <term>anapsyxis</term> <note>Greek: ἀνάψυξις, meaning "respite" or "breathing space"</note>, a breathing space, he hardened his heart and did not obey them. Behold the face of the man and his remarkable impudence. His mouth truly "plays the Egyptian" <note>Greek: αἰγυπτιαζειν, a term implying deceit or trickery associated with Egyptians</note>, making that saying true: *The Egyptians are clever at fashioning schemes.* Are you in your right mind? Should you not be constrained by new plagues, and those more severe? God therefore commands that, as Aaron extends his hand over the dust of the earth, there should be born <term>Kinnim</term> <note>Hebrew: כִנִּים</note>—a word whose proper meaning poses no small "cross" <note>a difficulty or puzzle</note> for Interpreters. The Vulgate renders this little word as *cynifes*, which are *subtle and tiny flies, yet they terrify the body upon which they settle with a most bitter sting*, according to Lyra*. They borrowed this opinion from Philo, who understands by *Kinnim* a most troublesome kind of fly, in whose writings we read: *That little beast, although it is very small, is nevertheless usually most troublesome; for it not only hurts the surface of the skin, sending in a hateful and harmful itching, but it even penetrates the inner nostrils and hurts the ears, and even the eyes, unless one is careful.* Some say winged worms similar to gnats are signified. The Seventy <note>The Septuagint</note> seem to aim at this kind of worm, translating it as <term>sknipas</term> <note>Greek: σκνῖπας</note>, from *sknipto*, to gnaw or scratch. For it is a little worm gnawing figs, or according to others, a little worm gnawing vines. Whence Origen writes that this animal is indeed suspended by wings flying through the air, but so subtle and minute that it escapes the sight of the eye unless one discerns sharply; yet when it settles, it bores into the body with a most bitter sting, so that one who cannot see it flying feels it stinging. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> understands them to be lice. Indeed, for the Masters of the Hebrews, <term>kinnah</term> denotes a louse, whence the plural is <term>kinnim</term> with the letter *yod* missing, instead of the full *kinniyim*; although there is also found *kinnam* or *hakinnam*, denoting that whole filth of lice, including pubic lice, which came forth from the struck dust of Egypt in such multitude and abundance upon men—

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Egyptian Plagues.</margin>
...men and beasts, so that they could no longer be turned away or driven off by any medicine. There is a certain herb called <term>pedicularia</term> <note>Stavesacre or Larkspur</note>, because it kills lice. The Greeks call it <term>agria</term> <note>wild</note>; Pliny says in *Book 23, Chapter 1* that its seeds free the head and the rest of the body from lice infestation, and Dioscorides says the same in *4. 156*: <note>original Greek: σμηχθεῖσα πρὸς φθειριάσεις καὶ κνησμοὺς καὶ ψώρας</note> "it is rubbed on for lice, itching, and scabies." But the experience of the Naturalists could do nothing against these tiny creatures sent by God as a punishment; no herb, no physician’s pot, indeed, not even the incantations of the Magi availed. For the power of the Magi, when it came down to producing the smallest and most contemptible creatures—namely, the lice—failed entirely. Hence they were forced to confess, <italic>“This is the finger of God,”</italic> <note>Exodus 8:19</note> that is, that the virtue and power of God stood in their way, preventing them from bringing lice into effect. Wherefore Augustine* rightly perceives, <margin>Book 3 on the Trinity, ch. 7.</margin> that this was done <italic>“so that it might be understood that whatever they had been able to do until now, they could only do by power granted from above.”</italic> And Prosper in *Book 1 on Promises and Predictions, 36, p. 48*: <italic>“The third plague of the Egyptians is the gnats vibrating through all the air, also distressing the Egyptians with a pestilential bite in the midst of the summer heats; in this plague all the learning of the magi failed, and they professed that the finger of God was in it; they themselves being also tormented, their cunning remained empty and vain.”</italic> Regarding this plague, though it was sharper and harder than the previous ones, no improvement was to be hoped for from Pharaoh; rather, his mind became more and more hardened, taking no account of what the Magi, albeit unwillingly, confessed. The cause of this obstinacy is by no means to be imputed to God, who does not approve of his stubborn and hostile front, with which he strengthens himself against God and His people. For how would He, by His own will, arm adversaries against Himself? Since He warned him so often, and knew he would not be obedient, by the just judgment of the Lord, the repeated commands—neglected by him—aggravated his sin and punishment. God did not immediately exact punishment from the impious King, so that the divine victory might shine more brightly in Egypt and be seen more clearly throughout the whole world, just as God says: <margin>ch. 9:16.</margin>
> For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I may show my power in you, and that my name may be declared in all the earth.

He wished there to be in Pharaoh an example of justice and severity, so that others might be invited to the fear of the Lord and true ways of living. A hard wedge is needed for a hard knot. Pharaoh, becoming more obstinate at the earlier plagues, deserved a more severe punishment, which God denounced for the morrow unless Pharaoh showed himself curable. But Pharaoh, impatient of correction and mindful of his name—that he is "Pharaoh"—thinks himself subject to no one, not even the God of Israel. Hence, in deed and name, he professes himself Pharaoh, as one who recognizes no legislator, no judge, nor any superior to himself. Therefore, a fourth pestilence, no less horren- <margin>ch. 8 v. 21.</margin> dous, is proposed under the name *Arob* <note>Hebrew: ערוב</note>, which the Vulgate explains as <italic>every kind of fly</italic>, plainly like the Greeks, who express it as <term>zoomyia</term> <note>animal-fly</note>, or <term>dog-fly</term>. Others also understand <term>Serpents and Scorpions</term>, and <italic>other animals</italic>, which the author of Wisdom seems to confirm in *chapter 17:9* when speaking of the plagues of the Egyptians: <italic>“For even if nothing troublesome had terrified them, yet being harassed by the passing of beasts and the hissing of serpents, they died trembling;”</italic> even the air, which can in no way be avoided, they

<column-break/>

refused to look upon. For such a great darkening did this multitude of venomous <margin>The Egyptian Plagues.</margin> and harmful animals of so many different kinds bring in, that they darkened the day at the noon sun. Hence they also have the name *Arob* from *Arabab*, <italic>“he mixed”</italic> or <italic>“it was darkened,”</italic> both because it was a dreg or mixture of insects or various animals collected from many species, and because, due to its immense multitude, it seemed to obscure the sun at noon. Josephus aims at this when he renders *Arob* as <term>beasts of all kinds or many forms</term>; nor does the Chaldean <note>Targum</note> disagree, while he excellently expresses it as *Arboni*, i.e., <italic>a mixture of insect animals</italic>, thus: a mixture of all kinds of living things, in which we do not even exclude the raven or *Oreb* <note>Hebrew: עורב</note>, as another Chaldean rendered it: but the raven alone is not sufficient, see D. And since they worship serpents and similar beasts as Gods, they were also worthy to receive this "favor" from them in return; whence the Author of Wisdom* says: <italic>“They worshipped indeed dumb serpents <margin>ch. 11:16.</margin> and beasts: and he sent upon them a multitude of dumb animals for vengeance.”</italic> They were worthy to suffer this punishment alone, separated from the Israelites, so that they might know that Jehovah had divided between the Egyptians and the Israelites, *Exod. 11:7.* <margin>Exod. 11:7.</margin> But you ask, what did Pharaoh intend, caught between the "sacred and the stone" <note>a Latin idiom meaning "between a rock and a hard place"</note>? He indeed, when he felt himself and his people, with no exception, struck by an <term>invincible disease of God</term> <note>original Greek: νόσῳ θεοῦ ἀμάχῳ</note> and the inevitable wrath of the Divine Power, fled to Moses and Aaron, promising mountains of gold, but with no other intent than to deceive them; <italic>“Go,” he said, “sacri- <margin>v. 25.</margin> fice to your God in this land.”</italic> But Moses, not content with this permission, rejected it for two principal reasons: *first*, because it was not permitted for the Israelites to make a sacrifice to God in Egypt:
> We will go a three days' journey, said Moses, into the wilderness, and sacrifice to Jehovah our God, as he told us.

On these words we cannot help but note what Augustine* notes: <italic>“The question is asked, how it is said to the people that God commanded <margin>Question 13 on Exodus.</margin> he would cast them out of Egypt into the land of Canaan; but to Pharaoh it is said that they wished to go a three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to their God by his command? But it must be understood that although God knew what He was going to do, since He foreknew that Pharaoh would not consent to letting the people go, that was said first which would also happen first if he let them go; for so that all things might happen just as the following Scripture testifies, the contumacy of Pharaoh and his people deserved it.”</italic> Thus he spoke. *Secondly*, because it was not expedient: <italic>“Behold,” he said, “we shall sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians before their eyes, <margin>v. 26.</margin> and will they not stone us?”</italic> The sacrifices of the Israelites are called an "abomination" to the Egyptians not simply, but in a limited sense. For the Egyptians worshipped bulls, rams, and goats as Gods. They venerated the bull in the form of Apis, about which Augustine* says much; <margin>Book 18 of City of God.</margin> the *Ram*, because Jupiter is adored among them in the figure of a ram; and *Goats*, because the Demons from whom the Magi drew their power appeared in the form of goats. Indeed, according to Herodotus *Book 2* and Strabo *Book 17*, all animals were Idols of the Egyptians. Pharaoh, however, when he saw that the matter did not turn out according to his wish, finally permitted that they should go...

So that Pharaoh might truly recognize the powerful hand of God, Moses and Aaron were sent to him to announce a very grave pestilence upon the cattle and living creatures, whose use he and the Egyptians could not do without. As Pharaoh persisted in his obstinacy, the pestilence was sent, so that all the cattle of the Egyptians perished—specifically those that were in the field, for it is clear from verses 19 and 20 of Exodus chapter 9 that not every single one perished universally—except for the cattle of the Israelites, which were kept safe both in the field and at home. raoh as God threatens the Israelites in *Leviticus 26:18: If you will not obey me, I will add seven times more to your punishments.* He now threatens Pharaoh with a seventh punishment, unless he repents and lets the people go. God sends this plague beforehand because he was now about to send a pestilence that would utterly remove Pharaoh and the Egyptians. Since, however, we do not read that a pestilence or other plague that would utterly cut off Pharaoh and the Egyptians was actually sent upon them, therefore these words: *For now I will stretch out my hand, and strike you and your people with pestilence*, etc.
<margin>v. 15.</margin>
from the earth, are to be explained not as an action but as a potential: *I will strike you, that is, I could strike or could have struck you.* In this sense, the
<margin>Chaldean Paraphrase.</margin>
expressed it: *since now it was near before me that I should have sent even the plague of my strength and struck you and your people with death, and so you would have been deleted from the earth.* Tremellius and Piscator read it thus as well. This reading agrees best, in the judgment of Pererius, with what follows immediately: *But for this cause I have placed you*, that is, I have made you stand and remain, so that I might show my power or virtue to you as you remain and live longer. Let us hear how piously Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, once wrote on these words in his *Commentary on Habakkuk, book 1, fol. 59. a.*: *We must not suspect,* he says, *that your "placing" him here is to make him evil. You did not so place him, nor any of the evil or strong men. Certainly, you did not make Pharaoh, nor Assur or Nebuchadnezzar, nor the most proud Haman, nor Antiochus, nor Herod evil, nor did you wish them to be proud; but since they were evil and proud, you placed them on high, and this for judgment; you established them as strong, and this for correction. You knew what kind of man he was, and because you knew what you wished to correct, therefore you placed him there, so that he might first become known, and then finally be corrected.* And in book 1 on Jonah, f. 6. a.: *God did not make Pharaoh to be evil, but since he was evil, He raised him up as King, so that He might show His strength in him.* After this rejection was made, Moses announced the seventh plague from God to Pharaoh,
<margin>v. 18.</margin>
*Tomorrow,* he said, *at this very hour, I will rain a very heavy hail;* and so that God might show him His *long-suffering* <note>Greek: μακροθυμίαν</note>, He urged Pharaoh and the Egyptians through Moses to meet the threat and bring their cattle under roofs in time if they wished them to be safe. Some obeyed this warning—if not out of sincere repentance, then out of fear of the immediate plague and their experience of the plagues thus far—and took their cattle under shelter. Then God sent, just as He had predicted, a very great hail:
<margin>v. 23.</margin>
*For Jehovah gave thunders and hail, and fire ran along the ground, and Jehovah rained hail upon the land of Egypt. And there was hail, and fire mixed with the hail, very heavy, such as there had not been in all the land of Mizraim <note>Egypt</note> since it became a nation.*
