# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Plagues of Egypt. ch. 9. 25.</margin>
*And the hail struck throughout all the land of Mizraim <note>original: "Mizraim" — the Hebrew name for Egypt</note>, whatever was in the field, from man even to beast; the hail also struck every herb of the field, and broke every tree of the field.* By these words, the severity of this punishment is described, which was greater and more bitter as Pharaoh’s obstinacy grew larger and worse. For in this plague three of the elements converge, namely air, fire, and water, <margin>v. 31. 32.</margin> by which the flax and the barley were battered, because the barley was green and the flax was in the stalk. But *the wheat and the rye were not struck, because they were late-ripening.* Pharaoh indeed grieves from the weight of such a great plague, but with a hypocritical grief rather than a saving one; for he does not keep what he promises regarding the dismissal of the Hebrews. Nor does that contrition—by which he confesses God to be just, but himself and his people to be unjust (that is, that these punishments are deservedly inflicted upon him and his people)—flow from a humble heart fearing God and enlightened by true faith. Rather, as he was an atheist, he was somewhat softened by the dread of greater punishments. Whence, when he enjoyed the free air again, he returned to his vomit, <margin>v. 33.</margin> and took away all hope of release from servitude from the Hebrews. Moses had obtained from God what he had pledged, namely the removal of the plague; he therefore performed what he promised: but Pharaoh does not perform what he promised. Wherefore Moses denounces a new punishment upon him unless he obeys: He says that locusts will come, <margin>ch. 10. v. 4.</margin> in Hebrew <term>ארבה</term> <note>Arbeh</note>, in the Greek Septuagint <term>βρῦχος</term> <note>bruchus - a wingless locust</note>. Concerning this kind of locust, the words of the Blessed Luther in his Biblical notes are worthy of note: *They were four-footed animals, known to us, yet like grasshoppers, which do great damage to vines, grain, and trees, like the beetles and caterpillars among us.* These would utterly consume the remaining produce of the year which had not perished in the hail. But Pharaoh was not moved even by this denunciation of a new punishment; wherefore Moses, weary of the Tyrant's stubbornness and obstinacy, went out. But the King’s impious Counselors were present, who, having had their minds changed for the better by the preceding plagues, began to exhort him to release <margin>v. 7.</margin> the people. *How long,* they said, *will this man be a snare to us? Let the men go, that they may serve their God; do you wish to know beforehand that Mizraim has perished?* The Greek renders this as <term>σκόλον</term> <note>skolon</note>, but it is <term>σκόλοψ</term> <note>skolops</note>, a thorn or a sharpened stake. The Counselors intend by this speech that he should let the people go, lest God cast them headlong into greater evils. The tyrant is moved by this speech of his followers, though not entirely overcome; having recalled Moses, he permits him to go with the men to sacrifice to their God in the desert, but leaving behind the children, wives, and all their belongings. Since Moses would not accept this condition, but insisted on the women and little ones, <margin>v. 9.</margin> saying: *We will go with our young and with our old: with our sons and with our daughters, with our flocks and our herds will we go, for it is a feast of Jehovah to us.* The Tyrant flared up in anger and cast them out. He could indeed cast out Moses and Aaron, the Ambassadors of God, but not the locusts, much less God himself, who, as he had threatened, sent the locusts by an East wind, consuming everything that had remained after the hail. For in such abundance and multitude did they cover the face of the earth,

<column-break/>

that they took away the sight of the ground, compare Psalm 78:46 and Psalm 105:34. When Pharaoh <margin>The Plagues of Egypt.</margin> feels himself constrained again, he returns to his former arts; he summons Moses and Aaron, whom he had expelled, before whom he humbles himself, acknowledging his sin and promising obedience. Although he did this with a hypocritical heart, yet for the fuller <term>φανέρωσιν</term> <note>phanerōsin — manifestation or revealing</note> of divine glory, <margin>v. 19.</margin> Moses prays for this plague to be taken away. At his prayers, God, by a contrary wind—namely a western one—takes away and destroys the locusts. Following closely upon this plague, since no improvement appeared in Pharaoh, the ninth followed: namely, <margin>v. 22.</margin> *gloomy and palpable* darkness. Moreover, this darkness arose not by the force of a solar eclipse—which is indicated by the span of time and its density (as some establish)—but also by the distinction made between the Israelites and the Egyptians. For it lasted for three whole days, and was so dense that one could not see another; and although it was spread through all Egypt, it did not seize the Israelites. An eclipse rarely exceeds the space of three hours, nor does it produce such great darkness that men cannot see each other; nor does it ever happen that for those dwelling in the same land, the light of the sun and stars shines for one, but not for the other. Therefore, nothing can be said so fiercely regarding the errors and darkness of Egypt that the magnitude of the Egyptian darkness would not far surpass it. The Author of Wisdom <note>referring to the Book of the Wisdom of Solomon in the Apocrypha</note> describes quite graphically that dark <margin>ch. 17 & 18.</margin> misery of the Egyptians in the darkness for three days: *For the whole world was illuminated with clear light, (ch. 17. v. 20. 21.) and was occupied with unhindered works. But over them alone a heavy night brooded, etc.* Compare Josephus, Book 2 of the *Judaic Antiquities*, chapter 5. Constrained by this darkness, Pharaoh recalls Moses and Aaron, whom he had previously expelled, and gives them the power to depart, yet on the condition that they leave their cattle in Egypt. But when Moses insists on the cattle and herds being sent away at the same time, saying: *You also shall give into our hand sacrifices and <margin>v. 25.</margin> burnt offerings, that we may sacrifice to Jehovah our God. Furthermore, our livestock shall go with us; not a hoof shall remain.* Driven by furies, *he breathes out a terrible force of fire* <note>original Greek: δεινὸν ἀποπνέει πυρὸς μένος</note>, <margin>v. 28.</margin> and forbids Moses all access to him: *Get away from me, take heed to yourself, see my face no more; for on whatever day you see my face, you shall die.* But to this threat, Moses intrepidly responds *like a lightning bolt from the gate* <note>original Greek: ὡς ἀστραπὴ ἐκ πύλου</note>—having first announced the tenth plague concerning the killing of all the firstborn—*You have spoken rightly, I will not see your <margin>v. 29.</margin> face again; and he went out from Pharaoh in the heat of anger.* This anger was not a sin, because it proceeded from zeal for divine honor, and from a detestation of the rebellion of the King of Egypt against God. Moses was angry not from a disturbance of mind, but he was stunned by the hardness of the King, and marveled that the wretched man, struck so many times, did not repent, as Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a medieval biblical exegete</note> says. But so that the Israelites, before they departed, might receive some reward for the labors with which they served the Egyptians for many years, God enjoins the Israelites through Moses *that each should ask from his neighbor, and <margin>ch. 11. v. 1.</margin> each woman from her neighbor, vessels of silver and vessels of gold, and thus they despoiled the Egyptians.* Justin <note>a Roman historian</note> also mentions this, though with little biblical truth,

# On Exodus IX, v. 18.

<margin>
The Egyptian Plagues.
Book 36, chapter 2.
</margin>
It is said that Moses, having become the leader of the exiles at their departure, carried away the sacred objects of the Egyptians, which the Egyptians were then forced to reclaim by arms. In truth, Moses had not taken their sacred objects, nor was that the reason the Egyptians pursued the Hebrews; rather, it was for another cause which the Book of Ancient Truth <note>The Bible</note> reveals to us. Meanwhile, it is clear from this that Justin—or rather Pompeius Trogus, who was earlier and from whom Justin copied his writings—had heard of the gold and silver vessels received as loans and carried away at God's command. Indeed, while God commanded this plundering, He did nothing unjustly. Certainly, the sole authority of God absolves them from the crime of theft or deceit. For by God's command, it is not permitted for any mortal to find fault or criticize; He who gave the law is also able to grant a dispensation from the law. Regarding this, Augustine says in *this place*: *It is a command of God, which was not to be judged but obeyed; for He Himself knows how justly He commanded it, and it pertains to the servant to obediently do what He commanded.* And Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a medieval exegete</note> adds: *It should also be considered that, regarding the persons involved, this ordinance of God was rational, because the Hebrews had served the Egyptians in many and very heavy labors, and had received no compensation for their work.* This <term>harmonizes</term> <note>original: συμφωνεῖ</note> with Sirach chapter 11:4: *The works of the Lord are wonderful, and His works are hidden among men.* In this way, that which the Lord promised to Abraham 400 years earlier was fulfilled: that his descendants, after suffering heavy servitude in Egypt, would go out with much substance, that is, with great wealth and riches.

<margin>Genesis 15:13, 14.</margin>
There remains that solemn and most holy night of the slaughter of the Egyptians and the liberation of the Hebrews which was to follow, which is called by the peculiar and singular name **Night of Watching** <note>original Hebrew: לֵיל שִׁמֻּרִים / Leil Shimurim</note>; neither this word **Watching** nor any other night is referred to by this title elsewhere. The Chaldean <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> expressed it simply as **a night to be observed** <note>original Aramaic: לֵיל נְטִיר</note>, or *a night for the Lord*, with which Blessed Luther’s version agrees: *The children of Israel shall keep it to the Lord, they and their descendants.* Hence the Jerusalem Targum says: *Four illustrious nights are remembered in the book of histories: The first, it says, is the night of creation, when the WORD OF THE LORD was manifested to create the world, which was hitherto crude and unformed with darkness spread over the face of the abyss: when the WORD OF THE LORD shone forth and illuminated that crude mass. The second night was that of the wonderful revelation made to Abraham, when the WORD OF THE LORD revealed Himself to Abraham between the covenantal sections of the slaughtered animals, through which a smoking furnace and a burning lamp passed, when a deep sleep and a dark and great terror fell upon Abraham (Gen. 15:12, 17). The third night was that of the liberation from Egypt, when the WORD OF THE LORD manifested Himself to the Egyptians at midnight and with His powerful right hand; He slew the firstborn of the Egyptians, but rescued the firstborn of the Israelites, to fulfill what the Scripture said: Israel is my firstborn. The fourth night is that of the consummation of the Age, etc.* Thus says the Targum.

<margin>Chapter 12:29.</margin>
Furthermore, in this last and tenth plague of the striking of every firstborn in Egypt, it should be noted that by the word "firstborn" is understood everything from man to beast that was ever the firstborn to its parents; for there are those who extend the term <term>firstborn</term> <note>original Greek: πρωτότοκον</note> to those who, the original firstborn having died, formerly succeeded to the right of primogeniture.

<column-break/>

<margin>
The Egyptian Plagues.
Wisdom 19:12, 13.
</margin>
They were slain from the firstborn of Pharaoh sitting upon his throne, even to the firstborn of the captive in the prison house, so that <term>in a single generation</term> <note>original Greek: πρὸς μίαν γονὴν</note> their most excellent offspring perished; the servant suffered the same as the Master—namely, from the most honored to the most lowly, all the firstborn died. Nor was it only the "sons of the family" still under paternal authority, but even their fathers, who had once been the firstborn to their own fathers. Therefore, a mixed slaughter of old and young was seen, and in the same house died the son, the father, and the grandfather, each of whom was a firstborn to their parents. Only the King was excepted, reserved for a greater punishment in the midst of the Red Sea, who did not perish in the common slaughter of the Firstborn. This happened to the firstborn at **midnight** <note>original Hebrew: חצי הלילה</note>, which the Chaldeans render as **the dividing of the night** <note>original Aramaic: ליליא פלגות</note>, and the Greeks as <term>the middle of the night</term> <note>original Greek: μεσούσης τῆς νυκτὸς</note>, when Jehovah Himself passed through Egypt and struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt. The Psalmist highlights and illustrates this immense plague taken upon the Firstborn of the Egyptians as a most wonderful work in Psalm 78:49: *He sent upon them the fierceness of His anger... by the sending of* **evil messengers** <note>original Hebrew: מלאכי רעים / malakhei ra'im</note>, namely either good angels, or Moses and Aaron, who announced those plagues to the Egyptians. Others render it *evil angels*; but the Hebrew syntax rejects that version, as it is not a case of agreement but of governance <note>A grammatical distinction in Hebrew</note>. For it says **messengers of evils**, not **evil messengers**. However, there are examples in the sacred texts where the "construct state" is used for the "absolute." Others who translate it as the "sending of evil angels" explain it by the gravity of the punishment, which occurs not without a great provocation of the Divine Majesty, so that harmful Spirits are sent to rage not against one or two men, but against an entire nation. Some think *Devils* are noted here, because they are called harmful angels; but this reasoning is very weak, since even good angels can harm the impious at God's command. By this, however, it is not denied that God executes His wrath through evil angels as if through executioners; we only intend that He does not always and everywhere use them to punish the impious.

<margin>2 Kings 19:35.</margin>
For who repelled the Assyrian from the siege of the city of Jerusalem by a great slaughter in his army, if not the Angel then given as the protector of the Church? Thus, to return to our purpose, the Angel, <term>the one destroying the firstborn</term> <note>original Hebrew: המשחית / original Greek: ὁ ὀλοθρεύων τὰς πρωτοτόκας</note>, who slew the firstborn, was not only the minister and executor of God's wrath against the Egyptians, but also provided for the safety of His people; hence Jehovah Himself is said to have "leaped over" <note>The root of 'Passover'</note> the doors of the Hebrews marked with the blood of the lamb. <margin>Exodus 12:13.</margin> See, if you please, Blessed Tarnovius, *Biblical Exercises* 735; *Sixtinus Amama, Antibarbarus Biblicus book 3, p. 806; D. Varen. p. 189 seq.* This huge slaughter, which pervaded all of Egypt—with no city, village, or house excepted—excited such consternation in Pharaoh and his servants that no time was given or found for seeking a remedy. We might apply here to the Egyptians, in the face of such implacable plagues, that line of Hercules (who was most impatient in his disease and despairing of human help) in Sophocles:

<margin>*Trachiniae* v. 1009.</margin>
> For what singer, what master of the craft
> of healing, is there who [could soothe] this calamity?

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Egyptian Plagues.</margin>
> Can one be shut out without Zeus?
> We would see a wonder from afar, Alas, Alas!
> Let me, the ill-fated one, go to my rest.
> Let me, the wretched one, go to my rest.
<note>original Greek: Χωρὶς Ζηνὸς κατακλήϊσαι... These lines evoke the tragic cries of the grieving.</note>

For those deprived of their dearest children and destitute of all help break out into wailing and lamentation. I seem to see the Egyptian parents deploring the sad fates of their firstborn with the words of Priam and Hecuba from the *Iliad*, book 22, verse 422:

> — Especially for me, above all others, he has caused grief.
> For he has slain so many of my sons in their prime.
> For all of them I do not mourn so much, though I am grieved,
> As for one, for whom sharp sorrow will carry me down into Hades.

And in the same place, verse 430:

> Child, I am wretched; why should I live, having suffered terribly
> Now that you are dead? You who were my boast by night and day
> Throughout the city, and a blessing to all.

In this terror and sad spectacle of death, Pharaoh does what those usually do who, despairing of better circumstances, act not as they wish, but as they are compelled to wish; he therefore sends messengers to Moses, asking that he depart quickly from Egypt with his people. And those who previously detained the Hebrews now urgently press the people to leave in haste. Thus the Hebrews departed from the house of Egyptian servitude in the month of Spring, the month of flowers, as the sadness of winter was passing away. Macarius says in Homily 47, page 511: "When the sons of Israel groaned to God because of their labors, then He visited them through Moses, and having struck the Egyptians with many plagues, in the month of flowers, when the sweetest spring season appears and the gloom of winter passes away, He led them out of Egypt." Many of the Egyptians who joined themselves to the Hebrews departed with them; <term>Ereb Rab</term> <note>Hebrew: ערב רב, "a mixed multitude"</note> went up with them, Exodus 12:38. The Chaldean translation understands this mixture as referring to foreigners or strangers. The Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> uses the name *epimiktos*, which is related to the Hebrew *ereb*, to mix, and more closely to *masak*; for they had mixed themselves into the assembly of the Jews. <margin>Oration 24, p. 417.</margin> This company of the promiscuous commoners was judged to be innumerable by the Old Interpreter, and our version has named them the "rabble-folk" <note>German: Pöbelvolck</note>. Among our scholars, the Blessed Frantzius explains that "great mixture" in this way: <margin>Palaest. 2. v. 25.</margin> *The miracles and words of Moses were so true and palpable that they moved a vast multitude of Egyptians; for very many—and almost, as we are accustomed to say of a maximum number, infinite—Egyptians joined themselves in religion and in the journey to the birthplace of the future Messiah with the Jews. They are called "mixed," and the passage in Numbers 11:4 proves they were not the commoners of the Israelites.* Whether these were pure Egyptians or also from other nations, they preferred to follow the departing Israelites rather than remain in Egypt, terrified by the miracles and wonders by which they learned to revere and worship the God of the Israelites, seeing also that the land of Egypt was so stripped and ruined by various calamities that they could no longer promise themselves a safe and comfortable habitation in it. They departed after Egypt had been struck by ten lashes, which the Blessed Rhodomannus rendered in excellent verse:

> By blood, and frogs, and gnats, and dog-flies,
> By the death of four-footed beasts, and blisters, and by hailstorms
> Carrying fire, and the devouring of locusts, by darkness, and by the fate

<column-break/>

> Of the firstborn; for which things even the unbending king was moved
> To send away the people, and to loosen the unseemly bonds.

<margin>The Egyptian Plagues.</margin> And Eugenius, Bishop of Toledo, in *Opuscula* D. 3. b., through single lines:

> The first plague turns the waters of the Nile into blood;
> The second created the croaking and rot of frogs;
> The third moved biting gnats from the dust;
> The fourth gave flies, fearsome in their sting and sound;
> The fifth also condemned all living things to death;
> The sixth fed consuming ulcers with a festering wound;
> The seventh vibrates a thundering murmur with hail;
> The eighth locusts, harmful to crops and foliage;
> The ninth prepares pitch-black darkness to be felt by touch;
> The last, which is the tenth, cuts off the first-fruits of offspring.

They departed in an immense number, six hundred thousand, not counting the little ones and the women. Having departed, they receive the law concerning the consecration of all firstborn to the Lord, and having received the law, they pitch camp near the Sea and Magdolum, a place which seems very dangerous for the Israelites, because they have the sea in front, high rocks on both sides, and behind them Egypt, grieving that it dismissed the Israelites who would no longer serve them. Pharaoh ascends his chariot with his nobles and all of Egypt to destroy the Israelites. He ascends, unmoved by those ten most wonderful miracles and made no better, about to attack the people of God with a hostile and bloody mind. But the Divine Majesty is accustomed to so moderate the attempts of the wicked that He turns their impiety into His own glory; and the destruction which they intend for others falls upon the ruin of the authors, but to the happiness and benefit of the good. He therefore allows Pharaoh loose reins—indeed, looser than before—so that he might go out armed with a ferocious mind and all his forces, whereby the glory of the Deliverer might be more illustrious, and it might become plain to all that the impious King with all his retinue perished by the most just and equitable vengeance of God. Whence the Lord instructs Moses concerning the future intention of Pharaoh as soon as he perceives the flight of the Israelites: *I will harden Pharaoh's heart and he will pursue them, and I will be glorified in Pharaoh and in all his army: and the Egyptians shall know that I am Jehovah. Exodus 14:4.* But he had to contend with the Lord, whose hand he had experienced so many times in Egypt; yet he, entirely immersed in Cyclopean recklessness, would have hissed at one warning of God's power, like Homer's Polyphemus:

<margin>Odyssey, book 9, v. 273.</margin>
> Fools! You have either come from far away, or you are a fool,
> You who bid me either to fear or avoid the gods.
> For the Cyclopes do not care for aegis-bearing Zeus,
> Nor for the blessed gods, since we are much stronger.

So also Pharaoh thinks himself more powerful than God, relying on his own strengths, doubting nothing of the prosperous success of his arms. But the mercy of God was greater over Israel, [snatching] the soul of His people from the lower hell of Egypt. For the more remarkable Pharaoh's cruelty was, the more illustrious the future mercy of God was to be. The more terrible the danger that loomed before the Red Sea, where there was great fear among the people and many an image of death, the clearer was the kindness of the Savior. # Exodus IX, v. 18.

<margin>The Egyptian Plagues.</margin>
...of the one who delivers. Plentiful is the redemption with God, and plentiful is His mercy. *The Egyptians whom you have seen today, you shall never see again forever. For Jehovah shall fight for you, and you shall remain silent.* <note>Exodus 14:13-14</note> Hence Jerome says in his commentary on *Jeremiah, chapter 32, column 668: The more fierce the vengeance upon sinners is, the more just it is, after the likeness of Pharaoh, who, though warned by ten plagues, was not punished <insert>into repentance</insert>, and persisting in his hardness, was at last overwhelmed by the waves of the Red Sea.* By the command of God, Moses uses the ministry of a staff as a lowly instrument to congeal the waters. The Israelites, having entered, had behind them the pillar of cloud, which provided light to the Israelites but darkness to the Egyptians, so that they did not dare to move from their place, fearing lest they fall into the hands of the Hebrews or into dangerous places. Meanwhile, along that path which the Israelites held until all, with none excepted, were staying in the very depth of the sea, Moses by God’s command extended his hand, and the sea returned <note>Hebrew: *le-eitano*</note>, that is, as the Chaldean and Greek translators rendered it, to its strength or its power, and it rushed upon the Egyptians. However, the return of the waters was preceded by the "disarming" <term>hypopiamos: a buffeting or wearing down</term> of the chariots and wheels. There are those who refer to this "entanglement" <term>sylleiōsin: a binding together</term> to the fact that the Egyptians, seeing the chariots proceed more slowly in the fermenting bottom, broke the ropes of the wheels and, mounting swift horses, betook themselves to flight, saying: *Let us flee from the face of Israel, for Jehovah fights for them against the Egyptians. Exodus 14, 25.* There are those who claim the confusion of the wheels arose from the voice of those crying out and urging flight. Truly, not even the lowest act of God the Avenger is seen in this "entanglement" of wheels and the "shaking together" <term>synkinēmati</term> of the camps. For whichever way they instituted their flight, whether backward or forward, they fell into the hands of God the Avenger; thus the reason is wondrous and veiled in mystery, that at the same time the sea flowed and ebbed, even while Israel had not yet struggled onto the shore! The ebbing sea blocked that way to the shore, so that the Egyptians, shouting as they headed for the shore from the dry (though gradually fermenting) bottom, fell into those collapsing walls of water while fleeing, and the sea rushed over them as they headed for the shore. Therefore the sea opened its jaws and swallowed Pharaoh with his whole army. The Robber wished to plunder, but the sea took the Robber for its prey. Skillfully, Tibullus names it *dark water* <note>Latin: *pulla aqua*</note>, which is defiled because of the mud and filth of every kind mixed in:
> *But where the region of the Velabrum opens, a tiny boat*
> *used to go through the shallows on dark water.*
You might call the water of the Red Sea *dark* after it buried the drowned followers of Pharaoh, who, submerged in the waves, suffered an end worthy of their crimes; for the dark color is the color of mourning, hence the *dark myrtle in Horace*; and thus *Pharaoh*, as Ambrose says in *Psalm 118, sermon 18, page 730, being merged in the waves with his people, is an example of worldly conversation, lest anyone should persecute the people of God.* For God is the avenger of the defiant, says Orosius (Book 1, Chapter 10): He suddenly divided the Red Sea, and with the margins of the stiffened waves widened on both sides, He suspended the sides erect in the likeness of a mountain, so that, provoked by the hope of an unimpeded path, the pious might enter the way of deserted safety, and the impious might enter the pit of unlooked-for death, the multitude of Egyptians being cut off with their King.

<column-break/>

<margin>The Egyptian Plagues.</margin>
Even now there exist most certain monuments of these things; for the tracks of the chariots and the ruts of the wheels are discerned not only on the shore, but even in the deep, as far as sight is permitted; and if by chance they are disturbed for a time by accident or curiosity, they are immediately restored to their former appearance by the winds and waves through divine power. The same things regarding the signs and monuments of Pharaoh's overwhelmed army on the shore of the Red Sea are read in Ivo of Chartres, *Chronicle page 2.* God had dealt with Pharaoh for a long time until then, so that, confounded by so many wonders and signs, he might return to himself, or if he would not, his hardening might be more clearly revealed and his lost nature exposed, while the glory of God might shine forth more and more before men, and His greatness be declared for the salvation of many. Hence Origen, when he treats "concerning free will" <term>peri tou autexousia</term> in his books *On First Principles*, <margin>Philocalia ch. 20, p. 276.</margin> explaining at length the Pharaonic hardness and the cause of his "stiffening" <term>sklērysmō</term>, says among other things: *He of an earthy nature is altogether disobedient to God. But if someone is disobedient, he has need of a hardening of the heart, and that not once but many times. Unless perhaps, since it was possible for him to be persuaded—and he certainly would have been persuaded, not being earthy, by being put to shame by the wonders and signs—God uses him to show the greatness of salvation to the many because they were more disobedient; for this reason He hardens his heart.* <note>Original Greek: Ὁ τῆς χοϊκῆς φύσεως... translated here into English.</note> In every act of the whole drama of the Pharaonic tragedy, God shows Himself as the God of mercy and the God of justice, the God of kindness and of wrath, who knows both the times for help and the fitting limit of punishments, *for God alone administers all things* <margin>Philo page 288.</margin> *and the seasons are under Him, and the appropriate helps, and the leadings, and the ways; He is the God and Father of all, who knows how He leads even Pharaoh through the necessary things and the drowning, the administration of Pharaoh reaching its conclusion.*

These miracles and wonders, by which Jehovah revealed Himself to all Egypt in astounding ways, were so illustrious that the fame of them was spread to all the inhabitants of the whole world, *Deuteronomy 2:25.* But Jehovah also wished to make His people, His Church, so famous, whom He ennobled with such a harvest of miracles: the pillar of fire, the split rocks, the divided waters of the Jordan, the sustenance of the Israelites for 40 years, the miraculous leading into the promised land, and so many enemies conquered. The fame of all these things penetrated to everyone at that time, and no series of ages, no day has obliterated the memory of them. Hence in Strabo, Numenius the Pythagorean, Berosus, Justin, and others, you will find the whole history of the leading of the Israelites out of Egypt described, although adulterated by very many fables; compare Diodorus Siculus, *Eclogues from Book 34, page 901.* Even Pliny himself calls Moses a Magician, from which it is clear that the name of this Leader of the Israelites was so famous in all the earth that it escaped the oblivion of posterity. Who would ever go so far as to deny the fame of Hebrew history, if they accurately weighed how the Church shone with such signal triumphs not only under Moses but also under Joshua—how the walls of Jericho fell by the sound of trumpets alone, and what other memorable things there were, all of which would be too long to review. Rahab herself is no weak witness to the fame of the victory of the Israelites and the drowning of the Egyptians in the Red Sea. *Joshua 2:9-10.*

# From Exodus XXIII. v. 14. 15. 16.

<margin>Jewish Festivals.</margin> Plutarch, in *Book 4 of Table Talk, Problem 6*, placed the origin of this word [Sabbath] in a Greek cry <note>original: "voce"; likely referring to the Bacchic cry 'Sabazios'</note>, nor is the derivation from the Egyptian word *Sabbo*—which denotes a disease of the groin—valid, though Apion defended it in Josephus, *Book 2 Against Apion*. For what good and for what end or use God the Lawgiver willed the seventh day to be sacred in each recurring week, the Holy Scripture is witness in *Exodus 20:10, 23:12, and Deuteronomy 5:14*. For the Jews were bound to abstain from all servile and daily labor, and God willed this day to be entirely destined and consecrated to sacred and divine worship. The more recent Jews, like the modern "circumcised ones" <note>original: "verpuli"; a derogatory Latin term for circumcised Jews</note>, are excessively superstitious regarding works not to be performed on the seventh day, as is evident from the Talmudic tractate *Shabbat*, as well as from the book *Orach Chayim*. For the Talmudists count 39 works <note>The 39 Melakhot or categories of forbidden labor</note> to which all other things prohibited on the Sabbath can be referred, as if to primary classes; they call these <insert>the fathers of work</insert> <note>original Hebrew: אבות מלאכות (Avot Melakhot)</note> or even <insert>offspring</insert> <note>original Hebrew: תולדות (Toldot)</note> for the foundations of works. Regarding the rest, they dispute with great subtlety, but they are not of such importance that we should stain this paper by reviewing them, since all these things savor of the "filthy wisdom" of Apella <note>A reference to Horace's "Credat Judaeus Apella," implying Jewish credulity or superstition</note>. Moreover, the New Testament Codex mentions the *Great Sabbath*, which in *John 19:31* is called <insert>the great day of the Sabbath</insert> <note>original Greek: μεγάλη ἡ ἡμέρα τῷ σαββάτῳ</note>, by which is understood the solemn day of the Sabbath upon which the Passover fell; as well as the *second-first Sabbath*, which in *Luke 6:1* has the name <insert>second-first</insert> <note>original Greek: δευτεροπρώτῳ</note>. Which Sabbath truly comes under this name is a learned dispute among the learned. Erasmus, in his *Annotations on this passage*, tells a charming story about a certain Doctor of Theology. Recently, he says, a certain Monk, who was also a Professor of Theology, was asked at a banquet by a certain scholar what the "second-first Sabbath" in Luke meant. He denied that any such thing was found anywhere in the Gospels, which he otherwise claimed to know well. When the other asserted it was in Luke, the brave Theologian challenged him to a wager: "I will lay down this cowl of mine," he said, "if Luke ever wrote such a thing." This matter of the second-first Sabbath, as an obscure thing, was not first questioned today, but also in olden times, as is clear from Chrysostom in *Homily 40 on Matthew*, Theophylact, Jerome, and others; so much so that today it is no wonder if the learned spend an hour or two investigating it. Martin Chemnitz and others with him understand it as the seventh day of Passover, which is called "second-first" because it is just as solemn as the first, and on it one must rest from all servile work. Nor are there lacking those who are persuaded that the feast of Pentecost itself is hinted at; since the Hebrews have three festivals more solemn than the rest—namely the feast of Passover, Weeks, and Tabernacles—they think the Feast of Weeks is understood, because it is *second* in terms of order, but *first* in terms of dignity, which it has in common with the other two. <margin>C. on this passage.</margin> See Blessed Friedlib; Hugo Grotius is of this opinion in his notes on this passage. There are those who think the second Sabbath is understood—second, I say, from that which is commonly called the first in the calculation of the four Preparations <note>Special Sabbaths leading up to Passover</note>, which they call <insert>Shekalim, Zachor, Parah, and HaChodesh</insert> <note>original Hebrew: שקלים וזכור ופרה & החדש</note>, because the Passover before the second from Christ's baptism fell on the 4th of March, and before the third on the 6th of the Calends of March,

<column-break/>

<margin>Jewish Festivals.</margin> and before the fourth on the 17th of the Calends of April; and in this Louis Cappel agrees, who fosters this opinion along with Johannes Cloppenburg, except that the latter understands the fourth Sabbath in the calculation of the four Preparations, which is called <insert>Shacharit</insert> <note>original Hebrew: שחרית; morning prayer</note>. Louis de Dieu, in his *Observations on this passage*, opines that the Sabbath is hinted at which lay between two other Sabbaths—namely the **first** day of Unleavened Bread and the Seventh—and followed immediately after it. For example, if Passover had fallen on a Thursday, the first day of Passover would have been the "first Sabbath"; that which followed in the weekly cycle, or as Epiphanius is accustomed to say, <insert>revolving in seven days</insert> <note>original Greek: εἰς ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας ἀνακυκλώμενον</note>, would be the "second-first" Sabbath, and the seventh day of the festival would be the "third Sabbath." There remains the opinion of Scaliger in *Book 6 of the Emendation of Times*, who, noticing the divergence of opinions in this business, unrolled the passage in *Leviticus 23 from v. 11 to v. 16* and found there that from the second day of Passover until Pentecost, 49 days are to be numbered. Then, that in the same place God commanded the people to offer a sheaf of grain <insert>on the day after the Sabbath</insert> <note>original Hebrew: השבת ממוחרת (mimochorat ha-shabbat)</note> of the feast day. From that second day of Passover, on which the sickle was usually sent into the harvest after the sheaf was offered, seven weeks were to be numbered; and among those, the Sabbath of the second week was the "second-first," <insert>six days after the first Easter-Day</insert> <note>original German: sechs Tag nach dem ersten Oster-Tag</note>. And thus, according to the mind of Scaliger, it is called the "second-first" Sabbath, as if it were the <insert>first Sabbath of the second day</insert> <note>original Greek: δευτέρας ἡμέρας πρῶτον σάββατον</note>, because it was the first Sabbath from those six Sabbaths which are usually numbered from Passover to Pentecost. Casaubon, Drusius, Martinius, Johannes Piscator, Dionysius Petavius, Calixtus, Schmidt, and Major approve this opinion of Scaliger with their own calculations. Mr. Frischmuth also has a specific disputation on this passage. It is pleasing to add a few things about the journey to be performed on the Sabbath, mention of which is made in <margin>Acts 1:12.</margin> A "Sabbath day's journey" is the distance which it was permitted for Jews to travel on the Sabbath day without violating their religion. Regarding this distance, the same opinion does not please everyone. However, the most common opinion of the Rabbis is that the space contains two thousand cubits. Since a cubit is a foot and a half, and a stadium is six hundred feet, four hundred cubits make six hundred feet or one stadium, and two thousand cubits make five stadia; hence it seems to follow that the Jews were permitted to undertake as much of a journey on the Sabbath as would be equivalent to half a German mile. Compare on the Sabbath journey Blessed Gerhard, Calixtus, Gualther, Buxtorf's *Talmudic Lexicon*, Johannes Jonston, Walaeus, and Louis de Dieu discussing this journey. But God willed not only the **seventh day**, of which we have spoken thus far, to be holy, but he also instituted other more solemn days in the Old Testament, on which he commanded the memory of his more illustrious benefits to be cherished and passed down to posterity. <margin>Commentary on this place.</margin>
See Blessed Friedlibius, or the Sabbath preceding Pentecost, which is the opinion of Hugo Grotius on this place. For example, if Passover had fallen on a Thursday, the first day of Passover would have been the <term>first sabbath</term> <note>Greek: πρῶτον σάββατον</note>; that which then followed weekly, or as Epiphanius is accustomed to say, <term>revolving in the seven days</term>, was the <term>second-first</term> Sabbath, and the seventh day of the feast was the <term>third sabbath</term>. There remains yet the opinion of Scaliger in *Book 6 of The Emendation of Time*, who, noticing the divergence of opinions in this business, unrolled the passage in *Leviticus 23 from v. 11 to v. 16* and found there that from the second day of Passover until Pentecost, 49 days are to be numbered. Then, that in the same place God commanded the people to offer a sheaf of grain, <term>the waving of the Omer</term> <note>Hebrew: הֲנָפַת הָעוֹמֶר</note>, after the feast day. From that second day of Passover, on which the sickle, after the sheaf was offered, was accustomed to be sent into the harvest, seven weeks were to be numbered, and among those, the Sabbath of the second week was the <term>second-first</term>, *six days after the first Easter-day* <note>original German: "sechs Tag nach dem ersten Oster-Tag"</note>. And thus, according to the mind of Scaliger, it is called the <term>second-first</term> Sabbath as if it were the <term>first sabbath of the second day</term>, because it was the first Sabbath from those six Sabbaths which are usually numbered from Passover to Pentecost. This opinion of Scaliger is approved by the calculations of Casaubon, Drusius, Martinius, Johannes Piscator, Dionysius Petavius, Blessed Calixtus, Blessed Schmidius, Blessed Hackspan, and Mr. Frischmuth in a specific disputation on this place. It is pleasing to add also a few things about the journey to be performed on the Sabbath, mention of which is made.

<margin>Jewish Festivals.</margin>
<margin>Acts 1:12.</margin>
A Sabbath journey is the distance which it was permitted for Jews to travel on the Sabbath day without violating their religion. Regarding this distance, the same opinion does not please everyone. However, the most common opinion of the Rabbis is that the space contains two thousand cubits. Since a cubit is a foot and a half, and a stadium is six hundred feet, and four hundred cubits make six hundred feet or one stadium, and two thousand cubits make five stadia, it seems to follow from this that the Jews were permitted to undertake as much of a way on the Sabbath day as would be equivalent to half a German mile. Compare on the Sabbath journey Blessed Gerhard, Blessed Major, Blessed Calixtus, Blessed Gualtperius, Buxtorf's *Talmudic Lexicon*, Johannes Jonston, and Walxus discussing this journey from Selden and Ludovicus de Dieu. But God did not only want the *seventh day*, of which we have spoken thus far, to be holy, but He also instituted other more solemn days in the Old Testament, on which He commanded the memory of His more illustrious benefits to be cherished and passed down to posterity. ### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
#### Page 182

<margin>Festivals of the Jews.</margin> These include the *Sabbath* and the *New Moon* <note>Latin: *Neomenia*</note>, the author of which is established as God—not without reason and the appearance of truth—in *Numbers 28:11* and *1 Samuel 20:5*. This was in memory of the light created by God, so that by this means the people of God might be called away from the superstitions and idolatry of the Heathens, who subjected the months to planets and other signs (see *Blessed Thummius, Treatise on the Festivals of the Jews and Christians, page 21*). There were five annual festivals: the *Feast of Passover, Pentecost, Trumpets, Propitiation <note>Yom Kippur</note>, and Tabernacles* <note>Latin: *Scenopegia*</note>. Of these, three were most celebrated. First, the *Feast of Passover*, given in remembrance of that wondrous liberation and leading out of the Israelite people from the house of Egyptian Servitude. Second, the *Feast of Pentecost*, as a perpetual testimony of the law promulgated on Mount Sinai amid lightning and the clangor of trumpets. Third, the *Feast of Tabernacles* (or *Skenopegia* <note>Greek: σκηνοπηγίας</note>), in which they gave thanks for the liberal blessing of all the earth's produce. Regarding these three primary Feasts of the Israelite people, because God said they must be celebrated three times each year, it is to be believed entirely and from the heart what *Sirach* <note>Ecclesiasticus 33</note> said many ages later: *that the Wisdom of the Lord thus distinguished them, and He ordained the times and festivities; some days He chose and sanctified above others.* Indeed, since the most grand feast of *Passover* is the first among those three and of greater importance, it must be discussed before the others. For in Egypt, when the Israelite people were to be liberated and GOD was about to send the Angel to kill the firstborn of the Egyptians, on that night when the slaughter was to occur, the Israelites were commanded to sacrifice a Lamb and smear the doorposts with its blood. Seeing this blood, the Angel passed over, and by this was prefigured the coming passage of the people into the land of Canaan. This done, God sanctioned the *Feast of Passover* as a memorial <note>Greek: *mnemosynon*</note> of this liberation, to be performed with certain ceremonies. The manner in which the Paschal Lamb was to be celebrated is described copiously in Exodus. The matter stands briefly thus: Each Father of a family was commanded to sacrifice a year-old lamb without blemish, to anoint the threshold and posts with the blood of the sacrificed animal, and to eat the flesh in his own home with his family. The preparation was such: the Lamb was not to be raw, nor boiled in water, but roasted by fire; no bones were to be broken, but it was to be whole. They used to eat it, prepared rightly, not reclining but standing, with loins girded, shoes on, and staffs in hand. They ate it in haste with bread that was not leavened, but unleavened <note>Latin: *azymis*</note>, with wild lettuce added, leaving nothing behind, and if they were not enough to eat the lamb, devoting the remainder to the fire. Since it is the common custom of writers to begin a treatment of things with etymology: men formerly famous for learning stumbled at the first stone by deriving the word *Pascha* from a language it does not recognize as its mother; for *Pascha* is not derived from "to suffer" <note>Greek: *paschein* / πάσχειν</note>. That would be the same as if we wished to derive the name of King Rehoboam from "to strengthen" <note>Latin: *roborare*</note> because the Scripture says clearly, as if alluding: *And when the kingdom of Rehoboam was strengthened and fortified, he forsook the law of the Lord (2 Chronicles 12:1).* Hence Isidore <margin>6 Origins 17. col 966.</margin> says: *The word Pascha is not Greek, but Hebrew; it is not from "passion," since "to suffer" is called paschein in Greek; but it is named from the Hebrew word Pascha, meaning "passage,"*

<column-break/>

<margin>Festivals of the Jews.</margin> because then the people of God passed out of Egypt; compare *Augustine on Psalm 68 and 120; Jerome on Ezekiel ch. 25.* Therefore, the view of *Justin in his Dialogue with Trypho, Ambrose, Lactantius,* and other ancients who seem to derive the name from "to suffer" <note>Greek: *paschein*</note> is allusive and pious, even if not genuine. The true root in the Hebrew language is *Pesach* <insert>פסח</insert>, which has the significance of passing over or leaping over; whence *Pesach* means transition, because God, while killing all the firstborn in one night, "leapt over" (so to speak) the Israelites alone, whose posts were sprinkled with the blood of the lamb; for *Pesach* signifies to leap from place to place. This Feast, which is called the "Festival of Passage" <note>Greek: ἑορτὴ διαβατηρίος</note> by *Basil*, *Diabateria* by *Philo*, *Hyperbasia* <note>The Over-stepping</note> by *Josephus*, *Hyperbasis* by *Symmachus*, and *Phasekh* by *Theodotion* and *Theodoret*, was celebrated by the Jews according to divine prescription for seven continuous days. Their beginning was the 14th day of the month *Nisan* (called *Abib* from the start), which is the first month of the sacred Ecclesiastical year; the end was the 21st day of the same month. Of these seven days, the first was the most solemn, and hence was called the *Great* day; the five following days were intermediate, and are called by the Jews *Chol HaMoed* <insert>המועד חול</insert>, that is, the secular days of the festival, and in their way are considered indifferent regarding labor. Finally, the seventh and last day likewise had to be solemn, and so a Sacred assembly was held on the first and seventh days. As for what concerns the history of the Paschal meal, it is woven together in *Exodus 12:14 ff.*, where it is recorded by whom and when it was instituted, for whom, what, where, how, and why. It recognizes no other author but God, who instituted this feast according to some calculations in the *Year of the World 2447; 791 years from the Flood; 430 years from the promise made to Abraham when he was called from his Fatherland.* It was at that very time when God was about to deliver His people from the heaviest servitude, and on that night *which is called the night of watchings for the Lord, because the Lord watched over the children of Israel in it, lest they be hurt by the Destroyer, so that He might afterward lead them out of the land of Egypt and bring them into liberty; it was to be eaten between the two evenings (Exodus 12:6).* What is understood by those "two evenings" is not yet agreed upon among the Learned. We, with Scaliger (*On the Emendation of Time, book 6*), think it means the time between the 9th hour (which corresponds to our 3:00 PM) and the 11th hour (our 5:00 PM), so that the "first evening" is when the Sun declines toward setting, and the "latter evening" is when it descends below our Horizon (see *Blessed Gerhard, Harmony of the Gospels; Blessed Thummius; Buxtorf's Hebrew Lexicon*). The communicating persons could only be the circumcised; hence foreigners had to be circumcised first, the Law saying (*v. 48*): *When a stranger dwells with you and will keep the Passover to the Lord, let all his males be circumcised, and then let him come near and keep it; and he shall be as one born in the land; for no uncircumcised person shall eat of it. (v. 49) One law shall be for the native and for the stranger who dwells among you.* Indeed, entire families of the circumcised were admitted, God saying (*v. 47*): *All the congregation of Israel shall keep it* <insert>כל-עדת ישראל יעשו אתו</insert>. It is clear that women were not excluded from this,

# Exodus XXIII. v. 14. 15. 16.

<margin>Jewish Festivals.</margin>
For they [the women] were also certainly part of the entire assembly of Israel; however, an infant, being destitute of speech and judgment, could not be admitted. Nevertheless, children were present who were able to ask: *What is this service to you?* <note>original Hebrew: מה העבודה הזאת לכם — a reference to the traditional Four Questions asked by children during the Passover Seder.</note> By this law, every Israelite was admitted, provided they ate the Passover in a state of purity. For when they celebrated the Passover in the wilderness of Sinai two years after the departure from Egypt, it happened that some had defiled themselves by contact with a corpse, preventing them from performing that sacred rite. They therefore went to Moses, indicating that they desired nothing more than to be allowed to offer the prescribed offering to Jehovah following the example of their brothers. Moses, unwilling to act on his own authority, brought the matter before God. God approved the petition, even to the point of appointing a new date by a fresh precedent, on which they themselves might slaughter and eat their Passover lamb (*Numbers 9:11*). And when King Hezekiah wished to restore the worship of God, which had been corrupted and interrupted through many ages (*2 Chronicles 30:18*), and the Passover was already being duly celebrated by his command, there were many in the assembly who had not been consecrated or purified according to the law, yet they celebrated their Passover without their uncleanness having been first purged. When the pious King became a participant in this, although he could have sought punishment for these delights <note>i.e., the unauthorized enjoyment of the feast</note>, he spared them out of a certain anxious kindness and prayed for them, saying with a gentle heart: *May the good Lord be gracious to everyone who has set their heart to seek God, the Lord, the God of their fathers, even if they are not cleansed according to the rules of the sanctuary.* The material or thing to be eaten was a lamb, whole, male, and a year old, taken from the common flock, and eaten entirely with its head and entrails; this was done both for the sake of the blood, with which the doorposts were to be smeared, and especially for the sake of the meat, which was to be eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. As for the arrangement, distribution, and preparation, this was first in the hands of the Elders, because before the Levitical Priesthood, every father of a family or Elder of a house—and after him the firstborn—had the right of priesthood; later, however, the lambs were prepared by the Priests and Levites. Regarding the former, as we said, it is written: *Moses called* <margin>2 Chronicles 35: 9. 10. 11.</margin> *all the elders of Israel and said to them (v. 21): Draw out and take for yourselves lambs according to your families, and slaughter the Passover.* <note>Hebrew: Pesach</note> Regarding the latter, the author of Chronicles says: *Conaniah, Shemaiah, and Nethanel his brothers; also Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad, the leaders of the Levites, gave to the other Levites for the celebration of the Passover 5,000 animals and 500 bulls; and when the service was prepared, the priests stood in their places and the Levites in their divisions according to the King’s command, and they slaughtered the Passover, and the priests sprinkled the blood with their hands, and the Levites flayed the skins.*

<margin>Deuteronomy 16:2.</margin>
The lamb thus prepared was not to be eaten except in Jerusalem, since God expressly restricted the celebration of the Passover to that place where he would make his name to dwell. Nor was this Passover feast a reciprocal social banquet, but the Father of the family, by God’s command, instructed his own while eating, teaching them especially about the type <note>The historical symbol</note> of the lamb and its antitype <note>The spiritual fulfillment</note>. "You know," he would say, "how harsh a servitude we served under Pharaoh, how he oppressed us with burdens of labor, and sought the death of our male children. You know that Moses and Aaron were sent with commands to Pharaoh to let his people go, adding the most

<column-break/>

<margin>Jewish Festivals.</margin>
severe punishments if he did not obey; and since he would not obey the warnings, all the firstborn in Egypt were put to death, and finally Pharaoh himself with his whole army was overwhelmed by the waters in the Red Sea. You know, finally, that before God killed the firstborn of Egypt, He commanded that they should slaughter a Lamb with certain ceremonies, and with its blood they should anoint both doorposts of the door with the lintel, so that they might be immune from the plague of the striking Angel." After these things were set forth and warnings added during the eating, the lamb was eaten by the Father of the family and his household members, with certain circumstances observed which were discussed above. And so, while they were conducting the Passover supper, it was not permitted for the Jews to go out reveling. For the Passover supper was to be performed *without revelry* <note>Greek: aneu kōmōn</note>. For the guests at the Passover feast were forbidden to go *Afikoman* <note>Hebrew: אפי קומן</note>, that is, *to the revelry* <note>Greek: epi kōmon</note>; which Scaliger <margin>Book 6 on the Emendation of Time</margin> wrongly explains as "dessert," where he cites those words from the ritual canon: *They do not depart after the Passover to the Afikoman* and interprets it with these Greek words: *not to dismiss the Passover meal with a revelry.* For this is not the sense of those Hebrew words; nor should the word *epikōmon* be taken there for "dessert," although more recent Jews have written it in that sense. It was not permitted to go from that feast elsewhere to revel, nor to betake oneself to the banquets of others—as was the custom among the Greeks, and no less among the Jews, but in other kinds of feasts than the Passover. This was also forbidden to them then. The Greeks and other Orientals, after they had feasted, were accustomed to go *to the revelry* <note>Greek: epi kōmon</note>, i.e., to move themselves after supper with a crowd to male or female friends, and to enter the house with noise and song, and there renew the feasting, which was also called by the single word *kōmazein*, and the Latins called it *comissari* from that; as in Terence's *The Eunuch*: *If ever she says, "let us let Phaedria in to revel," you say, "let us call Pamphila out to sing."* The Glosses rightly interpret: *To revel [comissatum], to the revelry [epi kōmon].* In Aristophanes this is called *to walk to the revelry*, and in one word *to revel*. In the Code of the Talmud, in the chapter on the Passover, there are two distinct words, not one: *Afikoman* [epi kōmon]. Therefore, by that canon, "desserts" were not forbidden at the Passover supper, but rather that one should not migrate from one banquet to another, which is *to the revelry*. The Hebrew words in which it is conceived clearly demonstrate this, as they stand in this manner: *They do not depart after the Passover to the Afikoman*; that is, *after the Passover they do not dismiss to the revelry.* For it is not permitted to explain it otherwise. The author of the Babylonian Gemara also correctly interpreted those words as being about the transfer and leading of a group from one assembly to another <note>Hebrew: m'chaburah l'chaburah</note>, *from one brotherhood to another brotherhood* <note>Greek: apo phratrias epi phratrian</note>, from a banquet in which one brotherhood has feasted to a banquet in which another is feasting. Namely, he does not want the Passover feast to be celebrated and eaten in two places. Which is clearly to go *to the revelry*. For a *kōmos* is the renewal of feasting at another's house by those who have already feasted at their own home. Whence the Grammarians also interpret *kōmos* as a "symposium" [drinking party]. However, it is not simply a banquet, but a reintegration of feasting after supper, at the request of arriving friends. Whence Epicharmus in Athenaeus says that from a sacrifice follows a feast, from a feast a drinking session, and from a drinking session a *kōmos*, i.e., a revelry. *From sacrifice, a feast; from a feast, drinking; from drinking, a revelry. And the reveler goes to the revelry.*

Later Rabbis, who did not understand that Talmudic expression which they took from the Greeks—as well as the custom itself of carousing, which is forbidden at the Paschal Supper—made one word out of two and, with the greatest ignorance, interpreted it as referring to dessert <note>original: "bellariis"; the author is likely critiquing the etymology of "Afikoman".</note>.
<margin>Simpl. Verinus Epist. ad Jul. Pacium p. 336. 342. 343. 344.</margin>

For the rest, those Paschal ceremonies placed before the eyes of the faithful, and impressed upon their minds, both an everlasting memory of divine benefits and the admirable holiness of the mysteries of religion, as well as the venerable and awesome Majesty of the eternal God himself. For the Passover was a sign, not only of *remembrance*, but also of *defense*, of *grace*, and of *eternal liberation*; since God had attached a saving grace to this sign, so that in this action, the benefits of eternal salvation might be offered sacramentally to those communicating through this medium of God. Thus, it was a sign not only by reason of its material part, but also by reason of its office regarding the entire sacramental action—namely, a sign of Jehovah rescuing from death, a sign signifying liberation, and a sign truly and really exhibiting grace. Hence, the solemn memory of the Egyptian liberation was in the Feast of Passover, but it was also a typical <term>anamnesis</term> <note>original: "ἀνάμνησις"; a ritual calling-to-mind or memorial sacrifice.</note> of that liberation by which God the Father, through the blood of His only-begotten Son, gathered and sanctified the Church for Himself. The weighty theologian Brentius <note>Johannes Brenz (1499–1570), a German Reformer.</note> instituted a comparison of both liberations, writing among other things:

> Truly the example of the Egyptian liberation is distinguished and memorable; for so that it might be diligently preserved, it pleased the Holy Spirit to institute two principal monuments of it. One is the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>, in the preface of which it is said: *I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.* Since the Decalogue was to be frequently commemorated, frequent mention of the Egyptian liberation was also held. The other is the anniversary feast day of Passover, distinguished not by only one simple kind of sacred rite, but by many and various ceremonies. However, it must not be felt that this feast day was only a monument of the past liberation from Egypt, but much more it was a monument of the future liberation through the Son of God, and that not from worldly tyranny, but from the slavery and tyranny of sin, Satan, death, and hell. Whence also the Paschal Lamb looked toward Christ the Son of God. The blood of the lamb, with which the doorposts of the Israelites were stained, foreshadowed the Blood of Christ, by which we are truly defended from the destroyer: but also the bones of the lamb, which were not to be broken, looked toward the bones of Christ; finally, almost all the ceremonies of the Paschal lamb and its feast day demonstrated Christ the Son of God and the liberation to come through him.

And so the antitype of the Old Passover was JESUS CHRIST, the Son of God, true God and true man, that great victim whose blood was to wash away the sin of the world. Our Christian Church, succeeding the Jewish people, celebrates the *memory of the true lamb*, by whose slaughtered blood the plague of divine wrath is turned away. By the sacrifice of this one, the wrath of the heavenly Father against death and sin (of which death is the wages) is appeased. As for the fact that we celebrate Passover in this turning year of Christ 1669, it is the one thousand six hundred and thirty-

<column-break/>

third Christian Passover of the New Covenant. Concerning which we could treat more extensively, but since we have some commentary on the New Testament under our hands, it results that in this, as in others, we are more brief.

We have heard thus far concerning the Passover, of which we have spoken indeed <term>with reverence</term> <note>original: "μετ’ εὐλαβείας"</note>, though not sufficiently for its dignity; yet having spoken with the best of intentions, let it now suffice. The next solemn feast after the Passover is called by the Hebrews <term>Shavuot</term> <note>original: "שבעות"</note>, by the Septuagint the <term>feast of weeks</term> <note>original: "ἑορτὴ ἑβδομάδων"</note>, *the Feast of Weeks*, because it was to be celebrated seven weeks after the prior feast, *Lev. 23:15, Deut. 16:10.* It is also called the <term>feast of harvest</term> <note>original: "חג הקציר"</note>, which then began, *Exod. 23:16*, likewise the <term>feast of firstfruits</term> <note>original: "בכורי"</note>, because then the firstfruits from the new crops were offered to God, *Exod. 34:22, Num. 28:26.* For at Passover they offered to God sheaves of firstfruits. In the New Testament it is called <term>Pentecost</term> <note>original: "πεντηκοστή"</note>, because it falls on the fiftieth day from the second day of unleavened bread, or because it was celebrated on the fiftieth day after the sickle was first put to the grain. Hence Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, early medieval encyclopedist.</note> says in *Origins, Book 6, 18, col. 968*: *Pentecost, just like Passover, is a celebrated day among the Hebrews, because it is celebrated after five decades [fifty days] of Passover; whence also it took its name. For <term>Pente</term> <note>original: "Πέντε"</note> in Greek is five, on which day according to the law the loaves of proposition from the new fruits were offered.* And because those fifty days are completed on the feast day itself, hence it was also called the <term>fulfillment of the days of Pentecost</term> <note>original: "πλήρωμα τῶν ἡμερῶν τῆς πεντηκοστῆς"</note>. By what ceremonies and rites this feast was to be celebrated, there is no need for us to inquire scrupulously, since they are expressly described—from which the more recent Jews depart, while they employ certain childish rites not commanded by God in the law. For they think this feast is primarily sanctified by these things: while among other things, they sprinkle the floors of houses, streets, and Synagogues with green branches, and they place the prize of this feast in these things, meanwhile neglecting the true use of this feast, which was the *memory of the giving of the law and the entry into the promised land*, which they were bound to celebrate with a grateful mind by the offering of firstfruits and two loaves baked from the new crops. In what month and day it was to be celebrated, we can easily guess. For it fell on the feast day of the month *Sivan*, and lasted at least for one day, out of which the moderns have made two, because they do not know which is the true day.

<margin>Num. 29. 1. seq.</margin>
At last we come to the final one among the major feasts, which was called by the Hebrews the <term>feast of tabernacles</term> <note>original: "חג הסכות"; Sukkot</note>, and simply <term>the Feast</term> <note>original: "חג"</note>, which was celebrated in the seventh month when the crops had been gathered. Since we have made mention of the seventh month, we wish to advise beforehand that the month *Tishrei* is understood, which was the first in the civil or political year, but in the sacred and Ecclesiastical year the seventh, and almost entirely festive among the Jews. For it was a time in which this month fell that was most suitable for celebrating feasts, because then all the fruits of the earth had been gathered from the fields; hence on the first day or New Moon of this month fell the <term>feast of the sounding of Trumpets</term> <note>original: "תרועה"; Teruah/Rosh Hashanah</note>, instituted by the command of God, either (as it pleases the Rabbis) in memory of Isaac being delivered from sacrifice; or (as Cajetan, Fonseca, and others think) in memory of the giving of the law; or (as others feel) as a greater preparation for the remaining feasts falling in this month. ...fell on the 10th day of this month, on which very day the High Priest, having solemnly washed and dressed in sacred vestments, first offered a calf for the sins of the people; having also been purified himself, he entered the Holy of Holies, atoning for the sanctuary, the tabernacle, the altar, the Priests, and the entire people. Whoever desires more on this feast of atonement may consult the Englishman *Sheringham* in his notes on the Talmudic book *Yoma* <note>Robert Sheringham (1602–1678) was an English scholar who translated the Mishnah tractate 'Yoma' (The Day) regarding Yom Kippur.</note>. These two were immediately followed by the Feast of Tabernacles ordained by God in *Leviticus 23:34, Numbers 29:12, and Deuteronomy 16:13.* Falling on the 15th day of the month of *Tishri*, it lasted as many days as Passover, namely eight. By the Greeks it is called <note>original: "σκηνοπηγία" (skēnopēgia)</note> *the pitching of tents*, because the Jews were accustomed to <note>original: "σκηνοῦν" (skēnoun)</note> *dwell in tents* or <note>original: "καλύβας" (kalubas)</note> *huts* made from the branches of all kinds of trees—primarily olive, myrtle, palm, cedar, etc.—and to <note>original: "πηγνύναι" (pēgnunai)</note> *fix* them in memory of that time when the Israelites were required to live in tabernacles in the desert <margin>Lev. 23. 34. 2. Macc. 1. 9.</margin> for 40 years. Hence *this* feast is called, according to the Septuagint, the *Feast of Booths* and in *Deuteronomy 12:16* the *days of tent-pitching*. It was, however, neglected from the time of Joshua (in whose time it was last celebrated) until the time of Nehemiah, under whose leadership it was excellently restored and celebrated, *Nehemiah 8:15.* We mentioned above that this feast lasted for eight days, yet with the law that the first and eighth of these days were most holy, on which all work was to be ceased and special sacrifices offered to God; the intermediate days were "half-feasts." Hence the last day was called <term>עצרת</term> (Atzeret) *the feast of restraint*, because the people abstained from all work and devoted themselves at least to sacred worship; it was also called <term>חג הגדול</term> (Chag HaGadol) *the Great Feast*, and the *Great Sabbath*, and <term>שמחת התורה</term> (Simchat Torah) *the Joy of the Law*, because on that day they read the final section of the Law and thus completed the Law. More on this feast below. By what ceremonies and rites modern "little circumcised ones" <note>A derogatory term for Jews used in the period.</note> celebrate this feast can be read in the Blessed <margin>Jewish Synagogue ch. 16.</margin> *Thuanus on the Festivals of the Jews p. 39 seq.* and *Buxtorf*.

<margin>
Deut. 16. 16.
</margin>
And thus far concerning the festivals which they call the "Major" feasts of the Jews, to be celebrated annually in Jerusalem as the place chosen by God, by Divine command: *Three times a year shall all your males appear before the Lord your God in the place which He shall choose: in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles.* Regarding the "Minor" feasts, whether they were instituted by God, by pious men, or finally by later Jews (we speak here of feasts instituted either divinely or by holy men), they could be celebrated in the places and cities where they lived. We add nothing of the festivals of the Heathens, whom it is established had their own holidays—both fixed, solemn, and perpetual, as well as private, extraordinary, and temporary—as is clear from the *legal title on holidays* <margin>Book 1, Satire 15.</margin> and others, except this: that they also celebrated their festival days with such devotion that they abstained from all servile work, as they judged that the days were profaned by it. The Egyptians, of whose religiosity <margin>Book 1, Saturnalia ch. 7, f. 52.</margin> Macrobius testifies, *celebrated their feasts with great reverence and modesty.* Among the Romans, holidays were held as very sacred, as is clear from the Twelve Tables. And Cicero explains that Roman law, *“Let them remove quarrels from holidays,”* with these <margin>Festivals of the Jews.</margin> <margin>On the Laws, book 2, p. 442, Vol. 4.</margin> words: *“The reasoning for holidays and feast days,”* he says, *“holds a rest from litigation for free men, and a rest from labor and toil for slaves.”* Hence Numa, the second King of the Romans, as recorded by the Blessed *Micraelius in his Synthesis of World History, book 2, f. 1, p. 336*, is said to have instituted that on working days, and especially on the priests' festivals, heralds should go through the city to command the citizens to rest and desist from domestic labors. So too the Athenians allowed no servile work to be performed on feast days. And when the *Anthesteria* <note>An ancient Greek flower festival in honor of Dionysus.</note> were held, it was permitted for both them and their slaves to participate, *having meanwhile been saved from work*. When the holidays were over, however, and they were called back to their accustomed tasks, the Masters addressed them thus: *“Out of doors, Carians, it is no longer the Anthesteria.”* The Heathens held their festivals in such veneration that if anyone did anything unworthy of the holiday, neglecting the precept, he was fined and had to give a "piacular pig" <note>An offering to atone for a ritual transgression.</note>, as Macrobius witnesses <margin>Book 1, Saturnalia ch. 16.</margin>. *Hence the Athenians are also said to have fined Ctesides because, while participating in the procession of the feast of Bacchus, he had struck one of his enemies with the whip he was carrying.* Modern Jews are so superstitious and stubborn in celebrating their festivals even today that, although it has been demonstrated to them a thousand times that the ceremonial laws cannot be adapted to the present state of the Church dispersed throughout the whole world, they refuse to turn away from their blind opinion. These "little circumcised ones" keep their festival days today not in spiritual exercises, but in a long babbling of words, in trifles, in gluttony, in bed-chambers and impurities, keeping holidays for themselves and not for God, serving the flesh and not the spirit. Thus the later Jews of this age are similar in this to their <term>προγόνοις</term> *ancestors*, who, as it is in <margin>ch. 29, 13.</margin> Isaiah, *honored God with their lips in the temple and outwardly, but retained neither innocence in their heart, nor truth in their mouth, nor continence in their flesh, but abused the New Moons and solemnities to satisfy the desires of the flesh, concerning whom God therefore said*: <margin>ch. 1, v. 14.</margin> *“I am full of loathing; your burnt offerings, your new moons, your solemnities, my soul hates.”* Every year they still feast in memory of the Passover, but sticking to the literal sense, they eat the lamb with wild lettuce. The successor Church celebrates the true Passover with a spiritual feast, full of joys, anointed with the oil of spiritual grace, commemorating the death of the Lord, the Lamb now sacrificed, until He comes, in Psalms and hymns and spiritual songs. Let us feast not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Let us serve God in Spirit and truth, and amid the tribulations of this world, let us await the glory of the heavenly kingdom with constant faith and hope, until we reach the eternal Sabbath! For then shall be fulfilled that of Isaiah <margin>Is. 66. v. 23.</margin> *chapter 66, verse 23, concerning the continuation of New Moon with New Moon and Sabbath with Sabbath.*
