# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

### Exodus XXIV. v. 3.

<margin>Legislation & Polity of the Jews.</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: ויבא משה ויספר לעם את כל־דברי יהוה ואת כל־המשפטים</note>
*And Moses came and told the people all the words of the Lord, and all the judgments.*
<note>original Greek: Εἰσῆλθε δὲ Μωϋσῆς καὶ διηγή沙το τῷ λαῷ πάντα τὰ ῥήματα τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ τὰ δικαιώματα.</note>
*Moses therefore came, and related to the people all the words of the Lord and the judgments.*

Since God wished the Hebrews to be most closely joined among themselves and to agree rightly, He brought forth certain laws, and ordered them to be delivered through Moses the Lawgiver—whatever of them pertained to morals, to ceremonies, or to the <term>forum</term><note>The "forum" refers to civil or judicial matters, as opposed to religious ones.</note> for the benefit of the Republic. Truly, in the Sacred Code of Laws, God the Legislator commanded many things holily, and promised many things bountifully and liberally. He commanded that the Jews should show themselves obedient and submissive to His word. He promised treasures, both heavenly and earthly. How many treasures of the riches of God's grace lie hidden in the kernel of the Law, which is the Messiah the Savior! He promised temporal things as corollaries of the grace of God already bestowed, and all these things under the envelope of the Laws, pertaining both to sacred rites and to other matters. For what are Laws other than the bonds and sinews regarding the worship of God, the purity of one's own conscience, and the observance of justice toward one's neighbor? They are, I say, the rule of discipline and public peace—if we love to speak of the laws of the forum—and the norm of all the counsels and actions of our life, as Chrysippus (praised by Marcian in the *Digest on Laws, law 2*) truly and gravely said: <note>original Greek: ὁ νόμος πάντων ἐστὶ βασιλεὺς θείων τε καὶ ἀνθρωπείων πραγμάτων...</note> *Law is the king of all things divine and human. It ought to be the protector of the honorable and the base, and the ruler and guide, and thus be the standard of the just and the unjust, and for those who are by nature political animals, it prescribes what must be done and forbids what must not be done.* For since the Law of Nature was almost obliterated because of the malice of men, and was in itself imperfect, a promulgated and prescribed law was added by God to this Law of Nature. This revealed Law is considered in two ways: *either simply and in itself*, as it was even before Moses, delivered to and observed by the Patriarchs; or *as it was solemnly promulgated through Moses*. Before this solemn promulgation of the Law, Moses, the supreme leader and likewise the supreme Prophet, following the counsel of Jethro, instituted that supreme and greatest <term>Sanhedrin</term><note>The high court or council of ancient Israel.</note> of seventy Elders, so that, while <margin>Exod. 18. 26</margin> the more serious matters were brought to him, they might judge small matters. Once these were established, the Law was brought forth amid thunder and trumpets <margin>Exod. 19. 14. 15.</margin> with great fear of the people, who were first ordered to be purified. For God had said to Moses: *Behold, I come to you in a thick cloud, so that the people may hear me speaking with you, and also believe in you forever.* He meant to say: I wish to prove to the Jews that you are my Envoy for giving my law to them through you, and when they themselves hear me speaking with you, it will be proven to them that I wish to give my Law through you. It was impossible, therefore, that any doubt about the Divine Law remained among the Israelites after they stood near the mountain, since in that standing at the mountain, the mission and office of Moses to give the law was proven to them, because they themselves heard the voice saying to Moses (*Deut. 5. 31. 32*): *Go, say to them, return to your tents, but you stand here with me, and I will tell you every precept, statutes, and judgments, which you shall teach them to*

<column-break/>

do in the midst of the land. As Moses thus received the Law, the sky flashed, the air <margin>Legislation & Polity of the Jews.</margin> resounded with great thunders, and the people were shaken with terror. Concerning this promulgation of the Law under the sound of thunder, Carolus Judæus says in the *Capitulary on Images*: *Moses, amid the terrifying blasts of trumpets and flashes of lightning and the overshadowing of a very thick cloud and the pyres of crackling fires, terrified and trembling, ascended the Mountain, received the Law, and as a true interpreter between God and men, showed the people the precepts promulgated by the Lord to be observed.* While Moses ascended the mountain, God descended upon Mount Sinai, and spoke with Moses on the very summit of the mountain in the sight of everyone. Who indeed could introduce with sufficient words GOD descending to the lands for the duty of instructing a nation! Let us use the words of Salvian saying: *and THE SON OF GOD accommodating Himself to earthly sights! A people of an innumerable multitude admitted into the fellowship of divine familiarity, prevailing in the honor of sacred friendship? Who [could describe] the thunders, the lightnings, the terrible sounds of the heavenly trumpets, and the tremendous crashing of the whole air on every side, the poles bellowing with sacred clangs, the fires, the glooms, the mists full of God, the Lord speaking face to face, the law resounding from the divine mouth, the letters carved by the finger of God, the rocky pages, the stone volume, the people learning, God teaching, and with men and Angels almost mixed, one school of heaven and earth?* It is my intention to hand down these sacred <term>thesmoi</term><note>Greek for "laws" or "ordinances."</note>, by which God partly tempered the Jewish polity, partly instituted morals, and partly the worship by which the Jews were distinguished from the nations, as if by a mark, a symbol, and a certain token, until the wall was torn down through the coming of Christ and they merged with the nations into one body; and to do so <term>syntomos</term><note>Greek for "concisely" or "briefly."</note>. Let us therefore look at this legislation of theirs, let us look at their <term>latreia</term><note>Greek for "worship" or "service."</note>. Now, there are three things around which the hinges of all laws, divine and human, turn: the worship of God, the purity of one's own conscience, and justice toward one's neighbor—all of which are contained in the Divine law. The Law, which is indeed called *Mosaica*, and is truly *divine* with Moses as the divine writer, is usually distinguished into these species: it is either *Moral*, *Ceremonial*, or *Forensic*. These are the accepted terms of distinction. That which is called the Moral Law is, in a stricter sense, the doctrine delivered by God and comprised in the Decalogue, such that it is subject to no exception, and is perpetual for all eternity; hence it is still observed by Christians, not insofar as it is of Moses or the Mosaic Law, but insofar as it contains within itself the morals and precepts of the eternal law flowing from the dictate of right reason. This Law is otherwise also usually called the *Law of Nature*, as being that which was implanted in the hearts of men at the original creation, repeated after the fall, and solemnly promulgated on Mount Sinai. Hence the Blessed Chemnitius <note>Martin Chemnitz (1522–1586), a prominent Lutheran theologian.</note> made a comparison between the Law of Nature and the Law of God. *This comparison is useful,* he says, *so that we may learn to love, venerate, and magnify moral sentiments that agree with the law of nature, wherever they exist and are read among Poets, Historians, Philosophers, and Legislators. Because they are divine right, and the truth of God divinely revealed.* And a little later: *Just as the Decalogue was distributed into two tables; so also Scripture, when [speaking] of the Law of nature...*

It categorizes the Mosaic Law into moral, ceremonial, and forensic types, noting that the moral law remains binding for Christians.</summary>

# From Exodus XXIII, verse 3.

<margin>Legislation and Polity of the Jews.</margin>
When [the author] speaks of [Divine] Scripture, he divides it into two tables. *The first is most beautifully described in Romans chapter 1 and is arranged, as it were, into certain precepts: namely, that there is a God, who is the eternal mind, omnipotent, invisible, the creator and sustainer of the world. That God must be acknowledged, and He must be obeyed according to the truth of the Law of Nature. The second table of the Law of Nature is posed negatively by the Philosophers: What you do not wish to be done to yourself, do not do to another. Christ, however, recites it affirmatively.* <note>Referring to the "Golden Rule" found in Matthew 7:12.</note>

<margin>Against the Jews, p. 100.</margin>
The same things are read in Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage, c. 155–220 AD.</note>: *I contend that before the law of Moses was written on stone tablets, there was an unwritten Law, which was understood naturally and kept by the Fathers; for from where was Noah found to be just, if the justice of the natural law did not precede him? From where was Abraham accounted a friend of God, if not from the equity and justice of the natural law? From where was Melchizedek called a Priest of the most high God, if there were no Levites who offered sacrifices to God before the priesthood of the Levitical Law? For thus, after the Patriarchs mentioned above, the Law was given to Moses at that time after they departed from Egypt, after an interval of many ages and spans of time.* These are his words. Moreover, God commanded many precepts to Israel, but those ten precepts of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>, which are the epitome of the Law of Nature, were

<margin>In the Augsburg Confession regarding the Magistrate, thesis 29, p. 409.</margin>
arranged by Blessed Lobechius <note>David Lobech (1560–1603), a Lutheran theologian.</note> as *elementary and fragmentary* <note>original: "στοιχειώδη καὶ κομματικά"</note>. God Himself spoke them with no ordinary pomp to all Israel as they listened; nor did He wish Moses—who otherwise had a great role in the promulgation of the law—to proclaim them, but God Himself spoke so that they might take hold more firmly. Their matter is the will of God, not indeed as it is considered within God, but as this norm of divine justice was revealed to men through outward proclamation. Thus, it is joined to the same, since it is fair and just that the will of God be done; and man, insofar as he is man and a rational creature, having his entire being through dependence on God, is bound in turn to refer all things to God—not according to his own judgment, but according to the will of Him from whom he has his being. This is his due

<margin>Deuteronomy 5:27.</margin>
obligation, as the people themselves confess in express words. But when it pleased God to enter into a yet more singular covenant with the Israelite people, so that the rigor of the law might be more clearly perceived from the start, He not only proclaimed the moral law in a more solemn manner with His own voice (though He did not dictate its fuller explanations), but He also increased both tables with an appendix, so that they might be all the more solicitous in the observation of the moral laws themselves. The appendix to the first table was the Ceremonial Law, which in the Old Testament is usually indicated by the name <term>Chukkim (Statutes)</term> <note>original: "חֻקִּים"</note>, a word derived from "imprinting an image." If we survey this, we will find entirely that the most significant part of its consideration is the prefiguration of Christ; upon His coming in the flesh, it gradually expired, and was completely abolished through the death of Christ. For that ceremonial Law was a Tutor leading to Christ (Galatians 3:24), which served the Moral law, and by which God commanded certain ceremonies and external rites as types of the Christ to be exhibited. These ceremonies, rites, and actions, which concerned both sacred persons and sacred things, all shone among the Jews, whom God had reined in,

<column-break/>

<margin>Legislation and Polity of the Jews.</margin>
as it were, so that under that great mass of very obvious rites He might call away the minds of the Jews, who were prone to superstition and the worship of false gods. Furthermore, by these rites God wished to depict the refinements of doctrine to the eye as if in a living image, and to exhibit them to be perceived somewhat by the senses. For circumcision warned of the corrupt nature of men, produced from natural seed, and that this required amputation; it also warned of the saving seed to come in the fullness of time, in which that which was lost in Adam was to be recovered. The purifications indicated the uncleanness to be purged by the washing of the blood of the Messiah, and the Sacrifices indicated the future expiation in the blood of Christ. Our study now descends to the forensic <note>Legal or court-related.</note> law; however, there is no need for us to "flash in the dark" <note>A metaphor for guessing or working without guidance.</note> while writing on the polity of the Jews, since the sacred writers have written everything diligently and not obscurely. As we release the chariots from the starting gates, immediately on the right side of the track there offer themselves so many laws, statutes, customs, rights, and sanctions of the Jewish republic, that to hand them all down would require great books. Indeed, great books by Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note> exist on these matters, and Cunaeus <note>Petrus Cunaeus (1586–1638), author of "The Hebrew Republic."</note> proceeds *briefly* <note>original: "συντόμως"</note> in these things. Since, therefore, the *ordinance* or *the entire constitution of the polity* <note>original: "θεσμὸν sive ὅλον τῆς πολιτείας σύνταγμα"</note> cannot be handed down by us, we shall at least pluck a *fragment* <note>original: "ἀποσπάδα"</note> from this so spreading tree. We wish, however, to premise some consideration of the judicial laws before we come to the special and distinct description of the Jewish government. Concerning what pertains to the judicial laws precisely considered: the ceremonial law looked to the immediate worship of God in the first table; likewise, the judicial law concerns the social interaction of men bound to that worship toward one another. And just as the former refers to the first table and the third commandment, so this refers to the second table and especially the fourth commandment <note>In the Lutheran numbering used here, the 4th commandment refers to honoring parents/authority.</note>, in which the duty of the Magistrate is treated, upon whom the constitutions of the polity still depend for their determination; this was also to be referred to in the Old Testament. It is

<margin>Deuteronomy 6:1.</margin>
called the *Judicial Law* <term>Mishpatim (Judgments)</term> <note>original: "מִשְׁפָּטִים"</note>, because it was clearly meant to be the norm of judgments, and to be kept and exercised in judgments. It is also called the Forensic Law by reason of its place, because the Jewish polity was like a lodging for the nascent Messiah and a school for the teaching Messiah, instituted for this purpose: that there might be a certain nation from which the Messiah would be born; likewise a certain place where He might teach, perform miracles, and fulfill the office of our redemption. The nerves of this polity, as it were, were the ceremonies and forensic laws, by which it was contained and distinguished from other nations until the coming of Christ. The matter with which the forensic laws deal are the actions of external life, insofar as this people had to be separated from others through worship. These laws are concerned with public worship, and especially with the preservation of ceremonies, so that transgressors were sometimes even to be punished capitally by the Political Magistrate—which was especially observed in the case of idolatry, lest it be disseminated among this people, whose forensic punishment is certainly peculiar to this people alone. They are concerned, then, also with conduct, both toward others, where they describe the system of wars and treaties, and of the Israelites toward one another, where it is prescribed, and the Magi-

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Jewish history, moving from general antiquity into the specific legal and political structures (Politia) of the Hebrew people across different historical eras.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Legislation & Polity of the Jews.</margin>
What the magistrate must do, and how subjects ought to behave toward both neighboring and domestic magistrates. To speak briefly, everything that must be observed regarding the civil conversation of men in public and private law, in politics, and in household management—all these things, as far as this people is concerned, are to be referred to these forensic laws. Having premised these things, the various states of the Israelites' government must be considered, and according to them, the entire system of government among the Israelites must be distinguished. For the Israelites lived far differently when mixed with a foreign Republic than they did in the Holy Land, when they possessed a Republic distinct with walls and towns. However, we must first consider what kind of government the people had *before entering the promised land*, while they stayed in Egypt. Truly, there was no <term>ὑπεροχὴ (hyperoche)</term> <note>original: "ὑπεροχὴ", meaning preeminence or authority</note>, dignity, or honor here, and whatever there was, it fell to them by the favor of Joseph. When we reflect upon and investigate the government, there was scarcely a shadow of it, and nothing else occurs to the mind but the fortune of Joseph; while he stood at the summit, the people lived comfortably, with the Egyptians indulging them in many things, incited to this by their zeal for Joseph’s favor. It is likely, in the *opinion of Menochio* <note>Giovanni Stefano Menochio (1575–1655), a Jesuit biblical scholar</note>, that they had at that time in the land of Goshen Judges and Magistrates from their own nation who would debate or settle disputes, pronounce the law, and administer public affairs, yet in such a way that they were subject to Pharaoh, whose supreme command was over all Egypt. They did not enjoy this prosperity for long, for after the death of Joseph, a King arose <gloss>who did not know Joseph</gloss>, whence they were tightly pressed by envy, hatred, malevolence, and tyranny, until they finally became bondservants of the Egyptians, by whom they were most harshly treated. The end of this calamity finally came when, by the singular mercy of God and under the leadership of Moses, they left Egypt and, asserted into liberty, began to live by the laws given by God. The counsels of God are hidden and admirable, and their depths are never to be explored by any human wits. In the miraculous leading out of the afflicted people, God's help emerges unexpectedly to the unexpecting Jews, and Pharaoh with a huge army is merged into the depths of the sea. With Pharaoh thus submerged, a polity gradually emerged, about which pagan writers have very little to say, and if there are any, they produce notable lies concerning their first origin and their laws and institutions. The notorious slanderer *Celsus* <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and opponent of early Christianity</note> says that the Jews were fugitives of the Egyptians, <term>ἀπ’ Αἰγύπτου δραπέτας (ap’ Aigyptou drapetas)</term> <note>runaways from Egypt</note>, indeed that they never did anything <term>ἀξιόλογον (axiologon)</term> or worthy of mention, <term>ἐτ’ ἐν λόγῳ ὤτ’ ἐν ἀριθμῷ αὐτές πό-τε γεγενημένως (out’ en logō out’ en arithmō autous pote gegenēmenous)</term> <note>original: "neither in word nor in number were they ever significant"</note>, *Against Celsus, p. 187. 192.*, and that they hid themselves <term>ἐν γωνίᾳ τῆς παלαιστίνης σύγκυψαντας παντεלῶς ἀπαιדεύτους (en gōnia tēs Palaistinēs synkypsantas pantelōs apaideutous)</term> <note>original: "huddled together in a corner of Palestine, completely uneducated"</note>, according to Origen, who refutes these slanders. But since the Sacred Pandects <note>A term for the Bible, comparing it to the Roman legal digests</note> teach otherwise regarding the Republic of the Israelites, let us hear the Jews, the witnesses of truth in this matter, who celebrate the <term>ἀξιώματα (axiōmata)</term> <note>principles or honors</note> of their former polity; and among them Rabbi *Shimeon*, who adorns the Israelite polity with this famous and elegant praise: <term>שלשה כתרים: כתר תורה וכתר כהנה וכתר מלכות (Sheloshah ketarim: keter Torah ve-keter kehunah ve-keter malkhut)</term>. *There are three crowns: the crown of the law, the crown of the Priesthood, and the crown of the kingdom.* Three illustrious dignities given to the Israelite people: *Priesthood, Kingdom, and Law*, as the most significant tokens of divine goodness and truth. From here, a very wide

<column-break/>

<margin>Legislation & Polity of the Jews.</margin>
field would open up to discuss the Judges, Kings, and those who presided over this people with the highest magisterial dignity until Christ; but we notice that it is not possible in the narrowness of this space to discuss everything more broadly. Therefore, we think it better to show the main points, just as we have reported in our historical *Breviary*. An opportunity will be given, if time permits, for these to be depicted in a better form. However, with Pharaoh thus submerged, the Israelite polity gradually emerged, and having progressed at first with small steps through the desert, it did not enjoy only one form of government. At first, the Jews wandered here and there through various stations, sometimes more joyful, sometimes sadder; Moses heard their cases and gave the whole day to litigants. But moved by the counsel of Jethro, Moses the Legislator chose strenuous men from all Israel to judge the people in the Republic, so that these, as leaders—captains of thousands, captains of hundreds, captains of fifties, and Decurions <note>leaders of ten</note>—might decide matters of at least moderate importance according to their smaller measure, but refer those of greater weight to Moses himself, to be judged as the supreme Prince of the Jews. This is clear to one reading chapter 17 in Deuteronomy and chapter 18 <note>OCR says XIII, but context implies XVIII</note> verses 20, 21, and following in Exodus. For God had chosen the Israelites as a peculiar people and made them superior to all nations *so that they might be a holy people to Jehovah their God*; and when, the time of exile having emerged, they were just about to enter the promised land under Joshua the Leader, Moses and the Priests of the Levite race said to all Israel: *Listen and hear, O Israel. Today you have become the people of Jehovah your God.* <term>היום הזה נהיית לעם ליהוה אלהיך (Ha-yom ha-zeh nihyeyta le-am l'Adonai Elohekha)</term>. *Indeed, they had long been received as the people of God, but by these words it is signified that He has now taken them more closely into a covenant as a people, and bound them more and more; for words that signify a thing often also indicate the increase of that thing.* After the death of the leaders Moses and Joshua, following the entry into the promised land, God governed His people in a threefold manner, as *Lyranus* <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a prominent Franciscan teacher</note> <margin>Deut. 26:19. <br/> Deut. 27:9. <br/> on Ezra ch. 1.</margin> once observed. First, through Judges: truly the virtues of Judges are commended three times in Deuteronomy <term>i. 1.</term>, namely *Equity*, that he may hear both sides; then *Integrity*, lest they accept persons or gifts; and finally *Strength of mind and constancy*, lest they fear power, threats, or hatred. Concerning these qualities, the texts in our Sacred law are venerable to read and to act upon, as Jehovah says: *Hear between your brothers <term>צדק ושפטתם (u-shefat-tem tzedek)</term> and judge righteously between a man and his brother and between his stranger (v. 17). You shall not recognize a face <term>במשפט (ba-mishpat)</term> in judgment. You shall hear the small as well as the great. You shall not fear the face of anyone <term>כי המשפט לאלהים הוא (ki ha-mishpat l'Elohim hu)</term>, because THE JUDGMENT IS GOD'S.* By which words there is required for judgment a man of proven faith and conscience, who fears God as present in judgments, who hears controversies accurately, and weighs the importance of things, whether they be cases of citizens among citizens, or citizens with strangers, or strangers with strangers; nor should he have any regard for persons in judgments, but should hear the poor as well as the rich, nor fear anyone, for *the Judgment is GOD'S*; because if any judge goes against this, with conscience removed, *the Devil is in the judgments*, as <margin>Deut. 1:16.</margin>

# From Exodus XXII. v. 3.

<margin>
Legislation & Polity of the Jews.
</margin>
<margin>
Judges in the preface, no. 8.
</margin>
As the jurist Henning Goeden piously speaks: besides the general Judge, there were four grades of offices in every city. The first was the *Zequenim* <note>Hebrew: זקנים</note>, or the Elders or *Senate*. The second was the *Rasché Aboth* <note>Hebrew: ראשי אבות</note>, for the leaders of the individual tribes were called the heads of the *Fathers*. The third was the *Schoterim* <note>Hebrew: שוטרים</note>, those who knew and spoke the law, whence they are called *Judges*. The fourth was the *Schophetim* <note>Hebrew: שופטים</note>, or those who executed the matters judged, whom you might call *Officers of the Court*; these offices are gathered from the Book of *Joshua*. The place of judgment and its ordinary seat were the gates, *For of old the Judges sat in the gates, by the will of the Lord, so that they might more easily settle the causes of all, and be found by the people without difficulty; so that you may know it is necessary that those who are made judges of the people be most ready to calm whatever question may arise*. In the gates themselves, correction was also carried out, because it is necessary that it be done in public where it reaches the people; for what is done for the sake of many must be recognized by many, as Francis Lambert comments <margin>chapter 23. 2.</margin> on *Amos chapter 5, folio 44. a. compare Philip the Presbyter on Job chapter 5, p. 15. and on chapter 29, p. 123.* And thus there was never a more blessed Republic under the sun, which had its center placed in God, with God Himself establishing it, instructing it with Laws, and directing it by Oracles. If one judges the form of the Hebrew Republic from the time of Moses until Saul according to the "political North Star" of that most political Aristotle—regarding where the sovereign power lies—that God-governed polity fits none of the Aristotelian forms, since the rights of Majesty or the "sovereignty" in the most important matters, such as the sanctioning of laws, the institution of Magistrates, and the declaration of wars, remained with God Himself. Whence, by a fitting name, Josephus calls this <margin>Against Apion, Book 2</margin> Republic a *Theocracy* <note>Greek: θεοκρατίαν</note>, in which the Holy Divinity reserved the more powerful rights of Majesty for Himself. This the Israelites ought to have preserved, just as Josephus introduces Moses speaking, or rather speaking well, in *Antiquities of the Jews, Book 4, chapter 8: "Let no passion for another polity take hold of you, but cherish this one."* They ought to have *cherished the present state* <note>Greek: στέργειν τὰ παρόντα</note>, and not absorbed the opinion toward a secular royal Monarchy, whence he says further: *"Let there be no desire for a King among you; let God be your kindred ruler."* But another thing pleased them; truly a great desire for having a King, not blushing to seek a higher throne than the polity established by God. Israel could not be kept from that desire even by the harsh laws proposed to them, even if they had seen God flashing in lightning: *They want a King, they clamor for a King, saying: "By no means, but there shall be a King over us, who shall go out before us. He will fight our battles and judge us."* Thus they asked for a King to be given to them, in which petition there were two sins: *distrust and audacity*. Distrust, seeking human protections and not resting in God alone. Audacity, seeking a new form of government in a Polity established by God. However, since the life and way of living of a King differs by a very great distance from an aristocratic state, Samuel predicts that their petition will be most difficult for them, and that royal society will be a burden, in these words: *This <margin>1 Samuel 8:11</margin> shall be the RIGHT OF THE KING who is to reign over you. He will take your sons and place them for himself in his chariots and among his horsemen, and they shall run before his chariot. He will also appoint for himself captains of thousands and captains of fifties,*

<column-break/>

<margin>
Legislation & Polity of the Jews.
</margin>
plowers of his fields, and reapers to reap his harvest, and smiths of his weapons and his chariots. (v. 12.) He will make your daughters his perfumers, cooks, and bakers. (v. 13.) He will take the best of your fields, vineyards, and olive groves and distribute them to his attendants. (v. 14.) He will take a tenth of your grain and your vineyards to give to his eunuchs and servants. (v. 16.) And he will take your male and female servants, and your best young men, and your donkeys, to use for his own business. He will take a tenth of your flocks, and you shall be his servants.* The right of the King is described far differently when he is forbidden *to multiply horses, wives, gold, or silver, but instead to worship God <margin>Deuteronomy 17:14, 15</margin> and observe His precepts*. The alliance of royal gravity with humanity toward subjects is most difficult, and rarely does a King show himself humane to his subjects. Samuel therefore wished to terrify the Israelites and strike fear into them regarding the character of Kings; for those who are oppressed by tyranny feel that no burden is heavier and *nothing is harder to fight than tyrants* <note>Greek: τυράννων δυσμαχώτερον οὐδέν</note>, and they are said to complain of the yoke. *You will cry out*, he says, *on that day from the face of your King whom you have chosen for yourselves, and Jehovah will not hear you on that day*. Since they are predicted to complain about the Royal right and cry out to the Lord <margin>v. 18</margin> concerning the injury inflicted, certainly if it were a true "right of the King," there would be no need for complaints; thus it is rash to establish that a "right of the King" properly so-called was granted to the King by God. Nor can a mere trifle be prescribed from what they take for themselves regarding *Mishpat* <note>Hebrew: משפט - judgment/custom</note>, since the word denotes not only *right and judgment*, but also *any custom and manner* received anywhere, even a detestable one. What Borrhaus writes here is pleasing: col. 344. *Since the rule of one is twofold: one in which "order" <note>Greek: τάξις</note>, that is, the order of legitimate administration is seen, which is conducted by virtue and not by lust; the other, in which the order of true governance is not kept, but all things are conducted according to the lust of the master. This right is tyranny, and it is mostly described here, where public matters are neglected as if they were someone else's, and private concerns are maintained. And this right is skillfully called "lawless" <note>Greek: ἀθέσμιον</note>, that is, an empire defined by no prescription or limits of right and laws. Those who exercise it carry that ruinous sentiment in their hearts and mouths: "So I will, so I command, let my will stand for reason."* On the contrary, if a King holds a kingdom, administering it not from the lust of the soul but *in a way dear to God and humane to men* <note>Greek: θεοφιλῶς καὶ φιλανθρώπως</note>, that is, he administers the kingdom so that God is given His honor and love toward men is declared, caring for the republic with the same or even greater diligence than his private affairs. God indeed requires such a King, who commands according to the sentiment of the Mosaic law, as is clear from Deuteronomy. But truly, because God knew His people were rebellious by nature, Samuel by His command foretold that they would have Tyrants instead of Kings, similar to the Kings who rule over profane nations. For the rest, whether the Israelites elected a King by divine mandate is a controversial matter: among the more recent authors, Cunaeus (Book 1 of *The Hebrew Republic*, ch. 14) and Schickard (in *The Right of the King* <note>Hebrew: משפט המלך</note>, ch. 1) defend the affirmative; and they prove this opinion of theirs from the Rabbis, among whom Rabbi Yehudah says: *Three things were enjoined upon the Israelites to do when they entered the holy land: to appoint a King for themselves, to cut off the Amalekites, and to build the chosen house, the Temple.* They furthermore urge the passage <margin>Deuteronomy 17:14</margin> *appointing, you shall appoint a king over you*...

"You shall set a King over you." These words, they say, contain a command from God that is not optional, but most serious, emphasized by the doubling of the word. <note>The author refers to the Hebrew grammatical structure of Deuteronomy 17:15.</note> But in truth, that phrase denotes not a command, but at least a greater certainty and evidence; for God had foreseen in the light of His omniscience that it would happen that the Israelites, weary of Aristocratic government by judges, would demand a King. Hence, in this place, He prescribes what ought to be done in that case and time, if ever the desire of having and creating a King should seize them. Truly, no necessity compelled them to create a King, nor is this an absolute command, but the speech is free, like that with which God addressed our first-formed ancestor: "From every tree of this garden <note>original: אכול תאכל</note> *eating you shall eat*," which the learned commonly explain as: *you may freely eat*, and it is purely and simply hypothetical. *If you say, "I will appoint a king over me, like all the nations have," you shall appoint him whom I shall choose from among your brothers.* For if the command had been absolute, the Hebrews would not have ceased to obey the command, nor would Gideon have rejected the Kingdom; for he, in Judges 8:22, replied to the people saying: *Rule over us, both you, and your son, and your son's son, because you saved us from the hand of the Midianites*, by saying: *I will not rule over you, nor shall my son rule over you, but the Lord shall rule over you.* Gideon was a Judge already ordained by God, and yet he speaks these things to those who were offering him full and pure power, and that hereditary into the second generation, so that they might lay aside these thoughts of royal power, leave all Lordship to the Lord God Jehovah, and rest content with the present form of government so constituted by God. These words provide a torch

There are those who say the Israelites had just causes, which they read in 1 Samuel 8:3, where it is mentioned that as Samuel inclined toward old age, his sons turned aside after greed, accepted bribes, and perverted judgment. Moved by these causes, the Elders of Israel approached Samuel in Ramah and said: *Behold, you have grown old, and your sons do not walk in your ways; appoint for us a King.* Concerning Samuel, while he joined his sons to himself in administering public office and appointed them judges, he acted partly rightly and partly otherwise. Rightly, in that he wished to consult the good of the Republic, because he himself, hindered by old age, could not travel around the regions. He therefore took his sons to himself, hoping they would emulate their father's virtue, and thus after his death would govern the Republic wisely and justly. # From Exodus XXIII. v. 3.

<note>original: "cat vetus Interpres; LXX. Κακὸν τὲ ἐλαίῳ"</note> The ancient Translator says; the Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> renders it: *Evil with oil.*

<margin>Legislation & Polity of the Jews.</margin>
Then Samuel took a flask of oil <note>original Hebrew: "את-פך השמן" (et-pach ha-shemen)</note> and poured it upon his head, *and kissed him, and said: Is it not because the Lord has anointed you to be prince over his inheritance?* By this question, a strong affirmation is pronounced; and as mention is made here of the oil vessel, the *Pach*, so the same word is used in *2 Kings 9:3* when it is recounted how Jehu was commanded by Elisha to be anointed as King over the ten tribes. However, by ancient law, the sons of Kings were not anointed, for they were considered anointed in their fathers, as Vatablus says regarding *2 Kings 11*; but when a controversy arose concerning the throne and the royal successor, the newly elected King was anointed, following the example of Solomon. Thus they also anointed Joash, the son of Ahaziah, because there was a controversy regarding the Kingdom; for Athaliah wished to reign. Furthermore, it was a custom among the Israelites that when a new King was inaugurated into office, the *Book of the Law* was delivered to him along with the regalia of the Kingdom, so that by this rite he might be reminded that the power entrusted to him must be moderated by *piety and wisdom*. This custom flowed from the Divine mandate in <margin>Deut. 17:18.</margin> where we read that for the King sitting upon his throne, there must be described a <note>original Hebrew: "משנה התורה" (Mishneh ha-Torah)</note>, which some explain as a *double of the law*, or a *double law*, so the sense is: *Let the King have two copies of the law, one which he may always keep at home, the other which he may carry with him wherever he travels.* The Chaldean <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> renders it *Targuno*, a *copy*, so the sense is: *He shall have with him a written or transcribed copy of this law; he shall take care to have a copy of this law described for himself.* The simplest explanation is gathered from *Joshua 8:32*: and he (Joshua) wrote there upon the stones this *repetition of the law*, that is, as the Septuagint rendered it both here and in *Joshua 8:32*: <term>this Deuteronomy</term> <note>original Greek: "δευτερονόμιον τοῦτο"</note>. See more in B. Gerhard’s *Commentary on Deuteronomy 17, p. 2055.* We intentionally omit the other ceremonies used in the inauguration of a new King, which can be read in *1 Kings 1:44 ff., 2 Kings 9:13, and 11:12.* In which last place that formula, *Long live the King*, is first read as being used, which Jean Gerson <margin>Vol. 4 of Works, n. 41.</margin> used when making a speech before Charles VI in the name of the University of Paris, beginning thus: *Long live the King, long live the King, long live the King. May he live physically; may he live politically and civilly; may he live spiritually and endlessly. We have been sent so that a discourse may be held by us concerning the Royal life, and his good and that of the whole Kingdom.* Indeed, he repeats that "Long live the King" often and explains it elegantly. Yet this formula seems to have arisen from the fact that it was customary, not only in the East but elsewhere, to swear by the fortune, health, life, or head of the King or Prince. Thus Joseph, according to the custom of the nation, dignifies Pharaoh the King with this honor, lest he seem to hold civil custom in contempt, saying <margin>Gen. 42:16.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: "חי פרעה" (Chai Paroh)</note>, *Pharaoh lives*, or, *by the life of Pharaoh*, asserting that the matter was as certain as the fact that Pharaoh lived among them. Aquila translated this differently than <term>Pharaoh lives</term> <note>original Greek: "ζῇ φαραώ"</note>. The Septuagint says <term>By the health of Pharaoh</term> <note>original Greek: "Nὴ τὴν ὑγιείαν Φαραὼ"</note>; for to live, <term>to live</term> <note>original Greek: "ζῆν"</note>, is to be well, to rejoice, to be happy. In the court of David, Uriah confirms the same established custom, swearing before Da- <margin>2 Sam. 11:12.</margin> vid by the life of the King: This custom did not stop in the East, but also passed to the Romans. There were solemn vows for Julius Caesar, and it was customary <term>to swear by his fortune</term> <note>original Greek: "τὴν τύχην αὐτὸν ὀμνύειν"</note>, to swear by his fortune and health—

<column-break/>

Dio, book 44, p. 275. This honor was also given to Augustus, <margin>Dio book 44, p. 275.</margin> and so that Tiberius might seem modest, <term>he allowed men to swear by his fortune</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐσυνεχώρει τοῖς ἀνθρώποις τὴν αὑτοῦ τύχην"</note> according to Dio. How familiar <margin>Legislation</margin> the rite of swearing by the Genius of the Prince was, <margin>& Polity</margin> Selden teaches in his notes on the *Arundel Marbles* <margin>of the Jews.</margin> Saul had a form worthy of empire and a kingdom <margin>1. 57. p. 696.</margin> sufficiently peaceful as long as he remained in the ways of the Lord, <margin>p. 148. 149. 150. 151.</margin> but when he turned away from God, he paid the due penalties for his defection. Under Kings David and Solomon, the kingdom was peaceful, with peace and concord everywhere, so much so that Ennius’s verse about the Roman Republic seems to find a place here:
> *The Roman state stands by its ancient customs and its men,*

This verse is praised by Cicero and by Augustine, as if spoken from an Oracle, *for neither could the men*, <margin>City of God, 2. 21. p. 133.</margin> they say, *unless the city had been so charactered, nor the customs, unless these men had presided, have either founded or so long maintained so great a Republic, ruling so justly and widely.* Regarding the Jewish Republic, one might say the same: *it stood by its ancient customs and men.* For the political order through laws and distinctions of lordships, through contracts and judgments, was a singular and immense benefit of God's work in the Jewish Polity, which showed God's illustrious grace toward the Jewish people. Whether you consider the *Magistracy*, the *Laws*, or the *Priesthood*, each was strengthened by divine authority. The laws and duties of the Magistracy and the ministries of the Priests scatter the highest rays of divine wisdom. In the consideration of this society, as much as we wonder at its wisdom and justice, so much do we detest the horrendous and sad confusions with which Satan and his instruments disturbed and deformed this political order. Divine Wisdom says in Solomon: *By me kings reign, and lawgivers decree just things.* Let it be said of the confusion and dissent of the Polity: *Through me, Satan, Kings reign badly, and Judges decree unjust things.* In this Jewish polity, if you consider the reign of the Kings, it must be confessed there was far more confusion than in the reign of the Judges; yet God did not cease to be present to the society of men, and to protect the order He instituted, lest it be utterly destroyed by the furies of Devils and evil Kings or external enemies; and indeed, He declared His judgment and presence by the punishments of the wicked, examples of which will be brought forward in their proper place. But after that division occurred following Solomon's death, with most Kings being impious and injustice becoming more powerful, the Republic could not exist without injury. For that older age, as its antiquity faded—to borrow the words of Augustine—not only neglected to renew the Republic with the same colors it once had, but did not even care to preserve at least its form and its outermost outlines. For what remained of the ancient customs by which the Jewish state stood? What arts were not devised to overturn and change the state in both Church and Polity? We do not know if more brilliant examples of religion being perversely applied among the arts of reigning can be found than in Absalom and Jeroboam: for when divine goodness had appointed a King here over the ten tribes of Israel, behold! the piety he owed to God, he corrupted and transferred into the arts of dominance: *For Jeroboam said (these are the words of the Holy Spirit) in his heart: now the kingdom will return to the house of David, if this people goes up...*

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>Legislation & Polity of the Jews.</margin>
*this man, so that he may perform sacrifice in the house of the Lord at Jerusalem, and the heart of this people will turn back to Rehoboam, King of Judah, and they will kill me and return to him.* <note>original Latin: "iste, ut faciat sacrificium..." quoting 1 Kings 12:27 regarding Jeroboam's fear.</note> Hence, to avert the danger he suspected and to strengthen the kingdom for himself, *he devised a plan, made two golden calves, and said to them: Do not go up to Jerusalem anymore; behold, your gods, O Israel!* <note>1 Kings 12:28.</note> Truly, it was not enough for him to have usurped religion as a tool of statecraft, unless he also perverted it entirely by introducing abominable Idolatry. But with what success? We shall hear again the eternal truth: *and for this reason the house of Jeroboam sinned, and was turned away, and wiped off the face of the earth.* <note>1 Kings 13:34.</note> Recognize with me, listeners! a negligence in wickedness and a stupidity in craftiness that is not easily described. Jeroboam knew the eternal Deity; he knew his empire had come to him by His goodness; he knew it happened because of the idolatry with which Solomon had polluted his own house; he had received the promise *that he would reign over all that his soul desired, if he walked in the ways of the Lord and kept his precepts.* Yet stronger than all these in his mind was a breeze of the slightest suspicion, so that for the stability of his kingdom he chose that which he had been taught by so many proofs—or at least ought to have been—would be his certain destruction. The same was the counsel of Absalom, and no more happy was the success: when everything necessary for the execution of the conspiracy against his father and his Empire seemed finished, he imposed a pretense of religion as a finishing touch. Hence he sought permission from his Parent to go to Hebron to fulfill the vows which he claimed, with a face composed into piety, he had offered to the eternal Deity. Nothing was more pleasing to the parent, nothing more joyful to the people, and if you consider the matter in itself, nothing more fitting to the spirit of unfeigned piety: but everything was directed by the traitor toward an opportunity for invading the kingdom. *For while he was sacrificing victims, a strong conspiracy was formed, and the people running together increased with Absalom.* <note>2 Samuel 15:12.</note> And indeed in this, the plan by which he had intended religion to be among the means of acquiring a kingdom did not lack success: but truly, its force soon collapsed. For, a little later, hanging from a tree and pierced through by three spears, he poured out his impious soul and lost the kingdom. A lesson was given to mortals that divine worship can never be usurped in vain, and that those who dare to count it among the deceptions of wickedness and villainy fall with a horrendous and irreparable ruin. We could not easily say how wonderful the state of the Jewish People was in the Babylonian captivity. In servitude they were not slaves; in captivity they were not captives. They lived in an unordered order, in a busy idleness, in a restless quiet, in a discordant harmony. The people wandered about <term>klaysigelos</term> <note>Greek: "weeping and laughing at once"</note>, <term>thrasydeilos</term> <note>Greek: "bold yet cowardly"</note>, <term>argotyphlos</term> <note>Greek: "idly blind"</note> and <term>living yet dead</term> <note>Greek: "zōn tethnēke"</note>. <term>Unfortunate yet happy</term> <note>Greek: "dystykhōn eudaimonei"</note>, because in the colony they were free, retained the <term>autonomy</term> <note>Greek: "autonomian" - self-governance</note> of their religion, and had their own Prince of the captivity from the Davidic lineage. When the years of captivity were finished, they returned to their fatherland, partly under Leaders from the family of David, partly under the Hasmoneans, partly under the Kings Herod and Archelaus—foreigners who had with them a bodyguard worse than the prince himself, collected from all nations, so much so that according to the testimony of Josephus, there were even German soldiers in that bodyguard—and partly under the Governors of the Romans, under whose rule there was less turmoil than when they were driven out, until

<column-break/>

<margin>Legislation & Polity of the Jews.</margin>
after a rebellion was made against the Romans, Titus, son of Vespasian, having utterly overturned Jerusalem, dispersed the Jews into the whole world, so much so that the ceremonial and forensic laws, which were once <term>truly laws</term> <note>Greek: "ontōs nomoi"</note>, are now <term>laws that are not</term> <note>Greek: "ouk ontes nomoi"</note>, namely, *null and void* laws. The <term>Justice</term> <note>Greek: "Dikē"</note> which was instituted by Moses and the Elders, which belonged purely to the Jewish court, is now <term>not in justice</term> <note>Greek: "mē endikē"</note>. We recognize, however, and feel that from the laws given to the Jewish nation there shines a most brilliant ray of divine wisdom, a ray of divine justice, and a mirror of divine goodness, indicating how much He loved this nation above others. Let the laws of Minos received from Jove, the constitutions of Lycurgus delivered by Apollo, the tables of Solon inscribed by Pallas, and those of Numa brought from Egeria, yield far to this. Minos was believed to have written laws from a conversation with Jove himself, who is called by Homer * ————— <term>the companion of great Zeus</term> <note>Greek: "Dios megalou oaristēs"</note>.
<margin>Odyssey 19, v. 179.</margin>
Hence Nicolaus of Damascus says: <term>Minos pretends that he learned from Zeus himself every nine years, going to a certain mountain in which there was said to be a cave of Zeus, and from there he always brought certain laws to the Cretans</term>. Who indeed does not see from these fictions that they have been corrupted by the cunning of the Devil from the history of Moses, the legislator of the Jews, who preceded Jove by several centuries? To such an extent has the skill of Demons imitated with its fictions this clemency of the Divine Majesty toward mortals (as Barthius says in *Claudian* p. 1261), yet in such a way that the greatest difference remained between truth and fictions. And thus far we have spoken of the Divine law with the demonstrative <term>Mosheh</term> <note>Hebrew: "Moses"</note> repeated three times * which is called <term>by excellence</term> <note>Greek: "kat' exokhēn"</note> <term>mitzvah</term> <note>Hebrew: "commandment"</note>, because it contains the principal part, which we call the moral law; partly <term>chukkim</term> <note>Hebrew: "statutes"</note>, *statutes* from <term>chakak</term>, which is *he engraved an image*, so called because everything in it is typical and to be referred to Christ, whom they represent; partly <term>mishpatim</term> <note>Hebrew: "judgments"</note>, *Judgments*, all of which, insofar as they savor of the promised land, vanished at the coming of Christ. *For the Law and the Prophets were until John*, says Christ himself,
<margin>Matthew 11:13.</margin>
by which he signified that the end of the Mosaic polity, the Levitical priesthood, ceremonies, and rites was already present, so that the end of John's ministry was the beginning of Christ's ministry.

The single tribe of Levi, consecrated to Ecclesiastical duties and destined for sacred functions, was divided into three orders: namely, the *Levites*, the *Priests*, and the *High Priest*, from which the Jewish hierarchy consisted. ...so that he might admit him, together with his offspring, into the supreme Priesthood and present him to the people. The succession of Aaron and his sons in this highest rank of honor is recounted by God with such care and so frequently—even while Aaron was still living—that one reads of hardly anything else repeated with such great solicitude. Regarding this pinnacle of authority, there are various accounts found throughout the sacred *Pandects* <note>original: "Pandectis" - a term for a complete body of laws or scriptures</note>. For Chapter 28 of Exodus concludes with these words: *it shall be a statute forever unto him and his seed after him* <note>original Hebrew: חקת עולם לו ולזרעו אחריו; Greek: Νόμιμον αἰώνιον αὐτῷ, καὶ τῷ σπέρματι αὐτῷ μετ’ αὐτόν</note>. Likewise in chapter 29:1 and following; Leviticus 8 in its entirety; Numbers 3:7, 10, 32, 39; chapters 17, 18, 20:26; 1 Chronicles 13:12, 13; chapters 20, 25, 26. From these it is clear that there was such love for that family of Aaron that God was moved chiefly by devotion to it. When this family was first mocked and despised by Korah and his accomplices, God—the Savior, steadfast in His purpose to preserve the consecrated order in its best state—cast Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, those three seditious citizens, into the underworld. For the earth, opening a chasm, swallowed them, their houses, and all the men of Korah (*Numbers* 16:31). Later, from the family of Eleazar, this highest honor passed for a time to the family of Ithamar, the cause of which the Sacred Scriptures do not explicitly state. The Hebrews think it happened because, when the crime against the Levite’s wife was committed (that sad history found in the *Book of Judges*), they were too negligent in their duty. Finally, in the time of Solomon, it was transferred back to the lineage of Eleazar, from which David appointed sixteen Princes, while from Ithamar he appointed eight, because the former was more numerous. Happy, therefore, was *Amram* <note>The father of Moses and Aaron</note> in such a Son, whom the Divinity Himself chose, so that he might observe His name in the highest priestly seat with great care, as a High Bishop, and possess the chief role in Ecclesiastical affairs. This heavenly office is the most narrow <note>exclusive</note> of all, for which reason its authority must be held as greatest. For what is more majestic than that *Aaron was separated to sanctify the most holy things, he and his sons forever, to burn incense before the Lord, to minister to Him, and to bless in His name forever*? <note>original Hebrew: אהרן להקדישו קדש קדשים הוא-ובניו לעולם להקטיר לפני יהוה לשרתו ולברך בשמו עד-עולם</note>

<margin>
1 Chronicles 23:13.
</margin>
Is there anyone who does not see here *the venerable dignity of Aaron* <note>original Greek: τὸ σεβάσμιον τοῦ Ἀαρών</note>? To the Roman Emperors was given a peculiar name of honor, so that they were called *Sebastoi* <note>August or Venerable ones</note>. But even if that purple power yields, can anything more venerable be said of our Aaron? While we assert the High Priesthood for Aaron, we remove it from Moses, protesting the error committed by the Jews who call Moses the *Priest of Priests* <note>original Hebrew: כהן הכהנים</note>, attributing the governance of the High Priesthood to him. But we do not recognize that High Priesthood in him, nor do we know of him having anything in common with the function of that Priesthood. The Jews studiously apply "pigments" <note>rhetorical embellishments</note> to obscure this most beautiful portrait of the High Priesthood, but since this space does not allow me *to wipe away* <note>original Greek: ἐξαλείφειν</note> the dye of the painters, we at least oppose them with the testimony of Josephus. He relates that the Israelites wanted to create Moses as High Priest, but he excused himself by the command of the Lord, who ordered Aaron to be consecrated High Priest because Moses was occupied with speaking with the Lord and the governance of the people—as Cornelius à Lapide recounted from him in his commentary on Leviticus 8:5. However, to represent the

<column-break/>

High Priest, we cannot do so more effectively than with the sacred words themselves. Truly, the narrative of Moses has expressed the ancient *High Priest* <note>original Greek: ἀρχιερέα</note> excellently and accurately; as much as one departs from this description, so much is diminished from the ancient glory. The ancient clothing and attire of him who once performed the High Priesthood was such: the High Priest used to be so adorned with garments, shining with gold and gleaming with gems, that he drew the gaze and thoughts of the entire people away from the rest of the priests and Levites *unto himself alone*. The supreme beauty of the High Priest affected the souls of the onlookers, charmed them with sweetness, and bathed them in joy. Indeed, in the conspicuous attire of the Priest and his singular holiness of life, the "best and greatest" Priesthood of the MESSIAH, the Priest of Priests, was to be observed in the innermost senses. All the splendor of the Priesthood blossomed from the majesty of the Messiah, from whose root all the delicious shoots and branches of the Priesthood flourished. Hence, that ancient legal ministry was honored with various insignia, gems, bands, and ribbons for the dignity of Him whom those signs represented. Sublime was the insignia with which Aaron's head was adorned; Plutarch himself describes the *Hebrew* High Priest as being "mitred."

Philo* delivers a more detailed explanation of this ornament when, describing the head-ornament of the High Priest, he expressly distinguishes the miter and the plate from the miter. For the miter, he says, was under the *petalon* (that is, the plate), so that the plate, which was golden, would not touch the head. Then he adds that the *cidaris* <note>a Persian-style tiara or turban</note> was added to the plate—that is, the upper part of the Pontifical crown. Concerning the plate, it was *made of much gold and precious stones* <note>original Greek: διὰ χρυσοῦ πολλοῦ καὶ λίθων τιμίων πεποιημένη</note>; *adorned with gold and variegated stones* <note>original Greek: χρυσῷ καὶ λίθοις πεποικιλμένοις κεκοσμημένη</note>. It consisted of precious material and a majestic form, and the more intricate its craftsmanship, the more excellent its significance. Each detail signifies nothing if not the heavenly; they signify the kingdom of Christ, which surpasses all kingdoms. The meanings of this weaving are the more noble as they are less understood by the ignoble; they are so majestic that they are not obvious to everyone. In the Sacred Language, the name *Tzitz* <note>original Hebrew: ציץ</note> occurs; whether it comes from the root *tzutz* (to flourish/bloom) or more correctly from *tzitz* (a flower/plate), lexicographers have not yet been able to agree. It is clear from many places in Scripture that the word *Tzitz* is equivocal <note>has multiple meanings</note>; compare Fuller, *Miscellanea Sacra*, Book 6, ch. 6, p. 708 and following. In other places of Holy Scripture, it comes described by other names: in Leviticus 8:9 it is called *the golden plate* <note>original Hebrew: ציץ הזהב; Greek: πέταλον χρυσόν; German: das guldne Blat</note>, which in *Exodus 39:30* is called *the holy crown* <note>original Hebrew: נזר הקדש</note>; according to Pagninus and Arias Montanus in *Leviticus 8:9*, *the holy Diadem*; and in *Exodus 29:6*, according to Tremellius, *the holy Crowning*, and according to Blessed Luther, *the holy Crown* <note>original German: die heilige Krone</note>, which Josephus also mentions (*Antiquities of the Jews*, 3.8) under the name of *pyleon* or *masnaempset*. Even if a diadem—as Hesychius observes, witnessed by Ursinus (*Analecta*, Vol. 2, Book 3, p. 107)—was *the king's wreath, an ornament of the head, or a crown* <note>original Greek: στέμμα βασιλέως, κεφαλιῶν κόσμος, ἢ ὢν στέφανος</note>; compare Caelius Rhodiginus (*Ancient Readings*, Book 24, ch. 6, p. 922) to whom the Diadem is called *royal attire* <note>original Greek: βασιλικὸν ἔνδυμα</note>; nevertheless, the *Tzitz* or *golden plate* <note>original Greek: πέταλον χρυσόν</note> among the Jews was the insignia of the High Priest alone, not of Kings, whose insignia were also the *Nezer* (2 Kings 11:12, 2 Chronicles 23:11) and the *Atarah* (2 Samuel 12:30, 1 Chronicles 20:2, Psalm 21:4). Thus, by this very plate, as the peculiar head-insignia of the High Priest, they were distinguished...

# 194 BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Clothing of Aaron.</margin> Kings were consecrated by the High Priest. Nor was it permitted for any common priest to adorn himself with this forehead-plate under penalty of death <note>original Greek: θανάτε (thanatou)</note>, which *Hottinger* proves in his *Book on Hebrew Law, section 99, page 128*, citing the *Gemara Zebachim*, the Englishman *Sheringham* on *Yoma chapter 6, page 168*, and *Rabbi Levi of Barcelona*. Furthermore, while it has been proven thus far that this head-ornament was unique and proper to the Jewish Pontiff, we do not deny that the priests of the gentiles <note>non-Jewish nations</note> adorned their heads with a certain peculiar covering. Through "cacozelia" <note>perverse imitation</note>, it can easily be said that it was taken from here and distorted into another form, so much so that the error of *Polydore Vergil* in *Book 4 of On the Invention of Things, chapter 7* is quite crude when he asserts that the Hebrew priests borrowed this head ornament from the Egyptians. Whatever the case may be, we still perceive a great difference between the head-ornament of the Jewish High Priest and those of the gentiles. *His* consisted of pure gold, for it was commanded to be made of <term>זהב טהור</term> <note>transliteration: zahav tahor; "pure gold"</note>, *Exodus 28:36*. *Theirs* was of various materials. Among the priests of the infernal rites it was made of *yew*; among the Mimallones <note>Bacchic revellers</note> it was of *ivy*, according to *Tacitus in Book 5 of his Histories*; among the Arval Brothers it was of *ears of grain*, according to *Macrobius in Book 1 of the Saturnalia*. Among the Gauls it was of *pine*, because Atys had castrated himself under a pine tree. In the Dionysian games it was *myrtle*; in the festivals of Ceres, *oak*; in those of Hercules, *poplar*; see *Virgil, Book 1 of the Georgics and Book 8 of the Aeneid*. The *Blessed Reader* will find more in *Saumbert*, and in the work of *Natale Conti*, which is in nearly everyone's hands. Our modern "Verpuli" <note>a derogatory term for Jews</note> use a silver plate in place of the gold one, which *Buxtorf* mentions in *The Jewish Synagogue, chapter 9*, from the version by *Germberg*:

> That book, he says, is always wrapped in a certain linen cloth, in which both certain Hebrew words and names are similarly sewn.

Then, on the outside, a certain linen cloth is hung around, similar to a small cloak, sometimes made of silk, sometimes of shagged silk or purple, and sometimes even made of pure gold. To this is attached a certain silver plate by a small golden chain, upon which is written *Kether Torah*, that is, *Crown of the Law*, or *Kodesch Ladodonai, Holiness to the Lord*. However, by divine mandate, the most holy name of the Most Holy Jehovah <term>קדש ליהוה</term> <note>transliteration: Kodesh l'YHVH; "Holy to the LORD"</note> had to be inscribed on this golden plate, *Exodus 28:36*. But in what manner and way were these two words written? Was it in two lines, so that *Holiness* was on the bottom and *of the Lord* on the top, to attribute honor to God and to teach that He is the highest and supreme over all things that exist in nature, as *Rabbi Levi* opines? Or was it in *one line*, according to *Rabbi Eleazar ben Jose* (from a plate seen at Rome) and *Rabbi Bahya*? We do not inquire too exquisitely into which opinion is correct; compare *Drusius on the difficult places of Exodus, chapter 52, page 217*. Furthermore, the name Jehovah, which adorned the forehead of the High Priest, taught the Pontiff that he ought to be joined in mind to God forever, concerning which *Photius* writes in *Epistle 162 to Amphilochius, page 219*: <insert>This name, both engraved on the golden petal and fastened with bonds to the high-priestly headband, brightens and adorns the forehead of the High Priest, at once showing something fearsome and venerable to those who see it, and at the same time enjoining that the High Priest must always be united with God, and never torn away from that connection and blessedness—</insert>

<column-break/>

<margin>The Clothing of Aaron.</margin> <insert>—down toward earthly things, and be carried away by the vanity of the world.</insert>
From the ornament of the head, we turn ourselves to the remaining clothing of the body. Historians relate of Alexander the Great that he wished to be painted not by just any painter, but only by Apelle, and sculpted only by Lysippus—the greatest artists—because he thought their art would bring him glory. Would that there were Lysippuses here to paint Aaron and to tint his sacred garments, which God designated for the Aaronic priesthood, with their deserved color. For God designated these sacred garments for Aaron himself so that the High Priest might be seen as decorous and glorious; He added ornaments of every dignity and majesty rather than mere coverings, and this above all for the splendor and glory of divine worship. That great beauty and that great apparatus which was seen in the Synagogue of the High Priest Aaron is most worthy of sight. In the consideration of the ornaments of the Pontifical body, there comes to us first the <term>כתונת</term> <note>transliteration: kethoneth; "tunic"</note>, *tunic*, which was put on first and adhered closely to the body, like the military shirts of old; it is said to be from the Ethiopian <term>כיתן</term> <note>transliteration: kitan</note>, which according to *Louis de Dieu* means *to cover*. Whence <term>תשבץ</term> <note>transliteration: tashbetz</note>, *checkered work*, from which this kind of garment is called the *checkered tunic*. Over this was thrown the <term>מעיל</term> <note>transliteration: me'il</note> *robe*, a garment shorter than the tunic and lacking sleeves: in its upper part was a "capitium" or opening, regarding which *Rabbi Rashi* notes *that of an undershirt*, through which the Priest thrust his head. In the lower part, in place of fringes, were pomegranates and golden bells, which warned the Priest not to be silent when it was time to rebuke; let him not keep silent about things that ought to be brought forward. For to ring the bell is to sound out, to speak freely, to exalt the voice of truth, not to hide the tongue when the wolf comes, and not to mutter when there should be a reprimand. Concerning this, *Gregory* says in *Part 2 of Pastoral Care, chapter 4*:

> Moses is commanded that the Priest entering the tabernacle be surrounded by bells; so that he may clearly have the voices of preaching, lest he offend the judgment of the heavenly spectator by silence; for it is written: Let the sound be heard when he enters the sanctuary in the sight of the Lord, and let him not die. For the Priest entering or leaving dies if a sound is not heard from him, because he provokes the anger of the hidden judge against himself if he walks without the sound of preaching.

*Alvaro Pelayo* also deals with this in *The Lament of the Church, 69, folio 98b*, as does *Jerome on Psalm 132, column 386*. The Superhumeral or <term>אפוד</term> <note>transliteration: ephod</note>, mention of which is made in *verse 6*, has its name from "girding." According to *Rashi* on *Exodus*, it was a girdle or wrap, the width of which corresponded to the width of a man's back, in the manner of a girdle called in the Italian language *Porzinth*, with which noble women are girded when riding on horses. So he says. It was the outermost garment, very short, lacking sleeves, and it somewhat tightened and constrained the looseness of the inner garments, almost similar to those linen togas which priests use elsewhere in our sacred rites. Nor was there only one Ephod. For there was another general Ephod, which they called the linen one, which was used in performing sacred rites not only by Priests and Levites, but also by others from the remaining tribes. Hence it is written of the Priests in *1 Samuel 22:18*: He slaughtered...

# From Exodus 28, Verse 2

## The Vestments of Aaron
<margin>The clothing of Aaron.</margin>
...gave on that day eighty-five men bearing the linen Ephod <note>original: "Ephod lineum"</note>; and concerning Samuel in 1 Samuel 2:18, that he ministered before the face of the Lord, a boy girded with a linen Ephod. Likewise of David in 2 Samuel 6:14, dancing with all his might before the Lord, and girded with a linen Ephod. Concerning this general Ephod, all feel—the Hebrews as well as the Latins—that it was simple linen and of the purest whiteness. Nor should it be overlooked here that among the Gentiles, linen was consecrated above wool for divine persons and things, which can be confirmed by many testimonies. Among these, the most principal is the view of Apuleius writing in his *Apology*, page 270:
> *Can it seem a wonder to anyone who has any memory of religion, that a man conscious of God through so many mysteries should keep certain sacred tokens at home? And wrap them in woven linen, which is the purest covering for divine things? For wool, the excrement of a sluggish body, pulled from sheep, was already a profane garment according to the decrees of Orpheus and Pythagoras.*
(Contrary to what Laërtius writes, that Pythagoras wore "a white robe of holy things" <note>original Greek: σολὴν λευκὴν ἐξ ὁσίων</note>), wool is considered profane clothing. But indeed, the cleanest crop of linen, arising among the best fruits of the earth, is used not only for the clothing and dress of the most holy Priests of the Egyptians, but also for a covering in sacred matters. 
<margin>On Osiris and Isis.</margin>
Plutarch writes similar things. However, the Hebrew Priests did not borrow from these Egyptians (as Polydore Vergil falsely thinks in *On the Invention of Things*, Book 4, Chapter 7), for they also had <term>linen breeches to cover the flesh of their nakedness</term> <note>original Hebrew: מכנסי-בד לכסות בשר ערוה</note> from the loins to the thighs; but they made them by divine command and ordination, not by imitation of a profane nation. The other Ephod, which we are dealing with in this place, was particular, and only the High Priest was permitted to wear it while performing sacred rites. Furthermore, it was woven from gold, scarlet, fine linen, hyacinth <note>blue</note>, and purple, so that by these colors alone he seemed, as it were, clothed in all the elements—by the whole world itself, by the entire universe of things—so that he might associate the lowest things with the highest, couple earth to heaven with prayers, and open the heavens. The fiery scarlet refers to heaven <note>or fire</note>, the hyacinth to the air, and the purple to the sea. Hence Jerome writes in his 2nd Epistle:
> *The hyacinthine color so pleased God that the Lord commanded the still-unrefined people and men unaccustomed to obedience through Moses, that as a sign of memory by which they might remember the precepts of the Lord, they should have insignias of hyacinth color with scarlet on each fringe of their garments, so that even when their eyes looked here and there by chance, the memory of heavenly commands might be born.*
We have contemplated thus far with what garments Aaron the Pontiff was honored, and with what colors he shone forth; for that High Priest surpassed the other priests in the splendor of precious clothing and the magnificence of ornaments. 
<margin>In the Pentateuch, folio 126.</margin>
For Bahya <note>Rabbi Bahya ben Asher</note> relates that *the priests had four lesser and common garments, but the High Priest was adorned with eight;* hence he was called the "Priest of many garments" <note>original Hebrew: בגדים מרובה</note>, especially then, when the sacred oil being lost, the "increase of Majesty" <note>original Hebrew: רבוי בגדים</note> from the robes and the anointing together was no longer instituted. Clothed in these garments, the High Priest was honored by the people like a King; indeed, he even represented an Angel, as Baal HaTurim says on Exodus 28, and in B. Hackspan on the *Kabbalah*, question 147, page 435, on the word "Angel" <note>original Hebrew: מלאך</note>.

<column-break/>

The word "Angel" <note>Malakh</note>, when numerically permuted by <term>Gematria</term> <note>The Jewish system of assigning numerical value to letters to find hidden meanings</note>, is...
<margin>The clothing of Aaron.</margin>
...There remains yet the most precious of the garments with which the High Priest was to be brought forth while he was about to enter the Holy of Holies. The Great Pontiff of the Jews used to wear on his chest twelve gems in an admirable series, which were woven and sewn into a small cloth, which the Latins call the *Rationale*, the Greeks the *Logion*, and the Hebrews the *Choshen*. It is the mark of a good Grammarian to be ignorant of some things here and to speak by divination, for here one deals more in conjectures than in certain arguments, and in the collection of little stones, the literary treasury is wonderfully poor. In this part, work must be done to fill the gaps with whatever supports are possible; for it is equally difficult to determine what they are not as what they are. It was worn nowhere else than on the breast, whence it is called the *Pectoral*, where the Heart, the home of Wisdom, resides. Nor was it otherwise or elsewhere that God was pleased to make His will known and manifest by certain signs when He was consulted by the people in doubtful times. Hence it was called the <term>Breastplate of Judgment</term> <note>original Hebrew: חושן משפט</note>, either because in it were the *Urim and Thummim*, from which judgment and demonstration were made as to what was fitting for man, and thus it gave the decision of forensic controversies; *or* because it expiated the abominable depravation of Judgment; *or* because each tribe of Israel had its own right in all the promises; or finally, because the future judgments of God were signified from it. Others suggest other reasons for this naming <note>original Greek: ὀνομαθεσίας</note>, the most powerful of which is that by this very thing the Pontiff and the people were warned of those things which were to be considered with the highest prudence and reason in their office, sacrifices, and Priesthood. This *Rationale* was a short cloth, showing two inches in length and one in width, and doubled, so that being set like a span upon a span, it created a quadrangular form. In it glowed twelve stones of wonderful price, arranged in four rows, so that in each little row three stones were placed.

### אדם, *Sardius, Sardion.*

The name of a precious stone so called from its redness, for the Hebrew name comes from *Adam*, "he was red," whence by the force of that etymology the Rabbis understand the *ruby*, which similarly took its name as a gem from redness; nor does the Chaldean Paraphrast disagree. To Josephus, it is the *sardonyx*. Augustine describes it as having a bloody and glowing or "fire-eyed" <note>original Greek: πυρωπώ</note> color in his commentary on *Psalm 86*, and similarly Gregory and Epiphanius: "it is fire-eyed in appearance and blood-like" <note>original Greek: ἐςὶ δὲ πυρωπὸς τῷ εἴδει καὶ αἱματοειδής</note>. And he compares the color to the Sardian fish, seasoned with salt and aged. Perhaps he meant the *Sarda*, as Petavius notes there. 
<margin>Book 37, chapter 7.</margin>
The *Sarda* stone is mentioned by Pliny in the class of carbuncles; but the color fits poorly that way. Otherwise, most things attributed to the *Sardius* by Epiphanius fit the Plinian *Sarda*. To Lucian it is the *Sardo*, commonly called the *Cornaline* <note>Carnelian</note>, which seems to have taken its name from flesh (*carne*), as if you were to say *carneolus*, from the color of flesh; for it has a faint redness, like the washings of meat, as Cesalpino notes in *On Metallic Things*, Book 2, 31, page 116. Plato made mention of the *Sardion* in the *Phaedo*, page 59, joining "these highly prized little stones, both sardians and jaspers" <note>original Greek: λίθιδια ταῦτα ἀγαπώμευα σάρδιά τε καὶ ἰάσπιδας</note>.
