# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Clothing of Aaron.</margin> He calls the stone a slightly paler Sardonyx <note>original: *Sardonycha*</note>, using the Greek *sardonyx* because it possesses a certain quality. They identify its place of origin as Babylonia. Regarding the Sarda, Cardanus says in book 7 of *On Subtlety* that it is a stone of red color; Scaliger adds in *Exercise 118* regarding carnelians <note>original: *corneolis*</note> that their appearance inclines toward a milky color like the filings of the kingdom of Cambay, and toward red. Carnelians are not preferred, nor are they of such value that we should place them in the first row and at the very forefront of the gems. As this stone stood first in order, so it undoubtedly stood first in dignity. It emitted rays with a fiery light and can best be compared to some flaming ruby. The <term>allegorical interpretations</term> are pleasing: it befits Reuben, because he was suffused with redness and shame after violating his father’s bed. It is also mentioned in Ezekiel 28:13, where he describes a garment interwoven with various gems, and in the first place he likewise puts the Hebrew *Odem* <note>אֹדֶם</note>, which the Latin and Greek explain as *Sardius*. In contrast to the Hebrew word, the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> uses *Samqan* from *Samaq*, meaning "to be red" or "to be ruddy." Nine gems are recounted by the Prophet, whose names occur identically in the High Priest's breastplate; the Greeks count twelve, and their interpreters say the stones of the breastplate are intended, which are computed at that same number. Jerome, Aquila, and Symmachus also adapt this text to those things found in Exodus and Revelation concerning gems.

->2. *Pitdah*, Topaz, *topazion*.<-

The second gem seems to most interpreters to be the *Topaz*, named after the island of Topazos in the Red Sea; however, not everyone explains its nature and color in the same way. Epiphanius attributes redness to it: "The Topaz is redder than a glowing coal, even exceeding it"; hence the Chaldean calls it *Yarqan*, meaning "to be green" or "to grow green." From this, some interpret it as an *Emerald*, which was highly commended by Pliny for those with sharp vision; this could be confirmed by Rabbi Jonah, who says this stone is called *Smerad* in Arabic. Elsewhere, Artemidorus makes the Topaz a transparent stone shining like gold, found on the island of Ophiodes. <margin>Book 4, ch. 3.</margin> "It is a transparent, gold-like stone flashing with light, which those collecting it see by night." Diodorus makes it similar to glass, yet with a golden color, leaving many notes on the search for Ophiodes and topazes. Cardanus notes in *Subtlety* book 7 that the Topaz of the ancients is not the same as ours. But we have no business with the degenerate order of topazes which jewelers call Chrysolites. Pliny <margin>Book 37, 7.</margin> extols the topaz most highly. Even the comparison of Job shows its value, who judges it worthy to commend most precious *Wisdom* by it in chapter 28:19, to teach that nothing man possesses can be compared in nobility, beauty, elegance, and goodness with Wisdom; among the most precious things, like gold of Ophir, Sapphire, Sardonyx, and Pearls, he names the stone *Pitdah*. "The Ethiopian topaz," he says, "does not equal it (wisdom)," Hebrew *Pitdat Kush*, Chaldean *Yarqat*, as also in Exodus 28:17, *Yarqan*. There is also evidence of it in Ezekiel, where the Greeks similarly understand it as *topazion*.

->3. *Bareqet*, Emerald.<-

If you derive the Hebrew name from *Baraq* <note>meaning "lightning" or "flash"</note>, this gem was named for its brilliance and resplendence, which the Emerald does not lack; hence the stone, if not an Emerald, would be very similar to an Emerald, which is not only

<column-break/>

<margin>The Clothing of Aaron.</margin> of the most pleasant appearance, but also the most lucid, so much so that it is said of it that it rendered images of things so accurately that the Roman Prince Nero watched gladiatorial bouts through an Emerald. For this reason, it seems to the Greeks to be named from *maiein* <note>to sparkle</note>, according to Erasmus in his *Letter of Jerome* to Fabiola, and Marbodus. <margin>folio 20. b.</margin> For in Hebrew *Bareq* and Chaldean *Barqa* are the same as "it shone," "it gleamed," "it glittered," or "it flashed like lightning"; whence *Baraq* means "lightning" or "flashing." And *Bareq* in Chaldean, as rendered here, is a precious stone named for its brilliance. Hence it appeared to some to be the *Ceraunius* <note>Thunder-stone</note>, as to Symmachus, according to Jerome; the word is *akeraunos*, "lightning," whence *keraunios*, "of lightning." For it seems to snatch the "brilliance of the stars" with its own splendor, to use Pliny's words (Book 37, 9). Nor does the Emerald lack brilliance; nothing is more pleasant to the eyes, nothing more useful. Above all, they are greener than watered grass, greener than all herbs, which is why they benefit the eyes because of their greenness. Theophrastus gave the emerald the third rank among stones, as related by Solinus (ch. 25) and Scaliger (Exercise 108, 4). Traces of the word appear to some extent in the word *Smaragdus*, which, if the first letter did not stand in the way, would be as clear as in the word *Jaspis* <note>Jasper</note>. But the word *Carbunculus* is also related, as Vatablus and others maintain, because it agrees with the Chaldean word *Bareqet* through a transposition of letters. It also occurs in Ezekiel, but with a change of vowels, *Barqat*, which the Chaldean preserves as *Barqata*—the Greeks translate it as *smaragdon*, whose inconsistency is also detected here.

->4. *Nofekh*, Anthrax, Carbuncle.<-

This interpretation of the *Carbuncle* pleased Philo, Josephus, and Epiphanius. The Chaldean goes a different way, explaining it as *Izmargdin*, an *Emerald*, as do the Belgians. Luther, however, translates it as *Ruby*. Rabbi Kimchi imagines a gem of black or dark color, saying *Nofekh* is large; his mind may be aided by Pliny, who says the Carchedonian carbuncles are of a larger appearance. The *Carbuncle* burns with a Phoenician <note>deep red</note> color and shines like a lamp or an ignited coal, concerning which hear some testimonies. Pliny and Marbodus <margin>folio 43. b.</margin> report wonders of its brilliance. In India, they say it has such great radiance that surrounding objects are illuminated no differently than by the brightness of the Sun.

->5. *Sappir*, Sapphire.<-

The name itself indicates it is a *Sapphire*, and the Chaldean, Luther, the Belgians, and all the interpreters we have inspected agree, and they constantly translate it thus in Ezekiel and Job. Also in the Arabic language, with only the letter *Nun* interposed. Regarding the color of this gem, they vary: some Hebrew interpreters say it is the color of the air <note>sky blue</note>, others red, others white. By Epiphanius it is called a "purplish stone," as if of a purplish color. It is among the number of red gems according to Aben Ezra, whose opinion can be confirmed because, when <margin>Lamentations 4:7</margin> a comparison to snow and milk was used to indicate the whiteness and splendor of the Nazirites, "redness" and brilliance are preferred for them (*Sappirim*): "they were more ruddy in body than carbuncles." From this, the sense will be clearer regarding the throne, which is said to be in the appearance of a *ruby* or *pyrope* <note>fire-red garnet</note>; and in Canticles 5:14, the bowels are said to be the brightness of ivory overlaid with *Sapphires*, which can best be applied, as is fitting, to the bloody passion of Christ. Job used it in chapter 28, where some understood *Sapphire*, others *diamond*, and Mercer *crystal*. Jerome used *glass*, and the Septuagint similarly *hyalos* <note>glass/crystal</note>. The Chaldean is *Asfirlina*, which from...

# From Exodus XXVIII. v. 2.

<margin>The Vestments of Aaron.</margin>
<margin>Rabboth on Lamentations, d. 1</margin>
In Latin, it is made *specularis* <note>original: "specularis" - like a mirror or transparent stone</note>, as if it were a mirror-stone, concerning which Marbodus writes on page 78 and Fuller in book 4 of his *Sacred Miscellanies*. Cardano places it next to the Diamond due to its extreme hardness; he noted its singular durability to such an extent that, when struck, it shattered the hammer and anvil while remaining whole. There is a tradition that *the Law was inscribed upon Sapphire tablets*; perhaps this is an allusion to the word *Sapiri* <note>Hebrew: ספיר</note>, as if the Law were "inscribed," and it was imagined that the Law appeared as fire in the hands of Moses because it was written on Sapphire tablets.

<margin>6. *Yahalom*, ἴασπις, *Jasper*.</margin>
Jasper seems to follow the Sapphire closely. But if we consult the Hebrews, a far different stone reveals itself. Ibn Ezra, a man of the highest authority among his people, determined this stone to be the *Diamond* <note>original: "Adamantem"</note>; his words are rendered by Petrus Ubbeelius of Worms in Marbodus, p. 80. The Belgians, Arias, and Luther base this on the etymology derived from *halam* <note>Hebrew: הלם</note>, meaning *to break, crush, or strike*. Similarly, Onkelos, with whom Paul Fagius agrees, suggests it is so named because it breaks all other stones and even pierces bdellium. However, Josephus and Epiphanius prefer *Jasper*, which also has its own hardness, so that the reasoning of the name might fit it. The color of Jasper is varied, as are its species. It reflects the color of *Emerald*, and that is the best kind according to 
<margin>Book 7 of the Thebaid.</margin>
Isidore. *Yellow Jasper* is attested by Virgil and Statius. Famous is the *Jasper* which antiquity saw in the armored likeness of Nero, the weight of which was eleven ounces. Pliny teaches how it may be adulterated, and after him Hermolaus in Marbodus, p. 89. Regarding its use in Medicine, certain people prattle on following Galen, things which a Christian ought not even to do, according to Vincent [of Beauvais] in his *Mirror of Nature* and Fuller in his *Sacred Miscellanies*.

<margin>7. *Leshem*, λιγύριον, *Lyncure*.</margin>
Leshem begins the third row. Here the water stands still <note>an idiom meaning "the investigation stalls"</note> because there is no available etymology to lean on, as we have seen through several examples by investigators of obscure gems. Josephus (who called it *ligurion*), the Septuagint, Jerome, Epiphanius, Pagninus, Luther, and Onkelos retain the "Ligurian stone." Here Fagius explains it as *Lyncure* <note>traditionally believed to be solidified lynx urine, often identified as amber</note> and likens it to the gem which the Jews call *Turckus* and *Lyncurer*. To others, it seems to be the *hyacinth*, in which they do not 
<margin>On Gems, book 2, ch. 30, p. 160</margin>
differ much from the Lyncure, as Anselmus Boëtius de Boodt discusses. Whatever it is judged to be by name, it is not equally clear what its nature is, for Epiphanius openly confesses, "we have by no means known its discovery," though he is otherwise not timid in offering his opinion. He says it is perhaps what they call *lagurion* in the common tongue. He preferred, however, to interpret it as *hyacinth*. Jerome is similarly undecided; searching whether it is Lyncure or whence it comes, he frankly admits it is not known to him from elsewhere. Nor is it a wonder that such a man, as Erasmus says, should perish among the writings of Theophrastus, Pliny, and others, where it is celebrated not so much for beauty as for utility.
<margin>Book 8, ch. 38 and Book 28, ch. 8.</margin>
For although he does not put faith in the Lyncure, he nevertheless explains here and there what others thought of it. They defiled the stone with fables who say it congeals from the urine of a lynx. So it was believed by Dioscorides and Solinus. But those who teach this think themselves too "lynx-eyed" <note>sharp-sighted</note>, for the reality of the thing convicts them of falsehood. Thus, Scaliger did not hit the mark either in what he recites from others regarding *Electrum* <note>amber</note>. Concerning amber, many things are 

<column-break/>

<margin>The Vestments of Aaron. book 2, ch. 15 and p. 321.</margin>
put forward by Aristotle and Aelian. Some of the ancients want the Lyncure to be our *Amber*, in which the Prussians take pleasure; compare Boëtius de Boodt.

<margin>8. *Shebo*, Ἀχάτης, *Agate*.</margin>
The method of etymology reveals either nothing or something quite obscure about this gem. Hence certainty is not established, and it would be slippery ground, as etymologies are often deceptive. Some want it named from the Achates, a river in Sicily. In Chaldee, this stone is called *Markia*, a word which according to Fagius seems to have some affinity with the stone commonly called *Turquoise*, to which Rabbi Kimchi attributes a hyacinth-like color. They derive it from *shabah* <note>Hebrew: שבב</note>, *to take or hold*, as if it were a "Stone worthy to be taken and held." If you derive it from the Arabic *shaba*, *to be similar or likened*, it must be said to emulate the forms and images of all things and to liken itself to various colors, like a certain Proteus. For it is of varied color: *white, reddish, saffron, ash-colored, green, black, variegated, blue*, so that you would not believe it to be a single stone, as observed by Cardano, 
<margin>book 7, p. 352</margin>
who reports that the colors of all other gems do not suffice for this one alone: it reflects groves, meadows, animals, rivers, flowers, and trees, with nature at play. Most famous in history is the Agate of King Pyrrhus, representing the nine Muses with Apollo in the middle striking his lyre, each with her own ornaments, so that nature then seemed to have competed with the painter; and this ought to be called a miracle rather than a gem, about which Marbodus writes:
> *King Pyrrhus is said to have worn an Agate on his finger,*
> *Whose flat surface depicted the nine Muses,*
> *And standing in the middle, Apollo touched his lyre;*
> *It was the work of nature, not of art:*

<margin>9. *Achlamah*, Ἀμέθυστος, *Amethyst*.</margin>
The origin of the name is *halam* <note>Hebrew: חלם</note>, *to be robust or to recover*, as if the gem were endowed with some power against something. In what that power lies is almost as obscure as the gem itself. It was believed to be effective against drunkenness and to give strength to the heart. Others say it stirred dreams, and they elicit this from the fact that *halom* signifies a "dream," as if he who wears the stone sees frequent dreams; so says Ibn Ezra in Marbodus. 
<margin>p. 80.</margin>
Fagius confirms this power in his commentary on Onkelos. The Chaldean has *Enegla* <note>Aramaic: עין עגלא</note> (the Germans call it *Onychel*, the Italians *Nicolo*), meaning "Calf's Eye"; not, it seems, because it took the shape and likeness of a calf's eye, but because by the mixture of colors, the *Achlamah* stone appeared to them to reflect a calf's eye. Thus to the Italians, the *Opal*, which imitates eyes with various colors, is called *occhio di gatto* or "Cat's Eye"; see Boëtius de Boodt, p. 192.

<margin>10. *Tarshish*, Χρυσόλιθος, *Chrysolite*.</margin>
*Tarshish* leads into the fourth row; its rank among gems is hardly clear to us, whence Pagninus retained the Hebrew name, and Rabbi David Kimchi did not define it, saying generally it was a gem of a blue color. The Chaldean, wishing to note the place from which it comes, writes *Tarshish, Yerka, and Parzam*, which sounds like "Thalassian stone" <note>sea-stone</note>, as if it came from the sea or reflected the blue color of water. This would fit the Beryl, which imitates the greenness of the *pure sea*, according to Pliny.
<margin>book 37, 5.</margin>
Most explain it as *Chrysolite*, as if you were to say "golden stone," in which way it is also rendered by the Latin in Ezekiel. The Greeks vary, rendering it here as *chrysolite*, but elsewhere as *carbuncle* and *hyacinth*. The color of Chrysolite is golden, as the word implies; it is *Turquoise* in our mother tongue.

11. שֹׁהַם <note>Hebrew: *Shoham*</note>, <term>beryllos</term> <note>Greek: beryl</note>, Beryl.
The Hebrew word did not sound familiar to Latin ears, unlike certain names of other nations (see verse 8), such as <term>Sapphire</term> and <term>Jasper</term>, which took on a Latin form from foreign languages. The Septuagint, and Epiphanius following them, change the order; placing the <term>beryl</term> in this spot, they put the <term>onyx</term> in the last place. Most interpreters maintain that this stone is the <term>onyx</term>. The Chaldean translates it as *burla*, which seems to be taken from the Greek *beryllos*. Josephus calls it a Sardonyx. They say it has the color of a human fingernail, from which it received its name, for <term>onyx</term> means "nail." The Sardonyx, moreover, is among the fiery gems, like the Sard, which it takes after in composition and color—having a hue like flesh placed under a nail, that is, reddish. Regarding this, see Marbodus. * Its preciousness is proved by the fact that Job commends it in his argument on wisdom, where the Greek text has <term>onyx</term>.

<margin>p. 120. b.</margin>
12. יָשְׁפֵה <note>Hebrew: *Yashfeh*</note>, <term>beryllos</term> <note>Greek: beryl</note>, Beryl.
The name *Yaspah* comes so close to the word for the gem Jasper that it is surprising the Septuagint and others—who usually stick to the literal letters—explained it as <term>beryl</term>; Pagninus follows them. Arias understands it as Jasper, as do the German translators, and also the Septuagint in Ezekiel, where others have <term>beryl</term>. The Chaldean Onkelos renders it *pantheri*, "panther-like," while Jonathan uses *apanturin*, as if to say a <term>panther-stone</term>, because it appears to be composed of many gems, according to Pliny.* In Ezekiel, it is written as *pantheron*, and thus it would be a species of variegated Jasper, for the Panther is an animal whose skin is <term>spotted</term>. As for the Beryl, according to Epiphanius, it is <term>glaucous [bluish-green], sea-dyed, having an appearance like the more watery hyacinths</term>. He says the color represents the sea or a diluted hyacinth. Indeed, "glaucousness" is attributed to the sea by the Latins, hence the "glaucous sea." Pliny wishes it to be seen as of the same nature as Emeralds.*

### The Use of the XII Stones.

The Priest's Breastplate, decorated with 12 gems for the number of the 12 sons of Israel, testified to the providence that God maintained toward the Israelite family. It pleased Jehovah—just as it pleased Him to have their names engraved on gems and hung upon the Priest's chest—to carry them in His own heart with benevolent love, provided they continued to walk in the Divine precepts. As a memorial and a seal of this ardent love, He willed their names to be carried on the breast of Aaron, and to be a certain monument of His divine presence and protection. I would not want you to think that these things, which were uniquely commanded by divine authority regarding the clothing, were produced from nothing. Here are the wrappings of no ordinary knowledge; here are the figures and emblems of hidden things spread throughout. As many gems as there are, so many are the hieroglyphics of wisdom. It is memorable what Josephus reported concerning the two Sardonyxes: that one of these, which occupied the Priest's right shoulder, would shine so brightly when the sacrifices were approved by God that the splendor appeared from afar. To understand the mystery veiled by the gems, it will be important to know the origin, shape, size, nature, power, and faculty of the stones. God willed to foreshadow the splendor of His divine grace through the image of the most elegant and precious gems, as if in a painting or a distinguished emblem. We would be greatly helped in knowing and 

<column-break/>

penetrating certain things more intimately if we were endowed with a certain knowledge of gems. We have need of a Solomon, so that from the very property of the stones the intellect might be opened, and the wrapping of mystery and allegory might be laid bare. As Augustine says*: "If the power and nature of gems are unknown, allegories proceed neither safely nor successfully." Among others who have applied their industry to this kind is Origen, and Jerome, who reviews the mystical interpretation of the Hebrews regarding Aaron's garments and the precious stones to be worn in his *Letter to Fabiola*. These senses, although sometimes suitable, in many cases (as Driedo notes*) have far different meanings, far removed from mystical senses. We see, therefore, various divinations brought forward; to wish to divine mysteries by these would be to "join night to night." Those who bring their own contributions to these <term>mysterious</term> symbols often introduce more than is actually in them. But enough of that. We have seen and contemplated the sacred garments thus far, described accurately even down to the smallest details—except for the shoes, of which no mention is made. Some gather from the silence of Holy Scripture that the High Priest was bound to walk with bare feet in that holy place. The High Priest himself represented Adam, whose soul was the image of God; on his ephod stood out the <term>Breastplate of Judgment</term> <note>Hebrew: *Choshen Mishpat*</note>, in which were placed the Urim and Thummim—"lights and perfections"—namely, full knowledge of God and creatures in the intellect, and perfect justice and holiness in the will. The <term>turban</term> <note>Hebrew: *Mitznefet*</note>, with the <term>flower</term> <note>Hebrew: *Tzitz*</note> or golden plate, on which was inscribed "Holiness to the Lord," was that grace with which God embraced the first man. These most ample gifts, most worthy of the High Priest of the Jews, these most august garments vanished when Christ the High Priest arrived, so that nothing remains of them but the name. We conclude, therefore, with the words of Jerome*:

<margin>City of God, book 2, ch. 16.</margin>
<margin>Ecclesiastical Writings, book 2, fol. 55.</margin>
<margin>Letter 128 to Fabiola, p. 99.</margin>

> It is said there is a book by Septimius Tertullian on the garments of Aaron, which has not been found by me to this day. If it should be found by you on account of the fame of the city, I ask that you do not compare my drop to his river; for I am to be judged not by the genius of great men, but by my own strength.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Exodus 32, specifically focusing on the creation of the Golden Calf and its historical connection to Egyptian worship of the bull-god Apis.</meta>

# Exodus XXXII, v. 4.

<margin>Calf-worship, or the adoration of the cast metal calf.</margin>
...from the ears of your wives, your sons, and your daughters, and bring them to me (v. 3). And the people did (having been provided with the tools for that purpose from the luxuries of the Egyptians) as he had commanded, bringing them from their ears to Aaron (v. 4). When he had received them, he formed them by casting-work, and made from them a **molten Calf**, and they said (and this indeed was much worse): *These are your Gods* <note>original: "Hi sunt Dii tui"</note> (*Elohim*, which can be understood as the one God of Israel) *O Israel, who led you out of the land of Egypt.* Thus, that people became entirely unmindful of all the benefits they had received from the Most High God in the desert, and through a perverse emulation, they came to imitate the Egyptians who worshiped Apis, and they prepared a Salian feast <note>A reference to the lavish banquets of the Salii, Roman priests of Mars; here meaning a decadent festival.</note>. For the Egyptians worshiped an Ox; from this, the example of foul superstition flowed to the Hebrews, who, wishing to have a symbol of the true Deity, desired a golden Calf, so that by the presence of that symbol they might imagine for themselves a sign of the divine Power present and going before them.

The question is asked: what appearance and what form did that *idol* <note>Greek: εἴδωλον</note> have? Secular history will satisfy this doubt, which tells of Apis, the idol of the Egyptians, which flourished in Egypt in the time of Isaac and Jacob according to <margin>Acts 7:41; City of God, Book 18, ch. 5.</margin> Augustine, and thus before the departure of the Israelites. Herodotus records it in this manner in Book 3, *Thalia*, p. 195: <margin>page 196.</margin> *This calf, called Apis, has these marks: being black, it bears a white square on its forehead, and on its back, the likeness of an eagle; in its tongue, the hairs are double; and on its tongue, a beetle.* <note>Greek: Ἔχει δὲ ὁ μόσχος οὗτος ὁ Ἄπις καλεόμενος σημήϊα τοιάδε; ἐὼν μέλας, ἐπὶ μὲν τῷ μετώπῳ λευκὸν τετράγωνον φορέει, ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ νώτου, αἰετὸν εἰκασμένον. ἐν δὲ τῇ γλώσσῃ, τὰς τρίχας διπλάς. ἐπὶ δὲ τῇ γλώσσῃ, κάνθαρον.</note> Valla translated these into Latin: *This calf, which is called Apis, has these signs: It is black in its whole body.* (The notes of H. Stephanus on this passage have *great* <note>Greek: μέγας</note> rather than *black* <note>Greek: μέλας</note> in our copies. Valla, however, added from his own: [in its whole body]) *having on its forehead a whiteness of a square figure, on its back the image of an eagle, a beetle under its tongue, and double hairs on its tail.* Ammianus Marcellinus in Book 21 depicts that ox as having the appearance of a crescent Moon on its right side, serene and shining. Pliny <margin>Book 8, ch. 46, p. 246.</margin> says: *The Ox in Egypt is even worshiped in place of a Deity; they call it Apis.* And Cicero, in the persona of Cotta, addressing Vellejus the Epicurean, <margin>Book 1, On the Nature of the Gods.</margin> says: *What do you think? Does not that Apis, the sacred ox of the Egyptians, seem a God to the Egyptians?* So also Tacitus on the customs of the Jews: *An ox is also sacrificed, which the Egyptians worship as Apis.* Lucian also mentions the same in his work on sacrifices: *Apis is a god from the herd, chosen over others for being much more beautiful and majestic than ordinary oxen.* <note>Greek: Ἔστι δὲ ὁ Ἄπις ἐξ ἀγέλης θεὸς, ἐπὶ τῷ προτέρῳ χειροτονέμενος πολὺ καλλίων καὶ σεμνότερος τῶν ἰδιωτῶν βοῶν.</note> The same in his book on Astrology: *Apis is to them the most sacred thing of the local mortals.* <note>Greek: ὁ Ἄπις αὐτοῖς χρῆμα ἱερώτατον τῶν χωρίων θνηέων.</note> Moreover, Jacques Bonfrère carefully notes in his commentary on Genesis 41, p. 303, that the Sun and Moon were shadowed forth by these marks: the Moon indeed by that white spot on the side in the manner of a crescent Moon; the Sun by the black color of the ox: see there if you please. It is not certain, yet it seems not absurd to say, that Aaron formed some of these *identifying marks* <note>Greek: γνωρισμάτων</note> with his tool: And *he formed the gold with a tool*, says Moses, namely *he shaped it with a stylus* <note>Hebrew: צָר אֹתוֹ בַחֶΡֶט</note>, or as the Septuagint has it, *he fashioned it with a graving tool* <note>Greek: ἔπλασεν ἐν τῇ γραφίδι</note>. It is established that the idol was molten; and it is an easy conjecture from here that the tools made the marks of Apis, or engraved some other such thing for the veneration of God. For we know of hardly any nation under the sun that indulged more in idolatrous representations and superstition.

<column-break/>

<margin>Calf-worship, or the adoration of the cast metal calf.</margin>
Indeed, the Jews, enticed by the vanities of the Egyptians, urged Aaron with wicked demands, so that with a *fretting spirit* <note>Greek: ἀσχάλλοντι θυμῷ</note> he yielded to their errors, and granted their *unrelenting custom* <note>Greek: ἀλύκτῳ ἔθει</note>, so that the worship of the Divine name might be represented through some external form. Thus the insane race, *darkened by Egyptian gloom* <note>Greek: ἀἰγυπτιακῷ ζόφῳ ἐπισκοτωμένη</note> (enveloped), wished to practice their religion, and to figure an image of darkness in the splendor of gold. This impiety St. Stephen, the first martyr and leader of the Martyrs of the New Testament, <margin>Augustine, Sermon 2 to the brothers in the Desert.</margin> judged worthy to be told even to fierce posterity, who had followed the footsteps of their ancestors' more vicious errors, in that grave Apology by which he rebukes the Jews <margin>Acts 7:41.</margin> and explains, as if tragically, their *mind-bending error* <note>Greek: τὴν φρενοκλινῆ πλάνην</note>. *They made,* he says, *a calf*—that is, an image of a calf—*and turned back in their hearts to Egypt.* By which words he signifies that they desired such symbols of the deity as they had seen among the Egyptians. For they had seen them perform *worship* <note>Greek: λατρείαν</note> to their Gods in Apis. These *demons* <note>Greek: δαιμονες</note> existed before Augustus Caesar, to whom, when he was in Alexandria after finishing affairs in Egypt, the inhabitants wished to show Apis; but seeing that bovine God, Caesar refused to approach, saying mockingly to them, *I am accustomed to worship gods, but not oxen,* <note>Greek: θεὺς ἀλλ' οὐχὶ βοῦς προσκυνεῖν εἴθισμαι</note> Xiphilinus <margin>page 64.</margin> where also are noted worthy portents which preceded that subjugation of Egypt and the subsequent cessation of the ridiculous Gods, where the historian says in that place, *the statues of the Gods were mournful*, and Apis himself gave out great and miserable bellows and shed tears; *his words are:* <margin>page 65.</margin> *the statues looked gloomy, and Apis bellowed lamentably and wept.* <note>Greek: τὰ τε ἀγάλματα ἐσκυθρωπασε, καὶ ὁ Ἄπις ὀλοφυρτικῶν ἐμυκήσατο καὶ ἐδάκρυσε.</note> It is established from Strabo <margin>Book 17.</margin> that Apis was twofold and had two names; when he spoke of Bubastus and the Bubastic prefecture, he adds: *Above them is the Heliopolitan district. There is the City of the Sun, situated on a notable mound, having the temple of the Sun, and the bull Mnevis, nourished in a certain enclosure, who is considered a god among them just as Apis is in Memphis.* <note>Greek: ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν ὁ ἡλιοπολίτης νόμος. ἐνταῦθα δ' ἐστὶν ἡ τοῦ ἡλίου πόλις, ἐπὶ χώματος ἀξιολόγω κειμένη, τὸ ἱερὸν ἔχουσα τοῦ ἡλίου, καὶ τὸν βοῦν τὸν Μνεῦιν, ἐν σηκῷ τινι τρεφόμενον, ὃς παρ' αὐτοῖς νενόμισται θεὸς ὥσπερ καὶ ἐν Μέμφει ὁ Ἄπις.</note> Plutarch testifies the same regarding Isis and Osiris: *The bull nourished in Heliopolis, whom they call Mnevis, is sacred to Osiris, and some consider him the father of Apis; he is black and holds the second honors after Apis.* <note>Greek: ὁ δὲ ἐν Ἡλιοπόλει τρεφόμενος βοῦς, ὃν Μνεῦιν καλοῦσιν, Ὀσίριδος δὲ ἱερόν, ἔνιοι δὲ καὶ τοῦ Ἄπιος πατέρα νομίζουσι, μέλας ἐστὶ καὶ δευτέρας ἔχει τιμὰς μετ' Ἄπιν.</note> Vossius <margin>Book on Idolatry, 29.</margin> teaches that the Heliopolitan Bull, which the wiser Egyptians held as a symbol of the Sun God, was in greater honor than the Memphite Bull, which they worshiped as a symbol of the Moon. Jeroboam, recently called to the kingship from Egypt, seems to have looked back to this double deity; he, together with the Israelites who lived in Samaria, separated from the Jews by civil discords, mindful of Egyptian superstition, erected two golden Calves, one of which he placed in Dan, the other in Bethel, 1 Kings 12:28. Where St. Ambrose <margin>Commentary on Romans.</margin> Bishop of Milan says: *The Egyptians worshiped a quadruped, which they called Apis, in the likeness of a cow; which evil Jeroboam imitated, instituting cows in Samaria, to which the Jews might sacrifice, and birds, which the Pagans have as Coracine rites (which were instituted for the worship of crows).* Furthermore, in Ezekiel 20:8, the children of Israel are written to have turned aside to the Idols of Egypt, not because they worshiped a calf as the Egyptians did, but because they transferred the images and external rites of the Egyptian Religion to the worship of the true God. And why say more? Whenever the Jews, having despised the law of Moses, [worshiped] certain animals and images...

they worshipped, they modeled themselves after the examples of the Egyptians. We will wonder at this less if we consider the nature of the people; for the vice of superstition, contracted through the constant contagion of Egyptian customs, exerted itself in the desert with Aaron’s connivance. According to their custom, they wished to represent and worship their own—that is, the true—God (for I do not believe the Israelites worshipped Apis himself <note>Apis was the sacred bull of Memphis in Egyptian mythology.</note>), who had led them out of Egypt, in the likeness of a calf. The Holy Spirit rebukes this most wretched "perverse imitation" <note>original: κακοζηλίαν (kakozēlian)</note> in Psalm 106:20, where it says: *they exchanged their glory* (God) *for the image of a bull that eats grass.*

This is the most common exposition of this passage, taught by the leaders of piety. Athanasius <margin>Question 50.</margin> says in the Council of Nicaea: *The Law is the Decalogue, which God delivered to them with a voice that could be heard before the people made the calf (that is, Apis).* Jerome <margin>Book 1 on Hosea, ch. 4.</margin> writes: *It seems to me that the people of Israel made for themselves a* <margin>Selden p. 136 seq.</margin> *calf's head in the wilderness to worship for this reason: Jeroboam son of Nebat fashioned golden calves so that they might preserve in their superstition what they had learned in Egypt—that Apis and Mnevis <note>Mnevis was another sacred bull worshipped at Heliopolis.</note>, who are worshipped under those figures, were Gods.* And Philo the Jew of Alexandria <margin>Book 3 on the Life of Moses.</margin> himself says: *Forgetting the true God, they began to emulate Egyptian fictions by making a young bull in imitation of the most sacred animal of that region.* And again: *A young bull was fashioned after the pattern of the Egyptian type.* Cyril of Alexandria explains it similarly in Book 2 of the *Glaphyra*, p. 278; as do Clement in Book 6 of the *Constitutions*, ch. 20; and Lactantius in Book 1 of *On True Wisdom*, ch. 10. Among more recent authors, the Blessed Luther <margin>Table Talk, chapter on Idolatry, folio 68a.</margin> teaches the same in these words: **The worship of the Jewish calf is taken and derived from the Egyptians, who honored an ox and the idol Apis. The people of Israel did the same, as St. Stephen points out.** The Blessed Chemnitz <margin>Part 4, Examination of the Council of Trent, p. 42.</margin> says: *When the Jews had seen the worship of Apis in Egypt, they transferred that image, by casting a golden calf, to the worship of the true God; they directed their worship not to the material or form of the calf, but to its prototype or the thing signified—that is, to the true God, who had led them out of Egypt;* and so forth. Gregory Francus <margin>p. 248 seq.</margin> feels differently in his *Sacred Lexicon*, confidently asserting that this "calf-making" <note>original: Μοσχοποίημα (Moschopoiēma)</note> was derived from a wicked imitation of the Cherubim placed upon the Mosaic Ark, to which he attributes a calf-like form; but he provides no evidence for this conjecture. He seems to have followed the author of the book *On the Golden Calf*, who, in order to have an excuse for Aaron, tries to thrust a Cherub upon us instead of a golden calf; for which he incurs the just rebuke of Jacob Bonfrerius <margin>p. 546 seqq.</margin> in this place, which you may read.

The construction of the Tabernacle.
</margin>
->Exodus 39, v. 32.<-
->And all the work of the tabernacle of the tent of meeting was finished.<-
->And all the work of the tabernacle of the testimony was completed.<-
->*Thus all the work of the TABERNACLE and the covering of the testimony (the tabernacle of the Church) was perfected.*<-

**T**he Tabernacle was the first public school of the Jews, a "contemplation of prayer or a place" <note>original: θεώρησιν τῆς εὐχῆς ἢ τόπον</note> according to Athanasius in his *Apology to Constantius*, p. 684; a workshop for practicing piety, a temple of true faith and invocation, a *theater* of confession and thanksgiving. When God commanded it to be made for Himself, He described its form to Moses by voice over forty days on Mount Sinai, explaining how everything was to be made; afterward, He placed a model of everything before Moses' eyes, saying: *Make it according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain.* <margin>Exodus 25:40</margin> We have set forth the construction of that ancient Mosaic Tabernacle—built with such skill and labor and shown to Moses on the mountain—for contemplation, more for the sake of the mysteries pertaining to the state of the Church than for the sake of the external structure. We present this admirable structure both because of the authority of God the revealer, and because of its own greatness, and because of the Sacraments which are exhibited for contemplation in the material idea. This Tabernacle is called in the holy language *Mishkan* <note>original: משכן</note>, a dwelling, from *shakan* <note>original: שכן</note>, he dwelt, resided, or *stayed*; whence in Exodus 25:8 God says, *and I shall dwell among them.* For God knew how prone the Israelites were to the worship of idols after the manner of other nations; He therefore established this for them as a kind of holy sanctuary, at which they might practice religion with what they call "external worship" and experience His divine power as most present. The Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> rendered it *skēnē* <note>original: σκηνὴν</note>, which properly denotes a "shady place" or "tent." For at first, a chamber was so named from the branches and foliage of trees leaning into one another, whether by art or by nature, as in that passage of Virgil: <margin>Aeneid, Book 1, p. 98.</margin>
> On this side and that, vast cliffs and twin rocks loom
> Toward the sky, beneath whose peak the safe waters
> Lie silent far and wide; then a scene of shimmering woods
> From above, and a dark grove overhangs with bristling shade.

Regarding this passage, Servius says: *Scena means a shading, and is called Scena from "skia" (shadow); for among the ancients, the stage had no wall, but they sought shade from foliage. Afterward, they began to assemble planks in the manner of a wall. The Scena, however, is the part of the theater facing the spectators, in which the royal palace stands. A passage from Cassiodorus also supports this:* <margin>Letter 4, 51.</margin> *The front of the theater is called the scena, from the very dense shade of a grove, where songs were sung with various sounds by shepherds at the beginning of spring.* The Greeks used this word, being more accurate, to signify the thing when they lacked another. Near the tabernacle and the temple there were no gardens, no woods or groves, because of the hindrance to Divine worship that would arise therefrom; whereas otherwise, worshippers of idols sacrificed on mountains and in woods. Moreover, God brought forth excellent craftsmen for this so holy a work: namely Bezalel, the grandson of Uri and Hur from the tribe of Judah, who possessed the skill, understanding, and knowledge of all mechanical craftsmanship divinely from the Lord, to work in gold, silver, bronze, gems,

# From Exodus XXXIX. v. 32.

<margin>
The construction of the Tabernacle.
</margin>
He was able to skillfully work gems and wood for the building of the Tabernacle of the Lord in the desert among the Israelites; to whom God added as a companion Aholiab, son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, and also increased the skill of other craftsmen, so that they might complete the work enjoined by the Lord upon Moses. For thus Jehovah spoke to Moses: <note>original: "Exod 31. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6."</note> *“See, I have called by name Bezaleel, the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah; and I have filled him with the* <gloss>Spirit of God</gloss> <note>Hebrew: Ruach Elohim</note>, *in* <gloss>wisdom</gloss> <note>Hebrew: Chochmah</note>, *and in* <gloss>understanding</gloss> <note>Hebrew: Tevunah</note>, *and in knowledge, and in all craftsmanship, to devise whatever can be made from gold and silver and bronze, and in the art of cutting stones for setting, and in the art of wood-carving, to work in every manner of work.”* Interpreters commonly recognize an *epimone* <note>a rhetorical figure involving the repetition of a point for emphasis</note> in this manner of speaking. But if we wish to distinguish these terms, we shall say that *wisdom* is a more general quality, which includes under itself as species *understanding* and *knowledge*, of which the former pertains to theory and the latter to practice: so that understanding is the same as what we call in German *Verstand* <note>Intellect/Understanding</note>: Knowledge is *Wissenschaft / Erfahrung* <note>Science / Experience</note>: or understanding joined with experience. And thus God himself places *Wisdom* in the mechanical arts, which the wiser among the heathens also recognize as a gift of Divine wisdom and prudence, which Cicero signifies with these words <note>original: "4. de Finib."</note> when he says: *“We wish that to all arts be attributed that which is called common prudence, which all who are in charge of any craft ought to possess.”* In this sense, Aristotle records that Phidias was called a *“wise marble-worker”* and Polycletus a *“wise maker of statues”* to signify the excellence of their art, writing in Ethics Book 6, Chapter 7: <note>original Greek: Τὴν σοφίαν ἐν ταῖς τέχναις... translated below</note> *“We attribute wisdom in the arts to those most exact in their crafts, such as Phidias, a wise stone-worker, and Polycletus, a statue-maker. In this context, we mean nothing else by wisdom than that it is the excellence of an art.”* He whom the highest God praises must be most experienced. The best praise is to be praised by Him who is the Praise of Israel. This happened to Bezaleel, whose calling is commended: <gloss>I have called by name</gloss> <note>Hebrew: Karati be-shem</note>. What this phrase means, we shall explain in the words of Flacius: <note>original: "Clav. Scriptura part. 1. col. 1298."</note> *“To call by name is to summon by name, i.e., specifically and separately and as if immediately, as when a master says to a crowd of servants: ‘Let someone from among you fly here quickly’; it is less than if he says by name, ‘Sofia, come here,’ or ‘Peter, follow me’; thus God commands Barnabas and Paul to be set apart by name for the work to which he called them in Acts 13, and does not say, ‘choose some for yourselves according to your own judgment.’”* He is called by his own proper and peculiar name, <insert>Bezaleel</insert>, which the Hebrews conjecture was given to him from a hoped-for future event, as often happens. Tanchumah <note>A collection of homiletic midrashim</note> fol. 42. col. 4. notes that it means, as it were, *“in the shadow of God.”* For he was to make the Ark, which was the <gloss>shadow</gloss> <note>Hebrew: Tzel</note> and protection of the Law of God to be placed within it. Buxtorf, in his *Exercises on the History of the Ark of the Covenant*, p. 25, relates a charming occasion for this <term>onomatomasia</term> <note>the naming of a person based on a characteristic or event</note> from the book Yalkut <note>original: "fol. 107. col. 2."</note> which we cannot help but recite here: Rabbi Samuel bar Nachman said; Bezaleel was so named because of his wisdom. For when the blessed God said to Moses: *“Go and tell Bezaleel: Make for me a Tabernacle, an Ark, and Vessels;”* Moses went and inverted the order of these, saying: *“Make the vessels, the Ark, and the tabernacle.”* Whereupon Bezaleel replied to Moses:

<column-break/>

<margin>
The construction of the Tabernacle.
</margin>
*“It is the custom of the world that a man first builds a house, then brings the vessels into it; but you say: Make the vessels, the Ark, and the Tabernacle. If I make the vessels first, where shall I put them? Perhaps God said it thus: Make the Tabernacle, the Ark, and the Vessels.”* Moses replied: <gloss>Perhaps you were in the shadow of God and knew this?</gloss> <note>Hebrew: Shema be-tzel El hayita ve-yadata?</note> The Mosaic Tabernacle was rectangular, longer than it was wide. For the length stretched from east to west for thirty cubits. The width from South to North was twelve cubits. The sides of this rectangle—namely the South, West, and North—consisted of a wall of planks; but the East side was entirely open to those entering. Furthermore, carpets placed as a roof covered the top of the Tabernacle. Each plank not only stood upright but was also connected to the walls with a certain common bond, which Moses mentions <note>original: "Exod. 36. 33."</note>, which they call the middle bar. Commentators vary on whether this was distinct from the others mentioned by Moses in Exodus 26:28; mindful of our purpose, we refer the Benevolent Reader to the most learned *Dissertation on the Middle Bar* by the Blessed Friedrich Müller. Furthermore, the Tabernacle is divided into three parts, namely the *Vestibule* or *Atrium*, the *Hall*, and the *Inner Sanctuary*. The first part of the Tabernacle, which is called the *Atrium* <note>the outer court</note>, was exposed under the open sky, defended by no roof or shade, but subject to rain, sun, heat, cold, and snow; it received indiscriminately not only the clean and unclean, the sacred and profane, but also animals of every kind, and in it, because of the sacrifices and perpetual offerings, there was a constant cycle of life and death. In this first class of the Tabernacle, there first occurred the *Altar of Burnt Offerings*, <gloss>Mizbeach</gloss> <note>Hebrew</note>, as if of the sacrificed, because sacrifices had to be burned on it daily. Concerning this, Augustine asks in Question 113 on Exodus: *“How could it be burned upon a wooden altar (for it was made of Shittim wood)?”* to which it is answered that it was overlaid with bronze, as is clear from verse 2 of chapter 38 of Exodus. This altar was a type of Christ, Hebrews 13:10; he is at once the priest, the altar, and the sacrifice, who offered our sins on the cross, 1 Peter 2:24, Ephesians 5:2. <margin>Exod. 30. 18. c. 38. 8.</margin> Additionally, a *bronze basin* <note>Hebrew: Kiyor nechoshet</note> was placed at the entrance of the second Tabernacle between the holy place and the altar of Burnt Offerings, full of water, in which those about to sacrifice were washed before they approached the sacred rites, so that they might perform the holy duties cleanly. This *basin* is said to have been made <gloss>from the mirrors of the serving women</gloss> <note>Hebrew: be-mar'ot ha-tzov'ot</note>; for thus the Vulgate translates: *“He also made the bronze basin with its base from the mirrors (from the mirrors of the fasting women)”* who kept watch at the door of the Tabernacle; so also Onkelos. This interpretation does not please the Blessed Frantzius <note>original: "de Interpr. Script. p. 40."</note>: *“In the Hebrew sources,”* he says, *“something else entirely is said, namely that he made the basin and its bronze base so that the Levites could look at themselves in it: not indeed from the mirrors of the women who gathered for work at the door of the Tabernacle, because there was no singular gathering of women at the door, and in the text the word for 'women' (which Pagninus puts) is plainly absent.”* Thus he says. Let everyone abound in his own sense; to us, the opinion of Rabbi Aben Ezra and Kimchi is more pleasing, who writes: *“It was the custom of all women to decorate their faces...”*

The second part or Hall, which was called the *Holy Place*, occupying the middle ground between the Vestibule and the inner shrine, shone entirely with the splendor of gold. For in its southern region was the *sacred lampstand*, distinguished by seven burning lamps; among these lamps, the one which occupied the middle summit of the lampstand had three lamps on each side. However, in the final conquest of the City [Jerusalem], it was carried away to Rome among other spoils by Titus and displayed in a triumph, as Josephus himself testifies in *The Jewish War, book 7, chapter 64.* Meanwhile, that famous Mosaic lampstand, which shone continually with seven lamps for the sacred use of the Jewish temple, symbolically prefigured Christ the Messiah according to the exposition of the Fathers. For Light arose through Christ, the Sun of Justice, who wished to announce the beam of his eternal light to the whole world by that lampstand, just as he says of himself: <margin>John 8:12.</margin> *I am the Light of the world. He who follows me does not walk in darkness.* The true Light, illuminating every man coming into this world, as witnessed by the "Eagle of the Evangelists" <note>A traditional title for St. John the Evangelist.</note> in chapter 1:9, and by the aged Simeon in *Luke 2:32, for whom a Light is prepared before the face of all peoples, for the revelation of the Gentiles* <note>original: *εἰς ἀποκάλυψιν ἐθνῶν*</note>, who at that time still dwelt in darkness, while the Jews dwelt in light. > ->What use is a Lampstand without the light of Christ?<-
> ->In perpetual darkness, you stubborn crowd, you lie.<-

His words are in *Stromata, book five, p. 240: The golden lampstand has another riddle, being a sign of Christ, not only in its shape, but also in the way it casts light in many ways and many parts upon those who believe in him, hoping and looking through the harmony of the prophets. They say there are seven eyes of the Lord, the seven spirits resting upon the rod blooming from the root of Jesse.* <note>Clement links the lampstand to the prophecy in Isaiah 11.</note> Gregory the Great in his *sixth Homily on Ezekiel* says: *It is Christ, in whom the nature of Humanity shone with the light of Divinity, so that he might become the lampstand of the world, by whose light the sinner might recognize his own*

Furthermore, in this second part of the Tabernacle was seen the *Table of the bread of proposition*, <term>Lechem Panim</term> <note>Hebrew: לֶחֶם פָּנִים</note>, the *bread of faces*, so called because they were before the face of the Lord in the presence of the ark and the mercy seat. Those loaves prefigure the Word of God to man, who lives not by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God, *Matthew 4:4.* These loaves are unleavened; whence later Christ warned his disciples to beware <margin>The construction of the Tabernacle.</margin> *of the leaven of the Pharisees* <note>original: *ἀπὸ τῆς ζύμης τῶν φαρισαίων*</note>, <margin>Matthew 16:6.</margin> which was hypocrisy and human tradition introduced under the plausible name of the *Elders*. Therefore, the word of God is pure and holy and must not be corrupted by our passions. Upon them was placed the clearest frankincense, for an odor of good fragrance to God. Now the word of God, if it is joined with faith in a pious heart, produces a sincere conscience, from which then flow pure prayers most pleasing to God. Moreover, because they were placed on a most clean table and eaten only by the Priests, it was figured who would be partakers of heavenly wisdom—namely, pure and holy minds; for the Lord did not wish that which is holy to be cast before dogs, *Matthew 7:6.* The third part of the Tabernacle was the most sacred and secret of all, which was called the *Inner Shrine, the adytum, and the Holy of Holies*; it was open to no one except the High Priest once a year, when he offered the blood of beasts for himself and for the sins of the people. <margin>Leviticus 16:34.</margin> In its inner recesses was hidden the *Ark*, which was destined for keeping the *tables of the Divine Law, the rod of Aaron, and the Manna.* This Ark of the Covenant was so called from the two stone tables written by the finger of God, because it contained within itself the covenant by which the Divine Power had bound the Jewish people to himself at Mount Sinai; it was covered inside and out with the purest gold. That Architect who first prescribed the form and use of the Ark of the Covenant is our God, for he spoke to Moses under that name in *Exodus 25:1, 10.* The assistant craftsman <margin>Exodus 37:1.</margin> was that distinguished artist *Bezalel*, who made the ark from Shittim wood; its length was two and a half cubits, its breadth a cubit and a half, and its height also a cubit and a half. Now the construction of the Ark and many other things fell in the year of the World 2454, before Christ was born according to the flesh in the year 1517, in which the Israelites were led out of Egypt. The material of the structure was *Shittim* wood, which the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> called *incorruptible* wood <note>original: *ἄσηπτα*</note>, because it would not easily rot. Since the Cedar-oil <note>original: *Cedrelatæ*</note> does not feel lines or decay, as Pliny witnesses in *book 16, ch. 11*, <margin>Pliny, Natural History book 16, ch. 11.</margin> and antiquity frequently used that species of wood, it is not unlikely that the ark was fashioned from cedar boards; for indeed the ark was worthy of Cedar, as it was the symbol of the covenant with God, and that transparent and most fragrant juice of the Cedar celebrated by Pliny...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>

</margin>
Two Cherubim covered and overshadowed this Mercy Seat <note>original: *Propitiatorium*</note> with their wings, which is why God is said to sit above the Cherubim (*Psalm 80:1*). As to what their *external form* was, the investigation of this has occupied the most ingenious men, yet no unanimous agreement regarding their accidental shape has been reached, nor is it ever to be expected. Men of no small reputation have asserted that they were <term>calf-shaped</term> <note>Greek: *Moschomorphous*</note>; 
<margin>
Commentary on Exodus 25:18, page 173.
</margin>
among our own scholars, the Blessed Friedlibius holds this view. Others think they had the form of four animals—namely a man, an eagle, a lion, and a calf—similar to the figure seen by Ezekiel, much like the <term>riddles</term> <note>Greek: *ainigmata*</note> or sphinxes fashioned by the Heathens. *Cornelius à Lapide* (in *Exodus* p. 536) concludes from *Clement of Alexandria* (*Stromata* book 5) that the Egyptians borrowed these from the Cherubim. There are those who prove they were fashioned in a *human* and *complete image of boys*, since it is established from *2 Chronicles 3:10* that Solomon fashioned others in the form of boys according to their likeness. In such a divorce of opinions, we do not see which side to join, choosing rather <term>to suspend judgment</term> <note>Greek: *to epechein*</note> in so abstruse and intricate a matter, especially since Josephus himself (*Antiquities of the Jews* book 3, ch. 6 and book 8, ch. 1) hesitates, saying they were <term>winged creatures, but in a form unlike any seen by men</term> <note>Greek: *zoa peteina, morphēn de oudeni tōn hyp’ anthrōpōn heōramenōn paraplēsia*</note>; *no one can guess or describe what species these flying animals were.*

This typical Ark of the Jews contained the Tables, the Manna, and the Rod: the mystical Ark of our Church contains in its Sacraments the divine Word, by which we are taught as if by tables, fed as if by manna, and directed and corrected as if by a rod. Nor does God merely contain this Word, but He bestows it through these same most holy Sacraments as through aids and divinely prepared instruments, by whose intervention the power of Christ’s merits is applied to all who receive them worthily. Hence, in the Mercy Seat and the Ark of the Covenant, let us not look with a faithful mind at the precious Shittim wood, nor the refined gold, nor the price of labor and the craftsmanship of both, but at the thing signified: namely, Him who is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world; who is the author of the eternal covenant with God the Father; who is the Protector of the Ark, that is, of His Church; who writes the Law upon it, and adds to it the more-than-golden ornament of His righteousness. For the depiction of the <term>Mercy Seat</term> <note>The lid of the Ark where atonement was made.</note> paints Christ and His passion. I. The *Ark of the Covenant*, in which the book of the covenant was placed, is the image of the true Church, with whom God made a covenant through His Word. The rings and poles by which the Ark was carried are the image of the Teachers in the Church, who sustain the burden of governance in the Church. The golden plate which covered the Ark, called the Mercy Seat, from which God spoke, signifies Christ the Mediator, *golden with His own blood* which He shed for the sins of men, on account of whom alone God is merciful to us. The two Cherubim above the Mercy Seat, looking at each other with faces turned toward the Mercy Seat, are a type of the Old and New Testaments, or the Prophetic and Apostolic doctrine, which agrees concerning Christ and His offices. The Ark of the Testimony was covered on the outside with curtains of goat's hair, rough and shaggy; but inside the curtains were of twisted linen and hyacinth, and purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, varied with embroidery work, so that inside everything was most beautiful. The Church has nothing grand on the outside; she dwells under skins, always fears the enemy, and is never secure. But inside, all things are beautiful and precious. *I am black,* she says, *but comely, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon.*

Song of Solomon 1:5.

But since we have so far contemplated the Ark of the Covenant—which was the dwelling place of the Divine presence, the salvation and glory of Israel, in which the Jews boasted greatly of old and even still today—it will be worthwhile to add a few points regarding its chronology, since it had no fixed seat before the temple was built but was moved from place to place. Hence, it is pleasing to note the chronology of the Ark of the Covenant: In the year 2455 from the creation of the world, the Tabernacle of the Ark of the Covenant was erected and dedicated with a solemn rite by Moses, with the cloud of glory overshadowing it <margin>Exodus 40:34</margin>. In the year 2494 from the creation, as the Israelites crossed the Jordan, the Ark was carried by the Priests into the land of Canaan; and not long after, it was carried around the city of Jericho by the command of the Lord until the walls of the city fell (*Joshua 3:13, 17; 6:6 etc.*). Just as the Israelites were led through the Jordan into the promised land under the leadership of Joshua, so we, under the leadership of Jesus Christ, enter into rest through the tribulations of this life <margin>Hebrews 4:1</margin>. Just as the walls of Jericho fell when the Ark of the Covenant was carried around them, so Jesus Christ, the author of the eternal covenant, destroyed the <term>strongholds</term> <note>Greek: *ochyrōmata*</note> or fortifications of Satan with the joyful clang of the Gospel (*2 Corinthians 10:4*). In the year of the world 2811, the Ark of the Covenant was in Shiloh, at which time Eli the Priest judged Israel. In the year 2850, the Ark was captured by the Philistines and finally restored the following year, concerning which restoration Nicodemus Frischlinus sings thus in his *Hebræidos*:
<margin>
Book 7, page 191.
</margin>

<margin>2 Samuel 6: 6, 7</margin>
Thereafter, the Bethshemites having been struck by the just judgment of God, it was deposited in Kiriath-Jearim in the house of Abinadab, 1 Samuel 7:1. In the Year of the World 2900, the Ark was brought into the city of Jerusalem by King David; and when Uzzah touched the tottering Ark, he was struck down by God*.

What could seem more holy than that Uzzah touched the tottering Ark with his hands and supported it against falling? Yet that intention so displeased God, that Uzzah incurred death as if he were a sacrilegious violator and profaner. This so harsh and unexpected punishment drove David off course, so that he changed his plan of bringing the Ark, depositing the Ark for three months in the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite. But afterward, the matter having been more diligently considered, and God’s blessing having been perceived as conferred upon the house of the Gittite because of the deposited Ark, David retracted his opinion and undertook the bringing of the Ark by the legitimate rite according to the law of Moses, and took care to have it brought into the city of David with religious pomp. There, full of divine joy, he adapted a religious dance to the <term>songs of praise <note>Original Greek: ἐπαινετικὰ (epainetika)</note></term> which were being chanted, showing openly and in public with what affection he worshiped GOD, with what fervor of gratitude he burned, and with what zeal he looked upon such a great benefit. On the way, Michal, his delicate and haughty wife, mocks him as he dances, judging it not to be according to the authority of a King to dance so, and not of a noble lineage to walk thus, subjecting him to her anger from her boiling over*:

<margin>2 Samuel 6:20</margin>
[How glorious was] the King today before the eyes of the handmaids <gloss>servants</gloss> of his servants, just as one of the most vain men uncovers himself. With a bold face she gazes upon the joyful David, and looks grimly, reproaching him with a hard mouth for his excessive ease and humanity, as if to say: What does it profit to be King? What does it profit to be famous for the nobility of my father's house, if you cast yourself down so and walk unkempt in the sight of all?

<column-break/>

<margin>The building of the Tabernacle. 1 Kings 8:9.</margin>
In the Year of the World 2981, the Ark was brought into the temple of Solomon and placed in the Holy of Holies*. In the year 3365 from the Creation of the World, 606 before the Incarnation of Christ, the Temple, set on fire by the leaders of Nebuchadnezzar, the Babylonian Monarch, burned down, after it had stood for 484 years. However, no mention is made of the Ark of the Covenant, nor of the rod of Aaron in that whole history, and specifically in the list of the Vessels of the temple, which were first taken away by the Babylonians, and then restored by Cyrus the Persian.

And it is likely that either the Ark, together with the rod of Aaron, the Tabernacle, and the Cherubim, as well as many other things, were consumed by age, and neither hidden in the earth by King Josiah through a special revelation of God with a few priests knowing, nor by Jeremiah the Prophet in a cave of Mount Nebo (who lived shut up in prison when the city was besieged by the Babylonians), which nevertheless pleases Joseph ben Gorion* and the <margin>Book 1, chapter 17.</margin> <margin>Ezra ch. 10.</margin> author of the book of Maccabees (2 Maccabees 2:1 ff; 4 Ezra ch. 10 v. 22), as well as others; but rather it was burned, and truly never restored nor ever to be restored. In this opinion, above others, is Epiphanius in the *Life of Jeremiah*, followed by Sixtus of Siena, *Sacred Library* book 8, heresy 12; Cornelius à Lapide, *Commentary on Exodus* ch. 25, p. 532; Marius, *Commentary on the Pentateuch* p. 546; Bonfrère, *Commentary on the Pentateuch* p. 489; Bellarmine, book 1, controversy 1, *On the Canonical and Apocryphal Books*, ch. 15, p. 68; and others, who all with one voice go on to assert that at the end of the world, after the conversion of the Jews, the Ark of the Covenant will rise again and come out from the Rock in which Jeremiah hid it. But as far as concerns Epiphanius, John Rainolds proves in many ways that his book is spurious in *Censure of the Apocryphal Books*, regarding Epiphanius, Vol. 2, lecture 138, p. 155 ff. Even today the Jews nurse themselves with the empty hope of restoring the Ark, which the Talmudists (Rabbi Levi, Ben Gerson, *Commentary on the Torah* p. 154, col. 4; Rabbi Abarbanel in his *Commentaries on Haggai* p. 277, col. 4) teach was absent in the second temple, in the day of the coming Messiah for which they hope in vain; compare Johann Frischmuth in his special dissertation on Jeremiah 3:14, regarding the restoration of the Ark of the covenant not to be hoped for.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The apparatus of sacrifices.</margin>
That the true invisible Church may be gathered and preserved by GOD within a visible assembly, let it be done through the sensible means of the Word—namely, public preaching—which began from the moment the Church began after the Fall in Paradise, and was continued thereafter. Later, however, divine kindness added the Sacraments, which look toward the same goal as the preaching of the Word: namely, that through their public administration the Church may be gathered, preserved, and recognized. The entire ceremonial Levitical worship was a part of worship in itself, being commanded by GOD; therefore, its transgression brought the guilt of even eternal death. Sacrifices held the principal place in that system, which, by reason of their "antitype" <note>The spiritual reality or person (Christ) prefigured by the symbol.</note> to be explained simultaneously through the Word, are reduced to the essential worship in the Old Testament.

Regarding these, I shall speak anew, though not of new things, and as briefly as I can. Let no one expect here the entire matter of sacrifice; if we strove to explain it as it deserves, the volume itself would hardly suffice. It is enough to have shown what they chiefly contain, what and how many they were, who instituted them, in what manner, and—what will be last—for what end and for how long they were instituted. For the entire treatment of sacrificial matters is full of the sweetest sermons and meanings; the magnitude of these things cannot be exhausted, and the revelation of this wisdom far surpasses the thoughts of all the wisest men and every edge of human intellect, unless the illumination of divine light is added. They were singular benefits exceeding all comprehension, which were represented in various ways by the apparatus of sacrifices; and indeed, in that region of Palestine, there had to be a certain seat for these actions. We shall touch upon the principal kinds of sacrifices and their main points.

<margin>Disputation 2 on Sacrifices, thesis 114.</margin>
However, so that we may provide a clear *systematic description* <note>original Greek: τεχνολογίαν (technologian)</note> of the Sacrifices, we think it must first be established that when the first man, through the first sin, had become an enemy of GOD—and all other men from that first sin—God, out of sole clemency, struck a covenant anew, promised a Savior, instituted rites, ordained sacred things, and commanded sacrifices, without which men could in no way be saved. And thus, immediately from the very beginning, GOD demonstrated the restoration and renewal of the covenant to the first man through sacrifices. Although no express mention occurs of any "Adamite" Sacrifice, it is nonetheless a pious conjecture of the Ancients that from the skins of sacrificial sheep, slaughtered and burned by divine command, garments were made and put upon Adam and Eve, *so that henceforth all sacrificial livestock might learn to be types, because without the garment of the innocence of Christ no one can be saved,* as the Blessed Frantzius says. And from there, taught and accustomed by Adam to the worship of Sacrifices, the two sons Cain and Abel are read to have brought Sacrifices. When GOD looked upon them both as they were offered—for Abel, the son of Adam, had brought from the firstborn of his flock and their fat, and indeed it is believable that a lamb was the chief among those gifts—it was pleasing to God, even if it is not expressed by what sign Abel's victim was approved. We read in Holy Scripture that other Sacrifices were approved and

<column-break/>

<margin>The apparatus of sacrifices.</margin>
consumed by flame sent down from heaven, just as the flame of heaven commended the Sacrifices of Moses, Aaron, Gideon, David, and others. That the smoke went into heaven from the sacrificial fire was written by Claudius Marius Victor in his poem, Book 2 on Genesis, verse 175:

> *Thus of old the pure Abel sensed beforehand*
> *The envy of his brother; for when the latter had sacrificed*
> *From his own fruit; the former with a snow-white lamb, soon straightway*
> *The smoke from the burned lamb ascended into the high heaven.*
> *But on the contrary, flying through the void from those fruits,*
> *The smoke returned to the earth from a fleeing Olympus.* <note>Olympus here refers to the sky or the dwelling of God.</note>

<margin>1. Sacred Miscellanies 3, p. 4.</margin>
Hence, concerning the different Sacrifices of Cain and Abel, Nierembergius speaks thus: *Cain's offering was lifeless, not a living victim, and because it was not living, lacking affection, it was not pleasing. Abel's victim was animate; he offered with affection, and himself rather than his things. Abel offered because he offered himself. Cain, who denied himself, offered nothing, although he offered gifts; because in offering these, and not himself, he offered nothing. Cain's gifts were without affection, without soul, without himself. Abel's were vivid, animated by affection, heart, and devotion of soul, with which he gave himself and all things. There was no offering from Cain, because it was not of himself. Abel's victim was the greatest, because it was of himself, because it was of all. He offers the most who offers himself, for he offers all things; yet he offers nothing who does not offer himself, because without oneself, "all things" are nothing.* Therefore, when Cain felt his burnt offering was unacceptable and less pleasing to God, he threw the blame for it upon his pious and innocent brother, and immediately thought of killing him. Speaking of his sin, Ambrose, in *The Calling of the Gentiles* chapter 4, introduces GOD speaking thus: *Abel did not harm you, nor did he hurt you by pleasing me. I despised your gifts by my judgment, not by his wish. For you performed a good work negligently. Your offering would have been right if your discernment had been right. Knowing to whom you offered, you ought to have known what you vowed. You did not divide worthily between me and yourself, since you kept the choicer things for yourself; compare the same.*

<margin>On Psalm 35, p. 477.</margin>
From this point, with sacred matters immediately sliding toward the worse after the fratricide under Cain, the School of Sacrifices was torn apart, and genuine Sacrifices remained with Seth, the successor of Abel. But the nation of Cain, with cunning and old-hand trickery, transferred the sacrificial doctrine to a dull resemblance; and in place of the pious ceremonies of Sacrifices, there succeeded an insane discipline of lies. From this, the sacred rites of the primeval institution gradually passed, through the snares of demons and the greedy wickedness of sacrifices, into various idol-madness, so that they twisted them into a dull art of soothsaying, baiting men (who were otherwise credulous) with certain crafty sophisms. They had received from their ancestors the doctrine that the Messiah to be sacrificed one day was signified by the Sacrifices. The priests turned this into *human sacrifice* <note>original Greek: ἀνθρωποθυσίαν (anthrōpothusian)</note>, lest they should seem to hand down anything other than what they had received from the ancients, even if all things were contrary to the tradition of the ancients. Meanwhile, the true and genuine use of Sacrifices remained with Seth and his descendants. For from Seth it went to Enos, from Enos to Cainan, from Cainan to Mahalaleel, from him to Jared, from Jared to Enoch, from Enoch to Methuselah, from him to Lamech, then to Noah,
