# From Leviticus VII. v. 37.

<margin>The apparatus of sacrifices.</margin>
The Holy Scriptures <note>original: "Pandectæ," here referring to the Bible as a complete body of divine law</note> testify that the first sacrifice after the flood was most pleasing to GOD in these words, *Genesis 8:21: The Lord smelled a sweet savor.* Because of the disobedience of our first parents, Adam and Eve, the Lord had smelled a foul odor; they had hidden themselves in fear, having slipped away from the face of God. But when they were commanded to appear, they were covered with clothing in their nakedness, received into grace in their confusion, set free from servitude as manumitted slaves, and joyfully commanded to perform holy rites through sacrifices, ready to offer pure victims free from blemish. There is no doubt that they offered them, even if the text passes over it in silence.

When the limits of the completed flood were reached, Noah offered a sacrifice of good odor; the divine Power approaching it with His celestial breath or celestial flames. For this is what "to smell" signifies; for GOD does not have nostrils, because He is Spirit, <margin>in the Chronicles of Melanchthon, p. 136.</margin> as Strigelius* says, but in the human manner He is said to smell when He ignites and consumes the sacrifices with celestial flames, which is a sign of divine approval or <term>eudokia</term> <note>Greek: εὐδοκία, meaning "goodwill" or "pleasure"</note>. <margin>On the rite of circumcision, p. 407.</margin> Hence Cyril* says:

> It is established that from Adam until Noah, sacrifices were acceptable to GOD, which until that time were celebrated without the distinction of the Law, by the divinely inspired institution of the first man. Those sacrifices were performed either in the blood of animals or in the burning of other offerings, not because GOD was delighted by smoke or the deaths of cattle, but so that the immutable judgment and the sentence pronounced against sin from the beginning might be understood.

But the descendants of Noah, scattered into diverse lands, gradually lost the celestial doctrine they had received from their holy ancestors and accumulated idols and deities. They did indeed retain some rites handed down by the Fathers, such as sacrifices. Naaman the Syrian, a witness greater than any proof, left this testified when, in *2 Kings 5:17*, renouncing the customary worship of false gods, he said to Elisha: >Your servant will no longer make sacrifice to foreign gods, but to Jehovah.< Upon these words of Naaman, the Blessed Lucas Osiander comments thus:

> From this remarkable miracle of health, I acknowledge that the GOD who is worshiped among you Israelites is the only true and eternal GOD, while the remaining gods of the Nations are nothing but vain and fictitious deities; wherefore I also shall hereafter worship only that true GOD, intending to sacrifice to Him. Therefore, since I cannot sacrifice in the Temple consecrated to Him, I desire at least to offer victims to Him upon that earth which He Himself consecrated for the habitation of His people.

Regarding the earth which the Syrian carried with him from Palestine into Syria, commentators vary as to what Naaman did with it; some asserting an altar was built from it, others that he worshiped the true GOD while standing upon it in the temple of Idols; compare Tertullian *on Idolatry, ch. 15*, Augustine *Sermon 207 on Time, which is about Naaman the Syrian*, the Blessed Johann Quistorp *Biblical Annotations on the Old Testament, p. 320*, Tirinus *Vol. 1 of Commentaries, p. 240*, and Cornelius à Lapide *commentary on this place, Vol. 2, p. 241*. If you desire testimonies from secular authors indicating various rites of sacrificing, you may have a few from Macrobius *Book 3 of Saturnalia, ch. 1, p. 81*, Porphyry *on Abstinence from Animals*, and Lucian of Samosata *in Prometheus, p. 223 and following*.

<column-break/>

Also Caelius Rhodiginus *Book 1 of Ancient Readings, ch. 10, p. 17, and Book 12, ch. 1, p. 428 and following*. <margin>The apparatus of sacrifices.</margin> All men not undeservedly think that these rites of offering sacrifice flowed from the most ancient example of Abel and Cain to the human race:

> For in any age, as Paul, Bishop of Burgos, truly writes in *The Scrutiny of Holy Scripture, part 2, dist. 3, ch. 11*, and among any nations of men, there was always some offering of sacrifices. That which is found among all is natural. Moreover, the reason for this thing is this: For just as in natural things lower things are naturally subject to their superiors, so also natural reason dictates that, according to natural inclination, men should show subjection and honor to Him who is above all, according to a manner suitable to man. This manner is that he uses sensible signs <note>physical objects perceived by the senses</note> to express an interior concept, just as he receives knowledge of invisible things from sensible ones. Whence it proceeds from natural reason that man uses sensible things, offering them to GOD as a sign of subjection and honor, in the likeness of those who offer something to their Lords in recognition of their Lordship.

It is therefore no wonder that the system of sacrifices, propagated from Adam—who by the command of GOD, and not by rash daring, offered <term>minchas</term> <note>Hebrew: מִנְחָה, grain offerings</note> from the fruits of the earth, and the firstborn of the flocks and their fat—was preserved until Noah, and thereafter after the flood among all the descendants of Noah, though not without the "appendix of the fig leaf" <note>a metaphor for human corruption or superficiality covering the original truth</note>. Indeed, the true rite of sacrifices remained with its proper use and purpose only in the family of Eber; the rest, however, were ignorant of their use and purpose, and thus, having lost the kernel, they retained the husk. If the sacrifices of profane superstition are examined, they will betray what they received from the first tradition of the most ancient Fathers; the closer they lived to them, the better "patches and fringes" they sewed onto their sacred rites, from which it will not be difficult to guess the quality of the cloth. They had neglected the pure grain, and wandering outside the true field of sacrifices, they had cultivated a field with a bad plow, whence many tares were brought in, which finally corrupted the whole field. Let us sift those sacred rites so that, if any pure grain remains from the old colony, we may save it—not as something necessary for us, but so that it can be shown from there that some grain of the ancient sacrifice survives in the rites of the gentiles. Let us shake out the crop of tares; let us winnow away everything superfluous and useless like chaff and needles, husks and awns, and all the dust, so that at least a small measure of pure grains from the immense harvest may come down to us, once all have been sifted.

In the general heap of sacrifices, while we begin the sifting for which the post-flood people provide us the opportunity, a clear image of pure grain is exhibited by what the Philosopher Aristotle sowed in his own Philosophical field: <term>For it is not likely</term>, he says in the Rhetoric, <term>that God rejoices in the expense of the sacrifices, but in the piety of those who sacrifice</term> <note>original Greek: Οὐ γὰρ εἰκὸς τὸν Θεὸν χαίρειν ταῖς δαπάναις τῶν θυομένων, ἀλλὰ ταῖς εὐσεβείαις τῶν θυόντων</note>. Nothing is lacking to this grain, except that it was not moistened by the dew of divine truth; I would believe this, if I did not [regard] Aristotle's authority...

If I had presented these laws, you would swear they had come forth from the field of Moses. You hear it taught that the divine Writers almost taught that God is delighted by the piety of those sacrificing, not by the expense of the sacrifices. Homer expressed this much more explicitly—which we can only utter with a groan—when he teaches that all prayers, libations, sacrifices, and other ceremonies tended toward this: that they might appease GOD, since no man can live or pass his time without God. For he says:

<margin>Odyssey, Book 3, line 46.</margin>

In the same manner, Zaleucus <note>A Greek lawgiver of the Locrians</note> says: God is not worshiped with expenditures, but with virtue and the choice of good and just works. Therefore, everyone who intends to be beloved by God must be good in both action and intention. <note>Original Greek: Οὐ θεραπεύεται ὁ Θεὸς δαπάναις, ἀλλὰ ἀρετῇ καὶ προαιρέσει τῶν καλῶν ἔργων καὶ δικαίων. διὸ ἕκαστον δεῖ ἀγαθὸν εἶναι καὶ πράξει καὶ προαιρέσει τὸν μέλλοντα ἔσεσθαι Θεοφιλῆ.</note>

<margin>Orations, Book 1, Chapter 11.</margin>
Mellissus reported this in fuller words: God is not honored by a wicked man, nor is he worshiped with expenditures, nor with the tragedies of those captured, but by the good intention of good and just works. <note>Original Greek: Οὐ τιμᾶται Θεὸς ὑπ᾽ ἀνθρώπῳ φαύλῳ, οὐδὲ θεραπεύεται δαπάναις, οὐδὲ τραγῳδίαις τῶν ἁλισκομένων, ἀλλ᾽ ἀγαθῇ προαιρέσει τῶν καλῶν ἔργων καὶ δικαίων.</note> The excellent lawgiver of the Locrians asserts that God is not worshiped by many expenses, but by virtue and the study of good works, and that God is to be worshiped not so much by will as by action; in whose very pious decree nothing is lacking except the Sun of divine revelation. But we must return from the husk to the kernel itself. In the family of Eber alone was the genuine rite and use of Sacrifices manifest, and from him to Abraham, to whom Jehovah appeared, saying: *To your seed I will give this land, and he built there an Altar to Jehovah, who had appeared to him.* <margin>Genesis 12:1.</margin> Furthermore, he moved himself to the mountain on the East of Bethel, and pitched his tent there and built an altar there. <margin>Genesis 12:8.</margin>

Returning from Egypt after the famine, he proceeded by his journeys to the place of the Altar, which he had made there in the beginning, and there he called upon the name of Jehovah. After the separation from Lot, he pitched the same tent in the oaks of Mamre, and built there an Altar to Jehovah himself. Similarly, Isaac, in the place of Beersheba, where Jehovah had appeared to him at night, built an Altar and called upon the name of Jehovah. <margin>Genesis 26:25.</margin> His son Jacob established an altar, and called it: The Mighty God of Israel. He is also commanded to make an altar to God in Bethel, for in this manner God speaks to him: *Arise, go up to Bethel, stay there: and make there an altar to GOD, who appeared to you when you fled from the face of Esau your brother.* <margin>Genesis 35:1.</margin> To what purpose, however, were the altars, if not for the sacrifices to be offered upon them? This reasoning for building altars reached the Gentiles as well: For the ancients, as Festus holds, performed sacrifices to the upper Gods on altars, of which matter many examples are read among the Poets; thus Silius, Book 12:

->Festive for Jove.<-

And the same in Aeneid 8, speaking of the Sacrifices of Hercules:

->Together all the first of the youths and the poor Senate<-
->Gave incense and the warm blood smoked at the altars.<-

Hence in the primitive Church it was considered a great crime against Christians that they had neither temples nor altars. For thus Caelius says to Minutius: *Why do they have no altars, no temples, no known images? Why do they never speak openly? Never freely*

*congregate? unless that which they worship and impress is either to be punished or is shameful?* So much did they then value the altars built in their shrines for offering sacrifices. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied in any way that sometimes altars were also erected for the taking of an oath; hence Cicero in defense of Flaccus: *Who, if he held the altar while swearing, no one would believe; what he wished, he proved unsworn through a Letter.* And Juvenal, Satire 13:

And so, intrepid, they swear by whatever altars. As also for that purpose, that all the wretched and the guilty might flee to them, which was called by the Greeks the *altar of refuge* <note>Original Greek: φύξιμοι βωμὸς</note>. Joab, the commander of David's army, sought that use of the altar when he fled to the horns of the altar as if to a most certain asylum, 1 Kings 2:29. ->In the middle of the city was an altar granted to none,<-
->Mild clemency placed a seat for the Gods,<-
->And the wretched made it sacred.<-

Nor should it be thought that these sacrifices of the Ancients were performed without prayers, but in the beginning of the world, piety itself and the pious intention of those sacrificing suggests that they poured out prayers to God during the sacrifices. For by these very things they intended to appease God and render him favorable to themselves; for that reason, there is no doubt but that they employed prayers during the sacrifice, so that God might wish to look upon their victims with merciful eyes and be delighted by them. Whence the rites of praying among the Heathens arose from the piety <note>Original Greek: εὐσέβειαν</note> of the godly in the use of sacrifices, which Athenaeus testifies were used in Book 6: *I, your servant, offer these things to you, and I sacrifice; I confess you as the author of holiness, and for sanctifying in this offering, that you may pour into it the power of your high and honored Spirit, so that through it we may obtain what we seek. But truly, just as this present thing is made yours by my offering, so that henceforth it lives and dies for you: so also may I be made yours, who through this offering and communion, through this, that I come to offer and sacrifice to you, profess myself to be of your family and worshipers.* Whence a great action consists in sacrificing and praying; for thus one replied to Socrates disputing with him about the definition of holiness <note>Original Greek: τὸ ὁσίου</note>: *I tell you simply, that if someone knows how to say and do things pleasing to the gods, both praying and sacrificing, these things are holy and such things save both private houses and the common affairs of cities. But the opposites of pleasing things are impious, which indeed overturn and destroy everything.*

# From Leviticus VII. v. 37.

<margin>The apparatus of sacrifices. Lev. 17, 14.</margin>
...mindful, and having applied his divine thought to it. Moreover, he elegantly says that they brought "substitutes for the soul" <note>original: τᾶς ψυχᾶς ἀντί-ψυχα</note>, since they offered the life of animals to God in place of their own souls; regarding this matter, he cites the words of the Divine Law: <term>The soul of all flesh is its blood, and I have given the blood to you upon the altar to make atonement for your souls. For the blood shall make atonement in place of the soul.</term> <note>The author translates the Greek Septuagint version of Leviticus 17:11 here.</note> God commanded that for the expiation of crimes, the blood of the animals being sacrificed should be placed upon the altar or poured at its base. This was not merely because blood is, in a sense, the "soul" of animals and thus appropriately sacrificed for the expiation of human souls, but because human life and blood ought to have been poured out and lost due to committed sins. The merciful and yet just Lord commanded that the life and blood of animals be offered to Him instead of the life and soul of man. After the law concerning sacrifices was brought forth, God wished to exercise His people with various ceremonies so that they would never cease thinking of the "Blessed Seed" <note>A reference to the promised Messiah</note>, and also to draw them away from those ceremonies which the neighboring idolatrous nations were accustomed to use. Hence *Tertullian* once responded to those inquiring:
<margin>2. Against Marcion.</margin>
> Let no one find fault with the burdens of sacrifices and the busy scrupulosities of operations and offerings, as if God properly desired such things for Himself, He who so clearly exclaims: "To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices to me?" and "Who has required these things from your hands?" Rather, let one perceive that industry of God, by which He wished to bind a people prone to idolatry and transgression to His own religion by such offices as were practiced in the superstition of the age; He did this to call them away from it, commanding things to be done for Himself as if He desired them, lest the people should fall into sin by making idols. But even in the very dealings of life and human conversation, at home and abroad, He distinguished the care of vessels in every way, so that these legal disciplines might occur everywhere, lest any moments be vacant from the respect of God.

Indeed, while the minds of the Jews were being corrupted in Egypt by that long cohabitation—to the point that they were almost ignorant of their ancestral religion and the covenant itself, but were falling away more and more each day toward Egyptian idolatry and the whole system of pagan rites—it then pleased the wise and merciful Lord to come to the aid of the collapsing covenant with certain supports. First, He restored the precepts of the ancient covenant itself, explained them more copiously, and inscribed them on stone tablets with His own finger. Then, He prescribed sacrifices with certain rites and ceremonies, which had been handed down through a certain divine revelation from Adam to all the godly until then. Moreover, the order of sacrifices in Leviticus—which in the Masora is called <term>The Law or Doctrine of the Priests</term> <note>Hebrew: תורת כהנים (Torat Kohanim)</note>, because it prescribes laws for the Priests and teaches what their duty requires—is described such that, with a distinction of victims added, one host is to be offered for the Priest, another for the people, another for the Prince, and another for the private citizen. Truly, six kinds of sacrifices are chiefly described in Leviticus, three of which are <term>propitiatory</term> <note>Greek: ἱλαστικὰ; seeking to appease God</note> (that is, typically so), and three are <term>eucharistic</term> <note>Greek: εὐχαριστικά; expressing gratitude</note>. There are those who list other species of sacrifices to be presented on the Hebrew altars: *First* was the burnt offering, under which were the Grain Offering, the Sabbath, and the New Moon. 2. Sacrifice for sin, *Sin-Offering* <note>German: Sünd-Opffer</note>. 3. Sacrifice for guilt, *Guilt-Offering* <note>German: Schuld-Opffer</note>. 4. Sacrifice of consecration,

<meta>This page continues the systematic classification of Jewish sacrifices, moving from expiatory offerings to grain offerings and peace offerings. It maintains the scholarly tone of a 17th-century theological treatise, citing both Rabbinic sources (like David Kimhi and Rashi) and Classical authors.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The apparatus.</margin>
Of the *expiatory* class of sacrifice, there was the "sacrifice for sin," called <term>Chatat</term> <note>Hebrew: חטאת</note> by the Hebrews <gloss>an offering or sacrifice for sin</gloss>. As seen in Isaiah 5:18, this was specifically for *involuntary* sin—not committed willfully, but through error or ignorance; in German, a *Sündopffer* <note>Sin offering</note>. This was *redemptive*, ransoming the penalty of a specific original fault, or some other sin of omission and ignorance. The third type was the "sacrifice for guilt," called <term>Asham</term> <note>Hebrew: אשם</note> by the Hebrews, an offering for trespass, named from the root <term>Asham</term> <note>to be guilty or to trespass</note>. This was offered for *voluntary*, actual sin; in German, a *Schuldopffer* <note>Guilt/Trespass offering</note>. This too was *redemptive* to ransom, as stated, the penalties of all actual sins. Regarding the word <term>Asham</term>, Rabbi 
<margin>Book of Roots</margin>
David <note>David Kimhi, a medieval Jewish grammarian</note> advises that it is almost always taken for the victim and offering which was poured out for a fault; whereas <term>Tzed</term> <note>Hebrew: צד</note> denotes a voluntary and gracious victim. Both words are joined in Proverbs 14:9, where Salazar (p. 1180) notes: *"The fool mocks sin,"* that is, *the victim for sin, and by mocking the victim, he delays or entirely fails to pay for the crimes committed. On the contrary, among the righteous there is favor,* that is, *a voluntary victim, while the righteous not only pour out the required pardon for their faults, but also pay a voluntary and gratuitous one.* Among the *Eucharistic* <note>Thank-offerings</note> types, the first was the "gift offering," called <term>Mincha</term> <note>Hebrew: מנחה</note> by the Hebrews; an offering, *a food offering/thanksgiving for life and sustenance*, an immolation, a libation. It is used for both a profane gift, which man gives to man, and a sacred grain offering, which was offered to God, as Buxtorf notes in his Lexicon under the word <term>Mincha</term>, which is the properly intended meaning; even if taken *broadly* it may encompass any offering, whether it was made from fruits or through the shedding of blood. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> attends to the 
<margin>on Leviticus 24:9 R. S.</margin>
proper meaning, whence he describes the Hebrew sacrifice thus: <term>Anything that comes from the produce of grain in general is included in the term Mincha</term>. And Sigonius, writing on the rites of the Jews, 
<margin>Book 3, ch. 1 on Jewish Matters</margin>
states among other things: *“Sacred things among the Hebrews were many; but offerings claimed the chief place among them. For these were of two kinds: one called by the name of sacrifice, host, and victim; the other by the name of gift and present.”* From which it is clear that the word <term>Mincha</term> in its proper and strict sense is noted only as an offering made from the fruits of the earth. The second is the "salvation sacrifice," called <term>Zevach Shelamim</term> <note>Hebrew: זבח שלמים</note> by the Hebrews, a victim of peace-offerings; *a thank offering/thanksgiving for certain benefits received*, which is also mentioned in Amos 5:22; it was offered to God for peace, safety, health, and benefits. It is called <term>Zeba Selomim</term> because in that sacrifice all things were required to be whole and sound, from the root <term>Shalam</term>, *to be complete, perfected, or to enjoy peace*. By the Greeks it is called a "salvation sacrifice," whence in 
<margin>Sirach 47:1</margin>
praise of David it is said: *“As the fat is set apart from the salvation offering, so was David from the children of Israel.”* The Vulgate version has *“from the flesh”* instead of *“from the salvation offering.”* However, by "the salvation offering," Osorius (following Jansenius) understands: *“The victim of the peace-makers, which was offered to the Lord for Salvation, of which the fat alone was burned; but the breast and the right shoulder belonged to the Priest.”* David is therefore said to be like the fat which had been consecrated to God in the sacrifice of peace-offerings, by which it was signified that, just as in that sacrifice the fat was separated from the rest of the meat and burned as a holy thing to God, while the meat was eaten by the Priest and the Laity; so David was separated from the children of Israel,

<column-break/>

even the righteous ones. The third was the "sacrifice of praise," by the Hebrews called the sacrifice of praise and confession, a *Lobopffer* <note>Praise offering</note> <term>Todah</term> <note>Hebrew: תודה</note>. This kind of sacrifice was presented—these are the words of D. Friedlieb in his *Commentary on this place, p. 196*—whenever someone wished to praise the Lord and give thanks for some sign, such as if someone had escaped a danger, for instance, if he had been freed from chains, or had recovered from a serious illness, or had obtained offspring from a barren wife. This kind of sacrifice (*says another author*) is numbered not among the most holy, but among the common ones. For it was permitted to eat of its remains, not only for the Priests, but also for the common people of the Israelites, provided they were sanctified according to their lawful rites. Next, two species of this sacrifice are recounted: One is called <term>Todah</term>, *a sacrifice of confession and praise*, by which the offerer confesses that he has received a benefit from God, and praises and commends the glory of God's mercy and goodness. The Septuagint translated this as "sacrifice of praise." The other is called <term>Nedavah</term> <note>Hebrew: נדבה</note>, i.e., *a vow or freewill offering*, when the offerer has not yet received the benefit from God which he hoped for, but either vowed a sacrifice in expectation of receiving the benefit, or brings a sacrifice of his own spontaneous will to excite and confirm his faith in the invocation of God's name for the desired and hoped-for salvation. For as there are various species of sacrifices, so they are allotted various names, of which two are principal among the Hebrews, namely <term>Tenufah</term> <note>Hebrew: תנופה</note> 
<margin>Lexicon p. 456</margin>
from the root <term>Nuf</term>, *he waved or moved*, about which Buxtorf notes under the word <term>Nuf</term>. It is often used for the special offering of certain sacrifices which was done by waving toward the East, West, South, and North, to show that sacrifices ought to be offered to the praise of the Divine name in the four parts of the world, as the ancient wise men of the Hebrews handed down in the *Talmudic Tractate Menachot, ch. 5, fol. 61, 62, and Tractate Sukkah 3, fol. 37*. The other is called <term>Terumah</term> <note>Hebrew: תרומה</note> from the root <term>Rum</term>, *he lifted up or exalted*; the former Blessed Luther translates as *Webeopffer* <note>Wave offering</note>—for *Weben* is to agitate or wave—but this latter he calls *Hebeopffer* <note>Heave offering</note>; he explains the difference at Exodus 35:22, about which Buxtorf’s Lexicon says on page 724: An offering which was given spontaneously to God, the Priests, and the Levites, for which there was neither measure nor estimation in the Law. Later, the wealthier gave one out of forty, the middle class one out of fifty, and the poorer one out of sixty, according to Rabbi Solomon on *Deuteronomy 18:4*. Commonly, two out of a hundred. Whence <term>Terumah</term> is said to be as if it were <term>Trei mi-meah</term> <note>A play on words: "Two from a hundred"</note>. If someone had gathered a barn full of sheaves of grain, he set aside a portion for the Priest out of fairness and goodwill, and afterward the whole barn was free for its master. Regarding these there were many Traditions of the Hebrews; see the Talmudic book *Terumot*, ch. 4. By a common name, however, they come from the root <term>Zevach</term>, which means to slaughter. By a similar reasoning, it is called *thysia* by the Greeks from the verb *thyein*, which means the same. The Hebrews also sometimes use the verb <term>Asah</term>, *he made/performed*. Similarly the Greeks, expressing the function of sacrificing, as Homer says:
<margin>Iliad book 2, line 400</margin>
> One sacrificed to one of the gods, another to another.
And again in Iliad book 1, line 315:
> They sacrificed perfect hecatombs to the immortals.
Which Hesychius maintains are "the completed sacrifices made upon the fulfillment of vows" or "those full in number."
Whom Virgil imitates in the Eclogues...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Jewish sacrificial laws, specifically focusing on the etymology of "immolation" and the physical requirements for sacrificial animals.</meta>

# From Leviticus VII, verse 37.

<margin>The apparatus of sacrifices.</margin>
"When I make a sacrifice of a heifer for the crops, you yourself shall come."
In Latin, nothing is more common than the word <gloss>to be immolated</gloss>. **Immolation** is named from the *mola* <note>salted flour</note> by way of synecdoche <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note>; for with "salted meal," as it was called, the victims were sprinkled at the beginning of the sacrifice. Now, the *mola salsa* was toasted grain sprinkled with salt, and because the victims were sprinkled with that <gloss>ground meal</gloss>, it was properly called "to be immolated" regarding the sprinkled victim. But afterwards, the meaning of the name was extended more broadly to the actual slaughtering which used to follow the immolation. Prudentius mentions this *:
<margin>Book 2 against Symmachus.</margin>
->*No bird, no happy victory through salted meal*<-
->*comes by entreaty.*<-
And Porphyry in Book 2 *On Abstinence* §. 6; Pliny, *Natural History* Book 12, chapter 18; Clauder *On Salt* chapter 3; Saubert the Younger *On Sacrifices* chapters 18 & 24. The Greeks call them *oulai* and *olai*, but also *oulochytai* and *olochytai*, from *ole* (barley) and *cheo* (to pour). Whence Eustathius says *oulai* are barley grains <gloss>mixed with salt, which they poured upon the animals being sacrificed before they were killed</gloss>. But so much for the types of sacrifices.

As for the **material of the sacrifices**, it was sometimes taken from inanimate things pertaining to human life, namely from crops, wine, and oil. In a burnt offering, however, it was a clean animal; whether a bird, such as a dove or turtledove; or a larger land animal, such as a cow, steer, or calf; or a smaller one from the goat kind, a buck or a kid; or from the flock of sheep, a ram or a lamb. Whence Johannes of Frankfurt, formerly a Professor of Theology at Heidelberg, in a certain Academic sermon held * on the Vigil of Epiphany (and still unpublished), while discussing among other things the sacrifices of the Jews, says: *“In the Old Law there were three kinds of legal offerings, namely Firstfruits, Hosts, and Victims, as is gathered from Leviticus and Exodus. Firstfruits are those first perceived from the crops and offered to God. A 'Victim' is the name for a sacrifice or offering for enemies already conquered, just as a 'Host' is named for enemies yet to be conquered; whence the verse:*
<margin>Year of our Lord 1423.</margin>
->*A Victim for the conquered is given, a Host for those to be overcome.*<-
It is manifest from the course of the Old Law that offerings were made of many things in particular, such as the sheep, ox, calf, cow, dove, turtledove, lamb, goat, fine flour, salt, oil, and frankincense. All of these designated a **mystical offering**: the sheep represents simplicity of heart; the Ox, the vigor of work or strength in the works of God; the Calf, spiritual joy; the Cow, the fertility of virtues; the Dove, the love of God; the Turtledove, bounty in the love of God; the Lamb, chastity; the Goat, the harshness of penance against the filth of sin; Fine flour, the purity of contemplation; Salt, discretion; Frankincense, the prayer of devotion, and in this manner for the others.

Furthermore, it was required in every offering that it be *tamim* <note>Hebrew: תמים</note>, perfect, whole, and without any blemish (Exodus 29:1, Leviticus 9:2). The Septuagint <note>Greek Old Testament</note> uses *amomos* <gloss>blameless/unblemished</gloss>. For the worshippers of God were commanded <gloss>to take, to bring forward, and to offer unblemished things</gloss>, immaculate and beyond all reproach, and to examine the victims beforehand lest there be any fault or spot in the whole body before they sacrificed. This kind of <term>anagnoseosmo</term> <note>critical examination</note> is elegantly called <term>momoskopein</term> <note>to inspect for blemishes</note>; for thus they are commanded in the law to seek out and sacrifice a lamb which is <gloss>unblemished</gloss>—to use a word frequent in Homer—in which <gloss>there are no spots or blemishes</gloss> (2 Peter 2:13). Chrysostom * uses that compound word, which common dictionaries do not have, regarding the faults of animals,
<margin>Homily 20 on Romans, p. 173.</margin>

<column-break/>

taking the metaphor from victims being recognized by their whole body. He also uses the same in Homily 17 on Hebrews. Therefore, *Amomon* is that which is without a spot, which is called *momos*, whence
<margin>The apparatus of sacrifices.</margin>
it cannot be doubted that the word *momos* <note>blame/mockery</note> has its origin. Hence also *amomon* is used for a pure spice. Thus *amomon libanon*, "sincere frankincense," and *amomon* simply in Dioscorides, Theophrastus, and Pliny. From this comes *kinnamomon* <note>cinnamon</note> as if it were *kinnamon amomon* <note>unblemished cinnamon</note>; for those who derive it otherwise will hardly escape the critic's mockery.

So also the Gentiles, in <gloss>imitation</gloss> of the true worship, accurately observed the animals they chose for victims. That it was not a common or cheap matter will be shown by many examples. Aristophanes * introduces a Megarian bringing for sale <gloss>pigs</gloss>
<margin>Act 3, scene 3, v. 15.</margin>
<gloss>mystical</gloss>, that is, pigs fit for sacrificing, which he calls "mystical" <gloss>because they are sacrificed in the mysteries of Demeter</gloss>, as the Scholiast says. The seller commends them for their fatness and beauty, saying *:
<margin>v. 17.</margin>
->*Hold them up again, see how fat and beautiful they are.*<-
But Dicaeopolis, when he saw they were without tails, says they cannot be sacrificed (v. 36). Whence in some sacred places and chapels there was a sign: *Let nothing made of hide be used*, so that nothing from a dead carcass be present, according to Varro. Ovid * explains it thus:
<margin>Fasti, Book 1, near the end.</margin>
->*It is not lawful to bring leather into that chapel*<-
->*Lest dead things violate the pure hearths.*<-
*Scortea*, that is, <gloss>leathern, made of skins</gloss>, which are made from hide and pelts. Therefore, all things in the sacrifices were required to be pure and immaculate; and daily so many most select cattle, which had been raised with great expense and trouble, were burned.

Truly, the number of victims at the universal gatherings must have been astounding when they came to Jerusalem from every land of Judea. A certain number cannot be defined, as it was greater or smaller according to the number of those who flocked to the celebration of the feasts. At one time Solomon sacrificed *twenty-two thousand oxen and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep for peace offerings* (1 Kings 8:63).
<margin>1 Kings 8:63.</margin>
Hezekiah, restoring the worship of God neglected by his ancestors, offers *seventy oxen, a hundred rams, and two hundred lambs* as burnt offerings (2 Chronicles 29:32).
<margin>2 Chronicles 29:32.</margin>
In the observation of the Passover, King Josiah showed singular munificence in this matter, and offered for victims *two thousand six hundred cattle, as well as three hundred oxen* (2 Chronicles 35:8). Noble and very memorable

was that celebration of the Passover which Josephus * records took place under Cestius Florus, where

two hundred fifty-six thousand five hundred hosts were counted. An almost incredible abundance, leaving the number of victims offered by Josiah many miles behind. Nor did the Gentiles show less liberality in their <gloss>worship of gods</gloss>; for Xenophon * records that Jason, the leader of the Thessalians, instituted a sacrifice of eleven thousand beasts: <gloss>nearly a thousand oxen, and over ten thousand sheep, goats, and swine</gloss>.
<margin>Greek History, Book 6, p. 408.</margin>
For the constitution of a sacrifice, however, not only was the "matter" required, but also the "form," that is, a certain action of offering commanded by God. To which we wish to refer first the persons destined and consecrated for this sacred duty. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<page-num>212</page-num>

<columns>2</columns>

Left Column:

<margin>The apparatus of sacrifices.</margin>
...but because out of pride and <term>meddlesomeness<note>original Greek: πολυπραγμοσύνη (polypragmosyne)</note></term> he dared to sacrifice, and to enter those inner sanctuaries which none but the Priests were permitted to enter. Furthermore, it was not permitted to offer sacrificial victims to God except in one place. For it was established as a holy and severe decree of God, that *the offering to the Lord should be made only at the door of the tabernacle*, Leviticus 17:8-9. And <term>BEWARE<note>Latin: CAVE</note></term> of the intention that *burnt offerings be offered in every place, but only in the place which God shall choose*.

<margin>Deuteronomy 12:13-14.</margin>
Plato, the wisest of the gentiles, also indicated that it is not permitted to perform sacrifices in private houses, but rather by establishing a common assembly in temples, writing thus in the 10th book of *Laws*: <note>original Greek: Εξωνόμω τοις σύμπασι κείμενος απλώς... translated below</note> "Let the law be simply laid down for all: let no one possess shrines in private houses; but when one is minded to sacrifice, let him go to the public buildings to sacrifice, and let him deliver the victims into the hands of the priests, whose care is the purity of these things. And let him pray along with them, and whoever else wishes to pray with him." In a few words he pours forth much of good precepts, designating the place, the worship, the worshiper, and the sacrifice. The place simply and without any limited formula of speaking. The sacrifice itself as proper and peculiar to the Priest. But the prayers are Common, for the Priest and the people. See further Saubert in his *Book on Sacrifices, chapter 14, page 315.*

<margin>Exodus 20:24. Exodus 30:1.</margin>
Refer here to the fact that Jehovah commanded Moses to build three altars: one of *earth*, one of *stone* (verse 25), and one of *wood*, as well as the instruments necessary for holy worship. The instrument of the Altar is called <term>Mizbeach<note>Hebrew: מזבח</note></term>, which Onkelos translated as *Madbecha* and Rabbi Solomon praises. Moreover, the instruments of the <term>Golden Altar<note>Hebrew: מזבח הזהב</note></term> and the <term>Golden Table<note>Hebrew: שולחן הזהב</note></term> are brought; the ash is carried away; and there is a <term>covering for the holy vessel of thin cast brass, having a handle<note>Hebrew: מזבח כסוי הקדרה של מתכת רק ולו בית יד</note></term>. They used that instrument, which Junius calls a *shovel*, during the sacrificing, while they moved the burning pile and collected and carried away the ashes with it. Jerome translates it as *forceps*. Pagninus as *brooms*. They had, besides, pots, brooms, bowls, three-pronged forks, lampstands, lamps, tables, dishes, spoons, covers, shells, basins, the "sea" <note>a large bronze basin</note>, incense burners, washbasins, knives, and small hooks, which they used for carrying water for the Sacrifices; mention is also made of <term>large basins<note>Greek: ὁλκίων (holkion)</note></term>.

<margin>Judith 15:13</margin>
The *Holkia* were indeed large basins made and fashioned in the likeness of great bowls, as Hesychius describes. There was also a use for *Holkia* in the baths. In Plutarch’s *Life of Alexander*, *holkeia*, jars, tubs, and alabaster flasks are joined together; compare *Casaubon on Athenaeus, book 5, chapter 5, page 343.* Nor did the Gentiles lack sacrificial vessels; they had the *axe* or *Scespita*, with which the victim was to be struck. The *Acerra* (incense box), in which spices were kept to wipe away the stench of the meat to be sacrificed; *Tripods*, upon which sacrifices are celebrated after the fire is lit; the *Lustral Vessel*, from which water was sprinkled on the sacrifices and on the bystanders for the expiation of crimes; the *Praefericulum*, a bronze vessel which Festus notes was used in the Sacrifice of *Ops Consiva*; the *Simpulum* or *simpuvium*, with which wine was offered in libations during Sacrifices, and six hundred other things which you may review at length in Saubert.

<margin>Book on Sacrifices, 8, 11, & 17.</margin>
Having viewed the instruments of libation—that is, the Sacrificial vessels, <term>spondeia<note>Greek: σπονδεῖα</note></term> being vessels, according to Suidas, <term>in which they pour libations<note>Greek: ἐν οἷς σπένδουσι</note></term>—the custom must be briefly tasted. For when the Priests were about to make a sacrifice of a male bullock, destined for a burnt offering, on the altar in the area of the inner court, it was performed in this manner: namely, that first, having slaughtered it, they would skin it, and sprinkle its blood around upon the altar, and piece by piece

<column-break/>

Right Column:

<margin>The apparatus of sacrifices.</margin>
they would cut it up on the tables standing in the same court; then they would place it upon the altar, and stir up the pile of wood in the fire, and pile the head and the fat from the pieces upon the wood placed on the fire. After this, they would wash the intestines and the feet in the ten bronze basins; and then finally they would burn all the pieces together on the altar. By the odor of this burned victim, provided they were done from an honest soul, the Lord is said to be soothed. We pass over more concerning other types of sacrifices for the present study. In almost the same way, the Heathens instituted their Sacrifices to appease their own Gods; the entrails of the victim—that is, the <term>cut-out and chopped parts<note>Greek: κὴ συγκοπτὰ</note></term>, sometimes cooked, sometimes raw—they cut into various pieces, and the first parts, which they offered to the Gods, they called *proficiae*, also *prosecta* and *prosectum*, as Vossius teaches in his *Etymology, page 414*, alleging the glosses of Philoxenus. Compare Arnobius, *book 7, page 290*; Martianus Capella, *book 1, page 5*; Macrobius, *7.12*; which an old Glossary interprets as <term>first-fruits for the sacrifice<note>Greek: ἀπαρχάς τῷ θυματ</note></term>. Add Nonius on the word *Prosecta*, and Turnebus, *Adversaria 15.7*. Thus it was sacrificed with care, and in the <term>practice<note>Greek: πραγματεία</note></term> of various nations there were various things. By an almost common custom, the Priests, having washed the victims—previously selected from an unblemished kind of animal—purified them with pure water, sprinkled them, and, having called out the vows, commanded the standing ministers, the *poppae* and *victimarii* <note>subordinate sacrificial officials</note>, to slay them. One held the standing victim, another struck it successfully, others drove in the sacred knives; the hide being pulled off, they soon cut it into members, and having tasted certain pieces, they offered those first-fruits to the sacrificers; and with wine poured over them, and frankincense and other perfumes given with a generous hand, the burning took place. When the Sacrifices on the altar were finished, parts or portions were distributed from the remains, which the Hebrews call <term>Manot<note>Hebrew: מנאות</note></term>, either to the Overseers of the Sacred Rites, or to the Household, or to all those who had offered.

<margin>1 Samuel 1:9.</margin>
As the examples testify. This custom of the Jews, the Devil, the "ape of God," emulated among the Pagans; for they themselves also prepared banquets from those sacred remains, which Herodotus said in *Euterpe, page 65*, where he deals with the Sacrifices of the Egyptians: <term>to set out a feast from the sacred things<note>Greek: δαῖτα προτιθέναι ἐκ τῶν ἱερῶν</note></term>.

<margin>Iliad, book 1, line 467.</margin>
Hence Homer accurately remembers the Feasts performed by the Achaeans after the sacrifices were finished, while he adds these verses:

# On Leviticus VII. v. 37.

<margin>The apparatus of sacrifices.</margin>
> *The Dorian youth, celebrating such feasts then,*
> *Sang a wide paean to God through the whole light of day,*
> *Appeasing the holy powers of health-bringing Phoebus.*
<note>The author quotes Latin verse referencing Greek (Dorian) customs to draw a parallel with religious feasting.</note>

The pious man Elkanah, husband of two wives, giving a sacrificial dinner (1 Samuel 1:5), gave a more lavish gift from these sacred remains to Hannah than to Peninnah; he gave to her in preference to the other a <term>מנה אחת אפים</term> <note>Hebrew: manah achat appayim</note>, <gloss>one portion of faces</gloss>, <gloss>a piece of two countenances</gloss>. Since I see interpreters going in different directions—among whom are the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament</note>—I truly do not know what face or what eyes, whether joyful or sad, I ought to attribute to Elkanah. The face is especially accustomed, as the <term>physiognomists</term> <note>Those who judge character from facial features</note> teach, and in this very face the eyes, to betray with what mind someone does this or that. If we rightly behold the face of Elkanah, he does not seem to have given a <term>splendid gift</term> <note>original Greek: ἀγλαὰ δῶρον</note> with a sad face to Hannah, for whom he was dying of love, even while she was suffering the envy of a rival wife. Indeed, for many years (<term>year by year</term> <note>original Greek: ἐνιαυτὸν, κατ᾽ ἐνιαυτόν</note> v. 7), the days and nights of Hannah were consumed in misery, weeping bitterly (v. 10) because of her sterility, which was a reproach in Israel, and for which she was mocked and afflicted by Peninnah (v. 6). Elkanah would certainly have increased this grief and bitterness of soul (v. 10) if he had given the portion with a sad face. Rather, he did so with a <term>rejoicing heart</term> <note>original Greek: χαιρομένη φρένα</note>, because he had appeased God with the sacrifice and the "calves of the lips" <note>a metaphor for prayer/praise</note>; and so that she might experience his benevolent and constant mind, he silently bids his Hannah to be of good cheer, and to speak with Homer and his—

<margin>Odyssey, book 13, line 43.</margin>
-> These things he gave, favoring her in friendship <-

Hence, having considered the words of the Greek Interpreter: <term>a single portion according to the face</term> <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὴν ἔναντι μερίδα μίαν κ’ πρόσωπον</note>. *And he gave to Hannah one portion according to the face*. It seems that the phrase "according to the face" should be referred not to the "portion" but to the person, so that the Interpreter wished to hint at the respect of persons held by Elkanah toward Hannah and Peninnah, since he favored the former more than the latter. Just as from this they say <term>to accept the face</term> <note>original Greek: λαμβάνειν πρόσωπον</note>, <gloss>to accept the person</gloss> <note>to show partiality</note>, when we consider something in someone that strikes us in the face, as it were, by which we deserve favor toward them. If you refer it to the "portion," the expression will not be unsuited to those things which could be compared with our vernacular, so that a "face-portion" is what is for us a <gloss>respectable piece / which was beautiful to look upon</gloss>, as Piscator and others translate; and this on the occasion of the feast performed after the sacrifice. But let us make an end of the things to be said. To what purpose now are so many sacrifices, so many slaughters of victims, such a mass of ceremonies? We answer you in a few words. They announced the future victim of the Messiah. They showed that our salvation must be expected from a slain victim. God had first given the hope of salvation to all men in those words: *I will put enmity between you (he addresses the serpent) and the woman, and your seed and her seed. He shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for his heel.* This revelation handed down a certain confidence of Salvation to be restored through the <term>Sacrifice of the Messiah</term>. It is the undisputed foundation, and the very first of the promises to all the descendants of Adam, who had perished together in Adam. The whole human race lay in a mass of perdition, whom He consoled by promising the blessed Seed, by whom the serpent and infernal Dragon must be overcome and crushed. The <term>death of a single victim</term> was to be expected, and through it true

<column-break/>

life was to be hoped for. All the offerings and all the victims denoted the image and shadow <margin>The apparatus of sacrifices.</margin> of this truly life-giving victim, and they were only useful to those offering them insofar as they were referred to that <term>unique sacrifice of the Messiah</term>.

Therefore, once the name of Christ was proclaimed, the name and authority of the <term>priests, high priests, and sacrifices</term> <note>original Greek: ἱερέων ἀρχιερέων & θυσιῶν</note> of the Old Testament ceased. Those who ruled the Churches afterward were called <term>Apostles</term>, <term>Bishops</term>, and <term>Presbyters</term>. Once assemblies of the faithful were established in individual cities, all memory of Judaic sacrifices was abolished and exterminated. No place was given any longer to sacrifices, nor to altars, nor to sacrificial vessels. Other names were given to the Ministers of the Gospel, the old ones being removed, lest the old priesthood, which was passing away into abolition, should seem to be renewed or patched up. The Jewish Law and ceremony were made ancient by a new law. The Priests, Pontiffs, and Levites were now called <term>Laity</term>, nor were any admitted as ministers of the altar unless from the lineage of Aaron <note>referring to the old system's exclusivity</note>. The curiosity of genealogies was exploded, nor did the priesthood remain attached to a certain family. The veil of the temple was removed; the middle wall of partition was removed by the leading-to <margin>John 10:16.</margin> and introduction of other sheep, namely the gentiles, into one fold*; which leading-in of the gentiles is universal, by which the gentiles were brought to the boundaries of the Church and so admitted that the middle wall of partition between Jews and gentiles was utterly removed <margin>Ephesians 2:14.</margin>*. From the ascension of Christ, that leading-in was done by the ministry of the Apostles, and that leading-in carries with it the abolition of the entire Mosaic antiquity, so that those Mosaic ecclesiastical ceremonies and political sanctions no longer bind Christians, a fact which the Apostles made witnessed to the Churches by a synodal decree*; for those constitutions were not <margin>Acts 15:24, 28.</margin> promulgated for the absolute perpetuity of the Church Militant, but only until the coming of the Messiah, and indeed to distinguish from all nations that people from whom the Messiah was to arise, whence even in the Old Testament the observation of them was not simply necessary for proselytes. Wherefore, since around the beginning of the New Testament those things ought to have vanished honorably as having reached their end, the Apostolic Church observed and omitted them indifferently, but fought strenuously against the necessity of them*, while the <margin>Galatians 5:2; Colossians 2:21.</margin> Jews vainly and obstinately resisted and wore themselves out in the observations of the Mosaic laws, whose heart is covered by a veil, concerning whom Paulinus speaks thus in *The 8th Birthday of St. Felix*, verse 25:

> *The Jews, retaining the nation in name alone,*
> *Through ancestral rites, but now through empty Sabbaths,*
> *Cherish the traces of an ancient, past fear;*
> *For in vain they practice the old law under a hollow image;*
> *But for us, because the Passover has fulfilled it,*
> *Christ is given as the one victim for all to the Father,*
> *And because the body of life is present, the shadow of the figure perishes.*

In vain, therefore, even today, in vain are all the sacrificial ceremonies, all the solemn rites in the Levitical sacred things, which were done and celebrated in their own time. He has already come long ago, at whose arrival that use of Sacrifices in the New Testament ought to have expired entirely: namely the Messiah, in whom all use of ceremonies was ended, Christ Jesus, the Alpha and the Omega, the head and the <term>colophon</term> <note>The finishing touch or crowning peak</note> of all those sacrifices and ceremonies.

It argues that Mosaic ceremonies were temporary measures intended only to point toward the Messiah and were rightfully abolished by the Apostles.</summary>

### Leviticus XVIII. v. 21.

-> And thou shalt not let any of thy seed pass through the fire to Moloch <-
<note>original Hebrew: ומזרעך לא-תתן להעביר למלך</note>
-> And of your offspring you shall not give to serve the ruler. <-
<note>original Greek: Καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ σπέρματός σου οὐ δώσεις λατρεύειν ἄρχοντι.</note>
-> Of your seed, you shall not give, that it may be consecrated to Moloch. <-
<note>original Latin: De Semine tuo, non dabis, ut consecretur Moloch.</note>

<margin>The unspeakable rites of Moloch.</margin>
That tragic and unspeakable <term>Anthropothysia</term> <note>human sacrifice</note> is forbidden to the Jews, lest they allow any of their offspring to be "brought over" to Moloch <note>Hebrew: לעביר המלך</note>, which they interpret as, *To be brought through the fire, or, to be brought over to the worship of Moloch*. The English Translator joined both in his version. Others say, "to be burned to Moloch." Moloch was worshipped by the immolation of humans, and also by lustration <note>purification ritual</note>, when they were led through the fire.

<margin>Deut. 18:10.</margin>
The Mosaic interdict aims at this: *There shall not be found among you anyone who purifies his son or daughter by leading them through the fire*. Where the Hebrew <note>מעביר בנו ובתו באש</note> is retained for Moloch. The author of the Book of Wisdom (ch. 12:5) calls them "merciless murderers of children" <note>Greek: τέκνων φονέας ἀνελεήμονας</note>, which the Vulgate rendered as: *Slayers of sons without mercy*.

<margin>2 Sam. 12:31</margin>
To this they refer <insert>the passage</insert>, and reading "their Moloch" <note>מלכם</note> instead of "our king" <note>מלכנו</note>, they explain it as referring to Moloch. As Pagninus cites from the Commentary of Rabbi David and Schickard approves in his *Dissertation on Hebrew Coins*; from whom Robertus dissents in his *Notes on Thiofridus of Echternach*, book 2, ch. 2.

Indeed, as is clear from what has been said, there were two types of this so immense and unspeakable human sacrifice. One, by which parents led their offspring through the flame of fire, and in this way purified them for the Deity, such as is forbidden in the passage of Deuteronomy cited above; called by some <term>Pyromanteia</term> <note>divination by fire</note>, which Benjamin of Tudela in his *Itinerary page 214* teaches was customary among the Persians, namely that there was *before the altar of the sacred houses a huge pit, in which for continuous centuries a very great fire burned, and there for the sake of expiation they purified their sons, yet without harm*, see the *Tarich* of W. Schickard, page 126 and following.

<margin>2 Sam. 12:31</margin>
To this some refer that deed of David which is read, who made the Ammonites pass through <note>Hebrew: במלכן</note>, which some explain as *Malcan* or the place where the Ammonites burned their sons to their idol Moloch or Milcom. Some read <note>במלבן</note>, as *through the brick-kiln, where bricks are baked*. So the Septuagint: *he led them through the brick-works*; the Vulgate Version: *He passed them through the brick-mold*. The Chaldean Paraphrase: *He dragged them through the streets*. Otherwise, by which they slaughtered and burned sons and daughters. However, there existed a divine Law against sacrificing humans, concerning which in Deuteronomy it says in these words: *Thou shalt not do so unto the Lord thy God; for every abomination which God hates have they done unto their gods; for even their sons and their daughters they have burnt in the fire*. Great was this savagery of the nations, a great abomination. For what speech can be equal to the most cruel slaughter of human victims? At these foul and shameful actions even a Scythian <note>traditionally viewed as the most barbaric of people</note> would be struck dumb, which are so abominable that they are shameful even to speak of. Who among men would not be stunned, to make from a human being an inhuman and senseless victim for the Gods! Who would not shudder at that cruel sacrifice <note>Greek: θυσίαν</note>, by which a man born for humanity rages against a man by the instinct

<column-break/>

and command of the Devil, who through oracles sought victims of this kind, cf. Strigelius in *Melanchthon's Dialectics, page 281.* A deed worthy of Moloch, and horrific to read, was that an infant was slaughtered having been dragged from the maternal womb, as Lucian testifies in book 6.

<margin>The unspeakable rites of Moloch.</margin>
> If by a wound of the belly, not where Nature called,
> The offspring is extracted, to be placed on hot altars.

Among all the abominations, therefore, which GOD loathed, none was more foul than <term>Teknothysia</term> <note>child sacrifice</note>. Therefore GOD also cursed this above other idolatrous cults, especially this one, as being singular and supremely abominable; hence specifically both in Leviticus and in Deuteronomy ch. 12:31, He condemns the child sacrifice which the Moabites performed for Moloch. What sort of minor deity Moloch was, Selden explains in detail in *Syntagma 1 on the Syrian Gods, chapter 6, pages 167, 193*, where from the dark mists of antiquity he inquires into his form and worship using the testimonies of the Rabbis. Yet nothing certain is established concerning the form of Moloch; for what Nicolaus of Lyra relates on *Jeremiah ch. 7 and Ezekiel ch. 16* and P. Fagius on *Leviticus* from the monuments of the Hebrews regarding a statue containing seven chambers is not approved by soundly learned men. The place of slaughter in Holy Scripture is called <term>Gehenna</term> <note>Hebrew: גיהנום</note> from <term>Gehinnam</term> or the roaring and laments of the boys while they were being burned, named thus, from which is derived <term>Gehenna</term> to signify the punishments of the age to come. In that place were the high places of Moloch and Baal built (*Jeremiah 19:5*); where the Jews gathered, burning their children with fire.

<margin>where 2 Kings 23:10</margin>

From the noise of the drums, the place seems to be named *Topheth*, from <term>Tuppim</term> <note>drums</note>, *Jeremiah 7:31.* Whence Euthymius says: *Topheth was a most pleasant place, which even today offers the delights of gardens, where they used to sacrifice to Demons upon an altar, and consecrate their children upon an unspeakable pyre or offer a burnt offering*.

<margin>in the book of Kings p. 282.</margin>
From the monuments of the ancients, Aben-Batrich traces the origin of this most savage rite back to the times of Serug; it was most in use among the Syrians, from there it passed to the Phoenicians (the colonists of the Syrians), and from these it migrated to the Carthaginians (the colonists of the Phoenicians) and other peoples of Africa, who transferred this most cruel institution to themselves, having fashioned a bronze statue of Saturn, where no differently than to Moloch the neighboring nations cruelly offered their infants, as Varro testifies in *16. Divine Matters* in Augustine's *City of God, book 7, p. 400.* For many nations persuaded themselves that they were delivered from public calamities by the offering of human blood, whence from every age and in almost the whole world, it is a dire kind of abomination among almost all nations. # From Leviticus XVIII. v. 21.

<margin>The unspeakable rites of Moloch.</margin> Philo of Byblos can prove this in the works of Eusebius, who handed down the following from Sanchuniathon in Greek on page 26: *It was a custom among the ancients in great dangers of calamities, in place of the destruction of all, for those ruling either a city or a nation to give up the most beloved of their children for slaughter as a ransom to the avenging spirits.* <note>original: "τιμωροῖς δαίμοσι" — literally "punishing demons" or spirits.</note> And Eusebius in his Oration in praise of Constantine Caesar says: *The Phoenicians used to sacrifice the beloved and only-begotten of their children to Cronus every year.* And Curtius in Book 4, speaking likewise of the Tyrians, records that human victims were offered to Saturn. For the worshippers of the Saturnalia, deceived by the ambiguity of a name—*phōs* <note>original: "φως"</note>, which signifies both "man" and "light" depending on a different accent—sacrificed some man annually to Saturn, when that sacrifice could just as well have been made by lighting lamps according to the Oracle, so that the Diabolical Saturn might be appeased. Therefore, he who was called Moloch by the Phoenicians, the Greeks and Romans call Cronus or *Saturn*, to whom they sacrificed in a similar way; from this it can be shown that the Oriental Deity is declared through Saturn. For just as men were sacrificed to the former by the Carthaginians, so to the latter, the Rhodians used to sacrifice some man to Saturn on the 16th of the Calends of November; which, having been observed for a long time, *was changed into a god*, as Porphyry in the cited place and Theodoret in *7. On Greek Affections* have handed down. Regarding the Carthaginians, more than <margin>cited book, chapter 38.</margin> one writer testifies; Dionysius of Halicarnassus says: *they say they also perform the ancient sacrifices to Cronus just as in Carthage, as long as the city remained, and it happens among the Celts to this day, and in some other of the Western nations, involving the slaying of men.* This fact concerning the Gauls and other Western nations (of whom more below), whom he records as *human-sacrificers* <note>original: "ἀνθρωποθύταις"</note> even in his own age (which falls in the reign of Augustus), is confirmed by the witnesses Caesar in *Gallic Wars 6.16* and Pliny in *30.1*. Plutarch reported the same in his *book on superstition, chapter 21.* But to return to the Carthaginians, Pescennius Festus says of them in his books of Histories <margin>Book 1, chapter 21.</margin> through Satire, as quoted in Lactantius: *The Carthaginians were accustomed to sacrifice human victims to Saturn; and when they were defeated by Agathocles, King of the Sicilians, they thought the GOD was angry with them; therefore, so that they might pay the penance more diligently, they sacrificed two hundred sons of the nobles.* Oh, the most cruel inhumanity of men, that these *human-sacrificers* should so utterly strip away their humanity! Of the Athenians we read that, for the sake of purifying their city, they again sacrificed two men; for in the Thargelia <note>An ancient Greek festival held in honor of Apollo and Artemis.</note> a purification of the city was celebrated annually, where two men were sacrificed—one for the men and one for the women—to cleanse them, as Helladius says in *Chrestomathy Book 3* in Photius *code 279, page 872*: *It was the custom in Athens to lead out two "scapegoats" <note>original: "φαρμακοὺς" (pharmakous) — ritual victims used as purifiers.</note>, one on behalf of the men and one on behalf of the women, led for purification.* Harpocration says under the word *pharmakō*: *They led out two men at Athens to be purifiers of the city in the Thargelia, one for the men and one for the women.* Tzetzes also mentions this in *Chiliades 5, chapter 23* and *Chiliades 8, chapter 239*, as does Michael Apostolius and Suidas under the word *peripsēma*. So, according to ancestral custom, Erechtheus, when he was sought in war by Eumolpus the Thracian, according to the response from the Seers that he would be superior if he sacrificed his daughter, with a cruel hand made her a victim for the safety of the Attic state; hence the mother Praxithea in Euripides speaks thus, as cited by Ly-

We do not possess that play, the name of which was *Erechtheus*, from which Lycurgus cites those verses. So it was with Codrus, so with Macaria, daughter of Hercules, so with Agamemnon’s daughter, Iphigenia; when the Painter could not represent the face of her father standing at the altar where Iphigenia was to be sacrificed, he veiled his head, so that the spectators themselves might judge the domestic grief of the paternal mind. So Polyxena, daughter of Priam, was slaughtered to appease the ghost of Achilles, who had demanded this victim. This was done in the Thracian Chersonese, which was situated opposite Troy, and Euripides set out the whole tragic matter and placed it before our eyes with wonderful skill in the complete play to which he gave the name *Hecuba*. Talthybius, returning from the army, tells the mother Hecuba by what rite and manner Polyxena was slaughtered by Pyrrhus (v. 521 ff.) and how noble she showed herself (v. 547 etc.), and how concerned she was that she should fall *gracefully and decently* (v. 569). Ovid describes these things gravely and <margin>13. Metamorphoses</margin> decently, in whose work the shade of Achilles demands Polyxena with these words:
> *Polyxena slaughtered pleases the ghost of Achilles.*
> *Then Polyxena,*
> *Snatched from the bosom of her mother, whom she now almost alone cherished,*
> *Brave and unhappy, and a maiden more than a woman,*
> *Is led to the mound, and becomes a victim at the dire tomb.*
> *She, mindful of herself, after she was moved to the cruel altars,*
> *And felt the fierce rites being prepared for her,*
> *When she saw Neoptolemus standing and holding the steel,*
> *And fixing his eyes upon her own face,*
> *Said: "Use now my noble blood,*
> *There is no delay: either hide the weapon in my throat*
> *Or in my breast." And at once she bared her throat and breast.*

So others also perished by the snares of that Bloodthirsty and lying Spirit, who delights in the destruction of men. Thus the grandson of Cadmus, Melicertes or Palaemon, was worshipped with the victims of boys on the Island of Tenedos; Itacius <margin>on Lycophron p. 47.</margin> says: *Melicertes, the son of Ino, was greatly honored in Tenedos, where they even sacrificed infants to him,* who was thereafter called *infant-slayer* <note>original: "βρεφοκτόνος"</note>. To Peleus and Chiron they also sacrificed a man, as Clement of Alexandria testifies in *Admonition to the Gentiles*. The Cyprians made a human victim to Agraulis, as Cyril has from Porphyry’s *On Abstinence from Animal Food* in *4. against Julian*. Regarding the <margin>Book 6 of the Gallic War.</margin> Gauls, Julius Caesar testifies that they were led to the same crime of madness, so that even men afflicted by more serious evils sacrificed humans. Cicero, in a fragment of his *Oration for M. Fonteius*, says: *If ever, led by some fear, they think the Gods must be appeased, they defile their altars and temples with human victims. So much so that they cannot even practice religion unless they first violate it with crime. For who is ignorant that they retain, even to this day, that monstrous and barbarous custom of sacrificing men?* Therefore, what sort of faith or piety can you think belongs to those who believe the immortal Gods can easily be appeased by the crime and blood of men? We see from this that this bloody <margin>Book 30, chapter 1.</margin> religion was displeasing to the more sensible Pagans; hence it is said in a Tragedy by Euripides that one should not "slaughter men" <note>original: ἀνϑρωποκτονεῖν</note> but "offer sacrifices" <note>original: ϑυηπολεῖν</note>. How much is owed to the Romans for removing these monsters, among whom killing men was considered most religious, yet for the world it was most unwholesome. Nevertheless, it is not to be excused that Augustus offered 300 men as victims on the annual day when Julius Caesar had been killed. But I return to the Gauls, of <margin>Book 1, chapter 21.</margin> whom Lactantius says: *The Gauls used to appease Hesus and Teutates with human blood.* Lucanus confirms this, adding a third, *Taranis*, in Book 1:
> And those by whom pitiless Teutates is appeased with dire blood,
> And Hesus, horrifying with his wild altars,
> And the altar of Taranis, no gentler than that of Scythian Diana.
What he calls "wild altars" here, he named "dire altars" in Book 3, verse 404, saying:
> Altars built with dire structures,
> And every tree purified by human blood.
For in their dire rites, the Druids chose groves of oaks, and they performed no sacred rites without that foliage, <margin>Book 16, chapter 434</margin> according to Pliny; in which they "offered burnt offerings of cattle and all kinds of wild beasts and men," <note>original: βοσκήματα καὶ παντοῖα ϑηρία καὶ ἀνϑρώπους ὡλοκαύτες</note> as written by <margin>Book 5, *Geography*, page 172.</margin> Strabo, who reports the same of the Samnites: that they consecrated to their Gods not only the fruits the year produced, but even offered their offspring when sterility threatened. Tacitus mentions of the Britons in the 14th book of his *Annals* that, under the victory of Suetonius Paulinus, *the groves of the Druids were cut down, sacred to cruel superstitions: for they held it lawful to kindle altars with captive blood and to consult the Gods through human entrails. Compare Quercetanus at the Library of Cluny, folio 39.* Regarding the Germans, the same Tacitus says in the 9th book of his *Annals*: *Of the Gods, they chiefly worship Mercury, to whom on certain days they hold it lawful to sacrifice even human victims.* He attributes the same to the Hermunduri, who consecrated the opposing army to Mars and Mercury, by which vow, says Tacitus (13.57.3), horses, men, and all things conquered (living) are given over to slaughter. The Icelandic Annals note that the Icelanders sacrificed men to the Gods, dashing them against a large stone. So too the Danes offered a man, as witnessed by Johannes Thomas in his *Oration on Christ*, page 34. Regarding the Swedes—

—and the rest of the inhabitants of the Scandinavian peninsula, Procopius reports that they sacrificed the first of their captives to Mars, believing this victim to be the most beautiful for the greatest of the Gods. "The most beautiful of their sacrifices is a man, whomever they have first taken captive. This one they sacrifice to Mars, since they consider him the greatest god." <note>original Greek: Τῶν ἱερείων σφίσι τὸ κάλλιστον ἄνϑρωπός ἐστιν...</note> Likewise, Jordanes records that the Goths always appeased Mars with the harshest worship, namely, by the deaths of captives. <margin>Gothic History, page 2.</margin> Eric of Uppsala, having reviewed the three most celebrated Swedish Gods, *Thor, Oden, and Frigga*, describes their worship, consisting of offerings and sacrifices, in these words: *To each of these three Gods were assigned Priests in their own order, to present the offerings and sacrifices of the people, and to serve continually in the ritual and sacrifices. Besides these, a certain general solemnity had been instituted to be celebrated with the highest ceremony every nine years, to which the entire multitude of all Provinces of the Gothic nation was bound to come and offer gifts; at which time living sacrifices of both men and beasts were offered, with whose blood they appeased the Gods. Their bodies they would hang in a nearby grove, believing the trees themselves to be divine and sacred from the death of those sacrificed, and for that reason they paid them the greatest respect.* Regarding this monstrous rite, one should also read Johannes Loccenius, *Swedish-Gothic Antiquities*, chapter 2, folios 32–33. We do not reproach the Scythians for that inhumanity toward men, as they certainly deserve the name of men in word but not in deed. Of them, Mela says (Book 2, chapter 1): *Mars is the God of all. To him, instead of images, they dedicate swords and banners, and they strike down men as victims.* The same people, according to Origen, <margin>Against Celsus, Book 5, page 252.</margin> slaughtered guests as victims for Diana; as they did all Greeks who came into their power, as noted by Appian (*Mithridatic Wars*, page 241). And Augustine mentions the same in *City of God* (18.12) and Boethius in *Consolation of Philosophy* (Book 2, prose 6, page 36) regarding Busiris, King of the Egyptians, who slaughtered guests for his Gods. Apollodorus reports of the same man <margin>Library, Book 2, page 105.</margin> that when the region had suffered from sterility for nine years, he sacrificed men after being warned by an oracle. The words of Apollodorus are these: "For Busiris used to sacrifice strangers on the altar of Zeus according to an oracle. For nine years of barrenness had gripped Egypt. But Thrasius, a seer who had come from Cyprus, said the barrenness would cease if they slaughtered a foreign man to Zeus every year. Busiris, having first slaughtered that very seer, then slaughtered the strangers who arrived." And so it happened to this advisor of cruelty according to the Greek verse: "Evil counsel is most harmful to the counselor." From this, it passed into a proverb: <margin>Note: The altar of Busiris.</margin> *The altar of Busiris*, of which even Virgil says: <margin>Georgics, Book 3.</margin>
> Or who knows not the altars of the unpraised Busiris?
And Claudian in *Against Eutropius*, Book 1:
> He who advised appeasing the Thunderer by killing a guest,
> First stained the altars of Busiris he had devised,
> And fell as the victim of the cruel rite he had spoken of.
Regarding the Ethiopians, neighbors of the Egyptians, Heliodorus relates that after defeating an enemy, they performed sacred rites with a human victim "according to ancestral law." <note>original: νόμῳ πατρῴῳ</note> Regarding the Africans, that most learned African Tertullian <margin>In the *Apology*, chapter 4.</margin> reports: *Infants were publicly sacrificed to Saturn in Africa until the proconsulship of Tiberius.* That Tiberius was undoubtedly not the Emperor, son of Augustus, but an African Proconsul. Hernán Cortés writes about this same city and the monstrosity of its inhabitants in his *Second Narrative* of the things seen by him; so that we may omit by design what the same Cortés, Marco Polo the Venetian (Book 2, Chapter 67, p. 395 and Book 3, Chapter 7, p. 399), and Amerigo Vespucci (Voyage 1, p. 161) narrate concerning the <note>original: *ἀνθρωποφάγοις* (anthropophagis) - man-eaters/cannibals</note>: But what is rightly to be deplored is that this kind of abomination could not keep its fixed seat only among nations ignorant of God; but having broken through the bars, it migrated to the very people of God and their leaders and kings: of which we have a notable pair of examples in Jephthah*, about whom we shall speak in his place.
