# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Feast of Tabernacles.</margin>
->Leviticus 23:34<-
->On the fifteenth day of this seventh month shall be the feast of tabernacles for seven days unto the Lord. <note>original Hebrew: בַּחֲמִשָּׁה עָשָׂר יוֹם לַחֹדֶשׁ הַשְּׁבִיעִי הַזֶּה חַג הַסֻּכּוֹת שִׁבְעַת יָמִים לַיהוָה</note><-
->On the fifteenth of this seventh month is the feast of booths for seven days to the Lord. <note>original Greek: Τῇ πεντεκαιδεκάτῃ τοῦ μηνὸς τοῦ ἑβδόμου τούτου ἑορτὴ σκηνῶν ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας τῷ Κυρίῳ.</note><-
->From the fifteenth day of this seventh month were the holidays of tabernacles for seven days to the Lord. <note>original Latin: A quinto decimo die menſis hujus ſeptimi erant feriæ tabernaculorum ſeptem diebus Domino.</note><-

The Jews celebrated with great joy the feast of <term>Skenopegia</term> <note>from Greek skēnē (tent) and pēgnunai (to fix/build)</note> or <term>Tabernacles</term> (Hebrew: *Chag HaSukkot*, or simply *Sukkot*), in the seventh month after the gathering of the fruits. This occurred on the 15th day of the month of Tishri (around the beginning of our September) and lasted for eight full days. During this time, they lived outside their houses in tabernacles <note>booths or temporary shelters</note> constructed from tree branches under the open sky. They spent those days joyfully in banquets and sacrifices, cooking, eating, and dancing, in memory of the time past when, having been led out of Egypt, they lived in tabernacles in the desert for forty years.
<margin>v. 43.</margin>
*Thus, they compared their present happiness with past misery through grateful memory: that while they once wandered as exiles in a squalid desert, they now possessed the kingdom of the land of Canaan; and while they then had neither houses nor fields, they now possessed and inhabited splendid cities and homes. On the first day of the Skenopegia there was a <term>holy convocation</term> (Hebrew: *Miqra-Kodesh*), on which
<margin>v. 35.</margin>
it was not permitted to do any servile work.* On this day, each person carried in their hand the <term>fruit of a beautiful tree</term> (Hebrew: *Peri Etz Hadar*), that is, of the most beautiful tree, as our Latin translator rendered it. Likewise, they carried <term>palm branches, branches of leafy trees</term>, and <term>willows
<margin>v. 40.</margin>
of the brook</term>, as a symbol of that ancient blessing. Describing this carrying of branches, Josephus in the 10th chapter of the 3rd book of his <term>Antiquities</term> says it was "entering mystically, carrying a willow with a branch of palm, together with the fruit of the Persian apple" <note>original Greek: εἰσελθὼν μυστικῶς, καὶ ἰτέας σὺν κλάδῳ φοίνικος πεποιημένην τῷ μήλῳ τῆς περσέας προσόντος</note>; which
<margin>on Lev. p. 700.</margin>
Bonfrerius translates as: *a branch of myrtle and willow with an elaborate palm branch* (Russinus says: "the tops of palms") with the addition of a Persian apple <note>likely referring to the Etrog or citron</note>. There were specific sacrifices and drink offerings to be offered each day, which are recounted individually in <term>Numbers 29 from verse 13 to the end.</term> The last day was the most famous because of the <term>holy convocation</term> mentioned in <term>Leviticus 23:36</term>, held without any servile work. This solemnity of the eighth day is called a feast of <term>Atzeret</term>, which the Septuagint <note>the Greek Old Testament</note> renders as
<margin>Question 32 on Leviticus.</margin>
*exodion* <note>a conclusion or exit</note>, which Theodoret explains * indicates "the end of the festivals" <note>original Greek: τὸ τέλος τῶν ἑορτῶν</note>. To the Latin interpreter, it is called a <term>Meeting and assembly</term>. That Hebrew word, if its etymology and root are considered, signifies <term>retention and conclusion</term>, from *Atzar*, meaning "he closed" or "he detained," because on that day the entire solemnity was closed, and the eighth day was like a closure of the solemn feast. In the same way, the day that closed the feast of unleavened bread was called <term>Atzeret</term> (<term>Deuteronomy 16:8</term>), as were other holidays appointed by the Church (<term>2 Kings 10:20, Joel 1:14</term>) and the <term>Feast of Pentecost</term>, which is celebrated solemnly at the end or conclusion of seven weeks. When it was the fiftieth day, it is called <term>Asartha</term> by Josephus in <term>Antiquities</term> Book 3, Chapter 10. This last day was holier and more devoted than the others, hence it was called the <term>Great Sabbath</term> (Hebrew: *Shabbat HaGadol*) and the <term>Joy of the Law</term> (Hebrew: *Simchat Torah*), because on that day they read the final section of the Law, and thus completed the Law. On that day also, if Paul Fagius is to be believed, they would circle the altar seven times, equipped with a bundle made of palm, myrtle, and willow branches, which they called a <term>Hoshana</term>, recalling the memory of the fallen walls of Jericho,

<column-break/>

<margin>The Feast of Tabernacles.</margin>
and they would shout: "Save now, I beseech thee, O Lord; O Lord, I beseech thee, send now prosperity" <note>original Hebrew: אָנָּא יְהוָה הוֹשִׁיעָה נָּא אָנָּא יְהוָה הַצְלִיחָה נָּא</note>. The Jews returning from Babylon celebrated that eight-day feast of the month of Tishri with a most famous rite (<term>2 Esdras 8:15-18</term> <note>Nehemiah 8 in modern Bibles</note>). For then, in all their cities and in Jerusalem, they sent out the voice of a herald, by which it was announced that everyone from all around should flock to Jerusalem to celebrate the feast of Skenopegia. It was proclaimed by the herald's voice that they should go to the mountain and bring olive branches, and branches of the pine tree (Hebrew: *alei-etz shemen*, "leaves of oil-wood," where the Septuagint understands cypress; the Old Latin interpreter says "branches of the most beautiful wood"), and myrtle branches, and palm branches, and branches of thick trees, to make tabernacles. And so the entire assembly that had returned from captivity made tabernacles, each on his own roof, and in their courts, and in the courts of the house of God, and in the street of the water gate, and in the street of the gate of Ephraim. *And there was very great gladness* (Hebrew: *vattehi simchah gedolah me'od*); and they kept the solemnity for seven days; and on the eighth day there was an <term>Atzeret</term> according to the custom. This festival had been interrupted from the times of Joshua until Nehemiah, but was grandly restored by him and Ezra. These tabernacles could be constructed from every kind of branch and could be fixed in any place, provided it was under the open sky, so that God could be celebrated and praised by all for the possession of the holy land and for the fruits collected that year. After these thanksgivings were completed, everyone returned from the tabernacles to their own homes. This solemnity of Tabernacles fell at the time of the <term>Vintage</term>, which is why it is also called the <term>feast of the seventh harvest and the collection of fruits</term>. Theophylact writes that it was a "Thanksgiving for the gathering of the fruits" <note>original Greek: Εὐχαριστήριον ἐπὶ τῇ συγκομιδῇ τῶν καρπῶν</note>, during which the Jews sang songs and hymns to proclaim the name of Jehovah for the many and great benefits to the human race, which had been festively and tangibly bestowed especially in that quarter of the year. Meanwhile, the Levites played on infinite instruments and the Priests sounded trumpets. For this use, three Psalms still exist—<term>8, 81, and 84</term>—in the venerable Book of Psalms, having the inscription <term>Al-Haggittith</term>. Some take the reason for this name from a musical instrument so called because it was first invented and constructed in Gath. Others want it taken from when the Royal Prophet [David] led the Ark of the Lord from the city of the woods into the house of Obed-Edom; thus *Githith* is a Gittite station or commemoration; for that reason, Junius and Tremellius translate it "at the Gittite station." A better reason for the name seems to be taken from the time of the vintage, so that <term>Al-Haggittith</term> refers to the winepresses, because *Gath* signifies a winepress. Hence Blessed Gesner thinks the name was given to these Psalms from the winepress, but he understands a mystical and metaphorical winepress, namely the ministry of the Gospel. It is certain, however, that Psalms 81 and 84 were sung in great solemnities to celebrate the admirable providence of Jehovah toward created things, and especially his inestimable goodness toward man. And by the solemnity described in Psalm 81, Blessed Luther specifically understands the Feast of Tabernacles. But since the Pagans at that very time of the vintage also conducted their own *thyrsa* <note>Bacchic processions</note>, so called from the Athenian month of Lenaeon...

# From Leviticus XXIII, v. 34.

<margin>
The Feast
of Taber-
nacles.
</margin>

...spoken in honor of Bacchus, and they devoted themselves to the vintage festival for several days with lavish joy and wantonness. Hence, Plutarch, in the 4th book of his *Symposiacs* <note>Table Talk</note>, problem 3, transforms this Feast of Tabernacles into the Bacchanalia. Because they carried branches in their hands at the time of the holy rites, that lying Greek thought the solemnity of the tabernacles was derived from his own triennial orgies. For when he made mention of the Jewish rites, he added this from his "cornucopia of lies": *“First, the greatest and most perfect solemnity of the Jews coincides in both time and manner with the rites of Bacchus; for what they call the fast, they celebrate in such a way that, at the height of the vintage, they set out tables on which all kinds of fruits are displayed, and they sit under tabernacles, especially those made of vine-shoots and ivy woven together; and the day preceding the feast, they call 'Tabernacles.'”* A few days later, they celebrate another festival, not obscurely but quite openly dedicated to Bacchus. *“There is also a solemn feast among them called 'Cradæphoria' <note>original: κραδηφορία - branch-bearing</note> from the carrying of vine-shoots, and 'Thyrsophoria' <note>original: θυρσοφορία - carrying the thyrsus, a staff topped with a pine cone</note> where, carrying thyrsi, they enter into the temple <note>original: εἰς τὸ ἱερὸν</note>; what they do inside, I know not. It is credible that the things performed are Bacchic revelry <note>original: βακχείαν εἶναι τὰ ποιούμενα</note>; for they also use small trumpets to call upon the Deity, just as the Argives do at the Bacchanalia, and others go forward playing harps, whom they call Levites <note>original: Λευΐτας</note>, whether from 'Lysios' <note>The Deliverer, a title of Bacchus</note> or from 'Evius' <note>A cry used in Bacchic rites</note>, the name having been derived from those invocations.”*

I am of the opinion, however, that the feast of the Sabbaths is not entirely foreign to Bacchus. For even now many call Bacchus "Sabbas," and they utter that cry while celebrating the orgies of Bacchus, as can be shown from Demosthenes (who in his 
<margin>
On the Crown
p. 150.
</margin>
Oration * formerly reproached Aeschines for raving with these cries, *euoi, sabboi*) and from Menander. *“They themselves bear witness to this talk; for when they observe the Sabbath, they especially invite themselves to drinking and drunkenness, or, if some more serious matter prevents it, they certainly have a custom of tasting unmixed wine.”* These things Plutarch pronounces concerning divine institutions less reverently than he ought, which is not at all surprising; for a pagan man does not perceive those things which are of the Spirit of God. He determined by a monstrous error that the rites of Bacchus were performed by the Levites, and he thinks they were named from the surnames of Bacchus. 

Much more ridiculous is the etymology by which he derives the name of the Levites from *Lysios* or *Evius*, than that which derives *Neptune* from *nando* <note>swimming</note>; especially since in *Evius* not even the first letter is the same as in *Neptune*. Just as he missed the mark in that, so too in thinking that the Sabbath arose from the Greek name for revelers, *sabos*, when it is actually from the Hebrew *shabat* <note>original: שבת</note>, meaning "to rest," not from a barbarian word by which Bacchus was once called. And so that he might disguise these vain and ruinous trifles with a greater similarity of words, and persuade people that the Jews were not at all averse to the cult of Bacchus, he corrupts *sabos* into *sabbas*, and claims that from this comes *sabazein*, which would mean to exult or dance, from which he finally trifles that the Sabbath of the Jews was named, and to this he fits his *cradephoria* and *thyrsophoria*. 

The thyrsus is assigned to Bacchus instead of a scepter, and it was a branch or spear adorned with the leaves of vines or ivy. The Gentiles used to employ such thyrsi of old when a victory had been won, as Plutarch shows in his lives of *Aemilius* and *Marius*; which things can be applied to the deed of Judas Maccabeus, who, after

<column-break/>

he had purged the temple and the city of Jerusalem from the filth of idolatry, <margin>The Feast of Tabernacles.</margin> celebrated the days with such gladness, as if they were feast days of tabernacles <note>original: σκηνωμάτων τρόπον</note>, carrying thyrsi and beautiful branches, and also palms, they offered up hymns to Him who had given success to the cleansing of His own place (2 Maccabees 10, v. 7). It was the custom in that Feast of Tabernacles <note>original: Scenopegico</note> to carry thyrsi made of palms and citrons, as Josephus attests <margin>13. Antiquities 21.</margin> * That carrying of thyrsi was a symbol of joy, and for that reason they were branches of delightful and precious trees, during the carrying of which they joyfully repeated "Hosanna," giving thanks to God and returning a hymn to Him who had given success. This was by no means done for Bacchus, for whom rites were performed with insane shouting, with torches and links set on fire, and with great impudence and wantonness. 

With the same ignorance, Apion derived the Hebrew word for Sabbath from the Egyptian language, and with equal impiety he raves against the observers of that day. *“After a journey of six days,”* he says (according to Josephus <margin>Book 2 against Apion</margin>), *“the Jews returning from Egypt were affected by ulcers of the groin, and for this reason they rested on the seventh day, and called that day the Sabbath, preserving the Egyptian word; for the Egyptians call a disease of the groin 'Sabbo.'”* In the Greek Basel edition, the word is *sabbatosis*, which reading the subsequent refutation suggests should be rejected; for Josephus, refuting these things among others, writes thus: *“The grammatical transposition concerning the name 'Sabbath' possesses much impudence or terrible ignorance. For 'Sabbo' and 'Sabbath' differ greatly from one another. For 'Sabbath,' according to the dialect of the Hebrews, is rest from every work; but 'Sabbo,' just as he says, signifies among the Egyptians a pain of the groin.”* 

Tacitus derives the origin of the Sabbath from elsewhere; for he thinks that honor is held by the Hebrews for Saturn, and he trifles something about the star of Saturn and the seven planets, being ignorant of the meaning of the name and of the blessed seventh day. But these are the slanders and "butubatz" <note>nonsense/gibberish</note> of the Gentiles, who ought to have known that they stole their *Sabbos* and the *saboi* cry of the revelers from the Jews, from the blessed name *Zeba* <note>original: צבא</note>, which was attributed to God, who is hence called *Jehovah Zebaoth* and *Lord of Sabaoth* (James 5:4, Romans 9:29). Concerning this, note: 1. This name *Zebaoth* <note>original: צבאות</note> is plural, signifying "armies" or "hosts," and noting all the creatures of God, because of the wonderful harmony and order in which they were created (Wisdom 11:12); several reasons for this naming are recited by the Blessed Ursinus in *Sacred Analecta*, vol. 1, book 6, p. 315. Hence these hosts of creatures and angels are commanded to praise God (Psalm 103:21, 148). 2. Therefore, the "Lord Zebaoth" is the same as that Lord and God of hosts, and the creator and mediator of the same. Next, it should be observed that the word *Zebaoth* is never used alone for God, like the other divine names, but always has another name of God attached and placed before it. More correctly, therefore, you will refer it among those names of God which are attributed to God in respect to His creatures, rather than those which are proper and essential to Him (cf. Flacius, *Key to the Scriptures* on the word "God"; B. Glassius, book 3, *Sacred Grammar*, Tr. 1, can. 3, p. 15). 

From this, however, they called their Bacchus "Sabazius," concerning whose worship among the Gentiles see Vossius, *On Idolatry*, book 2, ch. 14, p. 376-377; who also on p. 378 thinks the name *Iacchus* was twisted from *Saba* <note>original: סבא</note>, one of the names of God. That Sabazius Bacchus is truly a "Drunkard-Bacchus" from *saba* <note>original: סבא</note>, which is to be inebriated, from which comes *sabazein*. But...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<page-num>220</page-num>

<margin>The Feast of Tabernacles.</margin>
But we leave aside these <unclear>willingly placed stumbling blocks</unclear> <note>original Greek: ἑκὼν σκανδάληθρα</note>. When the Pagans heard that the Jews observed the seventh day with great religious devotion and called it the Sabbath, they called them "Sabbatarians" for the sake of mockery; an insult used by <margin>Martial, Epistles 4.4.</margin> Martial in *Epistle* 4.4, where he calls the Jews "gloomy Sabbatarians" whose breath reeks because of frequent fasts. He claims they do this uselessly, agreeing with Seneca, who—in a passage preserved by Augustine <margin>City of God 6.11.</margin>—criticizes the Jewish rites, especially the Sabbath: *that by interposing those individual seventh days, they lose almost a seventh part of their life in idleness, and are harmed by not attending to many urgent matters in time.* Persius, in *Satire* 5, line 184, says that "circumcised Sabbaths" <margin>Satire 14, book 5, v. 116.</margin> make the Jews turn pale because of their "Sabbatisms," and Juvenal mocks the *father who fears the Sabbath.* With the same scornful tone, Plutarch writes that on the Sabbath they <unclear>sit in unbent positions</unclear> <note>original Greek: καθίστας ἐν ἀγνάμπτοις</note>, and spend their days in sadness through neglect of worship and cessation of work. They write this because fasts were sometimes practiced on the Sabbaths with no change of clothing; hence Petronius says:

->And he burdens the Sabbath with the law of fasting.<-

<margin>Book 36.</margin>
The observation of the seventh day was very well known among the nations, and it seemed ridiculous to them. Justin perverts this slanderously, writing* at the beginning: *The Egyptians, when they suffered from scabies and leprosy, were warned by an oracle and drove him (Moses) with the sick out of the borders of Egypt, lest the plague creep to more people. Having become the leader of the exiles, he stole the sacred objects of the Egyptians; when the Egyptians sought them back with arms, they were forced by storms to return home. Thus Moses, having reached Damascus, his ancient homeland, occupied Mount Sinai. There, exhausted with his people by a seven-day fast through the deserts of Arabia, when he finally finished the seventh day, called the Sabbath in the manner of the nation, he consecrated it <margin>History, book 5, ch. 4.</margin> to fasting for all time.* Cornelius Tacitus* does not differ much from this tasteless fiction, saying: *The Jews testify to their long-ago hunger by their still-frequent fasts.* Thus we see how Satan, through his instruments, has tried to suppress the light of truth with infinite lies. That a rite of Bacchus existed within the Jewish sacred rites is the ultimate lie, and <margin>History, book 5.</margin> Cornelius Tacitus himself shows this is not likely due to the dissimilarity, saying*: *Their priests sang to the accompaniment of pipes and drums, they were bound with ivy, and a golden vine was found in the temple. Some thought Father Liber [Bacchus], the conqueror of the East, was worshipped, though the institutions do not agree at all; for Liber established festive and joyful rites, while the <margin>Book 3, ch. 5.</margin> Jewish custom is absurd and foul.* Regarding the golden vine, let it be noted from Florus, when he describes the victories of Pompey*: *The Jews, he says, tried to defend Jerusalem, but he entered this also, and saw that great secret of the impious nation revealed: a vine under a golden sky.* For this is how Lipsius corrects the text in *Elect.* 2.5, whereas the common copies have: "under a golden sky as it were." Josephus says in *Antiquities* 14.14 that he saw that vine, which Aristobulus had sent as a gift to Pompey, dedicated at Rome in the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus, with the inscription: *Of Alexander, King of the Jews.* Blind paganism, since it did not know the sacred mysteries of the Jews, conformed them to its own impious rites, as we have seen from the Feast of Tabernacles and other ceremonies.

<margin>The Jubilee</margin>
When God, the Best and Greatest, had finished the creation of the world in six days, He consecrated the SEVENTH day for rest, from which it received the name Sabbath, because on that day one must rest from all profane work by divine command. Nor did the Divine Being sanctify only every seventh day, but also every seventh year, so that all work of agriculture should cease; hence it is usually called <term>Shemitah</term> <note>Hebrew: שמטה</note>, *cessation*, or the *Sabbatical year*. This sabbatical revolution of years is called the *great week*. If we ascend from the seventh year to seven times seven, or forty-nine years, the nourishing Trinity also destined that year for sacred rest, which is called by the Hebrews the Year of <term>Jobel</term>, commonly *Jobelaeus* or *Jubilaeus*, but most commonly *Jubilaus* [Jubilee]. Some call its revolution the *greater week*, and it could be called the *greatest week* if we progress further to a period of seven Jubilees, so that it is constituted as a "Jubilee of Jubilees." After seven Sabbatical years, or forty-nine years, have passed, the following year, which is the fiftieth, was the Jubilee; although Scaliger, Calvisius, Alstedius, Petavius, and many others assert the forty-ninth year is the Jubilee—see them refuted in Wichmann, *Sacred Chronology* book 1, p. 19 ff., and B. Slevogt, *Philological Disputation* 4, n. 12. To treat the Jubilee year in order and not <unclear>disorderly</unclear>, we must first discuss where the Jubilee takes its name, then look into its types, origin, nature, and use. As for the first point, there are no small disagreements among the learned regarding this <term>onomatology</term> <note>the study of the formation of names</note>. Andreas Masius derives it from Jubal, the father and inventor of organic music and its instruments, than which nothing is more powerful for stirring up joy. Two of his instruments are celebrated: one, the <term>Kinnor</term> <note>Hebrew: כנור</note>, which they translate as a lyre; the other, the <term>Ugav</term> <note>Hebrew: עוגב</note>, which the ancient translator rendered as an organ. For he comments thus*: *The word Jobel first appeared, and was derived from the first inventor of musical instruments, Jubal; just as the Latin words "jubilo" and "jubilum" [to shout for joy]. I think these words signify those melodious sounds, grand indeed, but rustic, harsh, and wild, almost like howling, such as those early but imperfect instruments of the first craftsman produced; that is, like the hoarse blaring of trumpets and horns, though I am not unaware that in Varro, a "jubilum" is a rustic cry. I believe the year of remission was called the Jubilee because they spread the news of it far and wide as a festive and solemn time with blaring of that kind—* <margin>p. 104. On Joshua 6:4.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological discussion regarding the origins and meaning of the word "Jubilee" (Jobel) as found in Leviticus 25.</meta>

# From Leviticus 25, verses 4, 8, and 10.

<margin>Jubilee</margin>
The sacred Law commanded that [the Jubilee] be proclaimed to those spread abroad; for those who interpret *Jobel* <note>Hebrew: יובל</note> as either "remission" or "entrance/access" do so, if I am not mistaken, without any precedent. Furthermore, the Hebrew Doctors who trace the word back to the Arabic language seem to me to rely on quite uncertain conjecture. It appears clearly enough from the sacred words that those trumpets were horns, not those silver trumpets which Moses had long ago caused to be cast at God's command. But truly, it is most likely they were not rams' horns, since these are entirely solid, whereas a trumpet must be hollow so that it can be blown. Thus, Justus Ryckius also denies that this trumpet was made from a ram's horn, and maintains it was composed of an ox horn, yet with no suitable argument. Bochart seems to agree with this, likewise denying that horns which are not hollow could have been fit for this use. Indeed, I read in Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Book 2) and Varro (*On the Latin Language*, under "horns") that the people were summoned by the horns of oxen.

<margin>Sacred Miscellany, Book 4, Chapter 8</margin>
Others walk a different path and say that *Jobel* properly denotes a "ram," and figuratively a trumpet made from a ram's horn. they strive to prove this from Joshua 6:3-4, where "the horn of Jobel" <note>Hebrew: קרן היובל</note> is translated by the Chaldean <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> as "the horn of rams" <note>Aramaic: בקרן דכריא</note>. This is also based on the Arabic usage of the word, as is evident from *Rosh Hashanah* chapter 3, where Rabbi Akiva writes: "When I went to Arabia, I heard them call a ram *Jobel*." Compare Fuller, Forster, Avenarius, Chytraeus, Schindler, and Hottinger, who agree with them, contending that the word *Jobel* was formed from the peculiar sound which the trumpet of blast emitted. Among these, Hottinger (Dissertation 3, *Historico-Theological Analects*, p. 152) says: *“We recognize in the name Jobel an onomatopoeia <note>A word formed from a sound</note> which, as in other Oriental languages, especially Arabic, is not infrequent among the Hebrews. For our conjecture to be more probable, it must be known that the use of horns and trumpets among the Hebrews was most common—and sanctioned by divine law—for summoning assemblies, for kindling the spirits of soldiers for battle, and also for proclaiming the Jubilee. Lest the Israelites be confused by the blaring of trumpets and disturbed in the proper execution of their duty, the sound of the trumpets itself had to be distinct. Thus, to proclaim that great festival of the Jubilee recurring every fifty years, the Israelites used a 'trumpet of blast' <note>Hebrew: שופר תרועה</note>, but one which gave a certain and distinct sound, which Holy Scripture calls Jobel, that is, a jubilee.”* So he says. In this opinion, the Blessed Slevogt, in his peculiar dissertation on the Jubilee (§ 7), finds that those examples which the Blessed Forster produced from the Holy Code do not prove what he wishes. Let us note in this place what Cyril Franchus of Bologna, of the sacred Order of Servites and formerly primary Interpreter of Theology in the Gymnasium of Bologna, holds against that opinion. He published a work in 1608 on the Year of Jubilee, in which he shows by what beginnings it was instituted, at what times granted, how it was ordained for the Hebrew people in the Old Testament, and by what reasoning it passed from the Old Law to the Papal [traditions]. Regarding the name, he writes in chapter two, p. 2: *“Some think the explanation of the word, which some call the etymology, is derived from the clangor of the trumpets by which, in the seventh month by the command of God Almighty, the year of Jubilee was promulgated to all the inhabitants of the land; which*

<column-break/>

<margin>Jubilee</margin>
*interpretation I would not dare to condemn; yet, in my judgment, I would say it is less convenient, because those trumpets were ordained by God for the proclamation of the Jubilee, and even after—not before—the Jubilee was instituted; hence it must be said that the trumpets were instituted because of the Jubilee, not the Jubilee because of the trumpets.”* In chapter six, p. 7, he says this year could properly be called the "Year of Religion," for it was a year of lustration, a year of expiation, in which the Hebrews obeyed the precepts of the divine law with all zeal, by avoiding usury, laying aside private hatred, remitting debts, freeing slaves, and recalling alienated property to its former right. There are still others who think it is derived from *jabal* <note>Hebrew: יבל</note>, which enjoys the meaning of "bringing" or "leading back," or even "budding/sprouting." For whichever meaning you seize upon, the year will be deemed worthy of both words. Indeed, the grace [of the concept] would perish if you gathered some nonsense about a ram. The memory of "leading up" <note>Greek: ἀναγωγῆς</note> is handed down in those letters from the vernacular custom of speaking; whence the Jubilee is called a "leading up" <note>Greek: ἀναγωγή</note>, a "release from slavery" <note>Greek: ἀπαλλαγή δουλείας</note>, a "release from troubles" <note>Greek: ἀπόλυσις ὀχλήσεων</note>, a "restoration to the ancient state" <note>Greek: ἀποκατάστασις εἰς τὸ ἀρχαῖον</note>, a "joy over loans" <note>Greek: χαρὰ καταδανείων</note>, and indeed by the Seventy <note>The Septuagint Greek translators</note> it is called "remission" <note>Greek: ἄφεσις</note>, to signify the future "remission of sins in Christ" <note>Greek: ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν ἐν χριστῷ</note>. Nor do those displease me who seek the origin from "exultant joy." The word of most ancient memory explains the old rite of "leading back," and it is explained less clearly and solidly by professors of Jewish antiquities. For the "Year of Leading Up" <note>Greek: Annus ἀναγωγῆς</note>, because it "leads back to liberty" <note>Greek: εἰς ἐλευθερίαν ἐπανάγει</note>, and because it leads "back to inheritance" <note>Greek: πάλιν εἰς κληρονομίαν</note>—what else is it but a year of joy? And joy comes from the liberation and the holiday-keeping, as well as the liberty proclaimed throughout the region to all inhabitants. (We are attending to the matter in this discourse, not the word itself.) At this news, the inhabitant of the land was "overjoyed" <note>Greek: περιχαρὴς</note>, and the land itself kept holiday, and celebrated as if it were a "dedication festival" <note>Greek: encænia</note>. Many things supplied the material for gladness. It was "gladness" <note>Greek: Ευφροσύνη</note> because that year led everyone back to their old homes; "gladness" because there was a return to the ancient rights of inheritance, to the original conditions of living, to liberty; "gladness" because sins were remitted. How great the glory, how great the gap [bridged], how great the "leading up" <note>Greek: ἀναγωγή</note>! If a city or region is freed from the rule of barbarians, and all things are reduced to their former state of liberty, the old and young abound in joy, and they place that "leading back" in the highest degree of gladness. Then there is the congratulation of all good people, and they all share that congratulation among themselves. The "Year of Jobel" <note>Hebrew: שנת יובל</note> brought a greater fruit of common joy to the Israelites, namely the "Year of Leading Up" <note>Greek: ἔτος τῆς ἀναγωγῆς</note>, or, as Philo explains it, of "restoration" <note>Greek: ἀποκατάστασεως</note>. For it was a "year of restoration," a "year of emancipation," a "year of remission" <note>Greek: ἔτος τῆς ἀφέσεως</note> according to the sense of the Seventy, and a "year of liberty" <note>Greek: ἔτος τῆς ἐλευθερείας</note> according to Josephus. Whence some, among whom is Cornelius à Lapide <margin>on Lev. 25:11</margin>, want it derived from *jabal* <note>Hebrew: יבל</note>, "he brought" with joy; Morinus (*Biblical Exercises*, p. 219) derives it from the root in the Hiphil form *hobil* <note>Hebrew: הוביל</note>, "he brought, he led back, he reached," and judges the fiftieth year was called Jubilee from this, because it brought to each one the produce of his inheritance, and led each one back into his inheritance. We find that Gregory Nazianzen took it in this sense in his *Homily on Pentecost*, p. 262: *“The children of the Hebrews honor the week from the legislation of Moses; but the honor for them is not only in days, but it even reaches to years—”*

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
## Page 222

<margin>The Jubilee</margin>
I anticipate <note>original Greek: φθάνω</note>. On the one hand, there is the Sabbath among the days. On the other hand, there is the septenary of release among the years, occurring not only every seven years, but also after seven sets of seven years, similarly in both days and years. The weeks of days lead to the fiftieth, which they call a holy, convoked day <note>Pentecost</note>. The weeks of years lead to what they call the **Jubilee**, which likewise brings about a release: the freeing of slaves and the restoration of their possessions.

<margin>On the Holy Spirit, p. 437</margin>
And **Cyprian** states: *A week of years among the Hebrews makes fifty years, which they call the Jubilee, in which by the decree of the law there is a release of the land, freedom for slaves, and a restoration of possessions which sale had previously alienated; other such things return freely to the order of inheritance.*

<margin>Apology of David, ch. 8, p. 384</margin>
Likewise **Ambrose**: *In the Law you find that the Jubilee is the name for the cycle of fifty years, a very celebrated time in which debts are cleared, the liberties of the Hebrews are confirmed, and possessions are restored.* And so the learned clash over the etymology of this word. Leaving aside the naming conventions <note>original Greek: ὀνομαζλογίᾳ</note>, we approach the matter more closely; and since the Papal Jubilee was instituted in imitation of the Mosaic Jubilee, let us deal with the latter first. While we call it "Mosaic," we point the finger, as it were, to the fact that before this was instituted by Moses by divine command, none was in use. There are those who assert its origin began with the beginning of the world, including **Eusebius** in his *Chronicle*, **Bucholcer** in his *Chronology*, **Chytraeus**, and **Cornelius à Lapide**, who call this the "Jubilee of the World" to differentiate it from the Mosaic one.

<margin>Book 1 on the Jubilee, ch. 3</margin>
Others, with **Cosmas Montigianus**, seek the beginning of the Jubilee in the Law of Nature and refer it to the time of Noah, as if God established the covenant of reconciliation with Noah in the fiftieth year after the universal flood. Finally, others, among whom is **Hugh the Cardinal**, assign the first institution of the Jubilee to the victory of Abraham over the Kings, because Abraham reached his fiftieth year of age when those kings were conquered. But whatever the case, these are conjectures.

<margin>On Leviticus ch. 25</margin>
It is certain, however, that every such fiftieth year preceding Moses is called a Jubilee only *improperly and materially*. We find the primeval institution of the Jubilee properly and strictly <note>original Greek: κυρίως</note> so-called described in *Leviticus 25:4 and following.*

<margin>#</margin>
For after God had informed Moses concerning the laws and privileges of the *Sabbatical* year, He immediately adds the *Solemnities of the Jubilee feast*, and commands its proclamation to be made after counting <insert>seven Sabbaths of years</insert> <note>original Hebrew: שבתות שנים שבע</note>, or <insert>seven years seven times</insert> <note>original Hebrew: שבע שבתות שנים פעמים שבע</note>, that is, in the [fiftieth] year, and specifically, <insert>on the tenth day of the seventh month</insert> <note>original Hebrew: בעשור לחדש השביעי</note>. Since there was a double computation of the year among the Hebrews—one called the common and political year, because the Jews used it in civil matters, beginning from the month of **Tishri** (which corresponds mostly to our *September*), in which month the machine of the entire world is believed to have been created by God; the other, called the Ecclesiastical year, because its use was seen only in sacred and church matters, beginning from the month of **Nisan** (which corresponds mostly to our *March*), in which month the Israelites departed from Egypt. Compare **Buxtorf**, *Jewish Synagogue ch. 12*, and **Josephus**, *Antiquities of the Jews, Book 1, ch. 4.*

<margin>On 1 Kings 8:2</margin>
Hence **Rabbi David Kimchi** says: *Before the Israelites went out of Egypt, Tishri was the first*

<column-break/>

<margin>The Jubilee</margin>
month, because the world was created in Tishri; but after the Israelites went out of Egypt in the month of Nisan, that became the beginning of months, and Tishri is the seventh from it. And from this it happened that some placed the Jubilee in Nisan, others in Tishri. Those who follow the former calculation establish the reason or computation according to the common or civil year. The reasoning of the latter calculation has respect for the sacred or mystical year. Meanwhile, by the almost common opinion of all, the proclamation of the Jubilee year is placed and cast in the month of Tishri, which is the seventh of the sacred year, but the first of that common or civil year, corresponding to the autumn time. Compare **Cunaeus**, *On the Hebrew Republic, Book 1, ch. 6, p. 30*, and **Pererius**, who in his *Commentary on Genesis, Vol. 1, Book 1, p. 43, no. 121*, 

<margin>Thus he discourses on the time of celebrating the Jubilee.</margin>
discourses thus on the time of celebrating the Jubilee: *Furthermore, he says, although in the treatment of sacred matters and the celebration of festivals, Moses had established the beginning of the year in the springtime, this was not observed in all things. For in the celebration of the seventh year, in which rest was given to the land, and the fiftieth year, which was the Jubilee, the beginning necessarily had to be taken and computed from autumn. Otherwise, if it had been taken from the springtime, it would have been necessary that the crops and produce of the land of the sixth year, which were not ripe for harvest in Palestine in the month of Nisan, would utterly perish; which is against the Scripture, in which God promises that because of the rest of the seventh year He would give a tripled produce of crops, namely for the sixth and seventh [and eighth] years.* And this proclamation was not in one place, but in the whole land, or as **Aben Ezra** explains, <insert>in all its paths</insert> <note>original Hebrew: בכל מסלתה</note>. For this reason, **Maimonides** teaches in *chapter 10* that the celebration of the Jubilee was interrupted when the tribes across the Jordan were led away.

<margin>Leviticus 25:10</margin>
From the time, he says, that the tribe of Reuben, the tribe of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh were led into exile, the Jubilees ceased, because it is said, *you shall proclaim liberty in the Land to all who dwell in it*, that is, *you shall proclaim liberty in the Land at that time when all dwell in it, and for this reason: lest tribe be confused with tribe, but all dwell as they are ordained.*

<margin>In the place cited, ch. 6</margin>
**Cunaeus**, however, and others with him, place that interruption in the year of the desolation of the temple and city by the Assyrians, as well as the abduction of the King and all the Jews into the Babylonian captivity. By what ceremonies and rites the Jubilee was to be announced, **Moses** records in *verse 9*: *You shall sound the trumpet.* Of what material this trumpet was made is not yet agreed upon among the learned. **Cornelius à Lapide** fights for it being made of horn; **Tostatus** asserts the Jubilee trumpet was silver. He says: *Regarding this sound (which was heard at the announcement of the Jubilee), it must be said that it was made with silver trumpets, just as all other songs were made, etc.*

<margin>Lev. 25:4 ff; 2 Kings 25:9</margin>

Here the Jews have devised strange, even old-wives' superstitions—namely, in what manner and with what sound and tone this horn was to be blown—which we leave to them. # From Leviticus XXV. v. 4. 8. & 10.

<margin>The Jubilee</margin>
We turn ourselves to a most subtle <term>study <note>original: μελέτημα (meletēma)</note></term> of the privileges or benefits which God granted in the Israelite Jubilee. The Jubilee year was a year of release; in which slaves were gifted with liberty, debts were relaxed, and captives were sent away. Things alienated from their proper Master returned to their own right. The judgments of litigants were dissolved, and enmities were laid aside, so that there might be the highest rest for all, and tranquility of both body and mind. There were, however, two principal benefits which rendered the Jubilee year more celebrated than others. Namely, the *manumission* <note>The formal act of freeing a slave.</note> of slaves, and the *restitution of ancestral possessions to their former Masters* without any price or compensation, to which, by almost general opinion, is added the *remission of all debts*. Compare Flacius in his *Key to the Scriptures under the word Jobel*. 

But since, according to the opinion of the Hebrews, nothing is more absurd than to confuse the Jubilee year with the Sabbatical year—inasmuch as the former is distinguished from the latter by this: that in the Sabbatical year the remission of debts used to occur, but not so in the Jubilee—wherefore, according to their opinion, Maimonides says in <term>The Laws of the Sabbatical Year <note>original: הל' שמטה (Hilkhot Shemitah)</note></term> chapter 10: *The Sabbatical year excels the Jubilee in that the Sabbatical remits debts, while the Jubilee does not remit them; but the Jubilee excels the Sabbatical in that the Jubilee brings out slaves as free men and restores lands, and the Jubilee indeed restores lands at the beginning of the year, while the Sabbatical remits debts only at the end of the year.* 

Now, the Sabbatical year was every seventh year, in which, after six years of <term>farming <note>original: γεωργίας (geōrgias)</note></term>, the fields and vineyards were left uncultivated; that is, they neither sowed, nor reaped, nor pruned vineyards, nor gathered grapes, but whatever grew was common to all, and was gathered indifferently by anyone. *Exodus 23:10, Leviticus 25:3, etc.* Some begin the start or calculation of this from the first entry of the Israelites into the Promised Land, while others place it at the first cultivation of the fields and vineyards. And just as the Jubilee had the unique feature that lands were restored to their legitimate Masters at the same time as the manumission of native slaves with an awl <note>A reference to the ritual of piercing the ear of a slave who wished to remain with their master.</note>, 
<margin>Exod. 21:2 sq. Deut. 15:12.</margin>
*Exodus 21:2 sq. Deuteronomy 15:12.* So the Sabbatical year had the unique feature of the remission of debts along with the restoration of slaves to liberty without the awl, *Deuteronomy 15:2, etc.* 

Hence the benefits of the Jubilee consist chiefly in the liberation of Slaves and the restoration of lands to their legitimate Masters or possessors. For God willed that, in memory of the liberation from Egyptian captivity, slaves should be released and gifted with their former liberty, so that they might enjoy or rejoice in the same happiness as their masters; which the Hebrews feel was indicated by the phrase <term>he shall be with you <note>original: יהיה עמך (yihyeh immakh)</note></term>, *Leviticus 25:40.* Hence the Jalkut <note>A collection of Jewish midrash/commentary.</note> on this passage says: *He shall be with you in food, with you in drink, so that you do not eat fine bread while he eats bran bread, you do not drink old wine while he drinks new wine, you do not lie on a soft bed while he sleeps upon straw.* This, however, is not to be understood of all slaves indiscriminately, but only of those who were from the Hebrews. For of them it is said in *verse 10*: <term>every man shall return to his family <note>original: איש אל משפחתו תשבו (ish el mishpakhto tishuvu)</note></term>, that is, as Rabbi David Kimchi declares: <term>every slave sold in Israel <note>original: העבד הנמכר לישראל (ha-eved ha-nimkar le-Yisrael)</note></term>, whether he sold himself or was sold judicially. Since, however, slaves could also be released in the Sabbatical year, it must be carefully observed that the "awled" ones—who had their earlobe pierced with an awl—could not be freed in the Sabbatical year, 

<column-break/>

yet meanwhile in the Jubilee year, which also pertained to the <term>pierced ones <note>original: נרצעים (nirtza'im)</note></term>. 
<margin>The Jubilee</margin>
As for slaves bought from the Gentiles, they had to bear the yoke of servitude <term>forever <note>original: לעולם (le-olam)</note></term>, *through all the days of their life*; since the buyers possessed them by hereditary right, *Leviticus 25:46.* See, if you please, Tostatus on *this passage, question 24.* 

Not unlike this benefit is the custom of the Athenians, who in the Thesmophoria <note>A festival in honor of Demeter.</note> released captives from prison in honor of the Goddess, as witnessed by Meursius in *Attic Lectures, book 4, chapter 21, page 221.* And among the Samians, the *Eleutheria* <note>A festival of liberty.</note> were celebrated, dedicated in honor of Jupiter Eleutherius <note>Jupiter the Liberator.</note>, which slaves gifted with liberty celebrated. Hence Plautus in *The Persian*: 
<margin>Book 1, v. 29.</margin>
*Act out the Eleutheria royally.* Gerson also mentions, in an oration held at Marseille before Pope Benedict in the year 1403, some ancient institution of the Greeks called *Charistia* or "common grace," which was done for the common utility, not entirely dissimilar from the Jubilee year of the Jews. It is also pleasing to refer here to what Trigault says in *Chinese Annals, page 99*: that the King in the Chinese realm at certain times absolves the accused of the entire kingdom, which they call a public remission. 

It is pleasing to add a few more things regarding the custom of the Romans in manumitting slaves: Among the Romans, it proceeded from many causes, although Cicero posits at least three species of it. Namely, manumission either from sacred constitutions in the Holy churches—where liberty was conferred upon Slaves by Masters under a Bishop, and in the sight of the people, with some writing intervening for the memory of the deed, *Law 1, Code on those who are manumitted in the Church.* Then manumission was done by the *vindicta*, that is, a rod, with which the Praetor, striking the head of the Slave, said with solemn words: *I say that you are free*. Then, being led around in a circle by the lictor as a sign of free will and judgment, with all and singular knots of servitude broken, he was and was held to be free. Justinian makes mention of this manumission in *Law 'ego', Law 'Pater', Digest on manumission by rod.* And since this manumission is called *vindicta*, there are those who want it to be named after Vindicius—according to Livy, a slave of the Aquilii, but according to Plutarch in *Publicola*, a slave of the Vitellii—who, when he had revealed the conspiracy to bring Tarquin back into the city, was the first of all gifted with liberty, with Brutus conferring the *Vindiciae*. Others derive it from *vindicando* [vindicating], which is to claim into liberty. 

A third Manumission used to be performed in the Temple of Feronia, the Goddess of Freedmen, where with the head shaved (as was also done at other times), those who were hitherto slaves, now gifted with liberty, received a *pileus* <note>A felt cap symbolizing freedom.</note>. Hence, "to call to the cap" is proverbially *to call to liberty*, as found in Suetonius, Pliny, and Macrobius. As a sign of this, slaves wore caps during the Saturnalia and put on the shoes of the free-born, as witnessed by Porphyry. A sign of liberty was also a coin of Claudius having a seal which held a cap in the right hand, while extending the left as far as possible, spread out, with the inscription: *August Liberty*. Finally, this benefit could also be procured through a Letter signed by the Patron and five witnesses; for in that way, from the last will of the master, the slave attained liberty, *Law 'unica', section 'sancimus'*. Likewise also through a testament, even a less solemn one, that is, through codicils or through any other expression of will. Concerning these and other modes of manumitting, consult, if you please, Aulus Gellius *book 7, chapter 4*, and Blondus *book 4*.

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
The Jubilee
<term>Caelius Rhodiginus</term> <note>Lodovico Ricchieri, a Renaissance humanist</note> book 7, ch. 21 & book 25, ch. 22. <term>Rosini</term> book 1 of *Roman Antiquities*, ch. 20, p. 177. <term>Johannes Funger, Etymological Lexicon</term> page 1079.
</margin>
The second benefit of the Jubilee consisted in the <term>restitution</term> <note>restoration or returning</note> of fields or estates. Lands sold were redeemed in the Jubilee year, so that their possession returned to the original Lord. Regarding these, three laws were established by the Lord: the first concerns the price; the second the fruits of the earth; and the third, finally, deals with the condition of redemption, such that not only the Lord of the estate could redeem it, but also his kinsmen. For they were able to redeem the estates by paying the purchase price in this manner: they counted the years passed since the sale, so that if those years and the years remaining until the Jubilee were equal, half the price would be returned to the buyer in the redemption; but if they were unequal, the restitution would be made according to the proportion. However, account also had to be taken of the estate's improvement or neglect, as <term>Maimonides</term> <note>The influential 12th-century Jewish scholar Rambam</note> observes in the cited book, ch. 11. God thus willed that goods and possessions remain with those to whom they were assigned by law: He willed that they remain in the possession of the tribes and families, among the <term>clans</term> <note>original: "Stämmen"</note>, so that the ranks and growth of families might be preserved. In almost this same manner today are the <term>fief-estates</term> <note>original: "Lehen-Güter"</note>, which cannot be alienated without the permission of the <term>Feudal Lord</term> <note>original: "Lehen-Herrns"</note>. And so God, by this right of <term>recovery</term> <note>original: "relutionis"</note>, willed to take care lest the property of the Ancestors and their ancient estates pass to strangers; for which reason He willed the right of <term>pre-emption</term> <note>original: "προτιμήσεως" (protimeseos)</note> or <term>Family Retraction</term> <note>The right of a family member to buy back ancestral land sold to a stranger</note> to be introduced—even if the right of recovery still differs in many ways from Retraction—so that kinsmen, and those who are of the seller's family, may recover the thing sold by him for themselves. On this, see more in the Legal Consultants, who almost with one voice confess that the origin of the "right of retraction," as they call it, was drawn from divine law. <term>Boerius</term> in *Customs of Bourges*, title on *retraction of lineage*, § 1; and <term>Chassanée</term> in *Customs of Burgundy*, title on *retraction*, § 1, n. 1, verse "and it seems," states it is founded in divine law. And <term>Johannes Oldendorp</term>, formerly a professor at <term>Marburg</term>, says that Moses, by God's authority, brought this law to the Hebrews so that possessions would be reserved for individual families and could not be alienated outside of them forever, in his *Treatise on Law and Equity*, title 8, near the end. <term>Ernest Cothman</term> subscribes to these views in *Response* 42, n. 5, vol. 4. This right is beyond all controversy, having been instituted by the Creator of celestial and terrestrial things himself; compare <term>B. Reinking, Synoptic Treatise on Consanguineous Retraction</term>, p. 8. But if it happened that the seller, by the right of recovery, was unable or even unwilling to recover the sold estate for himself, the Jubilee year restored everything to him for free and without any price, even if the immovable things given or sold (for movable goods never returned to the seller) had changed buyers a hundred times; to which end <term>Maimonides</term> writes again: *Suppose someone sold his field to a first person, the first sold it to a second, the second to a third, so that it passed from one to another even a hundred times; nevertheless, the year of Jobel <note>Jubilee</note> restores it to the first Lord, because it is said in Leviticus 25:24: "In the year of Jobel the field shall return to him from whom he bought it, to him whose possession it was."* <note>The author cites Lev 27:24, but the text matches 25:24</note>. Yet these were the privileges and benefits of the year of Jobel, which vanished along with the solemnity of the Jubilee itself during the second temple and ceased to be in use. For how could they

<column-break/>

<margin>

</margin>
exercise those rights once the solemnity of the Jubilee itself had lapsed, which, by the testimony of the Jews themselves, vanished in the second temple? This is expressly confessed by <term>Maimonides</term>: *At the time,* he says, *when Jobel is in use, the law of the Hebrew Servant is also in use and observed, as is the law of buildings in walled cities, the law of vineyards, the law of fields, and the law of those who receive a stranger; the seventh year of the land and the remission of debts are in use wherever the Law requires. But at the time when Jobel is not in use, none of all those laws are in use. Only the Sabbatical year is usually observed in the Land, and the remission of debts annexed to it.*

The first of all to rival the Jewish Jubilee was <term>BONIFACE VIII</term>, who should be noted in capital letters, and that around the year 1300; from which time the "year of holiness" has been brought down to our times, and will be brought further as long as the world remains in the debt and veneration of Boniface, who had made such great profits. Since the beginnings were quite fruitful, <term>CLEMENT VI</term>, captured by the richness of the proceeds and more prone to the same, applied himself to the greater task of concluding within fifty years the Jubilee which had been extended to a hundred, and this *for the sake of gold*, as <term>Achilles Gassar</term> judges in his *Historical Epitome*, p. 219, Lyon edition. These fertile Jubilees, according to the etymology of <term>Bellarmine</term>,* made <term>SIXTUS IV</term>

Regarding its institutor, historians write: "he entered like a fox," and regarding the institution of this Jubilee, Krantz, book 4 of *Saxony*, 26, p. 94.

Theses concerning the Jubilee and the year of remission were publicly proposed at Wittenberg by Blessed Luther, in which he discusses its salutary use. <note>Martin Luther's "Theses on the Jubilee" (1517/1520s) often contrasted spiritual freedom with the sale of indulgences.</note> The jubilee of our current age brings much profit, but nothing of the Spirit. However, the faithful man in the house of Christ guards both the letter and the Spirit of the Jubilee. Likewise, Christians ought to observe the annual remission, although for them it is not every seventh year but perpetual. We ought, therefore, to give a loan to a needy Brother, seeking neither interest nor the principal; for the law of the year of remission demands that you not only emancipate a brother servant, but also provide him with travel funds. Since the Papal Jubilees do not have this—which is the very thing to be praised in a good Jubilee—let it be called an *Eleleum* <note>A Greek-derived term for a cry of lament or a "false" shout, contrasting with the joyful "Jubilee".</note>. For what kind of Jubilee is it where the Gehazi-ites <note>A reference to Gehazi, the servant of Elisha who took illicit payment; used here to describe greedy clergy.</note> rejoice over money, with a marketplace that is never satisfied? Each one watches for his own portion, colors it, *gains beautifully* <note>original Greek: κέρδει καλῶς</note>, while the other *is taken under* <note>original Greek: λαμβάνῃ ὑπὸ</note>. So much so that it can be said of those who prostitute the Jubilees in the words of Euripides found in Stobaeus: *that which is now called kindness by some is drunk and ruins an entire life into poverty.* The Jubilee of Christians consists in the gracious mercy of Christ, which is dispensed freely, conferred freely without a papal bull, without the "Holy Stairs," and without pomp. Bulls are often "bullate" <note>A Latin pun: "bullatis" means both "sealed with a bull" and "inflated/empty bubbles".</note> trifles, concerning which it would be the same as if <margin>Sal. 5. v. 19.</margin> it were said from the poet Persius:

> — so that my page may swell
> with bubbled trifles.

We marvel that Osorius said in *Volume 5 of his Works, page 864*, that the Jubilee is a "third Baptism," because something similar occurs in it. We wish that otherwise learned man had abstained from abusing the religious name of a Sacrament. Away, I pray, with all such spurious, supposititious, and fabricated Jubilees, where the common people, scattered in *parables* <note>original Greek: παραβολῇ</note>, follow custom rather than pious and religious zeal, saying what they are told to say, denying what they are told to deny, and embracing many absurd and inconsistent things which can hardly be enumerated here. Our highest Messenger after God, JESUS CHRIST—under whose patronage we spend every year in peace, secure in a Jubilee year—stirs our hearts with true obedience to Him, so that through the Guide we may reach the goal of truth. And since obedience is better than sacrifice, no one should glory in anything, since nothing is our own. We must glory in the **Only One**, the Leader of our salvation <note>original: "Jubelarcha", a hybrid term for "Ruler of the Jubilee".</note>, and His messengers, the twelve Apostolic men, from whose Creed we believe the remission of sins occurs. Let us glory with Saint Paul in nothing else but Christ, and Him CRUCIFIED. May God grant, I pray, that in this mortal life we may be held solely by the desire for eternal jubilation, holding the joys of the earth and the delights of the world in low esteem, and that we may finally be added to that rank of which David sang: BLESSED IS THE PEOPLE THAT KNOWS THE JOYFUL SOUND.

These are the names of the men whom Moses sent to spy out the land. And Moses called Hoshea the son of Nun, Joshua. <note>Original text provided in Hebrew, Greek (Septuagint), and Latin (Vulgate).</note>

The older a language is, the more *emphatic* <note>original Greek: ἐμφατικωτέρα</note> it is in the <margin>Sacred Onomatology.</margin> doctrine of names. Such is the Hebrew language, in which many contemplations of great and manifold importance are presented; especially, however, a great treasure is stored in the *storehouse* <note>original Greek: ταμιείῳ</note> of proper names. From this we can be led into various mysteries, since the deepest secrets often lie hidden in proper names, which cannot be perceived unless Hebrew etymologies are clearly understood. Hence, Theodore Bibliander <note>A 16th-century Swiss Orientalist and linguist.</note> rightly says in *On the Best Way of Explaining Hebrew*: *The Maker of things, moved by His immense goodness, formed man in His own image and likeness, and gave him the divine gift of reason; He also bestowed speech fit for explaining reason. By this, familiarity and commerce between God and man immediately intervened, and the force, property, and entire nature of all things were marked by the notation of words. The nature of all things was also distinguished by the most fitting symbols, so that it cannot be doubted that the Hebrew speech, attributed to the human race by the most wise and kind Creator, most greatly accords with reason and proceeds through the tracks of nature and truth.* Therefore, the notations of names are not to be undervalued, since powers lie hidden in them; for we regularly judge a thing from the calling of its name, and a person is presumed to be such as he is designated <margin>Law 4 on the Significance of Words; Law 7.</margin>. From this, much is taken from the notation or meaning, especially if the force of the word agrees with the thing it signifies; for it is well known that grave controversies are often settled by a true and suitable interpretation of a word. In his *Oratorical Partitions*, Cicero says, *many things are taken from notation. This occurs when an argument is drawn from a name, which the Greeks call etymology—that is, word for word, "true-speaking." We, however, avoiding the novelty of an unsuitable word, call this type "Notation," because words are the marks [notae] of things.* Therefore, Aristotle calls this same thing a *symbol* <note>original Greek: σύμβολον</note>, which in Latin is a *Mark*. But when it is understood what is signified, one should labor less over the name. The same Cicero <margin>in the Topics</margin> calls this the "argument from the mark." Aristotle, in the beginning of his book *On Interpretation*, called the words themselves *symbols*. Furthermore, all nations had a system for imposing names, lest unlucky names of ill omen be given. The Romans were so careful that soldiers and leaders with bad names were displeasing, as is evident from Cicero <margin>Book 1 on Divination</margin> regarding the purification of a colony; he says it was done by the one leading it out, and when the Commander, the army, or the Censor purified the people, those with "good names" were chosen to lead the sacrificial animals. The Consuls observed the same in a levy, so that the first soldier chosen would have a good name. That they were occupied here with great care so that names might be auspicious, you have in few words from the same author: among the good names were the Valerii, the Salvii, and the Statorii; he likewise reminds us of this in the name of Naevius, concerning...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<page-num>226</page-num>

<margin>Sacred Onomatology <note>The study of the origin and meaning of names.</note></margin>
...of whom the same author says in *Speech for Quinctius, Section 6*: *When I name the man, I feel I have said enough.* Among "bad names," Plautus counts *Epidamnus*, writing: *Therefore the name Epidamnus was given to this city, because almost no one turns aside to it without loss <note>Latin: "damno".</note>.* Thus, what Plato says in the *Cratylus* holds true here: that the giving of names was not the work of base or ordinary men. For parents, wishing for a good state of mind and body for their children, wanted to offer a good omen <note>Greek: "euphemiein"</note> through the bestowing of good names. When his parents gave Galen his name, it must be thought they did not do so randomly; for *galenos* means *tranquil, serene, calm*. What is better than a mind free from disturbances? What is better than that by which minds are cleared and quieted? Often, names become sad by the outcome of events and, so to speak, fatal, without the namer realizing it. The word *Abel* <note>Hebrew: "Hevel", meaning breath or vanity.</note> is an ill-omened word, not unlike that of Ajax, who himself feels in the Poet <note>Sophocles, in the play *Ajax*.</note> that his name fits his heavy misfortunes, as it was derived from the mournful cry *ai, ai* <note>Greek: "alas, alas".</note>.

->Alas, alas! Who would have ever thought that thus...<-

The Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator.</note> says: This too is an ancient custom, to express misfortunes through names. Thus etymologies are often prognostic, and arguments drawn from etymology are often not to be despised, as *Richter* learnedly says in *Economic Axioms, ch. 4*. Names imposed on children often hold their own power, according to that line of the Poet:

->*Names often fit their subjects.*<-

<margin>In the *Cratylus*.</margin>
And Plato affirms several times: *things well-named are like those things for which the names are set, and are images of the realities.* Therefore, what Cyprian writes to Pope Cornelius fits here perfectly: Mothers, he says, are accustomed to fit names to newly born infants at the very entrance of life, and to impose names from some preceding or surrounding causes, or from lineage, or from events, so that in those very first beginnings certain reminders might be prefixed. This was so that, for those entering life, their name would not be a source of ignominy if the transmission of their original nature strayed from the accustomed path, and if an unworthy succession, degenerating from the virtue of the Fathers, showed the face of a monster rather than a man. Names were not first imposed on things in a tumultuous or thoughtless way; but from the moment each thing was brought to Adam so that he might call them and impose proper names, it was provided by the first namers that there should be some reason in the words, that the names should interpret the thing and express some property of the person, by which they might either differ from others or share with them. Thus in the names of the Patriarchs—*Abraham*, *Isaac*, and *Jacob*—there existed signs of great things, and they spoke of things to come; nor did the namers lack a certainty of effects according to their own sense. For just as the Romans, in imposing names on their children, aimed for the children to have an incentive to always practice piety and virtue—as Carolus Sigonius discusses regarding Roman names, first names, and surnames and their singular reasoning in the booklet included by Sylburgius in *Roman History, Vol. 1, p. 340 ff.*—so no less did many Greeks impose names on their children based on the things in which they would later place their work and

<column-break/>

study, using it as an omen. *Most of the ancients,* <margin>Sacred Onomatology.</margin> says Eustathius in his commentary on Homer’s *Iliad, Book 2*, *gave names to their children anticipatorily, based on the activities the children were destined to pursue.* The Hebrew language, above all, is anxious to give names that fit the things according to their nature, whether by reason of matter, form, effect, or cause, etc. Whence they especially derived the imposition of their names from an event, either past or present (of which they were to be monuments), or future (the symbolic appreciation of which the named would receive as a best omen), so that the name might be an omen and a memorial <note>Latin: "nomen omen et monimen".</note>. You see, therefore, where the practice of naming tends, and to what considerations it invites us. When Socrates considers the name of *Agamemnon* in Plato, he thought it had been imposed by fate, *because this man is good at perseverance.* While he was going to capture Troy, he stuck there for ten years; the Philosopher felt this fate was hidden in his name. When he calculates the reason for the names of *Orestes*, *Atreus*, *Pelops*, and *Tantalus*, he thought the names were gathered not without an omen. When the Athenians considered the nobility of the name in *Nicias* <note>Derived from "Nike", victory.</note>, they portended a happy General, but the omen failed them, as the outcome of the Syracusan war taught them. Other words have failed, of whatever origin they were, whether good or bad. *Antiochus* was called *Epiphanes* <note>The Illustrious.</note>, yet was found out in impiety and madness. Thus our first Parents were deceived <margin>Genesis 4:1</margin> in their firstborn son Cain, to whom Eve, from a happy omen, gave the name of the most desired Messiah <note>Eve's exclamation "I have gotten a man from the Lord" led to the name Cain, from "qanah" (to get/acquire).</note>. Although the hope conceived by Parents for their sons may sometimes fail, *it is still sometimes a grace to praise someone from their names, their synonyms, and their epithets,* <margin>In *Theon*, regarding the "Preliminary Exercises" <note>A textbook on rhetoric.</note>, ch. 8, p. 103.</margin> as Theon says. For if we wish to consider what power and excellence of names exists in the nature of things, we will understand if we consider that, first of all, when the world was built and adorned, Adam, the prince of the human race, was set over it. He was appointed by God as the Lord and Administrator of all things which then existed in the sea, on the earth, and in the air; and it was given to him at the same time that, when all kinds of living creatures were brought to him, he could impose names on each fitting their nature. Whence Pythagoras not undeservedly established that he was the most skilled of the Wise, and indeed the most ancient, who first gave names to things so fittingly to their natures: *not only,* he says, *the most learned, but also the eldest of them, who established names for actions,* as reported by Theodotus in his *Excerpts*. <margin>History, fol. 348.</margin> In the beginnings, the entire genus of living things received their names in a long series from Adam the First-Formed <note>Greek: "Protoplaste".</note>, into whom from the very start of creation the knowledge of the Hebrew language was instilled. This was not natural, or arising from the principles or causes of human nature, but "preternatural," so to speak, because it was granted by the singular grace of God. Therefore, it was not propagated to children through natural generation, but it is necessary to learn it from Parents and receive it from the instruction of the breast. For no language after the Fall—neither Hebrew, nor Chaldean, nor Egyptian—is innate to any man, but it must be learned by learning, and languages must be learned as long as the world exists. # From Numbers XIII, v. 17.

## Sacred Onomatology
<margin>Sacred Onomatology <note>The study of the origin and meaning of names.</note></margin>
...if we wished to discuss this further, we would need a new book, especially since men of no small chair or reputation have performed this task before us, so that we can easily refrain from this labor. In proceeding, we place first the "onomathesia" <note>naming</note> of the First-Created, so that by considering the **onomatology** of the first man, we may always be reminded of our own beginning and origin.

Indeed, the nourishing Trinity, for a singular reason, assigned to the first of men the very lowly name **Adam** [אדם], as a lesson in humility. Named from the ground <note>Latin: *humus*</note>, and made from mud by the great condescension of God to His own dignity, man was made to be a living soul; and that he might be well, he was formed in the image of God. In the letters of **Adam** [אדם], the Cabbalists, through *Notarjekon* <note>a method of forming acronyms</note>, signify three princes: Adam the first-created through the letter *Aleph* [א], David through *Daleth* [ד], and the Messiah through *Mem* [מ]. Thus, according to the author Cyprian in his book *On the Mountains of Sinai and Sion against the Jews*, the first man received his name from the four quarters of the world, so that he was called **Adam**: **A** from *anatole* [ἀνατολὴ], i.e., the East; **D** from *dusis* [δύσις], the West; **A** from *arktos* [ἄρκτος], i.e., the North; and **M** from *mesembria* [Μεσημβρίαν], the South. Rabanus Maurus applauds this in *Book 1 on the Praises of the Holy Cross, f. 25* and *Book 2 on the Wood of the Holy Cross, l. 2. f. 66. b*, as does Cornelius Musso in the *Synod of Bitonto*. <margin>page 36.</margin> Adam, he says, was a vessel which that supreme Potter, sitting at His wheel, formed by taking mud from the four regions of the world. For this reason, he has four letters in his name, which in the Greek language speak of the four parts of the earth. *Therefore, while he fell broken and crushed, it is necessary that all of us, who were shattered with him as if by the mutual friction of vessels, be restored. This was indeed done by divine mercy, all the vessels having been gathered and fused together again into one by the fire of charity through Jesus Christ.* Certainly, in the judgment of Reuchlin, this is not to be blamed in the first author of this opinion, Cyprian, who wrote thus with a good heart and simple mind to stir up contemplation, even though it was never in the mind of the Author [God], or Moses; for in the Hebrew language, the name Adam imposed by God has only three letters. Furthermore, when the same holy man interprets Adam as "earth made flesh," he does so out of ignorance of the Holy Language [Hebrew], which he had not learned, just like many other holy Greek writers. So says Reuchlin. In the same way, among the Latins, *homo* [man] is said to be from *humus* [ground], not from *homou* [together], as Quintilian and C. Rhodiginus (*l. 2. Antiq.*) would have it. Scaliger (*de L. L. c. 28*) notes that Nonnus calls man "a simple thing from the androgynous dust." <margin>Oration on Cain and Abel, p. 33.</margin> And Basil of Seleucia says: *Adam was of double dust, and the earth was fashioned into the nature of men.* Adam, therefore, is common to all men and specific to the first man. In a broad sense, it encompasses both man and woman, so that sometimes it hints at both sexes together, *Gen. 1:27, c. 5:2*, although it is used separately for the male, and that more often, and occasionally for the female. Drusius makes this clear in his *Letter to Willem Baudartius (ad Sulp. p. 9. 10)*. Since these things are true, all the greater is the madness of a certain wicked "Light-shunner" <note>Lucifuga: one who avoids the light/truth</note>, born perhaps of a wicked woman or rather an abortion [*ektroma*], who dares to deny that the name of "man" [homo] applies to women. The womb of his mother was purer than the mouth of that wicked man! Blessed Gediccus answered that Alastor <note>an avenging spirit or demon</note> in a special book titled: *A Defense of the Female Sex, opposed to the most futile Disputation recently published, in which, the names of the author and printer being suppressed, it is blasphemously contended that women are not human beings, Leipzig 1595.* What no mortal has dared until now, this worthless slave dares with such foul and impious speech that he seems to have been raised in a pen among swine, worthy of being received with whips by harlots. With a filthy mouth, he boasts that he can prove from the Sacred Scriptures that a woman is not a human being, and that she is neither expressly nor implicitly called a human in them. Those trifles are easily dispelled by the fact that virgins are called "men" [Adam], *Num. 31:35*, a passage which Blessed Frantzius bids us to see and weigh carefully, because there virgins are most expressly called *Adam*, i.e., humans, so that it appears the disputation is vainer than vanity, as if women were not called humans in the Scriptures. Thus Christ is everywhere called the *Son of Man*, namely of His Mother Mary, the Blessed Virgin. The buffoon objects that Mary was a human not by nature, but by grace. Therefore, will the Messiah not be consubstantial with us who are humans by nature? Moreover, Adam, the first contemplator of the world, was made from the ground, not from the sun or heaven, but from the vilest earth, so that he might recognize himself as lowly and not seek high things. Mud is the beginning of our origin, and a daily mirror of our origin. From fragile mud comes smoke; because you see it daily before your eyes, remember, I pray, that you are mud and ash, and to be reduced to mud and ash. It was the custom to cast earth upon a grave, so that the origin from earth and the exit into earth might be noted. Bernard himself speaks of himself and this customary practice: *Clothed in priestly robes, I completed the usual prayers over him (the deceased Gerhard) with my own mouth; I threw earth with my own hands, according to custom, over the body of my beloved, which was soon to be earth.* Mindful of the ash, Bruno, Bishop of Meissen, ordered that when he felt death approaching, he should be placed outside his brothers upon ash, and there he lay humbly and breathed out his spirit with great contrition, as witnessed by Siffrid, Priest of Meissen, at the year 1304, p. 338. The word **Adam** [אדם] recognizes the root *adam* [אדם], "he was red," because the first man is believed to have been created from red earth. Whatever the case with this etymology, that name, says Blessed Simon Pauli, ought to be a constant sermon to us regarding our infirmity and immortality, and regarding humility, which, recognizing its origin from the dust of the earth and considering its own uncleanness and infirmity, truly fears God, does not exalt itself above others, keeps itself within the bounds of its calling, and seeks and expects help and happiness from God. Therefore, let him who hears, reads, or has the name of Adam always consider what it encompasses. Let him consider lest he be ignorant of his parent. Let it come to mind what our creation was in Adam. Man was created with the help of mud, and mud existed before man. So that the first man might take this to heart every day, God gave him the name Adam. Think then, little Adam, you who are proud and raise your crests beyond measure, whence you were born, and from what matter you were fashioned. Moses says, *God formed man* [אדם] *from the mud of the earth*. Why do you raise your crests above the mud? Recognize your birth, and ruminate on what happened in this miraculous birth. Recognize your Creator, from whose race you are descended. You are from mud, you live in mud, you are fed by mud. All things of the world are MUD, and if there were no mud, there would be no King, nor...

# SACRED ANTIQUITIES
