<margin>Sacred Onomatology <note>The study of the origins of names.</note></margin>
...neither emperor nor beggar. And into the mud—<margin>to the earth</margin>—into the very earth every man shall return, as Moses teaches in *Genesis 3:19*; and this by the force of the divine curse because of the preceding transgression of the Divine law regarding the forbidden tree. Adam, made from mud, truly became mud after the fall and the broken covenant, to whose violation all human miseries are imputed. Defiling himself and the entire race descending from him by his crime, that mud could not be washed away except through a new covenant, which was in Christ. Because no restorer could be found among mortals, Christ, the second Adam, was to be expected from heaven; He renewed the old mud of the ancient Adam and exchanged its dry and foul filth for a new richness, and its exhausted sterility for a new fertility.

->What Virgil says of *Aeneas* beholding the picture of Roman history formed upon his Shield:<-

> He marvels at it, and though ignorant of the events, he delights in the image.

The same may be said much more aptly of Eve, formed by God with wondrous workmanship and given to Adam. For this whole work is full of praise, so much so that wherever you turn your eyes, nothing offers itself but the image of a most perfect creature, the most perfect work of all works. A splendid image indeed, by which Adam, the <term>onomathetes</term> <note>Greek: "name-giver"</note>, though ignorant of the process of creation, yet not ignorant of the divine work, immediately knew his spouse intimately. This is shown by the name imposed upon her, *Eve* or *Chava*, from the root *chavah*: *he lived, he lived again, he was safe*. This denotes fertility or a living soul, which <term>onomatothesia</term> <note>Greek: "naming ceremony/act"</note> is expressly read in *Genesis 3:20*, where Adam is said to have called the name of his wife *Chava*, because she is the <term>mother of all living</term> <note>Latin: "mater omnis viventis"; Hebrew: "em kol-chai"</note>. She would have remained so, had she not allowed herself to be deceived by the fraud of the serpent; but having been deceived, she became the <term>mother of the dying</term>. Thus we received an inheritance from Eve, not of *Life* but of *Death*; we received from the eating of a single apple *Sin*, *Death*, and *Ashes*. She who was called *Mother of the Living* by Adam ought rather to have been called *Mother of the Dying*. To her, who could have lived forever, it was said: <margin>Gen. 3:19</margin> *Remember, O Man (Adam and Eve), that dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.* Weighing this more deeply, Broughton says <margin>in Concent of Scripture, p. 15</margin>: *On the occasion of the promise concerning the future blessed seed, Adam calls the woman LIFE; foreknowing that she, redeemed from death, would be the mother of children who through Christ would live eternally.* But if we go to the Rabbis, here too they admit their usual <term>lexe anothesia</term> <note>Greek: "senseless word-play"</note> and accept the Chaldean word *chivvah*, which means to indicate or to speak, as if the usual talkativeness of women were noted in her. One would have to be thoroughly soaked in Rabbinic liquor before acknowledging those <term>aloga</term> <note>Greek: "absurdities"</note> which *Baal Turim* nevertheless brought forth in these words: *Because she gives life, he called her name Chavah.* <margin>part 1. Philol. p. 303.</margin> To Majer, this seems a mere play of wit and a pleasant allusion to the character of the female sex, which can hardly restrain the tongue, nor press those words which the Poets call winged (<term>pteroenta</term>) behind the wall of white teeth once the feathers are plucked. But let those jesters play their shameful games. We wish none of this to be read here; much more shall we entreat those, if there be any who wish to read our writings, to spit upon those Rabbinic <term>adolechias</term> <note>Greek: "idle chatter/gossip"</note> regarding Eve's sad fall. Rather, we think the words of the excellent Polycarp Lyser should be reported here:

<column-break/>

In *Adam*, p. 319: *The ancients were not <term>aenigmatologoi</term> <note>Greek: "speakers in riddles"</note>, but often embraced many things in a single word; and just as the Jews had their Cabalas and the Egyptians their Hieroglyphics, in which, as if in enigmas and figures, they hid many mysteries of their religion; so Adam hid almost the entire sum of his faith and confession in this name of Eve. After he had noted the misery of the fall and the curse given therefrom, he noted from the blessing concerning the seed of the woman who would crush the serpent's head, that Adam seized upon those words, considered them attentively, and elicited from them that his posterity would live. Hence he called her whom he previously called Isha, "Eve," as if he had said: "You have indeed become the Mother of death by your fault, nor should any living person be born from you hereafter; but thanks be to GOD, the curse is lifted and the blessing restored, because God promised the seed which is to crush the Serpent's head, that is, which will take away that curse, THOU SHALT DIE THE DEATH, and in turn restore Life to us; and therefore you ought to be called Eve, because not only shall the living be born of YOU, but you are truly to be the Mother of those living forever."* <margin>Sacred Onomatology.</margin> These are pious meditations and to be piously observed by the pious: that Eve brought forth death before she brought forth offspring; she was the leader and teacher of transgression before she was the Mother of children. Basil of Seleucia <margin>Oration on Abel and Cain, p. 33</margin> introduces Adam and Eve as astonished at the first birth of Cain, as usually happens in a thing unexpected and never seen before, and therefore Eve called upon God the creator as a witness. *Having conceived, he says, she gave birth, not from the dust, not from a rib, but she sprouted from the belly. This overcame the parents with amazement. Eve saw a paradoxical sight, nature expanding with groans and bodies being enlarged, and she proclaims the miracle to the Creator as witness: "I have gained a man through God." She confesses the Maker, offering the work to God. She proclaims the Creator as the maker, not just a helper.* Eve feels the first pangs of childbirth when she brought forth Cain, a clearly "abortive" offspring <note>Meaning "failed" or "ruined" in a spiritual sense, rather than a miscarriage.</note>, in whom she first learns the curse of God by sad experience. Only Adam is present at the birth; he marvels at the bitterness of the pains; he hardly dares to move his hand amid the anxiety-bearing sorrows—he is Husband, Midwife, Servant, Father, and Godfather. Here at last Adam sees with trembling and wet eyes, and here Eve first felt within herself what profit there was in following the flattering voice of the serpent, and what it was to hear the thundering voice of God: <margin>Gen. 3:16</margin> *I will greatly multiply thy sorrow.* Those sorrows which He announced are now present with Cain, the son whom she brought forth in pain. Yet in these sorrows and torments, the anxious woman thinks of the Deliverer, of whom she had heard in the first promise. For she had learned from the mouth of the All-Wise Founder and most just Judge that a seed or son of the woman would one day be born, who would crush the head of the infernal Serpent, that is, the Devil, and overcome the force and power of hell: and thus he would be not only man, but also true God. Having heard this and fixed it most tightly in her mind as the foundation of life-giving consolation, she afterwards brought forth her <term>prototokon</term> <note>Greek: "firstborn"</note>. But once he was born, she began to make a poor application of the First Gospel <note>The "Protevangelium," the first promise of a Savior in Genesis 3:15.</note>, thinking that this son of hers was that promised seed of the woman, the Crusher of the Serpent's head...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of sacred naming conventions (Onomatologia sacra), specifically focusing on the naming of Cain and Abel as recorded in Genesis 4.</meta>

# On the Book of Numbers Chapter XIII, verse 17.

<margin>
Sacred Naming (Onomatologia sacra).
</margin>
...the Savior and <term>Redeemer</term> <note>original Greek: λυτρωτὴν</note> of the human race, and that she specifically was his chosen mother, that woman of whom God had spoken in the First Gospel <note>The "Protevangelium" refers to Genesis 3:15, the first promise of a Savior.</note>. Whence Eve, out of joy at the birth of her firstborn, exclaims, saying: *Genesis 4:1.* <term>I have acquired a man—the Lord</term> <note>original Hebrew: קניתי איש את - יהוה (Kaniti ish et-Jehovah)</note>, *I have acquired or possessed the man Jehovah*, and by that very act she bestows the name <term>Cain</term> <note>Hebrew: קן (Kain)</note> upon her firstborn son. For our venerable ancestors, especially those of the first age, were devoted to this: giving names to their children by which either a remarkable event might be noted, or an inexpressible outcome might be foretold. From the very first memory, the first humans Adam and Eve appear, who gave their firstborn the name *Cain*; but in the reasoning for this name there is some controversy and doubt among the learned. There is indeed no doubt as to the origin, for it comes from <term>to acquire</term> <note>Hebrew: קנה (Kanah)</note>, *he acquired*, but regarding the reason why he was called by it, not everyone is of one mouth and one language. Compare the Blessed Gerhard, *Commentary on Genesis chapter 4, page 128*; the Blessed Glassius, *Mosaic Christology, Dissertation 5, thesis 2, 3, page 143*; the Blessed Hackspan, *Theological Notes on Genesis chapter 4, page 101*. Let us hear our "Great Man" Luther on this matter, who * feels thus: <margin>Commentary on this place, folio 70, verso.</margin> *That Eve clings so tightly to the divine promise, and to the faith of the future liberation through her seed, she does rightly. For by this faith in the future seed, all the saints were justified and sanctified. But she errs in the specific individual; she believes Cain will be the one to put an end to the calamities into which Satan had cast man through sin. But she believes this by her own opinion, without a certain sign and without a certain word. The promise was indeed certain and true, but nothing had been signified regarding the individual—whether it would be Cain or Abel who was to be that Victor over the Serpent. Therefore, when she decides on the individual, Eve is deceived, and in vain she bestows such a proud and joyful name on her son. For the text shows that he was called Cain from the verb Kanah, which means to possess or acquire, so that by this name she might console herself against the evils received, and oppose the acquisition of life and salvation through the seed to the loss of life and salvation through sin and Satan. As if to say: I remember what we lost through sin, but now let us hope for and speak of nothing but recovery and acquisition. For I have acquired the man of GOD, who will acquire again for us that lost glory. The excessive certainty of the promise makes Eve hurry, and think this first son is the one of whom the Lord promised. But the miserable woman is deceived; she does not yet sufficiently see her own calamity—that from the flesh nothing but flesh can be born, and that through flesh and blood, sin and death cannot be conquered. Furthermore, she does not know the point in time at which that blessed seed, conceived by the Holy Spirit, is to be born into the world through a virgin.* In the same manner write the Blessed Heerbrand: *Eve,* he says, *the first <margin>Oration on the Nativity of the Lord, page 14.</margin> mother, when her firstborn was born, broke out into these words from excessive joy: I have acquired the man, the Lord Jehovah himself. And therefore she called him Cain, that is, a <term>treasure</term> <note>original Greek: κειμήλιον</note> or a wealth itself, judging that this promised seed was the Lord, the crusher of the Serpent's head. But the miserable mother was foully mistaken, though it was a pious error. She understood the matter from the published promise. But the error was committed regarding the person. For Cain was not the seed of the mother-woman (that is, the Virgin), but of the man Adam and a married woman. And the tragic outcome—which is the teacher of fools—following afterward, taught Eve to understand the divine Oracle more correctly.* And the Blessed <margin>part 1, page 105.</margin> Simon Pauli in his Method of the Places of Doctrine *:

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Naming (Onomatologia sacra).</margin>
*Eve, who is the first mother of all men, burning with faith in the promise of the coming seed, and seething with desire and expectation for the promised Redeemer, when her firstborn son Cain was born, exclaims: Now I have acquired a man, who is <term>Jehovah</term> <note>Hebrew: יהוה</note>, thinking she had already given birth to that promised Lord, endowed with a divine nature, who would both crush the head of the serpent and, having finished with sin and death, would restore true righteousness and eternal life in human nature. However, although Eve errs both regarding the Person and the point in time at which the promised Redeemer ought to be born, she nevertheless indicates her faith and her burning desire to see the Messiah; and at the same time, she accuses that sad stupor of our own hearts, which, colder than winter ice and harder than Caucasian rocks, can scarcely be moved to conceive some tiny spark or little flame of love toward the Messiah already revealed and born and given to us.* Certainly, it can seem a paradox that the first mother of all living, who was so clearly taught by Jehovah himself in person, should have made such a great error. But she wandered in this: that she thought she herself would be the Mother of the Mother <note>This likely refers to her thinking she was the immediate mother of the Savior mentioned in the prophecy.</note> in that specific instance, and that he would be born according to the common course of Nature; meanwhile, she felt correctly in this: that the Messiah would be true man and true God. She had heard that the Messiah would be the seed of the woman; that he would be the Son of a Virgin, she as yet did not know, or certainly did not consider. It is likely, therefore, that she looked back to the promise given after the fall concerning the seed of the woman who would crush the head of the Serpent, as if she saw in her son the one who would crush and destroy the serpent's head. If this was an error, it was a holy error, by which she manifested her most ardent desire, so much so that crying out she said: *I have possessed the Man-Lord*. But she possessed the first villain of the whole world, who, after the fall, stood as the cause of all sorrow and pain for his mother and father; he was <term>mud soaked in blood</term> <note>original Greek: πηλὸς αἵματι πεφυραμένΘ</note>, as the teacher Theodorus of Gadara had elsewhere said of the cruelty of Tiberius—one who lacked a sword, but not the skill and machinery for striking and killing. In him, truth was first corrupted, the way of life perverted, idol-madness introduced, and all laws, both divine and human, violated. Then, in place of punishment and vengeance, being cast out from the face of the Lord, he wandered on the earth. The eastern region of Eden, in which he settled, ought to be called the region of impiety on account of the "Cainism" established there. Indeed, Sedulius joins Cain and Judas the betrayer as a "noble pair of brothers," when <margin>Collection of the Old and New Testament, verse 9.</margin> he says:

> The brother was wicked, who once struck down the just;
> The betrayer of Christ was also a wicked brother.

Eve, as has been said thus far, applied that august name of the Messiah, <term>Jehovah</term> <note>Hebrew: יהוה</note>, to her firstborn Cain; but to the other, and indeed the fourth human inhabitant of the terrestrial globe, she gave the name <term>Abel</term> <note>Hebrew: הבל (Habel)</note>, commonly called Habel, which word by reason of its etymology signifies vanity, or a thing of nothing, abject and vain. And without doubt (as the Blessed Brentius thinks) he was so called by his parents because they looked down on him in comparison to Cain; as if to say: "this one is vanity, he is a man who will do nothing memorable; but the other, Cain, will bravely manage his affairs as the Messiah and Liberator of the world." Those who are worthy of their name are called <term>eponymous</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπώνυμοι</note> by the Greeks, as Sophocles testifies: *Pentheus, eponymous of misfortune* <note>A pun on the Greek 'penthos' meaning grief/sorrow.</note>.

It contrasts this "holy error" of faith with Cain's eventual status as the first murderer and a figure of vanity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of biblical genealogy and the etymology of the names of the first patriarchs, following the account of Adam and Cain.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
Page 230

<margin>Sacred Name-study.</margin>
That which could be said here of Abel *by name* <note>original: "ἐπωνύμως" (eponymously)</note>, as a man of his own name (as the expression goes in Spartianus), would be this: Abel was the fore-demonstrator of misery and necessities. Nothing could have been said more fittingly regarding the things that happened, nor more conveniently, than what the interpretation derived from that name designates. No other name, nor that first calamity of the age, was better suited by a speech than that heard from the most sorrowful Iphigenia in Euripides:
<margin>*Iphigenia in Aulis*, v. 1330.</margin>
> Truly it was a race of much toil,
> a race of much toil for mortals. <note>original Greek: "ἡ πολύμοχθον ἄρ’ ἦν γένος, ἡ πολύμοχθον ἀμερίων."</note>

How much more significantly, then—how much more effectively, how much more clearly, I say—did Adam bestow this name on him than on Cain! For after the first man had made a divorce from God, to whom he had pledged his faith in the covenant entered into, only then did he see into what vanity and misery he had cast himself. By this path and reason he gives the name to his Son, having experienced *Hebel* <note>original Hebrew: הבל</note>, vanity. Philo brings forward a secondary etymology from *Abel* <note>original Hebrew: אבל</note>, meaning "he mourned, grieved, or lamented," so as to derive *Hebel* or *Abel* from it—not strictly according to the name's form, but according to the reality. For the first man had cast himself, and at the same time all his sons and posterity, into mourning. The First-Created ones were cast into mourning because of the first fratricide
<margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, 11. 4.</margin>
perpetrated upon Abel; whence Eusebius thinks Abel was so named because he was the cause of immense sadness to his parents: *Abel is interpreted as "mourning," having become such through his suffering, and being himself the cause for his parents, who, seeing certain more divine forewarnings happening to their children, bestowed these names upon them.* <note>original Greek: "Ὁ μὲν Ἄβελ ἑρμηνεύεται πένθος..."</note>
<margin>Lyser, *Adam*, p. 366.</margin>
The Blessed Lyser aims at the first etymology, saying: *When the second son was born, he gave him the name of Abel, from vanity; for both parents remember the vanity which exerts itself not only in calamities, but also in thoughts and deeds; for we are all useless, and we walk in the vanity of our senses; whence those emphatic scriptural sayings in David were later taken: "Col Adam, Col Habel." Every living man is like Abel, altogether vanity, passing like a shadow. And Solomon: "Habel Habelim, col Habel." Vanity of vanities, and all is Vanity. Therefore the first parents confess and deplore Original Sin, because of which both they and this Son are subject to vanity and destruction.*
<margin>Nieremberg, *Sacred Miscellany*, 3. 1. p. 2.</margin>
Nieremberg looks toward both meanings, and we cite his words to this end: *He granted him the fitting name Abel, that is, vanity and vapor. Human joys are very brief and lack substance. All joy of mortals is vain. The happiness of the wretched is vain. What is not vain to man, when he himself is most vain, of whom it is said, "Every living man is altogether vanity"? All things belonging to him cannot but be vain, who is himself altogether Vanity. Abel also signifies mourning, born after the joy of the first-born Son, since mourning follows human joys, nor is there any happiness so lucky that no grief misfortunes it. No joy is without snares, no exultation without sorrow. Furthermore, Abel was the cause of mourning to his parents. In him were dedicated innocence, patience, and tears. He was the first of those of whom it was said: "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted." He is the leader of those who, desiring the heavenly city, mourn over the miseries of this habitation.* Moreover, both sons are an image of those things which are carried out daily in the world. Those who live piously experience the lot of Abel—

<column-break/>

namely hatred, envy, persecution, malevolence, and death. What else are the truly pious but Abel and *Hebel* <note>original Hebrew: הבל</note>: thin, wretched, abject, despised by the world, and held in hatred? But the impious are Cain, who take their name from "possessing," and they exercise dominion in the world, possess the goods of the earth, live in delights, and do all things according to their own desire.
<margin>Sacred Name-study.</margin>
Concerning the Son whom God had given to the First-Created in place of the slain Abel, Eve says: *God has appointed for me another Seed, instead of Abel, whom Cain killed.* It should be noted that "Seed" <note>original Greek: "τὸ Semen"</note> is spoken of here as one, though it is more often said of many. Thus "the seed of the woman" <note>original Greek: "τὸ σπέρμα τῆς γυναικὸς"</note> encompasses the Messiah alone in Genesis 3:15. So also regarding Ishmael in Genesis 21:13, the speech of God to Abraham is: *For he is your seed* <note>original Hebrew: כי זרעך הוא</note>, *because I will make the son of the bondwoman into a nation,* etc. The most beautiful name which she gives to her Son is *Seth* <note>original Hebrew: שת</note>, meaning "placed" or "founded," so called from "placing," which draws its origin from *shith* or *shuth* <note>original Hebrew: שית / שות</note>, "he placed, he founded." For this is that unique son in whom the promise of the future Messiah is founded, whose posterity could not be blotted out by the Cainites, and who was the unique *Staff* of his most afflicted parents, Abel having long since been extinguished by the sad fratricide, and the most wicked Cain, that most pestilential fratricide, having been turned to flight by God and rejected from the family of the pious. But Seth, when he had already completed his hundredth year, fathered a Son, whom he called *Enos* <note>original Hebrew: אנוש</note>. Now, Enos signifies *man*, and specifically a *wretched* one, by which name the pious man wished to remind himself of the miseries of this life, and to rouse himself to the hope of perpetual happiness by aspiring to the heavenly life. Whence Musculus says in his commentary on Genesis: *Enos signifies a man who is miserable, wretched, and calamitous. This seems to have been the understanding of Seth. Although he himself was placed and founded by God to be, as it were, the head of the generation of the pious, he nevertheless prudently recognized that his descendants in this age would be subject to various calamities and miseries. And indeed, until the end of the world, there will be no other lot for the elect while they live in this flesh than to be "Anashim," that is, wretched and afflicted.* But Eusebius in *Preparation for the Gospel* (if it is right to believe Gregor Frank in the book cited below, although in book 7, chapter 3, page 144, where Eusebius deals with Enos, none of these things can be found) derives Enos from *nashah* <note>original Hebrew: נשה</note>, from "forgetting," because he is quickly led into oblivion; and he proves this notation from Psalm 8:5, so that Enos is like one who is *forgetful* <note>original Greek: "ἐπιλήσμων"</note>. But this is an allusion rather than a true etymology. The true etymology of it is from *anash* <note>original Hebrew: אנש</note>, "he grieved, he was lethally sick, he labored under a desperate disease," the synonym of which is *nus* <note>original Hebrew: נוס</note>, whence comes the Greek *nosos* (disease) and *noseros* (sickly), as noted by Gregor Frank in his *Sacred Lexicon*. <margin>Root 207, p. 256.</margin> Nevertheless, this "wretched one" came to the aid of the world, and in it to the wretched and calamitous human race, by the public preaching and announcement of the divine word. For whatever he had learned about God from his Grandfather and Father within private walls, he communicated to many others, and strongly opposed the idolatry of the Cainites. For that reason it was said by Moses: *Then it was begun to call upon the name of Jehovah.* That is, the public Ministry was instituted, and as the Blessed Luther translates it: *At that time they began to preach of the name of the Lord.* A gymnasium or public school was first opened, says the Blessed Christian Matthias in *Patriarchal History*, p. 86, in which the true religion of God might sound forth, and the people might be instructed concerning the true Jehovah (that is, concerning the true God and the promised Messiah).

<summary>This page explores the etymological and theological significance of the names Abel, Seth, and Enos, linking their meanings to the human condition of vanity, mourning, and the eventual establishment of public worship.</summary>
<keywords>Abel, Seth, Enos, etymology, vanity, mourning, original sin, public ministry, Messiah, Genesis, Philo, Eusebius, Luther</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of sacred names (Onomatology) and the lineage of the early Patriarchs, focusing on the transition from Enosh to Noah.</meta>

# From Numbers XIII. v. 17.

<margin>
Sacred Onomatology <note>The study of the meaning and origin of names.</note>.
</margin>
For previously Adam, Abel, and Seth taught how to call upon the name of God, but they did so privately within their households. However, after Enosh grew up, the name of the Lord began to be called upon in groups within Church assemblies, employing rites that were not human inventions, but divinely instituted. For "will-worship" <note>original: θεοθρησκεία (theothreskeia); refers to self-imposed religious practice not commanded by God.</note> never pleased God, *Isaiah 1 v. 12, Matthew 15:9.* To this belongs the distinguished explanation of the Blessed Luther <margin>on Genesis chapter 4, verse 26.</margin> *Luther’s words are: "After confusion was brought into the house of Adam through Cain, the generation of the pious also gradually multiplied and a Church was prepared, in which Adam governed all things as a High Priest through the Word and sound doctrine. Moses says this began during the birth of Enosh; although his name signifies that the Church was then oppressed by a great calamity, God nevertheless raised it up again through grace and mercy, and added this spiritual blessing: that they should meet in a certain place to teach, pray, and sacrifice—things which had perhaps been forbidden or hindered until then by the Cainites."*

To Enosh was born a son, to whom he gave the name קינן <note>Kenan</note>, whose etymology some derive from קנה <note>kanah</note>, *he possessed*, as if he were the heir of the promise. Others derive it from קינה <note>qinah</note>, *to lament*, because it best suits the most miserable life of men. To him was born a son מהללאל <note>Mahalalel</note>, that is, *praiser of God* or *celebrator*, from הלל <note>halal</note>, *he praised*; this was bestowed by his parent Kenan because of the moderate state of the Church, which at that time began to breathe a little after its affliction. Following him <margin>Sacred History p. 20.</margin> is ירד <note>Jared</note>, *descending*, from ירד <note>yarad</note>, *he descended*, on account of a double descent of God—either of grace, or of glory and vengeance; or from רדה <note>radah</note>, *he ruled*, on account of the Church's happy <margin>Disputations on Scripture p. 181 ff.</margin> dominion in the world and its propagation, as Jodocus Capellus notes. חנוך <note>Enoch</note>, *consecrated* <note>original: μεμυημένος (memuemenos)</note> and *initiated to God*, from חנך <note>chanak</note>, *he dedicated*; an outstanding and most excellent type of Christ, whom <insert>*</insert> Blessed Glassius explains extensively and elegantly. מתושלח <note>Methuselah</note> *Mosaic.* <note>Referring to the Mosaic account.</note> *Then* למך <note>Lamech</note>, which they explain as *the dart of death*, derived from מות <note>mut</note>, *death* and שלח <note>shalach</note>, *he sent*. And the son whom he left here, Lamech, obtained his name from thinning out and poverty, since the poor, oppressed, and humble please God, while the proud and lofty displease Him. Certainly, the name bestowed upon Noah was not inauspicious, being suited to the outcome; he is recognized as a comforter in reality, concerning whom the words of *Lamech* sound thus: *Genesis 5:29.* זה ינחמנו ממעשנו — *This one shall comfort us from our work.* That the name fits Noah most correctly is clearer than needs pointing out; but the reason for the name given by Moses is not so clear. For if we weigh the name in a just balance, נח <note>Noach</note> comes from נוח <note>nuach, "to rest"</note> rather than from נחם <note>nacham, "to comfort"</note>, which is why the Greeks, moved by this, translated it: *This one will give us rest* <note>original: οὗτος διαναπαύσει ἡμᾶς (houtos dianapausei hemas)</note>, adhering strictly to the notation and etymology. But the Hebrews incline more toward the latter, so that it seems to them a loss of the letter ם <note>m</note> occurred. According to this, *Noah* denotes a *comforter* or refresher; according to the former, a *giver of rest*. Between these two there is a great kinship, for he who comforts does so by providing rest, and he who provides this has performed the office of a comforter excellently. This doubt invites us not to be content with these things but to be held by a desire for what the Interpreters have. While the accurate searcher of words, Mercerus, examines the text, he writes: *"Many difficulties occur here. First, the reason for the name given: which is brought here by Moses, does not seem to correspond to the name itself, namely נח, because ינחמנו (he will comfort us) is from the root נחם (to comfort); whereas the name is from the root נוח (to rest), where neither the root nor the meaning matches. For it seemed it should have been said, זה יניחנו (this one will make us rest) from our work. But the Hebrew word ינחמנו means to console, not to make rest. Or certainly, if we look at the logic of the word, he should rather have been called נחם (Nacham), the Comforter, to which the reason would fit perfectly: For this one will comfort us."* Having exploded the opinion of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note>, who explained the word through diaeresis, as well as the opinions of others, he proceeds: *“We say that here there is only an allusion of words, not a reason sought from the etymology of the name, because the verb נחם is close to the name נח in both sound and meaning; for when the reason for the name נח is brought forth as 'this one ינחמנו (will comfort us),' it is exactly as if he had said 'יניחנו (will make us rest),' because the sense falls back to the same thing, and he who consoles relieves the trouble."* Therefore he also subjoined the ablative with the preposition מ <note>from</note> having taken the verb ינחמנו into account; for with "he will console us," "from our labor" does not fit so aptly; as if to say: Consoling us, he will at the same time make us rest from our labor, he will provide us rest from our labor and hardship, he will lighten our labor.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred Onomatology.
</margin>
So also Jerome <margin>Questions on Genesis ch. 5.</margin> *“He called his name Noah, saying: He will make us rest from our works. Therefore, from the fact that under him all previous works rested through the flood, he was called Rest.”* He took these things from Origen, whom he is accustomed to imitate often for entire books; see Origen's Homily 2 on Genesis, where he accommodates those words of Lamech to the spiritual Noah, that is, Christ Jesus, who truly gave rest to men and bore the sins of the world. But regarding that: *“Because Jehovah cursed the earth.”* The earth itself paid the penalty because Adam sinned. Let us consider the words brought forth by the angry God Himself to Adam in *Genesis 3:17:* ארורה האדמה בעבורך, *Cursed is the ground because of you.* By clear signs, the words do not allow us to doubt that the earth was exposed to a curse on account of Adam, which we would not understand so clearly if we go to the Greek and Latin translations, who, led elsewhere by the similarity of the letters ר <note>R</note> and ד <note>D</note>, distort it with a foreign sound; for without doubt they read בעבורך <note>on your account</note> as something else, while one translator has: *In your work*, and the other *in your works* <note>original: ἐν τοῖς ἔργοις σου (en tois ergois sou)</note>. Which then shall we follow, this one or that? Neither. What Theodotion has alludes more closely: *in your transgression* <note>original: ἐν τῇ διαβάσει σου (en te diabasei sou)</note>, as if it were from עבר <note>avar</note>, which means to transgress. If they read it thus in their Codices, it was erroneously transcribed by the scribes. Whatever they devise of this and similar things is certainly not to be entirely despised, but with Mercerus we know that *“the simplest reading is what is read in Hebrew today, which we do not doubt was also held formerly, although it was either read differently (as often happens by the similarity of letters) or understood as* בעבורך *'on your account,' that is, your sin.”* What Bellarmine might devise here to veil the error <note>original: παράραμα (pararama)</note> of the ancient translator is weighed by Sixtinus Amama, until he finally ends in these words: *“These things are futile, and stuffed with blemishes.”* What Ludovicus Capellus might conjecture, the Anti-Critic Buxtorf <margin>& Vindication part 2, ch. 11, p. 784</margin> will show, where he also explains Jerome’s gloss. He [Noah] suffered no small calamities both before and after the cataclysm of the world. Before the flood, with great grief and sickness of mind, he saw the monstrous impiety of Lamech, arising from the progeny of Cain, who as the first polygamist violated domestic society and spread the union of two souls, which God had established between man and woman, into multiple loves, *Genesis 4:19, 23, 24.* He saw...

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Onomatology. Gen. 6:4.</margin>
...[Noah] beheld the untamed license, lewdness, and levity of the impious (*Gen. 6:2*). He saw the ferocity of the monstrous giants and the most cruel tyrants. Finally, he saw the accursed hypocrisy of all those who, under the title of "Sons of God," maintained a <note>original: "μόρφωσιν εὐσεβείας"</note> form of godliness while degenerating from true piety toward God; they devised and did nothing but evil. After the flood, he experienced the mockery and insult of his younger son Ham (*Gen. 9:22*). He saw and felt the tyranny and insolence of Nimrod (*Gen. 10:3*). He turned away from the foolish recklessness and pride of the sons of this age, who wished to build a great Tower whose top might reach heaven itself (*Gen. 11:3*). Finally, he deplored the confusion of tongues and the wretched dispersion of the nations. Truly, Noah sustained each and every one of these <margin>Gen. 11:7, 8.</margin> hardships of that morose age with incredible patience and constancy, not allowing himself to be broken by the deceit of heretics or the violence of tyrants. Instead, he bravely opposed the scandals and impiety of men, and cultivated true religion with such care that no one can doubt but that he labored with the greatest zeal for the 350 years he lived after the cataclysm to sow the true doctrine of divine worship among his sons and grandsons. So much so, that even those who separated from him could not help but retain some "fringes" of the doctrine they had received, although they greatly obscured it, as has been said by us elsewhere. Noah was the first parent of all men born after the flood, whose firstborn was <note>original: "ἢν"</note> indeed <note>original: "יפת"</note> Japheth, "the enlarged one," or he who was to be spread out. For this is the interpretation of the name, to which that word-play prophecy of Noah looks: <note>original: "יפת אלהים ליפת"</note> *May God enlarge Japheth* <margin>Gen. 9:27.</margin> a place of dwelling.

Wonderful is that blessing of Noah with which he adorned Japheth and his race. Regarding the meaning of "enlarging," they accept that *Japheth* comes from the Chaldee language now prevailing, which adopted it from the Hebrew language, about which Barth. Mayer <margin>2. Philol. S. p. 299.</margin> has this to say: *If the name Japheth took its name from "breadth," it must be said that Noah drew that word from Chaldaism. If we embrace this, the Chaldean language would yield nothing to Hebrew in terms of antiquity. But the answer is easy. The word <note>original: "פתה"</note> "pathah" has a double meaning: in the simple form (Kal), it means he enticed or was persuaded; in the intensive form (Piel), he enticed or deceived by flattering. But in the causative form (Hiphil), it obtains the meaning of "enlarging," which meaning flourishes most in the Aramaic language and is very frequent in it. Therefore, Noah did not use a Chaldean idiom, but the Chaldeans, after the confusion of tongues, translated this somewhat rarer meaning of the word "pathah" from Hebrew into their own idiom and used it most frequently, so that it now seems more Aramaic than Hebrew.* God enlarged Japheth and granted him a wider habitation in the world, which Fuller treats more extensively in his *Miscellanies*, showing how wide and ample a region fell to him. That breadth of nations was more fortunate because his gathering into the tents of Shem is predicted. Who could explain in worthy ways this divine benefit, which is encompassed in the name itself, and from which Noah elicited the matter of his blessing? Who could follow its utility, spreading itself most widely through all Japhetic possessions, with sufficient elegance <margin>Questions on Genesis.</margin> and richness of speech? We shall not even attempt to approach it, being content now with the words of Jerome:

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Onomatology.</margin>
From Shem the Hebrews are born, from Japheth the people of the Gentiles. Because, therefore, the multitude of believers is broad, the name "breadth" was taken from the width which is called Japheth. *But as for what he says, "And let him dwell in the tents of Shem," this is prophesied of us, who, after Israel was cast out, are occupied in the learning and knowledge of the Scriptures.* However many of us inhabit Europe, we are the sons of Japheth. Moses enumerates seven grandsons of Japheth: three from Gomer and four from Javan. Josephus makes the Gauls the descendants of the former: <note>original: "τοὺς μὲν γὰρ ὑφ' Ἑλλήνων, Γαλάτας καλουμένους, Γομαρεῖς δὲ λεγομένους, Γομάρος ἔκτισε" — "For Gomer founded those whom the Greeks now call Galatians [Gauls], but were then called Gomerites."</note>. William Camden agrees with this opinion when dealing with the first inhabitants of Britain, making them Britons themselves, whose words are: *Gomer, the eldest son of Japheth, gave both origin and name to the Gomerians, who were afterwards called Cimbri and Cimmerians in these furthest ends of Europe. For the name of the Cimbri or Cimmerians in a way filled this part of the world, and was most widely extended not only in Germany but also in Gaul. I have always thought that our BRITONS derived their origin from these Gomerians or Gomerites and brought the name as an argument of their origin; for they call themselves Kumero, Cymro, and Kumeri. From where else, I ask, should we think these names flowed, than from that Gomer, and the Gomerians in nearby Gaul, which was the seat of the ancient Gomerians?* From the other son of Japheth, Javan, come the Greeks: for you will derive <note>original: "Ἰάων"</note> Iaon and <note>original: "Ἰῶν"</note> Ion and Ionian with little trouble, just as <note>original: "מצד"</note> becomes Cimmerian. By translating the Hebrew letter <note>original: "נ"</note> "Nun" into a related letter, there come the <note>original: "כרתים"</note> Kittim, <margin>Gen. 10:4.</margin> who were so famous that the Prophets named the principal nations in Europe "Chittim."

Concerning Ham, the youngest of the sons of Noah, there is not much for us to say, except that which was said of old: *from white Ham is born the dark Cush*, the cause of which variety the interpreters commonly derive from the curse. Because Ham had held the simple and harmless nakedness of his father in mockery, therefore the mark of perpetual darkness and blackness, or certainly a lurid color such as is seen in that nation, was branded upon his firstborn and his grandsons. For the heat of the sun alone is prevented from being the cause of that blackness by the multitude of nations living under the same climate whom no such thing disfigures, says Gregor. Franc. *Lex S. p. 138. cf. Postell. Comp. Cosmogr. p. 17. 18. 37. seqq.*

Shem, if we follow the biblical order, is the first among the sons of Noah, not by birth, but by piety toward God and his parent; in the Hebrew tongue he is called "praised" or "celebrated." Since <note>original: "שמו"</note> *Shemo* in the sacred writings often <margin>Gen. 6:4.</margin> denotes the fame and celebrity of someone, <note>original: "אנשי השם"</note> *Anshe ha-shem*, *Men of name*, i. e., *most famous, most celebrated; Greek: ἄνθρωποι ὀνομαστοὶ, named men, i. e., noble, famous*. Luther explains it as *Famous People*. Otherwise *Notable People*. Whence Blessed Luther says of Seth and Shem: *Seth and Shem were in great honor among the people*. Among his descendants was <note>original: "עבר"</note> Eber, *one who passes over or a pilgrim*, from <note>original: "עבר"</note> *abar*, *he passed over*, so called, from whom the Hebrews descend (if we follow Augustine *City of God book 16 ch. 11* and others), and the Hebrew language, as it was propagated in his family through Peleg, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and the rest. For Noah, Shem, Eber and others never conspired in the wicked...

# From Numbers XIII, v. 17.

<margin>Sacred Onomatology (Study of Names).</margin>
<margin>Book 16 of The City of God, chapter 3.</margin>
They did not consent with the builders of the [Tower of] Babel and the confusion of tongues, and therefore they studiously preserved Hebrew as the ancient and primary language, holily cherished it, and transmitted it to posterity, as if passed through their hands from the Fathers, as the treasury of the true religion. Augustine treats this at length in several places*, where he especially urges, among other things, the words of Moses in *Genesis 10:21*, *Shem is the Father of all the children of Eber*. Whose firstborn received the name <term>Peleg (פלג)</term>, <note>Greek: Phalek (φαλέκ)</note>, because during the time of his birth the division of languages occurred, and the dispersion of Nations into all parts of the earth, *Gen. 10:25; 11:16; 1 Chronicles 1:19.* And thus the name was given not from a future event, as the Rabbis prefer in the *Seder Olam*, but from that which had already happened, <term>for he was born at the very breaking up of the settlement</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπειδὴ γὰρ τῷ ἀποδεσμῷ τῆς οἰκήσεως τίκτεται</note>, as it also seemed to Josephus in *Antiquities, book 1, chapter 7, page 15.* To whom the <term>breaking up</term> <note>Greek: ἀποδεσμός</note> or distribution of lands was occasioned by the diversity of languages, and the division of languages was caused by the *building of the Tower of Babel*.

We now make our descent to Abraham, that greatest Father of Christ, to whom, after the first-created parents, the promise of the Blessed Seed was first made*, omitting those who came before. He had a double name: <term>Abram (אברם)</term> without the letter <term>He (ה)</term> (that is, without the aspiration), which name signifies *Exalted or High Father*, from <term>Ab (אב)</term> Father and <term>Ram (רם)</term> *exalted, lofty, high*. But when <margin>Genesis 18:13.</margin> God instituted the Sacrament of Circumcision and entered into a covenant with Abraham, He changed his name and called him <term>Abraham (אברהם)</term>, inserting the letter <term>He (ה)</term>, which is the same as *Father of a multitude or Father of many Nations*; this letter <term>He (ה)</term> was taken from the word <term>Hamon (המון)</term>, *multitude*. Prudentius provides another reason for this etymology in his Preface*:

<margin>verse 2.</margin>
> ->Abram, fierce Father of a blessed seed,<-
> ->Whose name an added syllable increased,<-
> ->Called Abram by his parent, Abraham by God.<-

<margin>page 859.</margin>
Where the Glosses of Ivo* state: *The Hebrews say that God gave the letter* <term>He (ה)</term> *from His own name, which among them is the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter holy name of God, YHWH</note>, to Abraham, so that he who was previously called Exalted Father might afterwards be called the Father of many (it is understood) peoples or nations.* Compare on this matter the Bohemian *Hebrew Grammar, p. 54*; Venetus in *Problems, book 2, problem 8*; and from him Camartus on *Elias, ch. 4, p. 165*; Nieremberg *S.S. 97, 98*; Casaubon *Exercise 13, p. 188*; Crefoll. *Sacred Anthology, ch. 6, p. 165.* Basil—truly <term>Basileios</term> <note>A pun on his name meaning "Royal"</note>—writes that suitable names are a proof of the natural talent or virtue implanted by God in the pious Patriarchs, in his *Sermon on the Nativity of Christ: To those whom He gives names, the naming contains an indication of their underlying nature, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Israel. To each of these, the designation revealed the character or the specific excellence achieved by them rather than a physical trait.* This <term>change</term> <note>Greek: μεταβολὴν</note> made by <term>divine providence</term> <note>Greek: ϑείᾳ προνοίᾳ</note> (to use the words of Phaniss. v. 639) is imitated with detestable <term>perversity</term> <note>Greek: κακοζηλίᾳ</note> by the *Circumcised* <note>A derogatory term for contemporary Jews</note>, who, reading what was done by divine counsel regarding the changing of names, are accustomed to imitate it <term>superstitiously</term> <note>Greek: απνυ ϑριασμένως</note>, hoping for some help from it. For Menasseh <margin>On the Term of Life, book 1, section 8, p. 107, 108.</margin> Ben-Israel* teaches that it is familiar to the Hebrews to change a name when they are placed in extreme danger of life; and this is usually done by them in the synagogue with a certain singular ceremony.

Isaac, <term>Yitzhak (יצחק)</term>, <term>Isaac (Ἰσαὰκ)</term>, is a name of obvious significance, for since the reason for it is given by Sarah herself,

<column-break/>

it would be a matter of impudence to doubt it; for she said in *Gen. 21:3, 6*, <term>Tzahak (צחק)</term> *God has made me laugh. Whoever hears will laugh with me*. Anyone will see how fitting this is when the "laughter" that gave rise to this name is summarized. Abraham had laughed in *Gen. 17:17* upon hearing God's promise of receiving a son from Sarah. Sarah had laughed*, and then denied that she laughed. All laugh who hear that the old woman Sarah triumphed over all old women and conceived in a wrinkled womb, *Gen. 21:6.* And I do not know whether the laughter and mocking of Ishmael contributes to the present business? The use of the word <term>Tzahak (צחק)</term> is clear in the sense of laughing, or even deriding, whence comes <term>Tzahak</term>, *laughter*. This at least seems to deserve note: we find the name Isaac written either with a <term>Tzade (צ)</term> or with a <term>Shin (ש)</term>. From this arises a rule about the name Isaac, which Blessed Matthias gives in *History of the Patriarchs, p. 226*, saying: *When the name Isaac is written with* <term>צ</term> *it is a proper name and everywhere denotes Isaac the Son of Abraham; but when it is written with* <term>ש</term>*, it is found in four places of Scripture: in two it is used as a proper name, namely Psalm 105:8-9 and Jeremiah 33:26; but in two places it is a patronymic name and signifies the Israelite people descending from Isaac, Amos 7:6, 16.* How the History of Isaac is an image of the Savior is taught through long detours in his usual manner by Diego de Baeza in *Allegorical and Moral Commentaries on Christ, book 3, ch. 1, p. 186.*

Two sons were obtained in one birth from Rebecca his wife, the firstborn of whom is most well-known in Holy Scripture for his disobedience to his parents. # SACRED ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Onomatology <note>The study of the origins of names.</note></margin>
...that the name comes from "red," and if one wished to use the Greek term *iythapolia* <note>original: ἰυταπολιὰ; likely a reference to "grey-haired" or "changing color," here used to contrast with red</note>, one could greet as an "Edomite" anyone who walks about conspicuous with a red beard. We can more clearly place the Edomites before our eyes as being named from this source—from the one who cooked the red pottage—concerning which we provide the following observations written by Jerome*:
<margin>On Ezekiel, chapter 25, column 905.</margin>
*Edom the bloodthirsty, who lost his birthright because of the cooking of red lentils, and received his name from that (red) food. From him descend the Esauites or Edomites.* Jerome also says*:
<margin>In the same place, column 904.</margin>
*That Esau, Seir, Edom, Idumaea, and Dumah are called one nation, no one will doubt who has knowledge of the Scriptures.*

The other of the sons was יעקב, *Jacob*, whose name comes from the fact that, when he came forth in birth, he held the עקב *heel* of his brother Esau, as witnessed by Moses, the Chancellor of God, in *Genesis 25:26*: "And he called his name Jacob." Regarding this, Taubmann writes*:
<margin>4th Epigram, page 510.</margin>
> *The Hebrew mother is accustomed to call him Jacob*
> *Who secretly trips the one walking by placing his foot in the way.*

Later, when the brothers had grown up, *Jacob*, while Esau indulged in hunting, was תם *upright*, innocent, blameless, and perfect. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> uses *aplastos*, meaning not fake, without deceit or pretense. Symmachus uses *amomos*, without crime. Aquila uses *haplous*, simple; he cared for the household, practiced animal husbandry, and led a quiet life, which the ancient text implies by saying: *dwelling in tents.* The Septuagint says *oikon oikian*, tending the house and devoted to domestic management. The Chaldean Paraphrase says: He was a minister, that is, a student of the house of learning; he frequented the schools of Shem, Eber, and Abraham, who were still among the living. And then it happened that Esau, returning weary from the hunt, sold his birthright to his brother Jacob for a cooked dish of lentils, where the Targum reads *talu puhn*. But later, Jacob also snatched away the paternal blessing by the righteous plan of his mother, whence come the words of Esau complaining in *Genesis 27:36*: *Truly his name is called Jacob, for he has supplanted me <note>original: יעקבני</note> now two times.* The Septuagint: *Rightly was his name called Jacob, for he has tripped me now a second time.* He contemptuously calls Jacob a "tripper" <note>original: πτερνισμῷ</note> and twists the birth name to another meaning. To insult him, he uses the definition of the name and does an injury to his brother, distorting the name given for one reason as if he were a fraudulent supplanter; he accuses his brother of transferring the birthright to himself by deceit, even though he claimed it for himself through a contract of buying and selling. Furthermore, he speaks falsely that the blessing was due to him, since he had abdicated it himself by the law of the birthright. Thus he abuses the name of his brother, who had received his name from the *sole of the foot* <note>original: planta</note>, not because he was to be a supplanter, but because in birth he held the heel of Esau as he was coming out. So Cicero used a humorous definition when he said against Verres: *That his festival was rightly called the "Verrea," because Verres had "swept" <note>original: verrerit; a pun on the name Verres and the verb to sweep/plunder</note> all the places of Sicily, that is, he despoiled and preyed upon them.* This definition was devised by the Orator to mock Verres, because that festival was named from his name, not from his character and deeds. Regarding the betrayal and supplanting by a false friend, the Psalmist says in *Psalm 41:9*: "He has magnified the heel against me," which the Septuagint excellently renders: *They magnified the tripping against me.* Indeed, *tripping* <note>original: Πτερνίζειν</note> and *tripping up* <note>original: ὑποσκελίζειν</note> have the same force; whence these terms are specific to wrestlers, which Julius Pollux lists in *Book 3*: choking, turning, seizing, twisting, struggling, hooking, over-

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Onomatology.</margin>
turning, grasping, tripping up, and also flanking and laddering. Among those *wrestling-matches of names* appears "tripping up," which is when a wrestler, by placing his foot underneath, throws his antagonist to the ground, which the Latins express with the word *supplanting*. Whence writers use "to supplant" as a competitive word when they deal with wrestlers or all-round fighters: Seneca in *Epistle 13* says: *An athlete cannot bring great spirit to the contest who has never been bruised. He who has seen his own blood (shed), whose teeth have rattled under a fist. He who, having been supplanted, has borne the whole body of his adversary, and though cast down, has not cast down his soul.* Therefore, according to Jacob Perez de Valencia*, Jacob was called Jacob for three reasons:
<margin>On Psalm 136, page 943.</margin>
*Jacob is called Jacob, that is, supplantor, because he supplanted his brother Edom three times. First, when he pushed him out of the mother's womb, and thus was born holding the brother's heel. Second, when he stole the birthright from him for the food of lentils. Third, when he stole the blessing from him while he had gone to hunt for bodily food. And therefore he was called Jacob, that is, supplantor.* Philo is accustomed to call Jacob in his writings an "athlete" and an "ascetic," from the etymology of the name by which he is called a supplanter, and especially from the event itself, on account of the most glorious struggle with the Angel. In the Hebrew it is read ויאבק, which the Septuagint rendered as *epalaien*, he wrestled like a wrestler in the wrestling-ring. Rabbi Menahem derives it from the word אבק, which he thinks has a connection with the root for *dust* <note>original: אבק</note>; it will be "in the dust," so that the
<margin>Exodus 9:9.</margin>
sense is: "And a man was dusted with Jacob," that is, he went down into the arena with him. *Rabbi David Kimchi* explains it in almost the same way: They stirred up dust with their feet when they embraced each other in this struggle. *Rabbi Gerundinensis* thinks חבק is put for אבק, meaning he embraced, enclosed in his arms, and folded together, as wrestlers competing with each other are accustomed to do. *Aquila* and *Symmachus* translate it as "he rolled about," he turned and threw himself with him, as wrestlers are accustomed to throw and twist each other while one holds the other back and the other strives to free himself. *Rabbi Mordecai Nathan* says: When two wrestle, and one by strength throws the other to the ground, the dust, in Hebrew
<margin>In the Concordance.</margin>
*ha-abakut*, which they stir up with their feet, is called "pulverization." For it was once customary to sprinkle wrestlers not only with oil and ointment, but also with dust. Lucan deals with this custom of sprinkling dust when, speaking of Hercules and Antaeus, he sings:
> *He pours hot sands as an aid to the limbs.*
Martinus Roa* lists various reasons for this practice from the Ancients, among which the one sought from the
<margin>Book 6, chapter 18.</margin>
Gymnasiums by Lucan is especially pleasing: he thinks the use of dust was introduced lest, while the wrestler studied to grab the limbs of his adversary which were soaked in oil, his hands might slip with a greasy touch, and the antagonist, like an eel, might slip out of his hands; but, with the grip strengthened by the sprinkling of dust, they might hold them as tightly as possible. Whence such dust was also called *haphe* <note>Greek for "grip" or "touch"</note>. Compare Mercuriale *On Gymnastics, Book 1, ch. 8*, Onuphrius *On Circensian Games, p. 186*, and the Greek Lexicon of Robert Constantine under the word *haphe*. This contest of the Jacobaean struggle so pleased God, and He was so greatly delighted by it, that He celebrated him by this name, and bestowed upon him the most celebrated name of Israel. For so it is accustomed to happen, that men for famous deeds—

# Sacred Name-Lore
<margin>Sacred Name-Lore.</margin>
Those illustrious for their noble and praiseworthy deeds obtain august names, like marks and tokens of their virtues and heroic actions. Thus the victor Jacob received an honorable name from God as a prize <note>original: "brabejon" (Greek: βραβεῖον), a prize or award in a contest</note>; for he who was previously called Jacob <note>Hebrew: יעקב (Ya'akov)</note> from the supplanting of his brother Esau, was afterwards called by a new and more heroic name, Israel <note>Hebrew: ישראל (Yisra'el)</note>, following the second duel which he entered into with the Son of God—that great Angel of the Covenant of GOD—so that he might be strengthened against the dangers he feared, and by the victory he reported over the Angel. For these words were spoken to him by the Angel who had wrestled with him:

<margin>Gen. 32:28.</margin>
> Your name shall no longer be called only Jacob, but Israel, for you have behaved as a prince <note>Hebrew: שרה (sarah), to strive or have power</note> with God and with men, and you prevail in power:

The reasoning for the name is from the verb *sarah*, which signifies to exercise dominion, as if he were called a Prince and Victor of God, whom he prevailed over in the struggle. This is an example of a magnificent victory, and beyond all other victories, where the Lord of heaven and earth is conquered by His own weapons, where the antagonist provides the very strength by which He is overcome. God’s purpose, according to Vatable <note>François Vatable (d. 1547), a French humanist and Hebraist</note>, was to send His servant into various battles equipped with the confidence of such a remarkable victory, lest he waver in the future. He willed the name to be a sign of a victory achieved against the laws of nature. In vain, however, are those who interpret it as "the man seeing God," from *ra'ah* <note>to see</note> and *El* <note>God</note>, an origin commonly attributed to Philo, Nazianzen, Hilary, and Prosper; Augustine has it in *The City of God* and his commentaries on the Psalms. Didymus and Cassian also follow this. Yet the etymology is given in the context itself, which we have provided. Jerome, however, judges this origin very well and accurately in his commentary on Isaiah 44: "Properly," he says, "according to the Hebrews and the faithfulness of the letters, Israel is called 'the Upright One of God' <note>original: "rectus Dei"</note>; but 'the man seeing GOD' is not in the elements of the word, but only in the sound of the voice." Regarding the former, to use the words of Blessed Glassius

<margin>Book 4, tract 3, page 834.</margin>
in his *Sacred Grammar*, he derives the name from *yashar*, "upright" (whence *Jeshurun*, which is attributed to the people of Israel in Deuteronomy 32:15). But in the Hebrew word for Israel, the dot is not on the right, but on the left horn of the letter *shin* <note>שׂ vs שׁ</note>, so that it is *Yisra'el*: a matter expressed most clearly in the text. Regarding the latter [seeing God], it looks to the name *El*, which almost agrees with the Hebrew *ra'ah*; to which "he saw" seems to be added, so that with *El* it would be "the man seeing GOD." He rightly says, therefore, that this is not in the elements of the letters, for there *Israel* is without *ra'ah* from

<margin>Traditions on Genesis.</margin>
the beginning. And elsewhere the same author [Jerome] says: "Although they are of great authority and eloquence, and their shadows may overwhelm us—those who translated Israel as 'the man' or 'the mind seeing God'—we are led more by the authority of Scripture and the Angel, or GOD, who called him Israel, than by any secular eloquence." We conclude with the words of Blessed Luther: "It has been

<margin>On Genesis, fol. 168. a. b.</margin>
sought among all the Fathers what the significance of this word Israel might be. Jerome modestly complains that he is overwhelmed by the authority and learning of most eloquent men who explain this word as 'the man seeing GOD'; but he adds nonetheless that he would rather embrace the etymology of the Angel or of GOD than that of others, however eloquent. *Sarah* signifies to dominate, to prevail, to be a prince. In Isaiah 9, *Sar Shalom*, Prince of Peace. With the *Yod* placed in front, *Isarael*, the first *Aleph* is absorbed, and it becomes a proper name, just as in

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Name-Lore.</margin>
others because of the prefixed *Yod*, such as Josaphat, Jesus, Isaiah. Israel is a fighter, a prince, a Lord or Master of GOD. Everyone has sweated over explaining this word, because it seemed absurd that we should be called Lords and Victors of GOD. And indeed it is true, if we judge according to Philosophy. But in the Spirit and in Theology, it is rightly and piously said that God is conquered by us. Yet He is not conquered so as to be subjected to us, but His judgment, or His wrath and fury, and whatever stands against us, is conquered by our asking, seeking, and knocking, so that from an angry judge (as He previously seemed), He becomes a most loving Father." Then, after a few interjected remarks on how this victory still happens today, he continues: "These things are very learned and pleasant: that in Theology, Christians are called the *Sar* or *Sara* of God. Therefore, believers are Princes and Lords of God, because they wrestle with God and win. We do not dwell on the other etymology. For it sounds like nothing if the interpreter says 'Lord with GOD,' but it is expressly said here: 'You have struggled, you have fought with GOD and Men.' The Wrestler names himself not only God, but also Man, as if saying: 'With me, the God-man, being conquered, you have conquered.' He joins both. Previously, you overcame one man, your brother, by supplanting him, whence you obtained the name Jacob; but now you have emerged superior to both God and man at once."

Jacob, obeying the counsel of his parents to preserve his life and escape the cruel hands of his brother Esau, went into Mesopotamia to his maternal uncle Laban, by whom he was deceived ten times (Genesis 31:41), yet he obtained the divine blessing most abundantly both in the sheepfold and in the household. He became the parent of twelve sons and one daughter. From their number, the first was ראובן, Reuben; the fruitful Leah bore him and called his name Reuben; for she said, "He is to be so called because 'Jehovah has seen

<margin>Gen. 29:32.</margin>
my affliction'." Leah presents this son, given to her by God, against the insults of the family, her sister, and the neighbors, as if to say: "Behold, look upon the Son with whom the most merciful GOD has gifted me, and by him has testified that my affliction is His concern. Therefore my husband, invited by this blessing of God, will change his hateful mind toward me, and from now on will embrace me with more ardent love." The composition is from *ben*, son, and *ra'ah*, to see, as if to say "seeing a son" or "a son seen." Countless proper names occur in the Sacred Books composed with *ben*, which are written sometimes joined and sometimes separately, such as Ben-hadad (1 Kings 15:18), Ben-zoheth (1 Chronicles 4:20), Ben-chail (2 Chronicles 17:7), Ben-hur (1 Kings 4:7), Ben-hesed (v. 9), and Ben-hanan (1 Chronicles 4:20).

The second among the sons of Jacob born of Leah was named שמעון, Simeon <note>Greek: Σιμεὼν</note>, so called from hearing, namely from *shama*, he heard, as if to say "heard" or "son of hearing." By this naming, Leah, taught by clear signs and examples thus far, concludes that she has been heard by God: "Because," she said, "Jehovah heard that I was hated, He gave me this son also, and she called his name Simeon." To her firstborn she gave the name Reuben, from seeing, a son of vision, *a child to be gazed upon* <note>original German: "Ein Schaukind"</note>. The second she calls Simeon, from hearing. In the birth of both, the benefit and mercy of GOD is celebrated.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<page-num>236</page-num>

mercy, in that He not only saw her misery and affliction—from which the firstborn **Reuben** was named—but also heard and *answered* her groaning, from which the second was called **Simeon** <note>original: "exaudiverit" (heard/answered); Simeon is derived from the Hebrew root *shama*, to hear.</note>. To his posterity, by the force of Jacob’s prophecy in *Genesis* 49:5, 6, 7, no fixed lot was given in the
<margin>Joshua 19:1</margin>

We note in this place that "many-signified" <note>Greek: πολυσημαντον (polysemanton)</note> point which Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a medieval exegete.</note> mentions regarding the dispersion of the tribe of Simeon: *There is no poor man, nor schoolmaster, except from Simeon.* <margin>on Genesis chapter 49</margin>

**Levi**, לוי, *levvi*, the third born to Jacob by Leah, gave origin through Aaron, the brother of Moses, to the Levitical and Priestly race, by whom the Church was administered in the succession of time thereafter. The nature of the name is such that it does not imply a certain levity or thinness. Indeed, it was a most fitting thing for the purpose of suggesting and winning over [her husband], whence Leah, flattering herself in her "goodly offspring" <note>Greek: ευτεκνίᾳ (euteknia)</note>, said: *Now at last* לוי *my husband will be joined or coupled to me, because
<margin>Genesis 29:34</margin>
I have borne him three sons*; *therefore she called his name Levi*, that is, "joined" or "coupled." Leah rejoices in her heart, for while she brought forth so happily, Rachel—because her sister had more happiness than she wished—took grief from her sister’s "multitude of children" <note>Greek: πολυτεκνίᾳ (polyteknia)</note>, and
> eating her own heart, she avoids the tracks of men. <note>A poetic reference to Rachel's jealousy and withdrawal.</note>
It sank deeper into her soul because she was sterile. I believe no one is unaware of how common the prayer for "goodly offspring" <note>Greek: ευτεκνίας (euteknias)</note> was among all women in Judea. Hence Leah, behaving charmingly, boasts of her childbearing and calls the third-born **Levi**, which recognizes its first source in לוה *to borrow* or *receive a loan*, which in the Hiphil <note>A Hebrew verb form indicating causative action.</note> means *to give a loan*, and likewise, *to be added* or *joined*.

Leah, bearing a fourth son to Jacob, gave him this name: *This time I will celebrate* יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton/Jehovah</note>, *therefore she called his name Judah*. For when she had now obtained a fourth son, she broke out into thanksgiving; giving thanks to God, she imposed the name of Judah on the son
<margin>Genesis 29:35</margin>
as a perpetual memorial of the matter. Moreover, there is a twofold reason for this name. The mother names the son from the thanks paid to God, and credits it not to herself but to God alone that she bore four sons to her husband. Hence, for each of God's benefits toward her, she imposes on each of the sons a "memorial" <note>Greek: μνημονευτικόν (mnemoneutikon)</note> name, and one that is very grand and worthy of remembrance. **Reuben**, the firstborn, from God’s merciful vision; **Simeon**, from the longed-for hearing; **Levi**, from the friendly adherence and coupling of her husband; and finally **Judah**, from the praise and celebration due to God, she calls them, intending in this way to preserve the memory of God’s wonderful benefits toward her and transmit them to posterity. Moses also looked back to this in the blessing of the tribe of Judah
<margin>Deuteronomy 33:7</margin>
when he said: *Hear, O Lord, the voice of Judah*, that is, of confession, from ידה, *to confess, to give thanks*, whom
<margin>on Psalm 68, col. 741</margin>
Augustine follows, interpreting Judah as "confession." Jacob explains this name slightly differently in
<margin>Genesis 49:8</margin>
*Genesis 49:8: Judah, you (are) he whom your brothers shall praise.* There is an elegant play on words <note>term: paronomasia (a pun or play on words)</note> in the words *Judah* and *Jadah*. For *Yad* in the Hiphil means *to confess, to celebrate*. The sense of the words seems to be this: O Judah, you truly are Judah, that is, you have a name from celebrity, and you shall also have the omen of celebrity. For your brothers shall praise you, that is, they shall attribute singular praises of virtue, dignity, and power to you,

<column-break/>

and they shall proclaim you the author of their safety. With his wife, who was descended from the race of the Canaanites (whether
<margin>Sacred Onomatology</margin>
her name was *Shua*? or truly that of her parent? or truly called Bath-Shua? we wish to leave for others to discuss), he had an altogether unhappy offspring; for he raised three children from that marriage: **Er, Onan, and Shelah**. He himself, although he neglected his parent's authority in contracting the marriage, nevertheless used it in marrying off his sons. To the firstborn, **Er**, when he was 12 years of age (or according to others, 14), he gave **Tamar** as a wife; but God slew him on account of his impiety.
<margin>Genesis 38:6, 7</margin>
The daughter-in-law was immediately married off to the second son, **Onan**, so that he might raise up seed for his brother. But he also, either out of hatred for the wife or envy toward his impiously dead brother, corrupted his seed by pouring it on the ground, and thus refused to raise up seed for his brother. For that reason, he perished by a tragic kind of death from God in the same year of marriage as his brother.
<margin>Genesis 38:8, 9, 10</margin>
Such was the miserable end of the two sons of Judah from his Canaanite wife. But the third son, namely **Shelah**, whom he had promised to join to Tamar—though with vain hope, even if he were more fortunate in marriage (for Judah secretly transferred the blame for the premature death of his sons not to their impiety, but to the woman Tamar, and thence urged that the marriage be delayed under the pretext of age)—and he was called the father of many children, whence the family of the
<margin>Numbers 26:20</margin>
**Shelahites**; yet he lacked the chief blessing which was to be imparted to the seed of Judah. For he was removed from the genealogy of the Savior, who was to arise from the tribe of Judah; and it seemed better by divine providence to admit into the line of his generation the son of Judah, namely **Perez**, whom he had fathered by his daughter-in-law Tamar under the impression of visiting a prostitute (even if unknowingly), rather than to have anything in common with the race of the Canaanites, as Camartus relates on page 330. For when Tamar perceived herself deluded by her father-in-law, she in turn deluded him; having devised a bold and altogether shameful plan, she prostituted her body to her father-in-law because she had been defrauded of the hoped-for marriage to the third son.
<margin>Genesis 38:13 and following</margin>
Moreover, a great wonder occurred in the birth of Tamar, for it happened at the time she was giving birth (and behold, there were twins in her womb), it happened, I say, when she was giving birth, that one of them put out a hand, which the midwife took and bound a scarlet thread to his hand, saying: This one comes out first. But it happened, when he had pulled back his hand, behold, his brother came out, and she said: Why have you broken through? Let the breach be upon you. And he called his name **Perez**. When the namer saw this happen, he made the name so that by it the same thing is signified as if you said "son of the eruption," *The Breaker-Through* <note>German: Durchbrecher</note>, who anticipated Zerah by breaking out and bursting through the maternal womb, as it were, violently. "Breach" to the Hebrews is *Peretz* from *paratz*, *to break or burst*. Indeed, the tribe of Judah was the most fruitful and numerous of all, whence that saying: *The thousands of Judah, among the thousands of Judah.* That abundance can easily be gathered both from the census tables entered by Moses in the desert, and from when the whole number of Israel was observed through Joab and Abishai during the reign of David. It was not only populous, but also most famous, since the whole land of Canaan took its name from the tribe of Judah, both before and after the Babylonian captivity, and it even retained it. So also the whole family of Jacob, not only among the Sacred [writers], but even...
