# From Numbers XIII. v. 17.

<margin>Sacred Onomatology <note>The study of the origins of names.</note></margin>
...even among secular authors it is heard as such, although they clash with the truth both in terms of origin and the facts themselves; compare Tacitus, *Histories* book 5; Strabo, book 16; Dionysius, book 37; Justin, book 36, chapter 2. Even if, as Jerome says in his commentary on Psalm 108, column 328: *The Jews today are not named after that holy Judah, but after that betrayer of Christ, Judas.*

<margin>Meditations on the Lamentations of Jeremiah, p. 20.</margin>
We conclude our study, however, with the words of David Kyberus\*. *Judah is the proper name of one of the sons of Jacob born of Leah, whom his mother so named from confession or praise; for when he was born she said: "This time I will praise the name of the Lord," therefore, says Moses, they call his name Judah. Its root is* יהודה <note>Yehudah</note>, *but because the royal power specifically looked to the tribe derived from this very Judah, and it was adorned by God with many gifts above the others—as can be seen in the blessings of Jacob, where it is commended for royal dignity, for wars and victories, for the duration, security, and firmness of the kingdom, for the Messiah arising from there, and finally for the fertility of the land, not to mention the temple and the metropolitan city of Jerusalem, as well as the most famous Mount Zion, and innumerable other things which this tribe had above the rest—therefore, frequently in the sacred scriptures, Judah is taken for the whole people; whence also all Israelites are called Jews.* In this name the Jews also seek a greater dignity, as it contains within itself the letters of the name of God יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH</note>, which the same Kyberus discusses from Rabbi Abraham’s *Bundle of Myrrh*, pages 22, 23, 24.

Regarding the name יששכר, *Ioaschar*, Issachar: whom should we ask rather than the architect of the name herself, Leah, who said: *God has given me my reward,* שברי <note>original: "shabri"</note>, *after I gave my handmaid to my husband. And therefore she called his name Issachar.* As if to say: the most merciful God has abundantly compensated the loss of the mandrakes which I gave to my sister Rachel. For in exchange for the mandrakes <note>Dudaim</note> I received a son. In memory, therefore, of this reward, with which she had hired her husband, she called her son Issachar, that is, "son of reward"\*. <margin>Genesis 30:16.</margin> To the Hebrews, שכר <note>shakar</note> means to trade or to hire for a price, from which word comes שכר <note>seker</note>, "reward," and from that the Jewish word *Schachern* <note>To haggle or peddle</note>, to make a profit or gain.

<margin>Genesis 30:20.</margin>
In the name זבולון, *Zabulon*, Zabulon, Leah presents herself to us as an excellent Teacher, saying\*: *Now at last* יזבלני <note>yizbeleni</note> *my husband will dwell with me, because I have borne him six sons; therefore she called his name Zabulon.* Leah proved herself an excellent <term>child-bearer</term> <note>Greek: teknotonon</note>; the same diligence she applied in giving birth, she also brought to the naming of what she bore, and in both she left a remarkable lesson. For the prolific Leah wished by this naming to remind her husband of his duty: namely, that he should not dwell only with one sister while neglecting the other, but that he should divide his mind and marital affection equally between them. So that we may understand, זבל <note>zabal</note> signifies "to dwell," a word which occurs nowhere else but in this place; זבול <note>zebul</note> means "a dwelling," and to this pertains what Jacob says in Genesis 49:13 in the blessing of Zabulon: *Zebulon shall dwell at the haven of the sea.*

Rachel, most greedy for bearing children, moved both by womanly impatience—by which she bore her lack of children most bitterly, whence she erupted into these abrupt and brief words toward her husband, full of anger and impatience: *Give me children, or else I die*—and by envy, with which she envied her sister's

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Onomatology.</margin>
fertility, seeing herself as <term>barren and not producing children</term> <note>Greek: steiran kai me teknopoiousan</note>, she wished to be "built up" through her handmaid Bilhah, and to have her children as her own, to educate them and take care of them; hence her words: *Go in unto her; and she shall bear upon my knees, that I may also have children by her\** <margin>Genesis 30:3.</margin> The Hebrews explain these words thus: *that I may be stirred to bear and warmed to conceive.* Some take it this way: *That I may be as a midwife to her and she may bear for me, so that the offspring she is about to bear I may place upon my knees as if born of me.* For mothers are accustomed to cherish children born of them in their bosom, and in this manner to carry them upon their knees. A similar phrase occurs in Genesis 50:23 and Isaiah 66:12. At the persuasion and urging of Rachel, Jacob went in to Bilhah the handmaid, and from her he fathered a son, to whom Rachel gave the name דן, Dan, from the root דון <note>dun</note>, and דין <note>din</note>, and דנן <note>danan</note>, and דן <note>dan</note>; the meaning being: *GOD has judged my cause, and has also heard my voice, and has given me a son; therefore she called his name Dan.* By which words Rachel clearly testifies that this son was given to her by GOD, yet meanwhile she does not yet cast off her envious mind toward her sister, nor does she humble herself, but as if affected by a significant injury from her sister, she complains and implores the judgment of God the judge.

When the controversy over childbearing between the sisters was determined by the judgment of the immortal God, the excellent Rachel spoke when she had obtained a second son from her handmaid Bilhah: נפתולי אלהים נפתלתי עם-אחותי גם-יכלתי: *With great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed.* <margin>Genesis 30:8.</margin> To indicate a worthy and memorable wrestling, she intermingles the most illustrious name of God, and thinks she had cause to call the offspring נפתלי, *Nephthali*, Naphtali, from פתל <note>pathal</note>, "to wrestle," whence נפתול <note>naphtul</note>, "a wrestling." Rachel and Leah often differed, and that grudge had remained for a long time, but at last Rachel wrestled through. The sisters had waged war against each other in one house, and had consented to a duel. An internal war, and "more than a civil war." Isidore, *Etymologies* book 18, p. 1265: *A civil war is a sedition and the stirring of a tumult arisen among citizens. It is more than a civil war when not only citizens contend, but also kinsmen, such as occurred between Caesar and Pompey, when son-in-law and father-in-law fought each other; for in this battle brother fought with brother, and father carried arms against son.* Here it was fought fiercely between sister and sister. They conflicted with each other in heavy rivalry over the blessing of offspring. Finally, when Rachel's handmaid had brought forth offspring, she immediately sings a song of triumph <note>original: "paeana"</note> in the field: *With the greatest wrestlings I have wrestled, I have fought a huge contest, and with God's help I have held the field. Now at last I too stand firm. Shout for triumph! My house shall now be propagated through this recently born son, who someday shall be illustrious among us for the magnitude of his deeds and the dignity of his honors and life. Shout for triumph!* A truly pleasant victory, which was bloodless, without plundering, and without detriment to the conquered party. A pleasant outcome, where immediately in the field, before the army was dismissed, both the victress and the vanquished were joined again on both sides with equal goodwill, and from that day the vanquished lived with the victress in a somewhat fruitful concord.

Leah, when she ceased to bear, moved by her sister's example, substituted her handmaid for her husband in her own place, from whom she first obtained a son, whom she calls גד, Gad: *There comes* גד <note>Gad</note>, *a troop, others say prosperity,*

For the exultant Leah boasted of being increased by this son’s birth, and of the multitude that would follow him, as if she now so prevailed over her sister that she could even draw up an army from the abundance of her own children. Regarding this name, we have spoken more extensively elsewhere. At this point, however, it is worth noting what should be determined regarding Jacob’s polygamy, entered into at the persuasion and urging of his wives. Augustine answers for us: "Since," he says, "no law prohibited multiple wives for the sake of multiplying posterity, Rachel, being sterile, gave her handmaid to her husband so that she might receive children through her; and her elder sister, although she had already given birth, imitated her because she desired to multiply her offspring. Jacob is not read to have sought any wife besides one, nor did he use several except for the duty of begetting offspring while observing conjugal right; nor would he have done this unless his wives had demanded it, who had lawful power over their husband's body." Compare the same author, book 22, *Against Julian*, chapter 47.

The name **Asher** (Hebrew: *Asher*, Greek: *Asēr*) has a clear significance in its own language, and immediately indicates the reason for the name to those skilled in the language as being from *ashar*, "he made happy" or "blessed." Leah, increased by a second son from Zilpah the handmaid, immediately exalts herself in the procreation of children and proclaims a happy marriage and joyful success, saying: "In my happiness" <note>original: *be-oshri*</note>; for women will call me blessed; therefore she called his name Asher. The happy increase and promotion of the marriage itself is asserted. Asher was happy, and "blessed above the other sons is Asher. Let him be acceptable to his brothers, and let him dip his foot in oil," says Moses in Deuteronomy 33:24. He also receives a blessing from the dying Jacob: "From Asher, his food shall be rich, and he shall yield royal dainties."

God finally remembering Rachel, opened her womb, which had been closed until then, and gave her a son whom she calls **Joseph**, meaning "increase." Rachel, the giver of the name, provided light while she established the name so that it might be clearly seen: "May Jehovah add to me another son," she said. Therefore, she bestowed the name upon this son of hers from a good omen, because she hoped that more sons would be born to her after this one. Whence we can say, Joseph is an "addition" or "increase" <note>German: *ein Beygefügtes und hinzugethanen*</note> from the root *yasaph*, "to add." Elsewhere Joseph is also called *Yehoseph*, "the increase of the Lord" <note>German: *dess HERRN Vermehrung*</note> in Psalm 81:6. And the Patriarch Jacob alludes to this name: "A son of a fruitful or fruit-bearing (namely, a tree, i.e., a fruitful bough) is Joseph, a fruitful or fructifying bough." Luther translates: "Joseph will grow; he will grow as if by a spring." The history of Joseph is illuminated by a remarkable blessing with which the father advanced the son, so that he was not inferior to the father himself. In the formula of the blessing, like a little flower, is the word *berakah* (blessing), which intensifies the subject at hand and doubles all prosperity. Theodorus Bibliander says: "It is an *epitasis* (intensification) when the force of the meaning is intended by the addition of letters, and some weight is added to things, and the mind is stirred to understand even that which is not expressed, a virtue of speech which the Hebrews call *chizuk inyan*, the strengthening of the meaning; as in: 'Let the blessing come upon the head of Joseph.'"

<column-break/>

"Upon the head of Joseph," instead of simply "let it come," suggests a blessing that is not common, but increased and doubled, as if it were written "blessing, blessing"—universal happiness and whatever good exists anywhere. After many tribulations, Joseph experienced both the increase and the blessing of his family, concerning which see Augustine on Psalm 79 and Psalm 80.

**Benjamin** was so named by his father, but by his mother he was called **Ben-oni**. In his birth, the mother was overcome by the labor of childbirth; she imposed this name upon him at the very threshold of death, commending herself to God with ardent prayers in the recognition and trust of Jehovah. Since she was such a woman as Paul describes, "she shall be saved through childbearing." Regarding this name, the mother Rachel herself ends our worry, imposing the name amidst mortal birth pains and gasping words, by which she wished to express the weight of giving birth; for in giving birth she had very difficult labor, and it happened while she was in difficult labor that the midwife said to her, "Do not fear; for you have this son also." And it happened as her soul was departing (for she was dying) that she called his name Ben-oni. The birth was not quick, whence she aptly said: "Son of my sorrow," for *Ben* is "son," and—lest it deceive you—the word for sorrow <note>original: *ta'onitha*</note> must be known, for the difficulty of the birth and the sad departure do not allow it to be taken in the sense of "strength." The dying mother herself professes the explanation and places before our eyes the sad image of *dystokia* (difficult birth), so that it is necessary to take it for mourning, grief, and trouble, from which the word borrows its image, while the birth is truly an *on*—a burden and exhaustion—to the mother. However, the Father devised another name, by which he wished to depict and represent the future state of things, not the present; for he called him **Benjamin**, that is, "Son of the Right Hand," from which can be gathered the greatest love with which he embraced his Ben-oni, and in which he consoled the grief he had conceived from the death of his most beloved wife. The wife left a visible image to her husband in which he might weigh the image of human affairs; and while the husband contemplates the sad fate in her, he embraces the right hand of the son, kisses him, and loves him more ardently. Thus, nothing is so dear to a man (as Franco notes) except what is produced by pain; and what is wonderful, love is increased and sharpened by the difficulty of the experience, and by the necessity of suffering which is imposed on us before possessing. Hence it is that the same one who is the Son of Sorrow is also the Son of Love or of the Right Hand, which fits perfectly the sons of our nourishing mother, the Church, whom she has borne, bears, and will bear for God the Father.

The firstborn of Joseph among the sons of Jacob, numbered by the grandfather himself, was **Manasseh**, although the second in blessing (Genesis 48:18-20). Why Joseph wished to utter the name of his firstborn son in this way rather than another had no more suitable cause than to recall to his mind the rest from his previous labors. The name is a meditation on pleasure and present joy; therefore he called the name of the firstborn Manasseh, saying: "Because God has made me forget <note>original: *nasshani*</note> all my toil."

The passage in Genesis 48:15 declares this, where we hear the Grandfather blessing him thus: *Certainly his younger brother shall become greater than he, and his offspring shall be a multitude of nations.* This also seems to be alluded to in *Hosea* 13:15: *Though he (Ephraim) bears fruit among his brothers (the rest of the Patriarchs)*, that is, he has grown and been increased. Truly, it is not difficult to perceive the reason Joseph gave this name, since we have it from the Father himself; when he saw one offspring succeeding another from his wife's womb, he wished to express the joy of his soul by the name itself. For the words sound thus: *He called the name of the second son Ephraim, for he said*, <term>הפרני</term> <note>Hebrew: hiphrani</note>, *God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.* Therefore, because of this fruitful result, he offers "birthday words" to God for the fruit of the womb, and anyone can see, even from a basic greeting of Hebrew words, that <term>הפרה</term> <note>Hebrew: haphrah</note> means *to be fruitful*. Certainly, the name was born here—not without the favor of Mercury <note>A classical idiom meaning "with great eloquence or luck"</note>—so that it might be expressed both in the formula of blessing commanded by the Patriarch himself among the <margin>Gen. 48:20.</margin> Israelites: *God make you like Ephraim and like Manasseh,* and in that most ample <term>abundance of children</term> <note>Greek: euteknia</note> in which Ephraim flourished among his peers. For no tribe among the Israelites, except the tribe of Judah, was as populous and powerful as the tribe of Ephraim, to say nothing of the most glorious Judges and most powerful Heroes that this tribe gave to the people of Israel. Let the righteous in their tribulations remember Joseph and his two sons, to whom he gave names based on the outcome of events. Endure in patience what happens; sustain what presses upon you. Sometime, like Joseph, you will come out of the prison of your tribulation, and two sons will be born to you in the royal house: the first will be *Manasseh*, and you will say: *God has made me forget all my labors.* The second will be *Ephraim*, and you will say: *God has made me abound in all good things.*

We establish a special class for the **Leaders**, Judges, and Kings of the Israelite people, from whose number we review at least the principal ones on account of their famous deeds. First among them, worthy of the primary place, is <term>משה</term> <note>Hebrew: Mosheh</note>, *Mosche*, *Moses*, descended from the family of Levi. Scarcely has such a wonderful deliverance happened to any mortal as to the infant Moses; scarcely to any such a wonderful education in the Women's Quarters. Scarcely does it happen to anyone to be so dearly loved, guarded, and elevated by GOD. To no one else, who became so venerable by all his wonders and so entirely divinely inspired by his forty days of conversation with God, that his face shone. To no one else, who was buried by GOD himself. Saved <margin>Exod. 2:10.</margin> miraculously in the water, and more miraculously on the land. We far prefer the plan of the Egyptian Doris <note>A poetic reference to the Egyptian princess</note> regarding the preservation of the boy Moses, to the plan of the Greek Doris regarding the preservation of Danaë, the only daughter of Acrisius, and her little son. Mythologists write that the daughter, shut in a chest together with the infant born of her, was cast into the sea, <term>as a girl weeping over her misfortunes</term> <note>Greek: hōs apoloipathlia klaousa</note> <margin>Sea Dialogues Vol. 3 p. 33.</margin> <term>maiden</term>, <term>and the infant</term>; Lucian calls the chest <term>a small box</term>, mentioning that <term>the infant, most beautiful in his ignorance of evils</term> smiled at his mother when he was exposed; and in that Dialogue, Thetis says the same thing that Pharaoh's daughter said of Moses, a very handsome boy: <term>let neither the girl herself perish, nor the child, who is so beautiful.</term> That little boy is said to be Perseus, whom they say was preserved in the waters, and Lucian touches on the same fiction in

<margin>Sacred Onomatology.</margin>
the Dialogue of Triton and the Nereids, Vol. 2, page 62, where Triton says to the Nereids: <term>You know, I think, for what reason you saved Perseus, the child of Danaë, who was cast into the sea in a chest by his grandfather along with his mother, by spreading yourselves out beneath them.</term> This is an elegant coincidence of the name and the deed performed. Moses is found in the water and is drawn out from there, which is why he was called *Mosche*; for Pharaoh's daughter, when the infant came to her in the reeds of the water, took him and called his name *Moschen*, because she said, *for I drew him out of the waters.* The construction of the name is clearly given from <term>משת</term> <note>Hebrew: mashah</note>, which signifies "he drew out" or "led out." Because an Egyptian Princess imposed the name, you might say the Hebrews must yield their right regarding the origin of this word; for Josephus* affirms, from the Egyptian <margin>Book 1 against Apion.</margin> <term>Moy</term>, water, is the name. For this reason, this word can refer the cause of its meaning to both the Hebrew and the Egyptian language; and in this way Gregorius Francus said (Sacred Lexicon, page 65) that it is evident from this that *the Egyptian language was a dialect of Hebrew, although the Egyptians are called a people of* <term>a foreign tongue</term> <note>Hebrew: la'az</note>, *barbarous, Psalm 114:1, and their language unknown, Psalm 81:6.* The Hebrew <term>Mayim</term> (waters) in its grammatical form <term>Mey</term> is easily reconciled with Josephus's <term>Moy</term>. Compare Nieremberg on Holy Scripture, p. 167, in whose work on page 377 you will also find his life described in verse.

Moses, about to send scouts into the land of Canaan, changed the name of <term>הושע</term> <note>Hebrew: Hoshea</note>, *Osea* the son of Nun, into <term>יהושע</term> <note>Hebrew: Yehoshua</note> *Joshua*; and by a prophetic Spirit, foreseeing the excellent success of the affairs to be carried out by Joshua (whom God also later destined as the successor to Moses, *Num.* 27:18, *Deut.* 3:28). The word is splendidly composed of <term>יהוה</term> <note>The Tetragrammaton: Yahweh/The LORD</note> and <term>ישע</term> <note>Hebrew: yesha</note>, *salvation*. All things that the Holy Book brings forth concerning Joshua are splendid, but this will especially declare his splendor: that beneath that name lies the typical significance of our coming Savior, who will illuminate our minds with divine splendor. Concerning this, since other matters remain for us now, Blessed Gerhard treated it in his *Exegesis on the Person of Christ* § 18, and Blessed Walther with a more drawn-out thread. From the Catholics, however, we shall recite the words of Andreas Masius*: <margin>Preface to Joshua p. 5.</margin> 

> The most merciful God willed in the sixth polity (for the Church describes six polities there), which had been the goal of all the others after the first was violated, to exhibit to His people a presage all the more timely and certain, both through the name and through the deeds of Joshua. [The first leader, Moses] was heavier on account of the multitude and difficulty of the laws, but this second one was most desired and nearer; for in that state which existed under Moses' leadership, the mystery of the restoration of that heavenly inheritance through Jesus Christ, which our first Parent had lost, had been shadowed forth only in the darkest figures. # From Numbers XIII, verse 17.

The passage in *Genesis 48:15* clarifies this, where we hear the Grandfather <note>Jacob</note> blessing him thus: *Truly his younger brother shall become greater than he, and his seed shall be the fullness of nations.* This also seems to be alluded to in *Hosea 13:15*: *Though he (Ephraim) bears fruit among his brothers (the other Patriarchs)*, that is, he grew and was increased. We far prefer the account of the Egyptian Doris <note>A poetic reference to the Egyptian princess</note> concerning the preservation of the little boy Moses, over the account of the Greek Doris concerning the preservation of Danaë, the only daughter of Acrisius, and her little son. Because an Egyptian Princess imposed the name, you might say the Hebrews must yield regarding the legal right of this word's origin <margin>*Against Apion, Book 1.*</margin>; for *Josephus* affirms that the name is from the Egyptian *Moy*, meaning water. It is indeed consistent that the name should be from the nation in which he was born, but it is also fitting to affirm that neighboring languages influence and migrate into one another, so that often one word penetrates not only a neighboring language but even a distant one. For this reason, this word can refer the cause of its meaning to both the Hebrew and Egyptian languages; and for this reason, Gregorius Francus said in his *Sacred Lexicon, page 65*, that it is evident from this that the Egyptian language *was a dialect of Hebrew*, although the Egyptians are called a people of *strange language* <note>original Hebrew: לעז, *la'az*</note>, a barbarian people, *Psalm 114:1*, and their language unknown, *Psalm 81:6*. The terms *Moy* and *Moshe* are easily reconciled in the grammatical regime of *Moy* with Josephus's *Moy*. Compare Nieremberg *On Holy Scripture, p. 167*, in whose work on page 377 you will also find his life described in verse.

Moses, when about to send the scouts into the land of Canaan, changed the name of <note>original Hebrew: הושׁע, *Hoshea*</note> *Osea* the son of Nun into <note>original Hebrew: יהושע, *Yehoshua*</note> *Joshua*, and by a prophetic Spirit, foreseeing the best success of the affairs to be carried out by Joshua (whom God also later destined to be the successor to Moses, *Num. 27:18, Deut. 3:28*). The word is splendidly composed of <note>original Hebrew: יהוה, *Yahweh*</note> and <note>original Hebrew: ישע, *yesha*</note>, salvation; and all things are splendid which the Holy Book has brought forth concerning Joshua. But that will most greatly declare the splendor: that beneath that name lay the typical reason for our coming Savior, who would illuminate our minds with divine splendor. Concerning Him, since other things remain for us now, the Blessed Gerhard has treated in his *Exegesis on the Person of Christ*, section 18, and with a more drawn-out thread, the Blessed Walther. Truly, among the Papists <note>Catholic scholars</note>, Andreas Masius <margin>*Preface to Joshua, p. 5.*</margin>, whose words we shall recite: *The most merciful God wished, in the sixth polity (for he describes six polities of the Church there), which had been the goal of all the others since the first was violated, to exhibit a presage to His people so much more timely and certain, both through the name and through the deeds of Joshua. On account of the multitude and difficulty of the laws, the burden was heavier, but this other one, most longed for, was nearer; for how much that state which belonged to the leadership of Moses had been shadowed forth by only the obscurest figures, the mystery of restoring that heavenly inheritance through Jesus Christ, which the first Parent had lost. Therefore, He brought Hoshea, the Son of Nun, into the midst, and by His heavenly instinct commanded him to be called Joshua, that is, Jesus, so that he might foreshadow the Priest and Administrator of that last polity, Jesus Christ, not only by his deeds, but also clearly represent Him by his very name; for him whom the Hebrews call Joshua...*

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Onomatology <note>The study of the origins and meanings of names.</note></margin>
That he is called *Iēsoun*, Jesus, by the Greeks, no one can doubt who has looked even in passing at sacred history. *For as for the Talmudists*, and the Jews who follow these blind leaders, they record the name of our Savior not as *Yehoshua* <note>original: יהושע</note>, but precisely and with fewer letters as *Yeshu* <note>original: ישו</note>; these wicked men do this as an insult, and at the same time, so they are not forced to recognize the "type" <note>A "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a foreshadowing of Christ.</note> I have mentioned. And Emanuel de Naxera says: "Names, if properly bestowed, are brief definitions of things, so that what is required through lengthy investigation may be held in a summary meaning." To pass over other nations, it was a solemn custom among the Hebrews to bestow names upon their sons with great deliberation, and to fit them with names that were, by their very etymology, a prophecy of future things, and which would stir the memory of their ancestors while recalling fortunate or unhappy events. Examples need not be sought from afar; Joshua is present, whose name is an indubitable prophecy of his deeds and a favorable omen of the people's salvation. I find him ennobled by a double name. In the Book of Numbers he is called *Oshea*, but when sent to explore the fortifications of the enemy and the nature of the land, he changed the designation of *Oshea* to the name *Joshua*; and indeed, neither was given rashly or without counsel. Rather, since his parents sensed by divine inspiration that he was made entirely for the people's safety and produced for their benefit, they devised the name *Osee* <note>Hosea</note>, that is, "Savior," so that the omen of the name might be a comfort to the people and an incentive to the boy for noble deeds. The name *Osee* was surely very pleasing to all; upon hearing it, the hope of the wretched flourished and the uncertainty of their actions was removed. The name *Joshua* radiates with a new light of dignity and portends glorious things by its addition <note>The addition of the letter 'Yod', signifying the name of God (Yah), turning "Salvation" into "The Lord is Salvation".</note>.

<margin>
* Commentary on Joshua, p. 4.
</margin>
The name was given because of liberation, and how perfectly it agrees with his deeds is clearer than the midday sun. For while Israel, having scarcely been freed from Egyptian servitude, encountered the Amalekites with a hostile hand, behold, with Joshua as leader, they put the sons of Amalek to flight (*Exodus 17:13*). When sent with others from the desert to explore the land of Canaan, he not only freed himself along with Caleb the son of Jephunneh from present fate, but indeed the whole people (*Numbers 14:20*). Let his history be read, most fertile in prosperous successes: he led his countrymen into the land of Canaan, triumphing over all the inhabitants of the land of Canaan, and distributed the promised land among the Israelites. Whence Lactantius says: *“When he was first called Auses, Moses, sensing future things, ordered him to be called Jesus <note>The Greek and Latin form of Joshua</note>, so that since he was chosen as the leader of the army against Amalek, who was attacking the children of Israel, he might both overcome the adversary through the figure of his name and lead the people into the land of promise.”*

Just as he applies the remaining words that follow to him: *Dan shall be as a serpent by the way: as an adder in the path, etc.* For truly Samson was a snake in the way and an adder in the path to the Philistines. In Plato, Socrates praises Demodicus because he had bestowed the name *Theages* on his son, which he himself calls "beautiful and fitting for a sacred thing" <note>original Greek: καλὸν καὶ ἱεροπρεπές</note>. The bestowing of *Samuel*, a religious name, is even more to be praised and esteemed. Hannah, being sterile, asks God for offspring, on the condition that it please God. The most pleasant name of the female sex, *Hannah* <note>original: חנה</note>, is to be preferred to many others, and all the more so since her heart, consecrated to purity and grace, holds the favor of the most sincere love, so that there is no word or deed that disagrees with this heart. Lest we do injustice to this most honeyed name (for it sounds "gracious," *holdselig*, from *Chen* <note>original: חן</note>, grace), it will be more than enough to contemplate the piety of Hannah, the mother of Samuel. It is abundantly enough for her praise that, though an old woman and with God as her guide, she gave birth to Samuel—not indeed for herself, but as a most religious Priest for God, and a most incorruptible judge for the people. She was the wife of Elkanah, an Ephrathite, whose womb Jehovah had closed (*1 Samuel 1:5*), and Peninnah had reproached her for this sterility, "despising her" <note>original Greek: ἐξουθενεῖ αὐτώ</note>. But pious Hannah, weeping copiously, prayed to the Lord and made a vow that if a son were given by God, she would give him to the Lord (v. 10, 11). Samuel is given, and consecrated to God. A deadly war was being waged between the Israelites and the Philistines, the enemies of the Israelites <term>aspondei</term> <note>without treaty or truce</note> at that time, whose leader was Goliath, born of a public harlot according to the school of the Talmudists, and hence called *the man of the space between* <note>Hebrew: "אִישׁ הַבֵּנַיִם", often translated as "champion."</note>, which Capellus notes from the same sources, while taxing the ravings of the insane Jews.

The high-necked Goliath stands tall in the camp, better known to us by his reputation than by the naming of his name. He is the standout of the Philistine camp, Goliath is his name, of Gath, his height six cubits and a span. And he stood and cried out to the ranks of Israel, and said to them: *Why have you come out to set the battle in array? But we do not wish to follow uncertainties, and while we are <term>diazygo</term> <note>at a crossroads/separated</note> of uncertainty here, we shall seek more certain things about this Hercules of the Philistines, nor shall we let him slip away entirely. This <term>Pyrgopolinices</term> <note>A "tower-town-conqueror" or braggart soldier</note> goes around the army of the Israelites, and alone he trusts he can, if not repel, then at least put to shame the entire forces of his adversaries. <margin>1 Samuel 17:8, 9, 10.</margin> *Choose*, he cries, *a man from among you, and let him come down to me; then we will be your servants. Give me a man, and let us fight together.* O remarkable compendium of all masculine fortitude! He challenges a single adversary from the Israelite army and seeks to enter into a single combat with him. But what of the Israelites to this? Their hair stood on end and terror occupied their limbs, *for when Saul and all Israel heard these words of the Philistine, they were dismayed and greatly afraid.*

The adversary Galot became more ferocious from this (as the Quran calls him, for it is accustomed to invert proper names, just as it made Talot out of Saul, as Postel observes <margin>2. on the Concord of the East 13. p. 172.</margin>). Whatever strength he has, he displays again and again, and he approaches by coming morning and evening, and stood for forty days, waiting for a duelist, worried about nothing less than his own destruction. The army, not yet free, is kept from the field by great anxiety, *and all the men of Israel, when they saw that man, fled from his face and feared greatly.* By chance David was present, the son of Jesse, bringing some provisions to his brothers. Hearing the talk back and forth, he says to King Saul with masculine strength: *Let no man's heart fail within him.* Saul responds from an effeminate heart: *You are not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him, for you are a youth; but he has been a man of war from his youth.* Not at all deterred by this, David longs to be admitted to the single combat, trusting in God, by whose help he was pleased to undergo the danger of the contest for the safety of the whole army, saying: *The Lord, who rescued me from the hand of the lion and from the hand of the bear, He will rescue me from the hand of this Philistine.* Then Saul: *Go, and may the Lord be with you.*

David goes joyfully against the enemy; Goliath stands again with great gravity, and seeing David opposed to him, he mocks him as <term>not a worthy match</term> <note>Greek: "ὡς ἐκ ἀξιόμαχον"</note> for the Philistines, to whom nevertheless God had given <term>matchless power</term> <note>Greek: "ἀξιόμαχον... δύναμιν"</note>, saying: *Am I a dog, that you come against me with sticks? And he cursed by his gods, and said: Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the air and the beasts of the field.* David, with a calm countenance, warns the braggart how vain is the pride with which he stands in his gods and his strength, and stepping forward he puts his hand into his pouch, took from there a stone, which he threw with a sling, and struck the Philistine in his forehead; and the stone was fixed in his forehead and he fell.

However indignantly Goliath had previously taken being sought by the "pygmy" David, so the whole army of the Philistines took it hard that their Hercules was prostrated and conquered by David. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<page-num>242</page-num>

->**Sacred Onomatology** <note>The study of the origins and meanings of sacred names.</note><-

A notable proof is given by the sling of David: that the greater can be cast down and overthrown by the lesser, and that the greater can suffer defeat from those who are smaller in both power and dignity. For Dares <note>A reference to the Trojan boxer in Virgil's Aeneid</note> often challenges Entellus, and yet is subdued by him.

Solomon, raised to the royal throne above all the sons of David while his father was still living, takes his name from *Shalom* [שלום], peace. For *Shalom* is a word that announces and marks all prosperity and every kind of blessedness; it is much broader in scope than the synonyms usually accepted in any other language. Hence the Cabalistic Doctors feel that David conceived of something deeper regarding Solomon; according to their opinion, Reuchlin <margin>Book 1, Art of Cabala, folio 14. a.</margin> states: *David placed all hope in his seed, and for that reason called the son born of Bathsheba "Solomon," because he had heard and believed that the Messiah, through whom salvation would come to the world, would surely be the Prince of Peace according to the Cabala revealed to him. In his days there shall be an abundance of peace, until the moon be no more. Therefore, it was to be understood as referring to another of his seed rather than the son of Bathsheba; for that Solomon loved women, by whom his heart was corrupted so that he followed foreign gods, nor was his heart perfect with the Lord his God, like the heart of David his father.* Therefore, God raised up an adversary <note>original: "Satan"</note> against Solomon, so that he who possessed only the name of peace might not have perfect peace. For that promise concerning the perpetuity of peace in the time of Solomon was limited—namely, for as long as Solomon remained in the way of the Lord. Meanwhile, however, in the Holy Scriptures, this is not a fiction but the providence of the Divine Power, which willed the name to be a presage of the life to follow, especially if the person bore the type <note>A "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow Christ.</note> of Him to whom the reason for the name would truly fit. Thus Solomon was called *Peaceful* not because of total peace and public tranquility in his days, nor only because he was not a man of blood like his father, <margin>1 Chronicles 28:3</margin> but because he bore the figure of *Christ, the Peacemaker between God and men*, and who built for us the eternal temple, the Church, in which God dwells continually.

As a sort of crowning conclusion to Sacred Onomatology, we establish a review of the Prophets, in whose writings is found—scattered throughout—whatever divine doctrine, heavenly wisdom, and consolation is found in the remaining non-handwritten <note>original: "ἀχειρογράφοις" (acheirographois), likely referring here to the inspired canonical texts.</note> works. There exist in the Bible the historical books of Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles <note>original: "παραλειπομένων" (paraleipomenon)</note>, which provide many examples of pious and impious Princes, as well as of Divine grace and punishment. But in the books of the Prophets, all these things are set forth more illustriously, at greater length, and, I add, more accurately. For the Historical books are chiefly occupied with describing the deeds of the Israelite Leaders, and they mention other kingdoms only in passing and *as if by the way* <note>original: "ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ" (hos en parodo)</note>. The Prophetic writings, however, besides describing the character of the Israelite Leaders and the subject people more fully, wander out to foreign kingdoms; they both rebuke their wicked ways with sharp words and announce their *destined* <note>original: "εἱμαρμένας" (heimarmenas)</note> punishments. And what is equally greatest and most worthy of admiration: Daniel proceeds all the way to the end of all kingdoms and even of the entire world, depicting the four supreme empires in vivid colors. Furthermore, which should have been placed in the first position, they discuss so clearly and transparently the future

<column-break/>

->**Sacred Onomatology**<-

Messiah King, and the state of his kingdom on this earth, that one would have to be blinder than a mole to deny it. We observe in this our catalog of Prophets the same order we have maintained in the previous sections. The first place in the order of Prophets is occupied by *Nathan* [נתן], who, having been granted or given by a singular gift of God, received his name from the verb *nathan* [נתן], *he gave*. From this also the *Gibeonites* <margin>Joshua 9:22, 23, 27; cf. Ezra 8:20</margin> were named *Nethinim* [נתינים], *Nathinaioi*, *Nathiniaioi*, because they were surrendered to forced labors to be performed in the name of the assembly of God's people. *Joshua appointed them that day to be hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of Jehovah even unto this day.* His homeland was *Gabatha* or *Gibeah*, a priestly town, Joshua 21:17, where Eleazar the son of Aaron was buried, Joshua 24:34. He was David’s minister for Confession and courtly sermons, as is evident from his courtly sermon still *proclaimed aloud* <note>original: "ἀναφωνομένῃ" (anaphonomenē)</note> today in 2 Samuel 12:7.

Elias (Elijah) [אליהו], whose naming is composed of the name *El* [אל], "my God," and from the pronoun *Yah* [יה], "He," denoting the *Strong One of the Lord*. God gave him the strength of magnanimity and fortitude; out of *greatness of soul* <note>original: "μεγαλοψυχία" (megalopsychia)</note> he calls God *El*, i.e., his God, and believes this very one to be the true God. He who trusts in God approaches the business of the Lord undaunted and completes things that could be performed by no other human counsels or strengths. Johannes de Janua gives the same etymology in the *Catholicon*: *Hely* or *Heloy* or *Heloe* are *names of God among the Hebrews, and any one of them is interpreted as "my God."* So also Aegidius Camartus, in his learned treatise on the Prophet Elijah, <margin>Chapter 4, Section 5, page 152</margin> deals with the name of Elijah, saying it is composed of three names of God. Since he has, he says, *a name forged from the very names of God, there is no doubt that his connection with God was the greatest.* There are indeed often great and excellent titles among men, which Bernard calls "shadows of a great name" and "empty and vain images." But Elijah did not possess such a name in vain; he adorned its greatness with the splendors of great virtues. It must be explained in a few words how great the magnitude of this name is. This can be gathered first from the fact that it is forged from three names of God; for, as is clear from Jerome, *El* [אל] is placed among the ten names of God and signifies "the Strong" or "God." Also, another name of God is *Yah* [יה], which sounds like "Lord." The third name of God is *Hu* [הוה], and it is found in the sacred text: *Hu* itself is His name. From these three, indeed, consists the name of Elijah, which the Hebrews write *Eliyahu* [אליהו]. Although others may be called, such as Israel, Eliachin, Adonias, and six hundred others, you will hardly find another who has three names of God. Thus <margin>page 161</margin> *if you take the first two letters from the word Elohim [אלהים], namely EL [אל], and the first two of the word Jehovah [יהוה], namely YAH [יה], and add to them the middle letter of Jehovah, namely V [ו], then you have fashioned the complete name of Elijah, which is Eliyahu [אליהו].* He was a most fierce zealot for true religion and an *uncompromising* <note>original: "ἀπροσδεὴς" (aprosdeēs)</note> enemy of heterodoxy and the worship of Baal, whose prophets and ministers he killed to a man on Mount Carmel at the brook Kishon...

Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose (c. 340–397), Bishop of Milan.</note> explains this flight of his in this manner:
> Elijah flees the woman Jezebel, that is, the outpouring of vanity, and flees to Mount Horeb, which signifies "drying out," so that the flow of carnal vanity might be dried up in him, and he might know God more fully. For he was at the brook Cherith, which means "knowledge," where he might drink the flowing abundance of divine knowledge; thus fleeing the world, so that he did not even require food for this body, except that which the birds, as ministers, brought to him, although his food was for the most part not earthly.

Just as in an orchard, young saplings are usually planted next to aged trees so that they may grow up into their place, so that as the elderly trees wither and perish, newer ones may be present and continue the fertility of the garden with the abundance of their fruit. So it is in the Garden of the Church; thus Elijah succeeded, and entered into the harvest of his Teacher <note>Referring to Elisha succeeding Elijah.</note>, who

Regarding his true origin and the meaning of the name, he is called *Elisha*, because *Yisha-El* <note>original: ישע אל</note> means "the salvation of God," or *God saving*, and he is a type <note>A "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow Christ.</note> of Christ. Whence Augustine says in *Sermon on Time*, f. 1047: "We assert confidently and securely that Saint Elisha bore the image of our Savior." He is most famous for his miracles and other truly divine deeds, about which
<margin>
Sermon on the Desert, p. 75.
</margin>
Eucherius of Lyon <note>A 5th-century bishop and theologian.</note> should be read as follows: *Elisha, a follower of this eremitic life and virtue, became famous through the divine work of miracles; whom now the parted stream, now the floating iron, now the restored life, now the increase of oil made distinguished; and who finally, after many other things, proved the doubled virtue of the Master in himself even by this: that while the former, living, raised the dead, the latter, already dead, raised a dead man.*

Isaiah, by his name *Yeshayahu* <note>original: ישעיהו</note> or *Yeshaya* <note>original: ישעיה</note>, means "the salvation of the Lord"; for it is a word composed of *Yesha* <note>original: ישע</note>, "salvation," and the name *Yah* <note>original: יה</note>, which is the proper name of God, contracted from that Tetragrammaton *YHWH* <note>original: יהוה; the four-letter name of God</note>. For many of the Prophets received these two letters *Yah* at the end of their names, such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, Josiah, Zechariah, and the like, so that by that act they might show themselves to be adversaries and, as it were, declare war against the impious, who ended their own names with the names of their idols—such as Ethbaal, King of the Sidonians, and Jezebel his daughter, wife of King Ahab, from the idol *Baal*. This was noted from Peter Martyr on 1 Kings 16 by Aegidius Camartus in *On Elijah*, ch. 4, p. 169. Isaiah, moreover, is the *Salvation of the Lord*, as he displayed the salvation about to arise from the *Messiah* through his prophetic sermons with most joyful tidings, especially in chapter 52:10 and 57:1, so that pious Doctors have not hesitated to call him an Evangelist and an Apostle.
<margin>
Book 18 of The City of God, ch. 29.
</margin>
Whence Augustine writes of him: *Isaiah, among those things in which he rebuked the wicked and commanded the just, and predicted future evils to a sinful people, also prophesied much more than the others concerning Christ and the Church, that is, concerning the King and the city which He founded, so that by some he was called an Evangelist rather than a Prophet.* He refers to Jerome, who writes thus of him in his *Epistle to Paulinus*: *Isaiah seems to me not to weave a Prophecy, but a Gospel.* In the *Preface to the Commentary on Isaiah*, he says: *I will so explain Isaiah as to show him to be not only a Prophet, but an Evangelist and an Apostle.* Thus Amphilochius, p. 94, calls him a "clarifier" <note>original: σαφηνιστὴν</note>.
<margin>
ch. 48:25.
</margin>
And Sirach <note>The author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus.</note> calls him a "great and venerable prophet" <note>original: προφήτην μέγαν καὶ σε-λὸν</note>, or as others explain it, "faithful in his vision" <note>original: ἐν ὁράσει αὐτῷ</note> or prophecy. Truly Isaiah is the greatest of the seers, who, when he beheld Jehovah, the ruler of all things, sitting on a high throne (ch. 6:1), also perceived with his ears the divine music of the Seraphim, who celebrated the majesty of God with such great and incredible straining of voices that the lintels of the most august temple, shaken on both sides, tottered entirely (v. 3, 4), and the house, filled with a fiery exhalation, smoked; for one cried to another and said: *Holy, Holy, Holy is the Jehovah of hosts. All the earth is full of His glory.* And the lintels of the posts moved at the voice of him who cried, and the house was filled with smoke. Would that one of the Seraphim, who for this reason touched the lips of the failing Prophet with a burning coal (v. 7), would also touch my tongue, so that it might be able to speak the great things of God.

Jeremiah, born of his father Hilkiah from the tribe of Levi from the village of Anathoth, three miles distant from Jerusalem: has his name in Hebrew *Yirmeyah* <note>original: ירמיה</note>, from the loftiness and height of Jehovah; for *Ram* <note>original: רם</note> is "loftiness," with which origin the Romans strive to decorate their *Rome*, on account of its greatness, power, and splendor, which otherwise is said by the Greeks to be from *rhōmē* <note>original: ῥώμης</note>, from "strength," whence Jerome says in
<margin>
Book 2 against Jovinian.

*Powerful city, mistress city, city praised by the voice of the Apostle: interpret your name, Rome: it is either a name for strength among the Greeks, or for sublimity among the Hebrews.* Our Prophet certainly has both the name and the omen. He taught the great things of God with a great, brave, and firm mind; though he was perhaps the most unhappy of the prophets, he nevertheless sustained heavy persecutions in his office with a most level mind. He experienced as many persecutors as he had listeners—namely, the stubborn, the defiant, those who knew not how to repent, mockers, slanderers, and those plotting his death and destruction with great zeal. Hated by the King, delivered to prison, and even demanded for death by the common people. Exposed to such great dangers and calamities that, being but a man, he was cursed at the hour of his birth. But, having resumed his courage through the grace of God, he saw the conflagration of Jerusalem and the Temple, which he had predicted and later mourned in his lamentations. From the Talmudists, Epiphanius reports in *On the Lives of the Prophets* that Jeremiah took up the Ark and caused it to be swallowed into a rock, and that he would be the first to rise in the resurrection, and would come forth from the rock to be placed on Mount Sinai, and all the Saints would flow to it (Rivet, 3 Crit. 30, p. 368).

# SACRED ANTIQUITIES

<margin>

Of priestly lineage, the son of Buzi, and deported in the times of Jeconiah with those who were first of all carried away from the tribe of Judah. He was truly *Hezek* <note>original: חזק</note>, for he was strong—indeed, he prevailed over others in learning and genius, so that (setting aside the gift of Prophecy, which is incomparable) one might not undeservedly compare him to Homer, as the words of Master Friedlieb suggest, on account of his beautiful concepts, illustrious comparisons, and great knowledge of many things, especially architecture, and his prediction of the Church to be devastated by Gog and Magog before the final judgment.

Daniel, descended from royal blood, *Daniel* <note>original: דניאל</note>, from *Dan* <note>original: דן</note> "he judged" and *El* <note>original: אל</note> "God," sounds like *God shall judge* or *the judgment of God*. One can learn enough and more of his entire life from his own prophetic book, whom Ezekiel commends for the name of wisdom in chapter 28:3. Jerome, in his *Epistle to Paulinus*, calls him the "polyhistor" <note>A person of great and varied learning; original Greek: πολυΐςορα</note> of the whole world, whence Rhodom says:
<margin>
Book 3, Palestine, verse 921.
</margin>
> To the joyful Eusebius, Daniel is the greatest,
> Skilled in all things among the Hebrews and Assyrians,
> A counselor in Babylon and likewise in the Persian realms,
> Honored, venerable, and silver-haired. <note>Translated from the original Greek verse.</note>

But regarding what we should be advised of concerning *Daniel*, together with the names of Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, we shall grasp them in a single handful. These were religious and venerable names among the Jews, but when they came into the power of the Babylonians, their pious names were cast aside and idolatrous, ambitious ones were substituted by the Master of the Court. We shall use the words of Grynaeus: <margin>Prolegomena on Daniel, pp. 44, 45.</margin> *The sacred name of Daniel testified that God was his judge. But the profane name Belteshazzar signified "keeper of the treasure" or "treasurer" of Bel, the idol of the Chaldeans. The sacred name of Hananiah recalled the grace of God; but the profane word Shadrach denoted one exalted and overflowing with delights. The pious name Mishael signified one seeking his things from the strong God. But the ethnic name Meshach intended for itself one who excels in authority. Finally, the religious name Azariah celebrated God as the helper. The glorious name of Abednego signified either an "enlightener" or a "servant of Venus."* Daniel will be praised with praises as long as the memory of the Monarchies remains. A man beloved by God, he received from God many hidden things before the time and during the time of the four Monarchies concerning their fates and periods. He was truly *a light-bringer in deeds and words* <note>original Greek: ἐν ἔργοις καὶ λόγοις φωτάγω</note>, a title with which Amphilochius adorns him (v. 287) on account of his incomparable wisdom. Truly a *man of desires* <note>original Hebrew: איש חמודות; Greek: ἀνὴρ ἐπιθυμιῶν</note> (ch. 9:23), to whom all desirable and sought-after things were revealed and communicated, as Graser says (*in h. c. p. 14*), regardless of what Porphyry once, or the "circumcised" <note>A derogatory historical term for Jewish commentators who disagreed with Christian interpretations.</note> still prattle about his prophetic book, because it clearly contradicts their impiety and vain expectation of a future Messiah, whom they falsely and foolishly imagine for themselves.

Hosea had as contemporaries <note>original Greek: συγχρόνους</note> Jonah (2 Kings 14:26), Isaiah (Is. 1:1), Amos (ch. 1:1), and Micah (ch. 1:1), all of whom announced the destruction of the kingdom of Israel <margin>in Exegesis p. 164.</margin> according to the testimony of Blessed Gerhard. His name comes from "saving." For Hosea in Hebrew is *Hosea* <note>original: הושע</note> from *hoshea* "he saved." He bore this name partly because he announced salvation and the manner of salvation to the house of Israel, and partly because he spoke words concerning the Savior of the world,

<column-break/>

and partly because he was meant to be a type <note>A symbolic foreshadowing.</note> of the Savior.

<margin>
Sacred Onomatology.
</margin>
Joel, *Yoel* <note>original: יואל</note>, a word obscure and doubtful in its etymology because of the curious etymologies of many interpreters. Jerome translates it as "beginning." Philo thinks it is said as if *Yah-El* <note>original: יה-אל</note> "is God." Blessed Chytraeus interprets it as "Jehovah is God." There is one who derives it from the name *Jehovah* and *alah* <note>original: עלה</note> "he descended," not without error and confusion of letters. If there is room for conjecture, says Blessed Tarnovius, I would rather say that it is a name composed of the proper name of God, *Yah* <note>original: יה</note>, contracted so that it might better coalesce, and the verb *alah* <note>original: אלה</note> "he cursed," because he greatly emphasizes the curse of God and the punishment with which He afflicted the land. Unless you prefer to derive it from the unusual root *ya'al* <note>original: יאל</note>, which in the Hiphil form means "he willed" or "desired," as if to say *erasmon* <note>original Greek: ἐρασμὸν</note>, a "desire."

Amos, *Amos* <note>original: עמוס</note>, his name is from *amas* <note>original: עמס</note> "he loaded" or "imposed a burden," namely, *with heavy words*. He is a vehement Prophet, coming burdened with threats and reproofs to the stiff-necked people of Israel and their Princes, whom he argues against with much vehemence, and whom he reproves with a wonderful and most vivid style, as Francis Lambert says (*prolegom. p. 8*). Most of all, he indicated a "burden" to the enemies of the people of God: the Syrians, Philistines, Edomites, Ammonites, and Moabites. To these, the prophecy was a "burden" of miseries and damnation, the weight of which burden can be felt from the beginning of his book. He was among the shepherds *among the sheep-breeders* <note>original Hebrew: בנקדים; Greek: ἐν ἀποκείμ or ἐν νακκαρείμ</note>. Concerning which Gregory Nazianzen says: <margin>Oration on Pentecost, p. 263.</margin> *The most philanthropic One who enlightens the earth with the Spirit (he speaks of the Holy Spirit), if He takes a shepherd, He makes him a psalmist (he speaks of David), charming away evil spirits, and shows him as a king to Israel. If He takes a goatherd nipping sycamore fruit, He makes him a prophet.* <note>Translated from the original Greek.</note>

Obadiah, *Obadyahu* <note>original: עבדיהו; Greek: Ἀβδιῦ</note>, has his name from *avad* <note>original: עבד</note> "he served" and *Yah* <note>original: יה</note>, which is a contraction of the tetragrammaton *Jehovah*; it signifies "servant of God," which name he seems to have received from his office and industry, because he was an industrious servant and minister of God, whence Jerome says: <margin>In the Epistle to the Prophets, Vol. III, col. 439.</margin> *Obadiah the Prophet, which is interpreted as servant of the Lord, received his name from his service to God.*

The history of Jonah is most celebrated, containing the principal doctrine of the Church, since it both represents a type of Christ and sets forth an example of the dangers of the Church and its wonderful liberation. He was called Jonah, *Yonah* <note>original: יונה</note>; the name means "dove" from *yayin* or the feminine *yanah* <note>original: ינה</note>, because like a dove he was simple, pious, and mournful in the belly of the whale; or because he was forced to fly away like a dove, led by fear of danger, as if from the root *yanah* "he oppressed." Sent by God to announce repentance and punishment to the Ninevites, but disobedient to the Divine calling, he was consecrated to the sea waves by the judgment of the sailors' lots, whence he is called by Alcimus Avitus (*Book 4*) the "deposit of the world":

->And the sea, raging above all things, preserves<-
->The deposit of the world.<-

Micah, *Michah* <note>original: מיכה</note>, has his name either from the simple word *makh* <note>original: מיך</note> "he was thin/poor," on account of the thinness of his fortune, which is usually the companion of piety; or composed of *Mi* <note>original: מי</note> "who" and *ka*, either a suffix pronoun or an adverb of likeness (as pleases some, whom others contradict, since that adverb is always prefixed to other words, which dispute Blessed Tarnov— <meta>The text cuts off here; "Tarnovius" is the likely full name.</meta>

# Sacred Onomatology <note>The study of the origins and meanings of names in sacred scripture.</note>

<margin>
Sacred
Onoma-
tology.
</margin>
Tarnovius does not wish to adopt the view of those who embrace the former etymology or composition: *Who is like you?* <note>original: "quis tibi, sc. par?"</note> or *Who is here? Who is such?* Jerome explains it differently in *Epistle 103 to Paulinus*, where he interprets Obadiah as *servant of God*. And in *Volume 3, column 10*, he interprets Jonah as *most beautiful dove*; Micah as *co-heir of Christ*; Nahum as *consoler of the world*; Habakkuk as *strong and rigid wrestler*; Zephaniah as *observer and knower of the secrets of God*; Haggai as *festive and joyful*; and Zechariah as *mindful of his Lord*.

If you wish to interpret the Hebrew name נחום (*Nachum*), it has the same meaning as נחם (*consoler*), since both are derived from the root נחם (*he was comforted*). And here indeed the name is an omen, since his prophecy was a great consolation to the pious remnants of the Jews. Hence Rupert of Deutz says: *“Nahum is translated from Hebrew into 'consoler,' just as 'paraclete' is translated from Greek. And according to his name, which is Nahum, he consoles those who in this world are under pressure and suffer tribulation from men who are without God.”* That word in the *Niphal* <note>A Hebrew grammatical form indicating passive or reflexive action.</note> also means *he repented*, a meaning which is not foreign to this Prophet, seeing as he was also a Teacher of repentance.

<margin>
On Nahum f. 5 b. fol. 10, a.
</margin>
<margin>
In Epiphanius on the Lives of the Prophets p. 108.
</margin>
Hence the Blessed Zehner says: *“The name of the Prophet Nahum signifies Consoler, or Consolation; although he sprinkled his sermons quite sparingly with this [comfort], in other places he acts as anything but a Consoler, since he denounces a most heavy burden, a universal destruction <note>original Greek: πανωλεθρίαν</note> or slaughter, upon Nineveh, the Metropolis of the Assyrians.”* Rupert of Deutz institutes a comparison between Nineveh and Alexandria in *Book 2 on Nahum, f. 37. a.*: "That which is now called Alexandria was called No, and a long time later received its name from Alexander the Great of Macedon; it was always under its first name, that is, No, the metropolis of Egypt and most abundant in people. Finally, those who have handed down the history of Alexandria <note>original: "Alexandriæ memoriæ tradiderunt"</note> assert that it was the chief city." It is said therefore to Nineveh: *Are you more populous or powerful than Alexandria?* and the site of Alexandria is described, situated above the Nile and the sea, surrounded on all sides by waters and rivers. Moreover, that Ethiopia, Egypt, and Africa were in its defense shows the importance of the provinces and the city.

*Chabakkuk* or *Habaccuc* (חבקוק) is a name from חבק (*he embraced*); with the last letter doubled for emphasis, it denotes the *best embracer*. In Greek it is *Abbakum* (Ἀββακὺμ)—for so the Complutensian edition has it—others write *Abakum*, others *Ambakoum*, others *Abbakoum*, others *Ambakum*, as Eusebius always wrote it. And certainly the name is an omen. For as the Blessed Luther writes, in this prophecy he embraces his afflicted people, loves them and leans them into his arms, cherishing and sustaining them, just as a sadly weeping little boy is taken up in an embrace by his mother so that he may be silent.

*Sophonias*, *Zephanias* or *Tzephaniah* (צפניה) is a word composed of צפן (*he hid*) and יה (*Jehovah*); it sounds like him whom *God has hidden and protected*, and to whom, while hiding with Him, He revealed His hidden things and secrets, and showed the recondite treasures of His wisdom, which he in turn might show to others; as if you were to say "the Secretary of God," a title whose measure he most excellently fulfilled. Others derive it from צפה (*the north wind*), which they think the Prophet obtained from the force of the word predicated of him. Others truly, among whom is Jerome, lead it from צפה,

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred
Onoma-
tology.
</margin>
*he watched*, whence he explains Zephaniah as the *watcher of God*. *Compare Welthemer on Sacred Tropology, col. 1128.*

*Haggai* or *Chaggai* is a name among the Hebrews (חגי) which sounds like *festive, solemn, dancing* from חגג (*to leap, to dance, to keep a feast day*). He excellently fulfills the reason, measure, and omen of this name when he exhorts that the temple be restored, in which thereafter festive solemnities might be rightly performed.

*Zacharias* (זכריה, *Zecchariah*) takes its origin from the Hebrew זכר (*he remembered*) and the contracted four-letter name of God (יה), whose *mappiq* <note>A dot in the Hebrew letter 'He' indicating it should be pronounced.</note> usually falls away in compounds, so that it can be more easily distinguished from the proper name of God. This Prophet therefore has a name *from the memory of God*, perhaps because through him God wished to recall His memory to His people, and to testify that He Himself also remembered them; or because he himself held the divine promises in recent memory and recalled them daily to the people's memory.

<margin>
Malachi 4:2, 5
</margin>
The choir of Prophets, by the common opinion of the Ancients, is closed by *Malachias* (מלאכי, *Malachi*), which sounds like *angel or messenger of God*. From the Chaldean להך (*to send*), to which is related הלך (*to walk*), which is the characteristic of Envoys. The Prophet fulfilled the reason of this name in himself while he repeated the Evangelical promises concerning Christ himself—that great Angel of the eternal covenant—and concerning the forerunner or precursor of the Messiah, John the Baptist; he diligently insisted with the others that the time of the Messiah was at hand, in which the Gentiles were also to be called to the Church. Wherefore we give thanks to Almighty God, that He not only predicted the calling of the nations through the mouth of the Prophets of old in the Old Testament, but also that according to the kindness of His promise He has called the multitudes of the nations to the tents of Shem, and that the islands and fleets of the Ocean, the Northern and Eastern world, have brought their sons from afar.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

## Page 246

**Column 1:**

<margin>The size of the clusters of grapes in the land of Canaan.</margin>
The question of why wine was prohibited is settled in a dialogue held with a certain Jew, which can be read in the *Alcoran* <note>The Quran</note>, book 13. There were, says the mythologist, two Angels, **Harut and Marut**, sent long ago by God from the heavens to the earth to govern and instruct the human race, with these three prohibitions: that they should not kill, nor judge unjustly, nor drink wine. For a long time, therefore, having lived thus, they were judges by night throughout the whole world. One day there came to them a woman, by far the most beautiful of all women, who had a case against her husband. In order to win the judges to her side, she invited them to a feast; they followed. Busy with the preparations, she placed wine before the guests amidst the dainties and cups; she stood by serving, offered it frequently, and insisted they partake. What more? The woman's flatteries conquered; inebriated by the cups, they grew hot for their beautiful hostess and, overcome, demanded to lie with her. She promised on the condition that one should teach her the word by which they ascended to the heavens, and the other the word by which they descended. The condition was accepted. When she had learned it, she suddenly underwent an elevation and ascended to the heavens. When God saw this, having investigated the cause, He placed her as the morning star, the most beautiful among the stars, as she had been among women. But as for those two, having been called into judgment, God proposed that they choose between the punishment of this world or eternal punishment. They chose the former. They were therefore suspended by iron chains and lowered head-first into the well of **Babel** until the day of judgment.

Not content, this trifler <note>referring to the author of the legend</note>, in order to provoke God as if He were the author of his pretended prohibition, and to insult Christ—who Himself drank wine and graced the wedding in **Cana of Galilee** with the most flavorful and excellent wine <margin>John 2:7</margin>, clearly adorning us with precious <term>ganōsei</term> <note>original Greek: γανώσει, meaning "brightness" or "gladdening"</note> in like manner, and after a brief lack of wine filled all the water-pots to the brim, compensating for the delay with the magnitude and abundance of the benefit—he [the trifler] most impudently charges Him with sin against God's precept. Furthermore, he maliciously perverts the history of **David**, who fell into adultery and homicide but afterwards repented and chose one of three punishments <margin>2 Samuel 24:12</margin>, in a blasphemous manner. This blasphemy against such a noble gift of God was first offered by the Parent of Lies to **Tatian**, a student of **St. Justin** <margin>Bellarmin, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 49</margin>, a man otherwise not obscure among the Syrians. Among other errors he fostered, he established this one: that wine was an invention of the Devil; hence he did not admit it in the use of the Holy Supper, but substituted pure water for wine, as reported by **B. Pappus** in his *Epitome of Ecclesiastical History*, p. 235. This error was adopted by the **Encratites**, **Severians**, and **Manichaeans**, who all with one voice cursed the use of wine and detested it as the gall and filth of the Prince of Darkness; compare **Eusebius** book 4, ch. 28; **Irenaeus** book 1, ch. 34; **Epiphanius** Vol. 1, book 2. From their opinion **Hermolaus Barbarus** of Venice, Patriarch of Aquileia, did not depart much; although he acknowledged wine as a gift of God, he nevertheless taught that its use was altogether unjust, believing that God had everywhere given pure and clear water for man's drink. When he once by chance happened to have a conversation with a Demon, he asked nothing else of him but what was the meaning of **Aristotle's** <term>entelecheia</term> <note>original Greek: ἐντελέχεια, a technical term for "actuality" or "perfection"</note>, according to **Stratemann** <margin>*Historical Theater*, p. 892</margin>. Regarding the use of wine by the Antediluvians <note>those living before the Great Flood</note>, the Doctors do not agree; however, it is probable that even before the flood the Patriarchs ate grapes, just as they did other things springing from the earth. That the impious **Cainites** also abused wine before the flood is gathered from Matthew 24:38. Compare **B. Quistorp**, *Commentary on Genesis*; **Janus Cornarius**, *Theology of Vines*, book 1, ch. 1, p. 8. Concerning the origin and first cultivation of vines, the Pagans have invented various stories.

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

**Polydore Vergil**, book 3, p. 205, reports that some established that the vine was discovered near Mount Etna in Sicily; that when **Oristeus**, son of **Deucalion**, came there to reign, he by chance plucked a branch from its boughs, which he ordered to be planted, and from there the vine-sprouts were born, which he named *Oenous* from the name of a dog, which to the Greeks sounds like "wine." Others attribute the invention of the vine to the Egyptians, others to the Indians, others to the Greeks, with a teacher of planting vines leading the way, such as **Prometheus**, **Bacchus**, **Janus**, **Saturn**, or another. But from the Holy Books it is certain to us that the cultivation of the vine began under **Noah**, who was the first to plant a vineyard again in joyful soil, everywhere best for vines; and like a new Prometheus, he snatched the kindling of a little fire from heaven for the benefit of the whole human race. Hence, whatever the Gentiles prattle and trifle about the first Inventor of vines, all of it can with the easiest effort be applied to the history of Noah. Indeed, the Pagans themselves understood Noah by the name **Janus**, among whom we cite **Berosus Annianus**, who <margin>book 3</margin> discusses Noah thus: *Noah, before he departed from Armenia, where he first settled after the flood, taught them simple agriculture, and was the first of all to find vines and plant them, and taught how to make wine. For which reason they say he was called Janus by the ancients, that is, "Wine-bearer," which word took its origin from the Hebrew word Yayin, which signifies wine.* But ridiculous is the fable about the occasion given to the Father of the post-diluvians for planting a vineyard, as **Ezler** reports it <margin>*Introduction to Medical Magic*, ch. 4, p. 92</margin>: that Noah after the flood sent out a goat onto Mount Coricus in Cilicia, which, having devoured wild grapes and become drunk, began to attack the other animals with its horns; from this Noah recognized the power of the wild grape, and immediately planted it with the blood of a Lion to strengthen it, adding the "Spirit of Gold" and the mystic blood of a lamb so that it might lay aside its wild nature; it then produced excellent fruit, and he harvested it. Hence the Gentiles, as **Cornarius** notes in *Theology of Vines* book 1, ch. 3, fabled that the Aetolian shepherd **Staphylus**, while leading the she-goats of **Oeneus** to pasture, observed one wandering from the flock, more joyful than the rest, returning later to the stalls; having secretly followed her, he noticed her eating a grape on a remote stalk—a fruit unknown to him—which he took and brought to Oeneus. Oeneus, delighted by the pressed juice, and knowing it mellowed with age, offered it to **Father Liber** <note>Bacchus/Dionysus</note> when he was received in hospitality; Liber, showing Oeneus the cultivation of vines, named the wine *Oenon* after Oeneus, and the grape *Staphylen* after Staphylus the shepherd. By these wrappings of fables and names, the true and genuine history of the use of vines and wine after the flood was depraved and perverted; wherefore no less skillfully than elegantly **Daniel Heinsius** <margin>*Hymn to Bacchus*, v. 146</margin> mocks the Greeks who ascribe the invention of the vine to a Goat, when he sings in his own language:

->Those who to a Goat such a great thing as the finding of Wine<-
->Ascribe, they themselves must be Goats.<-

To the Greeks it is <term>Ampelon</term> <note>Greek: Αμπελον</note>, as if it were <term>empelon</term>, "from the shaking and stirring of the mind," because it vibrates and strikes the mind. To the Latins it is named either from *vita* (life), because it recreates the life of man, as **Mathiolus** teaches <margin>on Dioscorides, ch. 7</margin>, whence **Julianus Wauber**:

->Life differs little from the name of the vine; join<-

To others, it is from the fact that it invites (*invitet*) anyone to partake of the grapes, according to **Gregorius Horst** <margin>book 1, *On Herbs*, s. 6, § 13</margin>.
