# From Numbers XIII, v. 24.

<margin>The size of the cluster in the land of Canaan.</margin> He confesses that he cannot be satisfied by the sight of it: Do not the shoots, the branches, the layers, and the offshoots, he asks, bring it about that they delight anyone, not without admiration? The vine, which by nature is falling and, unless supported, is carried toward the earth, embraces whatever it has found with its tendrils, as if with hands, so that it may raise itself up; the skill of farmers restrains it with iron <note>original: "ferro" - referring to pruning shears or knives</note>, lest it grow wild with shoots and pour itself out excessively in all directions. What can be more joyful in appearance or more beautiful? Indeed, not only its utility delights me, as I said before, but also its cultivation and its very nature: the rows of supports, the joining and binding of the heads, the propagation of the vines, and that amputation of some shoots and the grafting of others which I mentioned. I say that the vine was created by God <note>original: "D. T. O. M." - Deo Ter Optimo Maximo, "To God, Thrice Best and Greatest"</note> immediately in the first <margin>Gen. 1:11.</margin> production of vegetables on the third day of creation; this is placed beyond all risk of doubt, and we assert without hesitation that it was known to those before the Flood, although before the Flood the use of wine was either meager or almost non-existent.

The men before the Flood, especially the pious and faithful, used either water or milk for drink. No luxuries of food or drink were known then. There was almost no other nourishment except from herbs, or fruits, or even, according to Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a prominent Italian theologian</note>, animals or birds. That most ancient life was ignorant of luxury—would that it were also ignorant of malice. But after the Flood, as human nature daily inclined and failed, Noah, the first Sower and Father of all post-flood nations, <margin>Gen. 9:3.</margin> having first been granted by God the eating of meat—which, however, Cajetan and Dominicus de Soto <note>Spanish Dominican scholastic philosopher (1494–1560)</note> prove by many arguments was customary before the Flood—discovered the use of Wine. For since he knew that wine softens sorrow, strengthens vigor, and heals diseases—all of which inconveniences, like those from Pandora's box, weary men after the Cataclysm—he bestowed diligent labor upon the cultivation of the Vineyard as a panacea <note>A universal remedy</note>; compare Horatius Augenius <note>Italian physician (1527–1603)</note>, Vol. 3, *Medical Consultations*, ep. 9. Joyful at this discovery, he takes a trial of the wine, which exhales its power and clouds the brain of the excellent old man. For nothing casts down strength as much as wine if it is taken immoderately by the healthy, or if it is taken by the sick when it ought not to be consumed. The authority of physicians recommends this matter, such as Theophrastus* <margin>On Characters, ch. 13.</margin>, and Zaleucus confirmed the same by a certain law, which law is found in Aelian, *Various History* 2, 37, p. 75, and Athenaeus 10, p. 170. Wine is indeed said to be created to gladden the heart of man, Psalm 104:5; indeed, it is said to be given for the solace of those mourning and those who are of a bitter <margin>Prov. 31:6.</margin> spirit*, which ends wine will achieve if the drink remains within the bounds of digestion and does not disturb digestion, whence a man can be strong and of good spirit, if the Spirits are refreshed thereby, sleep is won, and forgetfulness of cares is induced. To this pertains the Gloss on the law *si minor* 34... which we admit without difficulty concerning wine taken moderately <note>original Greek: "μετρίως" (metrios)</note>: He who drinks wine spends money for good uses, and because the soul, since it is Spirit, cannot dwell in a dry place. For wine, when used in moderation, exhilarates; beyond measure, it does not weigh down; hence <margin>ch. 34:33.</margin> it is called "the joy of the heart and gladness of the soul" by Sirach* <note>Referring to the Book of Ecclesiasticus</note>. And Pliny (23.1, p. 340) very elegantly commends the use of wine drunk moderately, saying: By moderate wine the nerves are helped, by more copious wine they are harmed; so also the eyes. The stomach is refreshed; the appetite for food is invited; sadness and care are dulled; urine and cold are

<column-break/>

expelled, and sleep is won. Furthermore, it stops vomiting; it mitigates swellings outside the body when applied with moist wool <margin>The size of the cluster in the land of Canaan.</margin>. Asclepiades pronounced that the utility of wine could scarcely be equaled by the power of the Gods. Just as wine taken moderately is a nourishing drink and has the power of nourishing, as the School of Physicians demonstrates everywhere (compare Bonamicus *On Nourishment* ch. 6, p. 273; Augenius, *Medical Epistles* Vol. 2, ch. 9, p. 511 and ch. 10, p. 513), whence it provides strength to the weary and exhausted, according to the saying of Homer*, <margin>Iliad 6, v. 261.</margin> "To a weary man, wine increases great strength." <note>original Greek: "ἀνδρὶ δὲ κεκμηῶτι μένος μέγα οἶνος ἀέξει"</note> It happens otherwise if our hearts are weighed down "in surfeiting and drunkenness," <note>original Greek: "ἐν κραιπάλῃ καὶ μέθῃ"</note> to use the words of the Savior*, whence comes a mass of torments, short sleep, and a confused head; for drunkenness does not <margin>Luke 21:34.</margin> refresh the Spirits, but dissipates them; nor does it dissolve cares, but increases them; indeed, it often dissolves the thread of moisture and heat in which our life consists. And who is able to recount the inconveniences of wine absorbed beyond measure?

The same to Eustochium* <margin>col. 178.</margin>: Wine and youth are the fire of pleasure. Why do we add oil to the flame? Why do we administer the fuel of fires to a glowing little body? So the same Presbyter, lamenting the magnitude of the sin of Lot perpetrated in drunkenness from excessive drinking of wine, says to the same Eustochium* <margin>col. 173.</margin>: Lot, the friend of God, saved on the mountain, and found alone just out of so many thousands of people, is intoxicated by his daughters; and although they thought the race of men had failed, and did this more from a desire for children than from lust, yet they knew that the just man Lot would not do it unless drunk; finally, he was ignorant of what he did; and although the will may not be in the crime, the error is in the fault. <meta>This page continues a discussion on the history and cultural perceptions of wine, moving from its biblical origins to classical Greek and Roman customs regarding its dilution and medicinal use.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<page-num>248</page-num>

<margin>The size of the grape clusters in the land of Canaan.</margin>
The Moabites and Ammonites are known as enemies of Israel, who, even unto the fourteenth generation and forever, shall not enter into the Church of God. Therefore, the Greeks, contemplating the harm and violence of wine taken immoderately, were by custom never used to drinking pure wine, but always diluted the wine with water, as Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of *The Deipnosophists*.</note> testifies. The Poet of Ascra <note>Hesiod, the Greek poet.</note> also aims at this: <margin>Book 10, ch. 5, v. 594.</margin>

> Pour three parts water, and the fourth let be wine. <note>original: "Τρὶς δ' ὕδατος προχέειν, τὸ δὲ τέτρατον ἱέμεν οἴνου."</note>

Indeed, according to the testimony of Athenaeus in the place cited, the Greeks held this custom of diluting wine, so that to two cups of wine they would add five of water; elsewhere, to four cups of wine, two of water, as Athenaeus cites from Menander:

> And yet it is much sweeter; or else they
> Would drink three of water, and of wine only one. <note>original: "Καί τοι πολὺ γ' ἐσϑ' ἥδιον, ἢ γ' ἂν πότε / Ἔπινον τρεῖς ὕδατος, οἴνου δ' ἕν' μόνον."</note>

We cite the words of Athenaeus himself, which go as follows: *And Diocles in "The Bees" says how one must drink wine mixed, both four and two; the mixture, then, this four to [something] or to [something else] perhaps reminded him of the celebrated proverb: either drink five, or three and four. For he says one should drink two to five, or one to three.* <note>original: "Καὶ Διοκλῆς ἐν μελισσαίς..." This passage discusses the specific ratios of water to wine favored by the ancients to avoid drunkenness.</note> Holy Scripture also mentions wine in *Song of Solomon* 7:2. The Hebrews interpret this as two parts water and one of wine, <term>two parts water and one wine</term> <note>original Hebrew: "שני חלקי מים ואחד יין"</note>; the Greeks call it a <term>rounded bowl, not lacking mixed wine</term> <note>original Greek: "κρατὴρ τορνευτὸς, μὴ ὑστερούμενος κράμα"</note>. *A rounded bowl, never lacking cups*, as the Vulgate Translator rendered it. That cooling of wine or mixing with water is in use in hot places: In all of Sicily it is performed by means of snow, which Cortefius notes in *S. Misc.* 6, p. 216, against Massiminus, can be used safely and without any danger to life. Hofmann notes in *S. Instit. Medic.* 25, § 7, p. 702, that it is a matter of great skill to temper wine so that neither the vinous quality perishes, nor the wine becomes either too strong or too weak; to which should be added Caldera on the use and method in *Tribunali Med.* sect. 2, ch. 2, p. 448, 449; Zacutus in *History of the Principal Physicians* book 4, hist. 10, p. 661, and book 6, hist. 13, p. 956; Balthasar Bonifacius in *I. Ludic. histor.* 16, p. 20, ch. 17, p. 21, and book 18, ch. 13, p. 724. For we experience, says Erasmus*, <margin>Vol. 5, p. 137.</margin> so many diseases and so many deaths arising among men from tainted wines. Others have removed all use of wine; Jonadab forbade all his posterity the use of wine, and he is praised in Jeremiah* <margin>ch. 35:18.</margin> by God Himself for both the obedience and the abstinence of his sons. Thus the use of wine is not always prohibited to the High Priest, but only at that time when he was about to enter to perform divine worship or to pray, *Leviticus* 10:9. Among the Locrians as well as the Carthaginians, it was a capital offense for those in the Magistracy to drink wine, unless a Physician had ordered it, as Aristotle testifies in book 1 of *Economics*, 5; Alex. ab Alex. 4, 6. And a drunk Prince among the Athenians was punished with death, as read in Laertius regarding Solon. The Egyptians acted more rightly, who did not deny wine to their Kings entirely, but at least offered a certain measure of wine, lest being out of their own control they might by chance fall into some vice of baseness, *Diodorus Siculus* book 2, ch. 3. For Huartus in *Examination of Men's Wits*, ch. 16, p. 516, establishes that a moderate drink of wine is necessary and very advantageous for the Magistrate and Leaders of War according to the common opinion of Physicians, since by no thing is natural heat more intensified, and no food exists

<column-break/>

which grants so much wit to a man, and yet takes it away if drunk immoderately, as the liquor of wine. For the ancients rightly withdrew the custom and daily use of wine from boys, *partly* because they are endowed with thin and loose bodies, *partly* because they can easily be inflamed due to the excess of innate heat, and *partly* also because they have weak nerves, for which wine is harmful due to convulsions, as the School of Physicians teaches at length. For this reason, Boys among the Persians were forced to be content with *water alone*, Xenophon in *Cyropaedia*, p. 6. And to this pertains the *Platonic Law* in Athenaeus*. <margin>Care must be taken that boys do not taste wine at all before their 18th year, p. 252.</margin> <margin>Book 10, ch. 11.</margin> *Care must be taken that boys do not taste wine at all before their 18th year, since fire is not to be brought to fire; from this time until the 30th year, it is to be granted to them moderately, yet so that in that time of youth they restrain themselves from the drinking of wine; but when they have exceeded the 40th year, and are initiated as Elders, let them drink more liberally.*

But we must return to Noah, the first <term>vine-planter</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀμπελοφύτω"</note>, many centuries older than Saturn and Bacchus: He, exhausted from daily labor and urged by thirst, drank rather largely, and being ignorant of the strength of wine, was intoxicated contrary to expectation. For the wines of Armenia are most noble, and of greater efficacy and power than those of the other regions of Asia. He does not sin at all, but falls into drunkenness ignorantly, unaware of the wine's strength. Therefore this drunkenness can be excused, says Blessed Gerhard*, <margin>on Genesis 9:21.</margin> because it was not of intemperance, but of inexperience; meanwhile, it ought not to be approved, because the act was in fault, though the mind was not. And Jerome to Eustochium, col. 173: *Noah drank wine, and was intoxicated. After the flood, in an age still rude, and the vineyard then first planted, perhaps he did not know that wine could intoxicate. After the drunkenness, the baring of the thighs followed, lust joined to luxury; for first the belly is distended, and so the other members are incited.* Jerome seems silently to accuse the excellent Old Man through the word *perhaps*, as if he had well known the strength of wine: But no suspicion of this thing can fall upon Noah, a just man, pious, and a herald of justice: For never afterward did he relapse into it, nor would Holy Scripture have been silent on that, which did not keep silent about this one instance of his intoxication. Hence, if he had intoxicated himself excessively from prior knowledge, it would have been done <term>out of deliberate choice</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐκ τῆς προαιρέσεως"</note>, which however cannot be said: For if such <term>deliberate choice</term> <note>original Greek: "προαίρεσις"</note> had been present, he could not have brandished such a heavy lightning-bolt of a curse against the petulance of Ham and his grandson Canaan. For that Canaan was an accomplice and partner in the paternal malice and impiety is probably gathered from the punishment inflicted. Whence the Rabbis, and from them Theodoret, hand down that Canaan first saw the nakedness of his grandfather; and mocked him, and soon pointed it out to his Father, who, when he ought to have rebuked his son, also came and saw the nakedness of his Father's private parts, and with mockery announced it to his brothers Shem and Japheth, cf. Pererius *Commentary on Genesis* p. 436. B. D. Gerhard *in the place cited*. B. Raup. *Commentary on Genesis 9* p. 57, B. D. Friedlib. *Commentary on this place* p. 51. Concerning the crime of Ham, Berosus fables thus: *Ham* <term>since he had attained the name Zoroas by studying Magic and sorcery. He hated his Father Noah, because he loved others born last more ardently, but saw himself despised: Therefore, having found an opportunity, when Father Noah lay soaked [with wine], grasping his genitals and silently murmuring with a magic song, he mocked his Father, and at the same time made him sterile.*

<meta>This page continues a discussion on the agricultural richness of the Levant and surrounding regions, specifically focusing on the history and botanical scale of viticulture (grape-growing) as described in classical and biblical sources.</meta>

# From Numbers XIII, verse 24.

<margin>
The size of the grape cluster in the land of Canaan.
</margin>

**H**e planted the first vineyard in that region of Asia which later took the name Assyria from his grandson Assur, the son of Shem. Because of the excellence of its wine, Asia once snatched the palm of victory from almost all other regions; today, by the Agarene law <note>The "Agarene law" refers to Islamic dietary prohibitions, as "Agarenes" was a historical term for Muslims.</note>, it lacks this precious liquid. Once famous was the *Byblian Thracian wine*, a fragrant wine from the Byblian vine, which was brought from Phoenicia into Thrace. This grew abundantly in Phoenicia, since Byblus was not far distant from Mount Lebanon. Festus also mentions it in *On the Meaning of Words, book 2, page 260*, calling it *Bublum*. Turnebus <note>Adrianus Turnebus (1512–1565), a French classical scholar.</note> suspects it should be written as *Byblinum*,

<margin>
Adversaria 29, column 1121.
</margin>

for Eustathius also writes it with a "y" (*byblinon*) in his commentary on *Homer, page 871*. Whatever the case regarding the spelling, this kind of wine was formerly praised as being "light-bearing" <note>original: ὀλιγοφόρον (*oligophoron*), meaning a wine that does not quickly intoxicate.</note>, whence it is also called by Theocritus in *Idyll 14, verse 15*, a "sweet drink" <note>original: πότος ἅδυς (*potos hadys*)</note>, such as a mild wine that is beneficial to the stomach—*a gentle, mild stomach-wine.* Nor was *Cabillonian wine* held in less esteem in Damascus of Syria, which only the Kings of Persia were accustomed to drink, according to Praefectus in *On the Nature of Wine, page 24*. And the Holy Bible makes mention of this Damascene wine. Ezekiel mentions it in *chapter 27:18*, which Tyrian merchants carried to the markets, "in the wine of Helbon" <note>original Hebrew: ביין חלבון (*be-yein Chelbon*)</note>. Others take *Chelbon* to be the name of the place where the best wine grew, such as B. Rauppius in his commentary on this passage. But Josephus de la Cerda, in his book on *Judith, page 109*, says: In Hebrew, *Chelbon* comes from the word for fat, *Cheleb*, that is, *milky*, and as I judge, *thick and with much juice for fattening; not because it had been spiced or was white, but because from the richest shoots, very frothy wines were cooked, which because of their abundance fattened the grapes swelling with richness.* In the time of Jerome, Damascus was still famous for its grapes; he writes on this passage: *From Damascus was brought the fattest wine and excellent wool, which we see even to this day.* An estate is praised in which there is a fertile abundance of oil and wine, not one which shines with lilies and flowers to feed the eyes: a field is pleasing which measures out the ornaments of interest <note>i.e., profitable yields</note>. Hence Quintilian

<margin>
Institutes of Oratory, book 3, page 386.
</margin>

writes elegantly on this sentiment: *Should I think a farm better cultivated in which someone shows me lilies, violets, and pleasant rising springs, than one where there is a full harvest or vines heavy with fruit? Would I prefer the sterile plane tree and clipped myrtles to the "married" elm <note>A Roman practice of training vines to grow up elm trees.</note> and fertile olives?* I shall restrain the rising peaks of the olive with iron <note>pruning</note>; it will spread itself more beautifully into a circle and immediately bear fruit for many. Judea—by which name the whole Promised Land is commonly known—that glory of the entire East, the grace of Palestine and the Prince of Provinces, abounded no less in "milk and honey" (*Exodus 3:8, 17*) than in the richest supply of the most noble wine. For just as Judea, indeed all of Palestine, once rejoiced in the most fertile vines everywhere, so today no vineyards are seen in Palestine; so much so that today, from the whole tract of Palestine, as Lyferus says in his work on *Josephus, page 498*, not even one donkey could be loaded with grapes, which was once done from a single vine. Formerly, the entire land of the Israelites was famous for the abundance of its wine. In the tribe of Judah is the Valley of *Eshcol* or the Valley of the Cluster, named for the grape or cluster of stupendous and unusual size, which the two men among the Spies carried hanging from a pole after it was cut in that place (*Numbers 13:24*). There are those who think that this cluster was taken from an Indian fig tree, as

</margin>

The temple of Juno at Metapontum stood with columns made of vine-wood. The city of *Eucarpia* in Phrygia is placed by Strabo in *book 12, page 397*; Stephanus, in his work *On Cities*, brings a witty reason for its name from Ephorus and Metrophanes, saying it was so called because of the excellence of the vine, which produces a grape so large that when placed on a wagon, it breaks the middle of it. Johann Forster says in his Lexicon: Thirteen years ago, there was a preacher at Nuremberg at St. Giles named Achacius, who had lived as a monk in the Holy Land for a full eight years. When he was sick and had nothing with which to quench his thirst—for he suffered from dropsy—he wished for himself each day only one single berry from a cluster of wine, with which he would abundantly quench his thirst. And when I, sitting by him as he lay ill, asked him how large the cluster was, he replied that it was of such size that it could scarcely be carried by two men, and that there was one cluster on one tree, and it grew only around Hebron, and was called in the language of the Barbarians *Musi*. This he said in the year '66 of the previous century; Gregory Francus considers him a witness of doubtful credit. Yet it is not so unusual for such large clusters to grow in certain regions. Nicolaus Radzivillius reported that in Rhodes they are found of such size that one extends to three-quarters of an ell, and the berries are equal to our plums. In the Island of Madeira, grapes

narrates that they are so large a man’s embrace cannot encompass them. *Strabo, Geography, Book 2, p. 50; Mercator, Great Atlas, f. 35.* This opinion of Strabo is confirmed by an eyewitness, Adam Olearius, in his *Persian Journey, part 3, p. 484.* He states that near *Astara* <note>A city on the border of modern Azerbaijan and Iran</note> he saw vines whose trunks were equal to the girth of a man, and that in *Margiana* (a province of *Chorasan*), vines are of the same magnitude as noted by Strabo—though he considers the claim that grapes are two cubits <note>About 3 feet</note> long to be far from the truth. In the islands of the Archipelago and Crete, Master Jonas *Deutshländer* observed a few years ago that clusters grow eight or even twelve times larger than ours. Nor is it uncommon to see such things along the banks of the Rhine, where others recall seeing clusters of two cubits. We must not overlook what Master Philipp Jacob *Sachs*, a member of the College of Natural Curiosities, mentions in his *Ampelographia <note>A treatise on vines</note>, p. 100.* Master Johann Michael Fehr, a physician from Schweinfurt, indicated to him by letter that in the year 1660, he observed in Franconia, near Schweinfurt in the village of *Forst*, a *grape of unusual size* produced from an *Albuoli* (or white vine, called Elbling). It grew from a thin shoot with a thick, round stalk that soon broadened, first into two larger wings, then into eight clusters of fair size, each with its own smaller bunches (called *Francis Dehrlein* in the local dialect). Its berries were then the size of millet seeds, except for the middle one, which was the width and length of a finger and surrounded by berries like an Egyptian Sycamore or an Indian fig. It stood straight without wings and promised a fruit of several pounds, which would be evident by autumn. He had seen it on June 21st. No less valuable was the vineyard of En-Gedi in the same tribe. En-Gedi was a city by the Dead Sea, as seen in *Joshua 15:62* and *2 Chronicles 20:2*, most fertile in balsam, palms, and noble wine; see also Adrichomius. Solomon mentions its vineyards in *Song of Solomon 1:14*, comparing the grace of the clusters of that place to the sweetness of the Heavenly Bridegroom and the abundance of sweetest consolation. En-Gedi, however, is a city where little trees sweat out balsam, and it is interpreted as the "fountain of the kid."</term> The tribe of Benjamin also flourished with most fertile vineyards, among which were the vineyards of Jerusalem, *2 Kings 18:31*; the vineyards in *Shiloh, Judges 21:20*; and Beth-Haccherem, which is like a village of vineyards (*Weinhausen*), *Jeremiah 6:1*. On the borders of Dan, Judah, and Ephraim, the vineyards of *Timnah* were famous, *Judges 14:5*. —the Holy Scripture testifies that the other tribes were not lacking in most delicate vines. In that part of Judea inhabited by the tribes of Ephraim, Manasseh, and part of Issachar (which was later called Samaria), the vineyards of Shechem are celebrated, *Judges 9:27*; the vineyard of Naboth, *1 Kings 21:1*; the vineyard of Gideon, *Judges 6:11*; and the vineyard of the city of Samaria, *2 Kings 6:27, Jeremiah 31:5*. In Galilee, both Upper (where the tribes of Asher and Naphtali were) and Lower (which Zebulun and the rest of Issachar received in the division of the Holy Land), many vineyards were seen, especially on Mount Tabor, Carmel, and Lebanon, as can be gathered from *2 Chronicles 26:10* and *Hosea 14:8*. The same must be said of the regions across the Jordan, namely Perea and Gilead, which fell to the tribes of Gad, Reuben, and the half-tribe of Manasseh; this was likewise a region most fertile in wine, as can be gathered from *Judges 11:33*. Thus the Holy Land, once most fertile in milk, honey, and wine, has today taken on a different face, partly from a curse and partly from the neglect and carelessness of its inhabitants. Where it once abounded with vines, it now abounds with thorns and briars; where once there were bushes and vineyards excellently cultivated, there are now horrid thickets. Hence the wines praised by the ancients are missing today, partly due to different cultivation and partly due to a natural defect in the earth. For just as the bodies of men change entirely, so the Earth, as it wears out in parts through constant cultivation, is deprived of its vital Balsam. We see vines still today coming forth happily in some places and degenerating in others; the differing nature of lands ensures that the products of the earth are not of the same vigor and value, even if they are of the same genus. Experience itself being witness, not every soil nourishes the vine, nor does every soil that nourishes it produce grapes of the same quality; hence, toward the East or South, it is thought to produce a more "heroic" wine than toward the West or North. *Merz in Oenopolia, ch. 3; see Faber, book 4 on Chymical Decrees, ch. 2.* The structure of the vine is wonderful; some classify it among trees, others among shrubs. In Crete and other islands, *vines are cultivated without any support*, immediately intertwining themselves. In Gascony, *the vine has a hard trunk* and immediately intertwines and supports itself with its branches, whence it is usually called the *upright vine*. But that which is *prostrate* immediately creeps along the ground, bringing forth most pleasant fruits. Among us, it is commonly supported by *props, yokes, or stakes* to promote the ripening of the grapes. Though it is slender and by itself not at all stable, it is nevertheless lovely; it cheers with the display of its shoots and leaves, the embrace of its tendrils, and the diversity and abundance of its swelling grapes—producing grapes here of a purple color, there in a display of grains, and elsewhere boasting a blackish veil. Hence, above other plants of the earth, God has deigned to honor the vine so much that He has compared the most powerful things of heaven and earth to it. From the vineyard and grapes come many expressions, similes, and other things of great beauty. He several times compares His Church to a vineyard, *Isaiah 5:1 ff., Psalm 80:15.* The author of the Church is God, who chooses a certain assembly from the whole human race, enlightens it with the knowledge of heavenly truth, and grants eternal blessedness to those remaining in true faith. Hence the Church has excellent comparisons: *a fruitful vine, planted in a well-watered place*, whose—

# From Numbers XIII. v. 24.

<margin>The size of the clusters in the land of Canaan.</margin>
...whose shoots are accustomed to grow to such a great size that royal scepters can be made from them, <margin>Ezekiel 19:10-11.</margin> *Likewise a vineyard, but given over to plundering by wild boars and forest beasts, Isaiah 5:5, Psalm 80:14.* Moreover, parables are most often taken from those things which are most common and familiar to everyone. Truly, because the region which the Israelite people once inhabited abounded in vineyards, <margin>Deuteronomy 8:8.</margin> for this reason God drew so many similarities from the vineyards of this region. Not only was the Holy Land a type <note>A "type" is a biblical person, event, or thing believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament.</note> of the true Church, but the Israelite people themselves were as well. Whence the Republic of Israel itself is compared to a vine planted by God, <margin>Hosea 10:1.</margin> for in that sense we understand those words <note>original Hebrew: גפן ישראל - "Gefen Yisrael," the Vine of Israel</note>. Thus, with a beautiful figure of a Vine, God describes the origin and growth of the kingdom of Israel, <margin>Psalm 80:12-13.</margin> and complains that it is miserably devastated by boars and wild beasts, that is, by enemies. Thus, no less truly than skillfully, Asaph uses rhetorical figures *regarding the transplantation of the vine* in the same Psalm, verse 8, to indicate the transition from Egypt into the land of Canaan; which at first grew most happily and extended itself over all the mountains and Cedars, even unto the sea and the river Euphrates. *God of Hosts, he says, turn us, and show the light of your face, and we shall be saved.* v. 8. <note>original Hebrew: גפן ממצרים תסיע - "Gefen mi-Mitzrayim tasiya"</note> YOU TRANSFERRED A VINE out of Egypt. You cast out the nations and planted it. <note>original Hebrew: ותשלח - "And you sent forth"</note>. You cleared the ground before it. You fixed (v. 9) its roots, and it filled the land. (v. 10.) The mountains were covered by its shadow, and the cedars of God by its branches. (v. 11.) You extended its branches <note>original Hebrew: קצירה - "its harvest/boughs"</note> unto the sea, and its shoots unto the river. <note>original Hebrew: ותשלח - "And you sent forth"</note>, which last words the Greek rendered: *and its young shoots even unto the sea, and unto the rivers.* Rightly here they explained the word <term>Katzir <gloss>properly meaning harvest</gloss></term>, from which Aquila understood "propping up," which the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> also use in expressing the Hebrew in Job; <margin>chapter 29:19.</margin> however, it is taken for the branch of a tree in Job 14:9, Isaiah 27:11; and in vines the <term>Katzirim</term> are the shoots or branches of the vines, which take their name from the human palm. For just as some shoots are "hearth-shoots" <note>original: "focanei," secondary shoots</note>, springing forth in the middle of a fork, others are fruit-bearing or cluster-bearing, while others are "barren" <note>original: "orbi"</note>, which produce nothing, <term>blind vines <gloss>German: blinde reben</gloss></term>. So indeed in the Church, such shoots are found, who possess nothing besides the name of "shoots," and bear no fruit in it; the cause of which sterility is in no way the vinedresser, just as in the spiritual vineyard it is in no way God. Paschasius Ratbertus writes elegantly on these words of the Psalm in his commentary on Matthew: <margin>chapter 20, column 825.</margin> *The vineyard of the house of Israel was transferred and transplanted from Egypt, which vineyard was called Sorek, that is, "the chosen one." In which vineyard clearly all that ancient and Hebrew people of God labored, whom the Father of the family himself, namely Christ, chose from the very beginning of the world, and established in the faith; and as if by a straight line through all the Fathers and Patriarchs down to the same Christ, he did not cease to instruct their genealogy and establish them in the faith, and through the same ones he never ceased to labor and cultivate that same vineyard. Even if truly he handed it over to be cultivated by Bishops and Priests—to speak of the present Church—as if to farmers, so that he might receive the fruits or tithes from their hands; for they are his hired, chosen, and designated workers, to do what belongs to vinedressers, lest the vines grow luxuriant into leaves, barren shoots, and tendrils, which bring nothing, but that*

<column-break/>

<margin>The size of the clusters in the land of Canaan.</margin>
they might produce clusters and bunches, from which wine may be drawn out, which makes God and men glad. What then, if instead of fruit only leafy shoots were found, if instead of grapes wild grapes are returned, and gall instead of wine in the field or spiritual vineyard? The <term>pampini</term> are the leaves with which the vine is clothed, and by which the fruits are covered and defended from excessive sun and other injuries of the air. Hence the verb *to prune* <note>original: "pampinare"</note> is to break off the tips and remove the luxury of the foliage, whence vines are said to be pruned, lest a too-abundant supply of leaves harm the clusters on the vines. Dominicus Chabræus describes the wild grape thus in his *Iconography of Plants*: <margin>Class 15, p. 111.</margin> *It is a wild version of the cultivated vine, with trunks, branches, jointed shoots, leaves, tendrils, flowers, and fruit, but it runs riot into a branchy and tree-like offspring, whence it becomes sterile, and brings forth smaller and rarer grapes, and even those it does not finish, but leaves them less tasty and immature.* Moreover, it is called *Labrusca* <note>Wild grape</note>, because it grows on the edges or "lips" <note>Latin: "labra"</note> of the land, according to Gorræus in his *Medical Definitions, book 3*; and it is distinguished into that whose grape never matures, but at least produces the flower called *Oenanthe*: And into that which has small, black, astringent berries. From the fruits of the wild grape, in the absence of the cultivated vine, the peasants in Sardinia press wines, as witnessed by Baccius in *On the Nature of Wines, book 5, p. 238*; and the inhabitants of the Lumellin territory, when the vineyards are troubled by hail, frost, or blight, make a vintage from the clusters of the wild grape, as Bernhard Saccus testifies in *History of Ticino, book 4, chapter 12.* In the spiritual vineyard, that is, in the Church, very often wild grapes are offered to God, the greatest <term>Vinedresser <gloss>Greek: ampelophyten</gloss></term> of all; mere and pure leaves are offered, even if he planted the vineyard in a fertile place and leased it to vinedressers to be diligently cared for; concerning which he complains in Isaiah: *I will sing,* <margin>Isaiah 5:1 etc.</margin> he says, *to my beloved the song of my cousin concerning his vineyard: my beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill. And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones, and planted it with the noblest and most excellent vines, and built a tower in the midst of it, and set up a winepress in it; and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes.* The Prophet implies that God planted this vineyard of his, that is, the Jewish Church, in a fertile place, that is, moistened by the dew of his grace and the Holy Spirit, and gifted it with innumerable physical benefits; he also surrounded it with a hedge and a stone wall, that is, he defended it with a faithful guard against physical and spiritual enemies; he planted it with the noblest vines, that is, he planted in it the most noble vine, Christ, *John 15:1, 5*, into whom the truly faithful are grafted like shoots so that they may bear fruit; he built a tower in its midst, that is, he guarded it with the watchful eye of his providence, indeed he took such great care of it that he could say: *What more ought I to have done for my vineyard, that I have not done?* <margin>verse 4.</margin> Notwithstanding this very diligent care, God complains that the vineyard produced not grapes but wild grapes; he expected grapes, that is, works pleasing to God and a life worthy of a reborn man, but he received *wild grapes*, that is, impious works, which by their foulness and bitterness, like wild grapes, offend and embitter God. He repeats the same complaint in Jeremiah, <margin>chapter 2:21.</margin> *I had planted you as a noble vine, entirely of the best seed. How then are you turned against me...*

In the Sacred Records <note>original: *Pandectis*</note>, false doctrine and life are compared with wine mixed with water.

It is a stratagem of innkeepers to deprave good wine and mix in water for the sake of ruinous profit. They destroy the wine and gain nothing, even if silver and gold are in the chest, and even if they think they have a profit. Those greedy gluttons, seekers of profit but losers of soul, seek for themselves filth from profit, ruin from destruction, and death from their inner greed. Thus sincere religion is corrupted by superstitions, and civil justice and honesty by iniquity and fraud, avarice and injustice, while the vinedressers seek their own profit and neglect what is the duty of each, whence for the Prophet to "mix wine with water" is to study deceits and frauds both in the perversion of religion and in the business of the State. To the Vineyards and the Vinedressers or Shepherds who

<column-break/>

demolish the vineyard, God threatens destruction—to the former because of the wild grapes, and to the latter because of their sluggish laziness in planting the vineyard. Vines are subject to many injuries, especially if the negligent cultivation of the Vinedresser is added, so that they often forestall fate and the limits of a proper age. From the shoots of the Vine are born little worms, which gnaw the ripening grapes unless the vinedresser cuts away or removes the shoots swarming with such worms at the right time; hence this removal is called <term>vermiculatio</term> <note>The process of clearing worms from plants.</note>. In the Sacred Records such a Worm is called <note>original: *תולעת* (Tola'at)</note>, *by the Septuagint "the worm" <note>original: *ὁ σκώληξ* (ho skōlēx)</note>.*

<margin>
The size of the clusters in the land of Canaan.

Among secular writers, it is called by **Pliny** (*Book 17, ch. 28*) the *Volvox*; by **Cato** (*On Agriculture, ch. 95*) the *Convolvulus*; by **Columella** (*On Trees, ch. 15*) the *Volucrum*; by **Plautus** (*Cistellaria 4. II. 63*) the *involvulus*, as it is that which wraps itself in the twisted leaf of the shoot and brings great harm to the ripening grapes. Otherwise, that little worm <note>original: *תולעת*</note>, which comes from the grain-fruit destined for the dyeing of garments—which Kings and Priests once used—is similar to a gnat and immediately flies into the air when the fruit is mature. From this is made the color with which scarlet <note>original: *Scharlach*</note> is dyed; compare *Exodus 25:4*, where the same word <note>original: *תולעת*</note> occurs in the Sacred text with another, <note>original: *שני* (shani)</note>, both of which the Septuagint rendered as "double scarlet." The Vulgate: *scarlet twice dyed*; Pagninus and Vatablus: *the worm of scarlet*; Junius and Buxtorf: *double-dyed scarlet*; the Chaldean Paraphrast: *a bright color*.

<margin>
Deut. 28:39.
</margin>

Because of the damage brought upon the vines and the vineyard, the vinedressers are bound to drink the *wine of fury*, <note>original: *כוס היין החמה*</note>, who previously drank the wine of iniquity, <note>original: *יין חמסים*</note>, *Proverbs 4:17*. It is

<margin>
Jer. 25:15.
</margin>

unmanageable and gloomy subject matter when we must deal with the wine of calamity, for which no desire arises, which even the pious drink in this life, albeit from the cup of paternal chastisement. The Psalmist deals with this wine of calamity and affliction in *chapter 60:3*: *You have shown your people hard things: <note>original: *השקיתנו יין תרעלה*</note>, you have made us drink the wine of staggering <note>original: *οἶνον κατανύξεως*</note>, others say the wine of horror.* Junius translates: *You had given us horror to drink like wine.* Arias: *the wine of perturbation.* Pagninus: *a soporific or sleep-inducing wine.* Some interpret the Hebrew word as madness and rage, so that you may understand the Israelites were so overwhelmed by their evils that they were uncertain of all things. And **Calvin** thinks the Prophet speaks specifically of a poisonous potion which deprives minds of sense and intelligence. The Psalmist indicates the calamity of the Kingdom of Judah by using a metaphor of the *wine of compunction*; this signifies that they were overwhelmed by such great calamities that they stagger and nod like drunken men, nor can they find where to stand or rest. This is an unpleasant cup even if it proceeds from paternal love, and more unpleasant to the impious, who read listlessly what is held in the Psalms concerning the bitterness of that wine, namely Psalm 75:8, concerning the cup of the Lord's fury, which the impious are forced to drink down to the dregs, from which the danger of loathing and satiety is not absent. *The cup,* says **Asaph**, *is in the hand of the Lord, <note>original: *כוס ביד יהוה*</note>, and the wine is pure, <note>original: *ויין חמר מלא מסך*</note>, full of mixture, he has poured out from it; nevertheless its dregs they shall suck out: <note>original: *ישתו כל רשעי-ארץ*</note>, they shall drink...*

# From Numbers XIII. v. 24.

<margin>The size of the grape cluster in the land of Canaan.</margin>
...all the sinners of the earth, all the impious of the earth shall drink. Let those be terrified by what is announced here concerning "pure wine," which is explained as *oinos akratos* <note>original: "οἶνος ἄκρατος" — unmixed wine</note> by the Greeks; that is, wine that is pure and separated from all mixture. In Hebrew, there is a word that signifies to redden or to be disturbed, for *chamar* <note>original: "חמר"</note> means to be troubled, turbid, and muddy, just as Aben-Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a medieval Spanish Jewish scholar</note> and Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the influential medieval French rabbi</note> explained here regarding turbid wine. That cup is full of an infusion of pure wine, or, if you prefer, turbid wine, by which the brains of the impious are disturbed while they are intoxicated. The wine was mixed, "full of mixture" <note>original: "πλήρες κεράσματος"</note>, for *masak* <note>original: "מסך"</note> means to mix and to pour out a mixture, for these actions <margin>Proverbs 23:30.</margin> follow one another, as it is held. This was said according to the custom of those nations who mixed water with wine. The Oriental peoples, on account of the burning temperature of their regions, were accustomed to temper the wine to be drunk with water; among them, "unmixed drinking" <note>original: "ἀκρατοποσία"</note> was a great disgrace. But to Vatablus <note>François Vatable, a French humanist scholar</note> a different meaning is indicated, namely that the wine is aromatic. For he compares the vehemence of God's wrath and fervor to aromatic wine, as if he were saying: God does not merely set simple wine before the impious, but with an added mixture so that it has more strength. But the former view pleases us more, since the Ancients, and especially the Greeks, and after them the Romans—living in hotter places and having wines that were more noble [potent]—mixed them with water, which they called "diluting." Regarding the author or the first parent of dilution, they tell various fables. Athenaeus (Book 2, Chapter 6) relates that Melampus was the first. Others make Staphylus, son of Sithenus, the author, according to Pliny (Book 7). The Greeks fable that the mixing of water was discovered by chance and accident, according to Athenaeus (Book 15, Chapter 5): *When Bacchus had brought vines into Greece, and men, charmed by the use of wine, fell down overwhelmed by it, a rainstorm came on and a cup in which a little wine had been left was filled with water; when the guests returned and tasted the diluted wine, they felt a mild pleasure that was not at all troublesome; afterwards they diluted their pure wine.* Indeed, it is established that the genuine cause of dilution among the Ancients was what we brought forward above: namely, that the wines were more potent than ours, and they themselves inhabited regions hotter than our soil. On this soil, we prefer pure wine to diluted wine by many <margin>Book 2, Epigrams.</margin> leagues <note>original: "parafangis" — a Persian measure of distance</note>, agreeing with the judgment of Owen*:
> Simple wine is praised, double beer is praised,
> Duality is good, but simplicity is best.

Lest we wander too far, we shall not stray if we mix the "mixing" of the Latins into this business and offer it in good faith. For "to mix" is elegantly used for "to pour," "to offer a toast," or to give a drink to someone. <margin>On Ends, 2. 67. b.</margin> Hence Cicero*: *He who mixes honey-wine for another, though he is not thirsty himself.* This phrase is taken from antiquity: for it was the duty of the boys who served the cups to dilute the wine with water; Juvenal refers to this custom:
> --- The boy, bought for so many thousands,
> knows not how to mix for the poor.

And Ovid, *Metamorphoses* Book 10, line 160:
> --- who even now mixes the cups,
> and serves nectar to Jove against Juno's will.

In Homer, the word *kerannymi* <note>original: "κεράννυμι" — to mix</note> is used in the same sense elsewhere, since the Ancients were especially accustomed to use wine for the purpose of libation; hence Minerva <margin>Odyssey, Book 3, line 332.</margin> urges Nestor to make a libation to Neptune and the other immortals*,

<column-break/>

--- mix the wine.
So also in the *Iliad*, Book 8, line 189:
"and having mixed wine to drink when the spirit urged."
<margin>The size of the grape cluster in the land of Canaan.</margin>
Where Eustathius simultaneously observes that *keran* <note>to mix</note> is derived from *keratos* <note>horn</note>; for the ancients, before the use of drinking cups, used horns instead of goblets. The dregs of the cup are mixed for the impious; for here he shall drink of the wine of God's wrath, which is mixed with pure wine in the cup, according to the words of the Psalmist: *The dregs of the impious* <margin>Psalm 75:9.</margin> *they shall suck up and drink.* To some, the words seem transposed, for "they shall drink and suck up," as if to say: they shall not only drink, but they shall drink it all down to the very last drop, even to the dregs. This is a common enough expression for the Hebrews, that the word which has more vehemence is placed in the first position. The sum of it is: they cannot escape drinking the cup offered by God down to the last drop. Of the same wine and from the same cup shall he drink, *who worships the Apocalyptic beast and its image, and receives the mark on his forehead or on his hand*, the Angel threatens* those who, against their conscience, profess their <margin>Revelation 14:9, 10.</margin> name among the followers of the Roman Pontiff and bind themselves to him by oath; since by this "image" of the beast is understood the Papal kingdom (compare *Revelation 13:16* and B. Gerhard, *Notes on Revelation, page 111*). Yet the godly cannot entirely escape this mixed wine, for tribulation is also given to the godly; which, although it be heavy, is still wine, because God always offers and mixes in consolation, nor does He pour the cup more fully than the nature and condition of the godly man can bear. Nor should this seem unusual to the godly, while they too are bound to perform their labors in the spiritual vintage, and to apply a vigorous hand in the pressing of the grapes; it befits them to be among those who
> --- pluck the grapes from the vines,
> and carry them in baskets, and hasten to crush them with swift feet
> upon the hollow rocks; the vintage glows
> on the highest hills, the grape is broken by frequent treading,
> and wet breasts are splashed with purple must.

Since in the Holy Scripture, "to gather the vintage" and "to tread the winepress" are attributed to both the godly and the impious, though in different respects. For "to gather the vintage" is frequently read in the Latin version of the Bible, and beyond its proper meaning, it notes metaphorically: 1. To send war and other chastisements, because in the vintage the vines are despoiled of their fruits, and the whole vineyard is left as if desolate*; *He has stripped me as in a vintage*, where Jerome adds: <margin>Lamentations 1:15.</margin> *The Lord is said to gather the vintage because, by the rule of justice, He has now decreed that they should reap the fruit of their labor.* A little more clearly, Cornelius à Lapide says: *He has stripped me*, that is, the Chaldean enemy has despoiled me of all goods, as a vineyard in the vintage is despoiled of all its fruit and good. 2. It is to take away or snatch away for the same reason*. He <margin>Psalm 76:13.</margin> cuts off [vintages] the spirit of Princes: *He is terrible to the Kings of the earth*, that is, He Himself takes away the courage and strength of heart from Princes, so that, despoiled of all nobility of mind, they tremble like little women; just as those despoiled of all godly honor and manly virtue; just as vines, after the vintage is finished, are seen naked, desolate, and deformed (Flacius, *Key to the Scriptures, under the word 'vintage'*). 3. It notes the exercise of the final judgment, because there the separation of the good and rotten grapes will be made. From this...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The size of the clusters in the land of Canaan.</margin>
The meaning must be explained from verses 18 and 19 of chapter 14 of the *Book of Revelation*, as the Blessed Dionysius interprets them in Volume 4 on *Revelation*, page 595. However, Luis del Alcázar argues that the vintage in that passage foreshadows the martyrdom of those who would embrace the faith of Christ. Blasius Viega, in his *Commentary on Revelation 14, section 2, page 752*, refers the vintage sickle to the young and the harvest sickle to the old. He adds this reasoning: because the elderly depart at a mature age, they are rightly compared to a dry harvest, which is already fit for reaping; but because the youth, still in their flowering age, represent a vineyard overflowing with the most beautiful clusters, they rightly belong to the vintage sickle. *These two sickles are to be referred not only to the Last Judgment, but also to the death of each individual.* These are his words. The pressing of the grapes follows the vintage. The vessel is called the wine-vat or small vat, in which the grapes are trodden, and afterwards the small vat full of trodden grapes is carried to the Lake <note>The "Lake" or *Lacus* refers to the receiving vat for the juice.</note>. The Lake, the Winepress (*Torculare*), and the Press (*Prelum*) are one and the same thing, the structure of which Cato describes in *On Agriculture*, chapter 18; Vitruvius describes it differently in Book 6 of *Architecture*, chapter 9. Regarding the ancient method of pressing new must, or treading grapes, which was varied and unknown in our age, <margin>Book 14, Natural History.</margin> Pliny himself shows this in several places, at which Hesiod also seems to aim before him in lines 609 and following. From the treaders of the grapes, they required that before they girded themselves for this labor, they should have their feet well cleaned; for it was not fitting for anyone impure to eat or drink in the winepress, nor to enter or leave it <margin>Book 12, chapter 28.</margin> too often, because nothing, as Columella says, draws a foreign odor to itself more quickly than wine. Hence Bacchus himself, who was depicted wearing *buskins* <note>High boots worn by tragic actors.</note>, is warned by Turnebus <margin>Adversaria 25. 30.</margin> to bare his feet, as in Virgil’s *Georgics*, Book 2, line 6:

->— — — *and stripped of your buskins*<-
->*Stain your bare legs with me in the new must.*<-

<margin>Book 2, Elegy 5, d. 4.</margin>
Jacopo Sannazaro imitated this passage of Virgil:
> But now lay aside your heavy robe and hairy buskins,
> And you too stain your tender feet in the must.
Regarding the modern use and method of pressing grapes, especially in Germany, I will say nothing, since it is known even to the blind. Jeremiah laments in his *Lamentations* <margin>Chapter 1, 15.</margin>: *The Lord has trodden the winepress for the daughter of Judah*: that is (as it is explained there), he did not tread clusters of grapes, but the men themselves, and even the primary nobles; he trod them down and crushed or bruised them, just as grapes are crushed by the treader. On this passage of Jeremiah, <margin>Column 1346.</margin> Paschasius Ratbertus speaks thus: *The winepress, according to the custom of Holy Scripture, is sometimes used for vengeance and the punishment of sinners; sometimes, in the gathering of new fruits, it is used for pains and torments, as it is in the present case, where Jeremiah, mourning the overthrow of Jerusalem, says: The Lord has trodden the winepress.* In Solomon’s *Proverbs* 3:10, abundance is attributed to the winepress: *The vats shall overflow with must,* <note>original Hebrew: וְתִירֹוֹשׁ יִקְבֶיךָ יִפְרֹוֹצוּ</note> and your vats shall burst with new wine, according to the version of Arias Montanus and Pagninus, <note>original Hebrew: וְיִקְבֶיךָ יִפְרֹצוּ</note> that is, they shall break out because of the plenty; they will weigh down the vats with their abundance, for the word <note>original Hebrew: פָרַץ (paratz)</note> denotes breaking through, and indeed with a certain force, a metaphor taken from overflowing waters. The Church is like a certain vineyard and winepress of God, where from the grapes of the doctrines, commands, and promises of God, through the ministry of the heralds of truth, the wine of wisdom, faith, obedience, and endurance in

<column-break/>

the cross must be pressed out, by which God is gladdened, the Church is helped, and the faithful are confirmed and preserved in faith and obedience. We are exhorted to the profession of the cross by the example of our Leader and Forerunner, Jesus Christ, who through his herald Isaiah <margin>The size of the clusters in the land of Canaan. Chapter 63: 2, 3</margin> asks in the name of the Church: *Why is your apparel red, and your garments like his who treads in the winepress?* To this question, which Isaiah brings forth in the name of the Church, the Savior responds and says: *I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the peoples no man was with me.* Some explain these words only regarding the passion of Christ, not regarding the subduing of the enemies of the Church, which still happens today and will happen until the last day, because Christ uses means in subduing tyrants and persecutors, such as the work of Moses, Cyrus, etc. But the Blessed Tarnovius <margin>Biblical Exercises, p. 432.</margin> responds well: *Christ effects this as the primary and principal cause, which does not exclude secondary and instrumental causes where a place is given to them. Thus we rightly say that God alone governs the world, which he does not do immediately, but usually uses the work of angels and men. Thus God alone performs miracles, yet it is not to be denied that the saints also performed miracles. God alone forgives sins, yet he uses for this the ministry of the Apostles and Teachers of the Church.* Compare the Blessed Friedlieb and Raupp in their *Commentaries on this passage*. It remains, therefore, that these words of Christ are to be understood not only of his passion, but also of the oppression of the enemies of the Church. Paschasius <margin>Lamentations 1:15.</margin> Ratbertus looks to both meanings: *When the Lord, as if ascending to the heavens, was asked by the Angels, "Why is your apparel red, and your garment like those of people treading in a winepress?" he is said to have answered: "I have <margin>Commentary on Lamentations, Book 1, col. 1346.</margin> trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there is no man with me." For this winepress, in which both punishments for the wicked and rewards for the good are trodden out, the Lord himself trodden alone, having no helper. For neither Angel, nor Archangel, Thrones nor Dominions, nor any of the heavenly powers, assumed a human body, and suffered for us, and trampled the opposing strengths and crushed them. The Lord trod the winepress on the day of his passion, so that rewards for the believers, and for the non-believers and persecutors, perpetual vengeance of captivity and the punishments of eternal damnation might remain.* And since we have such a Leader and High Priest, who did not refuse <note>original Greek: συμπαθῆσαι ταῖς ἀסθενείαις ἡμῶν — "to sympathize with our weaknesses"</note>, *Hebrews* 4:15. Who would blush to tread the winepress of the cross with him, to wash his garment in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape, *Genesis 49:11*, that is, to take up his cross and follow him, as he himself explains, *Matthew 10:38*. For wine is often used to describe afflictions, whence the Patriarch himself in a Prophetic Spirit wished to signify by this washing the multitude and magnitude of the sorrows and passions of Christ, just as it is a much greater thing to soak or wash clothes in wine than to sprinkle them with it. Blessed is he who washes his clothes in the blood of the lamb, that is, who is endowed with true faith in Christ and adorned with the crown of all virtues. He is a vine pleasing and fruitful to GOD, which does not bear the words of GOD in the Prophet Isaiah *chapter 5: 5, 6*: *I will take away its hedge, and it shall be eaten up; I will break down its wall, and it shall be trodden down. And I will lay it waste; it shall not be pruned...*

# From Numbers XIII. v. 24.

<margin>The size of the cluster in the land of Canaan.</margin>
And briars and thorns shall come up over it, and I will command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it. Truly a heavy and difficult judgment against the vineyard and the vine, whose fruits are wild grapes, and grapes of <term>ענבי רוש</term> <note>original: *inve rosh*</note> *grapes of poison* or *of gall*, that is, virulent, bitter as gall, and most sour clusters, <term>σταφυλὴ χολῆς</term> <note>Greek: *staphylē cholēs* - cluster of gall</note>, a sentence by which all temporal happiness is withdrawn, and unless one repents and returns in time, eternal happiness as well. These cannot expect the joyful vintage which is foretold in *Jeremiah 31:5*, when the Prophet says: <term>נטעו נטעים וחללו</term> <note>Hebrew: *natu netaim v’chillelu*</note>, *The planters shall plant, and shall play the flute*: Thus the Septuagint rendered <term>חלל</term> <note>the root *chalal*</note> as <term>αἰνεῖν</term> <note>Greek: to praise</note>, whom Luther followed: *They shall plant / and pipe thereto*; Zangerus poorly: *Earnestly they shall plant / and not gather.* This version of Zangerus does not fit, since the Prophet's whole discourse turns on joy, and consolation is directed to the captives, that they should return with joy to their own land. The Blessed Luther, and those who side with him, look to the custom of the Jews introduced into the vintage itself. For it is clear that the Jews sang in the vintage from *Judges 9:27, Isaiah 16:10, Jeremiah 48:33*, as in *Hosea 2:15*. Moab is threatened through Jeremiah (ch. 48:33) that they shall not tread with a <term>הידד</term> <note>Hebrew: *heydad* - a shouting cry</note>, a *shout of joy*. The Hebrew word <term>הידד</term>, which the Septuagint nowhere expresses, the Vulgate translates as *celeusma* <note>a rhythmic chant for rowers or laborers</note> or a *trumpet blast* or an *incitement to war*; among the Hebrews it signifies any clamor, but specifically in this place it denotes the shouting of those treading the winepress, as is clear from the cited places. For in the joy of the vintage, everything once resounded with songs, namely:

> While boys through the fields, and girls mixed with boys
> Running about, plunder the riches of Bacchus.
> While jar against jar, while basket against basket and floor
> Against floor, sickle against sickle, struck and struck back, they rattle.

Great joy was seen among all nations in the autumn at the time of the vintage, while some were seen lifting the clusters high, others carrying the gathered grapes in a heap, others bearing full baskets, others with well-washed feet entering the winepresses, squeezing and treading the grapes put in, others pressing with the wine-press, others with a hoarse whisper drawing off the foaming, fermenting must, others extracting the grape-skins so that the greatest part of the liquid could be cast into the vats beneath the press, others removing the foam risen to the lips, others putting the grape-skins into jars to make a drink for the household, others pouring new must into flasks and jars, and finally others greedily drinking:

</margin>
> ———— each for himself the cups
> That meet them they seize; what chance gave, use takes.
> That one hollows his hands, and turns his palms into cups.
> But he, prone, drinks from the vat, and with smacking lips
> He drains the must ————

Great was the joy therein, and a greater license than is proper was given then, as it is still given today to the Vintagers; concerning the license of the ancients, one should read Caelius Rhodiginus. Concerning that of the moderns, Ambrosius Leo in his *Description of Nola*, where he reports concerning the vintagers in the Kingdom of Naples at Nola, that even today they rail against anyone, even against Lords and Magistrates, with gestures and obscene words, yet they suffer no punishment for it, the custom of the place so allowing them. The song which the vintagers sang among the Gentiles was called <term>ἐπιλήνιος ᾄσμα</term> <note>Greek: *epilēnios asma* - a song of the winepress</note>, and this to Bacchus,

<column-break/>

the inventor of the vine, who was therefore called Lenaeus, was sung while the grapes were being pressed; Scaliger describes its manner in *Book 1 of Poetics, ch. 55* thus:

<margin>The size of the cluster in the land of Canaan.</margin>
> All the spring is pleasing, I drink new wine,
> I cure an old disease with a new one.

But to return to the Prophetic passage, from which we departed on the occasion of the rite of singing in the common joy of the vintage, most of the Interpreters translate <term>נטעו וחללו</term> as *to profane*, so that the sense is: *They shall plant vineyards, that they may take common use from them*. For they say the word <term>חלל</term> <note>chalal</note>, when used regarding the fruit of Vineyards or vines or trees, signifies to make their use *Common* or *Vulgar*, which was finally taken after the fruits had first been consecrated to God. For it was cautioned by divine law that trees or vineyards should not be picked within three years after they were planted; the fruit of the fourth year was to be consecrated to God alone; finally, the fruit of the fifth and following years was to be consumed for public use; hence it happened that vineyards and trees, after they had been consecrated to God, were said in the following years to be *profane*, that is, to be of profane and common use, just as <term>τὸ κοινὸν</term> <note>the common</note> and <term>κοινῶν</term> <note>common things</note> among the Greeks is taken for that which is not sacred, but of common and vulgar use. And thus Saa, Vatablus, Castro, Cornelius, Junius, Piscator and others explain it; compare the Blessed Hülsemann's *Commentary*. Yet neither opinion, as far as it seems to me, removes the other, but both seem conformable to the present place, since as a punishment God threatens the impious Israelites that they shall plant vineyards, but shall not profane them, or make them common, that is, so that all may eat of the fruit of the vine in that place and enjoy it; compare *Deuteronomy 20:6*. Furthermore, <term>חלל</term> in the Piel form, as Buxtorf teaches in his Lexicon, also signifies *to play the flute, to pipe, to dance*, although the former meaning is more frequent. Finally, since the <term>κοίνωσις</term> <note>koinōsis - making common</note> commanded by God, or, so to speak, the *restoration to the community*, was done with singular joy on the part of both the Lord of the vineyard, who made the vineyard common, and those who ate of the vine and made a plenty of grapes for themselves, it can very easily be conjectured from this that they harvested with almost the same rite and manner of singing, and gave thanks with a grateful soul to the <term>πολυηγέθι</term> <note>Greek: *polyēgethi* - much-rejoicing</note> God for the gifts of the vineyard. During the vintage and after the vintage, the <term>τὰ ληναϊκὰ</term> <note>Greek: *ta lēnaika* - festivals of the winepress</note> were celebrated in the field at the winepresses, and among the Romans the *Sacred Vinalia of Jupiter*, which were also called the *Rustic Vinalia*; compare Rosinus, *Roman Antiquities, Book 4, ch. 12, p. 107*; Marcellus Donatus, *Clarifications on Suetonius, ch. 40, p. 683*; Lipsius, *Second Cares on Tacitus, Book 1 of Annals, p. 58*; namely when the wine was first brought into the city, on the 19th of August, and it was offered as a libation to Jupiter as the Author of this good gift, concerning which Pliny, Varro (*On the Latin Language, Book 5*), and Ovid write:

> Autumn had come, stained by the treading of grapes,

The Devil, as a <term>κακόζηλος</term> <note>Greek: *kakozēlos* - wicked imitator</note> and ape of divine works, stole this rite of libating wine to himself along with other rites commanded in the Divine law. ...trained slaves, namely Heathens, so that they might celebrate their sacred rites with wine, for no other purpose—as Augustine testifies the Heathens thought—than because they knew both the Jews and after them the Christians *used wine, the former once in Sacrifices, the latter in the Holy Eucharist*, and thus they believed they were worshipping Bacchus and performing rites to Jupiter. Moreover, while the Romans celebrated the festival of the vintage, amidst various joys they also observed the rites of Venus; for they not only celebrated the *Vinalia* (called by others *Veneralia* <note>Festivals of wine and Venus</note> in honor of Venus as the *Protectress of Gardens*) on the 23rd of April, but even in those *Vinalia* which were sacred to Jupiter, they did not forget Venus. Indeed, among other playful and obscene acts, it was the custom for the Prince himself to go outside the city and devote himself to wantonness during this feast, as noted by Lipsius in the place cited above. The purpose of the godly was different: after giving thanks to God, the Best and Greatest, for the generous blessing of the vintage, they would gather their friends once the harvest was finished and enjoy the riches of the earth with them in gladness.
<margin>Song of Solomon 5:1.</margin>
To this the words of the Bride refer: *Come, my friends, and drink deeply, my dearly beloved.* <note>original Latin: "Venite amici mei, inebriamini Charissimi."</note> Happy is the intoxication to which we are invited by these most dear words! Concerning that intoxication to which the Bridegroom invites us, let us hear Ambrose in Sermon 13 on Psalm 118: *It is a good intoxication which causes a certain departure of the mind toward better and more pleasant things, so that our soul, unmindful of its loneliness, is cheered by the wine of delight.*

Wherefore He says to His people by a severe mandate: *You shall not do so to the Lord your God.* At the same time proposing a blessing... <margin>v. 4.</margin>

In several writers, there was the name *Yah* <note>original: יה</note> from the Hebrew *Yah* <note>original: יה</note>, <gloss>Iao and Iaoth</gloss>, as if the name *Iacchus* flowed from this source, and through the Aeolic digamma became *Bacchus*. It was a familiar habit of the devil to admit sacred names into the use of his superstitious rites—a matter we pursue more extensively elsewhere—and to transfer holy words, after the true knowledge of God was lost, into titles for fictitious deities. Doctor Thummius, in his commentary on *Matthew, page 40*, believes that every single surname of Jupiter was drawn from sacred fountains; and one should read Heinsius in *Aristarchus, chapter 1*, regarding the attributes of the true God wickedly transferred to Jupiter and Bacchus. While the Defender of Superstition <note>referring to the devil or pagan apologists</note> smeared on his own dyes, that color and splendor of the divine name gradually grew cheap and vanished. Thus was introduced—which was the first step and slide toward an open profession of impiety—the erection and veneration of images and idols under various concepts. By this very act, men easily forgot God and clung to external signs. How much the memory and recollection of God was abolished among the descendants of Cain is shown by their sacred rites, which were seen to consist of certain naked and external ceremonies on hills, in groves, and on mountains, where nothing was seen by which the Divinity, majesty, and power of God could be recognized. They fabricated and worshipped images of created things. When the Pagans did not see these in the assemblies of the Jews, and noticed a far different method of divine worship, they either defamed their mysteries or, if they perceived anything similar to their own rites, affirmed that the Jews had transferred it into their own sect. Jehovah had revealed to his people how much images displeased him, and how much a worship without likenesses pleased him; for a slide into the impiety of the neighboring nation was easy, which had made for itself a graven image and the likenesses of those things *which were in heaven above, and which were on the earth beneath, and which were in the waters under the earth*, so that it might adore and worship them. Therefore, He warned so diligently both in His law and through the Prophets that they should flee that nation along with all the profanity of idols. When Moses wished to turn the people away from idolatry, he said: *You saw no likeness on the day that the Lord spoke to you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire.* The most wise Lawgiver said this so that they would not be led by <unclear>desire</unclear> to make an image of the divinity and attribute the honor due to God to a created thing, as 
<margin>In the explanation of the 1st Precept.</margin>
the *Tridentine Catechism* rightly advises. Conversely, the Canaanites and as many as pleased themselves with ancestral superstition mocked the worship of the Jews as simple, and, being without the apparatus of images, as vile and contemptible. What trifles and <term>indifferent matters</term> <note>original: διαφορά</note> the gentiles handed down concerning the sacred things and ceremonies of the Jews cannot be told without amazement. In that historian, Lipsius praises his prudence, precepts, love of truth, and maxims without any confusion or harm, yet in such a way that he censures his impiety.
