<meta>This page continues the discussion of ancient misconceptions and slanders directed at the Jewish people by Roman and Greek authors, specifically addressing the false claims of animal worship.</meta>

# From Deuteronomy 12:3

<margin>Altars, statues, sacred groves, and idols. See book 5, chapter 3 of this work.</margin> The Egyptians are accustomed to worship [these]. Tacitus* invented this occasion for [Jewish] worship: that while they were wandering in the vast, waterless regions of Arabia and wasting away from thirst, they found springs by following wild asses <note>original: *onagris*</note> who were heading from pasture to drink; out of gratitude for this favor, they supposedly consecrated the likeness of such a beast. But a liar ought to have a good memory of what he previously said: for he also wrote that they count among the profane anyone who would fashion *images of the Gods out of mortal materials in human likeness*, much less that of a donkey. He also writes concerning *Gnaeus Pompey* entering Jerusalem: *From then on it became common knowledge that there was no image of the Gods within, the seat was empty, and the mysteries were void.* Among the Jews, according to the minds of the Pagans, since it was doubted whether there were ever swine [there], the pigs grew old; and by the ancient law, the Jews were forbidden from eating pigs. They grow old, they say, for since the pigs were not killed, they reached old age, to which Juvenal alludes when he mocks the Jews in passing in *Satire 6, line 160*:

> And ancient mercy grants long life to old pigs.

<margin>Book 12 of the Antiquities of the Jews, chapter 7.</margin> Antiochus certainly attempted everything against that nation and its law: *For having placed an altar in the temple (these are the words of Josephus), he slaughtered pigs, a sacrifice most foreign to the Jewish religion, and he compelled everyone, having abolished the worship of the true God, to venerate his own deities, and having built temples and altars in every town, to slit the throats of porcine victims in them daily. He even threatened heavy punishment if anyone circumcised their children, appointing men to enforce the mandates and even to compel by force those who refused to observe them.* What punishment would it be, I ask, if the pig had been a religious object to the Jewish people? Petronius also clings to the same lie, whose very sharp poem survives in the *Catalecta* as follows:

> Though the Jew may adore a porcine deity,
> And call upon the very tips of the donkey's ears. <note>original: *Cilli summas advocet auriculas*</note>

Good God! A porcine deity! That the Jews would be moved by reverence for such an unclean and hated animal; an animal whose mere image placed on the gates by the Emperor Hadrian was intended to drive the Jews away? Mocking the Jewish abstinence from swine's flesh, Plutarch disputes in *Table Talk, Book 2, Question 5*: *Whether the Jews abstain from its flesh because they venerate the pig or rather because they loathe it?* This insult regarding the worship of a porcine deity arose from the abstinence from pork commanded by the Law, <margin>Leviticus 11:7-8.</margin> *just as that regarding the donkey perhaps arose from the singular law of redeeming the firstborn of a donkey, which was misunderstood by the Gentiles, Exodus 13:13.* Regarding the other lie, Pithou reads *cilli* <note>from the Greek *killos*</note> so that it means a donkey. This reading is preferable to the following one, which reads *coeli* (of heaven). Heaven lacks ears, but the *cillus* (donkey) does not, which is why he adds "the tips." The Donkey has large ears, which is called *killos* by Julius Pollux in the *Onomasticon, Book 7*, by Hesychius in his *Glossary*, and by Johann Scapula in his *Lexicon, page 789.* This calumny concerning the worship of a Donkey's head owes its origins to Apion, who, according to Josephus in *Book 2 Against Apion*, was the first of all to charge the Jews with worshipping the head of a donkey: *Apion used to say*, says Josephus, *that the Jews had placed a donkey's head in the sanctuary and worshipped it religiously; he asserts this was revealed when Antiochus Epiphanes plundered the temple and found that head made of gold, worth a great deal of money.* Christians were also once accused of this deformed worship, having originated from the Jews in the mind and opinion of the Pagans; indeed, as Tertullian reports in *Apology, chapter 16*, a picture was circulated in Rome in his time in which some Deity was inscribed with donkey ears, one foot hoofed, carrying a book, wearing a toga, and <margin>Altars, statues, sacred groves, and idols.</margin> it was said to be the *God of the Christians*. See Kipping on *Pappus' Supplement, page 113 ff.*, Beyer on *Selden's Additions, page 225*, and *Vossius, Book 3 on Idolatry, chapter 75, pages 1135-1136.* But if you approve the common reading of *coeli* (heaven), he will be explaining it as worshippers of the ether and the clouds, according to the opinion of Juvenal:

<margin>Compare Cunaeus, On the Hebrew Republic, chapter 4.</margin> > They adore nothing except the clouds and the light of heaven.

God very often showed himself present to his people from the clouds; hence perhaps it is that these liars of liars babble that they worshipped clouds. Or they speak ironically, as if the Jews adore clouds when they look up while praying to heaven as the dwelling place of God; or because they address God by the name *Shamayim* <note>Hebrew: שמים, meaning "Heavens"</note>. Hence also the Jewish sect once called the *Coelicolae* (Heaven-dwellers). Regarding the donkey's head which they blather about with donkey-like stupidity, it could be guessed that the *worship of the golden calf* was being noted—for which some Fathers substitute the *head of the golden calf*—and the *donkey's head* was substituted for the calf's head in a matter not well understood. A single, very simple argument suffices for us, supplied by Tacitus, who records that the invisible creator of the world is understood by them without mortal materials, and they perceive one deity with the mind alone. The Law of God forbade them from living with those who despised the divine law and the one deity, whether they were Canaanites or other foreigners <note>original: *allophyli*</note>, whom God commanded them to avoid extremely as being alienated from religion—not out of hatred for the human race, as was charged against them, but out of hatred for idolatry, so that they might avoid idolaters. If those most infamous slanderers would weigh a little more carefully that religion which they boast of, they would undoubtedly spare the Jews. Cicero, ignorant of the heavenly scriptures, mockingly ridiculing the Jews conquered by Pompey, calls their sacred institutions a *barbarous superstition*. He says <margin>Oration for Flaccus, Vol. 2, page 512.</margin> *the Jewish religion is inconsistent with the splendor of the Roman Empire*. He calls Gnaeus Pompey, who first made Judea a tributary, *Hierosolymarius* (the man of Jerusalem), and praises him because, although he usually offered sacrifices wherever he went, *he denied worship to the God of Israel* alone, thinking it did not suit the majesty of the empire *that only one God should be worshipped*. He also passes judgment on the conquered people based on their present calamities and hardships, concluding that they are by no means *a care to God*, much less that men so distressed, poor, and few are loved by Him. But if someone were to ask you, not those who possess heaven, but those who merely tread the earth: have the shameful rites of these [Romans] contributed more to the splendor of the empire? What will you answer? Truly your worship in every state and form of your empire was ridiculous and erratic. King Numa, your first King and Lawgiver, who said he had slept with the Goddess Egeria, laid the "excellent" foundations of your Republic, if it please your Gods, for the splendor of the following empire. From the founding of the city, no image was seen in your temples for one hundred and seventy years, by the decree of Numa, as Augustine teaches from Varro in *City of God, 4.31* <note>OCR says 32</note>; and Eusebius has the same in *Preparation for the Gospel, 9.3*. Unless you wish to say that splendor comes from the veneration of many deities—

...of the deities, so that you dared to boast from this point in the *Speech on the Response of the Soothsayers*: <note>original: "Orat. de arusp. resp." referring to Cicero's *De Haruspicum Responsis*</note> *that your nation has surpassed all nations and all peoples in piety and religion.* If only Cicero had given the glory to God, and in place of and along with his oratory, had planted true piety! If only he had thundered in the argument of piety and put on the tragic buskin! <note>A metaphor for speaking with great dignity or solemnity.</note> It smacks of the deepest paganism and an ignorance of divine justice and counsel that he insults the calamities of the Jews; it moved the Orator, immersed in Roman affairs, when he saw the affliction of the Jews, and it moved other mockers to openly repeat what the Psalmist says of such buffoons <margin>Psalm 94:7; 115:2.</margin>: *The Lord does not see, nor does the God of Jacob understand. The Jews, as we who dwell in the Church know, when they ceased to be <term>theoproslykoi</term> <note>Greek: "those who flee to God"</note>, they ceased to be <term>theoproslokoi</term> <note>Greek: "those who look to God"</note>, and were handed over to the nations to be afflicted. Jeremiah 29:18.* <margin>Deuteronomy 28:37.</margin>

How this was fulfilled is evident only through an enumeration of the calamities of war and other distresses in which they were greatly entangled, and are still entangled to the reproach of all nations, which it is not the purpose of this section to review. We shall see here rather the chief cause of these calamities, which was <term>idolatry</term> <note>The worship of idols or false gods.</note>, and we shall briefly list the foreign Gods described for us by the Holy Book, along with the religious honor paid to them, which consisted in the veneration of images or any other ritual, whether in temples, private houses, on hills, or in groves. Something will be reviewed concerning each. That sentiment of Cicero is true and notable <margin>Tusculan Disputations, Book 1</margin>: *There is no nation so wild, none so barbarian, that it does not confess there is some God.* But as to who that true God is, errors were made everywhere among the nations, where each abounded in its own sense and wavered without the light of the divine word. Only

<column-break/>

in Judea was God known, *Psalm 76:1*, because there alone the word of God was shining. Those who turned away from this light could not help but fall into the pit of errors. Hence the world was filled with various Gods and <margin>Altars, statues, groves, and idols.</margin> various idols according to the diverse character and judgment of men. So that we may understand the idolatry of the ancients, with Scripture as our guide, it can be divided by its object: some is *heavenly*, some *earthly*, and some *aquatic*; for among the ancient Gods, some were believed to be heavenly, some earthly, and others aquatic or subterranean. Theodoret says in *Question 21 on Exodus, p. 80*: <note>The following is translated from Greek</note> *Both the Egyptians and the Greeks believed that some were heavenly goddesses, some earthly, and some subterranean; and that some ruled the earth, some the sea, and some had authority over the fields and the plains.*

And indeed, the first and most ancient of all appears to be <term>heliolatreia</term> <note>Sun-worship</note>, which worshipped heavenly things: the Sun, the Moon, and the rest of the stars. The Phoenicians *knew only the sun, the moon, and the other stars as Gods*, according to the testimony of Sanchoniathon. In this *one point* (says Natalis Comes <margin>Mythology, Book 7, p. 10</margin>) *the opinion of almost all peoples and nations first agreed: that when they saw those divine bodies which appear above—the Sun, the Moon, and the other stars—driven by perpetual motion, they called them* <term>Theos</term> <note>God</note> *from that swiftness and believed them to be divine. Nor was any nation found that first believed the Gods to be anything other than the celestial bodies themselves.* The author of the *Wisdom of Solomon* <note>Chapter 13</note> sharply attacks this impiety and identifies the first authors and inventors of impiety as those who worship <note>The following is translated from Greek</note> *either fire, or wind, or the swift air, or the circle of the stars, or the violent water, or the luminaries of heaven, the governors of the world* from verse 1 to 10. But if those poor interpreters of divinity had weighed a little more attentively the greatness of the appearance and the creature—that is, the excellence and beauty of the creation—they would have seen the author and maker *recognizably*, as the Old Interpreter says: <note>The following is translated from Greek</note> *for from the greatness and beauty of created things, their original author is seen by analogy* verse 5. Luther translates this: <insert>The Creator can indeed be recognized in the great beauty and works of the same, as in a picture.</insert> So much so that Plato, in *Book 10 of the Laws*, recognized divinity from the motion of the Sun. And Manilius in *Book 1*, considering the motion of the heaven and the course and order of the stars, concluded thus:
> And to me no reason seems so present,
> By which it is clear that the world is turned by divine power
> And is itself God.
But the greater part, with a relaxed mind depressed toward the earth, considered the works of the creator: <note>Greek</note> *because, attending to the works, they recognized the craftsman* verse 1. Here <term>prosekhein</term> <note>to attend/pay attention</note> is used with emphasis, and suggests that the irregular worshippers were not engaged with the highest attention and thought in knowing and seeking the creator through the creatures, by comparing the creature with the creator and the effect with its cause. <note>Greek</note> *For if they were so far able to know that they could aim at the world or the Lord of these things, how did they not find Him sooner?* verse 9. And this is that <term>ra’ah</term>, *to see, Isaiah 40:26*, with which the Prophet calls out to the idolaters, *that they should lift up their eyes on high and see who created these things.* He demands <term>anablepsin</term> and <term>epignōsin</term> <note>looking up and recognition</note>, a contemplation in which the intention and thought of the mind is applied to the sharpness of the eyes. Certainly by this <term>prosokhē</term> and <term>stokhasmos</term> <note>attention and conjecture</note> many Philosophers arrived at the knowledge of one deity, <note>Greek</note> *and from the good things that are seen they were able to know...*

significant form, it is in the shape of a *Mule*, according to the Babylonian Talmud; but if we believe the Jerusalem Talmud, it is in the shape of a *Peacock*. So too the Babylonian <term>סכות בנות</term> (*Succoth Benoth*), *Sefach*, and <term>ששך</term> (*Sheshach*), concerning
<margin>Jeremiah 25:26. Daniel 1:7.</margin>
the worship of the Goddess Sacea, see Selden, Book 2, Chapter 13. From the contagion of their neighbors, the Israelites adopted Gods, who upon their departure from Egypt and at their very entry into the land of Canaan served *Baalim* and *Ashtaroth*. This same impiety
<margin>Judges 2:11, 12, 13.</margin>
later invaded the most wise Solomon, who in his old age, enticed by foreign women, worshipped <term>עשתרות</term> (*Ashtoreth*), the God of the Sidonians, and <term>מלכום</term> (*Milchom*), the abomination of the Ammonites.
<margin>1 Kings 11:5.</margin>
The most detestable idol is called <term>שיקוץ</term> (*shikkuts*), "abominable" above others, because it required the sacrifice and burning of men, as will be discussed at length in its proper place. He also built a <term>במה כמוש</term> (*high place for Chemosh*) (v. 7), which was the Moabite idol, and perhaps the God of feasting, who was called *Komos* by the Greeks. They think Ashtoreth is Venus, because Cicero says:
> The Syrian Venus, conceived at Tyre, who
<margin>On the Nature of the Gods, Book 3.</margin>
is called Astarte, and who is said to have married Adonis.
Those who derive the etymology of her name from the stars (*astra*) are foolish. Mention is made of the temple and cult of Venus, where
<margin>2 Maccabees 1:13, 15.</margin>
she is called *Nanea*, and was worshipped in Persia, with whom Antiochus desired to "dwell together" <note>original: "συνοικεῖν" (synoikein), a euphemism for marriage or cohabitation.</note>. It is ridiculous that this King sought marriage with a Goddess, which Tirinus (p. 906) teaches was a custom among ancient Kings. Concerning *Dagon, Gad, Miplezeth, Jupiter, Hercules, Tammuz*, and others, they will be discussed separately in their own places. The general name for the Gods was *Baal*, which was applied to any false God; first recommended by this title are *Beelphegor* and *Beelzebub*, most filthy deities. For these and other foul Gods, altars and shrines were constructed, high places were consecrated, images and statues were erected, incense was burned, and victims were sacrificed. As far as *images and idols and likenesses* are concerned, they were fashioned *according to the whim of the molders*, as each person was inclined toward these or those Gods. This "personal invention" is indicated by Hosea
<margin>Chapter 13:3.</margin>
with this word: <term>כתבונם</term> (*kitvunam*), *according to their own understanding.* Or as the German says: *as they are able to devise it.* The Author of Wisdom (Chapter 13:10 ff.) pursues this elegantly, and Baruch exaggerates this insane custom,
<margin>Chapter 6.</margin>
where he excellently shows that idols are nothing (v. 1 ff.), that they can neither punish the wicked nor do good to the righteous (v. 33 ff.), and that everything done for idols and all those ceremonies and rites of worship are false and vain. "All things that happen among them are false," he says:
<margin>verse 44.</margin>
> Being made of wood and overlaid with gold and silver, it shall be known
<margin>verse 50.</margin>
hereafter that they are false.
(v. 50). For all things are full of superstition, having proceeded and been established by the most vain minds; and the authors and makers of the carvings are just as much <term>תהו</term> (*tohu*), *Vanity*, as the fashioned Gods themselves. See the description of their
<margin>Isaiah 44:9 ff.</margin>
manufacture (v. 12, 13, 14, 15, 16) from the craftsman's art, exactly as Baruch describes it, so that one might seem to have borrowed the sentiment from the other. Vain craftsmen, out of vain craftsmanship, fabricated vain idols of no importance, for a vain and empty purpose. Hence Jeremiah also
<margin>Chapter 10:3, 4, 5.</margin>
aptly depicted the crafted likenesses, how the Craftsman adorns them with gold and silver, and fastens them with nails and hammers, so that they must be carried...

# On Deuteronomy XII. v. 3.

<margin>
Altars, statues, groves & idols.
</margin>
...it brings and afflicts. Before this work *of hands, the idolater is undoubtedly at prayer, worshipping what his own fingers have made*, Isaiah 2:8; he bows himself down before a piece of wood, chapter 44:15. His lips vibrate with certain rhythmic numbers, and he worships an empty phantom in the place of God, saying: *deliver me; for thou art my GOD* v. 17.

<margin>
Arnobius, Book 6.
</margin>
The more sophisticated Pagans did not wish to be described this way, and they retorted to the Christian who reproached them for idolatry: *You err and fall into mistake; for we do not judge the bronze, nor the materials of gold and silver, nor the other things from which statues are made, to be in themselves religious divinities. Rather, we worship those within them, and venerate those whom the sacred dedication brings in, making them dwell in the manufactured images.* This was also the view held by Julian the Apostate, the <term>kerophylax</term> <note>original: κηροφύλαξ; literally "wax-guardian," a title used here perhaps mockingly or technically regarding temple duties</note>, when he replied to Artemius, the Duke of Syria:

<margin>
Surius volume 5 page 581.
</margin>
*The Heathens do not worship their images as if they were GODS.* Far from it. The rustic and simpler folk take it that way, but those who are possessed by a desire for wisdom, and who inquire accurately into the affairs of the Gods, know to whom they pay honor, and to whom the adoration of the images passes. But even so, not even he who holds a "good opinion" of God can wash away the stain. The sacred Writers cannot sufficiently rebuke the thoughtlessness and stupidity of the idolaters, who looked up to images as if they were full of divinity and animated.

<margin>
Lorin. on Wisdom p. 233.
</margin>
Moved by the occasion of the foul idolatry of the Egyptians and Canaanites, God forbade images to be introduced into his temple, so that genuine worship might stand as far as possible from the likenesses of the gentiles. The profane nations mocked the temples that were empty of statues for that very reason, as we said above; and, as we add here, they mocked the Christians for it, who it is certain for some time introduced absolutely no image into their temples, so that they too might seem to stand at the furthest distance from the likenesses of the gentiles. And from this, <term>atheism</term> <note>original: atheïsmus; in the early church, Christians were often accused of being "atheists" because they had no visible statues of gods.</note> was charged against them, because they could not show their God, they abolished the ancient cults of the Gods, and held no GODS besides one. There is no merit in likenesses, neither by reason of the material, by which they are called silver, golden, bronze, or wooden, nor by reason of the form, by which some are called

<margin>
Psalm 115:4 & 134:15-16.
</margin>
carved, others cast, others painted. The Psalmist says: *Their idols are* <note>original Hebrew: כסף וזהב</note> *silver and gold, the work of men's hands. They have mouths but they speak not.* He uses a fitting name <note>original Hebrew: עצבים</note> from <note>original Hebrew: עצב</note>, meaning pain, labor, or trouble, which manifests the nature of idolatry, which brings pain and terror to consciences, but no

<margin>
On Hosea page 514. b.
</margin>
relief. Luther says: *The word by which he calls idols here (chapter 4:17, where Tremellius translates "terrors") has its name from hardships. For not only is the life of idolaters full of hardship, because they leave themselves no leisure or rest, but certain calamity follows idolatry.* Peter

<margin>
On Samuel p. 210.
</margin>
Martyr says: *Idols are rightly called "pains" in Hebrew, because without any use they only torture, tear, and afflict consciences, and—what is the highest and greatest pain—they provoke the wrath and vengeance of God.* Truly, various troubles undergo both those who venerate idols and those who carve them. *The carpenter as a wood-cutter* <note>original Greek: ὑλοτόμῳ τέκτων</note> wanders anxiously in the forest to choose precious wood that does not feel decay or rot, *well-fashioned* <note>original Greek: εὔτυκτον</note>, Wisdom 12:11. Solicitous about material that can be handled and elegantly worked, he goes back and forth to cut down cedars for himself, and takes the holm-oak and the oak, the pine among plants, for a future *idol-making* <note>original Greek: εἰδωλοπόιησιν</note>, Isaiah 44:14. The cedar is a tree free from corruption and

<margin>
Pliny Book 13 chapter 11.
</margin>
decay, for eternity belongs to the material itself, and because of this

<column-break/>

<margin>
Altars, statues, groves & idols.
</margin>
the likenesses of the Gods were frequently made from it; and the roof of the Ephesian Diana was constructed with beams of cedar, as the same author testifies in Book 16, chapter 40. He takes from those trees to form an idol and outlines it *with a measuring line* <note>original Hebrew: בשכד</note>; he shapes it with a compass and makes it with axes, v. 13.

->*A trunk perhaps hewn*<-
*Venerate the divinity of the ancient tree of the Phallus,*
he is anxious, however, lest he make a mistake, which Horace mockingly and festively says:
> *Once I was a fig-tree trunk, a useless log,*
> *When the carpenter, uncertain whether to make a bench or a Priapus,* [Satires Book 1, Satire 8]
> *Preferred that I be a God. Thus I became a God, the terror of thieves and*
->*birds.*<-

After the idol has passed into its form, a great preparation was made there concerning the consecration, the worship, and other *youthful follies* <note>original Greek: νεανιεύματα</note>. The priests, *having their heads and beards shaved* <note>original Greek: τὰς κεφαλὰς καὶ τὰς πώγωνας ἐξυρημένοι</note>, Baruch 6:30. So that the icons might shine, *they smeared them with vermilion* <note>original: minio perlinibant</note>, just as Pliny (Book 33, chapter 7) recorded that among the Romans the face of the statue of Jupiter itself was accustomed to be smeared with that color on feast days. *They clothed them in purple garments*, Baruch 6:12, 57, 71; *they placed crowns upon them*, v. 9; *they wiped away the dust*, v. 12; *they lit lamps*, v. 18; *they offered gifts*, v. 28; *they hung ornaments in their ears*, *they burned incense*, 1 Kings 11:8, Ezekiel, Genesis 35:4, 20:18, and other such vanities.
Just as that worship of idols is condemned, so also the word of God condemns all things that serve it, such as the Priests, the high places, the groves, the altars, the statues, and finally all the instruments from which the idol was made. PRIESTS were appointed to appease the Gods, to preside over the solemn rites. These ministers of Idols are called <note>original Hebrew: כמרים</note>, *Chemarim*, as if you were to say "the blackened ones," because they were clothed in dark garments when they performed the rites; for the word is from <note>original Hebrew: כמר</note> or <note>original Hebrew: כמל</note>, which signifies *to be blackened, to be darkened*, and *it also signifies to burn*; for pseudo-priests are accustomed to grow hot with zeal and, as it were, to seethe with heat. *For their heart is in hot devotion, like an oven, when they sacrifice.* [Hosea 7:7]. Wolfgang Capito, in his commentary on Hosea p. 199: The idolatrous sacrificers were called *Chemarim*, as if "burning and glowing," because they were of burning and inflamed affections in worshipping their God. The *Chemarim of Baal* displayed this kind of religious fervor, who cut themselves *according to their custom with knives and lancets until the blood gushed out upon them*, 1 Kings 18:28; these Zealots Elijah killed at the brook Kishon, v. 40. Josiah, about to renew the covenant between God and the people, could do no other than first cast out of the temple of the Lord all the vessels that had been made for Baal, and for the grove, and for all the host of heaven, and destroy the *Chemarim*, the priests of the idols, whom the Kings of Judah had ordained to burn incense in the high places, and at the same time those who burned incense to Baal, to the Sun, to the Moon, and to the signs, and to all the host of heaven, 2 Kings 23:4-5. The Greek translators express the type of punishment—he destroyed—rendering it: *and he burned the priests* <note>original Greek: καὶ κατέκαυσε τοὺς ἱερεῖς</note>. In the text: <note>original Hebrew: השבית</note>, *he caused to cease*, i.e., *he abolished, he removed*, from the verb <note>original Hebrew: שבת</note>, *he rested, he ceased*, for which the Chaldean said in the same sense: <note>original Hebrew: בטל</note>, *to cease*. Perhaps the Greeks thought it was from the word for a spark. These blackened priests of the idols were cut off by the command of God, when Israel acted as an idolater, by the Chaldeans themselves. *I will stretch out*, says Zephaniah 1:4, *my hand upon Judah and upon all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and I will destroy from this place the remnant...*

<sig>Fff 2</sig>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

-> Altars, statues, groves & idols. page 630. <-
<margin>page 8 ff.</margin>
...while **Baal**, <term>את-שם הכמרים</term> <note>original: "et-shem ha-kemarim"</note>, the name of those who wear black garments. The Vulgate: *the names of the temple-attendants*. Luther: *The names of the Camarim*. The Septuagint: *the names of the priests*. Vatablus* <note>François Vatable, a 16th-century scholar</note> says the **Cemarim** were idol-worshippers, so called because they were clothed in black garments; as if to say, I will bring it about that not even a memory remains, not only of the idols, but also of the worshippers themselves along with their ministers. Tirinus* <note>Jacobus Tirinus, a Jesuit commentator</note> says the Hebrew **Kemarim** properly signifies "kindlers," namely of fire or incense, because they were mostly covered in soot, and were black in face and clothing. This would be what Baruch chapter 6, verse 20 says: their faces *grow black from the smoke* <note>original Greek: μελαίνεσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ καπνοῦ</note>. 2 Kings 23:5. Indeed, moreover, out of the greatest incentive of superstition, they used to sear themselves and imprint black marks with permanent characters upon their bodies for the sake of religion, so that they might exaggerate their fervor toward the Gods; these stigmas were like certain silent marks *for a seal of superstition* <note>original Greek: εἰς σφραγῖδα τῆς δεισιδαιμονίας</note>. Concerning this branding, hear Prudentius <note>A Roman Christian poet</note>:

> What when the one to be consecrated receives the Seals?
> They apply needles to small furnaces.
> With these they proceed to burn the limbs, and as they have fired them,
> Whatever part of the body the burning mark
> Has branded, they proclaim this thus consecrated.

Hence Vatablus and Mariana translate it as *the scorched ones*. Pagninus: *those dressed in black or mourning*. Our author elsewhere calls them soothsayers, and adds that they were appointed for sacrificing in high places; in Hebrew <term>lecatter</term> (<term>לקטר</term>), that is, for fumigating or burning incense to idols. The duty of the **Temple-attendants** <note>Latin: Aedituorum</note> therefore, besides the protection of the sacred temple—from which they seem to have received their name—was to cherish a perpetual fire in the temple, to burn incense to the idols, and to serve the Priest in the burning of victims, although they themselves were occasionally called Priests on account of the said fumigation of incense, which was a type of Sacrifice, as they are also called here by the Septuagint. These dark-clad men are also mentioned
<margin>chapter 10, v. 5.</margin>
in **Hosea**, as having exulted over the glory of the calf which was worshipped in Bethel. By the word <term>כבוד</term> <note>kavod</note>, glory, is understood a glorious worship, or that in which they gloried, enjoying fat victims. From this word it seems that Latin name, **Camillus**, was derived, by which the chief minister of the priests was denoted, as Macrobius explains in 3.8. The heart of those Priests is shown by the quality of their works, and their clothing reveals their actions. These filthy little sacrificers are judged unworthy of the title **Kohen** <note>Priest</note> by the Chaldean Interpreter, who in Genesis 47:22, Judges 17:5, and 18:4, 30, rendered it as **Komer** or **Komra** <term>כומר</term>, which word the Jews today also use for Monks shut up in a Monastery, from "inclusion," for the same notation is in the verb <term>כמו</term> <note>kamo</note> and has its nomenclature from "closing," like our **Cloister**. That **Camarina** <note>A marsh in Sicily, here used as a metaphor for a "sinkhole" of filth</note> of impieties can easily be judged by its foul odor. Through these ministers of idols and associates of idols, the worshippers used to seek oracles, which Satan sometimes gave through wooden images. Deceived by the responses of four hundred false prophets, Kings Ahab and Jehoshaphat proceed to battle against the Syrians for Ramoth Gilead, but Ahab, seduced by his own Prophets, perished miserably. The Devil, consulted by the Baallitic Prophets through auguries and sorceries customary to them concerning the outcome of the war, promised victory with a bad result, while there existed *a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets* <term>רוח שקר בפי כל-נביאיו</term>.
<margin>2 Kings 22:23.</margin>
The spirit of lies in the mouth of all his Prophets*, and the King, from a grave wound, gave back his spirit to him in whom

<column-break/>

<margin>Altars, statues, groves & idols. 2 Kings 1:2.</margin>
he had trusted (v. 34). Thus art is deluded by art. His son and successor Ahaziah, with equal impiety, consults concerning his health **Beelzebub**, or the God of flies*, but by the just judgment of God he perished with many others who were his advisors to consult the God of the Ekronites, and *his brother Joram reigned in his place*. The King of Babylon, that he might know things to come, <term>שאל בתרפים</term> <note>she'al ba-teraphim</note>,
<margin>v. 17. Ezekiel 21:21</margin>
*consulted the images*. Thus, so that the future might be open to them, the Israelites consulted <term>בעצו</term> <note>be-itzo</note>, *their wood*, that is, as the Commentator explains, <term>בצלם אעא</term>, *in the image of their wood*, or, *in their wooden idol*. The Chaldeans gloried in
<margin>Hosea 4:12.</margin>
their portentous idols after they had seen the captivity of the Jews, as if their Gods were the true Gods; but God predicts through Jeremiah their eternal and irreparable ruin: Behold the days are coming, said Jehovah, <term>ופקדתי על-פסוליה</term>, *and I will visit punishment upon her carved images, and in all her land the wounded shall groan*. God is said to "visit" when he is accustomed to take notice and pay the penalty for crimes, as to "visit sin" (Exodus 20:5, 32:24; Isaiah 26:21; Job 34:29; Lamentations 4:22); and the "time of visitation" <note>original Greek: καιρὸς ἐκδικήσεως</note> (Jeremiah 46:21, 49:8); the "days of visitation" <note>original Greek: αἱ ἡμέραι τῆς ἐκδικήσεως</note> (Hosea 9:7) denotes the time of retribution according to what the wicked have done. God will visit with his hard and great and strong sword, to speak with the Prophet*, upon Babylon
<margin>v. 52. Isaiah 27:1. Jeremiah 50:35.</margin>
by the hand of Cyrus and Darius, and the Persian sword went against the Chaldeans, and against her princes, and against her wise men*, <term>אל-הבדים</term> <note>el ha-baddim</note>, *against the liars*, as Vatablus translates Jeremiah 50:35, v. 36. By <term>בדא</term> <note>bada</note> (from "he lied") he understands *the diviners* <note>original Greek: τοὺς μάντεις</note>, or soothsayers, as the received versions have it, whose predictions and promises of future happiness had nothing firm or solid; whence God is said to scatter and make void the <term>אותות בדים</term>, *signs of the diviners*, *the signs of the fortune-tellers* <note>German: die Zeichen der Wahrsager</note>, Isaiah 44:25, where Rabbi Solomon explains them as: <term>הוזי בכוכבים</term>, *Astrologers*, who look at the stars. The Septuagint has: *Signs of ventriloquists*. Where Tirinus (page 627) says: God makes void and false the signs of the diviners, augurs, and soothsayers, e.g., the entrails of animals, the chirping or flight of birds, the appearance of stars, dreams, lightning, and other things from which they are accustomed to divine. Babylon was most famous for diviners, who established their judgments and observations in their various *idol-temples* <note>original Greek: εἰδωλείοις</note>, whence they are said <term>באמים יתהללו</term>, *to glory in images*, or, if you prefer, *to be insane*, to be carried away by an insane impulse.
<margin>Jeremiah 50:38.</margin>
The Vulgate: *to glory in portents*. Luther: *Trusting in their terrible idols* <note>German: Trogen auff ihre schreckliche Götzen</note>, expressing the emphasis which lies in the etymology, for images are called **Emim** from the terror which they strike into those who worship them, as if you were to say "terrifiers," for <term>אימה</term> <note>eymah</note> is terror and dread, <term>אמם</term> <note>amam</note>, to terrify, to strike terror <note>German: schrecken</note>; whence also the Giants, who were seen in the land of Canaan, are called **Emim**, i.e., formidable ones (Genesis 14:5, Deuteronomy 2:11, 12). Terror and great fear fell upon the land of Babylon, which was a <term>ארץ פסילים</term>, *land of carved images* <note>original Greek: γῆ τῶν γλυπτῶν</note>, *Idol-land* <note>German: Götzenland</note>, and whose *foolish* <note>original Greek: ἄφρονες</note> Priests were scarcely in control of their minds for fear; and who, as soon as war
<margin>v. 36.</margin>
and some evils had been brought in, consulted *among themselves, how they might be saved together with their idols* <note>original Greek: πρὸς αὐτὸς, πᾶ συναποκυβώσι μετ’ εἰδώλων</note>, Baruch 6:48. So Isaiah* says it will happen that men in great calamity will cast away their idols into the caves
<margin>chapter 2:20.</margin>
of moles and bats. The dens of these idols were either public or private. Private places for themselves at home...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of ancient religious laws and the transition from pagan sacred spaces to Christian ones, specifically focusing on the legal status of gods and the history of sacred groves.</meta>

# From Deuteronomy XII. v. 3.

<margin>
Altars, statues, groves & idols,
XII Tables ch. 2.
</margin>
...he erected for every worshiper. When the Romans saw that a confusion of religions would follow from the flowing multitude and the changeable minds of men, they did not allow other Gods to be received except those which public authority established. The law was set as follows: *Let no one have Gods separately, nor new or foreign ones, unless publicly adopted; let them worship them in private. Let them have shrines constructed by their fathers. Let them have groves in the fields. Let them preserve the seats of the Lares <note>household gods</note>, and the rites of the family and the fatherland.* An *apotheosis* <note>original: "ἀποθέωσις" — deification</note> of Christ was attempted by Tiberius, who advised the Senate with the prerogative of his voice regarding the acceptance of Jesus into the number of the Gods. However, Eusebius reports in *Ecclesiastical History, book 2, ch. 2*, that the Senate rejected it because it was an ancient custom that no one should obtain divine honor among them except by the opinion and decree of the Senate; for unless a God pleased the Senate, he would not be <margin>a. History of Civil Law p. 43.</margin> a God. Aymar Rivallius states: *Because of this law, Christ was not received among the Gods by the Romans in the times of Tiberius; for although Tiberius, having understood the divinity of Christ through Pontius Pilate, had brought this to the senate with the prerogative of his own vote, yet because that matter was not at all approved by the Senate, Christ was neglected.* By this law, Christians are also warned not to worship certain Saints unless they have first been approved by the authority of the Roman Pontiff and publicly received, which is provided for today by the constitutions of Popes Alexander and Innocent. Behold how great the religion of the Romans was, so that it did not even shrink from our own. And therefore, by the testimony of Cicero, the Romans prohibited the worship of any Gods whatsoever, lest they have a confusion of religions and bring ignorance of ceremonies to the Priests. And on pages 44 and 45: *The Law commands that there be shrines and groves of the Gods. Christians, following this Roman custom, have many temples of God and of heavenly men in the fields and cities.* A beautiful comparison. And this is what the Poet says in the Golden Verses:

> Worship first the gods as they are disposed by law. <note>original Greek: "Σεβᾶ μὲν πρώτως οἱ θεοὶ νόμῳ ὡς διάκεινται"</note>

Groves and Temples were public. Groves existed before Temples did, wherefore the first place of discussion will be concerning them. It was a most frequent and ancient custom of idolaters that, when they had erected some idol, they immediately planted a forest and a place for it, or dedicated a planted one in which divine matters might be duly performed; and so a forest and a grove stood out as the proper ornament and domicile of the gods of the nations. This is witnessed by the seat consecrated to Jupiter Hammon, made of a shady and dense grove, the image of whose site the Elzevir edition of Curtius shows us. And that other one dedicated to Jupiter *Aphlystius*, especially worshiped by the Greeks, among whom the traveling Xerxes, out of religious respect, abstained from that grove of Aphlystius when he was in Achaia, commanding the same to his troops, lest they violate the seat of the minor god; being more superstitious than P. Turullius, who is read in Dio *book 51* to have violated the grove of Aesculapius on the island of Cos by cutting down trees for the construction of ships. In Colchis was the temple and grove of Phrixus, famous in the old fable <margin>book I. c. 21.</margin> for the golden fleece, as Mela witnesses: *Phrixus is said to have brought the golden fleece of his ram into the Grove, and fastened it to a holm-oak in honor of Jupiter,* or, as Apollonius speaks in *Argonautica 2*: *hanging upon a shaggy oak* <note>original Greek: "λασίοισιν ἐπὶ δρυὸς ἀγκρεμένον"</note> to which ram's fleece the Argonauts are read to have set out. Apollodorus writes in *On the Origin of the Gods, page 15*, that a grove was consecrated to Mars. Thus trees were the temples of the deities, and by the ancient rite of the simpler folk...

<column-break/>

<margin>Altars, statues, groves & idols.</margin>
...they called a tree excelling for God, nor did they adore images gleaming with gold and ivory more than groves, and in them the silences themselves, as Pliny witnesses in *XII. 1*. Never was there a grove without religion and fear, on account of the present Gods and the souls of heroes dwelling in the shady groves, as Virgil speaks; and mention of them is hardly ever made by writers without them immediately adding a cult of astonished veneration, as Macrobius speaks *concerning the rites of Isis*. <margin>1. Sat. 20?</margin> Seneca in *Epistle XLI*: *If you come upon a grove thick with ancient trees that have surpassed the usual height, that loftiness of the forest and the secrecy of the place and the admiration of a shadow so dense and continuous in the open, creates in you a faith in a deity.* I know not what deity and vain superstition the Poet augurs from this, writing:
<margin>3. Fasti</margin>
> A grove lay beneath the Aventine, black with the shade of the holm-oak,
> Which, having been seen, you could say "a deity is within."

Indeed, Cornelius Tacitus witnesses that a similar veneration was paid to groves by the Germans, relating of the Semnones <margin>On the geography and customs of the Germans, ch. 39.</margin> that at a stated time they meet in a forest
<margin>A chance verse.</margin>
> Sacred by the auguries of the Fathers and by ancient dread,
> and publicly celebrate with a slain man
the horrendous beginnings of a barbarian rite; and in chapter 40: *a sacrificial terror and a holy ignorance.* That there was a marvelous superstition of groves and forests among our ancestors is witnessed even today by the traces not so much of places dedicated to sacred things in Prussia, of which I was an *eyewitness* <note>original: "αὐτόπτης"</note>, and elsewhere, as also by the names which remain to us from these forest assemblies, *Wallfarth / Wallen / Wallengen* <note>German terms related to pilgrimage/wandering</note>, concerning the modern pilgrimages of Christians to temples and sacred houses. Though the thing is lost, the words often remain; just as the temples themselves, which were workshops of a perverse religion, passed over into the Basilicas of the Christians. Moreover, the Germans embraced the deities in uncut places with a secret care of the mind and a trembling, as we have heard, and in them they built altars for the use of sacrifices, just as in the most celebrated grove of Zuttiber of the Sorbs and Vandals, which Bishop Wigwert, the third of Merseburg, utterly destroyed, as Ernest <margin>1. Chronicle of Merseburg 6.</margin> Brottuffus investigated. A similar superstition was preserved by the *Slavs*, whose most sacred grove Gerold, Bishop of Oldenburg, set on fire, being an assistant to the Canon of Bützow, Helmold, which the *Chronicle of the Slavs* by Helmold left behind. *Among the Myonenses on the peak of a mountain was a grove and altar of the Mild Gods <note>original: "Deorum Milichiorum"</note>*, to whom they offered nightly sacrifices, and meat to be consumed before the rising Sun, as Pausanias witnesses in *book x*. Clodius is accused by Cicero in the *Oration for Milo n. 86* of cutting down groves, the speech being turned by apostrophe to the altars and groves themselves, writing: *You, Alban hills and groves, you, I say, I implore and attest, and you, the overturned altars of the Albans, associates and equals of the sacred rites of the Roman people, which that man in headlong madness, having cut down and prostrated the most holy groves, had overwhelmed with the insane masses of his substructures.* Concerning the violated grove of Ceres, the fable of Erysichthon is well known. A grove of Neptune existed in Phocis. Of the Fates and Apollo, in Boeotian Paracephissia. Of Diana the Huntress in Attica. Of Saitis Minerva in Argolis. Of Jupiter Ceraunius in Laconia; and you will have a great forest of this superstitious material in the vast work *On Gardens* by Benedictus Curtius, *the whole of book 3 from p. 79 to 109.*

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Altars, statues, groves, and idols.</margin>
Chapter 13. This pagan error greatly occupied those provinces which God had given to the people of Israel, whose inhabitants used to sacrifice victims in shaded groves and on high hills, consecrating idols and performing every kind of divine rite. From this, the "Lucaria" festivals were named, which Festus discusses when writing about the Romans on page 85: *The Romans celebrated the Lucaria festivals in a grove, which was very large, located between the Via Salaria and the Tiber. And because the gods were believed to dwell there, they are called "pious groves" by Horace in Book 3, Ode 4, verse 6.* Therefore, since those Canaanites frequently erected their idolatrous altars and temples in pleasant groves and mountains, God <term>O.M. (the Best and Greatest)</term> universally prohibited anything similar from being introduced into the fellowship of divine worship, so that the Jewish nation would be further removed from all such imitation of idolaters, saying: <margin>Altars, statues, groves, and idols.</margin> *You shall not plant for yourself a grove* <note>original Hebrew: "Lo-titta leka asherah"; Greek: "Ou phyteuseis seautō alsos"</note>. God did not want the perimeter of His temple, or the place where the Tabernacle stood, to be planted with groves, nor the altar to be adorned with any tree, lest the people, prone to idolatry, should seem to practice it after the ritual of the Canaanites. Luther translates:
> You shall plant no grove of trees near the altar of the LORD your God, which you make for yourself.

It was neither permitted to plant them, nor to tolerate them even where they were found; for their cutting down and burning is expressly commanded, lest there be anything that could bend or <margin>Exod. 34:12</margin> provoke unstable minds toward idolatry. *Take heed,* He says, *lest perhaps you strike a treaty with the inhabitants of that region into which you are about to enter, lest perhaps they be* a snare <note>Hebrew: "lemokesh"</note> *in your midst.* The Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> says: *lest it become a stumbling block among you.* Luther: *That they do not become an offense among you.* Regarding the seduction of a son, lest he go after another god <margin>Deut. 7:4</margin>—namely, through the beautiful worship of the gods in verse 16—where the Septuagint has "a trap." Lest the people of God be ensnared, God carefully provided that groves, as stumbling blocks and snares, should be removed (verse 13). *You shall destroy their altars, and break their statues,* and you shall cut down their groves <note>Hebrew: "ve-et-asherav tikrotun"; Greek: "kai ta alsē autōn ekkopsete"</note>, and *root out their groves.* The word <note>Hebrew: "karat"</note> means *to cut off or lop off*, a verb used for wood in <term>Numbers</term> 13:24, <term>Judges</term> 6:30, 9:48-49, <term>1 Kings</term> 5:6, and <term>Job</term> 14:7. Corresponding words for cutting the same material are found in <term>Deut.</term> 19:5, 29:11, <term>Joshua</term> 9:21, <term>Jeremiah</term> 46:22, and <term>Ezekiel</term> 39:10. <margin>Deut. 7:5</margin> A synonym is used in the same prohibition: *These things you shall do. You shall destroy their altars, and break their statues,* and you shall hew down their groves. Luther here uses: *to chop down.* The burning of groves <margin>Deut. 12:3</margin> is commanded: *Burn their groves with fire.* The Septuagint retains "you shall cut down." Good kings obeyed this precept, cutting down the groves, and are praised for that reason. The worship of the grove had become so strong in the time of Manasseh that, not content with building high places and making groves, he even placed a carved image of the grove <note>Hebrew: "pesel ha-asherah"</note>, a *grove-idol*, in the very temple of the Lord (<term>2 Kings</term> 21:3, 7). For, having moved that image from a public grove, he placed it in the house of God and surrounded it with leafy trees, where women wove hangings. Josiah caused this grove, along with the carved image itself, to be carried out of the house of the Lord outside Jerusalem to the brook Kidron, and burned it there, and ground it to dust, and cast its dust upon the graves of the common people (chapter 23:6-7). These abominations of the nations

<column-break/>

<margin>Altars, statues, groves, and idols.</margin>
Hezekiah, the father of Manasseh, detested these things; he removed the high places, broke the statues, and cut down the grove (<term>2 Kings</term> 18:4). Rabshakeh was not ignorant of this, saying: <margin>Isaiah 36:7</margin> *Is it not he whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed?* He was mistaken in this, thinking that the high places and altars the King had removed belonged to their own God, rather than to foreign gods. And the King had said to Judah and Jerusalem: <margin>2 Chron. 32:12</margin> *You shall worship before this altar,* which is the legitimate one in the temple at Jerusalem. Long before, when Israel had fallen into these same crimes and the fields were oppressed by Midian for that reason, Gideon alone remained to resist, destroying the altar of Baal and cutting down the grove that was around the altar. <margin>Judges 6:25</margin> For this praiseworthy deed he was called *Jerubbaal* (v. 32), as if to say, *one contending with Baal.* For when the townsmen demanded the death of his son Gideon for the destroyed altar of Baal, Joash replied: *If Baal is a god, let him avenge himself:* <note>Hebrew: "lo yariv lo"</note>, which <term>Vatablus</term> explains as: *Let Baal litigate against him;* and Jerome: *let him seek vengeance from him.* As if to say: If Baal is a god, let Baal avenge himself on my son before tomorrow morning for this deed, and strike him with death. Let Baal judge with Gideon and pass sentence, as is usually done in criminal cases, where the lawsuit of the accuser and the sentence of the judge aim toward vengeance and the punishment of the guilty. If Gideon is guilty of treason against Baal, Baal is the one who can rightfully seek revenge. But Gideon was truly *Jerubbaal* (<term>2 Sam. 11:21</term>), who destroyed Baal as a "shameful thing" <margin>2 Sam. 11:21</margin> and put his worshippers to shame. He was also a man of his name, namely, a "cutter." The name *Jerubbaal* is best attributed to him who cuts down the idol, the idolatry, the altar, and the grove, and who overthrew the Midianites. With the same boldness, the Englishman Wolfred, while uprooting superstition in Sweden, said to the worshippers: *If your god Thorstan is powerful, let him avenge himself;* and at the same time, seizing an axe, he hacked the idol into pieces, and in this way freed the people from superstition, as witnessed by <term>Crantz</term> in *Metropolis* Book 4, Chapter 8. After the death of Gideon and his successors Tola and Jair, the Israelites joined new sins to the old ones (which we will discuss shortly) and served various gods: <margin>Judges 2:6, 10</margin> namely, the Baals and Ashtoreths, the gods of Aram, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the children of Ammon, and finally the gods of the Philistines, neglecting the worship of God. But when they repented, having first been oppressed and delivered by God into the hands of the Philistines and the children of Ammon, they cast away all the idols of foreign gods from their borders (<term>Judges</term> 10:16). To briefly recount the Israelites' proclivity toward idolatry from the beginning: after the death of Joshua and the elders who had seen all the great work of Jehovah which He did for Israel, and after that whole generation was gathered to their fathers, a new generation arose, says the author of the book of Judges (2:10), *which did not know Jehovah, nor the work He had done for Israel; they did evil in the sight of the Lord and served the Baals.* For the Israelites, seduced by the same lust for idolatry after they had mingled with the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, <margin>Judges 3:7</margin> served the Baals and the groves (the Vulgate says: *and Asheroth*). Therefore, the burning anger of Jehovah sold them into the hands of <margin>v. 8</margin> Cushan-rishathaim. This was the reward for sparing the nations against the prohibition of God...

# From Deuteronomy XII. v. 3.

<margin>Altars, statues, groves & idols.</margin>
...and they had joined themselves to them. But Othniel <note>The first Judge of Israel</note> conquered that King after they had been oppressed by eight years of servitude, and without doubt he removed by fire the groves which they had made. For the anger of God could not be ended otherwise than by executing that which had been commanded; so much so that it was necessary to root out, break in pieces, or defile with foul filth—to show detestation—the places where the dwellings of superstition had been, as well as the idols and other vessels of superstition. Moses ground (<term>shachaq</term> <note>original: שָׁחַק</note>, to grind to powder) the golden calf until it was minute dust, and scattered it upon the surface of the waters, Exodus 32:20. The mass melted by fire he reduced to powder by violent rubbing with a millstone. The Chaldean <note>Likely referring to the Aramaic Targum translation</note> suggests one who scrapes with a file. Thus the pious King Josiah, detesting the very place polluted by idolatry, threw there carcasses, dung, and other refuse, after the ashes of the idol and the grove—consumed by flames—were scattered <note>original: εἰς τὰς τάφας τῶν ὑψηλῶν</note> *into the graves of the common people*, that is, in the place where ordinary men were usually buried, 2 Kings 23: v. 6, 12, 14, 15, 16, so that it might no longer be held as a religious site. This was indicated by a peculiar instinct to Jacob, who demanded that not only the idols, but also their earrings, necklaces, and various other ornaments usually hung upon them, be handed over to him, so that he might bury them under an oak, Genesis 35:4. Christian Emperors, having stormed the seats of idolatry, used to remove idols, groves, and sometimes the temples themselves from the midst. Phoenicia, most celebrated for its ancient religion, worshipped in Groves, until by the consensus of the Emperors, craftsmen were sent there and the temples of the idols and the groves were destroyed, concerning which Theodoret writes in Book 5, chapter 29. Indeed, the gentiles themselves, if they did not find the victors favored their own rites, removed them from the midst. The Emperors of the Persians, having conquered Babylon, ground into the earth <term>all the carved images of her gods</term> <note>original: כָּל-פְּסִילֵי אֱלֹהֶיהָ</note>, <margin>Isaiah 21:9.</margin> which are named Bel and Nebo in chapter 46:1, in the prophecy concerning the ruin of the Babylonian gods. The Prophet saw in spirit, *Bel is bowed down and Nebo stoops*. There are two words in Hebrew, both indicating <term>bowing down</term>, <term>qaras</term> <note>original: קָרַס</note> and <term>kara</term> <note>original: כָּרַע</note>, from which, due to their bent shape, <term>hooks</term> <note>original: קרסים</note> are named. The Old Translator <note>The Vulgate</note> has: *Bel is broken, Nebo is crushed*; the Septuagint: <unclear>Bel has fallen</unclear>, Dagon is crushed. Luther: *Bel is bowed, Nebo has fallen.* Thus Shalmaneser the Assyrian, having captured the last King of Israel, destroyed the sacrifices, shrines, statues, Ephod, and Teraphim, Hosea 3:4; for it was not permitted for them to practice their idolatry in a foreign land. Thus the Magi of the Persians burned the temples of the Greeks when Xerxes broke into Greece, <margin>2. On the Laws</margin> because of the idols placed there, as Cicero witnesses. Why so? Because they were not imbued with the folly of Greek religions, and they judged that the divine power of the Gods could be enclosed in no place, accusing those of folly who erected images, temples, and altars. Herodotus records this in *Clio* <note>Book 1 of his Histories</note>, there: *The Persians have no custom of erecting statues, temples, or altars, but rather charge those who do so with folly.* Thus it pleased God <margin>Numbers 33:52.</margin> that all the images of the Canaanites should be destroyed and cut down. *Destroy*, He says, *all their pictures*, <term>and you shall destroy all their figured stones</term> <note>original: וְאִבַּדְתֶּם אֵת כָּל-מַשְׂכִּיֹּתָם</note>, <term>and all their molten images</term> <note>original: וְאֵת כָּל-צַלְמֵי מַסֵּכֹתָם</note> *you shall destroy, and all their high places you shall lay waste*. <margin>Deuteronomy 12:3.</margin> This is repeated, as we heard above, so that when they reached the land of promise, where those consecrations of groves and idols then flourished, they should not endure a grove near His altar, but wherever they found them, they should immediately break the idols,

<column-break/>

cut down the statues and groves, and shun the high places. Yet on the contrary, out of their stiff-neckedness, not content with their legitimate rites, they kept groves and shady places, <margin>Altars, statues, groves & idols.</margin> and performed their rites on high places, in groves, and, as the Scripture says, under every leafy and green tree. The trees chosen for this superstition were especially thick and shady, and rites were performed <term>under a thick tree</term> <note>original: ὑποκάτω δένδρου δασέως</note>, Deuteronomy 12:2; or *a shadowy tree*, Ezekiel 20:28; or *a screening tree*, Hosea 4:13; *a shady tree and under a thick oak*, Ezekiel 6:13. A tree excelling others was chosen for the pleasant shade they desired. For this use, the <term>Oak</term> and the <term>Poplar</term> were commended, because their shade was good, as the Prophet witnesses <margin>Hosea 4:12.</margin> when he writes: <term>Upon the tops of the mountains</term> <term>they sacrifice, and upon the hills</term> <note>original: עַל-רָאשֵׁי הֶהָרִים יְזַבֵּחוּ וְעַל-הַגְּבָעוֹת יְקַטֵּרוּ</term> <term>they burn incense, under the oak, and the poplar and the elm</term>, <term>under the oak and the white poplar</term> <note>original: ὑποκάτω δρυὸς καὶ λεύκης</note>. <term>Leuke</term> <note>Greek: λεύκη</note> denotes the white poplar, where in Hebrew it is <term>livnah</term> <note>original: לִבְנָה</note>, which tree is greatly spreading, pleasing in flowers, and delightful with shady leaves; it has leaves white on one side, whence it is called <term>leuke</term>, and *candida* <note>white</note> by Virgil. Called *Alba* by Horace in Epode 2, v. 10, whose shade the same commends in Odes Book 2, Ode 3, v. 9:

> *Where the huge pine and white poplar*
> *Love to join their hospitable shade*
> *With their branches.*

Stupid nations thought certain trees, whose shade was good, would be more pleasing to certain Gods. The poplar was sacred to Hercules. Theocritus in Idyll 2 calls it <term>the white poplar sacred to Hercules</term>. Virgil in Eclogue 7:

> *The poplar is most pleasing to Hercules, the vine to Bacchus,*
> *The myrtle to beautiful Venus, his own laurel to Phoebus.*

That religion of trees is very well known, especially if they were planted or stood in high places and hills, which were judged opportune for performing their rites; for with similar religion, high places dedicated to idols are read of among leafy trees. Concerning these, Eucherius says: <note>original: p. 203</note> *Scripture is accustomed to name "high places" those locations situated on the brows of hills, in which they either sacrificed to demons, or even to the Lord—enticed by the pleasantness of the places—offering victims against the prohibition, having abandoned the altar which was in the temple.* Whence it is often said in this book concerning the Kings who were less perfectly just: *Nevertheless he did not remove the high places*. That phrase, <term>only the high places were not removed</term> <note>original: רַק הַבָּמוֹת לֹא סָרוּ</note>, is read <margin>1 Kings 15:14.</margin> concerning Asa, who is said there not to have taken away the high places, though otherwise his heart was pious and perfect before Jehovah in the worship of the one God. He did not move the high places which he saw had been erected to the true God; but those which he saw consecrated to profane idols, he overthrew with the statues, groves, and all foreign worship, 2 Chronicles 14:2. So it is read in 2 Kings 15: v. 35 concerning Jotham, that he indeed laudably followed in the pious footsteps of his father Uzziah, *except that he did not take away the high places; the people still sacrificed and burned incense in the high places.* <term>Sacrificing and burning incense</term> <note>original: מִזְבְּחִים וּמַקְטִרִים</note>, that is, immolating and perfuming in the high places. It is believable that the pious Prince could not, due to the ferocity of the people, cut down and remove the iniquity of the high places, which the Septuagint seems to have hinted at by the word <term>still</term> <note>original: τὸ ἔτι</note>, where the Hebrew has <term>adhoc</term> <note>original: עוֹד</note>. Pious Kings (says Cornelius à Lapide) <margin>1 Kings 3 p. 112.</margin> permitted high places erected to the true God, or if they were established for idols, they permitted them because, due to the inveterate custom of the idol-worshipping people, fearing their sedition and rebellion, they were unable to hinder and remove them. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Altars, statues, groves & idols.</margin>
...those in which sacrifices were offered to the true God, not to idols; insofar as the more pious Kings did not permit them but overthrew them—namely David, Hezekiah, and Josiah. After the temple was built for God and a certain place was established in Jerusalem for public divine worship, so that the unity of the Jewish religion might be preserved in one temple, they ought to have utterly condemned the high places to which they had hitherto clung. Or, if they were unwilling, it would have been incumbent upon the Kings to keep the people from them with greater zeal and to have granted no dispensation. And this is <unclear>that</unclear> sin by which all the Kings of Israel and Judah sinned, except for those three Kings praised by Cornelius <note>Likely referring to the commentator Cornelius a Lapide</note>, for thus it is read in <margin>Ecclesiasticus 49:5</margin>: <term>Except for David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, all committed a trespass.</term> <note>original Greek: Πάρεξ Δαβὶδ καὶ Ἐζεκιΐου καὶ Ἰωσίου πάντες πλημμέλειαν ἐπλημμέλησαν.</note> He calls the tolerance of the high places a <term>trespass</term> <note>Greek: πλημμέλειαν - a fault or error</note>, an error which he says everyone wandered into except David <margin>1 Kings 3:3; 2 Kings 18:4; 23:8</margin>, who did not tolerate the high places, and Hezekiah and Josiah, who even shattered them as places unfit for sacrifices. For all others had either sacrificed in high places to God or to other gods, or certainly, when they could and should have, they did not remove them but tolerated them with a culpable tolerance. Hence, it is noted as a blemish in Asa and certain other even pious Kings, that whether through fear of offending the people or through neglect of stricter discipline, they tolerated high places of this sort, which the people—more inclined than was right toward elevated places—had chosen for the service of the true God. Therefore, there were two kinds of *High Places*: one where sacred rites were performed for idols with foreign worship, as in the time of Ahaz, Manasseh, and other impious Kings; the other, where they sacrificed to appease their own God, at which place of worship some pious Kings were accustomed to wink. Before the construction of the Temple, the offering had to be made <margin>Leviticus 17:3-4</margin> before the *Tabernacle*, where it is expressly forbidden for any animal to be sacrificed to God anywhere other than at the door of the tabernacle <insert>Hebrew: אל-פתח אהל</insert>. However, God occasionally permitted, for reasons known to Himself, for sacred rites to be performed in other places until a firm and stable temple was built. Thus Gideon, when he had destroyed the high places and groves, performed sacred rites to God on the <term>summit</term> <margin>Judges 6:26</margin> of a <term>rock</term>, and indeed using the wood of the grove <term>which he had cut down</term>.
<margin>1 Kings 3:2; Question 36 on Judges.</margin>
*In the time of Solomon the people sacrificed in high places* <term>Hebrew: בבמות, מזבחים - Bamot, altars</term>, because, as the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> says, <term>where were they sacrificing in the highest places? For the house for the name of Jehovah was not yet built.</term> <note>original Greek: ποῦ ἦσαν θύοντες ἐν τοῖς ὑψηλοτάτοις</note> God (says Augustine) <term>endured rather than forbade the custom of His people, by which they offered to the Lord their God rather than to foreign gods outside of His tabernacle, even thus hearing those who offered. Solomon himself is said to have loved Jehovah by walking in the precepts of David his father, except that he sacrificed and burned incense in the high places</term> in the cited chapter, verse 3. In the Hebrew: <term>only in the high places he sacrificed and burned incense</term> <note>original Hebrew: רק בבמות הוא מזבח ומקטיר</note>. Tirinus <note>A Jesuit commentator</note> says on this passage, p. 253: <term>this custom of sacrificing to God in more elevated places gradually grew strong because there was not one certain designated place, but sacrifices were made partly in Gibeon and partly in Jerusalem. By the Prophets, however, in grave necessity, they were made in several other places by a singular dispensation of God. In imitation of these, the people, more inclined than was right to the rites of the gentiles, claimed the same for themselves here and there. But David, throughout the whole time of his reign, strongly opposed this practice, so often forbidden in the Law, and left it in his commands to his son Solomon that he should oppose it in like manner; hence he is said here to have walked in the precepts of his father David, except that he walked in the high places.</term>

<column-break/>

After the construction of the temple, it was not permitted to perform sacred rites outside that place, except by some divine privilege, by which the most esteemed man of prophecy, Elijah, <margin>Altars, statues, groves & idols.</margin> sacrificed on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:23). God ordinarily willed the offering of victims and the burning of incense to be carried out only in the place He had chosen; and He had chosen the temple of Solomon. But often unmindful of this law, they forgot and sacrificed not in Jerusalem, but in Dan and Bethel, and on the hills and the peaks of mountains, as if they were closer to their God there. This superstition became so ingrained that at last these most wicked men vented their rage upon their own offspring, building the <term>high places of Topheth</term> <insert>Hebrew: במות התפת</insert>, <term>consecrated to Moloch, where they would burn their sons and daughters with fire</term>, which are called in chapter 32:35 <term>the high places of Baal</term> <margin>Jeremiah 7:30-31</margin> <insert>Hebrew: במות הבעל</insert>. The meaning of that word <term>Bamah</term> <insert>במה</insert> is <term>height and loftiness</term> <insert>Hebrew: גובה ורום</insert>, as explained by Rabbi Mordecai Nathan in the *Book of Paths* p. 102. It is taken for an eminent and high thing, such as high and steep citadels, or a <term>high altar</term> <margin>Psalm 18:34</margin>, as in the Talmudic books, from which comes the Greek <term>bomos</term> <note>βωμός</note>, *an altar, as if a high altar or area* in which sacrifice is made to the most high God, <term>high places</term> <margin>Deuteronomy 32:13</margin> according to the explanation of Vatablus, and finally <term>lofty groves</term> in which most nations used to erect their chapels and altars to perform their divine business. The higher a mountain was, the more sacred it seemed; hence names were given to the Gods and the Gods were worshipped on them. They write wonders about the height of Mount Olympus; what Xenagoras had found pleased him so much that he thought the matter should be testified to posterity in a poem on a monument erected at the summit, as noted by Plutarch in the *Life of Aemilius*; hence they gave Jupiter his surname. The Persians climbed the highest peaks of mountains to make offerings to the Gods. Herodotus recorded that this was sanctioned by law, writing: <term>They are accustomed to ascend the highest of the mountains to offer sacrifices to Zeus, calling the whole circle of the heavens Zeus.</term> <note>original Greek: Οἱ δὲ νομίζουσι Διὶ μὲν ἐπὶ τὰ ὑψηλότατα τῶν ὀρέων ἀναβαίνοντες θυσίας ἔρδειν, τὸν κύκλον πάντα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ Δία καλέοντες.</note> In Sicily, a <term>very high and elevated place</term> is said to be famous for the abduction of Proserpina, which was called <term>Enna</term>, <term>on the top of which was a level plain of land and perennial water; but the whole was cut off and separated from every approach. Around it were many lakes and groves, and the most joyful flowers at every time of year</term> (Cicero, *Against Verres*, Act 6). At Rome, the <term>Capitoline</term> hill was consecrated to Jupiter, from which the name <term>Capitoline Jupiter</term> remained. Regarding this, Virgil <margin>Aeneid</margin> says it was held in religious awe because of the thick thickets and forest, from which a certain divine horror was struck into the worshippers:
-> And he leads them to the Capitol, <-
> *Now golden, once bristling with woody thickets.*
> *Even then the dire religion of the place terrified the trembling rustics;*
> *even then they shuddered at the forest and the rock.*
> *"This grove, this hill with its leafy summit," he said,*
> *"(which God it is, is uncertain) a God inhabits. The Arcadians themselves*
> *believe they have seen Jupiter."*
A hill with a leafy summit is nothing other than a <term>Bamah</term> <insert>במה</insert>, where a <term>bomos</term> <note>βωμός - altar</note> was placed, which the Poet here calls a <term>rock</term>. For a rock, either rough or polished, served as an altar or hearth. Isaiah notes in chapter 65:3 that sacrifice was made to Gods upon brick altars <insert>Hebrew: על-הלבנים - upon the bricks</insert>, upon which stone monuments are also read to have been erected, incised with certain superstitious figures...
