# From Deuteronomy XII. v. 3. 269

<margin>Altars, statues, groves & idols. 2 Kings 23:15.</margin>
<margin>Leviticus 26:1. Numbers 33:52.</margin>
They were accustomed to consecrate altars for the purpose of sacrifice, which is called here *mizbeakh* <note>Hebrew: מזבח</note>, as if a "sacrificatory" from *zabakh* <note>Hebrew: זבח</note> "to sacrifice," where we read that the altar was on a high place. The Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> calls it a *thysiasterion* <note>Greek: θυσιαστήριον</note>, because a *thysia* <note>Greek: θυσία</note>, a sacrifice, was offered upon it. A stone of this kind which had been cut for an altar could not be turned to any other common use, among both the Gentiles and the Jews. The altars of the Gentiles are elegantly named by the writer of the Maccabean history "stones of defilement," **unclean** <note>Greek: ἀκάθαρτον</note> *or of pollution, an unclean stone / which, when they purged the temple,* they carried out to an "unclean place" <note>Greek: εἰς τόπον ἀκάθαρτον</note>. The Historian refused to call those stones *thysiasteria*, a word he reserved for the altar of *holocaust* <note>burnt offerings</note>, which Ezra had built long ago, and which was afterwards foully profaned by the Gentiles through the placement of a statue of Olympian Jupiter (1 Maccabees 1:57, 62). Therefore, because of that profanation, they did not wish to use that altar any longer, lest it might perhaps become *a reproach* <note>Greek: εἰς ὄνειδος</note> to them; yet they did not throw them away into a filthy place, as they had done with the altars of the Gentiles, but they stored those stones of the destroyed altar "in the mountain of the house in a suitable place" <note>Greek: ἐν τῷ ὄρει τοῦ οἴκου ἐν τόπῳ ἐπιτηδείῳ</note>, namely in some corner of a certain area in the temple, or perhaps outside the temple, to be kept for a while until something more certain should be answered concerning them by a Prophet to come: "until a prophet should appear to give an answer concerning them" <note>Greek: μέχρι τοῦ παραγενηθῆναι προφήτην τοῦ ἀποκριθῆναι περὶ αὐτῶν</note>, verse 46. Altars consecrated to the Gods were usually anointed with oil. The religious anointing of stones customary among the Heathens is believed to have originated from that stone which Jacob is said to have anointed and poured oil over at Bethel; from which Scaliger (*Notes on Fragments p. 198*) and Selden (*On the Syrian Gods p. 165*) derive the *Baetylia* <note>Sacred stones or meteorites</note>. Jacob set up a monument of a blessing, not a shrine, nor did he pour oil on the stone in the manner of idolatry, as if making it a God. That the Heathens progressed so far in superstition that they even worshipped anointed stones is testified by Arnobius (and there Elmenhorst p. 23), Prudentius (Book 1 against Symmachus), Pausanias in his *Description of Greece*, Lucian in *Charon*, and others. That stones were erected to the Gods has nothing strange about it. Hence there is a suspicion that the stone upon which Abimelech killed his brothers was sacred to *Baal-Berith*; as if some altar, dedicated to that GOD of the covenant (for *Berith* <note>Hebrew: ברית</note> means "covenant"), was in the same place where previously there had been an altar of the same idol, which his father Gideon had destroyed (Judges 6:28). Thus he would avenge the ignominy done to Baal, and the seventy sons—guilty, as it were, of their father's sacrilege—would appear slaughtered on that altar as pleasing burnt offerings to appease the offended deity. Altars were usually prepared for idols (Exodus 32:5, Deuteronomy 12:3, Judges 6:25, 1 Kings 16:32, 18:26, Isaiah 16:12, 2 Kings 3:2, Acts 17:26) and stones, statues, idols, or other signs were erected "for adoration" <note>Greek: εἰς προσκύνησιν</note>, before which the Israelites were cautioned by law not to bow down. Manasseh had gone against this law, having erected a statue to Baal in the temple at Jerusalem, which Josiah removed (2 Chronicles 34:4), but Jehoiakim or Zedekiah replaced it (2 Kings 23:37, 2 Chronicles 36:14). Nebuchadnezzar presented himself to be adored in a golden statue (Daniel 3:5), and when Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, Jewish men, refused to adore it, they were sent into the furnace of burning

<column-break/>

fire (v. 21) and were liberated from there by the great hand of GOD (v. 92).

<margin>Altars, statues, groves & idols.</margin>
Josephus mentions concerning Gaius Caesar <note>Caligula</note> that he ordered his image to be carried around through the Roman Empire so that he might be adored in it, saying that he was the brother of Jupiter. The Jews, resisting him under Petronius, suffered many punishments. Take other examples of that unbroken courage in that people. Apion accused the Jews because they did not set up statues of the Emperors; to which Josephus replied that the modesty of the Romans was to be praised in this, that they did not force their subjects to transcend their ancestral laws. Pilate placed statues of Caesar in Jerusalem, threatening the Jews with death unless they complied. But they declared they would rather undergo death than transgress the decrees of their law. Then Pilate, marveling at their obstinacy in their law, ordered the images to be removed. Similarly, when Herod, their King, to please the Emperor, had placed a **golden eagle** over the gate of the temple, certain young zealots, having formed a conspiracy and raised a riot, broke it and threw it down, crying out that it was against religion and the institutions of their ancestors, and that the occasion—when it was heard the King was near death—should be taken to avenge the injuries to the divine essence. But that turned out badly, for Herod survived long enough to hand them over, once captured, to be burned alive in flames. If they had been of such constancy in the times of the Kings, and had neglected to honor the memory of GOD or of Gods in high places with statues, images, or any other monument, the name of GOD would not have been profaned among the Gentiles, as if HE were a **God of the mountains**. From this, they thought the Gods of the Jews were more sublime and powerful because they presided over high and mountainous places. The Syrians besieging Samaria used this taunt when they were twice slaughtered by Ahab, where they cry out: **"The God of Israel is a God of the mountains and not a God of the valleys."** <note>Greek: Θεὸς Ἰσραὴλ καὶ οὐ Θεὸς κοιλάδων</note> *Their gods are mountain gods* <note>German: Ihre Götter sind Berg Götter</note> (*Elohei harim* <note>Hebrew: אלהי הרים</note>) *therefore they have overcome us.* They had begun this slaughter in mountainous Samaria, and they believed that the God of the mountains or of the heights had prevailed over the God of the Valleys. They do not attribute this misfortune to their own very bad morals, but say the victory happened because of the nature of some GOD who had power chiefly in the mountains; hence that saying: **The God of the mountains is the God of Israel; and the God of the valleys is ours.** They ascribed their fortunes and misfortunes to one of the Gods, and it was a common error that, according to the variety of places and operations, various deities held dominion in certain places and over certain kinds of things which they presided over. No place was believed by them to be devoid of some peculiar deity: there was no mountain which did not have its Jupiter, no hill which did not have its Goddess Collatina, no forest without its Sylvanus, no water lacking some Neptune; hence so many places consecrated to so many different Gods: **"Mountains and glens to Pan, meadows and blooming places to the Nymphs, shores and islands to the sea-gods; and of the others, as is appropriate to each God and spirit."** <note>Greek: ὄρη μὲν καὶ νάπας Πανὶ, λειμῶνας δὲ καὶ τεθηλότα χωρία Νύμφαις, ἀκτὰς δὲ καὶ νήσους πελαγίοις δαίμοσι· τῶν δ’ ἄλλων, ὡς ἑκάστῳ τι Θεῷ καὶ δαίμονι οἰκεῖον.</note> Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book 1. Hence Ovid introduced the Gods speaking.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<page-num>270</page-num>

<margin>Altars, statues, groves & idols.</margin>

> *We are gods of the fields, and those who rule in the high*
> ->*Mountains; empire over his own dwellings belongs to Jove.*<-
> <note>Original Latin: "Dii sumus agrestes..." A poetic illustration of the pagan belief in localized deities.</note>

Therefore the Syrians thought the God of Israel prevailed in strength in the mountains of Samaria, as if he were the tutelary Deity <note>A guardian spirit of a specific place.</note> of those locations; and they raise themselves up with some vain hope regarding the Gods of the valleys, whom they think will be more favorable to them. For this reason, leaving the mountains, they pitch their camps in the valleys, saying: *Let us go down into the valleys and level places, so that we may fight against them, and we shall prevail.* *That we must fight with them on the plain / what does it matter / we would win against them?* <note>Original German: "Dass wir mit ihnen auff der Ebne streiten müsten..."</note> It is incredible to say with what reinforcements, what troops, and what eagerness they drew up their battle line. But how they deceived themselves here also by trusting in the location is revealed in that very chapter, when, once the battle was joined, the small forces of the Israelites emerged superior in the plains, <margin>v. 29.</margin> striking down one hundred thousand Syrian infantry in a single day. <margin>1 Kings 18:27.</margin> Where then were the *Gods of the Valleys*? Either they were on a journey, or in pursuit, or asleep, or performing some other heavy business—to use the words with which the Prophet Elijah mocked the worshippers of Baal on Mount Carmel. This belief regarding the Gods of the mountains did not occupy the Syrians alone, but also the rest of the Gentiles, who placed their own spirits <term>genios: protective spirits or local deities</term> over mountains, valleys, cities, and other inanimate things. Hence among the Romans, *Nemestinus* was the God of the groves; *Collina*, the Goddess of the hills; and *Vallina*, the Goddess of the Valleys; these were held in no small worship (see Vossius, book 2 on Idolatry, chapter 62, page 640).

The wondrous desire with which the Israelites burned for the mountains and hills shaded by trees is expressed by the Prophet Isaiah using a word that signifies lustful craving, to show how greedily—all reason being set aside—these senseless men turned their minds to the mountains and the idols of the mountains and groves, not enduring even a little delay. Rebuking each of the idolaters, he threatens the punishment of confusion: <margin>ch. 1 v. 29.</margin> *You shall be put to shame* <note>Hebrew: מאילים</note> *on account of the trees which you have desired, and you shall be put to shame on account of the gardens* (<note>Hebrew: גנות</note>) (<note>Hebrew: מהע</unclear></note>) *which you have chosen.* The Vulgate <note>The standard 4th-century Latin Bible translation.</note> reads: *They shall be confounded by the idols to which they sacrificed.* For <note>Hebrew: אילים (oaks/trees)</note> he reads <note>Hebrew: אלילים (idols)</note> along with the Greek interpreters, who have: *they shall be ashamed of their idols.* <note>Greek: ἀισχυνθήσονται ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων</note> Luther: *They must be put to shame over the oaks.* <margin>Josh. 24:26. Gen. 35:4.</margin> By "oaks" are understood oak groves, as Vatablus explained here; for <note>Hebrew: אלה</note> means "oak," where it is read that Jacob buried the idols and their earrings under the oak (<note>Hebrew: תחת האלה</note>), so that he might root out from the minds of his household all the idolatry contracted in the house of Laban. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> and Vulgate: *under the terebinth tree.* <note>Greek: ἀπὸ τῶν τερεβίνθων</note> That holy man [Jacob] wished, in full detestation of idolatry, for the idols with all their ornaments to be buried deep in the earth as useless things, unfit for any other use. If the Jews had paid attention to these and other examples of their pious ancestors, they would not have been seized by a loathing for the legitimate

<column-break/>

sacred rites, which for a grave reason were divinely attached to a single place; nor would they have lusted after the groves and leafy oaks, pleasant and plausible to the eyes, which the Prophet reproaches them for when <margin>Altars, statues, groves & idols.</margin> he says, *which you have desired.* By this very word, their ardor for those superstitions is described—that they lusted for groves and chose gardens (<note>Hebrew: גנות</note>) to worship idols there and perform their sacrifices. He used this same word of desire in describing this very matter, saying: <margin>The Makers, ch. 44:9.</margin> <note>Hebrew: יצרי-פסל</note> *The makers of a carved image are all nothing, and their delectable things* (<note>Hebrew: וחמודיהם</note>) *shall not profit them.* Vulgate: *Their most beloved things.* Septuagint: *their heart's desires.* <note>Greek: τὰ καταθύμια αὐτῶν</note> Luther: *The idol-makers are altogether vain / and their precious thing is of no use.* <note>Original German: "Die Götzenmacher find allzumahl eitel..."</note> He condemns all images as useless, however precious and skillfully crafted, however much they may be desired. Tirinus <margin>Tirinus, The Molder, in this place, p. 626.</margin> says: *The molder and the craftsmen of the idol are all nothing, i.e., men of nothing, worthy of the name of no thing, inasmuch as they are so foolish as to think they form Gods with their own hands. And indeed their most beloved things, namely the idols formed by them, shall not profit them, but shall hinder them greatly, so that they ought rightly to be confounded for such great folly.* Great is the blindness of the eyes of the flesh, to be captured by the sight of variegated images and to be delighted by the ruinous invention of men and the fruitless labor of painters—by a figure stained with various colors, *on a colorful image with many kinds of colors*, <margin>Wisdom 15:4.</margin> the sight of which *comes into the lust* <note>Greek: εἰς ὄρεξιν ἔρχεται</note> of the minds of men, so that they desire the form of a dead image void of spirit. These words of Wisdom, <margin>v. 5.</margin> *it comes into lust and longing*, <note>Greek: εἰς ὄρεξιν ἔρχεται καὶ ποθεῖν</note> correspond to that prophetic word <note>Hebrew: חמד (to desire/covet)</note>, which GOD himself uses in the illustrious edict by which <margin>Deut. 7:25.</margin> He forbids even the material of the idol from being transferred to profane use. *The carved images of their Gods you shall burn with fire* <note>Hebrew: תשרפון באש</note>. *You shall not desire* (<note>Hebrew: תחמד</note>) *the silver and gold that are upon them* (<note>Hebrew: עליהם</note>), *nor take any of it for yourself, lest you be ensnared by it* <note>Hebrew: פז תוקש בו</note> <note>Greek: μὴ πταίσης δι’ αὐτό</note>, *that you do not get yourself caught in it.* <note>Original German: "dass du dich nicht drinnen verfahest."</note> Neither shall you bring an abomination (<note>Hebrew: תועבה</note>, <note>Greek: βδέλυγμα</note>) into your house, lest you be a cursed thing (<note>Hebrew: חרם</note>) like it. *You shall utterly detest it and utterly abominate it, for it is a cursed thing* <margin>v. 26.</margin>. GOD could not detest idolatry with a louder thunderbolt of words; it was so abominable to GOD that He would not even allow the cheap material of an idol to be taken for profane uses, let alone sacred ones. But, oh the malice of men! Abominable things became desirable things, <note>Hebrew: וחמודות</note> and the desire of the soul, <note>Hebrew: מחמד</note> <margin>Hosea 9:6.</margin> <note>Hebrew: לכספם</note> *which the Vulgate rendered: desirable for silver. Our [Luther's] version: Their dear idol-silver.* <note>Original German: "Ihr liebes Götzen-Silber."</note> <note>Hebrew: מחמד</note> denotes desire, and "desire of silver" is "most desirable silver," just as "desire of the womb" means "most desirable children" in the same chapter, verse 16, where Luther has: *The dear fruit of their body.* This desire and this appetite of the Israelite people to grow hot in this matter of foreign worship is expressed by the same Prophet Isaiah in chapter 57:5, as if from the womb, when idolatry grows hot...

# From Deuteronomy 12:3

<margin>
Altars, statues, groves, and idols.
</margin>
...brought forth offspring. He uses the parable of adultery to indicate the most intense zeal for idolatry, which was of no other heat and ardor than that of adulterers when they are accustomed to some adulteress or harlot. "You burn with lust," he says, "with gods under every green tree." The Hebrew: *ha-nechamim* <note>original: הנחמים</note>. The Vulgate: *Who console yourselves* (taken passively for "you seek consolation") in gods under every leafy tree. The Greek interpreters—whom the Latin [translator] can very often be observed to have consulted and sought consolation from for his own interpretation—have: *Those who call upon idols under thick trees* <note>original: Οἱ παρακαλοῦντες ἐπὶ τὰ εἴδωλα ὑπὸ δένδρα δασέα</note>. Luther: *You who run in heat to idols under all green trees.* The idolatrous impulse could not be better given by any other word than the verb *chamam* <note>original: חמם</note>, which Scripture is accustomed to use for the heat of coitus or conception, even of brutes (Genesis 30:9, 31:10, 41). And this "yoking together" of idolaters is expressed by the verbs for coupling, *tsamad* <note>original: צמד</note> (to couple or join, Psalm 106:28) and *chabar* <note>original: חבר</note> (to be associated or adhere, Isaiah 44:11 and Hosea 4:17). We would say: *Idol-Companions*, or *Idol-Stallions*, or *Idol-Calves*. For just as beasts of burden and horses are bound to the yoke, so the children of idols are coupled by the yoke of impiety. But what is the bed of this spiritual adultery? The seventh verse in Isaiah answers: *Upon a high and lofty mountain you have set your bed* <note>original: על הר - גבה ונשא שמת משכבך / ἐν ὄρει ὑψηλῷ καὶ μετεώρου ἐκεῖ σου ἡ κοίτη</note>. Luther: *You make your camp upon a high, exalted mountain.* A place or chapel placed upon mountains and decorated with altars is called *mishkav* <note>original: משכב</note>, a bed or couch, which is a verbal noun from *shakav* (to lie down, to lie with). Idolatry is usually described under the guise of adultery or prostitution, the "bed" of which is the groves and high places.

Musculus <note>Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563), a Protestant theologian</note> says: *He calls the temples and chapels placed on mountains a 'bed,' following the example of the ancestors who had sacrificed on mountains. They had a temple approved by God, assigned to His name and worship. Here they were to sacrifice, and nowhere else. But they had filled all the mountains and hills with temples, chapels, altars, idols, and sacrifices, meanwhile despising the temple of the Lord. It serves the metaphor of prostitution, in which he takes this rebuke, that he calls the temple or chapel placed on a mountain the bed of the adulteress herself; as if to say: You have become so shameless that you have brought the bed of your prostitution even onto the mountains, so that it might be in public view.* This madness grew so much that they not only worshipped their gods in public, openly under the sky, but even brought them into their houses for the sake of worship; which the Prophet indicates saying: *Behind the door and the doorpost you have set up your memorial* <note>original: אחר הדלת והמזוזה שמת זכרונך / ὀπίσω τῶν θυρῶν σου καὶ τῶν παραστάδων ἔθηκας μνημόσυνά σου</note>. </margin>
"Upon the mountain you have set your bed" of your adultery, namely an altar to idols. "Furthermore, behind the door of your house you have set your memorial," i.e., the image of your idol, so that both entering and exiting you might have a memory of it, and commend yourself and your belongings to its protection. "You have also enlarged and multiplied the bed of your adultery," i.e., you have erected many altars to idols. So that their entrance and exit might be happy and auspicious, the Jews, *mad for idols* <note>original: εἰδωλομανῶντες</note>, used to place *Lares* and *Penates* <note>Roman household gods</note> on the threshold of their houses. It was believed by the ancients that some Gods had a peculiar care for houses, who were called *Lares* and *Penates* by the Romans, just as others had care for cities. They called it a *Lararium*, where they stored domestic idols. In his *Lararium*, Alexander Severus had Apollonius, Christ, Abraham, Orpheus, and the deified Princes, according to Lampridius. On the day Germanicus died, temples were stoned, altars of the GODS overturned, and by some, the household *Lares* were thrown out into the street.

<margin>
Book 4, ch. 5 in A.S. ch. 29.
</margin>
Suetonius. Laban believed in tutelary gods, whence the wives of Jacob and his handmaids still retained something of the old ferment of idolatry (Genesis 31:19), where Rachel is said to have stolen the *Teraphim* of her father, which were his *Elohim*, his gods. They were images, doubtless marked with certain characters according to a certain constellation, which the superstitious Laban held as household gods and domestic *Lares*, seeking responses from them in doubtful matters; for that they gave responses to those who questioned them can be gathered from Judges 11:18, 18:5, Hosea 3:4, Ezekiel 21:21, and Zechariah 10:2. Rabbi Kimchi interpreted the images of Laban's gods in this sense; nor is the opinion improbable that Rachel stole these *Lares* who were aware of the future so that her father [would not find] her...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES.

<margin>
Altars, statues, & idols.
v. 32. 34.
</margin>
...by consulting [the idols], he might find out by which way they had fled. Nor was Rachel—as the female sex is a credulous sort—free from superstition; otherwise, she would have sooner thrown those idols into the Euphrates than hidden them under the camel’s straw, and that without Jacob’s knowledge <note>Genesis 31:34</note>. We are far from feeling, as some Church Fathers do, that they were stolen merely to deprive her father of the occasion and material for further idolatry. Rather, she took them so that she might have those household gods with her as guardians of her and her flight; this superstition still clung to her from the custom of her father’s house, and her husband could not suppress it in any other way than by burying them under the earth <note>Genesis 35:4</note>. Granted, she had some knowledge of the true God from her husband, yet by the custom and vice of her nation, she approached these idols to consult God in their presence and to expect help through them. Aben Ezra <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish scholar</note> conjectures that these idols had the form of a human, and he asserts that the *Teraphim which Michal placed in the bed in place of David* <margin>1 Sam. 19:13</margin> were of this form. In place of all other examples, we should look to the *Teraphim-worship* which began shortly after the death of Joshua, from the vow of a certain old woman, and on this occasion: A certain wealthy widow had *eleven hundred pieces of silver* taken by a thief, whom she *cursed* (Hebrew: *alah* אלה), that is, she devoted him to dire fates, imprecating misfortunes according to the superstitious custom of old women until he should return it, *Judges 17:2-3*. Terrified by these adjurations and curses, the son confesses the theft and restores the money to his mother. Lest those curses harm her son, she said, praying for prosperity: *Blessed be my son by Jehovah* (Hebrew: *Baruch beni l'Yehovah* ברוך בני ליהוה). And to show her mind was devoted to worship, and to gain for herself some reputation for religion, she had made from that silver by a *goldsmith* a *graven image and a molten image* (Hebrew: *pesel u-massekhah* פסel ומסכה; Greek: *glypton kai choneuton*), that is, two idols, one carved and hewn, the other cast by founding work. And so that there might be a place of devotion, she made a small shrine, appointing her son as priest, <margin>v. 5.</margin> who made for himself an *Ephod and Teraphim* (Hebrew: אפוד ותרפים), that is, as the Vulgate translation adds, *a priestly garment and idols*. This priest was called *Micah*, who first consecrated *one of his sons* as the priest of the Teraphim idol, and then appointed a *Levite* from Bethlehem as Priest, who had arrived by chance; for *that young man departed from Bethlehem in Judah to wander wherever he might find a place* (*like a young vagabond*) *and came to <margin>v. 8.</margin> Mount Ephraim as far as the house of Micah*, to whom Micah said: *Stay with me, and be to me a Father and a <margin>v. 10.</margin> Priest*. This office the young man gladly took upon himself, seduced by a small gift and a little salary, in hope of some <margin>v. 10. 11.</margin> honor; for he stayed with Micah and was to him as *one of his sons*, enjoying food and clothing, and receiving for an annual salary *10 pieces of silver*. This Priest was—you will be amazed—the grandson of Moses, the son of Gershom (Exodus 2:22), named Jonathan, *Judges 18:30*. The degenerate grandson of a most holy man. Six hundred men from the tribe of Dan snatched away this sacrilegious priest along with the Ephod and Teraphim while they were going to expand their borders, and they transferred him to the recently captured city of Laish to be a father and a Priest for their tribe, *Judges 18:16, 17, 19*. Micah took this robbery badly, and following them, he said: *You have taken away my gods* (Hebrew: *elohai* אלהי) *which I made for myself, and the priest*

<column-break/>

*and have gone away; and what have I left?* <margin>Altars, statues & idols.</margin> But Micah, seeing *that they were stronger than he*, <margin>v. 24. v. 26. v. 30.</margin> returned to his house with a heavy heart. But the sons of Dan set up the graven image (Hebrew: *et-ha-pesel* את-הפסל), which remained in worship until the time when the ark of God was taken by the Philistines under Eli the Priest at Shiloh, *v. 3, 1 Sam. 4:10*. The city of Dan became famous for the infamy of idolatry; for in that same city, after the Teraphim-worship had ceased, it was replaced by no less an idolatry: the *worship of the golden calf* by the hand of the impious Jeroboam. Learn from this how great was the ardor of the Danites for idolatrous worship, both public and private, and how great was the progress from small beginnings. Idolatry and heresy are never more to be feared than when they appear smallest. Think of Muhammadanism <note>The author uses the historical term for Islam</note>, how it unfolded from the contemptible beginnings of the false prophet Muhammad, who was no less a *man of his own desire* than this wandering Levite of Micah’s, and fulfilled his name, which comes from *mah* (מה), from *desire*. There is a greater desire to propagate impious doctrine among the impious than among the pious, among whom if there are zealots, that zeal is often stifled by a stronger hand. A proof of this is the whirlwind of the Danites, who snatched away a priest at their whim with all his priestly apparatus, and labored most strenuously for a new worship they had found, whose newly-found priest just as greedily took the office upon himself as he had from Micah; for the Scripture says *his heart was glad* because of that more lucrative <margin>v. 20.</margin> Superintendency. Another proof is the whirlwind of the Baal-worshippers, who propagated their rites with a great spirit, having scattered and dispelled the pious, among whom was *Elijah*, who thought the Church had come to its end; he later, as an excellent avenger, restored the clergy to the temples and faith to the people, addressing all the people: *How long will you limp between two sides? If Jehovah is God, follow him. But if Baal, follow him.* But what did all the people say to this? *They did not answer him <margin>1 Kings 18:21.</margin> a word*. No greater iniquity was ever seen than that which was under Ahab, who *set up an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal* (Hebrew: *mizbeach l'Baal beit ha-Baal* מזבח לבעל בית הבעל), which he had built in Samaria, and *planted a grove* <margin>ch. 16 v. 31. 32.</margin> (Hebrew: *et-ha-asherah* את-האשרה) *and added to his deeds to provoke Jehovah the God of Israel more than all the Kings of Israel who were before him*. Truly, it can best be <margin>v. 33.</margin> said of Samaria what was said of the city of Gilead, *Hosea ch. 6 v. 8*, which was contaminated with equal crimes. For it is called *the city of those who work iniquity* (Hebrew: *kiryat poale aven* קרית פעלי און). The Vulgate: *the city of those who work an idol*. The Septuagint: *a city working vain things*. (German: *a city full of idolatry*). Vanity, iniquity, and idol come under one name in Hebrew, *aven* (און), of which vanity the primary symbols were the Teraphim, *for the Teraphim speak vanity* <margin>Zech. 10:2.</margin> (Hebrew: *ki ha-teraphim dibru-aven*). Luther: *the idols speak vain trouble*. The Teraphim were a *work of vanity*, a work of shame and a work of trouble, whose words were *loose prophecy, inane and empty* (Hebrew: *nevuah rafah* נבואה רפה), as Rabbi Bechai calls it, as if the etymology were from *rafah*, *to be loose or slack*. The Teraphim were *teraph* (תרף), shame and filth in the shrine of Micah, which he had made for these images; yet he did not fear to call this place of filth and ignominy *the house of God* (Greek: *oikon theou*; German: *a House of God*). A little shrine... <margin>ch. 17:5</margin>

# ON DEUTERONOMY XII. v. 3.

## Altars, statues, sacred groves, and idols.
<margin>Altars, statues, groves & idols.</margin>
...separated for God, so that he might place the ephod and teraphim <note>household idols</note> in it. He made an ephod similar to the ephod of Moses in Exodus 28:2, just as other worshippers did in Hosea 3:4, and the Egyptians imitated the priests. Now, the Ephod was a religious garment, to which two stones taken from the Ark and placed in the <term>Choshen</term> <note>The High Priest's breastplate</note> were attached; these he names <term>the Urim and the Thummim</term>, which they translate as "illuminations and perfections," or commonly "doctrine and truth." Either the high priests wore it, or the lesser priests (1 Samuel 22:18), or the Levites (1 Samuel 2:18), or even laymen when performing a sacred function, as is read concerning David in 2 Samuel 6:14 and 1 Chronicles 15:27. The Pontiff, clothed in the Ephod and adorned with the breastplate or Thummim, would inquire of God regarding future or doubtful matters. Micah’s little priest imitated this custom; the Danites had asked him to consult God (<term>Elohim</term>) so they might know if they would proceed on a prosperous journey. He answered them: "Go in peace. Your way in which you walk is before Jehovah (<term>nechach Jehovah</term>)."
<margin>chapter 18, v. 5, 6.</margin>
He pretended to have received an answer from Jehovah when he had actually consulted his idol or teraphim—those household gods of his, *Hauß-Götzen* <note>German: house-gods</note>. Isaiah, censuring this vanity and madness in chapter 44:13, says that idols were fashioned <term>according to the form of a man</term>, <note>original Greek: "as the form of a man"</note>, *like a man's image*, according to the glory of a human <term>ke-tipheret adam</term>, that is, as a beautiful human, as the ancient Translator renders it, giving it a most elegant human likeness, *so that it may dwell in a house* <term>la-shevet bayit</term>, that is, to store it in a shrine, <note>original Greek: "to set it up in a small house"</note>, as the Septuagint well rendered it. Perhaps he intended to hint at the
<margin>p. 627.</margin>
household gods. Musculus <note>Wolfgang Musculus, a Reformer</note> says: *“That phrase, 'that it may sit in a house,' can notably refer to the Lares [household gods], whom everyone keeps in their home in such a way that the whole house is consecrated to their worship, and all their fortune is judged to depend on their whim.”* They kept the images of their gods <note>original Greek: "in small houses and in tents"</note>. The Author of Wisdom <note>Book of Wisdom 13:15</note> calls them "tents" when he says a shrine is built worthy of the idol, or according to its dignity, in which it may be enclosed. The Ephesians knew how to make "worthy little dwellings" for their Diana (Acts 19:24), a craft in which Demetrius the silversmith was then famous, who made <note>original Greek: "silver temples"</note> or silver shrines for Diana. The men of Babylon made <term>Succoth-
<margin>2 Kings 17:30.</margin>

<margin>in 4 Kings 26, p. 188.</margin>

Among the moderns, John Selden (Syntagma 2 on the Syrian Gods, ch. 7) and Gerhard Johann Vossius (Book 2 on Idolatry, ch. 22) and Hugo Grotius agree with this. However, there are others who, along with the Syriac, Arabic, and Septuagint translators, take this as a specific idol of the Babylonians—namely, Martin Luther in his version, the Vulgate, François Vatable, Santes Pagnino, Arias Montanus, Sebastian Münster, Johannes Piscator, Franciscus Junius, and Immanuel Tremellius, as well as the Hebrew commentators; see also Athanasius Kircher in *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*. <margin>ch. 6, 3.</margin>

The Jews had seen this done in Egypt in the worship of the Apis bull; hence, in the solemnity of the festival of the calf, they are said to have risen very early in the morning and offered burnt offerings, and brought peace offerings, and sat down <term>to eat and to drink</term>, and afterward rose up <term>to play</term> (Exodus 32:6). # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Altars, statues, groves & idols. Amos 2:8.</margin>
...they would feast joyfully, according to the ancient custom. A similar passage is: *they lay down beside every altar upon clothes taken in pledge, and they drank the wine of the condemned in the house of their gods* <note>original: אלהיהם (*Eloheihem*)</note>. Martin de Roa <note>Spanish Jesuit scholar, 1563–1637</note> suggests in *2. sing. 9.* that they pledged themselves to these gods with these garments, as if devoting themselves to them. The Israelites, seduced by Moabite and Midianite women, worshipped Baal-Peor (*Numbers 25:3*) and ate things sacrificed to idols, as the Greeks explicitly express: *the people ate of their sacrifices* <note>original Greek: ἔφαγεν ὁ λαὸς τῶν θυσιῶν αὐτῶν</note>. They are said to have eaten the sacrifices of the dead in *Psalm 106:28*, that is, victims offered to idols and false gods, who are rightly called *Dead Gods*, and a *dead idol* in *Wisdom 13:18*. They worshipped that for which a tomb could be shown, and it was customary to sacrifice to one who, while alive, had once sacrificed to the dead. They worshipped that which led its worshipper into death and to the underworld; for his soul could not die the death of the righteous, to use the phrase of Scripture <margin>Numbers 23:10.</margin>. This is what it means to eat the sacrifices of the dead <note>original: זבחי מתים (*Zivchei Metim*); Greek: θυσίας νεκρῶν</note>, "The eating of the offerings of dead idols," as our version has it. In the Chaldean <note>Aramaic Targum</note> they are called *property of the dead* <note>original: נכסי מיתיא</note>, the same as sacrifices of the dead, from the root *to slaughter and offer as a sacrifice*. To this, the translators of the Septuagint impertinently applied the precept about not eating meat with the blood (*Leviticus 19:26*), where the Law intended that one should abstain from strangled animals. *Do not eat upon the mountains* <note>original Greek: μὴ ἐσθίετε ἐπὶ τῶν ὀρέων</note>; they clearly read *mountains* <note>Hebrew: הרימ (*Harim*)</note> instead of *blood* <note>Hebrew: על-הדם (*Al-ha-dam*)</note>. Rabbi Moses Gerundensis <note>Nachmanides</note> refers this to a form of idolatry by which a covenant was made with the devil, in the 220th negative commandment of the Jews, concerning which see Peter Gregory *book 12, chapter 20, section 4*. Regarding these feasts, Virgil says in *book 8*:
> King Evander said: No empty superstition,
> Or ignorance of the ancient Gods, has imposed on us
> These solemn rites, these customary feasts,
> This altar of so great a divinity. Trojan guest,
> Saved from cruel perils, we perform these rites and renew deserved honors.
And a little later he mentions how the priests sang praises and deeds at the altar of Hercules.
> Then the Salii <note>Leaping priests of Mars/Hercules</note> come to the songs around the smoking altars,
> Their temples bound with poplar branches.
> Here is a chorus of youths, there of elders, who in song
> Carry the praises and deeds of Hercules.

<margin>Genesis 4.</margin> Idolatry entered the world through Cain, who, going out *from the face of God*, <gloss>defiled the worship of God</gloss> as the first of all men; which was afterwards restored through Cain's brother Seth by public exercise, with certain ceremonies and formulas of prayer established for that purpose. For then began the name of *Jehovah* to be called upon <margin>verse 26.</margin>, namely publicly through assemblies and Churches, through public prayers and sermons, through sacrifices and other rites and ceremonies. Learned men among the Hebrews gave an interpretation entirely contrary to this, as if the name of the Lord was then polluted and profaned by idols; an opinion I see pleases John Selden in *Prolegomena on the Syrian Gods, chapter 3, page 28*. But the word *began* <note>Hebrew: החל (*Huchal*)</note> does not descend from the root *to profane* <note>Hebrew: חלל (*Chalal*)</note>, but from the root meaning *it was begun*; and it refers to that invocation which was now performed at fixed hours in a certain assembly and with certain ceremonies; not that there was no invocation before, but that it was not of such a kind; almost in the same way it is said in <margin>1 Samuel 3:1.</margin> that *there was no open vision* in the time of Eli, i.e., manifest, by which it would be publicly known, not that

<column-break/>

it was entirely removed, but that it was obscure and very thin, which afterwards shone clearly and brightly in Samuel. Whence Johann Forster <margin>Altars, statues, groves & idols. Dictionary page 742.</margin> observes: "It should be noted that if the verb 'to call' follows the name of Jehovah, that is, to call in the name of the Lord, it means to invoke in the name of Jehovah, to preach, to profess publicly, to glorify, and to celebrate the name of Jehovah, in which indeed the true outward worship of God consists—namely, in invocation, thanksgiving, the preaching of the word of God, and confession" (for this phrase embraces these four kinds), in which the true and principal use of the name Jehovah consists. For the business of religion and vision had its intervals. Afterward, Enoch raised up the worship of God, who walked with God for three hundred years by leading a life of singular holiness, and *Noah was perfect <margin>Genesis 5:22.</margin> in the same walking with God*, who found grace in the eyes of Jehovah because of his zeal for piety <margin>Genesis 6:9, verse 8.</margin>, by which he deserved to be saved alone with his family, while all other men in the world were removed by the flood. And so that he might spread the grateful fame of God, immediately upon exiting the ark he built an altar to Jehovah, and took from every clean animal and every clean bird, and offered burnt offerings on that altar <margin>Genesis 8:20.</margin>. This sacrifice pleased God and he was appeased by it, having previously been offended by the human race because of idolatry and other immense sins; *he smelled a soothing aroma* <margin>verse 21.</margin>, so much so that what Ovid wrote of Bacchus in the 3rd book of the *Fasti* can be applied to this so holy man, the first theologian of the second world:
> Before your birth, altars were without honor,
> And grass was found in cold hearths.
> The Ganges remembers you, and the whole conquered East,
> Having set aside first-fruits for the great God.
> You first gave cinnamon and captive incense,
> And roasted entrails from the triumphed God.
The degenerate son of this Noah, Ham, disseminated impure worship among his descendants, whom Noah had cursed (*Genesis 9:25*). The sons of Ham were: *Cush, Mizraim, Phut, and Canaan* <margin>chapter 10, verse 6.</margin>. From Cush came the Ethiopians, from Mizraim the Egyptians (whence the land is called Mizraim, *1 Chronicles 1:8*, and the land of Ham, *Psalm 105:23, 27; 106:22*, and the tabernacle of Ham, *Psalm 78:51*). The origin of nearly all idolatries is believed to have flowed from the Egyptians, and from them to the Persians, Greeks, and other nations. Ammianus Marcellinus <margin>book 22, chapter 41.</margin> says: "If anyone with a vigorous mind wishes to unroll the manifold addition of understanding the divine and the origin of foreknowledge, he will find throughout the whole world that such learnings were carried around from Egypt." Herodotus testifies regarding the Greeks <margin>Euterpe</margin> that they brought the method of building temples and images and rites from the Egyptians. "They say the Egyptians were the first to recognize the names of the twelve gods, and that the Greeks took from them the altars, statues, and temples for the gods, assigning them first." He says the twelve gods were first worshipped in Egypt, then carried into Attica, and had a common altar which was called the *Altar of the Twelve Gods*. The Greeks followed the Egyptians, and the Romans followed the Greeks, for whom the twelve great gods were the gods of the major nations; and perhaps the Egyptians imitated the names of God which the Hebrews had attributed to God, as Taubmann conjectures <margin>on Plautus, page 442.</margin>. Whatever was in the institutions of the Jews, the Egyptians first, and then from them the Greeks and Romans, seem to have borrowed like an ape. Who can constantly deny, says Natalis...

It traces the geographical spread of idolatry from Ham's descendants in Egypt to the Greeks and Romans.</summary>

# From Deuteronomy XVI. v. 21.

<margin>
Altars, statues, groves & idols. Mythology, book as cited above, last page.
</margin>

Do you suppose *, that those laws which were given to the holy Hebrew men, first migrated to the priests in *Egypt*, and then from Egypt into Greece? <margin>canonical rules</margin> If such rules are found anywhere in pagan doctrine, they can certainly be <unclear>safely</unclear> observed in the rites of their sacrifices. Whatever the pagan has here that is similar, they are debtors to the Jews; Hence Augustine <margin>Book 22 against Faustus, ch. 17.</margin> * writes that the religious categories of the Hebrew sacrifices were sacrilegious imitations for the Pagans. This is most true, for the descendants of Noah, scattered into diverse lands, gradually lost the heavenly doctrine they had received from their holy ancestors; they indeed retained the ancient rites handed down by the Fathers, such as sacrifices, but they were ignorant of their use and purpose, and thus, having lost the kernel, they retained only the shell. The dull-witted Julian <note>The Emperor Julian "the Apostate," who sought to revive paganism.</note> affirmed that the sacrifices of the Jews differed in no way from those of the Ethnecs <note>Gentiles/Pagans</note>, as Cyril testifies <margin>Book 3 against Julian. Question on the City of God 21.</margin> *, when there is actually as much difference (as Augustine elegantly says *) *as there is between the gestures of men and those of an ape.* The Pagans offered sacrifices out of voluntary and arbitrary worship without faith, as the same Father teaches in *Book 20, ch. 5 of the City of God.* The sacrifices of the Jews, however, were a shadow and representation of the future passion of Christ, and in this respect most pleasing to God, as he shows in *Book 20, ch. 26* of the said book. In one or two ceremonies the Egyptians imitated the Hebrews, especially in circumcision and most of all in sacrifices; they thought that unless the things sacrificed were pure and select, they contributed nothing to the divine matter, and before they sacrificed, they washed their hands and feet. <margin>On Genesis, p. 341</margin> Nothing was more frequent (says Bonfrerius *) among the ancient gentiles—the Devil emulating divine rites—*than the washing of hands and feet before sacrifices, which, if any other things are, ought to be handled decently and reverently.* Frantzius makes this manifest with examples in *School of Sacrifices, Disputations 5, 7, 13, 19.* Danæus in *Antiquities of the First World, pages 239, 246, 247.* and most recently our friend Johannes Fabricius, in a special little book to which he gave the title: *The Devil is the Ape of God;* <note>original: "Simia Dei Diabolus"</note> but also those *theaters of oracles* which were instituted in honor of the Gods, and the responses made in them, the Devil as an Ape imitated from what he had seen used and employed among the people of God. For all this filth of Diabolical oracles was introduced by a wicked and sacrilegious emulation of the form of certain <unclear>manifestations</unclear> by which God spoke with the Fathers in certain places, making known his promises, as the Theologian Jakob Martini feels in *Special Part of Theological Topics, disp. 7. th. 95.* This glory of the Devil faded away at the coming of CHRIST, and the night of Ethnic errors passed away, the multitude of impure Gods being put to flight everywhere.

### DEUTERONOMY 16. 21.

-> You shall not plant for yourself an Asherah <note>A sacred tree or pole</note> of any kind of wood near the altar of the LORD your God, which you shall make for yourself. <-
-> You shall not plant for yourself a grove, any tree near the altar of the Lord your God, which you shall make for yourself. <note>original Greek: Οὐ φυτεύσεις σεαυτῷ ἄλσος...</note> <-
-> **You shall not plant a grove, nor any tree near the altar of the Lord your God.** <-

<margin>Groves consecrated to the Gods</margin>

Concerning their groves and the worship of them, we have said not a few things in a previous place; nevertheless, it pleases us to say certain things at present regarding the forbidden worship of groves. God forbade groves and woods within which, according to the custom of the nations, sacred rites were performed to idols. For because the Gentiles frequently erected their altars to idols in groves and shady places, to show a greater detestation of idolatry, and so that they might be further removed from all imitation of idolaters, God, the Best and Greatest, prohibited anything similar from being introduced into divine worship. See Philo the Jew’s book *On Monarchy, the second part near the beginning;* where he investigates the reasons why the Lord of his temple did not wish groves to be established.

It is a most well-known matter from the books of the Pagans that most of the ancient Gods were accustomed to be worshipped in groves. Regarding the grove of Ceres, the story of Erysichthon is well known; regarding the grove of Dictynna, see Antonius Liberalis; *regarding the grove of Dis <note>Pluto/Hades</note>* see Frontinus *. <margin>Stratagems book 1, ch. 11; book 1 on the Trojan War, p. 250.</margin> Regarding Pallas, see Pindar *Olympian 5.* Livy *book 35.* Regarding the grove of Diana, see Dictys of Crete *, in which Agamemnon, heedless of the religion that was in that place, had pierced a grazing doe with a javelin, as is narrated there by many: *The gentiles also dedicated every grove to Diana, because she is the Mistress of mountains, and of green forests, and of hidden glades, and of sounding rivers, says Catullus in his Secular Hymn.* Regarding the groves of the Germans, see Tacitus and Claudian *On the Praises of Stilicho, book 1.* The Abasgi and Druids venerated groves with the same superstition, on which matter see Petrus Faber’s *Semestria, book 3, p. 20.* Regarding the Lithuanians who pursued whole groves with divine worship, one may read Aeneas Sylvius in his description of Europe: Strabo, dealing with Abydos of the Thebaid, says there was a trench there, and around it a grove of Egyptian acanthus sacred to Apollo. That town was situated in the furthest part of the Thebaid, where *the oracle of the God locally called Besa formerly revealed future things,* as Marcellinus testifies in *book 19.* There is one who thinks that instead of "locally" <note>original: "localiter"</note> it should be read "from a grove of such a kind" <note>original: "a luco taliter"</note>. Indeed, they assigned Sylvans and Fauns * and other such deities to the woods just as they did to the heavens. <margin>Rhodiginus book 12, ch. 1, page 523.</margin> We would bring forward more examples, were we not of the opinion that the matter is manifest even to the moderately learned. This Pagan error, says Jerome *, <margin>on ch. 7 of Ezekiel and Jeremiah.</margin> occupied all provinces, so that they sacrificed victims at the heads of springs and in most pleasant groves, and the religion of every perverse superstition was maintained. Moreover, a grove was placed either around the shrines of the Gods or around the tombs of men; the traces of which thing, says Schindler, can still be seen in our linden trees planted in cemeteries. You will see examples in H. Kornman *On the Miracles of the Dead, part 9, ch. 7.*

It seems to P. Faber *Semestria book 3, ch. 1, p. 13.* that Astarte, the Goddess of Syria (of whom mention is frequent in Holy Scripture) was named from groves and woods (which are called *Ashera* and *Asherim* by the Hebrews) in which the pagans venerated that idol; consult him. Add Selden *Syntagma 2, ch. 2* *. <margin>p. 232 and following.</margin> Mention of groves is frequent in the sacred texts: the burning of which, and the overturning of the idols themselves, was done by the command of God; see *Exodus 34:13, Deuteronomy 7:5, ch. 12:3, Judges 6:28, 1 Kings 14:15, 23; ch. 15:13; ch. 16:33; ch. 18:19, 22; 2 Kings 13:6; ch. 17:10, 16; ch. 18:4.* (P. Faber *in the place cited, p. 15 & 16* thinks this passage should be understood as referring to the Prophets of the goddess Astarte) *ch. 21 v. 3, 7; ch. 23:4, 6, 14, 15.* where the grove in Bethel is set on fire by the command of Josiah (the word there is *Asherah*, which Selden thinks can also be taken for a calf *) *Isaiah 1:29.* (where the Vulgate <margin>Syntagma book 1, ch. 4, p. 143.</margin> version wrongly translates as *from idols:* for it is *Eylim* <note>Oaks/Trees</note> not *Elilim* <note>Idols</note>) *chapter 17:2, 8; ch. 27:9; ch. 66:17.* (on which place see Scaliger *in his notes on the fragments,* which are at the end of the book on the Emendation...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

Correction of times) Jeremiah 17:1, Ezekiel 20:28, Micah 5:14, Judith 3:12.

<margin>Groves consecrated to the Gods</margin>
Groves (*Luci*) are so called by the Latins because they shine (*lucent*) most brightly due to the frequency of sacrifices, as discussed by Isidore in Book 14, Chapter 8, and uniquely defended by the great Scaliger. <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a famous scholar of chronology and philology.</note> We spoke more regarding groves and tree-deities in the passage immediately preceding; likewise, you may find many details about groves in Lipsius’s commentary on Tacitus’s *Germania*.

### DEUTERONOMY XXII. 5.

->A woman shall not wear the garment of a man, nor shall a man put on a woman’s cloak, for<-
->whoever does these things is an abomination to the Lord your God.<-
->Greek: There shall not be the equipment of a man upon a woman, nor shall a man<-
->put on a woman’s robe, because an abomination to the<-
->Lord your God is everyone doing these things.<-
->*Latin: A woman shall not be clothed in a man’s garment: nor shall a man use<-
->a feminine garment; for he who does these things is abominable before God.*<-

<margin>A woman clothed in man's attire.</margin>
By this law, God Most High forbids the exchange of garments by which men and women misrepresented their sex. The most serious reason for this was not only so that one sex might be distinguished from the other by this mark of clothing, but also that a window might be closed against lusts and other dishonest actions usually committed through such confusion. Some of the Church Fathers explained this law mystically, among whom we cite Clement of Alexandria. <margin>Epistle 15.</margin> *What reason,* he asks, *does this Law have? It wishes us to be men by consent, and not to be effeminated in body, deeds, mind, or words.* And Ambrose: *I judge that this law spoke not so much of clothing as of morals, or of customs and acts, for one act becomes a man, another a woman.* However, some more curious interpreters of that law explain the text regarding the deceptive habit of dress as referring to a certain idolatrous fashion, which can be included under the general term <term>Keli</term> <note>Hebrew: vessel, tool, or garment</note>. They argue that what is forbidden here is for a woman to carry the <term>Keli Geber</term>, the "vessels" or "weapons" of a man—<term>Manns-Gewehr</term> <note>German: man's weapon/gear</note> as the edition of Jacob Liesvelt has it. They believe it refers to that worship where women exchanged weapons and clothes in veneration of the Goddess Venus, and men did the same in honor of Mars. They attempt to prove this from the fact that <term>To'ebah</term> <note>Hebrew: abomination</note>, which is mentioned here, is commonly used in the Scriptures when speaking of idolatry or anything pertaining to it. The leader of this exposition is Rabbi Moses Ben Maimon <note>Maimonides</note> in his work <margin>part 3, ch. 37</margin> *Guide for the Perplexed*, whom others follow. The Syrian Venus was thought to be a deity both masculine and feminine. They performed various solemn rites for her, and according to the ritual, they put on either male or female clothes. From this, surely, comes the light of the scripture which forbids the exchange of garments. Furthermore, by the precept concerning the habit of both sexes, some profane rite seems to be forbidden, both because a woman is prohibited from taking up the warlike weapons of a man—not just garments, which are specifically denoted by another name, <term>Simlah</term>—and because that solemn reason is added: <term>To'ebah</term>, that is, a thing accursed to the Lord, which usually regards idolatry in the sacred texts. Francis Vatablus on this passage says: <term>Keli</term> signifies instruments of war. It forbids women from going out to military service with men, after the custom of Oriental women, for they would expose themselves to the danger of violated chastity. At the same time, it is commanded

<column-break/>

<margin>A woman clothed in man's attire.</margin>
that a man should not use women's clothes, for the sake of protecting public decency and avoiding fornications; otherwise, a beardless youth could easily hide among women in female dress. To this also aim the writings on this passage by Nicholas of Cusa, a German by nation, first Dean of St. Florinus, then Bishop of Brixen and Cardinal, in Book 2 of his *Exercises in the Sermon: The Magi went.* There he restricts this prohibition in the divine law to idolatry, because women put on female clothes and weapons in honor of Mars, and men put on female clothes in honor of Venus, as cited by Philipp Camerarius in *Historical Meditations, ch. 29*. But since the law forbids wearing <term>Keli</term> (a general term) to both men and women, I do not know how it can be translated as only "Martial weapons" for the female sex, which she handles too awkwardly in a man's toga; nor were the things denied here unique to the Gods. Nor do those words accept the restriction that they should refer only to idolatrous customs. <term>Keli</term> here, as in Sirach <margin>v. 4. 45. v. 21.</margin> <term>ta skeue</term> <note>Greek: the vessels/garments</note>, is said of clothes; compare Numbers 31:50. <term>Keli tzon</term>, the vessel of a man, i.e., manly clothes, which is also explained by the more specific <term>Simlah</term> in this place. Thus, the opinion of the most learned Selden <margin>Book 2 on the Syrian Gods, 4</margin> regarding the warlike weapons of a man being forbidden to a woman is not to be approved, as Quistorp in *Biblical Annotations* and B. Danhauer in *Decalogue College* rightly disprove. In idolatrous rites, the exchange of clothes is indeed attested by the "Hybristica" <note>A festival involving cross-dressing</note> of the Argives, where women were dressed in male tunics and men in female fillets and veils, according to Plutarch in *On the Bravery of Women*. Regarding the Athenians, Macrobius <margin>Saturnalia, book 3, ch. 8</margin> says: *Philochorus also affirms in his history of Attica that the same (Venus) is the Moon: and that men sacrifice to her in female dress, and women in male dress.* Also, Julius Firmicus in *On the Error of Profane Religions* records that the priests of the Assyrian Venus disgraced the male sex with female finery. But the law is more general and of greater scope, which does not tolerate the promiscuous use of garments in either sex, even for sport. This divine law has its place not so much in military service as at home and in peace. God immortal did not want the distinction of the sexes to be perverted or confused, because it would be an execrable deed, most contrary to shame and chastity; for the best sign and guard of modesty is the clothing and the modesty of the habit, as the Poet hints: it is shameful for a woman to handle weapons, having abandoned domestic duties.

> What modesty can a helmeted woman provide,
> who flees from her own sex?

In the Council of Gangra, Canon 13, a woman is struck with anathema for using male garments. Philo explains the words of Moses in this spirit: The Law willed, he says, that a man should conduct himself in his dress as becomes a man, which since he carries it about day and night, ought to be such that it always reminds him of decorum and honesty. So also for women, adorning them according to their dignity, it forbids taking up male dress, removing far away both effeminate men and women who are more masculine than is right. And Flavius Josephus <margin>Antiquities of the Jews, book 4, last chapter</margin> says: <term>Beware especially in battles, so that neither a woman uses a man's equipment, nor a man a woman's robe.</term> Cases of necessity are exempted, where to avoid danger to life one might sometimes change sex with clothing <meta>neces-</meta>

# From Deuteronomy XXV. v. 5. <note>The author is actually discussing Deuteronomy 22:5, which forbids wearing clothes of the opposite sex.</note>

<margin>
A woman dressed in male attire.
</margin>
It was necessary to make an exception for the heroic courage found in certain women, whose deeds and the *shaping* <note>original: "σχηματισμος" (schematismos) - outward appearance or fashioning</note> of their sex under male habit are to be praised rather than blamed.

<margin>
In Pompey, p. 636.
</margin>
Hypsicratia, a woman of manly spirit, followed Mithridates (for whom she burned with passion) into war, using a Persian male robe. Plutarch recorded her courage in his writings with these words: *“She often endured much, being always manly and daring (for the King used to call her 'Hypsicrates' in the masculine); at that time, wearing the robe and mount of a Persian horseman, she did not despair of her body despite the length of the journeys, so that she might tend to the King’s body and his horse.”* <note>original Greek: "ύπεκαρτη πολλάκις... εξείκαζε"</note> Thus, this noble woman was not only present in Mithridates' expeditions, but followed the King of Pontus with indefatigable spirit and body after he was defeated by Pompey and fled through wild nations. You may read many examples of this matter in Ravisius’s *Officina*, Majolus p. 50, Meteranus book 21, and Gabriel Chappuys in the *History of Our Time*. Those who, out of softness or lust, whether male or female, counterfeit their sex and walk about in changed dress, incur deserved reproach—especially men who, out of softness, choose female attire for themselves. Wherefore Dominicus Mancinellus rightly inveighs against them in *On the IV Virtues*, ch. 6, v. 379:

->Let a man think it unworthy and ridiculous alike<-
->To take up feminine dress and soft gestures.<-
->What is more against nature or decency,<-
->Than for a man to live under a woman’s garment?<-

Sardanapalus, the last King of the Assyrians, was so corrupted by soft delights that, abandoning royal majesty, he as a man took up female habit and, counterfeiting a woman, hid away among girls and eunuchs. Suetonius criticized the *stola* <note>A long gown worn by Roman matrons.</note> in Caligula, which a man could not use without reproach; as Ulpian testifies in law 23, § 2, regarding gold and silver, upon which there exists a commentary of varied erudition by Lazarus Bayfius, published in Basel a hundred years ago.

<margin>
The legal consultant says: "Feminine items are those prepared for the sake of the mother of the family, which a man cannot easily use without blame, such as stolas, cloaks, tunics, head-coverings, belts, and mitres, which are provided more for the sake of covering the head than for ornamenting it, as well as small curtains and hoods. Common items are those used indiscriminately by a woman with a man, such as a hood or cloak of that kind, which either husband or wife may use without reproach."
</margin>

For in the Roman era, the *stola* was not numbered among male garments; among them, it was a sin to exchange the *stola* for the male *toga*, nor was it assumed except by one as effeminate as Caligula or Heliogabalus. "Does it not seem to you that they live against nature, who exchange dress with women?" says Seneca in Epistle 122. Those who wore the *mitra* <note>A type of soft headband or cap.</note> fell under the same reproach—a female ornament, shameful for men—which Turnebus, the most learned of the Gauls, proves from Lucan.

</margin>

### DEUT. XXII. 8.

->When you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof.<-
->If you build a new house, you shall make a crown for your dwelling.<- <note>Greek Septuagint translation.</note>
->*When you have built a new house, you shall make a wall for the roofs round about.*<- <note>Latin Vulgate translation.</note>

<margin>
Architecture in the East.
</margin>
It was the custom of architecture in Palestine, indeed throughout all Asia—whence one can read about flat roofs in Babylon in Xenophon p. 131, which are even still in use, as Olearius testifies in his *Travels* p. 278—to establish flat roofs at the top of the houses. For they did not rise into a peak or gable like our houses, which are seen pointed into a cone as if gabled, and where:

<margin>
The roofs have a peak, and rejoice in the highest summit.
</margin>
Lest those flat roofs be prone to falling, the outer spaces had to be surrounded by a breastwork <note>original: "peribolo loricato"</note> to avoid the danger of falling and homicide. Thus God cautioned by decree, lest bloodguilt be placed upon the house. <term>Damim</term> <note>Hebrew: דמים</note> denotes the guilt or fault of slaying, as in chapter 21:8 and elsewhere in the books. The roof was surrounded against precipices by enclosures, the height of which was three or four feet. That circuit is called <term>Ma'aqeh</term> <note>Hebrew: מעקה</note>, for which Onkelos <note>The famous Aramaic translator of the Torah.</note> substituted <term>Teika</term> <note>Aramaic: תיקא</note>, which in Greek is *theke* <note>θηκη</note>, a "case" or "sheath." That fence of the roof can also be called a *thrigkos* <note>θριγκος - a coping or eaves-cornice</note>, and Homer uses it:

<margin>
It can be called *thrigkos*, and Homer uses it. Odyssey book 7 v. 87 and book 17 v. 257.
</margin>
> From the threshold to the inner chamber; and around it a coping of blue.
> With a wall and copings, and the doors are well-fenced.

Where he describes the hall of Alcinous and the house of Ulysses: Philo calls it a *thorakion* <note>breastwork</note>. In place of *theke*, the Greeks formerly said *thebe* or *sibe*, meaning a "chest," as in *sibe papyro* for a wicker basket in Exodus 2:3. Casaubon writes in his notes to Athenaeus p. 245 that the Greeks borrowed this word from the Syrians. The Rabbis made the Greek *theke* their own by use, from which Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> explained the meaning of the word *Ma'aqeh* in his gloss on this place: namely, that the word *Ma'aqeh* denotes a fence around the roof, and Onkelos rendered that name as *Teika* because it is like a "case" (theca) which guards that which is hidden and preserved within it.

</margin>
Munster in his Dictionary.

Peribolus (circuit), *Chika*, *Ma'aqeh*, *Gephoth*. Salmasius says the Greeks properly call a *peribolus* a certain measure of land around a temple that is vacant, planted with vines or trees, enclosed by a wall, and dedicated to the God of the Temple. Hence "the peribolus of the temple" is frequently mentioned by Greek authors. It also happens that the Greeks use *peribolus* for the temple itself; thus "to throw a peribolus around" means to build a temple. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Architecture in the East.</margin>
...because it was customary for them to call every protruding edge or the extremity of any object, whatever its shape might be, a "crown" <note>original: *corona*</note>; hence the term "crown" <note>Greek: *stephanos*</note> also occurs in reference to city walls in Pindar:

->*Intending to build a crown for Ilium*<-
->And Anacreon: *Now the crown has perished from the city.*<-

The Greek interpreters call this kind of flat roof a *doma*; for they almost everywhere translate the word *gag* <note>Hebrew: גג</note>, which signifies a roof, as *doma*.
<margin>On Amos 7, p. 104.</margin>
Jerome: *Gag is translated into our language as doma, i.e., a roof.* An old Glossary: *Tectum* <note>Latin: roof</note>, *stegē, stegnon,* and *doma* <note>Greek terms for roof/dwelling</note>. Greece also used the term more generally for a dwelling; for *doma* is also *oikos* <note>house</note>, especially among the Poets; nothing is more frequent in the Prince of Poets <note>Homer</note>. The *Etymologicum Magnum*, page 293: *Doma*, a dwelling, from *domō* <note>to build</note>, *domēsō*, *domēma*, and by shortening, *doma*. Suidas, Moschopulus, and Varinus Camers record the same. Herodotus uses it thus in *Clio*, page 71. More specifically, *to doma* is said to be *the upper part of a house, the covering, the roofing of a dwelling*, the superior part of the house by which it is covered, in which
<margin>page 74.</margin>
sense Herodian uses *doma*, and the legal consultant Theophilus used it in a similar way in the *Institutes*, page 249.
<margin>Vol. 5, p. 584</margin>
Jerome, commentary on Daniel 6:10: *Domata are called in Latin Meniana, or roofs, or solaria and anōgeia, i.e., dining rooms.* Meniana (which is also often written with an *oe*) were named after Maenius, a Roman inhabitant; *solaria* <note>sun-decks</note> were those attached to houses. He writes the same in Epistle
<margin>Vol. 3, p. 91.</margin>
135 to Sunia: *In the Oriental provinces, that which is called a roof among the Latins is called a doma. For in Palestine and Egypt they do not have gabled peaks on their roofs, but domata, which at Rome they call either solaria or meniana, i.e., flat roofs supported by transverse beams. When it is commanded that we make a "crown" for the doma, this is commanded: that we make certain elevations around the circuit of the roof, lest there be an easy fall headlong.*
<margin>3. Travels 14, p. 262.</margin>
Salomon Schweigger: *The buildings in Egypt are not built according to the style of our land with tiled roofs; for in the entire Orient—Judea, Syria, Persia, Asia—they have no roofs, but instead of a roof there is a masonry floor, built like any other wall. It has a door on one side through which one can walk up from the house onto the floor to stroll, eat, and perform other matters. At the four corners, the wall continues upward about half a man's height, so that one can
<margin>book 1, ch. 33, p. 99.</margin>
look out over it, like a railing.* And Heberer in *Egyptian Servitude*: *The houses in Alexandria, as well as in other places in Egypt and Syria, have no roofs, but are entirely flat on top, so that one can walk upon them. From there, the houses receive light falling in from above.*

<column-break/>

<margin>Architecture in the East.</margin>
Jerome explains *doma* as a *solarium*, which was a place where one was accustomed to sun oneself, as P. Victorius shows in *Various Readings* 21, 13; nor should these be confused with those roofs which were inaccessible, unlike the *solaria*, concerning which see Heinsius in *Exercises on the New Testament*, page 152. Nevertheless, Jerome himself, if he is the author of the version, used the word
<margin>Isaiah ch. 2, v. 1.</margin>
in naming the place where Rahab hid the Israelite spies, calling it a *solarium*; because there he intended nothing other than the upper part of the dwelling exposed to the sun, and therefore the roof itself for the same reason, just as the same Vulgate translator in Judges ch. 16, v. 27 joined *the roof and the solarium, in which the Philistines watched Samson performing.* The Septuagint there has *upon the domata*. Otherwise, the name *doma* is found in the translator of Proverbs, verse 9 of chapter 21, and verse 24 of chapter 25: *It is better to sit in a corner of the doma* <note>Hebrew: *gag pinah*</note>—*upon the corner of the doma—than with a quarrelsome woman in a shared or very large house* <note>Hebrew: *be-veit chaver*</note>, i.e., *a house of society.* This Hebraism, I might add in passing, Symmachus elegantly expressed as *a house of companionships*, and no less unpleasantly the French translator: *in a house of (great) assembly.* The word *doma* also passed to other Latin writers. Aldhelm, in *Praise of Virginity*: *He is remembered to have burned in the very tiling of the doma by vengeful globes of flames.* The author of the *Life of St. Ulrich*: *Lest they be further soaked by rains from the domata.*
<margin>book 1, ch. 25.</margin>
The illustrious Welser does not explain it there, merely placing an asterisk. However, the *domata* of those regions were so prepared on account of their flatness that it was permitted to walk, stay, feast, sleep, and do other things of that kind upon them. This flatness is evident not so much from the testimonies already mentioned as from those to be said. A law was passed so that the owner would not be guilty of homicide if someone were cast headlong and fell. It was in the evening, when the heavy heat of the sun had ceased, that David rose from his
<margin>2 Samuel 11:2, 7.</margin>
bedchamber and walked upon the roof of the royal house <note>Hebrew: *al gag beit ha-melech*</note>, *upon the doma*, and saw a woman washing herself from the roof itself. Isidore, in book 15, ch. 3, understood this as a *solarium* when he writes: *A solarium, which lies open to the sun and the breeze, such as was the place in which David beheld and fell in love with Bathsheba washing.* We gather from Isaiah ch. 22, v. 1 that it was a customary kind of refuge to go to the roofs in mourning, where Jerusalem, which is called the valley of vision, is said to have ascended *to the domata* on account of excessive mourning and distress. *What has happened to you,* says the Prophet, *that you have all climbed to the roofs, full of commotions?* This was the gesture of mourners: that in the crossroads and squares (just as the Pharisees otherwise counted their prayers in public) and likewise on the roofs, they would stir up mourning, so that the public misfortune might be more widely spread; and their misfortunes, to use the words of Terence in *Hecyra* 3.3.28, *will happen on silent roofs, known to none*, which the words of Jeremiah do not allow us to ignore:
<margin>ch. 48, v. 38.</margin>
*Upon all the roofs of Moab and in its streets there shall be nothing but wailing, when I have broken Moab.* The roofs were also the hiding places of the house, where, as I might say from Plautus,
<margin>*Trinummus* 2.2.</margin>
*men would hide themselves secretively in fear and danger*, for those who feared danger either from an enemy or the attack of another would conceal themselves there. On the roof <note>Hebrew: *al-ha-gag*</note>, the spies who were sent...

# From Deuteronomy XXII. v. 8.

<margin>Architecture in the East.</margin>
When they had entered into Canaan under Joshua, Rahab the harlot hid the men in the stalks of flax in her inn <note>original: "διὰ τὴν τεκτονικὴν" - likely a reference to the structural layout or "by means of the construction"</note>. For thus the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> say of Rahab, hiding the scouts on the roof: *She brought them up to the roof, and hid them in the stalks of flax, which she had laid in order upon the roof.* The history is found in Joshua chapter 2, where in verse 7: *She herself caused the men to be hidden in the solarium <note>A sun-terrace or flat roof</note> of her house, and covered them with the stalks of flax which were there.* So says the Vulgate translator, who could have better translated it as *roofs*, into which the Innkeeper-woman had withdrawn the men to avoid danger, so that she might conceal them with the bundles of flax which she had stored on the roof. People were accustomed to hide there, as if in a safer part of the house, when they feared danger either from an enemy or the attack of another. The stalks of flax were set out there so they might be dried by the sun for future carding <note>original: "confusionem" - here referring to the processing of fibers</note>. The "armfuls of flax," as they are called by Josephus, and the bundles were the hiding places of the scouts. To explain this, one might look to what Plutarch mentions in *Dion* regarding those fleeing to hide on roofs, and that from the *Saracen History* of Elmacinus, written in Arabic, concerning Hakem, the King of Egypt. In book 3, chapter 6, among other impious *decrees* <note>original: "θεσπίσματα"</note> of his, that author recounts: *He seized certain women and killed them, and issued an edict through a herald that no woman should leave her house, nor ascend onto her roof; perhaps, lest they should hide there to avoid death. Just as we read in the same Elmacinus, book 2, chapter 20, that a certain Caliph named Cahir Billah, out of fear of the soldiers, fled onto the roof and hid there.* On the roof 
<margin>Plautus 3. 2. 14. in Truculentus c. 9. 25.</margin>
they frequently passed to and fro, for the sake of watching or conversing. That Samuel spoke with Saul *upon the roof* <note>original: "עלה אל הגג" (Hebrew) / "ὑπὸ τὸ δώματι" (Greek)</note> is proved by the first book of Samuel; where Vatablus says in his Notes: *He ascended upon the roof, namely, so that he might speak with him more familiarly. Moreover, they were accustomed to walk there especially after dinner, for the roofs were flat, not like ours. Nor was this common only among the Jews, but also among the Gentiles, to ascend roofs for the sake of watching.* Plutarch narrates a battle watched from a roof.

The Oenidae. <margin>book VII.</margin>

<margin>book 16.</margin>

<margin>Matthew 10:27.</margin>

<margin>On Matthew p. 503.</margin>
*He speaks according to the custom of the province of Palestine, in which there were walking-roofs above, on which they very often spoke to the people. Whence also the Lord commands the proclamations of the truth to be set forth on high, and to announce constantly whatever the holy preachers have heard from the Lord, not so much with the ear of the body as with the ear of the mind within.* Anselm on Matthew: 
<margin>f. 113. b.</margin>

<margin>Vol. 5. p. 365.</margin>
*Truly, what he says: "it shall be preached on the roofs," he speaks according to the custom of the Province of Palestine, where they are accustomed to reside on the roofs; for they do not make roofs raised with peaks in our manner, but make them level in a flat design. Whence the law prescribes that he who builds a new house should place a wall of the roof in a circle, lest innocent blood be shed there by someone slipping and falling headlong.* The same in *Questions on Kings* 13, folio 95b: In Palestine, just as in Egypt, they do not have peaks on the roofs, but rather flat roofs of houses are constructed, suitable for sitting or walking. Whence the Lord says in the Gospel: *What you hear in the ear shall be preached on the roofs.* For such a place is most suitable from which the word is preached, either to those standing near or to listeners placed below. Compare Salonius on the *Proverbs of Solomon*, page 1011. Papias the Vocabulist, 
<margin>Venice, year 1496.</margin>

He explains *upon the pinnacle* of the temple to mean that the Devil placed the Lord upon one of the four corners, which the high roof of the temple would have had, similar to wings; for every roof had four extremities which are called <term>Cenaphoth</term> <note>Hebrew: כנפות, meaning "wings" or "corners"</note> on the four sides of the roof. Villalpandus discusses this at length regarding those words of Ezekiel: *He has become the head of the corner*.

Constantin l'Empereur has shown that the roof of Solomon's temple, which those authors mentioned, did not have a completely flat surface (such as is known to have existed on the roofs of houses), but was somewhat vaulted and slightly sloping;

For I would prefer to explain it this way rather than simply "without a roof," as others do. Paschasius Ratbertus discusses the roof of Solomon's temple in Matthew, chapter 4, column 208: *In Palestine, the architectural custom—which is proven to have existed in Solomon's temple—is that it is kept flat across the whole top, and in a circuit (according to what the Law commanded) there are railings for a walkway, lest someone incautiously fall. Among these, surely, the seats of the Teachers were erected above the wing of the temple, so that from there, placed as if in a more eminent spot, the Teacher might speak to the people*. The same most wise King [Solomon] took care to build a <term>Xystus</term> <note>A covered portico or gallery</note>—if I may call it that—a gallery fortified with margins or borders, which led from the royal palace into the temple (1 Kings 10:13, 2 Chronicles 9:11). These two passages should be compared, since the same walkway is described by the words <note>Hebrew: מסלה and מסעד, meaning "highway" and "support/railing"</note>, which designate both the supports that were on each side of that raised path made of joined beams through which one ascended into the temple, and the lattices and railings which were above on each side of that underlying path, lest anyone fall.
