soft breeze when sick; for in those hot places, because the mild West wind blows sweetly at night, they set up beds under the open sky to catch the breeze. The Arab Tograus, a most learned poet, is my witness. Some sowed barley and other fruits on the roofs of houses. Botero testifies to this regarding northern peoples (*Treatise on the Origin of the Universe and Cities, f. 348*), whom he says preserved the roofs of their houses with very rich soil. He took this, however, from Olaus Magnus, who records it in Book 12, chapter 3. These roofs grew green by human industry; afterwards, grass also grew up spontaneously. We know that from this come metaphors and proverbial expressions in the Holy Scriptures. Isaiah chapter 37, v. 27, regarding the devastation of cities: *Their inhabitants shall be as the grass of the rooftops*, <note>Greek: ὡς χόρτος ξηρὸς ἐπὶ δωμάτων, "as dry grass upon the roofs"</note>. 
<margin>
Psalm 129:6.
</margin>
Thus the Psalmist is accustomed to compare *all who hate Zion* (or the enemies of the Church) to grass growing on such flat roofs, which withers quickly because of the dryness of the place and the vehement heat of the sun, in order to diminish the power of the enemies and signify that they are to be removed from the midst before they accomplish anything. Benedictus Arias Montanus, who converted the Psalms from the Hebrew truth into Latin verse, expresses it thus (p. 287):

> *May all whom hatred of Zion draws*
> *Be as grass upon the roofs, which withers*
> *Before it can even think of producing grain.*

Not without elegance, the Evangelist calls those who are <note>Greek: σεληνιαζομένους, "moon-struck" or "lunatics"</note> by the Syrian name <note>Hebrew/Aramaic: ברנשׂא, "son of the roof"</note>, alluding to their nature; for by this he signifies the disease itself or the lunatic spirit, so called as if it were a lover of roofs or addicted to roofs. This is not because it drives men out of the house into deserts remote from human conversation due to excessive melancholy (as Nicholas Fuller 
<margin>
Misc. 17.
</margin>
posits), but because it drives them out of the rooms of the houses onto the roofs. Louis de Dieu maintains that this is characteristic of lunatics (*Commentary on Matthew, ch. 4, v. 24*), where he explains how it happens and what the symptoms are; Dr. Jacob Horst explained this in a specific book on the causes and effects of Sleepwalkers—see him at that passage of Matthew, p. 22. I shall conclude with a proverb by which they indicated things that were absurd, unseemly, or preposterous, and it serves to show us that the word <note>Greek: δῶμα</note> is used for a flat roof even by secular authors:

->A goat under the builders, but he plays upon the rooftops in the temple.<-

# From Deuteronomy XXV. v. 4.

<margin>threshing</margin>
The ancient method, which is even observed today, was:
1. The threshing of oxen with a sledge; when the crops were crushed by the work of oxen drawing a dray, or a threshing-sledge, or a wagon. Specifically, the oxen were harnessed to instruments uniquely constructed for this purpose, which, when drawn over the ears of grain, left the kernels shaken out. 2. That instrument suited for threshing is named by the Hebrews <term>חָרוּץ</term> (*charutz*) and <term>חָרִיץ</term> (*charitz*), because it shakes out and cuts the grain from the ear and crushes it from the stalk. For its root <term>חָרַץ</term> (*charatz*) signifies to cut out or to cut up. It was a board roughened with iron and toothed, consisting of small rollers. It is called a <term>Tribulum</term> <note>A heavy wooden threshing board with flint or iron teeth on the underside.</note> by the Latins, which Varro describes in a way that entirely corresponds to the Hebrew word. He says <margin>1. On Agriculture 52.</margin> it is made *"from a board roughened with stones or iron, which, with a driver sitting on it or a heavy weight placed upon it, is drawn by yoked beasts to shake the grain from the ear; or it is made from toothed planks with rollers, which they call a Punic little-wagon."* He calls the threshing wagon by the diminutive form <term>ploſtellum</term> <note>A small wagon or cart.</note>, which Horace uses in *Satires 2.3. v. 157*. *Ploſtrum* is the same as *plauſtrum* <note>Latin for wagon</note>, just as *cautex* becomes *codex*, *clauſtrum* becomes *cloſtrum*, and *cautes* becomes *cotes*. The Phoenicians and Carthaginians were neighbors to the Jews, originating from Canaan; so it is likely that they also used a similar little-wagon. Indeed, since the Phoenicians and Jews often walk with equal pace in secular matters, he seems here to have hinted at the Jewish mode of threshing as well. This can also be easily gathered from certain passages of Scripture, such as <margin>Isaiah XLI, 15.</margin> where God declares the promised grace of His help through an excellent figure of speech regarding this toothed instrument, saying: *"Behold, I have made you into a dray, into a new threshing-sledge* <term>לְמוֹרַג חָרוּץ חָדָשׁ</term> <note>original: "le-morag charutz chadash"</note>, *having mouths or beaks. You shall thresh the mountains and crush them, and make the hills like chaff. You shall winnow them, and the wind shall carry them away."* By this metaphor, He promises future liberation to His people from their enemies, whom they shall crush and grind just as one grinds bundles of crops with a new and well-toothed threshing instrument. There is no lack of interpreters who here explain the name <term>חָרִיץ</term> (*charitz*) from the adjective form as *cut off* or *excised*, as if it were a passive participle. Thus our version <note>The German translation</note> says: *"I have made you into a sharp new threshing-wagon."* The teeth of the sledge or the iron nails were fastened as <term>Zacken</term> <note>German for "prongs" or "spikes"</note>, which are here called <term>פִּיפִיּוֹת</term> (*piphiyot*), "mouths," from the noun <term>פֶּה</term> (*peh*), "mouth," in that manner of speaking <margin>1 Samuel 13:21.</margin> by which the notches of files are called <term>פִּים</term> (*pim*), "mouths." This interpretation seems much more suitable, since no conjunction intervenes to allow it to be translated as: *"into a dray cutting, from* <term>חָרַץ</term> (*charatz*), *to cut or divide."* Moreover, the threshing-sledge was, to describe it in the words of Buxtorf <margin>Lexicon p. 265</margin> following Rabbi Solomon Jarchi, full of cuts or incisions, like the instrument of blacksmiths called a <term>File</term>, and it was dragged over the threshing-floor until the ears were cut off and the straw became chaff. Among the Talmudists, it is read that it was a wooden instrument made of beams, full of nails or teeth (blunt at the bottom), upon which an iron mass was placed for the sake of weight. It was drawn by oxen over the threshing-floor, and thus the grain was shaken out and the straw reduced to chaff. *Tractate Menachot ch. 3 fol. 22 and Tractate Zevachim ch. 14 fol. 116; compare Reuchlin p. 178.* Varro continues: *"On that little-wagon someone sits to drive the beasts that pull it, as they do in Hither Spain and other places."* Even now, this sitting upon the sledge is in use in certain places in the East;

<column-break/>

<margin>threshing</margin>
just as a certain citizen of Dresden in our own century experienced this transport during his tribulation, who, in the description of his Turkish captivity, places that kind of threshing vehicle before our eyes. The history is available described in German. It follows now that we treat the second mode of threshing, of which we just made some mention from the Talmudists: the threshing of oxen without a sledge, which was accomplished by the feet and hooves of the oxen alone. Regarding this, Varro says in the same place: *"Among others, it is rubbed out by a herd of beasts driven in and agitated there with poles, so that the grains are rubbed out of the ear by the hooves."* Columella <margin>Book 2, ch. 20</margin> embraced both modes of threshing, using the hooves of horses (whom he prefers to oxen) or oxen, if someone has many teams; but if few, by adding a threshing-sledge. He says, *"If it is suitable for the grain to be threshed on the floor, there is no doubt that the matter is finished better by horses than by oxen; and if there are few teams, you can add a threshing-sledge and a dray, both of which things crush the stalks very easily."* The *Area* <note>Threshing-floor</note> was a certain and defined space in the fields where the crops were spread for threshing. Eustathius on the *Iliad* says: *"The threshing-floor is the place in which the wheat is trodden."* Whence the grain of wheat shaken out in that place is quite elegantly called <term>בֶּן גֹּרֶן</term> (*ben goren*), "son of the threshing-floor," whose hairs are the awns <note>The beard-like bristles on grain</note>, Isaiah 21:10, where Tirinus says: <margin>p. 603</margin> *"You are my threshing, O Jews, and the sons of my floor, that is, grain shaken out by threshing on the floor; as if to say: I will not thresh the Babylonians, but utterly crush and destroy them. But you, O Jews, who are my people, I will thresh, I will winnow the chaff, I will separate the stalks and straw, and I will store the grains in the granary."* But others wish the words to be directed to the Babylonians, among whom is Jerome Oleaster. <margin>p. 411</margin> He calls the Prophet, in the person of the Lord, "Babel my threshing," because He was going to trample it just as a crop is trampled on the floor. And he is called "son of the floor," a man trampled and crushed like wheat on the floor. And Musculus says: <margin>p. 350</margin> The Prophet, under the person of **GOD**, calls Babylon his threshing and the son of his floor, after the likeness of threshing by which grain is accustomed to be threshed in the land of Judah by oxen driven over the floors. "Thus," he says, "I will trample and tread down Babylon by the Medes and Persians." The "son of the floor" is the grain that is rubbed and shaken out on the floor. Thus he calls the Babylonians. The former opinion is more probable, so that the Prophet turns his speech to the Jews, announcing to them the fate that would be theirs in the Babylonian captivity; and the pronoun "My" hints at this. Regarding the site and construction of the threshing-floor, Varro treats this in Book 1, ch. 51, which begins: *"The floor ought to be in a higher place in the field, where the wind can blow through it. This should be of a size proportionate to the harvest, preferably round and the middle slightly raised... paved, especially if it is clayey, lest it become full of cracks from the heat, and the grains get lost in its cracks, and receive water, and open doors for mice and ants."* Hesiod <margin>Works and Days v. 597</margin> relates the same regarding the place in which the floor is to be set, namely,

> In a well-aired place and on a well-rounded threshing-floor

Which Valla translates:

> Placed toward the winds and leveled with a huge cylinder.

And you will see the same words about a round threshing-floor in Homer <margin>Iliad 20, v. 495</margin> when he describes the threshing by oxen,

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES.

<margin>threshing</margin>
->As when one yokes broad-browed bulls<-
->To thresh white barley on a well-rounded floor<-
->And quickly it is thinned under the feet of the loud-bellowing bulls.<-
<note>original: Homer, Iliad 20.495-497. The author uses these Greek verses to illustrate the ancient method of treading grain.</note>

The "well-rounded" <note>Greek: *eutrochalos*</note> floor was rendered as a space leveled with a smooth wooden roller, which was rolled over it to round out the pavement; and that type of instrument was named from the effect of circular leveling as a **ma’agalah** <insert>מעגלה</insert>, from the verb **agal** <insert>עגל</insert>, *to round or rotate*, whence comes **agalah** <insert>עגלה</insert>, *a wagon*, from the roundness of the wheels; and **agil** <insert>עגיל</insert>, *an earring or round ornament*. Among the Latins it is called a *cylindrus* [cylinder], and Valla used this term excellently to investigate the "well-rounded floor," which, to become "well-rounded," was usually leveled with a cylinder. No doubt Valla was taught this by Virgil’s *Georgics*, where in book 1, verse 178, a description of the floor is given in reverse order <note>Greek: *kath' hysterologian*</note>:

> The floor must first be leveled with a huge cylinder,
> And turned by hand, and consolidated with clinging clay,
> Lest weeds come up, or it collapses, defeated by dust.

<margin>On Agriculture 6. 91.</margin>
Cato provides the method for making a floor \*. *Make a floor thus: Dig up the place where you are making it, afterwards sprinkle it well with olive-press dregs <note>Latin: *amurca*, a watery byproduct of olive oil production used as a natural pesticide and binder</note> and let it soak in. Afterwards break the clods well, then level it and beat it with rammers.* I add Columella, Book 2, Chapter 20, explaining the same thing in a similar way: *If the floor is made of earth, so that it is fit for threshing, let it first be scraped, then dug up, and after mixing straw with olive-press dregs, let it be smoothed.* In Judea, the threshing floor was called **Goren** <insert>גורן</insert>, and it appears in Genesis 50:10, Numbers 15:20, 18:27, and other places. Threshing floors were under the open sky, as has been said. This is shown by that famous floor of Gideon, where he asked for a sign of God’s gracious calling and liberation through a fleece *placed on the floor*. From this he would know—if the dew fell from heaven only on the fleece while the ground all around remained dry—that he would carry back victory over the enemies by his hand. And it was so; (**vayehi ken** <insert>ויהי כן</insert>) so that when the floor was dry, he found the fleece dewy. Again, when he prayed to God that only the fleece be dry and all the ground wet with dew, <margin>Judges 6:37</margin> *and God did so that night* \*, and so on to the end. This downpour of dew happened because the floor was out in the open, not in some barn whose roof rose high with a cover. That floor is elegantly called by the Chaldean [Aramaic] translator **Beit Idri** <insert>בית אדרי</insert> *house of the threshing floors*, not because it was a house, but because Orientals love to speak this way even where there are no traces of floors or ceilings; as with the Chaldean "house of drinking" \*, for a trough or vessel into which water is poured, <margin>Gen. 24:19</margin> "house of perdition" for a pit in Isaiah 14:15, <margin>Eccl. 12:4</margin> "house of burial" \*, and "house of fingers" for a glove. **Idri** is equivalent to the Hebrew *Goren*. Nor should we value less the floor of Araunah the Jebusite king, <margin>2 Sam. 24:18, 21, 24</margin> **Goren Aranyah** <insert>גורן ארניה</insert>, on which David, having built an altar, appeased God \*. It stood on the highest ridge of Mount Moriah, where later Solomon’s temple was founded, as is expressly handed down in 2 Chronicles 3:1, calling it with a slightly changed name the floor of **Ornan** <insert>ארנן</insert>. This was the noblest floor of all that ever existed; nor is any place given that reaches its degree of blessedness. How wonderful that the floor of a Gentile king was judged worthy for God to choose as the seat of His Church. This can be drawn as a type [symbol] of the calling of the Gentiles that would one day solemnly occur. But lest anything happen outside the space of the floor in which we are running, let us—

<column-break/>

—bring forth some handfuls from the "floor" of Scripture, which are suitable for our threshing here. <margin>threshing</margin> Clear mention of a threshing wagon is made by Isaiah in chapter 41, and above in 28:27, to indicate the heavier afflictions and chastisements with which God is accustomed to punish. The Hebrew itself must be set down here:
->**לא בחרוץ יודש קצח ואופן עגלה על-כמן יוסב**<-
Our version: *One does not thresh vetches with harrows / nor does one let the wagon-wheel go over the cumin.* The Belgian: *One does not thresh vetches with the threshing-wagon.* The Old [Vulgate]: *Gith <note>black cumin</note> shall not be threshed with saws, nor shall the wagon wheel circle over the cumin.* What is noted by **charutz** <insert>חרוץ</insert> we have said before; it is more convenient, as Solomon Jarchi notes, that it denotes a threshing sledge full of notches or incisions (which he explains by the example of a *file*), and it is dragged along in threshing until the ears are cut off and the straw turns to chaff. This is a harsh method of threshing stalks and ears, which usually do not yield unless treated roughly. To this the Seventy Men [Septuagint] seem to have looked, who rendered it: *not with hardness*. However, while the more stubborn kind of fruit is crushed, the thresher will not thresh with perpetual threshing (**lo adosh yedushenu** <insert>לא אדוש ידושנו</insert>), nor will he crush indefinitely with the wheel of his wagon (**galgal agalato** <insert>גלgal עגלתו</insert>) or with teeth or points (**pi charutz** <insert>פי חריץ</insert>) (as Kimchi explained that sledge in verse 28). But in those things which are cultivated, if they are softer, and as if frolicking with a feminine softness in both stalk and leaves, flowers and fruits—such as fennel (**ketzach** <insert>קצח</insert>) or cumin (**kammon** <insert>כמן</insert>)—one proceeds with a lighter arm, namely with some light staff. This excellent simile taken from threshing commends God’s moderation and, so to speak, His temperament in inflicting types of afflictions and calamities. For just as a good farmer knows the method of threshing, lest if he exceeds it he should harm the grain and be exhausted by threshing in vain; he also knows the distinction in threshing, by which he threshes smaller seeds one way and larger ones another; <margin>Tirinus \*. on this passage p. 610.</margin> So God distributes to each his exercises according to measure, nor does He impose heavier afflictions than we are able to bear. Tirinus says:
> In ruling the Synagogue [the Church], God behaves like a wise and provident farmer, who at the proper time works and subdues his field now with a plow, now with a hoe, now in another way; now he sows various seeds, now he cleans the crops, now he reaps, now he gathers the fruits, now he threshes; and legumes indeed, like gith and cumin, with a light rod or staff; but grains, which are more difficult to shake out, with the hooves of oxen or with wagons, after the manner of Syria, toothed and iron-shod.

As for the last words, they are, as I hear, for the interpretation of the Vulgate Translator, for which there is usually much anxious labor in Rome—which those who do not wish to become arrogant disapprove of. It is right to venerate, not adore, those who are below the majesty of their Monarch. He who wishes to undergo the service of a faithful servant, serves. That version will not satisfy the reader here, which has (and indeed from that very large Louvain edition): *Neither shall the "marshy wheel" <note>Latin: *rota palustri*. The author is mocking a typo in the Louvain Bible where "plaustri" (wagon) became "palustri" (marshy).</note> vex him, nor shall he crush it with his hooves.* Marshy wheels will perhaps be rotated in that most vexing war of the mice and frogs which Homer described for us. For the rest, I would wish satisfaction for the most learned translator Bonfrère, who on that prophetic passage strangely...

# From Deuteronomy 25:4

<margin>Threshing in Deuteronomy p. 1011.</margin>
...he does not write*: The Hebrew word *parash* <note>original: פרש</note> does not signify the hooves of oxen, as Jerome also testifies, but everywhere means a horse or a horseman; however, this passage cannot be understood as referring to horses or horsemen. For, as Jerome says regarding that passage, the Scripture could not speak of something that the province of Judea did not have. Indeed, it is clear enough from the added suffix that it signifies neither horses nor the hooves of oxen, but something pertaining to a wagon. Thus Jerome, translating with the Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> "with its hooves," understood something on the wagon that either reflected the shape of hooves or crushed the ears of grain in the manner of hooves. But I do not wish to be the herald of a future interpretation, lest in the valley of Mamre I seem a *Mamzer* <note>A Hebrew term for one of illegitimate birth; a wordplay on the location Mamre</note>. That which is in Hebrew *qetsach* <note>קצח</note> the Vulgate translates as *Gith* <note>Black cumin</note>, which Pliny (XX, 17) affirms is a type of legume called *Melanthion* because of its black seed; hence the Septuagint translated it "small black-flower," and Pagninus and Arias translated it as *Nigella*. In German: **Roman Coriander**. But concerning that *Gith*, we have nothing further to say than that nothing certain can be held regarding it, neither from the Sacred Codex, where it appears only in this place, nor from the Rabbis. One of them, Rabbi Kimchi, notes it is a species of legume useful for human food; another, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note>, says it is a seed similar to Cumin, except that it is black. What this or that man writes about *Gith* or *ith frith*, we shall leave aside, since not much utility results for us here, given that no or at least very little knowledge of exotic plants or shrubs can be made known to us. Rather, let us see what Isaiah writes further on this matter. The Prophet was not ashamed to insert a commonly known thing once and again into his prophecies, and to bring forth precepts for the correction and information of his people from a familiar and well-worn matter. Just as he compares the judgments of God and His works in the aforementioned chapter to the studies and labors of those plowing, sowing, and threshing, which we have explained; so also he indicated the severity of divine judgment against Moab and all enemies of the Church by a twin likeness. He says there in *verse 10*:

<margin>chapter 25.</margin>
*And Moab shall be threshed in Madmenah* <note>original: ודש מואב במדמנה</note>. The Translator: *Moab shall be threshed, just as chaff is threshed in a wagon*. The Septuagint: *The land of Moab shall be trodden down, in the way they tread a threshing floor with wagons*. Neither a wagon nor another instrument of threshing is expressed here from which a certain species of threshing can be distinguished with absolute certainty; for in the word *Madmenah*, neither a wagon nor a floor with wagons is admitted by the Interpreters, who explain it as a dunghill and manure; because *domen* <note>דמן</note> means manure*. The Chaldean <note>Targum</note>: The Moabites shall be threshed in their place, as *be-mabna* <note>במבנא</note> is threshed, that is, chaff in the mud. *Tibna* and *tebna* mean straw and chaff. Luther: **As straw is threshed, and like dung.** In which form it is said the King of Syria placed the Israelites in victory *as dust for threshing* <note>original: כעפר לדוש</note>.

<margin>Isaiah 9:22. Psalm 83:1.</margin>
<margin>2 Kings 13:7.</margin>
* **Like thresher-dust.** Septuagint: *as dust to be trodden down*. Vulgate: *as dust in the threshing of the floor*. We have frequently seen the verb *dush* <note>דוש</note> used for the trampling of grain, by the hooves of oxen or in a small wagon; and from there it remained in use for the Chaldeans, with the letter *daleth* changed into *zayin* <note>linguistic note on Aramaic/Hebrew shifts</note> in the term *charish*, meaning crushed or mixed wheat. But lest the examination of languages divert us from our purpose, the sense seems to be: Just as the threshing sledge crushes the straw or stubble so that it finally becomes a dunghill; so also Jehovah

<column-break/>

will strike the Moabites, and will subdue and grind down their pride. The Moabites are placed synecdochically <note>A part representing the whole</note> for all enemies of the Church, because they were the implacable enemies of the Jewish people, more hateful than other neighboring enemies. Tirinus*. In the eucharistic hymn, the saints give thanks to God that, having depressed their impious and proud enemies, they themselves have reached the port of salvation. But the Moabites, that is, the reprobate, are foretold to be threshed and trodden by the wagon of God's wrath. Jeremiah used the same likeness of threshing to indicate the destruction of Babylon*.

<margin>threshing</margin>
<margin>in this place p. 606.</margin>
<margin>chapter 50 v. 26.</margin>
Come against her from the utmost border, **open** <note>original: וערמו ערמות</note> **her granaries, tread her down like heaps** which are piled up on the floor to be trampled. Luther: **Open her corn-houses / throw them into a heap.** The old Interpreter aptly renders *salal k'mo-aremim* <note>סלל כמי-ערמים</note> as *to reduce into heaps*; *salal* notes to order and arrange, to build into a mound or heap, whence *solelah*, a piled-up mass, a *mound*. However, the Latin translator understood that word *aremim* <note>heaps</note> not as a heap of grain but of stones, translating it as *skorpizon*: *Take the stones from the way, and reduce them into heaps.*

<margin>and chapter 51 v. 33.</margin>
And in chapter 51 v. 33 he says: The daughter of Babylon is *like a threshing floor at the time of its treading* <note>original: כגרן עת הדיכה</note>. The Chaldean: *the time of her threshing or treading*, for in both places the verb *darok* or *dur*, to tread or trample, corresponds to the Greek *patein* <note>πατεῖν</note>, as when Eustathius above defined the threshing floor as the place in which grain is *trodden*, specifically by the feet of oxen. This name is used in both the Targum of Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum on the passage in Deuteronomy; for instead of *in its threshing*, they have *in the time of its treading*, namely of the ox, who, when he was crushing the ears and stalks, lest he fail from hunger in his labor, would eat from the handfuls as a reward for his labor. God established this law for oxen, so that they would not be bound by a halter or any other impediment during threshing, but that in that circling to crush the crops on the floor, their mouths would be free, not bridled or bound, and they might freely eat from that which they worked upon. From this, the Apostle Paul, having taken up an elegant likeness, preaches concerning the reward not to be denied to those who labor in the floor of the

<margin>1 Corinthians 9:9.</margin>
Lord*, relying on the praised passage of Deuteronomy. Sometimes they hung a basket from the neck of the beast so that it might eat from it, which we learn from *Terumot chapter 9*. This fodder-basket is called *kefifah* from its curvature, for *kafaf* means to bend. Those who were more attentive to the matter used to bind some instrument or a muzzle to the mouth of the threshing ox, by which the haltered beast would be entirely prohibited from snatching any ears during the threshing. This is established from Cato* and the proverb *An ox upon the heap*, which Suidas

<margin>on rural affairs s. 4 p. 143.</margin>
<margin>Suidas</margin>
understands as referring to oxen who tread the fruits on the floor but are hindered by a muzzle so that they cannot taste anything therefrom. They also covered the eyes of the ox with a skin, as explained in the *Aruch* at the word *malkut*; and *malkut* was also a small bag hung at the hindquarters to catch excrement, lest the grain prepared for threshing on the floor be defiled by it. They also smeared the nostrils with dung, so that the oxen, moved by the foul odor, would abstain from the ears, as Aelian testifies*.

<margin>4. History of Animals 25.</margin>
> They devise this trick, he says, and a very suitable one it is. For this animal, loathing the aforementioned smear, would not taste anything, even if it were pressed by the heaviest hunger.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
## Page 284

<margin>threshing</margin> of beasts of burden, called *machsom* <note>Hebrew: מחסום, meaning a muzzle</note> and by dropping the initial *ch*, it becomes *chasom*, from which by some transposition of letters comes the word *camus* <note>Latin: a muzzle or snare</note>; just as by a certain similarity the words *tachsom* <note>Hebrew: תחסום</note>, *taumen*, to bridle and to halter, agree. The Jerusalem Targum <note>An Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible</note> expresses it with this very word, for in place of our Hebrew *tachsom* it placed *tumonon*, where *Jonathan* <note>The Targum of Jonathan</note> also has *tumonon*; and this same term is used by the Talmudists regarding this very matter in <margin>Kelim ch. 10. Terumah ch. 9.</margin> the tractates *Kelim* and *Terumah*. It is customary for the mouths of animals to be closed and stopped up, especially to restrain their ferocity. The Hebrews indicate this with the word *chasam* <note>Hebrew: חסם</note>, which means *to close, to cover with a halter, to stop up*; as in the discussion of the baskets hung from the mouths of donkeys, which we call a **Muzzle** <note>original German: **Maul-Korb**</note>: *until you muzzle them* <note>Hebrew: עדי שתחסומו</note>. Thus, in Italy and elsewhere, it is customary to block the mouths of pack horses and mules so they do not leave the path for the sake of fodder, but proceed by following one another. By Eu- <margin>on Iliad 10.</margin> stathius it is called: *Pausikape*. For he says: *The Pausikape, according to Aelius Dionysius, is a certain machine like a wheel, by which the necks of beasts of burden are bound so that they cannot bring their forelegs to their mouths; and it seems from this account to be called pausikape as "stopping the feeding" or from "eating," which is to consume.* The Greeks call it *phimoun* <note>Greek: φιμοῦν, to muzzle</note>, whence the oxen threshing are said to be prevented from eating by a muzzle, according to Suidas. Having thus examined both methods of threshing, we can now consider a bit more attentively a certain kind of punishment, in which we read of men being crushed by iron threshing-sledges, or even by the hooves of oxen. Without a doubt, David afflicted the Ammonites with this very heavy and bitter punishment <margin>2 Sam. 12: last verse</margin> after the capture of Rabbah. The severity was truly great, not to say cruelty, to drive iron <margin>1 Chron. 20:3</margin> drags over the backs of the conquered so that they were cut apart and crushed. It was (the text says) *with the saw, and with iron threshing-drags, and with iron axes* <note>Hebrew: במגרה ובחריצי הברזל ובמגזרות הברזל</note>, as Arias translates it. The Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> says: *He led out the people with the saw and with iron threshing-sledges and iron axes.* The Vulgate: *Bringing out the people, he sawed them, and drove iron-bound wagons over them, and divided them with knives.* Luther: *He put them under iron saws and tines, and iron wedges.* And thus he did to all the cities of the sons of Ammon out of the heat of vengeance, because Hanun, King of the Ammonites, had insultingly received the ambassadors sent in friendship, <margin>2 Sam. 10:4</margin> and had sent them away mutilated in their garments and beards, not without mockery, against the law of nations which forbids harming ambassadors; <margin>Thebaid 2, v. 466</margin> for, as Statius says:
> A name sacred to peoples through the ages
> Is the Ambassador; to attack him with snares and silent steel [is a crime].
This shame and reproach of most foul mutilation, which erupted into a grave war, David wished to avenge with a more atrocious mutilation; so that those who had ignominiously cut the garments of the ambassadors through the middle even to their buttocks, should pay with greater ignominy and be cut through the middle by irons; those who had shaved their heads with razors, should themselves be truncated in the head or other members by knives and swords. With this same inhumanity the Damascenes raged against the inhabitants of Gilead, whom they had <margin>Amos 1:3</margin> threshed with iron wagons; wherefore, because of that great crime committed against the Jews, Jehovah says: *For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four, I will not spare it, because they have threshed Gilead with iron wagons.* <note>Hebrew: על-דושם בחרוצות הברזל</note> *Because of their threshing them with threshing-sledges of iron.* Regarding the "irons," the Septuagint understood and restricted this to pregnant women, whom they ripped open with iron tools; something which we read

<column-break/>

happened during the reign of Hazael, King of the Syrians, according to the prophecy <margin>threshing 2 Kings 8:12</margin> made by Elisha in Damascus in the presence of Hazael. Those interpreters aimed at that event, though nothing similar is found in the Hebrew text, for the word *baka* <note>Hebrew: בקע</note>, *to split or divide*, does not convince me that I must believe in a specific kind of cutting by a saw or threshing-sledge. Luther: *Because they threshed Gilead with iron tines.* Jerome on this passage; Tirinus: *The Syrians, in a most cruel spectacle, threshed the Israelites living in Gilead, prostrate on the ground, with iron wagons, that is, they crushed them with wheels that were iron and toothed underneath, just as ears of grain are accustomed to be crushed on the floor so that the grains are shaken out.* Some are pleased to think that this kind of punishment was inflicted on the citizens of the cities of Succoth by Gideon, *Judges 8:7, 16*, who explain that word *dashti* <note>Hebrew: דשתי, "I will thresh"</note> regarding the manner of crushing, in which he placed briars and thorns over their naked bodies prostrate on the ground, and drove threshing wagons over them, which would both drive in those thorns and, in a way, grind the flesh with the thorns fixed in. So Bonfrerius feels. *As the vintage*, in which the vines are stripped of their clusters, is used for hostile devastation and destruction, *Lamentations 1:12, 22; 11:20*. So also is *threshing*, in which the husks, chaff, and stalks are broken into small pieces. From this are taken those allegorical expressions. <margin>Micah 4:13</margin> *Arise and thresh* <note>Hebrew: דושי</note>, *daughter of Zion; for I will make your horn iron, and your hooves* <note>Hebrew: פרסותיך</note> *I will make brass, and you shall beat in pieces* <note>Hebrew: והדקות</note> *many peoples.* Tirinus: *Arise, and lift up your spirits, O daughter of Zion, and you also thresh, no longer with wooden flails or the horny hooves of oxen, but with iron and bronze wheels, and with saw-toothed wagons, pursue the prostrate enemies, lay them low, and cut down those who flee.* In the same form it is said that Ephraim *is like a heifer that has been trained from her youth and loved to thresh, Hosea 10:11*, and to subject others to herself, while refusing obedience to others. But this happiness and luxury of that petulant and well-fed heifer, and that empire, the more it shone, the more quickly it ceased; for she who was accustomed to thresh others, and to press her feet upon their necks, as an ox or a young cow is accustomed to do to a heap of grain, she herself experienced that threshing. I (He says) will pass over her fair neck. — *I passed over the goodness of her neck.* <note>Hebrew: עברתי על טובה צוארה</note> The Septuagint: *And I will come upon the beauty of her neck.* Luther: *I will ride upon his beautiful neck.* The *passing over of God* <note>Hebrew: עבר</note> is to declare His power and energy, according to the nature of the thing joined to it, as *the Lord passed through Egypt*, namely by killing the firstborn, and, *passing before the face of Moses*, namely by illuminating him with the knowledge of Himself. Thus *to pass over the neck* is to impose a yoke. Treading symbolically denotes dominion and rule over subjects and the conquered; for victors were accustomed, as a sign of dominion and victory, to go and place their feet upon necks, <margin>Joshua 10:24</margin> *to make enemies a footstool for their feet*, <margin>Psalm 110:1</margin> *to tread upon their high places* <note>Hebrew: במותימו</note>, *Deuteronomy 33:29*, where Jerome, the Septuagint, and the Chaldean understood "neck" and "throat." Hence it is said in *Luke 10:19* by Christ to the disciples: *I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy.* To which is similar what is read: *upon the asp and the basilisk you shall tread, you shall trample* <margin>Psalm 91:12</margin> *the young lion and the dragon.* Let us approach

# From Deuteronomy XXV. v. 4.

<margin>threshing</margin>
<margin>v. 12.</margin>
...now to the secular authors. It has been handed down to us by *Athenaeus* <note>Greek rhetorician and grammarian, c. 200 AD</note> that there was a horrific kind of punishment in which the maddened populace, having appointed oxen, crushed certain exiles in the manner of harvested grain: <term>Συναγαγὼν ( ὁ δῆμος ) τὰ τέκνα τῶν φυγόντων εἰς ἀλωνίας ( in areas ) ρᾶς συναγαγόντες συνἠλόησαν</term> <note>original Greek: "The people, having gathered the children of the fugitives into the threshing floors, gathered them together and threshed them."</note>. One might add the not dissimilar cruelty of Nero, who, on the *Appian Way*, suddenly crushed a boy with swift draft animals in a village, not unknowingly, as noted in *Suetonius, chapter 4*. But enough now of these two modes of threshing <note>referring to oxen and wagons discussed previously</note>. There remains yet a third, which is more obvious and more frequent in our own regions; for we (excluding the Italians and Spaniards) have nothing to do with that ancient threshing by means of a small wagon or the hooves of oxen; we shake out the grain with revolving clubs or poles fastened on one side with a movable wooden hinge. We call them <term>Flegell</term> <note>original German: "Flail"</note>, which peasants sometimes use to strike the backs of their enemies, as the Peasant Revolts attest. *Columella* mentions this mode of threshing:
<margin>Book 2 on Rural Affairs, ch. 21, p. 302.</margin>
*If the crop is harvested with sickles along with part of the stalk, it is immediately gathered into a heap or a shed and then, dried by the opportune sun, it is trodden out. But if only the ears are cut off, they can be carried into the granary and then, during the winter, either shaken out with sticks or trodden by cattle.* When the Israelites were pressed by a very sharp war by the Midianites for seven whole years, their threshing floors were destroyed and all their beasts taken away; and when Israel had sown,
<margin>Judges 6 v. 3.</margin>
Midian, Amalek, and the other children of the East would come up and devastate the fruit of the land as far as Gaza, leaving no sustenance in Israel, <term>שה ושור וחמור</term> <note>original Hebrew: "neither sheep, nor ox, nor donkey"</note>. In this
<margin>v. 2.</margin>
oppression, to provide for their lives, they chose inaccessible places and made for themselves dens and caves in the mountains, nor could the customary method of threshing in the open floors be held by them anymore because of that public plundering. The proof is that Gideon was shaking out and cleaning the
<margin>grain. v. 11</margin>
grain <term>גת</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Gath"</note> in a winepress. <term>גת</term> means a winepress, a place where grapes are squeezed, which perhaps was in the seclusion of some vine-bearing mountain, so that Gideon might hide there more conveniently; and thus it truly was a <term>גת</term> winepress, which comes from <term>גדד</term> <note>original Hebrew root: "gadad"</note>, meaning to act solitarily or to be in solitude. For those do not convince me who want there to have been a press or a wine-crusher in the large granary of his father where crops were usually stored. In that unhappy war, what was otherwise their custom was not permitted. In time of peace they threshed with oxen; now, with the beasts snatched away, they use sticks for threshing. *Isidore* noted this well in *Book of Judges, Question 2*: "Gideon, under an oak tree, beats the harvest with a rod and shakes the grain from the chaff." *Cornelius à Lapide* <note>Jesuit exegete, 1567–1637</note>,
<margin>p. 123 on Judges.</margin>
whose words these are: *He would shake it out, namely with a flail, just as the Belgians and others shake the grains from the ears by flailing. Otherwise in Palestine (as is still done in Italy) oxen threshed the crops by treading them with their hooves, and thus shaking out the grains, whence that saying: "Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treads out the corn." But Gideon threshed here with a flail because he did it secretly and hastily, lest he be caught by the approaching Midianites; and for the same reason he did it in a winepress, where grapes are usually squeezed and wine drawn from them. For this winepress was in a level place, and perhaps in a granary, as Vatablus <note>French Hebraist</note> wishes, where crops are usually flailed and threshed.* Otherwise, some kinds of
<column-break/>
herbs which consisted of a thin husk were subject to the threshing stick. Isaiah hints at this when he says: *A wheel is not sent over the cumin, but the cumin is shaken out with a rod.*
<margin>Threshing ch. 28:27.</margin>
The Septuagint <note>Greek Old Testament</note> says: <term>Οὐ γὰρ ἀμάξης τροχὸς ἐπὶ τὸ κύμινον, ἀλλὰ ῥάβδῳ ἐκτινάσσεται κύμινον.</term> <note>original Greek: "For the wheel of a wagon is not for the cumin, but the cumin is shaken out with a rod."</note> The Hebrew text is: <term>כי במטה יחבט קצח וכמן בשבט</term> <note>original Hebrew: "For the black cumin is beaten with a staff, and the cumin with a rod."</note>. In German: *The vetch is beaten out with a staff, and the cumin with a stick.* Neither the toothed threshing-sled nor the wagon wheel are driven over the black cumin and cumin to shake out its seeds; for that large and heavy instrument, which is called <term>חרוץ</term> <note>original Hebrew: "charutz," a sharp threshing instrument</note>, is unsuitable for the threshing of small seeds because of its violence. According to the diversity of grains and legumes, a diverse threshing is performed. From this diversity of threshing, GOD shows the diversity which He is accustomed to use in discipline and chastisement. Pharaoh and those like him, men of deplorable wickedness, are threshed with iron sleds. He threshes these with a rod; those with a stick. God does, as *Salvianus* says,
<margin>Salvianus, Book 6 on Providence.</margin>
what skilled physicians are accustomed to do, who provide different cures for different diseases; this one he burns and cuts to heal him; that one, as desperate, he leaves alone; this other one he treats with a gentle hand, whence *Prosper* says in his *Epigrams*:

> He consults for those to be saved even by His anger,
> Just as a Doctor heals wounds with wounds.

It remains for us to purify the floor and purge it of chaff, which is usually the final work in the collection of grain. The excrements of grain are the chaff, which are eliminated from the floors by a winnowing fan, like the impure members of the grains. For it was necessary, once the grains were well shaken out, to move and remove the empty chaos of the awns from the place, so that the fruit might be brought into the granaries as pure fruit. This is usually expressed by the words <term>מרה , זרה</term> <note>Hebrew roots for winnowing/scattering</note>. We read of that scattering in *Ruth 3:2*, that Boaz decided to winnow <term>את גרן השערים</term>, <term>τὸν ἅλωνα τῶν κριθῶν</term>, the threshing floor of the barleys. To winnow the floor of barley is to separate the grains of barley from the chaff, which had already been threshed and piled up in a confused mass on the floor. In speech, it is sometimes customary to attribute to the container what is owed to the contained. As if we say, *To winnow the barley-floor* <note>original German: "Die Gersten Tenne wörffeln"</note>, i.e., *the barley on the floor*. *To cut the oat-field*. Likewise: *to consume a spit of larks* <note>original German: "ein Spiß-Lerchen verzehren"</note>, *Veru alaudarum consumere*, that is, twelve larks fixed on a small stick or spit. Regarding this secretion of husks from the grains, one may read *Columella*:
<margin>Book 2 on Rural Affairs, ch. 21, p. 363.</margin>
*The ears themselves are better beaten with sticks and purged with winnowing fans. But when they are dry, the West Wind is considered excellent for this task, which blows gently and steadily through the summer months; however, it is the mark of a slow farmer to wait for it, because while it is expected, a cruel winter may overtake us. Therefore, the threshed grain on the floor must be piled up so that it can be separated by any breeze. But if for several days the air is silent on all sides, let them be purged with winnowing fans, lest after too much sluggishness of the winds, a vast storm make the labor of the whole year in vain.* And *Varro*:
<margin>Book on Rural Affairs, 52.</margin>
*Once threshed, those grains ought to be tossed from the ground with winnowing forks or fans when a gentle wind blows. Thus it happens that what is lightest in it, called the husk, is winnowed out away from the floor, and the grain, which is heavy, comes pure to the basket.* From this method of winnowing, expressions are likewise taken in the sacred texts. In the Prophet Jeremiah, GOD, about to indicate destruction to the Jews, says: *And I will winnow them with a winnowing fan*
<margin>ch. 15:7.</margin>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>threshing</margin> of beasts of burden, called *makhsom* [מחסום] and by dropping the initial *he*, *khasom* [חסום], from which by some transposition comes the word *camus* <note>a muzzle or noseband</note>; just as by a certain similarity they agree with *zamam* [זמם], **to bridle**, to curb and to halter, with which word the Jerusalem Targum <note>an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible</note> expresses it. For in place of our Hebrew *makhsom* it placed *khimumoni* where *Jonathan* has *khomamon*, and this very term is used by the Talmudists regarding this same matter in *Terumah, chapter 9*. The mouths of animals are usually shut and stopped up, especially to restrain their ferocity. The Hebrews indicate this with the word *khasam* [חסם], which is to close, to cover with a halter, to stop up; as in <margin>Kelim ch. 10</margin> regarding the baskets hung on the mouths of donkeys, which we call a **Muzzle** <note>original: *Maul-Korb*</note>: *until they are muzzled*. Thus, the mouths of pack horses and mules are usually blocked in Italy and elsewhere, lest they leave the path for the sake of fodder, but instead proceed by following one another. It is called by Eustathius <margin>on Iliad 10</margin> a *Pausikape* <note>Greek: Παυσικάπη</note>. For he says: *A Pausikape, according to Aelius Dionysius, is a certain device similar to a wheel, which is tied under the neck of beasts of burden so they cannot bring their forelegs to their mouth, and it seems this is called a Pausikape in speech as if "stopping the manger" or "stopping the gulping," which is eating.* The Greeks call it a *phimos* <note>Greek: φιμὸν, a muzzle</note>, from which oxen are said to be "threshing through a muzzle" to be prevented from eating, according to Suidas. Having thus examined both methods of threshing, we can now consider a little more attentively a certain kind of punishment, by which we read that men were crushed by iron threshing-sledges, or even by the hooves of oxen. Without a doubt, David afflicted the Ammonites with this very heavy and bitter punishment after the capture of <margin>2 Sam. 12, last verse</margin> Rabbah. It was certainly the greatest severity, not to say cruelty, to drive iron drags over the backs of the conquered, so that they were cut apart and crushed. <margin>1 Chron. 20:3</margin> It was (the text has) the **People** *with a saw, and with iron threshing-drags, and with iron axes*, as Arias translates. The Septuagint: *He led out the people and [cut them] with the saw and in the iron threshing-sledges, and with iron hatchets.* The Vulgate: *Bringing out the people, he sawed them, and drove over them iron-bound chariots, and divided them with knives.* Luther: *He laid them under iron saws and spikes, and iron wedges.* And thus he did to all the cities of the sons of Ammon out of the heat of vengeance, because Hanun, King of the Ammonites, had insultingly received his ambassadors sent in friendship, and had sent them away mutilated <margin>2 Sam. 10:4</margin> in their garments and beards, not without mockery, against the law of nations, which forbids harming ambassadors; for, as Statius says <margin>2 Thebaid v. 466</margin>,
> A name sacred to peoples through the ages,
> To attack an ambassador with treachery and silent steel.

This shame and reproach of most foul mutilation, which erupted into a grave war, David wished to avenge with a more atrocious mutilation; so that those who had ignominiously cut the garments of the ambassadors through the middle even to the buttocks, should pay with greater ignominy and be cut through the middle by irons; those who had shaved heads with razors, should themselves be truncated in the head or other members by knives and swords. With this inhumanity, it is said in <margin>Amos 1:3</margin> they raged with iron wagons; wherefore on account of that great crime committed against the Jews, Jehovah says: *For three transgressions of Damascus and for four I will not spare him, because they have threshed Gilead with iron wagons.* [על-דושם בחרצות הברזל את-הגלעד] *Because of their threshing in iron threshing-sledges.* The Septuagint understood this as being about iron tools, and they restrict it to pregnant women, whom they cut open with iron tools; that which sometimes

<column-break/>

<margin>threshing 2 Kings 8:12</margin> happened during the reign of Hazael, King of the Syrians, according to the prediction of Elisha made before Hazael at Damascus, and the interpreters aimed at that point, though nothing similar is found in the Hebrew, for the word *baka* [בקע], *to split, to divide*, does not convince me that I must believe in a specific kind of cutting, by saw or sledge. Luther: *Because they have threshed Gilead with iron spikes.* <margin>Jerome in this place p. 816; Tirinus</margin> Jerome and Tirinus: *The Syrians, in a most cruel spectacle, threshed the Israelites living in the region of Gilead, prostrate on the ground, with iron wagons, i.e., with wheels iron-clad and toothed underneath, they crushed them just as ears of grain are usually crushed on the floor, so that the grains are shaken out.* Some are pleased to think that this kind of punishment was inflicted on the citizens of the cities of Succoth by Gideon, Judges 8:7, 16, who explain that word *dosh* [דוש, threshing] as a manner of crushing, in which he placed briars and thorns over their naked bodies prostrate on the ground, and brought over them threshing wagons, which would both fix those thorns in and somehow grind the flesh with the fixed thorns. So thinks Bonfrerius <margin>As in this place p. 495</margin>. *Post-harvesting*, in which vines are stripped of their clusters, is used for hostile devastation and cutting off, Lamentations 1:12, 22; 2:20. So also is threshing, in which the husks, bristles, and stalks are broken small. From this are taken those allegorical expressions <margin>Micah 4:13</margin>. *Arise and thresh* (*doshi*), *daughter of Zion; for I will make your horn iron, and your hooves* (*parsotecha*) *I will make brass, and you shall crush* (*ve-hadakot*) *many peoples.* <margin>Tirinus in this place p. 836</margin> Tirinus: *Arise, and lift up your spirits, O daughter of Zion, and you also thresh, no longer with wooden flails, or the horny hooves of oxen, but with iron and bronze wheels, and iron-bound chariots, pursue the prostrate enemies, strew and cut down those fleeing.* In the same form it is said that Ephraim is *like a heifer that has been accustomed from her youth and loved to thresh*, Hosea 10:11, and to subject others to herself, but to refuse obedience to others. But this happiness and luxury of that wanton and well-fed heifer, and that empire, the more it shone, the sooner it ceased; for she who was accustomed to thresh others, and to press her feet on the neck, as an ox or heifer is wont to do to a heap of grain, she herself experienced that threshing. I (He says) will pass over her fair neck. [עברתי על-טוב צוארה] *I passed over the goodness of her neck.* The Septuagint: *I will come upon the beauty of her neck.* Luther: *I will ride over his beautiful neck.* The word *avar* [עבר], *the passing of God*, is to declare His power and energy, according to the nature of the thing joined to it, as *the Lord passed through Egypt*, namely by killing the firstborn, and, *to pass over the face of Moses*, namely by illuminating him with the knowledge of Himself. Thus *to pass over the neck* is to bring on a yoke. Treading symbolically denotes dominion and empire over the subjected and conquered; for victors were accustomed, as a sign of dominion and victory <margin>Josh. 10:24; Ps. 110:1</margin> to place their feet upon necks, to make enemies a footstool for their feet, and *to tread upon their high places* [במותימו], Deut. 33:29, where Jerome, the Septuagint, and the Chaldean understood the nape and the neck. Hence it is said in Luke 10:19 by Christ to the disciples: *I have given you power to tread upon* (*tou patein*) *serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy.* To which is conformable what is read in <margin>Ps. 91:13</margin> *upon the asp and the basilisk you shall tread* (*tidroch*). *You shall trample* (*tirmos*—*katapateseis*) *the young lion and the dragon*. Let us proceed...

# CONCERNING DEUTERONOMY XXV. v. 4.

<margin>threshing v. 12.</margin> Now we turn to secular authors. We have received from *Athenaeus* <insert>*</insert> a report of a horrifying type of punishment, in which an insane mob, having brought in oxen, crushed certain exiles in the manner of harvested grain: "The people gathered the children of the fugitives into the threshing floors and, having gathered oxen, drove them over them." <note>original: "Συνάγαγον (ὁ δῆμος) τὰ τέκνα τῶν φυγόντων εἰς ἀλονίας (in areas) βῶς συναγαγόντες συνήλασαν."</note> Add to this the cruelty of Nero, though the circumstance is quite different, when on the Appian Way he knowingly crushed a boy with swift draft animals in a sudden village encounter, *Suetonius ch. 4.* But enough now of these two modes of threshing <note>i.e., by the hooves of cattle or by heavy sleds</note>. There remains yet a third, which is humbler and more frequent in our own regions; for we (excluding the Italians and Spaniards) have nothing to do with that ancient threshing by wagon or the hooves of oxen; we shake out the grain with "versatile clubs" or poles fitted on one side with a swinging piece of wood. We call them *flails* <note>Latin: *Flagel*</note>, which peasants sometimes use to strike the backs of their enemies, as the Peasant Revolts testify. *Columella* <margin>Book 2 on Agriculture, ch. 21, p. 362.</margin> mentions <insert>*</insert> this mode of threshing: *"But if the crop is harvested in bundles with part of the stalk, it is immediately gathered into a heap or a shed and then, dried by favorable suns, it is trodden out. If, however, only the ears are cut off, they can be carried into the granary and then during the winter either shaken out with sticks or trodden by cattle."* When the Israelites were oppressed in a very bitter war by the Midianites for seven whole years, their threshing floors were destroyed and all their beasts taken away <insert>*</insert>, <margin>Judges 6 v. 3.</margin> *"and when Israel had sown, Midian came up, and Amalek, and the other children of the East, and they destroyed the fruit of the earth as far as Gaza, and left no sustenance in Israel, nor sheep, nor oxen, nor donkeys."* In this <margin>v. 2.</margin> oppression, to provide for their lives, they chose inaccessible places and made for themselves dens and caves in the mountains, nor could the customary method of threshing in the open floors be held by them any longer because of that public plundering. The proof is that Gideon <term>בגת</term> <note>Hebrew: *be-gat*</note> in a winepress shook out and cleaned the grain. <margin>v. 11</margin> <term>גת</term> <note>Hebrew: *gat*</note> is a winepress, a place where grapes are squeezed, which was perhaps in the seclusion of some vine-bearing mountain, so that Gideon might hide there more conveniently; and thus it truly was a <term>גת</term> <note>winepress</note>, which is derived from <term>גדד</term> <note>Hebrew: *gadad*</note> meaning to act solitarily or to be in solitude. For those do not convince me who claim there was a grape-treader or a winepress in the large granary of his father where the crops were usually stored. In that unhappy war, what was otherwise their custom was not permitted. In time of peace they threshed with oxen; now, with the beasts snatched away, they use sticks for threshing. Isidore rightly observed this in his Questions on Judges, Q. 2. a.: *"Gideon, under an oak tree, beats the wheat harvest with a rod and shakes the grain from the chaff."* Cornelius à Lapide, <margin>p. 123 on Judges</margin> whose words are <insert>*</insert>: *"He would shake it out, namely with a flail, just as the Belgians and others shake the grains from the husks by flailing the crops. Otherwise in Palestine (as is still done in Italy) oxen threshed the crops by treading them with their hooves and thus shaking out the grains, whence that saying: 'Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treads out the corn.' But Gideon threshed here with a flail because he did it secretly and hastily, lest he be caught by the approaching Midianites, and for the same reason he did it in a winepress, where grapes are usually squeezed and wine drawn from them. For this winepress was in a level place, and perhaps in a granary, as Vatablus wishes, where crops are usually flailed and threshed."* Otherwise, certain types of herbs

<column-break/>

which consisted of a thin husk were subject to the flailing stick. Isaiah hints at this <insert>*</insert> when he says: *"The wheel is not turned over the cumin, but the cumin is shaken out with a rod."* <margin>Threshing ch. 28:27.</margin> The Septuagint <note>Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> says: "The cart-wheel does not run over the cumin, but the cumin is shaken out with a staff." <note>original: "Οὐ τρέχει ἁμάξης σειραῖα ἐπὶ τὸ κύμινον, ἀλλὰ ῥάβδῳ ἐκτινάσσεται κύμινον."</note> The Hebrew text is: <term>במטה יחבט קצח וכמן בשבט</term> <note>Hebrew: *be-matteh yechabat qetsach ve-kammon be-shevet*</note>. *"The black cumin is beaten out with a rod, and the cumin with a staff."* Luther: <term>Vetch is beaten out with a rod / and the cumin with a stick.</term> <note>original German: "Wicken schlägt man aus mit einen Stab / und den Kümmel mit einen Stecken."</note> Neither the toothed threshing-sled nor the wagon wheel are driven over the black cumin and cumin to shake out its seeds; for that large and heavy instrument, which is called <term>חרוץ</term> <note>Hebrew: *charuts*, a sharp threshing instrument</note>, is unsuitable for the threshing of tiny seeds because of its violence. According to the diversity of grains and legumes, a diverse threshing is performed. From this diversity of threshing, GOD shows the diversity which He is accustomed to use in discipline and chastisement. Pharaoh and men like him of deplorable wickedness are threshed with iron sleds. He threshes these with a rod; those with a staff. God does <insert>*</insert> what skilled physicians are accustomed to do, who provide different cures for different diseases; He burns and cuts this one to heal him: that one, as if desperate, He leaves alone; this one He handles with a gentle hand, whence Prosper says in his Epigrams, <margin>Salvianus, Book 6 on Providence</margin>

> He consults for those to be saved even by His anger,
> As a Physician heals wounds with wounds.

It remains for us to purify the floor and purge it of chaff, which is usually the final work in the collection of grain. The excrements of the grain are the chaff, which are eliminated from the floors by a winnowing fan, like the impure members of the seeds. For it was necessary, once the grains were well shaken out, to move and remove from the place the empty chaos of husks, so that the fruit might be brought into the granaries as pure fruit. This is usually expressed by the words <term>זרה ,מורג</term> <note>Hebrew: *morag* (threshing sledge) and *zarah* (to winnow)</note>. We read of that scattering in *Ruth 3:2*, that Boaz decided to winnow <term>קשערים</term> <note>Hebrew: *se'orim*, barley</note>, the threshing floor of barley. <note>original Greek: "τὸν ἅλωνα τῶν κριθῶν"</note> *"To winnow the barley floor is to separate the grains of barley from the chaff, which in the floor was already threshed and piled up in a confused mass."* In speech, it is sometimes customary to attribute to the container what is owed to the content. As if we say, <term>To winnow the barley-floor, i.e., the barley on the floor.</term> <term>To cut the oat-field.</term> Likewise: <term>to consume a little spit,</term> <note>Latin: *Veru alaudarum consumere*</note> that is, twelve larks fixed on a small stick or spit. Concerning this secretion of husks from the grains, one may read Columella <insert>*</insert>: *"The ears themselves are better beaten with sticks and purged with winnowing fans."* But where they are dry <margin>Book 2 on Agriculture, ch. 21, p. 363.</margin>, let them be separated by the wind; for that purpose the West Wind <note>Latin: *Favonius*</note> is considered excellent, which blows gently and steadily in the summer months; yet to wait for it is the mark of a slow farmer, because while it is expected, a cruel winter may overtake us. *"Therefore, the threshed grain on the floor must be so piled up that it can be sifted by every breeze. But if for several days the breeze blows from all sides, let them be purged with winnowing fans, lest after too much sluggishness of the winds, a vast storm make the labor of the whole year in vain."* And Varro <insert>*</insert> says that when these (grains) are threshed, they ought <margin>Book 1 on Agriculture, 52.</margin> to be <term>thrown up from the ground with shovels or winnowing fans when a gentle wind blows. Thus it happens that what is lightest in it, and is called the husk, is winnowed out away from the floor, and the grain, which is heavy, comes pure to the basket.</term> From this mode of winnowing, figures of speech are likewise taken in the sacred texts. In the Prophet Jeremiah, GOD, about to indicate destruction to the Jews, says <insert>*</insert>: *"And I will winnow them with a winnowing fan"* <margin>ch. 15:7.</margin>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Threshing</margin>
(And I will scatter them with a winnowing fan) *in the gates of the earth*, <note>original: "in portis terræ"</note> namely, even to the farthest shores of the east and west, which are as it were the gates of the universe. Luther says: *I will winnow them out of the land with the winnowing shovel.* Varro says this is done when a gentle wind is blowing: for the labor is most pleasant when moderate breezes assist the ventilation, which is especially necessary for storing grain before it is brought into the granaries. The cleaner the grains are, the less they are devastated in the granaries by weevils; and the more the East and North winds permeate them, the less they will suffer from mice or worms. The Bactrians, Cappadocians, Thracians, and even now the Hungarians, use caves—which they once called *Syros*—with the ground covered in straw, as granaries, and thus they stored their crops underground. In our regions, however, custom has led us to use raised granaries, the sides of which are open with windows, so that the winds may pass through as desired and circulate beneath the floor.

When the entire harvest was finished and the fruits purified by winnowing and ventilation, it was the custom to provide a feast for the workers. This persists even to our own times, where, after the *aloasmos* <note>Greek: ἀλοασμῷ, "threshing festival"</note> is finished, a feast is given to the threshers, which is commonly called the *Staub-Wein* <note>German: "Dust-Wine," a traditional drink given after the dusty work of threshing.</note>.
<margin>Ruth 3:2</margin>
While Boaz was celebrating this day of joy with his threshers, Ruth the Moabite woman—acting on the advice of her mother-in-law, whom she piously revered and with whom she had traveled to Judea, longing to be counted among the true Church—approached him. By the power of the Divine law, <margin>Deut. 25:5</margin> she modestly requested marriage from him. Hence Boaz, a man described as *gibbor chayil* <note>Hebrew: גבור חיל, "a man of mighty valor" or "wealth"</note> or a most excellent man of the family of Elimelech, is called by Naomi <margin>v. 20, ch. 2</margin> *goelenu* <note>Hebrew: גואלנו, "our redeemer" or "kinsman-vindicator"</note>. This refers to our Redeemers or vindicators; as if to say, to Boaz, this *ish gibbor chayil* <note>Hebrew: איש גבור חיל, "man of great standing"</note> (for *chayil* generally denotes power, specifically here either diligence and courage of soul, or wealth and resources, as this whole history teaches), belongs the right of liberating us from childlessness and vindicating the name of my sons and Ruth's husband from destruction and oblivion by raising up seed and posterity for them. Indeed, the right of redeeming property included the right of marriage, *Deut. 25:5, Ruth 4:5*. But he who refused to fulfill what he was bound to do by this divine law had the shoe of his deceased kinsman's widow pulled from his foot, and *chalatz lo ne'alo* <note>Hebrew: חלץ לו נעלו</note>, which means *he drew off, he pulled off*.
<margin>v. 9</margin>
The Targum says *yishrei*, "and he shall loosen," for they used to fasten shoes to their feet with thongs. <margin>John 1:27</margin> The Jerusalem Targum says *shalaph*, "and he shall pull the shoe from his foot." The Septuagint <note>Greek Old Testament</note> added for the sake of clarity that she pulled off only one shoe: *and she shall loosen his one sandal from his foot.* It resulted in great ignominy for him who was a contemner of this divine law and refused to free the name of his kinsman from oblivion by marrying the widow and raising up seed. Hence he was deservedly called *yachaph*, "the barefoot one," and his house was called <margin>v. 10</margin> *the house of the one with the loosened shoe*. Targum Onkelos: "the house of the one stripped of his shoe"; Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum: "of the Sandal"; the Septuagint: "the house of him who had his sandal loosened." Luther calls it *the house of the barefoot man*, <note>German: "des Barfüffers Hauß"</note> that is, of the man whose shoe was pulled off by his sister-in-law, because she had

<column-break/>

<margin>threshing</margin>
pulled off his shoe and spat in his face. For such a man was deemed unworthy to wear a shoe—that is, to move among free-born men. In ancient times, it was a mark of servitude not to wear shoes, a servitude to which the Canaanite slaves were once condemned. Among the Romans, the footwear of slaves differed from others, for ages, sexes, dignities, and offices were all distinguished by dress, and especially by shoes.
<margin>Book 33, ch. 18</margin>
Hence Pliny says at the end: *And they are almost sent back with the laurel-wreathed fasces to the place from which they had come with chalked feet.* For slaves' feet were marked with a chalky sign. Ovid refers to this custom in *Amores*, Book 1, Elegy 7:

->Despise the empty name of the gypsum-whitened foot.<-

And Juvenal, Satire 1, v. 101:

->One who had recently come into this city with white feet.<-

So also Aulus Tibullus, Book 2, Elegy 3:

->I will speak of what is known; he himself holds the kingdom, whom the<-
->barbarian scaffold often forced to bear gypsum-whitened feet.<-

For slaves for sale were exposed on a scaffold <note>term: catasta, a raised platform where slaves were displayed for auction</note> marked in this way. Besides "barefootedness" <note>Greek: γυμνοποδίαν</note>, it was also once the custom for slaves to grow their hair long, as Aristophanes witnesses in *The Birds* when he says: *Being a slave, you grow your hair long.* P. Aemilius affirms the same regarding Charlemagne, Clovis, and Clotarius II: among the Lombards, hair was shorn as a symbol of servitude. To lay down the hair and beard was a symbol of surrender. Conversely, it was a sign of liberty if slaves wore a cap <note>term: pileum, the felt cap of liberty</note> during the Saturnalia and put on the shoes of the free-born, as Porphyry testifies; hence "to call to the cap" is proverbially "to call to liberty," according to Suetonius, Pliny, and Macrobius. Let us note the words of Blessed Luther in his annotations on this law: *The barefoot foot,* he says, *is a mark of ignominy and a cause of everlasting reproach,* as if the sister-in-law says: *You are worthy to be barefoot yourself, that is, without a family and subjects (who are signified by the shoe), since you make yourself barefoot by this one act of not raising up the family of your brother, so that the mark is similar to the act by which you sin.* Regarding the apparent contradiction <note>Greek: ἐναντιοφανὲς</note> that occurs between the law and the action of Ruth's kinsman, Blessed Gerhard <margin>Commentary on Deut. 25, p. 1528</margin> responds thus: Although the necessity of marrying the sister-in-law was joined inseparably with the power of entering the inheritance of the deceased (as is clear from Ruth 4:5), the Jews used distinct rites for the refusal of marriage and the renunciation of inheritance. For the refusal of marriage, the sister-in-law herself pulled the shoe from the refusing brother and spat in his face. For the renunciation of inheritance, the one refusing the marriage pulled off his own glove—or more properly, his shoe—and handed it to the next of kin who wished to marry the widow. Ruth obtained her wish, and when the next of kin renounced his right, she was taken in marriage by Boaz. By this act, Ruth deserved to be numbered among the ancestors of Christ the Savior, *Matthew 1:5*. Regarding Ruth's act undertaken on the advice of her mother-in-law, I will add a few things before returning to the matter from which I have digressed: it should be known that the advice of the mother-in-law and the deed of Ruth itself were legitimate in reality, though seemingly dishonest in appearance. Legitimate in reality, because in this way she wished to provide for her pious and obedient daughter-in-law...

# On Deuteronomy 25, Verse 4
## (Continued)

<margin>threshing</margin>an honorable marriage, toward which the law concerning the raising up of offspring <note>The Levirate law, where a relative marries a widow to continue a lineage</note> tacitly admonished her. Indeed, the daughter-in-law, knowing that her mother-in-law intended no evil for her, showed herself obedient to her mother-in-law in this matter as well. It had the appearance of something dishonorable, because it is not the custom for women to woo men, but rather for men to woo women. Thus, Ruth’s lying at the feet of Boaz had the appearance of evil, all the more so since she presumed to sleep at the feet of a drunken Boaz at night in a solitary place. However, the piety toward God of both was known to the mother-in-law; indeed, God himself prevented any dishonor from arising there. Hence the author <margin>Homily 1 on Matthew</margin> of the *Imperfect Work* found in Chrysostom <note>A famous 5th-century commentary on Matthew formerly attributed to St. John Chrysostom</note> judges this act of Ruth’s skillfully and quite piously: >*Unless the inspiration of God had been in Ruth, she would not have said what she said, nor done what she did. What is first praised in her? Her love for the race of Israel, or her obedience, or her faith? She desired to receive children from the seed of Israel and to become one of the people of God. Furthermore, her simplicity is shown because she entered under the cloak of Boaz of her own accord, and did not worry that he might spurn her as a righteous man would a wanton woman, or that he might lead her away and—what would be more serious—scorn her after deceiving her, as many do; but obeying the counsels of her mother-in-law with confidence that God would prosper her action, and knowing her own conscience, she knew that lust had not compelled her to this, but religion had urged her.* Thus he wrote.

However, it was not only among the Israelites that this festive day was customarily celebrated, so that a feast was prepared for the workers once the harvest and **threshing** were finished. The Greeks celebrated in honor of Ceres <note>The goddess of agriculture</note>, the inventor of grains (as they fabled), the <term>proerosia</term> <note>original: προσηρόσεα; "pre-plowing" sacrifices</note> according to Hesychius, commonly called <term>prochairetia</term> <note>original: προχαιρέτια; "pre-gratulatory" rites</note>, instituted by the persuasion of an oracle when famine pressed throughout all Greece; these were performed before they plowed for a happy outcome of the crops. The Athenians, according to Suidas, held their <term>haloa</term> <note>original: ἅλωα; "threshing-floor festival"</note> in the month of Poseideon, when they made the <term>first-fruits</term> <note>original: τὰς ἀπαρχὰς</note> offerings around the <term>threshing floors</term> <note>original: τὰς ἅλως</note> or areas; and that these lasted for several days can be seen from the letters of Alciphron the Philosopher, a native of Miletus, who lived in the times of Alexander. The Athenians themselves also had their <term>thalysia</term> <note>original: θαλύσια; harvest-home festival</note>, according to the Etymologist, celebrated after the crops were brought in; and these were not without a feast and the participation of servants, whom it was also permitted to attend. Among the Romans, this feast is called *Daps* <note>A sacrificial feast</note>, as Cato reports in *On Agriculture*, <margin>R. R. ch. 132</margin> where he describes how the feast ought to be conducted. >*To Jupiter of the Feast,* he says, *offer a cup of wine as large as you wish. On that day there is a holiday for the oxen, the plowmen, and those who make the feast. When it is time to make the offering, do thus: "Jupiter of the Feast, because it is right for a cup of wine to be offered to you in my house and family for the sake of this feast, be honored by this wine. Be honored by this feast being offered." Wash your hands. Afterward, take the wine: "Jupiter of the Feast, be honored by this feast being offered. Be honored by this wine." If you wish, give to Vesta; the feast for Jupiter consists of roasted meat and an urn of wine for Jupiter in a pure manner.* And this day was sacred to Jupiter of the Feast, a holiday and empty of work, which is why Ovid in the 6th book of the *Fasti* calls it the day of *Vacuna* <note>Goddess of leisure/rest</note>, because the servants were vacant from labors:

->Even now, when the rites of ancient Vacuna were held,<-
->They stand and sit before the hearths of Vacuna.<-

There was strenuous and splendid feasting during the Vacunalia by those at leisure and vacant from labor, and this in honor of Vacuna, who was believed to be a Goddess and presided over those who were vacant and at leisure. Varro writes that *Victory* was so 

<column-break/>

<margin>threshing</margin>called by the Sabines, and that those who conquer through wisdom especially rejoice in her. Porphyrio, in his commentary on *Horace*, records that she was worshiped by the Sabines and depicted under an uncertain form, so that some thought her *Minerva*, others *Diana*, and some even *Ceres*. The Gentiles performed sacred rites to their fictitious Gods both before and after the vintage. Before the vintage, sacrifices were made to Liber and Libera <note>Bacchus/Dionysus and his consort</note>; and they acted most holily with the pressing vessels, because the vintage rites, which were also called "rustic" <gloss>book 12, ch. 18</gloss>, were celebrated in honor of Jupiter, specifically when the first wine was brought into the city. The wine that was brought in was called <term>Calpar</term> <note>A sacrificial wine jar</note> and <term>Sacrima</term> <note>New wine for sacrifice</note>, as Rosinus reports in *Roman Antiquities* book 4, ch. 12, p. 107; also *Inferium*, because it was "brought in" <note>Latin: inferebatur</note> from the vats. This ritual of the Heathens is illustrated by what is read concerning the Shechemites <gloss>Judges 9:27</gloss>, who went out into the field gathering their vineyards and treading them, and they rejoiced, and entered the house of their false god, and ate and drank. Not without a feast, and that in the sacred house or shrine of their false god Baal-Berith, they finish the vintages, and at the same time they curse Abimelech, upon whom they vomit no small slanders, but with a truly unhappy outcome, as history witnesses. William Stuckius narrates in *Ancient Feasts* book 1, ch. 23: <margin>P. 94</margin> In Gaul and certain places in Germany, besides a license among the vintagers that is hardly to be tolerated, a feast is celebrated when the Vintage is finished, which they call the <term>Vintage Bath</term>, or the **Herbst-Bad** <note>German: "Harvest Bath"</note>; we ourselves have found that this custom still holds, though with that unbridled license abolished, although that feast goes by one name or another here and there. But enough has been threshed! And now let there be a holiday from our threshing, which was performed not with a threshing-sledge but with a pen! Those who desire more concerning threshing may consult those who have written professionally on *Rural Affairs*: among the ancients, the four men, namely Cato, Varro, Palladius, and Columella. Among the more recent, indeed, Jean Liébault, Pietro de' Crescenzi, Conrad Heresbach, Theodor Zwinger, and others.

->Arise, go over this Jordan, thou, and all this people,<-
