<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>I strive to deliver a **Chorography** <note>A description of a region or district</note> of the land of Canaan, made noble by the gathering of the twelve tribes. But while I strive, I can more easily wish for the strength than achieve it. I ask the reader, therefore, if he observes my wit here growing dull, or failing to penetrate the innermost chambers, to pardon it as if belonging to one <term>unskilled in geometry</term> <note>original: ἀγεωμετρήτῳ</note>, not indeed by his own fault but by the fault of his teachers. We have need of a leader and author for this way into the land of Canaan, under whose guidance we shall go and return. I wished for a guide <note>original: Hodegeten</note>, but such was my misfortune that he remains hidden outside our Hesse for now; meanwhile, I shall follow the tracks of the common Caravan, about to set forth from tribe to tribe. The Holy Spirit exhibits a liberal nomenclature of the places and cities occupied in the land of Canaan, from chapter 13 to 20 of the book of Joshua.

# SACRED ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
Sacred Geography

Volume of Orations, p. 677.
</margin>

...not as an idle and useless heap of facts, as Chytræus <note>David Chytræus (1530–1600), a Lutheran theologian and historian.</note> teaches in his commentary on *Joshua, p. 62*, warning us that this part of history should not be passed over listlessly or coldly. Whence the same Chytræus says: *Geography is the light of all histories in Holy Scripture; it indicates and measures by a certain method the sites and distances of the places in which the divine revelations were published and other deeds are written to have been performed.*

We commend Homer, who diligently and attentively considered the ships of the Greeks, accurately recounting the names and homelands of the Leaders, weighing the locations of the Boeotians, Locrians, Euboeans, Mycenaeans, Lacedaemonians, Pylians, Arcadians, Cephalenians, Aetolians, Cretans, Rhodians, Philaceans, Pheraeans, Methoneans, and others. It is even more fitting that we commend that conspicuous and illustrious narrative of Joshua, in which, as if on a tablet, he depicted Palestine, and within it the more powerful and noble places with a certain <term>geographic knowledge</term> <note>original Greek: "geographikēn epignōsei"</note>. Furthermore, the utility of <term>Chorography</term> <note>The description of specific regions or districts.</note> requires that we adorn our Biblical Antiquities with this part as much as possible. For once Chorography is read and known, it brings great light to the histories, whether you desire the Mosaic, the Prophetic, or finally the Evangelical ones. For those who approach Sacred History move through it more successfully and readily if they place before their sight the distances of regions and towns, the seats of the twelve tribes, and the metropolises of the Kingdom; whence they seem to themselves to be either companions of the travelers or guests of the inhabitants. Entirely, those places must be beheld in the mind in which God either revealed Himself by most certain testimonies, or showed remarkable proofs—whether of wrath or of grace—or which Christ Himself trod with His holy steps. From this, reminders of many great things can be made, and the slip of memory can be stirred and confirmed, if one proposes to oneself images and pictures, if one carves out spectacles as if radiating into the eyes and places them in view, representing the deeds themselves through the imagination of places. For geographical maps, as they are called, vehemently aid historical study; you might see the journeys of Moses leading the people out, and of Paul teaching all nations, as if present before you, if you inspect accurate tables. Formerly, <term>Tilemannus Stella</term> <note>A 16th-century German Renaissance cartographer.</note> published two maps: the first of Palestine, the second of the leading out of the people of Israel from Egypt. By these aids, it is enough to have indicated Palestine <term>from the margins</term> <note>original Greek: "apo margadōn"</note>; and diligent seekers will be able to arrive at intimate knowledge if they unroll the *Phaleus* of <term>Bochart</term> <note>Samuel Bochart, a famous 17th-century scholar of biblical geography.</note>, or the work of the Monk whom they commonly call Brocardus, who contemplated the Holy Land with great zeal and devotion in the Year of Christ 1280. Also, with the great curiosity he possessed, Saint Jerome once circled the entire coast of Palestine so that he might illuminate with his own eyes all its places, sites, and regions mentioned in Scripture, and behold in person what he had heard of while absent. Whence the same Father, in his preface to Chronicles addressed to Domnio and Rogatianus, strongly commends the itineraries established to the sacred places of Palestine. *Just as,* he says, *those understand Greek histories better who have seen Athens, and the third book of Virgil*

<column-break/>

<margin>

</margin>

*who have sailed from Troy through Leucas and the Acroceraunian mountains to Sicily, and thence to the mouths of the Tiber; so he will behold Holy Scripture more clearly who has contemplated Judea with his eyes, and has known the memorials of ancient cities and the locations, whether their names remain the same or have been changed.* But, since in this time of ours especially it is not granted to everyone to visit the Holy Land with their own eyes, we exhort the reader

along with Matthias Flacius* to always contemplate the maps of the Holy Land and compare them to the histories. If you should despise my warning, let the words of the Blessed Chytræus* move us to serious contemplation:

<margin>

> *Since the Land of Canaan was the true seat of the Church of God and of many illustrious revelations of God from the time of Abraham, and afterward the lodging of the nascent Church, and the domicile and school of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ—who in almost every mile of this region gave illustrious testimonies of His doctrine and miracles—let us know that God wills us to regard and contemplate with singular attention and diligence the towns and all places of this region in which God revealed Himself, and the Fathers, Prophets, Christ, and Apostles taught and confirmed their doctrine with the testimonies of miracles, and where other great things were done which the Holy Spirit described in the whole series of the books of the Church; and let us consider their sites and distances, and carry them fixed in the mind, placed before our eyes daily in the reading of the sacred books and in prayer.*

And again in *Joshua, ch. 13, p. 62*: No region in the whole world is more celebrated or more worthy of survey than Palestine, whose regions, peoples, and chief cities the book of Joshua enumerates. To behold and traverse in the mind this most noble region of the earth, which is the homeland of the ancient Church, and the various distant tribes, cities, rivers, seas, and mountains within it, and to consider the deeds done in individual places and to measure and distinguish the sites and distances of the places, is not only an ancient part of our condition and the sweetest part of geographic learning, but is also joined with singular pleasure and fruit, even if you have never departed from your own home.

God had pre-signified to Abraham (*Gen. 15:13*) that his posterity would serve in a foreign land for 400 years, and after the fourth generation would return with great wealth and glory to the land of Canaan. By the paternal providence of God, a Hero was being prepared who would lead the most afflicted people from the harshest slavery into sweet liberty, from a foreign and ungrateful land into the longed-for promised homeland. This was done through Moses, whom his most sorrowful parents had exposed on the River Nile, and his successor Joshua, by whose leadership and distribution they occupied the holy land <term>for the purpose of inhabiting and colonizing entire cities</term> <note>original Greek: "pros to enoikein kai exoikizein poleis holas"</note>, to speak with Dionysius, after the inhabitants were first utterly cut off, or killed, or expelled to dwell elsewhere.

By the excellent economy of GOD, therefore, the seat of the Israelite people was chosen among neighboring and most flourishing kingdoms—the Egyptian, Syrian, Babylonian, and Persian—which God willed to entice and insinuate Himself into, so to speak, so that they would not hold in contempt His kingdom, placed in such an eminent and illustrious location and introduced with stupendous miracles. # From Joshua 1, v. 2.
## Iii 3

Against the most powerful Assyrians, God nevertheless meanwhile established this kingdom—which seemed scarcely able to stand by its own ruined walls—with a mighty hand against any tyrants whatsoever, so that it stood firm. God, the most powerful arbiter of governing boundaries, establishes the borders of Judea <margin>Sacred Geography</margin> <note>original: *τὰ ὅρια τῆς Ἰουδαίας*</note>, and the region <note>original: *χωρίον*</note> which He adjudged to His Church, He defended from hostile invasion in various and wondrous ways. Tyrants, gasping for land everywhere and as if enclosing and besieging Judea, were not able—though they seemed capable of anything with an armed hand—to cross the limits placed upon their own kingdoms. Hence also God, for just causes, prohibited the neighboring kingdoms (which then adhered to other Gods) from entering, so that His people might be carried more vehemently toward Him, and so that there might be a greater impetus for foreign peoples to approach a kingdom so admirably and miraculously gathered. He willed that there be peace between both, yet He willed no covenant between them; He willed that there be one God between both, yet He willed no idol of God between them; so that among this His people, joined tribe by tribe, there might be a joining of souls, a charming and friendly society among all through mutual love: one soul, one mind, one God, one altar, one temple. Let us now approach the tribes, intending to see in order the principal dwellings of all, and to survey the "statues of Mercury" <note>A classical reference to boundary markers or guideposts</note> not so much from ancient as from recent memory—a task which requires more time, more eloquence, and more learning than our meager ability can provide. Meanwhile, although sufficient strength may be lacking, we shall encompass in a single overview <note>original: *σύνοψιν*</note> the regions, towns, villages, wandering rivers, ponds, and lakes mentioned in the Holy Volumes, so that the path of solid knowledge may lie open, and all things may seem level to the seeker, lest there be a need to wander through many writings or great volumes.

Abraham Ortelius, in his geographical names of places, followed the version of the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint</note>, as he mentions in the *Parergon* of his *Theatrum*, section on Sacred Geography. The map of Nicholas and Arnold Geilkerker, published by Jan Jansson in Amsterdam, 1631, accurately displays all the places of Palestine. Furthermore, a map published by the Jews of Amsterdam in Hebrew characters displays the places of the Holy Land. See the descriptions in Adrichomius, Ortelius, Reiner, Ziegler, Arias Montanus, Weissenburg, Bunting, Heidmann, and others. <margin>Encyclopaed. Epist p 117.</margin> The work of Franciscus Quaresmius on the places of the Holy Land is commended by Aloysius Novarinus; just as an accurate explanation <note>original: *ἐξήγησις*</note> of the places of the Holy Land exists in Jerome’s *Epitaph of Mother Paula*.

Palestine, however, contains within itself not only the Holy Land itself but also the surrounding regions. The most ancient name of this land is from Canaan, the son of Ham, whose sons distributed it among themselves (Genesis 10:19). It is called the Land of Israel from its inhabitants, the Israelites, who distributed it into twelve parts according to the twelve tribes, as Sacred History testifies. This is the most commonly used division according to the twelve tribes or the twelve sons of Jacob—with Ephraim and Manasseh substituted, of course, in the place of Levi and Joseph. Adrichomius judges that the part which is distinguished from the Perizzites, Jebusites, and others was properly and originally "Canaanite." But afterward, that whole land received the name.

<column-break/>

Regarding Palestine, it can be said for certain that it was the land of the *Pelisthim* or Philistines, who were confined <margin>Sacred Geography</margin> to only a few tribes, namely Judah, Dan, and Simeon. Ptolemy and other geographers call it Palestine from the Palestinians, whom the Holy Codex, as has been said, calls Philistines. Herodotus in *Polymnia* and Dio in Book 37 call that part of Syria which looks toward Egypt "Syrian Palestine." After the first inhabitants were driven out, a large part of whom became exiles in Africa, Eusebius <margin>Book 1, Chronicles</margin> rightly names the place of the Canaanites' flight the "Tripolis of Africa." Indeed, the remaining people of the stock of Anak were then cast out into Africa; and they settled in those places where Carthage later stood. Hence it is that Carthage is called *Cadreanech* by the Phoenicians, as if to say "the seat of the Anakim." (Heurnius, *Chaldeans* p. 32; Stuckius, *On Royal Law* p. 119). Witnesses to this are two stone columns in Tangier, surviving even two thousand years after the event, inscribed in the Phoenician language of that age with words sounding thus in Greek: *We are those who fled from the face of Joshua the robber, the son of Nun*; as Procopius testifies, as he himself describes in Book 2 of the *Vandal War*, f. 135. (Evagrius Book 4, ch. 18; Selden, *On the Syrian Gods* ch. 3, p. 18; Mornay ch. 26, *On the Truth of the Christian Religion*; Reinesius ch. 3, num. 11, 12, *On the Punic Language*). <margin>Greek</margin> But from where they were called "Phoenicians" is not sufficiently clear. Scholars seek the origin of the word "Phoenician" from Syriac in vain. For they were not called that by themselves, but rather "Canaanites." The Greeks, however, called them Phoenicians, as Aristotle relates in his *Marvelous Utterances*, because acting as robbers, they would kill men wherever they landed on a coast; for to the ancient Greeks, "to snatch" <note>original: *ἁρπάξαι*</note> was said to be "to bloody/redden" <note>original: *φοινίξαι*</note>, which the Scholiast of Aristophanes also noted regarding the *Acharnians*. For the same reason, the Carians were also called "Phoenicians" by Bacchylides and Corinna (cf. Grotius on Matthew 15:22, p. 285). For the Canaanites went around the sea and the dry land for the sake of business, and they surveyed all parts of the world suitable for trade; hence in Homer, the Phoenicians are called "famed for ships" and "greedy" <note>original: *ναυσίκλυτοι καὶ τρώκται* - Odyssey 15.415</note>; hence Eustathius says: *The Phoenicians being merchants, and sellers, and greedy, they enrich the poet everywhere.* For while they added profit to profit among the business of life, and were entirely occupied with matters of money-making and trade <note>original: *πραγματείας χρηματικῆς καὶ ἐμπορικῆς*</note>, because of this immense zeal, the name "Canaanite" passed to every man who spends his life in commerce, like some Canaanite who did everything for profit. Hence the Canaanites who inhabited the seacoast were properly called Phoenicians, as is gathered from the report of Moses' spies when they say, "the Canaanite dwells by the sea," <margin>Numbers 13:30</margin> whence the Seventy Interpreters <margin>Joshua 5:1</margin> render "Kings of the Phoenicians" for "Kings of the Canaanites," from whom we do not exclude the Philistines, neighbors of the same sea with the Tyrians and Sidonians.

After most of the inhabitants were driven out, as we have said, this land used to be called Judea, by which designation sometimes the whole Holy Land was understood, and sometimes a third part of it. For in the time of the New Testament, all Palestine this side of the Jordan was divided into these three parts: namely, Judea, Samaria, and Galilee. It is indeed the Holy Land (which is called holy for this reason: that holy men, Patriarchs, Judges, Kings, Prophets, and Apostles illustrated it with doctrine and many miracles, and so most...)

### SACRED GEOGRAPHY
<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
...they spent their entire lives in it; finally, since that Holy One of Israel himself was conceived, born, and educated here, and performed miracles in it, first taught his heavenly and holy doctrine here, suffered the most bitter death here for the eternal salvation of all men, was buried here, and here, having conquered all our enemies, rose again on the third day, and from here also, after first sending his Apostles into all the earth, ascended into heaven.) It is a most noble region, most abundant in the wealth of things necessary for the sustenance of life (*Deuteronomy* 8:7 ff.; chapter 11:7 ff.).

For there is no other region or province in the whole world which encompasses such remarkable, great, and numerous towns, forts, villages, etc., in so small a space. Indeed, as far as its width and length are concerned, there is no reason for us to boast: whence Jerome, in his letter to *Dardanus*, discussing its width and length, says: <margin>Letter 129, column 104, Volume 3</margin> *Let those answer me, who think this land possessed by the people of the Jews after they returned from Egypt—how much did they actually possess? Certainly from Dan to Beersheba, which extends scarcely one hundred and sixty miles in length; for the scripture does not testify that even David and Solomon, the most powerful Kings, held more, except for those whom they received into friendship after victory.*

For it had Syria and Arabia to the East; the desert of Paran and Egypt to the South; the Great or Mediterranean Sea to the West; and Mount Lebanon as its borders to the North. Its length from the North, from the city of Dan situated at the foot of Mount Lebanon (which was later called Caesarea Philippi and Paneas), stretches toward the south as far as the city of Beersheba in the tribe of Simeon, situated against the great desert, making more or less sixty-seven miles <note>The author uses "miliaria," likely referring to German miles or leagues, as 67 modern miles is too short for the length of Israel.</note>, each of which is to be measured by the space of one hour's travel.

The width, however, which is to be taken from the Great Sea in the West to the Jordan in the East, encompasses sixteen miles in some places, and eighteen in others. God had indeed established larger boundaries for the inheritance of the children of Israel, specifically four: from the Desert, which is called both Zin and Kadesh, and this from the south; the second from Lebanon, closing the northern region; the third from the Eastern Euphrates; and the fourth from the Great Sea stretching toward the west.

But God left many nations to test Israel, namely the five Lords of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, Sidonians, and Hivites living on Mount Lebanon: from Mount Baal-Hermon to the entrance of Hamath (*Judges* 3:3). Not to mention the Canaanites, Jebusites, etc., who remained in the midst of Israel, whom Solomon finally made tributary and reduced to forced labor (*2 Chronicles* 8:7-8; Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 8, Chapter 2). Hence there is no small controversy concerning the land of Canaan: whether all this land was granted as an inheritance, or whether only some part of it was an inheritance while another portion was tributary? Augustine (*Questions on Joshua*, 21) believes the land lying outside the borders of the seven Canaanite nations was tributary.

<margin>On Genesis chapter 15</margin>
Masius, and with him Pererius, consider it hereditary and their own property. This is agreed upon by Emmanuel Naxera, writing on *Joshua* chapter 1, page 9. I would settle this dispute thus: namely, that all that land was given as an

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
inheritance; but some part is called tributary by Augustine, not because he denied the right of inheritance, but because he looked at the outcome—for a significant part of that land was not the dwelling place of the Hebrews, but paid tribute to David and Solomon.

In the division of the Holy Land, twenty-two cities fell to the tribe of *Asher* <note>original: "Afer," a common early modern variant for Asher</note> by lot (*Joshua* 19:30). Among these, the most celebrated were *Ptolemais*, so named by an Egyptian King (also called *Acon* and *Ace*, but today *Acre*), formerly a colony of Claudius Caesar. A most fortified city, whence it could not be subjugated by the Israelites. It is maritime on two sides, having a notable harbor to the south, and in it a tower which they named after *Flies* <note>The "Tower of Flies" at Acre</note>. It was once both splendid and magnificent, with both public and private buildings. Today, just as all the East obeys the Turks, it was previously subject to the Saracens, by whom it was almost devastated, but finally restored.

From here, scarcely a hundred stadia <note>A Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet</note> toward the North, lies the mountain called the *Ladder of the Tyrians*, where on the same shore is seen *Tyre*, now called *Sur* <note>original: צור (Tzur)</note>, from the Hebrew and Syrian word *Tzur*, as Jerome witnesses on *Ezekiel* chapter 26, column 907; compare what we have noted on *Isaiah* 23:3. An ancient, powerful, noble city, and the mother of noble cities throughout various parts of the world. To Strabo it is called "the greatest and most ancient city of the Phoenicians" (*Book 16*). <margin>History of Jerusalem, p. 437</margin> If Fulcher of Chartres is to be believed, it was founded by the Phoenicians at the time when Gideon was judging Israel. Fuller (*Miscellanea*, Book 11) conjectures that the name "Tyrant" came from Tyre; concerning which derivation there is much discussion. Tyre, extremely powerful by land and sea, was once as busy as it was populous, whence much merchandise was carried to it even from distant places; thus the trade of the Tyrians was in "universals," that is, in every kind of merchandise (*Ezekiel* 27), so that in *Ezekiel* 23 they are said to be "clothed in universality," that is, in every kind of ornament. For the word there is *miklol* <note>original: מכלול</note>, which is also often written as *kalah* <note>original: כלה</note>, meaning "completion" or "totality," usable for that in which nothing is left out, just as in *Psalm* 50 it is called the "perfection of beauty." For this city, famous for its market and riches, is not undeservedly called "exultant" <note>original: עליזה (alizah)</note>. A city as elegant as it is noble: "exultant" in *Isaiah* 23:7; and Nineveh is the "exultant city" in *Zephaniah* 2:15; and Jerusalem is the "exultant city" where the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> reads "wealthy city." For there is nothing that preserves cities and regions longer, and makes them grow rich more conveniently, than the easy navigation of a deep sea or a great river. Voyages are the shortcuts of commerce. What we obtain on land with great expense and labor is done with far less by the benefit of the waters. The sea supplied Tyre with whatever could be found anywhere in the world, and in turn, Tyre supplied other places. Tyre sent out precious ointments, and there the perfumers and ointment-sellers devoted themselves to this trade. From here Greece received them, as Tibullus sings: <margin>Book 3, last elegy</margin>

> Long since, my temples soaked with Tyrian nard,
> I should have bound my hair with garlands.

And Horace (*Odes*, Book 2, Ode 7, line 8):

> ... and the boy [anoints] my hair
> with Syrian malabathrum <note>A fragrant plant oil</note>.

And Clement of Alexandria asserts that dyers first came from Tyre, "in Tyre and Sidon" (*The Instructor*, Book 2).

# From Joshua Chapter 1, Verse 2

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
...the dyers and the purple-merchants are especially drawn there, as are the shellfish themselves, because the purple dye flourishes from their blood <note>The author refers to the Murex snail used to create "Tyrian Purple."</note>. And he who desires to read more concerning its trade, let him read through the 27th chapter of Ezekiel. Who does not know how much Venice owes to her sea, by whose benefit she held the leadership of all cities existing under the whole world for so many centuries? The name of Antwerp would have perished six hundred times over, nor would it now be known where the Cimbri <note>An ancient Germanic tribe.</note>, about to invade Gaul, deposited their baggage, had not the Scheldt river perpetually defended the city against the strong teeth of biting time, says the learned inhabitant of that city, Goropius Becanus, in *Vertumnus, page 52.* Who does not know, he says in the same place, how much London must acknowledge its debt to the Thames, by whose benefit it has held the leadership of the entire kingdom for so many centuries? An equal happiness falls to Hamburg, the Queen of German cities, from its most favoring river. Thus Genoa, Alexandria, Amsterdam, Copenhagen, and Riga prevail by the convenience of importing and exporting. On account of the pleasantness of the place <margin>v. 9. 15.</margin> and the convenience of its site, it is praised by Hosea: *Ephraim is as I saw Tyre, planted in a pleasant place.* The Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament.</note>, by dividing one word into several, read: *Ephraim, in the manner I saw, presented their children for the hunt.* They seem to have read <note>original: לציד שתו לה בניה</note> "to hunt" and "to place," *4. Sacred Criticism 13. n. 4. p. 290.* Trusting in its fortifications and the fact that it was washed on all sides by the sea waves, it raised its crests beyond measure; whence Ezekiel, rebuking its pride with grandiloquent words and a sonorous—indeed, rather unusual—metaphor, describes the ruin <margin>26. 15.</margin> of Tyre. *Shall not the islands shake at the sound of your fall, when the wounded cry out, when the slaughter is made in the midst of you?* These things will be clearer by the light of our version. For thus says the Interpreter:

> What does it matter? The islands shall tremble when you shall hideously fall, from the noise of your fall, and your wounded shall sigh (howl), who shall be murdered within you.

He does not simply mean the islanders by a common metonymy <note>A figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it.</note>, as below in verse 18, but hyperbolically the islands themselves. Indeed, in <margin>chapter 28. 2.</margin> and following, he finally passes to the inhabitants. And concerning the Prince of Tyre, the Prophet says: *Thus said the Lord Jehovah: Because your heart is exalted, and you have said, "I am a God, I sit in the throne of God, in the heart <margin>v. 5.</margin> of the seas," though you are a man and not God, and you have set your heart as the heart of God.* These last words are repeated a little later, and the punishment is added: *Behold, I bring upon you strangers, the robust of the nations, and they shall draw their swords against the beauty of your wisdom, and they shall defile your splendor.* In <margin>v. 7, 8.</margin> they shall make you descend into the pit, and you shall die the deaths of those slain in the heart of the seas. Will you indeed say, "I am God," before your killer? But <margin>2. Iecar. 14. f. 72.</margin> you are a man, and not God, in the hand of the killer. <margin>v. 9.</margin> Upon these words, Josephus Albo <note>A 15th-century Jewish philosopher.</note> says: From this we can see that God visits the proud in that which is not their own; for if any glory because of a kingdom, God takes it from them and gives it to a <margin>Dan. 4. 14.</margin> humble man, so that it may be known by all that the kingdom is not man's, nor in his hand; and thus, if any glory in divinity, so as to make himself a God, God visits him and delivers him into the hands of a killer; for this is the true punishment of retaliation upon one boasting himself to be God, to show his

<column-break/>

shame, namely, that there is not such great power in him that he can snatch himself from death. And this is because <margin>Sacred Geography</margin> God is accustomed to raise the dead and snatch away those taken to death and liberate those inclined to slaughter, and to be eternal, the contrary of which is in this man; for God delivers him into the hand of the killer to show that he is not God, after power is given to a man to kill, and he has not the strength to rescue himself. For first Nebuchadnezzar, the Lord of the sea, conquered Tyre, and after a long interval Alexander the Great, who, having cast up a mound with incredible effort, joined it to the mainland, and having captured it, punished it severely, just as Isaiah said long ago in chapter 23:1 concerning the 70 years of calamity and its destruction. Afterward, however, it flourished again, although it could not recover its former power. Curtius writes concerning the state of Tyre in his own age: <margin>Book 4, ch. 4.</margin> Having therefore survived many misfortunes and been reborn after destruction, it now nevertheless, with a long peace refreshing all things, rests under the protection of Roman custom. In the following centuries it was also very well fortified with walls, towers, and bulwarks, not divided from the mainland, whence <margin>on Ezekiel 26 col. 910.</margin> Jerome says: *We read in Greek, Latin, and barbarian histories that Tyre was an island and had no entrance from the land, but afterward, by Nebuchadnezzar, King of the Chaldeans, or as some affirm, by Alexander, King of the Macedonians, mounds were cast up, and the place was prepared with siege engines and rams, and from an island it was made a peninsula.* Having cast aside the superstition and idol worship to which it had greatly adhered, it gave its name to Christ, whose faith it constantly professed, suffering itself to be broken by no storms of persecution nor turned away from it, until it was captured by the Saracens and forced to undergo the yoke of the infidels, who possess it still. Writers of the Holy Land formerly made mention of this city: William Bolumzele in his *Itinerary*, which exists as a manuscript in the Giessen Library; Ludolph, Parish Priest in Suchen, in his <margin>ch. 2. fol. 2. b.</margin> *Itinerary of the Holy Land*, extant in the St. Mark’s Library in Butzbach; Vincent of Beauvais in the *Speculum Historiale*; William of Tyre; Wilbrand of Oldenburg, Bishop of Paderborn and finally of Utrecht during the reign of Otto IV, in his *Itinerary of the Holy Land*; Johannes Phocas in his *Description of Phoenicia and Palestine*; Brocardus, who should be named in the first place; and Fulcher of Chartres in the *History of Jerusalem*.

Toward Lebanon, the river Eleutherus, flowing from the roots of Lebanon, pours itself into the Ocean; frequent mention of it is made in Josephus. Between it and Sidon was once seen Sarepta, called <note>original: צרפת</note> *Zarephath* by the Hebrews, famous in Holy Scripture for the son of a certain widow raised to life by Elijah, 1 Kings 17:22. It was rich from metallic veins, whence it received the name Sarepta from the smelting workshops, from the root <note>original: צרף</note> *tsaraph*, which is to smelt metals and purge them from dross. They say the ruins of the houses argue that it was great and splendid, and noble for its generous wine, concerning which Sidonius says: <margin>poem 17.</margin>

> I have no wines from Gaza, Chios, or Falernum,
> Nor those you might drink sent from the Sareptan vine.

Phocas affirms that a temple was formerly built here by Christians in honor of the Prophet Elijah, and he who... <meta>The catchword "and he who" indicates the start of the next page's text.</meta>

Of this city and temple
<margin>p. 125.</margin>

> We passed through Sarfente, which we call Sarepta, and because there is another Sarepta in Judea, for the sake of distinction it was said in the second book of Kings <note>The author refers to 1 Kings 17:9; in some older Latin Bibles, 1 & 2 Kings are called 3 & 4 Kings, and 1 & 2 Samuel are 1 & 2 Kings.</note> to Elijah the Tishbite: "Arise and go to Sarepta of the Sidonians." For this is that very one; it is a small city, not very well fortified, lying next to the sea in the middle of the borders of Tyre and Sidon, which our people also rule. Outside its walls, Elijah, seeing a widow gathering two sticks, asked her for something to eat; when he understood from her own profession that she was poor, he enriched her with oil and flour. In memory of this event, a tiny church was built in that place where the woman spoke, in which her footprints are visible today.

Sidon, now called Saida and Sageta, is a very famous city of the Phoenicians, four miles distant from Tyre, and similar to Tyre in most matters; whence in *Isaiah 23:3* it is called <term>Sacher Goyim</term> <note>Hebrew: סחר גוים, "the merchant of nations"</note>, since the Sidonians used to travel to distant shores for the sake of trading, being most skilled in navigation, and others came to them for the sake of merchandise, so that at that time they surpassed other nations in the industry of sailing and trading. It had as its founder the firstborn of Canaan, from whom it also took its name. It was first consumed by Nebuchadnezzar by famine, pestilence, and the sword. Then it was also conquered by Alexander, according to Curtius, and finally by Saint Louis, King of the Franks, as Herold reports in *History of the Sacred War, book 4, chapter 8.* Regarding this city, one may also read William of Tyre *History, book 11, chapter 14, p. 804*, Willebrand of Oldenburg in *Itinerary of the Holy Land p. 125*, and Brocardus *Description of the Holy Land p. 300.* Above Sidon, toward the same Mediterranean Sea, were *Tripoli, Antioch, and Beirut*; concerning the merchandise of the latter and of the Tyrians, one should hear Procopius:
<margin>Secret History p. 111.</margin>
> <note>original: "ἱμάτια τὰ ἐκ μετάξης..."</note> It was customary from of old for silken garments to be manufactured in the cities of Beirut and Tyre in Phoenicia. The merchants, local producers, and craftsmen lived there from the beginning. From there, it happened that this merchandise was carried into every land.

In front of the aforementioned cities, especially Sarepta and Sidon, lies *Anti-Libanus*, a mountain famous for the cultivation of vineyards, situated not far from the Great Sea, and in some places touching the sea. Brocardus *Itinerary p. 300.* Beyond it, in the plain of Lebanon by the river Eleutherus, was situated *Greater Cana*, not far from Sidon in Upper Galilee (or Galilee of the Gentiles), so called to distinguish it from Lesser Cana in the tribe of Zebulun in Lower Galilee, in which the Savior turned water into wine, as Masius maintains, and commonly with him many others on *Joshua 19:28.* Eusebius disagrees with this in his *Book of Places*, writing thus: "But Cana was in the tribe of Asher (for this is the lesser one) where our Lord and Savior converted water into wine." <margin>1 Kings 9:13.</margin>
Regarding this tradition, I note the words of the Spanish Bishop de las Casas, on the question: "Whether Kings or Princes can, by any right or title and with a safe conscience, alienate citizens and subjects from the Royal Crown and subject them to the jurisdiction of another private lord?" <margin>Solomon § 36, p. 46.</margin>

King Solomon granted these twenty cities into the possession of Hiram, King of Tyre, by this gift. When Hiram had seen them and they did not please him, he said: *"What are these cities which you have given me, my brother?"* And he obtained then that it should be called the land of Cabul, for the purpose, no doubt, that the whole land seemed of no value to the Tyrians. If we consider the Hebrew word, it should be compared with <term>Kebel</term> <note>Hebrew: כבל</note> which has the meaning of an iron shackle or iron chain. From this, the Rabbis understand it to mean a "muddy land" which holds back the feet by its tenacity and binds them as if with a shackle. I do not know how this note helps in understanding the history, as it could just as easily be told of sand as of mud; whence Fuller also doubts
<margin>Musc. 16</margin>
whether this land was considered sterile by the Rabbis because of marshiness or sand. He adds that Brocardus testifies that part or tract of Lebanon was fertile and cultivated beyond measure. If that were so, what was noted by the Rabbis would be of no use at all. It is certain the land was displeasing, but it is not so easy to guess why it did not please the eyes. Fuller surmises that the cultivation of the land was laborious and did not suit the luxury of the Tyrians; and that the wise King wanted to moderate their luxury by this means.
There were formerly many cities of great name in this tribe between the Eleutherus and Jiphtah-el. *Hazor* or *Asor*, which nevertheless, if we wish to follow Mr. Johann von Felden's map of the Holy Land, belongs to the tribe of Naphtali; compare *Joshua 19:36.* Jabin, the seat of the King of the Canaanites in these regions in the time of the Judges, was a most renowned city, concerning which Fulcher of Chartres says:
<margin>History of Jerusalem p. 434.</margin>
> Tyre is richer and nobler than all the cities in the land of promise, except for Hazor, which Jabin the King of the Canaanites possessed in ancient times, and which Joshua afterward destroyed with many others.

# From Joshua 1, v. 2. 293

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
...highly fortified for commerce; the former, however, was populous with an infinite number of people; the latter situated on the sea coast; the former placed in the plains. It had as a neighbor the noble city of New Giscala, mentioned in Josephus’s history of the *Jewish War*, book 4, chapter 4. At the roots of Mount Lebanon is placed Enoch, which Josephus calls Enosa, the most ancient of all cities the world holds. For this is believed to have been built by Cain, who is celebrated as the founder of seven cities by Philo in *Biblical Antiquities* <note>original: "Antiq. Bibl."</note> and by Bornitius in *On the Foundations of the State*, chapter 4, page 21. Cain was the first who founded a city on earth, and he lost the celestial city. On the other hand, pagan writers record that the method of first founding and later preserving cities was handed down and invented by the most ancient Jove; others make Cecrops the first to build cities (compare Danaeus, *Antiquities*, page 256 and following). Among other nations, the Greeks imagine the first construction of cities originated with them, as Stephanus relates in *On Cities*, noting that the Athenians called their city *polis* <note>original: "πόλιν"</note> and the citadel of the city *acropolis* <note>original: "ἀκρόπολιν"</note>. Scripture records that Cain, after killing his brother, fled into the land of Nod (Jerome <margin>column 307</margin> in his *Letter 48 to Sabinus* reads this as *Naid*, which Erasmus wrongly reads as *Naim*, explaining it as the city where the widow's son was raised by Christ) and built a city named after his son. But where this region of Nod is and where the city was built, we remain ignorant since Scripture is silent, contenting ourselves with knowing this: *the first founder of an earthly city was a fratricide, who, overcome by envy, killed his brother, a citizen of the eternal city wandering as a pilgrim on this earth*, as Augustine learnedly speaks in *The City of God*, book 15, column 810.

Having thus seen the cities situated at the roots of Mount Lebanon, it will not be inconvenient to say something of the mountain itself. The higher a mountain is, the more its summit is cold, abounding in perpetual snow and ice. We observe this on the highest peaks of the Alps, and those who travel the Pyrenean passes know it. Lebanon, the "Alps of the Holy Land," which girds it from the north and east, is seen covered in perpetual snow at its summit; yet it is adorned with cedars and other most beautiful trees, bright with medicinal and fragrant herbs, and rich moreover in the firmest and whitest marbles, as the eyewitness Johannes Phocas noted <margin>chapter 4, page 6</margin> in his *Description of Syria and Palestine*. He commends Lebanon for its various kinds of trees and fruits: *The all-beautiful and worthy of song in the scriptures. Lebanon is a massive ridge, draped from summit to foothills with drifts of snow like flowing curls, forested with pine, cedar, and cypress, and beautified by an abundance of other fruit-bearing plants.* <note>original Greek: "ὁ πάγκαλος καὶ ἀξίος... ὡραϊζόμενος"</note> Those who describe Lebanon usually take their argument from the origin of its name; since it often happens that a thing becomes clear through the origin of the word, I judge it right and good in this case to begin with that notion. Let us therefore be carried by the vehicle of the word to the summit of Lebanon, and since on its peaks snow appears whitening through the long course of years, I am inclined to believe the name was given from that. For they wish the name of the snowy mountain to be attributed to the Hebrew *laban* <note>original: "לבן"</note>, meaning *white*. Of this, Tacitus says: *Lebanon rises as the chief of mountains, marvelous to say, remaining shaded and faithful to its snows amidst such great heat.* The author of the *Jerusalem Itinerary*, cited by Drusius at

<column-break/>

Deuteronomy, page 530: *On the highest peak, as on the highest ridges of the Alps, there is perpetual snow, which is preserved with straw and carried in baskets to neighboring places sweltering in great heat, so that wine and other fruits may be tempered by the cold.* Rupert of Deutz <note>original: "Rupertus Tuitensis"</note> interprets it in almost the same way, saying: *Lebanon is interpreted as "whitening," and sometimes the Temple is understood by this name, as in Zechariah: "Open your doors, O Lebanon."* And in book 4 on Zechariah he says: *Lebanon, than which mountain that land had or has nothing higher, signifies the Temple in this place, than which that nation has nothing more august.* Besides a great abundance of the best frankincense, Manna is collected on Mount Lebanon and carried to Venice, not to mention the pastures; hence when Isaiah (35:2) paints the soul heavy with celestial goods and splendid with divine ornaments, he attributes the "glory of Lebanon" to it. It has two ridges: one is named *Antilibanus*, but the principal one is Lebanon, of which *Hermon* is a part, a mountain most celebrated in sacred song. Regarding this, Hilary says: *Hermon is a mountain in Phoenicia, the interpretation of which is "anathema" [a curse or set apart], for what is called Anathema by us is called Hermon in Hebrew. It is said, moreover, in a certain book of unknown authorship, that the angels who lusted after the daughters of men gathered especially on this high mountain when they descended from heaven. But let us pass over these things. For what is not contained in the book of Laws, we ought not to know; these things were mentioned only because the profession of the Prophet concerning this mountain of God reminded us of them. Certainly today the nations worship this mountain with profane religion, and they testify to the interpretation of its name, which is anathema, by that very impious seat of superstition.* <margin>Sacred Geography</margin> <margin>on Habakkuk book 2, folio 72a</margin> <margin>on Psalm 132, column 1058</margin>

Naphtali embraces almost all of Upper Galilee, the springs of the Jordan, and part of Mount Lebanon as far as Damascus. At the foot of Lebanon rise two springs, *Jor* and *Dan*, which flowing together into one constitute the *Jordan*. It first breaks forth small, but in the progress of its flow it acquires a wealth of waters, as Seneca says of the Euphrates and of our Rhine: *Look at the Rhine; look at the Euphrates; look at all the famous rivers; what are they if you judge them from where they flow out? Whatever they are, by which they are measured and named, they have acquired in their progress.* <note>original: "de Benef. lib. 4. 29."</note> Concerning its origin, we find diverse opinions in Josephus (*Antiquities* 15, ch. 13; *Jewish War* book 1, ch. 16; and book 3, ch. 18), to which we wish to refer the kind reader. From the source of the Jordan under Mount Lebanon for nearly a hundred miles, the Jordan itself has wide and pleasant fields and green meadows on both banks, with very high mountains placed here and there where these fields end, which extend even to the Dead Sea alongside the Jordan's stream. It passes through Lake Samachonites, which in ancient times they called the "waters of Meros" or "Meron" (Judges 5:23), and the Lake of Tiberias, which the Sacred Letters call the *Sea of Galilee* or *Chinnereth* or *Gennesaret*. Of this, Pausanias says <margin>in the Eliacs</margin>: *In the land of the Hebrews, I myself know a certain river, the Jordan, passing through a lake named Tiberias.* In Sicily, the river *Hipparis* flows through the Camarina marsh, *flowing through the middle of Camarina*, as the Scholiast of Pindar has it on page 42; which is also said of the Rhine in our Germany, flowing through Lake *Acronianus* <note>Lake Constance</note> in the same way.

It is also famous in the writings of secular historians, as witnessed by Pliny (Book 5, Natural History, ch. 15), Strabo (Book 16), Solinus (ch. 38), Tacitus (Book 5 of the Histories), and others. It is likewise famous for miracles and deeds, of which the Holy Scripture provides us a most abundant supply, so that there will be no need for our own materials here. It divides the land of Canaan into two parts, though unequal ones. The smaller part comprised two kingdoms, the Kingdom of Sihon and the Kingdom of Og, beyond or across the Jordan toward Arabia. Two and a half tribes held this smaller part, namely the tribe of Reuben, the tribe of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh; and this distribution was made while Moses was still living. The other part, and indeed the larger one, was between the Jordan and the Mediterranean Sea, whose inhabitants were the Palestinians. It comprised nine and a half tribes, and its division among the tribes was made by Moses' successor, Joshua, and Eleazar the High Priest of the Levitical worship. Therefore, on this side of the Jordan, the tribe of Naphtali received its lot. The furthest borders of Israel in Upper Galilee were closed by Hamath or Hemath, of which frequent mention is made in the books of Kings and Prophets—an ancient and fortified city assigned indeed to the tribe of Naphtali, which they were nevertheless unable to occupy because of the strong citizens descended from Amathaeus, son of Canaan, from whom the whole region received its name. It had its own King, who quite shrewdly obtained peace and a treaty from David. It was finally conquered by Solomon and fortified with a garrison, just like others in this region.

<margin>Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, 7.3 and 8.6.</margin>
It lost its ancient name under Antiochus, by whom it was called Epiphania, as Josephus witnesses. Not far away, situated by the Jordan river, was the city of Laish, or Laisa, or even Leshem by its ancient name, before it was occupied by the Danites (Judges 18:29). But after it came into the power of the Romans, it was called Paneas from the spring that washes it, and was established as the Metropolis of Iturea and Trachonitis. Greatly adorned and enlarged by Philip, son of Herod the Great, it was called Caesarea Philippi in honor of Tiberius Caesar, and a little later Neroniana; today, for several centuries, it has been known as Belinas. Toward the West in

<column-break/>

this tribe, there occurred between Laish and Riblah: Arama, Chinnereth (which King Ben-hadad conquered, <margin>Sacred Geography</margin> 1 Kings 15:20), Hazor, and other fortified cities. Situated on the bank of the waters of Merom was Riblah, where Pharaoh Necho, King of Egypt, led away Jehoahaz King of Judah into Egypt (2 Kings 23:33) and Nebuchadnezzar plucked out the eyes of Zedekiah (2 Kings 25:6-7). A spring named Daphne watered this city, famous for its very thick laurels, so much so that they recalled in some way that noble Daphne of Antioch (2 Maccabees 4:33). At the waters of Merom was also seen Harosheth of the Gentiles, in which lived Sisera, the commander of the army of Jabin, King of the Canaanites (Judges 4:2). Between Lake Samachonitis and the Sea of Galilee were cities of no small renown, of which Kedesh-Naphtali held almost the first place; assigned to the Levites and granted the right of asylum, this was the homeland of Barak, a most brave leader (Judges 4:6). Its ancient magnificence is shown there by great ruins and the most beautiful sepulchers of the ancients, says Brocardus <note>A 13th-century Dominican traveler</note>. <margin>T. J. p. 303.</margin> Arbel or Arbella occupied the middle ground between Riblah and Kedesh-Naphtali, from which the region <note>original: "ἐκχώρᾳ" - countryside/territory</note> takes its name. Famous there for its remarkable fortification was a cave, which Bacchides nevertheless conquered (1 Maccabees 9:2), and Josephus fortified it against the Romans when he presided over Galilee. Not far from that cave was Abela, also called Abel and Beth-maacah, whose name became famous from a siege (2 Samuel 20:15, cf. 2 Chronicles 16:4). Beth-shemesh, whose inhabitants were tributaries <margin>Judges 1:33</margin> along with the inhabitants of Beth-anath; it was named, if I am not mistaken, from a temple of the Sun therein, like the Baath of the Arabs situated by the Red Sea, which is corrupted from Beth-shemesh, and <note>original: "σὺν οἶκος ἡλίε"</note> "with the house of the sun," as Stephanus notes. There were besides Jabneel, Horem, and Safed situated on a very high mountain, all of which, as well as others whose catalog the Book of Joshua <margin>ch. 19:38</margin> shows us, belonged to the tribe of Naphtali. In later times, Capernaum or Capharnaum was situated on the shore of the Sea of Galilee in this tribe, a famous trading center and the primary city of the Decapolis; it had Christ as a citizen, whom it nevertheless held of little value, wherefore Christ predicts its destruction <margin>Matthew 11:23</margin>. Thus, once most flourishing, today it lies overwhelmed by its own ruins. For as Brocardus, an eyewitness, says <margin>ch. 4, § 7</margin>: *Capharnaum, glorious as he himself calls it, once a powerful city, is now so desolate that it has scarcely eight small houses, or rather I should say, huts.*

The tribe of Naphtali had neighbors, but across the Jordan (which was the boundary of both tribes), the half-tribe of Manasseh, which together with the tribe of Gad and Reuben had received the Trans-Jordanian lands as an inheritance from Moses himself. Concerning the Trans-Jordanian region, specifically regarding the location of the Canaanite land, we cite Johannes Pythius <margin>Treatise against Praedam, p. 23.</margin> when he explains the words of Moses: ("These are the words which Moses spoke across the Jordan") he writes thus: *You think that if the writer of this book had been in the stretch of the desert in the region of Suph between Paran, Tophel, etc., where Moses is said to have spoken these words, "across the Jordan," it is because he who spoke and he who wrote was not on this side of the Jordan, but across the Jordan; for that desert, and all the regions of the Moabites, have for many times past had this proper and most well-known name "Across the Jordan" with respect to the Holy Land of Canaan.* So that the scripture speaks, not respect-

# From Joshua 1, verse 2
## Kkk 2

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
With respect to the banks of the river, as in a crossing, or the actions of particular persons, the river itself is taken into account; but with respect to the regions, they retain their accustomed names. By its ancient name, that tract which the half-tribe of Manasseh received as a possession was called the *Land of Giants* and the *Kingdom of Bashan*. Within its borders was the Kingdom of Geshur, to which Absalom had fled (2 Samuel 13:37-38), and Damascus. Jair, the son of Manasseh, received a possession in the Region of Bashan around the thirty-eighth year from the Exodus, when Moses had set out to conquer the Kings Sihon and Og. The name given from antiquity was increased by a new denomination so that, once that Giant King was destroyed, it was called *Bashan, Havoth Jair* <note>original: "Havoth Jair" - meaning "The Villages of Jair"</note>, because that lot had fallen specifically to Jair, and was named by him for the fame and dignity of his name (Deuteronomy 3:14). Bashan בשן <note>Hebrew: Bashan</note> signifies *in the tooth*, or *in ivory*, or *in change*, or *in sleep*, or *in sleeping*; or *confusion* or *ignominy*, as Johannes à Leusden explains the Hebrew word in his *Sacred Onomasticon* <note>A dictionary of proper names</note> page 50. Jerome, indeed, in his commentary on *Isaiah 53, column 260*, explains it otherwise: *Bashan*, he says, *is a region across the Jordan, which the two and a half tribes possessed, and which is interpreted as most fertile and fat.* In the same region was Golan, a distinguished city in the regions of Bashanitis and Batanea, from which the region also took its name; which, with its suburbs, was a place of refuge for the Priests of the Levite line and for fugitives who killed a man unintentionally (Joshua 20:8). Just as Capernaum possessed the right horn <note>The northern/eastern side</note> of the Lake of Gennesaret where the Jordan enters; so the left was held by *Chorazin* or *Corotaim*, where Christ our Savior very often taught and bestowed many benefits upon it, though he announced an eternal woe to it along with the others (Matthew 11:21). On the same eastern shore of the pool was *Julias*, named after the daughter of Augustus Caesar, married to Tiberius—a woman most devoted to Venus—by Philip, who, when it was formerly a village of lower Gaulanitis, had surrounded it with a wall and granted it the rights of a city. Not far away was the mountain and *wilderness of Bethsaida*, in which Christ satisfied five thousand men with five loaves and two fishes. In its confines was the village of *Magdala*, which some call *Mageda*, others *Dalmanutha*, of which mention is made in Matthew 15:39 and Mark 8:10. And the region of the Gergesenes or Gadarenes, so named from the city of Gergesa, which had as its founder Gergesaeus, the fifth of the sons of Canaan: Also *Gadara*, situated on the same mountain, but removed a little further from the Sea of Galilee; this city was hated by Herod, whom they had accused of various crimes before Augustus Caesar, as well as by the Jews, since it preferred Greek institutions to the Jewish religion. It was not unknown to Strabo (Book 16), from which, according to Strabo, arose Philodemus the Epicurean (well known to Horace), and Meleager, and Menippus the <term>jester</term> <note>original Greek: παιγνιώδης - meaning playful or satirical</note>, and Theodorus the Rhetorician, whom Strabo says was his contemporary. Just as in this district was Jabesh, most famous for the very brave citizens of the city, of which mention is very often made in Holy Scripture (Judges 21:8, 1 Samuel 11:1, 31:11, 2 Samuel 2:5). Situated on the same shore was Hippos, or Hippene, a city not unknown to Pliny (Book 5, chapters 15 and 18), Ptolemy (Table 5 of Asia), Jerome (On Hebrew Places), and other writers. Neighboring this was Ephron, built on a high mountain,

<column-break/>

and founded almost at the extreme corner of the sea, where the Jordan flows out of it: sufficiently fortified and warlike, whence Judas <note>Judas Maccabeus</note> consumed no small amount of labor and time in capturing it; which, once taken, he plundered, burned, and utterly overthrew because passage had been denied (1 Maccabees 5:51). And these cities already enumerated in the tribe of Manasseh were almost all coastal, or certainly not far distant from the shore. Toward the mountains of Gilead there were other sufficiently fortified cities in this region, a catalog of which is supplied to us by 1 Maccabees chapter 5, where it lists the cities *Bosor, Alema, Chaspho, Maked*, and *Carnaim*. Also Pella, a city by the river Jabbok, concerning which see Deuteronomy 3:16 and Joshua 12:2, because it is the boundary of the region of the Ammonites, which the Patriarch Jacob crossed (Genesis 32:23); in which city the Christians saved themselves at the time of the destruction of Jerusalem. This city was founded by Seleucus, King of Syria, at the foot of Mount Gilead, and so named after the Macedonian city, the fatherland of Philip and Alexander.
<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
There were various mountains beyond the Jordan, namely Mount *Seir*, Mount *Hermon*, Mount *Lebanon*, and Mount *Gilead*, which nevertheless *all*, says Brocardus (Description of the Holy Land, p. 302), *are one continuous mountain, except that in different places they obtain different names.* Mount Gilead is the highest and seems to be the head of the others due to its prominence. In these mountains the Patriarch Jacob once struck a covenant with his father-in-law Laban (Genesis 31:47). Gilead is praised for its abundance of medicines and physicians (Jeremiah 8:21). Concerning that famous mountain across the Jordan, and the city clinging to it, let us hear Hosea (6:8): *Gilead is a city of those who work iniquity, defiled with blood.* First, it is said that there were makers of idols in it, for from the time an idol was established there, they thereafter learned not only to worship idols, but furthermore to become their manufacturers. Secondly, it is said to be "supplanted in blood," by which words they say two execrable types of crimes, with which that city was defiled, are insinuated: The first is homicide, for those men were, among other things, villainous and gasping for blood. The second is the infamous sin of luxury <note>In this context, "luxury" often refers to sexual immorality or excess</note>, by which, having fallen into every foulness, they defiled one another. Hosea comprehends both sins in one word, saying: *cursing and lying*. Concerning the triple meaning of Gilead, see Camartus on the deeds of the Prophet Elijah, chapter 5, section 8.
<margin>p. 224 seq.</margin>
There were furthermore in these mountains of Gilead, *Comon, Casphor, Gamala*, a city most fortified by the nature of its location, from which the surrounding region was called *Gamalitica*, in the storming of which Vespasian suffered a huge slaughter of his men, according to Josephus.
But it is time that, turning our backs on the mountains of Gilead, we sail again with our little boat across the Jordan into Lower Galilee, which in the lot of the promised land fell as an inheritance to the tribe of *Zebulun*. Situated on the coast and by the Mediterranean Sea in this tribe were the cities of *Sycaminum* (now *Ephsa*), and Zebulun, lying a little further from the shore, which Cestius the Roman General took and burned, according to Josephus (Book 11, Jewish War). In its border were *Gaba*, and *Cana*, surnamed *the Lesser*, otherwise of Galilee, in which Christ made wine from water (John 2:11). # SACRED ANTIQUITIES

A city most celebrated throughout the whole world, especially among Christians; for in this place Christ, the Deliverer of the human race, was conceived by virtue and the *overshadowing* <note>original: ἐπισκιασμῷ (episkiasmō)</note> of the Holy Spirit; here he was raised, and from this place he was named <note>i.e., Jesus of Nazareth</note>. Built almost in the middle of Lower Galilee was the largest and quite wealthy city of the Galilean towns, *Sepphoris, or Dio-Caesarea*, of which *Josephus* makes frequent mention in *Antiquities of the Jews, books 14, 17, & 18, and Wars of the Jews, books 2 & 3.* Also Hegesippus *book 1, chapter 30.* And <insert>Gath-Hepher</insert> <note>Hebrew: גת-חפר</note>. The glory of cities is not estimated by the magnitude of their walls, nor the splendor of houses and towers, nor the multitude of citizens, but chiefly by the integrity of the inhabitants; indeed, the strenuous deed of a single man can acquire celebrity for a city. Thence *Gath-Hepher* became known because it was the fatherland of the Prophet Jonah. It was distant two thousand paces from *Sepphoris* on the road leading to *Tiberias*, <margin>Prologue to Jonah</margin> according to the tradition of *Jerome*, and Jonah’s monument was shown there. *Shimron* <note>original: Semeron</note>, a city destroyed by Joshua, whose King fell together with others in the battle against Joshua, *Joshua 11:1, 12:20. Bethulia*, a city best known from the book of Judith, and *Dothan* <note>original: Dothaim</note>, mention of which is made in *Genesis 37:17 and 2 Kings 6:13*, not far from the torrent of the same name. *Rimmon* <note>original: Remmon, Rummon</note>, a name for several towns, which seems to have been bestowed from "pomegranates," situated on the bank of the torrent of *Dothan*. Not far from which was *Bethsaida*, a maritime city, the fatherland of Peter, Andrew, Philip, and other men most celebrated in Holy Scripture. Quite famous on account of the miracles performed there by Christ. Happy because of so many constant confessors of Christ; unhappy from incredulity, the punishment for which Christ foretold, *Matthew 11:21.* On the same shore was *Magdala*, the fatherland, as they say, of Mary Magdalene. *Tiberias*, formerly called *Chinnereth* <note>original: Cenereth</note>, which Fulcher of Chartres mentions.

<margin>History of Jerusalem, p. 402</margin>
> *It pleased our Princes to pass through the city of Tiberias next to the Sea of Galilee, which sea, gathered there from sweet water, has eighteen miles in length and five in width.*

Most fortified in these regions, not far from the Sea of Galilee, placed upon steep and abrupt rocks between Magdala and Tiberias, was *Jotapata*; it was so prepared by Josephus, the Governor of Galilee, that it had to be captured by Vespasian at last with incredible labor, or rather occupied by trickery; compare *Josephus, Wars of the Jews, book 3, chapters 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, & 13.* Between *Tiberias* and *Tarichea*, which others refer to the tribe of Issachar, not far from the shore was *Emmaus*, a distinct city, though *of the same name* <note>original: ὁμώνυμος (homōnymos)</note>, from that town in the tribe of Benjamin, not only ennobled by the victory of Judas Maccabeus, but especially by the deed of our Savior to be remembered, *Luke 24:13.* The last among the *Decapolis* <note>original: Δεκαπόλεις</note> was *Tarichea*, situated toward the East at the Sea of Galilee, a most fortified city, finally captured by Vespasian along with the remaining cities of Lower Galilee.

Between Mount Tabor, of which we shall speak immediately, and the Lake of Tiberias, according to the testimony of Jerome, begins the Region of *Sharon* <note>original: Sarona</note>, extending itself further from Caesarea all the way to Joppa. It is called by the Greeks *Saron, Saronas, and Asaron*. In Hebrew *Sharon and Ha-Sharon* <note>Hebrew: שרון & השרון</note>.

There was also a city of the same name, <insert>Sharon</insert> <note>Hebrew: שרון</note>, beyond the Jordan in the tribe of Gad at the river Arnon, *1 Chronicles 5:16.* Concerning the Region of which we now speak, the Holy Codex should be read: *1 Chronicles 27:29, Song of Solomon 2:1, Isaiah 33:9, 35:2, 65:10*, whence it is called *Asaron* from *Ha-Sharon* in certain manuscripts. That the region was

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
most fertile, level, and good for pasture, extending in a long tract between Caesarea of Palestine and Mount Tabor and Lake Gennesaret beyond Joppa, is shown by Geographers and testified by Jerome. <margin>Jerome, On Hebrew Places</margin> Even in his own age, there was a field there fit for feeding flocks, and the Map of Judea published in Amsterdam describes that region as *fat and oily* <note>Hebrew: דשן ושמן (deshen ve-shamen)</note>, and also vine-bearing, likewise productive of flowers, whence in *Song of Solomon 2:1* the rose of Sharon is mentioned; compare Louis de Dieu in *Acts*, p. 101; *Camerarius in Acts*, p. 258.

*Tabor* <note>Hebrew: תבור</note>, in Hebrew means *choice* or *purity* from the root *bar* <note>Hebrew: בר</note>, *pure*: or in Syriac *contrition* or *shattering*. According to Augustine’s interpretation in *Psalm 88, column 978*, it is *coming light*, and as Theophanes has it in *Homily 59, p. 403*: *Tabor is interpreted as the coming of light* <note>Greek: Θαβὼρ ἔλευσις φωτὸς ἑρμηνεύεται</note>. A word *of many meanings* <note>original: πολύσημος (polysēmos)</note>, simultaneously noting a city in the tribe of Zebulon given to the Levites, *1 Chronicles 6:77, 1 Samuel 10:3*, and a mountain in the same, which others however refer to the Tribe of Issachar, situated at the torrent Kishon <note>original: Cison</note>, which is distant fourteen miles to the North from Jerusalem, almost midway between the Eastern Jordan and the Western Syrian Sea. Famous for various events, especially by that illustrious manifestation of the Divine glory of Christ and his metamorphosis <note>The Transfiguration</note>, *Matthew 17:1 ff.* By *Josephus, Wars of the Jews, book 4, chapter 2*, it is called *Itabyrius*, by others *Tabyrius*; from the middle of the plain, it rises with a wonderful roundness on all sides to a height of 30 stadia. From the North, one climbs it with great difficulty. It had a plain on the summit of twenty-six stadia (others say 23), which space Josephus had formerly encircled with a wall in 40 days at the beginning of the Jewish war. But Placidus brought that mountain into his power by trickery. The aforementioned Monk <note>Brocardus</note> mentions the same, <margin>The Holy Land, p. 306</margin> saying:

> *There are on Mount Tabor still various ruins of palaces and towers, which today are the dens of Lions and other beasts. At the Southern foot of this mountain, opposite the village of Endor near the road which leads from Syria into Egypt, is the place where Melchizedek is said to have met Abraham with bread and wine as he returned from the slaughter of the four Kings.*

The side of the inheritance of Zebulon is closed by the *Kishon* torrent and the mountains of Hermon. At the Eastern foot, <margin>The Holy Land, p. 306</margin> says Brocardus, *of Mount Tabor descends the torrent Kishon, next to which Barak fought against Sisera and turned him to flight. Moreover, this torrent is gathered from rain waters which flow down from the mountains of Tabor and Hermon, and it is cast headlong into the Sea of Galilee.* The same author: <margin>at p. 307</margin> *From Acre it is four leagues to the torrent Kishon, where Elijah killed the Priests of Baal, and this torrent, having passed through a small space of land, enters the Great Sea <note>The Mediterranean</note> almost three leagues from Acre; and although we have said this torrent is carried into the Sea of Galilee, yet since the place of its origin is somewhat higher, it flows into different regions, namely partly toward the east into the Sea of Galilee, and partly toward the west into the Great Sea, and so there are two torrents and streams but taking their origin from one place. However, that Kishon which flows to the West gathers more water, because from Mount Ephraim and from places nearer to Samaria, and from the whole plain of Esdraelon, many waters flow together and are received into this one torrent.* Therefore the boundary of the tribe of Zebulon was the torrent Kishon, on the other side of which the inheritance of Issachar began. # Sacred Geography

### From Joshua 1, v. 2.

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
At the mouth of the Kishon torrent, where it empties into the Sea of Tiberias <note>The Sea of Galilee</note>, is **Cesion**, a city of the Levites. Not far from there was **Issachar**, a town not famous but obscure, except that it bore the name of the tribe's founder. More famous was **Bethsan**, otherwise called **Scythopolis**, because it was once restored by the Scythians. It was situated in a very pleasant location nearly in the middle space between the Jordan and the mountains of **Gilboa**. In this city, as Scripture witnesses in *1 Samuel 31:10*, the Philistines hung the bodies of Saul and his sons, who were slain in battle, from the wall of this city. Most well-known in this tribe <margin>Psalm 88:13</margin> were the **mountains of Hermon**, where animals were pastured for sacrifice in the Temple of Jerusalem because of the land's fertility, and **Gilboa**. Between these lay the **Valley of Jezreel**, and at the foot of Mount Gilboa, the city of the same name. In this city, Naboth was stoned by the order of Jezebel because of his ancestral vineyard; and here Jezebel herself, by the command of King Jehu, was thrown from a window and provided a feast for dogs (*1 Kings 21:13; 2 Kings 9:36-37*). David cursed the mountains of Gilboa, where Saul fell fighting for his country with his sons, praying that neither dew nor rain should moisten them (*2 Samuel 1:21*). Hence, there are those who believe David's curse was so effective that from that time neither rain nor dew has irrigated these mountains. But Brocardus <margin>ch. 7, § 10</margin> proves the contrary, taught by his own experience; he says that while staying overnight on these mountains in the month of November, he was soaked by dew beyond measure, and on the feast of St. Martin, he was thoroughly washed by the heaviest rains on the same mountain, and as he writes, he descended "soaked to the skin." The intervening valley is illustrious for the conflicts fought there. For there Gideon fought against the Midianites; Saul against the Philistines; Ahab against the Syrians; and in modern times, the Tartars fought there with the Saracens, as Brocardus writes (*T.S. p. 308*). The cities on this coast are not very famous. **Endor** is that city where Saul consulted the medium <note>original: "Pythoniffam"</note> (*1 Samuel 28:7*). **Nain** became known for the son raised from the dead by Christ before the city gates. **Shunem**, where Elisha, by the same means, raised the son of his nursing woman—a son previously obtained through prayer but then deceased (*2 Kings 4:17, 36*). Not far from there were **Jaramoth** and **Esdrelon** in the borders of the tribe of Issachar. Quite nearby was **Aphek**, most famous for the slaughter of the Syrians (*1 Kings 20:30*). On the sea coast was built the **Castle of the Pilgrims** <note>Château Pèlerin/Atlit</note>, fortified with great wealth by the Christians and famous in recent itineraries. **Mount Carmel** is most celebrated in both sacred and secular literature. It excelled in both beauty and abundance of fruit. It was held as sacred even by the pagans themselves. "Between Judea and Syria is Carmel," says Tacitus in *Histories, Book 2*, "so they call the mountain and the God; there is no image for the God, nor a temple. Thus the ancestors handed down only an altar and reverence." Suetonius in *Vespasian, ch. 5* mentions "consulting the oracle of the God of Carmel in Judea." And much older than these is Scylax of Caryanda: <term>Kamelos oros hieron Dios</term> <note>original Greek: "Κάμηλος ὄρος ἱερὸν Διός" — Mount Carmel, the sacred mountain of Zeus</note>. This signifies that it is both a mountain and a God, and the seat and sanctuary of a God. For there was no temple on it, as Tacitus indicates, but Mount Carmel itself was like the temple of the Deity, and indeed his body. For the God Carmel consisted of the spirit of the place and the vast body of the mountain. It is likely, however, that this opinion gradually crept in because Elijah

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
the Tishbite lived here and had a school, as John of Jerusalem recorded concerning the institution of the first monks under the Old Law. Indeed, we read that near there, at the Kishon torrent, 450 priests of Baal were killed by Elijah (*1 Kings 18*), and we know from *2 Kings 2 & 4* that Elijah's disciple Elisha fixed his seat here for some time. Because such great prophets chose this place for dwelling and performing sacred rites, it was long held as holy, and it was judged that worship would be more pleasing to the deity there (Vossius, *On Idolatry, 2.62, p. 640*).

The **half-tribe of Manasseh** across the Jordan possessed sixty large and excellently fortified towns; that land was called **Bashan** because of its fertility, according to Jerome. It was formerly inhabited by giants, whence it was called the **Land of the Giants** or **Rephaim**. It also contains **Trachonitis**, which is a region like a kingdom. On this side of the Jordan, this tribe obtained a very fruitful land between Issachar and Ephraim, which extends in length from the Jordan River to the Great Sea and the city of **Dora**. **Dora** (also called Dor or Adora), situated on the shore of the Western Sea, was besieged by Antiochus with huge forces (*1 Maccabees 15:13*) to bring **Tryphon**, who had fled to this maritime city, back under his power. On the same shore is seen **Caesarea Palaestina**, a most fortified and wealthy city. It is girded on the west by the Great Sea, and on the east by a certain fresh and deep marsh, in which there is a multitude of crocodiles and a great abundance of fish, according to Vitriacus (*ch. 56*). Herod Agrippa, fearing a revolt of the Jews, imposed this city upon the whole nation like a citadel; he adorned it entirely with marble buildings, both royal palaces and the houses of private citizens, and—what was most laborious—he added a harbor (named **Sebastus** in honor of Caesar) safe from storms. Here, while Herod was being hailed as a God by the people during games dedicated to Augustus, he was struck by an angel and died, according to Josephus (*Antiquities 19, ch. last; Jewish War 3.14*). Here Cornelius the Centurion was baptized by St. Peter (*Acts 10:48*). Here Paul, in chains, appealed to Caesar (*Acts 25:11*). It was also called **Strato's Tower**, **Flavia Colonia**, and by Pliny, **Apollonia**. On the same Mediterranean shore is **Capernaum**, and in the borders of this tribe is **Antipatris**, formerly called **Capharsalama**, built on pleasant soil and surrounded by a fertile grove and a river on every side. It was restored by Herod and so named in honor of his father, Antipater. Here Judas Maccabeus routed the forces of Nicanor (*1 Maccabees 7:31*). Here Paul was first sent by the tribune to be safe from the ambushes of the Jews, so that he might be sent further to Caesarea to Felix the Governor (*Acts 23:30*). Not far from the maritime cities of Caesarea and Dora was **Megiddo**, today called **Subimbre** according to Brocardus <margin>T.S. p. 307</margin>, situated in a plain by a certain torrent named **Kane** <note>meaning "Reed"</note>; a city famous for the memory of things that happened there. For Ahaziah, King of Judah, died in this city after being wounded by Jehu <margin>2 Kings 9:27</margin>, and Josiah, a most pious king, while fighting against Pharaoh Necho, expired there after being wounded—a sad fate for the Church and the Jewish state (*2 Kings 23:29*). In the same plain were situated the towns of **Adrademmon**, today called **Maximianopolis**, and **Gaber**, situated on a hill, on the ascent of which King Ahaziah was wounded.
