# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES.

-> Sacred Geography <-
<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
In this region, the Cave or *Mount of the Prophets* was also shown, so named because Obadiah, the steward of the wicked King Ahab’s palace, hid one hundred prophets here and sustained them with bread and water (1 Kings 18:4). Toward the Jordan in this tribe lay *Taanach*, where Deborah, with the help of Barak, defeated Sisera in a glorious victory; and *Thebez*, situated in a fertile place and distinguished by a strong tower, in the siege of which Abimelech perished (Judges 9:53). *Tirzah* or *Therza* was the royal seat of the Kings of Israel before Samaria was built (1 Kings 14:17; 15:33). Closer to the Jordan was *Ophrah* of Ephraim, not unknown for the history of Gideon and the fratricide of Abimelech. There was also *Aenon* near *Salim* in these regions by the Jordan, where John was baptizing (John 3:23). At the edge of this tribe toward the Sea of Galilee was the town of *Salem*, which some identify as the palace of Melchizedek. Jacob, coming here with his company, bought a portion of a field from the sons of Hamor, where he pitched his tents (Genesis 33:19).

The region of Gilead belonged to some extent to the tribe of Manasseh (Joshua 13:31), but for the most part it pertained to the tribe of Gad (Numbers 32:26; Joshua 13:25; 2 Kings 10:33). For after the two Kings of the Amorites, Sihon and Og, were defeated, Moses assigned all this land to the tribe of Reuben, the tribe of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, on the condition, however, that they should go armed before their brothers and help them in occupying the land of Canaan.

<margin>on Matthew 25, col. 1128.</margin>
*Mahanaim* or *Manaim* was the first city of the Gadites, situated not far from Ephron; it received its name from the "army of angels" <note>original: "acie angelorum"</note> whom the Patriarch Jacob encountered when returning from Mesopotamia. Regarding this, Ratbertus says: *Jacob met a multitude of the divine host, who relieved him of his fear of his brother and guarded him. Whence he called the place where they were seen Manaim, that is, the camps of God.* David stayed here in this city when he fled from the weapons of his wicked son Absalom (2 Samuel 17:27). Across the brook Jabbok was the place where Jacob wrestled with the Angel all night, and because he had beheld the face of the Lord, he gave the place the name <note>Hebrew: מחנים, Mahanaim</note>, "seeing God" or "the face of God" <note>The author here conflates Mahanaim with Penuel/Peniel</note>. This city, because it denied provisions to Gideon’s army, was destroyed by Gideon and its inhabitants killed (Judges 8:17). It was later restored by Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:25). Closer to the Jordan stood *Succoth* <note>Hebrew: סכות, Sukkoth</note>, meaning "tents," a name given by the Patriarch Jacob, who pitched his tents there when he met his brother Esau and was reconciled with him (Genesis 33:4, 17). In the borderland of this city and Penuel was the wilderness of *Mahanaim* and the forest of *Ephraim*, in which Absalom, with his forces, paid the deserved penalty for his sedition. Famous in this tribe were the cities of *Ramoth Gilead*, a priestly city and city of refuge, which Ahab, King of Israel, wished to seize against the will of God, but he fell wounded in battle. Then *Mizpah*, the seat of Jephthah the Judge, and *Rabbah*, the royal seat of the King of the Ammonites situated at the brook Jabbok, which in later times obtained and kept the name *Philadelphia* from its restorer, Ptolemy Philadelphus. Furthermore, there was *Lo-debar*, from where David summoned Mephiboseth, son of Jonathan and grandson of Saul, to live at his table forever. And *Tishbe*, the homeland of the Prophet Elijah, concerning which Camartus says in his *De Rebus Eliae*: *Since Tishbe is*

And in this sense Elijah would be called a Gileadite, as were Jair, Jephthah, Barzillai, and those very men who are said to have occupied the fords of the Jordan; for they all received their name from the region.* *Arnon* surpassed the others in this tract in fame, built among steep and rugged rocks; between it and Jazer was the region of *Tob* <note>Hebrew: טוב, "Good"</note>, into which Jephthah fled when expelled from his father's house, where he supported himself as best he could, having become a "leader of brigands" <note>Greek: λῃσάρχος, lestarchos</note> who gathered to him. It has springs constantly flowing, and on account of the slow-moving waters and irrigated fields—in which Isaiah predicted so many would be killed that its rivers would seem turned to blood (Isaiah 15:9). *Heshbon*, which nevertheless pertains to the tribe of Reuben, was a glorious city situated in the mountains, surrounded by a wall of fired brick, which a great number of villages served as their mistress. There was also a city of the same name among the Ammonites. For Moses had given the tribe of Gad half the land of the sons of Ammon (Joshua 13:25). Regarding how this agrees with the words of Moses in Deuteronomy 2:9, 19, the Blessed Bugenhagen provides a reconciliation, writing: *God had given the land to the Ammonites, just as God gave all nations their lands, though they be ignorant and ungrateful, as Moses sang. But the Ammonites, in addition to the lands they had previously occupied by God's gift, seized much land by wars and injury from the land of the Amorites, as it seems, across the brook Arnon [which is the border of the sons of Ammon] where Sihon, King of the Amorites, reigned. Therefore, the land of the Amorites, or part of the dominion of King Sihon, and certain adjacent places across the brook Arnon which the Ammonites had occupied by plunder and which did not belong to the land God had formerly given them, are called in the book of Joshua "half the part of the sons of Ammon," as being occupied and possessed by them.*

To *Ephraim*, the second son of Joseph, fell a territory that, although mountainous, was nevertheless very fertile, situated on this side of the Jordan: it is bounded on the East by the Jordan, on the West by the Great Sea, on the South by Benjamin, and on the North by the half-tribe of Manasseh. It had elegant cities, "level and flowery" <note>Greek: εὐπέδους καὶ ἀνθηρὰ</note>, as Strabo says of a certain city of the Bruttians (Geography, Book 6, p. 177). Because of its fertility, it is called in Isaiah 28:1 the "fat valley."

On the sea coast, this tribe had the city of **Apollonia**, which **Josephus** mentions in *Antiquities book 13, chapter 21* and *The Jewish War book 1, chapter 6*. Not far from there was **Sarona**, situated on a mountain, from which the adjacent region near the sea—being most fertile—took its name; for the plains were called the **Plains of Sharon**. There was also **Gophna** beyond the mountains of **Ephraim**, and **Beth-horon**, surnamed **the Upper**, <margin>1 Kings 9:18</margin> which **Solomon** fortified and within whose borders **Judas Maccabeus** carried off several notable victories, as witnessed by the first book of **Maccabees**. For there were two cities by the name of <note>Hebrew: בית - חורון</note> **Beth-horon**, one of which was called **the Upper** in the tribe of Ephraim, assigned to the Levites; the other, **the Lower**, seems to have fallen to the Benjamites, as the first book of **Chronicles** testifies in *chapter 7, verse 24*. The second book of **Chronicles**, *chapter 8, verse 5*, records that both cities were fortified by **Solomon** with walls, gates, and bars, where the words are: "And he built moreover **Beth-horon the Upper**, and **Beth-horon the Lower**, cities fortified with walls, gates, and bars" <note>original Hebrew: ערי מצור חומות דלתים ובריח; original Greek: πόλεις ὀχυρὰς τείχεσι, πύλαις καὶ μοχλοῖς</note>. However, in the history of the **Kings**, mention is made only of the Lower **Beth-horon** as being restored by **Solomon**, *1 Kings 9:17*.

They are mentioned by **Jerome** in the Letter of **Paula** <note>original: "phio"</note>. Setting out from there (Nicopolis or Emmaus), she ascended to **Beth-horon the Lower** and **the Upper**; by which words he records that Paula climbed up from Nicopolis (which was previously called Emmaus) to **Beth-horon**, and saw **Gibeon** and **Aijalon** on the right. Near to it was **Hyrcanium**, a very strongly fortified castle best known from the writer of Jewish affairs, **Josephus**. Toward the north is **Mount Gerizim**, the highest of the whole tract of Ephraim; since it is twin-peaked, one summit was named **Gerizim** and the other **Ebal**, the former destined for blessing and the latter for cursing, concerning which one should read **Moses**, *Deuteronomy 11:29*. Perhaps for that reason **Sanballat the Cuthean**, the Governor for **Darius King of the Persians** in these regions, was moved to build a Temple on this mountain to rival the one in Jerusalem, in which he made **Manasseh**, his son-in-law and brother of Jaddua, the High Priest. This provided the cause and source of the schism between the Samaritans and the Jews. This temple lasted over two hundred years, until **John Hyrcanus**, son of Simon (the last of the Maccabean brothers), brought an end to this schism; he destroyed both the temple and the nation of the Cutheans and the city of **Shechem**. Compare **Josephus**, *Antiquities of the Jews, book 13, chapters 16 and 17*, who in chapter 6 of the same book reports that when the Samaritans and Jews litigated before **Ptolemy Philometor** concerning the <term>superiority <gloss>original Greek: ὑπεροχῇ</gloss></term> of each temple, the King, having heard the case and with the unanimous consent of the litigants themselves, decreed the death penalty for the petty lawyers of the losing side. Not far from Mount **Gerizim** was **Bethel**, situated on a high mountain, in which **Jeroboam, son of Nebat**, placed one of the golden calves by which he made Israel to sin. From there, half a league toward the left, is another mountain named **Dan** above the city of **Shechem**, in which according to some the other golden calf was placed. But Saint **Jerome** thinks it was established in the city of **Dan**. Between these two mountains is situated the city of **Shechem**, which the Patriarch **Jacob**, when close to death, handed over as a legacy to his son **Joseph** as a benefactor, and thereby increased his wealth

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
beyond the others. "I have given to you," he said, "one portion (the city of Shechem) *above your brothers*, <margin>Genesis 48:22</margin> *which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and my bow*." But why did he grant that city to Joseph rather than to **Simeon** and **Levi**, its conquerors, or to **Reuben** the firstborn? They say the city, which had been associated with defilement, was given to the most chaste Joseph so that he might purify it by the example of his chastity. On this matter, one should read **Ambrose** *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs, chapter 3*. In this city, or near it, the holy Patriarchs **Abraham** and **Jacob** lived for some time by the **Oak of Moreh** <note>original Hebrew: אלון מורה</note>. Long afterward, <margin>Genesis 12:6</margin> **Abimelech** utterly destroyed it, *Judges 9:45*, even sowing it with salt. It was quite elevated, so that the view from there extended far and wide. On this mountain—from which, on account of wickedness and idolatry, God took away the Ark and the sacrifices—He delivered the inhabitants into the hands of the Chaldeans and finally the Romans. We shall say no more of the metropolis in this place than what we will say elsewhere, or only in the words of **Brocardus**, who has this to say concerning the site and <margin>T. v. 5. p. 312.</margin> circuit of the city of Jerusalem:
> Jerusalem, the city of the Most High God, is situated in a mountainous land. For there are mountains round about it, and it has fertile and good land in its circuit, except toward the east and toward the Jordan. It is situated from the South on the side of Mount Zion, and from the west it has Mount Zion; nor is its site changed today, as some falsely claim, since because of the fortification of the places it cannot be moved from its original site. It is indeed somewhat enlarged in width, but not in length, since it cannot be extended on the side of the citadel and Mount Zion; for that mountain towers over it, yet is enclosed within the walls of the city, being very spacious, so that it could almost provide the foundation for the city by itself. For it begins from the Water Gate or the Fountains of Siloam toward the East, and in its tract through the south all the way to the west it describes almost a semicircle, with a steep cliff surrounding and consolidating this semicircle. From the western part, where we said the ridge of the mountain begins, the Tower of David is situated on a certain hill of that same steep cliff, and it had at its back a certain abyss which comes from the southern part of Mount Zion, and reflecting in the corner of this tower, it turned toward the East and was divided into two deep valleys, one of which verges to the North, the other to the East, constituting another corner opposite to that corner on which the Tower of David rests. Hence the Valley, which descended from the Tower of David against the Northern side of Mount Zion as far as Mount Moriah (in which the Temple was), extended from Mount Zion and the whole lower city as far as the Brook Kidron, through the place where the Water Gate now is between Mount Zion and the Palace of Solomon, which was built on the Southern part of Mount Moriah; and in this way that abyss surrounded Mount Zion on every side, and this was the City of David. But now the abyss itself is entirely filled up, though traces of the former hollow remain. But the other...

# SACRED ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
*Indeed, the abyss or valley, which was divided by that [wall] near the tower of David, proceeded toward the North and formed the ditch of the city along its length, as far as the Northern Quarter; and above it on the inside was an overhanging height, which Josephus calls Arrum, which supported the city wall placed upon it, encircling the city from the West and coming as far as the corner gate, which was established in the corner of the city against the North and East corner; and there it curved again from the North through the East against the South outside the temple area, enclosing it and the gate of the spring near Mount Sion.*

Closer to Jerusalem one encounters Bethany, which signifies the village of humility and affliction, through which an entrance to the kingdom of heaven lies open to us, just as Christ penetrated to heavenly joys from the village of affliction: And Bahurim, a fortified town known for the cursed tongue of Shimei, *2 Samuel 16:5.* And in this tract is Anathoth, a priestly city, the homeland of the Prophet Jeremiah, *Jeremiah 1:1.* So also Ramah, not far from Shiloh, which Baasha King of Israel repaired and fortified, so that he might make incursions into Judea. Concerning this city, Brocardus <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and famous traveler to the Holy Land.</note> says: <margin>T. S. p. 309</margin> *To those going from Gibeah one league toward the South, the city of Ramah occurs, but what exists today is a village situated on a mountain to the left of the road leading into Jerusalem. There are also other villages in the holy land called Ramah, one near Tekoa on the road going to Hebron; another in the tribe of Naphtali not far from the village of Safed; a third in Shiloh, and all these villages lie on high hills; for Ramah is interpreted as "high place."* Gibeah or Geba was a fortified city in the tribe of Benjamin, to the North, of which we read in the books of Kings <margin>1 Kings 15:22</margin> that it was built from the ruins of the city of Ramah by King Asa; for when Baasha, King of Israel, had been driven away from fortifying the city of Ramah, then Asa gathered all Judah to destroy the fortification begun in Ramah: with no one exempt and no one immune from the labor, the Jews, obeying the command in a great crowd, flocked there and carried away the stones of Ramah and its timber, with which Baasha had made the fortification, and from them he built Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah. We learn from the prophecy of Zechariah that it was a border town of the Benjaminites, who, taking this place from the boundaries of the kingdom of Judah, writes in *chapter 14:10*: All the land shall be turned into a plain from Geba even to Rimmon <note>original: מגבע לרמון (mi-Geva le-Rimmon)</note> where the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> rightly has, *from Gabaan even to Remmon*, whereas in the former place they rendered it appellatively as "the hill." However, the Old Interpreter <note>Referring to the Vulgate/Latin translation.</note> in this place translated poorly as "the hill of Remnon," though he had translated well in the books of Kings: "Gibeah of Benjamin." Thus, either the translators were different in different books, both among the Greeks and the Latins, or they were inconsistent with themselves; since nevertheless the sense is clear concerning the same place, whatever else might seem to Jerome, who explains the words of Zechariah <margin>Vol. 6 col. 609</margin> concerning the hill of Remmon, for he says this is what Gibeah sounds like, where there was also a pomegranate tree. This was the homeland of Saul, the first King of the Israelites, where also that unspeakable crime against the Levite’s concubine was perpetrated, concerning which Jerome says in *Letter 27 to Eustochium*: <margin>91. 223.</margin> *In Gibeah, a city destroyed even to the ground, Paula paused a little, remembering its sin, and the concubine divided into pieces,*

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
*and the tribe of Benjamin, of whom three hundred men were reserved for the sake of Paul the Apostle.* Not far from there was Michmash, the seat of Jonathan, the brother of Maccabeus, *1 Maccabees 9:73*, and the rock of Rimmon, in which 600 men, the remnants of the Benjaminites, took refuge after all the Benjaminites had been cut down, from whom the tribe later regained its strength, *Judges 20:47.* Near the rock of Rimmon were the mountains of Bethel, known from the sacred writings, *2 Kings 2:23.* Not far from these was Bethel, a name given to the place from a most auspicious origin. Jacob had come into it, and hearing and seeing wonders, as if clouded by terror, he said, *Genesis 28:17, 19: How terrible is this place! This is none other than* <note>original: בֵּית אֱלֹהִים (Beit Elohim)</note> *the house of God, and he called the name of that place* <note>original: בֵּית-אֵל (Beit-El)</note> *Bethel, whereas Luz was the name of that city before.* Again we read of the same place <margin>6. 35. 14.</margin> *Jacob had set up a pillar in that place where God spoke with him, a stone pillar, and he poured a drink offering upon it and poured oil over it. Thus Jacob called the name of that place where God spoke with him, Beth-El.* To celebrate the place, he summons the most celebrated name of God and calls it the house or place of God. The word <note>original: בַּיִת (Bayit)</note> "house" is in very frequent use among the Hebrews, who are accustomed to apply it to signify various things, which should be mentioned by us in another place rather than this one. It is a common point that from the word <term>Elohim <gloss>God</gloss></term> is contracted <term>El <gloss>God/Mighty One</gloss></term>, just as <term>Eli <gloss>my God</gloss></term> and <term>Elohai <gloss>my God</gloss></term>. It is elegant through its very simplicity, by which we are reminded at once of true happiness and its practical use. Jacob erected an altar in this place because God had been revealed to him there. Afterward, according to some, Jeroboam erected a golden calf in this place, although it should rather be determined that he erected it in the Bethel of the tribe of Ephraim near Shechem. For some confuse both places, deceived by the name, which is read as having been given to many places. Charlemagne was also deceived by this in his *Capitulary on Images* <margin>Book 4, ch. 13, p. 512</margin>: *The city of Samaria, Luz, which received the name Bethel, i.e., the house of God, from the Holy Patriarch Jacob, and in which the same Patriarch saw a ladder touching from the earth even to heaven, and the Angels of God ascending and descending by it, afterward had golden calves as a stumbling block for the house of Israel, which the worst of Kings, Jeroboam, instituted to be worshipped there; and the place of which the holy man said, "Truly the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not"; and which, admiring with great awe, he said was terrible, and that there was nothing else there but the House of God and the Gate of heaven, afterward became the House of the Idol; and a cause of danger to the Israelite nation; neither the consecration of the Stone erected by the Patriarch, nor the anointing of the sacred Oil, nor the calling of the revered name restrained the wickedness of the unspeakable King Jeroboam from his perverse action, but he did not fear to pollute with idols the place which he knew was admired by so great a Patriarch.* That city which was formerly called Bethel, i.e., the house of God, and a place dedicated to worshipping God: that place, on account of King Jeroboam’s golden calf worshipped there, is called by Hosea <margin>ch. 4:15</margin> <note>original: בֵּית-אָוֶן (Beit-Aven)</note> *Beth-aven*, which Aquila and Symmachus <note>Ancient translators of the Old Testament into Greek.</note> interpreted as *an unprofitable house*, a house of vanity, <note>German: Eitelhausen/ Mußstatt/ Sundhoffen - "Vanity-town," "Useless-place," "Sin-village."</note>. Luther uses that word concerning the College of Canons that was at Wittenberg, which he wished to be reformed or abolished, writing to Georg Spalatin <margin>O. T. 2. Epist. f. 109. b.</margin>: *What is the Bethaven of All Saints but a brothel? And would that it were only a brothel. But it is sin,*

# From Joshua Chapter 1, Verse 2

...son, as Amos says of Amaziah, it is the king’s sanctuary <note>original: *sanctificatio regis*. See Amos 7:13</note>. Would that the Prince might also set his hand to the matter there. Certainly, these sins will weigh heavily upon her. Likewise to the same person on folio 111a: *How our Bethaven <note>House of Iniquity—a derogatory name for Bethel</note> might be changed regarding the scandal of our neighbor and the offense of the living, who could easily say? Especially if you call that a scandal or offense by which the impious Papists are offended. If you do not yet know, almost all the Priests there act not only impiously, but with a stubborn heart; despisers of God and men, they commit adultery almost every night, and with an impudent and hardened brow, they celebrate Mass in the morning. Now consider what this abomination deserves before God for the Prince and his people, by whose expense they are maintained.* Again to the same: *Now is the time to weaken that Bethaven, which has been tolerated until now with great scandal. God must not be tested further; therefore help, as I know you wish and as you are able, contribute.* From a letter of Luther to the Provost and Canons of All Saints' Church, which appears on folio 126b, 153. Not far from the town of Bethel was Ai (or Hai), a town which Joshua finally took by ambush, as his book testifies in chapters 7 and 8. Nearby is the Mountain of the Devil, where it is believed Satan tempted Christ the Savior after he was taken up. In these regions, the Quarantana <note>The Mount of Temptation, from the Latin *quadraginta* meaning forty</note> mountain and desert occur; on this mountain, Brocardus <note>A 13th-century Dominican traveler</note> maintains Christ was tempted by the Devil, but according to Saligniaco, it is the mountain where he fasted for 40 days. This entire tract took its name from Mount Quarantana near the city of Jericho. Truly, no more fitting name could be given to the city of Jericho—which was a little more than four miles from Jerusalem—because its site is seen to be such that you could not even fit a more convenient one to achieve all those things expected from the position of places. For the yield of palms and roses contributes greatly to the adornment of this city, and it seems to have received its name from the sweetness of the odors arising there, as it might be called <term>רוּחַ</term> <note>Ruach: to smell or breathe</note>, to smell, from the fragrance of the balsam which grows there with the greatest fertility; or from <term>יָרֵחַ</term> <note>Yareach: Moon</note>, the Moon, *Luneburg* <note>Moon-town</note>, by which Augustine intends a naming convention in Letter 119 to Januarius, column 565. That places are often named from the yield of fruits needs no proof. Thus Tappuah is named from apples; Rimmon from pomegranates; Batnae from pistachios; Luz from almonds. Pliny confirms this regarding Jericho in Book 5, Chapter 17 and Book 12, Chapter 25, stating that the entire tract was fertile with palms and groves of palm-trees. It is enough for us if it is established from the gardens of Scripture that the palms of En-Gedi and the roses of Jericho are praised (Sirach 24:14) and that Jericho is called the City of Palms (Deuteronomy 34:3; 2 Chronicles 28:15; Judges 1:16). It had mountains to the North and South, which stretched on both sides toward the Jordan. These mountains provided a secret hiding place, on Rahab's advice, for the spies sent out by Moses and Joshua; she persuaded them not to keep to the straight path toward the river crossing, nor to betake themselves there quickly, for they could thus be easily captured, but that it was safer to keep themselves among the windings of the mountains and the caves of the rocks. For she said to them:

> Go to the mountain, lest those who pursue you happen upon you, and hide there for three days until the pursuers return, and afterward you shall go your way.

It suffered a triple devastation and a triple restoration. For when Joshua, by divine command, burned it—

<column-break/>

<margin>Cursed be the man before the Lord who shall rise up and build the city of Jericho. Joshua 6:26.</margin>
<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
—adding a curse. However, this curse, which was by God's command, did not deter Hiel (1 Kings 16:34), in whom detestable ambition was so strong that not even the death of his sons could deter him from finishing the work against the will of God. Whether it suffered devastation under Nebuchadnezzar is not clear from the Sacred Scriptures or from Josephus. Herod the Great and Archelaus enlarged it, building there an amphitheater and a fortress, which Herod named Cypros after his mother's name. Overturned by Vespasian in the Jewish War, it is written to have been restored again by Hadrian; hence in Jerome's age (in *On the Sites and Names of Hebrew Places*), Jericho still existed, but built in another location. But by the time of Brocardus, it lay so devastated and cut down, perhaps by the arms of the Saracens, that he writes it had scarcely nine houses, nor did it deserve to be called even a small village, and all the monuments of the holy places were utterly destroyed. One league from Jericho toward the Jordan is situated Gilgal, once a famous city, where Joshua, having overcome the river, had his stationary camp, pitched the Tabernacle of the Lord, and celebrated the second circumcision there; they remained in that same place until they were healed. Saligniaco testifies that Gilgal is two miles from Jericho, and was once a famous city, but is now a village.

<margin>T. 9. c. 5. Matthew 3.</margin>
And Jerome, in Letter 27 to Eustochium, chapter 226, mentions both:

> *Having entered Jericho,* he says, *Paula saw the city which Hiel founded in Abiram his firstborn, and whose gates he set up in Segub his youngest son. She beheld the camp of Gilgal, and the heap of foreskins, and the mystery of the second circumcision; and the twelve stones, which, carried there from the bed of the Jordan, strengthened the foundations of the twelve Apostles; and the fountain once most bitter and sterile of the Law, which the true Elisha seasoned with his wisdom and converted into sweetness and abundance.*

He speaks of the fountain of Elisha, about which Josephus tells wonders in Book 5 of the *Jewish War*, chapter 4. Not far from Gilgal was Bethabara, which signifies "house of passage," where Joshua, the waters of the Jordan having been divided, crossed over with the people on dry feet. Bethabara was situated across the Jordan in the tribe of Reuben, which received its possession beyond the Jordan in the land of Moab, fertile with the best herbs and very suitable for feeding cattle; a place most memorable for various deeds performed there. Here the people of Israel were led across the dried-up Jordan, where six hundred thousand men fit for military service, excluding wives, children, maidservants, and beasts of burden, crossed while the Jordan stood like a cliff, where it was turned backward,

<margin>Psalm 114:3</margin>
as the Psalmist sings, until the people could cross. Where the Ark of the Covenant stood in the middle of the ford until the crowd crossed through the Jordan into the promised Palestine, as the history is described in three chapters in Joshua. The interception and slaughter of the Midianites also once made the place famous, as in the history of Judges 7:24. So too the crossing of Elijah and Elisha through the Jordan on dry feet (2 Kings 2:8, 14). Finally, that miraculous crossing was made more illustrious when John began his Baptism, and there baptized Jesus Christ, our Savior. Neighboring this in the tribe of Reuben, partly at the bank of the river...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
...partly not far from it, namely **Livias**, which Herod had built on the shore of the Jordan in honor of Livia, the mother of **TIBERIUS Caesar**; **Besor**; and **Shittim**, where the Israelites committed fornication with the daughters of Moab and Midian (Numbers 25:1). These places were not of such great authority and renown as **Bethabara**, which has been held in great honor by the pious at almost all times. <margin>On Hebrew Places</margin> **Jerome** is a witness to this fact: "Bethabara across the Jordan, where John baptized for repentance; whence even today many of the brothers—that is, from the number of believers—desiring to be reborn there, are baptized in the life-giving waters." <note>original: "vitali gurgite," literally "vital whirlpool" or "living depths."</note> What its modern appearance is, and the nature of the river in this place, **Bartholomew of Salignac** (that French knight and legal scholar) eloquently explains: "The Jordan," he says, "at the place where Christ was baptized, is marked by a ruined building: clearly a house with a far more famous title, where the Heavenly Father was present in a voice, the Holy Spirit in the appearance of a dove, and the Son in human flesh was to consecrate baptism as the remedy for human salvation and the gateway to the sacraments. Here, therefore, all we pilgrims entered the holy river and washed both our bodies and our souls: the former from filth, the latter from sins—an event of the highest joy and salvation; had not a sad accident disturbed our joys. For a certain French physician of our company, an upright man, when he entered the river a little too far, was seized by a **Crocodile** (you might call it a dragon or an uncertain beast) and swallowed up, not without the shared sorrow of our brothers."

Near the Dead Sea, where the Jordan flows into Lake Asphaltite <note>The Dead Sea</note>, **Machaerus** is seen, a most beautiful and fortified castle, of which there is frequent reading in **Josephus**. It was first built by Alexander, King of the Jews, because of the convenience of the location, but magnificently adorned and fortified by Herod. Josephus writes in *Antiquities* Book 18, Chapter 7, that John the Baptist was imprisoned and executed there.

Not far from here were the **Mountains of Abarim**, which run in a long stretch to the mountains of Gilead from the land of Moab, and separate the Ammonites from the Amorites. The higher part of these mountains is **Nebo**, and the summit itself is **Pisgah**, from which Moses, now near death, beheld the entire Promised Land from Beersheba even unto Dan, where also shortly after he died and was buried by God himself (Deuteronomy 34:5-6).

This place of encampment is famous because they stayed <term>at Abarim <note>Hebrew: בעברים (Be-Abarim)</note></term> (Numbers 21:11). Regarding the name, since it is uttered in the plural number, the cause is investigated. Anyone even moderately skilled knows it has the meaning of "crossing over" <term>Abar <note>Hebrew: עבר, to cross over</note></term>. **Schindler** says it is spoken in the plural, *Abarim*, either because it had two crossings, or because the Israelites crossed there. It seems to foreshadow no ordinary crossing, but an extraordinary one: that it was the "crossing of crossings," the goal of crossings, the end of the journey taken, from which there is now an easy passage into Palestine.

<margin>*</margin> For here was the final station in the plains of Moab by the Jordan. Likewise, in the region of this mountain was **Peor**, itself a very high and steep mountain, from which Balak showed Balaam the camps of the Israelites (Numbers 22:41). Moreover, in this tract were the more famous cities: **Heshbon**, situated on a mountain, formerly the seat of the King of the Amorites, later assigned to the Levites, whose pools were then on everyone's lips, to whose beauty the eyes of the Bride of Christ are compared (Song of Solomon 7:4). So also...

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
...**Kiriathaim**, a city formerly inhabited by the **Emim**, a robust, fierce, terrible, and giant race, whom Chedorlaomer nearly destroyed, whose descendants the Moabites exterminated, but the sons of Reuben rebuilt (Genesis 14:5, Deuteronomy 2:10, Numbers 32:37). Near the torrent were **Medeba**, **Baal-meon**, and **Kedemoth**, a city of the Levites (Joshua 13:21, 1 Chronicles 6:79), which is also called Jeshanah. Not far from Lake Asphaltite was **Lasha**, an ancient city, later called **Callirrhoe** in Greek, named from springs of entirely different natures flowing together, since various springs of water—hot and cold, sweet and bitter—flow out there. Here Herod the Great, tortured by a varied and foul disease, saw to it that he was carried, but in vain (cf. Josephus, *Antiquities* Book 17, Chapters 8 & 10, and *Jewish War* Book 1, Chapter 21).

After Paradise, the most beautiful tract was the land of **Sodom and Gomorrah**, also called the **Valley of Salt-pits**, praised for its fertility and pleasantness; for God himself has told us that the land was like the Paradise of God. A happy land because of the abundance and goodness of its fruits and other things springing from the earth, but ill-fated because of its most wicked inhabitants, the memory of which is held as unhappy and ill-fated even to this day, remaining from so many centuries ago.

When a quarrel arose between the shepherds of Abraham and Lot, Abraham allowed Lot a free choice of either keeping his tent or moving it elsewhere: "Choose," he says in Genesis 13:10, "whichever land you prefer, the rest is for you, and I will depart elsewhere." He, however, leaving the mountains, chose the most pleasant valley, where so many vices sprouted up that the region was destroyed by God through fire. <margin>On Abraham</margin> **Ambrose** says* he chose badly, as experience proved; for from there he was led into captivity, and finally all his substance perished there. This tract is also called the **Valley of Siddim**, in which the battle was joined where the Kings of Sodom and the others fell, and Lot was led away captive.

<margin>Genesis 14:8, 9, 10</margin>
Let us hear Moses speaking thus about this battle and the place of the battle*:
> But the King of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, and they fell there.

<margin>Genesis 14</margin>
War having been joined between the five kings (Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Bela) and the four kings (Chedorlaomer, Tidal, Amraphel, and Arioch) in the Valley of Siddim, Lot is captured with all his substance. Mention of that valley is made in verses 3, 8, and 10, and that word <term>Siddim <note>Hebrew: שדים</note></term> is not fully known to the Hebrews. After God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah with fire sent from heaven and ruined that whole tract, the entire Valley of Siddim, which abounded in wells of bitumen, was turned into Lake Asphaltite or the Dead Sea, which is called the Sea of Salt in verse 2. There is also mention of the **Valley of Salt** in the history of David, where from Pagninus's interpretation we read it translated thus:

<margin>2 Samuel 8:13</margin>
"David made a name for himself when he returned from striking Aram in the Valley of Salt, eighteen thousand being slain." David attained a famous name because he killed eighteen thousand Syrians in the Valley of Salt-pits. **Borrhaus** is mistaken here, writing*: <margin>column 498</margin> "The Valley of Salt is that which is also called the wooded valley, which the Lake of Asphaltite floods, which anciently, before Sodom was overturned, when it was well cultivated, was compared to the Paradise of God." He thinks that the Valley of Siddim, which became the Dead Sea, is to be understood here, and that the Valley of Salt, in which the Syrians and Edomites were destroyed by David, is the same as that valley in which Lot was captured. This was also formerly the opinion of **Epiphanius**...

# Sacred Geography

->From Joshua 1, verse 2.<-
**Lll 2**
<meta>catchword: Deuteronomy</meta>

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
...was the opinion of those who wished the "Valley of Salt" <note>original Greek: κοιλάδα τὴν ἁλυκὴν</note> to be what is called the "Dead Sea" <note>original Greek: τὴν νεκρὰν καλουμένην θάλασσαν</note>. In the time of David, that valley no longer existed, for it had been changed into the Dead Sea, and a battle could not be fought in the Dead Sea. That valley was in Idumaea, which is situated far from the Dead Sea. See Salmasius *in Solinum p. 613, 614.*

Abraham, with God granting him victory, liberated those led away by the enemy and brought them back; yet the people of Sodom and their allies did not allow themselves to be converted to a better way of life, but as Josephus testifies, *elated by riches and an abundance of money, they were as insolent toward men as they were impious toward God, inasmuch as they neither remembered his benefits nor welcomed strangers; finally, they even defiled themselves with mutual lusts.* Offended by these things, God decreed to inflict the due punishments for their pride, and to render their region so devastated that hereafter it would produce neither plants nor any fruit. Abraham intended to avert this disaster with his prayers, whence contending with GOD he said: For the sake of fifty righteous men forgive them, for the sake of forty, for the sake of thirty, and finally for the sake of ten. To whom God replied: <margin>Genesis 18:32.</margin> *If there be ten righteous men, I will not destroy these five cities for their sake.*

Therefore the cities themselves perished with their inhabitants; and the entire region, so much so that today, besides a lake—dreadful to look upon, exhaling heavy mists and foul-smelling smoke—not even a single trace remains, cf. *Fulcher of Chartres, History of Jerusalem p. 405. Varthema, Book of Navigation 10. p. 195.* Indeed, after the celestial fire of Sodom, nothing is shown to us but an example of impiety, and a most empty appearance of pleasures, which God left for us to contemplate in the *Apples* <note>The "Apples of Sodom," described by ancient travelers as beautiful fruit that turned to smoke and ash when touched.</note> which grow there, with the beauty of external form and a colored surface for show, concerning which Solinus aptly writes in chapter 44: <margin>Deuteronomy 2:13.</margin> *They shine for appearance, for a mere pretense of the outer skin contains within a soot-like ash, which, pressed by even a light touch, exhales smoke and crumbles into wandering dust.*

The valley of Shaveh and the city of the same name closed off the eastern region of the Asphaltite Lake <note>The Dead Sea</note>. Midian, the women of which city enticed many of the Israelites to the worship of Idols, *Numbers 25:14.* so also *Memrim* is near the torrent Zered, which descends through the valley of the same name into the Dead Sea, and which the Israelites crossed. Across the Zered river, the neighbors of the Dead Sea were the Arabs of Arabia Petraea, whose metropolis was *Petra* of the desert, a very ancient fortified city situated on a mountain. So called by the Greeks: But by the Hebrews *Sela*, and formerly, *Arce, Arcen* or *Arecen*: later *Rekem* and *Rekeme*. The Israelites once captured this, *Numbers 31:8. and Amaziah, 2 Kings 14:7. and he named it Joktheel.* And Aretas, King of the Arabs, held it in the time of Antipater, the father of Herod, as Josephus testifies in the 14th book of *Antiquities, ch. 9.* The Christian Princes of Europe, who had occupied Palestine five hundred years ago, and specifically King Baldwin, are said to have enlarged this city. Today it is held by the Sultan, who stores there the treasures of all Egypt and Arabia. From where this tract was called Arabia, authors go into a divorce of opinions. Scaliger thinks it received its name from the west, namely—

<column-break/>

—from *Ereb* <note>original Hebrew: ערב</note>, which signifies "evening" <note>original Greek: ἑσπέραν</note>, as in *Genesis 1:5. & Numbers 21:1.* where the Septuagint translates it as "of the west" or "the setting sun" <note>original Greek: δυσμῶν</note>. <margin>Sacred Geography Book I.</margin> In the same way the Arabs were the same as the *Essenes*. And for the same reason Scaliger thinks they are called "desert-dwellers" <note>original Greek: ἐρημικοὺς</note>. Truly in Homer these same Arabs are called *Erembi* <note>original Greek: ἐρεμβοὶ</note>, as found in Strabo. But if the Arabs were so called, it is as if the name of that nation had been sought from more remote sources. From the Persians? But their language is different. Nor would the Greeks have sought the name of that nation from more remote sources. From the Syrians or Babylonians? But these are to the south. I rather judge that they were first called Arabs who inhabit the desert of Arabia: Hence the name was attributed to others as well, for *Arabah* <note>original Hebrew: ערבה</note> means *desert, solitude.* Or it can be said to be like a "dregs of men," from *Arab* <note>original Hebrew: ערב</note>, meaning *mixture, mingling*, cf. *Vossius, On Idolatry 26. p. 186.* For suitably to this name of theirs, the Arabs even today live by plunder, retaining by tradition the ancient *nomadic and predatory* <note>original Greek: νομαδικὸν καὶ λῃστρικὸν</note> way of life. Whoever visits the Holy Land as a traveler experiences their robberies. The monk Malchus experienced the robberies of the Arabs on a journey, in whose life Jerome writes: <margin>From Beria Vol. 1. col. 340.</margin> *To those going to Edessa, a solitude is near the public road, through which the Saracens, with uncertain dwellings, always wander hither and thither, which suspicion gathers a crowd of travelers in those places, so that imminent danger may be avoided by mutual help. There were in my company men, women, old men, young men, small children, about seventy in number. And behold, suddenly the Ishmaelites, riders of horses and camels, rush in, with long-haired and banded heads, and half-naked bodies, wearing cloaks and wide boots. Quivers hung from their shoulders, vibrating loose bows; they carried long spears. For they had come not for fighting, but for plunder. We are seized, we are scattered, we are dragged in different directions.* A prophecy against Arabia is brought forth by Isaiah in chapter 21, whose slaughter he foretells will be in the desert. He exhorts the citizens of the city of Dedan to meet the fugitive and thirsty Arab with bread and water. Toward the south of the Dead Sea were the cities of the Arabs, *Dumah, Dedan, and Teman*, in the last of which *studies of wisdom* are written to have been cultivated of old, *Jeremiah 49:7.* Bordering these is Mount *Seir*, in which the Horites previously lived, whom the sons of Esau occupied after they were expelled and destroyed; they remained untouched by the sons of Israel in the time of Moses, as he himself asserts, *Deuteronomy 2:5.* Truly it was *Seir* <note>original Hebrew: שעיר</note>, a mountain of a long tract, fortifying Idumaea between the Asphaltite Lake and Egypt, which took its name from Esau, who had the surname *Seir*, because he had come into the light hairy or shaggy, and had lived here. Generally, the mountains which closed off Judea to the south are called the *mountains of Seir*; he who is bristly, shaggy, and hairy is called *Seir* <note>original Hebrew: שעיר</note>, such as a goat, which has its name from this, and elegantly *barley* is named *Seorah* <note>original Hebrew: שעורה</note> on account of the spikes or awns ending in hairiness. At that time the Israelites not only spared their Edomite brothers, but even, having sent legates to them from the King of the Edomites, they very humanely asked that they might be allowed to cross their borders without harm. But the Edomites refused this request of theirs, and met their brothers, the sons of Jacob, in arms. Hence, by the command of God, the Israelites turning aside, avoided their encounter, *Numbers 20:21. Deuteronomy 2:8.* inasmuch as God was going to give them nothing of their land.

However, in the time of David this was permitted, for he placed governors in Edom after the Idumeans were reduced to servitude. <margin>1 Chronicles 18:13</margin> Finally, Hyrcanus also compelled them to undergo circumcision, as witnessed by Josephus, who discusses their wicked character *thus*: <margin>The Jewish War, Book 4, Chapter 6</margin> *They knew they would be persuaded, being a tumultuous and disorderly nation, always hovering toward movements and rejoicing in changes, moved to take up arms by the slight flattery of those in need, and rushing into battle-lines as if to a festival.* <note>original Greek: ἤδεισαν πεισθησομένους... This quote characterizes the Idumeans as fickle and prone to violence.</note>

In the mountains of Seir is **Kadesh-Barnea**, from where Moses sent the scouts into Canaan; it is the southern border of the tribe of *Judah*, but to the west toward Egypt lies *Sihor*, the brook of Egypt. On its shore was built *Rhinocolura* (or as others prefer, *Rhinocotura*), so named from the mutilated noses of its inhabitants, according to the <margin>opinion of Strabo, Book 16; Diodorus, Book 1, Chapter 60; and Seneca, On Anger, Book 3, Chapter 20.</margin> <note>Rhinocolura means "cut-off noses"; legend says a king settled criminals there after mutilating them.</note> This city, along with other notable towns, was seen on the shore of the Mediterranean Sea, among which were *Raphia* and *Anthedon*, later called *Agrippias*. In these places are shown the spring of *Hagar*, where she fled from the house of Abraham when driven out with her son Ishmael, and the *Juniper of Elijah*, under which Elijah fled when avoiding the threats of Jezebel. Furthermore, this place is desert and uncultivated due to the multitude of sand—whence it is often called the *sandy desert*—both because of the lack of water and the heaps or mountains of sand, by which travelers are not infrequently overwhelmed. This desert, together with the western region as far as the tribe of Dan, fell as an inheritance to the tribe of Simeon from the portion of the tribe of Judah, because the portion of the children of Judah was too large for them. <margin>Joshua 19:9</margin> Near the brook Besor were the towns of *Gerar*, the royal city and metropolis of the Philistines, situated between Kadesh and Shur—two wildernesses, the latter of which joins Egypt, while the former reaches the desert of the Saracens. Frequent mention of it is made in the journey of Abraham toward the south country. For in this place Abraham lived for some time; here Isaac was born; and here Isaac himself fixed his tent after the death of his father. <margin>Genesis 21:32; Chapter 26:23</margin> **Beersheba** is also a town near the brook Besor, with a well of the same name, where the Patriarchs Abraham and Isaac spent many days of their pilgrimage. <margin>Volaterranus, Book 11; Ptolemy calls it Bersana.</margin> The barbarians now call this *Gibelin*, according to Volaterranus. Beyond it were the *Well of the Judge* and the *Grove of Abraham*. In the plains, the tribe of Simeon had cities that were less famous. *Bethul*, a city in the inheritance of the tribe of Simeon, is known by its name: for the word <term>בתול</term> <note>Bethul/Betulah</note> is a lovely term for a mature maiden of marriageable age. *Ziklag*, which Achish the Philistine once gave to the exiled David while he was earning wages in his army. <margin>1 Samuel 27:6</margin> The coastal shore was inhabited by the *Philistines* (corruptly called *Palestinians*): termed by the Greeks *allophyloi*, that is, foreigners; they were domestic and *implacable* enemies of the Israelites, whom David, that most pious King renowned for many naval victories, finally brought to order and made tributary to himself. They possessed cities celebrated for both their population and location, two of which were situated in the tribe of Simeon, not far from the Mediterranean Sea. **Gaza** takes its name from "strength," for

<column-break/>

it is called <term>עזּה</term> <note>Azza</note>, which signifies *strong*, and there is an elegant wordplay in Zechariah where the Prophet says *Azza is to be weakened.* <margin>Sacred Geography, Chapter 9, Verse 5</margin> Therefore, the name is not derived from <gloss>treasure</gloss> <note>original: "za-beu"</note>, as Mela thinks, writing: *In Palestine is the huge and very fortified Gaza (so the Persians call a treasury), and the name comes from the fact that when Cambyses sought Egypt with arms, he had brought the wealth and money of the war here.* <margin>Book 1, Chapter 11</margin> Mention of it is frequent and famous in Holy Scripture; it was finally overturned by Alexander the Great. But under Augustus and Nero it was restored in another location and became a famous trading center, to which goods were carried by camels from Arabia Felix. <margin>Pliny, Book 12, Chapter 14</margin> In the times of Constantine the Great, when it professed the Christian religion, it was called *Constantia* after the name of the Emperor's sister. Today it is *Gazera*, a large city of Palestine, twice as large as Jerusalem; called *Ajan* by the Syrians, it is governed under the tyranny of the Turks by a Captain or Pasha, who defends the city against the treacherous Arabs, as related by Thevet, who reported that the ruins of Samson's Palace were shown to him by a Jew. <margin>Cosmography, Book 4, p. 157</margin> The other Philistine city in this tribe is **Ashkelon**, built in a semi-circular shape at the very harbor of the sea, 720 stadia distant from Jerusalem, as Hegesippus determined. It was once noble and powerful, though its fortune varied. It was especially hostile to the Jews, for which reason Josephus son of Tobias once punished it severely (cf. Josephus). <margin>Antiquities, Chapter 4</margin> Robert mentions it: *Ashkelon is a distinguished city of Palestine, twenty-five miles distant from Jerusalem, which the foreigners once founded and called Ashkelon from the name of Celon, who was the grandson of Ham and son of Mizraim. It was always an adversary to Jerusalem, and although it is a neighbor, it never wished to be joined by any familiarity.* <margin>History of Jerusalem, p. 77</margin> And Brocardus: <margin>Brocardus, Description of the Holy Land, p. 321</margin> *To this day it remains situated on the seashore, having a semi-circular shape: strongly fortified, upon which now depends the whole strength of the Saracens.*

The inheritance of the **Danites** was divided from the tribe of Simeon by a certain brook, perhaps *Sorek*, where the most noble vines used to grow; it was bounded on the west by the seashore; from there it extended from Azotus, or near that city, as far as Joppa. To the east, toward the southern side, it stretched from Azotus beyond Eleutheropolis; and thus it turned back toward Kiriath-Jearim and from there to Joppa.

In the plains and far removed from the seashore in this tribe, *Eshtaol* (or *Astaol*) deserves mention, near which Samson was born and buried. <margin>Judges 13:24; 16:31</margin> Also the Philistine city **Azotus** or **Ashdod**, which was one of the five Satrapies of the Philistines. It is situated about six German miles from Jerusalem toward the West near the Mediterranean Sea, close to Ekron. Into this city the Ark of the Covenant was once carried by the Philistines into the temple of *Dagon*. <margin>1 Samuel 5:1</margin> In this place also Philip was found, after he had baptized the Eunuch of Queen Candace and was transported there by an Angel. <margin>Acts 8:40</margin> It was once a most noble city, famous for the temple of the idol Dagon, but now, almost destroyed, it has become a village. **Ekron**, the fourth city of the Philistines, was not far distant from the shore of the Mediterranean Sea; frequent mention of it is made in the sacred records. In it, superstitious nations worshipped the idol *Baal-Zebub*, to whom Ahaziah, King of Israel, sent to inquire for the sake of recovering his health. <margin>2 Kings 1:2</margin>

# From Joshua 1, verse 2.

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
Today it has cast off its ancient splendor, for according to the witness of Brocardus <note>A 13th-century Dominican traveler to the Holy Land</note> (T. S. p. 320), it has been turned into a small hamlet, though it retains its former name. On the borders of Judea, in the tribe of Dan, is situated **Modin**, the homeland of the Maccabees. Their famous marble monument is there, built by Simon, the brother of Maccabeus; it rises with seven pyramids from a square base to such a height that it can be seen by sailors. (Josephus, *Antiquities* book 13, ch. 11; Borchardus, part 8, ch. 7). Not far from there was **Themnas**, or Timnah, where Samson tore the lion apart (Judges 14:6). A little toward the North was situated **Kiriath-Jearim**, in which the Ark of the Lord remained for twenty years (1 Samuel 7:2). For the citizens of Beth-Shemesh had sent to the inhabitants of Kiriath-Jearim so that they might come and take the Ark of the Lord away to themselves (1 Samuel 6:21). **Beth-Shemesh** was a city in this tribe given to the Levites, not far from the sea, into whose field the Ark of the Lord had been brought back by young cows from Ekron; because the people of Beth-Shemesh inspected it too curiously, they paid a huge penalty for their curiosity (1 Samuel 6:19). There remains the fifth city of the Philistines, situated on a mountain not far from the sea to the West for those traveling from Jerusalem, whose name is <term>Gath</term> <note>meaning "wine-press"</note>, the homeland of Goliath, whom David, while still a youth, struck down with a sling, and of other men of immense stature (2 Samuel 21:19 ff.). To this place the Ark of the Lord was also brought after the Israelites were defeated, but when the Gathites felt the hand of the Lord, they sent it to Ekron (1 Samuel 5:9-10). Coming here, David escaped the snares of King Achish by feigning madness, a history which Josephus provides in detail in *Antiquities* book 6. It profited him to "play the fool in the right place," which Horace said was sweet. Thus the Roman annals testify that Lucius Junius Brutus, the first Consul, feigned stupidity so that he would not be killed by his uncle Tarquin the Proud, and from this he received the name "Brutus" <note>meaning "dull" or "stupid"</note>. Gath experienced the same fortune as the rest of the Philistines.

<margin>T. S. p. 320</margin>
For today, as Brocardus witnesses, it is a small hamlet called Modin or Vobim situated on a hill; compare also Jerome on Micah ch. 1, col. 332. While we persist in the unfolding of this city, a passage in Micah 1:10 occurs to us, much vexed by fate: *In Gath, announce it not.* We explain it simply thus: Just as David once (2 Samuel 1:20), seeing the kingdom had received a great wound with the death of Saul and his sons, wished this calamity could at least be hidden so that the sworn Philistine enemies of the Israelites would not find out and rejoice, insulting him and the people of God—lest this be added to the remaining evil—he said, "Tell it not in Gath." So also the Prophet in this place, in a similar or even heavier affliction, now uses these words and commands his listeners not to weep or wail at all (compare Amos 6:10). Saint Jerome, weighing the words of Micah 1:10, *In Gath announce it not with tears*, struggled with various difficulties in interpreting it and could not satisfy himself, which he confessed with a candid mind, twisting his pen into these words:

> *The Hebrew differs much from the translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint Greek version</note>, and both my translation and those of others are involved in such difficulties that if ever we—unworthy of the Spirit of God (though we always need His coming when explaining Holy Scriptures)—now especially desire Him to be present. And at the end he says: Thus far according to*

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
> *the Hebrew, as we were able and as it seemed to us, or certainly as we heard from the Hebrews, we have steered our little ship as if between sharp rocks and crags; whether it has entered the harbor or still tosses on the salt sea, it will be for the reader's prudence to judge. And afterward he adds: I beseech the reader not to think necessity is my will, nor to consider a long exposition as wordiness, but rather to marvel that I found anything at all in such rough places, rather than that I missed anything that ought to have been said.*

Gaspar Grajan, formerly a Master and Professor of the Bible in the Academy of Salamanca, marks the Vulgate translator with a censor's mark because he often translated Hebrew proper names with a common meaning; for he publicly declared this while commenting on Micah ch. 1, f. 40. <margin>Salamanca edition, 1570.</margin> Among other places which Santes Pagninus—a man most skilled in the Hebrew language—brings forward in his letter to Pope Clement VII to defend his opinion (against other learned men who have contended about this matter in books published in our time) that the Vulgate edition which the Church now uses is not Jerome's, this is one (Micah 1: *In Gath announce it not*), because he put adjectives or nouns in place of the names of cities, which the most learned Jerome would not have done. It usually produces no small obscurity in the Holy Scriptures if proper names are used as common nouns, or conversely, if someone thinks common nouns are proper names. Thus, one will more clearly understand the passage in verse 15: *His place was made in peace and his dwelling in Zion*, if he notices that in place of "peace," the Hebrew has: *His place was made in Salem*, which he immediately explained in other words (as we have warned frequently happens in the Psalms), *and his dwelling in Zion*. So in Genesis 33 it is held: *Jacob passed into Salem.* The translator thought it was the proper name of a place, when yet here it is a common noun, and should be translated: *Jacob came safe (or peaceful) to the city of Shechem.* He then brings forward other places, using also the testimony of Martin Martinez, who rebuked the same error of the Vulgate translator in his book *Hypotyposeon*, saying among other things: "He who knows this is a vice worthy of notice will find innumerable instances of this kind." A short distance from Gath to the west lay <term>Joppe</term> <note>Modern Jaffa</note>, a maritime and most noble city, now Jaffa, founded before the flood by Japheth the son of Noah, as they say; this fact about this most celebrated city was also known to secular writers (see Pomponius Mela book 1, ch. 11; Strabo book 16; Pliny, *Natural History* book 5, ch. 13). It was chiefly a dwelling for merchants, who lived there as if in a sort of marketplace. This port was once most convenient for the Jews, as is clear from the history of Solomon. For Hiram sent cedar beams from Lebanon by sea to Joppe, from where Solomon took care to have them carried by land to Jerusalem for the building of the Temple and his house. <margin>* fol. 111. a.</margin> Hence Bede says: *Joppe, a maritime city of Palestine, distant about forty miles from Jerusalem. Furthermore, Sidon and Tyre were most noble Phoenician cities, having Mount Lebanon in the vicinity; the children of the captivity, obtaining help from them, asked for cedar wood to be cut for them from Lebanon and brought by rafts over the sea to Joppe, from where they could again be carried by land to Jerusalem for the work of the Temple.* Here also Jonah boarded a ship...

The Prophet Jonah—from whom Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymo"</note> in *Volume 2, Apology against Rufinus, column 362* hears of the "Port of Jonah." This is a convenient port for all who set out from Europe to the Holy Land; from there, traveling by a land route through ***Ramah***, the homeland of the Prophet Samuel, they go up to Jerusalem.

The boundaries of the tribe of Judah are the Dead Sea to the East; Idumaea and Seir to the South; Simeon and Dan to the West; and Benjamin to the North.

Libnah, a city of the Priests, and *Lachish*, cities of the tribe of Judah, are very near to the mountains of Ephraim; they fix the limits of this tribe in a narrow space from the North. It takes its name from the moon or its white color <note>Libnah derives from the Hebrew root for 'white'</note>, regarding which Stephanus says: *Plinthine, a city of Egypt, named after the one in Samaria.* That is, *Plinthine is a certain city of Egypt having its name from that city which is in the borders of Samaria.* Stephanus thought the Egyptian Plinthine was named after the city of Libnah, whose history is recorded in sacred scripture, *Joshua 10:29.* Both are counted among the fortified cities which Sennacherib was about to occupy when he sent Rabshakeh to Jerusalem, *Isaiah 37:8.*

<margin>Jeremiah 34:7</margin>
So also *Lachish* was one of those fortified cities that remained safe from the arms of Nebuchadnezzar, to which is joined *Azekah*, to which Joshua once pursued his enemies, *chapter 10:10.* Not far from there was *Makkedah*, a city and a cave where Joshua trapped the five kings of the Amorites, whom he finally hanged from trees after the battle was finished, *Joshua 10:26.* Furthermore, in those same borders occurred *Sochoh*, where the Philistines pitched camp against Saul, and they had Goliath with them in their camp, *1 Samuel 17:1.* Toward the South, not far from the borders of Dan, is written to be *Emmaus*, a town ennobled not only by the victory of the Maccabees, but also by the wondrous deed of our Savior, *Luke 24.* Later it was called *Nicopolis* <note>City of Victory</note>, from a victory, it is believed, won by the Romans over the Jews; compare *Jerome on Hebrew Places; Salignac book 7, chapter 4.* Between Jerusalem and Bethlehem, at the borders of Benjamin and Judah, lies *Beth-zur*, a very well-fortified castle, first fortified by the Maccabees in such a way that it was the strongest castle in all Judea, according to Josephus, *Antiquities book 13, chapter 9.* From there toward Bethlehem, the tomb of Rachel was once shown, concerning which Bede says in his *Homily on the Feast of the Innocents: Rachel was buried near Bethlehem, just as the inscription of her monument remaining to this day testifies to the west of the city, beyond the road which leads to Hebron.* Bethlehem, which is also called Ephrata—from which its inhabitants are called Ephrathites of Bethlehem Judah, to distinguish them from the Ephrathites of the tribe of Ephraim, *Judges 12:5, 1 Kings 11:26*—was a city near Jerusalem, distant from it by about six miles, that is, a journey of perhaps two or three hours. It received its name from the fertility of the place, and it is the *House of Bread* <note>Hebrew: Beit Lechem</note>, where Christ, the Bread of Life, was born. Hence Jerome, in *Letter 27 to Eustochium, column 234*, makes Paula, a most noble Roman woman who established four monasteries there, speak thus melodiously <note>original: "ἐυφώνως"</note> upon entering Bethlehem:

> Hail Bethlehem, house of bread, in which was born that Bread which descended from heaven. Hail Ephrata, most fertile and fruit-bearing <note>original: "καρποφόρε"</note> region, whose fertility is God.

This place has always been holy and highly esteemed by pious and religious men, because the Savior of the world

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
uttered his first cries here, and here, being circumcised, willed to shed his blood for us. Hence, pilgrimage to it is frequent. Paula, a most noble matron, established two monasteries here so that by the constant devotion, especially of virgins but also of men, the memory of the divine benefit might be preserved. She is also said to have met her end here. Jerome, who also died here (whose cell, a workshop of prayers and meditations, they show there today), in order to serve God more conveniently according to his own judgment, sought Jerusalem and Bethlehem, having left behind the refined affairs of his homeland. Heliodorus was his chief companion on this journey, who also lived with him for some time in the desert. He stayed there among the monks in a strict way of life, promising himself that God would be more favorable because of such a rigorous life. "I," he writes to Theodora, "am the smallest and least of all Christians, and because of the consciousness of my sins, I inhabit the rocks of the Bethlehemite countryside."

<margin>Letter 29, column 251</margin>
Thus, out of a view of devotion and piety, he chose Bethlehem as his seat, and there, content with a small enough lodging, he devoted himself to prayers and readings. Concerning his second journey (for he went there twice) toward Bethlehem, he writes in *Apology 3 against Rufinus:*

<margin>column 362</margin>
> I entered Jerusalem. I saw many miracles, and what I had previously known by rumor, I confirmed by the judgment of my eyes. From there I hurried to Egypt, I surveyed the monasteries of Nitria, and among the choirs of saints, I perceived asps <note>metaphorical snakes/dangers</note> lurking. Immediately, with a quickened step, I returned to my Bethlehem, where I adored the manger and the cradle of the Savior.

Furthermore, he extols Jerusalem and Bethlehem here and there with various encomiums of praise; but while Jerome praises these cities and holy places so greatly, let us also consider what he himself says in his eulogy of the Bethlehemite countryside: *Each person praises most what he possesses.*

<margin>Letter 18, column 163</margin>
Today the town is greatly diminished, consisting of scarcely a hundred houses, and those meager, with few inhabitants, although the Church of the Nativity is held in great veneration even by the Muslims themselves. About a thousand paces from Bethlehem was the *Tower of Eder* or *Ader*, erected on account of robbers, lest they bring harm to the flocks and shepherds. Jacob withdrew to this place in his greatest grief, which he conceived from the premature death of his dearest wife, *Genesis 35:21.* It is also believed that the Angel appeared to the shepherds at this tower while they were guarding their flocks by night, and announced the Messiah born in Bethlehem, *Luke 2:8-9.* Toward the East, a certain castle was seen situated on a high mountain, named *Herodium*, which Herod had adorned with incredible beauty and named after himself. *Segor*, which is also *Zoar* and *Bela*, in the borders of Benjamin and Judah at the shore of the Dead Sea, is a small countryside to which Lot hurried with his daughters, and which the Lord spared for that man's sake, *Genesis 19:2.*

I underwent much labor to see it, but in vain: for the Saracens turned me away, saying the place was not without danger on account of serpents, worms, and fierce beasts living there; but later I found the matter was not so.* This place was once most fertile, whence from the vineyards of the most noble wine

# Sacred Geography
### From Joshua 1, verse 2, page 307

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
The vine of the Parents is celebrated by Solomon in *Song of Solomon* 1:14. **Engaddi** <note>Modern En Gedi</note> is the name of a mountain, a city (also called *Hazazon-tamar*), a valley, and a desert, in which David lay hidden while fleeing the fierce anger of Saul.
<margin>1 Samuel 24:1. T.S. p. 312.</margin>
Regarding Mount Engaddi, Brocardus <note>A 13th-century Dominican pilgrim and geographer</note> himself writes as an eyewitness: *The mountains of Engaddi are very high, presenting a wonderful arrangement, for they have such steep cliffs threatening to fall into the valleys below that they strike fear and terror into those seeing and passing them.* There was a small town in the tribe of Judah called **Thecua** <note>Tekoa</note>, the homeland of the Prophet Amos and of the woman mentioned in
<margin>2 Samuel 14:2. 2 Chronicles 11:6.</margin>
2 Samuel 14:2. It was fortified with walls by Rehoboam, 2 Chronicles 11:6. It abounded in pastures, providing a pleasant seat for shepherds, and Amos was among the *herdsmen* <note>original Hebrew: בוקרים (boqerim)</note>; God, who is wonderful in all His saints, is truly admirable in Amos the herdsman, whom He called from the Shepherds of Tekoa to feed the people of Israel with His holy word. Regarding
<margin>On Jeremiah ch. 6, col. 533.</margin>
this city, Jerome *says*: *We see with our own eyes every day that Tekoa is a small village situated on a mountain, separated from Jerusalem by twelve miles.*

Before we descend further in our progress, we must consider the city of **Keilah**, of which there is frequent mention in the Holy Scriptures. This city belonged to the tribe of Judah, <note>Hebrew: קעילה</note> *Ceila*, which Joshua mentions in the catalog of cities in chapter 15:44, and whose site was between Hebron and Lachish. We must mention the evil of the inhabitants
<margin>1 Samuel 23.</margin>
due to their ingratitude toward David; although he weightily delivered them from the siege of the Philistines, and while this benefit should have provoked them to gratitude, they would have handed him over to his enemy Saul had God not kindly averted the disaster. He underwent every danger for the defense of the citizens, yet at Keilah they perfidiously rewarded this faithful service. The history is worth telling so that their treachery may appear more significant, and the place may suggest an example of what should be thought of such people, how it must be prevented by pious prayers, and so that godly men in misfortune may know that trust must be placed in God's help. The people of Keilah were being besieged by the Philistines, and when David had received an answer from GOD
<margin>v. 4, 5.</margin>
that he should rise and go to Keilah, he went, defeated them, struck them with a great slaughter, and saved the inhabitants of Keilah. Meanwhile, it was announced to Saul by traitors that David had come to Keilah, wherefore he joyfully
<margin>v. 7.</margin>
exclaims in verse 7: *The Lord has shut him into my hands, since he has enclosed himself by coming into a city fortified with gates and bars*, thinking that by divine will he had come into his power, having entered a town fortified with gates and bolts and thus shut himself in. Therefore, he immediately assembles all his forces for
<margin>v. 8.</margin>
war and commanded all the people to go down to battle at Keilah to besiege David and his men then staying in the city. When David learned of this bloodthirsty plan, he inquired about the outcome through the Ephod <note>A ceremonial vestment used by priests to discern God's will</note> in these words:
<margin>v. 11.</margin>
"Will the men of Keilah deliver me into his hands?" And when he received the answer that he would indeed be delivered up, then David and his companions, about six hundred men, departed from Keilah to go wherever fortune might lead them. *For the people of Keilah did not believe themselves safe unless they showed the way <note>to Saul</note>.*

Nor should we pass over **Hebron**, a city most famous of all for its nobility and antiquity. So

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Geography</margin>
it is arranged in mortal affairs that we rejoice in societies; the larger they are, the greater the applause for the cities where they are rightly established. Hence the name seems best given to the city of Hebron, which was previously called *Arba* after a certain very famous man among the Anakim <note>A race of giants in the Bible</note>; because of the frequency of people and the more populous community, the namer seems to have placed a fitting nomenclature on the place—unless one prefers to derive it from a certain son of Caleb mentioned in 1 Chronicles 2:42. Even if we do not hit the mark, the name will not thereby become ill-omened. The name implies association or communion, for *chabar* <note>Hebrew: חבר</note> means to join, associate, or gather; and *chaber* means a companion, and *chaburah* means a society or fellowship. All these are worthy of a city far more ancient, a community established seven years before Zoan or Tanis, the royal city of Egypt, as Moses witnesses in Numbers 13:22. For it is believed to have been built by Heth, the son of Canaan, grandson of Ham. Indeed, in the times of Abraham, the
<margin>Genesis 13:2, 3.</margin>
Hittites possessed Hebron and the neighboring field, Genesis 23:2, 3. In the conquest of the land of Canaan, it fell to Caleb, and especially to the Levites, and it was one of those cities into which, by the will and command of the Lord, one could flee who had killed a man by chance and not on purpose <note>A City of Refuge</note>. In this city David also inaugurated his kingdom, and Absalom chose it as the place and seat of his sedition against his father. Today, from the Jewish War, it still lies demolished; its huge ruins on the mountain where it stood are even today the most certain witnesses of its greatness. But the new and modern city is nearby, where the valley of Mamre and the grove of
<margin>T.S. p. 319.</margin>
Abraham planted near it once stood, of which we shall speak immediately. Let us hear Brocardus on this matter: *Hebron, formerly called Kiriath-Arba, was situated on a mountain. Today, besides great ruins, nothing is seen here, but about three bowshots toward the South, though declining a little to the East, is the new Hebron built, specifically in the place where the double cave was; there were buried Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebecca, Jacob and Leah.* And from Jerome's *On Hebrew Places* we add, and *Adam the Great*, as is written in the book of Joshua: although some suspect he was buried in the place of Calvary. Hebron, therefore, provided hospitality to those first and greatest lights of the Church: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Regarding
<margin>Genesis 13:18.</margin>
Abraham, we read that moving his tent and tabernacle, *he dwelt by the oak of Mamre* <note>original Greek: κατῴκησε περὶ τὴν δρῦν τὴν Μαμβρῆ</note>. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> uses the verb *aposkenon*, which here means *to pitch a tent*; elsewhere it denotes stretching further, having tents at a long interval, or having a seat far removed. *He pitched his tent in Sodom*, but before that time *he set up his tent in Mamre*. This was a happy and blessed place, *Mamre* <note>Hebrew: ממרא</note>, where Abraham received the Angels as guests, where he was made a partner in the divine counsel. The most sacred shade of the tree was consecrated by these most venerable guests. We need not deal at length with the monument of the place, since it commends itself greatly not only for its fertility, from which it also received its name (for *mara* <note>Hebrew: מרא</note> means "he has become fat"), but also communicates its fame to the nearby place of Hebron, from which it was six stadia distant. Led by its fame, Constantine the Great took care to have a church erected there, about which from Eusebius and Baronius...

We shall add a few things concerning the **Terebinth tree** <note>The Terebinth or Turpentine tree (Pistacia terebinthus) is a large deciduous tree common in the Mediterranean, often associated with sacred sites in the Bible.</note>: *There is seen*, says Josephus <note>original: "S. de bell Iud. cap. 7." referring to The Jewish War</note>, *at the sixth stadium from the town, a very large Terebinth tree; and they record that it was created at the beginning of the world and has endured until now.* Concerning the same, Brocardus says: *The Oak of Mamre is still shown today before the entrance of Abraham's tabernacle. This place is also of great veneration among the Turks, who enclose it within a very fortified temple, and permit no Jew or Christian access to it. Not far from Hebron seems to have been *Dabir*, which was once called *Kiriath-sepher*, that is, the city of letters or the University and Academy of Palestine, as Adrichomius interprets and explains it. And *Mareshah*, both royal cities, were fortified with stronger garrisons by Rehoboam, son of Solomon (2 Chronicles 11:8), but were afterwards so destroyed by the injuries of wars that in Jerome's time they had obtained the name of a not very large village. By the same author, in the *Epitaph of Mother Paula* (Volume 1, folio 225), *Moresheth*, once the tomb of the Prophet Micah, is now called a Church.

This region, surrounded by high and rugged mountains, has the hill country of Judea to the west, at the feet of which is placed *Eleutheropolis*, a city famous in Jerome's age. *Jarmuth, Tappuah* and others: It also included vast wildernesses, named from neighboring places, such as the *Desert of Bethlehem, En-gedi, Ziph, Maon, Judah*, situated to the East toward the Asphaltite Lake <note>The Dead Sea</note>. Furthermore, in certain places it abounded with hidden and dark mountain caves, or steep and inaccessible rocks, in whose fortifications David hid, seeking in them the support and protection of his life; yet he was not so safe in them that Saul, carried away by anger and envy, did not search for him as he wandered in the mountains, successfully tracking the valleys and hills, so that he might hold the exile like a sparrow, or some other prey, and slaughter him with his own hands. Whence
<margin>Oration 3 on David, p. 145.</margin>
