And indeed, having gathered the armies of the kingdom, he sought out the one who would shortly be hidden. He tracked all the ravines and drove through them, and busied himself with the peaks of the mountains, an unjust hunter of the just.* And this
<margin>T. S. p. 322.</margin>
was the Holy Land, which, to use the words of Brocardus <note>*</note>, has such praise in Holy Scripture that it excels other lands in goodness and fertility, and leaves them far behind, since it is said to overflow with milk and honey, by which are understood all those things which this mortal life has need of. *The soil itself is most fertile for grain, since it requires the least labor in its cultivation and returns much fruit; for I have often seen with my own eyes the plow turned by only two oxen, and the fields have no need of manure, since by its own nature the earth itself is fat, and in most places requires very little external seasoning.* Today, however, the greatest part lies uncultivated, whence its modern face is wretched, bristling, and deformed. How miserably today the whole

<column-break/>

Let us recall to our minds that we have no stable and firm region or seat in these lands, but an eternal fatherland in heaven is to be expected, as Blessed Chytraeus <note>*</note> piously warns.

### JOSHUA 2:1
->The spies shall come into the house of a woman, a harlot.<-
->The two young men entered into the house of a woman, a harlot.<-
->*The spies entered the house of a woman who was a harlot.*<-

<margin>The infamous function of female innkeepers</margin>
**T**he Hebrews express both a harlot and an innkeeper by the word *Zonah* <note>Hebrew: זנה</note>; for it is either a noun from the participle of the verb *zanah*, "to commit fornication," or it seems to be a noun, though unusual to the Hebrews, from the verb *zun*, "to feed." Hence it happens that the interpretation of one is used for the interpretation of the meaning of the other by the Chaldee Interpreter <note>The Targum</note>, who rendered it *it-ta pundi-ta* <note>Aramaic: אתתא פונדיתא</note>, that is, *a woman host*, using a milder word which corresponds to the Greek *pandokeion* <note>an inn</note>; as if she were an innkeeper, a receiver of all newcomers. Such a woman is also described in those same profuse words in *Judges 16:1*, where Samson turned aside; where Vatablus's explanation is: *A harlot, that is, an innkeeper;*
<margin>For this reason it should rather be translated "innkeeper."</margin>
*for no mention is made that Samson loved her.* But to "go in to a harlot" in Scripture denotes to commit fornication and act the harlot. Therefore Samson committed fornication here, and perished in the embraces of a harlot who acted as an innkeeper; compare Cornelius à Lapide, page 173. Most of the Rabbis follow the Chaldee, denying that Rahab made a trade of her body, because they judge it shameful for their nation if it were said the Spies entered the lodging of that harlot Rahab, the hostess of Jericho; whom, on account of her performed duty of faithfulness, Joshua, the servant of the Lord,
<margin>chapter 7, verse 5.</margin>
caused to live in the land of Canaan <note>*</note>. Those who have a clear perspective on the force of the proper root *zanah*, "to commit fornication," and its proper and perpetual meaning and use in Holy Scripture, do not rise to the forced etymologies of the Rabbis; among whom many examples of cold interpretations can be found. Nevertheless, both expositions taken together will not lack their foundation; namely, that we may say of Rahab that she was both an innkeeper and at the same time a harlot, for which function innkeepers were not unsuited, who among the gentiles (such as Rahab was) received guests not only under a common roof, but also in a common bed. Hence Gilbertus Cognatus in his *Adages*, page 805: *The Hebrews name a harlot and an innkeeper by one and the same word...*

# On Joshua Chapter II, Verse 1
### Mmm
-> <note>original: "ישבי" (the inhabitants)</note> <-

<margin>The infamous occupation of female innkeepers.</margin>
...woman, because they are of the same kind; for those who work in inns are of common modesty <note>i.e., of loose virtue</note>, as stated in the Code of Justinian <note>original: "Constantin. l. quae adult. C. ad leg. Jul. de adult."</note>. For as Philostratus says in his *Letter to a Female Innkeeper*, "retail trade was almost synonymous with the rites of Aphrodite" <note>original: "καπηλεία erant ἀφροδίσια"</note>; and Xiphilinus declares in his life of *Avitus* that inns <note>original: "πανδοχεῖα"</note> were infamous. This is also demonstrated by Isocrates, Athenaeus, Aelian, Theophrastus, and Suetonius, from whom P. Faber, Casaubon in his *Notes on Theophrastus' Characters* (in the chapter "On Desperation," page 184, and "On Slander," page 365) have proven this. Therefore, Junius and Tremellius translated not ineptly: *They came into the house of a certain harlot-innkeeper*, implying she was both a public hostess and at the same time unchaste, as literature and experience often testify happens in such a way of life. Forster, in his *Dictionary* (folio 230), defines the Hebrew word *Zonah* <note>זונה</note> as a washerwoman, an innkeeper, a publican, a harlot for hire, and a prostitute; because in ancient times washerwomen and innkeepers were also notorious and simultaneously made money with their bodies. Chrysostom, in his second sermon *On Repentance*, calls this very woman a "hostess" <note>original: "πανδοκεύτριαν"</note>; for innkeepers usually made such a profit. See the law regarding adultery in the Code.

<margin>On chapter 23 of Isaiah, page 304.</margin>
J. Brentius notes: Although *Zonah* <note>זונה</note> signifies a harlot, it properly signifies a hostess who receives strangers with hospitality and serves them food for her price, such as Rahab was in Jericho. I believe, however, that the lifestyle of these hostesses and cooks was considered honorable in the beginning, until these women began to serve not only food but also to prostitute their bodies to guests. Hence *Zonah* began to be used for "to commit fornication." Flacius, in his *Key to the Scriptures* (folio 866), says: The reason that one word, *Zanah* <note>זנה</note>, signifies both—namely a female provider of food and a harlot—is that the things themselves or the trades are frequently joined. For hostesses are often harlots, and conversely, harlots often sell food and receive their lovers with hospitality. Thus, among the Romans, cookshops, brothels, inns, and similar places were full of harlots. While Thomas de Vio <note>Cardinal Cajetan</note> considers these things, he doubts which meaning

<margin>On this location, folio 4, a.</margin>
to rely upon. He says: "It is not clear whether this woman is described as a harlot or an innkeeper." For the Hebrew expression is ambiguous, and there are arguments on both sides; her duty testifies that she was an innkeeper, but the frequent use of this word among the Hebrews suggests she was a harlot. This also raises a difficulty: if she had been a harlot, these men <note>the spies</note> would not have turned aside to her for fear of suspicion and the arrival of other fornicators; a point which also caused a "scruple" for the very learned Schindler in his *Lexicon* (page 476). Nor do Lyranus, Pagninus, Arias, Titelmann, and others abstain from this view, who, led by preconceived opinions, maintain she was not a harlot. To these, Barradius objects that the Vulgate version is authentic (as he usually does), and I would wish they settle it with him. We, however, "shake a different oak" <note>a Latin idiom meaning to try a different approach</note>. The word *Zonah* <note>זונה</note> is clearly used for a harlot in Genesis 38:15, where Tamar is impregnated by Judah: *and he thought her to be a harlot* <note>original: "וחשבה לזונה"</note>, the Greek says *he thought her to be a prostitute* <note>original: "ἔδοξεν αὐτὴν πόρνην εἶναι"</note>, because she had covered her face; she was also called a "shrine prostitute" <note>original: "קדשה"</note> in verse 21, from the root *Kadesh* <note>קדש</note>, the meaning of which is "to sanctify" in some places and "to pollute" in Deuteronomy 22:9, noting the uncleanness and pollution of prostitutes; for the sense of "sanctification" is absurd here unless you wish to imagine an antiphrasis <note>using a word to mean its opposite</note>. Jephthah is said to have been *the son of a harlot woman* <note>original: "בּן־אשה זוֹנה"</note>, the Greek says *son of a prostitute woman*

<column-break/>

<margin>The infamous occupation of female innkeepers. Judges 11:1.</margin>
<note>original: "υἱὸς γυναικὸς πόρνης"</note>, *the son of a woman who was a companion* <note>original: "υἱὸς γυναικὸς ἑταιρούσης"</note>. In verse 2, the Chaldean <note>Aramaic Targum</note> has *the son of an innkeeping woman* <note>original: "בּן אִתּתָא פוּנְדָּקִיתָא"</note>, making her a tavern-keeper or perhaps a concubine. Two harlot women <note>original: "זוֹנוֹת"</note> came to Solomon litigating over a child in 1 Kings 3:16, where again the Chaldean translates with his word for "innkeepers" <note>original: "פוּנְדָּקִין"</note>. Thus, usage proves that Rahab was a *porne* <note>Greek: prostitute</note> or harlot; whatever Daniel Fuffelius might say, the author of the *Biblical Storehouse*, who thought Luther's translation should be corrected in this matter.

<margin>Page 771.</margin>
Against him must be opposed two witnesses distinguished by Apostolic authority: the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews (St. Paul) in chapter 11, verse 31, and James in chapter 2, verse 25, both approving the version of the elders <note>the Septuagint</note>; and thus the Syriac version has "harlots" <note>original: "זַנְיָתָא"</note> in both places. Furthermore, *porne* <note>πόρνη</note> by its usage in Matthew 21:31-32, Luke 15:30, 1 Corinthians 6:15-16, and Revelation 17:1, always signifies a harlot. In further confirmation of this, there are other things which Dr. Junius discusses regarding this harlot,

<margin>Book 3, Parallel 11.</margin>
especially this, when he says: *Since the proper root signifies nothing else properly than to commit fornication, and the Hebrew name from that related root never appears in this form where it can even probably be taken in another sense, I truly do not see why it is more necessary to reject the proper meaning of the root and the common, perpetual use of the Hebrew name in this argument, than to confess concerning Rahab what the proper notation of the word demands: that she was a sinner and had devoted herself to fornication. To which end, certainly, the occupation of those who receive foreign guests and make a profit from innkeeping is not inconvenient.* The accurate writer Bonfrerius also urges this same point: that suitable examples of this meaning <note>innkeeper</note> cannot be given in this place; for everywhere *Zonah* is taken for a harlot, and the verb *Zanah* is never taken otherwise than "to play the harlot." Nevertheless, Estius says, we do not deny she was an innkeeper; for among

<margin>On chapter 11 to the Hebrews.</margin>
the Gentiles, for whom simple fornication was not considered a sin, women practicing innkeeping, if they did not have husbands, simultaneously made a profit from the prostitution of their bodies. And it is sufficiently clear that Rahab was unmarried, or certainly a vigorous widow, which the attribute *Zonah* argues. For she only bargains for the safety of her father, mother, and sisters, and leads no more out with her. However, we feel that the Spies did not turn aside for the sake of fulfilling their lust or prostituting their modesty, but rather, being entirely ignorant that it was the house of a harlot, they were brought to Rahab's house. For who would have persuaded those strangers that Rahab was marked by the stain of some baseness? Rahab sold food, received any comers with hospitality, and did not deny love and the service of her body to whoever wished. For the sake of lodging, the travelers turned aside to her; we cannot say here that they were captured by her love and admitted by her, as we said of Samson visiting the innkeeper. They did not know it was a harlot's dwelling, but chose a dwelling that was contiguous to the gate and the wall. We end our speaking with the words of Georg Fabricius of Chemnitz, which are read in Volume 3 of *German Poets*, page 73:

> Rahab alone, though subject to infamous guilt,
> While she fears, desires to be part of God's people.
> Hostess to the saints, and hating her former ways,
> She snatches her own from the midst of a late death.

### JOSHUA IX. v. 3. 4. 5.

> And when the inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done unto Jericho and to Ai, they did work wilily, and went and made as if they had been ambassadors, and took old sacks upon their asses, and wine bottles, old, and rent, and bound up; and old shoes and clouted upon their feet, and old garments upon them; and all the bread of their provision was dry and mouldy. <note>original: Hebrew text of Joshua 9:3-5</note>
>
> And the inhabitants of Gabaon heard all that Jesus <note>The Greek form of Joshua</note> had done to Jericho and to Gai. And they also acted with craftiness, and having gone they provided themselves with food, and prepared themselves, and taking old sacks upon their shoulders, and old wine skins, both torn and bound up. <note>original: Greek Septuagint text</note>
>
> Those who dwelt in Gabaon, hearing all the things that Joshua had done to Jericho and Ai, and thinking cunningly, brought food for themselves, placing old sacks upon their asses, and wine skins torn and sewn together, and very old shoes, which as a sign of age were sewn with patches. <note>original: Latin Vulgate/Scholarly translation</note>

<margin>
Travels of the Eastern nations.
</margin>

**I**t is my intention, on the occasion of the aforementioned passage, to describe the foreign peoples of the East who have undertaken journeys. Among the Easterners, among the types of vessels prepared for containing provisions, they were accustomed to use sacks, skins, and baskets, which were of the most common use for those making a journey. A <term>Cophinus</term> <note>A sturdy traveling basket</note> is properly a woven vessel made of wicker, over which leather was usually drawn; such also was the <term>canistrum</term> <note>reed basket</note> woven from split reeds or wicker; or the <term>sporta</term> <note>wicker hamper</note>, which was made of Spanish broom; as the <term>Calathus</term> <note>tapering basket</note>, because it was woven from wood, which is usually called *kalon* by the Greeks. In Hebrew it is *dud*, *Gen. 40. v. 17. 18.* which Jerome thinks in his *Hebrew Questions* can more conveniently be called a <term>cophinus</term> than a <term>canistrum</term>. Likewise *dud*, as in *2 Kings 10. v. 7.* "in baskets" <note>Hebrew: *ba-dudim*</note> in Baskets or hampers, where the Targum <note>Aramaic translation</note> has *salaya sla*. <term>Utres</term> <note>Skin-bottles</note>, which were usually made from the skins of goats or other beasts, were vessels serving for the transport of wine, oil, honey, and other liquids. The <term>Saccus</term> <note>Sack</note> was intended for carrying merchandise, spices, grain, dry goods, and other utensils. In Hebrew *saq*, which word is common to many languages, remaining with many nations from that ancient mixing of many languages at the tower <note>The Tower of Babel</note>, since everyone intently watched his own sack during the departure. Joseph commanded his brothers, when they were to return to their Father for the first time, that besides the wheat with which their sacks were filled, provisions should also be given for the way, *Gen. 42. 26.* and a second time, when he had revealed himself, he provided travel-money for the journey, and by the King's command sent them back equipped with wagons, provisions, and gifts to bring their father and the whole family quickly, *chap. 45. v. 21. 22. 23.* Concerning sacks of merchandise, Juvenal says in *Satire 14, book 5, v. 269*:

> The reckless and vile merchant of the stinking sack.

Those vessels of people who commit themselves to a journey are called, in *Jeremiah 46:19*, "vessels of exile" <note>Hebrew: *keli golah*; Greek: *skeue apoikismou*</note>, the vessels of migration, which those migrating into exile would carry with them, whether they be those in which utensils and food are carried, or those which serve for carrying the weak and the little ones. Prepare for yourself, he says to Egypt soon to be laid waste by Nebuchadnezzar, *the instruments of deportation. For Memphis shall be a desolation, and shall be burned so that no one dwells there.* Luther translates best: *Wander-Geräth* <note>Travel-gear</note>. The French elegantly call it *equipage de chemin* <note>road equipment</note>. "Vessels" is often said of traveling instruments; sometimes of those of war, as concerning the Babylonians, *Jeremiah 51:20*:

<column-break/>

<margin>Travel of the Easterners.</margin>
**Y**ou have been a mace to me, instruments of war <note>Hebrew: *keli milchamah*, vessels of war</note>, *that I might shatter nations through you, and destroy kingdoms through you.* Utensils of war, and whatever is prepared for the use of a journey or a house, are designated by that word; hence those expressions: *to collect the vessels, to call for the vessels, to pack up*, concerning those who, being about to move, put their things together. Julius Caesar, in *The Gallic War, book 1*: *When the army is about to move camp, it is customary to call out that they should collect the vessels.* And in the same author it is said figuratively *to depart without the vessels being called* of those who leave without saying goodbye to the host. Cicero against Verres: *He had already moved camp from Sicily, and had collected his vessels.* The Romans called <term>Vasarium</term> all that apparatus, every instrument and furniture, with which Proconsuls and Governors about to depart into the provinces were equipped at public expense, lest they be a burden to the allies and provincials. Under that name, Piso had taken money counted out from the treasury for interest, about which Cicero says <margin>Speech against Piso, n. 85.</margin>: ->Why should I now explain the sum of his greed, which is entangled in infinite crimes? I will speak generally of those things which are best known. Did you not leave at interest in Rome the eighteen million sesterces, which you had credited to yourself from the treasury as if under the name of "equipment money" <note>vasarii</note>, in the sale of my head?<- Now let us inspect the journey of the Gibeonites. The Gibeonites, about to cunningly seek peace through Envoys to Joshua and the incoming Israelite enemies, so that they might add a look of good faith to their inwardly conceived fraud, took up every equipment and ornament which a long journey otherwise requires, and they deceived those who did not suspect anything sinister even in a dream, both by their appearance and by the falsehood of their words; namely, when they had heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and Ai, and had also perceived the plans of the rest of the Canaanites, who had gathered themselves together to fight against Joshua and against Israel with one voice, <margin>v. 2.</margin> they also wished to look out for their own lives, but by different means—not by attacking with force, but by deceiving with craft; not by conspiracy, but by shrewdness and tricks. The Canaanite kings, already declared enemies by the Israelites, do not want to become suppliants, nor do they want to appear to be of a stricken and dejected spirit, but they resolve to approach the matter with war and a great and brave spirit. On the contrary, the Gibeonites, with a broken and humble spirit, approach the matter by another way, namely *they went, and feigned that they had come as Ambassadors from a far country*, v. 4. 9. For so it is in the Hebrew text: *vayyitztayaru*, *they made themselves ambassadors.* They simulated an embassy, and persuaded by a false representation of external things. The Septuagint, according to the Roman Codex, has: *epesitisanto*, to suggest they had prepared food for themselves, in which sense the Old Interpreter <note>The Vulgate</note> says: *they brought food for themselves.* And the Chaldean <note>Targum</note> the same: *and they provided themselves with travel-provisions.* For *zid* is the same as the Hebrew *tzid*, by the change of a related letter into a related one. These interpreters read the original word with the letter Daleth. Luther: *Send a message.* The Spanish version: *They feigned themselves ambassadors.* So that the fiction might bear a greater appearance of truth, *they placed old sacks upon their asses* (upon the asses, not indeed upon the shoulders) *in which bread and other necessities for the journey were included, and wine skins torn and bound up because of age and rupture; finally, worn-out shoes, which as a sign of deformity were mended and sewn with patches*, as the old interpreter rendered *metullaot* <note>Hebrew for "patched"</note>.

For "bread" there underlies the word <term>לחם</term> <note>lechem</note>, which one may observe more than once in the sacred writings is sometimes used to denote every kind of nourishment; for because bread is the most common food <term>καὶ</term> <term>τὸ</term> <term>κυριώτατον</term> <term>πρὸς</term> <term>τὸ</term> <term>ζῆν</term> <note>and the most essential thing for living</note>, as Strabo speaks in book 16, and without which life can in no way be sustained; therefore its name is used to understand all food, just as by the name of "water" any drink is indicated; as Sirach says in chapter 29:25: *The beginning of life for a man is water and bread.* Castalio translates: *Our pouches are exhausted of bread.* Luther: *The bread is gone from our sack.* <note>original German: "Das Brod ist dahin aus unserm Sack."</note> The Vulgate: *Bread has failed in our baskets* <note>original Latin: "cistariis"</note>. If this reading is genuine, a *cistartium* is a <term>κίστη</term> <term>ἄρτω</term> <note>bread-chest</note>. You might call it a *Bread-store* <note>Greek: "Artotheke"</note> or a *bread-carrying chest*, a *food-carrying and dinner-carrying chest*, a *Sacciperium* <note>traveling bag</note>, a *bread-sack*. Also <term>σιπύυ</term>, or, as Pollux writes, 10. Onom. 36. p. 495. <term>σιπύα</term>, was called a bread vessel, or a storehouse for certain wicker baskets. By the Germans, a travel pouch is called a *Knapsack*. *Knappen* is an old German word, and it means to chew; just as *Wadsack* is as if it were *Weidsack*, from *Waiden*, to graze or feed. To the Belgians it is *Aetfack*; i.e., a sack of food. Understand, therefore, a pouch or *sacciperium* (which word Plautus uses in *Rudens* act 2. sc. 6.) in which the servant of Saul carried bread and other things necessary for sustenance. Nor is there reason for us to accuse the ancient Translator of barbarism. If the true reading is in the hands of the authors of the Royal Work, we must say that *sistarchium* is by metonymy the <term>σιταρχίαν</term> <note>sitarchia</note> of the Greeks, which word is from <term>σιτεύειν</term>, *to supply*, and <term>σῖτος</term>, *grain* or food; whence later Latinity aptly applied the name *sitarcia* to indicate food supplies, especially for those *traveling* <note>Greek: "hodoiporeunton"</note>. Apuleius in book 2 of *The Golden Ass* p. 160: *The ship of Venus alone requires this provision [sitarcia], so that in the night-long vigil both the oil for the lamp and the wine for the cup may abound.* He thinks oil and wine suffice for the nourishment of Venus, the abundance of which he wants supplied to the ship, so that lust may be kindled by wine, and the light of the lamp nourished by oil in nocturnal pleasure. Jerome also uses it in the *Life of Malchus* Vol. 1. p. 258: *Refreshed by new provisions [sitarciae], that is, by rations, we came at last on the tenth day through the desert to the Roman camps.* From this *sitarcium* is derived, to denote *some vessel for grain or bread*, which is a more refined and polished reading than *cistartium* or *sistarchium*, or *sitarchia*, concerning which Rangolius in *Samuel* p. 1111 notes these things: *The restorers of the ancient common reading have noted that it should be read 'Sitarciis', not 'cistartiis', which some read, deriving a word they did not understand as if from 'cista' [chest], whereas it is rather composed from* <term>σῖτος</term>, which denotes grain in Greek, and <term>ἀρκείν</term>, which is to suffice; whence the feminine noun <term>ἡ</term> <term>σιταρχία</term>, meaning provisions; and the neuter *sitarcium*, which signifies a pouch, a sack, or a vessel in which travel-provisions are stored for those on a journey. The word *sitarcia* encompasses rations, food, and nourishment prepared for the way; he who was in charge of these was called a <term>σιτάρχης</term>, *sitarchus*, a *Provisions-Master* <note>original German: "Proviant-Meister"</note>; just as there was a <term>σιτοστάσιος</term>, who was in charge of selling grain, and a <term>σιτοκόμος</term>, who looked after the grain and rations, whose function is called <term>σιτοκομία</term> by Arcadius the Jurist in the law *concerning duties*...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

*of gifts and honors*, and Ulpian mentions that "provisioning" <note>original: *sitocomia*</note> in his work *On the Vacations of Duties, book 2*. In Latin, it is called *Viaticum*—whatever is necessary for a traveler (to use a word from Apuleius), whether it be food or money to be spent on sustenance. In Hebrew, it is *Tzedah* <note>original: <hebrew>צֵידָה</hebrew></note> in Joshua chapter 1, verse 3, which the Greek translates as *provisioning* <note>original: <greek>τῷ ἐπισιτισμῷ</greek></note>. In Genesis 42:25, Joseph commanded his ministers to fill the equipment and vessels of his brothers with supplies, returning each man's money into his sack and giving them *viaticum* for the journey. It is used absolutely as *Tzedah* or *provisioning* in Joshua 1:11, where we read that Joshua, the leader of the holy war, about to move camp, first commanded by the public voice and edict of the *Shotrim* <note>officers or heralds</note> that everyone should prepare for the expedition and gather the necessary food for it. We see here that the translators disagree, which is a common marvel in other passages. The Hebrew words are: *Pass through the midst of the camp and command the people, saying: Prepare for yourselves provisions.* <note>original: <hebrew>עִבְרוּ בְּקֶרֶב הַמַחֲנֶה וְצַוּוּ אֶת־הָעָם לֵאמֹר הָכִינוּ לָכֶם צֵידָה</hebrew></note> Arias translates: *Pass through the innermost part of the encampment and command the people, saying: Prepare for yourselves Viaticum.* The Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> says: *Enter into the middle of the camp to the people, and charge the people, saying, prepare provisioning.* So it is found elsewhere, and fittingly, just as Thucydides similarly wrote in book 6, page 229: *having provisioned the whole army*, that is, *having taken travel-supplies*. The Vulgate <note>Latin Bible</note> says: *Prepare for yourselves food*. This is best understood by military custom, of which I add a single example from Frontinus, *Stratagems* 4.7: *Cato ordered a third part of the soldiers to prepare food and board the ships.* Luther translates: *Provide yourselves with supplies* <note>original: *Schafft euch Vorrath*</note>, where the Weimar Glossators <note>commentators</note> on page 191 say: *Provide yourselves with provisions and food. The Manna had not yet ceased, but it did not keep until the next day. Therefore, this is to be understood as the food which the Israelites could buy for money from the neighboring peoples.* The Dutch say: *Prepare for yourselves travel-food*. The French and Italian use the word *provision*, the Spaniard *Comida*. Some understand the Hebrew *Zeda* to mean Manna. From their perspective, Menochius writes on page 263: *Manna was still falling every day. They were therefore commanded to collect it more abundantly and prepare it by the usual grinding and cooking.* Procopius explained it thus, with the approval of Serarius. But they err regarding the manna, which could not be kept until the next day, and it was cautioned by command that it be gathered for one day, not two or three. Therefore, it must be understood as other things of which a supply could then be made, such as produce and grain, which are used for *provisioning*. Sulpitius Severus in *Sacred History* book 1, page 56, says: *Joshua, at the beginning of his assumed command, having sent messengers through the camp, informed the people that they should prepare grain.* Sigonius dislikes this in his notes on Sulpitius, page 115, as something invented by wit, claiming the text uses the word "food." As if these things were *contradictory*. Among foods, *grain* claims the first place for itself. Not only side-dishes were to be prepared for the way, but also *breads* from wheat or barley flour (Bonfrerius, page 5). And these were indeed available from the plundering of that whole region of the two Kings of the Amorites across the Jordan, which the Reubenites, Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh had just occupied. So much grain and other edibles could be obtained from here as was necessary for three days. The people obey the command and prepare for themselves a

<column-break/>

<margin>Travels of the Eastern Peoples.</margin>
*three-day military supply*, and equipped with this *three-day provisioning*, they advance against the enemy. Nor should it be said that *while they had so much provisioning, the Manna* failed them. To the food given from heaven, they added *local grain*, as they had also done previously (Deuteronomy 2:28) while staying among the Edomites and Moabites. The Manna finally ceased to fall *from heaven* on the 15th day of the month of Nisan, after they had tasted the new produce of the promised land (Joshua 5:11), as the text says: *in eating of the grain of that land.* <note>original: <hebrew>וַיֹּאכְלוּ מֵעֲבוּר הָאָרֶץ</hebrew></note> Martin Borrhaus writes: *Besides Manna, care is taken for the rest of the supplies; for Manna did not cease to fall until they began to eat the fruits of the sacred land, as is clear below from chapter five, lest anyone think the Manna expired along with Moses.* Thus, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon expires, who thinks not a collection of food but of weapons is signified. But since the Hebrew word always signifies edibles elsewhere, why or how would it lose that meaning here? Rabbi Kimchi understands it as side-dishes without bread, as if seasonings for the Manna, to which Quistorpius gave his assent, writing in his *Commentary on Joshua chapter 1*: <margin>page 225.</margin> *Tzedah* signifies any food except bread. This word also occurs in Genesis 42:25, *where Joseph commands his brothers to be equipped with viaticum for the journey.* Nor can it be manna, for that was collected for only one day, but here they are commanded to prepare for three days. Additionally, in Deuteronomy 2:6, they are commanded by God to buy food for a price and eat. With equal elegance, the Greeks called *Viaticum* "ephodion" <note>original: <greek>ἐφόδιον</greek></note>, which is used by *those walking the road*, whatever it may be. When a slave was granted freedom, God commanded he be given from the flocks, the threshing floor, and the winepress (Deuteronomy 15:13-14), where the Greek says: *to provision with viaticum*. The Hebrew is slightly different: *by placing, place it upon his neck*, that is, liberally supply from your sheep and cattle, from your grain and your wine. Elegantly, with Virgil in the *Aeneid* book 1, line 362, you might call it *aid for the way*:

> And aid for the way, he reveals ancient treasures 
> from the earth, an unknown weight of silver and gold.

Aulus Gellius observes in *Attic Nights* 9.1 that the Latins, in imitation of the Greeks, transferred the word *Viaticum* from the expense of a journey to the preparation of other things as well. Demosthenes used it thus regarding the "nourishment," so to speak, of the elderly. But lest we seek a travel-allowance when the journey is finished, as the proverb says, let us return to the royal road. In the same book of Samuel, chapter 21, the journey of David is described, who, pressed by great hunger, went to Ahimelech. The priest, before David would take the sacred showbread set before the Lord to drive away his hunger and that of his men, warns him first about ritual purity—that he should consider the state of his men, lest the limits of the law be exceeded in two ways: by giving sacred bread (which was not permitted to be eaten) to laypeople, and moreover to *unclean* laypeople. For it was a sin for the pure to touch the impure, and for anyone besides priests and Levites to eat the bread of the presence, a command found in Leviticus 24:9. To this David, the *prophet-king* <note>original: <greek>προφητοάναξ</greek></note>, pressed by the lack of supplies and *viaticum*, replied in verse 6: *Truly women have been kept from us since yesterday and the day before since we went out. But also the vessels of the young men were holy*, that is, our clothes, the baskets in which the bread will be received, and all our baggage we have taken care to sanctify, *after the manner of those*, adds Vatablus (page 169), *who wish to commit themselves to a journey*; and although the pilgrimage was for the sake of a profane matter...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES.
Page 314

<margin>Travels of the Orientals.</margin> —the salty plain, the stony mountains, or deep sands; and furthermore, no river, no human presence, no winter-torrents, no spring, no sown crop, no tree, no animal of flight or land. <note>The author quotes Greek here: ἡ ἁλμυρόγειος πεδιὰς... (the salty plain...)</note> Where there is neither a bite to eat nor a crumb to break / where there is neither dog nor cat / as we say: *neither wood, nor fodder, nor water*, Xiphilinus page 254. In such places, it is absolutely necessary to provide provisions for a long journey, as is still the custom today, especially on a most difficult, dry, and destitute route, where you can find nothing for sale neither by prayer nor by price, *unless you lead some Jesus with you, who might turn water into wine, and say to those stones that they become bread,* as was skillfully written by one who experienced it himself, Barthélemy de Salignac, Book 1, page 75. And those who have surveyed those places complain of that penury and other inconveniences, of whose testimonies we shall bring forward a few. Ludovico di Varthema, a Roman Patrician, described his varied and dangerous journey to the Egyptians, Arabs, Persians, Syrians, and Indians; in his first book of *Navigations*, as he titled it, he describes how, departing from Damascus, he sought Mecca with a Caravan. *He entered* (he writes in chapter 8, page 194) *upon his journey in the year of salvation 1500, dressed in the garment which the Mamluks are accustomed to use. After a journey of three days was completed, we arrived at a certain place named Mezarib. There we paused for three days, so that the merchants might take up the necessities for undertaking the journey, especially camels and many other things. Having completed,* chapter 10, page 195, *a journey of twelve days, we came down to the valley of Sodom and Gomorrah. Indeed, the Holy Page relates the truth. There remain yet the traces of the collapsed cities, a testimony of divine wrath. Having passed the cities by about twenty miles, about 33 of our men lay down from thirst; many were buried there half-dead in the sand, with only their foreheads uncovered. Having progressed a little, we reached a small mountain, at the base of which water was found, at the discovery of which I rejoiced greatly. There we made a station. On the dawn of the following day, several thousand Arabs appeared and demanded a price for the water drawn. When we responded that we would not pay, and that it was given as a gift of the Gods, a battle was immediately joined, as they shouted that we had drunk their waters.* That quarrels and fights have existed at springs, and often even slaughter, is encountered everywhere among others; and it is also related in Holy Scripture. There was a contention between the herdsmen of Lot, Genesis 13:7, over pasture and watering. *For that land could not bear them, that they might dwell together; for their substance was great, so that they could not dwell together, verse 6.* From this it is certain that disputes arose because the herds of oxen were larger and the flocks of sheep more numerous from the blessing of God than that part and portion of the land which they inhabited could suffice to feed so many flocks conveniently. To this was added that the Canaanite and the Perizzite then dwelt in *that land, verse 7*, who simultaneously were an impediment to extending the pastures; for lest they lack that wherewith to feed their own flocks, Abraham and Lot had to dwell more closely together. Thus it happens that, while riches grow, cares grow. Those whom the most joined and inseparable partnership of agricultural pursuits could not separate—not hunger, nor wandering, nor the enemy, nor any calamity—

<column-break/>

—another thing dissociates: the disagreement of the servants; the lack of pasture tears them away. For Abraham said to Lot: *Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee, or between my herdsmen and thy herdsmen; for we are BRETHREN, verse 8.* What could be said by Abraham more peacefully and more fitly for the pursuit of peace? What more convenient for settling a future dispute than to use these words: *Is not the whole land before thee? Separate thyself, I pray thee, from me. If thou wilt take the left hand, then I will go to the right; or if thou depart to the right hand, then I will go to the left, verse 9.* If you depart to the north, as the Chaldean explains it, I shall go to the south; and if you to the south, I to the north. Behold, Abraham leaves the choice to Lot, although he was the more powerful and the elder. He permits the option of choosing to his nephew, and for the sake of redeeming peace, he yields. Lest there be dissension between those joined by blood, a disjunction of places was pleasing, not of minds. Separation is pleasing to both sides, and it pleased Lot *to dwell in the cities of the plain and in the whole plain of the Jordan, because he saw that it was well-watered, verses 10, 11, 12.* He chose that well-watered and pleasant plain of the region which was around the Jordan, and was abundantly irrigated by that river; nor does Abraham envy him. This plain was near Sodom, and was, before that mournful destruction, *verse 10, very pleasant and well-watered from various springs of waters and rivers:* for since Sodom with the neighboring cities was overturned on account of most corrupt vices, the region around those cities is now dry and uncultivated, foul with soil, producing nothing fertile, especially devoid of waters, as Varthema testifies <margin>Travels of the Orientals.</margin> <margin>in the cited place, p. 196.</margin>*. Previously it had been entirely and on every side <term>משקה</term> <note>Hebrew: Mashqeh</note>, <term>irrigua</term> <note>Latin: well-watered</note>, <term>mastig</term> <note>Old German: juicy/moist</note>, <term>a marsh-land</term>, by the force of the word <term>שקה</term> <note>Hebrew root: Sh-Q-H</note>, which signifies to irrigate and to give drink; whence the Sodomites became insolent on account of the abundance of things. But after they defiled themselves with unspeakable crimes, by divine vengeance their fertile region, which had received its name from the five cities of the Pentapolis in Greek, *being struck from heaven, received a black soil dissolved into ash,* according to Solinus chapter 38. This ashy land with its burnt cities and lakes stinking of asphalt is described by Justin, book 36, and Strabo, book 16 of his *Geography*. *It is uncertain from whence*, says Tacitus book 21, *witnessing moreover, that the fields once fertile and inhabited by great cities burned by the casting of lightning; and the traces remain, and the land, parched in appearance, has lost its fruit-bearing power; for all things produced spontaneously, or sown by hand, whether they grew to the stage of grass or flower, or into their usual form, black and empty, vanish as if into ash.* But let us return to other deserted places, where fodder is rare and springs are rare. The Israelites, having gone out into the wilderness of Shur, which was exceedingly thirsty, walked for three days through the solitude, *and they found no water, Exodus 15:22.* Then arriving at Marah (so the place is called by anticipation) *they could not drink the water on account of its bitterness, verse 23, and they murmured against Moses, saying: What shall we drink? verse 24.* While the people were murmuring, Moses cries out to the Lord, verse 25, who showed a piece of wood, which being cast into the waters, all bitterness was turned into sweetness, verse 25. Then they were terrified by the harshness of the desert of Sin, through which they were to be led; for both provisions were lacking, and there was no water in that tract; *wherefore again the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron,* by saying...

# From Joshua IX. v. 3. 4. 5.

->**Travels in the East**<-

<margin>Travels in the East.</margin> with greater impatience: <margin>Exodus 16. v. 3. 4.</margin> *Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots, when we ate bread and were satisfied. Why have you led us out into this desert, to kill this whole assembly with hunger?* <margin>ch. 17. v. 1. 2.</margin> Having departed from here through their stages, they pitched camp in Rephidim, and again there was no water for the people to drink; wherefore the people, contending with Moses, said: *Give us water, so that we may drink.* To be distressed by the inconveniences of a journey is the greatest anxiety, especially where travelers are oppressed by hunger and thirst. The Israelites lost heart in the wildernesses and distrusted their God in the face of imminent necessity. Every need and every cry overflowed upon the afflicted Moses, as their leader. Such is the condition of leaders, that if any misfortune happens, it falls back upon their heads. We cannot sufficiently marvel at the wondrous "brutality" <note>meaning lack of reason or stubbornness</note> of the Israelites. God had attested to His almighty power through various miracles before their eyes in Egypt, and had confirmed it several times in the Red Sea and the deserts, so that He powerfully convinced them that He was—to speak with Paul—so near that He could be felt and almost touched with their hands. Damage is often caused more by the regions themselves than by enemies. When the Roman army under Augustus first reached Arabia, it was vexed more by the inconveniences of the region than by a hostile enemy. <note>original Greek: Ἡ δὲ γε ἐρημία καὶ ὁ ἥλιος...</note> *Indeed, the desert and the sun, and the waters having a certain weak nature, greatly distressed him (the army leader Largus, who had moved there from Egypt), so that the greater part of the army perished,* according to Xiphilinus, page 72. For this reason, neither Trajan nor Severus were able to subjugate that region later, concerning which see the same author, page 254. From the harshness of the eastern regions in most places, they perceive how much difficulty there is in waging war, and how much labor the opposing side will have. No Itinerary is read that does not reveal the arduous nature of traveling, especially through the lurid deserts, where everything is full of despair, so that a desired exit often scarcely appears. I will give here the words of that famous "Pilgram" (as I may call him) Bernhard von Breitenbach, a Noble Man, concerning the vast desert of Gazera: <margin>Itinerary f. 176. a.</margin> *A mile's way from Gazera we saw before us the great, terrifying wilderness, into which we then rode and first pitched our tent; we went far about until we found a little wood to make a fire with. One finds nothing else in those parts that grows or is green, but only dry little shrubs; these we tore out of the earth with the roots and made a fire from them. We also found there a deep well, but having no water at this time. And it is said that the Virgin Mary together with Joseph and JESUS had spent the night there and drawn water from it when they fled into Egypt. The following day we rode over a wide sandy plain, of which we could see no end, except toward the West, and came into a region which in the Arabic tongue was called Cawatha. Having pitched our tents there, we remained for the night and divided ourselves to search the land for wood, as before. There they also brought us water in small casks*

<column-break/>

<margin>Travels in the East.</margin> *from afar, which gave us little delight or cooling, for it was spoiled in the casks. Yet we had a little rain that night, which is very rare in those parts. Moving forward, we came into the true wilderness, in which no man has ever dwelt, and where the soil can neither be sown nor harvested; we found neither village nor city, neither house nor farm, neither fields nor gardens, neither tree nor forest, but only an unfruitful soil burnt by the great heat of the sun.* Now, even from this, consider how necessary travel equipment for food, clothing, and other most necessary things is in those places. From our sacred Antiquities, we have that travelers carried wine and water with them in skins and other vessels. Jesse, 1 Samuel 16:20, *took a donkey loaded with bread, and a skin of wine* <note>original Hebrew: נאד יין; German: Eschel Weins</note> and one kid from the goats, to send by the hand of his son David to Saul, whom he soothed by playing the lyre when he was raving. The Hebrew *donkey of bread* means one loaded with bread, a donkey with bread. In the same way, Sosibius said "three donkeys of loaves" for "the load of three donkeys," as observed by Casaubon on Theocritus. The Greek interpreters say that Jesse took a donkey and placed upon it a *gomor* <note>a dry measure</note> of loaves. For so it stands in the Complutensian and Royal editions: *Jesse took a gomor of loaves and a skin of wine.* But the Aldine edition has: *Jesse took a gomor of donkeys.* The *omer* was a type of measure containing the tenth part of an *ephah*. But the word *ne'ed* <note>skin/bottle</note>, which is also written *ned*, the Latin translator renders as *Lagena* <note>flask/bottle</note>; it seems to be so called because it is moved from its place and arrives from one place to another, for the verb *nud* generally denotes transportation; concerning this etymology see Avenarius's Hebrew Dictionary, page 481. *Nud* generally signifies commotion, swift agitation, and flight from place to place, and cannot be conveniently rendered by a single Latin word. *Ne'ed*, where *aleph* is written for *vau*, signifies a skin in which liquids are contained; these were sewn from hides so that they could be moved or transported from place to place. And Rangolius on Samuel, page 288: *Ne'ed* is a skin or hide in which wine or oil is usually carried, because it is moved from place to place. For *nud* properly designates flight, exile, and wandering, from the verb *nud* or *nad* which expresses "he migrated," "he fled," "he was moved," and similar things emphatically. Skins were made from leather. Lycophron calls a skin a "sewn vessel" <note>Greek: ῥαπτὸν κύτος</note>, writing in the *Alexandra*:

> I bewail you, O fatherland, and the giant
> divers of the Atlantic tombs, who once in a sewn vessel,
> like a four-legged Istrian boar
> solitary in a skin, having enveloped his body
> swam in the waves as if in a light boat.

I do not know, however, where Junius came upon "wooden skin" <note>Latin: uter ligneus</note>, while he explains the word *askopytine* in that way in chapter 10, verse 5, where it is read that the heroine gave to her maid *a skin-flask of wine and a jar of oil, and a bag of meal and of fruit-cake and of pure loaves.* For the last word, the Latin seems to have read "and of cheeses" while speaking of cheeses; or he found both in his Codex. *Askopytine* of wine, a wine-skin (so Vatablus and Castalio translate), a wine vessel; also

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
## Page 316

<margin>Travels in the East, book 10, ch. 20, p. 474.</margin>
...also in the *Onomasticon* of Pollux <note>Julius Pollux, a 2nd-century Greek grammarian</note> it is *counted among the number of wine-carrying vessels* <note>original Greek: ἀσκοφόρων ἀγγείων</note>. By Luther it is rendered: *A pitched skin full of wine* <note>original German: Gepicht Haut voll Weins</note>. By the Vulgate it is called *ascopa* <note>a leather bag or bucket</note>, and Arias Montanus does not correct this; this reading is also confirmed by a very ancient manuscript Codex of the Bible, a copy of which was provided to me by my closest friend, Mr. Balthasar Mentzer—the son of a great father, sharing both his name and his mind <note>original Greek: ὁμώνυμος καὶ ὁμόφρων</note>. I saw it written with the same characters in another parchment Codex in the Library of the Hamburg Chapter; nor is it read otherwise in the Louvain edition, which was most carefully corrected from ancient Codices. Other Codices do not recognize that reading, but have *ascopera* <note>a traveler's leather bag</note>, which Andreas Placus approves by his own calculation.

<margin>Biblical Lexicon, folio 112, a. 25, against 11.</margin>
There is a similar diversity of reading in Suetonius’s *Nero*, chapter 45: *an ascopa tied to the neck of another*, unless one reads it as *ascoma* with a change of letter as Turnebus does, because the Greeks say *askoma* <note>original Greek: ἀσκώμα, a leather padding for an oar-hole</note>. It is better if we read *ascopera*. The reading *scopera* is worthless, though Sabellicus saw it in so many Codices. *Ascopera* is named like Seneca’s *hippopera* <note>a saddlebag</note>, and it denotes there a bag made of bull’s hide, a sack <note>original Greek: ταύρειος ἀσκὸς, ἀσκὸς βόειος</note>, which in the language of the Tarentines is called a *molgos* <note>original Greek: μολγὸς</note>, according to Pollux, book 10, ch. 50, p. 503. John Xiphilinus uses this word in his *Epitome of Dio*, page 165, speaking of that same matricide Nero, in place of what Suetonius called an *ascopera*. The historian related that a sack was placed on a statue of Nero with this inscription: *I did what I could, but you deserved the sack*. This marked Nero as a parricide, and simultaneously the punishment for parricide of which he was worthy. For the penalty was that a parricide, sewn into a sack with a dog, a rooster, a viper, and a monkey, should be cast into the sea or a river.

With no less fame, we have received the celebration of the skin-bottle of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, from which Sisera satisfied his thirst, but which brought him death. For the woman intercepted Sisera, to whom no way of escape lay open, addressing him with flattering words: *Turn aside, my Lord, turn aside to me. Do not fear.* Sisera entered the tent to her, and she covered him with her cloak, or, as Tremellius prefers, *a shaggy blanket* <note>original Latin: stragula amphitapa</note>, which according to Isidore (book 9, ch. 26) are carpets shaggy on both sides. The new guest asks for a drink of water to quench the thirst he had contracted from flight. The hostess offers a <term>נאד החלב</term> <note>ne'ed ha-chalav</note>, a skin of milk <note>original Greek: ἀσκὸν γάλακτος</note>, and gives him a drink, *Judges 4:18-19*. Regarding this, in the Song found in the fifth chapter, verse 25, we read: *When he (Sisera) asked for water, she gave milk; in a bowl of nobles she offered butter.* The Septuagint punctuates this differently, and refers the bowl, which they call a *lekane* <note>original Greek: λεκάνην</note>, to the milk, not the butter. In the Hebrew it is <term>ספל</term> <note>sephel</note>, a word found only in this book, and indeed a second time in verse 38, where the Chaldean <note>Aramaic Targum</note> has <term>לקנא</term> <note>laqna</note>, to which *lekane* and *lagena* <note>flask/bottle</note> correspond; just as <term>ספל</term> (the word the Chaldean uses in verse 25) corresponds to *phiale* and *vial*. The Hebrew seems to harmonize with the word *Simpulum* <note>a small ladle used in sacrifices</note>, a word which delighted Junius, who translated: *In a simpulum of the magnificent ones she offered rich milk.* We do not wish to stir up verbal crowds, or "excite waves in a simpulum" <note>a Latin idiom similar to "a tempest in a teapot"</note>. We know where we stand in this legal matter.

To David, living in exile, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth <margin>2 Samuel 16:1.</margin> came to meet him with two saddled donkeys, which were loaded with *two hundred loaves of bread, and a hundred clusters of raisins, and a hundred cakes of figs, and a skin of wine*, according to the Vulgate translation. The Septuagint has *a pair of saddled donkeys, and upon them two hundred loaves, and a hundred raisins, and a hundred cakes, and a nebel of wine*. Hebrew: <term>נבל יין</term> <note>nebel yayin</note>, *Wine-skin*. *Nebel* among the Franks and others is a certain vessel, <term>נאד</term> <note>ne'ed</note>, a flask, and hence the Latin diminutive *laguncula*, Jeremiah 13:12, where it stands: *every bottle shall be filled with wine*. The Septuagint: *every skin <note>original Greek: ἀσκὸς</note> shall be filled with wine.* And: *All bottles <note>original German: Nebel</note> shall be filled with wine.* One must not remain here in the literal sense, but seek something deeper, regarding which Origen spent an entire homily, found in Volume 1 of his works, p. 671 ff. Tremellius and Grotius understand it as an earthen or potter's flask <margin>page 189.</margin>, to which those words in chapter 48:12 uttered against the Moabites should be traced, from the old version: *I will send to him decanters and spreaders of flasks, and they shall lay him low, and empty his vessels, and break their flasks.* Junius renders it: *I will send to him wanderers, who shall make him wander, and empty his vessels, and scatter their skins.* Hebrew: <term>נבליהם</term> <note>nebelehem</note>. The Greek interpreter understands *pottery* <note>original Greek: τὰ κεράμια</note>, and a reading more fragile than any potter's vessel is *horns* <note>original Greek: τὰ κέρατα</note>, which I see embraced by the Interpreter of the Greek Bible, who, hiding his name, sells a most diligent translation of them. The Hebrew <term>נבל</term> <note>nebel</note> drives out that word, about which the skilled Professor of this language, Johann Forster (p. 468), teaches: <term>נבל</term> *a vessel whether of leather or earthenware, so called because it is empty.* Just as <term>נבל</term> *signifies a fool, because he is empty of wisdom and virtues.* *You may translate it as a skin, if it is understood to be made of hides. But if it has the name of earthenware attached, or another word from which you understand it to be a potter's work made from earth, and easily subject to breaking, then it will be permitted to translate it as a flask, or a pitcher, or an amphora, or by another name, although it would be better to have some name in the mother tongue by which the etymology and meaning of the word might be properly expressed.* The variety of meaning is restricted by the evidence of the thing, to which a certain mark is added as it were, and for proof are the words of Isaiah: *He shall break it as the breaking <margin>Isaiah 30:14.</margin> of a potter's skin <note>nebel</note> when crushed.* Thus Tremellius translates harshly. The old interpreter better: (*it shall be crushed as a potter's flask is broken*) *with a very strong crushing.* The Septuagint says its ruin shall be like the crushing of an earthen vessel from a fortified potter's workshop. He well understands an earthen vessel, baked from clay by a potter, which is *kerameion* to the Greeks, *fidelia* <note>an earthen jar</note> to the Latins, *irden Krug* to the Germans, that is, a little earthen vessel, in French *vaisseau de terre*, or, as the Italian interpreter speaks here, *vaso di vasaio*, the Spaniard, *vaso de olleros*. In Columella 12. R. R. 38, *fidelia fictilis* <note>an earthen jar</note>.

# From Joshua III. v. 3. 4. 5.

<margin>Travels of the Easterners.</margin> **Flagon** (*Lagena*), from which comes "little flask," a vessel suitable for storing and carrying wines. Regarding Cretan wine, which we now call *Malvasia*, carried in flagons, Juvenal writes in *Satire 14, Book 5, line 270*:

> You who rejoice to have brought from the ancient shore of fertile Crete
> Raisin-wine, and flagons that are fellow-citizens of Jove.
<note>original: "Qui gaudes pingue antiqua de litore Cretæ / Passum, & municipes fovis advexisse lagenas." Juvenal suggests the wine jars are "citizens" of Crete because Jupiter was said to be born there.</note>

<margin>Genesis 21. v. 14. 15.</margin> Furthermore, the Hebrew word <term>חמת</term> <note>Chemet</note> is also used for a *skin* and a *flagon*. Abraham rose early in the morning and gave to Hagar the handmaid bread and a skin of water, <term>חמת מים</term> <note>Chemet mayim</note>, which the Greek translates as <term>ἀσκὸν ὕδατος</term> <note>askon hydatos - a skin of water</note>. The Zurich translators call it a *pitcher of water*. The Spanish: *un cuero de agua* [a skin of water]. Luther: *a bottle with water*.

It was truly a meager provision—*a skin of water and bread*—for one who was forced to journey through desert places, for whom even a donkey with moderate supplies would not have sufficed. Content with those things, she placed the provisions on her shoulder, departed, and wandered in the desert of *Beersheba*. When the water in the skin (<term>מן-החמת</term>) <note>min-ha-chemet</note> failed, the wretched mother, with a wail of lamentation, cast the child under one of the trees so he would not be utterly consumed by the heat of the sun—the infant whom she had led by the hand until then, now fainting with thirst, while she herself was equally exhausted by thirst. Luther on this passage says: *Moses describes a horrific history in few words. Mother and son had water for three or four days; they refreshed themselves in the solitude, but afterward the water failed. Death therefore hung over both, and indeed from thirst, than which nothing is more intolerable to nature.* That Egyptian handmaid was exposed to the greatest hardships of the journey after her drink failed, having no place in that sterile and waterless land from which to refill it. <term>Not only was the current scarcity difficult, but there was also a despair of future necessities.</term> <note>original Greek: Ἦν δ' ὁ μόνον παρελθὼν σπάνις χαλεπόν, ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς τὸν μέλλοντα χρόνον τῶν ἐπιτηδείων ἀπόγνωσις.</note> But what happened? When the thirst redoubled and the infant's final breath of fate was imminent, an Angel came and opened the mother's eyes; seeing a well of water, she went, filled the skin, and gave the boy a drink. <margin>v. 19.</margin> There is no greater complaint in those places than the lack of water, so much so that more perish from thirst than from hunger. In the description of Africa, Joannes Leo <margin>Book 1. c. 27 f 28. b.</margin> recorded that in the desert of Azoad there exist two monuments: one of a merchant, the other of a carrier of goods; the latter received ten thousand gold pieces from the former for a single cup of water, yet the water could not suffice for both to deliver them from death. The Prophet *Habakkuk* also seems to have spoken of a skin, according to the interpreter Junius: <margin>c. 2. v. 15.</margin> *Woe to him who gives drink to his neighbor, applying your skin, and even making him drunk.* *Vatablus* and *Pagninus* agree with this, following the Rabbis. He threatens woe to him who uses his skin to inebriate his friend. *Rabbi Abraham* calls it the "cup of deep sleep" in this passage. They claim Nebuchadnezzar did this so he might delight in the ridiculous behavior of the drunkards. Interpreters sometimes make places doubtful where doubt hardly appears. The ancient interpreter took the name <term>נאד</term> <note>Nod/Ned - heap or skin</note> to mean a skin, <term>in a similar way</term>, I believe, in Psalm 33 verse 7; for those words <term>ככנס כנד מי הים</term> <note>gathering the waters of the sea as a heap/skin</note> he rendered: *Gathering the waters of the sea as if in a skin*. Luther follows this sense: *He holds the water in the sea together like in a skin-bag*. This is not without the sense of the Masoretes and Greek interpreters. Thus the Chaldean Paraphrast took <term>נאד</term> for <term>גאד</term> in *Joshua 3. v. 13. 16.* where it treats the divided waters of the Jordan, which stood above <term>נד אחד</term>, *in one mass, one heap, in a pile*. The Septuagint, according to the

<column-break/>

Royal Codex: <term>as a heap</term> <note>Greek: ὡς σωρός</note>. Symmachus: <term>as a skin-bag</term> <note>Greek: ὡς ἀσκῶμα</note>. However, as this discourse concerns the Israelites—how, with the Ark sent ahead, the Jordan was divided and they crossed as if it were suspended in a mound <margin>Travels of the Easterners.</margin> or a mountain—so in the Psalmist the discourse is about the division and suspension of the waters of the Red Sea for those crossing through the midst of Israel. God opposed a mass and "valves," as it were, to the waters to keep back the waves, just as a dike is usually built to restrain water; hence Job, a master of grandiloquence <margin>c. 38. v. 8. 10.</margin>, writes of the creation and constitution of the sea: *Who shut up the sea with doors? I broke up the earth for it by my decree, and set bars and doors.* The force of the waters from the wind swells like a skin that is blown up by a bellows, and when the wind stops, it subsides; and lest it break out, it is contained as if in a skin. Basil on the said Psalm, p. 85: <term>He did not say, "gathering the waters of the sea as in a skin," but "gathering the waters of the sea as a skin." Consider for me the nature of a skin: now being blown out when the skin is stretched by the following wind, now being contracted when the wind recedes. So it is with the sea.</term> <note>original Greek: Οὐκ εἶπε, συνάγων τὰ ὕδατα τῆς θαλάσσης ὡς ἐν ἀσκῷ...</note> Theodoret, Question 1 on Joshua, p. 184: <term>The rush of the waters being held back, it was like a skin and rose to a peak.</term> By a new and rare usage, <term>to be like a skin</term> <note>Greek: ἀσκῷ</note> means to swell up like a skin-bag, whence the concretion of waters is called <term>a skin-like swelling</term> <note>Greek: ἀσκῶμα</note>, as is the tumor of an inflated skin, when the waters are piled up as if into a *skin* or *heap*. <term>נד</term> <note>Ned</note>, a heap or mound, is so called from <term>נוד</term> <note>Nud</note>, to be moved or agitated, because by motion and agitation something is gathered and comes together as one, just as sandy hills are accustomed to be driven and carried by the wind in certain maritime places or in deserts. John Forster in his Dictionary, page 482: <term>נד</term> *a heap, mound, mass either of sand or of waters, which is moved from place to place*. Authors tell wonders of the little mountains of sand heaped up by the wind. Diodorus Siculus, 2nd Library <margin>Hanover Edition, 1604</margin> page 136: *The places turned toward the west contain sandy plains of immense vastness; thus it happens that those making a journey there, not otherwise than on the sea, direct their progress by the signs of the celestial Bear [the stars].* Quintus Curtius *Book 7, chapter 4, num. 27. 28. regarding the land of Bactria*: *Sterile sands occupy a great part of the same land. The region, squalid with dryness, nourishes neither man nor fruit. But when the winds blow from the Pontic sea, they sweep up whatever sand lies in the plains. When this is heaped up, it looks from afar like great hills, and all traces of the former path perish. Therefore, those who cross the plains observe the stars at night in the manner of sailors, directing their journey by their course. Otherwise, if that wind which rises from the sea catches any, it buries them in sand.* And Book 5, c. 1. n. 29. 30: *The Euphrates carries deep mud. Sands heaped up from time to time, and clinging to the stones by which the bridge is supported, delay the river, which, being held back more sharply than if it flowed in a free course, dashes against them.* Describing the land of the Ammonites, Arrian in Book 3, c. 1, teaches that when the South wind blows, the sands are heaped up so that all traces of the roads where one must go are destroyed. He records that travelers follow the guidance of the stars, just as sailors do the stars at sea; Pliny in IV. 5, speaking of the Syrtis: *The journey is by observation of the stars through the deserts of clinging sand and through serpents.* As it happens, even more faith should be placed in the Poets. Lucanus <margin>Book 9, v. 495</margin>

> The most faithful Little Bear <note>The constellation Ursa Minor, used for navigation.</note> guides the Sidonian sailors.

<margin>Commentary on Genesis, p. 51.</margin>
Junilius, the African Bishop, was not ignorant of this when he wrote: *The lights are for signs, necessary for the uses of this life, which either the sailor observes in steering, or those traveling in the sandy deserts of Ethiopia; where, at the slightest impulse of the wind, all the tracks of the travelers that had been found are immediately leveled. Therefore, those going in those regions, no less than those who sail on the sea, need the signs of the stars by night and day.* You may see that there is danger in the sand as in the sea, and the journey through sandy tracts is steered almost as if in the waves of the sea; whence he describes the journey through the sands as if it had been performed in a maritime course. Vartomannus, <margin>Book 1, ch. 13, p. 199. <note>Ludovico di Varthema, a 15th-century Italian traveler.</note></margin> who informs us of this matter by his own example, writes: *I would not wish (he says) to consign to oblivion what I found in the sea nicknamed "of sand." In a sandy sea of this kind, we had a journey of five days and nights. Now it shall become known to you what kind of sea it is. They are open fields, which are strewn with white sands like dust. If by some sinister foot it should happen that those who travel there were carried by the South wind, as they are driven by the North, they would all fall overwhelmed by the sand; for even if they were carried by favorable breezes, they were nonetheless so enveloped by a dark whirlwind of sand that, with sight and distance taken away, one could not see another at ten paces. Because of this, the inhabitants are carried on camels enclosed in wooden cages, and in them they drag out their lives, led however by pilots, who are guided no differently than in a billowing sea by a compass and a chart. But when the Etesian winds blow from the north, then the sand is lifted on high, and is carried gathered into a mountain.* We have a memory of these things because of several sacred expressions, which seem to be taken from here. The prophet Habakkuk, in order to describe the numerous cavalry of the enemies coming for the destruction of the Jews, <margin>ch. 1, v. 8, 9.</margin> says: *His horsemen coming from afar shall fly like an eagle hastening to the prey. All shall come for violence, the faces of those approaching like the east wind (pestilential in those places) and he shall gather the captive multitude like sand.* Which words Wolfgang <margin>Exposition on Habakkuk, f. 17. a.</margin> Capito <note>A German Reformer and Hebrew scholar.</note> explains thus: *It is a hyperbole <note>original: ὑπερβολὴ</note>, which serves gravity and clarity. That part of Arabia which extends from the Syrians and Jews toward the south to the sea is sandy, upon which winds suddenly falling pile up vast heaps of sand. Just as, therefore, he says, the sand of that place is suddenly gathered in great numbers; so Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans unexpectedly heaped up a captivity of infinite nations. He indicates the speed of the arrival and also the swift deportation and depopulation by this illustrious simile; that as easily as the wind carries away thin sand to another place, so easily shall the troops of the Chaldeans lead away the people into captivity.* From which simile <margin>ch. 17, v. 13.</margin> Isaiah does not recede far, which is concerning the flight of the Assyrian enemies: *He shall flee far off, and shall be snatched away like dust (chaff, husk) of the mountains before the face of the wind.*

<column-break/>

He said, *of the mountains*, so that he might note speed most emphatically <note>original: ἐμφατικώτατος</note>, for winds <margin>Travels of the Orientals.</margin> are accustomed to be stronger above the mountains. Another passage of Silius almost passed by in the same <margin>Book 3, v. 653.</margin> where he describes the journey of Hannibal through the Syrtes <note>Dangerous sandbanks off the coast of North Africa.</note>, and the sands to be feared equally with the Syrtes, as dangerous:

> A land more violent than the seas almost swallowed us.
> To the end of the sky from the middle of the mouth are stretched
> Squalid plains. Nature denied a mound
> To the immense spaces, except that which the whirlwind, twisting hollow clouds,
> Constructed, heaped up with impacted sand.
> Or if the South wind, having broken its prison, ravaged the lands,
> Or the Northwest wind, scattering the sea over the ether,
> Fiercely invaded the plain receiving the battles,
> And in turn piled up mountains with heaped dust.
> We sailed these valleys by the observed stars.

We ought not to forget these things. The same is mentioned—which will help our opinion—by that unpublished Arabic *Travelogue* <note>original: Hodæporicum</note>, a copy of which was shown to me by a man both learned without ostentation and most kind without pretense, Mr. Jacob Golius, who teaches these letters and rites with profit in the illustrious Academy of the Batavians <note>Leiden University</note>, on whose guidance <note>original: ἀγωγῇ</note> I congratulate myself. I seem not to have done badly if, according to the nature of our undertaking, I say something from it here. When Hared, which the name implies, had mounted a camel for the sake of travel, he came first to Sana'a, a city of Arabia Felix <note>Modern-day Yemen</note>, like a thirsty bird, and having wandered <note>original: ἀλανηθεὶς</note> through the land, at last he came to a certain old man in a large assembly speaking sententiously and shrewdly about contempt for the world; having heard his grave speech, each of those listeners put his hand into his bosom, and they filled a skin-bag with their gifts. To be sure, the *machlin* <note>original: מחלין</note> was a small vessel made of leather, which they carried with them, so that they might draw water on the way, or fill it with wine, to quench thirst. Most elegant and full of graces is that travel of Ulysses, which Homer, the Parent of all antiquity and elegance, describes in a divine poem, the *Odyssey*. You may see Ulysses *having packed his things and arranged his bundles <margin>Odyssey 1, v. 229.</margin> putting on a cloak and a tunic, preparing a ship, and hastening by oars and sails through the courses of an unknown sea to his Ithaca.* Moreover, Calypso helped the maritime journey, preparing provisions and side-dishes for him as he was about to depart, <margin>Book 4, v. 266.</margin> provisions and meat <note>original: ἤϊα καὶ ὄψα</note> besides, as the Poet records, <margin>v. 265.</margin> *she sent in a skin-bag dark wine, and another large one of water.* The same man, brought down to the Lotus-eaters <margin>Odyssey 9, v. 196</margin> received from Maron, the priest of Apollo, a goat-skin bag of dark wine. Of dark wine? Aelian (History 12, 26) and Athenaeus (Book 1, p. 15) will teach that there were various kinds of Greek wines. These are the words of the latter: *Homer, praising dark wine, often calls it also "sparkling." For it is most potent, remaining in the habits of those drinking for a very long time. And Theopompus says that dark wine first came into being among the Chians.* Before those [Athenaeus 3, v. 247] which verses Athenaeus also reviews in Book 10, p. 168. For the mother of Nausicaa pours wine into a goat-skin bag, which she gave to her daughter together with a flask full of liquid oil, concerning which Homer speaks thus in Odyssey Book 6, v. 75. <margin>Odyssey 6, v. 75.</margin>

> And the mother placed in a chest heart-satisfying food,
> Of every kind, and in it she placed meat, and in it she poured wine
> In a goat-skin bag.
