# From Joshua IX. v. 3. 4. 5.

<margin>Travels in the East. Vol. 3. Life p. 394 +</margin> Artaxerxes did not reject the filthy leather skin of a certain Caunian, even drinking from it water that was already foul, according to Plutarch <note>Plutarch was a Greek biographer and philosopher</note>. Those who travel through the parched regions of the East are accustomed to carry skins full of water with them by the labor of camels; and this is usually done especially in long deserts, where sometimes for a journey of six or seven days not even a drop of water is found, unless it has been carried by camels in skins placed upon their backs, as witnessed by the history of Joannes Leo Africanus <note>A 16th-century Berber Andalusian diplomat and author</note> 1. Afr. 27. f. 28. a. Concerning the journey of Saint Anthony, Athanasius says in his life of the same, page 72: *A camel carried for them the loaves of bread and the water; for all that desert is waterless, and there is no drinkable water at all.* <note>Original Greek: Κάμηλόν αὐτοῖς ἐβάστᾰσε τοὺς ἄρτους καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ. ἄνυδρος γὰρ ἐρημός ἐστιν ἐκείνη πᾶσα, καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ὕδωρ πότιμον ὅλως.</note> Later, describing how they suffered from a lack of water (which he narrates was obtained miraculously, not unlike Samson), he says they filled whole skins and placed them on the camel: *And so, having drunk, they all revived, and having filled the skins, they sought the camel. Then, leading it and giving it water, they placed the skins upon it and continued their journey.* <note>Original Greek: Καὶ ἔτω πίοντες οἱ πάντες ἀνέπνευσαν, καὶ τοὺς ἀσκοὺς πλήσαντες ἐζήτησαν τὴν κάμηλον. ἀγαγόντες τοίνυν καὶ ποτίσαντες ἐπέθηκαν τοὺς ἀσκούς, καὶ διώδευσαν.</note> Furthermore, regarding the same use of the skin, an elegant testimony occurs in the fourth book of Quintus Curtius in the description of the most troublesome and vexatious journey which Alexander undertook to the oracle of Jupiter Ammon through fields that were extremely hot and sandy. I will set down the words themselves: *When the plains covered with deep sand opened up, they looked for land just as if they had entered a deep sea. No tree, no trace of cultivated soil met them. Even the water had failed, which the camels had carried in skins, and in the dry soil and burning sand there was none.* You may gather that the skins, as the eloquent writer says, were carried by camels and were therefore very large; just as today camels are designated for carrying larger skins, about which Thomas Treterus noted these things in the Jerusalem
<margin>page 153.</margin> pilgrimage of Prince Radziwiłł: *Eight thousand camels carry water from the Nile (he speaks of Cairo) from door to door, in two leather skins, each of which holds our common cask, hanging on either side.* Others who have visited those places write similar things, such as A. Heberer in *Egyptian Service* 8. p. 129: *Because the city of Cairo is exceedingly large, so that the inhabitants are partly far and partly near to the water of the Nile, in my time 18,000 camels and dromedaries were counted which carried water for sale from the Nile here and there into the city, not counting what was carried by men and donkeys.*
<margin>S. Itin. 15. p. 264.</margin> Salomon Schweigger says: *In Alexandria they use camels so that they carry well-water back and forth into the houses in two leather sacks on their backs, just as wine is also commonly carried in goat-skins.* Among the spectacles exhibited by the Egyptian King Ptolemy Philadelphus to show his pomp more clearly, was a skin of stupendous size, which six hundred men pulled on a chariot, *a skin containing three thousand measures, sewn from leopard skins*, concerning which Athenaeus should be consulted from the book of Masurius Callixenus.
<margin>Book 5. Deipnosophistae p. 60.</margin> You may also find men wandering through cities who carry good and always fresh water in certain skins, which they offer freely to anyone who asks, according to Joannes
<margin>2. On the Rites of Nations book 1. p. 153.</margin> Boemus. Those who make the journey through the Pyrenees mountains from France into Spain drink wine from skins, which often spoils and turns into little worms.

<column-break/>

<margin>Travels in the East.</margin> In Italy also there is the use of skins. Codrus Urceus, a man famous for learning and festive wit, alludes to this in witty rhythms concerning the feast of St. Martin, f. 66. a.
> He who wishes to carry with me,
> Though he may carry the truth with him
> Wines in full skins.
It happened that, when a journey was made through various places and deserted regions, the skins were sometimes loosened by mist, frost, and dew (which falls copiously around Mount Sinai), and sometimes by rain; they also developed cracks, being shriveled by heat and wind, and finally were worn out from long and constant use. However, they were sometimes accustomed to hang the moistened and loosened skins in the chimney flue so they would not rot, so that having been moderately dried out again, they might be repaired. From this you will understand the words of the Psalmist, Psalm 119 v. 83: *For I have become like a wineskin in the smoke.* <note>Original Hebrew: כִּי־הָיִיתִי כְּנֹאד בְּקִיטוֹר</note> The Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> says: *For I have become like a skin in the frost.* <note>Original Greek: ὅτι ἐγενήθην ὡς ἀσκὸς ἐν πάχνῃ</note> The Vulgate: *I was like a skin in the frost.* The Hebrew for frost is *Cephor*, as in Psalm 147:16, and thus they seem to have read it. Here, however, *Kitor* is *smoke*. The version does not seem so intricate, for since the word refers to vapor or smoke, from which frost arises when lifted into the air and constricted by the night cold, those who look upon that version as oracular can defend it. Hence also the Arab, who follows other versions, translates: *like a skin in the ice*, namely constricted and dissolved by the cold. Luther: *like a skin in the smoke.* Metonymically; for the skins were made from hides. In which sense Martin Opitz says in his metrical paraphrase:
<margin>n. 42.</margin>
> Like a skin shriveled by the smoke,
> So also sadness brings me to nothing.
> Yet I never forget the custom,
> That I meditate on your statutes.
The comparison is drawn from a *skin*, which is loosened and pulled apart by frost and rain, but is constricted and joined together by smoke or heat in a chimney, to exaggerate the magnitude of the calamities and hardships which he was enduring; for the sense is: I am scorched by adversities, I am exhausted by the constant heat of evils, and contracted into the wrinkles of miseries, like a skin hardened and parched by smoke. By very frequent fasting and the soot of hunger, my whole body is shown to be wrinkled and dried up, like a skin dried in a smokehouse; like a skin relaxed by frost, which the smoke in the chimney dries out and wrinkles. Plautus mentions this. Lucas Osiander paraphrases: *Just as a skin hanging in a very smoky place dries out; so from the long and anxious expectation of your help my skin has dried out, and no longer has moisture.* And Antonius Flaminius in his metrical paraphrase:
<margin>page 376.</margin>
->Before the magnitude of this<-
->Affliction, although<-
->My skin be greatly consumed,<-
->Like skins suspended at the hearth,<-
->Yet mindful of your law<-
->I pray to you.<-
Fittingly, the Holy Scripture has compared the gravest hardships, fear, dread, hunger, and those things which are deadly, with a smoked <unclear>mouse</unclear>, likewise with the blackness of the oven and the bronze pot, because calamities as it were burn the bones, blacken the skin, and exhaust all the limbs; for not only the soul but also the body wastes away with sadness and hardships. *A sorrowful spirit dries up the bones*, says Solomon. Nor in an alien way of speak—
<margin>Prov. 17. 22.</margin>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
### Page 320

<margin>Travels in the East. Chapter 1, scene 2, verse 31.</margin>
This manner of speaking in *Psalm 102, verses 3 and 6*, denotes extreme thinness with these words: *My bones are dried up like a hearth with constant heat. My bone clings to my flesh,* just as the character of the *Parasite* says in the plays of Plautus:
> I grow thin, I grow old, and I waste away, miserable.
> I am nothing but skin and bones from wretched leanness.

The fate of the Jews is elegantly expressed by the same sentiment through the metaphor of an *oven* <note>Latin: clibanus</note>, "lying in helpless wrath," in the Prophet *Lamentations, chapter 5, verse 10.* Now, an oven was a vessel in which bread, or even meat, was cooked by slow steam. Regarding the famished, *Joel chapter 2, verse 6* says: *They shall take on blackness like a pot.* This is similar to our saying: *The black hunger.* This *blackness is a sign* by which the *Psalmist* declares the magnitude of grief and affliction when he says:
<margin>Psalm 38:7</margin>
*I am bowed down, I am greatly depressed by the weight of sin and calamities: I walk black all day long.* Regarding this, *Mollerus* (p. 687) notes that some interpret the Hebrew word *Koder* <note>קודר</note> not as clothing, but as the blackness of the skin, as if to say: *The natural color has vanished from the face; for sadness deforms men with thinness and filth.* Therefore, to persist with our comparison: just as skins <note>leather bottles</note> develop cracks from being carried around constantly, and usually take on a black color from being frequently hung in smoke; so men are seen to become more slender and parched by the frequent infestation of calamities. A parallel comparison is found in Psalm 56, verse 9, where he prays to God to be mindful of his calamities and his fall; *that He might store his tears in His bottle, just as men otherwise store some good liquid of wine or oil in a skin or flask.* Place *my tears* <note>Hebrew: בנאדך</note> i.e., *in your bottle.* The Vulgate version has: *You have placed my tears in your sight.* *Johannes Campensis paraphrases it: Collect, I pray, my tears, and pour them into your glass, so that you may see how many they are.* The poet *Johannes Stigelius*, the most eloquent poet of his time, alluded to the song of the holy Psalmist in an Eclogue which he wrote under the name 
<margin>Year 1522.</margin>
of Daphnis to the Most Illustrious Prince of Saxony, John Frederick:
> He collects pious complaints as if in a certain bottle,
> And at last turns the tears of the righteous into joys.

<margin>In the Life of Theseus, p. 11.</margin>
There exists a verse of the Sibyl in Plutarch, which we can cite as a charming image of the dangers and the miraculous preservation of the Church and its members:
> *The skin-bottle is baptized (submerged), but it is not permitted for you to sink.* <note>Original Greek: Ἀσκὸς βαπτίζῃ, δῦναί δέ τοι οὐ θέμις ἐστίν.</note>

Which you may render poetically:
-> The bottle is dipped in the waters, but is never submerged. <-

<margin>On Joseph, p. 369.</margin>
*Such are the ends of the godly,* says Philo, *for even if they are tossed by waves, they do not fall forever, but rising up again, they stand firm and steady.* <note>Original Greek: Τοιαῦτα τῆς εὐσεβῶν... κἂν γὰρ κλιδῶσιν...</note> We say: God may let us sink, but not drown.
-> *That ship is tossed by the waves, but never sinks.* <-

By an illustrious metaphor, the clouds are called the *bottles of heaven* <note>Hebrew: נבלי שמים</note> 
<margin>Chapter 38:37</margin>
by Job; the Chaldean translation has "vessels." What form of speaking is more illustrious than this? From the clouds, as if from flasks or skins, waters are poured out abundantly. The Greeks call the clouds "rain-bringing" and "rain-birthing," just as the Latins say *imbriferam* or *pluviam* (rain-bearing cloud).
-> Who is called so wise <-
-> That he can count the clouds? Who can stop the water-skins <-

<column-break/>

-> In the high field of heaven, so that it retreats, <-
<margin>Travels in the East.</margin>
-> So that it cannot flow, when now the dust of the earth <-
-> Is to be watered, and turns into clods? <-

Knowledge of the skin-bottle also contributes much to understanding the simile taken from old bottles and new wine, which the Savior uses in *Matthew 9:17* in the conversation held with the disciples of John regarding fasting. What is said about the bottles, the Savior speaks according to the custom of Syria, where new wine was stored in fresh skins. In this sense, Matthias Flacius explains in a special treatise on the necessity of knowing various things for the understanding of the speech of Holy Scripture: *It was customary to carry wine, water, and other liquids in skins; hence their mention in the Old and New Testaments. They placed unfermented wine (must) in new skins because, due to its gassiness, it needed to be contained in a strong vessel; nor did the skins hinder it by their own rawness, or infect the must, which rejects rather than attracts influences by its own exhalation. Conversely, old wine does not require a strong vessel and is more easily affected by the vessel. Therefore, they put old wine into old skins. The Lord wishes to indicate that a proportion must be maintained between the discipline and the disciples: so that although beginners are treated with a softer discipline at the start, they will later necessarily have to endure harder things, which remain for them in great abundance.* The Arabs call a skin of this kind that has suffered decay *Daphna* or *Naphtu*, i.e., so that with its lining cut and broken, it can contain nothing. For that vessel is bound between two patches on both sides; and it has a small opening <note>term: verticillum - a small vent or stopper</note> through which the air of the wine may evaporate, according to Giggæus in his *Treasury of the Arabic Language*. Among the ancients, a friend was nicknamed "the body of a skin-bottle" <note>Greek: askos soma</note>, as the Glossary has it, or, as Festus prefers, "the neck of the bottle," through which wine is poured from the skin. From this, the words of Job in *chapter 19, verse 32* are illustrated: <margin>Chapter 19:32</margin> *Behold, my belly is like must without a vent, which bursts new flasks.* In Hebrew it is *Ob* <note>אוב</note>, which Mercerus and Pineda interpret as a skin-bottle, and they deduce from this that *Ob* was later used for a Python <note>a spirit of divination</note>, who is puffed up by an evil spirit like a skin-bottle. From the same word, the Latin *Obba*, a type of cup, can be derived; a word which pleased Castalio, so that he rendered "a jar of oil" as *obbam olei* in *Judith 10:5.* Persius uses it: <margin>Satire 5, line 148</margin> *The broad-bottomed cup exhales the smell of flat pitch.*

There are also proverbs and maxims taken from the skin-bottle by secular authors. The Greeks joke about a drunken man, saying he is a "mere skin-bottle" and a "mere sack." We say: *A full tap that has no bottom in its body: a wine-skin.* From bottles we move to Sacks, which they carried with them so that travelers' supplies were best managed. Sacks were of two different types, just as bottles were: some of smaller size, others larger. These were placed on beasts of burden, as appears in *Genesis 42, verses 25, 26, 27* in the history of the journey of Joseph's brothers, where Luther commended to us the word *Ametachath* <note>אמתחת</note> or *Sak* <note>שק</note> with a fitting etymology in his commentary on Genesis. *Ametachath* signifies a sack, from *Mathach*, i.e., by expanding; just as when the belly makes a fold among us, we call it in our language: *A Sack.* Likewise, a watery cloud, or the sails of ships when the wind blows through them, have a certain appearance of a sack. Thus a sack, when it is filled—

# From Joshua IX. v. 3. 4. 5.

<margin>Travels of the Eastern Peoples.</margin>
...is filled, expanded, and from that extension or swelling it is so named, because it is turgid and sinuous. Bags would also be suspended from the shoulders, and they are met with everywhere; concerning which, to add this as well, we have observed from Belon’s book 1, chapter 35, that the Monks (who call themselves by the beautiful name <note>original: καλοχέρες (kalogeroi), meaning "good old men"</note> *Good Elders*) among the Greeks on Mount Athos, having gone out from their monasteries at earliest dawn to work, carried tools for laboring; some a mattock, others a spade, others a sickle, and having a pouch hanging from the shoulder in which was twice-baked bread <note>biscotti or hard tack</note> and onions. Diogenes the Cynic took a "cup out of his pouch" <note>original: ποτήριον ἐν τῆς πήρας</note> when he had come to the fountain of Panope exhausted by thirst, which he finally threw away and scooped up water with his hands, having been taught by the servant boy Theon; concerning which see the complete Letter of Diogenes to Crates, *Letters* page 68. The same Philosopher carried a pouch on his shoulders and a staff in his hand, as is established from his same Letter to his father Hicetas and to Antipater, pages 70 and 76. The pouch hanging from the shoulder is the very *mantica* <note>a double-sided bag or portmanteau</note> which was suspended so that it could be seen in front of the chest and at the back at the same time, hence the Proverb: *We do not see the part of the bag that is on our back*. i.e., we immediately notice the smallest vices of anyone else, but we do not see our own enormous ones. Hence Aesop, according to Stobaeus, <margin>form. 21. p 180.</margin> said: *Each of us carries two pouches, one in front and the other behind; and into the one in front, we put the sins of others, but into the one behind, our own.* <note>original: Δύο πήρας ἕκαστον ἡμῶν φέρειν...</note> I hardly see the sense nor even a trace of the word *Cassidilis*, which our Latin Translator uses. <margin>Tobit ch. VIII. v. 2.</margin> *He brought out from his "cassidile" a piece of the liver.* Tell me, Phoebus <note>an appeal to Apollo/wisdom</note>, what might this be? In the Greek there is nothing to which *cassidilis* can be referred. I find, however, in the Glossary of Isidore: *Cassidilis: a pouch, a purse.* The parchment manuscript which I use reads *cassidile*, a reading which wonderfully approves itself to me, as it comes from *capsa* <note>a box or chest</note>. I reject *cassidile* as it is found in old Bibles. Andreas Placus in his *Biblical Lexicon* on the said chapter of Tobit, folio 109a, noted these things: *Cassidile, with the penultimate syllable lengthened as usage dictates, if it be a Latin word, is a pouch in which we store necessities.* Some think it belongs to a fowler. If it is from *cassis* <note>a helmet or a net</note>, it will be a pouch like a helmet or a hunting net. That kind is carried today by the *Ger-nel* <note>likely a regional term for a hunter or gatherer</note>. But lest the paper perish in vain, consult *cassidile* in Goldast’s Notes on the Alemannic Writers. <margin>vol. 1 p 220</margin>

To the categories of travel vessels we summon the *glossokomon* <note>original: τὸ γλωσσόκομον, literally a case for reeds/mouthpieces, but used for a money box</note>, John ch. XII. v. 6, where concerning Judas the betrayer: *And he had the money box, and carried what was put into it.* <note>original: Καὶ τὸ γλωσσόκομον εἶχε...</note> The little thief had opened the vessels of money, like that Gylippus the Spartan in Aelian and Plutarch. Some understand it as a leather purse; such as is generally a *bulga*, a leather bag, according to Festus; concerning which Lucilius in *Satires* book VI: <margin>page 161.</margin>
> Who has no beast of burden, nor servant, nor any companion.
> The bag and whatever coins he has, he carries with him.
> With his bag he eats, sleeps, and washes; all the
> Hope of the man is in that one bag.

And such were the portable coffers which someone from the flock of servants used to carry, toward which custom L. Pignorius writes in his book *On Slaves*, page 166, that the translator of John aimed in those words about Judas: *He was a thief and had the money-box.* The Arab has the word *tzuanch*

<column-break/>

which designates a chest in which alms are stored; as Paul Tarnovius notes. <margin>Travels of the Eastern Peoples. in Job p. 849</margin> What if others better understand it as a small box or some vessel in which he carried not only money, but also other necessities; just as Galen in *Fractures* 2.64 is a witness, that among the Attics a vessel was signified whose use was for preserving certain more secret things which travelers especially might use; which Hofmann, the other "Preserver of Galen," teaches us in his *Notes on Galen’s Use of Parts*. To this also belong the words of the Savior to the Apostles about to set out for the preaching of the Gospel, in St. Mark ch. 6 v. 8: *except a staff only; no pouch, no bread, no copper in their belts.* <note>original: εἰ μὴ ῥάβδον μόνον...</note> St. Luke ch. X v. 4: *Carry no purse, no pouch, no sandals, and greet no one on the road.* <note>original: Μὴ βαστάζετε βαλάντιον...</note> ch. XXII v. 35: *When I sent you without purse and pouch and sandals, did you lack anything?* and v. 36: *he who has a purse, let him take it, and likewise a pouch.* The Vulgate in both verses rendered it *sacculum* <note>small bag</note>. Beza rendered it *crumenam* <note>purse</note>. The Arabic usage is read several times as *al-ghirnah*, which in Valentin Schindler is explained as a pouch and bag in which travel provisions are carried. He does not permit a pouch, by which he hints that they ought not to be anxious about the necessities of the way, lest they hinder them in the course of the Gospel. Eucherius in his *Book of Spiritual Formulas* ch. 8 p. 238: *The pouch: anxiety for vices and the impediments of the world.* In the Gospel: *No pouch on the road.* Thus under the title of bag, pouch, or purse, he embraces whatever pertains to the necessity of life, and the Savior wished nothing to be present for them which might hinder the journey, *simply* (as Procopius excellently says) *he suggests to them what is well-equipped and light, making the journey easy for them.* <margin>in Isaiah 252.</margin> They used to carry belts <note>original: Zonas</note>, and in them coins. Hence the Lord: <margin>Matt. 10. 9.</margin> *Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor in your belts,* noting higher precepts *through a symbol*. Euclio the miser in his belt anxiously guarded his money, and hung a bag full of silver around his neck when he went to bed. The witty Plautus, writer of comedies, festively describes the madness of misers under the person of Euclio the "stingy-steward," *act 2. sc. 4. v. 22.*, how they shut up their coins tightly in chests and bags; and on the contrary, he thinks spendthrifts are driven by a certain madness whose coins cannot be contained in a bag; for as a "lymphatic" <note>frenzied/mad</note> man throws himself wherever his madness drives him, so the spendthrift loses his coins wherever *everyone* <note>original: πᾶς</note> snatches them into this or that tavern. Hence he festively called them "lymphatic coins." He calls a bag of money a *follis* <note>bellows or leather bag</note>, exactly like Juvenal. <margin>Sat. 14. lib. 5. v. 281.</margin>
> It is a great reward for the effort, so that with a stretched bag you can return
> home from there.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Travels of the Easterners.</margin>
and a necklace, until the payment of the agreed-upon wage was made. This cloaked friend <note>Referring to Tamar in Genesis 38</note>, easy of access and deceptive of face, does what she pleases; and as he departs, Judah sends the customary gift for such easy delights via a shepherd, *so that he might recover his pledge (v. 20).* But the outcome cheated his hopes, and Tamar concealed her womb under a false appearance until the daughter-in-law revealed herself to her father-in-law, who had called for her to be burned alive (v. 24). Love for offspring persuaded her to the deed, which she said: "Before you decree it must be expiated by my death, first recognize with your own eyes whose ring, bracelet, and <term>scipio</term> <note>A staff or scepter, from the Latin *scipio*</note> these are" (v. 25). Then, as *Ovid* sings in *Letters from the Black Sea, Book 2, 2:*

> *A calm and easy parent, ready with a pardon,*

The armed also had staffs with which to defend themselves from the incursions of enemies at home and abroad. *Ezekiel ch. 38:9:* They shall chop up and burn the weapons, the shield and spears, the bow and arrows, and the hand-staffs. In Hebrew: מקל (*maqqêl*). Luther translates this as: *Fauststange* <note>German: "fist-pole" or "hand-staff"</note>.

I would hardly hesitate to use this to illustrate the words of Christ, *Matthew ch. 10 v. 10*, in which he forbids, among other things, that the Apostles (whom he was sending throughout the whole world) should take a staff for the journey with which to arm themselves for defense; yet in *Mark ch. 6 v. 8*, he commanded that they take a rod for the journey, which relieves travelers. There is a Greek saying on this matter: *without a stick, do not walk* <note>original: ἄνευ ξύλου μὴ βάδιζε</note>, that is, as J. Lang, the abridger of Erasmus, explains in *Adagia loc. 51 p. 417*: do not be unarmed, but let there always be something at hand to drive away anyone who might seek to harm you. There are rhymes of the ancients concerning the traveler's walking-staff:

> *I am the glory in hands, I support the old man, I guide the steps,*
> *I am the terror to dogs, the weary man carries me as his leader.*

<margin>1 Kings 19:19</margin>
It would be a long story if I wished to speak of the *clothing of travelers.* A cloak was necessary for the journey. When Elisha was holding the plow-handle as a plowman, *Elijah cast his cloak over him,* by which ceremony he intended to signify that he should follow him and leave the plows behind.

<margin>2 Timothy 4:14</margin>
The Latins call it a <term>penula</term> <note>A thick, sleeveless traveling cloak</note>, such as the one Paul ordered to be brought to him, which he had left in Troas. They were accustomed to use it in rainy weather. Galba replied to one asking for a <term>penula</term>: *“If it does not rain, you have no need of it. If it rains, I shall use it myself,”* according to Quintilian, *Institutes 6.3.* Spartianus says in his *Life of Hadrian: He lost the penulas which the tribunes of the people were accustomed to use in rainy weather.* Varro in *The Divine Rod* says: *A man who possesses virtue should not seek a penula in the rain.* Hence Horace says in *Epistles I. 11 v. 18* that it is of no use to have a

> *Penula in the summer solstice, or a loincloth in snowy breezes.*

Just as they sometimes took up a cloak over the toga in the rain, so they threw on the *penula* to protect their clothes against the force of the rain. Just as today it is the custom for Hamburg women to protect themselves against rain and other discomforts of the air with a hood or a black cowl, with which they veil the head so that the path is scarcely visible to their eyes. This covering against the injuries of the air, or even the cold, was worn out of necessity. Martial, *Book 14, ep. 130*, says of the leathern or "conacean" *penula*:

> *Though you enter the road while the sky is ever serene,*
> *Let the leather cloak never be missing for sudden waters.*

And in the same book, *ep. 137*:

> *We are recommended for use in the amphitheater,*
> *When our cloak covers the freezing togas.*

<column-break/>

Their garments were very long and hung down even to the ankles; lest these should hinder one making a journey, they would gird them up and tuck the fringes into the belt, or throw them back over the shoulders, so that they might be more ready for a quick pace and for undertaking tasks. From this, the words of Elisha to his servant Gehazi are to be explained: *Gird up your loins, and take your staff in your hand, and go.* From this customary girding, various expressions are celebrated, and more famous than the rest is *to gird the loins* for making oneself ready, or preparing oneself to expedite a matter, *1 Kings 18:46, 2 Kings 9:1, Jeremiah 1:17, Nahum 2:1, Luke 12:35.* From here also elegant Arabic metaphors are derived, some of which can be read in the very well-furnished *History of Tamerlane*, published in Arabic by the Elzevir press. Tertullian, *Book 4 against Marcion p. 267: We ought to gird our loins, that is, be ready and free from the impediments of a fringed and rain-soaked life.* Regarding Eumaeus, Homer says in *Odyssey 14 v. 72: Having spoken thus, he quickly bound his tunic with a belt (zōnē),* and proceeded to go, so that he might more readily prepare the *xenia* <note>gifts for a guest</note>. To act with haste and make a hurried journey (to speak with Ovid), *he girds his garment to his breast.*

<margin>4. from the Bridge</margin>
I will not speak now of those going abroad being "petasated" <note>wearing a *petasos*, a wide-brimmed traveling hat</note>, of whom Lipsius treats in *On the Amphitheater ch. 19*; nor will I describe (for we shall strive for brevity) what the adornment of other nations was, and what their habit was when they applied themselves to a journey. Peter Victorius collected some things not to be despised in *Various Readings 1.24.* I wish now to assign one or two testimonies from the sacred writings concerning <term>tents</term>, <term>tabernacles</term>, and <term>carpets</term>, which they were accustomed to use in the East whenever they made a journey. The Patriarchs, always wandering on foot and tossed by various waves of pilgrimage—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—dwelt for two hundred years (not without the wise counsel of God) in tabernacles, <gloss>they came from nation to nation, and from one kingdom to another people,</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἄτερ οἴκου ἐξ οἴκου καὶ χώραν ἐκ χώρας μεταρχόμενοι</note> as the Psalmist described their transitory lodgings.

<margin>Psalm 105:13</margin>
Abraham, having left Egypt, went *on his journeys toward the south, toward the land of Canaan*,

<margin>Genesis 13:3</margin>
and he proceeded through his departures and encampments from the south even to Bethel, even to that place where previously, when he was entering Egypt, he had fixed

<margin>ch. 12:8</margin>
his tent; the Septuagint says: *where his tent was before.* <note>original Greek: ἦν ἡ σκηνὴ αὐτῷ τὸ πρότερον</note> *There where his hut first was.* <note>original German: Da am ersten sein Hütte war</note> The holy man does not change his ancient dwellings, but revisits the same places he had used when seeking Egypt. An old lodging, like an old guest and friend, is not to be changed rashly.

<margin>v. 5</margin>
Lot, traveling together on the same road, had *sheep and oxen and tents*, as the Roman edition genuinely has it, for "beasts" <note>Greek: κτῆνη</note> here does not accord with the Hebrew text. Jacob, in his going and returning from Mesopotamia, spent the night in fields and mountains; and indeed in his going, although he had the nearby city of Bethel, he nevertheless *lived in the open* <note>Greek: ἀγραυλεῖ</note> in a nearby field; in his return, he offered a feast on Mount Gilead to Laban and his companions.

<margin>Genesis 31:46</margin>
To which Jacob looked back, being accustomed to live in migrating houses: *The days of my pilgrimage are one hundred and thirty years, few and evil.*

<margin>ch. 47:9</margin>

# From Joshua IX. v. 3. 4. 5.

## The Pilgrimage of the Eastern Peoples. Matthew 2:13.

...by extension and dilation, as if he wished to indicate that he was not <margin>The Pilgrimage of the Eastern Peoples. Matthew 2:13.</margin> an exile in only one place, but wandered far and wide in an "exile of protraction." These words of the divine Psalmist could be repeated by the innocent Joseph when, with Mary the *Mother of God* <note>original: θεοτόκῳ (Theotokos)</note>, he lived as an exile in that "exile of protraction" and withdrew into Egypt, *having suffered many hardships* <note>original: πολλὰ κακοπαθήσας</note>. Joseph was poor; his trade was pitiable, his life subject to want. He had no skins full of wine, nor a multitude of servants, mules, or camels, nor the equipment of tents. His *journeying on foot* <note>original: Πεζοπορία</note> was full of poverty between Meshech and Kedar. The Kedarite "Tent-dwellers" <note>term: Scenitae (from Greek skenitai) — people who live in tents rather than permanent houses.</note> have no fixed seats; they easily move their tents and migrate to wherever better pastures call them. Hence they are called *Nomads* <note>original: Νομάδες</note>, that is, Wanderers, because they are devoted to the pastoral life. Concerning the Arabs, Diodorus Siculus writes in his 2nd Library, p. 95: *Of Arabia, the parts facing the south are called "Blessed"; but the interior is inhabited by a multitude of Arab nomads who lead a more peaceful life in tents, and these, rearing great herds of livestock, encamp in immeasurable plains.* He asserts the same wandering for pasture regarding the Troglodytes on page 111, saying: *The Troglodytes are called nomads by the Greeks, having a nomadic life from their livestock. Because of the excessive heat, when the pasture dries up, they flee to marshy and well-watered places.* Ezekiel testifies to this nomadic life of the Arabs when he describes their *merchandise from livestock* <note>original: ἐμπορείαν ἀπὸ τῶν βοσκημάτων</note> in chapter XXVII, 21: *Arabia and all the princes of Kedar, they were the merchants of your hand: with lambs and rams and goats your merchants came to you.* Truly the Arabs seek *one land after another* <note>original: ἄλλην ἐξ ἄλλης χώραν</note> for the sake of *following the herds of livestock* <note>original: ἕνεκα ἀγέλας τῶν θρεμμάτων ἐπακολουθέντες</note>, and they fix their tents there where there is grazing land; hence Isaiah, intending to signify desolation, says: *The Arab shall not pitch his tent there; nor shall shepherds rest there* (chapter XIII:20). So in Psalm 83:7, understand the "tabernacles of the Edomites and Ishmaelites or Hagarenes" in the same sense, according to the custom of the nation which lived under tents; to which they also refer Judges chapter 8:11: *And Gideon went up by the way of those dwelling in tents.* <margin>see</margin> <insert>the way of those dwelling in tents</insert> <note>original Hebrew: דרך השכוני באהלים</note>. The Targum defines the desert as <insert>the camps of the Arabs who dwell in tents in the desert</insert> <note>original Aramaic: משרות עכנαι לשן טבכוני במדברא</note>. Whence also the Proverb in Jeremiah chapter 3:2: *As an Arab in the desert*, and that Greek epithet: *Tent-dwelling Arabs* <note>original: Σκηνῖται Ἄραβες</note>, whom Benjamin [of Tudela] in his *Itinerary* p. 82, Drusius in *Observations* 11:15, and Fuller in *Miscellany* 2:12 describe. Nor has this custom ceased in the East, the traces of which were recognized many centuries later in the lands of those nations by those who saw and reported that they seek various places as the pastures <margin>Commentary on Isaiah book 50, ch. 21, p. 67.</margin> lead them. Jerome * says: *The nation of Ishmaelites, that is, Saracens, live in tents; they hold whatever seats the night compels them to, they who have herds and flocks and droves of camels, who have neither doors nor bars* (taken from Jeremiah 49:31). For they do not dwell in cities, but live in the wilderness. <margin>On the Life of Moses, p. 415.</margin> Philo * says: *The Arabs are livestock-breeders and they graze their herds—not only the men, but also the women, the youths and the maidens among them—not only those of the neglected and ignoble class, but even those of the very prominent.* The most noble of the Arabs to this very day live from pastures, and neglecting cities—which they call the dens of idle men and the

<column-break/>

prisons of the wretched— <margin>The Pilgrimage of the Eastern Peoples.</margin> they live in tabernacles, sometimes arranged in a circle, under the open sky. And since they are subject to the attacks of enemies almost daily, everyone equips himself with a spear, a horse, and a musket <note>term: sclopeto — an early modern firearm, showing the author is blending ancient history with contemporary 17th-century reports.</note>; especially those who do not recognize the Emperor of the Turks as their Lord. At the entrance of mountains, distinguished by valleys and hills, they are accustomed to build their tents so that they can hide more safely and more readily withstand the force and onset of enemies, as the Illustrious Golius, most experienced in exotic matters, reported to us. Therefore, it is permitted to measure ancient times even by modern custom. <margin>ch. 3:6.</margin> In the Song of Habakkuk *, the tents of Ethiopia are joined with the skins or tents of Midian, which refer to the history of Gideon and Othniel, by the consensus of interpreters. He says: *I saw the tents of Ethiopia in vanity, the curtains (skins)* <note>original Hebrew: ירגזו (shall tremble)</note> *of the land of Midian shall be troubled.* Take "skins" to mean tents, from which Midian, rushing out, used to infest the Israelites. How ridiculous is that Interpreter who made the "skin of the flayed Bartholomew" out of the skins of the land of Midian, as can be seen among the sermons of Jordanus! What could be said that is holier than this interpretation? It is established from many authors that tents were usually made from sewn skins. Livy (Book 5, Dec. 1) reported that the Roman soldier endured "under skins" <note>term: sub pellibus — a Latin idiom for being on active campaign in the field.</note> in work and labor, overwhelmed by snow and frost. Cicero (4th Academic Questions, 2) says a commander does not leave much of his sheep-skin tent in permanent camps, praising Lucullus because even in the occupation of military affairs he delighted in the reading of books. The same Orator *, accusing Piso of greed <margin>Oration against Piso, n. 87.</margin> for the treasure he collected from military equipment, says: *What? Do you remember that workshop of arms, when, having driven together all the cattle of the whole province, under the name of "skins," you renewed all that domestic and paternal profit?* Under the name of "skins" here, other instruments of war can also be understood generally, for the making of which skins were used, such as shields, breastplates, thongs for engines, and straps for spears. Annaeus Florus (History 1:12) indicates how great the affairs of the Veientes were by their ten-year siege: *Then for the first time they wintered under skins, and winter quarters were paid for by a tax.* There is a known story about a tent sent to Narses, King of the Persians. The people of Mesopotamia had sent him a gift of a tent made of camel leather, interwoven with gold by Babylonian art. The father asked his son Adarnasses whether it pleased him; the son replied it would be more pleasing if it were made of human skins. Alexander, in order to cross the Oxus river of Asia, used skins taken from tents as an aid, according to Arrian. But if we wished to transport everything, the skins of the land of Midian would not suffice. Naudé (Book on Military Study, p. 333) seems to have understood that expression, "to winter under skins," as referring to military clothing. The first author of skin tabernacles was Jabal; for he himself is said to have been <insert>the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock</insert> <note>original Hebrew: אבי ישב אהל ומקנה</note>, Genesis 4:20. The Septuagint: *the father of those dwelling in tents, cattle-breeders.* The name "Father" is used for the author and inventor, as in verse 21. So that livestock farming might be carried out more conveniently under the open sky, he devised movable tabernacles, which Abel (who was a *shepherd of sheep* <note>original Hebrew: רעה צאן</note>, Gen 4:2) and other men of livestock lacked before him; but this man was the Author for the "Men of Cattle," thus...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
The Travels of the Orientals.
</margin>
They are called in *Genesis 4:3* <note>The text likely refers to Jabal, the father of those who dwell in tents</note> as those living in tents made of skins while tending flocks, a method of pasturing that was thereafter adopted everywhere in Oriental regions by shepherds, and most especially by the Arabs. Moreover, the material of skins was suitable for enduring rainstorms, for they do not quickly soak up water; thus they were used for preparing tabernacles and other equipment. Shields were also fashioned from skins and wood, as well as other instruments of war, of which Gottfried Jungermann gives an account in his *Notes on Longus’s* <term>Pastoral Scenes</term> <note>original: ποιμενικῶν</note>. Hence, by metonymy <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole or a related concept</note>, "skins" is used *for tents and camps*.
<margin>
*2 Samuel 7:2*
</margin>
Pierius already noted this long ago in his *Hieroglyphics, book 34, folio 260*. In the Sacred Scriptures, the *Vulgate* reads: *The Ark of God is placed in the midst of skins*, which the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translate as *the Ark of God sat in the midst of a tabernacle* <note>original: ἐν μέσῳ σκηνῆς</note>. The *Hebrew* <note>original: בתוך היריעה</note> says *in the midst of the curtain, that is*, in a tent made of curtains and skins, to which the phrase *in the midst* <note>original: בתוך</note> in *2 Kings 23:7* corresponds, which they explain as the curtains of the grove. Just as by the same synecdoche <note>a figure of speech where a part stands for the whole</note> a "nail" or "peg" is taken for military tents which are fixed with pegs in *Zechariah 10:4*. The peg made the tabernacle firm and sustained the stretching of the veils; for that reason it was large and very sharp, and thus seemed suitable to Jael for piercing the head of Sisera in *Judges 4:20*. The word <term>curtain</term> <note>original: יריעה</note> which the Hebrews use signifies a hanging or a curtain; for an entire tent is constructed from several curtains which are joined by loops. Thus, for the same reason, it is called a *tentorium* [tent] by the Latins from the verb *tendo* [to stretch], because it is extended by ropes, curtains, and bent wooden poles; the word *tentum* is also found here in Florus *as Salmasius reads it, and Horace, Epode 12.12. Johannes Drusius in Habakkuk p. 812.* *The curtains of the land of Midian*
<margin>
*Isaiah 2, ch. 12* <note>Likely a reference to Habakkuk 3:7</note>
</margin>
signifies the tents of the Midianites, which were made of curtains, which the Hebrews call <term>curtains</term> <note>original: יריעות</note>. For it is a manner of speaking, as when tents of this kind are called "skins," for they were fashioned from skins. In the book of Song of Solomon *ch. 1:7*, the *Bride* (or the Church) says of herself: *I am black but beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem, like the tabernacles of Kedar, like the skins (derreis) of Solomon.* Wherefore Jerome *on Isaiah ch. 21, p. 67* says: *The book of Genesis teaches that from Ishmael were born Kedar and the Hagarenes, who by a perverted name are called Saracens. These dwell throughout the entire wilderness, of whom I think the Poet says* —

->*And widely wandering*<-
->*The Barcaeans*<-

An elegant metaphor concerning the Bride-Church taken from the tabernacles of Kedar and the curtains of Solomon. Moreover, it can be seen in *Genesis 31:33* that it was customary for women to inhabit tents distinct from the tents of their husbands, just as women also did not recline with men at the table or in the dining rooms. While the promise of a son, Isaac, was being made to her husband during the feast in *Genesis 18:9*, Sarah laughed from the door of her tent, which was behind the tent of Abraham (*v. 10*). So the frugal customs of the Orientals required. There were also those who fashioned tents from skins. We read of them in *Acts 18:3* that they were <term>tent-makers by trade</term> <note>original: σκηνοποιὸς τὴν τέχνην</note>, and that Saint Paul joined himself to them as a <term>fellow-craftsman</term> <note>original: ὁμότεχνον</note>. The Vulgate says: *They were of the tent-making art.* The Syriac: *They were makers of canopies.* The word <term>radidaya</term> <note>original: רדידיא</note> they explain as weavers, those making latticed works and the connections of tabernacles, fitting skins. To "fit skins" is to prepare them for the construction of tabernacles. Hence it is that Chrysostom, in his *4th Oration in Praise of Paul*,

<column-break/>

calls Paul a <term>tent-maker</term> <note>original: σκηνοποιὸν</note> and a <term>leather-cutter</term> <note>original: σκυτοτόμον</note>. This was a name derived from the verb <term>to cut</term> <note>original: τέμνειν</note>, which means *to incise or cut*, and thus
<margin>
The Travels of the Orientals.
</margin>
it is more expressly signified that tabernacles were usually fashioned from skins cut and fitted together. Finally, it is pleasing to note this custom, by which they carried tents with them for making a journey, from *Matthew 17:4*, where Peter, caught up outside himself, says: *Let us make three tabernacles*; when, because of the sweetness and abundance of the Spirit—as Burchard says *in his description of the Holy Land, part 1, ch. 6*—not knowing what he said on Mount Tabor, he asked for three tabernacles to be made. From which
<margin>
*in Notes on Matthew*
</margin>
passage Kirstenius argues, in the *Arabic version* edited by him, that the disciples of Christ, about to make a journey, carried tents with them according to the custom of Asians and Africans to ward off the injuries of the open sky. *In this place,* he says, *the Arabic text indicates not obscurely that the disciples, according to the custom of those regions, carried small tents or rather cloths, either woolen or linen, with them, so that necessity requiring it, wherever they had to spend the night in the mountains, deserts, or fields, or even by day in very rainy weather, they could be extended to defend them from storms, dew, or winter, even from frost, or in summer from the excessive heat of the sun. Therefore, Peter seems to ask here concerning these tents whether Christ wishes them to be extended, which the number three also suggests. For each of the Apostles could have carried one.* We leave this conjecture to be examined by the more learned. There is no need for us to bring disputes over it. Certainly, that this was characteristic of that nation is confirmed for us even today by their fierce descendants. Rather, it should be felt that Christ, when he traveled among us *taking the form of a servant* (as the Apostle says in *Philippians 2:7*), walked without tents; of which opinion we have some evidence in those words: *The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head*, and those sacred volumes which record his journeys and deeds for memory agree in this: that the entire stay of Christ on earth was full of poverty. Hence he abstained from such things, which to Kirstenius <term>seems unlikely</term> <note>original: δοκεῖ ἀπεικὸς ὑπάρχειν</note>. Agreeing with these things, Anastasius Sinaita, in the book titled <term>The Guide</term> <note>original: ὁδηγὸς</note>, *page 272*, wrote elegantly: <note>original: Πάλιν ἡ ἐπὶ γῆς τοῦ χριστοῦ διατριβὴ ἐν πτωχείᾳ καὶ πεζοπορίᾳ γέγονεν... (Greek text follows)</note> *Again, the sojourn of Christ on earth was in poverty and on foot; the Lord of heaven and earth, being without a house of his own, moved from house to house, being a guest and being fed by the women who followed him—He who grants life and food to all.* Since, therefore, it was among the ancient customs of travel to have tents, Oriental writers are accustomed to derive certain elegant expressions and metaphors from this. By this metaphor, the word <term>to dwell in a tent</term> <note>original: σκηνόω</note> was used concerning the conversation of the Son of God *in the flesh*, of which are the words of the Evangelist: *And he dwelt among us* <note>original: καὶ ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν</note>. Translated by Budé: *And he had his dwelling among us. He was in companionship with us.* To the

</margin>
just and those who live piously, the likeness of a tent is applied in *Proverbs 14:11*, as if to pilgrims and travelers or guests of this world; but to the impious, as to inhabitants of a house. Where Bede—whom they call "Venerable" for his elegance of doctrine and character—says in *Volume 4, page 919*: *A house is for a permanent stay; they are accustomed to use tabernacles on a journey.* The Israelites used tents in their travels; hence Balaam, although a pagan, exclaims: *How beautiful are your tabernacles*

# From Joshua IX. v. 3. 4. 5.

<margin>
The Pilgrimage of the Eastern Peoples.
</margin>

*How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, and thy tabernacles, O Israel! As the shady valleys, as gardens by the river’s side, as the tabernacles which the Lord hath planted.* <note>Numbers 24:5-6</note> He [Balaam] vows and blesses the people dwelling in tents, as the Spirit of God rushed upon him—the same people he had previously intended to curse according to the rash vows of Balak, who had devoted the Israelite people to destruction by an oath (to use the language of Apuleius). In memory of the miraculous preservation of the Church and the defense of the people of Israel wandering in the desert without a fixed seat, a feast was instituted which was commonly called the *Feast of Tabernacles.* In Greek <term>skenomata</term>, from <term>skene</term> and <term>skenoo</term>, meaning the fixing of scenes or tents. 

<margin>
Gen. 33:17.
</margin>
Places were even named from this. Where Jacob fixed tabernacles or huts for his cattle, it is called Succoth; <term>for his livestock he made booths</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Lemi asah Succoth"</note> says the text. The Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> says: <term>he made tents for his cattle</term>. The Chaldean version has a name equivalent in origin and sense to <term>Succoth</term>, which is from <term>shasak</term>, *to cover or overshadow* (from the Hebrew <term>sakak</term>), just as <term>sakak</term> and <term>sukkah</term>. Good pastures made for long journeys; Jacob rested in that place for some time, and the name remained from the huts, so that it was called Succoth—a proper place name which the Septuagint inappropriately rendered as a common noun. But correctly: Succoth. We would say *Hüttenstatt* [City of Huts], from which perhaps that district between Giessen and Butzbach is called *der Hüttenberg* because of its good pastures. Luther says on this passage: *The city of Succoth was so named then from the effect, because Jacob fixed a tabernacle there for his cattle, and built a house for his family.* 

<margin>

In this place they bake unleavened bread, and first pitch their tents, whence the place received its name. For Succoth is interpreted in our language as tabernacles or tents.* In the tribe of Gad there was a city of the same name (Judges 7:5) from whose inhabitants Gideon sought provisions in vain while he was swiftly pursuing the Midianites.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
Travel of the
Eastern
peoples.
</margin>
Horses were brought to Solomon at great expense, as can be read in 1 Kings 10:28–29. A horse imported from there cost 120 shekels—that is, by our calculation, 75 Imperial thalers—while a *chariot* (as the old Translator calls it, "a team") cost six hundred imperial thalers. Such was the cost of the luxury of Solomon's cavalry, which he purchased in great numbers against the edict which states: *When a King has been appointed, he shall not multiply horses for himself, nor lead the people back into Egypt, being lifted up by the number of his cavalry.* <note>referring to Deuteronomy 17:16</note> As for what kind of place that is in *Esther 5:10 and chapter 8*, the debate is still before the judge. In that verse, it speaks of the royal couriers of Ahasuerus, that they rode on *angaria* horses <note>original: "equis angariis," referring to the Persian postal system</note>, as the Vulgate translator has it; which were undoubtedly of outstanding fame among the Persians. Just as among the Norwegians there are *Reindeer*, and among the Spaniards *Lusitanian* horses, which are commended for their swiftness; and for that reason, the French Translator expressed them specifically in his version: *By the hand of the couriers on horseback, riding jennets, mules, and mares.* A Jennet is a horse of very fast gait, a Lusitanian horse, a Spanish *hemerodromus* <note>Greek: "day-runner"</note> horse, as Philibert Monnet teaches in his Lexicon. Of every kind of horse, those which the inhabitants of Spain call *Ginetas* excel in beauty and speed; as witnessed by Lanfius in his *Oration for Spain, page 186.* Our version <note>The German Luther Bible</note> has: *And he sent letters by riding messengers on young mules.* I see the Zurich version agrees with this, which similarly translates: *by riding messengers on fast mules.* Arias Montanus and the Italian version of Diodati explain them as *Dromedaries*. Dromedaries, however, are swift Camels, "Dromas" Camels; called by the specific name <term>dromades</term> <note>Greek: runners</note> from <term>dromos</term> <note>Greek: a race or course</note> because of the speed of their *run*, in which they especially excelled; for they had the swiftest steps, and grew tired more slowly than any other beast of burden; <term>dromakotatoi te hama kai okistai</term> <note>Greek: "at once most fit for running and swiftest"</note>. Jerome, *in the Life of Malchus*: *The day being spent, we set out toward evening, and we saw camels, which because of their excessive speed they call dromedaries.* The same *Father* <note>Jerome</note> teaches in his commentary on Isaiah 21, p. 67, that they excel for hastening flight following the example of the Saracens; and Flavius Vopiscus, in his life of Aurelian, mentions their swift help on the same occasion when describing the flight of *Zenobia*, Queen of the East: *Zenobia, being defeated, when she fled on camels, which they call dromas, and directed her journey toward the Persians, was captured by horsemen who were sent out, and brought into the power of Aurelian.* Zosimus, in book 1 of his history, p. 377, relates the same in these words: <term>Kamēloi tēn Zēnobian anabibasantes...</term> <note>Greek: "Camels, having mounted Zenobia (and camels are very fast, even surpassing horses in speed), led her out of the city."</note> The Dromedary is an ugly animal, smaller in stature than a camel, which we have seen led around Germany in these recent years. That name, brought down to us from ancient years, most nations still keep, for the Spaniards, Italians, Germans, French, and English use it. Mention of it is made in *Isaiah 60:6: A multitude of camels shall cover you, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah.* <term>bikre midyan</term> <note>Hebrew: the young camels of Midian</note>. Concerning these racing camels, Diodorus, in book 2 of his *Library*, p. 96, says: <term>Pleista kai diaphorōtata genē kamēlōn trephei hē Arabia</term> <note>Greek: "Arabia breeds many and very diverse kinds of camels"</note>, and when he had enumerated the kinds, he adds: <term>hai de anakōloi...</term> <note>Greek: "those which are short-legged and lean in build are runners (dromades), and they cover a very great length of road, especially for journeys completed through waterless and desert regions."</note> [No animal can be devised more useful for travel than the camel, ex-]

Schweigger, in his *Travels*, book 3, ch. 15, p. 264: In Turkey and other places, camels are commonly used here and there for travel, not only to ride upon, but also to carry loads and all kinds of merchant goods. In one day's journey, with its slow gait but wide steps, it completes 40 Italian miles, more or less, which make 8 German miles; and it carries a load of about 14 hundredweight. It also has this nature: it will not let more be loaded onto it than its strength can endure. For if one loads even one pound more than its strength extends, one can get it up from the ground (where it must lie down when one wants to load it) neither with good nor bad words, so that the camel drivers must immediately unload the excess of the weight by which it was overloaded. It can go without drinking for up to 4 days, and when it then comes to water, it drinks for its future thirst. Ludovico Varthema: *In feeding, each camel is given five barley loaves, uncooked, the size of a pomegranate. They are burdened with incredible weight, for they carry a double load, as much as two mules. Their drink is only every three days.* Regarding how suitable that animal is for travel and transport, no describer seems more fit than Leo Africanus *in his description of Africa, book 9, p. 290.* To take a few points from there, he says: The camel, a gentle and domestic animal, is found in the greatest abundance in Africa. When it is loaded with bundles, being struck on the knees and neck with a small rod and lying on the ground, as soon as it recognizes a sufficient weight, it raises itself. Being patient of hunger, they tolerate thirst so well that they can abstain from drink without discomfort for fifteen days. And since the Camel alone among quadrupeds has this, one does not wonder so much at the hump as at the back-carrying labors of the <term>nōtophorou</term> <note>Greek: "back-bearing"</note> animal. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Travel of the Eastern Peoples.</margin> Lest we be too tedious to our guest or reader with excessive length, we shall set down our baggage, being about to go to bed. (Among the Hebrews, travelers are called *devariatoribus*, from חנות <note>original: "chanot"</note> i.e., *to stay the night*, Gen. 32:21, Isa. 10:2, 9. The Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translates this as *to sleep*, *to camp*, *to remain*, *to lodge*, or *to rest*. For in these inns, both men and beasts rest from the hardships of the journey. From this comes מלון <note>original: "malon"</note>, the place which those turning aside occupy, Jer. 9:2. Among the Hebrews, <margin>2 Chronicles 32:28</margin> the word *urvah* <note>אורוה</note>, named from the taking of fodder, means a *stable* or manger, just as the Greek *kapne* comes from *kaptein* [to eat]; the Latin *Mansio* [mansion/station] comes from *manere* [to remain], for *menein* is to them what *Lun* is to the Hebrews. These stations, which Pliny also mentions, were arranged in certain places according to the availability of water for the use of camels and other beasts used in the East. Pliny, in book 6, says regarding the journey to India from Alexandria: *The camel-train proceeds from Coptos by stations arranged according to the watering places.* Herodotus <margin>book 5, p. 193.</margin> records that there are one hundred and eleven stations from Sardis to Susa, the royal city of the Persians. Those who were in charge of these stations, which the Greeks call *staseis*, were called *epistathmoi*, as the most learned man of his age, Guillaume Budé, shows in his *Later Annotations on the Pandects*, p. 197. Tobias, chapter 6, v. 1, says of the journey of Tobias: *he stayed the first night [station] by the river Tigris.* The Greek says: *and there they camped.* Apuleius, in book 1: *Having paid the stable-fee for the station, we took to the road.* Those words <margin>John 14:2</margin> allude to this custom: *In my Father’s house are many mansions [rooms]*, just as on earth there are many and various places for journeys; so in the house of God there are places of perfection: one glory for the Teacher of justice, another for another. In Greek, *monai*. In Hebrew, *megurim*. Servius, commenting on Virgil's *Aeneid* book 1, perhaps said because of this: *Magar in the Punic language signifies a villa.* I read that the same word is used for a station in a certain inhospitable desert in the *Travelogue* of Bernhard von <margin>p. 64, line 4.</margin> Breitenbach, whose words sound like this: *We came even deeper into a gruesome wilderness / there we pitched our tents at a sandy spot called Magare in Arabic.* We have said that the camel stations were formerly around springs. Just as today they pitch tents where fodder for the beasts and water-supplies can be had; which the Greeks call *hydreumata*, because the stations were arranged around *hydreia* or wells, at which those exhausted by fatigue or heat and thirst necessarily had to turn aside and *remain* [manendum], from which the Latin name is derived; because having finished a certain stretch of the journey, they rested around springs and watering holes. Jacob, having set out, came to the land of the East, *and saw a well in the field, and three flocks of sheep lying by it* Gen. 29:1-2. Springs were designated by specific names; just as we have from the Sacred Scriptures three springs of Isaac <margin>Gen. ch. 26, v. 20, 21, 22.</margin> called Esek, Sitna, and Rehoboth; we read that the patriarchs gave surnames to the wells, for which their servants, *lacking water*, sometimes found wells, and sometimes quarreled *due to the scarcity of water and wells.* In place of the proper names, *Esek, Sitna, Rehoboth*, the Vulgate <note>The Latin Bible</note> in its usual manner substituted *Calumny, Enmity, and Latitude*, by changing proper names into common nouns; Pineda collected all examples of this in his commentary on Job, ch. 42, v. 14. In the same chapter, v. 33, the well *Shibah* [Siba], which the servants of Isaac dug, is celebrated; from which the city later took its name, *Beer-Sheba* [Well of the Oath]; not otherwise than among all nations

<column-break/>

where many cities are said to be named after rivers, streams, and watered places. Thus in Judges ch. 7, v. 1, <margin>Travel of the Eastern Peoples.</margin> the spring of Harod is mentioned; later called, <margin>Thus Judges 7:1</margin> as Adrichomius notes in *Issachar num. 21*, *Tubania*; just as today a spring located not far from the village of Tor, a place famous for its port on the Red Sea, is called by the merchants stabling there, *El pozo dal Tor* [The Well of Tor]. And so many others. Breitenbach in his *Travelogue* <margin>Breitenbach in Travelogue f. 179. b.</margin> says: *To the port of the Red Sea called Tor, ships usually come from India within 16 days, bringing all spices and roots. As the day declined, we came to a place called Dronden, where we found water, therefore we stayed there that night; for at that place there are many living, clear springs welling up, where many palm trees grow; and as we believe, it was the place called Elim, where the children of Israel found 12 wells and 70 palm trees, of which one reads in Exodus ch. 15. However, there are very large peas (lentils) there, equal in size to hazelnuts, and they are called Pharaoh's peas.* Furthermore, it was a most ancient custom, preserved in the East even to our age, *to receive and also to dismiss* an arriving guest with a *kiss* and a hand-clasp: which is established to have been the custom of the Jews even in the time of the Savior, for, as Luke witnesses in ch. 7 v. 45, Christ worthily reproaches his host Simon because he had not even deigned to receive Him with a hospitable kiss; for they used *greetings* [aspasmous] with this rite, as we use an embrace and the offering of the hand, for the sake of honor and love. St. Augustine <margin>Question 78 on Genesis.</margin> says: *It was the custom, especially in the simplicity of the ancients, that relatives should kiss relatives (and disciples their Master, etc.).* So that from this rite it can be gathered what that manner of speaking in Psalm 2 regarding the "kissing of the Son" means; namely, it is metaphorical, from the old custom of receiving guests with a kiss and embrace. They were also accustomed to add a greeting or blessing to the kiss, full of affection. Hence it happens that by the same word *aspasmos* [greeting] both were signified, because they required mutual help. To the Hebrews, *Barak* [ברך] denotes *to bless*, and in approaching someone it is the same as *to greet*; in departing, however, it means *to say farewell*; and because in greetings the knees are usually bent, it denotes *to kneel*, whence *Berech* [ברך], *knee*, because the bending of the knees was added to blessings, and hence that word <margin>Daniel 6:11</margin> *Abrech* is rendered by the Interpreter: *Bow the knee.* To bless is to greet a friend received with a kiss with good words, and to pray for peace and the grace of God for him. David, in 2 Samuel 19, dismisses the noble Barzillai with a kiss. For thus you have in v. 39: *The King kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his place.* Raguel, weeping for joy, received Tobias with a kiss, Tobit 7:7, 9, and without delay, having slaughtered a ram, ordered a feast to be prepared, *and they sacrificed a ram of the flock and set out many meats* according to the custom of the Easterners, still used among them today. For to the greeting and blessing, as if attached, the duties of hospitality in slaughtering livestock adhered between friends. A famous example exists in Genesis ch. 18, where Abraham, inviting three men (i.e., Jehovah and two Angels) in v. 3, 4, 5, and preparing food, and slaughtering *a son of the herd* [a calf] in v. 6, 7, received them with hospitality in v. 8 and following. Concerning this *hospitality* [philoxenia] of the Patriarch, Philo in *On Abraham*, *having marveled at it as worthy...*

<margin>Scythed chariots used in wars.</margin>
Scythed chariots were formerly used in wars to cut through the enemy; for in earlier times the Canaanites as well as the Syrians, Arabs, and all inhabitants of Asia used chariots fortified with sharp iron; they specifically added very sharp iron scythes of about two cubits to the axles on both sides of the wheels, and thus with swift speed they made an attack into the middle of the enemy's column and armed ranks. Xenophon is a witness in *Book 6 of the Education of Cyrus*, describing their form; *He also
<margin>P. 90. 92.</margin>
equipped chariots* (<term>chariots</term> <note>Greek: harmata</note>) *both from captured chariots and from elsewhere, wherever they could be obtained. And he rejected and removed the old Trojan method of chariot driving, which is even now used by the Cyrenian charioteers. For in earlier times, the Medes, as well as the Syrians and Arabs and all inhabitants of Asia, used chariots in the same way that the Cyrenians do now. And in the same book: He took care to manufacture war chariots with strong wheels, so they would not easily be broken, and long axles; for things that are wide are less easily overturned; moreover, he made a seat for the charioteers like a tower constructed of strong wood; their height is up to the elbows, so that the horses can be driven from above the seats. He armed the charioteers entirely, except for the eyes; he also added iron scythes of about two cubits to the axles on both sides of the wheels: and likewise others below, turned from the axle toward the ground, as if he himself with his men were about to make an attack upon the enemy with the chariots.* But in this he errs, while it pleased Cyrus to attribute the invention of war chariots to himself, since here you see they preceded Cyrus's time by 900 years. For the Inhabitants of the Valley, or the Canaanites, who lived in the flat and level region, used these kinds of fighting vehicles, for which reason the sons of Joseph—that is, the two tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh—were afraid, and despaired of seizing the land from its ancient possessors. The Ephraimites and Manassehites allowed themselves to be distracted by various fears because they had seen the inhabitants of the land, the dwellers of the valley, armed for every danger, and the approaches closed to them, whence they tried to evade the danger of war, responding to Joshua: *We will not be able to go up to the mountains,
<margin>v. 16.</margin>
since the Canaanites who live in the flat land use iron chariots*; as the Vulgate translates better than the Septuagint, who were "nodding" <note>i.e., careless or sleeping</note> here. They distrusted victory with a cowardly fear when they saw the inhabitants were equipped with iron or scythed chariots, which they themselves lacked, and inhabited very fortified cities. But Joshua persisted in his opinion, praising them for their fortitude, so that he believed nothing so hostile, so fierce, or so atrocious could be presented that could not be turned aside and put to flight through divine help. They receive a public testimony of their fortitude in verse 17: *You are a great people, and great strength is yours.* v. 18: *You shall cross the mountain, you shall expel the Canaanite, although he has iron chariots, although he is strong.*

# From Joshua 17, verse 18.

<margin>Scythed chariots commonly used in wars.</margin>
God is accustomed to describe himself through *anthropopathism* <note>original: "Popathicè" [anthropopathice]; a figure of speech attributing human passions or actions to God</note>, as if avenging wrongs done to him in the manner of a General, who brings forth from his armory chariots, teams of four horses, and all the apparatus of war to aid in defense. David, when he had overcome certain enemies in war, sings praises to God in a truly beautiful hymn, the sixty-eighth Psalm; and to introduce the divine power, he chose to declare it through the chariots which were customarily used to break through the enemy. We shall provide the Hebrew words as they ought to be given, especially in obscure passages: <margin>v. 18.</margin> *The chariots of God are twenty thousand, even thousands of angels* (he says in verse 18 <note>Psalm 68:17 in modern English Bibles</note>). Arias translates: *Chariots, two myriads of God, doubled thousands.* Those who derive the word from *shanan*, which means *to repeat or to do something by turns*, translate it as *thousands of iteration*, which are namely repeated and multiplied. Our version <note>Luther's German</note>: *The chariot of God is many thousand times thousand.* The Dutch: *God's chariots are twice ten thousand / the thousands doubled.* But those who derive it from *shanan*, meaning *to sharpen and polish*, wish to indicate by that word a type of chariot equipped with scythes <note>term: scythed chariot; a war chariot with horizontal blades extending from the axles to mow down infantry</note>. With magnificent speech, he signifies the immense power of God, to whom belong, as it were, his own celestial chariots, in which he is carried *in abundance* <note>original: "en pleithei" (Greek)</note> of his glory and splendor, as the most powerful tamer of his enemies and the most present protector of his own people.

<margin>v. 17.</margin> *Why then, O adversaries†, do you look with envy* (*tirtzedun*) *upon the mountains of God*, and bring war against the holy city, which God holds most dear and protects with his presence like a warlike Leader? David testified that the Angel of the Lord *encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them*, Psalm 34:7. The example of Elisha testifies to this, when the Syrian enemies wished to seize him, 2 Kings 6:17. The Targum <note>Aramaic translation/commentary of the Hebrew Bible</note> explains the word *radad* or *ratzad* through *rakad*, *to dance or leap out*, and our local translator rendered it as *jumping* <note>original: "hüypffen"</note>; just as in Psalm 114:4 the mountains are said to have skipped, where for *rakedu*, the Targum <margin>Nahum 3:2.</margin> has *patazu*. Similarly, chariots are said to *leap*, where with a most beautiful *hypotyposis* <note>a vivid, lifelike description</note> he describes the siege and destruction of the royal city of Nineveh and the Assyrian empire, and represents as if in a living image the substance of the enemies—the Chaldeans and Medes—at whose arrival he graphically describes the chariots, horsemen, swords, and spears. He says in that verse that the *sound of the whip of the drivers and the leaping chariots* ring in his ears. The Hebrew words are worthy to be heard: *The crack of the whip, and the noise of the rattling of the wheels, and of the prancing horses, and of the jumping chariots.* A voice concerning the sound of the whip when the driver urges the horses, and concerning the sound of the wheels. The horse also *shakes the crumbling field with the sound of its four-footed galloping.* Regarding horses shaking the earth with their hooves, the word *dahrot* is used in Judges 5:22, which word is doubled to express swift motion and incitement. The grandiloquence of these words can be better perceived from our own language than any other, and therefore let it be heard with attentive ears: *There one will hear the whips crack / and the wheels rattle / the steeds cry out / and the chariots roll.* The Dutch have: *That is the clapping of the whip / and the noise from the thundering of the wheels / and the horses stamping / and the chariots jumping up.* With no less emphasis we read in chapter 2, verse 4: *The chariots roll in the streets / and rattle in the lanes.* The Vulgate: *In the streets the drivers of the chariots go mad, they shall walk hurriedly through the squares.* The Dutch: *The*

<column-break/>

*chariots rage through the alleys / as in the Notes: f. 125. b. The chariots shall roll and howl and thunder through the streets and paths of the city with such speed and rumor / as if the drivers and those sitting upon them were mad and raging.* The chariots in their swift course are as if scythed— <margin>Scythed chariots commonly used in wars.</margin> sarcastically, in the manner of hostile mockery. Luther: *Come on, sit upon the horses / race with the chariots.* The Vulgate: *the chariots are mad.* *Ha-rekhev ha-mithalelu*, to be mad; likewise: *to extol oneself with praises and to boast.* He exaggerates the Raving enemy and his swift efforts with notable words, so that the hostile impetus can be seen by everyone as if in a theater or some circus. The works of God are admirable and *even unto the highest*; and God is admirable in his <margin>Psalm 71:18.</margin> speech; nor can any mortal sufficiently consider or worthily enough praise him according to his dignity. The utterances of God are great utterances. In a human manner, the immortal God many times declares himself and his power through common expressions among mortals. The God of hosts does not lack celestial chariots, nor does he lack battle lines, and attendants ready for business. The chariots of God are twenty thousand, many thousands of Angels. There stand around, as Ezekiel says <margin>*</margin>, four youths to the chariot, <margin>chapter 1:15.</margin> each with four faces and four wings, flaming, sparkling, and making a horrendous crash in their flight. Above their wings is seen the extended sky, transparent like crystal, upon which is placed a sublime royal throne, and in it God residing with a human countenance, his body down to the loins like glowing brass, and all ignited below, and clothed around with a shining rainbow. O wonderful work of the wheels of the chariot of divine glory! How admirable are your works, O God, among us, you who carried up Elijah into heaven in a chariot of fire and horses of fire, 2 Kings 2:11, Ecclesiasticus 48:9. Seeing that chariot of fiery horses, Elisha cried out: <margin>*</margin> *My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its horsemen!* He uses a metaphorical kind of speaking taken from the present thing which he had seen, concerning his Teacher as the leader of the Church and the strength of the people; as if to say: My Master, my Master, where are you being snatched! Ah, you helped Israel more by your zeal and prayers than a great multitude of scythed chariots and horsemen. Concerning this expression, Tirinus <margin>*</margin> commented thus: <margin>P. 268.</margin> *By this proverb the Hebrews signify the highest protection and pillar in adversity; just as the Latins do when they call someone the anchor of the Republic, the pillar of the fatherland, the column of the house.* Furthermore, this talk is not of a rustic or urban chariot, but a military or scythed one. Whence for "driver" the Hebrew is *Perasau*, that is, his horsemen, namely those who fought from chariots in the battle line, as if one Elijah (just as formerly *one <margin>Exodus 17:11, 12.</margin> Moses*) were for Israel an entire military apparatus, which is figuratively signified by the symbol of the scythed chariot prepared for the slaughter of enemies. Joash used a similar acclamation when bidding farewell to the dying Elisha: (2 Kings 13:14) *My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its horsemen.* For such a one had Elisha been after Elijah; where the words of Flacius occur to us to be noted at the same time: *They used to use...*
