# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
### Page 332

<margin>Scythed chariots used in wars.</margin>
...formerly with scythed chariots, in whose power they most greatly trusted, believing they could break through or scatter an enemy's battle line.
By way of metaphor, however, Elijah (Elisha) is called the "chariot and horsemen of Israel," because he, through his teaching, exhortation to repentance, and his prayers, fought more strongly against all enemies than the Kings, Leaders, and soldiers of the Israelites. Among military writers, mentions of four-yoked, eight-yoked, and scythed military chariots <note>original Greek: τεθραρύμων καὶ ὀκταρύμων καὶ δρεπανηφόρων</note>, and of those fighting from chariots, are extant everywhere. Heliodorus, in Book 9, page 430, described an army line equipped with these scythed chariots: *“He himself took the center, being guarded for safety by a scythed chariot and by the phalanx on either side, and he placed only the armored cavalry in front of himself.”* <note>original Greek: Αὐτὸς δὲ τὸ μέσον... προέταττεν</note> Military chariots of this kind, used for cutting down the enemy, consisted of sharp iron scythes and were the strongest part of the army. The war-charioteer, having mounted the horses and being negligent of his own life, drives the horses into a gallop and makes an assault upon those in his way, carried wherever his fervor against the enemy sweeps him. When driven so persistently, the chariots made a huge noise from the iron instruments hanging from them. Mention of these is found almost everywhere. Regarding scythed four-horse chariots, we shall recite the words of Curtius*: <margin>Book 4, ch. 9</margin> *"Two hundred scythed four-horse chariots, the sole aid of those nations, followed. From the end of the pole, spears tipped with iron projected. On both sides from the rear they had directed three swords, and between the spokes of the wheels several points projected forward; other scythes then clung to the tops of the wheel rims, and others were lowered toward the ground, intended to cut off whatever came in the way of the spurred horses."* Compare the same author, Book 4, ch. 12, and the uncertain Author of the book *On Military Matters* in Dempster.

<margin>Book 2, ch. 6</margin> Diodorus Siculus*, citing Ctesias regarding the expedition of Ninus against the Bactrians, says: Ninus led out ten thousand scythed chariots with a little less than six hundred [thousand], seventeen hundred thousand infantry, and two hundred and ten thousand cavalry. His words are these: *“When the army was gathered from everywhere to Nineveh, of which Ctesias records in his histories, there were 1,700,000 infantry, more than 200,000 cavalry, and scythed chariots numbering a little less than 10,600.”* <note>original Greek: Συναχθείσης τῆς στρατιᾶς... ἑξακοσίων</note> So against Alexander Severus, Artaxerxes the King of the Persians came with one thousand eight hundred scythed chariots, as witnessed by Lampridius in *Severus*, ch. 55, p. 353. In the camps of the Carthaginians <note>referred to as "Poeni"</note> which were led out against Timoleon, four-horse chariots of a horrible appearance were seen prepared for battle <note>original Greek: τεθρίππα ἐκπληκτικῶς πρὸς ἀγῶνα κατεσκευασμένα</note>. This "rank of chariots" was passed by the cavalry, who went sharply and eagerly against the enemy, though they were far superior in number. By the heavens fighting alongside them, 70,000 Carthaginians were defeated by 5,000, as Plutarch narrates at length in *Timoleon*, p. 249, 250. In the siege of the city of Troy, Teutamus, King of the Assyrians, sent to Priam who was seeking help *“ten thousand Ethiopians, and as many Susians with two hundred chariots,”* led by Memnon, son of Tithonus, as reported by Diodorus Siculus, Book 2. In the battle of Mithridates with Nicomedes, King of Bithynia, Appian* says: <margin>Mithridatic Wars, p. 182</margin> *“The scythed chariots, falling upon the Bithynians with force, cut through and sliced them, some groups into two, others into many parts. The event terrified the army of Nicomedes, when they saw men cut in half*

<column-break/>

<margin>Scythed chariots used in wars.</margin>
*still breathing, or scattered into many pieces, or hanging from the scythes.”* <note>original Greek: δρεπανηφόρα ἅρματα... ἀπηρτημένους</note> Regarding the nine hundred scythed chariots of Sisera dispersed by Barak, one can read the Book of Judges, about which Rhodomannus wrote in *Palaestina*, Book 2, v. 156, p. 55:

->**The phalanxes unaccustomed to defeat**<-
> He laid low in the dust, and the leader of the warriors
> Who was terribly boasting in his iron-bearing vehicles,
> He turned Sisera to flight; and with a nail a woman pierced
> His head while he finally slept—a great light for the Hebrews.
<note>Translated from the Greek verse provided in the text.</note>

<margin>1 Samuel 13:5</margin>
Thus the Philistines are said to have gathered* against the Israelites with 3,000 chariots and 6,000 horsemen. This abundance of armed chariots is called into doubt by Cappel*, to whom three thousand chariots seem sufficient; for he suggests a slip easily occurred from *shelosh* <note>three</note> into *sheloshim* <note>thirty</note>. <margin>Sacred Criticism, p. 419</margin> Nor were "war chariots" <note>original Greek: ἅρματα πολεμηστήρια</note>, to use the words of Plato in the *Symposium*, p. 119, used only among the Easterners. In military affairs, the English <note>Britons</note> were formerly outstanding, prevailing not only in cavalry and infantry but also fighting equipped with chariots, which they called partly *corini* and partly *esseda*; they used this kind of fighting against Caesar the Dictator when waging war. Hence they are named *Essedarii* by historians; compare Pomponius Mela 3.6, Cornelius Tacitus in *The Life of Agricola*, Lucan Book 1 of the *Pharsalia*, and Xiphilinus on the Britons, p. 421. Olaus Magnus, Book 9, is witness that the use of these military chariots even reached the North. Felix Malleolus of Zurich, a legal expert who lived around the year 1434, testifies in the book he wrote *On Nobility* (found in Lavater’s commentary on Joshua, ch. 1, p. 49) that the Bohemians, in the war waged against the Germans after the Council of Constance, used four-horse chariots armed with iron tools, which, when necessity demanded, were joined by chains like the walls of a camp to withstand enemy attacks. Regarding the speed and violence of these chariots, Lucretius* records wonders:
<margin>Book 3, v. 643</margin>
> They say the scythe-bearing chariots lop off limbs
> So suddenly, amidst the heat of the slaughter,
> That the part which has fallen cut off
> Is seen to quiver on the ground.

Therefore, the fierce battles and the swift courses of chariots rushing toward the cruelty of Mars deserve to be reviewed here, just as Euripides graphically described them, so that they seem to stand before your eyes. Thus says the Messenger*: <margin>In The Suppliants, v. 666</margin>
> Horsemen were armed against horsemen,
> And chariots against four-horse chariots.

Later he reported the heat of the "bloody battle"*: <margin>v. 673 ff.</margin>
> The drivers of the four-horse vehicles
> Then began the battle,
> And having driven their vehicles past one another,
> They set the combatants in battle array.
> Some fought with iron, while others turned
> Their colts back toward the combatants.
> Seeing the panic, he who was the lord of the single-bridled steeds,
> Aided those who feared the mass of chariots.
> Those who in turn guarded the Cadmean cavalry,
> Joined their strength, and now they conquered, now were defeated.
> Seeing and hearing these things—for I was there
> Where the chariots and the riders contended—
> I cannot say which of the many miseries present there
> I should tell first: whether the dust rising to the sky,
> For there was much of it.

# From Joshua XVII. v. 18.

<margin>Scythed chariots used in wars.</margin>
> ...or the streams of blood, dark red with gore,
> scorched above and below by the thongs <note>original Greek: ἱμᾶσιν</note>,
> as some fell and others were crushed in their chariots
> onto their heads, tumbling violently to the ground,
> leaving their lives behind in bloody gasps.
<note>This is a fragment from a lost Greek tragedy, likely describing the carnage of a chariot wreck.</note>

Now, if you apply this horrific description to our sacred history, you will see more clearly the rush and impetus of that burning warfare which is hinted at briefly <note>original Latin: βραχυλόγως</note> in the Holy Scripture. Thus a comparison should be made where the heavy battles of the Israelites are strictly reviewed, and where great engines of war are hidden within certain very intense words. For this reason, these military chariots, on account of their speed, can be compared with the narrative of a chariot race which Sophocles described *quite skillfully*.

<margin>Electra v. 705</margin>
> At the sound of the bronze trumpet, they dashed forth. All at once,
> shouting to their horses, they shook the reins
> with their hands: the whole course was filled
> with the din of rattling chariots. The dust was carried
> upward: and all mixed together,
> they spared the whips not at all, so that each might
> pass the wheel-hubs and the snorting of the horses.

Euripides, in *The Phoenician Women* v. 799, introduces Mars <note>The Roman name for Ares, the god of war</note> as the author and inciter of war with chariots. Hence, when Eteocles, contending with his brother for the kingdom, hastens to swords and fires, to horses and chariots, he speaks thus in Euripides:

<margin>The Phoenician Women v. 524.</margin>
> For these things, let fire come, let swords come!
> Yoke the horses, fill the plains with chariots!

In the same play, the Chorus, comparing Mars and Bacchus, says that the former wanders about,

<margin>v. 799.</margin>
> ...with the chariot and the four-footed bits of single-hoofed colts.

Then, with an elegant structure of speech, he describes a bitter battle, how chariots mixed with chariots shook off the soldiers, the wheels leaped, and corpses were piled upon corpses:

<margin>v. 1196.</margin>
> But our men, seeing a favorable omen from Jove <note>Zeus</note>,
> drove out the frames of their chariots,
> horsemen and heavy infantry, and into the midst of the Argive weapons
> they joined their spears. All was a mass of evils.
> They died, they fell out from the chariot-rims.
> Wheels leaped, and axles crashed upon axles,
> and the dead were heaped up together with the dead.

As for the army being hedged about by chariots, he says of it:

<margin>v. 740.</margin>
> ...and there the people are fenced in round about with chariots.

Therefore, although chariots may loosen and scatter the ranks with a stormy force, they are nevertheless of no use in the mountains and in marshy places; for wooded places are impassable for wagons <note>original Greek: ἀναμάξευτοι</note>, through which carts cannot be driven. This was experienced by Porus, King of the Indians, to the great loss of himself and his men, when he fought unsuccessfully with chariots against Alexander the Great. *The greatest part of his strength*, says Curtius, *was in the chariots;*

<margin>Book 8, ch. 14.</margin>

<column-break/>

*each was carrying six men: two shield-bearers, two archers stationed on each side, and the rest were drivers, certainly not unarmed. Truly, there was scarcely any use for this aid on that day, for a rain more violent than usual had made the fields slippery and unrideable, and the heavy and almost immobile chariots were stuck in the filth and quagmires. Now the battle had moved on all sides, when those who drove the chariots, thinking it the last hope for their side, gave the horses their heads and*

<margin>Scythed chariots used in wars.</margin>
*began to rush into the midst of the danger. This evil was double-edged for both sides, for the Macedonian infantry were crushed in the first charge, and the chariots, sent through slippery and pathless ground, threw off those by whom they were steered. The horses of others, being terrified, plunged the chariots not only into quagmires and pits, but even into the river.* Porus *sees the chariots thus scattered* across the whole line, *wandering without drivers; those closest to his friends were abandoning the elephants, etc.* However, a remedy was found for resisting these military chariots, the method of which Curtius records: *The chariots, he says, which had disturbed the line near the front standards, had been driven into the phalanx; the Macedonians, with their spirits strengthened, received them into the middle of their column. The battle line was like a wall; they had joined their spears, and from both sides they stabbed those rushing blindly in; then they began to throw down the chariots and their defenders.* L. Sylla also found another method of stopping and turning away four-horse chariots: he fixed stakes in the ground, between which the soldiers would be safe from the coming chariots; this is recorded by Frontinus in *Book 2, ch. 3.* However, it is not sufficiently clear what the shape of the wheels was in such scythed chariots. Stewichius, in his commentary on *Vegetius*, shows an image of a scythed wheel, but in the judgment of Rader (on *Curtius*), it is impractical; Rader therefore shows another wheel, equipped with scythes, yet capable of turning. Petrus Redanus examines both images and says he does not understand how, as they are depicted, they could have been turned around, let alone how they could have run. But since these chariots belong to ancient times, that form of warring has ceased today—except that you may occasionally find scythed ships where necessity required them—and that terror of chariots has utterly vanished. Let us therefore make an end of these things with the words of *Savilius*, where among other things he discusses such chariots thus: *The manner of fighting from chariots is a thing celebrated not only in the fables of the Poets, but also recorded by the writers of sacred history; it should perhaps be ascribed to those heroic times as more proper to them, but it was exploded and rejected by other nations as if by the common consent of all (I except a few barbarian nations, always tenacious of those things to which they have become accustomed), because it was more difficult, and the cost of feeding and arming four (namely the fighter, the driver, and at least two horses) for one warrior to be equipped for battle was too high, and the failure of one would render the work of the rest useless.*

<margin>Book 4, ch. 15.</margin>
<margin>Commentary on 1 Maccabees 1:18, p. 222.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of biblical vows, specifically transitioning from general principles to the famous and controversial vow of Jephthah, comparing his situation to the sacrifice of Isaac by Abraham.</meta>

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Jephthah’s Vow.</margin>
...and returning in peace from the children of Ammon, I will offer him as a burnt offering to the Lord. <note>original: "holocaustum" - a sacrificial offering entirely consumed by fire.</note>

An example of obedience unheard of in all ages occurs in Abraham, to whom a son is promised to be born in his hundredth year (*Genesis 17:19*), in whom his seed is to be called and blessed (*Genesis 21:12*). Yet that same son, by a reversal of fortune, is commanded to be sacrificed to GOD as a burnt offering in the land of vision (*Genesis 22:2*). Is this bloody rejection not part of a terrifying decree? Abraham knew well that innocent blood must not be shed; he knew GOD is not appeased by human victims; he knew that the death of his son carried out by his own hand would be infamous with the crime of parricide; he saw that this oracle fought against all previous promises of GOD. Truly and gravely Chrysostom says <margin>Homily 25 on Hebrews chapter 11.</margin> <note>original Greek: "ἐνταῦθα δὲ οὐ τοὺς ἀνθρωπίνους ὑπερβῆναι μόνον ἐχρῆν λογισμοὺς..."</note> *In this matter, it was necessary not only to surpass human reasoning, but also to demonstrate something more; for the things of God seemed to fight against the things of God, and faith fought against faith, and the command against the promise.* Hence Cyprian, on account of this hitherto unheard-of example of obedience and faith in both the parent and the son, does not hesitate to count them both among the Martyrs. For he says this concerning the double Martyrdom <margin>page 518.</margin>:

> *Who would dare to exclude either the Patriarch Abraham or his son Isaac from the number of Martyrs? What executioner’s rack tortured the body more severely than the affections of nature tortured the Patriarch’s mind, when without hesitation at GOD’s command he prepared to sacrifice his only and uniquely dear son, in whom was his entire hope of posterity? What was lacking for the martyrdom of Isaac, who, without murmuring, allowed himself to be bound and placed upon the pyre? Nor did he tremble at the sword brandished over his neck?*

Jephthah, the Gileadite and consequently a Manassite, possessed "ancestral virtue" <note>original Greek: "τὴν πατρῴαν ἀρετὴν"</note>—these are the words of Josephus—he was a "mighty man of valor" <note>original Greek: "δυνατὸς ἐν ἰσχύϊ"</note>, a valiant hero. Driven from his home by the public hand, as can be gathered from verse 7, he lived for some time as an exile in the land of Tob. Then, with changing fortune (to speak with Tertullian), he was recalled—not without the hidden cords of divine providence—as the prince and head of the Gileadites, a <term>hindrance</term> <note>original: "ἐμπόδιον" (empodion) - an obstacle or barrier.</note> to Ammonite tyranny; a second Abraham, as Theophanes chooses to call him. Here he uttered and made a vow according to the custom of the Jewish homeland, for whom it was not unusual to pronounce vows, as is evident from *Genesis 28:20* and *Numbers 12:2*. Tertullian, in his 3rd book against Marcion, chapter 4, verse 110, writes:

> *Jephthah with firm faith, who with a harsh wound dared*
> *A vow, to declare a great price of war to God.*
> *Here because, what the Lord does not want, he had promised madly,*
> *There first meets him the pledge dear to his heart,*
> *Which by a sudden chance hoped for by none fell to him,*
> *That the promise might stand, he loosed the pious laws of a parent,*
> *The vow of a sin, a monstrous fear violently constrained,*
> *He obtained fame for a crime, praise for a wicked deed, as solace for a bereaved life.*

<column-break/>

<margin>Jephthah’s Vow.</margin>
There were, however, four types of sacred bonds, as they call them, among the Jews, which Ludovicus Cappellus brings forward from the Mishnah in the tractate *Nedarim*, and from the commentaries of Rabbi Nissim, Rabbi Asher, and Rabbi Solomon Jarchi on that same tractate. <term>Neder</term> <note>Hebrew: נֶדֶר</note> is called a <term>promise</term> <note>Greek: ὑπόσχεσις</note>, a vow or pledge made to GOD for obtaining some benefit, with a certain firmness and obligation toward that which was previously free to do or not do. The second is <term>Cherem</term> <note>Hebrew: חֶרֶם</note>, an <term>anathema</term>, or a thing devoted to slaughter and destruction, consecrated indeed without any mercy. The remaining two species, namely the <term>Nazirite vow</term> and the <term>oath</term> <note>Hebrew: שבועה (Shevuah)</note>, we omit, since according to the common opinion of authors, Jephthah’s vow is in no way referred to them. Now, however, we must proceed further and discern to which of these this devotion of Jephthah can be referred. We find two principal opinions concerning that vow. One group refers this act of Jephthah to a <term>neder</term>, a simple vow; hence they interpret the words of the vow, "it shall be the Lord's AND I will offer it," in such a way that the conjunction placed in the second position takes on the force of a disjunctive <note>Meaning "and" is read as "or".</note>. They are moved both by the words of the history itself, "and he vowed a vow" <note>Hebrew: וַיִּדַּר נֶדֶר (Vayiddar neder)</note>, and by other passages of Scripture where the letter "Vav" <note>The Hebrew prefix for "and".</note> acquires a disjunctive sense (*Genesis 26:11, Exodus 12:5, 21:15, Isaiah 10:14, 19:15, Jeremiah 44:28*). And so, they argue Jephthah included in his vow only what he thought was lawful to vow. If the vow had been specifically about a burnt offering, and he had intended to complete the sacrifice by vow, surely his only daughter, who was his delight, would have disapproved of the act, refused obedience, and the rebuke of the Levites would have followed. But now, since the daughter—as one capable of a vow of virginity—consents and does not refuse to take upon herself the vow made by her parent (however imprudently made), they prefer to understand it as virginity consecrated to divine use. The daughter, they say, could have—and it would have been lawful—broken the vow of virginity if she, as a maiden, had refused to accept it. How much more could she have done so if that vow had been about slaughter and the subsequent sacrifice? They proceed to argue indiscriminately: Jephthah did not vow that whatever first met him he would make a burnt offering. For how could he, when he knew very well that the sacrifice of sons and daughters was expressly and by name forbidden by divine law; likewise any other human, or from the animals a dog or another unclean animal! Who would believe he vowed so impiously, so thoughtlessly, so abominably? And if it had been so, he could and should have rescinded the vow in the case of evil promises. For a promise is impious which is fulfilled by a crime. Furthermore, they say it is not strictly necessary to insist on that disjunctive meaning, since even without it the same sense can flow through a convenient interpretation: there are two parts in this vow, one of which is general, extending more widely than the second, indeed including the second, which is the burnt offering—which itself is among the things consecrated to GOD, yet not everything consecrated to God...

# From Judges XI. v. 30. 31.

<margin>Jephthah’s Vow.</margin>
...to God is a burnt offering. First, therefore, the vow was general concerning everything that might meet him returning from his house, to be consecrated into divine service; but since an animal might meet him which, according to the law, was fit for an offering, he vows more specifically that he would offer it as a burnt offering. But his daughter met him beyond his expectation, and so that the vow might be fulfilled, and that she might appear to be consecrated to none other than God, he willed that she be and remain a perpetual virgin. This milder opinion is defended, besides the Rabbis, by the more recent authors Blessed Brentius, Franzius, Chytræus, Osiander, Schindler, Quistorp, Glassius, Fussel, and Hackspan; also Pellican, Munster, Broughton, Junius, Pagninus, Arias Montanus, Perkins, Grotius, Drusius, Heinsius, Tofanus, Piscator, and many others. Those, however, who refer this act of Jephthah to a composite vow, namely to <term>Cherem <note>Hebrew: חרם; a thing devoted to destruction or sacred use</note></term>, an anathema, agree in this: stating that the daughter was snatched from the living, but some contend she was only slaughtered but not sacrificed, while others say she was both slaughtered and sacrificed. To this last opinion a great number of the Fathers subscribe: Justin Martyr (Question 99), Tertullian (Against Marcion 3. 4), Nazianzen (Oration on the Maccabees), Ambrose (Book 2 on Virgins and On Offices 12), Jerome (Epistle 34 to Julian), Chrysostom (Homily on Jephthah), and Augustine (City of God, Book 1, 21). These are cited as a virtual cloud of witnesses by Blessed Balduinus (Book 2, ch. 8 on Cases of Conscience, title on Vows, case 4) and Dr. Calovius in his Disputations against Grotius on this passage. Among the more recent are Blessed Luther, Balduinus, Friedlieb, Dannhauer, Calovius, and Walther; also Martyr, Musculus, Salianus, Torniellus, Serrarius, and Cavanellus. These base the principal strength of their opinion on the text itself <note>original Greek: ῥητῶς; "expressly" or "literally"</note>. The Hebrew words are <note>Hebrew: והיה היוצא אשר יצא והיה ליהוה והעליתיהו עולה</note> *And it shall be, that whatsoever comes forth, which shall come forth, it shall be the Lord’s, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering.* The Old Interpreter <note>The Vulgate</note> rendered this sense: *Whosoever first comes out of the doors of my house and meets me returning in peace from the children of Ammon, him I will offer as a burnt offering to the Lord.* Two things must be noted here: first, that the phrase <note>Hebrew: זה אשר; "that which"</note> is not to be taken as strictly neuter, for since the Hebrews lack a neuter singular ending, Jephthah could easily have argued—when his daughter first met him—that he had been speaking of a masculine subject, not a feminine one. But since the vower did not say this, the words of the vow certainly include a human of either sex, as the event proves. Nor are walking or emerging beasts excluded, which by ordinary custom were used to be sacrificed, vowed, and consecrated. Therefore, the phrase is determined toward those kinds of things to which it is given to go out, walk, and come to meet someone. The second point, in which the Old Interpreter slips, is making a single statement out of a two-part vow; this omission is against the text, which has: *And it shall be the Lord’s, AND I will offer it up for a burnt offering.* Hence the patrons of this opinion usually render the prefixed *Vau* <note>The Hebrew letter 'and'</note> in its most famous, copulative sense, implying a subordination, so that the first part acts as the genus and the latter as the species, and indeed <note>original Greek: ἐξηγητικῶς; "by way of explanation"</note>, *it shall be the Lord’s in such a way that it is immolated in sacrifice*, absolutely, not condition-

<column-break/>

<margin>Jephthah’s Vow.</margin>
-ally, provided it were fit and suitable for sacrifice. Next, they urge that Jephthah’s mind was most severely wounded by his daughter’s <note>original Greek: ἀπάντησιν; "meeting" or "encounter"</note>. For Jephthah, about to go down with an army to defeat the Ammonites, had bound himself by a vow, and as one liable for that vow, he sought the enemy army, invaded the Ammonites, slaughtered and subdued them; and since this happy outcome was the condition of the vow made, being bound by it, when he returned home as Victor, his daughter met him first—ignorant of her father's vow, unaware of her own danger, leading dances and processions. When he sees her, how he is distracted by grief, how he tears his clothes for sorrow and groans "Ah, Ah," saying: <note>Hebrew: הכרע הכרעתני ואת היית בעכרי</note> *In bowing down you have bowed me down, and you are among those who trouble me, for I have opened my mouth to the Lord, and I cannot go back.* Here Lucas Osiander says: *You utterly darken my victory because of my vow; and though the Lord raised me up on high, you humble and depress me greatly; and whereas I promised myself much comfort from you, hoping to see your grandsons, sons, and daughters, it has happened that I shall receive more sadness from you than joy.* The Vulgate rendered these words: *You have deceived me and you yourself are deceived*, but they do not reach the sense, since according to the Lexicographers and Concordances, the word <note>Hebrew: הכרע; "to bow down/bring low"</note> is nowhere found with the meaning of "deceiving," even if Cornelius à Lapide intends to help the Vulgate interpreter and cloak his <note>original Greek: σφάλμα; "error" or "slip"</note>, saying: *You have deceived my hope of propagating a family through you. You are deceived because you thought I would be happy at your coming out.* Finally, they also urge the execution of the vow; for when the daughter returned from the mountains, where she had bewailed her virginity for two months, the execution of the vow is described, while it is said of the rigid and piously superstitious father: <note>Hebrew: ויעש לה את-נדרו אשר נדר</note> *and he did to her his vow which he had vowed.* Regarding the daughter: <note>Greek LXX: καὶ αὐτὴ οὐκ ἔγνω ἄνדρα</note>. The Old Interpreter: *who knew not man.* Arias Montanus: *And she had not known man.* Others: *And she knew not man.* Thus the assertors of perpetual virginity commonly translate it. But from Blessed Glassius himself, though he is of the opposite opinion, it is established that the past tense verb among the Hebrews sometimes has the meaning of the imperfect, pluperfect, or future. And hence from the <note>original Greek: συναφεία; "connection" or "context"</note> of the text itself, it is clear that the pluperfect meaning has a place here. In that way, "she had not known man" posits an act, not a vow of virginity or a custom of abstaining from marriage. Finally, even those words <note>Hebrew: ותהי-חק בישראל לתנות</note> *and it was a statute in Israel, to lament*, they lead in favor of their opinion. For those who defend the <note>original Greek: τἀκριβείαν ἀνυπερθέτως; "the strictness without delay"</note> extort this sense: *from this time the custom prevailed in Israel that the daughters of others also should be consecrated to God by this example*, and they fix the foundation of their exposition in verse 39. Others refer this to verse 36 in this way: *It was a statute, lest anyone hereafter vow a son or daughter to be sacrificed to GOD, as Jephthah did imprudently and inconsiderately.* These, however, leaving both these senses, refer it to verse 40, so that the annual ascent of the daughters of Israel is indicated, in this way: *And the custom grew from then on, that the virgins of Israel would meet every year <note>Hebrew: לתנות</note> to lament, or rather to celebrate (not to chatter, as Rabbi Kimchi fabu-*

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
# Page 336

<margin>Jephthah's Vow.</margin>
...fables are told) regarding Jephthah's daughter for four days. And thus we have repeated the most powerful arguments of both sides, finally adding our own judgment to the opinion of those who believe it is better to remain in doubt about uncertain matters than to litigate them. Therefore, they take up the defense of neither opinion, but rather embrace a cautious <term>epoche</term> <note>original: ἐποχὴν; a Greek philosophical term for the "suspension of judgment"</note>, as seen in **B. Gerhard, Vol. 7, Commonplaces, § 507; Cl. Sennert in a special Exercise held at Wittenberg in the year 1650; Meier on Perkins' Cases of Conscience, 2. 15. question 3; and Selden, Book 4 on the Law of Nature and Nations, 11, p. 553.** A vow similar to Jephthah’s was that of Alexander, who, having been warned perhaps to kill the first person who met him coming out of the gate, as witnessed by **Valerius Maximus, 7. 3. p. 297**, ordered a donkey-driver who happened to be the first to meet him to be dragged off to death. The donkey-driver, however, replied that his little donkey had actually met him first, and thus he freed himself. Would that Jephthah’s daughter had also had a little dog before her, by which she might have escaped her father’s utterly rash, unthinking, and illicit vow. We pronounce this vow of Jephthah rash and illicit due to the lack of requirements which are legally necessary to constitute a legitimate vow. For it is not enough that the person vowing has the power to vow, and that he vows freely—both of which were present in Jephthah’s vow—but there are several conditions and requirements that must necessarily concur for the legitimation of a vow. Among these is that the vower should vow prudently and with good premeditation, not imprudently and without prior consultation. That neither of these was present in Jephthah’s vow will be clear to anyone <term>accurately</term> <note>original: ἀκριβῶς</note> weighing it; for he did not consider: what if the thing coming out of the house were something cheap, unsuitable, or rendered unfit for sacrifice by the law of God? What if it were a donkey? What if a human? What if his daughter? Would such a thing coming forth even be pleasing to God? For no one vows or promises to another that which he knows to be unacceptable to them. To this is added the subsequent grief, the tearing of his garment, the lamentation, the sadness, etc., all of which more than sufficiently imply his imprudence, rashness, and precipitancy in vowing.

That custom held many peoples, and still holds many, to keep captives bound in loose iron shackles for grinding, or even for cutting stone, drawing water, agricultural labor, and other servile works. That the hero Samson, deprived of sight and stripped of his kingdom, was cast down to the mill to drive it around and crush grain with a pestle in prison, is a matter of almost no doubt to one who looks at *Exodus chapter 11, verse 5*, where the Lord says: "Every firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, even to the firstborn of the maidservant who is at the mill." This is understood more clearly in *chapter 12, verse 29* as referring to the prison or workhouse <note>Latin: ergastulum</note> and the mill-house, in which male and female slaves drove the hand-mill around. <margin>Iliad, Book 20, v. 105.</margin> A woman of the mill is a <term>grinding woman</term> <note>original: γυνὴ ἀλετρίς</note> in **Homer**, concerning whom see *Matthew*

*24:41 and Luke 17:35.* To this Salmuth refers in his *Notes on Panciroli, N.R. book 2, ch. 22*: "A girlfriend bought from the machines," namely, one who was from the mill-house or the mill. The Septuagint calls her a <term>female captive in the pit</term> <note>original: αἰχμαλωτίδα ἐν τῷ λάκκῳ</note>; for the mill was nothing else to captives but a prison and a pit, a <term>house in the pit</term> <note>original: οἶκος τῆ λακκῳ</note>, *Jeremiah 37:16*. In this sense, they called prisons in Athens <term>pits</term> <note>original: λάκκους</note>, as noted by *Ad. v. 24. Turnebus, and II. Parerg. 39. Gentilis*. The Lord Jehovah threatens the same as punishment in *Isaiah 47:2*, constituting for the Babylonians a part of their <term>utter destruction</term> <note>original: πανολεθρίας</note> as shameful and troublesome servitude, which is indicated metaleptically by the mention of the mill. Similarly, in *Exodus 6:6*, the entire Egyptian servitude was aptly designated by the translator with the single word "workhouse" <note>Latin: ergastulum</note>, which perfectly fits the Egyptian labors. The words of the Prophet are: *Take the millstones, <insert>rekhayim</insert>, and grind flour, <insert>kemakh</insert>*, by which he signifies that the Queen of Babel, the mistress and conqueror of kingdoms, would be subject to the most abject servitude, and indeed the very same in which the Hebrews themselves had once served. In this way, in *Lamentations chapter 5, verse 13*, the Prophet complained that the young men were led away to the mill; although the Latin translator does not think this should be referred to that servile ministry of grinding, but takes it in an obscene sense of pederasty: *They have shamefully abused the youths.* In this same sense he translates: *Let my wife be the harlot of another*, for which the Hebrew has: *Let my wife grind for another. Job 31:10.* This is properly explained by **Vatablus**, and more according to the sense: *Let her be taken from me and serve another.* Women in families where there were no slaves used to grind and make bread. Now, however, we have here many interpreters who take this word "grinding" used of Samson in the sense of the work of the flesh, <term>concerning intercourse and solemnly</term> <note>original: ἐπὶ μίξεως καὶ σεμνῶς</note>; for they say it is a euphemism, so that "to grind" denotes marital and obscene matters. This is the same figure of speech by which **Horace** spoke of "grinding away at other men's wives," *1. Although the thought of the comparison is ugly in that regard, **Baldus**, that ugly and un-Latin writer, recites the same in his *Catholicon*. # From Judges XVI. v. 21

<margin>Samson’s workhouse.</margin>
...that Samson might be called, and that he might play before them. According to some, this means he was forced to perform shameful and lustful acts before the eyes of the spectators; Villalpandus <note>Juan Bautista Villalpando (1552–1608), a Spanish Jesuit scholar known for his commentary on Ezekiel.</note> thinks this pleasure is indicated by the same word *to play* <note>original Greek: *παίξειν* (paizein)</note> in Exodus 32:6. Otherwise, for the Greeks, *to play* is a word of joy, used when jokes and musical delights are employed, as in Pindar’s *Olympian Ode 1*: *we play together* <note>original Greek: *ϲὺν παίζομεν*</note>, and there John Benedictus (p. 8); then it refers to *wickedness* when Venus <note>i.e., sexual acts</note> is practiced. In the same way, "to play" among the Latins—likewise "to grind" and "to knead"—are words of wickedness, as noted by Rittershusius on Oppian (p. 287), Paraeus on Musaeus (f. 97), Taubmann on *Plautus' Truculentus 2. 2.*, Drusius (5. *Observations 5.*), Torrentius on *Suetonius (p. 94)*, Lotichius on *Petronius (p. 34)*, Salmuth on Panciroli (1. 2. c. 22. p. 299), and Laurenburg in *Antiquarius (f. 130)*. By this definition, the Hebrews note and blame the Philistines' customs in those games and public spectacles—which were hardly modest and quite effeminate—as being directed toward the "game of Venus," as if they wished Samson to copulate with foreign women so that from so strong a man, strong sons might be created, according to that line of Horace: <margin>Odes 4. l. 4. v. 29.</margin> *The brave are created by the brave.* However, an accurate consideration of the event itself, as it is recorded, entirely dissolves and shakes off this interpretation. Regarding those **feasts** and games, just as the Scripture speaks *appropriately* and *properly* <note>original Greek: *πρεπόντως* (prepōntōs) & *κυρίως* (kyriōs)</note>, so it does regarding the comedies; nor does a *wicked deed* <note>original Greek: *ἔργον κακουργὲς* (ergon kakourges)</note> befit a pious hero. Nor would I think it should be attributed to Philistine customs—to speak from Terence’s *Andria* <margin>Act 1. sc. 1.</margin>—that Samson held a "Chrysis" <note>A reference to a courtesan character in Roman comedy</note> in a dense circle of youths and maidens, in whose minds the shamefulness of the act would have immediately settled. And therefore, we deservedly reject that sense as frivolous and shameful. Truly, the matter stood thus: in the prison was a mill of the region's delay, in which the bound Samson, fettered with two chains (for Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible.</note> has it that the word *nechoshtayim* in the dual number implies two chains), prepared the bound work, pushing the mill with his hands and his whole body. This was a most harsh and difficult labor, which Rabbi Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a prominent medieval Jewish biblical commentator.</note> notes as the custom here. That prison is called here the "House of the Bound," and *asurim* <note>Hebrew: "prisoners"</note> is in the reading, in the Scripture *Beit ha-Asurim*. So in 2 Samuel 20:3, *Beit Mishmeret*, the house of custody. It was that kind of the vilest and most abject slavery: to work while bound in workhouses <note>term: *ergastulum* (a Roman private prison for slaves)</note>, from which work they were called *ergastulians*, *places in which the bound work* <note>original Greek: *ἐρχεςήλιοι, τόποι ἐν ᾧ δεσμῶται ἐργάζονται*</note>. Surely nothing is more miserable and despised than a man who drives a mill around while in shackles. Samson was forced to serve this unworthy slavery until his tragic end of life, "and he ground" <note>Hebrew: *vayitach*</note>, as the Chaldean <note>The Aramaic translation</note> has it. You will read nothing more often among secular authors than that slaves underwent this most miserable lot of service; regarding this matter, it will be by no means unpleasant to read the commentaries of Lorenzo Pignoria and Titus Popma on slaves, where they deal with their workhouses and their use and condition among various nations. From this it also became common that, because of the most miserable lot of service, those who worked the mill were called *Asses*, as witnessed by Scaliger on *Catullus (p. 130)* and Meursius in *Critical Exercises*. To the Mill-house belonged sieves, asses, the millstone, and slaves, as I observe in <margin>p. 132.</margin> Julius Paulus, *Received Opinions, book 3, title 6*. Pollux (book 3, ch. 8, n. 2), describing the *hardships* <note>original Greek: *ταλαιπωρίας* (talaipōrias)</note> of slaves, says: *and so that the slaves are not punished, there are mills and seeking-places and husking-places and groat-crushing-places and [punishment] belts.* <note>original Greek: *καὶ ἵνα μὴ κολάζονται οἱ δῦλοι, μύλωνες καὶ ζητρεία καὶ λοιπεία καὶ χονδροκοπεία καὶ ζωντάι*</note> From this, some light will be shed on the words

<column-break/>

<margin>Samson’s workhouse.</margin>

No Apelles <note>A famous painter of ancient Greece, used here to mean a vivid describer.</note> ever painted that harsh treatment and lifestyle of slaves more clearly than Apuleius: <margin>Book 9, Metamorphoses.</margin> *Good gods,* he says, *what sort of little men were those, their whole skin painted with livid welts, their scarred backs more shaded than covered by a tattered rag; some with only a small loincloth covering their private parts; yet all were so tunicked (marked with known letters on their faces, so that each more shameful one could be recognized) and half-shaved of hair and their feet ringed; because they were bound with iron chains of rings, lest they flee.* Other examples from a more recent age are frequent in Plautus and Terence (in whose work Geta in *Phormio, Act 2, sc. 1, v. 18* complains thus:

And there are others, from which we could bring forth very many if there were a need. And even today this kind of prison remains among the Turks, by whom Christians are packed into workhouses and mills, as Nicolaus Clenardus <note>A 16th-century Flemish grammarian and traveler.</note> is an *eyewitness* <note>original Greek: *ἀυτοπτης* (autoptēs)</note>; in which <margin>Book 2, Letters, p. 62.</margin> man it was a matter of praise that he first—so that his work in spreading the study of humanity might shine more brightly at that time—betook himself to Salamanca out of a desire and love for the Arabic language, and even sought out Africa itself of his own accord, as he reported of himself in the cited place of his letters. The Ancients had various workhouses: Florus reports concerning Sicily (book 3, ch. 19): *The land, fertile in crops and in a way a suburban province, was held as the broad estates of Latin citizens (Lipsius reads "wealthier" [lautiorum], since the Latins were allies, not citizens).* Here, for the <margin>2. Elect. 15.</margin> cultivation of the field, the crowded workhouses and chained laborers provided the material for war. Moreover, those slaves, whether captured or bought for a price, were of the lowest condition, and were shown for sale marked with titles and signs, by which either their names were explained, or the price, and whatever else it was in the interest of the buyer not to be ignorant of. These were not exercises of pleasure or of passing time, but torments of the harshest slavery and of all one's strength, joined with the loss of life itself, which the "mill-slaves" or "bakery-slaves," as Pignorius calls them (book 2, *On Slaves*, p. 35, 36, 37), were forced to endure. Among the exercises of Pittacus, King of the Mitylenians, was grinding; for Laertius says of him, quoting Clearchus, *his exercise was to grind grain* <note>original Greek: *τότῳ γυμνάσιον ϲῖτον ἀλεῖν*</note>, whence Plutarch in the *Symposium* makes Thales speak thus: *I heard a foreign woman singing at the mill in Lesbos, "Grind, mill, grind, for even Pittacus grinds, who rules great Mitylene."* <note>original Greek: *Ἄλει μύλα, ἄλει, καὶ γὰρ Πιττακὸς ἄλει, μεγάλας Μιτυλάνας βαϲιλεύων*</note> He said the King of great Mitylene grinds, and he rouses himself by his example—though those who interpret *to grind at Mitylene* do so poorly, for *to grind* is used absolutely. Regarding this laborious exercise of the King, Clement says in the *Pedagogue*: *That Pittacus, the king of the Mitylenians, ground, using an active exercise.* What that King did for the sake of exercise, Samson is forced to do as punishment.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Samson’s Prison-house.</margin>
Samson could rebuke the Philistines for their tyranny over him and his people, drawing from Isaiah 5:15: *Why do you crush the faces of the poor?* <note>The author likely refers to Isaiah 3:15, "What mean ye that ye beat my people to pieces, and grind the faces of the poor?"</note> But regarding Samson’s prison-house, <note>original Greek: ὡς κατ᾽ ἐκβολὰν λόγου — "as a digression"</note> enough has been said.

### JUDGES XVI. 23.

<note>Hebrew: "The lords of the Philistines gathered together to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god, and to rejoice."</note>
<note>Greek: "The Satraps of the foreigners assembled to sacrifice a great sacrifice to Dagon their God, and to be glad."</note>

->The princes of the Philistines came together as one, that they might immolate magnificent victims to Dagon their God, and feast.<-

<margin>The Vain Victory-Song of the Philistines.</margin>
Samson, born to his father Manoah from the tribe of Dan, was a hero shining with virtue even in his youthful years. A Nazirite <note>A person consecrated to God by a vow, usually involving abstaining from wine and not cutting one's hair.</note> from the womb, he was divinely adorned with intrepid strength from that moment. At a time when the Philistines pressed the Israelites under a harsh yoke, he was stirred by God and fortified with singular courage to deliver his fatherland and the entire race of Jacob from that foul and <note>original Greek: ἀνελπίστῳ — "hopeless"</note> servitude. He attacked the Philistines in a thousand and almost countless ways of harassment, and to speak with the Poet:

> *Seeking an approach here, that in just war he might*
> *Beset the Philistines, and free the thin hopes of Syria from the foe,*
> *He joins a treaty by marriage.*

By entering into marriage with a Philistine woman, he took the opportunity to avenge his people and snatch them from the wretched yoke of slavery. Having achieved his wish with the consent of the parents on both sides, he joined himself to the Philistine maiden whom he loved; however, the consummation of the marriage was prolonged and delayed to another more convenient time, as his father-in-law pretended. When the term and day for consummating the marriage had passed, he proposed a riddle to be solved by the young men—whom Josephus calls <note>original Greek: νυμφοστόλους & ἑταίρους — "bridal attendants and companions"</note>—who had gathered to celebrate Samson’s nuptial rights. This was done before he rewarded them according to the custom of the nation, under the law and condition that if they solved it within <note>original Greek: ἑπταήμερον — "seven days"</note>, he would be bound to give them thirty <note>original Hebrew: סדינים — "sedinim"</note>, fine linens or linen cloths, as Pagninus explains; Luther calls them <term>shirts</term> <note>German: Hembder/Hemden</note>. The Rabbis explain this as linen for both night and day, with which we are covered night and day. Friedlieb adds that they were undergarments of precious linen. He also promised as many <term>tunics</term>: in the text we read <note>original Hebrew: חליפח בגדים — "changes of garments"</note>, or by a reversal of terms, *garments of changes*, that is, *changeable garments*, as Pagninus reads. These are garments which noble men and those eager for more elegant dress are accustomed to have with them, which they change from time to time with other more common ones, lest they gather dirt. If they failed, they would be bound to him. The lot pleased them, and they approved the condition Samson brought; however, the meaning was debated with various sayings, and none were able to solve the riddle until, by adding threats of burning the bride and her entire family home, they extorted the solution through the bride's tears. For Samson, who:

> *Had a heart not unyielding to the roars of a Lion,*
> *Has here a heart not unyielding to the groans of a girl,*

opened the riddle proposed to his companions to his bride, who in turn revealed it to them. Thus was solved Samson’s enigma, who in anger descended to Ashkelon, and <margin>v. 19.</margin> having killed thirty men there, gave the change of garments to those who solved his riddle, albeit by fraud. But when

<column-break/>

Samson’s wife was given to the bed of one of those whom he had chosen as friends, he seized from this an occasion for harming the Philistines, and from that day he began to infest them. His deeds are worthy of the cedar <note>A metaphor meaning "worthy of immortality/preservation."</note>, which he performed not from a private desire for revenge, but by divine instinct to avenge the calamities of his nation. He did not let the repudiation he suffered go unpunished, but by catching three hundred foxes from all sides, which he sent into the harvest of the Philistines to be burned with fire, he avenged the injury done to himself and his people. Regarding this stratagem, the Poet says:

<margin>The Vain Victory-Song of the Philistines.</margin>
> <margin>Volume 4 of German Poets, p. 127</margin>
> *Indeed, the hero son of Manoah did not let it go unpunished,*
> *For he encircled the forest glades with snares, and the foxes*
> *He caught, having searched through the deepest dens, and with fire*
> *He bound shimmering torches to their tails, tied to one another.*
> *But behold, the foxes themselves, fearing the flame of the shining light,*
> *Are driven into a madness; the fury, ignited, rages more than the fires*
> *Themselves, and drove them now here, now there,*
> *By which wandering all around, the cultivated fields of the soil*
> *Seemed suddenly to boil, and everywhere to settle into fires.*

Not content with this stratagem for greater things, he was equipped with greater strength, as if he ought to attack his enemy through tunnels alone. For when this damage was discovered, the Philistines entered into a plan to capture Samson, who was indeed bound by men from the tribe of Judah and handed into the hands of the Philistines. But when he saw the enemies, he found the <term>jawbone of an ass</term> lying before him; though stripped of weapons, he found it solid and, aided by divine virtue, killed a thousand Philistines, saying (as Adam Siberus expresses his words in a poem, whose <note>original Greek: προσευχαὶ — "prayers"</note> are found in Vol. 6 of German Poets, p. 134):

<margin>Judges 15:16.</margin>
> *This they wished; the bodies of a thousand men lie on the fields*
> *By the jawbone of a slow-walking little ass,*
> *A thousand lie; the rotting jawbone of an ass destroyed*
> *A thousand men: an ass kills a thousand bodies.*

The Philistines plotted revenge for this heroic deed, and thought they had the desired opportunity when our Hero <margin>Judges 16:2.</margin> was found entering Gaza. They surrounded him from ambush, and having bolted the gates through the night, they chose the morning hour to kill him. But he whom new ropes could not make defenseless was much less affected by the ambushes of the Philistines. For in the middle of the night he rose, tore the doors of the city gate with the two posts and the bar from their foundation, and having placed them on his shoulders, carried them to the top of the mountain facing Hebron, and thus eluded the snares of the Philistines. Finally, he was captured by an ill-fated and shameful love for the infamous Delilah, who made her living from a dishonest art. <margin>v. 4.</margin> The leaders of the Philistines approached her and hired her for a great price to inquire of him the causes of such incredible strength. He deceived her once or twice, but finally, overcome by the daily flattery of Delilah, the man otherwise insuperable in war revealed the secret of his strength to her. His head being shaven, he fell from the favor of the Holy Spirit; he was captured, bound, and—having first been deprived of the light of his eyes—was banished to the mill. Regarding this captivity, the Poet sings:

> <margin>Volume 4 of German Poets, p. 131</margin>
> *She cries out: "O Princes, bring weapons, shut him in chains!"*
> *Nor could Samson bring his strength to the battle,*
> *But he stretched out empty palms to the work of Mars,*
> *Nor did he have anything further of his accustomed virtue.*

# From Judges XVI, verse 23.

<margin>
The Vain Victory Song of the Philistines.
</margin>

> *Failing in strength, they drag him with a clinging rope,*
> *And plunder the clear honors of his hollow brow,* <note>original: "Perspicuásq; cava prædantur frontis honores" — a poetic reference to the gouging out of Samson's eyes.</note>
> *And leave the sockets empty, the light torn out,*
> *And so they shut him in the shrieking caves of the mill,*
> *That he might break the grain by the hard fate of labor.*

Samson’s strength deserted him, and he owed this misfortune to the reckless Delilah, who loves a spouse only to deceive him; she soothes him only to capture him. Captured, Samson lies in the darkness of the prison and the mill, bound too tightly to be freed. You would have seen a body covered in torn rags, every limb pressed by chains, and hands rendered useless and crushed by shackles. The girl had deceived him; she had promised one thing and delivered another. He had taken a wife in happiness, only to become a slave. <margin>Seneca, Controversies 5, p. 58. 8.</margin> He could have said: *I took a wife, and I sold my freedom.* By the precept of wisdom, whoever seeks a wife for himself <note>original: "Præcepto sapientiæ, sibi quis quæret uxorem"</note> (Seneca, Controversies 5, p. 58. 8.) should see *whether she loves her marriage, whether she values nothing more than her husband, whether she is compassionate, whether she is brave, and whether she can endure it together if any evil should befall her man.* If she is equipped with these virtues, she is well-endowed. None of these things could be found in Delilah. Therefore Samson was captured and held. He loved Delilah with some kind of blind passion <note>original: "nescio quâ Venere"</note>, and Delilah became the perfect instrument of betrayal. Just as Philotas was betrayed to Alexander for slaughter through his mistress Antigone, which can be read in Plutarch’s *Life of Alexander p. 692* and *Oration 2 on the Fortune of Alexander p. 339.* With a great heap of words, Samson’s immense and distinguished strength is proclaimed—he who tore a lion apart with his hands; who alone overthrew a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass; who carried away the gates of the city with their posts; and who inflicted countless lethal wounds on the Philistines—yet soft love inflicted a lethal poison upon him. For with Samson thus captured and Delilah the traitress, the Philistines gathered a solemn assembly, to which the Princes flocked from all the satraps of the Philistines; they raised shouts of joy, and amid feasts and frequent dances, they sang a Victory Song of this sort: <term>Our God <note>Hebrew: אלֹהֵינוּ (Eloheinu)</note> has delivered our enemy Samson into our hands.</term> Hence <term>he shall celebrate with festive assemblies and sacrifices</term> <note>Greek: πανηγυρίας ἀγῶσι καὶ θυσίαις ἐπιτελέσει</note> according to the usual custom of the mind. And lest anything be lacking from the festivity, the captive had to be brought out; for the Princes of the Philistines, whose spirits had more than once failed at the sight of Samson, now went exulting to the temple of the god Dagon and offered insolent sacrifices. Smoke rose to heaven; there was eating, drinking, playing, and triumphing. With festive applause, new joys were spread among the common people as Samson was led out from the house of prisoners, <term>so that they might insult Samson and the drinking party</term> <note>Greek: ὅπως ἐνυβρίσωσι τὸν Σάμψονα καὶ τὴν πότον</note>, as Josephus notes. From here, Samson was led out, shackled at the feet, providing material for jokes; he played before the Philistines. The Seventy <note>The Septuagint translators</note> say they insulted him with heavy taunts and surrounded him with mockery, which is tolerated more harshly than captivity itself by a man conscious of his innate virtue. Therefore, when the feast was prepared and magnificent victims sacrificed to their god Dagon for the defeat of their most capital enemy, Samson was called to play before them. <margin>v. 25. 28.</margin> <margin>v. 25.</margin> Summoned, he is forced to play; they mock him as a blind man, and they push the blind, unarmed man. *"Blind man,"* they cry, *"strike the Philistines! Eunuch, move the camps to the camps! On the scaffold, move the catapults to the walls! Chained one, walk in your chain! Drive away the little dog licking the puppy. Beware of the dog. Beware lest you fall."* With these and

<column-break/>

other quibbles, the mockers lead the blind Samson around; they surround him in crowds, now digging into his sides, now softening his head with a club. At the rich and varied dinner, they call him a "dinner-seeker" and a parasite; they lead him around and perform dances all about him. As he goes around without his usual strength, they reproach the "Light-Shunner" <note>original: "Photolygio"</note> with the same words a Guest once said to the blind Oedipus in Sophocles: (Oedipus at Colonus v. 72.) <margin>The Vain Victory Song of the Philistines.</margin>

> <term>And what help can come from a man who does not see?</term> <note>Greek: καὶ τίς πρὸς ἀνδρὸς μὴ βλέποντος ἄρκεσις;</note>

That he was mocked with various illusions of this kind, which we cannot even imagine, <term>is clear even to a blind man, and these things are known to the blind and the deaf.</term> <note>Greek: δῆλόν ἐστι καὶ τυφλῷ, καὶ τυφλοῖς κωφοῖς τε γνώριμα ταῦτα.</note> But Samson, though blind in his eyes, was not blind in his mind; his spirit was not yet struck down or dejected. And just as that Oedipus at Colonus responds nobly to the Messenger laughing at him, although he was in grief and squalor:

> <term>Whatever I say, I shall speak as one who sees all.</term> <note>Greek: ὃς ἂν λέγ᾽ ὀρθῶ, πάνθ᾽ ὁρῶντα λέξομεν.</note> <margin>v. 73.</margin>

But our Palestinian Oedipus <note>Samson</note>, attempting greater things, says to the Philistine mockers: *"You mock according to your lust and your judgment, but I am not mocked. You stir up laughter and raise guffaws to cause me pain. By acting the buffoon, you will provide sport and pleasure to the Princes, and you seek nothing from this comedy but a tragedy. The comic face of the jesters will soon have its epitaph and tragic catastrophe. The things I am about to do will not be blind, but seeing. You play the buffoon for the Princes; I shall go to the columns for you."* Just as Hercules once recalled his labors to mind when he was tortured by a disease fatal to him, seeking that former integrity of limbs with which he had overthrown the Nemean Lion. Thus he laments in Sophocles, looking at his torn and afflicted limbs: <margin>Trachiniae v. 1096.</margin>

> <term>O hands, hands,</term>
> <term>O back and chest, O dear arms,</term>
> <term>you are those very ones who once</term>
> <term>by force subdued the Nemean dweller,</term>
> <term>the herdsman's scourge, that unapproachable</term>
> <term>and monstrous lion.</term> <note>Greek: ὤ χεῖρες, χεῖρες... βίᾳ κατειργάσασθε.</note>

Cicero translating these in the 1st Tusculan Disputation:

> ->O hands, formerly victors,<-
> ->O chest, O back, O muscles of the arms,<-
> ->Was it by your grip that once the Nemean Lion,<-
> ->Gnashing, heavily breathed out his final breath?<-

That Hercules of Timnah, Samson, can be introduced in a similar way, since in captivity he is tortured more in spirit than in body, seeing himself mocked by the Philistines. As if to say: *"Now indeed I am mocked by those whom my victorious hand put to flight more than once. Before, no one dared to attack me; nor did anyone from our people take spoils with such praise. Yet not yet, not yet am I utterly defeated; some spirit returns to my womb, returns to my limbs. Not all virtue has dried up."* But to use the words of Sophocles v. 1114:

> <term>But know this well, even if I am nothing,</term> <margin>v. 1114.</margin>
> <term>and even if I crawl as nothing, I shall yet</term>
> <term>overpower the one who did these things, if only she comes here,</term>
> <term>so that she may be taught to announce to all that</term>
> <term>both living and dying, I took vengeance on the wicked.</term> <note>Greek: ἀλλ᾽ εὖ γέ τοι τόδ᾽ ἴστε... θανὼν ἐτισάμην.</note>

Sudden sorrow followed these joys of the Philistines, for they were singing of victory before the triumph. Samson, hearing the insults, taunts, mocks, sarcasms, and reproaches of his blindness from his enemies; feeling the slaps, the shoves, and the spitting, with death set before him, says: *"I shall not die unavenged; my last labor will be to destroy the..."*

For having said these things, the blinded Hero <note>original: "exoculatus," literally "de-eyed"</note> embraced with both hands the middle columns on which the vast theater-like house rested. He leaned forward with might, and the house fell upon the Lords and upon all the people who were in it; and the dead whom he killed as he himself was dying were more than those he had caused to die while he himself lived (v. 30). *Quick to meet death, and strong with gathered virtue.*
As Lucan grants us *words concerning our hero, who with gathered virtue (that is, collected or compelled by necessity) fell, overwhelmed by the ruin of his enemies, displaying even once more in his final breath the immensity of his strength, by which he first was able to crush his own killers by the very means of their killing,* as Augustine elegantly says in Sermon 107 *On the Season*: "his passion became the intersection of his pursuers." By a memorable example, he killed many more dying than he had slain living; he buried many more by his own funeral than he had heard of being buried before his funeral. Nor was there any rage against the dead man's body—again by a wonderful example—despite the Philistines' cruelty still persisting. The body, as it was found among the dense ranks of the dead, was carried away by his friends, brothers, and his father's whole house in a public and honorable funeral, and was laid to rest between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of his father Manoah (v. 31). To wash and anoint and put on more elegant clothing was the custom of the Hebrews, Greeks, and Romans, who anointed themselves before dinner and after baths, and would drench their guests—whenever they received them with care—with balsam and other fragrant ointments. # From Ruth, III. v. 3.

<margin>Washings and ointments.</margin>
...to pour ointment over themselves, not only the wealthy, but even those of the lowest rank and the poor; indeed, they even infused the bathwaters themselves with fragrant ointments. To perform this task, there were even <term>aleiptai</term> <note>Greek: "anointers"</note>, or <term>perunctores</term> in Latin; these were servants who anointed their Master in the baths and were appointed to that specific duty, as Victorius testifies in *Various Readings* 1.37. There, he bears witness that an ancient stone in Rome depicts an anointer holding a <term>guttus</term> in his right hand (this was a vessel full of oil from which the servant poured drop by drop), with a <term>strigil</term> <note>A curved tool for scraping the skin</note> engraved not far from it. From this, the place in the bath was called the <term>unctarium</term> <note>anointing room</note> or the <term>unctuaria cella</term>. This can also be sufficiently proven by the authority of modern Eastern peoples. The Turkish nation is most devoted to baths, the use of which is very frequent throughout all of Turkey: for they anoint the entire face and body most diligently, concerning which see Belon, *Observations* 3.34. That the Persian nation excelled in this kind of luxury could be supported by many examples. For among them, there was especially great use of ointments, as may be seen from the
<margin>Esther 2:12</margin>
example of Esther and her companion virgins. From this it is clear that it was the ancient custom of Kings to shut virgins away in <term>Gynaecea</term> <note>women's quarters</note> so that, after they had been adorned and polished there, they might then be called to the wedding. For we read that the girls whom King Ahasuerus wished to have present for his pleasure were anointed for six whole months with <term>oil of myrrh</term>, and then for another six months with <term>other spices</term>. Now, the use of myrrh ointment was for smoothing out wrinkles in the skin and for cleaning away blemishes and dirt; but other <term>pigments</term> and <term>spices</term>, as the Vulgate reads, were employed for smoothing and softening the flesh. There were "pigment-makers" <note>perfumers</note> who elaborately prepared these ointments by their art. Naomi refers to this custom, which was also common among the Hebrews, when she commanded that Ruth wash and anoint herself. We also find an example of this custom in the history of Judith, who, before she was to go to Holofernes, is read to have first anointed her face after washing it:
<margin>Judith 10:3</margin>
*And she washed her face with water, and anointed herself with thick ointment, and set a tire [mitre] upon her head, and put on her garments of gladness.* When David was enjoying his midday rest and, waking from sleep, walked upon the roof of his palace, behold, he saw Bathsheba, the wife of his faithful servant Uriah, *naked and washing herself* in a nearby garden; he sent a messenger to her and *went in unto her*, as the title of Psalm 51 says. Concerning Susanna washing in the garden and sending her maids to bring <term>oil</term> and <term>cleansing soaps</term> <note>original: smigmata</note>, read Daniel 13:7, where that memorable crime of the impure Elders attempted against the woman's modesty—as well as their own falsehood and the wicked impurity of their souls—is described and uncovered. In *Exodus* 2:5, we read of the descent of Pharaoh's daughter, named <term>Thermuthis</term> as they call her, who had gone forth with her attending companions to wash herself in the Nile. Some maintain that this was an expiatory washing, used for the sake of <term>hagneia</term> <note>Greek: "purity/sanctification"</note> in the sacred rites of the Gentiles. They worshipped the water of the Nile, according to Philo in *On the Life of Moses* page 465; hence he not unlearnedly con-

<column-break/>

-jectures on page 420 that the beginning of the plagues was made there, with the waters turned into blood for seven days. <term>For since</term>, he says, <term>the Egyptians have honored water exceedingly, he [God] first deemed it worthy to be called to the punishment.</term> He made the
<margin>Washings and ointments.</margin>
Nile red and turned its water into blood, so that those who saw it might themselves be "turned" <note>A wordplay on conversion</note>. In the treasures of King Hezekiah, 2 Kings 20, <term>spices</term> and <term>ointments</term> are recounted. Ecclesiastes 7:2 refers to the same: *A good name is better*, <term>than good ointment</term> <note>original Hebrew: mi-shemen tov</note>, as if to say that a reputation after death is more pleasing than the scent of the most fragrant ointment. By this very phrase, the Author also referred to the ritual of embalming corpses under the emblem of <term>mnemosynos</term> <note>Greek: "remembrance"</note>: *The corpses of the Gentiles were buried with laurel.* I believe Ecclesiasticus 24 says in the same sense: *I gave a sweet smell like myrrh*; for myrrh is numbered by Theophrastus among the "fragrant tears" <note>resins</note> which they use for ointments. Indeed, ointments were prepared not only for delight, but also for health: such as those listed by Pomponius: *Commagena*, *glaucina*, *irrina*, *rose*, *myrrh*, *colum*, and *pure nard*. (Law 21, *On Gold and Silver*). This is also related by Domenico Vigna of Pisa in his *Observations* (which are almost ridiculous) on Theophrastus's *On Plants*, where he also compared it with <term>Benjui</term> <note>Benzoin</note>, which is a resin from Java. For every fragrant resin is called <term>naka</term> <note>Hebrew/Arabic root for spices/resins</note> by the Arabs; concerning which Garcia de Orta in Book 1, Chapter 5, erred in the etymology of the name. Just as formerly among the kinds of myrrh, the *troglodytic* was most approved, <term>so called from the region of its birth</term> according to Dioscorides; Pliny reports in Book 12, Chapter 15, that the Sabaeans sought it from the Troglodytes. Dioscorides praises its <term>cleansing</term>, <term>drying</term>, and <term>astringent</term> powers in the cited place. One might call to this sense those words of the harlot in Solomon's Proverbs 7:17: *I have sprinkled my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon.* Salazar (page 517) understands these words to refer to the ointments themselves; for they were sometimes accustomed to stuff the coverings of beds with gathered flowers and leaves, and sometimes to soak them with ointments. He proved the same from those words of Canticles [Song of Solomon] 1:16: *Our bed is flowery.* Pliny mentions a most fragrant ointment made from cinnamon
<margin>Book 15, Ch. 7.</margin>
with which *the harlot perhaps had soaked her bed.* With no less luxury, even garments were ablaze with the scent of ointments; concerning this "woman's world" <note>the collection of a woman's finery</note>, I would like to add a passage from Psalm 45:8, where it says of the Virgins in the Vulgate translation: *Myrrh and stacte and cassia perfume thy garments, from the ivory houses* (here some understand the women's quarters, others ointment boxes), *whereby the daughters of kings have made thee glad in thy honor.* For they think the comparison is drawn from the Virgins shut in the <term>Gynaeceum</term>, so that they might be made cleaner with ointments and spices. Moreover, it is clear from many writers that the "woman's world" <note>Latin: mundus muliebris</note> includes mirrors, jars, and ointments. Julius Paulus in *Received Opinions* Book 3, Title 6: *Under the legacy of 'woman's world' fall those things by which a woman is made cleaner and more elegant, such as a mirror, a bronze vessel, small jars, also boxes (so the old books have it), ointments and the vessels in which they are kept; likewise the bathing chair and other things of that sort.*

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Washings and ointments.</margin>
In Psalm 104:15 <note>original: "Ps. 103. 16." following the Vulgate numbering</note>, wine is credited with gladdening the face with oil, that is, just as oil or even more than oil, because it serves to brighten the face beyond its other uses. From this common human custom, infinite figures of speech have been born in all writers; no one will understand these unless they thoroughly know the very nature, character, and, as it were, the spirit of things and rituals. For it is often arranged so that the meaning of words depends on the hidden nature of things, which serve as ladders to climb to the summit of more solid linguistic knowledge. Hence, "to make the face shine" is transferred from human custom to God to judge His mercy and kindness, as seen in other passages of the authors.

It is well known to those who handle theological matters that those who were mutilated, diminished, or "fined" in body (to use the word of Tacitus) were not admitted to the priesthood in the Old Testament. For the God of Israel ordained, *Leviticus chapter 21, verse 17 and following*, that those priests who suffered from some bodily defect—namely the maimed, the hunchbacked, the distorted, the bow-legged, the cross-eyed, the bleary-eyed, or otherwise deformed—should abstain from the sacrifices. An example concerning Hyrcanus is read in Drusius, *see Observation 2.* The Papal Canons decree the same, as Bisciola reviews in *book 4 of Subsicivae Horae, chapter 21, volume 1.* This same caution was observed by the Pagans, as Seneca the Declaimer advises in his 4th book, where he says of Metellus: *A priest must be whole. Metellus the Pontifex, when the temple of Vesta was burning, lost his eyes while rescuing the Palladium; the priesthood was denied to him.* And shortly after: *A priest of an incomplete body is to be avoided as a thing of bad omen. This is noted in the sacrificial victims; how much more so in a priest.* They also took care to use clothing free from every stain, so that the Priest might perform the sacrifice in a pure garment, as Virgil sang. Servius is a witness in his *Fragments* that in sacred rites *a garment is called "pure" which is neither associated with death nor has a stain from a dead man.* Nor was it permitted to touch the sacrifice unless one was clean, as that character in Virgil’s *Aeneid*, book 2, testifies of himself:

> You, father, take the sacred objects and ancestral gods in your hand;
> For me, having come from such great war and recent slaughter,
> It is a sin to touch them, until I have washed myself
> In a living stream.

Thus Telemachus, about to supplicate Pallas, washed his hands with sea water, lest he approach impurely or behave more unworthily than the law of sacred rites demanded. And indeed, this washing or purification of the body, most used before sacrifices, was twofold: one pertained to the *hands*, the other to the *whole body.* The former is properly called <term>chernips</term> <note>original Greek: χέρνιψ; water for washing hands at a sacrifice</note>, as Lily Gyraldus and Rhodiginus noted from Homer and Athenaeus; the latter is called <term>perirrhansis</term> <note>original Greek: περίῤῥανσις; a ritual sprinkling or lustration</note>. For they believed that any guilt was removed from them by that symbolic purification of the body—an external rite by which even Pilate, a most deceptive man, tried to remove the malice of his actions after committing such a detestable crime: for *having taken water, he washed his hands before the people, saying: I am innocent of the blood of this just man.* By this gesture, he signified the publication of the most unjustly delivered condemnation of the Savior through the washing water. Yet that vain boaster of simulated virtue was not therefore
<margin>Matthew 27, v. 24.</margin>

<column-break/>

innocent because he washed his hands; for he ought to have learned from his own Poet, he who rejected Christ the Teacher of truth:
<margin>Washings and ointments.</margin>

<margin>Ovid, book 2 of the Fasti, v. 45.</margin>
> Ah, too easy are you, who think that the grim crimes of slaughter
> Can be taken away by river water.

Concerning this rite, Anticlides writes in book 74 of *Returns*: *It was the custom of the ancients, which is still preserved, that those who had committed the slaughter of men or other animals should wash their hands in perennial water for the purification of the common guilt.* These same things are found in the Scholiast of Sophocles on *Ajax the Whip-bearer*: <note>original Greek: "It was a custom for the ancients, when they committed either a murder of men or other slaughters, to wash their hands with water for the cleansing of the pollution."</note> In Seneca’s *Mad Hercules*, Amphitryon says to Hercules:
<margin>Act 4, scene 1</margin>
> Son, first expiate your hands
> Dripping with bloody slaughter and the enemy's gore.

The same is alluded to in the final scene of the same Tragedy: *What Tanais, or what Nile can wash the right hand clean?* Hippocrates (if he is the author) in the book *On the Sacred Disease* says: *We designate the boundaries of the temples for the Gods, so that no one who is not pure may cross over, and as we enter we are sprinkled, not as if we are being defiled, but so that if we have any prior crime, we may be purified.* For this use, there were <term>perirrhantēria</term> <note>sprinkling bowls</note> and <term>loutra</term> <note>baths</note> in the temples; from these, those entering the temple sprinkled themselves, or were sprinkled by the priests, so that they might approach the Gods pure and chaste. I leave these ancient things and allow them to be trusted, or I shall be content with examples from our own memory.

For the same reason, the Turks today have fountains and cisterns at the vestibules and entrances of their temples, from which, before entering for sacred rites and public prayers, they are accustomed to cleanse their hands, feet, face, and all the organs of the senses; indicating by this that sacred rites must be performed with a pure mind, and that the mind must be cleansed of every stain by him who wishes to approach GOD, just as they themselves enter with a pure body; *and let it be observed that while chaste bodies are employed, it is much more to be observed in the mind*, as Cicero speaks in book 2 of *On the Laws*. In the deserts, however, if a supply of water is not given, those traveling abroad are permitted, according to the concession of the Muhammadan law, to use dust or sand with which to rub and cleanse themselves, as Leonhard Rauwolff records in *book 3 of his Travels, chapter 6, page 365.* This is also indicated by the Author of the *Refutation of the Ishmaelites*, which stands in the *Saracenica* that came forth from the Palatine Library by the labor of Sylburgius, page 29: <note>original Greek: "He commands those coming to prayer to purify themselves: with water, if it is present; but if it is absent, with earth."</note> Add witnesses greater than any exception, since they are eyewitnesses. Nicolaus Clenardus, in a letter given at Fez in the year 1541 to J. Latomus, which stands in book 1 of his *Letters*, page 62, reports thus: *Fez is divided into two parts. The old city is huge and populous. They say there are nearly 400 temples there and as many baths. For the Mahometans wash frequently, nor can they perform the hourly prayers without lustration, even if they have only broken wind.* Beware lest you laugh at their ceremonies, which are not ours. George Douza, in the description of his journey to Constantinople, page 73, to his Father: *They attribute very much to the washing of the body, thinking that frequent—*
<meta>The text cuts off mid-word "frequent-" (frequenti) at the end of the page.</meta>

# From Ruth III. v. 3.

<margin>
