</margin>
...that the filth of the soul is washed away by frequent bathing. Among them <note>The author refers here to Islamic customs</note> it is considered a monstrous crime to enter a temple with unwashed feet or genitals. You will also never see a Turk withdrawing for the requirements of nature without immediately washing his private parts afterward. Dionysius the Carthusian, in his *Refutation of the Alcoran* (Book 2, art. 20, p. 154), believes that Muhammad treacherously adopted this from the faithless Jews; just as that rite of taking off one's shoes before entering a temple flowed to them from the Jews. For they never enter their Mosques unless their shoes are first removed, or, to speak with the Muse of Juvenal in <margin>Satire 6.</margin> *Satire 6*, "with bare feet." In this regard, the Russians <note>original: "Rutheni," referring here to Eastern Orthodox Christians</note>, imitating the Greeks, also consecrate water with certain ceremonies; once this is performed, men and women alike are accustomed to plunge into the river from all sides without any sign of shame, and to moisten their idols with that water so that it may be well with the Divinities, while simultaneously testifying to the brightness and purity of their own souls. This madness of theirs was recorded in the *Historical Narrative of the Muscovite Journey*, which was—alas—fatal for the Most High Duke of Holstein, John. This was also testified to from <term>autopsy</term> <note>eyewitness observation</note> on page 20 of the *Russian Way-Gate* (which the Noble Melchior Goldast of Haiminsfeld saw to be published) by the most noble Jacob von Ulfeld, a man not only of high birth but of literate virtue among the Danes, of whom he has many like himself. No one is such a stranger to Hebrew Antiquities as to be unaware that in the most magnificent temple of Solomon there was a "brazen sea" or "molten sea"—namely, a most capacious vessel in which the Priests might wash. Its use was so that the Priests entering the temple might wash their hands and feet when about to ascend to the altar. The **DEVIL, THE APE OF GOD** <note>A common theological concept suggesting Satan mimics divine rites to lead people into idolatry</note> imitated this; for Lipomanus contends that these ceremonies were derived from the Law to the gentiles, which the industrious writer Villalpandus proved in <margin>Vol. 2, Explanation of Ezekiel, part 2, ch. 38.</margin> his work. The Law of God barred polluted Priests from sacred rites and the eating of sacred things until they were cleansed, nor did it admit those who were ceremonially unclean to handle or eat sacred things (*Leviticus ch. 21 & ch. 22*). The same was persuaded among the Heathens: that Sacrifices offered by the impure are not pleasing to the Gods. It is a most common theme among the authors of the Latin and Greek nations that they worshipped their Gods with external purity even in the victims. <margin>Book 2, On Abstinence.</margin> "The Divinity looks more to the character of those sacrificing than to the multitude of things sacrificed," says Porphyry. Furthermore, the gentiles were accustomed to hold feasts after the sacrifices were completed, using the remains of the sacrifice in honor of their Gods, as can be gathered from *Deut. 32:38, Judges 9:27, Baruch 6:31, 28, and 1 Cor. 10:21*; and from Aristotle's *Rhetoric* Book 3. As is clear from histories, the sacrifices were sometimes made quite liberally and with such an abundance of victims that all their meat could not be consumed at once in the sacred feasts. Then, therefore, whatever remained was sold in the meat market, and the money collected from this returned to the priests. Some carried a portion of the meat of the victims home, so that their household members, who could not be present at the sacred feast, might thus become participants in it. I add that Christians in the time of the Apostles at Corinth, having been invited, approached those feasts prepared from things sacrificed to idols; Paul rebukes them for this in *1 Cor. 10*, and exhorts those who had just now converted to the true God to stay away from the company of their feasting friends who had invited them, lest they be in the communion of Devils (v. 22). <margin>Washings & ointments.</margin> For that reason, it is clear from *Minucius* that the people of the Christian nation, faithfully taught afterward in both religion and piety, abhorred these profane foods; Minucius, reproaching the Christians for this religious scrupulousness, says: *You shrink from pre-tasted foods and cups already sipped.* Even now, both the Arabs and the Turks have their own votive victims called **Corban** <note>Sacrificial offerings in Islam</note>: the skin, head, feet, and a fourth part of the meat are given to the priest, another part is given to the poor, a third to the neighbors, and the remaining part the Sacrificers and their companions prepare for eating. These ceremonies of the Turks are also reported as <term>handed down from the fathers</term> by Barth. Georgievitz <margin>Book 2, ch. 1, R. T.</margin> and Benjamin of Tudela in his *Travels*. These are the ruins left from the decline of that more ancient custom of the Jews; for I have no doubt that this custom observed by the gentiles flowed from the sacrifices of the Jews, where by God's ordinance a portion was given to those who had offered them, so that eating before the Lord they might be gladdened together. In *1 Samuel ch. 1*, Elkanah, returning from the sacrifice, provides more lavish portions to his wives, Hannah, Peninnah, and others. Where the translation "a sad piece" <note>original: "ein Stück traurig"</note> is poorly rendered. The same was also solemn among the nations. No one will deny that they affected this ordinance of God in a spirit of rivalry, if they are familiar with examples of <term>perverse imitation</term>; I see that Bonfrerius has dealt with this in his work on the *Pentateuch*, and Wolfgang Franz in *On Sacrifices*. I would all the more wish there were someone who, in a specific book, would bring some Harmony into view here. It would be a wide field for industry and the exercise of wit. I hear there exists a book printed in Venice with this title, **THE DEVIL, THE APE OF GOD**, which, if it were available, many things would be at hand without effort, and we could add many other things, weaving them in like an embroiderer.

And it should be observed that while chaste bodies are required, it is much more necessary to preserve chastity in minds, as Cicero speaks in Book 2 of *On the Laws*. Indeed, in the deserts, if a supply of water is not given, those traveling abroad are permitted, according to the concession of Muhammadan law, to use dust or sand with which to rub and cleanse themselves, as Leonhard Rauwolff reports in *Travels*, Book 3, ch. 6. This is also indicated by the Author of the *Refutation of the Ishmaelites* <note>original: "τῆς Ισμαηλιτῶν"</note>, which stands in the Saracenic works that came forth from the Palatine Library through the labor of Sylburgius: <note>original Greek: "He commands those coming to prayer to purify themselves; with water, if it is present; but if it is absent, with earth."</note> Add to this witnesses greater than any exception, since they were eyewitnesses. Nicolaus Clenardus, in a letter from Fez dated 1541 to J. Latomus, reports: "Fez is divided into two parts. The old city is huge and populous. They say there are nearly 400 temples there and as many baths. For the Mahometans wash frequently, nor can they perform the hourly prayers without lustration, even if they have only broken wind." Beware of laughing at their ceremonies, which are not ours. Georgius Dousa, in the description of his journey to Constantinople, writes to his father: "They attribute very much to the washing of the body, thinking..."

# From Ruth III. v. 3. 343

<margin>Washings and ointments.</margin> It is believed that the filth of the soul is washed away by frequent bathing. Among them <note>The author refers here to "the Orientals," specifically Muslims and Jews in this context.</note> it is considered a monstrous crime to enter a temple with unwashed feet or private parts. You will never see a Turk retiring for the requirements of nature without immediately washing his private parts afterward. Dionysius the Carthusian, in his *Refutation of the Alcoran* (Book 2, art. 20, p. 154), believes that Muhammad treacherously adopted this from the faithless Jews; just as the rite of removing shoes before entering a temple flowed from the Jews to them. For they never enter their Mosques unless they have first taken off their shoes, or, to speak with the *Muse* of Juvenal in <margin>Satire 6.</margin> *Satire 6*, "with naked foot." In this regard, the Russians, imitating the Greeks, also consecrate water with certain ceremonies; once this is performed, men and women alike, without any sign of shame, are accustomed to plunge themselves into the river and moisten their idols with that water, so that it may be well with the Divinities, while simultaneously testifying to the brightness and purity of their own souls. This madness of theirs was recorded in the *Historical Narrative of the Muscovite Journey*, which was—alas—fatal for the Most Serene John, Duke of Holstein. This was also testified to from <unclear>personal observation</unclear> on page 20 of the *Russian Travelogue* by the most noble Jacob von Ulfeldt (which the noble Melchior Goldast von Haiminsfeldt saw to be published), a man not only of high birth but of literary virtue among the Danes, in which he has many peers.

No one is so much a stranger to Hebrew Antiquities as to be unaware that in the most magnificent temple of Solomon there was a "brazen sea" or "molten sea"—a most capacious vessel in which the Priests might wash. Its use was for the Priests entering the temple to wash their hands and feet when they were about to ascend to the altar. The Devil, the "Ape of God," <note>A common early modern trope: *Simia Dei*, the idea that Satan mimics divine rituals to lead people into idolatry.</note> imitated this; for Lipomanus contends that those ceremonies were derived from the Law to the Gentiles, which the industrious writer Villalpandus <margin>Vol. 2. Explanation of Ezekiel, part 2, ch. 38.</margin> proved. The Law of God barred polluted Priests from sacred rites and the eating of sacred things until they were cleansed, nor did it admit those who were ceremonially unclean to handle or eat sacred things (*Leviticus ch. 21 and ch. 22*). The same was persuaded among the Heathens: that sacrifices offered by the impure were not pleasing to the Gods. It is very common among the authors of the Latin and Greek nations that they worshipped their Gods with external purity even in the victims. "The Divinity looks more to the character of those sacrificing than to the quantity of things sacrificed," says Porphyry <margin>Book 2 on Abstinence.</margin>. Furthermore, the Gentiles were accustomed, after the sacrifices were completed, to hold feasts from the remains of the sacrifice in honor of their Gods, as can be gathered from *Deuteronomy 32:38, Judges 9:27, Baruch 6:27-28, and 1 Corinthians 10:21*; and from Aristotle's *Rhetoric* Book 3. As is clear from histories, sacrifices were sometimes made quite liberally and with such an abundance of victims that all their meat could not be consumed at once in the sacred banquets. Then, whatever remained was sold in the meat market, and the money collected from this returned to the priests. They would carry food away so that their household members, who could not be present at the sacred banquet, might thus participate in it. I add that the Christians in the time of the Apostles at Corinth were invited to and attended those feasts prepared from things sacrificed to idols; Paul rebukes them for this in *1 Corinthians 10*, and he discourages those who had just now been converted to the true God from the fellowship of feasting friends by whom they had been invited, <column-break/> lest they be in the communion of Devils <margin>v. 22.</margin> (*verse 22*). For that reason, it is evident from Minucius that the people of the Christian nation, having been faithfully taught afterward in both religion and <margin>Washings and ointments.</margin> piety, abhorred these profane foods; reproaching the Christians for this religious scruple, he says: "You shrink from the foods set aside and the choice drinks." Even now, both the Arabs and the Turks have their own votive victims, which are called *Corban* <note>original: "Corban" (sacrifice/offering)</note>: the skin, head, feet, and a fourth part of the meat are given to the priest, another is given to the poor, a third to the neighbors, and the sacrificers and their companions prepare the rest for themselves to eat. These ceremonies of the Turks are also reported as *handed down from the fathers* <note>original: "πατροπαράδοτοι"</note> by Bartholomaeus Georgievitz and Benjamin of Tudela in his *Itinerary*. These are ruins from the decline of that older custom of the Jews; for I have no doubt that this custom observed by the Gentiles flowed from the sacrifices of the Jews, where by God's ordinance a portion was given to those who had offered them, so that eating before the Lord they might be cheered together. Thus, in *1 Samuel ch. 1*, Elkanah, returning from the sacrifice, provides *choice* portions to his wives, Hannah, Peninnah, and others. Where it is poorly translated <note>original: "in vers. ein Stück"</note> as "a piece" or "sadly." The same was also solemn among the nations. No one will deny that they affected this ordinance of God in emulation, to whom examples of *perverse imitation* <note>original: "κακοζηλίας"</note> are known; I see that Bonfrerius dealt with this in his work on the *Pentateuch*, and Wolfgang Franz in his work *On Sacrificies*. I would all the more wish there were someone who, in a specific book, would bring together some harmony of rites here. It would be a wide field for industry and the exercise of wit. I hear there exists a book printed in Venice with this title, *THE DEVIL THE APE OF GOD*, which, if it were available, many things would be present without effort, and we could add many other things and weave them in like an embroiderer.

<margin>Dagon, Deity of the Philistines.</margin> Among those whom the Phoenicians established as Gods, the principal Deity of the Philistines was *Dagon*. We read in the *Preparation for the Gospel* by Eusebius (Book 1) that Dagon was one of the four sons of Heaven according to Sanchuniathon, where his interpreter Philo, who usually renders Phoenician names with Greek names, has it thus on *page 23*: "Dagon, who is Siton" <note>Siton (Σίτων) relates to the Greek word for grain/corn.</note>. To the Hebrews, <term>Dagon (דגן)</term> is *grain* (*Genesis 27:28, Deuteronomy 7:13, Psalm 78:24*); whence he thinks the name came to him, as if he were *Siton, the overseer of grain*, the God of grain, a *grain-producing Deity*, because he presides over the crops and makes the earth fruitful and produces various kinds of fruits; just as Ceres was believed to be the Goddess of crops, to whom they attribute a reaping sickle, which Apollonius <margin>4. Argonautica.</margin> calls a <unclear>straw-cutting</unclear> <unclear>sickle</unclear>.

-> She who first yoked the plowing neck of oxen, <-
-> and sent forth a lovely, prosperous life for mortals. <-

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

Hence the Psyche of Apuleius entreats and prays to the fruitful Ceres by the joyful ceremonies of the harvests, by the silent rites of the baskets, and by the furrows of the Sicilian soil. <margin>6. The Golden Ass.</margin> and other matters pertaining to the Deity of Ceres. If we consider the nature of the god Dagon more closely, a better derivation is from the Hebrew word *dag* [דג], meaning *fish*, which is named from *dagah* [דגה], signifying its multiplication and fecundity; thus it could have been more aptly rendered in Greek as <term>peri ichthyon</term> <note>original: "περὶ ἰχθύων" — concerning fish</note>, a fishy or fish-like God, who presided over the sea, like the <term>Neptune</term> of the Latins. This was the marine God to whom the people of Corcyra used to pray by sacrificing a bull, after which they would catch an incredible number of fish, as recorded by Pausanias <margin>in Phocicis.</margin> To him also is attributed by Manilius that celestial sign which bears the name of *the Fishes* [Pisces], <italic>in Book 2, where he reviews the celestial signs and the Gods to whom they were assigned.</italic>

<italic>And Neptune recognizes his own fishes in the ocean.</italic>
Hence Athanasius Kircher <italic>Vol. 1. Oedipus Aegyptiacus, synth. 4. c. 16. §. 1.</italic> prefers the opinion of Rabbi David Kimchi over others, who wrote concerning this Dagon: <italic>that from the navel downward he had the form of a fish, and from his navel upward the form of a man.</italic> Dagon was therefore like Neptune, to whom the Philistines performed divine rites so that he might favor them, bless their fishing, grant favorable voyages to their ships, and clear the sea of pirates. <margin>p. 241.</margin> Jerome, in his Questions, says: <italic>Dagon in Hebrew is the same as "dag," which means "fish of sorrow." He suggests that by dropping the letter Aleph [א], it is derived from "dag" and "on" [און], meaning mourning, from "anu" [אנו], to wail or be sad.</italic> Cornelius à Lapide, on 1 Samuel 5. Others everywhere derive Dagon from *Daga* [דגה], that is, *fish*, because this idol had the form of a fish. For since the Philistines were inhabitants of the seacoast, they devoted themselves to fishing, and therefore they fashioned and worshipped Dagon as the <italic>protector of fish and fishing.</italic> Furthermore, this idol was indeed in the likeness of a fish, but mixed with a human. Regarding its shape, they say it had the figure of a half-man and half-fish, from the navel to the lowest parts in the likeness of a fish; but in the upper part, in human likeness; just as Triton, the son of Neptune, was imagined,

<margin>Virgil, Aeneid 10.</margin>
> Whose shaggy front, as he swims, presents a man
> As far as the waist, but his belly ends in a sea-monster.

And in such a likeness are imagined the sea <term>Nymphs</term>, who are called <term>Nereids</term>, daughters of Nereus, the sea God, whom Orpheus calls the <term>renowned spirit</term> <note>original: "μεγαλώνυμον δαίμονα"</note>, and the <term>Naiads</term>, water Goddesses, with the head and face of a human, the rest a fish; whence the Poet says:

<margin>Horace, Art of Poetry, v. 4.</margin>
> <italic>A woman, beautiful above, ends in a fish.</italic>

Nor did Derceto differ in form, who was accustomed to be worshipped in a most noble temple among the people of Ascalon in Palestine; a woman in face, a fish in the remaining part, according to Diodorus Siculus, Book 3, ch. 2. Where, treating of her consecrated statue in Ascalon, he writes: <term>she has the face of a woman, but the rest of the entire body is that of a fish</term> <note>original: "τὸ μὲν πρόσωπον ἔχει γυναικός, τὸ δὲ ἄλλο σῶμα πᾶν ἰχθύος"</note>. So also Lucian, describing the temple, rites, and image of the Syrian Goddess <italic>Vol. 3. p. 686. seqq.</italic>, teaches those things about the image of Derceto which he saw with his own eyes: namely, that as far as the navel it was human, but from the thighs to the bottom it was in the form of a fish. <term>Of Derceto</term> (he says on p. 696) <term>I beheld the form in Phoenicia, a strange sight. Half indeed is a woman, but the part from the thighs to the tips of the feet extends as a fish's tail</term> <note>original: "Δερκετοῦς... εἶδος ἐν φοινίκῃ ἐθηησάμην..."</note>. Wherefore Ovid in Metamorphoses Book 4:

> Dercetis, whom the Palestinians believe inhabited
> The pools in a changed form, scales covering her limbs.

For her temple had been near Ascalon, next to

<column-break/>

a pool full of fish, because she was believed to have been turned into a fish; hence Pliny (v. 23) called her the "prodigious Atergatis," and the Syrians thereafter abstained from fish, worshipping them as Gods, which Diodorus holds in the cited place, and confirms by the testimony of Xenophon in Book 1 of the *Expedition of Cyrus*, describing the river Chalus, in which were seen fish of remarkable size, which the inhabitants did not allow to be harmed, regarding them as Gods. <margin>Dagon, Deity of the Philistines.</margin> Let us cite the words of Xenophon: <term>The river Chalus, being a plethron in width, full of large and tame fish, which the Syrians considered gods, and would not allow to be harmed.</term> <note>original: "Χάλον ποταμὸν... οὓς οἱ Σύροι θεοὺς ἐνόμιζον..."</note> So also Lucian: <term>They consider fish a sacred thing, and never touch fish.</term> <note>original: "ἰχθύας, χρῆμα ἱερὸν νομίζουσι..."</note> <margin>p. 697.</margin> Cicero in *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book 3: <italic>The Syrians venerate fish.</italic> Ovid in the *Metamorphoses* concerning Leucothoe and Palaemon, and in the *Fasti*, Book 2, says:

This Deity of the Syrians is the same as Venus; and is also believed to be the same as Dagon, notwithstanding that Dagon is called a God, not a Goddess, for <term>collectively</term> <note>original: "συλχηπτικῶς"</note> a masculine termination does not exclude the feminine, just as Venus herself is called a <italic>God</italic> [Deus] by Virgil. <margin>Aeneid 2.</margin> <italic>I descend, and with the God as my guide, I make my way through weapons and enemies.</italic>
That Dagon was fashioned in human form in his upper part is clear from the fact that they found Dagon, after his mechanisms were weakened, lying <italic>upon his face, with his head and both palms of his hands cut off, 1 Samuel 5:4</italic>, leaving only the body or trunk of the idol. In the lower part of the body, he undoubtedly had the form of a fish, hence no mention is made of feet, but only of the head and two hands, which, torn from the rest of the body, were found on the <italic>threshold</italic>; whence Rabbi Kimchi also notes that only the form of a fish was left in him. What the Septuagint [LXX] adds regarding both soles of the feet being taken away is added from outside the original source. For these are their words: <term>The head of Dagon and both the soles of his feet were removed upon the front of the thresholds, and both the wrists of his hands had fallen upon the porch.</term> <note>original: "Ἡ κεφαλὴ Δαγὼν καὶ ἀμφότερα τὰ ἴχνη τῶν ποδῶν αὐτοῦ..."</note> There is nothing in the Hebrew text about feet, for there it says: <term>the head of Dagon and the two palms of his hands were cut off</term> <note>original: "ראש דגון ושתי כפות ידיו כרותות"</note>. That house, which the strong hand of Samson overthrew, they maintain was the <italic>shrine of Dagon</italic>, which was so large that it held three thousand spectators of both sexes (v. 27). What then did the Hebrews do? They cried out as if to expostulate with God: "Why has the Lord struck us today before the Philistines?" Why did He not help His own? From the infamous and shameful punishment in the more hidden and obscene part of the body, with which the men of Ashdod were afflicted, they entered into counsel and made for themselves (as the Latin Bibles have in verse 9) "leathern seats" or cushions made of leathern material stuffed with feathers, so that they might sit more comfortably without pain; and afterwards <margin>* ch. 6 v. 2, 7.</margin> being warned by diviners and priests, they sent back the Ark on a new cart, and dedicated golden tumors <note>term: anus/emerods - likely hemorrhoids or swellings</note> and golden mice as a vow to the God of Israel. They were struck in their hinder parts, v. 6, so that their intestines rotted and protruded; therefore they paid five golden tumors (חמשה עפלי זהב) <margin>Author on the miracles of Holy Scripture, book 2, ch. 7</margin> for the expiation of sin. The disease of the buttocks was sent extraordinarily by God with horrendous torments, so much so that the cry of each city went up to heaven, v. 12. A wonderful and new disease, and full of novelties, it brings to our memory the companions of Agamemnon, once seeking Troy, who because of a disease infesting the buttocks were forced to stop and care for the skin of their buttocks; whence the city of Ionia, called *Pygelia*, preserved the memory of this matter, from *pyge* <note>original: πυγῶν</note>, meaning buttocks or loins, as Eustathius and Suidas record in the Iliad, p. 310. They imagine something similar regarding Venus, whose most ancient temple among the Ascalonites Herodotus records in book 1, who had afflicted the Scythians because of a robbery. Let us transcribe the words in full: "But those returning back, when they were in the Syrian city of Ascalon, after the majority of the Scythians had passed by without doing harm, a few of them being left behind plundered the temple of Celestial Aphrodite. For the temple in Cyprus originated from here, as the Cyprians themselves say." <note>original Greek: οἱ δὲ ἀναχωρέοντες ὀπίσω... κ.τ.λ.</note> In Scythia, where those retreating were in the Palestinian city of Ascalon, and a good part of the Scythians inflicted no injury, a few remaining plundered the shrine of Venus Urania, which was, among others (as far as I indeed know), the oldest. Since the house of the same Goddess which is in Cyprus came from this one, which even the Cyprians themselves report. Some interpret "mariscas" <note>term: mariscas - fig-like swellings or hemorrhoids</note> as shameful swellings in that more secret part. In Hebrew it is עפלים (Ophalim), which the Septuagint explains as "ulcers in the seats" <note>original: ἕλκη ἐν ταῖς ἔδραις</note>, Deuteronomy 28:27. The Chaldean has for it טחורים (Techorim), which if you look to the nature of the root, you would translate as "constrictions," for טחור means to constrict or contract. This constriction was to many a "destruction of death" <note>original: מהומת-מות</note>, a vexation of death, v. 11. Septuagint: "confusion of death" <note>original: σύγχυσις θανάτου</note>. Vulgate: "dread of death." Where: *a day of turmoil* <note>original: ein Tag des Getümmels</note>; "a day of disturbance" <note>original: ἡμέρα ταραχῆς</note>; "a day of slaughter." Vatablus: "a day of contrition." # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Dagon, the Deity of the Philistines.</margin>
Hence the Psyche of Apuleius prays to and entreats the fruitful <term>Ceres</term> <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture</note> by the joyful ceremonies of the harvests, by the silent secrets of the baskets, by the furrows of the Sicilian soil (*The Golden Ass*, Book 6), and other things pertaining to the Divinity of Ceres. If we consider the Divinity of Dagon more closely, a better derivation is from **דג** <note>Hebrew: *dag*</note>, *fish*, which is named from **דגה** <note>Hebrew: *dagah*</note>, due to its multiplication and fecundity; and from this, he could have been more aptly rendered as *perichthun* <note>Greek: "around the fish"</note>, a fishy or fish-like God who presided over the sea, like the <term>Neptune</term> of the Latins. This was the marine God to whom the <term>Cycyraeans</term> <note>Likely referring to the people of Corcyra/Corfu</note> used to pray by sacrificing a bull, after which they would catch an incredible number of fish, as recorded by <term>Pausanias</term> in his *Description of Phocis*. To him also is attributed that celestial sign which bears the name of *Pisces* by <term>Manilius</term> in Book 2, where he reviews the celestial signs and the Gods to whom they were assigned.

Neptune recognizes his own fish in the ocean. Hence <term>Athanasius Kircher</term> <note>A famous 17th-century Jesuit scholar and polymath</note> in Volume 1 of *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, syntax 4, chapter 16, section 1, prefers the opinion of Rabbi David Kimchi over others, who wrote this concerning Dagon: *below from the navel he had the form of a fish, and above from his navel the form of a man.* Dagon was therefore like Neptune, to whom the Philistines performed divine rites so that he might favor them, bless their fishing, grant a prosperous course to their ships, and clear the sea of pirates. Jerome, in his *Questions*, says: *Dagon is the same in Hebrew as "dag," which means "fish of sorrow." He wishes it to be said, with the letter Aleph removed, that it comes from "dag" and "on," meaning mourning, because it comes from "un," to wail or be sad.* <margin>p. 241.</margin> <term>Cornelius à Lapide</term> <note>A prominent Jesuit exegete</note>, commenting on *1 Samuel 5*. Others everywhere derive Dagon from **דגה**, *Daga*, that is, *fish*, because this idol had the form of a fish. Since the Philistines were inhabitants of the seacoast, they devoted themselves to fishing, and therefore they fashioned and worshipped Dagon as the *protector of fish and fishing*. Furthermore, this idol was indeed in the likeness of a fish, but mixed with a human. Regarding the form, they say it had the figure of a half-man and half-fish, from the navel to the lowest parts in the likeness of a fish; but in the upper part, in human likeness; such as <term>Triton</term> was imagined, the son of Neptune,

<margin>Virgil, Aeneid 10.</margin>
> ->Whose shaggy front, as far as the sides, shows a man as he swims,<-
> ->But the belly ends in a sea-monster.<-

And in such a likeness are imagined the sea *Nymphs*, who are called *Nereids*, the daughters of Nereus, the sea God, whom Orpheus calls the *great-named spirit* <note>original: "μεγαλώνυμον δαίμονα"</note>, and the Naiads, water Goddesses, with the head and face of a human, the rest a fish; whence the Poet says:

<margin>Horace, Art of Poetry, v. 4.</margin>
> ->A woman, beautiful above, ends in a fish.<-

Nor did <term>Derceto</term> differ in form, who was accustomed to be worshipped in a most noble temple among the people of Ascalon in Palestine; a woman in face, a fish in the remaining part, as witnessed by <term>Diodorus Siculus</term> in Book 2, chapter 2, where, dealing with her statue consecrated in Ascalon, he writes: *she has the face of a woman, but the rest of the entire body is that of a fish.* <note>original: "τὸ μὲν πρόσωπον ἔχει γυναικὸς, τὸ δὲ ἄλλο σῶμα πᾶν ἰχθύος"</note> So also <term>Lucian</term>, describing the temple, rites, and image of the Syrian Goddess in Volume 3, pages 686 and following, teaches those things about the image of Derceto which he saw in person: namely, that it was human as far as the navel, but from the thighs to the bottom it was in the form of a fish. *I saw the image of Derceto in Phoenicia,* (he says on page 696) *a strange sight. Half is a woman, but as much as extends from the thighs to the tips of the feet, a fish's tail stretches out.* <note>original: "Δερκετοῦς εἶδον ἐν φοινίκῃ ἐθνησάμην, θέημα ξένον. ἡμισέη μὲν, γυνὴ, τὸ δὲ ὁκόσον ἐκ μηρῶν ἐς ἄκρους πόδας, ἰχθύος οὐρὴ ἀποτείνεται."</note> Wherefore <term>Ovid</term> in *Metamorphoses*, Book 4:

> *Dercete, whom the Palestinians believe inhabited the pools*
> *In a changed figure, with scales covering her limbs.*

For her temple had been near Ascalon, next to

<column-break/>

<margin>Dagon, the Deity of the Philistines.</margin>
a pool full of fish, because she was believed to dwell in a fish; hence <term>Pliny</term> (Book 5, chapter 23) called her the "prodigious *Atergatis*"; and the Syrians for this reason abstained from fish, worshipping them as Gods, which Diodorus holds in the cited place, and confirms by the testimony of <term>Xenophon</term> in Book 1 of the *Expedition of Cyrus*, describing the river Chalus, in which were seen fish of remarkable size, which the inhabitants did not allow to be harmed, regarding them as Gods. Let us cite Xenophon's words: *The river Chalus, being a plethron in width, full of large and tame fish, which the Syrians considered Gods, and did not allow to be harmed.* <note>original: "Χάλον ποταμὸν, ὄντα τὸ εὖρος πλέθρου, πλήρη δ’ ἰχθύων μεγάλων καὶ πραέων, οὓς οἱ Σύροι θεοὺς ἐνόμιζον, καὶ ἀδικεῖν οὐκ εἴων."</note> So also <term>Lucian</term>: *they consider fish a sacred thing, and never touch fish.* <margin>cited place, p. 697.</margin> <term>Cicero</term> in *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book 3: *The Syrians worship fish.* Ovid, in the *Metamorphoses* concerning Leucothoe and Palaemon, and in the *Fasti*, Book 2, says:

> *Lest the timid Syrians violate the mouths of fish.*

This Deity of the Syrians is the same as *Venus*; and is also believed to be the same as Dagon, notwithstanding that Dagon is called a God, not a Goddess, for *grammatically* <note>original: "σχηματικῶς"</note> a masculine termination does not exclude a feminine one, just as Venus herself is called a *God* by <term>Virgil</term> in the *Aeneid*, Book 2:

> *I descend, and with a God as my guide, I make my way*
> *Between the weapons and the enemies.*

That Dagon was fashioned in the form of a man in his upper part is clear from the fact that they found Dagon lying on his face after the engines of war were destroyed, *with his head and both the palms of his hands cut off, 1 Samuel 5:4, leaving only the body or trunk of the idol.* In the lower part of the body, he undoubtedly had the form of a fish, whence no mention is made of feet, but only of the head and two hands, which were found torn from the rest of the body on the threshold; whence also <term>Rabbi Kimchi</term> notes that only the form of a fish was left in him. What the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> adds about both the soles of the feet being taken away, they add from outside the source text. For these are their words: *The head of Dagon and both the tracks of his feet were removed upon the front of the thresholds, and both the wrists of his hands had fallen upon the porch.* <note>original: "Ἡ κεφαλὴ Δαγὼν καὶ ἀμφότερα τὰ ἴχνη τῶν ποδῶν αὐτῦ ἀφῃρημένα ἐπὶ τὰ ἐμπρόσθια τῶν σταθμῶν, καὶ ἀμφότεροι οἱ καρποὶ τῶν χειρῶν αὐτῦ πεπτωκότες ἐπὶ τὸ πρόθυρον."</note> There is nothing in the Hebrew text about *feet*, for there it says: **ראש דגון ושתי כפות ידיו כרתות** that is, *the head of Dagon and the two palms of his hands were cut off*. That house, which the strong hand of <term>Samson</term> cast down, they maintain was the *temple of Dagon*, which was so large that it held three thousand spectators of both sexes (verse 27). <term>Isidore</term> is of that opinion in *Questions on Judges*. Concerning this, it is pleasing to bring forward the vernacular words of <term>Bernhard von Breydenbach</term>, who surveyed that place during his pilgrimage to Jerusalem:

> The city of Gaza is indeed twice as large and wide as Jerusalem / but in its buildings quite unlike it / and lies no more than two Italian miles from the sea / and was in former times the capital of the Philistines called Gaza / of which city one reads in the Book of Judges / that Samson, being there for his pleasure / and while he was in a house in which the lords and citizens ate and drank, moved and shook the two columns. That same house was a temple of the idol called Dagon / and one still sees today many old buildings of the ancient house.

That it was a temple is argued by the sacrifice of victims, which they did not ordinarily offer except in temples. Mention of this temple, existing in the city of Azotus, is made in *1 Maccabees 10:83-84*, as the place where fleeing enemies retreated.

# From 1 Samuel 5

<margin>Dagon, the Deity of the Philistines. see p. 83.</margin>
...fugitives for the sake of safety, as if to some guardian deity. In ancient times, temples were accepted as asylums by most peoples; but it poorly protected its clients, who established the shrine of Dagon as a refuge for their safety. For idol fell along with idol <note>The author refers to the destruction of the temple of Dagon by Jonathan Maccabeus (1 Maccabees 10:83-84), where the idol and those seeking sanctuary were burned.</note>; those who had fled there were also burned. The Greek text reads thus: *and they fled to Azotus, and entered into Beth-dagon, their idol, to be saved.* <note>original Greek: καὶ ἔφυγον εἰς Ἄζωτον, εἰσῆλθον εἰς βηθδαγῶν τὸ εἴδωλον αὐτῶν τοῦ σωθῆναι.</note> Beth-dagon, as the Vulgate retained it, is *Beth Dagon* (בית דגון), the house of Dagon. *Beth* (בית), house, is used for the seat and place of any thing, whether sacred or profane; as *Beth ha-Kapporet* (בית הכפורת), the house of propitiation, *the house of the mercy seat* <note>original Greek: οἶκος τὸ ἱλαστήριον</note>, 1 Chronicles 28:11, concerning the Holy of Holies; and *Beth Elohim* (בית אלהים), the house of God, Genesis 28:17, concerning the place where Jacob had seen the ladder, and from there, because of God's presence, he gave the place the name Bethel, the house of God. Where the Chaldean <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> has *a sanctuary to the name of the Lord* (מקדש לשמיה די). Beth-dagon is the same as *the temple of Dagon* <note>original Greek: τὸ ἱερὸν Δαγῶν</note>, as it is called in verse 84. Dagon could not protect his own idol; otherwise, he would have withdrawn himself from the flames applied by man—a mortal treating the "immortal" Dagon (as he was believed to be) badly, along with his seat and worshipers, as things went well through the cities captured here and there. Nor shall the Philistine object that the Ark of God was also taken away and brought into the temple of Dagon. We know it was brought in, but to the disgrace of the nation, which was vexed by a most bitter kind of disease, and the idol itself was also cast down once and again, with its head and hands cut off upon the threshold. They could not treat the Ark irreverently, which they found necessary to send back to the Israelites even with votive gifts. Nor would Israel ever have lost it, if they had listened to the voice of God. This happened by the just judgment of God, so that in that first encounter with the Philistines, God rejected the Ark of the Covenant and the tabernacle of Shiloh—that tabernacle where he dwelt among men (Psalm 78) and in which, through sacred rites and religious ceremonies, Jehovah was seen to converse familiarly among men. The Philistines were not ignorant of this all-powerful presence of God; for when they heard that the Ark had arrived in the camp of the Hebrews, they cried out in trembling: <margin>chapter 4:7</margin> *God has come into the camp* (אלהים אל-המחנה); and they groaned, saying: *Woe to us* (אוי לנו; Greek: *Οὐαὶ ἡμῖν*). And again: *Who shall deliver us out of the hand of these mighty Gods?* (מי יצילנו). They say *the mighty Gods* (האלהים האדירים); the Septuagint says *the stronger gods* <note>original Greek: θεοὶ στερεώτεροι</note>; the Latin says *sublime Gods*. To the Hebrews, *Adir* (אדיר) means magnificent regarding God, whose *magnificence and glory* (אדיר והדר) appeared and became known chiefly from the punishment of Egypt; and the Philistines themselves testify to this, saying: <margin>v. 8</margin> *These are the Gods (האלהים) who struck Egypt with every plague in the desert.* But what happens? That magnificence and glory of Israel, in which they boasted above all other nations, was transferred when the Ark of God was captured by the Philistines (v. 21, 22). Wherefore the daughter-in-law of Eli, who was the wife of Phinehas, expiring in childbirth, uttered her final words: <margin>v. 21, 22</margin> *The glory has departed from Israel* (גלה כבוד מישראל). **The glory is gone from Israel.** <note>original German: Die Herrlichkeit ist dahin von Israel.</note> And she called the infant *Ichabod* (איכבוד) in memory of the event, as if to say: "Where is the glory?" Not glory, or *dishonor* <note>original Greek: ἀδοξία</note>, as Josephus translates it. For the letter *Aleph* (א) is placed either for *Ain* (אין), "not," or for *Ai* (אי), "where." When the Ark was transferred to the Philistines, the *Shekhinah* (שכינה), the divine dwelling and presence, was transferred at the same time—all protection, all hope <margin>Dagon, Deity of the Philistines.</margin> of liberty—and it could be said by the Israelites:

> We were Trojans, Ilium was, and the great
> Glory of the Teucrians. <note>A quote from Virgil's Aeneid, lamenting the fall of Troy.</note>

What then did the Hebrews do? They cried out as if to expostulate with God: *Why has the Lord struck us today before the Philistines?* Why did He not help His own? But in truth, GOD finally struck the wanton enemies *in the posterior parts*, and gave them everlasting reproach (Psalm 78:66), by an infamous and shameful punishment in the more hidden and obscene part of the body. Afflicted by this, the men of Azotus took counsel and made for themselves (as the Latin Bibles have in verse 9) leathern seats or cushions stuffed with feathers, so that they might sit more comfortably without pain. Afterward, <margin>ch. 6 v. 2, 7</margin> being warned by diviners and priests, they sent back the Ark on a new cart, and dedicated golden "anuses" <note><term>Anos</term>: The author uses the Latin for "anuses" to describe the golden models of the tumors/hemorrhoids sent as a guilt offering.</note> and golden mice as a vow to the God of Israel. Mice had devastated the region (v. 5). Therefore, persuaded by their religion, they offered mice to appease God (v. 18). They were struck in their posterior parts (v. 6), so that their intestines rotted and protruded outward; therefore, <margin>Author on the Miracles of Holy Scripture, book 2, ch. 7</margin> they paid five golden "anuses" (חמשה עפלי זהב) for the expiation of their sin. The disease of the buttocks was sent extraordinarily by God with horrendous torments, so much so that the cry of each city went up to heaven (v. 12). This strange and new disease, full of novelties, brings to our memory the companions of Agamemnon, once seeking Troy, who were forced to stop because of a disease infecting the buttocks and to care for the skin of the buttocks; whence a city of Ionia, called *Pygelia*, preserved the memory of this matter, from *pyge* (πυγή), meaning buttocks or loins, as Eustathius and Suidas record in the Iliad, p. 310. They imagine something similar regarding Venus, whose most ancient temple among the Ascalonites Herodotus (Book 1) records, who had afflicted the Scythians because of a robbery. Let us add the full words: *But those who returned back, when they were in the Syrian city of Ascalon, after the majority of the Scythians had passed through without doing harm, a few of them who were left behind plundered the temple of Heavenly Aphrodite. This temple (as I find by inquiry) is the oldest of all the temples of this goddess. For even the temple in Cyprus originated from there, as the Cyprians themselves say.* <note>original Greek: οἱ δὲ ἀναχωρέοντες ὀπίσω... κ.τ.λ.</note> When the Scythians were retreating through the city of Ascalon in Palestine, and while the greater part did no injury, a few who remained plundered the shrine of Venus Urania, which was (as far as I know) the oldest. Indeed, the house of the same Goddess in Cyprus came from this one, as the Cyprians themselves report. Some interpret these as "mariscas," namely, shameful swellings in that more secret part. In Hebrew it is *Ophalim* (עפלים), which the Septuagint explains as *ulcers in the seats* <note>original Greek: ἕλκη ἐν ταῖς ἕδραις</note>, Deuteronomy 28:27. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<margin>Dagon, the Deity of the Philistines.</margin>
...lest they should perish from that affliction (1 Samuel 5:9-10). To avert this plague, they offered a guilt offering (1 Samuel 6:3) so that *the hand of God might be lightened from them, and from their gods, and from their land* (v. 5); for the hand of God had been against the city with a very great destruction <note>original Hebrew: *mehumah gedolah me’od*</note> (chapter 5, verses 9, 11). To turn away this most grievous destruction and affliction, they also added gifts and dedicated offerings <note>term: *anathemata* — objects set apart or consecrated to a deity</note>, which took the form of tumors and the shape of mice. This was clearly according to the custom of Atargatis <note>A Syrian fish-goddess</note>; when her suppliants adored her, they would dedicate golden and silver fish, as witnessed by Mnaseas in Athenaeus, *Book 8*. Greece feigned that Minerva <note>Athena</note> was born from *the head of Jupiter*, and Bacchus from his *thigh*, since they thought it fitting that Pallas, the inventor of arts, should be born from the brain, and Liber <note>Bacchus</note> from a shameful part of the body. One should not say that Baal generated Dagon from his head, nor from his side or thigh, but from the anus; for those foul offerings which they paid as required gifts prove that one must speak of the "birth" in no other way. By this ridiculous and filthy gift, they wished to bind the divine Deity to themselves and remove the danger from their borders. Now they supplicate the God whom they had previously despised, recognizing no power in Him. Now they enclose *golden vessels* <note>Hebrew: *kelei zahav*</note> (v. 15, ch. 6) in the Ark in hope of pardon—vessels into which they had perhaps previously cast dung in mockery. Thus, they rightly suffered in those very members with which they sinned, being worthy to endure such things and to labor in those members which they had offered to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity. Those who had previously submitted to Dagon, and had dedicated the Ark as a trophy or some 
<margin>1 Samuel 6:5, 2</margin>
victory gift, now, with a changed mind, recognize the God of the Hebrews as the Victor over their own god, Dagon. The Priests and Diviners <note>Hebrew: *kohanim ve-qosemim*; Greek: *hoi hiereis kai hoi manteis*</note> who had placed the Ark beneath their idol Dagon as a distinguished spoil, suddenly changed in the council of the Princes and spoke in another tongue: *And you shall give glory to the God of Israel* <note>Hebrew: *ve-natattem l'Elohei Yisrael kavod*; Greek: *Dosete tō Kyriō Theō Israēl doxan*</note>. 
<margin>1 Samuel 6:6</margin>
And as if the people were lingering, the priests rebuked them as sluggish, saying: *Why will you harden your hearts, as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? Did he not, after he had mocked them* <note>The scholar Arias translates the Hebrew *hit’allel* as "to mock," as do the Septuagint with the Greek *empaizein*</note> *let them go, and they departed?* They said this because there were some who advised against sending the Ark away. The priests flared up against them and terrified them with the example of the Egyptians; nor did they cease to quickly summon the Goldsmiths and command them to fashion five golden tumors and five golden mice, 
<margin>v. 4, 18</margin>
*according to the number* of the princes of the Philistines who ruled over the five satrapies <note>provinces</note>. There were five satrapies of the Philistine principality, and an equal number of mice as an expiation for the plague of tumors and mice with which they had been struck. They placed this expiatory gift in a *chest*, which is called an 
<margin>v. 8</margin>
*argaz*, and sent it away on a new cart without a driver, while the five satraps of the provinces watched to see which way the cows would go of their own accord—whether toward Israel or another way. An unexpected thing happened, providing a most certain proof of divine guidance: the cows, 

<column-break/>

leaving their masters behind, followed the true path among various roads without a leader or 
<margin>Dagon, the Deity of the Philistines.</margin>
driver. We see that nothing hindered them from continuing their way. They went where they ought, and where they ought, they stood (v. 14). However, the Philistines must have been of wicked character, for among so many demonstrations <note>Greek: *deigmatismois* — public examples or proofs</note> of divine power, Dagon remained preferable to them and far more excellent than the God of Israel, to whom they continued to pray. *The five Satraps of the Philistines saw these wonders, but they returned to Ekron on the same day, persisting in their old ways* (v. 16). But as a concluding flourish, let us hear Prosper <note>Prosper of Aquitaine, a 5th-century Christian writer</note>, who in *On Promises and Predictions*, book 2, pages 106-107, says: *While the sons of Eli the Priest acted wickedly, presuming to eat parts of the sacrifices that God had not commanded them, which should have been offered first to God and then to themselves; and also pursuing women coming to the temple, they committed outrages. Because of these crimes, an angry God sent the battle of a hostile nation upon them; in which not only were the people fallen, but those very Priests were slain. The Ark of God itself was captured by the enemies. For the God of Israel is so angry with sinning priests that He does not spare even His sacred places and vessels. But the enemies who had taken the Ark of God believed it should be treated with such veneration that they thought it should be placed in the temple of their god Dagon. Under whose power, on the following day, they saw their idol shattered and prostrate. But attributing this to chance, they fixed it with stronger and more powerful hooks. Finding it the next day broken and crushed before the Ark, they could not understand what it was, and the nation itself was struck with a heavy and atrocious plague. Nor were they able to escape the final punishment of this disgrace until they returned the Ark of God, which they had taken, with gifts attached.*

### 1 SAMUEL 31:9-10

<note>Hebrew text: And they cut off his head and stripped off his armor and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines... and they put his armor in the temple of Ashtoreth.</note>
<note>Greek text: And they behead him and strip him of his weapons, and send them into the land of the foreigners... and they dedicated the weapons of Saul in the temple of Astarte.</note>

*And they cut off the head of Saul, and stripped him of his armor, and sent into the land of the Philistines round about. And they put his armor in the Temple of Astaroth.*

<margin>On Dedicated Offerings.</margin>
The Hellenists <note>Greek-speaking Jews or scholars</note> called every consecration made to God—whether of a man, a beast, a field, or any other thing—an *anathema* (ἀνάθημα). However, there was a huge difference between *anathema* written with an 'eta' (η) and *anathema* written with an 'epsilon' (ε). The latter <note>anathema with epsilon</note> was a "curse," a thing hated by God and signifying ultimate detestation to the Hebrews, or something unworthy of this life, to which the word *cherem* <note>Hebrew: חרם — something banned or devoted to destruction</note> corresponds among the Hebrews (Joshua 5:17, 1 Corinthians 12:3, 16:21, Galatians 1:8-9). Thus the people of Jericho with all their goods were *cherem* to the Lord, an *anathema* to God (Joshua 6:17), that is, unworthy of this life. So Oedipus was an *anathema*, unworthy to live, namely "accursed." The former <note>anathema with eta</note> denotes a thing consecrated to God from a grateful heart; it is named from *anathenai*, "to hang up," or if you prefer, "to set aside," because it was a sin to return something once consecrated to profane uses.

# From 1 Samuel 31:9

<margin>Temple Offerings.</margin>
...from which comes that phrase of Plato in *Republic, Book 2: "dedicating offerings to the gods."* Among the Greeks, it also went by another name, *consecration* <note>original: ἀφιέρωμα</note>; to the Latins, a *votive gift* <note>original: donarium</note>. Allatius translates it as *offerings* <note>original: offerumenta</note>, not inelegantly, though not in pure Latin, in his *Excerpts* p. 355. Moreover, such donated items were *sacred goods* <note>original: ἱερὰ χρήματα</note>. Vallesius in his *Notes on Dionysius* p. 99, notes they were varied: but especially among the chosen people of God, it was most frequent and customary to hang up in the Temple of God the weapons taken from enemies in war and the spoils brought back from them, consecrating them to the living God. There is no small indication that the sword of Goliath, who was slain by David, was consecrated as a sacred offering to Jehovah, because Ahimelech, the priest in Nob, gave the sword of the giant Philistine—wrapped in a cloth and stored behind the Ephod—to David when he asked for it while fleeing the tyranny of Saul and lacking necessary weapons, as seen in *1 Samuel 21:9.* Josephus testifies to this in explicit words:
<margin>Book 6, Jewish Antiquities, 13.</margin>
*"David dedicated the broadsword of Goliath to God."* How David was later able to reclaim and use the sword, as a thing once consecrated to GOD, is not our purpose to inquire at this time; we refer the Blessed Reader to Abulensis on *1 Samuel chapter 21, question 21*, who argues at length against Lyra. The sum of his argument falls mostly to this: that this was done because of a case of extreme, pressing necessity, and with the intention of returning it to that place. Not only weapons, but other things acquired from conquered enemies were offered to God; hence we read that David sanctified to God all the gold and silver collected from all the subdued nations, *2 Samuel 8:10.* Judith offered the canopy of Holofernes and all the instruments of war as a sacred offering to GOD, the author of victory: *"she gave all the vessels and the canopy as an offering to the Lord,"* which last words Blessed Luther expressed notably as: *"that it should be banned [devoted] to the LORD forever,"* *Judith 16:23.* Prudentius looked to this rite when he sang of Chastity attacking Lust in his *Psychomachia*:
> Nor is she content to hide the purified
> Sword in its sheath, lest a covering of rust
> Should take hold: she consecrates its brilliance,
> Washed of foul filth, in the Catholic temple
> At the altar of the Divine font, where it may
> Gleam, shining with eternal light.
The Gentiles, shrouded in Cimmerian darkness <note>A metaphor for deep ignorance or spiritual darkness</note>, just as they dragged many laudable customs and rites of the Jews into a perverse imitation and their own abominable worship, so also in this matter—taught by the Devil, the ape of GOD—they imitated the Jews. Returning unharmed from war or battle, they hung the weapons taken from conquered enemies in the shrines of the Gods and dedicated the more noble spoils to them. When an enemy was conquered and regions subdued in the ancient Roman Republic, *triumphs* were held in the greatest glory, as were *trophies* and *ovations*. Various crowns were invented, various titles devised, statues erected, public proclamations heard, and temples and shrines magnificently built for the Gods, with sacrifices paid to the minor deities in thanksgiving. Festivals were established by decree of the Senate, as testified here and there by Livy and other writers of the Roman Nation. Hence Baptista Mantuanus writes:
<margin>3 Sylv. f. 61. a.</margin>

When Bacchus as victor penetrated to the Eastern Indians,

And great gifts to Jupiter; the ancients used to bring foliage into the temples.
He was the first to heap the altars with both spoils and gold.
Scipio, whose name was made by conquered Numantia,

The spoils of the Gallic leader. Agrippa, with proud

In the division of spoils, some went to the leader,

<margin>7th Aeneid.</margin>

Notable on this matter is a passage in Xenophon’s

Mamercus, the Tyrant of Catana, did this when, after routing several thousand cohorts, he dedicated shields to the gods, inscribed first with a shameful verse, which was:
->These shields, painted with mountains and chosen from gold and ivory,<-
->We captured with our cheap little shields.<-
->With gold, ivory, amber, and shining with purple,<-
->Behold, we took these shields with worthless ones.<-
Thus, this hanging of primary spoils in the shrines of the Gods prevailed everywhere among almost all peoples. And since it was believed that the gods were appeased by gifts and induced to help by presents, hence such a great and varied number of different offerings began. The sixth book of the Greek Epigrams contains nothing but the *offerings* <note>original: ἀναθήματα</note> of those who, having finished with some profession or at death, inscribed their tools to the gods. Hence there were offerings *proper* to Venus, namely hair; for which reason no one among the Troezenians, according to Lucian in *The Syrian Goddess*, entered into marriage without the consecration of these. Hence the Weapons of Minerva were hung up, *Herodotus, Terpsichore, in Stephens' Index 293.* Hence Neptune had his own peculiar gifts; Romulus dedicated a captured *bronze chariot* to Vulcan, see *Beyerlinck D. 356.* *The dagger of Scaevinus was consecrated by Nero at the Capitol, inscribed to Jupiter the Avenger*, see *Tacitus, 15th Annals.* A *Skeleton* was consecrated by Hippocrates to Apollo, compare *Meibomius on Hippocrates p. 32.* There were offered to Diana by hunters *horns, skins, bows, limbs of wild beasts*, and such other things. Hence the Scholiast of Aristophanes says: *"It was the custom for those hunting some prey to nail a part of the hunted thing—a head or a foot—with a peg to some tree in the forest itself in honor of Artemis."* Wherefore Lactantius says regarding Statius' *Thebaid 9: "In the grove of Diana or Sylvanus, some things are fixed [to trees], others are hung from the domes of temples by shepherds; teeth and horns are fixed, skins and other things are hung."* Apuleius on *p. 556 at the beginning of the Florida also makes mention of this custom: "It is the custom of religious travelers, when some grove or some sacred place is encountered on the road, to ask for favor, to place a gift, to pause..."*

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Temple Offerings.</margin>
...to sit by. Nor could a traveler more justly encounter a religious delay than by an *altar wreathed with flowers, or a cave shaded with foliage, or an oak burdened with horns, or a beech tree crowned with skins*. How very wealthy the temple at Delphi <note>original: "τὸ ἐν Δελφοῖς ἱερὸν"</note> must have been due to the abundance of offerings and gifts; seduced by the desire for its treasures, the Phocians with their leader, Philomelus, plundered the temple and carried off 60 tons of gold, which wealth had been amassed from the gifts of great Princes. From this, the words of Strabo in *Book 9* are to be explained: *Wealth, being an object of envy, is difficult to guard, even if it be sacred; certainly now the temple at Delphi is most impoverished.* That impiety resulted from the pillaging by the Phocians, from which was ignited the *Sacred War*; so called, lasting ten years. And thus far, the use and ritual of offerings among the Gentiles has been demonstrated and shown from profane <note>secular/classical</note> writers. From the sacred text, the matter is indeed manifest by the example of the Philistines, who, when they had overcome the forces of the Israelites with arms and killed their King Saul in battle, deposited his armor in the temple of Ashtoreth. For Saul, reduced to the power of the Palestinians, preferred a shameful death to flight, and chose rather *by his own hands* <margin>p. 467.</margin>—to use the words of Zosimus—to perish, and preferred to end his life with a miserable exit than to become a mockery to the Philistines, the most bitter enemies of the God of Israel and the Israelites. Saul, like that Ajax of Sophocles, being about to fall upon his sword, fixed the hilt in the excavated earth and covered it around with earth so that the sword might stand firm, upon which he prepared to lean. For that word <margin>v. 827.</margin> *perialo* <note>Greek: περιαλῶ, to fall upon or impale oneself</note> implies that with the point then turned toward himself, he would cast himself prone upon it, and he says:
> The slayer stands where it might be
> most sharp, if one has leisure even to consider it.
> It is fixed in the hostile land of Troy,
> newly sharpened by the iron-eating whetstone.
> I have fixed it well, arranging it
> most kindly for this man to die with speed;
> thus we are well prepared.

He perished therefore by the sword, the very same with which he had determined to kill David. His head was cut off with a sword, and to the great ignominy of himself, his people, and his God, it was hung up as an offering <note>anathema</note> in the temple of Ashtoreth. The enemy finally sings a song of victory, as if such a great victory had fallen to them by the help of their own gods. Let us bring forth the words of the text: *And they cut off Saul's head, and stripped him of his armor, and sent into their land round about to announce it in the temple of their Idols* (the house of their *etseb* <term>house of sorrows</term> <note>original: "בית עצביהם"</note>, of their terrors, i.e., idols) *And they put his armor etc.* In the word *bisser* <note>Hebrew: בשׂר</note> a joyful announcement of successfully managed affairs is noted, which the Greeks call *evangelion* <note>Good News</note>, whence they also translated here, *announcing good news*, as the Aldine edition has it; other editions: *bringing good news*. How fortune plays; Saul had previously erected a trophy <margin>1 Sam. 15:12</margin> (where the Vulgate has "triumphal arch"), now he himself becomes a trophy, and his head is carried around as a monument of victory through the regions, according to the custom of various lands, by which the spoils and arms of enemies are led in triumphs. When Goliath fell by David's hand, the Victor carried his head through the villages and hamlets in triumph, with women singing festive songs. The same was done with the head of Saul. The same happened later when Jehu ordered the seventy sons of Ahab to be killed, and *they put their heads in baskets* and sent them to the King (2 Kings 10:7), by which they redeemed peace. A similar thing is read in 2 Samuel 20:21 <margin>Temple Offerings. Book 6, Ch. 9.</margin> concerning the severed head of Sheba; and of Nicanor in 2 Maccabees 15:30, 35. So also of the Gauls in Diodorus, who tied the severed heads of enemies to the necks of their horses, and fixed the spoils spattered with blood to the doors of their houses with song and hymns. To say nothing now of the modern practice of the Hungarians with the truncated heads of Turks, fixing them on a pole, and vice versa. Finally, when Saul's head had been carried through all parts of the region, they fastened it in the temple of Ashtoreth, so that this happiness might be attributed to the gods. Thus it was the custom to bring spoils taken from enemies into the shrines of the gods; thus the abandoned arms of Alcaeus the lyric poet, fleeing in battle, were collected by the enemy and hung in the temple of Pallas (Herodotus *Book 5, p. 143*). So the spear of Achilles was hung in a temple (Dausqueius on Quintus Calabrus, p. 14). Saul therefore perished by that fate by which despisers of Divine solace are accustomed to perish. Things had gone badly with the Amalekites against the Divine precept, and having neglected the true God, the Devil was consulted through a devil—the Pythoness <note>Witch of Endor</note>, I think, or Apollo. This sin, therefore, was deservedly to be paid for by a sad death, both of himself and his three sons and his whole house, which had then gone out with him to battle. It is shown from this that blows for sin committed against God are severely expiated, either by the sent ministry of enemies or in another way. Every one of the Jews fled from this horrific event; the enemy followed the fugitive, exulted, insulted, and offered *Soteria* <note>sacrifices for deliverance</note> to his own Deity.
The head of the King (truly remarkable for the first King) is carried away, it was carried on a spear, his shield was sent for display; throughout the land, in the temple of the gods they were placed, and simultaneously, *the head was hung up according to religious custom*. The rarity of the victory demanded this, so that the glory of the deeds might be grandly publicized in the *temples of the gods Ashtoreth and Dagon*, and among the people. Thus Saul died by his own fault, *for his transgression which he committed against Jehovah, because he kept not the word of Jehovah, and also because he asked counsel of a familiar spirit. Because he inquired not of Jehovah, therefore Jehovah slew him, and turned the kingdom unto David the son of Jesse.* As he had lived, so (if I may joke sadly against the "letter of the grammarians") he "died-ed" <note>A pun on the Latin 'vixerat' (he had lived) and a made-up 'morixerat'</note>. He had fled the ignominy of this age, and by that very act ran into that of the next. When he had commanded his armor-bearer, "Draw your sword and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and mock me," he thought he had escaped ignominy; and if I am not mistaken, he feared at the same time the reproach of the divine name, for he feared lest the help of God and the presence of the empty Ark be thrown in his face. While we write these things, the Hebrew word *alal* <note>עלל</note> occurs, which word *our Translator <note>Luther</note> here renders "to handle shamefully" (schändlich umbgehen), and likewise "to mock"*, which Georg Witzel attacks in his *Censure of Luther's Translation, f. 70*, but without cause. For Buxtorf proves with many examples under the word *alal* that this word has the meaning of "mocking." Together with Saul, his excellent son Jonathan perished, but there is a great difference between the death of each. God is present for Jonathan, sustains him in death, and gives rewards after this life; Saul is extinguished without consolation, falls upon the sword, and falls into eternal punishments.

<margin>Sacred Music.</margin>
Just as God, by His own counsel, created different kinds of emotions, so He also willed that there be different signs of these different emotions in sounds, by which the animal spirit <note>The "animal spirit" in early modern medicine was thought to be a subtle fluid that carried sensations through the nerves.</note> might be delighted and nourished, just as the vital spirit is by spices and scents. Music, through harmonious and fitting rhythms, stirs human emotions; it draws, moves, and deeply affects them. Music, when it is harmonious, does not only affect the listener with pleasure and delight, but also penetrates wonderfully into the souls and hearts of those listening, and inflames the affections of true piety, faith, gladness, and burning joy in their breasts. Scaliger recites the cause of this matter in *Exercise 302. 2. Why are minds most greatly excited by sounds?* Because the spirits that move in the heart receive the trembling and leaping air into the breast, and become one with their own kindred substance. Thus the remaining spirits, placed in other parts of the body, follow and move the muscles or restrain them, according as the law of the rhythms either increases with incitements, or rests with a composed tenor, or imitates quiet with gentleness. Hence Dion Chrysostom skillfully says in *Oration 32 to the Alexandrians*: Music is an invention "for the sake of healing the passions of men, and especially to transform souls that are harshly and wildly disposed." <note>original Greek: θεραπείας ἕνεκα τῶν ἀνθρώπων τῶν παθῶν, καὶ μάλισα δη μετατρέφειν ψυχὰς ἀπηνῶς καὶ ἀγρίως διακειμένας.</note> But what point is there in commemorating the praises of Music, since none are found who do not desire it in the greatest measure? What joy would there be among men, what cheerfulness, what festivity, if Music did not exist? Nothing is more lovable than Music: consult the ears, if you deny it; or rather the heart, if you have a heart that loves the recreation of Music. It moves the senses, and gradually glides into minds so that it may settle there. Elisha, <margin>2 Kings 3:15.</margin> when he was somewhat moved in spirit against the King of Israel, ordered a minstrel to be called to him, so that by his musical harmony his mind, disturbed by the presence of the impious Israelite King, might be calmed and imbued with a spiritual song for prophesying heavenly things. For the highest and ultimate end of our Music is the glory of God. Philo, in his work *On the Service of Noah*, writes a report from the ancients that when the work of creation was finished, GOD asked one of the Prophets what he might desire; the Prophet replied that nothing was lacking except that they should sing praises to GOD. God then produced from the virgin Memory <note>original: Μνημη (Mneme)</note> a certain musical offspring called Remembrance. <note>original: Μνημοσύνην (Mnemosyne)</note> This is indeed a fable, yet its moral sagaciously indicates that glory must be rendered to God, and all things must be directed toward His glory. No art was perfect at its start, but just as an infant babbles before speaking perfectly, so it happens with the arts; so it is in mechanical things, and so it is in others, that one man first discovers, another

<column-break/>

increases, and this one perfects. Thus nothing was ever so crudely invented that it did not, through long successions, reach its <margin>Sacred Music.</margin> peak. <note>original Greek: ἀκμὴν (akmen)</note> We shall say the same of Music, which, like other inventions, changes itself for the better with time; hence Eupolis in Athenaeus: <margin>book 14.</margin>
->Music is a deep and<-
->complex thing. And it<-
->always finds something new for those who are able to love it.<- <note>original Greek: πρᾶγμα δ᾽ ἔστι μουσικὴ, Καὶ βαθύ τι καὶ κάμπυλον. Ἐξευρίσκει τε Ἀεί τι καινὸν τοῖς φιλοῦσιν δυναμένοις.</note>

->By the Gods, Music, like Libya,<-
->always brings forth some new<-

The first inventions of musical things were excessively crude, to which, with the passage of time, polishing and elaboration were added, so that now in our age nothing seems to remain to be done; for all things are so at their peak <note>original Greek: ἐν ἀκμῇ (en akme)</note> that Minerva was never more "Minerva-like." Let others proclaim as they please other eminent virtues in other ancients; while we pursue their sharpness of mind <note>original Greek: ἀγχίνοιαν (anchinoian)</note> in inventing with due praise, so let it be permitted to take the ultimate perfection of our latest age as an example. We take our example from the Italians, among whom the Muse of Music seems to have placed her palace, and from there wills that colonies be propagated through all lands and seas. But while we write these things, there twitches our ear the sweetest excellence and most excellent sweetness of the musicians born in our own Germany, in which matter Music seems, if not to snatch the palm from the Italians, at least to suggest a complete equality. <note>original Greek: ἰσότητα (isoteta)</note> Hence so many *sacred coins, so many Christian melodies, so many heavenly harmonies, sacred madrigals, ecclesiastical concerts, handfuls of sacred songs, sacred cymbals, sacred symphonies, melodic works, symphonic circles, and ecclesiastical songs* resounding the praise of God in one harmony; and thus what Scaliger says remains true, <margin>Poetics, book 5.</margin> that time is both the file and the law of the arts. The system of ancient Music is exceedingly intricate, and its origin far more intricate; for if we held the exact system of Ancient Music which the ancients used, especially the Hebrews, we would understand many sayings of Holy Scripture more clearly. But no one will be able to bring forth the Music lying hidden and as if buried in sacred things, since it has escaped even the ancient Rabbis and commentators; therefore we Christians are to be excused for our ignorance, since we have found the Jews to have been blind in these matters until now, which is an indication of an admirable and extreme neglect of their own domestic affairs. Only the memory of the name is left to us; the thing itself is utterly unknown, nor to be determined by any clear arguments on one side or the other. *Gaffarellus* wrote on the Music of the Hebrews among other philological works, praised by Leo Allatius in his *book on illustrious writings*, which we have not yet been permitted to see, <margin>p. 140.</margin> and many others with him. But we stick to the surface, we do not find the key, and like water-striders we scarcely touch it. What is written about the first moments of Music is foreign to that truth <note>original Greek: ἀνείθειᾳ (aletheia - likely a typo for truth)</note> which we desire here.
