# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Music.</margin>
The Sacred Annals have deigned to record very few things from that earliest age, yet they have preserved the memory of the inventors of music and metalworking. That musical <term>sagacity (Greek: agchinoia)</term> which the Sacred Annals attribute to Jubal—son of Lamech the bigamist, and the inventor and author of those who play the Lyre and the Organ—proves that certain remnants of <term>common notions (Greek: tōn koinōn ennoiōn)</term> <note>Basic innate ideas or instincts</note> remained in man after the Fall. He was the one who, so to speak, laid the first stone in the art of music, of whom the Poet says:

> *To Jubal was given the care to form the choir;*
> *Music created the singers' plectrums and tones;*
> *With twisted strings made from the guts of cattle,*
> *And with pipes for blowing, he distinguished them; the flute learned*
> *To be inflated by the winds; thus a slender origin began,*
> *Until organs grew into their immense form.*

How frequent the use of music was in all ages is manifest even from the history of Jacob. For when he had completed twenty years of servitude in Mesopotamia under his father-in-law, and was heading toward his homeland with his wives and children without his father-in-law's knowledge (while the latter was busy shearing sheep), he was overtaken on the road by Laban. Laban, arriving <term>beyond all reason and hope (Greek: pantos logou kai elpidos allon)</term> and accompanied by his kinsmen, <margin>Gen. 31:27.</margin> said to Jacob with a deceitful heart: *Why did you not tell me, so that I might have sent you away with joy and songs, with the timbrel and the lyre?* By these words it is clear enough that even at that time, both vocal and instrumental music were in use and accustomed to be employed for joyful festivities. Blessed Luther comments on these words of Laban thus: <margin>Commentary on Genesis, f. 141. b.</margin> *Laban displays great piety, humanity, and <term>natural affection (Greek: storgēn)</term> toward the children. "I loved you and my daughters so much, and embraced you with such services as I could, that you could find no fault in me; rather, you always found me most friendly. Therefore, now also, having called together all my friends and the inhabitants of this land, I would have escorted you honorably and splendidly with joy, with music, and with timbrels." For what would those joys and timbrels have been? Fetters, chains, prison, and perpetual slavery! Unless God had restrained his desires, he would have defrauded his son-in-law of all his goods; these, of course, are his "joys and lyres."* The author of the first song expressly mentioned in Scripture is Moses, who composed a new song for his people when they had escaped the hands of Pharaoh, King of Egypt. He instituted a day of festival and common joy, singing praises to the holy Power and Name of God alongside the children of Israel. He was followed by Miriam the sister, a <term>prophetess (Greek: prophētis)</term> and leader of the female troop. Her companion Elizabeth, the wife of Aaron, joined with those playing the psaltery; in the midst of young women playing timbrels, they led the dances, singing: *Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously magnified; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea, etc.* (Exod. 15:1). The music of the ancients is involved in many difficulties, especially regarding musical instruments, so that in investigating its differences, one often needs not just a "Delian swimmer" <note>A proverbial expression for someone who can navigate deep or difficult matters</note> but a Delian prophet. The music of the Jews perished along with their harps and psalteries, and it can only be reduced to its first principles with great difficulty. Hence arises the great discord among interpreters, and so many obscure and uncertain conjectures regarding the understanding of the words and speeches. This difficulty of knowledge arises partly from the things themselves, which have long since ceased to be used

<column-break/>

among mortals, being succeeded by other instruments, or even the same ones but greatly changed from their former condition and appearance; and partly from a lack of contemporary writers <margin>Sacred Music.</margin> from whom a judgment could be made about things past or changed. Hence, since it would be the mark of a headstrong and unintelligent man to define anything too stubbornly regarding this kind of instrument, or to adhere to any single opinion in matters that are highly contingent and not entirely necessary—which depend on the judgment of the human mind and can easily undergo change—we speak tentatively, as there is both a difference in notation and experience is deceptive. Franchinus (Book 1, *Theory* 4) establishes a threefold class of those practicing the musical art: one which acts with instruments; another which composes songs; and a third which judges the work of the instruments and the song. Whether the musician acts in speculation or in operation, and which part excels, we will now set aside and leave to those who have an abundance of skill in judging. Indeed, according to Boethius <margin>Book 1, ch. 34.</margin>, a musician is *one who, having weighed the matter with reason, assumes the science of singing not through the service of work, but by the command of speculation; and he who lacks speculation lacks the work.* Hence, some establish two kinds of musical organs, others three. Athenaeus (Book 4) calls some <term>wind instruments (Greek: empneusa)</term> and others <term>flutes (Greek: aula)</term>; for they are either inflated by breath or struck by the hand to produce sound. Those who consider musical instruments in a threefold way categorize them as: some <term>blown (Greek: emphysōmena or empneusa)</term>, which are filled by breath or inspiration; others <term>stringed (Greek: entala or enchorda)</term>, which are stretched with strings; and others <term>percussion (Greek: krousta)</term>, which are struck. To the first kind they refer the *Trumpet, Pipe, Reed, Clarion, Horn, Bugle, Lituus*, and those which today enjoy the specific name of "Organ" (*Orgeln* to us). To the second, the *Lyre, Cithara, Lute, Psaltery, Sambuca, Pandura, Barbiton, Nablium, Plectrum*. To the third, finally, the *Timbrel, Sistrum, Cymbal*, etc. Concerning these and other names of musical instruments, let us hear Angelo Poliziano (*Miscellanea* ch. 13, p. 238) discussing them thus: *There are many foreign names for instruments; just as Strabo relates in Book 10, among which the "nabla" is also numbered, that is, the Psaltery. But I also observed recently in the Prophet Daniel—with John Pico della Mirandola leading me into those recesses and sacred inner shrines of his studies—that there are even Greek and Latin-looking names for such instruments: although used much more corruptly by Chaldean authors, such as "carna" for horn, "cathros" for cithara, "sabuca" for sambuca, "psantorin" for psaltery, and "samphonia" for symphony. Indeed, the Frenchman Solomon says that "Nevel" is the Hebrew word where "psanterim" or "psaltery" is read. It is established that the name consists of three letters <term>נבל (N-B-L)</term>, from which "Navel" is also read in Isaiah and Amos, and then the form "Naulon," from which comes the Ovidian diminutive "Naulion."* We shall deal with these instruments according to the guidance of Holy Scripture as much as we are able. The author of Psalm 150, intending to invite the Jews and Gentiles to give thanks to God, recounts eight musical instruments with which he wishes thanks to be given to God: *Praise him, he says, with the sounding trumpet; praise him with the psaltery and lyre. Praise him with the timbrel and choir; praise him with strings and the pipe. Praise him with high-sounding cymbals.*

# On 2 Samuel VI. v. 5.

<margin>Sacred Music.</margin>
Because he recounts such a great number, it must have been a grand benefit; a point which Johannes Draconites <note>A 16th-century German theologian and reformer.</note>, referring it to the benefits of the Messiah, writes in *The Gospel of Christ*, E. 4. a.: He wishes to give thanks to God on account of the mercy promised in Christ then, and now exhibited; and since we know from the Chronicles that David instituted music of this kind for the glory of God and Christ, and that the singers, full of the Spirit of God, diligently sang Psalms to the Lord, I would especially consider Israel to be called by such instruments to give thanks to God for the benefits promised in Christ. Furthermore, the same interpreter, not unsuitably adapting those instruments to the Evangelists, Apostles, and ministers of the Church, writes: *Who will deny that by these various instruments are signified the Evangelists or ministers of the word? Though they are provided with various gifts of the Holy Spirit, they nevertheless preach the same Christ most pleasantly, just as different harmonies are accustomed to produce one most sweet concert. For Christ makes of one a trumpet in the Church, of another a psaltery, of a third a kithara <note>A type of ancient lyre.</note>, of a fourth a drum, and so on, so that the variety of gifts in the Commonwealth supports the harmony of doctrine and Christian life, no differently than many voices are accustomed to make one concert, and many members of the body serve one mind, as if the commander of the body.*

In the bringing up of the Ark of the Lord from the house of Abinadab into the house of Obed-edom, David and the whole house of Israel exulted with joy before the Lord, with all kinds of musical instruments sounding: namely *Kitharas*, and *Nablas* <note>Harps or lutes.</note>, and *Drums*, and *Trumpets*, and *Cymbals*, which the Vulgate renders as *Kitharas, and lyres, drums, sistrums, and cymbals*. David, <margin>2 Sam. 23:1</margin> the most prudent of Kings, the "Sweet Psalmist of Israel" <note>original: זמירות ישרֹאל (Zemirot Yisrael)</note>, commanded that God be praised with cymbals—not simply, but "well-sounding" cymbals, Psalm 150:5. A sounding voice pleases God when it is sweet, just as in the Canticles <note>The Song of Solomon.</note> Solomon writes that the voice of the Church sounds in the ears of Christ because it is sweet. A bellowing, lowing, and noisy voice is not the voice of the Church; nor should there be grating organs in the Church, but sweetly sounding ones. Since the cymbal is numbered among the well-sounding things by the divine Prophet, we shall begin with this word. It is excellently formed in various languages, and the Hebrew holds the first place here, which has *Tseltsel* <note>original: צלצל</note>, which others translate as *locust*.

<margin>Lexicon on this word.</margin>
<margin>2 Sam. 6:5.</margin>
Perhaps it is of another origin. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi.</note> writes on 1 Chronicles 13:8 that it is a "noisy locust," so called from its noisy voice, according to Buxtorf. *Hence "Tseltsel-kenaphim" <note>original: צלצל-כנפ-ים</note>, cymbals, from their tinkling.* The shape of the cymbals of the ancients is hidden from us today; it is most certain they were of a different appearance than ours. In the rites of the Gentiles, *cymbals and drums and rattles* <note>original: κύμβαλα καὶ τύμπανα καὶ κρόταλα</note> were very common, the initiations and toys of the Great Mother <note>Cybele.</note>. Whence in the rites of Bacchus and other gods were heard *those playing cymbals and those playing drums* <note>original: κυμβαλίζοντες καὶ τυμπανίζοντες</note>, as Arrian testifies. That there was a great difference in sound is testified by the words of Jerome against Helvidius, col. 19: *The drums sound, the flute cries out, the lyre chatters, the cymbal clashes.* <margin>Book 2.</margin> Whence Seneca, *Natural Questions* 2, 29: *You see how much more vocal empty things are than full ones; how much more those under tension than those relaxed. Thus drums and cymbals sound because the former strike the air resisting from the further side; the latter, driven against the air itself, do not tinkle unless they are concave.* The mallet strikes the convex and swelling part, and dashes the concave part against the air, as Lucretius says.

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Music.</margin>
->Taut drums thunder under palms, and concave cymbals<-
->all around, and horns threaten with a hoarse-sounding song.<-

From cymbals to drums, the use of which was very frequent in assemblies and public celebrations, as Sacred Scripture testifies, 1 Sam. 10:5, Job 21:12, Isaiah 30:32; compare Cocceius on Job, p. 248. They are made, however, as Augustine writes on Psalm 67, col. 712, from dried and stretched skin. From the Hebrew *Toph* <note>original: תף</note> comes the Greek *tympanon*, a drum, just as from *Lapad* <note>original: לפד</note> with a "mu" inserted comes *lampas*, a lamp, and from *Sindon* <note>original: סדון</note> comes *sindon* <note>fine linen</note>. The drums of the Syrians came from Greece to Rome, about which Juvenal says: <margin>Satire 3, v. 62.</margin>

> Long ago the Syrian Orontes has flowed into the Tiber,
> Bringing its language and customs, and with the flutist,
> Slanting strings, and its national drums,
> And girls commanded to stand for sale at the circus.

So from the Syriac *Abub* <note>original: אבוב</note> is derived *tibia* and *fistula* <note>flute/pipe</note>, and that word *ambubaja* in Suetonius' *Nero* c. 27 and Horace book 1, Satire 2. Where Acron says: *Ambubajae are what women flute-players are called in the language of the Syrians; for in Syrian a flute or symphony is called an ambubaja.* This also goes by another name, *Chalil* <note>original: חליל</note>, so called because it is perforated and concave, whence also to the Rabbis *chalul* <note>original: חלול</note> means concave. Among the ancients, as its use was very frequent, so its varieties were manifold, which we can read about in Scaliger’s golden books *On Poetics*. Among other differences were those made by age or sex. Hence *female and male flutes* <note>original: γυναικείοι καὶ ἀνδρείοι ἀυλοί</note>. The male ones were blown more strongly and gave a masculine sound; the female ones were the opposite. There could also be other differences, either by length, or by the number of holes, or by material. Its invention is commonly attributed to Marsyas, who is said to have invented the flutes and the *many-reeded pipe* <note>original: πολυκάλαμον</note>; see Scaliger, *Poetics* 20, and others. To say something of the Organ: *Organon* is as if *erganon* from *ergon*, a work. To the Latins, an "Instrument," not just any, but that which is preferred above all by way of excellence, and than which nothing is more effective for stirring up joy. Organs are now made from unequal tin pipes, an invention not very old, but very noble, says Fabricius in *Poetics*, p. 95. Around the year of Christ 757, *the first organ came into France, sent to King Pepin by the Emperor Constantine from Greece*, writes Marianus Scotus in his *Chronicles*. Aventinus testifies the same in *Annals* 3, p. 300. Bale says the same regarding this matter: *The Bishop of England, Vitellianus, he says, a native of Segni or Campania, a distinguished musician, introduced singing in churches around 660 AD, and applied Organs to human voices through harmonies*, according to that line of Mantuanus:

> To the signals he added organs cast from soft metal,
> Which might refresh the sacred rites on feast days.

In France, these musical organs first began to be manufactured around 828 AD at Aachen <note>original: aquas graneas</note> by the industry of a certain George, a Venetian priest, and at the expense of *King Louis*, as Aimoinus relates in book 14 *On the Deeds of the Franks*, c. 114. And Bruschius, in his notes on the *Monasteries of Germany*, says that George, Abbot of Salerno, ordered an Organ to be built in the basilica of his monastery, the largest and middle-sized pipes of which had a length of 28 feet and a circumference of 4 spans. What was added to these Organs around 1480 AD is indicated by Sabellicus where he says: *In the time of Pope Sixtus IV, a man of the musical art, of all who...* <margin>S. Enn. 10.</margin>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<page-num>352</page-num>

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>Sacred Music.</margin>
...who were ever among the most excellent without controversy. For many years, the Venetians had Bernhard, surnamed "the German" <note>original: "Theutonem"</note>, a testament to the genius of the land where he was born. He was the first to increase the musical measures in Organs, so that the feet might also assist the harmony by the pulling of cords, etc. However, when the Royal Psalmist mentions the organ with strings in *Psalm 150*, it is a most certain indication that David’s Organ is as different from our organs as the sky is from the earth. <margin>on Ps. 150.</margin> For "Organ," to use the words of Augustine, is a general name for all musical vessels, although custom has now prevailed so that those specifically called organs are the ones blown by bellows; I do not believe that type is meant here. For since "Organ" is a Greek word, as I said, general to all musical instruments, the Greeks also call this one to which bellows are applied by that name. However, calling it an "Organ" is a more Latin, common, and vulgar custom. Therefore, when he says "with strings and the Organ," it seems to me he wished to signify some instrument that had strings. Thus says Augustine. Regarding the lyre, the cithara, and the lute <note>original: "chely"</note>, the Poets make them one and the same thing when they wish, says Barth in his commentary on Statius, Book 1, *Silvae* 5, p. 133; they do not attend to the distinction, as often happens in other matters when the meter carries the mind away. Under the praises of the cithara, Pindar extols Music, which pleases the anger of the Gods, extinguishes Jove’s lightning, delights iron-hearted Mars, and soothes and tames wild animals. These are the words in his first Hymn:

<margin>v. 1.</margin>
> Golden lyre, rightful possession of Apollo
> and the violet-haired Muses,
> whom the step hears, the beginning of splendor,
> and the singers obey your signals,
> whenever you prepare the preludes
> of the choir-leading introductions,
> you even quench the pointed thunderbolt
> of ever-flowing fire.
> And the eagle sleeps on the scepter of Zeus,
> drooping his swift wing on both sides.
<note>This is a translation of the Greek passage from Pindar's First Pythian Ode.</note>

Taught by sacred texts, we know that David, by the sweetness of the sounds of the cithara, was able to dispel the mind of Saul when it was disturbed by melancholic fury (*1 Samuel 16:24*). This seemed a miracle to many in the past, and would seem so even now, unless we knew what that cithara was, as Johann Ferus writes in his second sermon on St. Boniface, folio 99. David, by plucking the cithara, sang divine praises, mercy, and truth, and invoked God himself; and by this song, by this sound, he was able to drive away the evil Spirit; otherwise, faith and the harmony of the cithara would have achieved nothing. Let Amphion of Thebes lay down his lyre here, let Arion of Methymna yield, let Orpheus of Thrace be silent—though they were illustrious musicians, though skilled in touching the lyre. That holy player of the Lyre, the Royal Prophet David, truly the <term>pleasant Psalmist of Israel <note>Hebrew: "na'im zemirot Yisrael"</note></term> of all, stops up your lyres and citharas. All the Davidic Psalms show the cithara of David was struck by the Holy Spirit. Hence, with an elegant compound word, Theophanes calls it the <term>Spirit-cithara <note>Greek: "pneumatokitharan"</note></term>. A species of the cithara was the <term>kinyra <note>Greek: "kinyra"</note></term>, from the Phoenician <term>Cinnor <note>Hebrew: "Kinnor"</note></term>, from which "Cinyra" comes, which Suidas notes was a name given to the King of the Cyprians; 
<margin>Hom. 12. p. 74. Il. 11. 20.</margin>
Homer also mentions it with praise:
> Which once Cinyras gave to him to be a guest-gift.

<column-break/>

Meanwhile, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint translators</note> use this word here, and that which follows, <term>naulon <note>Greek: "naulon"</note></term>, which in Hebrew is <term>Nebel <note>Hebrew: "Nebel"</note></term>, in place of which the Vulgate has "lyre" and Pagninus has "nablium." But what kind of instrument it was, we are ignorant today. What is the *diapsalma*? What is the *Psaltery*? What is *Alamoth*? What is *LeneZeach*? What are the titles? Whether they are other musical instruments or merely signs, our writers willingly confess their ignorance; see Augustine on *Psalm 3, p. 22; Psalm 42, p. 387; Psalm 58, p. 582.* Also Victor Strigel on *1 Chronicles 16, p. 452.* For there were various choirs of Musicians who sang in turn with different instruments. Sometimes the voice preceded the instrument, and the instrument maintained the proper melodies; sometimes the instrument preceded, and the voice sang along; sometimes both voices and instruments sounded together. Thus the Levites sang <term>with all kinds of fir wood instruments and all musical vessels</term>. Thus, in the bringing up of the Ark of the Lord, the same phrase is used of David and the people playing <term>before the Lord with all kinds of fir wood instruments and with sistrums <note>Hebrew: "mena'ane'im"</note></term>. The Hebrew name comes from "to move" (to be moved or shaken). Thus they are so named in the Hebrew *Sifra* because they move men to movement and dancing with a shrill sound, as Kimchi writes in his *Book of Roots*. Pagninus renders it "with things that move"; for the Hebrew word denotes frequent shaking through the doubling of the root letters. Whence Piscator of Herborn says of this musical instrument: *The sistrum signifies a musical instrument made of metal (such as bronze, silver, or gold), hollow, narrow, and curved, which when struck gave a sound; invented by the Egyptians and used by them in the rites of Isis, as well as in calling the people together, etc. It can be translated into German as an "Egyptian Clang-pipe" <note>original: "Clangrohr"</note>.* Amidst these common and universal joys, David—our Simonides, Pindar, and Alcaeus—is depicted dancing by Michal as if he were a most base person, where in the old interpretation the name "Scurra" <note>Buffoon/Jester</note> occurs. Regarding this word, Johannes de Janua writes: *Scurra: a glutton, a vain-talker. A scurra is especially said to be one who follows the court for the sake of food.* And in the second book of Kings: *And he uncovered himself, as if one of the buffoons were uncovered.* Scurrility is such gluttony, foulness, shameful play, and lewd words, which is commonly called "barrizare." David is mocked while he plays before the Lord to testify to the joy of his soul, which he took from the legitimate establishment of Divine worship. But *good is the play,* says Bernard in *Epistle 87*, *at which Michal is angry and God is delighted. A good play, which is indeed ridiculous to men, but provides a most beautiful spectacle to Angels. A good play, I say, by which we are made a reproach to the wealthy and a contempt to the proud.* Let us play with David, even if we are mocked; let us sing to the Lord songs of praise with him on this earth, and sing psalms to Him seven times a day. There remains another Music in heaven, the fame of whose melody cannot now be described by our tongue. This Triumphal Music in the Church Triumphant will be with full voice, in voice, without voice, in sound, without sound, in a voice and sound of perpetual exultation. Hymns, songs, and heavenly odes will be sung without annoyance, without labor, without interruption. There the voices of Angels and godly men...

<meta>This page continues a theological and historical commentary, transitioning from a meditation on heavenly music to a critique of the rebellion of Absalom against King David.</meta>

# On 2 Samuel XVII. v. 1

<margin>Sacred Music.</margin>
...with the highest harmony they will praise without ceasing, **Holy, Holy, Holy**. There, nothing will be in the voice that is not also in the mind. There, the affections shall sound and harmonize with the voices. There, the song of Moses shall resonate: *Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified* <note>Exodus 15:1</note>. There, from every tribe and tongue, and people and nation, there shall be one voice: *Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord of Sabaoth*. There shall be perfect Music, perfect joy, perpetual Music, by the taste of which the Church, being inflamed, sighs for that celestial choir and cries out: *Let us depart, let us depart hence to the Music which shall be in the heavens*. This is the prayer of the Church; let it also be mine.

### II. SAM. XVII. v. 1.

->And Ahithophel said to Absalom: "Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue David tonight." <note>Original: Hebrew text provided in source</note><-

->And Ahithophel said to Absalom: "I will choose for myself twelve thousand men, and arising I will pursue after David tonight." <note>Original: Greek Septuagint text provided in source</note><-

->*Ahithophel therefore said to Absalom: I will choose for myself twelve thousand men, and arising I will pursue David this night.* <note>Original: Latin Vulgate text provided in source</note><-

<margin>The Rebellion of Absalom.</margin>
Absalom, the worst son of the best parent, was so in name only, not in reality <term>Abessalon</term> <note>The author plays on the etymology of the name: 'Ab' (Father) and 'Shalom' (Peace)</note>. He is interpreted as "the Father's peace," not because he had any peace with his Father, but because the Father showed how much peace and patience existed in the face of the son's perversity; these are the words of *Gregory in the 7th Penitential Psalm, folio 39b*. The Father, a man after God's own heart, learned to endure hardships; the Son, a man after the world's heart, knew not how to endure them. The Father was a lover of peace. The son Absalom was most greedy for sedition and novelty on account of the virginal honor snatched from his sister by his brother Amnon; when the parent let him go unpunished, Absalom established a terrible example of cruelty upon him. He was plainly injurious to the laws of hospitality when he unhesitatingly crushed his brother—who feared no evil—with a wicked, albeit avenging, hand. Guilty of slaughter, he changed his native soil for exile and for a time withdrew from his parent's wrath. When Joab did not dare to directly intercede for Absalom, he suborned a clever woman, by whose indirect speech Absalom was reconciled to the Father; though barred for a time from the King's food and roof, he finally obtained the right to see the Father's face which had been denied him. After some time, he sought the paternal kingdom and scepter with a greater crime. He affects a kingdom which others, when offered, refuse. Rare indeed are the examples of such modesty, yet found in Gideon, who, when asked to rule, replied: *I will not rule over you, nor shall my son rule over you, but the Lord shall rule*, Judges 8:23. A wise response, as one who was not unaware of the burden of empire, according to the saying: *Many things are a care to a kingly man and a leader of armies* <note>Original Greek: πολλ’ ἀνδρὶ βασιλεῖ καὶ στρατηλάτη μέλη</note>. Just as the immodesty and headlong judgment of the common folk is noted, *Gordian* despised the honors of empire, and *Maximinus* despised them, but so that tumults might be prevented, both finally agreed: regarding both, one should read *Herodian, book 6, p. 248 and book 7, p. 268*. Frederick III, Duke of Saxony, gave the greatest thanks to the nobles (to use an example from our own age) for having offered him the Empire. Far different was the mind of our Absalom, who through right and wrong, through disturbances and tumults, invaded the scepters of his Father. For the sake of reigning, he thought justice should be violated, saying with Eteocles in Euripides:
<margin>Phoenician Women, v. 527.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>The Rebellion of Absalom.</margin>
> For if one must do wrong, for the sake of tyranny
> it is most noble to do wrong; in other matters one should be pious. <note>Original Greek: Εἴπερ γὰρ ἀδικεῖν χρὴ...</note>

What does ambition not devise! No one else is worthy of the name of Prince than he who has been held worthy by legitimate reason. Outside of this, so far is there from being a certain guardianship of status, that on the contrary, there is most certain not only danger but destruction. Absalom courts with ambition, thinking:
<margin>Homer, Iliad, book 6, 208.</margin>
> Always to be the best and to be superior to others. <note>Original Greek: αἰὲν ἀριστεύειν...</note>

Thinking all things beneath him, neither David his Father above him, nor his brothers beside him; and while he wishes to bear neither an equal nor a superior, he overturns both himself and the empire. Different was the mind of Titus toward his parent while subduing all of Judea; different was the observance of Gelon toward his parent, who considered greater glory for himself from piety toward his parent than from the dignity with which he was illustrated by the unanimous vote and consent of the people. There is an excellent testimony of this love in the *Excerpts of Polybius* gathered by the great collector Constantine Porphyrogenitus:
<margin>page 12.</margin>
> Gelon, having lived more than 80 years, set forth a noble goal: that in life, it is good to obey one's parent, and to value neither wealth, nor the greatness of kingship, nor anything else more than goodwill and faithfulness toward one's parents. <note>Original Greek: Γέλων πλείω τῶν π' βιώσας...</note>

Borrhäus (col. 529) recounts the causes for seeking the kingdom; see them there. However, so that he might become master of his desire, he meditates on various deceits, for it seemed advisable to him *to court and worm his way into the favor of the powerful*, to speak with Plutarch (*Alcibiades, p. 204*). His first step was in conciliating the favor of the common people, for he could proceed by no more convenient way than *to flatter the people*, says Aeschines against Ctesiphon. Absalom, therefore, acts in this matter as a true <term>demokopos</term> <note>A "people-pleaser" or "crowd-cutter"</note>; a *demokopos* is said to be a man who labors greatly for the grace of the plebeians, and through any zeal catches the popular breeze, creeping in by art so that he may conciliate the common folk to himself. Others wrongly explain it as an attacker of the people, an exhauster of the people, or likewise, popular labor. It is the same as an <term>ochlokopos</term> <note>A "mob-pleaser"</note>: to this also belongs the <term>demagogue</term>, who is accustomed to entice and creep up on the multitude with speeches; compare Budaeus 811 from Plutarch, Stephanus line 969, Reinesius *Various Readings* 9, p. 30. Such leaders of the people were Agesilaus, Pisistratus, and others. In the person of Agamemnon, I seem to see Absalom himself; a simulated humility is reproached in him by the Poet, by which he opened his doors to any of the commoners and enticed all with conversation, seeking with dyed manners to buy empire from the common folk. These are the verses of Euripides, *Iphigenia in Aulis, v. 337*, in which Menelaus thus pursues his ambition:

> You know when you were striving to lead the Danaans to Ilium,
> appearing not to want it but in your heart desiring it,
> how humble you were, grasping every right hand,
> and keeping doors unlocked for any of the townsfolk who wished,
> and giving a turn to speak to all in order, even if one did not wish it,
> seeking by these ways to buy ambition in the midst. <note>Original Greek: Οἶσθ' ὁτ' ἐσπούδαζες...</note>

Absalom does the same. It was the custom to salute Kings and the sons of Kings from a distance, so much so that even those far removed would prostrate themselves on the ground and roll at their feet. Majesty required not running to meet anyone, nor admitting into embraces, except those like oneself. So far was it from being permitted to touch the royal mouth with a squalid mouth. This would have been shameful and beneath majesty. The sanctity of the royal...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Absalom's Rebellion.</margin>
The prestige of a name has always been great among Orientals, and among the Persians so great that they venerated the face of their King as an <term>image of God <note>original Greek: εἰκόνα θεῦ</note></term>. It was no less so among the Jews, for whom nothing was more venerable than their King. Absalom could have taken a portion of this honor for himself. But what of that flatterer of the people? He did not maintain the distant expression of some ox-herd or shepherd, but at the mere sight of the lowliest person, he joined right hand to right hand, entwined arm in arm, and applied face to face as if with bonds of love. Thus, while David was unaware, he craftily stole away Israel, which is best expressed by the word <insert>stole <note>Hebrew: גנב (ganav)</note></insert> <margin>2 Samuel 15:6.</margin> where we read: <insert>And Absalom stole the hearts of the men [of Israel]</insert>. By fraud he captured the people and caused them to withdraw. If anyone pronounced him worthy of Empire at the beginning, the pretender admitted nothing less: *“Let my Father care for the Empire; let it be my Father’s role to reign,”* he would say, *“my only glory is to deserve the favor of my Father’s obedient subjects; it is enough for me to be regarded as courteous, pious, humane, and merciful.”* To him, flatterers doubtless replied: *“To deserve is a matter of virtue, to attain is a matter of fortune.”* Another would extol his form as worthy of the scepter, while disparaging the Father as morose and gloomy. *“The kingdoms are owed to him who casts them aside. May God preserve you for the Kingdom! Truly Royal offspring. Your safety is the safety of the kingdom.”* It was easy for those experienced in prudent practice to suspect what Absalom’s flatteries would lead to: namely, that evil was imminent for the Kingdom and the King. That smooth-talking and unusual benevolence toward the common people betrayed a mind greedy for rule. He had conceived a hatred for his Father; his old exile burned within him, the malice of which had not yet faded from his mind. The youth swelled with the hatred and pride of an impotent soul. David held an enemy in his own bosom and in his own embrace. With subtle art and wicked deceit, he had long ago begun the web which he then uncovered. He who had shed a brother's blood did not fear to pour out his Father's. Nor were there lacking henchmen for this crime, who day by day tickled his mind, which was most hungry for the kingdom. Ahithophel—a Jewish Cleon <note>Cleon was a populist Athenian general known for demagoguery</note>, <term>shaking and disturbing all of Judea <note>original Greek: σείων καὶ ταράττων πᾶσαν τὴν Ἰυδαίαν</note></term>, the torch and Fury of his fatherland—was the first and foremost director of evil counsels, and the only one to whom Absalom had opened the secrets of the conspiracy. Without doubt, he added fire to fire, saying: “Who is like you? Seize the kingdom which you hold in your hand. You will be received by the prayers of all. The faces of all are turned toward you.” It was deliberated how the Parent’s scepter was to be snatched away and the kingdom attacked. An opportunity was present, by no means to be neglected, for thrusting the Parent from the throne and intruding himself. For he had previously strengthened himself with the favor of the Common People, who possess neither reason nor sense (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Antiquities* Book 6). But that nature is unstable, seditious, and discordant, greedy for new things and opposed to quiet (*Sallust, Jugurthine War*). Indeed, a reciprocal love and mutual bond is required between <term>the ruler and the ruled <note>original Greek: τὸν ἄρχοντα καὶ τὸν ἀρχόμενον</note></term>. The subject is guarded so that he who guards may be loved. The guardian loves the subject so that he may be loved in return. Subjects are of a "bad flour" <note>a bad sort</note> who, at any breeze—not even an immediately flattering one—send a message of defiance to their Lords. Just as the inconstancy of the Israelite commoners is certain, so its cause is not simple. A common cause found everywhere is <term>fickleness <note>original Greek: πολυτροπία</note></term>, which, if not restrained by a bridle, is accustomed to break out into violence, as Phocylides says <margin>v. 93.</margin>:
-><term>The people are like water and fire, all uncontrollable things. <note>original Greek: λαὸς τοὶ καὶ ὕδωρ, καὶ πῦρ ἀκατάσχετα πάντα.</note></term><-

<column-break/>

When David was to be anointed over Israel, all the tribes of Israel came to him saying: <insert>*Behold, we are your bone and your flesh*</insert>. <margin>Absalom's Rebellion. 2 Samuel 5:1.</margin> But now, with Absalom <term>moving everything, disturbing everything, and troubling everything <note>original Greek: πάντα κινῦντι, πάντα θορυβῦντι καὶ ὀχλῦντι</note></term> in his Father's kingdom, the entire common crowd clings to him, having abandoned David, so that we can easily apply that verse of the poet Phocylides (v. 92):
-><term>Trust not the people; the crowd is fickle. <note>original Greek: λαῷ μὴ πίστευε. πολύτροπός ἐστιν ὅμιλος.</note></term><-
He who hunts for the favor of the Common People is skillfully called <term>a pleaser of the people <note>original Greek: δημοχαρής</note></term>, which properly sounds like "gratifying the people." Such a "Demochares" was Absalom: for he first enticed the people with his beautiful form, so that he might be greatly praised by men for it; for, as the *sacred words* <margin>2 Samuel 14:25.</margin> say, "Like Absalom <insert>there was no man so beautiful in all Israel to be praised greatly</insert>; from the sole of his foot even to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him." He was greatly praiseworthy, <term>exceedingly lauded <note>original Greek: αἰνετὸς σφόδρα</note></term>, or, as the Old Translator has it, *exceedingly comely*, so that, as Vatablus explains, men praised him vehemently, and he was worthy to be most highly praised for his beauty. Beauty is a quality worthy of commendation <margin>†24.</margin> in a man if it is graced by internal gifts of the soul. Nothing is more ardently desired than beauty, nothing more powerful to move the soul; and therefore, nothing is more suspicious. Beauty has detained many who were proceeding toward honest things and twisted them in the opposite direction. With beauty Absalom deceived his sister; he deceived the people. Absalom's exterior was smooth and mild, but his interior was most bitter. Absalom's beauty was more treacherous than it was fair. How light and unfaithful it was in Saul, the history of the King teaches; Borrhäus, commenting here on the words of the text, applied his example to Absalom: *“Praise comes from the beauty of the body, relying on which he seems to have affected the kingdom, knowing that Saul, commended for his beauty, had similarly reached the kingdom. These two and others are examples that minds often do not correspond to the beauty of bodies.”* Wherefore Isocrates skillfully said that those who had a beautiful body but a deformed soul had a good ship but a bad pilot. In both, Saul and Absalom, the image of hypocrites is figured, who, selling themselves by external appearance, ambitiously aspire to great things. As far as Saul's beauty is concerned <margin>1 Samuel 9:2.</margin>, he is called <insert>choice and handsome <note>Hebrew: בחור וטוב (bachur va-tov)</note></insert>, *chosen and beautiful, flourishing in age and handsome, and there was not anyone among the children of Israel more beautiful than he; from his shoulder and upward he was taller than all the people.* Both Saul and Absalom were <term>fair in form <note>original Greek: μορφῆν ἀεισοι</note></term>, but <term>most wicked in mind <note>original Greek: mente κάκισοι</note></term>, men who did not deserve to be commended for the beauty of their souls. Those are easily deceived who think that beautiful souls are clothed in beautiful bodies, and that deformed souls are surrounded by a baser appearance of bodies. The Jewish leaders, seeking men for themselves whose <term>appearance was worthy of sovereignty <note>original Greek: εἶδω- ἄξιον τυραννίδο</note></term>, looked only at naked beauty and stature of body, and they were deceived; for Saul perished in his sins, as we read <margin>1 Chronicles 10:13.</margin> <insert>in his transgression <note>Hebrew: במעלו (be-ma'alo)</note></insert>. So also Absalom died, pierced through in his transgressions. Absalom was of a mind least royal, although he sought the kingdom, and he was of a beauty unworthy of Empire; a premature hope of succession cast him down from Power. He was indeed of a most beautiful face, but of a far worse soul. Plato the Most Wise, in Book 7 of the *Republic*, wishes the Guardians of the Republic...

# From 2 Samuel 17, v. 1
## The Rebellion of Absalom

<margin>Absalom's Rebellion.</margin> ...not only ought they to be **most constant and most brave**, but also **most powerful**, and as much as possible, **most handsome**. Absalom was neither <note>referring to the moral qualities</note>; in his beautiful body dwelt a wicked nature, just as Marcus Lollius used to joke about Galba—who was famous for his eloquence, but whose physical appearance ruined the effect. <note>Macrobius, *Saturnalia* 2, ch. 6.</note> Each person should be measured not so much by external bodily gifts as by internal gifts of the soul, according to a very old proverb: *do not reckon the labor, but what is in it.* <note>Greek: μὴ λογίζου τὸν πόνον, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἐν αὐτῷ.</note> Nevertheless, praise is intensified and heaped up if the gifts of the soul are also commended by the gifts of the body. Although these things might perhaps be thought vain, they nevertheless acquire a great deal of veneration for a Prince, as Pliny testifies in *Epistle 10* and by the vote of Virgil:

<margin>5th Aeneid.</margin>
->*Virtue is more pleasing coming from a beautiful body.*<-
Hence that saying: *An appearance worthy of Priam's empire.* And Homer describes King Agamemnon thus:
->*In eyes and head like Zeus who delights in thunder.*<-
-><note>Greek: ὄμματα καὶ κεφαλὴν ἴκελος Διὶ τερπικεραύνῳ.</note><-
And the Latin Poet <note>Virgil</note> on the form of Prince Aeneas:
->*And he shone in the clear light,*<-
->*In face and shoulders like a God.*<-

Publius Scipio Africanus, besides the fact that by his very nature there was much majesty in him, was adorned by his long hair and a physical bearing not cultivated with refinements but manly and truly military. <note>Livy 28, ch. 35.</note> Furthermore, the firmness and height of his body, the honor of his head, and the dignity of his face, etc., showed Trajan to be a Prince far and wide, says Pliny in his *Panegyric*, ch. 4. The honor of the head, the dignity of the face, and long hair would have adorned **Absalom, if he had not overthrown himself by getting ahead of himself. When he thinned the hair of his head (v. 26 of chapter 14), for he used to thin it every year because the hair weighed him down, he would weigh the hair of his head at two hundred shekels by the royal weight.** Beauty, which was placed in the fit arrangement of the hair and its weight, is added to the handsome constitution of the body, so that there was veneration even in the extraordinary appearance of the hair. If his soul had been as rooted in virtue as his head was in the beauty of his hair, the dignity of the soul would have commended the grace of the body, and would have added the "vote of beauty" to his virtue—to speak with Latinus Pacatus <margin>Panegyric ch. 6 & 7.</margin>—and a most august appearance, if it is rooted in virtue, increases from one thing to another, and when equals are joined, both are greater. How badly, therefore, did the Jews act, who with the common rabble (according to Tacitus <margin>1st History, 7.</margin>) wished to compare a Commander to themselves by nothing but the form and grace of his body, despising that divine soul of David; in this they were similar to barbarian men, of whom (I use the words of Curtius <margin>6. 6. 7.</margin>) *veneration exists only in the majesty of their bodies, thinking none others capable of great works than those whom nature has deigned to gift with an extraordinary appearance.* But the Father <note>David</note> behaved worthily, because he did not judge his wicked son by the appearance of his face and the grace of his countenance, but on account of the criminal fratricide <note>the murder of Amnon</note> he wished him to wander in exile, and thereby provoke him to a better mind. But having been appeased by the intercession of the woman of Tekoa and Joab, Absalom is brought into Jerusalem from Geshur (v. 23, 24), and the King said: *“Let him turn aside to his own house, and let him not see my face.”* For two whole years he was not admitted to conversation or the sight of the King, and Joab is called to prepare an entrance for him. Joab did not want to come, although called twice, and from this, burning with rage—

<column-break/>

<margin>Absalom's Rebellion.</margin>
<margin>v. 28, 29, 30. Continued.</margin> —Absalom said to his servants: "Consider Joab’s property near my place, where he has barley; go and set it on fire." The servants carried out the command, and the crop of the field having been set ablaze, Joab came, saying: <margin>v. 31.</margin> *“Why have your servants set my property on fire?”* Joab, from whom the King shrank, also wished to abstain from his company, for he suspected Absalom’s nature was driven by ambition and tyranny. However, the damage inflicted forced Joab to approach him, and the wicked soul, which the beauty of the body covered, was betrayed by his evil deeds. The son of the King, who was aiming for great things, took it badly that he was being despised. Joab is then sent to the King to say: <margin>v. 32.</margin> *“Why did I come from Geshur? It would be better for me to still be there; and now I pray, let me see the King’s face; but if there is guilt in me, let him kill me.”* On these words Borrhaus says: <margin>col. 524.</margin> *“Lying hypocrisy betrays itself; for these were not the words of one loving his Father, but of one seeking an opportunity, under the appearance of friendship, to lay snares for him to invade the kingdom. He does not acknowledge the crime of his Brother killed through treachery—which was the act of one despising the divine law 'Thou shalt not kill'—and he despises the just expostulation of his father, nourishing hatred against him.”* That hatred soon broke out, which he covered with certain courtly ceremonies; for when he had come to the King, with a feigned appearance **he prostrated himself before him (v. 33) with his face upon the ground.** In the manner of the Orientals, with his face bowed to the earth, he paid honor to the King his Father, whose kingdom the hypocrite himself was seeking. The Father, ignorant of the plan, kissed Absalom, who was toiling at sedition against him and engineering a conspiracy. To that end, occupied in preparing chariots, cavalry, runners, and winning over the hearts of the Israelites, **he made for himself** <margin>Chapter 15, v. 1.</margin> **chariots, and horses, and fifty men running before him; and rising early in the morning, he stood by the way of the gate, and every man who had a cause to come to the King for judgment, he called and said: 'From what city are you?' And when he answered, 'Your servant is from one of the tribes of Israel,' Absalom said to him: 'See, your words are good and right; but there is no one appointed by the King to hear you.'** <margin>v. 2, 3.</margin> The Absalomic conspirator went about soliciting the multitude against his Father, and if anyone approached the King to seek justice on account of a controversy, Absalom was ready, asking what city he was from, or which of the Israelite tribes? And having heard his cause, he would affirm it was good and just, while remarking that there was no one present to listen. Moreover, the deceiver desired to be appointed judge of the nation, so that the disputes and causes of all might be brought to him, for he would render justice according to equity and the Good, saying: <margin>v. 4.</margin> *“Who will appoint me judge in the land, so that every man who has a suit or judgment* <term>אשר-יהיה-לו ריב-ומשפט</term> <note>Hebrew: "whoever has a dispute or judgment"</note> *might come to me, and I would do him justice.”* He could no longer hide his wicked heart, having used the kind simulation of amiable conversation up to this point; and that which had hidden deep within his breast, he soon poured out entirely in a quasi-fanatical fury. He persuaded the people that the eyes and pockets of his Father David were insatiable, that he could never be satisfied, that he was lavish in bribes and expenses, that the causes of the subjects were handled negligently, and that justice—the primary [virtue] of royal Majesty—[was lacking].

Hushai is sent to the court of the new King to offer his service and confirm his loyalty against David, so that he might fish out the plans of Ahithophel and, through the intermediaries Ahimaaz and Jonathan, report what Ahithophel prepared for David’s destruction. He resolved to catch out deceit and trickery with trickery—if it can be called "deceit" to be vigilant for one's own innocence. For after he knew he could achieve nothing by an open path, he wished first to try a <term>seemly deception</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀπάτη εὐπρεπὴς"</note>, to use a term from Thucydides, against a crafty enemy. Thus "one fallacy pushes out another," to use a Terentian phrase, and the fallacy of one man, Hushai, pushes out and eludes that of the other, Ahithophel. Cunning is repaid with cunning, and the Counselor who thinks to deceive another is himself deceived by a Counselor. Hushai was chosen because he was skilled in affairs and well-suited for such stratagems. David had barely finished praying:

---

<margin>
v. 31.
fol. 532.
</margin>
<term>O Lord, I pray, turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness</term> <note>original Hebrew: "סַכֶּל-נָא אֶת-עֲצַת אֲחִיתֹפֶל יְהֹוָה"</note>, and immediately a man of circumspect integrity, Hushai, is sent to intercept counsel with counsel. While I freely enjoy the fruits of this shared lineage, Borrhaus provides a small contribution; he says: *"This is an example of the divine care God has for the godly. As soon as David prayed, 'Make the counsel of Ahithophel foolish,' God immediately offered him Hushai, a man endowed with prudence, counsel, and eloquence, to oppose the craftiness of Ahithophel. He understood that 'one nail must be driven out by another'—that is, arts must be conquered by arts, and counsels by counsels. Therefore, although he knew the Lord renders the plans of devious men hollow, this present example proves that God also uses the ministry of men in such matters. Weighing this, David preferred his Friend to return to the city to dissolve Ahithophel's plans rather than keep him with him at the risk of both."* Here we have an image of the faithful and the unfaithful Counselor, even from one and the same court: one an inciter of disturbances and an instigator of dissensions, the other their extinguisher; one of unswerving integrity, the other of unswerving malice. One has a defamed name, the other the best reputation. One goes to seize the dignity and empire of his King; the other goes to preserve it. How great is the honor of the one who bore the name of Hushai, because he is called the FRIEND of David. Look into yourselves, you who are of the councils—this word was not recorded by the holy writer in vain. Look, you who are inner courtiers, for you who have inner admission to Princes are especially

touched by this most friendly title. By this name the Emperor <term>Titus</term> addressed his intimates; according to Suetonius, he chose Friends whose advice he and the Republic relied upon even after him. Consider these "Friends" not as those Titus held in domestic and private life joined by personal friendship, but those he loved and chose for the sake of public utility, by whose counsels he was guided. Thus Capitolinus says of Antoninus Pius: *He never decided on any acts unless he first referred them to his Friends.* Among this class of Friends to good Princes, there were certainly also the Jurists. The Divine Brothers <note>The Emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus</note> in <term>Law 17 of the Digest on the right of patronage</term> say: *Volusius Maecianus, our Friend, and a diligent seeker of civil law.* And shortly after: *When we were discussing this with Maecianus himself and our other friends skilled in the law.* But others also, to whom the Prince committed some part of the Republic to administer, were called his Colleagues, Companions, Friends, and even Parents. In this way, Emperor Alexander Severus calls <term>Ulpian</term> his "parent" in <term>Law 4 of the Code on hiring</term>. So too an Emperor is said to choose a "Father" for himself in the <term>Institutes</term>, regarding Eutropius the Patrician under Claudius:

Book 2, ch. 127.

A Prince cannot embrace everything by his own knowledge alone (Tacitus, <term>Annals 3. 69</term>). Rarely have eminent men not used great assistants to govern their fortune (Velleius Paterculus). I judge him who conducts everything by his own single opinion to be more proud than wise (Livy, <term>Book 44, ch. 22</term>). Certainly, the Emperor Justinian was not alone; when he administered everything by his own judgment (<term>αὐτογνώμως</term>), he threw the Republic into many disasters, says Zonaras.

<margin>
Vol. 3, p. 75. 14.
</margin>
Happy, therefore, is the court in which a good Prince has Counselors who observe the rules of justice. Unhappy is the court and kingdom where counselors indulge the evil inclinations of their Princes. Cambyses committed many deeds of foul monstrosity and madness, according to Herodotus (Book 3). But his Counselors gave no warnings; rather, they flattered him. He married his sister; when he asked the Jurists for advice on this, they replied that they had no law expressly allowing it, but they had found another law: that the King of the Persians might do whatever he wished. Furthermore, when he asked his Counselors if he was like his father Cyrus, they placed him far above his father because he had added Egypt to the Persian kingdom. What the Ahithophel-like flatteries, simulations, and counsels were is plain to see. We consider the Court of Absalom somewhat more deeply: we find in it hidden hatreds, perennial cares for evil, feuds, deceits, lies, frauds, lust for another's glory, arrogance, empty fear, false friends, factious men, the envious, and the treacherous! Behold, the court of Absalom was composed of such "Cadmean brothers" <note>A reference to the warriors who sprang from dragon's teeth and killed each other</note>! The court of Alexander Severus was most happy because of the integrity of his Counselors, *for he had friends who were holy and venerable, not malicious, not thieving, not lustful, not deceitful, not factious, not crafty, not consenting to evil, not enemies of the good, not cruel, not circumventors of him, not mockers who would lead him around as if he were a fool; but...*

It draws parallels between biblical counselors and the "Friends of the Prince" in Roman history, emphasizing the necessity of virtuous advisors for a stable state.</summary>

# 358 BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Absalom's Rebellion.</margin>
...holy, venerable, temperate, religious men who love their Prince; men who would neither laugh at him themselves nor wish him to be a laughingstock; who would sell nothing, lie about nothing, feign nothing, and never deceive the reputation of their Prince, but rather love him—as Aelius Lampridius reports in his *Life of Alexander Severus, page 223.* They turn to counsel: for just as great matters require great helpers—or as Heliodorus says, *great affairs require great preparations* <note>original Greek: τὰ μεγάλα τῶν πραγμάτων, μεγάλων δεῖται κατασκευῶν</note>—so do evil matters require evil helpers. What (curse it!) was this madness of Ahitophel, to do evil to one by whom he was not harmed even by a word? What was that wickedness <note>original Greek: κακουργία</note> by which he persecuted an innocent man with his advice, and one by whom he had been raised up with great favors? David composed a long complaint concerning this man's treachery in *Psalm 41*, where he laments that Ahitophel, who was previously among his most intimate friends, had now become a most savage enemy. Just as he was once joined to him in friendship, he had now become a Lycaon <note>A mythical king turned into a wolf; a reference to savage transformation</note>, forgetting past merits and attempting to snatch away the King's dignity, dominion, and life. For he was not content that by his advice Absalom defiled his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel to show the greatest contempt for David; rather, he directed his counsel toward removing David from the scene so that Absalom might possess affairs in peace. To this end, he offered himself as the leader to pursue and kill David. What Polydamas <note>A Trojan counselor</note> would have dared then to face this Hector? But behold: the Counselor of that Pretender-King, who could do everything, soon could do nothing. *All-powerful, then somewhat powerful, then weak.* <note>original Greek: Παντοδύναμος, ὁτιδύναμος καὶ ἐπιδανός</note> For his treachery finally found its own noose, and the supplanter is supplanted. For it is true what Sophocles says regarding a bad conscience in evil counsels:

<margin>Trachiniae, line 735.</margin>
> *In plans that are not honorable,*
> *there is no hope that can provide any confidence.*
> <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν τοῖς μὴ καλοῖς βελεύμασιν / εὐδ' ἐλπὶς, ἥτις καὶ θράσος τι προξενεῖ</note>

Thus, by the will and direction of God, the cunning man found one more cunning than himself. For when Hushai <note>spelled Chusai in the Latin text</note> was asked by Absalom to declare what he thought, he advised thus: *I counsel you that all Israel be gathered to you from Dan to Beersheba, like the sand of the sea for multitude, and that your own face go into the battle.* The reasoning of the counsel consisted in this: that he should collect all the Israelite forces and lead them himself in war. For in this way, the war would proceed more expeditiously. When Ahitophel was consulted about this expedition, he had said: *I will choose twelve thousand men.* On the contrary, Hushai advised that all Israel must be summoned, and that Absalom himself should be the leader. For the presence of the leader is noted in the word *paneka* <note>Hebrew: פניך</note> which signifies "face" and "countenance." Your face, he said, *shall go into the midst of the battle.* <note>Hebrew: הולכים בקרבם</note> The Old Version says: *You shall be in the midst of them.* The Septuagint: *Your face proceeding in the midst of them.* <note>original Greek: τὸ πρόσωπόν σε πορευόμενον ἐν μέσῳ αὐτῶν</note> They read the word *bekerev* <note>in the midst</note> with different vowel points. Thus Luther: *Your person shall march among them.* <note>original German: Deine Person ziehe unter ihnen</note> Nor does the Targum differ: *And you shall go at the head of us all.* <note>original Aramaic: ברש כלנא</note> Absalom was the head of the war, and Hushai wanted Absalom to rouse the men of war by his own "face" or presence. Ahitophel had urged that the army be committed to him, while Absalom stayed in the Palace.

<margin>Bornhaus, column 543.</margin>
Hushai advised the opposite, not indeed to help Absalom with his counsel, but to destroy the foul man, having obtained a space of time in which David might escape to safer places and Absalom might perish miserably in battle. He exaggerated to Absalom how much depended on the leader's

<column-break/>

presence. Everyone applauded this counsel.
<margin>Absalom's Rebellion.</margin>
But Ahitophel, the impious urger of waging war against David, to whom all affairs had hitherto been committed, when he felt himself neglected because of the new advice, took the unexpected counsel of Hushai as an occasion for despair. Having finally become a victim of a "sinister choking" <note>original Greek: συναγχώνης σκαὶὸς</note> and "self-condemned" <note>original Greek: αὐτοκατάκριτος</note>, he condemned himself and, with a broken spirit, hastened his own death. The Rabbis wonder what sort of sadness of mind he fell into, by which he was affected because his counsel had not succeeded; for they think it absurd to say of a wise and prudent man that he hanged himself. But that evil counselor strangled himself with a "noose" <note>anchone</note>, not a "sore throat" <note>synanche</note>. A witty allusion occurs here, which arose concerning Demosthenes: when he was reluctant to speak against the Milesians, he feigned a *sore throat* <note>synanche</note>, to which one of the people shouted that it was not a *sore throat* the orator was suffering from, but *silver-throat* <note>argyranche - i.e., he was bribed</note>; not the *jaundice* <note>original German: Gelbsucht</note>, but the *gold-lust* <note>original German: Geldsucht</note>, as noted by Gellius and Plutarch in the *Life of Demosthenes, page 857.* Pollux recorded that it was Demades who spoke that jest. In the same way, we say it was not a *sore throat* <note>synanche</note> that Ahitophel suffered, but the *noose* <note>anchone</note>. For while he saw that his bloody plans against his King did not succeed according to his heart's desire, the treacherous man laid violent hands on himself and perished by hanging. Thus the evil fell back upon his own head, and he who had broken faith with his throat was broken by the throat. Thus the testimony of the Verse holds true: *Whoever devises deceits against another, unknowingly builds the evil for himself.* <note>original Greek: Ὅστις καθ᾽ ἑτέρου δόλια μηχανεύεται, αὐτῷ λέληθε τὸ κακὸν ἀρχιτεκτονῶν</note> In this appears what the Roman Senate said in Livy:

<margin>Book 44, chapter 15.</margin>
*For the most part, fraud, even if cautious at the beginning, detects itself.* As Gunther writes:
<margin>Book V, 419.</margin>
> *The unspeakable engine of fraud was useless to the wretched,*
> *And destined for great evil; by a divine nod,*
> *The wicked enemy fell into the pit which he had dug.*

It is usually held and said, and indeed rightly, that a Counselor is the *Eye of the Prince* <note>Latin: Princeps Oculus</note>, if he is faithful. A certain Pseudartabanus, called the Counselor of the King of the Persians in Aristophanes, was called by the Greek envoys the *King's Eye*; laughing at this most beautiful title, Dicaeopolis says:

> *May a crow strike out*
> *that eye of yours and your envoy's with its blows.*
> <note>original Greek: ἐκκόψειέ γε / Κόραξ πατάξας τόνγε σὸν τῷ πρεσβέως</note>

He does not begrudge the title being given to those who conduct business faithfully in the councils of Princes, but he is angry when it is bestowed on one who would be a corrupter of the Republic. Since Ahitophel was such a corrupter of the Jewish Republic, he was finally sent by the just judgment of God *to the crows* <note>original Greek: πρὸς κόρακας - a Greek idiom for "to the gallows" or "to destruction"</note>, so that crows might pluck out the eyes of the crow who was gaping and seeking the treasures of the kingdom. Warned by the example of Ahitophel, let Kings and Princes learn here to live more cautiously and not to trust anyone too much; let even the noble courtiers, Counselors, and other Ministers be deterred by this example from perjury and treachery, lest they share the same shameful end as the treacherous Ahitophel and be further marked with eternal disgrace by historians. But Hushai, with unbroken faith, continues his most devoted will toward his King, and through mes—

# On 2 Samuel 17:1

<margin>
Absalom’s Rebellion.
</margin>
Faithful messengers report the plans that have been discussed so far in Absalom’s court. Both sides take up arms, and each individual augurs the best for a happy success. Truly, however, success in commands, fortunate plans, salutary governance, and victory are nothing if not the works and blessings of the one God. God teaches the hands <margin>Psalm 144:1</margin> for battle; if you do not stretch out your hand in trust of Him, you will give your hands over to the victor <note>i.e., surrender in defeat</note>. For what is your trust in horses and chariots? A horse is a vain hope for safety <note>original: *fallax equus ad salutem*, Psalm 33:17</note>. What is trust in the arm of man? Vain is the safety of man; God is in virtues. David, forced into battle, performs the duty of a good King; he assembles a modest army and leads them out, fighting with certainty that his plans and the right hand of his soldiers are aided by God. Yet, although Absalom was a man of such wickedness, the Father by no means wished for him to be killed. "Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom," <note>original Hebrew: <term>לאט לנער לי לאבשלום</term></note> he said, which the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> renders as: "Spare for me the young man" <note>original Greek: <term>φείσασθέ μοι τοῦ παιδαρίου</term></note>. The Vulgate: "Save the boy for me." Luther: *Deal gently for me with the boy Absalom.* That word <term>לאט</term> <note>Hebrew: *la'at*</note>, meaning "gently," is explained by Ludovicus de Dieu in his *Observations* (pp. 173-174), who teaches that the Rabbis also understood it this way, though he produces a new explanation which we leave to him. Regarding this leniency of David and his fatherly <term>affection</term> <note>original Greek: <term>στοργὴν</term>, referring to natural familial love</note>, Ambrose writes thus: <margin>Sermon 14 on Psalm 118, p. 302.</margin> *Concerning him who had defiled his Father’s house with shameful conduct, who sought his Father’s life in parricidal battles, the pious Father nevertheless said to those setting out for battle: Spare my son Absalom.* He was silent regarding the crime of his wickedness, but put forward the degree of piety and the name of their kinship, so that those about to fight, thinking not of the King’s Adversary but of his Son, might restrain the grief of wounded piety. Compare Hilary on Psalm 118, p. 500. This crime of Absalom had been preceded by a concern for his fame surviving after death, for which purpose he erected a column for himself so that his memory might be better witnessed. In the King’s Valley, which Josephus writes was two stadia from Jerusalem, he had erected a monument for himself during his life, for he said: *I have no son to keep my name in remembrance; therefore he called the monument by his own name, and it has been called <term>Absalom’s Hand</term> <note>original Hebrew: <term>יד-אבשלום</term>, Yad Avshalom</note> unto this day.* But another monument worthy of his crime remains for him to this day, which Scythianism, Barbarism, and the foreigner erect for him. For whoever passes by, whether of the foreigners or the inhabitants, even the Mohammedans themselves, throws a stone there with a curse, saying: *Cursed be the parricide Absalom, and whoever unjustly persecutes their parents, let them be cursed forever.* Furthermore, Absalom was well-haired, <term>beautiful-haired, long-haired, and with good locks</term> <note>original Greek: <term>καλλόθριξ, καὶ κατάκομος καὶ ἐυτρίχος</term></note>. Indeed, density of hair is believed to be a sign of strength; hence, while Aristotle ascribes the material of hair to heat and fatty moisture contained in the skin, he adds at the same time that its thickness contributes not a little to growth. From this, Goropius Becanus concludes <margin>4 Hieroglyphics, p. 52.</margin> that those who are vehemently hairy and have tough and abundant hair are robust, because the fatty and slow moisture renders the nerves most robust. By this contemplation of the hair, we are led in a way to knowing the temperament and recognizing the strengths of Absalom. The density of such moist material, cooked even to the point of tenacity, is an indication of a hot and dry temperament. A man of such a temperament is considered bold, who in any

<column-break/>

matter to be done or endured has suitable strength. The hairy Absalom takes pride in his hair, and because he sins through the pride of his hair, <margin>Absalom’s Rebellion.</margin> he is therefore punished through and in the same. There is nothing in the body by which one can be more easily held or hindered than by the hair. Absalom experienced this in his flight; for while riding upon a mule under the thick branches of a great oak, his hair became entangled in the oak. The Greek interpreters show him hanging there most clearly, where the Hebrew text has: *He was given <term>between the heavens and the earth</term>* <note>original Hebrew: <term>בין השמים ובין הארץ</term></note>, they translated: *He was hung between heaven and earth* <note>original Greek: <term>Ἐκρεμάσθη ἀνὰ μέσον τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ ἀνὰ μέσον τῆς γῆς</term></note>. Thus, hanging, he paid the deserved penalties, and thus the young man is overwhelmed by the force of the unrest he himself stirred up. For he is struck down by Joab, who acted as a prudent man; even if he wished to withhold his hand from the Son of David, he thought it better that the torch of conspiracy could not be extinguished unless Absalom expired. He knew his fierce spirit, which he decided must be crushed while the opportunity was so favorable, lest if conquered but living, he might rise again more terrible; and so:
> *He paid these penalties for his crimes, having driven out his Parent,*
> *Go now and lay snares for your father's goods.*
With a most lovely poem, George Fabricius of Chemnitz <margin>Vol. 3 German Poets, p. 96.</margin> emphatically described the whole rebellion of Absalom along with his tragic end, which, since it is worthy of preservation <note>original: *cedro dignum*, literally "worthy of cedar oil," used to preserve scrolls</note>, I have chosen to insert into our meditation:

> Absalom, stained with the incestuous blood of his brother,
> Had fled as an exile in haste from his native soil.
> His maternal uncle, the King of Geshur, received him in hospitality,
> Until the rapid anger of his injured Father should cease.
> After three harvests, his parent having been appeased,
> When he returned, he was shut up in the city of Jerusalem.
> Nor was it granted to the son to see the Father’s face,
> While the annual sun twice completed its full circuit.
> And when he entered the royal house by the lead of Joab,
> He received the pardon for his crime which they sought.
-> mind, <-
> Good deeds do not help the wicked: Absalom rages again,
> And seeks to hold the scepter against the will of God.
> The arms he moved before against his brother, the impious one now moves against his parent,
> While he is safe, he thinks himself less safe.
> He wins the favor of the people with words and fraud,
> And attempts to win over his father’s Leaders.
> Promises soothe those greedy for easy snares,
> And he has a title by which he protects his deeds.
> He usurps the holy and venerable name of Justice,
> And fraud lies hidden, covered by the name of honesty.
> And feigning that he wished to fulfill his vows,
> So that he might visit the holy sepulchers of the ancient fathers,
> The crime he had meditated breaks forth.
> For a new King is proclaimed in the city of Hebron,
> The rumor wanders frequently through the land of the Israelites.
> The common folk congratulate the swollen Tyrant on the given scepter:
> Alas for me, how brief a time that joy lasted.
> A great part of the grey-haired senate flows to the youth,
> Among whom the Chief was Ahithophel.
> The lowest crowd of the people aids this tumult
> And takes up arms under the auspices of the new King.
> When the injury reached the unaccustomed ears of the Father,
> The parent scarcely believed the crime of his innate enemy.
> He hurried his departure from the city of Jerusalem in haste,
> And commands chosen men to go with him.
> The best part of the city accompanies him wailing, and the Ark
> Of God is carried out, although the King forbade it.

<margin>Absalom’s Rebellion.</margin>

When we described Absalom, there finally came to mind from the Roman Republic Avidius Cassius, of whom Lucius Verus wrote in a certain letter found in Vulcatius <margin>p. 153.</margin> Gallicanus: *Avidius Cassius is greedy for power, as it seems to me, and as was already known under my grandfather, your Father; I wish you would order him to be watched. All our ways displease him; he is amassing no small wealth, and he mocks our letters. See what must be done. I do not hate the man; but see that you do not fail to consult the interests of yourself and your children, when you have such men among the high-ranking officers whom the soldiers gladly listen to and gladly see.* So it was with Absalom, a man not true to his name <note>Absalom means "Father of Peace"</note>, naming peace while about to invade the peaceful kingdom of his Father; he first amasses no small wealth for himself, marches surrounded by a long line of soldiers, offers his hand and mouth to subjects without distinction, and is such a man among the King's courtiers as the subjects would gladly see as King. Cassius revolted after the death of Verus and allowed himself to be hailed as Emperor of the East <margin>p. 154.</margin> with the consent of Faustina, the wife of Emperor Marcus [Aurelius], who already distrusted Marcus's health and feared she could not protect her infant sons alone, and that someone might arise who, having seized the royal station, would do away with the infants. Absalom, however, revolts before the death of his Father, led no doubt by the counsel of his Mother, who already distrusted and feared that after the King's death Solomon would be preferred, and that someone might arise who, after the departure of her husband, would take action against her son and the whole house. When Avidius had proceeded under the imperial name, he immediately made the man who had fitted him with the royal ornaments the Prefect of the Praetorium. As the Royal name of Absalom proceeded, he raised the Jewish Ahithophel, his Father's apostate Counselor, to the highest station, declaring him Prefect of the military army. But what was the progress of these movements? Marcus Antoninus, having learned of the rebellion,

<column-break/>

was not deeply angered, and having become the victor, <margin>Absalom’s Rebellion. p. 155.</margin> he did not vent his rage upon the authors privy to the defection, but asked the Senate that they not be severely punished. David, hearing of the defection, employs patience; he warns the leader of the army not to do anything severe against Absalom. Avidius is killed; the Praetorian prefect is slain. Absalom perished; Ahithophel perished. When Avidius's head was brought to Marcus, he did not exult, but grieved that the opportunity for mercy had been snatched from him. David grieves; for when the news of the death was heard, what a disturbance in that excellent old man, what consternation! For the stricken King ascended to the chamber over the gate weeping, crying out as he went: *My son, Absalom, my son, my son Absalom. Would that I had died for you, Absalom, my son, my son.* Behold the stupendous <term>storgē</term> <note>original: στοργὴν; Greek for "natural affection" or "parental love"</note>, which conquers even <margin>2 Sam. 18:33</margin> the rebellion of a son. A somewhat stricter judge might consider this an excessive affection. For is not the slaughter of a rebellious enemy joyful news?
> *For a dying enemy brings pleasures.* <note>original: ἔχει γὰρ ἡδονὰς θνήσκων ἀνὴρ ἐχθρός.</note>
And as Sophocles says in *Ajax*: *The sweetest laughter is to laugh at enemies.* <note>original: Γέλως ἥδιστος εἰς ἐχθροὺς γελᾶν.</note> Did he think it mattered that he should still live? But if to deceive enemies <margin>Plutarch, Laconian Apophthegms p. 209.</margin> *is not only just but also sweet and profitable,* it will be much more profitable to kill a warring enemy, for here that saying of Aeschylus will hold:
> *Once a man has died, there is no resurrection.* <note>original: ἅπαξ θανόντος, ὅτις ἔστ' ἀνάστασις.</note>
But if we consider those tearful drops shed by David with the veil of the heart removed, they will appear as drops of contrition and penitence. He deplores the death of a soul in his son, and the bite of conscience in himself, remembering that sentence set forth to him by Nathan: *The sword shall not depart from your house.* From this, judge the fountain of tears with which he waters his cheeks because of a death so sudden, by which his son was taken away without time to repent. Hence Conrad Pellicanus <margin>in Commentary, fol. 128 b.</margin> rightly explains those tears: *Caught in a great crime, he perished in body and soul, and that not without the fault of David. For it was so foretold by the Lord, that for his sin he would suffer evil from his own house. He grieved and wept that this was now happening, and was more bitterly afflicted in conscience because of the cause of the death, which he dared complain of to no one, than because of the evil itself; for he knew, while all others except Nathan were ignorant, that he himself had provided the cause for such severity in divine judgment; therefore he would have preferred to die alone in body, his Spirit being safe, than to experience such scandalous crimes of his sons, and so many deaths, and the misfortunes of his house and kingdom.* He grieved at the malice of his sons, of which he himself had been the cause. He wept that the sins of the sons were the punishments for the father's crimes. From this, now reflect on the tears, and learn to imitate them, you who have sinned greatly. Think in David of that line of Euripides: <margin>in Stobaeus, Oration 49.</margin> *Alas, great things suffer great evils.* <note>original: φεῦ τὰ μεγάλα, μεγάλα καὶ πάσχει κακά.</note> Think in Absalom of that same Poet: <margin>Oration 45.</margin> *No one who has campaigned unjustly has ever returned safe.* <note>original: Οὐδείς στρατεύσας ἄδικα, σῶς ἦλθεν πάλιν.</note>
