<meta>This page begins a detailed historical and theological description of Solomon’s Temple in Jerusalem, comparing its grandeur to the wonders of the classical world.</meta>

# FROM 1 KINGS VIII. v.13.

->1 KINGS VIII. v.13.<-
->Solomon said: I have surely built thee an house to dwell in, a settled place for thee to abide in for ever. <note>original Hebrew: אמר שלמה בנה בניתי בית זבל לך מכון לשבתך עולמים</note><-
->Solomon said: I have built a holy house to your name, prepared for you, and for your seat to dwell in it forever. <note>original Greek: Εἶπε Σολομὼν, Ἐγὼ ᾠκοδόμηκα οἶκον τῷ ὀνόματί σου ἅγιόν σοι καὶ ἕτοιμον, καὶ τῇ καθέδρᾳ σου τῇ κατασκηνῶσαί σε ἐν αὐτῷ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας.</note><-

> Building, I have built a house for your habitation, a most firm throne for you forever. <note>original Latin: Ædificans ædificavi domum in habitaculum tuum, firmissimum solium tuum in sempiternum.</note>

<margin>The Temple of Jerusalem.</margin>
When Pliny recounted the Wonders of the World, he maintained that all of them were far surpassed by those seen in Rome; among which he enumerates these principal ones: the Circus Maximus built by Caesar the Dictator; the Basilica of Paul; the Forum of the Divine Augustus; the Temple of Peace; and the Pantheon made by Agrippa for Jupiter the Avenger. Yet whatever most celebrated works ever existed in the whole world, they were surpassed by the glory of the Temple of Jerusalem. To wish to describe the magnitude, magnificence, <term>architectural skill</term> <note>original Greek: ἀρχιτεκτονικὴν</note>, and opulence of this City and Temple would be the work of a very long commentary. Someone once said of the city of Carthage that it was better to be silent about it than to say too little. The majesty of the Temple of Jerusalem, just as it surpasses the highest intellects, so it is greater than the narrowness of our pen, especially since it is the work not of human inventions but of the Supreme Architect, God. In this one city—which was the head of cities, the glory of all cities, the seat of religion, the theater of laws, the seat of the kingdom, and the throne of the Priesthood—was collected whatever of Majesty or piety could be beheld in all Judea. Here the truth of religion had fixed its seat; here the voice of God was as an Oracle. Great was the splendor there of the High Priest and the entire Hierarchical state. Great was the magnificence here of the Sanhedrin and its members. So great was the structure of the temple here, that famous geniuses in mechanics can scarcely extol it enough with words. Let Archimedes yield here, let Archytas yield, let Ctesibius yield—the most powerful engineers. Let Ephesus boast of its Temple, and proclaim that it had no equal in beams, flooring, or vaulting. Those ignorant of the Temple of Jerusalem will easily extol such things; however, those who are not ignorant of the city and the world will place them in no rank at all. Therefore, the temple must deservedly be placed among the wonders of the world, for no other equal to it will be given throughout the whole world, and it excludes and overshadows all others not only by the magnificence of its material and the variety of its art, but even by the very form of the building and its various treasures. That most wealthy, august, and famous temple, venerable even to profane nations, is worthy to be in eternal memory among all peoples, whether you look at its most magnificent beginning or its most terrible end. When Chrysostom* <margin>Oration on the Nativity of Christ.</margin> considers the matter from its first beginning and primary cause, he says: "When God delivered the Hebrew people from the Egyptian turmoils and the barbarian tyranny, seeing that they still held remnants of impiety and were terrified by all sensible things, and admired the size and beauty of temples, he commanded a temple to be built for them, surpassing all the temples on earth not only in the costliness of the material, nor in the variety of the art, but also in the shape of the building." <note>original Greek: ὅτε τὴν Αἰγυπτιακῶν θορύβων... ἀποκρύπτοντα.</note> Let us be permitted to enter the temple, whose porch we shall see first, admiring not from afar the magnificence that offers itself freely. Let us read judges who are not lowly, but sea-

<column-break/>

<margin>The Temple of Jerusalem.</margin>
soned veterans. Immediately there is a clear prospect, which the inner sanctuary will not provide. The view will be clearly seen, since by the confession of all spectators it lies open and bright without a telescope; for its majesty was so great and its brilliance so great, that it is scarcely within the power of man either to describe its value or to put its freshness into order; all those whose minds are imbued with even a slight knowledge of Sacred antiquity know this. Jerome Prado, Villalpando, Ribera, Adrichomius, and others—leading men in genius and learning—have illustrated this same seat of the Temple, so that it seems superfluous to take up <term>audacity</term> <note>original Greek: θρασύτητα</note> for oneself here and, as the saying goes, "write an Iliad after Homer." But since it is not for everyone to have those laborious books, or, even if they have them, to read them all through, I will briefly comprehend whatever others have handed down in sprawling spaces, and I will make an epitome, lest the summary of memorable things be missed. God had sought for himself David, a man after his own heart, who in the midst of his afflictions had collected all things required for the building of the temple, the catalog of which the Holy Scripture* <margin>1 Chronicles 28, 29. 1 Chronicles 28:3.</margin> recites; but he was unsuitable to build the habitation because he had shed much blood*. But he stood by his Son, and besides the wisdom and so many great riches which he bestowed upon him so that he might build, he commanded a temple, than which there was not, is not, and will not be on earth anything more august in holiness or magnificence—if you except the temple of the New Testament, in which the Messiah himself, of whom the Solomonic temple was a type, appeared and taught. He bought a place suitable for the building from Araunah the Jebusite for fifty shekels of silver*, which was in the other part of the city, named *Acra*, situated between both the lower and upper city, so that in this middle place it deserves to be called the crown and fortification of the city. We hold this part of the city to be most divine in every respect, by which, when it stands well, the whole city stands; and it is permitted to call it <insert>the middle city</insert> <note>original Hebrew: העיר התיכוני</note> by sacred testimony, 2 Kings 20:4. Solomon, now confirmed as King in the Israelite Kingdom after the death of his parent, brought forth all the preparation for the building of the house of the Lord, and sent out stone-cutters to polish stones, and craftsmen to cut timber on Mount Lebanon; he also committed the casting of vessels, the carving of panels, and the making of veils to the most ingenious artisans. And the work of such immense magnificence was begun by Solomon in the Year of the World 2833, on the second day of the second month, which for us would be a feast day in the month of May, or according to others, the twelfth of April. Solomon did not wish the foundations of the immense work to be laid on the second day of the month because of the holiness of the day, for every New Moon was sacred; lest, therefore, there should be unhappy beginnings for that stupendous structure, he wished to consecrate another day to that work. Thrice happy the day on which the most happy work began: Thrice happier the day on which it unfolded. It began, however, in the fourth year of the royal reign, in the 480th year from the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt, as the Holy Scripture itself indicates, 1 Kings 6:1-2, 2 Chronicles 3:2. In this very year, Solomon began to execute the most beautiful testament of his most beloved parent David concerning the building of a house to the Name of the Lord. Moreover, its foundations were made in that very place which had been shown to David and prepared for this matter by him. The foundations having been cast—

*The Blessed Gerhard* <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a prominent Lutheran theologian.</note> derives this word from *marar*, *it was bitter or sharp*, or *mor*, *myrrh, because that mountain was fertile in myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon.* Others derive it from *yara*, *he feared, so that it is the same as mora, dread or fear, because on this mountain—that is, in the Temple of Jerusalem built upon this mountain—the Lord ought to be worshipped, feared, adored, and reverence shown to Him; whence the Chaldean <note>The Aramaic Targum.</note> translates it: Go into the land of divine worship.* Or *because the Fathers worshipped God on the Mountain, as the Blessed Luther* says:

There are also those who want it derived from *ravah*, *to saturate or water oneself, because that mountain was very well-watered.* Finally, others from *ra’ah*, *he saw, chiefly for the reason that the Lord saw the obedience of Abraham and his son Isaac, and looked upon them; and the Blessed Gerhard and the Ernestine Bible seem to aim at this sense.* Since, however, this mountain was one of those three which overlooked the city from the east, and was distinct from Mount Zion by the Tyropoeon Valley, and from Mount Acra by the Kidron Valley, and moreover was situated outside the city for a long time until David enlarged the city and received it along with Mount Acra into the walls; compare *Bunting p. 37, 38; Adrichomius, Crellius, Friedlib, and others.* But this assertion—that Mount Moriah, where according to Scripture Isaac was to be sacrificed, was placed within the city walls by David—seems to be contradicted by what *Jerome* the Presbyter writes: that he learned most certainly from the Elders of the Jews that Isaac was sacrificed there, where Christ was later crucified. And so, by this admission, the prior assertion about the inclusion of Mount Moriah within the city walls falls of its own accord. But to remedy both views, *Diodorus Siculus* in his *Library* solves this doubt, writing: that Mount Moriah was divided into several hills and hillocks, and in its eastern part was Zion, in which the citadel of David was built, next to which Solomon began to build the temple; but another part of it remained outside the city, and that part was later called Calvary or Golgotha; see *Blessed Gerhard in the place cited p. 441; Blessed Glassius book 4, Sacred Grammar, section 3, p. 801.* In this place, therefore, and indeed in the threshing floor which David had purchased from Araunah, the ancient King of the Jebusites, *the King cast the foundations of the temple into the deepest depth of the earth from the strongest stones, which could resist every injury of time, so that, having grown together with the contiguous earth, they provided a floor and firmament for the substructures to be placed upon; and because of their unshakable solidity, they easily bore the mass of the building with its most sumptuous preparation of ornaments, which would hold no less admiration than those things which were*

<column-break/>

*elaborated by the craftsmen above for the size, beauty, and magnificence of the work,* and they built it up to the ceiling out of white stone, as Josephus writes in *Antiquities of the Jews, book 8, chapter 2, p. 110.*
<margin>The Temple of Jerusalem.</margin>
The superstructure was quite magnificent, made of the most polished white marble stones, fitting together so perfectly <note>original: "ad unguem," literally "to the fingernail," meaning with high precision.</note> that they seemed joined by nature rather than by art. Whence *Josephus:* The building of the temple was made of many skills and from stones cut sharp, joined together very harmoniously and smoothly. <note>original Greek: ἡ τῶ ναῶ, οἰκοδομία κ; πολλῶν τέχνων ἐκ λίθων ἀκροτόμων ἐγένετο συντεθέντων ἁρμονίως πάνυ καὶ λείως.</note> Nor were they brought from far distant places, which without doubt would have been noted. I do not know, however, from where that
<margin>on Ephesians 2.</margin>

And the Apostle sets down this figure.* But *Lyra* raves, and with him *Guilermus* in his *Postils, folio 49. a.* Like all other things, so this in particular is singular and altogether unheard of. There was no sound of a craftsman's tool in the structure. But how were no iron tools heard in the building? To be sure, none were used for the cutting and hewing, for these had been performed beforehand; but they were necessarily used for the joining and composition of the wood, stones, and beams among themselves. The fame of the matter reached foreigners, but was corrupted by falsehood and reported to the Mohammedans—a fiction worthy of that nation—as if the work had been begun and finished by the labor of *Demons*; compare *Alcoran, Sura 21.* What demons they mean would be foreign to our purpose and shameful to enumerate; as would also be the dream of the Jews, that by the help of the points of a little worm named *Shamir*, everything was bored through, however hard. These things cause weariness, and if you want trifles, *Schickard* will provide them in his *Tarich*. From the beginning and thereafter, the work always proceeded with the best and happy success, finally completed and finished in the twentieth year. Long before, David had shown the whole description of the temple, all the figures, all the arrangements, the <term>ground plans</term>, <term>elevations</term>, and <term>perspective drawings</term> graphically depicted in *1 Chronicles 28:11.* David had handed all these to his son Solomon with a lengthy commentary, so that he might complete the individual works through craftsmen. The son obeys the parent and builds, employing the hands even of the Gentiles themselves—Tyrians, and as Eusebius adds, Sidonians, Phoenicians, and Egyptians—to suggest the future mystery of the Calling of the Gentiles to the Church. Among so many and diverse nations, all things responded to each other beautifully and harmoniously. There was one mind of the craftsmen, one Spirit; and different people finished the same building, though in different ways, signs, and times, yet not with a different soul. How wonderful, I ask, is this one thing: that a King from a foreign people named Hiram helps the work with a liberal hand; the works of a most faithful man seemed worthy to God to be inserted into the prediction of eternity. # On 1 Kings VIII. v. I.
## The Temple of Jerusalem

->The Temple of Jerusalem<-

<margin>The Temple of Jerusalem.</margin>
By a foreign King of Tyre and the finest craftsmen, who knew how to cut and join stones, an admirable mass rose from a most abundant heap of wood and stone. Cedar wood was taken from Lebanon so that a temple worthy of cedar might be built. Worthy of the cedar was the number of workers, both overseers and others; the most pious King David had set apart the foreigners in the land of Israel to cut hewn stones to build the house of God, *1 Chronicles 22:2, 15.* Furthermore, there were 7,000 burden-bearers and 8,000 stone-cutters in the mountain.

<margin>1 Kings 5:16</margin>
Indeed, besides Solomon’s princes and overseers who were over the work, there were 3,300 who presided over the people and those who did the work. While
<margin>2 Chronicles 2:2, 18.</margin>
3,600 <term>ergodioktai</term> <note>Greek: ἐργοδιῶκται, "taskmasters" or "work-drivers"</note> are counted, Blessed Walther <note>Balthasar Walther (1558–1625), a Lutheran theologian and traveler</note> responds: These three hundred remaining foreign caretakers, over whom they had placed 150,000 workers, were arranged so that for every three thousand workers there was one overseer for every fifty; the remaining six hundred would further demand an account from these three thousand, each from ten of them. Therefore, these three hundred are included, even counting the three hundred who performed deputy duties. *Compare his Harmony on 1 Kings 5, page 413.*

<margin>1 Kings 5:13</margin>
Among the workers, Hiram, the son of a widow
<margin>1 Kings 7:14</margin>
from the tribe of Naphtali, excelled; his parent is called a Man of Tyre by origin, but because of many years of residency and <term>enoikesin</term> <note>Greek: ἐνοίκησιν, "dwelling within" or "habitation"</note>, he had left the Hebrew nation and land. Hiram’s parent lived in Tyre under that same fault, deprived of the public word and worship of God, from where Solomon summoned him as a Hebrew of Hebrews. Thus, by the wonderful providence and wisdom of God, it happened that Hiram was recalled not only to his fatherland and ancestral land, but even to the very structure of the house of the Lord; and so he was received back into the covenant of God, from which he had departed, as if by the right of <term>postliminium</term> <note>A legal term for the restoration of rights to a person returning from exile or captivity</note>. *Compare Blessed Hafenreffer, The Temple of Jerusalem, p. 14.* To ensure the fabric is treated <term>architektonikos</term> <note>Greek: ἀρχιτεκτονικῶς, "architecturally" or "according to the rules of art"</note>, we shall follow no other order than that prescribed for us by the rule of Holy Scripture. The most illustrious structure is presented to us divided into three parts, which we will consider through three words: *Ulam*, *Hekal*, and *Debir* <note>Hebrew: אולם (Portico), היכל (Holy Place/Nave), and דביר (Most Holy Place/Adytum)</note> as chapters and pillars. First, the outermost part toward the East is mentioned, which the inhabitants called in their own language *Ulam*. What was *Ulam* to them is called in Latin *porticus* (portico) or *vestibulum* (vestibule). Thus the words: — *The portico in front* <note>Hebrew: האולם על-פני</note>: and the *elam* (some say *elam*, others *ailam*) in front <note>Greek: καὶ τὸ ἐλὰμ... κατὰ πρόσωπον</note>. The Hebrews are accustomed to call the building of the gate the *House of the Gate* <note>Hebrew: בית-שער</note>. That, as well as all the space adjacent to it, is shown included in the single word *Ulam*, for which the Greeks here retain *elam*. The *Ulam* is described by its size and position. Its position was before the temple in the East, where the entrance opened. The entrance of the temple was in the Eastern part, no differently than in the Tabernacle, in imitation of which the temple was made. By the custom of other nations, the entrance opened from the West, but of this Temple at least from the East, for which cause Blessed Hafenreffer
<margin>In the place cited, p. 202.</margin>
adds this: *The Hebrews,* he says, *distinguish the quarters of the world such that they call the sunrise the front part, the sunset the back part, the South the right side, and the North the left side.* Concerning this distinction, one may see *Exodus 27:13, 26:18; Psalm 89:12, 13.* Most elegantly of all, we read this distinction perfected in all its

<column-break/>

<margin>The Temple of Jerusalem.</margin>
members in *Job 23:8, 9*: "Behold, if I go forward (that is, to the East), God would not appear; if backward (that is, to the West), I will not perceive him. On the left hand where he works (that is, to the North), I shall not see him; he will cover the right (namely, the southern region), nor will I be contained there." In these words, he continues, are contained all the parts of the distinction by which the quarters of the world differ. From this it is clear that the western quarter, which has no gate in the temple, is called the back part or region. For through the front things, which are spiritual, celestial, and divine, the entrance lies open; but through the back things, which are worldly, temporal, and fleeting, every access remains closed. *These things and more he says.* The *Ulam* is described by its dimensions, of which he makes only two, *length and width*, to which add the dimension of height from *2 Chronicles 3:4*, which is 120 cubits. It was therefore twelve times higher than it was wide, and six times higher than it was long. Above the foundation laid, the walls or sides of the house were raised, perpendicular indeed but not of the same thickness in height. From the interior face of the temple, it was level on every side, that is, *it was built straight up, without a ledge, so that nothing projected either at the bottom or the top*; but on the outside, it consisted of its own <term>migraoth</term> <note>Hebrew: מגרעות, "recesses" or "offsets"</note>, withdrawals, and contractions, *it had its ledges; the higher it went, the thinner it became.* Junius and Vatablus agree on this. *They call them retractions,* says the latter, *or restrictions or reductions, when the wall is drawn inward, so that the lower part of the wall is wider and projects more than the upper part, to accommodate the ends of the beams.* The windows were narrow on the outside but wider on the inside, so that the light passing through them might spread itself more within the walls and be more open for seeing to all those who were inside, and so that the view would not be open to everything for those standing outside. The Greeks call the doors or latticed windows <term>diktyotas</term> <note>Greek: δικτυωτὰς, "grated" or "net-like"</note> or lattices placed before the window <term>klinidas</term>. A "latticed window" <note>Greek: Θυρὶς δικτυωμένη</note> which was made of reticulated work, for <term>diktyon</term> means a net. Latticed windows and doors <note>Greek: Δικτυωταὶ θυρίδες καὶ θύραι</note> are called lattices from their resemblance to a net, from which it is also called *opus reticulatum* (reticulated work) by the Latins. Polybius calls them "transparent latticed doors" <note>Greek: θύρας διαφανεῖς δικτυωτὰς</note>. Paulinus, in Epistle 12 to Severus, calls it a "translucent screen." Latticed structures were in the temples of both Pagans and Christians, which enclosed the innermost parts of the sacred buildings. Servius: *Whence in sacred buildings and in tribunals we call the enclosures that keep out the crowds 'caulae' (folds).* The Capitularies of Charlemagne: *That part which is divided by lattices toward the altar shall be open only to the choirs of singing clerics*, hence today they call that part of the temple the "choir." All parts of the temple were so established that they could not have been better in form nor more beautiful in appearance. The floor of the roof was paved with stones solidly joined, yet not so solidly that certain grasses could not grow from the cracks and fissures of the stones. Under the image of these emerging grasses, the Psalmist
<margin>Psalm 129:6.</margin>
depicts the fortune of the wicked and the enemies of the Church. *They shall be,* he says, *like the grass of the housetops, which withers before it be plucked up.* Excellently, the suddenly perishing appearance of those little herbs shad— <note>original: "adum-" (catchword for "adumbrat" - shadows/foreshadows)</note>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
The Temple
of Jeru-
salem.
</margin>
...shadows forth the formidable power of the impious and their wondrous pride, which is no sooner born than it dies away for lack of earth and moisture and the heat of the sun. The entire building of the temple was made of hewn stone upon the highest ridge of Mount Moriah, 120 cubits high, so that from the very foot and base of the mountain to the highest <note>original: *στεγος* (stegos)</note> roof or height, it was 400 cubits according to the testimony of Josephus. The Psalmist alluded to this: *He built his sanctuary* <note>original Hebrew: *כמו רמים* (kemo ramim)</note> *like high places*. Wondrously, the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> reads *as of unicorns* <note>original Greek: *ὡς μονοκερώτων* (hōs monokerōtōn)</note>, reading *ramim* as *re'emim* <note>wild oxen/unicorns</note> or *remum*. <margin>Psalm 78:69</margin> Aquila translates it as *highly*, and Symmachus as *like high things*. This courtyard, which was the largest and most spacious of all, belonged to the people; in its center, Solomon made a bronze platform or pulpit, five cubits long, five wide, and three cubits high. On this, with bended knees and his face turned toward the Oracle <note>The Holy of Holies</note>, he prayed that God might deign to hear both his own prayers and those of others calling upon Him there. The Lord Himself, appearing to him shortly after by night, replied that He had heard him and would henceforth keep His eyes open and His ears attentive to the prayers of that place. Besides this, there was yet another courtyard built for proselytes and Gentiles; for since only Hebrews—and those who were holy and pure—were permitted to approach the upper areas (which we shall discuss in the following sections), this other area was established for impure Israelites and foreigners. It is in this sense that Solomon is to be understood. <margin>1 Kings 8:41-43</margin> From this courtyard Christ drove out those buying and selling (*John 2:14*). In this place He also acquitted the adulteress (*John 8:3*). Furthermore, many galleries and chambers, as well as lodgings, were prepared for various sacred uses of the Priests and pure Israelites, even though express mention of them is not made in the construction of the Temple. These were built by the command of David; they were lateral buildings surrounding the sides of the temple and were called <note>original Hebrew: *צלעות* (tsela'ot)</note> *side-chambers*. Because the guards and other ministers slept in them, and they served as <note>original Greek: *ταμεῖα* (tameia)</note> storehouses for things pertaining to sacred worship, they were called <note>original Hebrew: *יצוע* (yatsu'a)</note> *structures*, as Strigelius writes. <margin>1 Chronicles 28:11; on 1 Kings 6</margin>

*The second part*, or the inner courtyard, is called <note>original Hebrew: *החצר הפנימית* (he-chatzer ha-penimit)</note> *the inner court*, in which both the *exterior* and *interior* features must be considered. Regarding the exterior, we consider the *Dimensions*, which the text sets forth thus: *And the house which King Solomon built for Jehovah was sixty cubits in length, twenty in breadth, and thirty in height.* Then there were the *galleries* round about, as the Latin version calls them. <margin>1 Kings 6:5</margin> Added to these were wall ornaments decorated with various carvings of flowers, palms, and gourds. Regarding the *interior*, the following come into consideration: *the lampstand, the golden altar (or altar of incense), the table of showbread, the columns, the molten sea, the bases, the lavers*, and other instruments, which we shall treat in order. First, however, the *Lampstand* presents itself. After the fashion of the Lampstand which God showed to Moses in the desert, to be prepared from <note>original Hebrew: *מקשה* (miqshah)</note> *beaten work, not cast*, as some translate it, there were placed ten golden lampstands or candelabra, decorated with hearths, lilies, and lamps in mosaic style—five on the right and five on the left—with their flowers, lamps, and snuffers (*1 Kings 7:49; 2 Chronicles 4:7*). <margin>Exodus 25:31</margin> Since that Lampstand was so crafted that from the upright shaft three branches came out on each side,

<column-break/>

and thus the whole lampstand shone with seven lamps, it is easily apparent from this <margin>The Temple of Jerusalem.</margin> that these ten lampstands illuminated the Temple with 70 lamps—a most beautiful and pleasant sight for those beholding it. From this, the custom of introducing lights and candelabra into Christian temples began (see Volume 1 of the *Councils* in the *Life of St. Sylvester*; Baronius for the year 31; Spondanus no. 20 and for the year 57), the use of which has not been everywhere abolished in Protestant churches. In this part of the temple was also seen the *Altar of Incense*, which is also called the golden altar because it was entirely overlaid with gold. For God had ordered two altars to be made: one <note>original Hebrew: *מזבח* (mizbeach)</note> for burnt offerings, upon which sacrifices were burnt, which was made of bronze, twenty cubits long and wide, and ten high (*2 Chronicles 4:1*). The other was the <note>original Hebrew: *מזבח קטרת* (mizbeach qetoret)</note> *altar of odors*, so that incense might be burned upon it. This was placed near the wall and the veil which separated the Holy of Holies from the front Temple. It is also called by the ancient translator the *Altar of the Oracle* <margin>1 Kings 5:21</margin>, and in the Holy Language <note>Hebrew</note> <note>original Hebrew: *אשר-לדביר* (asher-la-devir)</note>, that is, *the Altar which belongs to the sanctuary*. It does not follow from this, however, that it was placed inside the Sanctuary or Oracle itself; rather, it was placed on the outer side, directly facing the temple door before the oracle. There the High Priest used to offer to God every day the incense which God had ordered to be made from four precious spices—namely frankincense, galbanum, onycha, and stacte, according to Hilary—from which a most sweet odor was produced. The *Table* was made of cedar overlaid with pure gold and surrounded by a golden crown; upon it, every Sabbath day, twelve most pure unleavened loaves were placed, which no one was permitted to eat except the Priests. We find that this table was made for the "bread of the presence" (*1 Kings 7:48*), but we have not found where it was located. I believe, however, says the Blessed Haffenreffer <margin>Luc. p. 22</margin>, by analogy with the Tabernacle, that it was located near the Altar of Incense. Furthermore, ten *tables*, which they call the tables of showbread <margin>2 Chronicles 4:8</margin> <note>original German: *Schaubrod*</note>—so called because they were before the face of the Lord—were placed in the same part of the temple, five on the right and five on the left. If we examine these more closely, we find they were multiplied to hold a greater quantity. The Lord ordered this table, along with the lampstand, to be placed not inside but outside the veil, so that they might be seen by all and hidden from no one who desires to be illuminated by the splendor of faith or satisfied by spiritual food, as Eusebius Emissenus says (*on Matthew ch. 5*). Whoever seeks an allegorical explanation of the showbread table from Peter of Celle and Ruusbroec may consult Nierenberg (*1. Ascetic Doctrine 5. ch. 50. p. 42*).

Two Columns, of the same form and beauty, of remarkable height and wonderful skill (*1 Kings 7:15; 2 Chronicles 3:15*), Solomon had ordered to be placed at the pillars of the inner vestibule. The one on the right, or toward the south, was called <note>original Hebrew: *יכין* (Yachin)</note> *Jachin*, from *kun*, meaning *He shall establish*. The other, on the left, was called <note>original Hebrew: *בעז* (Boaz)</note> *Boaz*, meaning *in it is strength* (so that *bo* is "in him" and *az* is "strength"). This word, says Rabbi Kimchi, is composed of two, because Solomon wished to signify by it that God had granted strength and firmness to this column, according to what is said: *God is the strength of His people*. The words of Rabbi Kimchi are: *The strength of the Lord...*

# From 1 Kings VIII. v. 13.

### The Temple of Jerusalem
<margin>The Temple of Jerusalem</margin>
The "Chariot of the House of Strength" <note>original Hebrew: *mirkebet bê 'az*</note>, which **Rabbi Levi son of Gershom** <note>A 14th-century philosopher and commentator known as Gersonides</note> writes in the same place is a great mystery. **Eupolemus** <note>An early Jewish historian</note>, cited in <margin>On the Preparation for the Gospel, page 192</margin> **Eusebius**, writes that these columns were covered in gold one finger thick; since they rose eighteen cubits, they cost over eighty-six million in gold, according to the account of **Villalpando** <note>A Jesuit architect and exegete</note> (Vol. 2, p. 2, book 5, ch. 37). The "Sea" or that molten reservoir, standing at the northern side of the inner court, rested upon twelve oxen; it was ten cubits in diameter, thirty cubits in circumference, and five cubits in height. From this, based on the proportion of the circumference to the diameter—which is three and one-seventh—**B. Haffenreffer** <note>Matthias Hafenreffer, a Lutheran theologian</note> concludes in the cited work that the rim of the reservoir or sea was not perfectly round or circular everywhere, but somewhat compressed at the sides. Otherwise, the circumference would have been thirty-one cubits, unless we prefer to believe that the redundant fraction was left out for the sake of brevity, expressing only the whole number. The capacity of this sea is said in <margin>1 Kings 7:25</margin> to be two thousand baths <note><term>Bath</term>: an ancient Hebrew liquid measure, roughly 22 liters</note>, but in 2 Chronicles 4:5, it is three thousand baths. Some seek a reconciliation in a difference of "bath" units; others suggest the first passage speaks of liquid measure and the second of dry measure (see **B. Hafenreffer**, **B. Schindeler** in his *Lexicon* p. 259, **B. Walther** in *Harmon.* p. 415, and **B. Glassius** in *Sacred Grammar* p. 73). This opinion is tolerable, unless perhaps—as **B. Walther** learnedly warns—it is moved by the fact that a "bath" is strictly a liquid measure. Furthermore, since this bronze reservoir or bath is called a "Sea" due to its vastness, **Philippus Lansbergius** in his <margin>p. 12</margin> *Commentary on the Diurnal and Annual Motion of the Earth* argues that it is described by the Holy Spirit in a popular manner, not an Archimedean one. His words are: *"We read that Solomon, among other instruments of the Jerusalem temple, made a bronze Bath, called a Sea for its vastness, whose diameter was measured by a cord of ten cubits, but its circumference by a cord of thirty cubits, where the proportion of diameter to periphery is set as 10 to 30, or 7 to 21. But Archimedes demonstrates in his circle-measurement, as we do in ours, that the diameter to the periphery is nearly 7 to 22, so that a difference of a whole cubit comes between the two measurements. If you ask which of these proportions is closer to the truth? I answer: the Archimedean is closest, resting on the most certain foundations of Geometry; not that which the Holy Spirit, intent on another purpose, was content to report in a popular and accepted manner. Therefore, it is evident even from this example that matters pertaining to Geometry must be demonstrated from Geometry, not from Holy Scripture."* **Libertus Fromondus**, a Professor of Theology at the Academy of Louvain, rightly opposes this crude assertion of Lansbergius <margin>Antarist. p. 38</margin>, saying that the proportion the Scripture sets down, though not Archimedean, allows a rough and mechanical calculation to be gathered from it; and from that example, if not precision, at least something close to precision can be fashioned from the Scriptures. It is also the custom of Scripture elsewhere to disregard small fractions that exceed a round number. <margin>Theol. Astron. Dialogue p. 12</margin> So also **Jacobus Du Bois** responds to these points, that in these words there is a *Synecdoche* <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole or a general number represents a specific one</note> of a round number for a slightly larger one, so that the dimension is not understood precisely, but "thereabouts," of so many cubits.

<column-break/>

Compare **Joh. Herbinius** in book 2 of *Exam.* p. 137, 138. In this part of the temple there were also ten bronze basins or lavers, placed upon <margin>The Temple of Jerusalem</margin> ten bronze bases, and so arranged that five bases with their basins stood at the left northern side and five at the right southern side of the inner court, so that the entrails and feet of the animals destined for burnt offerings might be washed and cleansed there. They held forty baths each, and five were placed on the right side and five on the left (1 Kings 7:38, 2 Chronicles 4:6). **Arias Montanus** reports here from the books of the *Mishnah* <note>original: *Misnaioth*</note>, that is, the ancient traditions: That there was a well in the Court of the Priests, closed with a movable lid, into which the ministers poured the water and the blood of the offerings, and once poured, it flowed through a channel all the way to the brook Kidron. On this matter there is total silence in the sacred texts, as they mention no such thing done for the sake of purity and cleanliness. Therefore, the Sea, and the twelve oxen under the sea, the ten lavers, the bowls, pots, basins, and all the vessels were of polished bronze, as the Sacred Codex <margin>1 Kings 7:44</margin> testifies. However, a different reading occurs here regarding the vessels. Those who wish to imitate the vessels of the Tabernacle read *hemmah* <note>Hebrew: "they"</note> according to the *Ketiv* <note>The written tradition of the Hebrew text</note>, or they prefer according to the *Keri* <note>The spoken/corrected tradition of the Hebrew text</note> that it be read *ha-elleh*, "these." So says **Pagninus**. **Jonathan** follows both readings in his Paraphrase, rendering it: *"And all those vessels according to the workmanship of the vessels of the tabernacle, which Moses had made, so Hiram made for King Solomon."* The **Septuagint** and the **Vulgate Version** omitted that word. From either reading, says **Cappellus** <margin>3 Crit. Sacr. 2, 7. p. 87</margin>, a sense arises that is not inconvenient, so it would be the same whichever you follow. But these are the things that were seen in the second part of the Temple, which, because the priests primarily occupied it, was called the Court of the Priests. Into that inner court or sanctuary, the Priests or Levites about to enter and perform the legal ceremonies were required to be pure and sober, abstaining entirely from their wives and unmixed wine; hence **Jerome** says: *"In the Old Law, those who offered sacrifices for the people were not only not in their own homes, but were purified for a time, separated from their wives, and did not drink wine or strong drink, which are accustomed to provoke lust."* Furthermore, they previously took off their profane clothing in the chambers prepared for that use, and put on sacred linen and fine white garments. When they were about to go out to the people in the outer Court, they took these off again and replaced them in a certain chamber assigned for those uses, and this by divine command (Exodus 28:43, cf. Ezekiel 44:18, 19).

The third part is the *Debir*, which the **Septuagint** translates as *to dabeir*, the Latins as either the *adytum* <note>The innermost sanctuary</note> or the *oracle*, and by a narrower nomenclature, the *Holy of Holies* <note>Hebrew: *Kodesh Ha-Kodashim*</note>. The place could not be commended with more majestic words than by the title by which God Himself is called, who is celebrated with the supreme eulogy of "Holy of Holies." It is called *Debir* from *dabar*, "to speak," because from there divine responses were given, according to Exodus 29:42. In Greek it can be called *semneion* <note>A holy place</note>, which the High Priest entered with great solemnity; by **Hesychius**, *semneion* is explained as a "sacred house." Into this oracular space, which the High Priest entered once every year, bringing there blood for himself—

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
The Temple of Jerusalem.

Within this space, both for himself and for the ignorances of the people, the most holy Ark was viewed with the Mercy Seat and the Cherubim, as we shall see in its proper place. As in the previous sections, so here we shall note in order: 1. the *dimension*, which was 20 cubits in length; regarding the height, it is a matter of controversy which we do not make our own here (See Ribera <note>Francisco de Ribera, a Jesuit commentator</note> on this passage). 2. The *Doors*, which were made of cedar wood. For the interior of the Temple, wherever the eye could reach, was adorned with cedar and olive-wood panels, decorated with various carvings of Cherubim and flowers, and most splendidly embellished with gold. The marbles appeared so dazzling to the sight that they seemed not to have been fashioned from earth but refined by heaven itself, so that the sacred things might appear even more sacred. A Veil, variegated with embroidery and illuminated with various colors, separated the Holy of Holies from the Holy Place. This was a *pastos* <note>original Greek: παστός</note>, a term usually applied to a curtain stretched before the doors or roofs of a bridal chamber, and the place itself was also called by this name.

<margin>
column 655.
</margin>
The Etymologist <note>referring to the Etymologicum Magnum</note> says: *pastos: a room within a chamber of varied workmanship, prepared as a bridal house.* Eustathius says: *Empasso means to embroider or weave in, whence the variegated hangings are called pastoi.* From this comes *pastophorion*, a place destined for a certain assembly of sacred men, as existed in the temples of Isis and other Goddesses, where the *hypastophoroi* <note>shrine-bearers</note> stayed. Dwellings adorned with such splendid veils gave rise to the reason for this name. Hesychius: *pastas: a porch facing the bridal chambers of nymphs. Pastophorion: that which carries the bridal veil, or an administration, or an assembly, or a flower-filled temple.*

<margin>
1 Kings 8:6.
</margin>
In the Holy of Holies, therefore, was the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord, which Solomon transferred into this house he had built from the tent on Zion (which David had prepared for the Ark in his city, after he had moved it from the house of Obed-Edom *2 Samuel 6:17; 1 Chronicles 15:1, 3*). Two Cherubim covered the Ark from above with expanded wings, with which they embraced the entire Inner Sanctuary <term>Adytum: the innermost sanctum of a temple</term>, *1 Kings 6:23 ff.* The Cherubim in this holier sanctuary were of the same measure and style, made of olive wood and overlaid with gold, each provided with two wings; with one wing they touched the walls on either side, and with the other they touched each other, protecting the Ark placed beneath them from above, while turning their faces toward the outer house.

part 1, section 4, Commentary on Ezekiel 1.

Regarding this support for the Ark, comparing *1 Chronicles 29:18* with *2 Samuel 15:1* and *Zechariah 6:2*, Pradus <note>Jerónimo Prado, Spanish exegete</note> feels thus: We believe Solomon made not only two Cherubim of material, but also a wagon with wheels or feet raised from the ground, upon which the Ark was placed, as right reason dictates. For it was unbecoming that the glory of the Lord should creep upon the ground, since other utensils had feet under them, or bases, lest they touch the pavement. And from *Exodus 25:12* <note>Hebrew: פעמתי - "corners" or "feet"</note> compared with *2 Kings 19:24, Judges 5:28, 1 Kings 7:30*, it is gathered that Moses did something similar, though narrower, so that the Ark of the Covenant had a table under it, into which were encrusted four "palms" or four feet, by which it was elevated from the earth. Therefore, in place of that table, Solomon seems to have made a vehicle fashioned of gold with either feet or wheels, upon which he might place the Ark with dignity. Thus he says. However, there was nothing in the Ark except the two stone Tables of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>, *1 Kings 8:9.* As for what is read in *Hebrews 9:4*, that there was the golden urn of Manna, the rod of Aaron, and the Tables of the Cove-

-nant, that is to be understood as being in the Tabernacle, but not actually inside the Ark itself. Indeed, both the rod and the golden urn were placed in the Holy of Holies near the Ark, but not in the Ark itself, as can be seen. *And Aaron placed it (the urn of Manna) before the Testimony* <note>Hebrew: לפניה עדה למשמרת - "before the testimony for safekeeping"</note>, that is, before the Ark, in the Holy of Holies. The same is read concerning the rod of Aaron in *Numbers 17:10.*

The Temple of Jerusalem. Exodus 16:34.

At incomparable expense—for some who calculate the costs of the temple reckon 137,672 tons <note>of gold/silver</note> and 10,075 crowns—the temple was built by Solomon within the space of eleven years; for he spent seven years in building the temple or house, and the remainder in preparing the utensils, *1 Kings 6:38.* Nor was there anything in the world that cost greater labor or greater expense, or which excited greater admiration in posterity. The Jews imagined that even if the rest of the whole world perished, Israel could not perish; and if Israel perished, Judea could not perish; and if all Judea perished, Jerusalem could not be endangered because of the temple of the Lord. They even threw this in the faces of the threatening Prophets, as in *Micah 3:11*: *Is not the Lord in the midst of us?* <note>Hebrew: הלוא יהוה בקרבנו</note> *No evil shall come upon us.*

<margin>
Epistle 57.
</margin>
It is therefore a great proof of God's mercy that He told Solomon He would place His name in the temple and dwell there. Augustine, explaining this with a certain interpretation, says: *God did not dwell in the man-made temple corporally, but overshadowingly, that is, by prefiguring signs. For in the body of Christ, which He assumed from the Virgin, He dwelt corporally as if in His own temple;* and he asserts elsewhere that when it is said in the Old and New Testaments concerning GOD’s dwelling on this earth made by the hands of men, it must be understood as having a certain singular and mystical significance; otherwise,

# From 1 Kings VIII. v. 13.

<margin>Absalom's Rebellion. chapters 2, 4</margin>
As previously stated, Solomon's temple was built with the greatest magnificence; however, when it was rebuilt by Zerubbabel <note>The leader of the first group of Jews returning from Babylonian exile</note>, it is said by Haggai: *Who is left among you that saw this house in its first glory? And how do you see it now? Is it not in your eyes as nothing?* <note>Haggai 2:3</note> How different was the Temple of Zerubbabel from that which Solomon had constructed. Five things were missing in the second temple, say the Talmudists, and according to their enumeration they are: 1. The Ark with the Cherubim. 2. The Urim and Thummim <note>Sacred lots used by the High Priest to determine God's will</note>. 3. The fire sent down from heaven. 4. The Holy Spirit or Prophecy. 5. The presence of the Divine Majesty. They claim this was hinted at by the Prophet Haggai through the word *evneh* <note>original: אבנה - "I will be glorified"</note>, where in the margin a *He* <note>The Hebrew letter ה</note> is added at the end; since *He* denotes the number five, they say those five things were indicated. But this is a fabrication which they devised regarding the missing letter *He*; see Constantijn L'Empereur in *Middoth page 154*, Amama on the *Keri and Chetib* <note>Traditional scribal notes on the Hebrew Bible text</note>, and Drusius on *Judges page 159*. Regarding the time when the Urim and Thummim ceased, Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note> does not agree with the Hebrews. For he says in Book 3 of *Antiquities, chapter 9*: "The breastplate and the sardonyx ceased to shine two hundred years before I composed this writing, because God was displeased by the transgression of the laws." <note>original Greek: Ἐπαύσαντο μὲν οὖν... translated here to English</note> Josephus finished those books, as he himself reports, in the 13th year of Domitian, which is approximately 93 of the Christian Era. It must be, therefore, that this oracle failed barely a hundred years before the birth of Christ. This is a *very great claim* <note>original Greek: λίαν μέγα αἴτημα</note>, and one that no one would easily grant to Josephus—a man otherwise of great authority in these matters—not even the Jews. For Don Isaac Abravanel expressly says in *volume 1, column 1*: "During the entire time that the second temple stood, the High Priest did not answer via the Urim and Thummim." <note>original Hebrew: היה הכהן בכל זמן בית שני משיב באורים ותומים</note>

Hence they imagine that the oracle of the *Bathkol* <note>literally "Daughter of a Voice" — a divine echo or heavenly voice</note> succeeded the Urim and Thummim, and was in use during the second temple. Nor was the Ark of the Covenant seen in the second temple after the Babylonian exile, although some claim it was captured by Titus and carried in triumph to Rome with other Temple ornaments—though how truly they saw this is their own affair. Yet the second temple did not lack its own ornaments; almost everything in it shone with the whitest and most polished marble, gold, silver, Corinthian bronze, gems, purple, and scarlet; for both the posts and the leaves of the gates shone with overlaid plates of gold and silver; in these, however, the craftsmanship often surpassed the nobility of the material, not to mention the gathering of both Jews and Gentiles from almost every region of the earth to perform sacred rites to the God of Israel, which was certainly greater in the second temple than the first. Above all others, the second temple was ennobled by the presence in the flesh of the Light of Lights, Christ, the Light of the Gentiles, so that in this respect it seems preferable to the first. But to finally bring our discussion to an end: in the most august temple of Solomon, pure gold, pure silver, and most precious gems reflected light, which so many thousands of other things cannot equal in splendor.

<column-break/>

The temples of the whole world were but a tiny thing, and like a shadow compared to it; and whatever things you wish to compare it to, you will find it equal to none. Its august appearance struck the eyes of onlookers, and displayed that beautiful external decoration of the temple, the altars, and the court, because of the presence of the venerable JEHOVAH, the Lord of lords, and because of the worship and sacrifice of the thrice-venerable God, because of the obedience of the people, and because as a type <note>A prophetic symbol or foreshadowing</note> it was a thing pleasing and laudable to God. An external appearance is nothing in itself if the beauty that ought to be within is absent. God turns His face away if our face clings only to external things and our opinion rests in them. In this opinion the Jews frequently sinned and dishonored the splendor of the decoration; being driven mad, they lost the internal essence, and because they clung astonished to the joints of the stones, finally not one stone remained upon another, as divine justice thus demanded. The temple shown today in Jerusalem is dross, and nothing but a scandal. In whatever part you look, it is a mockery. They wander out of the way and are carried outside the orbit of reason who approach it with the intent of worship. It is a filthy worship *and without piety* <note>original Greek: καὶ ἄνευ εὐσεβείας</note>. The typical temple has long since been abolished and overturned, and the place is now contaminated by the feet of strangers who have conspired for our destruction. The Rabbis are vainly expecting the construction of a third Temple, and that by the force of the words of Ezekiel, who *proposes a temple in hyperbolic words*, not built of stones, but far more august. For in the final parts of his Prophecy, the structure of the holy land, the City of Jerusalem, and the Temple is proposed by the grace of a vision in place of celestial and divine riches; and this for nine continuous chapters, from the 40th to the end of the book. He places the finishing touch upon his prophetic visions with this most august contemplation. While Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, 4th-century scholar</note> in *Epistle 82 to Marcella* calls it an "inexplicable building of the Temple," and B. Hafenrefferus <note>Matthias Hafenreffer, Lutheran theologian</note> undertook to explain its variety according to measure, he intrepidly pronounces that no one in this life can sufficiently give the spiritual significations of this vision.

<margin>Absalom's Rebellion.</margin>
<margin>chapters 40, 47.</margin>
<margin>page 107. Ezekiel's Temple.</margin>

"For since the obscurity of the text itself is so great," (I draw his own words), "such as I think occurs in such abundance and multitude of things hardly anywhere else in the whole volume of Scripture, who would dare to promise that he would give a full and perfect interpretation of its specific explanation, which is much holier and more sublime, and thus also much more obscure and intricate?" Meanwhile, it becomes every pious person to prepare his heart for Christ as a temple in which He may dwell, according to that saying of Christ the Savior in *John 14:23* and of Paul in *1 Corinthians 3:16*: *Do you not know that you are the Temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?* Therefore, with the Poet <note>likely a reference to a Neo-Latin Christian poet</note>, we shall finish this meditation <note>original Greek: μελέτησιν</note>:

# I. KINGS XV. 13. BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES.

### And also Maachah his mother, even her he removed from being queen, because she had made an idol in a grove. <note>original Hebrew: וגם את־מעכה אמו ויסרה מגבירה אשר־עשתה למפלצת׃</note>
### And he removed his mother from being leader, because she had made a gathering in her grove. <note>original Greek: Καὶ τὴν ἀνὰ τὴν μητέρα ἑαυτοῦ μετέστησε τὸ μὴ εἶναι ἡγεμένην, καθὼς ἐποίησε σύνοδον ἐν τῷ ἄλσει αὐτῆς.</note>
### *King Asa removed his mother Maachah, lest she should be a priestess in the sacred rites of Priapus.* <note>original Latin: Asa Rex Maacham matrem suam amovit, ne princeps esset in sacris Priapi.</note>

<margin>The Rites of Priapus.</margin>
The mother of King Asa presided over the *Miplezethic* <note>A term derived from the Hebrew word for the idol, often associated with "shuddering" or "horror."</note> rites, from which office her son removed her; he likewise burned the image of the deity and threw its ashes into the brook Kidron. In the Hebrew, the Ancient Interpreter understood *Miplezeth* to refer to <term>Priapus</term> <note>A Greek and Roman fertility god, often represented by a phallic statue</note>; who is well known from Pagan writers to have been the god of gardens, and of whose foulness there is more in their books than is profitable for the modesty of readers. The Zurich translators, in order to leave the judgment free to anyone, retain the Hebrew name *Miplezeth*. The same pleased Luther, who says in his notes: *Who this Miplezeth may have been is uncertain. Some say it was the idol Priapus.* <note>original German: Wer der Miplezeth gewesen sey/ ist ungewiß. Etliche sagen/ es sey der Abgott Priapus gewesen.</note> Other interpreters, looking to the word from which it is derived, translate it as a common noun. For Arias Montanus explained it as *Terrifying things*. Junius and Tremellius: *A horrible statue.* The French interpreter: *A puppet* <note>original French: Un marmouset</note>; which he immediately explains as *a scarecrow* <note>original French: un espoventail</note>; and it is said of it that it strikes terror or is a "fright-object" <term>μορμολυκεῖον</term> <note>mormolykeion: a Greek term for a hobgoblin or bugbear used to frighten children</note>; for *espouvanter* to them means: *to terrify, to frighten*. Piscator: *A loathsome idol.* <note>original German: Ein scheußlichen Gözen.</note> These versions square best with the Hebrew *Miplezeth*; for it is derived from *palatz*, "to be terrified, to dread, to tremble"; because all idols are to their worshippers
<margin>Jeremiah 50:38. Hosea 4:17.</margin>
*terrors and sorrows* <note>original Hebrew: אימים ועצבים</note>, as we have from the sacred texts. Therefore, Rabbi Levi Ben-Gerson aptly says the reason for the name is *because it brings trembling and many troubles to those who worship it* <note>original Hebrew: לפי שהוא מביא פלצה וצרות רבות לעובדיו</note>. For the *Miplezeth* brings pains and anxieties with it, rather than tranquility to the souls of the worshippers. Authors hold the same regarding Priapus, the terror and prohibitor of birds and thieves. Horace introduces Priapus as the guardian of the Esquiline gardens:
<margin>Book 1. Satire 8. line 3.</margin>
> Thence I, a god, became of thieves and birds
> The greatest Terror.

In the same manner, Virgil is to be explained in the 4th Georgic, line 110:
> And let the protection of Hellespontine Priapus, 
> guardian against thieves and birds with his willow sickle, keep watch.

And Propertius, elegy 1, book 1:
> Priapus terrifies the birds with his cruel sickle.

The statue of Priapus was erected either at the entrance or in the middle of gardens, than which nothing more shameful could have been erected. Those things which seem to pertain to the understanding of this garden-image and ancient observation could be explained at greater length, were they not exceedingly obscene. Several Epigrams by Tyrannius, Lucian, Leonidas, Apollonides, Argentarius, Erycius, and Antistius
<margin>Book 4. no. 87. following. p. 711.</margin>
exist in the *Anthology*, which I need not repeat here idly and offensively. In them, he is celebrated as the preserver of fruits, defender of the hut, guardian of vegetables, and likewise of vine-shoots. Some understand not Priapus but <term>Pan</term> <note>The Greek god of the wild, shepherds, and flocks, known for causing "panic"</note>,
<margin>column 739.</margin>
which Borrhaus also notes: *This idol is so called from the terror which it strikes. Therefore, there are those who render it as Pan, who was accustomed to be worshipped in gardens, and as far as terror is concerned, those are known as*

<column-break/>

*Panic terrors.* Among the translators, Castalio rendered it thus:
<margin>The Rites of Priapus.</margin>
*Maachah, his mother, he abdicated from power, because she had made a Pan in the grove, and he cut down that Pan, and burned it at the brook Kidron.* He gives the reason for his version in his Notes: *Since I think it should be translated as Priapus, the reason is that it is scarcely credible that Priapus was made by a woman; secondly, because this was placed in a Grove, which is more suitable to Pan, since Priapus used to be placed in gardens. Furthermore, because Miplezeth takes its name from striking terror, which fits Pan, whence it is called Panic fear.*
<margin>page 439.</margin>
The ancients contended that *Bel-Peor*, or <term>Baal-Peor</term>, was twin to Priapus. Jerome and all the Latin expositors following him explain it as *Priapus*. *Beelphegor* (he says on Hosea ch. 9 v. 10) *is the idol of the Moabites, whom we can call Priapus.* He also handed down this same thing on Hosea ch. 10 and in his first book against Jovinian. Moreover, Baal-Peor was the God of the Moabites, as is sufficiently clear from the horrific history found in Numbers 25:3, where we read that the Israelites, mingling themselves with the women of the Moabites and serving their Baal-Peor, were slain. For in Shittim, fornicating with the daughters of Moab, they adored their gods and set themselves apart for the shameful worship of the foul Baal-Peor. Isidore, in *Etymologies* book 8, ch. 11: *Beel-phegor is interpreted as the image of ignominy. For it was an idol of Moab named Baal upon Mount Peor, whom the Latins call Priapus, the God of gardens.* To Origen, it is called a *species of foulness*.
<margin>Homily 20 on Numbers.</margin>
Eucherius has the same in his interpretation of names, book 4, ch. 9, p. 290. And Jerome on Isaiah ch. 15, Vol. 5, p. 57, felt that the idol of the Moabites named <term>Chemosh</term> differed from Baal-Peor in name only: *In Nebo, he says, was the consecrated idol Chemosh, which by another name is called Beelphegor.* Apollinarius on Psalm 105, as it appears in the *Catena* of the Greek Fathers on the Psalms, compared him to Saturn; his words are: *The idol is Baal in the place of Peor. The Greeks call Baal 'Bel', whom they say is Saturn.* <note>original Greek: Εἴδωλον δὲ τὸ Βαὰλ ἐν τόπῳ φέγωρ. ἕλληνες δὲ τὸν Βάαλ βὴλ ὀνομάζουσι, ὅν φασιν εἶναι τὸν Κρόνον.</note> Chrysostom and Theodoret are of the same opinion, both on the said Psalm; compare Caelius Rhodiginus, book 3, ch. 3.
That idol, whatever it may be, took its name from Mount Peor,
<margin>Numbers 23:28.</margin>
of which mention is made, as Suidas (under *Beelphegor*), Theodoret (on Psalm 105), and others maintain; and perhaps Bel was accustomed to be worshipped on the mountain of that name. We read there that Balak, King of the Moabites, took Balaam to the ridge of Mount Peor so that they might sacrifice there. No one is ignorant that the altars of the Ancients were *high places* <note>original Hebrew: במות</note> or the ridges and peaks of mountains, whence also come the names of the Deities from the place; thus Baal-Peor would be *Jupiter of Peor*, just as he is called *Jupiter Olympius* from Mount Olympus, and *Jupiter Capitolinus* from the Capitol. Those who pursue letters within letters say the name comes from "denuding" and "opening." Just as Mercerus
<margin>page 2209.</margin>
in his Notes to the Lexicon of Pagninus: *Paar*, "to open," whence *Peor* and *Baal-Peor*, an idol among the Moabites, from opening and nakedness, because he was a God of foulness and lust, which in this language is signified by the name of nakedness. Our people called him Priapus, the voice being somewhat distorted; whose worship consisted in revelries and all lewdness and unbridled lust; whence also the mountain in Moab was named Peor, where there was both a temple of the God and worship. The greedy man worships gold, the glutton his belly, the lustful his penis and Beelphegor.* In these shameful sacred rites they contaminated themselves with promiscuous lusts and prostituted themselves with impudent gestures. It is known how the impure Spirit drove the wretched gentiles to flagitious rites, which can scarcely be heard with horror, let alone spoken. Foul and obscene were the Eleusinian mysteries instituted in honor of Ceres and Proserpina, which Tertullian describes at the beginning of the book *Against the Valentinians*. Those who were admitted swore silence, that they would divulge nothing. My pen hesitates because of the most obscene things, which we do not wish to betray to your ears, for I myself feel weariness in reading them, so that they ought to be hidden, and not published as I see even certain Theologians do; meanwhile, so that it may be known how they were not ashamed to seek noble worship and customs in these obscenities, we cannot pass these over, beseeching the Kind Reader that he might wish to read these with chaste eyes and a pure mind, and with detestation of the Devil. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Rites of Priapus</margin> There was a place near Tauromenium where men and women alike devoted themselves to sacred rites, and in honor and worship of the goddess, they publicly displayed large representations of the private parts. For so we read in the Vatican appendix of proverbs edited by Schott: *Naxian Shields*. <note>original: "Γέῤῥα Ναξιανά"</note> The Sicilians use the word "shields" <note>original: "Gerra"</note> to refer to the male and female genitalia; there was in Sicilian Naxos a boundary of "Aphrodite-by-the-Sea," in which large genitalia were dedicated. To this pertain the words of Nonnius: *Gerra, charms <note>original: "fascini"</note>, which are so named by the inhabitants of the Island of Naxos in the temple of Venus.* He actually confuses the locations here, Naxos of Sicily with the Island of Naxos; for it should be understood as Tauromenium, which was founded by those remaining from the Naxians, whence Bochart teaches it is called Naxos (Geography, book 2, ch. 26, p. 577). Fortunatus Licetus discusses the image of the male member hung around the neck as a protection against the "evil eye" <note>fascination</note>, as well as rings worn with a male member, <margin>ch. 24, p. 126.</margin> in his work *On Ancient Rings*, where among other things on p. 129 he says: *The ancients also prepared rings to ward off the evil eye, in whose bezel or setting they engraved an image of the male member; I recently received a very beautiful drawing of such a very ancient ring from a most learned man; from the place of the bezel a human hand seems to thrust out, etc.* In the famous rites of Isis, a *Phallus* <note>a representation of the male organ</note> was carried around, which they hung from the neck or tied to the loins, as Plutarch witnesses in his book *On Isis and Osiris*, p. 36. As the deity is, so is the object of worship <note>original: "σέβασμα"</note>; clearly, to obscene gods, a matching worship had to be offered. Gregory Nazianzen understood these filthy rites when he said there were ceremonies in which they worshiped not only with blood and the smell of burnt offerings, but also with truly foul actions and madness. By this impure rite, the Evil Spirit indeed wished to represent the symbols of generation, but also simultaneously to inflame minds toward filthy pleasure. For those foolish and impure festivals prove that as each person was affected by their own passions, so they sought gods to match those passions. A lustful man sought Venus and Priapus; a drunkard, Bacchus; a fierce man, <margin>Oration on Pentecost, p. 262.</margin> Mars. Whence Gregory Nazianzen says: *The Greek also celebrates a festival, but according to the body, and to their own gods and demons, some of whom are creators of passions according to those very people, while others were honored because of their passions. Therefore, even celebrating is a burden to them, so that the honor of the god is the act of sinning toward the one to whom the passion flees as if it were a matter of solemnity.* This very thing—that they sin in lust—just as they consider it an honor to themselves, so they think it is an honor to Priapus. The more lustful and well-endowed a man was, the more he thought <margin>see Idolatry p. 343. 7.</margin> he owed gratitude and honor to Venus and Priapus. What if something similar happened in the rites of Baal-Peor? Of this there can be no doubt. *It is not to be doubted,* says Vossius, *since those obscene figures had their own matching rites; namely, just as because Bacchus is the overseer of liquid, and especially of the vine-born kind, they drenched themselves in wine during his rites. And in the rites of Venus, they likewise indulged in sexual intercourse. So in the rites of Baal-Peor, who presided over generation, that was done which the day and the nature of the Deity seemed to suggest.* They treat "shameful talk" <note>original: "Αἰσχρολογήματα"</note> as "solemn talk" <note>original: "σεμνολογοῦσι"</note>, and they cover their diabolical rites with a veneer of solemnity. Thus, the gods are covers for vices, and the gods exist no less for vices than for virtues. Lucan laughed at these gods, as did every wiser person. Even the Pagans themselves laugh at the shameful Priapus, whom Horace describes farting

<column-break/>

and so terrifying two sorceresses with the noise <margin>Rites of Priapus</margin> of his belly that they fled into the city <margin>Satires, Book 1, Sat. 8, v. 45.</margin> out of fear:
> For like a bursting bladder, I let a fart,
> From my split-buttock fig-wood; but they ran to the city.

This brings to mind what the Rabbis dream up—who seem to have fallen asleep in a dunghill—concerning a certain foul baring of the buttocks and the voiding of excrement done in honor of Priapus. Rabbi Solomon Jarchi noted this opinion on Numbers 25:3, for whom the etymology of *Peor* is to denote the voiding of food remains. For they were accustomed to squat before the idol and offer the "excremental" Baal-Peor. This "dung-filled" explanation is refuted by Vossius the Elder (in the cited place, p. 342) and Vossius the Younger in his notes to the book of Rabbi Moses Maimonides, <margin>p. 37.</margin> both of whom also cite the opinion of Scaliger. He thinks there was another name among the Gentiles, and indeed a more honorable one for this deity, namely *Peor* or *Baal-Peor*, named after thunder <note>original: "βρονταῖος ἢ κεραυνίος"</note>, which the Jews deliberately changed into something more foul and contemptible. They were indignant that the noble name of "The Thunderer" or "The Lightener" (titles by which he is hailed by the Poets, especially Pindar) should be attributed to a Moabite Deity. As if Jupiter the "All-Giver" <note>original: "παγδρεὺς"</note> were made Jupiter the "Thunderer." Long before, Bucer handed down something similar, whose words in Psalm 105 are: *Scripture seems to have deliberately called the Gods by more foul and contemptible* <margin>2 Kings 1.</margin> *names. As when* it calls the God of Ekron *Baal-Zebub*, *that is, Master or Lord of the Fly. So also I think Baal-Peor was named from voiding, for "Peor" in Chaldean is said to mean to void. In Hebrew, however, it means to open. Thus he says.* But whatever the case regarding the name of the Deity, we do not attribute a foul name to him unless they actually celebrated the Deity himself with lewd and foul mysteries. The mythical fables of the Poets about the Gods sufficiently reveal the filthiness of the foul Deity; how obscene these are, and yet performed on stage, is hidden from no one! How unsuitable for men, let alone gods, to present Jupiter, the God of Gods, as a most obscene spectator of human forms, so often captured by love, cast into chains by the Titans, and barely escaping by the trickery and theft of Mercury! How unworthy of gods that Neptune and Apollo performed mercenary, slave-like labor for Laomedon! That Mars and Venus, caught in adultery by Vulcan, were entangled in adamantine nets and paid a penalty with their Uncle as a guarantor! Who would not shudder even to read what a stage of filthiness existed in the theater of the "Priapists." What monsters of depravity, what portents were carried out in rites of that kind, which anyone could hardly endure without nausea and horror! Those were dearer to him who exercised themselves in filth with less shame and greater impulse, as Horace says: <margin>Epistles, Book 4, Ep. 3.</margin>

> Those who, seizing uncertain Venus in the manner of wild beasts,
> The stronger man believed his own, like a bull in a herd.

The first and greatest applause was earned by those who had invented more exquisite allurements of lust, as what Juvenal writes concerning the worship of the "Good Goddess" <note>Bona Dea</note> comes to mind here: <margin>Satire 6.</margin>

> Lauffella, having set aside the crown, challenges the maids of the pimps.

Obscenities of this kind were present among their banquets, so that they used drinking cups which had the shape of the private parts—
<meta>catchword: parts—</meta>
