# From 1 Kings 15:13.

<margin>The Rites of Priapus.</margin>
<margin>p. m. 242.</margin>
...of those to be worshipped, although young girls served him, and as Juvenal says in *Satire 2*:

->He drinks from a glass Priapus.<-
<note>original: "Vitreo bibit ille Priapo." A reference to drinking vessels shaped like the phallic god.</note>

Pliny censures this foulness in the *Preface to Book 33 of his Natural History*: "It has become a pleasure to hide lusts within drinking cups, and to drink through obscenities." The shameless Ovid <note>original: "Naso"</note> describes in *Book 6 of the Fasti* how Priapus, approaching Vesta with stealthy step while she was overcome by sleep, was startled by the braying of a donkey—which things can only be read with a laugh. He is a deity worthy of having the Donkey as his sacred animal, as Ovid testifies in the same place. Augustine joins the *Rites of Priapus* and the *Rites of Bacchus* in *Questions on the Old and New Testaments, ch. 114, col. 830*, because they are of the same impurity, madness, and vanity. Regarding the Priapic rites of Bacchus, Livy reports things in *Book 9* that can neither be read without amazement nor recounted while preserving modesty. There also exist various poems addressed to Priapus, called *Priapeia*, which are unworthy of being read and most worthy of being burned; these are usually added to the works of Virgil like a sewer attached to a Palace. For those impure *Centos* <note>poems made of borrowed lines</note> are not by Virgil; he was called *Parthenius* <note>The Maiden-like</note> because of his chaste poetry and modest character. However, those immodest verses, patched together by various poets, were affixed to the shrine of Priapus in the gardens of Maecenas. Meibomius, in *Maecenas ch. 28, p. 174*, agrees with Gyraldus and others that those published by Joseph Scaliger in the appendix to Virgil under the name *Priapeia* originated from there. Baptista Mantuanus is nauseated by the *Priapeia*, writing in his poem against poets who speak immodestly:
<margin>7. Sylv 5. fol 102, a.</margin>

->Your Helicon is a Salmacis; give your vows to Priapus.<-
->Place incense on the Hellespontine hearths.<-
<note>Helicon was the mountain of the Muses; Salmacis was a fountain associated with effeminacy. Priapus was famously associated with the Hellespont.</note>

But let Priapus go, along with his beautiful little brothers: Cloacina <note>Goddess of Sewers</note>, Fear, Pallor, Fever, and the rest—not deities for those to be honored, but for those who honor crimes, whom Augustine brings forward in *City of God, Book 4, ch. 23*. A few things remain to be said regarding his worship. Indeed, even the most learned Hebrews hand down that the detestable worship of Peor was performed through shameful exposure; among them, most learnedly, Constant L’Empereur in his *Notes on the Codex Middoth, ch. 3, sect. 5, p. 116-117*. Let the reader's inquiry run quickly there regarding this singular method of worship, which consists of foul lusts among the Moabite women. Rivetus doubts this; consult him in his *Commentary on Hosea 4, p. 144 and ch. 9, p. 303*. Priests were employed for the insane and shameful rites of that Prostitute, if Jerome correctly gathers this from Hosea. For when he had previously set down certain things about the priests of Cybele, he added these: "Idolatry of this kind was in Israel, with the women especially worshipping Baal-Peor on account of the magnitude of his obscenity, whom we can call Priapus... It should be known, moreover, that in the present passage he calls the <lang="hebrew">קדשות</lang> <note>Qedeshoth: temple prostitutes</note> 'harlots,' that is, <lang="greek">ἱερεῖς</lang> <note>hiereis: priests</note> devoted to Priapus. Just as the <lang="hebrew">קדשים</lang> <note>Qedeshim: male cult prostitutes</note> were called priests of the Goddess Astarte; concerning whom Selden should be consulted regarding the *Miplezeth* and *Baal-Peor*." The Septuagint <note>LXX</note> calls them <lang="greek">τετελεσμένους</lang> <note>tetelesmenous</note>, that is, "the initiated," those taught the mysteries of demons, as Theodoret explains in *Questions on Deuteronomy 18*: those initiated into idols. In the same sense, "initiated" and "perfection" are used in *Psalm 105:29 and 106:28*: "And they were initiated to Baal-Peor." They were initiated or consecrated to Baal-Peor while they celebrated solemn and festive days for him. For <lang="greek">τέλη καὶ τελεταὶ</lang> <note>tele kai teletai</note> are the rites and ceremonies of the Gods, the purifications which, according to Plato, they called *teletai* because at the *telos*, that is, in
<margin>Syntagma 2, ch. 2, p. 237.</margin>
<margin>Syntagma 1, ch. 5 & Syntagma 2, ch. 5.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>The Rites of Priapus.</margin>
death, those sacrifices were made to the spirits of the dead. Some have seen the aforementioned Psalm as dealing with these sacrifices, and it pleased Apollinaris to express it thus in his *Paraphrase of the Psalms*:

> Those who, like Baal-Peor, were defiled by the rites,
> Tasted the nocturnal hecatomb of the dead.

To others, such as Theodoret and Lyra, it is established that they are called "sacrifices of the dead" because they were offered to false gods and inanimate idols. Where Bellarmine's words on page 694 are: "They ate the sacrifices of the dead, that is, they ate sacrifices offered to dead Gods, not to the living God, who alone is the true God. Moreover, they are called dead Gods either as the idols themselves, which being as if dead have eyes and see not, have ears and hear not; or as dead men, who were enrolled among the Gods by the pagans, such as Apis and Serapis in Egypt; Jupiter and Apollo among the Greeks; Romulus and others among the Romans." And from this comes <lang="greek">ὁ τελεσφόρος</lang> <note>ho telesphoros</note>, that is, the "leader of the mysteries," the "perfecter of the initiate." Concerning which *Deuteronomy 23:17* says: "There shall be no *telesphoros* <note>cult prostitute/initiate</note> among the daughters of Israel," etc., which words regarding the shameful imitation in the rites of idols are learnedly explained by Bonfrerius.
<margin>p. 1002 ff.</margin>

When interpreters find deities that are obscure *on account of their antiquity*, or suspect something from the name, they either explain them by those things which fit a known deity, or they guess from the actions performed, so that it is not entirely unknown. They did both in the case of the deity Baal-Peor: Baal is similar to Jupiter (see Augustine, *Schedules on the Gods of the Gentiles, p. 162*); Astarte is similar to Juno (the same Augustine). Other writers also take this liberty for themselves. Tacitus, the describer of our nation, says the Suebi worshipped Isis; and that Castor and Pollux were held in veneration by the Naharvali. When the Romans had observed the rites of the Germans and saw that certain things agreed with their own rites, they immediately applied the names of their own deities to them. For who would believe that the Germans of the ancient age had Castor and Pollux by those same names from the Romans? Therefore the Historian rightly adds: "They record the Gods as Castor and Pollux by Roman interpretation." The Germans worshipped Fire. Caesar says in *Book 6 of the Gallic War* that they counted Vulcan in the number of the Gods, for Vulcan was the same to the Romans as Fire was to the Germans. The Germans worshipped the deity Wodan, according to Paul the Deacon in *History of the Lombards, Book 1, ch. 9*; the Romans rendered this in their own language as *Mercury*. The Babylonians worshipped *Bel*; Jerome calls him *Saturn* in *Isaiah ch. 46, p. 171*. Likewise Philo, the translator of Sanchuniathon, shaped certain names of the Phoenician Gods according to Greek deities, and expressed in Greek words what Sanchuniathon had in Phoenician. If you desire examples, go to Vossius. And thus the Greeks and Latins explained some barbarian deity as Jupiter or Isis; that one as Juno or Ceres; another as Hercules or Mars or a Monster, and so in other cases. Henry Cornelius Agrippa says: "The supreme and unique act of reason is Religion, which from the beginning was commanded to man, namely the true and unique Spiritual worship of the one, only, and true God the Creator. But with reason corrupted, and the Serpent as Master, soon the whole of religion collapsed into nothing but the lust of the flesh. Men followed this as if it were the highest happiness, and the most filthy Priapus, the organ of primordial sin, was held as a GOD." To him...
<margin>l. c. p. 115.</margin>
<margin>Book 1 on Idolatry, 22.</margin>
<margin>2nd Epistle, p. 667.</margin>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<meta>Catchword: sacred— Isaiah.</meta>

<margin>The Rites of Priapus.</margin> They offered sacrifices; to him all the first temples were dedicated; his most filthy images were the first of all to be constructed. The first architects of religions—the Chaldeans, Egyptians, Assyrians, Babylonians, Arabs, Scythians, Phoenicians, and Ethiopians—worshiped him, as did all of Asia, Africa, and Europe; nor was it lawful for any man to become a priest who had not first been initiated into the rites of Priapus. This is that Belphegor <note>A Moabite deity associated with licentious worship</note>, the most ancient idol of all, which was also called Chemosh after Ham the son of Noah, according to the witness of Berosus; for this reason he was surnamed *Esenna*, that is, the "shameless" or "ignominious propagator." For he was the first to restore, after the Flood, this foul religion of depraved reason which had been received from those ancient Giants before the Flood. From this source came those Orgiastic, Bacchanalian, and Priapic rites, and all other most shameful ceremonies. From here Venus, Cupid, the private parts of Osiris, Pan, and the Satyrs were accepted as gods. Those foulnesses of idols and ceremonies utterly disgrace pagan rites, just as Augustine objects to and reproaches them. He reports such shameful and wicked things concerning the "fascination" <note>original: *fascino*, referring to the phallic amulet</note> of Priapus, and the filthiness of the rites of Father Liber <note>Bacchus</note> and Cybele (whom others called Berecinthia or the Great Mother of the Gods), that no one can read or hear them without amazement and blushing—that such detestable crimes began to be called the "mysteries" of the gods. From these we shall bring forth some of the dregs of the Unclean Spirit. In Book <margin>col. 355.</margin> VI, chapter nine* [of *The City of God*] begins thus: *“What of the very duties of the Divinities, so meanly and minutely divided, on account of which they say one must supplicate them for each one's specific gift—of which we have already mentioned many, though not all—are they not more akin to buffoonery than consistent with divine dignity?”* After various examples in which he exposed the ridiculous and obscene rites and duties, he finally adds, as if <margin>col. 357.</margin> an exceptional and highly dishonest example, that of Priapus, *writing:* *“What shall I say of this, when Priapus is there, excessively masculine, upon whose immense and most foul phallus the new bride was commanded to sit, according to the most 'honorable' and 'religious' custom of matrons?”* When they wish to excuse these and other things reported as lewd by distinguishing between writers and places, the answer to those solemn rites of vanity and obscenity is: *“Let them go on trying to distinguish with what subtlety they can the 'civil theology' from 'fabulous theology,' the cities from the theaters, the temples from the stages, the rites of the Pontiffs from the songs of the Poets—as if they could separate honorable things from the base, the true from the false, the grave from the light, the sacred from the playful, or the desirable from the rejected, etc.”* Concerning the Phallus or the male member, he who carried it was called a <term>Phallophoros</term> <note>Phallus-bearer</note>, and the procession itself was called <term>phallogogia</term> <note>the leading of the phallus</note> according to Theodoret, or <term>periphallia</term>, as is clear from Hesychius. And the song of the choir from Aristophanes is called the <term>Phallic song</term>. Among others, <margin>P. 530.</margin> Kircher writes thus in *The Egyptian Oedipus*: *“The Phallus or male member was a symbol of the fertility of the Sun, the all-seeing.”* Having joined its origin to the religion of the Egyptians and Greeks, he adds the cause of the widespread cult on page 531 in these words: *“Why, after the Egyptians, the Greeks and Romans (who drew these things from the Egyptians) always cultivated rites of this kind with such great zeal, I find to be because by this cult those evils which might hinder generation, or enchantments, were turned away; and also because of that part of the body from which the origin of all things comes. Another reason moved them, so that to turn away...”*

<column-break/>

<margin>The rites of Priapus.</margin> ...even to turn away impotence caused by sorcery and the sterility of women, they wore them in place of phylacteries <note>protective charms</note> around the neck, on the hands, on the belt, and in the ears. It is clear from hieroglyphics that for the same reason these were attached to animals and beasts, in which this phallic object occurs quite frequently. He adds that the Hebrews themselves, maddened by a foolish imitation of the Egyptians, turned to this to ward off sterility: "We assert that for the same reasons the Hebrew nation also embraced these most foul rites, and did so all the more willingly and greedily as they were more prone to every kind of superstition and all manner of filth of luxury. For since the Egyptians ascribed all the happiness of the earth, as well as the fertility of men and beasts, to the cult of this Priapus or 'Ithyphallus' <note>a representation of the erect phallus</note>, nothing was easier for a nation—among whom nothing was more shameful than sterility, and which, having loosened the reins of temperance, miserably threw itself into every kind of lust even under the pretext of honorable human propagation—than to adopt those rites for themselves. Under the mask of religion, they could do so safely and with impunity, and following the example of the Egyptians, they could turn away that shameful sterility, which was cursed in the Law, through the Priapic cult." Volcuinus, Abbot in Sedenbach, relates the "fornicating priests" to Belphegor in a *Homily which Wissenburg (or rather Flacius) saw to be published at Basel with other small works, regarding the Gospel of the Sowing of the Tares*: <margin>P. 742.</margin> *“Belphegor,” he says, “has his priests; Baal has his; Dagon has his. They serve Belphegor, that is, the God of Lust, who, bowing themselves to any luxury whatsoever, nourish a harlot in their house, reeking with the stench of libido even more than the laity.”* <margin>P. 746.</margin> Someone [asks], *“Is there anything greater or more enormous than to handle the daughter of Venus by night, and the son of the Virgin by day?”* He continues on page 749 and addresses each of these priests of the petty gods gathered into one bundle, as it were: *“To these three kinds of priests the Devil has betrothed his three daughters: namely, Pride, Avarice, and Luxury. Pride to the priests of Baal, that is, the ambitious who wish to rule. Avarice to the priests of Dagon, that is, the greedy and inquisitive. Luxury to the priests of Belphegor, that is, the shameless and lustful. O profane and detestable marriages! For what is born of these but monsters? The Church, the beautiful bride of Christ, suffers such monstrous nuptials and an enormous race. These are,”* <term>as much as it is lawful for one to say</term>, *“and to close with the words of Pliny (Book 28, ch. 6), things which it was right to report, though most of them only with 'honor being said' <note>a polite disclaimer like 'saving your presence'</note>.”*

The present paragraph bears witness that to the Sun—that illustrious star visible by its most bright torch—horses, chariots, and four-horse teams were dedicated in the time of Josiah. This was according to the custom of the Persians, or introduced through the Assyrians by superstition, as Tremellius* indicates, who dedicated chariots to the Sun. <margin>Chariots of the Sun. at ch. 45 v. 1 of Isaiah.</margin>

# On 2 Kings 23, v. 11.

<margin>Chariots of the Sun. book 7.</margin>And they consecrated them, as if "the swiftest thing to the swiftest of the gods," <note>original: "τò τάχιστον τῷ ταχυτάτῳ θεῶν"</note> as are the words of Heliodorus in the *Ethiopian Story*, book 10. Concerning this deed of Josiah, Josephus says in *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 10, chapter 3, page 334: "He searched the houses, the villages, and the cities, lest anyone might have something inside for the idol which they worshipped. Not only that, but also the chariots placed there by the kings, which his ancestors had constructed, and whatever else of that kind there was, which he found being worshipped as a god." In the expeditions of the Persians, the chariot of Jupiter <note>The Roman name used here for the Persian supreme deity, likely Ahura Mazda</note> used to go before with the horse of the Sun. Herodotus says: "Behind these ten horses was placed the sacred chariot of Jupiter, which eight white horses drew. Behind the horses followed a charioteer on foot, holding the reins." Quintus Curtius in book 3: "Then white horses drew the chariot consecrated to Jupiter. These horses of extraordinary size, which they call the horses of the Sun, followed." This seems to have been instituted by Cyrus, of whom Xenophon in book 8 of the *Education of Cyrus* records that he sacrificed horses to the Sun, with chariots proceeding before sunrise for the sacrificial procession. Herodotus says in his first book that the Massagetae likewise sacrificed a horse to the Sun; Xenophon says the same of the Armenians in book 4 of the *Anabasis*. Benjamin [of Tudela] in his *Itinerary*, page 107, relates something not entirely different regarding the inhabitants of Haoulam or Ceylon: "They venerate the Sun; and they have altars or great high places, arranged everywhere outside the city at a distance of half a mile. Thus in the morning they go out to meet the Sun: for on each of the altars or high places there is a sort of solar disk fashioned by magical arts; which turns with a very great noise when the Sun rises. Then each person, both men and women, holding their own censer in hand, offers incense to the sun," according to the interpretation of D. L. Empereur, who adds certain things in his Notes on page 214. Concerning the horses of the Sun, Isidore of Seville says in book 18, chapter 36: "Four-horse chariots, two-horse chariots, three-horse chariots, and six-horse chariots are named from the number of horses and the yoke; of these they consecrated the four-horse chariots to the Sun, the two-horse to the Moon, the three-horse to the underworld, and the six-horse to Jupiter. They join four-horse chariots to the Sun for this reason: because the year turns through four seasons—spring and summer, autumn and winter." Cassiodorus in book 3 of the *Variae* to Faustus, concerning the Circus games: "The two-horse chariot was invented in imitation of the Moon, the four-horse chariot in imitation of the Sun."

<margin>Ovid, book 2 of the Metamorphoses.</margin>> Meanwhile the swift horses Pyrois, Eous, and Aethon,
> The Sun's horses, and the fourth, Phlegon, fill the air with
> Flaming neighs, and strike the barriers with their feet.

<margin>Manilius, book 5.</margin>> And where Phoebus [the Sun] is in his four-horse chariot and Delia [the Moon] in her two-horse chariot.

<margin>Statius, book 6 of the Thebaid, v. 348.</margin>> Now nine times had the morning star sent down the dewy stars
> From heaven, and as many times the Moon had preceded the fires,
> A night-traveler with a changed horse.

Regarding this passage, Lutatius says: "The morning star rises both in the morning and in the evening; but with a changed horse. Moreover, the poets give four-horse chariots to the sun, two-horse chariots to the moon, and single horses to the stars." By the same number they attribute four-horse chariots to Pluto, which four black horses, breathing fire from their nostrils, used to pull. Likewise, horses are attributed to Neptune, by which he is carried through the sea. Concerning them, Homer says in *Iliad* 13, v. 23:
"He harnessed to the chariot his two bronze-hoofed horses, swift-flying, with flowing golden manes."
Where Eustathius lists the four horses of Neptune: Eriolen, Glancus, Enceladus, Sthenarus, and explains there why they were distinguished by these names. Others, however, think his chariot is pulled by seals and whales rather than by horses, the reason for which Natalis Comes recounts in *Mythology*, book 2, chapter 8, page 164. But to return to the fable of the horses and chariot of the

<column-break/>

Sun, antiquity attributed chariots to him because his rising and setting were more manifest. Sophocles introduces the Sun in a personification thus:
<margin>Chariot of the Sun. Ajax, v. 858.</margin>> "And you, O Sun, who drive your chariot through the steep sky,
> When you see my ancestral land,
> Checking your gold-backed reins,
> Announce my ruin and my fate
> To my aged father and my wretched nurse."

Claudian, in the first book of *In Praise of Stilicho*, ascribes exultation to the horses of the Sun:
> "Then the stars say that even the horses of the Sun
> Exulted in dances."

The ancient Greeks established two gates for the passage of the Sun, which Homer calls "doors" in the description of the cave of Ithaca, namely Cancer and Capricorn. For when the Sun reaches the final goal in Capricorn, he prepares his return. Perhaps from this arose the fiction of the two horses of the Sun, about which Tertullian says in *On the Spectacles*, chapter 5, page 86: "In the beginning there were two horses for the Sun, a white one and a red one; the white for winter because of the white snows; the red for summer because of the redness of the Sun." Some called these Phaethon and Lampon or Lamponta, though some preferred to ascribe them to the Dawn, among whom is Homer.
<margin>Odyssey, book 23, v. 246.</margin>"Lampon and Phaethon, the colts that carry the Dawn."
Regarding Phaethon, they tell the story that a desire came upon him to set the chariot of the sun on fire, and hence he was struck down by a lightning bolt. Plutarch in *On Contentment* says: "Phaethon, having ascended into heaven, wept if no one would hand over to him his father's horses and chariots." And Cicero in book 3 of *On Duties*: "The Sun said to his son Phaethon that he would do whatever he wished. He wished to be lifted into the chariot of the Sun. He was lifted up, and he, before he could stop, was consumed by the strike of a lightning bolt." Ovid described this fable copiously; Natalis Comes dealt with it most copiously of all in book 6 of *Mythology*, chapter 1, page 544 and following. Others attributed a four-horse chariot to him because of the four seasons of the year, and consequently four horses, whose names are Eous, Lampas, Pyrois, and Phlegon, whence the verse:
> "The four hours of light are called the horses of the Sun:
> This one grows red, this one shines, this one grows hot, that one is warm."

From this it is clear why horses, chariots, and wheels were attributed to the Sun; and from this Sophocles in *Antigone* v. 1180 is to be explained, where he said:
"But know well that the sun shall not complete many more
Competing circles of the wheel."
And the Scholiast explained it as "succeeding one another." The competing wheels of the Sun indicate the spaces of time, where by the course of the Sun the successions and varieties of the seasons occur, as if in a certain contest.
The Venerable Bede, in *Questions on the Book of Kings*, question 28, explains with an elegant conjecture why horses were attributed to the Sun: <margin>Volume 4, page 459.</margin> "This place shows that the Jews were enslaved to every kind of idolatry and superstition at all times, so much so that in veneration of the Sun, whom they believed to be a God in the manner of the Gentiles, they placed chariots and horses beneath the image of him they had made, and this in the courts of the temple of the Lord. For thus the Gentiles are accustomed to paint or make an image of the Sun, so that placing a young boy in a chariot, they join to it horses as if seeking the sky in their course. They fit the image of a boy to him for this reason: because the Sun, as if born daily with a new rising, falls into no old age through the ages." —

<meta>This page continues the discussion of biblical antiquities, specifically focusing on the transition from the story of Elijah to the reforms of King Josiah regarding solar worship, and the nature of Baal worship.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Chariot of the Sun</margin>
The Greeks, hearing from the Israelites (who were rumored to possess divine writings) that *Elijah* was translated to the heavens in a chariot with horses of fire, or perhaps seeing this very scene depicted on a wall, were deceived by the similarity of the names. Because the name <term>Elias<note>original: ἡλίας</note></term>, if the accent is shifted to the first syllable and the 'a' is changed to 'o', becomes <term>Helios<note>original: ἥλιος; the Greek word for the Sun</note></term>, they believed this designated the Sun’s passage through the heavens. Thus, they transformed a miracle performed by God into an argument for error—a fiction of human folly. The Jews themselves imitated these pagans, busying themselves so as not to appear any less foolish than the most foolish of the Gentiles. *Elijah*, carried up to the heavens, ascended <term>in a lamp of fire<note>original: ἐν λαμπάδι πυρὸς</note></term>, having been made a <term>charioteer of the elements<note>original: ἡνιόχ. τῇ τῶν στοιχείων</note></term>, as *Athanasius* skillfully puts it in his *Oration on the Assumption of Christ* (Vol. 2, p. 5). Hence, out of a <term>perverse imitation<note>original: κακοζηλίᾳ</note></term>, this venerable author believed the Greeks distorted the fiery chariot of *Elijah* being carried into heaven into the horses of the Sun. However, this is quite uncertain, even if *Chrysostom* himself anticipated the same conjecture regarding the similarity of the names in his *Second Sermon on Elijah*. For it is hardly credible that this was a Greek invention, since it is attributed to the Persian nation, whose language knows nothing of the affinity between the names of the Sun and *Elijah*. The Hebrew name actually signifies "My GOD is *Jehovah*." Compare Meursius, *Spicilegium on Theocritus*, pp. 150-151; Vossius, *On Idolatry*, Book 2, ch. 31, p. 464. It remains for us to say a few words on this passage regarding the manner of the horses and chariots of the Sun removed by King *Josiah*. Concerning the horses, the Sacred Codex uses the word <term>shabat<note>original: שבת</note></term>, which means *he caused to cease, he moved away, he removed, he abolished, he took away*; concerning the chariots, it uses <term>saraph<note>original: שרף</note></term>, which signifies *to burn, to set on fire, to cremate*. Regarding both, the Septuagint uses <term>burned up<note>original: κατέκαυσεν</note></term>. From this, a disagreement has arisen among interpreters: were these merely images, figures, or crafted likenesses of the horses and chariots of the Sun, or were they actually living horses and chariots in which they were carried while worshipping the rising Sun? *John Selden* explains them as cast images of horses and four-horse chariots consecrated to the Sun in *The Syrian Gods* (Syntagma 2, ch. 9), a view shared by almost all interpreters. But Rabbi David Kimchi, Rabbi Solomon Jarchi, and Levi Ben Gerson explain the passage as referring to horses and a chariot with which they led a solemn procession from the entrance of the Temple to the chamber of Nathan-Melech while worshipping the rising Sun; Sanctius follows them in this. They appeal to the first authors of this idolatry, the Persians, for whom a living horse was sacred to the Sun and usually sacrificed; likewise, the four-horse chariots were not painted images, but actual ones that used to precede the Persians on expeditions, as is clear from Herodotus above. They also appeal to the Sacred text. Regarding those specific horses, *Paulus Aringhius* says in *Subterranean Rome*:

<margin>Vol. 2, Book 5, ch. 17, p. 495.</margin>
> Those horses, which were dedicated at the entrance of the Jerusalem Temple near the chamber of Nathan-Melech and were later prohibited, were by no means lifeless or manufactured, but were certainly living creatures. They were studiously nourished there in stables so that at the appropriate times, when the customary sacred rites were to be performed, they might be sacrificed by the very hands of the priests in service to the Sun to whom they had been dedicated. Thus, thrown alive into the flames and consumed by the solar rays, they would be turned into a burnt offering for the sun.

This is clearly what the evidence suggests, and we may freely judge it so ourselves; for if the horses we mentioned were made of wood or some similar material

<column-break/>

<margin>The Chariot of the Sun</margin>
that fire could easily dissolve and consume—just as the chariot is said to have been consumed by fire—by the same logic, horses made of the same material and fitted to the chariot would be described as burned by fire. But the horses *were removed*, and only the chariot was burned. Therefore, the horses were rescued from the fire, having already been devoted to the flames by the insane superstition of men, and were transferred to better uses. So says that author.

-> I KINGS XVIII. 25. <-
-> <term>And they called on the name of Baal from morning until noon.<note>original Hebrew: ויקראו בשם-הבעל מהבקר ועד-הצהרים</note></term> <-
-> <term>And they called on the name of Baal from morning until midday.<note>original Greek: Καὶ ἐπεκαλέσαντο ἐν ὀνόματι τῷ Βαὰλ ἐκ πρωί-θεν ἕως μεσημβρίας.</term> <-

> They called upon the name of Baal from morning even until noon.

<margin>Baalitic worship.</margin>
That the error of "much speaking" <note>referring to repetitive, empty prayers</note> was deep-seated and practiced in the most ancient centuries regarding prayers and sacrifices (by which they thought the Divinities could be won over) is clearly gathered from the history of *Elijah*. When he spoke to the Prophets of Baal—who were pouring out harsh, hollow, and empty words to their gods with unrestrained liberty of praise—he said with prophetic irony: *Cry with a louder voice; for he is a god, and perhaps he is talking, or is in an inn* (the Hebrew is slightly different), *or on a journey, or surely he sleeps and must be awakened.* These foolish people believed that the Gods sometimes departed from their seats or were occupied with others; for this reason, they bound them with golden chains to ensure the favor and Spirit of the Gods remained in the idols. Thus the Tyrians, when pressed by siege, bound Hercules, and the Lacedaemonians bound Mars, so they would not flee. For the anxious vanity of the ancients wanted a divinity to preside over every city. The Gods of a place or city were called "Genii" by the Latins, hence the ancient inscriptions: TO THE GENIUS OF THIS PLACE. Regarding these guardians and protectors of cities, *Ovid* writes:

<margin>Fasti, Book 5, v. 136</margin>
> They also stand for us, and preside over the walls of the city,
> And they are present and bring help.

Sometimes they dreamed that the Gods had gone *abroad*. Homer feigns the absence of Jupiter in Egypt, on which see *Hoffmann*.
<margin>Various Readings, 1. 22.</margin>
Sometimes they also held the opinion that the Gods *sleep*; *Aben Ezra* dares to conjecture that this idea had settled in the minds of the Philistines, at whose wicked deeds the God of Israel had long winked, based on Psalm 78, v. 65. For he explains this verse and the following one as referring to the punishment with which God afflicted the Palestinians, the unjust possessors of the Ark of the Lord. I will first give the sense of the verses from the paraphrase of *Johannes Campensis*. v. 65: *And the Lord finally awoke, as one is accustomed to do who, overcome by wine, comes to himself after a long sleep, and being cheered again by wine, boldly attacks dangers.* v. 66: *wherefore he smote the behinds of his enemies.* The Rabbi says the Scripture speaks here according to the perception of the Philistines; namely, that to them the God of the Israelites seemed to have been sleeping and, as if overcome by a hangover, neglected to bring help to his people. But this explanation is "made of fig-wood" <note>meaning weak or flimsy</note>, and therefore we do not rely on it. The Philistines mocked the Jews as being devoid of law and Gods; yet divine vengeance finally found the Philistine scoffers, even if it was slow to snatch them for punishment. God had spared them until then for a heavier penalty, according to that most true maxim of Valerius Maximus regarding Dionysius:

<margin>Book I, ch. 1.</margin>
> The divine wrath proceeds with a slow step to its vengeance, and compensates for the slowness of the punishment with its weight.

# From 1 Kings XVIII. v. 25.

<margin>The worship of Baal.</margin>
...he compensates, for in a certain opinion, divine help long delayed in the eyes of men is like a sleep, which brings about the forgetting of all things; but divine vengeance does not sleep, *keeping watch over the wicked deeds of the ungodly* <note>original Greek: ταῖς τῶν ἀσεβῶν πονηρίαις ἀγρυπνῶν</note>. It follows closely that the superstitious Baalitic nation enclosed Baal within the heavens and walls; it is clear from the words of Elijah—by which he exposes the madness of their blinded minds—that they knocked at the doors of the heavenly Jove or Olympian Baal with a monstrous shout, as if he were in dreams. For that which was said in mockery by Elijah, a spectator of their rites, was taken seriously by those Baalites, as witnessed by those outcries and confused murmurs of the Prophets and Priests of the Phoenician Bel: *They cried therefore with a loud voice, and cut themselves, according to their ritual, with knives and lancets, until they were covered in blood.* In these shameful mysteries (as noted by Sedulius in *commentary on Romans 1, sheet 18*), they afflicted their own bodies with insults, *while they inflicted brands and burns upon themselves in the sacraments of the idols, so that, as if insane, they might be the avengers of their own sins upon themselves.*

<margin>p. 71.</margin>
In the worship of Isis, they cut themselves with small swords. The Carians, according to Herodotus in these words from *Euterpe*: *As many of the Carians as live in Egypt cut their foreheads with knives* <note>original Greek: Ὅσοι κωφῶν εἰσὶ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ οἰκέοντες, τὰ μέτωπα κόπτονται μαχαίρῃσι</note>. Regarding the priests of Bellona <note>The Roman goddess of war</note>, it is reported by Accone, an ancient author, that they cut their upper arms and shoulders, sacrificing their own blood to Bellona.

<margin>I. s. p. 381.</margin>
Lucian indicates laceration in the worship of the Syrian goddess. In that same manner, the priests of the noisy Baal cut themselves with a knife, to testify either to their grief arising from impatience, or to their zeal and love toward Baal in this solemn prayer; for while the people looked on, they bloodied themselves to appease Baal, because they believed the Deity was propitiated by blood, and especially human blood. Thus *that most holy high priest (of Cybele) offered up impure blood by also castrating his arms*, as Tertullian says in *Apology ch. 25, p. 41*. The cutting and bloodied wounding of limbs was a sign of love as well as mourning among Eastern peoples. I gather this from the words of Muhammad in *Surah 12 of the Quran, verse 31*, concerning Joseph, upon seeing whom certain women (whom Pharaoh's wife had summoned) *wounded their hands by cutting them*; as the Impostor <note>A common historical polemic term for Muhammad</note> imagines. This custom is familiar to the Arabs, Persians, and other peoples of the East, *as those who know say* <note>original Greek: ὡς φασὶν οἱ εἰδότες</note>. G. Fabricius in his *Book of Heavenly Victories to Johann Tetelbach*: *The monstrosity of worship followed the vanity of fictional deities, such that they thought God was appeased by slaughter and human blood. The Scythians sacrificed guests and strangers; the Kings of the Carthaginians and Moabites sacrificed their children; nor did Manasseh of Judah and Ahaz of Israel, Kings, abstain from these crimes. The priests of Cybele and Bellona raged against their own limbs with small knives and awls. The Baalites did the same, and their imitators, the Muhammadan Monks, do so to this day.* Regarding the Muhammadan peoples, the most ferocious since men were born, Salomon Schweigger in *book 2 of his itinerary, ch. 58, p. 197* and Wenceslaus Budowitz in the *preface of his Horologium, p. 4*, testify from *personal eyewitness* <note>original Greek: αὐτοψίᾳ</note>. Regarding the Jews, Christian Gerson in *part 1 on the Talmud, ch. 2, p. 16, 17* notes they were formerly forbidden to mourn the dead by shaving the head or cutting the flesh, *Deuteronomy ch. 14, v. 1, 2*. Upon which passage P. Fagius, the interpreter of Onkelos, says: *The nations used to wound certain parts of the body with a needle, or otherwise cut*

<column-break/>

<margin>— worship.</margin>
*them, and applied ink, which was done in the worship of their Demons. It is therefore commanded that they should in no way strike their flesh as the nations do, just like the priests of Cybele.* But it is our task to deal with the cutting of the body which was done by biting, or by a knife, or by any other iron tool, for the sake of worship. Concerning the fanatical worshippers of the Syrian Goddess, Apuleius says near the end of *Metamorphoses, book VIII: For a long time, with heads lowered, twisting their necks with slippery motions, and spinning their hanging hair in a circle, and sometimes attacking their own muscles with bites; and finally with the two-edged iron which they carried, they also dissected their own arms. Amidst this, one of them raved wildly and, drawing frequent breaths from his deepest heart, as if filled with the divine spirit of the deity, he simulated a wounded madness entirely, to which idolatry in Syria Baronius wrongly conjectures that Christ alluded in Matthew 6:7.* Julius Firmicus in *On the Error of Profane Religions, ch. 2*, concerning the lamentation for Osiris: *They wail with annual mournings, they shave their heads, so that, dishonored by the foulness of the head, they may bewail the pitiable fate of their King: they beat the breast, they lacerate the arms, they reopen the scars of both wounds.* Lucian in *On Mourning* mentions that the Greeks, at funerals or other unlucky events, bloodied their cheeks, where just as there are *reddened cheeks* <note>original Greek: φοινισσόμεναι παρειαὶ</note>, so in Homer there are *torn cheeks* <note>original Greek: ἀμφίδρυφοι παρειαί</note>, where it concerns women who had mangled their cheeks with their nails in grief. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The worship of Baal.</margin>
...understand) most opportunely for all. With great superstition in their ceremonies, the Baalites cried out to Baal; **four hundred and fifty men, prophets of the groves,** invoked the names of the Gods (*1 Kings 18:22, 25*). They worshiped and honored him with an ox, and around the altar, *they leaped upon the altars* <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ βωμῶν ἐσιλτάβαντ</note>; Luther's German translation says: *they hopped around the altar.* For the Hebrew word *Pasach* <note>פסח</note> signifies both to leap over and to limp. You might say in Greek, following Herodian (*Book V*): *the local women danced with him, running in a circle around the altars* <note>original Greek: περιϊόντα τοῖς βωμοῖς</note> (*running in a circle around the altars*) *carrying cymbals or drums in their hands.* In the sacred rites of the Mother of the Gods, Strabo describes the Priests (*Book X*) as acting *enthusiastically and in a Bacchic manner, with armed movement, amidst noise and clamor, and cymbals, and drums.* They were called Corybantes because, *striking their heels* <note>original Greek: κόρια κόπτοντες</note>, they moved forward dancing. Religious honor, due to the Gods, consisted chiefly in supplications, festivals, sacrifices, temples, altars, and statues. Baal had altars, images, statues, drink offerings, groves, high places, and shrines; as J. Herenchmid collected and observed from sacred writings in his *Sacred Kissing* <note>Latin: Osculologia sacra</note>; *see page 45.* Strabo writes (*Book III*) that the Celtiberians and neighboring peoples celebrated nocturnal vigils to a certain unnamed God by leading dances. What did Balak, King of the Moabites, do when he was in distress? He judged Balaam the Soothsayer, hired with many prayers and much money, most worthy to curse the people of Israel *over the victims* <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ τῶν τομίων</note>, <margin>on false embassies</margin> though he himself was worthy to perish a thousand times. Demosthenes (p. 209) said of such an imprecation: *pray to the gods to make some of them utterly destroyed, both in race and in ruin* <note>original Greek: ἔυχου θεοῖς, ἐξώλη ποιεῖν τινα αὐτῶν, καὶ γένῃ, καὶ ὄλεθρον</note>, so that all the gods might make them unfortunate. Balaam wanted seven altars erected for the supplication made to Baal, and sacrifices added—seven bulls and as many rams—by which they thought their vows would be heard. Where are those who attribute a pagan *magical* <note>Greek: μαγειῶδες</note> quality to the number seven? Perhaps so that he might draw favor from a higher sevenfold power; for he had otherwise experienced the force of that sevenfold number, says Fabricius <margin>Annals 31, p. 109.</margin> and Paduanius *in the Chain of Time, when he discussed the sevenfold number most extensively.*

> Build for me (these are the words of Balaam to Balak) seven altars here, and prepare for me seven bulls and seven rams. And Balak did as Balaam had commanded, and offered a bull and a ram on every altar.

Yet when it came to the words, no voice of one threatening or devoting to destruction was heard; for Balaam could not be corrupted by price. Despising the earthly King by whose reward he had been hired, he spoke according to the will of the heavenly Ruler, as stands in *Numbers chapters 22, 23, 24.* So far was he from devoting the Israelites to destruction with curses (which were done according to Ethnic custom and purpose), that he blessed them and, amidst the greatest praises, uttered that memorable and deservedly praised voice: *How beautiful are your tents, etc.* With such a curse <margin>1 Samuel 17:43</margin> that uncircumcised Philistine combatant <note>Goliath</note> devoted David—an untrained and unwarlike youth—to destruction, crying out with a stentorian voice: *Am I a dog, that you come against me with sticks?* "Dog" in sacred scripture became a proverb of contempt; and he cursed him by his gods, *to the shame of the gods* <note>original Greek: πρὸς αἰσχρή θεῶν</note>; which omen the Gods turned back upon him, *and he perished miserably, just as he deserved* <note>original Greek: ἐκεῖνον γε ὥσπερ ἦν ἄξιος κακῶς κακῶς ἀπώλετο</note>, as Demosthenes said of one who had perished at sea. See the formulas of dire imprecations in Brisson's learned work *On Formulas, Book I, p. 110.*

<column-break/>

However, as imprecations <margin>The worship of Baal.</margin> lose their force and power, they would pray that dire things might not happen; the Gods "averruncate" <note>term: averruncant - an ancient Roman religious term meaning to avert or ward off evil</note>.

> Gods, forbid these threats; Gods, avert such a misfortune.

Finally, one must note regarding the rites and prayers of the Baalites their *much-speaking* <note>Greek: πολυλογία</note> and *great fantasy* <note>Greek: πολλὴ φαντασία</note>, by which from morning until late evening, with a great jumble of words and a heap of titles, they busied themselves to earn the favor of the Divinities. And from these shoutings of long prayers, that saying of the Savior will receive mutual light: *When you pray, do not use many words* <note>Greek: μὴ βαττολογήσητε - "do not babble like Battus"</note>, *as the Heathens do: for they think that in their much-speaking* <note>Greek: ἐν τῇ πολυλογίᾳ αὐτῶν</note> *they will be heard.* <margin>Matthew chapter 6, verse 7.</margin> What kind of "babbling" and "much-speaking" this was, celebrated through their titles, we have investigated elsewhere, where it was noted that an immense number of Gods and Goddesses were worshiped with many, many names and surnames, which were proper and peculiar to each God. Or look at Baal himself now, how with various worship he passed into many names, neither great nor glorious. *In the Punic language, God is called Baal*, says Servius in his commentary on *Aeneid I, p. 262.* The Carthaginians took their voices, as they did their rites, from the Hebrews, for whom *Baal* <note>בעל</note> is Lord, and thence the Syrians *Bel* <note>ביל</note>, as in *Ezra 4:8.* To the Chaldeans, from the common letter L, it is *Bel* <note>Jes. 46:1</note>. Whence to the Greeks he is *Belos* <note>Βῆλος</note>, or with the ending omitted, *Baal* and *Bel*. The general title of the Gods was Baal, from which others were named with certain epithets, just as among the Latins you may find many Jupiters and Saturns; among whom, however, one most ancient claims the first place in the council of the Gods, from whose praise and fame that name was celebrated in other divinities. He who to the Greeks and Latins is Zeus and Jupiter, is to the Tyrians and Sidonians *Baal* <note>בעל</note>, whom the Greeks translate as *Belos*. Moreover, *Baal* is a common name for many Gods, since every God among them was called Baal. But that it was not the title of Jupiter alone, the *Alexandrian Chronicle* shows us, where you may read *that this glory of the name belonged to Mars.* To Mars <note>Greek: Ἄρει</note>, it says, *the Assyrians set up the first pillar and worshiped him as a god, whom until now the Persians call the god Baal, which is interpreted as Mars, the god of wars.* (There seems to be an error here, and instead of "god" one should perhaps read "Thurras" or something else.) Among the Assyrians also, Bel is called both Saturn and the Sun by a certain reasoning of the sacred rites, says the aforementioned Servius. Damascius has the same in the *Life of Isidore* in Photius, <margin>col. 242.</margin> <margin>P. 559.</margin> writing: *The Phoenicians and Syrians call Saturn El, and Bel, and Bolathen.* And also Procopius on *Isaiah p. 528*: *The Greeks also call Saturn Bel, to whom most people used to bring their dearest things as a sacrifice.* Know that regarding the God *El* <note>Ηλ</note>, the same is read in Servius concerning the name of the Assyrian Bel, saying: <margin>p. 254.</margin> *All in those parts worship the Sun, who in their own language is called Hel* <note>אל, El/God</note>, *whence by the Orientals* the name was attributed "by excellence" to the Sun whom they worshiped, from which also the Greek *Helios* <note>ἥλιος</note> was made. Eusebius, a man most highly praised in sacred and profane letters, holds the leading place in this matter, giving proof from the monuments of the most ancient writers that every nation—whether Phoenicians, Atlantians, Phrygians, or Cretans—had their own Jupiters and Saturns; and since Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are thus confused in fables...

<meta>This page continues a theological and historical analysis of ancient Near Eastern deities and biblical history, specifically focusing on the various titles of Baal and the Assyrian siege of Jerusalem.</meta>

# From 2 Kings 23:11

<margin>The worship of Baal.</margin>
<margin>1 Kings 15:13.</margin>
<margin>2 Kings 1:2.</margin>
<margin>Judges 8:33 & 9:4.</margin>
<margin>1 Kings 16:32, 33.</margin>
<margin>Tripartite History, Book 2, Chapter 20.</margin>
...so that neither Phoebus <note>The Greek sun god Apollo</note> himself could sufficiently distinguish them from himself, nor himself from them (these are the words of Selden, *Syntagma* 2, 1), and that numerous crowd of gods may be reduced by mythologists to the divinity of Apollo or the Sun; it is certainly no longer to be doubted that from one Bel, Baal, or Jupiter, invoked in the ridiculous manner of the ancients, innumerable titles were propagated. Hence, one may name a long series of epithets: *Baal-Shamayim* <note>original Hebrew: בעל שמים</note>, *Beel-Samen* <note>original Hebrew: בעלסאמין</note>, that is, as Philo of Byblos explains, "Lord of Heaven" <note>original Greek: κύριος οὐρανοῦ</note>. From Sanchuniathon in Eusebius, it is read thus concerning the Phoenicians: "They considered the Sun to be the only god, the lord of heaven, calling him Beelsamen, which among the Phoenicians is Lord of Heaven" <note>original Greek: Ἥλιον θεὸν ἐνόμιζον μόνον, οὐρανοῦ κύριον, Βεελσάμην καλοῦντες, ὅ ἐστι παρὰ φοίνιξι Κύριος οὐρανοῦ</note>. Jupiter had no other title among six hundred others; *Baal-Peor*, if he wishes to correctly maintain his name, will be that ill-omened and incestuous divinity Priapus, as we showed above at the asterisk. *Baal-Zebub* <note>original Hebrew: בעל זבוב</note>, the god of flies—if you translate it "at the foot" <note>original Greek: κατὰ πόδα; i.e., literally</note>—is Jupiter "the averter of flies" <note>original Greek: ἀπόμυιος</note> or "the fly-hunter" <note>original Greek: μυίαγρος</note>. In Ekron, a city of Phoenicia, this worship existed, as is read at the asterisk; the Jews adapted this Ekronite idol to the Prince of Demons, as is clear from Matthew 12:24, and that with a laudable "bad zeal" <note>original Greek: κακοζηλίᾳ; here meaning a mocking imitation</note>. In this matter, however, the wicked Pharisees are most worthy of the infernal whip, because they accuse the most holy Savior of casting out demons by the help of Beelzebub, through the instinct of Beelzebub. Concerning the etymology of the name, see Scaliger and Selden. *Muthumbal* in Plautus (whose Punic passages are explained by Selden, Petit, and Reinefius) is Pluto, the God of the underworld. These various surnames lie hidden in the plural *Baalim* <note>original Hebrew: בעלים</note>, when the Israelites are accused of having served "the Baals" <note>original Greek: τοῖς Βααλείμ</note>. The Shechemites used the general name of Baal at the asterisk. They abused this name to decorate the "naming ceremonies" <note>original Greek: ὀνομαθεσίας</note> of their Kings or illustrious Heroes, slightly changed, truncated, or even in full. For it often happened among the ancients that they bestowed the names of those they had transformed into Gods upon their Kings, and sometimes even upon private individuals; this can be seen from the nomenclature of Carthaginian leaders and Babylonian Kings in Otto Heurnius, *Ancient Barbarian Philosophy*, Book 2, Chapter 4; Reiner Reineccius, *Prolegomena to Julian History, Part I, p. 48*; and Vossius, *On Idolatry*, Book 2, Chapter 11, p. 364. There was a King of the Sidonians named *Eth-baal* (1 Kings 16:31), whose daughter Jezebel was married to Ahab, King of Israel; and at the same time, he learned idolatry from her, so that he served Baal and consecrated an altar and groves to him at the asterisk. So in the name of *Belshazzar*, we recognize the name of *Baal*, from which is contracted *Bel* <note>original Hebrew: בל</note>; and they judged no other title more fit to call Daniel in the Babylonian captivity than *Belteshazzar* <note>original Hebrew: בלטשצר</note>; concerning Bel and his treasure, a sign of superstition, though otherwise his birth and original notion were not ignoble. By a singular instinct, Gideon had destroyed the altar of Baal (Judges 6:32), from which deed of praise he was called *Jerub-Baal* <note>original Hebrew: ירבעל</note>, that is, the "adversary of Baal." Thus the Temple and shrines in which Baal was worshiped are designated by the linguistic usage *Beth* <note>original Hebrew: בית</note>, that is, "house," whence *Beth-Baal* (1 Kings 15), just as *Beth-Peor* is the temple of the God of Peor (Deuteronomy 34:6), and *Beth-Dagon* the temple of Dagon. Thus "house" <note>original Greek: δόμος</note> is used for temple by Dionysius Periegetes, who writes that Semiramis built a "great house" <note>original Greek: μέγαν δόμον</note> for Bel. And that which is celebrated as a "sacred place" <note>original Greek: ἱερόν</note> in Aphaca, Cassiodorus translates as "House" at the asterisk. In the same way, our ancestors made the names *Theoderic*, and by a more recent appellation, *Dietrich*, from *Teuth* and *Thied*, the idolatrous name of a God, just as we today use *Gotthard*, *Gottfried*, *Gottlieb*, or *Gottschalck* <note>German names incorporating "Gott" (God)</note>.

### 2 CHRONICLES 32:21

->And the Lord sent an angel, who destroyed every mighty man of valor, and the leader and the captain in the camp of the king of Assyria. <note>original Hebrew: וישלח יהוה מלאך ויכחד כל-גבור חיל ונגיד ושר במחנה מלך אשור</note><-
->And the Lord sent an angel, and he wiped out every powerful warrior, and ruler, and general in the camp of the king of the Assyrians. <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἀπέστειλε Κύριος ἄγγελον, καὶ ἐξέτριψε πάντα δυνατὸν πολεμιστὴν, καὶ ἄρχοντα, καὶ στρατηγὸν ἐν τῇ παρεμβολῇ τοῦ βασιλέως Ἀσσυρίων.</note><-
->*And the Lord sent an Angel, who struck every robust man and warrior and prince of the army of the King of the Assyrians.*<-

<margin>Isaiah 10:15.</margin>
<margin>Isaiah 10:5, 6, 7.</margin>
The prophetic comparison against the haughty mouth of Sennacherib must be noted: *Isaiah 10:15. Shall the axe boast itself against him who chops with it? Or shall the saw exalt itself against him who lifts it? How unbecoming it is for the axe, which is an instrument for cutting, to boast against the one cutting with it, and call itself the efficient cause, since he who cuts with it is the efficient cause.* Thus it does not befit the King of Assyria, with insane rashness, to ascribe the success of his victories to his own counsels and arms. For as far as the axe is from working or not working by its own will, rather than by the will of the man who works through it, so far was it from being in the Assyrian's hand to work his fortune, except by the will of God, who worked through him—to whom he himself was like the instruments, the axe and the saw, to the craftsman. But Assyria thought that he was the one who worked and subjugated peoples in fury according to his own pleasure, whereas God willed him to be nothing other than His instrument, and willed to work through him and send him to execute judgment on a deceitful nation and on the people of His fury; and therefore He said at the beginning of this matter at the asterisk: *Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger. I will send him against a deceitful nation, and against the people of my fury I will give him a charge. But he will not think so, and his heart will not so consider.*

<margin>2 Kings 18:13.</margin>
<margin>Isaiah 36:1.</margin>
<margin>2 Kings 16:7.</margin>
No other war was more formidable to the people of Jerusalem than that which Sennacherib, King of the Assyrians, brought against the city during the reign of Hezekiah; nor was there any other more admirable deliverance of the besieged. The Assyrian came with a most flourishing army against all the fortified cities of Judah <note>original Hebrew: על-כל-ערי יהודה הבצורות</note>, all of which, except Jerusalem, he devastated with fire and sword at the asterisk, with no one resisting. When this was finished, he decided to turn the entire force of the war against Jerusalem at the asterisk. "With a heavy army" <note>original Hebrew: בחיל כבד</note> (verse 17), "in great power" <note>original Greek: ἐν δυνάμει βαρεῖᾳ</note>, with a heavy army. The King of Jerusalem, feeling himself unequal to such a great army, sent ambassadors to meet him in the city of Lachish with mandates of this sort: *I have offended; depart from me; that which you put upon me, I will bear* (verse 14) <note>original Hebrew: חטאתי שוב מעלי את אשר-תתן עלי אשא</note>. These are words of fear from a somewhat timid King, otherwise good, who is led by repentance for his defection; for already from the time of Ahaz, his father, they had surrendered themselves to the Assyrians at the asterisk, when Ahaz, imploring the help of Tiglath-pileser, King of Assyria, against the King of Syria and the King of Israel, said through ambassadors quite slavishly: *I am your servant* <note>original Hebrew: עבדך</note> *and your son. Come up and save me from the hand of the King of Aram, and from the hand of the King of Israel, who have risen up against me.* Whence, until the fourteenth year of his reign, Hezekiah had remained tributary to him. Moved by this rebellion and stubbornness, by which he refused to pay the customary tribute, the Assyrian ascended against all the fortified cities of Judah; for the tyrant saw that once these were captured, his ascent toward Jerusalem would be easy. Therefore, having captured the cities according to his wish, he sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem, to whom the leaders Tartan and Rabsaris are read to have been joined. The King of Jerusalem sent his own legates voluntarily to the city of Lachish, where the army had encamped, to speak concerning the laws of peace; for Hezekiah did not wish to experience the doubtful hazard of war, promising anew a voluntary surrender and the payment of tribute. The King of Assyria accepted the conditions, imposing upon the King of Judah three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold—**300 hundredweight of silver and 30 hundredweight of gold** <margin>2 Kings 18:14-17</margin>. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sennacherib's war. Ezekiel 28:2.</margin>
Regarding the Prince of Tyre, because he boasted that he was a God, the Scripture says: *Because your heart is lifted up, and you have said, I am a GOD.* <note>original Hebrew: אל אני (El ani)</note> *Will you yet say before those who slay you, I am a GOD? But you are a man, and no God, in the hand of those who slay you.* From this we are permitted to see that God visits those who are proud in that which is not their own; for if they boast because of a kingdom, God takes it from them and gives it to the humblest of men, so that it is known by all that the kingdom does not belong to man, nor is it in his hand. Thus, if anyone boasts in divinity, so as to make himself a God, but God visits him and delivers him into the hands of a slayer, this is a true punishment against the one boasting to be a God, to show his disgrace—that there is not such power in him that he can snatch himself from death; for while he is delivered into the hand of the killer, he is shown not to be a Deity, since a man has power over him. The speech of the Heathens is wise: that bitter punishments are sent by God upon those who despise Him, and those who neglect the ceremonies and rites instituted by Him. It is necessary to examine how impiety toward the Deities and divine things displeased even those whose opinion was turned away from the truth of religion and perverse regarding sacred matters. The writers of Tragedy are especially elegant and grave interpreters of that religion; they are offended by this impiety, and each instructs particularly on this, as if on the greatest and first of matters. Oh, the tragic <term>deinotēs</term> <note>Greek: δεινότης - power, intensity, or terrible eloquence</note> of words! With what eloquent and grave speech does *Sophocles* strive to explain *Ajax son of Telamon*, and *Pindarus* explain *Capaneus*! Both were proud contemners of the Gods, and both are said to have been punished by the Gods for the nefarious crime of wickedness. How timely does Ovid discuss the monstrosity of *Pentheus*! As the subject demands, let us see what is handed down. One of the seven leaders who besieged Thebes was *Capaneus*, the husband of Evadne, who is said to have been struck by the lightning of Jupiter because of his contempt, when, having moved up the ladders, he wished to scale the Theban walls and occupy them even against the will of the gods; for he said not even the lightning of Jupiter could deter him from being able to take Thebes. In the pathetic buskin <note>A "buskin" refers to the high boots worn by tragic actors, symbolizing the tragic style.</note> of Euripides:

<margin>The Phoenician Women, line 1179.</margin>
> How can I describe how Capaneus raved?
> For he went with long-reaching ladders to the ascents,
> and boasted this much:
> That not even the holy fire of Zeus should hold him back
> from taking the city from its highest towers.
> And he shouted these things even as he was being pelted with stones,
> having curled his body under his shield itself,
> climbing the smooth rungs of the ladder.
> Already as he was overstepping the coping of the walls,
> Zeus strikes him with a thunderbolt. The earth
> rang out, so that all feared; and from the ladders
> his limbs were tossed like a sling, apart from one another.
> His hands and legs whirled like the wheel of Ixion,
> and his scorched corpse falls to the ground.

Regarding the impiety and blasphemy of Ajax against God, Sophocles' *Ajax* should be read, and it will appear to the inquirer how he rejected the warning of his Parent about imploring the help of God, but he himself hoped in his own spear, saying <term>hyperkompōs kai aphronōs</term> <note>Greek: ὑπερκόμπως καὶ ἀφρόνως - boastfully and senselessly</note>:

<margin>line 779.</margin>
> Father, even a man who is nothing might win
> victory together with the gods; but I, even without
> them, trust that I shall snatch this glory.

<column-break/>

<margin>Sennacherib's war.</margin>
Such proud speeches did that man boast against the Deity, who then perished frantic with the stirred-up wrath of the Deity against him, piercing himself with his own sword, after he had committed many most unworthy things in his madness. A similar blasphemy against the Gods by a certain Idas, trusting more in his spear than in God, exists in the *Argonautica* of Apollonius:

<margin>Book 1, line 457.</margin>
> Zeus does not help me
> so much as my own spear; may there be no
> deadly bane, nor unaccomplished labor
> for me who looks upon it, even if a god should oppose me.

Pentheus, the son of Echion by his wife Agave, daughter of Cadmus, spurning the rites of Bacchus, is said to have been torn apart by the wrath of the Deity, his mother and sister having been turned to madness; whence Cadmus, the King of Thebes, showing the corpse of the torn man to the spectators with a grieving mind, warned that by the example of Pentheus's calamity they should learn to feel piously and reverently toward the Gods:

<margin>Euripides, The Bacchae, line 1324.</margin>
> If there is anyone who looks down upon the spirits,
> let him look upon this man's death and believe in God.

Moreover, the Messenger had reported the best <term>gnōmē</term> <note>Greek: γνώμῃ - opinion or maxim</note> concerning divine things:

<margin>Ibid, line 1148.</margin>
> To be sober-minded and to revere the things of the gods,
> I think this is the most beautiful and wisest
> thing for mortals to possess, for those who use it.

Concerning the other Ajax—not the son of Telamon, but the one who was the son of Oileus, King of the Locrians—Homer handed down that he perished miserably in a similar way because of proud insults against God:

<margin>Odyssey, Book 4, line 504.</margin>
> He said that against the will of the gods he had escaped the great gulf of the sea,
> and Poseidon heard him shouting loudly.
> Immediately then, taking his trident in his heavy hands,
> he struck the Gyraeian rock and split it apart;
> it carried him into the infinitely surging sea.
> Thus he perished there, after he drank the salty water.

Excellent also is the sentiment of Sophocles concerning Jupiter, in the feast of boasting and vaunting:

<margin>Antigone, line 128.</margin>
> For Zeus exceedingly hates the boasts
> of a great tongue, and seeing them
> coming on in a great stream
> of the clanging of arrogant gold,
> he hurls them with brandished fire,
> as they were already rushing to shout
> victory at the very edge of the goals.

These things apply excellently to Sennacherib, already shouting with much pride, whom God destroyed with his whole army by the ministry of Angels, as if by <term>paltō pyri</term> <note>Greek: παλτῷ πυρὶ - hurled fire</note> or the brandished fire of lightning; and he who thought he was at the <term>akrōn balbidōn</term> <note>Greek: ἄκρων βαλβίδων - the very edge of the starting lines/goals</note> or the final goals of the fortune of War, fell <term>Tantalōtheis</term> <note>Greek: Τανταλωθείς - like Tantalus (struck down from a height of pride)</note> in extreme fear. You see now, what we say with the words of Herodotus concerning this headlong fall: *How God strikes with lightning those <margin>Polymnia (Book 7), line 136.</margin> animals that overtop others, nor does He allow them to show off, but the small ones do not even irritate Him. And you see how He always hurls such bolts against the greatest buildings and trees; for God loves to prune back everything that overspreads.*
Thus, in the middle of his course of happiness, by one blow all the glory of the house of Assyria fell, all power disappeared, and all the pride of the King vanished. In such a small space of time, the greatest confusion and greatest ignominy followed the greatest power of the tyrant, which he was forced to endure not only in Judea, but also among the rest of the nations, and even in his own land; moreover, he illustrated the glory of GOD, which he had blasphemed, by his flight and by his slaughter, by which he fell by the hand of his sons—
<margin>verse 38.</margin>

# From 2 Chronicles Chapter 32, Verse 21.

<margin>Sennacherib's war.</margin>
...of his own [sons], pierced by Adramelech and Sharezer while he was worshipping in the temple of his god Nisroch. He was finished by a kind of vengeance worthy of him and by a much more shameful death than if he had perished with the multitude.
> *He was saved alone from the slaughter for this reason: so that he might know the power of God, silence the mouths of blasphemers, and become a witness to that majesty which he had shortly before despised. Pharaoh also was preserved through the ten plagues of Egypt so that he might perish last, which is exactly what this man suffered. It was fitting for him to be punished in the house of his own god, to the shame of the god Nisroch, whom he had preferred over the true God—even after he had experienced the vanity of the former and the power of the latter to his own misfortune. Stripped of his camp, he hurried to Nisroch to implore new help there. To have entered was death; to have worshipped was his grave.* His burial <note>original: Ταφη (קבר)</note> in the idol's temple was testified by the Prophet Nahum, chapter 1, verse 14. It was fitting for a proud man to be punished by his own sons, who had been begotten by him, and against whom—if we believe the Rabbis—he himself had planned a slaughter in honor of his god. A death worthy of a tyrant, who, not satisfied with the blood he had shed, raged anew against the Jews in Nineveh, 
<margin>v. 37. Tobit ch. 1 v. 21, 22.</margin>

A slaughter worthy of a tyrant who blasphemes the true God and worships a false one, so that he might perish, killed by his own sons, in the very temple and worship of the false god. But as to why Sennacherib was killed by his sons, the Hebrew book of Tobit explains the cause this way, 
<margin>page 616.</margin>

To which his wise men and counselors replied: "Abraham, the ancestor of the Israelites, led his own son to be sacrificed so that he might win the favor of Jehovah his God for himself; for this reason He is fond of his posterity and has avenged His own." Then the King said that he would sacrifice two of his sons for the sake of Jehovah, so that through them he might acquire His favor and help. And thus was fulfilled the prophecy of the Prophet, which he had foretold in the thirty-third chapter: *Woe to you who plunder* <note>original: שׁוֹדֵד</note>, *O destroyer* <note>original: וְשׁוֹדֵד</note> *and shall you not suffer plunder? It was the law of retaliation <term>Lex talionis: the principle of "an eye for an eye"</term>, so that what he himself had committed against others, he himself should suffer the same from others. It was right that he who had exalted himself above God and men should himself be cast down. There was no greater day under the rule of the Jews than that one, when the greatest victor of almost the entire Asian world was defeated without battle-standards; and from that victory came rest for the land

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sennacherib's war. Ezekiel 28:2.</margin>
Concerning the Prince of Tyre, because he boasted that he was a God, the Scripture says \*: *Because your heart is lifted up, and you have said, I am a GOD <note>original Hebrew: 'El ani'</note>. Will you yet say, I am a GOD, before those who slay you? But you are a man, and no God, in the hand of those who slay you.* From this we are permitted to see that God visits the proud in that which is not their own; for if they boast because of a kingdom, God takes it from them and gives it to the most humble of men, so that it is known by all that the kingdom belongs not to man, nor is it in his hand. Thus, if anyone boasts in divinity, so as to make himself a God, and God visits him and delivers him into the hands of a slayer, this is a true punishment against the one boasting to be a God, to show his disgrace—that there is not such power in him that he can snatch himself from death; for while he is delivered into the hand of the killer, he is shown not to be a Deity, since a man has power over him. The speech of the Heathens is wise, that bitter punishments are sent by God upon those who despise Him, and those who neglect the ceremonies and established rites. It is necessary to examine how impiety toward the Deities and divine things displeased even those whose opinion was turned away from the truth of religion and perverse regarding sacred matters. Elegant and grave interpreters of that religion are especially the writers of Tragedy, whom this impiety offended, and who instruct particularly on this, as if in the greatest and first of matters, with a tragic <term>deinoteti</term> <note>Greek: 'terrible power' or 'intensity'</note> of words. With what eloquent and grave speech does Sophocles strive to explain *Ajax son of Telamon*, and Pindarus explain *Capaneus*! Both were proud contemners of the Gods, and both are said to have been punished by the Gods for the wicked crime of depravity. How timely does Ovid discourse on the monstrosity of *Pentheus*! As the subject demands, let us see what is handed down. One of the seven leaders who besieged Thebes was *Capaneus*, the husband of *Evadne*, who is said to have been struck by the lightning of Jove for his contempt, when, having moved up the ladders, he wished to scale the Theban walls and occupy them even against the will of the gods; for he said not even the lightning of Jove would deter him from taking Thebes. Euripides writes in the pathetic buskin <note>The 'buskin' or cothurnus was the high boot worn by tragic actors, symbolizing a grand style.</note>\*:
<margin>Phoenician Women, line 1179.</margin>
> How could I describe how Capaneus raged?
> For he went with long-reaching ladders to the ascents,
> and boasted so greatly:
> Not even the sacred fire of Zeus should hold him back
> from taking the city from its highest towers.
> And as he spoke these things, though being stoned,
> he crept up, huddling his body under his shield,
> climbing the smooth rungs of the ladders.
> And just as he was overstepping the coping of the walls,
> Zeus strikes him with a thunderbolt. The earth
> rang out, so that all were afraid; and from the ladders
> his limbs were sent flying apart from one another,
> his hair to the sky, his blood to the earth, and his limbs
> whirled like the wheel of Ixion, and his scorched corpse falls to the ground.

Concerning the impiety and blasphemy of Ajax against God, Sophocles' *Ajax* should be read, and it will appear to the inquirer how he rejected the warning of his Parent to implore the help of God, but he himself hoped in his own spear, saying <term>hyperkopos kai aphronos</term> <note>Greek: 'excessively and senselessly'</note>\*:
<margin>line 779.</margin>
> Father, even a man who is nothing might win
> victory with the gods; but I, even without
> them, am confident I shall snatch this glory.

<column-break/>

<margin>Sennacherib's war.</margin>
Such proud speeches did that man boast against the Deity, who then perished frantic with the stirred-up wrath of the Deity upon him, piercing himself with his own sword, after he had committed many most unworthy things in his madness. A similar blasphemy against the Gods by a certain Idas, trusting more in his spear than in God, exists in the *Argonautica* of Apollonius\*:
<margin>Book 1, line 457.</margin>
> Zeus does not help me
> as much as my spear; from it shall come
> a mournful destruction, nor shall the labor be unfinished,
> even if a god should oppose me.

Pentheus, the son of Echion and Agave (daughter of Cadmus), spurning the rites of Bacchus, is said to have been torn apart by the wrath of the Deity, his mother and sister having been turned to madness; whence Cadmus, the King of Thebes, showing the corpse of the torn man to the spectators with a grieving heart, warned that by the example of Pentheus's calamity they should learn to think piously and reverently of the Gods\*:
> If there is anyone who looks down upon the gods,
> let him look upon this man's death and believe in god.
<margin>Euripides, Bacchae, line 1324.</margin>
Moreover, the Messenger had brought back the best <term>gnomen</term> <note>Greek: 'judgment' or 'opinion'</note> concerning divine matters:
<margin>ibid. line 1148.</margin>
> To be sober-minded and to revere the things of the Gods,
> I think is the most beautiful thing, and the wisest
> possession for mortals who use it.

Concerning the other Ajax—not the son of Telamon, but the son of Oileus, King of the Locrians—Homer handed down that he perished miserably in a similar way because of proud insults against God\*:
<margin>Odyssey, Book 4, line 504.</margin>
> He said that against the will of the gods he had escaped the great gulf of the sea,
> and Poseidon heard him speaking loudly.
> Immediately then, taking his trident in his sturdy hands,
> he struck the Gyraeian rock and split it apart;
> one part stayed there, but the other fell into the sea,
> and it carried him into the vast billowing ocean.
> Thus he perished there, after he drank the salty water.

The sentiment of Sophocles is also excellent concerning Jove, in the festival of boasting and vaunting:
<margin>Antigone, line 128.</margin>
> For Zeus exceedingly hates the boasts
> of a great tongue, and seeing them
> coming in a great stream
> with the arrogance of clashing gold,
> he hurls them with brandished fire,
> as they were already at the very edge
> of the goal, rushing to shout victory.

These things apply excellently to Sennacherib, already shouting <term>alalazonta</term> <note>Greek: 'crying out' or 'shouting in triumph'</note> with much pride, whom God destroyed with his whole army by the ministry of Angels, as if by <term>palto pyri</term> <note>Greek: 'hurled fire'</note> or the brandished fire of lightning; and he who thought the fortune of War was at the <term>akron balbidon</term> <note>Greek: 'the very edge of the starting line/goal'</note>, fell <unclear>utterly ruined</unclear> in extreme fear. You see now what we say with the words of Herodotus concerning this headlong fall: *God strikes with lightning the creatures that stand out <gloss>Polymnia</gloss>, nor does he allow them to show off, but the small ones do not sting him. You see how he always hurls such bolts at the greatest buildings and trees, for God loves to cut down all things that excel.*
<margin>Polymnia, line 136.</margin>

Thus, in the middle of the course of happiness, by one blow fell all the glory of the house of Assur, all power disappeared, and all the pride of the King vanished. In such a small space of time, the greatest confusion and the greatest ignominy followed the supreme power of the tyrant, which he was forced to endure not only in Judea, but also among the rest of the nations, and even in his own land; moreover, he illustrated the glory of GOD, which he had blasphemed, by his flight and by his slaughter, in which he fell by the hand of his sons—
