# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
### Page 382

<margin>The war of Sennacherib.</margin> The terrified Egyptians urged the people to depart. <term>וַתֶּחֱזַק מִצְרַיִם עַל הָעָם לְמַהֵר</term> <note>Exodus 12:33: "And the Egyptians were urgent upon the people, to send them out of the land in haste."</note>; But to return to Sennacherib: Horace (Book 4, Ode 6, v. 1) calls Apollo the *great avenger of the tongue* <note>original: "magna vindex linguae"</note> which exalts itself with great boasting and glorious <term>grandiloquence</term> <note>Greek: μεγαληγορία (megalēgoria)</note> against the heavenly Powers—an arrogance for which antiquity invented the goddess Nemesis as the agent of vengeance. Because of such <term>boastfulness</term> <note>Greek: ἀλαζονεία (alazoneia)</note> and <term>haughtiness</term> <note>Greek: μεγαλοφροσύνῃ (megalophrosynē)</note>, they write that the proud Niobe, having dared to despise Latona, paid the penalty to the immortal gods; from her misfortune she learned, as Ovid witnesses:
<margin>Metamorphoses, Book 5, v. 3</margin>
> To yield to the heavenly ones, and to use humbler words.

And as Statius says in the *Thebaid*, Book 3:
> The impious daughter of Tantalus <note>Niobe</note> paid for her magnificent blasts of pride.

Callimachus, in his *Hymn to Delos*, calls this being <term>foul-tongued</term> <note>Greek: Κακόγλωσσον (kakoglōsson)</note>, which Aristotle (Ethics to Nicomachus, Book 7) describes as <term>not raising a hand against the gods</term> <note>Greek: μὴ χεῖρα πρὸς τὸς θεὸς</note>. The most glorious God of Israel was the avenger of the great tongue, the punisher of the proud tongue, and the vindicator of His people against Sennacherib. By his example and sad end, we are warned not to perish by recklessly boasting of our fortune, but to use prosperity and flourishing luck with modesty. See here, you proud ones, and learn from Sennacherib how vain you are, how inglorious in your glory, and how foolish in your wisdom. Sennacherib could scarcely contain or recognize himself; elated by success and driven mad by it, he denied peace to those who sought it. That Assyrian braggart <note>Latin: Thraso, a stock character name for a soldier</note> thought himself the invincible lord of nations, and even of those Gods whom he did not worship. Hence he spoke great and proud things, reviled the God of Israel, and by his insults provoked the wrath of God upon himself for his greater punishment; as Pindar aptly says:
<margin>Olympian Ode 9</margin>
> <term>To revile the gods</term>
> <term>is a hateful wisdom, and</term>
> <term>to boast out of season</term>
> <term>borders on madness.</term> <note>Translated from the Greek text provided</note>

Just as quickly as continued good fortune breeds a sense of security, so too does calamity suddenly cast one into despair, of which Aeschylus writes in *The Persians*:
<margin>In The Persians</margin>
> <term>Whoever is experienced in evils</term>
> <term>knows that when a surge of</term>
> <term>troubles comes upon mortals, they tend to fear everything.</term>
> <term>But when the divinity flows well, they trust</term>
> <term>that the same divinity will always blow a fair wind of fortune.</term> <note>Translated from the Greek text provided</note>

There was a stupendous <term>hardening of heart</term> <note>Greek: πώρωσις (pōrōsis)</note> in Pharaoh, that most dire and harsh Tyrant. The more Moses pressed him, the more the King persisted in tyranny. The more the Man of God sent plagues, the less that man of blood would let the people go. Despite so many plagues sent, removed, and sent again, he did not soften. After plague upon plague, each always heavier, he became angrier, not gentler, until God the Avenger followed the proud man from behind. Remember Goliath, who mocked the God of Israel; he was laid low to eternal infamy and reproach by the single cast of a single stone, and beheaded with his own sword. He paid the penalty, but did not wash it away; he is to be further punished by eternal fires, never to be fully expiated. You Great Men, whom God has raised to thrones, be warned by these sad examples: flee pride and insolence. A bad end follows the proud, and a death worthy of such impiety follows. Crimes are judged no less by the status of the person who commits them than by the act itself.

<column-break/>

Every crime stands out more when committed from a high place, and he who lives with wicked morals quickly loses his dignity. The oak tree falls with a heavier crash than the willow. The powerful are powerfully punished, and a stronger penalty follows the strong. ### EZRA 4:14

-> <term>כְּעַן כָּל-קֳבֵל דִּי-מְלַח הֵיכְלָא מְלַחְנָא</term> <-
-> <term>Καὶ νῦν ἐν ὡς ἅλας τὸ ναῦ ἡλισάμεθα.</term> <-
-> *Now because we have eaten the salt of the palace.* <note>Original: "Memores salis, quod in Palatio comedimus." This refers to the Persian officials' loyalty to the King because they were in his service.</note> <-

<margin>Salt as a symbol of friendship and covenants.</margin> Anciently, Salt was the primary symbol of covenants and friendship, which were ratified by the eating of salt on both sides: implying that whatever they said and contracted, they would keep as if it were preserved in salt. <term>Salt is a symbol of friendship</term> <note>Greek: Φιλίας οἱ ἅλες (Philias hoi hales)</note>, says Eustathius, <term>which is why it was set before guests before all other foods</term>. For among the ancients, salt and wine were usually employed only in sacrifices, atonements, covenants, vows, and those matters in which some divinity or secret power was thought to reside. (Compare C. Enselius, *Apparatus for Banquets*, Book 1, p. 10; Salmuth on Pancirollus, p. 59). Hence the "salt of the covenant" in *Leviticus 2:13*, which the Lord commanded to be used in all offerings He ordained for His people, as a covenant and a lasting statute. For sacrifices are symbols of a covenant. And in *Numbers 18:19*, <margin>Covenant of salt</margin> <note>Hebrew: בְּרִית מֶלַח (Berit melach)</note>, Jerome translates it as *Pactum salis* (Covenant of Salt): so named, says Forster, because it ought to be inviolable; for salt was anciently the symbol of friendship and pacts. Joachim Zehner explains the words of Ezra from this custom in his *Sacred Adages*, century 3, leaf 100. There was great reverence for the Prytaneum <note>the town hall or central hearth</note> among the Athenians, not so much because the magistrates met there for counsel, but because those who had served the Republic well were fed there <term>at public expense</term> <note>Greek: δημοσίᾳ (dēmosia)</note>. Perhaps from this comes the *public table and the salt of the city*, of which Aeschines speaks in *On the False Embassy*: <term>The salt of the city</term>.
<margin>Iliad, Book 1.</margin>
<margin>Vatablus</margin>
<margin>In the Dictionary, p. 442.</margin>
<margin>p. 250.</margin>

# From Ezra Chapter 4, Verse 14

<margin>Salt as a symbol of friendship and covenants.</margin>
He says that the public table is shared, as is the custom of the country. Anyone who committed an offense against the laws of friendship and agreements was said, in an elegant phrase, to "trample upon the salt," as Demosthenes says in *On the Crown*, page 167. For by these things friends were once united, and in ancient times companions celebrated mutual feasts among themselves, as Diogenes Laërtius also testifies in the *Life of Pythagoras*, and Theocritus agrees in his poem *Hylas*:

> Both companions always feasted at a single table.
->*Who as faithful friends always dined at the table.*<-

He is speaking of Hercules and Telamon. Likewise, Euripides in *Hecuba*, exaggerating the crime of Polymnestor, mentions the table shared by the right of hospitality and friendship:

> Having often shared a common table with me.
->*Often received by me at a shared table.*<-

Hence the Parian iambic writer Archilochus, reproaching Lycambes for a violated covenant which salt and the table had united, addresses him thus in Origen’s *Against Celsus*, book 2:

> You have cast aside a great oath,
> and the salt and the table.

That Lycambes, because he was lashed by such venomous iambic verses, hanged himself along with his daughters. Origen <margin>Homily 35 on Matthew</margin> twists this toward Judas the Betrayer, saying:

> Since he whom He received at the common table, and to whom He entrusted Himself—perhaps because he acted well at the beginning—himself betrayed Jesus who was embracing him with such honors; and he was mindful neither of the same salt, nor the table, nor the shared bread, but transgressing all those things for the sake of the promise of thirty pieces of silver, he handed over the giver of such great goods. And this is truly the characteristic habit of exceedingly wicked men: that after salt and bread, they plot against men who have done them no harm, with whom they have shared bread and salt.

Erasmus disapproves of this in Origen <note>Erasmus, *Adages*, page 47</note>, saying: *And I do not know whether Christ himself, the prince of our religion, alluded to this, as it seems to have been his plan to hide his deepest mysteries in very common things, foreknowing that this symbol, mocked by the Jews, would be embraced by the Gentiles.* Regarding salt being customarily set before guests in sacred rites, we read nothing explicitly; yet Philo pleases me, who, when describing the banquet of Joseph <margin>Genesis 43:16</margin> where he received his brothers, mentions salt, saying: He commands (in Joseph, page 377) the steward of the house to prepare a sumptuous lunch, and to bring the men in to share in the salt and the table. [Mr. Meursius added certain things to Lycophron, page 132. Salt was also a second symbol: a symbol of sterility; for the earth which produces or receives salt produces nothing else. From this came the custom in ancient centuries that salt was sprinkled upon land that was to be devastated; which was nothing other than to designate the place for perpetual solitude and unfruitfulness. We read that Abimelech did this <margin>Judges 9:45</margin> after the city of Shechem was destroyed because of the crimes committed there, to indicate total desolation. Theodoret, in Question 17, page 204, asks: "Why did they sow salt upon it? This signifies barrenness. For nothing grows from salt." Among the curses of God in Deuteronomy 29:23 and Jeremiah chapter 17, it is mentioned that if a land which had been fertile is turned into saltiness. The land

<column-break/>

<margin>Salt as a symbol of friendship and covenants.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 107:34</margin>
<margin>Genesis 13:10</margin>
moreover, the Almighty God turns a fruitful land into saltiness or a salt-waste because nothing is more sterile than salt, as a sign of His wrath; which is evident regarding the *Pentapolis* <note>The five cities of the plain, including Sodom and Gomorrah</note>, which He once turned from being most fertile into a most salty sea because of the sins of the Sodomites; the water of which also renders unfruitful and sterile whatever it touches, because of the saltiness it carries with it, as the flood has shown. Thus in Zephaniah chapter 2:9, it is predicted that the region of Ammon will be a place abandoned to nettles and salt pits. We read in Nauclerus <margin>In the life of Frederick</margin> that Frederick Barbarossa, an emulator of ancient ritual, saw to it that salt was sprinkled over Milan. To this point, passages concerning the nature of salt apply: Pliny, who in Book 31, Chapter 7, discussing the types of salt, its preparations, and medicines, says among other things: *Every place in which salt is found is sterile and produces nothing.* And in Chapter 9: *The nature of salt is inherently fiery, eroding all things, but binding, drying, and tightening bodies, even preserving the dead from putrefying so that they endure for centuries.* Aetius of Amida, on the differences of earths, Chapter 73: *It is common to all types of salt to heat, disperse, bind, dry out, and thicken the substance of those bodies to which they adhere: for they consume all moisture wherever they find it, and by binding the remaining solid substance, they pack it together; therefore they parch it.* Virgil, *Georgics* 2, line 238:

> But salty earth, and that which is called bitter,
> Is unhappy for crops: it neither softens by plowing,
> Nor does the vine keep its lineage, or the apples their names.

Matthias Flacius in *The Key to Scripture*: Salt denotes sterility in the earth: because, as *Pliny* testifies, salty places are unfruitful; on the contrary, sweet earth is fruitful, as *Virgil* testifies. For this outcome or meaning, *Abimelech* also, having overturned the city of Shechem, sowed salt in it to indicate that it ought to be perpetually deserted and uncultivated. From this it happens that other translations take our passage to refer to the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem. Also, since the Chaldean word *Melach* signifies both salt and, by extension, devastation, Kimchi in his *Book of Roots* translates it: *we cause the building of the temple to cease*, so that it becomes like the earth, *Melach*, that is, salty and waste. Dr. Luther, the Zurich translators, and Osiander follow this interpretation. Junius, in the first edition of the Bible according to the Hebrews, had rendered it: *Because we are demolishing the demolition of the temple,* that is, we were the cause for the temple in Jerusalem being destroyed. But in the revised edition, taking a "second voyage" <note>A Greek proverb meaning a second attempt or a change of course</note>, he translates it: *because we receive a salary from the King's Palace.* Buxtorf renders it in the same sense <margin>in his Lexicon, page 412</margin>; for to eat much salt in a court is to receive many benefits for a long time from Princes, to be greatly indebted to Kings, and to studiously prevent inconveniences and perform according to the King's pleasure, as Conrad Pellican once noted in his Biblical work. Sixtinus Amama, in his Review of the Dutch Bibles, rendered it with Junius: *Since therefore we have our Salary from the King's Palace;* <margin>page 199</margin> and in the notes he added that from this ancient custom flowed our words *Sold* <note>German/Dutch for pay</note>, *Besoldung* <note>German for salary/remuneration</note>, and the Latin *Salarium*; both from salt. After him, you may note that exactly the same thing is observed in the Edition of the Version of the Bible by order of the States General of the Netherlands...

### III. ESDRAS III. 6. <note>Referring to the apocryphal 1 Esdras</note>

> King Darius shall give him great gifts, and great prizes for victory, and to be clothed in purple, and to drink from gold vessels, and to sleep upon gold, and a chariot with a golden bridle, and a headdress of fine linen, and a chain about his neck.

> -> *King Darius shall give him great gifts: to be covered in purple, and to drink in gold, and to sleep upon gold, and a chariot with a golden bridle, and a linen Headdress, and a collar around the neck.* <-

<margin>The Cydaris, a royal insignia of the Persians.</margin>
In that futile and vain narrative of the three bodyguards of King Darius, written by the Pseudo-Esdras, mention is made of the "Cydaris of fine linen." The Cydaris was the insignia of the Kings of the Persians: for Brissonius, in *The Royal Apparel of the Persians, book 1, p. 7*, concludes from *Ctesias’s Persian History* that it was customary for a cydaris and a Diadem to be placed on the heads of those raised to the royal summit; he reports that the head of Ochus, though he was unwilling and reluctant, was bound with the diadem by the nobles of the Persian kingdom.

<margin>17. Onomasticon, ch. 13.</margin>

<margin>p. 50.</margin>
*Q. Curtius, book 3:* (They called the royal head insignia of the Persians the Cydaris; a blue band variegated with white went around this.) Curtius reports the same in book 6: that Alexander, having abandoned the customs and disciplines of his fatherland, wrapped a purple diadem variegated with white—such as Darius had possessed—around his head, and took up Persian dress. The Kings of the Persians wore earrings, *Arrian 6. 5. 15.* So too the Parthians: *Tertullian, On the Dress of Women, ch. 10; Athenaeus 3. 13; Juvenal, Satire 1. 104; Freinsheim 8. 9. 21.*

<margin>p. 105.</margin>
In Plutarch’s *Life of Artaxerxes, p. 1873*, it is said that Darius was granted the right *to wear the hidden cydaris upright* <note>Only the King wore the tiara/cydaris stiff and upright; subjects wore them folded forward</note>. Herodotus in *Thalia*, speaking of the Persians, says *they are shaded from the beginning, wearing hats and tiaras*, on which passage see *H. Stephens in the Appendix to the Thesaurus, part 2, p. 114.* Nectanebo, King of Egypt, *put on a woolen garment, and a diadem, and a proper cydaris*, according to Maximus Planudes in the *Life of Aesop, p. 82.* So Tigranes, King of the Armenians, an unhappy warrior against the Romans, came as a suppliant to Pompey and, having pulled the cydaris from his head, laid it at Pompey’s feet.

<margin>p. 637.</margin>
Plutarch in *Life of Pompey*: *When he came to Pompey himself, he took off the cydaris and prepared to lay it before his feet, and casting himself down most shamefully of all, fell at his knees.* Lucullus, the Roman General, had received the diadem of the same king when he routed him in a great battle, regarding which see *Plutarch in Life of Lucullus, p. 511.* Pancirollus (*book 1, ch. 9, p. 17*), Goropius Becanus (*Hieroglyphics, p. 186, 189*), and Cromer treat the Cydaris and tiara at greater length.

<margin>L.H.S. p. 61. Bayfius on Clothing, p. 59.</margin>
Furthermore, J. Lipsius, in *book 2 of the Annals of Tacitus*, learnedly and distinctly demonstrates the difference between the common diadem and the Persian one, to which the cydaris or tiara was attached. The Tiara, however, was an ornament woven from gold and pearls, with which the Great Men of the Persians bound their heads by permission of the King. Procopius calls it *an ornament of the head* in *Persian Wars, book 1*, and says it is the greatest dignity among the Persians. It was not permitted except by Royal leave, as Xenophon witnesses in *Cyropaedia, book 8*, to use a gold ring, nor a belt, nor a buckle, nor any other ornament of that kind. For only the Kings of the Persians wore the *tiara*, which covered the head, and the diadem, which was stretched across the forehead.

<margin>The Cydaris of the Persian kings.</margin>
By permission of the King, however, it was allowed to wear a tiara, whence Themistius says in *Oration 1 to Constantius, p. 20: It is not the Tiara that makes a king, nor the kandys, nor the mantle, nor the golden dagger, nor the twisted collars and bracelets, nor the rod-bearers and bodyguards and apple-bearers <note>The "Melophoroi," elite guards whose spears had golden apples at the butt</note>, nor some immortal number of dying soldiers. For all these things belonged to Cambyses the madman, and to Xerxes the boaster.*

<margin>Vol. 4, p. 540, on Zechariah 3:5.</margin>
The Venerable Bede, in *book 2 of his Exposition on Ezra, ch. 14*, writes that the cydaris is the same as the mitre according to the opinion of others; *Place*, he says, *a clean cydaris upon his head, which is called a mitre by many*; but they are in error, for even if the cydaris <note>original: "κίδαρις"</note> is also a head-binding, it is not therefore to be called the same as a mitre. *Suidas: Cydaris: a covering of the head. Either a fabric of hair, or a type of kamelaukion <note>a monk's hat or crown</note>, which is also understood as a tiara. Some say the cydaris is a felt skullcap, or a crown, or a turban, or the royal hat of the Persians, or the headband which the priests wear.* Origen also, *on Leviticus ch. 8*, expressly distinguishes them. *Therefore*, he says, *he first receives the cydaris, which is either a certain covering of the head or an ornament, and after this the mitre is placed upon him.*

<margin>Regarding the Mitre, which was threefold, see the same Brissonius, p. 31, and what he first delivers concerning the distinction between the mitre and the tiara; which Dempster notes in his work on Rosinus. The origin of the word is Hebrew, from "Keter" <note>original: "כתר"</note>, he encircled in the manner of a crown: whence also "citaris" is written, as Becmann asserts.</margin>

<margin>Who were called "Kinsmen" among the Persians.</margin>
In the same book, Chapter 4, verse 42, Darius, when he had perceived the speeches of these three youths, is read to have said to one of them: *Ask what you will, and I will give it to you, and you shall sit next to me, and you shall be called my kinsman.* These things must also be illustrated for us from antiquity. The Kings of the Persians had a cohort which consisted of ten thousand horsemen, whom *they called the Immortals*. The reason for the name was that in the place of those who died, or those who, suffering from a serious disease, had earned a discharge, others were substituted, the number always remaining whole; as shown by Herodotus, *who says they boasted themselves invincible by this name, History, book 11, ch. 15.*

<margin>Procopius, book 1 on the Persian War, book 7.</margin>
Athenaeus also mentions them in *book 12, and Pausanias, p. 265*; we shall treat them more fully below at *Esther 8:10*. Among their ranks thereafter, those who stayed closest to the King’s side were called the *Kinsmen of the King*.

<margin>p. 42.</margin>
Curtius mentions both orders in *book 3* in these words: *Next went those whom the Persians call the Immortals, numbering ten thousand; the opulence of their dress distinguished them more than other barbarians. They had golden collars, they had garments...*

# From 1 Esdras III, v. 6.

<margin>The Cydaris: a royal insignia of the Persians.</margin>
...they had garments decorated with gold, and long-sleeved tunics adorned even with gems. At a small distance followed those whom they call the "Kinsmen of the King," numbering fifteen thousand men. *Diodorus* also describes them in *Book 17 of his Library, section 1*, as does *Aristotle in his book On the Universe, chapter 6*, where he mentions the "foremost and most esteemed men of the Great King." The King also admitted these men to solemn feasts, whereas at other times he usually dined alone, as is clear from *Athenaeus*. In *Esther chapter 6, verse 8*, these royal honors and gifts are recounted: The man whom the King desires to honor must be clothed in royal robes, placed upon a horse from the King's own stable, and receive the royal diadem upon his head, etc.—all of which should be compared with our present text. Furthermore, *Procopius* mentions in *Book 1 of the Persian War* that even in his own time, no one among the Persians was permitted to use a gold ring, belt, or purple cloth without the King's favor. Regarding the royal throne of the Persians, see the notes by *Martin Roa, Book 2, chapter 3*. There are many other things in the books of *Ezra* and *Esther* explained and unfolded from Persian monuments by *Brissonius* <note>Barnabas Brissonius (1531–1591) was a French jurist and scholar whose work on Persian antiquities was the standard reference for centuries.</note>: such as the openings of Edicts and Decrees, which were almost always conceived in this manner: "The King says thus (these things)," an example of which is in *1 Esdras 1, v. 2*: "Thus said Cyrus, King of the Persians." Regarding this formula of words from *Herodotus* and others, see *Brissonius* <margin>Book 1, p. 140.</margin> concerning decrees sealed with the royal ring <note>original Greek: *daktyliō*</note>. *Esther 8, v. 8, 10* from *Xenophon* and *Curtius p. 141*. *Ecbatana*, the Royal City and Metropolis, *1 Esdras 6, v. 2* (where *Tremellius* translates it as *Achmetha*, see his notes); *p. 45, 46* regarding decrees, edicts, and records kept in chests and archives, *1 Esdras 5, v. 15, p. 142*. Regarding the King's scouts, *1 Esdras 3, 4, p. 130*; regarding the satraps and governors, *1 Esdras 4, v. 47, 48, p. 112*; the King's gifts, *1 Esdras 3, v. 6, p. 93*; the seven counselors, *1 Esdras 8, v. 12, p. 90, 91*; regarding the punishment of the cross <note>crucifixion or impalement</note> accepted among them, *Esther ch. 7 & 8* in the history of the hanging of Haman, *p. 161*; regarding the *Gaza* or royal treasury, *Esther 3, v. 9, p. 120 and following*; the *Megistanes*, who were the nobles and purple-clad elites of the Persians and Parthians, *p. 134*; and the *Saraballae* <note>trousers</note>, *Daniel 3:94*. <margin>page 42.</margin> These things and others, I say, are confirmed with many passages from authors by that incomparable man, most deserving of the gentler Muses, *Barnabas Brissonius*, in his truly royal work *On the Royal Government of the Persians*.

*Berosus*, *Megasthenes*, and others who included Persian affairs in their annals could also greatly assist us in directing the timeline of Persian history and understanding many other things in *Daniel* and these aforementioned books. However, they struck the same reefs upon which the works of so many excellent authors were shipwrecked. Nevertheless, some fragments of *Berosus* survive, preserved by *Josephus*, which are worth more than their weight in gold. But let us reject the "Berosus" and other imposters under foreign names which *Annius of Viterbo*, a Dominican friar, published many years ago; the learned have proved these to be illegitimate and supposititious offspring: *Joseph Scaliger*, *Chytraeus*, *Pererius*, *Rainoldus*, *Vossius*, *Gaspar Varrerius*, *Fr. Tilemannus*, *Calvisius*, *Casmannus*, and others. I thought it right to warn of this here, lest they deceive anyone. However, the testimonies of the Greeks in matters concerning the Persian Monarchy are of the greatest weight, as rightly judged by *Rainoldus* <margin>see p. 1477 ff. 1258.</margin> *Vol. 1, Censorship of Apocryphal Books 6, v. 1* and *Calvisius* in his *Chronological Introduction, ch. 40, p. 164*. For the Persians were the best known of all barbarians to the Greeks, as *Strabo* teaches near the end of *Book 19 of his Geography*. Yet the same *Rainoldus* rightly notes the lack of historical knowledge <note>original Greek: *anistorēsian*</note> among the Hebrews regarding Persian affairs in *Lecture 106, p. 1328*; see also *Casmannus in his Astrology, part 2, question 2, p. 83 ff.* and *Mayer's Dissertation on the 70 Weeks*.

### ESTHER I, 3.

->The army of Persia and Media, the nobles:<-
->and the illustrious of the Persians and Medes.<-
->*The Army of Persia and Media, the Princes of the Euphrates.*<-

The word *Parthemim* <note>Hebrew: *ha-partemim*</note> throws a blanket over the interpreters, many of whom argue for its various origins. Some think it is corrupted from the Greek *paratimoi* <note>honored ones</note>; and *Junius* derives it from the Greek *protoi* <note>first/chiefs</note>, with whom *Mayer* agrees. But *Rabbi Shelomo* <note>Rashi</note> writes that it is Persian in origin: "The word *Parthemim* is in the language of Persia." *Parthemim* are governors in the Persian language, like the *Adarpanes* in *Esther ch. 9, v. 3*, meaning "The Nobles." *Rabbi Joseph Kimchi* understands them as leaders living near the river Parath <note>the Euphrates</note>, because they were captains of the region around the Euphrates. *Hottinger* derives it from *par* (high, great) and *ruach* (spirit), as if you were saying "magnanimous heroes." In this explanation of this exotic word, he was perhaps preceded by *Louis de Dieu*, whose uncommon knowledge of Oriental languages has long been <margin>Notes p. 248.</margin> well-known, and was rightly held in high esteem during the time I was among the Dutch. If, as he teaches, the Persian *par* means high/great and *ruach* means spirit, we would easily believe that "magnanimous and exalted men" are denoted here. Certainly, the title "Magnificent" is great and not common; and the title of the Dutch, who are "Great in Spirit," *Hochmogend* <note>High and Mighty</note>, might if not equal, then at least match that *Parthemim* in some way. *Rabbi Kimchi* says: "*Paratimi* are Princes and Magnates illustrious by birth, and perhaps the same who are called the *homotimoi* <note>peers</note> or *kinsmen of the king* in Xenophon, or the King's relatives in Curtius, as Drusius prefers." We shall briefly repeat here from the earlier passage <margin>observation 14.</margin> what the "Kinsmen" were called among the Persians. The Kings of the Persians had a cohort consisting of ten thousand cavalrymen, whom they called the "Immortals." The reason for the name was that when any died, or were discharged due to a serious disease, others were substituted in their place, so the number always remained complete, as *Herodotus* shows. Within their ranks, those who stayed closest to the King's side were called "Kinsmen of the King." *Curtius* mentions both orders in *Book 3* with these words: "Next went those whom the Persians call Immortals, about ten thousand; no others were more honored by the richness of their barbarian dress. They had golden collars, garments decorated with gold, and long-sleeved tunics adorned even with gems. At a small distance followed those whom they call the Kinsmen of the King, fifteen thousand men." Hence *Junius* in his commentary on *1 Esdras chapter 4*, where *Darius*, having heard the speeches of the three youths, is read to have said to one of them: "Ask what you will, and I will give it to you, because you have been found wiser than your neighbors; and you shall sit next to me, and be called my kinsman." *Saint Jerome* renders them as "tyrants." Instead of *phorbōmēn*, he says, which *Theodotion* used, the Septuagint and *Aquila* translated "chosen ones." *Symmachus* understood "Parthians," taking the word as the name of a nation...

# From Esther Chapter I. verses 6, 7, 8.

<margin>
Persian Banquet Customs.
</margin>

> *Golden and silver couches were arranged upon a pavement laid with emerald and Parian stone.*
> *Moreover, those who were invited drank from golden cups... Nor was there anyone who compelled those unwilling to drink.*

IN that magnificent and sumptuous banquet celebrated at Susa, that great King Ahasuerus <note>Also known as Xerxes I</note>, a displayer of the riches of the glory of his kingdom, provided by edict against that barbaric custom of gluttony accepted among the Persians, lest one should compel another to drink; for originally, there were those who, according to the insolence of nations, would exhort one another to equal draughts. Therefore, through the Stewards of the house, whom he had appointed as Masters of the Measure <note>original: *Modimperatores*</note>, the King took care that no one should be prohibited from drinking what he wished, nor should anyone be urged toward strong wine, but each should drink cups at his own discretion. Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 11, Chapter 6, page 373: <term>The King commanded the servants not to force them to drink by constantly offering the beverage to them, as is the custom among the Persians, but to permit them and to treat each of the guests according to his own wish.</term> The Persians, by ancient institution, were of a more moderate diet and regimen, and they considered it shameful and an example of bad character to spit or blow one's nose, as Xenophon has recorded. It was the custom of Kings, 

<margin>
Sermon 42.
</margin>

according to the testimony of Serinus in Stobaeus, to dispute concerning modesty before food, and concerning temperance or continence of food and drink before drinking—to think of sobriety and the frugality of diet before eating. Many of the Ancients commend this sobriety in the Persians, and among these especially Xenophon, who calls them <term>mysteries of food</term>, by which he praises the Persians. Nevertheless, just as the rites and customs are not the same in all ages or places, so also the honorable institutions of the Persians were sometimes accustomed 

> *to fall into a worse state and, having slipped, be carried backward,*

which same thing Xenophon clearly testifies happened in Persia, where abuse had so prevailed that from morning until evening, whatever time there was, they often concluded with a single meal. Wherefore, by a most honorable institution, Ahasuerus protects the public discipline of morals and establishes—or, to describe the Hebrew word, ordains to be inviolably observed—that one should not compel another to drunkenness by drinking. When all had heard these things, they agreed that one should drink in the present banquet not unto drunkenness, but for pleasure, <term>Josephus: for delight</term>, and it seemed that it would be in each person's discretion how much he wished to drink, and truly no one was to be compelled beyond what he wished. In the Hebrew it is *Anas* <term>There was no one compelling</term>, i. is, one who would force (Forster notes on page 47 that this is a foreign word, though for a very weak reason). To be compelled by superiors does not excuse one, much less by equals, or what is even worse, by inferiors. *Anas* denotes *violence and impulse*, when a fellow-drinker is forced and compelled to a Bacchic battle. Often a young man tests his strength by drinking, engorging a great quantity of wine, and does violence to his own viscera and all that is contained in the belly and chest; whence he is compelled in later years to pay for the evil, where to his own hurt he experiences the evil contracted in youth, tenaciously sitting in his vitals, which can neither be forced out nor expelled by a Physician through the power of medicines. Thus force is conquered by force, and he who once conquered is now conquered and compelled by his own members, which he had once compelled. That compulsion is elegantly described in Sirach 31:37

<column-break/>

through the word *thlibein*, *to press, afflict, or wear down*, where in his Notes, Drusius mentions this place: <term>Do not press him (the guest) by demanding that he respond to you</term>; for that it was once customary in the East is clear from the law of the Persians, which expressly forbade this from happening, i.e., that one should compel another, of which mention is made in the history of Esther. He also writes in the Annotations on this place: *The drinking was according to the law, by which it was provided that one should not compel another to drink. But perhaps it should be distinguished and translated otherwise: And the drinking was according to the law, no one was demanding it, with this meaning: No one demanded a drink from another, no one compelled another, as was then the custom. If we disregard this, we shall follow the former, which seems to me altogether more probable, especially since the Hebrew word Dath is not used for "custom" in this book, as far as I know.* Sixtinus Amama agrees with this opinion, who thus translates the Hebrew: <insert>And the drinking happened according to this law: Let no one compel.</insert> where he added in the Notes: <insert>The sense of this golden law is this: that no one should compel another to "do justice" [match a toast], as drunkards are accustomed to do, but that one should let everyone drink as much as pleased him.</insert> Therefore the King commanded his ministers that *man and man* should not be compelled, to speak with the text, to mutual toasts, but it should be granted to each to drink as he wished. A salutary law! If it had been obeyed among other Kings of the Persians, not so much wickedness and engorging would have appeared in them; for Xenophon writes that they eagerly engorged unmixed wine in mutual contests of banquets and urged the rest to it, so much so that they often returned from the dining rooms, well-fed and drunk, on others' feet. Which violence or compulsion even today prevails greatly in the courts of Great Men, where if you do not obey the "great horses" <note>likely referring to high-ranking or heavy-drinking courtiers</note>, the courtly gluttons and big-mouths are accustomed to be provoked. But let Princes learn to be wise from this example of the Persians, and let them observe this command of Ahasuerus and exercise it in their own courts. Indeed, the edict of Ahasuerus is <term>worthy of speech and memory</term> <term>regarding the thirst for more wine</term>. For truly and skillfully did one of the Triumvirs of Greek Tragedy <note>Sophocles</note> say that to be compelled to drink is no less a grave evil than if one were compelled to endure sharp thirst; <term>to drink by force</term>, he says, <term>is by nature an equal evil to thirsting by force</term>, for you could hardly say which is more inhuman: to be driven away from drink when thirsty, or to be compelled to drink when not thirsty. Far more unlike Ahasuerus was the <term>heavy drinker</term> Alexander the Great, of whom Athenaeus writes in book 12 that he drove his guests to drink, and that he explored them with wine, which for that reason Horace calls a *gentle torture* for the <term>minds of fellow-drinkers</term>. Arrian, in book 7, implies this. If he had obeyed the precept of Androcydes, that young man would not yet have fallen, nor would he have killed his friends in drunkenness. They say that Mithridates proposed prizes for eating and drinking, and in both vices he bore away the palm, wherefore Plutarch in his *Table Talk* records him being called *Dionysus*, which passage Muretus treats. And I ask, what was done everywhere among the Greeks, conferring prizes on drinkers? (see Rango, p. 1298). Aemilius Portus, Matnesius, and R. Puteanus have written more concerning the <term>love of drinking</term> of the ancients, and many excellent things concerning drunkenness...

Let the drunkard’s inquiry run that way, and let him admit warnings that are healthy for both his morals and his health; above all, let him strive to imitate the frugality of the early Christians, about which Ter-
<margin>
page 879.
</margin>

They satisfy themselves in such a way that they remember they must worship God even during the night; they converse as those who know the Lord is listening," and so forth. Good God, how much this modern way of living differs from that pious custom of the ancient age! Today people eat, drink, and play as if there were no future judgment after death.

Taking the opportunity provided by Ahasuerus's <term>symposium</term> <note>original: συμποσίῳ; a drinking party or banquet</note>, it is pleasing to digress into the banquets of the Ancients, even if we have designated a special place for them below. Here also is revealed an ancient rite in that same royally furnished banquet, where gold and silver couches were placed upon a pavement of emerald and Parian stone, or on a floor of various colors with a mosaic pattern inlaid <term>very magnificently</term> <note>original: πάνυ λαμπρῶς</note>, upon which the guests would recline. For formerly they took their food on couches, <term>upon the bed</term> <note>Hebrew: עַל-הַמִטָּה (al-hamittah)</note>, as is said of Haman in Chapter 7, verse 8. Dr. Luther explained this in the same place, as well as in Chapter 1, verse 6, by looking to our own century and translating it as "benches." In the same form in Luke 22:14 and elsewhere, he rendered the word for sitting together as <term>he reclined</term> <note>original: ἀνεπέσε</note>; although that learned Translator was not ignorant of the fact that they took food not by sitting, but by reclining. It is the habit of translators to transfer the customs of their own age to the ancient usage of time, as Brentius also did in this passage. <term>Mittah</term> <note>Hebrew: מטּה; couch or bed</note> is so called as a "recliner" from the root <term>natah</term>, meaning "he inclined." Likewise, <term>kline</term> <note>Greek: κλίνη</note> is used by the Greeks from <term>klino</term>, "I recline," which little word is used both for a banqueting couch and for that in which one sleeps or lies ill. Xenophon notes that the Persians in his time were accustomed <term>to have more blankets upon their horses than upon their beds</term> <note>original: στρώματα πλείω ἔχειν ἐπὶ τῷ ἵππων ἢ ἐπὶ τῶν εὐνῶν</note>—
<margin>
Pad. 8. end.
</margin>
namely, <term>being careful to sit softly</term> <note>original: τὰ μαλακῶς καθίζειν ἐπιμελωμένους</note>. A little before, declaring their <term>luxury</term> <note>original: τρὐφὴν</note>, he had said it was not enough for them <term>to spread their beds softly</term>, but they also <term>placed the feet of the couches upon carpets, so that the floor would not offer resistance</term>. They delighted in soft bedding, loving to lie on golden couches with beautiful coverings magnificently decorated with woven work. Regarding such a couch which they used in
<margin>
1 Sam. 28. 32.
</margin>
banquets, the passage* about Saul must be understood, who "rose from the earth" where he had lain in a sorrowful spirit, and "sat upon the couch." So too in Ezekiel 23:41: "And you sat upon a most beautiful couch, and a table was prepared before it." Nor does the "lying upon ivory couches" of which we read in the Prophet Amos, Chapter 4, seem to bear any other interpretation; an explanation confirmed by the <term>context</term> <note>original: συνάφεια</note> of the text itself. Moreover, these small beds were of the most choice and precious kind; that they excelled in such nobility is suggested because they are called "gold and silver," that is, gilded with gold and interwoven with silver in embroidered work—a common way of speaking where a thing or material is covered with plates or interwoven with gold leaf. Germans speak no differently in their own language about garments and clothing worked with woven gold, which they call *ein gülden Stück* <note>German: "a golden piece"</note>. The Greeks call it <term>a garment shot through with gold</term> <note>original: ἱμάτιον διάχρυσον</note>. Andre-

It is established by various testimonies that there was great luxury and glory in the couches set up for dining rooms <note>term: triclinia; a dining room with three couches arranged around a square table</note>, as well as in the tables. Athenaeus, describing the wedding of Alexander—

That the ancients were accustomed to hold banquets on couches is clear not so much from sacred as from profane rites; namely, they reclined with the body so composed that, with the upper part of the body moderately bent and curved, the rest lay flat, and one would recline in the bosom of another according to the order. From this position, the ancients called it a "banquet reclining" <note>original: accubatio epularis</note>, as Cato testifies in Cicero*. "Our ancestors well named the 'banquet reclining' of friends a *convivium* <note>Latin: a living together</note> because it held a conjunction of life; better than the Greeks, who call this same thing either a 'drinking together' (<term>symposium</term>) or a 'dining together' (<term>syndeipnon</term>)." Just as in Tobit Chapter 2:3 and 9:8, the word for "reclining" seems to be taken in the same sense. So also <term>by the same reasoning</term> <note>original: ἀνὰ τῶν αὐτὸν λόγον</note> in the neighboring Syriac language, "reclining" is used for the banquet itself. For what the Evangelist calls the <term>master of the feast</term> <note>original: ἀρχιτρίκλινον</note>, the Syrian in John 2:9 calls <term>the head of the reclining</term> <note>Syriac: רֵישׁ מְסִמְּכָא (reish mesimka)</note>, the Prefect of the feast, from the root meaning "he leaned" or "he reclined." The same occurs in the language of the Arabs, for from the root *Wakaa* comes a verb in the 8th conjugation which denotes to lean, recline, or lie down, as the <term>students of such things</term> teach; and what is called "reclining" by these is
<margin>
Song of Sol. 1:11.
</margin>
more expressly called a "circuit" by the sacred author*, so named because there was a circle of those reclining; for <term>sabab</term> <note>Hebrew: סבב</note> is properly a circular reclining, from the root "to go around" or "move in a circle." Whence Rabbi Solomon says on 1 Samuel 16:11 that every sitting at a banquet is called <term>hasibbah</term> <note>Hebrew: הסבּה; the act of reclining around a table</note>. From this rite is drawn the metaphor of the <term>Bosom of Abraham</term>, serving as a hieroglyph of eternal blessedness, which the Savior describes under the guise of a banquet in the history or parable of <term>Lazarus</term>, whose soul is said to be carried by angels into the <term>Bosom of Abraham</term>, Luke 16:22. Under the person of Lazarus in the bosom of Abraham <term>the friend of guests</term> <note>original: τοῦ φιλοξένου</note>, he neatly depicts the state of the faithful departing from this life into eternal life, where those who are present are refreshed at the eternal table with Christ...

# From Esther Chapter I. verses 6, 7, 8.

<margin>Persian Banquets.</margin>
They eat of the refreshment, which one may, along with Bonaventure <note>St. Bonaventure (1221–1274), a Franciscan theologian.</note>, call the noble **dining room** <term>triclinium: a room with three couches for reclining at meals</term> of the entire most blessed Trinity. And from hell, he saw that in this divine dining room there were cups full of water on the table of Abraham, from whence he cries out: *Send Lazarus, that he may dip his finger in water, and cool my tongue.* The soul finds refreshment after so many labors endured in these lands in that heavenly upper room; of which Christ himself spoke figuratively in *Luke ch. XXII. v. 29* in this manner: *I appoint unto you a kingdom, as my Father hath appointed unto me* <margin>v. 30.</margin> *that ye may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.* And from that same metaphor of a banquet, the joys of the heavenly kingdom are **most beautifully** <note>original Greek: παγκαλῶς</note> expressed in those words: *Many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven*, namely, as if they were to be so dear to Abraham that all would recline as if next to him and in his bosom. This very happiness of the future life he expressed elsewhere by the name of **joy** <note>original Greek: χαράς</note>, in which word Lorenzo Pignoria, in his *Commentary on Slaves*, thought a great secret of some rite resided; though I do not know how much these things are approved by Abraham Scultetus <note>A German court preacher and theologian (1566–1624).</note>. Let the judgment be yours, reader. The Holy Spirit also foreshadowed this gladness with a wedding garment and crown: for this is a certain eloquence of saving doctrine, adapted to moving the affection of learners from visible things to invisible, from bodily to spiritual, from temporal to eternal. For the kingdom of God is not meat or drink, as Pagans and Muslims dream today, but *righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit*, as Paul warns when writing to the Romans. Furthermore, beds of this sort for reclining at banquets, as well as others arranged with *gold and silver*, as we have seen in this place, were spread with tapestries, even purple or other woven coverings, varied with wonderful colors, according to the wealth and **abundance** <note>original Greek: αὐτινοπίᾳ</note> of the host. You see here the **banquet-breeding** <note>original Greek: τὸ δειπνοτόκον</note> nature of the Persian nation, and their **soft bedding** <note>original Greek: τὸ μαλακῶς ὑπεστρώννυς</note>, which Xenophon censures in that nation in *Education of Cyrus, Book VII*, saying among other things: *they place their feet upon carpets on the couches*. Most highly praised were **silver-footed** <note>original Greek: ἀργυρόποδες</note> beds, and at the same time, as part of luxury, **gold-studded** <note>original Greek: χρυσόβακτοι</note> ones were placed. Likewise ivory ones, *Amos* <margin>2. Ped. 3. p. 160. 184.</margin> 6. v. 4. **Silver-footed couches** <note>original Greek: Κλίναι ἀργυρόποδες</note> are mentioned by Clement of Alexandria <margin>page 34.</margin> and Plutarch *in Lycurgus p. 47.* **Ivory-footed tables** <note>original Greek: ἐλεφαντόποδες τράπεζαι</note>, Lucian *in The Dream* mentions **ivory couches** <note>original Greek: ἡ κλίναι ἐλεφάντιναι</note>, Herodian p. 87. Couches were also adorned with tortoise shells; Pliny *IX, 11* says: *Carvilius Pollio instituted the practice of cutting tortoise shells into plates and covering beds and repositories with them.* Martial *XII, 54*:
-> Jeweled beds shine with the finest tortoise shell. <-
Athenaeus, *Book 1*, cited the comic poet Plato introducing certain people who would dine reclining on a bed supported by ivory feet. Which support of the beds he called **like a lentil** <note>original Greek: ὅμοιον φακῷ</note> in *Book X, chapter 1*, because it reflected the shape of a lentil; the famous Casaubon thinks they were also called **apples** <note>original Greek: μῆλα</note> from the same shape, and that from this author light is shed on the Vulgate version of *Proverbs 25:11, Golden apples in silver beds* <note>Modern translations usually say "settings of silver."</note>, from which Fernando de Salazar in his commentary on *Proverbs* and Martinius in his *Philological Lexicon* under the word *lenticula* have drawn. <margin>page 1450.</margin> **But precision regarding the ends of things is of no use.** <note>original Greek: ἀλλ' οὐδὲν ἡ ἀχειβολογία χρήσιμον, ἡ περὶ τὰ τέλων τῶν</note>. They reclined in such an order that he who reclined first, with the upper part of his body leaning on his left elbow (as did the others), would sit at the head of the bed with his head slightly

erected and his back moderately supported by cushions, so that he stretched out his feet behind the back of the second person. But he who reclined second turned his head toward the bosom and navel of the first, with his feet behind the back of the third, and so on; whence he who had reclined second reclined as if in the bosom of the first. In the same way the third was in the bosom of the second, the fourth in the bosom of the third. Now we understand how *one of the disciples is read to have reclined in the bosom of Christ*, since Christ, reclining in the upper part of the bed, had John next to him. Therefore he is said to have leaned back in the bosom of Christ; whom painters wrongly depict sitting with his head bowed before Christ, contrary to the custom of the ancients, from which it is clear that the Jews took food lying down no less than the Romans and Greeks. And it should be noted that Christ, as a God of **order** <note>original Greek: τάξιν</note>, nowhere rebuked customary things, but rather observed them seriously. For our Savior, when he was received as a guest by others, was accustomed to take food on a bed according to the received custom of the nation, to which he humanely conformed himself; this is evidently hinted at by the words of Christ to the disciples whom he had sent: *He will show you a large upper room furnished, a dining room equipped with couches.* And the passage in *Luke ch. 24 v. 30* argues this, where it is read of Christ having set out for Emmaus, while he reclined with them, **when he sat at meat with them** <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ κατακλιθῆναι αὐτὸν μετ' αὐτῶν</note>. Indeed, from Philo, who lived in the time of the Apostles, <margin>page 377.</margin> in his *Book on Joseph*, it is clear that the custom of reclining was then accepted; a custom which today we have almost entirely lost. For when he describes the banquet where the brothers were received, he says they sat together, **men not yet using the reclining posture in banquet gatherings** <note>original Greek: μήπω τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐν ταῖς συμποτικαῖς συνουσίαις κατακλίσει χρωμένων</note>. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<margin>Persian Banquets.</margin>
<margin>On old age.</margin>
-> Cicero* used to say: *I am truly delighted by the rules for presiding over feasts established by our ancestors, and by that discourse which, according to the custom of our forefathers, is led by the Chief Master over the cup.* <- The curators of this banquet defined how much should be given to each person, according to the law of Ahasuerus regarding feasting. **DINING ROOM ATTENDANTS**, who stood behind those dining and were ready at hand if they wished to command anything; concerning whom Dempster writes in his notes on Rosinus, book 5, page 874. In the sacred history, with which we are chiefly concerned, Mary Magdalene is said to have approached the feet of JESUS, that is, she stood like a servant from behind at the couch on which the feet of the reclining Christ were placed; for boys and servants stood at the feet of those feasting, hence they earned the name "around-the-feet" <note>original: *circum-pedes*</note> in Cicero, as well as "at the feet" or "to the feet." Such was the station of Mary at the feet of our Lord; which Painters and Sculptors, through I know not what ignorance, depict poorly, as can be seen more than once among others in the four Evangelists published in Arabic at Rome. No painter is good who is ignorant of ritual. Seneca* says: *As soon as it was light, the servant, who had stood at his feet while he dined, relates what he had said while drunk during dinner.* <margin>Book 3 on Benefits, ch. 27.</margin> Martial, Book 3, Epigram 23:
> Since you hand back all the scraps to the boys,
> Why is a table not placed for you at your feet?
Catullus *to his Boy:*
> Servant of the old Falernian wine,
> Pour out for me more bitter cups.

Moreover, since they feasted reclining on couches leaning on an elbow and arranged in a circle, they therefore washed after first taking off their sandals, lest the coverings be defiled. The vessel from which this was done is called a *podanipter* <note>Greek: ποδανιπτήρ, a foot-basin</note>. Amasis, King of the Egyptians, had a golden foot-basin, in which he himself and all the guests <note>Greek: δαιτυμόνες, a poetic term for guests</note> washed their feet every time (*Herodotus*). Among the Ionians and Poets, *daitymon* denotes a Guest. In Planudes' *Life of Aesop*, page 48, a rustic is noted as "having reclined with his very boots on." Whereupon Xanthus said to his wife: "Let her pour water into the basin and wash the feet of the stranger." She immediately, having poured water into the basin, went to wash the guest's feet. The rustic, once washed, was relaxed. From this you will understand what John the Baptist* says, that he was not worthy to loosen the strap or the thong of the shoes of Jesus the Messiah; for according to the custom of that region, they were shod in boots, and they used to take off or lay aside their shoes or sandals when entering a temple or a house or more splendid chambers to take food, or to do anything else, as the Mohammedans do today when they attend sacred rites; and those who were more honorable or wealthy had some male or female servant as a "sandal-bearer" <note>original: *sandaligerulam*</note> to carry those sandals or shoes, which was indeed the lowliest service. Therefore, one may gather from this how great was the dignity and majesty of Christ, and the humility and modesty of John the Baptist, when the greatest of all the Prophets judged himself unworthy to perform even the most abject service for Christ the God-man <note>original: *theanthropo*</note>. Thus, when in Exodus chapter 12 the Jews are commanded to eat the lamb in haste and to have shoes on their feet, some devise a reason for this precept because they were accustomed to recline at the table barefoot; and so, lest any delay be caused, under a certain type, the eating of the Paschal lamb was commanded in a

### Concerning that removal of shoes before reclining.

One should consult Ciacconius on the dining habits of the ancients; Balduinus on the ancient shoe, chapter 26; Nannius, *Miscellany* 4, 2; Drusius on Exodus chapter 20; Taubmann on Plautus' *Persa*, Act 5, Scene 2; Casaubon on Theophrastus' chapter *On Impudence*; Stuckius, *Antiquities* 2, 33; Lipsius in his work on servants, page 212. What of the fact that Christ himself, the Teacher and Prince of all*, taking the role of a servant upon himself for the Apostles, as if for beloved guests and companions, not only provided water for washing their feet, but washed them with his own hand, having first set aside his garments. I would not wish, nor do I think it right, to mix in here the Roman dining garment which they used while dining, which Cardinal Baronius attributes to the Savior. Casaubon rightly ejected it from these venerable dining rooms and this sacred foot-washing; rather, the *Girding* <note>original: *Praecinctio*</note> should be joined with this washing. For servants used to stand at the feet of their Masters tucked up <note>girded for work</note>, which we know from many places. Seneca, *On Benefits* 3, 26: *The servant who had stood at his feet while he dined.* Suetonius has this common expression in *Caligula* chapter 26 and *Galba* chapter 22 in this description of service. As for the girding, it appears to have belonged to those ministering from Luke 12:35, 37 and 17:8, where the word "to gird oneself" <note>Greek: διέζωννύω</note> indicates this. Eustathius, on this verse of Homer found in *Odyssey* 14, v. 72, testified that one was "girded in haste," saying: "so speaking, he quickly bound his tunic with a belt." Hence Phaedrus called the hall-servants "high-girded" <note>original: *alticinctos*</note> in Book 2, Fable 5, and Horace in *Satires* 2, 8: "a boy high-girded." The Savior himself, so that he might better prove his humility to the disciples according to the customs of the hospitable ancestors, girded himself with a *lention* <note>Greek: λεντίῳ</note>, that is, a linen cloth, when he performed the "servile work" <note>Greek: δούλιον ἔργον</note>, as Nonnus calls it, in the foot-washing. After the Paschal Supper was finished, Christ had risen to wash feet for the ordinary Supper, and "he laid aside his garments, and taking a linen cloth, he girded himself. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the feet," as is read in the said John, verses 4 and 5. Furthermore, after that foot-washing, they poured scented ointments and liquids over the heads, and sometimes the feet, of those reclining. The Author of the divine Song expressed this in chapter 1, verse 12; for where the King's reclining is described, it follows: *My spikenard gave forth its scent*, that is, while the King reclined, I anointed him with nard ointment. For the Orientals delighted in frequent scents and ointments, and they drenched their guests with balsam or other fragrant ointments whenever they received them sumptuously. A pious woman did not think Christ unworthy of this honor when, as the feast of Passover approached and JESUS was likewise reclining at the banquet, she took a pound of precious nard ointment, and having broken the alabaster jar in which ointments were best preserved, she poured it over the head of JESUS himself. So also in Luke 7:38, a sinful woman bathed the feet of JESUS with tears and ointment; hence Christ said to Simon*: *You did not anoint my head, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.* The anointing of the head was ordinary, whence also in Pliny...

# From Esther Chapter 1, verses 6, 7, 8.

<margin>Persian Banquet Customs.</margin>
...considers it excessive luxury that some would even anoint their feet, concerning which see Meursius in *Critical Exercises, book 2, chapter 16* and his notes on Lycophron, page 230. However, she anointed not only the head of Christ, but even his feet, so that nothing would be lacking to testify to her utmost humility of soul. The Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator</note> on Aristophanes' *The Wasps* says: <margin>Persian Banquet Customs.</margin> *It is an ancient custom for women to take care that the feet are not only washed but also anointed.* Indeed, these are the words of Aristophanes: *First my daughter washes me and anoints my two feet, and leaning forward, she kisses them.* From this custom also <margin>Chapter 6, verse 17.</margin> was spoken that saying of Matthew <term>*</term> <note>Matthew 6:17</note>: *But you, when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you do not appear to men to be fasting.* Jerome, Martin de Roa (*Singularities, book 1, chapter 5*), and Drusius (*Observations, book 3, chapter 10*) note that because people were not accustomed to recline at a meal unless washed and anointed, they are therefore commanded to do the same even when fasting. This was so they would appear to have already dined, rather than still being in a state of fasting; for those fasting or in mourning did not anoint their faces. Indeed, to truly appear to be mourning, the head was not anointed—this was a sign of grief and fasting; whereas <margin>verse 104, verse 15.</margin> *anointing* was a sign of joy and pleasure, which, according to the Psalmist <term>*</term> <note>Psalm 104:15</note>, makes the face shine. Joab commanded the woman he sent to the King on behalf of Absalom to neglect this (*2 Samuel 14:2*), so that she might appear in unfeigned mourning. Our Savior commanded not to neglect it, so that men would not notice the fast. For the Lord’s words are to be understood not absolutely but comparatively: namely, that it is better to anoint the head and wash the face, according to the custom of Hebrews holding a banquet, than to hypocritically display that work of fasting before men as if in a theater, selling one's own holiness like the Pharisees. They, to appear to men to be fasting, put on a sad countenance and wished to appear squalid, and they *disfigured their faces so that they might appear [to fast]*, to use the language of the Syriac <margin>On Matthew, folio 79, d.</margin> *codex, chapter 25, verse 18.* Anselm <term>*</term> <note>Anselm of Canterbury</note> says: *Banqueters, as Horace says, are accustomed to anoint their faces.* And it was the custom of the Palestinians to anoint the head and wash the face on festive days to represent the joy of the days; they are accustomed to soothe the flesh with oil and make it cheerful. Hence also, because the Palestinians used scents, oils, and fragrant ointments much in elegant banquets, the *specific* began to be taken for the *general* term; among them, to be anointed is said *instead of living in luxury, rejoicing, or being cheered*, as Schindler teaches in his Lexicon under the word *bush*, page 216. Crinesius also notes this in his *Syriac Lexical Disputation* from the ritual of the Orientals. Regarding the Romans, Greeks, and other peoples who held the same rite, testimonies are easily collected; Bulengerus teaches much about this anointing in *Diatribe against Casaubon, page 115 and following, and book 6 on the Roman Empire, chapter 75*; also Robierzyck on *Roman Luxury, 10, pages 88, 123*; Carrio in *Emendations, book 2, chapter 16*; Raderus on *Martial, book 3, epigram 60 and book 8, chapter 17*; Curtius page 531, and many others who have written on this custom. All these things serve simultaneously to explain the History of Esther, for in it we read that much time was spent on ointments to satisfy the King's pleasure. The young women whom King Ahasuerus wished to have present were anointed for six whole months with oil of myrrh, and then for another six months with other spices. Here one may also observe the ancient custom of confining virgins in the Gynaeceum <note>The women's quarters</note>, so that after they had been refined and polished there, they might then be called to the marriage; for in *erotic matters* they are rejected, as Cicero says to Atticus in *book 9*, if they are dirty and, as Terence says, "unclean with filth," unadorned and grimy. Therefore, the use of myrrh ointment was for rubbing out wrinkles of the skin and cleaning away spots and dirt; while other pigments and spices, as the Vulgate has it in that place, were used for smoothing and softening the flesh. It would remain, if there were space, to speak of the more honorable place for reclining at the table; concerning which Christ, from older teaching, informs the Pharisees in *Luke 14:7*, where it is called by the proper and elegant word *protoklisia* <note>original: πρωτοκλισία</note>, as if you were to say in a coined Latin word, *Praeaccubatio* <note>The chief seat at the table</note>.

### ESTHER II. 21.

-> Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs <-
-> The two eunuchs of the king, like the chief bodyguards. <-
-> *Bigthan & Teres, two Eunuchs of the King.* <-

<margin>Eunuchs.</margin>
The Eunuchs of Kings and Nobles in the East were prefects and ministers; they cared for and prepared what seemed necessary. Their use was very ancient among the Greeks and Romans, and indeed throughout the whole East and among all nations, who employed them indiscriminately in various offices. There were Eunuchs in the service of Pharaoh (*Genesis 39:1*) and of that King who adopted Joseph as a partner in the Kingdom <margin>Genesis 37:36</margin> <term>*</term>: Potiphar is mentioned as the *Eunuch of Pharaoh*, *Saris Pharao*, the *Master of the Soldiers*; who had a wife (*chapter 39:7*) and perhaps a daughter (*chapter 41:45*). Regarding him, Gordon says: *This Eunuch was not a castrate, but one of the King's intimate servants.* Indeed, he is the master of the soldiers. The *Septuagint* <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> calls him the *archimageiros*, the chief of the cooks or butchers. And why not also of the soldiers, since the Greek word for "to cook" can also mean "to kill"? For these are called Eunuchs not because they were castrated, but because—just as castrated men were chosen as guards for the inner bedchambers of Kings, usually selected for the guarding of the women's chambers—so also those who were placed in charge of the King's principal affairs, whether public or private, were often called Eunuchs; because this class of men excelled in loyalty toward their Masters. Therefore, they were called by the Syrians by a title meaning *Faithful* from their office. Theodoret on Genesis says: *They are named Eunuchs, not only those who are cut, but also those among the servants who are well-disposed toward their owners.* Some say, however, that the Egyptians were accustomed to have Eunuchs take wives for the sake of lust and wantonness. Eucherius in his books on Kings says: *It was a custom among the ancients to call the chamberlains and guards of the Palace 'Eunuchs,' who had wives and were not cut in their bodies.* Almost all the business of the kingdom was placed in the hands of the Eunuchs; hence they were called "Patricians" or "Fathers of the Princes," as found in Suidas under *patrikios*. Sozomen (*Ecclesiastical History, book 8, chapter 7*) and Nicephorus (*book 13, chapter 1*) note that these were called by the later Princes of the Eastern Empire *basileopatores* <note>original: βασιλεοπάτορες</note>, as if you were to say *Fathers of the Emperor*, a name devised by the Emperor Leo the Philosopher, according to Zonaras and Cedrenus. For even Corbulo was called the Father of Emperor Nero, as Xiphilinus reports from Dio in his *Nero, page 192, a.* Julian the Prefect of the city was called the Father of Commodus (*ibid. page 290, c.*), and Misitheus the Father of Gordian, according to Capitolinus in *Gordian, chapter 27.* Likewise, Metrodorus of Scepsis, the philosopher, was called the Father of King Mithridates, according to Plutarch in *Lucullus, page 506, a.*, since all the works of the kingdom were carried out under his leadership, counsel, and foreknowledge. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Eunuchs. chapter 18. verse 17</margin> Trigault, *Chinese Annals p. 133*. Bulenger, *On the Roman Empire p. 151*. In the fourth book of Kings <note>original: "IV. Reg."; in modern Bibles, 2 Kings</note> mention is made of a certain *Rab-Saris*, which is as if to say "Master of the Eunuchs," if you look at the etymology of the word; for *Rab* (רב) is Prince, and *Sarisim* (סריסים) are *Eunuchs*, from which the Rabbis derived the word *Saras* (סרס), which to them means *to castrate*. Our translation has *Arch-Chamberlain* <note>original: "Erzthämmerer"</note>. Junius, Piscator, the Genevans, and the Zurichers retained the word *Rab-Sar* itself. The servants of Kings were called *Eunuchs*. *Esther chapter 2 verse 21*. It is reported that eunuchs were doorkeepers and kept watch at the first threshold of the palace. Thus it is narrated in *chapter 1 verse 10* of the same book that seven eunuchs served in the sight of King Ahasuerus and stood at his table, according to the usual custom of the Persians, who always had eunuchs standing by and serving them; and this was by the institution of Cyrus, as Xenophon teaches in *Education of Cyrus, Book VII*. There was also a Prefect of the Eunuchs. The Prophet Daniel, of the lineage of King David, led away as a captive from Judea to Babylonia while still almost an infant, after he had added the language of the Chaldeans and their arts over a space of three years by the King's command, <margin>Daniel 1 verse 3.</margin> was summoned with his companions by the *prefect of the eunuchs* *Ashpenaz*, as the Vulgate version renders it (אשפנז); the Seventy <note>The Septuagint Greek translation</note> call him the *Chief Eunuch* <note>original: "Ἀρχιευνοῦχος"</note>. Luther: *Chief Chamberlain* <note>original: "Obersten Kämmerer"</note>. Zurich: *Master of the Palace*, so that he might stand around the King, *verse 19*. From the kingdom of the Ethiopians, we read that the *Eunuch of Queen Candace* was dyed with sacred baptism by Philip, <margin>Acts chapter 8 verse 27.</margin> where Philip Charles sharpens his teeth against Matthias Flacius because he asserts in his *Key to Holy Scripture* that the name of this eunuch, initiated into the pure religion, was the proper name of an official; since, however, not everyone's calculations agree on this; certainly the Ethiopian Interpreter is the authority in that same place that this eunuch was the *Governor of the city of Gaza*, which Louis de Dieu observes from the same source; indeed, Flacius himself does not assert it firmly. Our Savior in *Matthew chapter 19 verse 12* mentions three kinds of eunuchs; the first kind are *eunuchs from the womb* <note>original: "εὐνοῦχοι ἐκ κοιλίας"</note>, who are born unfit for Venus <note>unfit for sexual intercourse</note>; of the second kind are *those who were made eunuchs* <note>original: "οἱ εὐνουχισθέντες"</note>, who were castrated by men; the third are *Eunuchs in spirit*, so called figuratively; among whom the will has brought lust into order, who although they remain with a vigorous faculty for generating, nevertheless impose a perpetual chastity upon themselves by a votive abdication of sexual matters as a peculiar gift of God, so that they may be able to serve Him without hindrances. For it treats of those in that place who abstain from marriage, whether from a natural cause, or on account of castration performed by human labor, or because of a free purpose of the mind: as in <margin>Book 6 chapter 8 of the Ecclesiastical History</margin> Origen cut himself off, according to Eusebius, a deed which no pious person ever approved, nor did anyone imitate; except one or two of the Origenists; about whom Epiphanius writes, *They reject marriage, but not lewdness* <note>original: "Ἀθετοῦσι γάμον, ἀλλ’ οὐ λαγνείαν"</note>. However, there were eunuchs at all times—I speak of the castrated: which was done, sometimes for the purpose of making them more fit for the duties of the women's quarters <note>original: "gynaeceorum"</note>, and that they might be guardians of virgins, which we are taught from Heliodorus's *Ethiopian History Book IX, 452*, from which the name itself is derived: for it is from *eunē* (bed) and *echō* (I have/keep); which <margin>Exercise 277 Section 4.</margin> derivation is approved by Scaliger the Elder; sometimes as a punishment for debauchery or adultery: and that this was a very ancient custom appears from Plautus's *The Soldier* and Terence's *The Eunuch*. There were those who became such by origin of nature, and those who became so by disease or a disaster of the body; concerning

<column-break/>

<margin>Eunuchs</margin> whom (namely the *thlasiae*, *thlibiae*, and *spadones* <note>different technical terms for types of castrated men</note>) Paulus Aegineta treats in *Book 6*, where he teaches the method of effeminating, which the Greeks called *Eunuchism*. They claim Semiramis was the first to castrate males, of whom Claudian writes in *Book 1 against Eutropius, verse 331*:
> These, hands created; whether first Semiramis by craft
> Feigned a Man to the Assyrians, lest the shrill softness
> Of her voice and smooth cheeks might betray her.
> She joined these like herself to her, or Parthian
> Luxury forbade the shadow of downy hair to be born,
> And preserving the boyish flower for a long time, forced
> Youth, retarded by art, to serve Venus.
They tell of Cybele, that she, already an old and deformed woman, burned with love for Attis, a beautiful boy; and him whom she could not entice to debauchery, she unmanned. Others report that the old woman, when she heard that Midas, King of the Pessinuntians, had destined his daughter for Attis, impatient of a rival, then cut off his genitals. Hence it happened that the Priests of Cybele were castrated to the Phrygian sound of the flute. Tatian: <margin>Oration against the Greeks.</margin> *Rhea was she who, through the Phrygian mountains of Cybele, they say, caused the cutting off of genitals because of her beloved Attis.* And Servius on *Aeneid IX*: *The Great Mother instituted that every year in the sacred rites Attis should be mourned: and it was brought about that her worshippers should amputate their own manly parts, who are called archigalli.* Vossius pursues this castration at length in *On Idolatry Book I, chapter 20, pages 151-154*; and on *page 155* he relates that the name of the *Galli* was given to the Priests from this. Hence also some think the name of the *Gauls* <note>original: "Galli"</note> was given to the peoples of France, against whom Goropius Becanus <margin>2. Gall. p. 41.</margin> inveighs most heavily: *Who is so foolish, so devoid of common sense, as to think thus, that the Gauls, perpetual enemies of the Romans, would wish to accept or retain a name for themselves which the insult of their enemies had imposed? If anyone thinks so, I would say he certainly lacks not testicles, but a brain.* For this kind of the Castrated is subject to perpetual reproach, concerning which Xenophon says in *Education of Cyrus Book 7, page 116*: *Eunuchs are without honor among other men.* And it is established that they were of no value among the Gentiles from the fact that they detested the meeting of a Eunuch as an evil omen, as Lucian writes in *On the Unlucky Day*. Nor is the reason for this obscure, since either the origin of nature or a disaster of the body separated them as if exiled from both sexes, as Mamertinus writes in his Panegyric. Whence Hermotimus in Herodotus's *Urania* complains about that matter to Panionius, who had unmanned him and sent him among other gifts as a present to Xerxes, King of the Persians: *O most wicked of all men born,* he said, *who makes profit from a most nefarious trade! What evil did either I myself, or any of mine, do to you or any of yours, that you rendered me a "neither" instead of a man?* Camerarius reviews this history more fully in *Century I, chapter 99*; read it there. The Turks—to pass over things that are too ancient—still observe this mode of castrating, with the loss of everything the wretches have; otherwise they think it little safe to entrust their women to simple eunuchs, as Scaliger reports in *Exercise 104, Section 8*, A. Busbequius, who performed an eight-year embassy at Byzantium to the Emperor of the Turks, *Letter 3*, and Muretus *10. Various Readings 11*. V. Mendoza on *1 Kings 8:15, page 620 and following*. Lorinus on *Acts chapter 8*. Pererius on *chapter 37.*
