### ESTHER III. v. 2.

->And all the king's servants, who were in the king's gate, bowed and prostrated themselves to Haman.<- <note>original Hebrew: וכל-עבדי המלך אשר-בשער המלך כרעים ומשתחוים להמן</note>

->And all those in the court worshipped him.<- <note>original Greek: Καὶ πάντες οἱ ἐν τῇ αὐλῇ προσεκύνουν αὐτῷ</note>

->And all the servants of the King, who were occupied at the doors of the Palace, bent their knees and adored Haman.<- <note>original Latin: Cunctiq; servi Regis, qui in foribus Palatii versabantur, flectebant genua & adorabant Aman</note>

<margin>
The Persian custom of adoring Kings.
</margin>

We read that from the earliest ages, people attributed august titles to Kings, and likewise acts of veneration. Truly, as they are more eminent than other mortals, so they are more worthy of veneration. Furthermore, the venerations of the Eastern peoples, compared to those of the West, are even to this day more august and far more submissive, even to the point of superstition. Maro <note>The poet Virgil</note> alludes to this in the 4th book of the *Georgics*:

> Besides, Egypt and great Lydia, 
> nor the Parthian people, nor the Median Hydaspes, 
> do not observe their King in such a way.

As soon as access was granted, the worshippers would salute the King from a distance as if he were some Divinity; they would roll themselves at his knees with the whole body cast upon the ground. Every kneeling and bending of the entire body was a significant part and symbol of civil <term>adoration</term> <note>In this context, "civil" means social or political respect rather than religious worship</note>, which was so frequent among the Easterners that an inferior would show it to any superior. There are two words for submission among the Hebrews, *kara* <note>כרע</note> and *shachah* <note>שחה</note>, which appear together with *barak* <note>ברך</note> in <margin>Psalm 95:6.</margin> Aben Ezra <note>A famous medieval Jewish scholar</note> seems to have looked to this when he wrote: *And prostrating*, "Every man cried out before him: I will fall on my knees and adore." Buxtorf, in his *Hebrew Lexicon* under the word *barak*, lists four words by which the Hebrews describe the cult of honor: *kadad* <note>קדד</note> denotes the prostration of the whole body; *kadad* <note>also</note> the bowing of the crown of the head; *kara* <note>כרע</note> the lowering of the head with the upper body down to the knees; *barak* <note>ברך</note> the bending of the knees. The Talmudists hand down this distinction in the book *Shevu'ot*, folio 16, 2, and *Megilla*, folio 22. From these, they explain *shachah* as <term>proskynesis</term> <note>Greek for falling down to worship</note>, and in Latin as *adorare* (to adore), just as *kara* signifies bowing the head to the ground in the manner of those who give thanks for benefits received with a lowered head, or those who testify reverence by a lowering of the head when greeting or saying farewell. Thus *shachah* is to adore, to worship devotedly, not only with external gestures of the body but also with the affection of the soul. For when devotion grew, they did not only adore (*shachah*), but simultaneously with adoring they lowered their bodies. Thus Abraham, to whom three men are recorded to have appeared in <margin>Genesis 17:3</margin>, fell upon his face, *al-panav*, partly to show the honor due to divine majesty, partly to signify his own <term>ekdoteta</term> <note>Greek: surrender or lowliness</note> and unworthiness, and partly to testify to a humble and grateful soul by this inclination of the body. Jacob, in Genesis 33:3, bowed himself to the ground seven times toward his brother Esau who was coming to meet him, *vayishtachu artzah*; by this external exhibition of civil adoration, he wished to testify his devotion from a sincere, not hypocritical, soul toward his elder brother and honored Prince. There also occurs in verse 4 the word *vayishakehu* <note>and he kissed him</note>, which is punctuated out of the ordinary, in which a mystery seems to some to lie hidden, and among other things, by that very fact is noted the 

<column-break/>

hostile conversion of Esau's soul, as Mercerus and Sixtinus Amama in his *Antibarbarus Biblicus* have set forth. Regarding Moses, it is read* that having gone out to meet his father-in-law Jethro, *vayishtachu*, he bowed himself; the Septuagint says *prosekynese*. The Vulgate says "he adored," namely with a bent knee, his body being cast down at the other's feet, by which ceremony he declared his reverence and subjection toward him. We spoke above on page 133 regarding the <term>proskynesis</term> or "knee-bending" of Joseph's brothers. With the same cult, David venerated Saul—who was persecuting him without fault—when Saul entered the path from the cave (1 Samuel 24:9), with his face prone to the ground, and begged him not to listen to the words of those men who said he was plotting evil. And* before Jonathan, the son of Saul, falling prone to the ground, he adored three times: *he fell upon his face on the earth and worshipped three times*. Yet they fell in such a way that their foreheads touched the ground. Shimei did the same for David when he was restored to the kingdom (2 Samuel 19:18). Naaman the Syrian, when he had renounced idolatrous worship, indicated to Elisha (2 Kings 5:18) that he would bend his knees in the temple of Rimmon not with the intention of adoring Rimmon, but of serving his King, saying: "When my Lord enters the temple of Rimmon to adore, and he leans upon my hand" (for it is well known that Kings and other Princes had the custom of leaning on the shoulders of their servants or chief ministers, which Gregory of Tours relates of Childeric descending from his horse in book 6 of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 46), "if I adore in the temple of Rimmon, while he adores in the same place, may the Lord forgive me your servant for this thing." This reverence was done without sacrilege or, as Sulpitius says elsewhere, without the "wicked atonement of the mind," and the Apostle Peter in 1 Peter 2:17 calls it "honor." Indeed, among the honors of the Magistrate is the bowing which Naaman was bound to provide by reason of the office he held. For he was not permitted to be absent from the King's side by reason of his office, and therefore he asks: if the King, leaning upon his hand, falls down for the *worship of demons*, and he himself is also forced to bow, let not this external position of bowing be imputed to him as a sin by the God of Israel. There occurs in this place in the text the word *hishtachavayah*, a formative from the *Hithpael* of the verb *shachah*, and it intends such a bowing or adoration which is done with the spreading out of the hands and feet; the prince of Hebrew scholars, Buxtorf, writes in the monitoring conclusion of his Lexicon that this is the only example found in the Bible, and Valentin Schindler* notes the same regarding this word. They cast themselves prone to the ground not so much in civil as in religious worship, and when they touched it with their face, they raised themselves again, and once or twice more they bowed their bodies in veneration, following the example of Jacob, who bowed seven times, and David, who bowed three times. The Athenians despised this custom as unworthy of a free man, and the Turks turn away from it. For in a more recent age, the rite of salutation that was done with the submission of the forehead to the ground was forbidden by Muhammadan law, as something that belongs to the honor of God alone and not of men. Therefore, that honor is unusual among the Turks in civil conversation where the body is prostrated along with a kiss. For during prayer, they lean on the ground with the forehead applied to the earth at the same time, a custom reported to us by the eyewitness, the celebrated Jacob

</margin>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
### Page 394

<margin>The Persian custom of worshiping Kings.</margin>
Golius <note>Jacobus Golius (1596–1667), a famous Dutch Orientalist</note>, who formerly taught Arabic letters with great success in the Academy of the Netherlands, which is in Leiden. The Greeks call it *proskynesis* <note>original: προσκύνησιν</note>, which properly signifies the inclination of the body before another: and it is done either by falling on the knees, or upon the very face, as is clear from a comparison of Matthew 8:2, Mark 1:40, and Luke 5:12.
<margin>chapter 10:20.</margin>
Judith, coming into the sight of Holofernes, fell upon her face and worshiped him <note>original: προσεκύνησεν αὐτῷ</note>, that is, inclining and prostrating herself; she exhibited honor and reverence. For this is what *proskynein* signifies, which the Vulgate rightly translates in Job 9:38 as "to worship by falling down," so that it might more expressly indicate the rite of adoration itself. From there it is metaphorically transferred to the mind, so that religious adoration is signified; this can be declared by the example of the Magi in Matthew 2:2 and the Leper, in whom not only civil but also religious worship concurs. Moreover, the Magi seek the newborn Jesus in Bethlehem as a new King; they salute, worship, and honor him with gold, which is the symbol of Kingship, and with frankincense and myrrh, according to the ancient custom of the Persians, whose Kings are always accustomed to be worshiped with gifts, as Nicolaus of Lyra observed on this passage. For it was received among the Persians, either by law or custom, that no one could approach the Royal majesty without some gift. That which was thus accustomed to be offered to Kings in Persia, the Magi "from the East" offered to the young child Jesus, the future King of the world, as had become well known throughout the whole Orient. Regarding this as religious worship, Chrysostom says: *“They venerated this body lying in a manger, and coming from afar, they worshiped with much fear;”* and Toussaint explains it with us
<margin>on Acts chapter 20, verse 36.</margin>
in his *Commentary on this passage, page 27.* To which we subjoin Calvin:
> The internal affection indeed holds the first place in prayers; but external signs—kneeling, uncovering the head, lifting the hands—have a double use. The first is that we may exercise all our members for the glory and worship of God; secondly, so that our sluggishness may be aroused by this support, as it were. A third use is added in solemn and public prayer, because the children of God profess their piety in this way, and encourage one another to the reverence of God. Just as the lifting of hands is a symbol of confidence and ardent desire, so we fall on our knees to testify to our humility.

<margin>on 1 Kings 8, folio 62; 2 Chronicles 6:13.</margin>
Peter Martyr bears witness:
> In Chronicles, it is written that Solomon called upon God with bended knees and spread hands; not because the worship of God consists chiefly in external things, yet these are effective for inciting the mind and they invite due honors—and indeed not lightly—for pouring out prayers before God. By bending the knees, we testify to our subjection toward God.

He relates the same things about the gesture of Solomon praying in the same words elsewhere.
<margin>Common Places, class 3, chapter 13, section 12, pages 670–671; on Isaiah chapter 1, folio 28.</margin>
Thus Zacharias Ursinus:
> The stretching out of hands is a rite of suppliants. The lifting up signifies the One to whom they become suppliants: the God of heaven, that is, the true, omnipotent, and immense God. Although not commanded, it is nevertheless a gesture as if implanted by nature, which the ardent lifting of the soul to God, which it usually accompanies, demonstrates.

Why then are the minds of many so alienated from kneeling and uncovering the head when the thrice-holy name of JESUS is uttered? I remember hearing at Osnabrück a court preacher of the Count of Wittgenstein (then the Brandenburg Legate) railing against a religion so naked of external ceremonies and nauseated by kneel-

<column-break/>

<margin>The Persian custom of worshiping Kings.</margin>
ing and other symbols of worship. He was far more civil in the matter of piety than Caspar Olevianus, who formerly at Berleburg, in the court of the Counts of Wittgenstein, let out great bellows in his first sermons against kneeling and uncovering the head.

But our meditation now turns chiefly to the custom of the Persians in honoring their King. He committed a great crime who, about to approach the King of the Persians, did not intend to do so with a prostrate body; or if, about to enter the palace or the royal bedchamber while the King was absent, he did not uncover his head, he committed an unspeakable offense. The majesty of Kings among them was extraordinary, and Curtius testifies in *Book 5* that nowhere among nations were Kings worshiped with more sacred reverence and faith.
<margin>In the Life of Themistocles.</margin>
Hence Artabanus the Persian thus addresses Themistocles in Plutarch: *“To us, of many laws, this is the most beautiful: to honor the King, and to worship the image of God.”* <note>original: Ἡμῖν δὲ πολλῶν νόμων ὦ καλλίςος οὗτός ἐστι, τὸ τιμᾶν βασiλέα, καὶ προσκυνεῖν εἰκόνα θεοῦ.</note> So the rest of the Persian Princes, immediately sliding from their horses (as is the custom of the Persians), salute King Darius with their bodies prostrate on the ground, according to Valerius Maximus.
<margin>Book 7, chapter 3.</margin>
The Persians exhibited this peculiar honor to their Kings alone, as Curtius again left written in *Book 8*, saying: *“The Persians prudently worship their Kings among the Gods, for majesty is the safeguard of the empire's safety.”* The King was addressed by them as "the King of Kings" and "the Great King" in Aristophanes' *Acharnians, Act 1, scene 2, verse 23.* The Persians guarded this custom of theirs with religion, so much so that they considered it a sin to worship a foreign King with this kind of adoration. Heliodorus indicates this in *Ethiopics, Book 9*, where Orondates the Persian, stretching out his hands to Hydaspes, King of the Ethiopians, and raising his right hand, said: *“O King, because it is not accepted by us—a thing which is customary for Persians—to serve another King in this manner.”* <note>original Greek translated to English</note> This custom of worshiping Kings and leading men was very ancient, as Pighius relates on Valerius Maximus, Book 7, chapter 2. However, Arrian in *Book 4* reports that this veneration was instituted by Cyrus. Truly, if Arrian is discussing the worship to be exhibited to Persian Kings, we easily agree with him, since Cyrus was the first King of the Persian race to be so saluted, and he transferred the height of the Monarchy from the Chaldeans and Medes to the Persians. Otherwise, the prostration on the ground and adoration itself is many centuries older than Cyrus, as is evident from what has been said so far. Moreover, this *proskynesis* very often had joined to it the kissing of the pavement, by which they intimated their highest submission; hence it is said in a proverbial figure in Isaiah,
<margin>chapter 49:23.</margin>
"to lick the dust of the feet." The whole passage of the Prophet is: *“And Kings shall be your foster-fathers, and Queens your nursing mothers: with their faces cast down to the earth they shall worship you, and lick the dust of your feet.”* Thus in *Psalm 72:10*: "The King of Ethiopia shall kneel before him, and his enemies shall lick the earth." This figure is taken, says Simon de Muis in his *Commentary on the Psalms, page 382*, from the Orientals and Asians, who even today are accustomed, when they approach their King, to kiss the earth before him.
<margin>Chapter 7 of the Travels.</margin>
This is also testified by John de Mandeville, who many years ago stayed for a long time in those places: *“It is necessary,”* he says, *“that wherever a messenger first sees the Sultan, whether at the windows or elsewhere, he falls to his knees and immediately kisses the earth.”* Flacius, in his *Key* under the word "to lick," calls this a truly violent [expression]...

# On Esther III, v. 2.

<margin>The Persian custom of worshipping Kings.</margin> Jerome provides an interpretation of "licking" regarding this passage of Isaiah when he says: *This signifies that Kings and Princes wipe away and lick clean with their own speech whatever earthly work has clung to the feet of the Church.* Martial also seems to have alluded to this Eastern custom in Book 10, Epigram 62:
> And the foul, the humble, and the suppliant
> Kissed the soles of the embroidered Kings.
But to finally arrive at the passage prescribed for us, it is well known from the Book of Esther that when the proud Haman, son of Hammedatha, was proclaimed second after King Ahasuerus, the lone Jew Mordecai refused to show him the honor of kneeling that was performed by the other courtiers. He would neither bow before that braggart nor show him any reverence by external symbol. Mordecai refused <term>kolkeuein</term> <note>original: "κολκεύειν" — to flatter or fawm</note> in the manner of flatterers, <term>who throng the gates to be filled, and approaching, address them as masters</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀνὰ τὰς πυλῶνας ἔνθεν ἐμπλησθῶσι, καὶ προσελθόντες ὥσπερ δεσπότας προσείπωσι"</note>, as Lucian jokes about them. *You know, Lord*, he says in his prayer, *that I did not refuse to worship the proud Haman out of insult, nor pride, nor desire for glory.* (Namely, according to the custom among the Persians, who held their Kings in the place of gods, as Aeschylus testifies; Haman had commanded that he be adored in the manner of Kings.) *For I would gladly have kissed even the prints of his feet for the salvation of the Israelites; but I did this so that I might not prefer the glory of a man to the glory of God, nor worship anyone as my Lord except You.* Behold the reason of the pious man: <term>the man who does not bow down because of wisdom and the law within him</term> <note>original Greek: "διὰ σοφίαν καὶ τὸν οἴκοθεν αὐτῷ νόμον ὁ μὴ προσκυνῶν ἄνθρωπος"</note>, as Josephus has it in Book 11 of the *Antiquities of the Jews*, chapter 6. The Greeks were formerly averse to this kind of worship; hence Hermolaus, taking offense at Alexander the Great when he demanded a new ritual of approach for himself from his followers, addressed him with wonderful freedom: *You wanted the Macedonians to bow their knees to you, and to venerate you as a God.* Alexander also desired the Macedonians and the nations he had conquered to be fully persuaded, under threat of heavy punishment, that he was the *Son of Jupiter*; that Jupiter Ammon, or the "horned one," from which he still retains the name among the Arabs today, as Scaliger notes. Therefore, because of that insolence, he allowed them to lie prostrate on the ground in veneration. <margin>Book 6, § 6.</margin> Regarding this, Curtius says: *Regarding the ancestral customs and the healthily tempered discipline of the Macedonian Kings and their civil dress as too slight for his greatness, he emulated the Persian court and the height of the power of the Gods. He required them to venerate him on the ground, and sought to gradually imbue so many victors of nations with servile ministries and make them equal to captives.* For the high-minded Prince wanted new rites to be held for him; he thought he should be adored as a certain new Jupiter and Apollo, with bended knee and prostrate body. Callisthenes showed what he thought of this in his *Oration* against Anaxarchus. Furthermore, it is clear from Xenophon that the Persians also kissed the feet of their Kings, which is why Seneca, in *On Benefits* Book 2, calls the custom of kissing feet "Persian slavery." That ritual of <term>podophilematos</term> <note>original: "ποδοφιλήματος" — foot-kissing</note> passed from the Persians to the Jews, along with others, as is declared by the history of Mary Magdalene, the great sinner, <margin>Luke 7:38.</margin> who is read to have kissed the feet of Christ. Hence Gregory, with Lyra noting on this passage, says: *She kissed them, as one entirely burning for God in penance,*

<column-break/>

*because she had despised the Creator in her fault.* And <margin>Sermon 39.</margin> Chrysologus says: *That miserable woman, entirely suppliant, falling at the Savior's feet, signified her humility and penance by a great rain of tears poured out from the shrine of her innermost heart, so that Christ himself might be moved to mercy.* In the course of time, this most base form of kissing feet reached other nations as well. Dio records of Gaius Caligula in his life: <term>he kissed a few, but to most, even of his counselors, he offered either his hand or his foot to be worshipped.</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐφίλει ὀλίγους τοὺς δὲ πλείστοις, καὶ τῶν συμβουλευτῶν ἢ τὴν χεῖρα, ἢ τὴν πόδα προσκυνεῖν ὤρεγε."</note> Later, the Emperor Diocletian sanctioned this ritual of kissing by a special edict, *so that all, without distinction of rank, should kiss his feet while prostrate; he also displayed a certain veneration for them by decorating his shoes with gold, gems, and pearls.* Whence Seneca (*On Benefits* 2.12, p. 396), since Gaius Caligula had previously used the same practice, says: *What is insulting here, if a Man kissed gold and pearls, and would otherwise have chosen no other part of his body to kiss first?* No less insolent was Maximinus the Younger in demanding this worship of his feet, of whom Julius Capitolinus writes in the *Augustan History*: <margin>page 268.</margin> *That he might stretch out his hand, he allowed his knees to be kissed, and sometimes his feet, which Maximinus the Elder never allowed, who used to say: "The Gods forbid that any freeborn man should fix a kiss upon my feet."* A voice worthy of so great an Emperor! To which can be compared what Plutarch relates of Paulus Aemilius in his life, who addressed Perseus, the defeated King of Macedonia, as he lay on the ground embracing Aemilius's knees and uttering words unworthy of a Prince: *Why do you clear fortune of its crime by acting so that you seem unworthy not of your present fortune, but of your former? Why do you defile my victory and diminish my deeds by showing yourself degenerate and in no way worthy of having been a fit enemy against the Romans? Truly, the virtue of the fallen commands great reverence even among enemies; but cowardice, even if fortunate, is never without blame.* Having said these things, Aemilius raised him up, and taking him by the right hand, handed him over to Tubero. The ancient Romans considered it a disgrace and a vice, which they blamed in others and thought worthy of rebuke. Thus Pompey, as Plutarch testifies <margin>in *Pompey*.</margin>, when Tigranes, King of Armenia, wished to prostrate himself at Pompey's feet as a suppliant, Pompey prevented him and raised him up. Pliny praises the same in his *Panegyric* (p. 26) regarding the Emperor Trajan, *that he did not lower the embraces of citizens to his feet, nor return a kiss with his hand.* That insolent pride of the Roman See deserves the censor's rod, whereby the Successors of St. Peter (as they wish to be called) affect to imitate the tyrants Gaius Caligula and Diocletian—enemies of the Christian name—rather than the warnings of St. Peter <margin>1 Peter 2:13, 17; 5:3.</margin> to follow humility and subjection. They intend to fortify their insolence with testimonies of Holy Scripture and try to prove it from them "at the Greek Calends" <note>A Latin idiom meaning "never," as the Greeks had no Calends.</note>. The flattery of Poliziano is redundant in his *Oration for the Sienese* (Works, p. 306, 507) when he says that Alexander VI was raised plainly to divinity itself, and who sees all things except God as lesser and inferior to himself, so that even Kings and Princes themselves, humbled, do not only not disdain to adore his tracks and lick the dust of his feet, but even desire it as a distinguished gift. ### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Persian custom of worshipping Kings.</margin>
As Thomson responded to a foul flatterer in *The Defender of the Truth, p. 95*: "The Most Holy One," if it pleases the Gods, ordained by edict that all men, of whatever dignity and preeminence, as soon as they come into the sight of the Pope, must kneel before him three times at set intervals and kiss his feet. See, if you will, Lanius in *Oration for Italy, p. 696, 698* and *Oration against Italy, p. 754*; Mornay on *Temporal Monarchy of the Roman Pontiff, ch. 25, n. 6*; and Cyril Herdes, *The Guide of Pontifical Law, p. 5*. In this kissing of the feet, like Gaius Caligula <note>The Roman Emperor known for his tyranny and demand for divine honors.</note> and Diocletian, the Roman Pontiff offers feet adorned with gems and pearls, and on the surface of the shoe is woven a golden cross—plainly so that he may show the cross is being trampled under his own feet. Besoldus, *Practical Treasury, p. 149*, citing Angelus the Jurist; add Blondel, *Decade 2*; Platina in *The Life of Constantine*; Ravanellus, *Sacred Library, p. 466*. Indeed, Christopher Marcellus writes in the *Book of Ecclesiastical Rites of the Roman Church, book 3, section 4, folio 136* <margin>Venice edition, 1516.</margin>: "The Pope distinguishes four levels of honor: the mouth, the hand, the knee, and the feet. The mouth," he says, "only the Emperor is worthy to kiss; the hand, the Cardinals; the knee, the Bishops; the feet are kissed by the common and vulgar folk." However, the practice observed until now testifies to the contrary, if you except the Purple-clad Fathers <note>The Cardinals</note>, who alone are exempt from kissing the feet; in its place, they receive the Pontiff's right hand under the gold-embroidered ceremonial cloak with their mouth. Indeed, not even Emperors are exempt from the kissing of the feet, but from the time of Louis the Bavarian, as Bodin reports in *On the Republic, book 1, ch. 9*, they subject themselves to the Popes by such a symbol of reverence not only when present, but even when absent in their letters. We have a most evident example of this in the letters of Emperor Charles IV written to Innocent V, in which he mentions that he was elected to the imperial office by the common vote of all the states of the Empire, but asks for confirmation from the Roman Pontiff to obtain the Imperial crown; the letters begin: *After the kissing of the blessed feet.* The same is observed today in the letters of the Emperor to the Roman Pontiff, in which the signature reads: *I kiss the hands and feet of your Holiness.* And what these Princes of such high rank attest in letters, they have actually performed when the occasion arose. Regarding Charles IX of France kissing the feet of Pope Alexander VI, and Francis I, likewise King of France, at the wedding of his son Henry to Catherine de' Medici, kissing the feet of Pope Clement VII, one should read Paolo Giovio, *History, books 27 and 31*. A living, though silent, monument of papal arrogance also stands in Rome at the Castel Sant'Angelo, where an image of Emperor Charles V is carved in marble (who showed the worship of kissing the feet to Clement VII when he was crowned in 1530, and to Paul III when he returned from Africa). It displays this insulting inscription:

> From Libya the Roman Victor comes to the citadels,
> -> Caesar, and on snow-white horses he went in gold. <-
> He triumphed: but you, Paul, triumph more,
> -> For the Victor gives kisses to your feet. <-

But this is to the end that the See itself might more easily and conveniently grow and exalt itself, and proudly trample the necks of Christians with its feet, with no one resisting. Who is unaware of how indignant Gregory IX was with Frederick II, when by mistake he kissed his knees instead of his feet? Likewise, it is sometimes expedient, for the purpose of stirring men's minds toward true religion, that what had previously been held in honor among them should not be entirely removed, but applied to a similar worship by a holier institution.* And after he had recounted that the Roman Ethnic <note>Pagan</note> Priests were honored by the kissing of feet, and that Gaius Caligula offered his left foot to be kissed, and that Diocletian ordered the kissing of feet by edict, he adds: *That honor is today given to the Roman Pontiff, who admits those approaching to the sacred kissing of the feet; the other Bishops offer their right hand, turned away, to be religiously kissed by those approaching, which is known to be taken even from the Pagans.* Indeed, it is a Catholic observation and custom used by almost all men throughout the world since Adam, and there is hardly anything in which the more civilized rites of all nations agree more than in kissing. From the civility of the Orientals, it descended as a sign of more civilized submission to the Greeks, Latins, Italians, French, Spanish, etc. All kisses are pressed upon the lips, or the part of the face closest to the lips. It is one action, but often with a different spirit. For that man kisses flatteringly, this one treacherously, another hypocritically. # From Esther III. v. 2.

<margin>The Persian custom of adoration.</margin>
*To Amasa. With a wicked kiss Judas kissed Jesus.*
The holy kiss <note>original: "Osculum sanctum"</note> was performed to foster peace and charity; for it was the custom in the primitive Church that those receiving the Epistles of the Apostles would greet and kiss one another as a sign of concord, acceptance, and the fulfillment of admonitions. The kiss was not only a sign of love but also of reverence. We can note the custom of kissing the hands from Homer, and it is very ancient: Eumaeus received the returning Telemachus very humanely, *Odyssey 16, v. 15.*
<margin>Odyssey 23, v. 37.</margin>
> He kissed his head and both his beautiful eyes
> and both his hands.
Penelope, approaching Ulysses, hesitates within herself:
> Standing near, she might kiss his head and take his hands.
So Priamus, approaching Achilles, *Iliad 24, v. 478:*
> He took the knees of Achilles with his hands, and kissed his hands.
He uses the verb *kysai* and *kysas* in three places, from *kyein* or *kynein*, *to kiss*, which entirely agrees with the German *Küssen* and the ancient English *to Kisse*, as Meric Casaubon, son of Isaac, suggests in his Commentary on the Four Languages. In our century, it is still the custom in the greeting of Princes and Great Men to submit oneself by the kissing of the hand and to receive favor, which
<margin>Ventil. Philos. p. 9.</margin>
custom Balthasar Thomas believes *descended from that practice of greeting the Gods by kissing the hands, whose words I give you: This custom of kissing the hands of Men who are Princes and placed in illustrious positions leads its lineage from the impious and ridiculous religion of the Heathens, who, only upon the sight of something sacred, or in which they believed some divinity to be present, would bring the hand to the mouth; for they prayed to the Gods, whom they honored with these signs, with a thin murmur, that they might favor them. Besides the Heathen writers, the prayer of Job also testifies to this, by which he removes that impiety from himself. Sane men, however, when they noticed in Princes no obscure signs of divinity, began to hold this honor for them; and certainly since God holds Magistrates in such a place that He deigns them worthy of His own name and title, we shall rightly seem to testify to our observance and subjection by these signs. Therefore, this honor was once so proper to Princes that if anyone offered it to someone, he testified by that very act that the person was born of an illustrious place. An illustrious example of this matter is supplied by the most Illustrious Prince Otto of Hesse, who, while staying unknown in the court of Cleves, is said to have been recognized by this very honor deferred to him by a certain Hessian Nobleman.* We assert, therefore, that only Princes and those established in Magistracy are to be greeted with this honor; whoever does otherwise, and kisses everyone indiscriminately, we consider him further from civility than from flattering levity. We shall have to deal with the kiss more fully elsewhere by profession, so being content with these things, it pleases us to advise this further. Those who kiss do so with an embrace, and the more vehement the mutual love is, the tighter that embrace.
<margin>Tobit 7. 2. 7.</margin>
Raguel the Uncle, seeing the younger Tobit, says to his wife amidst joys: *How like the young man is to Tobit my cousin.* And when he knew it was the same man, he could not contain himself, but falling upon his shoulders *he leaped up, and kissed him, and wept, and blessed him.* Men of the first age were accustomed to greet one another not with empty ceremonies, as has badly become prevalent today. Joyfully they embraced each other; and they kissed more frequently. Joined as if by their chests, they clung to one another, and each received the other with his whole bosom. From this meeting and, as it were, entanglement of chests, it happened that one is designated by the other, as things which cohere by a sisterly bond, and

<column-break/>

have consented into a mutual pact, so that no divorce is to be made between them. From this mutual obligation, I should believe it happened that that phrase *Kiss the Son* <note>original: "נשקו בר" (Nashku-bar) from Psalm 2:12</note> was translated as *Lay hold of instruction* <note>original: "δράξασθε παιδείας"</note>.

For it sometimes pleased the translators not to stick to the words, but to take that sense which seemed to them to be within the words. Those rituals, therefore, from which the speech was taken, the Greeks wished to declare, and as much as was in them, to explain more clearly. The Latin followed the Greeks, as he translates everywhere: *Apprehend discipline.* Both from an elegant comparison, if it be rightly explained as it ought. Let that be compared:

But what of *paideia* (instruction)? Indeed, I can guess rather than assert that *paida* (child/son) was read, because *pais* often denotes a son. But let us remember the desires and loves of the bride, when impatient of delay, with a sighing soul she says: *Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,* and with the whole impulse of her heart. ### ESTHER III. 7.
-> He cast Pur <-
-> And he cast the lot. <-
-> *The lot was cast into the urn, which (in Hebrew) is called Pur.* <-

<margin>Divination by lots</margin>
A great and manifold use of Lots has prevailed at all times, which men used so that they might surely become more certain of things, and so that they might lean upon some hidden foundation in conducting affairs. In a doubtful matter, the Lot removed all doubt, and whatever matter came into doubt and dispute was immediately called a Lot, so that it might place the matter beyond doubt and dispute. The lot removed the hesitation of calling and election, and where it was doubted who rather or how one should be elected, the lot translated minds from hesitation to certainty. There was the lot-casting of provinces, the lot-casting of judges, the lot-casting of inheritances, and of many other things. There was the lot whose outcome the divine Power ruled. There was also where rashness and superstition prevailed, not reason, nor counsel. The chance of the lot is certain where the chance happens by divine judgment. Let us now cast lots, and first assign the permitted lots, following or executing that judgment in them which shall be for our benefit. Let the first be the urn of lots placed by God, into which the tokens were thrown, so that their judgment might be from the Lord.
<margin>Proverbs 16. 33.</margin>
The name of the Lot for the Hebrews is *Pur* <note>original: "פור"</note>,
<margin>Esther 9. 25.</margin>
borrowed from the Persians, from the root *pur* meaning to break, to crush, to abolish, because the lot breaks and abolishes
<margin>Proverbs 18. 18.</margin>
disputes, according to that saying of the Wise Man, or *Goral* <note>original: "גורל"</note>. Leviticus 16. 18. by which most often is signified the portion of a field which falls to someone by lot; hence the twelve portions into which the land of Canaan was divided according to the number of the tribes of Israel are everywhere called *Goralot*. Thus Judah says to Simeon:
<margin>Judges 1. 3.</margin>
*Come up with me into my lot* <note>original: "גורלי"</note>. For the Greeks, *kleros* is from *klan thein* (to break fate); whence *kleruchoi*,
<margin>p. 603.</margin>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>On Divination by Lots</margin>
...he rubs, more so with the right hand than the left, as one who is from the left. Thus, judgment is exercised through the casting of lots against Achan <margin>Joshua 7:18</margin>. Likewise, after the Canaanite nations were extinguished and destroyed, Joshua divided the land of promise by lot. In this division made by lot, a singular proof of divine providence shines forth: for most of the tribes received those regions which the Patriarch Jacob, dying 250 years earlier, had prophesied would fall to each <margin>Genesis 49, throughout</margin>. Divine counsel guided the lot which was cast before the people gathered by tribes for the sake of designating a King <margin>1 Samuel 10:19</margin>. For when the Jews, in an unusual manner, demanded a King be given to them, it was not easy to provide a King from the mass of so many tribes without contention, envy, or tumult. While this immense care weighed upon the mind of Samuel, to whose judgment the matter was committed, it pleased divine providence to settle the matter by lot. To choose a head not of one or two, but of twelve tribes—this was the work, this was the labor <note>original: "hoc opus, hic labor erat," a reference to Virgil's Aeneid regarding the difficulty of a task</note>. Indeed, Samuel felt a huge business, not free from danger, being placed upon his shoulders, where he thought it necessary to rule the minds of this majestic multitude (which desired a single head) with a certain practiced skill. To avoid animosity, he pronounced nothing himself; he defined nothing by his own will or that of the nobles, nor did he bind himself to the vow of the common people. Lest he should seem moved by favor, and lest sedition should arise, the matter was permitted to the lots. The lots then designated Saul; if he had been elected without lots, the matter could not have lacked envy—to say nothing of sedition—for Saul was from the lowest tribe and an ignoble family. The mouths of all, which they might otherwise have set against Samuel, were stopped by a single toss of the die. Most aptly, therefore, Samuel used the casting of lots, by which he avoided the slanders of all and won over the voices of everyone, so that <margin>verse 24</margin> all, exulting, greeted the King. **"LONG LIVE THE KING,"** they shout with the acclamation customary among them. Martin Borrhaus, *Commentary*, column 354: He used the lot to avoid emulation and envy, as honors and royal splendor usually excite envy, especially among equals. For kingship is among those things which are sought after with the greatest contention by ambitious men. Therefore, nothing was more congruent with the desires of all than to collect the wishes of all through that visible lot exposed to their eyes; and thus the designation of the King was terminated with a happy conclusion <note>original: "faustâ coronide," literally a 'lucky flourish' or 'finishing touch'</note>, and by a very brief compendium, the fate and sum, so to speak, of the entire Israelite order was gathered. Nor does the taunt of certain wicked men stand in the way <margin>verse 27</margin>: "What? Shall this man protect us?" The history of Jonah is worthy of admiration; he wished to flee <term>evil</term> <note>Greek: kakon</note>, moved by the <term>wickedness</term> <note>Greek: kakotēti</note> of the Ninevites. Hence, struck by panic terror, he did not want to go to them and preach the word of the Lord there. While he proposed to avoid <term>wrongdoing</term> <note>Greek: kakourgias</note> and render himself safe and secure from danger by this flight, he himself became a <term>wrongdoing man</term> <note>Greek: kakourgos anēr</note>. While he labored to escape one danger of death, he fell into a double one and experienced what is in the proverb: <term>he brings toil upon toil, toil in the sea, toil in the whale, toil on the island</term> <note>Greek: ponō ponon pherei, ponon en pontō, ponon en kētēi, ponon en nēsō</note>. But when, in that greatness of danger, the fugitive tried to hide himself in the ship of Tarshish, a great storm having arisen, the men said to their colleagues: "Come and let us cast lots, that we may know why this evil is upon us." And they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah. Here God moderates the lots by a singular economy, so that both Jonah's trans-

<column-break/>

<margin>Divination by Lots</margin>
gression might be made manifest, and the superstition of the sailors might be corrected. For the sailors knew the nature of the sea—these are the words of Jerome <term>he examined</term> <note>Greek: exetase</note> page 124—and sailing for so long a time, they knew the patterns of storms and winds; and certainly, if they had seen the usual waves arise which they had sometimes experienced, they would perhaps never have sought the author of the shipwreck, nor desired to avoid a certain danger through an uncertain thing. Nor should we immediately trust in lots following this example, or join that testimony from the Acts of the Apostles to this one, since the privileges of individuals cannot make a common law. For just as the she-ass speaks for the condemnation of Balaam; and Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar learn future things in dreams for the judgment of themselves, yet they do not understand God the revealer. Caiaphas also prophesies unknowingly that it was expedient for one to die for all. So also here, the fugitive is caught by lot, not by the power of the lots—and especially not by the lots of the Heathens—but by the will of Him who ruled the uncertain lots. Rupert of Deutz has the same regarding this example of Jonah <margin>Book on Jonah, folio 7. b.</margin>. The sailors knew the nature of the sea, and sailing for so long a time they knew the patterns of storms and winds; and certainly if they had seen the usual waves arise which they had sometimes experienced, they would perhaps never have sought the author of the shipwreck, nor desired to avoid a certain danger through an uncertain thing. Nor should we immediately trust in lots following this example, or join that testimony from the Acts of the Apostles to this one, where Matthias is chosen for the Apostleship by lot, since the privileges of individuals cannot make a common law. And Francis Lambert on Jonah, folio 111. b.: Let us not think it happened otherwise than by God's counsel that lots were cast, and through them Jonah was caught. The Lord loved him and did not want him to perish badly; therefore He willed all these things to happen. He who is the regulator of lots indicated through them the truth of the matter they sought, not to favor their superstition, but so that what He willed to happen to Jonah might be fulfilled. Thus He also regulated the lots for Nebuchadnezzar to His own glory. Here GOD moderates the lots by a singular economy, so that Jonah's transgression might be revealed and the sailors' superstition corrected. Rudolf Gwalther <margin>Homily 3 on Jonah, p. 149</margin>: (It is credible that the Heathen men, who a little before had called upon various Gods, also acted somewhat superstitiously in the lots; whom God nevertheless directed, because it was necessary for Jonah to be caught; where we are warned in passing that superstitious arts are not excused, even if sometimes the truth of a matter becomes known through them. For as God warned Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar and many others through dreams about future things, accommodating Himself to their weakness, yet He forbids His own to trust in dreams. So sometimes He also grants this to soothsayers and diviners by a just judgment, that they may truly explain the outcomes of things or other matters about which they are asked.) Moreover, the use of the prophetic urn among the Ancients in conducting affairs was varied. Those who were chosen to perform duties in the state or to rule provinces were selected by the judgment of the prophetic urn. Regarding the Romans, Tacitus records that they used the lot for embassies, lest there be room for ambition or friendships <margin>Histories, Book 4, ch. 8</margin>. Those drawn by lot from the number of Praetors to preside over the public records, when the departure of votes was suspected <margin>Annals, Book 13, ch. 29</margin>. Provinces obtained by lot or by the sending of the Prince <margin>Annals, Book 2, ch. 43</margin>. Nor was the use of lots unknown to other nations. The Athenians, Argives, Syracusans, Thebans, and Sicilians used them.

# On Esther III. v. 2.

<margin>Divination by lot</margin>...while Liberty stood unharmed; and in Asia among the Lydians and Persians. The Phrygians fled to this benefit, as Justin testifies in **book** 11; when they were destitute of a King, they were taught by an oracle that they should appoint as leader the one whom they saw entering the temple of Jupiter with a wagon upon returning home. Thus they hailed <term>Gordius</term> <note>The famous King Gordias of the "Gordian Knot."</note>, a ox-driver, as King. And just as in choosing Kings and Magistrates, so in dividing kingdoms and inheritance, the use of casting lots was most frequent among the Ancients. They say that Noah, after the flood, according to Hebrew tradition, distributed the entire world among his grandsons by casting lots, and adjudged to each a certain part of the earth. From this, it seems, was born the Poets' fable concerning the partition of the world among the Gods; for they, lest they should settle a dispute by arms after the bad example of brotherly contention, submitted the inheritance of their father's wealth to the lot, which attributed the sky to Jupiter, the sea to Neptune, the underworld to Pluto, and the air to Aeolus. Pluto, bearing this outcome of the lot with a troubled mind, complains in
<margin>book 1, The Rape of Proserpine</margin>Claudian:
> ->I suffer the third loss of the supreme lot.<-
And Neptune, when Aeolus stirred up troubles for him in his own kingdom, rebukes him quite vehemently <term>in Virgil's</term> Aeneid, book 1:
> ->Not to him was the empire of the deep and the cruel trident,<-
> ->But to me given by lot.<-
Nor was marriage entered into among the more ancient peoples without the sending of lots. The Romans and Greeks
<margin>Aeneid 3.</margin> took wives by the casting of lots, whence Virgil says of Andromache:
> ->O happy alone before others, virgin daughter of Priam,<-
> ->At the enemy's tomb, beneath the high walls of Troy<-
> ->Ordered to die, who did not endure those lots.<-
Furthermore, almost nothing was once undertaken without the judgment of lots. The officials of equestrian contests assigned places to the chariots by lot, as Sophocles says in <term>Electra</term> v. 710:
->The appointed judges<-
->Shook the lots, and arranged the chariots.<-
Homer also mentions these in <term>Iliad book 23</term> v. 352:
->And they went to the chariots, and cast in the lots.<-
->Again Achilles shook them, and the lot of Antilochus,<-
->Son of Nestor, leaped out.<-
So too in military expeditions, the use of the prophetic urn prevailed. Vespasian explored by lots whether a happy outcome would come to him in the expedition with the Jews, as Savile notes in Tacitus **p.** 244. Concerning the Germans, Caesar in **book** 1 of the Gallic War left it written: When Caesar asked the German captives why Ariovistus did not contend in battle, this cause was given: That among the Germans it was the custom that the matrons of the family should declare by lots and divinations whether it was useful to engage in battle or not; they said it was not divine will for the Germans to conquer if they contended in battle before the new Moon. Let us consult Homer, as a singular treasury of all ancient erudition, concerning the use of lots in the expedition of the Greeks. He is chosen by lot who should go down into combat with Hector, and the lots
<margin>Iliad book 3 v. 314</margin> are cast not into an urn but into a helmet:
->Hector, son of Priam, and noble Odysseus<-
->First measured out the ground, and then<-
->Taking the lots, they shook them in the bronze helmet<-
->To see which of the two should first hurl his bronze spear.<-
And when eight leaders prepared themselves to meet with Hector, Ajax is designated by lot to fight with Hector, <term>Iliad book 7</term> v. 182-183:
->And the lot leaped out of the helmet, which they themselves wished for,<-
->That of Ajax.<-

<column-break/>

<margin>Divination by lot</margin>So also Ulysses committed to the judgment of lots when he turned aside to Circe, his companions being divided into two parts, of which one, touched by the lot, had to go to Circe, <term>Odyssey book 10</term> v. 206:
->And they quickly shook the lots in the bronze helmet,<-
->And the lot of great-hearted Eurylochus leaped out.<-
Thus Nebuchadnezzar, deliberating on a military expedition against the Jews and Ammonites, commits to casting lots which would have the desired end. He shall stand,
<margin>Ezekiel 21:21, 23</margin> says Jerome, <italic>at the very crossroads, and according to the ritual of his nation consult the oracle, so that he may put his arrows into a quiver, and mix them together, inscribed or marked with names, to see whose arrow comes out, and which city he ought first to conquer.</italic> This the <term>Greeks call belomancy <note>divination by arrows</note> or rhabdomancy <note>divination by rods</note></term>. But what this kind of divination was among the Babylonians, interpreters vary. Some think the Babylonians polished <italic>arrows</italic>, or the iron of the weapons, so that they shone, and in that brightness as if in a mirror the diviners learned, as they are accustomed to look into the shining nail of the thumb. Others translate: <italic>he threw the arrows</italic>, and made them fly in the air, to see in which direction they fell, so that he might direct the army toward it. Thus also the Chaldean Paraphrase translated. Piscator thinks knives are meant, which they used for cutting up the cattle to be sacrificed. Friedlieb has the following: It was the custom of the Kings of the Chaldeans that, when about to go out to war, they prepared arrows by the work of magical Astrologers, inscribed the names of cities and nations which they wished to invade, and then, these being mixed together by a blind taking of the hands, whichever arrow they seized, they would first attack the nation or city of that arrow. Thus he says. But when the Prophet hints that <italic>the divination is in his right hand toward Jerusalem</italic>, it is nothing else than that the divination warns him that he must set out by the road situated to the right, which leads to Jerusalem. Whence Junius says: the lots were cast into the urn with the right hand. But since two lots had been compared between themselves, concerning the siege of the Jerusalemites or of Rabbath, it is credible that the lots were drawn out with both hands, so that whichever casting was to the right, that was seen to be commanded by divine power. Concerning this ritual of casting lots, Henricus Salmuth has the following in <term>Pancirollus, chapter on the buckle</term>: <italic>If anything is to be done, they perform the casting of lots thus: As if we imagine that in the Senate the plan of war must be discussed, and it is not agreed among the Senators against which city's conquest the army should first be led (which happened in the times of Michael, 35th Duke of the Venetians), they consider that they must recur to divine lots. Indeed, the names of the cities to be conquered are cast into a small urn; some young boy mixes them with his hand; then he brings one of the papers, which each contain the names of individual cities, to the Princes, and from the attacking of that one the war must begin.</italic>

For the rest, the ancients employed various rituals in casting lots, almost all of which Edo Neuhusius reviews in book 2 of *Sacred Prophecies*. The most ancient
<margin>ch. 19 p. 531 seq.</margin> method of casting lots is to be sought from the ritual of the Ishmaelites in the division of the promised land. These, as the Jews tell, took as many sticks as the number of tribes, on each of which they inscribed the specific name of the tribe; and again, having taken as many sticks, they inscribed the portions. All of these, divided into two parts, they offered to Eleazar the High Priest, who with his right hand [took] the stick with the name of the tribe and with his left the stick...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Divination by lots</margin>
...grasping the staff designated by the name of the portion of land, he joined those two staves together, and thus gave to each tribe its own portion according to the lot. *Neuhusius* (in the place cited) believes that papers were used on which were written first the names of the Tribes, then the Families, and finally the individuals. In this same manner **Achan** <note>Joshua 7:16-18</note>, guilty of the accursed thing, was drawn out for punishment, and **Saul** was brought forward for the Kingship. Regarding the Gentiles, they maintained various rituals in the conduct of divinatory lots. **Tiphramanteia** <note>original: Τιφραμαντεία; divination by ashes</note> took its name from the fact that the matter to be decided by lot was chosen by writing with a hand or staff in ash; that which remained unharmed after being tested by the force of the winds was selected. **Botanomanteia** and **sycomanteia** <note>divination by herbs or fig leaves</note> occurred when the matter was inscribed on sage or fig leaves and the leaves were gathered as sacred. For the leaves were placed under the open sky, and since they could easily be scattered by the wind due to their lightness and mobility, those leaves that remained arranged and in order were believed to have the power of an oracle. **Ceromanteia** <note>divination by wax</note> was done by melting a piece of wax at a fire, with the liquefied drops falling into water placed beneath; from their shapes, a response was finally elicited. **Cleromanteia** <note>divination by lots/dice</note> was performed by tossing small tiles or dice. In the times of the Trojans, casting lots was done with pebbles or fragments of wood: some marked with a certain character, others indeed **unmarked** <note>original: ἀσήμοις</note>. These were placed confusedly into a single urn, shaken, and drawn out in order among the diviners. Hence those terms in **Homer**: *to signify, to shake, to leap the lot, to clash with the lot*, namely *in the bronze-fitted helmet* <note>original: ἐν κυνέῃ χαλκήρεϊ</note>, in the iron helmet of Agamemnon. For the ancients did not always use buckets and urns, especially in war and games, which were called **hydriae** <note>water-jars</note>, and into which the stones and lots were cast; the word **hydrion** is also used in this sense. These words of Isocrates in *Trapezeticus* are to be understood regarding this: *For who among you knows that last year he opened the water-jars and removed the judges placed there by the council?* and again: *water-jars sealed by the prytanes and the choregi.* The use of these was frequent in Athens, whence there is such frequent mention of them in *Aristophanes* and *Xenophon's Hellenica, Book 1.* Indeed, the use of pebbles marked with a certain sign to distinguish them from the **unmarked** ones prevailed among the Greeks and Romans; these were cast into the urn in a certain number, after first placing an olive leaf inscribed with the name of Mercury, whom they believed presided over lots. Therefore, those about to draw a lot first removed the olive leaf: afterward, each person took one; and with the drawing repeated in order, they took second and third ones. Finally, when all were drawn, according to how each person excelled in the number of marked pebbles, he either took up a Magistracy, entered into an inheritance, or obtained the prerogative of some other benefit.

<margin>Cicero, Against Verres 4. c. 2.</margin>
**Cicero** is to be understood regarding this ritual: *As many as had been announced, so many lots were cast into the water-jar: whose name came out, he would hold the Priesthood.* **Plutarch** in his *Life of Lycurgus* testifies that the Spartans used balls made of bran instead of pebbles: when these were cast into a certain vessel, they cast lots to determine which guests were to be invited to the festive banquets or omitted. **Peucer** deals more extensively with other types of lots in his book *On Divination, p. 403 ff.* Regarding **grammatomanteia** <note>divination by letters</note>, before we finish this discourse of ours on lots, we shall say a few more things. The letter **Z** was inauspicious in lots, especially hated by Appius Claudius, concerning which see *Erasmus in his Adages, p. 759.* So **$\Theta$** <note>Greek letter Theta</note> was a death-bearing 

<column-break/>

sign, and an unhappy mark of the throat, which when inscribed on a pebble signified **"to be put to death"** <note>original: θανατωτέον</note>, as **Martial** witnesses.

<margin>Divination by lots, Book 2. Epigram 15.</margin>
> You know the deadly sign of the Quaestor, Castricus;
> It is worth the effort to learn the new $\Theta$.

> And Persius, Satire 4:
> And you are able to prefix the black $\Theta$ to a vice.

So the sign for being hanged was the diphthong **$\alpha\iota$**, representing a noose wrapped around the neck. This is what **Ausonius** prays for against a spendthrift Pedagogue:

> Wretched Teacher, may it be so for you and your obscenity,
> And may the split $\alpha\iota$ mark your name.

For **Tully** (Cicero), **C.** was the mark of condemnation <note>for *Condemno*</note>, while **A.** was for absolution <note>for *Absolvo*</note>. So **T.** among the ancients was also an omen of a foul thing in lots, denoting the gallows and the cross, the image of which is rendered by one hanging from the "unhappy tree": from the beam where the noose hangs, the transverse portion of the Letter represents the line of the hanging man. **Plautus** seems to have understood this letter as an indicator of the gallows when, in *Aulularia Act 1, Scene 1*, he says that **Staphyla**, the old woman and maidservant of the miser **Euclion**, would die with her breath cut off and make "one long Letter of herself" when she tightened the noose around her neck. Compare *Erasmus, Adages, p. 729.*

<margin>Ezekiel 9:4</margin>
However, among the Hebrews, this was sometimes a mark of safety, where the foreheads of groaning men were ordered by **Ezekiel** to be marked to grant immunity from punishment; for some Interpreters, especially **Arias Montanus**, introduce the sign **$\tau$** <note>the letter Tau</note> in this place. Whence **Baronius**, speaking of the sign of the cross in his *Annals*, says, *let it be enough for the present to know that among the Jews, as well as among the Gentiles, the figure of the cross was a sign of safety.* But since neither can be truly said by them—for it is beyond controversy among Christians that it is the sign of salvation—he is rightly corrected by **Casaubon**; see his *Exercise 16 on the Ecclesiastical Annals of Baronius, chapter 78.* The recklessness of diviners had also extended to the distinction of days. **Haman**, that most sworn enemy of the Jewish name and nation, sought through divination a fatal day for the safety of the Jews, whence by his command a lot was cast into the urn, which in Hebrew is called **Pur** <note>Esther 3:7</note>. *Pur* is a Persian word and denotes a divinatory lot; it is explained in the book of **Esther** by the word **goral** <note>Hebrew: גורל</note>, perhaps in the Susian language; among the Arabs it is *fur*, and in **Josephus** you have *phrouraias* <note>original: ἡμέρας φρουραίας; days of protection/lots</note>. For **Haman** had explored (to use the words of *Schickhard on the Jewish Bacchanalia, p. 9*) through lots cast into an urn, which month of the year was more inauspicious for the Jews. Since he had planned to extinguish that most numerous nation, dispersed throughout all Asia, with an unheard-of and monstrous daring, all at once as if with one blow, and since he himself—a man devoted to superstitious arts according to the Persian custom—feared lest some propitious star for the Hebrews might elude his cruel efforts, he inquired by the **Geomantic art** which month was least favorable to the Jews. He found the last month, called **Adar**, which was solemnized by no festival or sanctified by peculiar rites. Then, inquiring also for the day by magically cast projectiles, he elicited the thirteenth. Therefore, he destined this day, chosen by lot, for the public slaughter of the **Israelites** throughout the entire Orient, whence the name **Purim** was given to it. You might say "the festival of lots" <note>original: κληρωτήρια</note>, which name remained for the feast, instituted in memory of the **liberation** of the Israelites by **Esther** and **Mordecai**, by the authority of the High Priest **Joachim**, as **Philo** records, to be celebrated on the 14th and 15th of the month of Adar, so that the first day was more holy...

### From Esther III. v. 2.

<margin>Divination</margin>
...be celebrated more holily and solemnly than the second, because in those days the Jews avenged themselves on their enemies, and mourning and sadness were turned into gladness and joy, as can be read more at length in the Book of Esther. Modern Jews begin this feast with the reading of the Scroll of Esther; when it is finished, the Reader adds this blessing: <note>Hebrew: "Blessed art Thou... regarding the reading of the Megillah"</note> *Blessed be God, etc., who has sanctified us and commanded us to read the Megillah* <note><term>Megillah</term> — The Hebrew word for "scroll," specifically referring to the Book of Esther.</note>, and <note>Hebrew: "Blessed art Thou... who performed miracles for our fathers in those days at this time"</note> *Blessed, etc., who performed miracles for our fathers in those days, at this time.* During the reading, as often as the name of Haman is uttered, they curse him in this manner: <note>Hebrew: "The name of the wicked shall rot"</note> *the name of the wicked shall rot*, a formula they take by analogy from <margin>Proverbs 10:7.</margin>. Furthermore, when Haman's name is mentioned, they strike the benches on which they sit with fists or hammers, as if they were striking the head of Haman. When they come to the reading of the slain sons of Haman, they finish it without pause or distinction, but in one breath and gasp, because they fable that all of Haman's sons were killed in a single moment. When the reading is finished, they vomit forth curses against Haman and Christians alike, which you may read in Buxtorf's *Jewish Synagogue, ch. 29, p. 557.* They then celebrate this feast with banquets and noble wine, and in it they truly celebrate a "Bacchanalia" <note>A reference to the Roman festival of Bacchus, implying wild or drunken revelry.</note>; at the same time, they send gifts to one another, namely food and drink—disciples to Teachers, Masters to servants, the greater to the lesser—all according to the custom of Mordecai and the Jews of his time. Nor do they forget the poor among them; rather, so that they too might worthily celebrate this feast according to their condition, the wealthier send them <note>Hebrew: "Mannot Purim"</note> *Purim portions*, that is, Purim coins, which among us amount to three half-thalers, which they call *Lulis*. Sometimes, Purim coins are distributed indifferently among the poor in the Synagogue, whether they be Jews or Christians, although if you look at the letter of the law, they should be given only to Jews. But to return to the history of Haman: let us learn from it to act cautiously with Princes, and not always to trust their countenance. Things which princes wish to be hidden, even if we know them well, let us pretend not to know; nor should we pry into their secrets more deeply than they themselves wish. In Haman we see on how slippery a step the fortune of the court stands, and how all the power of those who think they can achieve everything with Princes through evil arts is on a precipice. This is the cunning of Satan, which shines forth in the example of Haman: to occupy the minds of men with a superstitious anxiety for foreknowing the future through sorcery, through <term>coccinomancy</term> <note>Divination using grain or seeds.</note>, through <term>geomancy</term> <note>Divination by interpreting markings on the ground or earth.</note>, and other trifles, to which he gives the appearance and color of a natural method; but, although sometimes some natural cause may underlie it, he offers poison under the gold of nature. A pious mind ought to stay as far away from this as it can be drawn away from pious meditations by such great craft. That old deceiver knows how to color ancient games and constantly heap them with new additions. It is a cause for grief that there are those among Christians who, without any fear or (as they think) loss of piety, are accustomed to use sorceries or other harmful follies, especially during feast days. On the vigil of the Feast of the Nativity <note>Christmas Eve.</note>, superstitious acts are committed with the greatest temerity. Let the words of the Disciples' sermon on the Eleventh Time be heard on this evil matter:

> There are some, he says, who ought to be saddened that they spent that night in gaming,

<column-break/>

nor did they pay any service of devotion to the newborn boy; who lived in gluttony and drunkenness; who consume that most sacred time with their unfaithful <margin>Divination</margin> sorceries and other unbeliefs; who in these twelve following nights practice many vanities; who say that a Goddess, whom some call Diana, in the common tongue *the Lady Holda*, walks with her army; who place heaps of salt and through this predict the future; who throw shoes over their heads; who girdle trees; and significantly, those who practice their sorceries with the crumbs and fragments taken from the table on the vigil of the Nativity of Christ. All these walk today like blinded and cursed owls in such clear light of this day. Thus he spoke. See what Thomas Gataker has disputed concerning Lots in a singular and learned book, which he would have contributed to the literary Republic in another language than English, had it not already been published, which is unknown to me. Furthermore, regarding lots both licit and illicit, see Delrio *4. Disquisitions on Magic, ch. 2, question 7, p. 508*; Lavater *on Chronicles, p. 92*; Robortellus *fol. 37*; Souter *on Gamblers, p. 139*; Salmasius *on the Climacteric Year, p. 791, 792*; Serrarius *on Joshua, part 2, p. 115*; Chytraeus *on Joshua, p. 47*; Junius *Animadversions 2, p. 361*; Aretius *1. Problems, p. 810.*

# ESTHER VIII. 10.

->And he sent letters by the hand of couriers on horses, riders of swift steeds.<-
->And they sent the letters by means of book-bearers.<-
->*He sent letters, swift runners, riding on postal horses, royal runners, born to the post.*<-

<margin>Angari</margin> That decree published at Susa, written in the King's name and sealed with his ring—by which that bloody edict of Haman, in which he had demanded the Jews for death, was rescinded—King Ahasuerus (whom they contend is undoubtedly Xerxes, comparing the Book of Esther with the writings of the Pagans: Scaliger, Genebrardus, Drusius, and Junius) took care to send to the Jews and others for the safety of the Jews, by the hand of Royal Couriers (Hebrew: *be-yad ha-ratzim*), through "book-bearers" (Greek: *dia bibliophoron*). The French Interpreter represents the Hebrew idiom: *By the hand of the horse-couriers.*

Tremellius, who is a *most wonderful steward of languages and histories* according to Dilherr <margin>Dialogue 1, Philippians 27</margin>, explains in his notes on this place: By these two words (Royal Couriers) are defined the <term>Angari</term> <note>From the Persian 'angaros,' referring to a mounted courier in the royal postal system.</note> runners, such as were stationed at fixed places in Persia, as Herodotus testifies in Book 8. For first they are called Royal Runners, from their function; in Persian, *Aschertani*, or, as Suidas calls them, *Astandae* for *Achafchtandae*, which sounds like "Royal flyers." Secondly, they are called "Born to the Post," that is, from men who were held in the servitude of the *Angari* and *Parangari* <note>The secondary or auxiliary postal service.</note>, or the broad-running service, because that service was hereditary and endured in families. Thus he spoke. For the Kings of the Persians were accustomed to have couriers and messengers stationed at certain posts, so that one might hand over the mandates to the other, that they might be carried more swiftly. For they divided their journeys into <term>parasangs</term> <note>A Persian unit of distance, roughly 3.5 miles.</note>: therefore the couriers and carriers, as they reached each parasang, would rest, and commit their burdens to others going further to be transferred in turns; as Agathias teaches <margin>Book 2</margin>.

Herodotus in *Urania* speaks of the Persian *Angari* in this manner: *The first one running delivers the commands to the second, the second to the third*, and so on. Suidas, whom Tremellius added in his notes: *Angari: those who are letter-carriers by succession; the same are also called angari.* And elsewhere in the same words: *Astandae: those who are letter-carriers by succession; the same are also called Angari.*

<meta>This page continues the discussion of royal administration and military structures, specifically focusing on official messengers and elite royal bodyguards across various ancient cultures.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES.

<margin>Angari.</margin>
The names are Persian. Regarding what "successive transmission" <note>original: *ex diadochês*</note> signifies, see it explained by *Suidas*, and in *J. Meursius, Critical Exercises, part 2, p. 177.* Compare *Rader on Curtius, book 3, ch. 5, p. 30; Drusius 12, observation 19; Brodaeus 6, Miscellany 6.* This Persian word passed first into the Greek, then into the Latin idiom; hence the *angarian* run <note>original: *angareion dromêma*</note>, the swiftest course of horsemen. An *angarian* fire <note>original: *angaron pyr*</note> is found in *Aeschylus* \*, referring to messenger torches by which news was announced. The passage is: "And beacon sent beacon here from the messenger-fire" <note>original: *Phryktos de phrykton deur’ ap’ angarou pyros epempen*</note>; as *Suidas* and *Eustathius* correctly read; not as others, "of the Angel" <note>original: *Angelou*</note>. *Becmann* in *On the Origin of the Latin Language* thinks this word perhaps migrated from the Greeks to the Persians because the letters 'l' and 'r' are easily exchanged <note>original: *eumetablêtoi*</note>.
<margin>in Agamemnon.</margin>
<margin>p. 183. Hanover Edition. Year 19.</margin>
So also *angarian* mules <note>original: *angaroi hêmionoi*</note>, which they use for carrying bundles and loads, or (as *H. Stephens* maintains) the mules which those swift messengers used. They called the stations *angara*, the lodgings and inns where the *angari* turned aside after completing their day's task. *Munster* in his *Chaldean Lexicon* defines *Angaria* <note>Hebrew: אנגריא</note> as a dwelling or small lodging. *Aristotle* in the book *On the Universe, ch. 6*, where he speaks of the Persians, mentions "day-runners, scouts, and messenger-bearers" <note>original: *hêmerodromoi te kai skopoi kai Angelophoroi*</note>. From this also comes that verb *Angareuein* <note>to compel into service</note> in the New Testament, *Matthew 5:41 and 27:31*, where *Beza* retains the verb *Angario*. The word *Angaria* was used by *P. Nigidius* in *Aulus Gellius, book 19, ch. 14.* See the *Justinian Code, Title on Angaria and Parangaria*, where *Cujacius* should be read in the *Commentary*. See also the previously praised *Brodaeus, Miscellany book 6, ch. 6.*

For just as Kings and Princes had their "after-runners" <note>original: *metadromous*</note>, so they also had their "body-guards" <note>original: *sômatophylakas*</note>, the guardians of both body and head, who were formerly called *Latrones* <note>robbers/guards</note>, because they covered the side <note>Latin: *latus*</note>. *Latrones* were also soldiers hired for the same purpose, from *latreuô*, "I serve," because they served for pay, as in *Plautus's The Braggart Soldier*:
> Today I must lead my Parasite to Seleucus,
> So that he may lead the *Latrones* whom I hired from here to Seleucus,
> To guard his palace.

In the Persian army, ten thousand select soldiers were called the *Immortals* <note>original: *athanatoi*</note>, for the reason that if any of them diminished the number through death or disease, another was substituted: there were never more nor fewer than ten thousand. They were distinguished among all by their special dress and were the most excellent of all, as *Herodotus* \* writes. *Pausanias (p. 265)* and *Athenaeus (book 12, p. 210)* also mention them: "For it is recorded somewhere that there was a troop of immortal soldiers and apple-bearers, and even a troop of elephants." <note>original: *historeitai gar pê hôsper agêma stratiôtôn athanatôn kai mêlophorôn, eti kai agêma elephantôn*</note>. An *agêma* was a column of elephants, horses, and infantry that preceded the King. And *Aelius Dionysius* in *Eustathius* explains *agêma* as a cohort of select cavalry and heavy-armed soldiers. Let us compare those *Immortals* of the Persians with the *Soldurii* of the Gauls, who were "those who die together" <note>original: *synapothnêskontes*</note> according to *Athenaeus*. Among the Sotiani, a Gallic people, the custom had prevailed that the King had six hundred of the more prudent men around him, whom they called *Siloduri* in their native tongue. They lived with the King and, bound by a vow, died together with him if any accident took the King. The words of *Athenaeus* are \**: "These Kings have those who live and die with them, this being their vow: that if anything happens to him with whom they rule, they shall share the same fate and way of life, and die together by the same necessity, whether the King dies of disease, in war, or in any other way." Such *Soldurii* are described in *Julius Caesar* \*, and these are Caesar's words: "From another part of the town, Adcantuannus, who

Their condition is this: that they enjoy all the benefits of life together with those to whose friendship they have dedicated themselves. If anything happens to them by violence, they either endure the same fate together or inflict death upon themselves; nor in the memory of man has anyone yet been found who, when the one to whose friendship he had devoted himself was killed, refused to die." They were sometimes accustomed to devote themselves to accomplish some task, of which *Titus Livy* leaves us a memorable example, relating that the *Etruscans* at Lake *Vadimone*, with their army in extreme danger, chose men by a "sacred law," so constrained that man chose man, and thus one bound himself to another, so that unless he proved himself an outstanding man in battle, he devoted his head to the infernal fires.
