# From Esther VIII, v. 10.
### Page 403

<margin>The Royal Couriers <note>original: "Angari"</note></margin> When an act is done, the difference in the cause distinguishes it: and it appears to be true what is commonly said: *when two people do the same thing, it is not the same thing.* Here someone plucks my ear and whispers with a gentle murmur: that the most faithful guard of a Prince is his own innocence; that this inaccessible citadel, this impregnable bulwark, does not need a fortification, as Pliny says in his *Panegyric*. These things are true; if he could trust the faith of others as he feels he himself ought to be trusted by virtue of being the best Prince. But this cannot be hoped for: the morals of men cry out against it, and experiments have so often turned out to the contrary: the most humane, and I might almost say Princes better than Trajan, have scarcely escaped the wicked hands of conspirators. And how many are there who could affirm of themselves what the magnanimous Eberhard I, Duke of Württemberg, said not without pride? For when, in the assembly of the Empire held at Worms, other Princes extolled various precious things of their realms, he boasted magnificently of this one thing: that he could rest safely in the lap of any of his subjects. *Zincgref, German Apophthegms, p. 161*. Yet it is not fitting to say he was therefore liable to suspicion, as if he did not trust his citizens at all. Clearly unhappy are those who, distrusting the faith of everyone, live in perpetual fear: as is reported of Dionysius: who, besides not daring to entrust his neck to a barber, taught his daughters to shear him; he even surrounded his bedchamber with a wide ditch, just like a camp, <margin>Book 16.</margin> according to *Ammianus Marcellinus*. Domitian was equal to him, who, always fearful and anxious, was moved beyond measure by the slightest suspicions; he even lined the walls of the porticoes in which he was accustomed to walk with Phengite stone <note>A translucent decorative stone used like a mirror</note>: so that by its splendor he could see through the reflections whatever was happening behind his back. *Suetonius, ch. 15*. If these men even enlisted the strongest and most robust soldiers, they would surround themselves with that terror in vain, because they are not hedged in by the charity and goodwill of the citizens: and they cannot even look securely upon those very hands to which they commit themselves. Seneca, *Book 1 on Clemency*. A beneficial Prince will not labor in this way, but uniquely so that *neither guards nor surrounding weapons protect him as much as love does.* But in truth, because whoever excels in some splendor is burdensome in their present life, especially to their peers and others with whom <margin>Book 6.</margin> they live: Thucydides says *there is no prince whom a heavy reputation does not graze: Julius Capitolinus in Marcus Antoninus:* nor can it happen that a prince pleases everyone, and even one ruling most justly does not incur the hatred of many, *Dio, Book 55*, which ends in conspiracies: prudently, not only those who sought the Princedom by arms retained it by arms (as Pansa and Hirtus <margin>Book 2, ch. 57.</margin> *advised Caesar*), but even those who obtained power by succession and ruled most mildly had attendants and ax-bearers <note>Lictors or bodyguards</note>, on account of the envy of power (as Gregoras indicates in *Book 9, ch. 5*). The most pious King David (to say nothing of the Pagans) had guards, the Cherethites and Pelethites, whose prefect was Benaiah son of Jehoiada. *2 Samuel, ch. 8*. After his father’s death, Solomon provided for himself a bodyguard, and divided the army into twelve cohorts, and ordered each cohort to accompany him for 30 days. *Josephus, Book 7 of Antiquities, ch. 15*. What of it? That weapons and youths with swords and spears are not only for the protection of the body, but are a certain solemn ornament of Imperial majesty, and were formerly the chief signs of a Prince, as Justus Lipsius notes

<column-break/>

on the words of Tacitus's *Annals* book 6, *guards, arms, and the rest of the court*.
<margin>The Royal Couriers.</margin> Which Herodian confirms: All the imperial POMP followed him (Gordian), whatever soldiers were present, and city youths of tall stature, in the likeness of those who accompany the Emperor at Rome. To these can be added what Tacitus has concerning our ancestors *in his book on the Customs of the Germans, ch. 13*: There is great rivalry among the companions as to who holds the first place with their Prince, and among the princes as to who has the most numerous and fiercest companions. This is dignity, these are strengths: to be always surrounded by a large globe of select youths, an honor in peace, an ornament in war. Above all nations, this honor was held by the Germans, that they protected the lives of Emperors and Princes, as if by ARMS and FAITH before all mortals, Tacitus, *Annals 13, ch. 54*. However, whether it was well done that foreigners themselves, with the natives removed, were employed for this duty, is debated. Most deny it, and place it among the marks of a tyrant, with whom I do not agree.

> Oh that my words were now written! oh that they were printed in a book! <note>Hebrew: Mi yitten apho ve-yikatevu millai...</note>
> That they were graven with an iron pen and lead in the rock for ever! <note>Hebrew: Be-et barzel ve-opheret...</note>

> *Who will grant me, that they be plowed into a book? with an iron stylus or a sheet of lead: or carved with a Chisel <note>original: "Celte"</note> in flint.* <note>Latin: Quis mihi det...</note>

<margin>Chisel <note>Celte</note>.</margin> We all know that in ancient times letters were inscribed on rocks and bricks, bronze, gold and silver, wax, copper, lead and wood, with an iron or even a bone stylus; namely, so that a perpetual record of them might exist, nor any day erase the memory of those letters by oblivion. In writing monuments, before the use of ink began—of which there were formerly various preparations, according to Pliny <margin>Book 35, 6.</margin> *either from soot, burnt resin or pitch, and cinnabar*—letters were carved with an iron stylus into either wood or stones, the use of which writing Josephus the Indian <margin>Navigation, p. 145.</margin> mentions is still used in his time among the inhabitants of the city of Cranganore in East India: *They write in no other way than with an iron stylus in the books of trees <note>palm leaves or bark</note>.* From this, the sacred Writers take forms of speaking to signify an exact and firm understanding. Let it be permitted to linger here a little. Solomon orders the precepts of his wisdom to be described *upon the tablet of the heart*, Proverbs 3:3, 6:3, 22:20. The Septuagint in the last place has *apograpsai*, which may be rendered, *engrave and carve*. The force of that word is the same when speaking of types or images; and from this meaning Cicero calls his philosophical books the *apographa* <note>transcripts/copies</note> of the Greeks. Moreover, he takes the expression from the fact that it was the custom to plow and carve those things which were most dear to the heart into tablets or plates of gold and silver, so that they might be hung at the breast. We read *the sin of Judah is written with a stylus of iron and the point of a diamond*, <margin>Jeremiah 17:1.</margin> <note>Hebrew: Hattat Yehudah ketuvah be-et barzel...</note>. Just as in Zechariah 7:11, we read that the obstinate Jews *made their hearts as an adamant stone* <note>Hebrew: Shamir</note>, *lest they should hear the law*. And the words to Ezekiel ch. 3:9, *As an adamant* <note>Hebrew: Ke-shamir</note> *and as a flint I have made your face*, denote constancy and immobility of mind, which can be conquered by no threats or reproaches. For whatever is hard and firm is compared to adamant by the Romans, Greeks, and Hebrews; for adamant on account of its hardness can scarcely be worked, as Pliny is witness <margin>Book 37, ch. 4.</margin>, *for he says all other gems...*

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Celte <note>A technical term for a chisel or engraving tool.</note></margin>
...that gems are worked with adamant <note>original: "adamante"; likely referring to diamond or an extremely hard mineral like emery</note>, and in general, bodies that do not yield to iron are conquered by adamant. Therefore, it is held by the Hebrews to be called <term>Shamir</term> <note>Hebrew: שָׁמִיר</note> as if it were a "preservable stone" (according to Buxtorf, *Lexicon page 822*) and indomitable by iron. For such is its nature, says Jerome in *commentary on Amos chapter 7*, that while it is itself indomitable, it nevertheless tames all other bodies; it cannot be diminished by any file, but on the contrary, it wears the file away. For the same reason, it is called <term>Adamas</term> <note>Greek: ἀδάμας</note> by the Greeks, meaning "untameable"; which Becmann (in *Origins page 317*) playfully derived from the Hebrew <term>Dazma</term> <note>דזמא</note>. Indeed, the Arabs, sharing the same root, called the diamond <term>Diama</term> <note>דיאמא</note> from its durability, as it is the victor over iron and fire. Hence, it also seems to be called <term>Chalam</term> <note>חלם</note> by the Hebrews, from the root meaning *to crush*, because it breaks all stones; yet it cannot be broken itself. This was the persuasion based on the various origins of its names—more clever than true. For Garcia ab Horto, a Portuguese (in *Aromatics 1. 47*), affirms that the Diamond does not reject the blow of a hammer, nor is it broken only when soaked in goat's blood; rather, it can easily be shattered and ground with an iron pestle. (*Certus section 3, Calceolarius page 204*). Indeed, it can even be engraved; an exam-

Therefore, the material of the diamond would not be so inconvenient for scratching with an iron stylus due to its hardness. > I know that my Redeemer lives,
> and on the last day I shall rise again from the earth.

In those words of Job, Jacques Bolduc of Paris seeks an elegant ladder consisting of four steps, thus: *Who will grant me that my speeches be committed to writing by some private and singular man, lest such useful doctrine perish entirely? But also, who will grant me that a notary or scribe, performing the public office of reducing history to order, might digest this history of mine and all the speeches I have uttered until now—especially those I am about to bring forth from Divine secrets—into a public instrument? Indeed, so profound and deep are these mysteries, and so profitable for posterity, that they ought to be inscribed with an iron stylus not merely on the common material of scribes, such as paper, or on parchments, or on tablets which can easily be gnawed away or consumed by age or erased; but on durable and perennial material, namely on lead plates (as is usually done for things contributing much to the public good and posterity); and even deeply engraved with a chisel into marble, flint, and other hardest materials, lest they perish in any way by age or the injury of time.* But we leave this ladder in its place, and we judge more solidly what Diego de Zúñiga of Salamanca advises in this passage: *In this place,* he says, *I think it should by no means be overlooked with what liberality and munificence God meets Saint Job in his vows and wishes. He himself wishes that his words be written in flint or a lead plate, lest any be ever erased by oblivion: but it was provided by God in a far better way. For after the ages of so many centuries, they have been celebrated by such frequent use of the whole Church, that the memory of them is most fresh, and the posterity of all ages will not be unmindful of his words.*

The material, which they claim Job called <term>Opheret</term> <note>Hebrew: עֹפֶרֶת; lead</note>, in which they used to write of old, was varied. We place engraving on stones at the forefront, which Josephus * testifies to be the most ancient, writing thus of the grandsons of Seth:

But lest their discoveries slip away from the knowledge of men...*

# Job XIX. 23. 24.

<margin>Celtes <note>Likely referring to a chisel or engraving tool.</note></margin> ...and they would perish before they could be thoroughly known; knowing that Adam had foretold a universal destruction of things, one by fire and the other by flood, they erected two columns and inscribed their discoveries upon both: so that, if it should happen that the brick one was destroyed by the flood, the stone one surviving would provide men with the means of learning and would display the inscriptions to be seen. For they say that the stone column dedicated by them still exists in our times in the land of Syria. The Holy God, the Creator of all things, chose the same material for recording the Ten Words <note>The Ten Commandments</note>, which he inscribed upon a "stony volume," as <margin>Book 1 of On the Government of God</margin> Salvianus calls it—that is, on stone tablets—and indeed with his own finger, *Exodus 24:12.* Nor is it any less clearly witnessed by Pliny that writing used to be done on lead, upon which even the work of Hesiod, titled *Works and Days*, was engraved, as Pausanias mentions in his *Description of Greece (Boeotia)*. Indeed, we read that this poem was so cherished by everyone that they set it before the youth to be learned by heart, transcribed in that manner in a leaden volume. In the previous century, Spain displayed leaden plates found by a singular stroke of fate on a certain mountain near Granada, which contained books written in the Latin language but in very ancient Arabic or Ethiopic characters; together with these, the bodies of the first Martyrs of Spain were found and offered for veneration. Whoever reads the sharp judgment of Blondel regarding these fabricated images (*Preface to the Apology against Chifflet, p. 46 ff.*) will marvel that there were men of great name who brought forth these wicked fictions as a hidden treasure of the Church. He aptly compares the example of the Annian Commentaries there, writing: *Why should we not decide that this very type of crime was committed by the Spaniards in the year 1588, to which Johannes Annius of Viterbo had knowingly and deliberately bound himself before the year 1500? For just as he, born to practice imposture upon his fellow citizens, had taken care to bury marbles inscribed with barbarian characters deep in the earth so that he might show them to the people of Viterbo when dug up again, and fascinate their minds with a fabulous appearance of antiquity, so certain Spaniards attempted to assert the antiquity of their Church by evil arts.* Of a similar disposition was *Alfonso Ceccarelli*, concerning whose various and nefarious tricks and impostures there exists a specific dissertation by Leone Allacci, appended to the fragments of Etruscan Antiquities—or rather fictions—which were examined professionally. Similarly, we say from Pliny that the ancients frequently wrote on <margin>Book 34, ch. 9</margin> bronze tablets. We read in the books of the Maccabees <margin>Book 1, ch. 8:22 & ch. 14:18</margin> that the words of the treaty struck between the Jews and the Romans were engraved on "bronze tablets" <note>original: "δέλτοις χαλκαῖς"</note> as a "memorial of peace and alliance" <note>original: "εἰς μνημόσυνον εἰρήνης καὶ συμμαχίας"</note>. Other monuments of treaties written in bronze are suggested by Cicero *Against Catiline*, Polybius *Book 3*, Dionysius of Halicarnassus *Book 3*, and Livy *Decade 4, Book 3 and Decade 1, Book 2*. The ancient laws of the Romans were engraved on oaken tablets, just as Dionysius mentions that by the order of Ancus Marcius, the commentaries of Numa concerning sacred rites were recorded. Dionysius of Halicarnassus *3, p. 178*: "He recorded them on tablets and set them forth in the forum for all who wished to look. There were no bronze pillars then, but both the laws and the descriptions of the sacred rites were carved on oaken boards." Under Servius Tullius, however, mention is made of a bronze column, a "bronze pillar" <note>original: "στήλης χαλκῆς"</note>, p. 230, in which public decrees were engraved. Laws engraved in bronze were displayed on tablets fixed in public,

<column-break/>

as Servius notes on those words of the Poet <margin>Celtes</margin>:
> He fixed the laws for a price, and refixed them. <note>A reference to Virgil's Aeneid regarding the changing of laws.</note>
And Tacitus: *They are now cut in bronze for the purpose of publishing the decrees of the people, fixed throughout the forums and temples.* For a law was first promulgated, then when it had been approved, it was engraved in bronze and stored in the treasury, and only then was it said to be "carried" <note>passed</note>; Ovid seems to have referred to this custom of engraving and preserving laws in *Metamorphoses Book 1*:
> — — — nor were the words remaining bound
> to the fixed bronze.
And Sophocles in *Trachiniae*:
> ...but I preserved it on bronze pillars,
> so that we might preserve the writing on a tablet. <note>original Greek: "στήλαις ἀλλ᾽ ἐσωζώμην χαλκῆς... ἐν δέλτῳ γραφήν"</note>
From this we have found that the Roman calendars were inscribed on bronze tablets by the care of Augustus. From the same bronze consisted the most famous Delphic Tablet, which was seen in the library dedicated to Minerva on the Palatine in Rome <margin>Macrobius, Book 1, Saturnalia 14</margin> in the time of Pliny, as Polydore Vergil reports from him. *Regarding the Laws of the XII Tables, it has been handed down to memory that they were engraved on bronze columns,* according to the testimony of <margin>Book 1, On the Discovery of Things, ch. 6</margin> Dionysius of Halicarnassus; Pomponius the Jurist teaches that these were also transcribed on ivory tablets and displayed before the rostra in Rome (*Law 1, Digest on the Origin of Law*). Thus Plato witnesses in *Critias p. 119* that laws were engraved in orichalcum <note>A golden-colored alloy, likely brass.</note>. Pignoria and Kircher have brought to light a very ancient bronze tablet carved with Egyptian hieroglyphic signs, illustrated with very learned notes. Gubbio still preserves in its palace nine bronze tablets in the Tuscan language with inverted Greek letter shapes; Baldus attempted to find the meaning of their use in a public writing; and Jan Gruter included it in his vast volume of most laborious Inscriptions, p. 142. Moreover, in the same work, we shall see illustrious examples of other monuments of lead, wood, stone, and others carved with a <margin>Celtes</margin> chisel. Furthermore, the ancients also wrote with golden letters, of which Sidonius Apollinaris is a witness in *Book 1*; and Dio relates this: *A decree made in honor of Caesar was inscribed as "silver pillars with golden letters"* <note>original: "ὡς στήλας ἀργυρᾶς χρυσοῖς γράμμασιν"</note>, *with golden letters on a silver pillar.* <margin>Book 44, p. 276 A</margin> And Seneca: *Let us not have silver into which an engraving of solid gold <margin>Epistle 5</margin> has descended.* For Trithemius is the authority regarding the Gauls <margin>Book 1, Short Annals of the Franks</margin> that they had public monuments of silver. Thus, a privilege given to the capital of the Vangiones <note>Worms, Germany</note> by the Emperor Frederick, inscribed on copper tablets, is seen fixed in the high church of Worms, a copy of which exists in Crusius *Annals of Swabia*. Regarding the "crated" <note>possibly wicker or framed</note> tablets of the ancients, one may see Salmasius *On Usury <margin>Salmasius, Höping, Püssel</margin> p. 421*, Höping *On Seals p. 67*, and Püssel *Adversaria 5, p. 40*. We would not wish to heap up the testimonies of the Ancients in a matter so well-worn. For what is it to heap these up? Except to labor so that the pages swell, and to fear lest the treatment be too brief. Truly, in a necessary matter, as Scaliger skillfully says, *not only is it useful to do this; but it is even negligence <margin>Epistle 90</margin> not to do it.* But to wish to prove a most common thing with testimonies is truly what the Greeks call "carrying wood to the forest" <note>original: "λύγον θῆκαι" - a Greek idiom similar to "carrying coals to Newcastle."</note>.

<margin>Celte.</margin>
...especially regarding the much-debated word *Celte* <note>original: "Celte" - a Latin term for a chisel</note>, which the Latin Translator of Job uses, and for which many Manuscripts have read *CERTE* <note>meaning "certainly"</note> in vain. For there is no doubt that the author of the Version wrote *Celte*; and those who substitute *certè* are certainly mistaken. The Lyon Bible published in the year 1522 correctly follows this reading, even though they placed *certe* in the margin. ### Job 31:26-27

<note>Hebrew text: "If I beheld the sun when it shined, or the moon walking in brightness; And my heart hath been secretly enticed, or my mouth hath kissed my hand."</note>

> Or do we not see the sun shining as it fails, and the moon waning?
> For it is not in their power, and if my heart was secretly deceived, or if placing my hand upon my mouth I kissed it,
<note>The author provides the Greek Septuagint version here.</note>

<margin>v. 26. If I saw the Sun when it shone, and the Moon walking clearly.</margin>
<margin>v. 27. and my heart rejoiced in secret, and I kissed my hand with my mouth.</margin>

<margin>Worship and adoration of the Sun.</margin>
<margin>Ovid, book 6 of the Metamorphoses.</margin>
Job, a man blameless and upright, and one who feared <term>GOD</term> (ch. 1, v. 1), a servant of <term>GOD</term> (ch. 42:7), professing his zeal and constancy in practicing humanity, piety, and various duties toward <term>GOD</term> and men—not without adding the gravest imprecations—also removes from himself every sin of superstition, idolatry, and violated Religion in seeing or enjoying [the lights of heaven]. He constantly detested in his soul all superstitious worship, especially of the celestial bodies, affirming that he never exhibited divine honors to the Sun or Moon by even the slightest gesture of the body. This was according to the custom of his age, which consisted in moving the hand to the mouth with the head bowed, and with a fearful murmur praying for peace and favor from these Lights. With the adoration of Baal (under whose name they say the Sun was worshipped) in 1 Kings 19:18, the kissing of hands is joined: "The knees which have not bowed

<column-break/>

themselves to Baal, and every mouth which has not kissed him." Or: "which has not adored him by kissing." Turnebus and Rainoldus think this is said in respect to an image or idol, which they were accustomed to kiss during prayers. Such also was the kiss in Hosea 13:2, where sacrifices are reproached which were made *with the kissing of Calves*; in the interpretation of which place our Greek Translator wanders astray with the phrase "for indeed" <note>original: "καὶ γὰρ"</note>. In divine worship, libations were made to the Gods for the sake of honor, a rite treated by J. L. de la Cerda *on Virgil* and Lælius Bisciola *Volume 1, book 7, ch. 14*. Since, therefore, the kiss or the act of kissing was a sign or adjunct of reverence and adoration, it happened that the thing signified took its name from this sign and was transferred to it. Thus, among the Hebrews, *kissing* is sometimes *adoration* itself, because the kissing of hands was a sign of subjection toward God. And so the Seventy <note>The Septuagint translators</note> interchange "to kiss" <note>original: "καταφιλεῖν"</note> with "to adore" <note>original: "προσκυνεῖν"</note> and vice versa, which Symmachus observed in this passage, just as we noticed in the said book of *Kings*. For where the Hebrew says: "and every mouth which has not kissed him," the Seventy rendered it, "every mouth which has not adored him." And much more clearly in *Hosea ch. 13, verse 2*, Aquila showed this exchange <note>original: "καταλλαγὴν"</note>; for while others of the Ancients had translated the Hebrew *nashaq* <note>original: "נשק"</note> there as "adoration," Aquila interpreted it as "kissing," where Jerome himself understands the kiss of the hand as a gesture of adoration. His words are: *Instead of what we translated as "adoring" according to Symmachus and Theodotion, Aquila interpreted it as "kissing" <note>original: "καταφιλοῦντες"</note>; that is, kissing repeatedly. Those who adore are accustomed to kiss their hand, which Job denies he did, saying: "If I kissed my hand, applying it to my mouth."* And in his commentary on Ezekiel, page 403: *Job says that among his other virtues he also had this: that never, while looking at the sky, did he kiss his hand—that is, he never adored creatures.* So in *Psalm 2, verse 12*, "Kiss the Son" <note>original: "נשקו בר"</note> is rendered both as "Adore the son" and "Kiss the son," i.e., by a kiss testify to your subjection. Aquila uses "kiss" <note>original: "καταφιλήσατε"</note>; Symmachus uses "adore" <note>original: "προσκυνήσατε"</note>; which could be called a kiss of piety, religion, or obedience. For there are various kisses—of piety, idolatry, benevolence, charity, subjection, reconciliation, and farewell—which Jacob Herrenschmidt treated in a special tract. For the kiss was a symbol of rendered obedience and compliance according to the solemn Hebrew mode of speaking, by which it is the same to *kiss the mouth of anyone* as to execute his precepts or commands, as in Genesis 41:40: *According to your mouth shall all the people be kissed* <note>usually translated as "ruled"</note>. The Vulgate renders this excellently: *At the command of your mouth all the people shall obey.* And indeed, according to this meaning, that translation of the Seventy seems to have arisen: "Lay hold of the discipline of the Son," that is, hear him, worship him, and be disciplined to his commands (if I may use the word from the Vulgate). From this obedience, they allusively derive the reason for the word <term>ADORE</term>, as if it were what Apuleius says in *Apology 1*: *to move the hand to the lips for the sake of adoring.* Flacius says in his *Key to the Sacred Scriptures* that they derive the name <term>adore</term> from *ad* <note>to</note> and *ora* <note>mouth</note>, so that *adoration* is as it were an *inclination to the mouth*; so called from the associated gesture of Eastern peoples, who, when about to show honor to Superiors, inclined their mouths to their feet and knees, or...

# Job XXXI. 26.

<margin>
The worship and adoration of the Sun.
</margin>
...they moved their hands to their mouths. Similarly, Hugo Grotius in *Explanation of the Decalogue, p. 35*: "Just as among Oriental peoples, veneration was shown by various forms of bending the body; so among the Greeks, it was shown by moving the hand to [the mouth], which is properly <term>proskunein</term> <note>original: προσκυνεῖν; to worship or bow down</note>, from <term>kuo</term>, and thence <term>kuneo</term>, which is 'to kiss.'" Nor does the Latin <term>adorare</term> <note>to adore</note> signify anything else; it is not derived from <term>orare</term> (that is, to pray), as unlearned men think, but from the fact that the hand is moved to the mouth <note>Latin: *ad os*</note>. However, Vossius does not grant his assent to this etymology. * So that by these words—<term>nashaq</term> <note>Hebrew: נשק; to kiss</note>, <term>kataphilein</term> <note>Greek: καταφιλεῖν; to kiss affectionately</note>, and <term>adorare</term>—it is intended by their origin to refer to the most accepted custom of the East, and from there to the act of divine veneration and <term>proskynesis</term> <note>the act of prostrating or bowing</note>; just as by the same figure of speech the word <term>gonupetein</term> <note>Greek: γονυπετεῖν; to fall on one's knees</note> is taken for "to bless," and many others, about which, since the evidence of the facts is present, there is no need for more words. The sense, therefore, would be: *"If when I saw the Sun and the Moon, I adored them, namely by moving my hand to my mouth and bringing it back for a kiss, this would have been an iniquity to be punished by the Judges. For I would have denied the mighty God above (v. 28),"* with respect to the capital punishment brought against idolaters in Exodus ch. 22:20 and Deuteronomy 17:5, 6, 7. For whatever glory is attributed to gods is taken away from God. Just as the Holy Spirit, when He wishes to designate His legitimate worshippers, says they have not bowed their knees before Baal, nor given a kiss, as a sign of obedience and reverence; so also Job, when he wishes to remove the stain of idolatry from himself, says he has not kissed his hand in veneration of the luminaries. For, as Jerome observes against Rufinus, Book 1, those who adore are accustomed to kiss their hand and bow their heads, which the Blessed Job denies he did to the elements and idols.

<margin>
4. Inst. Orat 7.
</margin>
<margin>
Vol 4 op. f 763.
</margin>
Bede, *Exposition on Job*, Book 2, ch. 14: *"Not only," says Job, "was I not delighted by the worship of any idols, but not even by the beauty and appearance of these great lights, nor as if adoring them did I kiss my hand in their veneration; nor did I worship the creature instead of the Creator."* Rainoldus, Vol. 2, *Lectures on the books of the Apocalypse*, page 1559: *"It is to be observed that the Ancients were accustomed, when they worshipped images, to bow their knees to Baal, and incline the body, and testify their love and submission by various gestures: so also sometimes to kiss the images themselves. But when the Sun and Moon were worshipped, and other distant creatures, they moved the hand to the mouth and kissed the hand as a sign of love. Because, therefore, he moved his hand to his mouth, so that the hand seemed to offer a kiss to the mouth, Job says: 'If my hand has kissed my mouth,' that is, if even by an external gesture alone I signify that I follow those heavenly creatures with love and obedience: or if I have worshipped them as God and Creator, since God has forbidden anyone to offer such worship, to bow the knee, to kiss the hand, or do anything of that kind to those inanimate creatures."* See the rest, which he disputes learnedly and at length in this place. Among mute animals, Pliny records that the Elephant pays honor to the rising Sun, when he says in Book VIII, 1, that there is in them a religion of the Stars and a veneration of the Sun and Moon. Aelian, in *History of Animals* 7.44, recorded that this is done with the trunk extended toward the rays of the Sun in these words: <note>original Greek: Τὸν ἥλιον ἀνίσχοντα προσκυνοῦσι Ελέφαντες τὰς προβοσκίδας εὐθὺ τῆς ἀκτῖνος, ὡς χεῖρας, ἀνατείναντες</note> "Elephants worship the rising sun, stretching up their trunks like hands straight toward the ray." Hence Ptolemy Philopator warned that the Sun should be worshipped as a God, having been 

<column-break/>

also warned of this by a dream, lest he sacrifice so religious an animal. "Elephants indeed," (he exclaims) "worship the gods, but do men doubt whether there are gods, and if they exist, whether they care for us?" Let us leave him to enjoy his persuasion. Concerning the rite of kissing hands, Pliny says in Book 28, chapter 2: *"In adoring, we bring the right hand back to a kiss, and turn the whole body around."* Lucian, in the *Encomium of Demosthenes* near the end, says: "Having saluted the God, I will follow voluntarily; I hoped it would be so, when he moves his hand to his mouth <note>original Greek: τὴν χεῖρα τῷ στόματι προσαγαγόντα</note>, I supposed nothing else than that he was worshipping." Demosthenes mocks the gaping Antipater, for he, moving his hand to his mouth as if to salute the God, at the same time drank the poison and died on the spot. He mentions the same rite in *On the Dance*, p. 104, thus: "They worship the sun, not as we do, by kissing the hand." The same in *On Sacrifices*. Apuleius in Book 4 of *The Golden Ass*, p. 50, depicts the beauty of Psyche in these words: *"Many citizens and numerous strangers, whom the rumor of the extraordinary spectacle gathered in busy crowds, were stunned by admiration of her inaccessible beauty, and moving their right hands to their mouths, with the forefinger resting on the upright thumb, they worshipped her with religious adorations just as if she were the Goddess Venus herself."* Minucius Felix, whose elegant book is circulated as the eighth of Arnobius, page 7: "Caecilius, having noticed the statue of Serapis (as the superstitious common people are wont to do), moving his hand to his mouth, pressed a kiss with his lips." Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 16, p. 33: *"Most of you, in the affectation sometimes even of adoring heavenly things, move your lips toward the rising of the Sun."* From these places it is clear that this rite of the Orientals in adoring with a kiss spread to the Greeks, Romans, and other nations, who for the most part emulated the Orientals, and that the custom of kissing the hand in showing honor to men seems to be derived and propagated from that superstition of the ancients who worshipped the Gods with this rite, as Muretus writes.

Book 10. Various Readings, ch. 1.

Tacitus in *Annals* 16 and Suetonius in *Claudius* called this "venerating with the hand." Martial, however, called it "saluting with the hand," when he says in *Epigrams* 8.65. The Sun, which I finally note, is called by Job <term>Or</term> <note>Hebrew: אור</note>, that is, "light" par excellence, because it illuminates all things with its light more than the Moon or other stars; which becomes evident even from the opposition made in this place. Thus the Septuagint understood it as solar fire or light, translating it so. The same is proven by the Egyptian word <term>Or</term>, or *Horus*, by which the Sun is named; <term>Or</term> among the Hebrews is "to shine" and "to illuminate." From there comes the Chaldean <term>Orya</term>, light, and the Latin *aurora*, and *aura* for splendor. Also from <term>Cham</term> <note>Hebrew: חם; heat</note>, which for the Hebrews is the Sun, you might not wrongly derive the name *Horus*, who for the Egyptians was the same as Apollo or the Sun, as Diodorus Siculus (Book 1, p. 15) and Macrobius (*Saturnalia* 21) testify; and from the same Hebrew word is the name *Cyrus*. Horus, therefore, is the Sun, and what is written by the Greeks with an omega [Ω]; and those can be rejected here who, deceived by the affinity of names, determine that the office of the God Horus was in placing the just boundaries of things, as if it were from <term>horos</term> <note>Greek: ὅρος; boundary</note>.

The allusion of Plutarch comes closer, writing: "In Horus is the power that contains and nourishes all things, the seasons <note>Greek: ὥραι; horai</note> and the temperament of the air." The Sun is called by Job (ch. 30:28) <term>Chammah</term> from <term>Cham</term>, heat, because the Sun is the source of heat; as Lucretius called fire "heat" by a metonymy of effect for cause. Elsewhere it is called <term>Shemesh</term> from its service, and <term>Cheres</term> from dryness.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The worship and adoration of the Sun.</margin>
Interpreters of the second class explain this metaleptically <note>a rhetorical figure where one word is substituted for another through a chain of associations</note>, as if *kissing the hand* were the same as the habit of hypocrites who commend, celebrate, and magnify their own work. That is to say, when Job denies that his hand was at his mouth for a kiss, he intended to signify that he never felt so arrogantly about his own virtues or works that his hand kissed his mouth—as if whatever help or ability he possessed, he had accomplished by himself, and had placed his hope and trust in himself because of his virtues. Flacius writes in his *Key to the Scriptures*, page 1075:
> *If my hand has kissed my mouth, stands for: if I have magnified my own works too much, and placed my trust in them.*

Whether Saint Job intended this, not a few doubt. Therefore, in such matters, we take nothing upon ourselves, nor do we wish to be the "Palaemons" <note>a reference to Remmius Palaemon, an arrogant Roman grammarian; meaning an ultimate, self-appointed judge</note> of the great Interpreters. However, let it be permitted to add that the former opinion concerning adoration, which explains the words literally, seems to have more favor in its camp, since among religious acts used in the worship of the Gods, the *Kissing of Hands* was not the least. But why this kissing of hands in sacred rites? <margin>Notes on Laertius.</margin> Isaac Casaubon asserts that it pertained to a certain veneration of silence, so that by their hand they might, as it were, impose silence upon their own mouth; they also placed the statues of their Gods in shrines accompanied by silence, because they thought the deeds of those gods, which for the most part were abominable, ought to be covered in silence, as Diego Covarruvias noted in book 2 of his *Emblems*, page 666. We think it truer that since worshipers often kissed the hands, feet, knees, mouths, and eyes of idols, when they feared to touch the Gods or Princes with a profane mouth, they did it from a distance by stretching out the hand and immediately bringing it back to the mouth. Truly, these are symbols of worship, and nothing is more frequent than to place the thing itself before the eyes through symbolic speech. The showing of the right hand was a symbol of a covenant and also of faith. How many phrases have been coined from this? Thus, the kissing of the right hand was a sign of worship. They prayed to the deities while touching their own right hand, and with the hand extended—as the sole pledge of their worship—they made a show of giving worship to the gods. They kissed with the right hand when they prayed, according to Stewechius, page 373, and they embraced the altar (compare 1 Kings 2:28). They wander in darkness, and although they know the brightness of the sun in its substance (which is fiery and lucid), and recognize its impassibility in its nature (which remains perpetual and incorruptible), and perceive its subtlety in its ray (which penetrates glass without obstacle), and feel its agility in its motion (because in one day it runs from East to West), yet they are blind in the very light of the midday Sun—those who venerate the Sun by the kissing of the right hand, who worship the creature with contempt for the Creator, and who, by the sight of the Sun's beauty, are carried away into its worship, neglecting the maker of such great beauty, whom they are not concerned to know. We, having dismissed that vanity and that vain superstition of the Sun, wonder at and admire instead the omnipotence and wisdom of God the Creator, venerating the Sun of Justice <note>original: "Sol justitiæ," a common Christological title</note>, who spreads his rays everywhere and distributes the strength of his brightness to each according to their measure and capacity, unless perhaps he finds hearts so thick and swollen with the pride of arrogance that they cannot be penetrated due to the obstacles placed in the way. I understand

<column-break/>

<margin>The worship and adoration of the Sun. chapter 9, 1. 2.</margin>
the Messiah, whom Isaiah predicted as a most shining Sun that would illuminate Galilee, Zebulun, and Naphtali. Here Jerome notes that the Hebrews interpreted the earlier words of that prophecy as referring to a double captivity—one under Tiglath-Pileser, King of the Assyrians, the other under Shalmaneser—but the latter part as referring to the light of Christ, so that the sense is:
> *In the first time, two tribes, Naphtali and Zebulun, were taken by the Assyrians and led into a hostile land, and Galilee was deserted and relieved of the weight of sins which the inhabitants committed; in the later time, it was burdened by Shalmaneser; but this people, who were led into captivity and who sat in darkness, are the first to see the great light of Christ.*

Among the wonderful works of God, the great light created by God on the fourth day is rightly placed, so that it may serve all living things with its light and rays; whence Philippus the Presbyter says in his commentary on Job, chapter 26, page 105:
> *We read in the beginning of Genesis that on the fourth day the Stars were placed by God in the firmament, and from then on we see the globes of the glittering stars, and the heat adorned by its unceasing course and the order of its shining disposition.*

Therefore, blessed Job says that the Spirit of God adorned these heavens with the wonderful beauty of lights. David also speaks not only of the beauty and grace of the heavens, but also of their power, saying: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the Spirit of his mouth." What David called the "power" of the heavens, Job called their "ornament," just as a fiery power exists in their grace and beauty, because by their light and heat the darkness of night and the rigor of cold are tempered. <margin>Through chapter 38, page 176.</margin> Thus, regarding the words of the same Job, *by what way is the light scattered, and the heat divided upon the earth*, Philippus the Presbyter continues:
> *Who among mortals can properly know what the path of the sun is, or with what ordered course it acts in the right climate of the heaven, scattering light upon the lands? Or how the heat is divided through the changes of the seasons or through the locations of all regions? So that it burns more in one place at the same time, while in another it is felt with tempered heat.*

A man who is occupied in the knowledge of the Sun of Justice, who lifts his eyes to his rays, and who kisses his right hand in his worship, is of as much preciousness in the eyes of God as the Sun is in the eyes of others. For a man to be admired for piety and virtues is of such exalted magnitude that there is nothing in heaven, and nothing under the sun so precious, that it surpasses the nature of virtue; and the virtuous Writer of sacred sentences declares this in these words: <margin>Ecclesiasticus 50:6, 7, 8, 9.</margin>
> *As the morning star in the midst of a cloud, and as the moon at the full; v. 7. as the Sun shining upon the temple of the Most High, and as the rainbow giving light in the bright clouds. v. 8. As the flower of roses in the spring of the year, and as lilies by the rivers of waters; as the branch of the frankincense tree in the time of summer. v. 9. As fire and incense in the censer. v. 10. As a vessel of beaten gold, set with all manner of precious stones. v. 11. As a fair olive tree budding forth fruit, and as a cypress tree which groweth up to the clouds.*

Nothing precious in the heavens, nothing on the earth, nothing under the earth is left out to which a holy Man may not be compared, to demonstrate that the just man is more precious than heaven and earth. A righteous and pious Man encompasses every value, every grace of human affairs. If you wish to take a comparison from the stars, he is like the morning star, graceful with the splendor of piety, watchful and awake before dawn for divine praises. More complete...

# Job XXXI. 20.

<margin>The worship and adoration of the Sun.</margin> ...more [radiant] than the full Moon; adorned with a circle of all virtues; drenching not bodies but minds with the light of doctrine like a more splendid Sun; more beautiful than a Rainbow, promising better hopes by his very sight; more fragrant than flowers and lilies by the fame of his holiness; more redolent than incense, refreshing others by his example; more glowing than fire by the heat of his charity; more precious than gold and gems by the ornament of great merits; greener and more fruitful than the olive tree in holy works; taller and more enduring than the cypress by the peak of highest contemplation and the perseverance of virtue.

### Job XXXVII. 7.

-> He seals the hand of every man, that all men may know His work. <-
<note>original Hebrew: בְּיַד־כָּל־אָדָם יַחְתּוֹם לָדַעַת כָּל־אַנְשֵׁי מַעֲשֵׂהוּ</note>
-> He seals the hand of every man, so that every man <-
-> may know his own weakness. <-
<note>original Greek: ἐν χειρὶ παντὸς ἀνθρώπου κατασφραγίζει, ἵνα γνῷ πᾶς ἄνθρωπος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀσθένειαν</note>
-> *He who places a sign in the hand of all men, so that* <-
-> *each individual might know their own works.* <-
<note>Latin translation of the above verses</note>

<margin><term>Chiromancy</term> for divination.</margin> By many signs, says Cicero, nature declares what she wants, what she seeks, and what she desires. Indeed, although man may be a <term>microcosm</term> <note>Greek: μικρόκοσμος; "a little world"</note>; small in name, he is nonetheless great and immense in estimation. Nor should it be thought that the Parent of Nature, who encompassed all the perfections of the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>the universe</note> in the microcosm as if in a summary, made anything in vain within man, the Lord of all created things. You commit yourself to an immense sea and undertake a task more than Herculean if you attempt to examine the most miraculous body of man, which is the seat of divinity and the most perfect exemplar of all miracles. For you will find as many miracles in one man as there are limbs. If you investigate the nature and character of a tender child, so many signs encounter you that you are scarcely equal to the burden and might succumb. Various are the signs from which the nature and character of a tender child can be perceived, and he who rejects each and every one of them is ignorant of the laws of nature and is injurious toward Nature, that kind mother. Nor do I think it entirely vain to conjecture character from <term>physiognomy</term> <note>the art of judging character from facial features</note>, such as from the shape, disposition, and habit of the face and the rest of the body, just as Aulus Gellius <gloss>*</gloss> testifies Pythagoras was accustomed to do. Concerning this <margin><gloss>*</gloss> Attic Nights, Book 1, ch. 9.</margin> method of conjecture, several philosophers have written entire treatises, some of whom attribute more to the signs implanted by nature than is fitting, while others discourse upon them at least with probability. For to attribute a certain necessity to this matter is altogether impious and frivolous; yet much was attributed in antiquity, both within and without the boundaries of the Church, to physiognomic signs and principles. For Aristotle wrote a specific book on Physiognomy. Polemon also, and Adamantinus the Sophist, handed down precepts concerning this art comprised of use and observations, and Hippocrates in Book 2 of *Epidemics* deals with this matter in many scattered places. For example: whoever are red-haired, with a sharp nose and small eyes, are bad; whoever are red-haired, flat-nosed, with large eyes, are good; and again, those who are large, bald, stammering, and endowed with a slender voice, are good; again, those with a large head, small eyes, and who stammer, are wrathful. And again, eyes that do not blink indicate the wrathful; and again, a large head, black and large eyes, having a thick and low nose, indicate the good. Nor today are these things neglected or esteemed lightly, insofar as they remain within the barriers of natural affections

<column-break/>

of the soul and the constitutions of the body, and <margin><term>Chiromancy</term> for divination.</margin> do not transcend their own hemisphere. For Physiognomy is a part of natural science or physics—physics, I say, to which it is subordinate rather than to Mathematics, except on account of principles taken from there, namely lines, figures, triangles, etc., which the <term>Chiromancer</term> <note>one who reads palms</note> considers alongside physical affection. It belongs to natural science while it considers the members of the human body: the face, eyes, nose, lips, ears, back, hands, and feet; hence, on account of the <term>study</term> <note>Greek: μελέτην</note> of the face it is called <term>Metoposcopia</term> <note>forehead reading</note>, because it conjectures certain things primarily from the face of a man; and on account of <term>Hand-management</term> <note>Greek: Χειρονομίαν</note>, because it observes the constitution of the hands, it is called <term>Chiromancy</term>. Indeed, even the son of Sirach praises Physiognomy <margin>ch. 13, v. 23.</margin> <gloss>*</gloss> saying: *A good face is the footprint of a good heart.* From the face, therefore, one can in a certain way judge the internal qualities of the soul. Natural affections arise from the mixture of seed and blood from which a man is conceived, which marks the habit of the soul; from these, one is usually able to conjecture probably about the temperament and consequently about the morals of the soul. Firmly, says Pompeius, Professor at Wittenberg, in his *Chirology*: *we judge concerning natural things following the vegetative soul, but not concerning animal things.* Regarding the marks of the face, judgment is brought, firstly, from similarity with other living creatures; for example, those with small eyes are esteemed *timid*, like monkeys and hares; those with large eyes, *stupid*, like oxen and donkeys; those who are very black are *timid*, like Ethiopians; those who are very pale are also *timid*, like women. So it is written of the companions of David in exile, that they were most robust men, their faces like the face of a Lion (1 Chronicles 12:8). From their faces, therefore, the fortitude of their soul was judged, such as is usually in Lions, whose ferocity the face itself shows. Then from the eyes, which are as it were the windows and indicators of the heart, the affection betrays itself with the first passions of the soul, whence Solomon <margin>Ecclesiastes 8:1.</margin> <gloss>*</gloss> writes: *The wisdom of a man shines in his countenance.* And again, Proverbs 17:24: *Wisdom shines in the face of the prudent, but the eyes of fools are in the ends of the earth.* Slightly downcast eyes mark a *modest* man; unmoving eyes, an *impudent* and *wrathful* one; frequently blinking eyes, a *pompous* or *insane* one; looking askance, a *deceitful* man and a *scoffer*; attentive eyes, a *deceitful* one (Proverbs 16:30). Winking eyes mark the same (Ecclesiasticus 27:25, Proverbs 10:10); the lifting up of the eyes marks a *proud* man (Proverbs 21:4). Therefore God reckons haughty eyes among abominable things (Proverbs 6:16-17). God has impressed similar marks also on other parts of the face and members of the human body, from which it is permitted to seek judgment *probably* concerning the temperament and morals of men—I said "probably" and "in a certain way," because bad temperaments and vices of nature can be averted, corrected, and changed through pious invocation to God, study, and diligent habituation, so that the mild may be made from the fierce, and the gentle from the wrathful. We have an illustrious example of this in Socrates, who, after he had been judged by the physiognomist Zopyrus from his bodily habit and face and openly pronounced a luxurious and lustful man because he did not have concave jugulars, and that he was slow and stupid, his disciples—to whom the incredible temperance of their teacher was known—partly [mocked]...

It cites various classical and biblical authorities to justify the study of the "microcosm" of the human body as a reflection of the soul.</summary>

...to those mocking the Physiognomist, he immediately restrained them and, supporting the physiognomist, replied: "He has divined the matter; I was all of these things, had I not corrected myself through the study of Philosophy and diligent practice." <note>This refers to a famous anecdote about Socrates, who agreed with a physiognomist's assessment that he was naturally inclined to vice, but had overcome it through reason.</note> Nor is it always and universally true that all those who possess a less comely bodily habit lack a good natural disposition. For often men of monstrous bodies are most gifted in genius, as is shown by the examples of Aesop and Ulysses; the former was of a plainly monstrous body, while the latter was somewhat deformed, just as Ovid <note>original: "Naso"</note> sings of him:
<margin>Book 2 of The Art of Love.</margin>
> Ulysses was not handsome, but he was eloquent.

Yet both were most wise, from which it is established how one must judge the pursuits or morals of men from the face by natural signs: namely, in such a way that to those natural marks are added those things which depend upon the human will, which frequently amend and change nature so much that no trace can ever be found of what those marks indicated. The same must be determined concerning the other part of Physiognomy, which they call **Chiromancy** <note>Palmistry</note>, which, if it contains itself within the barriers of natural causes, is rejected by no one of sound mind, nor are its predictions entirely disapproved. For it was not by chance, nor rashly, nor in vain that God placed lines in the hands, but for certain causes. For the lines and little mounds <note>original: "colliculi"</note> in the hands of men are indeed almost the same in appearance, but vary in their accidents. For they are either distinct, wide, deep, long, red, pale, or blackish, or bear some other color; or they are obscure, mutilated, small, interrupted, or dispersed into fibers more or less, which variety of accidents arises from the blood and the members to which they are subject. But the genuine cause of this thing is hidden from us, except that lines compacted into many channels, shortened, cut, intersected, thin, and split indicate a weakness of nature and a certain defect of the limbs, and consequently a shortness of life. If, however, they have a contrary path, they indicate firmer strength and a longer life. For a vivid and strong nature extends the lines further and makes them sufficiently manifest; but a weaker nature makes smaller and duller folds, due to a deficiency of either the matter or the **plastic power** <note>original: "$\pi\lambda\alpha\sigma\tau\iota\kappa\tilde{\eta}$" (plastikē) - the formative force in nature</note>, which for the same reason leaves some defect in the limbs themselves. Although the causes of this matter may be unknown to us, they nevertheless lie hidden in nature itself, and experience itself dictates them daily, so much so that the matter itself is the less to be doubted, even if we cannot point out sufficiently firm reasons, but at least we may conjecture probably from the marks and signs of the hand. For the human hand is the **organ of organs**; just as the face renders a probable conjecture or **estimation** <note>original: "$\sigma\tau\text{o}\chi\text{a}\sigma\mu\text{ò}\nu$" (stochasmon)</note> concerning the intellectual virtues, so the hand does concerning the active virtues. The hand relates to reason as an instrument relates to art, because just as reason is the art before all arts, so the hand is the organ before all organs. Therefore, says Vallesius <note>Francisco Vallés, a 16th-century Spanish physician</note>, nothing in man can equally indicate those things which pertain chiefly to reason as the hand; which, if it is quite large and described with many lines, and neither entirely smooth nor hairy, and consists of long fingers that are easily drawn together, denotes wisdom and good morals. But if it is shorter than is right, round, with short fingers, too smooth or very hairy, or having curved and long nails, distinguished by no lines or very few, 

<column-break/>

<margin>
Divinatory
Palmistry.
</margin>
it tastes of something bestial, and signifies a man who is rustic and servile, with unpolished morals: hands always contracted denote a timid and greedy man; but extended ones, a bold and liberal man. Thus much concerning the temperament and constitution of the body, and consequently concerning the shortness and length of life, may and can be probably conjectured from these external signs, provided that this **estimation** <note>original: "$\sigma\tau\text{o}\chi\text{a}\sigma\mu\text{ò}\varsigma$"</note> remains within the fences of natural causes and does not leap over them. To this is added that Aristotle and others gathered only probably concerning the constitution of the body from these signs, and proved their predictions more from use and observation of events than from art, and that for this reason: because Chiromancy consists only of probable precepts, not **demonstrative** <note>original: "apodicticis"</note> ones, and hence its reasons, which nevertheless hold the greatest part, are of no greater or better weight. For this reason, Cocles the Chiromancer <note>Bartolommeo della Rocca, known as Cocles</note> determined that a future Chiromancer has need, besides the precepts of the art, of a peculiar power of nature, which if one did not bring to the art, he would bestow his labor in vain on doctrine alone. And thus far we have discussed the true and legitimate use of Chiromancy. But since all disciplines and all things (though best in use) are changed in the progress of time, they are sometimes entirely overturned through abuse. Let the divine knowledge of the stars be an example for us, which is so depraved and corrupted by some that it is no longer called Astronomy, but **Astrology, Necromancy, and Geomancy**—these are the words of Johann Rudolf Lavater in his *Philosophical Disquisitions* <note>original: "disquis. Philosoph."</note>—and is expressed by many other new terms, invented because of the novelty of the thing. The same can be said specifically regarding the abuse of Chiromancy, from which, by a vain effort, they seek infallible oracles concerning a man's fortune, morals, pursuits, way of life, marriage, and finally diseases and the type or manner of death. For that reason, they place certain planets over the individual mounds of the hands, and from those imprinted characters they pronounce those things which are of the nature of the planets: to the mound of the thumb some attribute Mars, others Venus; under the index finger Jupiter, under the middle finger Saturn, under the ring finger the Sun, under the little finger Venus, others place Mercury; and they dedicate the tubercle of the hand to the Moon, but without any natural cause. Thus teach Andreas Tricassius, Bartolommeo Cocles, Johannes ab Indagine, Jean Taisnier, David Frölich, and others. We know indeed that certain and most important organs of man are ascribed to certain lines, such as the heart, which is the principle of the **vital spirits**; hence arises the **life line**, which if I find broken, I conjecture a short and less healthy life. The brain, which is the principle of the **animal spirits**; from there arises the **cephalic line** <note>head line</note>, which explains the nature of the brain. The liver <note>original: "Epar"</note>, which is the organ of blood and the principle of the **natural spirit**; whence that line is called the **hepatic line** <note>liver line</note>, indicating the constitution of the stomach or liver. The kidneys <note>original: "Renes"</note>, which are the principle of those things which complete the integrity of natural functions—that is, from them is the appetite for generation; hence comes the **renal line**, the **table line**, the **vesical line**, the **generative** or **spermatic line**, which speaks of the genital and vivifying nature, indeed of all those things which pertain to generation and conjugal works, etc. We are also not ignorant of the influences of heaven with the stars upon these lower things...

<summary>This page discusses the transition from physiognomy to chiromancy, arguing that while hand lines can naturally indicate physical health and temperament, their use for predicting fortune or planetary influence is a superstitious abuse of the science.</summary>

# Job XXXVII. 7.

<margin>
Divinatory Palmistry.
</margin>
But is it truly so, that for every mountain <note>likely a reference to the "mounts" or fleshy pads of the palm</note> in the hand of man a specific planet must be assigned? Or is it therefore permitted to judge apodictically <note>demonstrably or with absolute certainty</note> and infallibly concerning a man's fortune, life, and death from chiromantic signs and characters, as if the stars possessed an inevitable power over these lower realms, compelling and necessitating them? As if that which those signs indicate could not be changed and amended by a man's piety and habits? This is contrary to the mind and words of God the Creator, and against His will and direction; for it is He who wrote our days in His book before they existed, *Psalm 139:16*. Moreover, it can be said of no man that he has the days of his life written in his own hands <margin>chapter 31:16.</margin>, but that saying of the Psalmist remains true: *My times are in Your hands.* Hence, P. Winstrup in his *Epigrams, book 3, page 628*, writes to the Palmist:

> ->My fate and my health are not in my own hands:<-
> ->My fate and my health are in the hands of the Lord.<-

We therefore commend what *Moldenarius* writes in *book 2, chapter 9, page 136* regarding the method of proceeding in this art, when he says: *By the convenience of the offered inspection, before you look at the hand, first converse with the person whose hand is to be inspected; and in that conversation, attend most diligently to the face, the eyes, the color of the hair, the stature of the body, the quality of speech, the sound of the voice, and the agility or slowness of the body.* Furthermore, on page 140, section 7, he continues: *Before anything certain is announced, it must be signified that these indications carry no consequence of necessity; lest perhaps, if impending evils are indicated, one might lose heart, or upon learning of future happiness, one might "raise his crest" and become proud.* It should be noted that in a bad prognosis, the word "fear" or "dread" should be used, e.g., *it is to be feared that the wicked man shall be extinguished by a violent death.* Thus he speaks. Therefore, we praise rather than condemn the use of Palmistry when it remains within its own limits and contains itself within the principles of nature; we only condemn the excess of those who place all their effort, care, and labor into this one thing: to predict and divine the future outcome of events with certainty and infallibility from the inspection of hands and the consideration of lines, and who presume to prove this intention of theirs with the words of *Job 37:7.* Truly, they quite foolishly busy themselves defending their Palmistry from those words of *Job*, which has been brought down to us not without the dregs of Paganism. For if you inspect the Hebrew literature, you will find no argument there, as has been demonstrated by *Augustinus Steuchus, folio 256. b.*, *Tarnovius in Biblical Exercises, page 349* and following, and *Amama in Antibarbarus, book 3, page 679.* But they themselves appeal to the Hebrew text. For even if, they say, this saying is explained in various ways by ancient and modern theologians, and especially by the despisers of Palmistry, nevertheless, if we look back to the origin of the Holy Language—as I have consulted the most learned Hebrews on this matter, says *Goclenius in his book on Chirosophy, sections 15 and 16*—it cannot and should not be understood otherwise than as referring to the use and significance of the art of Palmistry. But in truth, if we look at the text and what precedes and follows it, not even a "grunt" <note>original: "ne gry quidem"; a Latin idiom meaning "not even a syllable" or "not the slightest bit"</note> is found from which we could gather that Palmistry is being discussed in this place. <margin>page 762 seq.</margin> *Dilherrus* persists in his *Academic Disputations, Volume 1*,

<column-break/>

Elihu continues in recounting the wonders of nature sustained and governed by God—especially meteorological effects—for the confirmation of God's wisdom, power, and justice, and to restrain the rashness of human audacity. The *Septuagint* <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated the words of Job thus: *He seals up the hand of every man, that every man may know his own weakness.* <note>original Greek: Ἐν χειρὶ παντὸς ἀνθρώπου κατασφραγίζει, ἵνα γνῷ πᾶς ἄνθρωπος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀσθένειαν</note> *Tremellius* translates verse 7: *He seals up the hand of every man, so that all may recognize His workers.* He adds to verse 6: *that is, by sending storms of this kind, He causes men to flee home from their work, where it is permitted for masters to review their works at leisure.* Verse 7: *that is, He prevents them from working, as if a seal were imposed.* A metaphor for the Hebrew: *The men of his work.* *Mercer:* *The violence [of the storm] shuts up every stone, so that man may not recognize all the men of his work.* He adds: *In the hand, He seals up the hand of every man*, that is, He shuts them up at home, forces them home, or so that they seek hiding places, so that they cannot do work in the field with their hand because of the rains and thunders. It should be understood as *molad* <note>Hebrew: birth/origin, here likely referring to a grammatical ellipsis</note> (something is to be understood), namely, so that he cannot go out, so that he may know all the men of his work, that is, those who do work for him in the field, or that he may know and visit his workers to see what they are doing in the field. This is the simple sense woven from the thread of the text. *Lavater:* *He shuts up every man in his hand, so that man may not recognize all the men of his work.* He adds: *When such fierce storms arise, men are forced against their will to keep themselves at home. Those who are outside look for hiding places or roofs to go under, or other covered places and receptacles under which they can be safe from the rain until it has passed. Nor can they go into their vineyards or fields to their workers and mercenaries; a thing which necessity sometimes demands: if anyone wants his workers to be vigorous and carry out the prescribed work. The mercenaries themselves, when a storm breaks, leave their work and flee here and there, wherever each one trusts he will be safe from the injury of the storm.* <margin>Divinatory Palmistry.</margin> *Vatablus:* *The violence shuts up every man, so that man may not recognize all the men of his work.* He adds: *By force (understand: the power of the rain) He seals every man, that is, He closes or shuts him up in his house (understand: God).* A teacher among the Hebrews says: *some also apply this to the rain, that it closes and prohibits every man from leaving his house, so that all men may know to take up work in the field.* "Lest he recognize," etc. That is, lest he recognize all his workers, that is, so that they cannot see what the men of their labor are doing. As if to say: God, by the abundance of rain, forces men to remain at home, so that they cannot go out to visit their workers. "To know": the word "not" is understood. We add a few things, continues *Dilherrus* in the place cited: (1) It is not unusual for the Hebrews to use "hand" (*yad*) for "place." See *Psalm 10:5*, where *Rabbi David* interprets "in his name" as "in their place." *Numbers 2:17*: *each shall set out in his place* <note>Hebrew: אל-ידו, literally "at his hand"</note>. Santes Pagninus under the word *yad* (hand): power, faculty, counsel, means, force, strength, potency, place, the hinge of a door, a part, a region, prophecy...

(3) For *ma'aseh* <note>Hebrew: מעשה, meaning "work" or "deed"</note>, such an ellipsis of the prefix *bet* <note>The Hebrew letter ב used as a preposition "in"</note> occurs in Exodus 19:12: *to all the border* instead of *at the border*; that is, take heed to yourselves that you do not go up. *Isaiah 58:13*: If you turn away your foot from the Sabbath, *doing* instead of *from doing*, that is, so that you do not do [your own pleasure]. <margin>p. 37.</margin>
: For the Father of the family, or the farmer working under the open sky in the fields, gardens, or vineyards, *Job 37:7*: He seals up the hand of every man <note>Hebrew: חתם, *chatam*</note>, so that he may recognize all the strengths of his work. This means: When God sends snow and rain from on high, as is clear from the preceding, He seals the hand of every Father of a family working under the open sky in the fields, gardens, and vineyards; that is, He prevents him so that he cannot proceed in the work he has begun, and as if a seal were imposed, He so shuts him in that he is forced to flee from his work to his home. From this it eventually happens that the Master of these peasants, servants, vine-dressers, gardeners, and mercenaries may recognize at home—namely by inquiring during the leisure time—how much each has labored in tilling the field, in planting the vineyard, or in executing the work; who has done his duty and who has not, and may either inflict punishment or return rewards according to their merits. Therefore, the Jesuit Christopher Castro errs, who in *Book 1 on the Prophets, chapter 20, page 20, column a*, used this saying to establish Palmistry. But while this exegesis of Job's words is not to the taste of the Palmists, they bring forward more arguments. They appeal to the Hebrews as the Librarians of the Old Testament, to whom "the oracles of God" were once entrusted (*Romans 2:2*), who explain this present passage <term>with one soul</term> <note>Greek: ὁμοψύχως, meaning unanimously</note> as being about Palmistry, according to the testimony of Buxtorf *in the Rabbinic Bible on Job*. But in this argument, a fallacy of the consequent is committed. For from the office of Librarian, you conclude too weakly to the true and genuine sense of some saying retained by the Librarian. The Hebrews still have the letter, but not the sense. How childishly they behave in explaining the sayings of Scripture we have said above on page 24; from which sayings I am pleased to repeat here at least the quip of Blessed Luther regarding the Rabbis: *That they are an animal without intellect.* But they seek another <term>refuge</term> <note>Greek: κρησφύγετον, a place of retreat</note> from the text of Job, namely that the literal sense and proper signification of a word is to be preferred by many leagues to the improper and secondary one. This is indeed so; one must stand by the proper acceptance and meaning of a word, which the words themselves give forth, as long as the <term>connection</term> <note>Greek: συνάφεια, the coherence or continuity</note> of the text requires it, and the preceding and following parts do not lead us, as if by the hand, to an improper meaning. As far as this passage of Job is concerned, neither the preceding nor the following parts favor the interpretation of Palmistry: For he had said in the preceding sixth verse that by God's command the rains and impetuous showers fall; in

the following eighth verse, he says that the beasts then enter into their coverts and dwell in dens. For what purpose and intention, I ask, would the intermediate seventh verse deal with Palmistry? Since the whole context stands on our side and signifies that men, just like beasts, seek safer and covered places when a storm comes on, we cannot yet divine that we have departed from the genuine meaning of the words which the connection of the text itself requires. Next, they call to the aid of their opinion other sayings of Scripture in which the phrase *to sign in the hand*, or something similar, occurs (*Exodus 13:9, Proverbs 3:16, 18:21, Psalm 39:6, 119:109, Isaiah 49:16*). But in truth, the patrons of Palmistry have the same vice in common with Aesop's wolf; for just as he repeated "SHEEP" at every letter of the alphabet, so whenever they find "to sign in the hand" and similar phrases, they quickly adapt it to their Palmistry project, not attending to what the Holy Spirit properly intended in those places. The Mosaic passage is plainly <term>irrelevant</term> <note>Greek: Ἀπροσδιόνυσον, literally "nothing to do with Dionysus," meaning off-topic</note>, since God is there dealing with a sign of a past event; but Palmistry is occupied with signs of future things. Furthermore, the text speaks only of the Jews, not of all men; yet signs and lines are in the hands of all men. In the remaining places, they commit the fallacy of the consequent. In the hand of God—that is, in Divine power—is our life absolutely and simply; therefore is it also in our hand? Finally, the new Palmists defend their opinion with the authorities of certain men; but if we must fight with authorities, the victory will be ours without further struggle. For that astrological Palmistry—which claims to predict certainly and infallibly from the inspection of hands health, sickness, misfortunes, journeys, marriages, Ecclesiastical and Political duties, offspring (and the sex and number of offspring), the multitude of brothers, sisters, wives, and husbands, losses of household property, damage to the goods of the body and fortune, wounds, favor among the great, diseases, the kind of death, homicides, incests, imprisonments, and whatever else will ever happen to a man—is disapproved of by all of sound mind, even by those who otherwise do not think so poorly of Palmistry. But whether you understand this as Physical or Mathematical, those who strive to prove it from Job and other Holy Scriptures are rightly said to be "washing a brick" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to labor in vain</note>, and are scarcely a farthing better than those who force Job, Moses, Aaron, Elijah, Enoch, David, Solomon, Daniel, Baruch, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, John the Baptist, all the Patriarchs and Prophets—and why not the Apostles too?—into the rank of Palmists and Magi. Concerning Moses, Luke is a witness <note>Acts 7:22</note> that he was *learned in all the wisdom and doctrine of the Egyptians*, where Clement of Alexandria *in the 1st Miscellany* understands the whole of Mathematics and Medicine. # Job XXXVII. 7.

<margin>
Divinatory Chiromancy.
</margin>
...had come into custom, there God raised up Moses, a man of the greatest learning <note>original Greek: πολυμαθεστατον (polymathēstaton)</note>, so that he might oppose superstitions using their own books, and as Strabo records, show that the Egyptians did not act rightly toward the divine with unworthy sacrifices and omens from the heavens <note>original Greek: θυσιαις αναξιαις και θοσημασι (thysiais anaxiais kai thosēmasi)</note>. He who asserts that he [Moses] was a Magician is injurious toward God himself. For such a predicate is not fitting for so holy a man; although it was otherwise good in itself, I judge that one must nevertheless abstain from it because of the evil reputation it holds today. Those who strive to prove Chiromancy <note>Palmistry or hand-reading</note> from the passage of Job 37 verse 7 achieve nothing; indeed, they are in vain, says Nicolaus Pompejus, Professor at Wittenberg, in *Chiromantia* Prolegomena canon 3. So also the Blessed Friedrich Balduin in book 3 of *Cases of Conscience*, chapter 6, concerning Divination, page 799, says: *Among Christians who devote effort to this art, they are accustomed to cite that passage of Job 37:7 for it. But this is nothing to the point. For the sense, according to the Hebrew truth, is: All men are in the hand of God, who are able to recognize His works and power from the storms. There is nothing here about signs and figures in the hands of men, which the Chiromancers observe.* We also bring to our side <margin>chapter 32 on Sacred Philosophy, page 241.</margin> Francisco Valles, who discusses the passage of Job thus: *Since we have accepted Chiromancy in good part; although those words of Job: "Who signs in the hand of all men, that individuals may know their works," may be interpreted chiromantically: yet another interpretation occurs to me, which is much more pleasing, namely, as Galen explains in the cited place: the hand was given to man as a rational and most wise animal. For it was equitable that to one possessing the art before all arts, that is, reason; should be given the organ before all organs, that is, the hands. Just as therefore the adze or saw makes the craftsman, and the mattock and sickle make the farmer remember his duty, so the hand reminds us of human duty. Therefore, even by gazing at his own hands, a man will recognize that he was born to exercise all arts, to adore God, to erect altars to God, to perform sacred rites, to write, and to teach all wisdom even to posterity: the Pythagoreans would say, to count, since the pebbles of the decimal numbers (which contain all numbers) are placed before the eyes in the fingers themselves. God therefore signed in the hand of all, that individuals might know their works, that is, what it behooves them to do, and for what they were born; surely he warns the ears that we were born to hear: the nostrils, to smell: the tongue, to taste: the eyes, to see. All these indeed are our works, but common with most creatures: but the Hand warns us of wisdom and divine worship, and reason, of counting, and of exercising all arts; which are the proper works of man.* To these we add Pineda, who in his *Commentary* on this place speaks thus: *Who closes the hand of all men, while he sends the showers, rains, snows, and thunders, of which there is discourse there, so that they may keep themselves at home as if on holiday, and recognize their own weakness. For "to sign" in Holy Scripture is sometimes taken for "to close," as in Daniel 12: "Close the word, and sign [seal] the book": and Deuteronomy 32: "stored up and signed [sealed] in my treasures," furthermore, "to sign in the hand" can be taken for "to sign the hand," that is, to close the hand, just as in Hosea chapter 4 it is said: "ask in the wood," for "ask the wood." According as all might know their works, the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint</note> have, "that every man may know his weakness."* M.
