# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Divinatory Chiromancy.</margin> ...practitioners do not yet agree among themselves in assigning the locations of the Planets, which is truly a sign that they are led in these assignments not by reason, but by mere <term>skhediasmois</term> <note>original: σχεδιασμοῖς; improvised or superficial sketches/conjectures</note> devoid of truth. Indeed, they cannot be led by reason, not even by a probable one, since it is impossible for the same location or mound in the hand to correspond to several planets that are <term>antikeimenois</term> <note>original: ἀντικειμένοις; opposed or contrary to one another</note>, because diverse and contrary things could be predicted from the same signs of the same location. For if one asks why they assign either Saturn, or Venus, or Mars to the thumb rather than any other wanderer <note>The term "erronem" refers to the planets, or "wandering stars."</note>, they either have no answer, or they bring forward nothing but ridiculous arguments, as Johannes Thaissner testifies in Book 2 of *Chiromancy*, chapter 1. Therefore, that Chiromancy must be vain which consists of contradictory principles and promises knowledge of things that are not supported by the principles of nature. We conclude, therefore, with the words of Father Caspar Schott, which appear in Book 8 of *The Physical Thaumaturge*, concerning Chiromantic, Astrological, and Physical Magic: <margin>p. 637 ff. ch. 3.</margin>

> *Astrological Chiromancy is therefore vain, (1) because it is held as such by wise men who weigh all matters with sincere judgment. (2) Because it is despised and held as a delusion by Agrippa, from whom one might have deservedly expected a judgment. (3) Because the Gypsies themselves, who practice it most of all for the sake of profit, have no faith in it; and many men in Rome confessed to me that those whom they call Gypsies there—who are nevertheless Catholics, live together in one street, and apply themselves to various arts and occasionally even to Chiromancy—have confessed this. (4) Because it is established by no reason, no certain and solid authority, and no firm experiments that certain planets are attributed to certain fingers and certain regions of the palm of the hand to preside over human diseases, characters, various accidents, business, journeys, and the like, or to announce various winds through various positions of lines and appearances of signs. For what reason could there be, or what experiment might show, that either Venus or Saturn presides over the thumb alone and its base, and not others? That they rule those alone and no others? Who has enclosed their empire within such narrow limits? The same must be said of other regions of the hand and other planets. Furthermore, what authority could persuade us of this, when Cardanus admits that the books attributed to the ancients are by no means theirs. (5) Even if reason, authority, and experience suggested that certain planets preside over certain fingers from locations on the hand, it is still not clear to chiromancers which ones they preside over, because, as we saw above, they disagree greatly with one another in the distribution of the planets. Nor do they disagree less in the meanings of the lines and signs, as is clear to those reading their writings. (6) The whole of Chiromancy under discussion relies on the doctrine of Astrologers, who attribute more to the stars than can or should be attributed, not without prejudice to human freedom; a doctrine which we shall show elsewhere to be vain. (7) If all who have such or such a line arranged in such or such a way in the hand must die a violent death—for example, if many thousands of men die in some battle, pierced by the sword, or struck by engines of war, or driven over precipices—all will have the said lines arranged in the same way; which nevertheless seems utterly incredible, since there are almost as many different arrangements of lines in hands as there are men: in their number, continuity, interruption, and entanglement,*

<column-break/>

<margin>Divinatory Chiromancy.</margin> *as anyone can recognize if he inspects the hands of many people. (8) If someone who has such or such signs must die by poison, for example, then the planet which works such an effect is not in the one who dies, but works in the other who is going to give the poison; but who would believe that the stars express in my hand what another person is going to do? Furthermore, either the other will offer the poison freely, or by necessity: to say the latter is not only false but impious and heretical; the former, however, can be predicted with certainty by no one except God alone, and to whom God has willed to reveal it. To believe that God has revealed this to the very babblers who practice Chiromancy is more than foolish. Deservedly, therefore, Astrological Chiromancy, no less than superstitious Astrology itself, is forbidden by the Church, as we shall see later, and therefore ought to be avoided by all right-thinking people.*

## Job XLII. v. 14.

-> Keren-happuch <-
-> <term>Keras Amaltheias</term> <note>original: Κέρας Ἀμαλθείας; The Horn of Amalthea or "Cornucopia"</note> <-
-> *Horn of Antimony.* <-

<margin>Horn of Antimony.</margin> The names of the Daughters of Job are recounted in this verse as follows: And he called the name of the first ימימה <gloss>Day</gloss>. The Vulgate, transcribing the proper name into a common noun, rendered it *Day*. And by the same fault, the Septuagint rendered it *Hemera* <note>Greek for "Day"</note>, I think, because Jemimah has an affinity with the Hebrew *Yom* <note>Day</note>. The name of the second was קציעה *Keziah*, and the name of the third was קרן הפוך; our ancient Translator rendered this *Horn of Antimony* <note>original: Cornu Stibii</note>, because *Keren* is a horn, and *Happuch* is *Stibium* <note>Antimony/Kohl</note>, a pigment with which women formerly used to paint their faces, whose world <note>i.e., their cosmetic kit</note> consisted, according to Ulpian, of mirrors, vessels, ointments, ointment jars, and similar things. There is an old tradition, found in Pliny Book 33, ch. 6, that *Stibium* served for beautifying and even for treating the eyes; and by an elegant etymology or rather allusion, it is so called by the Hebrews because the countenance and face are, as it were, "inverted" or changed by it, from the meaning of the verb *Haphak* <note>to turn/overturn</note>. The Septuagint translators in a similar way put down a Greek meaning, and one altogether inconsistent; namely, that one of the three daughters was called <term>Keras Amaltheias</term> <note>The Horn of Plenty</note>, an interpretation taken and adapted from custom and popular opinion, as being better known <term>eis parastasin tes eudaimonias</term> <note>original: εἰς παράστασιν τῆς εὐδαιμονίας; for the representation of prosperity</note>, as Olympiodorus noted on this passage: that is, to declare and represent the happiness of Saint Job, for whom God doubled all fortunes in his household affairs, giving him also most beautiful daughters, whose beauty is indicated in verse 15: namely, that they had no equals in beauty in that region. Whence the Chaldean, rendering the reason for these names, <term>eulogese</term> <note>original: εὐλόγησε; blessed/explained</note> that *Jemimah* was so called because she was precious like the day; *Keziah* because she was as precious as Cassia; and *Keren-happuch* because her face was abundant in splendor and beauty like an Emerald. Goropius Becanus, in *Hieroglyphics* book 13, called the stories about Amalthea and her origin "vain dreams." It is a strange <term>metamorphosis</term> <note>transformation</note> of *Keren-happuch* into the horn of Amalthea. No one who is a stranger to the literature of foreigners should follow this version: for it introduces the fictions of the gentiles, whose origin is here. There was once a tract of Libyan land...

# JOB. XLII. 14.

<margin>
The Horn of Antimony <note>original: "Cornu Stibii." This refers to the literal Hebrew name of Job's daughter, Keren-Happuch.</note>.
2. Library p. 116.
</margin>
It was exceedingly fertile in noble wines and other fruits, given as a gift to Amalthea, the daughter of Ammon, as Diodorus relates in the 3rd book of his *Library*, page 141. And Apollodorus says: *Amalthea was the daughter of Haemonius, who possessed a bull's horn. This horn, as Pherecydes says, had such power that it could provide food or drink, whatever one might wish for, in abundance and without effort* <note>translated from the Greek</note>. From this arose the poets' fables concerning the Horn of Amalthea; for fabulous antiquity invented Amalthea as the goat of Jupiter <note>Zeus</note>, by whom he was suckled after Rhea gave him secretly to Adrastea and Ida to be nourished. They say her horn abounded with a plenty of all things. It is also said that the adult Jupiter gave the other horn of this goat to the Nymphs as a reward for their service, after he had placed the goat among the stars; he added the faculty (in the affairs of the Aetolians) that whatever was desired by the one who held it, whether drink or food, would immediately be produced. Indeed, they say the shield of Jupiter was covered with the skin of the goat Amalthea, the shaking of which would stir up rains; concerning this shield forged by Vulcan for Jupiter, *see* Homer:

<margin>Iliad book 8, v. 310.</margin>
> — — And he held the aegis,
> Terrible, shaggy, and bright, which the smith
> Hephaestus gave to Zeus to carry for the terror of men, <note>translated from the Greek</note>

And Virgil in the 8th book of the *Aeneid* concerning the Arcadians, v. 353:

> (They believe they have seen Jupiter himself, when often his right hand
> Shook the darkening Aegis and summoned the storm-clouds.)

Servius explains in the same place that the *aegis* <note>Greek: αἰγίδα</note> is the skin of the goat Amalthea, by whom he was nourished. Hence Homer calls Jupiter *Aegiochos* <note>Greek: Αἰγίοχον</note>, the aegis-bearer, in *Odyssey* book 5, v. 103 and book 9, v. 275, not to mention Hesiod. For an explanation of the proverb, see Erasmus’s *Adages* regarding the Horn of Amalthea: which is similar to that of the "Celestial Goat" in Zenobius, *century 1, adage 26 and century 2, adage 48*, where you may consult Schott in his *Notes*, p. 7 and 39. Palaephatus, in his work *On Incredible Tales*, ch. 46, p. 156, handed down from some unknown mythologists that Hercules used to carry the Horn of Amalthea with him, by the benefit of which he obtained whatever he sought. But I think the Interpreters <note>the Septuagint translators</note> were looking toward the custom of speaking then prevalent in Greece, by which various names were bestowed upon the stars—most of which are defiled by some shameful fable. Because they had seen these names confirmed by long-standing use in the "decree of the Astrologers," they did not wish to overturn them, lest they offend against the established laws of time. Procopius

<margin>on Isaiah p. 206</margin>
says: *Through Orion he indicated the brightness of the stars. Otherwise, among the Hebrews, this star is called by a different name, but the translators rendered it according to the prevailing Greek custom. And in Job, the Scripture says: the Pleiades, the Evening Star, Arcturus, and the chambers of the south—again using the names as they are spoken by the Greeks.* Or as Agostino

<margin>on this passage f. 267.</margin>
Steucho says: *Why the Seventy <note>the Septuagint</note> said "Horn of Amalthea," I do not know. The Greeks teach what the horn of Amalthea is: the ancients called the abundance of goods the "Horn of Amalthea." They say Amalthea was the nurse of Jupiter, whom a goat suckled; Jupiter gave one horn of that goat to Amalthea, in which were contained all the good things anyone could wish for. But "Horn of Amalthea" is not in the Hebrew.* Let those who stubbornly defend the translation of the Seventy Interpreters take note. We cannot help but add from their version the passage in Job ch. 9, v. 9 concerning Orion, Arcturus, and the Hyades: whose specific names also do not seem to be present in the original sources;

<column-break/>

Nevertheless, they are read as translated by the presumption of the Vulgate translator, collected from knowledge of the books of the heathens, and sought from the most impure fables of men and beasts.

<margin>The Horn of Antimony.</margin>
*Who makes Arcturus and Orion and the Hyades, and the inner parts of the South. The LXX: He who makes the Pleiades, and the Evening Star, and Arcturus, and the chambers of the south.* The Interpreters, when the names of the stars had to be rendered, preferred to retain the very ancient Greek names (also accepted by the Latins) to which the age was accustomed, seeking names taken from fables about Gods and heroes. Since other words were not available, they thought it better to apply their own existing terms than to retain the Hebrew names. Moved by this reasoning, Jerome writes in *Amos*, p. 93: *When we hear of Arcturus and Orion, we ought not to follow the fables of the poets and the ridiculous and portentous lies with which they attempt to defame even the heavens. But the Hebrew names, which are called differently among them, have been translated into our language by the names of the fables of the heathens; for we cannot understand what is said except through those words which we have learned by use and absorbed through error.* The Hebrew text has:

-> He makes the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades, and the chambers of the south. <note>original Hebrew: עֹשֶׂה־עָשׁ כְּסִיל וְכִימָה וְחַדְרֵי תֵמָן</note> <-

I suspect here that Eucherius, who published *Difficult Questions on the Old and New Testament* and on Job, asks on page 257: *What does it mean that we read there Pleiades, Orion, or Arcturus, according to the custom of secular authors? He answers: Not that they are known by these names among the Hebrews, but so that the meaning of these constellations might be more manifest to us, the translator wished to call them by the names that heathen usage had devised.* So

<margin>Vol. 3, p. 61 from the book on the Priestly Vestments</margin>
Jerome also says: *Let the explanation not seem different to other nations. For if celestial things and the disposition of God are defamed by the names of idols, God's providence is not therefore to be denied—which runs, is carried, and rules all things by a certain law. For in Job we read of Arcturus and Orion, and Mazzaroth <note>Hebrew: מזלות</note>, that is, the Zodiac circle, and other stars: not because the names are the same among the Hebrews, but because we cannot understand what is said except through familiar words.* We shall go through the nomenclatures in a few words. Arcturus, Orion, and the Hyades are constellations in the heavens formed from various stars, marked with those fabulous names, as well as others, which the superstitious observation of the signs of heaven later provided as a cause for idolatry. They imagined Orion was begotten by three Gods—Jupiter, Neptune, and Mercury—in a manner that Ovid was ashamed to tell (let alone a Christian). If you wish to know the fable of Orion, you can seek it with little effort from the *Mythologies* of Palaephatus, ch. 5, p. 111. We only wish to observe a not unpleasant comparison of words. *Ayish* <note>Hebrew: עיש</note> is Arcturus or the Bear, if you wish to say a "gathering" or "collection" from Rabbi Levi, gathered like a wagon-load. That constellation, according to Ralbag <note>Rabbi Levi ben Gershom</note>, will be *an image in the spheres of the winds*. Hence *Ayish* is the "wagon" of seven gathered stars which are never separated, according to Aben-Ezra; they represent the form of a wagon and revolve in that manner. Thus we read that the Greeks called that star the *Wagon* <note>Greek: ἅμαξαν</note> in Homer:

<margin>Iliad book 18, v. 273.</margin>
> The Bear, which they also call by the name of the Wagon. <note>translated from the Greek</note>

To the Latins it is the "Wagon" <note>Plauftrum</note>, because it has a certain part...

<meta>This page continues a critique of divination, specifically focusing on the transition from the vanity of palmistry to the biblical interpretation of the names of Job’s daughters.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>
Divinatory Palmistry.
<note>original: "Chiromanteia divinatoria"</note>
</margin>
...designators do not yet agree among themselves in assigning the locations of the Planets, which is truly a sign that they are led not by reason, but by mere guesswork <note>original Greek: "στοχασμοῖς"</note> without any truth in the matter of these assignments. Indeed, they cannot be led by reason, not even once by a probable one, since it is impossible for the same location or "mount" in the hand to correspond to several planets, and indeed to planets that are opposites <note>original Greek: "ἀντικειμένοις"</note> to one another, because different and contrary things can be predicted from the same signs of the same location. For if it is asked why they assign either Saturn, or Venus, or Mars to the thumb rather than any other wandering star, they either have nothing to respond, or they bring forward nothing but ridiculous arguments, as Johannes Thaissner himself witnesses in *Palmistry, book 2, chapter 1.* Therefore, that Palmistry must be vain which consists of contradictory principles and promises knowledge of things that are not resting upon the principles of nature. We conclude, therefore, with the words of Father Caspar Schott, which appear in *book 8 of The Physical Miracle-Worker, concerning Palmistry, Astrological and Physical Magic:*

<margin>
p. 637 and following, chapter 3.
</margin>
> (1) *Because it is held as such by wise men who weigh any matter with sincere judgment.* (2) *Because it is despised and held as a delusion by Agrippa, from whom it rightly should have expected protection.* (3) *Because the Gypsies <note>original: "Zingari"</note> themselves, who practice it most of all for the sake of profit, have no faith in it; and many famous men in Rome from those they call Gypsies there—who are nevertheless Catholics, live together in one street, and practice various arts and occasionally even Palmistry—confessed this to me.* (4) *Because it is established by no reason, no certain and solid authority, and no firm experiments that certain planets are attributed to certain fingers and certain regions of the palm of the hand, to preside over human diseases, character, various accidents, business, journeys, and the like, and to announce various outcomes through various positions of lines and appearances of signs. For what reason can there be, or what experiment might show, that either Venus or Saturn presides over the thumb alone and its base, and not others? That they rule those alone and not others? Who has enclosed their empire within such narrow bounds? The same must be said of other regions of the hand and other planets. Furthermore, what authority could persuade us of this, since Cardano confesses that the books attributed to the ancients are by no means theirs?* (5) *Even if reason, authority, and experience suggested that certain planets preside over certain fingers from locations in the hand, it is still not clear to palmists which ones they preside over, because, as we saw above, they disagree greatly with one another in the distribution of the planets. They disagree no less in the meanings of the lines and signs, as is clear to those reading their writings.* (6) *The whole of Palmistry in question relies on the doctrine of Astrologers, who attribute more to the stars than can or should be attributed, not without prejudice to human freedom; we shall show elsewhere that this doctrine is indeed vain.* (7) *If everyone who has such and such a line arranged in such and such a way in the hand must die a violent death—for example, if many thousands of men die in some battle, pierced by the sword, or struck by engines of war, or driven over precipices—then they all had the said lines arranged in the same way; which nevertheless seems altogether incredible, since there are almost as many different arrangements of lines in hands as there are men—

<column-break/>

their number, continuity, interruption, and entanglement—as anyone can recognize if he inspects the hands of many.* (8) *If someone who has such and such signs must die by poison, for example, then the planet which works such an effect is not in the one who dies, but works in the other who is going to give the poison; but who would believe that the stars express in my hand what another person is going to do? Furthermore, the other will offer the poison either freely or by necessity: to say the latter is not only false but impious and heretical; the former, however, can be predicted with certainty by no one except God alone, and those to whom God has wished to reveal it; but to believe that God has revealed this to the very babblers who practice Palmistry is more than stupid.* Rightly, therefore, Astrological Palmistry, no less than superstitious Astrology itself, is forbidden by the Church, as we shall see later, and therefore ought to be avoided by all right-thinking people.

### Job 42:14.

->קֶרֶן הַפּוּךְ<-
<note>Hebrew: Keren-happuch</note>
->Κέρας Ἀμαλθείας.<-
<note>Greek: Keras Amaltheias (Horn of Amalthea/Plenty)</note>
->*Horn of Antimony.*<-
<note>original: "Cornu Stibii"</note>

<margin>
Horn of Antimony.
</margin>
**T**he names of the daughters of Job are recounted in this verse as follows: And he called the name of the first ימימה *Jemimah.* The Vulgate, transcribing the proper name into a common noun, rendered it *Day* <note>Latin: "Diem"</note>; and by the same error the Septuagint <note>LXX</note> rendered it *Day* <note>Greek: "ἡμέραν"</note>, I think, because Jemimah has a similarity with the Hebrew word for day, *Yom* <note>ימימה vs יום</note>. The name of the second was קציעה *Keziah,* and the name of the third was קֶרֶן הַפּוּךְ; our ancient Translator published this as *Horn of Antimony* <note>original: "Cornu Stibii"</note>, because *Keren* is a horn and *Puch* is *Antimony* <note>Stibium</note>, a dye with which women used to be painted and colored in the past, whose world <note>finery/toiletries</note> was contained, as Ulpian witnesses, in *mirrors, vessels, ointments, ointment jars,* and similar things. There is an old tradition, found in Pliny *book 33, chapter 6,* that *Antimony* was used for beautifying and even for treating the eyes; and by an elegant etymology or rather allusion, it is called so by the Hebrews because the look and face are, as it were, "inverted" and changed by it, from the meaning of the verb *Haphak* <note>הָפַךְ - to turn/overturn</note>. The Septuagint translators, in a similar way, put down a Greek meaning, and one that is altogether inconsistent; they say that one of the three daughters was called the *Horn of Amalthea* <note>The "Cornucopia" of Greek myth</note>, an interpretation taken and adapted from custom and common opinion, as if it were better known to them as a "representation of prosperity" <note>Greek: "παρασᾶσιν τῆς εὐδαιμονίας"</note>, as Olympiodorus noted on this passage; that is, to declare and represent the happiness of Saint Job, for whom **GOD** doubled all fortunes in his household affairs, giving him also most beautiful daughters, whose beauty is indicated in *verse 15*: namely, that they had no equals in beauty in that region. Whence the Chaldean <note>Targum</note>, rendering the reason for these names, explains: *Jemimah was so called because she was precious; Kezia, [because she was fragrant]; Keren-happuch, because she was abundant in splendor and beauty of face like an Emerald.* Goropius Becanus spoke vain dreams about Amalthea and where her origin was in *Hieroglyphics, book 13, pages 205, 208.* However, the transformation of *Keren-happuch* into the *Horn of Amalthea* is a marvel. No one would affect such a version who is a stranger to foreign literature: for it intends the fictions of the gentiles, whose origin is here. There was once a tract of Libyan land...

# Job XLII. 14.

<margin>Horn of Antimony.</margin>

page 141. And Apollodorus: <note>original Greek: Αμαλθεια ην Αιμονιου θυγατηρ...</note> *Amalthea was the daughter of Haemonius, who had a bull's horn. This horn, as Pherecydes says, has such power that it provides food or drink, whatever one might pray for, in abundance and without toil.* From this arose the poets' fables concerning the Horn of Amalthea; for fabulous antiquity invented Amalthea as the goat of Jupiter <note>Zeus</note>: by whom they say he was suckled after Rhea gave him to be nourished secretly from Adrastea and Ida. They say her horn abounded with a plenty of all things. It is also said that the adult Jupiter gave the other horn of this goat to the Nymphs as a reward for their service, when he placed the goat among the stars; he added to it the faculty (in the matter of the Aetolians) that whatever was desired by the one who held it, whether it be drink or food, would immediately be produced. Indeed, they say the shield of Jupiter was covered with the skin of the goat Amalthea, the shaking of which would stir up rains; concerning this shield forged for Jupiter by Vulcan,
<margin>Iliad 8. v. 310.</margin>

> —— and he held the tasseled aegis,
> terrible, shaggy, and bright; which the smith
> Hephaestus gave to Zeus to carry for the terror of men.

Servius explains in the same place that the *aegis* <note>Greek: αιγιδα</note> is the skin of the goat Amalthea, by whom he was nourished. Hence Homer calls Jupiter *aegis-bearing* <note>Greek: αιγιοχον</note> in *Odyssey book 5* v. 103 and *book 9* v. 275, to say nothing of Hesiod. For an explanation of the proverb, see Erasmus’s *Adages* regarding the Horn of Amalthea: which is similar to that of the "Celestial Goat" in Zenobius, century 1, ad. 26 and century 2, ad. 48, where you may consult Schott in his *Notes* p. 7 and 39. Palaephatus, in his work *On Incredible Tales* ch. 46, p. 156, added from I know not which mythographers that Hercules was accustomed to carry the Horn of Amalthea with him, by the benefit of which he obtained whatever he sought. But I think the Interpreters <note>The Septuagint translators</note> had respect for the custom of speaking then prevalent in Greece, by which various names were bestowed upon the stars, most of which are defiled by some shameful fable. Because they saw these names confirmed by the long passage of years in the "decree of the astrologers," they did not wish to overturn them, lest they offend against the established laws of the seasons. Procopius
<margin>on Isaiah p. 206.</margin>
says: *Through Orion he indicated the bright stars. Otherwise, these stars being named differently among the Hebrews, the translators rendered them according to the prevailing Greek custom. And in Job the scripture says: The Pleiades, the Evening Star, Arcturus, and the chambers of the south, again using the Greek names.* Or, as Agostino Steuco says, why the Seventy <note>The Septuagint</note> said "Horn of
<margin>on this place f. 267.</margin>
Amalthea," I do not know. The Greeks teach what the Horn of Amalthea is: that the ancients called an abundance of goods the "Horn of Amalthea." That Amalthea was the nurse of Jupiter, for whom she substituted a goat; Jupiter gave one horn of that goat to Amalthea, in which were contained all the good things one could wish for. But the "Horn of Amalthea" is not in the Hebrew. Let those who stubbornly defend the translation of the Seventy Interpreters take note. We cannot help but add from their version the passage in Job ch. 9 v. 9 concerning Orion, Arcturus, and the Hyades: whose specific names do not seem to be present in the original sources;

<column-break/>

<margin>Horn of Antimony.</margin>
Nevertheless, they are read as translated by the presumption of the Vulgate interpreter, gathered from knowledge of the books of the gentiles, and sought from the most impure fables of men and beasts. *Who makes Arcturus and Orion and the Hyades, and the inner parts of the South.* The Septuagint: *He who makes the Pleiades, and the evening star, and Arcturus, and the storehouses of the south.* The Interpreters, when the names of the stars had to be rendered by them, preferred to retain very ancient Greek names, also accepted by the Latins, to which the age was accustomed, seeking names from fables about dead Gods and heroes; for since other words were not available, they thought it better to apply their own which they had, rather than retain the Hebrew names. Moved by this reasoning, Jerome writes in *Amos* p. 93: *When we hear of Arcturus and Orion, we ought not to follow the fables of the poets and the ridiculous and portentous lies with which they attempt to defame even the heavens. But the Hebrew names, which are called otherwise among them, have been translated into our language by the names of the fables of the gentiles, because we cannot understand what is said except through those words which we have learned by use and drunk in through error.* The Hebrew text has:

-> He makes *Ash*, *Kesil*, and *Kimah*, and the chambers of the south. <-

Making *Hus* (or *Ash*), *Kesil*, *Chima*, and the inner rooms of the South. I admire here Eucherius, who published *Difficult Questions on the Old and New Testament* and on Job; he asks on page 257: *What does it mean that we read there, according to the custom of secular authors, Pleiades, Orion, or Arcturus?* He answers: *Not that they are known by these names among the Hebrews, but so that the significance of these stars might be more manifest to us, the translator wished to call them thus, as the usage of the gentiles had devised.* So also Jerome:

Arcturus, Orion, and the Hyades are constellations in the heavens formed from various stars, marked with those fabulous names, as well as others, for which the superstitious observation of the signs of heaven later provided a cause for idolatry. They imagined Orion was begotten by three Gods—Jupiter, Neptune, and Mercury—in a manner that Ovid was ashamed (let alone a Christian) to narrate. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Antimony Horn <note>original: "Cornu Stibii." Likely a reference to a specific star or constellation shape.</note></margin>
The "Horn of the Pole" <note>original: "Cornu temonis"</note> is called by the Germans *the Army Wagon* <note>original: "der Heerwagen"</note>; that is to say, the Chariot of Hermann. According to some, they retain this name because they believe those ancient Germans thought that Hermione, or Hermann—or even Arminius, that renowned and most brave hero of Germany, from whom the *Erminsul* <note>A sacred pillar-like object or idol of the Saxons.</note>, the idol of the Saxons, may have received its name—was deified after death and rests within this constellation. The Hebrew term *Kimah* <note>כימה - usually identified as the Pleiades</note> is explained as "the Pleiades" <note>original: "deiora"</note> by the Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> in Isaiah chapter 13, where Jerome (page 53) notes: "The Septuagint translated the Hebrew word *Kimah* as 'the Pleiades.' The Hebrew teacher whom I used interpreted it as *Arcturus*. We, following Symmachus in a general sense, have called them 'stars.'" And in Amos chapter 5 (page 92), Orion is called *Kesil* <note>כסיל</note> in Hebrew. Symmachus calls them simply "stars." Theodotio interpreted it as "the Evening Star." However, the Hebrew who instructed us in the Holy Scriptures thinks *Kesil* should be interpreted as "splendor" and signifies stars in general. It appears to us around autumn and is called by the peasants *Jacob’s Staff* <note>original: "der Jacobsstab"</note>. Orion was so named from the inconstancy and mutability of the weather and its shifting path. For *Kesil*, taken as a common noun, usually signifies someone inconstant or a fool. Forster (page 387) notes that the Targum <note>Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible</note> uses *Zikuka* for *Kimah*, from the word for "rushing," because it disturbs the sea and lands with varied storms and, as it were, uproots them from their deepest foundations—just as the Greek *orino* (to stir up) indicates the same. Or, as Sabinus (commenting on Ovid) prefers, it comes from *ourein* (to urinate/rain), because the rising and setting of this constellation stirs up storms; "Orion is harsh both when rising and setting," according to Aristotle. From which Virgil writes in the *Aeneid*, Book 4, line 52:

> While winter rages on the sea, and watery Orion.

And in Book 7, line 719:
> Where fierce wintry Orion is hidden in the waves.

And again:
> The cloud-bearing Orion of the waves.

For the rising and setting of this star was formidable to sailors because of the storms, hail, and tempests which, according to Pliny, come forth from the "horrid stars": Arcturus, Orion, and the Kids. Almost the same things occur in Virgil and in the Interpreter of Job, in the *Aeneid*, Book 3, line 516:
<margin>Book 18, chapter 28.</margin>

> He looks around at Arcturus, the rainy Hyades, and the twin Bears,
> and Orion armed with gold.

<margin>The same "sword" is mentioned near the end of Aeneid Book 1. See Disciol. Vol 2, Book 7, Ch 1.</margin>
There remain the Hyades; these stars Aratus correctly placed "in the forehead" <note>original: "en tō metōpō"</note> of the Bull; they are named from *hyein*, "to rain," because by their rising they stir up rains and heavy showers. Eucherius, in his *Spiritual Similitudes* (chapter 3, page 222), says: *The Hyades are named from the Greek letter U (upsilon), from whose shape they do not differ in appearance, and when risen they bring rains. For "hyetos" in Greek is called "imber" (shower) in Latin. Hence they call them "little torches" and "the moist ones," because at their rising and setting they usually bring many juices or rains.* Pliny observes this origin, for he says in Book 2, chapter 39, *the name of the "little pigs" <note>A common Latin folk-etymology for Hyades, "suculae," confusing it with "sus" (pig) rather than "succus" (moisture).</note> is rainy* and in Book 18, chapter 26, *cloudy.* And Ovid, in the 5th book of the *Fasti*, line 166, says:

> The face of the Bull shines radiant with seven flames,
> Which the Greek sailor calls the Hyades from the rain.

<margin>Book 4, Fasti, line 168.</margin>
The Pleiades, in Greek *Pleiades*, as if *Poleiades*, the "Seven Stars." Yet only six stars appear on the back of the bull. Ovid says:

> The Pleiades will begin to lighten their father's shoulders,

<column-break/>

<margin>Antimony Horn.</margin>
> Which are said to be seven, yet are usually six.

*Kimah* would have its name from the "gathering" <note>original: "synaxei"</note> and conjunction of those stars. For they are bunched together so that they occupy the smallest space. Whence Valerius Flaccus in Book 5 said *the globes of the Pleiades, and the clusterable star.* Their rising is the herald of summer and heat. *Kesil*, however, heralds the cold. Arcturus declares the name of the "rainy one." Francis Bacon, in Book 1 of *The Advancement of Learning* (page 25), explains the "Chambers of the South" as the Antarctic Pole, around which the stars are visible to those who live under the other pole, but hidden from us; therefore they are called "interior," as if concealed and remote from our eyes. See what they are in Fuller’s *Miscellanies*, Book 15.

->Psalm 50, verses 10, 11.<-

<note>Hebrew text: "For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle on a thousand hills. I know every bird of the mountains, and the moving things of the field are with me."</note>

<note>Greek Septuagint text: "For mine are all the beasts of the field, the cattle in the mountains, and the oxen. I have known all the birds of the sky, and the beauty of the field is with me."</note>

> For mine is every beast of the forest, and the animals on a thousand mountains.
> I know every winged creature of the mountains, and the wild beast of the field is with me.

Magnificent is the eulogy of the first historical man, Adam, for his exact <term>theriognosia</term> <note>The knowledge of the natures and characteristics of animals.</note>, in that he perceived the individual natures of animals from a mere glance at them and imposed names upon them that were fitting. The beasts approached the first man to receive names; these names were not haphazard, ignorant, or inept, but were most consistent with and accommodated to their very natures. This is confirmed partly by the nature of the Hebrew language itself, and partly—and most significantly—by the approval of the Supreme Creator. Adam, in his state of innocence, possessed exquisite knowledge according to the requirements of his status. He gave a most wise specimen of this knowledge, even in natural things, through his <term>onomathesia</term> <note>The act of naming or name-giving.</note>. By this, when all animals were brought to him—never having been seen before—he bestowed "harmonious" <note>original: "omophōna"</note> names upon them at first sight. Not even the fish were excluded, although no express mention is made of their approach to Adam.
<margin>Genesis 2:19, 20.</margin>
Hence Augustine, in Book 9, chapter 12 of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, when asking whether the names of fish were received from God or from the First-Formed man, responds: *It is by no means credible that in that same (Hebrew) language, the names of fish were instituted not by man but divinely, which man would later speak after God had spoken them; but it must be believed that as the kinds of fish were gradually known, names were imposed, etc.* And so God was the fabricator of the creatures, and Adam was their namer. God created the natures; Adam named them. Adam was the craftsman of names and words; God was the worker of things. God forms, but Adam names, and all the beasts are present at Adam's beck and call. Moses did not ascribe this obedience of the beasts to immediate divine power, nor to any ministry of Angels; rather, He who today gathers fish into the nets of fishermen and wild beasts into the snares of hunters, is the same who then exerted the secret force of His command over all living things.

# Psalm 50, verses 10–11.

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
For He bestowed [names] upon them and led them to offer obedience to man of their own accord. We have a certain trace of this in Noah, whom the cattle and birds followed voluntarily as he entered the Ark; yet none of the fish did so, inasmuch as the water of the universal flood did not extinguish them. Regarding this matter, let us hear Augustine in Book 1 of *The Wonders of Holy Scripture*,
<margin>Chapter 4.</margin>
reasoning thus: *The plague of that flood did not touch all things that can live in the waters; it brought death only to terrestrial animals. At this point, a question occurs to those searching shrewdly for a solution: Why do terrestrial animals succumb more to human punishment than aquatic ones, since they have no greater record of sins? Yet, in the sin of the first man, the earth from which he had tasted was immediately cursed: "Cursed is the ground in your work,"*
<margin>Cicero <note>The margin likely refers to a citation style or a specific edition of the text.</note></margin>
*etc. In this matter, it should be noted that the animals themselves, which ate from the cursed earth, could not be exempt from the curse, especially since the earth was cursed along with its animals. Therefore, another question arises: Why did God not also curse the waters in the curse of Adam? To which it is easily answered: because man did not drink water against the Lord's prohibition, but ate of the fruit of the earth. Beyond these reasons, God spared the waters from Adam's curse because He had prepared to wash away that curse through water—which was done in the flood, and is now granted through Baptism. For in water and the Spirit, all human crimes, both bodily and spiritual, are purged together. Aquatic creatures do not succumb to the punishment of the curse because they do not participate in the curse. And because of this, when the Lord had laid aside the curse of human death by rising again, He ate the flesh not of terrestrial but of aquatic animals, when, for the confirmation of the resurrection before the disciples, He ate a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb, etc.*

The reason why this assembly of living creatures gathered is clearly handed down by Moses: namely, so that along with the <term>giving of names</term> <note>original: ὀνομαθεσίᾳ (onomathesia)</note>, dominion over all things
<margin>Genesis 1:30.</margin>
might be handed over to man. Therefore, all animals approached Adam, and by that approach, they confessed their servitude. *This same man,* says Basil of Seleucia,
<margin>Oration 2, p. 11.</margin>
*by a secret signal of order, was carried toward all the animals, and they all flocked to Adam, acknowledging their slavery by their standing in line.* <note>original Greek: ἀποῤῥήτῳ τῆς τάξεως συνθήματι... "by an unutterable signal of arrangement..."</note> All living things approached and received names, venerating the Master by the name of their calling, recognizing under which Master they had been placed. Regarding this approach and the dominion of the first man over all creatures of heaven, earth, and water, Barlaeus speaks elegantly:
<margin>Heroic Poems 4, p. 363.</margin>

->*Our Father tended those orchards,*<-
->*Strolling in such a garden,*<-
->*He went, and held the lands and waves by his command,*<-
->*Alone he governed an unknown world with his scepters:*<-
->*The wild beasts recognized their Master, and the Lions*<-
->*Submitted their rage to the Man. The Panther with spotted back*<-
->*Obeyed, as did the lynxes darting their eyes from afar,*<-
->*And the swift tigers, and the bears with hoarse voices,*<-
->*And the wolf, and the elephant bristling with grim trumpeting.*<-
->*Whatever was of the quadrupeds, whatever the Air*<-
->*Brought forth, or the wide sea had armed with scales,*<-
->*They carry out the commands of one man. He does not refuse them,*<-
->*The Crocodile who lives on the Pelusian shores,*<-

<column-break/>

->*The Dolphins who plow the waves, and extend*<-
->*Iron-like snouts in the sea. Not the panting Whales,*<-
->*Not the high-flying eagle, though the armor-bearing bird of Jove,*<-
->*And destined to be preserved as the victorious emblem of the Latins.*<-
<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>

By this very act, Adam gave an illustrious proof of <term>Physiological Wisdom</term> <note>The study of the nature and functions of living things.</note>, for by natural light he saw into the natures of living things far more deeply than all anatomists have ever been able to achieve through countless dissections. As the author of the nomenclature, <term>having imposed their powers, he assigned names that were somehow neighboring to their nature</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπιθεὶς τὰς δυνάμεις... "applying their powers, he placed names close to their nature."</note>; that is, inspired by divine virtue and wisdom, he established the names of things. Now, after the Fall, that which Jerome says holds true: *We marvel at the Creator not only in the heavens and the earth, the sun and the ocean, elephants, camels, horses, oxen, leopards, bears, and lions; but also in the smallest animals: the ant, the gnat, flies, little worms, and that sort of kind, whose bodies we know better than their names; and in all of them we venerate the same skill.*
<margin>Epistle 3 to Heliodorus, col. 29.</margin>
Great indeed was that benefit and <term>dignity</term> <note>original: ἀξίωμα (axioma)</note> of the first man, but alas, by the deceit of Satan, that power was greatly diminished. Man fell from that <term>image toward the created thing</term> <note>original: πρὸς τὸ κτισθὲν (pros to ktisthen)</note> by the bite of Eve and Adam, which the tongue of the Serpent offered to them as something so sweet. This tongue of the serpent was poisonous, especially when Satan used that tongue. It cast the first man down from the place of delights, stripped him of the robe of immortality, deprived him of the grace of God, and led him to death. This tongue of the serpent was the subversion of man, as it emitted a foul breath and communicated a hellish contagion. The lying tongue spoke smoothly, and with a few brief words in a single moment, it infected the first humans—and in them, all humans—while it infected their ears. The tongue flatters to harm, lies to deceive, and offers the apple to intoxicate. Thus the noxious poison was dispersed among all inhabitants of the earth; the dominion which they possessed before the Fall by the grace of the Creator, they lost through the envy of the Corruptor. For before the Fall, the first humans and their descendants would have ruled over living creatures through the light of wisdom in the intellect, and then through the singular care and protection of God toward men, by which it would have been prohibited—either immediately by God or through Angels—that any harm be offered to man by animals. Finally, the majesty of the Lord shining in man himself would have deterred the animals themselves. But now, after the Fall, just as the image of God was lost, so too was the dominion, which was a certain part and consequence of that image. One may still observe a certain shadow of this dominion in the fact that fish, as Basil says,
<margin>Homily 9.</margin>
when a man walks near the water and they see his shadow, they tremble and take flight, like servants in a house thrown into an uproar, terrified by the unexpected arrival of the master. And the dominion which we exercise today over the brutes is not dominion, but rather tyranny; it is not spontaneous, because we exercise it through arts and snares. Whence Blessed Luther says on Genesis: *This leprous body still has, by the benefit of God, some appearance of Dominion over other creatures: but it is very small and far inferior to that first Dominion, where there was no need for art or deceits (as there is now), but simply for the divine...*

# SACRED HISTORY OF ANIMALS
<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>

The creature obeyed the voice when Adam and Eve were commanded to rule over them. Therefore, we retain the name and title of "Lord" as nothing more than a hollow label; the reality of that power is almost entirely lost. And yet, it is good to know and meditate on these things, so that we may sigh for that coming day in which those things we lost in paradise through sin shall be restored to us. Regarding this lost dominion over the beasts, let us also note what Hugh of St. Victor <note>A 12th-century Saxon canon regular and influential theologian</note> says:
<margin>
In the annotations on this place.
</margin>
*Because of sin,* he says, *man lost dominion over two kinds of living things: first, over the largest animals, such as lions, tigers, and panthers, so that he might understand that he had been deprived of that excellent power of lordship which he had received from God. Secondly, over the smallest and vilest little creatures, such as flies, gnats, etc., which can be tamed even less than those larger ones, so that we might recognize into what vileness man had fallen and been cast down because of sin.* Wherefore it is rightly said by Basil of Seleucia \*
<margin>
Oration 349.
Psalm 49:12.
</margin>
that man has been <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὸ κτηνῶδες ... μεταμορφωθῆναι</note> "transformed into the likeness of beasts," and with David, \* "Man will not abide in honor; he is compared to the beasts that perish" <note>original Hebrew: נמשל כבהמות נדמו</note>. The Psalter speaks here of the state of the present life and the men of this age, who measure the future by this life, or rather believe there is no life at all after this one which they enjoy. For a man placed in honor and wealth, honored only in the riches of the world while remaining destitute of knowledge and piety, is compared to cattle; nor does he take his wealth or honors with him, being plainly like the beasts of burden who have nothing remaining after death but to utterly perish and be given over to oblivion. Indeed, the whole strength of man is situated in the soul and the body, one of which he has in common with God, the other with the beasts. If man, degenerating from his noble lineage, clings to the brutish senses of his flesh (which he shares with the beasts), living in carnal delights and dead to God, he passes in a certain way into the nature of beasts, so that the words of Jerome in Letter 3 to Heliodorus are true of him: "Without the knowledge of his Creator, every man is a beast." And the Psalmist says: \*
<margin>
v. 49:21.
</margin>
*Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts and made like unto them.* Man is like God if, preserving the nobility of his dignity and honor, he mortifies the deeds of the flesh through the spirit. Regarding this foul and deplorable <note>original Greek: μεταμορφώσει</note> "transformation" caused by sin, Radulphus Ardens <note>A 12th-century French theologian and preacher</note> discourses elegantly in his Homily for the Easter Vigil: *Man, first blinded by the merit of his transgression, was made brutish, so that inclined in a bestial manner he tastes and seeks only the earth; and in it, dying, he is dissolved, according to that saying: Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to beasts as much in his vices as in his death.* This is why the Poets describe men being changed into cattle. For a man who, forgetting his divine origin, is devoted only to his throat <note>i.e., gluttony</note>, what else is he but changed into a pig? He who is entirely devoted to fulfilling his lust, what else is he but changed into a stinking goat? Similarly, men are said to be transformed into other cattle according to the likeness of their habits. He who is devoted to cruelty and blood, what else is he but changed into a wolf? The same things are read in Bernard's Sermon on our Beginnings, Middles, and Ends, discoursing thus: When you were in honor,

<column-break/>

O Man, you did not understand, whence you were compared to senseless beasts and made like unto them.
<margin>

</margin>

Blush, because instead of the company of Angels, you have the stronger company of cattle, not only in the necessity of the body, but even in the affections of the heart. You share the food of the earth with the beasts because you loathed the bread of Angels, the celestial bread. Not only that, but what is worse, the soul is crooked in an upright body; the human likeness remains in the body, but in the soul, the likeness of God has been changed into a bestial likeness. An example of divine wrath is proposed to us in Nebuchadnezzar, King of the Chaldeans, who, puffed up by pride and magnificence, was sent by God \*

They are certain images and patterns of reason, not reason itself; by the law of Nature they act without reason, and individual living things do only individual...

# From Psalm 50, verses 10 and 11.

<margin>Sacred History of Animals.</margin>
They exercise so much skill, from which the spider weaves, the ant collects crumbs, the birds build nests, and every creature acts according to that which they are driven by nature. They also have their own voices, by which they are distinguished from one another, as the saying goes:
> *The horse whinnies, and the elephant trumpets, but the donkey brays,*
> *The sheep bleats, the bull bellows, and the camel babbles,*
> *The pig grunts, and the dog barks, the little fox yelps,*
> *And the crow caws, and the goose cackles,*
> *And the ravens croak, the cuckoo calls, the swallow*
> *Twittered, the boar gnashes, and the owl chirps in the morning,*
> *The stork clucks at length, and rattles with its long beak,*
> *The magpie chatters, the sparrow chirps, and the cicada screeches,*
> *And the hen at once clucks, cackles, and squawks,*
> *The bee-eater chirps, the rooster crowed, and the snake*
> *Hisses, the hawks pipe, and the frog croaks,*
> *The crane cries, but the eagles scream, the wild bear growls,*
> *The mouse squeaks, the <unclear>tanas</unclear> screeches, and the lioness roars.*
<note>original: "Hinnit equus, barritq; elephas..." This is a traditional Latin "Carmen de Philomela" or a similar list used by grammarians to teach the specific verbs for animal sounds.</note>

In many external things, brute animals surpass us, says Augustine in *The City of God*, book 8, chapter 15, according to the distinction of the common verse:
> *The boar beats us in hearing, the lynx in sight, the monkey in taste:*
> *The vulture in smell, the spider surpasses us in touch.*

Hence they say that men learned grammatical letters from birds, according to the witness of Majolus (Volume 2, *Dierum Canicularium*, collection 2, page 153); from swallows they learned architecture, as Ludovicus Vives says (Book 1, *On the Transmission of Disciplines*, Volume 1, page 441). From the Egyptian Ibis they learned the enema, and from the Hippopotamus the practice of blood-letting, as recorded by Hugo Fridevallis in his *Treatise on Preserving Health* (Preface, page 7). There is in certain wild beasts and birds such industry that, not content with what nature gave them, they learn by art and instruction, and in this they train their offspring. Bears are said to shape their cubs by licking them. Deer exercise their fawns in running and teach them to meditate on flight; they lead them to the precipices of mountains, demonstrate the leap, and heal received wounds with dittany <note>A medicinal herb believed in antiquity to expel arrows from wounded animals.</note>. Eagles lead their chicks out for flight and teach them to look directly into the sun. The swallow builds its nest with art. Hence, in Aesop's Fables, little animals are introduced expressing the unique qualities, gifts, and arts of their nature: namely, the dog’s loyalty, the fox’s cunning, the lion’s nobility, the wolf’s ferocity, and the lamb’s simplicity. And so, in the smallest things, one can sometimes admire the greatest; God arranged the smallest things in nature so that they might yield to those which are most robust and strong. Thus the elephant yields to the weasel; the lion to the rooster and the mouse, so that the greater glory of God may appear in them, according to that saying of Solomon:

<margin>Proverbs 30:24.</margin>
> *There are four things which are the smallest of the earth, and yet they are wiser than the wise: namely, ants, hyraxes <note>original: "cuniculi" (rabbits/coneys), usually translated as rock hyraxes in modern Bibles</note>, locusts, and lizards.*

There are many things which are not valued by their bulk, but by their quality and virtue. Often in tiny things great powers lie hidden, which God the Creator, the *all-wise* <note>original Greek: ὁ πάνσοφος</note>, communicated to the most minute things according to His immense wisdom; however, the virtue of these things is not evident except by the effect, from which the cause must then be considered. The body of a viper is small, but it has a huge poison. The Torpedo fish may be small, but it produces astounding effects; when we weigh these with the right-hand scale of reason, we—along with Thiofrid, Abbot of Echternach—rightly exclaim:

<margin>Book 1, chapter 1.</margin>
> *Although God is great in great things, He works wonders more gloriously in the smallest.*

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred History of Animals.</margin>
But lest we seem to have wandered too far from the mark, like a horse with loosened reins leaping outside the track, we shall pull in the reins. It is worthwhile, however, to warn that no small difficulty stands in the way of him whose mind is set on reviewing the names and histories of animals. For we see many obscure, doubtful, and variously transmitted things circulated about animals; nor would there be such difficulty if the terms were not obscure and so variously explained. Two very famous men in the previous century acknowledged this difficult work: Johann Bugenhagen (who was commonly called "the Pomeranian" after his homeland) and Theodoric Sneppius. The former, in his commentary on Jeremiah 50:

<margin>folio 438. b.</margin>
*I do not dispute here with the Hebraists about the names of the wild beasts, which I cannot do, nor do I take it upon myself, nor does it profit the meaning at all. Certainly, no "convenient" wild beast is signified here, but robbers and murderers.* The latter, in his commentary on Isaiah 13:

<margin>page 226.</margin>
*I do not labor over the words, because it is uncertain which beasts the Prophet intends. Perhaps he understood those animals which are not found or seen in these regions of ours.* From the difficulty of names, I descend to the multitude of living creatures: for who shall count the armies of living things which the Creator of things has under the waters and in the waters, upon the earth, under the sky, and in the heavens? Under the earth, He has a huge army of hunting worms; in the waters, indeed, He nourishes a stupendous and remarkable crowd of larger and smaller fish, and immense whales, which neither Job nor the Psalmist can sufficiently praise. On the earth are found so many thousands, nay, myriads of beasts: namely, so many horrendous lions, rapid bears, most cruel tigers, most fierce panthers, rapacious wolves, gnashing boars, kicking horses, grim bulls, wanton goats, and most foul crocodiles with a flock of dragons and a twin-set of vipers and serpents. There, mice devour Bishops <note>A reference to the legend of the Mouse Tower of Bingen.</note>, lice devour Kings, and rabbits undermine mountains and houses. There are asps and basilisks, horned vipers and two-headed snakes, spotted snakes and thirst-snakes, the scorpion and the venomous spider. Innumerable troops fly in the air, which are armed against the Egyptians, whence even beetles and hornets are expressly called the "army of God" in Holy Scripture; compare B. Ursinus.

<margin>Volume 2, Vol. 1. Sacred Analects, page 315.</margin>
Ulisse Aldrovandi of Bologna, in his learned work on insects, recounts about a hundred genera of butterflies, all different from one another, almost seventy genera of flies, nearly fifty genera of caterpillars, forty of beetles, about thirty of locusts, thirty-five of Spanish flies, twenty-five of spiders, twenty of bugs, and about twelve of wasps. So that to build a history of animals is a work of immense bulk. Regarding the reptiles mentioned in the sacred books, Juan Camara Bustamante has discussed them appropriately. In the previous century, a laborious commentary on Biblical animals was published under the title *Ophio-ichthyo-biblos* (Biblical Book of Beasts, Birds, and Fish). Wolfgang Frantzius performed the same in this century in his *Sacred History of Animals*, and recently Johann Heinrich Ursinus—both of *blessed memory* <note>original Greek: ὁ μα카ρίτης</note>—in his *Nomenclature of Biblical Animals*. Furthermore, a few years ago, Samuel Bochart published a vast and precious work on animals titled *Hierozoicon*.

# SACRED BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

### Sacred History of Animals
### Genesis 7:2
Among various authors, even those who have written specifically about animals, there is a well-known division found in the Sacred Scriptures—to say nothing of others—between clean and unclean animals. This is first mentioned in the law <note>Genesis 7:2</note>. This division is not based on the inherent nature of the living creatures themselves, since everything God had created (Genesis 1:24) was **"very good"** <note>Hebrew: *tov me'od*</note>, not only individually but collectively, existing with such symmetry <note>Greek: *symmetria*</note> and perfection that nothing more noble could be imagined. Isidore deeply reflected on this in *Sentences*, Book 1, Chapter 11: *"If you shave the hair from a man's head,"* he says, *"you remove a small thing, but you bring foulness to the whole body; so too in the universe of creation, if you call the lowliest little worm an evil of nature, you do an injury to all of nature."* Rather, the distinction depends on the will of the Lawgiver. This was partly for sacred reasons, regarding sacrifices—in which only sheep, oxen, goats, doves, and turtledoves were to be immolated—and partly for secular and domestic reasons, regarding food. Exactly when this distinction began in eating habits is uncertain; compare Blessed Ursinus in his *Miscellanies on Clean and Unclean Animals*.

<margin>page 179</margin>
It is not our purpose here to be overly wordy. By divine command (Leviticus 11:2 ff.), it was a sin for the Jews to eat the flesh of certain animals, both for the sake of "Levitical pedagogy"—by which the Lawgiver wished to restrain this nation, otherwise too prone to idolatry—and for physical reasons. The Hebrews, as noted by Münster on Leviticus (compare Hermann Heinrich Frey’s *Book of Beasts* <note>Greek: *theriobiblion*</note>, p. 9), observe that the flesh of unclean animals prohibited by law produced a sluggish, putrid, and diseased body, such that the soul could perform nothing excellent—much as if a candle were placed in a dark lantern. The Sacred Pandects <note>A reference to the comprehensive body of Scripture</note> provide us with another division of animals:

<margin>Deuteronomy 4:16, 17, 18</margin>
Where, besides humans, animals are divided into beasts of the earth, birds under the heavens, creeping things on the ground, and fish under the earth in the waters. These categories are established both by the nature of the creatures and by the specific quality and "home" <note>Greek: *oikeia*</note> assigned to each by God the Creator; for every living thing lives in an element similar to its own nature. All things that breathe and live a sensory life through a sensitive soul live in the earth, air, or water. All creatures dwell "under the heavens." The labor and goal of our pen concerns those creatures which, though lacking a rational soul, are endowed with a sensing soul like ours. Thus, we shall deal first with those that dwell with us on this earth, called *terrestrial*; then those that live in the air, called *volatile*; and finally those that have their home in the waters, called *aquatic*. We shall follow the Holy Scripture as our guide <note>Latin: *Hodogetam*</note>, contenting ourselves this time with a description of those listed in the Sacred Codex according to alphabetical order.

**The Elk** <note>Latin: *Alce*</note> occupies the first place among terrestrial animals in this our study of Biblical animals. The word is of Greek origin: *alkē* <note>Greek: *ἀλκή*</note> signifies strength or might. To the Norwegians it is the *Elg* or *Elgar*; to the Germans the *Elend*—a name derived primarily from its very mournful and miserable cry, so much so that if it were not seen, one would think it was a crying infant. It is found in great numbers in the North, especially in Norway and Sweden, and sometimes in Prussia. Scaliger (Exercise 206, p. 660),

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred History of Animals</margin>
Gesner, and Lonicer in their *Books of Beasts* <note>Greek: *theriobibliois*</note>, as well as Vossius (Book 3 on *Idolatry*, ch. 63, p. 1068), confuse the Elk with the **Reindeer** <note>Latin: *Rangiferum*</note>. The Norwegians and Laplanders, among whom alone this animal is found, call it the *Ranger*, *Reiner*, *Raniger*, *Ruensthler*, or *Ruensboef*; but we call it the *Rhenthier* because of its speed. For Olaus Magnus (Book 17, ch. 26 ff.) and Torquemada (*Hexameron*, colloquy 6, p. 577) testify that it is of such speed that in one day it covers more ground than a horse does in nearly three, especially over snow and ice. Zeiler reports from Olaus Magnus that it can cover 15 German miles in a day's run.

<margin>Century 5, Letters, p. 169</margin>
For that reason, it is of great use to Northerners in winter for riding and pulling vehicles. Scaliger also attributes this swiftness to the Elk in the place cited; his words are: *"The Elk is almost entirely the shape of a deer, with branched horns, but they are thinner than a deer's, stretched further back, less branched, and covered in a kind of down. Hitched to a vehicle—which is two-wheeled and called a 'Sannia' by the Sarmatians—they write that it travels three hundred German miles in a twenty-four hour period <note>Greek: *nychthēmeron*</note> over the ice with an unhindered pace. Such strength, such swiftness, etc."* Vossius speaks similarly of this animal: *"The Elk,"* he says, *"covers as much ground in one day as a horse does in three. It is used by Northerners for pulling vehicles. And within a day and night <note>Greek: *nychthēmeron*</note>, even without food or drink, it covers 200 Italian miles (not 500, as you might read in Ulysses Aldrovandus, Book 1 on*

<margin>p. 781, Bologna edition, 1611</margin>
*Quadrupeds, ch. 32)."* This is also in Olaus Magnus (Book 11, ch. 36), where you may also read that in some parts of Sweden their use was forbidden, lest someone use them to betray the secrets of the kingdom to foreigners. However, with all due respect to such great men, we have learned from those who know Elks and have seen them in Northern regions that they are not of such great speed. Furthermore, Reindeer only have their dwellings in the very northern parts of Norway and Sweden (or as Torquemada writes, in Skritfinnia); they cannot survive in other regions that experience a milder climate, especially through the summer. This is testified by the letters of William the Wise, Landgrave of Hesse, to Tycho Brahe (Astronomical Letters, Book 1, p. 203): *"We arranged for Reindeer to be brought here from Sweden on two occasions, up to a hundred in number; they all fared well in winter and pulled vehicles over the ice in their usual way. But when the heat returned, every single one perished, so that we see clearly they cannot endure in these regions when summer and heat come on."* Tycho Brahe himself (p. 208) relates of them: *"There were indeed one or two Reindeer in Copenhagen <note>Latin: *Hafniæ*</note>, as I mentioned in my previous letters, but they could not survive the summer here or tolerate the heat, much less in Hesse <note>Latin: *Hassia*</note> or other places further south."* Elks, however, as is clear from the same letters of the most serene 'Atlas of the Hessians' to Tycho Brahe, can survive in these regions. *"As for the Elk,"* the Prince says in the same place, *"we kept a single one in our garden at Zapfenburg, which has fared well from the Feast of St. Martin until now..."*

# From Psalm 50, verses 10 & 11
## Cccc

**Column 1:**

<margin>Sacred History of Animals.</margin>
...it plays, leaps, and is in good spirits, especially when we are driven around in our carriage in our green deer park; it runs toward us as closely as it can and observes us just like a dog. However, its horns do not grow very much, nor do they protrude beyond the measure of a finger at this very time, etc. <term>Tycho Brahe</term> <note>The famous Danish astronomer (1546–1601)</note> writes back clearly the same thing in a letter in the cited place to His Serene Highness William: "Although <term>Elks</term> <note>original: *Alces*</note> trace their origin from *Norway* and *Sweden*, they can nevertheless endure here in *Denmark* for some time if they are well kept. I should think, therefore, they could also be kept in *Germany* without difficulty. For sometimes in the summer the air here is no less sweltering than there. I recently had one, when I was writing to Your Highness, from the region in Scania at my estate; and when I intended to have it transported to this island, it came to Landskrona, a town situated opposite this island, where it was kept in the Citadel for several days. It happened that while they were sitting at the table, it climbed the stairs of its own accord and gorged itself on a drink of strong beer (with which <term>Olaus Magnus</term> <note>Swedish ecclesiastic and writer (1490–1557)</note> also writes in Book 18 they are greatly delighted), so that in descending it fell from the stairs and broke one of its legs, which afterwards could not be healed by any diligence, and so it died in this manner."

Regarding the <term>Reindeer</term> <note>original: *Rangifer*</note>, they report that it has meat, especially the younger ones, that is delicate and well-flavored; likewise, the females provide no small abundance of milk, butter, and cheese for the household, which is why they are nourished in such numbers by the Lapps in *Schrickfinnia* <note>An archaic term for part of Lapland/Finland</note> as herds are elsewhere, as can be read in <margin>Book 10 on perfect animals, page 367.</margin> <term>Torquemada</term> in the cited place, page 577. I am pleased to give some description of it from <term>Cardanus</term>. He says they tame those captured in Lapland, for they are born there, and they are yoked to carriages; they cover 150 miles in a day in place of horses, for they are more robust in body, though with thinner horns than stags. And perhaps they have only two horns according to nature: more, however, as was said regarding rams, by chance. Or since they are branchy and supported by more frequent branches than stags, it was believed—falsely—that they have multiple rows of horns. Or just as in plants which sprout more abundantly, like apples and hazelnuts, branches and shoots come forth from the foot which were born from the suckers: so from the root of the two horns, shoots are born which ought to grow from the trunk, and in that way they present the image of many rows. In general, reindeer usually have three horns: two very long ones from the sides, and one small one in the middle; but all are branched. <term>Thomas Bartholinus</term> had intended to give us a more accurate description of this, had not Vulcan <note>A metaphor for fire; Bartholinus's library burned in 1670</note> envied this most learned writing on Norwegian animals along with the rest of the Republic of Letters this year. But let us finally return to the <term>Elk</term>. Aristotle has nothing on this, nor Pliny, to whom it was known by name only. However, <term>Julius Caesar</term> mentions it in <margin>Book 6, page 129.</margin> of the *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, where he describes the Hercynian Forest extending as far as possible toward the North, and reports that the Elk is found in it. But Scaliger thinks it is the *Machlin* which Caesar called the Elk. It occurs once in the Holy Scriptures, *Deuteronomy 14:5*, where in the catalog of clean animals allowed to the Jews for eating is the word *Zemer* [זמר]; concerning which word <term>Schindler</term> writes thus in the Le-

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

-xico under the root *Zemer* [זמר]: *Zemer*, זמר, is a branch-bearing animal, a mountain goat, or a fallow deer. <term>Pagninus</term> and <term>Arias</term> likewise translate it as mountain goat. <term>Martin Luther</term> <unclear>in</unclear> the sacred [text], but <term>Tremellius</term> and <term>Junius</term> (following the Latin translator of the Chaldean Paraphrase, who translates it as Elk) rendered it as *the Elk* <note>original: *das Elendt*</note>. <term>Tremellius</term> and <term>Junius</term> (following the Septuagint and the Vulgate, who, just as the Old Latin Translator and the Septuagint agree throughout the whole verse regarding the interpretation, so also in this name) understand it as καμηλοπάρδαλις, <term>camelopard</term> <note>The archaic name for a Giraffe</note>, regarding which verse <term>Borrhaus</term> well notes: col. 983. The translation of the Paraphrast is known; the interpretation of the Greeks and the Old Translator (following the Greeks) is known; nor is it obscure how the Hebrew interpreters here are unlike themselves, for it is an old complaint how they grope blindly in rendering the names of stones, animals, and plants. Leaving the complaint to the Ancients, let us look at the <term>Camelopard</term>, lest the Latin-Greek interpretation be unknown. The word is composed of *camelos* [camel] and *pardalis* [leopard], and the name comes from the fact that the animal is like a Camel in its head, but like a leopard with white spots distinguishing its reddish color, as Pliny teaches in these words: *The Ethiopians call it Nabin, with a neck like a horse, feet and legs like an ox, a head like a Camel, and white spots distinguishing its reddish color*, whence it is called <term>Camelopardalis</term>, more conspicuous for its appearance than its ferocity. And after him, <term>Dionysius the Carthusian</term> in his Commentary: *The Camelopard, although it is a leopard sprinkled with white spots, is yet similar in its neck to a horse, in its feet to oxen, but in its head to a Camel, and it is born in Ethiopia*. Hence Horace* thus <margin>Epistle 2, 1, v. 195.</margin> confuses the Camelopard:

> A panther of a different kind confused with a Camel.

<term>Bochart</term> denies that it was known to the Jews in the time of Moses. But even today it is a stranger in Egypt, brought from elsewhere (see Belon, *Observations* 2, ch. 49), so that it seems to have been permitted for food in vain; compare <term>B. Ursinus</term> *Nomenclature of Biblical Animals, page 124*; <term>B. Gerhard</term> *Commentary on Deuteronomy, ch. 14, p. 847*; <term>B. Franzius</term> *Sacred History of Animals, ch. 10, p. 106.*

### BOAR, *Wildschwein*; in Greek, *syagros* or *sys agrios*.

It is read once in the Holy Codex, Psalm 80:14. *Chazir mi-ya'ar* [חזיר מיער], *the pig of the Forest*, i.e., the Wild Boar. Varro, cited in Nonius, called it the forest swine; and Catullus, the *Grove-wanderer*. The same beast in the cited place in the Psalmist is immediately called the *wild beast of the field* [she-day ziyz], or as the Septuagint says, the *wild solitary one*, and the Vulgate *the wild singular one*; by which terms Hesychius, Suidas, and others teach the boar is described, and called *monios* [solitary] because it flees the company of others and lives by itself. *Ziyz* [זיז] is otherwise a general name, noting everything that moves by itself, from motion; for *zuz* [זוז] is *to move*, whence both <term>Rabbi David</term> and <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> interpret it as *creeping thing*. <term>Aben Ezra</term>, however, says *Birds*, winged creatures: but to the Chaldean it is the *Woodcock*; whose feet stand on the earth while its head reaches even to heaven; hence the Talmudic fable in *Bava Bathra folio 73, 2*, which <term>Johannes Buxtorf</term> recounts in *The Jewish Synagogue, ch. 36*. It differs from the Swine in that the latter is tame, while the former is counted among the wild animals. Juvenal* counts its meat among the delicacies of food along with hare <margin>Satire 1, v. 142.</margin>

> He serves boars, an animal born for banquets.

And Varro* says generally of pigs: The swinish <margin>Book 11 on Agriculture, ch. 4.</margin>
