# SACRED HISTORY OF ANIMALS
## ANTIQUITIES OF THE BIBLE

<margin>Sacred History of Animals.</margin>
...a genus bestowed by nature for feasting. For just as in hares the most flavorful parts are considered to be the front *shoulders* and the hind *thighs*, so the delicacies of the wild sow were the kernels <note>original: *glandula*; likely referring to the sweetbreads or neck glands</note> and the loins. Martial writes of both in *Epigrams, Book 7, 19*:

> Three times he demands the boar's kernels, four times the loin;
> And both thighs of the hare, and two shoulders.

Hence, during the Saturnalia <note>The Roman winter festival of unrestrained feasting</note>, the meat of the wild boar held the chief place among delicacies, as witnessed by the same Martial in *Book 14, Epigram 70*:

> That pig will make a good Saturnalia for you,
> Fed among the foaming wild boars upon the holm-oak.

The *wild boar or pig* is a symbol of the Chaldean nation; it is that "boar from the forest" mentioned by the Prophet <note>Psalm 80:13</note> laying waste to the vineyard, i.e., the Church. Just as wild boars are very often read to have devastated vineyards in the works of the Poets (hence the Erymanthian and Calydonian boars). Symbolically, the unruly common people are also indicated under the shroud of the boar. Hence that Calydonian boar, which was a bronze statue in the Hippodrome at Constantinople, attacking a Lion with bristling hair and lightning-fast teeth, signified the disobedient populace; Euphrosyna, the wife of Alexios Komnenos, being maddened by magic arts, cut off its snout. But Isaac Angelus, restored to power, transferred it to the Great Palace, hoping thus to keep the common people in their duty (Nicetas Choniates in *Alexios and Isaac, Books 3 and 4 of the Annals*). As I said, the Prophet refers to the enemies of the Israelites, rushing with impunity into the Promised Land and cruelly ravaging it. Although Augustine explains it specifically as the Romans, who utterly overturned the Republic of the Jews. "Therefore," he says, "that pig is an adversary, and they place in the pig, as it were, the uncleanness of the nations. For the Jewish nation was overturned by the nations: but that King who overturned it was not only an unclean pig, but also a Wild Boar." For what is a Wild Boar but a savage pig, a proud pig, etc.? Jerome explains it as the Devil himself. "In the boar," he says, "and the solitary beast, the ferocity of the Devil is understood, by whom the Synagogue was exterminated because of unbelief, etc."

CONCERNING THE SPIDER: although it is of the insect genus, its nomenclature warns us to deal with <unclear>it</unclear> briefly. It is called *Shemamit* [שממית] among the Hebrews, whence Proverbs 30:28: *The spider takes hold with her hands, and is in kings' palaces.* The Talmudists write it with a [ס] *Samekh*; whence "the terror of the spider is upon the scorpion" (*Shabbath*, folio 77, verso 2). For it enters the ears of the scorpion, whence it is a terror to it: "The spider was created against the scorpion"; namely, if anyone is struck by a scorpion, then a crushed spider applied to the wound cures it (compare Buxtorf's *Lexicon* under the word *Shemam*).
<margin>p. m. 824.</margin>
The spider is a little creature of very certain recognition, but it is very uncertain whether that word *Shemamit*—which the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated as *kalaboten* <note>original: καλαβώτην; a spotted lizard or gecko</note> (an animal which the Greeks today call <unclear>amianaton</unclear>, which is clearly from the Hebrew *Shemamit* that we have here, says B. Friedl. *Commentary on Proverbs 30*)—is intended there.
<margin>p. m. 718.</margin>
The Hebrew word *Arag* [ארג], *to weave or spin*, leads as if by the hand to the spider, no more clearly than the German *Spinne* comes from *nendo* (spinning) or weaving. To the Greeks, *arachnes* [ἀράχνης] seems to embrace the Hebrew *Arag* in its scope, and even more so the French *araigne*, preserving the letter *g*. Mention is made of the spider very often in the Sacred Scriptures, but quite inconveniently in the Septuagint version of Psalm 90:10, where that which is "finer than any web of spiders" is the Septuagint's "meditation" <note>original: παρεάχησις</note>. The words in the original text sound thus: *We have consumed our years like a moan* [כלו שנינו במו הגה]. Where, I ask, did "spider" creep in? In the Hebrew language, that word will never sustain the meaning of "spider," since it is *Hegeh* [הגה], *speech, talk, or a groan.* That version is clearly <note>original: ἀνδράχνης; possibly a scribal error for "spider"</note>, whether "spider" is taken in a proper or improper sense, nor does the context allow it. If this Septuagint version were rendered according to the sense: *Our years shall meditate like a spider;* or in German: *Our years vanish like a spiderweb.* But what strangeness of sense is this? And who would labor with such <unclear>idle talk</unclear> [ἀδολεσχία] that they would not see the sense becomes absurd in this way? The Hebrew *Kalah* [כלה] is explained as *to be consumed, finished, or perfected*, whence by a convenient exposition we can render it thus: *Our years, like a talk or speech, are consumed.* Or thus: *We have consumed our years like a story.* And in our language: *Our years pass away like a chatter* [German: *Geschwätz*]. Speech and thought pass quickly and swiftly, and the days of our life are transfixed in a moment, like speech, the end of which is nothing but some talk vanishing into the breezes. The time we live is but a point, and our days are swifter than speech, as the Septuagint has it in Job <margin>Job 7:6</margin>, where the Hebrew is *swifter than a weaver* [מרו ארג], others say *shuttle*, others *as a weaver's shuttle.* Indeed, the spider's web is a type of mortality and human frailty, which should be drawn not from this passage, but from others. For if you see a spider in your heated room <note>original: *hypocausto*; a room heated from below</note> or in another place weaving a web, think that there hangs before your eyes a symbol of the brevity of life and a picture of vanities and fragile things. Concerning these empty works, Isaiah says <margin>Isaiah 59:4</margin>: *They weave the spider's webs* [קורי עכביש יארגו]. And verse 6: *Their webs shall not become garments, neither shall they cover themselves with their works. Their works are works of iniquity, and the act of violence is in their hands.* The Septuagint here is good: *Their web shall not be for a garment, nor shall they be clothed by their works, for their works are works of lawlessness.* It captures the useless things of men, and indeed he most excellently calls their webs *spider webs*, which it weaves to catch flies; for what else do these people seek but empty glory, brute pleasure, and vain riches? Behold, they catch only flies. Nor truly shall they be clothed with these webs, from which they will not be able to fashion a wedding garment. While Ambrose is in these meditations <margin>in Psalm 38, p. 130</margin>, he says: "When you see some people studying to increase their resources, piling up powers, and affecting beauty, you shall say that passage of Isaiah: They weave a spider's web, which cannot be lasting, but is quickly torn, and all its work is dissolved. For it is not placed upon any solid foundation, but is suspended in a vacuum." All greedy people seem to themselves to be clever and industrious. "What is more clever, what more anxious than a spider? Which works it leads out and always stretches through the nights, and with no expense or cost finishes a garment, but all that it has made is vain." Thus the writer on vanities, Antonius à Burgundia, Archdeacon of Bruges, in *The Touchstone of the World* <margin>page 1</margin>, presents the spider's web in the first place as a symbol of vanity among vanities. He says, "The web, which the weaving spider makes for itself—being its own distaff, spindle, thread, and wool-weigher—is clearly established as so useless..."

...to be more useful than subtle; or rather, it is most useless precisely because it is most subtle. Nothing is more useless to true wisdom than the subtlety of the Sophists <note>Sophists were ancient Greek teachers often accused of using clever but fallacious reasoning.</note>. For this reason, the ancients depicted the spider as hateful to Pallas <note>Athena/Minerva, goddess of wisdom and weaving, who transformed Arachne into a spider.</note>. Lælius Mancinus, a Jurist, also calls to mind his own mortality through the image of the spider when about to compare

divine and human laws, writing: *While I write, a little spider is before my eyes, which completely eviscerates itself, meditating on nothing other than that web of hers, from which she may catch flies. A maidservant arrives, who with her brooms suddenly drags the web, the fly, and the learned animal down to the ground and crushes them with her foot.* Moses aptly says: *Our years shall be considered as a spider <note>original: "Anni nostri sicut aranea meditabuntur"</note>, that is, they shall be reckoned, and in the midst of meditating and busying ourselves, they are broken off.* We all hunt for flies; so do I, who see books from text, just as others see brooms daily, yet we do not believe it. Although the spider's web may be a symbol of vanity and almost of folly, its "delirium" should not be defrauded of its own praise and encomium. For not only does Aristotle commend its operation as <term>inspired by God</term> <note>original: θεόπνευστον (theopneuston)</note>, and records that men learned the art of weaving from the spider—whence also Democritus, according to Plutarch, says we are disciples <term>of the spider in weaving, and of swallows in building</term> <note>original: ἀράχνης ἐν ὑφαντικῇ, καὶ χελιδόνων ἐν οἰκοδομίᾳ</note>, which I hold in the same regard as the story of the Ibis, from which physicians learned the use of the clyster <note>An enema; ancient lore claimed the Ibis bird taught this to humans.</note>—but also its subtlety in weaving threads and drawing circles is truly admirable. Is there, I ask, any Geometer who draws equations and straighter lines from the center to the circumference? Is there any sailor who observes the weather better, whether cloudy, rainy, or serene, than the spider, since she does not weave in fair weather, but weaves when it is cloudy? Is there any guard more vigilant in watching for enemies than the spider is in watching for flies? Among the Caribs in the New World, as Joannes Eusebius Nierembergius

<margin>
Book 11, Natural History, chapter 26.
</margin>
records from the Spanish commentaries, there are spiders with long, sharp teeth and tiny legs, yet with a body so large that they equal half a citron; they weave a web with threads so strong that even sparrows and other birds are entangled in them. From these, a woman's hair-net can be woven. It can be washed and in this way becomes white. Justly, therefore, Solomon, the wisest of all wise men—to speak with Doctor <term>Tackius</term> <note>Johann Tackius (1617–1675), a professor of medicine and chemistry at Giessen.</note> in a public program, that incomparable master of the mysteries of natural things—when delivering certain ethical admonitions through numbers in Proverbs chapter 30, verse 24, says:
> There are four things which are the smallest on the earth, yet they surpass all the wise in wisdom. 1. The ants, a people not strong, who prepare their food in the summer. 2. The mountain mice <note>often translated as rock hyraxes or coneys</note>, a breed not powerful, dwelling in the rocks. 3. The locusts, who live without a king, yet they march out in beautiful order, as if under command and a signal. 4. The spider, which weaves and fashions her web, and dwells in the palaces of kings.

Leaving aside the first three, let the spider alone be worthy of consideration for this turn. I will not now record those things which Pliny discusses concerning the generation of spiders in book eleven, chapter twenty-four. Let it suffice to have recited in this place those things which seemed to me most necessary to be said. The spider laboriously begins her web, runs about for a long time and much, circles here and there, returns from the center to the circumference and from the circumference more often to the center; with greater mathematical science than any mortal could, she orders her threads, strengthens them, connects them, and

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred History of Animals.
</margin>
consumes herself while she completes that little wheel of manifold threads. She disembowels and eviscerates herself so that she may skillfully fashion that airy little tent of hers. To hang it high, to attach it, and to fasten it, she goes and returns six hundred times, nor does she spare her own vitals, but willingly spends them on this thinnest texture, either so that she may live in it, or so that she may more successfully hunt flies and live off their juice. Borellus reports that he discovered with a microscope that spiders are equipped by nature with eight eyes, sometimes six; so that I might perhaps think it arises from this: that spiders surpass us in touch, since they can see into all dimensions and differences of places and thus very easily guard against an imminent enemy. Truly, the power of the greatest Creator shines forth in great things: but who would not marvel at it more in the smallest things, in which there is sometimes such skill, such diligence, and such science that it seems to surpass all human ability. It has been observed by the curious, on the testimony of Drexel via Pineda: that the circular orb of spiders divides four crosswise wefts at equal intervals, which individual segments, interwoven with twenty equal threads, complete a checkered net with uniform meshes everywhere, so that when they have finished the whole web, that entire predatory orb is entwined with exactly eighty joints and patches, rounded for the destruction of flies. The webs of spiders are highly recommended against fevers, as well as for stopping the flow of blood; and it is memorable that a spider enclosed in a hazelnut and worn suspended from the neck is strongly recommended against the plague; against which, without doubt, the **Arachnites** <note>A "spider-stone," a stone supposedly found inside or produced by a spider.</note> will also fight, concerning which let me interject this story. In this current year, 1660, on the second day of Pentecost, Catharina Simonia, the maidservant of Mr. Johann **Köppel**, a very well-known pharmacist here in Giessen, being about to take down a spit by order of her mistress from a darker part of the chimney, felt something clinging to her hand and moving on it. When, anxious and curious, she began to look at what it was, she discovered a quite large spider rolling in the palm of her hand. Terrified, and wanting to free herself from that venomous animal by moving her hand here and there, when she had spent her effort in vain—the spider clinging more tightly to her hand and walking from the palm to the outer or convex surface of the hand—behold! it excreted a large part of either gore or an excremental liquid like curdled milk, so much so that it flooded the entire surface of the hand. She immediately said to her mistress: *"Oh! how foully that spider has defiled me!"* The mistress said: *"Go quickly, and free yourself from that gore!"* They both went into the courtyard of the house, and while the maid tried to wipe away that dross with a piece of wood, she found the material clinging more tenaciously to her hand and quickly hardened by the air; but in the middle of it, a blue mass fell to the ground with some resistance. When it was separated from the rest of the mass by washing with water, they found a stone of a clearly celestial color, which color, however, that **Arachnites** lost after being dried from the washing. It was of fifteen grains in weight: almost oval in shape. On the convex surface, it was polished like a bezoar stone <note>A stone-like mass found in the stomachs of animals, highly prized as an antidote to poison.</note>: but on its flatter part, it was marked with white spots and as if by a milky way...

<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

**History** is remarkable, as if some part of that milky matter had not yet been fully cooked out, so that it might be doubted whether that entire substance or curd could not have eventually hardened into a stone, if only the spider's body had been able to sustain the burden of carrying it. The spider then departed somewhere, happy with a swift pace, as if having given birth. It is a marvel! Neither Pliny, nor Albertus Magnus, nor Cardanus, nor Aldrovandus—all keen investigators of nature—nor others who have written about gems and stones, have handed down anything concerning a "spider-stone" of this kind. This history is most true, and I would wish that no one doubt it, since I have handled that stone many times with these hands of mine. Since spiders therefore seem to possess a bezoar-like <note>A bezoar is a stone-like mass found in the stomachs of animals, historically believed to be an antidote to poison.</note> or even a magnetic power—inasmuch as they are believed to draw venom to themselves from chambers—maids do an injustice to the little creature when it is made a prey to poisonous atoms; for they not only destroy its work, the web, with the stroke of their brooms, but also crush it with their feet when it is cast to the ground. From this, the actions of our lives can undoubtedly have an excellent hieroglyphic <note>In this context, a "hieroglyphic" refers to a symbolic or moral emblem found in nature.</note>. For while the hardworking little creature constructs either a funeral shroud for itself or a rope in which it is finally entangled and suffocated as if by its own bond, wretched mortals can learn by its example: exhausted by many labors to rise high, to overflow with pleasures, and to acquire and retain vast treasures for themselves, they often spend their talent and health in vain. In vain do they run about, grow weary, sweat, and weaken themselves like spiders by the exhaustion of their own vitals; for when they have done all, they possess only spiders' webs and a weaver's work fit for catching flies, and often carry a pebble or stone within their own vitals instead of delights, and die in their own work. The days they hoped would be joyful they find to be fatal, with what they hoped would be a palace turned into a tomb. Perhaps it will not be out of place to mention here: spiders are a sweet food and nourishment for hens; for even in the Court of Hesse-Darmstadt, a certain man of the Hessian nobility was known who hunted spiders no differently than wild game and devoured them as delicacies without any harm. The only thing that frightens most people away from spiders is the omen of some misfortune, namely when they emerge from their webs and either cling to a wall opposite a person or are carried down from on high before a person's face by a long thread drawn from the air. In what manner and by what instinct this happens, I most willingly remain ignorant; for who can explain every antipathy and sympathy of nature with precision? Yet even if an unusual and unexpected encounter with a spider portends something unfavorable and is a symbol of an enemy gaping at another with poisonous hostility, who shall accuse it of being the author of the misfortune? Unless one wishes to accuse a physician when he predicts a disease, or an astrologer and a rooster if they predict a storm. Concerning the Tarantula, which is of that genus of insects that kill with poison—a spider peculiar to Italy, especially Apulia, from whose town Taranto (as we now say for Tarentum) it took its name—they record this singular fact:

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals</margin>
If it bites someone, they remain in that state in which they were when bitten: one walking continues to walk, one dancing continues to dance, one laughing to laugh, one weeping to weep, one sleeping to sleep, until the poison has been driven from the body, as Alexander ab Alexandro records <note>original: *Genial. dier. l. 2. c. 17.* referring to "Genial Days," a work on ancient customs.</note>, along with Camerarius, and Gerhard Johann Vossius. But enough regarding the Spider.

**THE RAM**, an animal most celebrated in Holy Scripture on account of sacrifices, is called **Ayil** <note>original: איל</note> by the Hebrews, having a name derived from strength and power, as it is not only the male and leader of the sheep, but also rejoices in those horns above the others. Its use in sacrifices was great. In the sacrifice of Isaac, by divine command, a ram was substituted; indicated by the initial letters of the phrase <margin>Gen. 22:13</margin> "God will provide for himself" <note>original: אלהים יראה-לו (Elohim Yireh-lo)</note> in verse 8, it was found entangled by its horns among the thickets. For when Isaac was already twenty-five years old, if we believe Josephus, God tested the faith of Abraham and demanded that he sacrifice his only son—sought with so many desires, raised with so many cares, and shown by so many promises to be the father of a famous and great authority—on Mount Moriah. Abraham obeyed, and was just about to sacrifice his son on Mount Moriah when God called out that he should spare the only-begotten. Therefore, in his place, he sacrificed a Ram sticking there in the brambles, and being praised by God in the name of obedience, he received the promise of a most abundant posterity, and of the Messiah to be born from it. Concerning this, the "Circumcised" <note>A historical, often polemical term for Jewish scholars.</note> devise wonders, fabled that this ram had existed in that place from the beginning of the world specifically for the purpose of a victim, and was created during the six days of creation for the redemption of Isaac and destined for this use <note>original: *Pircke Aboth. c. 5. R. Salomon Jarchi in gloss.*</note>. There are those from the Christian school who assert that this ram was created immediately by God at that time, so that it might be a more illustrious testimony of divine providence. Most simply, with Blessed Gerhard, we believe it was brought from elsewhere from the flocks by divine ordination through the ministry of Angels, and remained entangled in the brambles of thorns by its horns. Augustine aims at this opinion <margin>ch. 14</margin> in his book *On the Miracles of Holy Scripture*:

> *It is asked,* he says, *whence was that ram in the solitude? Whether, as some assert, the earth brought it forth in 그 hour, just as it produced livestock in the beginning? Or, lest God be said to have created that work after the sixth day, we believe an Angel brought that ram from elsewhere,*

just as we believe an Angel transferred Philip from the Eunuch to Azotus, and as an Angel is said to have transferred Habakkuk to the Lions' Den to Daniel in Babylon. In the consecration of Aaron and his sons to the sacred office, God commands Moses to sacrifice a Ram, upon whose head Aaron and his sons are read to have laid their hands (Exodus 29:1, 10, 15, 19), and with its blood he should stain their ears, right hand, and right foot. That ram is called the **Ram of Fillings** <note>original: איל מלואים (Ayil Milluim)</note>, that is, the *ram of completions*. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translates this as *perfection* <note>original: τελείωσιν (teleiosin)</note>, i.e., *consecration and inauguration*; for the Greek word also denotes *to consecrate* and *to inaugurate*, whence Baptism among the Church Fathers is called *perfection* <note>original: τελείωσις</note>. For Gregory often uses this regarding Baptism in his work on the Maccabees: "The word of God is mystical, and very persuasive, at least to me among all those who love God, that no one before the presence of grace should be perfected..."

<meta>The catchword at the bottom, σθήναι (sthenai), completes the Greek word for "be perfected" or "be consecrated" on the following page.</meta>

# From Psalm 50, verses 10 and 11.
## Cccc 3

<margin>Sacred History of Animals, Book 5, chapter 3.</margin> ...of mortals, apart from faith in God, to obtain these things. And Eusebius in *Ecclesiastical History*: *Of those who were most perfect, having been placed in positions of authority, their remains were brought back.* <note>original: "Τῶν δὲ καὶ τελειοτάτων..." This Greek passage refers to the honor given to the remains of martyrs or holy figures.</note>

<margin>On the Latin Language.</margin> The **Ram** was also not excluded from the sacred rites of the Heathens; indeed, according to Varro, a Ram was sacrificed with solemn pomp during the *Agonalia* festivals: *The Agonal days,* he says, *during which the King sacrifices a ram in the Royal Palace, are named from 'agon' [the contest], because the Prince of the city was asked [interrogabatur], and the prince of the flock is sacrificed.* Finally, the Ram exhibits a figure of various things;

<margin>Daniel 8:3 and following.</margin> Under the type of the two-horned ram, the second Monarchy <note>The Medo-Persian Empire</note> is exhibited, of which *one horn* represents the Medes, and the other larger one represents the Persians, which grew far higher than the Median one, and pushed toward the West, toward Asia Minor and Syria; toward the North, toward Lydia, Cappadocia, Armenia, Iberia, the Chaldeans and Caspians; toward the South, toward Arabia, Judea, Egypt, and Ethiopia. Regarding the *prefiguration* <note>original: ὑποτύπωσις (hypotyposis)</note> of the Ram in the sacrifices of the Old Testament, I shall say nothing, but for the sake of brevity, I refer the Benevolent Reader to others who have treated the types of sacrifices professionally.

**THE DONKEY**, in Greek *onos*, from *oninein* [to help/profit], according to the Etymologist, just as *jumentum* [beast of burden] comes from *juvando* [helping]. In Hebrew *chamor*, according to *Rabbi Bechai on Genesis 2*, so called from <margin>Chamar</margin> carrying measures or heaps of grain. Others derive it from *chamar*, *to be red*; from the red color with which almost all donkeys in the Orient were endowed. Hence they were hated by the Egyptians and thrown off cliffs by the Copts, on account of the "Red Typhon" and their *donkey-like color*, according to Plutarch in *On Isis and Osiris*. The Donkey is an animal of the most abject nature and the most sluggish disposition; if you seek to gain utility from it, you must have clubs and whips at hand. Hugo Cardinalis <margin>on Luke 19.</margin> includes its properties in these verses:

> Food, bed, lazy, cross, voice, mind, burden, offspring,
> Clean, strong in the rear, the lecherous little ass.

To every kind of living creature its own food is familiar; for donkeys, thorns and thistles, and when it is led through grass, its mouth is restrained by a bridle lest it feed on the herbs; at home it feeds on chaff, even though it carries wheat to the mill and back. A good donkey lives on meager fodder, says Cornelius <margin>chapter 102, page 308.</margin> Agrippa in *The Vanity of Sciences*, and is content with whatever it gets, most tolerant of the penury of hunger, of labor, of blows, of negligence, and most patient of every hardship; of a most simple and poor Spirit, so that it does not know how to discern between lettuce and thistles; with an innocent and pure heart, and lacking gall, having peace with all living creatures, and patiently placing its back under all burdens. Donkeys are commonly accused of laziness and weariness, whence they exhibit a symbol of sloth; however, in Egypt and Palestine, donkeys seem to be exempt from this laziness and slowness, being called "trotters," which can cover 40,000 paces in one day without harm, as was also reported by Scaliger against Cardanus in *Exercise 218*. Indeed, in Arabia, Donkeys are found equal or superior to horses in speed. Regarding this matter, <margin>page 256.</margin> Xenophon writes in *Book 1 of the Expedition of Cyrus*: *And the donkeys, whenever someone pursued them, having run ahead, would stand still (for they ran much faster than the horse), and again when the horse approached, they did the same.* <note>original: "Καὶ οἱ ὄνοι..."</note> Indeed, the donkeys there, if anyone pursued them, would run ahead (since they were much swifter than the horse); likewise, as the horse came nearer, <margin>Book 1 on Job 1, page 425.</margin> they did the same. Origen writes the same regarding the speed of Donkeys

<column-break/>

in Arabia and Palestine: *That which History <margin>Sacred History of Animals.</margin> now attributes to horses and mules, donkeys nonetheless fulfilled; especially such as are in the region of Arabia, and the donkeys of the Palestinians, which are similarly swift as horses.* The common and almost daily use of donkeys for riding among the Palestinians distinguishes those of that region from our own, since, according to Scripture, not only commoners but even the more noble used this means of riding. Jair, to whom the office of judge fell after Tola (an obscure man) <margin>Judges 10:3, 4.</margin> among the Israelites, was an illustrious man, noble in power, majesty, and the command of cities, and also happy in the number of his children, for he had thirty sons, riding *upon thirty colts* <note>Hebrew: עַל-שְׁלֹשִׁים עֲיָרִים (al-shloshim ayarim)</note>, understand *donkey colts*, which meaning Piscator thinks holds place everywhere; compare *Zechariah 9:9, Genesis 49:11, Judges 12:14, Isaiah 30:6.* Although others understand this as excellent and young mules; others, however, as young horses. But since there was a small supply of horses in Palestine, and a great supply of donkeys and mules, the former opinion seems preferable to the latter. Thus in Judges 12:14, mention is made of another Judge, named Abdon the Pirathonite, who had forty sons and thirty grandsons, *sons of sons*, riding *upon seventy colts*. Not to mention that the chief wealth of the Orientals, especially the Arabs, was placed in the number of *donkeys* <note>Hebrew: חֲמוֹרִים (chamorim)</note>, as evidenced by the example of Job, <margin>chapter 42, verse 12.</margin> who before his ruin had five hundred female donkeys, but after the divine restoration, a thousand. Thus from the Midianites, the prey of the Israelites in donkeys alone was sixty-one thousand *donkeys* <note>Numbers 31:39, 45.</note>. Likewise the Reubenites with their confederates <margin>1 Chronicles 5:21.</margin> plundered two thousand *donkeys* from the Hagrites. The voice of the Donkey is to bray, whence it is said *onkasthai* from the braying, regarding which Camerarius writes in *Miscellany, chapter 3, page 10.* The female donkey of Balaam indeed had articulate speech, and that only from the power of God, for brutes do not by nature either produce articulate voices or understand those uttered by others. Porphyry <margin>Book on Abstinence.</margin> indeed attributes speech to animals, adding that Apollonius of Tyana, Melampus, Tiresias, and Thales understood and judged the speeches of brutes. Which some of the Hebrew Doctors also believed to be so, according to Abulensis, <margin>on 3 Kings 3.</margin> asserting that Solomon was expert in their voices. However, since articulate speech proceeds from mind and reason, and the meanings of words are not natural but by imposition, nothing will be gained here for animals; nor do the *Parrot*, or the *Raven*, or the *Starling*, or the *Magpie* commonly provide proof, which are taught with long labor to return some words obscurely, for these are not properly articulate voices, and, as Persius says: <margin>Prolegomena to Satires.</margin>

> Who expedited to the Parrot its "Hello"?
> Who taught ravens to salute with a hollow sound?
> And magpies to attempt our words?

Neither does that which Homer writes fit here, that the *horse* of Achilles spoke with its Hero <margin>Iliad 16, verse 404.</margin> and predicted his death; nor the elm tree of Philostratus, which he asserts spoke with an articulate and womanly voice to Apollonius the Philosopher. You may call it a Diabolical trick, or excuse it as a personification. Otherwise, it is most tolerant of labors...

conspicuous, as if some part of that milky matter had not yet been fully cooked out, so that it might be doubted whether that entire matter or curd could have eventually hardened into a stone, if only the spider's body had been able to endure the burden of carrying it. The spider then went away somewhere with a swift pace, joyful as if after giving birth. It is a marvel! Neither Pliny, nor Albertus Magnus, nor Cardano, nor Aldrovandus—all keen investigators of nature—nor others who have written on gems and stones, have handed down anything concerning a spider-stone of this kind. This history is most true, and I would wish that no one doubt it, since I have handled that stone many times with these hands of mine. Since spiders therefore seem to possess a <term>bezoardic</term> <note>Bezoars were stony masses found in the guts of animals, believed to be universal antidotes to poison.</note> virtue, or even a magnetic one (inasmuch as they are believed to draw venom to themselves from rooms), servant girls do an injustice to the little creature when it has made a prey of poisonous atoms; for they not only destroy its work, the webs, with the stroke of their brooms, but also trample it underfoot when it is cast to the ground. From this, without a doubt, the actions of our lives can have an excellent <term>hieroglyphic</term> <note>In this period, "hieroglyphic" referred to a symbolic or moral lesson drawn from nature.</note>. For while the most industrious little creature either builds for itself a funeral shroud or a rope in which it is finally entangled and suffocated as if by its own bond, miserable mortals can learn by its example: that they often spend their talent and health in vain, exhausted by many labors to emerge on high, to flow with pleasures, or to acquire and retain vast treasures for themselves. In vain they run about, grow weary, sweat, and are weakened like spiders by the emptying of their own entrails; for when they have done all, they possess only spiders' webs and the work of a loom for catching flies. Often, in place of delights, they carry a small stone or a pebble within their own vitals and die in their own work: the days they hoped would be festive, they find to be fatal, with what they hoped would be a palace turned into a tomb. Perhaps it will not be incongruous to mention here: that spiders are a sweet food and nourishment for chickens; for even in the Court of Hesse-Darmstadt, a certain man of the Hessian nobility was known who hunted spiders no differently than wild game and devoured them as delicacies without any harm. The only thing that frightens most people away from spiders is the omen of some misfortune, namely when they go out beyond their webs and either cling to a wall opposite a person or are carried downward from on high before a person's face by a long thread drawn from the air. In what manner and by what instinct this happens, I most gladly remain ignorant, for who has ever explained every antipathy and sympathy of nature with perfect precision? Yet even if an unusual and unexpected encounter with a spider portends something unfavorable and is a symbol of an enemy gaping at another with poisonous hostility, who shall accuse it as the author of the misfortune? Unless one wishes to accuse the physician when he predicts a disease, or the Astrologer and the rooster if they foretell a storm. Concerning the **Tarantula**, which is of that genus of insects that kill with poison—a spider peculiar to Italy, especially Apulia, from whose town *Taranto* (as we now say for *Tarentum*) it received its name—they record this singular fact: If it bites someone, they remain in that state in which they were when bitten; if walking, they continue to walk; if dancing, they continue to dance; if laughing, they laugh; if weeping, they weep; if sleeping, they sleep: until the poison has been driven from the body, as recorded by *Alexander ab Alexandro* in *Genial Days*, book 2, chapter 17; *Camerarius*, volume 2, *Historical Meditations*, chapter 81, page 458; and *Gerhard Johann Vossius*, book 4, *On Idolatry*, chapter 96, page 1634. But enough concerning Spiders.

**THE RAM**, an animal most celebrated in Holy Scripture on account of sacrifices, is called <term>Ayil</term> <note>original: איל</note> by the Hebrews, having its name from strength and power, since it is not only the male and leader of the sheep, but also rejoices in those horns above the others. Great was its use in sacrifices. In the sacrificing of *Isaac*, by divine command, a **ram** was substituted, indicated by the initial letters <margin>Gen. 22:13</margin> <term>A. Y. L. — Elohim Yireh-Lo</term> <note>original: א. י. ל. — אלהים יראה-לו</note> *God will provide for himself*, caught by its horns among the thickets. For when Isaac was already twenty-five years old, if we believe *Josephus* in *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 1, chapter 14, God tested the faith of *Abraham* and demanded that he sacrifice his only son—sought with so many desires, raised with so many cares, and shown by so many promises to be the father of a famous and great authority—on Mount *Moriah*. *Abraham* obeys, and was just about to sacrifice his son on Mount *Moriah* when God called out that he should spare the only-begotten. Therefore, in his place, he sacrificed a **Ram** sticking there in the briars, and being praised by God in the name of obedience, he received the promise of a most abundant posterity and of the Messiah to be born from it. Concerning this, the <term>Recutiti</term> <note>A derogatory Latin term for Jews, referring to circumcision.</note> feign wonders, fabled that this ram had existed in that place from the beginning of the world specifically for the sake of a victim, and was created during the very six days of creation for the redemption of *Isaac* and destined for this use, as in *Pirkei Avot*, chapter 5, and *Rabbi Solomon Jarchi* <note>Rashi</note> in his commentary on this passage. There are those from the Christian school who assert that this ram was created immediately by God at that time, so that it might be a more illustrious testimony of divine providence. Most simply, with *Blessed Gerhard* in his *Commentary* on this passage, it was brought from elsewhere from the flocks by divine ordination through the ministry of Angels, and remained entangled in the briars of thorns by its horns. *Augustine* aims at this opinion in book 1, *On the Miracles of Holy Scripture*: <margin>Ch. 14.</margin>
> *It is asked,* he says, *whence was that ram in the wilderness? Whether, as some assert, the earth brought it forth in that hour, just as it produced cattle in the beginning? Or, lest God be said to have created that work after the sixth day, do we believe an Angel brought that Ram from elsewhere, just as an Angel transported Philip from elsewhere to Azotus, and Habakkuk is said to have been transported by an Angel to the Lions' Den to Daniel in Babylon.*

In the consecration of Aaron and his sons to the sacred office, God commands Moses to sacrifice a **Ram**, upon whose head *Aaron* and his sons are read to have laid their hands, *Exodus 29:1, 10, 15, 19*, and with its blood he should stain their ears, hand, and right foot. That ram is called <term>Ayil Milluim</term> <note>original: איל מלואים</note>, which is to say, *the ram of fillings*. The <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translates this as *perfection*, that is, *consecration* and *inauguration*; for "to perfect" also signifies to consecrate and inaugurate, whence also *Baptism* is called *perfection* among the Fathers; for *Gregory* often uses it of Baptism in *Against the Maccabees*: *The word is secret, very persuasive, at least to me and all who love God, that no one before the coming of Christ was perfected—* <meta>The text cuts off here with the catchword "perfected."</meta>

**THE DONKEY**, in Greek <term>onos</term> <note>ὄνος</note>, <gloss>as if "useful"</gloss> <note>Greek: ὀνητὸς</note>, according to the Etymologist, just as *jumentum* <note>beast of burden</note> comes from *juvando* <note>helping</note>. Every kind of living creature has its own familiar food; for donkeys, it is thorns and thistles, and when it is led through the grass, its mouth is restrained by a bridle so that it cannot feed on the herbs; at home it feeds on chaff, even though it carries the wheat to the mill and back. A good donkey lives on meager fodder, says Cornelius Agrippa in *On the Vanity of Sciences*, and is content with whatever kind, most tolerant of the penury of hunger, of labor, of blows, of negligence, and most patient of all persecution; of a most simple and poor Spirit, so that it does not know how to discern between lettuce and thistles, innocent and pure in heart, lacking gall, having peace with all living things, and patiently placing its back under all burdens. Donkeys are commonly accused of laziness and weariness, whence they also present a symbol of sloth; however, in Egypt and Palestine, donkeys seem to be exempt from this laziness and slowness. These are called "trotters" <note>Latin: tollutarii</note>, which can cover 40,000 paces in one day without harm, as was also reported by Scaliger against Cardanus in *Exercise 218*. <margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
conspicuous, as if some part of that milky matter had not yet been fully processed, so that it might be doubted whether that entire substance or curd could have eventually hardened into a stone, provided the spider's body had been able to bear the weight. The spider then departed somewhere with a swift pace, joyful as if after giving birth. It is a wonder! Neither Pliny, nor Albertus Magnus, nor Cardano, nor Aldrovandus—all keen investigators of nature—nor others who have written on gems and stones, have handed down anything concerning a "spider-stone" of this kind. This history is most true, nor would I wish anyone to doubt it, since I have frequently handled that stone with these hands of mine. Since spiders therefore seem to possess a bezoartic <note>Bezoar: a stone-like mass found in the stomachs of animals, historically believed to be an antidote to poison.</note> or even a magnetic power—inasmuch as they are believed to draw venom to themselves from rooms—maidservants do an injustice to the little creature when it has made a prey of poisonous atoms; for they not only destroy its work, the webs, with the stroke of their brooms, but also crush it with their feet when it is cast to the ground. From this, without doubt, the actions of our lives can have an excellent hieroglyphic <note>In this context, a "hieroglyphic" refers to a symbolic or moral emblem found in nature.</note>. For while the most industrious little creature either builds for itself a funeral shroud or a rope in which it is finally entangled and suffocated as if by its own bond, wretched mortals can learn by its example: that having exhausted themselves with many labors to rise high, to abound in pleasures, and to acquire and retain vast treasures for themselves, they often spend their talent and health in vain. In vain they run about, grow weary, sweat, and are weakened like spiders by the emptying of their own vitals; for when they have done all, they possess only spiders' webs and the work of a loom fit for catching flies, and often carry a pebble or stone within their own vitals instead of delights, and die in their own work. The days they hoped would be festive, they find to be fatal, with what they hoped would be a palace turned into a tomb. Perhaps it will not be incongruous to mention here: that spiders are a sweet food and nourishment for hens; for even in the Court of Hesse-Darmstadt, a certain man of the Hessian nobility was known who hunted spiders no differently than wild game and devoured them as delicacies without any harm. The only thing that deters most people from spiders is the omen of some misfortune, namely when they go outside their webs and either cling to a wall opposite a person or are carried downward from on high before a person's face by a long thread drawn from the air. In what manner and by what instinct this happens, I am most content to be ignorant; for who has ever explained every antipathy and sympathy of nature with precision? Yet even if an unusual and unexpected encounter with a spider portends something unlucky and is a symbol of an enemy gasping for another with poisonous hostility, who shall accuse it as the author of the misfortune? Unless one wishes to accuse a physician when he predicts a disease, or an astrologer and a rooster if they foretell a storm. Concerning the Tarantula, which is of that genus of insects that kill with poison, a spider peculiar to Italy, especially Apulia, from whose town Taranto (as we now say for Tarentum) it took its name, they relate this singular thing:

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
If it bites someone, they remain in that state in which they were when bitten: if walking, they walk; if dancing, they continue to dance; if laughing, they laugh; if weeping, they weep; if sleeping, they sleep; until the poison has been driven from the body, as Alexander ab Alexandro records in *Genial Days, book 2, chapter 17*; Camerarius in *Historical Meditations, vol. 2, chapter 81, p. 458*; and Gerhard Johann Vossius in *On Idolatry, book 4, chapter 96, p. 1634*. But enough concerning the Spider.

## **THE RAM**, an animal most celebrated in Holy Scripture on account of sacrifices, is called **Ayil** <note>Hebrew: איל</note> by the Hebrews, having a name derived from strength and power, as it is not only the male and leader of the sheep, but also rejoices in those horns above the others. Its use in sacrifices was great. In the sacrifice of Isaac, a ram is substituted by divine command <note>Genesis 22:13</note>, indicated by the initial letters of verse 8: **Elohim yireh-lo** (God will provide for himself) <note>Hebrew: אלהים יראה-לו</note>, found entangled by its horns among the thickets. For when Isaac was already twenty-five years old, if we believe Josephus (*Antiquities of the Jews, book 1, chapter 14*), God tested the faith of Abraham and demanded that he sacrifice his only son—sought with so many desires, raised with so many cares, and shown by so many promises to be the father of a famous and great authority—on Mount Moriah. Abraham obeys, and was just about to sacrifice his son on Mount Moriah when God called out that he should spare his only-born. Therefore, in his place, he sacrificed a Ram sticking there in the brambles, and having been praised by God in the name of obedience, he received the promise of a most abundant posterity and of the Messiah to be born from it. Concerning this, the Circumcised <note>A historical term for Jewish scholars/rabbis.</note> feign wonders, fabled that this ram existed in that place from the beginning of the world specifically for the purpose of a victim, and was created during the six days of creation for Isaac's redemption and destined for this use (*Pirkei Avot, chapter 5*; Rabbi Solomon Jarchi in his *gloss on this passage*). There are those from the Christian school who assert that this ram was created immediately by God at that time, so that it might be a more illustrious testimony of divine providence. Most simply, with Blessed Gerhard (*Commentary on this passage*), we believe it was brought from elsewhere from the flocks by divine ordination through the ministry of Angels, and remained entangled in the brambles of thorns by its horns. Augustine aims at this opinion in *On the Miracles of Holy Scripture, book 1*:
<margin>ch. 14</margin>
> It is asked, he says, whence was that ram in the wilderness? Did the earth bring this forth in that hour, as some assert, just as it produced cattle in the beginning? Or, lest God be said to have created that work from the earth after the sixth day, do we believe an Angel brought that Ram from elsewhere? Just as the Angel transported Philip from the Eunuch to Azotus, and as the Angel is said to have transported Habakkuk to the Lions' Den to Daniel in Babylon.

In the consecration of Aaron and his sons to the sacred office, God commands Moses to sacrifice a Ram, upon whose head Aaron and his sons are read to have laid their hands (Exodus 29:1, 10, 15, 19), and with its blood he should touch their ears, hand, and right foot. That ram is called **Ayil Milluim** <note>Hebrew: איל מלואים</note>, as if to say "the ram of fillings." The Septuagint translates this as **teleiōsin** <note>Greek: τελείωσιν</note>, that is, *consecration* and *inauguration*; **teleioun** <note>Greek: τελειοῦν</note> also signifies to consecrate and inaugurate, whence Baptism among the Fathers is called **teleiōsis** <note>Greek: τελείωσις</note>. For Gregory often uses this regarding Baptism in *Against the Maccabees*: **"The word is still secret, yet very persuasive, at least to me and all who love God, that no one before the presence of grace is perfected—"** <note>Original Greek: Ἀπόῤῥητος ἔτι ὁ λόγος... τελειωθῆναι. The text cuts off at the catchword.</note>
<meta>catchword: —to be perfected,</meta>

# From Psalm 50, verses 10, 11.

<margin>
Sacred History of Animals, Book 5, verse 5, concerning L. L.
</margin>
...of mortals, apart from faith in God, to obtain this. <note>original: "θνητῶν, δίχα τῆς εἰς θεὸν πίστεως, τοῦτο τυχεῖν"</note> And Eusebius in *Ecclesiastical History*: *The remains of those even more perfect among mortals were brought back into the seats of power.* <note>original: "Τῶν δὲ καὶ τελειοτέρων, θνητῶν ἐν ταῖς ἐξουσίαις ἐπανεκομίσθη τὰ λείψανα."</note>
The **Ram** was also not excluded from the sacred rites of the Heathens; indeed, according to Varro, the Ram was sacrificed in the Agonalia with solemn pomp: *The Agonal Days*, he says, *during which the King sacrifices a ram in the Palace, are named from 'agon' [the struggle], because the Prince of the city was asked [interrogabatur], and the prince of the flock is sacrificed.* Finally, the Ram exhibits a figure of various things;
<margin>Daniel 8:3 and following.</margin>
Under the type of the two-horned ram, the second Monarchy <note>The Medo-Persian Empire</note> is displayed, of which *one horn* represents the Medes, and the *other, indeed the larger one*, the Persians, which grew far higher than the Median, and pushed toward the West, toward Asia Minor and Syria; toward the North, toward Lydia, Cappadocia, Armenia, Iberia, the Chalcidians, and the Caspians; toward the South, toward Arabia, Judea, Egypt, and Ethiopia. Concerning the <term>prototypes</term> <note>original: "ὑποτυπώσεις" - early symbolic models</note> of the Ram in the sacrifices of the Old Testament, I shall say nothing, but for the sake of brevity, I refer the Benevolent Reader to others who have treated the types of sacrifices professionally.

**THE DONKEY**, in Greek *onos*, from *oninein* [to help/profit], according to the Etymologist, just as *jumentum* [beast of burden] is from *juvando* [helping]. In Hebrew *chamor*, according to Rabbi Bechai on *Genesis 2*, so called from *chamor*, that is, from carrying measures or heaps of grain: Others derive it from *chamar*, *he grew red*, from the red color with which almost all donkeys in the East were endowed. Hence they were hated by the Egyptians, and cast down from precipices by the Copts, on account of the "Red Typhon" and their "donkey-like color," <note>original: "ὀνάδην τὴν χρόαν"</note> according to Plutarch in *On Isis and Osiris*. The Donkey is an animal of the most abject nature and the most sluggish disposition; if anyone seeks to gain utility from it, he must have clubs and whips at hand. Hugo Cardinalis <margin>on Luke 19.</margin> includes its properties in these verses:
> Food, bed, lazy, cross, voice, mind, burden, offspring,
> *The little donkey is unclean, strong in the rear, and lewd.*

To every kind of living creature its own food is familiar; for donkeys, thorns and thistles, and when it is led through the grass, its mouth is restrained by a bridle lest it feed on the herbs; at home it feeds on chaff, even though it carries wheat to the mill and brings it back. *A good donkey lives on meager fodder*, says Cornelius <margin>chapter 102, page 308.</margin> Agrippa in *The Vanity of the Sciences*, *and is content with whatever kind, most tolerant of the penury of hunger, labor, blows, negligence, and most patient of every perfection; of a most simple and poor Spirit, so that it does not know how to discern between lettuce and thistles; with an innocent and pure heart, and lacking gall, having peace with all living creatures, and patiently placing its back under all burdens.* Donkeys are commonly accused of laziness and weariness, whence they also display a symbol of sloth; yet in Egypt and Palestine, donkeys seem to be exempt from this laziness and slowness, being called "trotters," which can cover 40,000 paces in one day without harm, as was also reported by Scaliger against Cardanus in *Exercise 218*. Indeed, in Arabia, donkeys are found equal or superior to horses in speed. Concerning which <margin>page 256.</margin> Xenophon writes in *Book 1 of the Expedition of Cyrus*: *And the donkeys, whenever anyone pursued them, having run ahead, would stand still (for they ran much faster than the horse), and again when the horse approached, they did the same.* <note>original Greek: "Καὶ οἱ ὄνοι ἐπεί τις διώκοι, προδραμόντες ἀνειστήκεισαν..."</note> *Indeed those donkeys, if anyone pursued, ran ahead (since they were much faster than the horse); likewise, as the horse came nearer, <margin>Book 1 on Job 1, page 425.</margin> they did the same.* Origen writes the same concerning the speed of donkeys

<column-break/>

in Arabia and Palestine: *What horses and mules now perform, this the donkey animals nonetheless fulfilled; especially such as are the donkeys in the region of Arabia and of the Palestinians, which are similarly swift as horses.* The almost common and daily use of donkeys for riding among the Palestinians distinguishes those of that region from our own, since, as Scripture testifies, not only commoners but even the more noble used this means of riding. Jair, to whom the office of judge fell <margin>Judges 10:3, 4.</margin> among the Israelites after Tola (an obscure man), was an illustrious man, noble in power, the majesty of his riding, and the command of cities; nor was he less happy in the number of his children, for he had thirty sons, riding <insert>upon thirty colts</insert>, understand, *of donkeys*, which meaning Piscator thinks holds place everywhere for the word *ayir*, compare *Zechariah 9:9, Genesis 49:11, Judges 12:14, Isaiah 30:6*; although others understand it as excellent and young mules: others, however, as young horses. But since there was a small supply of horses in Palestine, and on the contrary a great supply of donkeys and mules, the former opinion seems preferable to the latter. Thus in *Judges 12:14*, mention is made of another Judge, named Abdon the Pirathonite, who had forty sons, and <insert>thirty sons of sons</insert> [grandsons], riding <insert>upon seventy colts</insert>. Not to mention that the chief wealth of the Orientals, especially the Arabs, was placed in the number of <insert>she-asses</insert>, as witnessed by the example of Job, <margin>chapter 42, verse 12.</margin> who before his plundering had five hundred she-asses, but after the divine restoration, a thousand. Thus from the Midianites, the prey of the Israelites in donkeys alone was one out of sixty thousand <insert>donkeys</insert> *Numbers 31:39, 45.* Likewise the Reubenites with their confederates plundered two thousand <insert>she-asses</insert> from the Hagrites. *The voice of the donkey is to bray, whence it is said 'onkhasthai' from 'onkan'*, *to bray*, concerning which <margin>1 Chronicles 5:21.</margin> Gataker writes in *Miscellanies, chapter 3, page 10.* The she-ass of Balaam indeed had articulate speech, and that only from the power of God; for brutes do not by nature either utter articulate voices or understand those brought forth by others. Porphyry indeed <margin>Book on Abstinence.</margin> attributes speech to living creatures, adding that Apollonius of Tyana, Melampus, Tiresias, and Thales understood and judged the speeches of brutes: which some of the Hebrew Doctors also believed to be so, according to Abulensis, <margin>on 3 Kings 3.</margin> asserting that Solomon understood the voices of all things. However, since articulate voice proceeds from mind and reason, and the meanings of words are not natural but from imposition, nothing will be gained here for the animals; nor will the *Parrot*, or the *Raven*, or the *Starling*, or the *Magpie* commonly provide proof, which are taught with long labor to return some words obscurely; for these are not properly articulate voices, and, as Persius says: *Satires, Prologue.*
> Who expedited for the Parrot its "hello"? <note>original: "χαῖρε"</note>
> Who taught ravens to salute from the hollow?
> And taught magpies to attempt our words?

Neither does that which Homer writes fit here, <margin>Iliad 16, verse 404.</margin> that the horse of Achilles spoke with his Hero and predicted death for him; nor the elm tree of Philostratus, which he asserts spoke with an articulate and womanly voice to Apollonius the Philosopher. You may call it a Diabolical trick, or excuse it through <term>personification</term> <note>original: "prosopopoeiam"</note>. Otherwise, the animal is most tolerant of labors...

# SACRED BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...most [patient]; hence it matters little to the donkey whom he serves, for no more can be laid upon him than he is able to carry. Thus Phaedrus in Book 1, Fable 15:
> ->*A timid old man was grazing a little donkey in a meadow:*<-
> ->*Terrified by the sudden shout of the enemy,*<-
> ->*He urged the donkey to flee so he might not be captured.*<-
> ->*But he, sluggish, asked: "Do you think the victor*<-
> ->*Will place double pack-saddles upon me?"*<-
> ->*The old man said no. "Then what does it matter to me*<-
> ->*Whom I serve, as long as I carry my pack-saddle?"*<-

The donkey is a symbol of servitude, since bitter labors must always be endured by him, and the harshest things must be borne; and for these he does not receive oats like a horse, but hard and rough fodder. No labor is more troublesome than the donkey's, nor more annoying due to its sluggishness, yet none is more patient under the lash. He does not kick back, nor raise his feet against an angry driver. He proceeds with a slow step and carries the sack placed upon him with great patience. Because of his portion of burdens and tributes, Issachar, in his descendants,
<margin>Genesis 49:14, 15.</margin>
is called by his father Jacob *chamor garem* <note>Hebrew: חמור גרם</note>, a *bony donkey*, that is, robust, strong in bone, and powerful. The Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> rendered this as "he desired the good," for instead of *chamor* (donkey), they read *chemed* (good desire); and for *garem* (bone), they read *garah* (he desired). In this prophecy, the tribe of Issachar is compared to a donkey, an animal fit for carrying
<margin>Commentary on this place, p. 847.</margin>
burdens but sluggish by nature. The tribe of Issachar was strong and "bony"—these are the words of Blessed Gerhard—in war (Judges 5:14) and in the wars which the Zebulunites waged for David (1 Chronicles 12:32). It signifies, therefore, that this tribe would be most tolerant of burdens and labors, performing nothing worthy of high praise, accepting the tributes imposed by the Israelite Kings, and resting in a peaceful place within its borders—that is, between the Sea of Galilee and Mount Tabor on one side, and the Jordan on the other, in the middle of the land of Canaan. Moses repeats the same prophecy in Deuteronomy 33:18. Regarding this
<margin>f. 75. b.</margin>
prophecy of Issachar's descendants, Victorinus Strigelius speaks thus in his *History of Joseph*: *Issachar had this prerogative over his other brothers: namely, a fertile land situated as if in the middle of the region. He is called a sluggish donkey by a Homeric metaphor, in which Ajax retreating is compared to a donkey slowly leaving the cornfields, even if he is fatigued by the blows of boys. For just as a donkey is driven with difficulty from good pastures—indeed, he prefers to endure any burdens rather than be deprived of the sweetness of the crops—so Issachar was a Theban farmer, who did not seek military glory and patiently bore the burdens imposed by Kings.*
<margin>Iliad, book 11, v. 557.</margin>
Strigelius refers to a similar passage in Homer, where he compares Ajax, "the great son of Telamon," to a donkey led into deep corn, but driven out of the corn by boys with blows only with difficulty. Then he calls him a "Theban farmer" by allusion, for the Boeotian field was far more fertile and produced sweeter fruits than the sandy and sterile Attic soil. While in the blessing of Judah mention is also made of the son of a she-donkey tied to a choice vine,
<margin>p. 267.</margin>
Bacon, in *The Advancement of Learning* (Book 8, ch. 3), acutely applies this to subjects of different conditions in various kingdoms, when he explores their fortune to judge the state of the Kingdom and Empire: *The blessing of Judah and Issachar will never meet in one; namely, that the same tribe or nation should be at once a lion's whelp and a donkey crouching between burdens.*

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
Nor will it ever happen that a people oppressed by tributes will stand forth as strong and warlike. Subjects are made into "donkeys" in various ways through different modes of exactions: through sacred taxes, "excises" as they are called, through tributes, subsidies, collections, and other nomenclatures newly devised by Tax-gatherers, of which a single page would hardly suffice to list each and every one. Jerome explains the "bony donkey" mystically, understanding by it the Gentiles, who, carrying Christ and offering gifts to Him, desire the safe rest of eternal life. His words are these: *Issachar, which is interpreted as "reward," refers to the people of the nations, whom the Lord purchased with the price of His blood. He is written as a strong donkey because previously the Gentile people were like a brute and luxurious animal, subsisting by no reason, but afterward they willingly bore the yoke of Gospel discipline. To lie down between the borders is to rest while waiting for the end of the world, seeking nothing of those things in the middle, but desiring the ultimate things. And the strong donkey sees rest and the best land when simple Gentility raises itself to the strength of good work and tends toward the fatherland of eternal life. Whence he also applies his shoulder to carrying, because when he desires to reach the promised rest, he willingly carries all the burdens of the commandments. Whence he was made a servant to tributes, that is, to Christ the King, offering the gifts of his faith and the presents of good works.* Under the old law, God exempted the donkey from sacrifices; when He ordered every firstborn to be killed in sacrifice, He spared only donkeys along with humans, permitting the human to be redeemed by a price, and a sheep to be exchanged for the donkey (Exodus 13:11).
<margin>Exodus 13:11.</margin>
From this arose the Gentile fable about the Jews worshipping a donkey in their sacred rites, although Tacitus and Plutarch write that the worship of the donkey originated from the fact that the Jews, with a donkey showing the way, found water while living in the desert of Arabia. The same calumny regarding the worship of a donkey's head was also brought against the Christians: *I hear,* says Minutius in *Octavius*, *that they, by some inept persuasion, venerate the consecrated head of a donkey, the most shameful of beasts.* Whence they were called *Asinarii* (donkey-worshippers), as Tertullian indicates in *Apology*, ch. 16. Indeed, from this, Christ was
<margin>Book 1, ch. 14.</margin>
depicted by a certain scoundrel (according to the same witness) with donkey ears, one foot hoofed, carrying a book, and wearing a toga with an inscription of this sort: THE GOD OF THE CHRISTIANS, ONONYCHITES <note>Likely meaning "donkey-hoofed"</note>. Regarding the last word of the inscription, these are the words of Gerhard Vossius (Book 3, ch. 75, p. 1136): the manuscripts do not agree. In the printed editions it is *ononychites*; but the MSS have *onochotes*, *onocholises*, *onochoutis*, *onochorfitis*, *onochotafis*. *Onocorsues* is preferred by some due to the authority of the Vatican MSS, which Francis Junius confirms is written there, meaning "from a donkey and a head" <note>Greek: apo tou onou kai korses</note>. Jacques Godefroy suggests *onochostes*, as if you were to say "priest of the donkey" <note>Greek: tou onou choetes</note>, a word fashioned from the fact that *choai* are sacrifices. Nicolas Rigault preferred *onokoites*, that is, "donkey-progeny." Others have devised yet other things. Balthasar Bonifacius deals with the head of the donkey as a consecrated deity in a specific chapter (Book 6, *Ludicrous History*, 30). Cosmas of Prague indicates in the *Bohemian Chronicle* that the Bohemians once sacrificed to a donkey. And Clement of Rome is the authority that the Scythians offered a donkey to Mars. Among the foods prohibited by God, donkey meat is also included.

It also addresses historical slanders against Jews and early Christians involving "donkey worship" (Onolatry).</summary>

# From Psalm 50, verse 10. II.

<margin>Sacred History of Animals, book 1, on the power of food, chapter 2.</margin>
...of the donkey, from the eating of which even the Saracens abstain, according to Avenzoar <note>original: "Theifer l. II. 2. f. 18."</note>, and those who do eat them are called "donkey-like" by Galen. The animal is known for its lustfulness, as the Prophet says: *with a passion for the bedding*
<margin>Ezekiel 23:20.</margin>
*of those whose flesh is like the flesh of donkeys.* The donkey is a lustful animal, endowed with a very large member for that purpose. Whence the Prophet, rebuking the insane lust of the Israelites, denotes its foulness by the nature of the donkey and the horse, which are most potent in that part. Jerome says on this passage: *She once raved for the bedding of the Egyptians, whose flesh is in the likeness of donkeys: and so large is the flow of seed, or the shameful parts so great, that they surpass the deformity of horses.* Peter Damian, Bishop of Ostia, holds nearly the same in his *Letter to the Hermit Brothers concerning the apparition of Pope Benedict in the monstrous form of a donkey and a bear after his death:* *Because that miserable man, from the very beginning of his Papacy until the end of his life, wallowed in the filth of luxury, it was not seen as incongruous for him to begin with the ears and end in the tail of a donkey. For the donkey is a luxurious animal, just as the Prophet designates when he speaks of one devoted to the uncleanness of the flesh: And their flesh is the flesh of the donkey.* And Bernard of Cluny <note>original: "Bernhardus Morlanensis"</note> in book 2 of *On Contempt for the World*:

> The Donkey-folk, forever drunk, live in luxury,
> While the sober life and chaste grace are reviled.
> Each one, like a beast or a leaping horse, whinnies toward crime;
> He leaps for Venus <note>Lust</note>, cherishes her, feeds her, and from this produces evil.

<margin>Jeremiah 22:19.</margin>
Those who live thus are worthy, indeed most worthy, of the "burial of a donkey," which God threatens against Jehoiakim, the most wicked King of Judah: <heb>קבורת חמור</heb>, *he shall be buried with the burial of a donkey*, that is, *an unburied burial*, as Cicero calls it in the first Philippic. It follows: *dragged and cast out beyond the gates of Jerusalem.* To be buried and to be cast out unburied like a donkey are opposites, and yet they are joined here to indicate the frustration of King Jehoiakim's hope for a royal burial and funeral rites.
<margin>2 Chronicles 36:6.</margin>
This was fulfilled by Nebuchadnezzar, who, having entered Jerusalem, bound Jehoiakim in chains to lead him away to Babylon, but later, having changed his plan, killed him and ordered him to be cast unburied outside the walls, as Josephus records <note>Antiquities of the Jews, book 10, chapter 8</note>. The burial of a donkey is the shameful discarding of a corpse. A dead body that perished by its own hand <note>Greek: αὐτοχειρίᾳ - suicide</note> was dragged from the house by ropes through the door or through a hole and pit dug under the threshold of the house where the person had brought death upon themselves; this is called a *canine burial* <note>dog's burial</note>, as noted in the gloss on the text in the chapter *placuit*, on the word "to burial" <note>Canon Law reference</note>, and there exists an addition to the gloss of Saxon Law <note>Landrecht lib. 2. art. 31.</note>. I believe what has been said so far is not "to fall from a donkey" <note>Greek: ἐξ ὄνου βαλεῖν - a proverb for something trivial or clumsy</note>, unless you think these things are "seeking wool from a donkey" <note>Greek: ἀπ' ὄνου ζητεῖν πόκας - seeking the impossible</note>. Ludovicus Vives relates a ridiculous deed
<margin>On the City of God, chapter 16.</margin>
in his notes on book 10 of Augustine: that in those times the people were so mindless that, led by vain errors, they believed the Moon had been swallowed by a donkey; for while a donkey was drinking from a river, as is its custom, the image of the Moon reflecting in the river had suddenly hidden itself behind an opposing cloud. For this reason, the poor donkey was driven into prison and, after a legal

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred History of Animals p. 31. Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer p. 72.</margin>
interrogation, was cut open so that it might return the Moon to the world. One sheep is not more like another than that fable of the "Verpuli" <note>a derogatory term for Jews</note> regarding Abraham’s donkey. For thus says Rabbi Eliezer: *Abraham rose early in the morning and took Ishmael, Eliezer, and Isaac his son: and he saddled the donkey (this donkey was the foal of that donkey which was created in the twilight of the Sabbath eve) as it is said: And Abraham rose early and saddled the donkey. This was the donkey upon which Moses sat when he came into Egypt, according to the text: Moses took his wife and his sons and set them upon a donkey. This also will be the donkey upon which the son of David <note>the Messiah</note> shall sit.* I wonder if anyone is so lacking in all sense
<margin>Zechariah 9:9.</margin>
as not to marvel at this most beautiful "agreement of donkeys," and not to marvel even more at how aptly donkeys match donkeys in the Rabbis' pairings <note>Greek: συζυγίες</note>. These and similar comments deserve Satire more than a modest speech; whence Willem Vorstius shrewdly observed:
<margin>Among the Animals, p. 207.</margin>
*This little fable about Abraham's donkey can rightly be placed among stupid and donkey-like ravings. A subject truly worthy of Rabbinic sharp-wittedness, that it should be exercised not only on the genealogy of men but even of this donkey. They make the parent of this donkey the donkey of Balaam, which they claim was created at the twilight of the Sabbath. It must be that this donkey of Abraham, Moses, and the Messiah is of a prodigious old age, or like the first serpent, sheds its old age every seven years.* But let us stop <note>Greek: παῦσα</note>, lest we give "a sheep instead of an egg" <note>Greek: ἀντ' ᾠοῦ ὃϊς - a proverb for a poor trade or non-sequitur</note>.

**ASP** <note>Latin: Aspis</note>, called *Pethen* <heb>פתן</heb> by the Hebrews, is a most venomous animal of the serpent kind. For there are various species of serpents, almost all of which Venantius Fortunatus

included in these verses:

> The viper, the chersydros, the seps, the dragon, the cenchris, the hybris.
The same in his poem on the joys of eternal life, verse 153:
> The viper, the seps, the dart-snake, the basilisk, the hemorrhöis, the asp,

The *Chersydros*, which Venantius also mentions, is the same as what is called the *Chelydros*. Others distinguish them, such as Lucan and the most ancient writers. A more recent age wrongly confuses them. It is called *chersou* because it stays in both water and land, *because it spends time in water and on dry land* <note>Greek: διὰ τὸ ἐν ὕδατι καὶ ἐν χέρσῳ διατρίβειν</note>, as the Interpreter of Nicander has it; for that poet, the *chelyndros* is a *drines* <margin>page 21.</margin> and perhaps *achelous* and *drys*, but the *chersydros* is the same as the *hydros*, which also lives on land. Solinus in chapter 2 testifies that Calabria is very crowded with *Chelydri*, where some editions have *chersydri*; Salmasius prefers the former (p. 86). But to the Asp, of which three primary kinds are reviewed: the *ptyas*, the *chersaia* (land-asp), and the *chelidonia* (swallow-asp), as Aegineta teaches from Galen (book 5, chapter 19; compare Gerard Johann Vossius, book 4 on Idolatry, 46, p. 1496). This species of serpent—I mean the asp—is not seen as frequently in Europe as in Egypt, on the banks of the Nile. It is established not only from the book of nature that this serpent is exceedingly poisonous. For the initiates of nature testify concerning its poison that its power is so great that it makes a wound altogether incurable, and such a great convulsion follows that the sick person can scarcely survive for more than a few hours. Furthermore, its bite is so tiny that it is hardly perceived by the senses, or looks like a pinprick. Finally, on account of the violence of the poison, it immediately seeks the heart and hastens death. Of these, the Libyan asp alone...
