# SACRED HISTORY OF ANIMALS

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
It is said to blind a man with its breath, as Aelian says in book 6 *On Animals, chapter 38.* Queen Cleopatra of Egypt, being aware of this fact, chose the bite of the asp as a milder kind of death than if she were to drink poison or fall upon a sword. The asp does not inject poison with its tail, as some say, but in the manner of other serpents, it breathes it into a wound made by its iron-like teeth from tiny hollows beneath the teeth, where it keeps the poison reserved in a small skin for those purposes.
<margin>Psalm 140:4</margin>
The Psalmist refers to this regarding slanderers: *The poison of asps is under their lips.* We also have information from the Holy Scriptures about this serpent, that it is exceedingly poisonous; in *Deuteronomy* 32:33 its poison is called <term>חֵמַת</term> <note>Hebrew: chemat</note>, *cruel*. This intensity is increased by the great cunning found in it: for they say the asp departs thirty days before the flooding of the Nile and hides itself in the grass or in the sand, so that only the protrusions of its head stick out, which are commonly called horns. When small birds see these (for they are similar to grains of wheat), they fly down as if to food, and thus perish miserably and are killed by the asp.
<margin>Genesis 3:1</margin>
Moses is a witness to its craftiness, where the serpent is called <term>φρονιμώτατος</term> <note>Greek: phronimotatos; most wise/prudent</note>, as the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> has it, or as Aquila says, <term>πανῦργος</term> <note>Greek: panourgos; knavish/clever</note>, which Jerome translates as *shifty* <note>Latin: versipellis; literally "changing skin"</note>. They do not have strong sight for reasons enumerated by Vossius in book 4 *On Idolatry, chapter 54, page 1490.*
<margin>Psalm 58:5</margin>
Meanwhile, their hearing is proven by the words of the Psalmist: *Like the poison of a deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not listen to the voice of charmers.* Cardanus believed and wrote many superstitious things, yet he did not believe the Asp could be restrained by incantation, in book 2 *On Poisons, page 953.* Those who write that diseases can be cured through words and characters try to prove this very thing from the Royal Prophet <note>King David</note>; since the asp, upon seeing one who wishes to charm it, stops its ears so as not to hear, and thus renders the song ineffective. From this they cry out that the power of the song is so great that even Asps dread it. But among those skilled in Nature, there is deep silence on this matter. And I believe this moved Grevinus to write in his first book on Poisons: *This can hardly be believed, yet it should not be entirely rejected, as he may have spoken in a poetic manner.* Indeed, the place from which that passage is taken is a poetic work; and it is more likely that the Psalmist does not mean a literal *stopping of the ears*, but signifies a <term>μεταφορὰν</term> <note>Greek: metaphoran; metaphor</note>; that the asp acts as if it despises the song, and has become plainly deaf to it. Therefore, the meaning of the Psalmist would be: So great is the fury of his enemies that it can no more be mitigated than an asp is moved by the song of a charmer. For his enemies are just as deaf as the asp is deaf to such a human song.
<margin>Jeremiah 8:17</margin>
As you may also read in *Jeremiah 8:17*: *Behold, I will send serpents among you, basilisks, for which there is no charm, and they shall bite you.* The highest conclusion from this is that it was customary for Magi to sing songs to Serpents: but, as I think, they will never prove from this that there is any power in that song, or that serpents know this by their shrewdness and thus craftily stop their ears lest they hear. See Vossius, book 1 *On Idolatry, 8, pages 61, 62* and also book 4, chapter 54, page 1490. Compare Scaliger’s *Commentary on book 2 of the History of Animals, 18, section 123.* Also B. Frantzius, *History of Animals, part 4, chapter 2, page 726*, who explains this text as an asp ruled by the Devil for the sake of the charmer. Although the voice of the charmer may be indomitable, as

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
is believable, nevertheless among the Egyptians it is customary for them to be tamed; for when called by boys, it comes out of its cages and approaches those calling. It is summoned by the snapping of fingers, and comes to tables where wine and honeyed morsels are laid out, which the asps eat; compare B. Frantzius in the place cited, page 724.
<margin>Isaiah 11:8</margin>
Isaiah seems to have looked toward this taming of asps when he mentions this most venomous and harmful kind of serpent to emphasize the happiness of the time under the Messiah, when even men of the most diverse character, who were otherwise ferocious, shall return to favor with a changed nature and worship God in the same Church. For when he says, *The nursing child shall play over the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the den of the adder (or basilisk);* by this figurative speech he understands that there will be the greatest harmony between the good and the bad.

### THE SILKWORM.

Nature reveals itself most especially in the smallest things. Nature produced the *bombyx* <note>The silkworm</note>, a lowly little animal that surpasses even the Phrygians, those most celebrated craftsmen. *Bombyx* is a Greek word, although scholars do not yet agree on its origin. For some derive it <term>ἀπὸ τὸ βομβεῖν</term> <note>Greek: apo to bombein; from "to buzz"</note>, which is the sound proper to bees and wasps, referring to the sound which silkworms make at the time when they have become butterflies. They say the sound is a <term>βόμβον</term> <note>Greek: bombon; a buzzing/booming</note>; whether it is made by the mouth or the wings, Francis Bacon of Verulam teaches in *Century 2 of his Natural History, section 175.*
<margin>Book 12 of the Etymologies, chapter 5.</margin>
Another derivation of the word pleases Isidore of Seville, who says: *The Bombyx is a worm of the leaves, from whose weaving silk cloth is made; it is called by this name because it is emptied out while it generates threads, and only air remains in it.* Among the Hebrews you will find no term suited to this, except that in *Leviticus 11:22*, <term>סָלְעָם</term> <note>Hebrew: solam</note>, which the Septuagint, and with them the Vulgate, Pagninus, and Vatablus, have translated as *attacus* <note>A type of locust</note>. Junius, however, translates it as *bombyx*. But the Talmudists write that a species of locust without wings is noted, in the *Book Chullin, chapter 3, folio 65.* It is so called because it delights in rocks, from <term>סלע</term> <note>Hebrew: sela</note>, *rock*. To others, however, the word is a root: they say this creature has a cavity, lacks a tail, and has an oblong head. To the Germans, it is the *Seidenwurm* <note>Silkworm</note>. Its synonym is *Ser*, from the *Seres*, that people of India <note>Ancient term for the Chinese</note>; the little worm is so called because it is not only found in great numbers among them, but also was spread from that people and region into all parts of the whole world. Regarding the Seres, the peoples of India, one should read Solinus, Stephanus, and Martinius in the *Philosophical Lexicon*; Alciatus in *Parerga, book 6, chapter 25*; and Abraham Peritsol in chapter 9. In the *Paths of the World*, he calls the kingdom of Serica <term>גָּדוֹל וְנִפְלָא</term> <note>Hebrew: gadol ve-nifla</note>, *great and wonderful*; his words are cited by Constantinus L'Empereur in his notes on *Benjamin of Tudela’s Itinerary, pages 208, 209.* Serica, unknown to Ptolemy, is today bounded by Cathay to the west, and Scythia, which is beyond the Imaus mountains. To the North by Great Tartary. To the south and East by India beyond the Ganges and the kingdom of China, which today the Tartars from the kingdom of Niuche <note>The Manchus</note> have entirely occupied; see Johann Neuhoff’s *Description of a Chinese Journey*. The city of Sera is today called Sindifu by merchants, and is located in the farthest parts of Serica toward the east; compare Cluverius, *Introduction to Geography, book 5, chapter 2*; Scaliger, *Exercise 158, section 9, page 530.* From these Seres, the peoples of India, the Persians, Medes, and Assyrians, as well as the Egyptians, formerly received [silk]...

# From Psalm 50, verses 10–11

<margin>Sacred History of Animals, Book 1. Persia.</margin> We have no doubt, for the ancient Greeks—who had little or no knowledge of the Chinese <note>original: *Serum*</note> and Indians—called that "Median clothing" which was later named "Seric" (silk). Thus Procopius says: *This is the raw silk from which they are accustomed to make the garments that the Greeks of old called Median, but now call Seric.* Suidas in his Lexicon says: *Seric is raw silk,* etc., citing the same words of Procopius; compare Bayfius *On Clothing, chapter 5.* But what is *metaxa* <note>Greek: *μέταξα*, a term for raw silk</note>? It seems the Greeks took this word from the ancient Romans, though writers vary on what it specifically indicates. But *Metaxa* seems to be not just any silk, but only that which is rough and raw; compare Scaliger in the work cited above, and Nicolaus Fuller, *Sacred Miscellany, Book 2, chapter 11, page 248.* Isidore, in *Origins, Book 19, chapter 29*, not inappropriately derives *metaxa* from *metago* (to lead around), from the circling of the threads, because raw silk was gathered into balls, as Bernardino Baldi teaches us in his commentary on Vitruvius. Among the Hebrews, there is an allusive word <term>meshi (משי)</term>, which the Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> renders as *trikhapton* (fine hair-like fabric), regarding which see Fuller in the place cited. And in Syriac, which comes closer to the Greek *metaxa*, is <term>makhsa (מכסא)</term>, meaning *ordered* or *adorned*. For silk is sought after primarily for adornment. Truly, we will cause no controversy for anyone regarding the Egyptians; Isaiah is a witness in *chapter 19:9* that silk was brought to them from India or the region of the Chinese for luxury: <term>And those who work in multicolored and excellent silks shall be put to shame.</term> The Septuagint translates this as *split linen.* The Vulgate separates these two words entirely. Tremellius translates it as *noble garments.* Castalio as *distinguished.* Munster as *lattice-work.* Others as *combed linens.* The first edition of Robert Estienne has *Silk.* In this matter, he followed Rabbi Kimchi as a guide, who explains it thus: <term>The finest of silk, and it is usually called "al-shariq" in the Arabic language.</term> Others, however, understand it generally as precious works prepared from linen and wool; compare B. Friedlib, *Commentary on this passage, page 786.* There is no doubt, therefore, that the use of silk reached other Orientals from the Indians, and from them reached the West, as Nicolaus Fuller laboriously proves in the cited work, page 249. To turn to more recent times, we owe the use of silk from silkworms <note>original: *bombycibus*</note> to monks among new inventions; regarding this invention, or rather transportation, Horatius Tursellinus, when he relates this history, adds in *Epitome of History, Book 6, 232*: *A noble invention, had the luxury of the material not had monks as its authors.* For the Greeks received it from the monks of India, who first brought those worms from India to Byzantium—specifically the eggs, which, placed in a basket, transformed into worms and produced silk. As witnesses to this matter, we call upon Zonaras, *History, Volume 3, in the Life of Justinian*; Procopius, *Gothic War, Book 2*; Theophanes in Photius, *C.D. 64, page 79*; and Alexander ab Alexandro, *Genial Days, Book 4, chapter 22.* From the Greeks, it then passed into Italy, especially in the times of Robert of Sicily, a King from the royal family of the Dukes of Anjou, who, having conquered Athens, Corinth, and Thebes in Greece, led away the craftsmen who made silk cloths as captives and settled them in the Sicilian city of Palermo. From there it happened that the weaving craft, which previously only the Greeks among Christians possessed, was shared with Roman talents, as Otto of Freising says in the *History of Frederick*, and Jacques Auguste de Thou, *Book 129.* From the Italians, it then reached France along with the silkworms, as is clear both from de Thou and Aldrovandi, *On Insects, Book 2, page 114*, and from the edict of Henry IV, King of France, who judged it best that silk should be produced on his own soil. Hence he began to think seriously about silk workshops, as de Thou reports of his institute. I shall say nothing of Holland <note>original: *Batavia*</note> and the Venetian empire, in which the method of making silk increases daily. For while the manufacture of silk took hold in Europe, in Persia—which is a region more fortunate in silk than others—a pound of silk today sells for only a florin, which was once sold for a hundred florins. In those regions of Europe lying toward the North, such as Germany, Denmark, and Sweden, there is no use of silkworms for making silk, except for those kept for pleasure. For the silkworm feeds on the leaves of the mulberry, which are not as plentiful in these regions as elsewhere, since it loves warm places; it grows on them as its most useful and healthy food, although they are also accustomed to be fed on elm leaves where mulberry is not available; compare Vida, *The Silkworm, Book 1, line 509*; indeed, even on lettuce, nettle, and bramble, as G. J. Vossius teaches in *On Idolatry, Book 4, chapter 69, page 1542.* Nor should we overlook what an anonymous author writes in the book titled *Adventures of Natural and Artificial Things in China and Europe, chapter 38, page 719*, concerning silk threads in the Chinese province of Shandong, which are emitted not by a silkworm, but by another worm similar to a caterpillar, not in an oval form, but in a thread drawn out at length, which attaches itself to trees and houses at the will of the wind, and from which the silk they call *byssine* is made. Truly, the play of nature is most miraculous in this most lowly little animal, as it turns now into a caterpillar, now into a butterfly. Like snakes, it sheds its old skin several times, and while it prepares to cast off its former slough, it falls into a three-day lethargy, which usually occurs every tenth day. When this is finished, it seeks food again as if renewed, from which it had previously abstained. Let us hear Hieronymus Vida on that matter in his *Work on the Silkworm*, which Scaliger <margin>in the *Hypercriticus*.</margin> calls the "King of Books":

<column-break/>

> Often you will see them turn away from their food untouched,
> And lulled in a heavy lethargy, as if in a stupor,
> Upon the boards: Here spare them, lest by chance some disease
> Should seize their bodies, or a plague invade the sickly race.
> Nature herself added this custom, this sleep to them:
> They indulge in slumber and rest upon their beds,
> And while they are lulled, a second and a third day passes,
> But when the third light has driven the night from things,
> They will rise together, and return to their joyful, familiar fodder.

The silkworm follows this lethargy with its head held high, and persists in the same *posture* <note>Greek: *σχέσει*</note> of body until, in the manner of serpents, it has shed its *slough* <note>Greek: *λεπιδείδα*</note> or old age, which Vida hints at in the following poem:

> Therefore I bid you observe them when they are swollen (nor is it
> A great labor to know): lest sleep seize them unawares:
> They themselves will give signs of their own accord, they will lift
> Their steep heads to the sky, and spurn the feast: then you will note
> Their sluggish hearts, their idle spirits, and unusual silence at the tables.

Within <unclear>two days</unclear> it grows to maturity, and after that space of time, it gradually abstains from food, and having acquired a certain luster, it emits from its mouth a very thin and fine thread, which we call silk: which, having been observed—

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
### Page 430

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
Once observed, those little worms are immediately to be separated from the others and enclosed in hoods or another vessel destined for that purpose. There, with marvelous skill, they weave their shells or little nests within three days, sometimes two, producing silk that is either white, yellow, or a mixture of white and yellow, with a thread so thin it almost escapes the sight, and of such extended length that you might say with Maro <note>The poet Virgil</note>:

<margin>Aeneid, Book 1, v. 372.</margin>
> You could encircle a city with the thread of a silkworm. <note>original: "Urbem bombycis possis circumdare filo."</note>

Their little nests, shaggy with many threads, represent the form of a *date-stone* <note>Latin: caryotae</note>, which is why among our people they have the name *Dattelkern* <note>German: date kernel</note>. In these, the worms lie half-buried for eight days and more, at which time they are rightly called *bombylii* <note>the pupa stage</note>. While they lie thus half-buried, silkworm farmers usually break away the silk from that revolving nest, which they also call a *cocoon* (the Greeks call it *koukoulion*), before the butterflies break forth. This "half-finished" state is soon followed by a new metamorphosis; for from the worms, by a new transformation, come forth winged and horned butterflies, differing in sex, called in Greek *nekydaioi* because they do not live long. Like the rest of living creatures, they seek mating, and from this mating the females lay very tiny eggs in great numbers, which are yellow at first and shortly after turn an ash color; kept until the following year, they are hatched at a certain time. Finally, when they have undergone all the turns of nature, the winged silkworms—or more truly butterflies—die shortly after, as Vida points out:

<margin>Book 2, v. 296. Vida</margin>
> They all indulge in mating, so that the female of the race
> May leave life behind for those whose fates are finished,
> And be able to preserve the kind and protect the lineage.
> After this comes the end of all their works and of their age.

St. Basil, Bishop of Caesarea, advises women to look upon this marvelous metamorphosis of the silkworm as an argument for the future resurrection when they wear silk. For by the same power that God makes butterflies out of caterpillars, He will also change our bodies into spiritual ones. The words of the Holy Father are worthy to be recorded:

<margin>Hexaemeron, Homily 8, p. 109.</margin>
> What do you say, you who do not believe Paul concerning the change at the resurrection, when you see many creatures of the air changing their forms? Such as is told of the Indian worm with horns; which first changes into a caterpillar, then becomes a pupa, and does not remain in this form but is winged with loose and broad petals. Therefore, when you women sit unrolling the work of these—the threads which the Seres <note>The Chinese</note> send to you for the making of soft garments—remembering the change in this animal, take a clear concept of the resurrection, and do not disbelieve the change which Paul promises to all.

What do you say? You who do not believe Paul regarding that change of those rising again, when you see that many of the creatures of the air change their forms; such as are also reported of the Indian worm, endowed with horns. This is first changed into a caterpillar, and progressing further becomes a pupa; nor does it persist in this form, but becomes a winged creature with soft and broad wing-plates. Therefore, when you women sit together, unweaving their work—namely the webs which the Seres send all the way to you to make those soft clothes—be mindful of that little animal's 

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
transformation into various forms, and from that, take a clear argument for the resurrection; do not withdraw your faith from the future transformation, which he announces will be common to all. He who desires more on this matter may consult *Hieronymus Vida* (cited above), *Alexander ab Alexandro* (Book 4, *Genial Days*, ch. 9), compare *Vossius* (Book 4 on *Idolatry*, ch. 66, p. 1529), *Lauremberg* (Philological Treasury, cent. 3, num. 72), *Dalechamps* (Notes on Pliny, Book 11, ch. 23), and *B. Franz* (Sacred History of Animals, ch. 10, p. 828).

-> THE OX <-, among the Greeks and Latins, includes both the bull and the cow; among the Hebrews, however, the word is *polyonymous* <note>having many names</note>. The common term is *Shor* (שור). In Chaldean it is *Tor* (תור), which among the Phoenicians (according to Plutarch) is *Thor*; "the Phoenicians," he says, "call the ox *Thor*." It is so named from its terrible or grim look, from *shur* (שור), "to gaze"; or because of its conspicuous and distinguished form, for *Shor* is "first," as Rabbi Bechai notes on Genesis 2, because specifically taken, oxen are the leaders of the herds, or because they easily endure the yoke, whence they are also called *me'alaphim* (מאלפים), "leaders," from *alaph* (אלף), "he learned" or "he taught." From this descends the Arabic *Alapha*, to join or couple, because it is necessary for oxen to be *yoked together* <note>Greek: syzygeis</note>. Whence also the Phoenicians called the ox *Alpha*, which gave the first letter to the Greek Alphabet. Thus *Bakar* (בקר) taken collectively denotes "a herd or Oxen," from *bakar*, "he sought out," because it seeks its companion with frequent lowing, according to Isidore (Book 12, *Origins*, ch. 1). Even if the Roman *Vacca* <note>Cow</note> seems to be taken from there with the 'R' dropped, as from *Masar* comes *Musa*, and from *Zonar* comes *Zona*. And in 1 Samuel 14:32, they are called *bene bakar*, "sons of the cow." We pass over other words, among which is *Egel* (עגל), which properly denotes "a calf or young bull," and also *Eglah* (עגלה), "a heifer or young cow" (Gen. 15:9, Isa. 7:21-22, Hos. 10:11, Lev. 9:2, 2 Kings 17:16, Judges 14:18). Although "calf" seems to be taken so broadly that it denotes the same as "ox," as in Virgil:

<margin>in Syllapag. 463.</margin>
<margin>Prov. 14:4.</margin>
> -- *A calf already curving horns on its two-year-old brow*.

Among the animals that were in daily use by the Orientals are numbered the *Ox, sheep, Camel, and Donkey*; whence these four animals are joined when Samuel, in the name of God, commands Saul the destruction of the Amalekites. But while Saul had spared Agag, and the best of the sheep and oxen, the word *ha-mishnim* (המשמנים) is usually rendered in different ways by the Interpreters. The Targum understands it as "fat oxen." In Hebrew, *ha-shemanim* means "the fat ones," from *shamen*, "fat." The Septuagint translators and the Old Latin version render it "foods" and "garments," taking *mishnim* for "changeable garments" from the root *shanah*, "to repeat" or "to change." Others: "and the second-rate," i.e., less excellent and fat, yet not lean and not contemptible. Rabbi Solomon: "the near ones," i.e., bodies having doubled flesh and fatness. Junius also translates it "secondary," adding in the notes: "Secondary, i.e., less excellent, but not lean and contemptible." That this is the genuine meaning of the Hebrew word, whatever others may say, is taught by the order of the letters and the vowel marks. So that it is secondary, "that which was next after the best" <note>German: daß das nächste nach dem besten war</note>, as Piscator of Herborn expresses the mind of his guide. Luther understands it as "the fattened ones" <note>Greek: ta sitista</note>, "what was fattened" <note>German: was gemest war</note>, nor anything other than "whatever was best and especially..."

<margin>1 Samuel 15:3.</margin>

# From Psalm 50, verses 10 and 11.

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
Castalio understands "history" as referring to the most choice or fat animals. However, the Chaldean Paraphrast <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation/interpretation of the Hebrew Bible</note> understands the Hebrew word *hamshumannim* <note>original: המשמנים</note> to mean those that are fat by their very nature. The following words, namely *al-hakarim* <note>original: על-הכרים</note>, seem able to be explained according to others as those fattened by human industry—specifically lambs—from the root *kar* <note>original: כר</note>, which among various meanings also denotes a pasture. Although others explain this word as young lambs or rams (that is, those older in years), others again as lambs of the second birth (that is, in their second year). Junius, however, translates it as *the leads of the sheep*, which he thinks were taken away so that the flocks, accustomed to their leaders, could be led away more easily. Saul thought he had done something pleasing to God when he made a selection of the animals, as is clear from his own response which he gave to Samuel in 1 Samuel 15:21, saying: "The people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the chief of the *devoted things* <note>original: *anathematis*</note>, to sacrifice to your God in Gilgal." He used the phrase *reshit hacherem* <note>original: ראשית החרם</note>, the *firstfruits of the devoted things*, that is, the more excellent animals which were meant to be destroyed and utterly wiped out. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> rendered this as *the first of the destruction* <note>original: τὰ πρῶτα ἐξολοθρεύματ@</note> or *the beginnings of the devoted thing* <note>original: τὰς ἀρχὰς τὰ ἀναθέματ@</note>. The Chaldean Paraphrast says *in the beginning of the devoted thing*, that is, before he began to destroy the animals. But this selection of oxen and other living creatures, made besides and against God's command, did not please God, as is clear from verse 11. Indeed, there was greater value in obedience to those things which God had commanded than in burnt offerings; meanwhile, even the *burnt offerings* <note>original: ὁλοκαύματα</note> themselves were fully pleasing when performed by God's command and out of faith. Hence, God himself instilled the use and manner of sacrifices in the first inhabitants of the earth, Adam, Abel, and Cain, as is established from the Book of Genesis <note>original: "book of creation"</note>; this practice later grew strong among all people, albeit for a different or even contrary purpose, until Moses, the leader and writer of the Levitical sacrifices, enclosed it within certain limits, rules, or canons.

Among the Levitical sacrifices, the sacrifice taken from the herd of cattle held a significant place—namely calves. Among clean animals, God the Lawgiver had not only destined the firstborn for himself, but also, through certain statutes and laws pertaining to the Israelite Commonwealth, Moses first made a *burnt offering* <note>original: ὁλόκαυμα</note> in honor of God from the herd of cattle:

<margin>
Exodus 22:30.
</margin>
<margin>
Exodus 24:5.
</margin>
> For Moses sent (to recite the words of Holy Scripture) *young men of the children of Israel, who offered burnt offerings, and sacrificed peace offerings of oxen to Jehovah himself,* *parim* <note>original: פרים</note>;

For the Hebrew *par* <note>original: פר</note> signifies a *bullock*, and *parah* <note>original: פרה</note> a *heifer*, which in German is *Par* or *young cow* <note>original: junge Kuh</note> which is not yet broken in or able to bear the yoke on its neck; compare Psalm 69:32, Job 21:10, Numbers 19:2, 1 Samuel 6:7, 10. The same word is found in Exodus 29:1 and Leviticus 9:2, where Aaron is commanded to offer for his sanctification a *par ben-baqar* <note>original: פר בן-בקר</note>, a *bullock, the son of an ox*; the Septuagint says *a young calf from the oxen* <note>original: μοσχάριον ἐκ βοῶν</note>, which some think was done in memory of the *calf-worship* <note>original: μοσχολατρείας</note> performed by Aaron and the people. Origen "the Man of Adamant," having fallen into not a few errors out of an excessive zeal for *allegories* <note>original: ἀλληγοριῶν</note>, understands by that bullock our proud flesh,

<margin>
Homily 1 on Leviticus.
</margin>
> *which if you wish to offer as a gift to the Lord, so that you may keep it chaste and modest, bring it to the door of the tabernacle, that is, where it can receive the hearing of the divine books. Let your gift be masculine; let it not know the female, let it*

<column-break/>

*reject lust, reject frailty, and seek nothing dissolute or soft.* Indeed, calves are *unyoked* <note>original: ἄζυγα</note> animals which, being in their first and green age, frolic through the meadows; they move about playfully among the grass and flowers, contending with each other in mutual games, and present a beautiful and pleasant sight. But while they are thus "calving about" <note>note: a play on the Latin 'vitulari', meaning to frolic like a calf</note>, stinging flies intervene, tormenting and pricking them so that they flee, hurrying away from the meadows and leaving behind their companion cows and bulls, thrusting themselves into brambles so they might be relieved from that annoyance. The Prophet compares the joy of the godly to the *leaping* <note>original: σκιρτῶμεν</note> of calves, saying:

<margin>
Malachi 4:2.
</margin>
> *But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and gambol as calves of the stall.*

He describes the *shining forth* <note>original: ἀναλάμψα</note> of true believers at the rising of the Sun of Righteousness with the phrase *they leap joyfully* <note>original: Σκιρτῶσι φαιδρὰ</note>, based on the image of an exulting and frisking calf, which makes them frolic and leap. We "act the calf" when we indulge in joy. Nonius defines *vitulantes* as those rejoicing, derived from the *benefit of a good life*, which in his judgment comes from *vita* (life). But one must not "calf about" like an unbroken heifer or those who *fight against the yoke* <note>original: ἀζυγομάχοις</note>, just as the Prophet rebukes and chides the stubborn and rebellious people, saying:

<margin>
Hosea 4:16.
</margin>
> *For Israel slideth back as a backsliding heifer,* *sorerah* <note>original: סוררה</note>, from the root *sorer* <note>original: סורר</note>, meaning stubborn or refractory.

Blessed Luther calls it a cow impatient of the yoke and unbroken, which cannot be restrained. To this the Prophet compares the *Israelites: For the word of God is that bond by which He has bound us, lest we wander from the truth and indulge the desires of the flesh. Israel had shaken off this bond, wherefore the Prophet compares them to an unbroken heifer, which is slow to become tame and pulls at the reins, being impatient of being held. The words of Ambrose in Sermon 8 on Psalm 118, page 654, fit here quite well: "The ropes of the wicked, by which sins are drawn as if with a long rope, and iniquities like the strap of a heifer's yoke. For an unbroken heifer tosses and shakes itself more when it is held; it neither yields to command nor is bound by a bond, but rather, when it is pulled back by the strap, it becomes more exasperated. Thus it does not submit even when forced, yet it is not free from bonds. Just as, therefore, the heifer pulls the strap of the yoke—which, even if not held closely, is still held and does not disentangle or free itself—so every sinner with unbroken morals pulls his iniquities. He thinks himself free because he is not subject to the yoke or subject to judgment, and he does not know that he has not been stripped of them, but rather, like that heifer, he entangles himself in the knots of his own sins."*

Isaiah repeats the same complaint about the men of his age in chapter 1, verse 3, comparing them to cattle partly through the ignorance of a dull nature and their own lack of knowledge: *The ox, he says, knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib: but Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider.* Nothing is more stupid than a perverse sinner who does not allow himself to be ruled. He is an ox, and a frolicking cow driven by a gadfly—indeed, more stupid than the ox and the ass in the mind of the Prophet. Regarding these words, Paschasius Ratbertus writes in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 11, column 536:

> *The Ox knows his owner and the Ass his master's crib. By the Ox are designated the Jews, who drew the very heavy yoke of the Law, and by the Ass the irrational Gentiles, burdened with excessive crimes. Both are called first to come to the faith and receive something special: the Jews the yoke of labor, which is proper to them, and the Gentiles, having laid down the burden of Camels, the lightness of the gentleness of Christ.* I am not...

# SACRED HISTORY OF ANIMALS
<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>

I cannot help but bring forward the words of Blessed Luther—which are no less worthy of being read than remembered—to highlight the blindness of almost all men and their abominable ingratitude toward their Creator. He says: 

> "Is it not," he asks, "the ultimate disgrace that by the divine voice the Ox and the Ass are—I do not say compared with us—but preferred to us entirely, because they perform their duty toward their owner, while we do not perform ours toward God? We ought therefore to uncover our heads before oxen and asses as if before our masters, whom we see have been set before us by divine providence so that we might learn by their example to revere our God."

For just as under the figure or name of "goring oxen" (*Exodus 21:28-29*) and "fat cows" (*Amos 4:1*), we are to understand the enemies of God and the Church—for which purpose we cite *Psalm 22:13, 68:31, and Isaiah 34:7*—even if the cited Psalm primarily deals with the persecutors of Christ our Savior (namely the Hierarchical Senate of Jerusalem and its leaders and accomplices), it is nevertheless not irrelevant to adapt the same passage to any members of Christ and his Church who are oppressed by "fattened bulls."

<margin>T 2 Latin. in this place.</margin>
Luther says: *Therefore the multitude, magnitude, height, wealth, favor, delights, and glory—that is, the whole world—opposes the Gospel of God and its ministers, who are solitary, small, few, humble, poor, cast down, despised, and hated.* By "fattened bulls," I mean <term>te'orei bashan</term> <note>Hebrew: תאורי בשן</note>, the bulls of Bashan, or the "mighty ones of Bashan." The Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> renders this as *fat bulls*. With an elegant metaphor using the word <term>Bashan</term> <note>Hebrew: בשן</note>, the Psalmist describes the enemies of Christ by drawing a similarity from the fertility of the land and the convenience of the pastures in Bashan. This was a mountainous region where the animals grazing there were fatter, stronger, and larger than others, just as Frisian and Polish oxen are held in higher value than others today. Amos uses the same metaphor in *chapter 4:1*: *Hear this word, you cows of Bashan, who are on the mountain of Samaria.* He understands the leaders of the kingdom of Samaria, whom he calls this way partly because of their luxury (since they neglected their duties and cared only for their own skin and fattened themselves), and partly because of their violence and abuse of power in oppressing the weak (just as cows nourished in Bashan were fatter and therefore more insolent). Both reasons are immediately added in the text. However, while he compares the men not to bulls but to "cows," he simultaneously notes their softness and effeminate habits. Otherwise, it is solemn and common in both Sacred Scripture and secular writing to compare the strong and powerful to strong animals. Among pasturing animals, the Bull stands out for its strength; hence, by a common Scriptural phrase, great men are compared to bulls because of their might and power (*Psalm 22:13, 31; 68:31; Deuteronomy 33:7*). Because of the wordplay <note>paronomasia</note> between <term>shorim</term> <note>Hebrew: שורים, oxen</note> and <term>sarim</term> <note>Hebrew: שרים, princes</note>, the Septuagint translated "oxen" as *the rulers*. There is a controversial passage in the first book of Creation <note>Genesis 49:6</note> due to a <term>disagreement</term> <note>Greek: διαφωνίαν</note> among interpreters: <term>ve-hirtsonam iqru shor</term> <note>Hebrew: וברגנם עקרו שור, "in their self-will they hamstrung an ox"</note>. The word <term>shor</term> is explained in various ways. Pagninus explains it as "a wall," following the Targum <note>Aramaic translation</note>, as if the Patriarch were referring to the wall of Shechem; but in Hebrew it is not *Shur* <note>wall</note>, but *Schor*, the former meaning a wall and the latter an ox, which is why the Septuagint reads *bull*. Others explain it as the driving away of cattle, so that "ox" is used as a part for the whole <note>synecdoche</note> for oxen or any herds; but the verb <term>iqer</term> <note>Hebrew: עקר</note> is never

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
used for the driving away of cattle. We, along with Blessed Gerhard and Blessed Friedlieb, think it can be most simply explained as referring to Shechem, the son of Hamor and the abductor of Dinah. For just as in the first part of the verse he dealt with the Prince who was the father of the city, so in this latter part he deals with the son of the Prince, because these were the Lords of the city. The Jerusalem Targumists explain it as referring to Joseph, whose beauty in the Mosaic blessing *is compared to the beauty of a firstborn ox* (*Deuteronomy 33:17*). Blessed Luther follows them, saying: *The firstborn ox is greatly commended in Holy Scripture because it feeds and cares for the Master. Nor was it permitted to sacrifice a plowing ox, because it was like the father of the family and the pillar of the house; even the gentiles abstained from plowing oxen. For they not only plowed, but also threshed. Therefore the works of the Ox are greatly praised in the law, etc. This, therefore, is what Jacob wants to say: "The one who fed us during such a long time of famine—not only Egypt, but also all of us who would have perished by hunger if not for him, and whom I loved uniquely because he was born in my old age and was most pleasing to all because of his excellent character and remarkable piety—this Ox they hamstrung," he says, "they did not kill him, but they would have prevented his freedom so that he would not be the firstborn or Father or King, and would not succeed me in my family. But now he has been raised to the height of dignity, to become the Father of Egypt and of my whole house."* Thus says Luther. Of such value was the firstborn ox of old that they were neither slaughtered in the house nor offered in sacrifice except in matters of great importance and weight. This is shown by the example of Saul, recently elected King, who, having learned of the siege of the Jabeshites and hearing of their extreme necessity, was compelled to take a pair of plowing oxen and cut them into pieces, sending them into all the land of Israel with this command: *Whoever does not come out after Saul and Samuel, so shall it be done to his oxen.* (*1 Samuel 11:7*). So too we think there is a certain <term>mystery</term> <note>Greek: μυστήριόν</note> when Elisha, anointed to the Prophetic office by Elijah, slaughters a pair of plowing oxen and cooks them with the equipment of the oxen (that is, the yoke and plow), to indicate that he was now called to a greater and more excellent kind of life and province (*1 Kings 19:21*). Likewise, Isaiah, speaking of the powerful in the same likeness (*chapter 34:7*), says: *The wild oxen shall come down with them, and the young bulls with the mighty bulls.* So Homer (*Iliad, Book 2, line 481*) compares King Agamemnon to a Bull:

<margin>Deuteronomy 33:17.</margin>
> Just as a bull in the herd stands out far above all,
> A bull (for he is conspicuous among the gathered cattle),
> Such did Zeus make the son of Atreus on that day,
> Conspicuous among the many and outstanding among heroes.

<margin>* 1 Samuel 11:7</margin>
And so <term>as if someone were returning to it and wishing to demonstrate it</term> <note>Greek: πῶς ἰχὼν αὐτὸ ἐπανιὼν καὶ ἐπιδεῖξαι βυλόμενῷ</note>, as noted by Dio, who says the Bull bears the image of the King and the kingdom, <term>because he rules and governs his own kind with goodwill, as one might say, and guardianship. For when a beast appears... he does not flee the pasture, but fights in front of the whole herd, helping the weak and risking himself to save the multitude; therefore he is the leader of the fierce and wild. Just so is the Ruler and King in truth, and worthy of the greatest honor among men.</term>

# Sacred History of Animals

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> They are designated by the names *chargol* <note>original: חרגול</note>, *solam* <note>original: סלעם</note>, *arbeh* <note>original: ארבה</note>, and *gazam* <note>original: גזם</note>, which are known to them today only by their Hebrew nomenclature. Mention is made of the others throughout the Sacred Pandects <note>A term for the Bible, comparing it to a complete body of law</note>, from which Ursinus, in his *Nomenclator* p. 164, enumerates ten of their names based on Bochart. Among these is <term>gob</term> <note>original: גוב</note> or *gobi*, which is translated in Chaldee as <term>goba</term> <note>original: גובא</note> from "height," or as others prefer, <term>gobi</term> is called a <term>collection</term> from the root *gabab* <note>original: גבב</note>, meaning "he gathered," because they come in great numbers. Hence in *Amos 7:1*: <term>And behold, he formed locusts</term> <note>original: והנה יוצר גובי</note>, where the swarm of locusts devouring the late-growth or autumn hay signifies the future depopulation and devastation of the Holy Land by the massive armies of the Babylonians, Assyrians, and Romans. The Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> reads here <term>offspring of locusts</term> <note>original: ἐπιγονὴ ἀκρίδων</note>. And in *Nahum 3:15*: <term>like the locust of locusts</term> <note>original: כגוב גובי</note>, that is, like great and very large locusts according to the Hebrews; thus Rabbi David Kimchi, Abraham, and Jonathan explain them as locusts of extraordinary size, while Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> explains them as an army of locusts. In *Joel 1:4*, three species of locusts are read: the first is <term>gazam</term> <note>original: גזם</note>, which the Septuagint translates as <term>caterpillar</term> <note>original: κάμπη</note> and the Vulgate as <term>eruca</term> <note>caterpillar/cankerworm</note>, from the root *gazaz* <note>original: גזז</note>, which means <term>to shear, shave, or cut off</term>. Hence Kimchi thinks the *gazam* is a worm that shaves off vegetables and especially cabbages. The second is <term>yelek</term> <note>original: ילק</note>, which takes its name from *lakak* <note>original: לקק</note>, meaning <term>consuming or devouring</term>, so that it is the same as <term>consumer, corrupter</term>, or <term>devourer</term>, because it wastes and destroys everything so that nothing is left. Thus in *Deuteronomy 28:38*: *You shall sow much seed in the field and gather little in, for the locust* <term>yelek</term> *shall consume it all*. The third species, or rather the middle one, is called <term>chasil</term> <note>original: חסיל</note>, from *chasal* <note>original: חסל</note>, <term>to lick or lap up</term>; it is so named because it consumes the greenery as if by licking it, as Rabbi Aben Ezra notes. Rabbi David Kimchi defines it in his commentary on *Joel* as a small winged animal like a hornet, but smaller, which depopulates the leaves of trees and devastates in great multitudes. The Chaldee translator renders this word variously. In *Joel* he gives *Coret*, meaning <term>cutting</term>. In *Nahum 3:15* he interprets it partly by the name *Sochala*, meaning <term>creeping thing or worm</term>, and partly *Kameza*, which also signifies a locust so named from "collection" or "gathering," because they fly in swarms or ranks. The Syriac version of the New Testament also uses the same word for the name <term>akris</term> <note>Greek for locust</note>.

The <term>Chaldee Paraphrast</term> interprets the same word as <term>Pirha</term>, as if you were to say *scouring* or *running about*, from the root *parach* <note>original: פרח</note>; <term>he moved, he ran about, he visited</term>, because it runs and leaps here and there, wasting the crops. From their paraphrase, it is gathered that the <term>yelek</term> is a type of locust that, besides its abundance and number, excels in swifter flight and extends further than the others, finishing off and consuming more fields more quickly. Hence the Psalmist says in *Psalm 105:34*: *He spoke, and the locust [Arbeh] came, and the cankerworm [yelek] without number.* And in *Jeremiah 51:14* it is read: *Surely I will fill you with men as with caterpillars [bruchis]* and in *v. 27*: *bring up the horses like the bristly caterpillars [yelek]*. The Septuagint usually renders this word as <term>bruchus</term> <note>wingless locust or beetle</note>, followed by Jerome, Pagninus, and almost all interpreters. However, since the Hebrew word is broader than the word *bruchus*, it denotes a genus of locusts that is prickly, feathered, and flying. According to Albertus <margin>book 26</margin>, the *Bruchus* is the first offspring of the Locust; when it becomes larger, it is called *Archalabus* (perhaps

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> *Attelabus*) and when it is perfected, it is a *Locust*. Lyranus also writes that the *Bruchus* and the *Locust* differ as the imperfect and perfect within the same species. The *Gloss* says the *Bruchus* is the name for the locust's offspring before it has wings; then, when it begins to fly a little, it is called *Attelabus*; but when it flies fully, it is called a *Locust*. The *Bruchus* is much more heavy than the *Locust* or *Attelabus* because, staying in one place, it eats the fruits down to the roots. So too Chrysostom, on the words *the Locust and the Bruchus came, etc.*, says: *The Locust and the Bruchus do not usually exist at the same time; for either the preceding locust gives birth to the Bruchus, or the Bruchus grows and turns into a locust.* Jerome observes the same distinction: to him, the *Bruchus* is a small animal unable to fly, devoted only to its belly; the *Attelabus* leaps rather than flies, having small wings; and the *Locust* is the perfected form with wings. And <margin>book 3 on Nahum, folio 40 a.</margin> Rupert says: *The Bruchus is a worm, capable of flight but sometimes weighed down by its own weight; because it is not sufficiently aided by its wings, it is pulled down and falls to the earth in weary flight.* In the cited passages, namely *Psalm 105:34, Jeremiah 51:14, 27, and Joel 1:4*, Blessed Luther translates the Hebrew word <term>yelek</term> as *Käfer* <note>German for beetle</note> to indicate the damage this genus of insects brings to herbs and crops. Chrysostom mentions this damage in the *Homily* titled "That no one is harmed except by himself": *Everything in existence,* he says, *has something by which it can be corrupted; as the moth harms wool, the wolf the flocks of sheep, the change to vinegar harms wine, bitterness corrupts the sweetness of honey, tares hurt the crops, hail harms the vineyard, and the army of locusts and caterpillars [bruchi] devastate the thickets and various plantations; and (lest the speech be drawn out too long by listing everything) various types of diseases bring corruption to every single body.* The *bruchi* are especially harmful to vines and cause great slaughter among them, as Prudentius indicates in the *Hamartigenia*:

> Either the Bruchus gnaws the budding shoots it has ravaged,
> Or the grape will be torn, plucked by wild birds.

Hence the people of Miletus used to sacrifice to Hercules because he had put to flight the *bruchi* that were gnawing and consuming their vineyards. To this point belong the verses of Theocritus, who <margin>Idyll 5, v. 110.</margin> introduces Comatas praying to the locusts not to consume his vines:

> *Locusts, you who are accustomed to leap over my wall,*
> *Do not harm my vines; for they are tender.*
> <note>original Greek: Ἀκρίδες αἳ τὸν φραγμὸν ὑπερπαδῆτε τὸν ἀμὸν, Μὴ μὲ λωβάσησθε τὰς ἀμπéλω· ἔντι γὰρ ἁβαί.</note>

And Caelius Rhodiginus (book 4, A.L. ch. 15) notes from a book on agriculture that a "Feast of the Bruchi" <note>original: τῶν βρούχων ἑορτήν</note> used to be celebrated by the ancients on the eighth day before the Calends of December. Since they come in such great numbers, they are called "armies"; hence Quintus Calaber compares the Trojans and their auxiliary forces to locusts, who fell upon the Greeks in as great a multitude as locusts fall upon the fields. This parable is frequent in the Sacred Pandects. When God is about to threaten the destruction of Babylon in *Jeremiah ch. 51 v. 14 & 27*, He predicts that enemies will come in such plenty and multitude that they would equal the number of caterpillars. Because of such a great multitude flying together and their audacity, Saint Jerome compares the rushing forces of the enemy to them—

# SACRED HISTORY OF ANIMALS

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> In the explanation of *Joel 2:9*, it is said: *At their face the earth trembled, they were moved;* which we should understand hyperbolically. It is not that the force of the locusts or the enemies is so great that they can move the heavens and shake the earth, but that to those suffering adversity, the heavens seem to fall and the earth to fluctuate because of the magnitude of their terror. Finally, because of the multitude of locusts covering the sky, the Sun and Moon will be turned into darkness, and the stars will withdraw their light, while the cloud of locusts placed in the middle does not allow the light to reach the earth. The prophecy concerning the <term>kakoezia</term> <note>Greek: "bad condition" or "malice"</note> of the Ninevites deserves the first line, which stands in *Nahum 3:15*, where the Prophet, by the names of locusts and <term>bruchi</term> <note>A type of wingless locust or beetle</note>, implies a triple kind of men: namely, the enemies, the merchants, and the Princes of the Assyrians, who hitherto have raged against everyone. But with the storm of enemies now imminent, he predicts that all are preparing their departure; compare Blessed Hasenreffer in his *Commentary on this place, page 76.* Regarding the second kind of men, Rudolf Gualther says: *Do you wish to know, O Ninevites, what your merchants are like? They are "bruchi," who indeed consult for themselves and their own affairs, but spend nothing for you for the defense of the Kingdom and the Fatherland. For as "bruchi" frequently occupy fields and meadows, and with insatiable greed devour the flowers of trees, herbs, and crops, but when they see there is nothing left, they suddenly fly away: so these now indeed come together to you in great troops, and carry out their business in your city, seizing both public and private wealth for themselves by merchant arts and usury, so that when they have made a profit and see danger looming over you, they soon betake themselves elsewhere, lest they be forced to undergo the common danger.* Rupert of Deutz <note>original: "Rupertus Tuitensis"</note> in *Book 3 on Nahum, folio 40 recto*, uses rhetoric in the consideration of the prophetic speech in a manner unusual for him, so that I think his words will be all the more pleasing to us here. *These are sentences of the kind "entering into the mud and treading the mortar, hold the brick," which grammarians or Rhetoricians call "concessive," having a beautiful mode of speech such that they prohibit in compulsion and compel in prohibition. Yet, lest they seem to be persuasions if not understood, some words are mixed in which clearly conflict, so that the listeners do not think that what is said is being commanded or persuaded. So it is clear here; for when he had said, "Enter into the mud and tread the mortar, hold the brick," he immediately added: "There the fire shall devour thee, thou shalt perish by the sword, the 'bruchus' shall devour thee." Where he said "gather," he soon added "as the bruchus"; where he said "multiply," he immediately added "as the locust." Continually he brought in a truly grand-sounding sentence, containing much reproach, saying: "Thou hast made thy negotiations more than the stars of heaven."*

### THE BUFFALO.
Among the clean animals allowed for eating is numbered the <term>Iachmur</term> <note>Hebrew: יחמור</note>. Regarding this name, Interpreters go into different opinions, nor is there consensus among them today. Tremellius, following Rabbi Yehuda—a most ancient writer of the highest authority among the Hebrews—explains it as *fallow deer*. This explanation does not please Drusius, who for that reason in his *Commentary on the more difficult places of Deuteronomy, chapter 17*, criticizes this opinion in more than one way. For he says: *The Interpreters from the Palatinate changed "Buffalo" into "fallow deer." Let us see if they are right. The fallow deer is a genus of wild goat. Rabbi Jonah*
<sig>Bbbb</sig>

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> (mistakenly called Rabbi Yehuda in Tremellius), the Hebrew Grammarian, says: *In the Arabic language, they call an animal similar to a large goat "Iachmur."* Yet Sylvaticus rendered the word *Iachmur* as *buffalo*. Also, <term>boubalos</term> <note>Greek: βούβαλος</note> is read in certain Greek versions; see the Roman edition. Nor does Josephus interpret it otherwise. What shall we conclude here? It is permitted to know that the buffalo is also of the goat genus. Indeed, in *1 Kings 4:23*, it is numbered among the more sumptuous foods of King Solomon, which cannot be understood of the common buffalo, which is called *boubalos*. *The "Iachmur" therefore is a genus of goat, not the fallow deer (which is called "dorkas"), but a large goat, which the Arabs call "Iachmur."* Here the Hebrew Hafcun stands in the way, who interprets it as a ferret, unless <term>binanim</term> is a ferret, about which I think more must be sought. The same cites a Talmudic Treatise on *Blessings*, in which are mentioned the *eggs of the Iachmur*. Forster and Kircher in their Concordances render it *wild ass*, perhaps moved by the word <term>chamor</term>, meaning *Ass*. But Luther, in Deuteronomy, translates it *Buffalo*; later in *1 Kings 4*, more correctly *Chamois*. Without doubt, it is an animal unknown in our lands, since the Arabs describe an animal of this kind, similar to a goat, as being almost red in color, frequent near the Euphrates, with serrated stag-like horns with which it cuts through bushes, often getting stuck in the tangles so that it betrays itself by its cry and becomes the prey of hunters; <margin>Oppian, Halieutica, v. 625.</margin> whence also Oppian calls that animal foolish, not only for that reason, but because it thinks it is hidden when its head is concealed in dense shrubs. Schindler, in his Lexicon under the word *Iachmur*, has almost the same as Johannes Drusius: *Chamar*, he says, according to the Hebrews, is an animal similar to a large goat. Furthermore, the Septuagint, as well as the Interpreter of the Chaldean Paraphrase, rendered it *boubalos*, buffalo, whom Gesner follows in *On Quadrupeds*, explaining this Hebrew *Iachmur* as *a buffalo, and neither the Reindeer, which is seen in Lapland (as Dalecampius thought in his notes on Pliny and Forster); nor <margin>Book 3, Observations, ch. 1, num. 10.</margin> the Bonasus, as Boetius suspects.* Add that the Hebrews also count the *buffalo* among the <term>pene meriam</term> <note>Hebrew: פני מריאים</note> or *fattened cattle*, whence the Arabs call it *almari*; compare Belon, *Observations 2, ch. 50.* And in *1 Kings 4:23*, it is referred to among the delicacies of the Royal table, which were no less than the Lucullian delicacies or the Apician refinements, by which are understood: peacock from Samos, Phrygian heath-cock, Melic cranes, kid from Ambracia, Chalcedonian young tunny, Tartessian moray eel, Pessinuntian cod, Tarentine oysters, Chian scallops, Rhodian sturgeon, Cilician parrot-fish, Thasian nuts, Egyptian dates, Iberian acorns, and whatever other kinds of edibles that profound gluttony devised and the throat sought out with a destructive search. Regarding the buffalo, one should also read Blessed Gerhard, *Commentary on Deuteronomy 14:5, page 845*; Blessed Ursinus, *Nomenclature of Biblical Animals, page 124*; and *Volume 2 of the Sacred Analecta, Book 1, 21, page 31.*

### THE CAMEL
To the Hebrews <margin>Esther 8:10.</margin> <term>Achashteranim</term> <note>Hebrew: אחשתרנים</note> is the only word in the Hebrew language given to this animal, although also according to the opinion of some Interpreters, especially Rabbi Solomon Jarchi, by *Achashteranim* they understand *very swift camels.* According to Aben Ezra, however, they are *mules*, whom most follow. The Greek and the Vulgate each retain the word in their own language. # From Psalm 50, verses 10, 11. 435

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...those that have a divided hoof, the camel, the hare, and the rock hyrax <note>original: "cuniculum," often translated as rabbit, but in a biblical context refers to the hyrax</note>, *because they chew the cud but do not divide the hoof, they are unclean to you.* And in the following verse: *Of their flesh you shall not eat, and their carcasses you shall not touch.* The chief riches of the Orientals consisted in a multitude of Camels, whence we read that Job lost three thousand Camels at the hand of the Chaldeans and received six thousand from the divine blessing.
<margin>chapter 42, verse 12.</margin>
Hence Robert, in the 7th book of the *History of Jerusalem*, page 65, records a battle in the East involving Hugh the Great and Duke Godfrey, in which, after the Armenians and Syrians were defeated, fifteen thousand Camels were found. For the Camel, although it is a twisted and callous animal—that is, as Aristotle says in *History of Animals* book 2, chapter 1: *it has a unique feature compared to other quadrupeds, the so-called hump upon its back* <note>original Greek: "ἴδιον ἔχει τύλον τὰ ἄλλα τετράποδα, τὸν καλέμενον ὕβον ἐπὶ τῷ νώτῳ"</note>—it has upon its back what they call a Tuber <note>a hump or swelling</note>; whence it is also named by Isaiah as sitting upon the *hump of camels.*
<margin>chapter 30, verse 6.</margin>
Their utility in Asia is as great as that of horses among us: nor is their virtue and strength in carrying burdens any less, as Botero notes in *Reports on the King of Persia*, title "Strengths," folio 203. But nature, so that she might assist commerce and provide for the convenience of human life in places lacking navigable water, endowed Persia and the neighboring regions with camels, which are most convenient there. For they carry heavier loads than horses and mules can carry, and they endure long in labor: they carry a load of a thousand pounds; they continue a journey for 40 or more days; and in dry and sandy places, such as Libya, Arabia, and Persia, where water and pasture are lacking, they drink only once every five days, and if necessary, they endure thirst for ten or more days. As for fodder, when relieved of their load, they are given a small amount of grass, thorns, or branches of trees. Therefore, there is no animal that endures labor longer or is of less expense; because of these conditions, it is most suited to the arid and dry regions of Asia and Africa, in which men suffer from a great lack of water: since a little suffices for the camel, yet it can carry a great quantity of supplies for the use of others. Truly, there are three kinds of them: men ride upon the smaller ones; the medium ones have two humps and are strong for carrying merchandise; the larger and thicker ones carry loads of a thousand pounds as we said, and whenever packs are to be placed on them, or taken off after a journey, they are accustomed to kneel at the command of the driver. Those which have two humps are commonly called *bikri* <note>Hebrew: בכרי</note>, *dromades*, or *dromedaries*, which are both more fit for carrying loads and swifter on a journey than camels. For although Dromedaries are smaller in stature, they excel in speed, so that it is said one can complete a hundred miles or more in a single day; compare Diodorus Siculus books 3 and 19, Zosimus book 1, and Philostratus book 2, chapter 3. Because of their speed, they are commended in more than one place in the
<margin>Isaiah 60:6.</margin>

Pandectis," a legal term here applied to the Bible</note>, since the Prophet predicts that the merchants of the Nations will come with Camels in troops, through what they call Caravans. *A multitude of camels,* he says, *shall cover you, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah*, that is, the peoples from the rising of the Sun, who are accustomed to use camels, are led to the heavenly Jerusalem of Christianity in as great a heap as there usually is of camels and dromedaries in Arabia, Syria, and the coastal places of the Red Sea. In the sacred text there, the word is *bikri*; the Chaldean translation

<column-break/>

has *Hogne*; which others interpret as the small or younger ones, whence the Proverb was born: *Many old camels carry the skins of the younger* Hogne; see Buxtorf in the *Talmudic Lexicon*. Bochart thinks the word was fashioned from the Greek *eugeneis* <note>meaning "well-born" or "noble"</note>, as if to say "excellent." The Septuagint <note>LXX</note> retains *camelos*. Pagninus translates it as *foals of camels*, and Luther as *runners* <note>German: "Läuffer"</note>. They have gained another name in the Sacred Scriptures from their swiftness; for the same Prophet calls them *bikkarot* <note>Hebrew: בכרכרות</note>, which, to use the words of B. Ursinus in *Nomenclature of Biblical Animals*, page 99, perhaps comes from *Kirkir*, "to dance" or "to leap," whence also *Carcar*, a weaver's shuttle. The simple *Car* signifies a *lamb or ram*, whence *kar* among the Ionians means "sheep." And perhaps the Latin *currus* (chariot) and *currere* (to run) come from this. The Vulgate has *Carrucas* <note>carriages</note> here, which Pagninus imitates, and Luther uses *runners*. This word is repeated in 1 Kings 4:28 and Micah 1:13, where the Hebrew is *rekesh*; the Septuagint has *chariots*. Pagninus in the former place has *mules*, in the latter, *very swift horses*. The Vulgate has *beast of burden*, and Luther in both
<margin>Isaiah 30:16.</margin>
places has *runners*; as also for **rekeb** <note>Hebrew: רכב</note>, *upon light followers*, he translates "on runners we will ride" <note>German: "auf Läuffern wollen wir reiten"</note>. The Camel is a hieroglyphic <note>a symbolic figure</note> animal in the Sacred Scriptures. For while under the Mosaic law the Jews are ordered to abstain from the flesh of the Camel and from touching and eating it, Hesychius understands this as the Scribes and Pharisees in the time of Christ sitting in the chair of Moses. To eat a Camel, taking it as *playing with pride*, is rightly understood; that is, the *Scribes and Pharisees eat the cud-chewer because they glory in the meditation of the letter of the law, and in the worship of the Sabbath, and of purification and sacrifices, and other similar things. But they do not divide the hoof, for they do not discern the spirit from the letter; therefore their knowledge is unclean.* Regarding every filth and foulness of sins,

Or when it forbids the Pig to be taken as food, it certainly rebukes a filthy and muddy life, or one rejoicing in the foulness of vices, placing its good not in the nobility of the soul, but in the flesh alone. Or with the hare, it accuses men reformed into women. Who would make the body of a weasel food? But it rebukes thefts. Who the lizard? But it hates a life of uncertain variety. Who the gecko? # SACRED HISTORY OF ANIMALS

<margin>
Sacred History of Animals.
p. 110.
Deut. 23:18
</margin>
In his *Nomenclature of Animals*, although the dog deserves praise for its loyalty and keen intelligence, it is nevertheless numbered among the most impure animals. This is so much the case that God forbade it by a severe mandate in His law: *“You shall not bring the hire of a harlot, or the price of a dog, into the house of the Lord your God for any vow: for even both these are an abomination unto the Lord your God.”* <note>Quoting Deuteronomy 23:18. The "price of a dog" refers to money gained from selling or trading the animal.</note>

Interpreters debate this "price of a dog" that must not be offered in the house of God. Josephus, in Book 4 of the *Antiquities of the Jews*, chapter 8, explains the price of a dog as that which was received for the breeding of female dogs, for which hunting dogs and sheep-guards were hired; "likewise," he says, "no one should take a reward for the mating of a dog, whether a hunter or a guardian of flocks, and sacrifice from this to God." <note>original Greek: ὁμοίως... ἐκ τούτου θύειν τῷ θεῷ.</note> Abulensis, Lyranus, and others explain it as the firstborn of a dog; since the firstborn of unclean animals (among which is the dog) could not be offered, they were instead redeemed for five shekels given to the Priest (Numbers 18:16). Others finally understand it as money obtained from any sale of a dog, which, due to the dog's impurity, should not be contributed to sacred uses. We believe this law regarding the price of a dog refers both to the impurity and foulness of the dog and to its worthlessness. Hence Blessed Luther says: *“This is the reason why the money for which a dog is bought is not to be offered: because the dog is considered the most worthless animal in the Scriptures, even serving in proverbs, as Abner says: 'Am I a dog's head?' (2 Samuel 3:8). Clearly, he could allege nothing more worthless. He who honors God with the price of a dog, therefore, despises God and holds Him cheap, as if he were offering the price of dung.”* These signs show a low opinion of God in the heart. Parallel to this are the words of Isaiah:

<margin>ch. 66:3</margin>
*“He who sacrifices a lamb is as if he slaughters—others translate 'breaks the neck of'—a dog.”* This refers to sacrificing according to the custom of the Gentiles, especially the Egyptians. They were the most superstitious of all and were occupied with the worship and veneration of dogs among other beasts, as Cicero testifies in Book 5 of the *Tusculan Disputations*: *“Who is ignorant of the custom of the Egyptians? Their minds are so imbued with the errors of depravity that they would sooner undergo the executioner than violate an ibis, an asp, a cat, a dog, or a crocodile.”* This agrees with the *History of Barlaam*, where it says of Egyptian superstitions: *“Some of them worshiped the sheep, some the goat, some the calf and the pig, the vulture and the eagle; others the crocodile, some the cat and the dog, the wolf, the monkey, the dragon, and the asp; others goats, garlic, and thorns.”* The same is read in Strabo (Book 15) and Diodorus Siculus (Library, Book 1). Juvenal, in his 15th Satire, mocks this foul Egyptian "superstition" <note>original Greek: Δεισιδαιμονίαν (Deisidaimonian) - literally 'fear of spirits' or superstition.</note> with his usual wit:

> Whole towns worship the dog; nobody worships Diana.

He refers to the people of Hermopolis, of whom Strabo mentions that they worship the "dog-head" <note>original Greek: κυνοκέφαλον (kynokephalon) - a cynocephalus or dog-headed deity like Anubis.</note>. Clement of Alexandria writes 
<margin>in the *Protrepticus*</margin>
that the dog was held in the highest veneration among the Cynopolites; hence, according to Herodotus, at the funeral of a dog they shave their entire body and head. It is a wonder they did not also erect epitaphs in honor of dogs. Well known is that playful epitaph by Justus Lipsius for his dog, whom he called "Sapphire," which is read in his *Centuries to the Belgians* (3rd Ep. 89). There is also the case of the Perusian dog, who, to serve his Master's interests, barked at

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred History of Animals.</margin>
thieves, but to please his Mistress, admitted her lovers without a bark; hence the Poet wrote:
->I barked at thieves, but was silent at the thefts of lovers,<-
->As I pleased the Master, so I pleased the Mistress.<-

In Genoa, in the Palace of the Prince D’Oria, specifically in the garden before the gate toward Milan, one reads the epitaph of a dog named *Roldan*. Five hundred florins were spent annually on his food; moreover, two servants were hired specifically for his service, who daily brought him food in silver vessels prepared for eating. This is testified by Johann Heinrich von Psaumern in his *Italian Mercury*, who disapproves of it out of righteous grief. We find such foolish affection for dogs even today among certain men and women who value a dog more than a human—truly "irrationally" <note>original Greek: ἀλόγως (alogos)</note> and without a mind worthy of a human. In ancient times, the "Maltese puppies" <note>original Greek: μελιταῖα κυνίδια (melitaia kynidia)</note> became a proverb; they were useful for nothing except being the darlings of wealthy matrons. If we consult the ancient writers of the Pelasgian race, they distinguish dogs into three types based on their duties. First were the "trackers" <note>original Greek: ἰχνευτικοὶ (ichneutikoi)</note>, which we call hounds—hunting dogs, very pleasing to nobles and the wealthy who devote themselves to the hunt. The second kind were the "house-guards" <note>original Greek: οἰκουροὶ (oikouroi)</note>, so called because they kept watch before the doors; Virgil (Georgics 3) and Hesiod (Works and Days) advise every head of a family to nourish such a dog:
->And do not spare the food to maintain the sharp-toothed dog<-
In feeding this one, he warns not to be too stingy with expenses, so that he may watch lest a man who sleeps by day enters the house by stealth and steals something:
->Lest ever the man who sleeps by day takes your goods.<-
In the third rank were the "Maltese dogs" mentioned above, named after the island of Melita, today Malta. Otherwise, dogs were praised in antiquity for their noble breeding, such as those from Arcadia, the Celts, Hyrcania, India, Laconia, Locris, and the Molossians. Hence in the Sacred Scriptures, the word *Zarzir* <note>Hebrew: זרזיר - often translated as 'greyhound' or 'strutting cock'.</note> is used, meaning "girt in the loins," 
<margin>Prov. 30:31</margin>
referring to a noble dog. Rabbi Levi interprets this as a hunting dog, "tender in the loins," meaning swift and fit for the chase, a view supported by Nicolaus Fuller. Since this word *Zarzir* occurs only once in the Sacred Books, it is interpreted variously: the Chaldean translates it as "Cock," followed by the Septuagint: "A cock walking in among the hens." Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus also say "a cock," though something seems missing to complete the sense. To others, this word suggests a "Leopard," because it is lean and strong in the loins. To others still, it should be understood as a "Horse," noble, pugnacious, and vigorous for war. Nor were there lacking those, as Rabbi Aben Esra mentions, who ascribed the nature of the *Zarzir* to the Bee, because the Bee is an insect endowed with extraordinary vigor and the promptest agility. In such a doubtful matter, we rightly suspend our judgment, content with a bare review of opinions. The dog surpasses all other animals in sagacity; "Nothing is more sagacious than dogs," says Isidore, for they have more sense than other animals; they alone know their own names, recognize their masters, and love them.

> *Among the quadrupeds, the dog is faithful,*
> *Among the quadrupeds, the dog is a delight.*

The dog is a wonderful animal: he attacks the unknown with barking and biting, he cherishes the known, loves the familiar, and soothes with fawning. He is a spirited animal, yielding easily to no one, admitting no one unless they are not an adversary to him. He barks boldly against an opponent. From this, he is established as a Symbol of the Teachers of the Church and of Bishops; and he who does not perform his duty is called a "dumb dog" by Isaiah, 
<margin>
Isaiah 56:10.
</margin>
where God says: *They are all dumb dogs, they are not able to bark; they are sleepers, lying down, loving*

<column-break/>

*to slumber.* It is against the nature of dogs to be dumb: *A dog is falsely called a dumb guardian,* says Columella <note>Roman writer on agriculture, 1st century AD.</note>, *for what man announces a beast or a thief more clearly with such great shouting*
<margin>
Book 7 on Rural Affairs, Chapter 12.
</margin>
*than that barking? What servant is more loving of his Master? What companion more faithful? What guardian can be found more incorruptible? What watchman more vigilant? Finally, what avenger and punisher more constant?* When ornaments had been stolen from the temple of Aesculapius in Athens, a dog followed the thief constantly, barking and not stopping, deterred neither by the striking of stones nor by fatty morsels; and this was seen as sufficient evidence to investigate the thief by the barking. When the thief was caught and tortured, he confessed, and punishment was taken upon him. Indeed, food was publicly decreed for the dog, as Aelian <note>Roman author of "On the Nature of Animals."</note> relates; 
<margin>
Book 7, History of Animals, Chapter 13.
</margin>
you will find more examples of the fidelity and watchful vigilance of dogs in his work, namely in Book 7, 21 and Book 9, 42. God requires the same vigilance from the Pastors of the Church, that they should not be dumb, but cry out incessantly: *It is not imperial,* says Saint Ambrose, *to deny the*
<margin>
Letter 29 to Emperor Theodosius.
</margin>
*freedom of speaking, nor is it priestly not to say what you feel. Nothing in a Priest is so dangerous before God, so shameful among men, as not to freely announce what he feels. For it is written: "And I spoke of your testimonies in the sight of Kings and was not confounded," etc. I prefer, therefore, O Emperor, to be good with you than to be in the company of the wicked. And therefore the silence of the Priest ought to displease your clemency, and his freedom please you. For you are involved in the danger of my silence, but you are aided by the gift of my freedom. Since the fault of my silence and dissimulation weighs me down and does not free you, I prefer that you judge me too troublesome rather than useless or more shameful. For it is written, as the Holy Apostle says: "Be urgent in season and out of season, reprove, entreat, rebuke in all patience and doctrine." We also have, therefore, One whom it is more dangerous to displease, especially since it does not even displease Emperors that each person enjoys his own duty, and you listen patiently to each one suggesting according to his office; indeed, you would correct them if they did not use the order of their service. Therefore, what you willingly accept in those who serve you as soldiers, can this seem troublesome in Priests, when we speak not what we want, but what we are commanded, etc.* It is certain that the state of the Church was greatly corrupted in the time of Isaiah, from his complaint about the silence and sleepiness of the Pastors, who see the wolf breaking into the sheepfold and do not cry out; scandals are stirred up, and they do not rebuke them; crimes roam, and they do not tax them; evil morals grow, and they do not wail; many live most wickedly, and they do not bark. People, whether Pastors, Teachers, or Bishops, are called dogs, says Johannes Goropius Becanus <note>16th-century Dutch physician and linguist.</note>, 
<margin>
6. Hermathena, page 124.
</margin>
since it is theirs to know and see what ought to be done in all things; then with a high voice and great courage to teach the truth, and to keep the wolves away from the flock they received to be guarded. God therefore accuses them because they not only do not teach and bark against the ignorant, but they themselves do not even see or know the truth. Then also, they are so far from guarding the grazing flock against wolves that they themselves perpetually gape for prey, with an avarice never to be satisfied. They do not have those things which are to be praised in a good dog, but those which are to be blamed in this animal: namely, voracity and impudence, and deep sleep instead of vigilance. An impudent animal...
