# SACRED HISTORY OF ANIMALS

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.

Iliad, Book 21, line 481.
</margin>
The dog is a [vile] animal, which is why it has become a term of reproach, so that a **shameless** <note>original: *ἀναιδὴς* (anaidēs)</note> man is called a **dog** <note>original: *κύων* (kyōn)</note>, as Hesychius testifies. In this sense, Homer uses the phrases **having the eyes of a dog** <note>original: *κυνὸς ὄμματ' ἔχων* (kynos ommat' echōn)</note>, **dog-faced** <note>original: *κυνώπης* (kynōpēs)</note>, and **dog-fly** <note>original: *κυνόμυια* (kynomyia)</note>. Thus, there is a heavy insult in these lines:
> How do you now dare, you fearless dog, to stand 
> against me?

<margin>
Iliad, Book 1, line 225.
</margin>
In the same author, Achilles reproaches Agamemnon for his impudence, as one who fears no one, cares for neither Gods nor men, and loves neither law nor piety:
> You drunkard, with the eyes of a dog and the heart of a deer.

It is a very great insult if any man is called a dog; because of his impudence, Aristogiton, the Athenian orator, was called "The Dog." The same is evident from the Sacred Scriptures in the example of Abner, 2 Samuel 3:8. "Dog" is a name of censure, which is why the *insult of the dog* is frequent among the Turks against Christians, as Scaliger testifies. And Ludovicus Romanus in *Navigation*, Book 2, page 209, writes: *The Muslims seized me, and having seized me, they put shackles on the cunning one. Someone addressed me with these words: "Christian dog, born of a dog."* Upon hearing the name "Christian," the Muslims immediately seized me. Then in chapter 5, page 211, he repeats the same insult cast at him by someone else: *"Christian dog, born of a dog."* In Asia, the Saracens were provoked by the insult of a single greedy Eunuch in charge of the treasury, who had called them "dogs"; they then spread the Muhammadan sect by arms through all of Arabia, Persia, and Syria with such speed that no plague, as Goropius Becanus records, ever spread with such sudden contagion. Similarly, Mestivoius, Prince of the Vandals, was so moved by the insulting name of "dog" that he not only renounced the Christian religion but also waged a bloody war against Margrave Theodoric of Brandenburg, who had insultingly called him a **Venetic Dog** <note>original: *Canem Henetum*</note>; see Georg Sabinus in the *History of the Life of Margraves Hugo and Theodoric of Brandenburg*, page 72 and following.

<margin>
Exercise 266, p. 808.

3. Francic. p. 89.
</margin>
### THE GOAT,
called by its proper name among the Hebrews **ez** <note>original: *עז*</note>, from which comes the Greek **aix** <note>original: *αἲξ*</note> and our [German] **Geis**. In Syriac it is *Izza*, from which comes *izan*, a goat-skin, according to Pollux in *Onomasticon*, Book 4, chapter 18. Because of its hair, as it is entirely hairy and shaggy, it is also called **sa'ir** <note>original: *שעיר*</note>, Leviticus 4:28, from **se'ar** <note>original: *שער*</note>, meaning **hair**. And a flock of goats, to which the army of the Israelites is compared, is called **izzim** <note>original: *עזים*</note>, from **azaz** <note>original: *עזז*</note>, **to be bare**, because due to their small number and scarcity, the land appeared almost bare, while the enemy covered the land with their multitude, as Johann Buxtorf has it in his Lexicon; or because it is not convenient to pasture large flocks lest they be infected by plague, as Ursinus teaches from Varro, *On Agriculture*, Book 2, chapter 3. It is found in the number of clean animals which the Jews were not only permitted to eat but also to offer in sacrifice under certain conditions, Deuteronomy 14:4. Thus, when God formerly made the promise of the covenant to Abraham regarding the hallowing of his seed in Isaac, He willed it to be fortified not only by the solemn seal of circumcision at the beginning, but also for the sake of confirmation, saying: *Bring me a heifer three years old, a female goat three years old, a ram three years old, a turtledove, and a young pigeon.* Augustine mystically explains this command in *The City of God*, Book 16, chapter 24, and interprets these three beasts as referring to the Jews: by the name of the heifer he understands

<margin>
1 Kings 20:27.

Genesis 15:9.
</margin>
<column-break/>
<margin>
Sacred history of animals.

On Psalm 104.
</margin>
those insofar as they are kept under the yoke of the law; but when they transgress the precepts of the law, he considers them to come under the name of the goat; while they allow themselves to be ruled, they are like the three-year-old ram. Elsewhere, *by the ram* he understands the Leaders; *by the heifer*, the Jews living under the yoke of the Mosaic law; *by the goat*, the converted Heathens or Gentiles, who hitherto had lived in the desert and thickets of Idolatry. Before the eighth or seventh day, a kid was not to be sacrificed to God, Leviticus 22:27. This is a most certain type <note>A "type" is a prophetic symbol or foreshadowing.</note> of the passion and death of Christ, which was not to be carried out in infancy: *I am of the opinion*, says Blessed Brentius, *that the Holy Spirit willed to signify, as if by a prophecy, that Christ was not to be offered or suffer death in his infancy and childhood, but in a perfect and manly age. It is also signified by this law that no man is a suitable propitiatory sacrifice for sins, because men are, by their age or virtue, softer and more tender than can stand in the judgment of God. Only Christ is of such adult perfection and strength that he can both bear the judgment of God and bring back victory from death and hell.* From a misunderstanding of this sacrifice of goats, or rather from the Devil's envy and **perverse imitation** <note>original: *κακοζηλίᾳ* (kakozēlia)</note>, goats began to be worshipped with divine honor in the city of **Coptos**, from which this name was given to all Egyptians. For the Coptites used to **revere** <note>original: *σέβειν* (sebein)</note> the goat, that is, to hold it as a God, because they thought it was the **plaything** <note>original: *ἄθυρμα* (athyrma)</note> or delight of Isis, as Aelian reports concerning them: <margin>History of Animals, ch. 23.</margin> **The Coptites worship female goats and place them among the gods; they say the females are the plaything of Isis.** <insert>The Coptites worship the females among the wild goats and attribute divinity to them; the males they eat, but the females they say are the delight and luxury of Isis.</insert> To Homer, on the island of Ios (his homeland and one of the Cyclades), the inhabitants performed sacred rites and offered a white goat in his rituals, as Agellius is witness to this matter in Book 3, chapter 11, and the epigram added to the image of Homer:
> Behold this white tomb of Homer; it indicates
> that the joyful people perform sacred rites for the dead at the altar.
That goats were excluded from the sacred rites of the Gentiles elsewhere seems to be indicated by the fact that among the Romans, as Plutarch testifies in *Roman Questions*, the priest of Jupiter <note>original: *flamini Dialis*</note> was forbidden by law not only from eating a goat, but even from touching it, and indeed even from naming it. Plutarch cites the cause of this in the place mentioned as the "sacred disease," which they also call the falling sickness [epilepsy], from which Hippocrates says goats and sheep suffer: **the disease of goats** <note>original: *τῶν αἰγῶν νόσος*</note>.

Question 111.
</margin>

or wild goat. Among the Hebrews, it has a name derived from beauty, grace, or ornament: **tsebi** <note>original: *צבי*</note>, **glory, grace, ornament**. With this title of honor, Judea is several times distinguished in the Holy Books, Daniel 8:9, 11:16, Ezekiel 20:6. In Latin it is *Dama*, which others derive from **deima** [fear], because they are timid. <margin>

confirm. Deservedly like a young gazelle, because the gazelle feeds in high places. It is called *Dorcas* <note>Greek: δορκάς</note> from "seeing." For the *Dorcas* has a very sharp sight. What is more fitting for Christ, who saw the Father, whom no one else has seen? Or if anyone has seen the Father in Christ, the Son himself revealed Him. Deservedly like a young stag; the young stag is like the Son, into whom the Father’s natural power has grown, so that hidden things are not concealed from him. Holy Scripture represents the coming of the Messiah for the salvation of men as swift and fast, and similar to a fleeing gazelle and a young stag, leaping on the mountains and skipping over the hills. <margin>Song of Sol. 2:8-9</margin> *Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills: My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag.* Regarding the first verse of the Song, let us hear the rhymes of Williram <note>Williram of Ebersberg, an 11th-century scholar known for his paraphrase of the Song of Solomon</note>, which go as follows:

> This strenuous one crossed all mountains and hills
> To him, boyish men cannot be compared:
> He who, carrying humanity, is the same Most High God.
> He himself took a leap from heaven into the virgin’s womb
> Into the field of the world he came after the virgin’s womb
> Then he underwent the cross, from there he leaped to the underworld <note>original: "phlegetonta," referring to the fiery river of Hades</note>.
> A victor from Hell, he sought heaven by leaping.

Regarding the second verse, St. Bernard says in Sermon 55 on the Song of Songs, column 951: For him whom he had just described as leaping and hurrying, he consequently compares to a gazelle and a young stag. Aptly indeed, because this kind of animal is swift in running and agile in leaping. Furthermore, the discourse is about the bridegroom, who is described as leaping and skipping over, having been made like a gazelle and a young stag. And this is the reason for the likeness. Add, however, lest any tiny portion of the likeness itself be empty, that the gazelle excels not only in the speed of its running, but also in the sharpness of its sight. The young stag is known to carry itself with a more rapid course. Through the young stag is expressed the desire of the one leaping; through the gazelle is expressed the judgment of the one choosing. From "leaping" and "ascending" <note>original: ἀναβάσει</note> onto the highest rocks they are named <margin>1 Sam. 24:3; Job 39:3; Ps. 104:18; Prov. 5:19</margin> where the Vulgate reads "Ibexes," and sometimes "stag," at other times "young stag": Luther translates it sometimes as "Roe" <note>German: Rehe</note>, sometimes as "Chamois" <note>German: Gembfen</note>. But you will more accurately translate it as "rock-goats" or "mountain goats." Just as you will more elegantly explain the term <term>לצב</term> <note>Hebrew: *tsbi*, gazelle</note> as the young of a doe or gazelle in Song of Sol. 2:9, 17; 4:5; 7:3; and 8:14. But what does he mean by the gazelles <margin>Song of Sol. 2:7</margin> <term>adjuration</term> <note>original: ὁρκισμός</note>? It is a pastoral oath, says Mercerus in his Commentary, folio 149. And the Bridegroom means to say: "May your vows turn out well for you, so that you may pursue gazelles and stags of the fields in a happy hunt and entangle them in snares." Osiander and the Rinberg Bible explain this <term>adjuration</term> <term>by the gazelles</term> <note>original: בצבאות / bi-tsba'ot</note> thus: *By those things which are most dear and pleasant to you, I adjure you, that you do not disturb my Church.* Blessed Luther seems to be distant from this interpretation, for he understands the gazelles and stags to be the holy Prophets, Leaders, and Kings among the Israelite people, who were exposed to all neighbors like stags in a field; as if he were saying: *By your ancestors, distinguished in faith and Spirit, I adjure you.* And the likeness fits: for he rightly depicts holy men among this people through simple beasts exposed to the injuries of all. Blessed Rauppius supplies and adds another from Hegesippus in his commentary on this passage. He explains these words and the preceding ones concerning the Church of the Old Testament and its ardent desire for the coming of the Messiah, in this way: *I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem,*

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
as many of you as belong to the Judaic or Old Testament Church, by the gazelles, by the dearest and most pleasant of all animals, that you do not rouse my beloved—that is, do not disturb the Church in its quiet and faithful expectation of the Messiah—with a false rumor, as if I have already come, until he pleases—that is, until the time for sending the Messiah has been fulfilled according to the divine promises, and she herself has greedily fulfilled and desired their completion. This explanation agrees in sense with the first. Finally, it must be noted that while the Septuagint <note>LXX</note> explains this passage of the Song, they have nothing to do with stags. For they say: <term>by the powers and by the strengths of the field</term> <note>original: ἐν ταῖς δυνάμεσι καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἰσχύσεσι τοῦ ἀγροῦ</note>; they did not follow the proper root of the words. Since for <term>gazelles</term> <note>original: צבאות / tsba'ot</note>, they assumed the root <term>to serve or fight</term> <note>original: צבא / tsaba</note>, and wanted it to be a noun for "military service" or "host." Likewise, in place of <term>does</term> <note>original: אילות / ayalot</note> they took <term>strength or fortitude</term> <note>original: איל / ayil</note>. But it is a common fault of theirs to wander and to depart <term>entirely</term> <note>original: διὰ πασῶν</note> from the original text. Symmachus, Aquila, and Theodotion are more correct: <term>by the gazelles and by the hinds of the field</term> <note>original: κατὰ τῶν δορκάδων καὶ κατὰ τῶν ἐλάφων τοῦ ἀγροῦ</note>.

THE STAG, from the catalog of clean animals which God permitted the Hebrews to eat, *Deut. 12:15; 14:5; 15:22*, is the chief animal among the horned creatures, whose strength, beauty, and dignity also consist in its horns; whence it is called by the Hebrews <term>Ayil</term> <note>איל</note>, from <term>strong</term> <note>איל</note>, because its chief strength is in its horns. Oppian also refers to this, where he says the beauty and the whole <term>horn</term> <note>original: κέρας</note> of the stag consist in its high head, large eyes, fat and colored back, and especially the horns, according to verse 194. <margin>Book 2 of *Cynegetica*, v. 177 ff.</margin>

> <term>A sharp-haired, highly-wrought, variegated branch of horns.</term> <note>original: Ὀξύκομον κεράων πολυδαίδαλον αἴολον ἔρνος</note>

Soon he also calls the horns <term>beautifully branched</term> <note>original: ἐυοζίδια</note>. To which Maro <note>Virgil</note> agrees in the 1st book of the *Aeneid*:

> *And the leaders themselves first, carrying their heads high
> With branching horns, he lays low.*

It is to be ascribed to Providence, or rather to Divine Wisdom, that the stag sheds its horns every year, specifically in the winter time, and in the spring new ones are born to it. If a cause for this must be given from nature, it is because they are earthy and dry, and thus easy to shed, because they do not grow from the skull but only adhere to the skin. He tests the firmness and consistency of the newly received horns against a tree, and does not come out into the open until they are sufficiently strengthened. The females are <term>hornless</term> <note>original: ἀκέρατοι</note>, without horns, and that by the most wise <term>all-encompassing</term> <note>original: πανοίκῳ</note> disposition of the Creator, lest the horns be troublesome to the females during the time of gestation. We do read of a <term>horned hind</term> <note>original: κεροέσσαν ἔλαφον</note> in Anacreon and Sophocles, whom Pollux reproves in Book 5, chapter 12, section 2. Furthermore, it is a very swift animal, but at the same time fearful, which Achilles refers to when, in Homer, he addresses Agamemnon thus: <margin>Iliad, book 1, v. 225.</margin>

> <term>You drunkard, with the eyes of a dog and the heart of a deer,</term> <note>original: Οινοβαρές, κυνὸς ὄμματ᾿ ἔχων, κραδίην d᾿ ἐλάφοιο</note>
> *Woe to me, bold in face and dog-like in countenance,
> And most cowardly with the trembling heart of a timid stag.*

According to Camerarius's version: *For as we say, "He has the heart of a hare" <note>German: er hat ein Hasen-Hertz</note>, in its place the Greeks said, "He has the heart of a stag."* To the Greeks it is called *elaphos* <note>ἔλαφος</note>, from *elaphros* <note>ἐλαφρὸς</note>, "light," whose greatest happiness very often consists in the wonderful [speed] of its feet...

# SACRED ANTIQUITIES

-> Sacred History of Animals <-

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 18:34</margin>
...speed, whence the Psalmist, taking a comparison, prays for happy success for himself by the "feet of a deer" <note>original: "cervorum pedibus"</note>. Plutarch provides another origin for this, who wishes the Greek word for deer <term>elaphos</term> to be derived <term>from driving away or chasing serpents</term> <note>original: "apo tou elaunein sive elan tas opheis"</note>. For Nicander writes in his *Theriaca, v. 142*, that deer draw out serpents with their nostrils and their breath:

> <term>They track them everywhere,</term>
> <term>Searching the clefts of walls and their winding dens,</term>
> <term>Urging them out with the terrible blast of their nostrils.</term>

By the name <term>trochmalōn</term> <note>clefts/hollows</note>, the Commentator understands <term>rough and rocky places, and the lairs of wild beasts</term>. Oppian in Book 2 of *Cynegetica*, Basil in the *Hexaëmeron*, and Martial subscribe to this:
<margin>Book 12, epigram 29.</margin>
> *Thus the breath of a deer sucks up the cold snake.*

Eustathius assigns this efficacy to the scent of the deer's horn; he says the deer first rub their horns against a rock and heat them by the friction, <term>so that by the vapor</term> <note>original: "ana-thumiasei"</note> they draw out the serpent. Vossius, in *On Idolatry, Book 3, ch. 73*, thinks the exit of the serpents from their caves comes not so much from the exhalation of the horn as from the scent, and both the expiration and transpiration of the deer; you may consult him there for more details. Athanasius and Eustathius derive the word <term>elaphos</term> <term>from taking/destroying serpents</term> <note>original: "apo tou elein tas opheis"</note>. There is certainly a stupendous <term>antipathy</term> <note>natural hostility</note> between deer and serpents, since deer either crush with their feet the serpents extracted from their caves, or tear them into many pieces, or finally devour them entirely. Indeed, from the eating of serpents, their insides become so heated that, parched with thirst, they seek springs at a very swift run to cool themselves. While by the instinct of nature, like a kind mother, they know well that drinking water before the digestion of the snakes would bring death upon them, they endure the thirst; and exhausted from their swift run, they "glocitate"—that is, they lament miserably—and when they reach the springs or waters, they do not drink immediately, but plunge themselves in and make noises. Once <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "pepsei"</note> is complete, the deer slakes the thirst which it had acquired either from eating the serpent, or from its very fast running, or from the danger of flight from the hand of the Hunter and the teeth of dogs. With an appropriate likeness, David depicts his ten-year flight from the hunter-driven deer <margin>Psalm 42:1</margin>, *which <term>pants for the streams of water</term> <note>original Hebrew: "ke-ayal ta’arog al-aphike mayim"</note>.* <term>It longs for the springs of waters</term>, gasping toward the fountains, or as Pagninus and Luther translate, *cries out*. The word <term>ta’arog</term> attributed here to the stag or hind, and to all beasts in Joel *ch. 1:20*, denotes something that befits animals; those who translate it as "to cluck/glocitate" seem too narrow, just as it seems too narrow what Ludovicus de Dieu brought here from the foreign soil of Arabia and Ethiopia in his *Observations, p. 330*. Let the longing of the thirsty deer, hastening at a very swift run to the spring of waters, be a hieroglyph of the sinful man who has hitherto wallowed in the filth of sins, but now desires with burning longing to be united with Christ and received into grace by Him, according to Jerome. *The death of the deer,* says that Father of Stridon, *is to draw in the discovered serpent with its nostrils, and after this, descending, to extinguish its thirst. Therefore the man of the Church, who lived long in a poisonous state, when he perceives himself full of the mud of fornication and the stench of idolatry, desires to come to Christ, in whom is*

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
the fountain of light: *so that washed by Baptism, he receives the gift of remission, etc.* St. Augustine applies this similarity of the deer's longing to the truly pious, and enumerates three properties of deer in which the truly pious ought to imitate them: namely, in swift running, then in the crushing of serpents, and finally in how, while swimming across a river, the deer place the burdens of their heads upon one another in turn. His words are:
> *Run to the fountain, long for the fountain, but do not run just any way; do not run like just any animal: run like a deer. What is it to run like a deer? Let there be no slowness in running; run tirelessly, long for the fountain tirelessly. For we find the mark of velocity in the deer. But perhaps Scripture did not want us to consider only this in the deer, but hear another thing. What else is in the deer? It kills serpents, and after the killing of the serpents, it burns with a greater thirst: having destroyed the serpents, it runs more sharply to the fountains. The serpents are your vices: consume the serpents of iniquity, then you will desire the fountain of truth more greatly. There is something else you may notice in the deer. It is handed down, and even seen by some (for such a thing would not be written of them unless it were seen before), that deer are said—either when they walk in their herd or when by swimming they seek deep parts of the land—to place the burdens of their heads upon one another in turn, so that one precedes, and those who follow place their heads upon him, and others following upon them, and so on until the line ends. But that one who was carrying the weight of a head in the lead, when fatigued, returns to the rear, so that another may succeed him to carry what he was carrying, etc. Thus by carrying what is heavy in turn, they both complete the journey and do not desert one another. Does the Apostle not speak to certain "deer" when he says: "Carry one another's burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ"?*

To which we add that regarding the deer chased by dogs, which, exhausted and thirsty, pants and runs to the waters to slake the thirst from its vehement running. Blessed is he who, amid the pressures and narrows of this life, glows with pious desires, and thirstily seeks the heavenly fatherland; having despised all the joys and desires of this world, he ardently seeks the full vision and enjoyment of God.

### THE HIND
In Hebrew <term>ayalah</term>, which rising early in the morning cares for her fawns, spreads a bed for them, provides and looks out so that they are in safety. Xenophon in *Cynegetica* says the Greeks call it <term>nebros</term>, as if <term>koimas</term> <note>one who sleeps/rests</note>, as one <term>who, sleeping in a cave</term>, does not dare to commit herself to the woods. Elegant is the <term>epigraphē</term> or inscription of Psalm 22, though not without a strange discord among interpreters: <term>Upon the Hind of the Morning</term> <note>original Hebrew: "al-ayelet ha-shachar"</note>. What <term>ayelet</term> is does not yet stand certain, if you look at the various interpretations. The Greeks translated it *for the morning help*, that is, to implore God's help in the morning; it seems that instead of <term>ayelet</term> they read <term>eyalut</term>, for this latter word is translated as *help* <note>original Greek: "antilepsis"</note>. In this place, as almost always, the Vulgate imitates the Greeks, reading *for the morning undertaking*. Junius and Tremellius walk almost the same path: *at the first dawn*. And in the Annotations: *at the beginning of the dawn, or at the strength of the dawn, that is, at daybreak, because namely at that time the dawn exerts its strength.* They wish the sense to be, therefore, that this Psalm was delivered to the Priests and Levites so that every single morning in the Church, as soon as the Dawn...

# From Psalm 22, verses 1 and 19.
<note>The header refers to Psalm 22, though the Latin text cites Psalm 50 (L) in error or follows a different numbering system; the content clearly discusses the "Hind of the Morning" from Psalm 22.</note>

<margin>Sacred History of Animals.</margin>
...should break forth and be sung, as was the custom for the priests and Levites to perform music according to the law (1 Chronicles 9:33; 23:5, 30). Others, however, explain <term>אַיֶּלֶת הַשַּׁחַר</term> <note>Hebrew: *Aiyeleth Ha-shachar*</note> as *strength*, as Rabbi Menahem does, cited by Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note>; Aben-Ezra translates it as the *strength of the rising dawn*. Others claim *Aiyeleth* is a *musical instrument*. Others a *song*. Some translate it as *upon the morning star*, because the entire Psalm is about Christ, the Light-bringer. The accepted reading is *upon the hind of the morning* or *of the dawn*. Moreover, Luther (T. 2. Lat. Jen. fol. 238), Flacius (*Key to Scripture*, col. 112, 113), Dr. Gerhard (*Harmony of the History of the Lord's Passion*, ch. 7, p. 310), and Dr. Franz (*Sacred History of Animals*, p. 163 ff.) all teach that Christ is symbolically called the *hind of the dawn* here. To this some also refer the Chaldean paraphrase <note>The Targum</note>, which says: *For the virtue of the perpetual and morning sacrifice, by which the end of this afflicted and slain hind seems beautifully expressed.* For the offering of Christ on the cross is, in the words of the Blessed Glassius, truly a perpetual and most perfect sacrifice (Hebrews 10:12, 14, 16). It is also a "morning" sacrifice, whose power and prefiguration began at the world's beginning after the fall of the first parents <note>Original: *Prophetarum*, likely a slip for *Protoplastorum* (first-formed)</note> (Revelation 13:8; Hebrews 13:8), of which the morning sacrifice itself, usually offered in the Old Testament, was a type (Numbers 28:4). Drusius explains the name *hind of the dawn* or *of the morning* such that the *hind of the dawn* is a *most beautiful hind*. For he says the Hebrews use *Dawn* to mean *beautiful*. And it is clearly a term of endearment. For those who love are accustomed to call their female friends *Hinds* in sweet address. Whence that saying: *A hind of loves, a doe of grace* (Proverbs 5:19, etc.). He understands this Psalm to be about Christ. Others explain it as denoting a hind which hunters especially pursue, capture, and slaughter in the morning time, while it goes out from its lair to pasture. In the same way, Christ went out with his disciples (like fawns) in Judea in the morning time—that is, in the very beginnings of his kingdom like the true divine light—to the pastures of life (not so much to seek them as to administer them to others), and was captured and killed by the devilish hunters and the Jewish "dogs," while the Apostles were meanwhile scattered like fawns. This seems to be hinted at in verse 17: *Dogs have surrounded me:* to which is added <term>εὐξηγητικῶς</term> <note>Greek: *exēgētikōs* — by way of explanation</note>: *The assembly of the wicked has besieged me.* They refer this to the morning time because Christ, in his very first infancy, endured Herod's persecution and the expulsion into Egypt (Matthew 2:14, 15), and because the Chief Priests, Scribes, and Elders of the people are recorded to have met in the morning for the condemnation of Christ (Mark 15:1). Furthermore, just as a morning hind is not captured and killed merely so that it is enough to have caught and killed it (the way wolves are usually killed), but so that it may be pleasant food: so Christ, in the sacrifice of the cross and death, was made for us the sweetest food of life and salvation, to be eaten both sacramentally and spiritually. Musculus says on this passage: "O truly deer-like flesh of Christ, far more savory to a faithful soul than that which the nobles of this world hold as a delicacy." And lest anything be lacking for a delicate flavor and taste, our hind was not simply killed but well-chased beforehand; just as great lords, by hunting and chasing before they capture and kill, are accustomed to make the venison sweeter, softer, and more delicate, etc. The same author says: And see how

<margin>Sacred Rhetoric, Book 1, ch. 8, p. 165, 166.</margin>
<margin>Book 10, Observations, ch. 3.</margin>
fittingly it matches the death of Christ, that even for a hind, when it is in the nets, its side is opened with a spear-point—a thing which Christ also endured on the cross. So much for the hind under the title of the morning. In the words of the blessing given to Naphtali, he is called <term>אַיָּלָה שְׁלֻחָה</term> <note>Hebrew: *Ayalah shaluchah*</note>, a *hind let loose*, which excels in its speed and thereby easily eludes a pursuer. *Naphtali*, said Jacob, *is like a hind let loose, giving elegant words.* <margin>Genesis 49:21.</margin> Concerning the same Naphtali, Moses agrees with Jacob in his blessing: *Naphtali, favored and full of the* <margin>Deuteronomy 33:23.</margin> *blessing of the Lord, possess the sea and the south.* These words of Moses and Jacob are interpreted to mean that the Naphtalites, placed in a safe and fertile region, would exult in sweet liberty like a hind enclosed by no nets, playing freely at pasture in grassy and pleasant glades; and by sweet addresses and the arts of humanity, they would win favor for themselves among all, and enjoy the blessing of God in peace. Masius explains it thus, <margin>on Joshua ch. 18, p. 298.</margin> neglecting the Rabbinic gloss of Rabbi Levi Gerson <note>Gersonides</note>, who restricts the universality of the blessing to *Barak*, who was a Naphtalite born in the city of Kedesh, and who easily and readily, like a swift hind, allowed himself to be sent by Deborah on the expedition against Sisera, and then, triumphing together with Deborah, uttered most sweet words from his mouth in a song of victory. "I see that this Jewish opinion pleases many," says Masius, "but to me it has always seemed most foolish. For who could be so thoughtless as to think that most majestic prediction of the Patriarch concerning the entire posterity of Naphtali was fulfilled and exhausted by the victory of one man—otherwise ignoble and obscure—and a few chanted verses? To this, the sacred narrative itself clearly testifies that Barak was not at all prompt for that expedition, but hesitated, and would not obey the commands of God which he had received from Deborah unless she joined herself as a companion in the danger; for which reason the glory of the victory was snatched from him by a woman. Furthermore, those verses were sung by Deborah (who seems to have been descended from Joseph) rather than by Barak the Naphtalite. Finally, it is surely absurd for a brave and bold commander to be compared to a Hind, the most flighty of animals, unless we think Jacob's predictions were intended for the disgrace of the tribe of Naphtali, not its glory; for certainly Barak is not obscurely accused of timidity by Deborah."

**CHAMELEON**, from the number of those which are four-footed egg-layers, and which are recorded by Moses in Leviticus 11:29, 30 among the creeping things, because they creep with tiny feet rather than walk. Among the creeping things, the animal <term>כֹּחַ</term> <note>Hebrew: *Koach*</note> was unclean to the Jews, which the Septuagint translates as <term>χαμαιλέων</term> <note>Greek: *chamaileōn*</note>, followed by the Vulgate, Pagninus, and Vatablus. Junius and Piscator want it to be a lizard, according to Rabbi Solomon. Luther translates it as *Mölch* <note>German: Salamander/Newt</note>. Concerning this animal *Koach*, a learned man among the Hebrews writes: Rabbi Jonah writes that *Koach* is the animal called *Chardun* by the Arabs, and is a species of toad. But Rabbi Solomon writes it is the animal commonly called a lizard. Germany does not know this animal, but it has its native soil in Asia and Africa, and more frequently in India. Pliny describes the Chameleon: *It is tall, <margin>Book 28, Natural History, ch. 33.</margin> always with a gaping mouth, the only one of animals that [lives] neither on food nor*...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
It is nourished by drink, and by no other, *than the element of air.* Whence also Ovid sings:
> ---- the animal is nourished by winds and the breeze. <note>original: "ventis animal nutritur & aurâ"</note>

However, experience cries out against Pliny, Ovid, and others; for it does not live on air alone, as was once thought, but since it has a gaping mouth and a very long tongue always covered in mucus, it captures flies, gnats, ants, beetles, locusts, and similar insects by this means and eats them. This is testified to by an eyewitness, G. Joh. Vossius (*On Idolatry, book 3, ch. 55*), in addition to Jul. Caes. Scaliger (*Exercise 196, section 4*), Joh. Brodaeus (*Miscellany, book 6, ch. 11*), and Petr. Bellonius (*Observations, book 2, ch. 24*). There is a similar reasoning regarding the opinion of the ancients about the colors white and black, which they denied the chameleon could assume; yet you may read in Aldrovandus and Ambrosius that a nobleman, having been gifted a chameleon, wrapped it in a shroud. Returning home and opening the shroud, because he did not look closely enough at first, he thought the animal had escaped; but inspecting the shroud more carefully, he found the animal matching and assuming the bright white color of the cloth. If this is true, what prevents it from also assuming a red color? Besides a skin capable of every color, it also has very mobile eyes and rotates them frequently; it has little flesh and little blood, and lacks a spleen. In this way, a Christian ought to have the skin of a chameleon, so that he can accommodate himself to the customs of all; he ought to have very mobile eyes, so that he can turn away from impending dangers from any side; he should say farewell to "flesh and blood" and not be carried away by their allurements; and he should consider himself far below the "spleen" <note>The spleen was historically associated with laughter and melancholy.</note> of worldly laughter, lest he be captured by the pleasures of this world or carried away to joy by its inducements.

CHOEROGRYLLUS <note>A Greek term for a "pig-piglet" or "hedgehog-pig."</note>, this is a strange word which is read in the Septuagint version <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> of *Leviticus 11:5*: "You shall not eat THE CHOEROGRYLLION." The Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible.</note> explained it as *Choerogryllium* (spelled with a *ch*). It is repeated in *Deuteronomy 14:7*: "these you shall not eat: the rough-footed one <note>The hare</note> and the choerogryllion." The Vulgate: *these you ought not to eat; the hare, the choerogryllum* (spelled with *oe*).
<margin>Proverbs 30:26.</margin>
"The choerogryllioi, a nation not strong, who made their houses in the rocks," etc. The Vulgate: *four things are the smallest of the earth, and they are wiser than the wise: the ant, a weak people who prepares its food in the harvest; the little hare, a feeble folk who places its bed in the rock,* etc. *Psalm 104:18*: "the rock is a refuge for the hares" (other copies here have: *choerogrylliois*). The Vulgate: *the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs.* First, we shall examine what a *choerogryllios* is; then, whether it can stand in each of those places. In the first case, no one helps us except Suidas, who says: "choerogryllios is a porcupine, a thorny-pig, that is, a land-urchin," in German *an Igel / a pig / hedgehog.* It is also read in the Scholiast of Aristophanes, but with a single 'l'—doubtless by error. That it belongs to the porcine genus is somewhat clear from the etymology, which is sought from *choiros*, "pig," and *grylle*, "a sound, a grunting"; which our people call *Frollen* or *Gryllen*: or *gry*, which likewise means "pig": so that it is composed

<column-break/>

of two names with the same meaning, just as *orchano* is from *orcho* and *thyno*, and *gepedon* from *ge* and *pedon*, noting the same thing. Furthermore, we do not see how the version corresponds to the Hebrew text, in which is the word *shafan*, which both the Targum and the Hebrew Schools constantly interpret as a *rabbit* or *little hare.* Jerome observes it is called an *agromun* <note>field-mouse</note>, because it is a mouse, as if uniform; perhaps from a black heat, which however varies for this animal according to the climate. For ours are white, reddish, or distinguished by both colors, as rabbits are varied. And Friedlibius thinks it signifies every fleeting animal living in darkness. Moreover, it cannot be said of *choerogrylliois* or hedgehogs that they hide themselves in rock; seeing as they have nests near vineyards and thorny hedges through autumn, and in hollow trees in winter. Regarding the rabbit, however, it is well known what Martial sings:
> the rabbit rejoices to dwell in excavated caves.

They are accustomed, moreover, to level excavated places with dust so they are not tracked. In the morning and evening they creep forth, and sitting in the entrance of the cave they look around: but when dogs press them, they immediately penetrate into the caverns, nor do they come out from there unless ferrets are sent in, which are hostile to the rabbit kind (*B. Frantz in History of Animals, book 1, ch. 19*). Regarding the hatred of these little animals, Varro of his age and Cicero of Germany, Erasmus, think the proverb of Plautus refers: "Go now, hunt hares, now you hold the *sictin*" (so he reads it himself, that is, the ferret), that is, since you now have a most desired opportunity of finishing this, do not let it pass.

DRAGON, in Hebrew *tannin*, a word and its meaning I have dealt with at length above <note>original: "Græce δράκων, pag 611"</note>
<margin>page 611</margin>
from which the Latins have their word *draco*. To some, *drakon* seems placed by transposition for *derkon*, from *derkein* or *edrakon*, "to see," because it is endowed with large eyes, but for those looking sharply; whence of old they were imagined as guardians of treasures where there was need for vigilance, an opinion which still commonly possesses the mind. Scaliger preferred it to be from "doing pain." "And why not 'doing medicine'?" says
<margin>Exercise 183, section 12.</margin>
Vossius (*Idolatry, book 4, ch. 58*), namely because they are harmless and healthy everywhere; yet in some places, if not every individual, at least some, are harmless snakes permitted to the inhabitants, as Scaliger testifies (*Exercise 183, section 3*) regarding the Bigerrones near the Pyrenees mountains, where some use the same bed and almost the same table. For they familiarly take food from those things which fell as scraps. But whichever etymology you assume, you act like Strabo. Concerning "love of worship" <note>original: "φιλολατρείᾳ"</note> it will be dealt with later more professionally and at length. It suffices here to have cited that history from Valerius Maximus (*book 1, ch. 8*) concerning the Roman veneration of the Dragon of Epidaurus, who nevertheless was that infernal serpent disguised in a vivid dream, leading the First-Created <note>Adam and Eve</note> to apostasy. In which it is a marvel to say, that although the serpent, having once exited the ship standing in the harbor, returned, and was received at Rome with great veneration and divine honors and worshiped, it entered into that place which they themselves had designated and consecrated. No one is unaware of the worship of the Dragon among the Babylonians from the sacred Apocrypha, to whom the Babylonians were compelled to offer much food daily; whether he was the deity Bel himself, or a symbol of the deity, is not...

# From Psalm 50, verses 10 and 11.

<margin>Sacred History of Animals.</margin>
...is not sufficiently clear. The entire matter is made doubtful and almost suspicious by the very different account given by the writer of those things annexed to the Holy Scripture called the Apocrypha of Daniel, and by that recent compiler Joseph, who is called Ben-Gorion, concerning this deed. The former places it under Cyrus, the latter under Darius. The latter mentions an iron instrument with saw-like teeth hidden under a coating of sulfur and pitch and reduced to the form of a *Mincha* <note>original: *Minchæ*</note>, which Daniel threw into the Dragon's mouth. The former mentions only pitch, fat, and a mass made from them. It is pleasing to add the words from Ben-Gorion, Book 1, Chapter 10: *But Daniel, departing from the King's presence, prepared iron instruments like the combs with which flax is cleaned, and joined them together internally, back to back, while their spikes protruded outward, filed and sharp all around; to these he applied various kinds of food, especially fat, grease, and other fatty things. He also applied a coating of sulfur and pitch to it, by which fuel the iron spikes and those saw-like teeth were hidden, and he gave it the form of a measured portion (In Hebrew <term>מנחה</term> Mincha, which is a gift offered to God.)* And when Daniel had thrown it into the gaping mouth of the Dragon, *the Dragon took it and devoured it with the desire of his soul; but when it descended to the interior of his belly, the fat and grease were dissolved by the iron spikes, and the points of the saw-like teeth entered the dragon's entrails and pierced them, and immediately the dragon began to feel immense pain, and collapsing, he died the following day.* Whatever the truth of these things, it is evident that this method of killing the Dragon used by Daniel was not miraculous but natural. For although there is no deadly power in pitch, nor in fat (for since he says simply "fat," it is likely it was not from some harmful animal, but a very common one), nor in hair (because if drunk when crushed into powder they only cause dryness), nor in a mixture of them; nevertheless it is certain (and I once happened to see this) that swallowed human hair-balls cause great harm to the stomach, and even a lethal cholera disease. I believe the cause is that due to their flexibility they move the nausea, but due to their thinness and entanglement they are not rejected, but stick continually and irritate. Now, since pitch and fat are sticky and plaster-like, they are naturally suited to block the passage of food; and when entangled with hair, they stuck much more tenaciously. Therefore, I believe it rightly happened that the balls given from that mass stuck firmly in the narrowest passages of the belly, and with those being completely blocked and no exit given for what was swallowed or for wind, the Dragon burst, as Vallesius says in *Sacred Philosophy, 81.* To say nothing of other things which Selden relates on this argument in *Syntagma 2, chapter 17, on the Syrian Gods.* Otherwise, it was a sign of good omen among the Nations when they saw a dragon present during a sacrifice; whence Homer elegantly describes the dragon which appeared portentously to the Greek fleet staying in the port of Aulis, from which the time of the war was predicted to Calchas:

<margin>Iliad 2, verse 308.</margin>
> Then a great sign appeared. A dragon with a blood-red back,
> Terrible, which the Olympian himself sent into the light.

<gloss>and the cheek of all was red with blood.</gloss>
<gloss>As it is here <term>daphoinos</term>, <term>the great red one</term>. So no less auspicious were the standards of the cohorts considered to be from a dragon, or those whose ensign was a dragon, called by the Greeks both <term>drakonteioi</term> <note>dragon-like</note>, as is clear from Leo's *Constitution 3*, and <term>drakontophoroi</term> <note>dragon-bearers</note>, which is also in the Greek-Latin Glosses. There is no slight conjecture that the Assyrians or Chaldeans—from whom Codinus in his *book on the offices of Constantinople, page 108* records the Greek Emperors received them—used these in military service in memory of Bel or the Dragon worshiped by Babylon.

THE ELEPHANT, in the East is everywhere called <term>Phil</term>, whence <term>Sendephil</term> is the tooth of the Elephant <note>ivory</note>, for which is read in <term>1 Kings 10:22</term> and <term>2 Chronicles 9:21</term> <term>שנהבים</term>, <term>Senhabim</term>, perhaps as if <term>Senhababim</term> with the middle syllable elided. No other of the animals living on land deserves the title of "Beast" more than the Elephant, as the Whales do in the deep sea, and the Eagles flying on high. This animal is <term>Anonymous</term> <note>unnamed</note> in the Pandects <note>a compendium of Roman law</note>, except that mention is made of its teeth in <term>1 Kings 10:22</term>, namely ivory, of which there was no use in Scripture before Solomon; whence concerning ivory palaces in <term>Psalm 45:9</term>, where <term>chambers</term> are understood, which were covered with exquisite work and ivory, and <term>2 Kings 20:13</term>; compare <term>1 Kings 22:39</term> and <term>Amos 3:15</term> concerning the ivory house, so called from ivory repositories in which precious garments and royal spices were kept. From the teeth of Elephants comes ivory, which are of such weight and size that in Ethiopia they use them to build stalls for cattle; compare Pliny *Natural History, Book 8, Chapter 5.* I saw, says Vartomanus in *Navigation, Book 6, Chapter 23, page 267*, very large ivory in the Island of Sumatra; these are the teeth of Elephants, weighing three hundred and thirty-five pounds. Or, according to the common opinion of Interpreters, it is understood by the word <term>בהמות</term> <note>Behemoth</note> in <term>Job 40:10</term>: *Behold now Behemoth, which I made with thee; he eateth grass as an ox.* Where by <term>Behemoth</term> the Septuagint and the Chaldean understand every terrestrial beast of vast size; but the Hebrews think only the Elephant is signified, whom Lyra, Thomas, and others follow. The context reveals that a monstrous animal of enormous body size is understood, and the Interpreters agree, concerning which Gregorius Francus says: *This name is worn by the mouths of all who know sacred letters; but its proper meaning is not equally obvious; yet from the subject matter and the very long description given here, it presents itself spontaneously to the minds and eyes of all, so that nothing can be held more clearly; for such a long enumeration of so many properties looks toward that. What? That it is called the primary work of the ways of the strong God.* <margin>Sacred Lexicon, page 174, no. 139.</margin> *Therefore, since the discourse is about animals, some of which are expressed in the preceding parts, it is immediately clear from this that it is brought forward here as an example, because it excels all the rest in strength of body, vastness, and length of life.* <margin>verse 14.</margin>

</margin>
surpasses others. Therefore, to indicate its excellence, it is expressed in the plural number and called *Behemoth* <note>original: בהמות</note>, although it denotes nothing other than an animal, whether wild or domestic. By way of supreme eminence and as a proper name, *Behemoth* can signify no other than the Elephant. All those properties enumerated in this chapter [of Job] fit this creature. Among quadrupeds, the Elephant holds the sovereignty, whence it is deservedly called *Aluph* <note>original: אלוף</note>, that is, the prince of animals or Leader, from *alaph* <note>original: אלף</note>, which in the simple verb form means "to learn," and in the intensive form "to teach," whence comes the Greek *alphein* <note>original: ἀλφεῖν</note>, to find, to devise, or to learn. From this word, Gregorius Francus and Samuel Bochart derive the Greek *elephas* [elephant]. Among the Chaldeans, it has the name *Pila*, from which the name *Barri* was given to the Elephant. They were also called *Luca* [Lucanian oxen] among the Romans, according to Varro <margin>Book 6 on the Latin Language</margin>, because they were first seen in Lucania during the war with Pyrrhus; however, by that word they commonly mean an ox. Whence the proverb of Ennius: *A locust will give birth to a Lucanian ox before that happens.* And Lactantius Firmianus in his book *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 3, says: "Can anyone, then, when he sees even Lucanian oxen with their massive bodies serving man, complain about God the creator?" It surpasses every single beast in magnitude and height; Job aims at this when he describes it in the plural, *Behemoth*, that is, as if it were the equivalent of all beasts together. Next, he notes that it is accustomed to rest and lie down under shady trees so that it may be safe from the heat of the sun. Under the shade, says Job <margin>verse 16</margin>, it sleeps in the secret of the reed and in moist places; the shades protect its shadow, the willows of the brook will surround it. Rabbi Levi and Rabbi Kimchi, in the *Book of Roots*, explain these words interrogatively. But both its habitat and the vastness of its body are hinted at by these words; for although it does not enter deep waters, it nevertheless keeps itself by the banks of waters and in marshy places. It loves the shade, whence it seeks tall and shady trees, so that under these it can protect and hide itself from the burning of the sun. Its strength is celebrated in these <margin>verses 11, 13</margin> words: *Behold now, his power is in his loins, and his strength is in the navel of his belly. His bones are like bars of bronze, his bones like a rod of iron.* By which Job hints that even those parts which are soft in other animals are hardest and strongest in the elephant, so much so that it surpasses the rest in the strength of its loins just as it does in its bulk. How great its strength is can be known from the fact that they carry towers, from which ten or even fifteen soldiers may hurl javelins or arrows, as is told in the first book of the Maccabees <note>original: "book of the Asmonaeans"</note>, chapter 6, verse 37, concerning a certain Elephant carrying 32 soldiers along with the Indian, the master of the beast, which was killed by Eleazar, son of Mattathias. Hence its use in wars is frequent, as history testifies; yet often they brought more danger to their own side than to the enemy (compare book 9 of Curtius). Furthermore, Job outlines its food and drink with these words <margin>verses 15, 18</margin>: *Surely the mountains bring forth grass for him, and all the beasts of the field play there. Behold, he will drink up a river, so that he does not hurry; he trusts that he can draw up the Jordan into his mouth.* The meaning is: although the Elephant is vast, it does not feed on flesh like other wild beasts, but on herbs, a plenty of which is supplied to it on the mountains. In the words describing its drink, some recognize a hyperbole [exaggeration] in poetic writing, which is not unusual. Others explain it to mean that it drinks intrepidly from a river without fear of anyone, not like a dog

<column-break/>

from the Nile, according to the proverb. Aristotle testifies in *History of Animals*, book 8, chapter 9, that an Elephant drinks nine Macedonian measures in one draught. As for the sacred matters which Philippus the Presbyter and after him Blessed Brentius explain mystically and apply to the Devil and his followers: by the "mountains" they understand proud and overly exalted men in whom the Devil dwells; by the "river" they understand men, and by the "Jordan" they understand the pious. The words of Brentius are: *The power of Satan is insatiable, for Satan absorbs the whole river, that is, the entire human population (for many waters are many peoples) and, trembling at nothing, devours everything. Nor does he keep his mouth from the Jordan, for he trusts that he will drink it all up.* The Jordan is the chosen people, for the Jews, a holy and chosen nation, lived by the Jordan. Therefore, Satan not only intends evil for the wicked, but also thrusts the worst things upon the good and pious. It surpasses other beasts in sagacity, whence it is called by Philostratus in the second book of the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, chapter 7, *an animal next to man in intelligence and counsel* <note>original: ζῶον ἀγχίνουν ἀνθρώπῳ κατὰ ξύνεσιν καὶ βουλὴν</note>. Concerning which Ludovicus Romanus writes in *Navigation*, book 4, chapter 10: "The Elephant is a very docile animal, and lacks little of human senses, and usually surpasses all beasts in strength. The Indians, about to enter wars, place pack-saddles on the elephant. These saddles are of the kind used by many in the kingdom of Ausonia; beneath the belly, twin iron chains cinch the saddles. Above the saddles on this side and that is a house, or if you prefer to call it a tower or a wooden cage; they join the cages to the neck with padding of some thickness, half a palm wide. Three men enter each cage. Between the two, an Indian sits on the back of the beast and speaks to it; for they have an understanding of their native speech and a memory of duties. It is certain that no other animal approaches closer to human senses, if you look at the pleasure of love and glory, conspicuous integrity, prudence, and that kind of character of which other animals are devoid. And so there are seven men who, about to enter battle, mount the elephant armored, carrying bows, spears, swords, and shields. The trunk of the elephant, which they call a 'hand,' is armored; to it is tied a drawn sword, two cubits in length, and of the thickness and width of a human palm; and thus equipped they fight. Where it must go forward or backward, the master warns it, whose voice the elephant understands. 'Strike that one,' says the moderator of the beast, 'spare that one, rage against others, abstain from others.' And the animal undergoes all commands, and fulfills them exactly, and they can be led by nothing to retreat; for that nation, with wonderful art, excites fires to terrify the beasts when they please. The animal fears these so much that it is terrified by nothing more. Because of this, when fires are seen, they flee most widely. What remains? In its established character and extraordinary strength, it surpasses all. I remember once seeing three elephants drag a very large Liburnian ship onto dry land." But we must hurry, lest if we linger too long on the Elephant, other animals might withdraw themselves.

# From Psalm 50, verses 10-11.

<margin>Sacred History of Animals.</margin>
...and he cheers his rider with his own alacrity; rather, he is so named from ruling his own kind, as Ursinus has it in his *Nomenclature* p. 99, because he is, as Nemesianus witnesses in the *Cynegetica* <note>A Roman poem on hunting.</note> *easy, easy, and,*

> *He obeys in submission to the guidance of the supple switch,*

He has many other common names with others, among which are *Rekheb* <note>original: רכב</note>, which also denotes a chariot, from *rakhab*, he rode or sat upon a horse; and *Rekush* <note>original: רכוש</note>, horseman and horse; *Abbirim* <note>original: אבירים</note>, Isaiah 34:7, namely "strong horses," *starke Gäul/Rosse* <note>German: strong nags/steeds</note> according to Dr. Luther. He found a panegyrist of his nobility in Job, *chapter 39:19*: *Have you given the horse strength, or clothed his neck with thunder? Can you make him afraid as a grasshopper? The glory of his nostrils is terrible. He paws in the valley, and rejoices in his strength: he goes on to meet the armed men. He mocks at fear, and is not affrighted; neither turns he back from the sword. The quiver rattles against him, the glittering spear and the shield. He swallows the ground with fierceness and rage: neither believes he that it is the sound of the trumpet. He says among the trumpets, Ha, ha; and he smells the battle afar off, the thunder of the captains, and the shouting.* Among the beasts of burden, which according to Augustine have their name from *helping* <note>Latin: "jumenta" from "juvare"</note>, the horse holds the preeminence; hence in every age of the world, men have placed no small effort in breeding horses. You might except only the Americans <note>Indigenous peoples of the Americas</note>, to whom this animal was unknown until the last century; hence, seeing a horseman—that is, a man sitting on a horse—they thought they saw a single individual, imagining for themselves new Centaurs, whom the Poets of old feigned to be men in the upper part and horses in the lower. This fable was born from the Centaurs, a people of Thessaly skilled in riding, who are said to have first discovered the method of fighting from horseback. The Thessalians were once famous for their cavalry, whence King Philip of Macedon, as Justin records, subjugated Thessaly to himself—not out of a desire for plunder, but so that he might join the strength of the Thessalians to his own army, and make one body of cavalry and infantry for an invincible force. An animal most well-known to us, and indeed most useful, it holds the first rank for war, the second for travel, and the third for transport. From ancient times, Nesaean horses from Media were supplied for their excellence, just as Oldenburg horses are in Germany.

<margin>17, 6, 6.</margin>
<margin>Book 11.</margin>
Strabo, mentioning a "meadow for horse-breeding" <note>original Greek: Λειμῶν ἱπποβότου</note>, adds: *As for the Nesaean horse, which the kings used, being the best and largest, some say the breed is from here, others from Armenia.* Stephanus says in *On Cities*: *Nesaeon, a plain, from which the Nesaean horses come to the Medes.* Spain was also celebrated of old and remains so today for its abundance and excellence of horses,

<margin>Book 44, ch. 3.</margin>
whence *many authors have related that mares conceive offspring from the wind*, says Justin, *which fable was born from the fecundity of the mares and the multitude of the herds; which are seen to be so great and so swift in Galicia and Lusitania <note>Modern Portugal</note> that they are not undeservedly thought to have been conceived by the wind itself.* The same could be said today of the Tartar horses because of their speed. The Ancients praised Arcadian, Iberian, Mauritanian, Gallic, and Parthian horses. Today, Spanish, Neapolitan, Turkish, Wallachian, Sarmatian, and Epirotic horses are in high esteem; to the latter, the Epirotics, Gratius gave the palm for racing in his

<margin>Cynegeticon v. 529.</margin>
> *—Who would dare to contend against the Chaonian [Epirotic] mares,*
> *which Achaia marks with the well-deserved palm?*

Virgil gives them the same praise in the *Georgics*, Book 1...

<column-break/>

> *India sends ivory, the soft Sabaeans their frankincense,*
> *But the naked Chalybes send iron, and Pontus the strong-smelling*
> *Castoreum, and Epirus the palms of the mares of Elis.*

<margin>Sacred History of Animals.</margin>
Nor should our Germans be deprived of their praise; though Cornelius Tacitus says they were not conspicuous for beauty or speed, nor trained to perform varied turns in the Roman fashion. But today you would not easily judge whether our Germans yield anything to the Italians in the skill of riding and turning horses, whether to the right or left, or driving them in a circle or orb, or even directing them in a straight course. Busbequius also commends, besides the Turkish horses (which one is not allowed to export from Turkey even if bought), the Syrian, Cilician, Arabian, and Cappadocian horses, which he kept for his own pleasure during his long and troublesome embassy, and he praises them for their memory. *I take in a pleasant sight,* he says, *when the sun is setting and each horse is placed in its own spot in the courtyard: called by me either "Arab" or "Caraman" or by whatever name, they respond with a neigh and turn their eyes toward me. For I am accustomed sometimes to go down and divide melon rinds among them with my own hand; hence that recognition.* They have this in common with dogs, that they know their own names and understand the voice of the household. Whence the Ancients gave specific names to the more noble horses: thus Adrastus's horse was **Arion**; Bellerophon's, **Pegasus**; Onemaj's, **Psylla** and **Harpinna**; Achilles's, **Xanthus** and **Balius** (the immortals) and **Pedasus** (the mortal); Pollux's, **Cyllarus**; Mars's, **Deimos and Phobos** <note>Terror and Fear</note>; Neptune's, **Ereopes and Glaucus** (that is, the force of storms and the Blue-Gray); Mezentius's in Virgil, **Rabus**; Pallas's, **Aethon**. It is well known among the common people that this custom of naming has been maintained both in the courts of Princes and among private individuals. Cyril, in Plutarch, discusses the character, docility, and memory of horses at length, and Pliny says:

<margin>Book 18, ch. 42. Natural History.</margin>
*So great is the docility of the horse, that the entire army of the Sybarites, the cavalry, was found accustomed to be moved in a kind of dance to the sound of a musical ensemble.* Aelian narrates this matter more fully in Book 16 *On Animals*, ch. 23; Athenaeus in Book 12 regarding the horses of the Cardians taught to dance to the flute; Solinus on the nature of Cappadocian horses, ch. 47. And to say in one word, as it were, what others have recorded most extensively regarding the virtues, magnanimity, fortitude, and love of horses, I am pleased to do so in the words of George Buchanan, a poet of no low rank in the previous century:

> *The Creator of things fashioned other animals for their specific*
> ->uses; the horse accommodates himself to all<-
> *uses. He pulls wagons, carries pack-saddles, carries chariots, cuts the earth*
> *with the plowshare, carries his master, whether swimming across*
> *rivers, or clearing a ditch with a leap, or if it is necessary to conquer*
> *rough ground in a race, or to surround the glades with dogs,*
> *or to gather his soft steps, or to turn in circles,*
> *or if he plays with free playfulness in the empty fields.*
> *But if wars call, a sharp vigor enters his trembling limbs*
> *for his master: and he vomits shared rages from his mouth and nostrils,*
> *and offers his noble breast to wounds, and takes up and puts down*
> *joys and sorrow in turn with his master: here, dutiful in every lot,*
> *as the ancients joined us in so certain a treaty...*

# SACRED BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
They might have believed that a mixed figure could coalesce, and that Centaurs were brought forth in the Pelethronian woods <note>A reference to Ovid or Virgil regarding the mythical origin of Centaurs in Thessaly</note>. It is not permitted to wander through such examples, since our task is to proceed <term>without dust <gloss>original: ἀκονιτὶ (akoniti), meaning without struggle or easily</gloss></term>, and to illustrate this so that it may be done with little effort—much of which the aforementioned Poet sang <term>as a model <gloss>original: ὡς ἐν τύπῳ (hos en typo)</gloss></term> concerning the praiseworthy qualities of horses. It has pleased the Holy Spirit that we should return to Sacred history, where not once, but very often in the Old and New Testament, <term>mysterious <gloss>original: μυστηριώδη (mysteriodē)</gloss></term> and celestial things are suggested to us under the symbol of the Horse. Zechariah <margin>ch. 1:8</margin> presents to us a man, whom he later calls Jehovah, sitting upon a red horse: *I saw by night,* he says, *and behold, a Man riding upon a red horse, and behind him were red, speckled, and white horses.* Who is this rider but Christ the Messiah, who is red in his passion and white in his glory? <margin>Rev. 19:11</margin> Hence he sits upon a white horse. Let us hear Jerome and Origen on both sayings. The former argues regarding the first: "The Man who ascended the red horse is the Lord and Savior, who, assuming the dispensation of our flesh, hears in Isaiah 53: *Why are your garments red?* etc." Origen <margin>Homily 2 on the Song of Solomon</margin> says this of the latter: "Someone might say the white horse is the body which the Lord assumed, and by which He, who in the beginning was the Word with God, was either clothed or carried. Another might say it is the soul which the Firstborn assumed; another might think both body and soul together are called a white horse because there was no sin; yet a fourth might say it is the Church, which is also called His body, appearing as a white horse, as if having no wrinkle or stain, which He sanctified for Himself by the washing of water, etc." The Man on the red horse is accompanied by a heavenly army, partly Angels, partly Apostles, and all the elect on horses of various colors, by which the attributes of the Angels are signified. The Messiah had sent out this heavenly cavalry, who, returning from the business committed to them, report, saying: <margin>v. 11</margin> *We have walked to and fro through the earth, and behold, all the earth is inhabited and is at rest,* that is, the whole earth enjoys peace and happiness, while the Church alone is pressed by afflictions; all is well for everyone on earth except the pious, for whom it goes badly. If anyone looks at external comforts—for they were in the harshest captivity for many years, and though finally liberated and restored to their own seats, they have so far been exercised by various evils, spending their lives in doubt and great misery between hope and fear. "This is the state of affairs," says the Choir of the elect with the Angels, "O Lord, do Thou in Thy immense wisdom discern what must be done, and enjoin us to execute it." Upon this concise report of the heavenly army concerning the miserable state of the Jewish Church at that time, the Angel of Jehovah is moved <margin>v. 12</margin>. Regarding who this was—since the preceding text sufficiently reveals and manifests Him to us—there would be no need to ask, were it not that we find <term>Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note></term> here, according to his custom, <term>Judaizing and Socinianizing <note>Accusing Grotius of interpreting the text through a Jewish lens or denying the divinity of Christ (Socinianism)</note></term>. It is Christ the Messiah, not a created angel as Grotius imagines (Michael), who, moved by the misery of his people, addresses his heavenly Father, saying: *O Jehovah of hosts, how long wilt Thou not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, against which Thou hast had indignation these seventy years?* As if to say: O eternal Father, Jehovah Lord of hosts, while profane nations destined for <term>the underworld <gloss>original: orco</gloss></term> because of their wickedness enjoy peace and leisure, it is a cause for grief that the nation which Thou hast given me as an inheritance, and which I have chosen as my only one, is ex-

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
posed to continuous disturbances and dangers; indeed, equity itself demands that, after Thou hast afflicted her long enough, Thou shouldst again <margin>Ps. 90:15, 17</margin> establish her, and let Thy beauty be upon her, and let Jerusalem herself and the remaining cities of Judah and the whole holy land be restored, since the seventy years of captivity have elapsed. How long, therefore, will You, who are love itself and the most merciful God, not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, against which You were angry because of past sins for seventy years now—the time You once predefined for the future destruction (2 Chron. 36:14, 15, 21; Jer. 25:3, 4, 5, 12; ch. 29:10) and which are for the most part completed in the captivity itself? Afterward, according to Your promise, the Jews were led back to their land, in which they have lived for some years now, but miserably. Where indeed is Your promise, Lord? *Thou shalt arise and have mercy upon Zion, for the time to favor her, yea, the set time, is come* (Ps. 102:13). Compare B. Ursinus, *Nomenclature of Biblical Animals*, p. 204. Zechariah has almost the same vision <margin>ch. 6:1</margin>, seeing four chariots: in the first red horses, in the second black, in the third white, and in the fourth speckled, i.e., of various colors. These four chariots with horses denote the holy angels and God's ministers and attendants, who in all four corners and parts of the world execute God's commands as quickly and easily as if they were the winds of the heavens (for He, by His admirable power, *makes His angels winds, and His ministers a flaming fire* <margin>Ps. 104:4</margin>). These, sent by God, come and return to the same after the demanded things are dispatched, and present themselves to that supreme Commander if He wishes to enjoin anything further (just as we read also of evil angels, 1 Kings 22:21; Job 1:6). Thus they proceed from where they had stood and were the executors of God's decrees (for "to stand" here often means to minister, as above in ch. 3:1 and 4:14); for they are always ready and prompt for their Lord and stand before the Ruler of the whole earth, observing His nod and awaiting His command (Matt. 18:10; Dan. 7:10). It will not be inconvenient if I briefly touch upon the horses of fire with the chariot of fire by which the prophet Elijah was carried up into heaven <margin>2 Kings 2:11</margin>. It is no wonder that Interpreters twist themselves strangely regarding the heaven into which Elijah ascended, while neglecting Holy Scripture and following their own <term>thoughts <gloss>original: νοήματα (noēmata)</gloss></term>. Some understand it as the Air. Justin and Emmanuel Sa understand it as Paradise. Gregory as some secret land. Jerome, Dorotheus, and Albinus as some celestial place, insofar as heaven is distinguished from the air. Most wondrous of all is <term>Becanus <note>Martinus Becanus, a Jesuit theologian</note></term>, who fluctuates strangely here <margin>in the appendix to the Disputation on Calvin's Purgatory, ch. 1, p. 44</margin>: "Enoch and Elijah," he says, "were translated not into heaven, which is the seat of the blessed, but into another place." But what is that place? Some interpret it as the earthly paradise from which Adam was expelled; others say they were there at the time of the flood, overwhelmed and destroyed; others say they dwell in some other pleasant place—nothing is certain, only this one thing is established: they were not snatched into heaven. But what is this <term>against the ancient sayings <gloss>original: πρὸς τὰ παλαíφατα (pros ta palaiphata)</gloss></term>! It is more certain than certain that Enoch and Elijah passed into the very seat of the blessed; where and what that may be, since Holy Scripture nowhere declares it, we shall not scrutinize, being certain that it exists, as the Blessed D. Friedlieb says. Regarding Elijah's <term>ascent <gloss>original: ἀναβάσει (anabasei)</gloss></term> into the heavens, Chrysostom feels thus: <margin>Vol. 1, Homily 6 on the ascent of Elijah</margin>
