# Sacred Animal History

<margin>Sacred animal history.</margin>
Among certain ancient Kings, it was the custom that if anyone had acted bravely for the King in war, and had not feared to expose both body and soul to dangers, he would be gifted with a chariot and other insignia of royal dignity. Therefore, earthly and mortal Kings were accustomed to remunerate those most devoted to them in this way. How much more did the almighty God—because he is King of Kings and Lord of Lords—will that his servant Elijah <note>original: "Heliam"</note>, who was zealous for Him with the total devotion of body and soul, should reach His kingdoms in a triumphal victory. This followed the sweat of many labors, the heaviest fatigues of dire persecutions, and the great and illustrious victories over such wars, bringing back the best spoils from the world and the devil, placed upon a fiery chariot and flaming horses. Compare Augustine, book 2, *On the Miracles of Holy Scripture*, chapter 22. Elisha also had fiery chariots and horses standing by and accompanying him while he passed through the camps of the Syrians unharmed, 2 Kings 6:17. Regarding both histories, let us hear Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose, 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note> debating thus:

<margin>Sermon 87.</margin>
Someone says: We have frequently heard that Angels descended to men; we also desire to hear when men migrated to celestial realms? The matter is manifest and placed ready at hand. Was not Elijah, the Master of Elisha, snatched up to heaven with Angels leading him, and placed upon a fiery four-horse chariot, ascending as a victor in a kind of triumph? For he had gone out as a victor, not over barbarian nations, but over worldly pleasures. Indeed, depraved morals are more grievous enemies than hostile foes, so that we may more easily understand that in this time, the malignancy of enemies can be conquered more readily than one's own morals. Therefore, Angels carry Elijah to heaven. The Angels who had carried the Master protected the Disciple, and they deferred those noble services, which they had once exhibited to the Father, also to the Son. For he is the spiritual son of Elijah; he is the heir of his holiness.

<margin>verse 10. 3.</margin>
God has His own horses and horsemen in heaven, sometimes sent for the aid of the pious, 2 Maccabees 3:25; 10:29; 11:8. He has, I say, His horses on earth. Zechariah shows us the Horse of glory; nor is a horse more commended by anything else than by glory—otherwise commendable for nobility, speed, and strength—the gifts of a war horse are all the greater if a victor sits upon it, if a warrior conquers, if a Victor triumphs. Blessed Luther <note>Martin Luther</note>, and with him Juan Nieremberg (*Ascetic Doctrine* book 9, ch. 82 ff., p. 66), explains this regarding the Apostles and other Ministers of God and the Church, who run faithfully, swiftly, nobly, and patiently for the glory of God and carry out His commands.

<margin>Song of Solomon 1:9.</margin>
The Mares in Solomon <note>The Song of Solomon</note> receive almost the same interpretation <note>original: "ἐξηγησιν" (exegesis)</note> and sense. Concerning which Ambrose speaks thus in Sermon 2 on

<margin>Psalm 118, page 608.</margin>
Psalm 118, page 608: In the Canticles we have it written: *I have compared thee, my love, to my mares in Pharaoh's chariots.* In this, while the likeness of the Church seems to be compared to the course of swift horses, her rich grace is estimated. You should not, therefore, take it that he designated a single Mare of the King, but absolutely for the Cavalry <note>original: "Equitatu"</note>. Pharaoh, therefore, as a most powerful and very wealthy King, had powerful horses, whence the Scripture says: *The chariots of Pharaoh*, as if the most powerful kind for the use of wars and the support of fighting. Along with Ambrose, Origen (Homily 2), Abbot Williram, Blessed Luther, and Osiander explain this regarding the Church, although Origen and Williram depart from Ambrose in this, while he and with him Luther and Osiander

<column-break/>

<margin>Animal history.</margin>
judge that by this likeness the Holy Spirit <gloss>Sanctum</gloss> pointed as if with a finger to the Cavalry of King Pharaoh, whose daughter King Solomon took in marriage. But those others think the Holy Spirit looked back with this likeness to the history of Pharaoh perishing with his army in the Red Sea. For Origen says in the cited place: The historical sense seems to show this: Just as then in Egypt, when Pharaoh, pursuing the people of Israel, proceeded in chariots and cavalry: And my cavalry—that is, the cavalry of my Lord the Groom—far excelled the chariots of Pharaoh, and was more excellent, inasmuch as it overcame them and sank them in the sea: so also you, my close Bride, excel all women, having been made like my cavalry, which, compared to Pharaoh's chariots, is certainly more powerful and more magnificent.

Truly, just as God the King of Kings has His horses in these lands, so Satan, the prince of the power of the air <note>original: "ὁ ἀρχων τοῦ ἀερος", Ephesians 2:2</note>, is not destitute of his own

<margin>Ephesians 2:2.</margin>
cavalry on this earth. For as we see an abundance of virtues in quadrupeds, especially in horses, so also in them the images of vices are not few. And what wonder? They are beasts. But for us, who are endowed with reason, it will be shameful if we do not surpass them by far. Such great heat of Venus <note>lust/sexual desire</note> is in most quadrupeds that it turns into madness, concerning which Maro <note>Virgil</note> writes in *Georgics* book 3, line 245:

> At no other time does the lioness, forgetting her cubs,
> wander more savage on the plains: nor do shapeless bears
> deal so much death and slaughter everywhere.
> Then the wild boar is fierce, then the tiger most wicked:
> Alas, then it is ill wandering in the lonely fields of Libya.
> Do you not see how a trembling possesses the whole bodies
> of horses, if only the scent has brought the familiar breezes?
> And now neither the bridles of men, nor savage whips,
> nor crags and hollow rocks, nor opposing rivers
> stay them, though they whirl mountains snatched by the wave.

<margin>Jeremiah 5:8.</margin>
Such is the madness of horses, as has now been proven from Maro; and Aristotle (History of Animals book 6, ch. 18 & 22) and Aelian (History of Animals book 4, ch. 11) have left the same testified. Thus, mystically, the impulse by which impious men are carried toward rapid lusts is likened to stallions maddened by the desire for females <note>original: "ἵπποι θηλυμανέισιν"</note>, which are called by the Greeks "irrationally raging" <note>original: "ἀλόγω λυσσώδειζ"</note>. While horses, relying on their own strength, tear the bridles and exhibit undue disobedience to their rider, they are called untamable and proud; so in Zechariah 12:4, they are most stupid: *I will strike every horse with astonishment, and his rider with madness.* Where the Seventy <note>The Septuagint</note> explain "astonishment" as "ecstasy" <note>original: "ἔκστασιν"</note>. Luther, however, translates it as "shy and stubborn" <note>original: "scheu und stüßig"</note>.

<margin>Psalm 147:10.</margin>
To this refer that verse of the Psalm: *He shall not have pleasure in the strength of the horse*, that is, if you explain it mystically regarding a man who trusts in his own strengths and works. Jerome understands such a horse to mean sinners, wallowing in the mire of vices and refusing to be ruled; "I think," he says, "the horses are sinful men, and the riders are demons who ride in them." If ever, therefore, we see some brother being an enemy and persecuting, let us know that he is a horse. Furthermore, the rider is the devil, who strikes us with his lance; the former runs and the latter strikes, but the horse itself is led by spurs, pierced, and rages against its will. This is the cavalry of the Prince of the world, Jeremiah 8:6; Revelation 6:4 ff.; 9:7, 17; Psalm 32:9, where we are warned not to be like—

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
...lest we be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding <note>Psalm 32:9</note>. The soul must be conquered and tamed, for it seeks to carry us away with a frantic riding. The pleasures of the world must be bridled and destroyed, lest they become wild and impatient of a ruler.
<margin>
On the 2nd Penitential Psalm, p. 243.
</margin>
Innocent III says: "There are two things that hinder discipline: pride and stupidity; for the proud, because of arrogance, do not wish to learn; and the stupid, because of imprudence, are unable to learn. The proud man is designated by the horse; the stupid man by the mule; from which he discourages us when he says: *Do not become like the horse and the mule.* The horse, that is, the proud man, must be bridled, lest he run too far through arrogance; and the mule, that is, the stupid man, must be whipped, lest he wander too far through imprudence."
<margin>
Micah 5:10.
</margin>
While the Jews placed more trust in horses and chariots, God threatens their destruction in Micah: *I will cut off your horses from the midst of you, and I will destroy your chariots.* Jerome explains the horses mystically as the unbridled horses of lust, raging with unrestrained force in the heart or soul, as if in a filthy stable. His words are: *O Israel, I will kill the horses from your midst, that is, the wanton impulses from the principal part of your heart, breaking forth like horses that have snapped their bonds; and your chariots, in which you pleased yourself in vices, joining sin to sin, as if you were carried in triumph in four-horse chariots.* Egypt is celebrated in Holy Scripture for the multitude of its cavalry, as its strength consisted chiefly in troops of horsemen,
<margin>
Isaiah 31:1.
</margin>
wherefore Isaiah announces woe to those who go down to Egypt, hoping in horses and having trust in chariots because they are many, and in horsemen because they are very strong.
<margin>
Isaiah 2:8.
</margin>
For the same reason, he had rebuked the Jews because, having spurned trust in God, they had filled their land with horses against the express command of God. For a law had been given to the King of the Jews regarding not multiplying horses for himself, nor leading the people back to Egypt to multiply horses, Deut. 17:16. God wanted the Kings of His people to be content with moderate forces, lest they trust in the great protection of equestrian troops, or place more hope in human defenses than in the help of God. Concerning Solomon, the most powerful King of the Israelites, it is established from 1 Kings 4:26 that he had forty thousand stalls of horses for his chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen; compare chapter 10:26.
<margin>
2 Chronicles 9:25.
</margin>
But in Chronicles, a far smaller sum is read instead of forty thousand stalls: that he had four thousand stalls of horses for the chariot, and twelve thousand for riding. The <term>Recutiti</term> <note>A derogatory term for Jews, literally "the circumcised"</note> twist themselves strangely in reconciling these <term>phainomenos</term> <note>original: φαινομένως; "apparently"</note> contrary passages. In the Gemara, they explain from Rabbi Judah that there were either forty thousand stables, each of which had four thousand stalls, or four thousand stables, each of which had forty thousand stalls.
<margin>
Defense of the King, p. 185.
</margin>
But what a multitude of Solomon's horses must necessarily arise from this interpretation and reconciliation! says Claude Saumaise. So great, indeed, that it defies belief. The expositions of other Rabbis are no better. The Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint (Greek Old Testament)</note> much more correctly took the forty thousand stalls to mean forty thousand horses, rendering it <term>forty thousand horses</term> <note>original: τεσσαράκοντα χιλιάδες ἵππων</note>. In Hebrew it is *urvot*. What are stalls, called <term>phatne</term> <note>original: φάτνη</note> by the Greeks, you might also call <term>hipponas</term> <note>original: ἵππῶνα; "horse-stalls"</note>.
<margin>
Commentary on the Bible, p. 431.
</margin>
B. Friedlieb answers most simply: In the latter passage, the groups of ten stalls are counted, where one stable often contained ten horses; but in the former, individual stalls are noted for individual horses. There were, therefore, four thousand groups of ten common stalls, each of which had ten individual stalls, from which forty thousand individual stalls are known. Whether Solomon actually transgressed the law or divine precept against multiplying horses is a matter on which the Rabbis do not entirely agree. Among our own, B. Gerhard thinks this was granted to Solomon by God through some special privilege, for the glory and splendor of the kingdom promised to him by God, which notable passage he cites from 1 Kings 3:13 and 2 Chronicles 1:12. Added to this is the fact that Solomon was equipped with that abundance of horses even at the time when he was still pleasing and acceptable to God, before the construction of the Temple. B. Friedlieb wishes Solomon to be excused by this: that the law was given with the condition that the King should not trust in them, which could not be said of Solomon; B. Walther also aims at this in his *Biblical Harmony*.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
There remain the horses of the Sun, which the Kings of Judah placed at the entrance of the Temple of the Lord.
<margin>
2 Kings 23:11.
</margin>
Concerning them, the author of Chronicles <note>The author actually cites 2 Kings here</note> says: Finally, Josiah abolished the horses that the Kings of Judah had given to the Sun, at the entrance of the temple of the Lord, near the chamber of Nathan-melech the Eunuch, which was in the suburbs, and he burned the chariots of the Sun with fire. Interpreters commonly explain this as images of the Sun and Moon suspended in the temple itself, as well as sculpted horses and chariots, rather than living horses consecrated to the Sun and offered in its worship. Whatever the mode of worship was, it is certain that this <term>heliolatreia</term> <note>original: ἡλιολατρεία; "sun-worship"</note> was instituted after the manner of the worship which the Persians, Armenians, Massagetae, and other peoples exhibited to the Sun. That the Persians were once accustomed to sacrifice a horse to the Sun is testified, besides Herodotus and Trogus, by Xenophon in the 8th book of the *Cyropaedia* and Ovid in the 1st book of the *Fasti*:

> The Persian placates Hyperion <note>The Sun</note> girt with rays with a horse,
> Lest a slow victim be given to the swift God.

But they especially offered a white one to him in sacrifice, because the sun is bright, as Philostratus testifies in the 1st book of the *Life of Apollonius*. Thus the Massagetae sacrificed a horse to the Sun because it was fitting to give the swiftest of all quadrupeds to the swiftest of the Gods, as Herodotus testifies at the end of book 1; and likewise the Armenians, concerning whom Xenophon should be read in the 4th book of the *Anabasis*. Thus horse sacrifices were in use among many nations, as Lipsius and others have long noted regarding Tacitus. To the Romans, the Horse was a victim not to the Sun, but to Mars, either because the Trojans were captured through its image, or because Mars was thought to be delighted by that kind of animal. Therefore, Florus tells of the Mysians; and Vitellius prepared a horse to placate the river Euphrates, according to Tacitus. Thus the Germans made much of horses for the sake of omens,
<margin>
On Germany, 10.
</margin>
concerning which Tacitus says: "It is peculiar to the nation to also test the omens and warnings of horses; they are nourished at public expense in the same groves and woods, white and untouched by any mortal labor; these, yoked to a sacred chariot, are accompanied by the priest and the king or prince of the state, and their neighing and snorting—"

<meta>This page continues the "Sacred History of Animals," moving from the worship of solar animals to the natural history and symbolic significance of the cat and the ant, drawing on classical, biblical, and patristic sources.</meta>

<header>from Psalm 50, verses 10–11</header>

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
...they observe the growling. No omen was more trusted, not only among the common people but among the nobles and the priests. For they think themselves the ministers of the Gods, and those animals to be their confidants. These are his words. We have spoken elsewhere more extensively on the worship of the Sun and its chariots.

**THE CAT**, called *ailouros* by the Greeks <note>original: "$\alpha\acute{\iota}\lambda o\upsilon\rho o\varsigma$"</note>, so named <term>because of its waving and moving its tail</term> <note>original: "$\delta\iota\grave{\alpha}\ \tau\grave{o}\ \alpha\iota\acute{o}\lambda\lambda\epsilon\iota\nu\ \kappa\alpha\grave{\iota}\ \kappa\iota\nu\epsilon\tilde{\iota}\nu\ \tau\grave{\eta}\nu\ o\grave{\upsilon}\ρ\grave{\alpha}\nu$"</note>. Aulus Gellius <margin>*Aelian, Natural History, book 6, ch. 8.</margin> teaches that their eyes grow along with the Moon. Herodotus, in his book *Euterpe*, refers to the cat or *ailouros* being worshipped by the Egyptians. Plutarch also mentions this in the 4th book of his *Symposiacs*, Question 5, as does Juvenal in his 15th Satire, verse 7:

->There they worship <term>cats</term>, here the fish of the river, there—<-

<margin>others read "the blue ones."</margin> Concerning this worship, Clement of Rome <note>an early Christian author</note> mentions it, or another ancient but substituted writer, <margin>Book 5, Recognitions.</margin> where he speaks of *gattas* or *cattas*, that is, cats; for as it says in the glossary, a *catta* is an <term>ailouros</term>, and a *katta* <note>original: "$\kappa\acute{\alpha}\tau\tau\alpha$"</note> is a cat. And according to Evagrius, Book 6, Chapter 24, <term>custom calls the ailouros a cat</term>. These obscure names for animals in Isaiah 13:21, chapter 34:14 <note>OCR says 24, but 14 is the likely reference</note>, and Jeremiah 50:39 provide us an opportunity to write about cats; there, to describe a terrifying solitude and devastation, the author uses the names <term>Ziyim</term> <note>original: "$\text{ציים}$"</note> and <term>Iyim</term> <note>original: "$\text{איים}$" — terms for wild desert creatures</note>. Who are they? For *Ziyim*, the Greeks sometimes used <term>leaping creatures, demonic beasts</term>, and even <term>demons</term> in Psalm 72:9. Others translate this as <term>Cercopithecoids, Monkeys, or Martens</term>. Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century scholar of biblical animals</note> understands them to be <term>wild cats</term>. For *Ziyim*, the Septuagint reads <term>onocentaurs</term> <note>mythical donkey-centaurs</note>, and the Vulgate reads <term>screech owls</term>, followed by Pagninus. For *Ochim*, others put <term>cats, monkeys, or weasels</term>. Jerome uses <term>Dragons</term>. The Greeks use <term>Echo</term>, a sound; the Syriac uses <term>daughter of a voice</term>; and the Arabic use <term>Echo</term>. Blessed Luther, the prince of translators, sometimes retained the Hebrew words themselves: *the Ziyim shall dwell there, and their houses shall be full of Ohim*; elsewhere he translates it as <term>monstrous beasts and birds</term>. Whence Junius renders it: *And the animal of the islands shall cry out*, which Piscator glosses as "A terrifying, foreign animal living in remote places." Let the reader find more in the works of the Blessed Ursinus.

**THE ANT**, named *formica* in Latin because of its "bearing of crumbs" <note>original: "ferendis micis"</note>. To the Greeks it is the *myrmex* <note>original: "$\mu\acute{\upsilon}\rho\mu\eta\xi$"</note>. In Hebrew it is <term>nemalah</term> <note>original: "$\text{נמלה}$"</note>, a name derived from "cutting seeds." This is that tiny animal which seems to possess more sense than other brute creatures. Indeed, almost all animals take no account except for present things. But ants look forward to future matters; for when hunger looms, they are wonderfully industrious in carrying food and storing up grain for themselves. When summer approaches, the ant prepares its caverns, goes out to labor, and at harvest time, when the crops are ripe:

->*then the wise one harvests the heap,*<-

<margin>Works and Days, v. 776.</margin> according to Hesiod; provident in domestic affairs, she plucks the mature grains from the ears and stores them in the earth, a quality which Baptista Mantuanus <note>a Carmelite poet</note> praises in this little creature in his 5th Eclogue:

> *Behold the tiny ant, a provident beast that stores*
> *In winter the goods found in summer's hollow dens;*
> *Lest the buried crops sprout again, she cuts them with her mouth.*

Jerome describes the <term>industriousness</term> <note>original: "$\phi\iota\lambda o\pi o\nu\acute{\iota}\alpha\nu$"</note> of ants observed and praised by Malchus the Monk in his *Life*: <margin>Volume 1, column 342.</margin> *I behold a swarm of ants bustling in a narrow path, bearing loads larger than their bodies. Some were extracting certain seeds of plants with their pincers; others were carrying out earth from the pits and blocking the flow of water with mounds. Mindful of the coming winter, lest the damp earth turn the stored seeds into*

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
*grass, they cut the seeds they had brought in. Others carried away dead bodies in a solemn funeral procession. What is more wonderful: in such a great column, those leaving do not get in the way of those entering; rather, if they saw someone had fallen under a bundle or load, they helped by putting their shoulders underneath. Why say more? That day provided a beautiful spectacle for me, whence I remembered Solomon, who sends us to the cleverness of ants to rouse our sluggish minds by such an example, and I began to seek the cells of the monastery and consider the similarity of those ants.* Concerning the burial which Jerome mentions in this passage on ants, it is certain that, besides humans, ants are the only animals of all that reverently care for their dead. They do not leave them in their caverns for the sake of cleanliness, nor do they throw them out heedlessly, but they carry them out and bury them honorably in the vicinity within the husks of grain. This is done by those closest to them, just as sons bury a parent in some honorable place or family tomb. Aelian <note>a Roman author of natural history</note> reports in Book 6, Chapter 50, about Cleanthes, who saw with his own eyes a dead ant being exported from a foreign cavern and brought back to its own people. At first, the carriers stood at the mouth of the foreign cavern, while the others looked on, and as if negotiating with the outsiders, they went back and forth until finally they brought a worm, which they gave to the strangers as if it were a ransom price. Concerning the social life and mutual work of ants among themselves, Dio <note>Dio Chrysostom, a Greek orator</note> discusses it thus: <margin>Oration 48, p. 535.</margin> <term>And indeed one may look upon ants with great pleasure, how they judge among one another easily, how they pass through, how they take up burdens from one another, how they give way to one another on the road</term>; whence he reproaches men for their dissensions and seditions, adding: <term>It is a shameful thing for men to be more foolish than beasts so small and senseless</term>. Compare the same in Oration 40, p. 495, where he takes instruction from ants for men who mutually revile each other and hinder one another from performing honorable deeds. Among insects, bees and ants are <term>the most industrious</term> <note>original: "$\epsilon\rho\gamma\alpha\tau\iota\kappa\acute{\omega}\tau\alpha\tau\alpha\iota$"</note>, as Aristotle testifies in Book 9 of his *History of Animals*, Chapter 38. Hence, since ants are not deterred from labor by the most burning heat, nor are they idle at night (which is a time granted for rest), nor do they allow themselves to be exhausted by the length of the journey or the roughness of the paths, but often carry their food over rocks and flint into their storehouses, the wisest of Kings, Solomon <margin>Proverbs 6:6 ff.</margin> sends us back to the ant, which neither borrows nor begs (as Basil the Great says of them in his *Hexaemeron*): *Go to the ant, O sluggard, and consider her ways, and learn wisdom, which, though she has no leader, nor teacher, nor prince, prepares her food in summer and gathers in the harvest what she may eat,* etc. Which Viexmontius rendered into an excellent poem in his *Method*:

> *Go, sluggard, learn labor from the tiny ant.*
> *She travels the path so often to store away*
> *A few grains for herself, while you roll here and there in your feathers.*

For it is not at all shameful to learn virtue and industry from brutes; since Christ in Matthew 6 discourages us from excessive worry about food by bringing forward the birds of the air, which neither sow nor reap. If our mind is truly fortified with humility, do not be ashamed to learn what you do not know, even from any young boy. And the first step toward knowledge is not to be ignorant of one's own ignorance.

# SACRED ANTIQUITIES OF THE BIBLE

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
...to be ignorant of. Concerning the **ant**, see Pliny, Book 11, Chapter 30, and Virgil, *Aeneid* 4, verse 402:

> And just as when ants pillage a huge heap of corn,
> Mindful of winter, and store it in their home,
> A black line moves across the plains, and through the grass
> They carry their prey, etc. <note>original: "Ac veluti ingentem formicae faris acervum / Quum populant, hiemis memores, tectoque reponunt, / It nigrum campis agmen, prædamq, per herbas / Convectant, &c."</note>

Much the same is found in Virgil's *Georgics*, Book 4, as cited by Lactantius in *On the Anger of God*, Chapter 7, and Ovid in *Metamorphoses*, Book 7:

> And the grain-bearing line, etc.
> —it is a frugal race, patient of labors,
> Holding fast to what is sought, and what is sought it saves. <note>original: "Graniferumque agmen... parcum genus est patiensque laborum / Quaesitique tenax, & quod quaesita reservat"</note>

So also Horace, *Satires*, Book 1, Satire 1, verse 33:

> The tiny ant (for she serves as an example) of great labor
> Drags with her mouth whatever she can, and adds to the heap
> Which she builds: by no means ignorant or incautious of the future.
> Who, as soon as Aquarius saddens the inverted year,
> Creeps out no more, but wisely uses those things
> Gathered before. <note>original: "Parvula (nam exemplo est) magni formica laboris / Ore trahit quodcunq, potest, atque addit acervo / Quem struit: haud ignara ac non incauta futuri. / Qua, simul inversum ut contristat Aquarius annum, / Non usquam prorepit, & illis utitur antè / Quaesitis sapiens."</note>

Ambrose, in his *Six Days of Creation*, Book 6, Chapter 4, says: "The ant is small, but it dares things greater than its strength; it is not forced to work by any servitude, but by a spontaneous foresight of purpose, it prepares in advance the future supports of its food." And a little later:

> No granaries are closed to it, no storehouses are impenetrable, no heaps are inviolable. The guard watches, and does not dare to prohibit the thefts; the owner sees his losses, yet does not seek revenge; the black line carries the prey through the fields, making paths through the company of travelers, and what cannot be grasped by their narrow mouths is carried as large grains upon their shoulders. The master of the harvest sees these things and blushes to deny such small, pious industry its modest gains. <note>original: "Nulla sunt ei clausa horrea... nigro convectat agmine prædam... Spectat hac dominus messis, & erubescit tam parca pia industria negare compendia."</note>

Thus far Ambrose. Marcus Aurelius, the Philosopher and Emperor, in the beginning of the 5th book of his *Meditations*: <term>At dawn, when you rise reluctantly, let this be ready at hand: I am rising for a human work. Should I then be disgruntled if I am going to do that for which I was made, and for the sake of which I was brought into the world?</term> <note>original: "Όρθρου όταν δυσόκνως ἐξεγείρῃ, πρόχειρον ἔστω, ὅτι ἐπὶ ἀνθρώπου ἔργον ἐγείρομαι..."</note> Xylander translates this into Latin as follows:

> In the morning, when you rise from sleep with difficulty, let it be ready for you to think that you rise to do a human work. Shall I then (you will say) approach with difficulty the doing of those things for which I was born, and for which I came into this world? Was I made for this, that I might lie in bed and keep myself warm? But this is more pleasant. Were you then born for pleasure, not for action? Do you not see the little plants, the sparrows, the ants, the spiders, the bees, each intent on its own duty? But you refuse to perform the duties of a man, and do you not hasten to that which agrees with your nature? But is rest not necessary? Certainly, but nature has set a limit to this, just as to eating and drinking. Yet you proceed beyond the limit and what is sufficient; but in doing things, you stay within the limit, etc. <note>original: "Manè cùm gravatim à somno surgis... non vides plantulas, passerculos, formicas, araneas, apes, singula huc suo intenta officio?"</note>

These things the Emperor and Philosopher said from the height of his Majesty. I do not wish to use a larger boundary; Bartolomeo Bonifacio treated the subject of ants in seven chapters in his *History of Play*, Book 9, Chapter 24, page 367.

**THE HE-GOAT**, called *Hircus*, as if *Hirtus* <note>meaning "shaggy"</note>, because it is shaggy and bristly of body, with a terrifying beard, threatening horns, and a heavy odor. Called by the Greeks <term>tragos</term> <note>original: "$\tau\rho\acute{\alpha}\gamma o\varsigma$"</note>, named either <term>from gnawing</term> <note>original: "$\dot{\alpha}\pi\grave{o}\ \tau o\tilde{\upsilon}\ \tau\rho\acute{\omega}\gamma\epsilon\iota\nu$"</note> due to the animal's voracity, or

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
<term>from having rough skin</term> <note>original: "$\tau\grave{o}\ \delta\acute{\epsilon}\rho\mu\alpha,\ \tau\rho\tilde{\alpha}\chi\upsilon\ \hat{\epsilon}\chi\epsilon\iota\nu$"</note>, according to the Etymologist. In Chaldaic it is <term>tsephir</term> <note>original: "צפיר"</note>, as in Daniel 8:5, 21 and Ezra 6:17, 8:35. In Hebrew, <term>ez</term> <note>original: "עז"</note> or <term>se'ir</term> <note>original: "שעיר"</note>, as in Genesis 30:35, 32:13, etc. The term <term>se'ir</term> is from its long hair or shaggy tufts, from the root <term>sh'ar</term> <note>original: "שער"</note>, meaning *to shudder* or *to be hairy*, as in Genesis 27:11 and Leviticus 4:24. For <term>se'ir</term> is properly "hairy" or "shaggy"; hence <margin>Isaiah 34:14.</margin> a woodland demon is so called, because it appeared in the form of a He-Goat in the woods and desert places, and by its terrifying appearance struck horror into those who saw it. It would make them "horripilate" <note>to have one's hair stand on end</note>, as some say, *so that people's hair stood on end* <note>original: "daß den Leuten die Haar zu Berge stunden"</note>. Luther in this place rendered it *field-devil* <note>original: "Feldteuffel"</note>, but in Isaiah 13:21 he used *field-spirits* <note>original: "Feldgeister"</note>. Pagninus translates it as "Demons" in both places. But Arias Montanus uses "Satyr" in the former, which word comes closer to the Hebrew. This is especially true if you compare these with Deuteronomy 32:17, where <term>shedim</term> <note>original: "שדים"</note> or "demons" is found, with which Leviticus 17:7 should be compared, even if <term>se'irim</term> is used there, since Pagninus renders both words as "demons." In both places, Moses rebukes the Israelites for the worship offered to Satyrs, whether to prevent them from doing harm or to drive away evils. That demons appeared in the form of a shaggy goat is indicated both by the word <term>se'irim</term> and by the fact that they thought they gained some majesty for themselves in this form among their own, as they are still accustomed to appear in the nightly gatherings of witches; see Remigius, *On Demonolatry*, Book 1, Chapter 23. Or perhaps because it was a foolish and very ancient opinion of mortals that Pan was the God of nature, whence they called him <term>the lord of matter</term> <note>original: "$\tau\grave{o}\nu\ \tau\tilde{\eta}\varsigma\ \ddot{\upsilon}\lambda\eta\varsigma\ \kappa\acute{\upsilon}\rho\iota o\nu$"</note> and <term>the whole of this universe</term> <note>original: "$\kappa\acute{o}\sigma\mu o\iota o\ \tau\grave{o}\ \sigma\acute{\upsilon}\mu\pi\alpha\nu$"</note>, as can be seen in Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book 1, Chapter 22, and Natalis Comes, Book 5, Chapter 6. He was typically depicted as a two-legged and shaggy goat. The Israelites learned this demon-worship from the Egyptians, who worshipped the goat with divine honors, as Diodorus Siculus records in Book 1 of his *Library*: <term>They deified the goat, just as they say Priapus is honored among the Greeks, because of his libidinous nature</term> <note>original: "$\tau\grave{o}\nu\ \delta\grave{\epsilon}\ \tau\rho\acute{\alpha}\gamma o\nu\ \dot{\alpha}\pi\epsilon\theta\acute{\epsilon}\omega\sigma\alpha\nu...$"</note> and because impure lust is more pleasing; <term>and this animal is prone to copulation: for it is fitting that the part of the body which is the cause of generation should be honored as being the beginning of the offspring of the nature of living things.</term> They included the goat among the Gods because of its genital organ: just as they say Priapus is held in veneration by the Greeks for that reason, etc. Clement of Alexandria writes that the goat was worshipped among the people of Mendes <margin>Admonition to the Gentiles.</margin>, as does Herodotus in his book *Euterpe*: <term>The Mendesians revere all goats, and the males more than the females, and of these the goat-herds have greater honors.</term> The Mendesians also attribute divine honor to the female goat, and more to the males than the females. And among those goat-herds, some are in the highest honor. He adds that if the chief of the goat-herds dies, a huge mourning occupies the whole region of the Mendesians. Indeed, it is gathered from this that their name comes from the worship of the shaggy one, because <term>Mendes in Egyptian</term> <term>signifies both a goat and Pan</term>. For the rest, since in Leviticus 17:7, Isaiah 13:21 and 34:14 the original text has the word <term>se'ir</term>, which properly means "hairy," some think that in these places, if we are to be precise, we should understand Satyrs, Fauns, and Sylvan spirits, which were not devils but terrifying brute animals. Thus, in both places in Isaiah, they are numbered among the brutes and other wild animals of which frequent mention is made among secular writers, which presented a human form in the upper part but a goat in the lower. Of these horrendous and monstrous forms the infernal Spirit made use...

# From Psalm 50:10-11
<columns>2</columns>

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
Matthew 25:33.
Homily 54 on Matthew.
</margin>

History shows that the Devil persuaded the Gentiles that he was a god through this form <note>the goat</note>, appearing through and in those satyrs to give oracles; he wished and commanded himself to be worshiped in them. From this, it is established that the Devil is especially delighted by the form of a he-goat, seeing as he is the "head of the goats" <note>original Latin: *caput hircorum*</note> who are to be placed on the left hand. Indeed, the naming <note>original Greek: *ὀνομασία*</note> of the impious is frequently taken from goats in the Holy Scriptures <note>the "Pandects," a term for the complete body of divine law; see Ezekiel 34:17-18, Zechariah 10:3, Matthew 25:33</note>. Hence, Chrysostom reviews the distinct types of goats. He says that the kids are sinful men because these vices are natural to goats: *Lust beyond all other animals, quarreling, and pride; for they always walk about striking one another, sometimes bumping with a shoulder, sometimes striking with a horn. Likewise, they are envious of one another, etc. Likewise, they are boastful and glorying, etc. Likewise, goats are much drawn by the greed of the throat; for on account of their gluttony, they walk through rocks and precipices, and hang themselves over cliffs. Likewise, the goat is loud and talkative above all others.* In all these vices, sinners abound, and therefore they are likened to kids. Thus, Hugo Cardinalis also compares hypocrites with he-goats *in his commentary on Psalm 49*, and he likens all the properties of the he-goat to them in this elegant poem:

->Wool, food, sight, blood, flesh, horns, offspring,<-
->The victim, the mountain, the vine, the tooth, the foot, the voice, the beard, lust.<-
->A short tail, a hide fit for the use of<-
->shoemaking,<-
->It lacks milk, it stinks, it is sent out, the he-goat chews the cud.<-

<margin>
Daniel 8:5, 8.
</margin>

So also the princes of the earth are compared to he-goats <note>Isaiah 14:9, 34:6; Jeremiah 51:40; Ezekiel 39:18</note>. Especially worthy of mention is the "he-goat of the goats" whom Daniel saw, which had a notable horn between its eyes; when this was broken, four horns arose beneath it toward the four winds of heaven. This signifies that after Alexander the Great—who was the *he-goat of the goats coming from the West over the face of the whole earth*—four kings would arise, each reigning at the same time in his own place: namely Antigonus in Asia, Seleucus in Syria, Ptolemy in Egypt, and Antipater in Greece.

<margin>
Leviticus 4:23.
Leviticus 16:5 and following.
</margin>

The he-goat was among the catalog of clean animals, which is why it was used extensively in the Mosaic sacrifices. Sin committed through error was forgiven through the blood and offering of a he-goat <note>Leviticus 4:23</note>. The sacrifice of atonement, to be performed once every year, consisted of a pair of he-goats. According to Leviticus 16:5 and following, one of these was to be offered to God as a sacrifice by lot, and the other, the "one sent away" <note>original Greek: *ἀποπομπαῖος*, meaning the Scapegoat</note>, was to be sent into the desert. This one was called *Azazel* by the Hebrews, *apopompaios* by the Greeks, and in Latin was known as the *Emissarius* <note>the Emissary or Scapegoat</note>. The Hebrews think that *Azazel* <note>עזאזל</note> is the proper name of a mountain near Mount Sinai; therefore, Rabbi Solomon says it is a strong and difficult mountain which obtained this name from that goat which was sent there. This opinion is confirmed by verse 10: *to send it to Azazel in the desert* <note>original Hebrew: *לשלח לעזאזל המדברה*</note>. From this, it appears that the goat was to be sent to Azazel, and thus the name belonged to both the goat and the place (compare Blessed Glassius, *Sacred Grammar*, Treatise 3, Book 4, page 763). Cornelius Agrippa mentions a certain demon by the name of *Azazel* who presides over the elements. Mention is also made of the demon Azazel in an ancient and learned poem cited by Blessed Irenaeus, which he writes was composed by a certain divine elder and Herald of Truth

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
In this place.
</margin>

against Marcus, the disciple of the heresiarch Valentinus. Among other things, he charges him that his father Satan, the "Azazel," supplied him with the power to perform his wicked deeds; you may see more on this in Marius. Those who subscribe to this opinion wish *Azazel* <note>עזאזל</note> to be derived from *az* <note>עז</note>, "strong," and *azal* <note>אזל</note>, "he went away." Others say it is a compound of *ez* <note>עז</note>, "goat," and *azal* <note>אזל</note>, "he went away," so that it means the *goat going away* or the *emissary*. The Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> rendered it *apopompaios*, as if you were to say, the "depeller of evils" or "the carrier away," because he carried the sins of the people—the cause of all evils—into the desert. From this, the Greeks called the gods they worshiped to drive away evils *apopompaioi*, *apotropaioi* <note>averters</note>, or even *alexikakoi* <note>warding off evil</note>. These were "averruncate" gods <note>gods who avert calamity</note> for repelling various evils, from which they were also called *lysioi theoi*, the expiatory gods (compare Platina, *On the Republic*, Book 2), though their primary author is debated. The Egyptians put forward Hermes, and Kircher affirms that the Syrians and Chaldeans received this from the Egyptians through the associates of Abraham (*Oedipus*, Volume 2, Part 2, Book 12, Chapter 6, pages 459, 469).

<margin>
On the Republic, Book 2.
</margin>

The Hebrews further relate, as recited by Fagius, that this scapegoat was pushed off a precipice from the very high mountain Azazel by the one who led him there. Meanwhile, that person held in his hand a scarlet thread, which was tied to the horn of the goat. If they had God as propitious and forgiving of sins, that thread was usually turned white soon after, as a sign of grace and benevolence. But if it remained scarlet and did not change, it was taken as a sign of God's anger. When the change was observed, a horn <note>the shofar</note> was sounded, so that those stationed in order all the way to Jerusalem might hear it; they themselves would immediately blow their horns, and thus within almost an hour, a great sound would be raised throughout the entire land of Israel. For this use, horn-blowers were stationed from Mount Azazel all the way to Jerusalem and thence through all Judea, so that in this way the whole people might break into praises of God. But if the horns remained silent and no sound echoed through the land, a year of mourning and repentance with fasting would be proclaimed.

<margin>
Question 22 on Leviticus.
</margin>

But I shall leave those circumcised men <note>original: *Verpulis*, a disparaging term for Jews</note> to their own fictions, dreams, and traditions, since Holy Scripture shows us a more certain path of comparison. This scapegoat <note>original: *hircus ἀποπομπαῖος*</note> was a type or image of none other than Christ the Satisfier and Mediator. Many among the people were reprobate; many were slain from heaven in the Lord's fury, many were rooted out for many crimes, as both God Himself and the Prophet Moses often complained about the stubbornness of this people. Nevertheless, the "evil-warding" goat carried out into the desert the sins of all—all, I say—who were among this people. Christ provided the same, which is why Theodoret *in Question 22 on Leviticus* explains these two goats (one of which was sacrificed at the door of the Tabernacle, while the other was sent into the desert) as the two natures in Christ. Thus, by the one who was slaughtered, the mortal nature is signified; and by the one who was let go, the immortal nature is signified. *These things,* he says, *bear the type of Christ the Lord, yet these two animals are not taken for two persons, but for two natures. Since Christ's mortality as well as His immortality could not be conveniently foreshadowed by a single goat, two were necessarily commanded, so that the one slaughtered might prefigure the passible nature of the flesh: while the one set...*

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence with the catchword "set free" (solvabatur).</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<columns>2</columns>

<margin>Sacred History of Animals.</margin>
...was intended to indicate the impassible nature of the divinity, etc. Next, the sins of the entire people were placed upon the head of the Scapegoat. Indeed, the Priest, placing both hands upon the head of the goat, would confess the sins of the whole people and, as it were, deposit them onto the head of the victim, so that it might become a *sin offering* <term>chatta: a Hebrew term for a purification or sin offering</term> for the people. Moreover, the form of the confession, according to Hebrew tradition, was as follows:
> O Lord, your people, the house of Israel, have sinned, they have acted wickedly, they have transgressed before you. I beseech you, O Lord, forgive now the sins and iniquities and transgressions by which the house of Israel has sinned, acted wickedly, and transgressed before you, just as it is written in the law of Moses your servant: "for on this day he shall make atonement for us, to cleanse you, and you shall be clean from all your sins before the Lord of the world," etc.
In this same way, the Heavenly Father cast the sins of the whole world upon Christ, who became a *purification* <term>katharma: a Greek term for a ritual scapegoat or someone sacrificed to avert disaster</term> and a curse for us, so that he might satisfy for our sins—and not for ours only, but for the sins of the whole world. (1 John 2:1-2).

**HYENA:** This is a beast somewhat lower than a wolf, but no shorter in length. It has a skin similar to a wolf’s, except that its hair is rougher and a mane extends across its back. From this it took its name, because its back is bristly like a pig's; for *ys* <note>original Greek: ὗς</note> signifies a pig or sow. Its head is joined to the spine of the back without any vertebrae; therefore, whenever it wishes to look back, it is necessary for it to turn its entire body. Its eyes frequently change into
<margin>XI. Natural History 37.</margin>
a thousand colors, as Pliny * testifies. It has serrated teeth just like a wolf's, and the structure of its teeth is a solid and continuous piece. They say it sometimes imitates human speech with its voice, though Vossius says <note>in Book 3 of *On Idolatry*, chapter 69</note> that this is fabulously attributed to it; he claims it barks like a dog so that it may devour men and dogs lured out by the sound. Regarding this, Philes says in his Iambic verses:
> *By craft the Hyena ensnares the dogs,*
> *And thus provides for the hunger of its hunting traps.*
> <note>original Greek: Ὕαινα δὲ τίκτει τὰς κύνας δόλῳ / θηρατικῶν τὸδ' ἱσίαται λυρίων.</note>
> *The Hyena entangles dogs with its cunning,*
> *Soon it feeds its hunger with their flesh.*

<margin>Book 7 on Animals, ch. 22.</margin>
Aelian * testifies the same regarding it: *The hyena and the animal they call the crocuta are indeed malicious. For the hyena approaches the farmyards at night and mimics the sound of people vomiting. The dogs, hearing this, approach as if toward a human, but the hyena seizes and eats them.* <note>original Greek: κακοήθης δὲ ἄρα καὶ ὕαινα ἦν... ἡ γὰρ ὕαινα πρὸς τὰ αὔλια νύκτωρ φοιτᾷ, καὶ μιμεῖται τὰς ἐμέτας...</note> The hyena and the crocuta are truly spiteful animals. The hyena approaches the stables at night and imitates those vomiting. The dogs who hear it approach as if toward humans, and
<margin>Book 8 Natural History, ch. 30.</margin>
it devours them after they are caught. And Pliny records the same things *: Many wonders are told of the hyena, etc. But especially that it imitates human speech among the shepherds' stables, and even learns someone's name, so that it may tear them apart once they are called outside. Likewise, it imitates a human's vomiting to entice the dogs it intends to attack. Solinus the Polyhistor <note>chapter 40</note> reports this slightly differently: it fakes human vomiting and devours the dogs enticed by these false sobs. It lives in caves and feeds on the carcasses of men and dogs. Regarding its capture, Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, the Imperial Ambassador to the Ottoman Court, reports in his *Turkish Letters* *:
<margin>Letter 1.</margin>
If anyone enters its cave (which can be recognized without difficulty from the pile of bones), as long as the person entering says, "JOCTUR JOCTUR UCALA" <note>Turkish: *Yoktur*, meaning "It is not here."</note>—that is, that the hyena is not inside—the animal imagines that it is not being seen, and therefore

<column-break/>

remains unmoved, even if a rope is tied around its leg. But when the hunter goes out and shouts that the hyena is clearly
<margin>Sacred History of Animals.</margin>
inside, the beast, understanding this, takes to flight; but because its leg is already bound, it is either captured in this way or killed. Compare Gesner *On Quadrupeds*, the chapter on the hyena; Scaliger *Exercise 292, no. 2*; and Bauhin *Book 2 on Hermaphrodites, chapters 2, 3, 4, 5, and 7*, who set forth the history of the hyena at length against the opinions of Bodin, Belon, and Marcello Virgilio, using the views of both the Ancients and the Moderns.

The son of Sirach gave us the occasion for writing about the hyena in chapter 13, verse 22: *What peace is there between a hyena and a dog?* <note>original Greek: Τίς ὑαίνῃ εἰρήνη πρὸς κύνα;</note> The word for "hyena" <note>original: ὑαίνης</note> is rendered in different ways by translators: by some as "hyena"; others as a "hyena-serpent"; others have "the voice of a serpent" in place of "hyena." Others finally, such as Pagninus and the most ancient version, put "Holy man" in place of hyena. But the new version is approved—whether it be by Vatablus or another—which renders it: *Whatever agreement there is between a hyena and a dog, such is there between the rich man and the poor man.* To clarify this simile, I add the words of the most learned Zehner *: For he says that it is 
<margin>Adages, page 362.</margin>
just as if a hyena were coupled with dogs. For Oppian shows in Book 3 of *Cynegetica*, verse 278, that wolves and sheep, and likewise hyenas and dogs, disagree most severely not only in life, but even after death.
> *---If you wear a piece cut from this animal [the hyena] around your feet,*
> *You will carry a great terror for powerful dogs.*
> *And dogs will not bark at you as you walk in those shoes,*
> *Even if they were barking just before.*
> <note>original Greek: τὰς μὲν τε διατμῆξαι περὶ ποσσὶν... Καὶ σε κύνες κείνοισιν ἐπαμβαίωτα πεδίλοις / Ἀντίον οὐχ' ὑλάωσι...</note>

> *But if you should construct a loud, resonant drum*

Vossius <note>Book 3 on Idolatry, ch. 60, p. 1056</note> notes that Rittershusius, a very learned man, was deceived by the translators of Aristotle, who had annotated this passage of Oppian to mean that not only by wearing the hyena's skin, but even if we prostrate ourselves before a dog, we can escape its bite. Vossius <note>p. 1105</note> considers it an Egyptian fiction that a man dressed in hyena skin cannot be wounded in battle. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the hyena from the previous page, specifically debating the translation of the Hebrew term 'tzabua' in Jeremiah 12:9, before moving into descriptions of the ibex, the lizard, and the lion.</meta>

<header>from Psalm 50, verses 10, 11.</header>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> ...a valley, a cave of the hyena, my heritage belongs to me. <note>The author is likely discussing Jeremiah 12:9, though the header refers to Psalms.</note> The translator Aquila follows this same reading. In the Hebrew, the word is <term>tzabua: meaning painted, dyed, or colored</term>. The scholars Arias and Pagninus translate it as *a speckled bird*. Menochius believes this is the meaning: Does my people deserve to be my delight, like birds painted with exotic colors and elegant beauty that are kept in cages at home? No, instead they have degenerated into a foul bird, to be thrown to the beasts. This is Menochius’s view. However, Mercerus and Drusius reject this interpretation as a fabrication and irrelevant; they, along with Rabbi Joseph Kimchi, Lyranus, and Osiander, prefer it to indicate an *owl*, toward which all other birds fly to kill it if it flies during the day. Jerome substituted the *peacock* for the *owl*: *Just as the peacock excels in the elegance of its feathers,* he says, *so also Israel possessed great beauty; but because she is ungrateful, she is given over to the plundering and prey of the nations.* Calvin understands it as an *unusual bird*, which by its strange appearance incites men against it, and even a *wild bird*, to which the Jews, who were most insulting toward God, are compared. But who, in such a great divorce of opinions, would easily take upon themselves the role of the reconciler?

**IBEX.** This is the word the Vulgate uses several times where the Hebrew has <term>ya'el: literally "the climber"</term>. You will find this word four times in the Biblical record: 1 Samuel 24:2, Job 39:1, Psalm 104:18, and Proverbs 5:19. Isidore thinks they are called *ibices* as if they were <note>original: "avices"</note> *bird-like*, because they live in high places like birds. Martin Luther translates <term>ya'el</term> sometimes as *roe deer* <note>original German: "Rehe"</note> and sometimes as *chamois* <note>original German: "Gembs"</note>. The word descends from a root meaning *to be of use* or *to profit*, which has a strong kinship with the word meaning *to ascend*. Both words are extremely well-suited to the rock-goats, which we commonly call *chamois*. Indeed, the root for *to ascend*, besides the meaning just mentioned, also signifies *to vanish into nothing, to perish, or to disappear*. Both of these meanings fit the rock-goats or ibexes perfectly. By nature, this beast has little prudence, which is why it allows itself to be easily deceived by the voice of a hunter, and thus "perishes" according to the second meaning of the root. Furthermore, it is a weak beast of no great strength, which, even if it is otherwise <term>oxyopes: sharp-sighted</term>, hardly notices a hunter standing right next to it. Its safety consists in leaping and ascending rocks that hunters cannot penetrate; thus, while they are *ascending*, they rightly acquire the name *ya'elim* <note>the plural of ibex</note> to their great benefit, because by leaping they help themselves and escape the danger of death.

**LIZARD.** This is listed among the egg-laying four-legged creatures that creep more than they walk, in Leviticus 11:29-30, under the names <term>chomet</term> and <term>tzab</term>. The Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> rendered the first as *Chameleon*, followed by the Vulgate and Pagninus; but Junius, Arias, and Piscator translated it as *lizard*. Luther calls it the *newt* <note>original German: "der Molch"</note>. The second term is interpreted by some as a *turtle*; Arias calls it a *slug*; Pagninus a *lizard*; and Luther a *slow-worm* <note>original German: "Blindschleich"</note>. This first reptile takes its name from "power" or "strength," whatever it may actually be, for <term>koach</term> means *strength, power, or faculty*. The lizard is very strong, a conqueror of serpents and land crocodiles, whom it drives out of their hiding places; for it does not dig for itself, but inhabits the homes of others after the inhabitants have been expelled. The second reptile lives in mounds of sand and immerses itself in them, moving here and there with a swift run, and then stopping suddenly. Hence, in the Talmudic writings, *Chometon* is sand, just as the Greeks call it <term>amathon</term> and <term>psamathon</term>.

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> **LION**, regarding which we may more rightly say what Martial sang of the Hare:

->Among the four-legged, the Lion is the first glory.<-

For to him, according to the common opinion of almost everyone, the sovereignty among wild beasts is granted; hence he is called the beast *by excellence*. Suidas says: *The natural sovereignty is as the Lion among animals and the eagle among birds; the man-made sovereignty is as a King over men.* And Oppian calls him in the third book of his *On Hunting*:

->the illustrious king Lion.<-
->the renowned king Lion.<-

<margin>History of Animals, chapter 31, verse 2.</margin> Hence Philo also attributes to him a *monarchy* among the beasts. Various names for the Lion exist for different stages of its life in the same passage of Job 4:10-11, which is an elegant example of poetic amplification in that book. In the first stage, it is called <term>gur</term>, in the second <term>kephir</term>, in the third <term>aryeh</term>, in the fourth <term>shachal</term>, and in the fifth <term>layish</term>, as recorded by Strigelius. Following this naming system, we organize what we are about to say concerning the Lion. <term>Gur</term>, a *cub*, comes from a root meaning *to gather or collect*, because cubs gather to their mother; from this also comes the Greek word for "I gather." In Jeremiah 51:38, this cub is said not to *roar* like an adult, but to *growl*, that is, to emit an unformed voice, not a true roar. This marks the first stage of the lion's age. For naturalists tell of the lion's cub that when first born, it is like an unformed piece of flesh, and in size it hardly exceeds a weasel. For two months it senses nothing and performs no vital function, until finally it is awakened by the roaring of its father and mother, and after six months it begins to stand on its feet. Since the cub cannot yet run out for prey, this "cruel" animal—by a divinely implanted <term>storge: natural parental affection</term>—offers necessary food to its cubs until they are able to go out and hunt for themselves. <margin>Job 38:39.</margin> Job refers to this: *Will you hunt prey for the lioness and satisfy the hunger of the cubs, when they crouch in their dens and lie in wait in their thickets?* A lioness's <term>horme: impulse or drive</term> is never sharper or more excited than when she has suckling cubs; she is then remarkably fierce, bringing prey to them while all others resist in vain, or even if her cubs have been snatched from her. Hence Virgil in the third book of his *Georgics*:

>At no other time, forgetting her cubs, does the lioness
>Rage more fiercely across the fields.

<margin>Medea, verse 187.</margin> Hence also the Nurse in Euripides' play compares Medea to a fierce lioness:

>And you, with the glare of a lioness who has just given birth,
>Look fiercely at the servants, whenever anyone
>Approaches to bring word.

Jacob compares his son Judah to a lion's cub, and in this, the political kingdom of the same is commended: he takes the likeness of the lion from the excellence of its sovereignty. For thus he depicted the strength and bravery of Judah and the stability of his kingdom: <margin>Genesis 49:9.</margin> *As a lion's cub,* <term>gur aryeh</term>, *Judah, you shall be formidable to your enemies, and you shall bring back ample spoils. From the prey, my son, you have gone up. He stooped down and couched as a lion, and as a great lion. Who shall rouse him up?*
Judah is a young lion / you have gone up from the prey /

...risen; which Luther’s version expressed according to the sense: *You have come up through great victory.* <note>original German: "Du bist hoch kommen durch grosse Sieg." Referring to Genesis 49:9.</note> He has knelt down and lain down like a lion, and like an old lion; who would dare to wake him? Using the figure of the lion, the text illustrates the future state of Judah, so as to place his heroic virtues and noble spirit more clearly before our eyes. Nor is this progression placed here in vain—the *young cub*, the *middle-aged lion*, and the *lion of the final age*—so that through these stages of age, the glorious growth of the kingdom might be shown. Whether you consider the beginnings of his kingdom, its progress, or its end, you will always "know the lion by his claws." <note>A Latin proverb, "ex ungue Leonem," meaning one can judge the whole from a small part.</note> For after the death of Joshua, the leadership <note>Greek: ἀρχὴ (archē)</note> was conferred upon the tribe of Judah by the unanimous vote and consent of the rest. When they first asked God for a prince and leader to continue the battle against the Canaanites, they received this 
<margin>Judges 1. 1. 2.</margin>
response: *Judah shall go up: behold, I have delivered the land into his hand.* Judah behaved as a middle-aged lion in the time of David and Solomon, during whose reign the kingdom was excellently established, strengthened by laws and peace, and the kings and neighboring peoples on all sides were subjugated. Hence, the Blessed Luther explains the lion having reached his prime <note>Greek: ἀκμὴν (akmēn)</note> as referring to David, who undoubtedly performed more and greater deeds than are even extant in *Sacred Scripture*. Even when he became an old lion, he did not entirely shed his lion-like eminence, but showed it in both spirit and eyes; although his strength was trimmed by the power of the Romans, from him would come the future Messiah, the most powerful, wisest, and most excellent King of all Kings of Judah.

**THE YOUNG LION**, <term>gur: גור</term>, denotes a lion of the second age, which, having now been weaned, runs out with teeth <term>aryot: אריות</term> roaring, *Judges 14:5*, to tear and procure prey for itself, *Job 4:10, Psalm 58:7*. It leaves its covert, *Jeremiah 25:38*, and learns to prey, *Ezekiel 19:5, Amos 3:4*. These are more spirited and bold, as they have not yet experienced human strength or snares; and because their boiling blood increases their audacity, they are more greedy for the blood they have recently tasted, and thus are fiercer than the old ones, and impatient of hunger, since they require much food for their nourishment and growth.
<margin>Psalm 34. 9. 10. 11.</margin>
Hence, Sacred Scripture compares the wealthy to young lions—those who are entirely occupied with providing for their own sustenance, yet in those very riches they are in need. They are usurers, violent men, trusting in their own strength, and seizing everything for themselves. The Psalmist uses an elegant contrast <note>Greek: ἀντιθέσει (antithesi)</note> between those who trust in God and those who trust in their riches: *Fear the Lord, you his saints, for there is no want to those who fear him.* <term>kephirim rashu ve-arevu: כפירים רשו ויעבו</term>, *The young lions shall lack and suffer hunger: but those who seek Jehovah shall not be deprived of any good thing.* The Septuagint and the Old Translator render it: <note>Greek: πλοὐσιοι ἐπτώχευϲαν καὶ ἐπείναϲαν (plousioi eptōcheusan kai epeinasan)</note>, *the rich have become poor and hungry.* Great confidence resides in these young lions, just as craftiness does in foxes; hence Pindar, in the fourth hymn of the Isthmian Odes, compares a brave man to a lion for his strength and to a fox for his prudence. The verses are:

->for courage is like<-
->the spirit of roaring lions<-
->in toil, but in cunning it is a fox<-
->that, stretching itself out,<-
->stops the whirl.<-

In this third regard, the Sacred Book compares the righteous man with the young lion: the man of a righteous and secure mind drives far from his soul every

<column-break/>

fear and anxiety with which profane men are troubled, being surely persuaded that he and all his affairs are the care of God, however things may finally turn out. Thus, because he awaits all outcomes with an upright spirit, he is said to be as confident as a
<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
<margin>Proverbs 28:1.</margin>
lion: *The wicked flee, although no one pursues; but the righteous shall be as a confident lion without terror.* This, therefore, is that incredible security of the pious mind which excludes all anxiety and desperation, while on the contrary the wicked fear even when no one is pursuing. Such was the young lion, <term>gur: גור</term>, in which Samson demonstrated the first trial of his heroic fortitude, which we shall describe as a "lion-killing" <note>Greek: λεοντοφονίαν (leontophonian)</note> in the sacred words: *Samson went down, and his father and his mother, to Timnath; and when they came to the vineyards of the town of Timnath, behold,* <term>kephir aryot shaag likrato: כפיר אריות שאג לקראתו</term>, *a young lion roared in his path. And the Spirit of Jehovah rushed upon him, and he rent him,* <term>vayishase’ehu: וישׁסעהו</term>, *as a kid is rent, and there was nothing in his hand; and he did not tell his father or his mother what he had done.* This was the first example of Samson's fortitude, free from danger, although he was armed with no weapons, nor had anything in his hand with which to defend himself against such a beast; so that we might more aptly apply the phrase "a mighty work of hands" <note>Greek: χειρῶν καρτερόν ἔργον (cheirōn karteron ergon)</note> to the lion-killer Samson, as Theocritus says of Hercules, the slayer of the Nemean Lion, who describes that contest with a notable vividness <note>Greek: hypotypoſi (hypotyposi)</note>, *Idyll 25, line 175*, where he speaks in the person of Hercules at line 266:

->I strangled him powerfully, pressing my strong hands<-
->from behind, lest he should tear my flesh with his claws.<-
->I pressed my heels firmly on his hind paws,<-
->standing on his tail, and I guarded his ribs.<-

If the fates of this Nemean Lion are compared, the fiction of the Nemean will be seen to spring from the history of the Timnathite lion. For just as Samson killed the lion armed with no weapons, so they tell fables of Hercules, that having seized the lion with his bare hands, he tore it apart with its own claws; and having thus pulled off the skin of the slain beast with its claws, he thereafter wore it as an invulnerable shield, as Euripides testifies in *The Madness of Hercules*:

->He wrapped the skin of the beast about his head<-
->the lion’s, in which he armed himself.<-

Our study now turns to the Lion that is of middle and full age; it is called <term>ari: ארי</term> or <term>aryeh: אריה</term>, a larger and more adult lion, having cubs and seizing prey for them, *Nahum 2:12*; spirited, *2 Samuel 17:10*; lifting itself up, *Numbers 23:24*. The name comes from <term>arah: ארה</term>, "to pluck," or <term>ra'ah: ראה</term>, "to see," just as "Leo" comes from the Greek <note>Greek: λάω (laō)</note>, "I see." Its characteristic is strength, just as the eagle's is speed, according to Phocylides:
<margin>line 110.</margin>

->God distributed a weapon to each: a nature that flies through the air<-
->to birds, to horses speed, and to lions strength.<-

From this fortitude, the Delphic Apollo gave him praise in Herodotus, *Book 5*:

->She shall bear a lion<-
->strong and eater of raw flesh.<-

Homer attributes the same epithet to him in *Odyssey 4, line 253*, and Calaber in *Book 5, line 247*, so much so that they write that even the tracks of an absent lion and even its very lair cause terror; regarding which there is that well-known saying in Plutarch, in the *Life of Marius*, near the end:

->For the lairs even of a departing lion are terrible.<-

Yet the Libyan lions prevail over others in strength; one of them will attack as many as two hundred horsemen, and even kill five or six. On account of this singular strength, <margin>Book of Epigrams, 62.</margin> Martial mentions them most particularly:
->Libyan lions rush at bulls,<-

->Alone in Libya, or scorched India,<-
->May I come face to face with the fierce lion.<-
<note>original Latin: "Casio veniam obvius Leoni." The word "caesius" often refers to blue or grey eyes, but here implies the terrifying gaze of the beast.</note>

The Lion takes its name from its ferocity, being called *Ari* <note>Hebrew: ארי (ari)</note> from *arah*, meaning "to pluck" or "to tear apart," because in its hunger it mangles and tears whatever comes in its path. For this reason, in Holy Scripture, powerful men and tyrants are called Lions. Hence, in <margin>Jeremiah 5:6.</margin> Nebuchadnezzar, King of the Babylonians, is called "a lion from the forest," <note>Hebrew: אריה מיער (aryeh mi-yaar)</note> who hastens to his prey with an open maw, formidable in his very roaring. Comparisons based on the nature of the lion are frequent; Homer employs them twelve times in a single book of the *Iliad*, to say nothing of the *Odyssey*. Not to speak of all of them, I cannot fail to mention one here <margin>Iliad, book 24, v. 41.</margin> regarding Achilles, whom he compares to a lion because of his savage ways, attacking a flock with a wild soul in hope of prey. Those verses are so composed that they rightly apply to our "Babylonian Achilles" <note>Nebuchadnezzar</note>, who, relying on "great force and pride," lost all mercy just like the Homeric Achilles, greedy for prey like some famished lion.
> Who has neither righteous thoughts nor a flexible
> mind in his breast; but like a lion knows wild things,
> who when yielded to great force and a proud spirit
> goes after the sheep of men, so that he may take a feast.
> So Achilles has lost pity, nor is there any shame
> in him, which both harms and helps men greatly.
<note>original Greek: "ῳ̈ τ’ αρ’ Φρενες εισιν εναισιμοι..." from the Iliad, describing Achilles' lack of mercy toward Hector's body.</note>

And like a mountain lion, devouring all things and leaving neither entrails, nor flesh, nor bones, with which <margin>Odyssey, book 9, v. 292.</margin> Homer compares Polyphemus:
> He ate like a mountain-bred lion, nor did he leave
> The entrails and the flesh and the marrowy bones.

<margin>Psalm 7:1–2.</margin> David, establishing a defense against sycophants and slanderers, among whom Shimei was the foremost, sketches the magnitude of his persecution with a simile drawn from the cruelty of a lion, seizing and tearing. He prays to God, the just judge, for liberation from his enemies and from the ways of these sycophants in these words: *O Lord my God, in thee have I put my trust. Save me from all them that persecute me, and deliver me; lest he seize* <note>Hebrew: כאריה (ke-aryeh)</note> *my soul like a lion, tearing it in pieces while there is none to deliver.* A roaring and mad lion in its hunger mangles whatever comes its way, tearing apart the sheep, a defenseless beast. Let there now be an <term>application</term> <note>Greek: νοησις (noesis), meaning a spiritual or deeper understanding.</note> to David, destitute of human help and every deliverer; hence he asks that he be snatched from the lions by God alone. See how even slanderers are compared to lions, and learn that every matter should be committed to God alone—the severe avenger of slanderers and the vindicator of innocence—especially when no protection remains in the lawful investigation of the magistrate. Stand then before God, hope in Him, and cry out:

->*Savior of the world: from the jaws of enemies*<-
->*deliver me, who with a savage mind*<-

->*cruelly mangles the defenseless flock;*<-

Thus he continues, in the person of the Messiah, to compare his enemies to famished lions who rush toward their prey with open mouths, terrifying in their very roar: <margin>Psalm 22:13.</margin> *They gaped upon me with their mouths, as a ravening and a roaring lion.* <note>Hebrew: אריה טרף ושאג (aryeh toreph ve-shoeg)</note> He uses the same lion-simile in *Psalm 10:9*, complaining of those who lie in wait on the public roads to rob passing travelers of their lives and goods; who, like a lion, treacherously oppress innocent men who possess some wealth, and when the opportunity arises, emerge from their hiding places so that they may fall upon the prey. *The wicked*, he says, *lurks in secret*, <note>Hebrew: כאריה בסכה (ke-aryeh be-sukkoh)</note> *like a lion in his den.* Jerome, at the end of the verse, reading it without the pronoun as "in a thicket": the Septuagint reads, *in secret like a lion in his fold.* *Why does he lurk, to catch the poor?* On account of such great ferocity and greed, the lion in the sacred texts is also commonly called *Shachal*, *Shachatz*, and *Lavi*. The first, *Shachal*, is read concerning the lion in <margin>Job 4:10, Proverbs 26:13.</margin> and is explained as "fierce" or "immense." There are some who think the lion is called *Shachal* as if it were *Shachar*, from "blackness"; for that black-colored lions have been observed even in Syria is testified by Oppian in book 3 of his *Cynegetica*, Pliny in book 8, chapter 16, and Aelian in book 17, chapter 26; although Aristotle believed all lions were tawny. The second term, *Shachatz*, marks any <margin>Job 28:8 & 41:25.</margin> immense and proud animal, but is used particularly of the lion in Job. The last, *Lavi*, although it may denote one that is old but younger than a <margin>Job 4:11.</margin> decrepit one, still having cubs, nevertheless properly signifies a lion named for its immensity <note>Psalm 75:5.</note> and ferocity, which no one dares to rouse or provoke <note>Genesis 49:9.</note>, and which has molars for teeth <note>Joel 1:6</note>; whence <margin>Gen. 49:9; Joel 1:6; Ezek. 19:2.</margin> the Lioness <note>Latin: Leæna</note> is also distinguished by this name for her ferocity and grimness.

A lion of decrepit age, whose strength has failed and who is no longer able to run, but hides himself in caves or lies down among the brushwood on his paws, feigning sleep and moving no limbs—the Hebrews call such a one *Laish* <note>Hebrew: ליש (laish)</note>, in <margin>Isaiah 30:6.</margin> (where Arias and Pagninus have "tiger"), still powerful in <margin>Proverbs 30:30.</margin> but who finally, for lack of prey which he cannot catch being <margin>Job 4:11.</margin> destitute of strength, perishes. Johannes Tzetzes is the authority for the idea that the younger lions feed their parents when they have grown old. Indeed, Plutarch records that lions worn out by old age are driven by the younger ones. There are some, however, who record that lions have greater strength in old age than in youth, and to this they apply that saying of Solomon in Proverbs 30:30, where the lion *Laish*, though worn by age, is given the epithet *Gibbor*, meaning "mightiest," and that line of the poet Hippothoon in his little verse in Stobaeus: "The old age of a lion is better than the prime of fawns," which words that old man in Aristophanes' *Wasps* also brings forward in his own defense: "And I indeed think that old age is better than many locks of youth." Among other virtues which the initiates of nature commonly attribute to the lion, not the least is *gratitude*, both toward aged parents...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the lion's nature, specifically its reputation for gratitude and clemency, before transitioning into a new section on the hare, detailing its biblical status as an unclean animal and its various symbolic and biological characteristics according to ancient and patristic authors.</meta>
