<header>ANTIQUITIES OF THE BIBLE</header>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>They show gratitude toward their benefactors, as evidenced by the example of Androclus, who pulled a thorn from a lion's foot, and whom the lion later spared at Rome, as recorded by Aulus Gellius (Book 5, Chapter 14) and Aelian (History of Animals, last chapter of Book 7). There is also their clemency, about which this verse was written:
> The noble wrath of lions knows how to spare the fallen.
<note>original Latin: "Parcere subjectis scit nobilis ira Leonum." A common medieval proverb reflecting the belief that lions would not attack a person who surrendered or lay prostrate.</note>

<margin>Book 8, Natural History, ch. 16.</margin>Pliny says: *The lion alone among wild beasts shows clemency to those who plead; it spares those who have been cast down, and when it rages, it growls at men before women, and never at infants unless driven by great hunger.* Daniel experienced this clemency of lions in Chapter 6:21, not by any seed of nature, but by a divine miracle; for the lions, forgetting their pressing hunger, spared him, showing reverence to a man who was a servant of God. Regarding Daniel's liberation, Rhodomannus <note>Lorenz Rhodomann (1546–1606) was a German humanist known for his Greek poetry on biblical themes.</note> writes thus:

<margin>Book 3, Palestine, verse 1065.</margin>> He also drew Daniel from the man-killing pit,
> and feasted upon the gaping mouth of the deep-roaring lions.
<note>original Greek: "Εἴρυσε καὶ Δανιῆλον..."</note>

<margin>Revelation 5:5.</margin>For this reason, namely both for its clemency and its greatness, Christ is called a Lion: *Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has prevailed to open the book.* For when none of the spirits could open the book, Jesus Christ was able to do so, which is a preeminent proof of strength. Thus He is called a Lion, just as He is later called a Lamb in verse 8 because of His innocence. Yet He is not called simply a Lion, but the Lion of the tribe of Judah, an indication that the Apostle John was looking back to Jacob's prophecy concerning the future Lion from the tribe of Judah in Genesis 49:9. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> adapts this to Christ: *The blessing of Judah is mystical, prefiguring all things pertaining to Christ. Since Christ was to appear from this tribe according to the plan of the divine arrangement, Jacob, inspired by the Holy Spirit, predicted through the things said to Judah not only the descent of the Lord to men, but also the Mystery, the cross, the burial, and the resurrection—in a word, everything.* The Lion's cub (Jacob predicts His kingdom: for it is always the custom of Scripture to suggest royal authority through the figure of this animal. *He lay down as a lion and a cub. Who shall rouse him?*) signifies the cross, the burial, and the resurrection. On this same passage, consult Origen (Homily 17 on Genesis), Ambrose (Book on the Blessings of the Patriarchs, ch. 4), Augustine (Book 16, City of God, ch. 41), and Julian Pomerius, Archbishop of Toledo (Book 1 against the Jews). In the same way, the Devil is compared to a lion by St. Peter, but not <margin>1 Peter 5:8.</margin> simply; rather as a *roaring* lion, that is, one who is starving, angry, rapacious, and desiring to devour men. Augustine says in his commentary <margin>On Psalm 103.</margin> on the 103rd Psalm: *The greater Lion is the prince of all such lions; what was said of him? Do you not know that your adversary goes about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour? They seek their food from God because no one can be tempted by the Devil unless God permits it. Why is this power given? Either for the damnation of the wicked or the testing of the godly. The Lord does all this justly, and the Devil has no power over anyone, or over any part of them, unless the One who has the highest and most sublime power grants it.* It is not our purpose to run through all the sayings of Scripture and review every instance where the lion is or can be compared in Holy Writ. This was done formerly by M. Heinrich Herman Frey in his *Thierbibel* <note>A 16th-century work "The Bible of Animals" by Frey.</note> and not long ago by Samuel Bochart; see their works.

### THE HARE

The hare is numbered among the unclean animals in Leviticus 11:5-6 and Deuteronomy 14:7, along with the rabbit. Because both the rabbit and the hare chew the cud and

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>do not divide the hoof, they shall be unclean to you. Juvenal includes the hare among the delicacies and luxuries of banquets:
<margin>Satire 11, v. 138.</margin>> The hare with a great sow’s udder, and boar, and antelope.

And Martial writes:
> Among quadrupeds, the first glory is the hare.

The shoulders from the front and the thighs from the back of hares are considered to have the most flavor; hence, the meat of hares that are only two, three, or at most eight months old is held to be much more savory and delicate, especially if they lived in mountainous places and fed on wild thyme and pennyroyal, as their meat is judged healthier than others and provides a more flavorful juice, more pleasing to the palate. Why God forbade the Jews from eating hare meat, the initiates of nature give this reason in addition to what has been mentioned: because the hare is a lustful animal—indeed, at times the same individual can both mate and be mated with. It is not that all hares are androgynous, as many have believed, but because many possess characteristics of both sexes. Clement of Alexandria explains this at length in his <margin>Book 2, The Instructor.</margin> *Pedagogue*, where he brings forward these causes for why the hare was forbidden by Moses: because the hare mates at all times, conceives every month, and "superfœtates" (conceives again while already pregnant), nor is it content with one mating, even conceiving while still nursing. After narrating these points at length, he finally adds: *The prohibition of this enigma exhorted us to abstain from vehement appetites, mutual congresses, intercourse with pregnant women, the corruption of youth, adultery, and the lascivious waste of seed.* <note>original Greek: "ἀπέχεσθαι τοίνυν..." Clement is using the biological "nature" of the hare as a moral allegory for human behavior.</note> Basil the Great provides us with another reason based on the hare's fertility; <margin>Homily 9 on the Hexaemeron.</margin> namely, that from the hare’s fecundity we can learn of God's goodness toward us, as they are more fertile than other beasts for our benefit. He says: *It is established that those animals which are easily captured are far more fertile than others; wherefore hares and deer, as well as sheep, give birth more often and bear twins and multiple offspring, lest the species fail when exposed as prey to those wild beasts that rejoice in blood and feed on flesh.* Then he compares the prolific hare to usury (lending money at interest): <margin>Sermon 2 on Psalm 14.</margin> *Why do you join yourself to a varied and excessively fertile beast? They say hares are of such a nature that they give birth, nourish, and conceive again all at once. So too is money given by usurers at one time; it gives birth to interest, and "superfœtates" by increasing. For you have not yet received it into your hands, and you are already demanding the profit of the current month. This, once given, produces another evil; that in turn another, until finally it is an infinite evil.* Among the Hebrews, the name is *Arnebeth* <note>Hebrew: ארנבת (arneveth)</note> from *eretz* (earth), because it crops the produce of the earth with such harm that they have sometimes brought about high prices for grain and famine for the inhabitants; consult Hyginus’s *Poetic Astronomy* regarding the hare, and Athenaeus, Book 9, Chapter 14. The hare is commended for its speed, for as Anacreon says in Ode 11: *There is no animal of equal size that is its match in the race.* To this end, nature formed its individual limbs to be most fit for running, so that it might more easily escape its enemies.

...could escape. Indeed, there is almost no animal exposed to such varied persecutions, and which has met with so many different fates. Besides dogs, eagles lie in wait for it, according to that saying of Xenophon: *they fear not only dogs but also eagles; for when they cross flat and bare ground, they are snatched up.* <note>original Greek: "πεφοβῆνται οὐ μόνον τὰς κύνας ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς ἀετούς. ὑπερβάλλοντες γὰρ τὰ σιμὰ καὶ ψιλά, ἀναρπάζονται."</note> Yet by the speed of its feet and the keenness of its ears and nose, it very often escapes the hands of its enemies. Because of this, it is the most timid of animals, and its great timidity caused it to be called simply *ptox* <note>Greek for "cowerer" or "one who crouches in fear."</note>—a name otherwise used generally for a fearful person—by Homer when he describes a hare hiding in the bushes for fear of an eagle with these words:
<margin>
Iliad, book 21, v. 676.
</margin>
> For even the swift-footed hare, though far off, did not escape him
> As it lay crouching under a leafy bush.

Referring to this, Pollux writes in Book 5, Chapter 12: *this animal is exceedingly cowardly, being easily startled and terrified, which is why it is named "the cowerer."* <note>original Greek: "δειλὰ ὑπερβάλλει τοῦτο τὸ ζῶον, ἐμπληκτόν ῥᾷστα γινόμενον καὶ ἀναπτυόμενον, ὅθεν καὶ πτῶξ ὠνομάζεται."</note> The timidity of the hare became a proverb. Albert of Stade relates a almost
<margin>
Chronicle, leaf 119, a. b.
</margin>
ridiculous story about Eric of Denmark, brother of King Canute, who gathered a multitude of Danes and, taking the royal title, began to attack Magnus (on account of the murder committed against his brother Canute). However, having been defeated quite often, he was put to flight, from which he began to be distinguished by the name Eric **Hasenforth** (Hare-foot). But a little later in Scania, the same Eric put Magnus to flight in battle and became famous through that victory; thus a new name was created for him, Eric "Emun," which means "the Memorable."

Similar to the hare is the *Rabbit* <note>original Latin: "Cuniculus."</note>, though smaller; yet it is stronger than the hare and, as it were, an "iron animal." It seeks out caves under the earth and hollows out the ground beneath mountains, just as Martial says:
> The rabbit delights to dwell in excavated caves;
> It has shown easy paths to its enemies.

<margin>
Book 8, ch. 59.
</margin>
And Marcus Varro is the authority cited in Pliny who says that a town in Spain was undermined by rabbits. Equal to this is what Strabo relates in Book 3: that rabbits (which he calls *lagideis* <note>Greek: "λαγίδεῖς," literally "little hares."</note>) overturned the houses and trees of the Balearic Islands, so that the inhabitants were forced to implore Roman assistance. In the Sacred Scriptures, the word <term>שפן</term> (*Saphan*) occurs in *Leviticus 11:5 and Deuteronomy 14:7*, where this little animal appears in the catalog of unclean creatures. Interpreters vary in explaining it. Most maintain it is the rabbit, because the rabbit is similar to the hare and is joined with the hare in the cited passages. Others translate it as the *mountain mouse* <note>likely the rock hyrax or marmot.</note>. The Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> calls it a *choirogryllion*. As for the *choirogryllum* (a word the Old Latin translator retained), some want it to be a hedgehog, others a porcupine, or a **Meerschwein** <note>literally "sea-pig"; in this era, it could refer to a guinea pig or a porcupine.</note>. Blessed Friedlieb says it is a general term signifying any fleeing animal that lives in hiding places. Blessed Luther everywhere translates it as **Kaninchen** (Rabbit); compare the cited passages with *Psalm 104:18 and Proverbs 30:26*, where the <term>שפן</term> (*Saphan*) is listed among the "wisest of the wise," because it places its bed in the rock and has its refuge in the cliffs. For it is accustomed to level its excavated places with dust so they are not tracked. In the morning and evening it creeps out, and sitting in the entrance of its cave, it looks around. But when dogs press upon it, it immediately penetrates into the caverns and cannot be driven out unless *viverrae* <note>ferrets.</note> are sent in, which are enemies to the rabbit kind.
<margin>
Book 3.
</margin>

<margin>
Book 8, ch. 55.
</margin>
on account of this same hunting; they are thrown into the burrows so that they may

<margin>

who delight in the hunting of rabbits in coastal places and call the ferret a **Frette**, we are certain they corrupted the Medieval Latin word *foretta* in this way. Gryphiander, in his *Treatise on Islands, chapter 32, no. 117*, considers that they are called **Freeter** from "devouring." Jerome explains this mystically of those who are penitent and timid because of committed sins, who, being convicted in their conscience, take their refuge in the Rock, which is Christ: *He who is timid,* he says, *has a refuge in the Rock; but the Rock is Christ.*

->**THE LOCUST**, called *akris* by the Greeks, but <term>הארבה</term> (*ha-arbeh*) by the Hebrews;<-
There are four kinds of locusts which were permitted to be eaten by divine law,
<margin>
Leviticus 11:22.
</margin>
of which the first place is held by <term>הארבה</term> (*ha-arbeh*), which the Septuagint and the Vulgate render as *bruchus* <note>a type of wingless locust.</note>. However, the Teachers are entangled in many trifles and difficulties when they deal with creeping insects, which, although small, present no small obstacles; so much so that Junius, noticing the intricate interpretation here, was pleased to note: *These kinds of insects are known neither to the Hebrews, nor to historians, nor to us; therefore we have retained the Hebrew words.* Thus we are pressed by the heavy authority of Junius, who is otherwise sharp-witted. Among the winged creeping things that walk on four feet, the first place is occupied by <term>הארבה</term> (*ha-arbeh*), which means "locust" to the Hebrews, and which they say is so named from "multiplying" <note>Hebrew root *rabah*.</note>. The reason for this shines forth elegantly from that passage: *The locust has no king, yet they all go forth in a troop.* <note>Proverbs 30:27.</note> Pagninus translates it thus, and Luther: **Locusts have no king, yet they go out together in heaps.** The Hebrew text has the word <term>חצץ</term> (*chatsats*), which presents a difficulty. Aben Esra explained it through <term>מבוקץ מאסף</term> <note>Hebrew for "arranged/gathered."</note> in the sense of a troop or company, as they collect themselves from everywhere and gather in ranks. Interpreters follow the sense of "in ranks," but Ludovicus de Dieu says this interpretation
<margin>
Notes, p. 415.
</margin>
rests on mere conjecture, since the word <term>חצץ</term> does not have that meaning of "collection" elsewhere, nor is any noun derived from it. He then opposes conjecture with conjecture and compares it with <term>חץ</term> (*chetz*), "arrow," and <term>חצץ</term>, "to shoot arrows," and translates: *The locusts have no king, yet they all go forth shooting forth like arrows.* Another species of locust in the cited place is called <term>סלעם</term> (*Solam*), a word that vexes interpreters with no less trouble. The Septuagint and the Latin interpreter, as well as Pagninus and Vatablus—to whom you may add Arias—translate it as *attacus* <note>a kind of locust.</note>. Junius calls it the *silkworm*. The Talmudic writers write that it is a species of locust without wings. In the tractate *Cholin*, it is said to be named
<margin>
q. 3. f. 65.
</margin>
because it delights in rocks, from <term>סלע</term> (*sela*), "rock." Others, however, say the radical <term>נ</term> indicates that this "bird" <note>used loosely for flying things.</note> has a baldness, lacks a tail, and has an oblong head. The third kind of locust is named <term>חרגל</term> (*Chargol*), which some count among the birds. According to the Hebrews, it denotes a certain kind of locust and is neither common nor very strong, although the Old Interpreter and the Septuagint rendered it as *Ophiomachus* <note>literally "snake-fighter."</note>, whom Pagninus, Arias, and Vatablus also follow. <header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...reported by a great author regarding the "opimachus" <note>A type of locust or "leaper."</note>, neither Aristotle nor any other reliable writer has recorded anything. Indeed, that author states quite freely that there is <term>nothing pure</term> <note>original Latin: "puroque"</note> or certain about it; even if such a creature existed, it would not be mentioned in this context. He cares little for the inconsistencies that might arise among his own peers if the author of the Old Translation <note>The Vulgate.</note> is not interpreted exactly as commanded. He reshapes many things, points out inconsistencies, and changes what needs changing, quite unconcerned about the haughty judgment of posterity. For all eternity, not even a hundred Councils of Trent will persuade us, nor those more sincere than themselves, to canonize that Vulgate version and receive it in such a way that no pretext <margin>Session 4, Canon 2, Council of Trent.</margin> would allow us to reject it. Meanwhile, we shall not overlook what Aristotle recounted in his book *On Marvelous Things Heard* <margin>Geneva edition, 1597.</margin> regarding a species of locust called the <term>scorpiomachum</term> <note>The "scorpion-fighter."</note>. It is a clever enemy of the scorpion that surrounds it, signals its anger with a chirping sound, leaps upon it, and triumphs when the adversary's sting is lost, devouring it once it is disarmed. His words are as follows: <note>original Greek: "Ἐν Ἄργει δέ φασι γίνεσθαι ἀκρίδα τινὸς γένους... ἀγαθὸν δέ φασιν εἶναι, πρὸς τὰς πληγὰς τῶ σκορπίω ἐπιφαγεῖν αὐτήν."</note> *In Argos, they say there is a species of locust called the scorpion-fighter. Whenever it sees a scorpion, it immediately stands against it. The scorpion does the same; the locust runs in a circle around it. While the scorpion raises its sting and turns in the same spot, the locust lets out a buzzing sound, causing the scorpion to lower its sting and eventually stretch out entirely as the locust continues to run circles. Finally, the locust approaches and devours it. They also say it is a good remedy to eat this locust after being stung by a scorpion.* This account by Aristotle is confirmed by a story told by Simon Majolus, Bishop of Volturara <note>A 16th-century Italian bishop and author.</note>. <margin>Beginning of Colloquy 10.</margin> He relates that his gardener, coming from the field, saw a locust seize a snake by the throat and kill it without a fight. Concerning the fourth kind, which they commonly explain as the <term>bruchus</term> <note>A wingless locust or beetle.</note>, we have spoken elsewhere. <margin>Theater of Insects, ch. 16, p. 123.</margin> Regarding the <term>chagab</term> <note>Hebrew: חגב, a generic term for a locust.</note>, we shall at least note from Mouffet <note>Thomas Mouffet, author of "Insectorum sive Minimorum Animalium Theatrum."</note> that the *chagab* does not merely nibble at crops or shear them, but breaks and crushes the stalk itself. In general, it should be noted that although the wiser Talmudists in the tractate *Chullin* (Chapter 3) dispute at length about these four species of locusts permitted for eating, these four types of animals are actually unknown even to the Jews themselves. Therefore, they do not have specific names for them but call them all by the common name "locusts," which is why Luther also retained the Hebrew names. Since the locust in Hebrew takes its name from *multitude*, because they fly in swarms and great numbers and consume everything in their path, it is a clear sign that they are undoubtedly created by a singular divine power. They are armed with an insatiable appetite and an unfillable nature for devouring as a punishment, as shown by the list of plagues in Egypt and countless examples from secular history, many of which were cited by the Blessed Franz in his *Sacred History of Animals*. We shall speak of the eating of locusts elsewhere, God willing. That a multitude of locusts is counted among divine punishments is well known from both sacred and secular history. *This plague*, says Johannes Brentius, *brings such destruction to regions that it is called by the pagans the* WRATH OF THE GODS. The Church Fathers treat and consider locusts symbolically. Gregory compares locusts to flatterers. *By locusts*, he says, *which harm crops more than other tiny creatures, the tongues of flatterers are represented. These tongues, by praising too immoderately, corrupt the minds of earthly*

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
*men who are producing some good fruit.* <insert>For the fruits of the Egyptians—the works of those who labor with their hands <note>original Greek: "χειροβόων"</note>—which the locusts destroy, occur when* <italic>the tongues of flatterers incline the heart of the worker to seek transitory praise. The locusts eat the grass when flatterers exalt the words of speakers with favors. They devour the fruit of trees when, with vain praises, they weaken the deeds of those who are already somewhat strong. And in Book 33 of his Morals, Chapter 39,</italic> Gregory applies locusts to the ambitious: *What is expressed by the locust, which flies in leaps, if not vainglory, which exalts itself with empty presumptions,* etc. Hugo Cardinalis <note>A 13th-century Dominican biblical commentator.</note>, partly following Augustine, explains locusts as slanderers: *The locust harms with its mouth and one devours the other. These are the detractors who devour crops and fruits while they are still in the blade or tender—that is, they consume and gnaw away the good of others while it is still in the beginning of its birth. Detractors are those who judge others and lick the blood of sinners.* In part, he applies this to ecclesiastical persons: *The locusts*, he says, *are the Bishops, Archdeacons, Deacons, and the like, who devour the whole people and eat their labors. When a locust gnaws and consumes one tree, it moves to another, and from that to a third: So do these Superiors, Prelates, Bishops, and Archdeacons; when they have consumed one part of the land, they move to another. In one night they consume one Priest, and the next day they leap to another. However, the tiny locust devours only what is around it: So these Minor and Rural Deans devour everything around them wherever they dare to extend their reins. These are the locusts of locusts, etc.*

## THE WOLF
THE WOLF, called *Ze'eb* <note>Hebrew: זאב</note> by the Hebrews, is named for its golden color, such as those found in Cilicia according to Oppian <margin>Cynegetica, Book 3.</margin> (from *ahab*, gold). Hence in Chaldean it is *Deba*, in Arabic *Dib*, and in Phrygian (according to Hesychius) *aithops* <note>Greek for "fiery-looking" or "burnt-face."</note>, a Wolf. The animal, as Pierius notes in his *Hieroglyphics*, was considered a good omen by some, but by others an ill-omened and pestilential creature, which is why it was once held as an augury of death. They predicted the slaughter the Jews suffered under Emperor Hadrian when wolves, along with hyenas, filled the city with their howling in great numbers. Similarly, wolves portended the destruction of Emperor Maximinus when about five hundred entered the city where he had retreated at the same time he had set out for Italy against Maximus and Balbinus. To the Romans, it was a sign of good omen, perhaps because some write that Romulus and Remus were raised and suckled by a she-wolf; for this reason, the wolf was the emblem of the first legion before the eagle. Aelian, citing Polemon in Book 12 of his *History of Animals* (Chapter 40), wrote that a wolf was even worshipped at Delphi because it gave a sign of stolen sacrificial gold that had been buried on Parnassus. The animal is otherwise rapacious and fierce, as well as deceitful. In Oppian, it is called "the night-wanderer." They prowl like hyenas, as the prophet Habakkuk (Chapter 1:8) compares them to the wolf that goes out in the evening, maddened by hunger for prey. Antonio de Guevara disputes at length (commenting on this from page 33 to 51) that the "evening wolves" actually designate hyenas. Conrad Gessner is of the same opinion when describing quadrupeds. <margin>Volume 1, folio 556.</margin> The hyena is indeed similar to a wolf, prowls mostly at night, and with an open mouth like a wolf,

# From Psalm 50, verse 10. II.

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
<margin>Book 4, Ode 4, verse 50.</margin>
"He comes forward to scout out ambushes around the sheepfolds," <note>original Latin: "Prodit, ut insidias exploret ovilia circum."</note> just as Virgil sings in the third book of his *Georgics*, verse 537. Because of its deceit, ferocity, and rapacity, this animal is particularly suited for describing human character. A rapacious man is compared to a wolf, just as Hannibal in the works of Horace compares the Romans to **rapacious wolves**, while calling the Africans "timid and fleeing deer"—alluding to Romulus, the founder of the name, who was nursed by a she-wolf, as noted by Acron in his *Commentary*, page 504. A simple man is compared to a sheep or a dove, a cunning one to a fox, a noble one to a lion, a filthy one to a pig, and a talkative one to a jackdaw. Thus, Horace in his second book of *Epistles*, verse 28, compares a soldier serving in the camp of Lucullus to a wolf; when driven by poverty after losing his travel money, the soldier, angry at the enemy, violently cast down a garrison of Mithridates' soldiers and plundered the fortress like a wolf, which tears apart everything in its path with a hungry and starving maw:
> After this, a fierce wolf, angry alike 
> At himself and the foe, sharp with hungry teeth.

<margin>2. Epigrams, last.</margin>
In the same way, Martial uses this likeness for rapacious and cruel men who demand immoderate interest. And Prudentius, in his *Psychomachia*, calls the heretics Photinus and Arius 
> Wolves of monstrous ferocity.

Hedio writes that wolves raged in a great pack in Switzerland during the war of Maximilian against that nation, and it was decreed that to exterminate them, a bell should give a signal whenever a wolf appeared so they could be destroyed by a common call to arms. Regarding this type of proverb, Tertullian observes in his book *On the Soul*: *Men are equated to beasts according to the qualities of their character, dispositions, and emotions.* And 
<margin>Chronicle Annals, folio 652.</margin>
<margin>On the Nature of Man, chapter 2.</margin>
Nemesius writes: <note>original Greek: "Εἰπόντος Πλάτωνος..."</note> *Plato stated that souls that are spirited, angry, and rapacious are clothed in the bodies of wolves and lions, while those devoted to excess take on the bodies of donkeys and such.* No less skillfully does Pisides write in his *Cosmorgia*:
> And the beast reveals the hidden thoughts; 
> Swine represent the lecherous, and wolves the robbers, 
> Wasps represent the wanderers, and leopards the quick-tempered.

<margin>2. Physiognomy.</margin>
With these things Adamantius does not disagree: <note>original Greek: "Ἔπασα ἤδη τοῦ θηλείου..."</note> *The nature of each is already evident in their forms, for their habits resemble those they represent. To the lion belong a spirited, brave, and noble appearance. To the leopard belong grace and anger, but also calculation and treachery.* To that citation from Prudentius regarding Photinus and Arius belongs this sentiment also, which is read in Ambrose: *Persecutors are wolves, and all heretics are wolves. They do not know how to teach; they are accustomed only to howl. But let no one be moved if he is in the midst of wolves. By the grace of Christ, even the wolf itself is changed.* Benjamin, the **rapacious wolf**, became the Apostle Paul—no longer an ambusher of Christ’s sheep, but a defender and guardian. *It is a pleasure to dwell with this wolf; through this wolf it has come to pass that we are safe in the midst of wolves. No one now fears the wolf when we pasture with these, just as it is written: Then the wolves and the lambs shall feed together.* It is very common among the Fathers to explain that prophecy of the Patriarch Jacob as referring to the Apostle Paul, as can be seen in Jerome (*Epistle 3 to Heliodorus*, page 27; *Epistle 23 to Marcella*, column 198), Augustine (*Sermon 13 on the Saints*, column 1194, volume 10), Cyprian, and others. For the prophecy concerning Benjamin is: <note>original Hebrew: "בנימין זאב יטרף"</note> *Benjamin is a wolf that ravages; in the morning he devours the prey, and in the evening he divides the spoil.* A **ravaging wolf** <note>original Greek: "Λύκος ἅρπαξ"</note>
<margin>Sermon 6 on Psalm 118, page 635.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
is what he is called because of the tearing apart of enemies and the destruction of the fortifications set against him. Jacob compared Judah to a noble lion, and here he compares the warlike Benjamin to a predatory wolf, plundering the Amalekites, Moabites, Ammonites, and other nations strong in war. <term>Saul</term> <note>The first King of Israel, who was of the tribe of Benjamin.</note> was a predatory wolf of this kind, regarding whose military deeds they wish to sound a war-trumpet. But as they extend the discourse to the other <term>Saul</term>, called <term>Paul</term> after his conversion, who confesses himself to be of the tribe of Benjamin, let them see how the name of the wolf could apply. Thus Jerome thinks, whose words are found in *Questions on Genesis*, column 354, volume 3: *Regarding Paul, there is a most manifest prophecy: that in his youth he persecuted the Church, and in his old age he was a preacher of the Gospel.* Let them also see how the distribution of spoil can be drawn to the sacrifices in the temple, just as the Paraphrast <note>Likely referring to the Aramaic Targum.</note> wishes for Jacob to have foreseen: that the Benjaminites would be famous for the sanctuary and the temple, and fortified by it, they would declare their strength. Jerome explains the Jewish opinion in these words: *The Altar, upon which the victims were sacrificed and the blood of the victims was poured at its base, was in the portion of Benjamin. This, they say, therefore signifies that the Priests sacrifice victims in the morning, and in the evening they divide those things which were gathered for them from the people according to the law.* Thus they place the bloodthirsty wolf, the voracious wolf, upon the interpretation of the Altar.

<margin>In the Philological Lexicon, page 4006.</margin>
**THE MULE**, called <term>Pered</term> <note>original Hebrew: "פרד"</note> by the Hebrews, from a root meaning "to separate," because it is separated and does not mix with others for the sake of breeding, or because its kind is separate; see Martinius on this. The Greeks always translate it as <term>hemionos</term> <note>original Greek: "ἡμίονον"</note>, from the words for "half" and "donkey," because it is an animal of two kinds, according to Varro in his second book *On Agriculture*, chapter 8. Otherwise it is called <term>hyris</term>, not from the word for "fluid," but because it has failed seed, being unfit for breeding; hence, from the common opinion of the Ancients, mules do not breed, but are bred. Aristotle argues at length against Empedocles and Democritus regarding the sterility of mules, saying in his second book *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 8, page 667: *The whole genus of mules is sterile.* And Theophanes adds: *The succession of the genus of mules does not come from one another.* Augustine subscribes to this in *The City of God*, book 15, chapter 26: *Certain animals have sex in such a way that they do not have offspring, like Mules.* Hence, for a mule to give birth was considered a bad omen among the Romans, as their annals testify. However, Pliny, Varro, and Columella testify that they are fertile in Syria and elsewhere. The name <unclear>Pered</unclear> is sometimes associated with mountains, being called "mountainous" <note>original Greek: "ὄρειος"</note> from the word for "mountain," because this animal is more fit for mountain work than others. For they are strong in labor, and it is well known how in Palestine, as well as in the mountainous and steep places of Italy and Spain, the use of these animals is very frequent. The Greeks called the donkey and the horse "bodily" <note>original Greek: "Σωματικὸς"</note> when they carried things on their backs, to which are added the "yoke-beasts." The Attics call the donkeys and horses that carry on their backs "back-bearers" <note>original Greek: "Νωτεῖς"</note>, and they are contrasted with "yoke-beasts" (that is, those used for wagons). Hence they are also called "load-carriers." The epithet for a mule in Hesiod, verse 45, is "toiling" <note>original Greek: "ταλαεργὸς"</note>, meaning hardworking. The Etymologist explains this word thus: *Toiling ones: those who are enduring and able to endure every labor.* The Donkey is a sorrowful and hardworking animal, and yet mules surpass donkeys; hence
<margin>Homily 1, page 6.</margin>
<margin>page 744.</margin>

# SACRED BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
There is a proverb: *How much mules surpass donkeys.* <note>original Latin: "Muli quantum asinis præstant."</note> This is an animal otherwise stupid and dull, which is why "mule" is used in contempt when we reproach someone for their stupidity or dullness. The husband of Lesbia is called a **Mule** in the works of Catullus, page 138:
> While her husband is present, Lesbia says many bad things to me;
> This is a source of greatest joy to that fool.
> Mule, you sense nothing; if she were silent, having forgotten us,
> She would be sane.

<margin>In the Commentary, p. 139.</margin>
Where Muretus notes: *There are those who take "mule" in this passage as the proper name of a man; I think those people were themselves mules.* Simonides, the lyric poet, was once asked by a man who had won a race with mules to celebrate the victory in a poem. Since the man offered too small a reward, the poet refused the task, saying he could not praise mules because the subject was barren. But when the reward was increased, he began to praise them and took up a more grand opening in this manner: "Hail, daughters of storm-footed horses." <note>original Greek: Χαίρετ' ἀελλοπόδων θυγατέρες ἵππων.</note> He passed over the fact that they were also daughters of female donkeys as being too lowly a detail. Augustine discusses mules in *The City of God*, page 860, questioning whether they were in Noah’s ark, since no mention of them is made before that time.

<margin>Genesis 36:24.</margin>
Holy Scripture first mentions them there <note>original Latin: "Primùm eorum meminit Scriptura S."</note>, but the passage is highly controversial. Indeed, many and abundant doubts tend to present themselves whenever one deals with things not heard of before or words heard for the first time, to such an extent that both cause anxiety in the minds of scholars. Regarding the interpretation of this passage, even as far back as the time of Jerome, there were as many opinions as there were interpreters. Some, reading the Hebrew <term>yamim</term> <note>often translated as "mules" or "hot springs"</note>, wished to believe that Anah found "gatherings of waters" while pasturing donkeys in the desert, which are difficult to find in such a place. Others interpreted it not as *yamim* but as "hot waters," influenced by the proximity of the Punic language. Some interpreted it as "wild asses," and some as "mules." Seeing these difficulties, the Greek interpreters defined nothing, leaving the word <term>yamim</term> untranslated, for which Symmachus and Aquila used "the gatherings." <note>original Greek: τὰς γαμεῖν.</note> Moreover, that man who is said to have found the <term>yamim</term> is called <term>Anah</term>, whom the Septuagint calls *Enan*; and I do not know from where

<margin>Iliad, book 2, line 852.</margin>
Homer * gets his information regarding the Eneti, from whom the race of wild mules is said to have originated:
> From the Eneti, where the race of wild mules originates. <note>original Greek: ἐξ Ἐνετῶν, ὅθεν ἡμιόνων γένος ἀγροτεράων.</note>

**THE MOUSE**, called <term>Akhbar</term> by the Hebrews, was forbidden to the Jews in the Law (Leviticus 11:29), but they later delighted in it against the law.

<margin>Isaiah 66:17.</margin>
Although this little creature may be born from scraps <note>referring to the ancient theory of spontaneous generation</note>, lives under roofs, and flees the light, it nevertheless very often steps into the battle line against the wicked. The tiny mouse threw Pharaoh's own court into fear, emerging from its hiding places into the open. Pliny (Book 8, chapters 29 and 57) is the authority for the fact that the inhabitants of Gyarus, one of the Cyclades, were once driven away by mice. He reports the same of others in Book 10, chapter 65: *Very many of them reached the Troad, and have already driven away the inhabitants from there.* Elian (Book 17, chapter 41) writes that the same happened to certain Italians, and Justin (following Trogus, Book 15) mentions it regarding the Abderites. Rutilius Rufus says of Cosa:
> It is said the citizens were once forced to migrate, 
> And deserted their homes, infested by mice.
Otherwise, great sagacity is usually attributed to animals, and especially to mice, which they say are animals highly endowed with the science of prophecy, so that you might say from this:
-> often a tiny mouse <-

<column-break/>

> Will give you a sad omen, who from deep beneath the earth
> Was held by no love, but burst forth into the open air
> From the pits, unmindful of life and habit,
> And left behind its little young and its sweet home.

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
Hence it is considered a most prophetic animal <note>original Greek: μαντικωτάτῳ</note> because it foreknows future events; for when a house is already rotting and about to fall shortly after, it foresees the danger first, and having abandoned the seats it inhabits, it flees with the greatest possible speed, according to the testimony of Elian in *Varia Historia* (chapter 11) and *History of Animals* (Book 9, chapter 19). Regarding the "Musoritae"—those who grant divine honor to mice—one may read Philastrius, though we do not know where he found it. This much is certainly true: mice were held in great honor by the inhabitants of the Troad because, during a war, they had destroyed the strings of the enemy's bows by gnawing them. Aristotle is the witness in the second book of his *Rhetoric*, and Herodotus produces a similar example in his second book regarding the King of Egypt, Sethos, whom field mice helped against Sennacherib, gnawing through the quivers, the bows, and the straps of the shields so thoroughly that on the following day, stripped of his arms, he took flight.

**THE SHREW-MOUSE**, called <term>Anakah</term> by the Hebrews, which the Septuagint renders as *mygale*. It is one of the egg-laying quadrupeds <note>an ancient biological error</note> mentioned in Leviticus 11:30, where Eugubinus says he does not know that kind of animal. Dioscorides writes elsewhere about the *mygale* (Book 2 and more than once in Books 7 and 8), as do Plutarch (Book 4, chapter 5), Aetius, and Nicander in his *Theriaca*, where he names the *mygale*. Some assign a reason for the name, suggesting it is generated from a mouse and a weasel, which is in no way likely, since there is no small antipathy between these animals. Commonly, the *mygale* is a shrew <note>original German: "ein Spigmans" [Spitzmaus]</note>. Luther renders the Hebrew word as "hedgehog" <note>original German: "Igel"</note>. Others want it to be a wingless species of locust. Bochart proves it is similar to the *stellio*, a type of lizard, regarding whose sharp screeching Pliny writes in Book 29, chapter 4. Münster also placed the "hedgehog" <note>original Latin: "ericium"</note> here based on a corrupted paraphrase of Onkelos. Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] suggests it is a "fiber" or a beaver. Perhaps it comes from the name of the *Castoris*, which Elian and Oppian fabulously claim is a sea animal that gives a mournful wail, sounding a prophetic "howl" that foretells swift death to whoever hears it.

**THE WEASEL**, the use of which is not small in catching both smaller mice and those we call rats, because on account of its slender body it even enters burrows that cats cannot penetrate. Among the Thebans, it was honored with divine worship because Galanthis, having been turned into a weasel, gave aid to Alcmene while she was in labor. Ovid tells this fable: *

<margin>Book 9 of the Metamorphoses, fable 6.</margin>
> The goddess powerful over the womb [Lucina], once the bonds were released, I am lightened myself. 
> Fame says Galanthis laughed, having deceived the divinity. 
> As she laughed, the golden-haired goddess seized her by her very hair 
> And dragged her, and as she tried to lift her body from the ground, 
> She hindered her, and changed her arms into forelegs. 
> Her old vigor remains, nor did her back lose its color, 
> Though her form is different from before. 
> Because she had aided the one giving birth with a lying mouth, 
> She gives birth through her mouth, and frequents our homes just as before.

This refers to the wondrous conception and birth of weasels according to the opinion of the ancients: that they conceive through their ears and give birth through their mouths, a belief held by the Egyptians and almost all...

### From Psalm 50:10-11

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
This was the opinion of all, which Aristotle * solidly refutes, because weasels do not have a womb for no reason, and furthermore, it is clear from anatomy that there is no path from the ears to the womb, nor from the womb to the mouth. <note>Aristotle is refuting the ancient myth that weasels conceive through their ears and give birth through their mouths.</note> Clemens of Alexandria mentions the same "weasel-worship" <note>original Greek: γαληλατρείας</note> among the Thebans in his *Exhortation*, as does Aelian in Book 4 of *On Animals*, chapter 5, where he cites the same cause.

<margin>Book 3, *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 6.</margin>
The weasel was forbidden to the Jews by the law of Leviticus 11:29. Procopius of Gaza gave this reason for the prohibition: God wished to deter man from the robberies and ambushes by which the weasel lives. It is a harmful animal that does not even abstain from human corpses; in particular, just as it is accustomed to suck out the eggs of hens, so it sucks out the eyes of the deceased, as found in Aelian, Book 15, chapter 11. The weasel is called *galē* <note>original Greek: γαλή</note> by the Greeks, in the explanation of which word there is a great error among the Greeks—not only those of the present day, but all who have flourished in literary studies for five hundred years. Indeed, they all think that *galē* is a cat, an error which Nicolaus Perottus boasts he was the first to detect in his *Cornucopia*.

<margin>Leviticus 11:29.</margin>
Concerning the word found in the Law of Moses, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translated it as *galēn*, followed by Jerome and Luther, who translated it as *Wiesel* [weasel]. But Bochart explains the Hebrew word *choled* <note>original Hebrew: חלד</note> as a mole, and produces various arguments for this opinion, which may be seen in his work.

**ONAGER** [Wild Donkey], a word of Greek origin, which the Seventy use separately in Job 39:5: *Who has sent out the wild donkey free?* <note>original Greek: Τίς δὲ ἐστιν ὁ ἀφείς τὸν ὄνον ἄγριον ἐλεύθερον.</note> In the original text, the word *arud* <note>original Hebrew: ערוד</note> occurs, noting a forest animal, free, having its name either from its running, because it is of such speed that no one can overtake it, or from its fecundity, because in those places where they live, entire forests are full of wild donkeys, from which they rush out into the crops. They are plainly untamable and never domesticated. *Who loosed the bonds of the free wild donkey, who laughs at the multitude of the city and does not hear the shouts of the driver?* says Job in the passage cited, by which he shows the untamable and utterly wild nature <note>original Greek: ἄγριον φύσιν</note> of this animal, whatever Varro or Pliny might say to the contrary, unless perhaps they are speaking of domestic wild donkeys. It lives in deserts, especially those of Africa, Assyria, Phrygia, and Arabia; however, Torquemada testifies that they are also found in Northern regions.

<margin>*Hexameron*, p. 579.</margin>
Simocatta notes in his *History* that its meat and haunches were among the types of delicacies for the Persians, and Olearius, an eyewitness, reported that this is still the case today in the Persian court. The male is jealous, whence he is said to castrate the newborn male foals with a bite unless the mother hides them, as Oppian reports in his *Cynegetica*. Because of its wildness and unsociable nature <note>original Greek: ἀσύνθετον</note>, Ishmael is called a "wild man" <note>original Hebrew: פרא אדם</note>, that is, one who loves solitudes and is intent on catching wild beasts. Thus Eucherius writes that the wild donkey represents the Hermit, both for its solitary life and its love of the desert <note>original Greek: ἐρημοφιλίαν</note>.

**ORYX**, <note>original Greek: ὄρυξ, Hebrew: תאו - *teo*</note>. Among the animals which the Jews were allowed to eat by law, Deuteronomy 14:5, of which mention is also made in Isaiah 51:20. In both places, Luther translates it as *Uhrochs* or *Waldoche* [Aurochs or Forest Ox]. What the oryx is, say the grammarians, is disputed: We take it for a wild ox. For it is to the Church like a wild beast; against which all exercise their hatred by hunting, snaring, and slaughtering it. But nevertheless, it will finally be

<column-break/>

delivered from all evils and its enemies will perish. In this, the History followed the Targum, which reads *torbala* <note>original Hebrew: תורבלא</note> in this passage, which the Latin interpreter of the Chaldean paraphrase renders as "Wild Ox." Certainly, a great obscurity is presented to us in the names of animals, and there is a wonderful diversity in explaining these names, such that there are many which cannot be thoroughly understood, and many we <unclear>hardly</unclear> see except in some part through the opinions of interpreters. Among these are *teo* and *arud*, the former of which Moses has in his writings, the latter Isaiah. That Mosaic animal seems to the Greeks to be the *oryx*, which is also known to the Latins by the same name, and is said to resemble a gazelle. Of it, Pliny says: There are gazelles, there are rock-goats, there are ibexes of wonderful speed. There are also oryges, which are the only ones said to be covered with hair pointing the opposite way, toward the head. Oppian mentions them in *On Hunting*:
-> ...and gazelles and oryges and shining roe-deer. <-
<note>original Greek: καὶ δόρκας ὄρυγάς τε καὶ ἀγλήεντας ἰόρκας.</note>
But Bochart * denies it can be counted among other types of goats, both because Judea did not nourish this animal, which the Greeks call *Dorkas*, nor can it be caught with a snare like that *teo* of Isaiah. Whence, with the Seventy and the rest of the Greeks and Jerome, he determines it to be the Oryx.

**OVIS** [Sheep], so called from the Greek *ois* <note>original Greek: ὄις</note> with a digamma interposed, as Beccmannus wishes; called *probaton* <note>original Greek: πρόβατον</note> by the Greeks, from "walking forward on feet" <note>original Greek: τὸ προβαίνειν διὰ ποδῶν</note>, because others follow the steps of the first, according to Eustathius and the Etymologist. Among the Hebrews it is "many-named," just as Ursinus counts twelve names for the sheep-flock in his *Nomenclature of Biblical Animals*. Sheep, a most gentle flock, whose utility Columella loves, are commended for their wool and milk, from which cloth and cheeses are made. Hence they are called "wool-bearing flocks" by Lucretius:

<margin>p. 108.</margin>
-> Wool-bearing flocks and the warlike offspring of horses. <-

<margin>Book 2.</margin>
By Apuleius, however, they are called "shining and flourishing with the color of gold." Since they are sometimes of various colors, they are usually named from it, just as Virgil says that sheep grazing will spontaneously become a scarlet color, when he sings:

<margin>Book 6, p. 79.</margin>
-> Of its own accord, the scarlet dye shall clothe the grazing lambs. <-
Vossius notes that this verse was correctly understood neither by Pliny nor by Servius. Baptista Mantuanus places the cause of different-colored sheep in the constellation of the sky itself, and in the different nature of the water and herbs:

<margin>Eclogue 10, folio 25b.</margin>
> Why are the flocks of the Mutinian field of dark fleece?
> Why does the Clitumnus have snowy ones? Why does Mantua
> -> excel <-
> In soft wool? And Verona, closest to Mantua?
> From where comes this multiple variation in the form of things?
> From nowhere else but from the heavens, from the grass, and the wave?
> It matters much, therefore, what pastures the flocks
> -> crop, <-
> What rivers they drink, and in what region they stay.

How much it contributes, however, what an animal is nourished by and in what region it lives, is evidenced by the fact that in the North, because of the extreme hardship of the cold, stags, wolves, bears, hares, and every animal of that kind are of a white color, as Torquemada testifies. Thus the oxen pastured at the Clitumnus are white, from Claudian in his *Panegyric on the Sixth Consulship of Honorius*:
-> Nay, it was a care to visit the sacred waves of Clitumnus, <-
-> Which provide white herds for the Latin triumphs. <-

### SACRED BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

**Column 1:**

<margin>Sacred history of animals. ch. 33.</margin>
In the same way, sheep turn black by drinking from a spring on the coast of the Erythraean <note>The "Erythraean Sea" refers to the Red Sea and sometimes the broader Indian Ocean in ancient geography.</note> Sea, as Solinus * testifies from Varro: <margin>The true Pelusiac mouth of Arabia belongs to the Red Sea, which Varro reports was named "Erythraean" after King Erythras, the son of Perseus and Andromeda, and not solely from its color. He affirms that on the shore of that sea is a spring which, if sheep drink from it, changes the quality of their fleeces; though they were white before, they lose what they were until the drink, and later turn black with a dusky color. Martianus Capella mentions the same thing in Book 6 on Egypt, though omitting the names of Varro and Solinus.</margin> Regarding the sheep of Crete, Oppian writes in Book 2 of *On Hunting* <note>original: *Cynegetica*</note>, verse 377, that they are yellow in color <margin>Book 5, p. 590.</margin> and four-horned, which Torquemada * also testifies regarding the rams of Greenland, which are commonly four-horned, and many even eight-horned. Thus, more credit should be given to Martial, a man of Spain, when he writes that in Spain the fleeces of sheep <margin>Genesis 30:37.</margin> are of a golden color. Moses * narrates what Jacob—a singular master of managing household affairs—did through a peculiar craft to miraculously increase his own property. He entered into a contract with his father-in-law Laban in this manner: the solid-colored sheep were to be separated from the variegated ones by a three-day journey, and whatever was born variegated from the solid-colored sheep (which Jacob kept in his own care) would fall to him as wages. Once the separation was made, Jacob took green branches from trees and shrubs and stripped away part of the bark while leaving part on, so that the rods appeared partly white and partly green or dark-colored. He placed these rods, prepared with this craft, in the watering troughs so that the sheep would see these multi-colored branches during mating, and thus, being pregnant, they would bear similar offspring. Furthermore, he turned the lambs already born with spotted fleeces toward the variegated sheep, so that from the mutual sight of them, multi-colored ones would likewise be born. Thus, in that matching of the flock, the variegated rods moved the imagination, the imagination moved the senses, and the senses moved the formative power. For Jacob knew <margin>Commentary on Genesis, p. 591.</margin>—to whom, according to Blessed Gerhard *, God had supernaturally revealed in a dream—that if sheep have multi-colored rods placed in their sight at the time of conception, they produce spotted lambs. He knew the secrets of nature and the sympathies of things; he knew God would bless him through this means, which the School of Physicians also widely teaches to be natural (compare Pliny, *Natural History*, Book 7, ch. 12; Francisco Valles, *Sacred Philosophy*, ch. 11). In this way, he increased the reward for his exhausted labor. Yet it must not be thought that the imagination of the livestock was the entire <margin>3 *On Idolatry*, 22 p. 833.</margin> cause of this matter. Indeed, as Vossius * writes: if its power were so great that the effect always, or even mostly, followed, then surely our own shepherds today, being skilled enough in their craft, would imitate the example. Therefore, this effect is not to be ascribed to imagination alone, nor to the peeled rods alone, but most especially to divine power, which by its own cooperation so increased the weak force of the secondary cause that what it could not do alone according to nature, it performed through divine blessing above nature. Hence Jacob himself ascribes that change to divine power and the special grace of God in Genesis 31:8, 9 <margin>Commentary on Genesis, folio 126.</margin> and following. To this, refer to what Blessed Luther writes *: God shows Jacob a singular craft by which he might correct and change nature. He takes rods from three trees and strips them, not that he

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

pulls the bark off entirely, but so that he might produce a certain variety of colors, white <margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> and black, so that in one part it appears white because the bark was removed, and in the other black where the bark remains. He places these in the water channels so that the sheep have the rods before their eyes and conceive while under their influence. It was an ingenious philosophy or magic by which he caused the sheep, in the heat of their lust, to procreate varied offspring under the influence of the varied rods; and thus, from a white or black flock, multi-colored and spotted ones were born. So, by art and wit, or natural magic, Jacob deceives the art—or rather the malice—of Laban. The Fathers say they learned this magic either through long use or from the instruction of their ancestors. For Jacob was undoubtedly taught by one of the Patriarchs, or by Divine instinct through the Holy Spirit. Again, at folio 130b: Neither the pact with his father-in-law nor the magic he used would have profited Jacob, since Laban changed the conditions so often and at his whim, had not the divine blessing been added, as he says: "The Lord brought it about so that he might not harm me. God has delivered me and increased my flocks. Indeed, He has snatched away the livestock from your father and given it to me." <note>original Hebrew: ויצל אלהים את מקנה אביכם ויתן לי ע"כ</note> There is a great emphasis in the word "snatched away" <note>The Hebrew verb *natzal* implies rescuing or plundering back something that was taken.</note>. He does not say He "received" or "took," but "God snatched away." God snatched away, that is, He delivered and saved; and the Holy Spirit wishes to signify that this livestock belonged by all right to Jacob and his wives, given by the blessing of God and acquired by their labors, because he had served fourteen years, and in this six-year period he was deceived ten times. Therefore, Holy Scripture says that which was owed to Jacob and his family was a "permissible seizure" and a "taking back." My art and cunning, he says, shown and approved by God, would have profited nothing unless God, by a singular force and power, had snatched away and liberated the livestock of your father like a captive—livestock which he himself had previously snatched from our jaws. All this that he held was ours; and what we now have, I did not acquire by art or industry, but by divine power, which snatched it with a strong hand from the hand of this Laban. Moses wished to signify this with the word <term>Jazel</term> <note>original: *yatzel*, meaning "he delivered" or "he snatched away"</note>, that the Lord blessed Jacob by snatching it back. Jacob had prepared three kinds of rods: first, <term>populi</term> <note>Hebrew: *libneh*, meaning white poplar</note>; then <term>amygdali</term> <note>Hebrew: *luz*, meaning almond</note>, as the Vulgate translates, or as others say, <term>coryli</term> <note>hazel</note> (indeed, from the Hebrew <term>luz</term> comes the Latin <term>nux</term> <note>nut</note>, by the common transition of two liquids, as in <term>lympha</term> and <term>nympha</term>); and finally <term>castanea</term> <note>Hebrew: *armon*, meaning chestnut</note>, as Solomon Jarchi thought with David the Sami; or the <term>platani</term> <note>plane tree</note>, as the Latin interpreter explained, favored by the Chaldean Paraphrast when he explains it as <term>dilbu</term>, which although Paulus Fagius renders as chestnut, truly denotes the <term>plane tree</term>, as (just as observed by Drusius) is also shown in the Arabic language, where <term>dilub</term> is the <term>plane tree</term>. Regarding the "variegated" and "spotted," the term <term>akod</term> is sometimes used in Genesis 30 and 31, where it concerns the spotted flocks of Laban and Jacob. The spotted goats are <term>nequddim</term> in Genesis 30:35, <note>original Greek: οἱ ῥαντοί</note> in the Septuagint, that is, "sprinkled," namely with various colors. Onkelos reads <term>regula</term> and Jonathan <term>reglin</term>, meaning they have a sign and mark on their feet, multi-colored lines around their legs. For they used to, and still do today, brand marks into the flock of sheep to distinguish the livestock of their master and to avoid troublesome disputes, about which Calpurnius * writes from the emendation <margin>Eclogue 5.</margin> of Fruterius, Book of *Verisimilia* 15, p. 47:

> *Also, boil weights of silver-lead with honey,*
> *And tough bitumen in a bronze pot,*
> Brand- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

<summary>This page discusses the natural and supernatural factors involved in the breeding of Jacob's variegated sheep in Genesis, blending classical natural history about the effects of environment on wool color with theological interpretations of "natural magic." It emphasizes that while Jacob used biological "sympathies" (visual stimuli), the ultimate success was a divine act of "snatching back" what was rightfully his from Laban.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of sheep and goats within the framework of sacred history. The previous page concluded with Jacob’s contract with Laban regarding the separation of solid-colored and spotted livestock. This page explores the linguistic and theological nuances of Jacob's breeding practices, the classical origins of animal sacrifice, and the symbolic connection between the sacrificial sheep and the Messiah.</meta>

<header>From Psalm 50, verses 10–11.</header>

<margin>Sacred History of Animals. *Tiberiad*, ch. 14, p. 160.</margin>
Imprinting names upon the sheep; for the bed,
The great possessor, will take the muddy ones from your shoulder.
But what should be made of the final *Vav* <note>The Hebrew letter ו</note>, which is drawn longer than usual in the word *ve-hattuphim* <note>Hebrew: וְהַטּוּפִים</note>, interpreted as "the late-born" or "feeble" ones? Buxtorf * treats this, writing: The larger final *Vav* marked in the word *ve-hattuphim* serves to highlight the shrewdness of Jacob, by which he ensured—through a fair agreement—that he would acquire a generous compensation for the many years of service rendered to his father-in-law. This final *Vav*, enlarged in writing, indicates that the end of that labor would testify amply to its beginning. Likewise, the *He* <note>The Hebrew letter ה</note> marks *ha-aquddim* <note>Hebrew: הַעֲקֻדִּים, meaning "the striped" or "bound"</note> as a "vengeance," namely, that this work would become a vengeance against the ingratitude of Laban. We might wish for a more moderate judgment regarding Jacob, whose pious and devoted soul toward God we know to be far removed from all craftiness and "vengeance" in the strict sense. Let us rather judge Jacob’s purpose along with Theodoret in *Questions on Genesis*, 88: *not trusting in the rods themselves, but awaiting divine care* <note>original Greek: "ουκ εν αυταις θαρρων, αλλα την θειαν επιμελειαν προσ- μενων"</note>. He peeled the rods, not placing his confidence in them, but expecting divine help. We also agree with the Blessed Luther, whose words are these: *First, he is excused by human law (Jacob), because it is granted to those who serve greedy and unjust masters—if they pay no wages but only seize, plunder, and pillage—that the servants may in turn take what is owed to them as wages: but in a proper manner, lest it be done to the Master's detriment. Thus the children of Israel despoiled Egypt, etc. Second, although there is trickery and deception, Jacob nevertheless did it by divine authority, because an Angel appeared and showed him that this natural magic was lawful. Jacob therefore learned it from the Angel or from the holy Fathers, who had great experience and knowledge of things. Truly, when God commands holy and faithful men to do something, that is without doubt holy and lawful.* Third, he says later, "God looked upon my labor and my affliction," etc. As the best and most faithful servant, he had no hope of grazing or gathering any property of his own because of the insatiable greed of his father-in-law. That was certainly no small calamity, by which he was moved to this "plunder," especially since divine authority was added, by which he was commanded to do this. "For Laban has felt more benefit from you," says the Angel, "than you can take from him. Therefore, you can rightfully use art and deception to take something from him—not as a theft, but as something granted and given by God." Thus Jacob is excused by both human and divine law, and by extreme necessity. The sheep is an animal of great utility, which is why it was held in divine veneration by the Egyptians for its usefulness, according to Plutarch in his book *On Isis*.

<margin>Plutarch, in his book *On Isis*.</margin>
<margin>Clement of Alexandria, *Admonition to the Heathen*.</margin>
Clement of Alexandria also reports this regarding the inhabitants of Sais and Thebes in his *Admonition to the Heathen*, as well as regarding the Samians. However, concerning the Samians, it seems the sheep were worshipped not as gods, but as votive offerings, if we may follow Aelian in Book 2 of *On the Nature of Animals*, chapter 40. From which Aristotle says: *A sheep found the sacred gold stolen from the Samians; and because of this, Mandrabulus the Samian dedicated a sheep as a votive offering to Hera.* <note>original Greek: "Σαμίοις χρυσίον (ιερόν) κλαπὲν πρόβατον ανεύρε, καὶ εντεύθεν Μανδράκορα ὁ Σάμιος τῇ Ἥρᾳ πρόβατον ανάθημα ανέθηκε."</note> We recall it being asked by the Pagans <note>original: *Ethnici*</note> which animal was the first destined for sacrifice; they were of the opinion that it was the swine. Varro conjectures this from the origin of the name itself, as well as from the ancient initiations of the Eleusinian mysteries and other ceremonial rites.

<column-break/>

<margin>Book 2 of *On Agriculture*, 4.</margin>
The swine (*sus*), he says *, is called *hys* <note>original: υς</note> in Greek, formerly *thys* <note>original: θυς</note>, from that word which is called *thyein* <note>original: θυειν</note>, which means "to sacrifice"; for the first beginning of sacrificing animals seems to have been taken from this type of livestock. Traces of this remain: that pigs are sacrificed at the festivals of Ceres; that when a peace treaty is struck, a pig is killed; and that a new husband first sacrifices a pig. The ancient Latins and even the Greeks in Italy seem to have practiced the same; for our women, especially nurses, call the female genitalia in young girls a "pig" (*porcus*), and the Greeks call it *choiros* <note>original: χοίρον</note>, signifying that it is worthy of the mark of marriage. Athenaeus * agrees regarding the origin:

<margin>Book 9.</margin>
> -> those who, in peace, as if in sacrifice, <-
> -> provided those things suitable for the offering. <-
> <note>original Greek: "οι δε συν ειρηνη, οιονει θυνη, τον εις θυσίαν επιτήδεια."</note>

But just as Abel was the first shepherd of sheep from the very beginning of the nascent world, who
> often placed a sacrifice from his flock upon the altars,
so the sheep was seen as the most suitable of all animals, a victim purer and more excellent than other living creatures to be offered in sacrifice to God; hence Prudentius *:

<margin>*Romanus*, verse 829.</margin>
> -> So that you might believe a firstborn offspring was brought <-
> -> To be offered to God on the dish of holy Abel, <-
> -> Chosen from the sheepfold, purer than the rest. <-

<margin>Genesis 3:15, 21.</margin>
That first sacrifice performed in Paradise after the Fall preceded this offering of Abel. For when the promise of grace for the new covenant had been made (Genesis 3:15, 21), God Himself made tunics for the naked humans from the skins of slaughtered sheep. It was there, certainly, that the first *sacrifice* <note>original: θυσία (*thysia*)</note> was performed; for Adam, in such great consternation of mind, would not have slaughtered even the smallest and cheapest little sheep without an express command and order from God. Therefore, among the animals, the Sheep first gave the type of God’s appeasement through the Messiah, who was to be sacrificed one day on the altar of the cross. The sheep is an innocent and weak animal, neither armed with horns <note>The author likely refers to ewes or the general nature of the species compared to predators.</note>, nor teeth, nor hooves, nor claws, nor protected by venom for its own defense; indeed, there is absolutely no impatience or resistance in it when it is led to the slaughter. Isaiah * describes the virtue of humility in Christ, who humbled Himself in all things, using the example of the Sheep, writing:

<margin>Isaiah 53:7.</margin>
> Like a sheep he will be led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he will be silent, and he will not open his mouth.

Christ, cast down by every kind of injury and insult, was found like a sheep, patiently enduring all things: hunger, thirst, cold, contempt, poverty, insults, wounds, death, and the cross. St. John * pointed his finger to the *Lamb* whom the Prophet had here foretold, saying: *Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world.*

<margin>John 1:29.</margin>
Pressed under the heaviest weight of the sins of the world, He is silent; dragged to the slaughter, He is silent, no differently than a lamb while it is shorn. Thus in Him we have the true Lamb of God, the true and most powerful sacrifice and effective victim, which alone reconciles sinful men to God—benefiting not only the Jewish people, but the entire world.

Flocks of sheep were very numerous in Palestine: Jacob, Moses, David, and Amos cared for flocks of sheep; they were *overseers of sheep* <note>original Greek: επιστάται των προβάτων</note>, and were later made *overseers and venerable leaders of men* <note>original Greek: επιστάται, σεβαστοὶ των ανθρώπων</note>. Hence come such frequent comparisons from sheep...

<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>Sacred history of animals. Ezekiel 34:2.</margin> In the Old Testament, we find the ministry of the Church described in Ezekiel under the likeness of a Shepherd of sheep. In this passage, the Lord censures and severely rebukes false teachers and pseudo-prophets, pronouncing a curse and destruction upon them for the scattering of the wretched sheep. The crimes of these shepherds could not go unpunished, nor could the calamities of the flock remain without the consolation of a new covenant. The crimes of the shepherds are these: <margin>v. 3.</margin> *To eat the fat, to slaughter the choice animals, to clothe themselves in the wool, but not to feed the flock;* <margin>v. 4.</margin> *not to strengthen those afflicted by disease, not to heal the sick, not to bind up the broken, not to bring back those driven away, not to seek the lost, but to rule over them with cruelty and violence;* <margin>v. 18.</margin> *to graze upon the best of the pastures, to tread the remains of the fodder underfoot, to drink the clear water and disturb the rest with their feet.* But the consolation for the sheep who have been so poorly fed thus far is this: *that He will seek the sheep, rescue them, lead them out, gather them from the lands, bring them into their own land, and feed them in good pastures.* The nature of the sheep as an animal is simple; it is easily led into wandering, cannot help or save itself, and if unguarded, it strays into thickets and briars. With a reckless leap into water or over a precipice, it easily allows itself to be led away by a companion. David, likening himself to a sheep, said <margin>Psalm 119:176</margin>: *I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant.* Let us hear Paschasius Ratbertus <note>A 9th-century Benedictine theologian</note> in his commentary on Matthew 18, column 741, regarding this confession <note>original Greek: ὁμολογήσει</note> of David. He says the Patriarch David felt that he had wandered and perished badly in Adam, and for that reason, he said: *I have gone astray like a lost sheep.* Because he knew that in that same Adam he had perished and wandered. The Prophet confesses his fall in that which he shares in common with all men. For no one has not died in Adam, except for Him who alone was found free among the dead. But since David had perished like a sheep—having wandered from the path in that first Adam—he therefore asks that the Good Shepherd seek him out. For no one is truly lost who perfectly recognizes his own error. What else is it to say, "seek your servant," but to seek a fallen and wandering sheep? Once a sheep is led into the wilderness, it does not return of its own accord, nor does it seek the Shepherd; rather, it is necessary that it be sought by him. When David fell into the wilderness of adultery and later <margin>2 Samuel 12:2</margin> murder, God brought him back by sending Nathan. Nathan corrected the vice in David's soul through a skillfully crafted story and an indirect approach. For a harsh and unpleasant rebuke often does harm, whereas a more concealed one is beneficial—especially in the minds of Great Men. In correcting them, that oblique method, instituted through a "metamorphosis" or parable, often achieves more than a "harshness of words" <note>original Greek: τραχύτητι λόγων</note>, such as the "rebuke of those who blame and accuse" <note>original Greek: ὁ τῷ μεμφόμενων καὶ κατηγορούντων ἔλεγχος</note>, which only exasperates them into further harshness and cruelty. For it is a disease of the human mind that it does not wish to be admonished or corrected for its wrongdoings; we can hardly bear to have our own blemishes pointed out to us by others. The Holy Spirit, knowing this stubbornness <note>original Greek: ἀυθάδειαν</note> and moroseness of character, transforms both the facts and the persons involved so that He might more easily and quickly instill what He wants us to know. This is done so that He may convict men, even those who are unwilling or careless, out of their own mouths. While they think something else is being said or done, their judgment—not yet corrupted by their own emotions—more willingly embraces the truth and pronounces what is just. By this prudent stratagem, Nathan, intending to admonish David for his crime committed against Uriah and his wife, proposed a parable and

<column-break/>

brought the King to the point where he condemned himself. <margin>Sacred history of animals. 1 Kings 20:39-40.</margin> Likewise, Ahab, an impious king, brought judgment against himself in a case proposed by a Prophet as if it concerned someone else, for which he was to be rebuked for letting Ben-hadad go. In this same way, Frederick, Bishop of Utrecht, corrected Louis the Pious. When the Emperor advised the Bishop at a banquet to conduct himself in his commissioned office in such a way that neither fear of danger nor hope of honor or profit should allow him to be turned aside from a hallowed and honorable course, the Bishop replied: "You advise rightly, Emperor; but tell me, is it better to catch this fish placed before us by the head or by the tail?" "By the head," said the Caesar. "In the same manner," said the Bishop, "it is right that you, the head of the Empire, be corrected first: that you cease from your incest and dismiss your kinswoman, the daughter of the Duke of Bavaria." The Emperor, not at all offended by this prudent freedom of speech, corrected his behavior, as reported by Johannes Trithemius in the *Hirsaugi Chronicle*. Secular writers of the gentile world also approve of this method of rebuke, giving counsel that in the manner of teaching and admonishing, persuasion should be established through the sweetness of a fable. Thus Pollux says in Book 1 of the *Onomasticon*: *Since the instructional style is dry and tedious, nothing should prevent adding the sweetness of a myth for the enchantment of the soul.* Agathias Scholasticus briefly expressed the same sentiment in his Epigram on Aesop:

-> Rough advice should be avoided. <-

The **LEOPARD**, called *Namer* <note>Hebrew: נמר</note> by the Hebrews—the female of which is called a Pardal or Panther—is an animal fierce beyond measure, extremely swift, and headlong for blood. <margin>John de Bado Aureo, *On Arms*, p. 13.</margin> Regarding this, John de Bado Aureo writes: *The Pardus is a very swift beast, patterned with white spots like a panther, headlong for blood, and often dies from a single leap. It does not differ in color from the Panther, except that the Panther has whiter spots. It is also a degenerate animal, because it mates with a Lioness, and from this adultery the Leopard is born.* <margin>Hosea 13:6-7.</margin> From the ferocity of this wild beast, Hosea draws a comparison with an angry God. To declare the severity of punishment, God puts forward savage animals and likens Himself to them. *I will be,* He says through Hosea, *to them like a great Lion, like a leopard by the way.* The Old Interpreter <note>The Vulgate</note> renders this "of the Assyrians," as do the Septuagint <note>original Greek: Ἀσσυρίων</note>. Rabbi Iarchi <note>Rashi</note> wants this to be the future tense of the root *shur* <note>Hebrew: שור</note>, meaning to see, look upon, or watch, so the sense is: *I will watch them like a Leopard, who lies in ambush by the way.* Rabbi Kimchi, however, wants it to be the participle of the root *shur*, meaning to step or walk, in this sense: *Like a Leopard walking by the way.* The Paraphrast Jonathan <note>The Targum</note> says: *Like a Leopard lying in ambush by the way.* For the initiates of nature <note>naturalists</note> testify concerning the Leopard—and Basil the Great drew from them—that among animals it is the most hostile to humans and the most greedy for human blood. It possesses such singular cunning that it climbs leafy trees by the royal highway, hides itself in them, and leaps unexpectedly upon passing men to tear and devour them. Basil continues, saying that those who seek to mock the fury of this beast show it the image of a man on paper, which it immediately attacks and shreds in a rage. It evades hunters with its speed, such that it can only be captured when lulled to sleep by wine or lust. Regarding its speed, Phaedrus says thus <margin>Book 3, Fable 41, line 8</margin>:
