# [The Leopard]
<note>The heading for the Leopard is implied by the preceding page and the content of the first section.</note>

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>

> When she has restored her weary strength,
> She frees herself from the pit with a swift leap,
> And hastens with a quickened step to her den.
> After a few days have passed, she flies forth,
> Slaughters the cattle, kills the shepherds themselves,
> And, laying everything waste, rages with an angry force.

<margin>
Jeremiah 13:23.
</margin>

According to the testimony of Lucian, the leopard has a variegated skin, "spotted in its color and marked with patterns" <note>original Greek: παρδαλωτοὶ τὴν χρόαν κεκατερισμένοι (pardalōtoi tēn chroan kekaterismenoi)</note>, yet it is beautiful and almost appears to be covered in eyes. Jeremiah looked to this when he sketched and prefigured the depravity of human nature by applying the likeness of the leopard, saying: *Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? Then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.* This is as if the Prophet had said: Just as the Ethiopian cannot change his skin, nor the leopard his spots, so you also cannot change the depravity and wickedness of your nature for the better so that you might do good. The depravity of a stubborn nature, which can will nothing good and act in no way rightly, could not be better understood. Nevertheless, the grace of God can change all things by illuminating the mind and renewing the will. 

Ambrose also explains it this way in Book 6 of the *Hexameron*, chapter 3. Regarding the appearance of the leopard, he says to the sons of the Scripture that the soul betrays its various impulses through the variety of its colors (referencing Jeremiah 13). For this is understood not only of the physical form, but also of the volatility of its fury: because the Jewish people, discolored by the dark, restless, and shifting changes of an unfaithful mind and spirit, could no longer hold the grace of a good purpose, nor move toward any improvement or correction, having once put on a beast-like ferocity. 

It is a hieroglyphic animal used to indicate the cruelty and speed of the Third Monarchy—that of Alexander the Great and his successors. Philippus Melanchthon <note>A German reformer and collaborator with Luther</note> writes of this symbol in more than one place:

<margin>
Daniel 7:end.
</margin>

> Behold the leopard of Pella <note>Pella was the capital of Macedonia and birthplace of Alexander the Great.</note>, than whom no other was more beautiful
> In the beautiful world that he had conquered, nor ever
> Did anyone perform similar deeds in fewer years.

And in Book 2 of his *Chronicles*, regarding the Third Monarchy, Daniel makes the Macedonian king like a leopard, which is not captured by armed hunters (for it evades their darts by its own speed), but rather when it is put to sleep by wine and lust. 

<margin>
Revelation 13:2.
</margin>

In the New Testament, the Antichrist is compared to a leopard because of his cruelty and hostility in "senselessness" <note>original Greek: ἀπονοίᾳ (aponoia)</note>. Having been taught this by his parent, the Devil—who rages against man made in the image of God because he cannot strike at the Creator himself—he acts like a leopard attacking a man, or even a mere image of a man presented to it on paper. Basil uses this same comparison in his *Sermon on Anger and Envy*, Volume 1, page 478.

### THE LOUSE

In the Holy Scripture, this is read in the plural as *kinnim* <note>Hebrew: כִּנִּים</note>, a word we discussed more extensively above on page 173. It is a "little beast" <note>original Greek: θηρίδιον (thēridion)</note> troublesome to all, both humans and almost all other living creatures. It is not nourished by meat, nor by miscellaneous fluids, but by the moisture of living flesh. However, natural philosophers disagree in its description, as can be seen in the work of Giovanni Tommaso

<margin>
Padua edition, year 1600.
</margin>

Minadous, in his *Consultation on the Disease of Errors*, page 4. While Aristotle writes that they are born "in the flesh" <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ σαρκίον (en tō sarkion)</note>, Minadous understands this to mean not the material but the location and seat where they are formed; he attributes their material substance to humid moisture. We see that lice are sometimes increased by divine vengeance or punishment. From their increase arises the disease we call *phthiriasis* <note>original Greek: φθειριάςιν</note>, the "louse-disease." This is not only a foul disease but also a miserable one, because a large part of a living man's body is eaten away by these most vile and tiny "little beasts" <note>thēridiois</note>. They then multiply so miraculously that they seem to gush forth from the depths of the body, and the victim is tormented by the external voracity of such tiny little enemies, which devastate even the internal organs unto death. Herod the Great died of this disease, as did others whom Vossius lists in great number in Book 4 of *On Idolatry*, chapter 67, page 1532.

<column-break/>

### THE PYGARG

The *pygargos* <note>original Greek: πύγαργος; literally "white-rump"</note>, or *dishon* <note>Hebrew: דִּישׁוֹן</note>. They explain the Hebrew word as referring to a certain kind of wild goat, not unlike a doe, but using the derogatory term—and as it seems, common usage—"to be a profligate" <note>original Greek: καταπυγεῖν (katapygein), a pun on the word for "buttocks"</note>. The Greeks and Latins use a compound word that gives the sense of an animal whose buttocks are white; for *pyge* <note>πυγὴ</note> means buttocks or haunches, and *argos* <note>ἀργὸς</note> means white. 

This word is ambiguous, referring either to wild or semi-wild animals of the goat kind, such as the *pygargus* and the *Strepsiceros* <note>an antelope with twisted horns</note> mentioned in Pliny,

<margin>
Book 8, chapter 53, page 125.
</margin>

or to types of birds, either eagles or herons. Aristotle, in Book 9 of the *History of Animals*, chapter 32, describes a type of eagle so named because of its whitening tail; in Latin, you might not ineptly call it a "white-tail" (*albicella*), a word coined in imitation of the "wagtail" (*motacilla*). Regarding this, Pliny,

<margin>
Book 10, chapter 3, page 143.
</margin>

while listing six kinds of eagles, says the second kind is the Pygargus, which lives in towns and fields and has a whitening tail. And Eustathius, in his commentary on Homer (page 804), says: "It is one of the three species of hawks called *pygargos*." 

However, in Deuteronomy 14:5, Moses is not yet dealing with kinds of birds, but with quadrupeds. Additionally, all eagles are classified among the unclean birds in Leviticus 11:13, whereas here he is discussing clean quadrupeds. The *dishon* is included in this class, and thus it is more correctly judged to be a species of goat, similar to a doe. Blessed Luther translates this as *Tändeln*, or perhaps elsewhere *Dämling*, which we call a *damhirsch* <note>a fallow deer</note>.

### THE RHINOCEROS AND THE UNICORN

These are distinct animals: the former is distinguished by two horns, especially on the nose; the latter has a single horn, black, in the middle of the forehead, two cubits in size. In the Holy Scriptures, it enjoys a single name, *re'em* <note>Hebrew: רֵים</note>, from *rum*, meaning he was high, exalted, or sublime. 

There is a difficult controversy among the learned regarding the word *re'em*, which the Septuagint and all the translators who follow them (as far as I have seen) explain as the "unicorn." Some consider the unicorn a fabulous animal, first invented by Ctesias. However, since Holy Scripture frequently employs learned imagery taken from the nature of the Unicorn, adapting them to the godly, the ungodly, and even to Christ himself with singular teaching and consolation, it must be real. Furthermore, a unicorn was exhibited in a spectacle by Pompey the Great, as Pliny (Book 8, chapter 20) and Solinus (chapter 43) testify. Titus and Domitian also pitted the same animal against an Urus <note>a wild ox</note>, a contest about which Martial (or another) wrote in the *Book of Spectacles*:

<margin>
Epigram 22.
</margin>

> Has he not lifted the heavy urus with his twin horn,
> just as a bull tosses practice balls into the stars?

Not to mention that one was seen by a certain friend of Julius Caesar Scaliger, which he mentions in his *Exoteric Exercises* against Cardano, Exercise 205.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

->### SACRED HISTORY OF ANIMALS<-

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
p. 659. ...so that it is beyond doubt that this animal is found in the nature of things. Regarding the Rhinoceros, to which Pausanias, in his writings on Boeotia, attributes a double horn—one on the nostril and another above it, which is smaller—this can be explained <margin>Deut 32:17</margin> by that Mosaic passage where two horns are expressly attributed to the *Reem* <note>Hebrew: רְאֵם; likely referring to the wild ox or rhinoceros</note>. However, others deny that this animal was known to the Jews because of the lack of an "exalted horn," which the Psalmist mentions in chapter 92:11. For this reason, <margin>Book 3, Sacred Animals, Chapter 1.</margin> Bootius <note>Anselm de Boodt, a 17th-century naturalist</note> opines that it is the *Urus* <note>The extinct wild ox or aurochs</note>, a wild ox not unknown in the North and the Hercynian forests <note>A vast ancient forest in Germany</note>; but whether it was known to the Jews is not clear to me. Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart, a famous biblical scholar of natural history</note> leans toward a species of mountain goat of pure whiteness that is accustomed to holding its head high, and concludes that the *Reem* is the *Oryx*, which sometimes approaches the size of an ox and is occasionally seen with a single horn (from which the Latins call it *Subulo*, from that horn); it is frequent in Egypt and hated due to superstition. We do not commit our ship to such a great sea of opinions, being content with the bare opinions of others regarding the *Reem*. Many things are described in the Sacred Scriptures by the word *Reem*. The Royal Psalmist, discussing the Messiah and his spiritual kingdom in chapter 29:6, says: *And you make them skip like a calf: Lebanon and Sirion like a son of unicorns.* Mystically, the Church Fathers explain the "son of the unicorns" as referring to Christ. It is helpful to bring forward Basil <note>Saint Basil the Great, a 4th-century theologian</note> for this opinion, who says the following in his first explanation of this Psalm: *The only-begotten Son, giving life to the world, is called the "son of the unicorn" when it is necessary to punish vices and the swelling power of the human race, and to overturn that wild and rabid force, as we learn in Job.* It should be observed, however, that Scripture uses the likeness of the unicorn for both: for sometimes it is praised, while at other times it is blamed, etc. It seems that the strength and nature of this animal, being ready for vengeance, is often referred to in Scripture by the likeness of something worse. But because of the loftiness of the horn it carries on its forehead, and its freedom, it is also taken in a good sense, etc. And finally, we find it used for glory in many places. Christ, however, is virtue itself, and therefore, as if having one horn—namely, the one power of the Father—he is called a unicorn. Thus, by the word <margin>Ps 22:21</margin> *Remim* <note>Hebrew: רֵמִים; plural of Reem</note>, the most ferocious enemies are sometimes described because of their untamable ferocity and pride. *Save me,* says David, *from the mouth of the lion* <note>original Hebrew: מִפִּי אַרְיֵה; original Greek: ἐκ στόματος λέοντος</note>, *and from the horns of the unicorns* <note>original Hebrew: מִקַּרְנֵי רֵמִים; original Greek: ἀπὸ κεράτων μονοκερώτων</note>, *deliver my poor or afflicted soul.* This fits with the violent nature of the animal, which <margin>Book 8, Natural History, Ch. 10.</margin> Pliny describes: *The Monoceros* <note>Greek-derived name for the unicorn</note> *is the fiercest of wild beasts, in the rest of its body similar to a horse, with the head of a deer, the feet of an elephant, the tail of a boar, a deep lowing sound, and a single black horn two cubits long projecting from the middle of its forehead.* Job mentions its strength and ferocity in chapter 39:12 and following. <margin>Origins, Book 12, Ch. 2.</margin> Isidore of Seville <note>A 7th-century scholar</note> writes of it that it is captured by the love of a beautiful virgin coming to meet it; it approaches her like a Maltese dog and, having laid aside all ferocity, rests and grows tame in her lap, and is thus bound. Vossius does not give credit to this report of Isidore's (Book 3, On Idolatry, ch. 60, p. 1056), but classifies it among Aesopic fables. That passage in Balaam’s prophecy is disputed due to the divergence of interpreters, whose words we cite here: *God himself is to be praised, who leads them out of Mizraim* <note>Egypt</note>, *who has the strength of a Rhinoceros.* Numbers 23:22 and 24:8. Indeed, Pagninus thinks it should be translated: *God led them out of Egypt; he is like the strength of the unicorn.* Vatablus: *God led them out of Egypt; he is like the strength of the unicorn*

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> *to him.* Tremellius: *The strong God is their leader out of Egypt; he is to him like the strength of the Monoceros;* and they support this version with these notes (p. 182): *He who rescued them from servitude against the will of the Egyptians, the same one fortifies them with strength against enemies, just as the unicorn is fortified; nor do diabolical arts have more power against him than poisons against a unicorn.* <note>Referencing the myth that a unicorn's horn could neutralize poison.</note> Luther and the Swiss <note>Refers to the Zurich Bible</note>: *God has led them out of Egypt / his joy [or strength] is like that of a unicorn.* <note>original German: "Gott hat sie aus Egypten geführet / seine Freudigkeit ist wie eines Einhorns."</note> Piscator: *God, who has led them out of Egypt, is to him like the powers of the unicorn.* <note>original German: "GOtt / der sie auß Egypten geführet hat / ist jhm wie die Kräfften deß Einhorns."</note> The Genevans: *The strong God, who withdrew them from Egypt, is to him like the forces of the unicorn.* <note>original French: "Le Dieu fort, qui les a retires d' Egypte, lui est, comme les forces de la licorne."</note> Castalio: *God, who led them out of Egypt, is endowed with the strength of a unicorn.* To what, therefore, does the oracle of Balaam look, represented by the likeness of the unicorn? Does it look to Egypt, or to God, or to the kingdom of the Jews? Some refer the strength of the unicorn to Egypt, saying that in the pronoun *lo* <note>לוֹ; to him</note>, respect is had for the word *Mizraim* <note>Egypt</note>; they argue that despite the latter being plural and the former singular, the construction is the same as in: *Exodus 14:25. And Mizraim said: I will flee from the face of Israel. Also there: Isaiah 19:16. Mizraim shall be like women.* From this the sense would be: Although the people of Egypt had great skill in incantations and sorcery, as well as immense strength, such as is the strength of the Unicorn, it nevertheless did not stop the Israelites from being able to be liberated from Egyptian power by a strong hand. This is the opinion of the Spanish Jew, Joseph [Albo], in the third book of *Ikarim* <note>The Book of Principles</note>, chapter eight, of which four books translated from the Hebrew language into Latin by Matthias Elias are kept in my possession. Origen explains it as referring to the Son of God (*Homily 16 on Leviticus*), to whose explanation Brentius adds, saying: *His strength is like the Rhinoceros, that is, most firm.*

### SCORPIO & SCORPIUS

This is a common word for the Latins and Greeks; the latter call it *skorpios* <note>σκορπίος</note>, to which Dioscorides adds the epithet *chersaios* <note>land-dwelling</note> to differentiate it from the sea-scorpion. They think it is named from *skaios herpein*, that is, because it crawls crookedly, or as others say, from *skorpizein ton ion*, which is to say, because it ejects venom. The Latins once had another name in common with this, *nepa*, which appears in Cicero <margin>On Ends, 134. b.</margin> when he says: *We see ducklings swim, blackbirds fly, oxen use horns, and scorpions* <note>original Latin: nepas</note> *use stings.* The Arabic verse agrees with this:

->*And the scorpion* <note>original Latin: nepaï</note> *presses upon the eyes and the chest with its feet.*<-

Although others write that both crabs and prawns come under this name, and Festus notes that in the language of the Africans, *nepa* signifies the constellation called Cancer, or as some wish, the *Scorpion*. Among the Hebrews it is *Akrav* <note>עַקְרָב</note>. Some think the [letter] *resh* is inserted, Pagninus says, from *akev* <note>עָקֵב</note>, "the heel," because when stepped upon it punctures and strikes. Avenarius thinks the Latin *Scorpius* is derived from the Hebrew. Nicander recently listed eight kinds of Scorpions, the first of which is not lethal and is without venom, such as Pliny writes is found in Italy (Book 11, *Natural History*, ch. 25), and Galen testifies can be eaten in Egypt without food <note>likely meaning as a snack or without side dishes</note> (Book 3, *On the Properties of Foodstuff*). In Africa, an immense and deadly multitude of Scorpions is found, so much so that Pliny <margin>Book 5, ch. 7.</margin> calls it the "dreaded animal of Africa"; nor is Asia immune from them. Indeed, they are found in great numbers in Egypt, where once the Ibis bird was worshipped because it [ate] scorpions and serpents...

...killed [pests]: In Persia, India, and other parts of the world, they establish their seats especially under stones, as is known even from the common proverb: *under every stone a scorpion sleeps* <note>original Greek: "ἐν παντὶ λίθῳ σκορπίος εὕδει"</note>. They are of a fraudulent nature and character, which is clear from what Clement of Alexandria writes <margin>Book 1 of the Miscellanies.</margin>—that if it does not succeed in striking a person, it goes away and returns with several others, hanging one from another like a chain, and thus they engineer an ambush; these beasts do not use a vague nod or signs through their shape, but, as he believes, their own proper dialect. The Scorpion bends itself in the manner of a bow, which is why Jerome calls a wound inflicted by it "arched" <note>original: "arcuatum"</note> in *Volume 3, Epistle 101, column 21.* And when a Scorpion stings, they say it lifts its tail, in which sense Lucilius says in Nonius:

->*Just as a mouse-trap is stretched, so the Scorpion stands with tail raised.*<-

The Scorpion brings death with the smallest strike and an imperceptible amount of material, unless its bite is prevented in time. No more effective means is found for treating this and drawing the poison from the wound than if a raw land-scorpion is crushed and applied to its own blow; or if it is eaten toasted, it will be a remedy for its own sting, as Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note> teaches in *Book 2, Chapter 13.* The Scorpion is a symbol of the Devil, to which Jerome alludes, saying:

<margin>
Epistle 23 to Marcella, column 199.
</margin>
> The serpent is condemned to the dust: the Scorpion envies your pious purpose, and with smooth speech about the truth, persuades you again to eat from the tree; let it be mocked and held as anathema as if for a sandal <note>Likely referring to treading upon the enemy</note>, and let it be said in its own biting wound (Erasmus wrongly reads "pure"): Get thee behind me, Satan.

The infernal Scorpion lays snares for us, in the likeness of the "crooked" <note>original Greek: "σκολιοῦ"</note> or terrestrial scorpion, about which Nicander sings in his *Theriaca* <note>A poem about venomous creatures</note>:

->*The unforeseen Scorpion, having lurked under a small crooked rock.*<-
->*The Scorpion stretched his snares beneath a small stone.*<-

For just as the Scorpion wounds the body with its sting to introduce poison through the wound, by which it kills the man: so also the Devil wounds the mind either with anger, pride, lust, or some other pleasure of the flesh, so that through this he may pour in the poison of his malice and kill the soul. Scorpions are innocent in appearance but deadly in the sting of the tail; smooth in the face, lethal in the tail: such are hypocrites, parasites, and all "false friends" <note>original Greek: "ψευδόφιλοι"</note>, about whom that passage of Ezekiel can be understood:
<margin>
Ezekiel 2, verse 6.
</margin>
*you dwell with scorpions* <note>original Hebrew: וְעִם-עַקְרַבִּים אַתָּה יוֹשֵׁב</note>. Pagninus <note>Santes Pagnino, an influential Hebraist</note> reads it as "with briers," that is, with crafty and harmful men, in which sense Basil explains it in *Homily 11 on the Hexameron* <note>A series of sermons on the six days of Creation</note>: *Why,* he says, *do you deny that hypocrisy is a beast? Whoever is composed for the crafting of calumny, and is of a sharp wit, should he not rightly seem to you a Scorpion?* And in truth, Scorpions are those who flatter with the head but wound with the tail and inflict a deadly wound: so those wicked men, composed of frauds, use flatteries and seem harmless, but behind their backs they carry that from which they pour poison: such were those of whom God said: *You dwell with scorpions.* Flee these like a plague and abstain from their company as much as you can; always keep with you, wherever in the world you may live, that saying of Sophocles in *The Captives*, which has become a proverb:

->*For in every stone a scorpion keeps watch.*<-

**SERPENT**, a general name for terrestrial creatures,

<column-break/>

encompassing many species under its embrace, such as the asp, viper, *water-snake, basilisk*, and *dragon*. The term "dragon-like" <note>original Greek: "δρακοντεινὰ"</note> animals at least denotes terrestrial snakes, because there are also aquatic snakes; hence the word *anguis* <note>snake</note> has a broader meaning than the word *serpens* <note>serpent</note>, as Vossius teaches in *Book 4, On Idolatry, Chapter 52*, against Blessed Franz, who writes that only aquatic ones are designated by the name *anguis*. The name of the serpent [*serpens*] comes from *serpo* [to creep], much like the Greek *herpo* <note>original: "ἕρπω"</note>; just as the name *anguis* comes not from *anguli* [corners] because it hides in caves (as some say), but from *ancho* <note>original Greek: "ἄγχω"</note>, meaning *I choke, I bind, I press*, since it is made with a constricted and pressed—or narrow—body: just as the words *narrow* [angustus], *corner* [angulus], and the disease *quinsy* [angina] descend from the same root. Or, if you prefer, seek its origin from *echis* <note>original Greek: "ἔχις"</note>, the male viper, with an 'N' inserted; as from *dakus* comes *densus*, from *bythos* comes *fundus*, and from *rhykane* comes *runcina*. In Greek it is *ophis* <note>original: "ὄφις"</note>, from the word *to see* <note>original Greek: "παρὰ τὸ ὀπτῶμαι"</note>, because it sees sharply and sleeps with eyes open. Others derive it from the Hebrew *ob* <note>Hebrew: אוב; often associated with mediumship or "spirit"</note>, which denotes a type of serpent, or from *tzapa* <note>Hebrew: צאפע; likely referring to a viper</note>, "python," which is a name for a Dragon. This word occurs in that divine prohibition against soothsayers; the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> rendered it as 
<margin>
Leviticus 20:27
</margin>
"ventriloquist" <note>original Greek: "ἐγγαστριμύθον"</note>. Arias and Pagninus translated it as "Python," the meaning of which, according to Aben Ezra, is one who brought forth oracles from a swollen belly, like a leather bottle. Or it comes from *to inquire* <note>original Greek: "πυνθάνεσθαι"</note>, because of the oracles which were sought from Pythons and Pythonesses; or from *to rot* <note>original Greek: "πύθεσθαι"</note>, which latter origin fits the story of Pythian Apollo. They tell a fable about him: that he killed the serpent Python (others say Typhon) with arrows not far from the Cephisus river, which flows at the foot of Mount Parnassus, as Dionysius writes in his book *On the Situation of the World*. And from that serpent, when it began *to rot* due to the sun's heat, Apollo was called "Pythian." In memory of this deed, the Pythian games were instituted by Pythian Apollo, which Ovid mentions in *Metamorphoses, Book 1*:

->*This the bow-bearing God—having never before*<-
->*used such weapons except against deer and fleeing goats—*<-
->*destroyed with a thousand arrows, his quiver nearly exhausted,*<-
->*while the venom poured out through the black wounds.*<-
->*And lest the passage of time should erase the fame of the work,*<-
->*he instituted sacred games with famous contests,*<-
->*called 'Pythian' from the name of the conquered serpent.*<-

But Ephorus describes this fable in another way: namely, that Apollo, after he came to earth, soon set out to the city of Panopea and slew the cruel and violent tyrant Tityus, and from the men of Parnassus, a man stained [with crime] named *Python*, surnamed *Dragon*, whom Apollo also dispatched with his arrows. And since during the fight it was shouted: *Io Paean* (that is, "Hail Apollo"), the custom prevailed again that in hymns of praise and songs of victory *Io Paean* should be shouted; hence he was called *Pythontios* by Orpheus. But leaving the fables to their fabled authors, among the Hebrews the general name for a Serpent is *Nachash* <note>original Hebrew: נחש</note>, which under different punctuation denotes "divination" <note>original Latin: "augurium"</note>; both owe their birth to the root *nachash*, meaning "he practiced divination" or "he conjectured." From this, "serpent-divination" <note>original Greek: "ὀφιομαντεία"</note> and the whole superstition of augury were born, which someone named *Ophion* is said to have discovered, as is clear from Apollonius, *Argonautica, Book 1, verse 303*, Nonnus in *Dionysiaca 12, verse 44*, and Claudian's *Rape of Proserpine, Book 3, verse 348*. From this, Aldrete in *Antiquities of Spain, Book 4* derives the name of the *Nasamones*, who were excellent diviners.

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

From this, the Devil is called **Ophioneus** <note>original: "Ophioneus," a name for a titan or demonic figure in Greek mythology</note>, the prince of the evil angels, and the author and inventor of all evil. *In more ancient literature*, says Coelius Rhodiginus <margin>Book 11, ch. 28, p. 29.</margin> *we have observed it handed down by Pherecydes that demons once fell from heaven (as our own doctrine contains), and were called Ophioneus, that is, the demonic serpent, who was the leader of the host falling away from the will of the Divine Mind.* Following this came <term>Ophiolatria</term> <note>serpent worship; from the Greek 'ophis' (serpent) and 'latreia' (worship)</note>. In the bosom of the Church long ago, the <term>Ophites</term> <note>a Gnostic sect that gave special importance to the serpent</note> or Ophiomorphs were born, who used to cultivate and adore that serpent through which Eve was first deceived <margin>Psellus, Ecclesiastical History, p. 328.</margin> as if he had been Christ. They attributed to it not only divine force and power, but even divine nature and essence. They attempted to teach that there was great power in the serpentine form from the fact that humans have intestines in their bellies coiled in the manner of serpents, and that Moses exalted the serpent in the desert, by the sight of which people were healed from other serpents. They even used to summon the same serpent whenever they were about to celebrate the mystic supper, and they did not believe the Eucharistic bread was complete until that summoned serpent had touched and tasted it. Behold a new fraud of the ancient serpent of Paradise established for his own honor and adoration! The Egyptians, among whom all <term>theriolatria</term> <note>the worship of animals</note> arose, offered divine worship to serpents, which Plutarch records *were strongly honored* <note>original Greek: "ἰσχυρῶς τιμᾶσθαι"</note> *History, book 12, and from him Aelian, On the Nature of Animals, book 17, ch. 5.* And at first, indeed, the serpent was commended to the nations as a symbol of the deity, and thus Maximus Tyrius writes in *Dissertation 38* that it was worshiped by the Indians. But while the worship was symbolic for the more prudent, it was literal for the simple and unrefined, and thus more pleasing and acceptable to that infernal serpent, because he saw his own instrument—which he first abused to deceive the first-formed humans—followed with such great veneration. In ancient times, the Prussians, Samogitians, and Lithuanians fell into this foul superstition of <term>Ophiolatria</term>, as witnessed by Erasmus Stella near the beginning of the first book *On the Antiquities of Prussia*; by Baron Sigismund von Herberstein in *Commentary on Moscovite Affairs*; and by Alexander Guagnini in *European Sarmatia concerning the Lithuanians*. Stephanus Zamofcius in *Analects of the Antiquities of Dacia* <margin>p. 45.</margin> whose full words we shall cite: *The snake was always held sacred by the Romans; and not only by the Romans, but also by the Greeks and Egyptians, for no other reason surely than that Satan, that ancient serpent, revealed himself to the nations chiefly in that image, lying that he was a savior to them. Thus today among the Samogitians, peoples of Sarmatia, serpents are said to be kept in houses as household gods.* Scaliger records the same of the Samogitians <margin>Exercise 183, section 2.</margin> *against Cardano*: *In Sarmatia*, he says, *there is a region either of the Ruthenians or very close to them, called Samogithia. In it are lizards larger than a foot and a half, thick and black, which the inhabitants worship as family gods. If anything unfavorable happens, they think the deity has been improperly worshiped, or received with worse or more meager feasts. Therefore they tend to it with more attentive care, by which they believe they will entreat for more prosperous circumstances.* The same Scaliger, in his *Commentary on book 2 of Aristotle’s History of Animals*, reports <margin>chapter 18, section 123.</margin>: *In the province of Calicut, there are serpents with a vast head, the size of a very large pig: they are worshiped as a deity by the King: therefore their power is greatest.* Thus that hellish horned serpent and

Therefore this is a promise, showing and exhibiting a remedy against the sin introduced by the Diabolical serpent. # SACRED HISTORY OF ANIMALS
### FROM PSALM 50, VERSES 10–11

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
ch. 51, p. 243.
</margin>

History teaches us, according to Fortunio Liceto <note>1577–1657, an Italian physician who wrote on the "spontaneous generation" of life</note> in the third book of his work *On the Spontaneous Origin of Living Things*, that those "fiery serpents" <note>original: שרפים (Seraphim), referring here to the venomous snakes in the desert</note> with which God punished the Jews on the borders of Edom were not unknown to the Pagans, but that they possessed a true knowledge of this history. His words are: *I believe that Agatharchides <note>a Greek historian and geographer</note> plainly read this sentiment in the sacred writings of Moses, the chronicler of the Most High God, and explained it. I am truly surprised that the most learned Vallesius <note>Francisco Vallés, a Spanish physician known as the "Divine Vallés"</note> did not observe or note this in his "Sacred Philosophy," as he discusses similar arguments there by design.* Augustine explains this mystically in his 12th Tractate on John, while asking: "What are the biting serpents?" and he responds: "They are the sins born from the mortality of the flesh. Who is the exalted serpent? It is the death of the Lord on the cross. For since death comes from a serpent, death was symbolized by the image of a serpent. The bite of the serpents is lethal; the death of the Lord is life-giving. The serpent is gazed upon so that the serpent may have no power. What does this mean? Death is gazed upon so that death may have no power." When the fiery serpents were killing the Children of Israel in the wilderness, at the Lord’s command, Moses erected a bronze serpent 
<margin>Num. 21:9.</margin> 
on a pole, and those who looked upon it *were delivered from the fiery serpents.* This is a remarkable thing reported about the bronze serpent: although it had been erected by God Himself through Moses, and a certain power and efficacy had been assigned to it for a time, and it was preserved for a time in memory of such a great benefit; yet, because of an encroaching abuse—where some worshiped it for its own sake, and others worshiped God in it, but through a self-chosen cult—it was destroyed by King Hezekiah <margin>2 Kings 18:4</margin> to stop the spreading superstition. Regarding this, Tertullian <note>an early Christian author from Carthage</note> says in his second book *Against Marcion*, p. 160: *The image of the bronze serpent, commanded of Moses by the Lord, did not belong to the category of idolatry, but was for the sake of healing those who were infested by serpents.* The "Type" <note>a prophetic symbol or foreshadowing</note> of this is well known from the words of Christ in John 3:15, a passage which 
<margin>Book 1, ch. 18, p. 179.</margin> 
Charlemagne <note>Charles the Great</note> refers to in his *Capitulary on Images*: *What that serpent signified—by the sight of which those wounded by serpents were healed—we have learned from the teaching of our Redeemer Himself, who said: "Just as Moses lifted up..." etc. When we look upon Him with a diligent mind and internal eyes, having overcome the deadly diseases of the temptations of evil spirits, we escape the dangers of eternal death.*

But to touch briefly on the species of serpents, it is known that in the Sacred Books twelve names and species are recounted, which are of the most difficult distinction and, due to the disagreement <note>original: διαφωνίαν (diaphōnian)</note> of interpreters, are of the highest uncertainty. Briefly regarding each: The **Viper**, called *Eph'eh* <note>original: אפעה</note> by the Hebrews in Isaiah 42:14, seems to be named from the cry it makes during birth. It can be categorized among the egg-layers because of Isaiah 59:5, where eggs are attributed to it, which it produces within the womb, from which little vipers are born and emerge. Although many testimonies of the Church Fathers support the idea that they emerge by bursting through the mother's belly, Johannes Brodaeus <note>Jean Brodeau, a 16th-century French critic</note> proves this is a fabrication in his *Miscellanies*. A passage difficult to explain is Psalm 91:13, where you will find four names joined together: *Upon the Shachal and the Pethen <note>original: שחל & פתן</note> you shall tread; you shall trample the Kephir and the Tannin <note>original: כפיר & תנין</note>.* Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart, author of a famous 17th-century study on biblical animals</note> proves these are names of serpents through many arguments, both from the conjunction itself and from the Greek translation of 
<margin>Ps. 140:4.</margin> 
the words "to walk and tread upon them," and from Job 4:10 and 38:39. Thus occurs the name of the serpent *Achshub* <note>original: עכשוב</note>, the **Asp** <note>original: πτύας (ptyas)</note>, which Bochart derives from the Arabic *Achasha*, meaning "to twist back," so that it is properly called an asp because it is twisted into a circle when it is angry and rises for a fight; from which also the name of a round shield 

<column-break/>

is "Aspis." **Zimmaon**, mentioned in Deuteronomy 8:15, is translated almost only by Jerome as "dipsas" <note>a snake whose bite was thought to cause unquenchable thirst</note>, though it properly denotes a dry place where there is no water. **Tzepha** <note>original: צפע</note>, a word read throughout Proverbs 23:32, Isaiah 11:8, 14:29, 59:5, and Jeremiah 8:17, is commonly explained as a **Basilisk** or **King-snake** <note>original: regulus</note>; the name appears to be fashioned from the sound of its hissing. Next is **Kippoz** <note>original: קפוז</note> in Isaiah 34:15, where Arias retains the Hebrew, Pagninus translates it as "hedgehog," but Bochart is entirely of the opinion that a serpent is meant, named for its "leaping" <note>the "arrow-snake"</note>, because it bites by leaping upward and launches itself like a dart. There remains the **Shephiphon** <note>original: שפיפון</note>, <margin>Gen. 49:17.</margin> since the others have been discussed elsewhere, which they explain as the **Cerastes** <note>the horned viper</note>; it has its name from "limping" because it crawls in a winding way and stumbles here and there. It does not differ much from the **haemorrhoid** <note>a species of snake</note>, from whose bite blood flows from every part of the body, concerning which Marcellus Virgilius's commentary on Dioscorides should be consulted.

**THE APE**, called *pithex* and *pithekos* <note>original: πίθηξ & πίθηκος</note> by the Greeks. They derive the Latin word *Simia* from *simos* <note>original: σιμός</note>, which denotes one who has a flat nose, or *simoprosopos* <note>original: σιμοπρόσωπος</note>, "one who has a bent-in nose." Others want *Simia* to be said as if it were *mimia* <note>from mimic</note>, which is why the later Greeks call it *mimo* <note>original: μιμὼ</note>, as is clear from Suidas. But the ape is called *mimo* because of its "mimicking" <note>original: παρὰ τὸ μιμεῖσθαι (para to mimeisthai)</note>, because among animals there is none that is accustomed to imitate everything so skillfully. Hence Ennius, cited by Beckmann, wrote:
> *The monkey, how similar to us, that most foul beast!*

For it is an animal exceedingly sagacious and docile, so much so that it even learns to play board games, which Pliny relates from Mucianus (who was three times Consul) in Book 8, ch. 54. In ancient times, they were even accustomed to be armed with a helmet and a small shield so that they might defend themselves from spears, to which Martial refers:
<margin>Book 14, dist. 202.</margin>
> *The clever monkey eluding the flung spears,*
And Juvenal in Satire 5, v. 154:
> *He who is covered with a shield and helmet, and fearing the whip,*
> *Learns to hurl a javelin from the back of a shaggy goat.*

They have a great physical analogy <note>original: ἀναλογίαν (analogian)</note> with the human body; hence, because they are so similar to humans, especially if you look at the feet and hands, they earned divine honor among the East Indians. This is attested by Balbi in his *Itinerary* (written in Italian) and by Maffei, who in the first book of his *Indian History* mentions a most beautiful temple consecrated to an ape. Thus Jan Huygen van Linschoten <note>1563–1611, a Dutch traveler and historian</note> narrates that when the Portuguese in the year 1554 captured the island of **Scylon** (commonly **Ceylon** or **Zeilan** <note>modern Sri Lanka</note>), in which the inhabitants point out the tomb of Adam, they were not content with having devastated it; they also proposed to plunder the temple on the peak of *Pico d'Adam* (or Adam's Peak). But they found nothing except a small chest distinguished by gold and gems, in which an **ape's tooth** was preserved. They carried this away, to the great grief of the local rulers. Ambassadors were sent by them who offered the Portuguese seven hundred thousand ducats for that tooth. The Portuguese were not averse to the sale, but they were dissuaded by their Bishop, Gaspar <note>Gaspar de Leão Pereira</note>, who said it was a wicked thing to foster the horrific idolatry of the Indians in this way. Consequently, he burned the tooth and threw the ashes into the waves of the sea.

Vossius <margin>Book 3, ch. 75, On the Gods of Idolatry.</margin> narrates the symbolic worship of apes among the Egyptians and Pithecusians <note>people of the "Ape Islands" near Naples</note> from Diodorus:
> *With good reason apes lived among the people, being considered gods among them, just as dogs are among the Egyptians. From the food prepared in the storerooms, the animals took their nourishment without hindrance whenever they wished.*

<sig>Iiii</sig>
<meta>catchword: whenever they wished (θέλοιτο).</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
## SACRED HISTORY OF ANIMALS

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>

In his work *On the History of Animals in Spain and Africa* (Book 3, p. 557), it is noted that the Devil is called **Ophioneus** <note>original: *Ophioneus*, a name derived from the Greek *ophis* for serpent</note>, the prince of evil angels and the author and inventor of all wickedness. We have observed, says Cœlius Rhodiginus <margin>Ancient Lessons, Book 28, p. 29.</margin>, that it was handed down by *Pherecydes* <note>An early Greek thinker from Syros, often cited regarding the soul and the cosmos</note> in the ancient records that demons once fell from heaven—a fact our own doctrine contains—and that their leader was named *Ophioneus*, that is, the *Demonic Serpent*, who was the standard-bearer of the host falling away from the will of the Divine Mind. From this followed *serpent-worship* <note>original: ὀφιολατρεία (*ophiolatreia*)</note>. In the bosom of the early Church, the *Ophites* (or *Opites* or *Ophiomorphs*) arose—sects who worshipped and adored that Serpent through whom Eve was first deceived, as if he had been Christ himself. <margin>Pappus, *History of the Church*, p. 328.</margin> They attributed to him not only divine force and power, but even a divine nature and essence. They attempted to prove the great power of the serpentine form by pointing out that humans have intestines in their bellies coiled in the manner of serpents, and that Moses "exalted" a serpent in the desert so that those who looked upon it were healed from the bites of other snakes. They even used to summon this same serpent whenever they were about to celebrate their mystical supper, and they did not believe the Eucharistic bread was complete until that summoned serpent had touched and tasted it. Behold, a new deception of the ancient Serpent of Paradise, instituted for his own honor and adoration! The Egyptians, among whom all forms of *animal-worship* <note>original: θηριολατρεία (*theriolatreia*)</note> arose, exhibited divine cults to serpents, which Plutarch (Book 12 of his *Histories*) and Ælian (Book 17 *On Animals*, ch. 5) report were *firmly honored* <note>original: ὀχυρῶς τιμᾶσθαι (*ochyrōs timasthai*)</note>. And indeed, the serpent was first commended to the nations as a symbol of divinity; thus Maximus Tyrius writes in his 38th *Dissertation* that it was worshipped by the Indians. But what was symbolic worship for the more prudent was taken literally by the simple and unrefined, and was all the more pleasing and acceptable to that infernal serpent, because he saw his own instrument—which he first misused to deceive the **First-formed Humans** <note>original: *Protoplastas*, referring to Adam and Eve</note>—being followed with such great veneration. According to Erasmus Stella, near the beginning of his first book on the *Antiquities of Prussia*, as well as Baron Sigismund von Herberstein in his *Commentaries on Muscovite Affairs* and Alexander Guagnini in his *European Sarmatia* regarding the Lithuanians, the Prussians, Samogitians, and Lithuanians once fell into this foul superstition of *serpent-worship*. <margin>p. 45.</margin> We shall cite the full words of Stephanus Zamoscius in his *Analects on the Antiquities of Dacia*: *"Among the Romans, the snake was always held sacred; and not only among the Romans, but also the Greeks and Egyptians, for no other reason than that Satan, that ancient serpent, manifested himself to the nations chiefly in that image, lying to them that he was their savior. Thus today among the Samogitians, a people of Sarmatia, serpents are kept in houses as tutelary household gods."* <margin>Exercise 183, section 2.</margin> Scaliger reports the same concerning the Samogitians in his work against Cardan: *"In Sarmatia,"* he says, *"there is a region either belonging to the Ruthenians or very close to them, called Samogithia. In it are lizards larger than a foot and a half, thick and black, which the inhabitants worship as family guardians. If anything unfavorable happens, they think the deity was not properly worshipped or was received with too meager a feast. Therefore, they care for it with more attentive labor, by which they believe they will entreat it for more fertile outcomes."* The same Scaliger, in his commentary on the second book of <margin>ch. 18, sect. 123.</margin> Aristotle’s *History of Animals*, reports: *"In the province of Calicut [India], there are serpents with vast heads, the size of a very large pig; they are worshipped as a deity by the King, and thus their power is considered greatest."* Thus that Stygian horned-serpent and masked snake uses hidden approaches, to use the words of Cyprian in *On the Unity of the Church* (col. 23): *"For such is always his cunning; such is the blind and lurking fallacy of circumventing man, with which from the very beginning he deceived us in our ignorance, and flattering with lying words, misled simple souls with incautious credulity."* Through the Serpent, the infernal Serpent poured the poison of his malice into the **First-formed Humans**, which he still exerts, and *the all-holy one in the marrow* <note>original: ἡ τῷ μυελίκτῳ παναγία (*hē tō myeliktō panagia*)</note> will remain until the final day. The deceiver Satan used the work of the Serpent, which is called **Nachash** <note>original: נחש (*Nachash*), the Hebrew word for serpent</note>—whether it had natural speech or walked upright on two feet, let others say; we have spoken on this elsewhere above on page 92—to deceive the First-formed. From this, the words of God are directed in different ways toward the natural serpent and the one that was not merely natural but possessed by a Demon. The first words indeed look to the natural *Serpent*, which are: <margin>v. 14.</margin> *"Because you have done this, you shall be cursed among all cattle and all the beasts of the field: upon your belly shall you go, and dust shall you eat all the days of your life."* The comparison with the other beasts of the field shows this, as does the punishment of walking on the belly and eating dust, which befit a natural serpent. God addresses it through a word of *malediction* <note>a curse</note>, which deprives it of some conceded good and inflicts punishment by the act itself. Yet this punishment is not to be sought primarily or ultimately in the natural serpent, but is directed toward another; for the Author of the deception himself ought to gather from the punishment of his instrument that he would not carry out his crime with impunity. Therefore, it follows by way of a prediction concerning a future thing: <margin>v. 15.</margin> *"I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. It shall crush your head, and you shall crush its heel."* This prediction, like the predicted event itself, cannot look to a serpent lacking reason, for it would be dealing with a matter common to other small beasts, which are also sometimes crushed by feet; indeed, it would deal with something that would never happen regarding larger serpents, where the opposite would rather occur. This is therefore a promise, showing and exhibiting the remedy against the sin introduced by the Diabolical serpent. Hence the serpent is a symbol of hatred and enmity, concerning which Artemidorus says in his second book of *The Interpretation of Dreams*: *a serpent brings enmity; just as it affects someone, so shall the enemy affect the one who saw it.* They speak of **Nachashim** <note>original: נחשים, plural of *Nachash*</note> as the serpents which God sent to punish the disobedient and murmuring Israelites in Numbers 21:6. The **Prester** <note>original: Πρηστὴρ (*Prēstēr*)</note> is a species of serpent, and indeed a most wicked one, which Pliny calls the *swelling-maker*. It is named from the word for "to burn" or "to inflame" <note>original: πρήθω (*prēthō*)</note> because of the fire of unquenchable thirst which it brings through its bite; it is the same as the *causus* <note>a burning fever</note> and the *dipsas* <note>a serpent whose bite causes intense thirst</note> for the same reason, which Dioscorides discusses in Book 7, ch. 14. Hence in the books of Moses they are called **Seraphim** <note>original: שרפים (*Seraphim*)</note>, meaning *fiery ones*, from burning and inflaming; for **Saraph** <note>original: שרף</note> means to burn, to kindle, or to consume. They are called such not because they were made of fire, but because by their poisonous bite and breath they inflamed and killed the Israelites. It seems that God raised up those *Presters* or *causonas* in the deserts of Arabia through the ministry of Angels, so that He might punish the Israelites with a just penalty equal to their sin; hence Tremellius translates the word *Saraph* as *Prester*. Ælian (Book 17 *On the Nature of Animals*, ch. 14) narrates how horrendous the death is for those struck by a *prester*, and Lucan shows the same in Book 9. Furthermore, from Plutarch and Agatharchides he teaches...

### FROM PSALM 50, VERSES 10, 11.

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
History teaches, as Fortunatus Licetus writes in Book 3 of *On the Spontaneous Origin of Living Things*, that those serpents <term>swarming creatures</term> <note>Hebrew: *sheratzim*</note> with which God punished the Jews on the borders of Edom were not unknown to the Pagans, but that they had a true knowledge of this history. <margin>G. st. p. 243.</margin> His words are: *“I believe Agatharchides clearly read this opinion in the sacred writings of Moses, the chronicler of the Most High God, and explained it.”* I truly wonder that the most learned Vallés, who treats similar arguments there by design, did not observe or note this in his *Sacred Philosophy*. Augustine explains this mystically in his 12th Tractate on John, while he asks: what are the biting serpents? And he answers:
> Sins arising from the mortality of the flesh. Who is the exalted serpent? The death of the Lord on the cross. For since death came from a serpent, death was figured by the image of a serpent. The death of serpents is lethal; the death of the Lord is life-giving. The serpent is gazed upon so that the serpent may have no power. What is this? Death is gazed upon so that death may have no power.

When the fiery serpents were killing the children of Israel in the desert, <margin>Numbers 21:9.</margin> at the Lord's command, Moses set up a bronze serpent on a pole, by looking at which *they were delivered from the fiery serpents.* This is a remarkable thing reported concerning the bronze serpent: although it had been erected by God Himself through Moses, and had been assigned a certain power and efficacy for a time, and was preserved for a time in memory of such a great benefit; nevertheless, because of an encroaching abuse—since it was being worshipped by some for its own sake, and by others as God within it, but with a self-chosen cult—it was destroyed by King Hezekiah. <margin>2 Kings 18:4.</margin> He did this to check the spreading superstition; hence Tertullian says in his 2nd book *Against Marcion*, p. 160:
> The image of the bronze serpent, commanded to Moses by the Lord, did not pertain to the title of idolatry, but was for the healing of those who were infested by serpents.

The type of this fate is known from the words of Christ in John 3:15, a passage to which <margin>Book 1, chapter 18, p. 179.</margin> Charlemagne refers in his *Capitulary on Images*: *What that serpent was, by the inspection of which those wounded by serpents were healed, we have learned from our Redeemer himself teaching us, who said: "As Moses lifted up," etc. For while we look upon Him with a diligent mind and inner eyes, we overcome the deadly diseases of the temptations of evil spirits and avoid the dangers of eternal death.*

But to touch briefly upon the species of the Serpent, it is well known that twelve names and species are recounted in the Sacred Books <note>original: *Pandectis*, here referring to the Bible</note>, which are of the most difficult distinction and, because of the <term>dissonance</term> <note>Greek: διαφωνίαν (*diaphonian*)</note> of interpreters, of the greatest uncertainty. Let us look briefly at each. The Viper, called by the Hebrews the <term>hissing one</term> <note>Hebrew: *eph’eh* <term>אפעה</term></note> in Isaiah 42:14, seems to be named from its cry during birth. It can be categorized among the egg-layers because of Isaiah 59:5, where eggs are attributed to it, which it brings forth within the womb, from which little vipers are born and emerge. Although the testimony of the Church Fathers is crowded with claims that the mother's belly is eaten away during their birth, Johannes Brodaeus proves this to be a fiction in his *Miscellanies* (Book 3, 28). The passage in Psalm 91:13 is difficult to explain, where you will find four terms joined together: *You will tread upon the* <term>lion</term> <note>Hebrew: *shachal* <term>שחל</term></note> *and the* <term>adder</term> <note>Hebrew: *pethen* <term>פתן</term></note>; *you will trample the* <term>young lion</term> <note>Hebrew: *kephir* <term>כפיר</term></note> *and the* <term>serpent</term> <note>Hebrew: *tannin* <term>תנין</term></note>. Bochart proves with many arguments that these are the names of serpents, both from the conjunction itself and from <margin>P. 1/140 4.</margin> the words *“to walk and tread upon these,”* as well as from the Septuagint translation of Job 4:10 and 38:39. Thus *the name for serpents <term>nachash</term> <note>Hebrew: <term>נחש</term></note> occurs; the asp, or <term>python</term>, a word which Bochart derives from the Arabic *Achafa*, meaning *to twist back* <note>original: *retorquere*</note>, so that the asp is properly said to be twisted back in a circle when it is angry and rises for a fight; hence the name of a round shield is also

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
*aspis*. *Zimmaon*, mentioned in Deuteronomy 8:15, is translated almost by Jerome alone as the *dipsas* <note>A serpent whose bite was thought to cause intense thirst</note>, though it properly denotes an arid place in which there are no waters. <term>Tzepha</term> <note>Hebrew: <term>צפע</term></note>, a word read here and there in Proverbs 23:32, Isaiah 11:8, 14:29, 59:5, and Jeremiah 8:17, is commonly explained as the *regulus* or *basilisk*; the name appears to be fashioned from its very sound. Then there is <term>Tzephioni</term> <note>Hebrew: <term>צפעוני</term></note> in Isaiah 34:15, where Arias retains the Hebrew, and Pagninus translates it as *hedgehog*, but Bochart is altogether of the opinion that a serpent is understood, named from jumping, because it bites by leaping upward and launches itself like a javelin. There remains the <term>Shephiphon</term> <note>Hebrew: <term>שפיפון</term></note> <margin>Genesis 49:17.</margin>, since the others have been dealt with elsewhere; they explain this as the *cerastes* <note>The horned viper</note>. It has its name from limping, because it creeps in a winding manner and staggers here and there; it does not differ much from the *haemorrhois*, from whose bite blood flows from everywhere, concerning which Marcellus Virgilius should be consulted in his commentary on Dioscorides.

The MONKEY is called <term>pithex</term> and <term>pithekos</term> <note>Greek: <term>πίθηξ</term> & <term>πίθηκος</term></note> by the Greeks. They derive the Latin word *simia* from <term>simos</term> <note>Greek: <term>σιμός</term></note>, which denotes one who has a flat nose, <term>snub-nosed</term> <note>Greek: <term>σιμοπρόσωπος</term></note>, *one who has an inward-curving nose*. Others want the monkey to be named as if it were a *mima* <note>a mime or imitator</note>, whence among more recent Greeks it is called <term>mimo</term> <note>Greek: <term>μίμω</term></note>, as is clear from Suidas. But it is called <term>mimo</term> <term>because of its imitating</term> <note>Greek: <term>παρὰ τὸ μιμεῖσθαι</term></note>, because among living creatures there is none that is accustomed to imitate everything so ingeniously; whence Ennius, as cited by Becmann, says:
> The monkey, how similar that most shameful beast is to us.
For it is an animal very sagacious and docile, so much so that it even learns to play at draughts <note>original: *latrunculis*, an ancient strategy game</note>, which Pliny relates from Mucianus, thrice Consul, in Book 8, chapter 54. They were also formerly accustomed to be armed with a helmet and a small shield <note>original: *parma*</note>, so that they might defend themselves from spears, to which Martialis refers: <margin>Book 14, distich 202.</margin>
> (The clever monkey eluding the flung spears,)
> And Juvenal in Satire 5, line 154:
> He who is covered by a shield and helmet, and fearing the whip,
> Learns to hurl a javelin from a shaggy goat.

They have a great <term>analogy</term> <note>Greek: <term>ἀναλογίαν</term></note> with the human body; hence, since they are so similar to man—especially if you look at the feet and hands—they earned divine honor among the East Indians, as witnessed by Balbi in his *Itinerary*, which he wrote in Italian, and by Maffei, who in the first book of his *Indian History* commemorates a most beautiful temple consecrated to a monkey. Thus Jan Huygen van Linschoten relates that when the Portuguese captured the island of *Scylon* (commonly *Ceylon* or *Zeilan*) in the year 1554—in which the inhabitants point out the tomb of Adam—they were not content with having devastated it, but also proposed to despoil the temple on the summit of *Pico d' Adam*, or Adam’s Peak. However, they found nothing except a small chest distinguished with gold and gems, in which *the tooth of a monkey was preserved*. This, therefore, they carried away, to the great grief of the local rulers. Ambassadors were sent by them to offer the Portuguese seven hundred thousand ducats for the tooth. The Portuguese were not averse to the sale, but they were dissuaded from it by their Bishop, Gaspar, who said it was a wicked thing to encourage the horrendous idolatry of the Indians in this way; and for that reason, he burned that tooth and cast the ashes into the waves of the sea. Vossius, citing Diodorus, relates the symbolic worship of monkeys among the Egyptians and the inhabitants of the Pithecusae Islands: <margin>Book 3, chapter 75, *On Idolatry*.</margin>
> Those [monkeys] from the seventy-four, being considered gods among them—just as dogs are among the Egyptians—received their food without hindrance from the prepared supplies in the storehouses whenever they wished. <note>original Greek: Τὰς ἐξ ἑβδομήκοντα καὶ τεττάρων τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, Θεοὶ παρ' αὐτοῖς νομιζόμενοι, καθάπερ παρ' Αἰγυπτίοις οἱ κύνες, ἔκ τε τῶν παρεσκευασμένων ἐν τοῖς ταμιείοις τὰ ζῶα τὰς τροφὰς ἐλάμβανον ἀκωλύτως, ὁπότε βέλοιτο.</note>

### SACRED BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> ...whatever it might wish. Parents even name their children after these animals, and most especially after monkeys, just as among us names are taken from the gods. For those who kill this animal, considering it the greatest of impieties, a prudent death penalty was established. Because of this, among some people, a saying took hold as a proverb used for those who are overly arrogant: *that they have drunk the blood of a monkey.* <note>The Greek text here reflects the same sentiment: "They have been given monkey's blood to drink."</note> Monkeys frequent the same houses as humans; they are held as gods among them, just as dogs were among the Egyptians. These beasts take prepared food from the larders whenever they please, with no one stopping them. Parents bestow names on their children derived mostly from monkeys, just as we do from the names of gods. Those who kill this animal are punished with the death penalty as being guilty of wicked impiety. Therefore, a proverb has taken the place of common speech among some, which is said against those who carry themselves magnificently: *You have drunk the blood of a monkey.* In European regions, they are not seen unless brought from abroad; likewise in Palestine, the animal was unknown before the time of Solomon, who took care to have them brought along with other merchandise from Ophir <note>A legendary port or region mentioned in the Bible, famous for its wealth and gold.</note>, according to 1 Kings 10:22 and 2 Chronicles 9:21, where they are called *Koph* <note>Hebrew: קוף</note>, likely from a root meaning "to go around." Symbolically, the monkey signifies flatterers, hypocrites, and finally the Devil himself, who is always accustomed to being "God's Ape" <note>A common medieval and early modern concept where the Devil tries to imitate or mock God's works.</note>; compare Wolfgang Franz, *Sacred History of Animals*, chapter 24, page 266.

**THE SPOTTED LIZARD (STELLIO)**, <note>original: "Stellio," a term often used for a gecko or a star-spotted lizard.</note> or *askalabotes* in Greek, is similar to a lizard; hence Luther, Munster, and Schindler simply interpret it as "lizard" in Leviticus 11:30, translating the Hebrew word *Anakah* <note>Hebrew: ענקה</note>. In Hebrew, it is also called *Leta’ah* <note>Hebrew: לטאה</note>, written with a capital letter *Lamed* in that passage to denote that one must be extremely careful, because it infects everything by touch alone. Bochartus teaches that the *Leta’ah* is similar to the *Stellio*, which clings fixedly to the ground; like the "alauda" <note>lark</note> according to Damiri—that is, like a spider while it hunts flies. It is not frightened by noise until it is crushed; and whatever it treads upon, it infects with poison. Among the Arabs, it is called *Wachara*, appearing to be a species of Salamander, whose malice is the greatest among all venomous things, as Pliny says in Book 29, chapter 4, and Book 10, chapter 67: it infects everything by touch alone. This passage is quite controversial due to the disagreement among interpreters; for in Proverbs 30:28, where the Hebrew reads *Semamit* <note>Hebrew: שׁממית</note>, the Greeks and Jerome translate it as *kalabotes* or *stellio*, a view which Bochartus supports with many arguments. Meanwhile, it must be admitted that the "Naming" here is stained with such obscure ink that it can hardly be discerned. We will search the word to see if any similarity appears that might represent it, even if it does not express it vividly. The Hebrew word, somewhat changed, came to the Greeks of a later age; for <margin>2. Observation 36.</margin> Pierre Belon, who brings forth many hidden things for us, reported a certain kind of lizard creeping on walls and catching flies, called *Samiamiton* in the common tongue of the Greeks. The Glosses say: *Askalabotes*, that is, a *samiamithi*. No doubt the word was brought into Greek from our Hebrew *Semamit*, which the Greek interpreters render as *kalabotes*; this, however, was made by dropping the first syllable from *askalabotes*, just as *skeleien* becomes *askaleien*, because *kalabotes* sometimes occurs when words are not preserved in their entirety. The language is wealthy and rich, but varied for show, without a clear middle or beginning, nor is it consistent like Hebrew; its form is not constant, so that one may see with admiration the play and variegated patterns of its forms. Hesychius says: *Kalabas, kalabotes...* <margin>column 386</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> ...a certain fish and a lizard. The Etymologist says: *Askalabotes*, a small creature like a lizard, crawling up the walls of houses. Hesychius also writes *kolotes*: *Kolotes, askalabotes. They also called it galeotes.* It seems to be very skillful at catching flies. Therefore *kolotes*, *galeotes*, and *askalabotes* are one and the same. <margin>column 154, column 458.</margin> What they add about the hunting of flies they attribute to this reptile, which lives in the cracks of houses and catches flies around the walls, and not only those, but also spiders. It was called *Stellio* by the Latins from the drops and spots with which it is colored as if "starred" (*stellatus*), for the spots depicted on its back shine; it is as if it were called *asterion* <note>star-like</note>. If you consult the interpreters, there are those who translate it as "spider." The Vulgate says: *The spider takes hold with its hands.* Osiander corrects this: *The spotted lizard relies on its hands.* Pagninus: *The spider grasps with its hands.* Luther: *The spider works with its hands.*

**THE PIG (SUS)**, in Greek *hys* or *sys*, whose origin Varro derives in Book 2 of *On Agriculture*, chapter 4, from *thuein*, "to sacrifice." He says: *The pig is called 'hys' in Greek, formerly 'thys', from that word which is 'thuein', meaning to sacrifice; for the first beginning of sacrificing seems to have been taken from that kind of livestock,* etc. To the Hebrews it is *Chazir* <note>Hebrew: חזיר</note>, from a root meaning "to return," appearing to be so named from "returning to filth," whence comes that saying: *The washed sow returns to wallowing in the mire*, 2 Peter 2:22. The Jews hated the pig, and other nations agreed with the Jews, yet it was a delicacy among the rest. It is established by the authority of Horace that the pig was sacrificed to the Genius, the Birth-god, and the Household God (Lar), when he says:

<margin>3rd book of Odes, Ode 17.</margin>
> — tomorrow you will tend your Genius with pure wine,
> And with a two-month-old pig,
> Together with your servants released from their labors.

And in Plautus’s *Pseudolus*, Scene "Go out," line 32: *For today is my birthday: it is fitting for you all to celebrate it. Make sure the ham, the neck-meat, the kernels, and the sow’s udder lie in the water.* Compare the same author in *Menaechmi 22*. This animal was sacred to the Cretans, but whether it was worshipped by them as divine is not sufficiently clear from Athenaeus, who in Book 9 says: *Everyone considers this animal worthy of the highest veneration.* The pig is an animal so hated by the Jews that they recoil from its usual name and call it "another thing" <note>Hebrew: "Davar Acher," a common Rabbinic euphemism to avoid saying the word for pig.</note>. <margin>Leviticus 11:7.</margin> By divine decree, the Jews abstained from the flesh of the pig, for the pig was held among the "unclean" animals, and thus it was neither for sacrifice (*thysimon*) nor for eating (*edodimon*). The Gentiles knew of the Jews' abstinence but did not know the cause, though they thought they did. Porphyry, in Book 1 of *On Abstinence*, thinks the cause of the abstinence is that pigs are not born in Judea: *For the pig is useful for nothing else than food. The Phoenicians and Jews abstained because it did not grow in those places at all.* <margin>Matthew 8:31.</margin> But this is an error, which the region of the Gadarenes refutes, in which there was a great herd of swine. Callistratus, in Plutarch’s *Table Talk* (Book 4, Question 5), is foolishly mistaken, thinking they did it out of honor, so that they might venerate the pig as the master of sowing and plowing; the Poet seems to refer to this veneration:

->The Jew may even adore the pig-god.<-

Tacitus asserts that the Jews avoided pig flesh out of fear of scabies, leprosy, or skin disease: <margin>Histories, Book 5.</margin> *They abstain from the pig in memory of a plague, because scabies once troubled them, to which that animal is prone.* We dealt with this more fully above on page 138. Plutarch, in *On Isis and Osiris*, writes that the bodies of those who drink pig's milk are infested with leprosy and scabby roughness: and the...

# SACRED BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

### FROM PSALM 55:10, 11

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...that the milk of pigs causes leprosy to break out on the body, as well as itchy roughness <note>original Greek: ὅ τι γάλα πιδίων ἐξανθεῖ τὰ σώματα λέπραν, καὶ ψωρικὰς τραχύτητας</note>. Thus Aelian writes in book 10, *On Animals*, chapter 16, following the opinion of Manetho: *I have heard that Manetho the Egyptian, a man who had reached the summit of wisdom, said that anyone who tasted pig's milk would be filled with white spots and leprosy.* <note>The author uses classical sources to explain the ancient health concerns regarding pork in the Near East.</note> On the other hand, physicians generally recommend the flesh of the pig because it generates the best blood, as Psellus testifies in book 2, *On the Method of Diet*, page 33; and Galen, along with other physicians, teaches that from it the greatest amount of blood and strong nourishment is added to human limbs. Vossius, in book 3 of *Idolatry*, chapter 66, page 1081, brings forward three reasons which we wish to insert into our little field of study: *As to why the pig was prohibited to the Jews,* there were primarily three reasons: *THE FIRST IS*, that this animal does not even abstain from human flesh, for which reason Aelian judges in book 10 of *On Animals*, chapter 16, that the Egyptians also abstain from it. But it is even more likely that God looked to this because in Genesis 9:4 He similarly forbade the eating of blood and strangled meat, the better to deter men from the shedding of blood. *THE SECOND* reason is that this animal delights in wallowing in the mire. Wherefore God wished to frighten men away from the mire and wallowing-place of sins. These two causes pertain to morals. *THE THIRD* pertains to nature: because in Judea, as in certain other lands of the East and likewise in Egypt, its pork would induce leprosy and skin blotches <term>vitiligines: a skin condition characterized by pale patches</term>; as is found in Plutarch’s *Symposiacs*, book 4, question 5. And the same thing, I believe, moved the Egyptians to abstain from it. Indeed, it has been reported by Manetho the Egyptian that pig's milk produces the same effect. You may also read in Herodotus's *Melpomene* that the Egyptians loathe the pig, besides those already mentioned. And these things show that the Jews abstained from the pig not out of veneration, but out of abomination. However, the Egyptians also turned away from its use for the sake of worship. Specifically, because the pig, by digging the ground with its snout, covers the seeds committed to the earth so that they are not devoured by birds. Besides the Jews and Egyptians, the Gallo-Greeks living in Pessinus loathed pork, according to Pausanias in his *Achaica*, as did the Scenite Arabs, as found in Solinus, chapter 46. Even today the Muhammadans abstain, as is clear from the Quran 33 and 34. In this, however, the Persians differ from the Turks. But neither do the Chinese—who are commonly, though poorly, called *Chinenses*—eat it, as is clear from Pereira and others who have recorded Chinese affairs; finally, the same is reported of the Tartars. And some of these, I believe, did so in imitation of the Israelites; others, however, because of the animal's uncleanness or to flee from leprosy. Thus says Vossius.

In the Sacred Scripture, no other reason or cause for the uncleanness of the pig is shown to us than this:
<margin>Leviticus 11:7.</margin>
> The pig also you shall not eat, because it divides the hoof and makes a split in the hoof, but it does not chew the cud, and it shall be unclean to you.

The Fathers <note>The "Fathers" refers to the early influential theologians of the Christian Church.</note> explain this mystically for those who are well-versed in the theory of Christianity, but when it comes to practice, nothing of "Christianity," so to speak, can be found among them. Whence Hesychius says: *He is said to eat the pig who has knowledge of divine things but does not use it well, and pollutes it with incongruous actions, and gives himself over to an unclean life. The pig is a filthy animal, it is greedy, it is shameless; wherefore the Jews were warned to be enemies of greediness and gluttony. By forbidding the pig, He forbids a life which belongs to profiteers and gluttons.* Tertullian, in his *Letter on the Foods of the Jews*, writes: *When He forbids the pig to be taken as food,*

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred History.</margin>
*He certainly rebukes a life that is muddy and filthy, and one that delights in the squalor of living things, placing its good not in the nobility of the soul but in the flesh alone.* Isaiah, in chapters 65:4 and 66:3, 17, complains about the Jews of his time, and among other things, he rebukes their sacrifices and compares them to the eating of pig's flesh and mice, the eating of which was expressly forbidden to the Jews. Jerome explains the words of Isaiah as referring to hypocrites and their works, who offered sacrifices to God without true faith in the promised Messiah, and who wished to cleanse their internal uncleanness with external purifications. His words are: *By these foods in this place, I think are to be understood those sacred rites by which hypocrites promised themselves the grace of God and eternal salvation: for just as the eating of flesh and mice is abominable to the Jews, etc., so abominable before God are the sacred rites which they thrust upon Him for the expiation of sins: and just as the Jew detests the eating of unclean animals, so God detests the sacrifices which impious hypocrites offer to attain eternal life by their own merits.* Great and clearly heroic was the faith of the pious confessors in their loathing of pig's flesh.
<margin>2 Maccabees 6 & 7.</margin>
The Jew Eleazar, a man venerable in age and piety, preferred to meet death rather than eat pig's flesh according to the edict of King Antiochus Epiphanes, so that he might give an illustrious proof of his confession—that he loved and professed that true doctrine handed down to the people of Israel by God—and so that by his example he might invite more Jews to the same constancy by this confession of his; for he knew that this was being done by the King so that an example of defection from the whole law might be shown. Such a mystical abstinence from the eating of pig's flesh is to be hoped for among Christians, who are indeed free from the ceremonial law if you look at the literal sense, but not from the mystical sense; yet, like the prodigal son, they nourish pigs and feed themselves with the same husks. *He is said to pasture pigs*, says Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquent preaching.</note>, *who nurtures filthy and unclean thoughts in his soul: and to eat the food of an irrational and wicked lifestyle, sweet indeed to one lacking in good things, because every work of fleshly pleasure seems sweet to the perverse, which is the seduction of desire and the corruption of life, which not only provides no strength and fortitude to the soul, but completely unnerves and oppresses it. He designates these kinds of pig-like and evilly sweet foods, which are the allurements of carnal delights, by the name of husks.* Compare Ambrose on Luke and Augustine in book 2 of *Evangelical Questions*, chapter 33, who understands by "the citizen" <note>Referring to the citizen of the far country in the parable of the Prodigal Son.</note> the Devil, the prince, 
<margin>Volume 2, Homily 24.</margin>
<margin>Luke 15:15.</margin> 
and by the "pigs" the remaining demons of an inferior grade. *One of the citizens of that region,* he says, *is some prince of the air belonging to the devil's army: his villa is the measure of his power: the unclean pigs are the spirits who are under him: the husks with which he fed the pigs are secular doctrines, ringing with sterile vanity, from which the praises of idols and of fables belonging to the gods of the gentiles resounded in various speech and songs, in which the demons delight.* Hugo Cardinalis, in Luke 15, recounts three types of pigs that are seen in the external assembly of the Church. First, *domestic pigs*, and these are public fornicators. Second, *wild pigs* or boars, who hide in the forest by day and come out at night; these are fornicating priests and hypocrites, who...
