# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...they hide in the day, but at night they do things that are not fitting, according to *Job 3 and Ephesians 5*. Thirdly, they are like porcupines, and these are the *Sodomites*, who shoot out the arrows of detraction sideways from themselves against the pursuing dogs—that is, the preachers.

**TACHAS.** A Hebrew word <term>תחש</term> <note>Tachash</note>, in the unearthing of which we have need of an Oedipus <note>A legendary riddle-solver</note>, or the sword of Alexander, to cut this knot among so many conflicting opinions of interpreters. It is mentioned in *Exodus 25:5, 26:14, 36:18, and 39:34, and Numbers 4:6-25* quite frequently. Most want <term>תחש</term> to be *badgers or martens*, in German *Dachse*. Hence Vatablus translates it as skins of martens and Pagninus as badgers, and Luther as *badger-skins* <note>original German: Dachsfelle</note>; with which the top covering of things we want to keep safe from rain is usually covered. Some of the Rabbis judge that this kind of animal was only known in the time of Moses: a clean, one-horned animal <note>original Greek: τῶ ὦτα</note>, multi-colored, and unknown today. Because of this, some leave the Hebrew word as it is and write *tassorum*, which is written in Hebrew as <term>thechasim</term>. The Chaldean Paraphrast <note>An ancient Aramaic translation</note> translates it as *Salgona*, that is, one rejoicing and delighting in its many colors. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translates it as *violet-colored skins* <note>original Greek: δέματα ἰανθίνα</note>; the Old Latin Interpreter as *violet*, or *purplish*, or *hyacinthine*. *Violet-brown skins* <note>original German: Violbraune Felle</note>. Hence Luther in *Ezekiel 16:10* translates it as *fine shoes* <note>original German: Gemische Schuhe</note>. Bochart <note>A famous 17th-century scholar of biblical animals</note> thinks it is not the name of an animal, but of a color, whether natural or produced by art.

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
**TALPA** <note>The Mole</note>, is a little animal that flees the light, which has no strength at all either to inflict violence or to avoid injury. Its only life is to hide in caves, whereby it represents the earthly man, who cannot endure the rays of divine light, according to Ezlerus in his *Introduction to the Signatures of Things, page 33*. Furthermore, it represents the deceptive man and the enemy of truth, who cannot bear the sun or the truth, but always lurks under the earth or in the dark. For just as darkness is scattered by the Sun, so is a lie put to flight by the truth. They maintain it is deprived of sight, to which Virgil refers in his *first book of the Georgics*:

> Or blind moles dig out their chambers with their eyes.

<margin>Commentary on Job 3, number 69, page 729.</margin>
But Fromondus <note>Libert Froidmont, a scientist and theologian</note> returns eyes to the mole, explaining Aristotle and Pliny. And so it is: as appears in a dissection after the skin is pulled back, there is a certain small orb of the eyes; compare *Aristotle’s History of Animals, book 1, chapter 9 and book 4, chapter 8*. Indeed, they see as much as is sufficient for them; for as Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner, a famous Renaissance naturalist</note> reports, they stand out from the skin like black points, the size of a millet or poppy seed, attached to a nerve. Hence, it is not deprived of the organ of sight by its nature, but by circumstance, because it always dwells under the earth. And what it lacks in sharpness of sight, Mother Nature has compensated twofold in the excellence of its hearing. In Greek it is called <term>σπάλαξ</term> <note>spalax</note>, from digging and hoeing, for <term>σκάλλω</term> <note>skallo</note> means "I dig." Hesychius says: *The digger, the mole, the earth-digger, the blind one.* And Aristophanes in *The Acharnians* joins together *moles, urchins, and cats*. To the French it is *Foyon* from *digging*. To us, from *throwing* <note>original German: werffen</note>, because it casts out the earth with its mouth: *Maulwurf* <note>The German word for mole</note>. Among the Hebrews it is called <term>חפר</term> <note>chaphar</note>, he dug, by a doubling of the second and third radical letters. it occurs in *Isaiah 2:20* <term>לחפר פירות</term> <note>to the digging of fruits/moles</note>. Kimchi <note>A famous medieval Jewish scholar</note> wants there to be two words, which according to some explanations signify a certain species <term>חפר פירות</term>, a bird that bores through fruit, or some other genus of insect, or something that digs pits or small trenches in the earth. Jarchi <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator</note> prefers it to be a single word

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
which he interprets as <term>תלפ</term> <note>talp</note>, moles, in which he follows the Chaldean Paraphrast. Aben-Ezra <note>A prominent medieval Spanish-Jewish scholar</note> takes up the office of the Masoretes <note>Scholars who preserved the Hebrew biblical text</note> when he judges that <term>ל חפר פירות</term> should be read as one word, so that there is a single term to signify moles. Several words occur written separately in the Biblical text which the diligence of the Masoretes, through their *keri* <note>marginal corrections to the text</note>, noted should be joined together; the curious critic Ludovicus Cappellus collected examples of these. But here the Masora noted nothing, so that the opinion or conjecture of Aben-Ezra might be seen as a certain irregularity by the Jews, for whom it is a matter of religion not to depart a hair's breadth from their Codices. The Vulgate translates it: *that they might worship moles and bats*. Hence B. Friedlieb asks: *How did the Israelites worship moles and bats?* and he answers: after the example of the Egyptians, who held even the vilest animals as Gods, according to Augustine in *The City of God, book 14, chapters 18 and 20*. But Vossius, in *On Idolatry, book 3, chapter 58, page 1041*, attributes at least this to the Egyptians: that they held the mole, due to its lack of eyes, as a symbol of a blind man.

**TEREDO** <note>The Woodworm</note>, in Greek <term>τερηδών</term> <note>teredon</note>, which is also <term>σκώληξ</term> <note>skolex, a worm</note>, hence Hesychius: *The teredo is a worm in wood.* And Suidas: *A wood-eating worm living in wood.* To the Latins it seems to be named from *rubbing* <note>original Latin: terendo</note>. To the Hebrews <term>רקב</term> <note>rakab</note>, which means *it rotted* or *it was putrid*, because the woodworm hollows out and destroys trees. And since in *Hosea 5:12* the woodworm and the moth are joined together and read as producing one effect, it is fitting to treat the moth here as well:

**TINEA** <note>The Moth</note>, in Greek <term>σὴς</term> <note>ses</note>, is a little worm that eats away at clothes, papers, and books; it is named from "holding" <note>original Latin: tenendo</note>, as Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, an early medieval encyclopedist</note> suggests, because it clings firmly to clothes and papers and lays them waste. Among the Hebrews it has a double naming: for it is called <term>סס</term> <note>sas</note>, from which the Greek *ses* comes, and <term>עש</term> <note>ash</note>, so called from "devouring," as Buxtorf notes in his Lexicon. Besides *ses*, they have the synonyms <term>βρῶσις</term> and <term>βρῶμα</term> <note>eating/food</note>, from which clothes consumed by moths are called *moth-eaten* <note>original Greek: σητόβρωτα</note>. Not only do clothes in chests experience these robbers and enemies, according to Horace:

<margin>Satires, book 3, line 11.</margin>
> ...for whom a coverlet
> rots in the chest, a feast for beetles and moths.

but even the *storehouses* <note>original Greek: ταμιεῖα</note> of books cannot be so tightly closed and guarded that moths do not enter and gnaw the books; hence Martial says:

<margin>Book 6, Epigram 60.</margin>
> *How many eloquent men will feed the moths and beetles.*

And in book 14, epigram 37:

> *Unless you give me books that are bound tight,*
> *I shall let in the moths and the cruel beetles.*

Hosea, in chapter 5:12, depicts the total devastation and *utter destruction* <note>original Greek: πανωλεθρίαν</note> of the Israelite kingdom using a double subject of comparison, and predicts the consumption and overthrow of both kingdoms, that of Judah and that of Israel: *And I will be like a moth to Ephraim, and like rot (a woodworm) to the house of Judah.* The Septuagint, as they usually do in various places, depart from the Hebrew text, reading: *And I am as trouble to Ephraim, and as a sting to the house of Judah*, whom the Vulgate imitates in its custom: *I am like a disturbance to Ephraim, and like a thorn to the house of Judah.* Tremellius thinks the Septuagint read <term>כעס</term> <note>indignation</note> (which in *Job 5:2* is also written with a "shin" at the end) instead of <term>כעש</term> <note>like a moth</note>, and for <term>רקב</term> (which signifies rot in general and the woodworm in particular), they read <term>דקר</term> <note>a sting/piercing</note>.

<meta>The catchword at the bottom is "bes," likely part of a word like "bestia" (beast) or "besonder" (special) continuing on the next page.</meta>

# SACRED HISTORY OF ANIMALS

<header>From Psalm 51, verses 10–11 <note>The header cites Psalm 50 in the Vulgate numbering, but the text below discusses the metaphors found in Hosea 5:12 regarding Ephraim and Judah.</note></header>

</margin>
...an ox or a goad. Whence also the Syriac: *I will be like a disturbance to Ephraim, and a disturbance to the house of Judah.* The Arabic of Antioch has it thus: *I am he who threw Ephraim into disorder, and I am like a biting thing to the house of Judah.* The Arabic of Alexandria: *And I will cast down Ephraim.* Luther: *I am as a moth to Ephraim, and as a maggot to the house of Judah.* <note>original German: "Ich bin dem Ephraim wie Motte / und dem Hauß Juda wie ein Made."</note> Dietenberger: *I am as a moth to Ephraim, and as a woodworm to the house of Judah.* <note>original German: "Ich bin dem Ephraim wie ein Motte (Schab) und dem Hauß Juda/ wie ein Holtzwurm."</note> God aptly compares Himself to a moth and a wood-borer, which attack cloth and wood covered with age, dust, and other filth, as can be seen in Pliny: <margin>Book 11, Natural History, chapter 35.</margin> In this way, God will consume Ephraim, who is stained with filth (by which name the Prophet denotes idols in verse 11). Moreover, the logic of this comparison is drawn partly from the form and *subject*. For just as both the moth and the woodworm consume even large timbers and precious garments secretly, with no one noticing, slowly and gradually; so God here hints that both these most ample kingdoms will be destroyed gradually and secretly, with no one on guard. It is also drawn partly *from the origin and the generating cause*. For just as little worms are born within the cloths and woods themselves, so the cause of their destruction and <term>πανωλεθρίας</term> <note>panolethrias: total destruction</note> did not originate from God, but from the sins of the people themselves. See the fulfillment of this prophecy in 2 Kings, chapters 15, 16, and 17. Gregory, in his *Moralia on Job*, applies this also to men devoted to pleasures, to whom God exists as a moth and woodworm: 1. in the soul through the bite of conscience; 2. in the body through the weakening of health; 3. in the goods of fortune through exactions, plundering, and the high cost of grain.

### GOAT-STAG
Called <term>אקו</term> <note>Akko</note> by the Hebrews, perhaps from the word <term>אקה</term> <note>akah</note>, *to cry out*. In the Talmud, it is called *Ikka*, the *common goat*. To the Arabs it is *Anack*, a *young she-goat*; in the plural: *Anouk*, hence the proverb: *Vuoak after nouk, that is, the she-goat after the camel*, which in Latin you would say is "to come from horses to donkeys" <note>An idiom for a significant downgrade in status or quality</note>. For the Syrians used goats for riding. To this genus belong the pygarg, the oryx, the chamois, the lachamur, the roe deer, the ibex, and the fawn, almost all of which are listed in Deuteronomy 14:5 and counted as permitted foods. Among the wild types of he-goats and she-goats, a place must also be given to this one, whence it is called a "wild goat" by some, a "chamois" by others, and <term>אקו</term> <note>Akko</note> by others; some call it a *unicorn*, and it is explained as a "roe deer" by Schindler, following the Targum. To the Greeks it is the <term>τραγέλαφος</term> <note>tragelaphos</note>, the *goat-stag*, that is, an animal similar to both a goat and a deer, having a mixed form of both. When Pliny treated deer in book eight, chapter thirty-two, he began the following chapter thus: *Of the same appearance, differing only in the beard and the hair on the shoulders, is what they call the goat-stag, born nowhere else than near the river Phasis.* Compare this with Aristotle, *History of Animals*, book 2, chapter 1, who mentions the *Hippelaphus* <note>Horse-deer</note>, which resembles a deer in form and a horse in its mane.

### THE WORM,
endowed by Mother Nature with weakness and a tiny body, appears meager in looks and contemptible in quality. Yet it should not be cheated of its own praise, both for the use it provides partly in food to nourish the body, and partly in medicine to recover health (than which nothing more excellent was ever given to the human race), and for its natural gifts. For that the worm moves so flexibly, and twists and turns itself in various circles, it owes entirely to God

<column-break/>

its author, as Aldrovandi astutely judges in book 6, *On Insects*, chapter 1, page 253. It has two names among the Hebrews. One is <term>רמה</term> <note>Rimmah</note>, a word that occurs in Exodus 16:24 in the description of the manna, which, when kept against God’s command, swarmed with worms. In verse 20 it is called <term>תולעת</term> <note>Tola'at</note>, but when it was kept by His command and lacked worms, it is called <term>רמה</term> <note>Rimmah</note>. Christ uses that word in the Psalms: <margin>Psalm 22:7.</margin> Whence some think <term>תולעת</term> <note>Tola'at</note> denotes a smaller and viler worm than <term>רמה</term> <note>Rimmah</note>, indeed the most abject of all, since the Messiah, to describe his supreme <term>κένωσιν</term> <note>kenosin: emptying or self-abasement</note>, uses that word instead of the other. Hence Tertullian, in his third book against Marcion, page 177, says of Christ's despised appearance: *Ignoble and unrecognizable in habit and aspect was Christ announced.* Isaiah is present here: *We announce Him, he says, before him like a little boy, like a root in a thirsty land, and he has no form, nor glory; and we saw him, and he had no form, nor beauty; but his form was dishonored, failing beyond all men; for although he was once timely in beauty according to David, beyond the sons of men, yet in this allegorical state it is spiritual grace. Otherwise, in his fleshly habit according to the same Prophet, He is a worm and no man, the ignominy and the non-entity of the people.* But we believe in <term>μυσελίδες</term> <note>muselides: mouse-like or small things/mysteries</note> nowhere unless we have the Holy Spirit as our leader and <term>ὁδηγόν</term> <note>hodegon: guide</note>. For indeed, we read of <term>תולע</term> <note>Tola</note> as the most excellent worm of all in the Sacred Books, <margin>Exodus 25:4, 36:8; Isaiah 1:18.</margin> referring to the "worm of the berry" <note>The cochineal insect used for dye</note>, which is also called absolutely <term>תולעת</term> <note>Tola'at</note> in Lamentations 4:5. And to return to the words of Isaiah, at the very beginning of the prophecy you hear the threatening and rebuking voice of God in verse 4: *Woe to the sinful nation, a people heavy with iniquity, a seed of evildoers, corrupting children; they have forsaken Jehovah, they have provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger, they have alienated themselves backward*, and many other things which follow in the same vein of sharp rebuke. But let the flow of mercy be added, and how the voice of anger and fury was immediately changed: <margin>verse 16.</margin> *Wash yourselves, wash yourselves, be clean, remove the evil of your works from the sight of my eyes, cease to do evil, learn to do good:* <margin>verse 17.</margin> *And: If your sins be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; if they be red*, <term>כחולע</term> <note>ka-tola: like the worm</note>, *like the little worm, they shall be white as wool.* Thus God, just and merciful, repeatedly changes His voice, now a merciful avenger, now austere to mild, according to the deeds of men. Now He coaxes with paternal love, entreating and consoling. Now He threatens, punishing and restraining. He acts with us just as we do with the "worms of the berry," which we nourish and protect. But as for the poisonous and harmful worms...
It is pleasing to say more in this place about the "worm of the berry" <note>The cochineal insect</note>: they say this little worm is born from the *coccus*, which is a dyeing grain adhering to a small, twiggy shrub like a lentil (according to Dioscorides and Mattioli, book 4, chapter 43), intended for the dyeing of garments which Kings and Priests used to wear. It is almost like a gnat and immediately flies into the air when the fruit is mature. From it is made the color with which "scarlet" <note>original German: Scharlach</note> is dyed; hence in Exodus 25:14 the <term>תולעת שני</term> <note>Tola'at Shani: crimson worm</note> was rendered by the Septuagint as <term>κόκκινον διπλοῦν</term> <note>kokkinon diploun: double scarlet</note>. The Vulgate has *scarlet twice-dyed*. Pagninus and Vatablus have *worm of the berry*: Junius and Buxtorf have *twice-dyed scarlet*. The Chaldean Paraphrast calls the color *bright*, and hence it is commonly called *crimson*...

# SACRED HISTORY OF ANIMALS
<header>474 BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> ...[the worm] because it becomes more brilliant than purple. Concerning this little worm, Scaliger writes thus in *Archilochus*:

> Why does the scarlet-clad, beast-like man walk,
> The stable-boy Tarrera, he swells and cracks with his cheeks,
> Listen, Tarrera, for it has come into my mind.
> This is the caterpillar of the foolish eater, the father
> Coccus of the tiny little worm dyed this.

**THE BEAR** <note>original Latin: *Ursus*</note> is so named as if from "pressing" <note>original: *urgendo*</note>, because it presses or weighs down heavily. In the old language of the Celts, the Bear was called **Baß**, whence, when the people of Bern struck a coin showing a bear on one side, that coin was thereafter called a **Baas**; this <term>naming</term> <note>original Greek: *onomatothesia*</note> still flourishes today; compare Glareanus *On the As*, chapter 16, page 21b and chapter 18, page 24b, and Stumpf. <margin>8 Hebrew Chronology 8, folio 253 b.</margin> In the Hebrew language <note>original: *lingua Eberina*</note> it is called *Dov* <note>original Hebrew: דב</note>, from the Arabic because it has a shaggy face. It is fierce and foul in appearance, whence Sirach 25:23 <note>in the Vulgate; 25:17 in English Bibles</note> draws a comparison between a bear and a woman of grim countenance; and with a sad and hoarse voice, whence "roaring" is attributed to them in Isaiah 59:11. It is a deceitful animal, which according to Oppian possesses <margin>3 Cynegetica, verse 145.</margin>
->—a deceitful heart, a shifty breast.<-
Because of its ambushes, it is dangerous to encounter (Lamentations 3:10, Amos 5:19) and should in no way be trusted, according to the warning of Martial, Book 6, Epigram 64:

> Though he be calm, and lick both fingers and hands.
> It is fierce and savage, especially when its cubs are stolen, Proverbs 17:12.

Hence Jerome says: They say, those who have written on the natures of beasts, that there is nothing among all wild animals more savage than a she-bear when she has lost her cubs or lacks food. <margin>6. 13. 8.</margin> Hosea must be cited in this place*, who introduces God as comparing Himself to a bereaved bear to signify His anger against idolatry. Furthermore, when it is hungry, it spares no labor to satisfy its hunger (Proverbs 28:15), and even dares to attack bulls (1 Samuel 17:34 <note>The text cites 1 S. 11. 7, likely a printer's error for 17:34, David’s struggle with the bear</note>). More ferocious than the rest, however, are those Northern and white bears, which the Dutch Argonauts <note>Refers to the Arctic expeditions of Willem Barentsz</note> experienced to their great misfortune in their expedition to Nova Zembla; though Torquemada writes in his *Hexameron*, page 586, that they can be tamed when they have not yet grown up. The Church Fathers explain <margin>2 Kings 2:24</margin> symbolically that example of the two bears tearing apart forty-two boys*, suggesting that the bears denoted Vespasian and Titus overturning Jerusalem in the forty-second year after the passion of Christ; compare Augustine, Book 12 *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, chapter 35, and Book 2 *On the Miracles of Holy Scripture*, chapter 22.

**THE FOX** <note>original: *Vulpes*</note>, called *Volpes* by Varro, as Aelius used to say, because it "flies with its feet" <note>original: *volat pedibus*</note>. In Greek, <term>fox</term> <note>original: *alōpēx*</note>, from "deceiving" and "the eyes," because it deceives the sight. Eustathius derives it from the words for <term>to wander</term> and <term>to deceive</term>. Whence "to play the fox" <note>original: *alōpekizein* and *vulpinari*</note> is said of one who perverts the truth and escapes through frauds and lies; this is said not from a hidden, but from the intent gait of foxes, according to Nonius. Thus Janus Gebhardus reads from the Palatine Manuscript. Hesychius says: <term>to play the fox means to deceive</term>. The proverb is well known: <term>to play the fox against another fox</term>. Thus the deceit and clever <term>concealment</term> <note>original: *perikrypsin*</note> of the Fox gave rise to a certain saying of Lysander, which he gave to those who criticized him for the deceits he used: <term>He said that where the lion's skin does not reach, the fox's skin must be sewn on there as well.</term> Plutarch in his *Apophthegms* felt that the fox's skin should be sewn on where the lion's was not suitable. This came to the notice of many men, and finally became a proverb about a calculated fraud by which someone finishes a business matter. Among the Hebrews it has its name from a cough,

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> which it imitates with its yelping, *Shu’al* <note>original Hebrew: שועל</note>, whence the proverb regarding coughing old men among the French: *The Fox's cough will lead you into the pit.* Marvelous is the craftiness and cunning of this animal; when it is hungry, and yet can bring nothing conveniently into its snare, and it sees birds flying by, it then feigns itself dead, and thus lures them to it, so that they descend as if to a corpse; these it finally seizes and satisfies its hunger. From this is taken the symbol of the fraudulent and crafty man, who are called "Fox-men" <note>original: *Vulpiones*</note> and "foxers." Such a one was Herod; such are false Teachers, the patrons of false opinions and heresies, <margin>Judges 14:5 <note>Corrected to Judges 15:4</note></margin> who are like the three hundred little foxes of Samson*, which had their tails tied together with a brand, by which part they brought fire to the crops, but they sought different directions with their heads; about which Serarius says much in question 8 on Judges 14. They delight in grapes, whence the fable of the fox and the grape, but with the devastation and ruin of the vineyard; hence Solomon in Song of Songs 2:15 warns to catch the little foxes that spoil the vines, the exhortation of which Abbot Willeram explains thus in his paraphrase on chapter 2, verse 119:

> The vineyard now blooms, let the Vinedresser now pray with petitions,
> That every little Fox may fall into the opposing snares;
> This cunning beast harms the ripe clusters.
> While the heretical foxes begin to crawl along crooked paths,
> Let the leaders of the Church immediately strike down the depraved dogmas,
> Lest they gain strength over time,
> And so the heresiarchs may cease with difficulty.

In the same way, Barlaeus in his 4th *Heroics*, page 590:

->You citizens, strive for the right path,<-
->To track the ways, and where subtle error<-
->Creeps in, and false Prophets sell their lies,<-
->Watch out, O Men, and do not trust in empty<-
->Witnesses. It is enough to have sworn by the words of one Master<-
->And to defend the cause with such a leader.<-

Origen understands by the little foxes the Devils, who lurk in the caves of the Church, and wander here and there through the field of the Church at night to seduce the simple from the simple truth of God. By the little foxes destroying the vineyards, St. Bernard understands, speaking according to the discipline of morals, evil doing harm under the appearance of good. Let us pay attention to them, he says in Sermon 64 on the Song of Songs, column 986, to those things said by the Bride about these small and crafty animals destroying the vineyards. I should call them "small" not in malice, but in subtlety. For it is by nature a crafty race of animal, and very prompt to do harm in secret; and it seems to me most fittingly to designate certain very subtle vices, cloaked in the appearance of virtues, the form of which I have already expressed for a little while by the examples previously brought to notice, though few. For they cannot harm otherwise, unless they lie that they are virtues by a certain similarity to virtues. We are hunters against Foxes and Wild Boars who lay waste the Lord’s vineyard—the former secretly, the latter openly—each in his own office which has been entrusted to him. The little foxes walk cunningly so that they may harm; the Holy Spirit calls you a hunter, <margin>Song of Songs 2:15.</margin> saying: *Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that spoil the vines; for our vineyard is putting forth buds.* The Wild Boar comes grunting from the woods and rages in the field of the Church, as the Psalmist writes in Psalm 80:14: *The wild boar of the forest has consumed it (the vine), and the wild beast of the field has grazed upon it.* Be vocal, that you may seize the hunting sword of the Word of God.

# FROM PSALM 50, VERSES 10–11
<header>ex Psal. L. v. 10. 11.</header>

...of God, and may you finish off that wild beast devouring the vine of the Lord.

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> Among these terrestrial (meaning tame) animals, the wealth of the first world of men—especially that of the Patriarchs—was placed. They were <term>rich in flocks</term> <note>original Greek: πολύρρεμμοι (*polyremmoi*)</note> and possessed much livestock. The Hebrew name <term>livestock</term> <note>original Hebrew: מקנה (*mikneh*)</note> is derived from the word for "acquiring," much like the Greek terms for <term>possessions</term> <note>original Greek: κτήματα (*ktēmata*)</note> and <term>cattle</term> <note>original Greek: κτήνη (*ktēnē*)</note> come from the verb <term>to acquire</term> <note>original Greek: κτάομαι (*ktaomai*)</note>. It is as if one were speaking of wealth and resources gathered together; and because the ancient and first inhabitants of the lands held their wealth almost entirely in livestock, the term is most often used for both larger and smaller cattle. Thus, the word <term>possession</term> <note>original Hebrew: משנה (*mishneh*)</note> properly signifies cultivation, yet it is meanwhile transferred even to <term>cattle</term>, because in these—as if in their chief possession—the labors of the Ancients were spent. Indeed, as we have said, in ancient centuries the entire census of wealth consisted of herds and flocks, and their efforts were occupied in making them numerous. That honest and upright method of increasing a household’s means was commended by the examples of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and other ancients. Job possessed a multitude of livestock, and his riches consisted of herds. <margin>1 Samuel 25:2</margin> Nabal, in 1 Samuel 25:2, had no small number of cattle, and his <term>dwelling</term> was in Carmel, a town near the wilderness of Paran. Pagninus translates this as: *And his cattle were in Carmel*. Arias: *His work*. Vatablus: *By his labor*. The Septuagint <term>from the Complutensian edition</term>: *his work was there*, but the Aldine edition says: *his flocks were there*. The Frankfurt edition: *his flock was there*. The Vulgate, however, says: *Flocks*. It was not only the wealth of the East that was placed in cattle, but also that of the West. For what the Holy Scripture testifies regarding the Easterners, Tacitus says of the Germans: *They are fertile in cattle, and these are their only and most pleasing riches*. Nor is this said of the Germans alone, but Justin testifies the same of the Spaniards: *The herds of Geryon, which in those times were considered the only riches*. Indeed, for the Romans too, their first wealth came from here; for where does the Roman word for money <note>original: *pecunia*</note> come from, if not from cattle <note>original: *pecus*</note>? The first of all Shepherds who ever lived in the world was the innocent Abel, and his first care was to offer the better cattle of his flock to God:

->From his flock he often placed a sacrifice on the altars,<-
->Now with a sheep, now with a fat calf he made an offering,<-
->More often still, he surrounded the Deity with great honor.<-

The second to be numbered among the Shepherds is Jacob. His service was long-lived and partly harsh, yet also—as it seemed to him—short because of his great love for Rachel. He voiced heavy complaints regarding the hardship of the pastoral life. <margin>Genesis 31:38, 39, 40.</margin> *Twenty years*, he said, *I have been with you; the ewes and female goats have not been barren, I have not eaten the rams of your flock, nor did I show you what was torn by beasts; I made good every loss, whatever was lost by theft. You demanded it from me; by day I was parched by heat and by night by frost, and sleep fled from my eyes*. A faithful shepherd deserves a better wage than fell to Jacob, who for his labors by day and night obtained nothing but the envy of his father-in-law Laban and Laban's children. For it is not without reason among all writers that those who exercise authority over other men are called Fathers and Shepherds. The duty of shepherds is not only to feed, but also to protect their sheep and to provide for them entirely. Whence the righteous man is commended because he cares for his beast: <term>A righteous man knows the soul of his beast</term> <note>original Hebrew: יודע צדיק נפש בהמתו (*yodea tzadik nephesh behemto*)</note>. That word <term>knows</term> <note>original Greek: γινώσκει (*ginōskei*)</note> is explained by the Greek translator in this History as <term>has pity</term> <note>original Greek: οἰκτείρει (*oikteirei*)</note>, or *to show mercy*. Castalio renders it: *The righteous man has regard even for his beast*.

<margin>Proverbs 12:10</margin> Concerning the beasts of the field and wild animals, power was given by God to Nebuchadnezzar over the beasts of the field and the birds of the heaven—and through him to all Princes of the earth—in Daniel 2:38. However, this was on the condition that they should not abuse that power and turn it into <term>wolfish cruelty</term> <note>original Greek: λυκανθρωπίαν (*lykanthrōpian*)</note>. For Princes sometimes sin by excessive cruelty toward their subjects when they discover they have struck down a wild animal. Regarding this, we had a cruel example a year or two ago of a man still living who was hedged in by the antlers of a stag <note>likely a reference to a specific contemporary punishment where a poacher was bound to a stag</note>. Worthy were the words of the pious Prince Frederick William, Administrator of the Electorate of Saxony, who said he had read through the Bible several times but had not yet found that a man should lose his life because of a wild beast. And Elector Christian II used to say: *I would rather have a faithful and wealthy farmer in the field than a fat stag who destroys the field*. Luther notes this in *The Babylonian Captivity*, page 119. Hunters receive little praise in Holy Scripture if we look at Nimrod, whence <margin>Sermon 8 on Psalm 118, page 655.</margin> Saint Augustine says: *We find no hunters among the holy men in the series of the Scriptures*. We believe this was said by Augustine with a grain of salt. Hunters also lean on their own praise in the Sacred Pandects <note>a reference to the body of law or collected scriptures</note>. Let us therefore remember and love Hunters—not such as those who gathered among the Aetolians to destroy the boar that laid waste to that region, leading to a cruel war between the Aetolians and Acarnanians—but those who shake men out of the hiding places of error like wild beasts, and reveal the light of truth when it is shaded by the difficulties of things like foliage. These are men who flee no labor for the sake of religion and faith, even if they must travel through the ridges of the Caucasus or the sands of Libya. God had long ago promised this to His Church, singing through the voice of the excellent Prophet Jeremiah that it would come to pass that He would one day send many Hunters whose task it would be to <term>hunt from every mountain and every hill and out of the holes of the rocks</term> those human minds captured by error and men living in the manner of wild beasts. <margin>Jeremiah 16:16</margin> Refer here to what is read in Ambrose on Psalm 118, Sermon 6, page 633: *The Hunters of the Lord are found on the mountains and on the hills, who track down those who are caught for life*. For thus God said through Jeremiah: <term>Behold, I send many Hunters, and they shall hunt them upon every mountain and every hill; and therefore the people of God are sought. The Lord has many skillful ministers for His operations; they are the same Fishers, the same also are Hunters and Reapers</term>.

The second class in our Sacred Zoology is made up of the Birds, created on the same day as the fish from the water, which concurred as the material through divine power to produce this specific being (concerning which we spoke more fully above on page 60). The Latin name for bird <note>original: *avis*</note> seems to owe its birth to the Hebrew <term>bird of prey</term> <note>original Hebrew: עיט (*ayit*)</note>, which in the Holy Language denotes a bird <term>or a flying thing</term>. It is a collective noun signifying every winged creature, whose root is <term>to fly</term> <note>original Hebrew: עוף (*ouph*)</note>, meaning *he flew* or *he fluttered*. Calepinus wants the bird to be named from <term>trackless places</term> <note>original Latin: *aviis*</note>, that is, from the more secret places in which birds especially delight. Others seek the origin in the idea that a bird is called such as if it were <term>without a path</term> <note>original: *sine via*</note>, because no one understands by what path it comes. Finally, there are those who dedu—

# SACRED HISTORY OF ANIMALS

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> 
Historians derive the word for bird from *arrival* <note>original Latin: *adventu*</note>, because they arrive every year, but this is not very precise <note>original Greek: ἀκριϐῶς (*akribōs*)</note>. Among the Greeks, the term <term>nestling</term> <note>original Greek: νεοσσὸς (*neossos*)</note> properly denotes a chick from an egg; the general term is <term>bird</term> <note>original Greek: ὄρνις (*ornis*)</note>, from the word meaning *to be carried with force* <note>original Greek: ὄρνυθαι (*ornuthai*)</note>. In the Holy Scripture, we read of <term>the birds of the heaven</term> <note>original Greek: τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ (*ta peteina tou ouranou*); original Hebrew: העוף השמים (*ha-oph ha-shamayim*)</note> in Matthew 6:26 and Daniel 2:38. These come from the words for *to fly* <note>original Greek: ἀπετομαι (*apetomai*) & πέταμαι (*petamai*)</note>, from which some believe the word for <term>wing</term> <note>original Greek: πτέρον (*pteron*)</note> was formed by a transposition of letters. The Latin word for wing, *ala*, comes either from the Greek for *a troop* <note>original Greek: ἴλαν (*ilan*) or εἰλεῖν (*eilein*)</note>, or from the Hebrew for *to ascend* <note>original Hebrew: עלה (*alah*)</note>, because a bird ascends into the air by means of its wings while flying. Birds are praised for their speed, specifically due to the benefit of wings; hence we read that wings are attributed to Angels, who are represented under winged images, as well as with the faces of men and beasts. A winged representation indicates, in a way, their supreme speed and eagerness in executing God’s commands, as they can fly down to us from heaven as swiftly as a flash of lightning. Hence the Cherubim in Exodus were made with wings, and Isaiah says the Seraphim flew to him. Daniel and Ezekiel also saw them as flying beings. Chrysostom, in his Homily *On the Incomprehensibility of God* <note>original Greek: περὶ τοῦ ἀκαταλήπτου (*peri tou akatalēptou*)</note>, says that Gabriel is described as flying *so that you may learn that he has come from the highest regions and from the dwellings above to human nature.* Because of his speed, Cyrus, <margin>Isaiah 46:11</margin> the first Monarch of the Persians, is compared to a bird. Regarding this passage, Brentius says: *He calls Cyrus a bird from the East because he would come with great speed from Persia into Babylonia, and because he would burst into Babylon just as a flock of birds is accustomed to rush upon a chosen spot in a field.* Thus, by an elegant metaphor, wings are also attributed to the soul, even by Plato <margin>in the Phaedrus</margin>. He speaks of *giving wings to the soul* <note>original Greek: Τὸ ἀναπτερῶν τὴν ψυχὴν (*To anapterōn tēn psychēn*)</note>, that is, *lifting the mind as if on certain wings.* And Basil, in his *Ascetica*: *For the soul, having received a vision of the truly beautiful, and being winged for immortality as if by a certain feather, drives as far away as possible the pleasures of the body that trouble it.* From this, Augustine also attributes two wings to the soul in his explanation of Psalm 138, which are the love of God and neighbor, as he explained in Psalm 103, where his words are: *On two wings all souls have their feathers, because all the commands of the Law are restricted, as it were, to two: the love of God and neighbor; supported by these, the soul, as if with free wings and with holy love, flies directly to God.* It is likewise familiar, especially to Homer and other Poets, to name Speeches and ships after their speed and to attribute wings to them, as in the Iliad, Book 1, line 201:
->And speaking to him, he addressed him with winged words.<-
<margin>in the Theriaca, line 814</margin> Thus Nicander commends ships for their swift oars as if they were wings, saying: *They depart like the wings of a ship,* which is the same as saying *they are driven like oars,* referring to the stroke of the oars so that the ship progresses with a rapid course. No less does Sophocles in *Oedipus the King*, line 185, compare the speed of a raging plague to a swift-winged bird <note>original Greek: εὐπτέρῳ ὄρνιθι (*eupterō ornithi*)</note>. Furthermore, birds cherish, cover, and defend their young under their wings. Hence, the *shadow of the wings* is used as a quite elegant metaphor for that singular providence by which God cares for, defends, and protects His own, as <margin>Psalm 36:8</margin> the Psalmist says: *How precious is your mercy, O God,* <note>original Hebrew: מה יקר חסדך אלהים ובני אדם בצל כנפיך יחסיון (*Mah yakar chasdecha Elohim u-vene adam be-tsel kenapecha yechesayun*)</note> *and the children of men hope in the protection of your wings.* So the shadow of the wings is put for God Himself caring for them,

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
and brooding over them like a bird. *Have mercy on me, O God,* <margin>Psalm 57:2</margin> *have mercy on me, for my soul hopes in you,* <note>original Hebrew: חנני אלהים חנני כי בך חסיה נפשי ובצל כנפיך אחסה (*Choneni Elohim choneni ki becha chasayah naphshi u-ve-tsel kenapecha echseh*)</note> *and in the shadow of your wings I hope.* Hence Jerome says: *Just as birds fly over their nests to defend their offspring, and if they see a snake, a man, or other birds approaching their chicks, they forget their weakness and fight with beak and claws, groaning with a chattering voice the pain of their breast: so the Lord will protect Jerusalem, and passing over it, He will deliver and save it.* In a similar manner, Hilary writes: *It is the nature of birds to overshadow the weakness of their chicks with their wings, and to defend them from the violence and wickedness of those flying by. This we recognize most of all in Hens, when they either cover or protect their brood gathered within their feathers. The Lord commemorates their habit as an example of His own concern, saying to Jerusalem: How often have I wanted to gather your children like a Hen, etc.* Therefore, the holy man hopes in the shadow of God's wings *until iniquity passes away, that is, while either the scandals of the world or the iniquities of the wicked pass, or while David himself escapes the weakness of earthly humility, as if from the cave of his dwelling and body in which he is now enclosed; and hoping under the shadow of God's wings, he is always intent on the duty of his hope, etc.* But without a longer prologue, mindful of our order, we shall consider the specific history <note>original Greek: ἱστοριογραφίαν (*historiographian*)</note> of each bird, beginning with the bird to whom not its own dignity, but the order of the alphabet, grants first place.

### THE HAWK
THE HAWK <note>original Latin: *Accipiter*</note> is so named from *taking* <note>original Latin: *accipiendis*</note> birds. To the Greeks it is the *hierax* <note>original Greek: ἱέραξ</note>, from which comes the term to scream like a hawk <note>original Greek: ἱεράζειν (*hierazein*)</note> in Aelian’s *History of Animals*, Book 7. To the Hebrews it is the *netz* <note>original Hebrew: נץ</note>, from a word meaning very swift flight, or because it is powerful in flying; hence in Homer it is called <margin>Iliad, Book 22, line 238</margin> *the swiftest of winged things*, where he compares Apollo to a swift hawk, a killer of doves <note>original Greek: φασσοφόνῳ (*phassophonō*)</note>:
---
->...like a hawk,<-
->swift, the killer of doves, which is the swiftest of winged things.<-
It is rightly counted among the birds of prey, about which Hesychius says: *The hawk is among the predatory birds, but it has something else for which it was listed by the Lawgiver: for it becomes tame and cooperates in predation.* Those who seem to be gentle and calm in sense, but are allied with the powerful, the greedy, and the predatory, imitate this bird. Or according to Hugo: *The hawk is a bird of prey, but being tamed by its master, it acquires prey for him; it signifies superiors and officials who violently snatch the goods of the poor for their masters, which they themselves cannot restore to the wretched.* As the tenth among the birds forbidden to be eaten, the sparrow-hawk <margin>Leviticus 11:16</margin> <note>original Hebrew: נץ (*netz*)</note> takes its place; Arias explains this as the goshawk, Luther as the *Sperber* (sparrow-hawk), and others say it is the lesser hawk. But in Job 39:26, Luther translates the same word *netz* as *Habicht* (goshawk), and Pagninus agrees with him; concerning this, Job says that it spreads its wings toward the south and flies, while others say it *grows feathers*. By these words, it is indicated that God instilled this cleverness in birds so that around winter they might seek suitable lodgings. Those who read "to grow feathers" interpret it as the hawk shaking off its old feathers and then spreading its wings to the Sun so that the pores of its body may be covered, and thus the new material of the feathers may come forth. This latter view pleases Lyranus, who says: *The hawk has a wonderful industry in its own renewal: when the south wind stands, which is a warm wind,*

### From Psalm 50, verses 10–11.

---

<margin>Sacred History of Animals, Book 31. Moralia, Chapter 32.</margin>
The bird spreads its wings against the heat of the sun so that its pores may open, causing old feathers and down to fall away so that new ones may grow in their place, allowing it to fly more easily. According to Gregory the Great, who speaks thus on this passage: *What does it mean for a hawk to grow feathers in the south wind, if not that every holy person grows warm by the touch and breath of the Holy Spirit? By casting off the habits of their old way of life, they take on the form of the New Man. To cast off the old feather is to lose the long-standing pursuits of deceitful actions; to take up the new feather is to hold a gentle and simple sense of living well. For the feather of the old way of life weighs one down, while the plumage of the new transformation lifts one up, making the flight toward God swifter as the bird is rendered lighter.* In light of this interpretation <note>original Latin: *exegeseos*</note>, this bird—which otherwise, due to its extreme greed, is an image of all the wicked and even of the Devil himself—becomes a symbol of the saints who strive for daily renewal. Hence, Philippus the Presbyter says: *It follows that we should understand this hawk in a positive sense. It represents the holy people who have changed for the better: those who have received the wisdom of God through conversion, so that they cease to prey and snatch, and stop feeding on the "flesh" of worldly senses. They have cast off the skin of the old man in Baptism so that, growing new feathers, they are renewed, just as the youth of the Eagle is renewed—especially when, holding the promise of the present and future life (signified by the wings), they turn toward the South, from whence comes the heat of faith and where they recognize Christ has come,* etc. Among the nobility, hawks are highly valued for the use they provide in hunting other birds; indeed, they are tamed for the destruction and ruin of simpler birds, hence the verse:

> We hate the hawk, for he always lives in arms. <note>original Latin: *Odimus accipitrem, quia semper vivit in armis.*</note>

In strength joined with equal cunning, they yield to no other bird. Regarding the Indians, Ctesias (as recorded by Photius) 
<margin>Codex 72, page 26.</margin>
relates: *They hunt hares and even foxes, not with dogs, but with ravens, kites, crows, and eagles.* <note>original Greek: λαγὼ οὓς δὴ καὶ ἀλώπεκας θηρεύουσιν, & τοῖς κυσὶν, ἀλλὰ κίραξί, καὶ ἰκτῖσι, καὶ κοράκαις, καὶ ἀετοῖς (*lagō hous dē kai alōpekas thēreuousin, ou tois kusin, alla kiraxi, kai iktisi, kai korakais, kai aetois*)</note>. This ancient method of capturing wild beasts and other birds by means of a hawk was known to both the Greeks and the Romans. Regarding the Greeks, specifically the Thracians, let us hear Aristotle in Book 9 of *History of Animals*, chapter 36, and in the book *On Marvelous Things Heard* <note>original Greek: περὶ θαυμασίων ἀκουσμάτων (*peri thaumasiōn akousmatōn*)</note>; likewise Pliny: *In the part of Thrace
<margin>History of Nature, Book 18, Chapter 8.</margin>
above Amphipolis, men and hawks hunt together in a kind of partnership. The hawks drive birds out of the woods and reed-beds, and as they fly above, the men strike them down.* In return, the fowlers share the catch with the hawks. Julius Firmicus writes the same of the Romans in Book 5, chapter 7: *They studied how to breed hawks, falcons, goshawks, eagles, and birds of this kind for hunting.* And in chapter 8: *They are breeders of hawks, falcons, and other birds pertaining to fowling.* The hawk is called *hierax* <note>original Greek: ἱέραξ</note> from its marvelous speed, because it "carries easily" <note>original Greek: ἱερῶς ῥᾳδίως (*hierōs rhadiōs*)</note>, that is, it flies swiftly. Because of this speed, as Horus witnesses, 
<margin>Book 2, Chapter 15.</margin>
a painted hawk denotes the winds, and among the Egyptians, it was a symbol of the wind. Diodorus Siculus writes in Book 2 that the hawk was worshipped as a God among them, and Eusebius adds the reason in Book 11 of *Preparation for the Gospel*: because it purges Egypt of horned vipers, scorpions, and other venomous animals. Concerning the people of Tentyra, according to Aelian (Book 10, *History of Animals*, chapter 24) and the people of Philae, according to Strabo (Book 17), on the borders of Egypt and Ethiopia, this

matter is well known. However, while Strabo mentions that this bird is worshipped by all of Egypt, one might doubt this, because Aelian, in the passage cited, after saying the hawks are worshipped by the Tentyrites, adds that the Coptites, on the other hand, revere crocodiles and often crucify hawks as the enemies of crocodiles. He offers this reason for both cults: *Some liken the crocodile to water, which is why they worship it; others compare the hawk to fire, and for that reason, they adore it.* <note>original Greek: εἰκάζουσι οἱ τὸν μὲν κροκόδειλον, ἐκείνοι ὕδατι, ἔνθεν τοὶ καὶ σέβουσιν. οἱ δὲ τὸν ἱέρακα πυρί· ταύτῃ τοὶ καὶ προσκυνοῦσι (*eikazousi hoi ton men krokodeilon, ekeinoi hudati, enthen toi kai sebousin. hoi de ton hieraka puri; tautē toi kai proskunousi*)</note>.

**THE BEE** <note>original Latin: *APIS*</note>, is named not as if it were "without feet" <note>original Greek: ἄπης (*apēs*)</note> as some prefer, but more likely descends from the ancient word *apo*, meaning "to bind" or "to weave." To speak briefly of the generation of bees, it is known from the common opinion of natural philosophers that bees are born from putrefying bulls, wasps from horses, and beetles from donkeys. Plutarch mentions that the more learned or wise were persuaded of this, saying: *The wiser men provide the account that bees flourish from the carcasses of oxen, wasps from horses, and beetles are brought to life from donkeys suffering the same fate.* <note>original Greek: οἱ σοφώτεροι διδόντες λόγον, ὡς μελίττας μὲν βόες, σφῆκας δὲ ἵπποι κολάσπαντες ἐξανθῶσι, καὶ θᾶροι δὲ, ὄνων τὸ αὐτὸ παθόντων ζωογονοῦνται (*hoi sophōteroi didontes logon, hōs melittas men boes, sphēkas de hippoi kolaspantes exanthōsi, kai tharoi de, onōn to auto pathontōn zōogonountai*)</note>. Similarly to Plutarch, Origen in *Against Celsus*, Book 4, page 210, taught that bees are born from the carcass of a cow, wasps come from a horse, and beetles from a donkey <note>original Greek: ἐκ βοὸς μέλισσαν, ἐξ ἵππου σφῆκα, ἐξ ὄνου δὲ κάνθαρον (*ek boos melissan, ex hippou sphēka, ex onou de kantharon*)</note>. A verse by Nicander from the *Theriaca* (v. 741) found in the *Anthology* and Suidas was often used for this purpose:

> The bull begets bees; the horse gives rise to hornets.

Ovid refers to the same in *Metamorphoses*, Book 15, verse 385:
> A thing known by experience: from the rotting entrails
> Flowers-gathering bees are born everywhere, which in the manner of their parents
> Inhabit the fields, favor work, and labor in hope.

It is established from Augustine, in *On the Trinity*, Book 3, chapter 8, that they conceive without any mating. He says: *Certainly, female bees do not conceive their offspring by mating, but they gather them with their mouths as if they were scattered across the lands.* By this example of the Bees, he intends to demonstrate the possibility

of the Virgin Mary giving birth: *Lest we leave this matter (the Birth of Christ) without an example from Nature in God’s creatures, we prove that many animals are born without the mating of parents. Just as bees grow without fathers, from the maternal body alone, and all such winged creatures conceive their young in this way.* Virgil felt no differently in the *Georgics*, Book 4:

This myth is created because Saturn, as we have said, is the God of time, which revolves back into itself forever. Thus, the bees, following the sound of brass, are said to have fed Jupiter with honey; for which reason Jupiter later granted them the ability to have children without any mating. Thus says Servius. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
Sacred History of Animals.
</margin>
...in our Belgic lands <note>Refers to the Low Countries, likely where the author is writing</note> bees feed. Meanwhile, we do not doubt that they reproduce. Some are pleased by the idea that from the "king" of the bees <note>Though we now know this is a Queen bee, historical naturalists referred to the leader as a King</note> both other kings and bees are born; and that from those bees which are not kings, other non-king bees are born, and from these, the drones <term>fucos: male bees that do not work or sting</term> are born, which do not reproduce. You may also read this in Aristotle, Book 5.

<margin>
Book 17 on the Treatment of Animals, Chapter 2.
</margin>
But it is more likely, though Albertus <note>Albert the Great, a medieval philosopher and scientist</note> denies it, that the genital seed is emitted by the king alone. Nor should it bother anyone that no one has seen these "kings" mating. For although bees do not copulate in a traditional sense, they still have a desire to propagate their kind; just as in certain other creatures that reproduce, there is only one sex, or none at all: such as the red mullet, eels, and purple-fish, as Julius Caesar Scaliger says in his 191st Exercise against Cardanus, Section 2. We have learned of the generation of this bee-king in these Belgic lands from those most skilled in the matter of beekeeping. The king of the bees emits seed into individual cells. This is a whitish follicle, from which emerges a small worm of the same color, resembling a poppy seed. Around this follicle, the bees surround a viscous moisture from the dew, likewise whitish. Certainly, this white part corresponds to the white of a hen's egg, while the royal seed corresponds to the yolk. Over the follicle, thus surrounded by viscous dew, a small bee broods like a hen, and cherishes it with its own heat. Thus the follicle swells more and more, until it becomes such a worm as we see born in fatty cheeses. Furthermore, though it is often slower, sometimes—provided the sky is clear—within the tenth or twelfth day, the skin of the worm is ruptured and a bee emerges, and a perfect one at that; having six feet and four wings, though somewhat paler, but shortly after becoming similar in color to the adults. Since, however, in our regions—to return to the first production of bees—nothing of the sort has been observed, nevertheless, from the carcass of another animal,

<margin>
Judges 14:8.
</margin>
specifically a Lion, the Sacred Code <note>The Bible</note> testifies that a swarm of bees emerged; whether it was in its womb, as Ambrose has it in *Letter 60*, or in its chest, as Josephus says, or in its head (that is, the skull), or in its mouth, as the Septuagint <note>original: *LXX*, the Greek Old Testament</note> and the Vulgate write, matters little. Some attribute this to a miracle produced by the singular providence of God, but there is no need to invent a miracle where none exists. In our regions, due to the harsher climate, we do not see bees born in the same manner as in warmer regions. Regarding the swarm of bees raised in the carcass of the Lion killed by Samson in the vineyards of Timnah, it is pleasing to add a few more things: That swarm of bees and the honey born in the mouth of the Lion killed by Samson is by no means a "rustic tale" <note>original Greek: *ἀγρὸς λόγος*</note>, but represents the greatest doctrines with honeyed sweetness. Borrhaus says it is relevant to understanding the secrets shadowed by the honey in the carcass of the Lion’s empire to have knowledge of the nature of bees: what care and industry they apply in shaping the honeycombs and wax, and in collecting the honey itself. Their Republic must be understood: how they have their King, whom they obey; how they expel the idle drones; how they consult for the common utility of the Republic; and other such things, the consideration of which in so small a creature opens a wonderful understanding of the riddle proposed by Samson to the Philistines. The Parent of Nature armed this little animal—though insignificant in appearance, and whose voice is said to be very weak and barely audible, a "buzzing" or "humming" <note>original Greek and Latin: *βομβεῖν*, *bombire*</note>, about which there is a famous verse by Theocritus:

This little animal, I say, he armed with stings, except for the King, who according to Aristotle, Columella, and Ambrose is without a spike; to which add what Antonio Herrera reports about bees in the American province <note>Likely referring to Central or South American stingless bees</note> truly lacking the sting of peace, who, as makers of liquid honey, do not fashion a honeycomb but make honey in the hollows of trees. To resist those who oppose them and their works, they defend themselves; whence Bernard says in his 2nd Sermon on the Advent of the Lord: *The bee has the sweetness of honey; it also has the puncture of the sting.* It is very easily provoked, of whose anger Virgil writes:
> "Their anger is beyond measure, and when hurt they breathe poison
> with their bites, and leave hidden stings behind,
> fixed in the veins, and lay down their lives in the wound."

One may learn of the strength and vengeance of bees from Aristotle, who reports that horses were killed by them.

In the same way, the townsmen of Belgrade <term>Alba Graeca: a historical name for Belgrade</term> removed and repelled Murad <note>Amurathem: likely Sultan Murad II</note> by throwing and releasing swarms of bees at the Turks, as Bonfinius has it in his *Decades*, Book 3, Chapter 4. From these examples, it is not obscure that the enemies of the Church are skillfully compared to irritated bees by the Psalmist in Psalm 118:12: *They surrounded me like bees*, and they blazed like fire among thorns. A bee burning with anger against someone circles, whispers, and finally stings—a light puncture indeed, but one which gives the bee itself to death; and thus, taking vengeance, it perishes and loses its own life. On this passage of the Psalmist, Osiander says: *Bees are held by such a zeal for vengeance that they would rather lose their life than not cause harm (for bees die when the sting is lost, which they leave in the wound). So the enemies of Christ—because for the most part their false religion and wicked morals are exposed and condemned by the ministry of the Gospel—persecute Christ in his members with such fury that they would rather perish than desist.* Compare Blessed Luther, Volume 5 (German) on this passage.

# FROM PSALM 50, VERSES 10, 11.

<margin>
Sacred History of Animals.
</margin>

...the yellow of honey, but a sting. And it shall come to pass, in that day the Lord shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria. <note>This refers to Isaiah 7:18. The author is interpreting the prophetic use of insects as symbols for invading armies.</note> Theodor Snepfius, in his *Commentary on Isaiah*, page 126, explains the sense of this prophecy, commenting as follows: He compares the Assyrians to bees and the Egyptians to flies for two reasons: first, because those regions abound with insects, especially in the marshes of the Nile; and second, to depict the multitude of enemies. For bees, when they leave their hives, fly in great numbers, and there is no doubt that the same applies to the wasps and flies of Egypt. The Prophet looked to the nature of bees and flies, which fly in swarms and fill every place, to show that no place in the Jewish kingdom would be free from the danger of war. Hugo <note>Likely Hugo of St. Victor, a 12th-century theologian</note> explains this regarding those who, weary of court life, retreat into monasteries: "The bee, which has honey in its mouth and a sting in its tail, represents the flatterer or the traitor; it is in the land of Assyria—that is, in the court of the powerful, where both treachery and flattery reign—but now they rest in the cloisters of monks and the chapters of canons." Among the natural gifts with which Nature has endowed this little creature, its mutual love and benevolence also stand out, which each shows toward the other. Regarding the concord and mutual aid of bees among themselves, let us hear the oration of

<margin>
Oration 48, page 535.
</margin>

Dio <note>Dio Chrysostom, a Greek philosopher and orator</note>: <note>original: "Μέλιτται μὲν ὁμονοῦσι..."</note> "Bees indeed live in harmony, and no one has ever seen a swarm in sedition or fighting with itself; they work together and live together, and provide and use their own food." A story recorded by Theodorus Clutius in Book 1 *On Bees*, Chapter 3—and from him by Vossius in the place cited—deserves mention. He had found in his garden a little bee nearly submerged in a pot of honey, and another so afflicted by rain that it lay on the grass as if lifeless. He placed both on his hand; warmed by his heat, they were completely revived. Indeed, as they recognized each other, they began to kiss and embrace in a friendly manner. And the cleaner one, which the rain had knocked down, began to clean the other, which was soiled with honey, limb by limb; she spent nearly an hour on this task. Then the one who had received the benefit moved her mouth to the other, and out of gratitude drew some honey from her own breast for her; the other drank it, and being satisfied, flew back to the hive since her help was no longer needed. Soon after, the one who remained balanced her wings for a moment, and when she saw she was fit for flight, likewise returned home. They show the same love to their King <note>Historically, the leader of the hive was thought to be male; we now know it is the Queen bee</note>, whom they carry and protect even when sick or worn out by old age, as Didymus writes in Book 15, Chapter 13. Indeed, they wage war for their king and meet death—

<margin>
Georgics, Book 4.
</margin>

—as Maro <note>The Roman poet Virgil</note> sings of this matter:

---
->...their bodies in war<-
> They offer up, and seek a beautiful death through wounds.

They maintain a similar society and benevolence with ants, just as Dio writes concerning the mutual society and benevolence of bees and ants:

<margin>
Oration 40, page 498.
</margin>

<note>original: "Οὐδὲ μύρμηκες..."</note> "Nor do ants, having others near them and often bringing in grain from the same threshing floor, quarrel over food, but they make way for one another and turn aside from their paths, and often work together. Nor do several swarms of bees, grazing in one and the same meadow, neglect their work to quarrel over the dew of the flowers."

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred History of Animals.
</margin>

All writers and all farmers commend the diligence and industry of bees. <note>original: "Συνεχῶς ἐργάζονται"</note> "They work continuously," says Aristotle, and no day is lost to them in idleness (to speak with Pliny), especially <note>original: "ὅταν εὐδία ᾖ"</note> "when the weather is fair." From this, Pliny (Book 10, Chapter 11) borrowed the idea that their column, if the temper of the sky be mild, proceeds to its labors. God showed the bees their way through the air, through the dewy grasses of the field, through the flowers of herbs, and through the peaks of mountains and hills, so that they might find the dwellings of their combs without wandering. Thus, we may say with Didymus: <note>original: "ἡ μέλιττα πάντων..."</note> "The bee is the wisest of all remaining animals, and the most ingenious, and a helper to man and a creature of understanding." By a buzzing sound—either double or triple—they are woken for work in the morning, and in the evening they settle themselves for sleep, which Virgil touches upon:

<margin>
Georgics, Book 4.
</margin>

> When the evening at last has warned them to leave the pasture
> Of the fields, then they seek their roofs, then they care for their bodies;
> A sound is made, they buzz around the edges and thresholds.
> Later, when they have settled in their chambers, there is silence
> For the night, and their own sleep occupies their weary limbs.

"Conjecture" or "aim" <term>stochasmos: a Greek term for purposeful planning or targeted effort</term> is also attributed to bees and ants by Plutarch in his book *On the Cleverness of Animals*, whose labor tends toward no other goal and looks to nothing else than:

> For they all, and every one, increase the common
> Work; but for one another in different ways
> There is no [individual] aim, nor care.

Bees, which are called "always-working" <note>original: "ἀειεργοί"</note> by Phocylides, are animals essential for the sake of food; for there is no creature so diligent and laborious that so ingeniously and skillfully stores and hides away nourishment for future use. It wanders through flowery fields and roams through the flowers of herbs to fill its storehouses, so that Engelmodus, Bishop of Soissons, not undeservedly sang of their diligence in his *Poem on the Praises of St. Radbert*, verse 96:

> And just as when the frost recedes while the West Wind blows,
> When the flowery earth brings forth the budding herbs,
> Painting the fields with distinct colors in the new spring,
> The youth of the bees, dispersed in the fields, exercises,
> Fearing the past labors of the shattered winter;
> They gather purple flowers and sip from the rivers.
> There is no delay, no rest, but they either shut the liquid honey
> In thin cells packed with nectar,
> Or with tough glue they build the hard foundations of the combs,
> Or arrange the saffron waxes in order.
> Frequent care burns, they offer up the purest honey.

And Corippus in Book 4:

> They settle on various flowers and the moist dew
> They gather with their mouths, and load their shoulders, and liquid waxes
> They fashion, and fix their sweet hearths in the pumice,

He said they have "hearths in the pumice" in imitation of Virgil, who said:

> They have dug out a hearth deep under the earth and are found
> Deep in hollow pumice stones and the cavern of a hollow tree.

And from this also Claudian, in his second book *Against Rufinus*, verse 470:

> The bees are stirred and cluster together, he who draws the sweet
> Honey by theft; they move their wings and aim their stings.

<page-num>480</page-num>
<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>

> And through the slender defenses of the rock they protect
> Their honey-combed homeland and beloved pumice caves,
> And cover the honeycombs with a leaning swarm.

The bee is a "geometric" little creature, and in it, architectural wisdom reveals itself above all else. Indeed, bees smear their hive with a plaster which you might call *kanōsin* <note>original Greek: κάνωσιν</note>, as if to say <gloss>a coating</gloss>, or *kommōsin* <note>original Greek: κόμμωσιν</note>, meaning a "gumming." They do this using bitter herbs to drive away other little beasts that are hungry for honey. But not content with this "gumming," they also apply *pissokēron* <note>original Greek: πισσόκηρον; literally "pitch-wax"</note>, so called because it is applied like pitch and is the beginning of the wax; as Pliny says, <margin>Book 12, chapter 7.</margin> it is a thinner kind of wax. Furthermore, they use a thicker material—not yet wax, but a foundation for the honeycombs—to block every entrance of cold or injury at the very threshold of the hive; for this reason, it is called *propolis* <note>original Greek: πρόπολις; literally "before the city"</note>, because it is found at the very entrance of the bee-city. Then, the shape of the cells also commends this building because, to use the words of the oft-cited Didymus, *tas thēkas hexagōnous poiei* <note>original Greek: τὰς θήκας ἑξαγώνους ποιεῖ</note>, "it makes the cells six-sided." Others say that bees divide their cells into three parts: the cell of the King <note>Early naturalists mistook the Queen bee for a King.</note> of the bees is more spacious, placed in a prominent location, and fortified with a more secure fence; then there are the adjacent cells of the more honored bees, who serve as the guardians of the kingdom and their public affairs, excelling the others in age, utility, and experience. This was handed down by Aelian in his book on animals: <term>Πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ ἐργάζονται τὰς θαλάμας τὰς τῶν βασιλέων... <note>original Greek: "For first they work on the chambers of the kings, and they are spacious, and they are higher up and appear more sovereign; for these, they show something like walls. They take pride in the royal dwelling... they divide them into three... for the oldest and most ancient dwell near the royal court, as if they were bodyguards and sentries."</note></term> Considering this wise <term>oikodomēn <note>building or architecture</note></term> of the bees, Pierre Du Faur <note>Latin: Petrus Faber (1540–1600), a French jurist and President of the Parliament of Toulouse.</note>, a Counselor to the King and President of the Senate of Toulouse, offered this political warning as a vow: *3. sem. 18. pag. 282.* "Would that our Princes today—and the civil and military magistrates who most imitate them—would weigh and follow the foresight, custom, rite, and even the counsel of such a little creature, though it has a wild nature! Would that they would seek and follow the opinion of the elders, distinguished by age and experience and approved as Patricians by deceased Kings in the chief business of the Republic, rather than yielding to the inexperienced reputation for virtue and faith held by youths and flatterers—as Rehoboam is said to have done to the great loss of himself and his subjects—and trusting the sum of the whole Republic without any selection, effectively commending the sheep to the wolves, as the saying goes. Would that they would desire nothing to be done by their own impulse, disregarding the judgment of their fathers' friends and other wiser men, or without a carefully sought opinion, merely for the sake of their own power."

From the home—about which Hesiod <term>Works and Days, line 301 and following.</term> bids us be concerned first—and as if from a city of birds, we proceed to the rule or governance of the bee-city. Among the Hebrews, the bee is called *Deborah* <note>Hebrew: דבורה</note>, either from its continuous buzzing (as if speaking), or from the wonderful leadership or order of its work, which descends from the root *Dabar* <note>Hebrew: דבר</note>; among its other meanings, this root also signifies to lead, to rule, or to set in order,

<column-break/>

whence Nebuchadnezzar, having returned to his senses, uses this word regarding the leaders of his kingdom, saying: *vachadabbāray* <gloss>my governors or leaders sought me out</gloss>, <margin>Daniel 4:33.</margin> It is a political animal, and they maintain a well-constituted republic among themselves. One must greatly admire the work of nature in bees: they have a King, and they obey one leader; they have honeycombs and homes; they carry honey and wax into the swarm as if into a common city and treasury. All gaze upon the King to serve him, for they are close at hand. When he flies out, they all fly out; when he fights, they all do battle; when he dies, they all raise a lament with a mournful sound. Once the funeral rites are celebrated, they all enter a new council, the citizens are called together, they deliberate, and a new King is chosen, who excels in form and size. From this, we see that this little creature is a lover of Monarchy and observes in its republic that form of governing which is the best of all. Regarding this, let us hear Alvaro Pelayo <note>Alvarus Pelagius (c. 1275–1349), a Franciscan bishop and influential political theorist.</note> arguing: <margin>* On the Lament of the Church, 40, folio 17. b.</margin> "In natural governance," he says, "we see all rule reduced to one, just as in a composite body one element dominates. In the human and homogeneous body, there is one principal member in the whole man. The Soul contains all elements. Even gregarious animals, such as Bees and Cranes, for whom it is natural to live in society, are subject to one King." So too Virgil, at the beginning of the fourth book of his *Georgics*, discusses the nature and customs of Bees; among other things, he sings of their Monarchy to Maecenas thus:

> I shall describe for you the wondrous spectacles of tiny things,
> The magnanimous leaders, and the customs of the whole race in order,
> Their pursuits, their peoples, and their battles.
> A labor on a thin theme, but the glory is not thin,
> If the unfavorable powers allow, and Apollo hears when called.

Basil <note>Saint Basil the Great, 4th-century theologian.</note> takes his starting point from the well-ordered politics of bees when about to deliver the encomium for Gordius the Martyr, and Ambrose <margin>Saint Ambrose, Hexameron, chapter 21.</margin> discusses most elegantly the properties and Republic of bees. I do not regret transcribing his words here one by one: "Now I shall explain how these creatures, like birds, seem to care for a kind of Republic and spend the ages of this life under laws. For this is the use of a Republic: that laws be common to all and that they be observed by common devotion; that all be held by one bond, so that what one understands is not permitted to him is not permitted to another, but what is allowed is allowed to all, and what is not allowed to all is not allowed to any. There is also a common reverence for the Elders <note>original Latin: Senatorum</note>, by whose counsel the Republic is governed; a common home of the city for all, a common duty of social life, one prescription, and one counsel for all. These are great things, but how much more excellent they are in Bees! They alone in every kind of living creature have offspring common to all; they all inhabit one mansion; they are enclosed within the threshold of one fatherland. Work is common to all, food is common, operation is common, use and fruit are common, flight is common. What more? Generation is common to all; the integrity of a virginal body is common to all, as is birth, since they are not joined by any coitus, nor are they undone by lust, nor are they shaken by the pains of birth. Suddenly they send forth a great swarm of children, gathering their offspring from leaves and herbs with their mouths. They ordain a King for themselves..."
