# From Psalm 55:10–11

<margin>
Sacred History of Animals.
</margin>

...govern <note>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on the bee's social order</note>, they create their own peoples for themselves; and though they are placed under their own King, they are nonetheless free. For they hold both the privilege of judgment and the affection of faithful devotion, because they love him as one appointed by themselves and honor him with such a great swarm. Now, the King is not chosen by lot, because in a lot there is chance rather than judgment, and often by irrational accident the very last person is preferred over those who are better. Nor is he designated by the common shouting of an ignorant multitude, which does not weigh the merits of virtue nor examine the advantages of public utility, but wavers with uncertain fickleness. Neither does he sit upon the royal throne by the privilege of succession or birth; for one ignorant of public life and uneducated would not be able to lead. Add to this the flatteries and luxuries which usually weaken either the natural age or the sharp edge of genius, as well as the instructions of eunuchs <note>original: "Spadonum"</note>, most of whom incline the mind of a King more toward their own profit than toward public use.

The King of the bees, however, is formed by nature with clear distinguishing marks, so that he excels in body size and appearance, and—what is most important in a King—in the gentleness of his character. For even if he has a sting, he does not use it for vengeance. For there are laws of nature, not written in letters but impressed upon hearts <note>original: "amoribus"</note>, so that those who possess the greatest power should be more lenient in punishing. But back to the bees: those who have not complied with the laws of the King punish themselves with a penitent condemnation, so that they die from the wound of their own sting. It is said that the Persian people even today observe this, so that for the price of a crime they themselves carry out the sentence of their own death. Therefore, none have such heavy laws toward their subjects as the Kings of the Persians. Neither the Indians nor the Sarmatian peoples observe such great reverence of devotion as the bees, so that none dare to leave the home or go out to any pasture unless the King has gone out first and claimed the leadership of the flight for himself.

Their progress is through fragrant countrysides, where gardens breathe with flowers, where a fleeing stream runs through the grass, where the banks are pleasant—there is the play of spirited youth, there is field exercise, there is the release from cares. The work itself is sweet, made from flowers; the first foundations of the camp are laid from sweet herbs. For what else is a honeycomb but a kind of military camp? Finally, the drone <note>original: "fucus"</note> is driven away from these stalls of the bees. What square-built camps could have as much art and grace as the structures of the honeycombs have, in which tiny and round cells are supported by their mutual connection to one another? For what architect taught them to compose those six-sided cells <note>original: "Hexagenia"</note> with such indistinguishable equality of sides, and to hang thin waxes between the walls of the houses, to pack the honey, and to swell with a certain nectar that bristles in the fabric of the flowers? 

You may see them all competing in their duty: some keep watch by seeking food, others apply a careful guard to the camp, others scout for coming rains and watch the course of the clouds, others mold waxes from flowers, and others collect the unsalted dew from the flowers with their mouths. Yet none lie in wait for the labors of others or seek a living by theft. And would that they did not fear the traps of robbers! However, they have their own little spears and pour venom amidst the honey if they are provoked, and they place their souls in the wound <note>A classical reference to Virgil's description of bees dying when they sting.</note> in the heat of vengeance. Therefore, in the middle of the valleys of the camp, that liquid dew is poured in, and gradually by the passage of time, it is thickened into honey; though it was liquid from the beginning, by the union of the wax and the scent of the flowers, it begins to smell with the sweetness of honey.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred History of Animals.
</margin>

Rightly does the Scripture praise the bee as if it were a good worker, saying: *Go to the bee, and see how she is a worker.* <note>The author quotes a common Greek/Patristic addition to Proverbs 6:8; the Hebrew Bible mentions only the ant.</note> Consider also how venerable a work she deserves, whose labor Kings and commoners take for their health; for it is desirable and dear to all. You hear what the Prophet says. He sends you, surely, so that you may follow the example of that little bee and imitate her work. You see how industrious and how pleasing she is. Her fruit is desired and sought by all, and no distinction is made for the status of persons; but by the grace of its creation, it becomes sweet with equal pleasantness for Kings and commoners alike. It is not only for pleasure but also for health; it sweetens the throat and heals wounds, and it pours medicine into internal ulcers. 

Thus, although the bee is weak in strength, she is strong in the vigor of wisdom and the love of virtue. Finally, they defend their King with the highest protection and think it beautiful to die for him. While the King is safe, they do not know how to change their judgment or turn their minds; if he is lost, they abandon the duty of keeping faith and they themselves tear apart their own honey, because he who held the leadership of the duty has been killed. And so, while other birds hardly produce a single brood in a year, bees create twin offspring and outweigh others with double fertility. 

And in the following chapter: The bees themselves sing something not unpleasant. For they have a pleasing sweetness in that hoarse murmur of their voice, which we seem to imitate first rather slowly with the broken sound of trumpets; no sound is judged more fit than this rattling for exciting spirits into vigor. And this grace remains in them, even though they are revealed to have no lungs or the function and use of breathing, but rather they feed on an airy breath. Finally, if someone pours oil over them, they are quickly killed, because they cannot draw in that airy breath through their blocked pores. Immediately, if someone pours vinegar over them, they revive at once, because the force of the vinegar is said to open those pores, which were blocked by the thickening of the oil, by its moisture.

Palestine is commended for its abundance of honey and milk, which is very often called *a land flowing with milk and honey* <note>original Hebrew: ארץ זבת חלב ודבש — Eretz zavat chalav u-devash</note>; see Exodus 3:8, chapter 13:5; Numbers 13:28, chapter 14:6, chapter 16:14; Deuteronomy 6:3, chapter 26:9, chapter 27:3, chapter 31:20; Joshua 5:6; Jeremiah 11:5, chapter 32:22. We believe this is said as a hyperbole and denotes the highest fertility of the region. For an abundance of milk and honey altogether proves a well-watered, fruitful land, abounding in joyful pastures and flowers, from which not only can herds and flocks fill their udders with milk, but also bees can fill their cells with liquid nectar. Ovid seems to have looked back at such great fertility of the blessed land when dreaming of the Golden Age:

> Then rivers of milk, then rivers of nectar flowed,
> And yellow honey dripped from the green holm-oak.

And Euripides in *The Bacchae*, lines 142 and following:

> The ground flows with milk,
> it flows with wine, it flows with the
> nectar of bees, and a smoke rises there,
> like that of Syrian frankincense.

Therefore, it must be a gross lie with which Strabo burdens Judea when he says: <margin>Book 16.</margin> *The place is not to be envied, nor is it something one would fight over earnestly. For it is rocky, though well-watered, but the land surrounding it is poor...* <note>original Greek: Οὐκ ἐπίφθονον τὸ χωρίον... The author takes offense at the geographer Strabo's dismissive description of the Holy Land's soil quality.</note>

<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred History of Animals.
</margin>

<margin>
Book 5, chapter 6, following.
</margin>

...cursed and waterless <note>original Greek: "ἀρὰν καὶ ἄνυδρον"</note>, a place not to be envied, nor worthy of much fate, over which one would greatly fight: indeed, because it is stony, though it is itself abundant in waters, it is such that the surrounding region is sterile and dry. But Tacitus, though younger than Strabo yet more a lover of the truth, attributes to the same place a **fertile soil**; and to add the testimony of Rabshakeh "in summary" <note>original: "ἐν περιοχῇ"</note>, that most bitter enemy of the Jews, who calls the promised land in 2 Kings 18:32: *a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive trees, oil, and honey* <note>original Hebrew: "ארץ דגן ותירש ארץ לחם וכרמים ארץ זית יצהר ודבש"</note>. Hyblaean honey was once the most highly celebrated, just as it came from Hybla Megara, a place not far from Syracuse, as Cicero writes in *Against Verres, Book 5.*

<margin>
Book 2, in Eutropius.
</margin>

Claudian also mentions it: 
> No one enjoys the true scents of spring,
> Nor spoils the Hyblaean honeycombs from their hiding places,
> If he fears for his brow, or dreads the brambles.
> The thorn arms the roses, the bees protect the honey.

In Poland, Lithuania, and Moscow—indeed, through almost the entire stretch of the North—bees make honey in the forests, in mountain caves, in small hives fixed to trees, and in pits in the ground. From this abundance, honey is usually made in great quantity, and from that supply they create a delicate and healthy drink which they call **Mead** <note>original: "Meth"</note>. On this subject, one should read Paolo Giovio *on the Moscow Legation*, page 542; Maciej z Miechowa, *European Sarmatia*, Book 1, page 515; and Sigismund von Herberstein, *Commentaries on Muscovite Affairs*, page 114.

Among all things which nature in her kindness has granted us to taste, almost nothing is either more pleasing or more healthful than honey. The bees first create the wax and the combs, then they place the honey within them; for this reason, in the writings of Athenaeus, honey is called the "fruit of the wax" <note>original Greek: "ὠκείων"</note>. For whatever they gather from dew and flowers, they vomit from their own mouths into the cells, filling them in one or two days. At the start, however, what they vomit into the cells is very diluted like water, but soon it begins to ferment <note>original: "fervescere," meaning to bubble or work</note>, just like new wine or freshly brewed beer, so that it may be purified in this manner. Once purified by the passage of time and more thoroughly "cooked" <note>concentrated by evaporation</note>, it becomes sweet, then it also thickens, and then it is called honey. Its use was varied among the Ancients, both in eating and in drinking, as well as in other things; regarding this, see Salvatore de Leone on Ecclesiastes chapter 11, verse 3, and Vossius, *On Idolatry*, book 4, chapter 79. Nor is its use any less in Medicine; it restores and recreates the strength, which we are taught by the example 

<margin>
1 Samuel 14:29.
</margin>

of **Jonathan**, who, having tasted the honey, confessed that the light of his eyes was restored to him—that is, he recovered his former strength, which had previously been weakened by hunger, so that his eyes could barely see and his knees could barely support him. That this comes from hunger is taught by the character Curculio in Plautus:

<margin>
Curculio, Act 2, Scene 3.
</margin>

*Darkness rises up, the knees sink from lack of food.*
From the sweetness of honey and its use, many and various metaphors are drawn in Holy Scripture. *How sweet were your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth* <note>original Greek: "ὑπὲρ μέλι τῷ στόματί μου"</note>, cries out the joyful David in *Psalm 119:103*, feeling the unspeakable sweetness and pleasantness of the divine treasure. Regarding this, **Hilary** writes: *Honey is sweet in the mouth, but not also in the throat; for outside the region of the mouth there is no sense of bodily flavors. But words are sweet in the throat, namely, entering into the soul and penetrating the innermost parts; not merely pleasing as food in the mouth, but sweet in that place*

<margin>
In this place, page 496.
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred History of Animals.
</margin>

where the sense of knowledge, prudence, and intelligence resides. And therefore the words are in the throat, and the honey is sweet in the mouth. But just as honey, through the illness of some fevers, softens those bitter things of the mouth that have occurred, so the infused words of God soften the bitterness of our soul and the sad fevers of unhealthy desires, provided they are not merely held in the mouth but swallowed by the throat. On the same *Psalm, Sermon 13, page 695*, **Ambrose**, reflecting on the honey-sweet taste and scent of the Divine word, writes thus: *What the honeycomb is, let Solomon teach us; for you said: Good words are a honeycomb of honey. Truly a good honeycomb, which the Church eats, smelling of the honey gathered by the spiritual richness of many Prophets, like bees.* This is the Honey of which he says: *I have eaten my bread with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk.* The mystical speech of the heavenly Scriptures is like Bread, which strengthens the heart of man, like the stronger food of the word; but persuasive ethical speech is sweet and softer, because the internal parts of the mind are soothed by ethical preaching. The lips of the preacher drip honey when, after hard falls or ruins, the limbs of the fallen soul are warmed again. There is also a more fervent power in the word, as there is in Wine. There is also a clearer speech in the form of Milk. But if you taste Honey, let your palate be Egyptian—that is, holding the sweetness in your sense, but recognizing the symbol with your intellect. For Honey indeed entices the taste, but if tasted too much, it harms the health. Nothing should be given to pleasure from which some disadvantage to health might arise. Honey taken in excess generates bile. Thus, things which are most sweet with too much love become sharp with too much excess. Therefore, let us use honey, but let us enjoy it sparingly. Rarer use is better use, and pleasures recommend themselves by being rare. Therefore, by a similar metaphor of the excessive use of honey, Solomon wished to recommend "nothing in excess" <note>original Greek: "τὸ μηδὲν ἀγὰν"</note> when he said in his *Proverbs* chapter 25, verse 16: *If you find honey, eat as much as is sufficient for you, lest perhaps you be filled with it and vomit it* <note>original Hebrew: "פֶּן־תִּשְׂבַּע מִמֶּנּוּ וַהֲקֵאתָוֹ"</note>. Continuing in the same metaphor, he says in verse 27: *As to eat much honey is not good, so the investigation of the glory of divine things is not glory.* The Old Translator has: *The searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory*; regarding the poor interpretation and abuse of this saying, see Wolfgang Franz, *Sacred History of Animals, part 4, chapter 8, page 783.* In the same way, Jerome draws this toward the pleasures of this world and the enticements of the flesh, and asserts that for this reason it was forbidden to be offered in sacrifices: *The lips of a harlot drip honey, which for a time fattens the throats of those eating, and afterward is found more bitter than gall;* whence they do not offer Honey in the sacrifices of the Lord, and, having rejected the wax (which is the guesthouse of honey), oil is lit in the temple of God, which is pressed from the bitterness of olives.

<margin>
Letter to Gaudentius, column 155, Volume 1.
</margin>

Finally, the Bee is an image of diligence, so that I may conclude with the Bee from where we began, according to the words of Solomon in *Proverbs 6: Go to the bee, and learn how industrious she is* <note>Note: This verse is found in the Septuagint version of Proverbs 6:8, though not in the standard Hebrew/KJV text</note>, a passage which Bochart explains at greater length. While she works not for herself but for others, she is a genuine symbol of the Pastors and Ministers of the Church, who also labor night and day, not for themselves but for God and the Church, by preaching, praying, and serving in other duties that belong to a true Pastor. Whence Cardinal Hugh skillfully compares Pastors with Bees:

### EAGLE
<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
Called *aetos* <note>original Greek: "ἀετὸς"</note> by the Greeks, according to the Etymologist and Eustathius, because it is "always going" <note>original Greek: "διὰ τὸ ἀεὶ ἰέναι"</note>; or from the Hebrew *ayit* <note>original: "עיט"</note>, a bird of prey. In the Holy Language it is *nesher* <note>original: "נשר"</note>, which Bechai (on Genesis 2) derives from the Chaldean *neshar*, meaning to fall or drop off. For every ten years, flying up even to the element of fire, it is scorched and falls into the sea, and then its life is renewed: hence that saying: *Your youth is renewed like the eagle’s* (Psalm 103:5). Finally, in its hundredth year, it falls and dies. Hence the Cabbalists say *nesher* <note>original: "נשר"</note> is an acronym <note>original: "notarikon"</note> for *falling, fire, air* <note>original Hebrew: "נפילה אש רוח"</note>. These are Rabbinic commentaries. Others derive it from *nasra*, which in Arabic means "to pluck with the beak." Others from *shur*, "to gaze," because it looks directly at the sun; for which reason they think the Eagle is called the bird of Jove or of God, because it is accustomed to stretch toward the burning torches of the sun in the heights and to seek the heavens. It is also said to carry its chicks toward the sun to distinguish the genuine from the spurious offspring: if a chick gazes at the sun with fixed eyes, the eagle retains it and acknowledges it as its own; but if its eyes blink, it casts it out as a bastard. However, Basil provides another reason for this:
<margin>Homily 8 on the Hexameron <note>A commentary on the six days of Creation.</note></margin>
> The eagle is said to be a most unjust bird in rearing its offspring. For when it hatches two chicks, it beats one with its wings and drives it away, thrusting it out and casting it down; it rears only the other for its own sake, out of a weariness for nursing. The one it gave birth to, it puts to flight; but they say the "bone-breaker" <term>ossifraga</term>, a bird of kindred sort, does not neglect the one cast out, nor allow it to perish, but takes it up and rears it together with its own chicks.

Ambrose, however, in Book 5, chapter 18 of his *Hexameron*, excuses and acquits the eagle of such lack of affection <note>original Greek: "ἀστοργίᾳ"</note>. He leans toward the former opinion, saying it becomes unkind not out of greed for nursing, but by a trial of judgment; compare the same in his commentary on Psalm 118, page 739. Pliny recounts six kinds of eagles, which you may see in his works. From his catalog comes the "bone-breaker" <note>original: "ossifraga"</note>, so called from breaking bones, which cherishes and feeds the eagle chicks cast from the nest; mention of which is made in Micah 2:3, although translators differ greatly in identifying this bird. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translates it as *phene* <note>original: "φήνην"</note>, followed by the Vulgate and others; Luther translates it as "Goshawk" <note>original: "Habicht"</note>. The German Jews call it the "Bare-foot Falcon," or a type of "Bearded Vulture" <note>original: "Gypaëto"</note>. It is the King of all birds, whom they fear and revere as King. Matthias of Miechów testifies:
<margin>1. Sermon 14, page 509.</margin>
> A certain bird has been brought that lives by prey, the size of an eagle but with longer wings and tail, resembling a hawk more than an eagle, which the Muscovites call *Kiczoth* and the Poles call *Byalozor* <note>The Gyrfalcon.</note> because of its whitening splendor, as it is whitish along the belly. All other birds of prey—hawks, falcons, and the rest—fear it so much that in its presence they tremble, fall, and are overcome.

So says he. In size, strength, and speed, it surpasses all other birds, for which it earned the insignia of empire. In the Scriptures, it is a symbol of Kings, such as Nebuchadnezzar, the most powerful King of the Chaldeans, and the Pharaoh of Egypt (Ezekiel 17:3, 7). To say

<column-break/>

nothing of its epithets among the Poets: for to Pindar it is the "chief of birds" <note>original Greek: "ἀρχὸς οἰωνῶν"</note>, and in the *Olympian Odes*, the "King of birds." So also it was believed to portend omens among the auguries. For as Tarquin was arriving at Rome, an eagle took off his cap and, when it had flown high, replaced it; from which his wife Tanaquil, skilled in augury, understood that kingship was portended for him.
<margin>Isthmian Ode 6.</margin>
Hence among the Gentiles, the sight of an eagle was considered a prosperous and happy omen. Many of the Latin poets state that the eagle gives joyful signs. Petronius says:
->- - - - the Delphic bird from heaven<-
> Gave all happy signs, and cleared the paths of the air.

Claudian, in *The Getic War*:
> All things agree with the words: the tawny armor-bearer
> of the Thunderer <note>Jupiter</note>, while all were watching the clear sky,
> entwined a water-snake <note>hydra</note> seized in its curved feet.

Sidonius in the *Panegyric for Anthemius*:
> Eagles have bound many; and through the sudden world,
> the handmaid wing played with the crowns to come.

By its strength, it conquers not only birds but even the dragons themselves, which it overcomes and kills, as Horace says:
<margin>Book 4, Ode 4.</margin>
->- - - soon into the sheepfolds<-
> its vivid impetus sent the enemy;
> soon the love of feast and fight
> drove it against the resisting dragons.

Among the arguments for its strength, they also include its long life <note>original Greek: "μακροβιότητα"</note>, because it lives for a very long time. The words of Holy Scripture in Psalm 103:5, Micah 1:15, and Isaiah 40:31 seem to attribute a long life to it. There are as many interpretations of these as there are translators, and as many opinions as there are heads. We do not deny that the eagle lives a long time, but to extend it to the five-hundredth year is something we think should be called fabulous, even if Antonio Agelli, Bishop of Acerra, asserts it; these are his words:
<margin>Commentary on Psalm 103.</margin>
> For the eagle, when it grows old, being scorched by the sun and dipping into a spring of water, is found young again. <note>original Greek: "Ὁ ἀετὸς γὰρ ὅταν γηράσῃ, καόμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου, καὶ καταδυόμενος εἰς πηγὴν ὕδατος, πάλιν νέος εὑρίσκεται"</note>

The eagle is renewed every five-hundredth year: scorched by the Sun and merged into a fountain of water, it is found a youth once more. Agelli fell into this error by trusting too much in the authority of the Rabbis, whose opinion we mentioned above. Furthermore, instead of "five-hundredth," one should read "hundredth." It is established by reason and experience that certain birds lead a long-lived life; but that they grow young again and recover the strength of their first age when they have reached extreme old age, I would hardly say of eagles. The Church Fathers, being "lovers of allegory" <note>original Greek: "ἀλληγορόφιλοι"</note>, transferred this passage of the Psalmist not unskillfully to the doctrine of **Regeneration**. Epiphanius refers it somewhat differently to the place of repentance. Nor should the exposition of Saint Augustine be passed over in silence, who suggests that a certain type of the future **resurrection** is prefigured here. Jerome agrees with him:
> That the saints grow young again, and having taken up an immortal body, do not feel the labor of mortals, but are snatched up in the clouds to meet Christ, and by no means hunger, because they have the present Lord as their food.

See Augustine’s words recited in Zehner’s *Sacred Adages*, page 110, and Herman Frey’s *Book of Birds*, page 109. In the loftiness and speed of its flight, it has no equal among birds, since it raises itself into the clouds; hence in Homer's *Iliad* (Book 10, v. 308) it is called "high-flying" <note>original Greek: "ὑψιπετήεις"</note>. Not only does it fly high and raise itself into the sublime, but also swiftly, wherefore...

...whence Apuleius * says of it: *The eagle, when it has raised itself most highly even to the clouds, carried away by its wings, travels all that space where it rains and snows, beyond which peak there is no place for thunder or lightning; it is in the very, as I might say, soil of the ether and the summit of winter. When, therefore, the eagle has lifted itself there, by a tilt of the element to the left or right, it glides with such a mass of body, turning its plucked wings where it pleases with a small rudder of a tail. Thence, looking down upon all things from afar with the untiring rowing of its feathers, and hanging for a little while in a lingering flight in almost the same spot, it looks around and seeks where best to hurl itself from above onto its prey in place of a lightning bolt: seeing at one glance and under the same impulse the cattle in the fields, the wild beasts in the mountains, and men in the cities, all unforeseen from the sky; it decides from where it might pierce with its beak, or where it might hook with its talons, whether a careless lamb or a fearful hare, or whatever winged or woolly creature chance has offered for food.* <note>original Latin: "Aquila cùm se nubium tenus... fors obtulit."</note>

<margin>Proverbs 30:19–20.</margin>
Whence Agur the Wise, in his "physical arithmetology" <note>A method of grouping natural observations by numbers.</note> after he had established "ethical arithmetology," enumerates: I. Five things <note>original Greek: "πράγματα"</note> that are inscrutable: the way of the eagle, the way of a serpent on a rock, the way of a ship in the sea, and the way of a man with a virgin, and the way of an adulterous woman. II. Four things that are hard to bear <note>original Greek: "δυσβάσταυτα"</note> or insupportable (verses 21, 22, 23). III. Four fleeting animals (verses 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29). IV. Four things that walk well, from verse 29 to 32. From this comes the Proverb in Aristophanes' *The Knights*, "an eagle in the clouds" <note>original Greek: "ἀέρος ἐν νεφέλαις"</note>. <margin>The Knights.</margin> It also builds its nest in high trees or rocks, partly so that the chicks are not harmed by smaller birds, and partly so there is no dispute over prey. Hence Job 39:27, 30: *Does the eagle mount up at your command, and make its nest on high? On the rock it dwells and makes its home, on the peak of the cliff and the stronghold.* And Jeremiah 49:16: *Though you make your nest as high as the eagle's, I will bring you down from there.* To this, refer what Cicero says in the second book *On Divination* regarding the same: *No bird,* he says, *flies more vehemently than that one.* Whence many similarities are drawn from the eagle, both from its speed (2 Samuel 1:23; Jeremiah 4:13; Lamentations 4:19) and from its other qualities, both praiseworthy and blameworthy. Great is the love of eagles toward their chicks, which is quite clear from their upbringing. For it is far from the truth, as is commonly thought, that the eagle rarely raises three chicks out of hatred; rather, this should be attributed to the heat of its temperament, because they require much food, which they lack when they are sitting on the eggs. Regarding the Patriarch Jacob, the Holy Pages testify that he commended the blessings and glories of his sons, not shrinking from comparing them to creatures as excellent as they are lowly. He compares Judah to a *Lion*, but Dan to a most vile *reptile*; Naphtali to a timid *Deer*; but Benjamin to a *ravenous wolf*. To declare His supreme love toward the Israelites, God compares Himself to an eagle. For in the third month after the children of Israel had gone out of Egypt, the divine voice renewed the memory of former benefits: how He not only destroyed their enemies with slaughter, <margin>Exodus 19:4.</margin> but even *bore them on eagles' wings*, testifying to His protection by this very noteworthy <note>original Greek: "ἀξιολόγῳ"</note> simile, in which He compares Himself to eagles carrying their chicks on their backs to protect them from the injury of other birds, and to carry the brood out of the reach of arrows. The same comparison is repeated in Deuteronomy: <margin>Chapter 32:11.</margin> *As an eagle spreads its wings, it took*

<column-break/>

<margin>History of animals</margin>
*him up and bore him on its shoulders.* For God to have wings (as Eucherius writes in his *Spiritual Formulas*) signifies that, in the manner of a bird, He gathers and cherishes His chosen ones like chicks under Himself, and protects them from the snares of the Devil and evil men. If we search the pagan books, I believe some explanation of this similarity can be found in Plutarch, <margin>Apophthegms, page 184.</margin> where Pyrrhus replied to his soldiers when they called him an "eagle": *Why should I not be an eagle, lifted up by your arms as if by swift wings?* <note>original Greek: "τί γὰρ ἐμέλλω, τοῖς ὑμετέροις ὅπλοις, ὥσπερ ὠκυπτέροις αἰρόμενος;"</note> On the Mosaic passage, Erasmus Marbachius <margin>Commentaries, page 148.</margin> writes: *He compares Himself to an eagle, which is said to carry its chicks on its back and to fly most highly, so that it may protect them from the injury of both men and other animals.* He says, "I bore you on eagles' wings," as if to say: *As an eagle carrying its chicks on its shoulders flies higher than can be reached by a javelin or harmed by anyone; so I have carried and led you, that you might escape safe and unharmed from all dangers of death.* Compare Zehner, *Sacred Similes*, pages 38, 39, 40. From the speed with which glorified bodies exist after this life, we have said that the saints are compared to eagles. In this similarity, Hugo <note>Hugo of St. Victor</note> is foremost in his *Commentary on Ezekiel*, chapter 1, who gathers into one bundle the qualities for which the saints, even while still in the Church Militant, are compared to eagles:

1. *Because the eagle,* he says, *sharpens its beak on a rock; and the righteous man sharpens his word and food after the example of Christ, who spoke nothing except what was useful.*
2. *In the heat of the Sun, it sheds its old feathers: so the righteous man, in the fervor of desire, puts off the old man with his deeds.*
3. *It is washed in a fountain so that it may be clothed in new feathers: so the righteous man in the fountain of contrition.*
4. *It is patient in hunger; so is the righteous man.*
5. *It looks studiously at its claws; so the righteous man at his final end.* <note>The Latin "novissima" refers to the "last things" or death.</note>
6. *It flies higher than other birds; so the righteous man through contemplation to the Lord.*
7. *The left leg is shorter; so for the righteous man, the care for temporal things is shorter, from which he seeks nothing except necessity.*
8. *It nests on high; so the righteous man through the contemplation of thoughts and desires places his eternal chicks.*
9. *In the nest it places the echite stone, which brings about birth and the hatching of eggs and guards the chicks: this is the memory of the cross of Christ.* <note>The "echite" or eagle-stone was a legendary stone believed to assist in nesting and fertility.</note>
10. *With an unflinching gaze it looks at the Sun; so the righteous man at the Sun of Righteousness.*
11. *It casts out degenerate chicks and trains the vigorous ones to fly: so the righteous man regarding his works or subjects.*
12. *An eagle with a black tail feeds its chicks more easily: so the righteous man, considering his past life, is more ardent in good works.*
13. *The domestic breeched eagle catches the hare: so those robust in continence can plunder others for the Lord.*

Thus says Hugo. Otherwise, in that vision of Ezekiel, interpreters mostly explain the eagle—than which no bird raises itself higher—as referring to John the Evangelist, who, flying higher than his predecessors, began his Gospel from the divinity of Christ. As Saint Augustine says in his *Prologue to this Gospel*, as well as in *Sermon 34 on John* and Book 1 of *The Consensus of the Four Evangelists*, to which also Sedulius refers in the last book of the *Paschal Work*:

> Flying in the manner of an eagle, John seeks the stars with the Word.

Saint Jerome agrees with Augustine in the *Preface to the Gospel of Matthew*, if you attend to the matter itself, although they differ somewhat in the distribution of the animals: *The first face, of a man,* he says, *signifies Matthew, because he began as if concerning a man...*

### From Psalm 64:10, 11.

<margin>Sacred History of Animals.</margin>
The history begins by setting forth the lineage: *The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.* <note>Referring to the Gospel of Matthew, symbolized by the "Man."</note> The second symbol is the **Lion**, representing Mark, in which the "voice of the Lion roaring in the desert" is heard in the first chapter: *The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.* The third is the **Ox**, representing Luke, because he began his account with Zechariah the Priest. The fourth is the **Eagle**, representing John, because, taking up the wings of the eagle and hastening toward higher things, he discourses upon the Word of God. There are also those who wish the four principal Fathers of the Latin Church to be understood through these four animals: specifically, that **Gregory the Great** is designated by the *Man*, as he excelled in adapting moral teachings to humanity in the Holy Scriptures. **Ambrose** is seen in the *Lion*, because of his incredible strength and constancy, by which he barred the Emperor Theodosius from the communion of the Church due to the massacre committed at Thessalonica. **Jerome** is seen in the *Ox*, who labored mightily in the "field" of the Church. Finally, **Augustine** is seen in the *Eagle*, because of his supreme sharpness of mind, by which he surpassed all others. However, this interpretation is foreign both to the spiritual mystery and the context. Because of their speed and power, the great men of the earth are also commonly compared to this bird in the Sacred Scriptures. Thus:

<margin>Hosea 8:1.</margin>
The speed of enemies is indicated, especially Nebuchadnezzar, as Jerome maintains: *Set the trumpet to your throat! Like an eagle he comes against the house of the Lord.* <note>original Latin: "Ad palatum tuum buccina sit..."</note> Pagninus translates this as *against the house of Jehovah.* He calls out the enemy to sound the signal for battle and attack suddenly. The Romans were accustomed to sending a herald to declare war on an enemy, who would hurl a spear into the enemy's territory as a symbol of hostility,

<margin>As reported by Gellius, book 4 of Attic Nights, page 576.</margin>
as reported by Gellius. Here, the trumpet of the Herald is represented, sounding out the battle as a sign and token of a hostile invasion and greed. This is shadowed in the fable of the Eagle snatching the tortoise in Phaedrus, Fable 37, at the beginning of which it is written:

> Against the powerful, no one is sufficiently protected;
> But if a wicked counselor is added,
> Whatever a man and his wickedness attack, it falls.

The Prophet looks toward the insignias of the enemies of the Jewish Church, which were the eagle—both of the Assyrians and the Romans, who utterly destroyed the temple of the Lord and overthrew the Holy City. How sharply the "dull-witted" Jews discern the eagle as the insignia of the Roman Empire is seen in how they interpret this saying: *The Lord shall bring a nation against thee from afar, from the end of the earth, as swift as the eagle flieth; a nation whose tongue thou shalt not understand; a nation of fierce countenance.* <note>Deuteronomy 28:49–50.</note> Regarding the "eagle" of the modern Jews, Menasseh Ben Israel, intending to explain the hieroglyphic of the eagle, writes:

<margin>I. 2. Concerning the determination of life, f. 3. p. 129.</margin>
It should be noted that the word "nation" is used three times here; for Jerusalem felt the force and power of the Romans on three occasions, since the eagle was the insignia of the Romans. First, when the Romans were called to aid Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, the sons of Alexander, against Pompey. Second, when Sosius brought help to Herod against Antigonus, the son of Aristobulus. Third, when the city was closed in siege by Vespasian and his son Titus, and was finally overthrown and utterly destroyed along with the temple. Therefore, when Moses says the nation would be "from a far-off land," understand Rome; and "from the end of the earth," take this to mean the many nations that Vespasian summoned to his aid from

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred History of Animals.</margin>
England, France, Spain, and other regions of the world. Just as the Rabbis are always "nodding off" <note>An idiom meaning they are making errors or being inconsistent.</note> when they look for praise for their own nation, so it is here: they have what they grab at, but the closer they get with their "looking glass," the further they are from the eagle. It happens to them as it does to infants who, when they are weaned, cling to a cup that takes the place of the breast, so that whatever they grab, they soon move it to their mouth as if it were a cup, and then drive it away. Since they were put to flight by the eagle of the Romans, whenever they hear of an eagle—even if it were from the furthest East—they immediately babble about the Roman eagle.

Although the eagle is the foremost of the other birds, it is nevertheless placed among the unclean birds and those <term>not fit to be eaten</term> <note>original Greek: "μή φαγείν"</note>. The reason for this is partly physical and partly mystical. The physical reason is that its meat is unhealthy; for it is difficult to digest, abounds in waste matter, and produces "black bile" <note>A reference to the four humors of medieval medicine.</note>. The mystical reason is that it lives by prey; for God wished to deter man from robbery by this example. And this reason for the prohibition was given by Eleazar to the Legate of Ptolemy Philadelphus, according to Eusebius:

<margin>Book 8 of the Preparation for the Gospel, ch. 3.</margin>
> *All the birds which we use are domestic and clean, nourished by wheat or legumes, such as pigeons, turtledoves, partridges, geese, and others of this sort. But those which are prohibited, you will find are predatory and nourished by the flesh of other birds; by snatching lambs and kids, they also do injury to men, both the living and the dead. All these He rightly named unclean, so that even from this He might deter us from robbery and slaughter, and exhort us to justice, and warn us to live most justly and peacefully, just as all the clean birds do, which do no injury to any other birds nor to anything else. Thus, by these as if they were symbols, He turns the understanding toward justice, etc.*

**THE OWL** (*Bubo*), not the least among the night-wandering birds, of which you will find such a description in Dionysius the Carthusian: *The owl is a base, foul, and funereal bird, a friend of the night, dwelling in tombs and caverns, sluggish, and hated by other birds, by whom it is torn to pieces if it is found by them during the day.* And according to the augurs, it portends evil, because it is funereal and mournful; it enters churches at night to drink the oil from the lamps; when it is attacked by birds, it turns on its back and defends itself with its feet; it hunts and eats mice and bats. It is placed among the unclean birds in Leviticus 11:17 and Deuteronomy 14:16 under the name <term>Tinshemet</term> <note>original Hebrew: "תנשמת"</note>, from <term>Neshef</term> <note>original Hebrew: "נשף"</note>, meaning darkness, obscurity, or twilight. By this, it is indicated that the bird is noted for delighting in darkness and loving to live in the dark. Arias in both places renders it as "night-wanderer"; Tremellius and the Chaldean Paraphrast as "owl"; Schindler as "a bat flitting in the twilight"; the Septuagint, whom Pagninus follows, as "ibis," although in Deuteronomy 14:16 the Septuagint and the Vulgate with them read "swan." Luther in both places uses "Uhu" <note>The German word for the Eurasian Eagle-owl.</note>. Thus the interpreters vary in a marvelous way, so that there are few things upon whose meaning they agree. This bird inhabits deserts—not just desolate places, but also dreadful and inaccessible ones—a monster of the night; compare Pliny, *Natural History*, book 10, chapter 12, of which the Poet says:

> The owl hoots with a horrendous, funereal song.

It is said to be so characteristic and native to Egypt that if it is moved elsewhere, it consumes itself with death <note>A reference to the belief that some animals cannot survive outside their native habitat.</note>; see Aelian, *On Animals*, book 2, chapter 38. It is an image and symbol of adulterers, of which Hugo says: *The owl is a bird...*

<margin>on Leviticus.</margin>

THE STORK, called <term>pelargos</term> <note>original: "πέλαργος"</note> by the Greeks, from <term>pelon</term> <note>original: "πέλον"</note> *black* and <term>argon</term> <note>original: "ἀργὸν"</note> *white*, because it has feathers that are partly white and partly black. In our language <note>The author likely refers to the scholarly language of the time or the Greek root.</note>, it takes its name from <term>storge</term> <note>original: "στοργῇ"</note>, that is, from the burning and pious mutual love that exists between parents and children, as well as between males and females themselves. To the Hebrews it is called <term>chasida</term> <note>original: "חסידה"</note>, meaning <term>beneficent</term> <note>original: "beneficus"</note>, although Luther translates <term>chasida</term> as "heron" <note>original: "Reiger"</note>.

Because it practices <term>chasidut</term> <note>original: "חסידות"</note>, or beneficence, toward its companions by sharing food with them," as the commentator adds. For name-givers usually direct their naming toward some singular <term>physis</term> <note>original: "φύσιν"</note> or nature of the living creatures. By a wise imposition, the name of the stork was given from *piety*, which is why Petronius calls it the "cultivator of piety" <note>original: "pietatis cultrix"</note>; for from <term>chasid</term> <note>the Hebrew word for 'pious' or 'kind'</note> it is called <term>chasida</term>, and it has become for us a symbol of piety and mercy. The Greeks also derived their word <term>antipelargein</term> <note>original: "ἀντιπελαργεῖν," meaning to reciprocate care, literally "to act like a stork"</note> from <term>pelargos</term> in a similar sense, to denote the care children owe their parents. Solinus refers to this: *Storks,* he says, *possess an extraordinary piety. For as much time as they spend nurturing their own young, they themselves are nourished in turn by their offspring.* However, greater piety toward parents is attributed to the *bee-eater* <note>original: "meropi"</note> than to the *stork*; for the latter is said only to feed its parents in old age, while the former does so even when the parents can still provide food for themselves. As a witness to this, we produce Aristotle himself, that most skillful investigator of natural things,

*History of Animals*, Book 9, Ch. 13.

Nevertheless, because of its piety, even if it is not constant, the bird is held in honor by almost all nations, especially among the Thessalians, of whom Clement of Alexandria in his *Exhortation* <note>original: "προτρεπτ."</note> records that they worshipped storks. Others mention the same regarding the Egyptians, citing Lucian in *The Council of the Gods*, whose words are these: <term>I am ashamed to mention the forms, and the apes, and the goats, and other much more ridiculous things, which I know not how have crept from Egypt into heaven.</term> <note>original: "Αἰσχύνομαι δὲ ἰδέας, καὶ πιθήκους εἰπεῖν... εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν."</note> Vincentius Opsopoeus rendered them thus: *I am ashamed to recount the storks, and the monkeys, and the he-goats, and things far more absurd than these; which somehow ascended from Egypt even into heaven.* Vossius, in *On Idolatry, Book 3, p. 1273, Ch. 100*, absolves both nations of the worship of <term>storks</term>. He clears the Egyptians in part, arguing that while "stork-worship" <note>original: "πελαργολατρεία"</note> might be established from this single passage, it actually arises from a confusion between the ibis and the stork; he believes Opsopoeus thought the ibis was a stork, as they at least agree in eating serpents. He thinks the Thessalians can be excused by the testimony of Pliny, who gives the reason* why, by Thessalian law, he who killed a stork was punished no differently than if he had slain a man: *Such great honor is given to them (the storks) for the destruction of serpents, that in Thessaly it was a capital crime to have killed one: and the same penalty was set by law as for homicide.* For a great <term>antipathy</term> <note>original: "ἀντιπάθεια"</note> seethes between storks and serpents, and it is a natural one, because storks search out the hiding places of serpents and devour them, and thus they purge gardens, fields, meadows, and courtyards of toads and snakes. Often, however, they are harmed by the serpents while they are gaping for them, and then they are said to seek out oregano and savory, which they apply to the wound and thus heal themselves. Their meat is fibrous, of bad juice, and difficult to digest; indeed, it is even considered pestilential, and this is for a reason sought from their diet, because they feed on frogs, lizards, toads, and serpents. # SACRED HISTORY OF ANIMALS
### From Psalm 55:10, 11

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...to have touched upon. In the Mosaic law, *their use was forbidden to the Jews, because regarding food they are exceedingly unclean; yet spiritually they represent a clean thing, so that the Israelites might be warned to restrain themselves much more from the impurities and pollutions of souls. They are a type of those who gape only for earthly riches, while meanwhile neglecting and utterly disregarding heavenly things.*
<margin>Leviticus 11:19; Deuteronomy 14:18</margin>

The stork, says Cardinal Hugo <note>Hugo de Sancto Caro (c. 1200–1263), a Dominican cardinal and biblical commentator.</note> in his commentary on Leviticus, *is a white, domestic bird; it eats serpents and purges its belly by inserting its beak through its rear. It signifies certain people who devour the injuries of their neighbors, but, being cruel to themselves, kill their own souls, casting out their own vitals with a most foul mouth.* It is a bird which, if you except its diet, has almost nothing for which it might incur any blame, being endowed with many notable likenesses of virtues. Indeed, they raise their chicks with great care and circumspection; with incredible care, as much as possible, they hatch the chicks and observe mutual turns in incubating, so that while the Father flies out, meanwhile the mother warms the eggs, and while the mother flies out, the father performs the duty at home. They train the hatched and growing chicks in flight, and go before them as leaders in flying, assisting the unskilled and resisting those things that threaten harm to their chicks. This is a symbol for Parents to raise, defend, and nourish their children with great and faithful care.

Furthermore, this bird is very devoted to chastity, and it punishes with a worthy penalty not only an adulterous mate but even a female guest who committed adultery <note>original: "μοιχευσᾶαν"</note> with an ungrateful servant while the Master was absent; Neander produces examples of this in his *Physics* and Aelian in *Book 8, Chapter 19*. It is a symbol for the pious to flee both bodily and spiritual adulteries. The Sacred Scriptures <note>original: "S. Pandectæ"</note> reveal that this is also a bird of a grateful spirit and one that returns favors <note>original: "χαιροεπιδοιαν," likely meaning "repaying joy" or "returning grace"</note>, and with them Aelian in *History of Animals, Book 8, Chapter 21*. 

<margin>Jeremiah 8:7</margin>
On the occasion of the departure and return of storks to warmer places as winter approaches us—as is the common opinion—Basil <note>Saint Basil the Great (c. 330–379), Bishop of Caesarea.</note> writes in his *8th Sermon on the Hexameron*: *The manners of storks, he says, you would say are not far distant from prudence and reason. Thus at one time they all come into our provinces, and thus again, when about to depart, they gather in a certain place, and from there they all withdraw on a fixed day as if by a prescribed law. Our local crows accompany and lead them like lictors <note>Attendants to Roman magistrates; here used as "guards."</note> and bodyguards. Indeed, as it seems to me, they even offer themselves as allies against their adversaries and enemies. The proof of this is: first, that in our provinces at that time no crow is seen at all. Then, when they return with wounds, they bring us clear signs of the help and fighting alliance. Who, I ask, prescribed the laws of hospitality among them? Who threatened them with the punishment for a deserted army, so that absolutely none withdraws from the forces and troops being led? Let those men hear this who do not indulge in hospitality, who shut their doors, and receive neither in winter nor at night pilgrims and strangers even for simple shelter: compare Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397), who also wrote a Hexameron based on Basil’s.</note> discussing this matter more extensively in Hexameron, Book 5, Chapter 16.*

THE DOVE, called <term>columba</term> in Latin, either because it "cherishes the loins" <note>original: "colit lumbos," a folk etymology suggesting frequent reproduction</note> by frequent birthing, or because their necks change colors with every movement <note>original: "conversations"</note>, or from "column" <note>original: "columna"</note> because they build nests in them, or from the "peaks" <note>original: "culminibus"</note> of houses and towers because they are accustomed to frequent and inhabit them. To the Greeks it is <term>peristera</term> <note>original: "περιστερὰ"</note>, which they claim is named from "loving excessively" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τὸ περισσῶς ἐρᾶν"</note>. To the Hebrews it is <term>Yonah</term> <note>original: "יונה"</note>; the origin of which Rabbi Immanuel judges to be from *yanah* <note>original: "ינה"</note>, "to seize," "to oppress," or "to snatch," because the dove is very easy to catch and often perishes as prey for rapacious birds. The STORK is called <term>pelargos</term> <note>Original Greek: πελαργὸς.</note> by the Greeks, from <term>pelos</term> <note>Original Greek: πέλος.</note> meaning black, and <term>argon</term> <note>Original Greek: ἀργὸν.</note> meaning white, because it has feathers that are partly white and partly black. By a wise imposition, the name was given to the stork from <term>piety</term>, which is why Petronius calls it the <term>cultivator of piety</term>; for it is called <term>chasidah</term> from <term>chesed</term> <note>Original: "חסד," meaning kindness or mercy.</note>, and has become for us a symbol of piety and mercy. Solinus refers to this: <term>"In storks," he says, "there is an extraordinary piety. I remember the same thing happened here in Giessen a few years ago, when two younger storks expelled the old ones from the nest, though it was not clear to me or others whether they were the offspring of the former ones. Yet because of its piety, even if it is not perpetual, the stork is held in honor by almost all nations, especially among the Thessalians, whom Clement of Alexandria in his <term>Exhortation</term> <note>Original Greek: προτρεπτ.</note> records as having worshipped storks. Others mention the same regarding the Egyptians, citing Lucian <term>in The Assembly of the Gods</term>, whose words are these: <term>I am ashamed to recount the ibises, monkeys, he-goats, and other far more ridiculous things, which somehow ascended from Egypt into heaven.</term> Vincentius Opsopoeus rendered it thus: <term>I am ashamed to enumerate the storks, and monkeys, and goats, and things far more absurd than these; which I know not how have ascended from Egypt even into heaven.</term> Vossius <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch classical scholar and theologian.</note> absolves both nations from the worship of <term>storks</term> <note>Original Greek: πελαργῶν.</note> in <term>Book 3, On Idolatry, p. 1273, chapter 100.</term> He partially excuses the Egyptians, suggesting that this "stork-worship" <note>Original Greek: πελαργολατρεία.</note> is established from this single passage, yet it may arise from a confusion between the ibis and the stork; for he thinks Opsopoeus believed the ibis was a stork, as they at least agree in their eating of serpents. He thinks the Thessalians can be excused by the testimony of Pliny, who gives the reason* why, by Thessalian law, he who kills a stork is punished no differently than if he had slain a man: <term>So great is the honor given to them (the storks) for the destruction of serpents, that in Thessaly it was a capital crime to have killed one; and the penalty by law was the same as for homicide.</term> For a great <term>antipathy</term> <note>Original Greek: ἀντιπάθεια.</note> seethes between storks and serpents, and it is a natural one, because storks search out the hiding places of serpents and devour them, and thus they purge gardens, fields, meadows, and courtyards of toads and serpents. Often, however, they are harmed by the serpents while they gape at them, and then they are said to seek out oregano and wild basil, which they apply to the wound, and thus they heal themselves. Their flesh is fibrous, of poor juice, and difficult to digest; indeed, it is even considered pestilential, a reasoning drawn from their diet, because they feed on frogs, lizards, toads, and serpents. Among the Romans, Sempronius Rufus, a man of praetorian rank, was the first to serve them at the table and place them among foodstuffs, concerning whom Horace writes: *

> The turbot was safe, and the stork safe in its nest,
> Until a praetorian author taught you otherwise.

Regarding this passage, an ancient commentator records that this epigram was made against Rufus when he suffered a defeat as a candidate:

> *That Rufus, the preparer of storks,*
> *Is here, more elegant than two vagabonds.*
> *He did not carry seven votes of the ballots.*
> *The people of the storks have avenged the death.*

Concerning the same bird and its consumption, Pliny should also be heard in <term>Book 10, Chapter 23</term>, whose words are these: <term>Cornelius Nepos, who died during the reign of the Divine Augustus, when he wrote that thrushes caught a little before were being fattened, added that storks were more pleasing than cranes; whereas now this bird is sought among the first, while no one wants that one—</term>

<header>From Psalm 50, verses 10–11 <note>In the Vulgate, these verses correspond to Psalm 51:10–11 in modern English Bibles; the text uses these creatures to illustrate spiritual purity and the care of the soul.</note></header>

<margin>History</margin> it [the stork] has touched upon literature. In the Mosaic law, the use of these birds as food was forbidden to the Jews because they were considered highly unclean, serving as a warning to the Israelites <margin>Lev. 11:19</margin> <margin>Deut. 14:18</margin> to restrain themselves much more from the impurities and pollutions of their souls. They are a type <note>In biblical interpretation, a "type" is a symbol or foreshadowing.</note> of those who gape only for earthly wealth, while meanwhile neglecting celestial things entirely. *The stork*, says Cardinal Hugh <note>Hugh of Saint-Cher (c. 1200–1263), a Dominican friar and biblical commentator.</note> in his commentary on Leviticus, *is a white, domestic bird; it eats snakes, and by inserting its beak into its rear, it purges its belly: and it signifies certain people who devour the injuries of their neighbors, but in being cruel to themselves, they kill their own souls, discharging their own guts through a most foul mouth.* If you disregard its diet, it is a bird that has almost nothing for which it might incur blame, being endowed with many notable images of virtue. Indeed, they raise their young with great care and circumspection; they hatch their chicks with incredible diligence whenever possible and take turns in brooding, so that while the father flies out, the mother warms the eggs, and while the mother flies out, the father performs the duty at home. They train the hatched and growing chicks in flight, going before them as leaders, assisting the inexperienced ones, and resisting those things that threaten their young with harm. This is a symbol for parents to educate, defend, and nourish their children with great and faithful care. Furthermore, this bird is very devoted to chastity, and will punish an adulteress—or even a guest who commits <term>adultery</term> <note>original Greek: μοιχεύειν (moicheuein)</note> with an ungrateful servant while the master is away—with a fitting penalty; Michael Neander in his *Physics* and Aelian in *Book 8, chapter 19* provide examples of this. It is a symbol for the pious to flee from both physical and spiritual adultery. The *Sacred Pandects* <note>A reference to the collection of sacred laws or scriptures.</note> and Aelian <margin>Jer. 8:7</margin> in *On the Nature of Animals, Book 8, chapter 21*, reveal this bird to be of a grateful spirit and free from <term>malice</term> <note>original Greek: κακοηθείαν (kakoeitheian)</note>. Regarding the departure and return of storks to warmer places when winter approaches us, as is the common opinion, Basil writes in *Sermon 8 on the Hexameron*: *The customs of storks... you would say are not far removed from prudence and reason. Thus, they all come to our provinces at one time; likewise, when the flock is about to depart, they gather in one place, and from there they all withdraw on a prescribed day as if by law. Moreover, our native crows accompany and lead them like lictors and satellites. Indeed, as it seems to me, they offer themselves as allies against their very adversaries and enemies. The evidence for this is: first, that in our provinces at that time, absolutely no crow is seen. Then, returning with wounds, they bring us clear signs of the help and combat they shared.* Who, I ask, prescribed the laws of hospitality among them? Who threatened them with the punishment of a deserted army, so that not one withdraws from the forces and troops to be led? Let those men hear this who do not indulge in hospitality and shut their doors, receiving foreign travelers with no shelter either in winter or at night: compare Ambrose discussing this more at length in *Hexameron, Book 5, chapter 16*.

THE DOVE is so named because it "cherishes the loins" <note>A folk etymology playing on the Latin *columbas* and *colit lumbos*.</note> by frequent birthing, or because their necks change colors with every movement, or from "column," because they build in them, or from the "summits" of buildings and towers, because they are accustomed to dwell and live in them. The Etymologist derives it <term>from the word "to swim/dive"</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τὸ κολυμβᾷν (apo to kolymban)</note>, from which comes <term>kolymbis</term> <note>original Greek: κολυμβίς</note>, the name of an 

<column-break/>

aquatic bird in Aristotle’s *History of Animals, Book 8, chapter 3* and Athenaeus, *Book 9*. <margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> Nor does Scaliger deny this in his notes *on Varro*, based on the gesture these birds make. But in almost all these delights of the Grammarians, <term>the matter remains sacred</term> <note>original Greek phrase suggesting the topic is beyond simple linguistics: ὑπὲρ ἱερὸν ὑπάρχει</note>. To the Greeks it is <term>peristera</term> <note>original Greek: περιστερά</note>, which they claim is so named <term>because of its excessive love</term> <note>original Greek: ὡς πρὸς τὸ περισσῶς ἐρᾶν</note>; to the Hebrews it is <term>Yonah</term> <note>original Hebrew: יוֹנָה</note>, the origin of which Rabbi Immanuel judges to be from <term>yanah</term> <note>original Hebrew: ינה</term>, meaning to seize, oppress, or snatch, because the dove is very easy to catch and often perishes as prey for raptors. Rabbi David [Kimhi] takes the origin of the name from the idea that <term>Yonah</term> <note>original Hebrew: יון</note> is a shortened form of <term>Yehoyonah</term> <note>original Hebrew: יהויונה</term>, meaning "the grace of God," because this bird, among others, was most pleasing to God and very celebrated in sacrifices. Others derive it from <term>yayin</term> <note>original Hebrew: יין</note>, wine, for there is a certain kind of wild dove which is called <term>oinas</term> <note>original Greek: οἰνάς</note>, that is, according to Gaza’s translation, a *vinago* [stock-dove]; in Syriac, it is a name composed of "vine" and "dove." *Charmiona* was the name of Cleopatra’s handmaid, according to Plutarch <margin>in the Life of Antony.</margin>. Others say it comes from the *Ionians*, that is, the Greeks, by whom it was carried into Asia, an opinion Bochart agrees with. Finally, others have thought it comes from <term>yaven</term> <note>original Hebrew: יון</note>, meaning mire and mud, against whom Rabbi Immanuel rightly inveighs; see Salazar <margin>Commentary on Proverbs 1:4, p. 34.</margin>. The color of the feathers—to begin with external splendor and beauty—is silvery, mixed with a pale gold. The eyes are chaste and lovely, and of such dignity that the eyes of the celestial bride are compared to the eyes of doves; we read this in <margin>2 Esdras 5:26; Song of Sol. 4:1.</margin> 2 Esdras 5:26 as being applied to the Jewish Church, though the unanimous opinion of all interpreters is that it should be understood as the universal Church. Thus says Abbot Williram <note>Williram of Ebersberg (d. 1085), a German Benedictine abbot known for his paraphrase of the Song of Songs.</note>:

> One dove, perfect in beauty for me.
> One beloved by her mother, her bringer-forth.
> Although from many persons and faces
> the people of the Church gather themselves, and in two
> orders, whether they complete the number of teachers
> to the end: yet this my assembly obeys the same
> Spirit, in whose gift she rejoices,
> preserving the beautiful dove-like duties of life
> and of her mother, whose name is the "vision of peace"
> now traveling abroad, a rival, for her strong, lovely
> -> father <-

> she still hopes for the heavenly citizens already joined to me.

This devout man refers at the same time to *Song of Solomon 6:7–8*, where the Bridegroom of the Church himself sings of the Church: *There are sixty queens, and eighty concubines, and young women without number.* But *verse 8*: <term>she is the only one</term> <note>original Hebrew: אחת היא (achat hi)</note>, <term>my dove is the only one</term> <note>original Greek: μία ἐστὶ περιστερά μου (mia esti peristera mou)</note>, <term>my perfect one</term> <note>original Hebrew: תמתי (tamati)</note>, <term>she is the only one of her mother</term> <note>original Hebrew: אחת היא לאמה (achat hi le-immah)</note>, <term>she is the only one of her mother</term> <note>original Greek: μία ἐστὶ τῇ μητρὶ αὐτῆς (mia esti tē mētri autēs)</note>, <term>she is pure to her who bore her</term> <note>original Hebrew: ברה היא ליולדתה (barah hi le-yoledetah)</note>, <term>she is chosen for her who bore her</term> <note>original Greek: ἐκλεκτή ἐστι τῇ τεκούσῃ αὐτὴν (eklektē esti tē tekousē autēn)</note>. He indeed established several particular Churches throughout the whole world, but from all these he established the one Catholic or universal Church, which he recognizes as his bride. Osiander proves Williram’s verses in his Paraphrase when he says: *It was signified that there are many Churches scattered here and there in the world, some of greater reputation and fame, others of less. But from all these is gathered one Church, the number of the Elect: this is most dear to Christ, whom he cannot hate; this is that one of which we say in the Creed: I believe in the holy catholic Church, the communion of Saints, etc.* But while the Bridegroom continues in this comparison in *chapter 4, verse 1*...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> ...and again, he grants his Bride dove-like eyes. Martin Luther <note>original: "B. Lutherus"</note> understands "eyes" in this passage to mean leaders and teachers. "The eyes," he says, "are the leaders and teachers": he calls them dove-like, which is to say, *distinguished by simplicity, for this is especially required in a Teacher, that he remain in the simplicity of doctrine and religion.* But let us observe here that this Bride has dove-like eyes in the presence of the Groom, for in the eyes of the world, nothing is judged more foul or deformed. For the wisdom of the flesh cannot judge this appearance; even if it sees and hears it, it still sees it as if through colored glass. Osiander, along with Williram in his Paraphrase, explains this as the faith and simplicity with which the Bride shines in the eyes of the Groom, or before the Groom, who is pleased by her purity of heart and Spirit. For the dove is celebrated for its purity, because it drinks only the clearest water, and does so specifically so that it can guard itself against hawks, whose image the water reflects. Regarding the Groom’s eyes, the Bride likewise <margin>Song of Solomon 5:12.</margin> sings: *His eyes are like doves by the rivers of waters, washed with milk, and fitly set*, as Pagninus and Arias read it. Others say *upon the fullness*, that is, as Mercerus <note>Jean Mercier (c. 1510–1570), a French Hebraist.</note> excellently explains: as if placed and enclosed in the bezel <note>original: "pala," the part of a ring that holds a gemstone</note> in which a gem is set—meaning neither protruding too far from the head, nor too deeply sunken, both of which are unsightly and deformed in eyes; but rather set in their sockets like precious stones in their settings. For <term>מִלֵּאת</term> (*malleth*) is *fullness*, and signifies the bezel that is filled with a precious stone. The meaning is that Christ’s eyes of mercy are so fashioned that he looks upon those who repent, but turns away from the impenitent. And while the dove is studious of purity and is greatly delighted by it, it is no wonder that it is also delighted by the purity of the Church's religion and life, and desires the water of no fountain unless it be drawn from the fountain of Israel, that is, Holy Scripture. To this, Abbot Willeramus <note>Williram of Ebersberg (d. 1085).</note> aims in his rhythms:

> Hence the eyes are like beautiful doves above all.
> Those which, washed first in milk, learn of the bitter river.
> Since a man is seen as a special grace to the Groom,
> From the Godhead he remains, that he may give spiritual
> Gifts to his dear ones; so that the harmony of peace
> And the duties of a dove-like life might delight them.
> Let them first strive to sit by the living streams
> Of Holy Scripture: but after the milk of history,
> Let them strive to love the rivers of sacred words,
> Searching out the hidden and deep meanings:
> In which they may see the hostile snares of Satan:
> In the manner of doves, which reside on the shore of the waters.

So that in this way they may recognize the approaching hawk. From this care and love which the Bride of Christ has for clean waters, there arise and proceed the praises which the heavenly Groom grants to his Bride, concerning <margin>4 Heroic Poems p. 592.</margin> which Barlaeus <note>Caspar Barlaeus (1584–1648), a Dutch polymath.</note> writes in his commentary on Song of Solomon 4:1:

> How my queen, excelling the Syrian girls,
> Proceeds with the most beautiful, honored face for me,
> Whiter than a swan, softer than a suckling lamb,
> Charming, playing with gentle, dove-like eyes,
> That you might believe her more truly mine, and that she
> Loathes the deceits and guiles of the wicked. Nothing in her mind is bloody,
> Nothing cruel or threatening. In all her limbs, clemency

<column-break/>

Shines forth, and her angers are broken by gentle pursuits. <margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> By flight she returns to her dovecote; she lives, however, not only in dovecotes where she has windows or holes in which she nests—as Scripture itself testifies in Isaiah 60:8—but also, for fear of the hawk, in the clefts of the rocks, as in Song of Solomon 2:14 and Jeremiah 48:28. This is a living likeness of the Church, which the serpent besieges from within and the hawk from without; that is, the heretics by their heterodoxy and the impious by their impiety, as well as the enemies outside who persecute the Church and shed the blood of the truly faithful. Williram understands the *clefts of the rock* to mean divine protection and the assistance of angels. Luther understands it as the pure exercise of religion in the Temple of Jerusalem, not on mountains and hills after the manner of the Gentiles. Osiander explains it as the persecutions where the faithful had to hide themselves in high cliffs and the hidden places of mountains for the sake of preserving their lives, as the first book of Maccabees and ecclesiastical history testify. *Come now, my dearest*, he says in his Paraphrase, *you who until now have found it necessary to retreat to hidden and remote places because of the storm of persecutions, so that you seemed not destroyed but banished from the world: come forward, make yourself seen in the world, restore public assemblies and divine worship (abolished by tyrants), let the voice of the preaching of the Gospel be heard, and the voice of Psalms, with which you praise God for the liberation you received, and for his benefits both physical and spiritual. Because divine worship is most pleasing to me, and your praises, which you sing to me, your God, are most sweet in my ears.* Barlaeus sticks to the same paraphrase: <margin>4 Heroic Poems p. 590.</margin>

> You who just now lay hidden, afflicted in the hiding places of rocks,
> As a dove is accustomed to do when the kite flies around,
> After the darkness I restore the day to you, more manifest to the world
> To be seen. Speak, to which Master do you wish to be indebted?

Christ is the Rock of Salvation; <margin>Matthew 16:18, 1 Corinthians 10:4.</margin> the faithful hide themselves in his wounds, and there is the safe habitation of the soul through meditation and imitation, says Manuel Sa <note>original: "Emanuel Saa" (1530–1596), a Portuguese Jesuit theologian.</note> in his notes on this passage, which we accept only in a sound sense—namely, concerning the hearing of the Word and the faith conceived therefrom. This is that bird which, sent out from the Ark, returned within the Ark, carrying in its mouth an olive leaf as a sign of the ceasing flood and of peace made between God and men, concerning which Avitus <note>Alcimus Ecdicius Avitus (c. 450–518), Bishop of Vienne and poet.</note> says: <margin>Book 4.</margin>

> Immediately he sends the white dove from its seat;
> Mindful of the command, she seeks the fields with rapid flight,
> and seeing the branch of the greening olive of peace,
> She plucks it, and carries it back in her gentle, white beak.

Regarding the dove as a messenger in Deucalion’s flood—indicating a storm when it entered the ark, but serenity when it flew out—what else should we say but that this was fashioned from, or rather borrowed from, the Sacred Book and the history of the universal cataclysm, and attributed to that particular flood which takes its name from Deucalion? Plutarch mentions this in *On the Cleverness of Animals, page 968*: *The mythologists say that for Deucalion, a dove sent out from the ark became a sign: returning inside when there was a storm, but flying away when there was fair weather.* Augustine <note>original: "Augustinus"</note> in his *6th Tractate on John* establishes a comparison between the raven and the dove: *The raven was sent from the ark and did not return; the dove was sent and did return. And if the ark figured the Church, it certainly seems that in this flood of the world, the (visible) Church must contain both types.*

It contrasts the dove's vulnerability to "hawks" (persecutors) with its safety in the "clefts of the rock" (Christ or divine protection).</summary>

<header>from Psalm 50, verses 10, 11.</header>
