...and the raven, that is, those who seek their own interests; and the dove, that is, those who seek the things that are of Christ. When Martin Luther was explaining this history regarding the herald of divine peace <note>The dove returning to Noah’s Ark with an olive branch.</note>—to speak with Tertullian* <margin>Against the Valentinians, p. 284.</margin>—he concludes that the olive branch is a type <note>A "type" is a person, thing, or event in the Old Testament seen as a foreshadowing of the New Testament.</note> of the Gospel, namely, the word of peace between God and man. He relates ten qualities of the dove that are most fitting for the Church of the New Testament, which pious antiquity included in these verses:

->*The dove lacks gall, harms not with its beak, and its talons*<-
->*Are innocent; it gathers only pure grains.*<-
->*It delights in waters, and flocking together, in swift flight*<-
->*It seeks safety; it raises the offspring of another.*<-
->*The male himself cherishes the young and sits upon the eggs,*<-
->*While preserving the chaste bonds of marriage.*<-

The latter part of these verses is also read this way:

->*It is frequent at the waters, and is carried through the air*<-
->*By swift wing; instead of a song, it moans with a mournful voice.*<-
->*It raises the chicks of another, and flies in flocks,*<-
->*And strives to build its nest in safe places.*<-

Indeed, the dove does not entirely lack gall <note>The "gall" or "bile" was historically associated with anger or bitterness.</note>, but it does not have bile as abundantly as other animals; therefore, it is false that doves are devoid of bile. Although they do not collect it in a vessel under the liver <note>The gallbladder.</note>, they nevertheless discharge it through a biliary pore to the intestines. Thus, Galen does not without merit mock the contrary opinion in *On Black Bile, chapter 9*, as does Aristotle in *History of Animals, book 2, chapter 15*, where he says that the gall is attached to the liver in some, but not at all in others; some even lack gall entirely. He notes that all birds and fish have gall, and in some fish it is placed in the liver, while in others it is attached to the intestine and hangs from the liver by certain continuous, extremely thin passages. In some, it even occupies both positions. Having said these things, he adds: <gloss>The situation is similar among birds; for some have [the gall] near the stomach. Some have the bile near the intestines, such as the dove, raven, quail, swallow, and sparrow. Others have it near the liver and the stomach at the same time, such as the hawk and the kite.</gloss> The matter is similar in birds. *Some indeed have gall near the stomach; some near the intestines, like the dove, raven, quail, swallow, and sparrow; some near the liver and the stomach, like the capriceps; some also near the intestines at the same time, like the hawk and the kite.* The dove is indeed very gentle, so much so that hardly any bird is found more gentle than the dove; yet, when it perceives its nest has been violated, then it becomes wild with a throat full of complaint and fierce pecks of its beak, as witnessed by Pliny in *Natural History, book 10, chapter 34*, and Aelian in *History, book 3, chapter 44*. The old translator <note>The Latin Vulgate.</note> inserts the Dove into the Prophecy of Jeremiah, *chapter 25, verse 38*: *Their land has become a desolation because of the wrath of the oppressor*, <note>Hebrew: *mipne charon hayyonah*.</note>. The Old Version: *Their land was made a desolation from the face of the wrath of the dove.* Luther: *Thus their land is destroyed before the wrath of the tyrant.* Zanger: *Their land is laid waste before the wrath of the doves.* There is a dispute here concerning the word *hayyonah*, which for Arias Montanus denotes a "devastator," from the root *yanah*, meaning to afflict, to oppress, or to inflict violence. The "wrath of the dove" does not fit here for the desolation of an entire territory, since it is a gentle animal and possesses hardly any wrath. We do not know what "enraged doves" might be flying around in the brain <note>A satirical comment on translators who take the literal "dove" meaning in a context of violent destruction.</note>. By the same error, in the words of Zephaniah, *chapter 3, verse 1*, <note>Hebrew: *Hoy mor'ah wenig'alah ha'ir hayyonah*</note>, where a city

<column-break/>

inflicting violence, or plundering, afflicting, and oppressing is noted, <margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> Zanger explains it as being about a dove, translating without judgment: *Woe to the rebellious and redeemed city* of doves. These are fragments <note>original: *ἀποσπασμάτια*</note> from the Vulgate version: *Woe to the provoking and redeemed city, the dove.* Luther: *Woe to the hideous, filthy, tyrannical city.* That the Prophet is speaking of Nebuchadnezzar is beyond controversy, but by what appearance of truth he should or could be called a "dove" here is something the interpreters sweat over, especially the defenders of the Vulgate. Jerome thinks he could be called a dove in the same way that Nebuchadnezzar is called a "servant of God." Others think he is so named because of his speed, and his "flight," as it were, to the slaughter. Others say the King of Babylon is so called because he carried the dove as a sign upon his military standards <note>original: *vexillum*</note>. For this was done in honor of Queen Semiramis, whom the Syrians worshipped in the form of a dove, as Diodorus writes in *book 3, chapter 8*. And Rupertus, in his *Notes to Besold, pages 39 and following*, reports that the Samaritans worshipped doves to gain the favor of the Assyrian King; compare *Ursinus, Volume 2, Analecta book 1, chapter 7, page 9*, regarding the cult of doves. Cardinal Hugo <note>Hugh of Saint-Cher (c. 1200–1263), a Dominican biblical exegete.</note> collected a great heap of yawning gaps <note>original: *ἀχασμῶν* (referring to far-fetched or empty explanations)</note>: *Just as in these regions the swallows*, he says, *fly down to warm regions and return in summer: and just as doves fly from Palestine toward the North in summer and return to Palestine in winter, so Nebuchadnezzar came from the North into Palestine to make a winter of captivity in it, and therefore he is called a dove. Furthermore, one may observe in the dove that it retains the same voice among birds in both adversity and prosperity, just as the sheep does among the types of four-legged animals. Regarding its cry, <margin>on Psalm 54, column 529, Volume 8.</margin> Augustine* writes: <note>original: "Columba pro figno dilectionis ponitur, & in ea gemitus amatur..."</note> > The dove is positioned as a sign of love, and in it, its moaning is beloved. Nothing is so familiar with moaning as the dove; it moans day and night, as if placed here in a world where one must mourn.

The voices of doves are called "murmurs" by some, and "groans" or "moans" by most. Scripture compares to them all sorts of suppressed sobs <margin>Isaiah 38:14.</margin> *Isaiah 38:14; 59:11. Ezekiel 7:16. Nahum 2:7.* but especially the gestures of the pious, who in the depths of distress express their pain only through a silent groan or frequent sighs, just as Hezekiah, when placed in his death-struggle, confesses concerning himself. In nature, the dove is simple, though not fatuous or foolish, yet it is rarely secure unless it remains in the rocks or its nests. Whence Bo<margin>Book of Animals 9, chapter 36.</margin>naventure *Sermon 53 on the Saints* teaches from Aristotle: that hawks are of three kinds that capture and hunt doves. Some capture doves only when they are sitting on the ground. Some capture them while flying. Others, again, capture them while the doves are letting themselves down into trees. But the doves can easily free themselves from the snares of all these and escape them out of an innate prudence. It escapes the first hawk by flying into the air. The second, by casting itself to the ground. The third kind, by raising itself back into the air again. Thus, by speed of flight, it escapes the snares of hawks—specifically when it observes its simple flight; but when it neglects this and beats its wings, or revels out of a certain pride and confidence, then it is easily captured and torn apart by the hawk. For they can be very easily seduced and thus captured, whence *Hosea 7:11* compares the Israelites to a <term>פותה</term> <note>Hebrew: *potah*; "silly" or "seduced"</note>, <term>אין לב</term> <note>Hebrew: *ein lev*; "without heart," meaning without understanding or sense</note>, *silly dove without heart*, as rendered by Arias and Pagninus; one easily trustful, who can be persuaded of anything, from the root <term>פתה</term> <note>Hebrew: *patah*; to be seduced, enticed, or persuaded</note>. Vatablus renders it: "one who easily casts herself into a net." The Greeks use *ἄνους* <note>Greek: *anous*; senseless</note>; Aquila uses *θελγομένη* <note>Greek: *thelgomene*; enchanted or beguiled</note>. Symmachus uses *ἀπατωμένη* <note>Greek: *apatomene*; deceived</note>. Luther uses *eine verlockte Taube* <note>German: "a lured dove"</note>. For just as it is a virtue in the dove that it harms no one, so it is a vice that it does not watch out for itself. Luther paraphrases this comparison from Hosea thus: > This simile, he says, is quite elegant, taken from domestic life: a dove is the most easily deceived of all birds, so much so that it forgets its own nest. So also Ephraim <note>A name often used to represent the Northern Kingdom of Israel.</note> became accustomed to a foreign nest, while deserting God and the temple; he seeks help not from God, whose name dwelt in Jerusalem, but from the neighboring nations, the Egyptians and Assyrians.

Jerome approaches this comparison in Hosea with another intention, and seeks the point of comparison in another property of doves. > It is asked why Ephraim was compared not to other birds, but to a dove? Other birds hasten to protect their chicks at the risk of their own lives, and when they see a hawk, a snake, a raven, or a crow approaching their nest, they fly here and there and throw themselves in, tearing with beak and talons, and testifying to the parent's pain with a plaintive voice. The dove alone does not grieve for her stolen chicks, nor does she seek them. And therefore Ephraim is rightly compared to her, because he does not feel that his people are being devastated piece by piece, but is negligent of his own salvation. In the swiftness of its wings, however, lies the dove's safety; hence the Psalmist <margin>Psalm 55:7</margin> *longs for the wings of a dove for himself, so that he might flee from his enemies and turn away from their insane violence.* Jerome applies these words of the Psalmist to Christ. *Not from another,* he says, *did I send the supreme flight for escaping death, but from myself: I have the power to lay down my life, so that I may return from the darkness to the heavens.* Moreover, in the dove, he designates a spiritual nature, just as was shown at the Baptism <note>The Baptism of Jesus, where the Holy Spirit descended like a dove.</note>. The dove is a simple animal, without gall <note>Ancient science believed doves lacked a gallbladder, making them symbols of lack of bitterness or malice.</note> and foreign to the malice of bile: it signifies the soul's kiss of charity, because the Church has two wings, that is, the two precepts of charity: namely, love of God and of neighbor. Elsewhere, however, he also explains this regarding the faithful, who, having neglected earthly things, desire *τὰ ἀνώτερα* <note>Greek: *ta anotera*; the things above</note> in mind and soul. There was frequent use of doves in sacrifices, yet only the young were offered, whereas turtledoves were only offered as adults. The method of slaughtering <margin>Leviticus 1:15.</margin> was unique: the throats were not cut with iron, but with the fingernail alone, which the Greeks call *ἀπονυρίζειν* <note>Greek: *aponyrizein*; to pinch off with the nail</note>, and Luther calls *abkneipffen* <note>German: "to nip off"</note>. Now, *ἀπονυρίζειν* signifies not only to break something off with a nail, but also to wound with a nail. Pagninus translates <term>מולק</term> <note>Hebrew: *molaq*; to wring off or pinch the head</note> as "and he shall twist," and the Vulgate as "with the head twisted back to the neck and the place of the wound broken, he shall make [the blood] run down." From such frequent use of doves in sacrifices—since the poor, lest they be without a sacrifice, offered young doves and turtledoves—an abuse <margin>John 2:14.</margin> arose *, when by the permission of the Priests, who had an interest in it, burnt offerings were for sale in the temple itself; from which the Priests confiscated a double profit for themselves, partly from the seller and partly from the buyer. The value of the dove's dung at five pieces of silver—that is, an imperial coin and a quarter—and its use is a matter of disagreement among authors. The "fourth part of a <term>cab</term><note>A 'cab' or 'kab' was an ancient Hebrew measure of capacity, roughly equal to 2 liters.</note> of dove’s dung" involves the Hebrew word <term>dibiionim</term> <note>original: דביונים</note>, a compound and similarly obscene term. According to the consonants, it would be two words: <term>chari yonim</term> <note>original: חרי יונים</note>, meaning the excrement of doves, or that which exits from the "opening" of doves. For <term>char</term> <note>original: חר</note> generally means an opening; by a figure of speech, it refers to the anus, the opening of the hindquarters from which waste exits. But because the word *dibiionim* is considered obscene, the Masoretes <note>Jewish scholars who standardized the Biblical text</note> substituted a reading in the margin using the word <term>dibyonim</term>, a word composed from <term>dub</term> <note>original: דוב</note>, meaning a flow, or dung or liquid manure flowing from doves according to Rabbi Solomon; or simply the excrement of doves according to Kimchi, and so on. Thus, the ancient Hebrews wished to preserve honor in the reading and pronunciation of the Holy Word of God, so that words which were obscene in common and secular use would not offend the ears of anyone in a sacred context. <margin>chapter 3.</margin> Hence the tradition read at the end of the Talmudic Book *Megilla*: "All words written in the Law which are obscene, they read them honorably." See examples in 2 Kings 10:27 and Isaiah 36:12. Junius translates it: *And a fourth part of the crop itself, which is in the cavity of the doves,* a version regarding which Piscator says he is doubtful. As for the use of dove's dung, there are some among the Hebrews who say they used dove's dung during times of siege to kindle fire due to a lack of wood. Others interpret it as those grains which were taken out of the crop of the dove’s throat, which they ate in time of famine. Bochart contends, citing many Arabic sources, that "dove’s dung" is a name for a certain kind of chickpea. Josephus, and many others who follow him along with Theodoret, believe that in such great poverty that dung served as a substitute for salt; without such seasoning, an ass's head would have been entirely tasteless, since that dung contains much saltiness and is therefore fit for seasoning food. Compare Hackspan’s *Philological-Theological Notes* on this passage. He commends the dove because it pleased the Holy Spirit to appear in its form as a witness <margin>Homily 12 on Matthew.</margin> during the baptism of Christ. Chrysostom* gives the reason for this when he says: *Why did He come in the form of a dove? This animal is gentle and clean: because He is the Spirit of gentleness, He therefore appeared in its form.* In another Commentary, Homily 4, he continues: *The Holy Spirit took the form of a dove because, above all animals, this one is the cultivator of love. For all forms of righteousness which the servants of God have in truth, the servants of the Devil can also have in pretense. But the unclean spirit cannot imitate the love of the Holy Spirit alone. Therefore, the Holy Spirit reserved this private form of love for Himself, so that the Holy Spirit might be recognized by no one’s righteousness or testimony as much as by the grace of love;* compare Ambrose, Sermon 21 on the Epiphany, Augustine, *On the Trinity* Book 2, Chapter 6, and *On the Christian Struggle* Chapter 22. We are not permitted to be too <margin>Commentary on Leviticus, column 607.</margin> lengthy in our praises of the dove; therefore, let this be the concluding summary from Martinus Borrhaus*: *How much praise is given to doves in the Holy Scriptures is not hidden. This bird was worthy to bring the news of peace when sent from the Ark, as it is considered a bird of mild temperament, simple and lacking in deceit, even by the testimony of the Lord: "Be simple as doves." Hence the Bride is compared to a dove: "Your eyes are as doves." In doves, a straight flight is also commended,* as the Prophet says: *Who will give me wings like a dove that I may fly?* And *among birds, the dove alone having feathered feet represents to us the Divine Spirit, who flies straight to us with an ardent affection of love, which is signified by the feet. For announcing and opening the oracles of eternal peace, He was sent to the apostles in the form of a dove. The dove was therefore assigned to divine sacrifice, so that by this sacred sign the Israelites might be reminded of patience, innocence, simplicity, modesty, peace, and love—virtues which they themselves should contemplate in Christ the victim and imitate. For it is said that among them, modesty is the first constant faith of marriage, which they never violate; they have singular patience toward a commanding mate, and a great love for their offspring. All these virtues you find in Christ and the Church.*

<column-break/>

<margin>

</margin>

-> **THE RAVEN**, named from the Hebrew *Erev* <-

Specifically, with the first letter <term>Ayin</term> (ע) pronounced more frictionally like a 'g', and later changing the 'g' into a 'c', it becomes *coreb* or *corev*, then *corv*, since the 'b' here is pronounced more softly like the consonant 'v'. And finally, with the Latin termination added, it becomes *corvus* (raven), which is denoted by this word. From the same word, by a transposition of letters, also comes the German *Rabe*. Aveharius links <term>Erev</term> (עָרֵב) to raven. The Latins, using 'c' for the Hebrew letter *Ayin*, say *corvus*, and the Germans by dropping the initial sound say *Rab* or *Rapp*; unless, as Vossius* says <margin>On Idolatry, chapter 85.</margin>, you would rather have this derived from the German and Dutch *rooven* or *rapen*, which means to snatch or seize. The Hebrew name is from *Erev*, which among other things also means to grow dark toward evening, to be obscured, or to grow shadowy. Thus the raven is named—called *korax* by the Greeks—by the Hebrews from its black color, and that is from its nature and constitution, or the "starlit" conditions of the sky in Palestine. Porphyry indeed thought that the blackness of a raven was an inseparable quality <note>original: ἀχώριστον (achōriston)</note>, separable only in thought, which not only Aristotle* <margin>On the Generation of Animals, chapter 6.</margin> refutes, but also experience itself, namely that white ravens are found in certain regions of the earth, such as in the Pyrenees mountains and the Alps, not to mention the Northern lands where cold is the mother of whiteness, as witnessed by Torquemada on page 615; in those places, the cold is of such power that it changes the skins of beasts; compare Scaliger, Exercise 59, page 213. Nevertheless, the Bride in Song of Solomon 5:11 is praised for the blackness of her hair. Indeed, the "raven-like" color among the Jews was a symbol of a man who is intrepid and spirited, according to the testimony of Lyra and Luther, whence also Horace in *The Art of Poetry*, line 37:

-> *To be admired for black eyes and black hair.* <-

By black hair, Luther understands the Priests, who were grave men, in whose face and gestures there was a pleasant severity: unless one prefers to take black hair as a symbol of being despised for one's external appearance, which I do not think is the case. Abbot Willeramus explains it as referring to all the faithful, blackened by the depravity of nature, but made white through the grace of God and the merit of Christ:

> But this unique one, through His Deity to the Father
> Having become man, made brothers and sisters for Himself,
> Who like locks of hair reclining on lovely necks,
> Both increase the number and cling tenaciously to the Bride,
> They grow green in hope and faith, they flower with the seed of virtues,
> and like the fronds of palms they strive for the heights,
> They trust not in their own strength, but by the origin of the flesh
> They count themselves black, unless Grace makes them white.

Hugo the Cardinal proceeds by another path, applying these words of Solomon to the human nature of Christ...

...the words: *The hair of his head*, <note>original: "Comæ capitis ejus"</note> it says, "refers to the body and soul of Christ clinging to his divinity (which is the head) through their union and covering it; these are compared to the branches of palm trees, which are used to crown victors, because through this union he conquered the Devil on the cross. These 'hairs' were black during the Passion, like a raven, because he had neither form nor beauty, as his flesh was scorched in the furnace of the cross by the fire of passion and tribulation," etc. Many things are found in Natural History which, due to the antiquity of the tradition, are difficult for scholars to ignore or reject. For this reason, **Georgius Rothagen** <note>A 16th-century rector in Magdeburg.</note>, former Governor of the Magdeburg School, wittily gave them the name **Truthful Lies** <note>original German: "Warhafftiger Lügen"</note>. These traditions are not retracted or removed by Ministers of the Church out of reverence for antiquity and a love for metaphors and comparisons. From this class of stories comes the one about the raven's *lack of natural affection* <note>original Greek: ἀστοργία (astorgia)</note>; for this reason, it is called a *child-hating* <note>original Greek: μισότεκνον (misoteknon)</note> animal by Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, a medieval encyclopedist.</note> in his *5th Book of Letters*. For they say the raven is very forgetful, and when it leaves the nest, it cannot return from the solitudes it loves (*Isaiah 34:11*); however, led by nature, it gathers things into the nest from which worms can be created to feed the deserted chicks. Opposing this opinion is what Pliny <margin>Book 10, Natural History, ch. 43.</margin> reports *concerning a raven of sharp memory, which in Rome every morning challenged and greeted Tiberius, Germanicus, and Drusus (the Caesars) and others* *by name* <note>original Greek: ὀνοματοδην (onomatoden)</note>. Others think the raven does not give food to its chicks until they begin to turn black, so that it may recognize them by their blackness. This was the opinion of Gregory the Great <margin>History of Animals, ch. 14, sect. 2, p. 448.</margin> in his *Morals, book 30, ch. 8*: *When the chicks are born, the raven plainly ignores providing food until they grow black with feathers; it allows them to suffer from hunger until its own likeness is seen in them through the blackness of the feathers, as they wander here and there in the nest and seek the help of food with open mouths.* But even this, as the Blessed Wolfgang Franz <note>A Lutheran theologian known for his work on animal symbolism.</note> skillfully judges, does not seem likely, unless you wish to say that ravens attended the school of Aristotle (or Porphyry) and there learned that blackness is an *inseparable accident* <note>A term from formal logic meaning a quality that cannot be removed without changing the nature of the thing itself.</note> of the raven kind, and that white ravens are found nowhere. Others attribute this entirely to divine providence: they believe the chicks are either fed by flies created meanwhile by God, or that food is brought to their mouths in a miraculous way by a certain breeze carried through the air, which they receive with gaping mouths and are thus nourished. Yet no animal is so devoid of common sense that it is not bound by some care for those it has sired and does not strive to provide them with what seems necessary. It is indeed true, and proven by the evidence of experience, that ravens, as Aristotle says <margin>Book 9, History of Animals, ch. 31.</margin>, *at the moment their young are able to fly, first cast them out of the nests, and then drive them out of the whole region.* This happens either because of the barrenness of the soil or because of age, since once they are more grown, they can provide food for themselves. Hence in the sacred scriptures (*Job 38:41, Psalm 147:9*), the "chicks of the raven" are understood to be the older chicks capable of feeding themselves; or, by a *synecdoche* <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole.</note>, it refers to the whole nature of birds, as Nazianzenus explains to Clenodius. But while they are not yet sufficiently taught the way to provide food for themselves, they wander with a cry; God treats the cry of these wanderers as a prayer, and thus for them—who would otherwise

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
perish—He provides food. Although the raven is an unclean bird, ill-omened, greedy and thieving, of a mournful color, with a deathly voice, rejoicing in corpses and gaping at foul places, and more ready by nature to snatch away than to bring back, yet by God’s command it becomes the steward and food-bearer for Elijah. God often acts through opposites, which is seen in the example of Elijah, whom in the desert <margin>1 Kings 17.</margin> *not gentle doves fed, but ravens—birds by nature greedy and gluttonous.* As Sedulius <note>A 5th-century Christian poet.</note> writes in his *Paschal Song, verse 154*:

> *Ravens once served as ministers to feed Elijah,*
> *Providing feasts without delay; the bird devoted to*
> *Plunder sated his hollow throat with a greedy beak.*

And yet, the raven receives its own praise because it was selected above others to feed Elijah. Augustine investigates the reason for this, saying: <margin>Book 2, question 17, On Miracles.</margin> *The ravens are commanded to serve the Prophet so that, evidently, that bird might be seen to purge the neglect and deception of Noah's time; while it was made a servant to him who had not sinned, even by the instruction of wild animals he now used their service. But where that raven brought those meats and breads from, He himself knows who committed such a duty. In this, however, it should be observed that the ravens received these things from the knowledge of some men or the industry of those unaware, who were preparing cooked breads and whatever meats in whatever way.* So he says. Ambrose, however, explains this whole history allegorically regarding the conversion of the Gentiles (see his *Commentary on Luke 3*). Other Fathers explain it as God's special providence toward the pious and faithful (*Basil, Sermon 3 on Divine Avarice; Augustine, Vol. 10, Homily 18 and Sermon on Time 146*).

Furthermore, the raven is a very well-known and very unclean bird, since it lives on corpses and loves to linger around gallows, seeking the flesh of those hanged, especially the eyes; hence the poet *Catullus*:

> *Let the raven devour the gouged-out eyes with its black throat,*
> *the dogs the intestines, and the wolves the remaining limbs.*

From this comes the most severe command of God, with the penalty of having one's eyes gouged out, concerning the honor and obedience to be shown to parents, so that it may be well with the children and they may live long upon the earth. To him who violates this command, *who mocks his father and scorns to obey his mother*, his eyes shall be pecked out <margin>Proverbs 30:17.</margin> *by the ravens of the valleys, and the young eagles shall eat them*, as the wisest of Kings <note>King Solomon, traditional author of Proverbs.</note> testifies. From this comes the proverb *to the crows!* <note>original Greek: ἐς κόρακας. A common ancient curse similar to "go to hell."</note> and *from a bad crow, a bad egg* <note>original Greek: κακῶ κόρακος κακὸν ὠόν</note>. Memorable also is that dream of the Egyptian Chief Baker in *Genesis 40:16*, who foresaw in prison ravens eating from the basket on his head; Joseph, interpreting the vision, indicated his death by hanging. Proportional things must be applied proportionally in dreams: it is the nature of ravens to seek the eyes and flesh of the hanged, to follow corpses, and to feed themselves on those foods toward which they are inclined and prone by natural instinct. Noah, a master of nature's secrets, well knew the nature of the raven, which is why he sent it out; for he knew it would fly back and forth seeking food from corpses. For after the peaks of the mountains were uncovered, he sent out the raven, which he knew would be lured by the smell of corpses.

<meta>This page continues the "Sacred History of Animals," moving from general bird lore to the specific biblical accounts of the raven and the quail. It focuses on the textual discrepancies regarding the raven's return to the Ark and the symbolic interpretations provided by the Church Fathers.</meta>

<header>from Psalm 55:10–11.</header>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...it could be enticed to fly further away if the earth, already stripped of its waters, were filled with the carcasses of animals. And yet the raven, the first explorer of the earth, <term>he shall return <note>Hebrew: *yashuv*</note></term>; he went forth and returned. He went out by going and returning, flying here and there, sometimes approaching the ark, sometimes leaving it. As long as he could feed himself on the carcasses floating in the water, he wandered freely and flew about cautiously, seeking a place of retreat either upon the ark or in the surrounding area, until the waters were dried up. He was carried around the ark, and whatever came to him as prey, he carried rapidly with him onto the roof of the ark. Indeed, I wonder what came into the minds of the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the influential Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> that they should add a negation in their translation: *having gone out, he did not return* <note>Greek: ἐξελθὼν οὐκ ἀνέστρεψεν</note>, and following them, the Latin version: *He went forth and did not return*, from which the suspicion might arise that the Hebrew text has been corrupted. But Agostino Steuco <note>A 16th-century Italian exegete and librarian.</note> rightly judges that *this passage is read corruptly among the Greeks, and the negation should be removed from the Latin and Greek codices*. He correctly believes that in the Latin version, the passage was corrupted either by scribes or by the long passage of time, such that commentators, greatly at odds with one another, have introduced the most fabulous interpretations. There is nothing that can better demonstrate the removal of the negative particle than its absence from six Latin manuscripts <note>abbreviated as MSS</note>, which we find noted in the Plantin edition of the year 1583. Christopher à Sacro Bosco <note>Christopher Holywood, an Irish Jesuit scholar.</note> also notes that there are Latin codices of great authority which read without the negation, just as it is found in the Hebrew. I have the Bible of the Louvain edition of the year 1547, revised and corrected by the Louvain theologians from thirty-five copies, which attaches an obelisk <note>A proofreading mark (†) used to denote doubtful or spurious text.</note> to the negation here.

<margin>Defense of the Council of Trent, part 4, ch. 5.</margin>
<margin>Sacred Criticism, p. 280.</margin>
But what did Cappel <note>Louis Cappel, a French Protestant scholar of Hebrew.</note> see? It seemed better to him that the negative particle be added; but that born Critic is sometimes, like the raven's nostrils, more delighted by cadaverous lakes than by the pure cisterns of Israel; compare Blessed Glassius <note>Salomon Glassius, author of *Philologia Sacra*.</note> book 3, *Sacred Philology*, Tract 3, canon 37, p. 351, and Tract 5, canon 12, p. 458; and Blessed Hackspan, *Philological-Theological Notes* on Genesis chapter 8, p. 139. In their allegories, the Fathers for the most part followed the Vulgate translator and established their allegories according to him. From this source flows the idea that all the animals of the Ark condemned the raven as treacherous, because he refused to announce safety to those who were still enclosed in the ark by his staying away. Concerning this, Theodotus <note>An ancient Christian poet.</note> sings in his *Eclogue* v. 77:

> *Every animal condemns the raven for his treachery,*
> *Because he would not be the messenger of safety to the enclosed.*
> *By her own choice, the dove brought a branch with green leaves*
> *In her mouth; Armenia remains as a witness.*

Similar to the raven of Noah’s ark are those who, having left the ark of the Church, cling to the carcasses of the age and the dead works of the world, and never return to the ark to serve the living God. Cyprian writes in this sense in his *Epistle to the heretic Novatian*: "Two birds are sent out from the ark, the Raven and the Dove. The raven truly bore the figure of impure men who will be in perpetual darkness along the broad way of the world, and of future apostates who feed on impure things and never turn themselves back to the Church; reading this, we find he was sent out and did not return further. Therefore, those who were found similar to this bird—that is, to the impure spirit—to the Church further..."

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
<margin>On Psalm 146, p. 644.</margin>
...they could not return, etc. Nor does Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century bishop and theologian.</note> think otherwise of the raven: "We remember that the raven was established in the form of a sinner when, having been sent out from the ark, he did not return. For since there was nowhere to stand, the waters being spread over everything, he—unlike the dove who later returned when she found no place of rest—did not return. Since the Ark there had the form of the Church, he who abandoned the Church when he could never stand anywhere else, is established as an example of a sinner in her; although he has no other rest in the world except that of the Church, he nevertheless prefers to linger in the vanities of the age." Ambrose <note>The 4th-century Bishop of Milan.</note> also introduces the raven allegorically, but he enters by another path; namely, that the raven, who has hitherto been a symbol of the sinful man and of one stubbornly persisting in sins, may now be the image of the faithful man, avoiding sins and never committing himself to the ship of sinners. These are his words: "Every righteous man, when he begins to cleanse himself, first repels from himself those things which are dark, impure, and reckless; for all impudence and fault is dark, and feeds on the dead just like a raven. But virtue is near to the light, which shines with purity and simplicity of mind. And therefore, fault is sent away and put to flight and separated from innocence, so that nothing dark remains in the mind of the righteous man. Then, the departed raven does not return to the righteous man, because fleeing fault seems to fit neither the probity nor the justice of all equity. Finally, the unjust man believes he has escaped as if from chains when the righteous man has separated himself from his company by a certain deluge of familiar corruption; like the raven, who, when he found dryness of the earth nowhere, did not return, but remained away."

<margin>On Noah and the Ark, ch. 17.</margin>
**THE QUAIL**, according to Festus, is so named from the sound of its voice. To the Hebrews, it is called <term>Shalav <note>שליו</note></term>, from <term>shalah <note>שלה</note></term>, "he was at leisure," "he rested," or "he lived quietly and in ease"; whence the <term>tongue of the quail <note>לשון השלו</note></term> means the same. For it sits in an abundance of grain, idle, secure, and devoted to sloth and luxury. Whence also "to quail-ize" (*coturniſare*) is the same as to indulge the gullet <note>i.e., gluttony</note>, from which the French and English *Gourmandise* also seems corrupted; see Minsheu, page 594. Because of their almost perpetual walking on the ground, they seem more like terrestrial animals than flying ones, since they not only do not nest on high, but gather briars on the flat ground and hatch their eggs among the crops and grasses. They never stay in trees, but always remain on the ground, and this is because of the weight of their bodies; for they are heavy birds. Hence they love storms and winds, so that they may be propelled more swiftly by them, rather than the tranquility of the air; whatever they lack in speed of flying, they supply with ease of running. The Greek Interpreters read <note>the word for quail as</note> *ortygometra* <note>ὀρτυγομήτρα</note>, not differing from the others except in size, being one of the leaders which accompany them when they are about to depart for other lands in the month of August because of the approaching winter season. For they write that four other birds join them on the journey, the first of which is the *ortygometra*, the greater quail, which in our language they call the <term>King of the Quails <note>German: *Wachtelkönig*; the Corncrake.</note></term>. The second is the *Lingulaca* or *glottis*, having its name from its very long tongue, which leaves them at the first lodging and returns on the second day to where it had previously departed. The third they call the *cynchramus*, a <term>shrieker <note>German: *Schreer*</note></term>, which is their most faithful and constant <term>guide <note>Greek: ὁδηγὸς</note></term>, and at night, when it is time to depart, by its voice and a peculiar sign...

...it rouses them and urges them to the journey; likewise, if they have wandered from the path, it calls them back with its own voice, which they follow once recalled. The fourth leader is the *Otus* or *Asio* <note>The Long-eared Owl or Scops Owl</note>, otherwise called the "night owl," because it is similar to the owl and has a certain appearance of wings around its ears. This bird is an inept leader and an image of fools; for it is a parasitic and boastful bird, prone to gestures, imitating dancers and others. Otherwise, the quail is a most prolific bird, which is said to lay sixteen eggs; authors testify that they give birth four times a year—twice among us, and twice in those regions to which they depart from us around autumn. Others add that the first offspring even hatch new chicks before their departure, whence the well-known proverb among bird-catchers: *He who kills a quail in early spring, kills a hundred quails.* From the Holy Scriptures, note Exodus 16:13, Numbers 11:31, Psalm 78:26 and 105:40, Wisdom 16:2 and 19:12; this is the bird that God sent down in great abundance twice upon the camps of the Israelites. While God sent the quails in such great abundance that they covered the camp, there are many among the Interpreters who believe they were created anew by God, especially since in Wisdom 19:10 they are called a <term>new creation <note>original Greek: νέα γένεσις</note></term>. Truly, this is not to be understood <term>absolutely <note>original Greek: ἁπλῶς</note></term> but <term>in a certain respect <note>original Greek: τῷ τὶ</note></term> regarding the people, who had previously experienced nothing of the kind. On this,
<margin>Book 1 of *The Miracles of Holy Scripture*, chapter 27.</margin>
Augustine* says: *nothing new or contrary to nature is contributed by the Lord, who seems to provide a created creature of birds, hidden in some remote corner of the world, for the necessity of His people: although it is written in the book of Wisdom: "They saw a new creation of birds shown to them," it was surely shown, not recently created.* What God once founded in the beginning with the rest of creation, He administered to His people in their time of need. The sending of the quails into the camps of the Israelites was indeed miraculous; meanwhile, it did not exclude all natural means, such as the wind in this miracle, as
<margin>Book 10 of the *Natural History*, chapter 23.</margin>
is clear from Pliny*: *They do not fly*, he says, *in a South wind, which is a moist and heavier wind. Yet they wish to be carried by a breeze because of the weight of their bodies and their small strength.* Hence that complaint of those flying is expressed by their labor. Therefore they fly most of all when the North wind blows, with the "quail-mother" <note>the *ortycometra*, often identified as the corncrake</note> as their leader. That African wind was divinely excited, as God was pleased to use such a medium in executing a supernatural work and bringing such an abundance of quails, which otherwise at that time—when winter was beginning here—stayed in Egypt in vast numbers. This bird is a lover of fighting, which is why quails used to fight in public spectacles; and from here, it is thought, arose the practice of the Phoenicians sacrificing quails especially to Hercules, as is found in Eudoxus of Cnidus in the first book of his <term>Circuit of the Earth <note>original Greek: γῆς περιόδῳ</note></term>. And Aristides, quoted in Philostratus, says that fierce men, preparing themselves for a fight, <term>take on the nature of quails <note>original Greek: ὀρτύγων ἀνάπλεως φύσιν</note></term>.
On the contrary, however, Aristophanes the comic poet* (in Athenaeus) attributes the opposite to them, saying of fearful men that they <term>have the soul of a quail <note>original Greek: ὀρτυγίας ψυχὴν ἔχειν</note></term>. Regarding their consumption, we must say: we do not conclude with Galen, Pliny, and Avicenna <note>famous ancient and medieval physicians</note> that the eating of quails is unhealthy, but we feel the contrary with Averroës. Nor is there reason for you to object regarding hellebore <note>a toxic plant</note>: since hellebore does not grow everywhere, and they also feed on other things; concerning which Lazarus Riverius <note>a 17th-century French physician</note> says in his *Institutes of Medicine*, Book 6, chapter 20, page 387: Concerning the Quail, there is

a controversy, since Galen, Pliny, and Avicenna report that those who frequently feed on quails are subject to spasms. Galen took the cause of this from hellebore <note>veratrum</note>, which quails are accustomed to eat. On the other hand, this opinion is rejected by others, whose leader is Averroës, asserting that the flesh of quails is most healthy and generates the best and most praiseworthy blood. This is most consistent with reason. For there are very few regions in which hellebore grows, but quails everywhere feed on the best herbs and grains. Nor does experience teach that those who eat quails are subject to epilepsy. Add that by a singular benefit of God they were granted to the Israelites of old in the desert, which would not have happened unless they provided the best nourishment. For although
heavy diseases arose among the Israelites from them, it is clear this happened from the abuse of that food, in which they gorged themselves so much that they could not sufficiently digest it; hence the greatest indigestion and putrefaction arose. It is at least a probable conjecture that diseases arose from the abuse of eating quails (Numbers 11:33) and that great plague, the genuine cause of which was obstinate murmuring and persistence. But then, says Augustine in the place cited above, God brought back quails for such a service—which previously, when contributed with Manna, brought nothing adverse to those eating—this time (the second time, to be sure) lest anyone think that the food of birds brought death to the people without the fault of murmuring; since in this vengeance, He kept those eating with a clean conscience unharmed, and when it was given with manna, it provided no inconvenience to the whole multitude. Therefore, to those desiring Egyptian meats even to the point of nausea and vomiting, God provides swarms of quails; and while they still persisted in their petulant murmuring and did not acknowledge God's goodness, He exercised His justice and, while the meat was still under their teeth, He killed those petulantly murmuring. What happened thus to the Hebrews regarding the flesh of quails, Jerome—more scathingly than became a religious man—applied to <term>dissoluteness <note>original Greek: ἀσωτίαν</note></term> in Letter 10 to Furia*, at which I do not doubt the noble widow Furia blushed: *What straits*, he says,

The dog returning to its vomit, and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mud.* This was said quite indecently out of excessive and foolish zeal against marriage and second vows. from Psalm 55:10, 11. 495

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...nature proceeded from the waters, but it acquired a habitation for itself in the air. Therefore, those who eat birds are reminded to lift their hearts from the lowest things to the highest, so that even though they live in earthly bodies, they may always seek heavenly things in spirit.

### THE HORNET

The HORNET, called *sphēx* <note>original Greek: σφήξ</note> by the Greeks, is hardly distinct from the wasp (which is also *sphēx* in Greek), except that it is marked with different yellow and black lines and is larger than the wasp, which is hairy. In Hebrew it is called *Zirah* <note>original Hebrew: צרעה</note>, perhaps by a transposition of letters as if from *razah* <note>original Hebrew: רזה</note>, meaning "from piercing." Indeed, hornets build nests underground and push out the earth just like ants; they make subterranean holes which their new successors make even larger after the previous ones have died. Thus, their greatest labor is located in constructing nests and piercing the ground. They do have this in common with bees: they build honeycombs, and something similar to honey is found in them, though scarcely a drop; hence the hornet is also called <term>honey-like <note>original Greek: μελιττοειδείς</note></term>.

<margin>Pliny, Natural History, book 11, ch. 20.</margin>
And if we believe Aristotle, they also have a leader, although Pliny thinks otherwise in Book 11 of his *Natural History*, chapter 21. There is a perpetual war and fight between hornets, wasps, and bees. Indeed, the animal is so harmful that its sting is rarely without fever; and authors say—these are the words of Pliny—that a man can be killed by thrice nine <note>27</note> stings. What's more, they do not only attack birds, but even four-footed animals. For this reason, God threatens in Exodus 23:28 and Deuteronomy 7:20 (compare Joshua 24:12 and Wisdom 12:8) that He would send hornets against the Canaanites. Whether this actually happened, and whether they were expelled from their seats by these insects, is not yet agreed upon among the Interpreters. Augustine, who should be heard first on this question, discusses the matter in his *Questions on Exodus*, Question 93: "We do not read that it was done (namely, that hornets were sent), neither in the times of Moses, nor under Joshua, nor under the Judges, nor under the Kings. And because of this, these wasps should perhaps be understood as the stings of fear by which the aforementioned nations were driven to give way to the children of Israel." Then, in Question 27 on Joshua, he holds the same: "Or perhaps by a figurative word, he wanted 'wasps' to be understood as the sharpest stings of fear: or secondly, as hidden spirits of the air, which they say in the Psalms are through evil spirits." However, he adds: "Unless perhaps someone should say that not everything that was done was written down; and that this was also thirdly done visibly, so that he wants them to be understood as real wasps." Blessed Martin Luther also explains this in his commentary on Deuteronomy as a silent fear sent by God into the Canaanites; he says: "For hornets to be sent before us among the nations is for the impious to be driven by the terror of the law and the deadly stings of conscience, so that they cannot hide themselves until they perish and are forced to confess their impiety." Furthermore, just as it was not in the power of the Israelites to release the hornets, so it is not our part to terrify any impious person; but it is God who disturbs and terrifies their hearts, so that, terrified like Paul, they may say, 'Lord, what do you want me to do?' Piscator understands it in the same way: "I will send my terror like a hornet." And indeed, it seems to be a proverbial expression, perhaps taken from that type of wasp or insect that usually attacks cattle; at the mere sound of its buzzing or whispering while flying, the cattle are struck with terror and flee as if they had been driven mad; nor can they be held back by any barriers. The same promise is repeated in Deuteronomy 7:20, in which place Piscator nevertheless adds: "Although nothing seems to forbid the name of hornets being taken here in its proper meaning."

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
For in this way, God sent hail upon the Amorites while Joshua was fighting them (Joshua 10:11). Likewise, at the prayers of Samuel, God sent a storm upon the Philistines who were about to join battle with the Israelites, by which he scattered and put them to flight (1 Samuel 7:9; compare the same in Joshua 24:12). Blessed Brentius acknowledges both opinions as probable: "Whether it is understood externally regarding those little beasts," he says, "or they are spoken of figuratively regarding sudden terrors, it is certainly manifest that the peoples of the land of Canaan were more terrified by divine miracles, so as to be stunned and conquered." This can be sufficiently gathered from the conversation Rahab had with the scouts (Joshua 2:9 onwards; compare with chapter 5:1). I add the learned things that Rivetus <note>André Rivet, a French Huguenot theologian</note> has on this passage; thus on page 113 of his *Commentary*: "From the word *tzara'at* <note>original Hebrew: צרעה</note>," he says, "which signifies being leprous, is derived *tzaru'a* <note>original Hebrew: צרוע</note>, a leper, and *tzir'ah* <note>original Hebrew: צרעה</note>, which some interpret as a hornet and others as a wasp. From this, some want there to be some affinity between the fly signified here and leprosy, either in color, or in stench, or because it infects lepers. It is, moreover, a large genus of fly, with a long body, inhabiting deserts, which has various colors similar to lepers, and representing their varieties to some extent; the Septuagint calls them *sphēkas* <note>wasps</note>. Rabbi David says it was an evil fly, emitting poison and striking the eyes so that they could not fight." He explains it as referring to real hornets, in which sense the author of the Book of Wisdom also understood it (chapter 12:8).

<margin>p. 115.</margin>
And he adds: "Although sacred history does not mention this thing, namely in what place and time it was done, since God promised it twice in the Law and the history of Joshua (last chapter, verse 12) testifies that it was done, it is right to believe that God sent hornets before his people, which infected, weakened, and wore down the Canaanites, so that they might afterwards be more easily conquered and destroyed by the people of God. For just as very small creatures are numbered among the plagues of Egypt, so the Canaanites seem to have been struck by the Lord through infesting hornets and wasps." In Ecclesiastical History, we read regarding the Persians besieging Nisibis, that James, the Bishop of the City, a pious man, called down bedbugs and fleas upon the enemies, by which they were driven away. Nor are there lacking in secular histories examples of certain peoples who were forced to change their seats by the smallest animals: mice, frogs, spiders, and similar things. Rivetus records these things. Pliny (Book 8, chapter 29) recounts inhabitants being put to flight and forced to change their seat by frogs; Justin (Book 15) by mice; Pliny (Book 10, chapter 15) by gnats; Pausanias in his *Description of Greece*. Likewise, one reads in Aelian that wasps drove the Phaselians from their ancestral seats in Phoenicia, where they occupied the Solymian mountains. But let us pause here, lest (as the proverb says) we "stir up the hornets," which are more bitter than wasps.

<margin>Book 11, ch. 28.</margin>
### THE GNAT

The GNAT <note>Latin: *culex*</note> is named from its sting <note>Latin: *aculeo*</note> because it sucks blood; so says Isidore in Book 12 of his *Etymologies*, chapter 8. And Augustine on Psalm 148: "Who gave the sting to the gnat so that it might suck blood? How thin is the pipe through which it sips." Thus, a "hoary gnat" is used as an insult for an elderly lover in Plautus's *Casina*, because he punctures the skin of beautiful women with his proboscis and draws out blood as if with a siphon, according to the interpretation of Turnebus (Book 16, chapter 3). Gnats seek human blood with great desire, whence in the summer time, by a certain marvelous affection of nature, they are able to smell the bodies of men even in the dark and from a distance.

<meta>This page concludes the discussion on the habits and moral symbolism of gnats—including accounts of fireflies in the Americas and the biblical metaphor of straining a gnat—before beginning a lengthy entry on the Swan, debating the reality of the "swan song."</meta>

<margin>
Sacred History of Animals.
Natural History, Book 12, Chapter 3.
</margin>

...in which. Truly, in no place do they infest men more than in Hispaniola <note>The island of Santo Domingo/Haiti</note> and the adjacent islands, as written by Juan Eusebius Nierenberg and by Vossius following him in *On Idolatry*, Book 4, Chapter 94, page 1627. In those places, gnats are found that so vehemently harass the inhabitants that they are forced to build low-lying houses with doors so small that a man can barely enter, and without any windows, lest the gnats get in. They do not dare to light lamps, because the gnats are accustomed to follow the light. But even when men take such precautions, the little beasts find a way to enter. However, God provides for those islands with a certain kind of beetle or flying creature, not unlike a small animal, which they call *cucuios* <note>The Pyrophorus or click-beetle, known for its bioluminescence</note>, which hunt those gnats. For this purpose, people are accustomed to catch the *cucuios* and bring them home. They catch them in this way: at the first twilight, they go out with a burning torch, shouting, "*cucuie, cucuie*." The simpler folk believe that the insects fly toward them upon hearing their name called. But if the shouting has any power at all, it is only that the insects are more easily roused by the noise. Once roused, they see the gnats around the torch, for these enjoy the light. Seizing such a fine opportunity, the *cucuios* fly toward them to catch them. Then they are struck with a garment or otherwise so that they fall to the ground, from where they are picked up while slightly faint, and once revived, are carried home. They fly through the whole house until they have gradually consumed whatever gnats were hiding there. When food becomes scarce, the people usually release the *cucuios* so that such a useful insect is not killed by hunger. In Egypt, to avoid the annoyance of gnats, people are said to spread out fishing nets at night, because gnats naturally fear nets. The Greeks call the insect <term>*konops* <note>original: κώνωψ</note></term> to differentiate it from the larger gnats, which are named <term>*empides* <note>original: ἐμπίδες</note></term>; in the *Greek Anthology*, Book 7, they are described as:

> *Sharp-witted gnats, shameless, siphons for the blood of men.* <note>original Greek: Ὀξυνόαι κώνωπες, ἀναιδέες, αἵματος ἀνδρῶν / Σίφωνες</note>

Among the Hebrews, the former species is called *Jabchufin*, to which they add the epithet "the red ones." Hence the custom of the Jews to strain their wine, lest they should swallow these unclean little animals; Christ seems to have referred to this custom when he calls the Pharisees those who "strain out a gnat and swallow a camel." <note>Matthew 23:24; original Greek: διυλίζοντας τὸν κώνωπα... καὶ κάμηλον καταπίνοντες</note> To strain is to examine food through a sieve so that no filth is mixed in, and to apply the sense of taste so that the food is not bad. The Pharisees "strained gnats," that is, they most strictly enforced the tiniest mandates of the Fathers while neglecting divine ones. The other species was called *Jatthufin* by them. We shall say more things pertaining to this, <term>with God's help <note>original Greek: σὺν Θεῷ</note></term>, in our *Illustration of the New Testament*. Finally, the gnat is a genuine image of detractors; for just as gnats arise from the wild fig tree and fly to the nearest cultivated figs—whose juice is suitable for nourishment, while the juice of the wild fig tree is unsuitable and raw, as Theophrastus says in Book 2 of *The Causes of Plants*, chapter 13—so detractors do not attack the lowest commoners and men of their own sort. Rather, they do not fear to attack the great, or to burden those who excel in virtue and innocence of life with slanders, according to the proverb: *Slander boldly, something always sticks.*

<margin>
Matthew 23:24.
</margin>

### CYGNUS, *Kyknos, swan, cycnus, olor, Schwan*

<margin>column 543.</margin>

The author of the *Etymologicum*, who seems to be negligent in his etymologies, derives this word from *klo* <note>original: κλῶ</note>, which he says is the same as *phono* <note>original: φωνῶ</note>, "to cry out," for the swan is a <term>shouting animal <note>original Greek: ζῶον κραυγικόν</note></term>. Furthermore, to dig deeper into the etymology, he says from the history of *klo* comes *klyo*, and hence *klyknos*, and through transposition and change of letters, it ends in *kyknos*. These things are said to be done miraculously, and it happens to him as it does to those who have no certain paths in marshy places: they seek paths now here, now there, yet they do not find them. He also seeks another path, thinking it can be derived from *kyklos* <note>circle</note>, though he devises no reason for it. The Swan delights in water and marshes, whence Aelian says in Book 17, *History of Animals*, 24: "The swan spends its time in lakes, marshes, and pools." <note>original Greek: Κύκνος διατριβαῖς λίμναις τε καὶ ἕλη καὶ τενάγη</note> It is distinguished by its snowy whiteness, from which the Poets take their comparison (see Theocritus, *Idyll* 16, verse 49, and the Scholiast there, page 132). It is *makrotrachelos* <note>original Greek: Μακροτράχηλος</note>, or long-necked, as Homer says in two places, but in one and the same verse:

> *Of geese, or cranes, or long-necked swans.* <note>original Greek: Χηνῶν, ἢ γεράνων, ἢ κύκνων δουλιχοδείρων</note>

The words *dere* and *deire* mean "neck"; *dolichos*, with a *u* inserted for the sake of the meter as *doulichos*, means "long." Both are poetic terms. It is a much-celebrated, though I believe fabulous, tale that the swan sings when it is just about to die. Because of this <term>reputation for music <note>original Greek: μουσικῆς δόξαν</note></term>, it is celebrated by Pausanias in his *Attica*, and from this Artemidorus takes a <term>dream-interpretation sign <note>original Greek: ὀνειροκριτικὸν</note></term> concerning a musical man in Book 2 of his *Oneirocritica*, 20, page 108. Great men like Plato relate that swans, when near death, sing sweetly out of pleasure and forgetfulness of the troubles of life; before we cite more authors, it is said that Socrates saw in a dream a *swan chick* fly from the altar which was consecrated to Cupid in the Academy and rest in his lap. Afterward, that swan sought the heavens with its feathers and ceased with a musical song. When Socrates related this in a gathering of men, Aristo arrived to present the boy Plato to the master Socrates. When Socrates looked at him, he said, "This, my friend, was that swan from the Academy of Cupid." Cicero, Aristotle, Oppian, Ovid, Martial, Dio Cassius, and Aesop (*Fable 210*) all agree with Plato; as do Martial in Book 13, Erasmus in his *Adages* ("the swan song"), Beroaldus in his *Commentary on Cicero’s Tusculan Disputations*, Book 1, Petrus Santeranus of Sicily in an epigram found in Erasmus’s preface to the works of Jerome, and Peter Comestor in his *Scholastic History*. But that this is entirely fabulous and false is asserted on the contrary by men of no low rank: Pliny (Book 10, chapter 23), Aelian (Book 1, *Varia Historia*, chapter 14), Bodin in his *Method of History*, Elmenhorst on Apuleius (page 383), Caelius Rhodiginus, Hoeschel in his *Notes on Horapollo* (Book 2, chapter 39), Albericus Gentilis (*L. Virg. chapter 17*), Tilemann in his *Philological Discourse* (page 97), Weitzius on Ovid’s *Tristia* Book 5 and on Virgil’s *Eclogue* 9 (verse 36). Dausqueius reconciles both sides in his *Notes on Silius Italicus* (Book 11, page 470). There is indeed an astounding consensus of writers on both sides, both denying and affirming that matter of the swans' melody at their end; and thus they are accustomed to interpret these by those, and those by these. But not even by that mutual effort do they open a way to the truth. Certainly, Aelian uses his phrase "it is common talk" <note>original Greek: τεθρύλληται</note> here, where we would say "it is widespread," so much so that it has passed into a proverb. Aristotle <margin>Book 9, History of Animals, chapter 12.</margin> makes swans "fond of song," as we have heard, and many of the most ancient writers agree with him. It is not so easy to entirely prove the old rumor false. But how, I ask, does it happen that no one hears that voice today? And what sweet song could there be for swans, when their voice is hoarse? As Virgil says <margin>Book 7, Aeneid.</margin>:

> *A cloud of hoarse birds pressing to the shores.* <note>original Latin: Urgens volucrum raucarum ad litora nubem</note>

Yet, perhaps by saying this, we will not please the <term>Venusian poet</term><note>Horace, born in Venusia.</note>, who—deceived by common opinion, unless it is a playful joke of the interpreter—writes about himself and his own poems. One may guess, rather than state with certainty, the Hebrew <term>onomatothesia</term><note>The act of naming or etymology.</note> of the swan. For the pens and minds of the interpreters are so discordant that there is scarcely such disagreement in the naming of any other bird. If you consult the <term>Septuagint</term><note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> and Latin versions, you will find three names by which the swan ought to be identified among the Hebrews. The Septuagint and the <term>Vulgate</term><note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note> with it translate the Hebrew word *ha-tinshemet* <note>original: "הנשמת"</note> as "swan" in Deuteronomy 14:16, which in Leviticus 11:17 they rendered as "ibis." Likewise, in Leviticus 11:17, the Septuagint renders *ha-tinshemet* as "swan," and Vatablus follows them with "swan," but the Vulgate renders it as "purple swamphen" <note>original: "Porphyrionem"</note>. But in Deuteronomy 14:17, the Septuagint translated it as "purple swamphen," and the Vulgate and Pagninus followed them. Thus, in Leviticus 11:17, the Vulgate expresses it as "swan," but the Septuagint as "purple swamphen." Furthermore, both versions are <term>anonymous</term><note>original: "ἀμώνυμοι" (likely a typo for "unnamed" or "inconsistent")</note> in their own translation of Deuteronomy 14:16, where they both rendered *ha-tinshemet* as "ibis." Behold the quicksands! Whoever wishes to commit themselves to these must do so at their own peril; we, not unaware of our own <term>inability</term><note>original: "ἀδυμαμίας"</note>, hardly entrust our pen to such uncertain and diverse ground. Instead, we imitate the swans in this: they do not dip their necks deeper into the water than natural instinct requires. Regarding this, <term>Basil</term><note>Saint Basil the Great, a 4th-century Church Father.</note> says: <margin>Homily 8 on the Hexaemeron.</margin> *If you observe how the swan, with its neck plunged into deep water, draws food for itself from the bottom, you will then clearly see the Wisdom of the Creator. You will find that the Builder joined a neck longer than its legs for this reason: so that, letting it down into the deep like a fishing line, it may obtain the hidden food therefrom.* <margin>Book 5, chapter 22 of the Hexaemeron.</margin> Those things read in <term>Ambrose</term><note>Saint Ambrose, 4th-century Bishop of Milan.</note> coincide with Basil: *Why the swan uses a rather long neck is obvious; because it is somewhat sluggish in body and cannot easily penetrate the inner parts of the waters, it extends its neck toward the prey so that, as if leading the rest of the body, it may seize the food it finds and tear it from the deep.* Add to this that the voice is sweeter and more melodious because it is modulated through a long neck, and it results in a far purer sound through longer practice. However, while the swan, according to the opinion of <term>Jerome</term><note>Saint Jerome, translator of the Vulgate.</note> on

the third chapter of Zephaniah, is placed among the unclean birds because of its upright stance and extended neck, for that very reason it is a symbol of those who are of a haughty spirit, which, as Hesychius says, God forbids. <term>Hugo</term><note>Likely Hugh of Saint Victor, a medieval mystic.</note> also points to this, saying: *The swan is a white bird, with an extended neck, large in body, but with black flesh: and it signifies those who, clothed in splendor, glory more than is right, while being black within with the blackness of sins, one of whom was the rich man in Luke 16.*

**THE ROOSTER** and **THE HEN** are called *alektor* and *alektoris* by the Greeks, either because it sleeps *without a bed* <note>original: "ἄνευ λέϰτρῳ"</note>, or because it rouses men *from bed* <note>original: "ἐϰ λέϰτρῳ"</note>. Among the Hebrews, if you consult the books of the Old Testament, they do not have a <term>unique name</term><note>original: "ἰδιώνυμοι"</note>, but are rather <term>unnamed</term><note>original: "ἀνώνυμοι"</note>. Nevertheless, they have flown into the inner sanctuaries of the Holy Bible—whether the Rooster earned this by its song or by its nobility, I do not know. For it is a very vocal bird, so much so that it is not silent even at night; its sonorous sound is heard even at a distance of a thousand paces, and indeed beyond. The ancients relate that the Rooster, by its song, strikes horror and is a source of terror even to the Lion, the strongest of animals: thus say Zoroaster in the *Geoponics* Book 10, Plutarch in his *Book on Envy and Hatred*, Aelian in *History of Animals* Book 6 chapter 22 and Book 14 chapter 9, Lucretius in Book 4, Pliny in *Natural History* Book 8 chapter 16, and Isidore in *Etymologies* Book 12 chapter 11. A great number of the Church Fathers followed these authors in their allegories. <term>Proclus</term><note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> reviews the cause of this matter, though it is legendary, and prophesies thus about the Lion and the rooster: <margin>On Sacrifice and Magic.</margin> *Furthermore, there are many solar animals, such as Lions and roosters, participating in a certain solar divinity according to their nature. Whence it is a wonder how much the inferior things in the same order yield to the superior, even if they do not yield in size or power. Hence they say the rooster is greatly feared by the Lion and almost revered; the cause of which we cannot assign to matter or sense, but only to the contemplation of the higher order. Namely, because the presence of solar virtue is more suited to the Rooster than to the Lion, which is apparent because the Rooster, as if with certain hymns, applauds the rising sun and calls to it when it turns toward us from the middle of the sky of the Antipodes. Sometimes certain solar angels have appeared, endowed with such forms; though they were without form in themselves, they appeared formed to us, who are formed beings. Sometimes even solar demons were seen with lion-like brows, who, when a Rooster was presented to them, suddenly vanished. This proceeds from the fact that things placed lower in the same order always revere the higher. Just as many people, looking upon the images of divine men, are accustomed by this very sight to fear committing something shameful. But we leave these fables to the fabulist.* For experience cries out against this fictional terror of Lions arising from the crowing of a Rooster, as <term>Philipp Camerarius</term><note>A 16th-century German scholar.</note> gives an example of this matter, saying: <margin>In Historical Meditations, Century 1, chapter 22, page 119.</margin> *In our times, in the court of the most Serene Prince of Bavaria, one of the Lions, with a miraculous leap, lowered himself into the courtyard of a nearby house, where, fearing nothing of the crowing or cries of the roosters, he devoured them along with many hens.* Or was it, as we said, its nobility? Moved by this, the Athenians—as Aelian writes in *Various History* Book 11, chapter 28—enacted by law *that roosters should contend publicly in the theater on one day of the year* <note>original: "ἀλεϰτρύονας ἀγωνίζεσθαι δημοσίᾳ ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ μιᾶς ἡμέρας τοῦ ἔτους"</note>. Furthermore, it was commanded by law to all young men *to watch the birds boxing until the point of total exhaustion* <note>original: "ὁρᾷν τὰ ὄρνεα διαπυκτεύοντα μέχρι τῆς ἐσχάτης ἀπαγορεύσεως"</note>.

...to see sheep or birds fighting, even to the point of fainting from excitement. You may see more regarding this law from Aeschines, Plato, and others in Samuel Petit’s *Commentary on Attic Laws*, page 84. Indeed, <term>Columella</term><note>A Roman writer on agriculture (c. 4–70 AD).</note> mentions this Greek custom in these words: *“Setting aside that study of the Greeks, who prepared every most fierce bird for contests and combat, we propose to establish the income of an industrious father of a family; not that of a trainer of hated birds, whose rooster-fighter often takes the entire inheritance as a gambling debt.”* And <term>Pliny</term><note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist.</note> reports in Book 19 of his *Natural History*, chapter 21: “At Pergamum, a public spectacle of roosters is presented every year, just like gladiators.” In the <term>Mosaic Law</term><note>The laws given to Moses in the Torah.</note>, it is commanded <margin>Leviticus 14:4</margin> that lepers, on the day of their cleansing, should offer <note>original Hebrew: "shetei tzipporim chayot tehorot"</note> *two small birds, living and clean*, along with cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop. <term>Arias and Pagninus</term><note>Famous 16th-century biblical scholars and translators.</note> explain that these birds should be understood as *sparrows*, but <term>Origen</term><note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD).</note> in his *8th Homily on Leviticus*, page 76, interprets them as *two hens*. His words are: (*“When the Priest has visited the leper, he commands that two living hens be taken for the one who is being cleansed, along with cedar wood, twisted scarlet, and hyssop.”*) These two hens seem to me to have a certain similarity to the two goats, one of which is offered to the Lord while the other is sent into the wilderness. For so it is here: out of two hens, one is sacrificed, and the other is released into the field. Therefore, the one who is being purged from leprosy gives some part to be cast away into the desert, while the other part is offered to the Lord for him. However, the hen offered for him is not yet offered at the altar like turtledoves or pigeons. For on that same day, the one being cleansed from leprosy is not yet made worthy of the divine altar; because of this, the Lawgiver commands that on the day he is cleansed, two hens are taken for his purification. I think, however, that the "understanding of the hen" is hidden there, through which the purification of the sinner is effected, regarding which it is written: <note>Matthew 23:37</note> *“How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were not willing!”* Nevertheless, the one being purified needs to be cleansed by cedar wood. For it is impossible for the leprosy of sin to be purged without the wood of the cross, unless that wood is applied, upon which the Savior (as the Apostle Paul says) stripped the Principalities and powers, triumphing over them on the wood. The things Origen discusses regarding the cleansing of the leper and his burnt offering are pious and most worthy of reading, though they are perhaps less strictly aligned with the literal text. Indeed, the word <note>Hebrew: "tzippor"</note> is a general name for all winged creatures, as <term>Aben Ezra</term><note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a medieval Jewish scholar.</note> teaches, but the context of Ecclesiastes 12:4 suggests it should be interpreted as a rooster and hen. Yet, it is not certain whether hens are meant by the "birds" in Leviticus 14:4, especially since other interpreters disagree. Hence, <margin>History of Animals 6.10, part 2</margin> the Blessed <term>Frantzius</term><note>Wolfgang Franz, author of a famous 17th-century work on animal symbolism.</note> at the end of his work rightly raises this question: why was the use of pigeons more frequent in Old Testament sacrifices, and why were roosters and hens not allowed to be admitted to them? To this he answers: Roosters are quarrelsome, pugnacious, boastful, and extremely lustful; they emit seed not only when they see females, but even when they see their own images standing before mirrors; they fight among themselves, and the conquered one submits to the male's lust; they even mate with each other when females are lacking. Hen manure is said to produce many useless weeds because they snatch up

<column-break/>

the grains of various seeds everywhere. Roosters and hens eat human waste, human vomit, spiders; they delight so much in sitting in dung, seeking worms, catching flies, looking for lice, and swallowing pebbles, needles, and coins; indeed, they do not even abstain from the intestines of slaughtered roosters and hens of their own kind. Therefore, the Lord wished to signify that the pious cannot holily sacrifice such animals to Him, and those who wish to keep the worship of God pure must be estranged from similar brawls, boastings, lusts, indiscriminate voracity, and impurities. These are his views on roosters and hens. However, their meat—especially that of hens and young chicks—is a wonderful help not only to the healthy but also to the sick, and is considered a significant delicacy among us, both because of its easy digestion and because it produces good blood and has less waste. <term>Petrus de Apono</term><note>Pietro d'Abano, a 13th-century physician.</note> is full of praise for it in his book on all types of medicine dedicated to Pope John XXI. Not to mention how easy it is to cook if a guest should surprise an unprepared host in the evening, as <term>Catius the Epicurean</term> suggests in <margin>Book II</margin> <term>Horace</term>:
> If an evening guest suddenly comes upon you,
> Lest a tough hen respond poorly to the palate,
> You will be wise to drown the living bird in mixed Falernian wine.
> This will make it tender.
The poet of Venusia <note>Horace</note> is referring to the meat of a hen, even one recently killed; he commands that since it might be quite tough, it should be submerged alive in <term>Falernian</term><note>A luxury wine from ancient Rome.</note> wine, or cooked with the herb sorrel or dock, which makes all meats tender. That passage in 1 Kings 4:23, where the author draws up a catalog of the foodstuffs consumed daily in King Solomon’s court to feed the royal household, troubles interpreters quite a bit. Among other foods, he names <note>Hebrew: "barburim abusim"</note>. Regarding what this might be, the opinions of interpreters are found to be quite different. Some derive *barburim* from a root meaning "to select" or "choose," and they translate it as *the most select*. But *abusim* means *stall-fed* or *fattened*. <term>Junius</term> translates it as *all the most choice fattened birds*. <term>Luther</term> says *fattened cattle*. The Greeks say <note>Greek: "pan ornithon eklekton pan nouadon"</note>, that is, *both selected birds and those from the pasture*. The <term>Vulgate</term><note>The standard Latin Bible.</note> says *fattened birds*. Pagninus says *fattened roosters*; Arias says *fattened capons*. For <term>Rabbi David Kimchi</term><note>A medieval Jewish grammarian.</note> writes that many believe them to be castrated birds, that is, capons. This is sought from the <term>Talmudic Pandects</term><note>The Talmud, specifically the tractate Bava Metzia, folio 86.</note>, where it is written that they are roosters who are fattened by force, with food being pushed into their mouths. It is well known from <term>Aristotle</term> that capons were a delicacy to the Greeks, so much so that it is surprising they lacked a specific name for them in Greece and called them <note>Greek: "alektruonas ektomias"</note>, or "cut-out rooster." Indeed, the Romans received the "cut-out" roosters from the Greeks; they call the castrated rooster a *capus* or *capo*, unless you wish to say the Roman word is of Greek origin, derived from <note>Greek: "koptein"</note> *to cut*, which the ancient grammarians Hesychius, Eustathius, and the Etymologist sometimes explain as "to eat," or "to eat greedily with an open mouth." <term>Baptista Platina of Cremona</term><note>A Renaissance humanist and gastronomist.</note> is quite generous in his praise of capon meat in his book on the science of the kitchen: <margin>Chapter on</margin> *“The praise of all birds,”* he says, *“as far as provisions are concerned, the meat of the chicken alone encompasses them all. For what do other birds bring to the kitchens that one capon does not have in itself, whether you want it boiled or roasted?”*
