who seems to yourself to be a <note>Hebrew: *geber*</note> strong man." See also <term>Luther's</term> version. Others, because the phrase <note>Hebrew: *ve-otkha atah*</note> ("and he will wrap you in a wrapping") follows immediately, apply the meaning of "covering," for the word <note>Hebrew: *atah*</note> signifies to cover or wrap (as in Nehemiah 3:15, from which <note>Hebrew: *atish*</note>, "dew," is named because it covers the herbs and grass). From this comes the doubled form, with the first radical letter <note>Hebrew: *tet*</note>, and the related noun <note>Hebrew: *taltelah*</note>, meaning a covering or garment. According to these scholars, the sense is: "Behold, Jehovah covers you with the covering of a man" (using an <term>enallage</term><note>A grammatical substitution of one form for another.</note> of the absolute state for the construct, "the covering of a man" instead of "a manly covering"), as the Blessed <term>Glassius</term><note>Salomon Glassius (1593–1656), author of *Philologia Sacra*, a key work on biblical linguistics.</note> teaches, on whose authority we rely. (Or as others supply: "with a covering, as much as can belong to a man.") And "he wraps you in a wrapping," that is, Jehovah alone raises you to this peak of honor and dignity. For just as dignity is recognized by distinguished clothing, so it is sometimes described in the Scriptures, as in Genesis 41:41 and following. "Of a man," or "as much as can be of a man," meaning the most ample dignity; for <term>Shebna</term><note>A high official under King Hezekiah mentioned in Isaiah 22.</note> was second only to the King. <term>Arias Montanus</term><note>A 16th-century Spanish Orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible.</note> embraces the opposite sense here in his book *On Hebrew Idioms*. For he translates it as "he will wrap you in a wrapping," meaning he will overwhelm you with confusion and reproach. But the preceding exposition is simpler. we have sent this ahead out of a study of the line from the most learned writing of Glassius (*Philologia Sacra*, Book 3, page 336), since we have read nothing clearer anywhere for explaining this text. Now we must hear the Verses and their Teachers, from whose class Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] here wonderfully explains the word <note>Hebrew: *geber*</note>: "And he will transport you <note>Aramaic: *ke-hadin tarnegola de-metaltel me-atar le-atar*</note> like a domestic rooster, which is transported from one place to another." He takes this from a certain Talmudic saying in which the word <note>Hebrew: *geber*</note> (in Chaldean/Aramaic <note>Aramaic: *gebra*</note>) signifies a domestic rooster. From this, one can now see from what "dungheap" that rooster flew into the Latin Vulgate version of this passage. This is to be ascribed to <term>Jerome</term><note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420), the primary translator of the Vulgate.</note> himself, who, as he himself testifies, having been taught by his Hebrew teacher, translated it thus. A "devirated" [castrated] rooster. And in the mystical exposition: "The rooster is a good <term>prelate</term><note>A high-ranking church official like a bishop.</note>, who guards and impregnates the hens—that is, the souls of his subordinates. That passage in Proverbs 30:31 experiences no better fortune. The Chaldean Paraphrase agrees with them: <note>Aramaic: *aknesha de-mizdarzez beynat tarnegolin*</note> "the rooster that is brisk among the hens." Otherwise, the pseudo-Jerome comments on this place: "Holy preachers, announcing the true morning amidst the shadows of this night, who are girded at the loins because they restrain flowing luxury from their members." In the same chapter of Proverbs, but in verse 19, the Rabbis repeat the same song regarding the phrase "the way of a <note>Hebrew: *geber*</note> man with a young woman," where in the *Midrash Mishle* [Commentary on Proverbs] they explain it as being about a rooster. It is also a wonder that Benito Arias Montanus, in his book *Joseph, or on the Secret Speech*, page 81, gave this note for the sake of the Latin version of Isaiah 22: "The rooster both knows the parts of the day and night and indicates them with its voice. For it announces noon and the middle of the night, just as it is written: 'Who gave the rooster intelligence?' Job 38:36. For this reason, it is accustomed to be carried by those making a journey or sailing, for the sake of indicating the time, just as it is written (Isaiah 22), 'as a rooster is carried away.' Whence it also expresses the image of a pilgrimage." And so Arias is contrary to himself while he explains the text in both places according to the truth of the Hebrew language. ...cockfighting <note>original Greek: ομαχίας, likely part of αλεκτρυονομαχίας (alektruonomachias)</note>, seeing birds fight even to the point of utter exhaustion. His words are: (*Moreover, when the Priest sees him (the leper), he commands that two living hens be taken for him who is being cleansed, and cedar wood, and twisted scarlet, and hyssop. It seems to me that even here these two hens have a certain similarity to the two goats, of which one is offered to the Lord and the other is sent into the wilderness. For so here, out of two hens, one is sacrificed, and the other is released into the field. I think, however, that even here there is a hidden understanding of that "Hen" through whom the purification of the sinner is effected, of whom it is written: "How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing?" Yet, he who is being purified needs to be purified through cedar wood. For it is impossible for the leprosy of sin to be purged without the wood of the cross, unless that wood is also applied on which the Savior (as the Apostle Paul says) stripped the Principalities and powers, triumphing over them on the wood/tree*), etc. The things Origen discusses regarding the cleansing of the leper and his burnt offering are pious and very worthy of reading, but they are perhaps less consistent with the literal text. To be sure, <note>Hebrew: צפר (*tsippor*)</note> is a general name for everything that has a wing, as <term>Aben Ezra</term> <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar.</note> teaches; but the context of *Ecclesiastes 12:4* suggests it should be explained as a rooster or hen. <margin>Sacred History of Animals, part 10, section 2.</margin> 
<term>B. Frantzius</term> <note>Wolfgang Franz (1564–1628), author of a famous work on animal symbolism.</note> at the end of his work raises this question: why was the use of pigeons more frequent in the sacrifices of the Old Testament, and why were roosters and hens not admitted to them? To which he answers thus: *Roosters are quarrelsome, pugnacious, boastful, and extremely lustful; they emit seed not only when they see females, but even when they see their own images standing before mirrors; they fight among themselves, and the loser submits to the male's lust, and they mate with each other when females are lacking. The hen is said to produce many useless weeds at the same time, because they everywhere* 

<column-break/>

*snatch up little grains of various seeds.* Roosters and hens eat human dung, human vomit, spiders; they delight so much in settling upon the filth of animals, seeking worms, catching flies, searching for lice, and swallowing pebbles, needles, and coins; indeed, they do not even abstain from the intestines of slaughtered roosters and hens of their own kind. Therefore, the Lord wished to signify that the pious cannot holily sacrifice such animals to Him, and those who wish to keep the worship of God pure ought to be strangers to similar quarrels, boastings, lusts, promiscuous voracity, and impurities. Thus says Frantzius regarding roosters and hens. Their meat—especially that of hens and young chickens—is a great delicacy among us, wonderfully helping not only the healthy but also the sick, both because of its easy digestion and because it generates good blood and has less waste, as <term>Petrus de Apono</term> <note>Pietro d'Abano (c. 1257–1316), an Italian philosopher and physician.</note> praises extensively in his book *On Every Kind of Medicine, addressed to Pope John XXI.* Not to mention how easy it is to cook if a guest should surprise one unprepared in the evening, which <term>Catius</term> the Epicurean Insubrian hints at in <term>Horace</term>:
<margin>Book 2, Satire 4</margin>
> If a guest should suddenly oppress you in the evening,
> Lest a tough hen respond poorly to his palate,
> You will be wise to drown it alive in mixed <term>Falernian wine</term><note>A prestigious wine from ancient Italy.</note>.
> This will make it tender.

The poet of Venusia [Horace] refers to the meat of a hen, even a recently killed one, and commands that since it is quite tough, it should be submerged alive in Falernian wine, or cooked with the herb of sorrel or dock, which makes all meats tender. That passage in *1 Kings 4:23* troubles the translators not a little, where the author draws up a catalog of the foodstuffs that were consumed daily in the court of King Solomon to feed the royal household. Among other things, he names the foods <note>Hebrew: אבוסים וּבַרְבֻּרִים (*abusim u-barburim*)</note>. What this might be is found to be quite different according to the opinions of translators. Some derive "choice birds" <note>Hebrew: בַּרְבֻּרִים (*barburim*)</note> from the root meaning "to select" <note>Hebrew: ברר (*barar*)</note>, and they translate it as *the most select.* But "fatted" <note>Hebrew: אבוסים (*abusim*)</note> they translate as *pastured.* <term>Junius</term> translates: *the most select of all fatted fowl.* <term>Luther</term> translates: *fattened cattle.* The Greeks translate: *fattened choice birds and pasture birds* <note>original Greek: σιτιστὰ ἐϰλεϰτὰ ϰαὶ νωμάδ’ων</note>. The <term>Vulgate</term> says: *fattened birds.* <term>Pagninus</term>: *fattened chickens*; <term>Arias</term>: *fattened capons.* For <term>Rabbi David Kimchi</term> writes that many thought they were castrated birds, that is, capons. This is sought from the Talmudic Pandects, in the *Tractate Bava Mezia, folio 86*, where it is written that they are roosters which are fattened by force, with food thrust into their mouths. It is well known from <term>Aristotle</term> that capons were a delicacy for the Greeks, so much so that it is surprising they lacked a proper name for them among the Hellenes, being called "castrated roosters" <note>original Greek: ἀλεκτρύονας ἐϰτομίας</note>. Indeed, the Romans received the "castration" <note>original Greek: ἐϰτομίαν</note> of roosters from the Greeks, and they call a castrated rooster a *capus* or *capo*, unless you wish to say the Roman word is of Greek origin and is derived *from "eating greedily"* <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ κάπτειν</note>, which the ancient grammarians Hesychius, Eustathius, and the Etymologist explain sometimes as "in mangers" <note>original Greek: ἐν ϰάνϑοις</note> and sometimes as "to eat from mangers" <note>original Greek: ϰανϑούς ἐσϑίειν</note>, to eat greedily and with a gaping mouth. <term>Baptista Platina</term> of Cremona is quite liberal in his praise of the meat of capons in his *On Honorable Pleasure and Health*: <margin>Chapter on the Hen.</margin> *The praise of all birds,* he says, *as far as meat is concerned, the single flesh of the chicken comprehends. For what do the other birds bring to the kitchens that one capon does not have in itself, whether you want it boiled or roasted?*

# From Psalm 50, verses 10–11

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>

A dish made of this bird <note>The rooster</note> is good for the stomach, soothes the chest, makes the voice resonant, and the body fat. As for what <term>Jarchi</term> <note>Solomon Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval rabbi</note> says, <term>Selden</term> <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English polymath and scholar of Jewish law</note> has treated the matter of the <note>original Hebrew: נחש (*nachash*, likely a transcription error in the original for *geber*)</note> more thoroughly elsewhere; meanwhile, in the <term>Talmud</term>, it denotes a wild cock or a poultry cock, just as <term>Rabbi David Kimchi</term> <note>A medieval grammarian and biblical commentator</note> fabulously recounts regarding <margin>2 Kings 17:30</margin> 2 Kings 17. On this matter, Solomon Jarchi and Selden (in *Syntagma 2, chapter 8*) have written extensively. We read in <term>Saubert</term>’s *On Sacrifices* (chapter 3, pages 54–55) that the rooster was considered a watchful bird and was dedicated to <term>Mercury</term> <note>The Roman messenger god, associated with vigilance</note>. <term>Pliny</term> (*Natural History*, Book 10, Chapter 42), <term>Alexander of Aphrodisias</term> (*Preface to Natural Problems*), and others have even devised the idea that there is a sense of religion or superstition within roosters and hens.

Thus far, as the occasion allowed, we have surveyed certain passages of Holy Scripture in which you will not expressly find the word "Rooster" used by all translators who revere the <term>Vulgate</term> <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note>. However, there remain places where the reading is consistent, namely *Job 38:36, Proverbs 30:31, and Isaiah 22:17*. To begin with the last of these, the Hebrew text reads: <note>original Hebrew: הנה יהוה מטלטלך טלטלה גבר (*Hineh Yehovah metaltelkha taltelah geber*)</note>, which means, *Behold, the Lord will cast you out* or carry you away with the "carrying away of a man"—that is, a manly, vehement, and forceful expulsion. Thus some Hebrew scholars, placing the root as *taltel* in the <term>Piel</term> form, or *hetil* in the <term>Hiphil</term> <note>Hebrew grammatical intensive and causative verb structures</note>, meaning to cast down or hurl. <term>Schindler</term> in his Lexicon says: *Behold, the Lord will hurl you with a hurling, O man, you who seem to yourself to be* <note>original Hebrew: גבור (*gibbor*)</note> *mighty.* See also <term>Luther</term>'s Version. Others, because the phrase "He will surely cover you" follows immediately, use the meaning of "covering," for the word *ataph* means to cover. <note>Nehemiah 3:15</note> (derived from *lut*, meaning dew, so called because it covers the plants and grass); from this, by doubling the first radical letter, we get *taltel* and the related noun *taltelah*, meaning a covering or garment. According to these scholars, the sense is: *Behold, the Lord covers you with the garment of a man* (using a grammatical shift where the absolute state <note>original Hebrew: טלטלה (*taltelah*)</note> stands in for the construct <margin>Can. 40, p. 160.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: טלטלת (*taltelat*)</note>), as the Blessed <term>Glassius</term> <note>Salomon Glassius (1593–1656), author of *Philologia Sacra*</note> records, from whom we take these points. (Or as others supply: "with a garment as large as a man's may be"). And "He clothes you by clothing you," that is, the Lord will roll you away from this peak of honor and pluck you from your dignity. For just as dignity is known by distinguished garments, so in the Scriptures it is sometimes described by them (*Genesis 41:41 and following*). Indeed, "as much as a man's can be," that is, most ample; for <term>Shebna</term> <note>The royal steward mentioned in Isaiah 22</note> was second only to the King. <term>Arias Montanus</term> <note>A 16th-century Spanish Orientalist</note> embraces the opposite sense in his *Book on Hebrew Idioms*. He translates it as "He clothes by clothing," meaning He will overwhelm you with confusion and reproach. But the preceding explanation is simpler. We have provided these linguistic details from the most learned writing of the Blessed Glassius (*Sacred Philology, Book 3, page 336*), as we have read nothing clearer for unfolding this text.

Now we must also hear the Jewish teachers <note>original: "Verpuli," a derogatory term for Jews</note> and their Doctors, from whose ranks Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> wonderfully explains the word <note>original Hebrew: גבר (*geber*, usually "man")</note> here: *And He transported you* <note>original Hebrew: טלטלת מאתר לאתר (*taltelat me-atar le-atar*)</note> from place to place, <margin>Please <note>The word "bitte" (please) appears here in German in the margin, likely a reader's note.</note></margin> like this poultry cock, which is transported from one place to another. He takes this from a certain Talmudic saying in which *geber* in <term>Chaldean</term> <note>Aramaic</note> signifies a poultry cock. From this, one can now see from which "dunghill" that poultry cock flew into the Latin Vulgate version of this passage. This is to be ascribed to <term>Jerome</term> himself, who, as he himself testifies, was taught by his Hebrew Master <margin>Comm. on Isaiah, Book 7.</margin> and thus translated it. His words are as follows: *All interpreted* <note>original Hebrew: גבר (*geber*)</note> *as "man." However, the Hebrew who instructed us in the reading of the Old Testament*

<column-break/>

translated it as "poultry cock." Just as, he says, a rooster is carried by the shoulders of a porter from a high place to another, so the Lord brought you lightly from your place. Both <term>Nicholas of Lyra</term> and <term>Hugo Cardinalis</term> <note>Famous medieval biblical commentators</note> blow the same trumpet, the latter saying on this passage: *Just as it is carried away, that is, easily and without labor or resistance. It is called a poultry cock, which leads the chicks just like a Hen.* And in the mystical exposition: *The rooster is the good prelate, who guards and impregnates the "hens"—that is, the souls of his subjects, etc. But the "gallinaceus" <note>A capon or non-breeding cock</note>, who cannot generate, is the prelate who does not know how to preach and leads chicks that are not his own. He who is carried to the market with his feet tied and his head turned toward the ground, so also is the evil prelate cast headlong into Gehenna <note>Hell</note>, with the feet of his affections tied and his head turned.* (*Matthew 22:6*)

The passage in *Proverbs 30:31* experiences no better fortune; the word *geber* is not found there, but rather another, namely <note>original Hebrew: זרזיר (*zarzir*)</note>, which the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated as "rooster" <note>original Greek: ἀλέκτωρ (*alektor*)</note>. The Chaldean Paraphrase agrees with them, saying: *The rooster, who is lively among the hens.* And the Latin Vulgate translator reads *The rooster girt about the loins*. Consult <term>Fuller</term>’s *Sacred Miscellany* (Book 6, chapter 14, page 649 and following) for more on this word; he treats the genuine meaning of this word at length and, with <term>Tremellius</term> <note>A converted Jewish scholar and reformer</note>, understands it to be a horse. Elsewhere, a pseudo-Jerome comments on this passage thus: *The holy preachers among the shadows of this night, announcing the true morning, who are girt about the loins because they restrain the flowing luxury from their members.*

In the same chapter of Proverbs, but in verse 19, the Rabbis repeat the same song regarding the phrase "the way of a man (*geber*) with a young woman," where in the *Midrash Mishle* <note>A commentary on Proverbs</note> they explain it as referring to a poultry cock. It is truly a wonder that Benedict Arias Montanus, in the book *Joseph, or on the Secret Speech* (page 81), gave this note in favor of the Latin version of Isaiah 22: *The rooster both knows the parts of the day and night and indicates them with his voice. For he announces midday and the middle of the night, just as it is written: "Who gave the rooster intelligence?"* (*Job 38:36*). *For this reason, he is accustomed to be carried by travelers and sailors for the sake of indicating the time, as it is written in Isaiah 22: "Just as a poultry cock is carried."* From this, he also expresses the image of pilgrimage. And thus Arias is contrary to himself, while in both places he explains the text according to the truth of the Hebrew language. No less in the cited passage of Job 38:36, where the Hebrew reads: *Who gave intelligence to the* <note>original Hebrew: לשכוי (*la-sekhvi*)</note>? Arias, by his own inversion, translates this Hebrew word as: *Who gave contemplation?* <term>Pagninus</term> translates it as "of the heart," Tremellius as "to the mind." The Vulgate again translates it as "to the rooster." On this passage, Jerome <margin>Comm. on Job.</margin> (or whoever else is the author) says: *I think the rooster is each of the saints, who in the night and darkness of this world receive faith, intelligence, and the constancy of virtue for crying out to God.*

Because of the supreme vigilance in which he excels, the rooster has deserved not only that his image be commonly placed by Christians upon the towers of churches, but he even provides a symbol for Bishops and all Pastors of the Christian flock to watch over the sheep committed to their faith. Let us hear <term>Gregory the Great</term> on this matter: <margin>On the Rooster, Moralia Book 30, chapters 4-7.</margin> *The preacher,* he says, *is like a rooster, who amid the darkness of the present life strives to announce the coming light by preaching, as if by singing; for he says, "The night is far spent," etc. The rooster received intelligence so that he might first know the times of the night...*

<meta>...ly [nocturnal]. This page captures the fascinating transition in 17th-century scholarship where philology (the study of language) meets theology. It shows how a single Hebrew word "geber" (man) could be transformed into "rooster" based on Aramaic dialects, and how that linguistic shift created centuries of art and architecture, such as the roosters on church steeples.</meta>

<summary>This page explores the biblical and linguistic origins of the rooster's symbolism, focusing on the Hebrew word "geber" and its translation in Isaiah, Proverbs, and Job. It explains how Jewish and Christian commentators interpreted the rooster as a symbol of the vigilant preacher or the "holy man" watching for the dawn of God.</summary>

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...he should shake off [slumber], and then finally emit the voices of awakening; for the holy preacher first considers the quality of life in his listeners, and only then forms a voice of preaching suitable for their hearing. For to discern the hours of the night is to rebuke the darkness of actions with an open voice of reproach. Intelligence is given to the rooster because the virtue of discretion is divinely shown to the Teacher of truth, so that he may know to whom, what, when, and how he should instill it. For the same exhortation is not suitable for everyone; often what harms some, profits others. When the rooster prepares to sing, he first skillfully flaps his wings and, striking himself, makes himself more vigilant. In the same way, when preachers set the word of preaching in motion, they first exercise themselves in holy actions, lest being sluggish in their own deeds they rouse others only with their voice. Instead, they shake themselves through sublime deeds before making others anxious to do well; they take care to punish their own sins with tears before they denounce the sins of others. They sound their wings before they emit their song when, before they bring forth words of exhortation, they proclaim through their deeds everything they are about to say. These and other properties of the rooster

<margin>On Luke 22.</margin>
<term>Cardinal Hugh</term> <note>Hugh of Saint-Cher (c. 1200–1263), a Dominican friar and cardinal known for his biblical commentaries.</note> included these in verses and applied them to Pastors:
> The rooster fights, he has spurs and a reddening crest,
> He strikes himself for the song, he scratches, and teaches the hours of night.
> The old one lays eggs, from which the <term>basilisk</term> <note>A legendary serpent-king. Medieval lore claimed that an old rooster could lay an egg that, when hatched by a toad or serpent, produced a deadly cockatrice or basilisk.</note> arises.
> He sits atop the Church, and stretches his beak into the breezes,
> Lifting his tail; these things the Master must note,
> He sires and calls to feed and to the high resting place.

Concerning the **Hen**, there are also many things that deserve to be said and have been said. First among these is her <term>storgē</term> <note>original Greek: στοργή — natural affection or parental love</note> and care. She does not merely hatch the chicks—during which time she often fasts for entire days while sitting on the eggs, or if she occasionally leaves the nest, she eats only a few grains in haste and immediately returns to the eggs—but she also defends them against the hawk <note>Latin: *milvus*</note> and any other enemies with such care, such affection, and such courage. She gathers her chicks and shadows them with her wings. This is a genuine

<margin>Matthew 23:27.</margin>
image of Christ the Savior, to whom He compared Himself with tears. Regarding this, <term>Augustine</term> <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD)</note> writes in *Questions on the Gospels* (Book 1, Question 36): *This kind of creature (the Hen) has a great affection for her children, so much so that when they are weakened, she herself becomes weak. And what you will find more difficult to see in other animals, she protects her children with her wings and fights against the hawk. Thus also our mother, the Wisdom of God, was in a certain way weakened by the taking on of flesh, protects our weakness, and resists the Devil, lest he seize us. In this defense, what the hen attempts through affection against the hawk, Wisdom perfects through power against the Devil.* Compare this with the same author on Psalm 58 and Tractate 15 on John; add also <term>Chrysostom</term> <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father.</note> in his 57th Homily on Matthew.

<margin>Homily 56.</margin>
The latter, in his subsequent commentary, also places the hen as a likeness of the Church. *For just as,* he says, *the chicks of hens wander through different places seeking their food, and are gathered to her by maternal voices, and again feed similarly, and are again gathered by maternal voices: so also the people of God, following fleshly pleasure and worldly desire, wander through various errors, whom Mother Church hastens to gather and entice through her Priests, sometimes by rebukes, sometimes by flatteries, as if by certain voices. 2. And just as a Hen having chicks does not cease calling the little animals, so that by her constant voice she may correct the wandering of her chicks: so also Priests must not cease in teaching, so that by the zeal and constancy of their teaching, they may amend the negligence of the wandering people. 3. And just as a Hen, having chicks, not only warms her own; but also treats the children of any other bird hatched near her as her own: so also the Church strives to call not only her own Christians, but whether they be Gentiles or Jews; if they are placed under her, she vivifies them all with the warmth of faith, generates them in baptism, nourishes them in the word, and loves them with maternal charity.* In place of a finishing touch <note>Latin: *Coronidis loco*</note>, I wish to add the verses of Henning Cunrad of Hamburg, found in Volume 2 of *German Poets*, page 991:
> The hen broods tirelessly on the warming eggs,
> Faithfully and wakefully hatching her own chicks.
> Softly she covers the hatched ones with embracing wings,
> And warms their naked bodies with secret heat.
> She picks suitable grains from everywhere for the led troop,
> And as leader, always directs the rewards with her voice.
> With a clucking throat she calls the scattered chicks,
> And the bird performs the diligent duty of a mother.
> Fiercely she stands against the hawk and greedy kite,
> And with beak and wings covers the unarmed line.
> Thus the <term>Word</term> <note>Greek: *logos*</note> nurtured us from the world's first origin,
> Renews us with the Breath <note>The Holy Spirit</note>, and purges hearts with water.
> He warms the troops gathered under the shadow of his wings by the word,
> He preserves, protects, honors, and loves them.
> He supplies the juices of heaven through the green meadows of the word,
> He increases and drives them by His command.
> He gathers the wandering far and wide, and recalls them under his wings,
> And brings back the seduced sheep with His voice.
> He fights against the violence of Satan and cruel Tyrants,
> A Leader in arms, a Brother by birth, a Father in love.

**THE JACKDAW.** The word <term>Anaphah</term> <note>Hebrew: אנפה</note> in Deuteronomy 14:18 is translated by Arias and the interpreter of the Chaldean version as **jackdaw** <note>Latin: *graculus*</note>. Others explain it differently, as even Arias himself is inconsistent, for in Leviticus 11:19 he renders the same word as an **enraged bird**; whether this applies to the jackdaw, let him see for himself. Tremellius renders it as **heron** <note>Latin: *ardea*</note>, Schindler as **kite** <note>Latin: *milvus*</note>. Luther calls it the **Heger** <note>A German name for a type of jay or heron</note>. Modern Jews call it the **Trapp** <note>Bustard</note>. This word owes its origin to the root <term>naph</term> <note>נאף</note>, which means "he snorted through the nostrils," and by metaphor "he was angry." Hence the Talmudists say, *The kite is an angry bird.* The Septuagint <note>LXX</note> in both places reads <term>charadrion</term> <note>Greek: χαραδριόν — a plover or stone-curlew</note>, followed by the Vulgate and Pagninus, who retain the Greek word, which is so called because it lives along the banks in all <term>gullies</term> <note>Greek: χαράδραις - charadrais</note>. Whence the Scholiast of Aristophanes says: *This bird is named because it spends its time in the gullies,* which the Comic poet himself implies when he says in *The Birds*: *The charadrii and other river birds brought water from below into the air.* The same bird *benefits those with jaundice* <note>Greek: ικτερικούς - ikterikous</note> *when it is looked upon,* as the same Scholiast notes. Among the Latins, the jackdaw <note>graculus</note> received its name from its sound, because it is extremely troublesome for its loquaciousness or chatter, especially during the time of mating. Hugh refers to this when he says: *The charadrius is a wordy bird and signifies the talkative,* as in James 3: *Every nature of beasts, birds, and serpents can be tamed, but no man can tame the tongue.* This bird is placed among the unclean birds, whence Hesychius says: *When he forbids the charadrius, he...*

...prohibits the intemperance of the tongue. Hence it is a symbol of talkative people, as Lauretus <note>Hieronymus Lauretus (d. 1571), a Spanish Benedictine who wrote an encyclopedia of biblical symbols.</note> notes from Tertullian or Novatian. Concerning this bird, let us hear Dionysius the Carthusian <note>Dionysius the Carthusian (1402–1471), a monk and influential mystic writer.</note>, who describes it in this way: *The Charadrius <note>A bird often identified as a plover or a stone-curlew; in medieval lore, it was said to cure jaundice by looking at the patient.</note> is said to be a bird of entirely white color, the lower part of whose thigh clears away the darkness of the eyes. This is said to be the nature of this bird: if it is placed over a sick person who is about to die, it turns its sight away from him; if over one who is to be healed, it fixes its sight upon him, as if applauding the healing; however, it is a bird of unclean nourishment.* Others attribute to it that it is stupid and hunts mice, and is a friend of the night like an owl, whence the proverb, *to imitate the charadrius*, or to live the life of a charadrius, said of one who hides and flees the light.

The CRANE, called *geranos* <note>original: γέρανος</note> by the Greeks and *agur* <note>original: עגור</note> by the Hebrews, is a bird named from the sound of its voice in the Latin, Greek, and Hebrew languages, because they are accustomed to "gruere" <note>An onomatopoeic Latin verb for the crane’s cry.</note>. It is found twice in the Holy Scripture and is commended for the order they observe in their departure. Because of this, they are often called the birds of Palamedes <note>A hero of the Trojan War credited with inventing various Greek letters.</note>, because Palamedes is said to have discovered certain letters from the order and shape they maintain while flying—especially the letter Ypsilon **Υ**, as Ulysses objects to him in the *Heroics* of Philostratus. Jerome, however,
<margin>
On the monastic life.
</margin>
maintains that by their flight they represent the Greek letter **Δ** (Delta), or rather **Λ** (Lambda); compare Cicero in the second book of *On the Nature of the Gods*. But whatever the case may be regarding this observation of letters in flight, it is established by experience that the bird is of no small sagacity and prudence, which Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman naturalist.</note> indicates in book 10, chapter 23 of his *Natural History*, where among other things he discourses on this bird: *When they set out, they act in concert; they fly high to look ahead; they choose a leader to follow; at the rear of the line, they have those stationed in turns to call out and keep the flock together with their voice. They keep watch during the night, holding a pebble in their foot; if it is loosened by sleep and falls, it proves their negligence. The others sleep with their heads tucked under their wings; the leader provides foresight with neck erect and gives warning,* compare Aristotle, book 9 of the *History of Animals*, chapter 10. It occurs in Isaiah 38:14 in the eucharistic prayers which King Hezekiah of Judah poured out to God because of his restoration to health and the lengthening of his life, where according to Arias <note>Benedict Arias Montanus (1527–1598), a Spanish orientalist.</note> and Pagninus <note>Santes Pagninus (1470–1541), a Dominican and Hebraist.</note>, following Rabbi Solomon, he notes the swallow <note>original: סוס (sus)</note>, but *agur* <note>original: עגור</note> for the crane; and to both is attributed the word *tsiphtseph* <note>original: צפצף</note>, which is a "squared" word, as it is called, from *tsaphaph* <note>original: צפף</note>, which in the Piel form means to cover or overspread; and hence *Ziphzeph*, that is, to speak in a covered and hidden speech, to utter something obscurely, to mutter. Compare that sense in Isaiah 8:2, 10:14, and 29:4. In the same way, Arias and Pagninus explain *agur* as the swallow in Jeremiah 8:7, though others say the crane.
<margin>
In the Hebrew Lexicon, page 504.
</margin>
Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a famous Hebraist.</note> notes, however, that in this passage it is not read as *sus* <note>original: סוס</note> but *sis* <note>original: סיס</note>, where Jonathan translates it as *kuznaya* <note>original: כוזניא</note>, which for the Rabbis signifies a crane. I have observed, moreover, in the Geneva Hebrew Bibles of the year 1619, published with the Latin version of Arias Montanus, that it is read as *sus*. I will leave this controversy to more learned men. This bird is praised for the time of its departure and return, and it is set as an example for the stubborn Jews who refuse to recognize the time of their visitation. Cranes are the visitors of winter, just as storks are of summer, as Pliny instructs us. The Church Fathers are prolific in commending this bird, especially for its vigilance, whence a "vigilant crane" among the Egyptians signified prudence; and for their prudence in flying, whence a flying crane among them denoted a man who was wise and

<column-break/>

taught in sublime things. Regarding the vigilance of cranes, Basil <note>Basil of Caesarea (330–379), a Greek bishop and theologian.</note> discourses thus, following Pliny in almost everything:
<margin>
Sacred history of animals. Homily 8 on the Six Days of Creation.
</margin>
> Cranes are accustomed to take turns keeping watch during the night; and while the others sleep, one remains awake and surveys everything, looking out with neck erect, providing security for each while they sleep. Then, when the defined time has passed, that one gives a clang and turns to take its sleep, while another succeeds it, and returns in part the security it received. One can certainly see this same order in their flight; for sometimes one takes up the duty of leading the others, and having performed this office for a set time, it retreats to the rear of the whole line, handing over the same duty of leading to the one who was flying first behind it, and so on.

Ambrose <note>Ambrose (c. 340–397), Bishop of Milan.</note> is more extensive regarding both of these properties in book 5 of his *Hexaemeron*, chapter 15, whose entire words I have chosen to write down because of the sweetness of the doctrine and the elegance of the language: *In cranes,* he says, *there is a certain natural republic <note>original: politia</note> and military service, while in us it is forced and slavish. How cranes, without orders and by voluntary habit, carry out a solicitous guard in the night! You may see the sentinels arranged, and while the other companions of the species rest, others go around and explore, lest an ambush be attempted from any side; and they perform the whole defense with tireless vigor. Afterward, when the time of the watches has been fulfilled and the duty performed, it settles itself to sleep, after first giving a clang to wake the sleeper to whom it will hand over the turn of duty. And the other willingly accepts its lot, and unlike our habit, does not refuse as being out of the way or too sluggish with sleep, but tirelessly shakes itself from its bed, performs its turn, and represents the favor it received with constant care and duty. Therefore, there is no desertion, because the devotion is natural. Therefore, the guard is safe, because the will is free. Those who fly also preserve this order and by this moderation alleviate all labor, so that they perform the duty of their leadership in turns. For one precedes and runs before the others for its restored time, and runs as if before the standards; then it turns back and yields the lot of leading the line to the next one. What is more beautiful than this: that both the labors and the honor are common to all, and power is not arrogated by a few, but is transferred to all by a certain voluntary lot? This is the duty of an ancient Republic and the image of a free city. Thus, from the beginning, having received this social order from nature through the example of birds, men began to practice it so that labor might be common and dignity might be common—that individuals in turns should share the cares, divide the duties, and partition the commands, so that no one would be without honor and no one immune from labor.* This was the most beautiful state of affairs; neither did anyone grow old in perpetual power, nor was anyone broken by long-term servitude, because the promotion was both without envy due to the order of duty and the reasoning of time, and the guard seemed more tolerable because it fell by a common lot. No one dared to press another with servitude when they themselves would have to undergo the mutual heights of honor as a successor. Labor was heavy for no one, as the dignity that would follow relieved it. But after the lust for dominating began to claim undue powers and refused to lay down those taken up—after military service began to be not a common right but a servitude—after power became not an order to be respected but a zeal for claiming—even the performance of labor itself began to be more harshly endured. And because it is not voluntary, it quickly leaves a place for negligence. How unwillingly men undergo the duties of the watches, how reluctantly...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
...everyone in the camp keeps watch more strongly against danger, because they are entrusted by a royal agreement to protect themselves. A penalty for laziness is proposed, and yet neglect often creeps in, and the watches are not kept. For *necessity*, which imposes obedience on the unwilling, usually brings about a sense of weariness. Nothing is so easy that it does not have some difficulty if you do it against your will. Therefore, constant labor turns away one's affection, and continuous, long-lasting power breeds insolence. Where can you find a man who would voluntarily lay down his Command and surrender the insignia of his leadership, willingly becoming the last instead of the first? We, however, contend not only for the first place but even for the middle, and we claim the first seats at a banquet, and if something is granted once, we want it to be permanent. Therefore, the cranes represent equanimity in labor and humility in positions of power. 

**They are warned to take turns in their guarding duties, but they are not warned to step down from their positions of power, because in the former case, the natural rest of sleep must be interrupted, while in the latter, it is a matter of voluntary and diligent service. Marco Polo the Venetian <note>original: Marcus Paulus Venetus; the famous 13th-century explorer.</note> records that while days appear to be of one color to us, there are diverse colors to be found elsewhere (*The Travels of Marco Polo, Book 1, Ch. 64, p. 359*). He says: There are (around the city of the Cianiganes <note>Likely referring to a city in China described by Marco Polo, such as Channiganfu.</note>) five kinds of cranes; some have black wings, like crows; others are white and bright, having full feathers and eyes of a golden color, like the "eyes" on the tails of our peacocks. Others are found there that are not unlike our own. Then there are others which are small but have long and very beautiful feathers, mixed with red and black. Fifth, there are cranes of a gray color, having red and black eyes, and these are very large.**

<margin>
Deuteronomy 14:12
</margin>
**THE GRIFFIN** <note>original: Gryphs</note> or Gryphus, among the Biblical birds, is referred to where the Hebrew reads *peres* <note>original: פֶרֶס</note>, according to the Septuagint and the Vulgate. Whether a bird of this name actually exists in nature is rightly doubted, and the arguments for the negative view are stronger than those for the affirmative. They imagine it living in the Rhipaean <note>A legendary mountain range in the far north.</note> or Hyperborean mountains of Asiatic Scythia; if this were so, it never reached Palestine or the neighboring regions. From its stature and body shape, it is more truly a monster than a bird or animal. According to Dionysius the Carthusian <note>A 15th-century theologian and mystic.</note>, it is a monstrous, four-footed bird, having a body shaped like a lion, with wings and a head like an eagle; it is very cruel, tearing apart living men whom it eats, and sometimes it seizes a horse with its rider, lifts them on high, and devours them. It has claws so large and wide that, as it is said, cups are made from them to be placed on the tables of Kings. It also places emeralds and jasper in its nest to protect against poisonous animals. So he says. Herodotus mentions (*Book 4, No. 13*) that the griffins are *gold-guards* <note>original: Χρυσοφύλακας</note> among the Scythian people called the *Arimaspi*. However, gold is not produced in the Rhipaean mountains or the entire North, as Joannes Michovius <note>Maciej Miechowita (1457–1523), a Polish scholar who debunked myths about Northern geography.</note> relates in his description of Asiatic Sarmatia. Vossius (*On Idolatry, Book 3, Ch. 99*) thinks the fable of the griffin originated with the Egyptians, where a deity was depicted in this or a similar form; having seen this figure, the Greeks gave the fictitious bird the name *grypos* <note>original: γρυπὸς</note> from its hooked beak—for one who has an aquiline nose is called *grypos*. You may see more on this there, to which you may add, if you like, more recent authors such as Ulisse Aldrovandi <note>A 16th-century Italian naturalist.</note>, Wolfgang Franz, Lelio Bisciola, and Friedrich Tilemann.

p. 1268.

THE OSPREY <note>original: Haliætus</note>, a Greek word retained by all the Latin translators I have read, except for Arias <note>Arias Montanus, editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible.</note>, who translates it in *Deuteronomy 14:12* as "the powerful-winged one"; Luther calls it the **Fisher** <note>original: Fischer</note>, but elsewhere the **Sea-eagle** <note>original: marina aquila</note>. Luther also uses the term **Diver** <note>original: Taucher</note>. The name *haliaietos* or *haliaetos* is derived from the sea and fishing, from *als* [sea] and *halieuo* [to fish]. Pliny (*Natural History, Book 10, Ch. 3*) reports it is a species of eagle with very clear eyes, which poises itself from on high, and when a fish is seen in the sea, it rushes headlong into it, strikes the water with its breast, and seizes it. Dionysius the Carthusian agrees with this: *The Haliætus, as it is in the books on the natures of animals, is a small bird, attacking, seizing, and eating small birds, whence some think it is a Sparrowhawk.* Aristotle mentions it (*History of Animals, Book 8, Ch. 3*) near the end: *The osprey dwells around the sea and dives into lakes,* where he also mentions other birds that *live around rivers and lakes, and around the sea.* In the Holy language it is called *azniyyah* <note>original: עָזְנִיָּה</note> from *azaz* [to be strong], because this bird is endowed with remarkable strength.

<margin>
Commentary on Leviticus 11.
</margin>
THE SWALLOW <note>original: Hirundo</note>, for which the Ancients used the name *Helundo*, or *chelidon* <note>original: χελιδὼν</note> (with the Greek X changed to H), or *Chelidonia*. Gaza <note>Theodorus Gaza, 15th-century translator of Aristotle.</note> calls it *hirundinaria* because the swallow heals the eyes of its chicks with it, according to Pliny, or because it blooms near its arrival, according to Theophrastus. According to Isidore, it is named from the sound of its voice, and because it does not take its food while sitting, but catches its meals in the air. Among the Hebrews, in the opinion of translators, it is the *agur* <note>original: עֲגוּר</note>. For according to some translators, the last of the unclean birds under the name *agur* in *Leviticus 11:19 and Deuteronomy 14:18* is the swallow. Then it occurs in *Jeremiah 8:7 and Isaiah 38:14* as *sus* or *sis* <note>original: סוּס / סִיס</note>, which words others translate as "crane," but the Septuagint translates as "swallow" <note>original: χελιδόνα</note>, whom Luther imitates. Finally, it comes under another name, unique to this bird, in *Psalm 84:3*: *deror* <note>original: דְּרוֹר</note>. It is so called because it seeks liberty so much that it would die sooner than endure slavery shut in a cage, and because it wanders freely among men, free from traps, as Dr. Geier says in his commentary on *Proverbs 26:2*. For there is an old superstition, which still clings tightly to the minds of the common people, that no one willingly harms a swallow, either because it is hostile to insects, flies, and spiders, or because it purges the air of flies, moths, crickets, and gnats. Buxtorf gives another reason for this name from the root *derar*, namely that the swallow is so called because it has the liberty of nesting in human houses, whence the *Talmudists* say: *The word deror signifies nothing but liberty* <note>original: אין דרור אלא לשון חירות</note> (*Rosh Hashanah, folio 9, 2*). And elsewhere: *Why is its name called the bird of liberty? Because it lives in a house just as in a field* <note>original: למה נקרא שמה צפור דרור? שדרה בבית כבשדה</note> (*Beitzah, folio 24, 1*). See also Rabbi Levi and Rabbi Aben-Ezra on *Proverbs 29:2*. It is the messenger of spring, whence the Rhodians, at the annual return of the spring swallow, sang in praise: *The swallow has come, has come, bringing the beautiful seasons and beautiful years,* according to Rhodiginus. And Aristophanes in *The Knights*:

Aristophanes, Scene 3, verse 182.
</margin>
> Look, boys, do you not see the seasonable swallow? 
> *Watch, boys, do you not see spring? The new swallow is here.*

### From Psalm 55:10, 11.

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
...the winter ends, and rain comes, and the swallow appears. <note>original Greek: χειμ. ἐπιτέλει, καὶ ὑετὸς γίνεται, καὶ χελιδὼν φαίνεται. A common ancient saying regarding the arrival of spring.</note> Furthermore, the swallow was used in hieroglyphic writings to signify the herald of the first dawn, and thus it represents vigilance, according to that common school verse used by monks:

> The swallow sings, the reed flourishes, the swallow heals. <note>original: Cantat hirundo, floret arundo, sanat hirundo.</note>

For the swallow is accustomed to spend the morning hours at windows with its chirping, and by the same means, it awakens those living in the house. For this reason, since this small bird is seen on the coat of arms of the Counts of Lippe, Justus Reuber <note>The text reads "Robigigrad," likely a Latinized name for Reuber or a similar scholar.</note> addresses Count Simon of Lippe in this way:

-> But what does the Swallow signify above the stars? Behold, you labor <-
-> To be a watchful Count for your people, night and day. <-

Indeed, it is a hardworking animal, and it applies the greatest effort in building its nest, which it constructs with wonderful art and skill. When it lacks sufficient mud for building the nest, it flies to the water and wets the tips of its wings, and afterward rolls itself in the finest dust; in this way, it procures for itself as much mud as it needs for the construction and completion of its nest. We shall describe the wonderful craftsmanship and ingenious structure of the nest itself, not in our own words, but partly in the words of Basil and partly in those of Ambrose. Thus
<margin>
Homily 8 on the Hexameron.
</margin>
Basil writes: Let no one deplore poverty, nor let anyone despair of his life or think that all is lost because nothing remains of his inheritance, if he considers the nature of the swallow, by which the swallow quite easily seems to help and provide for itself. For when it builds its little nest, it picks up straw in its beak and carries it to the place where the building is to be done. However, since it cannot carry mud in its feet, it first wets the ends of its feathers with water. Then, rolling itself in the finest dust, it procures the use of mud in this manner. Then, gradually joining the tufts together and binding the straws, using the mud just like glue, once the little nest is built, it finally nourishes its chicks hatched from the produced eggs. If any of these should have their eyes pricked, the swallow possesses a certain power of healing granted to it by Nature, by which it restores the sight of its offspring to its former health. <note>Ancient lore claimed swallows used the herb celandine—from the Greek "chelidon" for swallow—to heal their young's eyes.</note> Let these things teach you, let these things warn you not to be driven to any outrages or frauds due to the hardships of poverty: nor, when placed in the gravest calamities, should you lie down in total idleness with hope cast aside, with a weakened and broken spirit without action or any labor, but flee to God Himself. He who has bestowed such gifts upon the swallow will bestow much greater benefits upon those men who call upon Him with their whole heart and 
<margin>
Book 5, chapter 17 of the Hexameron.
</margin>
flee to Him. Ambrose is even more extensive in explaining the diligence and craftsmanship the swallow uses in building its nest, and he immediately adds how fiercely it defends its chicks against predatory birds. He says: Let us take a great lesson of maternal diligence toward children. The swallow, small in body but sublime in remarkably pious affection, builds nests more precious than gold for all the needy, because it nests wisely. For the nest of wisdom is more precious than gold. For what is wiser than to enjoy the wandering freedom of flying, yet entrust its little ones and its roof to the dwellings of men, where no one may attack the brood? For it is also a beautiful thing that from their first birth it accustoms its chicks to the habit of human 

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
conversation and makes them safer from the snares of enemy birds. Furthermore, it is remarkable by what grace it composes houses for itself without any helper, as if skilled in an art. For it gathers stalks in its beak and smears them with mud so that it can glue them together. But because it cannot carry mud with its feet, it dips the tips of its feathers in water so that dust may easily adhere to them, becoming slime, with which it gradually gathers stalks or tiny twigs and makes them stick, building the structure of the entire nest in that manner. So that, as if on the floor of a pavement, its chicks may move about within their home without injury, and no foot may get caught through the cracks of the weaving, nor cold creep in upon the tender ones. But this duty of industry is common to many birds. What is truly unique, however, in which there is remarkable care of piety and an insignia of prudent intellect and knowledge, as well as a certain skill in the medical art, is this: That if any of its chicks should be clouded by blindness or have their eyes pricked, it has a certain kind of healing by which it can restore their sight for its intended use. Let no one, therefore, complain about lack, because they have left their own home empty of money. The swallow is poorer, yet as an empty-handed bird, it abounds in industry. It builds and spends nothing; it raises a roof and takes nothing from its neighbor. It is not driven to harm another by want and poverty, nor does it despair in the grave weakness of its children. We, however, are affected by poverty, and the necessity of lack vexes us, and want forces many into outrage and impels them into crime. Also, in the pursuit of profit, we turn our intellect toward fraud, adapt our affections, and in the gravest passions, we lay down hope and, broken in spirit, we dissolve; we lie down improvident and idle, when one should hope more in divine mercy at the very time when human help has failed. To this belongs what Pliny reports concerning the Canopic or Heracleotic mouth of the Nile:
<margin>
Book 10, ch. 33.
</margin>
Swallows, he says, at the Heracleotic mouth of Egypt, oppose the wandering Nile with a mole <note>A massive structure or dam.</note> made of a continuous line of nests, impregnable, for the space of one stadium, which could not be completed by human labor. Pliny adds in the same place that in that same Egypt, near the town of Coptos, there is an island sacred to Isis, which the same swallows fortify with work so that the Nile does not tear it away; at the beginning of spring days, they strengthen its beak <note>Referring to the prow or point of the island.</note> with chaff and straw, continuing for three nights with such labor that it is established that many die in the work; this military service returns to them every year. Papinius <note>Statius</note> also mentions this work:
<margin>
Silvae, Book 3.
</margin>

> Under your leadership let it be known
> Whence the fertile license of the marshy Nile comes,
> Why the shallows fail, and the bank restrains the waves
> Marked by Cecropian mud. <note>original: Cecropio signata luto. "Cecropian" refers to Athens; swallows are often called Cecropian because of the myth of the Athenian princess Procne who became a swallow.</note>

Johann Baptista Pius notes here that "Cecropian mud" refers to the dam of the swallows, the reason for which name he provides, as does Boccaccio in Book 9, chapter 8. According to Cardinal Hugo's exposition on Isaiah 38, the swallow is a symbol of "painted" <note>feigned or false</note> friendship, according to these verses:

> Black, it fashions a home under the roof, yet it does not fall;
> Prey to none, it flies swift, and feeds in the air.
> It goes, it returns in summer, it gives the itch, it blinds with dung.

I have read these verses explained in this way in Hermann Frey's *Ornithobibl.* <note>Library of Birds</note>, p. 160: The swallow signifies a Flatterer for nine reasons. 1. Because it is black in the uncleanness of its own conscience, like the swallow. 2. Because the swallow fashions a house of mud, and the flatterer...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

...makes a great deal of noise about nothing. 3. Because the swallow does not destroy its own home, nor does a flatterer ever reproach his own master. 4. Because the swallow is prey to no other bird, and the flatterer is a friend to everyone. 5. Because it flies swiftly, and the flatterer very quickly carries rumors wherever they might please. 6. Because it lives in the air, and the flatterer feeds himself on the wind of vanity and human favor. 7. Because it departs in winter and returns in summer; likewise, the flatterer departs in times of adversity but returns in times of prosperity. 8. Because the swallow causes "the itch" <note>original: scabiem; likely referring to the irritation of its droppings or parasites.</note>, and the flatterer provides the "itch of excellence" to his listeners. 9. Because the swallow blinds with its droppings <note>A reference to the Book of Tobit, where Tobit is blinded by swallow droppings.</note>, and the flatterer blinds the eyes of self-knowledge in his listeners, and so forth. Thus he writes <margin>In the Exposition of Tobit.</margin> However, the same author also compares the bird to a man of integrity and honesty; finally, it is presented as an image of the Resurrection. Pliny writes truly about swallows in Book 10, Chapter 24: *they stay in the vicinity, seeking out the sunny recesses of the mountains, and are found there naked and featherless.* This is consistent with truth and experience, as they are found half-dead everywhere, both in the holes of the highest towers and in the caverns of lakes and ponds. By this, it is not denied that some, as winter approaches, retreat to warmer places that are more suited to their nature, but at least this is not done by all; for some remain, hiding themselves in the fissures of rocks or the hollows of decaying oaks, where they are sometimes found dead or clinging together in clusters.

**THE GULL** (*Larus*), among the Hebrews, has a name derived from swelling and the itch, <term>Shachaph</term> <note>Hebrew: שחף</note>, which Arias <note>Benedictus Arias Montanus, a 16th-century Spanish orientalist.</note> translates in both passages of Moses as *Phthiticum* <note>Related to phthisis, or wasting disease (tuberculosis).</note>, signifying that this bird is named after <term>Shachephet</term> <note>Hebrew: שחפת</note>, which means consumption—a disease by which the body wastes away and is weakened. The bird is so lean and light that it has many feathers but very little flesh; hence the name of the disease in Leviticus 26:16 and Deuteronomy 28:22. Whether this is a wasting away or a swelling with pustules, the Rabbis argue. Luther renders it as *Guckuck* (Cuckoo), a version which the Jews approve of in this instance because the cuckoo appears particularly "itchy" or mangy compared to other birds. It is also commonly called <term>Cepphus</term> <note>Greek: κέπφος; a term often used for a gull or a simpleton.</note>, from which comes the proverb: *O Cepphus!* and that line from Aristophanes: *Cepphi and doves are faithful to little foxes.* From this also comes <term>kepphotheis</term> <note>Greek: κεπφωθεὶς</note>, meaning "deceived by a harlot" (Proverbs 7:22). Others, including Tremellius, translate it as *asalo* <note>A type of hawk or merlin.</note>. The Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament.</note> rendered it as <term>ton laron</term> (the gull), with whom the Vulgate, Pagninus, Vatablus, and the Latin translator of the Chaldean Paraphrase agree. Concerning the Gull, Vatablus notes: "The gull is a small, black bird living near the water; it dwells both in the water and on land, and is also called a coot." By the common opinion of the initiates of nature, it is established that it is a bird that swims in the waters and flies over <margin>in the *Ixeutica*.</margin> the lands, as Oppian describes it, and Hesychius says *it is a predator of fish.* Aristotle mentions it in Book 5 of the *History of Animals*, Chapter 9: <term>the shearwater and the gulls breed in the rocks around the sea; but the gull breeds in summer, while the shearwater breeds at the beginning of spring.</term> <note>original Greek provided in text.</note> Pliny calls it a *Gavia* <note>A sea-mew or gull.</note>, saying, *Gaviæ nest in rocks, cormorants even in trees; Gaviæ give birth in summer, cormorants at the beginning of spring.* And Apuleius in Book 5 of *The Golden Ass*: *That very white bird, the gavia, which swims with its feathers over the sea waves, plunges itself down near to the deep bosom of the Ocean.* From this de-

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
lineation of the ancients flow the descriptions of others, such as Dionysius the Carthusian: *The gull is a bird, now flying in the air, now swimming in the water; it is a lazy, small, and fat bird, happily dwelling near waters; it cannot fly far or for long, so that a person running fast can catch it, and it is very moist.* And Hesychius says: *The gull is an animal living in both—that is, water and land—which flies like a bird but swims like an aquatic creature.* To which those who venerate circumcision and *Baptism* at the same time are not badly compared; to whom Paul says, *If you are circumcised, Christ profits you nothing.* And Hugo <note>Hugh of Saint Victor, a medieval theologian.</note> says: *The gull is an animal that now swims in the water, now flies over the land; and it signifies luxurious theologians, who now fly to heavenly things by inspecting the Scriptures, and now fly about in the waters of luxury, etc.*

**THE LITTLE DIVER** (*Mergulus*) or Cormorant (*Mergus*), <term>ichthyophagos</term> <note>Greek: fish-eater</note>, is a fish-eating bird which immerses itself deeply and for a long time in the waters, and from this "merging" it has acquired the name *mergus*. To the Hebrews, it is <term>Shalach</term> <note>Hebrew: שלך</note>, the root of which consists of the same letters and means "he threw away, cast out, or cast down"; because this bird throws itself with force from a height into the waters and plunges to the depth of a cubit, pulling out the fish it has spotted. Arias, Pagninus, and the Latin translator of the Chaldean version everywhere render the Hebrew word as *mergulus*; Tremellius renders it *mergus*, which is the same thing. Luther renders it *der Schwan* (the Swan). The Septuagint, however, in Leviticus renders the Hebrew word as <term>catarracten</term> <note>Greek: "the plunger" or waterfall bird.</note>, but in Deuteronomy as <term>nycticorax</term> <note>Greek: "night-crow" or owl.</note>; the Vulgate, as almost always, presents itself as consistent with the Septuagint in both places. The Greek word is <term>from the verb meaning to crash down</term>, which is <margin>Aristotle, *On Audibles*.</margin> *to fall down with great force and impact*, whence Aristotle says *when pursued, they crash down violently upon their heads*, rushing down from on high with force onto their heads—something he mentions regarding certain predatory birds, which he says are called *Diomedeas* by Juba; compare the same in Book 9 of the *History of Animals*, Chapter 12; Pliny, Book 10 of *Natural History*, Chapter 44; and Vossius, Book 3 of *Idolatry*, Chapter 82. Otherwise, Dionysius the Carthusian offers us such a description of the diver: *The diver (mergulus) takes its name from diving (mergendo),* he says, *because it frequently descends into the waters to swallow worms and small fish; when a storm is imminent, it hastens to the shore with a cry, and, as Isidore says, it is certain that a heavy and great storm is soon pressing when the divers seek the shore.* It is a symbol of the Devil, as Saint Martin has it in Severus Sulpicius, and of gluttons, about whom Hugo says: *The diver stays in the waters and submerges itself under the waves: and it signifies gluttons, who are absorbed by the pleasures of the flesh,* Philippians 3, *whose God is their belly, etc.*

**THE KITE** (*Milvus*). But despite the old books, says Vossius <margin>*Idolatry*, p. 1195.</margin>, it is rather *milvius*. Frantzius (p. 433) thinks it is so called from "softness" (*mollitie*), because it has a soft flight and also a soft voice, which is so thin that it is scarcely heard. To the Greeks it is <term>iktin</term> <note>Greek: ἰκτὶν</note>; compare Aristotle and Aristophanes in *The Birds*. Some translate the Hebrew <term>Da'ah</term> <note>Hebrew: דאה</note> or <term>Ra'ah</term> <note>Hebrew: ראה</note> as "kite," others as "vulture," some as "magpie," and some as "crow." It received its name from flying, for <term>Da'ah</term> means "he flew" or "he flutters," to which the poet refers:
> For the predatory kite flies near the highest stars.
And Martial in *Epigrams*, Book 9, 55:
> ---as much as a kite does not wander over the fields of Cures.
In Deuteronomy 14:13, the first word in the Holy language is <term>Ra'ah</term>, "he saw," which the Vulgate, Arias, and Pagninus render as *Ixion* or *Ixum*; however, others conclude, from the name...

### FROM PSALM 50, VERSES 10, 11 — 505

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
The terms *ra’ah* and *da’ah* <note>original Hebrew: ראה & דאה</note> are intended to denote one and the same species of vulture because of the similarity between the letters *Daleth* (ד) and *Resh* (ר). Indeed, Bochartus believes that scribes confused or swapped the *Daleth* and *Resh*, as has happened elsewhere; hence from *ra’ah*, meaning "he saw," we get the "kite-eyes" <note>original Latin: <term>mivini oculi</term></note> mentioned in Apuleius for the bird's keenness of sight. Others, however, wish to signify different birds by these words, so that *ra’ah* is a general vulture, while *da’ah* is the *iktinos* <note>original Greek: ἴκτινος</note>, a white and smaller vulture. The Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> in the book of Deuteronomy read "and the kite, and its kind," and so they either include the vulture and the kite under one word, *iktinos*, or they understand it under the name of the hawk. Blessed Luther expressed it with one name in that passage as "the vulture" <note>original German: <term>der Geyer</term></note>, but in Leviticus 11:14 he renders it as "the kite" <note>original German: <term>der Wenher</term>, likely *Weihe*</note>, and Arias calls it "the flying one." The rapacity of this bird is remarkable, for which it earned this description from Dionysius the Carthusian: *It is a bird of prey, complaining and troublesome, feeding on carcasses, lying in wait especially for domestic chicks; at first it is quite bold, but later more timid, not daring to attack wild birds. It is also shameless, since it not only preys on poultry chicks—to which the comic poet alludes in these <term>trochaics</term> <note>a type of poetic meter</note>:*

<margin>Plautus, *Paenulus*, Act 5, Scene 5.</margin>
> Hold me, please, hold me tight, my delight: I fear the kites.
> That is a bad beast: lest by chance it carries off your chick.

Furthermore, it even snatches meat from the butcher shop and food from the hands of children, and even fish from servants while they are gutting them. To this also belongs that line about snatched porridge in Plautus, Act 2, Scene 4:

> A kite snatched away the porridge long ago.

It serves as a symbol for many on account of its greed. By the Syrians, the Devil is called *da’itha* <note>original: דאיתא</note> because he is similar to the vulture in capacity and cruelty. Thus, because of the ambushes it uses in catching chicks, it is an image of robbers and thieves who gape at the goods of others. Hence Hugo Cardinalis <note>Hugh of Saint-Cher, a 13th-century theologian.</note> writes on Leviticus: *The kite is a bird of prey, always lying in wait, and it signifies robbers who do not trust in their own strength, but rather in ambushes.*

<margin>On Isaiah 34.</margin>
The same author says: *There the kites are gathered, one to another. In this world they gather so that they may snatch things together. Proverbs chapter 1: "Let us all have one purse," etc. But in hell the kites shall be gathered one to another, the robbers to the Devil, so that they may be punished together. For the Devil is a kite, which is why the act of "flying around" is attributed to him, which is the proper characteristic of the kite, etc.*

The FLY, in Greek *myia* <note>original: μῦια</note>, and perhaps the Latin *musca* is the Hebrew *zebub* <note>original: זבוב</note>. In Chaldean it is *dababa*, because it wanders with no fixed home, in the Scythian manner, making its home and bed wherever it is caught by night—as Lucian says in his *Praise of the Fly*. From flies, the idol of the Ekronites obtained the name Beelzebub (2 Kings 1:2). There is also "Jupiter the Fly-Averter" <note>original: Jupiter Apomyius</note> mentioned by Pliny (Book 10, ch. 28 and Book 29, ch. 6) and Pausanias in his *Arcadia* and earlier *Eliaca*. There are various species of them, which it is not our purpose to list here. God once punished the Egyptians with "dog-flies" <note>original Greek: κυνομυίαις</note>, as the Greek translates it, a various swarm of insects, about which we wrote above on page 174. And Bellonius <note>Pierre Belon, a French naturalist.</note> testifies that in Egypt, near the Pyramids, there is such a great abundance of flies that the air resounds with the murmur of their flying. It is indeed a lowly insect and, if you look at its external form, small; yet it should not be judged by the magnitude of its mass, but by its vigor and power, especially if it is sent extraordinarily by God as a punishment. 

<margin>Book 2, Observations, ch. 4.</margin>

<column-break/>

See Dauroultius (ch. 2), *Flowers of Examples* (title 1, History example 4, p. 194), and Baronius (Vol. 3, year 238, n. 1). Hence Augustine did not blush to prefer the fly to the Sun, because the fly lives and performs such actions (Book 1 *On Two Souls*, ch. 4).

<margin>Hexaemeron, ch. 11.</margin>
The opinion of Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose, 4th-century Bishop of Milan.</note> regarding such little creatures pleases us: *God does not struggle in great things, nor is He disgusted by the small.* Since the fly is a shameless little animal and harmful to the things it infects, sparing no table whether it belongs to a King or a cowherd, it is an image of parasites, slanderers, and little men of this sort of dregs; it is therefore a symbol of the "Gnathonic" <note>from Gnatho, a stereotypical parasite character in Roman comedy</note> chin and of feigned friendship. Parasites are like flies, which crowd the kitchens in a large swarm in summer, but in winter they withdraw entirely. There exists an elegant book by Plutarch which teaches how you can distinguish a flatterer from a friend. Hugo extends the icon of flies to sinners and all those wallowing in the mire of wickedness. For just as flies 1. arise from uncleanness, 2. cling to uncleanness and frequent unclean places, 3. circle and follow the scabby and the ulcerous, and 4. are troublesome, hostile, and tumultuous—so also are sinners, says Hugo. Augustine compares heretics to them in his book against Fulgentius the Donatist: *You dying flies, you Donatists, fly around through the members of the whole body; where they find a path through wounds, they sting the healthy, lick the sick, and from their wounds they pour out the worms of sins which bite the conscience, which end the soul, which nourish rot, and which spare not even the dead corpses themselves. Dying flies destroy the oil, and they are destroyed by the oil; for you Donatists do not live, you who breathe out the Holy Spirit.* Johannes Brentius <note>A German Protestant reformer (1499–1570).</note> applies the fly to the soldiers of our time: *Certain soldiers in this time of ours,* he says, *are like flies, who because of laziness are not fit for waging war, but only for defiling, contaminating, and devastating whatever places they travel to. For it is well known with what crimes and shames this class of soldiers is soiled, who wander about everywhere to harass the farmers. If you called these men flies, you would be saying less than they deserve; but you would rightly call them CATERPILLARS, WASPS, and HORNETS.* Now if Brentius said this and pronounced it truly regarding the soldiers of the previous century, what if he had seen and heard the abominable, detestable, and more-than-Devilish wickedness of the soldiers and their exercises of all impiety and disgrace in this century—especially during the time of the German Thirty Years' War? Would he not have proclaimed them worse than the Devil himself?

The OWL <note>original: NOCTUA</note> is named from the time of night, in which it sings, keeps watch, and flies. Among the Hebrews, if you look at the translators, it has many names. To the Greeks, it is called *glaux* <note>original: γλαῦξ</note>.

<margin>Leviticus 11:16.</margin>
It is in the catalog of those birds which are placed among the forbidden foods by Moses as unclean.

According to Rabbi David Kimchi in his *Book of Roots*, the *racham* <note>original: רחם</note> is an unclean bird, so called because it violently snatches other birds. For *racham* means to snatch violently or use force. The Seventy read *glaux* (owl) in this place, whom Pagninus, Luther, and the Vulgate translators follow, besides Arias, for whom it signifies a hawk. Tremellius prefers the swallow, but this fits least of all with the etymology. The owl keeps watch while other birds rest; it hunts its prey and sees best when the rest are blinded by the darkness.
