506 # SACRED HISTORY OF ANIMALS

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
Its sharp vision is not as strong at night as that of cats, whose eyes, owing to the dryness of their brains, are flaming and illuminate the nearby air with internal light as much as is needed—which cannot be said of the owl. Nevertheless, it sees well at night; it delights in the night, the twilight, and the dawn. For this reason, they compare it to wise men who acquire their learning through nightly study, vigils, and solitary contemplations. These are the ones who see alone in the darkness—that is, they can discern good from evil amidst errors—and who study while others snore and idle. Hence, they wish the owl to be under the protection of Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom.</note>, because "wisdom possesses its own brightness even in the darkness," says Fulgentius in his *Mythologies, Book 2, page 854.* And Francesco Petrar<margin>2 Invect. 8</margin>ca <note>A famous Italian scholar and poet.</note> says: *The most learned men consecrated the owl to Minerva, who among them is the Goddess of Wisdom. You wonder, you unlearned person, as these things are foreign to you; you would like to hear the reason for it. It is a hidden bird, and the wonder of winged creatures. It keeps watch by night and sees amidst the darkness; it flies while all others sleep. But you will cease to wonder if you begin to think on the person of Christ, who is the true God of wisdom and the Wisdom of the Father himself, of whom it was said in the hundred-and-first Psalm: "I have become like the night-raven in the dwelling." It delights in the darkness and loves it, but flees the Sun and hates its rays; hence it is also counted among the unclean birds, so that in that manner it may signify that the works of darkness must be fled. In this way, it is a symbol of those who flee the light of truth and are captured only by the love of darkness.* Hesychius says of the owl: *They assert that in the night its sight is sharp, but when the sun appears, it enjoys the use of its eyes less. Such are those who boast in the contemplation and knowledge of the Law <note>The Old Testament/Torah</note>, but are unable to grasp the light of the Gospel life.* Ambrose treats this type of the impious and the "light-fleers" <margin>Book 5 *Hexameron* chapter 24.</margin> more extensively with the owl: *The owl itself, just as it does not feel the dark horror of the nightly shadows with its large and gleaming pupils, so it carries out its flights unhindered the darker the night becomes, contrary to the habit of other birds. But when the day has risen and the splendor of the Sun is poured around, its vision is dulled, as if it wanders in some darkness. By this sign of itself, it declares that there are some who, though they have eyes for seeing, are not accustomed to see, and perform the duty of their sight only in the darkness. I speak of the eyes of the heart, which the wise of the world have and yet do not see; they discern nothing in the light, but walk in the darkness, while they search the shadowy things of demons and believe themselves to see the heights of heaven, describing the world with a compass and gathering the measurement of the air itself. Furthermore, those who have turned away from faith are entangled in the darkness of perpetual blindness; having the day of Christ and the light of the Church nearby and seeing nothing, they open their mouths as if knowing everything—sharp toward vain things, dull toward eternal ones—and through the long winding of dispute, they are "wise," yet unaware of their own ignorance. Thus, while they desire to fly away from their blindness with subtle speeches, they vanish in the light like dead things.*

### THE NIGHT-RAVEN
<margin>Deut. 14:16</margin>
This is a Latin word granted citizenship <note>A phrase meaning the word was adopted from Greek into Latin.</note> used by the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> in *Leviticus 11:17* and *Psalm 102:8*, where the Hebrew has *Kos* <note>original Hebrew: כוס</note>, which in Deuteronomy alone they rendered as *erodion* <note>original Greek: ἐρωδιόν, usually meaning a heron.</note>. The Latin interpreter of the Chaldean Paraphrase calls it a "falcon," which Arias <note>Arias Montanus, a 16th-century orientalist.</note> imitates. Tremellius, along with Schindler, calls it an "owl." Pagninus follows the Seventy in Moses, but in the Psalm he translates it as "great owl" <note>original Latin: <term>bubo</term></note>. As Blessed Tarnovius well warns,

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
the Interpreters fight bitterly among themselves over Hebrew words; and since the modern Jews are ignorant of those birds, and the ancient Rabbis did not describe them because they were very well known in the Holy Land, it is hardly possible to hand down anything certain. Just as with other names of trees, plants, fruits, birds, animals, and gems unknown to us, we adapt them to these lands of ours and to things familiar to us, etc. Concerning the bird *Kos*, let us hear Rabbi David Kimchi: *It is the name of an unclean bird unknown to us, and our Rabbi Solomon says it is that which they commonly call a falcon. But that which they call a falcon is found to be a domestic bird, which is guided by man and hunts other birds. And because the Scripture in Psalm 102 says: "I have become like the owl [or falcon] in the desert," therefore it is likely that it is a bird that lives in the wilderness.* Rabbi Aben Ezra writes of it thus: *There are some who think that this bird is called "Kos" in Hebrew from "hiding" and "concealing," because it flees the eyes of men and hides itself in desert places that are not inhabited, for "kasah" <note>original Hebrew: כסה</note> means to hide and conceal; hence the German Jews commonly interpret it as "Küttlin" <note>An archaic German term for a small owl.</note>.* It is established that it is a nocturnal bird, only slightly less deformed than a bat; nevertheless, David did not fear to take a comparison from it <margin>Ps. 102:8</margin> under his own name and that of the Church, which, like the <term>nycticorax</term> <note>The night-raven or night-owl.</note>, is harassed and oppressed by birds—that is, by the men of this world. Jerome, in this passage, compares the sinner with this bird due to its blackness, saying: *We know that the raven is black and has nothing white in itself; he wished to say hyperbolically that "I have become like the night-raven." If therefore it is black, how much more so in the night! So I have become because of my sins, comparing myself to them.* Scaliger also compares us to the same bird *1, Exercise 1, p. 4*, regarding eternal things, in the contemplation of which we are like that bird whose eye is too weak to endure the Sun. *For the understanding of eternal things,* he says, *the directed sharpness of our mind is as weak as the eye of the Night-raven is to those gazing at the Sun.*

### THE ONOCROTALUS
Named from *onos* <note>original Greek: ὄνος</note>, "ass," and *krotalos* <note>original Greek: κρόταλος</note>, "rattle" or "clapper," because by rattling with a discordant voice it resembles a braying donkey. From Jerome it is established concerning this bird: *There are two kinds of these winged creatures; one is in the waters, and its food is fish; and one is in the wilderness, and its food is poisonous animals; that is, serpents, crocodiles, and lizards.* He continues in his *Commentary on Zephaniah 2*: By the aquatic <term>onocrotalus</term> he undoubtedly understands the <term>bittern</term> <note>original Latin: <term>ardea stellaris</term></note>, so called from its elegant spots like stars, which lives in marshes among reeds and, with its beak inserted in the earth, imitates the braying of a donkey. By the <term>onocrotalus</term> of the wilderness, he understands the heron which, enclosed as if in the hollows of the highest trees in the forests, is heard to give forth a mournful voice similar to a goat's. From this, Dionysius the Carthusian took his description of this bird: *The onocrotalus,* he says, *is a bird similar in sound to a swan, and having as it were two bellies, in one of which it receives food—which is considered a small pouch of the throat—and in the other it digests them; of which, according to Isidore, there are two kinds, one aquatic, the other of the wilderness.* If you look at the disagreement of the Interpreters, its name among the Hebrews is uncertain and doubtful. Bochartus guesses that the *onocrotalus* is the Hebrew *Qa'at* <note>original Hebrew: קאת</note>, which otherwise is known as a name for a vessel;

just as the same bird is called **Truo** by the Latins, from the *trua* [a ladle or skimming-spoon], which is a vessel that serves as its throat, as Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, a Roman naturalist and author of *Naturalis Historia*.</note> notes. From this, the Arabs have a riddle: *What bird has its belly in its beak, and its eyes in its tail (or rather, at the very tip of its beak)?* The Vulgate translates the Hebrew word *ka’at* <note>original: כאת</note>—which Arias, Pagninus, Tremellius, and the Latin Interpreter of the Chaldean [Targum] rendered as "troglodyte" or "blackbird"—as the **onocrotalus** <note>A term used for the pelican or perhaps the bittern, named for its braying sound like a donkey (*onos*).</note>.
<margin>Natural History, Book 11, ch. 47.</margin>
There are also those who wish *ka’at* to signify the onocrotalus, both because it vomits up the water it holds in that throat-pouch so that it may select and eat the prey within it (according to Pliny in the cited place), and because it vomits up shells that have been softened and opened by the heat of its throat or stomach, so that it may pick out and devour the meat from the oysters. Furthermore, for us, the Onocrotalus is a **Crop-goose** <note>original: "Kropffganß," an early German name for the pelican.</note>, named for that womb-like pouch in its jaws. Adam Olearius <note>A 17th-century German scholar and traveler.</note> mentions in his *Persian Itinerary* that the inhabitants use it for fishing by tying its neck.

**THE SPARROW** [Passer], according to some, is named from "suffering" [*patiendo*], because due to its excessive lustfulness it suffers from the "falling sickness" <note>Epilepsy, known in Latin as *morbus comitialis*.</note>; for this reason, its life is so brief that it scarcely reaches the end of a two-year span. Avenarius, Scherus, Beckmann, and others teach that this Latin word has a Hebrew origin. Indeed, in the Holy Language, *zippôr* <note>original: צפור</note> (or *tzippôr*) is a bird, but by way of synecdoche <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole or vice versa.</note> it refers to the sparrow. It is a general name for all winged creatures or birds. More specifically, however, it is said of the common sparrow, and is commonly explained as a bird that is well-known and easily found. From this comes not only the German **Spar**, **Sperling**, and **Spass**, but also, by a transposition of letters, the Latin **Passer** and the Greek *psar* <note>original: ψάρ</note>, which means sparrow. For the grammarians establish the naming in this way: the root letters are *z, p, r* or *s, p, r*, leading to **Spar**, **Sperling**, and **Spass**. Then, from *zippor* or *tsippor*, by moving the letters, we get *pizor, pitsor, patsor,* and finally *passer*. And lastly *pzor, pifor, pfar, psar*. For *zippor* comes from the root *tzaphar*, meaning to fly away, to ripen, to hasten, or to be swift. The sparrow has a bad reputation for its lewdness, as Barlaeus <note>Caspar Barlaeus, a Dutch polymath and poet.</note> sings in his *Eclogues*:

->But will the playful sparrow show you the form of loving,<-
->And will he wish you to follow after his own laws?<-

<margin>Book 9.</margin>
Wherefore Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian.</note> says: *And sparrows are indeed prone to mating.* <note>original: καὶ οἱ στρουθοὶ δ’ εἰσὶν ὀχευτικοί.</note> And Terpsicles says: *To the living sparrows, it is natural to be driven toward sexual desire.* <note>original: τοῖς ἐμψυχόνοις στρουθοῖς, θηκατόφορος πρὸς ἀφροδίσia γινεῖσθαι.</note> Pliny also testifies that these little birds are the most lustful. And Rhodiginus calls the sparrow a "female-crazy animal." <note>original: θηλυμανές ζῶον.</note> For this reason, Sappho <note>The famous Greek lyric poet.</note> seems to say that Venus "rides upon it," according to Athenaeus; that is, Venus is carried by them. There is a passage by that poetess, which Athenaeus looked back to, in her *Hymn to Venus* found in Dionysius of Halicarnassus. In view of this, a sparrow is also attributed to Lesbia by Catullus. It is thus surprising that in Leviticus 14:4 and following, lepers are commanded after their purification [*katharismon*] to offer two sparrows for themselves. This is thought to be done to signify that the "sparrow-like lust" of the leper (for lepers, due to the sharpness of their humors, are strangely prone to lust) must henceforth be fled, along with the other pleasures of the world. For just as this bird dwells around the sacred temple, so by that offering it was signified that the cleansed leper was now received back and admitted to public society. It is hard to believe that a bird of such impure and impudent lust would be consecrated to God and offered in sacrifice, to persuade us of which the Vulgate version will be insufficient,

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
especially if one trusts Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a leading 16th-century scholar.</note>, who gathers from Nicander (a diligent observer of the ancients) that among the most ancient people, the *strouthos* <note>The Greek word for sparrow.</note> referred to a hen. Perhaps Origen Adamantius <note>An early Christian theologian from Alexandria.</note>—that illustrious light of the Alexandrian Church, as Lindanus calls him—referred to this as well.
<margin>Exercise 230.</margin>
<margin>Homily 8 on Leviticus.</margin>
The words of Origen were cited above. Unless, with Tostado <note>Alonso de Madrigal, also known as Abulensis, a Spanish bishop.</note> in his commentary on Leviticus 14, and Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan, a 16th-century cardinal and philosopher.</note> on the same passage, you wish to explain it thus: the sacrifices were made in the tabernacle, but the sparrow was killed outside. The priest performed the sacrifice, but he merely ordered the sparrow to be killed, and that for the purpose of anointing the leper. From this they conclude that the death of the sparrow was not a sacrifice, but merely a ceremony; see Vossius, *On Idolatry*, book 3. In the New Covenant, in Matthew 10:29, the sparrow is called a *strouthion* <note>original: στρουθίον</note>, and it is probable that no other bird is meant here than the little sparrow, with which Christ—as it is almost the most worthless and contemptible of animals, so much so that one can hardly value its price—makes a comparison. Yet God feeds it and does not permit it to fall to the ground or perish without His will. Augustine explains this parable more fully in *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 5:
> What the Savior says with His own mouth—that a single sparrow does not fall to the ground without God's will, and that He clothes the grass of the field which a little later is cast into the oven—does it not confirm that not only is this whole part of the world assigned to mortal and corruptible things, but even the most worthless and rejected particles are ruled by divine providence, etc.

Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, the "Golden-Mouthed" archbishop of Constantinople.</note>, that divine orator and contemporary of Augustine, says the same thing; for while the latter flourished in the Latin Church, the former taught at the same time in the Greek Church:
<margin>Commentary on Matthew, Homily 25.</margin>
"If a sparrow does not die or fall by chance, for the very reason that it is the work of God, how much more is a righteous man not placed in the hands of chance, since he is the image of God? Rather, he either dies having been delivered by God, or escapes having been freed by God. If in sparrows nothing is done without reason—two of which are worth a single copper coin—how much more is nothing done in you without me, since the price is my blood. If sparrows are held in such regard, how are sons to be held? Therefore, you should not fear men, because the power over you is not theirs, but God's. For the wicked cannot harm the saints whenever they wish, but only when God has granted them a time for harming, so that He may provide a crown for His saints." So he says. I hope it will not be troublesome if I add the agreeing words of Luther, that extraordinary instrument of God (as Beza calls him in his *Response to Saintes*):
> "It appears," Christ says, "that you, my disciples, are like sparrows born and treated for chance and sacrifice, who are killed most cheaply. Though you are slaughtered most cheaply, you are clearly just like them. But behold, unless God the Father willed it so, not one sparrow could be caught by all men, much less killed. But because it is the will of God, who delivers the sparrows, therefore they are caught, etc."

If therefore God numbers and cares for even individual sparrows in such a way that not even one would be caught unless He Himself willed it, how much more certainly does He number and care for you—not only as men but as my servants and believers—and He allows none of you to be afflicted without His certain knowledge and will, even though it may appear you are unknown and neglected by Him. Certainly, He who cares for a single, most worthless sparrow...

<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
[He] does not neglect, much less does he neglect any of you, etc. From the sound of "salacious little sparrows," which in Greek are called <term>titízein</term> <note>original: τιτίζειν, meaning to chirp or twitter</note> or *titissare*, impure men were called *Titi* in the works of Persius; see Rhodiginus, Book 9, ch. 10. On account of its lustfulness and other qualities of ill repute, Cardinal Hugo <note>Hugo de Sancto Caro, a 13th-century Dominican theologian</note> compares the sparrow to lustful Clerics in this poem:

->*Lascivious, in a soft nest, perishing by fire, falling,*<-
->*Swift, a rival, leprous, he fouls the altars,*<-
->*Eggs warm for Venus, thief of grain, from doves the temples*<-
->*He steals, hunts flies, small, and bites poorly.*<-

<margin>Ecclesiastes 10:5, 6.</margin>
With the phrase "stealing temples from doves," the aforementioned Cardinal refers to the passage: *There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, as it were an error proceeding from the face of the Prince: a fool set in high dignity, and the rich sit below*—that is, those rich in true spiritual riches. And this evil "proceeds from the face of the prince," that is, a major Prelate, "as if by error"—not truly by error, but through malice; but they feign error, saying they were deceived, because they previously believed them to be good when in truth they knew them to be evil. Modern practice is not a penny <note>original: "teruncio," a tiny Roman coin</note> better; the same happens today, as the common saying goes: *The bigger the fool, the better the fortune.* <note>original: "Je grösser Narz / je besser Pfärz." A German proverb suggesting that fools often attain the highest status or wealth.</note> Goodness has ceased to be among the simple attributes of Being, and is now relegated to disjoined or rather accidental relations: He is "good" who has "good gifts" <note>original: "gute Gaben"</note>—that is, he who gilds the Prelate's hands <margin>1 Kings 13:33.</margin> or, to speak with the Scripture, "fills" them. He is "good" who is from the class of the "crooked," notwithstanding the Divine law in Leviticus 21:21, which barred the hunchbacked, the <term>kampýlous</term> <note>original: καμπύλους, Greek for "bent" or "curved"</note>, or those spotted with other blemishes from sacred worship—though not from participating in the things of the saints. But what shall I say of blemishes? They are not believed to be tiny moles, much less full of blemishes, because they are high-born. Happy, therefore, are those to whom it falls to "know the downfall" <note>original: πτώσεως γινώσκει</note>, and even happier those "of the giving nature." <note>original: τῆς δοτικῆς. A play on Greek grammatical cases: the "fall" (genitive) and the "giving" (dative).</note> But why do you chirp, you talkative sparrow? Do you not know that line of the Poet:

->*It does not happen to every man to reach Corinth.*<-
<note>A famous line from Horace, meaning that not everyone can attain success or luxury.</note>

<margin>On Psalm 123, col. 966, p. 541.</margin>
The sparrow is a domestic bird and an inhabitant of buildings; it is not momentary or temporary, but remains without any change, as Hilary <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century bishop and theologian</note> says, or without observing the seasons; it stays out of fear of predators whose talons the sparrow dreads. Thus it groans over its fate alone, and sits alone without an avenger or patron. Hence David, making mention of the assaults and temptations he bore during the persecution of Saul, begins a consolatory Psalm composed by him with an imitation: <margin>Psalm 11:1.</margin> *In the Lord I trust; how say you to my soul: Fly to the mountain like a sparrow.* Then in chapter 101:8, he calls it a *solitary sparrow*, which Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine, a Jesuit Cardinal and counter-reformation scholar</note> explains as referring to just men, whose conversation exists in heaven even in the midst of the crowds of business. Finally, in Psalm 124:7, giving thanks to God for the liberation of himself and his people, he says: *Our soul is escaped as a sparrow out of the snare of the hunters.*

<margin>On Psalm 118, p. 500.</margin>
On these words of the Psalmist, Hilary comments: *In this forest of the world many snares are stretched out, many traps for life are prepared. Our speech, our thought, and our work always have snares lying nearby, when sometimes an occasion for anger occurs, an affection of grief, the necessity of complaint, or an opportunity for evil desire. The Devil and his angels, transgressors from the beginning and sinners from the start, always extend these snares. But he who is never unmindful of God,*

<column-break/>

even though snares are cast all around, has not wandered from the commandments; for always thinking of God, he flies away from these, as he says in the Psalm: *Like a sparrow freed from the snare of the hunters.* Thus, following Hilary, Saint Augustine says on the same Psalm: *Be even as a sparrow, so that with wise investigation you may foresee the snares and, having almost slipped away, you may say: Our soul, like a sparrow, is escaped from the snare of the hunters.*

THE PEACOCK, called <term>taōs</term> <note>original: ταὼς</note> by the Greeks. Both names are of uncertain origin. I would prefer, says Becmann, that both come from the Hebrew *tuki* <note>original: תכי</note>, meaning it was beautiful, graceful, sightly, handsome, or elegant, because of the bird's remarkable beauty and honor. For the parrot, peacock, and pheasant are commended for the beauty of their color, which is why Statius <note>Publius Papinius Statius, a 1st-century Roman poet</note> joins these birds in the second book of his *Silvae*:

> *That parrot, ruler of the green Eastern shore,*
> *Whom the Junonian bird with its jeweled tail*
> *Could not surpass in sight, nor the bird of warm Phasis.*

In a word-play on the name, Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger, a Renaissance scholar</note> describes the Peacock in his *Poems*, page 625:

> *The Greek voice gives you quiet unknown to lawsuits*
-><term>paūōn</term> <note>original: παύων, "stopping" or "ceasing"</note><-

-><term>paōn hos piskō</term> <note>original: παῶν ὃς πίσκω, a play on the Greek roots of feeding and peacocks</note><-

->*Avo* <note>Latin for "Hail," punning on "p-avo"</note><-

Among animals, the Peacock is most worthy of admiration, *the peacock so varied*, as Chrysostom says in his 12th Olympic Oration, page 194: *lifting and showing the beauty of its feathers, bending back its tail and placing it all around, like a beautiful theater, or like a sky imitated in a painting, varied with stars, while the rest of the body is wonderfully mixed with something very close to gold and dark blue*, and other elegant things he adds there in praise of the Peacock, which prides itself on the elegant appearance of its feathers and leads a parade. The Peacock presents itself as an image of the proud, swollen and puffed up because of its many-colored feathers. *Those are peacocks*, says Osiander <note>Lucas Osiander, a Lutheran theologian</note>, *who, adorned with excellent gifts, are proud of the same.* And Brentius: *Apes contain a perfect likeness of a human—in face, nostrils, ears, eyelids: they also have a thumb and joints, and even their internal organs are all according to the pattern. But peacocks expand their tails especially against the Sun, which thus radiates more brightly. It is handed down by authors not only as a glorious animal, but also as a malevolent one.* Such Apes and Peacocks are found even in the kingdom of Christ, which is the Church. *These are the hypocrites possessing a form of godliness but denying its power, who fast and disfigure their faces so they may be seen by men; who pray beautiful prayers in the street, and who, when giving alms, sound a trumpet before them so they may be commended by men.* In the Sacred Books, mention of it is made twice, as in Job 39:16: *The exultant wing of the peacock*, though others read "ostrich." Brentius is in this opinion above others: *Even if,* he says, *some say it is a peacock and others a nocturnal bird of horrendous cry, I nevertheless think it is the Ostrich-Camel [Ostrich], chiefly for this reason: that the things enumerated here about the nature of this bird generally agree with what has been written elsewhere about the Ostrich-Camel. </margin>
...finally given wings for this purpose: to help it while running; otherwise, they are not flyers, nor are they lifted from the earth. Their hooves are similar to those of deer, with which they spring forth with cloven feet, useful for seizing stones which they hurl with their feet behind them against those pursuing them in flight. They have a wondrous nature for digesting whatever is devoured without selection. But no less is their **stupidity**, for in such great height of the rest of the body, when they have hidden their necks in a shrub, they imagine that they themselves are hidden. Rewards are gained from them: their mouths, on account of their size, are used as certain vessels, and their feathers adorn warlike crests and helmets. This much Brentius <note>Johannes Brenz, a 16th-century Lutheran reformer</note> takes from Pliny.

In Hebrew occurs the word <term>Renanim</term> <note>original: רננים, often translated as "ostriches" or "peacocks" in Job 39:13</note>, and it takes its name from "clamping" or "crying out," for <term>Ranan</term> <note>original: רנן</note> means to sing, to acclaim, or to cry out. There is a dispute among interpreters regarding the grammatical structure, whether these words should be explained as a question, as Piscator <note>Johannes Piscator, a German Reformed theologian</note> asserts, saying: *Did you make the wings of the peacock and the ostrich?* Or truly, should that simpler and more common explanation be retained? I think it is more simply explained thus: *The wing of the peacock is exultant: is it not the wing of the stork and the ostrich?* that is, it is exultant. For the rest, we allow you to understand it as either the ostrich or the peacock, provided you note a bird well-feathered or plumed, as the words immediately following require. Moreover, God seems to imply this by these words: Just as any bird ought to be content with its own feathers, so also you and other men should perhaps be content with your own lot. Just as no one blames me because I gave more beautiful feathers to the proud peacock than to the pious stork, so you ought not to accuse me because I sometimes adorn the wicked with the goods of this life more than the pious. Among the goods which Solomon brought from Tarshish were <term>Thuchiam</term> <note>original: תכיים</note>, or *Peacocks*. So the interpreters commonly say.
<margin>1 Kings 10:22</margin>
<margin>2 Chronicles 9:21.</margin>
The origin of the name is hidden, unless perhaps by inverting the letters for <term>Thuchiam</term> you read *Guthiim*, the Cuthites <note>People from Cuthah</note>, just as Pheasants are named from the Phasis river, and African and Numidian birds and others are named from other places. And thus the Peacock is a *Median* or *Persian* bird, where the *Cuth* region is. There are those who read *Parrots* in this place; regarding both readings, to see which might prevail, see J. H. Ursinus, *Vol. 1, Sacred Fragments, pages 187, 276, and following.*

### PELECANUS.

While it is placed among the Biblical birds, it suffers no small loss in the naming process <note>original: "onomatothesia," the act of giving a name</note> due to the conflict of interpreters. Easier is the comparison which the Church Fathers establish between Christ and the Pelican; among the first of these, Augustine leads the chorus concerning the Pelican in his commentary on *Psalm 101, column 1135.* *The Pelican,* he says, *is born in that region such that it is an unknown bird to us. It is born in solitudes, especially those of the River Nile in Egypt. What is said, or even read, about this bird, let us not keep silent—not affirming anything rashly, but yet not keeping silent about what those who wrote it wished to be both read and said: Hear it in such a way that if it is true, it may be fitting; if it is false, it may not be held fast. These birds are said to kill their young children with blows of their beaks, and to mourn those same ones killed by them in the nest for three days; finally, they say the mother severely wounds herself and pours her own blood over the children, by which they, being bathed, return to life. Perhaps this may be true, perhaps it may be false: yet if it is true, see how it fits Him who gave us life by His blood, etc. He calls Himself a hen over her chicks in Matthew chapter 23, etc. For He has fatherly authority, He has motherly affection, etc. Therefore, this bird has a great resemblance to the flesh of Christ, by whose blood we are given life.* But how

<column-break/>

does it fit Christ that she kills her own children? Or does it not fit Him? *I will kill and I will make alive, I will strike and I will heal, etc.* <note>Deuteronomy 32:39</note> But let those who wrote it see to this; we ought not to establish our understanding on uncertainty. Let us rather recognize this bird in the wilderness, etc. I think it is understood here that Christ was born of a virgin, for He alone is thus <term>a solitude for God</term> <note>original: Deo solitudo</note>, etc. This bird is two-named among the interpreters of the sacred letters. <term>Qa'at</term> <note>original: קאת</note>, which has a place among the unclean birds in Moses, yet this voice is no less controversial than the following <term>Qippod</term> <note>original: קפד</note>, to which (with the peace of others from whom it is pleasing to depart this time) the word "Pelican" in no way corresponds. A doubtful opinion has drawn the mind of the interpreter, for from those the Vulgate translates it as *Onocrotalus* <note>The Great White Pelican</note> in Leviticus 11 
<margin>verse 11.</margin>
and Isaiah 34, but as *Pelican* in Psalm 101. These birds of ill omen clearly intend this: that we should consider, wherever mention of them is made, that no happiness is implied. It is a sacred art of speaking that in the description of horrid things, a fitting designation of the matter be made, either through birds that love pathless places, or through other animals—dreadful, vast, violent, and hated. The Prophet Isaiah recounts unlucky animals in his description of terrible calamities, and indeed specifically those of the infernal regions, according to the interpreter Brentius,
<margin>folio 462.</margin>
whose words are: *Just as the Prophet used the metaphor of bloody swords and horrible slaughter to describe the assembly of the Gospel, by which Christ, the Son of God, when He came into this land, would range as if with a sword against all the impious and unbelieving; so also the Prophet proceeds by the metaphor of pitchy rivers, always burning, and of unclean and ill-omened birds to describe the eternal punishment and everlasting horror which hangs over all the impious and unbelieving. Spiritual things are overshadowed by the names of physical things, and by the words of unlucky birds are signified the foulest Demons and the heaviest terrors, which will perpetually haunt the wicked.* By contemplation of the bird, as far as can be known by guessing, let us have faith that nothing is portended except what is unlucky, or what threatens ruin or a most present calamity. If we attend to the name <term>Qa'at</term>, the word yields nothing by its etymology, whence its interpretation is all the more difficult. It will be enough to have said that it is implied not just by this bird but by the others that not only the most powerful nations but also regions and cities will be most gravely endangered and will collapse. The context opens itself enough and proposes an example of the heaviest punishments, even if the words do not open themselves, concerning which I think it is better to discuss on both sides than on neither. Some call it the *onocrotalus*, others the *pelican*, others the *jackdaw*, others name it otherwise. If any place is to be given to our conjectures, <term>Qa'at</term> would be the **owl**, which hides itself in towers and obscure places of buildings, and with a somewhat hoarse and lamentable voice makes the night more horrible for men. As they shadow forth sad and adverse things by the voice of night in sacred writings, so also by the name of owls, which is called the "bird of the night" by Ovid:

> If ever they see the bird of night
> wandering in the light.

What the nature of this nocturnal or night-wandering animal places before our eyes is as clear as the fact that night is not clear. Surely this interpretation is better...

...interpretation seems to be what is assigned to the **Onocrotalus** <note>literally "donkey-rattle," usually identified as a pelican or a bittern</note>, which is an aquatic bird, perpetually wandering through marshes and the sea so that it may gorge itself on fish. It takes its name from the sound it makes when its head is submerged under the water, which is said to be similar to the braying of a donkey; for <term>onos</term> <note>original Greek: ὄνος</note> means "donkey," and <term>krotalos</term> <note>original Greek: κρόταλος</note> means "rattle" or "clatter." In German, it is called a *Snow-goose* or a *Crop-bird*. But what does the Onocrotalus have in common with those animals that live in ruins and caverns? Therefore, let us interpret the threatening prophecy or sermon as being about imminent punishments. But why do those who "rattle" the *onocrotalos* with I-know-not-what noise, also chatter about the "curam" and "coots," which are similarly aquatic birds living near marshes and lakes? None of these have secret chambers, nor do they have mournful cries, nor does their nature declare anything that shows the great terror of which our Prophet speaks. Therefore, whatever leads us by another way than that whose goal is established in the Prophet is by no means to be followed, as it is something that tries to snatch us away into paths of error. 

Furthermore, you will ask whether the **Cuckoo** can be understood, following Rabbi Kimchi, whom David de Pomis follows in his *The Growth of David* <note>original: צמח דוד (*Tzemach David*), a 16th-century Hebrew dictionary</note>, folio 163. a. But I do not know by what path they are led to the cuckoo, or by what naming-convention they devised this. I do not think a better interpretation can be devised for the name <term>Ka'at</term> <note>original Hebrew: קאת</note> than that which we have given. Examine the name, examine the nature of the cuckoo, and inquire whether you find any momentum here for explaining the prophetic passage. 

Examine also the name of the **Pelican**, to see if it might be the <term>Ka'at</term>? Those who follow Jerome make much of this explanation, as he translates those words of the Psalmist in **Psalm 102:7**: *I have become like a pelican of the desert* <note>original: דמיתי לקאת מדבר</note>. From the omen of the name <term>Ka'at</term>, an ill-omened genus of owls is noted, which we call **Kauz** <note>German for a screech-owl or tawny owl</note>, a name that approaches the Hebrew as closely as possible, and from there one may quite conveniently take something as an omen. The French call the owl *chonette*, which alludes to <term>Ka'at</term> just as much as our *Kauz* does. Names are accustomed to be derived from nation to nation, and are sometimes changed in wondrous ways, as the Doctors of linguistic harmonies teach more extensively. 

Relying on this demonstration, the name of the **owls** will easily indicate to anyone what singular quality it displays. It flees the day, and when the unseasonable night falls silent—to speak with the Poet—it does not fall silent. While other animals "pluck quiet rest in the black night," <note>original Latin: "nigra carpunt nocte quietem"</note> the owl is restless; it is wide awake,

<margin>
Virgil, Georgics, Book 1.
</margin>
and "is known for its services to the stealthy night."

<margin>
Ovid, Elegies, Book 1.
</margin>
It either catches mice or hunts the race of spiders, "It collects, and withdraws what it has found with fearful theft."

<margin>
Lucretius, Book 2.
</margin>
When the light of day shows itself with the morning star leading the way, the light-fleeing animal anticipates the day with a hurrying foot, shuns the Sun, and hides itself in blind caves. Thus, when the Prophets lift a "burden" against any nation (to use their phrasing), they amplify their symbols from this. We see the path open to the Pelican through the desert under the guidance of Jerome, but by what track, I do not see.

**THE PARTRIDGE**, the bird <term>perdix</term> <note>original Greek: πέρδιξ</note>, is that which varies its sound according to the diversity of locations, about which **Aristotle** says in Book 4 of the *History of Animals*, chapter 9: *Some of the partridges cackle, while others chirp.* <note>original Greek: τῶν περδίκων οἱ μὲν κακκαβίζουσιν, οἱ δὲ τρίζουσι</note> But instead of "chirp" [*trizein*], **Theophrastus** (cited in Athenaeus) reads "titibizein": *Theophrastus, in his book on the different voices of related animals, says that in Athens, the partridges on this side of Corydallus toward the city cackle, but those beyond it, chirp.* <note>original Greek: Θεόφραστος δ’ εν τῷ περὶ ἑτεροφωνίας τῶν ὁμογενῶν, Αθήνησί, φησιν, πέρδικας οἱ τάδε τὸ Κορυδαλὸ, πρὸς τὸ ἄστυ κακκαβίζουσιν, οἱ δὲ ἐπέκεινα, τιτιβίζουσιν</note>. Whence and when this change of sound occurs is not sufficiently clear; it pleases us that this bird "cackles" [*kakkabizein*] when it is more vocal, and "chirps" [*trizein* or *titibizein*] when it is less so, since the sounds *rei* and *ti-tu-xi* sound thin. And this is what Antigonus Carystius says in his *Collection of Wonderful Tales*, chapter 6: that the partridges sound differently... compare Vossius, Book 3, *On Idolatry*, chapter 88, page 1209. 

It is a clever and deceptive animal in seeking out its chicks by its own escapes, whence the verb "to act like a partridge" [*ekperdikisai*] was coined by Aristophanes in *The Birds*. Hence, it is called by **Aristotle** "cunning and malicious." <note>original Greek: κακόηθες καὶ πανοῦργον</note>. Led by this reasoning, **Basil** in his *Homily 8 on the Hexameron* compares this bird with the crafty minds of this age: "The partridge is a clever bird, astute and envious, and acts maliciously with hunters regarding the prey." 

He continues in the same comparison in his *Exhortation to Baptism*: "I have seen a wondrous art of the clever bird: when it sees its chicks still exposed to the danger of prey due to weakness, it offers itself to the fowler before them as if ready for the catch, so turning itself and distributing its gestures that it neither puts itself entirely in danger or in his hands, nor does it entirely snatch away hope from the one lying in wait. Thus, by turning between both, by occupying him, and by holding him back, it gives space for its offspring to flee at leisure, and at the last moment it flies away itself. Beware, therefore, lest you suffer similar things from the fowler, leaving certain things for uncertain ones, exchanging firm hope for vain things, etc." It makes two dwellings or receptacles for itself, as Aristotle writes in Book 6 of the *History of Animals*, if it is incubating eggs: *Partridges make two nesting-places for the eggs; the female sits on one, and the male sits on the other.* <note>original Greek: οἱ δὲ πέρδικες, αἵτε δύο ποιοῦνται τῷ ωῶν σηκὺς, καὶ ἐφ’ ᾧ μὲν ἡ θήλεια, ἐπὶ θατέρῳ δὲ ὁ ἀῤῥὴν ἐπωάζει</note>. And this is especially attributed to the female, because the male partridge is said to break the eggs of the female, whence he does not approach the eggs unless...

### From Psalm 55:10-11

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>

...unless by a convenient means of deceiving the male, so that he does not discover where the eggs are. Indeed, she even acts to lead man away from the eggs. In the Sacred Book, in two places—namely 1 Samuel 26:20 and Jeremiah 17:11—the Hebrew word *qara* <note>original: קרא</note> is found. Interpreters commonly explain this as the **partridge**, taking the name as an onomatopoeia from its cry, for *qara* means "he cried, called, or summoned." Regarding the latter passage, interpreters do not agree, as the Prophet says of that bird that it "gathers eggs it did not lay," a behavior which some deny of the partridge while others affirm it. Regarding the partridge, this latter point is asserted by **Ambrose** in his *Six Days of Creation* <note>original: *Hexaemeron*</note> book 6, chapter 3, and in his 48th Letter; by **Jerome** in his commentary on this passage; by **Augustine** in book 13 of *Against Faustus*; and by **Isidore** in book 12 of his *Etymologies* <note>original: *Etymologiae* or *Origines*</note>, chapter 7. However, nothing of this sort is found in the works of **Aristotle**, **Pliny**, or **Aelian**. It is a very elegant simile, which it is certain had passed into a proverb by the time of St. Ambrose, as seen in his 48th Letter. But in its application, a certain diversity is criticized, which some believe arose from the ambiguity of the Hebrew word *qara*. For this word specifically denotes the partridge, but in a general sense, it signifies any bird that makes a clucking sound. Those who follow the former interpretation apply it to the partridge, saying that it steals the eggs of another (that is, of another partridge) and sits on them, but gains no advantage from this labor, since the chicks, once somewhat grown, desert the nest of their nurse and follow their genuine mother. This could easily be applied to the greedy and their unjustly gained wealth—if that nature of partridges were supported by sufficiently firm authority. However, as **Zehner** <margin>Simil. S. S. p. 183.</margin> advises, although **Epiphanius**, **Augustine**, **Ambrose**, **Isidore**, and especially **Jerome** (who does not hesitate to cite Aristotle, Theophrastus, and Pliny as witnesses to his opinion) have recorded this in literature, yet since absolutely nothing on this matter is found in those classical writings, we leave it to each person's judgment how much faith they wish to grant this assertion. 

In my own judgment, Zehner continues, nothing prevents us from taking this to refer to the specific traits of each bird. For it often happens that a partridge lays eggs in great numbers but does not hatch them—either because she does not entrust them to a single place (as **Aelian** <margin>book 3, *History of Animals*, ch. 16.</margin> records), but carries them to another place as if migrating and finally forgets them; or because the eggs are soaked by dew and rain and rendered infertile, according to the same Aelian; or because the males, driven by an overwhelming breeding instinct, break them (as witnessed by **Aristotle**, **Aelian**, and **Pliny**); or finally, because the mother often rises from her sitting (as Aristotle writes) or is sometimes caught by a fowler. All these things fit well with wicked men who amass a great force of wealth through right or wrong, yet because of many intervening troubles, they cannot enjoy it—which is nothing other than, to use the words of **Quintilian**, "brooding over closed treasures." See also Blessed **Frantzius** in his *Sacred History of Animals* and **Vossius** in his *De Idololatria*. 

There are also those who write that the **Devil** was compared to a partridge by Jeremiah, as one who stole the nations from the Church, which finally return when they recognize the voice of their mother. Regarding this comparison, let us hear Ambrose:

> *That bird is said to be full of guile, fraud, and deceit, knowing the ways of deceiving a hunter and knowing the arts to turn him away from her chicks; she omits no attempt of craftiness by which she can lead the hunter away from her nest and dwelling. Certainly, if she notices him persisting, she will mock him as long as she can give her fleeing offspring the signal and the power to escape; once she senses they have evaded him, she then withdraws herself and leaves the hunter deceived by her slippery art.*

It is also said to be of promiscuous mating, such that they rush upon females with the greatest struggle and burn with wandering lust; hence the animal is thought to be impure, malevolent, and fraudulent, to be compared to the most deceitful adversary and deceiver of the human race and the author of impurity. The partridge therefore "cried out"—a bird that took its name from "destroying" <note>a pun on the Latin *perdix* and *perdendo* (destroying)</note>—that Satan, who in Latin is called the "Adversary." He cried out in Eve, Cain, Pharaoh, etc. With these voices, he gathered to himself peoples whom he had not gathered, and so on.

**PHILOSTORGOS** <note>literally "lover of offspring"</note>, a bird named among the Greeks for its supreme love for its offspring, a name which the Latins also retained. To the Hebrews, it sounds like **Racham** <note>original: רחם</note>, "the merciful one," from the root *racham*, which is "he loved," as if from the innermost depths; this word seems to be derived from *rechem* <note>original: רחם</note>, the "womb," which embraces the fetus with the most tender affection. Which bird this actually is, however, is not certain. Modern Jews want to identify it as the magpie. **Junius** and **Tremellius** identify it as the Bee-eater, which is the "most pious of all birds" because it feeds its parents, according to Aelian. But *Racham* properly signifies a "lover of offspring" <note>original Greek: φιλόστοργον</note>, not a "lover of parents" <note>original Greek: φιλοπάτορα</note>. **Schindler** interprets it as a vulture, or a "uterine eagle," an ossifrage <note>a bone-breaker eagle</note>. **Bochart** does not differ much from Schindler, showing from Arabic sources that the same things are attributed to the *racham* as the Greeks attribute to the vulture. **Plutarch** attributes a title of "Island-vulture" to the vulture in his *Life of Romulus*. Hence the Indians, Persians, and Iberians once cast the bodies of the slain or deceased to them, because, as **Silius Italicus** <margin>book 13, v. 470.</margin> sings:

> ...they believe they are carried to heaven and the gods above,
> if the hungry vulture plucks at the lying limbs.

Added to this is that, according to **Horus** <note>Horapollo</note>, the Egyptians signified a mother or a merciful person by a painted vulture; for Horus records a wonderful "love of offspring" <note>original Greek: φιλοστοργίᾳ</note>, that in a shortage of food, the mother, having cut her own thigh, offers her own blood to her chicks. **Bonfrerius** notes that in the Septuagint and Vulgate versions, the order of birds is changed, so that it is uncertain whether *racham* or *rachamah* signifies a swan, a pelican, or a purple gallinule? This reasoning perhaps moved Blessed **Luther** to put "the Stork," whose name is *Chasidah* <note>original: חסידה</note>.

**STRUTHIOCAMELVS** <note>the Ostrich</note>, an animal of amazing size, which, as Pliny mentions, exceeds the height of a rider sitting on a horse. Regarding this, **Galen** says <margin>chapter 20.</margin> that he heard a Sophist in his youth who, in a two-part speech, treated this argument: whether the Ostrich can be classified among the birds or not? In one part he contended it should be given a place among the birds, and in the other he attacked that idea; he finally concludes that it matters little for us to know whether it should be classified among the birds or not. Compare Aristotle, where he says it departs from the quadrupeds because it has wings...

<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...this seems to be the interpretation assigned to the *Onocrotalus* <note>The "donkey-clatterer," usually identified as a Great White Pelican or a Bittern</note>, which is an aquatic bird, constantly wandering over marshes and the sea to gorge itself on fish. It takes its name from the sound it makes when its head is submerged under water, which is said to be like the braying of a donkey; for in Greek *onos* <note>original: ὄνος</note> means "donkey" and *kotalos* <note>original: κόταλος</note> means "clatter." In German, it is called a *Schneeganß* <note>original: "Snow goose"</note> or *Kropffvogel* <note>original: "Crop-bird" or "Pelican"</note>. But what does the Onocrotalus have in common with those animals that live in ruins and caves? Therefore, let us interpret the prophecy or sermon about imminent punishments as a threat. Why would Onocrotaluses ring out with some kind of rattles, or why do coots and moorhens—similarly aquatic birds living near marshes and lakes—make such clattering noises? None of these have secret chambers or mournful cries, nor does their nature declare anything that would demonstrate the great terror the Prophet fears. Therefore, whatever leads us down a path other than the one whose goal is set by the Prophet should not be followed at all, as it would attempt to snatch us away into paths of error. You might further ask whether it could be understood as the *Cuckoo* following Rabbi Kimchi, whom David de Pomis follows in his work <term>The Growth of David <note>original: צמח דוד, Tzemach David</note></term> on folio 163. a. But I do not know by what path they are led to the cuckoo, or by what naming convention they devised this. I do not think a better interpretation can be devised for the name <term>Ka'at <note>original: קאת</note></term> than the one we have given. Examine the name, examine the nature of the cuckoo, and search to see if you find any momentum here for explaining the prophetic passage. Examine also the name of the *Pelican*, to see if it is the <term>Ka'at</term>? Those who follow Jerome make much of this explanation, as he translates those words in the Psalms, *Psalm 102:7*: <term>I have become like a pelican of the desert <note>original: דמיתי לקאת מדבר</note></term>. From the omen of the name <term>Ka'at</term>, an ill-omened genus of owls is noted, which we call *Kaus* <note>German: Kauz, a tawny owl</note>, a name which comes very close to the Hebrew, and from there one may quite suitably accept something as an omen. The French call an owl *Gallichonettæ* <note>A diminutive form of "chouette"</note>, which alludes to <term>Ka'at</term> just as much as our *Kaus*. Names are often derived from nation to nation and sometimes changed in wonderful ways, as the Teachers of linguistic harmonies teach more extensively. Relying on this demonstration, the name of the *owls* will easily indicate to anyone what singular quality it displays. It flees the day, and when the night becomes untimely—to speak with the Poet—it is not silent. While other animals take their rest in the dark night, the owl is restless and watchful,

<margin>Virgil, Georgics Book 1.</margin>
<margin>Ovid, Amores Book 1.</margin>
<margin>Lucretius, Book 2.</margin>
> and in the duties of the night, its stealthy nature is known.
> either it catches mice, or it pursues the race of spiders,
> it gathers, and things known are snatched away in fearful theft.

When the light shows itself with the morning star leading the day, the light-fleeing animal anticipates the day with a hurrying foot, flees the Sun, and hides itself in blind caves. Thus, when the Prophets lift a "burden" against some nation (to use their phrase), they symbolically amplify their words from this. We see that the path to the Pelican through the desert is open by the guidance of Jerome, but by what trail, I do not see. Luther’s version has: *I am like a Bittern in the desert.* Caspar Ammonius: *I have been like a bird of the deserts.* Piscator: *I am like a Spoonbill in the desert.* Castalio: *I resemble a wild Onocrotalus.* Junius: *I am like a Spoonbill of the desert.* With wondrous skill of speech,

The Church was then abandoned by all, hated by all, and affected by many injuries; under the cross, she implores the help and aid of God for the liberation and restoration of true religion. The "howler of the desert" <note>ulula deserti</note> shows the most pitiable misery, filling the desert with its wailing in a dark place. Thus the mournful Church laments with sighing wails,

Here the insatiable animal heaps everything, having a wonderful capacity; soon, the completed plunder is gradually returned from there into the mouth and brought down into the lower stomach in the manner of a ruminant.*

### THE PARTRIDGE

The bird *kordix* <note>original: κόρδιξ</note>, that is, the one that varies its sound according to the diversity of places, about which Aristotle writes in Book 4 of the *History of Animals*, chapter 9: *Of partridges, some cackle and others screech <note>original: τῶν περδίκων οἱ μὲν κακκαβίζουσι οἱ δὲ τρίζουσι</note>.* But instead of "screech" <note>original: τρίζουσι</note>, Theophrastus—cited in Athenaeus—reads *titubizousi* <note>cluck or twitter; original: τιτυβίζουσι</note>:

<margin>in Book 9.</margin>
*Theophrastus, in his book on the varied voices of related animals, says that in Athens, the partridges on this side of Corydallus toward the city cackle, but those beyond it "titubissate" <note>make a twittering sound</note>.* Whence and when this change of sound occurs is not entirely clear; it pleases us that this bird "cackles" <note>original: κακκαβίζειν</note> when it is more vocal, and "screeches" or "twitters" <note>original: τρίζειν/τιτυβίζειν</note> when it is less so, since these words sound thin and weak. And this is what Antigonus of Carystus says in his *Collection of Wonderful Tales, chapter 6*, that those appearing in the light sound one way, and those following tracks sound another; see also Vossius in Book 3 of *Idolatry*, chapter 8, page 1209. It is a cunning and deceptive animal in seeking out its young and in its own escapes, which is why Aristophanes in *The Birds* calls it "industrious" <note>original: ἐπιτηδεύουσα</note>. Hence Aristotle calls it *vicious and malicious <note>original: κακοήθης, καὶ πανῦργος</note>*, meaning crafty and mischievous.

<margin>History of Animals, Book 9, ch. 8.</margin>
Induced by that reasoning, Basil in his 8th Homily on the *Hexameron* <note>The Six Days of Creation</note> compares this bird with the clever wits of this world. The partridge is a clever bird, cunning and envious, and acts maliciously toward hunters regarding its prey. He continues in the same exhortation, specifically in the *Exhortation to Baptism*:

> *I have seen the wondrous art of this cunning bird: when it sees its chicks still exposed to the danger of prey because of their weakness, it offers itself to the fowler before them as if ready to be caught, turning itself and managing its gestures so that it neither gives itself up entirely to danger or hands, nor flies away completely. Beware, therefore, lest you suffer similar things from the fowler, leaving certainties for uncertainties, and exchanging firm hope for vain things, etc.*

It makes two nesting places or receptacles for itself, as Aristotle writes in Book 6 of the *History of Animals*, if it is incubating eggs: *The partridges, he says, make two nests for the eggs; the female sits on one, and the male on the other.* And this is especially attributed to the female, because the male partridge is said to break the female's eggs, which is why she does not approach the eggs, unless...

In the Sacred Scripture, in two places—namely 1 Samuel 26:20 and Jeremiah 17:11—the Hebrew word <term>קרא <note>Kore</note></term> is found, which interpreters commonly explain as the partridge. This is an <term>onomatopoeia <note>A word formed from a sound</note></term> taken from its cry, for <term>קרא <note>Kore</note></term> means "he cried, called, or summoned." Regarding the latter passage, there is no agreement among interpreters, as the Prophet says of this bird that it "gathers eggs it did not lay," a behavior which some deny of the partridge and others affirm. Concerning the partridge, this is asserted by Ambrose (Hexaemeron book 6, chapter 3 and Epistle 48), Jerome (in his commentary on this passage), Augustine (Against Faustus book 13), and Isidore (Etymologies book 12, chapter 7). However, nothing of this is found in Aristotle, Pliny, or Aelian. It is a very elegant comparison which, by the time of St. Ambrose, had clearly passed into a proverb (from book 7, Epistle 48). But in the application, as we said, a certain discrepancy is criticized, which some believe arises from the ambiguity of the Hebrew word <term>קרא</term>. For this word specifically denotes the partridge, but in its general sense, it signifies any clucking bird. Those who follow the former interpretation apply it to the partridge, saying that it steals the eggs of others (that is, of another partridge) and broods upon them, but gains no benefit from this labor because, once the chicks are somewhat grown, they desert the nest of their nurse and follow their genuine mother. These things could easily be applied to the greedy and their unjust riches—if that nature of partridges, which we mentioned, rested on sufficiently firm authority. <margin>Similar to Sacred Scripture page 383.</margin> However, as B. Zehner <note>Beatus Zehner, a 17th-century scholar</note> warns, although Epiphanius (Physiologist chapter 9), Augustine (On Pastors chapter 12), Ambrose, Isidore, and especially Jerome (Commentary on Jeremiah chapter 17) have recorded this in literature—Jerome even goes so far as to cite Aristotle, Theophrastus, and Pliny as witnesses to his opinion—nonetheless, since absolutely nothing on this matter is found in their writings (as we noted above), we leave it to each person's judgment how much faith they wish to grant this assertion. In my own judgment, Zehner continues, nothing prevents us from taking this as referring to the specific traits of each bird. For it often happens that a partridge lays a great number of eggs but does not hatch them: either because she does not entrust them to a safe place (as Aelian <note>original: Αἰλιανός, a Roman author of nature history</note> writes), but carries them to another place as if migrating and finally forgets them; or because the eggs are soaked by dew and rain (according to the same Aelian <margin>book 3, History of Animals, section 16.</margin> in book 10, chapter 35) and are rendered infertile; or because the males, maddened by lust, break them (as Aristotle book 9, Aelian book 3, and Pliny book 10 testify); or finally, because the mother often rises from her brooding (as Aristotle writes) or is sometimes even intercepted by a fowler. All these things fit well with wicked men who amass a great force of wealth through right and wrong, yet because of many intervening misfortunes, they cannot enjoy them—which is nothing other than, to use the words of Quintilian (book 10, chapter 1), "brooding over closed treasures." Compare B. Frantzius (Sacred History of Animals pages 420 and 421) and Vossius (On Idolatry book 3, chapter 85, page 1194). There are those who <margin>and that the Devil is compared to a partridge by Jeremiah</margin>

write that the nations stolen from the Church are like those who finally return upon recognizing their mother’s voice. Concerning this comparison, let us hear Ambrose in the book praised above: This bird is said to be full of guile, fraud, and deceit, knowing the ways to deceive the hunter and the arts to turn him away from her chicks; she does not omit any trial of craftiness by which she might stand her ground; she mocks him as long as she can give the sign and power of flight to her offspring, and once she senses they have escaped, she withdraws herself and leaves the hunter deceived by her slippery art. It is also said to be of promiscuous mating, such that they rush upon females with the greatest struggle and burn with wandering lust; hence it is thought to be an impure, malevolent, and fraudulent animal, to be compared to the most deceitful adversary and circumventor of the human race <note>The Devil</note>, the author of impurity. Therefore, the partridge "cried out"—taking its name from *perdiendo* <note>original Latin: "losing" or "destroying," a folk etymology for Perdix</note>—that Satan, who in Latin is called the "Opponent." He cried out in Eve, Cain, Pharaoh, etc. With these voices, he gathered to himself peoples whom he had not gathered, etc.

### PHILOSTORGOS,
a bird that received its name among the Greeks from its supreme love for its offspring <note>original: φιλόστοργος, philostorgos, "loving-affectionate"</note>, which the Latins have also retained. To the Hebrews, it sounds like <term>רחם <note>Racham</note></term>, "the merciful one," from the root <term>רחם</term>, which means "he loved" as if from the innermost bowels; this word seems to be derived from <term>רחם <note>rechem</note></term>, the womb, which embraces the fetus with the most tender affection. Which bird it actually is, however, is not certain. Modern Jews want it to be the magpie. Junius and Tremellius suggest the *Merops* <note>The Bee-eater</note>, which is "the most pious of all birds" <note>original Greek: εὐσεβεστάτα ὄρνιθον ἁπάντων</note> because it feeds its parents, according to Aelian. But <term>רחם</term> properly signifies "loving one's offspring" <note>philostorgon</note>, not "loving one's parents" <note>philopappa</note>. Schindler interprets it as the vulture, or the "uterine eagle," or the bone-breaker <note>The Ossifrage or Lammergeier</note>. Bochart does not differ much from Schindler, showing from Arabic sources that the same things are attributed to the <term>רחם</term> as the Greeks attribute to the vulture. Plutarch, in his life of Romulus and Roman Questions, attributes the title of Justice to the vulture. Hence the Indians, Persians, and Iberians used to expose the bodies of the slain or deceased to them, because, as Silius <margin>book 13, verse 470 and 340.</margin> sings:
> — they believe the soul is returned to the high heavens,
> if the unfed vulture plucks the lying limbs.

It is added that, as found in Horus <note>Horapollo, author of a treatise on hieroglyphics</note> book 1, chapter 11, the Egyptians used the vulture <term>glyph</term> to signify "mother" or "merciful one," for Horus reports in that place concerning its wonderful "parental love" <note>original: φιλοστοργία</note>, that in a scarcity of food, the mother, having cut her own thigh, offers her own blood to her chicks. Bonfrerius, in his Commentary on Leviticus, notes that in the Septuagint and Vulgate versions the order of birds is changed, so that it is uncertain whether <term>רחם</term> or <term>רחמה</term> signifies the swan, the Pelican, or the Purple Gallinule? This reason perhaps moved B. Luther to place "the Stork" there, whose name is actually <term>חסידה <note>Chasidah</note></term>.

### STRUTHIOCAMELVS <note>The Ostrich</note>,
an animal of stupendous <margin>chapter 20.</margin> magnitude, which, as Pliny records in book 10, chapter 1, exceeds the height of a rider sitting on a horse. Galen says that in his youth he heard a Sophist who, in a two-part speech, treated this argument: whether the Ostrich can be counted among the birds or not? In one part he contended that a place should be given to it among the birds, and in the other he attacked it; he concludes finally that it matters little whether we know if it should be counted among birds or not. Compare Aristotle, book 4 *On the Parts of Animals*, chapter 14, where he says it departs from the quadrupeds because it has wings...

By Buxtorf and Junius, the Hebrew word is explained as an *Owl* <note>original: "Ulula"</note>; by Pagninus as the *daughter of the owl*; by the Septuagint and the Vulgate as the *Ostrich* <note>original: "Struthio"</note>, with whom Luther agrees, translating it as *der Strauß*. It takes its name from its great cry, for this bird is said to be so noisy that it can be heard for half a league. It recognizes as its mother the word <term><hebrew>ענה</hebrew> <note>Anah</note></term>, which among other meanings signifies "he cried out" or "he shouted." From this, the Hebrew name found in the books of Moses is usually expressed as the "daughter of shouting." This bird lives in desert places (*Jeremiah 50:39, Isaiah 13:21, 34:13, 43:20*) and is mournful (*Job 30:29, Micah 1:8*), which agrees with another meaning of the root: "to be depressed." It is common near the Euphrates and in Arabia near Syria. It is called cruel, as is evident from the Lamentations of Jeremiah (*chapter 4:3*). In that place, regarding the word <term><hebrew>כיענים</hebrew> <note>Ki-ye-enim, "like ostriches"</note></term>, certain copies use a <term>diaeresis <note>a division of a word into two</note></term>, such as the Royal and Bomberg Bibles, which write it as <term><hebrew>כי ענים</hebrew> <note>Ki ayanim, "like the oppressed/mournful ones"</note></term>, though they place the undivided word in the margin. In the first manner, the Septuagint reads it as <note>original: "ὡς στρουθίον"</note> *like an ostrich*. The Vulgate reads: *Like an ostrich*. They understand it to be the *Struthiocamelus* <note>the scientific name for the ostrich, literally "camel-sparrow"</note>, and they describe it as <note>original: "ἀνάλγημον & ἄστοργον"</note> *unfeeling and without natural affection*, because it is accustomed to leave its eggs (*Job 39:15*); this can be applied here to mothers who abandon and neglect their children. When he says, "I will wail and howl," he shows the destruction decreed by the Lord. When he mentions the wailing of Dragons <note>or "serpents"</note> and Ostriches, it is as much as to say: Your region will be deserted, nor will anything be heard there, instead of the joy and jubilation of the people, except the wailing of serpents and the mourning of ostriches, who inhabit the deserts.* Wherever there is mention of Dragons and Ostriches in Scripture, it signifies devastation and horror.

### THE TURTLEDOVE.
A well-known bird of the pigeon family, taking its name from the sound it makes, according to Calepinus and Becmannus. The Turtledove is also named from its <term>distinctive voice</term> <note>Greek: *idiophōnia*</note>. It is the same among the Hebrews: namely <term>Tor</term> <note>Hebrew: <hebrew>תּוֹר</hebrew></note>. Those providing an <term>etymology</term> <note>Greek: *etymologountes* - explaining the origin of the word</note> form it from the root <term>tur</term> <note>Hebrew: <hebrew>תּוּר</hebrew></note>, which means to look, to inquire, or to track. Buxtorf says: *Tor, the turtledove, is so called from the voice it produces.* Kircher says: *Tor, the turtledove, is named either from the sound it makes or from its habit of circling.* Avenarius says: *Tor, the turtledove, is a bird named from tracking and searching for its mate. For they explain "Tor" as searching in a circuit or circle, investigating everywhere, exploring by going around, and inquiring.* **Johannes Eusebius Nierembergius** <note>A Jesuit physicist and mystic</note> writes: *In Hebrew the turtledove is called Tor, from the root Tur, meaning to think or meditate, because the turtledove seems to speak within itself, like those who speak to themselves while in deep thought.* The Greeks call it <term>trygōn</term> <note>Greek: <greek>τρυγών</greek></note>, from the sound of its song, for this bird is said to <term>coo or moan</term> <note>Greek: *tryzein*</note>. It is the herald of springtime (*Song of Solomon 2:12*), in which the turtledove gives forth its voice, which **Abbot Willeram** <note>An 11th-century scholar known for his commentary on the Song of Songs</note> interprets as the most sweet preaching of the Apostles:
> The noble voice of the turtledove has sounded in our land:
> The persuasion of the Apostles' words becomes frequent.
> It persuades the followers of Christ to have a chaste life
> With innocent minds and moaning desires,
> So that present groaning may give the joys of true laughter.

The **Gloss** <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, a standard medieval commentary on the Bible</note> intends the same meaning: *The voice of the turtledove is the voice of the Apostles or any preachers who, by their song, announce the departure of winter and the arrival of spring; who return a humble moan instead of a song; who are lovers of chastity; who always dwell on the ridges of mountains or the tops of trees; and though placed in the body, they have their conversation in heaven, mindful of their dwelling place and the homeland promised to them, etc.* This bird is commended above others for its chastity and continence. Hence, to express the highest continence, artists paint a turtledove sitting on a dry branch. For they say of the Turtledove that once its mate has died, it separates itself from the company of other birds and shows such signs of sorrow that it never allows itself to enter into a union with any other, but spends the remainder of its life without a mate in perpetual celibacy, flies alone, and never sits on a leafy branch—doing all those things which seem most fit to signify mourning

<column-break/>

and to express the sorrow of widowhood and solitude, even as seen in humans. Regarding its <margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> chastity and continence, let us hear **Ambrose** <note>Saint Ambrose, 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note> <margin>Book 5, *Hexameron*, chapter 19.</margin> discussing it thus: *The turtledove refuses to hope for a new union, nor does she break the laws of modesty or the bond of the husband who pleased her; she reserves her love for him alone, and for him she keeps the name of wife. Learn, O women, how great is the grace of widowhood, which is praised even in birds. Who then gave these laws to the turtledove? If I look for a man, I find none: for no man dared, since even Paul did not dare to prescribe laws for maintaining widowhood, etc.* Paul hopes for that in women which persists in turtledoves. And elsewhere he encourages younger women to marry, because our women can hardly fulfill the chastity of turtledoves. Therefore, God infused this affection into the turtledoves and gave them this virtue of continence—He who alone can prescribe what all should follow. *The turtledove is not burned by the flower of youth, nor tempted by the allure of opportunity. The turtledove knows not how to make void her first faith, knowing how to keep her chastity after the first lot of marriage has passed, etc.* This bird is deservedly placed among the sacrifices and lawful foods, the reason for which can be assigned in two ways: one physical, the other mystical. Indeed, the meat of the turtledove is of a good temperament, especially that which lives in the mountains, as **Galen** <note>The famous Greek physician of antiquity</note> <margin>Book 3, *On the Properties of Foodstuffs*, chapter 19.</margin> records. Indeed, because it produces a thin and dry juice, well-suited for generating spirits: hence **Nicolaus Massa**, a Venetian physician celebrated for many monuments in his art, was accustomed to call it "the food of the Wise." **Martial** <note>A Roman poet known for his Epigrams</note> indicates in Book 3, Epigram 60, that it once especially pleased delicate diners:

-> A golden, immoderate turtledove fills you with its haunches <-

-> Unless he meant to call it simply "great" by <term>synecdoche</term> <note>Greek: *synekdochikēn* - a figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note> of the part, for these were especially praised by **Juvenal** <margin>Satire 6.</margin> in Satire 6. <-
-> *Lacking a great turtledove,* <-
-> *And the crests of mullets.* <-

III.</margin> <term>and tenderness to the youth without hypocrisy, teaching like to be purified by like</term> <note>Greek: *kai hapalotēta tō neō anypokrisin, kai tois homoiois ta homoia didaskōn kathairesthai*</note>. Two turtledoves were taken for atonement, *Leviticus 15:29*, and they signified an expiatory victim. Worthy of mention and full of mystery is that rite in the offering of the turtledove, which God the Lawgiver specifically prescribed: for the Priest in the Old Testament was commanded to offer the turtledove upon the altar, and to nip off its head with his nail, and burn it on the altar, and press out its blood against the wall of the altar, and remove its crop with its feathers, and cast it near the altar toward the East to the place of the ashes, and split it with its wings and burn it on the altar, etc. A figure—though we may pass over the type most full of Christ's consolation this time—of faith and moral doctrine is given to us in it. **Brentius** <note>Johannes Brenz, a German reformer</note> says in his commentary on Luke: *The sacrifice of a turtledove or a young pigeon, besides the significance and admonition of faith, also contains moral doctrine and forms civil honesty. For they write of turtledoves and pigeons that chastity is their primary trait, and adulteries are unknown; they do not violate the faith of a spouse, and they keep a common home, unless as a celibate or widow they do not leave the house, and they bear masterful and sometimes even unjust behaviors.* Love
