<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...equal offspring to both, and providing solace and service to the mother from the male. Therefore, as in the laws of Moses, so that he might admonish spouses not only with words but with signs of their duty, he commanded the woman in childbirth to offer—not a partridge, which breaks its own eggs, nor a cuckoo, which lays in foreign nests and places its eggs under foreign brooders—but a turtledove or a pigeon, which are symbols of modesty, chastity, and conjugal love. Brentius <note>Johannes Brentz, a 16th-century German reformer</note> goes on to say elsewhere that the Church deserves the most sweet name of "Turtledove." He says: *It should be observed that the Psalmist calls the people of God, or the Church, a turtledove, and elsewhere a dove; because just as this little bird is destitute of all protection against the harpies <note>birds of prey</note>, so the Church of God is stripped of all human help against its enemies, both physical and spiritual, etc.* In his paraphrase of Psalm 76, Ostender lists three reasons why the Church can be compared to a turtledove: the first is "dove-like simplicity" (Matthew 10); the second is the love with which she pursues her husband, Christ; and the third is fertility, by which the Church daily generates spiritual children for Christ her Spouse through the mediation of the Word and the use of the Sacraments.

Among the <margin>Volume 2, Homily 26.</margin> Fathers, **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople</note> chooses to describe and commend the middle reason primarily: *The turtledove is a lover of the wilderness; when she dwells in deserted places, she summons the partner of her voice with delightful charms. Penetrating the valleys, she calls together her male feeding in the pleasant and wooded areas, and provoking him to fly from there, she urges him to make his approach to her swift. With a unanimous mind, they establish their nest in the uncultivated and rugged places of birds. Thence they provoke their chicks to fly without fear. Some assert that the turtledove is so chaste and such a lover of her partner that if it should ever happen that her male is captured by an eagle or a fowler, she does not join with another, but longs for him, waits for his arrival, and hangs in the expectation of his love, etc.* Such is every chaste Church; since her husband Christ was crucified and sits in heaven at the right hand of the Father, she does not join with another, but desires him, waits for him, and wishes to die in her longing for him. (Compare Ambrose, *The Six Days of Creation*, book 5, chapter 19; and Haymo’s *Exposition on the Song of Solomon*, chapter 1, page 11.)

**THE BAT**, since it flies at night, received its name from that fact, as Ovid says:
> *It flies by night and takes its name from the late evening.* <note>Latin: *Vesper* (evening) becomes *Vespertilio* (bat)</note>

<margin>On the Republic.</margin>
It is a foul little animal, about which **Plato** recites his famous riddle: *A man who is not a man, seeing yet not seeing, struck and yet did not strike, with a stone that was not a stone, a bird that was not a bird, upon a tree that was not a tree.* That is: a eunuch, who was dim-sighted, struck a bat with a pumice stone on an elder tree. In Varro's *Agatho* (page 306), he says: *I have become a bat, neither clearly among the mice, nor among the birds.* And in Aesop, the Bat responds to one weasel that he is a mouse, and to another that he is a bird. The reasons that prove it is a bird carry more weight; for to be a bird, it is enough if it flies, even if it does not lay eggs but is a live-bearing flyer—which should be noted against Macrobius (Book 7 of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 6), who places the bat among the quadrupeds. For he writes: *All flying things come forth from eggs, except one, which is of an uncertain nature; for the bat indeed flies with skin-covered wings, but it is not to be held among the flyers, because it walks on four*

<column-break/>

<margin>History of Animals, book 3, chapter 7.</margin>
*feet, and brings forth formed young, and nourishes those it generates with milk.* In the Holy Scripture, it is called עטלף <note>Hebrew: *Atalleph*</note> (Leviticus 11:20), and it closes the list of those birds which it was not permitted to eat. Bonfrerius notes this reason for the prohibition: that in some places large ones are found, which it is the custom to skin and season for food, such as those found and eaten in the city of Borsippa in Babylonia near Mesopotamia, according to Strabo (Book 16) and Scaliger (*Exercise* 236). But that bats are larger than eagles and prepared as sweet food—which Pigafetta also reported in Simon Maiolus (*Colloquy* 6)—let him believe and eat it who wishes. Isaiah (Chapter 2:20) predicted that idols must be thrown to the bats, which Eucherius explains with perhaps not enough sound sense, saying: *Bats are the monsters of idols devoted to darkness; as in the Prophet: "To worship moles and bats."* (See regarding this passage below, page 562.)

<margin>Formulary, page 7.</margin>
In India, among the Mexicans, Gryfaldus (Book 3 of the *Indian History*) reports that bats are adored and worshiped as a deity. But among the Syrian gods, they never found a place. Jerome, in that passage of Isaiah, understands them to be doctrines contrary to the truth. Thus, bats are an image of those who flee the light (Job 3:19–20), and in religion, they represent the "Neutrals," whom you hear praised today by the name of **MODERATES**, such as the Samaritans once were, as can be read in Josephus. We conclude with the words of Novatian (*On Jewish Foods*, chapter 3): *When God forbids the owl, He hates those who flee the light of truth; when the swan, those proud with high necks; when the plover, the overly talkative intemperance of the tongue; when the Bat, those seeking the darkness of night and error at once.*

**THE HOOPOE** follows the bat, a similarly foul bird. In the Hebrew language, its name is דוכיפת <note>Hebrew: *Dukiphat*</note>, which Arias <note>Arias Montanus</note> translates as "mountain cock" or "mountain craftsman," because of its works, according to Rabbi Solomon; because it is as if it were *Bor* and *Keph*—a wild cock and a rock—so says Bochart. Tremellius interprets it as a "heath-cock." Schindler as a "wild cock." The Targum <note>Aramaic translation</note> calls it the "mountain-dweller." Our fellow Jews explain it as an *Uhrhan* or "wood-grouse." But the Greeks call it *epopa*, and the Vulgate calls it the *Upupa* [Hoopoe], whom many more recent scholars follow, such as Widhopff. *Upupa* and *cucupha* are not far from the Hebrew *Dukiphat*, as Kircher notes (*Egyptian Oedipus*, page 328). There, Rabbi Solomon explains it as a "Wild Cock with a double crest," from which its name comes: *du-cephath*, "having crests." Kimchi and Aben Ezra follow him; Pagninus follows their version, saying the Hoopoe is a bird helmeted with crests emerging from its head. By some Greeks, the hoopoe is called the "wild rooster"; Aeschylus calls it a "bird of the wilderness"; Cyril, in his commentary on Zechariah, calls it "crest-loving and dung-collecting." And Jerome, on Zechariah 5, notes: *The Hoopoe (whose name we have drawn from the Greek, for they call it 'epopa' from the fact that it considers human dung) they say is a most filthy bird, always dwelling in tombs and human excrement. Finally, it is even said to make its nest out of it and to feed its chicks on the maggots of rotting filth.* He explains this as referring to those who wallow in the mire of lusts and eternal filth. Lyra adds to this:

<margin>In the *Moralia*.</margin>
*The Hoopoe nests in dung, therefore it designates those remaining in the stench of luxury/excess.* Hugo applies this to unchaste and harlot-favouring Prelates, the Hoopoe nesting in dung,

<page-num>p. 1508</page-num>
<header>from Psalm 50, verses 10, 11.</header>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...heart, it signifies prelates who build the Church’s nest for their own little nephews and kinsmen. <note>original: "nepotulus fuis & cognatis"; a critique of nepotism in the church hierarchy</note> Hesychius <note>An ancient Greek grammarian and lexicographer</note> explains this regarding those who love the sadness of the world which causes death. He says: *The Hoopoe is a mournful animal that loves grief; however, the sadness of the secular world produces death. For this reason, it is necessary for one who loves God to always rejoice, to pray without ceasing, and to give thanks in all things, because joy is the fruit of the Spirit.*

**T**he **Vulture**, named "vultur" from its slow flight <note>original: "à volatu tardo"</note>, is a well-known bird that flies slowly due to its great body size. In Hebrew, it is called *Ayah* <note>איה</note>, according to Arius, Pagninus, and the Vulgate. Rabbi Aben Ezra, however, translates it as a "kite" <note>a type of hawk</note> that lives on certain islands, so that it might agree with the word *Ai*, which signifies an island. Others translate it as a magpie, and some even as a crow. The Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> reads it as *gyps* <note>vulture</note> in both places in the books of Moses. It is different from the bird called *agyps* by Aelian and Pliny, which they translate as the "black vulture." It belongs to the category of unclean birds; it is extremely rapacious, feeds on carcasses, and has sharp vision. Hence, in the Holy Scriptures at Job 28:7, the eye of the vulture is praised—Luther translates this as *ein Geyersaug* <note>"a vulture's eye"</note>. For this reason, according to Horus in his *Hieroglyphics*, the Egyptians depicted a vulture to symbolize sharp sight. Osiander <note>A 16th-century German theologian</note> sets up a comparison between the sharpness of the vulture’s sight and human judgment in his paraphrase of Job, saying: *Even if vultures see quite sharply among other birds, they still cannot penetrate with their sight into those places from which gems and gold are produced—which are discovered by human diligence—yet man still does not comprehend the wisdom of God through the sharpness of his own natural talent.* 

Regarding this bird, it is a fabled belief that all vultures are of the female sex, and that they conceive without mating with any other bird. This is a very ancient opinion, perhaps arising from an Egyptian fable in which the vulture was the symbol of Vulcan and Minerva. For Vulcan was called "fatherless" <note>Greek: ἀπάτωρ</note> by the poets—as if to say he had only a mother—and Minerva was called "motherless" <note>Greek: ἀμήτωρ</note>, because she acknowledged only a father, hence she was also named *Hypatera* <note>born from the father</note>. From there, this idea flew into the Christian schools, and it was defended by Origen, Basil, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, and Ambrose. Among these, Basil and Ambrose did not hesitate to use this "conception without a male" to prove the Virgin Birth of the Blessed Virgin Mary against the pagans. In this instance, the saying applies: "to speak well, but to prove poorly." But however invalid this argument might be in itself, it was nonetheless effective against the pagan nations who were already convinced of it. Since, as we proved above, the Christians did not invent this story about the generation of vultures, but other pagans besides the Egyptians had approved the myth; compare Aelian’s *On Animals*. Furthermore, the masters of nature's mysteries report of this bird that it is rapacious, following armies in the hope of feeding on the carcasses of those to be slaughtered. This does not at all agree with the opinion of those who hardly admit that it lives off plunder. Let us hear Plutarch on this matter: <margin>Roman Questions, 93.</margin> *Hesiod says that Hercules rejoiced most of all when vultures appeared at the beginning of an action, deeming the vulture to be the most just of all*

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
*carnivorous creatures. First, because it touches nothing living, nor does it kill anything with a soul, as eagles, hawks, and nocturnal birds do. It must feed only on things that have already died. Second, it passes over the carcasses of its own kind. For no one has ever seen a vulture taste a bird, whereas eagles and hawks especially pursue and strike their own kin; and as Aeschylus says:*

-> *How can a bird be pure if it devours another bird?* <-

*Furthermore, this bird is the least harmful of all to humans, as it destroys no fruit, nor plants, nor does it harm any tame animal.* Thus writes Plutarch to show why the Romans used vultures most of all in their auguries <note>the practice of interpreting omens from the flight of birds</note>. However, Plutarch does not agree with Seneca, Martial, and Catullus, who use the example of the vulture when describing a rapacious man. For Seneca says: <margin>Letter 96.</margin> *If you are a vulture, wait for the corpse.* And Catullus in his 69th poem to Marius:

-> *He rouses the vulture from his white head* <-

And likewise Martial:

-> *Will this carcass belong to the vulture's cradle?* <-

These things were said against "inheritance hunters" <note>term: hæredipetas; people who flatter the wealthy in hopes of being named in their wills</note>, who neither work nor engage in honest commerce; they only hope to obtain something from the final will of the dying, contrary to that rule of Cato:

-> *Do not place your hope in the death of another.* <-

And so we have constructed a catalog of almost all the birds mentioned by the Holy Spirit in the Sacred Book. We have said something about them, for it was not our intention to write a full commentary on them; we have said only as much as the purpose of our work required. Various books exist concerning them, but what a long time and what long observation was needed so that something certain and worthy of reading might be gathered through daily experience. We lost in Adam what Adam the "Namer" <note>term: onomathetes; one who gives names</note> possessed. For he, without any new illumination but only by the goodness of his own nature, simply by looking at all living things, immediately had a thorough and known understanding of the nature of each creature, and from that he gave to each a name fitting and appropriate to its nature. What we still possess are the ruins of the divine image remaining from that great flood and shipwreck, which we ought to use rightly for the glory of God alone. From the wondrous creation of birds, we drink in the admirable power and wisdom of God. As Basil says: <margin>Homily 8 on the Six Days of Creation.</margin> *Absolutely, if the words of Holy Scripture are read ("Let the waters bring forth winged creatures above the earth under the firmament of heaven"), they seem to be very small syllables; but when the meaning of the words is investigated, then it is perceived how great is the Wisdom of the Creator: how many distinctions and how many differences the Maker himself conceived to be brought forth...*

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...how many genera and species He has separated among themselves, or how He has distinguished each one with its own proper and peculiar markings. There is no bird, even the very smallest in number, that does not lift its voice in praise of its Creator. This was noted by the most celebrated poet Johannes Stigelius, who introduces all and singular birds as if they were speaking, to incite man to join them in the praises of God. His poem is found in Volume 6 of the *German Poets*:
<margin>page 544.</margin>
> *O Traveler, who passes through these groves and cultivated greens,*
> *And by these white willow-thickets of the grassy soil,*
> *You hear the chirping of birds and their sonorous tongues,*
> *And the sweet melody scattered from their skillful throats.* <note>original: "docto gutture"</note>
> *Contemplate in your mind what we are, and from where we birds come;*
> *From this, there may be something that delights the soul.*
> *We live free from cares, a flock of pious birds*
> *Ignorant of fault and an innocent race.*
> *By singing we draw out as much of life as God grants,*
> *And our voice also celebrates the true God.*
> *So shall the most peaceful account of eternal life be,*
> *Bringing full joys before God to the elect.*
> *Golden simplicity will meditate on sweet hymns,*
> *Rejoicing to speak pleasing things to the present God.*
> *An innocent life, vowing eager minds in rejoicing,*
> *Will always be the rule of eternal justice.*
> *True wisdom, beholding God with full fruit,*
> *Being well-taught, will rejoice to hold the highest good.*
> *The Church, pleasing to God, rejoicing in sweet harmony,*
> *Will lead the perpetual joys of eternal peace.*
> *While we show this to you by the image of our song:*
> *How could we be harsh to your ears?*

The third part of sacred <term>zoology</term> <note>original Greek: "zoologias"</note> is constituted by <term>Ichthyology</term> <note>original Greek: "Ichthyologia"</note>, in which we must treat fish both in general and in the specific types that the Holy Scripture expressly names. In the first creation of living things, God indeed began with the fish, as they were more imperfect and less noble. For the best and most perfect Creator observed this order in creating living things: that He proceeds from the imperfect to the most perfect, and finishes there. Thus, He first turns Himself to the creation of fish, which are more imperfect than the rest, inasmuch as He even excluded them from sacrifices as being less fit, because very few of them can prolong their life for even an hour outside the element of water. After the production of fish was completed, He created the birds from the same element, using one and the same word: *let them swarm* <note>original Hebrew: "yishretsu"; from Genesis 1:20</note> or "let the waters bring forth." Regarding this phrase, since it was treated previously in *Sacred Physics* on page 60, we do not wish to repeat what has been done, but let us at least note those golden words of the Blessed Luther, which he brings forth in this passage from the <term>storehouse</term> <note>original Greek: "tamieio"</note> of the Holy Spirit: *"Here is seen,"* he says, *"what blessing properly is—namely, multiplication. When we bless, we do nothing except pray for good. But what we pray for, we cannot provide. But God's blessing sounds forth into multiplication and is immediately effective. This blessing, therefore, the Philosophers call fertility: namely, when complete and living bodies are produced from complete and living bodies—nothing like which is seen in trees, for a tree does not generate its like, but generates a seed, etc. This is a great miracle, but like other things, it has become commonplace through use. We see that the word of this day is still effective, that simply—*

<column-break/>

*—from the water, fish are generated."* For ponds and <margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> lakes give birth to fish, just as we see pike born in ponds where previously there were none. For it does not seem likely to me (as some trifle) that fish are caught by birds and, while carried in the air, drop their seed from on high into ponds and lakes, which later congeals in the waters. This, however, is the sole and true cause: that the water is commanded here to produce fish. This word is still effective and works these things. It is just as Luther, the <term>divinely inspired</term> <note>original Greek: "ho theopneustos"</note>, truly spoke: the liquid sea is that great <term>all-containing reservoir</term> <note>original Greek: "pantoche"</note> of the Lord, where God prepares a huge abundance of fish for the human race, which He eventually gathers at these shores or into those rivers according to His most free judgment and will. This has happened not only in our times, when certain species of fish enter and leave the sea—and what is more wonderful, almost every month new species are caught that were previously unknown, especially in maritime places—but it is also testified by that miraculous <term>catch of fish</term> <note>original Greek: "ichthyalosis"</note> by Peter and his companions. At the command of Christ, <margin>John 21:6.</margin> they cast the net on the right side, and by the power of the omnipotent word of Christ, one hundred and fifty-three fish were gathered into Peter's nets. They had spent the whole night before, but it was empty and without any benefit or fruit of labor. Peter had experienced a similar success and catch of fish earlier, though with the tearing of the nets, which Luke describes in chapter 5:6, and about which the Poet writes in Volume 4 of *German Poets*, page 1177:

> *Throughout the night Peter stretched his curving nets in the sea,*
> *But his hope and labor were in vain.*
> *But when, in the name of Christ, he trusted the nets to the waves,* <note>original: "vueris" (likely a typo for 'veris' or 'pueris')</note>
> *Already one boat cannot hold the prey.*
> *Nor is this enough: instead of scaly fish,*
> *He now draws men themselves into his nets.*
> *If you do what you do with Christ as leader and protector—*
> ->*Christ*<-
> *Do not doubt, you will soon obtain your wishes.*
> *Or if you see what you seek and desire being deferred,*
> *Gifts better than your wishes remain for you.*

Augustine explains that breaking of the nets symbolically in Book 2 of *Questions on the Gospels*, question 2: *"The fact that the nets were breaking,"* he says, *"from the abundance of fish, and the little boats were filled so that they were sinking, signifies that the Lord's multitude of carnal people* <note>original: "carnalium multitudinem"; referring to those focused on worldly rather than spiritual things</note> *would be so great in the Church that even if peace were broken by heresies and schisms departing from it, such a great loss of faith and good morals would remain and be in the future, that such a church would seem to say to Christ: 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man.' It is as if, filled with crowds of carnal people and almost submerged by their morals, the church in a way repels the governance of spiritual men, in whom the person of Christ especially shines. For men do not say this to the good ministers of God with the voice of the tongue—that they should repel them—but they urge them by the voice of their morals and acts to depart, lest they be ruled by the good. They do this all the more vehemently even as they defer honor to them; yet by their deeds they warn them to depart. Peter falling at the feet of the Lord signified their honor, but his saying 'Depart from me' signified their morals. Yet because the Lord did not do this—for He did not depart from them, but brought them to the shore after the boats were drawn up—it signifies that this will ought not to be in good and spiritual men..."*

...so that, moved by the sins of the crowds, they might desert their ecclesiastical duty to live more securely and peacefully. The same Father <note>St. Augustine</note> deals with both miraculous catches of fish in his *Book of Eighty-Three Questions*, where his words sound like this:
> *Before the Passion, it is said of a small net cast into the sea, that they caught so many fish they could hardly drag them to the shore and the nets were breaking. For they were not cast on the right side—for the Church of this time has many evil people—nor on the left, for it also has good people, but everywhere, to signify the mixture of good and evil. But that the nets were broken signifies that many heresies have gone out, with charity being violated. After the Resurrection, however, when He wished to foreshadow the Church of the future time, where all will be perfect and holy, He ordered the nets to be cast on the right side, and 153 large fish were caught. The disciples marveled that, although they were so large, the nets were not torn. Their size signifies the greatness of wisdom and justice, while the number signifies the discipline itself, perfected by both bodily administration and eternal generation. Augustine deals no less piously than skillfully with that fishing in Galilee at the Sea of Tiberias after Christ's resurrection:*

Tractate 122 on John.

*This is a great Mystery <note>original: "Sacramentum"</note> in the great Gospel of John, and it was written in the final place to be more strongly commended. Therefore, that there were seven disciples in this fishing signifies the end of time by their number of seven; for all time revolves in seven days. To this belongs the fact that, when morning came, Jesus stood on the shore, because the shore is also the end of the sea, and therefore signifies the end of the world. Peter dragging the net to the land, that is, to the shore, shows the same end of the world. The Lord Himself revealed this in Matthew 13: "So shall it be at the consummation of the world." But that is a parable of words, not an event. In an actual event, as in this place, it shows how it will be in the end of the world. Thus the Lord signified by the other fishing how the Church is now. That He did the first at the beginning of His preaching, but this one after His resurrection, shows that the first catch of fish signifies the Good and the Evil which the Church now has. This one, however, signifies only the Good, whom it will have eternally, when the resurrection of the Dead is completed at the end of this world. Finally, there Jesus did not stand on the shore when He ordered the fish to be caught; but ascending into one boat, which was Simon's, He asked, etc. (Luke 5). And there, because the catch of fish was in small boats, they did not pull the net onto the land as they did here. By these signs, and whatever others could be found, the Church in this world was figured there, and here the Church at the end of the world. Thus that happened before, but this after the Resurrection of the Lord, because Christ signified us as called there, but resurrected here. There the nets are not cast to the right, lest they signify only the good, nor to the left, lest they signify only the bad; but indifferently, He says, "let down your nets," etc., so that we may understand the good and evil mixed together. But here He says, "cast the net on the right side of the ship," to signify those who will stand on the right—the good alone. There the net was breaking to signify schisms; but here, because there will be no schisms in that supreme peace of the Saints, it pertained to the Evangelist to say, "and although they were so many," that is, so large, "the net was not torn," as if he were looking back to where it was torn, and in comparison with that evil...*

<header>508 (k) BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
...have been domesticated. Of these, such as chickens, geese, cows, sheep, pigs, and so on, we take no small care, but it is a care joined with great difficulty. Yet very often, to the great loss of our household economy, we encounter unexpected accidents and diseases among so many eggs, chicks, lambs, and calves, from which they succumb and miserably perish. Such evils in domestic affairs often surpass all our care, diligence, and prudence. As for wild animals, however—namely birds of the woods and fields, and fish—although they are deprived of these human aids, they nevertheless increase better and propagate better. They do not suffer or experience such great diseases or plagues because their generation and birth are committed to God alone, without human assistance or service. 

Here, God has adorned fish, like other living creatures, with *sight*: for eyes are the first things born in them, and the first to fail when they are dying. In the beginning, their ability to see is small or almost non-existent, but it grows with age. Therefore, if you except the shells <note>referring to shellfish or mollusks</note> about which <margin>Book 9, Chapter 30.</margin> Pliny *testifies: that shells lack sight and every other sense except for food and danger*, all other fish enjoy sight, though it may be hard and dull; yet there are some among them who see acutely, and for this reason are called "eyed." 

They are endowed with excellent *hearing*; and some fish are captivated not only by hearing but even by harmony. Concerning the Dolphin, Pliny records in his *Natural History*, Book 9, Chapter 8: *The dolphin is an animal not only friendly to man, but also to the art of music; it is soothed by the singing of a symphony, and especially by the sound of the water-organ.* <note>original: "hydraulis"</note> 

The same must be said of *taste*, which fish also enjoy; <note>original Greek: ιδιοις πολλὰ χαιρειν χυμοῖς</note> "they delight in many peculiar flavors," <margin>History of Animals, Book 4, Chapter 8.</margin> says Aristotle. *The instrument of taste is the tongue, for without a tongue we are hardly said to be able to taste. Therefore, if fish lack a tongue, they would also lack taste, which goes against experience.* For we use the tongue not only to form voices, but also to taste and direct food in the mouth. Hence, even if it has passed into a proverb, *more mute than a fish*, it is not permitted to conclude that because they are deprived of the benefit of a voice, and have no necks, nor tongues as distinct as other animals, they entirely lack a tongue with which to discern food and what kind of nourishment best suits their nature. 

Let us hear Aristotle on this matter in the book just cited: *But among aquatic creatures called fish, they indeed have a tongue as the organ of taste, but they have it obscurely and confusedly; for it is bony, not free-moving, nor detached. Indeed, in some of them, the palate is fleshy, such as in the river carp; so that to those who do not look closely, it seems to be a tongue.* <note>original: "At inter aquatilia..."</note> But in place of the phrase "those who do not look closely," Caesar Scaliger and Gaza <note>Renaissance scholars of Aristotle</note> read it as "those who *do* look closely," so that Aristotle would say the opposite about the carp—namely, that it has a tongue, even if it appears to be a palate. 

Vossius mentions in his *On Idolatry*, Book 4, Chapter 21, page 1363, that certain "vocal" fish are found, such as the sea-ox, the dolphin, etc. (compare Pliny, Book 9, Chapter 8). Regarding *smell* and *respiration*, many of the Masters of Nature deny that fish possess them; however, from the 

<column-break/>

side of those who assert it, the truth seems to us to stand more firmly, as Aristotle also asserts in <margin>History of Animals, Book 4, Chapter 18.</margin> his *History of Animals*, Book 4, Chapter 18. Indeed, experience also testifies that fish die in winter in ponds covered with ice unless holes are opened through which the external air may work its way into the internal parts of the waters. 

Finally, all are so endowed with *touch* that even those who seem to lack sight, hearing, and smell do not lack touch, as it is a sense simply necessary for life. Nor is the sagacity and cleverness in aquatic creatures any less than in other animals, if you look at certain internal senses; for Mother Nature, together with a Kind Mother, implanted in them the knowledge of guarding and defending themselves. Hence Ovid writes in his <margin>In the *Halieutica* <note>A poem about fishing attributed to Ovid.</note></margin> *Poem on Fishing*: 
> Fear of death is unknown to none: to all is given 
> To sense the enemy and the protection, and to know the weapons 
> And the strength and manner of one's own self. 

To this, Pliny adds in his *Natural History*, Book 8, Chapter 25: (*All animals,* he says, *are clever in this; they know not only their own advantages but also the weaknesses of their enemies: they know their own weapons, they know their opportunities, and which parts of their opponents are defenseless.* He continues in <margin>Book 9, Chapter 3.</margin> Book 9, Chapter 3: *The torpedo fish knows its own power, while not being numb itself; submerged in the mud, it hides itself, seizing the fish that swim over it unawares. Nor is the cleverness of the frog less, which in the sea is called the "fisher-frog" <note>the anglerfish</note>. It thrusts out little horns located under its eyes into the stirred-up mud, attracting small leaping fish until they come so close that it may pounce. In a similar way, the angel-shark and the turbot, having hidden their bodies, stick out their fins, appearing like little worms; likewise, the fish called the ray. For the stingray commits robbery from a hidden place, piercing those passing by with its stinger (which is its weapon).* 

Arguments for this cleverness include the fact that the slowest of fish are found with the mullet—the fastest of all—in their bellies. For more on the prudence of fish, see Ursinus, <margin>Analecta, Vol. 1, p. 172.</margin> *Analecta*, Volume 1, page 172. In addition to these modes of cleverness and sagacity, there is external armor, which Mother Nature has provided for them abundantly. Rich nature has armed them both on the head and on the rest of the body; some have sharp teeth, some have spines on the neck, and almost all have scales, except those of the cartilaginous kind, such as eels and large and small lizards <note>likely referring to sea-lizards or types of sharks/rays</note>. 

Concerning these weapons of fish, let us note the words of Pliny in <margin>Book 9, Chapter 12.</margin> Book 9, Chapter 12: *The coverings of aquatic creatures are many. Some are covered with hide and hair, like calves <note>seals</note> and hippopotamuses. Others with hide only, like dolphins. With a shell <note>cortice</note>, like turtles. With the hardness of flint, like oysters and shells. With crusts, like lobsters. With crusts and spines, like sea urchins. With scales, like fish. With rough skin, like the angel-shark, with which wood and ivory are polished. With soft skin, like the moray eel. Others have none, like the octopus.* 

From this distinction was taken the mandate in divine law, Leviticus 11:9 <note>The text says 11:8, but the specific rule for fish is 11:9.</note>, regarding the eating and not eating of fish; namely, the eating of those which have scales and fins was permitted, while the rest, which had none, was illicit and forbidden. Blessed Luther explains this divine prohibition mystically, saying: *By the fins, which are to fish in place of wings with which they steer their course, is signified the doctrine of faith, which by the Word of God rules and moves hearts in this world. The scales, however, are like the armor and ornament of their bodies, without which other swimming things are as if naked. They signify that faith is not idle, but active through the Spirit of charity. If, therefore, there are any with scales but without fins, they signify workers without faith and the word, like serpents. If any have fins...*

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...are domesticated. Of these, such as hens, geese, cows, sheep, pigs, etc., we take no small care, yet it is joined with great difficulty. Indeed, very often, to the great loss of our household management, we encounter unexpected accidents and diseases among so many eggs, chicks, lambs, and calves, from which they succumb and miserably perish; such evils in domestic affairs surpass all our care, diligence, and wisdom. But concerning wild animals—namely birds of the forest and field, and fish—although they are deprived of these human aids, they nevertheless increase better and propagate better. They do not suffer or experience such great diseases or plagues, because their generation and birth are committed to God alone, without human assistance or ministry. Here, God has adorned fish, like other living creatures, with *sight*: for eyes are the first things born in them, and the first to fail in them when they are dying. In the beginning, their power of vision is small or almost non-existent, but it grows with age. Thus, if you except the shellfish about which <margin>Book 9, Chapter 30.</margin> Pliny *testifies: "Shellfish lack sight and every other sense except for food and danger,"* all others enjoy sight, though it may be hard and dull; yet there are some among them who see acutely, and are therefore called "eyed." They are endowed with excellent *hearing*; and not only do they hear, but some fish are even captivated by harmony. *Concerning the Dolphin, Pliny records in Book 9, Chapter 8 of his Natural History: "The dolphin is not only a friend to man, but also to the art of music; it is soothed by the singing of a symphony, and especially by the sound of the water-organ."* <note>The hydraulis was an ancient pipe organ powered by water pressure.</note> The same must be said of *taste*, which fish also enjoy; for Aristotle says in <margin>History of Animals, Book 4, Chapter 8.</margin> they *delight in many peculiar flavors.* <note>original: "πολλὰ χαίρειν χυμοῖς"</note> *The instrument of taste is the tongue*, for without a tongue, we are hardly said to be able to taste. If, therefore, fish lack a tongue, they would lack taste, which is contrary to experience. For we use the tongue not only to form voices, but also to taste and direct food in the mouth. Hence, even if it has passed into a proverb, *“more mute than a fish,”* it is not permitted to conclude that because they lack the benefit of a voice, and have no necks or tongues as distinct as other animals, they entirely lack a tongue with which to discern food and what kind of nourishment best suits their nature. Let us hear Aristotle on this matter in the book just cited: *“Among the aquatic animals called fish, the organ of taste—the tongue—is indeed present, but it is obscure and indistinct, being bony and not free or mobile. In some fish, however, the palate is fleshy, such as in the river carp; so that to those who do not look closely, this seems to be the tongue.”* <note>original: "Ἐν δὲ τοῖς ἐνύδροις... δοκεῖν ταύτην εἶναι γλῶτταν"</note> But in place of *"those who do not look,"* Caesar Scaliger and Gaza read *"those who do look,"* so that Aristotle says the opposite about the carp—namely, that it has a tongue, even though it appears to be a palate. Vossius mentions in *On Idolatry*, Book 4, Chapter 21, that some "vocal" fish are found, such as the sea-ox, the dolphin, etc. (cf. Pliny Book 9, Chapter 8). Many of the Masters of Nature deny that fish smell and breathe; however,

<column-break/>

from the side of those asserting it, the truth seems to us to stand more firmly, which Aristotle also asserts in *History of Animals, Book 4, Chapter 18.* Indeed, experience also testifies that fish die in the winter in ponds covered with ice unless holes are opened through which the external air may work its way into the internal parts of the water. Finally, all are so endowed with *touch* that even those who seem to lack sight, hearing, and smell do not lack touch, as it is a sense simply necessary for life. No less is the sagacity and cleverness in aquatic creatures, if you look at certain internal senses, than in other living things; for the Parent of Nature, together with Nature as a kind Mother, has instilled in them the knowledge of protecting and defending themselves. Hence Ovid <note>referred to here as "Naso," his family name.</note> says: <margin>In the *Halieutics*.</margin>
> The fear of a bite is known to all; to all is given
> the power to sense the enemy and the defense, 
> and to know their own weapons and their own strength.

To this, Pliny adds in *Natural History*, Book 8, Chapter 25: *“All animals,”* he says, *“are clever in this, and they know not only their own advantages but also the disadvantages of their enemies; they know their own weapons, they know their opportunities, and which parts of their opponents are unarmed.”* He continues: *“The torpedo fish <note>The electric ray.</note> knows its own power, <margin>Book 9, Chapter 48.</margin> though it is not itself torpid; submerged in the mud, it hides itself, seizing the fish that swim over it unawares. No less is the cleverness of the frog-fish, which in the sea is called the 'fisher.' It thrusts out little horns from under its eyes into the stirred-up mud, attracting small fish as they jump about, until they come so close that it leaps upon them. In a similar way, the turbot and the rhombus, being hidden, stick out their fins in the appearance of little worms; likewise the fish called the ray. For the stingray acts as a highwayman from a hidden place, piercing those who pass by with its sting (which is its weapon).”* Arguments for this cleverness include the fact that the slowest of fish are found with the mullet—the fastest of all—in their bellies; compare Ursinus on the wisdom of fish in *Anal. Vol. 1, p. 172.* Added to these modes of cleverness and sagacity is their external armor, which Mother Nature has provided for them abundantly. Rich nature has armed them both on the head and on the rest of the body; some have sharp teeth, some have spines on the neck, and almost all have scales, except those of the cartilaginous kind, such as eels and large and small lizards <note>Likely referring to a specific type of fish or sea creature, not land lizards.</note>. Concerning these weapons of fish, let us note the words of Pliny: <margin>Book 9, Chapter 12.</margin> *“The coverings of aquatic animals are many. Some are covered with skin and hair, like calves and hippopotamuses. Others with skin only, like dolphins; with a shell, like tortoises; with the hardness of flint, like oysters and mussels; with crusts, like lobsters; with crusts and spines, like sea urchins; with scales, like fish; with a rough skin, like the monkfish, with which wood and ivory are polished; with a soft skin, like moray eels; others have none, like the octopus.”* From this distinction was taken the command in the Divine Law, Leviticus 11:9, concerning which fish were to be eaten and which were not; namely, the eating of those that have scales and fins was permitted, while the others, which had none, were forbidden and prohibited. Blessed Luther explains this divine prohibition mystically, saying: *“By the fins, which are to fish instead of wings, with which they rule their course, the doctrine of faith is signified, which by the Word of God rules and drives hearts in this world. But the scales are like the weapons and ornament of their body, without which other swimming things are as if naked. They signify, however, that faith is not idle, but active through the Spirit of charity. If, therefore, there are any that are scaly without fins, they signify workers without faith and the Word, like serpents. If they have fins...”*

### From Psalm 65:10, 11

<margin>
Sacred history of animals.
</margin>
...those that have fins but no scales signify people who possess the Word of God but produce no fruit or good works, such as the eel, the moray, and similar creatures. Others, having neither fins nor scales, represent those who have neither faith nor works, such as worms and leeches. It is not permitted to eat or associate with any of these <note>The author is referencing the dietary laws of Leviticus 11, applying a moral allegory to the types of fish deemed "unclean."</note>. The aquatic world provides no small proof of its strength through animals of vast size found in the sea alongside tiny fish. Among land animals, if you look at size, the Elephant excels; it is of such magnitude and strength that it carries wooden towers filled with armed men. Yet, in comparison with a whale, an elephant hardly equals a gnat. The whale is large enough to take a whole man into its belly, as seen in the example of Jonah. To this, we might add what is read in Jan Huygen van Linschoten’s *History of Voyages to the East Indies*:

<margin>
Vol. 1, ch. 48, p. 71. Dutch Edition.
</margin>
*He says that a Portuguese ship sailing from Mozambique toward the Indies, enjoying a favorable wind, was nevertheless carried backward for fourteen days. This was noticed by those who observed the height of the sun daily. This matter, he says, made the pilot and the others on the ship wondrously anxious; they could think of nothing else except that it was happening through the evil spell of magicians. Finally, a fish was found wrapped around the ship; everyone worked feverishly to push it away with poles and other instruments. However, it did not leave the ship until its tail was first cut off, after which the ship successfully completed the rest of its journey. They concluded, therefore, that the ship had been carried on the back of the fish, and because it was swimming in the opposite direction, the ship was driven backward for two weeks. The Viceroy of India ordered this event to be painted in his palace for eternal memory, adding the name of the pilot to whom it happened, as well as the year and month it occurred.* There is no doubt that the control of the rudder was rendered useless by this fish. For, as Linschoten says, the body of the fish was under the keel, but its head was under the rudder. From this, one can conclude how great the size and strength of this fish must have been—unless you wish to claim this fish was the *echeneis* <note>original: *echineum*. Known in English as the Remora or "suckerfish."</note>, called by the Greeks *from the holding of ships* <note>original: *ἀπὸ τοῦ ἔχειν τὰς ναῦς*</note>, or "ship-holders," because it stops or retains them. They also call it the *ship-ruler* <note>original: *ναυκράτης*, from *τὸ κρατεῖν τὴν ναῦν*, "the one who masters the ship"</note>, supposedly due to some hidden power. But it is not likely that this was an *echeneis*, because this fish is said to have *carried* the ship, and the ship did not merely stand still, but was driven backward for fourteen days. But whatever it may be, we gather from this without doubt <note>original: *ἀναμφιβόλως* (unambiguously)</note> that aquatic animals are far more wonderful than terrestrial ones, and that more and more marvelous traces of the power, wisdom, and goodness of God exist under the waters than among the animals of the land and air. Blessed Dilherr <note>Johann Michael Dilherr (1604–1669), a prominent German theologian and writer.</note> tells a story in the book titled *The Course of Time and the World*,

<margin>
p. 252.
</margin>
about a "man of the sea" or "water-man," who was captured in the Arctic sea by Danes sailing from Norway by means of a wide-brimmed hat <note>original: *petafone*</note>. After being brought onto the ship, he lay half-dead with great palpitations. While looking at him, certain noblemen praised and marveled at the admirable power of God and His stupendous variety in creating living things. To them, the man replied: "God is most wonderful, for He has far more marvelous creatures under the waters than on the land." So varied are the forms of fish and aquatic creatures, and so wonderful is their nature, that

one might not so much speak as stammer when describing it. This was not hidden from the pagans; indeed, they were seized with admiration for the Creator by the sight of so many and such varied species of animals. However, they did not follow this with the worship due to the Creator, but became worshippers of the creatures themselves, as the Teacher of the Gentiles, St. Paul, mentions of them in Romans 1:23. Among other animals, the Syrians and Egyptians—and following their example, the Lydians—attributed divine honor even to fish. Regarding the Syrians and Egyptians, Plutarch testifies that they abstained from eating fish due to a certain religious belief: *wherefore*, he says, *among the Egyptians, and not only the Syrians, but even among the Greeks, there was a part of holiness that involved abstaining from fish.* <note>original: *ὅθεν... ἡ παρ’ Αἰγυπτίοις μόνον, οὐδὲ Σύροις, ἀλλὰ καὶ παρ’ Ἕλλησι γέγονεν ἁγνείας μέρος ἀποχὴ ἰχθύων*</note>. Regarding the ancient Romans, whom they called the *Casci*, Ennius reports nearly the same (as attested by Varro in Book 6 of *On the Latin Language*): they abstained from fish because they appeased the goddess Carna, the protector of flesh and vitality, not with fish, but with bean mash and bacon. Ovid refers to this:

<margin>
Plutarch, *Symposiacs*, Book 8, question 8.
</margin>

<margin>

> *She is an ancient Goddess, nourished by the foods she used of old;*
> *She does not, in luxury, seek out foreign feasts.*
> *In those days, fish still swam safely for that people,*
> *And oysters were secure within their shells.*

Led by the authority and words of Plutarch, Vossius <note>Gerardus Vossius, a renowned 17th-century Dutch scholar.</note> denies that fish were actually worshipped among the Syrians and Egyptians, suggesting they were merely symbols of certain gods. But let the authority of Holy Scripture be greater for us, which testifies to this abominable *worship of beasts* <note>original: *θηριολατρείᾳ* (theriolatreia)</note>, a view supported by many pagan writers. For Xenophon, in Book 1 of the *Expedition of Cyrus*, testifies that the river Chalus was full of large, tame fish, *which the Syrians regarded as gods* <note>original: *οὓς οἱ Σύροι θεοὺς ἐνόμιζον*</note>; and he adds that they did not permit them to be harmed for that reason. Or, it was because Venus, fleeing from Typhon, transformed into a fish, about which Manilius writes in his *Astronomica*, Book 4:

> *Indeed, the Goddess of Cyprus <note>Venus</note> marked herself as a fish,*
> *When she fled into the Babylonian waves and was submerged,*
> *Escaping the raging Typhon, the serpent-footed one with winged shoulders,*
> *Hiding her fires from the underworld within scaly fish.*

Thus, for the slightest cause—or rather, a fable—the nations were once led into *superstition* <note>original: *δεισιδαιμονίαν* (deisidaimonia)</note> by the Devil. ->### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES<-

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...have been domesticated. Regarding these—such as chickens, geese, cows, sheep, pigs, and so on—we undertake no small amount of care, yet it is joined with great difficulty. Very often, to the great loss of our household management, we encounter unexpected accidents and diseases among so many eggs, chicks, lambs, and calves, from which they succumb and perish miserably. Such misfortunes in domestic affairs are so great that they exceed all our care, diligence, and prudence. However, concerning wild animals—namely birds of the forest and field, and fish—although they are deprived of these human aids, they nevertheless grow better and propagate better. They do not suffer nor experience such great diseases and plagues because their generation and birth are committed to God alone, without human assistance or ministry. Here, He has adorned fish, like other living things, with *sight*: for the eyes are the first things born in them, and the first to fail in them when they are dying. In the beginning, there is indeed little or no power of seeing in them, which nevertheless grows with age. Thus, if you except the shellfish, about which <margin>Book 9, ch. 30.</margin> Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist and author of the "Natural History."</note> *testifies: Shellfish lack sight and every other sense, except for food and danger*, all others enjoy sight, though it may be hard and dull. There are some among them that see sharply, and hence are called "sharp-eyed." They are endowed with excellent *hearing*; some fish are captured not only by hearing but even by harmony. Concerning the Dolphin, Pliny records in Book 9, ch. 8 of his *Natural History*: *The Dolphin is an animal not only friendly to man but also to the art of music; it is soothed by the singing of a symphony, and especially by the sound of the water-organ.* The same must be said of *taste*, which fish also enjoy; <note>original: "πολλὰ χαίρει χυμοῖς"</note> *they take delight in many peculiar flavors*, says Aristotle <margin>Book 4, *History of Animals*, ch. 8.</margin>. *The instrument of taste is the tongue, for without a tongue we are hardly said to taste. If fish lack a tongue, they would therefore lack taste, which is contrary to experience.* For we use the tongue not only to form voices, but also to taste and direct food in the mouth. Nevertheless, even if it has passed into a proverb, *more mute than a fish*, it is not permitted to conclude that they—since they are deprived of the benefit of a voice, have no necks, and do not have tongues as distinct as other living creatures—plainly lack a tongue with which to discern food, or to determine which kind of nourishment better suits their nature. Let us hear Aristotle on this matter in the book just cited: <note>original: "Ἐν δὲ τοῖς ἐνύδροις, καλευμένοις δὲ ἰχθύσι, τὸ μὲν τῶν χυμῶν αἰσθητήριον, πλὼ γλῶτταν ἔχουσι μὲν, ἔχουσι δὲ ἀμυδρῶς. Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ τὰ ἀπολελυμένως. Ἀλλ' ἐνίοις τῶν ἰχθύων ὁ οὐρανός ἐστι σαρκώδης, οἷον τῷ ποταμίων ἐν τοῖς κυπρίνοις. ὥστε τοῖς μὴ σκοπημένοις ἀκριβῶς, δοκεῖν ταύτην εἶναι γλῶτταν."</note> *But among the aquatic creatures called fish, as for the organ of tastes, they indeed have a tongue, but they have it obscurely and confusedly; for it is bony, not mobile, nor free. Indeed, in some of them, the palate is fleshy, such as in the river carp; so that those who do not look closely think it to be a tongue.* But in place of "those who do not look," Caesar Scaliger and Gaza <note>Famous Renaissance scholars and translators of Aristotle.</note> read "those who *do* look," so that Aristotle says the opposite about the carp: namely, that it has a tongue, even if it appears to be a palate. Vossius mentions in Book 4 of *Idolatry*, ch. 21, p. 1363, that certain vocal fish are found, such as the sea-ox, the dolphin, etc. (compare Pliny Book 9, ch. 8). Many of the Masters of Nature deny that fish smell and breathe, but from the

<column-break/>

side of those asserting it, the truth seems to us to stand more firmly, which Aristotle also asserts in *History of Animals, Book 4, ch. 18.* Indeed, experience also testifies that fish die in the winter in ponds covered with ice unless holes are opened through which the external air may work its way into the internal parts of the water. Finally, all are so endowed with touch that even those who seem to lack sight, hearing, and smell do not lack touch, as it is a sense simply necessary for life. No less is the sagacity and cleverness in aquatic creatures, if you look at some of the internal senses, than in the rest of the living beings; for the Parent of Nature, together with Nature as a kind mother, instilled in them the knowledge of protecting and defending themselves. Whence Ovid <margin>in the *Halieutics*.</margin>: <note>Ovid was a Roman poet; the "Halieutics" is a poem about fishing.</note>
> *Fear of death is unknown to all: to all is given*
> *To sense the enemy and the protection, and to know the weapons*
> *And the force and manner of their own being.*

To which Pliny adds in *Natural History*, Book 8, ch. 25: *All animals,* he says, *are clever in this; they know not only their own advantages but also the disadvantages of their enemies; they know their own weapons, they know their opportunities, and the weak parts of their opponents.* He continues: *The torpedo <note>The electric ray.</note> knows its own power, <margin>Book 9, ch. 42.</margin> though it is not torpid itself; submerged in the mud, it hides itself, seizing the fish that have crept up while swimming securely above.* No less is the cleverness of the frogfish, which in the sea is called the "fisher." *It thrusts out little horns from under its eyes in the stirred-up mud, attracting little jumping fish until they come so near that it may leap upon them. In a similar way, the monkfish and the turbot, though hidden, move their fins in the appearance of little worms; likewise the fish called the ray.* For the *stingray commits its robberies from hiding, piercing those passing by with its stinger (which is its weapon).* As evidence of this cleverness, the slowest of fish are found having the mullet—the swiftest of all—in their bellies; see Ursinus <note>Johann Heinrich Ursinus, a 17th-century scholar.</note> on the prudence of fish in *Analecta Polyhistorica, vol. 1, p. 172.* Added to these modes of cleverness and sagacity is the exterior armor, with which Mother Nature has abundantly provided them. Richly endowed nature armed them both on the head and on the rest of the body; some have sharp teeth, some have spines on the neck, and almost all have scales, except those of the cartilaginous kind, such as eels and large and small lizards. Concerning these weapons of fish, let us note the words of Pliny <margin>Book 9, ch. 11.</margin>: *The coverings of aquatic creatures are many. Some are covered with hide and hair, like calves and hippopotamuses. Others with hide only, like dolphins; with a shell, like tortoises; with the hardness of flint, like oysters and mussels; with crusts, like lobsters; with crusts and spines, like sea urchins; with scales, like fish; with a rough skin, like the monkfish, with which wood and ivory are polished; with a soft skin, like the moray; others with none at all, like the octopus.* From this distinction was taken the command in the divine law, Leviticus 11:8, concerning fish to be eaten and not to be eaten; namely, the eating of those that have scales and fins was permitted, but the rest, which had none, was forbidden and interdicted. The Blessed Luther <note>Martin Luther, the German Reformer.</note> explains this interdict of God mystically, saying: *By the fins, which are to fish in place of wings, with which they rule their course, is signified the doctrine of faith, which by the Word of God rules and drives hearts in this world. But the scales are like the armor and ornament of their bodies, without which the other swimming things are as if naked. They signify, however, that faith is not idle, but active through the Spirit of charity. If, therefore, there are any that are scaly without fins, they signify workers without faith and the Word, like serpents. If any have fins...*

<header>From Psalm 50, verses 10–11.</header>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...those that have fins but lack scales signify those people who possess the Word of God without fruit or good works, such as the eel, the lamprey, and so on. *Others that have neither fins nor scales represent those who are strong in neither faith nor works, such as worms and leeches.* It is not permitted to eat any of these, nor to have communion with them. No small proof of the strength of aquatic creatures is provided by animals of vast size which are found in the sea alongside tiny fish. Among four-legged animals, if you look at size, the Elephant excels; it is of such magnitude and strength that it can carry wooden towers filled with armed men. Yet, in comparison with a whale—which can take a whole man into its belly, as in the example of Jonah—the elephant is like a gnat. To this we may refer the account read in Jan Huygen van Linschoten’s <margin>Volume 1, Chapter 48, History of Voyages to the East Indies, page 71, Dutch Edition.</margin> *History of Voyages to the East Indies*: He says that a Portuguese ship sailing from Mozambique to the Indies, even while using a favorable wind, was nevertheless carried backward for fourteen days. This was noticed by those who observed the altitude of the sun daily. This matter, he says, made the pilot and the others traveling on that ship wonderfully anxious; they could imagine nothing else but that it was happening through the witchcraft of mages. At last, as he reports, a fish was found clinging around the ship; everyone therefore labored and sweated to drive it off with poles and other instruments. Yet it did not leave the ship until its tail was first cut off, after which the ship successfully completed the rest of its course. They gathered, therefore, that the ship had been carried on the back of the fish, and because the fish was swimming in the opposite direction, the ship was driven backward for two weeks. The Viceroy of India ordered this event to be painted in his palace for eternal memory, with the name of the pilot to whom it happened inscribed, as well as the year and the month in which it occurred. There is no doubt that the control of the rudder was rendered useless by this fish. For, as Linschoten says, the body of the fish was under the keel, but its head was under the rudder. From this it can be concluded how great the size and strength of this fish must have been—unless you wish to maintain that this fish was the *echineis*, called by the Greeks <gloss>from "holding the ships"</gloss> <note>original: "apo to echein tas naus"</note>, because it stops or retains ships; they also call it <gloss>the ship-master</gloss> <note>original: "naukraten"</note>, <gloss>from "mastering the ship"</gloss> <note>original: "to kratein ten naun"</note>, because it detains the ship, and that by some hidden power. But it is not likely to have been the *echineis* <note>The Remora, a small fish traditionally believed to be able to stop giant ships by clinging to them.</note>, because this fish is said to have carried the ship, and the ship did not just stand still, but was carried backward for fourteen days. But whatever it was, we conclude <gloss>unambiguously</gloss> from this that aquatic animals are far more wonderful than terrestrial ones, and that more and more marvelous traces of the power, wisdom, and goodness of God exist under the waters than among the animals of the land and air. Blessed Dilherr <note>Johannes Michael Dilherr (1604–1669), a German theologian and scholar.</note> tells a story in his book titled *The Course of Time and the World*, <margin>page 252.</margin> concerning a "man of the sea" or "water-man," as they call it. This creature was captured in the Arctic Sea by Danes sailing from Norway using a net; after being brought onto the ship, it lay half-dead with great palpitations. While some of the nobles looking at it praised and marveled at the admirable power of God and His astounding variety in creating living things, the creature responded to them: "God is most wonderful, for He has far more marvelous living things under the waters than on the land." So varied are the forms of fish and aquatic creatures, and so wonderful is their nature, that

<column-break/>

one might say we can only stammer, not truly speak, about it. Nor was this hidden from the pagans, but while they were seized with admiration for the Creator by the sight of <margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> so many and such various species of living things, they did not follow this with the proper worship of the Creator. Instead, they became worshippers of the creatures, as the Teacher of the Gentiles, Saint Paul, mentions concerning them in Romans 1:23. Among other living things, the Syrians and Egyptians attributed divine honor even to fish, and the Lydians followed their example. Plutarch <margin>* Book 8, Table Talk, question 8.</margin> testifies of the Syrians and Egyptians that they abstained from eating fish out of a certain religious duty: <gloss>whence,</gloss> he says, <gloss>not only among the Egyptians and Syrians, but even among the Greeks, the avoidance of fish became a part of religious purity.</gloss> Concerning the ancient Romans, whom they called the "Cheesemen" <note>An archaic term for the early Romans, possibly referring to their simple diet.</note>, Ennius records nearly the same thing (witnessed by Varro in Book 6 of *On the Latin Language*): they abstained from fish because they appeased the Goddess Carna, the protector of flesh and vital organs, not with fish, but with bean porridge and lard. Ovid refers to this in <margin>Book 6 of the *Fasti*.</margin>
> She is an ancient Goddess, and is nourished by the foods she used before:
> Nor does she seek out luxurious feasts.
> In that age, the fish still swam without fear of the people,
> And oysters were safe within their shells.
Led by the authority and words of Plutarch, Vossius <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch classical scholar.</note> denies that fish were worshipped among the Syrians and Egyptians, but were at least symbols of certain gods. But let the authority of Holy Scripture be greater for us, testifying of the abominable <gloss>worship of beasts</gloss> <note>original: "theriolatreia"</note>, with which many writers of the pagans also agree. For Xenophon testifies in Book 1 of the *Expedition of Cyrus* that the river Chalus was full of large, tame fish, <gloss>which the Syrians considered to be gods</gloss>; and he adds that for this reason they did not permit them to be harmed. To this also belongs the fable of Hyginus in entry 169 concerning Venus: <gloss>On account of this, the Syrians hold fish and doves among the number of the gods.</gloss> They pass down this reason for the worship of fish among the Syrians: that long ago, fish saved Derceto (whom they also call Dercen and Atergatis), the daughter of Venus, from the harm of the waters when she fell into the sea, as Theon writes on Aratus; or perhaps it was because of the metamorphosis of Venus into a fish while fleeing Typhon, about which Manilius writes in *Astronomica*, Book 6:
> Indeed, Cytherea [Venus] marked herself as a fish,
> When she fled into the Babylonian waves to escape
> The raging Typhon with his winged shoulders and snake-feet,
> And hid her own fires within the scaly fish.

### SACRED BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...those that are domesticated. Of these—such as chickens, geese, cows, sheep, pigs, and so on—we undertake a care that is not light, but rather joined with great difficulty. Indeed, very often to the great loss of our household management, we encounter unexpected accidents and diseases among so many eggs, chicks, lambs, and calves, from which they succumb and miserably perish. Such evils in domestic affairs often exceed all our care, diligence, and wisdom. However, concerning wild creatures—namely wild and field birds, and fish—even though they lack these human aids, they nevertheless increase and propagate better. They do not suffer or experience such great diseases and plagues because their generation and birth are committed to God alone, without human assistance or service. Here, God has adorned the fish, like other living things, with *sight*: for the eyes are the first things born in them, and the first to fail in them when they are dying. At the beginning, their power of sight is indeed small or almost nonexistent, yet it grows with age. Thus, although Pliny <margin>Book 9, Chapter 30.</margin> testifies: <note>original: "Carere conchas visu..."</note> *That shells lack sight and every other sense except for food and danger; yet all others enjoy sight*, though it may be hard and dull, there are some among them who see sharply, and are thus called "keen-eyed." They are endowed with excellent hearing; not only by hearing, but some fish are even captivated by harmony. Concerning the Dolphin, Pliny relates <margin>History of Nature, Book 9, Chapter 8.</margin> *that the Dolphin is a creature friendly not only to man, but also to the art of music, soothed by the symphony of song, and especially by the sound of the water-organ.* The same must be said of taste, which fish also enjoy; <note>original: "ἰδίοις πολλὰ χαίρει χυμοῖς"</note> *they take much pleasure in their own peculiar flavors*, as Aristotle says <margin>History of Animals, Book 4, Chapter 8.</margin>. The instrument of taste is the tongue, for without a tongue we are hardly said to taste. Therefore, if fish lack tongues, they would also lack taste, which is contrary to experience. For we use the tongue not only to form voices, but also to taste and direct food in the mouth. However, even if it has passed into a proverb, *more silent than a fish*, it is not permitted to conclude that because they lack the benefit of a voice, and have neither necks nor tongues as distinct as other animals, they entirely lack a tongue with which to discern food and what kind of nourishment best suits their nature. Let us hear Aristotle on this matter in the book just cited: <note>original: "Ἐν δὲ τοῖς ἐνύδροις..."</note> *Among aquatic animals, which are called fish, the organ of taste is indeed around the tongue, but they have it indistinctly. For it is bony and not free or loose. Indeed, in some fish the palate is fleshy, such as in the river carp; so that those who do not look closely might think this is a tongue.* But in place of "those who do not look," Caesar Scaliger and Gaza read "those who do look," so that Aristotle says the opposite about the carp—namely, that it has a tongue, even if it seems to be a palate. Vossius mentions <margin>On Idolatry, Book 4, Chapter 21, page 1363.</margin> that certain "vocal" fish are found, such as the sea-ox, the dolphin, etc.; compare Pliny <margin>Book 9, Chapter 8.</margin>. Many of the Masters of Nature deny that fish smell or breathe, but on the 

<column-break/>

side of those asserting it, the truth seems to us to stand more firmly, which Aristotle also asserts <margin>History of Animals, Book 4, Chapter 18.</margin>. Indeed, experience testifies that fish die in the winter in ponds covered with ice unless holes are opened through which the external air may work its way into the internal parts of the waters. Finally, all are so endowed with touch that even those who seem to lack sight, hearing, and smell do not lack touch, as it is a sense simply necessary for life. No less is the wisdom and cleverness in aquatic creatures, if you look at certain of their internal senses, than in other living beings; for Mother Nature, along with her Kind Mother Nature, has instilled in them the knowledge of guarding and defending themselves. Hence Ovid <margin>in the Halieutica (On Fishing).</margin> writes:

> *To all, death is an unknown fear: to all is given*
> *To sense the enemy and the protection, and to know the weapons*
> *And the force and limit of one’s own self.*

To which Pliny adds <margin>History of Nature, Book 8, Chapter 25.</margin>: *In this,* he says, *all animals are clever, and they know not only their own advantages but also the disadvantages of their enemies: they know their own weapons, they know their opportunities, and the weak parts of their opponents.* He continues: *The torpedo fish knows its own power, <margin>Book 9, Chapter 42.</margin> though it is not numb itself: hiding itself submerged in the mud, it seizes the fish which, swimming above carelessly, it has numbed.* Nor is the cleverness of the frog less, which in the sea is called the "fisher-frog" <note>likely the anglerfish</note>. It thrusts out little horns situated under its eyes in the stirred-up mud, attracting small fish that jump at them, until they come so near that it can leap upon them. In a similar way, the angel-shark and the turbot, having hidden themselves, stick out their fins with the appearance of little worms; likewise that which is called the ray. For the stingray <term>pastinaca: a venomous stingray</term> hunts from a hidden place, piercing those passing by with its stinger (which is its weapon). Proofs of this cleverness include the fact that the slowest of fish are found with the mullet—the fastest of all—in their bellies; see Ursinus <margin>Analects, Volume 1, page 172.</margin> concerning the prudence of fish. Added to these modes of cleverness and sagacity is their external armor, for which Mother Nature has largely provided. Rich nature has armed them both on the head and on the rest of the body; some have sharp teeth, some have stingers in their flesh, and almost all have scales, except for those of the cartilaginous kind, such as the eel and large and small lizards <note>likely referring to certain sharks or smooth-skinned fish</note>. Concerning these arms of fish, let us note the words of Pliny <margin>Book 9, Chapter 11.</margin>: *The coverings of aquatic creatures are many. Some are covered with hide and hair, such as seals and hippopotamuses. Others with hide only, like dolphins; with a shell, like tortoises; with the hardness of flint, like oysters and mussels; with crusts, like the lobster; with crusts and spines, like sea urchins; with scales, like fish; with a rough skin, like the angel-shark, with which wood and ivory are polished; with a soft skin, like the moray eel; and others with none at all, like the octopus.* From this distinction was taken the command in the Divine law, Leviticus 11:8, concerning the eating and not eating of fish; namely, the eating of those that have scales and fins was permitted, but of the others that had none, it was illicit and forbidden. Blessed Luther explains this interdict of God mystically, saying: *By the fins, which are for fish in place of wings, with which they steer their course, is signified the doctrine of faith, which by the Word of God rules and moves hearts in this world. Scales, however, are like the weapons and ornament of their body, without which other swimming things are as if naked. They signify that faith is not idle, but active through the Spirit of charity. If, therefore, there are any with scales but without fins, they signify workers without faith and the Word, like serpents. If any have fins...*

#### From Psalm 55:10, 11

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
Those that have no fins and are without scales signify those who have the Word without fruit or works, such as the eel, the moray, and so on. Others, having neither fins nor scales, represent those who are strong in neither faith nor works, such as worms and leeches. It is not permitted to eat any of these, nor to have communion with them. Animals of vast magnitude, which are found in the sea alongside small fish, provide no small proof of the strength of aquatic creatures. Among quadrupeds, if you look at size, the Elephant excels; it is of such size and strength that it carries wooden towers with so many armed men. Yet, in comparison with a whale, it hardly equals a gnat. The whale can receive an entire man in its belly, as seen in the example of Jonah. To this, one might add what is read in Jan Huygen van Linschoten’s <note>Jan Huygen van Linschoten (1563–1611) was a Dutch voyager whose writings provided Europeans with vital information about the East Indies.</note> *History of Indian Navigations*: * He says that a Portuguese <margin>* Tome 1, chapter 48, page 71. Dutch Edition.</margin> ship sailing from Mozambique to the Indies, even while using a favorable wind, was nevertheless carried backward for fourteen days. This was noticed by those who observed the height of the Sun daily. This matter, he says, made both the pilot and the others sailing on that ship remarkably anxious; they could not bring anything else to mind except that it was happening through the witchcraft of mages. Finally, as he reports, a fish was found wrapped around the ship. Everyone labored with great effort to push it away with a pole and other instruments. However, it did not leave the ship until its tail was first cut off; after that, the ship successfully completed the rest of its course. They concluded, therefore, that the ship had been carried on the back of the fish, and because it was swimming in the opposite direction, the ship was driven backward for two weeks. For the sake of eternal memory, the Viceroy of India ordered this event to be painted in his Palace, inscribed with the name of the pilot to whom it happened, as well as the year and month in which it occurred. There is no doubt, moreover, that the control of the rudder was rendered useless by this fish. For, as Linschoten says, the body of the fish was under the keel, but its head was under the rudder. From this, one can conclude how great the size and strength of this fish must have been—unless you wish to maintain that this was a <term>remora</term> <note>original: "echineum"</note>, called by the Greeks <term>from the holding of ships</term> <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἔχειν τὰς ναῦς"</note>, or by the name <term>ship-master</term> <note>original: "ναυκράτην"</note>, <term>because it detains the ship</term> <note>original: "τὸ κρατεῖν τὴν ναῦν"</note>; and this by some hidden power. But it is not likely that it was a <term>remora</term> <note>original: "ἐχενηίδα"</note>, because this fish is said to have *carried* the ship, and furthermore, the ship did not just stand still, but was carried backward for fourteen days. But whatever the case may be, we gather from this <term>without a doubt</term> <note>original: "ἀναμφιβόλως"</note> that aquatic animals are far more wondrous than terrestrial ones, and that more and more marvelous traces of the power, wisdom, and goodness of God exist under the waters than among terrestrial and aerial animals. Blessed Dilherr <note>Johann Michael Dilherr (1604–1669), a prominent German theologian and scholar.</note> tells a story in the book titled *The Course of Time and the World* <margin>p. 252.</margin> about a "sea-man" or "water-man" as they call it. This creature, using a wide-brimmed hat <note>The Latin "petasone" suggests a hat-like structure or perhaps a biological feature resembling one.</note>, was captured in the Arctic Sea by Danes sailing from Norway and brought onto the ship. After much palpitating, it lay half-dead. Some of the nobles looking at it commended and marveled at the admirable power of God and His stupendous variety in creating living things. To them, he responded: "God is most wonderful, for He has far more marvelous creatures under the waters than on the land." So varied are the forms of fish and aquatic creatures, and so wonderful is their nature, that

<column-break/>

one may not so much speak as stammer about it. This was not hidden from the Gentiles, but they were indeed seized with admiration for the Creator upon beholding so many and such varied species of living things; <margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> however, they did not follow this with the worship due to the Creator. Instead, they became worshippers of the creatures, as the Teacher of the Gentiles, Saint Paul, mentions regarding them in Romans 1:23. Among other living things, the Syrians and Egyptians also attributed divine honor to fish, and the Lydians followed their examples. Regarding the Syrians and Egyptians, Plutarch * testifies <margin>* Book 8, Symposiacs, question 8.</margin> that they abstained from eating fish out of a certain religious scruple: <term>Whence</term>, he says, <term>the abstinence from fish became a part of holiness not only among the Egyptians and Syrians, but also among the Greeks</term> <note>original: "ὅθεν... ἡ παρ' Αἰγυπτίοις μόνον, οὐδὲ Σύροις, ἀλλὰ καὶ παρ' Ἕλλησι γέγονεν ἁγνείας μέρος ἡ ἀποχὴ ἰχθύων"</note>.
