But truly, let the authority of Holy Scripture be greater for us, testifying to the abominable <term>worship of beasts</term> <note>original: "θηριολατρείᾳ"</note>, with which many of the Gentile writers also agree. For regarding the Syrians, Xenophon testifies in Book 1 of the *Expedition of Cyrus* that the river Chalos was full of large, tame fish, <term>which the Syrians considered to be gods</term> <note>original: "οὓς οἱ Σύροι θεοὺς ἐνόμιζον"</note>; and he adds that for this reason, they did not permit them to be harmed. To this also belongs the fable of Hyginus in entry 169 concerning Venus: *For this reason, the Syrians count fish and doves among the number of the Gods.* They report that this was the cause for the worship of fish among the Syrians: that long ago, fish saved Derceto (whom they also call Dercetan and Atergatis), the daughter of Venus, from the harm of the waters when she fell into the sea, as Theon writes on Aratus. Thus, from a very trivial cause—or rather a fable—the Gentiles were once led by the Devil into <term>superstition</term> <note>original: "δεισιδαιμονίαν"</note>. Regarding the worship of the Lydians, which they are said to have exhibited toward fish, we cite that passage from Varro, book 3 of *On Agriculture*, the last chapter. *Thus these men*, he says, *have partitioned fishponds, where they keep different species of fish separated, which they treat as if they were sacred and even holier than those in Lydia, about which you, Varro, used to say that when you were sacrificing, they came in a swarm to the edge of the shore and the altar at the sound of a Greek flute-player, because no one dared to catch them.* Many authors discuss this <term>fish-worship</term> <note>original: ἰχθυολατρείᾳ (ichthyolatria)</note> at greater length: Nonnus in *Dietetics*, book 3, chapter 2, page 285 and following; Selden in *Syntagma 2 on the Syrian Gods*, chapter 3; and Vossius in book 4 of *Idolatry*, chapter 51, page 1474 and following.

These generalities having been premised, we must descend to the special treatment of fish or aquatic creatures—those, I say, whose nomenclature and mention we find expressly in the Holy Scripture, where the first to present itself is:

<margin>Book 1, Part 2, chapter 36.</margin>
THE WHALE or SEA MONSTER. From the Greek <term>phalana</term> <note>original: φάλανα</note> comes the Latin *balæna* [whale], although there are those who prefer to call it <term>phallaina</term> <note>original: φάλλαινα</note>; they prove from Pliny that the *phalæna* is a small creature flying toward lamps, which is called *pyrausta*, *pyralis*, and *psora*, and originates <term>from leaping into the light</term> <note>original: ἀπὸ τὸ εἰς φῶς ἅλλεσθαι</note>, because it leaps as if toward the flame. We will start no dispute over the word. The Greek term is derived from the Hebrew <term>to swallow</term> <note>original: בָּלַע (bala)</note>, meaning he devoured, absorbed, or gulped down: for it swallows a man whole. Among the Hebrews, and especially in the Holy Scripture, two names are read by which this oversized aquatic animal is designated: For those which the Septuagint calls *cetos* [sea monsters] or *dracones* [dragons], the Hebrew Codices name <term>Tanninim</term> <note>original: תַּנִּינִם</note>. This word signifies not only fish, but also serpents, especially the larger ones which we call dragons. Just as terrestrial serpents that exceed common size are usually called dragons, so the larger or greatest fish in the Holy Tongue are called dragons; for example, Psalm 148:7: *Praise the Dragons (that is, whales) and all deeps, the Lord.* Then they are distinguished by yet another name, by which their magnitude is specifically hinted at, namely <term>Leviathan</term> <note>original: לִוְיָתָן</note>, which descends from the root <term>to join/increase</term> <note>original: לָוָה (lavah)</note>, whose meanings among others are to heap up, take on, increase, or add. We, following in the footsteps of the Vulgate Edition, will deal distinctly with the whale, the sea dragon, and the Leviathan. In the book of Creation it is said that God created the <term>Tanninim</term>, which

<margin>Genesis 1:21.</margin>

<column-break/>

the Greeks translate as <term>the sea monsters</term> <note>original: τὰ κήτη (ta kētē)</note>. Luther, in his commentary on Genesis, page 21, gives the reason why only these are mentioned there: <margin>History of animals.</margin> *So that we might know that such great bodies are the works of God, and that we, terrified by their magnitude, might not believe them to be ghosts; rather, from the creation of those great whales, we should infer that even the smaller fish were created by God.* No creature is of such power and such vastness as the whale; for the things reported by writers concerning the size of whales find almost no belief among those who have not gone to sea. For whales, as Basil and Theodoret say, when they raise their backs above the water, present the appearance of a huge island. And Pliny writes: *Whales of the Indian sea are four jugera in size; sawfish are two hundred cubits; while eels in the Ganges are three hundred feet long.* He continues in book 32, chapter 1, and reports concerning King Juba of Mauritania, who had written in his volumes to Gaius Caesar, son of Augustus, that sea monsters of six hundred feet in length and three hundred and sixty in width enter the Arabian river. There exists a letter concerning a certain whale sent to Polydore Vergil, in which it is narrated that in the year of Christ 1532, a certain whale was cast up by the sea waves near the shore, such that some part appeared outside the water, but the other part lay hidden within. And although it had been torn apart and devoured by cattle and for the most part, yet such a residue remained as a hundred huge wagons could scarcely carry. Furthermore, in length that whale had 30 ells or 90 feet; from the belly to the spine were 9 ells; the gape of the mouth encompassed six ells and a half; the jawbone was seven ells and a half; it had thirty ribs in its sides, each of which was twenty-one feet long and contained one foot and a half in circumference. Its bellies were like vast caves; it had two fins, each fifteen feet in length, and ten oxen could scarcely pull one out of the body. The length of the head from the beginning to the gape of the mouth encompassed 7 ells; similarly the tongue was 7 ells in length but 20 feet in width; the male genital was of prodigious size; the space between the eyes was 6 ells; the tail was forked and saw-edged, and in width it had 7 ells. Lyranus and Dionysius the Carthusian, on chapter 41 of Job, narrate that the tongue of a certain whale divided into pieces made the weight of 24 mules, and Francisco Mendoza examines the weight in his *Viridarium*, book 1, 81, page 229. Let him who wishes believe that they are of stupendous magnitude and so great that they almost exceed belief—so great, indeed, that they even represent a huge island. Olaus Magnus reports in *Northern Matters*, book 21, chapter 10, that larger ones than all others are found in the Arctic Sea. Torquemada in his *Hexameron*, page 597, notes that it is established from the Frankfurt Report of that year that a whale was caught in the year 1598 in the territory of Narbonne, which they commonly call "Provence," three hundred and twenty feet long and one hundred and sixty-two wide; moreover, with a throat consisting of a forty-five foot gap, so that a horseman sitting on a horse could have been hidden in its mouth. There are, however, various species of whale: the <term>physeter</term> [blower], <term>orca</term>, <term>pristes</term> [sawfish], <term>thynnus</term> [tunny], etc. The first takes its name from <term>blowing</term> <note>original: φυσᾶν (physan)</note>; the next from <term>rushing</term> <note>original: θύειν (thyein)</note> or from inflating; this one either from its impetus—for <term>to rush</term> <note>original: θύειν</note> has the same force as <term>to move violently</term> <note>original: ὁρμᾷν (horman)</note>—or its name is from the Hebrew <term>Tan</term> <note>original: תַּן</note>.

<header>from Psalm 55 verses 10, 11</header>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
Regarding the sea monster that swallowed Jonah, people ask more out of curiosity than for any practical benefit: what kind of creature was it? Holy Scripture adheres strictly and simply to the name *dag gadol* <note>Hebrew: "great fish"</note>, which the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> and Christ himself in Matthew 12:40 call *to ketos* <note>Greek: "the whale" or "sea monster"</note>. The Rabbis tell trifles about this, claiming that a male fish first received Jonah when he was thrown from the ship. They say that while he was in its belly, there was so much room that he did not yet feel driven to pray to God. Therefore, Jehovah supposedly commanded this male fish to vomit Jonah into the mouth of a female fish, which was full of offspring; thus, finding himself in narrow straits, the Prophet was forced to call upon God from his distress. But these are old wives' tales. For although in chapter 2, verse 1, Jonah is said to have been in the belly of a *dag* <note>Hebrew: masculine "fish"</note>, and later in verse 2 he is read at last to have prayed in the belly of a *dagah* <note>Hebrew: feminine "fish"</note>, this does not prove what these deceivers intend. As the commentators commonly teach, the names of animals, wild beasts, fish, and worms—of whatever gender they may be, whether masculine or feminine—often encompass both sexes under a single grammatical ending.

Similar to this fiction is another from Rabbi Bechai regarding the first creation of whales, when he fables: *Two whales were created by the Lord, a male and a female. Lest they should breed a numerous offspring by which the whole world would be devastated, the providence of God did not wish them to live together. Therefore, having taken away the strength of the sea, he named the male Leviathan; but his mate was slaughtered and preserved in salt for the banquet with which the righteous are to be cheered at the final resurrection. Consequently, the concluding phrase, "And it was so," which would signify they were established as they are now, was omitted, because the female whale did not survive.*

That the fish which swallowed Jonah was a whale is beyond doubt, hence Jerome states: <margin>on Jonah 2, p. 127.</margin> *In the Hebrew we read "great fish," for which the Septuagint translators and the Lord in the Gospel use the word "Whale," explaining the matter more briefly. For in Hebrew it is called "dag gadol," which translates as "great fish," which undoubtedly signifies a whale.* 

This opinion regarding the whale specifically so-called does not please Rondelet or Ulisse Aldrovandi <note>Famous 16th-century naturalists</note>, nor after them Pineda and à Castro, because of the narrowness of the throat and stomach. In their view, a whale could neither swallow a whole man nor contain him within itself. Therefore, they wish it to have been a *Cacharia* <note>Likely a Great White Shark or "Man-eater"</note>, also from the genus of cetaceans, which they also call a *lamia*. Homer also joined the "dog" <note>often used for sharks</note> with the Dolphin in *Odyssey* book 12, line 96:

> Both dolphins and sea-dogs.
> *Delphinasque canesque.* <note>original: Δελφῖνάς τε κύνας τε</note>

But it suffices for us that this fish was of the cetacean genus, and there is no need to know which specific species it was, as we read the common or general term used in the Holy Book. This term, as Aristotle records, includes that class of aquatic animals which brings forth live young rather than eggs, as witnessed by Aristotle in book 3, chapter 20 and book 6, chapter 11. With a wide-open maw, the whale swallowed Jonah, who had been given as prey, and in which he lay hidden for a three-day space. Certainly, this was a "living tomb" for Jonah, or a *taphos empsychos* <note>Greek: "living tomb"</note>, as Basil of Seleucia names it with the elegance of speech in which he excels in *Oration 1 on Jonah, p. 104*: *The sea,* he says, *carried him immediately in a living tomb, a swimming house-prison, lying in a chasm, living in a place of death, a hostel of the dead, not of the living, dwelling in a belly, the mother of death.* He elegantly calls the belly of the

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
whale a living tomb, a swimming prison, the womb of death, and a lodging for the dead. In this "hostel of the dead," Jonah stayed for three days; but since he was not suitable food for the stomach, the fish, moved by divine power, returned the swallowed prey. Jonah was struck with awe, not knowing how he had lived under the belly of the whale. Having emerged, he preached in Nineveh, and the Ninevites, led by penitence, were converted to God, who took pity on them. 

One must not venture into the vast sea of allegories which diligent and pious antiquity has collected from this whole history. The most important of them is the one we see rooted in the Holy Book itself, where Christ <margin>Matthew 12:40</margin> compares Jonah's three-day concealment in the belly of the whale with his own three-day burial. Regarding this, Ratbertus says in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 16: *Jonah was thrown into the sea amid raging winds, and was devoured by a whale or beast, and after three days was sent forth alive from the abyss and the belly of the beast. He was not retained by the whale, nor consumed in the abyss, nor digested by the conditions of food in the belly; but contrary to the nature of a human body, he escaped whole and unharmed into the upper air after three days, by the power of the Lord's prefiguration.*

The capture of whales is a marvelous thing. When signals are given by trumpet, as if for the storming of a city, all the subjects run together from every side to capture the whale. The whole region assembles for joy, as if drawn up for war with all kinds of military instruments: mattocks, forks, two-pronged hoes, cannons, anchors, spears, etc. Initially, the whale is provoked toward the shore, which it does with great force, and it rushes to those places that are not deep enough, and so it gets stuck and cannot swim away. Seeing this, the whale is dispatched with arrows and bullets until it dies. Then they approach with ships and, as if from the tallest great trees, they cut out many pieces of wood <note>referring to the massive bones or blubber</note>. There are also other stratagems which the Dutch and others practice today in capturing smaller ones around Greenland, about which others have written. 

Furthermore, these beasts grow so fat that eventually they can no longer see or hear. For then they are slow of movement and dull of sight. Their mouth is placed a little lower down, with which they snatch smaller fish. Regarding the whale's spines, with which the top of the back is rough and scabby, Dionysius says in his writing *On the Situation of the World*:

> and above the heights of the back
> a long ridge of spines is rough.
> <note>original Greek: τῶν δ᾽ ὑπὲρ ἄκρων / Τέτρηχεν νώτων ἐπιμήκετος ὁλκὸς ἀκάνθης.</note>

That is, *the ridge of spines which is roughened in length over the top of the back.* For the spines in such animals are quite horrific and rough to the sight. And its bones are of such great size and length that among the Fish-eaters <note>the Ichthyophagi</note>, situated between the Carmani and the Oritae, of whom Strabo speaks in book 15, they are used in constructing buildings. Pliny reports regarding the Arabs: <margin>book 9, Natural History, ch. 3.</margin> *They make roofs from the jaws of the beasts and seal them with bones; many of which have been found forty cubits in length.* 

Among the cetaceans is placed the Dolphin, which holds the first place among sea beasts for many virtues. It is commended for its speed, which is so great that no fish can escape it; yet this is very often its undoing. For as often as it pursues fish faster than is right, when it cannot stop its momentum, it hurls itself onto the shore, where its life leaves it along with the water on the third day, or even...

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
#### o.
<meta>catchword: Con,</meta>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
Regarding its speed and agility, let us hear from Pliny in his *Natural History, book 9, chapter 8*: *The dolphin is the swiftest of all animals, not just those in the sea; it is swifter than a bird and swifter than a dart. Indeed, were it not for the fact that its mouth is located far below its snout, almost in the middle of its belly, no fish could escape its speed. But the providence of Nature provides a delay, because they cannot seize their prey unless they are turned over on their backs.* He adds to this and proceeds in his description of the dolphin thus: *This is the primary reason that demonstrates their speed: when driven by hunger, they pursue a fish fleeing into the deepest depths and hold their breath for a long time; then, like an arrow shot from a bow, they spring up to breathe, leaping with such force that they frequently fly over the sails of ships.* Aristotle <note>History of Animals, book 9, chapter 16</note> and Solinus record the same thing about it: *Above all, the seas have nothing swifter, as they often leap over the sails of ships.* They say the dolphin lacks gall <note>original: "felle," referring to bile</note>, which is why it cannot be vehemently angry, or rather, its anger lasts only briefly while it glows with heat.

<margin>chapter 22.</margin>
It displays no small signs of love and gentleness, as witnessed by various writers. There is the famous story of Arion of Methymna, a player of the lyre <note>original: "Citharoedo"</note>, traveling from Tarentum to Corinth; a dolphin, said to be most devoted to music, is reported to have carried him across the sea to his homeland. And Aelian <note>History of Animals, book 6, chapter 15</note> tells of a certain boy whom a dolphin loved so much that when called, it would swim closer from the sea and allow the boy to ride upon its back. Indeed, the dolphin even observed the time when boys are usually dismissed from school, for at that time it would come closer to the shores. Because of this, some do not just claim that dolphins have voices, but even assert that they understand human speech and take delight in the name *Simon* <note>original: "Simonis," a common nickname for dolphins in antiquity</note>, a name given to them because of their "simian" or snub-noses <note>Latin: "simis" means flat or snub-nosed</note>. Pliny was of this opinion in 
<margin>book 9, chapter 8.</margin>
his writing: *Their back,* he says, *is curved, and their snout is snub-nosed.* For this reason, all dolphins recognize the name *Simon* in a wonderful way and prefer to be called by it. To this, Cardanus adds <note>On the Variety of Things, book 7, chapter 37, page 293</note>, whose words we cite in full: *Dolphins,* he says, *rejoice in the customary name of Simon, because the traces of custom, like a shape in wax, cling to animals. Thus, pigeons in certain islands of the New World used to be caught by hand, but now they are not; for through a long series of generations, they learned to flee from men. And my little dog, born of a father and mother accustomed to carrying things, learned to carry stones and iron in eight days; a wondrous thing, since you can hardly teach a dog of two months such logic, even with great labor. Nay, quite untaught, she carried it of her own accord, though she did not bring it back. Thus, the earlier dolphins, accustomed to being called by this name, left a trace in their descendants, so that even now they rejoice in this name.* But the most judicious Scaliger judges this matter quite differently and more accurately <note>Commentary on Aristotle's History of Animals, book 2, chapter 16, section 118</note>, saying: *Many things are told about dolphins that exceed our belief; we consider it ridiculous that the name Simon is pleasing to them because they are snub-nosed, so that even here Greece might not be without a lie.* Aelian <note>book 2, chapters 6 and 8</note> lists even more examples of the dolphin's gentleness, which may be read there. They are accustomed to come out to meet ships, playing together with exultation as if competing, and by their speed, they outrun even full sails. Ovid <note>original: "Naso," the cognomen of the poet Ovid</note> seems to hint at this:

> On every side they leap, and spray much brine,
> They emerge again, and return once more beneath the waves,

<column-break/>

> And playing in the form of a dance, they toss their
> Playful bodies, and blow out the sea from wide nostrils.

<margin>History of animals, book 18, chapter...</margin>
They are said to foretell storms at sea; hence, as Pliny records, when dolphins play in a calm sea, they predict winds coming from that direction; likewise, if they spray water in a stormy sea, they predict calm. Virgil says the same of Proteus in the *Georgics, book 4*:

> — around him the watery race of the vast Deep
> Leaping, scatters the bitter spray far and wide.

So also Seneca in *Agamemnon, Act 3, line 445*, regarding the play of fish in general:

> Then he who plays in the ebbing tide while the sea lies still,
> And leaps over the swelling sea with a curved back,
> The Tyrrhenian fish exults in every strait,
> And moves in circles, etc.

Thus they play when, after storms and tempests, the sea stands calm again, while <term>leaping over the sea</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπὲρ ἀλακαυχάοντες (hyper alakauchaontes), meaning to boast or exult over the sea</note>, as Oppian says <note>Halieutica, book 1, lines 460 and following</note>, they spring out and frolic as if in dances. While we are speaking of the play of aquatic creatures and their dancing, that passage from the Psalmist <note>Psalm 104:26</note> may be rightly applied here: *That dragon—in Hebrew it is Leviathan, that is, a whale or sea monster—which you have made to play in it.* Luther translates this: *There are whales, which you have made, so that they may frolic therein.* In the Hebrew text is the word <term>sachaq</term> <note>Hebrew: שׂחק</note>, which means to frolic, to be playful, to frisk like a calf, to play, or to exult. Besides this meaning, it also denotes laughing, mocking, or deriding, from which many explain it as "to mock him." In this sense, commentators say that "play" is attributed to the whale for this reason: because it rules the sea with its immense strength, so that for it, it is mere play to hunt and capture any living creature, to overturn ships, and to crush all the power of both men and beasts. The play of whales is tyrannical; as Jansenius says regarding this passage, it is mere sport; indeed, they even overturn vessels and sink them when they spout out a deluge of water. For this reason, the Indians hang large bells on the prow and stern of their ships, so that they may terrify the beasts with the sound, if one believes Philostratus in the *Life of Apollonius*. For Pliny says otherwise <note>book 9, chapter 3</note>: they are not terrified by voice, nor sound, nor blow, but by a great crashing noise, and are not disturbed except by a ruinous fall. The Church Fathers commonly focus on the latter meaning of the word <term>sachaq</term> <note>to mock</note>. For thus Augustine says: *Did He deliver him up to be mocked? That is, so that he might be made a laughingstock. We might think that God was mocking him, had not the Scripture in Job resolved the question; for there it is said, "to be mocked by my angels." Do you wish to mock the Dragon? Be an angel of God. But you are not yet an angel of God until you are such; if you hold to that course so that you may be, there are angels who mock the Dragon, so that he may not harm you.* For the Angels of the heavens are placed over the powers of the air. Jerome applies this to the Devil, who mocks men while he turns them away from God and casts them into the nets of crimes and outrages: *This is the Dragon who was cast out of Paradise, who deceived Eve, and was given into this world to mock us. For how many Monks and Clerics has he cast down, etc.* Lyra and others follow these Fathers. Regarding the Vulgate version of this passage, see Sixtus Amama <note>Antibarbara, book 3, page 853</note>.

# Sacred History of Animals
### from Psalm 50, verses 10, 11. page 508

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
60. Of these, the *concha* <note>a general term for shells or shellfish</note> is rather a shell and is always round, while the *strombus* <note>a spiral or snail-like shell</note> is likewise a shell but twisted into a long spiral. However, those which consist of two shells are primarily called by the name of *concha*; for this reason, Aristotle calls them "bivalves" <note>original: "Δίθυραι," literally "two-doored"</note>, which can be rendered as "two-gated," and thus oysters are also called by the name of shells, which were in great use among the Romans. Yet more frequently, shells are distinguished from oysters as "contrasted species" <note>original: "ἀντιδιῃρημέναι"</note>. Indeed, the shell of the *concha* is smooth and polished, or at least has ridges and teeth in a similar pattern, whereas the exterior of the oyster is scabby and rough. There are various species of shells in which pearls are accustomed to be born. That species which bears the "pearl-mother" <note>original: "μαργαρίτομητρα," translated into the German "Perlemutter" in the text</note> is etched with ridges and is more similar to a scallop than a fan-mussel, and it is also provided with certain transverse ridges inside. More open shells are called "hollows" <note>original: "κοῖλαι"</note> by the Greeks, about which Isidore says: *There are diverse kinds of shells, among which are the pearl-bearers, also called "hollows," because in them a precious stone is solidified.* Erotianus says in his Lexicon: *"Cheramida"* <note>original: "Χηραμίδα"</note> *is the hollow shell which we call a mussel.* And Galen in his Lexicon: *A "cheme" or "cheramida" is the more hollow and larger shell.* These "hollows" are not called so from the "heavens" <note>a pun in Latin between "cœlæ" (hollows) and "cœlum" (heaven)</note>, as if the stone were formed from the dew of heaven. For they say that they open at night—whence they are also called *myakes* <note>original: "μύακες"</note> from "closing" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῶ μύειν"</note>—so that they may conceive from the lunar sprinkling, that is, the dew; and as that pure and transparent moisture hardens, they give birth to that white little stone which we call a *pearl* <note>original: "margaritam"</note>. This is the opinion of Pliny <note>see Natural History, book 9, chapter 35, page 426</note>, Solinus, and Ammianus Marcellinus; compare also Bartholomaeus Anglicus <note>On the Properties of Things, book 16, chapter 62</note>. But while this might be true of land-shells, it is not likely for sea-shells. This is evident from what Isidorus Characenus relates in his description of Parthia <margin>book 3, chapter 14.</margin> quoted in Athenaeus: some shells are "deep-dwellers" <note>original: "ἐμβύθιοι"</note> which live at the bottom, and others are "surface-dwellers and visible" <note>original: "ἐπιπολάτιδες καὶ ἀναφανεῖς"</note> which are carried along and swim on the surface of the sea. I know, says Vossius <note>On Idolatry, book 4, chapter 46, page 1462</note>, what they might answer: that the shells have such wisdom that they seek the bottom as soon as they have conceived. But the objection is that the shells containing the largest pearls are created in the deep; such shells do not wander but cling to the bottom, so that it is often necessary for divers <note>original: "urinatores"</note> to submerge to a depth of twenty fathoms <note>original: "orgyarum," a Greek measure of about 6 feet</note>, as the same Isidorus says. Therefore, it is much more credible that both the animal and the little stone are produced from the same material, but the latter is created from a purer and more transparent moisture. As the animal grows, the stone also grows, or "the bone of its jaw" as it were—for the Ancients speak in both ways. It was reported to Pliny <note>book 9, chapter 35</note> that if it lightens, the pearls become smaller; he says this happens due to a kind of fasting. But the same author, along with Isidorus Characenus in the place cited above, judges that they are rendered larger by thunder, namely by the benefit of the rain that follows the thunder. For the same reason, truffles also become larger then, as Plutarch is fond of saying <note>Table Talk, book 4</note>. You might therefore elegantly call them "truffles of the sea," just as Matron the parodist calls the oyster in his "Dinner," whose verse can be read in Athenaeus <note>book 2, chapter 21</note>:

-> Oysters, those sacrificial truffles of the Nereid water. <-

And with a similar metaphor, Tertullian called them "apples of the sea" in *On the Apparel of Women, chapter 6*, who

<column-break/>

in the same place also clearly distinguished the shells in which the pearl is born from the pearl itself, saying: *If ambition fishes for anything from the British or Indian sea, it is a kind of shell—I will not say more pleasing in flavor than a purple-fish or an oyster, nor even a "poleride." For this reason, I have known shells as the apples of the sea. But if that shell develops a pustule within, it ought to be considered its defect rather than its glory. And although it may be called a pearl <note>original: "margaritum"</note>, nothing else is to be understood than some hard and round wart of that shell.* Properly speaking, "warts" <note>original: "verrucæ"</note> are prominent spots on the hands or other parts of the body, which sometimes neither fall off on their own nor are cut off without pain. Commonly called **Warts** <note>original: "Warzen," the German term</note>. Horace, not without charm, transfers this to other <margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> vices <margin>Sermons, Satire 3.</margin>:
> "Let him who asks that his own tumors not offend his friend,
> allow for his friend's warts; it is only fair
> for one seeking pardon for his own sins, etc."

In the same way and sense, Tertullian calls pearls a "wart" to describe the vice of pride, which the female sex is accustomed to practice with "unions" <note>original: "unionibus," a term for large, unique pearls</note> or pearls. Or he refers to the opinion of some who claim pearls are produced from a certain material of the shells, just as hail is formed in the clouds and stones in the kidneys. Regarding the method of catching pearls, writers report that in certain places in India, the shells are caught with nets because they swim in swarms, and like bees, they have a "king" surpassing the others in form and strength. When the fishermen know this, they turn all their industry toward the King. For unless the King is captured, the rest cannot be caught either, as they follow the fleeing king; but once the king is captured, the whole swarm stops and is taken. This is true of those shells which are called "visible," but for those that live at the bottom, and for the pearls which they have shed on their own and which have fallen to the bottom, there is need for divers who, using certain instruments, collect the "unions" or pearls. The "implacable" <note>original: "ἄσπονδοι," meaning those with whom no truce is possible</note> enemies of the shells are the sea-stars <note>starfish</note>, which eat and consume them. They lie in wait for the shells in various ways, but they primarily use this stratagem: when the shellfish open their shells, either because they need cooling or so that something pertaining to food may fall in (as Aelian records <margin>On Animals, book 11, chapter 22</margin>), the starfish inserts one of its legs or rays within the gaping shells of the oyster, preventing them from being closed, and then they feast on the flesh. Oppian describes this manner of ambush in his *Halieutics, book 2, chapter 2*:

-> Against them, the creeping stars of the sea <-
-> also devise a craft; for they too apply cunning to the oysters. <-
-> But they do not bring a stone as a companion and helper; <-
-> they, thrusting a very rough and sturdy limb <-
-> into the opened shells, manage to prevent them from closing and thus they feed. <-

*Thus you prepare snares for the shell, thus the crafty
Sea-star prepares frauds; but aided by no little stone,
It strives and with its rough feet separates the gaping
Shells, and feeds upon the soft flesh as if it were entrails.*
In sacred matters, how the shells with their offspring should be applied, others may see. *Channels,* says Bernard in his *Sermons on the Song of Solomon, Sermon 18, we have many in the Church today; but of shells, very few.* <note>St. Bernard's metaphor: a "channel" lets grace flow through it immediately without being filled, while a "shell" fills itself first before it overflows to others.</note>

# Sacred History of Animals
### Sacred History of Animals. New Edition.

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> ...likened to the shape of a land dragon. Furthermore, the skin of the Sea Dragon is not far removed from the form of the terrestrial Dragon. 3. The stings and spines of this fish possess a significant amount of venom, and finally 4. once captured, it casts itself onto the sand and, with wonderful speed, digs out a burrow with its snout. Here we must explain the words of the Psalmist <note>referring to King David, traditionally the author of the Psalms</note> in *Psalm 74:13–14*, where the word *tanninim* <note>Hebrew: תנינים, meaning sea monsters or dragons</note> is found. For the Vulgate <note>the standard Latin Bible</note> reads: *You crushed the heads of the dragons upon the waters.* Pagninus <note>Sante Pagnini, a Renaissance Bible translator</note> renders it: *the heads of whales.* Luther translates it: *you break the heads of the dragons in the sea* <note>original German: "du zerbrichst die Köpffe der Drachen im Meer"</note>. *You crushed the heads of the Dragon,* continues the Vulgate, *you gave him as food for the people of the Ethiopians.* These latter words of the Psalmist are quite controversial due to the various and diverse opinions of interpreters.

Luther, in his marginal note, explains the "heads of the dragons" metaphorically in this passage as referring to tyrants, such as Pharaoh was with his princes. From this, Osiander <note>Lucas Osiander, a Lutheran theologian</note> provides this paraphrase: *You destroyed the Tyrant Pharaoh and his princes. For a tyrant in the world is like a whale or a sea monster in the ocean. For in this way, he treats the other smaller and inferior fish cruelly according to his whim.* Generally, interpreters agree regarding the preceding parts, including Blessed Luther, as we mentioned in his marginal gloss, and the Nuremberg Bible. The Greek Scholia of Basil <note>Saint Basil the Great</note> state: *He calls the Egyptians "dragons," their "heads" the Princes, and the "greatest dragon" Pharaoh, who, having been submerged in the Red Sea with his army, became prey for the Ethiopians, who frequently waged war with the Egyptians.* 

This comparison with Pharaoh is frequent and fitting, especially since in *Psalm 68:31*, he is compared to a crocodile because of the Nile, the most famous river of Egypt, which nourishes crocodiles. Thus, in this place, he is compared to a whale or a sea dragon, either because he desired to oppress and utterly destroy the people of God with a ferocity similar to a sea monster alongside his nobles; or because he exercised tyranny on land as a dragon does in the sea; or because Egypt was adjacent to the sea and washed by it; or because a dragon or crocodile was depicted on the banners of the Egyptians, serving as an emblem of Egypt and its Kings. The Prophets use the same metaphor after the Psalmist in *Isaiah 27:1, 51:9,* and *Ezekiel 29:5, 32:2.*

However, when there follows "for the people of the wilderness" <note>Hebrew: לעם לציים, *le-am le-tsiyim*</note>, the Vulgate, following the Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, translates it as *you gave him as food for the people of the Ethiopians.* Regarding this phrase *le-am le-tsiyim*, which Arias Montanus translates as *the peoples of the solitude* <note>or wilderness</note>, he thinks it should be explained in this way: either you gave the kingdom of the drowned Pharaoh as plunder to the Ethiopians, *or* at least the corpses of Pharaoh’s men as prey and spoils to those living on the shores of the Red Sea. Others explain that God gave Pharaoh as food to the people inhabiting the desert while He made Israel take possession of his spoils. Junius and Tremellius translated it: *You gave food to the people themselves as they journeyed through the deserts.* The Weimar Bible <note>original: "Vinarienses"</note> understands *tsiyim* to mean wild beasts and birds, citing *Proverbs 30:25–26*, where both ants and conies <note>rock hyraxes</note> and mountain mice are called a *people* <note>Hebrew: עם, *am*</note>. Likewise, Piscator explains it as the corpse of Pharaoh, cast out from the sea and given to be devoured by the birds and beasts that inhabit the wilderness; the Dutch <note>original: "Belgæ"</note> say the same. The Chaldean <note>referring to the Aramaic Targum</note> explains it thus: *You crushed the heads of the dragons and suffocated the Egyptians in the sea: you crushed the heads of Pharaoh’s mighty ones, you gave them over to destruction for the people of the house of Israel, but their bodies to the dragons;*

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals. New Edition.</margin> Campensis says: *You threw him out to be devoured by the wild beasts and ravens, who are accustomed to live in desert places and feed on corpses.* Blessed Glassius <note>Salomon Glassius, author of *Philologia Sacra*</note> does not refer these words to the immediately preceding ones, but thinks they complete a thought on their own, and that the Psalmist is speaking of the Manna and the quails given as food to the people. 

Truly, just as the "head of Pharaoh" denotes his power, we think the following things should be explained most simply through metaphor. Since "food" is often taken to mean something sweet and pleasing, nothing else is signified than that God, by submerging Pharaoh and crushing his power, did something most gratifying for the Israelite people. By this, they not only refreshed their spirits, but they also obtained those rich spoils—which could stir and satisfy an appetite—which were stripped from the corpses of the drowned Pharaoh and his Princes after they had been cast onto the shore, as seen in *Exodus 14:30, Wisdom 10:18 ff., Deuteronomy 31:17,* and *Numbers 14:9.* Indeed, the *tsiyim* <note>wilderness dwellers</note> were the Israelites who wandered in the solitude of the Arabian desert, or in various parts of that wilderness, as Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish scholar</note> notes, through the desert of Etham, Suph, Paran, Kadesh, Sin, Moab, etc. From this, such a predicate can rightly be attributed to them, so that they are called "the peoples of the wilderness" <note>Hebrew: ציים, *tsiyim*</note>. 

The Vulgate and the Septuagint understood this as "the Ethiopians," those who live in the southern region of Egypt, whom they call the *Ichthyophagi* <note>Greek for "Fish-eaters"</note>, about whom Manilius <margin>Book 4</margin> writes:
-> *to bend the pliant oars* <-
-> *And sweep the calm sea with cast nets,* <-
-> *And to expose the captured peoples on their shores.* <-
From this, Claudian <margin>in Rufinus, line 377</margin> skillfully calls the fisherman a "sea-born plunderer":
-> *Thus the sea-born plunderer drives* <-
-> *The astonished fish to the shores, and draws together* <-
-> *The sparse windings of his nets, and gathers the gaping edges,* <-
who, among other edibles, also prepared their living from whales which the sea spewed out and left on the shores. They differed little from monkeys, as noted by Diodorus, Aben Ezra, and Agatharchides concerning the Red Sea. Theodoretus reports concerning the same that the Ethiopians, hearing of Pharaoh’s destruction, subjugated Egypt to themselves. See, if you please, Ursinus, Glassius, and Geier.

The LEECH <note>Latin: *hirudo*</note> or *sanguisuga* <note>literally "blood-sucker"</note> gets its name among the Latins from "sucking blood" <note>Latin: *sugendo sanguine*</note>, which nevertheless does not satisfy it, so much so that it sucks until it bursts. To the Greeks, it is the *bdella* <note>βδέλλα</note>. To the Hebrews, it is the *alukah* <note>עלוקה</note>. I bring forward the words of the Wisest of Kings <note>Solomon</note> regarding the leech, worthy of any fable: *The leech has two daughters, named Give, Give* <note>Hebrew: הב הב, *Hav, Hav*</note>. Symmachus renders this "Bring, Bring" <note>Greek: Φέρε, Φέρε</note>, or, as Pagninus translates it, "Affer, Affer." Luther: "Bring her, bring her" <note>German: *Bring her/bring her*</note>. The author of the Proverbs says this creature has two daughters who are themselves insatiable. 

The leech is a symbol of a greedy man, says Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf, a Hebraist</note>, whose daughters, into whom they are married, exhaust and diminish their resources. If ever he does a favor for a poorer man, he never does it for free, but always through his daughters *demands double back* <note>referring to "Give, Give"</note>, until that man is reduced to extreme poverty, which is denoted by the small letter <note>referring to the Hebrew letter *He* ה in the word *Hav* הב</note>. He extends this comparison with the leech to the parent of a greedy man...

<meta>This page continues the "Sacred History of Animals," transitioning from the physical description of sea creatures to the moral and allegorical interpretations of the leech and the Leviathan. It draws heavily on Patristic and Medieval authorities like Jerome, Gregory the Great, and Hugo Cardinalis to link these animals to the nature of the Devil and human vice.</meta>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> Jerome <note>St. Jerome, c. 347–420 AD, translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> provides a comparison of the leech: <note>original: "Sanguisuga Diabolus est..."</note> *The Leech is the Devil, who is unceasingly inflamed by a thirst for sinning and for urging others to sin. He has two daughters, because the allurements of the human race specifically imitate this ardor of the ancient enemy—namely, Lust and Greed. For in Lust, the more the reins are loosened, the more harmfully one is delighted.* Hugo Cardinalis <note>Hugh of Saint-Cher, a 13th-century Dominican theologian and cardinal</note> follows this metaphor of the leech as the Devil more extensively, reporting to whom this infernal and Stygian parent of vices betrothed his daughters: *The Leech is the Devil,* he says, *who perpetually burns with a thirst for sinning and suggesting sins; there are two daughters whom he generates in us by his suggestions: Avarice and Lust. The first daughter always cries out, "bring gold, silver, and possessions," with which it is impossible for the soul—or the chest, or the purse—to be filled. Therefore, the Soul of the Greedy man is always empty. The second daughter is similarly insatiable: because just as fire is not extinguished by adding wood, but rather increased, so Lust is nourished and increased by pleasures. The first daughter, the leech, plunders everyone, but she herself is plundered by the second daughter, because whatever Avarice collects, Lust scatters. Hence it often happens by divine judgment that a usurer, or a merchant, or anyone who has gathered much through Avarice, has a lustful son who scatters everything by living extravagantly. The Devil long ago married off these two most dear daughters of his: he gave the first to the Jews as if to the firstborn, and the second to the Gentiles; but the clergy of our time have seized both and illicitly joined themselves to them.* So says he.

# LEVIATHAN.

<margin>Book 4 of the Morals, chapter 11.</margin> **LEVIATHAN.** <note>Hebrew: לִוְיָתָן</note> This is a word of Hebrew origin which the Vulgate has retained in *Job 3:8, 40:20,* and *Isaiah 27:1.* it comes from *lavah* <note>Hebrew: לָוָה</note>, which among other meanings also signifies *he assumed, accumulated, added,* or *increased*, so that *Leviathan*, if you explain it in English, would be *addition, adjunction, adding-on,* or *supplement*. Regarding this meaning, let us note the opinions of some of the Fathers. For thus Philip the Presbyter <note>a 5th-century commentator on Job</note>, who applies this to the Devil, says: *Who did not stand in the truth, and exceeding the measure of presumption, added pride to himself, as if growing beyond the goodness of Nature into an immortal state by the disease of elation: therefore he is called an "addition," for a name made from a crime revealed the condition of the good nature which the good God had created.* Gregory the Great <note>Pope Gregory I, r. 590–604 AD</note> preceded Philip: *Leviathan,* he says, *is interpreted as the "addition of them": of whom, if not of men? Rightly is he called their addition, because after he brought in the first fault by evil suggestion, he does not cease to increase it daily with more grievous persuasions.* Or certainly, Leviathan is so named by way of reproach. *For he found those in Paradise immortal, but by promising the divinity of immortality, he pledged to add something to them beyond what they were: but while he smoothly claimed he would give what they did not have, he craftily took away even what they did have.* The same author continues: <margin>Book 33, chapter 12.</margin> *Leviathan is called the addition of those men to whom he once brought the fault of transgression, and he extends this daily through the worst suggestions even unto eternal death. While he multiplies their guilt by the interest of sin, he undoubtedly heaps up punishments without end or cessation.* Leviathan can also be called so by way of mockery. For to the first man, through crafty persuasion, he promised he would bring <meta>catchword: divinity</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin> divinity, but he took away immortality. Therefore, he could be called the "addition" of men through mockery, for while he promised to add to them that which they were not, he took away by deception even that which they were. So says he. Hugo Cardinalis, in his commentary on *Isaiah 27*, reduced these words of Gregory into a forceful summary: *The Devil is called Leviathan, that is, "addition": because he accumulates sin upon sin, suggestion upon suggestion, and deception upon deception.* Or by *antiphrasis* <note>a figure of speech where a word is used in a sense opposite to its proper meaning</note>: because when he promised to "add" to our first parents, he diminished what was promised. But Rabbi Levi, on *Job 3*, explains the word *Leviathan* as *their mourning* <note>Hebrew: אֶבְלָם</note>, as if the letter *nun* were an affix instead of *mem*. In that sense it is read among the Rabbis: *A woman shall not stir up her mourning on a festival day.* So say the Chaldean <note>referring to the Targum, the Aramaic translation</note> and Rabbi Aben Ezra, and some of our own people, says Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf, a famous 17th-century Hebraist</note> in his Hebrew Lexicon. However, Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a Dutch theologian</note> skillfully says that this meaning lacks an example. For what is cited from the Talmud is a proverb, "let not a woman stir up Leviathan on a festival day," and it is an allusion to this passage with a *misinterpretation* <note>original Greek: παρερμηνείᾳ</note>.

He solves the Gordian knot <note>an idiom for a complex problem</note> who, with a happy daring, extricates himself from so many interpretations of the Interpreters and either joins them together or offers the genuine meaning of the words of *Job 3:8* to the Blessed reader: For thus Job says in that place: <note>Hebrew: קֹבְבֹהוּ אֹרְרֵי יֹום הָעֲתִידִים עֹרֵר לִוְיָתָן — "Let them curse it who curse the day, who are prepared to rouse Leviathan."</note> The Septuagint <note>Greek Old Testament</note>: *But let him curse it who curses that day, he who is about to conquer the great monster of that day.* Symmachus: *those who are about to stir up Leviathan.* Aquila: *those prepared to rouse Leviathan.* The Vulgate: *Let them curse it, who curse the day, who are prepared to rouse Leviathan.* Pagninus and Arias Montanus <note>Renaissance Bible translators</note>: *Let them curse it, who curse the day, who are prepared to stir up their mourning.* Or as Arias says: *Let those who curse the day execrate it, being ready to stir up their mourning.*

The Targum <note>Aramaic paraphrase</note> and many of the Rabbis, joined by Christians like Mercerus, Drusius, Piscator, Tirinus, Mariana, and others, explain it thus: *Let them execrate it, those who curse the day, that is, the professional mourners who curse the day of one's death, whom they lament in a funeral, who are prepared to stir up their or his mourning, that is, those who are prepared to mourn the funerals of others.*

They place the foundation of their *interpretation* <note>original Greek: ἐξηγήσεως</note> in this: they want *Leviathan* to be a compound word from the Syriac name *levaya*, meaning "mourning," and the affixed letter *tav* instead of *nun*, which signifies "their."

The Nuremberg Bible interprets it thus: *Let the necromancers <note>magicians who speak to the dead</note> curse this day, who by their art can produce the devil, who is compared with Leviathan.*

Strength is added to this acceptance by what Plutarch <note>Greek historian, c. 46–119 AD</note> records concerning the Priests of Arabia and Egypt, that they were able to do much with magical aid; or this example from Plutarch demonstrates it, narrating that the Crocodile can be tamed by the Priests through the recitation of certain words, so that they offer themselves to be embraced. His words are: <margin>Volume 2, page 976.</margin> *The crocodiles not only recognize the voice of the priests when they call, and endure their touch, but opening their mouths they allow their teeth to be cleaned with hands and wiped with linens.*

Friedlieb, in his commentary on this passage, paraphrases it thus: *Let that day be ill-omened and detestable to fishermen because of the cloudy sky and storms.*

Schultetus provides another exposition of the words: *Let the illuminators of days pierce it or transfix it (from the word "or," meaning light), that is, lightnings, for these by their light as if...*

<meta>catchword: as if</meta>

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
...as if they illuminate the day even more by bringing new light to it; and *those who are prepared to rouse the whale* <note>Referring to Job 3:8</note>, that is, the violent winds and whirlwinds which, by agitating the sea, stir up the whales within it. This is therefore a poetic periphrasis <note>A roundabout way of describing something</note>, of which there are many in this book concerning storms. This is the view of Schultens <note>Albert Schultens, 1686–1750, a noted Dutch philologist and commentator on Job</note>. But if, by Schultens’ "illuminators," you understand magicians and sorceresses who possess divine-like power—for whom, according to common opinion, it is not difficult, as Propertius sings:

->*To be able to draw down the stars and rivers*<-
->*by means of Colchian magic songs.*<- <note>original: "Cytenæis ducere carminibus," referring to the witchcraft of Medea</note>

And as Seneca says in *Medea*: *though the wind was silent, the waves roared; the mad sea swelled.* From which Horace <margin>*Epodes, Ode 5, line 22, verse 6.*</margin> does not differ, where it is read:

->*— — — a dire curse*<-
->*is expiated by no sacrifice.*<-

Those who interpret the text as referring to necromancers <note>Those who communicate with the dead or demons</note> easily agree with Schultens. To this is added a fiction of the Greeks, who ascribed the causes of earthquakes to Neptune <note>The Roman name for Poseidon</note>, for which reason he is addressed by Hesiod in book 2 of *Works and Days*, verse 665, as:

->*— — — Poseidon the earth-shaker*<-
->*Neptune, the crusher of the earth.*<- <note>original: "Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων"</note>

This is because floods usually occur with earthquakes, which they imagined Neptune caused with his trident. The Sicilians believed that Mt. Etna was shaken and vomited fire whenever Enceladus <note>A giant from Greek mythology buried under the mountain</note>—the son of Titan and Earth, whom the poets say was struck by Jupiter's lightning and thrust under Etna—turned onto his side. Regarding this fable, one may read Claudian in book 1 of *The Rape of Proserpina*, Virgil in the 4th book of the *Aeneid*, and Sabinus in book 1 of *Caesar Germanicus* regarding Henry VI. There are others, moreover, who interpret this as referring to those men who invoke Satan out of desperation, just as Virgil describes those in such a state of despair:

->*If I cannot bend the Heavens, I will move Hell.*<- <note>original: "Flectere si nequeo Superos Acheronta movebo," from Aeneid VII, 312</note>

With this interpretation coincides that of Delrio <note>Martin Delrio, a 16th-century Jesuit demonologist</note>: "You who are in the habit of cursing certain days, and who are ready to invoke dire imprecations upon yourselves and others with every third word, and to summon the evil demon from hell with ill-omened voices: come here, come here, and heap as many evil words as you can upon this day of my birth." Among the ancients, Philip the Presbyter <note>A 5th-century commentator</note> understands "those who curse" to be the faithful, who curse their own transgressions and the author of them—namely the Devil—with all manner of dire threats. While they themselves resist and oppose his will as much as they are able with the help of the Holy Spirit, they rouse him against themselves, so that he gathers and stirs up all his strength to overwhelm them.

<margin>book 4 of the Moralia, chapter 10.</margin> But Gregory the Great <note>Pope Gregory I, c. 540–604 AD</note> walks another path, saying: *In these words it is clearly shown that the future destruction of the Antichrist at the end of the world is foreseen by the holy man [Job]. For the Evil Spirit, who by his merit is Night, pretends to be Day at the end of the world: when he shows himself to men as if he were God, when he attributes the brightness of divinity to himself, and exalts himself above all that is called God or is worshipped. He therefore curses the night who curses the day, because He will then destroy the spirit's malice, who by the illumination of His coming will also extinguish the power of his strength.* God presents Himself as the praiser of the Leviathan in Job, chapter 40, verse 20 and following, and describes him by his principal parts. He discusses his strength in verses 20 and 21, exaggerating it by saying: *Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook, or press down his tongue with a cord?*

<column-break/>

<margin>History of animals.</margin> *Will you put a hook in his nose, or pierce his jaw with a spike?* Other fish are caught with a hook, the hook penetrating their tongue and thus they are pulled out by the cord to which the hook is tied. But you will not be able to catch the whale in that way, nor carry him around tied with a cord through his nose pierced by a needle or a reed. For he has a tongue so large and powerful that Olaus Magnus <note>A 16th-century Swedish writer and cartographer</note> reports it has been seen to be 21 feet long (*History of the Northern Peoples*, book 21, chapter 9). Gregory the Great <margin>book 33, chapter 8, ibid.</margin> applies these words of Job to Christ, by whom the Stygian <note>Hellish</note> Leviathan was caught on a hook; for in our Redeemer, while he bit the bait of the body through his henchmen, he was pierced by the spikes of His divinity. The following verse, 22, reveals the ferocity and cruelty of Leviathan: *Will he make many supplications to you? Will he speak soft words to you?* He takes a comparison from men who are conquered and fear one more powerful than themselves, who are accustomed to soften his anger with prayers; even beasts imitate this in their own way, even the Elephant, as Pliny proves by example in book 8 of his *Natural History*, chapter 7. But the whale reveals himself as a suppliant by no gesture. The same is indicated in verses 23 and 24, as it is the conquered, not the victor, who are reduced to slavery and hand themselves over to the service of someone—unless you say this refers to Magicians and Necromancers, or those who have bound themselves to the Devil by a certain oath or pact, of whom Isaiah 28:14 speaks, who have struck a covenant with death and hell. Job continues in the demonstration of his strength in verses 25 and 26: *Will companions feast upon him? Will they divide him among the merchants? Will you fill his skin with barbed irons, or his head with fish spears?* The Vulgate reads *gurgustium* <note>a small hut or bait-shack</note>. Arias <note>Arias Montanus, a 16th-century orientalist</note> reads "in the armpit." For *Haberim* <note>the Hebrew word for "companions" or "merchants"</note> is either a certain type of vessel in which fish are caught or kept once caught, and thus verse 26 is to be explained by hypallage <note>a reversal of the natural order of words</note>, meaning: "Will you fill huts with his skin, or the wicker basket with his head?" Gregory the Great explains the Leviathan being cut up in this way: <margin>book 33, chapter 9 of the Moralia.</margin> *This Leviathan is cut into pieces as often as his members are separated from him by the sword of the divine word. For when the wicked hear the word with truth, and, struck by holy fear, withdraw from the imitation of their friendly enemy, he himself is divided in his body, since those who had wickedly clung to him are pulled away.* Philip the Presbyter says the same: *The friends and merchants are to be understood as the Saints and all preachers of truth. Indeed, the body of this Dragon is cut and divided when, through these same preachers, many people are separated from his multitude of the lost and brought to the faith of Christ.* He continues in verse 27: *Lay your hand upon him; remember the battle, and you will do so no more.* Or as the Vulgate says, *you will not add to speak further.* Schultens explains these words in this way: "If you dare to attack it with your hand, be certain that you are entering a very great struggle which you cannot finish." Thus also Vatablus <note>François Vatable, a 16th-century French scholar</note>: "If you once lay hands on him, that is, if you attack him, you will never fight another; for he will kill you." But Piscator <note>Johannes Piscator, a 16th-century German theologian</note> glosses it thus: "But come now, since you cannot take the whale by force, make a trial to see if you can take it by gently handling and stroking it with your hand; do not proceed to remember the war, that is, do not proceed to act hostilely with it to capture it." In the following chapter, verses 3 and 4, he discusses the formation of its limbs and its covering. *I will not be silent about its limbs, etc.* The word *Adi* <note>Hebrew 'adi'</note> otherwise signifies "garments," but here it means large limbs like bars; compare Job 18:13, Ezekiel 19:14, and Hosea 11:6. <meta>This page continues the theological and naturalistic examination of the Leviathan from the Book of Job (though the header cites Psalm 41, the text refers to Job 41). It focuses on the creature's mouth, teeth, and scales, moving from literal anatomical descriptions to allegorical interpretations involving Satan and the Antichrist.</meta>

### from Psalm 41, verses 10, 11 etc. 508

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
The commentator Piscator <note>Johannes Piscator, 1546–1625, a German reformed theologian</note> understands "garment" to mean the sea in this sense: who can pull him out of the sea, with which he is covered as if by a cloak? But this exposition is less consistent with the context—namely, that "to strip off one's garment" means to pull him out. Our Schultens <note>Albert Schultens, a Dutch philologist</note> better explains the "doubled bridle" as referring to the two rows of teeth, upper and lower, between which we are accustomed to thrust a bridle into horses. Regarding Satan, Brenz <note>Johannes Brenz, 15th-century Lutheran reformer</note> says: *Satan does not wish to be seen in his own true form, but hides himself under the mask of Goodness: only the Lord, however, will strip the bridle <note>original Greek: τὸν χαλινὸν</note> from this Beast.* Similarly, it is the *spiritual man who, through the Spirit of the Lord, understands the crafts of Satan (1 Corinthians 2).* These points agree with Gregory the Great, who in *Moralia in Job, Book 33, Chapter 28,* speaks thus: *This Leviathan tempts the religious mind in one way, and the minds devoted to this world in another: for he throws before the wicked the evils they desire, but lying in wait for the good, he mocks them under the appearance of sanctity. To the former, as if to his own familiars, he manifests his iniquity; but to the latter, as if to strangers, he cloaks himself under a pretext of honesty, so that he may introduce the evils he cannot do publicly under the veil of a good action. In the very work of iniquity he performs, he is clothed in the appearance of sanctity, and unless by divine grace, the garments of his simulation cannot be stripped away. But God inspires the minds of His servants with the grace of the most subtle discretion, so that, with his malice revealed, they may see his face, which he hides covered under the habit of sanctity.* He continues in verse 5 <note>Job 41:14</note> with the description of the parts, specifically the teeth and the mouth. *Who has opened the doors of his face? Terror is in the circle of his teeth.* His strength is made plain by the power of his teeth, which, because of their size, strike horror into any who look upon them. By the teeth of the Leviathan, Gregory understands heretics and teachers of false dogma, who propagate their heterodoxy with the help of the "secular arm" <note>Government or military power</note> and compel listeners to accept it. For so *the coming Antichrist will obtain the very highest powers of this age; raging with a double error, he strives to draw the hearts of men to himself, both by sending out preachers and by bowing them through the stirring up of political powers. Well does the Lord add concerning this Leviathan, saying: Terror is in the circle of his teeth.*

<margin>book 33, chapters 28, 29.</margin>
For by changing the name, he wished to signify these teeth in another way, which he previously called "doors." Therefore, perverse preachers are his doors, because they open the entrance to perdition. They are his teeth because they crush those whom they catch in error away from the solidity of truth. Because they tear apart the life of the reprobate by biting, they slaughter those led away from the integrity of truth in a sacrifice of falsehood. The preaching of these men could easily be despised by listeners, but the terror of secular powers added to it exalts this preaching above human judgment.* The perverse powers of this age protect the wicked preachers of the Antichrist. From the commendation of the mouth, the divine Writer descends to the scales, which he praises again for their strength in verses 6, 7, and 8 <note>Job 41:15–17</note>. *His scales are his pride, shut up together as with a close seal. One is joined to another, that no air can come between them. They are stuck together, they hold onto each other, and cannot be separated.* This is a praise of the Leviathan based on the connection and harmony of its members, especially the scales, which he calls shields; for the scales in which they take pride are like robust bucklers joined so tightly that not even the thinnest breath

<column-break/>

can penetrate them. Elsewhere, the teachers of natural history

record that the whale has smooth skin and lacks scales. Therefore, either the density of its skin is described metaphorically—suggesting it is so great that it is as if the creature were clothed in a coat of mail, or walks like a horse in full armor—or this must be understood as the scales of the head, or those bony shields which encircle the mouth like scales. For the preceding and following passages show that the head is being discussed. Perhaps there is also a certain species that has scales, just as Arrian reports in *Indica*, book 8, from the account of Nearchus, that a whale of 50 cubits <note>About 75 feet</note> was seen in India with a scaly hide so thick that it equaled a cubit in depth, with oysters and algae growing on it. Schultens, in this place, explains this symbolically, as does Brenz: *This is a description,* he says, *of the condition of the impious. For they are "strong shields," that is, most powerful in the world not only in secular but in spiritual power; they are strong in the sword and hypocrisy, in doctrine and tyranny, in authority and command. Furthermore, they are bound together most tightly, for Princes and Bishops are so joined by treaties among themselves that no man can dissolve that knot (the "Holy League").* From external qualities, he proceeds to those which primarily concern the senses, namely sight, both for us and for others:
<margin>verses 9, 10, 11, 12.</margin>
*By his neesings <note>An archaic word for sneezing</note> a light doth shine, and his eyes are like the eyelids of the morning. Out of his mouth go burning lamps, and sparks of fire leap out. Out of his nostrils goeth smoke, as out of a seething pot or cauldron. His breath kindleth coals, and a flame goeth out of his mouth.* Every detail threatens the forge of Vulcan and breathes the ashes of Etna <note>References to Roman mythology and the volcanic mountain in Sicily</note>, which the divine Writer discusses regarding the respiration or breath of the Leviathan. The "sneezings" mentioned in verse 9 are explained by Piscator as the spouting of water into the air. Regarding this, Pliny says in *Natural History*, book 9, chapter 6: *Whales have their mouths in their foreheads, and therefore, swimming on the surface of the water, they blow out clouds into the sky.* Thus it creates a splendor while the whitening water is dispersed in the air. Schultens stays closer to the text, saying that by "sneezing" or "strong respiration"—since that is a more violent movement—any violent motion and concussion of the creature is noted, which strikes the eyes with a certain splendor by the reflection of the sun's rays, as if a new light were emerging from the waves.
<margin>book 21, chapter 5.</margin>
From this, Olaus Magnus <note>1490–1557, a Swedish writer and cartographer</note> writes concerning the Norwegian whales that their eyes shine like huge flames, so that seen from afar by fishermen, they appear to be massive fires. The same spirit comes out of its nostrils, namely a fiery and flaming one; for it is full of hot and fiery moisture, and for that reason it has a seething breath, so much so that its breath makes <term>גחלים</term> <note>Hebrew: "gechalim," meaning burning coals</note> glow. Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, c. 1270–1349</note> notes here: *Just as water grows hot in a pot because fire is applied, so air is breathed in the lungs by the heat of the heart existing nearby. Its breath is so great and hot that it can kindle coals.* And he speaks of the whale in the manner of a great bellows by which fire is kindled in a great furnace. ...whoever does not do this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul. <margin>Book 33 of the Moralia, ch. 34.</margin> Gregory the Great <note>original: "tanæ commotione," likely referring to the disturbance or movement of the beast</note> discusses how the beast enters a damned man and, through him, dominates the reprobate. He moves himself with such power that he might disturb the members of the Lord—even the elect, if it were possible; he uses such signs and wonders that, through the power of miracles, he seems to shine as if with the light of a fire. *Chapter 35.* Gregory discusses the eyes of the Leviathan, and by them he understands the counselors of Satan. While these counselors foresee through perverse machinations how things ought to be done, they provide a shown path to his wicked workers, and are rightly compared to the "eyelids of the morning" <note>Job 41:18</note>. For we take the eyelids of the morning to be the final hours of the night, in which the eye opens as if just then, while already showing the beginnings of the coming light. Therefore, the worldly-wise who cling to the perverse malice of the Antichrist are like the eyelids of the morning: for the faith which they find in Christ, they treat as a night of error, and they promise that the veneration of the Antichrist is the truth. The lamps proceeding from the mouth of the Leviathan are explained by Gregory (in the same place) as false preachers, who set the minds of their listeners on fire for the love of treachery, so that they may delight in falsehood and errors. <margin>Book 34, ch. 1.</margin> By the name of the "neck," Gregory understands the arrogance of the Devil: *What is designated by the neck of this Leviathan,* he says, *except the display of pride? By this, raising himself against God, he is puffed up with a simulation of holiness and the swelling of power. In the neck of this Leviathan, therefore, power is said to dwell, because his joined power supports that pride. For whatever is then proudly exalted, whatever is craftily devised, is also carried out with the strength of secular power. As Daniel says: "deceit shall be directed in his hand" <note>Daniel 8:25</note>; indeed, deceit is in the hand, and fraud is in the power: because everything that he wickedly desires, he is also able to carry out strongly for a time. Deceit is said to be "directed" because the malice of his fraud is hindered by no difficulty.* By the "limbs" <note>or "members"</note>, Philip the Presbyter <note>A 5th-century commentator and student of Jerome</note> and Gregory understand the associates of Satan, who, devoted to carnal pleasures, cling to the Devil and are most closely joined with him. Finally, the divine Writer reaches the description of the heart, and says of it in chapter 41, verse 15 <note>Job 41:24 in modern bibles</note>: *His heart is firm as a stone; I say, firm as a lower millstone.* The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> reads: "like an unhammered anvil" <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ ἄκμων ἀνήλατος</note>. The Vulgate reads "as the anvil of a smith," but poorly, which Oleaster <note>Jerónimo Azambuja, a 16th-century Portuguese Dominican</note> also disapproves of. For three reasons, the chest of Satan is compared to a millstone: partly because of its great strength, partly because of his perseverance in malice and perversity, and partly because of his anger and hatred toward the human race. Gregory, following the Vulgate, offers this simile: *On an anvil, other vessels are formed, but the anvil itself is not changed into another vessel by so many hammer-strokes. Rightly, therefore, is this Leviathan compared to an anvil, because we are shaped by his persecution of us. He himself is always being struck, yet is never formed into a useful vessel. We leave him to the eternal strikes of punishment, while we, struck by the hand of the heavenly craftsman during his temptation, pass through like little vessels formed by him; for we are hammered in him so that we may come to the use of the heavenly house.* Let these things be said. The *FROG* <note>Latin: Rana</note>, says Varro <note>Roman scholar, 1st century BCE</note> in *Book 4*, is so named from its voice: but this is more obscure than the Greek names. Others derive it from the Hebrew *ranan*, "he cried out, he sounded with a joyful and clear voice, he shouted." Or from *renan*, which is the same. Thus also Peacocks are called *renanim* from their clamor and triumphant song, from the same root *ranan*, that is, "he sang, he chanted, he hummed, he cried out, he cheered, he shouted." By the Hebrews it is called *tsephardea*. By the Greeks *batrachos*, whence *batrachizein* <note>to croak like a frog</note>. *Koax* fits frogs perfectly, whence comes Aristophanes' *brekekekex, koax koax* <note>from his play "The Frogs"</note>, and the Latin *coaxare* and *quaxare* <note>to croak</note>. Because of their excessive croaking, they are annoying to everyone, except for the frogs of Seriphos <note>A Greek island</note>, of which Pliny writes in *Book 8, ch. 58*, which are mute because of the excessive moisture of the water; and the Cyrenaic frogs, which are also not vocal because of the bitterness of the water, according to Virgil in *Book 3 of the Georgics*. In the Holy Scriptures, Egyptian frogs are mentioned in *Exodus 8:3, Psalm 74:45, and 105:30*, about which we spoke above on *page 173*; and mystical frogs in *Revelation 16:13*, by which false teachers and Sophists are indicated, concerning whom consult the Theologians. Among the Muslims, frogs are held in great value, so much so that it is a sin to kill a frog, because they praise God night and day by croaking, and because, when Abraham was cast into the fire by Nimrod, they poured out water from their mouths to sprinkle him and extinguish the fire.

*THE FISH OF TOBIAS*; It is customary to inquire more curiously than certainly about that fish with which Tobias healed his father's blindness <note>original: "suffusionem," referring to cataracts or leucoma</note>. And those whom history does not name, people presume to name as if they themselves had been present when the smoke from the fish's heart drove the Demon away to the farthest parts of Egypt: *for when the demon smelled the odor, he fled into the highest parts of Egypt* <note>Tobit 8:3</note>. Concerning the power of that fish against Demons, Paulus Merlogus <margin>l. 131. 132</margin> in *Antiquities of the Hebrews, book 4, section 5, no. 44*, discusses it; reviewing three opinions, he embraces the one that ascribes it entirely to supernatural efficiency—that the Demon was driven away by a small portion of the heart placed over coals and resolved into smoke. The smoke, however, only had the status of a sign; upon seeing it, the wicked Spirit was routed by divine power, the energy having been miraculously communicated to the smoke. Franciscus Vallesius believes that fish was the *galeocynon* <note>possibly a type of dogfish or small shark</note>, which others call the *Callionymus* <note>The Stargazer fish, known for its large gall bladder</note>; see <margin>Sacred Philosophy, book 3, ch. 42.</margin> Hoffman in *Book 3 of Galen, on the use of parts, ch. 3, n. 129, p. 40*, by whose gall they say sight was restored to the elder Tobias. For this fish is accustomed to linger around the shores and even sleep in the sand during the day, whence it was called *hemerykoites* <note>"day-sleeper"</note> by Oppian in *Halieutics, book 2, v. 203*. Vossius <note>Gerardus Vossius, 1577–1649</note> in *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry, book 4, ch. 39, p. 1432*, feels this opinion is not absurd, where he cites the testimony of Rondeletius <margin>Book on marine fish, 1.</margin> who says he has often cured cloudiness and scars of the eyes with the gall of the stargazer and the frog-fish. It is mere presumption, which has no foundation in the truth of the matter. Regarding the *Callionymus*, Pliny indeed testifies in *Natural History, book 28, ch. 11*, that its gall heals scars and consumes superfluous flesh of the eyes; since he had not yet discovered any other power in it, it sufficed for him to pass these things down.
