# SACRED HISTORY OF ANIMALS
### From Psalm 50, verses 10–11

**Column 1**

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
"They are demons" <note>original Greek: δαίμονές εἰσί</note> according to certain interpreters; how they are divided into ranks and depart into various paths is learnedly recorded by Stephan Clotzius <note>Stephan Klotz (1606–1668), a German Lutheran theologian</note> in Book 10 *on the Worship of Angels, chapter 13, page 337 and following.*

And let these remarks suffice concerning the fish of Holy Scripture—the fish, I say, which the water of the universal Deluge <note>The Great Flood of Noah</note> did not kill. <margin>Book 1 of the Miracles of Holy Scripture, chapter 4.</margin> Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers</note> provided the reason for this, saying: *The plague of the flood did not touch all things that can live in the waters; it brought death only to land animals.* In this place, a question arises for those searching shrewdly and in need of a solution: *Why did the land animals succumb more to human vengeance than the aquatic ones, since they did not commit more sins?* Yet, in the sin of the first man, the earth from which he had tasted was immediately cursed: *Cursed is the ground because of your work,* etc. In this matter, it must be noted that the animals themselves, which ate from the cursed earth, could not be exempt from the curse, especially since the earth was cursed along with its animals. Therefore, another question arises: *Why did God not also curse the waters in the curse of Adam?* To which it is very easily answered: because man did not drink water against the Lord’s prohibition, but ate from the fruit of the earth. *Except for these reasons, God spared the waters from the curse of Adam because He had prepared to wash away that curse through water, which was done in the flood, and is now granted through Baptism; for in water and the Spirit, all human bodily crimes are purged along with the spiritual ones.* For aquatic creatures do not succumb to the vengeance of the curse, because they do not participate in the curse. *And by this, when the Lord had laid aside the curse of human death by rising again, He did not eat the flesh of land animals but of aquatic ones, when, to confirm the resurrection before the disciples, He ate a piece of roasted fish and a honeycomb, etc.*

Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 672–735 AD), an English monk and scholar</note> explains this roasted fish mystically in this way: *What do we believe the roasted fish signifies, but the suffering Man <note>referring to Christ</note>? For He deigned to be hidden in the waters of the human race, willed to be caught by the snare of our death, and was as if roasted by tribulation at the time of His passion. But He who deigned to become a roasted fish in His passion, became a honeycomb to us in His resurrection. Or did He wish to prefigure the tribulation of His passion in the roasted fish, and express both natures of His person in the honeycomb? For a honeycomb is honey in the wax; honey in the wax is divinity in humanity. Thus our Redeemer indicates His own nature, so that He might pave the way of imitation for us who follow. For behold, in His food, He willed to join the honeycomb to the roasted fish, because clearly those...*

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
*...He receives into His body for eternal rest, who, while they feel tribulations for God’s sake here, do not withdraw from the love of internal sweetness. The honeycomb is taken with the roasted fish because those who here undertake affliction for the truth are there satisfied with true sweetness.* As an example for us, fish are proposed here and there in the sacred writings, so that we may learn from them what we ought to do. <margin>Ezekiel 47:9.</margin> To Ezekiel, water—indeed, two torrents—was shown in a vision in the temple, in which there was a great multitude of fish, and many fishermen spreading their nets there. By the name of fishermen, the Apostles and their successors are understood and prefigured, and by the form of fish, men are understood. Whence Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), Bishop of Milan</note> says in *Book 5 of the Hexameron, chapters 6 and 7:* *You are a fish, O man. Listen, for you are a fish. The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind. But when it was filled, etc.*

*Therefore, there are good and bad fish: the good are kept for their value, the bad are immediately burned. Neither do the nets entangle the good fish, but lift them up; nor does the hook kill it, but it drenches it with the blood of a precious wound, in the confession of whose mouth a good price is found, by which the Apostolic tribute and the tax of Christ can be paid. For so it is written, etc. Matthew 17. Therefore, O good fish, do not fear Peter’s hook; it does not kill but consecrates. Do not despise yourself as if you were worthless because you see a weak body; you have in your mouth that which you may offer both for Peter and for Christ. Do not fear Peter’s nets, to whom Jesus says: "Lead into the deep and let down your nets." For he does not cast them to the left side, but to the right, just as he was commanded by Christ. Do not fear his embrace, for it was said to him: "From now on you will be making men alive." Therefore he sent his nets and embraced Stephen <note>St. Stephen, the first martyr</note>, who was the first to ascend from the Gospel having the shekel of justice <note>original: "staterem justitiæ"</note> in his mouth. Nor should it move you that I have put "the Gospel" for "the Sea." The Gospel is that upon which Christ walked; the Gospel is that by which, though Peter may have faltered, he did not deny Him, when through the right hand of Christ he found the protection of his station. The Gospel is that from which the martyr ascends. The Gospel is the sea in which the Apostles fish, in which the net is cast, which is like the kingdom of heaven. The Gospel is the sea in which the mysteries of Christ are prefigured. The Gospel is the sea in which the Hebrew escaped and the Egyptian was destroyed. The Gospel is the sea in which is the Church, the bride of Christ, and the fullness of divine grace, which is founded upon the seas. Leap over the waves, O man, because you are a fish: let not the things of this world oppress you...*

(X. BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES.)

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred history of animals.</margin>
*The history of this wave: If there is a storm, seek the high and deep waters; if it is calm, play in the waves; if there is a gale, beware of the rocky shore, lest the raging tide dash you against the cliffs.*

### Psalm 68, verse 31 <note>In most modern Bibles, this is Psalm 68:30.</note>

->Rebuke the beast of the reed.<- <note>original Hebrew: גער חית קנה</note>
->Rebuke the beast of the reed.<- <note>original Greek: Ἐπιτίμησον τῷ θηρίῳ τοῦ καλάμου</note>
->Rebuke the wild beasts of the reed.<- <note>original Latin: Increpa feras arundinis</note>

<margin>The use of reeds in warfare.</margin>
There is a divergence here in the verbal interpretation rather than the meaning, about which it is not difficult to decide. The word *chayat* <note>original Hebrew: חית</note> undoubtedly signifies not only a "beast," but also, among other things, a "company" or "assembly." *Schindler* <note>Valentin Schindler, a 16th-century Hebraist</note> teaches that this is a metaphor derived from wild beasts gathered together in one place: *Rebuke the congregation of the reed*, that is, "the reed-bearing assembly," using a common Hebrew idiom. The Arabic version, which usually follows the Greek Septuagint, here departs from it and translates: *Rebuke the beasts which you have possessed.* This is an incongruous use of that word <note>original Hebrew: קנה (kaneh)</note>, which can mean "to possess" in both Hebrew and Arabic; however, the word used by the Psalmist refers to a "stalk" or "reed." Metonymically, it refers to spears and lances made from reeds, which is why the Arabic word *Alkanu* signifies a spear-shaft. Therefore, the divine author undoubtedly intends an army equipped and armed with spears and lances—a nation armed with arrows. *Johann Lonicer* <note>1499–1569, a theologian and professor at Marburg</note>, the first Professor of Greek Language at the University of Marburg, in his Greek exposition of this Psalm (page 72), says: *He calls "beastly enemies" the "beasts of the reed," those who use long reeds—that is, arrows made of reeds and spears.* Spears and arrows were once made from reeds; for in certain regions, reeds grew to the size of trees so that <margin>Book 16, section 36.</margin> javelins could be made from them. As Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> records, many used reeds instead of spears, and throughout the entire East, wars were waged with reeds; even now in the East, they arm soldiers with them to keep enemies at a distance. On *Bals Island* <note>Likely refers to an island in the East Indies, possibly Bali</note>, they carry "arrow-vomiting canes," from which they blow smooth, slender little arrows fashioned from reeds and tipped with poison, as can be read in the *History of the East Indies, part 3, chapter 39.* China <note>original Latin: Sina</note> abounds in a greater plenty of these reeds than other regions of the East Indies. Just as they are of various sizes, they are also of various colors, though they are primarily seen in green. Although their hardness rivals iron, the Chinese adapt them to their ingenuity so skillfully that they know how to fashion from them membranes or parchment papers, carpets, and other very fine items. If you look at their thickness, it is so great that in some parts of China they equal an urn or a barrel in girth; they use the thinner ones in war as spears tipped with sharp iron, while the thicker ones are used for constructing buildings. India also produces reeds of such size that even small boats and skiffs can be fashioned from them, which *Salmasius* <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), a French classical scholar</note> confirms from Cristóvão da Costa <note>A 16th-century Portuguese physician and botanist</note> on pages 1021 and 1299 of his work on Solinus. Virgil, in Book 4 of the *Aeneid*, verse 43, writes: *The lethal reed sticks in her side*, meaning an arrow, which he also calls the "winged" and "flying reed" in Book 5 and Book 7: *And through the entrails came the reed.* He understands it to mean an arrow, which is why it is called "reeden" in these words of the Poet:
> He clothes the reeden arrows, ready for the contest.

<column-break/>

Ovid uses the same metonymy in *Metamorphoses*, Book 10, verse 16: <margin>number</margin>
*And fragile hazels, and the ash tree useful for spears.*
and again in Book 12, verse 181:
*He sent the ashen spear with all his mind’s strength.*
Just as in the sacred texts <note>likely referring to Nahum 2:3</note> "the fir trees are shaken" <margin>margin</margin> (Arias Montanus translates this as "the fir trees are poisoned"), these terms are elegantly used for spears and arrows made of wood. *Antonio Thylesio* <note>1482–1534, an Italian humanist</note>, describing the *Reed* in his *Poetic Works* (page 61), sang:
> You arm it with iron, and it twists rapidly through the air
> The Cretan archer fixes the high-flying birds beneath the clouds
> Or the mountain-wandering beast, driven by its errors, or the wounded
> Enemy falls from a distance, struck by that thrown weapon.
With this mind, *Arias Montanus* <note>1527–1598, a Spanish Orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible</note> paraphrases:
*It is better to scatter the spear-bearing crowds, the strong bulls,*
*Among the peoples, the herds of young bullocks.*
*Sixtinus Amama* <note>1593–1629, a Dutch Hebraist</note> in his *Biblical Antibarbarus*, Book 3, page 787, says: *Others better understand this as referring to the Egyptians, the enemies of the Israelites from every age.* Egypt, moreover, abounded in reeds and sedge; I think no one is such a stranger to natural history as to be ignorant that Egyptian reeds were always the most highly praised. *Sedges and reeds are used hieroglyphically to represent Egypt.* And Augustus, on a coin minted to mark his victory over Antony and Cleopatra, placed a Crocodile with a reed to represent Egypt. *D. Rivetus* <note>André Rivet (1572–1651), a French Huguenot theologian</note> says the same thing in his commentary on this passage (page 413), also citing, if I am not mistaken, Augustus's coin. *Abraham Scultetus* <note>1566–1624, a German professor of theology</note> takes a slightly different and narrower view; he feels this refers to the reed-thicket near Pharaoh's palace, and to the robbers and assassins <note>original Latin: Sicarios</note> who often infest that region. You will find the explanation in his *Oration on Joining Philology with Theology*, which he owes to *Guevara* <note>Antonio de Guevara</note>, so that it seems not so much spoken by Scultetus as written by Guevara. It appears in the same words in the writer of the *Theological Paratitla*, suggesting the "beast of the reed" is the King of Egypt, whose soldiers and leaders the Psalmist appropriately calls *Bulls and calves* in contempt, because they lie in wait for godly men like beasts. <margin>Book 1, chapter 10.</margin> Heliodorus <note>Author of the ancient Greek novel *Aethiopica*</note> writes that the places among the Nile marshes destined for shepherds were always infamous for robberies and plunder; thus the robbers pounced on others like wild beasts. *Xiphilinus* (page 272) mentions a rebellion that occurred while *Marcus Antoninus* was ruling in Rome, moved in Egypt by *Robbers called the Herdsmen* <note>original Greek: Βουκόλοι καλούμενοι</note>. It is clear that this concerns a certain cruel enemy of the Church; therefore, the royal Prophet asks God to subdue the adversaries or the company of spear-men who repeatedly try to destroy this kingdom by taking up arms. We shall conclude this discussion with the words of *B. Friedl.*: *Destroy the reed-throng, that is, the reed-bearing or arrow-armed crowd.* <margin>Compare page 67.</margin> The latter noun serves in place of an adjective. The Hebrew word primarily signifies a reed in a marsh, in a lampstand, in a writer’s hand, in a measurer’s hand, or in the hand of a balancer—a "steelyard" scale. From this comes the name of *Cana* in Galilee, where Christ graced the wedding with His presence and miracle. Under this metaphor, however, false teachers and their followers are understood, as Luther notes. Especially that beast of the reed, or the one coming out of the waters, the Anti-Christ of Revelation 13, verse 1. This one the Lord Jesus shall destroy with the sword of His mouth (2 Thessalonians 2:8).

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological examination of the Psalms, moving from Psalm 68 to Psalm 110. It transitions from discussing the "beast of the reed" to the symbolic and cultural significance of the "right hand" as mentioned in the famous messianic opening of Psalm 110: "Sit at my right hand."</meta>

->Psalm 110:1.<-
->Sit at my right hand.<- <note>original Hebrew: שב לימיני (Shev li-ymini)</note>
->Sit at my right hand.<- <note>original Greek: Κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν με (Kathou ek dexion me)</note>
->*Sit at my right hand.*<- <note>original Latin: Sede à dextris meis</note>

<margin>The place of the Right Hand.</margin>
**T**hat the right hand held great authority over the left among the ancients, and that much virtue was believed to reside in it, can be proven not by one but by infinite examples from antiquity. Alexander ab Alexandro <note>A 15th-century Neapolitan jurist and scholar</note> conjectures in Book 2, Chapter 29 of his *Genial Days* that there was a certain religious sanctity in right hands; for it is the right hand, he says, that we extend if we promise something will happen by our given word. Among the ancients, the <term>dexiosis</term> <note>original: δεξιοθεσία; the ritual joining of right hands</note> was the symbol of the most certain and inviolable faith. It was customary among the Persians and Parthians to solemnize that which they wished to remain firm and untainted with the right hand, as if it were a pledge of faith. Josephus <margin>Jewish Antiquities, Book 12.</margin> is a witness to this matter, reporting of Artabanus, the King of the Parthians, that he swore to Anilaeus the Jew—*having extended his right hand* by his ancestral gods—that his brother Asinaeus would have safe passage to him. <term>He gave his right hand, which is the greatest pledge of confidence among the barbarians in those parts for those who have dealings with them. For no one would deceive after the giving of the right hand, nor would anyone doubt to believe if such a pledge of security were given, even after a suspicion of wrongdoing had been established.</term> <note>original Greek: δεξιὰν ἔδιδε... καθεστηκότων</note> And therefore, even when Artabanus was urged by his commander of the soldiers to kill Asinaeus, he refused to allow this against a man who had trusted himself to his faith, confirmed by the giving of the right hand and the taking of an oath. And in Xenophon, Gobryas praises the right hand of Cyrus: *For he tells no lie, he says, concerning those things which he has promised.* It is well known that the same was observed among the Romans, as seen in Ammianus Marcellinus, Book 21, concerning a certain Nebridius. When he alone refused to conspire against Constantius, and fled to Julian out of fear of the soldiers who had drawn their swords against him, he humbly begged that Julian might extend his right hand to him for the sake of relieving his fear. Julian said to him: "What special thing will be reserved for my friends if you touch my right hand?" Plutarch records of Marius that when he was cruelly raging against his own citizens with innumerable slaughters, and his attendants were killing everyone they met, those he wished to save he made safe by extending his right hand or by giving a greeting. To this we may also look to the fact that the Kings and Emperors of Germany were formerly accustomed to send their gloves to establish peace and to validate actions where they could not be present in person, as is clear from the *Saxon Mirror* <note>The *Sachsenspiegel*, the most important law book of the German Middle Ages</note> or Saxon Law. The right hand was also offered for the sake of love and peace. This is the aim of Pythagoras’s warning: *The right hand is not to be extended to just anyone*, silently hinting that one should not rashly admit someone into a pact of friendship and familiarity. For just as the <term>dexiosis</term> <note>original: ἀδεξιοθεσία (here likely meaning the ritual act itself)</note> was a sign of peace and friendship, so too, even today, to seriously deny or intentionally withdraw the right hand from one who expects it is usually a clear and infallible sign of open rivalry and enmity. The right hand was also counted among the symbols of happiness, just as the left was called a sign of unhappiness and misery, about which the Palm-readers <note>original: Chiromantæ</note> speak with full

<column-break/>

lips. If you spoke of the <margin>A throne of honor [Greek: τιμῆς θρόνος], or the place of the right hand.</margin> right hand as a place of dignity, you would say nothing contrary to the rites and customs of the ancients. We shall bring to light certain expressions from the Holy Scriptures taken from the right and left. In Ecclesiastes <margin>Chapter 10:2.</margin> there is a passage extremely well-suited to our purpose:
> A wise man’s heart is at his right hand; but a fool’s heart at his left.

The meaning is: a wise man, by his heart (that is, by his counsels), manages his affairs skillfully, quickly, and successfully. On the contrary, a fool, by his heart (that is, his counsels), manages his affairs awkwardly, with difficulty, and unsuccessfully. Therefore, the right hand is a symbol of things successfully managed; the left of things managed unluckily. Nor should it be thought that the Wisest of Kings <note>Solomon</note>, otherwise a most sagacious and skilled teacher of natural things, is speaking here of the physical location of the heart in the human body. For that is the same in all and every man, both foolish and wise, and it is placed neither to the right nor to the left, but in the middle, generally leaning toward the left—a matter we leave to the Physicists and Anatomists to examine. But in this place, as we have said, the right hand is a sign of the favorable administration of one’s affairs, and the left is a sign of unfavorable and less prudent management; so that he who manages his affairs well and successfully seems to have a heart situated on the right side of the body. Patriarch Jacob also indicated a distinction of dignity, honor, and pre-eminence by the example of the right and left <margin>Genesis 48:17.</margin> when, as a sign of pre-eminence and greater dignity over his brother (even though he was the firstborn), he placed his right hand on Ephraim, Joseph’s second-born, but his left on Manasseh, <term>the first in birth</term> <note>original Greek: τῇ γενεᾷ προτέρῳ</note>. And for that reason, when warned by Joseph whether he might have done it by mistake, he replied:
> I know, my son, I know: he also shall become a people, and he also shall be great; but truly his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations.

This task must be carried out by us with great care. Benedictus Arias <note>Arias Montanus, a 16th-century Spanish orientalist</note> collected more on the meaning of the right and left hand in the book *Joseph*, or *On Arcane Speech*, which you may consult. Regarding whether the Right or Left is the more honorable place, Philologists struggle among themselves. Regarding the words of the Psalmist: *Sit at my right hand*, they are accustomed to cite the custom of arranging seating to the right or left. This is a comparison drawn from the custom of Kings, who placed those they wished to treat with honor at their right. Aelius Antonius Nebrissensis <note>Antonio de Nebrija, a Spanish Renaissance scholar</note>, who was an advisor to Cardinal Ximenes, Archbishop of Toledo, in preparing the Complutensian Biblical Work, discusses whether the left place was more honorable to the ancients. *Since among all nations,* he says, *it is a most common custom that he who sits or walks [on the right side]...* <margin>Question 3, Annotation chapter 39.</margin> *he wishes to understand what we read in Psalm 109 <note>Psalm 110 in modern numbering</note>: "Sit at my right hand." For since that Psalm is understood in the literal sense to refer to Christ, and these are the words of the Father to the Son, what could be said more incongruously, or what could be more unseemly, than that the Son should occupy the primary place? Not only here, but in a thousand other places, Holy Scripture testifies that Christ sits at the right hand of the Father; and although He is equal to the Father by nature, yet insofar as He is the Son and insofar as He is man, He ought to yield the primary dignity to the Father. While I was reflecting on this with myself, a certain*
suspicion <note>Catchword for the next page</note>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the symbolic "place of the right hand" in Psalm 110:1. Having established the right hand as a pledge of faith in the previous page, the author now addresses a scholarly controversy: whether the left side was actually considered more honorable than the right in certain ancient cultures and church councils.</meta>

<margin>The place of the Right Hand.</margin>
I suspect that there was another order of seating among the ancients than that which exists in our times, such that, evidently, he who sat on the left was more powerful than he who sat on the right. Joining Nebrissensis <note>Antonio de Nebrija, a Spanish Renaissance scholar</note> is Caesar Baronius <note>A cardinal and ecclesiastical historian</note> in his *Annals*, Volume 2, Year 213, number 6, where he brings forward two arguments from antiquity for the cause of Nebrissensis. The first he took from the custom used by the Romans in <term>apotheosis</term> <note>original Greek: ἀποθεώσει; the process of deifying a deceased emperor</note>. Regarding this, he says that an image made to look as similar as possible to the deceased Emperor was set out in the royal vestibule upon a very large and sublime ivory bed covered with gold cloth; on the left sat the entire Senate clothed in black garments, while on the right sat the matrons whom the dignity of their husbands or parents honored. This was because among the Romans the left side, as Plutarch <note>In *Roman Questions* 78</note>, Varro <note>In *On the Latin Language*, Book 6</note>, and others affirm, was considered of better auspice and therefore held to be more worthy.

<margin>Vol. 3, Year of Christ 325, num. 57, 58.</margin>
$\alpha$. Baronius proposes a second argument regarding the order of seating in the Council of Nicaea <note>The first major ecumenical council in 325 AD</note> in favor of the excellence of the left side over the right. To understand the order of seating, he says, no truer reasoning can be supported than that sought from the example of affairs in other Holy Ecumenical Synods. For of those four older general synods, only the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon <note>Held in 451 AD</note> remain entire. In its first session, the nature of the bishops' assembly in a Synod is clearly demonstrated, as these words are read there:

> While the most magnificent and glorious Judges and the most ample Senate were presiding in the middle before the railings of the most holy altar, the most Holy and Reverend Bishops and the Vicars of the most God-beloved, Holy, and Reverend Leo, Bishop of the ancient city of Rome, and Anatolius, the most religious Archbishop of the royal city of Constantinople, and Maximus, the most religious Bishop of Antioch, etc., were sitting on the left side. And a little later: On the right side, likewise, sat Dioscorus, the most religious Bishop of Alexandria, and Juvenal, the Bishop of Jerusalem.

Since these things are found arranged regarding the site and order of seating in the Synod of Chalcedon—and without doubt they followed the ancient and customary order of things, namely, that which the Fathers did when they sat in the Council of Nicaea, as well as those of Constantinople and Ephesus—who would not understand that the left place was esteemed by them to be holier and more worthy? So he says. This opinion also appealed to Robert Bellarmine <note>A highly influential Jesuit theologian</note>, who opposes this sentiment of Nebrissensis to the argument of our own theologians <note>referring to Protestants/Lutherans</note> regarding the real communication of Divine Majesty derived from the "sitting at the right hand" in Book 3 of *The Incarnation of Christ*, chapter 15. Compare on this opinion Drusius, *Epistolary Questions* 117, and Binius, Volume 1 of the *Councils*, page 314.

<margin>Vol. 2, *Leisure Hours*, Book 2, ch. 5.</margin>
This opinion of Nebrissensis is pleasing to Lælius Bisciola*,

<column-break/>

and he praises it as ingenious and solid on page 748, citing other authors: Bartholomew Cassanæus in *Catalog of the Glory of the World*, part 3, consideration 2; Cornelius Jansenius in his *Commentary on the Harmony of the Gospels*, chapter 150; Giovanni Tommaso Minadoi of Rovigo in his *History of the Turko-Persian War of 1577*; and Abbot Joachim in part 1 of his *Exposition on the Apocalypse*, chapter 2. In the progression of his work, however, he opposes arguments from antiquity to each individual argument that the former brings for the superior place being on the left. Finally, on page 758, he concludes, though hardly consistent with himself: "These things can rightly be objected to Nebrissensis, yet I do not reject his explanation, but praise and approve it; and perhaps it should be distinguished thus: that only in sacred and divine matters was the left superior, while in other human and civil offices the right was more honorable; and yet I still hold this as uncertain." Hermann Lignaridus follows the same opinion in his *Academic Delights*, chapter 45. There were also ancient divisions of opinion on this between Justus Lipsius and Johannes Goropius Becanus; the latter deems the left more honorable, the former the right. Their arguments are found in *Elections*, Book 2, chapter 2 and *Letters*, century 1, epistle 90. Bisciola* also responds to the arguments of Baronius: "From this ancient rite," he says, "as it is in the ancient Order of the Roman Church, they sat in that local arrangement so that the Bishops were to the left for those entering the Church, and the priests to the right; so that when the Pontiff—that is, the Pope—sat and looked toward them, he would have the Bishops on his right and the Priests on his left." Furthermore, it is established from the modern custom of the Orientals, especially the Turks, that they prefer the left to the right and hold the place of the left as more honorable than the right. Thus the left is more honorable at the court of the King of the Tartars; for Marco Polo <note>original: Paulus Venetus</note> writes of King Kublai <note>Book 2, chapter 13, p. 367</note> that the pomp observed in the King's Banquets is celebrated in this order: The King turns his face toward the south, having on his left the Senior Queen (the principal wife), and on his right his sons and grandsons and those of the royal lineage. Besoldus notes this same thing from Baronius Budovicius's *Horologium*, page 51, in his *Consideration of the Mohammedan or Saracen Sect*, page 10, where he says that Muhammad teaches that all who obey the Quran are most dear to God and will be placed on the left in the final judgment of God. This is because with God the left side is in greater honor (contrary to all the testimonies of Scripture, which were very often confirmed by Muhammad himself; see *Sura* <note>original: Azoar</note> 37). Because of this, even now, all Turks exhibiting reverence to someone in walking, sitting, or riding, offer the left side. These things may be observed from the daily custom of the Turks, which, since it draws its origin from the Agarene law <note>The "law of Hagar," a term used for Islam</note>, cannot prescribe a law for us regarding the ancient custom of the Orientals. Instead, we should follow the guidance of Holy Scripture, which pronounces the right hand more honorable than the left. Regarding this opinion, Baronius finally agreed—stepping away from the "left-hand" supporters <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῶν εὐωνύμων (from those on the left)</note>—in Volume 2 of his *Ecclesiastical Annals*, Year 213, number 7, where he confesses that among the Hebrews the right was superior.

<margin>The Right Hand is the place of the Hebrews.</margin>
<margin>Comm. on Epistle to the Hebrews, num. 2.</margin>
And Francisco Ribera* distinguishes between common preference among nations and among the Hebrews. Regarding the preference for the left among many other nations, he agrees with Goropius and Antonio; however, he denies that among the Hebrews the left was more powerful than the right. But Benedictus Pererius, in his *Commentary on Genesis* chapter 48, records that among the Hebrews the right part was held to be more honorable according to nature. This controversy is treated at greater length by B. Dorscheus in *Pentadec. Disputation* 13, thesis 17; and B. Danhauer in volume 10, chapter 15; B. Dilherr in *Dialogues*; Cornelius à Lapide on Proverbs 3; Rivetus; and Gomarus. Therefore, to sit at the right hand among men signifies having a more honorable place; but with God, it is to preside over all things with equal divine power, omnipotence, authority, and kingship. Since this "Sitting," attributed to Christ as a man, transcends the limits of philology, it includes certain mysteries about which philologists are partly concerned, but theologians are very much preoccupied.

<summary>This page explores the historical and theological debate over whether the right or left side was the seat of honor in antiquity, referencing Roman, Ecumenical Council, and Eastern customs before concluding that Scripture and Hebrew tradition prioritize the right hand as a symbol of divine power.</summary>

Using Proverbs 17:6 and 18:22 as a foundation, the author explores the "Household Crown," discussing the necessity and virtues of a good wife through the lens of classical philosophy, Rabbinic tradition, and early Christian fathers.</meta>

<header>From Proverbs 17, verse 6. Chapter 18, verse 22. 509</header>

### Proverbs XVII. v. 6. Chapter XVIII. v. 22.

->Children's children are the crown of old men, and the glory of children are their fathers.<-
<note>original Hebrew: עטרת זקנים בני בנים ותפארת בנים אבותם</note>
<note>original Greek: Στέφανος γερόντων τέκνα τέκνων, καύχημα δὲ τέκνων πατέρες αὐτῶν.</note>
->*Children's children are the crown of old men, and the glory of children are their fathers.*<-

---

->Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth favor from the Lord.<-
<note>original Hebrew: מצא אשה מצא טוב ויפק רצון מיהוה</note>
<note>original Greek: Ὃς εὗρε γυναῖκα ἀγαθὴν, εὗρε χάριτας, ἔλαβε δὲ παρὰ Κυρίου ἱλαρότητα.</note>
->*He who finds a wife finds a good thing, and has drawn benevolence from Jehovah.*<-

<margin>The Household Crown.</margin>
**T**HERE are three principal goods: *To be well-born; to be well-married; to be well-died.* <note>That is, to have a "good death" or a blessed passing.</note> One ought not to be called "well-born" if he is not "well-married." A wife should be chosen with the eyes, the ears, and the hands: with the eyes, that she may be of a comely face; with the ears, that she may be a lover of virtue and honesty; with the hands, that she may be wealthy. That is indeed a rare "three-leaf clover," <note>original: *trifolium*</note> but it must be sought from God through legitimate means. Hence Aristotle says in his *Economics, book 1, chapter 3*: <note>original Greek: Πρώτην εἰσαγωγὴν κατὰ γυναῖκα ἐπιμέλειαν</note> "The first introduction and primary care concerns the taking of a wife," for without her, a home can in no way exist. For he who lacks a wife does not have a fixed home, and if he does have one, he dwells in it not as the Father of the Household, but as a traveler in an inn. For a wife is the firmament of the house, as Afranius writes in *The Stepson*: *A wife is the firmament of any family.* And Rabbi Jose <margin>in the Tractate Shabbat, folio 118a.</margin> skillfully called his wife "his house" <note>original Hebrew: ביתי</note> because she is the "foundation of the house," <note>original Hebrew: עיקר הבית</note> as the commentator explains there. For domestic affairs, over which the wife ought to be set, cannot go well unless they are established, governed, and composed by the prudence, care, and industry of the principal woman, who is called the Mother of the Household. Therefore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> wants the first care to be concerning the wife, as the second foundation and "fence" of the house; for a house without a wife is a garden without a fence, a chamber without a key, a ship without a keel. He who plants vines soon fortifies them with a fence, lest they be devoured by beasts; how much more is it right to provide a woman, the fence of the house, lest the family estate go to ruin. This is what Sirach <note>The author of the Wisdom of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus</note> meant when he said, *chapter 36, verse 27*: <note>original Greek: Οὗ οὐκ ἔστι Φραγμὸς, διαρπαγήσεται κτῆμα, ὅπερ ἔστι γυνὴ, ὃν οὐκ ἔχει πλανώμενος</note> *Where there is no fence, the possession will be plundered; and where there is no wife, the wandering man groans.* Most accurately and expertly is the wife called the "fence of the house," and a "fenced estate" is where a woman is in the home. If the fence is removed, it is inevitable that the house falls into plunder. What he says about the "wandering man" is stated in contrast to the preceding verse, where he mentions marriage in these words: *He who has acquired a wife begins a possession, a helpmate like himself and a pillar of rest,* which Drusius <note>Johannes Drusius, a Flemish Protestant Hebraist</note> translates: *He who has acquired a wife has the beginning of a possession, a help suited to him and a column of repose.* For marriage is "rest," as the <margin>Chapter 1, verse 9.</margin> author of the book of Ruth expressly names it, in which we lead a quiet life (*Sirach 26:2*), and it is the "harbor of youth," which Plutarch mentions somewhere. The Hebrew word *Chuppah* <note>original Hebrew: חופה</note>—used for the nuptial chamber in *Psalm 19:6* and *Joel 2:16*—aims at this same meaning; there, as if in a harbor, the bride lies safe with the bridegroom, and in the harbor

<column-break/>

she sails, as it were; for the Hebrew word for "harbor" is *Choph*, from the root *Chafaf*, <margin>The Household Crown.</margin> meaning "he protected," because it is a protection for ships from the winds. So also is marriage; if the heat of desires carries youth into the deep of lust, it is a remedy for incontinence and a harbor for youth on account of the tranquility of the mind, which is then free from all disturbance. For before marriage, the young lover wanders about "wandering" <note>original Greek: πλανώμενος</note> and never rests; and as there are tides in the sea, so in the mind of the youth, in the midst of a sea of desires, are disturbances. For the mind, driven by love, always wanders, and can neither suffer nor endure; it never ceases to desire, as Plautus says of this: <margin>Cistellaria, Act 2, scene 1, line 4.</margin>

> I am tossed, tortured, driven, goaded; I turn, wretched, on the wheel of love.
> I am breathless, carried away, distracted, torn apart; I have such a clouded mind, 
> where I am, I am not; where I am not, there is my mind.

Therefore, so that the young man may be free from cares and be found an upright father of a household, let him above all be solicitous to provide himself with a wife who is *a healer of the troubled soul, a diligent increaser of the home, and a provident nurse of children*; that he may also have her as a partner in prosperity and uncertainty, a consort in both adverse and fruitful times. For the house requires the mutual support of the male and female, which Xenophon <margin>Economics, chapter 7.</margin> also teaches in these words: "I think that a wife who is a good partner in the home is a perfect counterbalance to the man for the sake of the good. For possessions come into the house for the most part through the actions of the man." He elegantly calls the wife a "counterbalance" <note>original Greek: ἀντίῤῥοπον</note> to the man for the sake of the good, for the wife is the other part of the husband and, as it were, a "yoke-mate" <note>original Greek: ἀντίζυγος</note> who both adheres to him perpetually and aids and consoles his labors, and performs for him services which he cannot do for himself in the "fellowship of life, in the procreation of children, and in the management of the house," as Chrysostom says. <margin>Homily 20 on Ephesians, p. 870, Volume 3.</margin> Hence in the Sacred Scriptures, Eve, and with her every wife, is called a "helper," <note>original Hebrew: עזר</note> *Genesis 2:18, Tobit 8:8.*
*A Helper / so that the woman shall help and advise the man in the house / as says the author of the Dialogue, printed in Munich 1520 by Johann Schobser, with the title: The Well of Counsel.* For there is much protection for a man in the Mother of the Household, that she be at hand "like unto him," <note>original Hebrew: כנגדו</note> as the Greek interpreters faithfully rendered it, or, as Onkelos and Jonathan <note>Aramaic translators of the Torah</note> say, "in his presence," <note>original Aramaic: כקבלה</note> that is, that she might be an inseparable companion of life who adheres to the husband himself, "as one coming forth with him," <note>original Aramaic: כד נפיק בה</note> as the *Jerusalem Targum* explains that phrase "like unto him." Thus is the wife described, and her duty: that she be "one who moves around with the man" (*Sirach 25:2*), who is moved, as it were, at the nod of the man like an inseparable companion; that she be like a merchant ship (*Prov 31:14*) because she brings many benefits with her; the "light of the house" (*Sirach 26:19*); the "relief of the man" (*Ecclesiastes 4:11*). Nor is there any other solace for the upright except from marriage, which Agrippina says in Tacitus <margin>Annals, Book 4, 53.</margin> when requesting a husband from Tiberius. From this, the wife is also called the "harbor of the man" who has fallen into sorrow, according to Naumachius in *Stobaeus's Sermons*:
*For to a man who is busy, a wife is a consolation.*
Which Gregory Nazianzen, in his *Admonitions to Olympias*, said by changing one word:
*For to a man who is busy, a wife is a harbor for mooring.*
Whence, according to Chrysostom, even marriage itself is called a "harbor" and a "refuge" and a "consolation" for those...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Household Crown" from page 509, focusing on the virtues of a good wife and the importance of her character and lineage in ensuring a happy domestic life.</meta>

<page-num>510</page-num>
<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<column-break/>

<margin>The Household Crown:</margin>
"A woman is the greatest of evils, and yet she is a harbor," <note>original Greek: μέγισον κακῶν, καὶ γ’ ἀλιμένιν ἐσιν ἡ γυνὴ</note> says John Chrysostom in his *26th Homily on 1 Corinthians, page 415*. For if some accident or a heavy illness pins a husband to his bed, she is ready at hand to sit by him, to console him, to offer her hand, to call the physician, to prepare remedies, and to do everything possible so that he might be restored. *But woe to him who is alone when he falls, and has not another to lift him up*, as it says in Ecclesiastes 4:10. Thus, when a man falls—if any sorrows or inconveniences happen to him—the companionship of a wife softens and takes away half of the misfortune. Valerius Maximus (Book 4, chapter 6), drawing from Plutarch’s *Life of Pompey*, records this of Hypsicratea, the wife of Mithridates: <note>Hypsicratea was the queen of Pontus who famously accompanied her husband Mithridates VI into exile, dressing as a man to stay by his side.</note> her great loyalty in harsh and difficult circumstances was to Mithridates "the greatest consolation and the most pleasant relief." For there is nothing so adverse that it does not become less so through her, and nothing so joyful that it does not appear brighter through her conversation. "For the companionship of those joined in marriage is more dear; good things are sweeter together, and difficult things are lighter with one another," <note>original Greek: φιλαίτερον γὰρ κοινωνία συζυγέντες, ηδιώλα τὰ ἀγαθὰ σὺν ἀλλήλοις, ὦ τὰ δυσχερῆ κουφότερα μετ’ ἀλλήλων</note> as Lucian says in *The Loves, page 206*. 

So too for Cicero, his most faithful wife Terentia was his only consolation in adversity, as will be clear to anyone reading the letters he sent to her in haste; though I often look for the "Cicero in Cicero" there, for I see the Philosopher so softened and dejected that he wrote nothing but womanly letters, filling everything with complaints. Even the most afflicted Terentia did not find in her husband "a limitless help of strength," <note>original Greek: ἄσπετον ἄλκας ἀ’ νύης</note> that great relief from cares which Briseis praises in Achilles in the works of Quintus Calabrus.
<margin>Book 3, verse 563.</margin>

Elizabeth, the wife of Christian II, King of the Danes, preferred to be the companion and partner of all her husband’s hardships and exiles rather than to flourish in a kingdom, peaceful and safe, without her husband; as David Chytraeus testifies in his *Oration on Marriage*. See other examples in the elegant treatise written in Dutch on the *Excellence of the Female Sex* by Johan van Beverwijck (Book 3, chapter 5). Moreover, if joyful things happen to a husband, the pleasure is doubled because it is poured into the bosom of a most sweet spouse; nor is there any greater charm for men than from charming little wives. For it is the wife’s part to "gladden the man," <note>original Greek: εὐφραίνειν τὸν ἀνδρα</note> as in Sirach 26:2; and "it is not fitting for Juno to be gloomy toward her Jupiter," as Plautus says. Likewise, Martial (Epigrams 10.47) numbers among the parts of a happier life:

-> a bed not gloomy, yet modest. <-

Therefore, if you wish to live in cheerfulness and fulfill the years of your life in peace, above all things provide yourself with a *good wife*, as Ben-Syra warns in his *Proverbs, page 62*: "A good wife—blessed is the man; the number of his days will be doubled." <note>original Hebrew: אשה טובה אשרי איש מספר ימיו כפלים</note> She is called a "good heart" there, which in the same sense the Latins call a "good wife" (*uxor bona*)—that is, dutiful, compliant, and frugal, who cares for domestic matters well. He who finds such a woman "finds a good thing," as the Wise Man testifies. Cicero used the term this way in *Philippic 3*: "The father of your wife, a good woman, was a certain Bombatio."
<margin>Book 3, Annals.</margin>
Ennius says: *

-> A good woman washed and anointed the body of Tarquin. <-

The best part of a house and the beginning of possessions is a GOOD WIFE, to be preferred above all riches. "Of all things, the best is a noble marriage bed," <note>original Greek: τῶν πάντων ὁ δ’ ἄριςος, γενναῖον λέχος</note> says Menander in *Andromeda*, where in the word "noble" (*gennaion*) there is the meaning of a generous nature, applied to all things that are excellent by nature. With this agrees that saying of Simonides found in Clement of Alexandria: "A man gains no prize better than a good wife." With an elegant 

<column-break/>

metaphorical misuse of the word (*catachresis*), <term>Catachresis: The use of a word in a way that departs from its traditional meaning, here calling a wife a "prize" or "booty."</term> he says there is no better "plunder" than a good and provident wife. He seems to have taken this maxim from Hesiod (*Works and Days, verse 700*):
> For a man wins nothing better than a good wife,
> nor anything worse than a bad one.

The more beneficial a part of the house the wife is, the more accurately one must provide—according to the Philosopher—lest we receive a bad one. For as the poet of Ascra <note>Hesiod</note> immediately added:
> ...of the bad wife, nothing is more chilling.

It is no small part of human happiness and blessedness to have a "favorable marriage," for it was not said without reason in the tragedy of Euripides, in the words of Orestes (verse 601):
> For those mortals whose marriages are well established,
> life is blessed. But for those that do not turn out well,
> they are unfortunate both within the house and without.

And Lucian says in *The Loves, page 236*: "Marriage is a life-benefiting and blessed barrier for men, whenever they are fortunate in it." But so that things may turn out according to one's wish, they warn us first to properly consider the birth and lineage; for it is likely that from the good, good children are born. 
<margin>Aristotle, Book 1, Rhetoric.</margin>
Aristotle says: * "It is likely that from the good, a good person is born, and one who is well-raised will be such." It is not consistent with nature for a woman who is well-bred and educated to be otherwise than an imitator of her ancestral virtue. He who is of sound mind should, above all things, diligently inquire into the quality of the wife and the life of her father and mother, remembering the saying:

-> *The fierce eagle does not* <-
-> *beget the unwarlike dove.* <-

Children greatly imitate the character of their parents, as Juvenal defines it (*Satire 6, verse 235*):

-> *Shall a mother pass on honest character,* <-
-> *or any other than what she herself possesses?* <-

The same Euripides urged in *Andromache (verse 619)* that a man about to marry should first consider with whom he is contracting an alliance, and from what house he receives a wife:
> ...do not take into your house
> the foal of a bad woman, for she will turn out
> like her mother. Consider this for me,
> you suitors: take a daughter from a good mother.
<margin>page 712</margin>
Where the Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator on the text.</note> notes: * "For children from bad mothers are molded by their mothers' insults, and they bring their mothers' designs into their marriages." These words have so affected me that I cannot yet leave that Poet, whose concluding exclamation to the play should be known to all who are about to marry; it is of such a kind (verse 1279) that it deserves a great "Bravo!"
> Therefore, one must marry from the noble,
> and give one's children to the good, if one counsels well,
> and have no desire for an evil marriage bed,
> even if she brings an immense dowry to the house.
> For they would never fare badly from the gods.

Those who give "the first care" to the largest dowry (the "immense dowries" he mentions), while neglecting the most excellent part, consult the interests of their household in the worst way. Thus it happens that in the midst of wealth, they often become destitute. A man is not to be judged by his wealth if he prefers riches over a wife. It is the part of an upright man to inquire first into the piety and education of her whom he is to marry; and the rest, by God's blessing, will easily be added. This man's hope will not fail him; he will establish a safe house, a rich house, a righteous house; and furthermore, divine mercy will add...

# Proverbs XVII. v. 6. Chapter XVIII. v. 22.

<margin>The Household Crown.</margin>
> As piety is the form, so beauty in turn joined
> to piety, may they perform equal service in an honorable body.

How negligent and improvident most people are in choosing a mother of the household from good stock <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῶ γένους</note> is a complaint made by Phocylides (lines 191 and following), calling those people foolish who seek out noble horses and strong bulls, but are completely lazy when it comes to seeking a noble wife. Let us bring forth his verses in full:

> You seek well-bred horses for your house,
> and long-necked bulls, and wide-ranging hounds.
> But as for marrying, the foolish seek out a "good" woman <note>meaning a woman of high social status rather than high character</note> without thinking.
> <note>original Greek: Ἵππους δ᾽ εὐγενέας δίζεσθ᾽ μὲν κατὰ οἶκον, Ταύρους δ᾽ ὑψιτένοντας, ἀτὰρ σκυλάκων παναχείας. Γῆμαι δὲ, ἢν ἀγαθὴν ἐπιδαίμονεν ἀφρονέοντες.</note>

Following exactly the same sentiment, Theognis <margin>lines 183 and following</margin> rebukes that shameful custom where men take greater care over the breeding of sheep and pack animals than they do over the procreation of children. His words to Cyrnus are:

> We seek out rams and asses, Cyrnus, and horses
> Of noble breed, and a man wishes them to spring from good stock;
> But a good man does not hesitate to marry the base daughter of a base father,
> If she brings him much wealth.
> <note>original Greek: Κριὸς μὲν καὶ ὄνες δίζημεθα Κύρνε, καὶ ἵππους Εὐγενέας, καί τις βούλεται ἐξ ἀγαθῶν Βήσεσθ᾽, γῆμαι δὲ κακὴν κακῶ ἐ μελιδαίνει Ἐσθλὸς ἀνὴρ, ἢν οἱ χρήματα πολλὰ διδῷ.</note>

Regarding these verses, we cannot provide a better paraphraser than Xenophon, whose words we add for the sake of clearer meaning, as they appear in Stobaeus <margin>Sermon 86</margin>, which is about Nobility. "For his reasoning seems to me to be correct regarding the poetry. For he begins first from the lineage. For he thought that a man, like anything else, could not be good unless those who generated him were good. He decided to use other animals as examples, those which are not raised randomly, but are cared for with skill so that they might be born most noble." He shows this in these verses: *rams and asses*, and what follows from Theognis, where note that he used "without harm" <note>original Greek: ἀβλαβῶς</note> in place of "to mount." <note>original Greek: βίσεσθαι</note> Therefore, be a cautious merchant, lest in marriages you look only at gold and copper while despising nobility of mind and character. If we seek noble dogs and horses from good ancestry, if in vines, trees, and seeds the best variety is calculated; much more so should a wife be sought from the best stock. In purchasing a field, we consider the nature of the soil in which we wish to sow. You should care more for this regarding a future spouse, from whom you desire to "sow" children; for here "one must consider from what sort of women the best children might be born to you, with whom we unite to produce children," as Xenophon advises in *Memorabilia*, book 2, page 432. For the kind of spouse you have, such will be the offspring you obtain; there is a certain hidden transition of the soul's affections into the bodies, and again of the bodies into the soul, "for there is a mixing of soul with soul," <note>original Greek: εστὶ γὰρ πρόσμιξις ψυχῆς τῇ ψυχῇ</note> according to Hippocrates, *On the Regimen of Health*, book 1, page 15. If we are careful when buying slaves, cattle, and houses, how much more so when we are to take a wife; which is also required by St. Chrysostom <margin>Volume 8 of his Works, page 81</margin> in his discourse on women and beauty; and more extensively by Stefano Guazzo in *On Civil Conversation*, book 3, page 276; and Anton Mokerus in *On Pious and Liberal Discipline*, book 1, chapter 4. According to Cardanus in *On Gaining Utility from Adversity*, book 3, chapter 3, page 931, seven things must be considered in the choice of a wife: a healthy body, age, a form prone to generation <note>fertility</note>, qualities of the mind, education, relatives, and dowry. Read about these in that same place, and at the same time remember regarding the whole book that he teaches many things for which it would have been better for him to have been obedient to this precept of Horace in *The Art of Poetry*, line 183:

<column-break/>

->yet do not bring onto the stage<-
> things worthy of being done within, and remove many things
> from sight.

<margin>The Household Crown.</margin> From natural desire and instinct, not from choice, says the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>, comes the conjugal society. Nature does not just invite men to fellowship <note>original Greek: κοινωνίαν</note>—those who are truly men—for in all of them there is by nature an appetite and impulse toward "pairing" <note>original Greek: πρὸς συνδυασμόν</note>; hence it is elegantly called a "tyranny of nature" <note>original Greek: τὴ φύσει τυραννὶς</note> by Chrysostom (Volume 3, page 492). From this necessity of male and female comes "pairing" <note>original Greek: συνδυασμός</note>. "For it is necessary for those who cannot exist without each other to be paired," in *Politics*, book 2—words which St. Thomas Aquinas refers specifically to conjugal society. Thus, certainly, nature itself joined male with female, and not either of these with their own sex; which the author of the book *On the Universe* (who goes by the name of Aristotle) expressed in these words: "just as nature brought together the male to the female, and each to its own kind." <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ τὸ ἄῤῥεν συνήγαγεν (ἡ φύσις) πρὸς τὸ θῆλυ, & ἑκάτερον πρὸς τὸ ὁμόφυλον</note> For humans in both sexes are generated by this law of nature, that they seek and generate their like, live like with like in society, and leave behind others of the same kind after them. Valerius Maximus, book 9, chapter 9, number 1: "Nature writes for us the law of being born, just as the law of begetting." Compare this with the words of the Emperor’s *Institutes on Natural Law, the Law of Nations, and Civil Law*, which says that the union of male and female descends from natural law. "Natural law is," (he says) "that which nature has taught all animals. For this law is not unique to the human race, but belongs to all animals born in the sky, on the earth, and in the sea. From this descends the union of male and female, which we call marriage; from this the procreation of children, and from this their education." Theophilus the Paraphraser translates it this way <note>into Greek</note> on page 10: "An example of natural law is the union of male and female, which we call marriage, and the upbringing of those who are born," etc. <note>original Greek: Παράδειγμα δὲ φυσικῶ νομίμῳ, ἄῤῥενός τε καὶ θηλείας συνάφεια, ὅπερ ἡμεῖς γάμον προσαγορεύομεν, καὶ ἡ περὶ τὰς τεχθέντας ἀνατροφή</note> Aristotle, to prove the Political axiom that "the city exists by nature," begins from man; regarding whom he teaches in *Politics*, book 1, chapter 2, that it is by nature that an animal is civil and born for society: "a political animal by nature" <note>original Greek: φύσει πολιτικὸν ζῶον</note>; which Stobaeus also has in the same words in *Ethical Extracts*, book 2, page 195: "a social animal" <note>original Greek: κοινωνικὸν ζῶον</note> in *Eudemian Ethics*, book 7, from the beginning, and "a lover of others" <note>original Greek: φιλάλλολον</note>, in Stobaeus, same place, page 185. From this, Antonius Codrus <margin>Sermon 4</margin> infers: If man is a political animal, i.e., civil; what civil life is more beautiful, what union more beautiful, than that from which "two are in one flesh." For it was so wisely instituted by God that man should not be alone (Genesis 2:18), but there should be two humans, male and female, necessary for generation and the preservation of the species, living "into one flesh" <note>original Greek: εἰς σάρκα μίαν</note> <margin>Matthew 19:5</margin> through the mingling in marriage; and "into one soul" <note>original Greek: εἰς ψυχὴν μίαν</note> through the joining of mutual love and the association of affections and the inseparable companionship of the whole of life. Truly, nothing greater can be said than such a communion of body and union of spirit, where two seem to have passed into one, and who have the same "to will" and the same "not to will," which is ultimately a firm marital union. Union of the body without communion of the spirit is a sugared poison. Chrysostom discourses elegantly on this matter in Volume 4, page 157, in his last homily on Corinthians: "God devised that he might divide the one into two from the beginning, wishing to show that even what is divid—" <note>the text cuts off mid-word</note>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

...to be divided, and for one to be sufficient for procreation. <note>original Greek: διαιρεθῆναι καὶ εἰς μὲν εἶναι ἀρκεῖν πρὸς τὴν γέννησιν</note> And Clement in his *Constitutions* <margin>Household Crown, Book VII, chapter 3.</margin> says: *There shall be two in one flesh. For man and woman are equal in Nature, in shared mind, in union, in disposition, in life, and in manner; but they are separated in form and number.* <note>original Greek: Ἔσονται δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν. Ἐν γὰρ ἴσῳ ἀνὴρ καὶ γυνὴ τῇ Φύσει, τῇ συμπανοίᾳ, τῇ ἑνώσει, τῇ διαθέσει, τῷ βίῳ, τῷ τρόπῳ κεχωρισμένοι δέ εἰσι τῷ σχήματι καὶ τῷ ἀριθμῷ.</note> Luther (Volume 7, Jena edition, page 253a) writes: **God** created man and woman in such a way that they should come together with pleasure and love, with will and from the heart; thus, bridal love and the marital will are natural things implanted and given by **God**. For this reason, the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle</note> spoke excellently, taught by the law of nature, saying that nature could not be fulfilled by a woman without a man, nor a man without a woman; and therefore this domestic society was established by necessity, both because it was necessary for the propagation of the human race and because it contributes greatly to a pleasant life. As he also says <margin>Politics, Book 1, chapter 2.</margin> all humans are carried toward political society by a certain innate force of nature, a natural impulse and inclination—which the Greeks, as they do with everything, aptly call *hormēn* <note>original Greek: ὁρμὴν</note>—as the supreme Divinity disposes. He says "the impulse toward such fellowship is in all by nature. But he who first established it is the cause of the greatest goods." <note>original Greek: φύσει ἡ ὁρμὴ ἐν πᾶσιν ἐπὶ τὴν τοιαύτην κοινωνίαν. ὁ δὲ πρῶτος συστήσας, μεγίστων ἀγαθῶν αἴτιος.</note> In much the same sense, the Stoics say that "the primary impulse of a living creature is directed toward self-preservation, Nature having made it dear to itself from the beginning." <note>original Greek: τὴν πρώτην... ὁρμὴν ζώου ἐκκειμένην τὸ τηρεῖν ἑαυτὸ, οἰκειούσης αὐτῷ τῆς Φύσεως ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς.</note> Which Cicero, in the fourth book of *On Ends*, translates: *We are commended to ourselves, and we have this first appetite from nature, that we should preserve ourselves.* What union could exist that is holier or more pleasant, what society safer, what unity closer or more chaste, than that of husband and wife? In this chaste fellowship <note>original Greek: κοινωνίᾳ</note>, *all things are common*; the place they inhabit; the *table* where they take food together; the spring from which they draw water; the *hearth and fire* where they warm themselves; the *bed* in which they refresh themselves at night, exhausted by daily labors; the fields from which they procure what is necessary for the sustenance of life. For the sake of these things, they help one another *for the sake of living well* <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὸ εὖ εἶναι</note>, where love is instilled in the beloved; each of them is the same as the other, one spirit in twin bodies, two bodies in one conforming mind. One grieves with the other's pain, and one rejoices in the other's joy. One depends on the other and rests in the other, and to speak with Catullus regarding *Acme and Septimius* (line 20):

> They love, and are loved, with mutual souls.

They share the same chest, the same riches, the same poverty; a common increase in profit, and a common fortune. To her, who is joined to us by such a bond of charity, we entrust ourselves no less than to our own selves, making her the most faithful treasurer of the house and the partner of every fortune; indeed, even the Mistress of our body, according to 1 Corinthians 7:4, for as it stands there, *the husband does not have authority over his own body.* <note>original Greek: ὁ ἀνὴρ ἐκ ἰδίου σώματὸς ἐξουσιάζει.</note> For marriage makes one common body out of two, so that there is a mutual right of one over the other *for the purpose of procreation.* <note>original Greek: ἕνεκα τῆς τεκνοποιΐας.</note> It is therefore not so much a *fellowship of bodies* <note>original Greek: κοινωνία τῶν σωμάτων</note>, from which the procreation of offspring flows, as it is a *fellowship of character and resources.* <note>original Greek: τῶν ἠθῶν καὶ χρημάτων.</note> Pollux says: *Marriage may be called a joining together, a meeting of man and woman, a cohabitation, a possession, and a fellowship for the sowing of children.* <note>original Greek: ὁ γάμος καλοῖτ᾿ ἂν καὶ συνδιασμός, καὶ σύνοδος ἀνδρὸς καὶ γυναικὸς, καὶ συνόικησις, καὶ σύνεξις, καὶ κοινωνία ἐπὶ παίδων σπορᾷ.</note> <margin>3 Onomasticon 3. section 4, page 138.</margin> Aristotle records that this society and friendship is a truly sacred thing, made not by human means but by divine means *under the deity*. <note>original Greek: ὑπὸ τῷ θείῳ</note>

<column-break/>

And Hierocles, in his *Book on Marriage*, <margin>Household Crown.</margin> celebrates it as "the first and most fundamental of fellowships." <note>original Greek: πρώτην καὶ στοιχειωδεστάτην τῶν κοινωνιῶν</note> Even that impious jester Lucian, in his *Affairs of the Heart* (page 196), cannot help but acknowledge something divine in this union when he writes: *Nature, having sown a common desire in both sexes, has yoked them to one another by a holy law of necessity.* <note>original Greek: Κοινὸν ἀμφοτέρῳ γένει πόθον ἐγκατασπαμένη (Φύσις) συνέζευξεν ἀλλήλοις θεσμὸν ἀνάγκης ὅσιον.</note> <margin>page 750.</margin> Plutarch also, in his *Dialogue on Love*, believed it was *according to a most sacred yoking*, <note>original Greek: κατὰ ζεῦξιν ἱερωτάτην</note> indicating that this mutual bond of charity and benevolence is most holy, such that it cannot easily be torn asunder by any external injuries. This is also proven by the names and words by which marriage is compared to a bond, and a very close one at that. For a man is said *to be glued* <note>original Greek: προσκολλᾶσθαι; Latin: agglutinari</note> to his wife (Matthew 19:5), whom God *has yoked together* (verse 6). <note>original Greek: συνέζευξεν</note> From this comes *syzygia* <note>meaning a pair or a union</note> and *those under the yoke*, referring to persons who have married; and Aristotle uses *syzeuxis* in the same sense in *Politics*, Book 7, chapter 15, and the verb *syzeugnynai* <note>to yoke together</note> regarding the marital union in chapter 16; likewise *parental yoking* in the same chapter, page 212. This also occurs among the Hebrews with the word *immar* <note>original: אמר</note> which corresponds with *yoking* and *joining*; for it means *I join in marriage, I combine.* From this comes the noun *conjugium* <note>marriage/joining</note> in the *Bereshit Rabba* <note>a collection of ancient Jewish explanations of Genesis</note>, section 58, at the beginning. Also among the Latins, marriage is called *conjugium* from *jugum* <note>yoke</note>, because the male and female are *under an equal yoke* (Martial, *Epigrams*, Book 4, 13, line 8) and *joined together* into one flesh for an inseparable life-partnership; for the prefix "con-" means "together," just as those who are in a single yoke are in a *shared yoking*. <note>original Greek: ἐν ὁμοζυγίῳ</note> <margin>Law 4, section 1, Digest on the Law.</margin> They are bound and gathered together *to love one another with an equal yoke*, and to bear the labors of a single household with combined strength. Hence Juno, *from the yoking of the female to the male*, was called *Zygia* <note>The Yoker</note>, or *Juga* and *Jugatina* by the Latins, because they believed she joined marriages together, as Festus testifies, and as Virgil sings in the *Aeneid*, Book 4, line 59:

> To whom the yoking chains are a care.

That yoking bond, as the same poet names it in verse 16, Plutarch calls "the most secure bond of youth"; <margin>Book on the Education of Children, page 13.</margin> which our Johannes Fischart rendered in our native tongue: **Marital marriage is the most secure fettering and the best bit that one can put on youth.** This is appropriate; for lust in young people *has a slippery nature*, <note>original Greek: ὀλισθήσασαν ἔχει Φύσιν</note> (Greek Anthology, Book 2, 7, line 3) *and for one who is yoked under the bonds of marriage, mad desires and impulses that are hard to restrain and certain erotic distresses disturb them*, as Basil says in his *Epistle to Gregory of Nazianzus on Solitude*. *This childish luxury must be bound with nuptial shackles*, as Apuleius says in the *Metamorphoses*, Book 6, page 279. Arnobius, in the 5th book *Against the Heathen* (page 97), said *to bind a young man with a wife.* Horace calls love a *pleasing shackle* in his Odes (Book 1, Ode 33, and Book 4, Ode 11), and Lipsius in his *Miscellaneous Epistles* (Century 1, Epistle 3, page 7) spoke of *chains and a prison regarding nuptials*, that is, he admitted the bonds of marriage. 
Statius, in his *Wedding Song for Stella and Violantilla*:

> — — he submits to laws and has bitten the bit.

Gregory the Great, in his 17th Homily on the Gospels (page 660): *When we see someone wandering and unstable, he must be warned to study how to restrain his iniquity by marriage, so that through that which is permitted, he may learn to overcome that which is not permitted.* By this counsel was the daughter of Plautianus given to Bassianus Caracalla, a fierce youth, by his father Severus, *wishing to sober him with marriage*, as Herodian testifies; <margin>Book 3, page 76.</margin> for he thought nothing more fit to conquer the spirit of a raging youth. We indeed allow ourselves to be easily entangled by this bond,

# FROM PROVERBS 17:6 AND CHAPTER 18:22

...but the more easily it is cast in, the more tenaciously it clings. <margin>The Household Crown.</margin> "For nothing is more tyrannical than these bonds," says Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquent preaching</note> in Volume 3, Homily 20 on Ephesians, page 862. <margin>Household Management, chapter 3.</margin> "For it is underlying us in others," says Aristotle. * There are some, including Muretus <note>Marc-Antoine Muret, a 16th-century French humanist</note>, who believe the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> is referring us back to his books *On the Soul*. But it seems more consistent that other examples are proposed here, which might serve as evidence that certain unions are required for natural propagation. This is especially visible in the propagation of irrational animals, as he says: "just as with each of the animals," for the appetite for generation is naturally implanted in all living things, and all animals follow their desires. Plutarch discusses this elegantly at the beginning of his booklet *On Affection for Offspring*, page 493 and following. <note>original Greek: περὶ τῆς εἰς τὰ ἔκγονα φιλοστοργίας</note> He proves there with the best reasoning that brute animals should be counted among those creatures that cherish natural union and the raising of offspring. He further testifies that many brute animals use the sexual union far more moderately and cherish their offspring with greater "piety" <note>term: piety (naturalis pietas) — here referring to the innate sense of duty and affection between parents and children</note> than many humans do, citing the examples of kingfishers, partridges, hens, bears, and the like, in which the full image of natural affection shines forth. Cicero <margin>Book 2, On Duties.</margin> says: "Common to all living things is the appetite for union for the sake of procreating, and a certain care for those which have been procreated." And in chapter 54: "It is common by nature to all living things that they have a lust for procreating." The Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> leads us by the hand to this same meaning <margin>Politics, Book 1, chapter 1.</margin> where he says it should not be thought that a woman seeks a man, or a man a woman, by deliberate counsel, choice, or institution, but that this union happens by a natural impulse which is common not only to humans but also to the rest of the animals, and even to plants. "First, there must be a union of those who cannot exist without each other, such as the female and the male for the sake of generation; and this is not from choice, but just as in other animals and plants, it is a natural desire to leave behind another such as itself." <note>original Greek: Ἀνάγκη πρῶτον συνδυάζεσθαι... οἷον αὐτὸ, τοιοῦτον καταλιπεῖν ἕτερον.</note> Thus also in *Ethics*, Book 8, chapter 14, section 48, he says that friendship between man and wife is natural and common to all living things. And there in section 53, he says humans live together first for the sake of begetting children <note>original Greek: τεκνοποιΐας</note>, and then for the sake of the needs of life <note>original Greek: τῆς χρείας τῶν εἰς τὸν βίον</note>. In animals and plants, therefore, as the Philosopher says, there is a natural desire to leave behind another like itself. "For the most natural of works in living things is to make another like itself: an animal an animal, and a plant a plant, so that they may participate in the eternal and the divine." He affirmed the same thing <margin>On the Soul, Book 2, chapter 4.</margin> where he does not say "in animals," but "in living things," <note>original Greek: ἐν τοῖς ζῶσιν</note> which can be said of both animals and plants. One cannot correctly say "animals themselves" regarding things that come from the earth; for plants are "living things," but not "animals." <note>original Greek: τὰ φυτὰ ζῶντα, non ζῶα</note> The male partridge chirps in the presence of the female; the horse whinnies to the mare; which is why Plautus <note>Roman comic playwright</note> humorously makes a servant whinny at the sight of a little maidservant. * ] <margin>to page 74. b</margin> Scaliger discusses this at greater length in his commentary on Aristotle's *On Plants*, page 25. Those learned in Nature write that there is a certain society and a desire for propagation even in plants. Pliny attributes sex and marriage to trees in Book 13, chapter 4, where he says among other things: "Nature teaches most diligently that there is both sexes in trees—or rather in everything the earth brings forth, even herbs." He reports in the same chapter that the female palm

<column-break/>

becomes sterile without contact with the male, which ought to be planted not far away; <margin>The Household Crown.</margin> and Theophrastus <note>Greek philosopher known as the father of botany</note> writes <margin>On Plants, Book 3, chapter 27.</margin> that its fruit does not last unless the flower of the male is sprinkled on it with its dust <note>term: dust — an early observation of pollen</note>; see Scaliger on this, page 205. Claudianus <note>Late Roman poet</note> writes elegantly in his book *On the Marriage of Honorius*:

> The leaves live for Love, and in turn every
> Happy tree loves; the palms nod to mutual
> Pledges; the poplar sighs from the poplar’s touch.

Ammianus Marcellinus, in Book 24, says the palms themselves are said to be "married," and their sex can easily be discerned. He adds that females produce when smeared with the likeness of the males, and they say they delight in mutual love. Ambrose, in his *Hexameron* <note>A series of homilies on the six days of Creation</note> (Homily 5, chapter 13), writes that the female palm inclines herself toward the male and, as it were, desires his embrace. There is also, marvelously, sex in the fruits themselves, and a distinction of sex in the trees; for you may see the palm that produces dates frequently bending its branches and lying beneath, showing a form of desire and embrace toward that tree which country boys call the male palm. Michael Glycas <note>12th-century Byzantine historian and theologian</note> records the same in his *Annals*, Volume 1. Indeed, who does not find their ears filled with wonder at the amorous affection of the palm tree—how the female, though separated by a distance, nevertheless lowers her branches to the male, and then returns again to her upright form, as if having enjoyed the fruit of the union? Theophylact <margin>Letter 18.</margin> Simocatta <note>7th-century Byzantine historian</note> says: "The palms also swell with natural love, and the male desires the female; the male is entwined by love, and weaves his foliage into the beloved," and so forth. The myrtle loves the embraces and joints of the olive, and their branches and twigs are better bound together by a sort of hidden necessity; Scaliger skillfully calls this the "marriage of roots" in his notes on Theophrastus, page 189. Theophrastus, having said there that there is a "friendship" between the olive and the myrtle, adds concerning the roots: "He says the roots of the trees entwine with one another like men." <note>original Greek: τάς τε γὰρ ῥίζας συμπλέκεσθαί φησι τῶν δένδρων ἀνδρεδίων.</note> The roots rejoice to be intertwined <note>original Greek: συμπλέκεσθαι</note>, to be coupled in a single bond, to be entangled and joined. The solitary almond tree is said to be less fertile. Pistachios produce more abundant fruit if the male and female are connected; the poplar and the elm are "married" to vines; <margin>Epigrams, Book 4, 13, v. 5.</margin> hence Martial writes on the marriage of Pudens and Claudia:

> Nor are elms better joined to tender vines.

Catullus, in his *Marriage Song*, verse 49:

> As a widowed vine which grows in a bare field,
> Never raises itself, never brings forth a sweet grape,
> But bending its tender body with prone weight, etc.
> But if by chance it is joined to the elm as a husband,
> Many farmers and many bullocks have tended it.

Ovid, in *Amores* Book 2, Elegy 16, and *Metamorphoses* Book 10:
"The Elm loves the vines, the Vine does not desert the elms."
"The leafy vines, and the elms clothed by the vines."
Statius:
->a vine allied with a branch of the same age<-

Horace, *Epistles* 2, 9, 10:

> Therefore he marries the tall poplars
> With the mature growth of the vines.

Johann Stigelius <note>16th-century German poet and scholar</note> imitated this in his poem to King Henry VIII of England and France, verse 128.

<summary>This page explores the concept of marriage as a natural law, demonstrating that the "impulse" for union and procreation exists throughout all nature, from humans and animals to the "marriage" of trees like palms, elms, and vines.</summary>
