# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Household Crown.</margin>
*The elms do not suit the vines themselves so well,*
*Nor does the Bindweed so well embrace and love the crocus* <note>original: "Tam bene conveniunt non ipsis vitibus ulmi, / Tam bene non Smilax ambit amatque crocum." These lines compare natural plant pairings to human marriage.</note>
*As well as the beautiful Anna is joined in your*
*embraces.*

Regarding the "marriages" of the vine and the fig tree, Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle, often called the "Father of Botany."</note> writes in Book 5, Chapter 5: "Among plants of the same kind, those that sprout together and are raised together become companions to one another, just as was said of the climbing vine and the fig."
<margin>Book 2, Chapter 24.</margin>
This author transmits the idea that there are friendships and, conversely, enmities among plants. There is such harmony between the olive and the vine that an olive grafted onto a vine produces both grapes and olives; this mutual "sympathy" <note>original: συμπάθεια (sympatheia) — an interconnectedness of nature</note> beautifully depicts an image of mutual benevolence, desire, and care in a sweet and peaceful marriage. Furthermore, the male is the animal that procreates in another, while the female is the one that procreates within herself; yet this cannot happen without the work and intervention of the man. As the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in his book *On the Generation of Animals*, Book 2, it is impossible for the female without the male, or the male without the female, to complete the work of generation. Lucian, in his *Affairs of the Heart*, page 196, writes: "Since it was impossible for anything to be born from one alone, nature devised a dual nature for each, granting the males their own discharge of seeds, while revealing the female to be a kind of vessel for the offspring." <note>original: "Ἐπεὶ δ' ἦν ἄπορον... τὸ θῆλυ δ' ὥσπερ γονῆς τι δοχεῖον ἀποφήνασα."</note> Yet with God every word is possible, by whose efficacy even a Virgin was made a mother. Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>A 16th-century French theologian and humanist.</note> comments on this passage: From a male without a female, our first parent Eve came forth; and there was only one woman who, without a male, brought forth <note>original: "profudit" — literally "poured forth." The author adds a warning: "abstine lector" (stay away, reader) from this harsh and unusual phrasing regarding the birth of Christ.</note> the Savior of men. Truly, this was not by the power of nature, but by the working of divine virtue, to whom the impossibility of nature is a possibility, and whose possibility is nature's impossibility. Otherwise, it is unheard of for a woman to have produced offspring without the intimacy of a man; as Nonnus writes in the *Dionysiaca*, Book 48, verse 834:
<margin>folio 124. b.</margin>
"I have not seen, nor have I heard, that a virgin gives birth." For no woman is ever said to have produced a child without the partnership of a man, according to Plutarch in his *Marriage Precepts*, page 145. Orestes, in Euripides' tragedy of the same name, expressed this by a comparison taken from the field in verse 553:
> The field, receiving the seed from another,
> But without a father, a child could never be.

For this reason, their society is necessary, "by a necessity of their own." <note>original: "ἐξ ἀνάγκης αὐτῶν ἡ κοινωνία" (ex anankēs autōn hē koinōnia)</note> Thus, I am ashamed of that delirious opinion which Bonifazio Simonetta <note>A 15th-century Italian author.</note> attributes to the Platonists, writing: "The Platonists said that the formative virtue in women is sometimes strengthened without a male, and a woman may be impregnated and give birth from herself. Such strengthening occurs through the stars in the first and fourth climates, where the power of the constellations is more effective." Quite recently in France, an opinion was spread and even approved by the judgment of great men that a certain woman conceived and brought a child into the light solely from the imagination of sexual intercourse; about which someone in Belgium published a witty discourse. The Saracen Muhammadans believe a virgin can conceive without a male, as Ribadeneyra reports in Book 1 of his *Life of Loyola*, Chapter 3; and Viciennus <note>Likely referring to a source on Islamic customs.</note> records that those so born are called *Nefefogli*. Averroes <note>The famous 12th-century Andalusian philosopher.</note> says in his *Collectanea* that a woman can conceive without a man, as Lindhout mentions in his *Introduction to Physics*, page 9. However, J. Wier <note>Johann Weyer, a 16th-century physician known for his work on witchcraft and medicine.</note> teaches in Book 3 of *On Demons*, Chapter 22, page 334, that without coitus and the seed of the male and female, neither a human nor any perfect animal can be born or conceived.
<margin>Book 4, Epistle 9, folio 67. a.</margin>

<column-break/>

Whether this happens "irrationally," <note>original: ἀλόγως (alogōs) — without the guidance of reason</note> as Aristotle seems to think in the cited place, this "coupling" of male and female occurs just as in other animals, and "for the sake of procreation alone," <note>original: τεκνοποιϊας μόνής χάριν</note> through the use of generation, by a blind impulse and wandering lust, so that they may perpetuate their species. Hence some wish for them to be called "wild beasts" (*ferae*), because they are carried along without reason (*sine ratione ferantur*); but this is a mere allusion; for the word comes from the Aeolic *phēr*. Thus, brute animals mate with no reason guiding them and only by the impulse of nature, "to the extent that they participate in nature," as Aretinus <note>Leonardo Bruni, an Italian humanist.</note> obscurely translates it. "To the extent that their nature allows," according to Camerarius. <note>Joachim Camerarius, a 16th-century German scholar.</note> To whatever the nature of each living thing inclines, there it is carried to procreate with the full force of desire. Plautus, in the *Menaechmi*, says that this kind is captured by its own fault. They are not led toward attaining offspring except by the guidance of nature, as is also asserted in *On the Soul*, Book 2, Chapter 4. This impulse and instinct in beasts is called "natural drive" (*hormē*), <note>original: ὁρμὴ (hormē)</note> which is given to animals so they may move themselves toward those things they know to be fit and suitable for them by natural instinct. That which "prevails" in irrational creatures happens "irrationally" in rational living beings who mate not only for the sake of "begetting children" <note>term: teknopoiia (τεκνοποιΐα) — the biological act of procreating offspring</note> chastely and moderately under the mastery of reason, but also for the sake of "health in life," or "for preservation," <note>original: σωτηρίαν (sōtērian)</note> as it is called in the *Politics*, Book 1; which he later says was "for the sake of benefit"; they associate for the sake of what is useful. The highest end of marriage, toward which nature and reason look, is the procreation of one's like. Authors attribute "begetting offspring" (*teknopoiia*) to both beasts and humans, but "rearing children" <note>term: paidopoiia (παιδοποιΐα) — the specifically human task of raising and educating children</note> to humans alone. To "make" (*poiein*) is used to describe the act of procreation, just as the word "to do" (*facere*) is used absolutely by Plautus in *The Little Carthaginian*. "To make a woman," as Tatius says; "to make a wife," according to Hesiod's *Theogony*. "To make a wife for oneself," in Apuleius' *The Golden Ass*. "To make children," in Aristotle and Chrysostom. "A child-making wife," in Euripides' *Andromache*, meaning a prolific woman. In Hebrew, "child" (*yeled*) is as if to say "one who is made," from the root meaning "he worked" or "he made." That the word for "offspring" (*teknon*) is said of the young of beasts and the cubs of animals can be confirmed by more than one testimony. Regarding wasps, see Homer's *Iliad*; as well as the word "offspring" (*tekos*). <margin>Iliad, Book 16, line 265.</margin>
> "There were the fledglings of the sparrow, helpless children."

The same is in *Iliad*, Book 2, line 311. Plutarch, in his *Life of Pericles*, mentions people carrying "the children of dogs and monkeys in their bosoms," and in *On the Delay of Divine Vengeance*, he speaks of "the offspring of bears and the children of wolves and monkeys." In Aesop's Fables, "begetting offspring" is used of a fox; just as Varro speaks of "making chicks," <margin>Book 3, Chapter 3. On Agriculture.</margin> whose words are: "Nor do they generally make eggs and chicks in the farmsteads, but in the woods." The Germans say: "to make young" (*Junge machen*). But this is never used in that sense for humans. It is established, however, that some animals are "wild" (*agria*) and others are "tame" (*hēmera*), as the author of *History of Animals* notes. You might elegantly call the former, with Pindar in the *Nemean Odes*, "beasts ignorant of justice," <note>original: ἀνδροδίκας θῆρας (androdikas thēras)</note> who, because of their natural ferocity, attack anyone they meet without foresight or restraint. For it is certain that tame and domesticated animals, though "irrational" (*aloga*), are endowed with more prudence and foresight regarding their livelihood; just as tame animals are by nature better than wild ones. "For the tame are better in nature than the wild," <margin>* Politics, Book 1, page 11.</margin> according to the *Politics*, Book 1. The same author calls them "herding" and "scattered" beasts, which Cicero also discusses.

It seeks to demonstrate that the virtues of household management—loyalty, foresight, and cooperation—are rooted in the natural law observed even in irrational creatures.</meta>

# FROM PROVERBS XVII. v. 6. CHAPTER XVIII, v. 22.

<margin>The Household Crown.</margin> ...gathered together and solitary, from *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 5. Others explain <note>original: ἀγελαῖα (agelaia)</note> "herding" as *social or political animals*; on this see Montecatinus, *pages 59 and 79.* In the books of Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 2nd-century Roman author who wrote in Greek about the nature of animals.</note> regarding those who love, many things are found concerning the faith, circumspection, attention, and cunning of animals, which will serve as a commentary here. Such as: the modest mating of camels *VI, 60*; their chastity toward their mothers *III, 47*; the reverence of elephants toward the elderly *VI, 61*; their religious devotion to the sun *VII, 44*; their love and piety toward their offspring *IX, 8*; their hatred of adulterers *II, 15*; and their <note>original: εὐπείθεια (eupeitheia)</note> obedience *II, 11*. Also the love of dogs for their masters *VI, 62*; the love of hawks for their females *II, 43*; the chastity of turtledoves and pigeons *III, 44*; the ingenuity of the hedgehog *III, 10*; the wisdom of bees *I, 11* and their prudence *V, 11*; the piety of the kite *II, 47*; the love of the pelican for its parents *III, 23*; the diligence of ants *IV, 43* and their <note>original: ὑπόγειον οἰκοδομίαν καὶ οἰκονομίαν (hypogeion oikodomian kai oikonomian)</note> underground construction and household management <note>The term "economy" here refers to the systematic management of resources and the home.</note>, *ibid*. See also the very elegant booklet by Plutarch, in which it is debated <note>original: πότερα τῶν ζῴων φρονιμώτερα, τὰ χερσαῖα ἢ τὰ ἔνυδρα (potera tōn zōōn phronimōtera, ta chersaia ē ta enydra)</note> *which animals are wiser, those of the land or those of the water*, which is found in Volume 2 of his Works, *pages 959 to 985*, where he celebrates the natures and talents of those animals living on land and in the water with mutual praise. The same author, in the booklet *On the use of reason by irrational animals* <note>original: περὶ τὰ ἄλογα χρῆסθαι λόγῳ (peri ta aloga chrēsthai logō)</note>, teaches from the mastery of nature alone that many brute animals possess qualities worthy of admiration. And see also the ninth book of Aristotle's *History of Animals*, which deals almost entirely with the character of animals (or <note>original: περὶ τῶν ζῴων ἠθῶν (peri tōn zōōn ēthōn)</note> *on the ethics of animals*, as cited by Athenaeus *VII, 7*).

In domesticated animals, mutual aid, affections, and mutual efforts appear more clearly than in others. For even brute beasts have their own quasi-Republics, their own customs, and finally their own economy; for indeed, even in them appears a certain stroke of <term>prudence</term> <note>In this context, prudence refers to the practical wisdom of providing for future needs.</note>, as they procure those things necessary for their own sustenance. Hence it is *written*: <note>original: καὶ τῶν θηρίων ἔνια φρόνיμά φασιν εἶναι, τὰ περὶ τὸν αὑτῶν βίον ἔχοντα φαίνεται δύנהμιν προνοητικήν (kai tōn thēriōn enia phronima phasin einai...)</note> "And they say some of the wild beasts are prudent, those which appear to have a power of foresight regarding their own life." <margin>Ethics, VI, 7.</margin> A likeness of this economic prudence is found in the ant, which gathers in summer to endure life in winter. Therefore, it is a symbol of a good farmer and a provident bailiff, for according to that saying of Titinnius in Nonius: *The rustic man is indeed very like the ant*. Horace *testifies to what can be done by labor and industry in these verses*: <margin>Satires 1, line 33.</margin>

> For the tiny ant is an example of great labor,
> It drags with its mouth whatever it can, and adds to the heap,
> Not ignorant and not reckless of the future it builds.

Regarding the friendships of animals among themselves, see *Sirach XXIII, 20*: <note>original: Πᾶν ζῷον ἀγαπᾷ τὸ ὅμοιον αὐτοῦ (Pan zōon agapa to homoion autou)</note> *Every animal loves its own kind*, which is also found in the Talmud, *Bava Kama, folio 92, 2*: <note>original: כל עוף למינהו ישכון (kol oph le-mino yishkon)</note> i.e., *Every bird dwells near its own species.* For animals of the same kind embrace one another. Here one might also add <note>original: ἐν πλάτει (en platei)</note> "at length" Isaiah, who writes in XXXIV, 14: the wild animals shall meet with the terrifying creature, and the hairy one shall call out to his neighbor. "Neighbor" refers to a companion among the Hebrews. Xenophon in *Oeconomicus, chapter 17*: *The gods made horses most pleasant to horses, cattle to cattle, and sheep to sheep.* <margin>folio 67. a.</margin> There is also a <term>friendship for the sake of utility</term> <note>original: διὰ τὸ χρήσιμον φιλία (dia to chrēsimon philia)</note> in the plover and the crocodile, in Herodotus, *Euterpe, page 73, at the beginning.* Also in the pea-crab with the small shrimp, about which see Muretus *V, Various Readings 10*; Scaliger on *Theophrastus's History of Plants, Book 2, chapter 13, page 151*; and in vipers and scorpions, according to Themistius, *Oration 4 to Valens, page 75.* <margin>Idyll IX, 31.</margin> Most famous are the verses of Theocritus concerning social animals:

<column-break/>

<margin>The Household Crown.</margin>
*Cicada is friend to cicada, and ant to ant,*
*Hawks to hawks.*

Nazianzen in *Precepts to Virgins, line 110*:
*Few are friends to the few, as deer to deer,*
*And lynxes to lynxes.*

In the Philosopher's <note>Aristotle</note> books on the history of animals, there is a most pleasant and beautiful narrative on the nature and properties of living creatures; in the first part, he explains the differences between animals that arise from their life, actions, and character, and says at the end of the chapter that he will speak of the character of each animal after discussing their <note>original: δι' ἀνεικείας (di' aneikeias)</note> conflicts; this he carried out in the ninth book, where he relates in *Chapter 1* the enmities and friendships of animals; and because he had said the characters of animals differ among themselves according to <note>original: δειλίαν, πραότητα, ἀνδρίαν, ὑπομονήν (deilian, praotēta, andrian, hypomonēn)</note> *cowardice, gentleness, courage, patience, etc.*, he demonstrates this specifically through the examples of sheep in *Chapter 3*; of cattle, whose <note>original: ἑταιρείας καὶ συνήθειας (hetaireias kai synētheias)</note> *companionship and intimacy* he commends in *Chapter 4*; of deer in *chapter 5*; of bears and panthers in *chapter 6*; of swallows and doves in *chapter 7*; of partridges in *chapter 8*; and others that follow. Just as he commends the "marriages" of animals there, so he holds the same in high praise in these books on household management. In Book 6 of the *History of Animals*, regarding fish: <margin>chapter 13.</margin> *Most fish have both males and females.* *Book IX, chapter 48*, regarding Dolphins: *The males live together in pairs with the females.* Theodorus Gaza <note>A 15th-century scholar who translated Greek scientific works into Latin.</note> translates: *The males live in pairs with the females.* Solinus says of the same, *They live as spouses*, in *chapter 12*. Pliny said they *conduct marriages*; in the same way he wrote of serpents: *They mostly wander in pairs, nor is there life except with a mate.* And just as dolphins live as spouses, so they also often follow each other in harmony, so that what the Philosopher said here regarding social animals shines forth most in their <note>original: βοηθείας καὶ εὐνοίας καὶ συνεργίας (boētheias kai eunoias kai synergias)</note> *assistance, goodwill, and cooperation with one another*. To such an extent that they follow each other perpetually for the sake of protection, which he recorded in the said *Book 9, chapter 48* with these words: *And some of the large dolphins always follow the small ones for the sake of protection.* Therefore, in contemplating the character of animals, we praise with Theodorus Gaza (from his preface to Aristotle's books on animals) that from here are supplied even to us humans *examples of all duties, and images of virtues are offered with the supreme authority of Nature, the parent of all things;* which he deduced more extensively in the same place through the examples of storks, eagles, ants, bees, dogs, elephants, and doves. Indeed, let us produce witnesses even greater than Gaza himself. Ambrose <note>The 4th-century Bishop of Milan.</note> wants humans to be formed and reformed by the use and example of animals in his *Hexaemeron, Book 5, chapters 17 and 18, and Book 6, chapter 9*, and Aristotle says they exhibit <note>original: μιμήματα τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης ζωῆς (mimēmata tēs anthrōpinēs zōēs)</note> *imitations of human life* in *History of Animals, 9, 7*; or "likenesses of virtues," as Cicero says in Book 1 *On Ends*. Doves teach both chastity and concord. Pliny, *X, 31*: *Modesty is first for them, and adultery is known to neither. They do not violate the faith of a spouse, and they keep a common home. Unless celibate or widowed, it does not leave the nest.* The Crow teaches the same, regarding which see Aelian, *On Animals, 3, 9*; Poliziano, *Miscellanies, chapter 67*; Junius, *Miscellanies 1, 1*. Aelian, in *History of Animals, 5, 48*, says it is a mark of extreme shame that men do not love one another, when animals devoid of reason form friendships among themselves, <note>original: φιλίαν μὲν τοῖς ζῴοις πρὸς ἄλληλα εἶναι (philian men tois zōois pros allēla einai)</note> *that there is friendship among animals toward one another*, where he recites many examples of mutual labors. And elsewhere among other things he especially commends *Ants*, *Book 2, chapter 25.* <margin>Book 2, chapter 25.</margin>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Household Crown.</margin>
...so that they may help one another in their labors, and with the highest honor and modesty—<note>original: πάνυ αἰδημόνως καὶ πεπεισμένως (pany aidēmonōs kai pepeismenōs)</note> very modestly and obediently—yield the way to one another. Certainly in the ant, which Aelian (Book 2, Chapter 25) calls a "noble housekeeper," man has a supreme example of thrifty household management. Even the Sacred Writer praises this, 
<margin>Proverbs 6:6.</margin>
when he commanded the sluggard to go to the ant as a teacher of life. No less an example and specimen of well-conducted economy is found in bees; thus Ischomachus, in the example from Xenophon, teaches his wife that her duty is to remain at home and manage the household. They have a King <note>Historically, the queen bee was often mistaken for a king.</note> whom they obey; 
<margin>Book II, Chapter 6.</margin>
they distribute tasks, with some going out and others staying home. They go out (as Pliny writes) to work and labor, and no day is lost to idleness when the weather permits. For this reason, the author of the *Great Etymologicum* (page 578) thinks that "the bee" <note>original: τὴν μέλισσαν (tēn melissan)</note> is so named from "care" <note>original: παρὰ τὸ μέλειν (para to melein)</note>, <note>original: οἰκονομικὸν γάρ τὸ ζῶον καὶ ἐπιμελὲς εἶναι</note> for the animal is economical and diligent. There were even philosophers who, seeing the bees' wonderful administration of their Republic, the docility of elephants, and other such things, attributed to every living creature a small portion of reason according to its lot, such as Porphyry in his book *On Sacrifice* (Book 3). Plutarch also took up this question in his dialogue *Gryllus*, where many things are told concerning the customs, characters, and history of various animals. See G. Vossius, *Physiology*, Book 3, Chapters 50, 60, 61, 84, 85, and Book 1, Chapter 66, where he treats the prudence, sagacity, concord, and similar traits of the elephant, bees, dove, and other creatures. Add to this Jer. Wilde *On the Ant*, Chapter 11, and Laur. Cupraeus in the *Theater of the Microcosm*, Book 1, page 33 and following. Truly, male and female are joined not only for the sake of existing, but for the sake of living well; they procreate children not only to pay their tribute to nature, but also to receive benefits therefrom. For marriage was instituted not only for the procreation of offspring, but also for the sake of mutual aid. Hence the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> writes in *Ethics*, Book 8, Chapter 12: <note>original: οἱ ἄνθρωποι οὐ μόνον τῆς τεκνοποιΐας χάριν συνοικοῦσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν εἰς τὸν βίον</note> "Men live together not only for the sake of procreating children, but also for those things necessary for life." 
<margin>Ethical Extracts, Book 2, page 195.</margin>
And Stobaeus says: <note>original: φύσει πολιτικὸν ζῶον ἄνθρωπος. πολιτεία δὲ πρώτη, σύνοδος ἀνδρὸς & γυναικὸς κατανόμῳ ἐπὶ τέκνων γενέσει, & βίου κοινωνίᾳ</note> "Man is by nature a political animal. The first state is the assembly of man and woman according to law for the birth of children and the fellowship of life." Thus it must be held that no requirement for the procreation of offspring is greater than the <term>synergia</term> <note>Working together or cooperation.</note> of minds—a sweet harmony, so that they may communicate all things between themselves <note>original: ἐν ὁμονοίᾳ μετὰ τῆς τε οἴκου κηδεμονίας (en homonoia meta tēs te oikou kēdemonias)</note> in concord with the care of the house, and strive together in mutual duties to acquire household resources by which they may be preserved and live a pleasant life. For there is nothing more excellent than when a man and woman manage a house in concord of counsel, as Homer, the Father of Wisdom, also warns: 
<margin>Odyssey, Book 6, line 182.</margin>
> For nothing is better or more noble 
> than when a man and wife hold a house 
> being of one mind in their thoughts.

"The one salvation of individual homes is to think the same thing," says Aristides in his *Oration on Concord*. This is by far the most efficient way to live well in a household, if <note>original: συγκαταζῶντες (synkatazōntes)</note> living together (as Plutarch said of spouses in the *Amatorius*, page 910) they embrace each other with mutual love, raise their children in the fear of God, instruct them in honorable customs, rule them with accurate discipline, provide for necessities, and direct their male and female servants toward dutiful and honorable tasks. Two things make a house: Stone 

<column-break/>

<margin>The Household Crown.</margin>
and wood; but three things adorn and preserve it: the piety of religion, the concord of those living within, and the justice of virtues. Just as the mutual love of spouses is the foundation of household management, so is their disagreement the disturbance of the entire house. St. Chrysostom, in a certain homily which is found 
<margin>Volume 8, Column page 78.</margin>
in his works, says: <note>original: Μηδὲν ἔσω γυναικὶ ἀνδρὸς τιμιώτερον, μηδὲν ἀνδρὶ γυναικὸς ποθεινότερον... (Mēden esō gynaiki andros timiōteron...)</note> "Let nothing be more precious to a wife than her husband, and nothing more desired by a husband than his wife. This concord of a wife with her husband holds our life together; it holds the entire world together. For just as when the foundation is shaken, the entire building falls, so when marriages are in strife, our whole life is overturned." The same author, a little later on the same page, teaches that neither riches, nor honors, nor any other names of human happiness can cheer us if the spouses disagree with each other, <note>original: ὅταν πρὸς ἀλλήλους ζυγομαχῶσι (hotan pros allēlous zygomachōsi)</note> "when they fight against each other under the yoke." Even an entire house cannot hold those in discord. These were the words of Leon of Byzantium, who was sent to Athens to settle a sedition: "I am fat, my wife is fatter; and yet, though we are such and so large, a small bed holds us when we are in concord, but the whole house cannot hold us when we are in discord." Therefore, Euripides said rightly in *Medea*, line 14:
> The greatest salvation comes 
> when a woman does not stand apart from her husband.

Where that cooperation and concord are violated, a battle arises, and the house totters. Chrysostom says (7, 3, page 93): "When a wife is in strife with her husband, nothing will be healthy in the house." Not without reason did the ancients place Persuasion and the Graces over the marriage chamber, to indicate that the life of spouses together ought to be mild and sweet—<note>original: ἥμερον καὶ γλυκεῖαν συμβίωσιν εἶναι (hēmeron kai glykeian symbiōsin einai)</note> to be a gentle and sweet living together—so that by persuading, they may obtain from one another what they desire, neither fighting nor being contentious (as seen in Plutarch’s *Advice to the Bride and Groom* at the beginning). There one may also read this beautiful precept: "Therefore, a woman must not trust in her dowry, nor her lineage, nor her beauty, but in those things that most touch her husband: her conversation, her character, and her conduct; she must provide these not as harsh or annoying daily things, but as well-harmonized, painless, and delightful." She who is endowed with such character follows her husband with her eyes and gaze if he wishes to go out to the country; she mourns him when he is absent and always wishes him to be present; she receives him as a friend when he returns, embraces him, coaxes him, welcomes him with a little kiss, prepares the hearth, and readies the meal with a cheerful spirit. Such a <note>original: συμππεριφερομένην (symperipheromenēn)</note> compliant wife is recommended to us by the Sacred Scriptures, one who cheers her husband through obedience and endearments; and in expressing this, it uses the very elegant verb "to accommodate oneself" <note>original: συμππεριφέρεσθαι (symperipheresthai)</note>, Sirach 25:2; likewise "to gladden" and "to be gladdened," which embraces all the delights of life. By this, the joy of the groom toward the bride is expressed (Isaiah 62:5), of the husband toward the wife (Deuteronomy 24:5), and of the wife toward the husband (Sirach 26:2). For there is no greater joy on earth than in a <note>original: ἐπιεικεῖ (epieikei)</note> virtuous woman. A wife is as a treasure and a most precious thing. Hence Clement of Alexandria says:
<margin>The Tutor, Book 3, page 258.</margin>
> Neither gold, nor tyranny, nor the luxury of wealth 
> possesses such distinct pleasures 
> as the righteous mind of a noble man 
> and a pious woman, who thinks with courage.

A thrifty spouse provides many good things to her husband so that it may be well with him; a depraved one brings destruction and grief to the man, and sinks the husband's weak spirit just as storms sink a rotten ship.
> A good wife has a certain delight in herself, 
> but a bad one always brings a bitter life.

<summary>This page explores the concept of "household economy" as a natural and moral virtue, drawing parallels between the organized labor of ants and bees and the spiritual concord required in human marriage. It emphasizes that domestic peace and mutual cooperation between husband and wife are the essential foundations for a stable society and a happy life.</summary>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<header>Proverbs 17:6. Chapter 18:22.</header>

---

<margin>The Household Crown.</margin> How great a blessing is a good and prudent woman, and how great an *evil* is a wicked and frivolous one; this can scarcely be expressed in words by writers. Many bitter sayings have been poured out regarding the malice of women, a collection of which was gathered by Tiraquellus in his *Laws of Marriage*. As Fulgentius says (*Mythology*, Book 1), "Nothing is higher than a kind spouse; likewise, nothing is more cruel than a hostile woman. To the extent that a spouse is joined by law, she is either as sweet as honey or as toxic as gall with malice. She is indeed either a perpetual refuge or a perennial torment."

<margin>v. 1223.</margin> Theognis says nothing is better than a good woman: 
> "Nothing is sweeter than a good wife." <note>original Greek: Οὐδὲν, κυρ' ἀγαθῆϛ γλυκερώτερον ἄλλο γυναικόϛ</note>

But a bad wife scowls when her husband is happy, and when he is serious, she plays and laughs; Plutarch recorded an example of such a woman in his *Advice to Bride and Groom*, calling her an "ill-mannered" <term>ill-mannered: ἀκαίρου (akairou), one who acts at the wrong time or lacks tact</term> woman. If the husband asks for food, she says there is no fire; if he desires bread, she shows him a stone. If a friend comes to the house, she behaves like a chick seeing a <term>kite: ἴκτι (ikti), a bird of prey</term>, lest she be forced to offer anything. They do not want what you want; but where you do not want them, they come of their own accord. <gloss>Here, you shall be like a Sphinx: by pretending not to want what you actually desire, you will have her most obedient, for she will think she is defying your orders—following the advice of Jerome Cardan in his book *On the Uses of Adversity*.</gloss> Doctors are similar in this provocation: a wife's "illness" is sometimes cured by "contrary medicines." "Mutual affection" <term>mutual affection: Αντιφίλησιϛ (antiphilesis)</term>, which Aristotle <margin>Ethics, Book 8, Chapter 2.</margin> teaches is required in friendship, must be most effective and firm in marital love. Nothing is more poisonous than the mutual hatred of spouses, just as nothing is more powerful than mutual love. Therefore, "To be loved, be lovable," as Ovid writes, and as Phocylides says, "cherish your wife" <note>original Greek: στέρχε τεὴν ἄλοχον</note>. If she is ever a bit moody or lacking in charm—either by a flaw of nature or due to the weariness of the home—something must be forgiven of this "weaker sex." In all friendships, mutual "equity" <term>equity: ἐπιείκεια (epieikeia), a sense of fairness and leniency</term> bears and overlooks certain follies of friends, as the saying goes: *Know the habits of a friend, do not hate them.* This must be done most of all in this marital yoke, where the highest degree of friendship exists. Let the husband’s whole will be in the wife, and the wife’s in the husband with the same affection and zeal; let the husband’s soul be bound to the wife’s soul (as was said of the friendship of Jonathan and David in 1 Samuel 18:1), so that "equal-souledness" <term>equal-souledness: ἰσοψυχία (isopsychia)</term> appears to all, along with "the will following the desire in the same way" <note>original Greek: τὸ μετὰ ἐπιθυμίαϛ θέλημα ἐν ὁμοίῳ</note>. Thus, one spirit is made from two, breathing for the same household goals—above all, commending themselves and their affairs to God in prayer, so that their minds are joined as one in God. For common prayer, the same spirit and the same affection are required for the same vows. For the common management of the home, it is required that the wife not only conform herself to the husband’s will, but be entirely transformed into it; and it is incumbent upon the husband to do the same. Oh, what pleasure, what security of the home comes from this uniform peace of mind! Thus it will be well for the house. But where a wife is moody and hateful, there are days of sadness and bitterness, and the sweetness of pleasantness is turned into the bitterness of wormwood. Thus she will be a heavy *burden* to the husband, and it will be ill for the house that has a wife endowed with hateful habits, who is said to "move the earth" (and much more the house) by the writer of

<column-break/>

<margin>The Household Crown.</margin> Proverbs (Chapter 30, v. 23). There she is called "hated" <note>original Hebrew: שנואה (shenuah)</note>, that is, hateful or invisible, or as Symmachus has it, a "hated woman" <note>original Greek: μεμισημένη γυνή</note>. Such a woman was in the house of Job, who, instead of soothing his pains, doubled his sickness with her reproaches to her pious husband. *Do you still persist in your integrity?* she said; to which sarcasm that most patient man replied (Chapter 2:9-10), *You speak as one of the foolish women* <term>foolish women: μία τῶν ἀφρόνων γυναικῶν (mia tōn aphronōn gynaicōn)</term> *speaks.* Tobit had a barking wife whose cursed tongue reproached him for his acts of charity (Chapter 2:22). Demænetus in Plautus’s play had an troublesome and inconvenient wife. The poets tell tales of Hercules being afflicted and destroyed by three women: Iole, Dejanira, and Omphale. If a bad woman’s mind is in a ferment, reason is conquered by the boiling spirit, and then:
> "The charioteer is carried away by the waters and the chariot does not hear the reins." <note>A quote from Virgil's Georgics describing a loss of control.</note>

<margin>Proverbs 19:13.</margin> Regarding those litigious women, Solomon spoke most aptly: *The brawling of a wife is a constant dripping.* The good Socrates felt the most bitter drops of this dripping; for his wife was Xanthippe, the worst of the worst, "the most difficult of all who have been or will be" <note>original: τὰν ὅσῶν ἐι τῶν γεγενημένων & τῶν ἐσομένων χαλεπωτάτη</note>, according to the praise in Xenophon <margin>Book 1, Chapter 17.</margin> (*The Symposium*). She was exceedingly moody and quarrelsome, stirring up anger and trouble by day and night, as Gellius testifies. Many today still have their own Xanthippes and Andromaches at home as "Teachers of Patience," whom neither Prometheus could reshape, nor Vulcan re-forge, nor Orbilius correct with the lashes with which (according to Tiraquellus) stubborn wives were once punished. If you experience such women, whose malevolence cannot be softened by any charms, you must be a Socrates: consider that you have a domestic exercise in patience. Jerome Cardan suggests other arts for correcting stubborn women (*On the Uses of Adversity*, Book 4). Learned men often complain, as Xylander did, that they have wives who burn out the mind with cares and bring on a swift old age. To say it from the *Anthology*:
> "For she burns out a man with cares, and withers him,
> and brings a premature old age upon his youth."

Happy are those who have "warless beds" <term>warless beds: ἀπολέμουϛ εὐνὰϛ (apolemous eunas), meaning a marriage without fighting</term>. Monica, the mother of Augustine, never had any quarrel with her husband, as her son left written concerning his mother (*Confessions*, Book 9). Macrinus lived with his wife for thirty-nine years without a quarrel or offense, according to Pliny.
<margin>Book 8, Letter 5.</margin>
> "For what is more painful and worthy,
> than when a wife feels kindly toward her husband in the grief of old age?"

Let a wife be placid and peaceful, as Plautus says, "charming," "kindly," and "fleeing from strife" (Proverbs 21:9). For it is better not to have wives than to have pugnacious ones, who often cause men to snatch themselves away into a secret chamber to meditate on the patience of Job (who even today is a "proverb to the people," Job 17:6) and the constancy of Socrates. Socrates bore the harsh habits of his wife very patiently, as recorded by Diogenes Laertius; for when he was doused with water, he said: "Did I not say that Xanthippe thundering would also bring rain?" <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔλεγον ὅτι Ξαντίππη βροντῶσα καὶ ὕδωρ ποιήσει;</note> A wife owes her husband a "quiet eye" <term>quiet eye: ὄμμα ἥσυχον (omma hēsuchon)</term>, a "silent face" <term>silent face: ὄψιν ἀφρωνῆ (opsin aphronē)</term>, and a gentle greeting.

It draws on biblical examples like Job and Tobit alongside classical figures like Socrates and Xanthippe to emphasize that domestic peace is the ultimate "Household Crown."</summary>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<page-num>518</page-num>

<margin>The Household Crown. Enchiridion, chapter 55.</margin>
*Hecyra 4, 1. v. 8.* reverence, *Epictetus*. **A husband, in turn, ought to <term>condescend: συγκαταβαίνειν (synkatabainein), to yield or accommodate oneself to another</term>, by granting his wife both her due <term>honor: τιμὴν (timēn)</term> and gentle conversation, as it is fitting to address the tender sex;** this was once advised by that otherwise stern judge of morals, Chrysostom, in his *Homily 3 on Ephesians, page 872,* with these words: <note>original Greek: Μηδέποτε ἁπλῶς αὐτὴν κάλει, ἀλλὰ μετὰ κολακείας, μετὰ τιμῆς, μετὰ πολλῆς ἀγάπης, τίμα αὐτὴν, & οὐ δεήσεται τῆς παρ’ ἑτέρων τιμῆς.</note> "Never call her simply by her name, but with words of endearment, with honor, and with great love; honor her, and she will not feel the need for honor from others." Certainly, skill must be applied even to nurturing love, which further fosters mutual goodwill. For in this way is earned what Hierocles calls <term>truest and genuine goodwill: ἀληθινωτάτη καὶ γνήσιος εὔνοια</term> in *Stobaeus, Oration 67*; he adds in the same place that <note>original Greek: μηδὲν οὕτω φορτικὸν εἶναι τῶν ὄντων, ὥστε μὴ ῥᾷστον εἶναι συμφρονῆσαι γε ἀνδρὶ καὶ γυναικί</note> "nothing in existence is so burdensome that it cannot be easily harmonized by a husband and wife acting in one mind." But it must also be said that among these roses of lovely society, there are also many thorns. Just as every good in this life we lead is joined with misery, so too is the good of marriage. By trust in the presence of God, every evil is overcome. Often, therefore, you should remember this word: *God said, Genesis 2:18.* An honorable wife, a partner in both prosperity and calamity, takes up the common cares with her husband in this yoke; she is not broken in spirit, even if the pleasure and sweetness of marriage sometimes turn bitter, or if pains and troubles are often mixed with its joys. Regarding these turns of fortune, see Nazianzen’s *On Virginity, v. 631 and following*; Clement of Alexandria’s *Stromata, book 2, page 422*; and Basil’s *Letter to Gregory Nazianzen*, which begins: <term>I recognized you: ἐπέγνων σέ</term>, where he lists the disturbances and cares in both lives, the celibate and the married. But know that those troubles are wiped away by greater benefits and pleasures.

-> *Let all a wife’s care rest in her chosen spouse.* <-

The entire force of private household management lies in a fertile and fruitful marriage, in which, through the wife—as from a fertile root—the mortal name of the house is rendered immortal by succession and offspring. The Author elegantly called the <term>procreative: τεκνοποιητικὴν (teknopoiētiken)</term> union a <term>service to nature: λειτουργίαν τῇ φύσει (leitourgian tē physei)</term>, as if it were a matter of rightly ministering to nature if effort is given to children. <note>original Greek: ταύτῃ γὰρ συνόικησις, παίδων ἕνεκα</note> "For this reason is cohabitation, for the sake of children," says Plato in *Laws, book 1, page 620.* <note>original Greek: συνέρχεται γὰρ τῷ θήλυ τὸ ἄῤῥεν κατὰ φύσιν τεκνώσεως, καὶ τῆς τοῦ γένους διαμονῆς, ἐφειδὴ γὰρ ἑκάτερον γεννήσεως</note> "For the male joins with the female according to the nature of child-bearing and the preservation of the race, since each is for the sake of procreation," as recorded in Stobaeus, *book 2, Ethical Eclogues, page 195.*

<margin>Pedagogue, book 2, ch. 10, p. 194.</margin>
Hence, Clement of Alexandria defines <term>marriage: γάμος</term> as <term>the appetite for child-making: ἡ παιδοποιίας ὄρεξις</term>. There he also very appropriately says that <term>the mystic rites of nature are being performed: τὰ μυστικὰ τῆς φύσεως ὄργια ἐκτελεῖσθαι</term>, which he later states more openly: <term>the encounter of marriage is being fulfilled: τὴν ἔντευξιν τοῦ γάμου τελεῖσθαι</term>. He says that <term>not coming together for the sake of begetting children: Τὸ δὲ μὴ ἐἰς παίδων γονὴν συνιέναι</term> is <term>to insult nature: ἐνυβρίζειν τῇ φύσει</term>. To the Greeks, <term>liturgists: Λειτουργοὶ</term> are ministers who serve the public, as in the State or the Church, or who manage a business from which some happiness returns to the public. In this way, the procreation and education of children is a species of

<margin>Politics, book 7, ch. 16, p. 213.</margin>
<term>liturgy: λειτουργία</term> for Aristotle, where he writes: <note>original Greek: ἐπεὶ ἡ μὲν ἀρχὴ τῆς ἡλικίας ἀνδρὶ καὶ γυναικὶ διώρισται, πότε ἄρχεσθαι χρὴ τῆς συζεύξεως, & πόσον χρόνον λειτουργεῖν ἁρμόττει πρὸς τεκνοποιίαν</note> "Since the beginning of the age for a man and a woman has been defined, when the union should begin, and for how long it is fitting to serve the liturgy of procreation." So too Clement of Alexandria in *Stromata, book 2, page 459,* writes that marriage has <term>its own liturgies and ministries: ἰδίας λειτουργίας & διακονίας</term>, which are important to the Lord, namely <term>caring for children and a wife: τὸ κήδεσθαι τέκνων & γυναικός</term>. Gregory Nazianzen expressed this <term>procreation: τεκνοποιίαν</term> in the Epitaph for Gorgonia as <term>serving nature: τὴν λειτουργεῖν τῇ φύσει</term>. Liturgy is that effect whereby a man gives back to nature

<column-break/>

<margin>Household Management.</margin>
what he borrowed from nature, by producing and nourishing offspring similar to himself. Plato in *book 7* says that those who give effort to children <term>are subservient to nature: ἐξυπηρετεῖν τῇ φύσει</term> and <term>hold fast to eternal nature: τῆς ἀεννάου φύσεως ἀντέχεσθαι</term>. This is nothing other than the Aristotelian <term>serving as a liturgy</term>. In one word, the <term>procreative: τεκνοποιητικὴ</term> act is called the "child-effecting" <term>living-together: συν-αυλία (syn-aulia)</term> (this is what he calls the <term>marriage union: σύζευξιν γαμικὴν</term> in *Politics, book 7, ch. 16*), which usually makes spouses dearer and more pleasing to one another. For children are a kind of bond in marriage—<term>children seem to be the bond: σύνδεσμος τὰ τέκνα δοκεῖ εἶναι</term>, as it says in *Nicomachean Ethics, book 8, ch. 12*—and the minds of the spouses are more closely coupled through children, as if by certain pledges. *Childbirth reconciles the minds of spouses, says Seneca in Hercules Oetaeus, v. 407.* This is what **Leah** wished to imply in *Genesis 29:34*, proclaiming a most happy <term>child-bearing: τεκνογονίαν</term> when she says: **"Now my husband will be joined to me"** <note>Hebrew: יִלָּוֶה אִישִׁי אֵלַי</note>. Which the Seventy Interpreters render: <term>at this time my husband shall be with me: ἐν τῷ νῦν καιρῷ πρὸς ἐμὲ ἔσται ὁ ἀνήρ μου</term>. That is, as Jerome explains, "not uncertain of my husband's love for me, he will be my companion in this life and his affection will lead and follow me even unto death: for I have borne three sons." A <term>child: τέκνον</term> is a great light of happiness; <term>not to die childless: μηδ’ ἄπαιδα θνήσκειν</term>, as Aeschylus testifies; <note>original Greek: καὶ γάμον τινὰ οἰκτείρουσιν οἱ Ποιηταὶ ἡμιτελῆ & ἄπαιδα, μακαρίζουσι δὲ τὸν ἀμφιθαλή</note> "and the Poets pity a marriage that is half-finished and childless, but they bless the one that blooms on both sides," as Clement testifies in *Stromata, book 2, page 422.* Rachel, because she lacked children after several years of partnership with her husband, begins a quarrel with

<margin>Politics, book 1, ch. 3. In Agamemnon, v. 750. Genesis 30:2.</margin>
her husband, saying: **"Give me children, or else I die"** <note>original Greek: Δός μοι τέκνα, εἰ δὲ μή, τελευτήσω ἐγώ</note>. <term>The request of the women: γυναικῶν δὲ ἡ αἴτησις</term> (says Chrysostom, *Volume 8, page 78*) is <term>irrational: καὶ ἀλόγιστος</term>, as if it were up to the husband whether she were fertile. The procreation of offspring is a gift of the Most High God, by whose

<margin>Genesis 1:28.</margin>
blessing we increase and multiply. This was known even to the Heathens, who desired <term>goodly offspring: εὐτεκνίαν</term> for themselves from the Gods. In *Idyll 18* of Theocritus, when the young women pray for Helen, they ask Latona for *happy offspring (v. 51)*, Venus for *equal love (ibid.)*, and Jove for *riches (v. 52)*. A house is built through children, *Exodus 1:21*, for whose sake a wife is given, and for this reason also a woman marries: to become a mother of children, who are called the *most desired of the womb, Hosea 9:16.* Hence also, from the name of the "mother" with the omen of taking up offspring, it is called **matrimony**—named for a future and hoped-for event—and every matrimony is entered into with the vow of undertaking children. Thus, the formula of marriage was usually entered into the matrimonial records: **FOR THE SAKE OF SEEKING CHILDREN** <note>Latin: LIBERORUM QUÆSENDUM GRATIA</note>. Regarding this, see *Brissonius, book 6, On the Formulas of the Roman People, page 542 and following; Cujacius on Novel 22, last chapter; Friedrich Lindenbrog on Terence’s Adelphi, page 643.* The justice of using marriage is this: **"that spouses should mingle at the proper time, not for the sake of fulfilling lust, but with the aim of substituting offspring,"** as Fulgentius says in *Letter 1, on Marriage and the Vow of Continence, page 350.* The prescription of reason must be observed here by every means, and modesty, like the light of reason, must be fixed in the mind. Regarding this, Clement of Alexandria prescribes the best

<margin>Pedagogue, book 2, ch. 10.</margin>
laws for Christians, which begin thus on page 187: <note>original Greek: συν-κοίας τὸν καιρὸν μόνοις τοῖς γεγαμηκόσι, ἀπολεί-λειπται σκοπεῖν. τοῖς δὲ γεγαμηκόσι, σκοπὸς ἡ παιδοποιΐα. τέλος δὲ, ἡ εὐτεκνία.</note> **"The time for lying together is left for only the married to consider. For those who are married, the aim is child-making; the end is goodly offspring."** Nature does not always grant the time <term>for the marriage encounter to be fulfilled: τὴν ἔντευξιν τῷ γάμῳ τελεῖσθαι</term>, *ibid. page 194.* Shame forbids saying more. It was given by the Creator so that the species might be extended through the work of individuals as a certain image of eterni- <note>catchword: eternity</note>

### From Proverbs 17:6 and Chapter 18:22
<page-num>519</page-num>
Rrrr 2
->Philo-<-

<margin>The Household Crown.</margin>
The **Crown of eternity** is so named because of succession. For it is through the hope of posterity and the preservation of memory that men take wives, so that in this marriage, through the circuit and cycle of generation—<term>in this eternal way: $\tau\alpha\text{ύ}\tau\eta$ $\tau\tilde{\eta}$ $\text{ἀ}\text{ϊ}\delta\text{ί}\text{ῳ}$</term>—they may receive eternity within this fleeting mortality. In this way, mankind may always exist <term>according to the species: $\kappa\alpha\text{τ}\text{ὰ}$ $\tau\text{ὸ}$ $\text{εἶ}\delta\text{ος}$</term>, since they cannot exist eternally <term>according to their individual number: $\kappa\alpha\text{τ}\text{’}$ $\text{ἀ}\text{ρ}\text{ι}\theta\mu\text{ὸ}\nu$</term>. For Nature, which could not create man as an immortal individual, strives to make the species immortal as far as it is able; through the mutual commerce of the sexes, it preserves the whole even as individuals perish. Indeed, *the difference of sex and the act of procreation have no other purpose than that the kinds of living things, which are otherwise bound by the condition of mortality, might be preserved through mutual succession*; as Lactantius teaches in his book *On False Religion*, 8, and in his book *On the Workmanship <margin>p. 517.</margin> of God*, chapter 12: *How truly wonderful is that ordinance of God, that for the preservation of each kind, he engineered the two sexes of male and female.* Junilius, in *The Parts of the Divine Law*: <margin>book 2, ch. 4.</margin> *General governance consists in succession, as men or cattle and other things which perish by death or corruption are renewed by the likeness of those being born again. As some are born from others, the human race exists, in a certain way, eternally.* Lucian, in *The Loves*: <margin>p. 196, Vol. 4.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἡ ἱερὰ τῶν ὅλων φύσις τὴν ἑτέραν φθορὰν ἄλλῳ γένεσιν ἐμηχανήσατο, καὶ τῷ θνήσκοντι τὸ τικτόμενον ἀντεμήσατο, ἵνα τοῖς παρ’ ἀλλήλων διαδοχαῖς εἰς τὸν ἀεὶ χρόνον ζῶμεν.</note> "The sacred nature of the universe engineered birth for every destruction, and substituted the one being born for the one dying, so that through successions from one another we might live for all time." And a few lines later: "The interactions of men with women have, until now, guarded human life through immortal successions." Theophilus, the paraphrast of the *Institutes of Civil <margin>page 81.</margin> Law*: "Nature, seeing each individual animal consumed by death, engineered immortality for them through marriage and the child-rearing that follows." There is no one who is not moved by the sweetness of perpetuity and eternity, so that the life he received from his parents, he may in turn <margin>6. On Laws.</margin> hand down to posterity like a burning torch. Plato: "One must hold fast to the ever-born nature by leaving behind children's children." The same author, in book 4 of *The Laws*, treating the age at which a wife should be taken, writes to the same effect.
<margin>Sermon 73. f. 408. b.</margin> Also in the *Symposium*, as cited by Stobaeus: "Zeal and love for immortality and happiness together follow for everyone through all time." This zeal and this love dwell most strongly in heroic and illustrious men—to make their lineage eternal. There is an excellent passage on this matter in the *Panegyric dedicated to the Emperors Maximian <margin>page 84.</margin> and Constantine*: "We give you the greatest thanks in the name of the public, because by acknowledging children and desiring grandchildren, you provide for all future ages by prolonging the series of your lineage. Thus the Roman state, once tossed by the diverse impulses and fates of various rulers, may finally grow together through the perpetual roots of your house; so that its empire may be as immortal as the eternal offspring of the Emperors." This is true piety: to give the nations an example of preserving the human race, so that they may more eagerly seek marriages and educate children, so that the Republic suffers nothing for the lack of posterity by substituting successions for individuals. For families must strive for this, especially the illustrious ones, lest oblivion cut them off. <margin>book 6, Letter 48. f. 155. b.</margin> Bonifazio Simoneta to Ludovico Sforza: *An exalted man without children is not truly happy.* You, Divine

<column-break/>

<margin>The Household Crown.</margin>
Ludovico, *will grace your happiness through the fruitfulness of marriage, since you will be immortal through it. Know that the fathers of households are made perennial and become immortal; even if individuals are corrupted, the species is perpetuated through successors.* Certainly, a sick father near death, seeing his sons standing around him, does not seem to die to himself; for he sees, in a way, in his offspring the seeds of his future immortality. Because by leaving children, he grows young again in them and is, in a sense, reborn; and while he departs, he does not perish, but leaves behind another new self like him. Thus, he should no longer be counted among the mortals, <term>becoming superior to death and all corruption: $\kappa\rho\epsilon\text{ί}\tau\tau\text{ο}\nu\alpha$ $\gamma\iota\nu\text{ό}\mu\epsilon\nu\text{ο}\nu$ $\theta\alpha\nu\text{ά}\tau\text{ου}$ $\kappa\alpha\text{ὶ}$ $\pi\text{ά}\sigma\eta\varsigma$ $\delta\iota\alpha\phi\text{ο}\rho\tilde{\alpha}\varsigma$</term>, having been made greater than any perishing thing, and unconquered as it were by death itself. Whence Virgil Wallendorffer exclaims: "O society, which <margin>Conclusion 13, folio 14a.</margin> establishes the homes and cities of all; it best preserves the human race so it does not perish through the length of time."
Furthermore, a father "dies" in his sons when one of them perishes, and if all die, then it is the death of the family, and the immortal man is rendered mortal. Hence, the excellence of this blessing is rightly extolled by the title of **Crown**, because in truth a great ornament is added to the elderly—<term>glory: תפארת (*tiferet*)</term>, honor, support, and delight—if through God’s blessing they see before them grandchildren growing up as witnesses to the glory of God, ready to propagate the glory and name of their ancestors. Conversely, from the presence and surviving life of venerable parents and ancestors, no small honor redounds to the children, by whose regard many are promoted and raised to higher things. And Divine providence shines most clearly in these things, upon which the society of man and woman rests. Therefore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says it was established by the Creator God himself that the male be joined with the female. Johann Faber on this passage: *There are those who accuse Aristotle of impiety, because he denied that divine providence diffuses itself into these lower regions around the lunar sphere; their opinions have spread even to Ambrose and men of the Church.* But if he had felt that way, he surely would not now say: <term>Thus they are provided for by God: $\text{Ο}\text{ὕ}\tau\omega$ $\pi\rho\text{ο}\kappa\text{ο}\nu\text{ό}\mu\text{ου}\nu\tau\alpha\iota$ $\text{ὑ}\pi\text{ὸ}$ $\tau\text{ῶ}$ $\theta\epsilon\tilde{\varphi}$</term>. Truly, for Aristotle, who recognized God as the cause of the universe, how could he deny that God is the author of marriage? He speaks wisely, or rather divinely, in the seventh book of the *Eudemian Ethics*: <margin>book 2 of the Politics.</margin> <term>In the whole, God and all things are moved by Him; for in a way, all the divine is within you: $\text{Ἐ}\nu$ $\tau\tilde{\varphi}$ $\text{ὅ}\lambda\omega$ $\theta\epsilon\text{ὸ}\varsigma$ $\kappa\alpha\text{ὶ}$ $\pi\tilde{\alpha}\nu$ $\text{ἐ}\kappa\epsilon\text{ί}\nu\omega$ $\kappa\iota\nu\epsilon\tilde{\text{ῖ}}$, $\pi\tilde{\omega}\varsigma$ $\pi\text{ά}\nu\tau\alpha$ $\gamma\text{ὰ}\rho$ $\tau\text{ὸ}$ $\text{ἐ}\nu$ $\text{ὑ}\mu\text{ῖ}\nu$ $\theta\epsilon\tilde{\text{ῖ}}\text{ο}\nu$</term>. With the same divine sentiment, he writes near the end: <term>By nature, therefore, there is an impulse in all toward such fellowship; and he who first established it is the cause of the greatest goods: $\Phi\text{ύ}\sigma\epsilon\iota$ $\text{ο}\text{ὖ}\nu$ $\dot{\eta}$ $\text{ὁ}\rho\mu\text{ὴ}$ $\text{ἐ}\nu$ $\pi\tilde{\alpha}\sigma\iota\nu$ $\text{ἐ}\pi\text{ὶ}$ $\tau\text{ὴ}\nu$ $\tau\text{ο}\iota\alpha\text{ύ}\tau\eta\nu$ $\kappa\text{ο}\iota\nu\omega\nu\text{ί}\alpha\nu$. $\text{ὁ}$ $\delta\text{ὲ}$ $\pi\rho\tilde{\omega}\tau\text{ος}$ $\sigma\text{υ}\sigma\text{ή}\sigma\alpha\varsigma$, $\mu\epsilon\gamma\text{ί}\sigma\tau\omega\nu$ $\text{ἀ}\gamma\alpha\theta\tilde{\omega}\nu$ $\text{α}\text{ἴ}\tau\iota\text{ο}\varsigma$.</term> Thus Xenophon in chapter 12 of his *Oeconomicus*, when about to explain the causes why marriage was instituted, says through the persona of Ischomachus: <term>This yoke, which is called female and male, God has joined together: $\tau\text{ο}\text{ῦ}\tau\text{ο}$ $\tau\text{ὸ}$ $\zeta\epsilon\tilde{\upsilon}\gamma\text{ο}\varsigma$, $\text{ὃ}$ $\kappa\alpha\lambda\epsilon\tilde{\imath}\tau\alpha\nu$ $\theta\tilde{\eta}\lambda\text{υ}$ $\kappa\alpha\text{ὶ}$ $\text{ἄ}\rho\rho\epsilon\nu$, $\text{ὁ}$ $\theta\epsilon\text{ὸ}\varsigma$ $\sigma\text{υ}\nu\text{έ}\theta\eta\kappa\epsilon\nu$.</term> These are certainly golden words of Aristotle and Xenophon, of which even a Christian would not be ashamed. Therefore, let them be all the dearer to us, as they are rarer among the pagans; and on that account, a Christian will rightly marvel that Aristotle, a pagan man ignorant of true piety and religion, progressed this far. Aristotle wrote few things indeed about the providence of God. But to know what he felt, look to Tommaso Giannini, in his book *On Demons*, chapter 26, page 427 and following. He knew...

It synthesizes views from Christian fathers like Lactantius and pagan philosophers like Aristotle and Plato to argue that marriage and succession are divinely instituted for the preservation of the human race.</summary>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<page-num>520</page-num>

<margin>The Household Crown.</margin>
The Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle or the general consensus of ancient thought</note> and all more sensible men believe that the fidelity of marriage, the love between spouses, and the fertility of nature come from God. For this reason, those about to enter marriage would ask the gods during sacred rites for their favor, so that the gods might turn the event to good. "Go home," says the parent to his son who is about to marry in the works of the Comic Poet <note>original: "ap. Comicum"; referring to the Roman playwright Terence</note>, "and pray to the gods that you may bring home your wife." Juno was the sponsor of the marriage between Dido and Aeneas. Quintus Smyrnaeus <note>original: "Q. Calaber"</note> records in his third and fourth books that the marriage of Peleus was a matter of concern for the immortal gods. The sublime and lofty poet Statius writes in his first book of *Silvae*, in the wedding song for his friend Stella, that the goddess Venus was the matron of honor <note>original: "pronubam"</note> for Stella and Violantilla:

<margin>v. 11.</margin>
> The mother of Aeneas <note>Venus</note> herself leads the bride by the hand,
> she who comes down with shining eyes and a sweet, blushing modesty,
> she herself prepares the marriage bed and the sacred rites.

Catullus, celebrating the lawful marriage of Julia and Manlius under the name of the god Hymenaios <note>the god of marriage</note>, says:
<margin>fol. 74 a.</margin>
> Without you, no house is able
> to give children, nor can a parent
> be named for his lineage; but it can
> if you are willing.

The Athenians performed prayers and sacrifices to the gods for the sake of offspring, as the author of the *Great Etymologicon* records on page 768; he also writes on page 220 that a <term>wedding sacrifice: γαμηλίαν θυσίαν</term> was made to Juno, Venus, and the Graces. Likewise, Pollux in his *Onomasticon* (Book 3) records that <term>preliminary wedding rites: προτέλεια καὶ προγάμεια</term> were made to Juno, Diana, and the Fates. When Protesilaus neglected to perform the <term>sacrifice: θυσίαν</term> to the gods of marriage, his house was begun in vain, as Catullus says in his epigram to Manlius:
<margin>v. 75.</margin>
> As once Laodamia came, burning with love for her husband,
> to the house of Protesilaus,
> a house begun in vain, since not yet with the blood of a sacred
> victim had that hero appeased the heavenly ones.

Antonius Muretus reads this as "received in vain," while Turnebus and Scaliger approve the reading "begun." If we compare our own sacred rites, we read that the sacraments of the marriage bed are begun in vain—to use the words of Arnobius—without the help of God, as seen in *Psalm 127:1*: <term>Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain: Ἐὰν μὴ κύριος οἰκοδομήσῃ οἶκον, εἰς μάτην ἐκοπίασαν οἱ οἰκοδομοῦντες</term>. With this agrees the line of Euripides in *Melanippe*:
<margin>Speech 70.</margin>
> <term>Those who rush into a marriage not ordained by fate</term>
> <term>labor in vain.</term>

A wife is from God, who is the joiner of good love. Thus also in *Proverbs 19:14*: <margin>on Prov. 19:14.</margin> <term>A prudent wife is from the LORD: אשה משכלת מיהוה</term>. The Septuagint <note>the Greek Old Testament</note> translates this as: <term>from the Lord a woman is fitted to a man: παρὰ κυρίου ἁρμόζεται γυνὴ ἀνδρὶ</term>. Here, instead of the Hebrew word for <term>prudent: משכלת</term>, the translator seems to have read <term>appointed or betrothed: משכרת</term> by a simple slip of the pen (changing the letter *Mem* to *Resh*), which is how the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> translator reads it: <term>desponsata: מזמנא</term>. For among the Chaldeans and Syrians, the root <term>m-k-r</term> means "to betroth"; from this, the Greek <term>fitted: ἁρμόζεσθαι</term> is understood in *2 Corinthians 11:2*. It is from God if anyone receives children. God places the solitary in a home, and the unique—<margin>Ps. 68:6.</margin> <term>those of a single way of life: μονοτρόπους</term>—he <term>makes to dwell in a house: יחידים</term>, that is, he makes those who were without children the parents of many. "God makes the barren woman dwell in a house as a joyful mother of children." Just as a happy marriage is from God, so also that marriage is happy in which God dwells. There are two <margin>Ps. 113:9.</margin> words for the spouses, <term>Man: איש</term> and <term>Woman: אשה</term> (*Ish* and *Ishah*), which contain within them the name of God, <term>Yah: יה</term>. If the letter *Yod* <note>י</note> is taken away from "Man" and the letter *He* <note>ה</note> from "Woman," there remains only <term>Fire: אש</term> (*Esh*) without God <note>Yah</note>, meaning God and every blessing are absent—as the Hebrews playfully observe <note>referring to a famous rabbinic wordplay: when God is removed from a marriage, only the fire of conflict remains</note>.

<column-break/>

### Proverbs 25:11

-> <term>Apples of gold in settings of silver is a word spoken on its wheels: תפוחי זהב במשכיות כסף דבר על-אפניו</term> <-
-> <term>A golden apple on a sardius necklace, so is it to speak a word to those it fits: Μῆλον χρυσὸν ὁρμίσκῳ σαρδίῳ, οὕτως εἰπεῖν λόγον ἐπὶ ἁρμόζουσιν αὐτῷ.</term> <-
-> *Golden apples in silver beds, is he who speaks a word in its time.* <-

<margin>Apples.</margin>
Great is the power of speech delivered in a timely and suitable manner, and great is its dignity, utility, and grace. Thus the wise man, not content to compare it only to a golden apple, adds further the silver engraving, so that the comparison might appear all the more pleasing and illustrious. A word *spoken in its place is like golden apples in silver dishes.* The word <term>in settings: במשכיות</term> they translate as "in engravings," that is, in vessels skillfully crafted with mosaic work, which, just as they attract the eyes of the spectators, so do words delivered *according to their proper modes.* To speak aptly and to speak timely—this, finally, is truly speaking; compare Cartwright on this passage, page 1089. The quality of the speech is commended by the fact that it is *spoken upon its wheels* or according to the proper ways in which it ought to be said. Here, by a grammatical repetition <note>polyptoton</note>, the terms <term>dabar and dabur: דבר ,דברי</term> are appropriately placed together: "a word spoken." But in the words that immediately follow—<term>upon its wheels: על-אפניו</term>—there is some difficulty. For the word <term>upon: על</term> is <term>multivalent: πολυσημον</term>, meaning *upon, near, according to*, etc. The latter word is commonly derived from <term>wheel: אופן</term>, which Solomon mentioned above: *he turns the wheel over them*, <margin>chapter 20.</margin> by which a certain kind of punishment is indicated (also in *2 Samuel 12:31*). Here, however, by a figure of speech <note>synecdoche</note>, it refers to any kind of condition. In this place, it is taken metaphorically, and thus is the same as speaking ornately, or as Cajetan explains: *upon topical places, upon rhetorical colors, upon modes of speaking: for these are the wheels of speech*, upon which the speech is carried to persuade and instruct. Jansenius agrees with this: but, as Del-Rio rightly judges, <margin>vol. 2, question 236.</margin> what is missing is the right occasion for speaking and a time suitable for the speech, which, along with the other circumstances, is worthy of observation when holding a conversation. With these things presupposed, the word <term>wheel: אופן</term> seems to be taken more broadly here, so as to signify at once the *mode, circumstance, form, condition, status, where, how, when, why, and before whom one should speak*. To be sure, one must consider the people to whom you speak, whether they are capable of understanding, whether they are paying attention, etc. Likewise, the place and time: do happy words fit a moment of sadness and mourning? Does silence befit the occasion more than speech? Does a simple form of speaking accomplish more than a figurative one? Is austerity or gravity appropriate here, or rather a gentle persuasion, and other similar things? According to these circumstances, then, a "word spoken" will be uniquely lovely, pleasant, profitable, precious, and dearer than gold. Hence, Blessed Dannhauer aptly says in his dedicatory epistle for his homilies: *A word, a saying, or an oration concerning the specific matter at hand, bound with every harmony of rhythm and mode, smooth and rounded as if by certain swift little wheels—if it is brought forth seasonably, maturely, in its proper place and time—it happens to be just as pleasing as it kindles the desire to listen. Just as golden apples, ripe, timely, from the autumn, produced in silver or in an emblematic engraved vessel or table, affect the palate and sharpen the hunger for eating.*

# From Proverbs 25, Verse 11.

<margin>
Golden apples.
</margin>
...propriety. Compare Tarnov's *Exercises, page 1175*, and Zehner’s *Century 1, Adage 58*, where they rightly observe that timely speech is pleasant and welcome for two reasons: *first*, in itself, because it smells of a wisdom more excellent than any gold; and *second*, because it is brought forth aptly and fully within its own "circumferences" or circumstances—that is, at the proper time and place. This is exactly like apples which, though naturally beautiful in themselves (so much so that the ancients completely abstained from eating them to preserve them), gain even greater grace if they are placed upon silver vials or platters. A similar expression exists in Sirach <margin>chapter 20, v. 22.</margin>: *A fool, even if he speaks something good, is of no consequence, for he does not speak it* <note>original Greek: ἐν καιρῷ αὐτῆς</note> *in its proper time*; that is, he does not know how to bring it forth at the opportune moment or adapt it to the present matters and persons. You will find a collection of parallels from secular authors regarding timeliness in *Del-Rio, volume 2, adage 236; Zehner, in the place cited; and Quistorp’s Biblical Annotations on this passage.* It is a singular prudence, among so many different human temperaments, to give each person a speech that is not necessarily always pleasing, but is nevertheless suitable. If you are dealing with a superior, you must use judgment so that you speak in accordance with their dignity and authority; if with an inferior or commoner, the same skill in speaking must be observed, directing it toward the present state, place, and other circumstances. This is what it means <note>original Greek: εὐκαίρως λέγειν ἢ λαλεῖν</note> "to speak or chatter opportunely," which Stobaeus treats in his *Sermon 34.* The opportunity of speaking is compared <margin>26.</margin> <term>bamaskiyot kesep</term> <note>original Hebrew: במשיכות כסף</note>, *to silver figures*—that is, things made of silver. The word <term>maskit</term> comes from <term>shakah</term>, *to look at or look forward*, which is Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note>; for where the Hebrew uses <term>hishkiph</term>, the Chaldean says in the Ithpehal form <term>istaki</term> (with the letter *Samech*). When applied to the mind, it means *to imagine or think*. Here you will find a wonderful disagreement among commentators regarding this word. Pagninus and Junius translate it as *with silver figures*. Arias says *in transparent cases of silver*. The Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> says *in a likeness of sardius* <note>original: ἐν ὁμοιώματι σαρдίου</note>, *in a small mountain or puppy-shaped setting of Sardius stone*. Symmachus and Theodotion say *in conspicuous silver things* <note>original: ἐν περιβλέπτοις</note>. The Vulgate says *on silver beds*; Luther says <note>original German: silberne Schale</note> *silver bowl*. There are some who interpret it as silver lattices or grates, through which those beautiful works might be seen, as we see done in the houses of the very wealthy. Vatablus looks to this, explaining it as a *case* in which precious stones are hidden so that they might be seen; these were made of silver and had holes through which those golden apples were visible. The reason for this diversity of opinion is easily gathered from the different meanings of the word, which can denote either a mental image or a physical one. Hence it will be most fitting, <margin>Commentary on this passage, p. 1395.</margin> says Doctor Geier, to understand it as some artistic figure representing a sea shell or another vessel that can hold golden apples like a case. Whether that receptacle is latticed and perforated so that the beauty of the apple shines through the cracks, or whether it is solid but aptly decorated with beautiful images, it lends greater grace to the offered item, which is already quite capable of moving the appetite on its own. In a word: silver platters or vials are indicated—not plain ones, but adorned by the goldsmith’s art with beautiful figures or images of whatever kind they might be. Elsewhere, <term>maskit</term> generally signifies the sculpted or painted image of any thing.

<column-break/>

<margin>
chapter 26, 23.
Golden apples.
</margin>
Sirach has a nearly identical comparison: *a golden column on a silver base, etc.*, where some explain "golden columns" as the boards of the Tabernacle covered in gold (discussed in Exodus 26:15 and following), whose bases are said in that same place to be silver. Stöcker, in his sermons on this passage, takes it to mean the two columns of Solomon, which he concludes probably had silver bases based on Jeremiah 52:21. Friedlieb adds in his commentary that Sirach—who in the preceding verse commended the face of a godly woman—here briefly touches upon the rest of the body, comparing beautiful feet on silver bases to golden columns, which he identifies as the two sides of the breast. However, he is looking not so much at the physical proportion and composition of the limbs as at the suitability and harmony of character and life. Hence, although feet are otherwise the foundation of the body, he says in an inverted order: "beautiful feet upon steady breasts." By "steady or constant breasts" he means the soul, which allows itself to be moved from virtue by neither calamity nor reward; upon this the feet—that is, one’s actions—rest. But we must return to the very elegant proverb of the wisest King of Kings. Johannes Ximenius, in the disputation he published on citron apples, believes that the Sage <note>Solomon</note> had in mind the memory of a certain amulet of Isis with the inscription *Urim and Thummim*. Taking a metaphor, he says, from the amulet of the Egyptian goddess Isis (by wearing which they judged themselves safe from all evil and poison, and which bore the inscription *Thummim and Urim*, words they interpreted as: "The true voice, the guardian of being, the just and the decorous"), the Holy Spirit substituted a truly good and perfect amulet for the superstitious one. This new divine amulet, derived from God Most High, is more certain than if you wore a citron with its leaf and the inscription *Thummim and Urim* hanging from your neck in silver capsules. He writes this <note>original Greek: ἀμοχθί</note> "without effort." For what, I ask, does this invention have to do with Agur <note>a speaker in Proverbs</note>? What is the point of preserving these pagan symbols, charms, "turning-away" spells of the guardian spirit, papers painted with magic signs, or plates inscribed with astral marks—"seals" or "little seals" as Prudentius calls them—rings, earrings, or "phylacteries of the gods" as Augustine calls them? These were worn as amulets by those searching into secrets, those wishing to acquire bodily strength, those warding off evils, or those practicing illusions and performing wonders. To preserve some sort of nonsense here through <note>original Greek: συγχύσει</note> "confusion" is to pollute a divine matter. Regarding the amulets of the Gnostics, Cabalists, and Muhammadans <note>Muslims</note> made from Indian letters and secrets, the "Universal Amulet," and the Seals of Saturn, Jupiter, and the Talismans <note>original: Telesmas</note> of Solomon, let others be consulted. I wish to add one or two points <note>original Greek: ἐκ περιόδου</note> "in passing." The Muhammadans attribute much to their Quran, and no less to amulets marked from the same. Likewise the Jews, whom the Arabs rival (and their leader Muhammad as well), have devised certain hieroglyphic marks, charms, seals, signs, and characters for driving away and curing diseases, repelling enchantments, and so on. Such is the one they display on a square piece of parchment containing the 6 words beginning at Deuteronomy 6:4: <term>Shema Yisrael, Yehovah Eloheinu, Yehovah Echad</term> <note>original Hebrew: שמע ישראל יהוה אלהינו יהוה אחד</note>, "Hear O Israel, Jehovah your God is one Jehovah." Likewise, in another from Exodus chapter 13, the first...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
### Page 522

<margin>
Golden apples.
</margin>
...the first ten verses, with "crowned letters," which they call *Tagin* <note>Hebrew: תאגין. These are decorative flourishes or "crowns" drawn on certain letters in a Torah scroll</note>; see Buxtorf’s *Rabbinic-Talmudic Lexicon*, page 2562; Schickhard in *The Law of the King*, page 41; Hottinger on *Oriental Coins*, page 169 and following; and Johann Ulrich Wallich on *Turkish Religion*, page 4.
