Acts 19:18, 19.
</margin>
And to this subject may be referred the *Ephesian letters* <note>original: "literae Ephesiae," ancient Greek magical formulas used as charms</note>, as they were commonly called in proverbs—known to the Greeks as *periapsis* <note>amulets worn around the neck</note> and to the Latins as *curiosa* <note>curious or magical arts</note>. The Magi commanded those possessed by demons to read these to themselves and to recite the Ephesian names, as witnessed by Plutarch in *On Progress in Virtue*. In his *Symposia*, book 7, question 5 at the end, he cites the words of Androcydes the Pythagorean, who said that those "much-celebrated Ephesian letters" served as symbols. Among the herd of heretics, the Simonians formerly used such amulets, signs, and characters, about whom 

<margin>
Book 1, chapter 20
</margin>
Irenaeus writes: *They use exorcisms and incantations. Love-potions and drawing-charms, and those called "Paredri" <note>assistant spirits</note> and "Oneiropompi" <note>senders of dreams</note>, and whatever other magical arts*—read "perierga" <note>superfluous or occult things</note> as Gutius advised—*are zealously practiced among them.* The authors of such books are listed in Tertullian as Osthanes, Typhon, Dardanus (from whom come the "Dardanian arts"), Damigeron, and Nectabis—perhaps Nectanebo, the King of Egypt?—and Berenice. More on the Ephesian letters is discussed by Clement of Alexandria in *Stromata*, book 5; Theodoret in the *Preface to the Epistle to the Ephesians*; Junius in his *Notes on the New Testament* regarding the passage in Acts; Thomas Canter in *Various Readings*, book 1, chapter 18; Erasmus in his *Adages* under the title "Imposture," page 305; Dilherr in *Eclogues 8*, page 454; Quistorp in his *Biblical Annotations* on this passage; and Cornelius a Lapide in his commentary. All these things are like a rotten catfish on a silver platter. For this reason, Martin de Roa rightly rejects the opinion of Ximenes, cited above in 

<margin>
Unique Parts of Holy Scripture, part 2, chapter 2.
</margin>
this passage, with these words: *Who has ever read that the ancient Egyptians carried golden apples enclosed in silver boxes as an amulet? But even if they did carry them, did not the Indians, Persians, Medes, Babylonians, Romans, and even the Hebrews themselves—and nearly all nations—have their own amulets or phylacteries, which were intended to avert evils? Why then would Solomon overlook what was common and daily to him, and travel so far to seek such forced and absurd amulets for his faith? And what medical power, so hidden and so potent, resides in a timely word?* But there is no reason for us to linger long in refuting these fictions, since they betray themselves as quite absurd, and as the saying goes:

> There is no oil in the olive, and no hard shell outside the nut. <note>A proverbial way of saying an argument has no substance.</note>

It is beyond dispute <note>original: "ἀναμφίλογον"</note> that the Wise Man was not referring to the amulets of Isis. However, whether he understood apples crafted from gold—as Martin Del Rio holds with the ancient Hebrew interpreters—or truly meant citrons or quinces, which are real fruit—as Ferdinand de Salazar and Martin de Roa maintain—these deserve to be called "golden" because of their color, grace, and beauty. Virgil mentions them:

> I have sent ten golden apples; tomorrow I will send another ten.

And another from the rank of the "Swan-like" poets:

> For thus do apples yellow with a noble color, 
> That they surpass true metal with their own gold.

We easily tolerate that each person may abound in his own opinion. It is certain, as experience testifies, that apples entice the eyes with their charm, the nose with their scent, the palate with their taste, and the hand with their lightness. Even if these lack 

<column-break/>

true gold, they are nonetheless more pleasant than gold to those eating them, for they sweetly suppress both hunger and thirst; thus they both help and delight at the same time, to say nothing of the medicinal virtues of "golden apples," for which the School of Physicians should be consulted. Furthermore, the Hebrew word *Tappuach* <note>Hebrew: תפוה</note> denotes both the tree and the fruit: the former in Joel 1:12 and Song of Solomon 8:5 and 2:3; the latter in Song of Solomon 2:5 and 7:9, just as *malum* <note>apple</note> does among the Latins.

The sense of the proverb, which we touched upon briefly from the beginning, is truly and genuinely this: Just as golden apples placed in silver engravings and elegantly crafted vessels are more delightful to the sight, so too a timely word <note>original: "σermo εὔκαιρος"</note> brings great grace in all matters, but most especially in giving advice. To speak and act is beneficial when the nature of the time demands it, *for that which is untimely is everywhere painful.* Indeed, just as things said according to the occasion—which is the very flower of time—are best, so those said or done after the occasion has passed are faulty and useless. For opportunities (*kairoi*) <note>Greek: καιροί</note>, as Demosthenes says, *do not wait for our slowness.* Pindar, in *Pythian Ode 9*, says that *Opportunity holds the peak of everything.* That is, according to the Scholiast’s interpretation on page 304, one must speak both great and small things according to the opportune moment. The Psalmist also praises this "timeliness" in the pouring out of prayers to God in *Psalm 32:6*: "Every saint shall pray to you in an opportune time" <note>original Hebrew: לעת מצוא; Greek: ἐν καιρῷ εὐθέτῳ</note>, namely, at the time when evil happens. "But in a flood of many waters, they shall not reach him," meaning when the deluge of divine wrath breaks out, then you cry out too late and in vain. The Greeks frequently use *Kairos* to mean the suitable moment for doing something, so that it may be done rightly, conveniently, and aptly. Hence Hesiod says: *Opportunity is best in all things*, which Theognis and Phocylides echo in the same words. Phocylides said "to serve the opportunity," which Cicero explains: *It is necessary to serve the time, and not to lose the time when it is given.* In this manner, Gregory of Nazianzus also instructs:

<margin>
To Nicobulus, verse 101.
</margin>
> Let us grasp the opportunity, which a wise man
> can catch. To seek it later will be a vain endeavor.

Sophocles elegantly calls that momentum of things to be done "the peak of deeds" <note>original: "ἔργων ἀκμὴν"</note> in the prologue of *Electra*:

> It is no longer time to hesitate, but the peak of deeds.

Our Sacred Writer speaks primarily of that occasion which is a part of time, holding within itself the suitable opportunity for speaking or remaining silent. Of this, Isocrates speaks best in *To Demonicus*: *Make two occasions for speaking: either about things you know clearly, or about things it is necessary to speak. For in these alone is speech better than silence, but in others, it is better to be silent than to speak.* Emperor Basil, a very diligent imitator of Isocrates, was not ignorant of this sentiment when he discussed speech and silence to his son toward the end of chapter 35. There is a time where the silence of a speech is superior, and a time where the speech is superior to silence; Euripides hands down this sentiment in *Orestes* and commends it to the youth. Plutarch, in *On the Education of Children*, says: *A timely silence is wise, and better than any speech.* For nothing is pleasing that is untimely, but all things are beautiful in their time <note>original: "πάντα δὲ καιρῷ καλά"</note>, as Sophocles instructs. This is shown with even more illustrious wisdom by the *Book of Proverbs*, which is nothing other than Christian Ethics, proposing various maxims full of richness and

## Proverbs 26, Verse 7.

->As a stone tied in a sling, so is he who gives honor to a fool. <note>Hebrew: כִּצְרוֹר אֶבֶן בְּמַרְגֵּמָה כֵּן־נוֹתֵן לִכְסִיל כָּבוֹד</note><-

<margin>
The heap of Mercury.

**W**ith this most weighty proverb, in which Solomon rebukes the reckless and thoughtless ease of conferring honors, titles, and offices, he says the same thing as the mime writer Publilius Syrus: *“Dignity in an unworthy man is a place of disgrace; for honor paid to the unworthy does not honor him, but dishonors him.”* Regarding this sentiment, 
<margin>
Book 7, Epistle 29.
</margin>
Pliny writes: *“This title especially reminded me how hostile and inept were the things that were sometimes thrown into this filth, into these dregs: onto a freedman unworthy of such great honor.”* The unworthy are compared to mud, filth, dregs, and trash. Hence Salvianus writes in *Against Avarice*, book 2, page 68: *“Nothing is more shameful than for anyone to be excellent in rank and contemptible in worthlessness. For what else is leadership without high merit but a title of honor without a man? Or what is dignity in an unworthy person but an ornament in the mud?”* For this reason, Pope Benedict XII used to call those who were unworthy of honors "mud," just as he said nothing was more important to him than that those promoted to ecclesiastical ranks and the Cardinalate should be not only eminently refined in virtue, but also most outstanding in the knowledge of sacred and civil law. He said he did not wish *“to decorate mud,”* a saying which Bucelinus praises as worthy of immortality in his *Benedictine Calendar*, volume 3, page 302.
<margin>
folio 239, column 2.
</margin>
Bernard of Clairvaux agrees in his *Second Book on Consideration to Pope Eugenius*: *“It is a monstrous thing,”* he says, *“a high rank and a low mind, the first seat and the lowest life, a high-sounding tongue and an idle hand, much talk and no fruit, a grave face and light actions, huge authority and wavering stability.”* To this is conformed what you read in Dio Chrysostom’s *Orations*, 11, page 162: *“There is no disease more grievous, neither in an individual nor in a city, than when someone who is ignorant thinks himself most wise.”* <note>original Greek: Τοῦτο μηδὲν ἔστι νόσημα χαλεπώτερον, μήτε ἐνὶ, μήτε πόλει, ἢ ὅταν τις ἀμαθὴς ὤν, σοφώτατον ἑαυτὸν νομίζῃ.</note> Jodocus Eichmann of Calw, a Doctor and Preacher of Heidelberg, calls those "horned asses" who come to high church offices through Simony <note>buying church offices</note> or other perverse ways, being neither wise

<column-break/>

nor suitable, as cited in Johann Melber’s *Preacher’s Vocabulary*, book 4. We cannot be too lengthy *on a matter so well-known*, especially since here the "mound of Mercury" <note>original: "Mercurii tumulus"</note> reminds us how useless are the things thrown into this filth. This mound was held in such veneration that no one passed it without at least touching it with a stone, if they had nothing else, *“as a sign of the honor they held for Mercury, or because they had nothing else to offer him,”* as Cornutus says in *On the Nature of the Gods*. Thus, the Vulgate translator took an allusion from the *throwing of stones at the statues of Mercury* <note>The Hebrew word for "sling" or "stone-heap" was interpreted by the Latin translator as a reference to the "Herms" or stone heaps dedicated to Hermes/Mercury found at roadsides</note>, which were once erected "throughout the lands" <note>original: κατὰ χώρας</note> to show the way to travelers. These were called "Mercurials" after Mercury, who was believed to be the god of wanderings, roads, and journeys; travelers honored him as the protector of streets and ways with heaps of stones. Just as superstition is fertile, so it fathered many Mercurys. Cicero enumerates many and affirms that the Mercury of the Egyptians was held in such high regard that they feared to speak his name. He distinguishes another from this one, whom they called Thoth <note>original: Thoyt</note>, the inventor of letters and laws in Egypt; Conring identifies him with the Phoenician Tanuth in *On Paracelsian Medicine*, pages 5, 6, 7, 32, and 33. concerning which Plutarch says: *“He said that the number especially belongs to the fourth day.”* <note>original Greek: Ἔφη μάλισα τὸν ἀριθμὸν τῇ τετράδι ἀνάκειται.</note> And for this reason, the "workmanship of his statues was square," <note>original Greek: τετράγωνος ἡ ἐργασία</note> according to Thucydides. Even the fourth day of the beginning month was consecrated to him, for Plutarch also says in the same place: *“Many record that the god was born on the fourth day of the month.”* Various fables concerning Mercury thus sprouted according to the different brains of this or that person, as each was bolder or more ingenious in invention. In these fables, due to uncertainty and the illusions of demons, the arguments lie open to any comment of the mind. The chief invention of Mercury is mentioned by Plato in the *Phaedrus and Philebus*: 
<margin>

Because of this, Julian "the Apostate" <note>the Roman Emperor who tried to reverse the Christianization of the Empire</note> always rose in the middle of the night to pray to him in secret, according to Ammianus Marcellinus, book 16. The Gauls made him the inventor of all arts, as Julius Caesar teaches in his *Gallic War*, book 6. He is called the inventor of the first elements of writing by the Phoenicians, according to Sanchuniathon in Philo, book 1. The Egyptians attributed all their wisdom regarding the stars to Mercury, according to Strabo, book 17, when he discusses the Theban priests. <meta>This page continues the discussion of cultural and religious markers, moving from the symbolic "sling stones" of Proverbs to a detailed historical and linguistic examination of "The Heap of Mercury" and its relationship to ancient road-marking traditions and biblical prophecy.</meta>

<page-num>524</page-num>
<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>The Heap of Mercury.</margin> Magius, in his *Critical Treasury* <note>page 1422</note>, writes that when God heard of the ways and journeys, there arose heaps of stones which people had made for Mercury in obscure paths. To the Greeks, these were called *hermaies* <note>original Greek: ἑρμαῖες</note> and *hermaioi lophoi* <note>original Greek: ἑρμαῖοι λόφοι—meaning "Heaps of Hermes"</note>. Regarding this, the Scholiast of Nicander says: *hermakes are stones piled up in honor of Hermes.* <note>original Greek: ἑρμακες, λίθοι σεσωρευμένοι εἰς τιμὴν τοῦ ἑρμοῦ</note> And Isidore notes in his *Glossaries*: *Of Mercury: a mass of stones on the peaks of hills.* Vincentius Chartarius of Reggio, <margin>On the Images of the Gods, page 224.</margin> according to the translator Verderius, states: *Travelers used to accumulate heaps of stones by the statues of Mercury, so that each person added a single stone, implying that the God should be honored with whatever thing was ready and at hand; or because it seemed to clear the road so other travelers would not stumble on the stones, or because the heap of stones made the statue of the God more noticeable to those passing by.* Roads were marked by stones, and through them certain intervals were counted; hence, it is familiar among Roman writers to speak of the "first stone," the "second," the "twentieth," and so on. For where there were no *Herms* <note>pillars topped with a head</note>, it was the custom for several stones to be heaped together to serve the same turn and purpose; compare Camerarius in his notes on *Sophocles' Oedipus* <note>page 338</note> and Mutius in Herodotus <note>Book 4</note>. Travelers passing by these gathered stones, whether out of a certain piety or superstition, increased them daily, so that they eventually grew into a small mound. What sort of *Herms* these were is not unknown: Macrobius is the authority that most images of Mercury were figured in a *square* stance. Plutarch attributes a *square* stance without hands or feet to Mercury. And if we believe Plato, Hipparchus first showed the use of them to the Athenians. These Mercuries or *Herms* were quadrangular; the upper part represented the form of Mercury, while the lower part showed road inscriptions, which is why it is called "four-cornered Hermes" <note>original Greek: ἑρμᾶς τετραγλώχις</note> in an epigram by Leonidas, because it had four points or sharp-angled corners. Regarding this quadrangular Mercury, Ulpian writes in his commentary on Demosthenes' *Oration against Leptines*: <margin>page 141.</margin> *Herms are square pieces of wood or stone having ears, with the head of Hermes above, and inscriptions on the flat surface below.* <note>original Greek: Ἐρμοῖ, ξύλα ἢ λίθοι τετράγωνοι ὦτα ἔχοντες ὦσιν ἑρμᾶ ἐπάνω, κάτω δὲ ἐν τῷ πλάτει τὰ ἐπιγράμματα</note> And Thucydides <note>Book 6, chapter 206</note> says: *There were many stone Herms in the local fashion of square workmanship.* Even the *Termini* <note>boundary markers</note>, over which Mercury was believed to preside (hence he was called *epitermios* or "guardian of boundaries"), were erected in a square shape; for the stone rose from the earth narrower at its lowest part, but wider at the top, being of a quadrangular shape on both sides, upon the summit of which, as we have said, a human likeness of Mercury was placed, expressed as far as the chest. These square images of Mercury stood in Athens in the temples, and also in the vestibules of private houses; some time before the Sicilian War, they were defaced and hacked about the head, and the *Hermokopidai* <note>original Greek: ἑρμοκοπίδες—literally "Herm-choppers"</note> were unknown, about whom Thucydides reported these things: <margin>Book 6, page 430</margin> *As many stone Herms as were in the city of the Athenians (there are many in the local square workmanship both in private porches and in sacred places), most had their faces hacked around in a single night; and no one knew who had done it, but they were sought out publicly with large rewards.* But as to why the Mercurial likeness was made in a square form rather than a round one, the Scholiast of Thucydides explains: <margin>page 430.</margin> *Hermes is Reason [Logos],* he says, *and he is sacred to Truth. Because of this, they also constructed his images in a square and cube-like fashion, hinting that such a shape, on whichever side it falls, is stable and upright on every side. So too is Reason, just as Truth is similar to itself from every side. But falsehood is many-colored and many-branched.* <note>original Greek: Ἐρμῆς λόγος ait, καὶ ἀληθείας ἵερος ᾖ... τὸ ψεῦδος δὲ πολὐχων καὶ πολυσχιδές</note> Demosthenes deals with the violators of these statues and the rewards established for judgment in his *Against Meidias*. The fact that violators of the Herms were held as sacrilegious shows immediately that there was once a great and entirely august veneration for that kind of statue. A well-known example in the common crowd was that of Alcibiades, who was cast into great danger of his life at the very time he was acting as commander with Nicias and Lamachus for the fleet about to attack Sicily. Plutarch described at length in his *Life of Alcibiades* how he was both accused and condemned in his absence because of the mutilation of the Herms, and how his accomplices were punished with the ultimate penalty; compare Thucydides <note>Book 6, pages 431, 448, and 453</note>. It was common for either a deed or some useful life-maxim to be carved into these. Cimon's victory was carved into the square statues of Mercury, though his name was concealed, as Plutarch testifies <margin>in Cimon, page 482.</margin>: *The people permitted him to dedicate the stone Herms. These, although they nowhere revealed Cimon's name, seemed to the men of that time to hold an excess of honor.* Therefore, at three-way and four-way crossroads and other most frequent places, Mercurial statues were once erected in honor and veneration of Mercury, the guardian of roads and a God of the Gentiles. These were imitated by the overly superstitious religiousness and "demon-fear" <note>original Greek: δεισιδαιμονία</note> of earlier centuries out of a mere habit of "idol-madness" <note>original Greek: εἰδωλομανίας</note>. An example of this is provided to us by the letters on a certain terminal consecration stone, which we have in the original manuscript, and which I am pleased to include here word-for-word:

<column-break/>

<margin>The Heap of Mercury.</margin>
> I, Thomas, by the grace of God and the Apostolic See, Bishop of Vice-Campania and Vicar General in pontificals for the Reverend Father in Christ and Lord, Lord Jacob, by divine mercy Archbishop of the holy see of Mainz. We make it known to all that in the year 1508, on the fifth day of the month of September, we have solemnly consecrated this present itinerary stone in the name of God, to the praise of Almighty God and in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, the blessed Elizabeth, the blessed James, and the blessed Apollonia, granting from above the customary Episcopal indulgences in the usual manner.

Jeremiah seems to refer to such "guide-stones" in chapter 31:21: <term>Tsijonim</term> <note>Hebrew: צִיֻּנִים</term> <term>Set up signposts [Tsijonim], make for yourself guideposts [Tamrurim]</term> <note>Hebrew: הַצִּיבִי לָךְ צִיֻּנִים שִׂמִי לָךְ תַּמְרוּρִים</note> where <term>Tsijonim</term> signifies *statues* or stones, such as are usually erected and placed in fields to indicate the way. Or, in one word: *Herms*, as Junius and Tremellius translate it. <term>Tamrurim</term> <note>Hebrew: תַּמְרוּרִים</note> indeed denotes eminences; or as Rabbi David Kimchi explains it, high markers, *lofty statues*, by which travelers (to use Salvian's word) are guided. For in this place, God foretells and promises liberation to Ephraim, who was once turned away from Him and for that reason led into the Babylonian exile, and who is now the enemy's captive. And lest he doubt this divine promise, God commands at the same time that signs be set up—not because He approves of the idolatrous actions of the Gentiles who consecrated their signs to Mercury, but so that, taking occasion from their common custom, the people of Israel might—setting aside the reason of false worship—look toward their future...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into "The Heap of Mercury," transitioning from classical definitions to the theological interpretation of biblical prophecy and a wide-ranging survey of "stone-heaping" traditions across the Jewish, Islamic, and Northern European worlds.</meta>

<page-num>525</page-num>
<header>From Proverbs 26, verse 7.</header>

<margin>The Heap of Mercury.</margin> ...let it remind us of the future and certain return; let it be erected so that we may know the way by which we were led away from the blessed land to Babylon, and the very path by which we must return. However, all these things must be understood mystically. For Ephraim (that is, the Ten Tribes) never returned from captivity, as Saint Jerome notes. Instead, they are commanded to meditate upon and prepare for a return to their cities which they deserted—not physical cities, but spiritual ones; namely, to the true Churches of God, which are to be established in the name of Christ in every province throughout the whole world. Yet these words could also be understood literally in this way: *Return from Assyria to your own cities in Samaria; where you will see and rejoice that Christian Churches have been raised up, flourishing with all spiritual goods.* For these were the first to receive the Apostles and Christianity, as is clear from *Acts* 8:14. Therefore, the Prophet addresses Ephraim and the Samaritans above others, inviting them to this joy. To explain <margin>Hebrew Questions, book 1, question 66.</margin> that phrase of the Old Translator <note>likely referring to the Vulgate or a related commentary</note>, Johannes Drusius and Johannes Buxtorf (in his *Chaldean-Talmudic Lexicon*, page 1263)—those leaders of Jewish antiquity and secret learning—trace the phrase back to the writings of the Hebrews. They explain Solomon’s words thus: *If anyone throws a stone onto a "Mercury,"* regarding which there is also a Talmudic gloss in the *Treatise on Idolatry*: *There are nations that worship a heap of stones, which they call "Mercury."* The worship is of this kind: *whoever passes by throws a stone onto that heap.* Such worship is touched upon by Rabbi Moses Maimonides in his *Book on Idolatry* (chapter 3, number 2); Rabbi Elias in *Tishbi*; Rabbi Nathan in the *Lexicon of Law*; and Rabbi Ishmael in the *Gemara*. Truly, whatever the more recent Rabbis might write or imagine regarding the worship of Mercury, I do not believe that in the time of the pious Solomon this manner of worshipping Mercury was known among the Israelite people—certainly not to the extent that Solomon would have alluded to it in this sentence as a thing known to all Israelites. Compare Dionysius Vossius in his notes on Maimonides; Selden’s *On the Syrian Gods* (Syntagma 2, chapter 15); Drusius (Decade 5, Hebrew Proverb 6); Grotius’s *Annotations* on this passage; Rupert in *Flowers* (page 132); and Hermann Conring (page 66). Vincent of Beauvais, in his *Historical Mirror* (book 24), teaches that this was observed by ancient custom among the Arabs and Indians; his words were fully transcribed by Caspar Barthius in *Adversaria* (book 9, chapter 5), and reviewed by Scaliger in *On the Correction of Time* (book 5, pages 486–487) and Vossius in *On Idolatry* (book 2, chapter 32, page 475). Sophronius, in the *Spiritual Meadow* (chapter 155), records that the Muslims worshipped Venus and offered human sacrifices to her, as do Evagrius in his *Ecclesiastical History* (book 6, chapter 33) and Dauroultius in *Flowers of Examples* (title 19, example 10, page 42). I read in Vincent <margin>book 21, chapter 60.</margin> of Beauvais, who reports from a dispute between a Christian and a Turk, that these same people performed an expiation for Venus using raised stones outside the city of Mecca. He says it was an ancient custom of two Indian nations, called the Zenchia and Alarachum, to circle the images of demons while naked and bald with great howling, to kiss the corners, and to throw stones onto a heap, which was built up as if in honor of the Gods. They did this twice a year, at the beginning of spring and autumn. This custom, having descended from the Indians to the Arabs, was found by Muhammad to be celebrated in his time at Mecca in honor of Venus. 

<column-break/>

He did not abolish it but approved it, <margin>The Heap of Mercury.</margin> even though he had removed the other delusions of idolatry. Indeed, it is said that this was usually shown *to Venus alone*, such that small stones were thrown backward from beneath the genital members, because Venus was thought to rule especially over those parts. He reported that this is still done in the temple at Mecca; and since the throwing was done by naked men, some instituted a rule that those throwing the stones should cover their loins at least with a small linen cloth, so that, being completely stripped, they might not imitate the shamelessness of dogs. This madness, which to Christians is a "devising of the mind" <note>original Greek: ἐπινενόησις—an invention or mental construct</note>, Muhammad is deservedly believed to have left intact and safe—while commanding other cults of demons to cease—*lest he leave his Lady Venus, in whom he boasted himself to be most powerful, entirely without honor.* Nor do I hear that the traces of the old custom of piling stones have vanished among them today. I also know that many heaps exist in Courland <note>a historical region in modern-day Latvia</note>, a region once most fertile in superstition, with which they formerly honored the Gods; and even now, some persevere in that superstition. In Denmark, I have seen heaps of stones of significant size thrown here and there in the roads and fields, which they once erected in honor of the dead, and perhaps also of the Gods. It would have been a sacrilege <note>original: piaculum</note> to have removed or even cast out those stones, even many years later. Apuleius describes such roadside superstitions at the beginning of the first book of the *Florida*: *Nor would a traveler find a more just cause for a religious delay than an altar wreathed with flowers, or a cave shaded with leaves, or an oak burdened with horns, or a beech tree crowned with skins, or even a small hill consecrated by a fence, or a trunk fashioned by a blade, or a turf smoking with a libation, or a stone anointed with oil.* <note>original: unguine delibutus</note> Janus Gruter (page 390). Sacred stones were also consecrated by Numa <note>the legendary second king of Rome</note>, regarding whom Dionysius of Halicarnassus <margin>book 2, Antiquities, 133.</margin> says: *Having ordered each person to mark his own property and set stones on the borders, he declared the stones sacred to Jupiter of the Boundaries.* <note>original Greek: Κελεύσας ἑκάστῳ περιγράψαι τὴν ἑαυτοῦ κτῆσιν, καὶ στῆσαι λίθους ἐπὶ τοῖς ὅροις ἱεροὺς ἀπέδειξεν ὁρίῳ Διὸς τοὺς λίθους.</note> "Jupiter of the Boundaries" <note>original Greek: ὅριος Ζεύς</note> is mentioned by Pollux in the *Onomasticon* (book 9, page 418) and by Plato in the *Laws* (book 8, page 914). If we wish to cross over into Arabia, we shall see that there arose, by a most severe custom, a new mass of stones which was placed in the fields of an enemy. Ulpian mentions this by the name *skopelismos* <note>original Greek: σκοπελισμὸς—the crime of "stoning" a field as a threat</note> in the law *Sunt quaedam* regarding extraordinary crimes. He says: *Many enemies are accustomed to "stone" the estate of an enemy, that is, to place stones as a sign that if anyone should cultivate that field, he would perish by a cruel death through the snares of those who placed the stones; which thing holds such fear that no one dares to approach that field, fearing the cruelty of those who performed the "stoning" (skopelismon).* Some apply the words of Job <margin>chapter 5, verse 23.</margin> regarding the *covenant made with the stones* to those stone mounds or rocky signs placed in an enemy's land; in explaining this expression, we shall no longer be stuck. Certainly, that punishment began long after Job, so that this "stoning" <note>original: σκοπελισμός</note> would be entirely foreign here. One may indeed compare them, but one cannot say it was alluded to there, since those things began only many centuries later. Can an infant testify about things that happened before he was born? Suidas is the authority that the Arabs worshipped an unshaped black stone as Mars. This passage is praised by Elmenhorst in his notes on Arnobius (book 6, page 112). What "The Heap of Mercury" or "a stony Herm" <note>original Greek: ἢ λίθινος ἑρμὸς τὰ ἑρμᾶ</note> means when applied to those who bestow honor upon a fool with entirely useless labor is briefly narrated by Justus

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "Heap of Mercury," moving from mystical interpretations of prophecy to the specific philological and cultural origins of the phrase as found in Proverbs 26:8. It contrasts the classical Roman/Greek understanding of Mercury statues with the Hebrew linguistic roots related to stoning and slings.</meta>

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
The Heap of Mercury, Epistle 5, Century 5. Miscellany.
</margin>
Lipsius * Mercury, the protector of roads, and called by the Greeks *enodios* <note>original: "ἐνόδιος", meaning "of the road"</note> or *odegos* <note>original: "ὁδηγὸς", meaning "guide"</note>, was depicted at crossroads or triple-ways in a pillar-like form, often as a rough, square stone which the Greeks called *Hermas* <note>statues known as Herms</note>. These were signs and indicators of the way; and where those were not present, they would pile up several stones to serve the same function and use. Thus, these few stones, thrown or arranged there, were increased by the piety or superstition of travelers. The Hebrew sage <note>Solomon, in Proverbs</note> says of this: *to give a benefit or honor to the foolish and unworthy is like someone wanting to throw a stone into such a heap; for while it is a benefit to a traveler, no one acknowledges it because the giver is unknown: likewise, you lose the benefit you confer on a foolish, unworthy person.* J. Selden (Syntagma 2, 15) and Vossius (Book 1, p. 474) wrote in the same vein. Johannes Arboreus leads us a different way in his *Commentary on Proverbs* (folio 91b) when he writes: *Mercury is imagined to be the God of commerce and the interpreter of the Gods, therefore called Hermes by the Greeks, from "hermeneuein" <note>original: "ἑρμηνεύειν", to interpret</note>. He taught the wrestling school, invented the lyre, and because the gentiles, addicted to their superstitions, were accustomed to give the highest honor to Mercury—which nonetheless should be given only to the one true and greatest God—and consecrated a sacred shrine to him, the honor given to the unlearned and foolish is compared to that given to Mercury, because both are vain and empty. And he who throws a stone into a heap of material from which a temple to Mercury is built is like him who gives the highest honors to the most speechless and lazy person, since in both cases the effort is useless and ineffective. They put Mercury in charge of commerce; for they thought he had the greatest power over profit, money, and trade, as Caesar says in Book VI of the Gallic Wars.* Looking toward this, Nicolaus Lyra understands the "heap of Mercury" as counting-stones or little pebbles: *Mercury is called the God of reasoning among the gentiles. Reasoning is called "calculation," in which they used to use little pebbles in ancient times.* However, while reading the Hebrew text, I have not yet happened to see this Mercury; rather, the word <term>Margemah</term> <note>Hebrew: מרגמה</note> implies something else. This word appears only in this place and nowhere else in the Sacred Code, such that it must be applied to Mercury, despite whatever Johannes Goropius Becanus might mutter in his more-than-silly trifles <note>original: "nugis plusquàm Becceselenicis"</note>, in which that fool delights.

<margin>
1. Hieroglyphics, page 14.
</margin>
The word <term>Margemah</term> has caused much trouble for many, and it is a wonder what cold and ridiculous things some have dreamed up regarding it. Indeed, regarding their controversy, I gather that the word was foreign to them, and therefore I am not at all surprised that great disputes have arisen over its interpretation. I praise those who translated it as "the heap of Mercury." For among the ancients, mounds of stones were usually gathered on the roads to show the way to the traveler; those who passed by and were warned by their benefit to keep the right path would add a stone, by which the heap—the road-guide—would gradually grow. Solomon says, therefore, that he who gives honor to a fool gains no more favor with him than he who throws a stone into a heap of Mercury, which understands nothing at all of what it receives. To this day in Spain, there are very many heaps of this kind, not a few of which I saw while traveling from Merida <note>original: "Augusta Emerita"</note> to Guadalupe. I think it unworthy to bring up how Becanus compares <term>Margemah</term> with "Marckmann" in his 

<column-break/>

tasteless way, by which he usually prefers his Cimmerian darkness <note>a proverb for total ignorance</note> to the Hebrew light. We oppose him with what Johannes Stephan Menochius, a theologian of the Society of Jesus, asserts against that "heap of Mercury" (though it is supported by a pile of so many interpreters): *That ritual,* he writes, *is found only in the Latin Vulgate edition; for the Hebrew seems to mean something else, as will be clear to those consulting the interpreters.* Therefore, I would not easily assert that the ancient Jews had this custom, but rather that our Latin translator wished to explain the mind of the Wise Man by a more recent ritual and custom that fit the matter. Among almost all, however, it is confessed that <term>Ragam</term> <note>Hebrew: רגם</note> means to overwhelm with stones, hence <term>Regamah</term> is a collection of stones, and <term>Margemah</term> is the "stoning" or "overwhelming" which is done with stones. It almost always has the noun "stone" <note>Hebrew: אבן, Eben</note> attached; hence, in one word, the Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> everywhere expresses it as *lithobolian* <note>original: "λιθοβολίαν", stoning</note>, and once in Numbers 14:10 as *katabolein* <note>original: "καταβολείν", to strike down</note>. From this, <term>Ragam</term> denotes a criminal who must be punished by public execution—that is, the overwhelming of stones (Leviticus 20:2, 27; 24:14, 16, 23; Numbers 15:35, 36; Deuteronomy 21:21; Joshua 7:25). It also refers to a hated man, such as Joshua and Caleb when they urged the march against the Canaanites, whom the whole congregation of Israelites thought to stone (Numbers 14:10); likewise Adoram, the legate of Rehoboam (1 Kings 12:18; 2 Chronicles 10:18), and Zechariah (2 Chronicles 24:21); compare Joshua 8:29 and 10:27 concerning those strangled and thrown into a pit and covered with stones. From this comparison, Dr. Geyer (Commentary on this place) and Ursinus (Volume 2, Sacred Analects) conclude that by <term>Margema</term> is most simply understood such a heap of stones that remains from such an execution, and is deservedly held as mournful and detestable. This was most aptly rendered into our language and usage by Blessed Luther as the *Rabenstein* <note>German: "Raven-stone," a traditional name for a place of public execution or a gallows hill</note>. From this they further infer: just as it would be plainly indecent, absurd, and damaging to throw a precious stone—which in the judgment of the ancients showed the majesty of nature's things compressed into a small space, as Pliny witnesses—*into a common pile of such mournful stones*, when it is worthy to be held in the highest price and worn for honor's sake; and since in this way all its value is lost and it profits no one further; so it is also indecent, absurd, shameful, and damaging to confer honor—so precious a thing—upon a fool or an inept man who will abuse it. So they say. Along with Rabbi Solomon and the Septuagint, others understand <term>Margemah</term> as a *sphendonen* <note>original: "σφενδόνην", a sling</note>, including Kimchi, Lyranus, Cajetan, Pagninus, Buxtorf in his Lexicons, Junius, the Dutch version, Piscator, Quistorp, and others, who translate <term>Ragam</term> as "to throw, to hurl, to aim with a sling" (2 Samuel 16:13; Lamentations 1:18, 2:14; Esther 5:14). Thus they translate <term>Margemah</term> as a sling, a machine made of ropes by which stones are emitted by rotating, and the meaning emerges: *Just as a stone is tied by a slinger in a sling only to be immediately thrown and lost, so the foolish glory and honor given to a man quickly vanishes, nor is such a foolish direction of honor permanent.* Johannes Draconites, Professor at Marburg, in his *Pentaplo* (folio 97a):

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological investigation into Proverbs 26:8 and transitions into a "Sacred Botany" commentary on Ecclesiastes 2:4–5. The previous page explored the classical Greek and Roman concept of "Mercury’s Heap" (stone markers for travelers) as a lens for the Proverb; here, the author evaluates various interpretations of the "stone and sling" before moving to the creation of plants.</meta>

<margin>
The Heap of Mercury.
Chiliads 4, Century 7, num. 4, page 974.
</margin>
...is not *understood*, but rather despised, and it becomes a disgrace. A simpler sense is seen by Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), a famous Renaissance humanist</note> who translated the Adages, saying: *The most clever opinion of those authors is that they refer to the foundation of a sling. For your service to a fool is not only lost, but it even remains to your own harm; just as if you were to bind a stone into a fool's sling, you have given him the means with which to strike you.* Others take "stone" not as just any rock, but as a gem or another precious stone, hence Aben Esra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a Spanish Jewish scholar</note> says: *As the binding of a precious stone in a heap of common stones, so is the showing of honor to a fool.* The word "stone" is used *preeminently* <note>original: "κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν"</note> for a precious stone, which was also the opinion of Luther. Moschopulus <note>A Byzantine grammarian</note> writes: "the stone" <note>original: "ἡ λίθος"</note> instead of "precious stones" <note>original: "τῶν τιμίων λίθων"</note>. This is also seen among the secular authors. Plutarch, in his *Precepts of Marriage*, writes: "with gold and stones" <note>original: "χρυσῷ καὶ λίθοις"</note>, meaning *gold and gems.* So too Synesius in his 3rd Epistle, page 160: "he bound gold and stones" <note>original: "χρυσία καὶ λίθους ἔδησεν"</note>—that is, he had fitted himself with gold and gems. Junius and his assistant Tremellius <note>Reformed theologians known for their Latin Bible translation</note> understood this as a military engine used for shaking walls, rendering it: *He who applies a stone to a ballista <note>a large ancient catapult</note>: so is he who grants honor to a fool.* Piscator, as usual, follows their wording. Martin Luther, however, and Johann Forster explain it as a *polyandrion* <note>original Greek: "πολυανδρίῳ", a mass grave or burial place</note> or cemetery, where the corpses of the lowly and the condemned were covered with a massive heap of stones. The Glosses state: A slaughter-place is a *polyandrion*,
<margin>folio 766.</margin>
a heap of corpses <note>original: "σωρὸς νεκρῶν"</note>. Papias says: *Polyandrion* is a mound of the dead. Forster’s words in his Hebrew Lexicon are: *It speaks of a precious stone thrown into a mournful heap of stones, which was destined to overwhelm the condemned, and was therefore an abomination to this people.* Both explanations of the word agree with the reality of granting unworthy dignity to a fool, even if the interpreters, who decide by their own arbitrary judgment, do not agree on the specific word. Laurence Ramirez in his *Pentecontarch* (chapter 49) and Ferdinand de Salazar on this passage (pages 735 to 747) are very laborious in their usual way to reconcile both translations. They are in vain, and the reason escapes them much if they bring in the winged God of eloquence <note>Mercury/Hermes</note> to mock the honor of a fool as merely empty. We believe that Mercury should be cast out of the Hebrew territory <note>original: "pomœrio", the sacred boundary</note> with pitchforks.

### Ecclesiastes 2: 4, 5.

<note>Hebrew: "I made for myself gardens and parks and planted in them every tree of fruit."</note>
<note>Greek: "I made for myself gardens and paradises, and I planted in them every kind of fruit tree."</note>

->I planted for myself vineyards; I made for myself gardens and paradises, and I planted in them trees of every fruit.<-

<margin>Sacred Botany.</margin>
God, the first Maker of all things, alone through His eternal word and the Holy Spirit fostering all things, willed to produce the first types of things in their first individuals extraordinarily and *without seed* <note>original: "ἀσπερμάτως"</note> from the earth: herbs, shrubs, and trees without the assistance of rains and without human cultivation. For there were no rains, but mention is indeed made of a "vapor," where the Hebrew has *Ed* <note>אד</note>. For what the Greek and Latin versions say—that *a fountain emerged from the earth*—which led Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (672–735)</note> to anxiously inquire how a single fountain could irrigate the whole world, is of no consequence. Indeed, *Ed* properly signifies vapor, which is why Aquila <note>a 2nd-century translator of the Bible into Greek</note> rendered it as "mist" and "moisture" <note>original: "ἐπιβάδα & νοτίδα"</note>, which vapor moistened and irrigated the earth in place of rain. From the most fertile womb of Earth and Water, at God's command and by the power He imparted,

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Botany.</margin>
various herbs and trees, various minerals, various animals, and various fish were produced. For the sacred voice of God *said* <note>original: "ἔφη"</note>: *Let the earth bring forth grass yielding seed, etc.* This is contained in the word *Tadshe* <note>תדשא</note>, with which He concluded the works of the third day. Regarding why trees and plants were created before the sun and the celestial lights, but animals after, Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397), Bishop of Milan</note> in his inquiry writes as follows: <margin>3rd Hexameron, 6</margin> *Many are accustomed to say that unless the milder heat of the Sun warmed the lands and fostered them with its rays, the earth could not germinate; and for this reason, the Nations grant divine honor to the Sun, believing that by the power of its heat it penetrates the depths of the earth and fosters the scattered seeds, or relaxes the frozen veins of the trees. Let the herb be born before the light of the Sun is made; let its prerogative be older than the Sun. Lest the error of men grow strong, let the earth germinate before it receives the sun's favor. Let all know that the Sun is not the author of living things. It is younger than the herbs, younger than the grass.* Josephus de la Zerda expresses the same sentiment in his *Academy* (3, section 4, number 33, page 59): Why did God bring forth gardens and humble tamarisks and tender herbs before the creation of the Sun and the Sun's splendors? On the third day, relaxing the earth, He made trees, soaking the veins with fertile heat and moistening them without flowing liquids, painting the earth with a multicolored tapestry. He delayed the lights of heaven, the shining choirs and hosts of stars, until the fifth day, as if the thickets were more noble, or their primacy in origin was unlearned before the rising of the Sun. Indeed, it was not so much the honor of the field as the honor of the Divine Power that drove such a precocious creation of plants. If the Sun and stars went first, the human mind, prone to sin, would attribute the birth of plants to the fervent and kind offices of the Sun, and would believe the earth received the fostering of the glowing light to expand into fruit-bearing wood. Trees turn green without the help of the shining creature, and fruits burst forth from the deserted soil, so that the unity of God might remain secure, and no plurality be introduced into the divinity by thinking the Sun is God. Truly, from the beginning, plants were produced immediately from the earth before they arose in the earth in a natural way, according to the Mosaic saying: *Let the earth bring forth a sprout, an herb producing seed, and a fruit tree.* And hence, concerning the immediate production of plants, Moses says: *Let the earth sprout a sprout;* concerning the second way: *The earth produced.* Hence Augustine interprets this as referring only to the power handed down by God and received by the earth, so that the sense of the first words is: *Let the earth have the natural power of germinating and bringing forth plants and bringing them to maturity.* Of the latter words: *The earth received the natural power of producing plants, which thereafter would be born by the ordinary law of nature from the seed itself.* Therefore, all that the earth produces from its most fertile womb is not produced by some random reason, but proceeds from the heavenly Power, who moderates all things in heaven and earth, and who pours out Wisdom *over all His works* (Sirach 1:9). Plants are ordered by God with marvelous art, displaying an illustrious and most express testimony of Divine Wisdom and goodness, *and these things indicate the craftsmanship of some wise and life-loving Creator* <note>original: "καὶ ταῦτα σοφῷ τινι καὶ φιλοζώῳ δημιουργῷ τέχνημα εἶναι ἐνδείκνυσι"</note>; even a single herb brings God before us. And thus in plants, God is seen as the *originator of life inherent in every sprout* <note>original: "γενεσιουργὸς ἑκάστῳ βλαστήματι ἐνυπάρχοντος"</note>, as Origen says, *by the skill found in the roots and the leaves.* <margin>Philocal. c. 2. p. 61.</margin>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Botany.</margin>
...and the potential fruits, and the differences of qualities. <note>original: "καὶ τὰς ἐνδεχομένας καρποὺς, καὶ τὰς διαφορὰς τῶν ποιοτήτων"</note> Three species of plants are recounted by Moses, the first of which he calls *deshe* <note>Hebrew: דשא; refers to young, unsown grass or sprouts</note>, that is, **unsown herb** or voluntary growth; the second *eseb* <note>Hebrew: עשב</note>, **sown herb**, or that which comes forth through cultivation; and the third *etz* <note>Hebrew: עץ</note>, **Tree**, under which name **Shrubs** also seem to be understood. Others distribute them into at least two kinds: *eseb* and *etz*. The Greeks translate the latter as *xylon* <note>original: "ξύλον"; wood or tree</note>, by which they encompass trees, shrubs, and similar things; the former they translate as *chortos* <note>original: "χόρτον"; grass or fodder</note>, in which category are grains, herbs, flowers, and so on. Specific mention is made of the **Seed**, which God willed to be within each species so that, through its intervention, the species might be preserved, which otherwise would perish in their individual members. From this follows God's approval, and thus the creation of the third day is concluded. Therefore, the generations of plants from the almighty and wonderful ordination of God are today both marvelous and varied: they are produced either spontaneously, or by seed, or by root, or by tearing away <note>cuttings</note>, or by branch, or by sprout, or by the trunk itself. The spontaneous plants, and those which come forth under a temperate and mild zone, hold the primary place. Nature plays in the fields with wonderful gestures, and the mildness of the air makes the appearance of the stems lovely. Just as a place happens to have various temperatures, so it produces many diversities in plants. This plant loves this region, that one loves another, and not everything grows everywhere. Some love to inhabit cold places, some chilly ones. Some are native to certain places, so that they utterly reject other lands. Egypt has its own peculiar **plants** <note>original: "φυτὰ"</note>, as does Arabia and Judea. **Frankincense, myrrh, balsam, cinnamon, and cassia** are assigned as if peculiar to themselves in those regions verging toward the east and south, yet they by no means wish to travel toward the North. There are also the faults and diseases of plants caused by the defect of a region. Each place has its own property in producing plants, its own praise, and its own benefit. However, frequent disputes arise from the lack of similarity among things of different kinds in plants, the confused variety of names, the diversity of languages, the negligence of authors in describing them, and the ignorance of some, which makes the study of plants most difficult and obscure. Botanists differ greatly in the names of herbs, a fact which even the single *Phytopinax* <note>A famous botanical "Index of Plants" (1596) by Gaspard Bauhin</note> or Botanical Index of Bauhin leaves well-attested; in it, you will find so many various names for one and the same herb collected into one. From this come such frequent disputes in every age; hence Pliny, **in the preface to Book XIV**, deplores that few in his time knew the names of those things which had been commemorated by Hesiod a thousand years before. *So much more fertile,* he says, *was the care of the ancients, or more successful their industry. Nor in this our century is there peace among the Sons of the Botanists.* Truly, it is a most obscure business among both the Ancients and our own people, no less laborious and full of weariness, to compare the histories of plants and to weigh their faculties and powers. Even those who seek herbs with diligent and burning zeal—whether those found in our Scripture, or those described in Dioscorides or Theophrastus—are afflicted by no small difficulties. A plant that was once most well-known to everyone is often unknown to modern Botanists. Not infrequently we see those who examine the names of plants in the books of Theophrastus <note>The "father of botany" (c. 371–287 BC)</note> deprived of their aim and fruit, for those names are known today neither to Doctors nor to other learned men, the names having been changed

<column-break/>

surely by later generations, and because similar things are hardly found in another author on the same subject. This complaint about the obscurity of ancient plants is as widespread as the contemplation of plants itself extends into every part of the three divisions of the world. One man here censures Mesue <note>A reference to influential medical writers of the Islamic Golden Age</note>, another hisses at Serapion, and that one over there picks at Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), author of *De Materia Medica*</note>. Botanists tread this path of contention, and when in the progress of their journey they come upon herbs, what seemed at first sight to be Rhapontic <note>a type of medicinal rhubarb</note> to one, seems the exact opposite to another; and while they linger in the struggle, someone stands by and exclaims with Brasavola <note>Antonio Musa Brassavola (1500–1555), an Italian physician and botanist</note>:

<margin><note>Examination of Herbs, page 4</note></margin>
> *O wondrous error of the moderns, and wondrous laziness of the pharmacists! For so many centuries they have been deceived in this herb, and are now deceived, yet they refuse to learn; even if the thing itself is brought before their eyes, they recognize the truth, but with a certain malignant spirit they deny the truth, and would rather persevere in that stubborn ignorance of theirs than acknowledge the truth.*

Those words of Theophrastus, so often used, testify concerning the ancients: **so to speak**, or **to speak in general terms** <note>original: "ὡς εἰπεῖν, ὡς τύπῳ εἰπεῖν"</note>; yet no one was a better Botanist—a rational one, if I may say so—than Theophrastus. **Dioscorides** was indeed anxious in his botanical study, yet he was occasionally a guest on foreign soil, testifying sometimes by the word **to record based on inquiry** <note>original: "ἱσορεῖν"</note> that he spoke entirely from the faith of others, that he followed the reports of others, and described plants not seen by himself. We also attest to the reliability of modern Botanists, who are nevertheless closer to the truth because of their voyages and their own industry, as they see with their eyes the native places of those plants and grasp with their hands the plants which were perceived by the ancients only by hearsay and listening. Yet how often do they still disagree! How little they remember their own points! Hermolaus thinks one way, Dalechamps another, Bauhin another, and others differently. On one side stands Dodoens, on another de l'Obel, and on that side Mattioli <note>References to 16th-century European botanists</note>. While I wander through these **errors** <note>original: "πλανὰς"</note> of opinions, I have judged it better to restrain my pen, lest it commit some insolent fault, rather than to enter an inexplicable Labyrinth. But truly, since it is not my intention to describe all the plants of all lands in this study, but only those which that desired Garden of Palestine supplies to us, it will be enough if, while others are closed off, the desired Garden of Palestine lies open to us. Palestine is so excellently cultivated with plants by the singular goodness of nature that it could challenge the other parts of the rest of the world. King Solomon—pronounced the Wisest not by the praise of Apollo, as Socrates was, but by the decree of the true God—preferred the Gift of Wisdom over all the Goods of earthly and temporal happiness. Being instructed by its virtue from heaven (at his own request), he not only wrote distinguished parables and composed a natural history of all vegetables, from the cedar upon the mountain even to the moss upon the wall, but also, with that science of natural things in which he excelled, he built vineyards, gardens, and paradises, and planted in them trees of every kind and fruit. Indeed, what the industry of Solomon performed here, as a most experienced physicist and botanist, requires no further deduction; only compare **Song of Songs** 8:12 and following, and 6:1, 10. Mention is made of the royal gardens near the two walls in 2 Kings 21:18, 25:4, and Jeremiah 39:4. Regarding the enclosed garden of Solomon, situated among very rugged mountains in a most pleasant valley, with most fertile soil and adorned with the most decorative trees, see if you please...

# Ecclesiastes 11:4–5

<margin>Sacred Botany.</margin>
As noted in the *Travels of Cotovicus, page 243*, we might believe that the rarest herbs, the most delicate flowers, the noblest vines, and trees of every kind—both domestic and exotic, brought from other parts of the world and distant islands—were found in the vineyard, garden, and paradise of Solomon. Indeed, his plantation was a compendium of all the rarest plants. However, we extend the vision of our mind beyond his physical garden, for we wish to include in this "Biblical Garden" whatever **plants occur in the Sacred Code**. Although the herbs in this biblical garden may seem lowly and contemptible at first glance, do not blame the gardener or despise the garden. Look not at the appearance, but at the virtues; look not at the flower, but at the excellence of the flower.

> ->Though small in appearance, no little herb is despised,<-
> ->in which a great use does not simultaneously dwell.<-

While an entrance into these sacred fields is prepared for us, and while our mind intends to visit the most pleasant gardens, meadows, and parks, the groves, forests, and all the valleys, plains, hills, and mountains painted in their native and varied colors; behold, there is offered to us the *Biblical Arboretum* of Johann Heinrich Ursinus, as well as his *Phytology*, *Herbarium*, and *Aromatic Garden*. We also have the *Sacred History or Contemplation of plants, trees, and herbs occurring in Holy Scripture* by Adrianus Cocquius. Having seen and surveyed these works, we feel it would be a religious offense to "write the Iliad after Homer" <note>A Latin proverb meaning to redo a task already completed perfectly by another.</note>. Yet, so that we do not appear to have contributed nothing <note>original: "ἀσυμβόλως"</note> to the matter, we shall at least show what purity the **Violet** possesses, what modesty the **Rose** holds, what purple the **Violet** promises in the garden, and what beauty the **Mandrake** offers in the bed. With the Blessed Ursinus, we hope that what we have omitted here out of necessity, another may supply, and eventually complete for us a "Sacred Botany"—an exceptional science of pleasure and utility—perfected in all its parts and shared for the public good.

In the catalog of obscure plants belongs that "Apple of Discord" <note>A reference to Eris, the Greek goddess of strife; here referring to a plant that causes scholarly debate.</note> whose name is *Dudaim* <note>Hebrew: דודאים; typically translated as mandrakes</note>. It is the custom of botanists to introduce plants that grow under a foreign sun by comparing them to plants of our own world, wherever they seem to possess similar or identical characteristics. Hence, to some, these are **Mandrakes**; to others, **Violets**; to others, **"Lovely Flowers"**; to others, **White Lilies**. To Mattioli, they are the **Plantain** <note>original: "Musa"</note>; to Clusius, the **Nutmeg-tree** <note>original: "Pala"</note>; see also Fuller (book 6, *Miscellanies*, ch. 6), Levinus Lemnius (ch. 2, *Biblical Herbs*, p. 15, 18), W. Stuckius (*Antiquities of Banquets*, book 1, ch. 8, p. 313), and Ursinus (*Biblical Herbarium*, book 2, ch. 6, p. 136). Even for the Blessed Luther, they sounded like **Lilies** in his first version, but when he observed the word more diligently, he dismissed the lilies. Still not understanding what the word meant, he chose to retain the original Hebrew word. And truly, as many as have attempted to explain that word in such great light have found themselves tied in knots. I marvel at the obstinate persistence of the scholar Witzel <note>Georg Witzel (1501–1573), a controversial theologian</note> in pursuing such minutiae, where, seized by an angry pen, he writes:

<margin>Compare folio 7. b.</margin>
"The German [Luther] has devised this 'eating' without any basis. Could he not have said more with certain Jews about 'figs'? For what great thing is it that one gives someone a few, or what great reward can it be? If it were a matter of guessing, another could say they were oranges <note>original German: "Pomeranzen"</note>." It is easier to criticize here than to understand. This is the common consensus of interpreters: if a botanical

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Botany.</margin>
term cannot be recognized from its roots, either the Hebrew word itself should be retained, or, if you prefer, one should allude to it with some related interpretation, so that a very likely reason for the word can be held in some way for that which cannot be known for certain. We see that the greatest botanists here do not agree on the reason for a single distinction, so that it is still unknown whether any botanist can provide an herb that explains both the dignity and the powers of the *Dudaim*. Therefore, while the ancient interpreters hear the Garden Minerva <note>A metaphor for botanical wisdom</note> telling them nothing certain, they invite us to contemplate a moral sense. One proposes the sweet scent of the herb to the ministers of the Church, so that, stable in faith and firmly rooted, they may scatter the sweet-smelling odor of a pious and upright life. However, it is not our purpose now to unroll this, and though he weighs this name with Witzel so as not to count it among the *lilies*, let him first settle the matter with Franciscus Georgius, who criticized Jerome for explaining *Dudaim* as **Mandrakes**. Let him further settle it with Oleaster, who feels the same and conjectures that *Dudaim* is a certain kind of **white lily**. How they support their conjecture has been explained by Bonfrerius,

<margin>Commentary on Genesis, page 252.</margin>
who does not want Jerome's authority to be diminished. In such a doubtful matter, we wander in the "common error" and wish the *Dudaim* to be understood as **Mandrakes**, moved chiefly by these reasons: 1. because mandrakes have the appearance of breasts, from which *Dudaim* has a linguistic connection with *dadim* <note>Hebrew: דדים</note>, which signifies **breasts**. 2. because they are fragrant and beautiful; that the *Dudaim* is a fragrant, lovely fruit, pleasing to the eyes, mouth, and smell, is gathered sufficiently from *Song of Solomon 7:13-14*. And as Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> testifies, they are "golden in color" <note>original Greek: "κεχριζοντα τῆ χροῖα"</note>, and thus pleasing to the eyes; and "fragrant in a heavy way" <note>original Greek: "εὐώδη κατὰ βαρύς τινος"</note>, that is, moderately, not violently scented. Therefore, they are not unpleasant to the nostrils. The first mention of *Dudaim* in the Sacred Books <note>original: "Pandectis"</note> occurs in *Genesis 30:14*. For the two sisters, Rachel and Leah, married to Jacob—of whom Leah had surpassed Rachel in the number of children—by her more blessed fertility, provoked an envious spirit in her sister no less than in the husband they shared. Rachel's sterile womb, envious of her sister's fecundity, demanded that Leah give her **some mandrake apples**, which she perhaps believed were not unsuitable for conception. Reuben, Leah's son, had brought that apple to his mother upon returning home from the wheat harvest, and Leah granted it to Rachel, who sought it with great passion, on this condition: that on the following night, she might enjoy the embrace of her husband, whom Rachel might otherwise accuse of idleness <note>or lack of attention</note>. For the sisters shared the husband's bed by turns, and since it was the night for Rachel's turn <note>original: "ἐπ’ ἐνυτνίῳ," likely referring to the marital bed schedule</note>, Leah, knowing the powerless mind of her sister, exchanged that night and bought it in trade for the *Dudaim*. Why Rachel so instantly lusted for the *Dudaim* of Reuben, I confess I do not know, unless perhaps because of the rarity of the fruit and the delight and pleasure of its burning scent. For if anyone wishes to say she desired them so greatly for the sake of Venus <note>as an aphrodisiac</note>, that pious woman would certainly seem too deceptive; nor would she have granted Leah the husband's embrace, but would have sought it herself after eating the mandrake, especially since it was...

<margin>Sacred Botany.</margin> <note>original Greek: φιλότεκνος — child-loving or desiring offspring</note>. For this reason, we incline more toward the opinion of those who believe that Rachel desired these mandrakes so greatly because of their most delicate scent and taste. Josephus does not depart from this view in his *Antiquities of the Jews, Book 1, Chapter 19*. He says: "When Reuben, the eldest of Leah’s sons, brought mandrake apples to his mother, Rachel saw them and <note>original Greek: παρεκάλει μεταδῶναι οἱ ἐπιθυμίας τῷ βρώματος γενομένη</note> begged her to share them, being seized with a desire for the food." Experience testifies that mandrakes are taken for food, especially in hotter regions where, as they grow, they correct excessive coldness <margin>On Biblical Herbs, chapter 2.</margin> (compare with Lemnius), even if they cannot be eaten in colder climates without danger. Thus, the opinion of Augustine seems very probable to us: he concludes that the *Dudaim* <term>Dudaim: The Hebrew word for mandrakes, often associated with "love-apples."</term> were not sought for the sake of conception—since *Leah* did not give them to her then for that reason—but because of the rarity of the fruit and the delight of its fragrance. There are those who assert that this fruit was fit for love-potions. But truly, it is not pleasing to affirm such a thing about this pious woman. Even if we easily concede that Rachel was initially raised among ethnic <note>pagan</note> rites and customs, we consider it a sin to say that, after being associated with a holy man for so many years as a most holy woman, she would have desired the *Dudaim* for the sake of a pagan love-potion. For she had no need of a love-potion, she whom her husband loved so boundlessly; nor would Leah have conceded if she thought this remedy would take anything away from herself, but rather she would have used it herself to win her husband's goodwill. Nor did this pious woman need this fruit to open her womb, since she began to conceive and gave birth to Joseph toward the end of the second seven-year period <note>Genesis 30:22</note>. For in the first years of the second seven-year period, Leah bore four children: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah <note>Genesis 29:31 and following</note>; but toward the end of this <note>original Greek: ἑπταετίας — seven-year span</note>, Rachel, freed from the reproach of sterility by God’s own power, gave birth to Joseph. Meanwhile, Leah having become exhausted <note>literally "effete" or past child-bearing</note> at the beginning of the following six-year period, Jacob again fathered two sons, Gad and Asher, by Zilpah. From this time, on the occasion of Reuben bringing the mandrakes, Leah—who had ceased bearing for a while—conceived again with her sister's consent. Thus, it is consistent with the truth that Rachel did not accept the *Dudaim* from her sister without a plan, so that she might use them as a remedy for a weak womb, seeing as she had already been made fertile with one offspring. Nor did this most pious woman abolish the ignominy of a sterile womb by a love-potion, but by prayer. This is indicated by the faithful prayer and speech of thanks to God by that holy matron: *God has taken away my reproach* (because sterility was held as a place of reproach in the Old Testament, <note>Isaiah 3:28; Luke 1:25</note>) and she called his name Joseph (which means "he shall add" or "may he add," not from the present participle in the *Kal* stem, but from the future of the third conjugation *Hiphil*, to denote something to be added rather than something already added, as the reasoning for the name and the fuller spelling *Yehoseph* in <margin>Psalm 81:6.</margin> proves) by saying: *May the Lord add to me another son* <note>See Blessed Gerhard's Commentary on Genesis 30, page 572</note>. Therefore, the *Dudaim*, which are perhaps called by a dual name because they are of two sexes, or two types (oblong and round), we compare by symbolic meaning and wish to relate them among the most powerful fruits of the Holy Spirit: namely, Faith and Charity. <margin>Psalm 4:9.</margin> Hence comes that sleep of Grace, and so that we may be a sweet odor

in Christ <note>2 Corinthians 2:15</note>. For in the book of Nature, if even a single lovely and pleasant page concerning herbs and plants is weighed, it cannot be but that a man, at once astonished and rejoicing, thinks upon what the elegant verses of *Stigelius* advise:

> *For surveying the miracles of the painted field that meet me,*
> *While I gaze upon the riches of birthing Nature.*
> *Either a plant demonstrates the Divinity to me from its herbs,*
> *Or a single herb brings back the presence of God.*

If ever the pious Fathers sacrificed the Paschal lamb, saw its flesh roasted, and ate of it, they beheld through spirit and faith that Lamb of God, sacrificed already—if you look at His merits—from the foundations of the world being laid; and by trust in Him alone, they raised themselves up and were comforted. So too, there is no doubt that Holy Rachel, when Reuben brought the first apples of fresh mandrakes, desired them not in a womanly way, but in a holy way. For God, who took care to commit these things to memory, wished to warn us: that the *Dudaim* <note>spiritual fruits</note> ought to be preferred above all the goods and pleasures of the world <note>Luke 10:41–42</note>. By these, Theodoret understood Divine Doctrine—namely, of the Law and the Gospel—and others interpreted it not much differently (see Cornelius à Lapide on the Song of Songs). Let these things said suffice concerning the Mandrakes. The Holy Code mentions two Roses above others: namely, the Rose of Jericho—doubtless the most beautiful, most remarkable, and most fragrant <margin>Sirach 24:18</margin>—such as those of Paestum were of old. Those meadows of Jericho were once most blessed, so that

Today, however, because of divine a curse and the neglect of cultivation, that place is subject to eternal abomination. There is also the Rose of *Ha-Sharon* <note>the Sharon</note> in Sharon <note>Song of Songs 2:1</note>. But these words, like the following ones, are more suitably attributed to Christ, the Spouse of the Church. Hence Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux</note> says: *Lest the bride should ascribe to herself the flowers with which the bed and the beautiful chamber seemed decorated, the groom asserts that he himself is the flower of the chamber, and that the flowers do not truly come from the chamber, but from the field; and it is by his gift and by participation in him that they shine and smell sweet.* I am the rose of the field, and the lily of the valleys. <term>Shushan</term> <note>original Hebrew: שושן</note> is called a <term>lily</term> from the word <term>shesh</term> <note>original Hebrew: שש</note> meaning <term>six</term>, because it consists of six petals. For this reason, the Hebrews called the lily the flower of six leaves. From this also descends the Greek word <term>syson</term> <note>original Greek: σῦσον</note>, which specifically denotes a lily. Likewise, the capital of the Persians, <term>Susa</term>, obtained its name from this, because lilies are accustomed to grow there in great abundance, as witnessed by Athenaeus in Book 12. To the Germans, it is called <term>Lilgen</term> from <term>lilies</term>, which seems to be derived from the Greek <term>leiria</term>, as if from <term>leia</term> meaning <term>smooth</term> or <term>glatt</term> <note>German: smooth/flat</note>; or perhaps because they <term>flow abundantly</term> <note>original Greek: λίαν ῥέασι — lian rheasi</note>, due to the outflow of their divine scent. Great are the uses of the most noble Roses—whether red, white, provincial, or Damascene—but there is no space here, nor the occasion, to enumerate <term>bundles of roses</term> <note>original Greek: φακυλλειὰς ῥόδων</note>. They receive all this clothing and utility from God, the Creator of all things, who dressed them in such splendid garments. Antiquity concealed this in fables: that when Hercules secretly sucked the breasts of the sleeping Juno, a "milky circle" <note>the Milky Way</note> was created in the sky, and from the milk that fell to earth, white or shining lilies arose. For this reason perhaps Nicander called the lily—which stands out among other flowers like the <term>Moon among the lesser stars</term>—the <term>Ambrosia</term>, because it obtained its color from the ambrosial milk on one hand, and its scent on the other. Regarding the premature death of Roses and Lilies, the author of the Book of Wisdom writes: <term>Let us crown ourselves with rosebuds before they wither</term> <note>original Greek: Στεψώμεθα ῥόδων κάλυξι πρὶν ἢ μαρανθῆναι</note>. The poets aim at this same point when they call the lily "brief." Thus Horace says:
<margin>
chapter 2, 7.
Book of Odes 36.
</margin>
> Let not roses be lacking for the feasts,
> Nor long-lived parsley, nor the brief lily.
And Valerius Flaccus in the 6th book of the *Argonautica*, taking a simile from lilies, says:
> Lilies shine through the colors of spring like white,
> Especially those whose life is brief, and all whose
> beauty blooms but for a moment.
Indeed, the Lily and the Rose flourish for a short time; and while the lily shows yellow tips in the middle of its cup, pleasing in beauty and scent—delighting the eyes and pleasing the nostrils—in the very moment it delights, it folds its petals, withers, decays, and gapes open. While it smells from afar, standing proud on its stalk, once plucked it dies in one's hands and breathes its last breath. It scarcely blooms before it perits. Thus Fumanellus, in his work *On the Powers of the Rose*, seems to have correctly described the rose when he says: <term>The rose is a flower born red from thorns, of pleasant scent, budding first enclosed in a grainy husk, which soon</term>
