<term>swelling and rising into green buds, gradually gapes open and spreads, leading a life of a single day.</term>
So too is the brief life of man, whence the glory of the rich man is called <term>as the flower of the grass</term> <note>original Greek: ὡς ἄνθος χόρτου</note>, in James 1:10. <margin>James 1:10.</margin> For man and all human things are like flowers in their birth, their state, and their passing: they are born from the earth, like the blite herb; they flourish in the earth with great variety, differing properties, and swift fleetingness.
-> - Old age, joined together, presses upon those reaching youth. <-
Finally, they return to the earth, yet with the hope of surely rising again, where they shall inhabit an eternal and ever-green or blooming garden. In that place, the fertility of the trees restores us, and the blooming grace of the roses delights us. There, the greenness of the shoots beckons us, and the abundance of the vines and figs pleases us. There are the Vales of Tempe <note>a valley in Greece famous for its beauty</note> in which, if we enter the shade of the groves, there offers itself in the very midst—among an infinite abundance of flowers—the <term>Queen of the Groves</term>. In her description, Isaiah and the rest of the Prophets, who are already the gardeners and possessors of this holy garden, show us an extraordinary shoot which is for our salvation and restoration, and they discuss its individual branches. Let us now look upon this sprout in the painted space of the garden with the intent eyes of the mind, and let us refresh ourselves in its fragrant shade, for it is the area where <term>the shoot comes up, and a root from the parched ground</term>. <margin>Isaiah 53:2.</margin> In the earthly Paradise we had lost the Tree of Life; in the heavenly one, a new tree is shown which removes the poison that was brought in. Concerning this, Jeremiah says: <margin>chapter 23:5.</margin> <term>Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous branch.</term> In that time Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell confidently. It is an elegant comparison by which the Church is compared to a garden, and the pious and just man to a tree. The voice of the Divine Spouse is heard here: <margin>Enclosed garden, Song of Solomon 4:12.</margin> <term>A garden enclosed is my sister, my spouse; a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed</term>; your plants are a Paradise. The Bride is like an enclosed garden, a garden of delights or a Paradise, a garden planted with choice plants and arranged with the gardener's art for every elegance and pleasantness; and like a fountain, gushing forth the clearest and tastiest waters—and indeed a sealed fountain, lest the purest waters be infected by turbid mud or defiled by filth. Jerome Osorio discusses this aromatic garden in his *Paraphrase of the Song of Solomon*: <margin>p. 31.</margin> <term>You are a garden in which all the plants are of that kind which are healthful; and they produce the sweetest fruits, just as are the pomegranates and other fruits whose taste is sweet and whose appearance is most pleasant; nor indeed are fragrant trees lacking in it. For the henna</term> <margin>Henna</margin> <term>blooms there, along with nard, and saffron, cane and cinnamon, frankincense and myrrh, and aloes, and whatever other trees are held in price, measured out in a wonderful order.</term> With an elegant metaphor, I say, he compares the Teacher and the just man adorned with virtue to a tree heavy with fruit and abundant in leaves, and specifically to a palm tree: <term>The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree</term> <note>original Hebrew: צדיק כתמר יפרח</note>, Psalm 92:12. The Greek Septuagint reads: <term>The righteous man shall blossom like a phoenix</term> <note>original Greek: Δίκαιος, ὡς φοῖνιξ ἀνθήσει</note>. Tertullian, in his book *On the Resurrection*, incorrectly took this to mean the Phoenix bird, translating: <term>The righteous shall flourish like a Phoenix</term>, when he ought to have said <term>like a Palm</term>. A tree is indicated there, not a bird—and a mythical one at that—which fable the common people follow, but not Holy Scripture. By a similar error in Plutarch, someone wrongly imagined the "brain of the Phoenix" and translated it so, rather than the "pith of the palm," which is called the <term>enkephalos phoinikos</term> <note>original Greek: ἐγκέφαλος φοίνικος — literally 'the brain of the palm'</note>, as noted by Muretus, Reinesius, and Vossius. Isidore of Pelusium <note>A 5th-century Greek abbot and prolific letter writer</note> also writes regarding the words of the Psalms: *Just as a noble tree, when weighted with fruit, is adorned with leaves, gladdening the farmer, delighting the traveler, and providing rest to those who pass by; so is it good for one established on the teacher's throne, when he is adorned with virtue and bears fruit in his speech, for he both gladdens God and benefits men.* <note>original Greek: Ὥσπερ εὐγενὲς δένδρον, αἰτ, ὅταν τῷ καρπῷ βριθῆται... Οὕτω καλὸ εἰς τὸν διδασκαλικὸν ἱδρυθεὶς θρόνον...</note> In this way, both the proud and the **boastful** <note>original Greek: μεγαλήγοροι (megalēgoroi)</note> are often compared to tall trees; but they are also compared to them when they fall with a great crash, like lofty trees. Homer compares Simoisius, the son of Anthemion, who was killed by Ajax son of Telamon, to an **elm**, which a carpenter

Among the Latin poets, Virgil, Horace, and others have fashioned their verses with a similar elegance of comparison. Regarding the fall of Troy, Virgil writes:

Hence Celada <note>Didacus de Celada, a 17th-century commentator</note> writes on the Book of Ruth (number 173, p. 315): *A tree is called blessed not merely because it bears fruit, but because it has given its fruit; otherwise, a tree that bears fruit but does not give it is unhappily sterile, and makes others sterile.* He elegantly applies this to men who, whether out of pride or greed, fall before their time and leave behind no fruits of virtue, only riches.

It is also familiar to God to explain and designate future events through various signs, which He usually takes from common things in the world. He delights to speak in terms of **gardening** or **building** <note>original Greek: κηπευτικοῖς ἢ οἰκοδομικοῖς (kēpeutikois ē oikodomikois)</note>, a notable example of which stands at the very beginning of the Prophecies of Jeremiah, where Jehovah Himself speaks to the Prophet: *Behold, I have put my words in your mouth.*
<margin>
Chapter 1, v. 9.
</margin>
*Behold, I have set you today over the nations,* <term>to root out and to pull down, and to destroy and to throw down, to build and to plant</term>. <note>Hebrew: לנתוש ולנתוץ ולהאביד ולהרוס לבנות ולנטוע (li-ntosh ve-li-ntotz...)</note> In this heap of words, it should be noted that four grim verbs—**root out**, **pull down**, **destroy**, **demolish**—are followed by two joyful ones: **build** and **plant**. Some of these refer to construction, others to planting, to indicate that good things cannot be built unless the evil are destroyed, and the best things cannot be planted unless the worst are eradicated. For there is a need at times for instruments that eradicate the evil seeds sprouting against the truth in the minds of men; and a need at times for those who pull down every structure built upon false dogmas, so that everything may be constructed which leads to the glory of God, the edification of the Church, and the planting

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred Botany.
</margin>
of the heavenly kingdom. When God saw the insane structures of the Jews, the Prophet Jeremiah was sent to demolish every high thing that exalted itself against God, and every arrogance rising against the temple of God. He was also sent to plant the "planting of divine agriculture" in the place of those uprooted, and to build the "glorious structure of God's temple" in the place of those demolished; *so as to plant the plantation of the Lord's divine farming in the land of those uprooted, and to build God's building and the temple of God's glory in the place of those torn down,* as I might say with Celsus <note>Origen's "Against Celsus," book 4, p. 166</note>. God uses more words to declare adversity than prosperity, to indicate the laborious necessity of destruction and eradication; and this language recurs throughout the prophetic discourse to grant greater authority to His decrees: *Behold,*
<margin>
Chapter 45, v. 4.
</margin>
*those whom I have built, I will destroy; and those whom I have planted, I will root out, even this whole land.* The land, as great as it is, is the Holy Land, which is compared to the soil in which things are built and destroyed; it is like a garden in which trees are compared and plants are rooted out. The Jewish people, truly, are compared to a building and to trees sown in a garden; from which you may also understand those words: *If you will indeed remain in this land, I will build you and not destroy you; I will plant you and not root you out; for I repent of the evil that I have done to you.* <margin>Chapter 42, v. 10.</margin> Thus God is accustomed to comfort in the midst of anger, and when appeased, to plant good plantings again.

God also showed, as if in a garden, the branch of an **almond tree**, which comes forth quickly; *and the word of Jehovah came to the Prophet, saying: What do you see, Jeremiah? And I said: I see an almond rod.* (v. 12). In the sacred language, it is <term>maqqel shaqed</term> <note>Hebrew: מַקֵּל שָׁקֵד - literally 'rod of almond'</note>. The Septuagint reads "a staff of nut-wood"; Theodotion reads "of almond," followed by Tremellius, Vatablus, Piscator, Pagninus, Arias, and others. Aquila and Symmachus interpret it as a "waking rod," which the Vulgate follows, reading **a vigilant rod** <note>Latin: virgam vigilantem</note>; from this, Viegas thinks Jeremiah saw a rod with eyes, and others think he saw a **comet**. But the Hebrew word *shaqed* is more correctly translated as **almond**; for among the Hebrews, *shaqad* means "he was diligent, he watched, he matured," for they say of the almond tree that it matures its flower and fruit quickly. Indeed, the almond blooms first of all, in the month of January; and in March it produces mature fruit, as witnessed by Pliny (Book 16, ch. 25) and Olympiodorus, who says that those who study agriculture observe that *the almond is the first tree to bloom and the last to lose its leaves.*

There remains a related passage most worthy of exposition and consideration, Numbers 17:1 and following, concerning the dry rod of Aaron, which by a miracle puts forth leaves and bears fruit: almonds. For when the <term>leaders of the congregation</term> <note>Hebrew: נשיאי עדה (nesi'ei edah)</note> and <term>men of renown</term> <note>Hebrew: אנשי-שם (anshei-shem)</note>—that is, the primates of the other tribes, especially Dathan and Abiram of the tribe of Reuben (the firstborn of Jacob, from whom the dominion and priesthood, which once belonged to the firstborn of the family, were taken away because of his foul incest with his father Jacob's wife)—bore it poorly that this honor was taken from them and transferred to the Aaronic family by hereditary and perpetual right. Korah associated himself with these men, and is called the author of the sedition; Dathan and Abiram perhaps found in him a partner for the conspiracy against their cousins Moses and Aaron. For Kohath had begotten Amram and Izhar...

### Ecclesiastes II. v. 4. 5.

<margin>Sacred Botany.</margin>
...and Izhar; Amram was the father of Moses and Aaron, while Izhar was the father of Korah <note>Korah, also spelled Core, led a famous rebellion against Moses's leadership</note>, *Exodus 6:18.* Thus, Aaron and Korah were the sons of two brothers. They stirred up a sedition, but they were punished with horrendous penalties: some of the conspirators were swallowed by the earth, *Numbers 16:31*, others were consumed by fire, *v. 35*, and finally, others were carried off by a plague, *v. 39.* However, so that God might demonstrate by a fatherly sign and proof that Moses had conferred this honor and the office of the High Priesthood upon Aaron not out of private daring or brotherly affection, but by divine command, He ordered in the following chapter that the prince or leader of each tribe should present his staff with the inscription of his name <note>original Greek: ἰδέαν (idean), referring here to the distinguishing form or appearance of the name</note>, and that all of these should be deposited in the sanctuary; and further, that on the rod of the tribe of Levi, the name of Aaron the High Priest should be carved. The Princes of the families carried these rods or staffs as insignias of their principal dignity, especially when administering justice, as it seems likely; for such was the custom of old, just as the *fasces* <note>bundles of rods symbolizing power</note> were used among the Romans, and *scepters* among other nations. The Heathens used to boast that they had received this custom from the Gods. Thus Minos in Crete, according to Hesiod:

> *Holding the scepter of Zeus, with which he also ruled the cities.* <note>original Greek: Ζηνὸς ἔχων σκῆπτρον, τῷ καὶ πολέων βασίλευε</note>

Which Plato in *Minos* judged to be the *instruction* of Jove. Not only did Magistrates carry their rods, but also Priests; from this the Magi had their *rods* <note>original Greek: ῥάβδους (rhabdous)</note> made of laurel, called *aisakas* <note>original Greek: ἀισάκας</note>; the Augurs <note>Roman religious officials who interpreted omens</note> had their curved *Lituos* <note>curved staffs</note>; and from this the Bishops have their *croziers* <note>term: peda—the shepherd's crook used by a bishop to symbolize his role as a pastor</note>, staffs that are sharp at the end, straight in the middle, and curved at the top, about which Hoelzlinus writes in his *Prolegomena to Apollonius’s Argonautica, p. 34*, and Stengelius in *Pomona, chapter 10, p. 133.* But to return to the rods: these were not recently cut from trees and still green, but had been carried in the hands of the Princes for a long time and were thoroughly dried out, in which—if you consider natural forces—no hope of blossoming again remained.

<margin>The Chain of Francesco Zephyro <note>A 16th-century Italian commentator</note></margin>
It is the opinion of nearly everyone that each of these was from the common almond tree, and Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century theologian</note> shows this by two arguments: first, because people of that nation used staffs from that tree most of all, as it was a tree that excelled in putting forth straight and tall shoots or branches, so that walking sticks for the elderly and scepters for Princes could be cut from it. Secondly, because this tree presented a symbol of vigilance, which is required most of all in a Prince. Whence the Egyptians, as Clement of Alexandria observed, used to paint an eye on the top of a rod, intending to signify that this eye ought to be the guardian of justice, just as it is for the whole body. Diodorus mentions of the Phrygians that they were accustomed to paint the Sun on a rod, noting by this symbol the empire and rule of the Sun over this universe. Finally, the outcome confirms Cyril's opinion, since Aaron's rod produced *almonds* <note>original Hebrew: שְׁקֵדִים (sheqedim)</note>, for which the Targum Onkelos <note>an ancient Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> has the related word *almonds* <note>original Aramaic: לוזין (luzin)</note>. Jonathan, however, uses the word *lechin*, which some translate as *nuts*, and others as *almonds*.

<margin>Book 4, A. l. c. 4</margin>
Regarding this rod of Aaron, one may read in Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note>: *From the rod of Aaron, they saw both a shoot and a branch having grown forth, and—what was more wonderful—ripe almonds, since the rod was made of wood of this kind.* <note>original Greek: ἐκ δὲ τῆς Ἀαρῶνος, βλαστός τε καὶ κλάδος ἀναφύσας ἑώρων. καὶ καρπὸν ὡραῖον, ἀμύγδαλα δ' ἦν...</note>

<column-break/>

Regarding this miraculous production, let us further hear Moses, who first testifies concerning the dry rod of Aaron that it *brought forth a bud*. In the Holy Language <note>Hebrew</note> there exists the verb *parach* <note>original Hebrew: פָּרַח</note>, *it flourished, it germinated*, which others explain as being about the buds or little pods which later burst into flowers, moved by the argument that the almond tree puts forth berries and flowers before its leaves. But it can be understood without absurdity as the budding of leaves, in the sense that this rod first produced leaves and then flowers, contrary to the nature of the almond tree, which increased the miracle. Secondly, it *made a flower to bloom*. In Hebrew, it is *tsits* <note>original Hebrew: צִיץ</note>, from the root *tsits* or *tsuts*, which properly signifies the flower of any plant or tree. And finally, that it *brought forth almonds*; just as the buds were suddenly turned into flowers, so the flowers were immediately changed into fruits. In the Holy Language it stands as *reddidit sheqedim* <note>original Hebrew: גמל שׁקדים — "it yielded almonds"</note>. The root is *gamal* <note>original Hebrew: גמל</note>, *he requited, he repaid, he weaned*, and metaphorically *he ripened*, when it is applied to the fruits of trees, which, when ripening, are as if they are being weaned. The Jerusalem Targum says: *it weaned the nut-son of nuts*, or the almond-son of almonds. The meaning, therefore, is that it had almonds brought to full maturity, just as boys are complete and grown when they are weaned. And thus, from Aaron's rod, it *miraculously bloomed again* <note>original Greek: τερασίως ἀναθήλησε</note>. A tree that has been cut down, and a trunk or branch cut from the tree and stump, can never *bloom again* <note>original Greek: ἀναθηλεῖν</note>, which we shall describe in the words of the Poet <note>Homer</note> speaking of the scepter of Achilles:

<margin>Sacred Botany. Iliad 1, v. 234.</margin>
> *Truly by this scepter, which shall never put forth leaves or shoots,*
> *since it first left its stump in the mountains,*
> *nor shall it bloom again, for the bronze has stripped it*
> *of leaves and bark.* <note>original Greek: Ναὶ μὰ τόδε σκῆπτρον... φύλλα τε καὶ φλοιόν</note>

What Mother Nature was therefore not strong enough to achieve by herself, the Parent of Nature <note>God</note> performed miraculously in this dry wood by His extraordinary power and virtue. For it is probable, says the Blessed [Johann] Gerhard <note>A prominent 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> in his *Homilies, part 1, p. 209*, that this previously dry rod presented to the sight of the Israelites buds, or foliage, and flowers together with the fruit, and that not all the buds were changed into flowers, nor all the flowers into fruits. Furthermore, this rod was never thereafter dried out, but always remained germinating, flowering, and fruit-bearing; that is, the flowers, leaves, and fruits born on it by a divine miracle did not wither, but always remained green and vigorous. This was because it was meant to be a perpetual memorial of the dignity of the priesthood of Aaron’s family, which had been confirmed—a fact that could not be so certainly confirmed to posterity by a dry rod as by a green one. In the same way, the manna was kept without any corruption or rot in a golden jar as a perpetual *memorial* <note>original Greek: μνημόσυνον (mnēmosynon)</note> of the miraculous feeding that had happened to the ancestors in the desert. But why God chose this kind of miracle, Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose, the 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note> gives this reason:

<margin>Book 10, Epistle 82.</margin>
> *That flowering rod of Aaron,* he says, *what else does it show, except that the priestly grace never withers, and even in the greatest humility, it possesses the flower of the power committed to it in its office.*

For the right of the firstborn was signified by the almond rod; for among the rest of the sons, it is like the almond, which is the first to bloom among trees; and that right, along with the attached Priesthood, was assigned to Aaron by divine will.

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Botany.</margin>
And because the almond tree is the last among trees to lose its leaves, according to Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize Torah with Greek philosophy</note> in *Book 3 of the Life of Moses*, this can therefore be applied to the perennial vigor of the Aaronic Priesthood, which was destined to endure until the times of the Messiah. Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397), an influential Bishop of Milan</note> adds in the same place that this sign of the flowering almond occurred **when Aaron was already an old man and approaching death**; for he was at that time at least eighty-six years old. This was meant to signify that the older people and the **priestly line—though decayed by the long-standing rot of infidelity—would, in the final ages of the world, be reformed by the imitation of the Church. Through a revived grace, they would send forth the flower that had been dead for so many centuries.** Finally, it remains for us to hear: from where was this rod of Aaron cut? The Rabbis fabulate that it was taken from the Tree of Life, which was situated in Paradise. For thus does Rabbi Simeon son of Jochai discuss it in the book called <margin>Book 6 on the Secrets of Catholic Truth, final chapter.</margin> *The Assembly of Measures* <note>original Hebrew: "Mikhal ha-Middot"; this likely refers to a Midrashic or Kabbalistic source cited by Petrus Galatinus</note> as quoted in Galatinus: "That rod, which blossomed and put forth buds in the desert, was cut from that tree which God showed to Moses in the desert so that the bitter waters might become sweet. And this tree was cut from the Tree of Life, which was placed in Paradise by the hands of Angels. They sent it to Adam when he had sent his son Seth to Paradise to implore God’s mercy for his sin. And the Angels told Seth to plant this tree; as soon as it bore fruit, the mercy of God would descend upon him, and the gates of heaven, which had been locked, would be opened. Seth received this tree—or rather, a branch of the tree—and planted it in the desert. Moses later found it in the desert and cut his rod from it, which is why it is called the 'Rod of God.' When Israel came to Marah and could not drink those waters (for they were bitter), God showed Moses this tree to make those waters sweet. And this is that tree upon which Moses placed the bronze serpent, through which God intended to save the entire world and send His mercy upon Adam. When the King Messiah comes, then this tree will bear fruits by which, for a second time, bitter waters will be made sweet, and they will purge the first sin and all the offenses that men have committed or will commit." There are those who assert it is the same as the rod of Moses that performed miracles, among whom is Estius in his *Commentary on Chapter 9 of the Epistle to the Hebrews*; he confirms this from *Numbers 20:9.* But Bonfrerius contradicts him, asserting that not only Aaron’s rod, but also Moses’s rod (the performer of miracles), were kept before the Lord in the Tabernacle. Cornelius à Lapide <note>A renowned Jesuit exegete (1567–1637) known for his encyclopedic commentaries</note> denies this regarding the latter, saying it is uncertain where the rod of Moses went. He seems unmindful of Baronius, from whom Stengelius relates that in the city of Sens, at the Church of the Blessed Martyr Stephen, a part of the Rod of Moses is found among other relics. Nor is it improbable, according to Rodulfus Glaber, that the Rod of Aaron is preserved in the Lateran Basilica. It would be better if it were observed there with the due worship and in the manner prefigured by this rod. For the first bud, says <margin>Homily 9 on Numbers.</margin> Origen, and after him Augustine in *Sermon 69 on Time*, is **the first confession in Christ; second, it piously puts forth leaves when the reborn person receives the gift of grace and the sanctification of the Spirit; from there it produces flowers when it makes progress and is adorned with the sweetness of character, pouring out the fragrance of mercy and kindness; finally,**

<column-break/>

**it brings forth the fruits of justice, by which one may not only live oneself but offer a way to others by bringing forth from within the words of faith and the knowledge of God.**

->Ecclesiastes 10:16-17.<-
->Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child... Blessed art thou, O land, when thy king is the son of nobles.<- <note>The source provides this text in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, all conveying this central theme of leadership.</note>

---

**Nothing** under the sun is more excellent or a more beautiful gift from the immortal Prince, God, than a good, wise Prince who is most like God. If virtue and the wisdom of governing are joined with piety, and if external prosperity is joined with that wisdom, what a great protection and what a great refuge is found in Princes! Therefore, the wisest King of mortals rightly exclaims: *Woe to you, land, whose King is a child. Blessed are you, land, whose King is a son of the white-robed ones.* <note>The author uses "white-robed" to translate the Hebrew *horim*, usually rendered as "nobles."</note> With a very moving complaint, he deplores the calamity of those kingdoms where Kings sit at the helm who are children either in age or in sense. They govern according to their own lust, neglect the cares of governance, and being unable to rule themselves, are greedy for vain things and entirely devoted to feasting and other vices customary to the court. The etymology of the word *na'ar* <note>נער</note> (**child**) fits these people best of all; it is derived from the word for "shaking off," because they shake off all discipline and the yoke of virtues. He wishes the **child** King to be understood more in terms of sense and character than age. For childhood, at least when considered in terms of age, is not so much to be blamed (even if we do not deny that it is extremely dangerous in the governance of others), since there have existed excellent Kings even in childhood. Such was Solomon, whom some calculate to have been twelve and others seventeen when he was raised to the heights of Imperial power; likewise <margin>2 Chronicles 24:1.</margin> Joash was seven, and <margin>2 Chronicles 34:1.</margin> Josiah was eight when they began to reign. Thus Tirinus cites Charilaus of Sparta and John of Castile as young Kings, drawing from Plutarch’s *Second Oration on the Fortune of Alexander*, and from Mariana and Ribadeneira’s *The Christian Prince, Book 1, Chapter 10.* Therefore, <margin>same as Chapter 13</margin> it is rather understood as a child at least in mind or intellect, who is unskilled and unfit to take up the scepters of Empire. Hence Rehoboam is called a child, **tender-hearted**, <note>original Hebrew: *lebab rak*</note> that is, imprudent, soft, timid, and effeminate, even though he was forty-one years old when he began to reign (*2 Chronicles 12:13*). To such a one is opposed the candid, noble, and <margin>2 Chronicles 7.</margin> generous Prince, whom he calls the son of **the white-robed ones** (*horim* <note>חורים</note>) as much by contrast as by description. This word is found used only in the plural, designating both **nobles**—those put in charge of the government of some city or domain (*1 Kings 21:8; Nehemiah 2:16*)—and **Princes** (*Isaiah 34:12*). It descends from the root *hur* <note>חור</note> (**to be white**), from which also comes "white," and therefore signifies men walking in white, splendid garments for the sake of authority, or otherwise most distinguished, famous, or illustrious above others by reason of their wisdom and virtues. For the color white has the most light compared to others; for this reason, the Roman **Candidates**, who sought honors in the assemblies, and other more honored citizens, used—

The Prince used to wear a white garment <note>original: "veste candido"</note>, compare Justus Lipsius <note>A famous Flemish philologist and humanist (1547–1606)</note>, Book 1, *Miscellanies*, chapter 13, concerning the court. He is one procreated from noble and generous parents, and through the holiest precepts and the most shining examples, he is instructed and shaped to hold the tiller of the kingdom excellently and with the highest praise, directing it wherever he wills. The brilliance of lineage and race indeed adorns a kingdom, but by itself it does not suffice for leadership unless it is supported by one's own virtue;*

-> *For lineage and ancestors, and those things we have not done ourselves,* <-

Neither should it be thought that commendation is drawn from the pedigree alone—that someone owes their origin to noble or illustrious parents while otherwise leading a wicked or childish life (according to the proverb: *the sons of heroes are a nuisance*). Rather, in the Hebrew phrase, the word "son" is redundant in its own way, so that *a King who is the Son of Nobles* is the same as *a Noble King*. Just as the sons of Greeks are Greeks, the sons of men are men, and the sons of doctors are doctors; hence Blessed Luther translates it very aptly: *whose King is noble* <note>original German: "dessen König Edel ist"</note>. For a soul noble by birth must also be cultivated by the nobility of virtues, without which the name of nobility is empty, or a noble can only be called an *abortion*. The same appeared true to the pagan Juvenal

-> *Though old wax busts decorate your halls on every side,* <-

Many nobles are indeed "well-born" <note>original Greek: "εὐγενεῖς" (eugeneis)</note>, but few are "truly noble" <note>original Greek: "γενναῖοι" (gennaioi) — implying noble character rather than just status</note>. They disgrace the dignity of their race who are not truly noble, even if they are well-born; for Sophocles wisely wrote: *Shameful deeds are done shamefully by those of noble birth.* <note>original Greek: "τῶν αἰσχρῶν αἰσχρῶς τοῖς καλῶς πεφυκ-- σι"</note> Above all, however, a son of royal youth must be properly educated and instructed in every branch of learning. Procopius, in Book 1 of the *Gothic War*, records that the Goths resisted their Queen when she tried to have her son, Athalaric, instructed in the liberal arts, for the reason that a Prince imbued with literature might become less fit for moderation <note>The Goths reportedly believed that too much schooling made a warrior weak or "civilized" in a way that hindered their martial spirit</note>. But this is a barbarian sentiment: for reason itself dictates that he who must preside over all ought also to excel all in virtue. Cyrus, in Xenophon's *Education of Cyrus*, Book 8, is a witness to this matter, saying that *it is fitting for no one to rule who is not better than those he rules.* <note>original Greek: "μηδενὶ ἀρχειν, ὃς οὐκ ἂν βελτίων τῶν ἀρχομένων"</note> But how will this happen to him unless he has 
<margin>
Book 12, chapter 2.
</margin>
learning as his helper? For as Quintilian says: *Although virtue takes certain impulses from nature, it must nevertheless be perfected by learning.* And Seneca explains it graphically and fully enough: *Even if it matters more to us to become braver than more learned: yet one does not happen without the other; for strength comes to the mind from no other source than from the good arts and from the contemplation of nature.* Therefore, as much as depends on a skilled Pilot, just as much depends on the future Governor and Prince of the Empire. For what else is a King or Magistrate but a Pilot? Hence, not only the person but also the office of holding the tiller of the Republic requires that a Prince-to-be be faithfully imbued with letters, which he may use in all his affairs like a "Thread of Theseus" <note>A reference to the thread Ariadne gave Theseus to navigate the Labyrinth; here, education is the guide through the complexities of statecraft</note>. He piously exhorted his son to listen to his teacher Aristotle and to devote diligent effort to Philosophy, adding this praise: *so that you do not commit many of the things I regret having done.* For the excellent Prince knew that saying of the Comic poet was most true: *Those who have learned letters see double.* <note>original Greek: "Διπλῆν ὁρῶσιν οἱ μαθόντες γράμματα" — meaning they have a deeper insight or "second sight" into reality</note> After piety, which is the foundation of all things and with which all things must begin and end, the study of law along with the diligent reading of history is extremely necessary for a young Prince. By this very thing, when we demand a knowledge of Law in a Prince, we do not mean that there is no difference between a Prince and a Jurist. A Prince ought to know the laws insofar as they are generally derived from the ethical fountains of honesty and equity, how some chapters depend on others, and how they are adapted to the public state. But as for that sea of disputations and subtleties which concerns specific types of deeds and private law, it is enough if he has a "taste" of it for the sake of forming judgment. It is necessary for Jurists to enter and swim through that sea, because they are at the Prince's side for the purpose of settling cases and giving each his due. It is not our place now to prescribe the method of training younger Princes; let it suffice to have advised on what is necessary for true nobility and happy governance. Authors like *Thomas Aquinas, Giles of Rome, Erasmus, Osorius, Foxius, Natta, Omphalius, Roseus, Marettus, Frachetta, Bellarmine, Ribadeneira, Scribonius, and Wimpheling* inform the Prince. For a most wicked scoundrel, endowed with no virtue, no prudence, and no fear of God, can focus on these solaces. He can carry a horn hanging from his neck, ride a horse wildly like a madman, circle through the thickets and fields on his nag, lift a clamorous voice into the air, lie in wait for wild beasts, or pursue them even with great risk to his body and life, and strike them down with bow and spear, or slaughter them with a hunting-pole.* How much depends on a good and properly educated Prince can scarcely be expressed in words. For just as according to Solomon a bad Prince *destroys* <note>original Greek: "κατεσκάπτει"</note>, he is also called *lawless* <note>original Greek: "παράνομος"</note>, about whom he also says: *When a King listens to unjust speech, all those under him are lawless.* <note>original Greek: "Βασιλέως ὑπακούοντος λόγον ἄδικον, πάντες οἱ ὑπ' αὐτὸν παράνομοι"</note> For as the King is, so is the flock, according to that saying of Herodian: *For the subject always loves to live according to the mindset of the ruler.* The goodness of a kingdom, says Giles of Rome <margin>On the Rule of Princes, ch. 2, p. 44.</margin> in *The Rule of Princes*: *depends on the goodness of those who are in the kingdom, and especially on the goodness of those ruling in it; for just as the health of the natural body depends on the health of the heart and the principal members, because the heart and principal members must flow into others and rectify them; so the goodness of a kingdom depends on the goodness of all citizens, but most of all on those who rule and dominate in the kingdom.* For the Prince is over the people, but the Law is over the Prince. 536 BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
The Prince with his court.
</margin>
The state of a Prince is most fortunate when all people obey the Prince, and the Prince himself obeys the Laws. For Laws, enacted from a sense of equity and honor, look to no other end than the better advancement of the common good. Therefore, no Prince is released from the laws. That common saying, *The King is above the law*, <note>original: "Rex supra legem"</note> tends toward this: not that he may establish or abolish political decrees according to his own whim, but that by the guidance of right reason, he may hold the tiller of the Republic with dignity and utility. Hence, in the consecration of a King by Divine mandate, the book of the Law was placed into the King's hands, so that he might know he is not a King outside the Law. Princes are ordained to protect Judgment and Justice. Judgment, as Blessed Brentius <note>Johannes Brentius (1499–1570), a German reformer</note> says in his commentary on Isaiah chapter 1, page 29, is to punish the wicked and to restrain the evil from inflicting injury upon the good. Justice is to defend and protect the good and the righteous, lest they be oppressed by the more powerful and the unjust. Such are, and ought to be, the duties of Kings and Princes; thus they are not outside the Law. Above all things, true piety toward God adorns a Prince. When Agapetus <note>A 6th-century deacon of Constantinople who wrote a "mirror for princes" for Emperor Justinian</note> described the duty of a good Prince to Emperor Justinian, he most excellently and wisely began with the worship and honor that Princes owe to God; for nothing more sublime can be said than what he says on <margin>p. 185.</margin> "above all the glories of the kingdom, the crown of piety adorns the King." <note>original Greek: ὑπὲρ πάντα τῆς βασιλείας τὰ ἔνδοξα, τῆς εὐσεβείας τὸ στέμμα τὸν βασιλέα κοσμεῖ.</note> Therefore, that sentiment of Cosimo de' Medici, found in Machiavelli on page 364, is worthy of sulfur and fire: *Empires are not preserved by "Our Fathers."* <note>original: "Imperia per Pater noster non conservari" — Machiavelli suggests that states cannot be governed solely by religious piety or prayer.</note> For it is a truth so well-tested that Kings reign by God and under God's guidance, and that Republics and Kingdoms are established and governed through Him, that the divine oracles through Isaiah (60:12) have denounced destruction and present ruin to any nation and kingdom that does not serve Him. Thus, he who does not have a people united by a consensus of law, equity, and—what is the head of the matter—Religion, cannot even be said to have a Republic. Therefore, in a Republic, as in all other things, it is necessary that the observance, worship, and highest veneration of the Supreme Deity religiously, purely, and with integrity precede all sanctions and every discipline of living, if we wish the society to be safe and unharmed. Piety is the firmest bulwark of Kingdoms. The heathens, it is true, used to extol the virtues of their Princes and Great Men to an immense degree with boastful eloquence. But these commendations savor of the profane vanity of the heathens, who, as Bacon <note>Francis Bacon, English philosopher and statesman</note> shrewdly noted, *weighed shadows as if they were larger than the body.* <note>original: "corpore majores pensabant"</note> But <margin>8. on the advancement of learning 3. p. 228.</margin> true religion and Christian faith seek the reality itself, by impressing upon the minds of men that charity which is most fittingly called the *Bond of Perfection.* Hence Isocrates, quite piously, comprehended the virtues of a good Prince in few but very select words, as if in a single bundle, regarding King Evagoras of Cyprus, when he affirmed of him: "That he governed the city in a manner beloved by God and with love for humanity." <note>original Greek: ὅτι θεοφιλῶς καὶ φιλανθρώπως πόλιν διῴκει</note> In these words, he included everything praiseworthy that could be said of him. For every Prince ought to look to these two things: just as a Magnet always turns itself toward the pole, so a Prince in his governance ought primarily to reconcile to himself the favor of God and the love of his subjects. We have spoken thus far of piety toward God; as for what concerns the love and benevolence of subjects, this is exceedingly useful, indeed necessary, for a Prince in conducting his affairs. This

<column-break/>

<margin>The Prince with [his court]</margin>
benevolence of the subjects toward the Prince and his state is a ready inclination and love. This can be acquired through a triple power: *Gentleness, Beneficence, and Indulgence.* The greatest power lies in Beneficence, which Gentleness and Indulgence build up. The former shows the kindness of the mind in words and deeds, and provokes service through courtesy and conversation, yet without compromising the leader's honor and keeping his majesty inviolate. Hence, the best Prince is he who does nothing for his own sake, but desires the Republic to be kept safe and sound for the sake of those who are under him. He will not send his subjects under the yoke of *Arithmetical severity*; <note>A rigid, equal punishment or tax regardless of circumstances</note> nor will he promulgate all his commands according to *Geometric lenity*; <note>A proportional mercy that might be too soft</note> but rather by a harmonic proportion, which is the surest remedy for the inflamed minds of citizens and creates the sweetest harmony in the Republic. Thus a King bears the name of Parent because of his fatherly care for his subjects; for it is never fitting to exercise command otherwise than if he loves his subjects in a fatherly manner and provides for them with utility. For as Dio <note>Dio Chrysostom, Greek philosopher and orator</note> says <margin>Oration 55.</margin> "The care of kings is fatherly and guardian-like, with benevolence and friendship, since it is never otherwise fitting for a man to stand at the head and rule, unless he does so with love and wisdom, just as Zeus is called the father of men above all." <note>original Greek: τὴν τῶν βασιλέων ἐπιμέλειαν... ὁ Ζεὺς ὡς ὑπερφορὰ πατὴρ τῶν ἀνθρῶπων καλεῖσθαι.</note> To this belongs Gropius's play on the word *Saal* <note>German for "hall" or "room"</note> by which, as is known to our countrymen, the more distinguished hall of a court dedicated to the most important public affairs is called. (2. Francisc. p. 47). Neither the house of a King nor any other Prince deserves this name unless the safety of the people resides within it. From *Saal* for preservation comes *Saalich* <note>A wordplay on the German 'selig' (blessed/happy) and 'Salus' (safety/health)</note> for him who is preserved, and for that which preserves, so that that which makes one happy and he who is happy are named by the same word. Would that all who move in the court were themselves happy and made others happy, so that the Court might finally be truly called a *Saal*, and the *Courtier* might not only be a subordinate, but also *Saalich* (that is, bringing salvation or safety) to all others. This is his view. To preserve this same title of a fatherly name, it is also required that the Prince does not burden, trouble, or exhaust his subjects beyond what is fair with taxes, extra taxes, impositions, super-impositions, poll taxes, manual labor, and similar things, as the laws of the Theodosian Code <note>A collection of Roman laws compiled in the 5th century</note> openly forbid: <margin>book 11. titles 6, 7 & 8.</margin>
> He does not weigh down his provincial subjects with heavy extortions, plundering, etc.; rather, from princely liberality, he remits debts owed to the private treasury if he can do so without harming the right of the Republic.

It is indeed just and fair to pay taxes to the Magistrate, but it is equally fair that subjects are not flayed by them—subjects who scarcely have moldy bread and who can barely quench their thirst, yet are forced to pay, pay, pay, often for the luxury of the ruler. How many coins are scraped together today from tears! How many subsidies are devised from unheard-of things! Long ago, Caligula <note>Infamous Roman Emperor known for his cruelty and extravagance</note> practiced new and unheard-of taxes, omitting no kind of thing or person upon whom he did not impose some tribute (Suetonius, chapter 40). And there is no lack of "Caligulas" today, and flatterers are present who cry out that new contributions are constantly necessary lest luxury suffer any detriment. *When kings go mad, the Greeks are punished*, <note>original: "Cùm delirent Reges plectuntur Achivi" — a quote from Horace's Epistles</note> and there are hateful Advisors present, who, lacking no plan of their own, shout their approval. They advise the Prince to constantly impose new tributes and taxes...

But since the condition of a Prince is such that he cannot encompass all things by his own knowledge alone—as Tacitus says in the 3rd book of his *Annals*, section 69—his most heavy labors, by which he manages the world, require administrative aids (as noted in *Annals* 12.5). He therefore has need of counselors; but in distributing honors and powers among his ministers, he must remember that precept of the Teacher of Wisdom: *the common safeguard of a Principality is to make no one man so great that he becomes a superior or an equal,* as Aristotle says in *Politics*, book 5, chapter 11. Otherwise, the Prince might later allow himself to be led by that man,
->*like a wooden puppet moved by another’s strings.* <note>A quote from Horace, Satires 2.7.82</note><-
Hence God himself appointed and joined instructors and monitors to Kings: Samuel for Saul, Nathan for David, Elijah for Ahab, Elisha for Jehoram, Jeremiah for the successors of Hezekiah, and for Solomon—though he was the wisest of all Kings, most consulted in taking counsel, and most prompt in performing actions—a college of Prophets and others excellent in learning and piety. Among these, Zadok and Ahijah the Shilonite shone forth, who handed down precepts of moral virtues for the correct governance of the Republic and, with learned pens, laws for living rightly, which a slow-to-follow posterity among Christians and barbarians alike still admires. Hence Polydamas, not without merit, reckons among the gifts of God a young man who is:

For a wise plan <note>Greek: Σοφὸν ἐπιβούλευμα</note> is the foundation and prop of a Kingdom; whence Sabellicus <note>Marcantonio Sabellico (1436–1506), historian of Venice</note> says of the Venetian Magistrate on page 287: *All the arduous and distinguished business of the Republic is sanctioned by the Senate: peace, war, truces, treaties, privileges, and prerogatives, from the Senate itself,*

<margin>The Prince with his court.</margin>
flow as if from a primary fountain of the Republic. Thus, even in a Monarchical state, nothing ought to be defined or determined without the foreknowledge of Counselors, who are rightly called the preservers and lovers of the public good. For he alone fulfills the duty of a Counselor who is known to surpass others in a seasoned knowledge of all things, both private and public; one who, through long and daily experience of affairs, is practiced in governing the community in both peace and war. Indeed, it befits a Counselor to speak things that are just and true. He ought to be a "Veronensian," not a "Placentinian." <note>A pun: "Veronensis" sounds like *verus* (true/truth-teller), while "Placentinus" (a person from Piacenza) sounds like *placere* (to please/a yes-man).</note> A Placentinian says what his Lords gladly hear. A Placentinian is a cook for those men; he must have his Lord’s palate so that he may speak accordingly. Placentinians speak according to the opinions and whims of their Lords. Such Placentinians were the counselors of Cambyses; when he was marrying his sister Atossa and asked for a legal judgment, they responded that they could find no law that permitted a brother to contract marriage with a sister, but they had found another law: that the King of the Persians may do whatever he pleases. Measuring himself against this standard, Cornelius Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a famous polymath and occultist who often fell out of favor at court</note>, having lost favor at court and intending to conform himself to courtly favor, expressed his opinion thus:
<margin>Epistle 59, book 4, p. 835.</margin>
*Now, as I am called back to court by new counsels, hear the laws I have prescribed for myself. To play the courtier rightly, I shall flatter exceedingly; I shall be stingy with faith, ambiguous in words, obscure in counsel, and like an oracle, double-tongued; but I shall pursue profit and prefer my own advantage above all. I shall cultivate no friendship except for the sake of gain. I shall be wise only for myself; I shall praise no one except artfully; I shall disparage anyone, but to my own profit; I shall push out those I can, and I shall sit on many chairs at once. Courtiers, guests, and others who bring no profit, I shall despise as barren trees. I shall trust no man’s word, nor rely on any man’s friendship. I shall interpret everything in the worst way and meditate on revenge. I shall only observe and adore the Prince, but I shall flatter him, agree with him, and play the parasite only out of fear or for my own gain. With these decrees, I shall return to the court.* The things he offers in another letter are so bitter that they cannot even be read here.
<margin>Epistle 72, p. 855.</margin>
Besides Counselors, at the Prince’s side is the Court Preacher and Confessor. What his duty should be, let us write not in our own words, but in those of Erasmus of Rotterdam in book 2 of *The Method of Preaching*, page 761: *The Preacher shall instruct the courtiers that in their delights they should remember sobriety; that they should be simple and not at all deceitful; that they should take care not to be deceived, and themselves deceive no one; that they should not basely flatter Princes; that they should not suggest ill-fated counsels; and that they should not think more is permitted to them because they are courtiers, but rather live more incorruptibly because they are exposed to the eyes of all.* But sometimes court preachers prefer to soothe with praise rather than to rebuke; indeed, what is worst of all, they think the honorable and dishonorable deeds of Princes pertain not to the judgment of a Bishop, but only to God (see Paschasius Radbertus on Matthew, chapter 14, column 611). Solomon was a great courtier, the unique mirror of courts; performing the duty of his own "Ecclesiastes" <note>The Preacher</note>, he refused to flatter the Court. He spoke many things about the Court which a courtly Preacher would not want to say, fearing for his own house. While the Court wallowed in a slough of pleasure, and the ordinary Preacher kept silent, he—the extraordinary Preacher (otherwise a rare animal)—cried out: *I have seen servants sitting upon horses, and princes walking like*

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Prince with his court.</margin> ...just like *servants upon the earth* <note>Referring to Ecclesiastes 10:7: "I have seen servants upon horses, and princes walking as servants upon the earth."</note>—that is, unworthy and insolent men. These are people who, though they abound in the help of relatives and grow fat on wealth and power, are snatched up and promoted to the functions of the Church, the Court, the Palace, and the Schools. Meanwhile, the pious—who are worthy of promotion due to their nobility of soul and other gifts of the mind—are subjected to the cross, despised, and trampled underfoot (*Ecclesiastes 10:7*). This "Tranquil Suetonius of the Church" <note>A likely satirical nickname for a contemporary figure or preacher</note> behaves this way because of a house and a Tusculan estate <note>A reference to a luxury villa, after Cicero’s famous estate</note> given to him, because of which he calls himself the *Lord of Espe*. Otherwise, he is quite reckless in his speaking and writing, yet on this occasion he is fit neither to write nor to speak; he is incompetent in all speech, even though the court is full of eloquent stable-hands, cobblers, and innkeepers. Regarding such a courtly preacher, Bernhard of Geist <note>Bernhardus Geystensis, a medieval poet known for the satirical poem *Palponista* (The Flatterer)</note> wrote:

<margin>1 Flatterer, line 298.</margin>
> *When he has finished the sacred rites, if perhaps he later asks,*
> *Being full of hot air, vain, and ambitious,*
> *“How did I sing? How did I feed you with my teaching?”*
> *Stand there with a stupid look, pretend you don't know how to speak.*
> *Then suddenly burst forth, and break the silence with these words:*
> *“You speak like an angel! You bring us news like an angel, you sing like an angel!*
> *Your tongue is soaked in sweetness, and the flavor of your voice!*
> *The common people sobbed, and watered their faces with weeping.”*

Then the preacher, wanting to seem like an Anchorite or a Hermit, says: "I almost bound myself with a sacred vow in my whole heart." Kings and Princes cannot do without other such ministers in their sight. But what truly is the Court? It is a difficult matter to describe courtly vices without the good suffering for it, or to distinguish them separately so that the bad are not mixed with the good and held in the same regard. In the court, the *greedy* man finds wealth, the *ambitious* man finds honors, and the *flatterer* will have in abundance whatever he desires if he simply mimics the face and expressions of the Lord. The *glutton* will find sumptuous feasts here, provided by a splendid table. The *libertine* finds mistresses. The *slanderer* finds "Theonine teeth" <note>original: "dentes theoninos"; a classical idiom for bitter envy or backbiting</note>. The *proud* man finds clothes painted with gold. The *critic* finds censors. Indeed, it is a rare man in the courts who is a stranger to the court—who is separated from the stain of the court, who has nothing in common with it, who claims nothing of the court for himself, whom the lust of the harem <note>original: "gynecæi"</note> does not inflame, whom the greed of the Chamber does not prick, whom the envy of the law court does not waste away, and whom the glittering care of secular business does not worry. This fits the saying of Emperor Maximilian I, that there are three kinds of men in courts:
> *In the King's court, there is little law.*
> *Those who are good are always sheep.*
> *Those who are evil are always in royal favor.*
> *If there are any others, they are always drunk.*

Courtly vices are placed in high positions, and the court politician knows how to cover his own vices with the "cloak of courtliness" or treat them as jokes. This is so much the case that if the phrase "live unnoticed" <note>original Greek: "λάθε βιώσας" (lathe biōsas); a famous Epicurean maxim</note> ever applies, it applies amidst the turmoils of the court. The courtier knows how to put on many faces and covers his whole soul with a drawn veil: it is convenient for him to be simultaneously deaf and blind, yet also sharpest in hearing and sight. With sweet speech, he knows how to "speak similar things, but think dissimilar things" <note>original Greek: "ὅμοια λαλεῖν, ἀνόμοια φρονεῖν" (homoia lalein, anoimoia phronein)</note>. With a sighing voice, slightly blushing cheeks, well-measured steps, and a neatly gathered cloak, he buys the Prince's favor for himself. Regarding the court, Bernhard of Geist published "Leonine verses" <note>A form of medieval rhyming Latin verse</note> under the title *The Flatterer* (*Palponista*), edited by Christian Daum, from which we take these lines: In order to please the court, he says among other things:

<margin>Line 132.</margin>
> *Begin to stroke the Lords, and learn to rub them.*
> *How he can please through various arts of praise—now for him who is of small stature (line 204), now for him who*

<column-break/>

is tall (line 212 through 228), now for him who is skinny (line 228 and following), and now for the fat man (line 235 and following):

> *Soon also give praises to the fat man with a double-tongued mouth.*

And there are other things not unpleasant to read, which prove what was said before (line 67):
> *The life of the Palace is a crime, and the ruin of souls;*
> *The Court is the death of Virtue, and the health of the soul.*
> *How, or why, I wish to note with brevity.*
And line 78:
> *Countless crimes are committed at the court, with Megaera <note>One of the Furies in Greek mythology, representing jealousy and envy</note> as the mother;*
> *There is no true peace of mind there,*
> *The illicit life, always conscious of itself, trembles,*
> *These evils surpass the fact that the court spreads nets for the soul.*

Truly, there are three vices that occupy nearly every Court: *Adulation, Sycophancy,* and *Envy*. If "faith is nowhere safe," certainly that "nowhere" begins in the Courts, where the simple man is easily captured and the deceptive man is eventually deceived, even when he thinks he has taken precautions. In the words of their lips are guile, fraud, slanders, sycophancy, extortions, and violence. Here, the prudent man considers that he must beware; *the wise man fears, but the fool rages and is confident.*
<margin>Proverbs 14:16.</margin>
The prudent man is cautious, and because of the many-sided envy, he does not think double caution is superfluous. The wise man fears that a "Scorpion" is "hiding under every stone"—as Alcaeus <note>A Greek lyric poet</note> says—and he cannot escape all the traps of the Courtly Scorpions with enough caution and prudence; rather, he is very often hurt by their stings, or even crushed. Thus, courtly envy crushed the most faithful courtier, Seneca. Let us look at the words of the court preacher Polycarp Lyser <note>A Lutheran theologian (1552–1610)</note> regarding him, which he has in the book where he described the *Persian Court*: *When Nero had ascended to the height of the Roman Empire, he had by his side Seneca of Cordoba, a most sharp and prudent philosopher, as his tutor. According to his advice, he administered everything that had to be done. Hence, the first years of his government were so happy and pleasing to his subjects that the "first five years of Nero" passed into a proverb. But there were certain Roman "little parasites" who envied this honor and favor of the Emperor toward Seneca, a Spaniard and a foreigner. Therefore, they attacked Nero with words, pretending that it was not Nero but Seneca who was the Emperor. They urged him to remove Seneca and take up the rudder of the empire himself. To be brief: they so battered Nero that he decided he wanted to remove his tutor from human life, so that all might understand that he alone could rule without a tutor’s advice. Seneca was therefore given the choice to pick whatever kind of death he wanted. But after this guardian was removed, Nero degenerated into such a beast, into such a tyrant, and into such a deformed monster of a man, that all historians confirm with one voice that there has never been a more foul disturber of the State. This was the fruit of courtly envy: that the whole Roman Empire was disturbed by it.* Thus, courtly favor can be lost more easily than it can be obtained, and that man is to be proclaimed happy and numbered among the great examples of great fortune who has prudently sailed past the rocks of the Courtly Sirens and, in time, withdraws himself into voluntary exile, taking himself to the countryside under the pretext of failing health. Comines <note>Philippe de Commines (1447–1511), a writer and diplomat at the courts of Burgundy and France</note> was a courtier, and in the midst of the splendid business of the court, he says...

### Ecclesiastes 10:16-17

<margin>The Prince with his court.</margin>
According to Schleidanus in book 10 of *The Gallic War* <note>original: "de Bello Gall." Referring to Johannes Sleidanus (1506–1556), a famous historian of the Reformation</note>, nothing is more excellent than a Prince, and indeed he is the most fortunate of all men. However, we have a notable example of courtly weariness from the previous age in Joachim von Beust, an intimate counselor to Augustus, Elector of Saxony. Although he wielded great authority with the Elector, serving as his very soul, once he obtained his dismissal in his old age, he retreated to his castle at Planitz. He treated it as his Patmos <note>A reference to the island where St. John was exiled; von Beust viewed his retirement as a spiritual sanctuary</note>, finding solace for his old age there. He began to collect and write *Pious and Useful Commentaries on the Gospels and Feast Days*, as well as a *Handbook on the Art of Dying Well*—works he could never have completed at court. For this, he was praised by the Court Counselor David Pfeiffer, who, out of detestation for the inconveniences of court life, placed this poem at the front of the book:

<margin>16</margin>
->*While the mockery of the vain world wears us out,*<-
->*And the restless court keeps us anxious and unquiet.*<-
->*O miserable ones, whom the luck of the court puffs up,*<-
->*Forgetful that change is inherent in all things.*<-
->*Fortune often lifts up high-ranking ministers,*<-
->*Only to crush them with a heavier fall.*<-
->*Thus once the Macedonian <note>Alexander the Great</note>, with his throat constricted,*<-
->*Died hanging before the gates of Memnon.*<-
->*Thus was the love of Thallus turned into Augustus's anger,*<-
->*His legs broken, a ruinous end to his favor.*<-
->*Thus for you, Sejanus, dragged by a hook through the city,*<-
->*A letter sent from Capri brought your death.*<-
->*Thus Burrus, once most dear to the cruel Nero,*<-
->*Finally hated, drank the dire poison.*<-
->*Thus were the eyes of Belisarius cruelly torn out;*<-
->*The highest place gave them this, as did the fickle Court.*<-
->*These examples warn us that the friendships of the powerful are not stable,*<-
->*And that each man should live for himself.*<-

We could say many other things about the instability of the Court and of Princes, if the truth of that matter were as safe as it is clear, and if the freedom of speaking were as secure as it is dangerous. What benefit, then, does a courtier have in courtly life? A pious courtier moves through the court as any other pious man moves through the world. He contemplates a miserable and fleeting life; he does not care for things that appear good but are vanishing; he judges as vain those things that present themselves to the eyes with a magnificent appearance but do not satisfy. He "possesses the court, but is not possessed by it," and he lives in it as if not living there. He discovers that these things are the mockery of empty shadows if the court changes its Prince. Whatever is put before him, he fears it to be deceptive; he esteems it as something in decline and clings to none of it. For who would fix his love on that which he understands to be a deception, and which he himself must soon leave behind? Such, then, is the unhappiness of courtiers. Nor is the difficulty of those who reign any less—carrying the "splendid misery" of golden crowns—since a good Prince is by no means immune to courtly troubles. Indeed, the difficulty of ruling is known to none more than those upon whom the kingdom rests.

<margin>Note the examples of Moses and Saul from the Sacred Scriptures, who declined political leadership because of its difficulty.</margin>
Suetonius reports that Otho, the Roman Emperor, said: *“You do not know, my friends, what it is to govern the empire of the Romans; believe me, who has tried it, I would now rather die at a wall than command.”* Themistocles and Demosthenes confirm the same. The former, upon hearing that some were seeking public office, said: "If you were to show

<column-break/>

<margin>The Prince with his court.</margin>
me two paths, one leading to the grave and the other to the tribunal <note>the seat of a judge or official</note>, I would much more gladly enter the one that leads straight to the grave." The latter said to the young men who were his friends—since he already knew how much envy, fear, slander, and danger are to be expected when entering public affairs—that if he had to choose between two options, he would sooner go into exile than to the tribunal. Thus Dionysius, the Tyrant of Sicily, represented the "happiness" and whatever else the court promises to Damocles by means of a shining sword hanging by a thread or a single horsehair, looming over Damocles’ neck (see Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 5, p. 258). Lucian explains the same misery in *The Dream*, where the Rooster <note>In Lucian's satire, a rooster (who was once a king in a past life) talks to Micyllus the cobbler</note> speaks to Micyllus:

"I ruled," he said, "a region by no means small, fertile in all things, and crowded with inhabitants; nor was it lacking in cities of especially admirable beauty. Furthermore, it was blessed with navigable rivers and a harbor-filled sea. Added to this was a huge army, a most distinguished and excellent cavalry, a large bodyguard, triremes, a force of money greater than could be counted, a vast abundance of silver vessels, *and all the other equipment of power* <note>original Greek: καὶ ἡ ἄλλη τῆς ἀρχῆς παρασκευὰ</note>, and all that tragedy of the Principate and its apparatus beyond what can be described. And so, when I went out, most people worshipped me, thinking they were looking at some God; others ran together, pushing one another; some, having climbed onto the roofs, thought it a great thing if they could clearly see my four-horse chariot, my cloak, my diadem, and the heralds walking before and those following behind. I, meanwhile, conscious of my own state, felt that *the reins lifted me and tightened* <note>original Greek: ἐπῆρέ με ἡνία καὶ ἔσφιγγεν</note>; I judged those people worthy of pardon because of their ignorance, *but I pitied myself* <note>original Greek: ἐμαυτὸν δὲ ἠλέουν</note>, for I seemed very much like those giant Colossi that Phidias, Myron, or Praxiteles built. For each of them, as far as *outward things* <note>original Greek: τὰ ἐκτὸς</note> appear, is Neptune himself or Jupiter, wonderfully beautiful, composed of gold and ivory, holding a thunderbolt, a lightning bolt, or a trident in his right hand. But if you were to duck your head and look at *the inward things* <note>original Greek: τὰ ἔνδον</note>, you would see certain bars, pegs, and nails protruding inside, as well as wickerwork, wedges, smeared pitch, and other such deformity dwelling within. I omit mentioning *the multitude of mice and shrews* <note>original Greek: μυῶν πλῆθος καὶ μυιαλῶν</note> that sometimes live in them."

A KINGDOM, surely, seems to be a thing of this kind. On this subject, I cannot help but use the words of Goropius Becanus <note>Johannes Goropius Becanus (1519–1572), a Dutch physician and philosopher</note> in his *Gallic Antiquities, page 75*. A good Prince, he says, "The matter stands thus: he who commands others is oppressed by a perpetual servitude, by which he is forced to look out for the advantages of those over whom he exercises power. He sells his whole self for meager tithes and taxes; he gives his whole self into slavery. Labors are constant, there is no rest from cares, anxieties are perpetual; complaints must be heard, petitions read, lawsuits settled, injuries avenged. Scarcity of food is feared; the care of guarding the borders causes torment. The plans of neighboring Kings must be explored, the armory equipped, and fortresses fortified. The methods of raising money cause agony. Why say more? There would be no end if I tried to enumerate all the torments of Kings and superiors." These things he feels...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

A good Prince feels the delights within governance only alongside his court. A good Magistrate is bound to endure these many troubles. When Solomon weighed these things, he could find no sweetness or pleasure in them, except for this: he saw in all things vanity and affliction of spirit, and that nothing remains firm under the sun in which one might trust; and that in honor, power, and high office, there is nothing but labor and hardship in which a person's mind might find rest.

->Song of Songs 1:5<-
->I am dark and beautiful<- <note>original Hebrew: "שחורה אני ונאוה"</note>
->I am black and beautiful<- <note>original Greek: "Μέλαινά ειμι ἐγὼ, καὶ καλή"</note>
->*I am black, but beautiful.*<- <note>original Latin: "Nigra sum, sed formosa"</note>

<margin>The abuse of the Song for secular purposes.</margin>
The soul of a good man is a garden full of the delights of virtues, and thus a second Paradise, in which myrrh is harvested—namely, the mortification of the limbs <note>the practice of self-discipline or "dying" to worldly desires</note> along with the spices of virtues; in which the rose is gathered, reddened by the blood of martyrdom; in which the apples of the valleys shine, moistened by heavenly teachings; in which pomegranates sprout, owing to the fragrance of good deeds. Thus, it is not without reason that, when about to speak to us concerning the Song of Solomon, I might *preface it* with the words of Radbertus in his *Life of Adelhard, Abbot of Corbie* <note>Paschasius Radbertus (c. 785–865) was a Carolingian theologian; Adelhard was a cousin of Charlemagne and a prominent churchman</note>. 
<margin>column 1643.</margin>
For there is nothing in this song by the wisest of Kings that does not breathe a sweet understanding, with the most joyful fruit, the most pleasant flower, and the most chaste speech and style; nothing is more beautiful to the sight, sweeter to the smell, or more pleasing to the ear. And to speak first of the style of speech in this Song of Solomon: there is a character of wonderful discourse in the Song, seizing the reader with sweetness and delights as if by a love-potion. There is a certain living and active kind of speaking, and not even all the charms of oratory can reach that divine artistry of speech. How elegantly the speech now rises, now sweetly smiles, playfully jokes, and aptly flatters! Everywhere it allures the listener with new emotions, here it detains the lover, there it binds the beloved. In every place there are mosaic-like emblems and figures; everywhere a golden thread <note>literally "golden stud" or "purple stripe"</note> of purple is interwoven. In such variety, the sweetest scent of all emerges abundantly from the little flowers and shrubs, through which divine love breathes. Lilies breathe between them, always sweet, always lovely, and greater than themselves. The whole texture is like a meadow painted with spring colors, budding with native gems and fresh little flowers, so that the reader always has something to admire and somewhere to rest, and never lacks for more. If you look at the mysteries of the Song, they declare God not only as a lover but as our friend, regarding which Bernard says in *Sermon 1 on the Song*: 
<margin>column 732.</margin>
*Solomon, divinely inspired, sang the praises of Christ and the Church, the grace of holy love, and the sacraments of the eternal marriage; at the same time, he expressed the desire of the holy soul and composed a song of marriage, exulting in the Spirit with a joyful, though figurative, eulogy. Doubtless, he veiled his face like Moses—a face perhaps no less shining in this part—because at that time there was no one, or very few, who were capable of beholding that glory with an unveiled face. Therefore, because of its excellence, I believe this nuptial*

<column-break/>

*song is distinguished by such a title that it is rightly called the Song of Songs in a singular way, just as He who is sung of is singularly called King of Kings and Lord of Lords.* Let us further note, before we say more about the matters it treats, the praise for the style of the Song which Francisco Mendoza <note>a 17th-century Spanish Jesuit and biblical commentator</note> *presents: The style of the Songs,* he says, 
<margin>Volume 1, page 289, On Kings</margin>
*is sublime, blossoming from various tropes and figures, such as befits songs of victory or those adorned with palms and laurels, to which genre most of the songs of Scripture are referred.* Indeed, the words of the Song are to be understood in a more elevated sense, just as Paschasius Radbertus viewed them and applied them to Adelhard, Abbot of Corbie, writing in his life (columns 1668, 1669): *A holy white-haired age adorned him with snowy brightness, and like a lily upon rosy garments, the hair of his head shone here and there like the fronds of palms above his skin.* (Song of Songs 5). Whatever beauty had been bestowed upon him, he took care to make it ascend by directing it upward to God. *His eyes, like doves over streams of water washed in milk,* because his whole gaze is believed to have been simple and intent only on God, not mixed with the gall of lusts, but washed in the true innocence of the mind. *Furthermore, his cheeks were like a bed of spices planted by the perfumers*—namely, by the holy Doctors—adorned with every flower of doctrine and the scents of virtues. *His hands were like turned gold, expressing the form of holiness, and moving swiftly in a circular motion toward every good deed, full of hyacinths, shining like the sky as he stored up treasures in heaven, hands which were filled with many gifts. His belly was of ivory, distinguished by the orders of virtues. His throat was most sweet because of the honeycomb of eloquence, and he was altogether desirable for his uprightness of character and extraordinary charity.* If we look at the things contained in this sacred song, they are sublime and full of divine mysteries. For if we diligently unroll this sacred Song, we will find nothing taught in it more carefully or accurately than to teach us God's supreme love for mankind; indeed, it describes the humanity and kindness of God toward the human race as if with a painter’s brush. The whole Song, in its entirety, breathes nothing but love and benevolence. It overflows with the benefits bestowed by God upon men; it commemorates individual benefits with individual words and strives to show them clearly and openly in every way. Concerning this matter, let us hear Alvaro Pelagio <note>a 14th-century canon lawyer and bishop</note> in book 2 of *The Lament of the Church*, chapter 4, page 7: *Just as the Song of Songs of Solomon excels other songs, in which the Groom, Christ, and the Bride, the Church, enjoy sweet embraces; so also the Lamentations of Jeremiah are figuratively, over the Church, the Lamentations of Lamentations, in which the absence of the Groom, Christ, from the Bride, the Church, is deplored with many tears because of great transgression.* So too Jerome, in *Letter 7 to Laeta on the Education of a Daughter*, says of this book: *So that that* 
<margin>column 60.</margin>
*young recruit of Christ <note>referring to a young student of the faith</note> may learn the Song of Songs last and without danger; lest if she reads it at the beginning, she be harmed by not understanding the wedding song of spiritual marriage beneath carnal words.* Following in these same footsteps, Joachim Vadianus <note>a Swiss humanist and reformer (1484–1551)</note> says in book 4 of *On the Eucharist*, page 115: *If you look at the literal letter of Solomon's Songs, what are they other than a love poem, filled with charms and allurements? So that not without reason the Jews*
