### Song of Solomon 1:4

<margin>
The abuse of the Song for secular purposes.
</margin>
...they did not permit the reading of this book except to those of a more advanced age. But truly, if we apply the Spirit drawn from the Scriptures rather than abandoning them, we find that *the entire Scripture contains no conversation of the faithful soul or the Church with its Groom, Christ, that is more ardent, pleasant, or sublime than this Song of Solomon.* Therefore, there is nothing scandalous in its matter or style, nor anything discordant to the ears of a chaste mind—despite what the "Enthusiasts" might breathe against the Spirit. These are the people who treat the book of Job as a mere fable, and likewise Ecclesiastes and the Song; they suggest that the former teaches Epicureanism <note>a philosophy often misunderstood in this period as simply seeking physical pleasure</note> and the pursuit of pleasure, while the latter is merely a composed amatory poem. There is nothing obscene in this Song, nothing in it that tastes of worldly Venus <note>the Roman goddess of lust and physical love</note>. The divine and chaste writer maintains a perpetual <term>allegory</term> <note>original: ἀλληγορίαν; a story where characters and events represent deeper spiritual meanings</note> concerning Christ and His Bride, the Church. What madness of impiety and an insane mind it is, then, to drag the praises of the heavenly Bride and Groom into the infernal "Petronian sewer"! <note>A reference to Petronius Arbiter, a Roman author known for the "Satyricon," a work filled with scandalous and "filthy" content</note>. According to Suetonius, 
<margin>
In Tiberius, chapter 58, page 205.
</margin>
it was a capital offense under Emperor Tiberius *to bring a coin or a ring impressed with the image of the Emperor into a latrine or a brothel.* Thus, it is a wicked custom, worthy of sulfurous fire, for even certain idle theologians to count the most sacred words of this Song among their jokes. In the year 1566, a certain Catholic doctor of the English nation, named *Heskinst*, released a book titled *The Parliamentary Assemblies*, and in it, he gave this horrendous judgment on the Song of Solomon: *How little incentive to virtue seems to be in the Songs of Solomon? Indeed, how impious and lewd they appear at first glance, instilling lewdness rather than piety! What, I ask, can the unlearned find in many of these sentences that does not provoke petulance rather than tend toward the building up of piety? Nor are the other parts any better; rather, the whole book is like this.* And *Possevinus*, in his *Sacred Apparatus* (Volume 3, letter T, under the word Th. Harding), approved that book by Heskinst with great praise. Conringius, in *Hermet.* page 25, notes the impiety of the Chemists <note>Alchemists</note> who explain the Song of Songs as a work about the refining of gold. And there is one person (whose name I hold in high regard, and for that reason, I shall spare his name here) who, in his commentary on Petronius—where there is nothing but the filth of the unchaste—treats the most sacred and chaste <term>foolishness</term> <note>original: μωρολογία; here used ironically to describe how secular critics view divine wisdom</note> of the Holy Spirit as something sordid. From among many, take these words, which by the common consent of interpreters are understood to refer to the Bride, the Church: *I am black, but beautiful.* This author, who is now <term>anonymous</term> <note>original: ἀνώνυμος; nameless</note> to us in his commentary on Petronius—would that he had remained <term>anonymous</term>!—explains this "dark blackness" as that of the Egyptians, because the Shulammite was the *Egyptian daughter of King Pharaoh. For the Egyptians and Syrians are somewhat black and dark.* This is surely to offer ghosts instead of reality, and to consume the gifts of intellect granted by God on frivolous things. It is a wonder that such <term>blindness</term> <note>original: ἀβλεψία; a failure to see or foresee</note> could fall upon that philologist! For with little foresight, he twists the most weighty and divine meanings of the Song into the lewd speeches of lovers. For those things handed down by Petronius in this genre are both impious and lewd, and therefore ought to be loathsome to Christian interpreters. For "who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?" * to speak from the book of Job. Let the Song be silent in the Master of Wickedness, 
<margin>
Chapter 14:4.
</margin>

<column-break/>

Petronius; and let Petronius, that Master of Ignorance who wrote filthily about the vices and corrupt morals and loves of the Romans in the ages of Tiberius and Nero, be silent regarding the Song. The divine writer of the Song is not occupied with human loves (as that interpreter thought) but with divine loves. We desire their explanation to be pure, untainted, and virginal, not the harlot-like style of Petronius. And what does the "Egyptian Shulammite" mean in this place? For if the Song were about the daughter of Pharaoh, or some Shulammite girl, those comparisons found in *Chapter 4:1 and Chapter 7:2*, and in other places, would be absurd and monstrous. And although the name of God is not explicitly written in the whole book, equivalent and more appropriate names occur—namely, Brother, Friend, Beloved Groom—to establish that the mystical Bride of Solomon is described here, which is the Church of Christ. And what business, I ask, does an Egyptian Shulammite have with the "daughters of Jerusalem" whom the divine Author addresses? For the Bride says of herself: *I am black, but beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem,* <insert>I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon</insert> <note>original Hebrew: "שחורה אני ונאוה בנות ירושלם כאהלי קדר כיריעות שלמה"</note> *like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains* (<term>skins</term>) <note>original Greek: δέρρεις</note> *of Solomon.* Luther glosses this as: <gloss>like the tapestries of Solomon</gloss>. Book 1, chapter 3.

In this way, the Jews exaggerate their calamities in the Prophet, *Lamentations 5:10: Complaining that their skins are blackened like an oven, contracting blackness from the face of the storms.* I am unsightly in the sight of the world; but inside, I shine with the various gifts of the Holy Spirit. Augustine writes aptly on these words of the Song in his commentary on Psalm 118:

> I am dark and lovely, O daughters of Jerusalem. Dark through fault; lovely through grace. Dark through vice, but lovely now through the washing in which every sin was bathed away. I am dark because I have sinned; lovely because Christ now loves me.

The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord.* Therefore, the beauty and loveliness in which the Bride of Christ excels is not her own, but the Groom's; hence in *Chapter 4:5, 6, 7*...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Abuse of the Song for secular purposes.</margin>
6.7. Nearly the same praises are attributed to the Bride as to the Groom, because she is an imitation of him; and although these qualities are not the Bride's *own* <note>original: ἰδίαι</note>, they are given and communicated to her by the singular grace of the Groom himself. The Groom himself commends the beauty of his Bride in chapter 4, verses 1, 2, and 3. He praises her for the decorum and elegance of her face, which Barlaeus <note>Caspar Barlaeus (1584–1648), a Dutch polymath and poet</note> proposes with precision and grace in his 4th *Heroic Poem*, page 593:
> *Innocent simplicity shines upon her brow,*
> *And constant to the truth, her thoughts are deep and dense.*
> *From her lips distill teachings opposed to unspeakable*
> *Vices; and her face glows red—with the blood of the Groom*
> *Destined to die, her face glows red. The Faithful are her outstretched towers;*
> *Hope is her helmet, salvation her breastplate, trust her shield;*
> *Her breasts are the fountains of justice, and the will*
> *Of my Father, both ancient and new. Like a neck, the Prophets rise,*
> *And display my rages to the sinning people.*

Thus, in the following chapter, the Bride of the Church proceeds to the praises of her Groom and his beauty, with which his whole body shines:
> *He is mine, whom I alone worship; with a charming brightness*
> *His head glows more than gold, and higher than the very*
> *Leaves of palms, his hair rises from his brow;*
> *His locks are illustrious in their blackness. The eyes he darts forth*
> *Surpass the very chaste eyes of doves;*
> *Eyes which, beside the bright gliding waters,*
> *Receive a pure brilliance from the cleansing river.*
> *As distinct herbs smell sweet in their own beds,*
> *So his cheeks stand by a distinct law. Lilies*
> *Flowing with myrrh yield to his lips. Each hand*
> *Holds gems and the grey-green beryl. Throughout his core*
> *A white ivory shines through, upon which a beautiful sapphire*
> *Strays in blue marks; like a house high*
> *Upon fearless columns, the husband’s legs*
> *Are golden, nor does his face fall short of the honor of Lebanon.*
> *A flattering tongue plays beneath his honey-flowing palate,*
> *And his clear throat sings with learned melody.*
> *Such were his eyes, such his hands, such his face.*

This is an elegant translation drawn from the "tents of Kedar" and the "curtains of Solomon"; so that one member might respond to the other through a mutual transposition of words. The *tents of Kedar*, which turn black exposed to the heat of the sun, snow, and rain in the open air, correspond to the blackness of the Bride; but the skins or *curtains of Solomon*, shining with gems and gold, which were made from <term>יריעות</term> <note>Hebrew: yerioht</note>, that is, curtains, correspond to her beauty. Thus the order of the words should be understood as: *I am black like the tents of Kedar, but beautiful like the tapestries of Solomon.* And so the words are restored to their proper order by an elegant <term>transposition</term> <note>original: μετάϑεσει; a rhetorical device where words are reordered for clarity or effect</note> common in Holy Scripture; compare Blessed Glassius, *Sacred Philology*, book 4, tract 2, page 749, and Cornelius à Lapide in his *Preface to the Pentateuch*, canon 13. But as to why the divine Writer uses this similarity, let us hear what Joseph de la Cerda responds in *The Academy*, book 4, chapter 1, number 38: <margin>page 90.</margin> "Why is it," he asks, "that she reveals herself as similar to the tents of Kedar—that is, of the Arabs and Hagarenes—and to the curtains of Solomon, to paint herself as lovely, though she seems somewhat black in her skin? The secret lies in this: if you look at the tents of the Arabs from the outside, they are filthy from their location, black from the heat, and, touched by rains and sprinkled with much dust, they present a foul skin to the eyes. Therefore, leather is their material, suited to the lashes of the weather; yet inside, they burn with a peaceful beauty, variegated with painted perfumes, woven with gold, weighted with gems, a work of many colors elaborated by a Babylonian finger. Thus, if you turn the skin or leather over or unroll it, a rich beau-

<column-break/>

ty and shining workmanship strikes the gaze." From the order of the ancients, let us hear Willeram, Bishop of Merseburg <note>An 11th-century scholar and head of the Ebersberg monastery</note>, who sings thus in his *Paraphrase on the Song*, verse 30: <margin>Abuse of the Song for secular purposes.</margin>
> *Though I seem dark, like the blackening camps of Kedar,*
> *I am exceedingly beautiful, like the curtains of Solomon.*
> *Dark indeed from blows, but shining with the honor of goodness.*
> *I endure great evil among the sons of darkness,*
> *Yet adorned within by the beauty of virtue,*
> *I shall strive to be held as the temple of the true Peacemaker.*
> *O you neighbors, see why I am so dark!*
> *Because of too much sun, I lose my beautiful color.*
> *The glory of virtues grows pale in the heat of evils.*
> *While I am pressed by the wicked, I have no times of peace.*

But the interior beauty becomes even greater amidst these pressures. Then, in his own Germanic tongue <note>referring to Old High German</note>, with Latin words intermixed, the same Abbot added: "I am black like the shelter of Kedar, and I am beautiful like the tent of Solomon." <note>original: Ich bien Salo famo thiu hereberga Cedar, ande ich bin avon vvathelich famo thiu gezhelt Salomonis</note> (Kedar is interpreted as *darkness*. He was the son of Ishmael, from whom the Ishmaelites come, who have no houses but only wild-skins and other unlovely shelters. By Kedar, the "sons of darkness" are signified, about whom I complain.) In these words, our "shelter" is expressed as *Herberg* (an inn), while "wild-skins" are *huts in the wilderness* <note>original: Hütten in der Wildnüssen</note>, as an anonymous author, a man very knowledgeable in our ancient language, explains in the same place <margin>page 10.</margin>. We have the exposition of this Willeram, Bishop of Merseburg, who flourished 550 years ago, edited by Paul Merula with notes; it is truly excellent and not "barbarous" for that time. That edition lacks the author Willeram's preface, which Martin Opitz first shared from a manuscript book of Michael Flandrinius, a Senator of Wroclaw, in his *Notes on the Old Teutonic Rhythm of St. Anno, Archbishop of Cologne*, pages 3 and 4. As a bonus, we add what Athanasius says in his *Synopsis of Holy Scripture*. While excerpting from the Song of Solomon those parts concerning the calling of the Gentiles, he referred that blackness to the tents of Kedar; for in a dialogue, the city of Jerusalem seems to have contended with the Kedarites. His words are: <margin>page 95, Volume 2.</margin>
> "Jerusalem, when the twelve tribes or nations were formed in the circumcision of faith, says in wonder to the bride from the Synagogue: 'She who comes like the dances of the camps'; for they came not from one but from every nation, leaving behind their own camps, and putting away their swords, and henceforth thinking thoughts of peace. The Church of the Gentiles now responds to the Jerusalem Church: She from the Gentiles, seeing Jerusalem as if blaming her, defends herself, saying that her calling was not from the beginning. 'I am black and beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon. I am black, but I am under the sun itself. For even if I am uncircumcised,' she says, 'yet I have renounced idols, and I have gone out from the house of my mother, just as Abraham did.'"

The same author says those words were spoken under the persona of Christ the Groom, pertaining to this: *You are beautiful, my friend, how sweet, how lovely, just like Jerusalem; stupendous, as an army's battle line is drawn up.* This was also observed by Nicolaus de Lyra <note>a prominent 14th-century Franciscan teacher</note> in his book against the Jews, which I read in manuscript from our library: "According to all the Hebrew Doctors, wherever the name of Solomon is placed in the book of the Song, under...

# Song of Solomon, Chapter 1, Verse 4.

<margin>Abuse of the Song for secular purposes.</margin>
By this name, we must understand God Himself, who is the "Great Solomon"—that is, the "Peaceful One"—who brings about peace and harmony among creatures through the connection of the parts of the universe. As it is said: *He who makes harmony in his high places.* <note>original: "Qui facit concordiam in sublimibus suis." A reference to Job 25:2.</note> For this reason, scholars say that this book deals with God and the Synagogue under the names of Solomon and his Bride or Friend; just as Catholic Doctors <note>Early Christian theologians and teachers</note> say that the same book, under these names, deals with the union of Christ and the Church.

The divine Writer alluded most especially to the graceful beauty of the peoples of the East so that he might set the mysteries of divine love, as it were, before our eyes. Thus, what the listeners cannot grasp through a simple command might be held through metaphor and examples, as Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), known for translating the Bible into Latin</note> says somewhere in his commentary on Matthew. Furthermore, blackness—especially of the eyes—is considered a delight even now among Oriental peoples, who are accustomed to staining their eyelids with a lovely blackness using a salve <note>collyrium</note> made from a certain Persian stone. This is noted not only among them, but also among other Western peoples, as Meursius <note>Johannes Meursius (1579–1639), a Dutch classical scholar</note> observes in his *Theological Gleanings* <margin>* s. 17.</margin>. * In the same way, Lucian <note>A Syrian-Greek satirist of the 2nd century AD</note> long ago in his *Affairs of the Heart* (p. 222) and Cyprian <note>Bishop of Carthage, 3rd century AD</note> in *The Dress of Virgins* (p. 363) noted eyes painted with an encircling blackness, and mentioned a black powder among other facial cosmetics. Cornelius Gallus <note>A Roman poet, though the work cited here was later attributed to others</note> traces this beauty of lovely blackness in a girl as a primary and most excellent quality in his last Lyric poem (though Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a famous Renaissance scholar</note> says it is the work of some inept fellow) not without skill:

> Open, girl, your starry eyes,
> And your curved, black lashes;
> Open, girl, your rosy cheeks
> Drenched in the red of Tyrian purple.

Solomon, beyond all doubt, wished to express these things as they truly are, worthily of faith; he did not intend to look upon foreign women with that love which wastes away in <term>irrational pleasure <note>original: ἀλογίσῳ ἡδονῇ (alogistō hēdonē)</note></term>, as Josephus <margin>l. 8. A. l. c. 2. p. m. 272.</margin>, the native historian of the Jews, puts it. And let us add a few points to these. In Chapter 2, verse 8, the Groom is introduced by the Bride, who until now has expected the Groom's arrival with great desire. In this place, however, let all thoughts of the gestures and dances used in choruses be absent. When the Bride describes the Groom "leaping," she implies by that very word his eagerness and readiness in undertaking the work of the Redemption of the human race. Hence, concerning the leaping and bounding Groom, Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397 AD), Bishop of Milan</note> says in his sermon on Psalm 118 <margin>Sermon 6. p. 633.</margin>: * "He leaps upon the heights, that he may ascend upon the bride. For the Bride's chamber is the tribunal of Christ. He leaps over the Church, he leaps across the Synagogue. He leaps over the Gentiles, he leaps across the Jews. Let us see him leaping: He leaps from heaven into the virgin, from the womb into the manger, from the manger into the Jordan, from the Jordan onto the cross, from the cross into the tomb, and into heaven from the sepulcher." Thus, immediately in Chapter 1, verse 4, the Bride asks to be introduced into the chamber, and having obtained her wish, she says: *The King has introduced me into his chambers.* Away with all vanities in this place! For by "chambers," some understand the Church, others eternal life. Both interpretations can be joined together, since the Bride speaks in the plural number, as if she were being led from one room into another—that is, from the Church Militant <note>The Church on earth</note> into the Church Triumphant <note>The Church in heaven</note>. Concerning this introduction, let us hear Ambrose again: "The Church was introduced into the chamber of Christ, no longer

<column-break/>

<margin>Abuse of the Song for secular purposes.</margin>
merely as one betrothed, but as one married; she has not only entered the bridal chamber, but has also obtained the keys through a lawful union. The 'chamber' of the Church is the treasures of the knowledge of the Sacraments; the body of Christ was previously closed. The King introduced her into all the interior mysteries; he gave her the keys, that she might open for herself the treasures of the knowledge of the Sacraments and throw open the doors previously closed; that she might know the grace of him who rests, the sleep of him who died, and the power of him who rose." Let us therefore turn our eyes away from vain things, and let us look here upon sacred eloquence with a chaste mind, much as Cicero viewed human eloquence as a virgin: let us keep her at home, fenced in by a liberal guard, and let us reject these unknown and impudent suitors. Let us protect her as a grown virgin, chastely, and keep her as much as we can from the rush of lovers. You should beware of taking sacred things into your hands with the same spirit with which you take up the *Attic Nights* of Gellius, the *Satyricon* of Petronius, Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, or Aesop's *Fables*. In such a presumptuous approach, there is no art, no fitting argument, and no safe faith. Therefore, take care not to follow the manner of a certain otherwise most learned Interpreter, and think to yourself: "What does a pig have to do with marjoram?" <note>A Latin proverb, "Quid sus cum amaracino," meaning someone who cannot appreciate or is unfit for something fine.</note> What does Horace have to do with the Psalter? What commerce is there between Christ and Aristotle, between the Evangelists and Maro <note>Virgil</note>, or between the Apostles and Cicero? Saul’s armor does not fit David. One must <term>practice philology <note>original: φιλολογεῖν (philologein)</note></term> within its proper bounds, nor is it permitted to rashly sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land. For this reason, we commend its reading along with Barlaeus <margin>4th Heroic Poem, p. 583.</margin> * in this way:

> You, Impiety, who are wont to sprinkle a stain
> Only upon chaste voices, and who wickedly gnaw
> At the oracles of the gods, and spit upon
> The festive songs of the innocent prophet—stay far from here!
> Those words are not open to the wanton,
> Nor is that petulant eloquence, or lewd Paris
> With his half-man entourage, worthy of these praises.
> Those who cannot give their hearts to divine things
> Did not sing this celestial melody.

Therefore, we ought to grant this honor to the Song of Songs: to believe that whatever is written or handed down in it is spiritual. Saint Augustine, writing on the *Catechizing of the Uninstructed*, warns the student that if he hears anything in the scriptures that sounds carnal, even if he does not understand it, he should nevertheless believe that something spiritual is signified. On this account, he praises the twelve Apostles who remained with Christ when many of the other disciples, offended by the Discourse on the eating of His flesh, left Christ and walked with Him no longer. Let us say with the ancient Hebrews: "Far be it, far be it, that this Song should be about obscene things!" It is rather a metaphor; unless it were of great dignity, it would not be written in the Catalog of Holy Scriptures. Moved by the <term>mysteries <note>original: μυστήρια (mystēria)</note></term> contained in this book, they diligently took care that no one should be admitted to the reading of the Song of Songs—just as with the first chapter of Genesis and the Prophecy of Ezekiel—unless they had first reached the "priestly age" <note>Usually thirty years old</note>. For they were concerned lest a youthful mind, not yet sufficiently prepared for such sublime things, might receive these "lover’s" passages in a sinister or improper way. Hence many of the Doctors have advised that the exposition of this book should be deferred until old age, as a solace for Christian seniority and a "viaticum" <note>provisions for a journey; here, spiritual preparation for death</note> for a pious departure. Gregory Nazianzen <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople</note> had received this custom, and Jerome likewise in his Letter to Laeta concerning the education of her daughter, where he tells her what...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the proper interpretation of the Song of Solomon, warning that it should be the final book studied to avoid carnal misunderstandings. It then transitions into a new section on the Wisdom of Solomon and the importance of Sacred Chronology in understanding the history of the world and the timing of the Messiah.</meta>

<margin>Abuse of the Song for secular purposes.</margin>
...prescribes what should be read from the sacred scriptures: *Lastly, let him learn the Song of Songs without danger, lest if he reads it at the beginning, he be wounded by not understanding the wedding songs of spiritual marriages beneath carnal words.* <note>original: "Ad ultimum sine periculo discat Canticum Canticorum..." This is a famous pedagogical rule attributed to Saint Jerome regarding the order of biblical study.</note> The approach to reading this sacred book correctly is open to those who, burning with celestial love, love the Groom of innocence and the Bride of heavenly modesty. For in vain, as Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot who wrote 86 sermons on the Song of Solomon.</note> says in *Sermon 79 on the Song, page 171*, does one who does not love approach to hear or read the song of Love, since a cold heart cannot grasp fiery eloquence. For just as someone who does not know Greek does not understand a Greek speaker, nor someone who is not Latin a Latin speaker, and so on; so the language of Love will be foreign to him who does not love; for he will be like *a sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal.* <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:1.</note> One must be equipped with the strength of piety when reading this amorous Song, lest he get stuck in the "bark" or surface of the words. *Because if he,* says Sanctius <note>Caspar Sanctius (1554–1628), a Spanish Jesuit commentator.</note> in *Prolegomena 12 on the Song*, *who has not experienced the sweetness of divine love, approaches the song of Love unsuitably, he will be even less fit if obscene love titillates his senses and if impure filth is not unpleasant to him. For he who accustoms his mind to shameful loves, when the appearance of love occurs—even chaste love—and names common to both types of love are used, he easily turns his mind and thought toward that love with which he was already long ago imbued. For almost everyone feels or judges things according to whether his mind is affected chastely and piously, or wickedly and basely.*

### Wisdom of Solomon VII. 17. 18. 19.

> For he himself gave me an unerring knowledge of the things that exist, to know the structure of the world and the activity of the elements. <note>original Greek: "Αὐτὸς γάρ μοι ἔδωκε τῶν ὄντων γνῶσιν ἀψευδῆ..."</note>
> The beginning, the end, and the middle of times; the alternations of the solstices and the changes of seasons; the cycles of years and the positions of stars.

> For God gave to me a true knowledge of those things which are in nature, so that I might understand the constitution of the world and the force of the elements. <note>The author provides both the Greek and Latin versions of these verses from the Book of Wisdom, attributed to Solomon.</note>
> The beginning, the end, and the middle of times, the change of the solstices and the variety of seasons.
> The circuits of years, and the locations of the stars.

<margin>The system of Years and Months.</margin>
The eternal Creator of things governs all things most wisely by His eternal wisdom, and moderates both night and day. He grants times through successions without Himself undergoing change. He moves the world, yet is not moved; He holds every place, yet is not held; He changes time, yet is not changed; He makes wandering things firm, yet He Himself does not wander. Indeed, by a singular counsel and a salutary institution, He distinguished the times and ordained the Days, Months, and Years. He placed distinctions between months and years, not so much to show the difference between eternity and the long-lasting nature of this world, but so that in the Church, through the series of years, it might be known in what order and in what ways He revealed Himself—when He gave the promises and the Law, and at what time the <term>Messiah</term> <note>The "Anointed One" promised in Jewish and Christian scripture.</note> was to come, and finally, what the end of all ages and all times shall be. Hence, the prophetic predictions do not only define the matter

<column-break/>

and the event that will follow after several centuries, but they also accurately present to us the persons and other circumstances, whether of place or time. Isaiah prophesied that Cyrus, after two hundred years, would grant the exiled people a return to their fatherland and supply the expenses for the restoration of the City and the Temple. The event, which is recounted in the first book of Ezra, responded to this prediction. Thus, **Sacred Chronology** brings time into view, and by establishing certain intervals of time and even specific moments, it brings a great light to the <term>God-given books</term> <note>original Greek: "Θεοδότοις βιβλίοις" (theodotois bibliois), referring to the Holy Scriptures.</note>, makes the reader more eager, puts to flight the evasions of adversaries regarding the doctrine of the Messiah, and altogether lights a lamp for history. It declares when individual acts were done, individual words spoken and written, and when the Authors of the sacred books lived, through certain intervals of time.

By this very fact, however, we in no way deny the difficulty of knowing Sacred Chronology. For this subject, due to human <term>blindness and wandering</term> <note>original Greek: "τυφλότητα καὶ ῥεμβασμὸν" (typhloteta kai rhembasmon).</note>, is entangled in almost indissoluble knots, as even the most accurate chronologists confess. How greatly, I ask, do the chronologists disagree when they place their calculation on the <term>abacus</term> <note>A counting board; here used metaphorically for mathematical calculation.</note>, inquiring how many years the Creation of the world and the beginnings of things preceded the common era of Christ! There are almost as many calculations as there are counting-boards; as many systems of arithmetic as there are heads. Bellarmine counts 3,984 years; Torniellus 4,054; Salianus 4,057; Gordon 4,001; Petavius 3,983; Henry Philippi 4,040; who even in his *2nd Question on Genesis chapter 1* reported forty-two different opinions. <note>These men were 16th and 17th-century scholars—Jesuits, Franciscans, and theologians—who specialized in "universal histories" and biblical timelines.</note> If you ask Palaemon Baronius, he replies in his *Apparatus, note 118*, that to sit as an arbiter and to seek to define the oldest question of all with a broad sentence is not a task for his present leisure, nor is such a great work within his strength. If you go to the most industrious chronologist Dionysius Petavius, he replies in his <margin>Rationes Temp p. 2. c. 1.</margin> *The number of years that have flowed from the founding of the world to this age is gathered by no certain reasoning, but by probable conjecture.*

Thus, opinions move in different directions, while meanwhile the certain distinction of years and days shown to us by God remains. God, the <term>Ruler of Time</term> <note>original Greek: "ὁ χρονοκράτωρ" (ho chronokrator).</note>, willed this to be a mark for the Church so that men might know the world is not eternal, but had a beginning at some point. For unless a series of years existed from the very beginning of the world, we would be dreaming, nor would we be certain of things; or we might think, with Aristotle and Democritus, that the world is eternal in the past. But so that we might know the beginning of the world and that there would also be a certain span for the world’s duration, the distinction and series of years was handed down, lest we be ignorant of our origin and end in this world. Moreover, God reminds us of the world’s beginning through the revelation of the word **Bereshit** <note>Hebrew: "In the beginning," the first word of the Bible.</note>, the very first word of all in the Sacrosanct Codex, concerning the absolute beginning of time and of all things created in time. For the Sacred Literatures open **TIME** to us immediately in the very entrance-hall, as we have said, which according to Tertullian <margin>* book against Marcion, p. 133.</margin> *is the judge and measurer of beginnings and ends. They hand down its division into DAYS, so much so that in this world we are unable to explain the world with its parts and the things that happen in it without a graphic partition; so that both Chronography and Chronology are commended to us immediately with the very beginning of the world.*

### Wisdom VII. 17. 18. 19.

<margin>The logic of years and months.</margin>
This was given as a testimony of the order which the most wise, almighty, and most beneficent author of the ages observed, especially in the accurate distinction of time, so that humans placed in the middle of the world might better grasp all things that are ordered by time, measure, and weight. For indeed God, who is the author not of confusion but of order, when no matter previously existed, produced from nothing a certain rough and undigested bodily mass, which Moses marked with the names *heaven, earth, and water*. In the *first three days*, He distinguished these three bodies, and in the *following three days*, He completed each with its own adornment. Thus, in *six distinct days*, He finished the entire machinery of the world—which is why the term <term>Hexaemeron</term> <note>From the Greek 'hexa' (six) and 'hemera' (day), referring to the six days of creation described in Genesis.</note> is so celebrated. God preferred to create the world and its parts successively and in order, rather than suddenly and all at once, to show as Creator that He is a God of order, and to encourage His creatures to complete and carry out all things in an orderly fashion. Those who believe that God created everything simultaneously and suddenly in a single moment are in error. God could certainly have done so, but we must examine what He actually did by the light of Holy Scripture, which openly testifies that those six days in which the work of Creation was finished were natural days, not mystical or allegorical ones. The parts of passing time are therefore *years, months, days, and hours*, by which every age of this world distinctly glides away. The circle of the year requires a course of *twelve months*, and the year perpetually turns and returns around this group of twelve. Eternity extends to eternity, yet time does not relate to the logic of eternity in any way. Nevertheless, eternity contains all times, and such a perpetual flow of time could not endure unless it received its stability from the immobility and firmness of eternity itself. Leaving eternity aside, our discussion will be on the measurement of times, whose parts are years, months, and days, and the smaller particles of days are hours. The parts of the year are *months*, the portions are days, and the small portions are *hours*. Plato says that among those things in nature, there are first things, middle things, and extreme or final things. For such is the order of things: whoever can see the beginnings, progresses, increases, and ends is to be considered a philosopher—that is, a wise man. In this present passage, the Author (whom *Johannes Costadius* <note>A 17th-century scholar; the reference is to a book published in Breda.</note> shows to be Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher often traditionally associated with the authorship of the Wisdom of Solomon.</note> in a learned little book) speaks of the whole course of time, in which a continuous series from the beginnings to the end is observed by the Wise Man. From this, *Osiander* <note>Likely Lucas Osiander the Elder or Younger, Lutheran theologians known for their biblical commentaries.</note> thinks the author intended to describe alterations, generation, corruption, and the like, about which physicists learnedly differ based on physical principles. However, the series and the <gloss>connection of the words</gloss> <note>original: "συνάφεια" (synápheia)</note> is an indicator that Philo wanted to point out that Solomon was incomparable in the faculty of Mathematics. To him was known everything regarding the exact disposition of the profane and sacred year, and he had such perfect knowledge of natural things—the heavens, the stars, the sea, the earth, etc.—that even if he did not possess the absolute and perfect knowledge that belongs to God alone, he had a determined science. He knew the <gloss>composition of the world</gloss> <note>original: "σύστασιν κόσμου" (systasin kosmou)</note>, the arrangement or makeup of the Earth, and the <gloss>operation of the elements</gloss> <note>original: "ἐνέργειαν στοιχείων" (energeian stoicheion)</note>; namely, how the elements send forth their powers and virtues into these lower things which

<column-break/>

<margin>The logic of the year.</margin>
lie beneath them. Thus, the Author attributes to Solomon the knowledge of how time began with the first creation and the motion of the heavens, the Sun, the Moon, and the stars; how it has proceeded in its course until now; and how it will finally cease. He also knew the dimension of each time according to the past, present, and future, which would be nothing without calculation. For if we lacked the distinction of numbers, we would wander blindly in time regarding what times, days, and months were. There would be a darkness and confusion of things. Indeed, years could not be numbered, nor the series of times distinguished, unless the boundaries of years, months, and days were observed as defined by the motions of the Sun and Moon. Therefore, the consideration and knowledge of the motions of the Sun and Moon are necessary for maintaining a certain logic of the year and the series of times. Hence the Author also attributes to Solomon the <gloss>changes of the solstices</gloss> <note>original: "τροπῶν ἀλλαγὰς" (tropōn allagas)</note>. I say *turnings* <note>original: "τροπῶν" (tropōn)</note>, for the Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible translation of the time.</note> reads it as "manners" <note>original: "τρόπων" (trópōn - with a different accent in Greek, changing the meaning from 'solstices' to 'customs' or 'ways').</note> and translates it as *changes of manners*, but this is against the context and beyond all reason. For the word *turning* <note>original: "τροπὴ" (tropē)</note> is used even among secular authors, though not without an addition like "winter" or "summer," because at those times the Sun changes its course. Thucydides says, *around the winter turnings of the sun*; that is, around the winter solstice. Theophrastus says, *after the winter turnings*; that is, after the solstice. <margin>Book 7. 6, 1. 15.</margin> Also *under the turnings* and in his book on Animals, *after the sun's turnings*. Even if these specific modifiers were not added by the Author, they belong to this passage, as the underlying subject matter absolutely requires it. Furthermore, he attributes to him the <gloss>changes of the seasons</gloss> <note>original: "μεταβολὰς καιρῶν" (metabolàs kairōn)</note>; that is, of the year. What time can do is well known to those who live within time. There is no one who does not know that time tames and changes all things. Because of this trait, time was called *all-subduing* <note>original: "χρόνος πανδαμάτωρ" (chronos pandamatōr)</note> by a certain poet. Ovid beautifully expressed this same violence:
> Time, the glutton of things, and you, envious old age,
> You destroy all things, and with the teeth of time,
> Little by little, you consume everything with a slow death.

He also mentions the <gloss>circuits of the years</gloss> <note>original: "ἐνιαυτῶν κύκλος" (eniautōn kyklos)</note>, which people commonly call the "revolution of the years." Regarding the year, as the primary part of time, it is made by the circuit of the Sun, just as the month is made by the Moon. However, the form and division of the year is not one and the same among all people. Servius writes that among the most ancient people, the year was divided into two parts, *winter and summer*, and he cites the authority of Virgil who sang:
> Now venerable Pales, now we must speak with a great voice.
> Beginning in the soft stalls, I command the sheep to pluck 
> the grass, until soon leafy summer is brought back.

In this passage, he extended winter until summer began. He is said to have included spring under the name of summer in this verse:
> But truly when happy summer comes with calling West-winds.

Yet in the *Georgics*, he also mentions three parts of the year—namely Autumn, Spring, and Summer—omitting Winter. But whatever the case may be regarding the division of the Ancients, the form of the year has been so manifold and diverse among different nations, and even among the same peoples at different times, that it would be laborious to recount them all. It is the most common custom of nations to record the history of their deeds...

## BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The logic of years and months.</margin>
...[world] of things done is circumscribed by a number of years, in which if an error is committed, even history itself is sometimes called into doubt. We shall illustrate this matter with an example. The Egyptian kingdom, according to Manetho of Sebennytos, a priest of Heliopolis, had thirty-one dynasties before Alexander. He lived in the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus and composed the entire ancient history of the Egyptians in three volumes. Indeed, he extended his history as far as the conquest of Egypt by Alexander the Great and the defeat of Darius Codomannus at Arbela. Thus, from the beginning of the Egyptian Empire until Alexander, he counts more than five thousand years. This will not be true unless you understand it "collaterally"—that is, in such a way that different kings reigned at the same time in different parts of Egypt. From this comes the need to consider the multiple methods of the year among the Egyptians, regarding which one should read Vossius <note>Gerardus Joannes Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch classical scholar and theologian.</note>, *On Idolatry*, Book 1, chapter 28, pages 207–212, where you will find not only the Egyptian years explained but also Scaliger defended against Petavius and others. Just as there is great diversity among nations in days and months, so it is with years. The Hebrews began the year at the vernal equinox; the Asians at the autumnal; the Greeks at the summer solstice; the Latins in winter; and thus in one way the Jews, in another the Greeks, in another the Romans, and in another still others began their year.

Let us first deal with the Jews, the most ancient among the more famous nations. The ancestors of the Jews used solar years before and around the time of the flood, not lunar months. This is most clearly evident from the history of the Deluge, in which the span of a year is described to us most exactly. For when Noah, in the 600th year of his life, had entered the Ark, mention is then made of the seventh and tenth months of that same year. Afterward, in the following year (which is the 601st of Noah's life), on the 27th day of the second month, he went out of the Ark again, having stayed in it for a full solar year. For from the 17th day of the second month of the 600th year of Noah’s life until the same day of the same month in the following year (601), a lunar year of 354 days is comprised; to which are then added 10 <term>epacts</term> <note>original: "επακται" — additional days added to the lunar year to synchronize it with the solar year.</note> days, during which he is read to have still remained in the ark, so that a full span of a solar year is completed. However, after the departure from Egyptian servitude, solar years began to be in use, since they took the beginning of the year from the new moon which most closely precedes the vernal equinox.

The Greeks began to calculate their years according to the festivals of the Olympic games; for before the institution of the Olympic games, the account of years among the Greeks, like everything else, was wrapped in the greatest veils of darkness. Hence Varro attributes three intervals of time to the Greeks. The first is called by him <term>adelon</term> <note>original: "αδδηλον" — uncertain or obscure.</note>, meaning uncertain—specifically for the Gentiles from the creation of the world until the universal <term>kataklysmos</term> <note>original: "κατακλυςμον" — the Great Flood.</note>. The second is <term>mythikon</term> <note>original: "μυθικον" — mythical or fabulous.</note>, from the flood to the beginning of the Olympiads. The third is <term>historikon</term> <note>original: "ιςορικον" — historical</note>, from the first Olympiad onward. The Olympic games were celebrated around the summer solstice, and always at the full moon, on the 15th day of Hecatombaion, the first month of the Athenians, which corresponds to our June. Thus we said above that the Greeks began their year at the summer solstice, though with some, albeit small, differences among themselves. For some

<column-break/>

began the year of their <term>Tetraeteris</term> <note>A four-year cycle used in Greek calendars.</note> immediately from the conjunction of the Sun and Moon. Others added two more days, looking toward the <term>doxa</term> <note>original: "δόξαν" — here likely referring to the appearance or "opinion" of the moon's phase.</note>. Others began from the full moon, when the Moon turns its entire illuminated part toward the earth; meanwhile, among all, the Luni-Solar year prevailed. Indeed, the Solar and Lunar years differ by eleven days, which are called by the Greeks <term>epaktai</term>, that is, intercalary, inserted, or super-added days. For the Lunar year contains twelve months, of which six are "full" and the other six are "hollow," as they call them. A full month contains thirty days; a hollow one twenty-nine. If you reduce these numbers into one sum—that is, if you multiply six hollow and six full months—the sum 354 will be produced. Add eleven days to these, and the Lunar will equal the Solar year, in which the Sun by its motion traverses the entire Ecliptic, returning precisely to the same point from which it departed.

As far as months are concerned, they are not the same among all people. That the months of the Greeks cannot coincide perfectly with ours is true and well-noted, says Brodaeus in his *Annotations on the Greek Epigrams*, page 178. Nor are the seasons of the year the same at one time among all. In Egypt, Spring flourishes in the months of January and February; Summer begins in March and lasts until the end of August; Autumn is in September and October; while Winter is completed in November and December, about which those skilled in astronomy treat more fully. For the logic and proper distribution of years and months depends on the laws of astronomy; neither the cycle of the year nor the course of hours and days is established without this field. Nor, without a proper distribution of time, is the order of civil business or the solemnities of sacred rites possible. To this end, Plato, in his *Republic* (and Book 7 of *The Laws*), decreed that the divine circuits of the Stars, Sun, and Moon must be learned, because in respect to these it is necessary to arrange the whole state regarding the order of days into a month, and months into a year. The Sun describes the most pleasing transitions of days and nights—which in Sacred Scripture is called a <term>nychthemeron</term> <note>original: "νυχθημερον" — a period of 24 hours, from the Greek for 'night' and 'day'.</note>, that is, the time integrated from a natural day and night, and is now called by the single name "day"—and the spaces of days, months, and years by its motion so elegantly that we use its course no differently than Pythagoras used numbers and figures, Orpheus used fables, or the Egyptians used hieroglyphs.

So that there might be a certain law and knowledge of the hours, this was managed by various devices, and from this <term>Horologia</term> <note>Clocks or sundials.</note> were born—first of unpolished, then of more refined workmanship, as taught by Paul Scherlog, whom you may see regarding the Sundial of Ahaz in *Hebrew Antiquities*, volume 2, chapter 1, section 7, page 246. To this, join Petavius * <margin>* on the Gospel of John, p. 275.</margin> Scripture mentions the sundial or solar clock of Ahaz, which was placed in Jerusalem by that King, on which the shadow moved back ten degrees at the request of Hezekiah and the command of the Prophet. No one until now has doubted that these degrees were indicators of those parts of the day which they later called hours. Salmasius thinks of this sundial just as he does of the solar clocks of the Babylonians and Egyptians in his notes on Pliny (page 657): namely, that they pertained only to astrologers, Chaldeans, and mathematical calculations, and that the day on it was divided into twelve equal parts or "equinoctial hours," not into "popular" or <term>kairikas</term> <note>original: "καιρικας" — 'seasonal' or 'temporal' hours, which varied in length depending on the time of year.</note> hours. But it was not the custom to display those machines publicly and in the forums of cities...

<margin>

...instruments for discerning the times, which were accessible for use only by astrologers and <term>genethliacs</term> <note>those who cast horoscopes based on the time of birth</note>; and there is an additional specific argument drawn from the Jewish people, to whom the use of horoscopes and astrology was most severely forbidden. Therefore, even if Ahaz—an unpraiseworthy Prince inclined toward the rites and institutions of foreign nations—could have used and publicly displayed a horoscopic and astrological instrument in imitation of the Babylonians, Hezekiah would never have done so. Instead, he would have removed this famous and notable object along with the remaining traces of idolatry and superstition. Nor would God have wished to use it through the Prophet to provide an illustrious specimen of His power, lest the value of that miracle seem to come from illicit arts. It is not for nothing, therefore, that days, months, and years are so accurately recorded in Scripture; nor are the times consecrated to God shown to us without reason. The rest of the seventh day is not superfluous, by which a great and wonderful rest in heaven is hinted at. The religious observance of the new month must be honored with venerable auspices, through which the sacrament of the heavenly festivity is noted by Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), a prominent bishop and theologian.</note> as being figured as if in a mirror (on Psalm 118, page 469). Venerable is that year in which, after six years of servitude, the Hebrew is set free; in which, after much labor, the field rests, its fruits being left for the <term>proselyte</term> <note>a convert or stranger</note>, the poor, and the beasts of the earth; and in which all debts were forgiven to the Hebrews. One must note the religious practice which occurs in the first month from the tenth day until the fourteenth, and then until the twenty-first. Also, that solemnity of the seventh month, whose memorial was in the trumpets, and the atonement on the tenth day of that month, and after the fifteenth day, the joy of eight days in the tabernacles—and how in these both the first and the eighth days were holy. Furthermore, in every single day we have a model of the four-fold year; for the day corresponds to the whole year by a certain proportion or analogy, so that the morning time is like Spring, midday like summer, evening like autumn, and night like winter, as Galen records in his commentary on Hippocrates’ *Epidemics* (page 452). David also expressed the principal times of the day to denote that one must always pray, and that there ought to be a daily exercise of prayer at specific hours, when he says in Psalm 55:17: *Evening and morning and at noon I will utter my complaint and moan, and he will hear my voice.* May God preserve us in time, until time fails, into that age of ages where there is no time; for there, as Augustine says on Psalm 88 (column 982), *no one expects the future, no one loses the past, but the days of heaven are always present.*

<margin>
The origin and progress of idolatry.
</margin>
The Lord our God is One God, not tolerating foreign gods alongside Himself, and utterly abhorring invented divinities. Who could tell us all the names of the divinities, who could enumerate those monstrous dogmas of the deities, who could examine that entire idolatrous <term>Pantheon</term> <note>the collection of all gods of a people</note>? It is gross stupidity, when you have more than the One God, to fashion so many other gods—to invoke and adore that which does not exist, which is neither one nor many. The invocation of the One God is as far removed from the worship of idolatry as the great error of many gods is from that which belongs to the One God alone. How favorable God was to Israel when He addressed them: *Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one* (Deuteronomy 6:4). For the essence of God is communicable to no one outside of God, and the essential Majesty of God existing outside of God is incommunicable; for every <term>Other</term> <note>original Hebrew: *acher*</note> is excluded (Isaiah 42:8). For just as there can be no other God, but there is only one; so also His glory and His essence are one. For as soon as essential divine glory and majesty are attributed to someone, immediately by that very act they are established as a God, or regarded as a God. Hence Jehovah, having called Moses to Himself in a more secret discourse, delivered the moral law; He likewise delivered ceremonial and judicial laws to be brought to the Israelite people. And indeed, He had given a command in the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> about not worshipping foreign gods; afterward, as if by an appendix (Exodus 20:23), He repeats the law about not making gods of silver or gold. Although this had been included under the first precept of the Decalogue, it nevertheless seemed right to God to repeat it, as He knew full well the nature and genius of the people, who were too prone toward idolatry. Hence He emphasized almost no command to them as often as this one about avoiding foreign gods. And so that He might all the more drive the opinion of <term>image-worship</term> <note>original Greek: *eikonolatreias*</note> out of the minds of men, God did not wish to appear to them in any visible form or assumed shape, but in thick darkness and a dark cloud (Exodus 19:9), lest they take the opportunity to make any carved image or likeness to represent God for themselves, as Moses expressly hints in Deuteronomy 4:11. But truly, even if a drive to venerate some God is implanted in the human race from its very cradle, and no nation or type of men has ever existed so wild or horrid that it was not held by the religion of some divinity (whether true or fictional), it usually happens in the matter of religion that he who has once begun to be deceived is deceived often. He who has once stepped away from the path and neglected to follow the trail that guides his journey, follows instead into precipices and pathless places with error as his leader. Since the <term>starting points</term> <note>original Greek: *hormētēria* - often used to mean a base of operations or stronghold</note> of vices come from one vicious person, with vices following one another in turn, one impious man sometimes infects others, as if from a root...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<page-num>548</page-num>

<margin>The origin and progress of idolatry.</margin>
...from the root, the entire root, so that a wicked nation might sprout from there. The envious malice of Cain, the forerunner of all idolatry, corrupted his entire posterity until the Flood, both in religion and in morals. For his sons strenuously continued along that path of idolatry which their Father had begun to enter. The sons of his sons and their descendants, swept away into the depth of idolatry <note>original Greek: "εἰς τὸ τῆς εἰδωλολατρείας βάθος"</note>, eventually reached such a point that they even sacrificed human blood—indeed, the gore of their dearest children—to the Gods! Concerning idolatry, many have treated the subject sufficiently and copiously up to this point, most notably in four books by Gerard Johann Vossius <note>Gerard Johann Vossius (1577–1649) was a Dutch classical scholar and theologian; his work "De theologia gentili" is a massive study of pagan religions.</note>, so much so that in writing these matters, there seems to be a need for contraction rather than a more prolix repetition. Hence, as we are about to discuss the Gods whom we know to have belonged to blind Gentility from the Old Testament, we shall first bring forth a general description of them by the force of this passage which we have premised, and afterward we shall arrange a special catalog of the <term>Deasters</term> <note>minor or false gods</note> according to the Holy <term>Pandects</term> <note>a complete body of laws or, here, the complete collection of Scriptures</note>. *Idolatry* is a most fertile thing, which to Tertullian is known as the *highest crime of the age* <note>original: "summus seculi reatus"</note>; it does not stand still at those beginnings from which it arises, but like a Plane tree, it propagates itself into great and spreading branches. The first opinion concerning "Gods" was cast before our First Parents in Paradise by Satan: *You shall be like GODS* <note>Genesis 3:5</note>. This ancient persuasion, never-ending among our ancestors—which is called by Plutarch the "ancestral and ancient faith" <note>original Greek: "Πάτριος καὶ παλαιὰ πίστις" from Eroticos, page 756</note>—the devil propagated immediately after the Fall, the true religion having been obscured in a wretched manner by various shadows of error, and various idolatries and heresies having been introduced time and again. God considers the First Parents in the height of perfect wisdom, by which they knew God and His essence and will most exactly. The devil did not wish to rest until he led those first inhabitants of most happy Paradise away. He led them away, and from this, the most miserable condition of the entire human race was infected. The fallen were indeed kindly received into grace and sufficiently instructed concerning those mysteries in which the restoration of the human race to eternal life is contained, the <term>Protevangelium</term> <note>The "First Gospel" or the first messianic prophecy in Genesis 3:15</note> having been given concerning the Seed of the Woman who would crush the head of the serpent. But meanwhile, great power remained to the Devil, since after that calamity of the fatal fall, the human race, infected by sin, can incline toward every kind of falsehood and error in religion and very easily turn aside from the royal road of truth. Wickedness is successful against the cultivators of true religion if piety is cast away. Satan was successful against Cain, while Cain, despising the admonitions of God and his Parents, neglected the study of religion, and—plucking himself away from the <margin>Genesis 2:14</margin> root of the holy stock—as Lactantius says, *founded new customs and institutions for himself according to his own will.* Ancestral credulity persuading toward idolatry led Cain and his followers, and with him everyone except the house of Noah alone, into various modes of worshipping God, so that it was necessary to radically extirpate this thick and indolent <unclear>nursery of idol-madness</unclear> with the waters of the universal flood. After the flood, the world having been purged of the unclean idolaters, within a few years most people, even in the family of the pious, followed idolatry after losing the true religion. For Satan then took on infinite forms of masks; he walked and seduced among this people under the mask of this minor god, and among that people under the mask of another, so much so that

<column-break/>

<margin>The origin and progress of idolatry.</margin>
from the flood until Abraham, a space of a thousand years and more, one does not read clearly of anyone worshipping God, as <margin>City of God, Book 16, Chapter 12</margin> Augustine observes; his words: *Let us see the progress of the City of God, even from that turning point of time which occurred in the part of Abraham, from which its knowledge begins to be more evident, and where clearer divine promises are read, which we now see fulfilled in Christ. As we have learned by the indication of Holy Scripture: Abraham was born in the region of the Chaldeans, which land belonged to the Assyrian kingdom. Among the Chaldeans, however, even then impious superstitions were prevailing, just as through the rest of the nations. Therefore, there was the one house of Terah, from which Abraham was born, in which the worship of the one true God, and as far as is credible, in which alone the Hebrew language had remained.* These are his words. But more powerful is the opinion of those who establish that Abraham, together with Terah and Nahor, was an Idolater; for so God addresses the Israelites in Joshua 24:2: *Across the river, He says, your fathers lived from the beginning, Terah the father of Abraham and Nahor, and they served foreign Gods. Therefore, I took your Father Abraham from beyond the river and led him into the land of Canaan.* The Hebrews indeed, and those of the Christians who follow them, establish that Abraham, while he was still in Chaldea, sharply attacked idolatry, to which Nimrod compelled the men subjugated to him by violent means; and therefore, when he refused to worship fire, he was cast into a fiery furnace but was divinely preserved unharmed like the three companions of Daniel. However, this tastes of a fable which authors report concerning the divine liberation of Abraham from Ur of the Chaldeans; the Vulgate translator even seems to err in this error concerning the punishment of fire, who translates *Ur of the Chaldeans* <margin>Antiquities Book 1, Ch. 8</margin> as the *Fire of the Chaldeans* <note>The Hebrew word "Ur" can mean "light" or "fire."</note>, since it should rather be explained concerning the worship of fire. Indeed, the entire Theology of the Chaldeans was in the contemplation of the celestial bodies and their veneration, and the greatest of all was the worship of fire, which the <term>Rambam</term> <note>Rabbi Moshe Ben Maimon, also known as Maimonides (1138–1204).</note>—so called by his initials—shows from the most ancient monuments of the Asians in his *Moreh Nevukhim* <note>The Guide for the Perplexed</note>, whose words Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English jurist and polymath who wrote on Syrian gods.</note> transcribed in Latin (*Syntagma 1, 2, chapter 8, page 321*); compare also Sixtinus Amama, Fuller, and Gyraldus. From this worship of fire, God called Abraham forth and brought him to the true divine worship; as one who did not have it from the sight and consideration of the marvelous workmanship of heaven and earth—an error which Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), the Jewish-Roman historian.</note> fostered, discussing Abraham thus: *Since he was considered wise above all others because of his exceptional virtue, he dared to uproot the commonly received persuasion concerning God and turn it for the better. Therefore, he was the first of all to preach with a clear voice that there is one God; this indeed he gathered from the observation of the earth and the sea, and from those things which he saw happening around the Sun and Moon and the remaining stars.* After the flood, the first of men occupied Chaldea and its neighbors; nor does Ursinus doubt that idolatry was born there and transplanted into the entire world. From the Orientals, therefore—the first inhabitants of the earth—whatever the remaining peoples have of divine and salvific knowledge flowed; from them also, whatever they have of impious superstition took its origin. In the East the first men were created. In the East the Church was first born and cultivated.

# Wisdom 13: 1, 2, 3.

<page-num>549</page-num>

<header>Wisdom 13: 1, 2, 3.</header>

<margin>The rise and progress of idolatry.</margin>
The Church. That region first held mankind; it first held religion and piety, and it was the first to possess learning. From there, just as people were propagated elsewhere, so too was erudition. Greece owes its doctrine and its fame to the East—Greece, which confesses that it received its letters from Cadmus the Phoenician, a neighbor of Syria. Read John Selden’s <term>treatise on the Syrian Gods</term> <note>John Selden (1584–1654) was an English polymath whose "De Diis Syris" was a foundational work in comparative mythology.</note> and the first chapter of Heinsius in his *Aristarchus*; you will admit that almost all the religion of the Greeks, Egyptians, and Latins flowed from the East, and that not even the names of the Gods can be understood from any other source but the East. However, among the Gentiles, there was a great abundance of Gods and a vast variety of names, and yet among so many Gods, there was no true GOD. If you inquire into the origin of these Gods, some are from the elements of the world, some from the names of Kings, and some from men—whence you might rightly say they arose <note>original Greek: "ἐκ προσωποπαθείας"</note> <gloss>out of human personification or passion</gloss>—and some are from stones, metals, and wood. When the Gentiles attribute the origins of the Gods to this or that family, it is done to cover up the ignorance of their true births. Boccaccio reduced the genealogies of these beings into a single body more successfully than could have been hoped for in that century, according to the judgment of Vives <note>Juan Luis Vives (1492–1540), a Spanish humanist commenting on Boccaccio’s "Genealogia Deorum Gentilium."</note>, even if he is often excessive and dull in interpreting the fables. Nimrod was consecrated as a God after his death; they called him Baal without doubt, or in the contracted form, Belus. Satan acted early in this regard, so that he might turn the mortality of Kings and Princes into divinity, and persuade people to worship dead Kings and Princes, whom he had led the wretched commoners to believe were changed into Gods. This practice prevailed for many centuries, so much so that even while they were still living, they were worshiped beyond the human lot. Thus, Alexander allowed himself to be called the son of Jupiter Ammon. Agesilaus laughed at these follies; for when divine honors were being deferred to him and he was hailed as a God, he replied: "He who provides my <term>chamber pot</term> <note>original Latin: "matula"; a witty way of saying his servant knows he is a mortal with bodily needs.</note> denies this." Menecrates the Physician, as Athenaeus testifies in Book 7, used to claim he was Jupiter, the giver of life, leading about with him a retinue of "saved" patients who followed this "Jupiter" as if they were the <term>Council of Gods</term> <note>original Latin: "Dii Consentes aut Selecti"; the twelve major Roman deities who advised Jupiter.</note>, having bartered their service for the health he had given through medical aid. When these men were invited to a banquet, King Philip—having ordered food to be placed before the other guests—gave them nothing but incense, until, mocked and deluded by the fumes, they rushed out from the middle of the hall. The records of human deeds, or things concerning God, the world, and whatever excellence the world possessed, were thus polluted by the figments of <term>idol-mania</term>. Hence,
<margin>Book on False Religion, book 1, p. 39.</margin>
as Lactantius says, individual peoples worshiped with the highest veneration the founders of their own Nation or City, whether they were men distinguished for bravery or women wonderful for chastity. Thus, the Egyptians worshiped Isis; the Moors, Juba; the Macedonians, Cabirus; the Carthaginians, Uranus; the LATINS, Faunus; the Sabines, Sancus; and the Romans, Quirinus. Therefore, the whole body of Heathenism was colored by a grand paintbrush, but not with the same face. There were innumerable types of Sacred Rites in false religion, and innumerable Gods. There was Zeus <term>Herkeios</term> <gloss>of the courtyard</gloss>, <term>Nemesios</term> <gloss>of retribution</gloss>, <term>Eleutherios</term> <gloss>of freedom</gloss>, and <term>Xenios</term> <gloss>of hospitality</gloss>, and this was due to distinct actions; hence not only were human forms attributed to the Gods, but also the modes of human actions. As Aristotle says:
<margin>Politics, book 3.</margin>
<note>original Greek: "ὥσπερ τὰ εἴδη ἑαυτοῖς (θεοῖς) ἀφομοιοῦσιν οἱ ἄνθρωποι, οὕτω καὶ τοὺς βίους τῶν Θεῶν."</note> <gloss>Just as men model the forms of the gods after themselves, so too they do with the lives of the gods.</gloss> Plato, at the end of Book 2 of the *Republic*, strongly rebukes this custom of attributing forms, lives, and actions similar to humans to the Gods without any discrimination, and he attacks the poets as the greatest au-

<column-break/>

thors and cultivators of this practice, teaching how cautiously we ought to deal with such matters; compare Montecatini on Book 1 of Aristotle’s *Politics*, p. 45. There were two different ranks and grades of these Heathen "godlings": some were among the "Greater" <note>original: "ἐν μείζοσι"</note> and others among the "Lesser" <note>original: "ἐν μείοσι"</note>. They made those the Gods of the "greater nations" who were foremost in age and worship, in respect to whom the later kind of Gods were to be held as if they were deities of "lesser nations." The Greeks, and the Latins following them, numbered these twelve foremost Gods, whom Ennius included in two verses:

<margin>The rise and progress of idolatry.</margin>

->Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, Venus, Mars,<-
->Mercury, Jove, Neptune, Vulcan, Apollo.<-

Regarding the Egyptians, Herodotus mentions that they made eight primary Gods and twelve secondary ones, who were either images or ministers of the others, like "dish-serving" Gods. In the first rank are Osiris and Isis, and that great Serapis, and Anubis, and Canopus, and Horus, and Typhon—about whom a few things cannot be said, and many things ought not be said. Serapis—lest we allow these Gods to pass by entirely unmentioned—had a most famous temple in Alexandria, in which the statue of Serapis himself was so vast that it brushed one wall with its right hand and the other with its left. This monster was said to be composed of every kind of metal and symbol, crafted with such art that a small ray of sunlight, directed through a window, would illuminate its bronze lips while the people watched. There was also an image of the Sun in the same temple made of very fine iron, which, drawn by a magnetic stone inserted into the ceiling, was lifted up as if to salute Serapis. The error and rumor of the common folk had hallowed such a massive bulk, everyone being persuaded that if a human hand touched this statue, the earth would instantly gape open and dissolve into chaos, and the sky would fall headlong. This is related by Haymo in Book 10 of *On the Memory of Christian Matters*, chapter 8, following Rufinus. Nor was the worship of Serapis—who is the same as Osiris according to the common opinion of the wiser historians (compare Diodorus Siculus, Book 1 of *Ancient History*, ch. 2, p. 32; Plutarch’s *On Isis and Osiris*, and others)—contained within the borders of Egypt alone. Rather, the Rites of Serapis were also transferred into Rome itself, and a magnificent "Serapium" <note>A temple dedicated to Serapis.</note> was built there, as Marcus Tullius [Cicero] testifies in Book 3 of *On the Nature of the Gods*, and Marcus Aurelius Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle*, and Eutropius at the end of Book 7 of his *Roman History*, and others whom you may read in Dempster, *Roman Antiquities*, Book 1, p. 57 and Book 2, ch. 22. Regarding Canopus, Rufinus relates a story worthy of laughter in Book 11, ch. 26 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. They say that once the Chaldeans, carrying around fire as their God, had a conflict with the Gods of all the provinces; whoever won would be believed by everyone to be the true God. The Gods of the other provinces consisted of bronze, or gold, silver, wood, or stone, or whatever material would undoubtedly be destroyed by fire. Because of this, fire was prevailing everywhere. When the Priest of Canopus heard this, he devised a clever trick. Water-jars <note>original: "Hydriae"</note> are usually made of clay in Egypt, covered everywhere with frequent and very tiny holes, so that as the turbid water sweats through, it is rendered more refined and pure. He took one of these, plugged the holes with wax, and even painted it over with various colors on the outside—

...having painted a jar and filled it with water, he established it as a God. He then took an old carved image of Canopus <note>In Egyptian mythology, Canopus was sometimes identified as a pilot of Menelaus; here, the author recounts a legend where a priest used a water-filled jar to trick rivals.</note>, said to be the pilot of Menelaus, and carefully fitted the head on top. After this, the Chaldeans arrived and a conflict ensued. A fire was lit around the jar, and the wax that had been used to plug the holes melted. As the jar "sweated," the fire was extinguished, and thus, through the priest's trickery, the Egyptian Canopus emerged victorious. What can we say of the Gods of the lesser nations, except to expose their mockeries? A more insane nation under the sun has never been seen, nor any more arrogant, so that it may rightly be said of them what Gregory wrote: <note>original Greek: βδελυκτοὶ τῆς πλάνης, βδελυκτότεροι τῆς εὐτελείας τῶν προσκυνουμένων καὶ σεβομένων</note> <gloss>they are abominable for their error, and even more abominable for the worthlessness of the objects they adore and revere</gloss> (where "the objects revered" is taken in the passive sense). Indeed, *among the land animals*, they worshiped dogs, cats, sheep, wolves, lions, she-goats, he-goats, mice, spiders, mongooses, crocodiles, and serpents; *among the birds*, eagles, griffins, ibises, and hawks; *among aquatic creatures*, the sharp-nosed fish, the scale-fish, the latus-fish, and eels; *among plants*, garlic and onions. But there was no limit to their insanity! For besides these foulest animals, they did not blush to worship as Gods certain things shameful to mention, which cannot be named without a prefix of apology. For as Clement, the Roman Bishop, testifies (though he is an author of doubtful reliability) in the 5th book of his *Recognitions*, they worshiped the sewer and the sound of intestinal gas; and as Diodorus Siculus writes

<margin>

(granting pardon for the saying), they performed sacred rites to the private parts as if they were the cause of the creation of animals. Nor were others far removed from this obscene worship. Certainly, the Romans, the masters of the world, numbered among their Gods and Goddesses Stercutius <note>From the Latin "stercus," meaning dung; he was the god of manuring.</note>, who discovered the method of fertilizing fields; and Caca, who gave Hercules evidence regarding the theft of the oxen; and Cloacina, who was found in the sewer by Tatius, King of the Sabines. Certainly, the obscene noise of the belly was considered *an augur of the best omen* among the Greeks, whom one might call—in the words of the Homeric Hymn—a <note>original Greek: ἀτάσθαλον ἀγγελίωτην</note> <gloss>reckless messenger</gloss>,

O shameful religions! O unspeakable ceremonies! Truly, Egypt did not entirely abstain from the worship of *Fire* either; for the Chaldeans and Assyrians pursued this with the greatest veneration under the maternal name *Orah*, which the Hebrews call *Or* <note>original Hebrew: אור, meaning light</note>. The Persians and Medes later followed under the name *Urismas* (from *Or* and *Chasda*), which signifies holy and divine Light, for which they had built a special shrine called a *pyreion* <gloss>fire-temple</gloss>. The Greeks called it Vulcan, who in Greek is named *Hephaestus*. The Romans used the name Vesta, by the authority of Numa Pompilius. To this, the Egyptians performed sacred rites through a Power named *Seraphim*, which means something *flaming, ignited, and shining*. And so, Fire was held as the *Greatest of Gods* among almost all nations, as Alexander ab Alexandro testifies in *Genial Days*, and Stuckius in his *Description of Gentile Sacred Rites*. Nor did they hold the Sun in less honor; hence the

Kircher is of this opinion in his work on *Hieroglyphic Obelisks*, explaining it from the words of Radaki and Benjamin: *I believe,* he says, *that these images and "chamanim" derived their name and etymology from Cham himself. For Cham is the same to the Chaldeans as heat, or even the Sun itself, "chamma," that is, the heat warming and penetrating the entire world.* Hence, I believe the name *Hammon* also flowed from this, by which the Egyptians symbolically hinted at the fertility of the Sun. Consult Vossius on this matter in *On Idolatry*, who renders the *chamanim* as fire-temples or fire-precincts—that is, enclosures in which you sing your songs by the perennial fire. There is nothing outside the Sun that presents the power and wisdom of God more clearly to our eyes. No image expresses God better than the Sun. *God placed his tabernacle in the Sun, and His throne is like the Sun.* Whence Goropius Becanus says:

> By the stupendous sight of the Sun and its clarity, intolerable to our eyes, which fills the whole world in a moment of time, we are swept away by majesty to behold with the eyes of the mind the author of such a great star, endowed with such beauty and infinite power. Truly, nothing meets the human senses that has more strength to instill the thought of Him who is alone, than the Solar star striking and stunning the eyes of the body with its immense light, and instilling such admiration as I could express with no words. Certainly, God seems to have fashioned a certain embodied image of His goodness and beauty when He fabricated the Sun. Let the vision not rest in the beauty and power of the Sun, but proceed further to the Creator Himself. If men had always done this, no mortal would have ever worshiped the Sun as God; though those who fell into this error are infinitely more excusable than those who worshiped statues, the work of vile craftsmen, as Gods. For if any embodied thing were to be worshiped, certainly this most beautiful solar orb would deserve the first place in this category.
