### Wisdom of Solomon 13:1, 2, 3
<page-num>551</page-num>

<margin>The origin and progress of idolatry.</margin>
Cicero mentions this in the fourth book of his *Academic Questions* <note>Tome 4, chapter 47.</note>. Nor were the planets and stars excluded from divine worship, specifically the entire <term>circle of stars</term> <note>Greek: kyklos astron</note>, which in the *Holy Scriptures* is called the "host of heaven" <note>Deuteronomy 17:3</note>. Even the Jews numbered these among the gods at times <note>Amos 5:26, 2 Kings 23:5</note>. Indeed, the most learned of the Hebrews believe that the first things men worshiped as gods were the celestial fires. This opinion is supported by the tradition of Abraham, who is said to have migrated specifically to flee such worship, and by the history of Job, taken from the most ancient times <note>Job 31:26, 27, 28</note>. See also Deuteronomy 4:19 and 17:3. After the stars—or rather, simultaneously with and through the stars—Kings and Queens were called "Divine" and worshiped with divine honors, the more so as they became more majestic in the eyes of the people. This was the flattery men showed their kings, even after death, by enrolling them among the gods. The most ancient record of star-worship is found in Sanchuniathon <note>A Phoenician author whose works are known through later fragments</note>, who teaches us that the Phoenician King <term>Konos</term> <gloss>Kronos</gloss> was consecrated into that star which the Greeks (having been taught by the Phoenicians) called <term>Kronos</term> and the Latins called Saturn. Likewise, Astarte was consecrated as the star of Venus; and later among the Egyptians, Osiris became the Sun and Isis the Moon. See Hugo Grotius in his *Explanation of the Decalogue* <note>pages 27, 28</note>.

Truly, I think paganism was never more foolish than when describing the divinity of its gods. It was a matter of shameless impudence and the thickest, most beast-like ignorance to subject the power of the gods to other powers—to subject their "Thrice-Great" Jupiter, four times powerful, to a mere human through some unknown means, as if the human were mightier! What is this folly of <term>invocations and enchantments of the gods</term> <note>Greek: ekkleseis einai kai goeteias theon</note>, by which, as Plutarch records in his *Roman Questions* <note>page 278</note>, the Romans believed they had led over some of the enemy's gods to their own side? Pliny reports <note>Book 28, chapter 2</note> that in sieges, it was the custom of Roman priests before all else to "call out" the God who protected that town, promising him the same or a grander temple and worship among the Romans. The more recent scholar Reuchlin <margin>*On the Miraculous Word, Book 3, chap. 6*</margin> describes it in these words: *It was once a custom observed by the Romans that whenever they besieged a city, they would accurately seek out the city's true name. Upon learning it, they were accustomed to "call out" all its protective Gods with a certain song/incantation, and thus finally conquer it. Because of this, no one dared to betray the secret name of the city of Rome, lest they suffer the same fate from their enemies. From this we see that the specific names of things are of no small use in incantations.* Fearing these "callings-out," the Tyrians are said by Plutarch <note>page 279</note> <term>to have bound their statues with chains</term> <note>Greek: desmois agalmasi peribalein legontai</note>. Perhaps not without reason could one accuse Balak of this same stupidity when he called upon Balaam to "call out" the God of the Israelites with <term>sorceries</term> <note>Greek: goeteiais</note>. But truly wretched are the gods of the Nations, who are so placed at the whim of men that, willing or unwilling, they could be summoned away, led off, taken captive, and transported from nation to nation. Their followers were so convinced of this that they would carefully guard their divine images, lest the deity be forced to depart along with them. Nor could the worshipers feel otherwise, since the gods themselves testified to it. For Juno, in the first book of Virgil’s *Aeneid*, complains thus about the gods of the Trojans:

> A race hateful to me sails the Tyrrhenian sea,
> Carrying Troy into Italy, and their conquered household gods.

And the worshipers said the same of themselves; for Aeneas says of himself:

<column-break/>

> Take up, O pious Aeneas, the household gods snatched from the enemy,
> Which I carry with me in my fleet.

<margin>The origin and progress of idolatry.</margin>
Again, the same is said of Panthus the Priest, as he joined the gods in flight:

> Panthus, son of Othrys, priest of the citadel and of Apollo,
> Carrying in his hand the sacred relics and the conquered gods, and his little grandson,
> Runs distractedly toward the shores.

God reproached the Ammonites for this insanity and threatened the <term>captivity</term> <note>Greek: aichmalosian</note> of their gods, as through Jeremiah <note>49:3</note>: *Cry out, daughters of Rabbath! Gird yourselves with sackcloth and go about the hedges, for Milcom shall be led into exile, his priests and his princes together.* Likewise in Amos 1:5: *Milcom shall go into captivity, he and his princes together.* For this reason, God did not allow the Ark to be carried into captivity along with the two tribes, lest it be said that the God of the Israelites had now been captured.

We have spoken so far of the times when these superstitions gradually arose and obscured the true doctrine of God; now we shall briefly present from our Holy Bibles how they eventually increased and infected the nations neighboring Judea, and even the Jews themselves. Foolish antiquity thought that the more surnames a god had, the more illustrious he was. Jupiter is burdened with so many epithets that he is more weighed down than any donkey. And to say nothing of epithets for now, the same little godling has so many famous names and deeds attributed to him that, if we look closer, we find nothing but a confused mess of one single thing and a miserable <term>concoction</term> <note>Greek: kykyema</note>.

We observe, however, that the names of most gods owe their origins to the Hebrew language. *Cronus*, for example, comes not from the Greek word for "time" <note>chronos</note>, but from the Hebrew <term>qaran</term> <gloss>to shine or radiate</gloss>. *Saturn* is not to be derived from "fate" or "sowing," but from the Hebrew <term>charan</term> <gloss>he hid</gloss>, just as the God is called *Latius* or *Latinus* from "hiding" (*latendo*), and his seat, the Saturnian land, is called *Latium*. From the same source (to prove the impious novelty of these ridiculous superstitions), the gods of Samothrace were called such by the corruption of the name "Satraces" (by inserting the letter 'm'), as if they were "abstruse and unknown" (for their names were unknown to the common people). They were also called <term>Gibborim</term> <gloss>mighty ones</gloss> in the Hebrew tongue, which the Greeks followed by calling them <term>Kabeiroi</term> <note>the Cabiri</note>, as the Latin interpretation in the *Book of Spectacles* shows, calling them "Divos potes" or "Powerful Gods." Thus, just as *Saturn* is to the Latins, so *Satrax* or *Samothrax* is the "abstruse and unknown" God to the Greeks and Ionians—the very kind Paul encountered among the Athenians. And what shall we say of Jupiter? It is certain that among the Latins, his name was translated <term>by a most unholy blasphemy</term> <note>Greek: di' anosiōtatēs blasphēmias</note> from the most holy name of *Jehovah* to the height of impiety. Among the Greeks, the name comes from the flashing and reflecting force and greenness of things. What of *Mars*, if not from <term>mari</term> <gloss>bitter or provoked</gloss>? What of *Hermes* and *Mercury*? *Hermes* is from <term>chalaph</term>, a <gloss>traveler treading and wearing down the roads</gloss>. *Mercury* is from <term>makar</term> <gloss>he sold</gloss>, a seller and merchant; but the Latins inserted the letter 'r' earlier to soften the name for their own people. Likewise, *Luna* (the Moon) was made from the Hebrew <term>laban</term>, so called for its whiteness. Of *Pallas*? The Greeks may forgive their own derivation from "brandishing" <note>pallein</note>, and instead derive their Pallas from the Hebrew <term>palal</term> <gloss>to roll or mediate</gloss>. Of *Ceres*? Some derive her name from "bearing" <note>gerendis</note> fruits and ears of grain, but...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<page-num>552</page-num>

<margin>The origin and progress of idolatry.</margin>
...the name of Ceres is nothing other than <term>gir</term> <note>Hebrew: גיר, usually meaning lime or chalk, but here linked to the grain-ear</note>, a word of purely Hebrew origin which Moses uses in *Leviticus 2:14* to signify a green ear of corn. Similarly, who could deny that the Roman Quirinus and the Sabines' Curin were named for their brilliance, much like the Greek <term>Kronos</term> <note>original: Κρόνον</note>? For even the iron of spears and swords is frequently called <term>chaz</term> <note>Hebrew: חז, meaning flashing or glittering</note>, "glittering," by Ezekiel and the poets. Likewise, what of Adad? Or what of Adarcate, whom some call Atergatis and others Derceto? It would exceed all bounds to investigate every instance where insane, foolish, and impious antiquity clothed its idols in Hebrew—that is, the most ancient—words, so that a fabricated antiquity of names might inspire religious awe. For the Egyptians, Phoenicians, Syrians, Assyrians, Arabs, and others, from whom these things flowed to the Greeks and Tuscans, used these arts to recommend their idols to posterity. They transmitted them to foreign nations adorned with holy words that feigned a sense of sanctity. Thus, all had idols of their own making, but names borrowed from others.

But let us set these aside and deal more specifically with those "godlings" <note>Latin: *Deastris*, a diminutive, dismissive term for pagan gods</note> explicitly mentioned in the Old Testament. *Adramelech*, which they interpret as the *cloak of the King*, or the *grandeur or power of the King or of counsel*, and *Anamelech*, which they say means the *affliction or response of the King*, were the idols of those people whom Shalmaneser,
<margin>2 Kings 17:31</margin>
King of the Assyrians, led from Sepharvaim into Samaria. The former took the form of a *peacock* or a *mule*, while the latter took the form of a *horse*, a *pheasant*, or a *quail*. The scholar John Selden, in his work *On the Syrian Gods* <note>original: *syntagm. 1. c. 6. pag. 171*</note>, reduced these to a single deity—namely, the very ancient Moloch of the Ammonites—since the Scripture testifies in the cited passage that they *burned their children in the fire* <term>to the</term> <note>Greek: τοῖς</note> Adramelech and Anamelech, the *gods of Sepharvaim*. The idol of the Hamathites was *Ashima*, having the form of a *wild goat* according to the common opinion of the Hebrews, as seen in *2 Kings 17:30*. The Goddess of the Sidonians, having the likeness of a *sheep*, is mentioned in *1 Samuel 31:10* and *1 Kings 11:5*; she is called <term>Astarte</term> <note>original: Αστάρτη</note> by the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, but <term>Eustarte</term> <note>original: ἐυςάρτη</note> by the author of the *Alexandrian Chronicle*. Among the Phoenicians and Syrians, the Moon was called *Astarte*, who is
<margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 1</margin>
called the daughter of Heaven by Sanchuniathon in the works of Eusebius. This description undoubtedly fits no one better than the Moon. There you may also read: <term>"Astarte placed a bull’s head upon her own head as a sign of her royal status."</term> <note>original: ἡ δέ Αστάρτη ἐπέθηκε τῇ ἰδίᾳ κεφαλῇ βασιλείας παράσημον κεφαλήν ταύρου</note> The bull's head is the symbol of the Moon, so that the Moon, curved into horns, might be represented by its horns, just as among the Egyptians *Isis* was recognized by her horns, through whom the Moon was likewise signified. Indeed, the Phoenicians proclaimed *Astarte* to be Venus, as the same Sanchuniathon testifies. This is confirmed by Procopius in his commentary on *1 Kings 7*, noting that Aquila translates the phrase as <term>"the statues of Astarte,"</term> <note>original: τῆς Αστάρτης ἀγάλματα</note> where the Septuagint has: <term>"the groves of Asharoth,"</term> <note>original: τὰ ἄλση Ασαρώθ</note> adding: <term>"Perhaps they named Aphrodite from the stars."</term> <note>original: ἔςω δέ καί ὗτος τῆν Αφροδίτην ἐκ τῆς ἀςίρης παρονομάσαντες</note> He interprets it similarly in *4 Kings 23* and *3 Kings 16*, where he adds that she was worshiped by the Sidonians and that groves were planted for her. This corresponds perfectly to the *Diana* of the Romans, as Gerardus Vossius says in *On Idolatry*. Suidas states: <term>"Astarte, who is called Aphrodite by the Greeks."</term> <note>original: Αστάρτη, ἡ παρ' Έλλησιν Αφροδίτη λεγομένη</note> Lucian, in his work *On the Syrian Goddess*, says: <term>"I believe Astarte to be the Moon."</term> <note>original: Αςάρτην ἐγώ δοκέω σεληναίην ἔμμεναι</note> For the Hebrews, <term>Astarte</term> is *Ashtaroth*, as in *4 Kings 23:13*, where Solomon is said to have built a temple to Ashtaroth, the idol of the Sidonians; the Septuagint uses <term>Astarte</term>. Similarly, in *1 Samuel 31:10*, the temple of Ashtaroth is called an <term>Astarteion</term> <note>original: Αςαρτεῖον</note> by the Septuagint. However, in *Judges 10:6*, the Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate also use *Ashtaroth*. Herodian says in his fifth book that the Carthaginians received <term>Ourania</term> <note>original: Ουρανίαν</note> or the "Celestial Deity" from Dido the Phoenician, and she is believed to be the Moon, called elsewhere the <term>Astroarchen</term> <note>original: Αςροάρχην</note> or "Ruler of the Stars."

<column-break/>

Therefore, the Greeks corrupted the word *Astarte*, as Vossius notes. Astarte is none other than the Venus of the Greeks and the lover of Adonis. Cicero says in the third book of *On the Nature of the Gods*: *The fourth Venus was conceived in Syria and Tyre, who is called Astarte, and she is said to have married Adonis*. Vossius <note>page 412</note> notes that the first defection of the Israelites from the true worship of the true God, as seen throughout the History of the Judges, was toward Baal and Ashtaroth. Thus, in *Judges 2:13*, they are said to have *forsaken the Lord and served Baal and Ashtaroth* after the death of Joshua and the Elders. In the following chapter, verse 7, it says: *they forgot the Lord their God and served the Baalim* <term>and the Asheroth</term> <note>Hebrew: והאשרות</note> and the groves. Hence, the Septuagint translated it: <term>"and they served Baal and the groves."</term> <note>original: καὶ ἐλάτρευον τῇ Βαὰλ καὶ τοῖς ἄλσεσι</note> Whether *Asheroth* or the "Groves" were the same as *Ashtaroth* is a point on which not everyone agrees. Selden demonstrates in his second volume that many goddesses were worshipped under the name of Astarte or Ashthoreth, so we may be brief on this matter. Certainly, Jupiter "of the groves" was named by the Rhodians, and Bacchus by the Boeotians, after their sacred groves. Likewise, Diana of the Woods and Diana of the Ardennes—like the goddess Albunea of old—were named after the groves where they were worshipped. The same was in use among the Romans; for them, hills and high places were sacred for altars and shrines, just like the groves. Cicero, intending to show that the death of Clodius was carried out by divine plan in a place famous for its religion, addresses the altars in an elegant apostrophe as if they were living beings, as can be seen in his oration *In Defense of Milo*.
<margin>Item number 8.</margin>
Adam of Bremen also mentions in his description of Scandinavia that *the grove (near the temple of Uppsala) is so sacred to the pagans that every single tree in it is believed to be divine due to the death or decay of those sacrificed there*. 

Regarding Baal or Baalim, of whom frequent mention is made in the Holy Scriptures, we spoke above at *1 Kings 18:25*. This name was common to many gods of both sexes. Just as Jupiter was called Ammonius, Capitolinus, or Cretensis according to the place, so among the Syrians, Baal-Peor, Baal-Berith, Baal-Zebub, Baal-Zephon, and Baal-Moloch denoted one and the same idol, which acquired various or distinct names based on the diversity of locations (see Selden, page 200). We shall discuss Bacchus at greater length at *1 Maccabees 6:7*. Bacchus is <term>many-named</term> <note>original: πολυώνυμῷ</note> according to the 29th Epigram of Ausonius:

> ->*Ogygia calls me Bacchus.*<-
> ->*Egypt thinks me Osiris.*<-
> ->*The Mysians name me Phanaces.*<-
> ->*The Indians believe me to be Dionysus.*<-
> ->*The Roman rites call me Liber.*<-
> ->*The Arab people call me Adoneus.*<-
> ->*The Lucaniacans call me the All-God.*<-

Furthermore, Georgius Hornius, in the second book of his *History of Philosophy*, derives the name Bacchus
<margin>Chapter 9, page 110.</margin>
from <term>bakah</term> <note>Hebrew: בכה</note>, which is the same as <term>to seek</term> or <term>to search out</term> <note>Greek: ζητέω or μαίωμαι</note>. Bacchus was so named from the study of searching out hidden things. To this is added the fact that they make Bacchus the grandson of Cadmus, who is known to have first brought philosophy into Greece. The idol of Babylon destroyed by Daniel
<margin>Daniel 14</margin>
bore the name *Belus*, <term>Belos</term> <note>original: Βῆλ@</note> to the Greeks and *Bel* <note>Hebrew: בל</note> to the Hebrews. 
<margin>Deuteronomy 34</margin>
Due to the diversity of rituals and locations, he acquired distinct surnames, such as the Babylonian, the Phegorian (who is mentioned in Scripture), the Phoenician (who was also called the Sea-God), and the Sidonian, in whose rites the priests used to bite their own limbs...

# THE ORIGIN AND PROGRESS OF IDOLATRY
<page-num>553</page-num>

<margin>
The origin and progress of idolatry.
</margin>
...priests, as seen in *1 Kings 18:28*. These are "dung-gods" <note>Latin: *stercoreos*, a derogatory term used by biblical writers to mock idols</note>; see Selden, *Syntagma 2, chapter 6*. All these names, however, denote the same "godling" <note>Latin: *deastrum*, a dismissive term for a pagan deity</note>, just as in reality Jupiter Olympius, Jupiter Latialis, and Jupiter Cretensis were the same, or as Apollo was called Clarius, Delphicus, or Selinuntius depending on the location. Regarding the Israelite idol mentioned under the name Chiun <note>Hebrew: כיון, often associated with the planet Saturn</note> in *Amos 5:26*, the late Glassius has collected various opinions on what it truly was in his *Sacred Grammar, book 4, treatise 3, page 868*; you may consult them there. As for the idol of the Philistines, which had a very famous shrine in Ashdod, the renowned city of Palestine, and where the Philistines placed the Ark of the Covenant after defeating the Israelites (*1 Samuel 5:4*), we have recently re-examined this in the passage cited above, to which we refer the reader. Mention is also made of the temple and cult of Diana—or perhaps Nanaea—in *2 Maccabees 1:13, 15*, who had various names. For she was called Latona, Lucina, Juno, Trivia, and Luna. When Catullus had reviewed these names in his *Epigram 35*, he added:

> <margin>p. 119.</margin> *Be you by whatever name pleases you, O Holy One.* <note>Original Latin: *Sis quocunque placet tibi, Sancta, nomine*</note>

Gad <note>Hebrew: גד, meaning "luck" or "fortune"</note> was a military idol, which some interpret as Mars, others as Jupiter, others as Fortune, and others as the host of heaven or "the numbers." We have stated our own opinion on this word in our notes on *Genesis 30:11*. We shall be more detailed concerning Hercules, Jupiter Olympius, and Jupiter Xenius <note>The "God of Hospitality"</note>, and their sacred rites, when we reach *2 Maccabees 4:19 and 6:2*. The idol of the Ammonites, a people of Coele-Syria, was *Moloch*, in whose honor and worship children were burned. This idol was assigned various names in the Sacred Scriptures: he is called *Malchom* in *Amos 5:26*; but to Moses in *Leviticus 18:21, 20:2, 3* and in *2 Kings 23:10* he is *Molech*; and *Milcom* in *1 Kings 11:5, 33* and *2 Kings 23:13*. Writers commonly attribute seven chambers to this idol based on Hebrew monuments, which we shall describe in the words of Paul Fagius <note>A 16th-century Hebraist</note>: *"Moloch was a hollow image having seven chambers. They opened one for an offering of fine flour; another for turtledoves; the third for a sheep; the fourth for a ram; the fifth for a calf; the sixth for an ox. But for him who wished to offer his own son, the seventh chamber was opened. The face of this idol was like the face of a calf. Its hands were spread out to receive from those standing by, and meanwhile they danced while the boy was burned in the idol by a fire kindled within, beating drums so that the boy's wailing would not be heard."* Fagius took this from the book *Yalkut*, whose author is Rabbi Shimeon. However, Vossius <note>Gerard Vossius, a prominent Dutch scholar</note> asserts in *On Idolatry, book 2, chapter 5, page 329*, that it cannot be firmly established from the Scriptures that the Ammonites sacrificed children to their Moloch. Yet, since in *2 Kings 23:10*, Tophet—which was in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom—is said to have been destroyed by Josiah so that no one might make his son or daughter pass through the fire to Moloch, we firmly conclude from this that this most savage kind of worship spread from the Ammonites to the Jews. Indeed, Tophet is named from the word *toph* <note>Hebrew: תף</note>, meaning a drum, because the neighborhood resounded with drums during the sacrifices so that the pitiable lamentations and heavy wailing of the children would not be heard by their parents. There are, however, some who maintain that children were not entirely burned to Moloch, but were initiated and consecrated through fire, moved by that phrase read in *2 Kings 23:10* and elsewhere: "to lead through" or "pass through the fire" <note>Hebrew: להעביר באש</note>. Compare Schindler in his *Lexicon, column 1009*; Junius, *Works, volume 1, column 1002*; Flacius, *Key to Scripture, column 1228*; and Selden, *On the Syrian Gods, Syntagma 1, chapter 6, page 167*. Hence it is called by Vossius in the place cited "februatio"—that is, a kind of purging or expiation—by which infants were either led or carried through the space between two huge fires by priests,

<column-break/>

or by the parents themselves <margin>The origin and progress of idolatry.</margin> following the priests' instructions. Nevertheless, Vossius correctly asserts in the same place that, in addition to this "februatio" <note>purification rite</note>, there was also the "vivicomburium" <note>burning alive</note> of these most dear pledges <note>i.e., children</note> in the rites of Molech, specifically based on *Psalm 106:36-37*: "And they sacrificed <note>or slaughtered, from the Hebrew *zavchu*</note> their sons and daughters to demons." Furthermore, the accounts of Saturnine sacrifices recorded by Ludovicus Vives in his *Commentary on Augustine's City of God, book 7, chapter 19*, can be linked to this idolatrous cult of burning children. For Saturn among the Latins (called Kronos by the Greeks) is generally considered to be the same as Molech. Infants or boys were the common victims for both, and those unspeakable rites migrated from Syria into Europe, just as they did into Africa. Pescennius Festus, as quoted in Lactantius <margin>Divine Institutes, book 1, chapter 21</margin>—who exploded false religion better than anyone, and who, according to Jerome, crushed the follies of the nations and the fictions of the gods—reports concerning the Carthaginian colonies of the Tyrians that: *"The Carthaginians were accustomed to immolate human victims to Saturn; and when they were defeated by Agathocles, King of the Sicilians, they believed the god was angry with them. Therefore, to pay the penance more diligently, they sacrificed two hundred sons of the nobility."* Those who lacked children of their own would buy them from the poor to slaughter them. Likewise, among these foul rites of the Carthaginians, there was a solemn use of flutes and drums so that the laments of the boys or parents would not be heard during the slaughter, a fact Plutarch testifies to in many places in his book *On Superstition*. Diodorus Siculus in his *Library, book 20*, Justin in his *History, book 18*, Cyril *Against Julian, book 4*, and Eusebius in *Preparation for the Gospel, book 4* (citing Sanchoniathon), all provide more information on this matter regarding the Carthaginians. Porphyry records almost the same regarding the Rhodians in the second book of *On Abstinence*, and from him, Theodoret in the seventh book of *Greek Affections* says: <margin>The origin and progress of idolatry.</margin> "For in Rhodes, on the sixth day of the month of Metageitnion <note>roughly August/September</note>, a man was sacrificed to Saturn. This practice, having prevailed for a long time, was changed into a custom: for they would keep one of those who had been publicly condemned to death until the Saturnalia." Those who desire more may consult Vossius, *On Idolatry, book 2, chapter 5, page 328*, and Selden, *Syntagma 1, chapter 6, page 167*. Furthermore, the Jews are accused of abandonment in "preparing a table for Gad" and "filling a drink offering for Meni" <margin>Isaiah 65:11</margin>. There are many different opinions regarding what is understood by *Meni* <note>Hebrew: מני</note>. The word *Meni*, which signifies "number," either denotes, according to some, the celestial forces, the host of heaven, or the vast multitude of stars which were held in the place of gods and were worshipped long ago and everywhere, according to the late Glassius in his *Sacred Rhetoric, treatise 2, chapter 2, page 526*. It is also taken as a common noun by Friedlibius, such that it is the name of a certain idol worshipped in Phrygia and Armenia, according to the testimony of Strabo and Iamblichus in his *Life of Pythagoras*. The same Friedlibius writes, following Jerome, that in all the cities of Egypt—and especially in Alexandria—it is the custom on the last day of the year and of their final month to set a table filled with various kinds of feasts and a full cup of mixed wine, as an omen for the fertility of either the past or the coming year. The Israelites did this same thing for all their idols...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of pagan deities mentioned in the Bible, moving from the general concept of "dung-gods" to specific historical figures and regional idols of the Egyptians, Babylonians, and Assyrians, often drawing on classical historians like Herodotus and Strabo to explain their origins.</meta>

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<page-num>554</page-num>

<margin>The origin and progress of idolatry.</margin>
...worshiping portents <note>Latin: *portenta colentes*. A reference to the bizarre animal-headed gods of Egypt.</note>. *So he says.* From this, a conjecture not to be disregarded might be made: that this custom in Egypt emanated from the first King of the Egyptians, who is called *Menis Thinites* by Manetho the Egyptian, and was said to have been snatched away by a hippopotamus; in Diodorus he is *Menas*; in Herodotus, however, he is *Men*, as in the *Euterpe* he writes: "that Men was the first to rule the Egyptians," and soon after, "to this Men, who became the first king." Josephus, however, in Book 8 of the *Antiquities*, chapter 6, calls him *Minaeus*, and Vossius conjectures in *On Idolatry*, book 1, chapter 17, page 197, that the sacred bull was his symbol, since according to Aelian in *On the Nature of Animals*, book 11, chapter 10, that bull is called *Mnevis*.

Regarding the *Miphlezeth* <note>Hebrew: מפלצת, a term for a "shudder" or "horrific thing."</note>, which some interpret generally as an *idol*, others as a *terrifying thing*, others as *Priapus* <note>A Greek god of fertility, often depicted with permanent arousal.</note>, and others as a "horrid statue" of Maacah, the mother of Asa—which King Asa removed, as the Scripture testifies—we have dealt with this above at the passage in *1 Kings 15:13*. Isaiah mentions a Babylonian idol in chapter 46 under the name *Nebo* or *Nabo*: *Bel has fallen, Nebo has collapsed*. In translating this, the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> substituted "Dagon was crushed," but Symmachus read it as *Nebo*, and Aquila and Theodotio called him *Nabo*. It is likely that the names of the Babylonians flowed from this idol: Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuzardan, Nabonetus, Nabonassar, and others; for it is so obvious that the names of Gods were bestowed upon Princes as a good omen that there is no need to list them further. The idol of the Cuthites, *Nergol* <note>Nergal</note>, mentioned in *2 Kings 17:30*, is in the opinion of the Rabbis a "wood-hen," a Jewish opinion which Selden rejects in *Syntagma 2, chapter 9*, and instead explains the name as "the fire" <note>Greek: τὸ πῦρ</note>, a fire most religiously preserved in perpetuity by the Cuthites.

<margin>book 15.</margin>
For Selden is entirely of the opinion that the Cuthites are from Persia—whom Strabo confirms were *neighbors of the Cuthi, a river of Persia*, and were named after this river—where they had a sacred fire. The idol of the Avites or Hivites, mentioned in *2 Kings 17:31* as *Nibchaz*, or the same as

<margin>Syntagma 2, ch. 9.</margin>
*Nabaam*, is given the form of a dog by Rabbi Kimchi and Jarchi. Selden mentions this where he judges *Nibchaz* and *Tarshac* to have been the same idol. There was a deity of the Assyrians called *Nisroch*, mentioned in *Isaiah 37:38* and *2 Kings 19:37*, in whose temple Sennacherib gave vent to his blasphemies against the true God of Israel. The Septuagint calls him *Mesorach* in the Book of Kings, but in Isaiah they call him *Nasrach*; nothing else is read about him in these places. The Syrian idol *Rimmon* from *2 Kings 5:18*—the word *rimmon* (רמון) in the sacred language signifies a "pomegranate"—is thought by Nicolaus Serarius to denote Venus, because fruits were dedicated to Venus, and her images were very often made with that fruit, as if she were named *Pomona* or "The Apple-One." Selden (*Syntagma 2, chapter 10*) thinks *Rimmon* is more likely derived from *rum* (רום), meaning "high" or "exalted," so that it is the same idol of which Hesychius says: "Ramas, the Most High God" <note>Greek: Ραμάς ὁ Ὕψιστος Θεός</note>. *Sesach* <note>Sheshach</note> seems to be the name of both a King and a city in *Jeremiah 25:26* and *51:41*. Jerome gives a hidden reason for this name: that *Sesach* becomes *Babel* through that permutation of letters which they call <term>Atbash</term> <note>A substitution cipher where the first letter of the alphabet is replaced by the last, the second by the second-to-last, and so on.</note>, where the last letter of the alphabet is put for the first, the second-to-last for the second, and so on. Thus, for B and L (the 2nd and 12th letters from the start), the letters S and C are placed (the 2nd and 12th from the end), as Emanuel Sa notes from Jerome on this passage. Others, however, think the initial letter here is doubled and the name is taken from the Goddess *Saca*, whom the Babylonians worshiped, from which *Sesach* would be,

<column-break/>

as Junius writes, "celebrating a feast day" in the Babylonian language. Strabo mentions the "Days of the Saceans" <note>Greek: ἡμέρας Σακέων</note> in Book 11 of his *Geography*, as do Valerius Maximus (Book 2, chapter 6) and Athenaeus in the *Deipnosophists* (Book 14), where he cites Ctesias and Berosus, whose records do not survive today. The words of Athenaeus are as follows: "Berosus, in the first book of the *Babyloniaca*, says that on the nineteenth day of the month of Loi, a festival called the Sacea is held in Babylon for five days. In these, it is the custom for masters to be ruled by the commands of their servants; one of them presides over the household, dressed in a robe similar to the royal one, who is also called a <term>Zoganes</term> <note>A temporary "king" or leader of the revels during the festival.</note>. Ctesias also mentions the festival in the second book of the *Persica*."

<margin>Is. 21:5</margin>
The late Glassius thinks this festival is also mentioned in *Isaiah 21:5* and *Jeremiah 51:39, 57*. He says that "the Prophet intended to note mystically by the word *shethu* <note>Hebrew: שתו, meaning 'drink ye' or 'they drank'</note> the time of the capture of Babylon, namely when the festival of Sacea was to be celebrated." But does this have anything in common with the banquet of Belshazzar mentioned in *Daniel 5*? On this, see the late Johann Behm in his *Manuscript Chronology, page 230*, where he takes the negative view. Compare John Selden, *Syntagma 1, On the Syrian Gods, chapter 13*, where you will find the cult of the Goddess Sacea described more at length. The name *Succuth* <note>Hebrew: את סכות</note>, mentioned in *Amos 5:26*, is considered by the late Luther in his marginal notes, by Chemnitz in the *Examination of the Council of Trent* (part 4, page 678), and by Schindler, Arias Montanus, Vatablus, and others, to be the name of an idol, with the reason for the name derived from "protection," "covering," or "defense." On the other hand, others follow the Septuagint, who explained it as a "tabernacle" or "tent" <note>Greek: σκηνὴν</note>,

<margin>Acts 7:43</margin>
especially since Luke follows their interpretation. Hence Selden understands this as a *litter* <note>Latin: *lecticam*, a portable carriage for an idol.</note> in which they carried the image of the Deity. Such litters or chariots upon which the statues of the Gods were placed were called *thensae*; they were covered all around with linens stretched in the likeness of a chamber or shrine, and Panvinius (*On Circensian Games, book 2, page 87*) thinks they were called *tensas* from this stretching. On this matter, compare Servius in his notes on Virgil's *Aeneid 6*, Eustathius on *Iliad 1*, Herodian (book 5), Macrobius's *Saturnalia* (6.23), and Strabo (book 4). Into the cities of the Samaritans, whom he had led away elsewhere, the king had ordered colonies to migrate from Babylon, Cuth, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim (*2 Kings 17*). From these, the Babylonians made for themselves *Succoth Benoth*. What this was, interpreters have "passed over with a dry foot" <note>A metaphor meaning they ignored it or treated it superficially.</note> as something of obscure origin, as Johann Frischmuth rightly complains in his *Disputation on the Queen of Heaven, section 2*. Nor do those who have mentioned it agree with one another. Luther, the Vulgate, Vatablus, Pagninus, Arias Montanus, Münster, Junius, Tremellius, and others take *Succoth Benoth* to be an idol proper to the Babylonians, with whom the Hebrew commentators agree. What kind of idol it was, however, is not yet agreed among them. The Rabbis commonly trifle with the idea of it being a "hen"; but the word "sculpted image" <note>Hebrew: סכות, referencing a carved idol</note> in the last verse of this chapter implies it was some kind of statue, where *Succoth* is also expressly placed...

<header>Wisdom 13:1, 2, 3. 555</header>

<margin>The origin and progress of idolatry.</margin>Benoth is called <gloss>Succoth</gloss> <note>Hebrew: סכות</note>, a carved image, from the root <gloss>Sakki</gloss> <note>Hebrew: סכה</note>, which according to Rabbi Nathan in the *Hebrew Concordance* is sometimes taken to mean <gloss>the language of branching off</gloss> <note>Hebrew: לשון פסק אדי שינות; a technical grammatical reference to the derivation of the word</note>. Furthermore, there are those who interpret that *Succoth Benoth* <note>Literally "Booths of the Daughters"</note> as an idolatrous shrine consecrated to the Assyrian Venus—who was indeed received by the Babylonians with divine honor and worship, as is evident from Herodotus in *Book 1, p. 330* and Strabo in *Geography, Book 16, p. 493*. Among the ancients cited for this opinion is Eucherius of Lyons, a Bishop in Gaul, in his *Commentary on 4 Kings 26* <note>Modern 2 Kings 17:30</note>; and among more recent scholars, Hugo Grotius on this passage, Vossius in *On Idolatry, Book 2, ch. 22, p. 413*, and Selden in *Syntagma 2, ch. 7, p. 308*, who establishes his opinion using many authorities from the ancients. As for our own view on *Succoth Benoth*, it will be clear from the following brief remarks. If we look at the text accurately, it suggests that the Samaritans made gods for themselves and placed them in the "houses of the high places," to which *Succoth Benoth* is immediately joined without any other word intervening, being placed in that same house. This is inferred by the <term>textual connection</term> <note>Greek: συνάφεια (synapheia); the way the words fit together in the sentence</note> itself. Now, if you take *Succoth Benoth* to be a "shrine" according to the latter opinion, the conclusion seems far too forced—that a shrine was placed inside a house of the high places. But if you understand it as the idol itself, it is clear how it could be brought into a sanctuary, and thus the meaning of the words <insert><gloss>in the house of the high places</gloss> <note>Hebrew: בבית הבמות</note></insert> will be plain. This is the same point urged by Athanasius Kircher in *Egyptian Oedipus, Vol. 1, Syntagma 4*, who indeed contends in that place that it was an image of a hen, and specifically a celestial one nesting in the sign of Taurus. We cannot agree with him on this matter, since the text does not reveal what kind of idol it was, nor by what rites it was worshiped; nor is there a need to inquire sharply into those things buried in deep oblivion, as their investigation would be more laborious than fruitful. Finally, near the end, we see the final letter of the abominations of the nations, <gloss>Tav</gloss> <note>Hebrew: ת</note>, by which is expressed in sacred writings (among other things) that shameful idol of the Israelite people, *Thammutz* <note>Tammuz</note>, whom some interpret as Bacchus and others as Adonis. We shall say what we think of him at the passage in *Ezekiel 8:14*. There remain the <gloss>Teraphim</gloss> <note>Hebrew: תרפים</note>, a word most intricate in both its etymology and its meaning. It is found eight times in the Holy Books: *Genesis 31:19; Judges 17:5 and 18:14; 1 Samuel 15:23; 2 Samuel 19:13; 2 Kings 23:24; Ezekiel 21:21; Hosea 3:4; and Zechariah 10:2*. Concerning the name, there are those, as Martin Luther mentions in his *Commentary on Genesis 31:19*, who derive it from <gloss>to heal or cure</gloss> <note>Hebrew: רפא (rapha)</note>, as if you were to say: "healing saviors," that is, Gods. Such Teraphim were "Good Spirits" [Genii] among the Gentiles. Thus the "Good Spirit" of Socrates is said to have been his Savior and helper. Such also was the one who, according to Dio Cassius, snatched Trajan from the immediate danger threatening him during the earthquake at Antioch and led him outside. Henry Salmuth, in his notes on *Pancirolli, Book 2, Title 1*, has an image of this kind which can be seen at Rome, regarding which are the following verses:

<margin>ch. 18.</margin>
> Who are you, joyful boy? A Spirit: Why does the right hand hold corn,
> The left grapes, and why does the crown have a poppy?
> These are three gifts of the Gods: Ceres, Bacchus, and Sleep,
> For by these and by the Spirit, you mortals live.

Others derive the word from <gloss>to cease, to fail, or to be slack</gloss> <note>Hebrew: רפה (raphah)</note>, among whom is Rabbi Judah in the *Zohar* (the Kabbalistic commentary on the five books of Moses), to

<column-break/>

whose opinion Martin Luther seems to move toward in his *Commentary on this passage*. But omitting the derivations of others, the opinion of Rabbi Jose seems more probable to us, who thinks that <gloss>Teraphim</gloss> descends from <gloss>disgrace or foulness</gloss> <note>Hebrew: חרפה (cherpah)</note>, even if this reasoning seemed less favorable to Laban and other worshipers of Teraphim, who would try to cast them off as if they were a <term>demon that wards off evil and drives away misfortune</term> <note>Greek: δαίμων ἀλεξίκακος καὶ ἀποπομπαῖος (daimōn alexikakos kai apopompaios)</note>. Nor is the meaning of <gloss>Teraphim</gloss> any easier than its etymology. Regarding the Mosaic passage, it is not so difficult to guess, since Laban himself says later in *verse 30*: <gloss>Why have you stolen my gods?</gloss> <note>Hebrew: למה גנבת את-אלהי</note>. From this it appears they were idols or images with which and through which Laban was accustomed to worship God with his family, which Rachel knew how to venerate, so that she diligently used them as gods.

-> O, truly, Divinities worthy of such a place! <-

In what form the Teraphim were, however, has not yet been sufficiently established. For if you examine more deeply what the Jews write about Teraphim, it will appear that they do nothing but run wild with conjectures hardly worth mentioning. It is characteristic of them to pile up trifles in their own affairs; what wonder, then, if they have little wisdom in matters savoring of paganism. We are pleased with what Vorstius writes: *Various descriptions of Teraphim are circulated among the Hebrews, but all are worked out with little or no probability. Rabbi David Kimchi thinks they were images made by astrologers, such as clocks or <unclear>sympathetic instruments</unclear> <note>Greek: συιάτθεια (a likely misspelling of 'sympatheia')</note>, and that they predicted the future. Others suggest they were bronze instruments serving the distinction of times and hours. Aben Ezra observes they were images adorned with human faces, suitable for receiving the influence of celestial bodies; but he admits he cannot explain what kind they were. Whatever the case, it is manifest that the use of Teraphim flourished among idolaters, and that they gave responses to those who consulted them.* What Rabbi Eliezer relates about the horrendous construction of the Teraphim—and after him Tanchuma, the Targum of Jonathan, Elias Levita, and others—contains nothing certain, but is drawn from a cesspool of traditions. We do not wish to add more regarding the idolatry of the Israelites, lest we cross the lines of ancient modesty, while that antiquity preferred to be hidden rather than spread abroad. Truly, how much care God took that Israel should not worship idols is plain from this: He forbade the creation of Angels to be described by Moses, lest an occasion be given to the idolaters for worshiping Angels. In the Temple, He did not want figures of the Sun and Moon; nevertheless, they worshiped the Sun, Moon, Stars, calves, and the most vile animals just like other nations. Of these, the Greeks (judging by Dionysius of Halicarnassus) were the most insane of all in the worship of the Gods, because they both believed and taught all manner of shameful fables about their Gods. The Romans were hardly better; while they contracted the whole world into one city, they made Rome the epitome of all idol-manias and granted citizenship to the Gods of all conquered nations—excepting Judea, and with the Christ of the Christians being rejected. Nevertheless, the worship of Christ is propagated daily under every sky, to the great decrease of ethnic superstition, so that we may say in the words of Blessed Hunnius: *The miraculous propagation itself of the Gospel doctrine is the most illustrious argument that it was not invented by human means, but clearly by divine power* in the world...

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The origin and progress of idolatry.</margin>
...worshipping monsters. Thus he says. From this, a conjecture not to be despised might be made: that this custom in Egypt emanated from the first King of the Egyptians, who is called *Menes of Thinis* <note>original: "Menis Thinites"</note> by Manetho the Egyptian, and was snatched away by a hippopotamus; in Diodorus he is *Menas*; but in Herodotus he is *Men*, as in the book *Euterpe*, where he says *Men was the first to rule the Egyptians* <note>original: "τὸν Μῆνα πρῶτον βαſιλεύſαντα Αἰγυπτίων"</note>, and soon after, *to this Men, the first king.* In Josephus, however, in *Antiquities Book 8, chapter 6*, he is *Minaeus*, whose symbol Vossius conjectures <note>*On Idolatry, Book 1, ch. 17, p. 197*</note> was the sacred bull, especially since that bull is called *Menis* by Aelian <note>*History of Animals, Book 11, ch. 10*</note>.

Regarding the **Miphlezeth** <note>Hebrew: מפלצת</note>, which some interpret generally as an *idol*, others as a *thing of terror*, others as *Priapus* <note>A Roman god of fertility, often represented by a phallus</note>, and others as the *horrendous statue* of Maacah, the mother of Asa—which the Scripture testifies King Asa removed—we have dealt with this above at the passage in *1 Kings 14:13*. Isaiah mentions a Babylonian idol in chapter 46 under the name *Nebo* or *Nabo*: *Bel has fallen, Nebo has collapsed*. In translating this, the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> substituted *Dagon shall be crushed* <note>original: "συντρίψειν Δαγών"</note>, but Symmachus read it as *Nebo*, and Aquila and Theodotion called him *Nabo*. It is likely that names among the Babylonians flowed from this idol, such as Nebuchadnezzar, Nabuzardan, Nabonetus, Nabonassar, and others; for it is so obvious that names of gods were imposed on princes for good omen that there is no need to list them. The idol of the Cuthites was *Nergal*, mentioned in *2 Kings 17:30*. According to the mind of the Rabbis, this is a "Wild Hen," a Jewish opinion which Selden rejects <note>*Syntagma 2, ch. 9*</note>; instead, he explains the term as "the fire" <note>original: "τὸ πῦρ"</note>, the fire most religiously preserved forever by the Cuthites. For Selden is entirely of the opinion that the Cuthites were from Persia—where Strabo <note>in <margin>Book 15</margin></note> confirms a sacred fire existed—and that they were named after the river Cuth in Persia, near which they lived. The idol of the Avites or Hivites, mentioned in *2 Kings 17:31*, was *Nibchaz*, also called *Nabaam*. Rabbi Kimchi and Rabbi Zarchi attribute to it the figure of a dog. Selden mentions it <note>in <margin>Syntagma 2, ch. 9</margin></note>, where he considers *Nibchaz* and *Tarthac* to be the same idol. There was a deity of the Assyrians called *Nisroch*, mentioned in *Isaiah 37:38* and *2 Kings 19:37*, in whose temple Sennacherib offered his blasphemies against the true God of Israel. The Septuagint calls him *Mesorach* in the book of Kings, but in Isaiah they call him *Auphach*, nor is anything else read about him in these places. The Syrian idol *Rimmon*, from *2 Kings 5:18*, means "pomegranate" <note>Hebrew: **רמון**</note> in the sacred language. Nicolaus Serarius thinks Venus is denoted here, because apples were dedicated to Venus and her images are very often consecrated with that fruit, as if she were named "Pomona" or "The Apple One." Selden <note>*Book 2, ch. 10*</note> thinks *Rimmon* is more likely derived from the word for "exalted" <note>Hebrew: **רום**, *rum*</note>, so that it is the same idol of which Hesychius says: *Ramas is the highest God* <note>original: "Ῥαμάς ὁ ὕψιστος Θεός"</note>. *Seshach* seems to be the name of both a King and a city in *Jeremiah 25:26 and 51:41*. Jerome gives a hidden reason for this name: that **Seshach** <note>Hebrew: ששך</note> becomes **Babel** <note>Hebrew: בבל</note> through that permutation of letters which they call **Atbash** <note>A substitution cipher where the first letter of the alphabet is replaced by the last, the second by the second-to-last, etc.</note>, where the last letter of the alphabet is placed for the first, the second-to-last for the second, and so on, and vice versa. Thus, for B and L (the 2nd and 12th letters from the start), the letters S and Ch <note>Shin and Kaph</note> are placed, which are the 2nd and 12th from the end, as Emanuel Sa notes from Jerome on this passage. Others, however, think the initial letter is doubled here, and the name is taken from the goddess Saca, whom the Babylonians worshipped, from which *Shesh* would be,

<column-break/>

as Junius writes, "celebrating a festival day" in the Babylonian language. Strabo mentions "the days of the Sacae" <note>original: "ἡμέρας Σακέων"</note> in *Geography, Book 11*, as do Valerius Maximus, Athenaeus, and the *Deipnosophists, Book 14*, where he cites Ctesias and Berosus, whose records do not survive today. The words of Athenaeus are as follows: *Berosus, in the first book of Babylonian History, says that on the 16th day of the month of Loi, a festival called Sacaea is celebrated in Babylon for five days. During these days, it is custom for the masters to be ruled by the commands of their servants, and for one of the servants to lead the house, dressed in a robe similar to the royal one, and he is called "Zoganes." Ctesias also mentions the festival in the second book of Persian History.* B. Glassius <note>in <margin>Book 4, Grammatical Error 3, 1</margin></note> believes this festival is also mentioned in *Isaiah 21:5 and Jeremiah 51:39, 57*. He says, *Therefore, by the word Seshach, the Prophet wanted to mystically note the time when Babylon would be captured—specifically, when the festival of Sacaea was being celebrated.* Now, does this have anything in common with the *Banquet of Belshazzar* mentioned in *Daniel 5*? On this, see B. Johann Behm in his *Chronology Manuscript, p. 230*, where he argues the negative. Compare John Selden, *Syntagma 1 on the Syrian Gods, ch. 13*, where you will find the worship of the goddess Sacea described at greater length. The name **Succoth Benoth** <note>Hebrew: סכות בנות</note>, mentioned in *Amos 5:26* <note>The author likely means 2 Kings 17:30</note>, is considered by B. Luther in his marginal notes, B. Chemnitz in *Examination of the Council of Trent, part 4, on Images, p. 678*, Schindler, Arias Montanus, Vatablus, and others, to be the name of an idol, with the reason for the name derived from protection, covering, or fortification. On the other hand, others follow the Septuagint, who translated it as "tabernacle" <note>original: "σκηνην", skene</note>, especially since Luke <note>in <margin>\* Acts 7</margin></note> follows their interpretation. From this, Selden understands it to be a *Litter* <note>A portable carriage</note> in which they carried the image of the deity. Such litters or chariots, upon which the statues of the gods were placed, were called *Thensae*; they were covered all around with linens stretched out like a chamber or shrine, from which Panvinius <note>*Book 2 on Circensian Games, p. 87*</note> thinks they were called *Tensae* <note>meaning "stretched"</note>. Compare on this matter Servius in his *notes on Virgil’s Aeneid 6*, Eustathius on *Iliad 1*, Herodian *Book 5*, Macrobius *Saturnalia Book 6, 23*, and Strabo *Book 4*. Into the cities of the Samaritans, whom he had led away elsewhere, the king had ordered colonies to migrate from Babylon, Cuth, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim (*2 Kings 17*). From these, the Babylonians made for themselves *Succoth Benoth*. As Johann Frischmuth <note>*Disputation on the Queen of Heaven, section 2*</note> not unfairly complains, interpreters pass over what this was with a "dry foot" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to skim over a difficult subject without depth</note>, as if it were of obscure origin. Nor do those who mention it agree among themselves. B. Luther, the Vulgate, Vatablus, Pagninus, Arias Montanus, Münster, Junius, Tremellius, and others accept *Succoth Benoth* as an idol proper to the Babylonians, with whom the Hebrew commentators agree. However, it is not yet established among them what kind of idol it was. The Rabbis commonly babble that it was a hen; but the word **pesel** <note>Hebrew: פסל</note>, meaning *carved image*, which is placed in the last verse of this chapter, hints that it was some kind of statue, where the name *Succoth* is also expressly...

### Wisdom of Solomon XIII. 1. 2. 3.

<margin>
The origin and progress of idolatry.
</margin>

**Succoth Benoth** <note>Hebrew: סכות בנות</note> is the name given to a carved image, from the root *sakath* <note>Hebrew: סכת</note> which, according to Rabbi Nathan in his Hebrew Concordance, is sometimes taken to mean a "carved image" <note>original: "לשון פסל"</note>. That is to say: *there are, moreover*, those who interpret "Succoth Benoth" as an idolatrous shrine consecrated to the **Assyrian Venus** <note>Also known as Mylitta</note>, who was received with divine honor and worship by the Babylonians. This is evident from Herodotus <note>*Book 1, p. 330*</note> and Strabo <note>*Geography, Book 16, p. 493*</note>. Among the ancient writers, Eucherius of Lyon, a Bishop in Gaul, is cited for this opinion <note>*Commentary on 4 Kings 26*</note>; among more recent scholars are Hugo Grotius, Vossius <note>*On Idolatry, Book 2, ch. 22, p. 413*</note>, and Selden <note>*2nd Syntagma, ch. 7, p. 308*</note>, who established his opinion using many ancient sources.

What we ourselves think of Succoth Benoth will be clear in a few words from what follows. The text, if we look at it accurately, implies that the Samaritans made gods for themselves and placed them in the **houses of the high places** <note>Unauthorized shrines built on hills</note>, to which "Succoth Benoth" is immediately subjoined without any other intervention, being placed within the house of the high places; for the context <note>original: "συνάφεια"</note> of the text itself suggests this. Now, if you take Succoth Benoth to mean a "shrine" according to the latter opinion, the conclusion seems too harsh—that a shrine was placed inside the "house of the high places." But if you understand it as the **idol itself**, it is clear how it could have been brought into a sanctuary. Thus, the meaning of the words "they made Succoth Benoth" <note>Hebrew: ויעשו סכות בנות</note> will be plain. This is also urged by Athanasius Kircher <note>*Egyptian Oedipus, Vol. 1, Syntagma 4*</note>, who indeed contends in that place that it was an image of a **hen**, nesting in the celestial sign of Taurus <note>Referring to the Pleiades, often called the "Hen and Chicks"</note>. We cannot agree with him on this point, since the text does not reveal what kind of idol it was, nor with what rites it was worshipped. There is no need to inquire so sharply into things buried in deep oblivion, as such an investigation would be more laborious than fruitful.

Finally, toward the end, we see the final letter of the pagan abominations, **Tav** (ת), by which is expressed in the sacred writings, among other things, that foul idol of the Israelite people, **Tammuz**, which some interpret as Bacchus and others as Adonis. What we think of him, we shall say at the passage in Ezekiel 8:14. There remain the **Teraphim** <note>Hebrew: תרפים</note>, a word most intricate both in its etymology and its meaning. It is found eight times in the Sacred Books <note>Genesis 31:19, Judges 17:5, 18:14, 1 Samuel 15:23, 2 Samuel 19:13, 2 Kings 23:24, Ezekiel 21:21, Hosea 3:4, Zechariah 10:2</note>. As concerns the naming, there are those, as the Blessed Luther mentions <note>*Commentary on Genesis 31:19*</note>, who derive it from *rapha* <note>Hebrew: רפא</note>, meaning "to heal" or "to cure," as if you were to say: **health-giving saviors**, that is, Gods. Such Teraphim were like the **Good Genii** <note>Guardian spirits</note> among the Gentiles. Thus, the "Good Genius" of Socrates is said to have been his savior and helper. Such also was the one who, according to Dio Cassius, snatched Trajan from the present danger threatening him during the earthquake at Antioch and led him out. Henry Salmuth <note>*On Pancirolli, Book 2, Title 1*</note> has an image of this kind which can be seen at Rome, regarding which are the following verses:

->Who are you, happy boy? A Genius. Why does your right hand hold grain,<-
->Your left grapes, and your head a curved poppy?<-
->These three are gifts of the Gods: Ceres, Bacchus, and Sleep,<-
->For by these you mortals live, and by your genius.<-

Others derive the word from *raphah* <note>Hebrew: רפה</note>, meaning **he ceased, he failed, or he was slack**, among whom is Rabbi Jehuda in the *Zohar* (the Cabbalistic commentary on the five books of Moses), to 

<column-break/>

<margin>
The origin and progress of idolatry.
</margin>

whose opinion the Blessed Luther seems to lean <note>*Commentary on this place*</note>. But to omit the derivations of others, the opinion of Rabbi Jose seems more probable to us, who thinks *Teraphim* descends from *turpah* <note>Hebrew: תורפה</note>, meaning **ignominy or foulness**, even if this reason would seem less acceptable to Laban and other worshippers of Teraphim, who would treat them as **a demon that wards off and turns away evil** <note>original: "δαίμων ἀλεξίκακος καὶ ἀποπομπαῖον"</note>. 

Nor is the meaning of the Teraphim any easier than the etymology. Regarding the passage in Moses, it is not so difficult to guess, since Laban himself says later <note>verse 30</note>: *Why have you stolen my gods?* <note>original: "למה גנבת את־אלהי"</note> From this it appears they were idols or images which Laban used to worship as God, and which Rachel knew how to "venerate" so much that she used them as a seat <note>Rachel hid the idols in a saddle and sat on them to hide them from her father</note>, 
->*O divinities truly worthy of such a place!*<-

What form the Teraphim took has not been sufficiently established. For if you examine more deeply what the Jews write about the Teraphim, it will appear they are merely indulging in conjectures, scarcely worth mentioning. It is characteristic of them to pile up trifles in their own matters; what wonder then if they have little wisdom in matters savoring of paganism. 

<margin>
Observations on Eliezer, Pirke p. 219.
</margin>

Vorstius writes: *Various descriptions of Teraphim are circulated among the Hebrews, but all are produced with little or no probability. Rabbi David Kimchi thinks they were images made by astrologers, like clocks or **shadow-trackers** <note>original: "σκιαθήρια"</note>, and that they predicted the future. Others please themselves with the idea that they were bronze instruments serving the distinction of times and hours. Aben-Ezra observes that they were images adorned with a human face, fit for receiving the influence of celestial bodies; but you recognize that he cannot explain what kind they were. Whatever the case, it is manifest that the use of Teraphim flourished among idolaters and gave responses to those who consulted them.* 

The things Rabbi Eliezer delivers regarding the horrendous construction of the Teraphim—as well as those in Tanchuma, the Targum of Jonathan, Elias Levita, and others—contain nothing certain, but are drawn from a heap of traditions. We do not wish to add more regarding the idolatry of the Israelites, lest we cross the lines of ancient modesty, since that antiquity preferred to be hidden rather than spread abroad.

However, how much care God took so that Israel would not worship idols is plain from this: He forbade the creation of the Angels to be described by Moses, lest an occasion be given to them for the idolatry of worshipping Angels. In the Temple, He did not want figures of the Sun and Moon; nevertheless, they worshipped the Sun, Moon, Stars, calves, and the vilest animals like other nations. Among these, the Greeks, in the judgment of Dionysius of Halicarnassus, were the most insane of all in the worship of the Gods, because they both believed and taught all the foulness of fables about their Gods. The Romans were scarcely better: while they contracted the whole world into one city, they made Rome the epitome of all "idol-manias," and granted citizenship to the Gods of all conquered nations—excepting Judea, and having rejected the Christ of the Christians. Yet the worship of Christ is propagated daily under every sky with great decrease to ethnic superstition, as we may say in the words of the Blessed Hunnius:

<margin>
Hunn. Marp. Disp. 1. th. 77. seq. p. 13.
</margin>

> *The marvelous propagation of the Gospel doctrine itself is a most illustrious argument that it was not invented by humans, but by clearly divine power...*

BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES.

<margin>The origin and progress of idolatry.</margin>
...was introduced into the world; for all the monuments of pagan antiquity testify that before the birth of Christ, all nations were idolaters, serving those who by nature are not Gods, and desiring nothing else but their Jupiter, Mars, Apollo, Minerva, Neptune, Mercury, and other false Divinities, which occur everywhere in the writings of the pagans. This superstition, over the duration of many centuries, had driven such roots into the world that they thought the contempt of their idolatrous religion should be avenged by military force; hence the proverb was born: *For altars and hearths* <note>original: "Pro aris & focis"</note>. He would be extremely impious who did not shudder at these things, who did not recognize the power of Satan in the "sons of Darkness," and who did not give eternal thanks with his whole heart to God, because He has translated us into the Kingdom of the son of His love by the unexpected ministry of the Apostles of our Lord.

### Isaiah 1:18

-> "If your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; if they be red <-
-> like crimson, they shall be as wool." <-
<note>original Hebrew: אם-יהיו חטאיכם כשנים כשלג ילבינו אם-יאדימו כתולע כצמר יהיו</note>

-> "And if your sins be as purple, I will make them white as snow; and if they be <-
-> as crimson, I will make them white as wool." <-
<note>original Greek Septuagint: Καὶ ἐὰν ὦσιν αἱ ἁμαρτίαι ὑμῶν ὡς φοινικιῶν, ὡς χιόνα λευκανῶ, ἐὰν δὲ ὦσιν ὡς κόκκινον, ὡς ἔριον λευκανῶ.</note>

-> *If your sins be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and though they* <-
-> *be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.* <-
<note>original Latin: Si fuerint peccata vestra, sicut coccinum, ut nix dealbabuntur, & rubra, sicut vermiculus, veluti lana erunt.</note>

<margin>Scarlet and Crimson.</margin>
No one who reads the Sacred Tables of the Old and New Testament will doubt that emphatic expressions are frequently adopted to signify the atrocity of sin and sinners; so that by the very frequency of these names, we might be reminded of our own infirmity and misery. Indeed, here the Prophet Isaiah has excellently compared the atrocity and guilt of the sins of the Jewish people with the juice or blood-red color of *scarlet and crimson* <term>vermiculus: literally 'little worm', referring to the kermes insect used to make red dye</term>, and their washing with snow and wool. The Hebrews are accustomed to use snow, ivory, fine linen, wool, milk, and silver more frequently to indicate a white color. A white color is an indication of purity of soul; black is for those mourning; scarlet for those sinning or wounded. Moreover, the Prophet could not have compared Sin better than with the color of scarlet; nothing on earth is more sharp, especially when "twice-dyed," which they call *dibaphum* <note>from Greek 'dibaphos', meaning twice-dipped</note>. It is understood emphatically in this place, for it is placed in conjunction with the word *shani* <note>Hebrew: שני</note>, "twice-dyed scarlet," as in Exodus 25:4, 39:3, and Leviticus 14:4. The scholar Vatablus rendered it "crimson of the worm" and "the worm of crimson," and handed down at that passage that in Scripture such conjunctions mean the same thing. *Shani* comes from *shanah*, which signifies "to iterate" or "to repeat." Horace mentions this "twice-dyed" fabric:

<margin>Epodes, Ode 12, verse 21, Book 1, p. 27.</margin>
> Fleeces of wool twice-steeped in Tyrian murex.
<note>The murex is the sea snail from which ancient purple dye was extracted.</note>

<margin>Note that the name *shani*, that is, scarlet, is according to the Hebrews from the root *shan* which signifies a tooth or ivory. But because a tooth or ivory are not red in color, I would think it rather to be from the root *shanah*, which is to double, and signifies here an intense red, which our people call crimson. *Shanah* therefore sounds like double-dyed or geminated; for purple was dyed once and then again, so that it might be more splendid and clear. Therefore, the description of the transgression of the house of Israel, as well as hu-</margin>

<column-break/>

-man misery, will take light from the description of scarlet and crimson, and the explanation of its metaphor, which will emerge as follows: *Even if your sins were so great and atrocious that they seemed impossible to be deleted by any means—just as a cloth dyed in a scarlet color, to which the blood of the worm born from the kermes berry is applied, cannot be washed out by any means to recover its original color—nevertheless, if you perform penance, I will so delete your sins by the blood of the Messiah, and wash away the filth through the bath of regeneration, that you shall appear whiter than wool.* This comparison of sin with scarlet is most elegant, and can be illustrated by a grammatical narration of scarlet. The words transferred from "Scarlet" carry a particular emphasis. The woman sitting upon the scarlet beast in Revelation 17:5 <note>original: μυστηριωδῶς, 'mysteriously'</note> hints at Babylon the Great, the mother of fornications and abominations of the earth; for that scarlet color intends the significance of tyranny and bloodthirsty monstrosity. From the same phrasing, the ingenious poet Virgil paints the bloody wars of Messala in the *Ciris*:

> Great robes are adorned with giant trophies,
> Horrid battles are painted with blood-red scarlet.

Homer used a similar formula concerning the death of the priest Hypsenor, which he elegantly calls "purple death" in the *Iliad* (Book 1, v. 83): "Purple death and strong fate seized him." Because his corpse, with a wounded shoulder and the other hand cut off, was red with blood. So Virgil in *Aeneid* Book 9, v. 349, spoke of a "purple soul" <note>meaning the lifeblood</note>; and Ovid in *Metamorphoses* Book 2, v. 11, spoke of "Punic gore" regarding the spilled blood of Coronis struck by an arrow: "she soaked her white limbs with Punic gore." In this passage of Isaiah, the atrocity of sins is exaggerated by the scarlet color and the so-called "worm" for greater detestation; and their free remission is commended by the color of wool, as by the Psalmist by snow (Psalm 51) for the greater encouragement of sinners. Scarlet designates the fiery sins of lust, the sins of homicide (of which the hands of the Jews were full), the sin of tyrannical cruelty, and the like, according to the witness of Rupert <note>Rupert of Deutz, a medieval theologian</note>. Wool signifies the white cleanliness of the soul, which is obtained from the fleeces of the lamb Jesus Christ, per Jerome and Augustine. Scarlet has an exuberance of red color as wool has of white. Excellent descriptions of the kermes and the "worm"—from whose blood-red juice the dyed wool takes on a shining red color—exist in Pausanias in his *Description of Greece*, Dioscorides (Book 4), Pliny (Book 24), and others. Both the berry itself and the worm itself, when present, are suitable for red tincture; if they are added to the color of purple, it renders it more pleasant to the sight and sharpens it remarkably, as Pliny shows in Book 21. The same author in Book 10 mentions two kinds of shellfish containing the flower for dyeing clothes: one named "purple" and the other "buccinum." To excite the color of the red murex more illustriously, wools prepared with scarlet were imbued with Tyrian red, from which mixture existed *hysginum*, that burning kind of reddish purple of which Pliny speaks. Pausanias makes the plants *kokkon* and *hysge* the same, from which it would follow that the scarlet and hysginum colors do not differ. But Salmasius refutes this. The Greeks call *kokkos* (the berry or grain) that which dyers use...

Selection 18.

<margin>Scarlet & Crimson</margin>
...is called. **Coccus**, or the grain of the **Coccus**, that is, of the shrub which in Greek is called *ho kokkos* <note>original: ὁ κόκκος</note>, so that *kokke* <note>original: κόκκ$\eta$</note> is used for both the reddish grain and the shrub itself. It pleased Minsheu in his *Guide into Tongues* to derive **Coccus**, on account of its power in dyeing, from the Hebrew word *koach* <note>original: כוח</note>, which denotes *strength and power* among the Hebrews. Dealing with the difference between **Scarlet** and **Purple**, Brodaeus, in his *Miscellanies*, book 8, shows that these are not only confused with each other, but not infrequently also with the red color of purple or the murex snail, and likewise with *ostrum* <note>a term for blood-red or purple dye</note>, concerning which Gellius writes in book 2, chapter 26, and indeed with any red that is exceptionally beautiful and brilliant. Because of this mutual sharing of colors and various mixtures, I believe that in the sacred texts, what Saint Matthew calls a "scarlet cloak" <note>original Greek: $\chi\lambda\alpha\mu\grave{\upsilon}\varsigma$ κoκκίνη</note>, which the soldiers used to mock Christ, is recorded by Mark and John as a "purple garment" <note>original Greek: $\dot{\iota}\mu\acute{\alpha}\tau\iota o\nu$ πoρφυρ$\tilde{\tilde{\upsilon}}\nu$</note>. Just as in Horace, the same cloth is called both "dipped in scarlet" and "purple" in book 2 of his *Satires*, describing dining couches:

<margin>Matthew ch. 27 v. 28</margin>
<margin>Satires 6 v. 102</margin>

->*where the cloth, dipped in red scarlet,*<-
->*shone brightly upon the ivory couches.*<-

Here too the interpreters vary, and to reconcile them one by one due to the confusion of colors is a superfluous labor. What the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> called *phoenikoun* <note>original: $\phi\omicron\iota\nu\iota\kappa\omicron\tilde{\upsilon}\nu$, meaning crimson or Phoenician red</note>, the Vulgate translates as **scarlet**, and with him Castellio; for when the Greek interpreters of Theocritus explain *phoenikon* as *kokkinon* <note>scarlet</note>, they called that part of Syria where the best purple was made **Phoenicia**, and the inhabitants of Tyre and Sidon **Phoenicians**, whose merchandise was purple, as will soon be shown regarding Isaiah 23. Hence they use the term *to phoenikoun* for any red color. Procopius in his commentary on this passage (page 27) says: "He cleanses us, who were *rubefactos* (*made red*) <note>original Greek: πε$\phi\omicron\iota\nu\iota\gamma\mu\acute{\epsilon}\nu\omicron\upsilon\varsigma$</note> with blood, through the bath of rebirth, and promises the kingdom of heaven." Luther translates the word as: **Blood-red** <note>original German: "Blutroth"</note>. The English as **Scarlet**. The Zurich translators, however, render *kokkinon* as: **Burning like purple** <note>original German: "Brūnend wie ein Purpur"</note>, which is to say (unless I am greatly mistaken) of a fiery or inflamed purple color; for Juvenal in his second Satire also makes the scarlet color **fiery**, as if it did not differ far from the redness of fire. Gregory, in his 16th Homily on Ezekiel (page 230, volume 2), affirms that **Coccus** glows with the appearance of fire; therefore Valerius Flaccus in the *Argonautica* also called it **burning**, just as one says **burning murex**. Corippus, in *The Praises of Justin*, book 2, line 4, writes: "radiating with burning scarlet," and Silius, speaking of one dressed in splendid clothing who (as he says in book 4, line 66) "shone with gilded murex," notes that the color is said to "burn" by Virgil in the fourth book of the *Aeneid* (line 53) because of its pre-eminent brilliance:

<margin>Idyll 2 v. 2</margin>
<margin>17. 8.</margin>

->*And the wools burned with Tyrian murex.*<-

In German, you would say of this color: **Fire-red** or **Light-red** <note>original German: "Feuerroth / Liechtroth"</note>. In Greek, it is *pyrros* <note>original: πυρρ$\grave{o}\varsigma$</note>, the color attributed to fire; for you will often find fire called *kyphon* red. Marcellus Virgilius, the interpreter of Dioscorides, rendered it as **vermiculum** <note>little worm</note>; a word, as he says, used by Columella, who in book 2, chapter 6, dealing with types of seeds, said among other things: "Emmer wheat, which is called reddish *vermiculum*." And Saint Jerome, in his interpretation of Leviticus, when he found in the Hebrew *thola'ath shani* <note>original: תולעת שני, "worm of scarlet"</note> and in the Greek "spun scarlet" <note>original: $\tau\grave{o}$ κόκκιν$\omicron$ν κ$\epsilon\kappa\lambda\omega\sigma\mu\acute{\epsilon}\nu\omicron\nu$</note>, translated it as **vermiculum**, as the Vulgate also has it here, which the French interpreter imitates. Concerning the nature and generation of the "little worm" from which the name comes, I bring forward the words of Renodeus. "The whole grain," he says, "is indeed pregnant with a blood-red gore, which after perfect maturity

<margin>Medical Disputations bk. 1 ch. 17</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Scarlet & Crimson</margin>
having been confined for some time in a small membrane, turns into **little worms**, leaving the thin skin almost empty: which, when they have grown, sometimes become winged and fly away." (Pausanias writes in the same place: "if it should reach the air having spread its wings, the fruit becomes winged immediately.") "However, before their procreation, the mentioned liquid is usually studiously drawn out for the preparation of the Syrup of Kermes <note>a medicinal syrup made from the kermes insect</note> or for dyeing silk. The generation of these little animals is hindered, or rather quickly induced internally, by the mere sprinkling of vinegar, by which the dead little bodies are collected and compressed into a vermilion mass called **Scocletium**; Pliny calls it **Cusculium**." Johannes Forster had already taught this long ago in his Hebrew Dictionary (folio 329). I will add as a finishing touch the words of Matthias Flacius (whom Richard Montagu calls "a man of a certain prodigious industry and a monstrous glutton for books"), which appear in his *Key to the Sacred Scriptures* (1681): "There was a kind of little worm from which they prepared purple, wherefore the Hebrews call that color **Tholaah**, 'the little worm'; perhaps they distinguish the shells themselves, from which the same color was usually made, by this name. Thus some think the Italian name **Scarlato** [Scarlet], by which the same color is now called, comes from the Greek *skolex* <note>original: $\sigma\kappa\omega\lambda\acute{\eta}\xi$, meaning worm</note>, as if it were *skolekion* <note>a little worm</note>. Thus also the Italians call the same color from the 'worm' **vermiglio** [vermilion] (which the French also call **vermeillon**). That very deep and blood-red color was to the Hebrews a symbol of a spiritual stain, that is, of sin; just as, on the contrary, whiteness and brightness were a sign of innocence both to them and to other nations. Therefore God says: *If your sins be like the little worm* <note>referring to crimson/vermiculum</note>." Julius Scaliger, in his *Poems* (page 352), skillfully calls the **Coccus** "the father of the tiny worm"; for in the coccus a red worm is born, from which the color is also called **vermiculus**. Strigelius says *thola* <note>original: תולע</note> signifies both the little worm and the purple color, because the dyeing **coccus** is a grain growing from the holm oak, which turns into a little worm, which they call *skolekion*. From this the color is scarlet, and they think the word **Scharlach** [Scarlet] was made from the Greek word *skolekion*. See the noble Lord Claude Salmasius commenting excellently on the **Coccus** in his *Plinian Exercises*, in which he will remove doubts for the scrupulous more than enough, as is his custom.
