# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Gentile-influenced Judaism</margin>
...is consuming, *a strong and jealous God*. Again, he commands them to avoid the abominations of the nations, where in verses 10 and 11 he enumerates their impious rites in detail and lists nine specific kinds under their own names:
<margin>Deuteronomy 18:9</margin>
1. **Human sacrifice** <note>original Greek: ἀνθρωποθυσίαν</note>. 2. **Soothsayers**. 3. **Astrologers** <note>literally "Planetarios," those who predict by the planets</note>. 4. **Augurs** <note>those who interpret signs or omens</note>. 5. **Sorcerers**. 6. **Knot-tyers** <note>original Greek: συνδέοντας συνδεσμοῦς</note>, who hang amulets around the neck or use other charms. 7. **Ventriloquists** or those seeking an oracle from a "Python" spirit. 8. **Diviners and Haruspices** <note>ancient priests who interpreted the will of the gods by inspecting entrails</note>. 9. **Necromancers**, who use magical arts to summon and consult the shadows of the dead. He adds the reason in verse 12: because all who do these things are *an abomination to Jehovah*. God had issued this command with such severity because the Egyptians, Assyrians, and Babylonians were particularly devoted to these kinds of magical divinations; they believed, through long observation of the stars, that they could foretell what would happen to anyone and the fate into which each person was born. Their profession is condemned by God throughout the Holy Scriptures. In Leviticus chapter 18, verse 3, God spoke to Moses, saying: *I am the Lord your God. According to the practices of the land of Egypt, where you dwelt, you shall not do; and according to the practices of the land of Canaan, to which I am leading you, you shall not do* <note>original Greek: Ἐγὼ κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ὑμῶν. Κατὰ τὰ ἐπιτηδεύματα γῆς Αἰγύπτου, ἐν ᾗ παρῳκήσατε, οὐ ποιήσετε, καὶ κατὰ τὰ ἐπιτηδεύματα γῆς Χαναάν, εἰς ἣν ἐγὼ εἰσάγω ὑμᾶς, οὐ ποιήσετε</note>. God exhorts the Jews that, if they come into the land of Canaan, they should not act according to the works of those for whose sake He had spat out the inhabitants of the land, nor should they walk in their laws. Instead, they were to overturn their altars, break their statues, burn their sacred groves, and cut down their carved idols, as is clear from the 
<margin>Deuteronomy 12:2, 3</margin>
explicit command.* That the Canaanites possessed the most depraved religion and morals can be read and is eloquently explained in the Book of Wisdom, chapters 12 and 13. The colonists of the Canaanites, the Tyrians—"a bad egg from a bad crow" <note>original Greek: κακῶ κόρακι κακὸν ὠὸν, a proverb meaning bad parents produce bad children</note>—were notorious for frauds and perjuries, so much so that "Punic faith" eventually became a proverb for **villainy** <note>original Greek: πανοργίᾳ</note>. To the Hebrews, the **Canaanites** <note>Hebrew: χαναναῖοι</note> were strictly those who inhabited Sidon and Tyre and the adjacent maritime coast, as is evident from Numbers 13:30, Joshua 23:8, and Judges 1:31. However, the command is repeated so many times in Moses and the Prophets: *Observe my commandments and my edicts*. He wanted His own mandates to be observed, not those of others; and that phrase was added so often: I AM THE LORD YOUR GOD. He, the thrice-high God, thundered from heaven: 
<margin>Deuteronomy 6:13</margin>
*You shall fear the Lord your God, and Him alone shall you serve*. And in Isaiah 42:8: *I am the Lord, and this is my name: I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to carved idols*. Just as it is commanded: 
<margin>Ezekiel 20:18, 19</margin>
*Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers, nor observe their judgments, nor defile yourselves with their idols. I am the Lord your God. Walk in my statutes, and keep my judgments, and do them.* They were forbidden from joining in marriage or making a covenant with the seven nations, as seen in Exodus 34:2. Already in the time of Abraham, the morals of the Amorites were greatly corrupted, yet they had not yet filled up that measure of sin which divine goodness had seen fit to wait for, as Moses teaches us in Genesis 15:16. God testifies in Leviticus 18:24 that He would avenge the crimes of the Canaanites with His hand after a very long time of patience (namely, after their sacrilegious rites, incestuous lust, and beastly cruelty had reached their peak). Nor had He separated the Israelites from the nations for any other reason than to prevent them from following their customs and institutions, knowing very well how easy and reckless 

<column-break/>

a change of their native customs and rites would be for them. He had given them one tabernacle and one sanctuary so that there would be no occasion for inventing multiple gods, but so that in this way they might foster unity of religion while slaughtering their sacrifices at a single altar and performing other duties to encourage mutual agreement. For it is right, as read in Acts chapter 4, verse 32, that the heart and soul of the multitude of believers should be one. But the Jews, disregarding the grave warnings of GOD, did not look toward God but looked down upon Him, going after foreign gods, just as 
the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin Scripture predicts in Deuteronomy 4:28 and 28:64: that the Hebrews would serve *other gods* <note>original Greek: θεοῖς ἑτέροις</note>. Here, the Chaldean paraphrase <note>the Targum, an Aramaic translation/expansion</note> must be set aside, as it changes the sense by diverting this crime of idolatry to the nations when it translates: *You shall serve the peoples who serve idols*, a translation that looks to the idolaters rather than the idols. Scarcely had they left Egypt when they took an example of foul superstition from there in the **worship of the Golden Calf**; we have seen how they defiled themselves with this in the desert. It is well enough established that the Jews scattered among foreign nations defiled themselves with their idolatry, even from 2 Kings 17:33, 
<margin>2 Kings 17:33</margin>
where we read that they fell away from the religion of the True God and adopted foreign gods. Indeed, customs were introduced by neighboring idolaters to the contempt of the living God: the **Remphan** of the Chaldeans was adopted, the **Baal and Astaroth** of the Sidonians, the **Dagon** of the Phoenicians, and the **Chemosh and Moloch** of the Moabites and Ammonites; soothsayers, augurs, and astrologers were summoned, and high places, groves, and the rest of the nations' trifles concerning gods were passed down to posterity. I will provide the words as they appear in the Greek: *According to the custom of the nations from whence they were carried away* <note>original Greek: Κατὰ τὸ κρίμα τῶν ἐθνῶν, ὅθεν ἀπῴκισαν αὐτοὺς ἐκεῖθεν</note>. This happened primarily due to political considerations, because they saw neighboring nations flourishing in wealth and some sort of honors, while they themselves were often pressed by poverty. Therefore, seeking the favor of the nations, the Jews introduced religion based on "reason of state" that might benefit the region's prosperity, as the author of the Book of Maccabees speaks so openly on this matter: 
<margin>1 Maccabees 1:11</margin>
*Let us go and make a covenant with the nations that are round about us: for since we departed from them many evils have found us* <note>original Greek: διάδωμεθα διαθήκην μετὰ τῶν ἐθνῶν τῶν κύκλῳ ἡμῶν, ὅτι ἀφ' ἧς ἐχωρίσθημεν ἀπ' αὐτῶν, εὗρεν ἡμᾶς κακὰ πολλά</note>. The nations worshipped many gods; they despised and harassed the Israelites, who were content with only one and were few in number. For that reason, they were also hated by the Romans and Greeks, as witnessed by *Cicero in Pro Flacco, Justin in book 36, Dio in book 37 page 41, and Horace in Satire 9*. Furthermore, the worship of the true God was more severe; but false religion was a provider of pleasures and had almost everything that is pleasing to the flesh, by which they falsely thought their minds would become lofty and bold for undertaking great things bravely. We shall make a summary of our work, reciting those things which are recorded in the Sacred texts concerning **Jewish-Paganism**; **let us return** <note>original Greek: ἐπανερχώμεθα</note>. To arrange the matter more deeply, let us consider the state of the Church before the flood, as it was: 1. Under Abel, *whose brother Cain went out from the face of 
<margin>Genesis 4</margin>
God*, that is, he left the place of the Church in which God had appeared to him, and sought another dwelling for himself, leaving behind his parents and other pious people. By this secession, the first division of the sons of God and the sons of men was made; which defection, as it is the fountain of vices, was followed by the impious pursuits of Cain, through which he devoted himself entirely to robberies, and having collected from everywhere companions acquired through banditry, he...

# II. 6. AMITIA <note>Likely a heading relating to historical periods or "Amicitia" (friendship/alliance), though the text focuses on the "Ethnico-Judaismus" or the mixing of pagan and Jewish customs.</note>

<margin>Gentile-influenced Judaism</margin>
...to them, as Josephus reports in Book 1, *Antiquities of the Jews, Chapter 3*, they lived a life of crime and, to hide themselves safely, they fortified themselves with walls and built cities, being plagued by a guilty conscience. This genealogy of the impious flourished greatly before the world and spread itself abroad; from them come those called the Giants, the **men of old** <note>Hebrew: מתי עולם (Methei Olam), meaning men of the world or men of ancient renown</note>, that is, the most famous men from ages past, namely from the time of Cain and Lamech. And so that this lineage might increase more quickly and prevail over the godly, Lamech became a *bigamist* <note>original Latin: biuamus, likely a typo for bigamus</note>, and the profanation of the divine name grew to such an extent that the godly Enoch found it necessary to restore and propagate the ministry of the Church. For it is clear from the Book of Creation <note>Genesis</note> that doctrine and the true worship of God had been almost obscured by the idolatry and tyranny of the Cainites before this Enos <note>The author here seems to conflate Enos and Enoch in the context of restoring worship</note>. Thus, there was a need for a restoration or reformation, as well as a separation of the "sons of God" from the "sons of men," as they are called in Chapter 6; hence it is said: *in whose time men began to call upon and preach the name of the Lord*. For they did not only imitate the vices of those who came before, but even surpassed them, so that Epiphanius, in the preface to his *Anchoratus*, rightly calls the customs and way of life of that age "Barbarism." This relates to that most grave complaint of the Holy Spirit concerning the malice of the early world, when He says all flesh was corrupted and every power of thought was evil. We may vividly depict this human malice with the words of Alcimus Avitus, a man highly learned in the divine scriptures and most skilled in secular letters, from Book 4, *On the Flood of the World*, verse 13:

Consistent accounts are found in the fictitious *Antiquities* of Berosus, which were compiled by Johannes Annius of Viterbo. Whatever their reputation may be, it seemed not unworthy to bring forward a **small fragment** <note>original Greek: ἀπόσπασμάτιον</note> from them. "Before the famous disaster of the waters, by which the whole world perished, many ages passed away, which were faithfully preserved by our Chaldeans. These men, trusting in the vastness of their bodies and their strength, oppressed others with invented weapons; and serving their lusts, they invented pavilions <note>original Latin: papiliones, possibly referring to luxury tents or 'social butterflies'/parasites</note> and musical instruments and all manner of delights. ...many preached and prophesied, and they carved in stone warnings of that destruction of the world which was to come. But they, being accustomed to malice, despised everything, even as the wrath and vengeance of the heavens pressed upon them for their impiety and crimes. The spurious Berosus of Annius intended this to stand as the beginning of his first book. God had long endured the progress of so many crimes, and at last He balanced the gravity of the sin with the gravity of the punishment in the *universal flood*, from which we know only Noah was snatched away. After the first race of mortals was removed and the lands were covered by the floodwaters, scarcely better times followed; for when the languages were divided, they went throughout the world. Let us consider the post-flood state of the Church under Abraham and Jacob. It was not immune from all worship of idols. Abraham himself had once been an idolater; afterward, he "won souls for God," but not through Gentile arts, as Origen says. Among the Chaldeans, a superstition regarding the worship of the Sun was practically their own, so that the Jews write that when Abraham left his homeland of Haran and came into *Ur of the Chaldeans* <note>original Latin: Ur Casdim</note> under the dominion of the Chaldeans, he found everyone serving the Sun as a God. Rabbi Moses <note>Maimonides</note> found this recorded in the histories and books of the nations, as reported by Rabbi Menasseh Ben-Israel in Question 40 on Genesis, pages 55 and 56. To the impiety of idolatry, which Ninus had increased, was added the pestiferous vanity of astrological divination, of which the Chaldeans were the parents and masters. Under Jacob, we read that he said to his household and to all who were with him:
<margin>Genesis 35:2</margin>
*Put away the foreign gods that are among you, and purify yourselves, and change your garments.* No sooner said than done, for they gave him all the *foreign gods which they had, and the earrings which were in their ears; and Jacob buried them under the terebinth tree which was near the city of Shechem*. Furthermore, Rachel his wife had stolen the household gods <note>term: Teraphim; small statues used for domestic worship or divination</note> *of her father Laban, which Jacob her husband saw to it were buried under the oak. 
<margin>Genesis 31:22</margin>
Laban the Syrian, a most ancient idolater, calls them his gods, saying to Jacob: Why have you stolen my gods? To which Jacob, who had proven his piety and faith to Laban with notable evidence, replied: Let him with whom you find your gods not live.* But Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen them; she had deceived her father by hiding the idols under the camel's saddle and straw. Again, Laban said to Jacob: *May the God of Abraham and the Gods of Nahor, the Gods of their father, judge between us.* He wished to hold out to Jacob a religion that was not only of his father but of his grandfather, or even older; which Joshua also testifies in Chapter 24, when he addresses Israel in the name of God: *Long ago your ancestors lived beyond the Euphrates River, Terah the father of Abraham and the father of Nahor, and they served other gods.* Under Moses, God had prohibited the ridiculous deities of the Egyptians in the gravest warnings to the Israelites, set forth in Deuteronomy Chapter 4, verse 15 and following: *Take careful heed, for the sake of your souls, lest you act perversely by making for yourselves a carved image of any figure, the form of male or female, the form of any beast that is on the earth, the form of any winged bird that flies in the sky, the form of any thing that creeps on the ground, the form of any fish that is in the waters under the earth. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Gentile-influenced Judaism</margin>
*...which the Lord your God has distributed to all the peoples under the whole heaven.* <note>Deuteronomy 4:19</note> What did they do? They made gods according to the custom of the Egyptians, to whose religion they conformed their own in the golden calf. Rebuking them for this, Moses speaks thus: *You have sinned a great sin; now I will go up to the Lord; perhaps I can make atonement for your sin.* <note>Exodus 32:30</note> Here the word *perhaps* does not imply doubt, but rather sharpens their concern, showing the gravity of the sin, and yet lifting them up with some expectation of God's grace. For indeed, these very people, to whom God had said, *You shall be to me a kingdom of Priests and a holy nation,* <note>Exodus 19:6</note> not long after addressed Aaron with one voice, saying: *Make us gods.* <note>Exodus 32:1</note> They had seen the Egyptians worshiping their God in the image of an ox or a calf called **Apis**; therefore, they also wished to worship that true God, by whom they had been led out of Egypt, with these rites and in this image. Indeed, God said of the Israelites at the beginning of the second year after the exit from Egypt: <margin>Leviticus 17:7</margin> *They shall no longer sacrifice their sacrifices to Demons <note>often translated as "satyrs" or "goat-demons"</note> after whom they have gone whoring*—that is, whom they were accustomed to worship at the time they offered burnt offerings to the golden calf and committed spiritual adultery in it. They had contracted this stain of an evil mind in Egypt from long association. Hence Theodoret <note>a 5th-century Christian theologian and bishop</note> writes in his commentary on *Leviticus, p. 105*: <note>original Greek: Ἐπειδὴ χρόνον συχνὸν ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ διατετελεικὼς ὁ λαὸς θύειν δαίμοσιν ἐδιδάχθη, συνεχώρησε τὰς θυσίας, ἵνα ταῖς δεισιδαιμονίαις ἐλευθερώσῃ. ὅτι γὰρ ταύταις ἔχαιρον μαρτυρεῖ τὰ περὶ τὸν μόσχον γεγενημένα.</note> "Since the people, having stayed a long time in Egypt, were taught to sacrifice to demons, [God] permitted sacrifices [to Himself] so that He might free them from their superstitions. For the events surrounding the calf bear witness that they delighted in these things." Truly, the Israelites, born and raised among that barbarian nation, had also absorbed Gentile customs of sacrificing to demons and impure spirits, and of worshiping celestial signs as gods. This is frankly written by the most learned of modern Rabbis, **Menasseh Ben Israel** <note>a famous 17th-century Portuguese rabbi and scholar</note> in his *Reconciler on Leviticus, p. 181*. God promised He would cure the Israelites of these idolatrous diseases in Exodus chapter 15: *None of the diseases I imposed on Egypt will I impose on you*, according to the same Rabbi on page 128. Therefore, after the Israelites—who had neglected God's commands even regarding circumcision—were circumcised in the promised land of Canaan by God's command, God said to <margin>Joshua 5:9</margin> Joshua: *Today I have taken away the reproach of Egypt from you.* That is, every kind of abuse, superstition, rebellion, and other sins to which you clung in Egypt and on the journey through the desert. Theodoret well notes in *Questions on Joshua, p. 186*: <note>original Greek: Ὁ τῶν ὅλων ἔφη Θεὸς: ὅτι τῇ σήμερον ἡμέρᾳ ἀφεῖλον τὸν ὀνειδισμὸν Αἰγύπτου ἀφ' ὑμῶν. δηλοῖ δὲ ὁ λόγος τὴν τῆς Αἰγυπτιακῆς δουλείας & δυσσεβείας ἀπαλλαγὴν, καὶ τῆς ἐπηγγελμένης γῆς τὴν ἀπόληψιν.</note> "The God of all things said: 'Today I have removed the reproach of Egypt from you.' This saying indicates the release from Egyptian slavery and impiety, and the taking possession of the promised land." Yet depraved thoughts always entered their minds; God also complains about this to Samuel in 1 Samuel 8:8, saying: *According to all the works they have done from the day I led them out of Egypt even to this day, namely leaving me and serving foreign gods, so they are doing to you as well.* For that reason, it is likely that the Devil, when he contended with Michael over the body of Moses (whom God buried in a place unknown to the Jews), struggled so that his body might be revealed to the Jews for worship and idolatry. For since God saw the Israelites were strongly inclined toward idolatry, it is probable He wished his grave to remain unknown lest they honor Moses with divine worship. The same is said of the Angels, whose

<column-break/>

<margin>Gentile-influenced Judaism</margin>
creation Moses kept silent about, <note>original Greek: διὰ τὸ φιλείδωλον καὶ πολύθεον τῶν ἀνθρώπων, μάλιστα δὲ τῶν Ἰουδαίων</note> "on account of the love of idols and polytheism of men, and especially of the Jews," as **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom, an influential Early Church Father</note> teaches in his commentary on Genesis. Once peace was restored, prosperity birthed luxury; and the people, unmindful of the discipline of their customs, began to take wives from the Gentiles, gradually following foreign habits and accepting the profane worship of Idols. God had previously warned the Israelites of this in Deuteronomy 7:4 and 20:18, unless they put the nations they encountered to total destruction; for God did not want the mixing of His people with the Gentiles for that purpose. But in a later age under the judges, they were *mixed among the Gentiles*, into whose marriages and kinships they had passed, and *they learned their works and worshiped their idols, as they are reproached in Psalm 105:20-21 and recounted to their shame in Judges 2:11 and following.* Specifically, they first offended God most gravely with a certain type of idolatry; for immediately after Joshua was taken from among the living, another generation arose that did not know the Lord or the work He had done for Israel. The children of Israel, therefore, did evil in the sight of the Lord and served the **Baalim** <note>the plural form of Baal, a Canaanite deity</note>, that is, all kinds of idols of the nations *throughout the cities and villages.* For the Hebrews seem to use that word indifferently for all the idols of the Gentiles, primarily because **Bel** or **Baal** was the first to whom a statue was consecrated, from which rite idolatry thereafter crept into the common people; thus the whole body of idolatry is now named after the head. The Angel of the Lord continues in the same place: *And forsaking the Lord God of their fathers, who led them out of the land of Egypt, they went after other gods, after the gods of the peoples who were around them, and they adored them and provoked the Lord to anger. And having forsaken the Lord, they served Baal and Astaroth.* We know from this why they did not come into full possession of the land as had been promised; concerning which <margin>Questions on Joshua, p. 19</margin> Theodoret says: <note>original Greek: Ἔγνωμεν δὲ καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν, δι' ἣν κατὰ τὴν θείαν ἐπαγγελίαν ἐκ ἀπάσης τῆς γῆς, τὴν δεσπότειαν παρέλαβον. ἀνασάμενοι γὰρ τῶν δυσσεβῶν ἐθνῶν τὴν συγγένειαν καὶ μιμησάμενοι τὴν ἀσέβειαν, τῆς θείας ἐγυμνώθησαν προμηθείας, καὶ δουλεύειν αὐτοῖς ἠναγκάζοντο.</note> "And we have known the reason why, according to the divine promise, they did not receive lordship over all the land. For having embraced kinship with the impious nations and imitated their impiety, they were stripped of divine providence and forced to serve them." In this manner, while serving Baal and Astaroth under **Othniel**, the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, and therefore the anger of the Lord burned against them, so that He sold them into the hands of **Cushan-Rishathaim**, and they were pressed under the King in an eight-year servitude. Finally, Othniel, the third leader of the Israelites, liberated the people from these hardships and the yoke. In Judges 10:6, the sevenfold gods worshiped by the Israelites after the death of Jair are listed: *And the children of Israel again did evil in the sight of the Lord, and served Baalim and Astaroth, the gods and goddesses, the gods of Aram, the gods of Sidon, the gods of the Moabites, the gods of the children of Ammon, and finally the gods of the Philistines, and they forsook the Lord and did not serve Him.* Thus there was almost no neighboring tribe or nation whose superstitions they are not read to have followed; wherefore the Lord delivered them into the hands of the Philistines and Ammonites, by whom they were most cruelly afflicted in an eighteen-year servitude. There is no space to relate the long series and catalog of various sins. Therefore we shall consider the **Times of the Kings.** The Kings, contrary to common custom and necessity, were sought after the manner of other nations (1 Samuel 8:5), and the Republic was not made better by this, for then especially...

## II. 6

<margin>

Foreign worship flourished most greatly, especially in the <term>high places</term> <note>Hebrew: 'bamot'; elevated sites for sacrificial worship</note> of the altars which God had so often commanded to be destroyed. Although that one high place in Jerusalem had already been chosen by God—not so much to preserve the authority of the public priesthood (lest everyone be a priest to himself like that fellow Micah <margin>Judges 17:10</margin>), but rather to remove every contagion of idolatry. For this reason, even the pious kings are often rebuked by the Prophets on this account: that while they had reformed other things, they had not removed the high places. Saul, the first King of Israel, immersed in the opinions of the gentiles, consulted a <term>medium</term> <note>original: 'Pythonissam'; a woman possessed by a spirit of divination</note> regarding the future success of a war; he ordered Samuel to be raised by her, or rather, his shade to be summoned. 1 Samuel 28:11. For those things which are done by the tricks of magi are proven to be illusions <note>original: 'phantastica esse'</note> in the Canon Law (case 26, question 5), where this passage concerning Samuel is explained. Even the most wise King Solomon, after being led <note>original: 'en xenois' (among foreigners)</note> by the love of foreign women for whom he was dying of "unreasoning pleasure" <note>original: 'alogō hēdonē'</note> as often happens, was led away to gentile gods. He built shrines for them in Jerusalem—**first wise, then wicked** <note>original: 'prōta sophos, metepeita kakos'</note>. *For when Solomon was now worn out with old age, his wives turned away his heart after other gods, so that his heart was not sincere before the Lord his God, like the heart of David his father. For he went after Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Sidonians, and after Milcom, the abomination of the Ammonites. He built a high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab, on the mountain facing Jerusalem, and for Molech, the abomination of the children of Ammon. And in this manner he did for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods.* I will send that fabled tradition about Solomon to the <term>Anticyras</term> <note>A classical reference to places where hellebore was grown to treat madness; meaning the idea is insane</note>—which I wish Josephus had not repeated—as if the wise King had used the magic art to acquire foreign trees for his orchards, established incantations against diseases, and revealed a method of conjurations. Books under the names of Enoch and Solomon are circulated regarding these things, as noted by Rodrigo de Castro in *Political Medicine, book 4, chapter 3*. Why would it be necessary to summon demons for counsel, only for the glory of the wisdom granted to him by God to be foully stained?

Gregory speaks elegantly on this, as reported in the Canon Law: *Solomon, he says, was led to this point by the immoderate use and persistence of women, that he built a temple for idols; and he who had previously built a temple for God, through the persistence of lust and even having his faith undermined, did not fear to build temples for idols.* After the death of Solomon, the kingdom was divided—which a furious God had foretold through a Prophet—between Jeroboam and Rehoboam. With their interests divided between retaining and expanding the kingdom, they wore each other down for 260 years; while the empire was divided, they were different in their minds, and Judah and Israel contended with each other in almost perpetual wars. And indeed Jeroboam, the first King of the Israelites, as soon as he took up the scepters of command, not only abandoned the Lord himself but also made all Israel sin by leading them to images of gods. For so that he might seem to follow the example of the Fathers worshiping at Bethel, he established <margin>1 Kings 12:28</margin> golden calves in Dan and Bethel for the sake of sacred worship. One can read of this, and indeed of the plan he entered into, saying to the people: *It is enough for you to have gone up to Jerusalem until now. Behold your gods, O Israel, who led*

*you out of the land of Egypt.* Furthermore, he made a house of high places and appointed priests of the high places in Bethel (verses 31, 32). The Prophets changed the old name of the place, Bethel <note>"House of God"</note>, into **Bethaven**—that is, the "House of Wickedness"—because of King Jeroboam's golden calf worshiped there. This was so the people would understand that the impious worship of the calf was being censured, which one might rightly call the head of all idolatry, following Rupert of Deutz (*On the Victory of the Word of God*, book 5, ch. 2). *You,* says the Prophet to the King, <margin>1 Kings 14:9</margin> *have plotted evil above all who were before you: for you have gone and made for yourself other and molten gods to provoke me, and you have cast me behind your back.* Imbued with superstition, Rehoboam imitated the religion of his mother Naamah the Ammonitess, placing altars and shrines everywhere and dedicating groves on hills to profane deities—which was the most common form of "impiety" <note>original: 'asebeia'</note> among the pagans in this regard. He made Israel sin; this phrase is commonly used in Scripture regarding the idolatrous Kings of Israel. *And Judah did evil in the eyes of the Lord, and they provoked him above all that their fathers had designed in the sins which they committed. For they also built for themselves high places, statues, and groves on every high hill and under every leafy tree; there were even <term>catamites</term> <note>Male cult prostitutes</note> in the land, and they did according to the abominations of the nations.* Hence an angry God sent **Shishak** <note>original: 'Sefacum'</note>, the King of Egypt, against them to avenge the injury brought upon Him. Coming to Jerusalem in the fifth year of Rehoboam, Shishak departed after plundering all the treasures and votive offerings. There was, moreover, war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all their days. Nor did this evil plague invade only Jeroboam and Rehoboam, but it also succeeded into their lineage; for nearly all their sons succeeded no more to their patrimonies than to their vices. *Abijam,* <margin>1 Kings 15</margin> *the emulator of his father Rehoboam, walked in all the sins of his father which he had done before him.* That king of "terrible speech" <note>original: 'terriloquus'; a literal translation of the Hebrew name 'Ahab' as interpreted by some scholars</note> (as he seems to be called in Hosea 13:1), **Ahab**, <margin>1 Kings 16:32</margin> surpassed all his predecessors in idolatry. Led on by Jezebel of Sidon, his wife, he introduced the worship of Baal into Israel and forced others to that worship. *For he considered it a light thing to walk in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat; he took as his wife Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal, King of the Sidonians, and went and served Baal and worshiped him. He even erected an altar for Baal in the shrine of Baal which he had built in Samaria. Furthermore, he made groves; Ahab added also to those things by which he might provoke the Lord God of Israel, more than all the kings of Israel who had been before him.* Elijah, the Prophet of that time, greatly mourning the condition of the Church, said that the Israelites had abandoned the covenant of God, destroyed His altars, and killed the Prophets with the sword. He said that he alone was left, and they were seeking to kill him too. To whom the Lord <margin>1 Kings 19</margin> said: *That He had left for Himself in Israel 7,000 whose knees had not bowed to Baal.* Ahaziah <note>original: 'Ozochias'</note> consulted <margin>2 Kings 1</margin> the gentile idol **Baal-Zebub** about the outcome of his illness, neglecting the oracle of God. Joram indeed removed the statue of Baal which <margin>2 Kings 3</margin> his father had made. Nevertheless, he clung to the sins of Jeroboam, who made Israel sin, and did not depart from them. Ahaz, in favor of the King of Assyria, is read to have removed many things pertaining to the worship of God, and he walked in the way of the kings of Israel; he even passed his son through the fire according to the abominations of the nations. Paganized Judaism.

...**above the hills, and under every leafy tree.** King Manasseh sacrificed his son to <term>Moloch</term> <note>A Canaanite deity associated with child sacrifice by fire</note>, placed detestable idols in the temple of God, and rebuilt the <term>high places</term> <note>Elevated shrines for unauthorized worship</note> that his father Hezekiah had destroyed. He erected altars to Baal and made a <term>sacred grove</term> <note>original: 'lucum'; often associated with the goddess Asherah</note> just as Ahab, King of Israel, had done. He worshipped and served the whole host of heaven; he even built altars in the house of the Lord, constructing altars for the entire heavenly militia in the two courtyards of the Lord's house. He passed his son through the fire, devoted himself to the art of fortune-telling and omens, established mediums and diviners, and practiced evil in the eyes of the Lord. 

Idolatry was finally the ruin of both kingdoms, Judah and Israel. For Israel was cut off by Shalmaneser, King of the Assyrians, and the ten tribes were led away into a near-perpetual captivity. Judah was weakened by Nebuchadnezzar the Babylonian, under whom they paid the penalty for their impiety with heavy punishment. Finally, a "finishing touch" of most sorrowful destruction was added by the Romans, and the fulfillment of the prophecy of Christ (*Matthew 24:15*) took place when the temple was burned by Titus and the Romans, the city destroyed, and the people deported and scattered, so that they ceased to be a nation. 

Nor did the traces of this corrupt mindset disappear until the very <term>total destruction</term> <note>original: 'panolethrian' (Greek)</note> of their political state, as can be confirmed from the books of the *Maccabees* and other *New Testament passages*. For first, under the reign of the Seleucids, they sought linguistic conformity with the gentiles and pursued it with great zeal; concerning this <term>confusion of tongues</term> <note>original: 'glottosynchusei' (Greek)</note> consult Majer, *part 1, prod. philol. sacr. page 214 and following*. *Nehemiah*, that most fierce censor of foreign idioms, is remembered to have cursed his fellow countrymen who used foreign speech; he also struck them, plucked out their hair, bound them by an oath, and devoted them to a curse, so that they would no longer allow room for the strangeness of an exotic language—that "filth of speech" contracted from profane marriages with neighbors. For they had taken foreign wives, including those from *Ashdod* (with whom they spoke the Ashdodite tongue), where the scripture records that Dagon was primarily worshipped. Ezra had seen Jews taking wives from Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab, and their children—hybrids of mixed race—likewise had a mixed language, speaking half-Jewish and half-Ashdodite. 

They emulated the gentiles no less in their names or <term>naming conventions</term> <note>original: 'onomathesia' (Greek)</note> shortly before the start of the Maccabean rule, so that they changed their ancestral and Jewish names for gentile ones—that is, they exchanged them for Greek and foreign names. Thus, *Jesus* became *Jason*, and likewise *Onias* became *Menelaus*, as we have learned from Flavius Josephus in *Book 12, Chapter 6 of the Antiquities of the Jews*. Indeed, that depraved man *Jason* himself sought the high priesthood in Jerusalem by offering money to King Antiochus, on the condition that he might also **enroll the people in Jerusalem as citizens of Antioch** <note>original: 'tous en Hierosolymois Antiocheis anagrapsai' (Greek)</note>. In other customs and rites, they left nothing undone that could be desired by their depraved minds. They requested permission from King Antiochus for a *Gymnasium* and an *Ephebia* <note>A Greek educational institution for young men, often involving athletic training in the nude</note> to be established **according to the laws of the nations** <note>original: 'kata ta nomima tōn ethnōn' (Greek)</note>, that is, according to the custom of the Greek gentiles, as shown in *1 Maccabees chapter 1, verses 14–15 and 2 Maccabees chapter 4, verses 9 and 14*. Regarding this, see what Peter Faber writes in *Agonisticon, Book 1 chapter 22 and Book 3 chapters 27–28*. They **made themselves**

Gentile Influence.

**uncircumcised** <note>original: 'praeputia sibi attraxere'</note>, neglecting the circumcision instituted by God, **and they made foreskins for themselves** <note>original: 'kai epoiēsan heautois akrobystias' (Greek)</note>, which Paul calls **to pull over** <note>original: 'epispasthai' (Greek); referring to the surgical reversal of circumcision</note> in the Jewish context. Sixtinus Amama, in his *Notes on the 41st Letter of Drusius*, shows from Epiphanius and Celsus that this was done through medical art. Furthermore, lest they be unlike the Greeks in any way, the impious priest *Jason* (*2 Maccabees 4:12*), wishing to please Antiochus, **led the best of the youths under the Greek hat** <note>original: 'kratistas tōn ephēbōn hypo petason ēgen' (Greek)</note>, so that they abandoned their own caps and wore the <term>petasos</term> <note>A broad-brimmed Greek hat associated with the god Hermes</note>. This is the explanation of Matthias Martinius in his *Lexicon Philologicum, page 2632*, and it pleases us more than the version of the common translator, though Peter Faber fights for that one in *Agonisticon 3.27*. 

There was such a burning passion for Greek manners and the adoption of foreign institutions—**because of the extreme impiety of the wicked and hardly-a-priest Jason—that there was no longer any inclination among the priests toward the duties of the altar. Instead, despising the temple and neglecting the sacrifices, they ran to enjoy the shameful spectacles exhibited in the wrestling arena and the discus competitions. Holding their ancestral honors as nothing, they considered Greek glories to be the most beautiful,** as the Zurich translators render it. I say nothing of the *Prayers for the Dead*, of sacrifices and other things brought into Judaism from gentile rites, regarding which see Blessed Chemnitz, *Examination of the Council of Trent, part 3, page 185 and following*. 

Thus, before the Redeemer came from Zion, these were truly the most desperate times. Religion, piety, the worship of God, and sacred things had veered off into utter impiety and profane atheism. After the tyranny of Antiochus and the paganism introduced into the religion of God by Menelaus, Alcimus, Jason, and others, there finally arose the Pharisees (who were imitators of the Stoics), the *Sadducees* (who were Epicureans), and the *Essenes* (who shared traits with the Cynics). Whoever wishes to know the character and life-customs of these men exactly should consult Montacute, *Apparatus 7, Origin of the Church, pages 240 to 275*. **Such was the state of the Jewish Republic at last, both in matters concerning God and the Law, and also in those pertaining to the state and civil government.** It had changed gradually, and from a most beautiful and excellent Republic, it became the worst and most shameful, with the Pharisees occupying the Seat of Moses. During the reign of Herod, they pushed men wherever they wished and led them away from wherever they chose through a feigned holiness, for which they were rebuked more than once by our Savior. Rightly, therefore, we might exclaim:

### Isaiah 2:20

<margin>Casting away idols.</margin>
The reader should consider the text more accurately; whether one explains the words <term>ironically</term> <note>original: "εἰρωνικῶς" (eirōnikōs)</note>, as if spoken to the blind and bleary-eyed; or whether one narrates that the Israelites will cast away their silver and gold idols, which they made for themselves to worship, into the caves of moles and bats. Nor anywhere, that I know of, would you read that moles and bats were worshipped by any nation—not even by the most superstitious Egyptians—unless you except the Americans, about whom one reads in Paulus Gryfaldus’s *History of the Indies, Book 3*, that they worshipped the bat as a deity. However, we are not unaware that Ramban <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nahman, a medieval Jewish scholar</note>, in *The Guide for the Perplexed, 30*, relates that seven bats, seven mice, and seven reptiles were offered to the Sun. The Old Version <note>The Vulgate</note> has it differently, namely that <term>one beetle, seven mice, and seven flying creatures</term> were offered. Jerome, in his *Commentary*, page 15, says regarding the <term>moles</term>, which we have interpreted from the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> as "Vain things" <note>original: "τοῖς ματαίοις" (tois mataiois)</note>, Aquila translates as "diggers" <note>original: "ὄρυγας" (orygas)</note>, Symmachus as "unfruitful things," and Theodotion used the Hebrew word itself, <term>Hapharpheroth</term>. The Hebrew words <term>לחפר פרות</term> <note>lachpar paroth</note> are used for moles because of their "digging of the earth," from the root <term>חפר</term> <note>chaphar</note>, to dig or dig out, because they pile up the excavated earth over themselves with their snout. Hence, I believe, Aquila translated it as "diggers," which signifies the act of digging, from the Greek verbs for "to dig" or "to dig through," which Aelian used regarding the digging of moles <margin>History of Animals, 17.10</margin>. *For the mole* <term>makes burrows</term> <note>original: "ὀρύγμαῖα" (orygmaia)</note> *and always* (these are the words of Jerome) *digs the earth and carries out the soil, and eating the roots from beneath, it is an animal harmful to crops, which the Greeks call* <term>aspalaka</term> <note>original: "ἀσπάλακα"</note>. The word <term>Aspalax</term> is said by the Etymologist, page 161, to come from <term>span</term>, that is, from "pulling away," because it always pulls back the earth and digs with its snout. *For this animal,* he says, *tears up the earth and makes a depth, and thus it enters.* Through the <term>moles</term>, to which the bats are joined, the Blessed Glassius <note>Salomon Glassius, a Lutheran theologian</note> in his *Sacred Rhetoric, book 1, chapter 2, page 330*, notes those who are spiritually blind and ignorant of God, since the former live in a dark place under the earth, while the latter fly and move about in the time of dark night; as if to say, those converted to Christ will leave their idols, which they stubbornly worshipped, to the blind and the unfaithful; they themselves will serve the Lord in heavenly light. Others understand by this metaphor a concealment born of contempt and shame. Whence the Blessed Schnepfius <note>Johann Schnepf</note> says in his *Commentary*: *He compares the expense bestowed upon idols and their veneration with the foul and infamous casting away of the same; for they made images of gold and silver, and even worshipped them and placed them in conspicuous spots; indeed, they built sumptuous temples for them. But now they are cast away, and indeed into sewers and the holes of moles. Before they boasted of them, now they blush if mention is made of them, and they act only to hide them: before they raised them to heaven, now they hurl them into the most contemptible little cracks: before they numbered them among the Gods, now among the bats, than which little animal nothing can be found more contemptible, more hateful, or more lowly.* <margin>p. 562.</margin> The Blessed Quistorp <note>Johann Quistorp</note> in his *Biblical Annotations* says: *This means that idols made of gold and silver, which were once held in great value, will be cast into the lowliest places, such as holes in the earth where moles and bats live.* Georg Witzel, who fiercely defended the Vulgate Version, relaxed his fervor somewhat here in his *Annotations on Luther’s German Bible*, published in Leipzig in 1556 <margin>folio 4. b. part 2</margin>, writing: *This place is not one of the easiest in the Prophet. According to the translation of the Septuagint and Jerome, it is spoken regarding the worship*

<column-break/>

<margin>Casting away idols.</margin>
*of these disregarded, ridiculous, and shameful little animals. We shall stick with that, however many others think differently, whom I nevertheless do not despise in their own way.* What is the difficulty here? In a manifest sense, the Prophet means that idolaters, blinder than moles and bats, will cast away their images into the gaps and <term>holes of the earth</term>, where moles spend a perpetual night, and into walls, where the hiding places of bats are, so that they might be able to flee from there more unhindered. This is a very fitting allegory from the habits of light-shunning animals for idolaters, who because of their blindness cannot endure the light of truth and seek the darkness of error. Therefore, "to worship" refers to the idols alone, not <term>to the moles</term>, as the punctuation in the Hebrew shows after the verb, where simultaneously <term>in common</term> <note>original: "ἀπὸ κοινοῦ" (apo koinou)</note> from the preceding verse the word <term>cave</term> must be repeated; as it is supplied by Osiander, and also by Luther in his German version, with which the Piscatorian version was observed to coincide. The gods of the gentiles were struck dumb before the majesty of Christ and threw themselves into the caverns of moles. The gentiles, having bid an eternal farewell to their ancestral superstitions, laughed at the oracles which fell silent when Christ was born, and cast away their idols, shining with gold and silver, into the lowliest places, such as those of bats and moles. Those who, having abandoned the springs, chase after the streams, superstitiously turn themselves into all forms so that they might support a struggling interpreter from antiquity—even if he sometimes says things that are foreign and less pertinent to the text.

> *The daughters of Zion are lifted up, and they have walked with outstretched throats, and beckoning with their eyes; they went walking and dancing, and they stir up the noise of rattles with their feet.*

<margin>Female adornment.</margin>
### IF we consider the very beginnings of clothing, it was <term>skin</term>, from which God fashioned garments for Adam to cover the nakedness of his body. The ancient monuments of the elders testify clearly enough that clothing was simple and without the luxury of artifice. First there were garments of skin, followed by those of <term>linen, wool, and silk</term>. The manner of dressing and clothing was not the same everywhere, but different for different nations; from this diversity of considerations, one name was given to this, another to that, and one person gave one name to this or that. The finery of the Persians was one thing, that of the Macedonians another, and that of the Phrygians another. The habit of the Romans was one thing, that of the Greeks another; the latter, because they invented the cloak, were called <term>palliati</term> <note>cloak-wearers</note>, while the former, who wore the <term>toga</term>, were called <term>togati</term>. In the progress of time, luxury grew everywhere among the nations, and the craftsman established the production of various forms. No one is unaware that the <term>Phrygians</term> excelled above the rest, being famous no less for the making of images than for the variety of garments, so much so that even now the <term>Phrygian garment</term>, which is decorated with a needle <note>i.e., embroidery</note>, and <term>phrygiones</term> <note>embroiderers</note>, who make it, are so called. Thus the <term>Seres</term> people <note>the Chinese</note> gave us <term>Silk</term>. King Attalus discovered the <term>Attalic</term> garment, that is, one which has gold woven into it. Clothing was once a matter of modesty...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
Women's
Cosmetics.
</margin>
<margin>
Book 1 p. 5.
</margin>
...a sign of austerity, today a sign of luxury. Regarding the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, who appointed Ephors <note>magistrates</note> to daily inspect the citizens' clothing so that nothing inappropriate to a decent appearance would be introduced, Aelian commends their moderation in his *Varia Historia, Book 14, Chapter 7*. Thucydides also writes *in these words*: "The Lacedaemonians were the first to use moderate clothing and the current style, and in other respects those who possessed greater means settled into a way of life as equal as possible to the common people" <note>original Greek: "μετριαισθῆτι και ες τον νυν τροπον πρωτοι λακεδαιμονιοι εχρησαντο, και ες τα αλλα προς τους πολλους οι τα μειζω κεκτημενοι, ισοδιαιτοι μαλιστα κατεστησαν"</note>. By these words, he teaches that among the Greeks, the Lacedaemonians were the first to be content with frugal food and appearance, and the wealthier among them also adopted and maintained a standard of living equal to the common folk and the masses. They loved an ornament in which simplicity was apparent, but others noted this as an "affected cheapness," and Aristotle in his *Ethics* classifies it as <term>boastfulness</term> <note>original Greek: "ὡς αλαζονικον"</note>, as if there were too much pride in having so little. Lycurgus <note>the legendary Spartan lawgiver</note> established these laws regarding dress; among others, he passed a law that no young man should use more than one garment for the whole year, nor should anyone walk about more elegantly than another, as Justin testifies in *Book 3, Chapter 3*.

Now, since one kind of cosmetics is "civil" and another is "effeminate"—the former aiming for an honorable bodily grace within modest behavior, while the latter employs dyes and pigments, sprinkles powder on the hair, and composes sweet-smelling perfumes—the Ephor of the Jewish people, Isaiah, attacks that vain and dishonest display of clothing with the gravest words. For there was no part of the body about which the Jewish women were not proud; they competed with one another in *stride and finery*, and with great inward swelling of the soul, they looked down on each other with disdain. Hence the Prophet predicts God's wrath to the women of the Jewish nation: "instead of perfume there shall be a stench, instead of a belt a dissolution <note>or a rope</note>, instead of curled hair baldness and a bare scalp, instead of a fine tunic a girding of sackcloth, and burning of the skin instead of beauty."

In former times, women were accustomed to add heirlooms, necklaces, collars, pearls, gems, and other ornaments to their delicate bodies, so that specific limbs might be adorned with them, and the eyes and minds of spectators might be delighted by these <term>splendid things</term> <note>original Greek: "αγλαϊσμασι"</note> as if by a <term>charm</term> <note>original Greek: "θελγητρω"</note>. In the same way today, our own foolish women walk about <term>clothed in expensive garments</term> <note>original Greek: "πολυτελεις εσθητας ημφιεσμεναι"</note>. If we look at their variety, nothing is more difficult than to write about the dress and finery of women. As minds are varied, so are the types of clothes and ornaments. The age has changed, and the habit has changed; if only the morals would change for the better! Silken garments, all-silk, and watered-silks are considered nothing unless they shine with gold and gems, or are adorned with chains. Today, she who dressed and adorned herself in the Spartan fashion might tomorrow use the Asiatic style. Thus, dress has never remained unchanged in the memory of any nation, nor of a single kind; and because of these changes, which existed once and still do, we cannot be certain of the nomenclature. Regarding Hebrew terms, the Nomenclators suggest that Hebrew writers must be consulted if we wish to draw out the inner power of the words. But even here, there are sometimes "Davuses" <note>slaves or meddlers from Roman comedy</note> and skeptics, especially regarding those words which remain even though the objects themselves have disappeared. The names by which the Prophet expresses women's ornaments are obscure because the "woman's world" <note>fashion/paraphernalia</note> common at that time has become obsolete. Today, the Jews themselves are ignorant of the terms for these garments, and it is troublesome to track them down, especially for ears

<column-break/>

<margin>
Women's
Cosme-
tics.
</margin>
not accustomed to such luxuries. We will set down some, if not all, of these terms, and propose what is suggested to us <term>visually</term> <note>original Greek: "καθ' ὄψιν"</note>. To maintain some order, let us follow the <term>cosmetic items</term> <note>original Greek: "τα κοσμητικα"</note> according to the parts of the body.

Starting from the top of the head: they exposed carefully arranged hair to the delight of onlookers. Isaiah mentions the *crisped hair* of the Jewish girls, the substitute for which, as a punishment, is *baldness*. The structure of the hair was varied with artistry; their wanton styling was either into a point or another form: *subtle, woven, added-on, interwoven with gold or gems, and formed with many allurements*. Tertullian <note>an early Christian author</note>, who was very well-versed in more elegant literature, calls curled hair <term>botronatum</term> <note>cluster-shaped</note>. This is derived from <term>cluster</term> <note>original Greek: "βοτρυς" and "βοτρυχος"</note>, meaning <term>plaited hair</term> <note>original Greek: "τειχες πλοκαμωδεις"</note> rounded like a neat cluster of grapes. Those <term>spirals</term> <note>original Greek: "ελικες"</note> and windings are elegantly likened to *grapes*, and that entire structure of hair, luxuriant with many such neat curls, is a *cluster or cluster-shaped*, "as if lying in clusters" <note>original Greek: "ὡς εν βοτρυσι κειμενη"</note>, appearing on the head no differently than several grapes crowded and heaped together in a bunch. This <term>cluster-like</term> <note>original Greek: "Βοστρυχωδης"</note> composition is a <term>lock of hair</term> <note>original Greek: "βοστρυχος"</note>.

The Etymologist <margin>column 201.</margin> says: "*Bostrychos* <note>a lock</note> is the *plaiting of hair*, from the word for *cluster*. For *botrychos* is *bostrychos*, that which is *cluster-like* in its shape, or that which is *hung like a cluster*." He explains the same with two testimonies, one from Sophocles and the other from Apollonius, whom he does not name. The first is from *Electra*:
-> "a freshly-cut lock of hair." <note>original Greek: "νεωρη βοστρυχον τετμημενον"</note> <-
The other is in the *Argonautica, Book 2, line 679*:
-> "the clustering locks rushed over his shoulders." <note>original Greek: "πλοχμοι βοστρυοεντες επερρωσοντο κιονθι"</note> <-
In common editions, it is "clustering" and "rushed." The words of Tertullian, however, appear in the book he wrote *On the Apparel of Women*: "Let Isaiah not rebuke any garment of purple, let him not reject any little moons <note>crescent ornaments</note>, let him not beat back any cluster-shaped hair."

The term <term>lock</term> <note>original Greek: "Βοστρυχος"</note> occurs twice in the *Song of Solomon*, where in the Hebrew <margin>chapter 5, verses 1, 2.</margin> it is <term>locks</term> <gloss>tzammot</gloss> and <term>curls</term> <gloss>kevutzot</gloss>, meaning "neat hair." The word <term>locks</term> <gloss>tzammot</gloss> is expressed in various ways by the Hebrews in this place. Some say that "hair" or *curls* are signified by it; so say Genebrardus, Pagninus, Clarius, Vatablus, and others. Some wish it to mean a *veil* and a covering for the face, as Rabbi David <margin>in the Book of Roots</margin> says Rabbi Jonah felt; Aben Ezra also feels this way, and Ghislerius proves it here on page 601. The Septuagint and Symmachus translated it thus: "outside of your silence" <note>original Greek: "εκτος της σιωπησεως σου"</note>. Ghislerius thinks that by the name "silence," they understood such great beauty of the bride that it moves those who see it with stupor and their minds with admiration, making them as if mute; he thinks they either read it as <term>your stupor</term> <gloss>tammushtcha</gloss> or <term>your silence</term> <gloss>damat-cha</gloss> from the root <term>to be silent</term> <gloss>dum</gloss>.

Indeed, <term>bostryx</term> and <term>bostrychos</term> refer to hair that is combed and curled or crisped with an iron, more often used for women's hair than men's. How much the hair of Samson was worth is known from the Book of Judges, which commends "the seven locks of his head" <note>original Greek: "τας επτα βοστρυχους της κεφαλης"</note>; for which one also reads in the same place, "the seven braids of his head" <note>original Greek: "τας επτα σειρας της κεφαλης"</note>, as if the curls hung like little chains. The <term>kalamis</term> <note>original Greek: "καλαμις"</note> was the hair-pin used for distinguishing and holding the hair, hence the <term>curling iron</term> <gloss>calamistrum</gloss>, which Servius interprets as a larger needle, which they used to twist the hair after heating it; it differs from the hair-pin, as the author teaches...

### Isaiah 3:16, 17, etc.

<margin>
Women's
ornaments.
</margin>
As Salmasius teaches in his notes on *Solinus, page 761*, specific and dedicated young handmaids were employed for these ornaments. Jerome is a witness to this in his *23rd Letter to Marcella, column 199*. Nor was Greece ignorant of "women with curled hair" <note>original Greek: βοστρυχιζούσας γυναῖκας</note> or hair "arranged in clusters" <note>original Greek: βοστρυδὸν κοσμέας</note>. Hesychius says in column 149 that "clustered" <note>original Greek: Βοτρυδὸν</note> refers to hair held one after another, like grapes in a cluster that are held close together and in a twist, or joined together. In Lucian, curly hair is called "spirals" <note>original Greek: ἔλικες</note> and "locks" <note>original Greek: βόστρυχοι</note>, *Volume 4, page 205*. And the handmaids who dyed the hair of delicate matrons with medicinal tinctures and sprinkled them with fragrant powder were called "psekades" <note>original Greek: ψεκάδες; literally "sprinklers"</note>, according to Budé. This custom of adorning the hair went by yet another name among the Greeks, called "korymbos" <note>original Greek: κόρυμβος</note>. A *korymbos* denotes anything at the highest point or protruding, which is why Herodotus uses it for the peak of a mountain when he says: "they fled reaching for the peak of the mountain." It was frequently used for pleated womanly hair; for they used to grow "hair crowned with a golden headband" <note>original Greek: κόμην χρυσῷ στρόφῳ κεκρωμυλώμενων</note>, to use the words of Suidas—that is, hair peaked with golden clusters. They seem to have been hairs fashioned and peaked into the appearance of a grape or a cluster; for *korymbos* occurs in reference to the berries and clusters of ivy. Regarding this hair ornament, the Scholiast on Thucydides says: "krobylos" <note>original Greek: κρώβυλος</note> was a type of braid or hair-weaving; for men it was called a *krobylos*, but for women it was a *korymbos*. Just as the members of the body become more perfect and charming through the cultivation of fine clothing, so the head is decorated by the shine of the hair, which is natural. Take away the foliage of a tree, and the whole tree is unpleasant. Take away the hair of a human head, and all beauty withers. This ornament of the head is obvious and clear to all, by which the brain is protected and clothed, so that it is not troubled by cold or heat. Just as nothing is fouler in a woman than a head stripped of its hair, so nothing is more charming than a head with a full mane of hair, as much in a male as in a female—insofar, clearly, as it is the natural grace and beauty of the hair that is born with the human. However, when it exceeds moderation, especially in males, that custom is to be blamed. Hence the Apostle [Paul] condemns the wanton custom of growing hair long in the manner of women as a proof of softness in men, requiring modesty in Christians by saying in *1 Corinthians 11:14-15*: *If a man has long hair, it is a disgrace to him.* <note>original Greek: Ἀνὴρ ἐὰν κομᾷ, ἀτιμία αὐτῷ ἐστι.</note> This opinion of the Apostle we shall explain not with our own words but with those of the Blessed Balduinus: <margin>Commentary on this passage, p. 440.</margin> *Nature for the Apostle Paul here is the same as the custom of that place and time, which they call a second nature. For even if natural reason and the constitution of the body suggests that women grow longer hair than men, yet no one would easily say it is done against nature if men also wish to grow longer hair. Certainly, the hair of Absalom is commended in 2 Samuel 14:26.* On the other hand, a great disgrace are hairs and manes that are adulterated or artificial, which the Greeks call "phenake" <note>original Greek: φενάκη</note> and "pinene" <note>original Greek: πινήνη</note>, meaning a "helmet placed around made of hair," which is convenient not only for women, but also, as Eustathius says, for "effeminate men" <note>original Greek: γυναικοζουμένοις ἀνδράσιν</note> who have been stripped of their own hair. And Xenophon says in his *Education of Cyrus, Book 8, 5*: *To see him adorned both with eye-paint and with the application of color and with false hair.* <note>original Greek: κόραις προσθέτοις</note> Regarding this "addition" of hair, let us hear Clement of Alexandria in the 3rd book of *The Pedagogue, sentence 11*, calling

<column-break/>

<margin>
Women's
ornaments.
</margin>
a woman adorned with "foreign hair, and through them (the hairs) another head." And Tertullian says: *You attach, besides, I know not what monstrosities of flimsy and woven hair-pieces, now in the manner of a cap, as a sheath for the head and a lid for the crown, now as a mound suggested at the back of the neck.* <margin>Book on the Veiling of Virgins, chapter 7.</margin> And a little later: *Be ashamed of these pollutions, lest you subject a Christian head to the spoils of someone else's head—perhaps an unclean person, perhaps a criminal and one destined for Gehenna <note>Hell</note>.* Jerome says nearly the same thing in his *2nd Letter, 8, to Demetrias, column 69, Volume 1*, writing: *When you were in the world, you loved the things of the world: to polish your face with rouge, and to paint your mouth with white lead; to adorn your hair and build a turreted crown with alien hair.* Hence Prudentius sketches the "turreted" crown thus in his *Psychomachia*:

> The turreted head is piled up high with twisted
> Hair, so that the added mass increases the built-up
> Curls, and the steep forehead carries a lofty peak.

As much labor was once applied to adorning the head as we find applied today. Seneca, in his book *On the Brevity of Life*, <margin>chapter 12, p. 707.</margin> seems to sketch this excessive anxiety over hair with these words: *What? Do you call those people "idle" for whom many hours are passed at the barber, while whatever grew the previous night is snipped away, while a consultation is held over every single hair, while either a disarrayed mane is restored or thinning hair is forced from here and there onto the forehead? How angry they get if the barber was a little too negligent, as if he were shearing a real man! How they flare up if anything is cut from their "mane," if anything lies out of order, unless everything has fallen back into its proper rings! Who among them would not rather the Republic be disturbed than his hair? Who is not more anxious about the beauty of his head than about his health? Who would not rather be more groomed than more honorable? You call these people "idle," who are occupied between the comb and the mirror.* The female sex is "body-loving" <note>original Greek: φιλοσώματον</note>, occupied in caring for the adornment of the body, which "body-love" they testify to with various ornaments with which they weigh down their soft and delicate bodies during the day. In adorning the head, the woman has worked more than is right; presently she prides herself on it with gold, gems, and silks. Regarding Judith, that heroic woman, it is read: that she fitly arranged the hair of her head. This some interpret as she made "grains" <note>original Latin: Grana</note>: What is this? Grains are hairs bent into a circle and scattered. Hence the Council of Braga prohibited: *Neither shall they let down "grains" in the pagan rite.* Moreover, the author of the book adds that she placed a *mitra* <note>turban or headdress</note> upon it. A *mitra* is an item in the woman's world, signifying an ornament or covering of the head, as demonstrated with many examples by Charles Paschasius in *On Crowns, book 4, chapter 20, p. 266 and chapter 21, p. 270*. God described the glory and splendor of His people with a many-colored thread and style through Ezekiel, chapter 16:10, a metaphor taken from the most splendid cultivation and ornament of the body. I shall begin to describe the matter using the hand of the Vulgate translator: *I washed you with water, and I cleansed your blood from you, and I anointed you with oil; And I clothed you with diverse colors, and I shod you with violet-colored leather, and I girded you, and I clothed you with fine linen.* In this place, the Hebrew uses the word "shesh" <note>original Hebrew: שש</note>. In what sense "shesh" is used is not known without ambiguity. Theodotio thought it sufficient if he put *mesi* <note>original Greek: μεσὶ</note>. Symmachus put "garment" <note>original Greek: ἔνδυμα</note> too generally. Aquila put "flowery" <note>original Greek: ἀνθιμον</note>. The Seventy <note>the Septuagint</note> used the artful word "trikhapton" <note>original Greek: τρίχαπτον; literally "woven of hair" or "fine net"</note>.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
**Page 566**

<margin>Women's cosmetics.</margin>
The word *trichapton* <note>original Greek: τριχαπτον</note> refers to a hair-net or hair-ornament, signifying a certain thin fabric that was drawn over the hair. Jerome translated it as "subtle" <note>fine or thin</note> and asserted that the seventy translators <note>The Septuagint</note> composed a new word for this novel item. He says: *When I diligently searched for what the word "trichapton" meant, which the Septuagint translated, and could find neither its use nor its etymology from any of the Greeks, I finally learned it was composed by the Septuagint.* It is a shadowy word if it was unknown even to the Greeks themselves. What, then, shall we bring forward to understand it? Suidas writes of this *trichapton*, as does the author of the *Etymologicum* (column 768): *Trichapton* is a silken weaving <note>original Greek: τὸ βομβύκινον ὕφασμα</note>, a highly prized garment. Hesychius says in column *trichapton*: a silken weaving fastened over the hair of the head <note>original Greek: βομβύκιον ὕφασμα ὑπὲρ τῶν τριχῶν κεφαλῆς ἁπτόμενον</note>. They understand it as a silken web in which loose hair is wrapped. Martial calls this kind of reticulum <note>small net</note>, which is usually drawn over the hair, a *capillare* <note>hair-cap</note> in *Epigrams, Book 3, 82, line 28*. Reuchlin <margin>2. On the Explanation of Words, page 249.</margin> understands it to be a silk garment woven with a subtle warp and woof, so fine that it either equals or surpasses the thinness of hairs. The Hebrews are ignorant of what the word *shesh* <note>Hebrew: שש; usually "fine linen"</note> signifies or what its origin is. But if the Septuagint were the first architects of the Greek name, it can be expressed by its composition as a textile either woven from hair or fit for covering the hairs of the head. To Theodoret, it was surely *a braid made of hair which is placed around the heads of women*. And to a certain Greek scholiast, it is a braid <note>original Greek: πλέξος</note> in which the hairs are entwined. Thus, the meaning of the Greek word must be deduced through its structure so that we may understand the sense of the passage in some way.

To adorn their foreheads, women wore images of *lunulae* <note>little moons or crescents</note>. These were *saharonim* <note>Hebrew: שהרונים</note>, "little gifts," or crescents, because they were round like the moon. In Hebrew, *sahar* <note>Hebrew: שהר</note> means roundness, from which the Chaldeans called the Moon *Sahara*, "the round one," because it is full. The Targum <note>Aramaic translation of the Bible</note> has "reticulated ornaments" <note>original Aramaic: כככא</note>. Arias translates it as "necklaces." The same word *Saharonim* is read in Judges 8:21, where the Targum calls them "collars" <note>original Aramaic: ענקא</note>. Schindler explains them as "women's mirrors," round like the moon, and spectacles. Moses describes this forehead ornament with a general term in Genesis 35:4: *Nezem* <note>Hebrew: נזם</note>, which signifies a silver, gold, or gemmed ornament for the nose or ear. One kind hangs from a thread tied to the forehead; the other is inserted into the ear and hangs from it. Regarding this, Blessed Luther says <margin>Commentary on this passage, folio 196 a.</margin>: *The word Nezem itself signifies a little moon or a golden semi-circle, like a crescent moon, with which they adorned the forehead from one ear to the other, like a diadem. Today we call them* 
-> Pearls, or golden borders and hairbands. <-
<note>original German: Perlein/ oder gülden Porten und Haarband</note>
Aaron also had a *Nezem* among his priestly ornaments. Later, kings used them and made diadems from them. It was customary at that time to adorn the heads of statues with such crescents out of reverence for the divinity, so they might have some appearance of holiness. *Although, according to Lyra's opinion, it is also possible that priests used them.*

Since physical beauty for the most part pertains to the sense of sight—for that living splendor shining in the body reaches the vision, consisting of the proper symmetry of parts, which two things joined together create beauty—nevertheless, through this external sense, beauty is perceived confusedly. It is rightly judged by common sense, and most exactly by reason. That living splendor

<column-break/>

arises from the proper measurement of the whole body and its individual parts, and from the harmony of the joints, <margin>Women's cosmetics.</margin> parts, and colors of the body. Its consideration must be one thing in the female sex and another in the male. A man’s beauty consists more in a defined mass and a fit and decent proportion of limbs than in sweetness of color or the effeminate use of clothing. A beard adorns a man, to the cultivation of which Lycurgus did not exhort in vain. Regarding color, women are praised if it is natural, without deceit, and if it is mixed in a certain proportion—florid, vivid, rich, and full. Hence, "dark-eyed women" <note>original Greek: μελανόφθαλμοι</note> are in favor with almost everyone for their grace and charm. Horace commends Lycus for the blackness of his eyes <margin>Odes, Book 1.</margin>:

> And Lycus with his black eyes, and with his black 
> -> hair handsome. <-

Homer praises Chryseis as the "glancing-eyed maiden" <note>original Greek: ἑλικωπίδα κώρην; Iliad, Book 1</note>, which the scholiast explains as "black-eyed" <note>original Greek: μελανόφθαλμον</note>, from which she is "noble," for *helikon* <note>original Greek: ἑλίκον</note> means black. She is also called "dark-browed" <note>original Greek: κυανώφις</note>, a girl endowed with black eyebrows in Theocritus <note>Idyll 13, verse 18</note>; compare Tiraqueau, *On Matrimonial Laws*, 2, number 38. If nature does not show itself here, women seek art to bring on color, laying hands on the Creator by staining the face with rouge and seduction, and by applying a plaster coating. On the medication of the face, there exists an elegy among Ovid’s works, beginning thus:

> Learn what care commends the face, girls,
> And in what way your beauty must be preserved.

For the female sex is very studious of beauty and rejoices exceedingly to be seen in this way—by combing, dressing, rougeing, and polluting the face with seductions. But to smear the skin with medicines and to stain the cheeks with white lead from the apothecary’s storeroom <note>original Greek: ταμιείῳ</note> belongs to prostitutes, who are accustomed to wear a face for sale. Those who expose their breasts put forward what they carry inside. Such was Jezebel, smearing her face with pigments; and that painted old woman in Aristophanes <margin>Plutus, Act 5, Scene 5, verse 1</margin>:

> For now she is like a shopkeeper's wares,
> But if this white lead is washed away,
> You will see the rags of her face clearly revealed.

They have an itch themselves and they provoke and invite others; by exposing their bellows to the air, they betray that they have a fire inside to be blown out. They rejoice to turn cold into heat and to break the ice of the cold-hearted. They labor with all their might to induce a form and skin upon themselves more beautiful and excellent than God the Creator intended; yet, as experience witnesses, they bring upon themselves a more deformed skin. They scandalize Christian eyes with this very dye, says Jerome <margin>Letter 2, column 195</margin>: *those who paint their faces and eyes with rouge and certain dyes, whose plastered faces, deformed by excessive whiteness, mimic idols; if by chance a teardrop breaks out from the improvident, it flows down in a furrow. Not even a number of years can teach them that they are old women; they build up their crowns with borrowed hair and polish past youth over aged wrinkles; finally, they are composed as trembling little maidens before a flock of grandchildren.* Let a Christian woman blush if nature compels decorum, or if care of the flesh causes lust. Hence Paula, the wife of Toxotius, often wept with tears because she had worn a painted face, and when Jerome discouraged her from excessive weeping <margin>Letter 27 to Eustochium, column 228.</margin>
-> she said: <-
