<meta>This page continues the discussion of feminine adornment based on the prophecies of Isaiah, moving from hairstyles to cosmetics, veils, and breast-bands, while contrasting ancient modesty with the perceived decadence of early modern fashion.</meta>

### ISAIAH 3:16, 17, etc.

<margin>Worldly adornments of women.</margin>
She says: *The face must be humbled, which I often painted with purple dye, white lead, and antimony <note>Antimony, or stibium, was used as a dark eyeliner in antiquity.</note> against God's command; the body must be afflicted, which once indulged in many luxuries.* To preserve the beauty of the face, women in the past used *sun-shades* <note>original: "umbellae"</note> to protect themselves against the heat of the sun, as we learn from *Martial, Book 14, Epigram 28*. For this reason, Eastern women walked about veiled; hence Sarah was commanded by Abimelech to cover herself with a veil when he said: *Is this (the silver) (or this husband) a covering of the eyes for you?* <note>original Hebrew: הִוא־לָךְ כְּסוּת עֵינַיִם; referring to Genesis 20:16</note>. Regarding these words, Vorstius notes in his *Observations on the Pirke* (p. 211): it was a fitting sense, and consistent with what preceded, *if it is said that Abimelech wished to suggest by this figure of speech that Sarah should henceforth be veiled, as a symbol of subjection and marital authority, by which her modesty might be preserved safe from the snares and violence of others.* The word *pargod* or *pargoda* <note>original Hebrew: פרגודא ,פרגוד</note> signifies a *curtain, veil, or tapestry* in the Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> on Exodus 26:31, 33 and Job 26:9; likewise a cloak that serves as a veil, or a broad tunic. Among the Talmudic writers, it is also read as a specific type of garment. From this, Buxtorf derives the word *Paragauda* <note>original Greek: παραγαῦδι</note>, a term used by both Latins and Greeks, whether they borrowed it from the Hebrews or the Hebrews from them. Martinius struggles greatly in investigating its etymology. Among the Greeks, this face-covering goes by more than one name: they are called *prosopia* <note>original Greek: προσώπια</note>, with which women covered their countenances. Also *prosopeion* <note>original Greek: προσωπείον</note>, from which Hesychius says: *prosopeion: what is now called the woman’s mask* <note>original Greek: προσωπείον, ἡ νῦν καλουμένη τῶν γυναικῶν προσωπίς</note>; the French call it a *masque*, whence the Hebrew *palshamesh* <note>original Hebrew: פלשמש</note> as if from *palash* <note>original Hebrew: פלש</note> meaning *to cover*. From the face we come to the adornment of the neck. That word *ha-netiphot* <note>original Hebrew: הנטפות</note>, which the Prophet mentions in verse 19, some interpret as *neck-chains*, others as *pearls*, others as *vessels*. But why vessels? They say they are vessels in which milk or balsam is stored; in Hebrew *nataph* <note>original Hebrew: נטף</note> means "to drip," whence comes that which usually drips from the myrrh tree; called *stakte* <note>original Greek: στακτὴ</note> by the Greeks. And from this they bring forth the phrase *tas netiphot* <note>original Hebrew: טס נטפות</note> to explain it. Rabbi Kimchi observes that the Arabic word *Natef*, with the Arabic article, refers to a pure pearl or pure *bdellium* <note>A fragrant resin resembling myrrh.</note>. But how the Greek *stalagmos* <note>original Greek: σταλαγμὸς; a drop or earring</note> fits, we do not know. If we turn to *nataph*, how far-fetched it will be, unless we understand "unions" <note>Large, high-quality pearls.</note> which, around the edges, resemble falling drops of water or icicles. Truly, Caecilius called a type of earring a *Stelagmium*, and Salmasius notes in his commentary on *Solinus* (p. 1334) that earrings of this shape are called *stalagma* <note>original Greek: σταλαγμα</note> by the Greeks. Among the ornaments of virgins in *Jeremiah 2:32*, the *breast-band* is also recorded, concerning which Paschasius Rat-
<margin>on p. 44. column 1296.</margin>
bertus says: *With breast-bands, the entire ambition of the chest is covered, and the slackness of the breasts is composed, and then the vitals are bound tight lest the belly swell too broadly.* But there are some bands with which Virgins are adorned, and others with which matrons, as we have said, are constricted. Today, this distinction of bands has ceased, since the barriers of modesty have been broken down; out of a loathing for Germanic simplicity, our women wish to be commended by French fashion, with such luxury that they sin most greatly on the very threshold, since they extend their naked necks and naked breasts even below the nipples. Regarding the swelling breasts of girls, Aristotle says in *History of Animals, Book 7, Ch. 1*: *In females, the rising of the breasts occurs, and what are called the 'reeds' break forth.* <note>original Greek: τοῖς θήλεσιν ἥ τε ἔπαρσις γίνεται τῶν μασῶν, καὶ τὰ καλάμινα καλέμενα καταρρήγνυται</note>. Gaza translates this: *The breasts rise in women, which is called 'to brother' [fratrare], and what are called the menses break out.* "To brother" <note>term: fratrare; an archaic Latin term for the swelling of breasts in puberty.</note> refers to the swelling of the breasts, as does "to sister" <note>term: sororiare</note>. For so Sextus Pompeius teaches: *Breasts are said to 'sister' when they first swell.* Plautus used it thus, in these verses from Scaliger’s emendation: *Then the nipples first began to 'brother'; I meant to say, they 'sistered'—why waste words?* Nonius says a *Strophium* is *a short band that restrains the virginal swelling of the nipples.* Hence Diodorus Siculus in *Book 3* spoke of *projecting breasts*, *downward-hanging*, and *lifting up* <note>original Greek: ἐξέχοντας μαστὸς, κασεδής, μετειωρίζειν</note>; see Gebhard's *Ancient Readings, Book 2, Ch. 13*. These bands having been cast aside today, one may now see the slashed garments of "slashed monsters," which skillfully represent to us their own "slashed" souls: breasts naked down to the halfway point, and those who lack breasts fill the empty space with rags and other things of that kind, lest anything be missing that could provoke immodesty. Johannes Huss <note>The Bohemian church reformer (c. 1369–1415).</note> once complained about these clothes in his *Book on the Abomination of Carnal Priests and Monks*, whose words we may quote:

<margin>Worldly adornments of women.</margin>
> *For now one may see, he says, women—and a little while ago much more immodestly—walking about in public so dressed, all of them, that it is or was almost impossible for a beholder not to burn with lust, incited by their naked flesh. Women wear their garments so cut away from above, and equally wide at the openings, that anyone might clearly see their gleaming flesh almost to the middle of their bared breasts. They do this everywhere, in the temples of God before priests and clerics just as in the marketplace, but even more so at home. And that part of their breasts which remained covered was, as was said a little before, made to protrude so artfully and pushed up that they appeared like two horns upon their chests.*

Thus far his words. Today our virgins, even those who seem modest to themselves, cover certain parts of the body in such a way that they appear through thin linen, so much so that they seem to desire to be seen and touched. Against this madness of baring the nipples and breasts, François Lambert <note>A French Protestant reformer (1486–1530).</note> of Avignon wrote in his book *On Sacred Marriage*, which (as Gesner calls it in his *Library*) he sent with a most brilliant and useful prologue to Francis, King of France. I wish the French would heed his words, for from them that poison and "malignant habit" <note>term: cacoëthes; a medical term used here metaphorically for a bad custom or itch.</note> of naked flesh passed to the Germans, whose dress was formerly more refined and bashful. *Christian wives,* he writes on *folios 61b and 62a, should strive especially for that adornment which indicates a Christian heart. This is chiefly situated in works that agree with the word of piety, namely, that which proceeds from a magnificent adornment of the heart—that is, from faith. But the precious adornment of gold, gems, and the like, where it is especially dearly loved and sought, belongs to the heathens rather than to Christians. Therefore, a decent and moderate adornment befits the wives of the faithful. For what use is such superfluous dress to those who profess the Cross, which all Christians do? It should be enough if they please God and their husbands, and that the Church of God is not offended by them, but rather built up.* It is a matter of great difficulty to define, in such things, how much ornament each person should have. The conditions of men are various. Likewise, the customs of regions are various. Therefore, let each be dressed according to their condition and the custom of the region, unless the custom itself...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Worldly adornments of women.</margin>
...is corrupted. Indeed, a garment must be considered "corrupt" when there is excess in its style, price, or quantity. The style is excessive when it looks more toward lust than toward decency, such as when clothes are made so that others can see the breasts and flesh. The price is excessive when it is not decency or utility that is sought, but the glory of costliness. The quantity is excessive when many garments are kept where two, three, or at most four would suffice. Certainly, only pride causes such excesses. Afterward, the author warns above all those who serve in the ministry of the altar and the Church to take care that their wives and daughters are not caught in this excess. However, it cannot be expressed with words sufficiently mournful how many today are prepared for pride and lust; let those pompous men listen to the words of the theologian Lambert <note>Likely Francis Lambert of Avignon (1487–1530), a Protestant Reformer.</note>: *Those who are Priests or Evangelists are the leaders of the people; it is necessary for them to ensure with all diligence that they teach the people not only by word, but also by deeds, and show themselves in all things as an example of a truly Gospel-centered life. Therefore, in their own adornment and that of their wives, and in all else, let them maintain such a middle ground and temperance that they show neither laziness and ignorance through neglect, nor levity, arrogance, and pride through excessive effort and novelty.*

**Bracelets** <note>original: "Armillæ"</note> are the proper decoration of the arms, which are called "arm-pieces" by some ancient writers, from which comes the French *bracelet*. A "dextral" is that which adorns the right hand. "Brachials" <note>from the Latin 'brachium' meaning arm</note> embraced the entire length of the arm including the shoulders, while "dextrals" covered only the wrist. Among the *ornaments of the wrists* <note>original Greek: κοσμήματα τῶν καρπῶν</note>, Pollux <note>Julius Pollux, a 2nd-century Greek grammarian.</note> lists *wrist-bands, armlets, and bangles* <note>original Greek: τὰ περιχάρπια, ψέλια, χλιδῶνας</note>. According to Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist.</note>, an *armlet* <note>original Greek: Ψέλιον</note> is a *decoration of the hand*, though Strabo expands the term, applying it to both the wrist and the arm. Polybius refers to *hand-bands* <note>original Greek: Περιχείρους</note> as armlets. *Bangles* <note>original Greek: χλιδῶνες</note> were looser and used by the more delicate, named from *luxury or softness* <note>original Greek: χλιδὴ</note>. Bracelets <note>original: "Armilli"</note>, although they look to the shoulders <note>original: "armos"</note> by the force of their origin, nevertheless passed to the hands, which in a broad sense includes both the arm and the outer hand. Hence, the term "brachials" fits both parts. Xenophon, in Book 1 of the *Education of Cyrus*, relates that the Medes wore *armlets around their hands* <note>original Greek: τὰ ψέλια περὶ ταῖν χεροῖν</note>. They were most often made of gold, which is why the Gauls are called *gold-bearers* <note>original Greek: χρυσοφοροῦντες</note> by Strabo in Book 4. Scylax, in his *Circumnavigation*, notes that Ethiopian women made their armbands out of ivory: *their women use ornaments of ivory armlets* <note>original Greek: αἱ γυναῖκες αὐτῶν χρῶνται κόσμῳ ψελίοις τοῦ ἐλέφαντος</note>. From a passage in Juvenal’s *Satire 9*, some guess they were even made of amber: *to whom you might send large ambers,* namely bracelets or spheres made of amber. Bracelets are also counted among pledges, which is why Judah said to Tamar: *What pledge shall I give you? She answered: Your signet ring and your bracelet, and the staff you have in your hand.* Genesis 38:18.

<margin>Chapter 10:3, 4.</margin>
Regarding Judith, the author testifies that *having put off the garments of her widowhood, she put on festive clothes, in which she used to be adorned when her husband Manasseh was alive, and she took sandals for her feet, and bracelets, armbands, etc.* Among the singular ornaments are *bangles* <note>original Greek: χλιδῶνες</note>, which are usually attributed to both the neck and the arm. Hence Hesychius says: *Bangles are ornaments which women are accustomed to wear around their arms and necks* <note>original Greek: χλιδῶνες, κόσμοι, ὧν αἱ γυναῖκες περὶ τοῖς βραχίοισιν εἰώθασι φορεῖν καὶ τοῖς τραχήλοις</note>. So in 2 Samuel 1:10: *and the bracelet that was on his arm* <note>original Hebrew: וְאֶת-הַצְּעָדָה אֲשֶׁר עַל-זְרֹעוֹ</note>, where the Septuagint reads *a bangle upon the arm* <note>original Greek: χλιδὼν ἐπὶ τῷ βραχίονι</note>. Soft cultivation of clothing and excessive preparation show a soft soul and lustful manners. Those who wish to entrap men with their allurements have 

<column-break/>

delightful steps, lustful clothing, and immodest gestures. Frivolous bodies are accustomed to decorate the frame with theatrical colors; there are wrinkles, and they betray by an external pattern the evil that lies hidden within, spending the whole day on the grooming of now this, now that limb. Since this is so common, a name—though perhaps not as common—has arisen: *laikastheias* <note>relating to harlotry or lewdness</note> according to the Etymologists, who are convinced it comes from the intensive particle *la* and *kazo*, meaning "I adorn." Perhaps our words "Ross! Ratz!" <note>Likely contemporary German slang for something tawdry or flashy.</note> come from that unseemly adornment. Eustathius, commenting on Homer, says: *harlots (laikastriai) are derived from the verb laikazein (to act lewdly). The verb itself becomes "laikastikon" and "kazein," which means to adorn one’s beauty improperly* <note>original Greek: λαικάστριαι, τουτέστι, πόρναι... τὸ κάζειν, ὅ ἐστι κοσμῆσαι τὴν ὥραν ἐκ δεόντως</note>. Aristophanes, quoted in Athenaeus Book 13, writes that the Peloponnesian War flared up for the Greeks *out of three harlots* <note>original Greek: ἐκ τριῶν λαικαστριῶν</note>: Simaetha and two Aspasias who were snatched by the Megarians. Among the vicious types of clothing, the Prophet also recounts those which revel in a *Syrma* <note>A long, trailing robe or train.</note>, whose tail sweeps the ground. A flowing and superfluous garment seemed intolerable to Isaiah and not to be endured at all. The flaunting of such a garment argues for a certain "softness," which the comic poet Plautus also noted in *The Little Carthaginian*, writing: *Surely this is the race of women with their trailing tunics.* God allows adornment for women, but not *costly and excessive* <note>original Greek: πολυτελῆ καὶ περιττόν</note>; He wants them adorned with moderation, not sumptuously. He wants them to please their husbands with modesty rather than makeup, with temperance rather than gold, with piety rather than emeralds. A woman who pursues piety does not seek adornment in sumptuous clothes, but in the management of the home and the education of children. The ornaments of an honest matron are honest manners, not robes sweeping the ground nor stoles woven with gold. Melissa writes to Clareta (folio 65b) that she permits no other *good order* <note>original Greek: εὐκοσμίαν</note> than this: *The ornament of a woman who wishes to please her own husband is her character, and not her robes. For it is beautiful for a free woman to be modest for her own husband but not for her neighbors. You should have a blush on your face as a sign of modesty instead of rouge, and goodness and decency and sobriety instead of gold and emeralds.* <note>original Greek: τᾶς ποθ' ἕνα τὸν ἴδιον... σωφροσύνην ἀντὶ χρυσοῦ καὶ σμαράγδου</note>. A woman adorned in that way is best adorned for her husband. But those who walk in a winding *Syrma* sweeping the earth with hanging borders—indeed, with tails following behind—cover their tracks like foxes, and wherever they go, they stir up dust like a whirlwind of a storm. Isaiah graphically described their luxury in dress and its punishment. The Pope drags a long *Syrma*, which he is accustomed to wear if a Legate of either the Emperor or a King is present when they go on foot to the church. Balthasar Mentzius saw this in Rome, where he stayed for three years; he saw the Legate of Emperor Maximilian, Count Nicolaus von der Arche, standing by to carry Pope Pius V's train as a sign of obedience and reverence toward the Vicar of Christ, as he reported in his *Genealogy of the Margraves of Brandenburg*. Alcibiades <note>A famous Athenian statesman and general known for his flamboyance.</note> used to walk proudly with a long trail of purple clothing, whose birth, wealth, prosperity, vigor in battles, crowd of friends and servants, prudence, elo...

### Isaiah 3:16, 17, etc.

<margin>Worldly ornaments of women.</margin>
<margin>In Plutarch's *Life of Alcibiades*, page 198.</margin>
...when Plutarch had commended the eloquence of Alcibiades, he added also his vices, among which were luxury, revelry, love affairs, and the purple garments he dragged through the forum, <note>original: "συρτὰς ἐσθήτων ἀλυγώτων ἑλκομένων δι' ἀγορᾶς" — "trailing garments of unwashed clothes dragged through the marketplace"</note>. He very aptly uses the word for "trailing," as it is characteristic of women to show such pride. For Greek women used to wear long robes with a **Train** <note>original: "Syrmate"</note>, from which comes the frequent epithet in Homer, "tunic-draggers" and "robe-draggers" <note>original: "ἑλκεχίτωνες, ἑλκεσιπέπλος"</note>. Hence the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> in this passage uses the phrase "by dragging" <note>original: "τῷ σύρειν"</note> not without emphasis; regarding this, the Lexicon of Scapula says: "Snakes *drag* <note>original: "σύρουσι"</note> their bodies because they move by drawing themselves along." In Plutarch's *Life of Antony*, it is also used for those who use rakes to pull stubble or similar things into a pile, and for those who sweep filth on a floor with brooms, as seen in Aristotle, Dioscorides, Hesychius, and Theophrastus. From this comes **Syrma**, a specific name for a garment that is dragged. It refers to a certain long robe which those who wear it seem to drag behind them as they walk, according to Pollux. For this reason, Blessed Martin Luther translated the Hebrew word <term>שוליו</term> <note>shulav — hems or trains</note>—which others think is the same as a drum or moving to a drumbeat (expressed elsewhere in Hebrew as moving the feet rhythmically)—as "wagging" or "tailing" <note>original: "Schwäntzen"</note>. Following this, Forster says in his Lexicon that it refers to the thudding or striking of a longer garment against the ground. The Church Fathers and other Doctors of the Church explained it in the same way. Cyprian <margin>On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins, p. 10.</margin> says: "Let chaste and modest virgins avoid the attire of the unchaste, the clothing of the immodest, the insignias of brothels, and the ornaments of harlots. Isaiah, full of the Holy Spirit, also cries out and rebukes the daughters of Zion, adorned with gold, silver, and fine clothing; he reproves those abounding in ruinous wealth and departing from God through the delights of the world. 'The daughters of Zion are haughty,' he says, 'and walk with heads held high, with glancing eyes and mincing steps, dragging their tunics and playing with their feet.'" Cyril, in his *Commentary on Isaiah*, says: "At the same time they drag their tunics and play with their feet; it is likely they do this to perfect their 'elegance,' though it is a profession of harlotry and an extreme proof of abomination." Basil the Great says on this passage: "By the gait of their feet, dragging their tunics and letting their robes hang to their ankles, they showed their inclination toward fulfilling lust." And shortly after: "That a woman takes more pleasure in herself and indulges more luxuriously is proven by that soft gait with the garment dragged along the ground." Similar things are read in Clement of Alexandria, Fulgentius, Chrysostom, Ambrose, and Bernard's letter to the Virgin Sophia. Therefore, what Isaiah said against the proud women of his age can be applied to our own time, which is far too ingenious in inventing new types and forms of clothing. For a long time, a type of flowing dress has prevailed among our women, which sweeps the ground with a train; I saw such dresses used by the more honorable women in Ulm, and it is reported to be in use elsewhere. Alvarus Pelagius mentions them <margin>On the Lament of the Church, book 2, chapter 76.</margin>: "Today," he says, "noble women magnify their fringes, as do certain vain and boastful Spaniards who leave their arms bare and carry long cloths for show. The Devil rides upon their trains <note>original: "Suppara"</note>, as a certain saint once saw." Hence the verse:
> -> Wear long trains, if you wish every mouth to be silent. <-
Johann Geiler von Kaysersberger also mentions these "tailed garments" in his *Mirror of Fools*, section 4.

<column-break/>

<margin>Worldly ornaments of women.</margin>
In *The Bells* <note>original: "Nola"</note> 7, p. 17, where he says: "The seventh bell is outside the person, or rather, decorating oneself beyond the feet, head, and body. How can this be done? It is done first through long tails, which they drag behind them in the mud, especially women and even some priests and prelates. Under this bell are the ladies who have long tails behind them, covering the earth with precious clothes while not caring for the nakedness of Christ in the poor; with their tails they collect fleas and stir up dust for men. It is to be feared that the Devil rests in their tails." So also Bernardino of Siena, in his *Sermon 47 against Painted Women*, censured women who carried tails on their garments: "Now all of Italy is full of tailed women. Nothing else remains to be done for them to appear as complete animals. They have tails and horns; for in some parts, horns have even come to women in various numbers <note>A reference to the 'hennin' or horned headdresses popular in the 15th century.</note>. Those tails hung mostly on precious garments, not cheap ones," as he says in the same work. "Tails are commonly made on expensive wool or silk garments, not on the cheapest cloths, for that would be a deformity in the eyes of the world." Hence Erasmus writes <margin>In the Preacher, book 1, p. 301.</margin>: "Nor were there lacking heralds of the Word who cried out against the tails which common women, provoked by the example of the great, had begun to drag behind them, shouting that demons rode upon them." Concerning that "riding upon them," see *The Garden of the Soul's Roots* <note>original: "der Seelen Wurzgart"</note>, printed in Ulm by Conrad Dinckmut in 1488, chapter 20. Jewish women did not just arrange their eyes, necks, and heads with care, but also their loins and feet. For they walked with luxury, and "virgin feet" were held in high honor among the Jews, according to the writings of Rabbi Moses ben Maimon <note>Also known as Maimonides.</note>. The Hebrew word is derived from the name <term>עכס</term> <note>akas</note>, which signifies a "fetter" or "shackle," and verse 18 teaches it is taken for an ornament of the feet in which they took pride. Some think this alludes to the laws of rhythm and the patterns of steps observed in dances, or to the shackles used by veterinarians to modify the gait of horses and pacers until they are accustomed to the patterns. From the school of the Rabbis, Kimchi understood it as the sound made while walking; these are his words: "The gait of those women was not modest and steady, as that of matrons ought to be, but unsteady and loose. With both eyes and feet, they showed what they carried in their hearts. With necks held high, they displayed the elation of their souls, for it is the mark of a humble soul to walk with the head bowed. By the winking of their eyes, they made public the lewdness they kept hidden in their impure breasts." Kimchi says: <note>original: "שיחבלו בהן הנואפים" — "so that adulterers might be snared by them"</note> "Unchaste eyes are the messengers of an unchaste heart." A soft gait is the attendant of a dissolute soul. They seem to have made a sound while walking, though it is uncertain whether they wore little bells or rattles on their feet to make them ring. For those anklets <note>original: "Periscelides"</note> were chained, so that they could produce a sound or tinkling during the gait. Hence the Talmudists in the tractate *Shabbath*, chapter 6, relate the same: they were bound with small golden chains like bracelets to moderate their steps, lest they stride too far, or <note>original: "בתוליהן תפסחנה" — "damage their virginity"</note>. <meta>This page continues the discussion of feminine vanity and luxury, shifting from the "trailing robes" of the previous page to footwear, jewelry, and the moral implications of fashion as seen through the lens of biblical prophecy and classical history.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<column-break/>

<margin>
Worldly ornaments of women.
7 Turcogr. p 496. <note>original: "Turcogr." — refers to Martin Crusius's *Turcograecia*, a 16th-century work on Greek culture under Ottoman rule.</note>
</margin>
As you might say with Apuleius, even shoes were adorned with gems; regarding these, Novarinus and Raderus comment on Martial 12.49. Crusius, following Gerlach, notes the pride of Greek women even in their footwear, and one can see the same in Italian women in Bosquier (p. 188), who use a raised type of shoe to appear taller in stature. In the past, shoes were also made with neatly cut slits and holes, which were called "slotted" <note>original: "σχιστὰ" (schista)</note> because of that elegance. Pollux testifies that a certain "lavish and delicate" <note>original: "πολυτελὲς καὶ θρυπτικὸν"</note> type of footwear went by this name. Even today, "finely-split" <note>original: "λεπτοχιδεῖς" (leptochideis)</note> or segmented shoes are in use among more delicate women; through the thin incisions or slits, silk or some other precious material placed underneath shows through. Papinius (Silvae, Book 5, 2) mentions the "little moons" <note>original: "lunularum" — crescent-shaped ornaments worn on the shoes of Roman patricians</note> on the shoes of the upper class, as do Juvenal (Satire 7) and his ancient commentator, Martial (Epigrams, Books 1 and 2, ep. 29), and others. Moreover, in Isaiah, God threatens to take away and banish that delightful luxury, and especially the luxury of the feet and their pride (v. 18). Let us bring forward here what Alvarus Pelagius writes regarding these words of Isaiah:

<margin>
2. on the Lament of the Church. 76. fol. 205. b. <note>Alvarus Pelagius was a 14th-century bishop known for his critiques of contemporary morals.</note>
</margin>
> *In 그날 [that day] the Lord will take away the finery of their shoes and the little moons. The "little moon" is a type of necklace; specifically, they are golden beads hanging down in the likeness of the moon—hence "lunulated" means adorned with little moons. And "torques," that is, a twisted band, a golden circle around the neck descending from the throat to the chest. And "monilia" [necklaces]. A "monile" or "munile" is an ornament for a woman's breast—not like those of the immodest Spanish women, many of whom, especially the commoners, uncover their chest and breasts—it is meant to "fortify" <note>A wordplay in Latin between "monile" (necklace) and "munire" (to fortify/protect).</note> the woman's chest so that sinners cannot put their hand into her bosom. And "armillas," that is, collars or bracelets for the arm, specifically for the right hand; these were originally for men, named from the "virtue of arms" <note>A pun on "arma" (weapons/arms) and "armilla" (bracelet).</note> granted to them. And "mitras." A "mitra" is a Phrygian cap protecting the head, such as the head-covering of devout women. And "discriminalia" [hair-dividers]. These are the pins with which divided hair is tied back, which "discern" [separate] the head from the man, or the hairs from one another. And "perichelides" [anklets]. A "perichelis" is a woman's ornament around the arms, or rather around the legs, by which their gait is adorned. And "murenulas." A "murenula" is a woman's ornament woven from brass or metal in a certain playful, winding pattern in the likeness of a lamprey <note>original: "murena" — a type of eel-like fish</note>, which is fitted to adorn the neck. "Olfactoriola." An "olfactorium" is a woman's perfume vessel in which scents are carried. And "inaures" [earrings]. An earring is a ring that was once worn in a pierced ear. And even now in Spain, it is worn by many Christian ladies on the forehead, but more so by the women of the Saracens and Jews.*

What, then, is a woman adorned beyond measure, if not that statue of Nebuchadnezzar? Its head is golden because of the golden ornaments; its chest silver, adorned with necklaces. But if you wish to know the foot of the statue, you will find it is clay. According to the Oppian Law in Rome, as recorded in Livy, no woman was to use a garment of varied colors, nor have more than half an ounce of gold, nor ride in a horse-drawn carriage in the city or town (or within a mile of it) except for the sake of a sacrifice; nor was she to use superfluous finery or hang more than an ounce [of gold] from her ears. A chaste and modest woman rejects those superfluous ornaments, as she can obtain the glory of perfect modesty without them.

<column-break/>

So Tertullian discusses this, though in an obscure passage: <margin>Worldly ornaments of women. Book on women's dress.</margin> *And if any modesty can be believed to exist among the Pagans, it is established as so imperfect and unformed that, although it may hold onto itself somewhat in the mind, it dissolves into license in its outward habit. Due to the vanity of the nations, they seek "solace" (from feminine ornaments and necklaces, as he says in the book "On the Cloak," that they "console the neck with necklaces," because in these things beauty-loving <note>original: "φιλοκόσμος" (philokosmos)</note> women establish their comfort) and thus escape the reality of it.* Susanna, the illustrious Hebrew woman and the glory of true modesty, teaches women that an unaffected appearance is the more beautiful ornament of their beauty. By her example, let us restrain ourselves from the luxury of clothes; let us not carry our thoughts to France or England to bring back the pomp of dress from there. While the spirit of the Israelites lingered on foreign clothes and lifted its mind from the land of Israel to the mountains of Moab, it happened by the just judgment of God that they became prey to those they imitated. Suit yourself with the national footwear in humility of soul, and flee the "nets" <note>Likely referring to decorative hairnets or veils.</note> of foreign women. Future changes are often indicated by an external change of clothes, or names, or similar things. *The matter of names is small and silent in itself, just like clothing, but both are indicative of great and noteworthy events, which one can learn from history; they show that when these things change, it is demonstrated that the previous laws have been altered along with them,* as Camerarius writes in his Homilies (p. 287). With what face and what finery virgins and women now walk about is such that it is obvious to the eyes and obvious to the tongues—not for the sake of slandering, but for judging rightly. For what good man would not detest that shameless nakedness, even in the very middle of winter? Clothing ought to be used for utility and modesty: for utility, to ward off the harm of the cold; for modesty, because it ought to veil those things that provoke the lack of restraint in young men. But if we look at the finery of our age, in most cases the dress is not meant to guide the eyes of young men, but to solicit them, so that what is forbidden might be desired. Clothing is no longer a covering for chastity, but a snare and a trap. Parents—indeed, the very overseers of laws and sacred rites—raise their daughters not as if they were bringing them up for chaste marriage or keeping them for unpolluted nuptials, but as if they were pimps raising their girls for some kind of profit. There was a wonderful zeal for modesty among the Jewish people, who did not think modesty would be safe unless it was most strictly guarded, both at home and abroad. Consider their living quarters, for from this one can understand their morals. The virgins stayed at home in a secret chamber; we shall not speak of widows or wives. That house was like a cloister and a training-ground for modesty; it was the "women's quarters" <note>original: "γυναικωνίτις" (gynaeconitis)</note>. If they went out, they went with their faces covered. They did not move about in public with curled hair, soaked in perfumes, with lascivious eyes, bare necks, exposed breasts, and immodest tongues. But now, the face, the dress, and the gait solicit the minds of both young and old.

### ISAIAH 7:20

> In that day the Lord will shave with a razor hired from beyond the River—with the king of Assyria—the head and the hair of the feet, and it will also take away the beard. <note>original Hebrew: "ביום ההוא יגלח אדני בתער השכירה בעברי נהר במלך אשור את־הראש ושער הרגלים וגם את־הזקן תספה"</note>
> 
> In that day the Lord will shave with the drunken razor beyond the river, the king of the Assyrians, the head, and the hair of the feet, and will take away the beard. <note>original Greek: "Ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ ξυρήσει κύριος ἐν τῷ ξυρῷ τῷ μεμεθυσμένῳ πέραν τοῦ ποταμοῦ, βασιλέως Ἀσσυρίων, τὴν κεφαλὴν, καὶ τὰς τρίχας τῶν ποδῶν, καὶ τὸν πώγωνα ἀφελεῖ." Note that the Septuagint uses "drunken" (memethysmenō) instead of "hired."</note>
> 
> *In that day the Lord will shave with a hired razor among those who are across the river, by the King of the Assyrians, the head and the hair of the feet and the entire beard.*

<margin>Shaving is a sign of captivity and servitude.</margin>
Isaiah, the foremost and easily the prince of the Prophets, was denouncing the most severe judgments of God upon the family and kingdom of the impious King Ahaz <note>King of Judah (c. 732–716 BC) who, fearing an alliance between Syria and Israel, turned to Assyria for help rather than trusting God.</note> because of his infidelity, discord, and rebellion. When pressed by the Syrians and Samaritans, Ahaz had implored the help of the Assyrians against God's command. Isaiah does not merely speak of these punishments in general terms but, in the prophetic manner, carefully recounts every detail that will happen to stir the emotions (*pathos*), so that the condition of the conquered seems not just narrated, but placed right before the eyes. He predicts destruction through those who are across the river (the Euphrates, which cut off Assyria)—that is, as he soon explains by way of interpretation <note>original: "ἐπήγησιν" (epegēsin)</note>, *by the King of the Assyrians*. He expresses their innumerable forces and ranks using a comparison drawn from swarms of flies and bees in verse 18. He compares the swift inhabitants of Egypt, as well as the Philistines and Edomites, to flies; but he compares the Assyrians, who were trained in military discipline, to bees because of the vehemence of their anger. As Virgil writes in the 4th book of the *Georgics*, bees are easily provoked to anger by a slight whistle, just as the enemies in Deuteronomy 1:44 and Psalm 68 are compared to irritated bees. At the same time, he alludes to the character and nature of the regions of Egypt and Assyria. It is well known from the books of geographers that Egypt is infested with flies, gnats, and other insects born from the mud of the Nile, while Assyria is noted for its beekeeping. Procopius <note>Procopius of Gaza (c. 465–528 AD), a Christian sophist and exegete.</note> (p. 120) says the bee is attributed to Assyria "because of its warlike nature and its use of a sting." <note>original: "διὰ τὸ πολεμικὸν κέντρῳ κεχρῆσθαι"</note> Johannes Brentius <note>A German Reformer (1499–1570).</note> calls the Egyptians "fly-like" <note>original: "μελισσοειδεῖς"</note> flies because of the great multitude of flies on the banks of the Nile; <margin>page 77.</margin> but he calls the Assyrians the bee, because Assyria abounds in bees and honey. Andreas Hyperius <note>A Flemish Protestant theologian (1511–1564).</note> says: "The Fly is a metonymy for Egypt, the Bee for Assyria: either because flies are most frequent in the former and the latter abounds in bees and honey, or because the Egyptians and Assyrians will flock to the army of the King of the Assyria in a great swarm like flies and bees." He continues to describe that total destruction <note>original: "Πανωλεθρίαν" (panolethrian)</note> looming over the kingdom of Judah allegorically or symbolically through the hired razor, because the Lord was going to "hire" the labor of the Assyrians to punish the Hebrews, as if for a wage. The Hebrew <margin>page 121.</margin> "with a hired razor" <note>original: "בתער השכירה"</note> was translated poorly by the Septuagint as "with a great drunken razor." <note>original: "ἐν τῷ ξυρῷ τῷ μεγάλῳ τῷ μεμεθυσμένῳ"</note> On this, Procopius says: "He calls it a drunken razor, a sword that shears unsparingly and is struck with the blood of those who fall." Some, however (interpreting the word "drunken"), explain it as a mercenary force, which the future kingdom of the Assyrians would be fond of. The literal text knows nothing

<column-break/>

<margin>Shaving is a sign of captivity and servitude.</margin>
of a "drunken razor" soaked in the blood of the slain, but rather of a hired razor summoned for a price. Thus, Aquila and Theodotion <note>Two 2nd-century translators of the Hebrew Bible into Greek.</note> more correctly translate it as "hired, a razor hired for a price." <note>original: "μεμισθωμένῳ, navaculâ mercede conductâ"</note> This phrasing hints at the King of the Assyrians in three ways: 1. In respect to Ahaz, who had hired him with much gold and silver when the Republic was in straits and great turmoil. Despairing of protecting it, the King sent for the Assyrians—ignorant of what he was asking—to bring help, "giving his hand" to Egypt and the Assyrians, to use the language of Lamentations chapter 5. For it is customary for treaties to be sanctioned by the mutual joining of hands. 2. In respect to the Assyrians, who allowed themselves to be hired for war for the sake of shameful profit. And 3. In respect to GOD the judge (which is more to the point), who had decreed to execute judgments upon the people using the labor of the Assyrians as if it were hired. For this reason, he is called later "the Lord’s saw," and in chapter 10, "Assyria, the rod of the Lord’s anger." Just as a *razor* leaves the whole body smooth by stripping it of hair and robbing it of all ornament, so the enemy, carrying everything away, plundering, slaughtering, and burning, is quite aptly said to perform the *function of a razor*. This shaving *from the crown of the head to the feet* indicates that both the lowest and the highest would feel the edge of the razor. This horrendous desolation is then expressed as if in a picture: one who was wealthy in livestock before the calamity will barely be able to nourish a young cow and *two sheep* (v. 21); one who previously cultivated the land with twenty plows will barely have a cow. For after that storm—namely, the Babylonian war—the prophet predicts such solitude and scarcity of men in the kingdom of Judah that a single cow or a few sheep will suffice to feed an entire family. For families that were once large would then be reduced to the greatest straits, most having been killed in war or led away into slavery. Just as GOD compared the *Chaldean to a hunter* (Jeremiah 16) who would hunt the Jews from every mountain, hill, and crevice of the rocks, so here he compares the Assyrian to a barber, who will shave the Jews' head, the hair of their feet, and their entire beard. The shaving of the head was a symbol of enslavement. <margin>Cyril on Amos, page 682.</margin> "A very dishonoring and most shameful thing for the head," <note>original: "Ἀτιμοποιὸν δὲ σφόδρα καὶ αἰσχιστὸν τὴν κεφαλὴν"</note> as is abundantly clear from both sacred and secular literature: victors of old ordered the heads of the captives they led away to be shaved, and sometimes the captives themselves cut their hair as a voluntary sign of mourning. Hence, the Prophets so often threaten the Israelites with future baldness. Thus Isaiah in chapter 3, verse 16, describing the punishment for the pride of the daughters of Zion, says: "The Lord will make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion, and the Lord will lay bare their secret parts." There, instead of "will make bald" <note>original: "חשפ"</note>, the Septuagint reads a root meaning "to make handmaids" <note>original: "חשׂף"</note>, for the words are related in their letters as well as their meaning. The uncovering of secret parts is the showing of shame. Some interpret "their hair" <note>original: "הפתהן"</note> as a baldness of falling hair, which the Septuagint translates as: "instead of the ornament of gold, baldness." <note>original: "ἀντὶ τοῦ κόσμου τῆς χρυσείας φαλάκρωμα"</note> He said "to strip" with an elegant metaphor; for the poet himself called the hair and the beard a "garment," and called one "unclothed" <note>term: "investem" — a Latin term for a youth whose cheeks are not yet covered in downy hair</note> whose cheeks no down had yet clothed. The Prophet threatens them with two things: *Baldness and the stripping* of those parts which nature intended to be covered. By this, he indicates that he wishes to reveal and bring into public view their shame...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
### Page 572

<margin>Shaving as a sign of captivity and servitude.</margin>
Shaving signifies filthiness or ignominy; <note>original Greek: τὸ δὲ τῆς φάσεως παθητικὸν ἴσων</note> for the passive sense of the expression perhaps implies that "to strip" does not only mean to make naked or to uncover, but also to expose, to indicate, or to behave unseemly <note>original Greek: ἄσχημονεῖν</note>. We see this in Ezekiel 16:7 and 22: "naked and disgraced" <note>original Greek: γυμνὴ καὶ ἀσχήμων</note>, referring to a shameful and infamous woman. In this sense, it is expressed more clearly elsewhere: *I will uncover your private parts and show the nations your nakedness, and the kingdoms your shame. For by whatever things a person sins, by those same things they are punished.* Therefore, if you ask why God said such a punishment must be inflicted upon them, I will answer that the penalty is suited to the crime. Among the Roman Emperors, Caligula—a notorious adulterer and glutton—died by a sword driven through his private parts, so that the cause of his death was evident. We also read in 1 Esdras 1:23 that the Jews were punished with the stripping of hair as a penalty.

<margin>Jeremiah chapter 48.</margin>
God also threatens the people with captivity, even using these words in verse 40: *Every head shall be bald and every beard shall be shaved, because the servants and surrendered subjects of the nations were compelled by custom to be shorn with a razor so that they might serve.* <note>original Greek: Οὐκ ἀνομοίως</note> Not dissimilarly, the same prophet says: *Cut off your hair and cast it away, and take up a lamentation.* The Prophet threatens the proud people with captivity and reduction to servitude. I do not agree with those who read "cast it away" as "driven to the cross," as Scheck explains that word in *Præmes. Epist. 13* and Cameron in *Plautus p. 285*. Likewise, Ezekiel in chapter 27 marks the mourning over the ruin of Tyre by the shaving of the head. In the burden of Moab, Isaiah predicts *baldness on all heads and the shaving or cutting off or diminishing of every beard*, as the Hebrew root <term>gazaz</term> <note>Hebrew: גזז, meaning to shear or cut off hair</note> shows in 

<margin>chapter 47:5.</margin>
chapters 15 and 7. Jeremiah threatens the Philistines with the same baldness, saying: *Baldness has come upon Gaza; Ashkelon is cut off.* Indeed, when Ezekiel 29:18 recounts that "every head was made bald and every shoulder was stripped of hair" during the siege of Tyre, it refers to the labor of the soldiers. He affirms that the shoulders of those carrying burdens were rubbed bare, a point noted by Rader in his commentary on *Curtius 4.2.16*, and by Freinsheim after him. In Psalm 68:22: *God will crush the heads of his enemies, the hairy crown of those who walk in their sins.* The Chaldean <note>The Aramaic Targum, an ancient paraphrase of the Bible</note> translates this as: *He will pluck out the hairs of the man who walks in his crimes.* As Lorinus notes on this passage, this implies a shameful balding that involves both pain and the ignominy of slavery. In Deuteronomy 32:42, captivity and the uncovering of the head are joined and explain each other, as God predicts the future slaughter of the enemies of the people of Israel. So 

<margin>Micah 1:16.</margin>
Micah also describes the magnitude of mourning and slaughter: *Make yourselves bald and cut off your hair for the children of your delight; enlarge your baldness like the eagle (when it sheds its feathers in old age), for they have gone into captivity from you.* The word <term>gazaz</term> means he cut back or shaved; Luther rendered it as <term>abschären</term> <note>German: to shear off</note>; but in Job 1:20, on a similar subject, he used <term>ausrauffen</term> <note>German: to pluck or tear out</note>. Among secular writers, Propertius speaks openly in Book 4, Elegy 12, verse 37, regarding Africa being led in a triumph:

> I call the ashes of your ancestors to witness, O Rome, which you must honor,
> Beneath whose titles Africa lies shorn.

This was a sign of triumph, for the hair of conquered enemies was shorn. Claudian also says in his first book against Rufinus, verse 379, and in his work against Eutropius: *Let shorn Sicambria serve under our standards.* Lucan says in the *Pharsalia*, Book 1, verse 442: *And now, shorn Ligurian.* In the books of the *Basilica* <note>A code of Byzantine law</note>, shaving takes the place of a civil penalty. 

<margin>Constitution 105.</margin>
The Emperor Leo decreed: *Those who have shared in this, if they are rich, let them be subject to the same fine; but if they are poor, let them be beaten with whips and ignominiously shorn* <note>original Greek: καὶ ἀτίμῳ κουρείᾳ</note>, *and be*

<column-break/>

ordered into exile. Isocrates, in his funeral oration celebrating the memory of those who fell at 
<margin>Shaving as a sign of captivity.</margin>
Salamis, said that "it was fitting for Greece to shave her hair at the tomb of those who died at Salamis, as if liberty were buried together with their valor," as cited in Aristotle's *Rhetoric*, Book 3, chapter 13. He says they ought to stand shorn at their graves, because liberty was buried along with those men; for in liberty, they used to grow their hair. To illustrate this passage of the Prophet, someone impertinently drags in a passage from Persius, Satire 3, line 61:

> And where the Stoic porch, painted with trousered Medes, 
> Teaches those things over which the sleepless and shorn youth
> Keep watch, fed on husks and great helpings of porridge.

With elegant imagery <note>original Greek: ὑποτυπώσει</note>, the youth of the Stoics, who were indifferent to elegant fashions, are called *shorn youth*, 
<margin>Some manuscripts: tonsa (shaved).</margin>
because they did not grow their hair long but recommended themselves by a close-shaved skin; thus a Stoic was shaved right down to the skin. To be "shaved to the skin" <note>original Greek: ἐν χρῷ κείρεσθαι</note> is said by Lucian in mockery, as noted by Turnebus in *Adversaria* 23.23 and 15.17; but we do not wish "to shave to the skin," as the proverb says <note>A metaphor for being overly meticulous or harsh</note>. Pomponius Laetus, writing on the triumph of Diocletian, says: *It was the custom for those liberated from captivity to follow the chariot of the triumphator with shaved heads as a proof of their preceding servitude.* However, just as the shaving of hair was a proof and sign of servitude, so the growing of it was a sign of liberty; for among the Gauls, Goths, and Greeks, to grow hair was a sign of freedom, as Dempster teaches in his commentary on Rosinus, Book 10. Traditionally, the glory of hair was a symbol of manly strength and fortitude. When the Argives, who previously had long hair, were defeated by the Spartans, they vowed they would not grow their hair again until they had recovered Thyrea, according to Herodotus, Book 2. But we may rightly doubt whether this explanation, taken from the ritual of the ancients, can apply here to the matter of servitude; for to what end would the shaving of the hair, the feet, and the entire beard be done? Therefore, a good portion of translators explain it as referring to men of the highest and lowest condition: just as in chapter 19:14, by the "head" they understand the Princes, and by the "feet" the craftsmen and the common rabble. For the Jews, the "beard" signifies the Priests and Counselors. In this way, the Assyrian will lead away both noble and ignoble captives, and will plunder and destroy the kingdom of Israel from top to bottom, which can be compared to a human body. The "Barber," 

<margin>In *Against Heresies* 7 and in the *Prologue to the Prophets*, p. 31.</margin>
says Cornelius à Lapide, is a hieroglyph for God, who through the Assyrians—as if by a razor—shaved the beard and the hair of the feet, that is, the Princes and the commoners of the Jews. And again: *By the riddle of the razor shaving the hair and beard, he describes the Chaldeans killing both the common people and the Princes of the Jews.* Robert Stephanus, in his notes to the 1557 edition of the Bible, offers a different view: The ancient Hebrews shaved the hair of the head and the pubic region, but not the beard, according to the custom of the region where the beard was held in the highest esteem. The hair of the head represents the Leaders. The pubic hair represents the common soldiers. The beard is King Sennacherib, who was killed by his sons after returning to his homeland. However it is explained, it is certain that the shaving and shearing of the head and beard intend a change of fortune and status. This is done symbolically, according to the common and widespread style of Scripture, in which one may observe mysteries under certain symbols concerning human actions, habits, positions, gestures, and the affections of bodies and souls...

<header>Isaiah 11:11, 12.</header>

Tonsure <note>The ritual cutting or shaving of hair.</note> includes various meanings introduced by certain customs. For example, *shaving the head and beard* was a sign of mourning, just as covering the head indicates the judgment of those condemned, and elsewhere it is a sign of confusion and shame. For what was said by Dionysius Thrax <note>A Greek grammarian who lived around 170–90 BCE.</note>, the ancient grammarian: <note>original Greek: ἐσήμαινον γ' ἔν τι διὰ λέξεως μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ συμβόλων ἔνιοι τὰς φράξεις; "Some signified their expressions not only through speech, but also through symbols"</note>, is especially true of the Hebrews and their neighbors. Thus, some of the Prophets had their heads *bruised*; others *took up iron horns*; others bound themselves with shackles.

-> Isaiah 11:11, 12. <-

> <note>Hebrew original of Isaiah 11:11-12</note> It shall come to pass in that day that the Lord shall set His hand again the second time to recover the remnant of His people who are left, from Assyria and Egypt, from Pathros and Cush, from Elam and Shinar, from Hamath and the islands of the sea. 
> He will set up a banner for the nations, and will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.

> <note>Greek (Septuagint) original of Isaiah 11:11-12</note> And it shall be in that day, the Lord shall again show His hand to be zealous for the remnant that is left of the people, which shall be left from the Assyrians, and from Egypt, and from Babylon, and from Ethiopia, and from the Elamites, and from the rising of the sun, and from Arabia. 
> And He shall lift up a signal for the nations, and He shall gather the lost of Israel, and He shall gather the dispersed of Judah from the four wings of the earth.

> *<note>Latin (Vulgate) original of Isaiah 11:11-12</note> And it shall be in that day, the Lord shall set His hand a second time to possess the remnant of His people, which shall be left from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.*
> *And He shall lift up a banner to the nations, and shall assemble the fugitives of Israel, and shall gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four quarters of the earth.*

<margin>The gathering of the Nations to the Church.</margin> The divine Prophets predicted that the glory of the second house would be far greater than the first; this oracle must be referred entirely to the spiritual glory which, in the last times, was brought by Jesus Christ—who is more than Solomon. He led into the Church the superstitious Greeks, the proud Romans, the fierce Dalmatians, the barbaric Germans, the rustic Scythians, the wild Britons, and other monstrous nations; the armed were made unarmed, the ferocious became mild, so that the word of Isaiah was fulfilled: *The wolf and the lamb shall feed together.* <margin>Wisdom 11:6.</margin> For we have the first prelude of the calling of the Nations in the example of Abraham, whose migration from Ur of the Chaldeans must be observed. He, together with his father Terah and the rest of his kindred, was led out of Ur, a city of the Chaldeans (Genesis 11:31), and stayed in Haran; and since even here he was devoted to the idolatrous cults to which he had been accustomed in his fatherland (Joshua 24:2), he was called out from Haran as well by a singular command of God. He was called out in such a way that he did not change his seat with his entire kindred, but rather, having deserted his kindred and his father’s house, he followed the God who called him. He followed, and not only did he lack a fatherland and say farewell to parents and agnates <note>Relatives on the father's side.</note>, but primarily he deserted and fled the idols which he had served until then, and which his parents had carried with them from Ur of the Chaldeans. For this reason, he is called by the Apostle "the father of us all" <note>original Greek: πατὴρ πάντων ἡμῶν</note>, Romans

<column-break/>

4:16, specifically in respect to his calling and faith. <margin>On the gathering of the Nations to the Church.</margin> In this respect, Saint Peter also, through a certain apostrophe <note>A rhetorical figure where the speaker addresses an absent person or personified object.</note>, calls the nations: "a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for His possession" (1 Peter 2:9). <note>original Greek: γένος ἐκλεκτὸν, βασίλειον ἱεράτευμα, ἔθνος ἅγιον, λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν</note>. For Holy Scripture agrees wonderfully regarding the calling of the Nations, and the prophetic oracles are confirmed by the words, deeds, and examples of the Apostles. We have just heard what Saint Peter wrote about the calling of the Nations; let us hear what the Creator of the Nations says to Jonah. Jonah is commanded to go away to the Ninevites—who were Gentiles by profession and strangers to the true faith—and to cry out with a loud voice: *Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.* <margin>Jonah 2:4.</margin> For God did not wish to establish His kingdom by the sword, but by the Word and the Spirit. Therefore, the Apostles did not use the labor of Princes and Kings in establishing the Church; indeed, those rulers rather enacted laws for destroying the followers of the Christian name and for utterly eradicating faith in Christ, according to that prophetic word: *Why do the Nations rage, and the people plot vain things? The Kings of the earth stood up, and the princes gathered together into one against the Lord and against His Christ;* which the Apostles allege in their thanksgiving <note>original Greek: εὐχαριστία</note> to God from Psalm 2:11 [and] Acts 4:26, until the Kings and Princes of the earth submitted their crowns and scepters to the Divine throne and power. Just as Nebuchadnezzar testified to his submission by a law passed regarding the punishment of all in his kingdom who *blasphemed the God of Israel* <margin>Daniel 3:96.</margin>; just as also the King of the Ninevites, having heard the preaching of Jonah, compelled his entire city to appease the Lord. To this may rightly be referred that prophecy of Isaiah 49:23 concerning the gathering of Princes and Kings to the Church: *And Kings shall be your foster fathers, and their queens your nursing mothers.* By this very fact, the calling and collection of not only Kings and Great Men, but with them all the Nations into the Church, is suggested. Indeed, Tertullian, Jerome, and other interpreters deduce from the words of Malachi that the preaching, celebration, and invocation of the Divine Name would be everywhere in all regions of the earth. Tertullian several times acknowledges and proclaims—with Malachi as the herald—that spiritual prayer would occur in the New Testament with the offering of a pure heart and a holy life, along with a great celebration of the Divine Power, such as: *From the rising of the sun even to its setting, <margin>Tertullian, 3. Against Marcion, page 182.</margin> my name is glorified among the Nations, and in every place a sacrifice is offered to my name, even a pure sacrifice.* That is, the return of glory, and blessing, and praise, and hymns. In the fourth book against the same [Marcion], page 187: *He destined other more powerful offices of sacrifices, and indeed among the Nations,* as Malachi says: *My will is not in you, says the Lord, and I will not receive your sacrifices from your hands, because from the rising of the sun even to the setting, my name is glorified among the nations, and in every place a sacrifice shall be offered in my name, even a pure sacrifice, namely, simple prayer from a pure conscience.* The same in the book *Against the Jews*, page 104: *Through the Prophets, the Spirit predicts that it will come to pass that in every land or in every place sacrifices shall be offered to God, just as He says through Malachi the Angel <note>In this context, "Angel" refers to Malachi's name meaning "My Messenger."</note>, one of the twelve Prophets: I will not receive sacrifice from your hands, because from the rising sun even to the setting, my name is made famous among all nations, says the Lord of all...*

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<column-break/>

<margin>The gathering of the Nations to the Church.</margin>
...the Almighty. Undoubtedly, the preaching of the Apostles was destined to go out into all the earth. We read that God is to be honored not with earthly sacrifices, but with spiritual ones, as it is written: *A contrite heart is a sacrifice to God.* <note>Psalm 51:17</note> *And elsewhere: sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High.* <note>Psalm 50:14</note> Thus, spiritual sacrifices of praise are designated, and a contrite heart is shown to be a sacrifice acceptable to God. In this way, Jerome demonstrates—from this prophetic oracle—that the Church of the New Testament, under the splendor of the Messiah, was to be spread throughout the whole world from the rising of the sun to its setting. He writes: *Let the word of the Lord be directed to the Priests of the Jews, who offer the blind, the lame, and the weak for sacrifice, so they may know that spiritual victims will succeed fleshly ones. By no means will the blood of bulls and goats be offered, but incense—that is, the prayers of the saints—shall be offered to the Lord. And this shall be offered not in a single province of the world, Judea, nor in a single Judean city, Jerusalem, but in every place. The offering will by no means be unclean, as it was from the people of Israel, but clean, as in the ceremonies of the Christians. For from the rising of the sun even to its setting, the name of the Lord is great among the nations,* <note>Malachi 1:11</note> as the Savior says: *Father, I have manifested your name to men.* <note>John 17:6</note> The same author notes: *In every place incense and clean burnt offerings are offered to God, marking the fulfillment of the prophetic word.*

<margin>On chapter 52 of the Commentary on Isaiah.</margin>
All the ends of the earth shall remember and return to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in His sight. According to that Psalm: *I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession.* <note>Psalm 2:8</note> By this very thing, the greatness of the Gospel’s kingdom is foretold; its preaching reaches out in every direction even to the furthest nations of the world. And so, the entire Council of Prophets foretold the Calling of the Nations across the world and throughout the ages. Yet no one is more frequent or clearer than Isaiah—that most noble narrator of the Gospel calling rather than a mere prophetic one. (Charlemagne honored the Prophet with this praise in his *Capitularies*, book 3, regarding Images, 14, p. 371). Isaiah, in his eleventh chapter, provides a most abundant sermon regarding the kingdom or Church of Christ, which is to be gathered from all peoples; because of its most ample doctrine and sweetest consolation, it truly deserves to be called the "Gospel of the Nations." For these things of which the Prophet speaks cannot be understood as the liberation from Babylon, since only two tribes—Judah and Benjamin—were brought back from Babylon, whereas here the discourse concerns a universal remnant from all the tribes. Furthermore, the places mentioned here cannot be restricted to Babylon. Therefore, this prophecy is to be understood not as some external return, but as a spiritual restoration and liberation of both the Nations and the Jews, who are converted to the Church through the preaching of the Gospel. For Isaiah testifies in chapter 60:1 that there is no light except in the Church, speaking of those who did not receive the faith of the Gospel: *Behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and thick darkness the peoples. But the Lord shall arise upon you, and His glory shall be seen upon you.* Shortly after, he adds concerning those who, having left behind their ancestral superstitions, believed the Gospel and sought to be received into the bosom of the Church: *And the Nations shall walk in your light, and Kings in the brightness of your rising.* Since,

<column-break/>

<margin>The naming of the Nations.</margin>
however, the "Nations" appear under various <term>terminology</term> <note>original Greek: ὀνομαζολογία (onomazologia); the study of names or terms</note> in Holy Scripture, we consider it worthwhile to review the principal authentic names in both [testament] languages. The primary designation in Holy Scripture in the original language is <term>Goyim</term> <note>original Hebrew: גּוֹיִם; nations or peoples</note>, by which are denoted all worshippers of idols, the unfaithful, the unbelieving, those foreign to the true religion, those lacking true knowledge of God, and those living outside the Church; this meaning is accepted <term>for the most part</term> <note>original Greek: ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ</note> in the Sacred letters. Modern Jews use that name to call and, as it were, distinguish all who are not of their assembly and addicted to their superstition—that is, all non-Jews—even though the same word is also used for the Jews themselves, either with or without an epithet, as in *Genesis 12:2, Exodus 19:6, Isaiah 11:12, 2 Samuel 7:23, Jeremiah 27:8.* They are also distinguished in the Sacred letters by another name, namely <term>Gerim</term> <note>original Hebrew: גֵּרִים; sojourners or proselytes</note> from the root <term>Gur</term> <note>original Hebrew: גּוּר; to dwell as a stranger</note>, which specifically refers to those who, although they were not of Israelite seed, nevertheless practiced the same sacred rites, as in *Leviticus 16:29, Deuteronomy 31:12, Joshua 8:33.* These were counted among the Jews by the law of hospitality, *Lev. 19:33, ch. 21:35*; they enjoyed the privilege of the city of refuge, *Num. 35:15, Jos. 20:9*; and they were permitted to eat the paschal lamb, *2 Chronicles 30:25.* According to traditions, it was not fitting to associate with them familiarly until they had been fully admitted into a deeper communion of religion and sacred things—a distinction that some Jewish-Christians still thought should be kept, as seen in *Acts 11:3.* The reason for denying social interaction for a time was this: occasionally a grudge would grow between them, leading the ancient Rabbis to say: *It would be good for us if we were not forced to receive so many proselytes, who hinder us greatly; for since they are not practiced in our ceremonies, they seduce the Israelites with their works,* which you can observe in the incident of the golden calf and the "graves of craving" <note>Kibroth Hattaavah; see Numbers 11:34</note>; compare *Sebastian Münster’s Hebrew notes on Matthew, ch. 23, page 128.* Also well known is the saying: *In the presence of a <term>proselyte</term>, even unto the tenth generation, do not despise a Syrian,* that is, a gentile (see *Paul Fagius in his exposition of Hebrew sentences, p. 127*). The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> uses the word <term>ethnos</term> <note>original Greek: ἔθνος; nation</note>, with the same and equal meaning as the Hebrew, as well as <term>ethnikos</term> <note>original Greek: ἐθνικός; heathen/gentile</note>, hence *Ephesians 4:18*, <term>nations darkened in understanding</term> <note>original Greek: ἔθνη ἐσκοτισμένοι</note>, where the plural masculine epithet "darkened" <note>original Greek: πεπορωμένους</note> refers back to the sense and meaning [of the people] rather than the grammatical form [of the neuter noun "nations"], as are the words of Camerarius on this passage, p. 105. It refers to a <term>synthesis of meaning</term> <note>original Greek: Synesin; a grammatical construction where agreement is according to sense rather than strict syntax</note> (Rudolf Goclenius prefers to speak of this in his *Greek Philosophical Lexicon*, p. 222). The Vulgate <note>The Latin Bible translation</note> translator imitates the same in *Matthew 28:19: teach all nations, baptizing them*, and similarly *<term>all the nations, upon whom my name is called.</term>* <note>original Greek: πάντα τὰ ἔθνη, ἐφ᾽ οὓς ἐπικέκληται τὸ ὄνομά μου.</note> This Greek phrasing is not infrequent, especially in Holy Scripture, where the relative pronoun does not agree in gender with the antecedent noun.

Among the Latins, the words *Nations* and *Gentiles* have various meanings and interpretations. The Romans called "Gentes" <note>Nations</note> all foreign peoples who had not been initiated into the Roman Empire, and those who presided over those assemblies they called "Presidents of the Nations," or <term>hyparchs</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπάρχας</note> in Greek. Likewise, Christians use the name "Gentiles" for all those groups who live outside their Commonwealth—that is, any infidel and worshipper of idols, differing in worship from the people of God and lacking the "token of faith" <note>the sign of baptism</note>. It is in this sense that the title of Arnobius's *Disputations* <note>Against the Heathen</note> should be understood. Often the term is used for a family among writers, and those born from the same family and same stock into various families...

### Isaiah 11:11–12
### Page 375

<margin>The gathering of the Nations.</margin>
The expansion of the "Nations" <note>original: "Gentium propagati"</note> led to the French term *gentilhomme* (gentleman), which some might think was translated from the Latin *nobilis* (noble). Nicolaus Perottus—who was otherwise infamous for his false interpretations <note>original: "ψευδερμηνείας"</note> in his *Cornucopia* on Martial, page 307—calls those "gentiles" who persisted in the "gentile" way, that is, in the faith of their ancestors, and did not change their religious worship. However, this pair of words does not seem to move in step regarding their meaning; one usually has a broader significance than the other. Indeed, the *Ordinary Gloss* <note>A standard medieval collection of biblical commentaries</note> often explains the word "Nations" by using "Gentiles," essentially explaining a broader term through a more specific one, and examples of this occur in many places. Otherwise, if one explained the same thing with the same word, it would be mere babbling <note>original: "ἀδολεσχία"</note>. But the "salvation of Greece" <note>a proverb for a decisive solution</note> does not rest on this. It seems that the ancient Christians preferred to say *gentiles* rather than *gentes* (nations), and *Ethnics* <note>heathens</note> rather than *ethnē* <note>original: "ἔθνη"</note>, though the scholar Drusius admits in his work on Sulpitius (page 236) that he does not know why. According to the power and arrogance <note>original: "καὶ αὐθαδείᾳ δύναμιν"</note> that Pope Sixtus V claimed for himself in issuing new definitions, "gentile" is the same as "excellent." In his book *On Chastity*, where he compares the holy cohabitation of spouses—oh, what a great outrage! <note>original: "proh grande nefas"</note>—to the breeding of pigs and dogs, he says: "To marry is common to almost all men; there is nothing 'gentile' <note>distinguished</note> about wanting to practice what everyone does, and to have that which even the worst people obtain. But to say nothing of humans, even wild beasts and cattle and birds marry; there is nothing great about having something in common with pigs and dogs. Rather, follow the life of God and His Angels entirely." This is cited and approved by Gretser in his *Virgidemia*, page 48.

But oh, what an impious mouth that the Devil should shut! To those shameful examples of men, it is "gentile" to commit fornication with the Jesuit Coster or to keep a concubine at home (even if done with heavy sacrilege), rather than following the Apostle's precept to have a wife to avoid fornication. It is "gentile" for Archbishop Johannes de la Casa of Benevento not only to practice the diabolical sin of sodomy, but to praise it to posterity under the parable of the "oven" through a euphemism <note>original: "καθ’ ὑποκόρισμα"</note>. It is "gentile" for Robert Gaguin to argue about the purity of the Virgin Mary, and after his praises of her, to mix in many sexual matters in a single breath, embracing lewd hostesses and harlots and exalting them to the sky in obscene language. It is "gentile" for the Italian Giordano Bruno to celebrate <note>original: "πανηγυρεῖν"</note> concerning the Devil, their leader. But these monsters of men are perhaps more than "gentile," they are beyond the pale. In this place, we are investigating the meaning of "Nation" which is called <term>Goyim</term> <note>original: "גוים"</note> by the Hebrews. Omitting other synonyms, this term simultaneously includes all those endowed with true faith in God, whether they are children of Abraham by blood or by faith. On the contrary, the <term>Bnei Nechar</term> <note>original: "בני נכר"</note> are the "alien" or "spurious" ones—all those who do not profess God with true faith. In this way, the term is used of the Jews in Psalms 18:44-45 and 143:12. There, Johannes Bugenhagen <note>a primary Reformer and associate of Luther</note> writes on Psalm 17, page 105: "*Alien children*, that is, those who ought to have been sons, having the promises and the testament; I say they ought to have been sons through faith, but they lied to me, that is, they denied the truth. Therefore they are aliens, that is, illegitimate. They have grown old, meaning they remained in the oldness of the flesh." And Clarius on Psalm 142, page 742, says: "They are *alien children*, meaning not of the family of God, though they boast of being sons, of whom it is said in Isaiah 1:2: *I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me.*" Read that whole chapter to understand who the alien children are.

<column-break/>

<margin>The gathering of the Nations.</margin>
Namely, those who boast that they are the people of God but impiously seek righteousness for themselves against God through their own works—which is the "right hand of iniquity." They teach things that are the "doctrine of vanity and lies," the doctrine of the dead, speaking lies in hypocrisy, having their consciences seared with a hot iron. Thus he says. Alexander Alesius <gloss>in his commentary</gloss> explains <term>Bnei Nechar</term> <note>original: "בני נכר"</note> in a completely opposite sense and translates it as "known sons." And in the Leipzig edition of 1554, he says in his exposition of Psalm 18, folio 87b: "Although the root <term>Nechar</term> <note>original: "נכר"</note> has two meanings, namely 'to know' and 'to alienate,' since the Greek and Latin translators rendered it: *A people whom I have not known has served me, as soon as they hear of me they obey me*, the logic of the antithesis <note>original: "ἀντιθέσεως"</note> forces us to admit the other part should be translated: *The known sons fall away from me; the known sons are bound and limp in their chains.*" Gessner translates it as "Sons of separation"; Tremellius as "Foreigners"; Castalio as "A strange race"; Johannes Campensis, more for the sense than the literal word, calls them "Deserters."

How great the praise of the Hebrew nation is, and how much glory it had above all other nations of every age, is witnessed by those words which God suggested to Moses when He was about to lead His people out of the dire Egyptian labor-camp, to say to Pharaoh: *Thus says the Lord:* <margin>Exodus 4:22</margin> <term>Israel is my son, even my firstborn</term> <note>original Hebrew: "בני בכרי ישראל"; Greek: "Υἱὸς πρωτότοκός μου Ἰσραήλ"</note>.

The exalted name of "firstborn" does not exclude a "second-born," as Jerome explains most clearly <note>original: "μηδινῶς"</note> when he writes <gloss>in his commentary on Isaiah 1:1</gloss> <margin>on Isaiah 1:1</margin>: "If Israel grows proud that he is the firstborn, let him understand he is called firstborn because a second group of sons is signified from the Nations. For he is not called 'Only-begotten,' which would exclude other brothers, but 'Firstborn,' to show that others would follow." And yet, according to the *mysteries of the scriptures*, it is not the firstborn who receive the inheritance, but the second. Cain was the firstborn, but Abel's *gifts pleased God.* Ishmael was the firstborn, but Isaac *received the inheritance.* Esau was the firstborn, but *Jacob the supplanter snatched away the father's blessing.* Reuben was the firstborn, *yet the blessing of the seed of Christ was transferred to Judah.* Thus, by their own failure, they lost the right of primogeniture; they lost their privileges and immunities, the priesthoods ceased, the scepter was taken away, the prophecies ended, and in their place, the Kingdom of God was transferred to the Nations. Even the Jewish Rabbis noted that this would happen regarding Psalm 75:11, as Petrus Galatinus <margin>Book 9, ch. 19</margin> cites their words when discussing the "ten horns of the Jews" that were cut off. He says: "There were ten horns or dignities of the Jewish people. 1. The horn of Abraham. 2. The horn of Isaac or the dignity of the promise. 3. The horn of Jacob or the dignity of the kingdom. 4. The horn of Moses or the dignity of speaking with God. 5. The horn of prophecy. 6. The horn of the law. 7. The horn of the priesthood. 8. The horn of the Levites. 9. The horn of Jerusalem. 10. The horn of the Messiah. But when Israel sinned, all these horns were taken from them and given to the nations of the world."

Concerning the calling of the nations, there is a parable in the Talmud, in the tractate *Sanhedrin*, chapter *Helec*, stating that it would come to pass that "a horse would be placed at the manger of a limping ox." Rabbi Jacob and Rabbi Solomon, explaining this, say that God would substitute the Heathens for the Jews who carried the Law. Nor indeed, even if the Jews later return to a better state, would the Heathens therefore...
