# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The gathering of the Nations into the Church.</margin>
...gathering the Nations, or driving them back. In the same passage it says, *a stone of stumbling to both houses of Israel, and a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem* <note>Isaiah 8:14</note>; compare Mornay’s *On the Truth of the Christian Religion* <note>Philippe de Mornay (1549–1623) was a French Protestant writer</note>, *chapter 30, page 493, 558, Volume 4, Giessen Disputations 4, thesis 57, page 99.* These are therefore Jewish dreams regarding the seat of their Church in Judea being perpetual and immovable; those who imagine the promises of the divine presence and help given to the Church are absolute to themselves, as if they were not circumscribed by certain limits of faith and obedience. Hence, when they were about to attack Jeremiah, they thought to strike him with this weapon: *Jeremiah 18:18, Come, let us devise devices against Jeremiah; for the law shall not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet.* Blinded by this opinion, even when the calling of the nations was at hand, they attacked Paul, who asserted the calling of the nations while the Jews were rejected by God: *Saying then, Romans 11:1, Hath God cast away his people?* Truly, St. Paul in Romans 9:24—where he explains the causes of the rejection and abdication of the Jewish people, as well as the free adoption of the Nations in their place (which he confirms by the prophecies of Hosea and Isaiah)—removes every occasion of offense from the objection that God might have revoked or made void the promise made to Abraham and his seed, and thus might be unstable or unfaithful in His promises. He answers thus: This promise was made to the descendants of Abraham, not the carnal ones but the spiritual ones, founded in the Messiah Christ; since the nations received Him with joy, it was not unworthy for the nations, once idolaters, to be preferred over the Jews. The Jews are therefore rejected and are wanderers, or rather now fugitives upon the earth, by that same curse which fell upon Cain for his great sin; and it happened to them as is said in *Hosea 9:17, My God will cast them away, because they did not hearken unto him: and they shall be wanderers among the nations.* They are rejected, I say, but not utterly repudiated, so that one should completely despair of their conversion to Christ the Messiah; for God still has His remnants among them, or some small seed, about which Zechariah prophesied above others in *chapter 8:23* and *Isaiah 65:8.* Therefore, they should not be hindered in their conversion, but rather helped according to one’s strength, which Blessed Luther <note>Martin Luther, the primary figure of the Protestant Reformation</note> beautifully taught in *Volume 8, German Jena edition, folio 93.* Hence Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, an 8th-century English monk and scholar</note> says in his *Commentary on Luke, book 3, chapter 32*: *Do not trouble him* <note>original: "Noli vexare illum"</note>; this is said today to those who see the state of the Synagogue so destitute that they do not believe it can be restored, and therefore they do not think they should pray for its resuscitation. But what is impossible for men is possible for God. While we meditate on the rejection of the Jews, let us at the same time be stirred to adore such great kindness of the Messiah, and to detest the evasion and stupendous malice of the Jews. Let us recall the name *Christ*, and from this our own surname <note>i.e., "Christian"</note>, a contemplation which should lift us to the supreme benefit of the anointing. Adhering to this, let us ruminate on these words with Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the famous Dutch humanist and theologian</note> <margin>Catechism on the Creed, 3, page 959, Volume 5.</margin> in the name *CHRIST*, which is frequently emphasized in the Evangelical and Apostolic writings: the

<column-break/>

<margin>That he might restore the Jewish nation, now everywhere rejected and exiled, to liberty and a kingdom; and with this vain hope, that unhappy nation consoles itself in its calamity.</margin>
foolish and stubborn incredulity of the Jews is reproached, who even to this day wait for their Messiah. For whom the Latins call the *Anointed* <note>original: "unctum"</note>, the Greeks call *Christ* <note>original: "Christum"</note>, and the Hebrews call the *Messiah*. However, they expect a King abundantly furnished with wealth and other worldly supports, who might restore the Jewish nation, now everywhere rejected and exiled, to liberty and a kingdom; and with this vain hope, that unhappy nation consoles itself in its calamity. But the Christian faith teaches us that this is truly that one and only Messiah, promised long ago by the Prophets, who would liberate—not one nation, but the true Jews throughout all the regions of the world (that is, those professing the name of Christ and circumcised in heart)—not by physical arms, but by His own blood from the tyranny of Satan, and, having forgiven all sins, would restore them to true liberty, and finally admit them as co-heirs and sharers of His heavenly kingdom. The surname of Christ was given so that no one should play around or expect another Messiah. Thus far Erasmus. Meanwhile, we give thanks to God, who called us into His marvelous light and to the true faith in Christ; let us resolve to die in that faith, and pray to God that He never allows us to be blinded in spirit.

### Isaiah XIII. last verse.

-> And the wild beasts of the islands shall cry in their desolate houses, and dragons in their pleasant palaces. <note>original Hebrew: וְעָנָה אִיִּים בְּאלְמְנוֹתָיו וְתַנִּים בְּהֵיכְלֵי עֹנֶג</note> <-
-> And onocentaurs shall dwell there, and hedgehogs shall make their nests in their houses. <note>original Greek: Καὶ ὀνοκένταυροι ἐκεῖ κατοικήσουσι καὶ νοσσοποιήσουσιν ἐχῖνοι ἐν τοῖς οἴκοις αὐτῶν</note> <-
-> *And the owls shall answer there in its houses, and Sirens in the temples of pleasure.* <note>original Latin: Et respondebunt ibi ululæ in ædibus ejus, & Sirenes in delubris voluptatis</note> <-

<margin>Sirens and Onocentaurs.</margin>
**R**egarding the destruction of Babylon, that greatest of cities, and of the Chaldean nation itself, the Prophet Isaiah prophesies both elsewhere and especially in the thirteenth chapter. When interpreters explain that chapter, they agree on the matter itself, but they assign uncertain names to certain things. To explain the names of *birds and other animals, as well as plants*, which are read in the books of the Hebrews, is a difficult task <note>original: "dura provincia"</note>, so that one must sometimes say here: "Get out, I am Clusius to you." <note>original: "Exeste, Clusius ego sum vobis" - likely a reference to Charles de l'Écluse (Clusius), a famous botanist, used here to mean "I am a scholar of these things, but even I am baffled."</note> This is not surprising in matters so remote from the age of those writers, where Interpreters often find it necessary to plead the fault of ignorance "through the sacrifice of the unknown" <note>original Greek: Διὰ τῶν θυσιῶν τὸ ἄγνωστον</note>, because the names among the Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins are sometimes extremely confused. Thus we are forced to guess from the genera and species of animals, as Luther says <margin>Volume 2 of the Epistles, folio 171a.</margin>, after which Bibliander <note>Theodore Bibliander, a Swiss reformer and linguist</note> (*On the Best Kind of Grammar, page 45-46*), Chytraeus (*On Leviticus, page 216, 225*), Franz (*History of Animals, page 582*), Casaubon (*On book 9 of Athenaeus, chapter 13*), and others complain about the same difficulty in finding the terms for animals. But while they agree on that difficulty, they disagree when some Interpreters rake up explanations for those words from the filthiest fictions of the heathens. Among these, the Vulgate interpreter <note>St. Jerome, the translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> seems to me to have behaved with little accuracy <note>original Greek: εὐστόχως</note>, to say nothing of the [unclear Greek phrase]. While he wishes to dispel the darkness, he creates darkness, bringing in from some cold Pagan poem I know not what Satyrs, Fauns, Pans, Sirens, and other such hairy and shaggy gods. Not once does the good Interpreter run onto this rock; thus I think that which was written by Caesar in his first book *On Analogy* should be kept in memory <margin>Gellius, book 1, chapter 10.</margin>: *that one should avoid an unusual word just like a reef.*

# Isaiah 13: Final Verse

<margin>
Sirens and Onocentaurs.
</margin>
...avoiding those unheard-of and unusual words in such a way that you will find no trace or palm-print of them in the sacred text. Let us test this in Isaiah.
Among scholars, there is much dispute over what ought to be understood by the Hebrew name <term>Tannim</term> <note>Hebrew: תנים</note>. On this point, they differ from one another as much as the four elements. The Ancient Interpreter <note>The Vulgate</note> translates it as *Sirens*; in the same way, the Septuagint <note>The early Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> and Suidas translate the word in Job 30:29 as referring to Sirens; however, the Latin translator renders it as *Dragons*. In other places, these same translators take the same word to mean Sirens, as in *Isaiah 34:13 and 43:20; elsewhere, they take it as Dragons, such as Isaiah 27:1 and 51:9. But in this chapter, 13:22, they translate it as the hedgehog*, which is an animal endowed with a prickly skin, and is called by the elegant compound <term>akanthochoiros</term> <note>Greek: ἀκανθόχοιρος, literally "thistle-pig"</note> by Hesychius. 
<margin>p. 54.</margin>
Jerome, commenting on this passage, says: *Only the Septuagint translated it as <term>Sirens</term> and wild beasts.* And for the Hebrew <term>Tannim</term>, only the Septuagint translated it as <term>onocentaurs</term> <note>A mythical creature, half-man and half-donkey</note>. They are called Sirens, which we have interpreted as either certain monsters or surely as great dragons. Through all these, signs of vastness and solitude are shown, because the depopulation of the once-mighty city is so great that, due to the multitude of demons and beasts, no shepherd dares to enter it. The same author <note>Jerome</note> notes that where the Septuagint said, "hedgehogs shall make their lairs in their houses," and the Hebrew 
<margin>p. 76.</margin>
uses <term>Tannim</term>, the translators Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion interpreted them as *Sirens*, signifying that they are either certain beasts or demons—following the error of the heathens—who sing sweetly and deceive men who cannot pass by the shipwreck of this world with closed ears. Procopius, on page 215 of his commentary, says: <term>Some have interpreted them as Sirens, birds known for their sweet song; others say the Hebrew edition means the owl.</term> <note>original Greek: Τινὲς δὲ Σειρῆνας ἐξηγήσαντο, τὰ ἐυοσμεῖν εἰδότα πτηνὰ ἢ καλά, γε φασὶ τὴν Ἑβραίων ἔκδοσιν τὸν γλαῦκα.</note> The Hebrew word signifies animals of a serpentine appearance and form more than <term>owls</term> or <term>screech-owls</term>; and since Dragons are numbered among the species of serpents, this word was pleasing to Luther, Castalio, Tremellius, the Zurich translators, the Worms Bible, and the English and French versions, who all understand the word *Thannim* as a type of Dragon. Regarding <term>Tannim</term> (which is said by syncope <note>A linguistic shortening</note> for <term>Tanninim</term>), this much is certain: Scripture assigns it to animals inhabiting places remote from human habitation, as in Jeremiah 9:10, <term>a dwelling of dragons</term> <note>Hebrew: במעון תנים</note> (in desolate places), to indicate the solitude and vastness of Judea. Likewise, in Malachi 1:3, it is said the mountainous region of the Edomites was laid waste and its heritage given <term>to the dragons of the wilderness</term> <note>Hebrew: לתנות מדבר</note>. And in Psalm 44:19, he calls the place of desolation the <term>place of dragons</term> <note>Hebrew: מקום תנים</note>, which Symmachus interprets as <term>an uninhabited place</term> <note>Greek: τόπον ἀοίκητον</note>, because dragons live in desert places and there give forth a lamentable mourning. Therefore, this same phrasing fits perfectly here to indicate the Babylonian desolation: namely, that Babylon is to be changed into an uncultivated and inaccessible place, filled with dragons and feral beasts. This is exactly what the outcome proved, since it possesses nothing of its old form but ruins and the dens of wild beasts; for at this time, the whole city lies in ruins and has become <term>a great city that is a great desert</term> <note>Greek: μεγάλη πόλις μεγάλη ἐρημία</note>, inaccessible because of the habitats of venomous beasts. 
<margin>Isag. hist. mill. p. 109.</margin>
Dresser <note>Matthäus Dresser (1536–1607), a German humanist</note> asserts that these are called by the Persian name *Eglo*, and that they are larger than lizards, two-headed, and variegated in color. Indeed, Jerome testified that in his own time, all kinds of beasts were within the circuit of the walls of Babylon,

<column-break/>

and Benjamin of Tudela testifies no differently in his *Itinerary*, page 76 (see the notes of Constantijn L'Empereur on page 199). Even now, the great Babylon, near Baghdad, is so extinguished that hardly a trace appears, having nothing except the scars and vestiges of ancient calamity, so that one might say: *Now there is a cornfield and a dwelling place for dragons where Babylon once was* <note>A parody of Ovid’s "Iam seges est ubi Troia fuit"—"Now there is a cornfield where Troy once was."</note>. Regarding these ruins, Pliny testifies in *Book 6, chapter 26*, as does Wenceslaus Budovviz, a Bohemian Baron, in his *Letter on Chronology* in the work of Bucholcer. Where there were once palaces, there are now caves and hiding places for dragons and wild beasts. Ill-omened owls shrieked where previously joyful musicians had sung. Satyrs danced where 
Satraps <note>High-ranking Persian officials</note> once danced. Hear this, you who devote yourselves to leisure and luxury in splendid palaces, surrendering your limbs to delights. Hear what end awaits you. Babylon was ruined by pleasures. This is an example of changed worldly fortune. Hence, Ambrose 
<margin>3. On the Faith, 1.</margin>
recorded that Jeremiah said of Babylon that the "daughters of Sirens" would dwell in it, to show that the allurements of Babylon—that is, of secular confusion—are to be compared to the ancient fables of lust, which like rocks on the shore of this life seem to sound a certain sweet song to capture the minds of young men. But from where does the word *Siren* come? It seems to have proceeded from a place where "mice gnaw iron" <note>A Latin proverb, "ubi mures ferrum rodunt," referring to a land of impossible or strange things</note>. But we are not surprised by the Latin Interpreter now, since the word <term>Ya'anah</term> <note>Hebrew: יענה, usually translated as ostrich</note> is rendered as <term>siren</term> by the Greek interpreters in the verse preceding the last. The Latin and the Septuagint often agree. It is known to all who have even lightly tasted the <term>creations of myths</term> <note>Greek: μυθευμάτων πλάσματα</note> that the Sirens were passed down as fables by the poets. Some understood by the name of Sirens the pleasures of Venus, others musical allurements, and others the shrill places of the sea where ships perish; for this reason, the sweetest and most delightful song, suited for ensnaring men, is attributed to them. Similar things are frequently taken from the Sirens. Æschines says against Ctesiphon: <term>He likens my nature to the Sirens, it seems; for he says that those who listen to them are not charmed by them, but destroyed.</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀφομοιοῖ με τὴν φύσιν ταῖς Σειρῆσιν, ὡς ἔοικε. καὶ γὰρ ὑπ' ἐκείνων οὐ κηλεῖσθαί φησι τὰς ἀκροωμένας ἀλλ' ἀπόλλυσθαι.</note> Hence Eustathius says that Pindar called them <term>enchantresses</term> <note>Greek: κηλίδωνας</note> because of their allurements, which clearly would make <term>those listening forget their food out of pleasure, and thus waste away.</term> <note>original Greek: τὰς ἀκροωμένας ἐπιλαθέσθαι τῶν τροφῶν ὑφ' ἡδονῆς, καὶ οὕτως ἀφαυαίνεσθαι.</note> (page 1709, on Homer). Athenaeus recorded the same in Book 7. It is doubtful, however, whether Pindar attributed this epithet of "enchantresses" to the Sirens, or whether he meant some <term>terrible demons</term> <note>Greek: δεινὰ δαιμόνια</note>. Regarding the Sirens, Fulgentius says: 
<margin>2. Mythology, p. 1867.</margin>
*The Greek Sirens are called 'drawing' creatures, for <term>syrein</term> <note>Greek: σύρειν</note> in Greek means 'to drag' or 'to draw'.* *For the allure of love is drawn in three ways: either by song, or by sight, or by habit. For some things are loved for the beauty of their appearance; others even by a seductive habit. Ulysses both heard and saw the Sirens—that is, the allurements of delights—which means he recognized and judged them, and yet he passed by nonetheless. Therefore, because they were heard, they died; for in the mind of a wise man, every pleasure of the passions dies.* According to some, the Sirens emblematically designate Venuses or pleasures, from which, unless one takes care or uses them sparingly, it is to be feared that he may perish and be overwhelmed by their sea and whirlpools. They are said to entice people to themselves by the sweetness of song and kill those who have been enticed—the <term>Sirens</term>, or truly the <term>draggers</term> <note>Playing on the Greek words Seirenes and syrenes</note>. Hence, Tiberius wanted to be informed by the Grammarians about the song of the Sirens; while he harassed them with strange questions, he also added this one about the Sirens...

It examines whether these terms represent actual creatures, poetic descriptions of animal sounds, or are merely remnants of pagan folklore used to fill gaps in understanding the Hebrew text.</meta>

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
Sirens & Onocentaurs.
Suetonius' *Tiberius*, ch. 70.
</margin>

...stated, of which Suetonius says: \* *He took the greatest care to know the history of fables, even to the point of silliness and ridicule; for he even tested the Grammarians with questions of this sort: Who was the mother of Hecuba? What name did Achilles have while disguised among the Maidens? What were the Sirens accustomed to sing?* But to apply this <term>myth-making</term> <note>original: λογοποιϊαν</note> to Isaiah, or to seek a deep meaning in it, would be like "shearing a donkey" <note>an idiom for a fool's errand or seeking something that isn't there</note>. For it is not fitting, since the voice of the Sirens is said to be sweet, charming, and melodious, whereas the <term>Tannim</term> <note>Hebrew: תנים, usually translated as jackals or dragons</note> or <term>Jaanoth</term> or <term>Jeenim</term> (for it is found in both forms) to which Isaiah refers, is horrible and wailing, as is typical of birds and wild beasts inhabiting the desert. From this, the meaning of the word <term>anah</term> <note>Hebrew: ענה</note> must be derived, from a resonating voice and a mournful howling, for <term>anah</term> signifies to sing or to cry out; hence in Exodus 32:18, we find the "voice of those who sing" <note>original: קול ענות</note>. You could not inconveniently translate it as a "howler" or a "screech-owl," which is a species of owl—birds that love solitude, which are also mentioned by Micah in chapter 1, verse 8: *I will make a lament like the Dragons, and a mourning like the daughters of the owl.* For in Hebrew <term>benot ya'anah</term> <note>Hebrew: בנות יענה</note> means "daughters of the owl," referring to owls, as also in Leviticus 11:16, Job 30:29, and in the passage of our Prophet which we are now discussing, verse 21. Likewise in Psalm 147:9, <term>bene orev</term> <note>Hebrew: בני עורב</note> means "sons of the raven," referring to ravens. Those who do not understand this Hebrew idiom attribute some kind of <term>unreasonableness</term> <note>original: αλογιαν</note> to ravens regarding their chicks—an opinion of the followers of Albertus Magnus that Rollenhagius rightly mocks in his *True Lies*, as he calls them, chapter 21, page 239. Indeed, many things are sanctioned based on the faith of a straying antiquity that are otherwise false and contrary to the senses themselves. Many such things can be found in the Ancient Interpreter <note>The Vulgate</note>, whoever he may be, which depart from the truth of the Hebrew text no more than screech-owls depart from Sirens; and yet you find people everywhere who mark everything coming from him with a "white line" <note>an idiom for unconditional approval</note>, under I know not what pretext of piety. Hence Nierembergius argues in his *Natural History*, book 5, chapter 13, pages 79–80, that the Ancient Interpreter understood "aerial Sirens," not "aquatic" ones—as if Satyrs, Fauns, and other such monsters were authenticated by the Vulgate Interpreter as having been in Noah's ark! But since in every literary battle one must flee to the original truth, without consulting which nothing should be settled, any fair judge of matters will judge the Vulgate Interpreter accordingly. That Translator, in the face of linguistic complexity and difficulty, sometimes flees to the fables of the pagans, which could not even win belief from the Pagans themselves; and yet today they allow themselves to be pressured by those who adore every blemish in that version. But Nicetas is here, who gives his opinion on such a version, stating that truth lies hidden under those fabulous names, when he writes on Job 42:14: *When Scripture mentions the "Horn of Plenty," or "Sirens," or the "Valley of Titans," it only signifies the utility intended by those fables, rather than offering us any falsehood.* Jerome, in his *Epistle to the Galatians*, 

<margin>
Volume 9, page 170.
</margin>

chapter 3, says: \* *It is taken from common opinion*—the "Valley of Titans" in the books of Kings, "Sirens" and "Onocentaurs" in Isaiah, "Arcturus," "Orion," and the "Pleiades" in Job, and other similar things, which terms certainly have their causes and origins in pagan fables. But I do not think it necessary to take words from the most trifling theology of the pagans and their abominations when other words are available. 

<margin>
Aelian, *On the Nature of Animals*, book 17, ch. 9.
</margin>

What necessity is there to force the words *And the desert-dwellers shall meet with the island-dwellers* (chapter 34, verse 14) into "Onocentaurs," whom Aelian himself calls into doubt?

<column-break/>

This is surely "joining griffins with horses" <note>an idiom for an impossible or absurd mixture</note> and "asking for water from a pumice stone." The words of the text are as follows:

<margin>
Sirens and Onocentaurs.
</margin>

> *And the desert-creatures shall meet with the island-creatures, and the hairy one shall cry out to his companion.* <note>Hebrew: ופגשו ציים את איים ושעיר על רעהו יקרא</note>

Centaurs, Onocentaurs, and Hippocentaurs are imagined as half-man and half-beast. The Interpreter <note>The Vulgate</note> in another place, Jeremiah chapter 50, verse 39, rendered the Hebrew words for "desert-creatures" and "island-creatures" as *Dragons with murderous Fauns*. In that passage, some read "Fatui" <note>fools/prophetic spirits</note> instead of "Fauni" <note>Fauns</note>, as the Roman Correctors note. Nothing is more foolish than that reading, unless you call Martianus Capella to your aid, who writes in book 2, page 41: *The very earth, which is impassable to men, is filled with choirs of long-lived beings who, inhabiting forests, groves, lakes, springs, and rivers, are called Pans, Fauns, Satyrs, Sylvans, Nymphs, and Fatui or Fatuæ or Fanuæ—named from 'fatu' or the prediction of the future*, not from stupidity. Those whom the Septuagint called "Onocentaurs," Aquila calls <term>trichiontas</term> <note>Greek: τριχιωντας, "hairy ones"</note>, for he usually tries to press the Hebrew words into a precise form. But it seems Aquila brought in that term <term>trichiontas</term> to express the Hebrew <term>sa'ir</term> <note>Hebrew: שעיר</note>. Now, <term>sa'ir</term> comes from the word for "hair" <note>Hebrew: שער</note>, as if you were to say "hairy ones," such as the goat-footed Satyrs of the Poets and the goat-footed Pans in Propertius (Book 3, Elegy 17) and the "deceitful Fauns." Hence Rabbi Kimchi writes in his *Book of Roots* that the Devil is called *Sahit*, who is accustomed to show himself to be seen and adored in the form of a hairy goat. Rabbi Moses Maimonides confirms the same in the third part of the *Guide for the Perplexed*, chapter 47. It is therefore taken to mean horrifying ghosts; Luther and Mercer note that the name remained for Mount Seir in Genesis 36:8 for this reason. So that it might be said of those mountain-dwellers what Lucretius says: \*

<margin>
Book 4.
</margin>

> *These places the neighbors imagine are held by goat-footed Satyrs and Nymphs, and they say the Fauns are there.*

In Leviticus chapter 17:7, God forbids the Jews from sacrificing to "the hairy ones" <note>Hebrew: לשעירם</note> in the manner of the Pagans. The Greek version translates this as "to vain things" <note>original: τοῖς ματαιοις</note>, meaning empty and futile gods. The Chaldean version uses <term>shiddim</term> <note>Aramaic: לשדס</note>, which some derive from the root for "to devastate," while others derive it from the Arabic word for "dominion," and thus <term>shed</term> means "Demon" (Deuteronomy 32:17), who is the true "Apollo" of the pagans. Aquila again translates it as <term>trichiontas</term> ("hairy ones"), for <term>sa'ir</term> means "hairy" or "goat." Thus Satyrs, Fauns, and Pans are depicted with hooked noses and hairy bodies. And so it is in this passage of Isaiah; and Vossius conjectures in his *On Idolatry*, book 1, chapter 8, page 58, that the word "Satyr" becomes "Sahir" by the change of a single letter, by which a "hairy one" is noted, likewise a "goat" in Leviticus 4:23, and <term>by metonymy</term> <note>a figure of speech</note> a "Demon." Brentius, in his commentary on Leviticus, conjectures that Satyrs were worshiped in Egypt, and that the Jews adopted their worship from there—an opinion also followed by Francois Vatable. Sebastian Münster understands them to be "hairy Fauns." Junius accommodates the term to "Scops owls," deformed birds of the owl kind; consult his Notes. That version by a learned man displeased Johannes Wouwer; see him in his *Syntagma on the Interpretation of the Bible*, page 14. The Vulgate, and those who side with it, takes "hairy ones" to mean Sylvan ghosts—think of Pans, Fauns, Satyrs, and that whole choir of butting fictions which pagan antiquity fashioned in the images of dancing, hairy, goat-like demons, as we have seen. Indeed, it was a common belief among the Ancients that Demons, Fauns, and Satyrs wandered through deserted and dark places, and the Vulgate Interpreter...

<meta>This page concludes the discussion of the "hairy ones" or "satyrs" mentioned in Isaiah 13, shifting from mythological interpretations to early modern natural history (identifying them as primates). It then begins a new commentary on Isaiah 18, focusing on the geographical identification of Ethiopia and the metaphor of "shadowing wings" as a reference to naval power.</meta>

<page-num>579</page-num>
<header>Isaiah 13, last verse. 579</header>

<margin>Sirens & Onocentaurs.</margin>
alluded to this. Lucretius, in book 4, attributes "night-wandering noise" to Satyrs. Eucherius, in book 2 of *Formulas of Spiritual Intelligence*, chapter 9, page 291, states: *The hairy ones* <note>original: "Pilosi"</note> in Isaiah are types of demons. Some of the most learned have thought these were *Incubi* or *Satyrs*, or certain *wild men of the woods*. Matthias Flacius annexed that book of Eucherius to the first part of his *Key to Scripture*, but Sixtus of Siena, in his *Library*, book 4, under the entry "Eucherius," denies it is actually Eucherius’s work. Nicolaus the Minorite, in his *Mammotrectus* <note>a 15th-century pedagogical tool for clergy</note> on Isaiah, says: *The hairy ones are monsters in the likeness of men, whose form begins with a human face but ends in a beastly extremity.* Or they are *incubus demons*, or *woodland demons*. Interpreters here pile up many fables concocted by pagan antiquity regarding Satyrs, Fauns, and Onocentaurs <note>mythical creatures, half-man and half-donkey</note>; however, lest we seem to distract the reader—who is occupied with weightier matters—with trifles, we shall remember the common proverb: *Hands off the slate* <note>original Latin: "Manum de tabula" — a phrase meaning to stop working on something that is finished or to avoid over-complicating it</note>. 

See, if you please, Juan Eusebio Nieremberg in his *History of Nature*, book 5, chapters 8, 9, and 10, pages 76–78. We command these shaggy and hair-bristling Satyrs and Onocentaurs to be excluded from Sacred matters; those terms "smell of the goat" <note>an idiom for something coarse or offensive</note> and are like mouse-droppings mixed into pepper. No one can easily provide firm explanations for the names of these beasts, in which we know Luther himself felt stuck, by his own confession. Hence he says in his *Scholia*: *The business here for the grammarians concerns the names of things that have now fallen out of use; just as in almost all languages, there is great obscurity in the names of things.* What the Latin calls *Demons* and *Onocentaurs*, the Hebrews call *Ziim* and *Iim*. Some take *Ziim* for what we call a *marten* <note>German: "Marder"</note> and *Jim* for a vulture. I think the *Hairy One* <note>Latin: "Pilosum"</note> is a Satyr or Faun. The <term>Lamia</term> <note>a female mythological monster</note> they call in German a *Kobold* or *Schretlin* <note>household spirits or goblins</note> / spirits wandering in houses and subjecting themselves to the service of men. 

But these things, as I said, are uncertain. We will not allow our eyes to be deceived by the mask of Onocentaurs and Satyrs, as if they were actual Satyrs, when they are merely ill-omened beasts. Andrea Cesalpino, in his book *On the Investigation of Demons*, chapter 14, folio 158b, claims that Fauns, Sylvan spirits, and Satyrs were born from the intercourse of the Devil, and that giants also arose from this. A Satyr was allegedly captured not far from Apollonia, a city of Epirus, according to Sabinus. Antonio Donato, in his *Treatise on Simples* <note>medicinal herbs</note>, page 118, displays a "marine Satyr" of wondrous form. An *Indian Satyr*, with a shaggy head, shoulder, and back, was brought from Angola to Frederick Henry, Prince of Orange; it was called in the Indian language an *orang-outang*, that is, a *man of the woods* <note>Latin: "homo Sylvestris"</note>, an image of which Nicolaes Tulp provides in his *Medical Observations*, book 3, chapter 56, page 275.

### Isaiah XVIII. v. 1. 2.

> Woe to the land shadowing with wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia:
> That sendeth ambassadors by the sea, even in vessels of bulrushes upon the waters.
> <note>original Greek (Septuagint): Οὐαὶ γῆς πλοίων πτέρυγες ἐπέκεινα ποταμῶν Αἰθιοπίας... "Woe to the land of ship's wings beyond the rivers of Ethiopia..."</note>
> <note>original Latin (Vulgate): "Væ terra inumbranti alis..." "Woe to the land shadowing with wings..."</note>

<margin>Egyptian Districts.</margin>
Isaiah prophesies in this entire chapter concerning the peoples of Ethiopia, in whose aid the Jews trusted against the Assyrians, and he denounces the slaughter they are to receive from Sennacherib. Others prefer to interpret this prophecy

<column-break/>

against the Egyptians, but they are mistaken, for <margin>Egyptians.</margin> the "burden of the Egyptians" is described in the very next chapter. Arias, Malvenda, Delrio, Bozius, Lumnius, and others interpret this as referring to the Indians; but a *Woe* <note>original Hebrew: "Hoy"</note> could not be intended for them here, because they never harmed the Jews, as Tirinus notes on page 600. The Prophet sets the whole matter before our eyes with such illustrious words that it seems not merely to be told, but to be happening. 

He begins with a threat. *Woe to the land*, he says—that is, Ethiopia—which can be gathered from the following description: *which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia*. For that nation is overseas with respect to Judea. It is not uncommon in Holy Scripture to describe places by their rivers. *The land by* (for some explain the Hebrew *eber* this way) *the rivers of Ethiopia*, because it is washed and flowed through by rivers, and is famous for its cities along the reaches of those rivers. Thus *Rabbah*, because it was surrounded and fortified on all sides by waters, whether stagnant or continually flowing, is called the *city of waters* <margin>2 Samuel 12:27</margin>. Likewise, Ausonius somewhere calls Alexandria the *house of the river*. 

With respect to Jerusalem and Judea, Ethiopia is properly situated beyond the seven streams of the Nile, which streams shall be shown below to be called "rivers." That region had resolved to send *naval* forces as an aid, as if they were allies. The Prophet describes the multitude of these ships with a hyperbolic and very elegant expression: to indicate the vast number of ships, he calls it *the land of shadowing wings* or *the land shaded by wings*. This refers to the shadow made by the sails of the fleets, such that the sea and the shore were made dark. For many interpreters wish for the phrase *tziltzal kenaphayim* <note>Hebrew: צִלְצַל כְּנָפַיִם</note> to contain the sense of shadowiness. The root *tzalal* means to overshadow, to make dark, or to cover; from which *tziltzal* is formed by doubling the letters. 

The edge or extremity of a thing is also usually denoted by the word *kanaph* (wing); as in the *hem of a cloak* in 1 Samuel 24:5, and regarding the *borders of garments* in Numbers 15:38, Deuteronomy 22:12, and Haggai 2:12. In this way, Tremellius is of the opinion that the mountains surrounding Ethiopia like fringes are meant; he translates it as *shadowy of borders* and thinks it alludes to the multitude of mountains. For he says in his notes: *Whose borders are enclosed by the greatest and most shadowy mountains, such as Strabo testifies exist everywhere toward the Red Sea.* 

However, the Prophet intended to illustrate, as I said, the multitude of ships, whose sails he calls *wings*. He implies that the ships, full of wind, fly across the seas by their sails as if by *wings*, overshadowing the shores and the sea itself. In a boat or ship, the sails are like wings, by which the ships fly out no differently than birds with wings; because of this "rowing of wings," ships are called *sail-fliers* <note>Latin: "velivolae"</note>. Hence the Targum says: *they extend sails like an eagle flying with wings*; and the Septuagint well translated it as *wings of ships*. The Greek *pteryx* is mostly used for the wings of birds. So too *kanaph* in Psalm 55:7 refers to the wing of a dove. Procopius says on this passage: *He calls the sails "wings of ships." For the ships are propelled like winged things when the winds blow into them.* <margin>page 88</margin> Jerome says: *Understand the wings of ships as the sails by which they are suspended and drawn.* Among more recent scholars, Oecolampadius *calls it the land of the shadowiness of wings, or shadowing with wings, that is, with the sails of ships, because of the frequency of harbors and ships, since they cast a shadow with their sails. Sails are called wings because by them, as if by wings, ships go and fly through the sea.* <margin>folio 125a</margin> Wolfgang Musculus, page 325: *He calls Ethiopia the land of shadowy wings because of the multitude...*

<meta>catchword: ...of [multitude]</meta>

The author argues that the "shadowing wings" mentioned in the prophecy against Ethiopia refer to the vast number of sails in the Ethiopian naval fleet.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Isaiah 18, moving from the geographical identity of Ethiopia to a deep linguistic and historical analysis of "shadowing wings" and the "vessels of papyrus" used by the Egyptians and Ethiopians.</meta>

<page-num>580</page-num>
<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>Egyptian Districts.</margin>
...the multitude of ships that come to her for the sake of trade. For by "shadowing wings," one should understand the sails of ships, which are to ships what wings are to birds; and in the meantime, they provide shadow for those sailing. Thus, it is a "land shaded by wings" because it is darkened by the sails of fleets as if by wings, which cast a shadow over the shores, seas, and rivers with their sails. Therefore, Luther translates it: <margin>folio 18. b.</margin> *That travels under the sails in the shadow.* <note>German: "Das unter den Segeln im Schatten fähret."</note> The critic of our version, Georg Wicelius, gives his assent, rendering it: *O Land / of which the wings are a shadow. That is / such a land in which so many ships go / that it is shadowed and covered by the ships' wings or sails.* <note>German: "O Land / des ein Schatte die Flügel sind. Das ist / ein solch Land / darin so viel Schiff gehen / das es gleich von der Schiff flügel oder Segel beschattet und bedecket wird."</note> Sails are the "wings" of ships, which the wind expands. A "wing" is also attributed to the Dawn in *Psalm* 139:9, so that the speed of the Sun may be indicated, which reaches the furthest places in its swift course. The Vulgate translator rendered the Hebrew word *tziltzal* <note>צלצל</note> as "cymbal"; the meaning of that word depends on the root *tzalal* <note>צלל</note>, and by its sound—a fitting onomatopoeia <note>a word that sounds like what it describes</note>—it gives itself over to the elements by doubling. Among the Hebrews and Chaldeans, it is the same as "to tinkle" or "to make a sound like a small bell made of metal"; it is used for the *tingling of the ears* <margin>1 Samuel 3:11</margin> where the angry Divinity says *he will do a thing (a dire matter and horrendous to hear) in Israel, which whoever hears, both his ears shall tingle.* Regarding this, Cornelius à Lapide (page 236) says: *The metaphor is drawn from one who suddenly hears a tinkling cymbal, or the roar of a large cannon, or a great thunderclap, whose violent sound strikes through and causes a tingling that lasts a long time in the ears of the listeners.* A similar phrasing comes from the same verb in 2 *Kings* 21:12 and *Jeremiah* 19:3. From this same verb, "tingling" is attributed to the lips in *Habakkuk* 3:16, where it says *my lips tingled* <note>original: "tzalalu sephathai"</note>, meaning they throbbed and made a sort of clear sound. Truly, I believe nothing so elegant, so charming, or so grave can be uttered by any Greek or Latin writer that cannot be said with equal strength by the Hebrew nation. These sacred expressions have sinew and bone, and they carry the banner of their own strength without trembling. My ears and lips tingle whenever I see the most hardworking critics, with their eyes sent out toward the whole battle-line of secular literature, finding nowhere a better-equipped or more elegant armory than in this "Western Hellespont" <note>A metaphor for the study of Hebrew in the West as a gateway to wisdom</note>. Cymbals sound in our ears to those we wish well. *Tziltzal* sounds like "cymbal" and "rattle." Where the prophetic singers occupied themselves with divine praises, they had before them the *lyre*, the *psaltery*, the *flute*, and the *harp* (1 *Samuel* 10:5). The sacred text designates those musical instruments, heard in that divine college of singers, with these words: *and before them a psaltery, and a timbrel, and a pipe, and a harp.* <note>1 Samuel 10:5; Hebrew: ולפניהם נבל ותף וחליil וכנור</note> <margin>1 Samuel 18:6.</margin> The Chaldean version has the name *tziltzalin* in the plural for the word "flute." Likewise, in that victory song in 1 *Samuel* 18:6, where Goliath had been conquered in the duel, for the Hebrew "with three-stringed instruments" <note>original: "beshalishim"</note> we find "with cymbals" <note>original: "betziltzalin"</note>; here the Septuagint <note>Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> says "with cymbals" and the Vulgate "with sistrums" <note>a metallic rattle used in ancient Egypt</note>. Luther translates: *with violins.* Vatable: *in songs.* It was, however, an instrument of three strings, by the power of its name, for it comes from *shalosh* ("three"), which seems to have a similarity with the *Pandura*, an instrument most commonly used by Italians today. It is also in *Psalm* 150:5, where the people are stirred up to proclaim the power of God *with loud cymbals* <note>original: "betziltzelei shama"</note>. *With well-sounding cymbals / with well-sounding cymbals.* <note>German: "mit wohlklingenden Cymbeln"; Latin: "in Cymbalis bene Sonantibus."</note> From this it is now clear why the Vulgate version interprets "the cymbal of wings," upon which words various explanations are published. Some speak of

<column-break/>

trumpets and bugles. Sanchez on this passage: <margin>Ethiopian ships</margin> Ethiopian ships are called "cymbals" or "cymbal-like" because the Ethiopians, and after them the soft Egyptians, were accustomed to sound bugles and pipes while sailing. And Jacobus Tirinus (page 600) says: *Woe to the land of Ethiopia, which is the cymbal of wings*, that is, *which has the wings of its armies, both land and naval, tinkling like a cymbal—that is, making an empty and futile sound, resounding with bugles, pipes, and trumpets, but bringing nothing of help or benefit beyond the sound.* J. Carpentejus wishes to suggest here that the worship of Apis <note>the Egyptian bull deity</note> by the clangor of the sistrum <note>rattle</note> is meant, which he expressed in heroic verse:
> <margin>Book 2, Meter 83.</margin>
> Woe to you, who celebrate the return of Apis with rattling sistrums,
> Beating castanets and empty cymbals.
Truly, this sistrum rattles poorly, and the clangor of the cymbal is empty; and this abnormal explanation is worthy only of a pipe and a rattle. Let us bypass another no less ridiculous explanation about the Troglodytes <note>legendary "cave-dwellers"</note> "cymbalizing" while speaking, which we read in Pineda. <margin>Pineda on this passage.</margin> Others put "skiff" <note>original: "cymba"</note> for "cymbal" <note>original: "cymbalum"</note>, and wish the version had been: *Woe to the land of winged skiffs*, using a Hebrew idiom to mean "provided with winged skiffs," that is, with sailing vessels; for in the same way it follows: *in vessels of papyrus*, that is, made of papyrus. But what if I take the reason for this name from the noise and creaking which an entire fleet makes in the heat of the sea (a rising flood?) where wave pushes wave, and the winds lean into the sails, a great sound is made. The King of Ethiopia had sent his ambassadors and auxiliary soldiers into the sea, and toward the sea and the Nile, in *vessels of papyrus*. Who was that King? Some understand him to be Tirhakah <note>Pharaoh of the 25th Dynasty</note>, who, while Sennacherib was away, had declared war on Assyria through ambassadors and, having drawn up his battle line, had attempted to invade so as to hinder him in invading Judea; about this invasion we read in 2 *Kings* 19:9 that the Assyrian heard this sad news: *Behold, Tirhakah has gone out to fight against you.* While Sennacherib sought the lands of others, his own were disturbed at home. But what are those *vessels of papyrus*? In the Hebrew: *in vessels of rushes* <note>original: "bekele-gome"</note>. By the name "vessels," the Hebrews understand any instrument, and here it denotes the vessels of sailors, that is, ships and skiffs. *Reed ships*, Luther translated. The word *gome* <note>גמא</note> denotes both a *cane*, which grows like a tree in Oriental places, and a *rush*; indeed, it received its name from the fact that it rises in waters and marshes and drinks or sucks up the juice; for *gama* means "he drank, he swallowed up." From rushes, little boats were prepared, which they used to smear with bitumen; of such a kind was that papyrus vessel, that little rush box in which Moses—the delicate infant of divine hope and elegance—is read to have been exposed (Exodus 2:3) by his mother, who took a *basket of rushes* <note>original: "thevath gome"</note>, an ark made of rushes or reeds in the manner of a small skiff, shaped so it could float easily on the waters. She smeared it *with bitumen and pitch* so the water would not enter, placed the boy in it, and thus exposed him to the river Nile, but *in the flags* <note>original: "be-suph"</note> or reeds near the bank of the river. *Suph* <note>סוף</note> denotes both the content (the seaweed or algae) and the container (the place planted with sedges, reeds, algae, or rushes), as is common at the banks and extremities of rivers; from which its name also seems to come, *suph* meaning "to end," and *suph* and *supha* in Chaldean meaning "end, extremity." <header>Isaiah 19, verse 1 and following.</header>

Egyptian Districts.

...with the paraphrase. That little ark was placed *in the midst of the rushes* <note>original Hebrew: בכלי גומא (*biklei gomeh*)</note>, as Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the reputed author of the Aramaic Targum</note> has it, so that the infant would not be swallowed up; for if the ark had come loose from the bank, it would have been carried away and overturned by the river in the deep. Josephus <note>a first-century Jewish historian</note> calls that ark a "woven vessel of papyrus" <note>original Greek: *πλέγμα βίβλινον* (*plegma biblinon*)</note>. It is not unknown that ships and boats were made of papyrus and reeds, even from the current custom among the Indians. The papyrus tree provided material *both from its bark and leaves for writing paper, the thinner inner bark of the tree being separated into leaves with a needle*, as Pliny testifies in *Book 7, chapter 56*. For this reason, the Septuagint <note>The "LXX," the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> thought that "papyrus letters"—that is, paper letters—had been sent; in the same way they took the Hebrew word for *papyrus* in Exodus 2:3 and Job 8:11. It was also used as wood for ships, for Pliny states in that same passage that ships were made on the Nile from *papyrus, rushes, and reeds*; he also mentioned "papyrus ships of the Nile" in Book 6, chapter 22, and repeats in Book 13, chapter 11, that "vessels are woven from the papyrus itself." Herodotus <note>the Greek "Father of History"</note> testifies in Book 2 that the Egyptians made vessels from rushes. Hence Lucan in Book 6:

<margin>
Exodus 2:3.
Job 8:11.
</margin>

->*So when the Nile holds all things,*<-
->*The Memphis boat is constructed from thirsty papyrus.*<-

"The Memphis boat is constructed from thirsty papyrus." Plutarch also mentions this same use in *On Isis and Osiris*, where he adds that it is believed crocodiles do not harm those carried on such rafts, perhaps because they move more swiftly than other ships and escape the animal's anger. Propertius, speaking of Charon's boat <note>the ferryman of the dead in mythology</note> in Book 2:

<margin>
Book 2.
</margin>

->*Now the oarsman may sit under the Stygian reed.*<-
<note>"Stygian" refers to the river Styx in the underworld.</note>

In India, reeds are so firm and tall that individual ships could be made from single segments between the joints. Pliny confirmed this with these words: *The Indian reed has the size of a tree. Single segments even serve the purpose of boats.* They grow mostly around the Acesines river. Now the Acesines is the same river that Stephanus calls the Tanais. Staurabates, King of the Indians, made up to four thousand ships from reeds against the power of Semiramis. Diodorus says of it: *He constructed river boats from reeds, with four wheels. For India, along the rivers and marshy places, produces a great quantity of reed, the thickness of which a man could not easily embrace.* <note>original Greek: Ἐκ τῇ καλάμῳ κατεσκεύασε πλοῖα ποτάμια... περιλάβοι.</note> Agathias, in Book 5 of the *Gothic War*, reported that a fleet of 150 ships compacted from reeds was prepared by the Huns. These vessels were light upon the face of the waters, and their use was to make a swifter journey; hence the ambassadors of the Ethiopians, who were equipped to hasten their journey, used them so they might reach their destination more quickly; and there were the "Catadupae" in Ethiopia, where the waters of the Nile rushed with a great roar among the obstructing rocks, which reed ships could navigate with a more agile course. These are the few things we wished to sample, sending the reader eager for a fuller *examination* <note>original Greek: *ἐξετάσεως*</note> to Martinus Roxa’s *Singularia*.

### Isaiah 19, verse 1 and following.

<margin>
The Burden of Egypt.
</margin>

->The Burden of Egypt<- <note>original Hebrew: משא מצרים (*Massa Mitzrayim*)</note>
->The Vision of Egypt<- <note>original Greek: Ὅρασις Αἰγύπτου (*Horasis Aigyptou*)</note>
->*The Burden of Egypt.*<- <note>original Latin: *Onus Ægypti.*</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>
The Burden of Egypt.
</margin>
**I**N the burdensome prophecy of Egypt, in which destruction is predicted for this nation—which traces its origin to Mizraim, the son of Ham <note>Mizraim is the biblical name for Egypt</note>—both for its pride and its superstition, many things must be observed from the *writings of ethnic history*. We shall attempt to show *briefly* <note>original Greek: *συλλαβήδην*</note>, according to the three parts of the first section of this chapter, the internal disturbances by which Egypt was to be shaken; for unless one learns the location and customs of the region from *archaeology* <note>original Greek: *ἀρχαιολογία*, here meaning ancient history</note>, which the Prophet described as concisely as he did skillfully, I know it will be difficult to arrive at an understanding of the matter. That understanding of ancient rites is useful, for those who lack it must often hallucinate, doubt, and pass over many things in the Prophets. For prophecies issued against the nations often adopt certain things from the customs of those nations, without the knowledge of which we would achieve nothing. We shall treat each in order.

<margin>
v. 1.
</margin>
*THE BURDEN OF EGYPT: Behold, the Lord riding upon a light cloud, and he enters Egypt, and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence.* A series of illustrious paraphrases of Egypt's greatest calamities follow, through which Jehovah places the matter so clearly before the eyes that it seems not merely to be told, but to be happening. Just as the Prophets use a sublime style of speaking, with frequent metaphors, allegories, and figures, so it is in this chapter. The Egyptian nation was greatly troubled by the sudden onset of the Assyrian army, so that the heart of Egypt melted <note>original Hebrew: *masas* (מסס)</note>, that is, *it was loosened* <note>original Greek: *ἐξηλύθην*</note>, as Homer also said, *it delighted the soul* <note>original Greek: *θυμὸν τέρψε*</note> and in the same book line 136, *the heart in its manhood* <note>original Greek: *κατ' ἠνορέην ἦτορ*</note>) in its interior, an internal sedition having arisen among them—some wanting to surrender themselves voluntarily to the enemy, others resisting—and so while they split into two factions, it happened that *its spirit was emptied in its innermost part*, all counsel and help failing. The first paraphrase is taken from the speed of the clouds. Therefore, *The Lord sits upon a light cloud.* For which Aquila <note>a 2nd-century translator known for his hyper-literal Greek version of the Hebrew Bible</note> has: *Behold the Lord mounts upon a light thickness.* <note>original Greek: ἰδὲ κύριος ἐπιβαίνει ἐπὶ πάχους ἐλαφροῦ.</note> That translator is often accustomed to render the etymologies of words, as Jerome testifies to Pammachius, and to express word for word, which he also did here; because a cloud <note>original Hebrew: *ab* (עב)</note> is called such from its thickness and density, for *abah* <note>original Hebrew: עבה</note> means *it was thick*, and *ab* means density, hence Aquila’s *pachos* <note>original Greek: πάχος</note>, "thickness," for a cloud. So elsewhere *abah* is rendered *willing ones* <note>original Greek: *θεληταὶ*</note>, because *abah* means *he willed*; and the Moon <note>original Hebrew: *lebanah*</note> is rendered *the white one* <note>original Greek: *λευκὴ*</note>, because *laban* means *white*. A cloud is a symbol of speed in sacred matters; and when attributed to God, it indicates the bitterness of taking vengeance and a sudden execution because of a crime brought before him. The authors—Jerome, Thomas, Haymo, Hugo, Lyranus—interpret the "light cloud" <note>original Hebrew: *qal ab* (קל עב)</note> as the very swift army of the Assyrians, of which the Lord was the Leader, as it were, who sent them most quickly against the Egyptians, so that like a thick cloud they might vibrate lightning—that is, weapons and arrows—at the enemy. Tremellius and Piscator explain this from the "critical meteorology" of a superstitious nation, which would consider clouds as most unlucky; especially since Egypt is very little troubled by them, and when they appeared, the inhabitants were so foolish and credulous and unskilled in things that they persuaded themselves that something calamitous or unusual was imminent or even "at the doors," which the priests then had to declare regarding the nation's fate. It was known that clouds were unlucky, a divination about which Damascius nevertheless reports in the *Life of Isidore* in Photius (code 242, page 554) *was not at all known to the ancients, even by hearsay*, and that *divination by means of clouds* <note>original Greek: *τὴν διὰ τῶν νεφῶν μαντικὴν*</note> was found under Leo, the Roman Emperor, an opinion to which we do not give assent. *Cloud-chasers* <note>original Greek: *νεφελοδιώκτας*</note>, or *persecutors of clouds*, are explained...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Isaiah 19, shifting from the physical description of Egyptian vessels to the theological and political "Burden of Egypt," specifically focusing on internal division and the administrative structure of the Egyptian districts or "Nomes."</meta>

<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>

<margin>The Burden of Egypt.</margin>
...to Balsamon in his commentary on the 61st Canon of the Council of Trullo, regarding diviners, concerning which see Delrio in the 6th book of *Magical Disquisitions*, section 2, question 1, page 928. However, I doubt whether I would dare to assert that this specific allusion pleased the Prophet. We simply estimate that God's arrival is described using an **anthropopathic metaphor** <note>Attributing human physical movements or emotions to God to make a concept understandable.</note> taken from the clouds; for Scripture is accustomed to attribute clouds to God as vehicles, according to this human-like description, to denote His power and incredible speed in executing judgments. For this reason, the adjective *light* is added—meaning *swift* by way of a **metalepsis** <note>A figure of speech where one word is used in place of another through a chain of associations.</note>. This means: The Lord Himself, the strong judge in Israel, comes most swiftly and unexpectedly to punish the Egyptians with a sinister blow by the hand of Sennacherib <note>The Neo-Assyrian king who invaded the region.</note>. It is as if He flies swiftly upon the clouds, and neither the threatening crags of the mountains in Egypt, nor the marshes, nor the filth of the desert, nor vain oracles, public supplications, or the futile consultations of ancestors, sorcerers, and diviners, nor the depths of the sea or the Nile, will be able to stand in His way.

<margin>verse 2.</margin>
**And I will confound Egypt with Egypt, and they shall fight, every man against his brother, and every man against his companion; city against city, and kingdom against kingdom.** Here is described a seditious faction—than which there is no more harmful plague—and the mutual envy of the inhabitants, which the Greeks elegantly call **androphthonia** <note>original Greek: ἀνδροφθονίαν; literally "the slaughter of men."</note>. This state of public affairs, as such things tend to be fertile in disaster, brought with it **uprising and the shattering of the fatherland** <note>original Greek: ἀνάστασιν καὶ ἀνδροπολισμὸν πατρίδος</note>. Hence, once the ancient dignity and glory of the Republic were lost, there followed at that time uncertain domains and errors of counsel (verse 3). Indeed, the affairs of the Egyptian citizens were confined within narrow limits by a multitude of lawsuits and internal disturbances; within the same house, nation, and family, man rose up against companion, and kinsman against kinsman **with weapons** <note>original Greek: τοῖς βελέσεσι</note>. By the just and ineffable judgment of God, they fell by mutual wounds, while one transferred his guilt to another, and he to a third. Thus it happens that if external enemies do not present themselves, or if they are despised, the violence of minds is armed against itself; citizen attacks citizen, and like the **Cadmean harvest** <note>A mythological reference to warriors who sprouted from the earth and immediately killed one another.</note>, they finally fall in mutual slaughter. The speech of Micipsa in Sallust’s *Jugurtha* (page 65) is well-used and not in vain: *“By concord small things grow; by discord the greatest fall.”* To the same effect is that passage in Dionysius of Halicarnassus (*Roman Antiquities*, Book 4): *“Unity is the cause of strength for the weak, but mutual envy causes lowliness and weakness even among the strongest.”* For what house is so stable, what city so firm, that it cannot be utterly overturned by hatreds and disagreements, as Cicero says in his work *On Friendship*. Nor does that saying of 

<margin>Matthew 12:25.</margin>
Christ differ: *“Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand.”* In the same vein is that word of Sopho-

<margin>in Antigone.</margin>
cles:
> For there is no greater evil than anarchy.
> It ruins cities, and turns
> households into ruins.

As for what the Hebrew says—that **kingdom fought against kingdom** <note>original Hebrew: ממלכה בממלכה (*mamlakha be-mamlakha*)</note>—the Septuagint has most skillfully rendered it: *“they divided the Nomes”* <note>original Greek: νομοὺς διέμον</note>. Epiphanius looked to this version when he wrote against the Basilidians: *“The Egyptians call the surrounding district or territory of each city a Nome.”* For thus, by the ancients, a province, administration, or prefec-

<column-break/>

ture was called a **Nome** <note>The administrative districts of ancient Egypt.</note>. Procopius also intends this, saying: *“For they called the lands Nomes.”* The "Solons of Egypt" <note>The wise lawgivers of Egypt, compared to the Athenian statesman Solon.</note> rightly understood and prudently considered that there is nothing that holds a Republic together more strongly than the proper ordering of Prefectures according to certain laws and constitutions. For it is clearly established that to this end the ancient Egyptians divided their land into prefectures, which they called **Nomes**, and those who presided over them were called **Nomarchs**. Moses and David, Proclus and Pliny, explain clearly who those people and places were. Among the Hebrews—to begin with the "better Muses" <note>A scholarly way of referring to sacred Scripture.</note>—they are called **officers** <note>original Hebrew: הפקידים (*ha-phekīdīm*), as in Esther 2:3</note> in Genesis 41:34; these were the dispensers, grain-supply managers, and judges appointed by the King's edict over all Egypt. The Vulgate rendered this: *“And he appointed servants over the land,”* while the Septuagint says: *“and let him appoint toparchs over the land.”* A scholarly annotation explains this as **overseers** <note>original Greek: ἐπισκόπους (*episkopous*)</note>; not badly, since Arcadius the Lawyer also calls an *Episcopus* (Bishop/Overseer) one who is in charge of bread and other saleable goods. To this we add the **princes** <note>original Hebrew: חשמנים (*chashmannim*), Psalm 68:32</note>, whom they understand as Prefects, Governors, or Nomarchs. Aben Ezra also saw this, interpreting it as **magistrates** <note>original Hebrew: סגנים (*seganim*)</note>. David Kimchi says in his *Book of Roots* that they are **great princes and leaders** <note>original Hebrew: שרים גדולים ונגידים</note>, a title full of weight and honor. Commonly, though not vulgarly, those skilled in the language translate **leaders** <note>original Hebrew: נגידים (*nagidim*)</note> as Dukes or Princes, for it is commonly used in the sacred texts with the meaning of "principality." In this loftier sense, the orders of principalities are found in four words—a significant number—in Proverbs 8:15 and 16: **kings, rulers, princes, and nobles** <note>original Hebrew: מלכים, רוזנים, שרים, גברים</note>, from which Kimchi thought the term **princes and nobles** <note>original Hebrew: שרים ונדיבים</note> fit the explanation of the *chashmannim* well enough. The Septuagint has **ambassadors** <note>original Greek: πρέσβεις</note> or Elders. Hesychius defines it: *phrearis, elders, kings, rulers, honored ones.* Thus, even the Latin *Senior* and the French *Seigneur* are words not only of age, but of honor. Now we shall explain the Nomes. A **Nome** is *primarily a place of pasturage*, as Eustathius records on Homer. In Topography, it denotes certain regions; he notes the same where he mentions the "Nomes of the Libyans." Jerome mentions the *“Heliopolitan territory, which the Egyptians call a Nome.”* Proclus, in his commentary on the *Timaeus*, teaches that a Nome is so called *“from the land having been distributed.”* For thus, he says, the Egyptians called the divisions according to the large parts of Egypt. Plato had narrated in the *Timaeus* that the **Saitic Nome** was in the Delta, whose Goddess's name was **Neith** in Egyptian, but **Athena** in Greek. Ancient Glosses state: *“A district [Pagus] is a toparchy, a region, a Nome.”* Pliny, in Book 5, chapter 9, interprets Nomes as **Prefectures**. Thus, discussing Egypt: *“The highest part bordering Ethiopia is called the Thebaid. It is divided into the Prefectures of towns (which they call Nomes).”* He differs in the number of Nomes from those who place ten in the Thebaid. Strabo, in Book 17, mentions the Sethreitic Nome, and also calls the Sabaeans and Minaeans in Arabia Felix "Nomes." The same author of natural history (Pliny, 36:13) mentions the Egyptian labyrinth in the Heracleopolite Nome as being most precious. Herodotus, in *Euterpe* (page 126), dealing with the provinces or prefectures contained in the region and tract of Egypt: *“They were arranged into the Egyptian Nomes.”* In the same book (page 69), Amasis, the King of Egypt, is mentioned as *“being of the Saitic Nome, from the city... of the Nome which is Siuph.”* Where Valla interprets this as "the tribal districts." Pliny, in his 10th Book of Epistles, letter 5...

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Isaiah 19, moving from the physical "burden" of God's arrival to the internal collapse of Egyptian society, specifically focusing on its administrative districts (Nomes) and the futility of its religious practices.</meta>

<page-num>585</page-num>
<header>Isaiah XIX. v. 1. following.</header>

<margin>
The Burden of Egypt.
</margin>
Trajan mentions the **Memphite district** <note>original Greek: νοµῷ µεµφιτικῷ</note> in a letter, which Johannes Maria Catanaeus correctly explains as the Memphite Prefecture, though others have mistaken the word for "law." In his correspondence with Pliny regarding Harpocras, the Emperor Trajan wrote: *You must make known to me from which district (nomos) he comes.* Among these prefectures or districts were the Sethaitic, Thebaic, Memphite, and Coptic. The Coptic District was named after Coptos, a city in the Mareotic region of Egypt <note>According to Pliny, Book 5, Chapter 9</note>. The Heliopolitan District took its name from Heliopolis <note>Strabo, Book XVII</note>. After discussing Bubastus and the Bubastic Prefecture, Strabo adds: <margin>Book 17, page 354.</margin> **Above it lies the Heliopolitan district.** Strabo also mentions the Egyptian town of Oxyrhynchus and the district of the same name: **On the opposite bank is the city of Oxyrhynchus and the district of the same name.** In Pausanias <margin>p. 6.</margin> we find the *Arsinoite prefecture*; for there he uses the term **district** <note>nomos</note>. In Epiphanius, a certain Egyptian prefecture is called the **Prosopite district**. Vitus Amerbachius, in an inexcusable slip, translated this as: *The Law, which takes its name from a person.* Chalcidius made the same error when translating Plato's *Timaeus*, where it says: **There is a certain district called the Saitic at the delta of the Nile**; he translated it as *The Saitic Law.* Sais is one of the cities of Egypt and the capital of the Saitic district. The governor who presided over a district was called a **Nomarch** <note>nomarchēs</note>, and the dignity of the prefecture itself was called a **Nomarchy**. You see what errors can occur if we are ignorant of the sacred rites, regions, and the specific magistracies of each nation! Even the Royal Interpreter of the Bible <note>likely referring to the editors of the Polyglot Bibles</note> threw mud on the text by foolishly following the Septuagint's rendering: *Law against Law.* For the accent alone distinguishes the meanings, as Eustathius teaches in his notes on Homer: **Nómos (accented on the first syllable) is that which grants justice; but nomós (accented on the last syllable) is a place of pasturage, and among the Egyptians, a district.** I have judged it worthwhile to include the commentaries of Oecolampadius on the sense of these words. I do so gladly because, in the century in which he lived, he is found to have occasionally explained the divine prophecies of Isaiah quite successfully where they depend on ancient customs, ceremonies, or geography. Indeed, <margin>18 E/f,</margin> Luther himself wrote to Nicolaus Gerbelius: *I am very glad that Johannes Oecolampadius is professing Isaiah at Basel, although I hear it displeases many. But such is the fortune of Christian doctrine. Through that man, Christ will give us some light on the Prophets.* Oecolampadius writes as follows: <margin>folio 104 b.</margin> *By "kingdoms" here, understand the Prefectures of Egypt, which are called "districts" (nomoi) by the Egyptians. Just as the Septuagint says here: "and district against district." This refers to one prefecture against another, such as the Alexandrian Thebaid, Ptolemais, Memphis, Arsinoitis, and others.* Oecolampadius knew Greek well enough here; <margin>Letter to Brixius, Book 19, p. 643.</margin> a praise written of him by Erasmus. We can find more on this in Paulus Leopardus, Lalius Bisciola, and Martini’s *Philological Lexicon* under the word *Nomos.* I also hope that Athanasius Kircher’s *Treatise on the Hieroglyphic Apparatus* will be fruitful, where we find a description of the geography of both ancient and modern Egypt, along with descriptions of the individual districts and famous cities. Regarding the fulfillment of this divine oracle, one should consult Brentius, who illustrates the history using Herodotus and Diodorus Siculus.

<margin>verse 3.</margin>
*And the spirit of Egypt shall fail in the midst thereof, and I will destroy the counsel thereof: and they shall seek to* <margin>The Burden of Egypt.</margin> *the idols (**ha-elilim**), and to the charmers (**ha-ittim**), and to the mediums (**ha-ovot**) and to the spiritists (**ha-yiddeonim**).* The prophet affirms that the spirit of the Egyptians will be troubled (as the Septuagint has it), and in the time of their affliction, they will be reduced to such inexplicable straits that they will consult every kind of oracle and prophecy. When Scripture wishes to indicate a total loss of courage and lack of counsel, it says *the heart melted and there was no spirit remaining,* as in Joshua 5:1 regarding the Canaanites trembling at the arrival of the Israelites. It was a common custom among all nations that, when placed in public danger, they would do nothing without seeking omens. Instead, they fled to the oracles of their petty gods, who were consulted for authority on what to do or omit. They went to the priests of these mysteries, to soothsayers, and to diviners <margin>1 Sam. 5:2.</margin> (of which there were infinite and diverse kinds) to explore the will of the gods. As Juvenal says, <margin>Satire 6, v. 584.</margin> they sought the *frequent clicking of tongues* so that the fates might be sung to them. Thus, with great devotion to frivolous things, the Baalites implored Baal, the Moabites Moloch, the Philistines Dagon, and the Babylonians Bel. The Moabites consulted Chemosh and were put to shame by him, just as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel, in which they had confidence (Jeremiah 48:13). They had placed their hope in the deity Chemosh (1 Kings 11:7), but the prophet predicted they would be frustrated in this at the destruction of the Moabites, saying in verse 7: *And Chemosh shall go into captivity, his priests and his princes together.* Every nation has a refuge in its own gods and their oracles and idols, yet it is entirely in vain. All these idols are *Elilim*—that is, "vanities," less than nothing, "hollow forms under the image of a face," as Virgil speaks (Aeneid 4.24), and as shown in 1 Samuel 12:21 and 1 Corinthians 8:4. The very origin of these manufactured images <margin>Jeremiah 10:3.</margin> is weak, having proceeded from the hand of a craftsman. Consequently, <margin>Hosea 13:2.</margin> names are inserted into the divine books for idols based on their "effect" (or rather their "defect"), which Kircher explains in his work on the use of Hebrew-Greek Concordances. Among these are *Elilim* and *Eloha*, because they deceive the expectation of the idolaters who trusted they would be helped and preserved by them. To show that all the gods of the peoples are false and vain, having no power at all compared to the true God, the maker of heaven and earth, the Prophet David says: *All the gods of the peoples are idols (**elilim**),* which the Greek translates as **demons** <margin>Psalm 96:5.</margin>; Paul seems to have taken his explanation in 1 Corinthians 10:19 from this. Isaiah (chapter 44) says both the makers of carvings and the gods themselves are vain. In chapter 41, he argues against the gods of all nations, proving they are not gods because they cannot announce the future. *Who is like Me? Let him declare what is coming and shall come to pass.* In chapter 14, he counts the heavens (which they worshipped as gods) among the vanities of the nations. Zechariah spoke emphatically to the Jews, saying the Teraphim <note>household idols</note> speak vanity, diviners see lies, and dreams tell false comfort. We say no less truly of the Egyptians here: that monstrous idolatry and its authors have been an ancient, fatal evil for the nation and a famous cause of sedition and discord...
