<meta>This page continues the discussion of Isaiah 19, shifting from the political divisions of Egypt to its religious landscape. It examines the "burden" or prophecy against the Egyptian idols, contrasting their perceived power with the reality of their vanity as described by Church Fathers and classical authors.</meta>

<page-num>584</page-num>
<header>584 BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>

<margin>The Burden of Egypt.</margin>
Our Prophet rightly mocks the advisors and administrators of Egypt as "burdensome comforters." Baruch, in chapter 6, excellently demonstrates that idols are nothing (verses 1 and following) and that they can neither punish the wicked nor benefit the good (verses 33 and following). Barnabas and Paul, in *Acts 14:15*, called Jupiter and Mercury "vain things" <note>original Greek: µαταῖα</note>, whom the people dreamed had descended from heaven in human likeness. If anyone seeks more references regarding the famous gods and idols of the nations, they should consult the highly detailed works of John Rainolds and Gerard Vossius on Idolatry.

It is truly a wonder that nowhere else in the world existed greater religious confusion or fouler idolatry than in Egypt. To this day, no nation on earth has been so foolish or vain as to live under such shameful idolatry—worshipping God under the image of an Ox, a Crocodile, a cat, an Ibis, and other living creatures. They even believed that onions and other garden plants nurtured some divine power within them. Thus, the Roman poet Juvenal <margin>Satire 15.</margin> rightly calls them *demented Egypt* <note>original: "dementē Aegyptum"</note>. Juvenal himself was once a diligent observer of Roman superstitions (as discussed above on page 136). You can see that the Egyptians suffered even more horrific mockeries, consecrating all manner of filthy things, which Saint Paul alludes to in *Romans 1:23*.

Certainly, Egypt, to which the Prophet writes, was a sewer of every kind of god and a workshop of various superstitions. From there, these practices grew and were exported to various nations. The Phoenicians and Egyptians were the first to turn deceased men, from whom they had received notable benefits, into gods; and from them, polytheism <note>original Greek: πολυθεότης</note> passed to the rest of mortals. This is how Philo, the interpreter of Sanchuniathon, derives it, as reported by Eusebius in the first book of *Preparation for the Gospel*, page 23: <note>original Greek: "Οἱ παλαιότατοι τῶν βαρβάρων..."</note> **The most ancient of the barbarians, and especially the Phoenicians and Egyptians, from whom the rest of mankind received it, considered the greatest gods to be those who had discovered things necessary for life or who had in some way done good to the nations.** Later, this superstition gradually extended further, as will be discussed in its proper place.

In this land, as Pope Leo the Great says regarding Rome <margin>Sermon 10 on the Apostles.</margin>, whatever had been established anywhere by vain errors was collected and held with the most diligent superstition. Augustine says in a certain place: **There is no greater, more superstitious idolatry than that of the Egyptians; for the Egyptian flooded the world with such fictions as the Apostle later describes. For when he had said: "Into the likeness of an image of corruptible man," he added, "and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of serpents."** Have you ever seen in other temples an image with a dog's head, or a bull's head, or the fictions of other irrational animals? These are the idols of the Egyptians.

At this point, I cannot pass over a prophecy concerning Egypt which I observed in Hermes Trismegistus's *Asclepius*, which has been proven by an admirable outcome. In the addresses to Asclepius (found among the works of Apuleius edited by Elmenhorst, page 90), he relates that Egypt is an image of heaven and a model for the whole world, because idols of every kind were most religiously worshipped there without measure or limit. Yet, like a prescient seer, he predicts their destruction, saying: **Then this most holy land, the seat of shrines, shall be a tomb and full of the dead. O Egypt, of your religions only fables will remain, and they will be incredible to your descendants; only the words inscribed on stones will remain...**

<column-break/>

**...telling of your deeds, and the Scythian or the Indian or some such person shall inhabit Egypt.** 

<margin>The Burden of Egypt.</margin>
We take an example, if not the fulfillment, of this prophecy from the words in verse 1: **The idols of Mizraim <note>Mizraim is the Hebrew name for Egypt</note> shall be moved at his presence.** These words are playfully cited by those who wish to prove that all the idols of Egypt collapsed at the entry of the infant Christ and the Virgin Mary—an event about which the hardworking chronicler Baronius <margin>Volume 1, Year 1, number 42 and following.</margin> is intensely concerned. 

Epiphanius, in *Lives of the Prophets*, page 54, records that Jeremiah predicted this fall of idols to the Egyptians, writing: <note>original Greek: "Οὗτος ὁ προφήτης σηµεῖον ἔδωκε..."</note> **This prophet gave a sign to the priests of Egypt, saying that all their idols must be shaken and all handmade things fall together when a child-bearing virgin with a god-like babe should arrive in Egypt.** On page 418, Cerda de Angelis committed a slip of memory, wishing to attribute this to Isaiah; for we read here "the handmade things shall be shaken," words which Procopius (page 265) applies to the boy Christ dwelling in Egypt. 

If such grand miracles had occurred, the Evangelists would not have passed them over in silence. Oecolampadius says on this passage: **It is legendary <note>original: "fabulosum est"</note> that the boy Christ performed signs in Egypt and that the idols collapsed, because the beginning of his signs was in Cana of Galilee.** However, it is true that He sanctified that land through His visitation, primarily through the Apostles, as it was neighboring Judea. The idols fell through the preaching of the Word; moreover, however much it once excelled in superstition, it later flourished just as much in religion. The idols tottered far more then than they did during the Assyrian invasion; indeed, they utterly collapsed.

Whether the idols collapsed when God approached via the Assyrians, I do not know, for the words do not clearly indicate it. A similar passage is found in the public sacred monuments which God ordered to be placed when He said to Moses and Aaron in *Exodus chapter 12, verse 12*, shortly before the people's departure from Egypt: **I will pass through the land of Egypt this night, and will smite all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and beast; and against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment: I am the LORD.** At that very time, the abominable worship of animals <note>term: theriolatry</note> and magical incantations were most prevalent. 

Scripture does not detail what those judgments of God against the unnamed gods of Egypt were. However, the Rabbis torment themselves over this, saying that on that night the statues of the gods fell everywhere and all the deities of the Egyptians perished. Nicholas of Lyra <margin>on Isaiah 19, note 1.</margin> says: **The Hebrews say that on that night all the wooden idols of Egypt were suddenly rotted, all the metallic ones were melted and poured onto the ground, and all the stone ones were shattered into pieces in detestation of idolatry.** 

It is not new for God to execute judgment on man-made idols. Thus we understand what is read in *1 Samuel chapter 5, verses 3 and 4* concerning Dagon, the idol of the Philistines, which could not stand before the Ark of the God of Israel (the arrival of which they dreaded, as seen in the preceding chapter 4, verses 7 and 8) but suddenly fell to the ground. Likewise, Bel was broken and Nebo was crushed; their images were given **to the wild beasts and cattle** (*Isaiah 46:1*). The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translates it thus: **Bel fell, Dagon was crushed** (read *Nebo*, as it is in the Roman edition) **their carvings were given to the beasts and the cattle.** Regarding idols shattered by the Typhon wind after the flood, which Said Aben Batrich records, see Selden’s *Prolegomena on the Syrian Gods*, page 48. The Egyptians fabricated such images, I should helpfully note, according to the influences of the stars...

It highlights the legend of idols collapsing upon Christ's entry into Egypt while weighing the historical and theological interpretations of such "judgments" against false gods.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of Egyptian religion, moving from the physical worship of animals to the more complex "science" of magic and astrology. It connects Egyptian practices with the Biblical story of Laban’s household gods and the training of Moses and Daniel, while critiquing the spiritual vanity of these "elemental" arts as described in Isaiah 19.</meta>

### Isaiah 19, verses 1 and following.

<margin>The Burden of Egypt.</margin>
They believed that the spirits of the stars were enclosed in these objects, as Marsilio Ficino teaches in his book *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens*, chapter 13. Just as demons were known to sometimes occupy human bodies—speaking, moving, and performing wonders through them—they believed that celestial spirits performed similar feats through images. They held that a divine spirit was attached to and, as it were, struck into the matter, so that the spirit itself might stir all things. Among these are the <term>Teraphim</term> <note>Hebrew: teraphim</note> of Laban, mentioned in the history of Jacob. Based on the belief that a divine spirit was enclosed within them, some choose to call them <term>gods</term> <note>Hebrew: elohim</note>. Regarding these, Laban and his daughter Rachel (who had secretly stolen the Teraphim) could have said what Laodamia said of the wax image of her husband Protesilaus, who had set out for Troy, as recorded by *Ovid*: *
<margin>Epistle 13, verse 155.</margin>
> Believe me, there is more here than what the image seems to be.

The famous vocal statue of Memnon is well known from the writings of Juvenal, Tacitus, and Pliny. There were various forms of these magical constellations or <term>elemental</term> <note>original Greek: stoicheiomatikōn</note> images, which the Hebrews call <term>Teraphim</term>, the Greeks <term>elements</term> <note>original Greek: stoicheia</note>, the Arabs <term>Talisman</term> (which comes from the Greek word <term>telesma</term>), and the Latins <term>Sigilla</term> (Seals). When you look into these, you will find nothing but the coldest of trifles, which you cannot read without feeling pity for such a foolish religion. On this subject, one should consult Selden's *On the Syrian Gods*, Scaliger’s *Epistles*, Delrio’s *Magical Investigations*, Leunclavius’s *Turkish Records*, Buxtorf’s *Chaldean-Rabbinic Lexicon*, Naudé’s work on military study, Grotius’s *Explanation of the Decalogue*, and Gaulmin’s *Notes on Psellus*. Regarding man-made idols that demons entered, it is read in the *Zohar* that these began during the time of the Flood and the division of the Tower of Babel; for then, it is said, demons descended and gave oracles and answers through images. If you wish to see the Hebrew words, consult Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel, a teacher in the Amsterdam synagogues, in his third book *On the Resurrection*. We have also seen from Philo that the worship of gods and idolatry first flourished among the Egyptians. Lucian also confirms this: * <margin>Book on the Syrian Goddess, page 687.</margin> <note>original Greek: The Egyptians are said to be the first of men we know to have gained a concept of the gods, to have built temples, and to have appointed sacred precincts and festivals.</note> The first idolatry, however, arose from the worship of celestial bodies, in which they went immensely astray. Diodorus Siculus is a wealthy witness to this: *
<margin>Library of History, book 1, page 7.</margin> <note>original Greek: The people in ancient Egypt, looking up at the world and the nature of all things, were struck with awe and wonder, and supposed there to be two eternal and primary gods, the Sun and the Moon, the former of whom they called Osiris and the latter Isis.</note> Among these same Egyptians, and from them the Chaldeans, were the cradles of <term>magical evil-arts</term>; from this source, as if from a fountain of all <term>wickedness</term>, began those fashionings of images we just mentioned. From here, oracles were introduced by the instinct of the Devil, along with prophecies, omens, and all types of false beliefs. Then, from the actions, passions, and forms of the four elements, they curiously derived <term>pyromancy</term> (fire-divination), <term>aeromancy</term> (air-divination), <term>hydromancy</term> (water-divination), and <term>geomancy</term> (earth-divination). To maintain the order of their sacred rites, there were <term>interpreters</term> <note>original Greek: exēgetai</note> for each kind of divination, who would act

<column-break/>

<margin>The Burden of Egypt.</margin>
and advise on what was beneficial for the State. The Prophet says all these things will be consulted in vain by those who gave themselves entirely to auguries and traced all actions and fortunes back to the stars as if they were first principles or "weak elements." The Egyptians are said by writers to have been the first of all mortals to comprehend the course of the heavens and stars, and all celestial movements, through their study and greatness of mind. For they are recorded as the first to have provided a form of living and a discipline of morals, the first to have invented the plow and farm tools, and the first to track the oblique course of the Sun itself, as can be consulted in Dionysius Periegetes. After these, as it is related, the Chaldeans—colonists of the Egyptians—received these arts and learned <note>original Greek: the practices concerning each way of life</note> from them. Among the liberal arts which it was in the public interest to learn and practice, they especially cultivated Arithmetic, Geometry, and Astronomy. It is believable that Daniel and Moses learned all of these (leaving aside the superstitions), as it is said of the latter in *Acts 7:22* that he was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians; and of the former in *Daniel 1:17* that he was given <note>original Greek: understanding and wisdom in all literature.</note> Procopius says: <note>original Greek: The Philistines seem to have invented omen-reading, just as the Chaldeans invented astrology, the Egyptians incantations and sorcery, and the Cretans bird-watching.</note> Diodorus Siculus writes: <note>original Greek: The Chaldeans have the greatest reputation in astrology of all men, because they have devoted the most care to this study.</note> They write that the Egyptians and Chaldeans received this Astronomy from the descendants of Seth, who inscribed the elements of the arts they discovered on two columns. <margin>Josephus, Antiquities, Book 1, page 8.</margin> However, who does not know from ancient tradition that in the course of time, it was defiled by infinitely many magical and diabolical deceptions? This Astrology, first cultivated among the Egyptians and Chaldeans, gave birth to a superstitious form of Medicine and Theology; for it handed down <term>magical evil-arts</term>, <term>demonic rites</term>, and <term>other unlawful secret-acts</term> <note>original Greek: magikas kakotechnias, daimoniōdeis teletas, kai allas athemitous arrhētorgias</note>. We await a specific book by Gilbert Gaulmin on this magical Theology of the Orient. Those first practitioners of superstition, in times of calamity, would betake themselves to the <term>Augurs of the heavens</term>, who, by observing the times, professed to know and certainly predict what would happen to anyone. Thus, in *Daniel 2:2*, the King commanded *that the diviners, magicians, sorcerers, and Chaldeans be called.* Here, the "Chaldeans" are named for their art, not their ethnicity—meaning Mathematicians and Astrologers. The God of Israel, who renders the signs of diviners void and drives the soothsayers mad, elsewhere threatens the coming destruction <margin>Isaiah 44:25.</margin> and addresses the city of the Chaldeans thus: <margin>Isaiah 47:13.</margin> *Let the observers of the heavens stand now and save you* (<term>LXX: the astrologers of the heaven</term>). In the Phoenician language they are called <term>zophasmin</term>, which Philo says means <term>watchers of heaven</term> <margin>cited in Eusebius, book 1.</margin>, which can be traced back to the Hebrew (the mother of Phoenician), for <term>tzaphah</term> means "to watch" and <term>shamayim</term> "heavens." Luther translates this as: *the masters of the course of heaven* <note>original German: die Meister deß Himmelslauff</note>; those contemplating the heavens and calculating the months to announce what will come upon you. In these words, Marsilio Ficino <margin>Volume 1, Basel edition.</margin> testifies in his *Book on Astrology, page 287*, that the vanity of the Chaldeans is accused—those who think that from the movements of the celestial orbs and the courses of the stars they can foresee the future and perceive human fates...

## BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<page-num>586</page-num>

<margin>
The Burden of Egypt.
</margin>
...or to drive them away, if they are evil, using magical amulets; or if they are good, to strengthen their influence. Next, the prophet hints at the uncertainty of their observations when he says in verse 11: *Therefore evil shall come upon you, the origin of which you do not know;* <note>Latin: "veniet igitur malum, cujus nescis ortum"</note> that is, a disaster that neither Mars nor the "cold star of Saturn" <note>A poetic reference to the planet Saturn, often associated with misfortune in ancient astrology</note> forewarned you about. *Then calamity shall fall upon you which you will not be able to expiate* <note>To "expiate" in this context means to use rituals to avert a predicted disaster</note> through the selection of auspicious hours, astrological images, or other superstitious devices intended to push it away. They were accustomed to "expiate" a crime if they thought they had committed one against the gods; "with sacrifices and incantations, if any wrong has been done by themselves or their ancestors, to find a remedy." <note>Original Greek: "θυσίαις τὲ καὶ ἐπῳδαῖς, εἴ τέ τι ἀδίκημα τὸ γέγονεν αὐτὸ ἢ προγόνων, ἀκεῖσθαι"</note> These are the words of Plato in the second book of the *Republic*. You might call these the "appeasements of heavenly wrath," as Livy does in the 5th book of his history; and from his 8th book, we see "victims slaughtered to ward off the anger of the gods." For they used these specific words: *expiating*, *managing* <note>Latin: "procurandi"</note>, *averting* <note>Latin: "averruncandi"</note>, and *appeasing*. Evils, especially those signaled by portents, were "managed" through prayers and supplications organized by the art of soothsaying; these rituals were called *Depulsa* <note>The "driving away"</note> or *expiations of portents*, as is clear from Valerius Maximus. Who would not conclude from these sayings that our prophet was referring to the oracles, prophecies, and auguries of the Egyptians? It is as if he looked at them and said: Where are your gods? Let them announce what is to come in the future, and we shall know if they are gods? As he says in chapter 41: where now are your augurs and astrologers, who boast that they know, like Homer’s Calchas in the *Iliad* (Book 1, line 70):

-> Things that are, things that shall be, and things that were before. <-
<note>Original Greek: "τά τ’ ἐόντα, τά τ’ ἐσσόμενα, πρό τ’ ἐόντα"</note>

And like Virgil’s Sibyl:

-> *What things are, what they have been, what soon shall be drawn on.* <-
<note>Latin: "Quæ sint, quæ fuerint, quæ mox ventura trahantur"</note>

Indeed, the gods were not enough for the Egyptians to ward off public calamities; when abandoned by their gods, they turned to the **Magicians** <note>Latin: "Magos"</note>, who were thought to be closest to the gods in wisdom and full of divine inspiration. But finding no counsel even among them, they submitted themselves with superstitious anxiety to the **Pythons** <note>Spirit-mediums or oracular priests</note>, who were also believed to possess something of the divine in their fortune-telling. Finally, with their minds conquered by superstition, they turned from the heavens to the earth and consulted auguries. They turned with incredible worry to the lowest sorts: namely, diviners, dream-interpreters, augurs, and soothsayers—a treacherous and plague-like race of men, deceptive to those who hope in them, whom Ennius graphically describes in Cicero’s first book *On Divination*. If anything unusual happened, it was immediately referred to the soothsayers, who would teach what the gods were forewarning or what they demanded. If anything had to be done abroad or at home, they sought auspices, and from there they promised themselves future success. Xenophon says in his *Symposium*: "All cities and all nations ask the gods through divination what they should and should not do." And: "They signal to me, sending messengers, omens, dreams, and birds, what I must do and what I must not do." <note>Original Greek: "σημαίνουσί μοι, πέμποντες ἀγγέλους, φήμας καὶ ἐνύπνια καὶ οἰωνὸς..."</note> *Also in Book 8:* "It was signaled to me both in sacrifices and in the heavens and in birds and in omens what I should do and what I should not." This vanity was described and refuted in entire books long ago by Augustinus Niphus, the philosopher of Sessa, which Dr. Rudolf Goclenius saw fit to have reprinted at Marburg. However, there was great reliance throughout the whole East on Magicians and Illusionists; therefore, they are placed in the first rank here and are called <term>Hartummim</term> <note>Hebrew: חרטמים - sacred scribes or magicians</note>. Translators render this name in various ways: Castalio calls them *soothsayers*, Tremellius *illusionists*, and the Vulgate *diviners*,

<column-break/>

where that same ancient translator uses the word in *Deuteronomy 18:11* for prophets who wish to predict the future, a word which the French language has retained with a slight change, for they call them *devin*. The Glosses say: "Diviner, a prophet." <note>Original: "Divinus, μάντις"</note> <margin>book [? illegible]</margin> Origen, in *On First Principles* translated by Rufinus: *“They call them diviners, from whom responses are brought forth by the embodiment of those Demons who preside over them, through verses modulated by art.”* Cicero in *On Fate*: (*Chrysippus, sweating over a falsehood, puts his hope in the Chaldeans and other diviners.*) There are also the *Arioli* <note>Soothsayers</note> <margin>pre-eminently</margin> <term>Yidde'onim</term> <note>Hebrew: ידענים - "knowing ones" or wizards</note>. They are called "know-it-alls" from the word <term>yada</term> <note>Hebrew: ידע - to know</note>; they are named this "pre-eminently" from their knowledge of hidden and secret things, just as the <term>Hakhamim</term> <note>Hebrew: חכמים - wise men</note> are called Magicians from their wisdom. The Elders translated this elsewhere as *incantatores* (enchanters), whom the Scholion explains as "those who lead out [spirits] through enchantments and the invocation of demons." Elsewhere they are *teratoscopos* (interpreters of prodigies), but here they are *gnostas* from the force of the Hebrew word: *knowers* or *diviners*. Regarding the word <term>Hartummim</term>, we have said some things elsewhere: the Egyptians, masters of superstition, held the conviction that nothing should be done unless a prophetic word first came out of the mouth of some Magician. It is well known what kind of Magicians first existed in Egypt. For Egypt itself, foolishly curious and credulous, has always nourished "some monster"—as is said elsewhere of Africa—and has always produced masters of the more secret magic arts of various kinds and wonderful talent. The certainty of this matter is clear from the Pentateuch, where we are abundantly taught how the Egyptian Magicians fascinated the eyes of Pharaoh. It is known from that book which extensively records the deeds of King Pharaoh that the first of the Egyptian Kings made use of Magicians. This was an ancient trick of the Devil, and Magic was not the least of the evil arts. In the time of Joseph <margin>Genesis 41</margin> *Pharaoh summoned to himself* <term>all the Hartummim of Egypt</term> <note>Hebrew: כל חרטמי מצרים - all the magicians of Egypt</note>; it appears they cultivated that infamous Magic composed of incantations and prepared songs. Perhaps we would know more from many documents if the work of *Apollonides*, a writer on Egypt, still existed—a book titled *Semenuthi* (mentioned by Theophilus of Antioch in Book 2) in which he treated the origins of Magic and its study and practice among the Egyptians. Pliny also testifies to this in Book 30, Chapter 1, where he deals with magic; he says that *Moses* was a practitioner of it in the same place. This passage should not be skipped. There is, he says, "another faction of Magic, depending on Moses and Jannes and Jotape, who were Jews, but many thousands of years after Zoroaster." This is a lie worthy of a pagan author. From it, however, we gather this "memorable fact": that the fame of that noble history narrated in Exodus—concerning Pharaoh, the most cruel persecutor of the pious nation beloved by God—had reached the gentiles, albeit through false rumors, as is the custom of the gentiles. It is also clear that Pliny understood *Jannes and Jambres* (whom Paul names in 2 Timothy 3:8 as the strenuous antagonists of Moses in that wonder-working of the time). The Talmud in the tractate *Sanhedrin* calls them <term>the heads of the magicians</term> <note>Hebrew: ראשי החרטומים</note>, whom we discussed above. Moses says that the wise men and sorcerers were summoned by Pharaoh to overturn the Jewish religion and bring shame upon the true God of the Jews; they resisted the power of God operating through Moses with their fictitious rivalry and magic arts. And indeed, those men misused a rod for incantations and for making deceptive and illusory transformations, just as in Homer...

### ISAIAH 19, VERSE 1 AND FOLLOWING
<page-num>587</page-num>

<margin>The Burden of Egypt. In the Odyssey, Book 10, verse 238.</margin>It is said that Circe, with a simple wand <note>Greek: *rhabdō*</note>, struck the companions of Ulysses and turned them into swine. They also changed water into blood, along with other "specters and deceptions" <note>Greek: *phasmata kai phenakismoi*</note> described in Exodus chapter 8, where you may read how the imposture of the magicians was detected and their knowledge confounded. However, incantators were accustomed, when they could achieve nothing by trying all other means, to finally use the *Prince of Demons*, such as Beelzebub, *Matthew 12:24*—on which point, see what the illustrious Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian famous for his Bible commentaries</note> noted from secular sources on page 232.

**Verse 5.** <note>original Hebrew: וְנִשְׁתּוּ-מַיִם מֵהַיָּם וְנָהָר יֶחֱרַב וְיָבֵשׁ</note> *And the waters shall fail from the sea, and the river shall be wasted and dried up.* In these and the following words, the Prophet threatens not only an unhappy harvest of crops, but also the abandonment of trade and the total failure of merchandise. Indeed, by the drying up of the "sea" and the rivers, he understands that all commerce and fishing will cease—activities in which they took great pleasure, always intent on gain and the catch—so that the region becomes a desert. Just as Virgil speaks <margin>Eclogues, 1</margin> hyperbolically of the "dryness of the sea" (meaning the bay of the sea into which the Nile discharges itself) and the desolation of the "river" (meaning the Nile itself and its embankments).

For Egypt was irrigated by the flooding of the Nile at fixed times of the year. Therefore, when that irrigation failed, the shores and fields would dry up, with the heat of the Sun scorching everything. By way of excellence <term>exochēn</term>, the Nile is called *the river* in *Genesis 15:18 and 41:1*. By the same figure of speech <term>antonomasia</term>, the People of Asia call the *Perath* or *Phrath* "the river," which the Greeks call the Euphrates. Similarly, *Suetonius, in his life of Augustus (chapter 67), simply called the Tiber "the river."* Even Curtius, when he names <margin>41. 8.</margin> "the stream" <note>Latin: *amnem*</note> without qualification, means the Nile (*Book 4, ch. 8, no. 7*); and likewise Athenaeus (*Book 9, ch. 9*) and Philo—in passages soon to be produced—call the Nile "the river" by way of excellence.

Because of this benefit from the Nile, Egypt abounded in the best grain, earning it the name *the granary of the world*. Neighboring nations, in their own poverty, betook themselves here. Thus Abraham, in a shortage of crops in Canaan, fled there to obtain food (*Gen. 12:10*). On this, *Philo says of Abraham (p. 246):* "Due to the failure of crops which lasted for a long time—sometimes because of great and immoderate rain, sometimes because of drought and storms—the cities in Syria, pressed by constant famine, were emptied of their inhabitants, as different people scattered to different places in search of food and to provide for their necessities. But hearing of the ungrudging abundance and prosperity in Egypt—the river flooding the plains at the right time with its surges—he brought his whole household there." <note>original Greek: "καρπῶν ἀφορίᾳ καὶ τῇ συχνὸν χρόνον γενομένῃ... πυθόμενοι δὲ τὰς ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ ἄφθονον εὐθενίαν καὶ εὐετηρίαν..."</note> Egypt itself received Jewish guests during times of hunger as if it were a second fatherland. While famine pressed upon the whole earth, grain was carried from Egypt into the land of Canaan (*Gen. 43:1*). Jacob, finally compelled by the lack of food, went down there with all he had (*chapter 46:1*). 

We read that from this river, to foreshadow drought and sterility (and the following "lack of grain" <note>Greek: *sitodeian*</note>), seven fat cows and seven thin cows ascended; for from the Nile alone comes both abundance and sterility. An overflow of 16 cubits portended fertility, while 6 or 9 cubits portended sterility. Without a doubt, for seven years there was no rise of the Nile, or certainly a very small one below 12 cubits or even five, and the deep rivers failed. On this matter, Philo says:

<column-break/>

<margin>The Burden of Egypt.</margin>
*In his book "On Joseph" (p. 368):* "In the former years, there was great and ungrudging fruitfulness, with the river flooding the fields every year and the plains enjoying fertility as I said before. but after these, a contrary seven-year period will come, bringing difficult want and a scarcity of necessities, with the river not rising and the land not being enriched." <note>original Greek: "ἦσαν ἐν τῷ πρότερω, πολλὴν καὶ ἄφθονον ἔχουσα εὐκαρπίαν... μητ’ ἀναχομένου τοῦ ποταμοῦ, μήτε τῆς γῆς λιπαιναμένης."</note> 

That prediction of famine was truly Prophetic, as Luther notes. Oecolampadius <note>Johannes Oecolampadius (1482–1531), a Protestant Reformer and Hebrew scholar</note> says <margin>on Gen. ch. 45, f. 611 b.</margin> on this passage (fol. 129a): "We should not assume a miracle here, as if the sea and all rivers were to be literally dried up; but because Egypt is most blessed by its waters, when it loses that blessing, it is said to lack rivers. This is especially true because it is not irrigated by heavenly rains like other lands, but by the inundation of the Nile to 14, 15, or 16 cubits. If it rises by fewer, it feels famine, as Pliny testifies." 

The desolation of the land is described by this penury of waters, as if it were so vast that it lacked water entirely, just as was said above regarding Moab. *The Nile is called here by various names*: sometimes the sea, sometimes the river, sometimes a stream, or streams. For that river is divided into seven mouths, and it is called a "sea" not only by the general name by which Hebrews call all gatherings of waters "seas," but also because, according to historical accounts, there was once a constant opinion that it took its origin from the Ocean sea. It is said, therefore: *And the waters of the Nile shall fail from the sea, that is, in the very mouths of the sea, and thus the river itself shall be a solitude and dry.* The Nile lands, elsewhere called "fields" <note>Latin: *Arva*</note>, used to respond generously to the prayers of the farmers. 

Some attribute this drying up to the insane constructions built on the Nile; for twelve minor kings <note>the "Dodecarchy" mentioned by Herodotus</note>, who are said to have reigned after the death of Sethos, are reported to have diverted its waters—even to the point of dryness—into the *Lake of Moeris* (which they say is called the "lake of pleasure" in *verse 10*). They were led by mere whim to complete this along with their pyramids and labyrinth. Whether it was so—whether this dryness arose from natural causes or from the diversion of the Nile into the lake and other pleasure projects—it is certain that great losses were given to the Egyptians from this, which are discussed in *verses 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10*. 

For the Prophet continues in **verse 6**, saying: *The rivers of Egypt shall be dried up.* <note>original Hebrew: יֶחֱרָבוּ יְאֹרֵי מָצוֹר</note> Arias <note>Benito Arias Montanus (1527–1598), a Spanish orientalist</note> translates: *The rivers of fortification shall be dried.* The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translates: "Every gathering of water shall be dried up." They understand a "gathering of water," as if the word comes from *atsar*, which means to collect, just as treasures (called *otsarot*) are collected. Similarly, in *chapter 37:25*, where King Sennacherib of Assyria says he dried up with the sole of his feet "all the rivers of the besieged places" <note>Hebrew: *kol yeore mazor*</note>, they translated it: "every gathering of water." 

Vatablus <note>François Vatable (d. 1547), a French humanist and Hebraist</note> translates "rivers of fortification" there (though in our current passage he has "Rivers of Egypt"). But the same Greek interpreters, in *2 Kings 19:24*, take the same words in the same story differently, and understand them as "rivers of containment," "rivers of the station," or "rivers of the siege." Luther understood them as "Lakes." The Vulgate translation says "rivers of the embankments," because embankments are like *mazorot* (fortifications) or bulwarks of the collected waters. For the word *Mazor* sounds like "fortification," so that *Yeore Mazor* can be called "rivers of fortification," *Wassergraben* or *Wallgraben* <note>German: Moats or trench-ditches around a rampart</note>. By changing one letter, the word becomes *Mazud*, meaning "fortress." The former comes from *tsur* (to besiege), the latter from *tsud* (to hunt or seek), just as wild beasts are sought with a hunting net, which is why both *mazor* and *mazod* are used. If we wish to take the matter literally, it will signify that, once besieged, all water was taken away...

<summary>This page analyzes Isaiah 19:5-6, explaining how the prophecy of the Nile drying up signifies the total collapse of Egypt's agriculture, trade, and fishing. The author compiles biblical, classical, and linguistic evidence to show that the Nile was Egypt's sole lifeline, making its failure a divine judgment of catastrophic proportions.</summary>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<page-num>588</page-num>

<margin>The Burden of Egypt.</margin>
...water, so that extreme necessity is indicated; it is even said that the rivers were dried up everywhere by the multitude of the army, and all the crops, grasslands, and seedlings were lost. Indeed, it is customary for everything to be exhausted and consumed when a very numerous army approaches, and just as this does not happen with water naturally, it is managed with great effort. Thus Xerxes, when he led his forces into Greece, dried up rivers. This was recorded in literature by Herodotus in Book 7, Justin in Book 2, and Juvenal. All the hope of Egypt was in the inundation of the Nile, for even today that land is irrigated not by rains, which it lacks, but by the Nile, and by the channels led from the Nile, and by the pools which the receding Nile leaves behind. Along the banks of this river and its streams were the best and richest grasslands *for the feeding of animals*, which in *verse 7* are called <note>Hebrew: *edoth*</note>. The Latin translator <note>The Vulgate</note> *took this word in the sense of stripping or nakedness*, translating it: *the bed of the river shall be laid bare from its source, for* <note>Hebrew: *arah*</note> means *to be made naked*. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> renders it elegantly: *the green things around the river*, for the Hebrews understand by <note>Hebrew: *edoth*</note> "the green things," *that is,* greenery and grasslands. From this, Luther translates: *The grass by the waters.* Musculus <note>Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563), a Protestant reformer and commentator</note> on this passage, page 332, says: *This is the second loss* (the drying of the grass) *which Egypt was to suffer through drought. It signifies that there will be such a great drought that the grasses will wither not only in drier places, but even at the very banks of the rivers and streams. To express this, he did not simply say: "The grasses shall wither," but "the grasses near the rivers," even "at the very banks of the rivers shall wither." Hence the greatest loss to the livestock and the entire province.* Thus also the lack of reeds and rushes is enumerated in verse 6: <note>Hebrew: *kaneh v’suph*—reeds and rushes</note> withered; likewise the papyrus, of which the aforementioned <note>Hebrew: *edoth*</note> speaks. Junius thought the word came from <note>Hebrew: *or*</note>, *skin*, as if those strips or membranes of papyrus were called "little skins"; for it was artistically cut into many layers and sheets, as Pliny teaches, whose words are: *From it* (papyrus) *paper is prepared, by dividing it with a needle into very thin but as wide as possible strips <note>Latin: *phyluras*</note>.* The Septuagint has "all green things." Who is so unread in history as to be ignorant that Egypt abounded in reeds and rushes in its marshes and the banks of the Nile? It was in the reed-beds of the Nile that the infant Moses was exposed, in *an ark of rushes or a basket of bulrushes, which was smeared with pitch and bitumen*, as we read in Exodus 2:3. Pliny says in the same place: *Papyrus grows in the marshes of Egypt, or in the still waters of the Nile where they stagnate after overflowing.* See Panciroli, page 609. The Old Translator calls that reed-bed a *Papyrion*, because the papyrus shrub grew up on the bank. Thermuthis, the daughter of Egypt <note>Pharaoh's daughter</note>, had come here to wash herself, choosing a place among the shadows of the papyrus and reeds where she might be less seen, *and her maidservants walked along the river bank; and seeing the little ark in the middle of the reed-bed, she sent her handmaid—for she was a King’s daughter—and took it (verse 5).* From this, Rabshakeh, the commander of Sennacherib's army, in his speech to Hezekiah <margin>2 Kings 18:20.</margin> alludes to the nature of that region when he speaks of the flimsy help of the Egyptians: *You trust in a staff of reed*, that is, you fix your hopes on those who can offer no protection. This proverb can also be confirmed by the usage of the Greeks, among whom *fig-wood* <note>Latin: *lignum ficulnum*</note>, as something very fragile and weak, gave rise to several proverbs; for *the wood of the fig tree is easily broken, weak, and powerless*, says the Scholiast on Theocritus. Hence the same poet in Idyll 10 calls a man "fig-like" <note>Greek: *andras sukinous*</note>, meaning soft and useless; and they use "fig-like help" <note>Greek: *sukinen epikourian*</note> for 

<column-break/>

empty assistance, and a "fig-wood dagger" <note>Greek: *sukinon makhairan*</note> for a false accusation—on which see Erasmus. Jeremiah, chapter 51, verse 32, says, *and they burned the pools with fire*. Arias Montanus, avoiding hyperbole, translates this as *reeds*; because pools full of rushes and reeds are understood. But <note>Hebrew: *agamim*</note> are *pools* and marshes (Exodus 7:19; Isaiah 14:23, 42:25), whereas <note>Hebrew: *agmonim*</note> are the rushes that grow in the pools (Isaiah 5:5). The Nile is called "papyrus-bearing" by the poets, for in it grows *papyrus, from which paper is constructed.* Mounds and embankments used to restrain the waters of the Nile, and so the Prophet seems to have said: *where the rivers shall be removed, they shall be thinned, and the streams of the embankment shall be laid waste*; regarding which, see Cujas <note>Jacques Cujas (1522–1590), a French legal scholar</note>. When the Nile floods through Egypt, lagoons remain which the natives call *Birchas*, as noted by Prosper Alpinus in his book *On Exotic Plants*, page 214. In these grows the plant *Lotus*, called by the inhabitants *Arais and Nil*, a description of which you have in the said book. It could be called the *Nymphaea Nilotica* <note>The Nile water lily</note>.

**And the fishers shall mourn, and all those who cast a hook into the river shall lament: and those who spread a net upon the face of the waters shall languish.** In these words, the failure and loss of trades, especially fishing, is recounted. Among the riches of Egypt was *Fishing*, on account of the Nile and the nearby sea, which is why they had fish-ponds and preserves (<note>Hebrew: *agmei nephesh*</note>, *pools of the soul*, that is, of refreshment) in which they kept fish for that purpose. Therefore, when that drought looms, the Prophet says *even the business of the fishermen shall cease*. Theodore Snephus on this passage, page 399, says: *By the waters, understand the abundance of things, and by the works of the fishermen and those who work with flax, understand by Synecdoche <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note> all merchants and craftsmen, whose arts, trades, commerce, and profits have collapsed in these civil wars.* The fishing of the Jews living in Egypt is well known; they were gripped by a longing for it while living in the desert, when as rebels, tired of the food sent from heaven, they clamored for the meat-pots and fish of Egypt. Well known from Plutarch is the story of Mark Antony fishing, whom Cleopatra deceived with a salted fish, advising him that he should leave fishing to the Egyptians, while he himself should "fish" for cities and kingdoms.

**And they who work in fine flax, and they who weave nets, shall be confounded.** The Hebrew says: *Those weaving perforated works*, that is, latticed hangings. The embroiderers shall mourn when they no longer see the earth supplying them with enough for their clothing and the decoration of their wise men, nor *variegated weavings*. Added to fishing was *wool-working* or the weaving of fine linen; for Egypt produced excellent and subtle flax, as Pliny testifies, from which the thinnest cloths were made, almost like the *Cambric cloth* <note>German: *Kammertuch*</note> among us. Its use was in sacred vestments. Jerome on Ezekiel chapter 43, page 546, says: *The Egyptian priests use linen garments, not only on the inside, but also on the outside.* Apuleius, in the last book of the *Metamorphoses*, speaking of the ceremonies of Isis, writes thus: *Then flow in the crowds initiated into the sacred rites, men and women of every rank and age, luminous in the pure whiteness of linen garments*; for when they performed divine service, they were dressed in white and luminous with pure brightness, as the man from Madaura <note>Apuleius</note> says here. Cicero in *On the Laws*, book 2: *A white color is especially fitting for God, both in other things and most especially in textiles.* Regarding those who wear linen, see Beroaldo on Suetonius’s *Tiberius*, pages 292, 378; Raphelengius in his *Observations on the Riddles of the Ancient Poets, folio 51*; see also Junius, *Animadversions 4, note 29*; and Winsemius’s *Sirius*...

# THE BURDEN OF EGYPT
<header>Isaiah XIX. v. 1. seqq.</header>

<margin>
The Burden of Egypt.
Library of Proverbial Sayings, book 238.
</margin>
p. 40. We teach the use of Egyptian linen in the treatment of polyps <note>a type of tissue growth</note> based on Hippocrates, *On Diseases*, page 29. Fine linen was also used in the distribution of honors and virtues. Thus Pharaoh clothed Joseph, the son of Israel—as the Vulgate and the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> record—in a robe of fine linen. *Shesh* <gloss>usually refers to a garment of fine linen</gloss>, which was a badge of high office, given as a sign that the wearer should be treated with honor by others; likewise, it was the adornment of brides, as in Ezekiel chapter 16: *I clothed you with fine fabrics*, as Jerome translates from the Hebrew. <margin>p. 423.</margin> The Septuagint has: *and I wrapped you in trichaptos* <note>original: καὶ περιεβαλόν σε τριχάπτῳ</note>, where the aforementioned Father <note>Jerome</note> noted*: "When I diligently inquired what the word *trichaptos* meant, which the Septuagint translators used, and could find neither its use nor its etymology among any of the Greeks, I finally learned it was a word composed by the Septuagint. For new things, new names must be forged; it was a garment of such great fineness that it was believed to possess the thinness of hairs and locks of hair." Thus, seeing that the word expresses the thinness of the garment, they translated it more precisely for *trichaptos*. He says the same regarding Zechariah chapter 14, page 286: we should understand *trichapta* as thin garments which are so beautiful and delicate that they seem like hair. Luther, in his commentary on Genesis chapter 36, folio 492. a., says: "The great nobles in the East used fine linen, just as today the Turks use a turban of fine linen. For the Romans, the badge of office was purple and the toga; for the Easterners, it was fine linen." The *Cydaris* <note>a royal headdress</note> of the Persians was made of fine linen, concerning which see above. Jerome also mentions that fine linen garments were familiar to the Jewish Priests, as noted by Josephus in book 6 of *The Jewish War*: "Jerusalem is not only clothed in various colors and shod in hyacinth-blue, but is also girded with fine linen, from which the thinnest threads are woven into the Priest's garment." *Shesh* is a species of the most excellent and delicate Egyptian flax, as Ibn Ezra writes on Exodus chapter 25, verse 4. Piscator rendered it in the same place as: *Egyptian Flax*. From this was made the garment the Greeks call *sindon*; according to Pollux in book 7, chapter 16, it was also called *othone* or *othonion*. Luther, in the Gospel of Luke, translates it as *costly linen*. Furthermore, this Hebrew word *shesh* occurs twice in Esther chapter 1, verse 6, with more than one meaning; in the first instance it denotes fine linen, but in the second, marble columns, *columns of shesh*, as the Chaldean <note>Aramaic Targum</note> has it; conversely, *shesh* also means marble. In Proverbs chapter 7, verse 16, *etun Mitzraim* <note>linen of Egypt</note> denotes Egyptian linens, or embroidered tapestries of fine linen, used by the harlot or adulteress <gloss>a spread-out linen cloth</gloss> <note>original Greek: λαινίς ἐντετὲν</note>. Junius says: "I have spread my bed with cords, with painted tapestries from Egypt, I have sprinkled my couch with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon." For Egypt was famous for the most elegant tapestries and textiles, which were extremely delicate; Pliny in book 7, chapter 56, is the authority for the fact that their invention is owed to the Egyptians. Lucan, in book 10, verse 161:

<margin>
Ezekiel 16.
p. 422.
</margin>

> Her white breasts shine through the Sidonian thread,
> which the Nilotic needle has compressed with the comb of the loom,
> and has loosened and thinned the warp in a wide-spread veil.

<margin>Epigram VI, book 10, v. 7.</margin>
Thus in Martial*, a "Nilotic tunic" is a tunic embroidered by the Egyptians, as Turnebus observes in *Adversaria* 30, observation 30.

<margin>p. 471.</margin>
"When the knight and the plague [clothed] in a Nilotic tunic..." Ezekiel chapter 27:7 teaches that the best and most variegated fine linen was exported from Egypt: *Fine linen with embroidered work from Egypt was your sail.* Here Jerome notes*: "Fine linen is grown most abundantly in Egypt, from which the sail of a Tyrian ship is woven, which is hung from the mast, and its covering, which provides a shade in the heat of the sun and in calm waters for the sailors and passengers." In the Hebrew, there is a word which Arias Montanus translates with a coined term as "fine linen of embroidery" <margin>The Burden of Egypt.</margin> <note>original: byssum de recamatione</note>. To understand this more fully, see above at Psalm 139 where we discuss *rqm* <note>embroider</note>, from which they conjecture the word *butz* <note>fine linen</note> was derived along with the art itself. They attribute the glory of weaving to the Egyptians, and Mercer notes at Pagninus, column 1419, that the Israelites brought this name with them into the Promised Land. It would indeed be a wonder if the ancient Hebrews lacked such a small abundance of words to define such textiles; I see nothing in them to make me believe that *hempen cloth* <gloss>spartinon</gloss> was not granted along with a word whose force the Jews themselves were not ignorant of; especially since we can refer it entirely to the Hebrew *butz*. That these same Egyptians excelled in linen-working five hundred years ago is testified by Benjamin the Jew <note>Benjamin of Tudela</note> in his *Itinerary* near the end, which Constantine L'Empereur edited more correctly after Arias Montanus. There, he commends the *Egyptian linen* <note>original: λίνου Αἰγύπτιον</note> celebrated throughout the whole world for making nets: "The inhabitants of Sunbat <note>a city in the Nile Delta</note> bring the best flax, and weave nets or *coropta* (Empereur translates this as 'white nets'); and with this merchandise they are distributed through the whole world." Scylax the Geographer alludes to this Egyptian trade in his *Periplus*, which Isaac Vossius recently refined after Hoeschelius; he calls it "a pure white and variegated cargo." Silius, in book 3, verse 370, joined the looms of the Arabs and Pelusian linen together. We also gather that Egypt was fertile in flax from Holy Scripture; for in Exodus chapter 9, verse 31, the first account of flax is given, and mention is made of the flax and barley being damaged when that horrible hail fell. "The barley and the flax were then in their greenness." The Jews in the Constantinople version translate: *The barley was ripe and the flax was in the stalk.* Junius: *The barley had its soft ear.* *Abib* is the ear of corn with a green stalk. An ear is called *mutica* <note>beardless</note> if it lacks an awn <note>the bristle-like growth on barley</note>, according to Varro in *On Agriculture*, book 1, chapter 49. But that ear which is not beardless, in barley and wheat, has three containing parts: the grain, the husk, and the awn. The Emperor Gallienus alluded to this same fertility; indeed, when they reported that Egypt had revolted from the Roman Empire, he replied: "What? Can we not live without Egyptian linen?" Trebellius Pollio writes that Gallienus joked in this way about all the regions famous for their yield of fruits which he had lost. John Leo* <note>Leo Africanus</note>, in *On Africa*, book 8, writes: "Although all of Egypt is most fertile, the province of Sa'id surpasses the other parts in the abundance of every kind of legume, animal, poultry, and flax." Marc. Frid. Wendelin, in *On the Wonders of the Nile*, page 191, writes: "Besides the abundance of crops, Egypt supplies a very great quantity of flax every year, which it owes to the fertility of the Nile; and this flax is most excellent, being distributed into various parts of the West." That Egypt is rich in flax is also gathered from Isaiah chapter 19, verse 9, and Esther book 1, verse 6, regarding which Pliny writes that it has the least strength but brings the most profit. If a land abounds in rivers, it is a great benefit; for from there the merchant brings in useful goods, the farmer makes a rich harvest, the fisherman and the weaver weave precious works from flax, and every field flourishes rich with cattle. From this, it seems to have happened that a "river" is beautifully used as a metaphor for fertility, plenty, and exuberance.

The author draws on classical historians and naturalists like Pliny and Herodotus to illustrate the Prophet's warnings.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>
The Burden of Egypt.
</margin>
water, so that extreme necessity is indicated; it is even said that the rivers were dried up everywhere by the multitude of the army, and all the crops, grasslands, and sowings were destroyed. Indeed, everything is usually exhausted and consumed when a very large army approaches, and if this is not done by water, it is managed with great effort. Thus Xerxes, when he led his forces into Greece, dried up rivers. Herodotus (Book 7), Justin (Book 2), and Juvenal have left records of this. All the hope of Egypt lay in the flooding of the Nile, for even today that land is irrigated not by rains, which it lacks, but by the Nile, and by the channels led from the Nile, and by the pools that the receding Nile leaves behind. Along the banks of this river and its streams were the best and richest grasslands for the pasture of animals, which in verse 7 are called *aroth* <gloss>Hebrew: ערות, often translated as meadows or open fields</gloss>. The Latin translator took this word in the sense of "uncovering" or "nakedness," rendering it: *the channel of the river shall be laid bare from its source*, for *arah* means "to be made bare." The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> elegantly translates it as: *all the green things around the river* <note>original: τὸ χλωρὸν πᾶν τὸ κύκλῳ τοῦ ποταμοῦ</note>, for the Hebrews understand *aroth* to mean "green things," i.e., greenery and grasslands; hence Luther's translation: *The grass by the waters* <note>original: Das Gras an den Wassern</note>. Musculus says on this passage (p. 332): *This is the second loss* (the drying of the grass) *with which the Egyptians were to be afflicted through drought. It signifies that the drought will be so great that the grass will dry up not only in the drier places, but even at the very banks of the rivers and streams.* To express this, he did not simply say: *The grass shall wither*, but *the grass near the streams, indeed at the very banks of the streams, shall wither. Hence the greatest loss to the livestock and the entire province.* Thus also the lack of reeds and rushes is recounted in verse 6: *the reed and the flags shall wither* <gloss>Hebrew: קנה וסוף קמלו</gloss>, as well as *papyrus*; Junius thought that *aroth* referred to this, from *arah*, "skin," as if those thin leaves or membranes of papyrus were called "little skins"; for it was artistically dissected into many skins and layers, as Pliny teaches, whose words are: *Paper is prepared from it (papyrus) by dividing it with a needle into very thin but as wide as possible layers* <note>original: philyrae</note>. The Septuagint has *every green thing*. Who is so unread in foreign history that they do not know that Egypt abounded in reeds and rushes in the marshes and banks of the Nile? In the reed-beds of the Nile the infant Moses was abandoned, in *an ark of bulrushes or a basket of rushes*, which *was smeared with slime and pitch*, as we read in Exodus 2:3. Pliny says in the same place: *Papyrus grows in the marshes of Egypt, or in the still waters of the Nile where they overflow and stagnate.* See Pancirollus, page 609. The Old Translator calls that rush-bed a *Papyrion*, because the papyrus shrub grew up on the bank. Thermuthis, the daughter of Egypt <note>Pharaoh's daughter</note>, had come here to wash herself, choosing a place among the shadows of the papyrus and reeds where she could be less seen, and her maidservants walked along the river bank; and seeing the little ark in the middle of the rush-bed, she sent her maid—for she was a King’s daughter—and took it (v. 5). Rabshakeh, the commander of Sennacherib's army, alluded to this nature of the region in his speech to Hezekiah <margin>2 Kings 18:20</margin> when he spoke of the Egyptian help being like a fig-tree: *You trust in a staff of a broken reed*, i.e., you fix your hopes on those who can offer no protection. This proverb can also be confirmed by the usage of the Greeks, among whom *fig-wood* <note>original: lignum ficulnum</note>, being quite fragile and weak, gave rise to several proverbs; for *the wood of the fig tree is weak and powerless in the mountains*, says the commentator on Theocritus; hence the same poet in *The Laborers* (Idyll 10) calls a soft and useless man a *fig-man* <note>original: ἀνδράσκινον</note>, and uses *fig-tree help* <note>original: συκίνην ἐπικουρίαν</note> for

<column-break/>

empty aid, and they use *fig-tree knife* <note>original: συκίνην μάχαιραν</note> for a false accusation; see Erasmus on this. Jeremiah (chapter 51, v. 32) says: *And they have burned the reeds with fire.* Arias Montanus, avoiding hyperbole, translates this as *reeds*; because pools full of rushes and reeds are understood. But *agamim* <gloss>Hebrew: אגמים</gloss> are "pools" and marshes (Exodus 7:19; Isaiah 14:23, 42:25). *Agmonim*, however, are the rushes that grow in pools (Isaiah 58:5). The Nile is called *papyrus-bearing* by the poets, for in it grows *papyrus, from which paper is prepared* <note>original: πάπυρος, ἀφ’ ἧς ὁ χάρτης κατασκευάζεται</note>. Dams and mounds used to restrain the waters of the Nile, and so the Prophet seems to have said: *when the rivers shall be removed far away, they shall be thinned, and the streams of the mound shall be wasted;* concerning which see <margin>In the commentary on Isaiah 19:8.</margin> Cujas. When the Nile has flooded Egypt, lakes remain, which the natives call *Birchas*, as noted by Prosper Alpinus in his book on exotic plants (p. 214); in these grows the herb *Lotus*, called by the inhabitants *Arais* and *nil*, the description of which you have in said book. It could be called the *Nymphaea Nilotica* <note>The Blue or White Egyptian Water Lily</note>.

*And the fishers shall mourn, and all they that cast an angle into the river shall lament, and they that spread nets upon the waters shall languish.* In these words, the failure and loss of trades, especially fishing, is recounted. Among the riches of Egypt was *Fishing*, because of the Nile and the nearby sea, wherefore they had ponds and preserves (*pools of the soul* <gloss>Hebrew: אגמי נפש</gloss>, i.e., of refreshment) in which they kept fish for that purpose; therefore, when that drought came, the Prophet says the business of the Fishermen would also cease. Theodore Snepf on this passage (p. 399): *By the waters, the abundance of things is understood, and by the works of the Fishermen and those who work in linen, by synecdoche, all merchants and craftsmen are understood, whose arts, trades, commerce, and profits lay idle in these civil wars.* The fishing of the Jews living in Egypt is well known <margin>Numbers 11:5.</margin>, for which they felt a longing while staying in the desert, when the rebels, out of disgust for the food sent from heaven, demanded the pots and fish of Egypt. The story from Plutarch about Mark Antony fishing is well known: Cleopatra, having deceived him with a salted fish, warned him to leave fishing to the Egyptians, and that he himself should fish for cities and kingdoms.

*And they shall be confounded who work in various linens, and they who weave nets.* Hebrew: *Weavers of hole-filled works*, i.e., reticulated hangings. The embroiderers will mourn when they see that the earth no longer supplies them with *various woven fabrics* <note>original: τὰ ὑφάσματα ποικίλα</note> for the clothing and adornment of their wise men. To fishing was added the linen trade or the weaving of fine flax <note>byssus</note>; for Egypt produced excellent and subtle flax, according to Pliny, from which the thinnest cloths were made, almost like the *Cambric* cloth <note>original: Kammertuch</note> among us. Its use was in sacred vestments. Jerome on Ezekiel chapter 43 (p. 546): *Egyptian priests use linen garments, not only on the inside, but also on the outside.* Apuleius, in the last book of the *Metamorphoses*, speaking of the Isiac ceremonies, writes thus: *Then a crowd flows in, men and women of every rank and every age initiated into the divine rites, luminous in the pure whiteness of linen garments*; for when they performed divine service, they were dressed in white and were luminous with pure whiteness, as the man from Madaura <note>Apuleius</note> says here. Cicero (Book 2, *On Laws*): *The color white is especially fitting for God, both in other things and most especially in textiles.* Concerning those who wear linen, see Beroaldus on Suetonius’s *Tiberius* (f. 292, 378); Raphelengius in his observations on the riddles of ancient poets (fol. 51); and Junius (4th animadversion, 29); Winsemius’s *Sirius*...

On page 40, we taught the use of Egyptian flax in the treatment of Polyps, citing Hippocrates’ *On Diseases*, page 29. There was also a use for fine linen <term>byssus; a high-quality fine flax or linen cloth</term> in the distribution of honors and virtues. Thus, Pharaoh clothed Joseph, the son of Israel—as both the Vulgate and the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> record—in a robe of fine linen. The Hebrew term is *shesh* <note>Hebrew: שש</note>, meaning garments of fine linen, which was a mark of high office; it was given as a sign that he should be treated with honor by others. Likewise, it was the adornment of brides, as seen in *Ezekiel, chapter 16*. Regarding these finer points of phrasing, Jerome translates from the Hebrew, while the Septuagint has: *and I clothed you in woven hair* <note>original Greek: καὶ περιβαλόν σε τριχάπτω</note>. On this, the Church Father Jerome <margin>p. 423.</margin> wrote: *When I diligently searched for what the word "trichapton" meant—which the Septuagint used—and could find neither its use nor its etymology among any of the Greeks, I finally learned it was a word coined by the Septuagint translators. For new things, new names must be forged. It refers to a garment of such great fineness that it is believed to have the thinness of hair.* Jerome continues: *Where I saw the thinness of the garment expressed, I translated it more precisely than "woven hair."* He says the same in his commentary on *Zechariah chapter 14, page 286*: *Let us understand "trichapta" as thin garments which are so beautiful and delicate that they seem like hair.* Luther, in his commentary on *Genesis chapter 36, folio 492 a*, notes: *The great nobles in the East used fine linen, just as the Turks today use a cap of fine linen.* While the mark of a Roman was purple and the toga, for Easterners it was fine linen. The *cydaris* <term>a royal Persian headdress</term> of the Persians was made of fine linen, about which see above. Josephus, in the sixth book of *The Jewish War*, mentions that fine linen garments were familiar to the Jewish priests. Jerome adds: <margin>on Ezekiel chapter 16, page 422.</margin> *Jerusalem is not only clothed in various colors and shod in hyacinth-blue leather, but is also girded with fine linen, from which the thinnest threads are woven into the Priest's garment.* The Hebrew *shesh* is a species of the most excellent and delicate Egyptian flax, as Ibn Ezra <note>A celebrated medieval Jewish scholar</note> writes on *Exodus chapter 25, verse 4*. In the same passage, Piscator rendered it as *Egyptian Flax* <note>original German: Ægyptisch Flachs</note>. <margin>il 18.</margin> From this was made the wrap which the Greeks called *sindon* <note>original Greek: σινδών</note>; according to Pollux (Book 7, chapter 16), just as *isis* was a type of *othone* <note>original Greek: ὀθόνη; fine linen cloth</note>. Luther, in the Gospel of Luke, translates this as *precious linen* <note>original German: köstlich Leinwad</note>. This Hebrew word *shesh* also occurs twice in *Esther chapter 1, verse 6*, but with different meanings: in the first instance, it denotes fine linen, but in the second, it refers to marble columns—*columns of shesh*—as the Chaldean translation has it; thus *shesh* can mean marble. In *Proverbs chapter 7, verse 16*, the phrase "Egyptian cord" <note>Hebrew: אטון מצרים</note> denotes Egyptian linens or fine linen tapestries embroidered with a needle, used by the "strange woman" <note>the "adulteress"</note>. She says, *I have spread my bed with cords*—that is, *I have covered my bed with colored tapestries from Egypt; I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon*. Egypt was famous for these most elegant tapestries and textiles, which were of the finest quality. Pliny (Book 7, chapter 56) credits the Egyptians with their invention. Lucan, in his *Pharsalia* (Book 10, verse 161), writes:

> Her white breasts shine through the Sidonian thread,
> Which the Egyptian needle has compressed with the comb,
> Releasing the warp and thinning the threads in the wide web.

<margin>Epigram 6, Book 10, verse 7.</margin> Thus in Martial, a "Nilotic tunic" is a tunic embroidered by the Egyptians, as observed by Turnebus in *Adversaria* (30.30).

<margin>p. 471.</margin> Ezekiel (chapter 27:7) teaches that the best and most variegated fine linen was brought from Egypt: *Fine linen with embroidered work from Egypt was your sail.* Jerome comments: *Fine linen grows most abundantly in Egypt, from which the sail of the Tyrian ship is woven; it is hung from the mast and provides a covering that offers shade to the sailors and passengers in the quiet heat of the sun.* In the Hebrew text, Arius Montanus...

<column-break/>

...translated this with the invented term *fine linen of recamation* <note>referring to needlework or embroidery</note>. To understand this more fully, see above at *Psalm 139*, where we discuss the root *rqm* <note>Hebrew: רקם; to embroider</note>, from which some speculate the word *chori* <note>Hebrew: חורי; white or noble cloth</note> is derived, along with the art itself. Those who grant the glory of weaving to the Egyptians note that the Israelites brought this skill, along with the name, with them into the Promised Land, as Mercer notes on Pagninus (column 1419). It would indeed be strange if the ancient Hebrews did not have a sufficient supply of words to describe such textiles; I see no reason to believe they were not granted the *art of weaving* <note>original Greek: ὑφαντικὴν</note> along with the vocabulary, the meaning of which the Jews themselves were not ignorant of, especially since we can relate it entirely to the Hebrew *chur* <note>meaning white</note>. That these same Egyptians excelled in linen-making five hundred years ago is testified by Benjamin the Jew <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a medieval traveler</note> in his *Itinerary* near the end, which Constantine l'Empereur edited more correctly after Arius Montanus. There, he commends the "Egyptian Aliboa," famous throughout the world for making nets: *The inhabitants of Sunbat grow the best flax and weave nets or "trichapta" (L'Empereur translates this as "white cloths"); and this merchandise is distributed throughout the whole world.* Scylax the Geographer alludes to this Egyptian merchandise in his *Periplus*—recently edited with corrections by Isaac Vossius after Hoeschelius—calling it *a cargo of fine and variegated linens*. Silius Italicus (Book 3, verse 370) joined the textiles of the Arabs and Pelusian linen together. We also gather from the Holy Scriptures that Egypt was fertile in flax; in *Exodus chapter 9, verse 31*, the first account of flax is given, and mention is made only of flax and barley when that horrible hail fell. *The barley and the flax were then in their greenness.* The Jews in the Constantinople version translate: *The barley was ripe and the flax was in the stalk* <note>original German: Der Gerste war zeitig / und der Flachs stengelecht</note>. Junius translates: *The ear was in the barley.* The Hebrew *abib* <note>אביב</note> is the ear of grain green with its stalk. An ear is called *mutica* <note>beardless</note> when it has no awn <note>the hair-like bristles on grain</note>, according to Varro (*On Agriculture*, Book 1, chapter 49). However, that ear which is not beardless, in barley and wheat, has three parts: *the grain, the husk, and the awn.* Gallienus Caesar alluded to this same fertility; indeed, when they reported that Egypt had revolted from the Roman Empire, he replied: *What? Can we not be without Egyptian linen?* Trebellius Pollio (chapter 6) writes that Gallienus joked in this way about all the regions he had lost which were commended for their produce. Leo Africanus <margin>Africa, chapter 8, folio 159 a.</margin> writes: *While all of Egypt is most fertile, the province of Sa'id nevertheless excels the other parts in the abundance of all kinds of legumes, animals, poultry, and flax.* Marcus Friedrich Wendelinus, in *The Wonders of the Nile* (page 191), writes: *In addition to the abundance of crops, Egypt provides a very great supply of flax every year, which it owes to the fertility of the Nile; and this flax is most excellent, being dispersed into various parts of the West.* That Egypt is rich in flax is also gathered from *Isaiah chapter 19, verse 9* and *Esther chapter 1, verse 6*. Though it has the least strength, it provides the most for sports and luxury; this does not only give splendor to Egyptian fashion, it is a great benefit; for from it the merchant brings useful goods, the farmer makes a rich harvest, the fisherman and the weaver weave precious works from flax, and every field flourishes, rich with livestock. Hence it seems to have happened that the river is beautifully used as a metaphor for fertility, abundance, and exuberance.
