<meta>This page continues the exposition of Isaiah 19. While the previous page discussed the physical and economic collapse of Egypt (specifically the textile industry), this page moves to the intellectual and political downfall of the Egyptian leadership, focusing on verse 11 and the vanity of their vaunted "ancient wisdom."</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The origin of Egypt.</margin> How can you say to Pharaoh: *“I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings”?*

In this second part of the chapter, which contains a rebuke of the entire administration, the prophet convicts the Princes of Tanis <note>Tanis, or Zoan, was a major city and often a seat of royal power in ancient Egypt.</note> and Pharaoh’s counselors of <term>δοξομαθησοφίας καὶ κενεῆς οἰήσεως</term> <note>original Greek: "a wisdom based on mere opinion and empty conceit"</note>. He argues against those calling themselves *Sons of ancient Kings and Sons of the Wise*. He warns that they should not be consulted because of their foolish and vain self-persuasion. None of those whom he pronounces as dullards—despite their appearance of wisdom—could help with their counsel; as Sophocles wrote in his *Oedipus*, good counsel does not take root in a wicked mind. For when God takes away the mind, there is no place for counsel or judgment in political affairs. *Those things that are destined by fate, though signaled, are not avoided*, says Tacitus in his *Histories*, Book 1, Chapter 18. *When the fates lay their hands upon a man, his senses are dulled and blunted,* writes Ammianus Marcellinus in Book 4. It is quite marvelous in the governing of a Republic that men who were previously prudent, when abandoned by God, are reduced to madness. They publish brutish decrees against God and His anointed ones; when divine help fails, they rush headlong into every <margin>Homer, Iliad 16, line 689.</margin> disgrace of folly—indeed, to their very destruction, <term>καὶ κῆρα κακὴν μέλανος θανάτοιο</term> <note>original Greek: "and the evil fate of black death"</note>. These pernicious authors of counsel were wise too late, even worse than the Phrygians <note>A reference to the proverb "The Phrygians are wise too late," meaning they only learned from their mistakes after the damage was done.</note>. For when headlong counsels can neither be recalled nor restored to their original state, Livy testifies in Book 31 that a swift repentance follows, but it is a late and useless one. *One ought to consult and provide promptly while the ship is safe, lest it be overturned.* After the waves have overcome it, the effort is in vain, as Julius Caesar writes in his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, Book 5. God threatens this same punishment upon the Edomites, rendering their efforts entirely fruitless and their deliberations empty, exterminating their *Wise Men*—that is, their counselors—as seen in *Isaiah chapter 29, verse 14*: *And the wisdom of the Wise shall perish.* Similarly in Obadiah: *Shall I not in that day, says the Lord, destroy the wise men from Edom?* The same is said in Jeremiah chapter 49, verse 6, regarding the slaughter of that same Idumæa; this is <term>φρονέοντας εἰς ἀφροσύνην ἀναβάλλειν</term> <note>original Greek: "to cast those who think into foolishness"</note>, to make the counsel of the wise foolish. If that which they enter into is <term>ἄνευ θεοῦ</term> <note>original Greek: "without God"</note>, it does not succeed. In this sense, the Hebrew word <term>הולל</term> <note>transliterated: holal; referring to making someone act like a fool or a madman</note> is written by Job <margin>Job 12:17.</margin> regarding judges who become foolish. The Vulgate renders it: *God leads counselors to a foolish end, and judges into a stupor.* The word <term>מהולל</term> <note>transliterated: meholal</note> here and in Isaiah 44:25 means *he renders inglorious, he makes brutish, he turns into madness, he infatuates.* Counselors, just as they are called "wise," ought to be so; otherwise, it may be said of them: <term>Κενοὶ κενὰ βουλεύονται</term> <note>original Greek: "Empty men plan empty things."</note>. He who does not act with wise counsel is a fool, and he who acts imprudently (<term>ἄφρων</term> <note>original Greek: "senseless/insane"</note>) is mad. Therefore, it is not only those who wear bells <note>A reference to the traditional "fool's cap" or jester's bells.</note> who are fools. Even those to whom jurisdiction is committed are often fools, as Seneca witnesses in *On Benefits*, Book 2, Chapter 35, while they think they are giving wise counsel to a failing Republic, though their advice is often most foolish. This evil folly gripped the people and the great Kings of Egypt and their counselors; trusting too much in their own strength, they seduced themselves and others, as if to say: *“Hey there, Egyptian! Where has that prudence gone that you have boasted of for so long since ancient times? Your so-called wisdom is now folly. Your science, in which you trust, has been found foolish before God. Your whole Republic will now collapse, since some lack the spirit and others the counsel to strengthen it.”* The Egyptian nation boasts of its antiquity even to the point of madness;

<column-break/>

for it was insolent and elated above all other nations of the world. Hence it says: *“I am descended from the stock of ancient kings.”* Not only was it proud above others, but it was also superstitious, attributing to itself the invention of religion—something a pagan might concede if the claims were only slightly exaggerated. But Pomponius Mela writes that their histories span more than thirteen thousand years, and that they are so ancient that since their beginning, the stars have changed their courses four times. Crinitus records these words in his *De Honesta Disciplina* (Book 8, Chapter 2, folio 31a) and leaves it, as he says, *to be judged by the readers*. Plato says in the *Timaeus* that they alone preserved the philosophy of many ages, and that they had been skilled in Astronomy for a hundred thousand years. This lying rumor does not deserve an investigation into what kind of "years" these might be; rather, one may laugh along with Augustine in *The City of God*, Book 8, Chapter 40. However, it should be noted that in the Holy Scripture, the Egyptians are adorned with the praise of *wisdom* when the discussion concerns physical things and other arts in which they excelled. For when the Bible wishes to praise King Solomon for his wisdom, it says in *1 Kings 4:30–31* that Solomon’s wisdom surpassed the *wisdom of all the people of the East and all the wisdom of Egypt*. Likewise, it is affirmed of Moses in *Acts 7:22* that he was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. Regarding this glory of theirs, an ancient describer of the world says on page 18: <term>ἄνδρας ὁρᾶς ὑπὲρ πάντα κόσμον Αἴγυπτον περιόντας</term> <note>original Greek: "you see men surpassing the whole world traversing Egypt"</note>. As far as the knowledge of the nature of various things is concerned, so many Egyptian obelisks testify to it, adorned with such inscriptions: <margin>Pliny, chapter 9.</margin> *“The works of Egyptian philosophy contain the interpretation of the nature of things.”* It was their custom to present their sacred and natural doctrines through hieroglyphic letters—that is, through symbols, allegories, enigmas, and other such signs—as well as on pyramids and obelisks; an entire volume on this by J. Pierius <note>Likely referring to Giovanni Pierio Valeriano Bolzani’s famous 16th-century work *Hieroglyphica*.</note> exists. Through these, they handed down what was to be said about the Gods and about the institutions of life and death. These were the exclusive coverings of science: he who devised them ingeniously and spread them was finally deemed worthy of the throne of Wisdom. They kept the common people far away, leaving them nothing but *to wonder* (<term>τὸ admirari</term>). A person could be admitted, but not fully initiated. There were many things that could be understood more than they could be expressed, and many things that could be expressed less than they were understood. In this way, the Wise Man (Sophos) pleased himself; but while the Sophos seeks secrets too subtly, he understands nothing at all. That is to act foolishly, not wisely. Truly, not only the Egyptians delighted themselves with this smoky pride of antiquity and wisdom, but all Pagans generally boasted of antiquity and the wisdom and institutions of their ancestors. In contrast, they looked down upon the Jews. Hence Josephus, in order to defend the antiquity of his nation against all others, left to posterity two distinguished books, titled <term>περὶ ἀρχαιολογίας</term> <note>original Greek: "Against Apion" (though often grouped with his "Antiquities of the Jews")</note>, which trace the history of his nation—both sacred and profane—from its very cradle. It always seemed dangerous to the heathens <term>τὰ ἀκίνητα κινεῖν τῆς περὶ θεῶν δόξης, ἣν εἶχον</term> <note>original Greek: "to move those things that are immovable regarding the opinion they held about the gods"</note>, as Plutarch has it in his *Amatorius*. He says no clearer argument can be found than this: <term>ἀρκεῖ δὲ ἡ πάτριος καὶ παλαιὰ πίστις ἧς οὐκ ἔστιν εἰπεῖν, οὐδ’ ἀνευρεῖν τεκμήριον ἐναργέστερον</term> <note>original Greek: "The ancestral and ancient faith is sufficient, than which it is not possible to speak of nor to find a clearer proof."</note>. By this argument, Cicero defends himself in *Pro Milone* (n. 64) regarding the *wisdom of the ancestors*, and in Books 2 and 3 of *On the Nature of the Gods*. But back to the Egyptians...

<summary>This page analyzes Isaiah 19:11, critiquing the vanity of Egypt's political advisors and their obsession with ancient lineage. It contrasts Egyptian claims of extreme historical antiquity and symbolic "hieroglyphic" wisdom with the biblical perspective that true wisdom is a gift from God.</summary>
<keywords>Egypt, Pharaoh, wisdom, antiquity, Isaiah 19, hieroglyphics, Josephus, Plato, Solomon, Moses, political counsel, divine judgment, Tanis, pride</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Isaiah 19, transitioning from the intellectual vanity of the Egyptian priests to a broader discussion of their national reputation for deceit. It then moves to Isaiah 23 to discuss Tyre and its relationship with Egypt and the merchant trade.</meta>

# Isaiah 19:1 ff. Isaiah 23:3

<margin>The Burden of Egypt.</margin> We must return to the Egyptians. They, as any nation is a boaster of its own affairs, placed themselves above other nations and mocked the Greeks. As a Priest of Sais once said: *“O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children, nor is there any such thing as an old man in Greece; for you are young in soul, having no ancient belief rooted in long tradition, nor any knowledge grown hoary with age,”* as can be read in Plato’s *Timaeus*. Elated by this wisdom they attributed to themselves—which they sold as being of the highest antiquity—they called themselves "Wise Men," or, as the Hebrews say, *Sons of the Wise*. The people of Heliopolis were considered the wisest of all, according to Herodotus in his *Euterpe*, where he writes on page 56:

->The Heliopolitans are said<-
->to be the most learned of the Egyptians.<-

And there was a proverb, mentioned in Synesius's *On Baldness*, that said *wisdom overflows among the Egyptians*. In truth, they were otherwise barbarians in their knowledge of divine things, and of all nations, they were the most dull-witted regarding superstition. Thus in Psalm 114:1, they are called a *barbarous people*, <term>lo'ez</term> <note>Hebrew: לועז, meaning a people of a strange or foreign tongue</note>, because they were rude and fierce, unmitigated by any religious institutions. Reuchlin says, <margin>Book 1, On the Word; Book 4.</margin> *“I believe the Egyptians were called barbarians <note>lo'ez</note> as a term of contempt, because they refused to be called barbarians; this term here signifies rudeness and stupidity.”* Traces of this ancient stupidity are found in the animals they worshipped. They were foolish and insane regarding religion, which is why the title God assigns in Deuteronomy 32:21 can be applied to them: <term>beni nabal</term> <note>Hebrew: בני נבל, "sons of folly"</note>, a *senseless nation*. The term <term>lo'ez</term> is usually said of those who do not acknowledge the true God, such as the impious and the Atheist in Psalm 14; and Job says of his "atheistic" wife in Chapter 2:10, *“You speak as one of the foolish women.”* Every age has noted the character of this diverse nation. Vopiscus, at the beginning of his *Life of Saturninus*, says: *“The Egyptians are a windy, frantic, boastful, injurious, and utterly vain people, always desiring revolution.”* Diogenianus says: *“The Lydians are wicked, but the Egyptians are second to them,”* as found in Erasmus (2.10.38). Phlegon of Tralles, in an Epistle, criticized them for their levity of mind (see Peter Crinitus <margin>Book 2, On Honest Discipline, ch. 10.</margin>), and they are ill-reputed elsewhere for wickedness and imposture. Indeed, even among the Comic poets, the word <term>aigyptiazein</term> <note>Greek: "to act like an Egyptian"</note> means to be a *rogue* or to act deceitfully, according to Synesius and Eustathius in his commentary on Homer's *Iliad*. From this malice and fraudulence, the Prophet Isaiah took a proverb in Chapter 19:2 <note>The text says cap. 12. v. 12, likely a scribal error for 19:2</note>: *“Egyptians against Egyptians,”* signifying that like-minded people—perverse with the perverse—are set against one another (as Zenobius testifies). The Scholiast on Theocritus (Idyll 15) says, *“The Egyptians are deceitful.”* Pharaoh ennobled this adage by his own example, <term>sphodra aigyptiazomenos</term> <note>Greek: "acting excessively like an Egyptian"</note>, for not even ten plagues could bring him back to his senses. He was always weaving new and stupendous schemes; as the proverb in Zenobius says regarding the *most wicked Egyptians*, <margin>Century 3, 37, p. 36, Schots edition.</margin> which can be further illustrated with examples from Arnold Clapmar’s *On the Secrets of State* (Book 3, ch. 3) and testimonies from Erasmus and Frenshemius.

<column-break/>

->And by great waters the seed of Sihor, the harvest of the River, is her revenue; and she is a mart of nations.<-
<note>Hebrew: Isaiah 23:3</note>

->*In much water, the seed of the traders, as the harvest of those brought in, are the traders of the nations.*<-
<note>Greek: Septuagint version of Isaiah 23:3</note>

->*In many waters is the seed of the Nile; the harvest of the river is its fruit, and it has become the trade of the nations.*<-
<note>Latin translation of the same verse</note>

<margin>The Nile</margin> Tyre, a most ancient city, *the first city of the ancient Phoenicians*, was the world’s most noble Egyptian marketplace <note>The author links Tyre's trade to Egypt's exports</note>. It was vast and reached remote places through both sea and land empires; because of the glory of its ornaments, its wealth, power, and sweetness of delights, Ezekiel 28:12 calls it the *seal of perfection*. And Isaiah, in verse 8 of this chapter, calls it <term>ha-ma'atirah</term>, that is, *the bestower of crowns* upon its own people, excelling in wealth and power like a crown among others, crowning its merchants and inhabitants with great riches and making them like Princes and Kings. For there follows in this description of Tyre's trade: *“Whose merchants are princes, whose traders are the renowned of the earth.”* The Phoenicians were the first among neighboring nations to tempt the sea, just as Thucydides says the Corinthians were among the Greeks.

->*And first they were carried through the waters,*<-
->*They surveyed the sea, and were the first to teach*<-
->*how to carry the world's commerce in hollow ships.*<-

Rufus Festus Avienus affirms this in his metrical paraphrase of Dionysius Periegetes. The Greek verses are found on page 551. Surely the Tyrians must have been of great courage if they were the first explorers of the sea for the sake of profit; as Horace rightly said, *“oak and triple brass were around the breast of him who first committed a fragile raft to the cruel sea.”* Truly, as Dionysius says, those who pant for trade in peaceful ships are *prodigal of their souls, not sparing their lives, so that they might seize boundless wealth.* That the Tyrians were no ignoble or obscure "sons of the earth and sea" is shown by the example of the most famous Admiral <margin>1 Kings 9:27</margin> Hiram, the renowned King of Tyre <margin>in the time of David.</margin>, whom the Septuagint calls *Cheirama*. Joppa was the port of Judea to which the Tyrian sailors brought timber from Lebanon on rafts, which was then carried to Jerusalem by land (1 Esdras 3:7). The author of Proverbs (31:24) testifies to the trade of the *Canaanites*. From their ancestor Ham, the son of Noah, they were perhaps devoted to negotiation due to their proximity to the sea; hence Aquila <margin>Zechariah 14:21</margin> understood the word <term>Kena'ani</term> (Canaanite) to mean <term>emporos</term> (merchant), a reading followed by Jerome, who says: *“For Canaanite, Aquila translated 'merchant,' and we have followed him in this place.”* The elders in the same passage of Solomon expand on the profits of the Phoenicians, for where the Hebrew text speaks only of Canaanites, they translate: *“She made linen and sold it to the Phoenicians, and girdles to the Canaanites.”* Thus it seems the Septuagint specifically called the Tyrians and Sidonians *Canaanites*. Our prophet expressly calls the citizens of Tyre "Canaanites" in verse 8. Stephanus says, *“Khia is what Phoenicia is called.”* Here *Khia* comes from *Kena* <note>The root of Canaan</note>, with the *nun* omitted, which the Hebrews admit is an addition. It is very likely that the Canaanites, driven out by Joshua, moved for the most part into Phoenicia.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
## Page 592

<margin>

of Egypt.
</margin>
So too in other places: that which in the Hebrew <note>Joshua 5:1</note> is "the Canaanite" <note>original: הכנעני</note>, they have translated as "the King of Phoenicia" <note>original: βασιλεὺς τῆς Φοινίκης</note>; and in verse 12, that region of Jericho near the Jordan is to them the "land of the Phoenicians" <note>original: χώρα Φοινίκων</note>. Likewise in Job 40:25, they make the Canaanites "the nations of the Phoenicians" <note>original: Φοινίκων ἔθνη</note>. Whatever the case may be regarding the Canaanites, it is established concerning the Phoenicians from all history that they excelled in the glory of commerce and in naval discipline. Eustathius, in his commentary on Homer’s *Odyssey*, says: *The Phoenicians are called men "famed for ships," as histories know, and they were the first or chief among them.* <note>original: Οἱ Φοίνικες ναυσίκλυτοι λέγονται ἄνδρες...</note> Scylax, in his *Periplus* on page 51, writes: *The merchants are indeed Phoenicians,* <note>original: Οἱ δὲ ἔμποροί εἰσι μὲν Φοίνικες</note> where he further describes the Ethiopian trade with the Phoenicians. Diodorus, in the 5th book of his *Library*, page 217, says: *The Phoenicians were skillful from ancient times at finding profit.* <note>original: Δεινοὶ ὑπῆρξαν οἱ Φοίνικες...</note> Therefore Ezekiel, about to describe them as "mighty masters of the sea-faring ships," began to speak thus to Tyre and the Tyrian "masters of the sea" <note>original: θαλασσοκράτορας</note>: *All the princes of the sea will descend from their usual places,* "the rulers of the sea" <note>original: ἄρχοντες τῆς θαλάσσης</note>, <note>Hebrew: נשיאי הים, which Arias Montanus translates as "the prelates of the sea" in verse 17</note> *and taking up a lamentation over you, they shall say to you: "How have you perished, you renowned city who dwell in the sea, who were strong in the sea with your inhabitants, whom all feared?"* And in chapter 27, verse 4: *In the heart of the seas* <note>Hebrew: בלב ימים, as in Exodus 15:8 or Psalm 46:3, for which Jonah 2:4 uses "in the heart of the seas," בלבב ימים</note> *are your borders.* Verse 9: *All the ships of the sea and their sailors were yours to conduct your trade.* Arias <note>Arias Montanus, a 16th-century Spanish orientalist</note> translates: *to your spreading forth.* The Greek codices add, *from the west of the west,* <note>original: ὅτι δυσμὰς δυσμῶν</note> to indicate that their commerce reached even to the most remote peoples, separated by the whole world. In the book of Isaiah, at this place in verse 4, it is called the "stronghold of the sea" <note>original: מעוז הים</note>, that is, a most fortified marketplace by the sea, the "fountain of all famous merchants" <note>original: πηγὴ πᾶσιν ὀνομαστῶν ἐμπόρων</note>, just as we know the city of Venice to be today: a supreme marketplace of wealth brought by land and sea, which deserved to be called a "paradise of delights," as Ezekiel said of Tyre. Later ages adorned Tyre with the same praises. Its inhabitants are celebrated as "masters of the sea"; Quintus Curtius, in his 4th book, about to write of the siege of Tyre by Alexander the Great, celebrates it as memorable for both fame and size above all the cities of Syria and Phoenicia. *Founded,* he says among other things in chapter 41, *by Agenor, for a long time it made not only the neighboring sea, but every sea its fleets visited, part of its own dominion; from which "Tyrian seas" became a proverb,* which Afranius teaches in Festus, where these words regarding the Carthaginians, "most skilled in naval matters," <note>original: nauepctices peritissimis</note> are read: *The Carthaginians, originating from Tyre, were so powerful at sea that navigation was dangerous for all mortals.* Ammianus Marcellinus writes: *The region of Phoenicia lies against Mount Lebanon, full of graces and beauty, decorated with great and beautiful cities, among which Tyre excels in charm and the fame of its name, along with Sidon and Beirut.* Regarding the same Tyre, an ancient describer of the world, first brought to light by Jacques Gothofredus, says: *Leading the trade of all with fervor, it is greatly prosperous; for there is almost no city of the East more crowded in commerce, and it has wealthy men who are powerful in all regions.* <note>original: πάντων ἐμπορεῖαν ζέσως ἄγω[ν]... </note> Cicero, in his 3rd book *On the Republic*, found in Nonius, writes: *Commerce itself teaches that the Greeks received from the Phoenicians both measurement and coinage as well as trade: the Phoenicians first brought, with their commerce and merchandise, avarice and magnificence and insatiable desires for all things into Greece.* This commercial use of the sea gave the Tyrians immense wealth, and the density of the people

and the splendor of the buildings greatly increased the city. From this it can easily be understood what the Prophet means by: *Tyre the crowned*, or, as Junius translates, *the crowner*, whom Piscator followed, translating: *The Crowner / she who crowns her own*, as the Genevans explain it. Castalio and the Italian version of Diodati have, *the crowned city* <note>original: città coronata, civitas coronata</note>, which is also how the author of the version of the Prophets published in Worms in 1525 (on which edition see Luther's judgment in the Jena German edition, volume 5, folio 143b) interpreted it: *the crowned City* <note>original: bekrönte Stadt</note>. Pagninus and the English render it actively: *the crowning city*. To this phrasing agrees what the ancient "Descriptor of the World" says on page 16 in praise of Egypt, *that it is crowned by the river called the Nile* <note>original: εἶναι ἐστεφανωμένην ποταῷ, ὃς καλεῖται Νεῖλος</note>. *He calls Tyre crowned,* says Jerome on this passage, page 71, *because just as a King raises his head adorned with a diadem among a great multitude of men, so Tyre, shining and lofty with wealth, gleaming with gold, gems, silk, and purple, was esteemed a queen among all nations.* Tyre is said to be named thus because it was built on a rock and sea-cliff, since *Tzur* <note>original: צור</note> signifies a rock or cliff; from which the Syrians derive *Tur*, a mountain. That it was situated on a rock is testified by Rauwolf and Breydenbach in his *Remarkable Travels Across the Sea*, folio 32a, whose words I will add: *The city of Tyre was larger than Acre, and was surrounded by strong walls and stout towers, having a round form, lying in the heart of the sea upon a large rock, and surrounded by the sea on all sides, except only at the front of the city, where it was joined to the land as wide as a stone’s throw by Nebuchadnezzar, and afterwards Alexander the Great; yet it had a high wall 25 feet thick, protected by 12 strong towers, which led up to the mighty castle of the city lying on the rock, upon which the city is also built; which castle was so secured that one might have believed the whole world could not have won the castle by force, though it is now indeed entirely destroyed.* With an elegant pun <note>paronomasia</note>, Zechariah writes of Tyre, that Tyre, *Tzor* <note>original: צור</note>, *built* <note>original: construxisse</note> a "stronghold" <note>original: מצור</note>, and from this some think Egypt was called *Mizraim* <note>original: מצרים</note>. Rabbi David thinks this is because of the very strong cities she had everywhere near the water conduits. That Tyre is called "fortified" is found in 2 Samuel 24:7. Aquila and Symmachus observed this better from the Hebrew *mivtzar tzor* than the Septuagint translators, who have *mazar Tyre*; however, in Joshua 19:29, the same translators render "the fortified city of Tyre" <note>original: עיר מבצר צר</note> as "the city of the stronghold of the Tyrians" <note>original: πόλιν ὀχυρώματος Τυρίων</note>. Here, however, I would like philologists to consider the "straw-man" etymology of Johannes Annius, which he spewed out in his edition of Berosus, folio 39a: *The Syrians and Hebrews, from the leadership of Phoenicia and the sea, call Tyre 'Zor'; for 'Or' <note>original: הור</note> signified a hill and a mountain. 'Zi' truly has its derivation from 'dignity of counsel,' as the skilled Talmudists assert. Hence 'Zor' is the consular hill.* For Tyre is a small island in the manner of a great and wide hill. This I do not understand, nor perhaps did he who wrote it. Those who have made their way to the *Patricius Philogeronton* <note>A scholarly reference, likely a work on ancient things</note> teach from Aulus Gellius (book 14, chapter 6, page 468) that Tyre was anciently called *Sarra*, which name agrees with the Hebrew *Tzor*, the sibilant letter being changed into *Thau*, and this then into *Samekh*; which we see happen in other similar letter-swaps <note>original: ἀντίστοιχον</note>, so that from *Tzur* comes both *Tyrus* and *Sarra*, by the usual exchange...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Mediterranean geography and commerce, specifically focusing on the relationship between Egypt and the Phoenician city of Tyre, centered on the linguistic and physical characteristics of the Nile River.</meta>

# ISAIAH 23:3

<margin>
The Nile of Egypt, p. 78, 12.
</margin>
On this matter, see the fourth volume of the *Miscellany*, chapter 11; Fuller, the third volume of *Questions*, chapter 48; and Drusius. Just as *Tanis*—once the seat of Pharaoh and a famous Egyptian city celebrated for signs and miracles—was derived from the Hebrew **Tzoan** <note>original: צען</note>. The Greeks and Latins do not have the "Ts" sound, and therefore they do not allow the sibilant here. Similarly, the **Shin** <note>original: ש</note> of the Hebrews and Arabs often loses its sibilant sound when it passes into other languages. From *Sarra* <note>an ancient name for Tyre</note>, the word *Sarranus* is used by Virgil:
<margin>Virgil, Georgics, Book 2.</margin>
> *That he may drink from a jeweled cup and sleep on Sarran purple.* <note>original: "Ut gemma bibat & Sarrano dormiat ostro." Sarran purple refers to the famous Tyrian dye.</note>

On this, Servius <note>a 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note> notes on page 129: *What is now called Tyre was once called Sarra, named after a certain fish that is abundant there, which they call 'Sar' in their own language.* This claim by Servius about the "Sar" fish deserves as much credit as his claim about the Sarrastes people (whom he argued in his notes on the *Aeneid*, Book 7, were named after the river Sarnus in Campania)—which is to say, none at all. **Tyre** <note>called Sor in Hebrew</note> is commended to us for the abundance and fertility of its purple dye, since, as Pliny witnesses, its entire fame consisted of the shellfish and the purple dye. Hence, Juvenal commends the *Sarrana* tapestries, dyed with the redness of the Tyrian murex <note>a sea snail used to make purple dye</note>, and Columella in Book 9, chapter 4, calls purple violets *Sarranae*. Furthermore, clothes dyed with Tyrian purple are simply called *Tyrian*, as Barth proves from Ovid and Martial. The Tyrian murex is well known from Virgil (*Aeneid* IV, 53) and Horace (*Epistles* 12, 5); its color, as Pliny says in Book 9, chapter 36, was *radiant when looked up at.* Because the garment was dyed twice in that color, it was called *Tyrian dibaphos* <term>dibaphos: twice-dyed</term>.

The Prophet <note>Isaiah</note> teaches that Tyre abounded in grain and provisions usually imported from Egypt, while Egypt received silk and purple cloth from the Tyrians. From this, some believe the word *Scharlach* <note>Scarlet</note> is derived, as if it were *Sarlachen*, meaning cloth (in Dutch, *Lack*) from Sar <note>Tyre</note>; just as *Seiden* <note>Silk</note> for silk is said to have first been brought from Sidon, which is today called Saida. The "Seed of Sihor" <note>original: שיחור</note>, that is, the Nile, as the Old Interpreter translates. Jerome says: *Where we read "Seed of the merchants," it is written in Hebrew "Seed of Sihor," which is understood to be the Nile, because it has turbid waters with which the crops of Egypt are irrigated.* Oecolampadius notes on this passage: *The harvest of the river. This means the same as the seed of the Nile, because it is not rain, but the seed of the Nile that fertilizes Egypt; therefore the fruits of Egypt are called the seed and harvest of the Nile. He means, therefore, that various goods were stored in Tyre, and thus it was the marketplace of the whole world.* This is the scope of the passage, for it will be of little help to bring forward a few common facts about the Nile, a river most celebrated by writers. Among rivers, the first glory belongs to the Nile, which is easily the first of all the greatest. Silius Italicus says in Book 16:

<margin>Pliny, Natural History 5, 14.</margin>
<margin>3. On the History of Clothing, 3.</margin>
<margin>Waser, On Hebrew Coins, book 1, num. 4, p. 100.</margin>
> *As Phoebe [the Moon] surpasses the stars, and the Sun surpasses the lights of his sister, and as Atlas surpasses the mountains, so the Nile surpasses the rivers.*

Plutarch, in his book *On Isis and Osiris*: *There is nothing for those under the heavens like the Nile.* <note>original: Ουδέν εν τω μὴ δι’ υπ’ τίοις ως ο Νεῖλος.</note> In the Scriptures, this river is called by more than one name. The common appellation is **Yeor Mitzraim** <note>original: יאור מצרימ</note>, the "River of Egypt." Rabbi Solomon and Rabbi Kimchi take it this way in Genesis 15:18. What if from **Nehel** <note>original: נהל</note> comes *Neel*, contracted to *Nel*, and thence *Nilus*, just as from *Baal* comes *Beel*, *Bel*, and *Belos*? Certainly, the source of the Nile in Ethiopia was called *Nuchul*, according to Malachi 3, chapter 10. Heliodorus, in Book 9, page 444, derived it from a Greek source wittily, but in vain. The other name is more specific: **Shihor** <note>original: שיחור</note>. The Nile would be called *Shihor* from the nature of the thing, because it is blackish and turbid, from **shachar** <note>original: שחר</note>, meaning *to be black* or *to become black*; or because it fertilizes the fields by depositing silt during its flood, carrying turbid waters full of mud to be poured over the lands. For this reason, the Old Interpreter undoubtedly understood it to be the Nile, just as

<column-break/>

<margin>The Nile of Egypt.</margin>
Drusius conjectures in *Observations* 9, 18, that in Jeremiah 2:18, "turbid water" refers to the water of the Nile; Pagninus also holds this, and Osiander follows him. Hence Jerome, on Jeremiah chapter 2, verse 18: *The Latin Interpreter retained the Hebrew word, saying: "And now what do you want in the way of Egypt, that you should drink the water of Sihor?"* Where Jerome notes on page 266: *For 'Scornos' we have translated 'turbid,' which the Hebrew word signifies, for which the common edition has 'Geon.' Since he had previously (v. 16) mentioned the sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes, who defiled Israel to the crown of the head, he now clearly names Egypt itself, and no one doubts that the Nile has turbid waters.* And on Ezekiel, page 482: *Jeremiah forbids us to drink the turbid waters of Egypt, saying: "What to you and the way of Egypt, that you should drink the water of Geon?" For which in Hebrew it is written Shihor, which word is translated as turbid and muddy waters.* He repeats this in chapter 47, page 558, and in Habakkuk chapter 2, page 192. 

But Matthew Beroaldus (*Chronology* 3, 7, p. 86) and Chytraeus (*On Joshua* c. 13, p. 64) raise a dispute about this: *Shihor, which takes its name from the blackness of its waters, is not the Nile, but another small river below Gaza and Raphia, which is called Rhinocolurus by Ptolemy, and flows into the Mediterranean Sea at the town of the same name.* This coincides with Joshua 13:3, where the Vulgate again has: *From the turbid river that waters Egypt*, which they explain as the Nile. However, it is not the main channel of the Nile that is understood, but that Pelusiac branch of the Nile which runs toward Judea and thence into the Phoenician sea; it is otherwise called the "Brook of the Wilderness" (Amos 6:14) and the "Brook of Egypt" (Isaiah 27:12). Virgil alludes to this in the *Georgics*, Book 4, line 291:

> *And he fertilizes green Egypt with black sand.*

In the same way, the Nile was called **Melas** <note>meaning "Black"</note> by the Greeks for the same reason, and by the Latins **Mela** and **Melo**. From this, Egypt was called **Melakolos** <note>original: μελάκωλος, likely meaning black-limbed or black-earthed</note>, as Posidippus noted in *Miscellany* chapter 10. Scaliger, in his notes on Festus, says: *The Greeks, knowing that the Nile was called Shihor by the Egyptians themselves (that is, 'black'), rendered it with their own equivalent word 'Aigyption' [Egyptian], since 'Aigyptios' means 'black'.* Selden teaches the same in *On the Syrian Gods* 4, page 148; Fuller in *Miscellany* Book 2, chapter 8, page 208; and Vossius in *Institutes of Oratory* 4, 12, section 5, and *On Idolatry* 2, 74, page 692, where he conjectures that the name *Osiris* (by which the Nile was also implied) is from the Hebrew *Shihor* through a transposition of letters. *Seiris is what the Nile is called by the Ethiopians,* says Dionysius in his *Periegesis*. Fuller, in the place cited, conjectures not unlearnedly that the star **Sirius**—which we call the "Dog Star"—is named after it, so that *Sirius* is the same as *Neilaios* or the "Nile Star." This is because, at that same very hot time of summer, the Dog Star rises and the Nile increases most abundantly, as if the fires of the star drew out the waters of the river, and both raged together in harmony: one on earth, the other in the heavens. Let these things said about the various names of the Nile suffice. 

We will add a few things about its origin. In Ethiopia, the Nile is called **Chascapusch**, meaning "flowing out of darkness"; **Chascacura**, "source flowing from darkness"; or **Chafcatzaphes**, "overflowing from darkness," because the head of the Nile is hidden. Indeed, the origin of the Nile was so unknown to the ancients that it became a proverb "to seek the head of the Nile" <note>original: "illum Nili caput quærere"</note> for one who seeks something impossible to find. Whence Herodotus writes in Book 2, that neither...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
The Nile of Egypt, book 22.
</margin>
...of the Egyptians, nor any of the Africans he encountered, who claimed to know the sources of the Nile. And *Ammianus Marcellinus* <note>a 4th-century Roman soldier and historian</note> says: *The origins of the springs of the Nile, as it seems to me, just as has happened until now, future ages will also remain ignorant of.* Hence, in former times, there was no small obsession among Kings to investigate the origin of the Nile. The Kings of the Egyptians, Persians, and Macedonians—and finally the Roman Emperors—all sought certainty on this matter, but in vain. This is recorded regarding Alexander the Great, Cambyses, Juba, Dicaearchus, Ptolemy Philadelphus, and others by Arrian in book 6 of the *Expedition of Alexander*, Herodotus in the cited book, Pliny in book 5, chapter 9, and Strabo in book 17. Nero, likewise anxious about the origin of the Nile and investigating its headwaters, as Seneca says
<margin>
Natural Questions, Book 6, Ch. 8.
</margin>
, had sent a Tribune with Praetorian soldiers, as Pliny also mentions in book 9 of his *Natural History*, chapter 29. Lucan, in book 10 of his poem, excellently indicates this "lust" of Kings for knowing the springs of the Nile:
> *Whatever desire you have to know the Nile, O Roman,*
> *The Pharians <note>Egyptians</note> and Persians had it too, and the Macedonian Tyrants.*
> *No age has not wished to pass down this knowledge*
> *To the future: but nature still conquers by remaining hidden.*
> *Greatest of Kings, Alexander, whom Memphis adores,*
> *Envied the Nile, and sent chosen men through the furthest lands*
> *Of the Ethiopians: the red zone of the scorched sky*
> *Held them back; they saw a steaming Nile.*
> *Sesostris came to the setting of the world, to the furthest reaches,*
> *And drove Pharian chariots over the necks of Kings:*
> *Yet he drank from your rivers, the Rhone and the Po,*
> *Before he drank the Nile from its source. Madly toward the sunrise,*
> *Cambyses reached the long-lived peoples,*
> *But failing in feasts and fed by the slaughter of his own men,*
> *He returned while you, O Nile, remained unknown. No lying fable*
> *Has dared to speak of your source: wherever you are seen*
> *You are sought, and no nation has the glory*
> *Of claiming the Nile as its own.* <note>original: "Qua tibi noscendi Nilum..." This passage from Lucan's Pharsalia emphasizes that even the greatest conquerors could not find the river's source.</note>

Certain modern figures have shared this same desire with the ancient Kings. Breidenbach and Johannes Tucher of Nuremberg record that the Sultans of Egypt and the Turkish Emperors attempted the same, but with the matter left unfinished. Finally, in the last century, around the year 1520, King Emmanuel of Portugal sent ambassadors to the Great King of the Abyssinians (whom they call Prester John); among them was Francisco Alvares, who was also enjoined by the King to describe the rising of the Nile, which he performed with praise. Thus, in our time, the springs of the Nile have been discovered, its marshes seen, and those who live beside it are known. Hence, Paolo Giovio <note>Paulus Jovius</note>, in book 18 of the *History of His Own Times*, accurately describes the origin of the Nile based on the report of Peter the Abyssinian, a most learned man: *From immense and most rugged rocks, which are called the Mountains of the Moon,* he says, *the springs of the Nile break forth in a frequent and copious gush, in a place profoundly hidden, which is called Beth—that is, "the desert"—in the Abyssinian tongue. From these springs, innumerable small streams flow through the expanses of the Kingdom of Gojjam, sometimes scattered, sometimes joining together into a freshwater marsh that is by far the largest in the whole world. From this great marsh, the Nile pours out, at first gently, then rapid and headlong.* From the excessive 

<column-break/>

force of the waves, the Nile is called a <term>cataract [katarrhaktēs]</term> <note>original: καταῤῥάκτης; a waterfall or down-rushing</note> where it flings itself down among the precipices of rocky places, about which Strabo writes at the beginning of book 17. And Marcellinus,
<margin>
* Marcellinus
</margin>
speaking of the Nile, explains the cataracts as *steep cliffs*; he was not deceived, as a certain learned man thinks, for he was himself a Greek speaker. And according to Eustathius's commentary on Dionysius's *Description of the World*, <term>cataracts</term> <note>original: καταῤῥάκται</note> are *rocky places where rivers, finding their flow checked, leap over them.* Nor was Aristotle ignorant of this headlong flow of the Nile from very high mountains; in *On the Heavens*, book 2, chapter 9, he writes that the inhabitants of the place where the Nile flings itself from the highest mountains lack the sense of hearing because of the magnitude of the sound. From this it is clear how closely the Ancients penetrated to the springs of the Nile. Orosius, in book 9 of the *Deeds of King Emmanuel*, agrees with Giovio, as do more recent geographers, even if they still seem to disagree on certain points.

Thus, once the origin of the Nile has been shown, the opinion of certain ancient theologians (though very common) regarding the springs of the Nile originating in Paradise falls by itself. To have merely recited it is to have refuted it. I wish at least to bring forward what Rudolph, a parish priest, records in his manuscript *Oriental Itinerary*: *The Nile, a river of Paradise,* he says, *passes through Egypt and near New Babylon <note>Old Cairo</note> and Damietta, and falls into the Mediterranean Sea near Alexandria. It is larger and wider than the Rhine, and very turbid, because it sometimes enters the earth or the mountains and is not seen for two or three miles, then exits again, and enters again, until it comes into Egypt; then it passes directly through.* To this, subjoin Fulcher of Chartres:
<margin>
The Geon, which corresponds [to the Nile].
</margin>
*I can wonder, but never wonder enough, how or in what way this river Geon <note>the biblical Gihon, often identified with the Nile</note>, which is also the Nile, and which is read to flow out of Paradise with three others, seems to recover its rising again, since it has the Red Sea on the eastern side and 'Our Sea' <note>the Mediterranean</note> on the west where it falls. For it has the Red Sea positioned between itself and the East, where we understand Paradise to be, from which it emerges. How then does it take up its rising again beyond that Red Sea, and how does it cross that same sea, or not cross it? I am amazed. We have similarly learned of the Euphrates, that it has its rising in Armenia and passes through Mesopotamia, and does not pass further from the city of Edessa than, I think, twenty-four miles. Let him who wishes seek, let him who is able learn; for I have often studied to learn this by inquiring from very many people, but I was by no means able to find someone who could explain this to me. I commit the reasoning of this to Him who wondrously established the waters above the heavens, and who makes them be drawn from the mountains and hills and valleys, and provided many-pathed ways for them in their courses through hidden passages, and finally leads them into the sea and back again in a marvelous way.*

Thus the Nile rises in Ethiopia after a very long journey; in part it falls violently through cataracts, in part it flows gently, and it cuts through the entire torrid zone from south to north. Having finished its course through Egypt, it finally discharges itself through seven mouths into the Mediterranean Sea. Pliny, in book 5, chapter 10, enumerates seven mouths of the Nile: the nearest to Alexandria is the *Canopic*, then the *Bolbitic*, the *Sebennytic*, the *Phatnitic*, the *Mendesian*, the *Tanitic*, and the last, the *Pelusiac*. Hence, to Maro <note>Virgil</note> and Catullus, it is the *Sevenfold Nile*.

> From the sevenfold Nile, also bore seven rivers on his shield.

And in the same book of the *Metamorphoses*:

<margin>

Hence in **Isaiah 11:15**, seven streams seem to be named, among which in <term>Numbers 34:5</term>—concerning the divine assignment of the Israelite territory—the <term>Torrent of Egypt</term> <note>often identified as the Wadi El-Arish or the Pelusiac branch of the Nile</note> is mentioned; specifically the Pelusiac mouth, it seems, which marked the border of the land of Israel from Egypt toward the sea. For this was the boundary of the rivers of Palestine; therefore in the sacred writings, as said above, the Nile is called now the sea, now a river, now streams, now a brook, now rivulets <note>original: "ἐπ’ ἐῤῥύῳ ἢ ἐπ’ ἀπείρῳ" — as a flowing stream or as a boundless expanse</note>, because of the various parts of which it consists. Refer here to that passage of the Prophets where it is called the river and the streams *par excellence* <note>original: "καθ’ ἐξοχὴν"</note>. Whence in <margin>Ezekiel 29:3</margin> it says of Pharaoh: *You sit in the midst of your rivers, and you say, "The river is mine."* Where **Jerome** <term>p. 482</term> comments in this way: *He speaks according to the location of the province, as if to a King who trusts in the inundation of the Nile, and does not greatly desire rains from heaven, and thinks himself the author of his own being.* Or he boasts that the river—that is, the <term>Nilometer</term> canals <note>original: "διωρυχὸς"</note>—and the streams of the **Nile** were made by him. And <term>Psalm 78:44</term>: *And he turned their rivers into blood, and their flowing waters, so they could not drink.*

<margin>
p. 288.
</margin>

On these words of the Psalmist, **Folengius** <note>Giambattista Folengo, a 16th-century Benedictine monk</note> says: *You should know that "rivers" is used here in the Hebrew manner for the Nile, which alone floods all of Egypt; though we would not want it to escape your notice that Egypt is intersected by trenches receiving the streams of the Nile in every direction, so that it is navigable everywhere. Therefore, it will not be improper for these trenches to be called "rivers" on account of their width and the flow of their waters; for where we read "their rains," they have "their streams."* For flowing down from Ethiopia all the way into Egypt, when it reaches the city of Syene <note>modern Aswan</note>, it begins to be called the Nile by its inhabitants; from there, passing through Egypt toward the North and finally divided into many parts, it is carried into the sea by seven mouths, irrigating the whole of Egypt and filling it everywhere with a marvelous fertility. Whence in <margin>book 1 of the Images</margin>, **Philostratus** says: *The Egyptians have the mouths of the Nile, but the Ethiopians have its springs.* This river is the largest of all, as **Aulus Gellius** records in <term>book 10, chapter 7</term>: *Of all the rivers that enter the seas where the Roman Empire is, which the Greeks call the "inner sea" <note>the Mediterranean</note>, the Nile is the greatest; Sallust wrote that the Danube is next in size.* In which book of **Sallust** this was placed, and in what words, is uncertain. This, I say, is that greatest and most noble river of all, which nature brought forth, as **Seneca** says in <term>Natural Questions, book 4, chapter 2</term>, so that it would flood Egypt at that time when the earth, scorched by the greatest heat, might draw the water deeper; drinking as much as might suffice for the annual drought. Whence the **Etymologist** <term>p. 602</term> says: *The Nile overflows every year and waters all of Egypt.* And the **Ancient Descriptor of the World** <term>chapter 18, p. 16</term>: *The Nile waters the whole face of the earth and makes all things bear fruit, without rain.* **Philo** in his *Life of Moses* <term>p. 410</term> says: *The river of Egypt, overflowing and pouring out at the height of summer, floods and turns the fields into lakes; and the fields, needing no help from above <note>rain</note>, supply an abundance of all kinds of goods every year.* For the Nile renews the earth every year, granting the exhausted soil new fertility

<column-break/>

and making it rich. It is a wonder, therefore, that the Nile <margin>of Egypt.</margin> at the same time seems to flood the whole of Egypt, and while everything in the plains of Egypt is scorched by the heat of the Sun, water is supplied to the river. A marvelous sight of the earth! Is that water from the high peaks of the mountains, with the Sun melting the snows above? If so, yet it would not be so great as to pour out such a vast quantity, and that during the summer. From that annual inundation of the Nile, not only did the Egyptians and the Israelites (while they lived in Egypt) determine the beginning of the year, counting it in the same way, but when God led them out, He restored the genuine calculation of years and ascribed the beginning to the springtime, <margin>Exodus 12:2</margin> <term>Exodus 12:2</term>.

Furthermore, since it was necessary to measure the fields because the boundaries and limits of the lands were confused <note>by the flooding</note>, some claim that **Geometry** was first born from this; but the idea that the method of measuring fields took its origin here is very weak. We place greater faith in **Josephus**, who testifies to the most ancient doctrine of the stars, studied most diligently by the Patriarchs, and clearly teaches that its first inventors were Adam, Seth, Noah, and their followers—for they had the longest lives. Afterwards, however, it is the common opinion of the **Doctors** that the Astronomical art was brought to the Egyptians and Chaldeans by **Abraham**.

The harvest proceeded according to the proportion of the Nile's flooding; for when the Nile overflowed too much, it damaged the crops, and there was a scarcity in Egypt, as **John Mandeville** says in <term>chapter 9</term>. I once saw his manuscript *Itinerary* at Sorø in Denmark, in the library of **Stephanus Stephanius**, and I have not laid eyes on it since; it is, however, I believe, published, since **Tilemann** <margin>Philosophical Discourse p. 237</margin> writes that the author should be read with judgment, because he overflows with fables.

Hence they observed a certain measure of degrees <note>on the Nilometer</note>, to which the surges of the river used to reach, sometimes higher and sometimes lower, and from there they predicted the fertility or barrenness of the year, as **Strabo** witnesses in <margin>Strabo, book 17, Geography.</margin> <term>book 17 of his Geography</term>. For just as the Romans regarded the flooding of the Tiber as an evil omen for all things, and still do; so the Egyptians, on the contrary, regarded a proper flood as most auspicious. Thus, the Nile is to them a true **Horn of Amalthea** <note>a cornucopia or horn of plenty</note>, by whose liquid the whole land of the Egyptians is nourished, and from which most copious water is poured out in a healthy inundation to the surrounding lands. From which the abundance of all fruits comes forth as if from horns: oh, admirable horn of plenty! The Nile is the <term>conduit</term> <note>original: "ἀγωγὴ"</note> of Egypt, from which, as if from a channel, water is copiously poured into the fields. With the Nile irrigating, the joyful fertility of the plains and the most generous abundance of all things flows forth. What, I ask, can be said or thought of more marvelous than this water? Oh, blessed inhabitants, for whom this river flows! The world has no similar example, unless the lake of **Curzenfis** <note>likely Lake Cerknica in modern Slovenia, famous for its seasonal disappearance</note> seems to have some kinship, regarding which see **Hulsius**.

Hence, not without cause, the Ancients went into praises of the Nile; **Cicero** <margin>book 2, On the Nature of the Gods, p. 322</margin> says: *The Nile irrigates Egypt, and when it has held it overwhelmed and covered for the whole summer, it then recedes, leaving the fields softened and coated with silt for sowing.* And from here perhaps comes the proverb: *Egypt carries a brick* <note>original: "Αἰγύπτιος πλινθοφόρος"</note>, which **Erasmus** <term>T. 3. 5. 48. p. 741</term> explains from Suidas and Aristophanes as referring to base people of the lowest sort and to labor...

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Nile of Egypt.</margin>
...with most troublesome labor, to which work the Hebrews were driven by Pharaoh; they were assigned to carry away the mud from the Nile’s inundation and to bake bricks from that same mud. And **Minucius Felix** in his *Octavius* (p. 37) says: *The Nile tempers the dryness of Egypt, the Euphrates cultivates Mesopotamia, and the Indus is said to sow the East and water it.* **Claudian** <margin>Epigram 6.</margin> not without elegance attributes "serene rains" to Egypt, hinting at the Nilotic irrigation which refreshes the region under a clear sky; just as in other places, rains from a cloudy sky fertilize the earth with their moisture:

> Egypt is fruitful without a cloud, and serene rains
> It alone possesses: secure from the pole, not needing the wind.
> It rejoices in the waters it carries itself, and overflows with the Nile.

For the Nile river irrigates the land so much that it has no need for rains; the Egyptian does not care for rain, but the Greek does. The Egyptian desires with a vehement longing the flooding of the terrestrial Nile, whereas the Greek desires the celestial flooding. The Greek hungers badly when the heavens stand still; the Egyptian hungers badly when the Nile does. There is a festive saying of the Egyptians, who, when they heard that all the land of the Greeks was drenched by rain and not by a river like their own, said that the Greeks, being at some point cheated of a great hope, would starve miserably. This is found in **Herodotus** (Book 2, chapter 13), whose words are: <note>original Greek: Πυνθανόμενοι, ὡς ὕεται πασα ἡ χώρη τοῦ Ἑλλήνων... "Learning that the whole land of the Greeks is watered by rain, but not irrigated by rivers as their own is, they said that the Greeks, being at some point cheated of a great hope, would starve miserably."</note> This speech means to say: <note>original Greek: ὡς εἰ μὴ ἐθελήσει σφίσι ὕειν ὁ θεὸς... "that if God should not wish to rain for them but should use a drought, the Greeks will be overtaken by famine, for indeed they have no other resource for water except from Zeus alone."</note> Rain is rare or almost non-existent in Egypt, though that rain does sometimes fall is indicated by those things extant in **Psalm 105:32** and **Zechariah 14:18**. Indeed, in almost the entire five-year period in which **Veslingius** <note>Johannes Vesling, a 17th-century botanist and traveler</note> stayed in Egypt, he observed that it rained only twice or thrice around Memphis, as he records in *Alpinus on Plants* (page 4). For the rest, he commends that tract of land above all others. *I have marveled from my soul*, he says in *Observations on Plants* (p. 44), *at the cultivation and pleasantness of the Pelusiac port, possessing all things by the benefit of its Nile, with which it challenges—to speak with Virgil—the pleasant greenery of the fortunate groves and the blessed seats.* In other regions, commendation comes from the sky. Herodotus in *Melpomene* reports that the Libyans, commending their region in the part where Cyrene is, said the sky was "pierced," as if all fertility and abundance of things flowed down from there. Egypt prefers the waters of the flooding Nile to all the goods of heaven and earth; enriched by their large and just inundation, it has no such need for rains, a fact I shall confirm also by the testimony of **Kimchi** and others. For thus says **Rabbi David Kimchi** <margin>on Isaiah 19:5.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: נהר נילוס הוא משקה הארץ עד שלא יצטרכו לגשמים "The river Nile waters the land so that they do not have need of rains."</note> **Valerius Flaccus** testifies the same in the 5th book of the *Argonautica* (line 423):

> There the year is fat without rains.

And so also **Mantuanus** in his *Parthice* (Book 1, chapter 3):

> Egypt knows no rain, but wide every year
> when the sun presses the humid arms of the watery Cancer,
> the Nile irrigates the fields.

But because it waters a <term>nitrous</term> <note>referring to the high salt/mineral content of the soil</note> and parched soil, **Heliodorus** (Book 9, p. 423) called it a "counter-imitation of heaven." Regarding this, one may see the words of **Philo** (p. 465), that is: *the country is not watered like others, but*

<column-break/>

*is accustomed to be flooded every year by the overflows of the rivers.* <margin>The Nile of Egypt.</margin> The Egyptians conceptually fashioned the Nile as a god because it was a "counter-imitation of heaven." Regarding this, **Seneca** says in *Natural Questions* (Book 4, chapter 2): *The Nile brings both water and earth to a sandy and thirsty soil; for since it flows turbid, it leaves all its sediment in the dry and gaping places, and whatever richness it has brought with it, it deposits in the parched areas; it helps the fields for two reasons: both because it inundates them and because it coats them with silt.* I add also the most elegant passage of **Pliny**, which stands in the *Panegyric* he wrote to the Emperor Nerva Trajan: *Egypt, in nourishing and increasing seeds, has so boasted that it owed nothing to rains and the sky. Indeed, always drenched by its own river, and not accustomed to grow fat from any other kind of water than that which it had carried itself, it was clothed in such great harvests that it competed with the most fertile lands as if it would never yield.* **Theocritus** proclaims the same benefit of Egypt alone in *Idyll 17* (line 77), writing to Ptolemy Philadelphus, King of the Egyptians:

> <note>original Greek: Μυρίαι ἀπειροί τε, καὶ ἔθνεα μυρία φωτῶν... "Countless continents and countless nations of men bring to ripeness the harvest increased by the rain of Zeus. But none produces as much as Egypt brings forth when the Nile, welling up, breaks the moist clod. For no river has become like the Nile, neither to cast down silt, nor to increase the wealth of the earth."</note>

These passages can serve as a commentary on **Deuteronomy chapter 11, verse 10**. For Egypt alone sees rarer clouds and is devoid of the wildness of rains, as we have in the writings of Moses, where God promised the land of Canaan seasonal rain in these words: *The land to which you are entering is not like the land of Egypt, in which the Nile is the sky, from which they lead out irrigating waters through furrows and ditches by the hand and industry of men in the manner of gardens; but it is mountainous and expectant of rains.* In the Hebrew and Greek text: *drinking waters from the sky.* God commends the Promised Land for its celestial irrigation; to it He promises rains of blessing from above (**Ezekiel 34:26**), so that from there the bread of the earth's fruits might be most abundant (**Isaiah 30**). In contrast, Egypt was irrigated from below by the flooding of the Nile; nor, as **Tibullus** said <margin>Book 1, Elegy</margin>, does the grass supplicate to Rain-Giver Jove, but content with its own rivers, it asks for no rains.

> In the Nile alone is there such confidence in the harvest.

**Isocrates** gave this hidden treasure of the Nile to be seen in distinct words: <note>original Greek: Ἔωρα γὰρ Βύσιριν... "For he [Busiris] saw that other places were not seasonably or harmoniously situated relative to the nature of the whole universe, but some were flooded by rains, and others destroyed by heat, while the land of Egypt, situated in the most beautiful part of the world, was able to produce the most and most varied goods, and was walled by the immortal wall of the Nile, which by nature provides her not only defense but also sufficient food, being invincible and hard to fight for those plotting against her, but easy to navigate and useful for many things for those dwelling within her."</note> And **Pomponius Mela** in *On the Situation of the World* (Book 1, chapter 9, p. 16): *A land devoid of rains, yet wonderfully fertile, and a most prolific mother of men and other animals. The Nile effects this, the greatest of the rivers flowing into our sea.* And after a few words: *Overflowing even in the summer season, it irrigates with waters so effective for generating and nourishing that, besides being full of fish and begetting Hippopotamuses and Crocodiles—vast beasts—it even pours life into the clods, and from them [creates] vital organs out of the soil...*

### EGYPTIAN ANTIQUITIES CHAPTER VIII. 3.

<column>
<margin>The Nile of Egypt.</margin>
...shapes vital things. **Haithonus**, in his work *On the Tartars* (chapter 54, page 471), says of the Nile: *This river rises once a year, and begins to rise from the middle of August until the feast of Saint Michael <note>September 29th</note>, increasing daily; and when it is at its full height, then men first allow the waters to flow through prepared channels and streams, and all the fruitful lands are irrigated, and the water stays upon the face of the earth for 40 days. Then it begins to decrease and dry up, after which the seeds are sown, and they grow only by the irrigation of the river, because it does not rain in those parts, so that winter is scarcely distinguished from summer.* The Nile is equally steady and fertile, in which both gentleness and utility compete, concerning which **Claudian** says of the Tagus in his work *Against Rufinus*:
> The Nile flows gently, yet it stands out
> More useful than all others, confessing no banks with a murmur.

<margin>On Deuteronomy, p. 810.</margin>
From this, as **Drusius** notes, the Rabbis made a distinction between two types of fields: one of Egypt, the other of the land of Canaan. The former they call <note>Hebrew: ארץ השקא, Eretz HaShikya</note> "the land of irrigation," and the latter <note>Hebrew: שדה בעל, Sadeh Baal</note> "the field of the Lord" <note>meaning a field watered by rain from heaven rather than human effort</note>. Moses continues in verse 14: *He will give the early and late rain for your land, that you may gather in your grain, your wine, and your oil;* by which he teaches that Canaan is not irrigated by the muddy and turbid water of the Nile, but is enriched by the blessing of the one God, through rain given from heaven. Both benefits are from God, and not from another, let alone from a Demon—as **Philostratus** <margin>On the Life of Apollonius.</margin> writes, citing **Pindar**, that there is a certain Demon who presides over the rising of the Nile: <note>original Greek: Πολλὰ καὶ θεῖα δαιμόνων ᾄδεται... "Many divine stories of spirits are sung, for which reason a spirit was hymned by Pindar at Thebes, who stands over these springs for the sake of the Nile's proportion."</note>. Furthermore, by this exceptional gift, Egypt served as the public granary of the World if other regions were in need. Under **Joseph**, neighboring nations flocked here as if to a sanctuary to temper the evil of poverty (*Genesis 41:58; 42:2, 3*). There was a delay in the <term>σιταγωγία</term> <note>sitagogia: the organized transport of grain by sea</note> performed from here every year. For the Romans cultivated the grain trade with great zeal, so much so that when they saw Egypt abounded in wheat, they took care to transport the grain from there:

<margin>2 Maccabees 28.</margin>
**Josephus** also mentions this regarding Egypt, which every year sent grain to Rome and paid more in tribute in one month than Judea did in a whole year; his words are: <note>original Greek: Τὸ δὲ ἐνιαύσιον παρ’ ὑμῶν... "The annual tax from you [Jews] provides more to the Romans in one month, and besides the money, grain for four months to Rome."</note>. It imported enough grain for four months of each year, which he calls <term>σίτον μηνῶν τεσσάρων</term> <note>grain for four months</note>. To this end, so that transport might be easier, they took care to have channels led from every region of Egypt into the Nile at public expense, by which the abundance of grain might be carried to Alexandria, and finally to Rome. They also took the greatest care that those channels be maintained, under a law that if anyone broke the dikes of the Nile, they would be punished by death—see **Wilhelm Bossardus**, *On the Magistrates of Athens*, chapter 15, page 510. Hence came the provisions and the Alexandrian fleet; and "the shipmasters of the transport of the Alexandrian city," as found in **Gruter's** *Roman Inscriptions* (4, f. 114), "warehouses for Egyptian cargoes." For this reason, the Nile is called "grain-bearing" by **Martial** (Book 10, 74), because it fertilizes the ears into harvests, and:
> The grain-bearing seed surrounds the river’s edge,
> And the reaper,

That the increase and flooding of the Nile, and consequently the fertility of the year, were judged by the color of Sirius rising in the East, is proven from the *Oracles of Apollo* by **Salmasius** in his *Plinian Exercises*. Furthermore, **Haithonus** writes about the <term>Nilometrium</term> <note>Nilometer: a structure for measuring the Nile's water level</note> (ch. 54, p. 471): *The inhabitants of the land of Egypt placed a certain marble column in the middle of the river before the city of Meser <note>Old Cairo</note>, and on that column they made marks, and when the river rises to its full height, they look at those marks on the column; and if the water has risen to the highest mark, then they know they will have an abundance of fruits; but if it has risen less, they know by those marks that the opposite must happen, and according to this, they set the prices of goods.*

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Nile of Egypt.</margin>
Finally, the Egyptians and others living along the Nile, because of the flooding of this river—by which the fields were sometimes buried under new mud—were accustomed to use a line or a gnomon <note>a measuring rod or tool</note> to measure out the spaces of the fields. This was done so that each person would know what belonged to him amidst the confusion of boundaries caused by the rising Nile. Regarding this custom of measuring, see Waferus in *Ancient Measures*, book 1, chapter 7. Because of this, Sanchez suspects that the phrase in Isaiah 18:2, <note>Hebrew: גוי קו קו, *goy kav kav*</note> "a nation meted out line by line," refers to them. However, Cornelius à Lapide rightly observes that this interpretation is weak and has nothing to do with Isaiah's intent. The metaphor is actually taken from architects, who use lines and plumb-lines to measure precisely what needs to be cut from wood. Similarly, the Prophet teaches that the region of the Ethiopians has been, as it were, measured and marked out by God for future devastation; Daniel Arcularius, formerly a Professor at Marburg, explains this excellently. One may also consult Wendelinus in his learned book on the wonders of the Nile.

### Isaiah XLV. 3.

-> <note>Hebrew: ונתתי לך אוצרות חשך ומטמני מסתרים</note> "I will give you the treasures of darkness and hidden riches of secret places." <-

-> <note>Greek: Καὶ δώσω σοι θησαυροὺς σκοτεινοὺς, ἀποκρύφους ἀοράτους ἀνοίξω σοι.</note> "And I will give to you dark treasures; I will open for you hidden, invisible things." <-

-> *“I will give you hidden treasures, and the secrets of hidden places.”* <-

<margin>Cyrus’s wealth and victory.</margin>
So says Jehovah to his anointed, Cyrus; who, according to Herodian (Book 6, chapter 6), was the first to transfer the empire from the Medes to the Persians. The history of Cyrus is known even to seven-year-old boys; it is enough for us to recount it briefly. He was a king no less victorious than he was wealthy. He was victorious: for he drove his grandfather Astyages (for Cyrus was his grandson by his daughter) from his kingdoms; he defeated Croesus, the wealthiest King of the Lydians; he defeated Darius (or Nabonidus) the Mede, the most powerful King of the Babylonians, in battle and expelled him from the Babylonian kingdom; indeed, he subjugated all of Asia. This was the 29th year of his Empire (see the *Tables of B. D. Helvicus*), at which time he could truly say: <margin>1 Esdras 1:2.</margin> *“The God of heaven has delivered all the kingdoms to me.”* He was also wealthy. The riches of the incredibly wealthy Croesus fell to him as victor, which gave rise to a proverb among the Greeks; as did the vast and hidden treasures of the Babylonians. Pliny (Book 33, chapter 3) says: *“Cyrus, having conquered Asia, found 34,000 pounds of gold (let the reader consider this!), besides golden vessels and wrought gold, including golden leaves, a plane tree, and a vine. From this victory, he carried back 500,000 talents of silver and the mixing bowl of Semiramis, which weighed fifteen talents. He records that an Egyptian talent weighs 80 pounds.”* On this same subject are these hendecasyllable verses by Sidonius Apollinaris:

> I do not speak of Cyrus, grandson of Astyages,
> Nourished, they say, by the teat of a dog,
> Whose greed not even the treasury 
> Of Lydian Croesus could satisfy.

The same Prophet in chapter 44 graphically describes Christ, the Savior of the human race from sin, death, and hell, through the figure of Cyrus, the liberator of the Jewish people from Babylon. There, everything will be clearer (as Scultetus rightly advises in his *Delights of Prague*), <margin>page 6.</margin> if we compare what Herodotus, Xenophon, and others relate about Cyrus with the words of Isaiah. However, it is 

<column-break/>

<margin>The *Cyropaedia*</margin>
hardly unworthy of notice here that the recently mentioned Xenophon described Cyrus not as he actually was, but as he ought to have been. He did not write the *Cyropaedia* <note>The Education of Cyrus</note> of Cyrus the Elder with historical accuracy; rather, he intended that education in the fictional person of Cyrus to be merely an elegant portrait or image. This is taught to us by the epitomizer of Scaliger in *Introduction to Chronology*, chapter 26, page 100; see also Antonio de Guevara's commentary on Habakkuk 2. These and other things, I say, must be learned from the histories of the pagans, which narrate that Cyrus was the conqueror of nearly the entire East. Thus, what Andreas Franckenberger says elsewhere is true: *“No one will explain the prophetic oracles without a multifaceted knowledge of Greek and Latin pagan history.”* But I shall stop, lest I be forced to hear the saying: *“He is teaching the eagle to fly.”* Furthermore, we shall deal more extensively with Cyrus in the section on Daniel’s Four Monarchies.

### Isaiah XLVII. 13.

-> <note>Hebrew: יעמדו-נא ויושיעך הברי שמים החזים בכוכבים מודיעים לחדשים מאשר יבאו עליך</note> "Let them stand now and save you—the dividers of the heavens, the gazers at the stars, who predict by the months what shall come upon you." <-

-> <note>Greek: Στήτωσαν δὴ καὶ σωσάτωσάν σε οἱ Ἀστρολόγοι τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, οἱ ὁρῶvτες τοὺς ἀστέρας, ἀναγγειλάτωσάν σοι, τί μέλλει ἔρχεσθαι ἐπὶ σέ.</note> "Let the Astrologers of heaven stand and save you, those who look at the stars; let them announce to you what is about to come upon you." <-

-> *“Let the augurs of heaven stand and save you, who contemplate the stars and calculate the months, so that from them they might announce your future to you.”* <-

<margin>Astrology.</margin>
Since in human affairs there is nothing more admirable or greater than the knowledge of great things—which those who have attained it are believed to stand above unrefined men just as they themselves are above the rest—and since that part of all Philosophy is Astronomy, which most uplifts minds to the knowledge of the greatest and heavenly things, we thought it would be worthwhile if I were to briefly condense the motion and powers of the heavens and set them before your eyes from our sacred texts. For why would God have produced those heavenly bodies with such wisdom, in such number and order, and with such diversity of colors and magnitudes, unless he had assigned a specific power to each? Every single day we are taught what the heavens and heavenly influence can do in herbs, in living creatures (both rational and irrational), and in fruits. Not all herbs grow in all places, and when transplanted, they often lose their potency because they do not have their original sky; sometimes they do not keep the same leaves, the same stalk, the same flowers, or the same fruits. Thus God distinguished things so that some enjoy this sky and others another. We are taught by daily experience what the cycle of the heavens can do in stones and minerals, and in living beings. There is vast room for discussing Astrology—for formerly **Astronomy** and **Astrology** went by the same name; however, a more curious age has distinguished them more conveniently, so that **Astronomy** observes the motion of the stars, while **Astrology** explains and observes the effects and influence of the stars. It is a vast subject, but one to be passed through briefly and as a summary among the thickets of the woods and the briars of a rugged path. Therefore, one cannot deny the effect of the heavens on these lower things, which is certainly very great, so much so that God himself recounts those powers to Job...
