### Book XLVII. 13.

<margin>Judicial Astrology.</margin>
<margin>Job 38:33.</margin>
God shows that He alone, through His works, is the one who can moderate the course and effects of the heavens. For thus Jehovah spoke to Job: *“Do you know the laws of the heavens? Can you establish its dominion on the earth?”* <note>original: "Nunquid nosti leges coeli? Nunquid pones dominatorem ejus in terra."</note> Johannes Brentius <note>A 16th-century German theologian and reformer</note> explains these words as follows: No one knows the statutes of the heavens, or, as they are called, the "influences," nor can any man be a herald or messenger of the heavens to announce and command them, as if by some lordship, to revolve now here, now there, or to provide this or that virtue from themselves. You may gather from this the nature of the dominant stars and their power. Among the Hebrews, there is an affinity between the words *mazzal* <note>Hebrew: מזל; original: "מזל"</note> and *mashal* <note>Hebrew: משל; original: "משל"</note>; the latter signifies power or "dominion," while the former refers to a "star" or "flow," because they provide a flow of their powers and qualities to lower things. Compare this with Ezechiel à Castro in *The Licking Fire*, book 2, chapter 14, page 152. The Planets operate in both the macrocosm <note>the universe</note> and the microcosm <note>the human body</note>. Just as the Sun excels all other stars in light, it is also superior in its forces. By its presence, the powers of the neighboring fixed stars are excited and, as it were, fanned into action, becoming fit for work; however, the "erratic" stars <note>the planets</note> are dulled and blunted when the Sun approaches. Chief among the heavenly bodies are the seven Planets, which wander so unequally that nothing is more equal, so inconstantly that nothing is more constant, and so mutably that nothing is more changeable. The Creator God has given each its own orbit in which it moves by its own motion; once God fixed these, they always run and return without change. For this reason, Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note>, in his book *On the Decalogue*, is displeased that some stars are called "erratic" <note>wandering</note>, since they never leave their order, and nothing in heaven is subject to error—a point the Mathematicians discuss at length. Nor can anyone who neglects the mathematical disciplines make successful progress in the Holy Scriptures. This is perhaps why our age produces so few who devote their study to those sacred books, which can only be supported by the aid of Mathematics. Who, I ask, will sufficiently understand or explain the Book of Job, in which almost the entire "host of the stars" is enumerated? Regarding this, Francis Bacon says:

<margin>Bacon, *On the Advancement of Learning*, p. 254.</margin>
> If anyone diligently examines that extraordinary book of Job, he will find it full, and as if pregnant with, the mysteries of natural philosophy. For example, regarding cosmography and the roundness of the earth, it says: *He stretches out the North over the empty space, and hangs the earth upon nothing*; where the hanging earth, the arctic pole, and the convexity of the heavens at the extremities are clearly hinted at. Again, regarding Astronomy and the constellations, it says: *By his spirit he has garnished the heavens; his hand has formed the crooked serpent.* And in another place: *Can you bind the sweet influences of the Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?* Here, the fixed configuration of the stars, always distant from each other by equal intervals, is most elegantly described. Likewise, in another place: *Who makes Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades, and the chambers of the south.* Where again he hints at the depression of the antarctic pole, designating it by the name "chambers of the south," because the southern stars are not seen in our hemisphere. Thus says Bacon.

The Poets tell fables, though the celestial circuits were not unknown to them; indeed, Homer, the prince of Seers and Philosophers, both throughout his work and specifically in the fifth book of the *Odyssey*, used a few verses to describe the primary features of the heavens: the Pleiades, Boötes, the Bear,

<column-break/>

<margin>Judicial Astrology.</margin>
and Orion himself, and the motion by which he introduces the navigating Ulysses; he expressed it as briefly as he did learnedly in these words from *Odyssey* 5, line 272:

> Gazing at the Pleiades and late-setting Boötes,
> And the Bear, which they also call by the name of the Wagon,
> Which turns in its place and watches Orion.
> <note>original Greek: "Πληϊάδας τ' ἐσορῶν τηλεὰς καὶ ὀψὲ δύοντα Βοώτην, / Ἄρκτον θ' ἣν καὶ ἅμαξαν ἐπίκλησιν καλέουσιν, / Ἥ τ' αὐτοῦ στρέφεται, καί τ' Ὠρίωνα δοκεύει."</note>

The Poets, I say, tell the fable that the seventh star of the Pleiades, named Electra, refused to be seen any longer after the fall of Troy, because Dardanus, the founder of the Trojan race, was born of Electra; as Hyginus notes in *Astronomy* and Ovid in *Fasti*, book 4. Vossius <note>Gerard Vossius, a Dutch scholar</note> also mentions this in *On Idolatry*, book 2. Nor was the virtue and power of the stars over these lower things hidden from them; hence Homer periphrastically attributes *sthenos* <note>Greek: σθένος, meaning "strength" or "might"</note> to Orion, speaking of his force and efficacy. For the Sun, the Moon, and all the stars flow from the highest peak of heaven into the elements; thus their influence is upon us, which is why a person may be rendered either more vigorous or weaker by that influence. To Venus is attributed the power to produce cheerful and eloquent manners when joined with Mercury. To Jupiter, the granting of peaceful manners and a well-moderated temperament. To Saturn, the stirring up of quarrelsome and crafty natures; and so it goes for the other stars. Since no sane person can deny these powers of the heavenly bodies over lower things, one must entirely agree with Aristotle:

<margin>*Meteorology*, ch. 2.</margin>
> This lower world is governed by the superior motions (*phorais*). <note>original Greek: "φοραῖς"</note>

It is also necessary that we acknowledge their great use in medicine, agriculture, household management, and navigation. For an Astrologer <note>here meaning a scientific astronomer</note> can know future events that happen necessarily from natural causes, such as the rising of the sun, eclipses, and others; for these are detected in their own causes. Many things are known not with certainty, but by very probable conjecture. Thus the Physician observes "critical days" from the stars. The Farmer and the Sailor observe the planets in those matters which clearly have their causes in nature itself. However, those things which depend simply on divine providence or on the will and free choice of man—such as the particular or accidental outcomes of human lives—of these there is no knowledge from the stars, and no true prediction. For that reason, Judicial Astrology <note>fortune-telling via stars</note>—the degenerate daughter of a beautiful mother—which presumes to speculate on the outcomes of men from the observation of stars, is frequently read as prohibited in the Holy Scriptures as a pagan folly. Isaiah, the Evangelist among the Prophets, mocks the Chaldean Astrologers in the name of God; though they professed knowledge of the future from the stars, they could foresee neither the general calamity of their Babylonian homeland nor their own personal ruin. The Chaldeans were once famous for the Mathematical arts; hence Simplicius writes that Callisthenes, at the request of Aristotle, sent to Greece the observations of the Chaldeans from 1,903 years before the time of Alexander. That would be about two hundred years before the birth of Abraham, shortly before the construction of the Tower of Babel. Compare Vossius, *On Idolatry*, book 2. Manilius, in the beginning of his *Astronomicon*, attributes the purpose of Astronomy to the Kings of Egypt:

<margin>Commentary 4 on Aristotle's *On the Heavens*, book 2.</margin>
> Regal minds were the first deemed worthy to be moved,
> Touching the heights of things nearest to heaven.

If we believe Eusebius, the Patriarch Abraham in Egypt—

ANTIQUIT. BIBL.

### Column 1

<margin>The Nile of Egypt.</margin>
Finally, the Egyptians and others living along the Nile, because of the flooding of this river—by which fields were sometimes buried under new silt—were accustomed to using a **line** or a **gnomon** <note>A measuring rod or surveying tool</note> with which they measured the areas of the fields. This ensured everyone knew what belonged to them amidst the confusion of boundaries caused by the rising Nile. On this custom of measuring, see Waserus in *The Ancient Measures, book 7.* From this, Sanchez suspects that in Isaiah 18:2, where it mentions <term>line by line</term> <note>Hebrew: *kav kav* (קו קו)</note>, it refers to these people. This is a cold interpretation and has nothing to do with Isaiah, as Cornelius à Lapide <note>A prominent Jesuit exegete</note> rightly observes. The metaphor is taken from architects, who measure precisely with lines and plumb-lines what must be cut from the wood. Similarly, the Prophet teaches that the region of the Ethiopians had been, as it were, measured and marked out by GOD for devastation; Daniel Arcularius, formerly a Professor at Marburg, explains this excellently. See also Wendelinus in his learned book on the wonders of the Nile.

### Isaiah 45:3

->And I will give you the treasures of darkness and the hidden riches of secret places.<-
->And I will give you dark treasures; I will open to you hidden, unseen things.<- <note>original Greek: Καὶ δώσω σοι θησαυροὺς σκοτεινοὺς, ἀποκρύφους ἀοράτους ἀνοίξω σοι.</note>

> *I will give you hidden treasures, and the secrets of private places.*

<margin>The wealth and victory of Cyrus.</margin>
**S**o says Jehovah to his anointed, Cyrus; who, according to Herodian (book 6, chapter 6), was the first to transfer the empire from the Persians to the Medes. The *History of Cyrus* is known even to seven-year-old boys; let it suffice for us to recount it briefly. He was a King no less victorious than he was wealthy. He was victorious: for he drove his grandfather Astyages from his kingdoms (for Cyrus was his grandson by his daughter); he defeated Croesus, the wealthiest King of the Lydians; he defeated <unclear>Darius</unclear> or Nabonnedus the Mede, the most powerful King of the Babylonians, in battle and expelled him from the Babylonian kingdom; indeed, he subjugated all of Asia. This was the 29th year of his Empire (see the *Tables of Blessed David Helvicus*), in which he could truly say: *The God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms.* He was wealthy. The riches of the most opulent Croesus fell to him as victor, which gave rise to a proverb among the Greeks; as did the vast and hidden treasures of the Babylonians. <margin>1 Ezra 1:2.</margin> Pliny says in book 33, chapter 13: *Cyrus, having conquered Asia, found 34,000 pounds (let the reader reflect on this) of gold, besides golden vessels and wrought gold, including a golden plane tree and a vine. From this victory, he carried back 500,000 talents of silver, and the mixing bowl of Semiramis, which alone weighed fifteen talents. He records that an Egyptian talent weighed 80 pounds.* On this same matter, here are the verses <note>Hendecasyllables: a classic poetic meter of eleven syllables</note> of Sidonius Apollinaris:

> *I speak not of Cyrus, grandson of Astyages,*
> *Nurtured, they say, on the teat of a dog,*
> *Whose greed could not be satisfied*
> *Even by the treasury of Croesus the Lydian.*

The same Prophet in chapter 44 describes Cyrus, the liberator of the Jewish people from Babylon, as a graphic type of Christ, the awaited Savior of the Human race from death and hell: where everything will be clearer (as Scultetus rightly advises in his *Delights of Prague*) <margin>page 6.</margin> if we compare what Herodotus, Xenophon, and others report about Cyrus with the words of Isaiah. However, it is

<column-break/>

hardly unworthy of notice here that the aforementioned Xenophon described Cyrus not as he actually was, but as he ought to have been. <margin>The Education of Cyrus</margin> The *Cyropaedia* <note>Greek: Παίδειαν; "The Education of Cyrus"</note> of *Cyrus the Elder* was not written as historical fact; *he wished, in the fictional persona of Cyrus, for that "education" to be merely an elegant picture and image of a rightly educated and legitimately ruling Prince*; as the epitomizer of Scaliger teaches us in the *Introduction to Chronology*, chapter 26, page 100; see also Antonio de Guevara in his *Commentary on Habakkuk 2*. These and other things, I say, must be learned from the histories of the nations, which narrate that Cyrus was the master of nearly the entire Orient. It is so true, as Andreas Franckenberger says somewhere: *No one will explain Prophetic oracles without a multifaceted knowledge of Greek and Latin secular history.* But I stop here, lest I be forced to hear the saying: *He is teaching the eagle to fly.* Especially since we shall deal more extensively with Cyrus in the section on the Four Monarchies of Daniel.

### Isaiah 47:13

->Stand now and let the astrologers of the heavens save you, those who gaze at the stars and announce month by month what is to come upon you.<-
->Let them stand now and save you, the Astrologers of heaven, those who look upon the stars; let them declare to you what is about to happen to you.<- <note>original Greek: Στήτωσαν δὴ καὶ σωσάτωσάν σε οἱ Ἀστρολόγοι τοῦ οὐρανοῦ...</note>

> *Let the augurs of heaven stand and save you, who contemplate the stars and calculate the months, so that from them they might announce your future.*

<margin>Astronomy and Astrology differ.</margin>
**S**ince in human affairs nothing is more admirable or greater than the knowledge of great things—which those who have attained it seem to stand above unlearned men just as they are believed to excel others—and since from the whole of Philosophy, Astronomy is that part which most lifts minds to the knowledge of the greatest and celestial things, we thought it would be worth the effort if I briefly condensed the motion and powers of the heavens and placed them, as it were, before your eyes from our sacred texts. For why would God have produced those celestial bodies in such number and order, with such diversity of colors and magnitudes with such wisdom, unless He had assigned to each its own peculiar power? What the heavens and celestial influence can do in herbs, in living creatures (both rational and irrational), and in fruits, we are taught by the passing of every day. Not all herbs grow in all places, and when transplanted they often lose their strength because they no longer have their original sky; sometimes they do not keep the same leaves, the same stalk, the same flowers, or the same fruits. Thus God has distinguished things so that some enjoy one sky, and others another. What the cycle of the heavens can do in stones and minerals, and in living beings, we are taught by daily experience. This is a vast subject for discussing Astrology (for formerly **Astronomy** and **Astrology** went by the same name; but a more curious age distinguished them more conveniently, so that Astronomy observes the *motion* of the stars, while Astrology explains and observes the *effects and influences* of the stars), but it must be passed over briefly and by compendium among the thickets of the woods and the briars of a rugged path. Therefore, it cannot be denied that the heavens have an effect on these lower things, which is certainly very great, so much so that God Himself recounts those powers to Job,

<margin>
Judiciary Astrology. <note>The practice of predicting human affairs and terrestrial events by the positions of the stars.</note>
Job 38:33.
</margin>
...and God shows through His works that He alone is the one who can moderate the course and effects of the heavens. For thus Jehovah spoke to Job: *Do you know the laws of the heavens? Can you set their dominion over the earth?* Brentius <note>Johann Brentius, a 16th-century German reformer and theologian.</note> explains these words as follows:
> No one knows the statutes of the heavens, or, as they call them, the "influences"; nor can anyone among men be a herald or messenger of the heavens, to announce and command them, as if he were their master, to revolve now here, now there, or to offer this or that virtue from themselves.

From this you may gather the nature of the ruling stars and their power. Among the Hebrews, there is an affinity between the words <term>Mashal</term> <note>Hebrew: משל, meaning "to rule" or "dominion"</note> and <term>Mazzal</term> <note>Hebrew: מזל, meaning "star" or "constellation"</note>. The latter derives its power from the former, which signifies "dominion"; yet the word for star also flows from <term>Nazal</term> <note>Hebrew: נזל, meaning "to flow"</note>, because they provide a "flow" of their strengths and qualities to lower things. Compare Ezekiel by Castrio in *The Licking Fire*, book 2, chapter 4, page 152. The Planets operate in both the macrocosm <note>the universe</note> and the microcosm <note>the human being</note>. Just as the Sun surpasses all stars in light, so it is superior in power. By its presence, the powers of the neighboring fixed stars are excited and, as it were, fanned into action, making them fit for work; however, the "erratic" <note>wandering</note> stars are dulled and blunted by the Sun's approach. Foremost among the stars are the seven Planets, which wander so unequally that nothing is more equal, so inconstantly that nothing is more constant, and so changeably that nothing is more changeable. A proper orbit is given by God the Creator, in which each is moved by its own motion; and what God once fixed, always runs and returns without change. Hence, Philo, in his book *On the Decalogue*, does not like certain stars to be called "erratic" <note>wandering</note>, since they never leave their order, and nothing in heaven is subject to error—a matter discussed at greater length by the Mathematicians. Nor can anyone successfully progress in the Sacred Code while neglecting Mathematical disciplines; perhaps this is why our age produces so few who devote their study to those sacred books, which are aided only by Mathematics. For who, I ask, will understand or explain Job with enough learning—a book in which almost the entire host of stars is enumerated? On this, <margin>Francis Bacon, *The Advancement of Learning*, p. 250</margin> *Francis Bacon* says:
> If anyone diligently unfolds that extraordinary book of Job, he will find it full, and as if pregnant, with the mysteries of natural philosophy; for example, regarding cosmography and the roundness of the earth in that passage: "He stretches out the North over the empty space, and hangs the earth upon nothing"; where the hanging earth, the arctic pole, and the convexity of the heavens at the extremities are clearly hinted at. Again, regarding Astronomy and the constellations in these words: "By His spirit He adorned the heavens, and His hand guided the winding serpent." And in another place: "Can you bind the glittering stars, the Pleiades, or can you loosen the belt of Orion?" Here, the unmoved configuration of the fixed stars, always distant from each other by equal intervals, is most elegantly described. Likewise, in another place: "Who makes Arcturus and Orion and the Hyades and the chambers of the South," where the stars of our hemisphere are mentioned. Thus he speaks.

The Poets also tell fables, for the celestial motions were not unknown to them. Homer, the Prince of Seers and Philosophers, both throughout his work and in the fifth book of the *Odyssey*, expressed the primary celestial forms—the Pleiades, Boötes, the Bear,

<column-break/>

<margin>
Judiciary Astrology.
</margin>
and finally Orion himself—and the movement by which he introduces the sailing Ulysses, briefly and learnedly in these verses from *Odyssey* 5, line 272:
> Looking at the Pleiades and late-setting Boötes, 
> and the Bear, which they also call the Wagon by name, 
> which turns in its place and watches Orion. <note>original Greek: Πληϊάδας τ' ἐσορῶντι καὶ ὀψὲ δύοντα Βοώτην, Ἄρκτον θ', ἣν καὶ ἅμαξαν ἐπίκλησιν καλέουσιν, Ἥ τ' αὐτοῦ στρέφεται, καί τ' Ὠρίωνα δοκεύει.</note>

The Poets, I say, tell fables that the seventh star of the Pleiades, named Electra, refused to be seen any longer after the fall of Troy, because Dardanus, the founder of the Trojan race, was born of Electra, as Hyginus cites in *Poetic Astronomy* and Ovid in the *Fasti*, book 4, line 167. See also Vossius, *On Idolatry*, book 2, chapter 30, page 456. Nor was the virtue and power over these lower things hidden from them; hence Homer, speaking periphrastically in *Iliad* 18, line 486, attributes <term>sthenos</term> <note>Greek: σθένος, meaning "strength" or "might"</note> to Orion, speaking of his force and efficacy. For the Sun, Moon, and all the stars flow from the highest peak of heaven into the elements; thus their influence is upon us, which is why a person may be rendered more vigorous or weaker by that influx. To *Venus* is attributed the production of cheerful and eloquent manners when joined with Mercury. To *Jupiter*, the granting of peaceful manners and a well-moderated temperament. To *Saturn*, the stirring up of quarrelsome and crafty dispositions; and so with the other stars. Since, therefore, no sane person can deny these powers of the celestial bodies over these lower things, we must entirely confess with Aristotle <margin>* Aristotle, *Meteorology*, book 1, ch. 2.</margin> that: *This lower world is governed by the upper movements (<term>phorais</term> <note>Greek: φοραῖς, referring to the rotations or carrying motions of the spheres</note>);* It is also necessary that we acknowledge their great use in medicine, agriculture, economics, and seafaring. For an Astrologer can know future things that happen necessarily from natural causes, such as the rising of the sun, eclipses, and others; for these are detected in their causes. Many things are known not with certainty, but by very probable conjecture. Hence the Physician observes "critical days" from the stars. The Farmer and the Sailor observe the planets in those matters which clearly have their causes in nature itself. But those things which depend simply on divine providence or on the will and free choice of man—such as the particular or fortuitous events of men, or from other external causes—there is no knowledge of them from the stars, and no true prediction. For that reason, *Judiciary Astrology*—the degenerate daughter of a beautiful mother <note>The "beautiful mother" refers to Astronomy.</note>—which presumes to speculate on the outcomes of men from the observations of stars, is read as being so often forbidden in the Holy Code as a filth of the gentiles. Isaiah, the Evangelist among Prophets, in the name of God mocks the Chaldæan astrologers; though they profess a knowledge of the future from the stars, yet they could foresee neither the common calamity of their Babylonian homeland nor their own. The Chaldæans <note>Ancient Babylonians famous for their early developments in astronomy and mathematics.</note> were once most famous for their mathematical arts and renowned for their ancient science of the stars. Hence Simplicius <margin>* Commentary 4 on Aristotle's *On the Heavens*, book 2.</margin> writes that Callisthenes, at the request of Aristotle, sent to Greece the observations of the Chaldæans from 1,903 years before the time of Alexander. That would be about two hundred years before the birth of Abraham, shortly before the construction of the Tower of Babel. Compare Vossius, *On Idolatry*, book 2, chapter 47, page 563. Manilius, in the beginning of his *Astronomica*, attributes the purpose of Astronomy to the Kings of Egypt:
> Royal minds were the first deemed worthy to be moved,
> touching the heights of things closest to heaven.
If we believe Eusebius, the Patriarch Abraham taught astronomy in Egypt...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the origins and classifications of astrology, specifically exploring its movement from Egypt to other nations and its condemnation in biblical law as distinguished from natural astronomy.</meta>

<page-num>600</page-num>
<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>Judiciary Astrology.</margin>
Upon coming to Egypt, he <note>Referring to Abraham, who according to some traditions taught the Egyptians.</note> first taught the Egyptian priests mathematics. Egypt then established what was essentially a second school for this study, so highly favored by the Pharaohs that public land was assigned to the priests as a salary for their mathematical profession. From that time on, the Egyptians handed down the discipline of birth-charts <note>original: "genethliacam"</note> along with the art itself, such that they attributed their own Deities to the sky and stars, who would act when summoned by their influence. From such a division of the heavens, and the belief in the presence of Deities in individual parts, the opinion spread from the Egyptians to other nations. Indeed, along with the art itself, it "swam across" from Egypt into Greece under the leadership of Thales and Pythagoras, and from there into other regions; even today in China and Persia, all things are conducted according to the judgment and counsel of Astrologers, as witnessed by Botero in his *Reports on the Empire of the Great Khan of Tartary*, near the end.

Moreover, it requires no great effort of proof to note that those Astrologers who pronounce from the stars what will happen to men are understood by the term <term>Hobere shamayim</term> <note>Hebrew: הוברי שמים, "those who divide or gaze at the heavens"</note>, meaning "heaven-watchers" <note>Greek: ουρανοσκόπους</note>, and by <term>Chozim bakokabim</term> <note>Hebrew: החוזים בכוכבים, "seers of the stars"</note>, meaning "astrologers" <note>Greek: αστρολόγους</note>. The Hebrews agree on this unanimously, except that to Rabbi Kimchi, the word *Hoberim* seems foreign. Piscator explains *Hoberim* as "associators of the heavens—that is, the stars—to establish a certain constellation or star," from which he builds this paraphrase: *Those who make known their predictions by the months: let them save you from those things which are about to come upon you.* He pronounces their science "maimed, vain, and futile," which is evident from the ironic phrasing and the announced punishment in Isaiah 47:14. Finally, he numbers them among the enchanters, <term>Chakamim, Lammadaim, and Mekashephim</term> <note>Hebrew: חכמים ולמדעים ולמכשפים</note>, the "wise men and sorcerers," *Psalm 58:6*, who are also called <term>Meonenim and Menacheshim</term> <note>Hebrew: מעוננים ומנחשים</note>, "soothsayers" (Deuteronomy 18:10), whom the Septuagint calls "those practicing divination" <note>Greek: μαντευομένους μαντείαν</note>. By this name are understood those who, through sorcery or a pledge, investigate the successful outcome of their proposal; hence the Chaldean Paraphrast translates it as "one practicing sorcery." The <term>Yiddoni</term> <note>Hebrew: ידעוני, often translated as "wizard" or "familiar spirit"</note> were those who gathered responses from the clouds or stars, or considered this day favorable and that day unfavorable. The <term>Menachesh</term> is one who watches the flight of birds and notes their chirping to augur something about the future; and the <term>Meonen</term> is one who, by magic art, changes a thing before one’s eyes—a thing in which the Chaldeans were distinguished, as were the Magicians of Pharaoh who turned rods into serpents; all of whom are abominable to God, *Deuteronomy 18:9*. Close to our Prophet is that passage in *Jeremiah 10:2*, where God forbids His people to depend on astrological observations, but rather bids them to be of good courage, since they have nothing to fear from the signs of heaven. "The signs of heaven are the stars," as Piscator explains, which God placed in the sky to be signs of seasons, *Genesis 1:14*. More precisely, with Ravanellus, we explain them as the constellations of the celestial bodies—that is, the movement, site or position, qualities, conjunctions, and oppositions of the stars or constellations, which are "prognostic" signs <note>Greek: προγνωστικά</note> of certain things. Consequently, these are the prognostications and predictions which the Astrologers of the Chaldeans sought from the constellations of the stars, fearing them more than God Himself. But God commands the Jews to dismiss these customs of the nations, adding this reason: <term>Chuqqot ha-shamayim hebel hu</term> <note>Hebrew: חקית השמים הבל הוא</note>, "because the laws, statutes, or disciplines [of the heavens] are vain, futile, and of no moment." He calls them most vain—
<column-break/>
<margin>Judiciary Astrology.</margin>
—the predictions of the nations, because they claimed for themselves the knowledge of future events, which is attributed to God alone in the sacred writings. *Let them approach*, says God, *and tell us what things are to come; tell the things that were before, and we will consider them, and we will know their later outcomes. Or teach us the things that are to come. Announce the things that will happen afterward, and we will know that you are Gods.* Indeed, the Chaldeans were so superstitious that they dared to predict from the stars of heaven any accidental outcomes of things, or anything hidden and unknown to men, <margin>Isaiah 41.</margin> <margin>Ambrose says of them: They are Chaldeans who explore the courses of the stars with the zeal of vain superstition, and bring the impious errors of paganism. Flee from these, lest they seize you, lest they entangle you in the heavy snare of captivity.</margin> whence Ambrose says of them: (They are Chaldeans who explore the courses of the stars with the zeal of vain superstition, and bring the impious errors of paganism. Flee from these, lest they seize you, lest they entangle you in the heavy snare of captivity.) This most cursed class of people clearly attributed its own quality to each planet, by which it is carried into earthly things through its "particular nature" <note>Greek: καὶ ιδιοτροπίας</note>. They explain the "particular natures" <note>Greek: Ιδιοτροπίας</note> of the Planets so variously that you might emerge from them "wandering" <note>Greek: πλάνας, a pun on the Greek word for planet</note> and be led "into the errors of others" <note>Greek: εἰς ἄλλων</note>. To say nothing of the "temperament" <note>Greek: συγκρασία</note> of the Planets, by which it acts "from one to another and in one upon another." For they are accustomed to consider the "configuration" <note>Greek: Συχηματισμὸς</note>, and the various mixtures, and from them to judge the outcomes and the "mixing and temperament of fellowship and powers" <note>Greek: μῖξιν & σύγκρασιν κοινωνίας καὶ δυνάμεων</note>. If a physician sees Mercury associated with "malefics" <note>planets believed to cause harm</note>, he says there will be dry diseases. But in truth, nothing in heaven is malefic; all things are beneficial. Those first "prostitutors" of Astrology, rather than its "institutors," judged the stars of Saturn and Mars (as they call them) to be malefic; but those of Jupiter and Venus to be benefic. Mercury, however, they deemed versatile, prone to both good and evil. For that insane opinion of the "astrologasters" arose from the Egyptians, who joined both the Mathematical and Medical arts; for this reason, the Greeks called them "medical-mathematicians" <note>Greek: ἰατρομαθηματικός</note>. These men cured the sick after inspecting the position and figure of the stars. They would not give a purgative, nor provide food, nor apply cupping-glasses, unless the stars decreed it; and this "dizziness of the brain" flowed down to other Medical-Mathematicians as well, whence Juvenal’s Satire 6, line 573:

> — — *If the corner of a rubbed eye itches,*
> *she asks for eye-salve only after inspecting her birth-chart.*
> *Though she may lie sick, no hour seems more*
> *suitable for taking food than the one Petosiris has given.* <note>Petosiris was a semi-legendary Egyptian priest and astrologer.</note>

On this subject, Ludovicus Vives <note>Juan Luis Vives (1493–1540), a Spanish scholar and humanist.</note> elegantly discusses the use and abuse of Astrology in Medicine: *Some, as if they had the stars in their counsel, observed the days, hours, and moments of whatever they did, as if they would undertake nothing except by the advice of the stars. Others showed the "middle finger" to the stars and professed they would cure even if the stars were unwilling. While the stars do not do everything in our bodies (for the tempering of the elements accomplishes much), they do not do nothing either; yet neither are all the things they do known, nor are they nothing.* Indeed, the science of the stars is useful to the Physician, provided that all superstition is absent, through which he is taught to recognize even the changes of "critical days," which are referred to among the primary "criteria" <note>Greek: κριτήρια</note> of diseases by common and unanimous opinion. Their variation, however, comes solely from the motion of the moon; for since every seventh day the moon moves to a sign of a contrary nature to the one in which the disease began, Physicians conclude—realistically and probably—that the disease will remit if that sign is contrary to the disease. But if the sign into which the Moon passes is...

<margin>L. Vives, *On the Causes of the Corruption of the Arts*, p. 190.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the critique of judicial astrology, moving from its historical origins to specific theological and logical arguments against its use, particularly regarding its application to the life of Christ and the errors found in the calculations of its practitioners.</meta>

<page-num>601</page-num>
<header>Isaiah 47:13.</header>
<sig>Ddddd 3</sig>

<margin>Judicial Astrology.</margin>
...is familiar, they conclude that the strength of the disease is growing, and in all this they commonly have experience as a witness. We experience a similar, if not greater, abuse of the sky and stars in Astrological and Birth-chart <note>original: "Genethliacis," referring to the casting of horoscopes based on the moment of birth</note> prognostications; nor is there any place where "works of total wickedness" <note>original Greek: <greek>πανεργήματα</greek></note> hide themselves more within the parts of the visible world. The greater the abuse, the more piety forbids seeking protection for the fleeting affairs of human actions in the stars. Regarding this masked art, 

<margin>Perkins, *Golden Chain*, p. 80.</margin>
Perkins* writes that the abuse of the sky and stars is greatest. *All "houses" of the celestial figures are made from the signs of the fictitious Zodiac of the "First Mover," <note>In the older Ptolemaic system, the First Mover or "Primum Mobile" was the outermost sphere that moved all others.</note> which can have no power. This artifice does not arise from experience, because the same constellation of stars never happens twice; and even if it could happen, no observation could have been made, because the force and influence of the stars is confused in the air and on the earth. It calls the minds of men away from the consideration of divine providence, while all things are thought to proceed from the motion and position of the stars. Nothing is more shameful, nothing even more dangerous than that superstition of vanity.* Not so long ago in France, J. B. Gaffarel <note>Jacques Gaffarel (1601–1681), a scholar known for his "Unheard-of Curiosities" regarding celestial alphabets.</note> came forward with a French treatise, as a "seeker of novelties" <note>original Greek: <greek>καινοτόμῳ</greek></note>, in which there is such a devotion to empty and vain things that his "vain speech" <note>original Greek: <greek>κενολογία</greek></note> equals the most vain of all writers on vanities. They must be very impious who believe that Christ's birth, passion, etc., could be known beforehand from the observation of the stars, and that the web of his fates could be predicted from the birth-chart position of the heavens. For they say that he had to die by the punishment of the cross because, in his nativity, Mars was in the House of Death. <note>The eighth house in a horoscope, traditionally associated with death.</note> They say he was born in a stable because Capricorn held the "Bottom of the Sky" <note>the *Imum Coeli*, the lowest point of the chart</note>; that he was King of the Jews because the horoscope was in Libra; that he was a Prophet and Priest because in the ninth region of the sky Saturn was in the sign of Gemini, according to the testimony of Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, a famous Renaissance philosopher who actually wrote a massive critique *against* judicial astrology.</note> from 

<margin>Book 5, ch. 14.</margin>
Albumasar of Ascalon, Pierre d'Ailly, and others*—a superstition which Cardano also followed in his Commentary on Ptolemy. But what could be more injurious to the person of the Redeemer? Surely His unsearchable majesty should have completely bound their minds so that they did not attempt this, since both the Birth and the conception of the "Giant of dual substance" <note>A poetic reference to Christ's dual nature as God and Man.</note> happened outside the normal order of things. Also foul are the things that Brother Pelbart of Temeswar babbles about some monthly observations or other, so that he might extract knowledge of the new King born in Judea from astrological science. Pierre d'Ailly is of the same sort in other matters, when he dared to recall most memorable histories from sacred and profane sources to the calculation of Astrology, and to give the causes of individual events from the position of the stars, even though the events themselves are distant from those constellations by a very long interval of years. He supposes the Flood to have happened in the Year of the World 2242, and he gives its "fatuous" <note>A play on words: "fatualem" (fatuous/foolish) vs. "fatalem" (fated/fatal).</note> rather than fatal cause from some conjunction or other of Jupiter, Saturn, and Cancer, when the beginning of Aries was in the horoscope. Yet it is established from the sacred scriptures that the Year of the World 1656, not 2224, was the year of the universal cataclysm. It is no wonder that the Heathens attributed such power to the stars, as they took the place of Deities for them. These people, according to the testimony of Aegidius 

<margin>ch. 8, p. 47.</margin>
Romanus in *On the Rule of Princes*, book 2.2,* were too curious concerning the judgments of the stars; for they never wished to start wars, nor begin any works, unless an "unconsidered degree" <note>A technical term regarding the specific degree of a zodiac sign rising on the horizon.</note> was ascending and the condition of the sky had been inspected.

<column-break/>

From this murky fountain, other things could not help but flow. Hence the Latin Astrologer in Book 1, having admired the motion of the sky and the course and order of the heavens, concludes:

<margin>Judicial Astrology.</margin>
> And no reason seems so present to me,
> By which the world lies open by divine power.

Nothing is more common in the still-heathen world than to search in the stars for what good or evil is portended. The Chinese are most dedicated to investigating celestial matters; their mathematicians contemplate the sky day and night to see if anything new or unusual might appear in it, so that they may warn their King and announce to him what good or evil it portends, as witnessed by Trigault. <note>Nicolas Trigault (1577–1628), a Jesuit missionary to China.</note> He describes two Colleges of these mathematicians, whose function is illustrious in the kingdom: one is in the Court of Nanjing, the other in Beijing. Their knowledge was occupied with the calculation of Eclipses and with certain trifles from judicial astrology; compare the same author on Chinese matters, pp. 159, 162. But it is deplorable to find among Christians such "sky-walkers," <note>original: "cerobatas"</note> soothsayers, and windy prophets, whom the Greeks call "birth-chart casters" <note>original Greek: <greek>γενεθλιόλους</greek></note>. By inspecting the theme and the position of the upper and lower planets, or by observing the horoscope of any man, they dare to know beforehand or predict the origins, growth, changes, and falls of republics, or the fortune and affections of the body and soul of individual men. They consider births and predict "concerning each individual man" <note>original Greek: <greek>καθ’ ἕνα ἕκαστον τῶν ἀνθρώπων</greek></note> about their life spans, body shape, injuries to limbs, diseases, the quality and sicknesses of the soul, and about fortune—both in recreation and in honors—the procreation of children, the prosperity of friends, travels, the type of death, and other such things. Such an Astrologer sits with the spheres and the movements of the celestial spheres in his hands, dividing them into parts and portions and tiny segments, so that he may obtain the true planetary and fatal hours, by which he may craft his <term>astrological outcomes</term> <note>original: "apotelefmeta," technical predictions or results of a horoscope</note> without error through clocks and horoscopes. But let such "little astrologers" <note>original: "Astrologastri," a derogatory term for hacks</note> be far, far away. Giovanni Battista Riccioli* reckons three abuses of the stars: the adoration by the gentiles, the rashness of the birth-chart casters, and vain boasting. Concerning the second abuse, he says:

<margin>In the *New Almagest*, preface, fol. 6b.</margin>
*Birth-chart casters, from the position of the stars, have dared to predict not only a propensity toward morals or a way of life based on the natural temperament of the humors, but even future contingencies and events that depend on the pure freedom of the will of one or many. It is a class of men, as Tacitus says, which will always be forbidden in the city and always retained; he would have spoken more truly if he said "in the world." Though they are a thousand times false and deceptive, if once or twice they divine by chance rather than by art, they gain more in fame from one rash success than they do infamy from so many most obvious lies. For the earth does not cover the errors of "little astrologers" as it covers the errors of Doctors; the sky covers them, yet they can be convicted of manifest falsehood everywhere.* Against these people there exist the most wise decrees of the Sacred Canons, the Councils, and the Supreme Pontiffs, especially Sixtus V and Urban VIII. Let us hear the judgment of Apollonius of Tyana regarding "little astrologers," as recorded in Philostratus: Men, he says, who serve the law of nature, if they did nothing by their own judgment or will...

It cites both secular authorities like Tacitus and religious ones like Pope Sixtus V to condemn the practice as superstitious and fraudulent.</summary>

<meta>This page provides a historical and theological critique of "judicial astrology"—the practice of predicting the future based on the stars. It traces the origins of this art to ancient Egypt and examines its condemnation in biblical texts, while also discussing its later application in medicine (iatromathematics).</meta>

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Judicial Astrology.</margin>
Arriving in Egypt, he <note>Likely referring to Abraham, whom many Renaissance traditions credited with bringing mathematical knowledge to Egypt.</note> first taught mathematics to the Egyptian priests. Egypt then established what became, as it were, a second school for this art, so highly commended by the Pharaohs that public land was assigned to the priests as a salary for the profession of mathematics. From that time, the Egyptians passed down the discipline of birth-charts <note>original: "genethliacam"</note> alongside the art itself, to such an extent that they attributed their own deities to the heavens and stars, believing these gods were called forth to act by their influence. From this division of the heavens and the believed presence of deities in individual parts, the opinion spread from the Egyptians to other nations. Indeed, along with the art itself, it "swam across" from Egypt to Greece under the leadership of Thales and Pythagoras, and from there to other regions; thus, even today in China and Persia, all things are conducted according to the judgment and advice of astrologers, as Botero <note>Giovanni Botero (c. 1544–1617), an Italian thinker known for his work on the Great Cham of the Tartars.</note> testifies in his *Reports on the Empire of the Great Cham of the Tartars* near the end.

Moreover, noting that those who pronounce what will happen to men based on the stars are meant by the Hebrew phrase *Habre shamayim* <note>original: "הברי שמים," literally 'dividers of the heavens' in Isaiah 47:13</note>, understood as "sky-gazers" <note>original Greek: <greek>οὐρανοσκόπους</greek></note>, and by "those who gaze at the stars" as "astrologers" <note>original Greek: <greek>ἀστρολόγους</greek></note>, the Hebrew scholars unanimously agree. However, to Rabbi Kimchi <note>A famous medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian.</note>, the word *Havro* seems foreign; Piscator <note>Johannes Piscator, a 16th-century German Reformed theologian.</note> explains it as *associators of the heavens*, that is, of the stars, for the purpose of establishing a certain constellation or heavenly body, from which they construct this paraphrase: *Those who make known their predictions by the months, and would save you from those things which are about to come upon you.* He pronounces their science to be "maimed, vain, and futile," which is evident from the ironic phrasing and the punishment denounced in verse 14. Finally, he numbers them among the "enchanters, wise men, and sorcerers" <margin>Exodus 7:11</margin>—those who are also called "diviners" <margin>Deuteronomy 18:10</margin>, <note>original: "קסמים" (Qesamin)</note> whom the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> calls "those practicing divination" <note>original Greek: <greek>μαντευομένους μαντείαν</greek></note>. By this name, they are understood as those who explore the success of a proposal through lots or stipulations; the Chaldean Paraphrast <note>A reference to the Targum, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible.</note> renders this as "exercising lot-casting." There are also those who gathered answers from the clouds or stars, or considered one day favorable and another unfavorable; those who watched the flight of birds and paid attention to their chatter to augur the future; and the sorcerer, who changes something before one's eyes by magic art. In this last matter, the Chaldeans were famous, as were the magicians of Pharaoh who turned rods into serpents—all of whom were abominable to God <margin>Deuteronomy 18:9</margin>. Close to our Prophet is that passage in *Jeremiah 10:2*, in which God forbids His people from depending on astrological observations, bidding them to disregard them, since they have nothing to fear from the signs of heaven. *Signs of heaven are the stars*, as Piscator explains, which God placed in the sky to be signs of the seasons <margin>Genesis 1:14</margin>. More precisely, with Ravanellus <note>Petrus Ravanellus, author of a 17th-century biblical dictionary.</note>, we explain them as constellations of celestial bodies—that is, the motion, site, or position, the aspects, conjunctions, and oppositions of stars or constellations, which are "prognostic" <note>original Greek: <greek>προγνωστικά</greek></note> signs of certain things. Consequently, the prognostications and predictions which the Chaldean astrologers sought from the constellations of the stars, they feared more than God himself. Yet God commands the Jews to dismiss these customs of the nations, adding this reason: *because the laws, statutes, or disciplines of those nations are vain, futile, and of no moment.* He calls the 

<column-break/>

predictions of the nations most vain because they claimed for themselves the knowledge of future events, which is attributed to God alone in the sacred texts. *Let them come forward,* says God, *and tell us what is to happen; tell us the former things, and we will consider them and know their outcome. Or declare to us the things to come. Tell us what is to come hereafter, so that we may know that you are gods.* Indeed, the Chaldeans were so superstitious that they dared to predict any chance events, any hidden things unknown to men, from the stars of heaven. <margin>On Psalm 4.</margin> Hence, Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose (c. 340–397), Bishop of Milan.</note> says of them: *They are the Chaldeans who explore the courses of the stars with the zeal of vain superstition, and carry the impious errors of paganism. Flee from these, lest they seize you, lest they entwine you in the heavy snare of captivity.* This most cursed class of people assigns to each planet its own quality, so that you might emerge from it as a "wanderer" <note>original Greek: <greek>πλάνης</greek></note> and be carried into sublunary things by "private motion" <note>original Greek: <greek>ἰδιοπορίας</greek></note>. They explain the "private motions" of the planets so variously that you might emerge as a "wanderer" and be led into "error" <note>A pun on the Greek word *plane*, which means both planet and error.</note>. We say nothing of the "blending" <note>original Greek: <greek>συγκρασίᾳ</greek></note> of the planets, by which *one* acts upon *another*. For they are accustomed to consider "configuration" <note>original Greek: <greek>Σχηματισμὸς</greek></note> and various mixtures, and from these to judge the outcomes, the "mixing," and the "blending of fellowship and powers." If a doctor sees Mercury associated with "malefics" <note>In astrology, planets thought to have a negative influence, like Saturn or Mars.</note>, he says there will be "dry diseases." But in truth, nothing in heaven is malefic; all things are beneficial. Those first practitioners, rather than founders, of astrology judged the stars of Saturn and Mars (as they call them) to be malefic, but those of Jupiter and Venus to be Benefic. Mercury, however, they considered versatile—prone to either good or evil. For from the Egyptians arose that insane opinion of the "astrologasters," who joined the two arts of mathematics and medicine, whom the Greeks call "iatromathematicians" <note>original Greek: <greek>ἰατρομαθηματικούς</greek>, literally 'physician-mathematicians' or medical astrologers.</note>. These people cured the sick by inspecting the position and figure of the stars. They would not give a purgative, they would not provide food, they would not apply cupping glasses, unless the stars decreed it; and this "dizziness of the brain" flowed down to other iatromathematicians, as Juvenal says in *Satire 6, line 573*:
> If the corner of a rubbed eye itches,
> she asks for ointment only after inspecting her birth-chart.
> Though she lies ill, no hour seems more suitable
> for taking food, except that which Petosiris <note>A legendary Egyptian priest and astrologer.</note> has given.

Hence, Ludovicus Vives <margin>S. cor p. 190</margin> <note>Juan Luis Vives (1493–1540), a Spanish humanist and scholar.</note> elegantly discusses the use and abuse of astrology in medicine:
> *For some, as if they had the stars in their council, whatever they did, they observed the days, hours, and moments, as if they would undertake nothing except by the advice of the stars. Others showed the "middle finger" <note>A gesture of contempt in antiquity.</note> to the stars and professed they would cure people even if the stars were unwilling. While the stars do not do everything in our bodies—for the tempering of the elements accomplishes much—they do not do nothing at all. And what they do effect, let it not be said that all is known, nor that nothing is known.*

The science of the stars is indeed useful to the Physician, provided that all superstition is absent, through which he is taught to recognize even the changes of "critical days" <note>Specific days in the course of a disease when a change for better or worse was expected.</note>, which are referred to by common and unanimous opinion among the first "criteria" <note>original Greek: <greek>κρίτήρια</greek></note> of diseases. However, their variation arises from the motion of the moon alone; for since every seventh day the moon passes into a sign of the opposite nature to that in which the disease began, Physicians conclude—realistically and probably—that the disease remits if that sign is contrary to the disease. But if the sign into which the Moon passes is...

It also examines "iatromathematics," critiquing the extreme reliance on astrology in medical practice while allowing for the Moon's natural influence on "critical days" of illness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a theological and historical critique of judicial astrology, moving from its ancient origins to its "abuses" in the medieval and early modern periods, specifically addressing the vanity of predicting human fates and even the life of Christ through the stars.</meta>

# Isaiah 47:13

<margin>
Judicial Astrology. 4. l. 22. 23.
</margin>
...it was common for the forces of a disease to grow when joined together, and in all these things, they generally have experience as their witness. We experience an equal, if not greater, abuse of the heavens and stars in astrological and birth-chart <note>original: "Genethliacis"</note> prognostications. Nowhere do the deceptions <note>original Greek: <greek>πανεργήματα</greek>, meaning 'all-working' or 'shifty' works</note> of the visible world hide themselves more; and the greater the abuse is, the more piety forbids seeking a defense for the fleeting affairs of human actions in the stars. Regarding this masked art, Perkins <note>William Perkins (1558–1602), an influential English Puritan theologian.</note> writes in his *Golden Chain* <margin>Armill. aur p. 80.</margin>: "The greatest abuse is of the heavens and stars. All the 'houses' of the celestial figures are made from the signs of a fictional Zodiac of the First Mover, which can have no power. This art does not arise from experience, because the same configuration of stars never occurs twice; and even if it could occur, no observation could have been made, because the force and influence of the stars is confused within the air and the earth." They call the minds of men away from the consideration of divine providence while they claim everything proceeds from the motion and position of the stars. Nothing is more foul, nothing even more dangerous than that superstition of vanity. Not long ago, J. B. Gaffarel <note>Jacques Gaffarel (1601–1681), a French priest and scholar of the occult and Kabbalah.</note> came forward in France with a French treatise, in a revolutionary manner <note>original Greek: <greek>καινατομῶς</greek></note>, in which there is such a devotion to empty and vain things that his "hollow-molding" <note>original Greek: <greek>κενοτυπία</greek></note> equals the vainest of the vain writers. <margin>psal. 1. 64.</margin> Those who thought the birth, passion, and other events of Christ could be known in advance from the observation of the stars must be exceedingly impious, believing that the web of His life could be predicted from the birth-chart position of the heavens. "For that reason," he says, "He had to die by the punishment of the cross because, in His birth-chart, Mars was in the House of Death. He was born in a stable because Capricorn held the lowest point of the sky. He was King of the Jews because the horoscope <note>In this context, 'horoscope' refers to the Ascendant, the sign rising on the eastern horizon.</note> was Libra. He was a Prophet and Priest because Saturn was in the sign of Gemini in the ninth region of heaven." This is according to Pico della Mirandola, citing <margin>lib. 5. c. 14.</margin> Albumasar, Cecco d'Ascoli, Peter d'Ailly, and others—a superstition also followed by Cardano in his *Commentary on Ptolemy*. But what could be more injurious to the person of the Redeemer? Surely His unsearchable majesty should have completely blinded their minds so they would not attempt this, since both the birth and the conception of the "Giant of double substance" <note>A poetic reference to Christ's two natures, divine and human.</note> occurred outside the natural order of things. Also foul are the stutters of Brother Pelbart of Temeswar <note>A 15th-century Hungarian Franciscan preacher.</note> regarding I-know-not-what monthly observations, as he tried to derive the Magi’s knowledge of the new King born in Judea from astrological science. Peter d'Ailly is of the same sort in other matters, as he dared to recall many memorable stories from sacred and profane history to the calculations of astrology, and to provide the causes of individual events from the position of the stars, even though the events themselves are separated from those constellations by a vast interval of years. He supposes the Flood happened in the year of the world 2242, and he provides a "fated" rather than a true cause for it from some conjunction of Jupiter, Saturn, and Cancer, when the beginning of Aries was in the horoscope—even though it is clear from Sacred Scripture that the year of the world 1656, not 2242, was the year of the universal cataclysm. It is no wonder the pagans attributed such power to the stars that they took them for deities. For these people, as Aegidius Romanus testifies in *On the Rule of Princes* <margin>v. 8 f 47.</margin>, were too curious about the judgments of the stars; they never wanted to begin wars or start any works unless a favorable degree was ascending and the condition of the sky had been inspected.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Judicial Astrology.
</margin>
From this murky fountain, other errors could not help but flow. Hence a Latin astrologer, in his first book, having admired the motion of the sky and the course and order of the heavens, concludes:

> *And to me no reason seems so present,*
> *Which reveals that the world is ruled by divine power.*

Nothing is more common in the still-pagan world than to search in the stars for what good or evil is portended. The Chinese are most devoted to investigating celestial matters; their mathematicians contemplate the sky night and day to see if anything new or unusual should appear in it, so that they may warn their King and announce to him what good or evil it portends, as Trigault <note>Nicolas Trigault (1577–1628), a Jesuit missionary to China.</note> testifies. He describes two colleges of these mathematicians, whose function is illustrious in the kingdom: one is in the Court of Nanjing, the other in Beijing. Their knowledge was occupied with the calculation of eclipses and certain trifles from judicial astrology; compare the same author on *Chinese Matters*, pages 159 and 162. But it is deplorable to find among Christians "air-walkers" <note>original: "cerobatas"</note>, soothsayers, and such windy prophets, whom the Greeks call birth-chart casters <note>original Greek: <greek>γενεσιαλόγους</greek></note>, who, having inspected the "theme" and position of the higher and lower planets, or having observed the horoscope of any man, dare to foreknow or predict the births, growths, changes, and falls of republics, or the fortune and affections of the body and soul of individual men. They consider births and predict for *each and every man* <note>original Greek: <greek>καθ' ἕνα ἕκαστον τῶν ἀνθρώπων</greek></note> concerning their lifespan, the shape of their body, injuries to their limbs, diseases, the quality and sicknesses of the soul, and fortune—both in family life and in honors—concerning the procreation of children, the prosperity of friends, travels, the type of death, and other such things. Such an astrologer sits, holding in his hands and dividing the spheres and the motions of the celestial spheres into parts, portions, and tiny particles, so that the true planetary and "fated" hours may be pointed out, by which he may complete his "outcomes" <note>original: "apotelesmata," a technical term for astrological results</note> without error through clocks and horoscopes. But let such petty astrologers be gone, far gone. Giambattista Riccioli <margin>in the preface to the New Almagest, folio 6. b.</margin> recounts three abuses of the stars: the worship of the pagans, the rashness of birth-chart casters, and vain boasting. Regarding the second abuse, he says: "Birth-chart casters, from the position of the stars, have dared to predict not only a propensity from the natural temperament of the humors toward this rather than that manner of life; but even future contingencies and events depending on the mere freedom of the will of one or many. A class of men which, as Tacitus says, will always be forbidden in the city and always retained." He would have more truly said "in the world." Though they are false and deceiving a thousand times, if once or twice they divine by chance and not by art, they gain more fame from one successful rashness than infamy from so many most obvious lies. For it is not as with physicians, whose errors the earth covers; the sky does not cover the errors of petty astrologers, but their manifest falsehood can be proven everywhere. Against these men there exist the most wise decrees of the Sacred Canons, Councils, and Supreme Pontiffs, especially Sixtus V and Urban VIII. Let us hear the judgment of Apollonius of Tyana regarding petty astrologers in Philostratus: "Men," he says, "who serve law and nature, if they did nothing by their own judgment or will..."

<meta>This page continues the critique of judicial astrology, contrasting the "superstitious" belief in fate dictated by stars with the biblical view of the heavens. It then transitions into a discussion of sacred rhetoric and the relationship between sacred and secular ("profane") literature, specifically examining the poetic structure of Isaiah.</meta>

<page-num>602</page-num>
<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>
<columns>2</columns>

<margin>Judicial Astrology.</margin>
...they would act, but with the stars acting as their charioteers, they would not clearly be men—that is, rational living beings—but would instead seem like the playful tricks of illusionists, or ridiculous puppets moved by strings. Therefore, the Emperors <note>Refers to the Roman Emperors who codified laws against magic and astrology.</note> had just cause—as seen in the *Code on Sorcerers and Astrologers <note>original: "Cod. de Malef. & Mathem."</note>, laws 5 and 7*—why they restrained this reckless and superstitious class of people with more severe edicts and decrees. An astrologer <note>original: "Mathematicus," which in late antiquity specifically referred to those who cast horoscopes.</note>, who had predicted life events to the people from the stars, performed public penance in the Church under Augustine; in Augustine's books there still exists the sermon which he delivered to the <margin>Volume 8, on the Psalms, column 631.</margin> people after the assembly, *in which these words appear: "That man used to say that it was not his own will that committed adultery, but Venus; and it was not his own will that committed homicide, but Mars; and it was not God who performed justice, but Jupiter; and many other sacrileges of no small weight. How many Christians do you think he took money from? How many bought a lie from him?"* He then brought forward the history from the Acts of the Apostles concerning the burning of wicked books, and adds that the volumes brought by the astrologer, which he had used, were then to be burned, *so that with those books sent into the fire, he himself might pass into a place of spiritual refreshment.* The good Melanchthon <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560), a colleague of Luther who famously defended astrology.</note> was too devoted to astrological predictions, as his letters sufficiently testify. The Blessed Luther often drove him to distraction with sarcasm, asking whether those who are drowned in a ship, or killed in danger, meet this fate because of their own birth-chart <note>original: "Genesi"</note>, or whether it should truly be attributed to the hour they boarded the ship? Moses informs us better regarding the purpose and office of the stars, from which nothing falls to the practitioners of birth-charts: *He says the duty of the stars is to divide the day and night, light and darkness, to shine in the heavens and illuminate the earth, to serve as signs, and to distinguish seasons, days, and years.* No protection is stored here for divinatory astrology regarding the lot and fates of men; even if there were, it would far transcend our grasp. *For the ability to truly grasp from the movement of the stars the things concerning each person—whatever they may be doing or suffering—is something much greater than what is possible for a human,* says Origen in Eusebius's *Preparation for the Gospel, book 6, chapter 9.* <note>Translated from the original Greek text cited in the source.</note>

---

<margin>Isaiah 51:17.</margin>
->Wake yourself, wake yourself, stand up, O Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of His wrath; you have drunk the dregs of the cup of trembling and drained it.<- <note>Hebrew original: התעוררי התעוררי קומי ירושלם אשר שתית מיד יהוה את-כוס חמתו את-קבעת כוס התרעלה שתית מצית:</note>

->Arouse, arouse, stand up O Jerusalem, who has drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his anger; the cup of ruin, the bowl of anger, you have drunk and emptied.<- <note>Greek Septuagint original: Ἐξείρει, ἐξείρει, ἀνάστηθι Ἱερουσαλὴμ...</note>

->Awake, awake, rise up Jerusalem, who have drunk from the hand of Jehovah the chalice of his fury; you have drunk and squeezed out the dregs of the chalice of trembling.<- <note>Latin original: Suscitate, suscitate, surge Hierusalem...</note>

<margin>Sacred-Secular Parallelism.</margin>
Theological matter, says Ramus <note>Petrus Ramus (1515–1572), a French humanist and logician.</note> in his *On the Christian Religion, pages 1 and 2*, is varied, distinguished, and adorned by every variety of argument and every kind of speech: by divine oracles, prophetic responses, poetic songs and psalms, and historical examples. For the style of speech in Prophetic literature is frequent in this: that the sense which the first part of a verse expressed, the latter part either exhibits in other <margin>verse 9.</margin> words, or refers back to the same or a similar thought, or responds with a contrary one. This present passage from Isaiah is emphatic, to which there is a clear parallel

<column-break/>

from the same chapter of the Prophet: *Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the Lord; awake.* Considering those words, the Blessed Brentius <note>Johannes Brenz (1499–1570), a German Reformer.</note> writes: *Observe here for me the pleasant rhetoric of the Holy Spirit and His weighty eloquence. For in this part of the sermon, He could have said those things simply: Just as the Lord once liberated His afflicted Church from Egyptian tyranny, so He has now also liberated her from all her adversities and adversaries. But He is not content with this simple narration; He rises into grandiloquence and shapes the speech with various figures. Who could sufficiently weigh the copious, eloquent, and indeed the rhetoric composed for moving and teaching in the illustrious sermons of Isaiah through each chapter! Yet the speech does not run toward ostentation, for the Spirit of the Lord, who spoke through him and through other Prophets, used that kind of speaking which flows plainly and from the nature of things for explaining necessary matters: divine things divinely, earthly things earthly, tragic things tragically, and mystical things in a mystical manner.* As for the "copiousness" <note>Abundance or richness of style.</note> which is most seen in the Prophets (whom they call the "Major" Prophets), the more tragic things <note>original Greek: <greek>τὰ τραγικώτερα</greek></note> are not described so copiously (to use the words of the Blessed Snepfius <note>Theodor Snepf (1532–1586), a Lutheran theologian.</note> on Isaiah 13, page 225) *so that the Prophets might pursue ornaments and little flowers of figures and the vain glory which the ethnic orators sought, but so that they might set forth by those examples of divine severity, as if in a mirror, what men should expect if they are unwilling to obey the Lord's warning.* For the authority of Holy Scripture is greater and our religion more august than can be known by the human mind or compared with the writings of these [secular] men. You will detect the difference where they labor on the same argument, whether of consolation or of prayer. Notwithstanding this, it is helpful here, having compared the tables of Holy Scripture and the pagans <note>original: "Ethnicorum"</note>, to notice where the faculty of speaking was equal and the style of speaking almost the same. For let the comparison of sacred and profane literature enjoy a pure and illustrious brevity, says Strigelius <note>Victorinus Strigel (1524–1569), a Lutheran scholar.</note> in his *Hypomnema, 299.* Truly, the humanities are nothing, and profane philosophy is nothing, if they disturb the foundation of Theology; they ought to build a step toward Theology, not destroy Theology. Therefore, we shall water the sacred gardens with little streams sought from the light of nature. In the previous century, the Englishman John of Wales <note>original: "Johan Galenfis," a 13th-century Franciscan scholar whose work was printed in the 16th century.</note> wrote <margin>book</margin> a *Comparison from Sacred and Profane Authors*, collected and published at Strasbourg in 1550. While we also, O literate world, hand over to you these sacred-secular parallels so that you may read and judge. We do not think we have gone astray,

> By teaching here twin arts at once,
> The sacred and the profane together;
> The profane and the sacred as one.

We deliver a harmony together, though not in an identical way; for even here that much-repeated <note>original Greek: <greek>πολυσθρύλλητον</greek></note> logical rule will prevail: *Every analogy limps.* If anything is discordant <note>original Greek: <greek>ἀνάρμοστον</greek></note>, it is simultaneously rejected and eliminated. He who teaches us from your world to teach twin labors with more refinement shall bear twin honors:

->*Of the arts and of learned piety.*<-

We would have given more refined things if our library had been better equipped and time had been more indulgent. Truly, *repetition* <note>original Greek: <greek>παλιλογία</greek></note> is a figure by which, when the same word or name is repeated, different things are not understood...
