...they are joined, but the same thing being signified is expressed more vehemently. There is also another type of "Doubling," which can be called **Synonymous**, where a repetition of a thing occurs but using different words. The Hebrews of old noted that this was done to strengthen the meaning, as the Rabbis say: <term>כפל הענין במלית שנית לחזק הענין</term> <note>original: "kefel ha-inyan be-millit shenit lehazzek ha-inyan"; translates to: "A doubling of the matter with a second word to strengthen the matter."</note>. Examples of this are found in Exodus 15:26, Isaiah 32:13, 52:13, Jeremiah 13:17, 48:29, and elsewhere. Among the Greeks, this is usually called <term>ἐπεξήγησις</term> <note>epexegesis: adding words to clarify or further explain a point.</note>. Furthermore, this doubling produces a superlative degree, beyond which there is no further level; the Hebrew writer intended nothing else by this duplication than to express that which is "very" good or "very" bad. Jeremiah says: <margin>See chapter 24:3.</margin> <term>תאנים הטבות ,הטבות מאד</term> <note>te’enim ha-tovot, tovot me’od</note> "I see figs, figs, good, very good," and I see figs, <term>רעות ,מלות מאד</term> <note>ra’ot, ra’ot me’od</note> "bad, very bad." The Greek version <note>The Septuagint (LXX).</note> there has: <term>ἐσῦκα τὰ σῦκα, τὰ χρηστὰ χρηστὰ λίαν, & τὰ πονηρὰ πονηρὰ λίαν</term> <note>"the figs, the figs, the good [are] very good, and the bad [are] very bad."</note>. While Holy Scripture uses this doubling, we rightly conclude with Augustine (commenting on Psalm 74 and Psalm 94) that repetition in the words of the holy tongue is not a desire for talkativeness, but possesses the power of a firmament <note>i.e., it provides a solid foundation or certainty.</note>. Among these repetitions, however, the most prominent of all occurs at the very beginning of Genesis, where it is said three times concerning the **Image***, where the word <term>ברא</term> <note>bara: "he created"</note> is repeated three times, <margin>Genesis 1:27.</margin> while the word <term>צלם</term> <note>tselem: "image"</note> is repeated twice. Of no less importance is that repetition read in Deuteronomy 2:27: <term>בדרך בדרך אלך</term> "in the way, in the way I will go." Some take this to refer to the speed of the journey, as if the sense were: "I will proceed without ceasing, without any hesitation, with a swift step, I will proceed continually by the same way," because the repetition of a noun signifies emphasis and clarity, or even continuation (see Deut 16:20, 2 Kings 4:19, 2 Samuel 18:33, Psalm 133:2, Jeremiah 4:19). But from the underlying explanation, "I will not turn to the right nor to the left," and especially from comparing the parallel passage in Numbers 21:22, <term>המלך בדרך</term> <note>ha-melekh ba-derekh: "on the King’s highway"</note>, it is gathered that the meaning is: "I will proceed by the public and well-trodden royal road." Hence the Greek translators rendered it, <term>ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ πορεύομαι</term> <note>"I travel in the way"</note>, and the Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> says, "I will proceed by the public way." Blessed Martin Luther translated it as: *where the road goes, there I will go* <note>original German: "wo die Strasse gehet / will ich gehen"</note>. Not unlike this is the sentiment found in Claudian (Book 3, *On the Rape of Proserpina*):

> I will go, I will go, wherever my feet, wherever
> chance shall command.

How copious and eloquent Isaiah was through his individual chapters could be taught with little effort: <term>רזי-לי רזי-לי</term> <note>razi-li razi-li</note> "Woe is me, woe is me!" <note>Literally "leanness to me," though often translated as "my secret is mine."</note>. Others: "My wasting away is mine." But at the end, it is not the first-person suffix, concerning which Avenarius <note>Johann Avenarius, a 16th-century Hebraist.</note> writes on the word "secret." Luther says: *How thin I have become!* <note>original German: "Wie bin ich so mager!"</note> <margin>Chapter 24:16.</margin> Zangerus, for what mystery we know not: *My secret I keep with me.* * Highly illustrious in that same passage is the coupling of words where the Prophet says in verses 19 and 20: <term>רעה התרעעה הארץ</term> "The earth is utterly broken by breaking." <term>פור התפוררה ארץ</term> "The earth is utterly dissipated by dissipating." <term>נוע תנוע ארץ</term> "The earth shall certainly shake itself by shaking." Luther’s version here seems to be "thin" <note>i.e., lacking the full weight of the original Hebrew.</note> when he paints the emphasis—which he otherwise usually does most heavily—with a light brush. In verse 3: <term>הבוק תבוק הארץ</term> "The earth shall be utterly emptied by emptying." The interpreter <margin>page 366.</margin> Blessed Sneppius * comments on the words in this way: Isaiah achieves the description of the greatest perturbation of things through a certain synonymous variety, repeating so many words so that the Jews would understand that although many and various calamities have existed for them—by which the Republic was, as it were, shaken and shattered—

<column-break/>

yet they have never received any such misery and <margin>Parallelism</margin> calamity as that which would be in the future, which he prophesies here. To cast away idolatry, Hosea exhorts in the name of God (2:2) with these words: <term>ריבו באמכם ריבו</term>. The Greek says: <term>κρίθητε πρὸς τὴν μητέρα ὑμῶν, κρίθητε</term> <note>"Plead against your mother, plead."</note>. The Old Latin: *Judge your mother, judge.* Vatablus: *Expostulate with your mother, expostulate.* The Chaldee Paraphrase: "Rebuke the assembly of Israel, and say to her." The word is repeated emphatically to signify vehemence and to hint at the many types of idolatry. Indeed, the word <term>ריב</term> <note>rib</note> otherwise denotes to dispute (whether privately or publicly) with adversaries, or to "plead a cause."* <term>הנני רב את-ריבך</term> "Behold, I am about to plead <margin>Jeremiah 51:36.</margin> your cause." So too in Judges 11:25: <term>הרב רב עם ישראל</term> "Did he certainly contend with Israel?" So in Psalm 119:154: <term>ריבה ריבי</term> "Plead my plea" <note>i.e., "Plead my cause."</note>. Concerning the diminishing of royal dignity, it is said three times in Ezekiel 21:27: <term>עוה עוה עוה אשימנה</term>. Vatablus: "A subversion, a subversion, a subversion I will make it." The Vulgate and the Greek put it twice: <term>ἀνομίαν, ἀνομίαν</term>, "Iniquity, iniquity." Blessed Luther: *I will make the crown nothing, nothing, nothing.* <note>original German: "Ich will die Cron zu nicht / zu nicht / zu nicht machen."</note> Marinus explains the word <term>עוה</term> <note>avah</note> in this place as a "crookedness," "inclination," or "deviation." By this triple repetition, certainty and a long duration of time are indicated, and the meaning is increased to "perverse, indeed most perverse." Others take this triple doubling to refer to the three more significant slaughters of the Jews, the first by the Babylonians, the second by Antiochus, the third by the Romans; this last one finally brought total destruction <note>original: "panoletriam"</note> to the people. For he had arrived (as is in the text) whose judgment it was, and to whom the crown was handed over in the most eminent way—namely, our Savior, JESUS—which time is determined here by the Prophet; compare Junius. See another reason for this triple repetition in Blessed Chemnitz, *Harmony of the Gospels*, chapter 3, page 119, and Blessed Glassius, *Sacred Grammar*, book 3, page 18. Still worthy of mention is the passage in Jeremiah 43:11, where under a type is proposed the defeat to be brought upon the Egyptians by Nebuchadnezzar, with a truly notable "epizeuxis" <note>A rhetorical device where a word is repeated for emphasis, with no words in between.</note> and repetition: <term>והכה את-ארץ מצרים אשר למות למות ואשר לשבי לשבי ואשר לחרב לחרב</term>. "And he shall strike the land of Egypt: those who are for death, to death; and those who are for captivity, to captivity; and those who are for the sword, to the sword." Blessed Luther, following the sense, repeats it thrice: *whomever it hits* <note>original German: "wen es trifft"</note>, as can be seen in his version of this place. In this way, Holy Scripture also tends to join its verbs to a conjugated or cognate noun, and this most often with the accusative case, so that an <term>αὔξησις</term> <note>auxesis: rhetorical amplification or growth.</note> and vehemence of the thing may be declared, or a most worthy <note>original: "ἀξιώτατον"</note> object noted. Let these few examples from many stand as testimony: "to sow a sowing" <note>σπείρειν σπόρον</note> (Lev 26:16, Eccles 11:6, Jer 35:7); "to sow a seed" (Deut 11:10); "to reap a reaping" <note>θερίσειν θηρισμὸν</note> (Lev 19:9). Hebrew: <term>צידה ציד</term> "to hunt a hunt" <note>Lev 17:13</note>; "to brick bricks" <note>πλινθεύειν πλίνθους</note> or "in burning for a burning" <term>בשרפה לשרפה</term> (Gen 11:3); "to work out a wrath in wrath" <note>קצף קצף</term> (Zech 1:15); "to fast a fast" (2 Samuel 12:16); "to celebrate feasts" <term>חג תחוגו</term> (Nahum 1:15); "to desire desires" (Proverbs 21:26). In this same style Ennius wrote: *Desiring desired things, he desires desirously*; Plautus (*Casina* 2.3.49); "to ask an asking" (1 Samuel 1:27, 1 Kings 2:16, 20, 2 Samuel 3:5), and what is the same, "to petition a petition" (Judges 8:24); such as "to ask a question" in Plutarch’s *Against Colotes*. "To be jealous with jealousy" <term>בקנאו את-קנאתי</term> (Numbers 25:11); "to be astonished with an astonishment" (Gen...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred-secular parallelism.</margin>
<note>The author uses the term "parallelism" here to describe how Biblical (sacred) and Classical (secular) authors use the same grammatical patterns.</note> In Genesis 27:33 and 2 Kings 4:13, where the Hebrew says <term>יחרד חרדה</term> <note>original: "yecherad charadah"; literally: "he trembled a trembling"</note>, we find a "trembling of trembling." Similarly, "to flash a lightning flash" <note>original: "ἀστράπτειν ἀστραπήν"; Hebrew: "ברק ברק" (barak barak)</note> appears in Psalm 144:6. We see "to sleep a sleep" in Psalm 76:6 <note>original: "נמו שנתם" (namu shenatam)</note> and 1 Samuel 2:22. Other examples include "the baldness of the bald" in Ezekiel 37:11; "to sacrifice a sacrifice" in Jonah 1:16 and Psalm 56:13; and "to sin a sin" <note>original: "ἁμαρτίαν ἁμαρτάνειν"; Hebrew: "חטא חטא" (chata chata)</note> in Lamentations 1:8, meaning a "sin has been sinned." We find "to vow a vow" in Genesis 28:20, Leviticus 27:2, Numbers 6:2, Deuteronomy 12:11, Judges 11:30, 2 Samuel 15:7, and Jonah 1:15. The Roman playwright Plautus uses this same expression: "to vow vows" <margin>Amphitryon 3. 2, 66.</margin>. The phrase "to reign a kingdom" in 1 Samuel 8 is a rare and specific usage meaning "to create a king." Further examples include "to split a split" in Mark 2:4; "to burden with burdens" in Luke 11:46; and "to divide a care" in Romans 12:5. We can see from this that this form of speech began at the very cradle of the world among the Hebrews. More recent Greek authors use this same form so similarly that, were it not for the timeline, one might think they were born of the same birth. They are entirely of the same color and character.

Let us begin with the Poets, whose style of speaking is fresh and original, and we shall give first place to Homer, the father of poets. Indeed, the prince of poets seems to seek a crown of laurel from this very style. "To speak a word" <note>original: "Εἰπεῖν ἔπος"</note> appears in the *Iliad* book 1, line 108, and Euripides uses it in *Orestes* line 1. We also find: "to bear children" (*Iliad* 2.313); "to speak in assemblies" (2.788); "to sweat sweat" (4.27); "to wield spears" (4.324); "to sleep a sleep" (8.506); "to feast a feast" (9.70); "to counsel counsels" (10.415); and "to perform funeral rites" (24.285). "To sit on a seat" appears in the *Odyssey* 5.3. Euripides, in *Orestes* line 461, says "to pour libations"; in *Medea* 549 "to bring a bringing" <note>meaning to bring a message</note>; in *The Suppliants* 116 "to wage a campaign"; and in line 193 "to tell a tale." In *Helen* 1047, he says "to flee a flight." Sophocles writes "to hate a hatred" (*Philoctetes* 59); "to praise a praise" (1375); "to laugh a laugh" (*Antigone* 557); "to work a work" (390); "to revere with piety" (955); "to pray prayers" (433); "to bind with bonds" (*Ajax* 62); and "to wail wailings" (316). This last one is parallel to the Scriptural phrase "to lament a lamentation" in 2 Samuel 1:17, "to wail a wailing" in Ezekiel 27:32, and "to weep a weeping" in 2 Samuel 13:37, where the Hebrew says <term>בכו בכי</term> <note>original: "bachu bechi"</note>.

But we must proceed. "To talk nonsense" <note>original: "Λῆρον ληρεῖν"</note> is found in Aristophanes’ *Plutus* (Act 2, Scene 5), which Plautus renders as "to chatter trifles." We find "to knead a cake" in *The Knights* (1.1.55); and "to walk a walk" <note>original: "βάδον βαδίζειν"</note> cited by Eustathius from an old comic book—it is just as if someone said "to way a way" or "to step a step." Hesiod says "to give a gift" (*Works and Days* 81). Aeschylus says "to be sick with a sickness" (*Prometheus* 383), for which the Sacred Scriptures use "to be ill with an illness" in 2 Kings 13:4. We also see "to marry a marriage" in Aeschylus (line 738), and "to perish a destruction" in Oppian’s *Halieutica* (line 263).

Nor are the Poets the only ones who love to speak this way. Aristotle said "to fear a fear" in his *Eudemian Ethics*. The Holy Writers say the same, such as Jonah (1:10), David in Psalm 53:5 where it says <term>פחדו פחד</term> <note>original: "pachadu pachad"; "they feared a fear"</note>, and Luke concerning the intense fear of the Shepherds (2:9).

The same Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> said "to serve a service" in his *Politics*, as did his student Theophrastus in his golden book *Characters*. The translators of the Septuagint <note>The Greek version of the Old Testament</note> used this in Numbers 8:24; what is beautifully translated from the Hebrew as "to war a warfare" means to perform a duty and exercise oneself in it. The New Testament does not depart from this, saying "to war a warfare" in 1 Timothy 1:18, as Beza notes. <margin>page 443.</margin> Arrian speaks of "serving a service" when describing Alexander mourning Hephaestion. In *Politics*, we find "to rule a ruling" and "to rule the greatest rulings." Similarly, Chrysostom <note>An early Christian preacher known as "Golden-Mouthed"</note> uses "to love a love" in his 30th homily on 2 Corinthians. We also see "to labor a labor" in Euripides’ *Hecuba*.

<column-break/>

This same phrase was used by Suidas concerning the leadership of Barbarius Philippus, by Aeschines in his speech *Against Ctesiphon*, and by Xenophon in *The Constitution of the Athenians*. Compare this with "to rule a ruling" <note>original: "משל משל" (mashal mashal)</note> from Daniel 11:3. Also "to travel a travel" in Lamentations 3:57, which is rendered the same way. Plato says "an appearance appeared" in his *Symposium*. Cicero writes "to love a love." We find "you judged the judgment" in the Vulgate Bible <note>The Latin Bible</note>. So too "to lie a lie" in Demosthenes (page 661); "to file a counter-plea" in the same author (598); "to abound in abundance" (365); "to fight a sea-battle" (Epistle 110); and "to danger a danger" in Isocrates’ *Oration to Philip*. "To fight a fight" is used in *Archidamus* and by Demosthenes, Plutarch, and Homer in the *Iliad*. Not far from this is "to war a war" in the *Iliad* (8.121). We see "to win a victory" in Josephus’ *The Jewish War*. "To progress a progress" appears in Plutarch, and "to capture a capture" in Juba. "To live in a house" <note>literally: "to house a house"</note> is in Theophrastus and Aristotle’s *Economics*. Aeschines often used this figure of speech; his works include "to buy a buying," "to clothe a clothing," "to impose an imposition," and "to insult an insult." Galen and Alexander of Aphrodisias said "to have the fire of a fever," as noted by Stephanus.

<margin>Vol. 3, p. 634.</margin> We see the Hebrews are no more successful or "well-aimed" in this than the Greeks, especially the Athenians, for whom this speech is considered a specialty. Hence, the scholar Suidas calls it the **Attic Figure**. I present his words to you: "The Attic figure is to say 'I fenced a fence,' using the name of the thing itself for the action. Examples include 'to insult an insult,' 'to talk nonsense,' 'to be mad with a madness,' 'to flee a flight,' 'to serve a servitude,' and 'to rejoice a joy.'"

Eustathius says the same regarding Homer’s *Iliad*: "It is spoken in the Attic way to say things like 'you spoke a speech,' 'I slept a sleep,' and a thousand other such things." This is elegantly said to happen "by internal sensation" <note>original: "κατ’ ἰδιοπάθειαν"</note>, because the verb, as it were, experiences its own body. Theodore Gaza, who is considered the Prince of Grammarians of his age, calls these **Overlaying Verbs** <note>original: "Ἐπιβατικά"</note> in his *Introduction to Grammar*: "Let us take," he says, "'I fight a fight,' 'I live a life,' 'I serve a servitude,' and all such things, as 'overlaying' verbs."

But leaving the Greeks, let us test this among the Latin writers. Among these, the Comic poets especially decorated their writings with it. Such things are found in Plautus <note>various citations from *Persa*, *Miles Gloriosus*, *Captivi*, *Aulularia*, *Curculio*, *Rudens*, and *Trinummus*</note>. He uses "to serve a servitude" in *Pseudolus* and "to fight a fight." This was also used by Gellius. In Plautus, we find "to dream a dream," "to plot a plot," "to buy provisions," "to perform piety," and "to live a life." Livy uses "to deceive a deceit." Terence, in *The Eunuch*, has "to play a game," which is also in Plautus’s *Mostellaria*. Boethius and Virgil use "to rage a rage." Cicero and Caelius use "to rejoice a joy." Similarly, Gellius says: "To rejoice a joy..."

<meta>The catchword "genni-" at the bottom suggests the next page begins with a word like "gennimata" or a similar Latin/Greek derivative relating to "offspring" or "production."</meta>

<summary>This page catalogs the use of cognate objects (pairing a verb with a noun of the same root) across Hebrew, Greek, and Latin literature. The author argues that this "Attic Figure," common in the Bible, is also a hallmark of the greatest classical poets, philosophers, and orators.</summary>

<keywords>cognate accusative, rhetoric, linguistics, Homer, Plautus, Aristotle, Attic Figure, Biblical Hebrew, Greek grammar, translation studies</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "cognate objects"—grammatical structures where a verb and its object share the same root—and transitions into a broader defense of studying "pagan" or classical literature to better understand the Holy Scriptures.</meta>

# Isaiah 51:17

<margin>Sacred-secular parallelism.</margin>
...genuine. The Roman playwright Terence, in the final scene of *Andria*, line 8, writes: "To joy a joy solidly" <note>original: *Solide gaudere gaudium*</note>. We can interpret Jonah 4:7 in the same way: <term>a great joy</term> <note>original Hebrew: *שמחה גדולה* (simchah gedolah)</note>, where the Greek Septuagint translates it as "to joy a joy" <note>original Greek: *χαίρειν χαράν*</note>. However, a synonym is used in 1 Kings 1:40, "to be glad with gladness" <note>original Greek: *εὐφραίνεσθαι εὐφροσύνην*</note>, where the Syriac translation <note>original: *חרין חדוה* (chadin chadutha)</note> uses the same form. To use a word from Plautus, I might compare this to "to breakfast a breakfast" from his play *The Rope* (2.6.24) or "to think thoughts" <note>original: *cogitationes cogitare*</note>. Even the legal scholars, such as Scipio Gentilis, mention this same way of speaking—using phrases like "to act an action," "to caution a caution," "to stipulate a stipulation," or "to part a part."

I am being somewhat brief with these Latin examples, which the commentator Donatus (on Terence’s *The Eunuch*) claims "smack of Archaism" <note>An "archaism" is a conscious use of old-fashioned or obsolete language.</note>. In this, Donatus hardly seems wise to me, as if only those who love the dead, obsolete language of the ancient past would speak this way. We recognize this as an ancient figure of speech, along with Julius Pomponius, but not an "antiquated" one. The best masters of Latin and Greek spoke this way. Therefore, I am ashamed of that "Master of Salamanca" <note>Referring to a Spanish academic, likely a critic of the Jesuit scholar Juan Luis de la Cerda.</note> who rejects these expressions as futile and useless, calling them mere "pleonasms" <note>Redundancies</note> and claims they are only useful if something else is added to them. In this, he rightly deserved the criticism of his countryman, Juan Luis de la Cerda, for making such a significant error.

While we were busy illustrating this mode of speaking from secular writers, we unexpectedly stumbled into a deeper question: *Is it actually permissible to do this? Indeed, should a Christian man even open the writings of the Pagans for such a purpose?* There are those who believe the reading of Pagan authors is entirely fruitless. This error seems to be shared even by the "greater gods" of the church, including the authors of the Fourth Council of Carthage, who published this decree: *A Bishop shall not read the books of the Gentiles.* Gratian, the compiler of church laws, also included this in his collection. Clement of Rome likewise commands everyone to abstain from all books of the Gentiles, calling them inventions of the Devil. Cornelius à Lapide writes that Clement established this based on the doctrine of the Apostles. However, since they wrote for the needs of their own era—when it was not safe to allow just anyone to read Pagan works—and since many things can be said in a relative sense that cannot be said absolutely, we believe their words should be interpreted kindly. As Chrysostom says in his homily on Colossians, these warnings were meant relatively compared to the Holy Scriptures, 
<margin>Chrysostom, Homily on Colossians.</margin>
which alone are the "base of knowledge" and the "medicine for the soul."

Nevertheless, we maintain that their books can be read with profit and that Christians can "water their own gardens" from those streams. We prove this, first, *by a survey of several passages of Holy Scripture.* We will easily show in this current essay that we cannot advance toward a richer understanding of many passages without first reading secular writers and drawing from them a knowledge of history and rituals.

Secondly, we see this *from the examples of the Sacred Writers themselves.* Consider Moses, 

<column-break/>

who from his childhood was liberally educated in the royal court of Pharaoh. <margin>Secular parallelism.</margin> Having a noble and polished mind, he was "learned," as Stephen <note>Stephen is called the *Primicerius* or "first-ranking" of the martyrs.</note> reports, "in all the wisdom of the Egyptians" <note>original Greek: *πάσαν σοφίαν αἰγυπτίων*</note>, and yet he is celebrated as "beloved by God" <note>original Greek: *ἠγαπημένος ὑπὸ Θεοῦ*</note>. His example shows us, as Daniel Greser (formerly the Superintendent of Dresden) writes, that the literature of the Gentiles is not to be despised as useless for the work of piety. 

Consider also DANIEL and his companions, <margin>Caussin, *Elogia*; Augustine, *Sermon 2 to the Brothers in the Desert*; Sirach 45:1.</margin> who were trained in the language and literature of the Chaldeans (Daniel 1:4, 17). On this point, St. Jerome notes: *If Daniel refused to eat from the King’s table or drink his wine so as not to be defiled, surely if he knew the wisdom and teaching of the Babylonians were themselves a sin, he would never have consented to learn what was forbidden.* 

Consider St. PAUL, who was highly skilled in reading secular authors. He cites testimonies from Epimenides (Titus 1:12), Aratus (Acts 17:28), and Menander (1 Corinthians 15:33). Weighing this carefully, the Venerable Bede writes on 1 Samuel 14:29: *It confuses the sharp minds of readers and makes them falter when one thinks they should be entirely prohibited from reading secular literature; for one may take useful things found there and treat them as one's own. Otherwise, Moses and Daniel would not have been allowed to be educated in the wisdom of the Egyptians—though they detested their superstitions and luxuries. Nor would the Teacher of the Gentiles (Paul) have included the verses of poets in his writings.* But Bede adds a caution: *One must gather a rose among sharp thorns much more carefully than a lily among soft leaves; it is much safer to seek healthy counsel in the Apostolic pages than in the Platonic ones.*

Some also apply the command in 1 Timothy 4:13, "Attend to reading" <note>original Greek: *προσέχε τῇ ἀναγνώσει*</note>, to this topic. Peter Stevartius notes that, according to the mind of the Holy Fathers, this recommends to Timothy not only the study of sacred books, but also human wisdom found in philosophers, poets, and historians. The same is said of the wise man in Sirach 39:4, that "he will travel through the land of foreign nations and test the good and evil in all things." We leave these particular interpretations to stand on their own merits.

<margin>Allegorical Exposition of Samuel, book 2, volume 4, page 303.</margin>
<margin>page 368.</margin>

Thirdly, we see this *from symbolic "types"* which some scholars apply here. 
1. In Deuteronomy 21:12, a "foreign wife" is told to shave her head and—as the Latin translator puts it—"circumcise her nails" <note>Hebrew: *תעשה* (ta'aseh); Greek version: *περιονυχίζειν* (perionychizein)</note>. Philo follows this reading. Just as a foreign woman, before being taken into a home and marriage, had to have her hair shaved, her nails trimmed, and the clothes of her captivity removed, so too must secular literature be "shaved and trimmed" when we wish to transfer it to our own use. We must cut away the superfluous, the irrelevant, and any impious parts, as St. Jerome and John of Damascus explain. Thus, there is no obstacle to a great partnership, provided this "captive" Pagan philosophy and philology—wherever it teaches things less than healthy—has its hair shaved, nails clipped, and garments cast aside, and is then led to its "husband," Holy Theology. Let it serve her perpetually as a freedwoman, so that it does not enslave her.
2. The same is symbolized by the vessels borrowed from the Egyptians and contributed to the building of the holy Tabernacle...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
Sacred-secular parallelism.
Vol. 4, f. 43
</margin>
**Augustine** writes in *On Christian Doctrine*, Book 2, Chapter 40, that by the example of the Hebrews <note>Referring to the "Spoils of the Egyptians," where the Israelites took gold and silver from Egypt to build the Tabernacle.</note>, we are reminded—as **Gregory of Nyssa** says in *The Life of Moses*, p. 506—that we must not neglect the riches of learning possessed by the pagans. We are commanded to take from them Moral and Natural Philosophy, Geometry, Music, Logic, and the other sciences in which those outside the Church flourish. If possible, we should strip those who misuse these tools and transfer them to better uses. One might also count among these the * spoils taken from enemies by David for the construction of the Temple.

<margin>
Gregory of Nyssa on Zephaniah, p. 262.
</margin>
4. **From the testimony of the Fathers.** Let **Saint Augustine** stand alone from among many; in Book 2 of *On Christian Doctrine*, he treats this very theme, from which I wish to gather some gleanings. In Chapter 28 of that book, he discusses *History*. He argues that history is of great value in explaining Scripture, and that knowledge of it greatly helps us understand the holy books, even if it is learned outside the Church during one's childhood education. He uses himself as an example: he, like almost everyone else, drew nearly all his secular knowledge from the pagans. He suggests that what was learned from them previously should not be unlearned, but rather used more profitably.

Chapter 29 deals with the use of *Geography, Physics, and Astronomy.* He states that knowledge of these is valid for solving the riddles of the Scriptures when used in a legitimate and lawful way. They should not be used as signs for superstitious remedies or devices, such as *hanging herbs around the neck*—a practice disapproved of even by the more sensible Pagans, as **R. Gualtherus** teaches. For example, some say: "If you hang this herb from your neck, your stomach will not ache," an example used by **Augustine**. Yet elsewhere, in his *7th Homily on John*, Augustine was somewhat indulgent toward such presumptions (as **Chemnitius** puts it), saying: "When your head aches, we praise you if you place the Gospel at your head." (Compare Fabricius’ *Commentary on the Christian Poets*, p. 129). Of a similar superstitious nature are certain "Characters" <note>Magical symbols or sigils.</note>, which **Gregory** calls *Phylacteries*. (The glosses here state: *These are papers on which incantations are written; the word is clearly a distortion of the Jewish Phylacteries,* as **Gualtherus** notes in ch. 1, p. 339). These and other types of incantations and invocations for healing the body must be avoided all the more prudently by a Christian, since they originate from pagan superstition, regardless of how effective they might seem to be. (Compare ch. 20). Regarding Astronomy, he notes its abuse and the fruitless intentions of those who try to draw suspicious and ominous conjectures about our actions and future events from it. He commands that this most persistent error of the *Horoscope-casters* <note>original: *Genethliacorum*</note>, who sing of foolish fates, should be fled from like a madness. (Compare ch. 21, 22, and 23). In these chapters, he attacks this impious curiosity with many arguments, saying among other things: *All arts of this kind, whether trifles or harmful superstitions, arise from a certain pestiferous society of men and demons, like an unfaithful and deceitful pact of friendship; they must be utterly repudiated and fled from by the Christian.* **Gratian** thought this passage important enough to include in his *Pandects* (Decretals), case 26, question 2.

<margin>
Homily 10 on Micah ch. 3, p. 318.
Part 2, Book 1, Ch. 9, p. 131.
</margin>

<margin>
C. Caussin, *Eulogies*, Book 4, ch. 35.
</margin>

Chapter 31 deals with the use of *Logic* <note>original: *Dialecticae*</note>. He teaches that one must beware of the lust for quarreling and the childish ostentation of deceiving an opponent with "catchy" conclusions condemned by Holy Scripture itself. He cites a certain Philosopher’s sophism <note>A "sophism" is a clever but false argument intended to deceive.</note> said to a companion: *“What I am, you are not. I am a man. Therefore, you are not a man.”*

<margin>
Sirach 37, v. 29.
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred-secular parallelism.
</margin>
This sophism, proposed insultingly by a Logician from Plato’s school, was very wittily repaid by Diogenes, as recorded in **Apuleius**, Book 18, *Attic Nights*, ch. 13 (which you should consult). Near the end of the chapter, Augustine accurately distinguishes between the *truth of logical connections* (which he shows in ch. 32 were observed by men, not invented by them) and the *truth of the statements themselves.* He proves that the former can be learned even in schools outside the Church, but the latter must be sought in the holy ecclesiastical books. For a detailed explanation of this Augustinian distinction, see **Cornelius Martini** in his *Logical Analysis* and **Gutkius** in his *Discourse for Peripatetic Logic, at the beginning.*

<margin>
Analysis p. 70 ff.
</margin>

Chapter 37 treats *Eloquence* <note>Rhetoric/Public Speaking</note>, the goal of which he teaches is "to persuade." This faculty is not blameworthy in itself, even though false things can be persuaded through the perversity of those who use it badly. **Saint Isidore** writes most elegantly in his *Letters*, Book 5, Letter 281: <note>original Greek: τοιαῦτα σοφίας ἡ μὲ λέξις πεζὴ...</note> "The language of Divine Wisdom is indeed humble, but its meaning is heaven-high. If the outward phrasing is not brilliant, perhaps the speaker is at fault. But if one can grasp the meaning and use the phrasing wisely, he is judged most sage. For eloquence can be the heaven of super-mundane wisdom, if it is subject to it like a body to a soul, or a lyre to a singer—innovating nothing on its own, but interpreting those heaven-high thoughts. But if it should flip this order, and when it ought to serve, it thinks it can rule or rather tyrannize, it is right that it be expelled." Let us add the Latin translation, though it may correspond less to the luster of the Greek: "The speech of Divine Philosophy (Wisdom) in the sacred letters is indeed humble, but the sense is sublime and clearly heavenly. The speech of external writers is surely splendid, but the subject matter creeps upon the ground. If, therefore, anyone is able to attain the sense of the former and the elegance of the latter, let him be considered most wise. For eloquence can be an instrument of heavenly science if it is subjected to it like the body to the soul, and like the lyre to the lyricist—innovating nothing privately, but interpreting its meditations. But if it inverts this order, and when it should serve, it wishes to rule or rather to command, it is just that it be expelled."

<margin>
Schott, *Letters*, vol. 5, p. 81.
</margin>

In Chapter 39, however, he requires a very diligent caution regarding these doctrines found among the pagans: *let no one, seeking the blessed life, dare to follow securely any doctrines practiced outside the Church of Christ as if they were the path to attaining that life.* This view entirely pleases us, and we wish it to be observed throughout this whole discussion. He also commands that the error be absent by which men seem to think they have learned the truth of the blessed life itself merely because they have learned these subjects (p. 6, 37). He commands that boastfulness be absent (ch. 39, p. 143; see also ch. 38, p. 144; ch. 42, p. 153; ch. 43, p. 153; ch. 18, p. 106). In summary: Following Saint Augustine in Chapter 19, we distinguish between the superstitious and the non-superstitious. He teaches that the former must be avoided (p. 20), among which he includes consultations with demons, the worship of idols, various omens, and a thousand other most vain observations, *many fables and falsehoods.* (See ch. 25 and 26). He advises in Chapter 40 that superfluous things should be cut away, but necessary things should be put to the just use of preaching the Gospel, for the service of the one God, and in obedience to Christ. There, using the examples of Moses, Cyprian, and others, he shows that it is permissible for Christians to be imbued with the doctrines of the philosophers, provided they are purified for our religion.

<margin>
Hele- p. 140.
</margin>

<margin>
Sacred-secular
parallelism
</margin>
...that they may use things that have been adapted and prepared. We may grasp all of these points in a single, elegant rule from the same Father <note>Saint Augustine</note>, which he provides in the same work, drawn from the figures and polished vessels of the Egyptians: *If those who are called philosophers—especially the Platonists—have by chance said things that are true and suited to our faith, these are not only not to be feared, but should be claimed for our use from them, as if from unjust possessors.* <note>original: "Philosophi qui vocantur... in usum nostrum vendicanda." A famous defense of integrating Platonic philosophy into Christian thought.</note>

From these points, the "what" and the "why" <note>Greek: τὸ ὅτι (the fact) and τὸ διότι (the reason)</note> of our inquiry shine forth, which the aforementioned Father treats with great learning and insight. His primary aim is to instruct the person who, having abandoned the "idol-madness" of the nations, has given his name to God and departed from pagan society. Specifically, it instructs how such a person ought to use "Egyptian spoils" after their conversion—that is, the doctrines of the nations—which we may very effectively adapt for our own use. For the matter remains the same, even if the people involved have changed.

Anyone desiring more on this type of question should see **Saint Basil the Great** in his specific sermon *To Young Men on the Utility of Greek Literature* <note>Greek: πρὸς νέους</note>; it will be worthwhile to bring some points from there to this discussion: *Just as we pick flowers in a rose garden but leave the thorns behind, so must secular authors be handled; having breathed in their fragrance, let us guard against what is harmful* <note>Greek: οἷον ῥόδισμον καπνωσάμενοι, τὸ βλαβερὸν φυλαξώμεθα</note>. That is to say, we should pluck what is useful and beware of what is noxious—a point he illustrates with the example of bees. He further states: *Secular disciplines bring both ornament and no small degree of assistance*, both in the explanation and the propagation of heavenly doctrine. This Father, truly Great, even taught Rhetoric for a time after receiving baptism; he fulfilled this duty so magnificently that Libanius, the most celebrated Sophist, submitted his own speeches to Basil's critique. See also **Jerome** on Daniel chapter 1, who himself read Quintilian and Cicero, as he mentions in his *Preface to Daniel*. He confesses in his *Preface to Job* that he had been occupied among grammarians and philosophers since infancy, and he disputes this at length in his *Letter to Magnus, the Roman Orator*. **Reinhart Lorchius**, in his notes on the *Exercises of Aphthonius* <margin>$\star$ Egenolph edition, year [15]78.</margin> $\star$ folio 72 and following, shows that the ravings of those who claim Jerome was whipped with lashes because of his secular books (especially Cicero's) are empty. **P. Mosellanus** discussed this extensively before him. Philipp Carolus—once a professor at Altdorf but now an apostate—ought to have known this before presenting these stories to his listeners as true history. For Jerome himself confesses in his *Apology against Rufinus*, Book 1, that it was a *mockery of the night* <note>original: "Noctis ludibrium" — meaning it was a dream or a nightmare, not a literal event or a divine prohibition.</note>. Therefore, the Canon Law (Distinction 37, chapter 7) does not have even the slightest support in this example when it says: *We read of the blessed Jerome, that when he read the books of Cicero, he was corrected by an angel because, as a Christian man, he was attending to the fictions of the pagans.* Consider also Damascene, the "Lamentation" <note>Monodia</note> of Nazianzen (that "Christian Demosthenes"), Tertullian, Justin, Cyril, Prudentius, Isidore, etc., whose testimonies were collected with critical judgment <note>Greek: ἐπικρίσει</note> by Nicolaus Selneccer in his commentary on Romans chapter 2, page 93; and among the more recent, our own Dr. Gerhard in the preface to the *Catholic Confession*, part 1; Dr. Meisner in *The Babylonian School*, part 3, question 7; and Claude d'Espence <margin>$\star$ On excellent works, p. 986 ff.</margin> $\star$ in his treatise *On the benefit to be perceived from reading the books of the nations*. See also Benedict Aretius in *Theological Problems*, part 2, the section on reading secular writers, folio 235; and Camillo Ricchieri of Rovigo in his

<column-break/>

preface to Book 19 of the *Readings* of his uncle, Ludovico Ricchieri. See also C. <margin>The Queen of Heaven and the Cakes</margin>
**T**he lights of the upper spheres—the Sun, the Moon, and the rest of the army of the stars—were designed by the supreme goodness of the Almighty for the *service* of mortals, not for their worship. That these bodies attained divine honors among superstitious pagans can be confirmed by a hundred witnesses; and if anyone desires proof of this, truly:
-> He is asking for the sun to be shown to him. <note>A proverbial way of saying something is blindingly obvious.</note> <-
The Highest God, the architect of heaven and earth and the moderator of things celestial and terrestrial,
> *Gave to man a face turned upward, and commanded him to behold the sky*
> *And to lift his upright countenance to the stars.* <margin>Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 1, line 84.</margin>
He did this so that man might marvel at that admirable work of the heavens, studded so diversely with the lights of the stars; not so that he might take those celestial bodies—members of the world visible to the eye—for Gods. <margin>$\star$ Deuteronomy 4:19.</margin> $\star$ Lifting his eyes to the sky, let him see the sun, the moon, and all the stars of heaven, which the Lord created for the service of all nations, and not be deceived by error into adoring them. God willed for the lights to exist for the alternation of days and <margin>$\star$ Psalm 19:1, Genesis 1:14.</margin> nights, not as Deities. Even **Plutarch** was able to notice this when he said in his book *On Isis and Osiris*: *Let us not worship the elements: the sky, the Sun, or the moon.* These are mirrors in which we behold the singular art of Him *who founded and adorned the world.* Nor is the world anything other than His temple. Furthermore, **Lactantius** testifies in Book 6, chapter 20, that it is far more noble and worthy of a human being *to behold the heaven rather than carved things* <note>wordplay in Latin: "caelum" (heaven) vs "caelata" (carvings/engravings)</note>, and to admire this most beautiful structure of the sky, adorned with the twinkling lights of stars like flowers, rather than things painted, fashioned, or set with gems. Nothing in physical things is greater or more wonderful than the sky, whether you consider its *mass*, its *beauty*, its *efficacy*, its *speed*, or its *stability*. Of the heavens it is singularly said: *The heavens declare the glory of GOD.* The heavens and the celestial bodies recount the glory of GOD in an orderly way; they declare it not so much by their magnitude, light, and splendor, as by their motion: *The heavens declare the glory of El.* <note>Hebrew: הַשָּׁמַיִם מְסַפְּרִים כְּבוֹד אֵל</note>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the ancient history and cultural context of the Bible, moving from the use of secular learning to a specific case study: the origins of astral worship (the Sun, Moon, and stars) and the ritual offerings associated with them.</meta>

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<page-num>608</page-num>

<margin>The Queen of Heaven and ritual cakes</margin>
"What is man?" says the Royal Prophet in Psalm 8, verse 5 <note>original: "Ps. 8. v. 5."</note>, where the word *visited* <note>Hebrew: פקד (*paqad*)</note> is used emphatically. Indeed, it signifies not only that God "looked upon" him, but also that He "counts" and "numbers" him, as the Greek translators in the Septuagint have further emphasized. In this sense:

->Nature provides God's monuments in a thousand ways,<-
->Imitable by no artist's skill or devotion throughout the world.<-

<margin>Jeremiah 2:28</margin>
How broadly the worship of the Sun and the rest of the stars spread throughout all antiquity can be inferred even from the Sacred Scriptures. From these, we see that the Jews themselves—as men of corrupt morals prone to superstition—worshiped the brilliant stars of heaven under various names, with diverse rites, ceremonies, sacrifices, and drink offerings made of wine and flour, at consecrated statues and altars. Isaiah 65:11 says the Jews offered a drink offering to "Gad" <note>A Canaanite god of fortune or luck</note>, to the whole crowd of gods or the "host of heaven," setting the table and consecrating a drink offering to "Meni" <note>A god of fate or destiny</note>. Jerome notes that they sacrificed to the stars and filled their tables with a multitude of gods. The Prophet adds that, just as they had a similar taste for these things <note>original: "similes haberent labra lactucas," a Latin proverb meaning 'like lips like lettuce,' or 'like people like food'</note>, they would soon face a matching punishment. Just as they manufactured a vast number of gods according to the number of their cities, so *the Lord would number them for the sword and for slaughter* <note>Isaiah 65:12</note>. He would make them bow down just as they had bowed down to the stars, following the custom of the neighboring nations. For as Plato testifies in the tenth book of *The Laws*, at the rising and setting of the Sun and Moon, the Greeks and all barbarians practiced prostrations and adorations upon the earth. Our Prophet <note>Jeremiah</note> says in chapter 19, verse 4, that the Jews had made the holy place "alien" by profaning it and practicing foreign rites within it. And in chapter 7 (verses 17–18), chapter 8 (verse 2), and chapter 44 (verse 17), he teaches most gravity that the Jews—worshiping the things of God instead of God himself—credited the harvest of the earth not only to the sky, the sun, the moon, and the whole host of heaven, but even worshiped them with idols of wood and stone (where he calls the wood a "lesson of vanity"). "Do you not see," he says in verse 17, "what they do in the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem? The children gather wood, the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead the dough to make <term>cakes</term> <note>Hebrew: כונים (*kavanim*); Greek: *popana*</note> for the <term>Framework of Heaven</term>." <note>original: "Machinae cœlorum"</note>. This Hebrew phrase <note>original: כונים למלכת השמים</note> means "cakes for the work of the heavens" according to some, or "cakes for the **Queen of Heaven**." By this title, they believe the Moon is meant, which, shining with the clearest light, appears to preside over the "host of heaven" like a Queen. Beza uses this title or epithet in his notes on Luke chapter 32.

<margin>In Joshua c. 2. 116. p. 290.</margin>
Serarius argues against this, though few names suit the Moon better than "Queen." Just as the Sun is the "Lord" <note>Hebrew: *Baal*</note>, so the Moon is the "Lady" <note>Hebrew: *Baalah*</note>, from which the Greek names *Beltis* and *Baaltis* may be derived (on this, see Vossius, *On Idolatry*, book 2). The Septuagint translates this here as "the host," but elsewhere as the "Queen of Heaven." Thus Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek lexicographer</note> says: "When the Scripture speaks of Manasseh, saying he worshiped the 'host of heaven,' it refers to the sun and the stars." This phrasing is drawn from military custom, for the stars are drawn up in the sky like soldiers in a battle line. Hence the "powers of heaven" in Acts 7:42 and Matthew 24:29 refer to the "army of the heavens," which are the stars. Similarly, the word "power" <note>Greek: *dynameos*</note> is used for an army and military forces in the works of Demosthenes, Xenophon, and others. Therefore, when attributed to the sky, it denotes the Sun, Moon, and stars, because each stands at its station like a

<margin>Psalm 19, v. 5</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>R[abbi]: The Moon is the image of the lower world.</margin>
soldier and a brave man in an army to perform his assigned duty. Just as in an army, the Sun in the heavens is the King or Commander to preside over the day, the Moon is the Prefect or Lieutenant to preside over the night, and the leaders—Orion, Arcturus, and the other constellations—are the officers and soldiers. The Jews who turned to paganism honored this heavenly ornament, army, virtue, troop, or "host" (as the Septuagint and Vulgate render it in different ways) with cakes, by imprinting and forming images and figures upon them. The Greeks call these <term>kaunones</term>, retaining the Hebrew name, for those cakes, kneaded with wine and oil, are called <term>Kavanim</term> by the Prophet <note>original: כונים</note>, from a root meaning "to prepare" or "to arrange," because they were prepared with great care. Hesychius says these were "breads mixed with oil." Suidas records the same, noting the name was derived from the singular Hebrew root *Kun*. Forster relates it to a root meaning "to burn." Solomon Jarchi <note>The medieval commentator Rashi</note> writes that these cakes bore the image of a certain great star, which they honored with the name "Queen of Heaven." Nicholas of Lyra asserts they were round loaves in which the image of the Moon or a star had been pressed.

<margin>In G[enesis?] v. m.</margin>
Franciscus Junius translates them as <term>popana</term> <note>ritual sacrificial cakes</note>; the Hebrew word, he says, signifies certain "molded" offerings which had specific forms pressed into them corresponding to the idols to which they were offered. This type of cake was adopted by the Romans and Egyptians from the Greeks, called *Lucientes* ("shining ones") or by the diminutive *lucunculi*; the Etruscan *Lucumones* were the greatest experts in these superstitions.

<margin>See Ancient Laws.</margin>
Regarding the Athenians, it is clear from Proclus (the interpreter of Plato) that they employed many people in the shaping of cakes for the gods; on this, see Casaubon and Downes. Aristophanes, in his play *Plutus*, calls these cakes *psaista*, which according to Suidas are "barley meal soaked in oil and wine, which are burned for the gods." In the same sense, they explain the words of Hosea 3:1 regarding the cakes offered in sacrifice: "The Lord loved the children of Israel, yet they look to other gods and love <term>raisin cakes</term>." <note>original: "coitiones cum uvaecis" / "pemmata meta saphidon"</note>. The Hebrews read "flagons of grapes." Saint Jerome writes here: "Instead of 'cakes' <note>Greek: *pemmata*</note>... we can call them in Latin 'pancakes' or 'crusts' which are offered to idols, and in Greek are called *popana*."

<margin>Isidore</margin>
Saint Cyril agrees in his commentary on the same Prophet: "They desert God for foreign gods, to whom they bring cakes with raisins, perhaps even honey-cakes; for they brought such cakes as a sacrifice to demons." There was a festival in Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> in honor of Hyacinthus (whom Apollo is fabled to have loved) where <term>pemmata</term> <note>sweet cakes</note> were traditionally offered. Athenaeus describes this Hyacinthia festival: "The Spartans perform the sacrifice of the Hyacinthia over three days... because of the mourning for Hyacinthus, they neither wear crowns at their feasts nor bring in bread, but they give cakes and things that follow from them."

<margin>Book 2, c. 24.</margin>
Macrobius says the Greeks called these *pemmata* or *tragemata* <note>sweets or desserts</note>, which our ancestors called *bellaria*. Juvenal mentions *popana* in his sixth Satire. The "offering to Meni" is explained in Isaiah 65:11, where I cite the words of Scultetus: Those who, along with the common crowd of interpreters, follow Jeremiah in identifying the "Queen of Heaven" [as the Moon], spread themselves out...

### JEREMIAH VII. 18.
<page-num>609</page-num>

<margin>The Queen of Heaven and ritual cakes</margin>
We are cast into a whirlpool of conjectures when we try to determine which specific deities are meant by the *Queen of Heaven* or *Urania* <note>The Muse of astronomy, often identified with celestial goddesses</note>, who were supposedly summoned from the heavenly fates to provide aid. Many scholars apply the words of Philastrius <note>A 4th-century bishop and writer on heresies</note> to this ritual. In his work *On Heresies* (chapter 15), where he imagines much for himself, he makes the *Queen of Heaven*, the *Celestial Goddess of the Africans*, and the *Fortune of Heaven* one and the same. Regarding the subject of the *Lamentations of Jeremiah*, he says: "There is," he writes, "a heresy among the Jews that invokes a Queen, and even the Fortune of Heaven, whom they also call the 'Celestial One' in Africa; they did not hesitate to offer sacrifices to her in the time of the Prophet Jeremiah, for which reason Jeremiah wrote his Lamentations." From this, the learned scholars Reinesius, Salmasius, and Selden have argued quite skillfully that these deities are related: *Astarte*, the *Celestial Goddess of the Carthaginians*, the *Venus* of the Latins and Greeks, *Minerva*, *Juno* (whom they called "the prosperity and seat of cities" <note>original Greek: εὐωνίαν & ἕδραν πόλεων</note>), *Belisama*, *Lucina*, *Io*, the *Mylitta* of the Assyrians, the *Lilith* of the Hebrews (from which comes the *Alileth* of the Arabs), the *Muta* of the Persians, and the *Syrian Goddess* of Hierapolis. Satan has worked strenuously among the children of this world so that the worship of the *Sun* and *Moon* might be recommended to them under various names. The Phoenicians and their Carthaginian colonists worshiped a *Celestial God*, who is *Baal Shamin* <note>Hebrew: בעל שמין, meaning "Lord of the Heavens"</note>, and a *Celestial Goddess*, who is *Baalat Shamin* <note>Hebrew: בעלת שמין, meaning "Lady of the Heavens"</note>. This is the *Melekhet ha-Shamayim* <note>Hebrew: מלכת השמים</note> of Jeremiah; there is little doubt that this title refers to the *Moon*, just as the first name refers to the *Sun*. From distant shores and the times of the ancients, that worship of the Sun spread, becoming so confused and broken into multiple and disparate naming conventions among different nations that it is difficult to find an end to them.

<margin>Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods, Book 3</margin>
Cicero recounts that there were several *Jupiters*, *Saturns*, *Mercuries*, *Suns*, and *Vulcans* among different nations and at various times. Seeing the customs of that age, who could not cry out: *“O the spirit of that ancient and iron age!”* Among the pagans, we have *Macrobius*, who reduces the gods of the ethnic peoples back to the *Sun* in his *Saturnalia* (Book 1, from chapter 17 to the end), where he shows at length that the names *Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, Liber, Horus, Osiris*, and many others signified the *Sun*. Certainly, in natural theology, the chief gods are referred to the *Sun* and the *Moon*. From this, they affirm that *Janus* is the same as the *Sun*, and that all gods are expressed under the name of *Janus*. Hence, they note that *Apollo* and *Diana* were carved in place of *Janus*; and sometimes the face of another god, such as *Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, Minerva, Ceres*, or *Hercules*, was added, since all these gods are referred back to *Janus*.

<margin>Book 6, page 15</margin>
Ludovicus Demontiosus, in his work *The Gallic Fame*, teaches from the secrets of the ancients that *Hercules* is the same as the *Sun* and *Janus*, and that his twelve labors denote the twelve signs of the *Zodiac* traversed by the *Sun*. For anyone who desires to know more fully and exquisitely the reduction of the gods to the *SUN*, the most industrious work of *Vossius*, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, will serve above all others. In his second section, he shows abundantly that the *Sun* was worshiped by the Phoenicians, Moabites, Assyrians, Babylonians, Syrians, Arabs, Egyptians, Greeks, Romans, and finally by other nations throughout almost the entire world under various names and rites. By *Molech*, the *Sun* is understood, as Peter Faber proves in his *Semestria*. That most celebrated prince of gods, *Jupiter*, was the *Sun*, according to Macrobius (chapter 23), and *Saturn*, the most noble 

<column-break/>

<margin>The Queen of Heaven and ritual cakes</margin>
god, was the same as the *Sun*; for the Phoenicians and Assyrians decreed that *Saturn* was the same as the *Sun*, and worshiped him under the name of *Heli*; as Salmasius observed from Damascius, Servius, and Photius in his *Notes on Vopiscus's Aurelian*. Among the Celts, it also seems that *Saturn* was called by the native name *Hellus*. Certainly, it is conjectured that *Apollo* or *Phoebus* (that is, the *Sun*) was worshiped by the Celts under the name *Helenus*, partly because it is said that a temple of his existed at Frankfurt am Main, where the *Druids* performed sacred rites to him; hence the name given to the place was *Helenopolis*. As for the "Helenus" that Trithemius thrusts upon us (citing Hunibald, who published the eighteen-volume *Annals of France* under King Clovis) as the Trojan leader and founder of that city, those who write the *Annals of the Germans* know him to be a fiction. Some have doubted whether the name *Belenus* was a corruption for *Helenus* <note>original Greek: ἀντὶ τοῦ Helenus</note> in Tertullian’s *Apology* and Capitolinus’s *Life of Maximinus*. Franciscus Junius also saw this in his *Notes on Tertullian*, thinking *Belenus* was said instead of *Hemelum*, meaning the *sky* <note>German: Himmel</note>, who was worshiped by the Germans alongside *Hertus* many centuries ago.

<margin>See Spelman in his Glossary, p. 351</margin>
For P. Pithoeus, Scaliger, Ausonius, Caspar Bruschius, and several others assert that *Belenus* was a deity of the Germans. What is the origin of this name, I ask? A certain learned man thinks it is named from "the arrows" <note>original Greek: τὰ βέλη (*ta belē*)</note>, as if it were a Greek name—a derivation that seems no more sharp than Herwart’s theory on the Celtiberian god *Endovellicus*, supposedly named from "within" and "arrows" <note>original Greek: ἔνδον (*endon*) and βέλη (*belē*)</note>.

<margin>Book on the Wonders of Baths</margin>
Tertullian, in his *Apology*, makes *Belenus* the god of the Noricans when he says: "Every province and city has its own god: as Syria has Astarte, Arabia has Dysares, Noricum has Belenus, and Africa has the Celestial One." Critics handle this passage like cobblers handle leather or potters handle clay. Marcus Donatus reads it as *Bellenus* and considers him to be *Mars*, whom they put in charge of war (*bellum*). Just as antiquity fabricated *Bellona*, the goddess of wars, establishing her as the sister of *Mars*. Egnatius reads *Fellenus* and says he is the tutelary god and presiding deity of the people of Aquileia; for inscriptions formerly erected there and brought forward by Pighius and Gruter testify that his shrine, *Tibilenus* as others read it, was at Aquileia. Thomas Reinesius, a most sagacious investigator of Celtic antiquities, deduced *Bellinus* from *Baal* and *Bel* adjectivally <note>original Greek: ἐπιθετικῶς</note> with a Latin termination through an ingenious conjecture. Scaliger thinks it is a Gallic word denoting *Apollo*. If there are other conjectures with which scholars are accustomed to butt heads, we do not care for them now; if your curiosity cannot be satisfied, you may consult Vossius. To return to our path from this digression <note>original Greek: παρεκβάσει ἀνίωμεν</note>, we must not overlook what the same author of the *Apology* says:

<margin>ch. 16. 33.</margin>
"The Persian nation worshiped the Sun depicted on a linen cloth; for they especially venerated the Sun as their presiding deity, as Herodotus wrote in his first book..."

<margin>
The Queen of Heaven and poems
</margin>
...the interpreter <note>referring to Herodotus</note> says in these words: They have a custom of climbing the highest mountains to sacrifice victims to Jupiter, calling the whole circle of heaven "Jupiter"; they sacrifice to the Sun and Moon, and to the Earth, fire, water, and winds; and they have performed these sacred rites to the Sun from the very beginning. They also sacrifice to Urania <note>the Celestial Goddess</note>, having been taught this by the Assyrians and Arabs. The Sun is called "Mitra" by the Persians. Curtius, in his fourth book, invokes the Sun as "Mitra" (though others incorrectly write "Mars") as the sacred and eternal fire. Regarding the Assyrians, Macrobius writes in chapter 23 that they celebrated the Sun with the greatest ceremonies under the name of Jupiter, whom they nicknamed "the Heliopolitan Zeus." The Egyptians worshipped the same Sun under the name of Osiris, as we have already relayed from Diodorus; and they called the Sun "Osiris" and the Moon "Isis" for a specific reason based on the names. Following the same Egyptian thought, Eusebius in *Preparation for the Gospel* (Book 1, Chapter 9) explains the fable of Isis and Osiris as representing the Sun and Moon, as Vossius specifically taught in his work *On Idolatry*.

Regarding the Germans, Caesar writes in Book 6 of the *Gallic War*: "They count only those among the number of the gods whom they can see and by whose resources they are clearly helped: the Sun, Vulcan <note>Fire</note>, and <margin>Vol. 4, page 104.</margin> the Moon; they have not even heard of the others by rumor." Regarding the Indians <note>of India</note>, Lucian, in his book *On the Dance*, says that when they rise in the morning to adore the Sun, they salute the Sun with a dance: "They stand," he says, "facing the east and greet the sunrise with a dance, wordlessly posturing themselves and mimicking the dance of the god" <note>original Greek: Ἐκείνοι πρὸς τὴν ἀνατολὴν στάντες, ὀρχήσει τὴν ἀνατολὴν ἀσπάζονται, σχηματίζοντες ἑαυτοὺς σιωπῇ καὶ μιμούμενοι τὴν χορείαν τοῦ θεοῦ</note>. Similar are the "Worshippers of the Heavens" <note>Latin: *caelicolae*</note> mentioned in the Theodosian Code regarding Jews and Heavenly worshippers, about whom one may consult Lipsius’s notes on Tacitus, Scaliger, Baronius, and Selden. Today, the Indians <note>of the Americas</note> worship what appears in the sky; for instance, the Tapuyas <note>a tribe in Brazil</note> venerate the stars of the Pleiades, as our late friend Marcgraf teaches us in his *Natural History of Brazil*. But we have wandered enough; let us return to the main points and get back in step, as they say, lest the addition to the bag be larger than the bag itself, or "lest the episode becomes many times larger than the main chapter" <note>original Greek: ἢ οὕτω γε ἐν τῷ ἐπεισοδίῳ πολλαπλάσιον ἔτι τὸ κεφαλαῖον</note>. See also Philipp Cluverius in *Ancient Germany*, who provided an excellent chapter on the worship of the stars from the authority of the ancients, and G. J. Vossius, a man of great genius, judgment, and learning, who did much to collect the opinions of the ancients on Solar worship; consult his second book on *Idolatry*, where he laboriously devotes fifteen entire chapters to confirming this matter.

### Jeremiah XVI. 5. 6. 7.

> For thus says the Lord: Do not enter the house of mourning, nor go to lament, nor bemoan them; for I have taken away my peace from this people, says the Lord, even loving-kindness and mercies.
> Both the great and the small shall die in this land; they shall not be buried, neither shall men lament for them, nor cut themselves, nor make themselves bald for them.
> Neither shall men break bread for them in mourning, to comfort them for the dead; neither shall men give them the cup of consolation to drink for their father or for their mother.
<note>The source provides the text in Hebrew, Greek (Septuagint), and Latin</note>

<column-break/>

...they shall not be buried, and they shall not be wailed for, they shall not gash themselves for them, nor shall they make incisions, nor shall they be shaved.
And bread shall not be broken in their mourning for consolation over the deceased, nor shall they drink the cup of consolation for his father and for his mother.

> *For thus spoke Jehovah: Do not enter the house of mourning, nor shave in order to wail, nor condole with them; because I have taken away my peace from that people, said Jehovah, even mercy and compassions.*
> *And the great and small shall die in this land: they shall not be buried, nor shall they wail for them, nor shall they cut themselves, nor shall they make themselves bald for them.*
> *And they shall not stretch out their hands because of mourning, to console them over the dead, nor shall they give them the cup of consolations to drink over their father and over their mother.*

Who is there that does not realize that nothing in the whole world is more changeable than the customs of nations? Various and ever-shifting laws and rituals concerning the dead succeed one another; Lilius Gyraldus will show that nothing is more variable, as he briefly recounted the various rites of burial in his elegant book dedicated to Carolus Militius, a nobleman of Meissen. From this, one may recall how many ways and how multifariously these funeral institutions have varied, so much so that what was an honor to one nation seemed a disgrace to another, and what seemed ridiculous to one appeared solemn to another. As many legislators as there are, so many are the laws. One man thought the most blessed kind of burial was not to be buried at all, or to be buried without a name. Another thought the memory of the dead was not cared for except with magnificent structures and various kinds of ambitions. One opinion is that it matters little whether bodies are dissolved by earth or by smoke; another holds the opposite. It is the custom of this nation to cremate the body with fire, and of another to preserve it forever. For one, funerals were mourned; for another, they were feasts, solemnized with games and song. On this side, the Egyptian commanded what, on the other side, the Greek forbade. Lucian records these various rites *on mourning*, noting that the custom was for the Greek to burn, the Persian to bury, the Scythian to eat <note>a reference to the ancient belief in Scythian cannibalism/ritual consumption</note>, and the Egyptian to embalm. Thus, institutions are as varied as the nations themselves. Indeed, sometimes a single nation is endowed with different laws as well as different customs. Some mourned with voices and carried out the funeral with specific wailings; others rejected this. Yet most were unanimous in certain rites. A ritual common to almost everyone, and common to nearly all ancient peoples, was that in mourning and heavy grief, whether public or private, they would change their clothing, tear their garments, beat their breasts, cut their hair, and sprinkle themselves with ashes; by these symbols, those ancients most often testified to their sorrow. Our own sacred annals persuade us that this was the practice among the Hebrews, providing the examples that follow. It is pious and laudable to grieve with those who grieve and to weep with those who weep. Those Stoic precepts of *apatheia* <note>original Greek: ἀπαθείας — a state of being unmoved by emotion</note> forbid all mourning and command the Wise Man never to be moved, neither to be touched by mercy or pain, nor to be stirred by anger. We are taught otherwise about the condition of humanity and the stirrings of the soul by the law and the example of Christ. It is the mark of men well-disposed by nature to lament at funerals, especially those of the people we held most dear in life. Pretu...

<meta>This page transitions from discussing the worship of celestial bodies to an exploration of mourning customs and the concept of "piety" or "duty" toward the dead, drawing from Greek, Roman, and Hebrew sources to contextualize Jeremiah 16.</meta>

# Jeremiah 16:5, 6, 7

<margin>Funeral rites.</margin>
Antiphanes, above all others, praised friends whose final fates must be lamented, but <note>original Greek: μετρίως & inmoderate</note> moderately and not immoderately, nor in a disorganized or indecent manner. His verses are indeed timely and relevant, and they deserve to be read:
> One should mourn for relatives and friends with moderation.
> For they have not died, but have simply gone ahead
> upon that same road which it is necessary
> for all of us to travel.

David mourned and wept for Jonathan, being moved beyond measure by his premature death. Love elicited these tears, and the spectators attributed them to love, saying <note>original Greek: δεικτικῶς</note> expressively: *See how he loved him.* This is the first duty of humanity toward the deceased, for which the eyes of Christians rightly shed tears and their souls pour out sighs. The speech of Anaxagoras upon the news of his son's death was austere: *I knew I had fathered a mortal.* Even more austere seems that statement by Ennius: *Let no one honor me with tears, nor conduct my funeral with weeping.*

Better is the sentiment of Solon, who sought to have his death honored by the tears of his friends; this is contained in a distich <note>a two-line poem</note> recited by Plutarch and Stobaeus in their <margin>Comparison of Solon and Publicola, Discourse 121.</margin> works:
> May my death not come unwept, but may I leave behind
> pain and groans for my friends when I have died.

By this, he declares that he does not wish his death to be devoid of the grief and lamentations of his friends, as witnessed by Cicero in his work *On Old Age*; the Orator also suggests this sentiment in verse in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, page 191:
*Let my death not lack tears; let us leave*
->Grief to our friends, so they may celebrate the funeral with a groan.<-

By the praise of this wise man—as Cicero calls him—proper rites ought to be celebrated for those who die by the common law of nature; for that reason, he prayed that if he were to live no longer, his funeral should be escorted by tears. But if the example of that Legislator <note>Solon</note> does not move someone, let him hear the Son of Sirach <note>author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus</note>, where there is a greater abundance of thought and greater force: according to the custom of the age in which he lived, mourning for the dead <margin>Sirach 22:10, 11, 12.</margin> was carried out for seven days. This had been introduced by the custom of his nation: that there was no funeral which did not include lamentation, a heap of dirges, and other very open signs of mourning and grief; and even today among the remnants of that nation, it is common to be moved by specific gestures over the deceased. Regarding this lamentation, he commanded again in chapter 38:16, 17, 18, that it should be intense, and the funeral should be conducted according to one's dignity with bitter weeping and fervent wailing. He expresses this in charming words that can move one to tears: *My son, shed tears over the dead, and begin the mourning as one who has suffered bitterly; cover his body according to funeral custom, and do not neglect his burial, etc.* This is the first duty of humanity toward the dead, which we pay to nature as something owed and solemn. For it belongs to human mercy to weep for the calamities of others, and to testify to a sympathizing soul through the honorable care of a funeral. On the contrary, it is unjust to utterly neglect these final duties. Indeed, even those to whom the voice of divine law was unknown were not ignorant of this, and they showed it at least by the honorable name of "pious duty." I speak of the Romans, who called those religious duties paid to the dead *Justa* <note>The "Just" or "Rights"</note>, because they were performed by right for those who, while living, had deserved well of human society. By the best right, funeral processions and services are owed to those who have deserved well of us, according to Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book 6, line 664:
->*And those who made others mindful of them by deserving well.*<-

<column-break/>

<margin>Funeral rites.</margin>
What the Greeks thought is declared even by the name *enagismos* <note>sacrificial offerings to the dead</note>, by which they express *theia nomima* <note>divine customs</note> with <note>original Greek: ἐναγῶς</note> purity and veneration. The word *hagia* means a sacred thing, to which veneration is due. According to their view, *enagizein* is to perform *enagismous* <note>sacred rites</note> for the dead. The *Onomasticon* <note>a Greek dictionary</note>, page 76, lists *emba* and *enagismata*. Suidas defines *enages* as that which is venerable and holy; *hages* as a sacred object of veneration; and on page 899 <margin>page 898.</margin> defines *enages* as venerable, or even devoted. *Enagizein* means to bring sacred libations or to sacrifice to those who have passed away. If we look for the words and phrases by which Sacred Scripture commends the *enagismon* and the rights of funerals, one word occurs out of many: *Chesed* <note>Hebrew: חסד, often translated as loving-kindness or mercy</note>, which presents under a single view the just and rightly owed works of humanity. Everything offered to honor the deceased is included in the word *Chesed*. Naomi, bidding farewell to her daughters-in-law, used these words: *Go, return each of you to her mother's house; may the Lord deal kindly with you, as you have dealt with the dead and with me.* <margin>Ruth 1:8.</margin> She could not have expressed the daughters-in-law's duties of kindness toward herself, their mother-in-law, and their husbands with a better word. The Hebrew word has a broad meaning, and it should be known that there is no word in the Latin language that properly expresses and exhausts its force. Drusius notes this here on page 32, writing: *The duty that someone grants to their father-in-law is properly called "Piety" by the Latins. For there is piety toward parents and those in the place of parents. But even the duty performed by a wife for her husband is called "Chesed" by the Hebrews. Therefore, that name has a broad scope, and it cannot be quite conveniently expressed by a single Latin word, since in common usage "piety" is not found in God, but is directed toward God.* For no one, I think, would speak thus: *May the Lord act piously toward you,* or *May He exercise piety toward you.* Those who examine the words note that in its primary and proper meaning, it signifies the same thing for the Hebrews as *storgē* <note>natural affection</note> does for the Greeks; Forsterus <margin>page 286.</margin> prefers to interpret it by this name, so that it denotes that affection of piety and charity with which parents are naturally touched toward their children, and they in turn toward their parents; which a brother feels for a brother, a husband for a wife (and she reciprocally for him), and a friend for a friend. It can and will be permitted, as the logic of the speech and the convenience of the thought requires, to be rendered variously: now as *charity*, now as *piety*, now as *benevolence*, now as *mercy*, now as *gratitude*, now as *sanctity* or *goodness*. We see Roman writers use the notable word "Piety," by which we are reminded how much they favored those who observed the laws of final necessity. Cicero, in the second book *On Laws*, says: *Parents and children of both sexes, and also other relatives by blood or marriage, are to be mourned according to the measure of piety and the endurance of one's own soul, as each person wishes.* A wife who mourns her husband is said to "provide the just rites of religion"; she who does not was pronounced "infamous," and he who knowingly married her contracted a "stain of shame." Statius, according to Gevartius (page 4), says that Antigone was "pious" because she committed her brother to the earth against the royal edict which intended him to be unburied. While the Chorus passes judgment on this deed, it feels that the pious girl acted piously, but while it considers the right of the Magistrate, it does not entirely approve of the act; with an elegant <note>original Greek: βραχυλογίᾳ</note> brevity seasoned with two maxims, it says:
> To act piously is a kind of piety.
> But power, to him who cares for power,
> is in no way to be transgressed.
And when she was condemned to death for this deed, she said that for the sake of her piety she had to endure the guilt of impiety...
