<meta>This page continues the discussion of funeral rites and the moral obligation of "piety" (duty/devotion) toward the deceased, moving from classical Greek examples to the biblical concept of "Chesed" (mercy/lovingkindness) as shown in the stories of Ruth, Jacob, David, and the prophet Ezekiel.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Funeral rites.</margin> ...must be maintained, as witnessed by Sophocles in *Antigone, verse 1040.*
> <note>original Greek: Την δυσσέβειαν εὐσεβὲς ἐκτησάμην.</note> **Through piety, she says, I have acquired the charge of impiety, and because of a pious act I am held guilty of a crime.**
Indeed, in the same work she cries out at *verse 1058*:
> <note>original Greek: Δια πρὸς οἵων ἀνδρῶν πάσχω Την ευσέβιαν σεβολάλα.</note> **See what I suffer, and from what kind of men, for revering piety.**

Sacred history describes the deaths, mourning, funerals, and sepulchers of so many pious men so accurately for this reason: so that through them we might be reminded of the piety and mercy we owe to the departed. Far be from us the mark of infamy and impiety; rather, let "mercy" <note>original Greek: ἔλεος (eleos)</note> be present. It is for this that those two young women <note>Ruth and Orpah</note> are commended by the Greek translators, who translated the word *Chesed* <note>Hebrew: חסד, meaning lovingkindness or loyal mercy</note> here, as they commonly do elsewhere, to make the meaning of the words clearer: *Go, return each of you* <note>Hebrew: אשה (ishah), meaning woman or each one</note> *to her mother's house. May the Lord deal kindly with you, as you have dealt with the dead and with me.* They showed mercy toward their dead husbands, Mahlon and Chilion, with a devoted heart and a merciful spirit, by paying the due funeral honors and <term>burial rites<note>original Greek: κηδεύσια (kedeusia)</note></term>, and by abundantly showing through other duties of this kind how dear their husbands had been to them while they lived. For this reason, their <term>natural affection<note>original Greek: στοργὴν (storge)</note></term> as daughters-in-law is praised, because they observed the honors due to the tombs of the dead. They were not <note>original Greek: ἄστοργοι (astorgoi)</note> devoid of natural affection or alienated from the feeling of charity. Whatever piety, whatever humanity, whatever charity required, they showed it profusely at and after the death of their husbands. Hence their mother-in-law <note>Naomi</note> says they deserved well of the dead, praying for them to have rest and an end to their miseries through another, happier marriage. Thus, *Chesed* implies an applied zeal and a supreme love for their husbands, with whom they had lived without quarrel or strife, whom they had kindly nursed during illness according to the law of marriage-charity, and whom they honorably mourned and buried after they departed this life. And this same grace, most praiseworthy even when not between blood relatives, is usually called mercy. As when Jacob said to his son Joseph: <margin>Genesis 47:29</margin> *If now I have found grace in your eyes, put, I pray, your hand under my thigh, and deal with me in* חסד <note>Chesed</note>, *mercy and truth, that you will not bury me in Egypt.* With what dutiful piety and with what funeral procession the son took care of the burial is declared in its proper place, so that it is abundantly clear how very observant he was of the burial and the funeral bed. As the father bargains with the son regarding his burial and his translation to the land of Canaan, so the son carries it out, performing for the father the benefit he requested. David also blesses the men of Jabesh Gilead because they had delivered Saul to burial, in 2 Samuel 2:5, where he addresses them thus: *Blessed be you of Jehovah, who have shown this mercy toward your lord, toward Saul, in that you have buried him.* Afterward, he himself transferred the bones of Saul, 2 Samuel 21:14. He testifies that this duty was acceptable to God, and that God approves of those who, by such piety and kindness, committed the remains of Saul to the earth. When Sulpitius had performed this kindness for Marcellus, who had lost his life from a wound and for whom the Athenians had erected a marble monument, Cicero says in his *Epistolae ad Familiares*: *Thus, whatever our duties were, on account of our association and kinship, we performed them all for him, both living and dead.* Mercy is also shown to the dead when the children of the deceased are helped,

<column-break/>

likewise their relatives and kin. Jonathan, about to commend himself and his family to David, says: <margin>*While I yet live*</margin> *you shall not only show me the mercy of the Lord—* 1 Samuel <margin><note>The margin incorrectly says ISA.</note></margin> *but also when I am dead. You shall not cut off your mercy from my house forever, no, not even when Jehovah has cut off the enemies of David every one.* Having given their right hands, they mutually pledge and promise that they will keep all the laws of friendship intact and protected. By the same bond with which they began to be joined, they wished to proceed. Nor did Jonathan think it shameful for himself to be moved by concern for David’s miseries; nor does David, after the death of Jonathan, forget this benefit, according to 2 Samuel 9:1. Mindful of the covenant struck with Jonathan—as one who knew that a royal throne is stabilized by faith and piety but dissolved by perfidy—David said: *Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake?* and in verse 17 <note>likely referring to v. 3 or v. 7</note> he says he wishes to provide the *mercy of God* to the son of Jonathan, who was Mephibosheth. By this, he indicates that Kings and Princes, through their beneficence and <term>good deeds<note>original Greek: ευεργεσία (evergesia)</note></term> toward the afflicted, come closest to the likeness of God. By a certain special grace, Mephibosheth was happily provided for, to whom the King said: *Fear not, for I will surely show you kindness for the sake of Jonathan your father, and will restore to you all the land of Saul your father, etc.* While all the rest of the lineage of Saul was destroyed, the posterity of Jonathan remained until the Babylonian exile. So true is what Theocritus said:
> **Better things happen to the children of the pious, but not to the impious.**
But what shall be made of those testimonies where God forbids signs of mourning to be made? To Ezekiel, God prohibited that he should wail or weep for the death of his wife. He forbids <note>Hebrew: לא תעשה (lo ta'aseh)</note> it to be done, lest the corpse be escorted with funeral pomp; He prohibits him from changing his clothes or putting on the appearance of a mourner, for the word of Jehovah came to him: <margin>*</margin> *Son of man, behold, I take away from you the desire of your eyes with a stroke; yet you shall neither mourn nor weep, nor shall your tears run down.* <margin>*</margin> *Cease to cry, make no mourning for the dead, bind your turban (for so the usual head covering is called) upon you, and put your shoes on your feet, and do not cover your lips, and do not eat the bread of men.* The Prophet's wife dies; he does not indulge in mourning as he had been commanded, he does not pay the funeral dues, nor does he show any sign of sadness to the people, who asked the reason for it, saying: <margin>*</margin> *Will you not tell us what these things signify, that you are doing?* What those things signified is explained by the Prophet from verse 21 to the end of the chapter. Typically, these things indicated that such a sudden destruction would happen to the city, just as a sudden calamity had fallen upon the Prophetic house through the death of a most desired wife whom he had ardently loved; and it would also happen that their own tragic death, and that of the city, wives, and children, would be such that the enemies would not allow them to perform the proper funeral rites. For this reason, God commanded the Prophet, on the day of his wife's funeral—whom God had snatched away by a sudden death—that he should not weep, nor show the usual signs of grief, nor observe the customary ceremonies. Doubtless, as Pintus says on this passage <note>page 290</note>, it was so that the Jews, stunned by the wonder of such an unusual thing, might ask him the cause of such a portentous and unaccustomed novelty, and thus understand that a supreme calamity was hanging over them. He ardently loved his wife, the Prophe—

### Jeremiah 16:5, 6, 7. Page 613. Funeral Rites.

<margin>
marginal note: Ezekiel 24:15.
</margin>
The Prophet <note>Referring to Ezekiel, whose wife died suddenly as a sign to Israel</note> found a sweet relief from his sorrows in funeral rites, but this was snatched away by a great blow. In the Hebrew, the word is <term>maggephah<note>Hebrew: מַגֵּפָה, meaning a plague, slaughter, or sudden stroke</note></term>, which the Old Translator <note>The Vulgate</note>, Junius, and others translate as "plague" or "stroke." The Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> uses <term>disturbance<note>Greek: ταραχὴν (tarachēn)</note></term>, which an interpreter renders as "sharpness" or "distress." The term <term>phalanx<note>Greek: φάλαγξ</note></term> does not fit here. It is worthy of note that he uses four words—<term>mourn and weep</term>, <unclear>cry and lament</unclear> <note>Hebrew roots: אבל (avel), דמע (dama), בכה (bakhah), and ספד (saphad)</note>—to wail, weep, shed tears, and groan. These words, which suggest a shared conspiracy of grief in a mutual bond, are not heaped together in vain; the speech rises in its somber tone. The same reality is expressed in various ways through several forms, and by this emphatic description, the Prophet is forbidden—whether by voice, groan, or other signs of sorrow—from testifying to the immense pain he felt at his wife's death. It increased his grief that he could not deplore his grief; and what was truly bitter was that he could not even use tears and other reliefs for his sorrows. To prohibit tears only increases the heart’s tears. *Therefore, it must be,* says Villalpando,

<margin>
page 311.
</margin>
\* that the Prophet was afflicted with the most bitter pain and immense sorrow when he was forbidden to weep, sigh, or sob. Hence, in the *Panegyric of Theodosius*, we read: *It is some relief for calamities to have given tears to evils, and to have eased the breast with sighs.* And Ovid says in the first elegy of the fifth book of *Tristia*:

> Strangled is the grief that is shut in, and it seethes within,
> And it is forced to multiply its own strength.

A marvelous prohibition from God! He was not allowed to mourn his most devoted wife with the customary ceremonies—a thing allowed to others. God forbade him the very mourning for the one whom He had struck with the heaviest grief; He prohibits tears and inhibits the signs of sorrow. But marvel at the justice of God, who is wonderful in His works. God first snatches away the wife, and the wretched Prophet is not permitted to weep. He commands *silence* upon the grief, something which Seneca says *cannot be commanded* \* and that there is no greater cause for being moved than being unable to weep, as he also says in the first book of *Controversies*. Let admiration be shown to these divine commands; let not unmercifulness be ascribed to Him, much less cruelty. The less you grasp the understanding of the work, the more reverently you should admire and venerate the counsel of God. The wickedness of the Israelites cost the divine Prophet dearly—namely, the loss of his most beloved wife. This loss designated God’s lack of mercy toward the people. Do not curiously scrutinize why He afflicted the Prophet, and not another, with a domestic plague. It is enough that you know these things were divinely ordained as a type <note>A "type" is a historical person or event that foreshadows a future spiritual reality</note>. Among mortals, it is a sign of inhumanity and lack of mercy not to mourn, not to pay the proper rites, not to care for funerals, nor to permit them to be cared for. For this reason, Cicero condemns the cruelty of Piso in his *Speech against Piso, no. 17*, because he did not allow the Senate to mourn the calamity of the Republic or change their garments: *Are you the one,* he says, *whom your own cruelty pleases? You, who when the Senate decreed that its grief and pain should be declared by a change of clothing, and when you saw the Republic mourning with the grief of its most distinguished order—O our merciful one! (spoken ironically)—what do you do? What tyrant in all of Scythia ever did this: that he would not permit those whom he afflicted with grief to mourn?* You leave the sorrow, but you take away the signs of sorrow. You snatch away tears not by consoling, but by threatening. Thus we can say that God took away the signs of sorrow by which pain and mourning are indicated, and snatched away tears. The heathens were so bold in their calamities that they reproached the Gods for unmercifulness and accused them of cruelty if anything happened. Hence Virgil: \*

<margin>
Controversies 3, 3.
4. 16.
7. 17.
7. 19.
Eclogues 5.
</margin>

->And embracing the piteous body of her son,<-
->The mother calls both the Gods and the stars cruel.<-

So also Tibullus in book 1, elegy 4:
->Cruel Gods! — — — he has put off his young years.<-
->The fates gave no delay to such beauty.<-

<margin>
page 151.
</margin>
By a similar divine interdict, mourning is forbidden to the Prophet Jeremiah. For God commands Jeremiah that he should not perform any kind of kindness or mercy toward the dead. *Do not enter,* He says in chapter 16:5, *into the house of mourning, and do not go to lament, nor go about for their sake.* This was in place of a punishment; God wished to indicate by this <term>wrath<note>Greek: ὀργῇ (orgē)</note></term> to the Jews, who were despisers of Him, how unworthy they were to be lifted up by prophetic consolation. He adds this most heavy penalty: *I have taken away my peace from this people, as well as my lovingkindness and mercies,* because they had turned away from God through idolatry; He takes back that grace with which He had previously favored them. Therefore, this prohibition was given to Jeremiah as a sign, *so that,* as Castrius notes from Hugh, *he might express by his own act the future solitude and unhappiness, which would be so great that no one would remain to provide those things which are granted to the dead and the mourners by the common law of nations.* He did this so that, by this threat, he might lead the people to whom he spoke back to a better way of life. What was that penalty? That hard fortune which was to come under the <term>surface<note>Greek: ἐνδέρματι (endermati), perhaps referring to the "hide" or "yoke" of captivity</note></term> of captivity, where they were sharply vexed, stripped of their fatherland and goods, their houses burned, their wives ravished, their children killed, and they themselves cast out from all their fortunes. This was the aim: that he might terrify them with the future punishment, so they would dread it and avoid it, and he persuaded them toward a better mind. However, although interpreters differ in the explanation of the words, they coincide in the sense. And, to review a few: the Old Translator and those who <term>agree with him<note>Greek: ὁμόψηφοι (homopsēphoi)</note></term>, among whom he seems to hold the helm, generally take the name <term>marzeah<note>Hebrew: מַרְזֵחַ</note></term> to refer to a feast, whereas the Hebrews, Pagninus, and Vatablus translate it as *mourning*. The same word, with slightly different vowel points, appears in *Amos 6:7*, where Pagninus and Vatablus understood it as mourning, but the Old Translator understood it as "factions." The Septuagint says: <term>do not enter into their assembly<note>Greek: μὴ εἰσέλθῃς εἰς θίασον αὐτῶν (mē eiselthēs eis thiason autōn)</note></term>.

<margin>
In this place, folio 352 b.
</margin>
An anonymous author renders it: *Do not enter into their dances.* From which Zwingli \* notes the Septuagint translated <term>marzeah</term> as <term>thiasos<note>Greek: θίασον, a term for a ritual procession or assembly</note></term>. Jerome translated it as "house of feasting," since the word <term>bayit<note>Hebrew: בית, house</note></term> and the preposition can signify *in*, *within*, and *into*; hence in this place it was not necessary to translate it as "into the house." We have combined the preposition with the verb ("do not go to the assembly"), by which the aforementioned <term>thiasos</term> or "assembly" could be taken as something outside a house or under another preposition. Moreover, the Prophet understands by <term>marzeah</term> either public banquets or public dances, both of which "assembly" encompasses. The word <term>thiasos</term> generally denotes an assembly and a gathering. Specifically, it refers to an assembly of those skipping and leading dances. Likewise, an assembly of those feasting, and the feast itself. The word is "doubtful," to speak with the jurists, and it mostly prevailed in the sacred rites of Bacchus, to whose peculiar minor deity that name was given, so that they called those Bacchic dancers and the companions of the insane choir <term>thiasōtai<note>Greek: θιασιώτας</note></term>. Hence Suidas on page 1322: <term>Thiasōtai are properly those around Dionysus, and thiasos is a dance, a sacred dance, and a crowd gathering for a purpose; or finally, the honor of the gods</term>, or as Harpocration has it, <term>for a rite and the honor of the gods</term>. Hesychius says: <term>Thiasos is a banquet and a crowd. Not only the Bacchic kind, but also the laboring kind. Thiasos is a dance</term>.

These restrictions served as a "type" or sign of the impending divine judgment and the withdrawal of God's mercy from the people of Israel.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the ritual prohibitions placed upon the prophets, specifically focusing on the terminology of mourning assemblies and the use of prophetic signs (actions rather than words) to warn the people of Israel of their impending exile and the cessation of all social joys.</meta>

# ANTIQUITIES OF THE BIBLE

<margin>Funeral rites.</margin> A <term>thiasos<note>Greek: θίασος (thiasos). Historically, this referred to a ritual procession or group, often associated with the worship of Bacchus/Dionysus</note></term> is a composition or gathering of a choir, or a simple crowd; sometimes it refers to a Bacchic revel or a swarm of women. *Thiasotai* are those who meet and dine together in houses. *Thiasotai* are also dancers. Regarding the Greek interpreter, we are almost amazed that he used the word *thiasos* to express the Hebrew word <term>marzeach<note>Hebrew: מַרְזֵחַ, typically referring to a mourning feast or a cultic association gathering</note></term>. For, as far as I know, while that word is usually applied by the Greeks to joyful matters, to attribute it to a mournful assembly such as the Prophet describes would be "waterless" <note>Greek: ἄνυδρον (anydron), meaning dry, unfitting, or lacking substance</note>, since there is not a trace or footprint of that name in such a context, if I have used my eyes correctly. Pollux places this word in the category of "convivial things" and proves it to be a gathering of those playing and rejoicing, <margin>6. Onom. 15 p. 271.</margin> hence in his 9th book he joins it synonymously to <note>Greek phrases translated</note> "a group of teachers and a choir of students." This is also apparent from Plutarch’s *Antony*, in which dancers, lyre-players, and actors are combined into one triumphal assembly, along with "the whole *thiasos* of Asian spectacles." There was no feasting here in the Prophet’s account, nor do the members of the *thiasos* or the dancers offer worship. There is no orchestra here, no stage-acting; all is sadness. For it was a multitude and a "swarm of mourners," and what was intended was the gathering for libations or "mourning meals," as the Interpreter I mentioned undoubtedly understood. However, I lack examples of its use that would allow the word to worthily hold its place. To call this sad synod and "mournful gathering" a *thiasos* is harsh and forced. Much must be granted to antiquity, and words in the Sacred Writer should not be too heavily scrutinized when the matter itself is clear. The matter is indeed perfectly plain: the Prophet's argument deals with mourning, whose ceremonies he describes step by step, and whose calamities Jehovah sets forth through a certain type. Let us look at each of these in the order they were proposed. So that God might place future evils before the eyes of the people, he forbade the Prophet from marriage, decreeing in verse 2: *“You shall not take a wife, nor shall you have sons or daughters in this place.”* Precepts and warnings had been so neglected by the blind people that God used to present their punishments through certain external actions—showing the coming fates as if to be seen by the eyes and felt by the hands—to bring into their sight what they had excluded from their minds. For God taught not only by word but warned of the future by signs. Hence Isaiah walked about with naked feet (chapter 20:2). Jeremiah was ordered to buy a linen belt (chapter 13), to break a pottery jar before the people (chapter 19:10), and to put bonds and yokes on his neck (chapter 27:2). Ezekiel was ordered to pack the gear of an exile and go out (chapter 12:3-4). Whence Gregory says: <margin>on Penitential Psalm 6, folio 39. b.</margin>

> Prophecy occurs in three ways: namely, by words, by deeds, and by dreams. The very actions of the ancient Fathers are prophecies for us; while they are doing one thing, they are hinting at another, revealing hidden things to us as if through the language of their work.

Therefore, God used to invite the people with such credible pre-figurations of the mind when invitations through sermons proved useless; if not by words, then by external acts that met the eye, he left stings in their souls. For in that deplorable blindness of mind and hardness of heart—to use the words of Horace: <margin>Ars Poetica 180.</margin>

> Things dropped through the ear stir the mind more slowly,
> than those which are subjected to the faithful eyes.

Therefore, He wished to teach the people not only with ears but also with eyes, through what I might call "silent sermons." For what Jew could fail to be moved by the sight of Isaiah walking *naked and barefoot*

<column-break/>

through the streets? (Isaiah 20:2). Who would not be moved when Jeremiah, surrounded by bonds and chains, preached to the Kings? (chapter 27:2). What Jew would not have been stunned when Hosea (chapter 1), by the admirable command of God, took a *“wife of whoredoms,”* that is, a woman of many fornications who had exposed herself to the lust of all? To what purpose was this? To show through this the most effusive Idolatry of the Synagogue, which was most devoted to spiritual harlotries, no differently than a prostitute addicted to fornications. And why was Ezekiel forbidden from mourning for his wife? When you meditate on these things, let not the "novelty of the work" weaken your mind, but rather consider the "majesty of the Worker," which is above human sense. The dignity of divine works exceeds the narrowness of the human mind; if the divine ordering does not subject itself to our intellect, must the wonderful Economy of heavenly things therefore be called into doubt? Far from it. It is the same with Jeremiah: he is not to take a wife and not to be present at the gathering of mourners. Clearly, while God commands this, He shows His divine judgment; and while these things were done by the Prophets, the fame of the unusual matter grew. For what Jew would not have vehemently desired to know and learn the cause of a thing so new, unusual, and utterly "inhuman"? Since the Jews were eager for the propagation of families, they were most inclined toward marriage, and he who was unmarried or celibate was marked with reproach. This was a "specimen" of future fortune, and a "mirror" of the coming celibacy in the captivity—namely, that there would be no joys of weddings, no delights of children. When they saw Jeremiah withdrawing himself from the company of virgins and women, and abstaining from both joyful and sad *thiasois* (societies), and doing so contrary to customary practice, there arose from this an easy and obvious question about this "solitary living" <note>Latin: monotropia, from Greek μονότροπος, meaning living alone or following a single way of life</note> that was unusual in their Republic. When they saw him living by his own rule—not entering the houses of mourning, not bewailing the dead, not consoling the sad, not grieving with them, nor performing other ministries of prophecy accustomed until then—they were struck with wonder and demanded his reasons. Here the Prophet, without any figurative circumlocution, in his own person encompassed much in few words. He openly told the unyielding people what he had typically carried out in himself, and he brought the sentence of exile. He pointed out the adversities in exile with these clear words: <margin>verse 8.</margin> *“Thus says Jehovah of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am about to cause to cease from this place (of exile), before your eyes and in your days, the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride.”* <margin>verse 6.</margin> *“When the great and the small have died in this land, they shall not be buried, nor shall they lament for them, nor shall anyone cut himself or make himself bald for them.”* <margin>verse 7.</margin> *“Neither shall they break bread for them in mourning to comfort anyone for the dead.”* You have here the "sad sackcloth," and the role the Prophet played in it. Now, so that the prophetic speech may be clearer to you, consider also the funeral preparation of the Jews, and what those of other nations were. It was said above that mourning is described step by step, in its own order and most fittingly to the "type." For it proceeds from the highest to the lowest, beginning with those who ensure all things are done in order, and descends to the other ceremonies used at that time. The first thing, therefore, is that those who are in mourning, before the funeral is carried out, [must seek] from the masters of the funeral...

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Jeremiah 16:5-7, transitioning from the definition of the "thiasos" or mourning assembly to the specific roles and rituals involved in funeral rites, particularly the function of funeral directors and the significance of mourning attire.</meta>

### Jeremiah XVI. 5.6.7. 615

<margin>Funeral rites.</margin>
They also shaped funeral ceremonies. Tremellius perceives that those individuals are designated by the word when he translates: *Do not enter the house of the funeral director, nor go there to lament.* Men skilled in solemnities were chosen to organize everything necessary for mourning; they took care that nothing was omitted, so that everything was done according to ritual, and they assigned each person their place in the procession. Those who presided over the funeral in this manner were called curators, but the Romans called them <term>designatores<note>Latin: funeral directors or marshals who arranged the rank and order of a procession</note></term>. They were called "designators" because they presided over the establishment of the funeral pomp, prescribing to each person their place and order of marching. Those who cite Festus on this point, I wish they had "designated" it more clearly, for there is neither a trace nor a footprint of that name present, if I have used my eyes correctly. Funeral games—truly mournful and fatal—were usually held at the burial mounds themselves to appease the souls of the dead. Those who presided over these were called *Designatores*, who designated what, in what manner, in what order, and what was to be done.

<margin>Adelphoe Act 1, Scene 1.</margin>
Donatus, in his commentary on Terence’s *The Brothers*, says: *They are called Designatores who preside over funeral games. I believe for this reason: that in the games themselves, new things are made* (he had said that "to designate" means the same as to make something new) *and things to be watched; at the same time, the crowd is held back.* Tertullian mentions this game in *On Spectacles*, Chapter 10: *From the temple and the altars,* he says, *and that wretchedness of incense and blood, one goes amidst flutes and trumpets to two most filthy judges: the Designator of funerals and the Soothsayer.* He elegantly calls him the *judge of funerals*, whom Cicero, in his second book *On Laws*, calls the *Master of the funeral*, because he presided and directed. The remaining things are customary, *that the funeral be announced, if there are any games*, and the Master of the funeral uses an <term>accensus<note>A subordinate official or attendant</note></term> and <term>Lictors<note>Officers attending Roman magistrates, here acting as funeral guards</note></term>. The Lictors, dressed in dark clothing, served the Designator, who also presided in a dark garment, while the people watched similarly in dark clothing. As Horace says to Maecenas:
<margin>1st Epistle, 7. v. 5.</margin>
> *Maecenas, I will come; while the first figs and the heat*
> *Adorn the Designator with his black lictors.*

He explains "the fig" crudely as a sign by which the Designator was recognized in funerals; compare Kirchmann. It is a sign of autumn, not an insignia of the designator, as the Poet indicates; we have said more on this in the *Commentary on the Aphorisms of Hippocrates*. There were also funeral prefects in Athens, through whom feasts were customarily prepared at the homes of the deceased's relatives. We make the second place for <term>mourning garments</term>. It was common to indicate the interior state of the soul by exterior clothing. A sad soul gives signs of itself through a sad face and dress. The blackness of color was preferred over others in more mournful cases, just as whiteness was in more joyful ones. Hence, to be present in places of weeping while wearing a white garment was considered <term>entirely out of place<note>original: ἀπροσδιόνυσον (aprosdionyson), literally "nothing to do with Dionysus," meaning irrelevant or inappropriate</note></term>, since, as Ovid witnesses:
<margin>Tristia, Book 1, v. 6.</margin>
> *That color is not suitable for mourning.*

*Let your garments be white,* says Ecclesiastes (9:8), *and let oil poured on your head not be lacking.* A person's distinct condition requires distinct clothes. A maiden rejoices in the greenness of the color green. The robe of the royal girl Thamar was of many colors (2 Samuel 13:18). More elegant and colorful clothing is pleasing, so that it may attract the eyes of young men; for she strives to please the young man no less than a married woman her husband (1 Timothy 2:9). A widow, who spends her life in sorrow, usually wears certain garments of widowhood. Thamar, lest she be recognized by the dress of a sad widow, <margin>Genesis 38:14.</margin> having put off her garments of widowhood,

<column-break/>

<margin>Funeral rites.</margin>
covered herself with a veil and arranged her dress in the manner of harlots. Judah is deceived by the prostitute’s attire, and the clever woman deceives him after she perceived she was being mocked, under the pretext of a prostitute. A father-in-law sins with his daughter-in-law; he imprudently, and she prudently. Prudently in the act of fornication, imprudently in the act of incest. He does not know she is his daughter-in-law, who was too eager for offspring—which the Greeks call a <term>theeisron<note>original: θέεισρον, a charm or means of attraction</term></term> here, and the Latin follows. She drives away the reproach of her widowhood <term>skillfully<note>original: τεχνικῶς (technikos)</note></term> by her schemes. Judah, who thought he wanted to mock his daughter-in-law who was hoping for marriage, because of the immaturity of his third son, she mocks by the deception of her dress. She assumes the persona of a harlot so that she would not be recognized. Having taken a <term>peplum<note>A shawl or wrap</note></term>, which is called a <term>tza'if<note>Hebrew: צָעִיף</note></term>, she covers her face (for it is established that the *tza'if* was a head veil, Genesis 24:65) and sits in a public place of the road in that finery of women who are no longer in mourning. By this very act, it is suggested, as Augustine observes (Question 129 on Genesis), *that even in the times of the Patriarchs there were certain and specific garments for widows, certainly not the same as those of married women.* That widows were dressed in sadder clothing and married women sometimes in more joyful ones is also clear from the example of Judith, who wore <term>widow’s garments<note>original: ἱμάτια τῆς χηρεύσεως (himatia tes chereuseos)</note></term>. It was fitting for a widow, if she wished to be a true widow, to carry about the sadness and severity of life in both her face and her appearance, in a dress full of shame and modesty. Thus, it could be said of her what Jerome said of the widow Salvina: *In your husband's tomb you buried all pleasures together; the face once smeared with purple dye and white lead, you washed with tears over his bier; the dark tunic and black shoes you took up, laying aside the white garment and gilded slippers.* From this, the black color of widows is gathered. Dark clothing has prevailed in the mourning of men even to this day; however, our women today wrap themselves in white veils. Formerly, there was variation in the Roman Republic; sometimes black prevailed, sometimes white, the cause of which change Lipsius investigates.

<margin>On Tacitus's Annals, p. 124.</margin>
Indeed, from the dark clothing customary in mourning, David and the Prophets took their figures of speech when they wished to describe calamitous things. In Malachi (3:14), the Jews complain that they have walked <term>in black<note>Hebrew: קְדֹרַנִּית (qedorannit)</note></term>, in the manner of mourners, out of fear of the Lord of Hosts; compare Tarnovius on this passage. Eliphaz, rebuking Job for his broken spirit, explains the wonderful judgments of God and the secrets of His providence, among which he recounts that He sets the humble on high, and <term>those in black<note>Hebrew: קֹדְרִים (qodrim), i.e., mourners</note></term> (Job 5:11) are exalted with safety. He humbles the fearful so that He may lift them up; He afflicts so that He may sublimate. "He strikes down the high and lifts the humble," says Aesop. The Prophet David placed nothing randomly when, in Psalm 35:14, to signify the greatest distress of soul, he chose to use this word: *As one mourning for his mother, I bowed down in black.* He says he walked with his head lowered, just like one who weeps for his mother's funeral and grieves at a maternal tomb in dark clothing. They show grief by the sign and habit of mourners, who walk with head cast down and give sad signs dressed in dark garments. He uses the participial name <term>qoder<note>Hebrew: קֹדֵר</note></term> from the verb <term>qadar<note>Hebrew: קָדַר, to be dark or black</note></term> and the verb <term>shahhah<note>Hebrew: שָׁחַח, to be bowed down</note></term>, because mourners are seen walking about with lowered faces and heads bent forward. Moreover, he mentions the *Mother* to increase the sense of the speech, because children usually groan more heavily for her than for a Father. The Septuagint and the Old Interpreter omitted this.

It follows the previous discussion regarding funeral organizers by examining the external signs—such as black garments and the absence of anointing—that signify internal sorrow.</meta>

<page-num>616</page-num>
# ANTIQUITIES OF THE BIBLE

<margin>Funeral rites. Book 1, folio 120 a.</margin>
Augustinus Steuco <note>Agostino Steuco (1497–1548) was an Italian humanist scholar and Old Testament exegete.</note> notes that the Hebrew word for a sad person is *qadar* <note>original: קדר</note>, which signifies black, dark, or gloomy. They suggest this is either because color and brightness depart from those in sorrow, or because of the dark clothing <term>pullam<note>Latin: "pullus" refers to dark-colored, somber cloth worn specifically for mourning</note></term> that mourners adopt. Let us hear a similar lament in Psalm 38:7: *I am bowed down, I am greatly humbled; all day long I walk in blackness* <note>original: שחוחתי עד-מאד כל-היום קדר הלכתי</note>. Johannes Campensis <note>Jan van Campen, a 16th-century Hebraist</note> translates it as: *Weighted down by the burden of sin, I am humbled beyond measure. All day long I walk about in a sad, mourning habit.* Pressed by extreme evils, filthy with grief and a dark countenance, he seeks no other remedy for his mounting troubles than to become a suppliant to God with a soul cast down through repentance, lifting his eyes upward. Thus, dragging out a miserable life, he testifies to the magnitude of his inward pain through an expression drawn from his external gait, gesture, and dress. A stooped gait is fitting for grief, a fact to which Propertius perhaps alluded:

<margin>4. Elegies.</margin>
> — *Who saw you stooped at our funeral?*
> *Who saw the dark toga grow warm with tears?*

He reviews external things so that the internal things, which lie hidden, might be brought into view. The description sufficiently shows that the holy man was oppressed by extreme narrowness, a speech which the most Illustrious Landgrave of Hesse, Maurice <note>Maurice "the Learned," Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel (1572–1632), was a patron of the arts and a composer</note>, expressed more clearly than other poets in his *Psalter* (k. 2) in this manner:
> *Bent and hunched I go, stumbling,*
> *and with head lowered I wander, mourning*
> *my sad fates.*
> *A great sorrow has consumed my limbs,*
> *and sickness weighs upon my whole body,*
> *and I, miserable, am changed; and for my disease*
> *there is no cure.*
> *I wail sadly, I complain and I strike my breast,*
> *and from the very depths of my heart*
> *I pour out tears to Jehovah*
> *from a sick breast.*
> *My heart trembles, the strength of my soul fails,*
> *my vigor is broken, my fortitude*
> *languishes, and an abyss of night has veiled*
> *my eyes in shadows.*

These are symbolic expressions drawn from dark garments to indicate the affliction of the soul; just as, conversely, others are drawn from white garments to denote cheerfulness of soul and innocence of mind. For white is the color of those who rejoice. Such is the passage in Ecclesiastes:

<margin>6. 9. 8.</margin>
*Let your garments be white, and let oil not be lacking for your head.* Some interpreters feel these are the words of Epicureans <note>referring to a philosophy emphasizing earthly pleasure and comfort</note>. The Chaldean <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> interprets it differently as *fair* or *beautiful* <note>original: שפירן</note>, translated by P. Costus:

<margin>Page 45.</margin>
*At all times let your garments be white and pure from every stain of sin; and acquire a good name, which is not unlike the finest oil, so that most happy omens may redound upon your head, and good things may not fail you.*

Anointing belongs to luxury, not to mourning. Thus, the woman of Tekoa, feigning mourning, adopts a face of sadness; she does not anoint herself with oil but puts on mourning clothes, and imitates those grieving over sad events so that she might intercede for Absalom before David in 2 Samuel 14:3. By the instinct and instruction of Joab, she simulates grief. He says to her, *Feign mourning* <note>original: התאבלי</note>, pretend, wear garments suitable for mourning, do not anoint yourself with oil, but represent the image of a woman who has lived a long time in grief for the dead. In sad times, the ornament of joy ceased, anointing ceased, and when

<column-break/>

mourning ceased, anointing was resumed. This is how David, rising from grief in 2 Samuel 12:20, washed and anointed himself and changed his clothes. That appearance <note>original: σχῆμα (schema)</note> of the woman was mournful <note>original: πενθίμον (penthimon)</note>, and all other things were composed to move and soften the King. As easily as a common woman imitates false sorrows, so easily is the King swayed, whom the woman’s mournful appearance, the tears poured down her cheeks, her somber speech, and her widowed condition immediately led to compassion. You might say with Catullus: *False little tears from the hair of Berenice, a feigned lament in a marriage song.* Just as the woman of Tekoa was sent by Joab, so was a daughter sent by Periander to her brother Lycophron; she, having been taught the most seductive things by her father, finally persuaded her brother to return to Corinth, from which city he had been cast out, according to Herodotus.

<margin>Herodotus, Book 3.</margin>
<margin>Book 2.</margin>
That sex is capable of exciting compassion and can easily feel-with-words <note>original: λογωπαθεῖν (logopathein)</note> and mourn with the sentiments of others, according to that line of the Poet:
-> *To weep, they trained their eyes.* <-

In observing mourning, Mordecai was religious, rejecting the more elegant garment sent by Esther; he thought it unfitting to wear a more joyful habit when he was devoid of joy given the dangerous state of the Jews. In the court, a decree had been made that a people who had committed no crime should be removed from the midst. Therefore, he does not accept the sent garments, lest he be criticized like the one in Salvianus (Book 6, *On Providence*): *The city is blackened by fire, and you assume a face of serenity.* A decree altogether barbarian and cruel, unheard of for ages, had been established by the King for the slaughter of the Jews. Terrified by this fatal news, Mordecai rent his clothes, wrapped himself in sackcloth, and, sprinkled with ashes, proceeded to the Queen, filling all places there with much wailing and lamentation. A huge horror was everywhere:
-> *Mourning everywhere, fear, and many a phantom of death.* <-

In mourning, and in the changes of fortunes and minds, faces are changed, clothes are changed, and garments are changed. They exhibited themselves in cheap, sad, worn, despised, unsightly, filthy, foul, and squalid habits—those who were mourning the sadder events of death or other calamities. Such was the habit of those mourning for the dead, of **penitents** for sins, of **supplicants** for punishments, and of **defendants** for crimes. Sacred history is no less abundant in examples than profane history. The people of Israel, having heard the evil word of an angry God, gave themselves to mourning in Exodus 33:4: *they mourned* <note>original: יתאבלו</note> and *no one put on his ornaments*, according to Junius’s translation. No one dressed in their customary way (as the old translator has it), neither in daily nor festive clothing, nor in precious ornaments, which were used in times of joy. This fits the text where it reads: *And no man put*, i.e., what the Septuagint <note>LXX</note> conveniently explained here: *they mourned in mourning-garments* <note>original: κατεπένθησαν ἐν πενθικοῖς</note>. The translator renders it: *They mourned in mournings*, but according to the custom of the Latin language, which here conforms to the Greek, he would have rendered it more aptly as: *in lugubribus* <note>in mourning-clothes</note>. He says they mourned in mourning clothes, namely: hair-cloth, sackcloth, and cheap habit. They laid aside gold, gems, rings, necklaces, and every more elegant garment; with a filthy and dark garment, they declared the pain of a repentant soul. They laid aside the ornament of their attire (as the Chaldean well expresses it) and changed their white clothes for black. This change pleased God, because it signified that a change of life was coming; for He is accustomed to change His sentence when a sinner changes his life. He commands in verse 5: *Lay aside your ornament...*

# ANTIQUITIES OF THE BIBLE
### Jeremiah 16:5, 6, 7

<margin>
Funeral rites. Book 1, folio 120 a.
</margin>
...your ornaments from you. The children of Israel obeyed and stripped themselves of their ornaments at Mount Horeb. **Johannes Brenz** <note>A 16th-century Lutheran reformer and theologian.</note> comments: *God’s threats call the Israelites not to destruction, but to repentance; therefore He commands them to declare their repentance through external proofs, so that it might be clearly seen that they acknowledge their sin and feel grief for their impiety. He says: "Put off your ornament now, that I may know what to do with you," that is, let each one put on mourning clothes, so that by their external habit they may publicly declare the sorrow of their soul.* Among the Jews, fasting, <term>sackcloth<note>original: "cilicium," a coarse cloth often made of goat's hair, worn as a sign of penance or mourning</note></term>, and ashes served this mourning. The angry Deity permits this, not as if some requirement of holiness were satisfied by these things. He did not grant sackcloth so that it might satisfy His justice for sins. Sackcloth was used by the Israelites so that the internal detestation of sins committed might be covered by external signs. This harsher dress was not a part of holiness required for the amendment of life. Sitting in sackcloth is a "good work" only if it is done well—that is, from a good heart. A deed is judged good only from its entire cause; it is not good if one necessary thing is missing, or if one thing is added that ought to be absent. When the more elegant care of the body was set aside, so that a public sign of repentance and confession of faults might exist, they signified by sackcloth how greatly they grieved for the sin of infidelity they had committed and for the offense against the most high God. They stripped off the garment of pleasures and put on another garment reflecting a changed mind. The former betrayed wickedness; the latter displayed repentance. This example, says 
<margin>
On Exodus, column 592.
</margin>
**Wolfgang Borrhäus** <note>Also known as Wolfgang Musculus, a Reformed theologian.</note>, *combined with fasting and prayer, is observable throughout all turbulent ages regarding guilt and offenses. Indeed, it would be especially necessary in our own time, in which we are so far from reducing our old physical refinement and luxury that it actually increases daily—a clear sign of souls not yet prepared for repentance.* Good Borrhäus, if you could see the luxury of dress today, I believe even harsher words would escape you. One would wish, along with you, that the whole Christian world would compose itself not only after the example of the Israelites, but especially in imitation of the King of the Ninevites. There would then be fewer calamities and punishments. Let us look upon the King rising from his throne. *He is conquered by God through humility; he confesses himself more a sinner than a King. He forgets he is King where he stands in awe of God, the King of all; nor does he remember his own power where he acknowledges divine power. He forgets he is King while he casts away the purple and sets aside the crown. Instead, he is clothed in sackcloth and haircloth, persists in fasts, and remains in prayers.* Thus **Maximus** <note>Maximus of Turin, a 5th-century bishop and theologian.</note> discusses the King of the Ninevites in his *Sermon on the Litanies and the Fast of Nineveh*. He cast off his royal cloak, <insert><note>original Hebrew: "vayasir" (וַיָּסַר)</note> and he removed</insert> and with it all the insignia of royal dignity. He put off his royal vestment and anything that had even the appearance of ornament; moreover, he stripped off his glory, as some translate it, which he had known—like that Roman Emperor—to be a banner of pride and a nest of luxury. He admitted no other clothing but sackcloth, by the wearing of which he decided to declare the sorrow he had conceived from the coming danger. No more illustrious example can be drawn from all memory. He is a King worthy to be the model by which Princes and Kings live today, and which the Great Men of following ages should follow.

<column-break/>

The Romans also used to do this; if danger was present, or imminent, or feared for their city, no elegance of dress was seen, nor did the majesty of the countenance appear. Thus, at one time, the most distinguished order of the Senate declared its mourning and sorrow by a change of garment; and for the sake of one citizen (**Cicero**) both all good men by private consent and the entire Senate by public counsel changed their dress, as noted by Cicero in his *Speech against Piso, no. 17* and *On behalf of Sestius, no. 27*. And Ninnius urged the common people <note>original Greek: "ὥς καὶ ἐπί τινι κοινῇ συμφορᾷ, μεταβάλλειν"</note> *to change their clothes, as if at some common calamity*, as **Dio Cassius** <note>A Roman historian of Greek origin (2nd-3rd century AD).</note> noted in *Book 40*. Indeed, the Senators <note>original Greek: "ἡ βουλευτικὴν ἐσθῆτα καταθέμενοι, τὴν ἱππάδα, ὥσπερ ἐπὶ μεγάλῳ τινὶ πένθει, συνέβαινον"</note> *putting aside their senatorial dress, assumed the equestrian robe, as if in a time of great mourning*. As if in a public calamity and great mourning, says the Historian, by which he clearly marks the custom of the Romans, who decided that garments must be changed during common danger and great mourning of the Republic. And if it were not clear from this place, it would be made plain from **Plutarch** <margin>Life of Camillus, p. 148.</margin>, where the common people devoted to the faction of Manlius, after he had been condemned to chains by the Senate, <note>original Greek: "γενομένην τὰς μετέβαλε τὰς ἐσθῆτας, ἀφ' οὗ γὰρ ἔγνωσαν ὅτι συμφοραῖς μεγάλαις ἐδημοσίαις"</note> *changed their garments once they realized they were in the midst of great public calamities.* The Senators and the leading Knights loved Cicero as a proven man of the Republic and a caretaker in adversity, so much so that amidst the rages of Clodius and his accomplices, when exile loomed over him, they vied with each other to intercede for him, and they attested to the sorrow they had drawn from his danger by a change of clothing. Cicero himself also changed his dress during the danger and sought the people as a suppliant, but all in vain; Plutarch is the witness, whose words we shall describe <margin>Life of Cicero, p. 876.</margin>. *The face of the Republic was wretched at that time because of the storms of sedition tossed about for Cicero's sake.* <note>original Greek: "κινδυνεύων καὶ διωκόμενος, ἐν ἐσθῆτι μεταλλάξας καὶ κόμης ἀνάπλεως περιϊὼν ἱκέτευε τὸν δῆμον· πανταχοῦ δ' ὁ Κλώδιος ἀπήντα κατὰ τὰς συνόδους, ἀνθρώπους ἔχων ὑβριστὰς πρὸς αὐτὸν καὶ θρασεῖς, οἳ πολλὰ μὲν χλευάζοντες ἀκολάστως εἰς τὴν μεταβολὴν καὶ τὸ σχῆμα τοῦ Κικέρωνος, πολλαχῆ δὲ πηλῷ καὶ λίθοις βάλλοντες ἐνίσταντο ταῖς ἱκεσίαις."</note> *Being in danger and pursued, having changed into mourning clothes and with his hair unkempt, he went about entreating the people; but everywhere Clodius met him at the assemblies, having insolent and bold men with him, who, mockingly and immoderately jeering at Cicero's change and appearance, and often throwing mud and stones, obstructed his pleas.* To the injuries and insults of Clodius, he adds the condolences of the Equestrian order and the Senate, which they also testified to by their external clothing. And indeed, first, almost the entire equestrian order <note>original Greek: "συμμεταβαλεῖν τὰς ἐσθῆτας"</note> *changed their garments along with him*, and they followed him indiscriminately <note>original Greek: "κομῶντων καὶ συνεκτευόντων"</note> *growing their hair long and joining in the supplication*. But the greatest proof of sadness was that many of the Fathers <note>A title for Roman Senators.</note>, when they could obtain nothing in the curia because of the fury of Clodius, poured out into the streets <note>original Greek: "καταρρηγνύμενοι τοὺς χιτῶνας"</note> *tearing their tunics* and crying out. Furthermore, they gathered, as **Dio Cassius** <margin>Book 56.</margin> records, <note>original Greek: "οἱ μᾶλλοί τ' ἱππάδα στολὴν ἐνδεδυκότες, οἱ δ' ἄρχοντες ἢ βουλευτικῶν πλὴν ἡματίων ἢ περιπορφύρων."</note> *most having put on the equestrian robe, while the magistrates put aside their senatorial robes, except for the cloaks or the purple-bordered ones.* The Senators appeared in equestrian dress, and those who held the dignity of a Magistrate set aside the <term>praetexta<note>The "toga praetexta" was a purple-bordered toga worn by Roman magistrates as a sign of their rank.</note></term>, which was the insignia of their office. And similar to this change of garments through public mourning is that which **Livy** <margin>Book 43.</margin> left described in the accusation of Claudius the Censor: *First Claudius pleaded his case, and when eight out of the twelve centuries of knights had condemned the Censor, along with many others of the first class, immediately the leading men of the City, in the sight of the people, set aside their gold rings and changed their dress, so that they might go about as suppliants to the common people.* But let these things said about the change of garments suffice; it was also a most ancient custom to rend one's clothing in mourning. Moreover, the tearing used to be done at the first impulse of sorrow, by which those ancients showed that their soul and heart were being broken by grief...

<summary>This page explores the biblical and classical tradition of changing garments (mutatio vestis) and wearing sackcloth as an outward expression of inward repentance or public mourning. It highlights the King of Nineveh as a primary biblical model and provides extensive Roman historical parallels, such as the Senate's support for Cicero through the adoption of mourning dress.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of mourning rituals, specifically focusing on the "tearing of garments" (rending) as a sign of extreme grief, moving from general biblical examples to specific Hebrew terms for clothing and ending with the introduction of sackcloth.</meta>

<page-num>618</page-num>
<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>Funeral rites.</margin>
Funeral [rites] and [garments] were also shown to be torn apart. The clothing was typically broken in the customary manner from the neck down to the middle of the chest; this was done sometimes to the tunic, sometimes to the cloak (for the clothing of the ancients was twofold), and sometimes to both. The first rudiments of this custom are seen in the house of Jacob; for we read that Reuben did so in Genesis 37:29, and Jacob in verse 34, from whence this custom passed to his descendants. A heavier affliction could not befall that most holy man, the weight and violence of which was so great that he refused to accept consolation (v. 35), due to the vehemence of his pain and the nature of sorrow, which is usually healed by time and not before its time. Yet he so restrained himself that he committed nothing scurrilous, as those do who, while mourning, tear their cheeks, strike their heads, and perform other womanly acts of that kind. He kept himself within bounds, uttering no unseemly lamentations or disordered wailing. Nevertheless, there were certain signs of his grief; having heard from the lie of his sons that his son was torn by a wild beast, and so that he might believe it, those most deceitful men showed him the blood-stained garment. Upon seeing it, he was cast into a more bitter mourning; it lanced his heart more than the Roman people were once lanced when shown the head of Cicero. The wicked sons cast their father into a long-lasting mourning (v. 34), *and they tortured the father more cruelly than their brother, for they forced him to mourn for twenty-two continuous years. It is a wonder how it could happen that among the brothers of Joseph not even one was found who, in so long a span of time, might lift the father’s spirit with better hope and indicate that the brother lived somewhere; for between the selling of Joseph and the descent into Egypt (in the judgment of many) twenty-two years intervened. Let us therefore learn tolerance in adversity. Thus says Blessed Luther.* <note>Martin Luther, the German Reformer, whose commentaries on Genesis are frequently cited here.</note> Moreover, the Holy Scripture testifies that he mourned his son for the full twenty-two years—this refers to the internal grief of the heart, which he did not set aside in so great an interval of time, rather than to the usual order of mourning among them, which they observed according to custom for the dead on certain days and within certain limits. Thus it is established from Genesis 50:10 that Jacob's sons mourned their father for seven days, whence the <term>circumcised<note>original: "Recutiti," a term used by Latin authors to refer to Jews, often with a derogatory nuance in the period, here referring to Jewish commentators.</note></term> dispute variously about both the beginning and the end of mourning. Among them, Maimonides (chapter 6, section 1) maintains that according to the opinion of the Scribes, one must mourn for a full thirty days. To this belong the things which Antonius Margaritha <note>A 16th-century convert from Judaism who wrote "Der Gantz Jüdisch Glaub" (The Whole Jewish Belief).</note> reports <margin>p. m. 62. *The Jewish Faith.*</margin> regarding the Jews: that the children, having returned from the funeral, sit on the floor barefoot for seven days, and are not permitted to end their mourning or wash themselves before the thirtieth day; compare Buxtorf, *The Jewish Synagogue*, chapter 35, page 433. For the rest, that seven full days were used among the Jews for continuing mourning according to ancient custom <margin>Sirach 22:13.</margin> is witnessed by Sirach, with whom the things that Josephus records in Book 17 of his *Antiquities*, chapter 10, regarding Archelaus agree: that he himself <note>original: "ἐπὶ με ἑβδόμην ἡμέραν πένθος τὸν ἐν τῷ πατρὶ τιμῶν"</note> celebrated the mourning of his parent for seven days, for <note>original: "τόδε γὰρ διηγορεύει τὸ νόμιμον ἳ πατρία"</note> the ancestral custom required so many days. And this custom they call <term>Halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai<note>original: "הלכה למשה מסיני"</note></term>, that is, the custom of Moses from Sinai, as something which they had received through oral communication derived from Moses. We said above that there were two types of garments among the ancients that underwent tearing. The internal garment, with which frugal antiquity was alone content, as defined by Blessed Luther on Genesis 37, was a linen shirt—tight, narrow, covering all the limbs

<column-break/>

of the body down to the ankles, not with flowing sleeves, but tight and without folds, *so that the priests might be unencumbered for the work of sacrifices and slaughtering, just like our butchers.* The external garment, as described by Blessed Schindler and others, was the uppermost robe, longer, without sleeves, more ornate and honorable, assigned indeed to priests, kings, and prophets. This the Hebrews called <term>me'il<note>original: "מעיל"</note></term> from the root <term>ma'al<note>original: "מעל"</note></term>, *he prevaricated/trespassed*, because both this and the word for garment, <term>beged<note>original: "בגד"</note></term>, from <term>bagad<note>original: "בגד"</note></term>, *he acted perfidiously, he was rebellious*, serve as a perennial monument of that most pestilential rebellion in Paradise, no differently than a rope seen around the neck of a gallows-bird or a criminal. By the Greeks it is called the <term>himation<note>original: "ἱμάτιον"</note></term>, from which they commonly explain the tearing of the clothes of Job and his friends as referring to the outer garment. For Job, having heard of the simultaneous slaughter of his people, tore his <term>robe<note>original: "מעילו" (me'ilo)</note></term>, which indeed Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Dutch theologian.</note> understands as the inner garment; but he is opposed by Aquila, who translates it as "he threw off [his cloak]," and by Theodotion, who uses "outer garment," as well as the Septuagint, who use "cloaks." He wrongly thinks these last could have better translated it as "tunic." They refer it to the inner garment when Hushai the Archite came with his <term>tunic<note>original: "כתנתו" (kethonetho)</note></term> torn and dirt upon his head because of the deplorable fate of David (2 Samuel 15:32). As also the tearing of Tamar, daughter of David, who, having been defiled by incestuous intercourse by her brother Amnon, tore her <term>tunic of many colors<note>original: "כתנת הפסים" (kethoneth ha-passim)</note></term>, reaching to the ankles, and as a sign of great mourning for her stolen modesty, she wailed without ceasing with her hands placed upon her head, and lamented in a pitiful way the virginity taken from her by her brother. This horrible news reached David, who, although he was greatly displeased (v. 21), yet being too indulgent toward his firstborn son, left this crime unpunished. But his brother Absalom avenged such incest, killing his brother through his servants; hearing this, David tore his garment (v. 31). The fratricide having barely been committed, he [Absalom] intended parricide with a fiercer mind, taking up impious arms against his father, to whom the father, likewise a little too indulgent, warned Joab to spare him when defeated. But Joab, despising the King’s command, sent the sword into the author of the Parricide. That victory was tearful to the King, and the fall of his son even more tearful. He tore his garments—which we do not read that he tore at his daughter’s shame—*for he was naturally affectionate and felt even more compassion toward him* <note>original: "φύσει γὰρ ὧν φιλόστοργος καὶ πρὸς ἐκείνον ἔτι μᾶλλον συμπαθῶς εἶχεν" (Josephus, Antiquities, Book 7, chapter 10, page 235).</note>. He who had received the news of the slain Uriah with a glad side, now receives the news of Absalom sadly; indeed, having climbed to the higher part of the city, *he wept for his son, beating his breast and tearing his head and tormenting himself in every way* <note>original: "ἀνεϰλαίετο τὸν υἱὸν, τυπτόμενός τὰ στήρνα, ϰαὶ τὴν ϰεφαλὴν σπαραττόμενος, ϰαὶ παντίως αὐτὸν αἰϰιζόμενος"</note>, crying out: *My son, would that it had happened to me to face death with you!* Nor did this custom of tearing clothes prevail only among the ancient Jews; rather, it can easily be deduced from Homer, Virgil, Herodotus, and others that this was a common rite for almost all ancient peoples. This has been done before us by Kirchmann (Book 2 on Roman Funerals, ch. 17), Dilherr (Philological Dialogue 1, p. 41 ff.), Brisson (Book 2 on the Persian Kingdom, p. 256), Octavius Ferrarius (Part 2 on Clothing, Book 4, ch. 4), Daille, and others. Furthermore, regarding clothes changed in mourning, this pertains to **Sackcloth**. For in sorrow and mourning, a cheaper and thicker kind of garment was assumed, which is designated by the Hebrews by the name <term>saq<note>original: "שק"</note></term>, or sack. Of what material it was is not yet certain. Whether woven...

It establishes that these rituals were not unique to the Hebrews but were shared across many ancient cultures like the Greeks and Romans.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the examination of mourning rituals, moving from the act of tearing one's clothes to the specific garments worn during periods of grief and repentance, namely sackcloth and haircloth.</meta>

<page-num>619</page-num>
<header>Jeremiah 16:5, 6, 7. 619</header>

<margin>Funeral rites.</margin> Whether this cloth was woven from the shaggy hair of bucks and goats, or from the hair of horses or camels, or from some other material, is of no great importance to know—though the Catholic commentators <note>original: "Pontificii"</note> are quite long-winded in unearthing this "mystery," if you can believe it, in order to justify the hair-shirts worn by their monks. It is certain that the garment was soiled, cheap, thick, and rough, covering the body and cinched at the waist. This is evident from the fact that it was the "dress of the humble," <note>original Greek: "$\sigma\chi\tilde{\eta}\mu\alpha \tau\tilde{\omega} \tau\alpha\pi\epsilon\iota\nu\tilde{\omega}\nu$"</note> used as a shaggy contrast to softer and looser clothing. Latin writers sometimes translated this as *cilicium* <note>a hair-shirt</note>, so named because it was first produced among the Cilicians, who became known to the world not so much for their shaggy goats and bucks as for these "Cilician" cloths.

<margin>Varro, *On Agriculture*, book 2.</margin> Varro says: *The goat provides hair for nautical use, for war engines, and for craftsman's tools. They are sheared because they have long hair in a large part of Phrygia, from whence hair-cloths [cilicia] and other things of that kind are usually brought.* Isidore, in book 19 of his *Origins* <note>his encyclopedia of etymologies</note>, chapter 26, notes that these hair-cloths are woven from goat hair, though he errs twice: first by saying they are of Arabic origin, and in book 14, chapter 3, by noting the name was drawn from a certain Cilix, born of a Phoenician.

<margin>Job 1:20.</margin>
<margin>col. 1458.</margin> Suidas writes: *Hair-cloth [kilikia] is the shaggy hair of goats. Some goats are born in Cilicia, and thus the things woven from their hair are called "kilikia."* Hesychius says: *Kilikioi are shaggy goats, and the hair-cloths woven from them are called kilikia.* The historian Procopius likewise records that screens were held up against those throwing javelins, *protective coverings made of rough hair-cloth, which they call "kilikia."* Dr. Leonhard Rauwolff <note>A 16th-century German physician and botanist</note> mentions a certain garment worn by himself and his companions in his *Travels to the Orient, part 2, chapter 1, page 133*:

<margin>1 Samuel 13.</margin>
> In addition, we put on an outer garment made of a coarse weave, called *Messa* in their language, which is very common among the Moors <note>Arab/Middle Eastern peoples</note>; it is mostly woven from goat hair, or sometimes from donkey hair. It is quite narrow, without sleeves, and short, not reaching down to the bend of the knee. Since these garments vary, the rougher ones (especially those with white and black stripes) are used for such clothing, while the coarsest are used for tents and grain sacks in which they carry their provisions, etc.

To this, Rauwolff adds that this clothing reminded him of those cheap garments the ancient Jews used in mourning, which they then called *Sacks*. We do not wish to depend too superstitiously on the phrasing or the origin of the word, nor to search everywhere for how the "sack" <term>saccus; a garment of mourning</term> agreed with or differed from the hair-shirt <term>cilicium</term>. We leave such legalistic hair-splitting <note>original Greek: "$\phi\iota\lambda\omicron\delta\acute{\iota}\kappa\alpha\iota\omicron\nu$"</note> to the works of Heinsius, Meursius, and Casaubon (the last of whom believes it cannot be proven by Holy Scripture or any other firm argument that the "sack" was a garment woven specifically from the hair of bucks and goats), lest we provoke laughter in a somber matter, as some do here. For what need is there to get entangled in "hairy" trifles? The first appearance of this somber habit and the first trace of the word *Saq* <note>Hebrew: שַׂק</note> is in the story of Joseph in *Genesis 37:34*, where the father, mourning his lost son, *clothed himself in hair-cloth*, as our translator chose to render it. Augustinus Eugubinus says: *What does it matter that the Hebrew says 'he was clothed in a sack,' unless one wants to weigh and distinguish this matter too scrupulously—that the hair-shirt was sewn from horsehair or similar material, while the sack was from hemp and that which grows from the earth? But these things are easily confused.* To that end...
<margin>folio 139. b.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Funeral rites.</margin> ...Schindler aims his focus, thinking the material was wool or *hempen* (*Pagninus* adds: *or of skin*) which one puts over the flesh. For once the more splendid garments were stripped off or torn, they covered the body or cinched the loins with a sack in place of an undergarment—the cheapest, densest, and roughest of clothing. Indeed, it is enough to note that it was an unrefined or bristly garment, a cheap and disordered way of dressing that, like a common sack, lacks all ornament and imitates the shape of a sack in some way. Rabbi David Kimchi observes that it signifies not only the shaped sack, but also its material and any cheap wrapping. This type of garment was usually cinched around the loins or girded at the loins. For the "Sack" is paired with the verb *vayechegor* <note>Hebrew: וַיַּחְגֹּר</note>, meaning *he girded*, as seen in *2 Samuel 3:31* where David says to Joab and all the people: *tear your clothes, and gird yourselves with sackcloth.* This phrase occurs frequently in the Holy Scriptures: *Isaiah 15:3; 22:12; 32:11; Jeremiah 4:8; 6:26; 49:3; Ezekiel 3:24; Amos 8:10; and elsewhere.*

<margin>2 Samuel 3:31.</margin> Refer also to what is read concerning the servants of Ben-hadad in *1 Kings 20:32*. The Syrians, having been defeated by the Israelites in a great battle, took counsel out of necessity and said: *Behold, we have heard that the Kings of Israel are merciful; let us, they say, put sacks on our loins and ropes on our heads.* They carried out this plan they had devised, girded their loins with sacks, and the plan succeeded for them; they obtained from the enemy life and favor for their King, and an amnesty <note>original Greek: "$\dot{\alpha}\mu\nu\eta\sigma\acute{\iota}\alpha\nu$"</note> and mercy for themselves. The King [Ahab] even broke out into a cry hardly unworthy of a King: *If he is still alive, he is my brother.* Ben-hadad, who once threatened Ahab with slavery and chains, now confesses himself a servant. Certainly, this was a worthy voice for a Syrian to confess the glory of Israel, but it was an impious voice for the King of the Israelites to call Ben-hadad—who was a stranger to the covenant of God—his "brother." He showed himself merciful to the enemies of God against and beyond the command of God himself, by whose help he had won two remarkable and glorious victories over the Syrians. This was not because the impious King [Ahab] was worthy of such great favors, but because God had determined to vindicate the glory of His name against the blasphemies of the Syrians and to punish the most arrogant King of the Syrian nation.

In a similar way, we see in *Judith 4:8 and 8:5*, *she placed sackcloth upon her loins.* The loins, which are otherwise the seat of lust and pleasures, are covered with cheap wrappings, becoming instead the seat of pain and sorrow. For the sack changes pleasure into harshness and delights into sadness. The sack is the external habit not so much of one mourning at a funeral, but of one who is a penitent. The penitent, wishing to move God to compassion, displays external signs proceeding from internal grief; by these, he shows what his mind is toward sin and toward God. Thus David, with the Elders, *covered in hair-cloth, fell prostrate on their faces to turn away the punishment and appease the wrath of God.*

<margin>1 Chronicles 21:8, 16.</margin> Thus Job is read in *16:15* to have *sewn sackcloth over his skin*, where it is worth noting that sometimes the sack was taken up *immediately* against the flesh, after all ordinary clothes were torn and cast off. The example of the most wicked King Ahab can be easily referred to here, as he tore his garments, covered his flesh with hair-cloth, and slept in the sack (*1 Kings 21:27*). For having heard the heavy threats from Elijah, *he tore his clothes, and put a sack over his flesh* <note>original Hebrew: "עַל בְּשָׂרוֹ"</note>.

It explores the material origins of these garments in Cilicia and their theological significance in the stories of David, Ahab, and Ben-hadad.</summary>
