<meta>This page continues the discussion of mourning rituals, moving from the tearing of garments to the use of sackcloth, the sprinkling of ashes, and the practice of shaving the head as expressions of grief and repentance.</meta>

<page-num>620</page-num>
<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>Funeral rites.</margin> ...his **own**. In a similar way, Jehoram, during the siege of Samaria, *2 Kings 6:30, tore his clothes: and as he passed by upon the wall, the people looked, and behold, he had sackcloth <note>original Hebrew: "בשרו מבית", literally "upon his flesh within"</note> underneath upon his skin.* Sometimes, however, the sackcloth was worn over the inner garment, which is how we interpret what is read of Hezekiah in *2 Kings 19:1* and Isaiah 37:1; of David in *1 Chronicles 21:16*; and of the King of the Ninevites in *Jonah 3:6*. Opposite to this "girding" of sackcloth is the phrase used for those setting aside mourning and receiving repentance from God, who are told to *loosen the sackcloth*, so that it no longer binds or restricts them. *Isaiah 20:2:* "Go and," says the Prophet, "loosen the sackcloth from off <note>original Hebrew: "ואפתח שק מעל"</note> thy loins," that is, so it no longer weighs upon them. *Psalm 30:11: "Thou hast loosed my sackcloth and girded me with gladness."* The actions of the Saints are usually taken up through imitation; thus, when the Prophets call the people to ashes and hair-shirts, their intention was none other than to exhort them to serious sorrow. Those who were upright and religious used these external signs, to which they had been accustomed since childhood, with the greatest devotion of soul to signify their grief for sins committed. But the hypocrite, when "repenting," displays external filth while retaining internal filth; therefore God mocks them and warns those who relied on these bare ceremonies—<margin>Joel 2:13.</margin> *that it is hearts, not garments, that must be rent.* There were foolish men who thought that by sprinkling a little dust on their head (a ceremony already mentioned <unclear>fati-tim</unclear> <note>likely "passim" (everywhere) or "affatim" (abundantly)</note>), or by throwing some torn and squalid rag over their body, or by lying on the ground once or twice, they were purified of crimes committed against God. As that ancient custom of the forefathers grew old, the custom of repenting through hair-shirts, ashes, and sackcloth also ceased. Even the Jews today have left behind those sacks with ashes; they do not wear hair-shirts, nor do they wallow in ashes anymore. Meanwhile, we do not banish physical exercises; we simply deny they are a strict necessity. For it is not at all necessary, nor commanded by law, that for one to live holily and innocently, one must wear sackcloth, wallow in ashes, or sleep on hair-shirts. The best garment of the soul is the sackcloth of humility. Let us be clothed in this, let us come forth dressed in this, having stripped off the hair-shirt of feigned uprightness and cast away the cloak of the "old man." Those who are students of antiquity, I would wish, should be stung by the Spirit within rather than by the roughness of bristles without; they should tear their hearts, not their clothes—or at least their hearts along with their clothes—and lacerate their minds along with their hair, sprinkling themselves with the ash of true repentance. For all these things were observed in the repentances of those recorded in the writings of the Old Testament. Among the signs and proofs of mourning, the *sprinkling* of ashes was prominent; for just as in prosperous times and when things went according to one's heart, people were sprinkled with scented powders, so those in mourning, by sprinkling ashes, wished to show from their prosperous state that they were now the most unhappy and abject of all. Moreover, the ash they sprinkled was to be sought either from the hearth or from another corner of the house where it was kept. This ritual prevailed among almost all peoples. Joshua, when the Israelites were beaten by the inhabitants of Ai, *chapter 7:6, tore his clothes, falling on his face, and together with the elders of the people, sprinkled dust upon his head <note>original Hebrew: "יעלו", literally "caused it to ascend"</note>; so too that fugitive from the fatal slaughter of the Israel-*

<column-break/>

ites, in which the sons of Eli perished, arrived with torn clothes and *earth upon his head <note>original Hebrew: "ואדמה על ראשו"</note>, 1 Samuel 4:12.* Likewise Tamar, the daughter of David, because of the violence brought upon her by her brother Amnon, *put ashes on her head <note>original Hebrew: "תתן אפר על ראשה"</note>, 2 Samuel 13:19.* We find the same traces of this ritual among the pagans. Homer mentions it regarding Laertes, the father of Ulysses, in *Odyssey book 24, line 315:*

> With both hands he took the dark dust
> and poured it over his grey head, groaning deeply.

The Poet relates almost the same thing in the same words regarding Achilles mourning Patroclus beyond belief in *Iliad book 18, lines 23–24:*

> With both hands he took the dark dust,
> and poured it over his head, and defiled his beautiful face.

In the same way, Virgil describes the Latin Father [Latinus], defiling his hair with a spray of ash and dust:

---
-> he deforms his white hair with filthy dust <-
---

And in *book 12 of the Aeneid, line 609:*

> *Latinus goes with his robe torn,*
> *stunned by the fate of his wife,*
> *defiling his white hair sprinkled with filthy ash.*

Kirchmann deals with this ritual of sprinkling ash at greater length in *book 2 of "On Funerals," chapter 12.*

Nor did the ancient age stop at those rituals we have recounted so far. In mourning, the head was to be veiled and deprived of its former ornament; regarding this ritual, Flaccius says in his *Key* under the word *Bread: In funeral mourning, they covered the mouth with a linen cloth and wrapped the head, especially when going out in public.* The plucking and tearing of the hair of the human head—which is its grace and ornament according to the Sacred Code itself, *2 Samuel 14:26 <note>The text cites 14:15, likely referring to the description of Absalom's hair which begins in this chapter</note>*—was also practiced; thus Ezra testifies of himself, *chapter 9:3, that he tore his garment and plucked out the hair of his head.* The narrowness of the paper does not permit me to bring forward the secular examples of Achilles, Priam, Hecuba, and others from Homer, Sophocles, and Ovid; see, if you please, Ravanellus under the word *Hair*. Sometimes a total shearing and shaving followed the plucking. This was a sign of freedom among the Gauls, Goths, Greeks, and many other peoples who were accustomed to growing their hair and beards, but among those same people, it was a mark of the greatest ignominy and abjection (cf. Dempster in *Roman Antiquities*, pages 1704, 1707, 1709; B. Finckius, *Illustrious Questions 54, page 314*). However, among the Assyrians, Persians, Egyptians, and others, such shaving was a sign of the highest and greatest sorrow; hence the Persians shaved not only themselves, but even their wives, children, horses, and pack animals—which Plutarch, in his *Life of Alexander*, testifies was done by Alexander the Great to his mules and horses after the death of Hephaestion. Likewise, the Egyptians laid aside their *beards* in mourning and shaved the hair of their heads. But God commands the Jews to mourn without the shaving of the head or the cutting of the flesh, adding the reason that they are children of God and a holy people:

> You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead. <note>Deuteronomy 14:1</note>

He prohibits the ritual which the pagans held in mourning the dead, from whom the Jews were required to separate themselves in worship and customs. Finally, He makes a prohibition in *Leviticus chapter 19:27–28*, commanding them not to make any cuttings for the dead, nor to imprint any marks. Shaving the crown, plucking the beard, mangling the body, and branding marks were common among neighboring nations, who disfigured themselves by shaving the head, tearing out the beard, and lacerating the cheeks and chest.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of mourning rituals from the previous page. While page 620 focused on the tearing of garments and the wearing of sackcloth, this page examines the more extreme physical expressions of grief: the cutting of the flesh and the shaving of the head and beard.</meta>

<page-num>621</page-num>
<header>Jeremiah 16: 5, 6, 7.</header>

<margin>Funeral rites.</margin>
These profane rituals and customs of the pagan nations did not befit the people of Israel, who were not to mourn like those who had no hope of the resurrection. <note>The author refers to 1 Thessalonians 4:13, a New Testament passage often used to distinguish Christian/Jewish mourning from pagan practices.</note>
<margin>1 Thessalonians 4:13.</margin>
* Vatablus <note>François Vatable, a 16th-century French scholar known for his notes on the Hebrew Bible.</note> translates: *You shall not round the hair of your heads, nor shall you mar the edges of your beard. You shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead, nor print any marks upon you.* These same instructions are repeated in chapter 21, verse 5: *They shall not make baldness upon their head, neither shall they shave off the corner of their beard, nor make any cuttings in their flesh.* The Law marks as grim the custom of shaving the hair and beard, as well as cutting the flesh. Superstitious nations used to lacerate certain parts of the body with a needle or nail, or cut themselves with small knives. This laceration of the body was done so that by showing their blood, the mourners might satisfy the spirits of the underworld, as Servius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil.</note> testifies. 
<margin>Virgil, Aeneid, Book 4.</margin>
The Egyptians, in their lamentation for Osiris, used to cut their flesh. Julius Firmicus <note>A Christian author of the 4th century who wrote against pagan religions.</note> is a witness to this in *On the Error of Profane Religions*, page 5: *In their inner shrines they have a buried idol of Osiris. They mourn this with annual lamentations; they shave their heads so that, having dishonored their heads with this ugliness, they may bewail the wretched fate of their King; they beat their breasts, they tear their upper arms; they reopen the scars of old wounds, so that through annual mourning the deadly and miserable destruction of his death is reborn in their minds.* Lucian <note>A Greek satirist of the 2nd century.</note> asserts that the Greeks bloodied their cheeks during funerals: 
<margin>Volume 1, On Mourning, page 788.</margin>
"There is wailing over the dead, and shrieking of women, and tears from everyone, and breasts being beaten, and hair being torn, and cheeks becoming reddened with blood." <note>Original Greek: Ὤμωγαὶ ἐπὶ τέτις, καὶ κωκυτὸς γυναικῶν, καὶ παρὰ πάντων δάκρυα, καὶ στέρνα τυπτόμενα, καὶ σπαραττόμενη κόμη, καὶ φοινισσόμεναι παρειὰὶ.</note> Just as there are "bloodied cheeks" there, so in Homer 
<margin>Iliad, Book 5, line 393.</margin>
one finds "cheeks torn all around," <note>Original Greek: ἀμφidρυφεὶς παρειὰὶ.</note> when he speaks of women who, in their mourning, had mangled both cheeks with their nails. Euripides described these same heavy rituals with these words: 
<margin>In Hecuba, line 653.</margin>
> And upon her gray head the mother,
> For her dead children, places
> Her hand. She tears her cheek,
> Making it bloody with her nail,
> Setting herself to the tearing.
> <note>Original Greek: Πολιόν τ᾽ ἐπὶ κρᾶτα μάτηρ... δίαιμον ὄνυχα.</note>

Where, with the epithet "bloody," he amplifies the mourning, and by the nail being bloodied again and again, he marks the weight of the grief. It was customary for women to tear their cheeks with their nails, which was forbidden to them by the Law of the Twelve Tables <note>The earliest code of Roman law, c. 450 BCE.</note>, which states: *Women shall not tear their cheeks.* A woman in Quintilian's *Declamations* (10), mourning her son, holds out her arms to the judges with her face torn and mangled and her breasts bruised. Anna is introduced with such a face in the mourning for Dido: 
<margin>Virgil, Aeneid, Book 4, line 674.</margin>
> Defiling her face with her nails and her breast with her fists.

And it was not only in mourning, but in any grief or ill success—whenever something unfortunate happened—that incisions were made. This is argued by the words of the Prophet Jeremiah (41:5) in the description of the sorrow of eighty men who are said to have come from three distinct towns belonging to the kingdom of Samaria—namely Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria—with *shaven beards, torn clothes, and mangled faces.* The Hebrew words are: <note>m'galchei zaqan v'q'ruei b'gadim u-mitgod'dim</note> "shaven of beard, and torn of garments, and cutting themselves." Vatablus says in his notes (page 351): *Literally: shaven in beard and torn in garments and cut. He calls them torn or mangled or lacerated in face, evidently by knives or nails, which were signs of mourning and sorrow.* 
<margin>Book 4, page 936.</margin>
Münster <note>Sebastian Münster, a German cartographer and Hebrew scholar.</note> says: *Although it was prohibited in the Law that the Jews should cut their bodies, being forgetful of the Law and accustomed to the manners of the nations, they did not restrain themselves from this error in times of extreme sadness.* 

<column-break/>

<margin>Funeral rites.</margin>
The Hebrews mark this incision with two words, namely *gadad* <note>Hebrew: גדד</note> which in the *Hitpael* form means "he cut and lacerated himself," and *sharat* <note>Hebrew: שרט</note> meaning "he lacerated." From this comes the word for the incision itself, *sharetet*, which they made with nails, knives, or small lances, as is evident from 1 Kings 18:28 concerning the priests of Baal, who cut themselves with *knives and lances*. <note>Original Hebrew: בהרבות וברמחים; Greek: ἐν μαχαίραις καὶ ἐν σειρομάσταις.</note> Herodotus <note>Famous Greek historian, known as the "Father of History."</note> called this "cutting oneself with knives" in his book *Euterpe*. Through interaction with the gentiles, that harsh custom was adopted by the Israelites, which is clearly gathered from the words of Jeremiah: 
<margin>Chapter 16, verse 6.</margin>
*Both the great and the small shall die in this land. They shall not be buried, neither shall men lament for them, nor cut themselves, nor make themselves bald for them.* The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> explains the word for "cut" as "making incisions on the arms." Therefore, it was the custom at that time to create baldness and cut the upper arms in mourning. Hence the poet Choerilus called the Jews *trochokeidas*, meaning "those with hair shorn in a circle." One might rightly say this custom was sadder and worse than the funeral itself, where the living appeared more miserable than the dead. 

Let us now see the shaving and plucking of the beard and hair. The custom of putting aside hair in mourning prevailed in almost the whole world. Herodotus says in Book 2: "Among other men, it is the law to shave their heads when in grief, especially those whom the grief most touches." It is well known that among the Jews, this ritual of shaving was introduced through customs contrary to God's command, which has ceased among them today. The Moabites, a people neighboring the Jews, had the shaved head as a sign of mourning, which becomes clear from the words of Isaiah prophesying the lamentation of the Moabites: *Moab shall howl; on all its heads shall be baldness, and every beard shall be shaven.* (Chapter 15:2). The Septuagint translates this poorly as "all arms are cut," for in the Hebrew it says: *every beard is diminished.* <note>Original Hebrew: כל-זקן גרועה.</note> This same baldness was predicted for the Philistines 
<margin>Jeremiah 47:5.</margin>
through these words: *Baldness is come upon Gaza.* It indicates a future mourning of the greatest kind, and the removal of all joy. 

The Prophet Ezekiel gave a sign of mourning and the greatest sorrow by baldness when he introduces the sailors wailing with a loud voice over the destruction of Tyre, sprinkling their heads with dust and bringing baldness upon themselves. *They shall cry bitterly, and shall cast up dust upon their heads, they shall wallow themselves in the ashes. And they shall make themselves utterly bald for thee.* (Original Hebrew: הקריחו אליך קרחה; Greek: ξυρήσονται ἐπὶ σὲ φαλάκρωμα) *and they shall gird themselves with sackcloth.* 

From profane authors, there is a mountain of testimonies. Queen Isis, upon receiving the news of the death of her husband Osiris, immediately cut off her hair and put on a robe of mourning. Plutarch in his book *On Isis and Osiris* says: "She cut off one of her locks there and took up a mourning robe, where the name of the city even until now is Coptos." <note>Plutarch suggests the city name Coptos comes from the Greek word "kopto," meaning to strike oneself in grief or to cut.</note> Hence the ministers of Isis were bald, which is why Juvenal says in *Satire 6*: 
> He who is surrounded by a linen-wearing flock, and a bald flock.

Briseis, having "shorn her locks," mourns Achilles in the works of Quintus Smyrnaeus <note>Referenced as Calaber.</note>. 
<margin>Book 3, line 685.</margin>
<margin>Xiphilinus, page 365.</margin>
The Emperor Macrinus, having suffered a defeat, walked about having "shaved both his head and his entire beard, and having taken a gray garment instead of the purple." It was considered a sad disaster if a shaven head was shown to anyone, and therefore this sign indicated either mourning or slavery. The victor made the vanquished bald; the master made the slave bald. Hence the "baring of the heads" in Deuteronomy 32:42. An enemy would shave the beard of an enemy for the sake of ignominy; for the beard is the ornament of a man. By the shaving of the beard, the ambassadors...

<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>Funeral rites.</margin>
...the servants of David were dishonored, as seen in 2 Samuel 10:4. <note>In this biblical episode, the Hanun of the Ammonites shaved off half of the beards of David's messengers to shame them.</note> In a similar way, Nehemiah punished the husbands of foreign women in chapter 13:25 by striking them and pulling out their hair; surely, as Barthold Majerus <note>A 17th-century theologian.</note> notes (Part 2, *Philol. Sacra*, p. 120), this was done so that those enemies of the native tongue and decency would be known to all, marked by the public disgrace of infamy and baseness. But thus far we have contemplated the rites of mourners regarding the deceased; it remains for us to touch briefly upon what the ancient age performed in the house with the corpse before it was carried out—a topic that perhaps should have been discussed first. Among the duties to be performed for friends while they were still sick, visitation was held in high regard among the Jews, as Maimonides <note>The influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> discusses in <margin>ch. 14, § 1.</margin> When they finally breathed their last, the first duty was to close the eyes, decently compose the limbs, and carefully wash the body. Nature herself dictates these first offerings to the dead; for it is not right to look upon eyes strangely rolled back, limbs dreadfully distorted, or bodies defiled by the filth of the deathbed. Our steward of primeval antiquity, while he diligently describes funeral accuracy for us, does not indeed (as far as I know) designate that first task in the final office of closing the eyes; yet this *krypsis* <note>original: κρύψις, "hiding" or "closing."</note> was an arbitrary necessity in such a matter, looking toward specific rites rather than common ones. For what man would not close the eyes of a dying man, unless he were savage in his ways or a barbarian in mind? The customs of a more cultured people are: *to shut the eyes*, <margin>Odyssey, Book 24, v. 186, 189.</margin> *to straighten and stretch the limbs, and to wash the bodies*. For as Homer says, *this is the honor of the dead*, <note>original: ὃ γὰρ γέρας ἐστὶ θανόντων</note> that bodies should not be neglected. Thus, in those more cultured times, it was the honor of the deceased to have the eyes immediately pressed shut, the mouth and other limbs composed, and the body purified by washing. It was considered inhumane not to perform these things; hence Homer shows the shade of Agamemnon complaining to Ulysses of the cruelty of his wife Clytemnestra, who refused to even close his sharp eyes with her hands as he breathed his last. *

<margin>Odyssey, Book 11, v. 424.</margin> <note>The OCR incorrectly attributes this to the Iliad.</note>
> ...nor did she endure, though I was going to the house of Hades,
> to close my eyes with her hands, nor to shut my mouth.
> There is nothing more terrible or more dog-like than a woman.

Polynices requires this duty from his mother just as he is drawing his final breath in Euripides' *Phoenician Women*, 460:

> Fit my eyelids together with your hand, 
> Mother; and he himself places it upon his eyes.

And so that after death his limbs might be decently shaped and composed, rather than just his eyes, Hippolytus, already breathing out his miserable life, entreats his father Theseus in *Hippolytus*, v. 1444:

> Alas, alas, the darkness already overtakes my eyes.
> Take hold of me, father, and straighten my body.

And amid those sobbing sighs, he repeats as he closes his own light, v. 1457:

> My struggle is finished, for I am perished, father.
> Hide my face quickly with my robes.

And the chorus concludes, following the heavy grief of the many-teared scene:

> This common grief has come to all the citizens
> unexpectedly;
> there will be a flood of many tears.
> For the reports of the great, worthy of grief, 
> take a stronger hold on us.

### Jeremiah 16:8

-> <term>The House of Feasting</term> <gloss>The house of drinking</gloss> You shall not enter <gloss>you shall not enter</gloss> to sit with them <gloss>to sit together with them</gloss> to eat <gloss>to eat</gloss> and to drink <gloss>and to drink</gloss> <-

---

When, after the defeat and capture of the Persian King, Lucius Aemilius Paulus wished not only to preside over but even to be present with the cooks and arrangers of the triumphal feast, his friends wondered at it. He responded that it required the same skill to arrange a battle line against enemies as it did a banquet for friends. Intending to bring this commander's voice from the battlefield into this literary wrestling-ground, and from the general's tent into the Academy: since we have thus far dealt with the funeral rites among the ancients, we wish that we might, with no less industry, now arrange a literary banquet for the friendly reader. There have always been, and still are, various kinds of banquets, both public and private; they were primarily derived from five principal acts of human life: namely, birth, education, the undertaking of an office, marriage, and Death. Birth feasts were either held immediately after delivery, <margin>Book 3.</margin> whence they were called *puerperalia* [childbirth feasts], or "Repotia" according to Ausonius (as noted by Turnebus), or they were repeated annually on the day of birth itself. These were in use among the Egyptians, Persians, Jews, Greeks, Romans, and Germans, as Stuckius proves more at length in *Antiquities of Banquets*, book 1, ch. 16. Cicero mentions this banquet in the second *Philippic*; Plautus in the *Captives* (Act 2, sc. 2) and in the *Pseudolus* (Act 5, sc. 2); and Seneca in *On Anger* (book 2, ch. 37). For the ancients were released [from labor] to cultivate with some religious observance the day that had opened the way to life for them, and to celebrate it with festive banquets. Hence the Persians celebrated it with chief veneration, and during the solemn feasts they indulged their *genius* <note>The divine spirit believed to accompany a person through life.</note>, serving what was rarest, including camel and horse meat, lest they should seem to have met for the sake of something simple <margin>Herodotus, book 1.</margin> or common. Whence Herodotus says: *They consider that day the most to be honored of all, on which each was born; on this day they think it right to set out a more plentiful feast than others. On it, the wealthy among them set out an ox, a horse, a camel, and an ass, all roasted whole in ovens; while the poor among them set out the smaller kinds of cattle.* Thus the son of Antony, as Praetor, celebrated the birthday of Augustus, Julius, and himself with both Circensian games and a hunt (*and with horse racing and the slaughter of beasts*); he even received the Senate itself at a banquet on the Capitoline, as Dio records in book 54, p. 617. So too the birthday of Maecenas <note>A famous Roman patron of the arts.</note> was celebrated by Horace with a birthday banquet, <margin>6</margin> to which the poet invites his Phyllis with these verses:

> *That you may be summoned to new*
> *joys, the Ides must be spent by you,*
> *the day which divides April,*
> *the month of sea-born Venus:*
> *Rightly it is a solemn day for me, and sacred*
> *almost more than my own birthday, because from this*
> *light my Maecenas begins to count*
> *his flowing years.*

If we consult the Sacred Pandects <note>original: *Pandectas*; the author uses this legal term to refer to the Bible as a complete body of divine law</note>, we find that no one observed their birthday except for Herod and Pharaoh; Paschasius Ratbertus <note>A 9th-century monk and theologian.</note> writes in *Book 7 on Matthew, column 613*, that as their impiety in treachery was equal, so was their celebration for the sake of pride. However, it is easily seen that Ratbertus was misled by the name of Pharaoh and thus fell into error. Regarding the banquet for weaning and teething <note>Refers to celebrations marking a child's early milestones.</note>, we add nothing, but wish the kind reader to be referred to Stuckius <note>Johann Wilhelm Stucki, a 16th-century scholar who wrote on ancient dining customs.</note> in *Ancient Banquets, book 1, chapter 17.* In the taking up of both sacred and political office, banquets were celebrated by the custom of almost all nations. Thus, feasts were in use not only among the Jews of old during the inauguration of the High Priest and other priests, but also among the Romans during the initiation of Pontiffs and augurs. Compare Macrobius, *Saturnalia, book 3, chapter 13.* But to add something regarding our own century, we might include here those initiations of monks, priests, and nuns which, no differently than weddings (the name by which they are even designated), are celebrated with the most profuse feasts, and even with wanton games and dances. I believe it was from these that those feasts originated which are established during the harassment of new students <note>original: *Neophytorum Studiosorum*</note>—those who, fresh from the crossroads and the schoolmaster’s rod, frequently arrive at the University—commonly called *pennalizations* <note>original: *pennalizationes*; a historical term for a harsh form of student hazing where freshmen were treated as servants.</note>. By a good and auspicious omen, the most Serene Princes and States of the Roman Empire proscribed this custom from their universities a few years ago. I suspect they were moved by the example of the School of Berytus <note>Modern-day Beirut, which housed a world-famous law school in late antiquity.</note>, lest our own universities perhaps suffer the same end as the once-flourishing School of Berytus experienced. There, to omit other crimes, the harassment of new recruits was so great that the Emperor Justinian was compelled to restrain it by a public edict written to Salaminius. When the Emperor’s most severe threats found no place, God suddenly, in the dead of night, overturned the foundations of the city, laid low the walls, and scattered the houses. So great a slaughter of men occurred that, as Agathias <note>A 6th-century Greek historian.</note> testifies, more than three thousand students perished miserably, not to mention the common folk. See Alsted in *Scholarly Anthology, Oration on the causes of the corruption of schools, in the Encyclopedia, p. 2790.* Leaving aside those banquets related to marriage and funeral feasts, the location of banquets deserves special commendation and observation. We shall describe this using the occasion of the courtyard of the garden of King Ahasuerus's palace from *Esther 1:5–6.* Everything in this hall was magnificent; the preparation was magnificent and sumptuous. The *pavements shone with marble*, the *couches with gold*, the *walls with hangings*, the *bodies with robes*, and the *atria with vessels*. All things were clean, all things bright, refined, splendidly prepared, properly placed in their order, everything generous and sumptuous; and as Plautus says in *Pseudolus* <note>A comedy by the Roman playwright Titus Maccius Plautus.</note>:

> All things turned, scrubbed, spread, elegant, and cooked. <note>original: *Versa, prasterga, strata, lautaq, coctaq, omnia.*</note>

The pavement drew its splendor from the pride of marble and displayed itself with bright columns that illuminated the courtyard with solid marble. At this first sight of the marble work, the remaining splendor of the royal banquet was, as it were, tasted in advance. To show exactly what the ornaments of that banquet were like, and so that the multi-colored marble of the pavement might become more brilliant, the divine writer did not even wish to pass over what was trodden underfoot. The words of the text are as follows: <term>bahat-ve-shesh ve-dar ve-sochereth</term> <note>original Hebrew: בהט-ושש ודר וסחרת; terms for various precious stones and marbles used in the palace of Esther 1:6.</note>. Among these, Arias <note>Benito Arias Montano, a 16th-century orientalist.</note> renders the last parts thus: *A pavement of crystal and marble and Parian and shining stone.* Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius, a Jewish convert and Hebraist.</note>: *A pavement of porphyry and marble, built both on the ground and in the emerald and Parian stone surroundings.* The Zurich translators: *A pavement laid with Parian and multi-colored marble stone.* Blessed Luther: *Pavement of green, white, yellow, and black marble.* The Genevans: *A pavement of porphyry, marble, alabaster, and choice marble.* Those words—*bahat*, *shesh*, *dar*, and *sochereth*—indicate precious stones almost unknown to us. By *bahat* they understand porphyritic marble, which is marble sprinkled with red spots—red marble. There is nothing more obscure than the history of stones, gems, herbs, and animals, especially to us who are as far removed from a certain understanding of them as we are certainly removed from the places where these exotic things usually originate. However, though the names of the stones and other things may be obscure, the banquet of Ahasuerus is not obscure; to be commended for its magnificence, the external splendor of the walls and pavements is described so accurately. The walls were proud with their hangings, curtains, and tapestries within golden rings of ornament. The courtyard was decorated here and there with white, fine linen, and hyacinth-colored hangings, which were suspended by purple cords of fine linen over silver rings that were supported by small marble columns. Furthermore, it is common knowledge that pavements were *laid with various stones* to give them splendor, and it requires no proof. Yet, lest we seem to have proven nothing, I add a few things about pavements made of multi-colored marble. Tullius <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> says: *I despise magnificent villas and marble pavements and coffered ceilings.* See Lambinus, p. 154, vol. 2, on Horace, *Satires*, 2.4. Furthermore, he arranged his narration in such a way (though we insist on an inverted order) that he reveals the *couches of the Royal Dining Room, shining with gold and silver.* <term>mittot zahav va-kesef</term> <note>original Hebrew: מטות זהב וכסף; couches of gold and silver.</note> It will not be irrelevant here to inquire about the beds that reveal themselves to us within the scope of Holy Scripture. Two kinds of beds are mentioned: those in which people slept, and those on which guests reclined at banquets. Both are called <term>mittot</term> in Hebrew from <term>natah</term>, which means *to stretch out*, *to recline*, or *to lean*; whence <term>mittah</term> is a *recliner* <note>Greek: ἀνακλιντήριον (*anaklinterion*)</note>, a bedding, or a couch upon which a person reclines, leans, and stretches himself out. Sleep and rest were taken in bedroom beds. However, feasts and courses of food were taken on dining room or reclining couches. It is used for *bedroom* beds where it is said that Jacob bowed himself at the head of the bed to give thanks to his God; for he was lying so that his head was raised. Since he was unable to rise due to weakness, he nonetheless composed himself in the form of one praying with a bowed face. The Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> read *Matte* (staff) there, not *mittah* (bed). Likewise, it is used for a dining couch in 2 Kings 4:10, though there are those who explain it otherwise, which I would like them to prove. The prophet Ezekiel spoke of dining couches in chapter 23:40, censuring the idolatry of the Israelites by drawing an allegory from ruined harlots for whom they put on makeup and lure. *Behold,* he says, *they come immediately, for whose sake you wash yourself, paint your eyes, and adorn yourself ornately.* He alludes to...

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
Preparation of banquets.
</margin>
...according to the custom of prostitutes, who before feasts are accustomed to wash themselves, comb their hair, and apply makeup, so that they may please their lovers, as Villalpandus <note>Juan Bautista Villalpando (1552–1608), a Spanish Jesuit scholar known for his commentary on Ezekiel.</note> and Stuckius <note>Johann Wilhelm Stucki, author of a famous work on ancient dining customs.</note> note along with him. The Prophet continues in verse 41: <term>על ערש כבוד ישבת</term> <note>original Hebrew: *al eresh kevod yashavt*</note> *you sat upon a stately bed*, and a table was set <term>לפניה</term> <note>original Hebrew: *lifneha*</note> *before her*, that is, it was prepared right in front of the bed itself. As Blessed Martin Luther translates: *You sat upon a magnificent bed, before which stood a table prepared.* Regarding this, the Weimar Paraphrasts <note>A group of Lutheran theologians who produced an explanatory Bible in the 17th century.</note> write: *You sat down at the table with your lover and received them magnificently. Everything was prepared for pleasure.* In this same way, an adulterous woman is described by 
<margin>Proverbs 7:16.</margin>
Solomon * who, in every form of luxury, invites the young man she has caught with a kiss to her table and to a skillfully built and adorned bed, saying: > *I have decked my bed with coverings of tapestry, with carved works, with fine linen of Egypt; I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon.*
The young man obeys the prostitute, accepts her terms, and follows her suddenly, *going like an ox to the slaughter*. It was not so much the clothing as the bed that was made for lust and luxury, as it is the custom of prostitutes to show outward beauty to capture and inflame the inner heart. For this reason, they use faces painted with antimony and pigments and decorated ornaments, and they set such an elegant table by the couches so that they might enlist lovers, inflamed by food and wine, into their ranks; therefore, these dining couches of prostitutes should be fled like traps and nets. Ezekiel assumes such a <term>ὑποτύπωσιν</term> <note>original Greek: *hypotyposin*, meaning a vivid sketch or outline</note> and character to depict that monstrous passion for idolatry among the Israelites, especially and fittingly through the custom of feasting at a table while reclining on a couch—a form of banqueting that undoubtedly came to the Jews from the Assyrians or Chaldeans.
<margin>Amos 6:4.</margin>
Amos mentions this several times in chapter 6, verse 4, when he says: *Woe to you who lie on beds of ivory, and stretch yourselves upon your couches.* These words prove he is speaking of the dining couch, as they are followed by descriptions of the luxury of banquets in food, music, drink, and ointments; according to the old version: *You who eat lambs from the flock, and calves from the midst of the stall. You who sing to the sound of the harp.* Tables crowded with various kinds of food around the couches were not enough; the sound of flutes, harps, and lyres had to be added, so that not only the ears but the belly would be soothed. By the custom of banqueters, harpers and singers were brought to the feasts. Thus the word <term>נגש</term> <note>original Hebrew: *niggash*, meaning to approach or bring near</note> suggests that musical ensembles were employed, which do not belong in a *bedroom*, but in a 
<margin>chapter 23:42.</margin>
dining room, where everything rang with songs and harmonies. Hence Ezekiel says *, *The voice of a multinational multitude was with her.* So the old translator renders it, but Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius, a 16th-century Hebraist.</note> translates: *to sing according to the rule of the harp.* Therefore, translate <term>שכב</term> <note>original Hebrew: *shakhav*</note> as *to recline*, for which the Old Translator has *to sleep*, and <term>סרח</term> <note>original Hebrew: *sarach*</note> means *to abound or overflow with plenty*, and from that—which usually follows abundance—*to act wantonly*, which the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> rendered as <term>κατασπαταλᾶν</term> <note>original Greek: *kataspatalan*, to live luxuriously or decadently</note>, 
<margin>chapter 2:8.</margin>
an emphatic word. Amos also mentions * pledged garments; for when proper couches were not available, their place was supplied by blankets, garments, tapestries, or other things found in nature. *They lay themselves down upon garments taken in pledge*, says the Prophet, *beside every altar, and the wine of the condemned* (prepared from the goods of those condemned because they refused to worship idols with

<column-break/>

them) *they drink in the house of their Gods*. Here the Septuagint uses <term>περιπετάσματα</term> <note>original Greek: *peripetasmata*</note>, meaning they prepared blankets from sewn garments to spread on the beds where they reclined. Hence Blessed Luther writes: *At all the altars they feast upon the pledged clothes, etc.* And the Dutch: *They lay themselves down by garments.* This refers to the altar upon the pledged clothes. The Prophet attacks the depraved impudence with which they celebrate festivals in their idolatrous temples during feasts, piling tyranny upon idolatry. Pledged garments are those taken as collateral. The Chaldean version says *on Beds*. (Compare Jerome's commentary on Ezekiel, page 289.) The Prophet continues *, *Those who sit in Samaria in the corner of a bed, and in the leg of a couch.* The Vulgate has: *Who dwell in Samaria in the corner of a bed, and in the couch of Damascus.* He seems to have noted those who were soft and overflowing with luxury, who took the seats of honor on the couches. I say *seats of honor*, for the word <term>בפאת</term> <note>original Hebrew: *bi-feat*</note> means at the head and corner of the bed, in the primary place, as Villalpandus prefers. Blessed Luther translates: *They have a bed in the corner, and a couch in Damascus.* And the Dutch: *Those who sit in Samaria, in the corner of the bed, and on the frame of the pot, etc.* And in the gloss: *Some understand these to be the luxurious and banqueting Israelites, who lived carelessly and threw God's well-intended warnings of coming misery to the wind. The Hebrew word is 'Demecheck,' which is found nowhere else in Holy Scripture. Some take it from 'Dammecheck,' that is, Damascus, and translate it as a couch from Damascus, or a Damascene or Syrian magnificent carriage.* This is an obscure passage; therefore the Septuagint retained the word <term>משק</term> <note>original Hebrew: *mesheq*</note>, writing it as <term>ἱερεῖς</term> <note>original Greek: *hiereis* ("priests"), likely a transcription error in the original OCR/source for *Damaskos* or similar</note>. Indeed, it should be written thus, as Jerome well noted. The Chaldean version reads <term>ערש</term> <note>original Hebrew: *eresh*</note> regarding the strength with which the people insolently exalted themselves from the covenant with the Damascenes. I hardly doubt that the custom of reclining at the table is being alluded to, whose antiquity we need not doubt. Older than that, but less comfortable, was the custom of sitting; since this seemed more bothersome to some nations before tables were invented, it was changed to that mode of reclining, where beds were spread for those dining. This method was much more delicate and comfortable for the body. The body was leaned and the head reclined upon a blanket or pillow, with the feet stretched out behind. Originally, where simplicity of diet and manners flourished, beds were simple and without luxury. However, as the luxury of the age grew, they sparkled with gold, silver, ivory, and other things. The examples of the Patriarchs provide a simple way of living and dining; they did not know that custom of reclining on beds. The pious Patriarchs consecrated only their <term>χαμαιτυπία</term> <note>original Greek: *chamaitypia*, literally "hitting the ground," referring to sleeping/sitting on the earth</note> and sat sometimes upon the bare earth without elaborate equipment. It was according to this ancient simplicity that Christ fed the people <term>ἐπὶ τῷ χλωρῷ χόρτῳ</term> <note>original Greek: *epi tō chlōrō chortō*</note> *upon the green grass* (Mark 6:39). Thus also Virgil mentions a grassy seat, and Macrobius in *Saturnalia* book 3, chapter 6. Leaving aside turf and herbs, animal skins became the material for seating, which is why Judith is said to have sat on *skins* when she came to Holofernes' dinner; in Greek these are called <term>κώδια</term> <note>original Greek: *kōdia*, fleeces or skins</note>, just as today pillows are sewn from the skins of goats and other animals and placed on benches so that we may sit more softly upon them. Ovid also mentions these:
> *He who could add skins was rich,*

# Jeremiah 16:8.

<margin>The preparation of banquets. Odyssey, Book 3, verse 38.</margin>
Thus in Homer, the kindness of Pisistratus <note>Son of Nestor, appearing in the Odyssey as a model of hospitality.</note> toward strangers is commended, as he placed them on soft skins for the feast,
> on soft fleeces upon the sands of the sea, <note>original Greek: κώεσιν ἐν μαλακοῖσιν ἐπὶ ψαμάθοις ἁλίῃσι</note>

Where Eustathius <note>A 12th-century scholar and archbishop known for his commentaries on Homer.</note> praises the frugality of the ancients and reproaches the luxury of the subsequent age. Plato also refers to this in *The Republic*, Book 2, page 600, where he describes men
> having provided barley cakes and loaves upon some reeds or clean leaves, reclining upon mats spread with bryony and myrtle, they themselves and their children feasted, drinking wine and singing to God, pleasantly spending time with one another. <note>original Greek: μᾶζα καὶ ἄρτους ἐπὶ κάλαμόν τινα παραβαλόμενοι, ἢ φύλλα καθαρά, κατακλινέντες ἐπὶ στιβάδων ἐστρωμένων μίλακί τε καὶ μυῤῥίναις, εὐωχεῖσθαι αὐτοί τε καὶ τὰ παιδία, ἐπιπίνοντες τοῦ οἴνου καὶ ὑμνοῦντες τὸν Θεὸν ἡδέως ξύνοντες ἀλλήλοις.</note>

That greatest of Philosophers, in order to instruct the Republic in frugal living, by prescribing a rule of diet, praises a sober life as much as he condemns a delicate one. This form of Republic flourished among those first men of the age, much more illustrious, much purer, and much simpler. They and their children sought their delights, before the use of skins prevailed, upon reeds or clean foliage, on <term>stibades</term> <note>From the Greek *stibas*, a bed of straw, rushes, or leaves spread on the ground.</note> made from various kinds of herbs. Therefore, bedding and couches were usually composed of reeds, herbs, and tender foliage in that ancient and simple age; the Greeks called them *stibades* and *stibadia*, hence in Theocritus: *
<margin>Idyll 13, verse 32.</margin>
> Stepping out onto the shore, they prepared their meal in pairs
> at evening. Many of them spread one bed on the ground,
> for a meadow lay there, a great source of bedding.
> From there they cut flowering rush and deep galingale. <note>original Greek: Ἐκβάντες δ' ἐπὶ θῖνα, κατὰ ζυγὰ δαῖτα πένοντο δειλινοί. πολλοὶ δὲ μίαν στορέσαντο χαμεύναν, λειμὼν γάρ σφιν ἔκειτο, μέγα στιβάδεσσιν ὄνειαρ. ἔνθεν βούτομον ἔζυ, βαθὺν δ' ἐτάμοντο κύπειρον.</note>

->Which Eobanus renders thus:<- <note>Helius Eobanus Hessus (1488–1540), a German Latin poet.</note>
> Here indeed, having departed to the nearby wide shores,
> they diligently prepared a brief evening meal
> in pairs; the majority lay down on beds
> spread upon the ground, for a vast plain
> extended its wide grassy fields all around;
> from here they cut the sharp flowering rush and deep galingale.

Hence the Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator.</note> of Theocritus, page 112, says: *They call "stibades" a grassy covering made of vegetation.* From these, the Latins took their customs, and the word *Torus* <note>A couch or bed.</note> implies something similar, which to Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a Roman scholar and writer.</note> refers to a bed made of twisted herb (*herba torta*), just as a *toral* is that which would be thrown over it. Aristophanes calls a bed of rushes a *stibada schoinou* <note>original Greek: στιβάδα σχοίνου</note>. Spartan youths used to make their beds or bedding from stalks and reeds, concerning which Plutarch says: *The young men slept together on mats (stibades), which they themselves brought from the reeds growing by the native Eurotas.* <note>The river Eurotas in Sparta.</note> *Stibadokoiteon* <note>original Greek: Στιβαδοκοιτέων</note> was said of that manner of reclining on a couch, when they lay upon herbs spread on the ground either to sleep or to feast. The host took care to have the *stibadium* <note>A semicircular dining couch.</note> prepared, hence Virgil:
> They built up couches, and feasted on rich banquets.

Athenaeus speaks of the same in Book 4: *They make tents, and in these, mats from vegetation. Upon these they spread carpets, on which those reclining feast.* <note>original Greek: Σκηνὰς ποιοῦνται ἐν δὲ ταύταις στιβάδας ἐξ ὕλης. ἐπὶ δὲ τούτων τάπιδας ὑποστρωννύουσιν, ἐφ' αἷς τοὺς κατακλινθέντας εὐωχεῖσθαι.</note> And a little later: *he commands reeds for those who work for themselves.* <note>original Greek: τοῖς δ' αὐτόροις ἐπιτάττει κάλαμον.</note> An unnamed author in Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> says: *coming to dinner, he reclined on mats, not on barbarian carpets.* <note>original Greek: παρελθὼν ἐπὶ τὸ δεῖπνον, κατεκλίνετο μὲν ἐπὶ στιβάδων, οὐκ ἐπὶ ταπίδων βαρβαρικῶν.</note> In Philostratus, Book 2, the King of the Indians reclined on a festive bed made of straw, and next to him were five of his kinsmen. Let us also hear Dion Chrysostom in the *Euboica*: *we feasted for the rest of the day, you reclining on leaves and skins, upon a high mat.* <note>original Greek: εὐωχούμεθα τὸ λοιπὸν τῆς ἡμέρας, ὑμεῖς μὲν κατακλινθέντες ἐπὶ φύλλων τε καὶ δερμάτων, ἐπὶ στιβάδος ὑψηλῆς.</note> The custom of the Jews was almost the same
<margin>p. 805.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>The preparation of banquets.</margin>
during the Festival of Tabernacles <note>Sukkot.</note>, where they cut branches from trees to build the small huts where they would feast. However, this rough and unrefined custom did not last long, but was gradually refined when they later stuffed herbs into cushions and laid them beneath themselves. Hence it is called a *stibas*, because it served as stuffing made from herbs. This word later remained as the name for a specific herb especially suited for this purpose due to the softness of its leaves; thus to Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Alexandrian grammarian.</note>, a *stibas* (as he writes with the accent on the second-to-last syllable) is *a kind of grass*, and indeed *a composition*, from which *stibazo* <note>original Greek: στιβάζω</note> refers to that positioning, whence it is said *to gather and collect wood for the fire*, to *pile up* (*stibazein*) in Ecclesiasticus chapter 8, and *to pile up upon the altar* in 1 Kings 12. And because these beds were first made from collected leaves and herbs, they received the name *lectus* <note>A bed or couch.</note>, according to Varro, from *legere*—the "gathering" or "collecting" of straw and herbs. But a derivation from the Greek *lektron* <note>original Greek: λέκτρον, meaning bed.</note> seems preferable, from which comes *lectisternium* <note>A religious ritual involving a banquet offered to deities who were represented by their statues reclining on couches.</note> and *lectica* <note>A litter or sedan chair.</note>. Similarly, *torus* was named from "twisted" (*tortis*) herbs, as Servius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil.</note> prefers in his notes on the 5th *Aeneid*, page 393, because the ancients either sat or reclined upon a heap of herbs. Apuleius’s words seem to refer to this etymology: *Psyche, reclining sweetly in tender and grassy places on a couch of grass itself.* This cheaper way of living became established early on, and gradually, as human luxury increased, a softer way of reclining succeeded it. Thus Servius wrote that even in his own time, the ancients did not have *stipadia*—he does not refer to the most ancient and archaic people, whom it is established did have them, but because they had fallen out of use since the earliest times—he says the ancients of the tribe of brothers feasted on three couches, referring to those verses of Virgil: *
<margin>1st Aeneid.</margin>
> When she arrives, the Queen is already on her proud tapestries.

Later, as skins also became outdated, beds were made of feathers, and for the more noble, they were made from the feathers of rarer birds—at first without frames, and later adorned with frames or boards. Lampridius writes of the Emperor Commodus that *he did not recline except on couches that had hare’s fur or the under-wing feathers of partridges.* Hence Apuleius, in Book 10: *A bed translucent with Indian tortoiseshell, with a heap of feathers.* Beds prepared with careful arrangement usually held three guests, sometimes four or fewer. The first mention of <term>Triclinia</term> <note>A dining room with three couches arranged in a U-shape.</note> appeared, and indeed was first brought to Rome when Asia was conquered, as Pliny testifies, *but they were made of bronze*. <margin>Book 33, chapter 11.</margin> Later, with increasing luxury, beds were then covered with purple blankets, which is why Amos, as we heard above, reproached the Samaritans and the inhabitants of Jerusalem for the luxury of their bedding. Ordinarily, there were three beds placed around a circular dining table, so that a space remained between each bed: three beds enclosed about two-thirds of the table. A larger space was left between the highest and lowest bed, so that it might contain one-third of the table's circumference; this vacancy was for bringing in or taking away food. Sometimes a single bed surrounded two-thirds of the table. If three beds surrounded it, it was properly called a *Triclinium*. However, only three guests usually reclined on each bed, and this was the ordinary manner; hence Cicero censures the luxuriously foul banquet of Piso in *Against Piso*, number 27, because five people were on a single small bed, as if it were not fitting for Roman dignity...
<margin>Book 33 chapter 11.</margin>

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES.

A banquet was suitable for a gathering, and yet it could be inconvenient for the fellow diners. When the table was set, it was not with shellfish or fish, but with many dishes of slightly tainted meat, etc. The Greeks were crowded, five to a small couch, often more; he himself sat alone, etc. If anyone else describes this order best, it is **Horace**, from whom we shall taste only as much as is sufficient. He elegantly describes the banquet of Nasidienus, in which, however, certain things were less than elegant. These verses show three people dining together on one couch:

->I was the Highest, and near me was Viscus of Thurii, and below,<-
->if I remember correctly, was Varius.<-
->On the second couch were reclining<-
->with Servilius Balatro<-
->Vibidius, whom Maecenas had brought as "shadows."<-
->On the third couch<-
->Nomentanus was above the host himself, and Porcius below.<-

Nasidienus the host lay in the middle between Nomentanus and Porcius, just as Fundanius was in the middle on the first couch, and Maecenas was in the middle of the middle couch, as the more honored man; for the middle couch was the one that stood in front and to which honor was deferred by the host. From this comes that **Double Triclinium** <note>A dining room with two sets of three couches.</note> which Perpenna established, whose arrangement Servius brings forward from Sallust, where on the first or highest couch lie Maecenas, Antonius, and Versius—the first in the superior position, the second in the middle, and the third in the inferior. On the second and middle couch, only two recline, Fabius and Sertorius. On the lowest were Perpenna with two others. However, Lambinus arranged it differently in his notes on Horace, attributing three guests to the first couch. Therefore, three couches <margin>13. N. A. 11</margin> contained nine guests, which number **Gellius** <note>Aulo Gellius, a 2nd-century Roman author of the 'Attic Nights'.</note> praises from Varro as being "full." 

But they did not stick so strictly to this number that they did not dare to go above or below it at times. Often only two would recline on two couches placed in the first position, and this for the reason that if some guest arrived unexpectedly, there would be a place to recline. **Plutarch** noted this in his *Table Talk* (Book 5, Question 5), saying that no one would be so ridiculous as to not leave some empty place on the couch so that there would be room for a newcomer. Indeed, there were usually three to a place and couch. Thus, seven guests were frequently accustomed to meet, so much so that as the number nine fell out of use, a banquet of nine people almost became a "brawl" [convitium], since it is very well known regarding the number of guests: "seven is a banquet, nine is a brawl," as **Capitolinus** says in his life of Verus. And **Ausonius**, subtracting one from the number, says:

->For six make a proper banquet<-
->With a King; if more, it is a brawl.<-

<margin>1. Satyr 4</margin> But **Horace** also testifies:

->You may often see four dining on each of the three couches.<-

And thus twelve on three couches. Indeed, what is rarest, even five. In that banquet of Christ, **Baronius** <note>A 16th-century Cardinal and historian.</note> conjectures (at Year of Christ 34) that five reclined on some couches and three on others. Also in use were **biclinia** <note>Two-couch arrangements.</note>; indeed, sometimes a single couch added to a table is read about. It was called a <term>monolektron</term> <note>original Greek: Μονόλεκτρον</term> or <term>monoklinon</term> <note>original Greek: μονόκλινον</note>—a "single-couch"—or, to speak from its resemblance to the letter C, it was often called a <term>Sigma</term> <note>The lunar sigma of the Greek alphabet resembled a Latin 'C'.</note>, about which **Chrysologus** says: <margin>Sermon 93, p. 85</margin> *The Pharisee, bright in his clothing, first in distinction, swelling in the very eyes of Christ, about to please man and not God with his feasts, is festive and poured in,* and it was called <term>Sebaston</term> <note>meaning "venerable" or "Augustan."</note>, perhaps more from its first

<column-break/>

letter than for any other sense. The more honored place of this arrangement was the right horn, and the nearest was the left horn, which the words of **Sidonius** (Book 1, Epistle 2) show. We add no more, referring the Benevolent Reader to **Buxtorf's** *Disputation on the Supper*, where he deals at length with the reclining of the Hebrews. 

In ancient times, especially among the Orientals, who for that reason are called <term>philomyroi</term> <note>original Greek: φιλόμυροι, "ointment-lovers."</note>, there was a very great use of ointments; for those received at a banquet were anointed on almost every single limb of the human body, hence "dripping hair," that is, anointed and perfumed, is read in Lucan (10. v. 184, p. 272); and in Horace, "anointed and scented hair" (Book 1, Ode 29, v. 7-8 and Ode 11, Book 2, v. 13); "a scented head" (Book 2, Satyr 7, v. 55). In **Nieremberg** (History of Nature, Book 8, 12, p. 137), some of the Indians wash the feet of guests. **Valerius Maximus** (Book 2) records that the Ionians were the first inventors of these things. 

Among the Jews also, Holy Scripture testifies that guests came to banquets washed and anointed. For Christ reproves the Pharisee <note>Simon the Pharisee, in the Gospel of Luke.</note> because he had not anointed His head with oil when he had invited Him to lunch, as if to say: *You have indeed invited me, Simon, but how coldly you think of me, and what kind of guest you take me for, external signs show. For you have not even shown me those common duties which are usually performed for accepted guests and honorable men: you gave no water for my feet, no oil for my head, nor a kiss for my mouth.* Nor was this rite of anointing unknown to the Romans: **Fabullus** had dismissed his guests well-anointed indeed, but hungry, from the dinner, at whom **Martial** (3, 3, 10) joked mockingly in this epigram:

> I confess, you gave good ointment
> To the guests yesterday: but you carved nothing.
> It is a false thing to be well-anointed and to starve.
> He who does not dine and is anointed, Fabullus,
> Seems to me to be truly dead.

"Dead," he says, for the dead were also anointed by the Romans before they were given to the funeral pyre. Regarding the various uses of ointments, which have fallen out of use today, see **Rigalt** on Artemidorus, **Villalpandus** on Ezekiel 23, **Casaubon** on Suetonius, **Conring** on Hermetic Medicine, and **J. Baptista Casalius** on profane Roman rites. 

No less care was applied by the Ancients in crowning their guests, of which they made **Janus** the first author, calling him <term>Stephanoton</term> <note>original Greek: Στεφανωτόν, "The Crowned One."</note>, as **Athenaeus** testifies. These crowns were used in sacrifices, contests, games, victories, triumphs, weddings, inaugurations, and funerals. Moreover, the crowns were made of ivy (Pliny, Book 16, c. 1), or of nard (Pliny, Book 21, 3), or of myrtle (Horace, Book 1, Ode 4), or of roses (Horace, Book 2, Ode 3), or of laurel (Suetonius in the Life of Tiberius), or of linden-bark [phylura] (Ovid, Fasti Book 5), or of parsley (Horace, Book 2, Ode 7), or of lilies (Athenaeus), or finally from other flowers and herbs, about which see **Stuckius** <margin>Book 3, chapter on banquets</margin> and especially **Charles Paschal's** tenth book *On Crowns*. 

Besides the courses and the most delicate preparations of food, banquets were seasoned either with the sweetest music (compare Stuckius, Book 3, chapter 20) or were enlivened by other convivial games, which **Pollux** (Book 9) and **Plutarch** (Table Talk, Book 7, q. 8) described copiously. But above all, the "food of the mind" and the sweetest seasoning of the banquet was applied: mutual conversation. For in olden times, banquets were established with such frugality that they did not indulge in gluttony, nor join night to day and day to night by drinking, but spent time in honorable and cheerful conversation...

<meta>The text cuts off here, with the catchword "and cheerful" [original: & hilaria] indicating the start of the next page.</meta>

# Jer. XVI. 8. 627

<margin>The preparation of banquets.</margin>
...and they refreshed themselves with joyful entertainment. For this reason, it was the custom of the Persians to consult on serious matters over their cups, as noted by Strabo in *Book 15*. The Greeks, after they had feasted magnificently, would decide on matters of war as if their spirits had been revived, according to Athenaeus in *Book 4, Chapter 5*. This was also the custom of the Germans: they would confer at banquets over their drinks regarding peace, war, treaties, alliances, friendships, betrothals, and pacts, as Tacitus writes in *On the Customs of the Germans*. Alexander ab Alexandro writes the same regarding the Britons in *Genial Days, Book 5, Chapter 3*, and regarding the Bactrians in *Book 5, Chapter 21*. <note>See also Plutarch, *Symposiacs*, Book 7, questions 9 and 10; and Stuckius, *Ancient Customs of Banquets*, Book 3, Chapter 19.</note> Truly, what the conversation of learned and prudent men ought to be in banquets is easily learned from the "banquets" <note>The *Symposia* or dialogues set at meals</note> of Plato, Xenophon, Plutarch, and Macrobius. In these works shines that ancient and honorable rite of gatherings and conversations, which, as <margin>In the *First Book of Offices* by Cicero, edited by Betulejus, page 112.</margin> Betulejus reminds us, *can serve as an example for those studious of such decorum and provides material for an invitation that should not be despised.* Hence, Athenaeus, in the books he calls *The Dinner Philosophers* <note>original: "δειπνοσοφιστὰς" (Deipnosophistae)</note>, deals for the most part with "literate banquets," teaching by what method and at what time it is appropriate to propose problems at feasts, and both proposing and discussing many "convivial knots" <note>original: "gryphos," a type of intricate riddle</note> and jests <note>original: "syrpos," obscure or dark riddles</note>. This is also the purpose of Plutarch’s books of *Table Talk* <note>original: "symposiakōn"</note>, which prove through many arguments that one must philosophize even amidst the dainties. For it pleased those who were wiser than the common crowd not to compete with wine-cups, but with clever questions, and to season their banquets not only with a variety of courses, but also with the pleasantness of problems and inquiries.

<margin>Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, Book 18, Chapter 2.</margin>
But what happens today in our Universities? If any student discusses something over his cups, immediately another is there to mock his "philosophical nature." Yet let it be done learnedly, not, as they say, "letting the mind go slack." Rather, let us learn from Gellius, who praised the Athenian celebration of the <term>Saturnalia</term> <note>A winter festival characterized by relaxation of social norms, here used to describe a scholarly holiday.</note> as being conducted with a "literate mouth": <margin>Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, Book 18, Chapter 2.</margin> *We were celebrating the Saturnalia at Athens,* he says, *quite cheerfully and modestly; not, as the saying goes, letting our minds go slack, but soothing and relaxing them a little with the pleasant and honorable allurements of conversation. Several of us who had come from Rome to Greece, and who attended the same lectures and the same Teachers, used to meet for the same dinner. Then, the one who took his turn to manage the dinner would set as prizes for solving a question a Greek or Latin book by an ancient writer, and a crown woven of laurel. He would propose as many questions as there were people present, and when he had set them all forth, lots would decide the order and place of speaking. Thus, the question solved was rewarded with the crown and the prize; if it was not solved, it was passed to the one who succeeded by lot, and this was maintained in turn around the circle. If no one untied the knot of that question, the prize itself and the crown were dedicated to the God whose festival it was. The things sought after were of this kind: either a sentiment of an ancient poet, charmingly obscure but not anxious, or a search into an older history; or the correction of some decree of Philosophy that had been wrongly publicized; or the solution of a sophisticated trap; or the hunt for an unexpected and rarer word; or the time-tense in a clear word that was nevertheless most obscure.* Let Gellius be followed by <margin>Book 6, Chapter 19.</margin> Julius Pollux, who says that the *Gryphus* <note>The "Knot" or Riddle</note> and the *Enigma* belonged to fellow-drinkers, not so much for the sake of a joke as for the sake of cleverness; and the prize was a portion of meat, while the penalty was a cup of salty brine. But here are the very words concerning the Banquet: <note>original Greek: "τῶν μέντοι συμποτικῶν αἰνιγμ. τὸ γρῖφον..."</note> *Of the symposiac enigmas, the "gryphos" [knot-riddle] had an element of play. But the "gryphos" also had seriousness, and for the solver, it had a prize of a portion of meat; but for the one unable to solve it, it was to drink a cup of brine.*

Regarding the prize or "honorary gift" <note>original: "γέρας" (geras)</note>, as Pollux calls it: just as Samson offered thirty linen garments and as many tunics as a prize to those who solved the enigma proposed, so also the Gentiles were accustomed to give prizes to those who solved an enigma or a proposed question during a meal. To this also belongs what Josephus writes in *Book 1: Against Apion*: that Solomon, the King of Jerusalem <note>original: "Solymæ"</note>—whose wisdom was contained within the same regions and boundaries as the course of the sun—and Hiram, King of the Tyrians, used to propose problems and enigmatic questions to one another, and they established that the one who emerged victorious in solving them would receive a monetary fine from the other.

Furthermore, let Pollux be accompanied by the author of *The Dial of Princes*, writing thus about Alexander the Great: <margin>Book 2, Chapter 27.</margin> *Among the other books of Aristotle, there is a certain one titled "Babylonian Questions"; where it is said that while Alexander reclined at the table, various disputations took place, with Alexander proposing them, the Princes of Persia standing by, and Aristotle delivering the judgment.*

However, the ancients did not always propose enigmas at banquets; sometimes they were accustomed to bring books to the family table and refresh the guests by reading, and to establish a peaceful conversation based on what they observed during the reading. This we have learned clearly again from Aulus Gellius. <margin>Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, Book 2, Chapter 22.</margin> *At the table of Favorinus in a family banquet, it was customary to read either an ancient poem by a Lyric Poet, or history, partly in the Greek language, at other times in Latin. Thus, a Latin poem was being read there involving the "Iapyx" wind. The question was asked: what wind is this? From what places does it blow, and what is the reason for such an infrequent word?* Seneca, the Master of Wisdom, reports the same in *Epistle 64*: *We had various talk at the banquet; then a book by Quintus Sextius the Elder was read, etc.* Cornelius Nepos says in the *Life of Atticus*: *Dinner was never held without some reading, so that the guests were delighted no less in their minds than in their bellies.* Pliny writes: <margin>Book 3, Epistle 5.</margin> *Over this dinner a book was read, notes were taken, etc.* Join to these the things which <margin>Book 7, Epistle 36.</margin> Chytreus himself collected from the books of the ancients on page 377; we do not wish to plunder his collections. Thus, in the past, <term>Sacred Reading</term> <note>original: "lectio sacra"</note> during meals was common for Clerics and Religious orders, as seen in Cyprian, *Book 2, epistle at the end*; the *Council of Africa, chapter 6*; the *Third Council of Toledo, chapter 7*; and *Burchard, Book 2, chapter 169.* So at Tübingen in the Stipendium College, at Leipzig in the Pauliner College, and elsewhere, while the other students are taking their lunch or dinner, one ascends the pulpit and reads several chapters from the Holy Bible. Stuckius writes in *Ancient Banquets, Book 3, chapter 18*, that this is also observed in the literary schools of Paris <note>original: "Lutetiæ"</note>, where while the rest are dining, one reads the commentaries of famous men.

Now let those step forward who deny that one should philosophize amidst the wine-cups—those who judge it better to introduce music and other playful things which serve the indulgence of the spirit rather than the sharpening of the wit, and who think Philosophy and the conversations and inquiries established from it should be omitted. They argue that we cannot be free for such serious matters at that time, nor are those matters suitable for playing along. But the response to these people...

Nor do we wonder at those who dare to demand such things, since the sum of their desire is to <margin>Preparation for banquets.</margin> soften the spineless soul, to insolently drain pleasant allurements, and to loosen broken senses. Thus, among the men of our age, that which John of Salisbury <note>original: "Saresberiensis"</note> complained about regarding his own century has now justly taken hold in banquets: *Without measure,* <margin>Book VII, chapter 6. Polycratics.</margin> *he says, they drink to a measure; and he prevails over the others who, either by gluttony or by trickery, prostrates or conquers his fellow drinkers.* And, as the previously praised author of the *Dial of Princes* <note>original: "Horologii Autor" - referring to Antonio de Guevara</note> redoubles with words well worth noting: <margin>Book 3, chapter 20, number 530. Dial of Princes.</margin> *Banquets are not now established by philosophers, but by gluttons; not for disputing, but for quarreling; not for explaining doubtful matters, but for tearing apart the lives of others; not for confirming old friendships, but for beginning new contentions; not for learning any doctrine, but for making a trial of delicate food. And what is worst: if ever the old men compete with the juniors at the table, it is not over who might speak the weightiest opinions, but who might drain the most and largest cups.* But we shall send these slaves of Bacchus <note>Followers of the god of wine/drunkenness</note> to the "Land of Sickness" <note>original: "Morboniam" - a common early modern Latin idiom for "the devil" or a place of ruin</note>, and we shall further consider what kind of guests they ought to be when speaking with one another? We do not praise those who defile their food with the heaviness of contentions and disputes, who are so full of arts that unless they have spewed something out, they cannot take in any food. Rather, we praise with both hands those whom the most learned of the Romans, Varro, once selected: whose conversations were not about anxious or twisted matters, but were pleasant and inviting, and useful with a certain charm and pleasure, from which the intellect might become more beautiful and agreeable. *This will surely happen, he says, if we talk together about the kind of things that pertain to the common use of life, about which there is no leisure to speak in the forum or in the conducting of business.*

Let us see, however, in a few words, the <term>Chidah</term> <note>original: חִידָה</note> of Samson, that is, a problem, a riddle, or a "griphe" <note>A clever or complex puzzle</note>, which in Hebrew was proposed in this way: <margin>Septuagint: "Out of the eater..."</margin> "Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness." <note>original Hebrew: מֵהָאֹכֵל יָצָא מַאֲכָל וּמֵעַז יָצָא מָתוֹק; Greek: ἐκ τοῦ ἔσθοντος ἐξῆλθε βρῶσις, καὶ ἐξ ἰσχυροῦ ἐξῆλθε γλυκύ.</note>

Since, indeed, the elegance and force of a riddle is placed in antitheses and opposites, and in the first part of this puzzle the antithesis and contrast appear beautifully ("out of the eater came food"), it was once thought that instead of "from the strong" <note>original: "me-az" (מֵעַז)</note>, it should read "from the bitter" <note>original: "me-mar" (מֵעַז - likely a scribal comparison/error mentioned here)</note>. But there is no need for this change, since the word *az* is also explained as a honeycomb, sharp, etc. And Josephus, recounting the history of Samson, brings forth the problem thus: *The all-devourer produced sweet food from itself, even though it was altogether unpleasant.* Book V, Chapter X. We could bring forward many other delights of the feast, did we not fear the stomach of more delicate men, concluding this meditation on the banquets of the ancients with that concluding shout of the Spartans, who, when they received a guest or a youth into their communal meals <note>original: "phiditia"</note>, would say while pointing to the doors:

->word goes out.<-

Just as the history of rings escapes the notice of the common people, so their origin is almost entirely obscure and hidden to the learned. We do not care that they are said to have come from Prometheus, since, as Pliny testifies in *Book 33, Chapter 1*, that is fabulous; meanwhile, their use has been celebrated from ancient times. Thus we read in sacred history, even before the destruction of Troy, that Judah gave to Tamar his daughter-in-law (whom he thought to be a harlot) a ring with a necklace and a staff as a pledge when she asked for payment for their union (Genesis 38:18). Likewise, Pharaoh took the ring from his own hand and placed it on Joseph's hand, and having adorned him in a robe of fine linen and a gold chain around his neck, he placed him in the second chariot in dignity (Genesis 41:42; Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 2, Chapter 3). If we consult secular history, Dionysius of Halicarnassus is a witness in *Book 4* that even the Sabines in the time of Romulus were devoted to the ornament of rings. *And a love of these things, he says, entered them: both the bracelets which they wore on their left arms and the rings. For the Sabines were wearers of gold, being no less luxurious than the Etruscans.* At what time and from whom the use of rings reached the Romans is not sufficiently clear; however, in the time of Hannibal, their use was so great that, according to Livy in *Book 3* of the Second Punic War, Mago, who had been sent to Carthage as a messenger of the victory at Cannae, after reciting the series of events, poured out a huge heap of gold rings in the vestibule of the Senate House to prove such joyful news. Then he added in words, so that it might be a sign of a greater slaughter, that no one except a Knight and their chief men wore that emblem. And finally, not long after the city's founding: *Livy says, the elections of Flavius held such indignity that many of the nobles laid aside their gold rings.* The material of rings was varied; for some consisted of simple metal: iron, gold, or silver. Fortunatus Licetus, in his treatise *On the Rings of the Ancients*, displays forty diagrams of rings drawn in bronze. Others truly were of mixed metal. These could be seen either without a gem, whence they were called <term>apeiroi</term> <note>original: ἄπειροι - meaning "infinite" or "boundless," referring to a plain band</note>, about which Aristotle says in *Book 3 of Physics, Chapter 9*: *For they say those rings are "infinite" which do not have [a stone].* Indeed, they say those rings that lack a setting are <term>apeiroi</term>. Hence, in the story of Gyges, which Marcus Cicero translated from Plato into the third book of *Offices*, it is read: *When he turned the setting of that ring toward his palm.* The Latin word <term>Pala</term> <note>The bezel or setting of a ring</note> is infrequent, which Cicero rendered as <term>sphendone</term> <note>original: σφενδόνην</note>, which in Plato is the name for the mass by which the gem of the ring is enclosed. Others, however, had a gem remarkable for some figure, though not all. Especially, however, signet rings enjoyed images. Thus Georgius Longus, in his work on signet rings, records that at first plain let...

Thus, according to Plutarch, Pompey's ring was engraved with a *lion carrying a sword* <note>original: "λέων ξιφήρης"</note>. Likewise, when Nero was taking the auspices, Sporus offered him a ring as a gift, the engraving of whose gem was the *Abduction of Proserpina*, according to Suetonius. Thus, it was not unusual among the Pagans for rings to be decorated with images of gods or goddesses; see Höpping, *On the Law of Insignia*, chapter 10, number 137 and following. An exception was made for signet rings, upon which they considered it a religious violation to engrave the forms of gods and goddesses, according to Macrobius; hence the saying of Pythagoras: *Do not wear the image of God on a ring.* <note>original: "ἐν δακτυλίῳ εἰκόνα θεοῦ μὴ περιφέρειν"</note> Just as the material of rings was varied, so too was their use. In ancient times, the ring was a mark of free birth <note>term: "ingenuitas" - the status of being born free rather than enslaved</note>, not only among the pagans but also the Hebrews; hence in the Gospel, after the Father saw his prodigal son return, he commanded: *Put a ring on his hand.* It was also a symbol of liberty; thus, slaves were granted both freedom and a ring at the same time, according to *Novel 78* <note>A law from the "Novellae Constitutiones" of Justinian.</note>: *Therefore we decree, if anyone manumitting a male or female servant should declare them Roman citizens (for it is not permitted otherwise), let him know by this law that he who has received freedom shall immediately possess the consequent right of both gold rings and rebirth, and he shall no longer necessarily demand this from the emperors.* <note>The text provides this law in both Greek and Latin; the English here covers the meaning of both.</note> The ring was also a sign of a pledge given, primarily a wedding token and down-payment <note>term: "arrhabo" - a deposit or earnest money securing a contract</note>. Concerning this as a symbol of betrothal, and indeed on the finger of the Bride which is next to the smallest, let us hear Josephus de la Cerda:
