Therefore, it seemed to the ancients that this finger should be encircled by a ring as if by a crown. If you transfer these ideas to the betrothal rite, you will easily guess the cause: for the crown is a symbol of marriage. Therefore, so that the heart surrendered to the marriage may be sealed, and marital chastity may be assigned to affection, for that reason the "finger of the heart" is crowned with the nuptial symbol—that is, the ring. These are his words. On which hand the ancients wore their rings is attested by this present passage in Jeremiah; among the Hebrews they were worn on the right hand, which agrees with the testimony of Sirach 49:13 <note>Sirach is also known as Ecclesiasticus.</note>: *How shall we magnify Zerubbabel? > ...often noted
> With three rings, now living as an ancient on a bare left hand,
> He lived inconsistently.

The reason for this was primarily twofold: partly because the right hand has greater use in performing tasks than the left, as Attejus Capito clearly testifies in Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book 7. Later, the custom of a more luxurious age began to engrave figures on precious gems, and certainly all this imitation provoked a situation where they boasted of the increased price they had paid for the stones to be carved. Hence it happened that the use of rings was removed from the right hand, which is involved in much business, and relegated to the left, which is more idle: lest the precious stones be broken by the frequent movement and duty of the right hand. Partly, it was because those who first invented rings, due to the novelty and strangeness of the thing, were ashamed to wear them in the open; hence they put the rings on the left hand as if more hidden, so that if they wore them openly, they would not incur the criticism of others. Pliny provides us with this reason:

The people of Gaul and Britain are said to have used the middle finger. Now this finger alone is excepted, while all the others are weighed down. Read more in Kirchmann, *On Rings*, chapter 4, p. 20. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES 630

<columns>

<margin>The ornamentation of rings.</margin>
Regarding the kings of the Egyptians, Jews, and Persians, the matter is clear from the sacred text: *Genesis 41:42, 1 Chronicles 21:8, Esther 8:8.* Thus, as Curtius witnesses in *Book 6, Chapter 6*, Alexander the Great used to seal the letters he sent to Europe with the *gem of his old ring*; however, for those he wrote to Asia, *the ring of Darius was impressed.* <note>Alexander used his personal ring for Greek affairs and the captured Persian royal seal for Eastern administration to maintain continuity of authority.</note> But why, in the primordial language <note>Hebrew</note>, is a signet ring called *tabba'at* <note>original: "טבעת"</note> while nature is called *teva* <note>original: "טבע"</note>? Franz Tidicaeus, in his preface to *The Human Horizon*, believes this is the cause: In man, he says, the signet of divine majesty is carved, a thought which the admirable power and hidden *energy* <note>original: "ἐνέργεια"</note> of the Holy Tongue produces in these words. For this tongue calls nature *teva* from the root *tava* <note>original: "טבע"</note>, meaning "immersed," "fixed," or "impressed," because nature is, as it were, a certain character of divine power deeply fixed in created things. Indeed, the German word *Tief* <note>German for "Deep."</note> seems to be derived from this root. In the same language, a signet ring is called *tabba'at* (*Genesis 41:42, Esther 3:12*) from the same root, undoubtedly because through it some small image of arms or other things is impressed into wax or similar material, which serves as a sort of monument of the ring's owner and his binding symbol. Nor should we overlook in this place the insane custom of certain evildoers who proclaimed that rings—which the Greeks called *pharmakitas* and *goēteumenous* <note>original: "φαρμακίτας καὶ γοητευμένους" meaning rings associated with drugs, charms, or sorcery.</note> and the Arabs call *Talisman*, according to Scaliger in his *French Letters*—were marked with certain characters and endowed with peculiar power. Egypt especially possessed this trait: it applied its mind to the evil art of divinatory superstition above all other nations, led by its own King Necepso, whom Firmicus mentions in *Book 4, Chapter 16 and elsewhere*. From this, they also engraved the figures and names of the signs of heaven and other images onto their amulets and *periaptois* <note>original: "περιάπτοις" meaning charms worn around the neck or limbs.</note>; on this, see Salmasius, *On the Climacteric Years, p. 565.* For the evil demon persuaded credulous men to engrave the likenesses of pagan gods on rings, thus alluring men to the worship of idols, as if the images of those gods worn on a ring would be salutary. Gorlaeus exhibits many such examples in his *Dactyliotecha* <note>A famous 17th-century catalog of engraved gems and rings.</note>: namely, numbers 2 and 159 with Hercules; 55 with Pan; 60 with Aesculapius; 70, 75, and 178 with Mercury wearing his winged hat; 76 with the horn of Amalthea; 100 with Venus; 112 and 158 with Jupiter; 155 with a Satyr; and 177 with Apollo. From these, they attributed various efficacies to rings so consecrated (or rather, cursed by evil custom): against incantations, against envy and slander, against the bites of wild beasts, against diseases, and against loss in cards, dice, and other matters. Thus Isis is said to have worn a phylactery <note>A protective amulet.</note> when she realized she was pregnant, which Plutarch says bore an inscription denoting the "true voice." Curiously, he did not provide the Egyptian name itself which held that meaning. Goropius Becanus exhibits the image and form of this amulet in *Hieroglyphics, Book 4, p. 49.* Isis had hung it on herself while carrying Harpocrates in her womb; the same Becanus asserts (*p. 51*) that Harpocrates' image was also worn from the neck by many people to make him propitious. Similarly, the image of Alexander the Great expressed in gold or silver was once believed to help [the wearer], as Pollio recorded in *The Thirty Tyrants, ch. 13, p. 260.* Yet it is a matter of grief, as Weyer notes, that far too many people still live with impunity among those bearing the 

<column-break/>

Christian name who use such rings against demons, against diseases of the soul and body, and for preserving the strengths of the mind and body. They claim that these rings have a wonderful power and virtue divinely instilled in them, just as the rings consecrated by the Kings of Britain were believed to be an *averter of evil* <note>original: "ἀλεξίκακον"</note>; Linacre sent some of these to Budé (see *Letters, pp. 24, 26*). <note>Refers to the "Cramp-rings" hallowed by English monarchs, believed to cure epilepsy and cramps.</note> So too, books are still circulated under the name of Solomon that are impious and magical, concocted by unknown impostors. Regarding these, Licetus says: *The book which was commonly circulated under the name of the Ring of Solomon, and was so called, was deservedly condemned by the Church because it taught the impious and nefarious magic of invoking and summoning demons and confining them in rings; it is falsely attributed and ascribed to Solomon by professors of magic so that they might gain authority for that treatise.* Delrio feels the same about similar works that stand under titles like *The Little Key of Solomon* and *The Incantations of Solomon*; though I would not dare to absolutely deny that these volumes could have been made by Solomon after he fell into idolatry; nevertheless, many futile things are said to be contained in those books which do not seem to have been written by a learned man, however impious. But Epiphanius, near the end of his writings against heresies, records that all such use of phylacteries is forbidden to Christians, and Chrysostom (*Homily 12 on 1 Corinthians*) calls this evil custom a *satanic comedy*, severely taxing those Christians who imitate this evil practice. Therefore, the blindness of those who assign such great virtue and efficacy to these *sorcerous* rings is to be deplored. Some of the Pagans were saner than these; for Aristophanes speaks thus of such a ring being effective against the "bites of a sycophant" in *Plutus, Act 4, Scene 3, v. 34*, where Dicaeus answers a sycophant threatening judgment:

> I value you at nothing; for I carry this ring,
> bought from Eudamus for a drachma.

Cario interjects that the ring is not so great as to be a remedy against the bite of a sycophant (*v. 36*):

> But it is not proof against the bite of a sycophant.

Verses by Antiphanes found in Athenaeus agree, advising about a ring of the *sorcerers* against stomach pains:
<margin>*Book 3* / *Athenaeus*</margin>

> I have an ailment, and may I not have it! But if a pain
> twists me around the stomach or navel,
> I have a ring from the best maker for a drachma.

These verses receive interpretation from Alexander of Tralles, who handed down the method of making a ring against colic, and from him Johann Kirchmann in *On Rings, ch. 21, pp. 227–229.*

<meta>This page continues the philological investigation of biblical terms, shifting from the ornaments of rings to the nature of punishments mentioned in the Book of Jeremiah, specifically focusing on the term "Nervus" (shackles or stocks).</meta>

# Jeremiah, Chapter 29, Verse 26

<columns>

<margin>The Shackle.</margin>
**The Shackle.** The Hebrew word is *tsinoq* <note>original: צינוק</note>; for some think the name is composed of *tsan* and *yanaq*, as if you were to say a "sucking boat." Scholars search for what this might be and where it came from as anxiously as that stingiest of misers, old Euclio, searched for his bag of gold. They write that this type of punishment was as follows: a guilty man, enclosed between two small boats, was fed with milk and honey, his eyes constantly turned toward the sky, so that his entire face would be covered by a swarm of settling flies. Artaxerxes ordered Mithridates "to die by being placed in the boats" <note>original Greek: ἀποθανεῖν σκαφευθέντα</note> in this manner of torture because he had congratulated himself on the death of Cyrus; as Plutarch relates, an example of cruelty which I would like to present in full.

<margin>In Plutarch's *Life of Artaxerxes*, page 1863.</margin>
For the King wanted it to be believed for certain by everyone, both Greeks and barbarians, and to enjoy this glory: that in the clash with his brother Cyrus, he had killed him, dealing and receiving a wound. He did not allow anyone else to be admitted into the fellowship of that victory, so that he might place a greater fruit in the perpetuity of his praise. However, when Mithridates the Persian was attending a certain splendid banquet, Sparamixes, the most powerful of Queen Parysatis's eunuchs—who was not ignorant of the truth—after first admiring the man's good fortune and the gifts he had received from Artaxerxes, provided an opportunity for the man, now drunk, to eloquently profess, while not in full control of his mind, that Cyrus the King's brother had been killed by his own hand. "For," he said, "I did not throw my weapon without a strike as Artaxerxes did; but when I had missed the eye by a little, I hit and pierced Cyrus's temple and laid him low, from which wound he subsequently died." The eunuch immediately reported this lack of tongue-control and Mithridates's boasting to Parysatis, and she reported it to the King. Therefore, Artaxerxes, being indignant, ordered him to be killed "between the boats," a kind of punishment which Plutarch describes most accurately. They take two boats, he says, which fit together; in one of these, the one to be punished is placed on his back. They then place the other boat on top and fit it so that the head, hands, and feet stick out, but otherwise the whole body is hidden. Food is offered to the one thus enclosed; and if he refuses to eat, they force him by pricking his eyes. When he eats, they pour a mixture of milk and honey into him in place of a drink, and they always position him so that he has his eyes facing the sun. Furthermore, his whole face is covered by the multitude of flies constantly settling on it. And since he performs those functions within the boats which a man enjoying food and drink must do, maggots and worms swarm from the putrefaction and corruption of the excrement; these, creeping into the intestines, consume the body. When it is finally clear that he is dead, the upper boat is removed, and they see the flesh indeed devoured, while swarms of such small creatures cling to the intestines. By this most exquisite and atrocious punishment, Mithridates was greatly tortured for seventeen days on account of his boasting while drunk and the revelation of secrets, until he was consumed by a slow death. Antonius Gallonius notes (*On Martyrdom, chapter 1, page 21*) that this punishment of the boats was also used against Christians. It is called *Scaphismus* <note>original Greek: Σκάφευσις</note> by Eunapius (*In the Life of Maximus, page 83*) and is a punishment customary among the Persians; regarding this passage, Martinius sings the same song as Junius in his *Philological Lexicon, page 3443*, as does Quistorpius in his *Biblical Annotations, page 655*.

<column-break/>

<margin>The Shackle.</margin>
Who would dare to say that such a horrendous kind of punishment was employed by a Jewish Priest, or even alluded to by that name? I do not believe it was ever known in Israel either by name or in reality, and for that reason, no strength shall be drawn from the notion of a name that ought to be based on actual practice. We count it among the virtues of philologists to be ignorant of certain things in etymology; for how much is there that they do not know? Truly, those who hunt for the etymology of any words whatsoever cannot help but be mostly foolish and deceptive, especially regarding terms made obsolete by long use and the changes of things and men. What Mercerus said on Rabbi 13 will rightly have a place here: *We are often ignorant of the causes of names, where I think it is better to profess our ignorance than to divine rashly.* On that account, the version by Piscator also takes a beating (against which Paulus Roderus wrote), who in his own way thinks he knows better here than the other translators; for with a curious and monstrous word, he rendered it as *Saugschiff* <note>German: "Sucking-ship."</note>, a word which I do not think is worth a trifle, nor will any German understand it unless a thick explanation flows from Plutarch. Speak with Germans so that they may see and understand you, following the example of our Luther. But I much prefer our Latin Translator, who here, as in Chapter 20:1, 2, uses the more honest word <term>Nervus</term> <note>A term originally meaning sinew or nerve, but used in Latin for shackles or stocks made of such material, or later, iron.</note>, which receives the force and strength of its translation from Rabbi Kimchi, who says that *tsinoq* is an instrument by which the hands are constrained, "a closed vessel for the hands" <note>original Hebrew: כלי סגור לידים</note>. Indeed, we have declared elsewhere that many words of good value and ancient mark are in the Vulgate Version, which the present word, *Nervus*, also confirms. By this word, the ancient Latins indicate some kind of bond prepared for restraining the neck or the feet; for in ancient times, bonds for the necks and feet were made from the sinews of animals, just as were chords, ropes, and whips. However, the word did not keep its original material, like infinite others; for it was also transferred to iron and wooden bonds, with the old word retained but not the material. In Jeremiah chapter 20:1: "And he sent him into the *nervum*." Where Jerome says (page 311): "Instead of the *nervus* which we said, the Seventy and Theodotion translate it as *cataracten* <note>A trapdoor or grate.</note>. Symmachus uses *sanisipion* or *streblowterion*, both of which signify instruments of torture. We, however, have said *nervum* in the common way." This kind of torture is also mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 16) when the Apostles Paul and Silas were given into the custody of the prison. Sextus Pompeius Festus, in *On the Significance of Words* (page 121, Scaliger's edition), says: *We also call the iron bond by which the feet or even the necks are impeded a 'nervus'.* Isidore confirms the same in Book 5, the last chapter, in so many words: *A 'nervus' is an iron bond by which the feet or necks are impeded.* Plautus, the best master of speaking, used it in the *Aulularia* (Act 4, scene 10, verse 13): *But I believe the Gods wanted me to die in the 'nervus' at my house,* that is, as Lambinus explains, "to throttle my throat with an iron noose at my own house." In the *Asinaria* (3.2.5), he joins together "shackles, chains, collars, fetters, and yokes"; and the same Comic poet in Festus (cited above) says: "By Pollux, you prove your neck is for the shackle of a treacherous head!" Tertullian, writing to the Martyrs detained in prisons, 

<margin>To the Martyrs, chapter 2.</margin>
writes elegantly and forcefully: *The leg feels nothing in the shackle when the mind is in heaven.* Cato, in Gellius (Book 11, last chapter): *Thieves of private thefts spend their age in the stocks and shackles; thieves of public thefts in gold and purple.* Terence in the *Phormio* (4.4.14): *When the silver...*

<meta>This page continues the philological investigation into the nature of ancient punishments and restraints, specifically transitioning from the Persian "boat" torture mentioned on the previous page to the various forms of the "nervus" (shackle or stocks) found in Biblical and Classical texts.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<columns>

<margin>The Shackle.</margin>
...they will repeat; for our sake, it will instead go into the *shackle* <note>original: nervus</note>. 
The Glossary defines the *shackle* as a "wooden foot-fetter" <note>original Greek: ξυλοπέδη</note>. Both terms appear in Job 13:27 and chapter 33:11: "He puts my feet in the stocks" <term>בסד רגלי<gloss>in the stocks [my feet]</gloss></term>, which Aquila translates as "in the wooden foot-fetter" <note>original: ἐν ξυλοπέδῃ</note>, the Septuagint as "in a hindrance" <note>original: ἐν κωλύματι</note>, and Jerome as "in the shackle" <note>original: in nervu</note>. If you break the Greek word down into its simple parts—"wood" <note>original: ξύλον</note> and "fetter" <note>original: πέδη</note>—we find it refers to bonds for the feet. Let us look at both. The word for "fetter" <note>original: Πέδη</note> appears in Psalm 105:18 and 149:8, where the Chaldean translation uses "chain" <term>שירא<gloss>chain</gloss></term>, which is the Greek word *seira* <note>original: σειρά</note>; indeed, many Greek words were adopted by the Chaldeans and Rabbis, and some were even derived from them, as carefully collected by Buxtorf in his Chaldean-Talmudic Lexicon, though he omitted this one under the entry for "chain." In Aristophanes' play *Plutus*, "fetters" and "stocks" <note>original: πέδαι & χοίνικες</note> are mentioned together, both signifying the shackles with which the feet of criminals in prison and slaves in the workhouse were bound. The "wood" <note>original: Τὸ ξύλον</note> is taken simply to mean the stocks in Acts 16:24, when the Apostles Paul and Silas were placed in prison custody. Chrysostom (if he is indeed the author, for there is 
<margin>Volume 4, page 808, Eton edition.</margin>
great controversy among scholars about this) in his 35th homily on Acts, explained it as the *shackle*: "he secured them in the wood, as one might say, in the shackle" <note>original: ἠσφαλίσατο εἰς τὸ ξύλον, ὡς ἀν εἴποι τις εἰς τὸν νέρβον</note>. The same author also explains a term for "unbinding" by the Latin word *nemus* <note>original: νέμερον</note> in homily 22. In Aristophanes' *The Clouds*: "Then bind his neck in the wood." Nicodemus Frischlin, who translated that poet’s verses into Latin in the style of Plautus and Terence, translates this on page 339 as: "And bind his throat tight with the wood." A commentator on Aristophanes explains it thus: "The 'wood' refers to the prison, or what they call the 'foot-shackle' <note>original: ποδοκάκην</note> and 'foot-twister' <note>original: ποδοστράβην</note>." As for the word "foot-shackle" <note>original: ποδοκάκην</note>, it is not found in the Greek editions of the Bible we have today. However, a commentary on the aforementioned passage in Job 13 used it where the Vulgate had the word *nervus*. Ulpian, commenting on Demosthenes' Oration against Timocrates (page 235), says it is a certain instrument of torture in which the accused is twisted with hands and feet bound: "The foot-shackle is a torture instrument in which one is racked, with hands and feet bound." It was also called a "wooden collar" <note>original: ξύκαλον</note> or even "wood" <note>original: κᾶλον</note>. Scaliger, in his notes on Festus (page 102), says the ancient Athenians simply called the shackle "wood," which is why those bound by law were called "wood-legged" <note>original: ἐγκαλοσκελεῖς</note> in Athenian law. To this same meaning belong the "pillory" <note>original: κύφων</note> and the "collar" <note>original: κλοιὸς</note>. The Etymologist (page 349) says the "pillory" <note>original: Κύφων</note> is a shackle named from the act of "bending down," used to signify a curve; just as the Hebrew word "to bend" <term>כפף<gloss>to bend</gloss></term>, from which Casaubon derived that Greek word. Aristophanes in *Plutus* (2.4.62): "O drums and pillories!" Frischlin brought the word into Latin, translating it as *Cyphon* (pages 101, 111). Lucian in *Menippus* lists: "racks, pillories, and wheels." 
<margin>In Volume 5 of Chrysostom, page 769.</margin>
Boethius describes this type of punishment in these words: "The *pillory* is a bond or yoke made of wood or iron, of such weight that, when placed on the necks of the guilty, it presses them down and curves them, not allowing them to lift their heads." I understand the words of Manasseh in his prayer to refer to such a bond: "I am bowed down by many iron chains" <note>original: πολλῷ κλοιῷ σιδηρῷ</note>. So he says. Torments used of old to extract the truth included the wheel, scourges, the rack <note>original: equuleus</note>, and the branding iron. Regarding the wheel, it is recorded in the *History of the Maccabees* concerning the seven brothers, that the third and fourth were driven and stretched upon the wheel; Cerda describes this torture at length in his commentary on Virgil’s *Aeneid*. Regarding the "drum" <note>original: tympanum</note>, it is read 

<column-break/>

in the story of the aged Eleazar, whom the soldiers 
<margin>2 Maccabees 6:19, 28.</margin>
tried to force to taste swine’s flesh, "leading him to the drum" <note>original: ἐπὶ τὸ τύμπανον ἄγοντες</note> so that they might beat him with whips. For it follows at the end of the chapter: "being about to die from the stripes," that is, when he was near failing from the torture of the blows. The Apostle seems to have looked to this type of torture in Hebrews 11:35: "Others were tortured" <note>original: Ἄλλοι δὲ ἐτυμπανίσθησαν</note>, or "Others were stretched out." That is, so that the body, being most forcefully stretched, would be more sharply tormented by whips, as it follows that they experienced "mockery and scourging." The Etymologist (page 771) explains the "drum" <note>original: τύμπανον</note> as "the public wood by which those handed over are dealt with." The drum was a piece of wood on which the guilty were beaten while stretched out. Hence the term "to drum to death" <note>original: ἀποτυμπανίζειν</note>, meaning "to stretch out with drums and strings," as Seberus notes on Pollux (page 177). Finally, let us see what the "collar" <note>original: κλοιὸς</note> is. This word appears in Deuteronomy 28:48, 1 Kings 12:4, and Ecclesiasticus 6:26, referring to an instrument applied to the neck and hands, or even feet, as punishment. This can also be shown from Jeremiah 27:2, where God commands the Prophet to make for himself "bonds and collars" <note>original: δεσμὰς καὶ κλοιὺς</note> and place them around his own neck; likewise from Xenophon 
<margin>Cyrus, Book 3, page 29.</margin>
when he says: "from then on, he was already in a collar, both his hands and his neck in a collar, being whipped and goaded." The Etymologist (page 521) says the "collar" <note>original: κλοιὸς</note> signifies "the irons which the condemned wear." An old Greek-Latin Lexicon defines it as: "a collar, a rack" <note>original: boia, eculeum</note>. Jerome, on Jeremiah 27:2, says: "In common speech they call collars 'boiae'." Thus Drusius translates it in Ecclesiasticus 6:31. Festus (page 25) says: "The *boia* is a type of bond, said to be both wooden and iron." Scaliger adds (page 31): "The *boia* is a collar, and 'to put on a boia' is to place a collar around someone." Often in old manuscript histories it is read, "Take the boia from my neck." Aldhelm, in *Praise of Virginity*, writes: "For the slander of the Bishop and the infamy of the clergy, let them bind boiae on the neck and shackles on the legs." Hesychius defines it as "a neck-bond, a collar, or a torque." The word for "torque" <note>original: μανιάκης</note> appears in Daniel 5:5, 31, where the Chaldean has "necklace" <term>מניכא<gloss>necklace/torque</gloss></term>, and in Ezra 3:6. Philo’s Glossary says: "a collar is the torque of the condemned, which is commonly called a boia." But I should also like to remember a crime once solemn among the Arabs, which they called "skopelismos" <note>original: σκοπέλισμον</note>, which was a capital offense. It is contained in this law in the Digest on extraordinary crimes: "Many enemies are accustomed to 'stone-mark' <note>original: σκοπελίζειν</note> the field of an enemy; that is, to place stones on it as a sign that if anyone were to cultivate that field, they would perish by an evil death through the ambushes of those who placed the stones; a thing which causes such fear that no one dares to approach that field." I dare to say that virtue and honesty are in a way "stone-marked" by those who offer scandals to others—that is, they are made hateful, so that men of small spirit do not dare to approach them. These people indeed commit a capital crime to be punished by eternal death. Salazar on Proverbs 3:23 (page 241) and Crinitus (page 141) discuss this. I think there are enough testimonies to explain the executioner's rack, the collars, and other types of torture. However, nothing is more unknown than "skophismos"—indeed, it is foolish if you 
distort things to that point.

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of physical restraints and punishments to the ritualistic "ratification of covenants," exploring the ancient practice of "striking" a treaty through animal sacrifice and symbolic division, a theme introduced by the legal consequences of breaking the covenant in Jeremiah 34:18.</meta>

### Jeremiah 34:18

<margin>
"I will give the men who have transgressed my covenant, who have not performed the words of the covenant which they had made before me, when they cut the calf in two, and passed between the parts thereof." <note>original Hebrew: נתתי את-האנשים... This verse describes the ritual of walking between the divided pieces of a calf as a way of sealing a binding agreement.</note>
</margin>

> "I will give the men who have passed over my covenant, the calf, which they made into two parts, and passed through the midst of its parts." <note>original Greek: Δώσω τοὺς ἄνδρας... from the Septuagint.</note>

> "I will give the men, who transgress my covenant, the calf, which they cut into two parts, and passed between its divisions." <note>original Latin: Dabo viros... from the Vulgate.</note>

<margin>
The Ratification of Covenants.
</margin>
In the Holy Language <note>Hebrew</note>, a covenant generally goes by the name <term>Berith<gloss>covenant</gloss></term>, which denotes any testament, alliance, or pact. This can be a "naked" agreement without ceremonies—such as the one between God and our First Parents after the Fall in <margin>Genesis 3:15</margin>, established with these words: *The seed of the woman shall crush the serpent's head*. Or, it can be "clothed" in certain ceremonies, solemnities, and promises. Among the Latins, these distinctions are more accurately defined, as seen in Popma <margin>Book on the Difference of Words, p. 86 & 137.</margin> Meanwhile, the translators of the Septuagint <note>the Greek Old Testament</note> almost everywhere translate this Hebrew word as <term>diatheke<gloss>testament/covenant</gloss></term>. Aquila—whom some say is the same as Onkelos, the famous Chaldean scholar who wrote the commentary on the Pentateuch—interprets it as <term>syntheke<gloss>binding agreement</gloss></term>. The Syrian interpreter uses *praestha*. The Septuagint frequently retains the word <term>chatheke<gloss>statute</gloss></term>, though in <margin>Romans 9:4</margin> it is read as "the law." Regarding the root of the word, it is either <term>bara<gloss>to choose</gloss></term>, or <term>barah<gloss>to cut down/consume</gloss></term> (though this also implies choosing), or finally <term>karat<gloss>to cut asunder</gloss></term>, through a transposition of letters. This last one is because of the ceremony observed in ancient times when entering into covenants. For it was the custom among the Ancients that while establishing treaties, they would first take oaths (which were not of the same kind for everyone, as we will show below); afterward, they would pass between the parts of a slaughtered animal. By this ritual, they prayed for a similar destruction upon themselves if they became covenant-breakers—as if to say, "May God do this to me, unless I keep the covenant, so that I too am cut into parts, just as this animal has now been torn apart." Hence, in the Sacred Scriptures, one often reads "to dissect a covenant," which does not mean to violate or break it, as people commonly mistake, but to *strike* or *make* a covenant (compare Buxtorf’s Lexicon on the root <term>bathar<gloss>to divide</gloss></term>). This ritual of making a pact was used both by the Chaldeans and by the Jews themselves. Regarding the Chaldeans, Blessed Matthias shows this in the section on the Old and New Testaments. Regarding the Jews, the matter is clear both from this passage in Jeremiah and from Genesis 15:9–10, where God observes the same custom of ratifying a covenant through the sectioning of animals in the Abrahamic pact. In that passage, God commands Abraham to split the animals and pass through the segments. Once this was done, God Himself, under the symbol of a smoking furnace, passed through the middle of the divisions, indicating that whoever broke the covenant would be so divided (see Theodoret on this passage). It is entirely likely that Saul had something similar in mind when, having divided his oxen throughout all the land of Israel, he made a covenant with the Israelites as a King initiated before the Lord; he wanted to recall this to their memory by adding this mandate: unless someone rushed to the King's banner, the same would happen to his oxen (1 Samuel 11:7). And thus, it was once customary to ratify covenants through the slaughter of certain animals. History testifies that this ritual, like others, eventually passed to other nations, though with many profane corruptions added. Regarding the Romans, the matter is clear: they were accustomed to entering covenants by the slaughter of some animal, especially a pig <note>original: porcus</note>, as Quintilian mentions in Book 8, Chapter 3; hence some want the word <term>foedus<gloss>covenant</gloss></term> to be named from *feriendo* (striking). Others from *foedando*, that is, the "foul" <note>original: foede</note> killing of a sow. There are also those who derive the word for covenant from the *fetiales* <note>a college of priests who acted as heralds/diplomats</note>, because through them covenants were once ratified. Let us hear Livy on this matter: <margin>Book 1, decade 1.</margin> *"Covenants," he says, "are made with various laws, but all in the same manner. We have received the following account of how it was done, and there is no memory of a more ancient treaty. The Fetial priest asked King Tullus: 'Do you command me, O King, to strike a treaty with the Pater Patratus [the chief herald] of the Alban people?' Upon the King's command, he said: 'I demand the sacred herbs [sagmina] from you, O King.' The King replied: 'Take them pure.' The Fetial brought pure grass from the citadel. Afterward, he asked the King: 'O King, do you make me the royal messenger of the Roman people, the Quirites? And my vessels and companions?' The King answered: 'I do so, provided it be without fraud to me and the Roman people.' The Fetial was Marcus Valerius. He appointed Spurius Fusius as the Pater Patratus, touching his head and hair with the sacred branch. The covenant was then carried out with many words uttered in a long song, which is not worth recounting here. The laws having been read, he said: 'Hear, O Jupiter; hear, O Pater Patratus of the Alban people; hear, O Alban people! As those things were publicly read from first to last from those tablets or wax without evil intent, and as they have been most correctly understood here today: the Roman people will not be the first to defect from those laws. If they should defect first by public counsel or evil intent, then you, O Jupiter [Diespiter], strike the Roman people just as I shall strike this pig today; and strike them all the more, as you are more powerful and mighty.' When he had said this, he struck the pig with a flint stone."* This is according to Livy. Others differ from him only in that they write a sow <note>original: porca</note> was used instead of a pig; thus Suetonius in the Life of Claudius, Chapter 25, reports: *"He struck a treaty with kings in the forum by slaughtering a sow."* Virgil feels the same way, as shown by these words: <margin>Aeneid, Book 8.</margin>

> *Armed before the altars of Jupiter, and holding the sacrificial bowls,*
> *They stood, and joined the covenants by slaughtering a sow.*

But concerning the method of "striking" a covenant and the slaughtering of the sow, more can be found in Cicero (On Invention, Book 1), Marcellus, Donatus (On Clarification, p. 4), and Taubman’s commentary on the Virgil passage just cited, as well as on Plautus’s *Rudens* (Act 4, scene 6). And thus, the custom of ratifying covenants with blood once prevailed among almost all peoples. Catiline, according to Sallust, carried around human blood mixed with wine in bowls to the associates of his conspiracy, and they each tasted it one by one so that they might be more faithful to one another. Likewise, Plutarch reports in the *Life of Publicola* that the sons of Aquilius, Vitellius, and Brutus met for the sake of Tarquinius to betray their country; they tasted the blood of a slaughtered man and, having touched the entrails, took a great oath. So too the Arabs: whenever they made a covenant with others, a man standing between the two parties would strike the palms of those making the covenant near their thumbs with a sharp stone; then, taking a tuft of wool from the clothing of each, he would smear the blood on seven stones placed in the middle, invoking Urania and Dionysus during the smearing. This being done, the same man who had been the mediator...

<column-break/>

# ANTIQUITIES OF THE BIBLE

<margin>The sanctioning of covenants.</margin> When a covenant was being contracted between friends, one might act as a surety for a guest, or perhaps for a citizen, if the matter was being conducted with a fellow citizen. Those who contracted these friendships deemed it just to observe the covenant, as noted by Polydore Vergil in *On Discovery*, book 4, chapter 15. That this was also a common custom among the Scythians is testified by Lucian in his dialogue titled *Toxaris, or Friendship*, where their covenant and oath—which he calls the greatest of all—is recounted. *For,* says that Scythian in Lucian’s work, *as soon as we have pricked our fingers and let the blood drip into a cup, and have dipped the tips of our swords into it, and both of us together move it to our lips and drink, there is nothing that can thereafter pull us apart.* You may see this Scythian custom of making a covenant described in different words in Herodotus, books 4 and 5. Radamistus, the son of Pharasmanes, King of Iberia, used this custom of making a pact to deceive his uncle, Mithridates, the King of Armenia. For, as Battista Fregoso reports in book 9, according to the custom of that nation, the thumbs of both parties had to be tied together, and both had to taste the blood drawn from them. The man who had been assigned the duty of binding them, pretending that the ties had fallen to the ground, instead entangled Mithridates' feet and thus captured him along with his wife and children. And because he had promised that he would harm him neither with iron nor poison, he smothered them with cushions until their breath was cut off and they died. He believed that by this observance—that he had killed them neither with iron nor poison—the crime of his treachery was hidden.

<margin>8. 2. ch. 2. The Learned Banqueters.</margin> Posidonius <note>a Stoic philosopher and historian</note> writes concerning the Germans in Athenaeus’ work. He says that during their symposia <note>social gatherings</note>, after they have embraced kindly, they cut the veins in their foreheads and drink the blood flowing down, mixing it in a cup, believing they have reached the highest peak of friendship once they have mutually tasted each other's blood. It is well established from 2 Kings 10:15 that the extending of hands had the same force among the ancients, where Jehu says to Jehonadab: "Give me your hand." By these words he seeks not subjection, but a partnership, either to be entered into then for the first time, or to confirm for the future a partnership already begun; compare Caspar Sánchez on this passage.

<margin>Book 12 of the Annals.</margin> Tacitus <note>the Roman historian</note> also testifies to this where he says: *It is the custom for Kings, whenever they enter into a partnership, to entwine their right hands and bind their thumbs together, tightening them with a knot. Soon, when the blood has flowed into the extremities, they elicit the gore with a light prick and lick it in turn. That is considered a secret covenant, as if consecrated by mutual blood.* And we believe it was entirely from this that the practice arose which we see on ancient coins: clasped hands with the inscription *Fides* <gloss>Faith/Loyalty</gloss>, or *Amicitia* <gloss>Friendship</gloss>, or *Foedus* <gloss>Covenant</gloss>. Furthermore, covenants were sanctioned among the ancients not only by blood, but also in other ways; the Romans primarily swore with a raised sword, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus records in book 9. Beatus Rhenanus reports the same in book 1 of *German Affairs* concerning the Quadi, a people of the Germans: that they swore by their drawn blades, which they held in the place of deities, just as the Scythians did. Additionally, they were accustomed to confirm covenants by touching the earth and the altars of the gods, as can be seen in Virgil’s *Aeneid*, book 4, and in Cicero’s *Speech for Flaccus*. Likewise, Polybius in book 3 testifies that covenants struck between the Carthaginians and the Romans were usually bolstered by <term>Jovem Lapidem<gloss>Jupiter the Stone</gloss></term>. We recite his words here: <note>original Greek: Ἔστι δὲ τὸ διὰ λίθου τοιοῦτον... — The oath by the stone is as follows: taking a stone into his hand, the one making the oaths concerning the treaties, when he has sworn by the public faith, says these things: "To me, if I keep my oath..."</note>

<column-break/>

"...may all good things happen, but if I should think or do anything otherwise, while all others are safe in their own homelands, under their own laws, in their own lives, sanctuaries, and tombs, let me alone be cast out in such a manner as this stone is." And having said these things, he throws the stone from his hand. That is: *The Herald or the <term>pater patratus<gloss>chief priest of the Fetials</gloss></term>, having taken the stone into his hands when the covenant between the parties had been agreed upon, spoke thus: "If I perform this covenant and this oath rightly and without malicious deceit, may the Gods grant me all things happy; but if otherwise, either I or my intentions change, while everyone else remains safe in their own fatherlands, under their own laws, in their own homes, in their own temples, and in their own tombs, may I alone perish, just as this stone shall fall from my hands," and having spoken thus, he threw the stone from his hand at the same time.* In Plautus, at the end of the *Aulularia*, Lyconides swears to his slave in this way, saying: *If I knowingly deceive you, so may Jupiter cast me out from my goods—the city and citadel being safe—as I do this stone.* Nor should it be passed over in silence that the Romans were not permitted to strike a covenant after midday; likewise, that from the beginning of the city, <term>myrtle<gloss>myrtus</gloss></term> was used for the sacred greenery <note>verbena</note> in peace pacts. Likewise, the Romans ordered covenants to be inscribed on bronze tablets or on a column in the Temple of Jupiter Capitoline for a perpetual memorial of the matter, or to be recorded in the Annals and the Calendars <note>Fasti</note>. Similarly, the Greeks sometimes consecrated those covenants at the Isthmian or Pythian games by erecting inscriptions to endure for all time, or they deposited them, carved on bronze tablets, in the Temple of Olympian Jupiter or the Acropolis of Athens. Among them, those who struck covenants, acting as interpreters and arbiters of peace, were called <term>spondophoroi<gloss>libation-bearers/treaty-messengers</gloss></term>, as in Pollux, book 8; whom Dionysius of Halicarnassus calls <term>eirenodikai<gloss>judges of peace</gloss></term>, whose duty among other things was to guard the sacred rites concerning treaties, to make peace, and to annul a peace already made if it did not seem to have been done according to the sacred laws. Or as Plutarch says in *Roman Questions* concerning those called <term>Fetiales<gloss>priests of treaties</gloss></term>, they are expected to be like peacemakers or libation-bearers. They were primarily called this because covenants were sanctioned <term>epi spondon<gloss>over libations</gloss></term>, over the entrails and the burning sacrificial victims, for which reason one should read Homer regarding those heralds who were employed to draft and make the agreed pacts between the Trojans and the Greeks:

> They brought together the faithful oaths of the gods, and mixed wine 
> in the bowl, and poured water over the kings' hands. <note>Homer, Iliad, book 3</note>

Where Eustathius explains <term>horkia<gloss>oaths</gloss></term> as <term>ta sphagia<gloss>the sacrificial victims</gloss></term>, that is, the victims to be slaughtered for making pacts. And in the *Iliad*, book 3, verse 245:

> Pure libations, and the right hands in which we trusted.

Thus, Sacraments and covenants were bolstered and confirmed by the libation of wine and the giving of the right hand; from which it came to pass that the word <term>sponde<gloss>libation</gloss></term> was accepted not only for the libation itself used in making covenants and truces, but also for the covenants, pacts, and truces themselves. Hence in Xenophon, *Hellenica*, book 3, it is asked: *whether they wish to have a truce or war?* And this rite of making and sanctioning a covenant in the midst of and with sacred rites has prevailed even to our own times, so that it is not unusual for covenants and pacts to be confirmed by the receiving of the Holy Eucharist. Thus the peace between Henry IV <note>Holy Roman Emperor</note> and Pope Paschal was solidified, as Sigebert testifies. And when the grudge that had arisen in Paris between Charles IX and Cardinal Guise was laid to rest, each took the body of the Lord as a testimony of reconciliation. So when...

## Jeremiah 44:30

->Behold, I am giving Pharaoh Hophra<- <note>original Hebrew: הנני נתן את פרעה חפרע</note>
->Behold, I give Hophra.<- <note>original Greek: Ἰδὲ ἐγὼ δίδωμι τ’ Οὐαφρῆ</note>
->*Behold, I will deliver Pharaoh Hophra.*<- <note>original Latin: *Ecce ego tradam Pharaonem Ephree.*</note>

<margin>
Pharaoh Hophra.
</margin>
It was explained above that the Egyptians named their kings "Pharaohs." This specific designation ended with Apries, whom the Prophet Jeremiah calls Hophra <note>original: Cophra</note>, who was the last of the Pharaohs to be delivered into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon. Herodotus, in his second book, calls this Pharaoh "Apries" (changing only the vowel points). He recounts that this king was so filled with pride that he did not fear to boast that he possessed a kingdom too powerful to be overthrown or snatched from him by any force, whether divine or human. The outcome showed that he did not say this with impunity. Indeed, the Egyptians revolted against him because of a disastrous expedition to Cyrene. Herodotus says that the prefect Amasis was sent to appease them, but Amasis instead won over the rebels, seized the kingdom himself, and—at the demand of the Egyptians—put to death Apries, who had been held in custody. Therefore, the one the Prophet names Hophra <note>original: חפרע</note>, the renowned historian is accustomed to call Apries <note>original: Ἀπρίης</note> by a slight inflection of the name.

Driven by this discrepancy, as if by a war of words, a certain <term>Dictator <note>Likely referring to the great scholar Joseph Scaliger (1540–1609), often called the "dictator" of the republic of letters.</note></term> began to call the critics to his side, asserting that the vowel points of the Hebrew word had not been correctly placed by the <term>Masoretes <note>Jewish scholars who standardized the text and pronunciation of the Hebrew Bible.</note></term> (who were otherwise miraculously careful critics of the Hebrew). He argued it should be read as "Haprea" <note>original: חפרע</note> so that it would agree with "Apries." <margin>Book 2, 97.</margin> Certainly, this shows little critical insight for such a great man, whose authority many revere. When Cicero saw that the authority of Cato stood in his way in the case of Lucius Murena, he said, *"Remove the name of Cato from the case; set aside and disregard his authority,"* believing that the defense drawn from Cato’s authority was very weak. They say that Cato the Younger obeyed his <gloss>tutor</gloss> and did everything commanded of him, but only in such a way that he required a reason for every single thing and inquired into their logic, as Plutarch witnesses in his *Life*. Thus, I especially apply this here: *one must bring forth the cause of all things and inquire into the "why."* <margin>Book 2, 98. 70.</margin> When in a case we are conducting on behalf of God's Scripture, the authority of some Scaliger or another "critic of critics" is thrown at us: take away the name, and bring in the reason! Let this secular author yield to the Sacred Writers, who more than once name persons and places with different markings than the secular authors do. It is not uncommon for the names of certain cities, regions, and persons to be found written in a different way than they appear in the Sacred texts. Should you then reform the accepted reading in the Scriptures to match the secular ones? The Romans were often accustomed to adopt Hebrew and Greek words by varying them slightly, not measuring them by the same letters, syllables, or sound, as the judges of the Latin language prove. Those called *Indigetes* are called *indigentes* by Stephanus, *indigetoi* by Ptolemy, and *Endigetes* by Avienus. So too with the Bruttii: they are called *Brutii*, *Brettii*, or *Brentii*; and Santes, Sannites, Saunnites, or Samnites; and Abraham is called *Abraas* or *Abraames*. There is also Bogud, called *Bogos*, and infinite other examples. Every language pronounces foreign names in its own way, and it is no wonder if the Romans change Greek names, the Greeks change Latin ones, and the Hebrews change "barbarian" ones when they record them, each inflecting them in their own manner, often omitting or changing several letters. I will not even mention how vowels in names are read in more than one way, but change according to the variety of dialects. One may laugh at those who are offended by any slight mutation of vowels, especially in exotic words, which the Greeks and Romans pronounce in various ways.

Nebuchadnezzar was the "Hercules of the East," whose fortune in war God had favored against the Tyrians, Egyptians, Ethiopians, Jews, and other nations. Nor did He enrich him with the spoils of the Egyptians alone, but he also added to his power and subjected to his dominion—besides Egypt—Ethiopia, Syria, Edom, Persia, Media, and Armenia, of which Habakkuk says <margin>ch. 1:9</margin>: *He shall triumph over the kings of other nations, and tyrants shall be a laughingstock to him.* With so many victories and triumphs, Nebuchadnezzar did not so much grow as he became swollen with pride, so that from a King he became a Tyrant, doing more than he had in his mandates. For he entered Judah with great cruelty, and having subjugated it, he practiced innumerable examples of cruelty upon the citizens and inhabitants of Judah. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
The Babylonian Captivity.
Introduction 2. *Sacred Tapestries* <note>original: *Stromata sacrorum*</note>, page 38.
</margin>

Eusebius Nierembergius <note>A 17th-century Spanish Jesuit and mystic author</note> writes on this same subject: "To the most monstrous vice of a proud soul," he says, "what more fitting mirror can we present than Nebuchadnezzar, the King of Babylonia and Tyrant of Jerusalem, who was a monster of fortune? He was the most fortunate among mortals, yet the most arrogant among Kings. His success brought him a false love of greatness, rather than a true one. Not inappropriately, this most powerful Tyrant represented the most powerful vice, one to be feared not only in evil deeds but even more so in good ones; in the former he acts as a King, in the latter as a Tyrant." He continues to describe the tyranny of Nebuchadnezzar and his haughty cruelty toward the conquered in *Sacred Tapestries* 2, book 6, page 36, and following. Not infrequently, an injury serves as an entrance for fortune, and one man’s success marches over the losses of another. The fiery young Nebuchadnezzar took up arms against the King of Judea (Jehoiakim), who ruled only by permission, and whom necessity and force had made a reluctant ally of Egypt. Jehoiakim had committed no sin against the Babylonian, yet he had sinned greatly against God. Therefore, Nebuchadnezzar, stirred by divine vengeance and his own greed, laid waste to Judea with a success as great as his wickedness. Unmindful that Josiah had fallen to the Egyptians while trying to maintain his faith and friendship with the Babylonians, Nebuchadnezzar plundered the kingdom of Josiah's son, Jehoiakim—claiming no right other than that Jehoiakim, coerced by Egypt, had not served him, though he lacked the power to do so. But those who believe they can do anything judge the inability of others as a fault of will, not of power. Since they think everything is owed to them, they believe that impossible obedience is being willfully denied. The King of Babylon then raised Zedekiah to the royal throne, who kept faith neither with his God, as he ought, nor with the King of the Chaldeans, whom he deserted while relying on the arms of the King of the Egyptians. Egypt had thus encouraged the disobedience of the Jewish King, who in his hope for Egyptian aid had despised divine oracles. Egypt, more generous with promises than with troops, had fueled Zedekiah's defiance. This is not even to mention his own crimes, by which he had provoked divine vengeance. Thereafter, Nebuchadnezzar moved his forces from the punishment of Tyre to the punishment of Egypt, and like a lightning bolt he flew through Egypt, wasting and pillaging it. Next, he approached the Ethiopians and subjected a large part of Africa to his empire, carrying his arms successfully in every direction. This most arrogant of kings, Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, puffed up by so many triumphs and victories, did not acknowledge to whom he owed his success, but ascribed it to his own power and counsel, 
<margin>Daniel 4:27</margin>
saying: > Is this not great Babylon, which I have built as a royal residence by my mighty power and for the glory of my majesty! <note>original Latin: *Hæc est Babylon magna, quam ego ædificavi in domum regni, in robore fortitudinis meæ, & in gloria decoris mei!*</note>
Then, having constructed and erected a statue, he wished divine worship to be offered to himself, demanding that he be adored like a second Lucifer <note>The "Light-Bringer," referring here to the pride of the fallen morning star</note>. Vain desires tormented Nebuchadnezzar; the lust for glory tortured him, goading him to such an edict of tyranny that he subjected those who neglected to adore the statue to the punishment of a furnace burning with fire. But while the foul ambition for adoration burned within him, the fire of the furnace refreshed those three holy men, who preferred to die in the Babylonian furnace than to deny the true God and adore the false idol of the Babylonians. It was no different for 
<margin>Daniel 6:7</margin>
Daniel himself; he ignored the impious command of Darius (crafted by the counsel of courtiers for Daniel’s destruction) which forbade adoring any God for thirty days under penalty of being cast into the pit of li-

<column-break/>

-ons, but he did not cease to call upon his God daily. Concerning this, Augustine says in *Against Faustus*, book 20, chapter 21, column 375, Volume 6:
> Proud spirits plainly demand the worship due to Divinity—the Devil and his angels do so, as seen through all the temples and sacred rites of the gentiles. Their likeness is expressed even in certain proud men, just as we hold the memory of certain Kings of Babylonia.

For this reason, holy Daniel endured accusers and persecutors because, after the royal edict was proposed that nothing should be asked of any God by anyone except from the King alone, *he was caught adoring and praying to his God, that is, the one and true God.* They were accused before the King and tried for the crime of treason for neglecting the royal edict, and once convicted, they were cast into the furnace burning with fire. These men, lifting a suppliant voice to God, felt God’s present help. Seeing this, the Tyrant himself was moved; he not only ordered the men to leave the furnace but even established a capital penalty for anyone who showed contempt for that God, who had given such an illustrious proof of power and majesty. In the second year of his reign and his Monarchy, after he had forged one kingdom out of many kingdoms of Asia and Africa, he saw a dream. He was warned by it to set aside his haughtiness and submit himself to God, the Author and Giver of Monarchy. Yet, disobedient to the divine warning, he returned to his former mindset, raising himself above God and attributing everything to his own hand. Consequently, as much as he raised himself above men through arrogant pride, so much was he cast down below men through punishment. He immediately became like a brute, growing wild and attacking those he met with ferocity, such that it could be said of him what Dionysius of Halicarnassus says of Tullus Hostilius: *“Such a man, though thinking himself strong in spirit, was corrupted in his mind by his body.”* <note>original Greek: *ὧδέ τις γνώμης θ’ αὑτῶ καρτερὸς εἶναι μένων, ἀλλὰ διαφθαρεὶς τῷ σώματι τὰς φρένας.*</note> Regarding this singular metamorphosis, Pacianus Barnesius writes in *On Patience*: *That Babylonian King was consumed by seven years of squalor. A lion’s mane grew on him, his hair went uncombed and a barbaric horror overflowed; with long, curved claws, his terrifying hands mimicked eagles, while he ate hay in the manner of an ox, a ruminator of pale grasses.* Likewise, Paulinus, Bishop of Nola, elegantly composes the foul form of Nebuchadnezzar out of a lion, a vulture, and an ox. Nierembergius provides a terrible picture of this in *Sacred Tapestries* 2, chapter 22, page 73, and he correctly notes that the king turned out *like* a beast, but was not an actual beast; he lived a life equal to a brute, not having lost his human form, but being deformed in appearance. Sacred Scripture, he says (chapter 23, page 73), *did not say that Nebuchadnezzar was transformed into a beast in physical nature; it only indicates he was deformed from the human, attributing to him a beast-like sense rather than a beast-like species.* Just as some people have believed themselves to be donkeys, cats, wolves, or roosters due to a damaged faculty of imagination, so the Babylonian King thought himself a beast, perhaps an Ox. *He who sinned in his thoughts is likewise punished in his thoughts. Most justly, he who thought himself a God is punished by considering himself a beast. He who had sinned by valuing himself above human dignity is tortured by believing himself below the human condition.* He is rightly weighed down by Melancholy, he who used to leap with the joy of fleeting success. It is necessary for the fortunate to remember their mortal nature, since they can descend into a bestial condition, lest they trust in unfaithful fortune. Jeremiah chapter 29, verse 26.

<margin>The Babylonian Captivity.</margin>
This pride is evident in Nebuchadnezzar, who, more arrogant on his high throne than any supreme monarch served by the most powerful kings, became through madness more foolish than a foolish man. Stripped of his royal purple, he wandered like a beast <note>A reference to the biblical account in the Book of Daniel where the king lived as an animal for seven years</note>, so that one hardly knows which to marvel at more: the heights to which the King ascended, or the depths to which he fell. Truly, the King’s descent was unheard of in human history; he lived for seven years a life more wretched than any misery. Previously, Nebuchadnezzar was wise in his own folly, fearing no ruin for his kingdom, but dreaming that it stood upon a solid foundation. Yet the end of the tyrant showed how even great power and wealth can be exhausted, even if the empire is vast. Where is that empire now? It perished as quickly as it had grown. It perished utterly, all its forces destroyed; the court of Nebuchadnezzar testifies that nothing is permanent in kingdoms, especially the proud ones. After he had paid the well-deserved penalties for seven years according to the divine decree, he returned to himself and his people, saying:

<margin>Daniel 4:34.</margin>
> *Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and exalt and glorify the King of heaven; for all His works are truth and His ways are justice, and those who walk in pride He is able to humble.*

Theologians count him among those converted to God; see Leonhard Hutter <note>A prominent 17th-century Lutheran theologian</note> in his *Epitome of the Book of Concord, page 1072,* and the Zurich theologians in their *Confession, page 17.* No doubt many of the leading men of the Kingdom followed him, including Nebuzaradan <note>The captain of the guard under Nebuchadnezzar</note>, as seen in *Jeremiah 40:1 and following.*

But let us finally return to the most calamitous <term>fall</term> <note>original: ἅλωσιν (*halōsin*), meaning the capture or sacking of a city</note> of the Jews, from which we have strayed in this overly long digression. The captivity was imminent, as the blindness and fury of the Jews were immense; no one would allow sound counsel or healthy warnings into their hearts, but with eyes and ears closed, everyone rushed toward their own destruction. No one among the Trojans believed the prophecy of Cassandra, and that was by the direction of Apollo. *“It was done by God’s command,”* says Virgil in the second book of the *Aeneid,* and Tryphiodorus writes:

<margin>Josephus, *Antiquities*, chapter 1, page 417</margin>
-> <term>For regarding the fall,</term> <-
-> <term>he spoke as both a good and excellent prophet.</term> <-

The same happened to Jeremiah and other prophets in that age, whom the Jews harassed and afflicted in every way. They would not listen to the voice of the Lord through them, nor walk in His law which God set before them through His servants the prophets, as Daniel confesses in his prayer in **chapter 9, verse 10.** But they were held captive under the doctrines of demons and the snares of vices long before they were led away as captives to Babylon. God predicted that the leaders would be led into the Babylonian captivity in squalor, the common people with their hands bound: mothers piteously following their lost liberty with tears, and infants dying as they swallowed the flowing tears of their mothers. Indeed, God declared His wrath toward the disobedient people through many various punishments, but chiefly by the *Babylonian Captivity*. By this, not only did they perish by many kinds of death, but even the *City of Jerusalem*, along with the *Temple*, was devastated, and the remnants of the people were led away into the most wretched slavery. This was the gravest wrath of God; no sadder tragedy was ever seen on the stage of the Jewish world, nor was a more marvelous resolution witnessed than the catastrophe <note>In the theatrical sense of a final resolution</note> at the end of the seventy-year period. Since we cannot depict the various acts and interludes of this event with a rhetorical brush, shaped for an <term>outline</term> <note>original: שׂרט (*seret*), a Hebrew term for an incision or engraved line</note>, we shall instead, with a sort of continuous theological picture—

<column-break/>

<margin>The Babylonian Captivity.</margin>
—outline the <term>engraving</term> <note>original: שׂרט (*seret*)</note> of the greatest suffering of the Jewish Church and Commonwealth. Indeed, the first lines must be drawn from the causes of that captivity. For what God desired in that people, He Himself clearly expressed through the mouth of His prophet:

<margin>Isaiah 48:18.</margin>
> *Oh, that you had heeded my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea.*

But what did they do meanwhile? *They did not incline their ear, but walked in their own counsels, in the imagination of their own evil hearts.* Finally, they turned their backs to Him, not their faces (*Jeremiah 7:24*). From that time, God’s decisive sentence was passed regarding the well-deserved destruction of the people, in *chapter 15, verse 6* of the same prophet: *“You have forsaken me, you have gone backward; therefore I will stretch out my hand against you and destroy you; I am weary of repenting.”* Regarding the final punishment of the King himself, *Jeremiah 22:24* says: *“As I live, says the Lord, even if Coniah <note>Another name for King Jeconiah or Jehoiachin</note> son of Jehoiakim king of Judah were the signet ring on my right hand, yet I would pluck you off.”* We see from this, clearer than the sun: contempt for God and His mandates was the fuel and the torch of all that calamity. "Indeed, what more has the Lord required of you," says Micah, "but to do justice, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?"

<margin>Chapter 6, verse 8.</margin>
The prophets exhorted them very frequently, especially that divine seer Jeremiah—sometimes even through sensible signs. When he predicted the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, he carried wooden chains around his neck to signify that the people were to be led into captivity bound in chains. Sometimes, and indeed most often, he warned through words, especially the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin who were addicted to idolatry and many crimes. He admonishes, rebukes, reprimands, and threatens them toward repentance so the imminent Babylonian captivity might be avoided, but he gains nothing by his exhortation. They continue to sin; Nebuchadnezzar, the avenger of sins, arrives from Chaldea as the exterminator of these two tribes, just as previously in the time of Isaiah the ten tribes fell to the Assyrian enemy. The frantic people stopped their ears to the lips of Jeremiah as he cried out: *“Walk in the good way” (Jeremiah 6:16).* But they shouted: **“We will not walk in it.”** Therefore, they had to walk to Chaldea and pay the price there. While the prophet Jeremiah was busy in his sermons, telling them to prepare for captivity, that they must be led to Babylon, that they should not resist the will of God, and to hope for nothing else but being captives—behold, he is twice seized and cast into a very deep prison, which in the Holy Language is called a <term>pit</term> <note>original: בור (*bor*), meaning a pit, cistern, or dungeon</note> or a hole, in *chapters 27 and 28* of his prophecy. When he recounts the saddest events of his miseries in his Lamentations, he says among other things: *“They have cut off my life in the pit.”* Not only was he shut in prison, but he also had false prophets contradicting him and promising the opposite. For in the fourth year of Zedekiah, Hananiah <term>prophesies falsely</term> <note>original: ψευδοπροφητεύει (*pseudoprophēteuei*)</note>, saying that within two years God would break the yoke of the King of Babylon and bring back Jeconiah and all the deportees. Jeremiah predicted to him that because of that false prophecy, he would die that very same year—a prediction that was confirmed by the event itself. Nor were there lacking those in Babylon who resisted Jeremiah. The first among them was a certain *Ahab*, and the second was *Zedekiah*,

<margin>Jeremiah 29:22.</margin>

...to whom the Prophet predicts the future, saying that Nebuchadnezzar would make such an example of them that they would become a formula for a curse. And it is by no means to be doubted that this happened to them when they withdrew from their service to the King; for he who was not going to spare his own Chaldeans (*Daniel 2:5*), would have spared these men much less. There was, besides these, a certain man in Babylon named *Shemaiah*, who had written to Jerusalem that Jeremiah should be thrown into the stocks because he had indicated in his letters to the deportees that the captivity would be long, which is read in *chapter 29:26*. To this man, the Prophet sends a harsher response from the mouth of the Lord, calling him a Nehelamite, whose family perhaps descends from Naham, *1 Chronicles 4:19*. Therefore, just as he was pretending that those taking notice of Jeremiah should imitate Jehoiada; so the Prophet, criticizing him, perhaps indicates he should be called a "dreaming" Nehelamite <note>The author is making a wordplay on the Hebrew name 'Nehelamite' and the word for 'dreamer'</note> rather than a Nahamite, as noted by Hugh Broughton in *Concent. p. 111* <note>Hugh Broughton was a prominent 16th-century English scholar of Hebrew</note>. Regarding this Nehelamite, he says that he shall perish in Babylon with his entire family. This Divine Seer <note>Jeremiah</note> had endured these miseries and calamities which, during the reign of Zedekiah—to whom God threatens total destruction because of his oath and faith violated even toward the impious Nebuchadnezzar—they felt were doubled.

<margin>Ezekiel 17:19.</margin>
For after King Jehoiachin was bound in chains and cast out to Babylon, deprived of both his power and his liberty, Nebuchadnezzar handed over the humble and mournful kingdom to Jehoiachin's uncle, Mattaniah. He ordered him to be named Zedekiah, so that he might remember he was a client under a Chaldean Patron. However, when Zedekiah did not remain faithful to the oath he had sworn, a provoked Nebuchadnezzar—having collected troops from every side and having performed a divination at the fork in the road by casting arrows, so that he might incite his fury through superstition—inundates Judea with slaughter and blood. He besieges Zedekiah in Jerusalem, interrupts the siege for a time due to the arrival of Egyptian forces, but after overcoming the Egyptians, he returns to the city and captures it. He strips the miserably blinded Zedekiah of his majesty, his children, his eyes, his liberty, and his honor. Jehoiachin was actually happier in the Babylonian captivity than Zedekiah was when he was granted the throne of Jerusalem. Jehoiachin, though a prisoner, was restored to some royal majesty in the seat of his captivity and shone on a higher throne than the other Satraps <note>provincial governors</note> of the Babylonian Court. Zedekiah, reigning in Jerusalem, was deprived of his eyes and his kingdom because of his treachery and died, *drinking the dregs of all ages*, as they skillfully say in their Chronology which the Jews call the *Seder Olam* <note>original: "Seder Olam," a 2nd-century CE Hebrew language chronology</note>. That is, he paid for the sins of previous centuries; and he entangled his nation in bitter servitude. For having entered the city, Nebuchadnezzar despoiled it of its men and treasures; he transferred to Babylonia all Jerusalem, and all the Princes and all the strong men of the army—ten thousand captives. He left nothing in the most celebrated metropolis of all Judea except the poor of the land, and those whose weakness or age caused the victors to look upon them with disgust. Transferred into captivity, they were subjected to foreign Kings: Nebuchadnezzar, Evil-Merodach, and others until the destruction of that supreme Babylonian Monarchy. In that seventy-year exile they sat <term>without a King <note>Hebrew: "ein melekh ve-ein sar"; Greek: "ouk ontos basileōs, oude archontos"</note></term>, as in *Hosea 3:4*, and without a prince. They had no altars there; the Sabbaths and solemnities ceased, and for this reason—

<column-break/>

—Jeremiah laments in *Lamentations 2:7*: <term>The Lord has cast off His altar; He has abhorred His Sanctuary <note>Hebrew: "Zanach Adonay mizbecho nier miqdasho"; Greek: "Apōsato Kyrios thysiastērion autou, apetinaxen hagiasma autou"</note></term>. Regarding the phrase "He has cast off His altar," Ratbertus <note>Paschasius Radbertus, a Carolingian theologian</note> says in column 1379 that God is said to have cursed His sanctuary because He despised all the sacrifices of the Law and the Altar, along with all the utensils in which victims were offered, and delivered them—together with the City and the people—into the hands of enemies to be plundered along with the fortifications. The Lord cast off the Altar upon which they offered their victims because the altars of the heart within were profaned by crimes, and the altar of the mind and conscience was polluted; and once this temple was violated, none other than unclean Spirits had occupied the seat. Nothing more miserable than this Babylonian captivity ever happened. Judea was then not far from total destruction. For the Jews were exiles from their ancestral home; they deplored their once-flourishing homeland and city, and they could have said with Hecuba in Euripides' play *deploring her fallen Troy*:
> O forms of houses, once happy homes!
> How we have come to nothing, though we were
> Formerly proud, and then indeed we were puffed up:
> One of you was rich in his dwelling,
> Another called noble among the citizens by law.
> These things are nothing.
<note>The author quotes the Greek tragedy *Hecuba* to compare the fall of Jerusalem to the fall of Troy.</note>

They had also once claimed for themselves what the Trojans in Troy—proud of wealth and fortune—boasted: that they were invincible, and that their city was one of the "unassailable cities" <term>a city of the unassailable <note>Greek: "tēs aporthētōn polin"</note></term> *[v. 906]*; but soon *these things were nothing*, whence the Chorus in *v. 909*, deploring the distresses of the city, says that the crowns of the towers have been shorn and cut off, and the city has been blackened by a most miserable stain of sooty smoke:
> From the towers your crowns are shorn,
> and with the soot
> of smoke you are colored with a joyless stain.

The Babylonians increased this misery of theirs, laughing meanwhile with a "Sardonic laugh" <note>A bitter or mocking laugh</note> and mocking the captive Jews, from whom they demanded a song and hymns according to *Psalm 137:3*. *"Rejoice,"* they said, *"sing us something of Zion."* With dire sarcasm they said: "Where are those promises now regarding your Deliverer, the Messiah? Sing to us, I pray, something of the kingdom of Christ, about to arise in Zion, as your Prophets sang; sing to us something of your Savior." The Jewish Church and State were forced to swallow these and other blasphemies in captivity, pouring out Psalm 137 against its Babylonian destroyers and Edomite mockers, in which it sends forth an imprecation against Babylon, speaking confidently: *O happy one, you devastated Babylon, who will retaliate against you for the injury you did to us. O happy is he who shall seize your little ones and dash them against the rock.* On these words the Blessed Draconites <note>Johannes Draconites, a 16th-century theologian and reformer</note> comments, adding this scholarly note at *folio 136, b.*: *It is both a prayer and a prophecy against the Babylonians, flowing from the word of God and faith. For just as Babylon is said to be "devastated" because God predicted through the Prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Habakkuk that Babylon would be devastated forever; so he calls the Medes "blessed" here because, according to the word, they were going to devastate Babylon most successfully. When, therefore, he asks that what was done to Zion be retaliated upon Babylon, he asks and prophesies nothing else than that Babylon be devastated according to God's...*

...word, so that it devastated Judah itself; let us prove this with God himself saying: *Indeed, I will repay Babylon for all the evil it did to Zion.* And again: *As Babylon has done, so do to her.* (Furthermore, when he says that the children of Babylon are to be seized and dashed against the rocks, he means nothing else than that the Babylonian kingdom will be so destroyed by the Medes that not even a boy or girl would survive through whom the kingdom could flourish again; let us also prove this by his own words, saying: *I will stir up the Medes against Babylon, so that they strike down their young men with bows, and have no mercy on the fruit of the womb, nor spare the children. Babylon shall be overturned like Sodom and Gomorrah, so that no one shall live there forever.*) Thus he spoke. That evil of captivity, greater than any other evil, did not lack noble tears. <margin>Section 9, 1.</margin> "Oh," the Prophet Jeremiah lamented, "if only someone would grant that <note>original: "quis daret"</note> **my head were waters, and my eye a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the calamity of my people.**" For what has happened to Judah in a long time that was so bitter to see, so mournful to hear, or so pitiable in reality, that it could seem comparable in any part to this present calamity? This supplied the Prophet with such abundant material for mourning and wailing; it provided it to the common crowd of subjects scattered through all the cities, villages, and towns of Babylonia, sitting by the rivers in filth and tears, beating the shores with constant weeping and untiring groans. In the Babylonian captivity, the Jewish State <note>original: "Politia Judaica"</note> was plainly filled with bitterness, or rather afflictions and adversities, so that there was nothing but bitterness, as it is said in Lamentations <margin>Jerome vol. 619.</margin> chapter 1:4: <note>original Hebrew: ויהי מר-לדי</note> "and it was bitterness to me," which is to say, in Jerome's translation, she is oppressed by bitterness itself. To emphasize the weight of this captivity, they even pay attention to the smallest details of the text, as Rabbi Solomon <note>This refers to the medieval commentator Rashi</note> says on Lamentations 1:6 regarding the word *rodpheha* (her pursuers). He says a sharper persecution is hinted at because while elsewhere it is written without the letter *vav*, here it has it. His words: <note>original Hebrew: שמעתיה חסר וזהו מלא שנדופין שלמה</note> "Every *Rodeph* <note>pursuer</note> found in the Bible is deficient (that is, written without the letter *vav* but keeping the *holem* vowel), but this one here is full (that is, it has the letter *vav* with the *holem*)." Jeremiah, though absent in body, was a spectator of this misery of the people led into captivity, not without human compassion. To bear witness to this <term>sympathy</term> <note>original Greek: συμπαθεια — shared suffering</note>, he wrote the Lamentations. For this reason, he was called "<term>sympathy</term>" by Amphilochius <margin>on Lamentations book 3, column 1433.</margin> verse 285. He marked these verses in alphabetical order, not without mystery nor without the "intelligence of ink," as Ratbertus says. In the book of Lamentations, the Prophet describes clearly what the cause of that Jewish captivity was; for he says in the first chapter: <note>original Hebrew: חטא חטאה ירושלם</note> **"Jerusalem has sinned a sin, (v. 8) therefore she has become a mockery."** And later in the same chapter, verse 18, he explains what that sin was: **"The Lord is righteous, for I have rebelled against his mouth"** <note>original Hebrew: כי-פיה מרית</note>. The tragedy of Jeremiah's Lamentations is nothing other than a perfect image of Jewish malice, and a sermon on the judgment of God punishing those who despise Him and demanding vengeance for neglected virtues. It is a most heavy complaint reaching into every part of life, almost stamped as a sign to guide and stir the souls of men and to curb their desires; for there is scarcely a testimony more worthy of being set forth
