**Column 2**

in this misery of the age—if only they would pay attention when warned—so that they might learn justice and not despise God. <margin>The Babylonian Captivity.</margin> Philastrius, in chapter 15, provides another reason for the writing of the Lamentations. He says, "There is another heresy among the Jews: they worshipped the Queen, whom they call the Fortune of Heaven, and whom they also call 'The Celestial' in Africa. They worshipped her in the time of the Prophet Jeremiah, for which reason Jeremiah wrote his Lamentations, that is, his Threni." In these, the Prophet deplores the calamities of the Jewish people, the devastation of the kingdom, its end and destruction, and the leading of the Kings into captivity. He adds consolation: **"It is the mercy of the Lord that we are not consumed, and his compassions do not fail."** Likewise, Ezekiel raised up the people who were dismayed in the Babylonian captivity with the sweetest promises of a longed-for return to the Fatherland (ch. 36:24) and by presenting the true Shepherd, namely the Messiah, the Son of David (ch. 34:23). Bright examples of divine protection toward the Jewish Church appear, as God wonderfully protected and preserved His Church among so many bitter enemies, among so many traps and horrible attempts of tyrants. Hence Bullinger appropriately says on 2 Corinthians 12, page 333: "The glory and truth of Almighty God seemed in the Babylonian captivity to be altogether afflicted, worn down, and obsolete; but in truth it was never so illustrious," which is proven by the history of Daniel. For Daniel alone, a miserable man, a servant and a captive, more than once conquered Nebuchadnezzar, the most powerful victor and Monarch of the whole world, and thus crushed idolatry. Therefore, let no one despair. God's power is made perfect through weakness. Let us only proceed in true humility of soul, in the simplicity of Scripture, and in the truth of faith. From this source, it was a great joy and consolation to the captives that certain ones from their own family were raised to governorships. Among these, Daniel stands out. He was dear and accepted by the Babylonian kings not only in his youth during the time of Nebuchadnezzar, but also in his manhood, and even in his extreme old age in the times of Darius and Cyrus. He was established in authority, as he briefly indicates in chapter 6, the last verse. He was a Satrap in the province of Susa, which was then subject to the Babylonians; a part of Persia, Susa, which either voluntarily or by some other event not expressed in sacred or profane history, was then under the Babylonian empire. There is also no doubt that a good part of Media was then under the Babylonian kingdom, especially since Nebuchadnezzar had a wife from Media, according to the historian Berosus. However, the greatest consolation of all, which should have been placed first, flowed to the captives from the reading of the sacred scriptures. For Jehoiachin <note>referred to here as Jechonias</note>, when he surrendered himself to the command of God despite the adversity, did not prevent the sacred and political records from being carried with them into Babylon. The entire nobility of the Kingdom, departing with the Prince, did not want to leave behind at home their most precious wealth—those things whose use they could not do without—so that they might at least be consoled in their exile by the reading of the divine writings. Regarding this, Bugenhagen says: <margin>on the last chapter of Jeremiah, folio 450 a.</margin> "The fact that Jehoiachin, King of Judah, is exalted in Babylon after the thirtieth year of captivity—there could have been other human reasons for it there, but God did this so that he might preserve the seed of David, from whom Christ was to be born according to the promise." Did not Daniel read Jeremiah? Did not Cyrus recognize his name in the prophecy of Isaiah...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the Babylonian Captivity, specifically focusing on the literary and prophetic record found in the Bible versus apocryphal accounts like the Book of Baruch. ### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

**Column 1**

<margin>The Babylonian Captivity.</margin>
...[is his] name contained? Did not Isaiah prepare consolation for the captives in Babylon—found from chapter 40 to 49—by which the Jews might be kept in the faith of the one God and not defect to "Chaldaeism"? <note>The author uses "Chaldaeism" to refer to the Babylonian religion, astrology, and culture.</note> Did not Jeremiah send a letter, found in chapters 29, 30, and 31, to the captives in Babylonia through the envoys of Zedekiah, and likewise a prophecy against the Babylonian kingdom, which appears in chapters 50 and 51? Nebuchadnezzar himself, holding the highest honor for education and talent, took care that the Jewish youths were liberally educated, and he permitted the captive people some form of commonwealth, including courts and assemblies within his Empire; and though frequently provoked by the treachery of Zedekiah, he displayed severity rather than cruelty. He also most diligently commended Jeremiah to the primary commander, Nebuzaradan, who treated the Prophet humanely and approved of his teaching with high praise, so much so that he seemed not a leader of enemies but a herald and panegyrist of "Hebrew Philosophy." <note>The author uses "Philosophy" here in the classical sense of "divine wisdom" or "theological system."</note> Furthermore, he left it to the Prophet's judgment whether he wished to remain in Judea or not, the former of which the Prophet chose. 

Hence, we are very poorly informed about this Babylonian captivity by the holy author of the book of Baruch, so that it is a wonder that there are those who wish to "turn their nose" <note>original: "nasum tornare"; a Latin idiom meaning to treat something with critical disdain or, conversely, to try and "shape" it into something acceptable.</note> at this apocryphal writing. The Canonical Prophetic Scripture clearly testifies that Jeremiah and Baruch were left in Judea by the Babylonians after the city of Jerusalem was captured; and that they were then led away into Egypt by Johanan, as Jeremiah himself testifies in chapter 43:6. On the contrary, at the beginning of this book, Baruch is said at that time (chapter 1, verse 1) to have been in Babylonia and to have read this book to the Jewish captives there. The Canonical Scriptures hold that the Jews were in this captivity for seventy years (Jeremiah 25:11, 29:10; 2 Chronicles 36:21). In contrast, Baruch says in chapter 6, verse 2: *Upon entering Babylon, you shall be there for many years and a long time, even for seven generations; but after this, I will lead you out from there in peace.* <note>original Greek: "Εἰσελθόντες εἰς Βαβυλῶνα ἔσεσθε ἐκεῖ ἔτη πλείονα καὶ χρόνον μακρὸν ἕως γενεῶν ἑπτά. μετὰ δὲ τοῦτο ἐξάξω ὑμᾶς ἐκεῖθεν μετ' εἰρήνης."</note> Seven generations would amount to 700 years; for according to the custom of Scripture, a "generation" <note>original: "seculum"</note> signifies 100 years, or the lifespan of one man (Genesis 15:15). He also says the city of Jerusalem was captured and burned at that same time (chapter 1, verse 2). Canonical Scripture teaches the opposite (2 Kings 25:7 and the last chapter of Jeremiah), where the conquest of the city is written as having occurred in the 11th year of Zedekiah, in the 4th month, on the 9th day. The burning, however, is written as having taken place afterward, in the 5th month, on the 15th day, in the 19th year of Nebuchadnezzar. 

Considering these and other inconsistencies and irreconcilable points <note>original Greek: "ἀσύμφωνα καὶ ἀσύστατα"</note> within it, Melchior 

<margin>Book 12, chapter 6.</margin>
Canus <note>Melchior Canus (1509–1560) was a prominent Spanish Dominican theologian.</note> writes: *The Church has not placed the little book of Baruch among the number of sacred books so tested and firmly that it is an established truth of the Catholic faith that it is sacred, or that it is an established heresy to say it is not sacred. This little book does not produce certain and constant truths of the Catholic faith.* 

The Jewish Church, bolstered by these means of consolation during the captivity, responded with a masculine voice to the Chaldeans who were soliciting them toward apostasy: 

<margin>Jeremiah 10:11.</margin>
*These gods, who did not make the heavens and the earth, let them perish from the earth and from under these heavens.* 

Most miserable was the appearance of the Jewish Church and Commonwealth at that time, so much so that very few thought the old polity could be restored after so long an interval. Yet was it restored so that the ancient Laws and form of government were reinstated together? That return was therefore a great miracle, because, while the Jews were being crushed under the heavy yoke of

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

different Kings, God, by His wonderful providence, restored them through the Persians, and willed them to be gifted with their former liberty and returned to their dear Fatherland. So that this liberation may be better understood, it is necessary to know a portion of Babylonian and Persian history; he who neglects to learn this finds the sweetest sayings and sacred prophecies to be mere darkness. For those who are ignorant of the sequence of times and Monarchies grope in the dark; to make this known, God has wonderfully preserved the history of all times. 

We confess with a plea for indulgence and deplore with Bonfrerius <note>Jacques Bonfrère (1573–1622), a Jesuit biblical scholar known for his work on geography and chronology.</note> the obscurity of Sacred Chronology, and with him, we rightly count among the other "rough patches" <note>original: "salebras," referring to rugged or difficult paths.</note> the 70 years of the Babylonian Captivity and the 70 Weeks of Daniel. 
> What is more obscure, he says, than the seventy years of the Babylonian captivity—where they are to begin, and where they are to end?

Thus he spoke. However, I think these rough patches can be crossed with little effort if, with Scaliger, Calvisius, and others, <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger and Sethus Calvisius were famous 16th/17th-century scholars who revolutionized the study of historical chronology.</note> we establish that these 70 years are to be started from the deportation of Jeconiah described in Jeremiah 29:1. Since the captivity was destined to last 70 years, and its beginning can be placed at no more convenient time than when the surrender and deportation of Jeconiah took place, we rightly cast the beginning of the captivity into the first year of Jeconiah's deportation. Thus, its end falls in the first year of the Monarchy of Cyrus. In this way, by the time of his reign, the tribe of Judah had been in exile in Chaldea for a full 70 years, and once those were completed, they were led back to the Fatherland by the command and permission of Cyrus, according to the divine promise. It was then that the good news was brought and published to the Jews in Babylon (Isaiah 52:11, Jeremiah 51:6): "Depart from Babylon!"

With how much congratulation from everyone, I ask, was this voice received? They saw the book of the Lamentations of Jeremiah thus closed and folded away, and their sadness turned into gladness, with such great sorrow changed into joyful things. Joyfully they girded themselves for the journey, about to see their ancestral homes again and to build the Temple and the city. With as much desire as they had held during the captivity to see their fatherland, in such numbers did they set out on the journey to their home to restore the ancient rites and that Temple which Solomon, the wisest of Kings, had once built. Just as the Jews had been led away into captivity at different times, so also were they liberated and sent back into Judea at various and distinct times: many with Zerubbabel, and then many also with Ezra after the Temple was already built. Many also remained in those regions to which they had been dispersed, even after the Temple was rebuilt and the polity somewhat restored; some for one reason, others for another, did not return to the fatherland. 

How many still remained in the Persian Kingdom is shown by the history of Esther, when Haman accuses Mordecai and the rest of the Jews of being disturbers of the kingdom. The names of those who had returned from the Babylonian captivity to Judea were recorded in a specific little book, which was compiled for that purpose; about which one reads [in the Bible], where in the Hebrew it is *Sefer Ha-Yachas* <note>original: ספר היחס</note>, the "Book of Genealogy." The Greek translators of the Septuagint sometimes translated the verb of this Hebrew name, *le-hityaches* <note>original: להתיחש</note>, in the books of Chronicles as "to be genealogized" <note>original Greek: "γενεαλογεῖσθαι"</note> (to be enrolled by family), and sometimes they used the nouns "genealogy," "census," or "lineage" <note>original Greek: "γενεαλογίας, καταλογισμὸς, κατὰ γένεσις"</note>. This captivity of Babylon and the restoration to the ancestral city is a shadow and figure of the victories and triumphs of the Church, which knows not how to be conquered...

### Baruch I. 29.

> They roar, crying out before their gods, like those at a feast for the dead. <note>original Greek: "Ὠρύοντο δὲ βοῶντες ἐναντίον τῶν θεῶν αὐτῶν, ὥσπερ τινὲς ἐν περιδείπνῳ νεκρῶν."</note>
> They roar while shouting in the presence of their gods, just as at a supper for a dead man. <note>original Latin: "Rugiunt autem clamantes coram Diis suis, sicut in cœna mortui."</note>

<margin>Funeral feasts. Continued in the supplement to Genesis ch. 21, p. 124.</margin>It was a widespread custom among the pagans to establish funeral banquets in honor of the deceased, in which they primarily recited the praises of the dead, according to Zenobius, and greeted the *Manes* <note>The spirits of the dead in Roman religion.</note> with a mournful cry. For that mournful voices were heard in these gatherings <note>original: "μεγάλῳ ἀλαλητῷ," with a great shouting</note> is confirmed by the present passage, which describes the wailing <note>original: "τὸ γοῶδες"</note> as the gnashing of a lion or the howling of a wolf. The word for "roaring" <note>original: "τὸ ὠρύεσθαι"</note> is used playfully in Psalm 21:13, 103:22, Jeremiah 2:15, Ezekiel 22:25, and Zephaniah 3:4; it is attributed to the lion, where in the Hebrew it is <term>Sha'ag<gloss>to roar or groan</gloss></term>. From there it is transferred to the Chaldeans, who wailed miserably before their gods, just as mourning is usually heard at the funeral supper of some deceased person. For the nations were accustomed to place food and drink upon the tombs of the dead, or rather to carry it in, adding an unusual shouting; hence these things that were carried into the tomb were called *inferiae* <note>Latin term for sacrifices or offerings to the gods of the underworld or the deceased.</note>, and were called *choai* by the Greeks from the act of pouring. Regarding <margin>In Orestes, verses 112 and following.</margin> the funeral banquet offered to the *Manes* and the ancestral preparations among the Nasamones, a people of Africa, these were nothing other than the cult of the ancestral spirits. <margin>On the Soul, ch. 57, p. 261.</margin> Concerning them, Tertullian writes: Heraclides of Pontus, or Nymphodorus of Amphipolis (who wrote on the laws and rituals of barbarians, according to Clement's *Exhortation to the Heathen* and the fifth book of his *Miscellanies*), or Herodotus writes that *the Nasamones capture their own oracles by staying at the graves of their parents.* The passage in Herodotus is in his book *Melpomene*. The Greeks call this a <term>perideipnon<gloss>a funeral banquet or "supper around the grave"</gloss></term>. Varro, in his *Meleagris* cited by Nonius, says: *Having performed the funeral with a song of praise (lausie) at the tomb according to ancient custom, we prepared a Silicernium, that is, a funeral feast, from which, having dined, we depart saying to one another, "Farewell."* Jerome <margin>p. 302.</margin> on Jeremiah chapter 16:4: *It is the custom for mourners to bring food and prepare a banquet, which the Greeks call perideipna, and are commonly called Parentalia by our people, because the proper rites are celebrated for parents.* <margin>page 32.</margin> The same author on Hosea 9: *The Greeks call the suppers of mourners "suppers of the dead" (nekrodeipna). We can call them Parentalia, from the fact that they are sacrificed to dead parents.* The Etymologist, p. 699, defines the *perideipnon* as the feast that takes place for those who have died. Pollux, in his *Onomasticon* 8.7.4, calls them "gatherings for mourning, a funeral feast," and hence the verb *perideipneo* is used for the funeral banquet after the burial of Abner in 2 Samuel 3:35. Eustathius, commenting on Homer's *Iliad* book 23, verse 680, distinguishes between the feast that was held at the tomb and that which was held after the burial; he says the former is called *taphon* <note>funeral/burial rite</note> and the latter is called *perideipnon*. In this sense, some explain the words of Tobit 4:18: *Place your bread and your wine upon the burial of the righteous,* where it refers either to the burial or the sacrifice. This too <margin>Book 3.8.13.</margin> is taken from this rite in Sirach 30:19: *Good things hidden <margin>Sermon 7.5.</margin> in a closed mouth are like offerings of feasts placed around*

<column-break/>

a tomb <note>original: "θέματα βρωμάτων παρακείμενα ἐπὶ τάφῳ"</note>. The same is found in Hosea 9:4, such as the *bread of mourners*, which was eaten in grief. Epiphanius <margin>Topic 505.</margin> testifies to feasts brought to the pyre and the tomb with a greeting to the deceased such as: *Arise, eat!* <note>original: "Ἀνάςα, φάγε"</note>; I was told that the Lithuanians still observe this custom in their cemeteries when I was living among them; and Stuckius wrote the same regarding the Livonians in his *Antiquities of Banquets*, page 75. Regarding the Americans, see Lerius in his *History of a Voyage to Brazil*, page 269; Barthius in his *Adversaria*, page 1874; and concerning the Turks, Bartholomaeus Georgieviz in his book on the ceremonies of the Turks, page 15, testifies that they frequent tombs and bewail their fate, having called friends and relatives to feasts and banquets. After the solemnities of the tomb were completed, "hail and farewell" was said, as noted in the *Notes on the Poem regarding the Pilgrimage and Blessed Death of the Most Serene Prince Henry, Landgrave of Hesse*. Our late colleague Bachmann <margin>page 153.</margin> noted this with many examples. More can be learned about sepulchral feasts and the funeral supper from Bisciola, Volume 1, *Subcisive Hours*, book 11, chapter 4; Stuckius in his book *On Banquets*, 25; Lipsius on Tacitus's *Annals* book 6, note 18; Kirchmann, *On Roman Funerals*, book 4, chapters 5 and 6; Kornman, *On the Miracles of the Living and the Dead*, part 7, chapter 36; Louis Guyon, *Various Readings*, book 5, chapter 3; Serrarius on Tobit chapter 4, page 86 and following; Villalpando on Ezekiel chapter 24, page 513 and following; Jan Dousa, *Plantin Explanations*, book 1, pages 73 and 74; and Santorellus in his book *On Preserving Health*, 46, pages 152 to 157.

### Baruch VI, v. 42. 43.

> The women sit in the roads surrounded by cords, burning olive stones.
> When one of them is pulled away by someone passing by and sleeps with him, she mocks her neighbor because she was not considered worthy like herself, and her cord was not broken. <note>These verses describe the ritual prostitution associated with the Babylonian goddess Ishtar or Mylitta.</note>

Jeremiah—or whoever is the author of the Epistle—described the harlots placed under Bacchus <note>The author uses "Bacchus" here to refer to the Babylonian deities associated with fertility or excess.</note>, warning his fellow countrymen who were just about to go to Chaldean Babylon against all the abominations of the Chaldeans, so that they would not follow the idols and vices of the Venus of those nations; he also mentions the *women surrounded by cords*. The words of the Vulgate are: *The women sit in the roads surrounded by cords, burning olive stones.* Verse 43: *When one of them is pulled away by someone passing by and sleeps with him, she mocks her neighbor because she was not considered worthy like herself, and her cord was not broken.* Here, unless the reader knows the customs of the Babylonians from the writings of the pagans, he will hardly understand the context <note>original: "τὰ συνεχόμενα"</note> of this Epistle written in Greek. It was an ancient and infamous custom of Babylon that virgins were prostituted before marriage; for it was sanctioned by public edict that no woman should enter into marriage until she had first been a hireling and had paid the tribute of her body to Venus once in her life. Herodotus relates this in his *Histories*: *The foulest of the laws among the Babylonians is this: every native woman must sit in the temple of Aphrodite once in her life and have intercourse with a foreign man.* Those nefarious sacred rites in the prostitution of modesty, as you hear, were performed at the temple of Venus—

BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
Babylonian harlots consecrated to Venus.
</margin>
...the rites were performed, and those women who were being initiated to that most filthy Goddess were anointed with ointments, their temples bound with knots and wreaths of rushes, as the Historian <note>Likely referring to Herodotus.</note> clearly relates. He mentions a double kind of cords: one with which the women's heads were crowned, and another by which tents were made and stretched out. In ancient times, harlots used to carry cords or thongs in their bosoms and under their clothes, which they would throw around the necks of those they claimed were held by their love, as is indicated in the *Satyricon* of Petronius and the *Epidicus* of Plautus. From this, perhaps, we might have guessed that these were the ropes with which women were surrounded in the streets to "drag in" <note>original Greek: "ἐκ τοῦ ἑλκύσθαι παριόντας," meaning to pull in passersby.</note> those going by, had not Herodotus suggested otherwise, by whose guidance we shall untangle the bonds of these cords. For the words of the same author are as follows:
<margin>
In Cleio <note>The first book of Herodotus's *Histories*.</note>, page 51.
</margin>
Many women sit in the precinct of Aphrodite <note>The Greek equivalent of the Babylonian goddess Mylitta or the Roman Venus.</note> wearing a crown of cord around their heads. Some are arriving, while others are leaving. There are pathways stretched with ropes <note>original Greek: "Σχοινοτενέες δὲ διέξοδοι," cord-stretched passages.</note> running in every direction through the women, by which strangers passing through make their choice. Once a woman sits there, she does not return home until one of the strangers, having cast silver into her lap, has had intercourse with her outside the temple. These words, which are clearly identical to this passage in Baruch, sound thus to Latin ears in the translation of Martinus de Roa:
> Women having wreaths of cords around their heads sit at the temple of Venus. And some indeed come, while others depart. Moreover, tents stretched out with rush ropes on every side provide a path to the women, from which passing guests choose. After a woman has come there, she does not go back home until some guest, throwing silver into her lap, has lain with her far from the shrine.

By this girding, they indeed professed their trade, and at the same time indicated that, being sacred to the Goddess Venus, they carried a virginity for sale; they simultaneously asked the newcomers to "break the belt" <note>original: "ζώνην rumpant"</note> and loosen that rush-made belt of virginity. For whether these "cord-stretched passages" <note>original Greek: "διέξοδοι σχοινοτενέες"</note> (as Herodotus calls them) are understood as leading to the <term>Succoth-benoth<note>original Hebrew: סכות בנות. Literally "Booths of Daughters," a term used in 2 Kings 17:30 for the shrines where this ritual took place.</note></term>, the "tabernacles of the daughters," or as other loin-cloths, the explanation points to the same thing. Nor is it perhaps inconvenient to say with Olympiodorus that by "cords" <note>original: "σχοινία"</note> are indicated the loin-cloths of the private parts, which those naked harlots placed around that part which they prostituted to anyone willing. His words are found in the *Greek Catena* <note>A collection of biblical commentaries.</note> on Micah, edited by Ghisler: "He says 'cords' for the loin-cloths. For they cover only the parts of shame, leaving the rest bare to call out to lovers." Rushes grew most excellently in Arabia and Babylonia, which is why they were celebrated above others, 
<margin>
On Virgil's Eclogues, p. 58.
</margin>
as noted by Barth*; thus their use could be common for making wreaths, cords, tents, and other coverings. Olympiodorus wished to imply a covering of the private parts, though I do not know if it is probable that they made such things of rushes over the chest and belly. Our first parents used an apron to veil their nakedness from fig leaves (Genesis 3:6), and today similar lower-body coverings <note>original: "perizomata"</note> are commonly made from the foliage of trees in Holstein by bath-attendants, which they call *Quaest*. But what these "cords" <note>original: "σχοινία"</note> signify is difficult to perceive.

Selden* says, regarding "putting on cords": "what it was, is not sufficiently clear. It might equally refer to those slender cords or thin ropes from which their crowns were woven, just as it might refer to the ropes that divided the spaces for each one; for the material of the wreaths..."

<column-break/>

"...were thin cords," as Herodotus and Strabo testify. The testimony most relevant to our subject is found in Strabo, which coincides with that of Herodotus. Herodotus testified that these impure Babylonian brothels at the temple of Venus (Baruch says "in the streets," i.e., of the temples and shrines) made their beauty mercenary and abominable—to use the Prophet’s words*. For this reason, next to the temple of the Babylonian Mylitta or Venus, there were many diversions or tents separated by cords—"cord-stretched passages"—of which there is obscure mention in Baruch and none in Strabo. Similarly, there is no mention of the "lovers' sorcery" in Herodotus, which Rodericus à Castro—a Jewish physician very well known throughout Europe—suspects lies hidden under these words, "to burn the husks" <note>original: "θυμιᾶσαι τὰ πίτυρα." The "husks" or "bran" mentioned in Baruch 6:43.</note>. I will quote his full words so you may recognize the author’s thought:
> Herodotus reports that it was the custom of Syrian women to sit at the shrines of Venus so that, according to the law, by sitting at her temple once in their life they might have intercourse with foreign men, nor would they return home until some guest had had his way with her after leading her apart from the shrine. No one was permitted to reject a guest, whoever he might be, who first led her away. Therefore, Jeremiah <note>Referring to the author of the Letter of Jeremiah/Baruch 6.</note> discourages the people of God from this Babylonian custom and from the burning of olives, which the Babylonian women—added to their magical trifles—used as a philtre <note>A love potion or charm.</note> so that they would not be forced to keep watch there for long. This was especially used by those who were recommended neither by wealth, nor beauty, nor noble birth; and when those "bones" <note>The pits or kernels of the olives.</note> were burned, they prayed that guests might be scorched by love for them in the same way.

You see the conjecture of the Portuguese <note>Rodericus à Castro.</note>, which I am easily persuaded he borrowed from elsewhere. The same exposition is approved by Jacobus Tirinus*, whose very words I produce:
> Women, both married and unmarried, publicly exposing their chastity to anyone willing, sit in the streets of the temples surrounded by ropes, that is, by a girdle or "Zone" as if a virginal one, testifying by this sign that they are sacred to Venus. Meanwhile, they set fire to "bones," that is, the hard and bone-like kernels of olives. This was a type of philtre or sorcery by which those devilish women—who were recommended by neither beauty, nor birth, nor wealth—tried to enchant the hardness of suitors and kindle the flame of concupiscence in them, adding an imprecation that just as those "bones" were scorched by fires, so might guests be scorched by love for them. They used the olive rather than the kernels of other trees so they might more certainly and clearly testify to the flames of their lust, since olive kernels, being more oily and fatty, burn more vehemently.

How well this holds up, let others judge. It cannot be held for certain that the word "husks" <note>original: "πίτυρα"</note> refers to the leaves or kernels of olives. Let the more curious see what Martinus de Roa* records, who discusses the cords and

### Ezekiel V. 5.

> Thus says the Lord Jehovah: This is Jerusalem; I have set her in the midst of the nations

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Jerusalem.</margin>
...the dwelling and temple of God, in which God would reveal himself, repeat the promises concerning the Messiah, and spread them far and wide among other nations. To that end, Jerusalem was built to be the city where assemblies ought to be held, *Psalm 122:3.* This place had been consecrated from ancient times by a remarkable divine revelation, when Abraham wished to offer his only-begotten
<margin>Genesis 22:2.</margin>
son Isaac as a burnt offering; yet Isaac, being ignorant of the whole matter—both of the sacrifice and the symbolic meaning <note>Isaac is often viewed as a "type" or foreshadowing of Christ.</note>—questioned his father, saying: *Behold the father, the fire and the wood; where is the victim for the burnt offering?* To which the father replied: אלהים יראה <note>original: "Elohim Yireh"</note> *The Lord will provide.* From this word *Yireh* <note>provide/see</note> some maintain the name of the city Jerusalem was formed; for, as they write, in an older naming it had been called *Salem*; but afterward, by a combination, it was called Jerusalem, because God would there "provide" for Himself a victim who could procure the lost peace between God and man. This <term>nomenclature</term> <note>original: "ὄνομα θεσίαν" (onoma thesian)</note> derived from "peace," most commentators reject, regarding which let us hear
<margin>on John 10 p. 178.</margin>
Masius, who, joining the errors concerning this name of Jerusalem by the Hebrew, Josephus, and the Greek Stephanus, writes thus: *The stories that Josephus babbles are trifles, when he says this name was bestowed by Melchizedek, who added the "sacred"* <note>original: "τὸ ἱερὸν" (to hieron)</note> *to the old Salem because of the temple he built there. As if Melchizedek spoke Greek! Elsewhere (Antiquities 7.3) he says it was because of the wall with which he surrounded the city; for he claims the Hebrews call walls "hieron." These things are so tasteless that I would sooner think they were sprinkled into his books by the detractors and adversaries of Josephus rather than written by such an erudite man, did I not notice him hallucinating to such an extent elsewhere in the explanation of Hebrew names that he might rightly seem ignorant of his own language, and educated and learned only in Greek. Stephanus of Byzantium also errs greatly, writing that this city took the name of the Solymoi from the Solymi mountains; for the Solymoi, whom even Homer mentions, are to be sought in Pisidia near Telmessus, as Strabo, a most diligent writer, attests. For surely, if the name of the Solymoi was ever adapted to our city by good writers, who would not think it was corrupted from the ancient Salem rather than taken from distant mountains?* To this, Agostino Steucho <note>A 16th-century Italian exegete and librarian.</note> entirely agrees where he
<margin>on Genesis chapter 14.</margin>
shows: Salem is not this Jerusalem, but a town near Scythopolis, which even in the time of Saint Jerome was called Salem, and where the palace of Melchizedek was shown, demonstrating its magnificence from the size of the ruins of the ancient building. Formerly, on account of the inhabiting Jebusites, it was called *Jebus*, whence Adrichomius <note>Author of "Theatrum Terrae Sanctae," a famous 16th-century geographical work on the Holy Land.</note> in his *Theater of the Holy Land* wishes it to have been called *Jebus-Salem*. But that naming by Lysimachus in Josephus (Book 1 *Against Apion*) is truly unlearned and entirely tasteless, as he thinks Jerusalem was named from "sacred" and "plundering" <note>original: "ἱερὸν & συλᾶν" (hieron & sylan)</note> because the Israelites once plundered the temples of the nations and brought the spoils to Jerusalem. Jerome (Letter 17 to Marcella, column 153) seeks a certain mystery in these three names with which it was marked, namely יבוס, שלם, ירושלים <note>Jebus, Salem, Jerusalem</note>; *Our whole mystery,* he says, *is native to that province and city (Jerusalem). In the three names, it demonstrates the faith of the Trinity. It is called Jebus, Salem, and Jerusalem. The first name*

<column-break/>

means "trodden down," *the second* "peace," *the third* "vision of peace." *Indeed, we arrive at the end little by little, and after being trodden down, we are raised up to the vision of peace*, from which Solomon, that is, *the peaceful one*, was born in it, and *his place was made in peace*. But whatever the case may be regarding the name Jerusalem, it was by far the most distinguished and famous city of the entire Orient, as Pliny affirms, with whom Tacitus also agrees. As soon as the Ark was moved to Jerusalem, the city, clothed in new virtue, breathed majesty; and when it later received the Temple, it could boast of it above all others that ever would be or had been. For what greater happiness could there be for a city than to receive a name from God himself, whence it was called יהוה שמה <note>original: "Jehovah Shammah"</note>, *The Lord is there*; what most useful and delightful meditations these names provide, Haffenreffer teaches in his *Commentary on the Temple of Ezekiel, p. 150 ff.* Hence, it was decorated with various names on account of the presence of God and His Temple. It was called the *City of God, the Holy City, the city of perfect beauty, and the joy of the whole earth, Lamentations 2:15. It was the gate of the people of God.* For in it were the Temple, the Priests, the royal power, and the Sacrifices; rightly, therefore, was it called the *Gate of the people of God*. For in ancient times, judgments were exercised in the gates of cities, and there also were the city's defenses, weapons of war, provisions, etc. Hence, the gates of cities were fortified with very high towers and strengthened by a strong garrison of soldiers. And what greater happiness could there be for this city, or what more honorable things can be said of it, than what God says of it: *Glorious things are spoken of thee, O Jerusalem.* In it sounded the doctrine of the mysteries of God, and from there its glory is extolled, just as it is said of the inhabitants in Hosea 8:12: *I have given to them the honorable things of my law.* How great a benefit of God, that He established this city to be a certain seat of doctrine and like an Academy, which, situated like a citadel on a steep mountain, might be seen from all sides and illuminated by miracles and happiness, so that from there the voice of doctrine might be carried to the nations in every direction. In it was the Temple, and in the Temple the Ark of the Covenant, and in it and near it God was present according to grace; whence it merited the name of the holy city, both because of the true worship of the true God and because of the peculiar protection of God. Happy, therefore, is the city for which God is the guardian. The Phaeacians in Corcyra <note>Modern-day Corfu.</note> were protected by the guardianship of the gods, in the boast of Nausicaa, the daughter of the King of the Phaeacians, in Homer's *Odyssey, Book 6, v. 201*:

> *There is no such man alive, nor shall there be,*
> *who would come to the land of the Phaeacian men*
> *bringing hostility, for they are very dear to the immortals.*
> <note>original Greek: "Οὐκ ἔσθ' οὗτος ἀνὴρ διερός βροτός..."</note>

From this, the Phaeacians are called by the same author *near to the gods* <note>original: "ἀγχίθεοι" (anchitheoi)</note> and *equal to the gods* <note>original: "ἰσόθεοι" (isotheoi)</note>, blessed and equal to the gods, as the ancient scholars interpret. This could truly be said of Jerusalem in the past, which God very often snatched from the hands of enemies, as history attests by the slaughter of Sennacherib <note>The Assyrian king whose army was destroyed outside Jerusalem.</note>, so that here that sentiment of Jerome (Letter 17 to Marcella, column 153) rightly has its place: *As much as Judea [excels] other provinces, so much does the city of Jerusalem [excel other cities]...*

# Ezechiel 5:5

<margin>Jerusalem.</margin> Jerusalem is more sublime than all of Judea; the glory of the entire province is claimed by its Metropolis, and whatever praise is found in the members is all referred back to the head. Therefore:
> O flower and glory of cities!
> Hail, O streets of the blessed people of Jerusalem!
> Here Jehovah placed a spot for sacred things;
> Here He chose His fire and His hearth;
> Here, here was the conspicuous tribunal,
> The sacred tribunal of the house of David. <note>This is a poetic tribute to the city's spiritual and royal importance.</note>
As for the appearance of the city of Jerusalem, its great preparations, its citadels, walls, temples, streets, and gates—to teach these things is a field of contemplation so vast that although many of us have completed studies on it, more will always remain than can be grasped by the eyes of the mind, let alone the body. It was situated in the middle of Judea, like a center or a navel <note>original: "umbilicus"</note>, among mountainous slopes, yet with a view of irrigated valleys and most fertile plains that was by far the most pleasant. Thus, in its fortifications, buildings, the number of its inhabitants, and every other glory that usually adorns a city, it never yielded to any other. But the greatest grace, which has happened to no other people under the sun, was in the divine appearances, prophecies, and God’s answers; then, truly and most importantly, it was the most blessed of cities through the manifest presence of the <term>Son of God</term> <note>The second person of the Trinity in Christian theology.</note>, our Lord <term>Jesus Christ</term>, in the flesh—by His teaching, miracles, burial, resurrection, ascension into heaven, the sending of the Holy Spirit, and the mission and preaching of the Apostles. That it was situated in the middle of Judea is attested by <margin>The Jewish War, Book 3, Chapter 2.</margin> Josephus, who, in describing *Judea*, says among other things: *In its middle (Judea) is Jerusalem; whence some, not without reason, have called that city the navel of the land.* God also placed it in the midst of the nations so that the great works of God might appear in its surroundings, since at that time no part of the world was more noble in its population than the regions closest to its circuit. For concerning Europe, especially Latium <note>The region of Italy including Rome.</note> and Germany, they were at that time scarcely known due to the rarity and scarcity of people, nor were they of such name as to be counted among the nations. Hence the Rabbinic scholars, as reported by Buxtorf in his *Chaldean and Talmudic Lexicon* (p. 2054), say the world is like an eye, the white of which represents the Ocean that surrounds the whole world. The black part is the world itself, and the pupil, which is in the black, is Jerusalem, and the image seen in the pupil is the Sanctuary. So they say. Otherwise, antiquity believed that Delphi embraced the middle of the earth. From this comes that fable of the two eagles sent out by Jove to explore the middle of the world, which the interpreter of Pindar records: namely, that one flew from the east and the other from the west, and they met at Pytho <note>Another name for Delphi.</note>; as a monument to this event, two golden eagles were later dedicated there. Plutarch mentions this embassy of eagles <margin>On the Obsolescence of Oracles, beginning.</margin>
Ovid also remembers the same:
-> and in the middle <-
-> of the world, Delphi sat without a ruler. <note>original: "Et orbe in medio positi caruerunt præside Delphi."</note> <-
And the author of a certain poem:
-> Pallas protects the Cecropian citadels; <-
-> Pythian Delphi is the navel of the world. <-
As for why they called it the "navel" <note>original: "umbilicus"</note>, taking the comparison from the navel of the human body, Varro indeed

<column-break/>

does not admit this, but he did not entirely persuade everyone, even though we believe with him that it was not the physical center of the earth, just as the navel is not the exact center in us. However, that the place was called the <gloss>navel</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ὀμφαλὸν" (omphalon)</note> is not to be denied, nor is antiquity to be attacked for believing Delphi to be the middle of the earth, even if it was not. <margin>Jerusalem.</margin> Livy was also of this opinion, writing thus: *The Gauls plundered Delphi, once the common oracle of the human race and the navel of the world.* <margin>Volume 4, p. 434.</margin> All those who have left descriptions of the Holy Land attest that the city of Jerusalem stood in a higher place than any other in all of Palestine. Among the older authors, one may consult Fulcher of Chartres in his *History of Jerusalem* (p. 397), describing the expedition of Emperor Henry in A.D. 1059; William of Tyre, *History*, Book 8, chapters 2 and 3 (p. 746); Willibrand of Oldenburg, *Itinerary of the Holy Land* (p. 146); the Anonymous Florentine on the *Investiture of Bishops* (p. 858); and Masius, *Commentary on Joshua* 11 (p. 212). Its <gloss>mountainous surrounding on every side</gloss> <note>original Greek: "συμπεριφορὰ ἔνθεν καὶ ἔνθεν ὀρεινὴ"</note> and its <gloss>construction</gloss> <note>original Greek: "κατασκευὴ"</note> are worthy of sight, namely the mountains <gloss>on the outside</gloss> <note>original Greek: "εἰς τὰ ἔξω"</note> and the mountains <gloss>on the inside</gloss> <note>original Greek: "εἰς τὰ ἔσω"</note>. It was situated in the mountains, and its foundations were in the mountains: <gloss>His foundation is in the holy mountains</gloss>, <margin>Psalm 87:1.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: יסודתו בהררי קדש (Yesodato be-harerei kodesh)</note>. This is surely a glorious proclamation, by whose <gloss>excellence</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ὑπεροχῇ"</note> the prophet Micah was moved to exclaim: *What are the high places of Judah? Are they not Jerusalem?* (Micah 1:5). And again: *The mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established at the head of the mountains, and it shall be higher than the hills.* <margin>Chapter 4:1.</margin>
With these words, the Prophet, full of the Holy Spirit and joyful, breaks forth suddenly, describing under the type of a mountain the Church of the New Testament, whose beginning would be in Jerusalem, in Sion, which place God had chosen above all the heights in all Israel. To show this praise as if from the foundation, let us go and walk around, surveying the mountains. <gloss>Walking around</gloss> <note>original Greek: "Περιϊόντες"</note> first within the city itself, we see two taller mountains, the first of which is **Mount Sion** in the furthest part of the city toward the south, truly steep and rugged. With divine help, King David took this and, after his own name, called it a stronghold, diligently fortified and adorned. For thus the Sacred Scriptures testify: *David took the stronghold of Sion; this is the City of David.* And again: *David dwelt in the stronghold of Sion, and called it the City of David: and he built all around from the Millo and inward.* (2 Samuel 5:7, 9). Of which we speak in the words of Euripides in *Hecuba* (v. 629):
-> <gloss>O form of the house, O once happy homes.</gloss> <note>original Greek: "Ὢ σχῆματ’ οἴκων, ὦ ποτ’ εὐτυχεῖς δόμοι."</note> <-
Besides this citadel of David, Josephus <margin>Antiquities, Book 15, Ch. 11.</margin> testifies that Herod built two magnificent palaces, giving the name of Caesar to one and Agrippa (who was married to Julia, the daughter of Caesar Augustus) to the other. And since this mountain surpassed the other mountains of the city in height, it happened that over the deep valley—once called Mello and later the Tyropoeon <note>The "Valley of the Cheesemakers" in ancient Jerusalem.</note>—which lay between the lower city and Sion, a bridge and certain steps were constructed, providing an easier path for those going up the mountain and down from the mountain into the city. The other mountain in the city to be extolled with no less praise than the former was **Moriah**, where Abraham, by the command of God, once intended to sacrifice his son Isaac (Genesis 22:2). On this Mount Moriah, King Solomon the Most Wise [built] a most magnificent Temple to God...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Jerusalem.</margin> ...[the Son of God would enter the] temple of God, in which God would reveal Himself, repeat the promises concerning the Messiah, and spread them far and wide among other nations. For this purpose Jerusalem was built, to be a city where assemblies should be established, as mentioned in *Psalm 122:3.* This place had been consecrated of old by a remarkable divine revelation, when Abraham intended to sacrifice his only-begotten
<margin>Genesis 22:2.</margin>
son Isaac as a burnt offering; Isaac, however, ignorant of the whole matter—both the sacrifice and its symbolic meaning <note>Isaac is often viewed in Christian tradition as a "type" or foreshadowing of Christ.</note>—questioned his father, saying: *Behold, Father, the fire and the wood; where is the victim for the burnt offering?* To which the Father responds: *God will provide.* <note>original Hebrew: אלהים יראה, "Elohim yireh"</note>. Some maintain that from this word *yireh* <note>meaning "will provide" or "will see"</note> the name of the city Jerusalem was formed; since, as they write, in older times it was called *Salem*; but later it was called *Jerusalem* from a combination of the two, because God would provide for Himself a victim there who could restore the lost peace between God and man. Most commentators reject this "divine name" <note>original Greek: ὄνομα θεῖον</note> derived from peace; on this matter let us hear
<margin>On Joshua 10, page 178.</margin>
Masius, who, linking the errors concerning this name Jerusalem by the Hebrews, Josephus, and the Greek Stephanus, writes thus: *“They are trifles, these stories Josephus tells, when he says this name was given by Melchizedek, who added ‘The Sacred’ <note>original Greek: τὸ ἱερόν, "to hieron"</note> to the old Salem because of the temple he built there. As if Melchizedek spoke Greek! Elsewhere, in the Antiquities of the Jews (Book 7, Chapter 3), he says it was because of the wall with which he surrounded the city; for he claims the Hebrews call walls ‘hieron.’ These things are so tasteless that I suspect they were sprinkled into Josephus’s books by detractors rather than written by such a learned man, unless I had noticed him hallucinating so much in the explanation of Hebrew names elsewhere that he might rightly be seen as ignorant of his own language, and educated and learned only in Greek. Stephanus of Byzantium also errs greatly, writing that this city took the name from the Solymi mountains; for the Solymi, whom Homer also mentions, are to be sought in Pisidia near Telmessus, as Strabo, a most diligent writer, testifies. For surely, if the name of the Solymi was ever applied to our city by good writers, who would not think it was corrupted from Old Salem rather than taken from distant mountains?”* Augustinus Steuchus agrees entirely with this, where he
<margin>On Genesis chapter 14.</margin>
shows that Salem is not this Jerusalem, but a town near Scythopolis, which was still called Salem in the time of Saint Jerome; he identifies the palace of Melchizedek there, demonstrating its former magnificence by the size of the ruins of the old building. Formerly, because of the Jebusite inhabitants, it was called *Jebus*, from which Adrichomius, in his *Theater of the Holy Land*, wants it to have been called *Jebus-Salem*. Truly foolish and altogether tasteless is that naming by Lysimachus (quoted in Josephus, *Against Apion*, Book 1), who thinks Jerusalem was named from *hieron* <note>temple/sacred</note> and *sylan* <note>to plunder</note>, because the Israelites once plundered the temples of nations and brought the spoils to Jerusalem. Jerome, in Letter 17 to Marcella, looks for a certain mystery in these three names with which it was distinguished, namely *Jebus, Salem, and Jerusalem* <note>original Hebrew: יבוס, שלם, ירושלים</note>; *“Our whole mystery,”* he says, *“is native to that province and city. In three names it demonstrates faith in the Trinity. It is called Jebus, Salem, and Jerusalem. The first name [means]...”*

<column-break/>

<margin>Paul.</margin> ...trodden down, the *second* peace, the *third* vision of peace. Through Latin we reach the end, and after being trodden down we are raised up to the vision of peace, since Solomon (that is, the peaceful one) was born in it, and his place was made in peace. Whatever the case may be regarding the name of Jerusalem, it is by far the most distinguished and famous city of all the East, as Pliny affirms, and Tacitus agrees. As soon as the Ark was moved to Jerusalem, the city was clothed with a new power and breathed majesty; and when it later received the Temple, it could boast of it above all others that ever would be or had been. For what greater happiness could there be for a city than to receive a name from God Himself, whence it was called *The LORD is there* <note>original Hebrew: יהוה שמה, "Jehovah Shammah"</note>? Haffenreffer teaches what useful and joyful meditations these names offer in his *Commentary on the Temple of Ezekiel*. Hence, because of the presence of God and His Temple, it was decorated with various names. It was called the City of God, the Holy City, the city of perfect beauty, and the joy of the whole earth (*Lamentations 2:15*). It was the gate of the people of God. For in it were the Temple, the Priests, the royal power, and the Sacrifices; therefore it was rightly called the *Gate of the people of God*. In ancient times, judgments were carried out in the gates of cities, and there too were the city's defenses, weapons of war, provisions, and so on. Hence the city gates were fortified with very high towers and strengthened by a strong garrison of soldiers. And what greater happiness could there be for this city, or what more honorable things can be said of it, than what God says: *Glorious things are spoken of thee, O Jerusalem.* In it sounded the doctrine of the mysteries of God, and from there His glory is extolled, as He says of the inhabitants in Hosea 8:12: *I have given them the honorable things of my law.* How great indeed was God's benefit, that He established this city to be a certain seat of doctrine and like an Academy, which, situated like a citadel on a high mountain, might be seen from everywhere and illuminated by miracles and happiness, so that from there the voice of doctrine might be carried to the nations in every direction. In it was the temple, and in the temple the Ark of the Covenant, and in it and near it God was present according to grace; thus it earned the name of the holy city, both because of the true worship of the true God and because of God's special protection. Happy, therefore, is the city for which God is the guardian. The Phaeacians in Corcyra were protected by the guardianship of the gods, as Nausicaa, daughter of the King of the Phaeacians, boasts in Homer's *Odyssey* (Book 6, line 201):

-> There is no man alive, nor shall there ever be, <-
-> who comes to the land of the Phaeacian men <-
-> bringing hostility, for we are very dear to the immortals. <-
<note>original Greek: Οὐκ ἔσθ᾽ οὗτος ἀνὴρ διερός βροτός, οὐδὲ γένηται, ὅς κεν Φαιήκων ἀνδρῶν ἐς γαῖαν ἵκηται δηϊοτῆτα φέρων, μάλα γὰρ φίλοι ἀθανάτοισιν.</note>

This is why the Phaeacians are called by him "close to the gods" <note>original Greek: ἀγχίθεοι</note> and "equal to the gods" <note>original Greek: ἰσόθεοι</note>—blessed and equal to the gods, as the ancient commentators interpret. # Ezekiel 5:5

<margin>Jerusalem.</margin>
Judea is more sublime than all the surrounding lands, and the glory of the entire province is claimed by its Metropolis; whatever praise exists in the members is all referred back to the head. Hence:

-> *O flower, O glory of cities! Greetings,* <-
-> *O streets of the blessed people of Jerusalem!* <-

<note>original Latin: "O flos, ô decus urbium! Platea / Salveto ô Solymum beatiorum!..."</note>

As for the appearance of the city of Jerusalem, its great preparations, what its citadels, walls, temples, streets, and gates were—to teach these things is a vast field of contemplation. Although many of us have poured our studies into this field, there will always remain more things than can be grasped by the eyes of the mind, let alone the eyes of the body. It was situated in the middle of Judea, like a center or a navel, among mountainous slopes indeed, but with a view of irrigated valleys and most fertile plains that was by far the most pleasant. Thus, in its fortifications, buildings, the density of its inhabitants, and every other glory that usually adorns a city, it never yielded to any other city. But most of all, it was the most fortunate of cities because of a grace that has befallen no other people under the sun: through divine apparitions, prophecies, the oracles of God, and then truly and especially the manifest presence of the <term>SON OF GOD</term> our Lord <term>JESUS CHRIST</term> in the flesh—His teaching, miracles, burial, resurrection, ascension into heaven, the sending of the Holy Spirit, and the mission and preaching of the Apostles.

<margin>Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book 3, Chapter 2.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 87, 8.</margin>
That it was situated in the <term>middle of Judea</term> is attested by Josephus. In describing *Judea*, he says among other things: *The middle of it (Judea) is Jerusalem: whence some, not without reason, have called that city the navel of that land.* God also placed it in the midst of the nations so that the great works of God might appear in its surrounding circuit; for at that time, no part of the world was more noble in the density of people than the regions closest to that circuit. For concerning Europe, especially Latium <note>the region around Rome</note> and Germany, they were scarcely known at that time due to the scarcity and infrequency of their peoples, and were not of such a name that they would be counted among the nations. Hence the Rabbinic scholars, as reported by Buxtorf in his *Chaldaic and Talmudic Lexicon, page 2054*, say that the world is like an eye: the white represents the Ocean, which surrounds the whole world; the black is the world itself; the pupil, which is in the black, is Jerusalem; and the image that is seen in the pupil is the Sanctuary. This is their view. In other ways, antiquity believed that Delphi occupied the center of the earth. From this comes that fable of the two eagles sent out by Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> to explore the middle of the world, which the interpreter of Pindar relates: namely, that one flew from the east and the other from the west, and they met at Pytho <note>Delphi</note>, and in monument of this event, two golden eagles were later dedicated there. Plutarch mentions this embassy of the eagles:

<margin>Plutarch, *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*, at the beginning.</margin>
Ovid also mentions the same:
> *And Delphi, placed in the middle of the world, lacked its protector.*
<note>original Latin: "Et orbe / In medio positi caruerunt præside Delphi."</note>

And the author of a certain lewd poem says:
> *Pallas watches over the Cecropian citadels,*
> *Pythian Delphi is the navel of the world.*

Because they called it the "navel," taking the comparison from the navel of the human body, Varro indeed

<column-break/>

<margin>Jerusalem.</margin>
does not admit this, but he has not entirely persuaded everyone, even if we believe with him that the middle point of the lands was not there, just as the navel is not precisely the center in us. However, that a place there was called the <term>navel</term> <note>original Greek: ὀμφαλὸν, "omphalon"</note> cannot be denied, nor should antiquity be attacked for believing Delphi to be the center of the lands, even if it was not. Livy was also of this opinion, writing thus: <margin>Livy, Decade 4, page 434.</margin> *The Gauls plundered Delphi, once the common oracle of the human race, the navel of the earth.* All who have left descriptions of the Holy Land attest that the city of Jerusalem stood in a higher place than any other in all Palestine. Among the older authors, one may consult Fulcher of Chartres in his *History of Jerusalem, page 397*, describing the expedition of Emperor Henry in A.D. 1059; William of Tyre, *History, Book 8, chapters 1, 2, and 3, page 746*; Wilbrand of Oldenburg, *Itinerary of the Holy Land, page 146*; the Anonymous Florentine *On the Investiture of Bishops, page 858*; and Masius in his *Commentary on Joshua 11, page 212*. Its <term>surrounding by mountains on this side and that</term> <note>original Greek: συμπεριφορὰ ἔνθεν καὶ ἔνθεν ὄρεσιν</note> and its <term>sloping vista</term> <note>original Greek: κατανευν</note> are worthy of sight—namely, the mountains <term>on the outside</term> <note>original Greek: εἰς τὰ ἔξω</note> and the mountains <term>on the inside</term> <note>original Greek: εἰς τὰ ἔσω</note>. It was situated in the hill country, and its foundations were in the mountains: *His foundations are in the holy mountains* <note>original Greek: οἱ θεμέλιοι αὐτὸ ἐν τοῖς ὄρεσι τοῖς ἁγίοις; original Hebrew: יסודתו בהררי קדש</note>, *Psalm 87:1.* This is a glorious proclamation indeed, moved by whose <term>excellence</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπεροχῇ</note> the Prophet Micah exclaims: *What are the high places of Judah? Are they not Jerusalem?* (Micah 1:5). And again: *The mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills.*

<margin>Micah 4:1.</margin>
With these words, the Prophet, full of the Holy Spirit and joy, bursts forth abruptly, describing under the type of a mountain the Church of the New Testament, whose beginning would be in Jerusalem, on Zion, a place which God had chosen above all high places in all Israel. So that this eulogy may be shown as if from its foundation, let us go and walk around, about to survey the mountains. <term>Going around</term> <note>original Greek: Περιιώντες</note> first within the city itself, we see two higher mountains, one of which is <term>Mount Zion</term> in the furthest part of the city toward the south, truly steep and precipitous. King David, aided by divine help, captured this and called it, after his own name, carefully fortified and adorned. For thus the Sacred Scriptures testify: *David took the stronghold of Zion, this is the City of David.* And again: *David dwelt in the stronghold of Zion, and called it the City of David: and he built all around from the Millo and inward,* *2 Samuel 5:7, 9.* Of which we say, in the words of Euripides in *Hecuba, verse 629*:

> *O form of houses, O once-happy homes.*
<note>original Greek: Ω σχῆματ᾽ οἴκων, ὦ ποτ᾽ εὐτυχεῖς δόμοι.</note>

<margin>Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book 15, Chapter 11.</margin>
Besides this citadel of David, Herod—according to Josephus—built two magnificent palaces, one of which he named for Caesar and the other for Agrippa, who was married to Julia, the daughter of Caesar Augustus. And since this mountain exceeds the other mountains of the city in height, it happened that a bridge and certain steps were constructed over the deep valley (once called the Millo and later the <term>Tyropoeon</term> <note>meaning "the Cheesemakers' Valley"</note>) lying between the lower city and Zion, building an easier path for those going onto the mountain and from the mountain into the city. The other mountain in the city, to be extolled with no less praise than the first, was <term>Moriah</term>, on which Abraham once intended to sacrifice his son Isaac at the command of God, *Genesis 22:2.* On this Mount Moriah, the most wise King Solomon [built] the most magnificent Temple to God...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Jerusalem.</margin>
...first built, about which more will be said later. In the region opposite the temple, that is, to the south, were two most lavish palaces: one of which King Solomon built for himself, and the other for his wife, the daughter of Pharaoh, on that same mountain. Near the first of these to the west was his very famous Tribunal or Throne. To the east of the second was the House of the Forest of Lebanon, of which mention is made throughout the <term>Sacred Scriptures</term> <note>original: "S. Pandectis," a term often used for the Bible, comparing it to a complete legal code</note> and in Josephus’s *History*. In the northern part, however, the Maccabees had in their time built a very strongly fortified citadel on a steep and high rock named Baris, which Herod later magnificently adorned and named Antonia after the <term>Triumvir</term> <note>Mark Antony</note>. In this fortress, the Priestly Robe <note>the high priest's vestments</note> was usually kept, and Roman soldiers stood guard, watching to ensure the Jews did not stir up any riots in the temple. Indeed, this Antonia fortress was a most formidable defense, raised up with four towers reaching high into the sky, separated from the Temple only by a bridge, which the besieged sometimes broke down so that an attack could not be made on them from Antonia, as Josephus testifies in Book 14 of *Antiquities*, chapter 8, and Book 15, chapter 14, and frequently in *The Jewish War*. There was also a certain subterranean passage led from the fortress into the temple, through which soldiers could secretly emerge into the temple without the Jews' knowledge. Whether this was that Tower of Strato, which Josephus mentions 

<margin>13. Antiq. 18.</margin>
as a dark passage between the Temple and Antonia, in which Antigonus was killed by his brother’s guards, we leave undecided. Having seen the two primary mountains, a third occurs within the city itself named Mount Acra, which contained the lower city and within it the citadel of the Maccabees (which King Agrippa later held), as well as the palace of Bernice, and those of Helena and Antiochus Epiphanes, besides other public places which we omit for the sake of brevity. On the fourth mountain, named Bezetha, was seen the "New City," fortified, as they say, by a triple wall, in which the large and splendid Palace of Herod was seen, surrounded by its own fortifications (see Josephus, *Jewish War*, Book 6, chapter 6). Famous in this new part of the city were the towers Phasael and Mariamne, built by Herod the Great in memory and honor of his brother and wife, excelling in beauty, height, and solidity. To these should deservedly be joined another tower rising from the middle wall and reaching toward the sky with a double peak, which Herod named Hippicus after his friend. Having surveyed the mountains within the city, three particularly noted mountains occur outside the city, of which frequent mention is made in the Sacred Scriptures. Outside the walls was Mount Calvary or Golgotha, designated for the punishment of criminals, where the Blessed Seed <note>Jesus Christ</note>, numbered among the cursed, died nailed to a cross for the sins of the whole world, according to the witness of the New Testament Scripture. Neighboring this was Mount Gihon, celebrated both for the anointing of Solomon as King and for the victory David achieved on this mountain over his enemies (2 Samuel 5:18, 1 Chronicles 14:12). The last of the celebrated mountains in history, especially the New Testament, was the Mount of Olives, located five <term>stadia</term> <note>about 1,000 yards or 0.6 miles</note> from the city, where our Savior spent several nights before His death; where He also predicted the destruction of the city, not without tears; and where finally, on the fortieth day after His glorious resurrection, while His disciples watched, He returned to His Heavenly

<column-break/>

Father in heaven, where He rules and governs everywhere present in the midst of His enemies. Having viewed the mountains, we descend into the valleys. Among these, the first place is held by the Valley of Jehoshaphat, which was so wide and deep that the eyes of those looking down from the roof of the temple or the towers on the outer wall, which rose to a great height, would grow dim with dizziness. But later this valley was filled with the ruins of walls, houses, and other things and leveled with Mount Moriah, as Brocardus <note>a 13th-century Dominican traveler</note> also mentions:

<margin>*The Valley of Jehoshaphat surrounded the city on the Eastern side, descending below the Mount of Olives; and although it is still deep, it is nevertheless much filled in. For the Romans, as Josephus says, attacking the city from that side, cut down the olives and other trees and, having made mounds from them, filled it. But also later, after the city was captured, Aelius Hadrian ordered the ruins of the citadels and the temple to be thrown into the Brook Kidron, and Mount Moriah to be leveled, and the city to be sprinkled with salt, things which can be seen to this day.*</margin>
It was also called the Valley of Kidron after the brook flowing through it, which, pleasant in its waters and banks, with green trees frequent on both sides, eventually emptied itself into the Dead Sea. Near this was the Valley of Tophet or Gehenna, very well known from Old Testament history because of the crimes and idolatry committed there. From the other side of the city were seen the Valley of Rephaim and also Baalpharasim, so named from the victory which David had won over the Philistines in this valley (2 Samuel 5:18, 1 Chronicles 14:12), near which was Mount Gihon with its spring of the same name, flowing from upper and lower sources into the Brook Kidron. We return into the city to describe the most famous towers and gates of the city of Jerusalem. The wall that enclosed only the northern side of the city is said to have been marked by 90 towers, among which is numbered the Tower of the Ovens, in which a perpetual fire shone for those traveling at night, so they would not easily wander from the path. Near this, in the very corner of this side where the walls turn to the east, was a tower raised to a great height, which was called the Corner Tower. On the eastern side was seen the Tower of Hananeel, mention of which is also made in the books of the Prophets (Jeremiah 31:38). Besides this, on the eastern wall, there was also the Tower of Siloam, by whose collapse in the time of Christ 18 people were crushed (Luke 13:4). In the western corner of the city, where the walls turned to the north, the Psephinus Tower stood out above the rest, octagonal, placed on a steep and high rock, 70 cubits high. It was believed to rise to such a height that on a clear day, Arabia, the sea, and the furthest borders of the Jewish territory could be seen from its peak (compare Josephus, *Jewish War*, Book 6, chapter 2). Thus far we have seen the city, although we are without the thread of Ariadne <note>meaning they are navigating a complex "labyrinth" of history without a perfect guide</note>. Let it suffice to have pointed it out as if with a finger from a distance, and to have ascended enough, though perhaps not abundantly so. Let us now follow the paths that lead us to the GATES,

> Twelve in number, with which they say it shone.

Let us carefully consider the leader and the manner of proceeding. Beginning to the west, he shows the first gate, called by the name of fish: <note>Hebrew: שער הדגים, "Sha'ar Ha-Dagim"</note> the Fish Gate.

> Below the steep peaks of Mount Zion,
> The gate was called by the name of the cold fish.

Hence Jerome, in his commentary on Zephaniah: *They called it the Fish Gate because it led to Lydda <note>original: "Diaspalim," likely a corruption of Diospolis/Lydda</note> and Joppa, and was closer to the sea than all the other ways of Jerusalem.* Indeed, Bede proves that it 
<margin>On Nehemiah.</margin>
faced the West in this way: *The Fish Gate was the first of the gates to the west of Mount Sion; the words of Chronicles seem to agree with this opinion, where it is written concerning Manasseh: He built an outer wall for the city of David to the west of Gihon from the entrance of the Fish Gate as far as Ophel.* Nehemiah records the place that Bede intends, noting those who restored the gate after the return from captivity. *The sons of Hassenaah built the Fish Gate; they laid its beams and set up its doors, its bolts, and its bars.* Through this gate, the disciples walking toward *Emmaus* encountered Christ as their companion and teacher, according to Luke; King Solomon is said to have paved this road, leading both to Emmaus and to Gaza and Joppa, with flint stone for a more convenient path for travelers. Nor did this gate go only by this name in the Sacred Scriptures, but it was also called the *Gate of David*, whence Brocardus writes:
<margin>Description of the Holy Land, p. 316.</margin>
*The first was the Gate of David, which was on the side of Mount Sion toward the west, where there was a corner of the lower city opposite the Tower of David, specifically in the place where two ravines began from one, one turning toward the North and the other toward the East, where a vaulted roof <note>original: "testudo"</note> was also made beyond one valley, through which there was an exit and entrance from that gate.* This gate was also called the Fish Gate, because through it was the way to *Joppa* and other maritime places, from which fish were brought in. It was also called the Gate of the Merchants, *because through it was the road to Bethlehem, Hebron, Gaza, Egypt, and Ethiopia; for it led to the fuller’s field next to Mount Sion, where to the left one went to Hebron, and to the right toward Joppa. And this same road, after a short interval, divided again, for to the left it led into the valley of Rephaim below the fortress of Beth-zur toward Philistia and Gaza, and from there into Egypt and Ethiopia, from which Merchants brought various wares.* From this gate toward the south, a tower of exceeding height and magnitude enclosed the city of David; it was named the *Tower of David* by its founder, which, along with the other fortifications of the city, felt the violent wrath of the victor. However, for those returning from captivity, another tower of that name was built, doubtless upon the foundation of the earlier tower; for Johannes Phocas, an observer of the new tower made of common stone, rightly calls into question whether it was truly the tower of the ancient building when he writes: *Description of Palestine, ch. 14, p. 20. The so-called Tower of David lies in the northern part of the city, and it is a most massive tower; and although this is accepted by some as the Jerusalem of David, to me at least, I think there is reasonable cause for doubt. For by sight, Josephus records that such a tower was made of white stone. Both the Temple and the other two towers built later by Herod in the names of Phasael and Mariamne were such; but this one is seen standing in common stone, and perhaps*
<margin>Description, p. 313.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Jerusalem.</margin>
*the tower now seen is rebuilt upon the most ancient foundations.* Near to this, toward Mount Calvary, was the *Old and Judiciary Gate*, through which the Savior was led to his punishment. Concerning this gate, and the entire Judiciary Way <note>the Via Dolorosa</note>, along which He carried the cross on His shoulders from the Palace of Pontius Pilate all the way to this mountain, it is worth consulting those who have left records of the state of the ancient city, and to look upon the maps representing it, as Christopher Heidman writes in his *Palestine*, p. 31. There was also in this part, even closer to *Golgatha, the Gate of Genaith* <note>the Garden Gate</note>; because it was enclosed on all sides by the walls of Herod’s palace and his royal garden, and thus did not lead into the city by a public way, there was almost no use for it. From that side where a very strong wall closed the northern side of the city, there were three gates in all; one of which was met by someone going from west to east, named the *Gate of the Women’s Towers*: in which region the Romans had their camp; however, where it received its name has not yet been determined by scholars of the Holy Land. Another was the Gate of *Ephraim*, by which they made the journey to Samaria. Finally, in the very corner of this side stood the *Corner Gate* and the *Gate of Benjamin*, by which one goes to Bethel and into the desert. The Holy Scriptures make mention of this gate not in one place but in several distinct ones: *Jeremiah 37:13, 38:7; Ezekiel 48:32; Zechariah 14:10.* Jeremiah mentions in *chapter 20:2* the Upper Gate of Benjamin, which was in the house of Jehovah, which had a prison attached to it, where Jeremiah was placed. That this was distinct from the other gate, the specific words seem to imply. The word <term>עליון</term> <note>Hebrew: Elyon</note> is explained by interpreters as "lofty," so that it is understood as the Lofty Gate, *the high gate* <note>original German: "das hohe Thor"</note>, mention of which 
<margin>2 Chronicles 23:20.</margin>
is made *which was in the house of Jehovah, that is, in the enclosures or building that belonged to the temple itself.* For this place should not be understood as the first building of the people’s court, but as the additions joined to the people’s court after the time of Solomon. From the Eastern part of the city, one encountered the *Dung Gate*, so called because a certain stream, rising from the old pool that was in the marketplace, carried the filth of the city, washed away by rainwater, through this gate into the brook Kidron. Regarding this Gate, one may read Nehemiah *chapter 2:13, 3:13-14.* Further to the south, one reached the *Gate of the Valley* or *Valley Gate*, which leads into the Valley of Jehoshaphat, both because it led there and because the livestock to be sacrificed in the temple were driven through this gate into the livestock market near this gate. Concerning this, let us hear Brocardus: *From the area of the temple toward the North is the Valley Gate, which leads into the Valley of Jehoshaphat, and this is also called the Sheep Gate, because through it were introduced the flocks to be sacrificed in the temple.* 
<margin>Description of the Holy Land, p. 314.</margin>
To those entering the Valley Gate or Sheep Gate, there appears on the left the *Probatica Pool* <note>the Sheep Pool</note>, in which the Nethinim <note>temple servants</note> washed the sacrificial victims, which they handed over to the Priests to be offered in the Temple; and this is shown to have had five porches, in which the sick lay, waiting for the moving of the water. To the right, however, is shown another *Great Pool*, which was called the *Inner Pool made by Hezekiah; for by blocking the upper spring of the waters of Gihon, he diverted its waters and directed them toward the west of the city of David, and cutting through the rock with iron, he introduced the waters through the middle of the city into the Valley.*

Indeed, the spring of the waters of Gihon, which was not far from the fuller's field, he channeled into the upper pool which is above the swimming pool of Siloam <note>original: "Silohe"</note>. King Ahaz <note>original: "Achaz"</note> began this work, but he did not complete it. Isaiah speaks of this pool and this spring and its location: *Go out to the end of the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the fuller's field.* It is called the "Upper Pool" in relation to the swimming pool of Siloam, which, being lower, received the waters from the spring of Siloam. And lest you be mistaken about these pools, note that the first and most important pool in Jerusalem was the Sheep Pool <note>original: "Piscina probatica"</note>, having two porticos, which Solomon built for the service of the Temple. The second was next to it toward the North, called the "Inner Pool," which Hezekiah <note>original: "Ezechias"</note> made. The third was the swimming pool of Siloam, which was beneath the Mount of Olives and beneath Mount Zion near the field of Aceldama <note>original: "Hakeldemah"</note>; it held water from the spring of Siloam, which Hezekiah also constructed. The fourth was the Upper Pool, which Hezekiah also made; and these were not lined with stone <note>original: "incrustatæ"</note> as some seem to think, since the city itself was higher than the source from which this pool drew its waters, namely from the spring of Siloam and the lower spring of the waters of Gihon. Both pools are at the foot of Mount Zion. These pools also receive water from the lower Gihon spring, which rises beneath the Fuller’s Field.
