and again, the *Sixth Gate* faced South and was placed next to the brook Kidron <note>original: "Cedron"</note>; it was called the Sheep Gate <note>original: "porta Gregis"</note> because through it the flocks to be sacrificed were led into the temple, and the Sheep Pool was not far from it. It was also called the Valley Gate, because the road through it led into the Valley of Jehoshaphat; and the Dragon Fountain Gate, named so after that spring. The Ninth Gate, the Golden Gate, was placed over the brook Kidron and faced South; it was so named because it shone with overlaid gold. This was more a gate of the Temple than of the City, as it provided a shortcut to the Mount of Olives. Through this gate the Savior of the world, riding on a young donkey, entered the city and the temple in a solemn and hitherto unusual procession for Him, accompanied by His disciples and a shouting crowd of people, a few days before His death (Matthew 21:7). The tenth was called the Gate of the Fountain or of the Waters, obtaining this name because it led to the pool and spring of Siloam. It was also called the Horse Gate, because horses were led through it to be watered. This was located between Mount Zion and Mount Moriah, directly facing the Mello Valley (also called the Tyropoeon), and it led most conveniently via a bridge built across the Kidron to the Mount of Olives; it was through this gate that the Jews, having captured CHRIST in the garden, led Him back into the city at night. Toward the South was the King's Garden Gate, providing entrance at least into the City of David or the Royal Palace; and the gate of the High Priest's Palace, providing an exit from that palace alone into the Valley of Gihon. And these were the twelve gates that stood open for those entering and exiting. Regarding the Gates of the Temple, that one stood out which, because of its magnificence, was named "The Beautiful Gate" <note>original: "Speciosa"</note>; at which Peter and John,

<column-break/>

by a word, healed a man lame from the day of his birth (Acts 3:2 and following). This gate was 30 cubits high and was entirely overlaid with Corinthian bronze, which was considered more precious than gold. We do not wish to add more regarding the Temple. And such was the holy city, which God had chosen for Himself and His name as a special seat out of all the cities of the earth; many brilliant praises and excellent privileges of it exist throughout the sacred writings. However, whatever we have said so far about the city of Jerusalem, there is no city—if we survey Bethlehem—to which we attribute more, even by the majesty and example of that divine oracle in which Bethlehem is preferred over so many thousands of cities of Judah and even over the Metropolis itself, because of the "coming forth" of Him whose "origins are from eternity." Who would not prefer this homeland of our Savior to Rome, or Susa, or even Jerusalem? Truly, Jerusalem underwent various shifts of fortune; after the death of Solomon, it was exposed to the violence of the Egyptians, Syrians, and Israelites because of its crimes and idolatry. It was, however, liberated several times, as that memorable slaughter of Sennacherib before Jerusalem testifies. From this, the Jews, attributing this to their own strength, boasted of their Jerusalem what the Trojans said of their Troy: that their city was *an unconquerable city* <note>original: "ἀπορθήτων πόλιν"</note> (Euripides, *Hecuba*, line 894), and that they themselves were invincible. Thus the Jews were glorifying themselves when Nebuchadnezzar, having temporarily lifted the siege to meet Pharaoh, turned him to flight and returned to the siege of Jerusalem. There was no beauty left in Jerusalem, all glory was gone, as the Prophet Jeremiah mournfully deplores in Lamentations <note>original: "thren."</note> chapter 1, verse 6: *From the daughter of Zion all her beauty has departed.* On this, Ratbertus <note>likely Paschasius Radbertus, a 9th-century theologian</note> says: *Jerusalem, besieged from without, had lost all the grace of its beauty and pleasantness; within, with its treasures plundered, its temple and priesthood destroyed, and suffering from famine and pestilence, it was sustained by no one’s help; for its princes and rulers, their strength dissolved—as Moses had foretold in his curses—were meditating in fearful sluggishness not on defense, but on flight.* For it had been so determined that Jerusalem should fall into the power of Nebuchadnezzar, as Jeremiah had often predicted. Thus Nebuchadnezzar, besieging the city with a powerful army, finally subdued it after years and took it by storm. Regarding this, Rhodomannus <note>Lorenz Rhodomann, a 16th-century humanist</note> writes:

> Subdued by war and hunger, he beheld the city,
> A city dear to the Gods, and revered by mortals;
> Whose wealth the soldier then plundered, carrying all away.
> The spear mowed down the men, the fiery torch devoured the houses,
> And with its treasures the temple perished, though filled with sacred things,
> The power of Vulcan’s fire and the enemy’s violence snatched away the gifts;
> Thus things varied and precious were lost, nor did God repel the ruin.

<margin>Jerusalem.</margin>
After the Babylonian exile, the city began to be restored, as witnessed by the History of the Maccabees and by Josephus, up until its final <term>utter destruction</term> <note>original Greek: "πανωλεθρίᾳ"</note>. For Jerusalem, which was once the <term>holy city</term> <note>original Greek: "πόλις ἁγία"</note>, became in the time of Christ the <term>Holy City</term> <note>original Hebrew: "עיר הקדש" (Ir Ha-Kodesh)</note> only in name; as seen in *Ezekiel 22:2*, due to a filth of the worst morals flooding the city and a "wild" religion under the hypocritical sect of the Pharisees, whose future slaughter Christ followed with his own tears. And so the City, once the princess among cities, could not—due to that ingratitude toward God's grace—but be valued at a cheap price, lose its happiness, and become the dregs of cities. Great men had fallen into great calamities after violating some Divinity, which gave rise to the proverb: <term>The evils of the Magnesians</term> <note>original Greek: "Μαγνήτων κακά" - a phrase used to describe total ruin</note>. Strabo records that these people flourished in wealth but were utterly overthrown by the Trerians, a Cimmerian tribe; he also mentions that this proverb was taken from Archilochus. Hence Theognis says in verse 603:

<margin>v. 603.</margin>
> <term>Arrogance destroyed the Magnesians,</term> <note>original Greek: "Μάγνητας ἀπώλεσεν ἔργα καλήβρεις"</note>
> <term>Such as now possesses this holy city.</term> <note>original Greek: "Οἵα τὰ νῦν ἱερὰν τήνδε πόλιν κατέχει"</note>

One might best attribute these verses to the city of Jerusalem, which, by violating the Divine Power, brought horrendous evils upon itself, so much so that the <term>Evils of the Jerusalemites</term> <note>original: "Ἱεροσολυμιτῶν κακά"</note> could be said of great misfortunes even more than those of the Magnesians. For Christ, who alone could penetrate the depths of the future, had predicted the fates of that most ungrateful city. The rays of those fates were seen not long before the actual demolition when, before it was besieged by Titus, the Sicarii <note>a splinter group of Jewish zealots known for using hidden daggers</note> secretly slaughtered whomever they pleased. Then the Zealots (as Josephus calls them) took control; their leaders, fighting for supremacy in both Galilee and Judea, tore the people into factions, tasted mutual slaughter, and forced them to obey wicked orders until Titus arrived. He shut them all within the Metropolis and, on the same day that Nebuchadnezzar had once captured it, he subjected it to fire (compare Eberus's *Calendar, pp. 280, 283*). According to Josephus (*The Jewish War, Book 7, Ch. 10*), Titus was very anxious to preserve the Temple from destruction, but he desired to save it in vain, for God did not consent. He could not prevent any soldier from throwing in fire against his will to destroy it—yet he followed its overturning with copious tears, just as Scipio did at Carthage. After the city was thus overturned and the remnants reduced to perpetual slavery, Vespasian, the Triumphant Conqueror of Judea, ordered a coin to be struck as a sign of the subdued nation with this inscription: <term>JUDAEA CAPTA</term> <note>Latin: "Judaea Captured"</note>. A woman was added, sitting at the roots of a palm tree, for victory was signified by palms, as the conquered brought palms to the victor. He also struck a coin with the inscription: <term>TRIUMPH OVER THE JEWS</term> <note>original Latin: "TRIUMPHUS DE JUDÆIS"</note>, as recorded by Jacobus de Strada (*Epitome of Antiquities, p. 50*). Hence, an inscription for Titus on account of the destruction of Jerusalem is read in Smetius (*folio 154 a, number 5*):

Jerusalem is now truly a heap of ash, she who was before the garden of the world; she who was once the <term>ornament of the world</term> <note>original Greek: "κόσμου κόσμος"</note> has now become the sewer of the world. Behold, O Jews, behold, I pray, that horrendous judgment of God upon your once-flourishing city, your capital; count the many years of your exile, look into yourselves, and acknowledge the vengeance of Jehovah. Let these things make you wiser; learn piety having been warned, and do not despise the Messiah, lest an "Iliad of woes" <note>a proverbial term for a massive series of disasters</note> finally overwhelm you in the future age. This is, therefore, the city of greatest vicissitudes, for having been occupied twenty-three times by various kings or leaders, she often rose from her ashes, and still shows some shadow of her former greatness. For in vain did Constantine the Great and other subsequent Christians, and even the Jews under the influence of Julian the Apostate, attempt to rebuild the city or the temple. There remains, and still is, a shrine of the Saracens, even if they were driven out from there so many times by the Christians; and the Sultan, a worshipper of Muhammad, lives there, as Alvarus Pelagius writes in his own time (*The Lament of the Church, Book 1, Ch. 67, fol. 90*). And so the words of our Savior remain firm and protected regarding the perpetual desolation of this city. To be sure, modern-day Jerusalem is inhabited, built in another location, by both Turks and Jews—though the Jews are not permitted to enter Mount Moriah (once dedicated to Solomon's Temple) under penalty of death—as well as by Christians of various nations on account of the tomb of Christ our Savior. Concerning this, Brocardus says: <margin>* Church T. 5, p. 315.</margin> *We grant the primacy to the Lord’s Sepulchre. This church is round and has a round opening in the middle, under which the Lord’s tomb stands in the open air, with no roof covering. The cave containing the Lord’s tomb is several feet long, and although some parts are covered in marble, the inside is still seen bare, just as it was at the time of the Passion. The door leading into this cave is placed on the East and is very small. When you enter the cave, the tomb is placed to the right, that is, against the northern wall of the cave, made of grey-colored marble, being eight feet long as is the cave itself; there is no celestial light in that crypt, but several lit lamps make it bright. In front of the cave of the Lord’s tomb is another crypt of the same size and shape, separated from the first only by an intermediate wall, and one descends to this one first, then through the door of the intermediate wall one comes into the cave of the Lord’s tomb.* For the rest, what Statius sang concerning Virgil, we might say more regarding the imitation of the prophecies of the Prophet Ezekiel, his building of the city with the Temple, and the division of the holy land:

This is shown by the Prophet in *chapter* 45 at the beginning, and in *chapter* 47 from verse 13 to 30, and in *chapter* 48. In this division—before any portion was granted to any of the tribes—a sufficiently large portion from the middle of the land, extending through the entire length of the territory and measuring twenty-five thousand cubits wide, is designated as a holy offering to the Lord. From this offering, a *sacred central square* <note>original Latin: "medium quadratum sanctum"</note> of twenty-five thousand cubits is granted to the Priests and the Temple, along with the Levites and the city. <margin>Rites of Adonis.</margin>
Frequent in the Sacred Books <note>original Latin: "S. Pandectis" - referring to the Bible as a complete body of divine law</note> are the complaints regarding the Synagogue of the idolatrous Israelites, loosening the spiritual bond of marriage and its foul harlotry. The voice of Isaiah in chapter 1, verse 21, says: *How has the faithful city become a harlot?* Jeremiah testifies in chapter 3:1–3 that God gave a bill of divorce to Israel—once a beloved bride—on account of her idolatry, describing her spiritual fornication: *You had a harlot’s forehead; you refused to blush.* An abominable image of these crimes is shown to the Prophet Ezekiel, and the things that are to come are revealed by the Lord, not without the splendor of divine glory. Specifically, the Prophet seemed to be snatched up by the hair <note>original Latin: "vertice suspenso" - literally "suspended by the crown of the head"</note> through the void from Chaldea to Jerusalem and introduced into the temple. There, among other shameful acts, an image of *Baal* was being worshipped by the townspeople, the ancestral rites having been driven out. Then, there were the images of every kind of animal, which stood depicted everywhere on the walls; Jaazaniah the Priest, son of Shaphan, and seventy of the elders stood around them, worshipping with

<column-break/>

burning incense. Then the Hebrew women, with the solemn wailing and shrieking of the Egyptians, were lamenting Tammuz, or Adonis, the delight of Venus. Finally, about twenty-five men, with their backs turned toward the temple, were adorning the rising Sun, or *Mithra* <note>Mithra was the Persian god of light and the sun</note>, with worship and honor in the Persian manner. Since all these things were done to offend and provoke God with such immense sacrilege, He then foretold that He, in turn stirred by fury and wrath, would spare no one. What does "Tammuz" mean? What is this word? What difficulty <note>original Latin: "scrupi" - literally a sharp stone or grit, metaphorically a source of unease or a puzzle</note> does it involve? Jerome interprets it as Adonis, that youth desperately loved by Venus and honored with solemn mourning. *The one whom we* (he writes on page 402) *have interpreted as Adonis, both the Hebrew and Syrian language call Tammuz; whence, because according to the myths of the nations, in the month of June, the lover of Venus and a most beautiful youth was killed and is said to have lived again afterwards, they call that same month of June by the same name, and they celebrate an anniversary solemnity for him, in which he is mourned by women as if dead, and afterwards, reviving, he is sung of and praised.* It is said that Adonis was the son of Cinyras, King of the Cyprians, whom Venus loved excessively for his exceptional beauty, and whom, when he died from a boar's bite, she mourned with most abundant tears. Ovid and Theocritus treat this myth at length. From these, John of Salisbury writes: *Venus mourns Adonis, killed by the teeth of a boar, always having commerce with the hunt.* Add to these Apollodorus, *book 3, page 194: "Adonis, while still a boy, was killed by a boar during a hunt due to the anger of Artemis."* <note>original Greek provided in the text</note> In honor of Venus, women then instituted this mourning annually; Jerome conjectures that the Hebrew women imitated them with similar folly. Since the explanation of "Tammuz" was uncertain, and the Greek customs were well-established, the Translator preferred to embrace the usage regarding Adonis rather than retain the Hebrew word. Hence he wishes the Tammuz of the *Easterners* to be similar to Adonis, *in the Greek language* <note>original Greek: "κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα φωνήν"</note>. Procopius feels no differently, where, bringing forward this passage in a long-winded tale, he adds after *Thammuz, "which is Adonis."* <note>original Greek: "ὅπερ ἐστὶ τὸν Ἄδωνιν"</note> It was granted to the memory of Venus that the festive solemnity of the Adonia should be acted out by almost all peoples. Just as in Phrygia, Cybele and her loved one Attis were worshipped, so elsewhere were Venus and her lover Adonis. *Servius* says: *Virbius is a deity joined to Diana, as Attis is to the mother of the Gods, Erichthonius to Minerva, and Adonis to Venus.* The female worshippers of Venus mourned the dead Adonis on one day with loud wailing and the mournful sound of flutes; on the other day, they received him with acclamations as if he were restored to life. He was also called *Gingras* in the language of the Phoenicians. *Pollux* 4.10: *"The language of the Phoenicians calls Adonis 'Gingras,' and the flute is named after him."* <note>original Greek provided in the text</note> And *Athenaeus*, following Democlides, handed down that he was called *Gingras* by the Phoenicians: *And the flutes* which they used were called by the same people *gingroi* from the mourning for Adonis, because flutes of that kind *sounded sharp and moaning* <note>original Greek: "ὀξὺ καὶ γοερὸν ἐφθέγγοντο"</note>, and for that reason were used for lamentation. Bion of Smyrna composed a most sweet Epitaph of Adonis, which, along with the Idylls of Moschus the Sicilian, for the benefit of literature, Adol-

### ->The Rites of Adonis<-

<margin>The Rites of Adonis.</margin>
Adolphus Mekerchus, in Bruges, Flanders, at the press of Hubert Goltzius. In this work, in the same manner as in *Theocritus* in the *Adoniazusae* <note>original: "Adoniazusis," a poem describing women at an Adonis festival</note>, where shorn-haired "Loves" <note>cupids or personifications of desire</note> mourn tender Adonis with groaning. <margin>On the Syrian Goddess</margin> Lucian <note>original Greek: τύπτονται ἐκάστε ἔτε@ καὶ θρηνέυσι, καὶ τὰ ὄργια ἐπιτελέυσι</note>: "They beat themselves every year and lament, and perform the sacred rites." Ptolemy, concerning the Easterners who fall under the northern triangle <note>original Greek: καὶ μυςήριά τινα μὴ θρηνῶν ἀποδιδόντες αὐτοῖς</note>: "and rendering certain mysteries to them with mourning." Similarly, examples of mourning are found in the rites of Leucothea in *Aristotle's Rhetoric, Book 2*. <margin>Plutarch, Life of Camillus.</margin> *Plutarch, Life of Camillus;* in the Rites of Hyacinth in *Ovid's Metamorphoses;* <margin>On the Aeneid, Book 4, line 511.</margin> and *Athenaeus*, Book 4. In the rites of Isis, *Servius* and *Macrobius* write, where the latter says: *It is no secret that Osiris is nothing other than the Sun; nor is Isis anything other than the earth or the nature of things: and the same logic applies to Adonis and Attis.* Regarding Attis, he said that Cybele had <margin>Book 3.</margin> loved him, according to Strabo, where he records that the Phrygians testified to their worship through wailing, laments, and other signs of honor, and that this was done <margin>On the Aeneid, Book 9</margin> annually; Servius attests to this with these words: *So that a perpetual memory of Attis might remain, the Great Mother instituted that he be mourned annually in her rites.* In ancient times, they also worshipped Diana of the Crossroads <note>Diana Trivia</note> in the <margin>On Eclogue 3.</margin> crossroads with howling. On this, Servius says: *It was the custom that the country folk would howl through the crossroads and three-way paths, and sing a certain mournful song in honor of Diana, in imitation of Ceres, who was searching for the abducted Proserpina at the crossroads.* Luther, in his version, retained the name "Thammuz," to which he added this marginal note:
<margin>On the Trifles of Courtiers, p. 19.</margin>
> Thammuz is said to be the idol Adonis, of whom the poets and heathens have written much, and who was Lady Venus's lover; therefore the women lament him. It means Bacchus the wine-god, just as among us we have Saint Urban <note>St. Urban of Langres, the patron saint of vine-dressers</note>.

Luther plausibly understands this as Bacchus, whom they placed over the vines, just as a later age did with *Saint Urban*, concerning whom see <margin>History of Images, Book 3, ch. 19.</margin> Molanus; from this it would appear that those rites of Bacchus were celebrated first and foremost in the East by women. To understand this more accurately, see *Daniel Heinsius, Sacred Exercises on Nonnus, ch. 1*, so you may know that not so much the worship, but the names of the cults, having taken their beginnings in the East, were finally carried to neighboring nations. Heinsius himself testifies concerning the name of Adonis, derived from *Adon* <note>Hebrew: "Lord"</note>. Hesychius (p. 21) <margin>Sacred Exercises on the New Testament, Matthew 26:7, p. 79.</margin> says: *Adonis is called "the gazed-upon one" <note>original Greek: τὸν θεατόν</note> by the Phoenicians,* which very closely approaches the Hebrew. For the Byblian Venus was of great value to the Phoenicians. No one has handed this down more learnedly and explicitly than Lucian, who, being a Syrian by nation, inquired into everything from the priests themselves and others. The Assyrian Juno is called by him "The Syrian Goddess" by way of excellence, about whom he wrote an erudite dissertation. For here, when about to explain the rites of Adonis among the people of Byblos, he narrates that to represent the grief of Venus over Adonis (who was killed by a boar), they bloodied themselves with flagellation, and the women performed parentalia <note>funeral rites</note> for him because of his head. *I saw,* he says, *at Byblos a great temple of the Byblian Aphrodite, in which they perform the rites for Adonis.* <margin>On the Aeneid, Book 9</margin> And Ammianus Marcellinus says in Book 19: *The female worshippers of Venus are often seen weeping in the solemn rites of Adonis.* Compare *Hottinger, Smegma Orientale, p. 179.* Certainly they say that Osiris (whom we shall now link to Adonis) <margin>Book 4.</margin> is Dionysus, and all the Egyptians worship him in the same way, as witnessed by Herodotus in *Euterpe*. Hence many interpreters refer the Tammuz-rites to the rites of Osiris,

<column-break/>

<margin>The Rites of Adonis.</margin>
which we read were performed annually with similar mourning. Maternus Firmicus says: *This is the sum of the Isiac mystery. In the inner shrines they have a buried idol of Osiris.* <margin>Julius Firmicus, Book on the Error of Profane Religions.</margin> They lament this with annual wailings and shave their heads. Plutarch also teaches that the Egyptians mourned the lost Osiris every year; he proves in the same place that the Bacchus of the Greeks is the Osiris of the Egyptians, and Vossius approves of this. According to the same <margin>The same Plutarch p. 69. 72. 2. Idolatry 14. P. 377.</margin> Plutarch (Table Talk, Book 4, ch. 5), Adonis is Bacchus. We know that the name of both Isis and Osiris was one, though appearing in multiform <margin>Idolatry 74</margin> appearance, with varying ritual and a manifold name. This explanation regarding Osiris is made more favorable by the fact that many Egyptians and Egyptian-Jews were in Judea at that time; and Osiris himself was called *Ammuz* by the Egyptians, which very closely approaches the name Tammuz, from which Plutarch says the name of Jupiter Ammon was corruptly derived. And even in this sense, the insightful interpreters Junius and Tremellius explain it, based on Eusebius and others: *The word Ammuz,* they say among other things, *which Herodotus and Plutarch use, we do not doubt is derived from a corrupted 'Tammuz,' the word having a double meaning. First, among the Egyptians, it signifies 'hidden' and 'occult,' as Manetho of Sebennytos interprets in Plutarch. For this reason, his rites were secret. Secondly, it signifies the fourth month, with the solemn feast for Tammuz or Osiris, who was sought after by the priests, the ministers of Isis, with the greatest wailing and lamentation.* These interpreters are followed, as is his custom, by *Johannes Piscator*, who in his version retains "Tammuz" and understands by that name Osiris. What the common people of the Egyptians attributed to Osiris (or Ammuz), the Hebrews to Tammuz, the Babylonians and Syrians to Salambo—that is what the ancient Phoenicians, and from them the Greeks and Romans, attributed to the Threnodes <note>mourning songs or mourners</note> of Adonis. From these—the Syrians and Phoenicians, or even the Egyptians—it is easily established that other Jews accepted the *Adoniasmus* <note>the ritual mourning for Adonis</note> or the rite of solemn lamentation over Adonis, though under a different name. This is especially so when those who teach that these rites stem from an innate religion lead the way. Let *Martianus Capella* lead, who in *Book 2 of the Marriage of Philology* says that the Sun, Serapis, Mithras, Dis, Attis, Ammon, and Adonis are all the same. *Macrobius* explains the same in Book 21: that the same thing was celebrated under different names, and hence to him Osiris is the same as the Phoenician Adonis and the Phrygian Attis. Indeed, different things were worshipped under one name. Thus, under the name of *Osiris* came the Sun and the *Nile*. Indeed, the order of rites and names is very often swapped, just as with *Bacchus*, and the rites of ancient memory undergo various changes through places, times, and persons. This error of cults happens in many cases, just as times themselves are fleeting, especially when empires are overturned and changed. Thus, today there are rites in the East that existed long ago when the world was barely born, and others that are no more. Nor is it unusual for gods to stand before us under various names in various nations with a single cult. Take an illustrious example here: The rites accustomed to be performed for Adonis by the Greeks, and for Tammuz by the Jews, seem to be the same as those called "Salambo" by the Syrians. The Syrian cult of Salambo, very similar to Adonis, reached the Europeans by the authority of Heliogabalus, as Satan made sport of these things. For the Syrians [lamented] Salambo with every lamentation and tossing...

<meta>This page continues the scholarly investigation into the identity of the idol Tammuz, further linking him to the Greek Adonis. The author transition from historical/mythological identification to the physical orientation of worship described in Ezekiel 8:16, contrasting Jewish, Pagan, and Christian practices of facing East or West.</meta>

<margin>The Rites of Adonis.</margin>
The historian Lampridius, in his *Life of Elagabalus* <note>original: "Heliogabali," the Roman emperor known for bringing Eastern sun-worship to Rome</note>, testifies that Elagabalus introduced this cult to the Romans. This is even more clearly established by Julius Firmicus, who writes in chapter 10 of his book *On the Error of Profane Religions*: *In most cities of the East—though this evil also crossed over to us by the authority of Elagabalus—Adonis is mourned as the husband of Venus, and his killer and his wound are displayed.* A plausible conjecture by Thomas Reinesius, in his *Examination of Lusitanian Inscriptions regarding the God Endovellicus*, suggests that the name Salambô <note>original: "Σαλαμβὼ"</note>, as Hesychius calls it, or Salambus, is not at odds with the Arabic *Al Tammuz*. He suggests that the name of the deity *Salammûs* or *Salambas* emerged from this, having been received by the Greeks and Latins from Easterners with an added letter "S." He asserts without hesitation that these names—Salamba, Salambûs, or Salammûs (due to the linguistic similarity between the labial sounds 'b' and 'm')—and *Thammuz* (which the Arabic version of Ezekiel renders as *Al Tammuz*) are the same, one being a distortion of the other. Indeed, if the initial "S" is removed, the latter reveals itself most clearly. Nor is the addition of the letter "S" unusual; it is proven by many examples which demonstrate that scholar's singular skill in etymologies. John Selden (in *Syntagma 2, chapter 10*) and Gerard Vossius (in *On Idolatry, Book 2, chapter 4*) demonstrate how closely the deities Adonis and Tammuz agree with one another. Petrus Castellanus also learnedly explains the ritual of the Adonian rites from Greek authors in his *Treatise on Greek Festivals*. However, the accounts found in Rabbinic records <note>historical Jewish commentaries</note> concerning Tammuz—claiming he was a man among the Prophets whose idol was mourned at the beginning of the first month of Tammuz after his death—are no more true than the claim that *Succoth Benoth* (mentioned in 2 Kings 17) was an image of a hen with her chicks, which the Rabbis foolishly imagine. The Rabbis are almost entirely ignorant of this unexamined branch of learning <note>original Greek: "ἀνεπισκεψίας παιδείας," referring to the critical study of history and mythology</note> which investigates the antiquities of the Gentiles, as we have shown elsewhere through examples of their trifles. But what smells like garlic to everyone else smells like musk to these [Rabbinic] gates <note>A metaphor suggesting that what others find offensive or false, these writers find pleasant or true</note>. These "Judaizers" laugh at the fables of the Gentiles, yet they do not see the bag of faults hanging on their own backs <note>A reference to Aesop's fable where people see others' faults but not their own</note.

### Ezekiel VIII. v. 16.

->They bowed down eastward to the sun.<-
<note>original Hebrew: משתחויתם קדמה לשמש</note>
->They worship toward the east to the sun.<-
<note>original Greek: Προσκυνοῦσι κατὰ ἀνατολὰς τῷ ἡλίῳ.</note>
->*They were worshipping at the rising of the sun.*<-
<note>original Latin: *Adorabant ad ortum solis.*</note>

<margin>The custom of praying toward the east.</margin>
It was an ancient superstition of the Gentiles to turn themselves toward the east during prayer, and to frequent and solemnly celebrate their superstitious pagan cults at the rising of the sun. We have a clear example of this here among the Jews, who were conforming themselves to the Pagans in this business of superstition. Thus the Lord showed this abomination of the House of Israel to the Prophet, who, caught up in the spirit from Babylon to Jerusalem, saw the abominations and idolatries that the Jews were then committing in the Temple of the Lord. From the institution of divine law, it is certain that the Hebrew nation turned toward the west while praying; they did this to show that they were not worshipping the rising sun, but the Lord of the sun, as Anastasius of Nicaea says in his 18th question on the Scriptures. For this reason, they placed their altars at the setting of the sun during the construction of the Tabernacle and later the Temple, as can be read in the layout and topography of the Tabernacle in Exodus chapters 25, 26, 27, 36, and 40.

<column-break/>

Likewise, the delineation, form, and situation of the Temple can be understood from 1 Kings, chapter 6. The Sanctuary faced the west, and therefore they necessarily prayed toward the west. God, the Best and Greatest, seems to have done this for that reason: lest, if they worshipped facing the east, they might appear to be venerating the sun itself. Rabbi Moses Ben Maimon (called Rambam from his initials) explicitly discusses this in his work *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "More Hanebuchim"</note>; these are his words: *Our Rabbis in the Gemara expressly teach (as translated by Buxtorf) that Abraham our Father designated the west as the location for the Holy of Holies. The reason for this, in my judgment, is that since the common superstition of that time was to worship the sun and hold it as God, all men undoubtedly turned toward the east. Therefore, the Patriarch Abraham turned toward the west on Mount Moriah (that is, in the sanctuary), so that he would turn his back to the sun.* For are you unaware of what the Israelites did when they apostatized and declined into those ancient errors? Their descendants (says the Prophet) turned their backs to the Temple of God and their faces toward the east, and they bowed themselves to the rising sun, or toward the east to the sun itself. This is an observation worthy of great wonder and note.

It is clear from many writers that the Romans and other nations were accustomed to perform their purifications <note>original Greek: "καθάρματα"</note>, washings, expiations, prayers, and similar sacred rites with their faces turned toward the rising sun. King Numa, the High Priest of Rome, commanded his subordinates to offer their short prayers toward the rising sun, as ancient writers like Plutarch (in his *Life of Numa*), Juvenal (in *Satire 6*), and Apuleius (in books 1 and 2) testify. They worshipped facing the rising of the great sun, according to Herodotus, book 1. Vitruvius, in book 4 on architecture, chapters 5 and 8, dealing with the structure of sacred buildings, says: *The statues placed in the inner chambers ought to face the western region of the sky, and the altars toward the East, so that those who approach the altar to immolate or perform sacred rites may look toward the Eastern part of the sky and the statues themselves may appear to behold the supplicants and sacrificers as they rise. Indeed, even before Vitruvius, Clement of Alexandria declares this was in use (Stromata, book 7), testifying that the most ancient temples faced the west so that those standing with their faces toward the images might be turned toward the East.* With these accounts agrees what Hyginus Augustus says in *On Establishing Boundaries* near the beginning: *Boundaries are directed according to ancient custom, which is why not every measurement of fields faces East rather than West. Facing East like a sacred building: for the ancient architects correctly wrote that Temples should face the East; later it was decided to turn all religious worship to that part of the sky from which the earth is illuminated.* Boundaries are constructed in the same way. Virgil, in the 12th book of the *Aeneid*:

->*They, turning their eyes toward the rising Sun,*<-
->*Offer the salted grain from their hands.*<-

The ancient Christians also prayed toward the east, unlike the Jews, toward their own Sun—the Sun of Righteousness. They even constructed their Temples in such a layout that the part in which the priests were situated, which they call the choir, always faced the East. Because of this, as Tertullian writes in his *Apology*, the Pagans thought that Christians worshipped the Sun,

### Ezekiel 21:21, 22, 23

<note>original: Hebrew text of Ezekiel 21:21-23</note>
For the King of Babylon stood at the fork of the road, at the head of the two ways, to practice divination: he shook the arrows, he consulted the idols, he looked at the liver. 
At his right hand was the divination for Jerusalem: to set up battering rams, to open the mouth for slaughter, to lift up the voice with shouting, to set battering rams against the gates, to cast up a mound, and to build a siege wall.
And it shall be to them as a false divination in their eyes, to those who have sworn oaths; but he will call to mind their iniquity, that they may be taken.

<note>original: Greek (Septuagint) text of Ezekiel 21:21-23</note>
Because the King of Babylon shall stand on the ancient road, at the head of the two ways, to practice divination, to shake the rod, and to ask of the carved images, and to look at the liver. 
On his right hand the divination was against Jerusalem: to cast a rampart, and to open the mouth in a cry, to lift up the voice with a shout, to cast a rampart against its gates, to cast up a mound, and to build siege engines. 
And he himself is to them as one practicing divination before them; and he himself, calling to mind their injustice, shall bring it to remembrance.

<margin>
Divinations and Sorcery.
</margin>
If a city and its Republic turn toward great glory and benefit when administered by the wisest laws, and if public safety is preserved by legitimate means—removing everything that seems detrimental to its future as opportunely and timely as possible—then truly greater will be the glory and fame of the Church. For the Church is the City of God, which God himself founded; he wrote the laws for governing her, and he protects and defends her as the Bride, friend, and Sister of his Son <note>Song of Solomon 2:7, 10; 4:12; 5:1</note> and preserves her as his own body <note>Ephesians 2:19</note>. For in adorning, gathering, and preserving his chosen people for himself, God has employed innumerable means and used various methods from the first days of the world until now. Long ago, he raised up Prophets in the midst of his people, who are called <term>Nebiim <gloss>prophets</gloss></term>, either from the word <term>Naba <gloss>he prophesied</gloss></term>; or from the word <term>Bo <gloss>he came</gloss></term>, because a prophet deals with things to come; or from <term>Bin <gloss>he understood</gloss></term>, because he understands future things which God reveals and manifests to him from heaven. For this reason, in ancient times, a Prophet was called a <term>Ro'eh <gloss>seer</gloss></term>, as is evident from 1 Samuel 9:9, because they are said to see into heaven. John of Damascus <note>a 7th-century monk and scholar</note> refers to this when he calls Prophets <term>hypsanophoitas <gloss>those who walk through the heavens</gloss></term>, and Gregory of Nazianzus calls them <term>theoglossous <gloss>speaking with the tongue of God</gloss></term> and <term>pneumati theio keknēmenous <gloss>moved by the divine spirit</gloss></term>; whence also Dio-

<column-break/>

nysius the Areopagite <note>a Christian theologian of the late 5th century</note> calls them the expositors of <term>tēs hieras theoparadotōn nomothetas <gloss>the laws divinely handed down</gloss></term>. Indeed, God suggested his will to the Prophets not in one single way, but, as Saint Paul records: <note>original: Greek quote from Hebrews 1:1</note> *In many parts and in many ways, God spoke long ago to the fathers by the prophets.* There are those who reduce the predictions of the Prophets in the Old Testament to five modes:

1. They make the first <term>Be-mar'ah <gloss>by vision</gloss></term>, when God revealed a matter in visions to the Prophet.
2. <term>Be-chalom <gloss>in a dream</gloss></term>, which happened to Jacob making his journey into Mesopotamia <note>Genesis 28:12, 13</note>.
3. <term>Be-chidot <gloss>in a riddle</gloss></term>, when one thing is seen and another is implied, such as the vision of Jeremiah <note>chapter 1:11, 13</note> seeing a shapely branch and a boiling pot; or Peter in the New Testament <note>Acts 10:11, 12</note>; and join to this the vision of John <note>Revelation 10:10</note> eating the book.
4. <term>Be-temunah <gloss>in a figure</gloss></term>, to which you may refer the vision of Ezekiel <note>chapter 1:5</note> and other Prophets.
5. <term>Peh el-peh <gloss>by divine address</gloss></term> <note>literally "mouth to mouth"</note>, in the way God addresses the Angels, and as he spoke to Moses and a very few others. Compare the *Exegesis* of Blessed Gerhard <note>Johann Gerhard, a Lutheran scholastic</note>, the *Sacred Philology* of Blessed Glassius, and the *System of Theology* of Doctor Calovius.

Others make three modes by which God used to address the Prophets of the Old Testament: namely, when he sent dreams to them, as was done for Abraham <note>Genesis 15:12</note>; or when he spoke with them with a sensible voice through Angels; or even when he employed spiritual speech within the mind and imagination. Many examples of this kind of vision or prophecy are found in the Holy Code, which they say Saul was looking for <margin>1 Samuel 28:6</margin> when he spoke with the disguised Samuel <note>the Witch of Endor episode</note>, saying: *That the Lord answered him no more, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by Prophets, when he went to consult Him.* See Cornelius à Lapide <note>a Jesuit commentator</note>.

Beyond the Prophets as extraordinary means of consulting God, after the Levitical worship was established, God gave answers through the High Priest. The priest was clothed in the <term>Choshen Ephod <gloss>Breastplate and Ephod</gloss></term>, in which were the <term>Urim and Thummim <gloss>Lights and Perfections/Truths</gloss></term>, through which oracles and answers were given by God <note>Exodus 28:30</note>. The use of these also existed in the Second Temple, as can be gathered from Ezra 2:63, Nehemiah 7:65, and Josephus in *Antiquities* Book 3, chapter 9. Josephus testifies that the Essene stone and the Sardonyx only ceased to shine two hundred years before he wrote this, God being angry due to the transgression of the laws; but Cunaeus and others maintain that they were entirely absent from the Second Temple.

Some confuse the pectoral (breastplate), which consisted of twelve gems, with the Urim and Thummim, but the placement and storage of it contradicts them. For the Urim and Thummim were one thing that was *placed*, and the pectoral was another thing *in which* it was placed. For that pectoral was a certain garment to be fastened to the ephod, adorned with twelve gems of stupendous and admirable color, upon which the names of the twelve Patriarchs were skillfully inscribed. The Septuagint renders this pectoral as <term>logion <gloss>oracle</gloss></term>, as if you were to say "prophetic" or giving answers. The Vulgate uses <term>rationale <gloss>rational breastplate</gloss></term>, following the Greek word, perhaps because since divine answers were issued through it, it did not seem to be an irrational thing, but something powerful in reason and intelligence. Luther calls it the <term>Amptschildlin <gloss>little shield of office</gloss></term>, because it belonged solely to the High Priest.

For David interrogated God through Abiathar the High Priest, not because he himself put on the breastplate, as some conclude from this passage. The <term>Urim and Thummim</term> <note>Sacred objects used by the High Priest to determine God's will; the names roughly mean "Lights and Perfections."</note> were translated by the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> as **"revelation and truth,"** <note>original Greek: δήλωσιν & ἀλήθειαν</note> by the Vulgate as **"doctrine and truth,"** and by Blessed Luther as **"Light and Right."** It seems Blessed Luther looked to the opinion of those who believe the answer was given through the *Urim and Thummim* by an extraordinary flashing of the gems, or by the protrusion and sparkling of the letters of the inscribed names. Those letters which composed the words of the answer would shine more than the others, so that the message could be read, as it were, from that remarkable sparkling of the letters on the Priest’s breastplate. We shall explain the whole matter using the words of Rabbi David Kimchi:

<margin>
On Judges chapter 20.
</margin>
*“He who wished to inquire about a public matter,”* he says, *“or some grave business, came to the Priest. He, clothed in the Ephod, stood before the Ark of the Lord. In the Ephod, or breastplate, were enclosed twelve precious stones, in which the names of the twelve tribes were inscribed; the names of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were also added, so that all the letters of the alphabet were present on those stones. It was necessary for the inquirer to turn his face toward the Priest and ask—not so openly that the voice could be heard, nor so obscurely that he only thought the request in his mind—but in the same manner as Hannah is read to have prayed in the first book of Samuel, only moving her lips, without saying anything that could be heard. Then the oracle was returned to the Priest in this fashion: by the power of the Holy Spirit, certain letters on the breastplate stood out, either by rising up or by glowing, in which the Priest read the oracle and the will of God; and these are those Urim and Thummim which the Priest carried on his chest.”*

<margin>
Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, Book 3, ch. 9.
</margin>
Before Maimonides and Kimchi, Josephus favored this opinion, writing thus on the matter: <note>original Greek: ἐπίστετε θαυμασιώτερον ἐγώ...</note> *“I will tell of something even more marvelous: for through the twelve stones which the High Priest wears sewn into the breastplate (the 'essen'), God would foretell victory to those about to go to war. For such a brilliance flashed from them, even before the army had moved, that it was clear to the whole multitude that God was present to help.”*

<margin>
Annales, Tom. 2, year 2544, sec. 550.
</margin>
However, Rabbi Solomon, DelRio, Serarius, Ribera, Salianus, and others deny that any external revelation was made to the High Priest. Instead, they believe that when the High Priest, clothed in the Ephod, consulted God, the will of God was made known to his mind by an internal revelation. This opinion is contradicted by the fact that a specific method of consulting God through Urim and Thummim is described in Holy Scripture (as is clear from comparing *Exodus 28:30, Leviticus 8:8, Numbers 27:21, 1 Samuel 28:6, and Deuteronomy 33:8*), and it is expressly distinguished from dreams, visions, and prophecies in *1 Samuel 28:6*. In such an uncertain matter, we do not start a quarrel with either side, acquiescing to the very weighty judgment of Blessed Gerhard in his *Theological Explanations*: that no one today knows exactly the true mode of divine revelation through Urim and Thummim. See also Blessed Meisner, Blessed Gerhard, Blessed Dilherr, M. Stolterfoht, P. Cunaeus, and Sixtinus Amama. From this was distinguished the method which occurred 

<column-break/>

through the <term>Kapporet</term> <note>The "Mercy Seat" or golden cover of the Ark of the Covenant.</note>, the covering of the Ark of the Covenant, or before the propitiatory. That *Kapporet* or covering was a plate of solid gold placed upon the Ark like a lid or cover; it also served as the base upon which the Cherubim stood fixed. From this place, God very frequently spoke to the Israelites, especially in the time of Moses (*Exodus 25:21, Numbers 7:89*). This oracle was given by a vocal response and a sonorous voice from heaven, which the Hebrews called the <term>Bath-kol</term> <note>Literally "Daughter of a Voice," referring to an echo of the divine voice.</note>, the "daughter of a voice." A voice of this kind falling from heaven, says M. Laurentius Fabricius, Professor at Wittenberg, was also heard in the New Testament. Thus, while Christ stood in the Jordan, a voice was heard from heaven. Thus, a divine revelation occurred to Paul as he set out for Damascus. Thus, the voice said to Peter: *“Eat.”* And Blessed Gerhard observes that this type of oracle was always heard after the era of Prophecy during the time of the Second Temple, citing the Jerusalem Targum on Genesis 38. However, Dr. Calovius restricts it to Moses alone, saying it no longer had a place after Moses, to whom alone that specific revelation had been promised.

Nor should we wrap in a veil of silence that type of divination or oracle which occurred through **lots**, which was no less common among the Israelite people. Thus Joshua discovered the lawbreaker and the author of the curse (*Joshua 7:18*). Thus Samuel instituted the lot in choosing a King (*1 Samuel 10:20*). Saul inquired by lot into the transgressor of his command (*1 Samuel 14:40, 42*), to pass over other examples discussed more fully above. Through these and other kinds of divine revelation and oracles, God intended both our information and our salvation, namely, that we might guard ourselves against everything that could in any way be an obstacle to our salvation. Whence Lactantius speaks fittingly: *“Some of the Prophets,”* he says, *“were Princes or even Kings, who announced God’s message with a singular divination, the same as the others.”* And a little before, more clearly: *“Prophets,”* he says, *“are therefore sent by God to be both heralds of His majesty and correctors of human depravity.”* See also Dr. Palladius and Gisbert Voetius.

If ever the Devil has abused divine works to overturn the kingdom of God and acted as **"God's ape,"** he certainly did so in this subject we are now discussing. For that "master of a thousand arts" <note>A traditional epithet for the Devil.</note> emulated each and every kind of divine divination and oracle, and most cleverly and craftily deceived men. With exquisite study and a singular "wicked zeal," he abused almost the same means by which God once instituted and established true religion, striving to procure authority and sanctity for his own idolatrous worship. Therefore, we rightly recognize the Devil as the author and inventor of so many kinds of divination among the gentiles, since according to Thomas [Aquinas], *“all [pagan] divination proceeds from the operation of demons, either because demons are expressly invoked to manifest future things, or because demons thrust themselves into true inquiries.”*

For Aristotle, discussing the causes of why the Sibyls <note>Ancient prophetesses who uttered oracles in a state of frenzy.</note> and others become ecstatic, attributes these things to heat or a natural imbalance. For he speaks on this matter thus: *“Many people, because that heat of the seat of the mind is nearby, are entangled in diseases of madness and become possessed; whence Sibyls, and followers of Bacchus, and those inspired by a divine spirit arise, since they do so not from disease, but from a natural imbalance.”* Much less do we agree with the Epicureans <note>Philosophers who generally believed the gods were indifferent to human affairs and that the world was made of atoms.</note>, who held everything predicted about the future to be trifles and old wives' tales; hence they rejected all types of divining, saying there was nothing to it but the foolishness of the common people or the impostures of priests, devised and thought up under the pretext of piety and religion to subdue the ignorant masses. Coelius Rhodiginus writes in support of this view (though his mind was not precisely inclined to their affections):

<margin>

*“If the origin of oracles is first to be searched out with a curious investigation, I seem to have discovered through constant reading that they were not established or propagated by Gods or Demons, but were begun in the beginning by certain crafty and money-seeking men. The most famous of the Greek sages—the Peripatetics, Cynics, and Epicureans—followed this opinion; by them, the vanity of oracles was not only made public in writing, but it was also shown what a progeny of evils sprouted from there. Evidence for this is the responses of wicked men, practiced in the fountains of greed for both imposture and slaughter, who were far too skillful at adapting their answers to either possible outcome. These answers were eventually stuffed together or (as that man says) woven with patched-up deceits, after emissaries had wandered anxiously through the cities like certain spies <note>original: Coricæi, a reference to the inhabitants of Corycus known for eavesdropping.</note>, of whom they had quite a few as administrators and partners in their crimes. In order to demonstrate that the origin of oracles should not be referred to Gods, nor to Demons, nor to heroes, but to entirely natural causes, he flees to the singular quality or temperament of the earth and attributes all power and faculty of divining to it. Just as one piece of land is more fertile than another, this one abounding in a harvest of grain, that one in veins of metal, another in kinds of cattle—and this from a diverse mixture of the primary qualities and the position of the sky—so he thinks certain parts of the earth are endowed with such a temperament that they make men prophetic. *“Even more certain responses came forth,”* he says, *“the more sharp, pure, and refined the earth was; nor does he judge that oracles eventually grew old for any other reason than*

After these things, the Delphic Oracle earned no small fame; it was also commonly called the Pythian oracle, either from the word <term>punthanesthai</term> <note>Greek: πυνθάνεσθαι, meaning "to inquire" or "to learn by asking."</note>, or from the slain Python—a serpent which, as the poets tell the story, Apollo killed with arrows in his earliest infancy. From this, the city itself began to be named <term>Pytho</term>, though otherwise its name was Delphi (compare Alexander ab Alexandro, book 6, *Genial Days*, chapter 2, page 819; Simon Majolus, book 2, *Dog Days*, page 136). They say this city held the "navel" of the whole world; see Turnebus’s notes on Plutarch’s *On Oracles*, page 81, and Tiraquellus in his *Notes on Alexander ab Alexandro*. Cicero seems to have looked toward this when he wrote: *“I come to you, O holy Apollo, who occupies the certain navel of the lands, from whence first escaped the superstitious, wild, and fierce voice.”* Indeed, Chrysippus filled an entire volume with your oracles—some false, as I believe; some true by chance, as happens very often in any speech; some twisted and obscure, so that the interpreter needs an interpreter and the matter itself must be referred back to the lots; and some ambiguous, which must be referred to the rules of Logic. Hence, in the Delphic temple, as Blancardus reports <margin>Odyssey book 6, verse 296.</margin> from book 6 of Strabo in his *Annotations on Quintus Curtius* (book 4), the "navel" was shown covered in bandages to demonstrate that this place was at the navel—that is, in the middle—of the earth. The Pythian oracle had this peculiar trait: it did not give responses every day, nor every month, but observed certain intervals of time, as Servius reports on the *Aeneid* (book 4) and Alexander ab Alexandro. Thus, when Alexander the Great came to Delphi at a time not permitted to consult Apollo, the priestess excused herself based on the law of the unusual time. But Alexander, paying no attention, began to drag the reluctant priestess with him into the temple. The priestess herself, overcome by Alexander’s persistence, cried out: *“You are invincible, my son!”* Having received this response, Alexander was satisfied and said he needed no other oracle, since he had obtained the answer he desired, as Tiraquellus observes from Plutarch in his *Notes on Alexander ab Alexandro*. <margin>On Divination, book 4, page 231.</margin> (Compare Peucer’s *Commentary on Divination*, page 231). # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Divinations and fortune-telling.</margin>
Alexander of Naples provides many examples concerning ghosts and things of that sort in book 2 of his *Genial Days*, chapter 9, and book 4, chapter 19. So does Hieronymus Magius in his *Miscellany*, 4.12, and Lavater in his work *On Ghosts*, etc. Pliny also mentions some in book 7, *Letters*, 27, where there is an excellent debate regarding specters and nocturnal apparitions—which are variously called phantasms, phantoms, apparitions, idols, lemures <note>spirits of the restless dead</note>, manes, or shadows—as to whether they are truly something, or merely empty and vain things that take shape from our own fear. Although in such an ambiguous matter it might be better to imitate the Socratic <term>epexontas</term> <note>original: ἐπέχοντας; those who suspend judgment</note>, and the uncertainty of the Academic school is safer than the sworn dogmas of the other sects, yet so many examples have been observed and recorded—not only by the common folk, who can deceive and be deceived, but even by great men—that it leaves little room to doubt the reality of certain specters. God uses these either to test the faithful or to punish the unfaithful. That these are not the souls of the deceased is beyond doubt. Blessed Nikolaus Selnecker discusses apparitions and specters excellently in his *Analecta* (H. 4. b.): *“It is true that many spirits wander about and are often seen; and examples are not only read about, but we ourselves have known examples, and have heard and seen specters.”* Concerning these, the Pagans had said: *“The Shades are something; death does not end all.”* <note>A quote from the Roman poet Propertius.</note> However, we have a rule *expressed in the Word of God*: *“You shall not seek the truth from the dead; for the Lord abominates all these things.”*

<margin>H.S.a.</margin>
The question is also asked: *“Are those wandering spirits truly the souls of certain dead men, as the Pagans think, or are they rather entirely evil, demonic, and damned spirits?”* When Chrysostom defines this question, stating that they cannot be the souls of the deceased, he adds his own view: It can indeed happen that a Demon appears in the form of a dead man, as examples everywhere testify. For instance, there is a castle in Denmark where King Valdemar is often seen. He had said that even after his death he could never be satisfied with hunting; thus, he is often spotted sitting on a horse, leading black dogs to the hunt, and blowing a hunting horn. Similar things are often heard elsewhere. But all these are diabolical mockeries with which Satan imposes upon men, terrifying them and making them fearful. Often the Devil occupies a certain place, castle, house, territory, or chamber, and does not easily depart from there, as we ourselves have known. Since it is established that such apparitions of the dead are mere traps of Demons, we ought to place no faith in them. Furthermore, the Devil has maddened the Gentiles in countless other ways, so that there was neither number nor end to their divinations, all of which it is not our purpose to review.

<margin>2. On Witches 12. col. 196.</margin>
Dactylomancy <note>From the Greek 'daktylios' (ring) and 'manteia' (divination)</note> was a type of divination performed with rings constructed according to a certain position of the sky or enchanted, as Ammianus describes in book 29; they divined by moving them over a tripod while reciting certain words. Wierus says: *“It is called Dactylomancy when sorcerers divine using rings fashioned at certain positions of the heavens or consecrated by a diabolical rite.”* The *Ring of Gyges* is celebrated by the Poets; they mention he found it on the hand of a certain corpse, and by its power, the kingdom of Lydia was obtained. From this, a proverb arose, so that the *“Ring of Gyges”* <note>original: Γύγου δακτύλιος</note> was said of fortunate people, which Erasmus discusses in book 1, *Adages*, 96 (pages 56-57), drawing from Lucian, Plato, and Cicero. You will find various types of this practice in Peucer and others, some of which are captured in these simple verses:

<column-break/>

->From the earth is the divination called Geomancy made;<-
->But Hydromancy looks to water; Pyromancy looks<-
->To fire; but Chiromancy is done for you by the palm.<-

Furthermore, it was believed by the Gentiles that there were almost no evils that were not first announced and predicted by their own signs, portents, and omens. Hence Dio Cassius says in book 53 (page 595): *“For it is always likely to signal something before such evils.”* <note>original: Φιλεῖ γάρ πώς ἀεί τι πρὸ τῶν τοιούτων κακῶν προσημαίνειν.</note> Because of this, they were beyond measure both fearful and superstitious. For they were accustomed to make conjectures from the sudden movements of the sea and other novelties concerning it, whether seen or heard—the kind of divination by which Jonah was tested. Regarding this <term>episēmasia</term> <note>original: ἐπισημασίᾳ; a significant sign or omen</note>, Plutarch says in the *Banquet of the Seven Sages*: *“Not indeed unexpectedly, but from afar, a ripple was seen coming down along the headland amid cloudiness and calm, bringing a certain foam and swell with its rushing sound, so that everyone was bound to rush to that place, running down in wonder.”* To this, you may refer what they conjectured regarding the entry of animals which were thought to be ill-omened. Terence says in *Phormio*, Act 4, scene 4, line 25: *“A strange black dog entered the house. A snake fell from the roof-tiles through the skylight. A hen crowed.”* This was seen as an omen of an unhappy marriage. By the entry of the strange black dog, they predicted a mark of future adultery; by the fall of the snake from the tiles, that one of the spouses would perish by poison. By the crowing of the hen, they pronounced that the husband would live according to his wife’s command, or that the wife would survive her husband. They judged the same regarding dreams, whence they tried to avert danger with a sacrificial victim whenever monsters or portents—or even sinister dreams—seemed to portend or threaten, and this was done according to the counsel and prescription of the Augurs and Haruspices <note>Roman priests who interpreted the flight of birds or the entrails of animals</note>. They called this "tending to the portents"; likewise, they were accustomed to "tend with larger victims," and the Romans used to be wonderfully superstitious in this matter, appointing fifteen men <note>The 'Quindecimviri sacris faciundis'</note> to approach and inspect the Sibylline books for that reason. Cicero says in book 1 *On Divination*: *“Since great power seemed to reside in interpreting and tending to monsters, they applied all this science from Etruria to the discipline of the Haruspices.”* And in the second book: *“Chrysippus placed it as one of the duties of divination to foreknow how signs, which are portended by the Gods to men, should be tended to and expiated.”* Hector, in Homer, despised the vanity of auguries, responding gravely to Polydamas, who was refusing the fight for fear of an omen: *“There is one best omen, commanded by God: to bravely defend the fatherland.”*

> You bid me be persuaded by long-winged birds,
> Whom I do not heed, nor do I care for them,
> Whether they go to the right toward the dawn and the sun,
> Or to the left toward the misty gloom.
> Let us be persuaded by the counsel of great Zeus,
> Who rules over all mortals and immortals.
> One omen is best: to fight for one's country.

Augustinus Niphus teaches what antiquity wrote and felt about auguries in a special treatise, which Rudolf Goclenius saw to be reprinted at Marburg. From this, Accius says concerning the wordy tricks of the Augurs, in Nonius under "divination":

->They enrich the ears with words<-
->Of others, so that they may enrich their own homes with gold.<-

### Ezekiel 21: 21, 22, 23.

<margin>Divinations and fortune-telling.</margin>
At the end of his first book *On Divination*, Cicero suggests that this class of men should be "heard rather than listened to" <note>Cicero implies we should acknowledge their existence as a historical fact without actually obeying their advice.</note>. Nevertheless, Tibullus, in his *Elegies* (Book 2, Elegy 5), relates the practices of augury and haruspicy <note>the inspection of entrails</note> to <term>divination</term> <note>original: μαντικὴν</note>:

<margin>Jonah 1:4.</margin>
> You see things far in the future; the Augur, devoted to you,
> Knows well what the bird, foreseeing fate, sings.
> And you rule the brave; through you the haruspex senses the future,
> When God has marked the slippery innards with signs.

The Italians were excessively devoted to the inspection of entrails and <term>liver-reading</term> <note>original: ἡπατοσκοπίας</note>, about whom Herodian writes in Book 8: "The Italians trust this inspection most of all." To these, join the Chaldeans, who were otherwise most practiced in divinations. Diodorus Siculus narrates that it was their business to turn away evils from men and bring about good things through auguries and certain incantations, to interpret dreams and wonders, and to hold most skillfully those things pertaining to the observation of sacrifices. They indicated an imminent death for Alexander the Great if he were to enter Babylon; concerning this prophecy, I present the Greek of Diodorus (Book 17, page 622) as I read it: "When he was three hundred stades <note>about 34 miles</note> from Babylon, the people called Chaldeans, who had achieved the greatest reputation in astrology and were accustomed to foretelling the future through a certain eternal observation, sent forward the oldest and most experienced among them. Having known through the <term>divination of the stars</term> the king's coming death in Babylon, they ordered them to report the danger to the king and to urge him by no means to make his entry into the city. They said he could escape the danger if he rebuilt the tomb of Belus, which had been destroyed by the Persians, and, halting his planned route, passed by the city." But Alexander, at the instigation of certain philosophers who defended the dogmas of Anaxagoras, held this omen of the Chaldeans in contempt, as Diodorus indicates in the cited passage. From our Prophetic passage, it is clear how much value the Chaldeans placed on <term>sorcery</term> <note>original: γοητείαν</note> and <term>divination by lots</term> <note>original: κληρομαντείαν</note>. To sorcery is commonly referred <term>sacrificial inspection</term> <note>original: ἱεροσκοπία</note>, by which a conjecture was made from the consideration of victims and the things done around them. The Latins called the observers of such things by the special names *Extispices* and *Haruspices*, which the Greeks called <term>liver-readers</term> <note>original: ἡπατοσκοπίαν</note>. Although signs were sought not only from the entrails, but also from the victims themselves before they were slaughtered, from the flame and smoke, from the flour, frankincense, and wine consecrated for libations; from which arose <term>fire-divination</term> <note>original: πυροσκοπία</note>, <term>smoke-divination</term> <note>original: καπνομαντεία</note>, <term>incense-divination</term> <note>original: λιβανομαντεία</note>, <term>wine-divination</term> <note>original: οἰνομαντεία</note>, <term>barley-divination</term> <note>original: κριθομαντεία</note>, etc., and likewise <term>human-sacrifice divination</term> <note>original: ἀνθρωπομαντεία</note>, which, according to the author Heliogabalus <note>a Roman Emperor known for religious eccentricity</note>, was established from the internal organs of slaughtered men. However, the origin of all <term>sacrificial inspection</term> <note>original: ἱεροσκοπίας</note> and the <term>art of sacrifice</term> <note>original: θυτικῆς</note> among the Pagans owes its beginnings to those rites which, from the start,

To those nations where the memory of rituals did not flourish through false tradition, there was added the cunning of the Demons whom they worshiped. Therefore, partly from <term>perverse imitation</term> <note>original: κακοζηλίᾳ</note>, by which the world is accustomed to imitate the Church in certain things, and partly at the instigation of the Devil, various sacrifices and various rites were observed even among the Pagans, as Rivetus concludes in *Exercise 42 on Genesis*, page 212. He did this to draw the Pagans more into his camp and to have them more ready and prepared for his pursuits. The Etruscans make the author of the art of inspecting entrails a boy named Tages. As Cicero recounts from the Etruscan books, when the earth was being plowed and a furrow had been pressed deeper, Tages suddenly appeared with the look of a boy but the wisdom of an old man, and addressed the one who was plowing. At this sight, when the plowman was struck dumb and gave a great cry of wonder, a crowd gathered, and in a short time all Etruria assembled at that place. Then the boy spoke many things to the many listeners, who caught all his words and committed them to writing. His entire speech was that in which the doctrine of the *haruspex* is contained. But there is no doubt that this Tages was the Devil himself, clothed in a boyish habit and <term>outward forms</term> <note>original: χέσεσι; likely a corruption of σχήμασι (schemasi)</note>, who, by altering several things from the true doctrine of Sacrifices, introduced this custom of inspecting entrails, which Lucan also mentions:

### ANTIQUITIES OF THE BIBLE

<margin>Divinations and lot-casting.</margin>
...Nothing was decided privately or publicly in the Senate unless the consensus and approval of the augurs was obtained. Hence, whatever they declared to be just, good, and favorable was held as such; but whatever they called unjust, unspeakable, flawed, or ill-omened was immediately deemed completely void and undone. Thus, among the Romans, their dignity was so great that they were enrolled in the Senate as messengers and interpreters of the Gods, and were numbered among the Fathers of the Roman People. Compare Peucer in his *Commentary on Divination, pages 374 and following.*

Both the sacred and profane pages <note>referring to the Bible and secular literature</note> testify that the use of <term>lots</term> <note>original: sortium</note> was of great importance in antiquity. The choice of two rams was committed to the divination of lots, one of which, touched by the lot, was to be sacrificed to God (*Leviticus 16:8*). By lot, the Promised Land was divided among the Israelites by God's command (*Joshua 13:2*). By lot, Joshua searched out Achan, the <term>transgressor</term> <note>original: παραβάτιν</note> of the Divine law (*Joshua 7:14, 18*). Saul was chosen as King by lot (*1 Samuel 10:21*). Likewise, there is frequent mention of the casting of lots in secular literature. Among the Romans, Praetors and the presiding officers of public trials were chosen from the decuries by lot. So too among the Athenians, the same custom was observed in electing the <term>Council of Five Hundred</term> <note>original: τοῖς πεντακοσίοις</note>, whose election was usually done <term>by lot</term> <note>original: διὰ κλῆρον</note>. Thus, as Homer testifies, the Princes going into the holy war met among themselves by lot according to rank, specifically by casting lots into a helmet:
<margin>Odyssey, Book 10, line 206.</margin>
> We quickly shook the lots in a bronze helmet,
> and the lot of great-hearted Eurylochus leaped out.
<note>original Greek: κλῆρος ἐν κυνέη χαλκήρεϊ πάλλομεν ὦκα / Ἐκ δ' ἔθορε κλῆρος μεγalήτορος Εὐρυλόχοιο.</note>

Our ancestors long ago, according to Cornelius Tacitus (*Book 10 on Germany, chapter 10*), were most devoted to divination by lots: *They observe auspices and lots, he says, above all else. The custom of the lots is simple: they cut a branch from a fruit-bearing tree and slice it into twigs, marking them with certain signs and scattering them randomly and by chance upon a white cloth. Then, if it is for a public consultation, the priest of the community—or if private, the head of the family—prays to the Gods, and looking up to heaven, picks up three twigs one by one, and interprets them according to the marks previously impressed upon them.* This use of lots still flourishes today in Persia among the Muslims, which Adam Olearius mentions in these words:
<margin>Persian Journey, Book 3, chapter 28, page 631.</margin>
> Among their superstitious arts and prophecies, I do not consider the least to be that they wish to explore future things through lots, just as I encountered such soothsayers in Isfahan at the Meidan <note>The central square or marketplace</note> or great market, sitting with their wares laid out. These are of two kinds, namely Remal and Falfir. The Remal is similar to a <term>geomancer</term> <note>One who predicts the future using patterns on the earth or dice</note>; he uses six or eight dice pulled onto two copper wire-rings and prophesies through the lot. The Falfir, however, works in another way: he has 30 or 40 thin boards, a good inch long and wide, lying before him, which are written upon on the bottom side. On one of these, one must place money and ask his question about the matter he desires to know. Whatever the soothsayer first notices here is considered quite certain; he pulls the money along with the little boards, speaks several words meanwhile, and examines the writing. Then he has a very long and wide book, three or four fingers thick, whose pages are painted with angels, devils, dragons, and all kinds of animals and creeping things in gruesome

<column-break/>

and unpleasant forms. This he takes in hand, reaches in several times, and murmurs continuously; finally, he catches a certain figure, holds the mentioned writing against it, and prophesies. I have gone there several times when I had the inclination and seen that veiled women came and asked how it fared with their sons and husbands who had traveled away, whether they would return soon, and whether the husbands might bring other wives with them. Likewise, they asked about good and bad luck: some went away with happy news, some with doubtful reports. Thus he writes. However, just as there were formerly different types of lots and various distinct purposes, so too were there various instruments for them. Lots were captured by tossing <term>tesserae</term> <note>small tablets or dice</note> and knuckle-bones on which certain characters and figures were carved; this species was called <term>cleromancy</term> <note>divination by lot</note>. Next was <term>astragalomancy</term>, done from the throwing of knuckle-bones. <term>Geomancy</term> from points and figures established by lot. <term>Hydromancy</term> from the color and other qualities of water. <term>Onomancy</term> and <term>arithmomancy</term> from names and numbers. <term>Logarithmantia</term>, by which oracles were fabricated from numbers—specifically numbers converted into words and conversely words resolved into numbers. <term>Tetramancy</term>, when the matter about which divination was being made was inscribed with a finger in ash, and this was exposed under the open sky so that whatever letters were left behind might teach the outcome; Peucer treats all these more at length in his *Commentary on Divination, page 399.* These lots were observed with great religious devotion, and much faith was placed in them by the ancients. Especially among the Pagans, the Delian, Lycian, Praenestine, and Antiatine lots, among others, have no small fame; those wishing to consult them were not permitted to approach unless they had first been purified by solemn rites and initiated with peculiar ceremonies. *At Bura, a town in Achaia, Peucer reports, there was an Oracle of Hercules made of knuckle-bones and a tablet <note>original: abaco</note>, where one wishing to consult about any matter, after offering vows and prayers to God, threw four knuckle-bones. When the President of the Oracle inspected their position and figure, he found what would happen expressed in letters on the tablet according to the bones; all the bones were skillfully fashioned from the bones of sacrificial victims.* The more accurately the outcome answered the prophecy, the greater the value placed on the lots. Thus, the Antiatine lots were made famous by the death of Gaius Caligula, whom they once warned to beware of Cassius, by whom he was killed, as Suetonius writes in *Caligula, chapter 57.* Thus they prepared greater fame for themselves the greater the person and the more celebrated the event. Tiberius Caesar ennobled the lots at the fountain of Aponus <note>a hot spring near Padua</note> of Geryon; while still a private citizen, consulting this oracle about Augustus's successor, he threw golden knuckle-bones into the fountain of Aponus and discovered from the collection of numbers that the succession and empire would be his, as the same Suetonius testifies. Nebuchadnezzar used lots together with <margin>Ezekiel 21.</margin> <term>belomancy</term> <note>divination by arrows</note> so that he might be informed by the casting of lots about a successful outcome. The lots were cast with the right hand into an urn. However, as Junius says on this passage, when two lots were compared with each other concerning the siege of Jerusalem or Rabbah, it is believable that the lots were drawn with both hands, so that whichever lot was in the right hand was seen to be commanded by divine power. A certain place was destined for this business, from which the King of Babylon...
