### Ezekiel 21. v. 21. 22. 23.

<margin>Divinations and lot-casting.</margin>
The King of Babylon, according to the Prophet, is said to have stood "at the mother of the way at the head of the two ways" <note>original Hebrew: *el-em haderekh berosh shenei haderakhim*</note>, that is, at a crossroads. How much significance sorcerers attribute to such locations is clear from their own practices and various books. In this place, he performed "divination by shaking arrows" <note>original Hebrew: *kilkel bakhitzim*</note>; the word <term>oracular shaking</term> <note>original: קלקל, kilqel</note> is translated by Pagninus (following Arius Montanus) as "he polished the arrows," while the Vulgate <note>the standard Latin Bible</note> has "mixing the arrows," and Junius and Piscator read it as "sharpening the knives." This is because the root word <term>qalal</term> <note>original: קלל</note> means to be "vile" or "lightly esteemed," but in the intensified form <note>the Hiphil or Piel stems</note> it can mean to curse or blaspheme; when the first root letter is doubled, it becomes *kilqel*, which means to wash, wipe, or polish. 

Interpreters do not agree on what kind of divination this actually was. Some think the Babylonians polished their arrows or the iron of their weapons until they shone, and the diviners sought knowledge in that brightness as if looking into a mirror, similar to how some look into a polished thumbnail. Others translate it as "he threw the arrows," making them fly into the air to see in which direction they would fall, so he could lead his army that way. This is also how the Chaldean Paraphrast <note>the Targum</note> translated it. Piscator <margin>Commentary on this place, page 877.</margin> thinks it refers to the knives used to cut up the sacrificial cattle. B. Friedliebius writes the following: "It was the custom of the Chaldean Kings that when they were going out to war, they would prepare arrows with a magical rite through the work of astrologers. They would write the names of the cities and nations they wished to invade upon them. Then, after mixing them together, they would draw one blindly; whichever arrow they took, they would first attack that nation or city." See Jerome’s commentary on this passage, and add the Nuremberg Bible, where it is reported slightly differently according to Junius; Luther also has the same in his marginal notes.

The circumstances sufficiently show that this type of divination belongs to the category of <term>casting lots</term>. Whether it was used by <margin>p. 403.</margin> other nations is not certain. It is counted among those types of idolatry that happen "by chance," and is called "divining" <note>original Hebrew: נחש, nakhash</note>, a word used in the First Book of Kings (20:33) regarding the servants of King Ben-hadad of Syria sent to King Ahab of Israel after their defeat.

That this divination was not performed without a curse upon the enemy seems to be suggested by the root word *qalal* in its intensified form, which very often has the meaning of "cursing" (Leviticus 20:9, 24:14; Jeremiah 15:10), just as its opposite, "blessing" <note>original Hebrew: ברך, barakh</note>, is found in its respective sense (Daniel 2:19, 4:13; Proverbs 20:21, 22:9; Psalm 113:2, and elsewhere). Terrible imprecations <note>formal curses</note> are common enough among the ancients. Priests and prophets used to call down "Dirae" <note>furies or dire curses</note> upon enemies and hostile places. Theopompus, as cited by Plutarch in *The Daemon of Socrates*, tells of a priest named Cabirichus who could not be turned away from his destructive plans of cursing; he was killed with a sword because he favored tyrants to the ruin of his homeland and spoke on behalf of enemies. He said: "Lie here with those you flattered; for you shall not wear a wreath in a liberated Thebes, nor shall you sacrifice to the gods any longer, since you frequently called down many curses upon your fatherland while making vows for the enemy" <note>original Greek: Ἐνταῦθα (ἔφη) κεῖσμαι... εὐχόμενος</note>. 

Cambyses also called the Persians to witness by the royal gods that they should obey his commands. For there was a prayer and a curse: that for those who obeyed, the earth would bring forth fruit, and their wives and livestock would give birth for all time while they enjoyed <margin>p. 173.</margin> freedom; but for those who did otherwise, the opposite would happen (Herodotus, 

<column-break/>

*Thalia*, chapter 65, page 188). So too among the Lydians, a command was given with a curse if it was not fulfilled: <margin>Divinations and lot-casting.</margin> "For those of us who are dying, we charge you and all others to take vengeance on this Agoratus as a murderer" <note>original Greek: Ἀποθνήσκοντες γδ᾿ ἡμῖν... ὄντα</note>. 

Balak, King of the Moabites, <margin>Numbers 22:5, 6.</margin> wanted to keep the Israelites out of his territory with a "bolt of execration" <note>a formal curse</note>, so that they might become "accursed and defiled" <note>original Greek: ἐναγεῖς καὶ μιαροί</note>. At that time, Balaam held great authority in that eastern region, of whom it could be said what Homer said in the *Iliad* (Book 1, line 69) regarding Calchas:
-> "The best of bird-diviners," <-
who was born under a lucky star for prophecy, a seer known for many examples, as it says in the same place:
-> "Who knew things present, future, and past," <-
-> "Through the art of prophecy, which Phoebus Apollo gave him." <-
Balak summoned him to hurl the "bolts of the Furies" <note>deadly curses</note> at the people of Israel; for he said, "I know that he whom you bless is blessed, and he whom you curse is cursed." Although Balaam might deserve praise because he refused to curse or execrate them in his own way despite the King’s flattery or anger, he is nonetheless to be blamed because, as a fickle man, he wavered toward human favor on both sides. Wishing to oppose the Israelites but not being able to, he went hunting for money and honor, "speaking while being transformed into a prophet among the gods," to use the words of Philo in Book 1 of *The Life of Moses*. Furthermore, he gave Balak the advice to destroy Israel by the help of prostituted young women, enticing the Israelites to fornication and idolatry, which is why he perished by the sword of the Israelites along with the Midianites (Numbers 31:8). 

A curse <margin>Numbers 31:8.</margin> was a sad and infamous thing; Plutarch says, "A curse is something ill-omened and gloomy" <note>original Greek: Ἐςὶ... κατάρα δύσφη- μον καὶ σκυθρωπόν</note>. However, the manner of cursing varied according to the customs of different peoples. Who would doubt that curses were commonly used by the Greeks and Romans? Among the Greeks, the "weapon of the curse" flourished; and when Alcibiades was to be cursed by the decree of the Athenian people, a priestess was praised "for not being willing to curse Alcibiades when ordered" <note>original Greek: μὴ θελήσαζα καταράσαθαι...</note>, according to Plutarch <margin>Roman Questions 44.</margin>. That priestess was Theano, daughter of Menon, as the same Plutarch reports in *The Life of Alcibiades*. 

There exists another example of curses hurled at the wicked in the case of Crassus, found in Plutarch’s *Life of Crassus*. He was believed to have been made subject to "Dirae" <note>horrible curses</note> by the Tribune of the Plebs, Attejus, in this manner. Attejus's attempt against Crassus—who was bringing war upon the Parthians despite the warnings of the Priests and Augurs—was famous. Attejus ran ahead to the gate through which Marcus Crassus, dressed in his general's cloak, intended to leave Rome. There he lit a fire; when Crassus arrived, Attejus threw in incense, performed libations, and called down atrocious and horrifying curses upon Crassus’s head, invoking monstrous and foul gods. He adds from ancient tradition that so much power is attributed to the horror of those secret "devotions" <note>ritual curses</note> that no one against whom they are conceived can escape them; therefore, it is not lawful to call them down for just any reason. Aeschines called a curse conceived in specific words a "delimited curse" <note>original Greek: διοριζομένην ἀρὰν</note>. For these curses were made with specific words and ceremonies. Thus, "incantations" were performed with less equipment than "devotions"; the former were done through words alone without other sacred rites, while the latter also involved sacrifices...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>

</margin>

...they stood in need of sacrifices and sacred songs, specifically if they were imprecating curses <note>original: *diras*, formal ritual curses</note> in a public capacity. It is abundantly clear that in other cases, curses were made with bare words alone. Thus Eumenes, having been betrayed by his own army—which had bound itself to his word by oath four times in a single year—prayed for every kind of evil upon them, saying (as witnessed by Justin *): *“Do I speak these curses and funeral offerings against you?”* <note>original Latin: *Has vobis diras atque inferias dico?*</note> So too a centurion, as recorded by Tacitus in the *6th book of the Annals, 24. §. 3.*, imprecated composed curses against Tiberius in these words: *“That just as he had filled his house with the slaughter of his daughter-in-law, his brother's son, and his grandsons, so might he pay the penalty to the name and race of his ancestors and to posterity.”* Compare the same author in *Book 14 of the Annals, c. 30. §. 2.* regarding the Druids, who poured out curses with hands raised toward heaven. Likewise, Antigone, as she is about to die, imprecates her judges: if she suffers unjustly, she prays that they might suffer as much evil as they are unjustly inflicting upon her; but if her actions are disapproved by the Gods, she wishes for forgiveness to be given to those who destroy her. Sophocles records this in *Antigone, verse 922*:

> But if these things are good in the sight of the gods, 
> after suffering our fate, we may realize we have erred; 
> but if these men are the ones erring, may they suffer no more evils 
> than those they are unjustly doing to me.
> <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ' εἰ μὲν τάδ' ἐστὶν ἐν θεοῖς καλὰ / Παθόντες ἂν ξυγγνοῖμεν ἡμαρτηκότες· / εἰ δ' οἳ δ' ἁμαρτάνωσι, μὴ πλείω κακὰ / πάθοιεν, ἢ καὶ δρῶσιν ἐκδίκως ἐμέ.</note>

Where the phrase *doing unjustly* <note>original Greek: *δρῶσιν ἐκδίκως*</note> means to act against right and merit, just as *justly* <note>original: *ἐνδίκως*</note> means rightly and correctly. Thus the imprecation of Theseus is said to have destroyed his son Hippolytus in the works of Euripides *, from which the son exclaims:

<margin>
Hippolytus
the Crowned,
v. 1241.
</margin>

> — — — Oh, my father’s miserable curse!
> <note>original Greek: Ὦ πατρὸς τάλαιν' ἀρά.</note>

For the parent Theseus had made prayers to Neptune that he might destroy his son; compare the cited work at verses 1315, 1324, 1362, and 1378. We hold from the sacred scriptures that the dire vows and imprecations of parents infallibly strike disobedient children. The son of Sirach <note>The Book of Ecclesiasticus</note> says in *chapter 3:11*: *“The blessing of the father establishes the houses of the sons: but the curse of the mother roots out the foundations;”* so that we may pass over in silence here the examples of punished disobedient children which Hondorfius, Titius, and others have collected in great number. In Theocritus, in the *Bucoliasts*, the Cyclops imprecates Telemus, who had predicted to him that his eye would be torn out by Ulysses:

> But that prophet Telemus, who sings of hateful things, 
> let him carry those hateful things home, that he may keep them for his children.
> <note>original Greek: Ἀὐτὰρ ὁ μάντις ὁ τήλεμος ἔχθρ' ἀγορεύων / ἐχθρὰ φέρει, πότε οἶκον, ὅπως τεκέεσσι φυλάξῃ.</note>

Telemus the seer, who sings all harsh things to me, let him carry the curses home, so that his children may endure them. Agamemnon repeats nearly the same curses in Homer *, devoting them to the Trojans:

<margin>
Iliad
v. 162.

Curses were also used in other matters, such as on consecrated statues against anyone who might move them from their place, as found in Philostratus’s *Life of Herodes Atticus*. For no consecration of any significant importance was made without the addition of *curses* <note>original Greek: *ἀρῶν*</note>, which Salmasius notes in several observations on the *Augustan History*, and in his *Discourse on the consecration of the Temple in the field of Herodes Atticus, p. 9–10, Paris edition, 1619.* In this same way, after Popery was purged from the borders of Hesse, Philipp the Magnanimous—a Prince greater than all praise—wished the monastery of Haynau to be a common hospital for all eternity, where in the great dining hall these rhymes are read:

> And what I have founded here /
> That such shall not be abolished /

<column-break/>

> and whoever does so, may Your hand punish him /
> With poverty, sickness, sin, and shame /
> Until he recognizes Your good pleasure /
> And does it; let everyone say Amen:
> <note>original German: Und was ich hie gestifftet hab / Daß solchs nicht werd gestellet ab / und wer das thut/den straff dein Handt / Mit Armut/Kranckheit/Sünd und Schand/ / Biß daß er deinen Wolgefall / Erkenn und thu / sprecht Amen all:</note>

But it was no less frequent among the Ancients to cast back curses upon those who had vomited them out without just cause. Hence, the most solemn formula of imprecation among both the Latins and the Greeks was to hurl those very things back upon the heads of those who had prayed for evil. In that garden of the Muses and Graces, Plautus, in his *Poenulus*, when the advocates had said that Mars was angry at Lycus, Lycus retorts: "MAY THAT BE ON YOUR OWN HEAD." <note>original Latin: CAPITI VESTRO ISTUC QUIDEM</note> From this also, if a curse had slipped out from someone unintentionally that offended another's mind, or if someone had imprecated something against another for which he later asked favor and pardon: if he wished to appease and satisfy the person, he would wish—in their presence—that those things he had said against them might fall back upon his own head.

This can be most clearly demonstrated from the Prince of Stoic Philosophy, Seneca, who, after discussing the frequent and nearly public custom of accusing others, relates this little story about Rufus: *“Rufus,”* he says, *“a man of Senatorial rank, had wished during a dinner that Caesar might not return safe from the journey he was preparing; and he had added: that all the bulls and calves wished the same. There were those who listened to these things carefully. As soon as it was light, the slave who had stood at his feet while he dined told him what he had said while drunk during the meal. He urged him to get ahead of Caesar and report himself. Following this advice, he met Caesar as he was coming down. And since he swore he had a ‘bad mind’ the day before, he wished THAT IT MIGHT FALL BACK ON HIM AND HIS SONS, and he asked Caesar to forgive him and return into his favor.”* 

The same Seneca, in *On Benefits, book 4, chapter 31*, says this regarding Mamercus Scaurus, the Consul, a most foul man: *“I will relate,”* he says, *“a saying of his (meaning M. Scaurus) against himself, which I remember being circulated and praised in his own presence. When he had used an obscene word against Pollio Afinius as he lay there, he said he would do that which he preferred to suffer, and when he saw Pollio’s brow contract: ‘Whatever I have spoken as a curse,’* he said, *‘BE UNTO ME AND MY OWN HEAD.’”* He used to tell this saying of his own himself; thus Seneca. We read almost the same formula in other authors. That servant of luxury, Ovid, in his *books*:

> Why do you dig out the eyes of your undeserving sons, Phineus? 
> That punishment IS DESTINED TO RETURN UPON YOUR OWN HEAD.
> <note>original Latin: Pœna REVERSURA EST IN CAPUT ista TUUM.</note>

In the same author's 19th *Epistle*, the wretched Acontius breaks out into these words:

> I am tormented at times because I am the cause of pain to you, 
> And I think you are being harmed by my cleverness. 
> I pray that the perjuries of my mistress MAY FALL UPON OUR OWN HEAD: 
> let her be safe through my punishment.
> <note>original Latin: IN CAPUT NOSTRUM domina perjuria quæso / EVENIANT: pœna tuta sit illa mea.</note>

Cicero also, in *book 7 of the Letters to Atticus*: *“When he had said many evil things,”* he says, *“they say, 'ON HIS OWN HEAD'.”* <note>original: *suo capiti*</note>. Likewise: *“from which since he is a stranger, let him omen it ON HIS OWN HEAD, provided we are safe.”* Caelius, in *Epistle 1 to Cicero, book 8 of the Letters to Friends*: *“May the people of Subustri (WHICH BE UPON THEIR OWN HEADS) scatter you and let you perish by the 9th day before the Kalends of January.”* But he who is delighted by these pleasantries should consult the most learned Barnabas Brissonius in his most elegant work on the formulas of the Roman Forum...

### Ezekiel 23:24.

-> They shall come against you with chariots and wheels, and with a multitude of people; they shall set against you buckler and shield and helmet all around. <- <note>This translates the provided Hebrew, Greek, and Latin versions of the verse.</note>

We shall describe the arms of the ancient people in parts, as each aspect of their warfare seems worthy of memory, and as much as Ezekiel provides in a handful of knowledge regarding ancient weapons <note>original Greek: *ὅπλων*</note>, explaining first the types of transport, then the weapons themselves. So that his rebuke of the crimes with which Israel and Judah had polluted themselves might appear more forceful—having neglected the true worship of God—he sets before them, as if from a high watchtower, the manner of vengeance to be viewed most clearly <note>original Greek: *ἐμφανικώτατως*</note>. He recounts the great and terrible gathering of neighboring nations, whom he leads forth with all their armor, saying: *“Behold, I will rouse your lovers (with whom you have committed fornication like an adulteress through wicked forms of worship) against you—those from whom your soul is alienated—and I will bring them against you from every side, so that they may attack you with combined forces; namely, the Chaldeans and all the Chaldean governors to whom the care of conducting the war will be entrusted, the Satraps and Leaders together with all the Assyrians, young men of excellent form, Princes and Magistrates, all of both branches of the military, Centurions and most famous soldiers, all of whom ride on horses.”*

At the first glance, the obscure titles of the Commanders and Leaders present themselves, which those who are able to weigh military names with a more exact judgment might better express. We shall set forth the versions of these and others. *Behold, I raise up your lovers against you, from whom your soul has departed, and I will bring them against you from all around. The Hebrew words are *Pekod, Shoa, and Koa* <note>original Hebrew: *פקוד ושוע וקוע*</note>, which Aquila translated as *overseer, and tyrant, and noble*. Jerome says on this passage: *Where the Hebrew has Pekod, Shoa, and Koa, many understand these to be Eastern nations; though we find names of this sort neither in the books of Kings, nor in Chronicles, nor even in Jeremiah (who describes the captivity of Jerusalem), nor in any other place of Holy Scripture. Nor is it strange, since the Seventy [the Septuagint] placed the Hebrew names themselves there, and Symmachus and Theodotion also agree on the same words.* Tremellius and his inseparable follower Piscator understood these to be specific peoples of the Assyrian kingdom, introducing the new names of the *Pekodites, Shoahites, and Koahites*. Yet it was no less frequent among the Ancients to cast curses back upon those who had vomited them out without just cause. Hence, a most solemn formula of imprecation among both the Latins and the Greeks was to hurl those very things back onto the heads of those who had prayed for evil. In the works of Plautus—that garden of the Muses and Graces—in the play *The Little Carthaginian*, when the advocates said that Mars was angry with Lycus, Lycus retorts: **MAY THAT BE UPON YOUR OWN HEAD.** From this also, if a curse escaped someone’s lips by mistake which offended another’s mind, or if someone imprecated something for which he later asked for favor and pardon; he, wanting to appease and satisfy the other, would wish in their presence that those things he had said against them might fall back upon his own head.

This can be most clearly demonstrated from Seneca, the prince of Stoic philosophy, who, after discussing the frequent and nearly public habit of accusations, recounts such a story about Rufus: *Rufus, a man of Senatorial rank, had wished during a dinner that Caesar might not return safely from the journey he was preparing; and he added that all bulls and calves wished the same. Having used an obscene word toward Asinius Pollio, he had said he would do that which he preferred to suffer; and when he saw Pollio's brow furrow: "Whatever evil I have spoken," he said,* **LET IT BE TO ME AND MY HEAD.** He used to tell this story of himself.

> *Why do you dig out the eyes of your undeserving sons, Phineus?*

> *I am tormented sometimes that I am the cause of grief to you,*
> *And I think you are harmed by my cleverness.*
> *I pray that the perjuries against my lady* **MAY FALL UPON OUR OWN HEAD:**
> *let her be safe through my punishment.*

Cicero also writes in Book 7 of his *Letters to Atticus*: *When he had said many evils,* **THEY SAY, UPON HIS OWN HEAD.** Likewise: *...from which since he is a stranger,* **LET HIM PROPHESY UPON HIS OWN HEAD,** *while we remain safe.* Caelius, in the first letter to Cicero in Book 8 of the *Letters to Friends*: *You withdrew yourself on the ninth day before the Kalends of January* (**MAY IT BE UPON THEIR HEADS**) *that they might be scattered and perish.* But he who is delighted by these pleasantries should consult the most learned Barnabas Brissonius <note>A French jurist and scholar (1531–1591) known for his work on Roman legal formulas.</note> in his most elegant work *On the Formulas of the Roman Forum*...

...in the first book. No one who has even lightly tasted the sweet writings of Demosthenes <note>A famous Greek orator of the 4th century BCE.</note> would deny that this formula is frequent among the Greeks. We read in his work: *May the gods turn these things upon your head.* <note>original Greek: Θεοί σοι ταῦτα τρέψειαν εἰς κεφαλήν</note> Likewise, in his oration *On the False Embassy*: *instead of you, he must turn it upon their heads.* <note>original Greek: ἀντὶ εἰς κεφαλεὺς ὑμᾶς αὐτῶ δεῖ τρέψαι</note> Phalaris <note>A Sicilian tyrant known for his cruelty and his "bronze bull."</note> writes in his letters: *I cast these things back upon your head.* <note>original Greek: τρέπω εἰς κεφαλήν σοι ταῦτα</note> To these one may add Aristophanies; in his work, when Dicaeopolis had commanded a Megarian to *rejoice* <note>original Greek: χαίρειν</note> and the latter replied *that is not the local custom for you*, Dicaeopolis prays *that it might fall back on his own head*, in this manner:

->*Now may it be turned upon my own head for my meddling.*<-
<note>original Greek: Πολυπραγμοσύνης νῦν ἐς κεφαλὴν τρέποιτ' ἐμοί.</note>

Where the Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator on classical texts.</note>, as Muretus <note>Marc-Antoine Muret, a 16th-century French humanist.</note> observes, relates that this was also an Athenian custom. We find nearly the same formula of imprecation in the Sacred Scriptures. In *Joshua 2:19*, the spies of Joshua establish a covenant with Rahab in these words: *And it shall be, that whosoever shall go out of the doors of thy house into the street,* <margin>his blood on his head <note>Hebrew: דמו בראשו (damo berosho)</note></margin> *his blood shall be upon his head, and we will be guiltless: and whosoever shall be with thee in the house,* <margin>his blood on our head <note>Hebrew: דמו בראשנו (damo berosho)</note></margin> *his blood shall be on our head, if any hand be upon him.* In *1 Samuel 1:16*, David says: <margin>your blood upon your head <note>Hebrew: דמיך על ראשך</note></margin> <note>Septuagint Greek: τὸ αἷμά σου ἐπὶ κεφαλῆς σου</note>—that is, *your blood be upon your head*. So too Solomon in *1 Kings 2:37* to Shimei: *on the day thou goest out, and passest over the brook Kidron, thou shalt know for certain that thou shalt surely die:* <margin>your blood shall be on your head <note>Hebrew: דמיך יהיה בראשך</note></margin> <note>Septuagint Greek: τὸ αἷμά σου ἔσται ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλήν σου</note>—that is, *your blood shall be upon your head*. Hence David, looking toward this formula, says in *Psalm 7:17*: <margin>his labor returns on his head <note>Hebrew: ישוב עמלו בראשו</note></margin> <note>Septuagint Greek: Ἐπιστρέψῃ ὁ πόνος αὐτὸ εἰς κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ</note>—that is, *his sorrow shall be turned upon his own head*. To this we can also refer *Judges 9:57* and *1 Samuel 25:39*. Furthermore, they devoted not only others, but sometimes themselves. A very clear example of this is provided to us by the faithful scribe of Jesus Christ, Saint Matthew, in *Chapter 27:25*, where all the Jewish people boldly break out into these most cruel words that can never be fully atoned for: *His blood be on us, and on our children.* <note>original Greek: αἷμα αὐτοῦ ἐφ' ἡμᾶς καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ τέκνα ἡμῶν</note> Those perverse Judeans should have been mindful of that saying of their wise men, which is found in the *188th Book of Precepts, Chapter 2* (cited by Johannes Drusius <note>A Flemish Protestant orienalist and exegete.</note>): <margin>Book 1, Precepts, page 54.</margin> *Judgments involving money are not like judgments involving souls. In money judgments, if a man gives money to his fellow, he is cleared; but in judgments of souls, his blood and the blood of his descendants hang upon him until the end of the world.* This formula of imprecation seems to remain from that common formula of swearing among the Greeks, who used to swear by the head. Regarding this, the most learned Bartholomaeus Majerus wrote, and our Savior Christ prohibited it in *Matthew 5:36* when He said: *Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black.* But before we depart from this, we cannot help but add what the wisest of the Rabbis, Aben-Esra <note>Ibn Ezra, a 12th-century biblical commentator and polymath.</note>, writes concerning the Egyptians: <margin>Book 1, Sacred Philology, page 227.</margin> *They used to swear,* he says, *by the head of the King, and whoever violated that oath was punished by the head [execution], nor could he redeem himself with any amount of money.*

We shall describe the arms of the ancient people piece by piece, as each part of their military service seems worthy of memory, and we shall provide as much knowledge as possible regarding the nature of the ancient <term>hopla</term> <note>weapons/armor</note>; since these do not exist today, it is sometimes necessary to employ conjecture rather than certain reason. *Ezekiel* presents the ancient military in a single handful, as it were, explaining first the types of transport and then the types of armor. The Greek Translators themselves hesitate regarding these names, and they supply us with three Hebrew terms as if they were things they did not fully understand. Tremellius and his inseparable follower Piscator <note>16th-century Protestant biblical scholars.</note> understood these as specific peoples of the Assyrian kingdom, introducing the new names of the *Pekodites*, *Shoahites*, and *Koahites*. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Military of the Orientals.</margin>
The English, Zurich, Worms, Genevan, Italian, and Belgian peoples agree on this. The simplicity of the Latin has translated these as "noble tyrants" and "Princes." Luther renders it: *Head-People / Princes and Lords.* Castalio: *Prefects, Emperors & Illustrious.* Osiander: *Captains, Satraps, strenuous men.* Pagninus: *Prefect, & Prince & Duke.* Vatablus: *Prefects, Princes & Dukes.* Münster: *Prefect, powerful one, and tyrant.* It is well known, says Blessed Glassius <note>Salomon Glassius (1593–1656), a Lutheran theologian and biblical critic.</note> in *Book 4 of Sacred Rhetoric, tract 3*, what these interpreters were looking for in the Hebrew words *Shoa* and *Koa* <note>original: שוע & קוע — titles of Babylonian officials in Ezekiel 23:23</note>. But regarding *Koa*, there is doubt. Pagninus says in his Lexicon: *It is possible that it belongs here* (to the root *Kua*), *the
<margin>Ezekiel 23:23.</margin>
noun Toar, meaning a noble and honorable man.* * A leader or wealthy and honorable man: Rabbi Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish grammarian and commentator.</note> says: *Pekod, Shoa, and Koa* are names of *Toar* <note>meaning titles or descriptions</note> which apply to the princes who are mentioned by name in Jeremiah: Nebuzaradan, Nebushasban, Serezer, Rabmag, and the others recorded there. Forsterus <note>Johann Forster (1496–1556), a Hebrew scholar.</note> in his Lexicon derives *Koa* from *Ka'aka*, which signifies a brand or sign impressed upon
<margin>Leviticus 19:28.</margin>
the body; * *Ka'aka* (he says) refers to a man distinguished by such marks, as was the custom of the Babylonians, so that their leading men were distinguished by such marks impressed into the flesh. But let us step away from our discussion of titles and turn to military instruments, contemplating each in order. First, we must speak of vehicles and chariots, in which either the necessities of war were carried, or from which the fighting was done. Here, the gloss of Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius (1510–1580), a prominent Jewish-Italian convert and Hebraist.</note> presents itself, which is rarely found among the couriers. He says *three types of transport are posited: first, scythed chariots; second, wagons or covered carriages, which were vaulted for the comfort and protection of the passengers; third,* "hog-wagons" <note>original Greek: χοιραμαξῶν — likely a light, narrow cart</note> *or light chariots, if you wish to speak with Festus about a very light kind of chariot,* in which sometimes a single man could be held, standing in a narrow box to wage battle from there. Those who have the leisure to be occupied with the "litters of wagons" <note>original Greek: φορείοις ἀσχολζεῖν</note> may weigh which chariots and carriages he describes. From the category of wagons, we will restrict ourselves to the scythed chariots, which others call "iron-clad" <note>original Greek: ἐγχοινῶς — meaning fitted with points or spears</note>, so that we might exercise our memory, having become well-versed in the ancients <note>original Greek: παλαιωθέντες</note>. The military of the ancients relied very heavily on scythed chariots. These were equipped with iron scythes on both sides of the wheels, about two cubits long, with which they charged at full speed into the middle of the enemy line to cut through and break the armed ranks. The Canaanites of old, who lived in the flat and level country, used to use this kind of fighting vehicle, and for this reason, the sons of Joseph—the two tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh—feared them with a cowardly dread, despairing of seizing the land from its ancient owners,
<margin>Joshua 17:16.</margin>
while * they say from a reluctant spirit: *We shall not be able to ascend to the mountains, nor to cut down those forests which you have assigned as our inheritance, since the Canaanites, who live in the land of that valley, and those in Beth-shean and its villages, and in the valley of Jezreel, use iron chariots.* The Ephraimites and Manassehites allowed themselves to be distracted by various fears because they had seen the inhabitants of the valleys armed for every danger, and their own path blocked in the mountain passes from which they might escape the hazards of war; they distrusted victory once they noticed the inhabitants were equipped with iron and scythed chariots, which they themselves lacked, and that they lived in the most fortified cities. But

<column-break/>

Joshua, the edge of the military, persisted in his opinion, praising his fellow soldiers for their ancestral fortitude, so that he believed nothing so hostile, so fierce, or so atrocious could be offered that could not be turned aside and put to flight through divine help. They received a public testimony of fortitude: * *You are a numerous people, and great is your strength. You shall cross the mountain, and you shall expel the Canaanite, even though he has iron chariots and even though he is strong.* Go with a lucky foot, carry your banners forward without trembling, despise the vastness of the place and the monstrous nature of the chariots; even if the enemy has placed his defensive protections in them, do not fear. Lean upon divine help, for with that support, you will not only easily cross those mountains and forests, but you will also subjugate all the lowland cities of the Perizzites and the Rephaim, though they be most fortified. The descendants of Joseph had complained about the narrow spaces of the seat assigned to them and the straitness of their borders, and had said in protest: *Why have you given me only one lot for a possession, since I am a numerous people, and one tribe could scarcely suffice to possess it?* However, since we have said much on this passage of Joshua above, we do not wish to be more prolific here. Among the military garments designed for the protection of the body, the first place is occupied by the *breastplate* (lorica), so named from the thongs (loris). Although today it consists only of iron, formerly it was usually made of leather thongs, as we see in the ancient statues of Emperors. Diodorus attributes linen ones to the Athenians, given by Iphicrates instead of bronze ones. Plutarch, in his Life of Alexander, testifies that Alexander was accustomed to wear such a thing, as were the Greek heroes in the *Iliad* Book 2, line 539, where it is said of Ajax, son of Oileus, that he wore a linen thorax <note>breastplate</note>,

->—— he was small, wearing a linen breastplate. <-
<note>original Greek: ὀλίγος μὲν ἔην, λινοθώρηξ.</note>

The Poet also brings in the Achaeans dressed in bronze breastplates in the *Iliad* Book 2, lines 47, 163, and elsewhere.

->—— by the ships of the bronze-clad Achaeans <-
<note>original Greek: κατὰ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων</note>

The same Poet testifies this concerning Agamemnon, *where among other things his breastplate is described as having* ten paths of black cyano <note>original: "cyano" — likely lapis lazuli or a dark blue steel</note>, *twelve of gold, and twenty of tin*, but "path" (oimos) is used metaphorically in this place, and it seems to signify the lines and spaces drawn across the thorax, according to the opinion of Stephanus. In the Sacred Books, Goliath (*1 Samuel 17:5*) walks armed in a steel helmet, in an iron shoulder-piece, and in a scaled breastplate, which the Septuagint translated as "a breastplate of chain-links," <note>original Greek: θώρακας ἁλυσιδωτὸς</note> <note>original Hebrew: שריון קשקשים - literally "breastplate of scales"</note> that is, chained or *branched* breastplates, at which Statius undoubtedly aims with these words,

> *Thin chains repeat the manifold breastplate.*

In Dio Cassius, regarding Macrinus, we find "scaled breastplates" <note>original Greek: θώρακας τὰς λεπιδωτὸς</note>; in Plutarch's *Lucullus*, an "iron breastplate" <note>original Greek: θώρακα σιδηρᾶν</note>; in Virgil, *a breastplate triple-woven with gold,*

> *A breastplate woven with hooks, and triple-threaded with gold.*

because, since it was woven with iron hooks and scales, it was furthermore adorned with three threads running through it. Thus he also called a breastplate "double-threaded" in *Book 12 of the Aeneid*. The garment which was worn over the armor was the *Sagum* (military cloak): for the Romans had certain garments destined only for military duties, which Polybius clearly indicates were given to the soldier from the public treasury, and we see this noted several times in Livy. ### Ezekiel 23:24. Page 665

<margin>Military of the Orientals.</margin>
The military cloak <note>original: *sagum*</note> was as much the proper dress for wars as the toga was for peace; hence you may frequently find in Cicero such phrases as *to go to the military cloak, to put on the military cloak, the city is in its military cloaks, to return to the toga*. This type of garment was followed by the *Lacerna* <note>a sleeveless open cloak worn over the tunic</note>, see also the *fringed pallas*, which once only soldiers used, as the Scholiast of Persius notes—who correctly added the word "once," because city-dwellers later began to wear the *lacerna*, as Salmasius showed at length and learnedly in his notes on the *Augustan History*. There he also discusses the nature of the *penula* <note>a heavy traveling cloak</note>, which differs in no way from the *lacerna* themselves, not even in their use in war, wherefore "cloaked slaves" <note>original: *Servi penulati*</note> are mentioned by Seneca in his *3rd book On Benefits, chapter 28, equipped in the dress of soldiers, and indeed not of the common sort*; see also Philippus Rubenus, *2. Elect. 12*, and Gabriel Naudé on *Military Study, book 1, pages 327–328, Roman edition, 1637*. The Prophet describes the enemies of the Jews as being equipped with, among other weapons, the *shield* <note>original: *clypeo*</note>. Frequently one instrument is named to imply all of them. Thus, by the name of the shield and the word for the helmet positioned in this place, all instruments of war are to be understood. Plutarch uses this same synecdoche <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note> regarding Crassus, who was unskilled in military matters, citing the Comic poet: *A man most excellent in other things, except in [matters of] the shield.* <note>original: Ἀνὴρ ἄριστος τὰ ἄλλα, πλὴν ἐν ἀσπίδι</note> Furthermore, the weapons of the ancients were varied: some were protective <note>original: σκεπαστήρια</note> for covering the body, such as greaves <margin>Iliad 11. v. 17, 18.</margin> and leggings, concerning which Homer says:

<margin>Iliad 11. v. 14.</margin>
->First he placed the greaves around his legs,<-
->Beautiful ones, fitted with silver ankle-guards.<-

<margin>Iliad 11. v. 17.</margin>
To this category should be referred the breastplates <note>original: *thoraces*</note>, the helmet or headpiece <note>original: κόρυς or περικεφαλαία</note>, and the various types of shields <note>original: *aspis, sakos, thyreos, scutum, clypeus*</note>. Other weapons were defensive <note>original: ἀμυντήρια</note> for repelling attacks, such as the lance, the spear, the javelin, and the sword. Regarding shields, the distinction between the *clypeus* and the *scutum* deserves note. An *aspis* is properly a *clypeus*, circular in shape, whence the city *Clypea* in Africa (called *Clupea* by Pliny) formerly took its name *Aspis* from the shape of a shield. The *thyreos* is a *scutum*, oblong in shape, as Turnebus teaches in many places in *Adversaria, book 9, ch. 27*, as does Aldus Manutius in *book 2 of Inquiries by Letter*. As Homer in *Iliad 5, v. 428* makes shields well-rounded and bossed <note>having a central decorative knob</note>, Eustathius notes on page 966 from ancient sources that not all shields were circular or well-rounded, but some were "stretched" <note>original: ἐπιμήκεις</note>, derived from the word meaning to extend or expand; from this is derived the *aspis* that is oblong, and the *aspis* that is not extended in length but gathered into a circle. Thus Virgil imagines that under the forehead of the Cyclops Polyphemus lay a single huge eye, *like an Argolic shield or the lamp of Phoebus [the sun]*; on this matter one should read Sylburgius’s preface to Pausanias. There was not just one <margin>Iliad 4. v. 16.</margin> material for shields among the ancients, concerning which see Alardus’s notes on Flaccus, page 418. For shields were constructed from leather, either alone or with wood added; compare Lipsius, *On the Roman Military, p. 143*, and Basil’s *2nd Sermon on Fasting*. Reading about leather shields, and indeed those made of bull-hide <note>original: ταυρείων</note>, is frequent among the ancients. Homer says of a shield covered in bull-hide:

<margin>Iliad 11. v. 18.</margin>
->And he struck, and did not miss, against the shield everywhere equal<-
->made of bull-hide.<-

<margin>6. Anth. 25. n. 5. v. 1. p. 925.</margin>
Concerning a shield made from bull-skins in the *Anthology*:

->A shield of bull-hide, a defense for the skin, which many times<-
->has tasted the spear of the enemy in its guts.<-

They used to layer several skins over one another so that the shields would be stronger. For this Homeric passage teaches:
<margin>Iliad 17. v. 141</margin>

<margin>Iliad 1. 479.</margin>
->around his shoulders he placed a four-layered shield.<-

<column-break/>

<margin>Military of the Orientals.</margin>
And Hesychius explains—undoubtedly looking back to this passage—that "four-layered" <note>original: τετραθέλυμνον</note> means four-fold, placed from four folds, that is, upon a foundation or having four layers one upon the other, composed of four skins. Whence Ludovicus Romanus <note>Ludovico di Varthema, a 15th-century Italian traveler.</note> reports concerning the soldiers serving under the Sultan of Arabia and using leather shields: <margin>2. Navigation, 4. p. 210.</margin> *Entering wars they use circular shields. These consist of two buffalo hides, with four small rods running between them, which, by some sort of cement, do not allow the hides to slip apart. Multiple paintings decorate shields of this kind, making it so that you would believe nothing is more beautiful to see, and nothing is more suited for avoiding blows; they do not exceed the size of the mouth of a jar. For a handle they have only as much of a plank as the hand itself can grasp, and they secure it with twin nails*. Homer is a witness to the variegated shield of Achilles, stating that it was equipped with five layers, *Iliad 18, v. 481*:

->and there were five layers of the shield itself,<-

Thus in *Iliad 20, v. 275*, he also mentions five folds: "since," he says, "the club-footed god [Hephaestus] forged five folds." In the fight of Ajax with Hector, he recounts the shield of Ajax having seven skins in its weaves, wherefore he calls it a "seven-fold ox-hide shield," *Iliad 7, v. 245*, because the striking Hector penetrated to the seventh skin.

->And the unwearying bronze went through six folds, cutting them.<-
->But in the seventh hide it was held.<-

According to Suidas, the "folds" <note>original: πτυχαὶ</note> are called the different plates of the shield laid upon one another. Polybius hands down the method of making shields common to the ancient Romans in *History, book 6, p. 468*. Shields were also made of bronze, hence Livy in *book 1*: *Arms were twice ordered: helmet, shield, greaves, breastplate, all made of bronze*. Virgil in <margin>1. Aeneid.</margin> *Aeneid, book 1*:

->A great shield made of hollow bronze, the equipment of Abas<-
->and book 2:<-
->and he binds the bronze shield to his left arm<-

Ovid says of the shield of Achilles in *Metamorphoses 12*:

->He spoke, and sent the spear destined to stick in the curve of the shield<-
->against the descendant of Aeacus, which broke both the bronze and the next<-
->nine layers of ox-hide, yet it was stopped by the tenth circle.<-

By metonymy, "bronze" is used here for the "shield." Hence Festus says: *The term "proffered bronze" in Ennius signifies a shield held out before oneself*. Likewise Hesychius: *a clattering shield, for it has an overlay of bronze*. Polyhaenus also mentions "bronze-covered shields" in *book 7*. Thus Virgil commends the shield of Pallas from this fact, <margin>Aeneid, book 10</margin>

->- - - A shield with so many layers of iron, so many of bronze,<-
->while the bull-hide goes around it so many times.<-

There was a double benefit from this: the hardness of the metal blunted the point of the thrown weapon, and the flexibility of the leather broke the throw and the blow; compare Dasque's annotations to Quintus Calabrus, p. 77. The custom of honoring shields was also frequent among the ancients; for shields were dedicated in shrines for the proclamation of illustrious men, which Philo (p. 782) calls the "honors of shields." In time of peace and when war was finished, they were hung in temples; hence "to hang the shield" in Suidas means to make peace. Likewise, in honor of these men, military standards were decorated with shields, whose images were superstitiously adored, as Grotius witnesses in his notes on the *New Testament, p. 407*. From this, their use prevailed among almost everyone. Concerning the Goths...

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
# Page 666

<margin>Military of the Orientals.</margin> Regarding the Goths, Olaus Magnus writes in *History of the Northern Peoples*, book 8, chapter 5, page 263: "It is the most ancient custom of the Gothic nobility to attend the public assemblies of Princes with such insignia—namely, the helmet, spear, and shield—and to defend the liberty and justice of the fatherland with arms of this kind." Concerning the Indians in the city of Chaul and neighboring regions, Vartomannus reports in *Voyages*, book 4, chapter 3, page 228: "They are quite ready for war; in battles they use the sword, bows, reed spears, and circular shields." He writes the same regarding the people of Calicut in book 5, chapter 11, page 241. Furthermore, a certain Greek law contributed to the greater veneration of shields; it provided that those who lost their sword or spear were not punished, but those who lost their shield were fined. Thus, the dying Epaminondas <note>a famous Theban general</note> asked whether his shield was safe. And Spartan women, when sending their sons off to military service, were accustomed to say, "Either with this, or on this," <note>original: ἢ σὺν τούτῳ, ἢ ἐпὶ τούτῳ</note> meaning that their sons must return either with the shield (victorious) or carried dead upon the shield. For shields were of such height that, as Homer witnesses in the *Iliad*, book 8, verse 646, the whole body was protected from the top of the head to the very bottom of the feet against incoming arrows:

-> "which he himself wore, a defense reaching to the feet against javelins." <-
-> <note>original Greek: τὴν αὐτὸς φορέεσκε, ποδηνεκὲς ἔρκος ἀκόντων</note> <-

Homer praises the Shield of Achilles, fashioned by Vulcan, in many words, as does Hesiod for the shield of Hercules; see these descriptions in their proper places. But let the *Shield of Achilles* yield, let it yield from here—the shield on which Vulcan is said to have depicted the entire variety of the stars, and then added all the parts and duties of peace and war. A deeper meaning underlies this, as Homer imagines God as the author of the shield and the engraver of the celestial orbs and even the world itself. Theologians may take from this a "knowledge of God" <note>original: γνώστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ</note>; likewise, mathematicians may find an argument for their science. Let the *Shield of Ulysses* yield, upon which was engraved a dolphin, a music-loving animal. Let the shield of Aventinus yield, which:

-> "bears the emblem of his parents: <-
-> a hundred snakes and a hydra encircled by serpents." <-

The guardianship of the Angels, with which God protects us, is a shield superior to the seven-fold shield of Ajax celebrated by Homer. King David the Prophet, most experienced in every kind of warfare and weaponry, delighted greatly in his Odes in the emblem of the *shield and buckler*, the sword, etc., by which he celebrated his confidence in Divine protection. Through the laws of these military instruments which he saw before his eyes, he recalled to mind divine protection, drawing hope in the midst of the difficulties and hardships of life that he was covered and defended by a divine shield. Hence the wisest of Kings <note>Solomon</note>, commending God’s protection in *Song of Solomon* 4:4, compares it to the tower or armory of David, in which hang a thousand shields and all the bucklers of the mighty. Upon these words, Haimo writes on page 57 of his commentary on this passage: *By "a thousand shields" are understood the innumerable protections of divine defense, with which the Holy Church is enclosed and defended.* Let us also hear Ludovicus Crefollius in *Sacred Anthology*, final chapter, page 539, on this passage: *When the Wise Man wished to sketch the inexplicable power of the divine shield, he gives the holy soul a thousand shields from the tower—that is, hanging from the neck—which clearly surround the heart and breast, the home of the soul and the tabernacle of grace. Here the learned Solomon expressed the custom of nations when he equipped his heroine as if covered by the protection of the weapons of heaven. For the peoples in the East,*

<column-break/>

*when going out to war, suspended their shields from the neck by straps and threw them back over the left shoulder until they came to hand-to-hand combat,* as Herodotus is the witness. Therefore, he says a thousand shields hang from the neck of the Bride—that is, innumerable ones—yet the firmness and strength of these is surpassed by this single shield of the Deity. Regarding this shield-bearing Tower, Barlæus also sings in *Heroics*, book 4, page 593:

> Your cheeks glow, O Bride; your neck is most like a tower,
> Which stands completely open for war; a valley so iron,
> Fortified in so many ways. You may see from afar in a long line
> The hanging shields of ancestors, and shields fastened
> To new shields, the bucklers of leaders, and spears with bows,

And long swords, and blades fixed to hollow breastplates.
Among shields and bucklers, the <term>pelta</term> <note>original: πέλτη; a light, crescent-shaped shield</note> occupies a significant place; it is a shorter shield, having no strap, which archers and light-armed soldiers used. Whence Plutarch in *Artaxerxes*: "having fastened on his quiver and carrying his pelta." And regarding Alexander's fortune: "Ptolemy held the pelta over him," protecting and guarding Alexander with the pelta. Hesychius and Suidas say it is a shield that does not have a rim or boss <note>the central protruding knob</note> on its circumference. Virgil called them *crescent-shaped peltas* because their form reflected the likeness of the waxing moon; hence in *Aeneid*, book 1:

-> "She leads the ranks of the Amazons with crescent peltas." <-

Quintus Calaber introduces Penthesilea protected by a shield like the orb of the moon, in *Fall of Troy*, book 1:
-> "In place [of another] she took up a divine shield, like a moon, in place of a single one." <-
Where the word *aspis* <note>usually a large round shield</note> is used loosely for *pelta* by Calaber, as Dausque notes on this verse, page 19. For the *aspis* is a full circle, as is known from Eustathius’s etymology; the Amazonian pelta is a half-circle. Therefore, Arrian considerately attributes to the Amazons "axes instead of spears, and peltas instead of shields" in book 7. Hesiod <note>likely a mistake for Pliny or similar naturalist</note> in book 12, chapter 5, says of fig leaves: "The width of the leaves has the appearance of an Amazonian pelta." And Isidore Clarius says: "The pelta is a very short shield in the manner of a half-moon." Furthermore, the Prophet describes the enemies of Jerusalem as helmeted. That was a beautiful sight, and fearsome to the enemy, says Polybius, primarily because of the shape, such as appears everywhere in the monuments of the ancient age. They were open in the front, says Lipsius, with some protrusion of iron, but turned back, whence they were also called *Silae* by Festus: "*Silus* is the name for one with an upturned nose, whence helmets were also called such from the similarity to the *Sila*." The images of the ancients testify that helmets were once made primarily from the hides of wild beasts; hence in Homer a helmet is called <term>ktideēn</term> <note>musteline</note>, made of weasel-skin, in *Iliad* 10, lines 335, 458; where manuscripts read *ktideēn* for <term>kyneēn</term> <note>canine</note>, made of dog-skin, in *Iliad* 8, lines 176, 187, by which epithet the helmet of Agamemnon and Ajax is celebrated; and <term>taureiēn</term> <note>taurine</note>, made of bull-hide, in *Iliad* 10, line 268. The helmet of Diomedes and Ulysses consisted of such hide, "without a cone and without a crest," which was called a *kataytyx*. For helmets were usually adorned with crests and a feathered peak, as Polybius has it, whence the helmet of Paris is called "horse-haired" <note>original: ἵпπειos</note>, crested from horsehair, in *Iliad* 3, verse 337; and Lycon in *Iliad* 16, verse 338, struck the "cone of the horse-haired helmet" <note>original: ἱппоκόμος κόρυς</note> of Peneleos. Regarding the various ornamentation of helmets, see Lipsius in the cited place. So also, finally, a helmet is called "caprine" <note>original: αἰγείην</note>, of goat-skin, by Homer in *Odyssey* 24, verse 230. Whence also Suidas:

Suidas <note>a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> mentions the *alopekia* <term>original: ἀλωπεκία; a fox-skin cap</term> (as Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius, a 16th-century humanist scholar</note> writes) as a type of helmet <term>original: ἡ περικεφαλαία</term>, literally "fox-like" <term>original: vulpina</term>. Even Propertius * says:
> And a helmet adorned with a shaggy wolf-mane.
> <note>original Latin: Et galea hirsuta comta Lupina juba</note>

Eventually, however, bronze helmets came into common use, as recognized by the historians Livy and Dionysius, and they were forged from various other materials. When Camillus <note>a Roman general</note> led his soldiers against the Gauls and their massive swords, he "forged," in the words of Plutarch in his *Life of Camillus*, "helmets for most of them that were entirely of iron and smooth around the edges, so that swords would either slide off them or be broken." <note>original Greek: ἐχαλκεύσατο... κράνη τοῖς πλείστοις ὁλοσίδηρα καὶ λεῖα ταῖς περιφερείαις, ὡς ἀπολισθαίνειν ἢ κατάγνυσθαι τὰς μαχαίρας</note> Yet, because of old habits, the ancient name was nonetheless retained, as Eustathius <note>a 12th-century scholar and archbishop</note> indicates in his commentary on the *Iliad*, book 3, with these words: "The name has not yet fallen out of use; even a head-protector made of any other material is called a *kyneen* <note>literally 'dog-skin'</note> because of the ancient practice, just as we still call iron weapons 'bronzes' because of the old ways." <note>original Greek: τὸ δ᾽ ὄνομα οὐκ ἐκλέλοιпεν... κυνέην καλεῖται διὰ τὴν παλαιὰν χρῆσιν... χαλκέα φαμὲν, διὰ τὸ ἀρχαῖον</note>

<margin>Isaiah 59:17</margin>
In wondrous ways, Isaiah * depicts God wearing a helmet; regarding this description, see Osorius, Volume 5, page 714. When the prophet Nahum was set to explain the struggles, calamities, captivity, and total desolation of the Ninevites, he predicted in the name of the Lord <term>original: Jehovah</term> that soon there would be heard the sound of the whip, the noise of the rumbling wheels, the horses shaking the earth, and jumping chariots; moreover, the horseman raising himself up, the glittering sword, and the flashing spear (Nahum 3:2-3). You hear seven "voices" or sounds here: 1. the sound of the whip; 2. the sound of the rushing wheel; 3. the sound of the snorting horse; 4. the sound of the charging chariot; 5. the sound of the ascending horseman; 6. the sound of the glittering sword; 7. the sound of the flashing spear. The fury of the combatants is described by this seven-fold number in such a way that the famous painter Apelles could hardly depict it better with his brush. Jerome says that this description of an army preparing for battle is so beautiful and "picture-like" that any words of his own would seem cheap by comparison. We touched upon earlier how much force the scythed chariots had when their horses were driven into the enemy with a whip, causing great slaughter. For there was great use of horses, camels, and elephants in war, even if infantry might seem superior to cavalry; compare Riccius, *On the German War*, page 270.

<margin>Lipsius, Book 3 on Roman Military, page 253</margin>
Despite this, the cavalry was immense among the Orientals, especially the Egyptians, Syrians, and Assyrians, when waging war. Hence Shishak, King of the Egyptians, is recorded to have marched against Rehoboam, King of Judah, with sixty thousand horsemen (2 Chronicles 12:3). From the Syrians who aided the Ammonites, forty thousand horsemen were routed, as reported in 2 Samuel 10:18. Among the Israelites, infantry was the prevailing condition of military service; none of the Kings among the Israelites ever had such a large force of horsemen in arms except Solomon, of whom the author of 1 Kings 10:26 reports that he had one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the King in Jerusalem. For the rest, the dignity of military service among both the ancient Romans and others consisted in the cavalry, and they therefore attributed a great deal to equestrian exercises, regarding which one should see Lipsius, *On the Roman Military*,

Dialogue 7. As concerns camels and elephants, Curtius (Book 8, chapters 12-13; Book 9, chapter 2) is a witness that their use in battles was not small. Regarding camels, one may read Vegetius, *On Military Matters*, Book 3, chapter 23, page 56. Furthermore, God threatens with a flaming sword and a flashing spear. In Homer *, the sword is called *phasganon*.

<margin>Iliad, Book 1, line 190</margin>
> "and he, drawing his sharp sword from beside his thigh."
> <note>original Greek: ἡ δ’ αὖτε φάσγανον ὀξὺ ἐρυσσάμενος παρὰ μηροῦ</note>

According to the Etymologist, the word *phasganon* <note>sword</note> is derived from *ganymai* <term>I shine</term> and from *phao* <term>I kill</term>, so that the sword's form and its final purpose are indicated simultaneously. This definition fits perfectly with the epithet given to the sword by the Prophet in this passage. Thus, in Psalm 7:13, God is said to be "polishing his sword" <term>original Greek: στιλβῶν μάχαιραν</term>, that is, "making it bright, wiping it so that it glitters," and by extension, so that it flashes. The word for sword, *gladius*, was said by Varro <note>a Roman scholar</note> to come from *clades* <term>slaughter</term>, and its use was widespread everywhere. When a war ended, swords were hung in temples as dedications to the Gods (Bartholinus on Claudian, page 1355). For this reason, the Sword of Goliath, with which David had killed him, was guarded with great care. It was wrapped in a cloth with the Ephod—that garment of such great dignity—and David considered himself blessed to have that very sword in his hands; for he immediately fled, safe and undaunted with it, from the face of King Saul (1 Samuel 21:9-10). In the past and even today, the sword is carried before Kings during their investiture, a ritual mentioned by Boeckler in *History of the Baltic Regions*, page 174. When God punishes with sharp vengeance in temporal penalties, He is described "as one drawing a sword" <term>original Greek: ὡς ξιφουλκῶν</term>, and is accustomed to sending pestilence and famine. These three are joined in three prophetic sayings, such as Jeremiah 14:12 and Ezekiel 6:11, where these words are read:
-> "Alas, on account of all the evil abominations of the house of Israel, <-
-> who shall fall by the sword, and by famine, and by pestilence." <-

As for whoever is far off (verse 12), he shall fall by the sword <term>original Greek: ἐν ῥομφαίᾳ πεσεῖται</term>; and whoever remains and is besieged shall die by famine <term>original Greek: ἐν λιμῷ συντελεσθήσεται</term>. Later, in chapter 7:15: "The sword is outside, and pestilence and famine are within." He who is in the field shall die by the sword, and him who is in the city, famine and pestilence shall consume. Therefore, in the Holy Scriptures, "devouring" <term>original: voratio</term> is very often attributed to the sword (Deuteronomy 32:42; 2 Samuel 11:26, 12:25, 18:8; Jeremiah 11:30, 47:10, 14; Isaiah 12:27, 31:8). By the same metaphor, a "mouth" is attributed to war by Homer *:
<margin>Iliad, Book 19, line 313</margin>

To which Eustathius adds: "Seeing something new, if he calls the warriors the 'mouth' of war as they eat each other up." So Cicero * says: "She was snatched and preserved from every royal attack and from the very mouth and jaws of the whole war." <margin>In defense of Archias.</margin> "Close-fighting weapons" <term>original Greek: Ἀγχίμαχα ὅπλα</term> are swords and spears, with which we fight at close quarters as well as from a distance. Regarding swords, being the most ancient and common type of weapon, there can be no doubt. However, since there is more than one type of sword, we think they should be discussed distinctly. From the Assyrians came that type of sword called the *acinaces* <note>a short, curved scimitar</note>, which all of Asia has used constantly for so many centuries. For they fought by hacking rather than stabbing, since their military was almost entirely cavalry. The Israelite *chereb* <note>Hebrew for sword</note> seems to have been not a curved *acinaces*, but a straight sword, which they could use for both stabbing and hacking, like Europeans. ...curved, not unlike sickles, which they call *Copidas* <note>original: Copidas; from the Greek 'kopis,' a heavy curved knife or cleaver</note>, and with which they would strike at the limbs of great beasts. This weapon is frequently attributed to the Persians and Barbarians by Xenophon in *The Education of Cyrus* (Book 2, Chapters 6 and 7); see also Plutarch’s *Life of Alexander*. Justus Lipsius discusses the origin, use, and excellence of the Spanish sword in Book 3 of *Roman History*, Dialogue 3. The use of spears and lances is also of great antiquity. The *Spear* <term>original: Hasta; the traditional Roman spear</term> was a sign for declaring war, according to Barthius in his notes on Claudian (page 1336). Cluverius writes about the lances of the ancient Germans in *Ancient Germany* (page 296). They were fashioned from cornel wood, hazel, or even ash, which Ovid mentions in
<margin>
Book 10 of *Metamorphoses*, line 16.
</margin>
*And fragile hazel and ash useful for spears.*
Hence, at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, the gods are imagined to have been present with gifts: "And Chiron gave to Peleus an ashen spear, Poseidon gave the horses Balios and Xanthos, Hephaestus a sword, and the others gave various things," as recorded by Apollodorus in Book 3 of his *Library* (page 189). Moses testifies regarding Phinehas in Numbers 25:7, that taking up a lance, he pierced through the Israelite and the Midianite woman. Regarding this deed, Jerome writes to Sabinian: "Beware, lest Phinehas transfix you with his spear while you are fornicating with a Midianite woman, you who have polluted a brother and kinsman more than the Virgin Tamar." On this passage, Erasmus observes that some manuscripts had *fero hasta consigat* <note>may he pierce with a wild spear</note>, some *ferro hasta* <note>with the iron of the spear</note>, and some *syromaste* <note>with a javelin</note>. Jerome would have written it thus, were it not for a single letter needing correction. For the Seventy <note>the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> use that term in Numbers chapter 25. Hesychius <note>an ancient Greek lexicographer</note> defines it: *Seiromastes* <term>original: Σειρομάστης</term> is a type of javelin. *Seiromastes* means a spear-bearer and a type of lance. The same author later says: *Seiromastes* is the shaft of a lance, a long sword. *Syromastes* is an iron tool which tax collectors carry, having a wooden handle. Add to this Meursius in his *Greeko-Barbarian Glossary*. Jerome himself says to the priest Riparius against Vigilantius: "For I have read of the *Stromastes* <note>likely a corruption of Seiromastes</note> of Phinehas, the austerity of Elijah, the zeal of Simon the Canaanite, and the severity of Peter in punishing Ananias and Sapphira." Basil, in his work *On Anger and Enmity*, invokes the same history: "He used his anger as was necessary by driving the *seiromastes* through both of them." These points are from Gronovius’s *Observations* (chapter 19, page 201). Truly, the spears of the ancients were not of a single length. Those used by the Macedonians were very long and strong, which Alexander the Great called for according to Curtius when he had to fight against elephants and their drivers. Among the Romans, there were three types of spears: The *Amentated Spear* <term>original: Hasta amentata</term> was named from the *amentum* or strap, made in such a way that it could be thrown with greater force. The *Handled Spear* <term>original: Hasta ansata</term> took its name from the *ansa* or handle. The *Skirmisher’s Spear* <term>original: Hasta velitaris</term> was named for the *Velites* <note>light-armed Roman infantry</note>, which they threw from a distance. The principal duty of the *Velites* was to hurl javelins. Polybius calls such a spear a *grosphos* <term>original: γρόσφος</term>, and from this, he calls the *Velites* "javelin-fighters" <term>original: γροσφομάχοι</term>, whence some apply that line of Homer
<margin>
Book 8, section 14.
</margin>
to this:
<margin>
Odyssey, book 4, line 631.
</margin>
<margin>
...hurling javelins...
</margin>
<note>original Greek: αἰγανέῃσιν ἱέντες</note>
On which his commentator Eustathius says: "The ancients say that the *aiganea* is the *grosphos*, a small javelin, and one must ask whether the term has been corrupted." Livy (Book 31) and Ovid in *Ibis* testify that the *Velites*, after hurling their spears, engaged in hand-to-hand combat.

> And as the spear of the skirmisher seeks the soil full of yellow sand,
> Not yet warmed at the start of the battle.
> <note>original Latin: Utque petit primo plenum flaventis arena / Nondum calfacti velitis hasta solum.</note>

<column-break/>

There are, however, those who understand the poet to be speaking of the equestrian training ground rather than a battle; see Salmasius in *On Roman Military Matters* (page 176). Lipsius, however, in Book 3, Dialogue 1 (page 102), thinks that "skirmisher" <term>original: velitem</term> is used here for "javelin-thrower." For this purpose, one may read Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century encyclopedist</note>, who numbers the skirmishers among the gladiators: "The fight of the *Velites*," he says, "was such that they would throw missiles back and forth; their combat was varied and more pleasing to spectators than the rest. They were called *Velites* from a city of the Etruscans called *Veletes* <note>referring to Veii</note>." So says he. Whatever the case may be, the ambiguity, as is manifest, lies not in the thing itself but in the name. We must speak of those *Velites* whom Livy records among the light-armed soldiers, and whose invention and institution is recounted by Valerius Maximus (Book 2, Chapter 3) in this manner: "The use of *Velites* was first invented in that war in which the Commander Fulvius Flaccus besieged Capua. For since the cavalry of the Campanians, by frequent charges, could not be resisted by our cavalry because they were fewer in number, the Centurion Quintus Navius chose the most agile-bodied men from the infantry, armed them with seven short, curved spears and a small shield, and taught them to mount behind the cavalry with a swift jump and then drop down with a quick movement, so that the infantry, placed within the cavalry battle, could more easily strike the men and horses of the enemy with their missiles. This novelty in fighting weakened the only hope of the treacherous Campanians. Therefore, honor is still held for its author, Navius." Thus says he. And these were placed in the first line among the Romans. In the second were the *Hastati* <note>spearmen</note>, who were reserves for the *Velites*. In the third were the *Principes* <note>leading men</note>, who served as reserves for the *Hastati*. In the fourth and final line were the *Triarii* <note>third-rankers</note>, who, placed as reserves for the *Principes* behind everyone else, closed the rear line; consult Salmasius, *On Roman Military Matters* (chapter 12, page 133). Before these *Velites*, *Slingers*, *javelin-throwers*, and *Archers* were in use. Concerning the *Slingers* <term>original: Funditores</term>, they took their name from the *sling* <term>original: funda</term>. In the Holy Scriptures, a simile of the sling is used to describe the wretched state of the wicked: "The soul of your enemies shall be slung out from the middle of the hollow of a sling." <note>1 Samuel 25:29</note> That is, the Lord will cast away the life of enemies as if with a sling and will exterminate the wicked from the land of the living. Our version: *The soul of your enemy will be slung with the sling.* <note>original German: Die Seele deiner Feind wird geschleudert werden mit der Schleuder.</note> In Hebrew it is *Kaph ha-kela* <gloss>original: כף הקלע; palm of the sling</gloss>. Rabbi Solomon says in his gloss on this passage that the "palm of the sling" is a piece of leather made wide like a palm in the middle of the sling, where the stone is placed. The Benjamites are celebrated for their sling throwing; seven hundred of them could throw stones with slings at a fixed target so accurately that they could even hit a hair (Judges 20:16). Nor should David be deprived of his praise in the art of throwing, who struck the Philistine Goliath in the forehead with a stone thrown from a sling, so that he fell upon his face on the ground (1 Samuel 17:49). Among the pagans, the Balearic slingers are held to be no less skilled than they are strong. Diodorus Siculus says of them: "They throw stones much larger than others, and with such force that the missile seems to be carried as if from a catapult." They sent stones or leaden missiles from the sling so intensely and robustly that they broke through shields, helmets, and every covering of armor. Again he says: "They crush shields and helmets and every protective weapon." Nevertheless, Livy prefers to these the Roman invention used in the storming of the Samians. His words are these: "One was invented to restrain the hardly..."
