...it is a matter of no small record. One hundred slingers were summoned from *Aegium, Patras, and Dyme*. From childhood, according to the custom of their people, they practiced by hurling rounded stones—the kind that usually cover the shores mixed with sand—with slings out into the open sea. Thus, they used that weapon at a greater distance, with more certainty, and with a more powerful strike than the *Balearic* slinger. Their sling is not made of a single strap like the Balearic and other nations' slings, but consists of a triple pouch <note>original: scutale; the part of the sling that holds the projectile</note> hardened with frequent stitching, so that the bullet does not wobble in the throw due to a loose strap, but, being balanced when it sits, it is discharged as if shot from a bowstring. Having become accustomed to shooting through small circular hoops from a great distance, they would wound not only the heads of their enemies, but whatever part of the face they had targeted. With those slings, they restrained the *Samians*, preventing them from breaking out so frequently or so boldly; to such an extent that the Samians would plead from the walls for the *Achaeans* to withdraw for a little while and watch them fight the Roman outposts in peace. The *Carduchi* <note>The Kardouchoi, a people mentioned by Xenophon, often identified with the ancestors of the Kurds</note> hurled stones and lead spheres with such skill that they never failed to hit the intended target, which Suidas wrote in these words: *The Carduchi are the best slingers with both stones and lead spheres, which they hurl accurately at the mark.* <note>original Greek: Καρδοῦχοι σφενδονῆται ἄριστοι λίθοις τε καὶ μολυβδίναις σφαίραις, οἷς ἐξακοντίζουσιν ἐπίσκοπα.</note> Regarding slingers in Arabia who were hostile to him and his

<margin>
Military of the Orientals.
Varthema, Navigation Book 2, p. 228.
</margin>
allies, *Vartomannus* <note>Ludovico di Varthema, a 15th-century Italian traveler</note> relates that he calls the *Banduin* <note>Bedouins</note> an inhospitable people who, by stones projected from a sling, prevented his ship from the shore. *For a response,* he says, *stones were thrown by the sling. That kind of people is called the very inhospitable Banduin; there were nearly a hundred of them who joined hands with us from a distance, vibrating stones in their slings. For the space of an hour, they fought. They were unarmed, if you except the slings, and they went about naked.* A type of weapon closely related to the sling was the *Bow*, by which arrows are sent forth. They wish the name to be derived from *arcendo* <note>Latin: "from fending off"</note>, because it fends off the enemy from a distance. The bow is said "to be trodden," from the verb <term>דָּרַךְ</term> <note>darakh; literally "to tread or step on"</note>, for the reason, as *Rabbi Solomon* <note>Rashi, the medieval Jewish commentator</note> writes, that it was the custom of the ancients, when they wished to string their bows, to tread upon them with their feet or place them between their feet, so that they could more conveniently draw the string. See, if you please, *Peter Martyr's Commentary on Lamentations ch. 1 v. 4* and *B. Tarnovius' Commentary on Psalm 7:13.*

<margin>
1 Samuel 25:29.
</margin>
The bow was very frequently used, and is still used, by the Orientals. Hence, in his blessing to *Joseph*, Jacob extols his happiness by a comparison taken from the bow. *He dwelt,* it says in *Genesis 49:24, in the strength of his bow, and the arms of his hands were made firm.* But the Vulgate <note>The standard 4th-century Latin Bible</note> takes it in the opposite sense: *The bonds of his arms and hands were dissolved.* For <term>וַיָּפֹזוּ</term> <note>vayafothu; "were made strong/supple"</note> it reads <term>וַיָּפֻזּוּ</term>, from the root <term>פָּזַζ</term>, which means to be scattered. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> is no better: *Their bows were crushed with might, and the sinews of the arms of their hands were loosened.* <note>original Greek: Συνετρίβη μετὰ κράτους τὰ τόξα αὐτῶν, καὶ ἐξελύθη τὰ νεῦρα βραχιόνων χειρῶν αὐτῶν.</note> Our version <note>referring to the German or Protestant translations</note> puts it best: *Yet his bow remains firm, and the arms of his hands are strong.* <note>original German: So bleibet doch sein Bogen fest / und die Arme seiner Hände starck.</note> The strength of the place is described, as well as that of the soldiers, and what is most excellent, that of *Joseph*, whom he makes like a vigorous archer whose bow does not grow weak, nor are his arms lowered or his muscles relaxed; everything tends toward indicating that although *Joseph* would have monstrous and bitter enemies, he would nevertheless conquer them by the help of God. Joseph's bow is opposed to the enemy's bow as being stronger, by which a firm kingdom is symbolically

<margin>
Psalm 18:34.
</margin>
suggested. Thus *David*, singing a song of victory to God and extolling His guardianship and protection, writes: *He teaches my hands for battle, and my arms, so that I may break bows of bronze.* Knowledge of military matters was formerly

<margin>
Hec. 4:19.
</margin>
<column-break/>
chiefly in the skill of the bow, and it defined the bowman. To bend the bow and direct shafts with the bow was an Oriental art. For this man, a bow of horn; for that one, iron; for another, steel. But was it also of bronze? Those who are engaged in examining and explaining the material of weapons acknowledge that bronze was the first of all, and deny that iron existed before bronze. *Drusius* <note>Johannes Drusius, a Flemish Protestant scholar</note> wishes to be considered learned and a leader here, as he questioned others on this cause in vain in his *Questions*. Others correct the Vulgate version and, neglecting bronze as being unsuitable, understand the bows to be iron or steel. They say the Hebrew text indeed indicates bronze by its name, but this requires that another kind of metal be implied. Hence *Castalio* in his *Notes*: *In Hebrew it is 'bronze,' but bows are not made of bronze; it is put for 'metal,' and further for 'iron,' if it concerns an iron thing, as in Homer 'chalkos' <note>Greek: bronze/copper</note> is used for iron.* But, as we said, *Drusius* affirms that the Hebrew word first and properly signifies bronze, and furthermore he fights for the idea that weapons were first fashioned from bronze. Concerning the translations, it should be known that they by no means agree. For the Septuagint has: *You made my arms a bronze bow.* They forge a steel bow; for steel <note>original: chalybs</note> is iron forged twice, and *chalkotypoi* are those who handle steel. *Campensis and Castalio understand an iron bow; Junius and the English, a steel bow; Luther, Ammonius, and Piscator, a bronze bow.* To whichever thing the word is applied, Vulcan by his heat brings it about that the bow emerges from it; it is his to know how and be able to do so, for which reason he is called a smith of bronze. Truly, the Ancients used bronze in the manufacture of weapons, a certain tempering being applied to harden it, as Proclus notes on those words of Hesiod:

<margin>
Hesiod, *Works and Days*, v. 149
</margin>
> Their weapons were of bronze, and of bronze were their houses;
> they worked with bronze, for black iron did not yet exist.

Concerning that use of bronze in weapons, let us see further what *Lucretius* says:

> Ancient weapons were hands, nails, and teeth,
> and stones and likewise branches broken from the woods;
> later the power of iron and bronze was discovered,
> but the use of bronze was known before that of iron.

<margin>
Book 8, ch. 11, p. 1028.
</margin>
*Isidore* affirms the same: *The sound of cymbals or bronze things, and the point of iron tools in cultivating fields; and thus bronze, because the ancients cultivated the earth with bronze before iron was invented.* *Amerigo Vespucci* relates the same thing about the Indians discovered by him: *They lack iron and other metals, but in place of iron they arm their arrows with the teeth of beasts or fish; these they also frequently char, so that they may be stronger.* They are surely most certain in the art of the arrow, so that whatever they wish, they strike with their missiles; and in some places, the women also stand out as the best archers. For the rest, the chief strength of the oriental military stood in the *Archers*, against whom the *Shield-bearers* <note>original: Scutarii</note> were placed. Now an arrow consists of a reed, iron, and barbs on both sides. The reed is fixed to the iron, which is pointed. It is easily driven in, but it is removed and pulled out with great difficulty, as *Celsus*

<margin>
Celsus, *On Medicine*, Book 7, p. 96, 97.
</margin>
teaches, whose words are: *Missiles which have stuck inside bodies after being driven in are often ejected with great trouble. And there are certain difficulties from their types; certain ones from those places into which they have penetrated.* And after a few more words: *Nothing is so easily buried in the body as an arrow, and the same sits very deep. Moreover, these things happen because it is carried with great force...*

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
Eastern Warfare.
</margin>
...and because it is in a narrow space. Whence also the explanation of the scriptural words: *Thy arrows stick deep in me* <note>original German: "Deine pfeile stecken tieff in mir"</note>. And they do not only penetrate so tightly, but in ancient times they were sent out in such a large quantity that they were said to overshadow the sun itself. We find that secular writers also used this famous hyperbole. Pliny says <margin>Book 16, ch. 36</margin> that the sun itself is obscured by the frequent and dense shooting of arrows. From this comes the "cloud of weapons" in Lucan, Book 4, line 773. For where war is waged with arrows, "you would think a rain of arrows and javelins was descending through the air," says Paulus Venetus <note>A reference to Marco Polo, often cited in the early modern period as Paulus Venetus</note> (Eastern Regions, Book 4, p. 362). Florus mentions a sea covered with sails when describing the huge fleet of Antiochus (2.8). Xiphilinus, recording the eruption and conflagration of Vesuvius in Campania, says it spread as far as Rome and overshadowed the sun. "It even entered Rome," he says, "and filled the air above it, and cast a shadow over the sun" <note>original Greek: Εἰσῆλθε, δὲ καὶ ἐς τὴν Ῥώμην, καὶ ἡ ἀέρα ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς ἐπλήρωσε, καὶ τὸν ἥλιον ἐπεσκίασε</note>. Hence among the Hebrews, it received the name *Qeshet* <note>original Hebrew: קשת</note>, from *qashash*, meaning "to cut" or "to divide," because arrows sent from a bow cut through the air by passing through it very rapidly, and seemingly darken it. Among the Easterners, however, the use of archers—whom the ancients used to call *Arquites*—was more frequent than among others. Ovid meant these by the name "Aurora" <note>The personification of the Dawn, used here to represent the East</note> in Book 3 of *Tristia*, elegy 10, in these verses:

->and by the far-flying arrow<-
->whom neither the Ebro, nor the East, safe with its arrows,<-
->sustains.<-

Thus the Ephraimites were famous for the art of archery,

->and with skilled arrows<-
->to pierce with a certain dart, however distant.<-

Which commendation in the Hebrew tongue is *those armed with the bow* <note>original Hebrew: נושקי רומי קשת</note> <margin>Psalm 78:9</margin> where the Septuagint reads: "the sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting with bows" <note>original Greek: υἱοὶ Ἐφραῒμ ἐντείνοντες καὶ βάλλοντες τόξοις</note>. And David ordered the Jews to learn the art of archery (2 Sam. 1:18), because Saul and Jonathan had been wounded by very skilled archers. The wise Leader of the people had seen that the arts of war were necessary in well-governed states; since he felt the enemies excelled in these, he commanded that the Jews be taught the art of the archers. Besides these, the Scythians, Parthians, Cretans, Magnesians, Armenians, Germans, and English are commended for this study, as Daniel Scruterius teaches in *Palamedes*, book 3, ch. 13. The Gortynian arrow is celebrated by Lucan <margin>Book 6</margin>.

->Behold, the Gortynian reed is stretched<-
->by a Dictaean hand.<-

So called from Gortyna, a city of Crete, which was famous for the use of arrows. Thus all Cretans were celebrated for this art of arrows. For "Crete went forth in its prime with a multitude of archers," (Xenophon, *Hellenica* 4). "Cretan archers followed." Horse-archers <note>term: Hippotoxotai; cavalry who shoot while riding</note> using swift horses harassed the enemies and suddenly fled. Many very skilled archers could be brought forward, if there were need. Philoctetes is celebrated in Homer as "well-knowing the bow," <note>original Greek: τόξων εὖ εἰδὼς</note> who was in command of seven ships <margin>Iliad book 2, line 718</margin>.

Of these Philoctetes was the leader, well-knowing the bow,
of seven ships; and fifty rowers in each
had embarked, well-knowing how to fight strongly with bows.

Teucer was "the best of the Achaeans in archery," according to Homer (Iliad 13, line 313), regarding which passage Plutarch says, "Homer has made Teucer famous because of his archery." The Persians and Parthians were skilled in shooting arrows, who, according to Justin

<column-break/>

Book 41, ch. 2, and Herodian, Book 6, teach archery with great industry. Let us hear Herodian in that place: "They do not use bows and horses only for the purpose of making war, as the Romans do, but from childhood they are brought up with them and live by hunting, whether they ever put away their quivers or dismount from their horses, they are always using them, either against enemies or against wild beasts." The historian Agathias writes of the Aligern Goths in Book 1 that an arrow sent by hand immediately pierced through a whole man through his shield and breastplate; and, what is marvelous, if they had fallen upon a rock or some other hard thing difficult to break, they broke all of it by the violence of the impact. Procopius left written the same thing in Book 1 of the *Persian War* concerning the archers of his age: "an arrow sent with such force that neither any breastplate nor shield could resist it." Arrows were in such high esteem in that great age of the Ancients, "and perhaps it was not by good counsel that they were so entirely abandoned," says Lipsius in Book 5 of *Roman Military Affairs*, Dialogue 20. Nor is it unusual in both sacred and secular literature to describe punishments sent by God through divinity with this kind of weapon. Homer, describing the plague sent by divinity to punish Agamemnon, introduces Apollo equipped with arrows so that he might shoot at men; he even calls the god one who acts "through the archery art,"

->But then he sent a sharp arrow against them,<-
->And struck; and the funeral pyres of the dead burned constantly.<-

The divine wrath is depicted for us with a more elegant description in Psalm 7:12: "If you do not turn, he will whet his sword; he has bent his bow and made it ready." <note>original Greek: Ἐαν μὴ ἐπιστραφῆτε, τὴν ῥομφαίαν αὐτοῦ, σιλβώσει· τὸ τόξον αὐτοῦ ἐνέτεινε, καὶ ἡτοίμασεν αὐτό</note>. To make it more apparent how great that divine anger <note>term: theomenia; the wrath of God</note> is against the impious, further describing God vigorously equipped, he says: "in himself he has prepared" (v. 13) "the instruments of death; his arrows he has crafted for those who are burning." He threatens certain destruction unless the evil and impious repent. *Romphæa* <note>a large sword or pike</note>, the bow, the fiery darts, are elegant metaphors for punishments, and an elegant Hebraism in the words *keley-mavet* <note>original Hebrew: כלי-מות</note>, called "deadly weapons," or "vessels or instruments of death." Tarnovius explains this elegant progression thus: *The first likeness is taken from an armed soldier rushing eagerly against enemies, to indicate the severity and power of the Supreme Judge, who so detests the crimes of the wicked that if, when he calls them to repentance, they refuse, he declares himself their open enemy, setting his angry face against them, and punishes them both near at hand with the sword and from a distance with arrows sent from a very strong bow, so that clearly no place of escape remains.* Thus the chosen David had felt the arrows from the quiver of the Lord in himself, complaining in Psalm 38:3: *Thy arrows have sunk into me* <note>original Hebrew: חציך נחתו בי</note>. "Your arrows were fixed in me." <note>original Greek: τὰ βέλη σου ἐνεπάγησάν μοι</note>. The Vulgate: "Your arrows are fastened in me." For just as arrows strike the body, they wound and cause anguish. Similarly Job complains about the arrows sent from the bow of God: *The arrows of the Almighty are with me* <note>original Hebrew: חצי שדי עמדי</note>. "Strong arrows are in my body." <note>original Greek: βέλη ἰσχυρὰ ἐν τῷ σώματί μ’ ἐστιν</note>. The Vulgate: "The arrows of the Lord are in me." Job groans and laments about those arrows which the Lord, as if an enemy, had sent through his limbs to wound him. Whence Vatablus says on this passage (p. 9): *The arrows of the Almighty, that is, very sharp ones, just as the "mountains of God" and "Cedars of God" stand for the highest, he calls the lethal wounds by which he was being finished "very sharp arrows".* Other metaphors concerning arrows in the Holy Scriptures...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of ancient military equipment and personnel, specifically shifting from weapons like bows and arrows (discussed previously) to the identity and physical nature of the "Gammadim" or guards mentioned in the prophecy against Tyre in the Book of Ezekiel.</meta>

<page-num>671</page-num>
<header>Ezekiel XXVII. v. 11.</header>

<margin>Eastern Warfare.</margin>
We intentionally omit those things we have previously proposed by conjecture regarding the weapons of the Ancients. As Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606) was a renowned Flemish philologist and humanist who wrote extensively on Roman military history.</note> says in his preface to *On the Roman Military*: *I speak knowingly and with experience when I say there is nothing that more hinders or delays the progress of youth than an ignorance of ancient warfare*. For who would dare to categorize the weapons of the Ancients, which changed almost as often as the moon and are known by little more than their names? **Aulus Gellius** <note>A 2nd-century Roman author of "Attic Nights."</note> in *Book 10, ch. 25, p. 238*, recounting various kinds of weapons, lists some in this order: *The spear, the javelin, the heavy siege-dart, the half-siege-dart, the all-iron dart, the Gallic spear, the lance, the hunting spear, the barbed dart, the three-pronged dart, the strap-thrown dart, the Germanic pike, the mid-weighted dart, the barbed club, the long Thracian sword, the scorpion-dart, the scribones, the sicleses, the javelins, various swords, the curved dagger, the long-sword, the tongue-shaped blade, daggers, and the belt-knives*. In these military matters, most of which are now obscure, we adopt the words of Constantine <note>A reference to the Byzantine Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus and his "Life of Basil."</note>:
<margin>In the life of Basil, ch. 33, p. 87.</margin>
<note>original Greek: ἐπεὶ ὁ χρόνος ἤδη ῥεύσας διὰ μέσου πολὺς τὰ καθ' ἕκαστα τῶν ἐξ ἀρχῶν διὰ τὸ μεταξὺ σιγῆς, οἶον ἠμαύρωσε...</note> "Since much time has now flowed by in the interval, it has, as it were, obscured the details of things from the beginning because of the intervening silence. Thus, we are no longer able to know or describe the types of battle lines, the methods of attack, the deployments and contractions of phalanxes, or the timely use of stratagems, nor can we continue to explain these twenty-seven parts to everyone for all time."

### Ezekiel XXVII. v. 11.
-> וגמדים במגדלותיך היו <-
<note>original Hebrew: "And the Gammadim were in your towers."</note>

<gloss>Guards were in your towers.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Φύλακες ἐν τοῖς πύργοις σου ἦσαν</note>
<gloss>Pygmies, who were in the towers.</gloss> <note>original Latin: Pygmæi, qui erant in turribus</note>

<margin>Battle of the Pygmies.</margin>
Those who claim that a tiny people, lowly of body, who can scarcely be distinguished from the noise and clatter of cranes <note>A reference to the classical myth of the "Geranomachia," the perpetual war between Pygmies and cranes.</note>, are the subject here, usually cite this passage of Ezekiel—where the *Gammadim* <term>Gammadim: A mysterious group mentioned in Ezekiel 27:11; interpretations range from a specific tribe to "midgets" to "brave warriors."</term> are mentioned among the military men of the Tyrians—based on the assumption of the Vulgate version, and they do so against the true meaning of the Scripture. *How well* (these are the words of Tremellius) <note>Immanuel Tremellius was a 16th-century Jewish convert and leading Hebraist.</note> *this playful interpretation fits with military affairs, let them see for themselves. We, however, believe the Gammadim are named from the "cubit" (Hebrew: gomed), but because there was a region of Phoenicia projected into the sea in the shape of a cubit/elbow, which was later swallowed by the sea, we think it was called Gammade*, as Pliny writes. *But what if we understand them to be robust and muscular men based on the etymology of the word? Certainly, that would be the most fitting interpretation*. "The eye speaks," says Caspar Waser in Book 1, *On the Ancient Measures of the Hebrews*, chapter 6. Marcus Marinus himself, in his *Noah's Ark*, folio 102. a, thinks it is the name of a certain nation, perhaps called the Gammadensians. Sixtinus Amama <note>A 17th-century Dutch Hebraist.</note> feels the same way.
<margin>Commentary on Psalm 159.</margin>
Those who understand them as "midgets" produce nothing but trifles. The Rabbis understand them as dwarfs. For Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish exegete and grammarian.</note> writes that they were dwarf-like men of small measure, citing for this sense the passage in
<margin>page 260.</margin>
*Judges 3:16*, where it says <note>original Hebrew: גמד ארכה</note>, i.e., *a cubit was its length*, regarding the double-edged sword of Ehud, the length of which was a cubit. He says the *Gammadim* <note>original Hebrew: אנשים לדה קדה קטנה</note> were men of small stature. And Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki), the foremost medieval commentator.</note> notes that some explain the Gammadim were <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: גנסין ונכנסו במדת אמה</note>, that is, dwarfs (*nanafin*) who would fit into the measure of a cubit. *Gamm*
<margin>6.4.</margin>
or *Gamad* means a "dwarf" or <term>nanos</term> <note>original Greek: νᾶνος</note>. The Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible.</note> has "Cappadocians," as if it read *Cappadoces*. But what use would such little men be to the Tyrians, who were quite vast in both body and countenance? Unless, perhaps, they were present for the pleasure that a witty people might take in mocking them; or perhaps they were provided with food and wages to mock the enemy, or to cry out that the enemy was present, just as geese were once kept on the Capitol <note>A famous Roman legend where the honking of sacred geese alerted the guards to a Gallic night attack on the Capitoline Hill.</note> to signal if thieves were
<column-break/>
coming. But in the extreme difficulty of affairs with which the Tyrians were then pressed, it was of great importance whom they
<margin>Battle of the Pygmies.</margin>
admitted to deter the enemy—men who would provoke fear, not laughter and jokes. Certainly, for the inhabitants of Tyre, anyone who advised bringing in these midgets as garrison soldiers would have seemed to be a madman among the sane, or like a drunkard reveling among the sober. I believe those men who imagine lowly people here have fallen asleep thinking of the battle lines of the cranes and Pygmies, and from there have taken the Pygmies, who prefer shameful flight over war. In a playful contest, one may play and laugh, but one should not act seriously in ridiculous matters, nor ridiculously in serious matters; "neither should one be serious about jokes, nor rejoice in serious things with jokes," as Isocrates <note>An ancient Greek rhetorician.</note> instructs. For there was no need for the shadow-boxing of Pygmies at a time when men were devoted only to serious matters, and Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire and metalworking.</note> was intent on forging swords and missiles. For what, I ask, did the Tyrians in a most fortified city have to do with Pygmies? What use were Pygmies, who are quite inept with shields, among guards most learned in war? Why would shields be hung around the towers, if not as indicators of the armor of the brave? The towers were evidence (*tekmēria*) of strength as well as of the strongest men, about which testimonies exist in *Canticles 4:4, Judges 9:51, Judith 1:14 & 7:5, and 2 Samuel 11:20, 24*. Jerome says in his commentary on Isaiah ch. 2, p. 14: *A tower is built either for the fortification of a city, or for a lookout, so that an enemy coming from afar may be seen*. Tyre was "tower-crowned" (*epipurgos*); since the Gammadensian warriors are said to be stationed in its towers, we must interpret them as pugnacious soldiers, as was seen by Lalius Bisciola and Carranza, rather than by that
<margin>Exhortation to Demonicus, p. 16.</margin>
conceited Vizeius, who seems to think himself very wise in his notes on Luther's version. For in ancient times, the more robust soldiers were usually stationed *on the walls*, and especially *in the towers*, to hurl iron and fire at the enemy, wounding them not only with the blow but with the flame itself. Pygmies would have accomplished no more in those towers (which "City-Takers" <note>The "Helepolis" was a massive ancient siege engine.</note> were meant to overturn) than Terentian Sophrona <note>A character from Terence's play *Phormio*, often used as a type for a weak or elderly person.</note> would have. Indeed, there is almost no doubt that Aquila <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek, known for his literalism.</note> himself looked to the strength of these guards in his version. For that translator is accustomed not so much to translate words as the etymologies of the words themselves, which, as he observes in many terms, can also have a place here. For *Pygmaios* <note>Greek: "Pygmy"</note> descends from *pygme* <note>Greek: "fist" or "forearm"</note>, just as according to some *Gomad* comes from *gamad*, a "cubit"; it is as if to say "cubit-men" or "those strong in the cubit," <note>original German: *Männer die stärcke in ihren Fäusten und Armen hatten*</note> "men who had strength in their fists and arms," since strength consists in the arm; just as in an ancient Lexicon, *pygmas* is explained as *pechyaios*, "one a cubit long," or strength in the hand. Whence Josephus says of Nimrod <note>original Greek: τολμηρὸς καὶ τὴν χεῖρα γενναῖος</note> that he was "bold and noble of hand." Thus, they seem to be called "cubit-men" from their strength, just as the Hebrews describe the strong by the fist, calling them <note>original Hebrew: בעלי אגרופין</note> "Masters of the Fists," who are powerful in their fists and elbows, bold men ready of hand. For it is common for names to be derived from those members in which the sinew of strength resides, such as *omokratēs* <note>Greek: "strong-shouldered"</note> in Sophocles' *Ajax*, line 206:
<margin>T. 2. subc. l. 4. c. 1. on childbirth c. 17.</margin>
<margin>Eunuch, Act 5, sc. 3, v. 4.</margin>
<margin>Judith 9:9.</margin>
<margin>Antiquities of the Jews, Book 1, ch. 5.</margin>

<margin>The Battle of the Pygmies.</margin>
> Towering above the Greeks with his head and broad shoulders,

Compare this with Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius (1500–1574), a German classical scholar.</note> on Sophocles, page 48. I am therefore nearly convinced that the ancient Interpreter <note>A reference to the translator of the Vulgate (St. Jerome) or earlier Greek versions.</note> was looking toward this meaning rather than toward that race of people

<margin>on this passage, page 427.</margin>
found in poetry, of which Jerome says: *Whether they are Pygmies, that is, warriors and most ready for war; from the word "pygme," which in the Greek language is translated as a contest.* "Pygme" <term>Pygme: A Greek unit of measure based on the fist or forearm.</term> denotes a hand contracted into a fist. Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> on page 654 says: *Pygme, a wrestling match, a closing of the fingers.* Truly, if these Pygmy warriors had been tiny little men acting as guards, they would have lost the citizens rather than saved them; it would have been ridiculous to have such <note>original Greek: ἀνθρωπάρια μικρὰ</note> "diminutive mannikins" in a tower as guards, when they themselves would have needed guards. For I do not see how the weak Pygmies and the warlike Tyrians belong together here; it seems to me that those who imagine little men here instead of the "Gaminadais" <note>The author likely refers to the "Gammadim" mentioned in the Hebrew text of Ezekiel.</note> are trying <note>original Greek: ἀκροθύνια τῷ πυγμαίων κολοσσῷ ἐφαρμόζειν</note> "to fit the ornaments of a colossus onto pygmies," adapting the smallest things to the greatest. Who would not laugh at the crude fiction of Ctesias <note>A Greek physician and historian from the 5th century BCE.</note>, who narrates in his Indian histories (excerpted by Photius) that *the Pygmies have beards down to their feet and hair down to their knees, which they use in place of clothing*? I shall not even mention the other tales produced by

<margin>*Iliad* book 3, page 372.</margin>
Eustathius in his commentary on Homer <note>Eustathius of Thessalonica was a 12th-century scholar.</note>, where the greatest of Greek poets described that dire and lethal war of the Pygmies with the cranes, who were the thieves of their grain; it is best to hear it from him, in *Iliad* Book 3, verse 1:

> But when they were arrayed, each company with its leaders,
> The Trojans came on with clamor and a cry, like birds,
> Even as the clamor of cranes arises before the face of heaven,
> When they flee from winter and unspeakable rain,
> With clamor they fly toward the streams of the Ocean,
> Bringing slaughter and fate to the Pygmy men;
> And in the early morning they bring on the evil strife.

Other most vain things are told: for they say that in the springtime they go out with great ceremony and full armor to destroy the eggs and chicks of the cranes; that this expedition takes three months to complete; and that rams and goats serve as their horses. If anyone wished to inspect the armor of the Pygmies, they would find <note>original Greek: ζωνίδια καὶ λογχαρίδια τῷ κύπῃ κεκρυμμένα</note> "little belts and tiny spears hidden in a cup," like in the war of the Apameans against the Larissaeans mentioned by Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, writing c. 200 CE.</note> in Book 4, citing Posidonius. For if a Pygmy obtained the armor of Achilles, do you think—to use the words of Lucian <note>A 2nd-century satirist; the passage is from *Against the Ignorant Book Collector*.</note>—*that he would immediately become both handsome and strong, and leap over the river, and check the very flow of the stream with the slaughter of the Phrygians, and slay Hector, and Lycaon, and Asteropaeus, when he could not even carry the ashen spear on his shoulders?* Surely the same thing would happen to him as happened to Thersites: he would be mocked as he limped behind his shield, <note>original Greek: καὶ δὴ στόμα καλαπίπτει ὑπὸ τὸ βάρος</note> "and indeed his face falls forward under the weight," being unequal to carrying the burden; as if he were peeking his head out from his helmet like a mouse from a bundle of flax, barely dragging his breastplate over his hunched back. Would this full set of armor not provoke laughter, just like the armor of the mice and frogs in Homer <note>Referring to the "Batrachomyomachia" or Battle of Frogs and Mice, a parody of the Iliad.</note>? Certainly, it would disgrace the work of the armor-makers as well as its owner. Concerning Dwarfs

<column-break/>

handling weapons with a strong hand, which even the cranes marvel at while Mars laughs, one can read Statius <note>A Roman poet of the 1st century CE.</note> in *Silvae* Book 1, line 57, where he describes the battles of Dwarfs in a gladiatorial show:

> Here a bold rank of Dwarfs comes forward,
> Whom nature, having finished their brief stature,
> Bound once and for all into a knotty globe.
> They deal out wounds and join their right hands,
> And threaten each other with death—with what hand?
> Father Mars and bloodstained Valor laugh;
> And the Cranes, destined to fall in wandering raids,
> Marvel at the more ferocious Dwarfs.

Nor does Naso <note>Ovid, the Roman poet (Publius Ovidius Naso).</note> pass over their deeds, but in *Metamorphoses* Book 6, fable 2, verse 21, he sings:

> Another part holds the wretched fate of the Pygmy mother,
> Whom Juno commanded to be a crane after she was defeated
> In a contest, and to declare war on her own people.

But because these things lie somewhat obscurely beneath the "husk" of a Pygmy changed into a crane, we should take up those things which are clearer. I think those lines are from Juvenal <note>A Roman satirist.</note>:

> To the sudden birds of the Thracians and the sounding cloud,
> The Pygmy warrior runs in his small arms;
> Soon, unequal to the foe, he is seized and carried through the air
> In curved talons by a cruel crane.

The contest of the Pygmies with the Cranes was described in an elegant poem which Laurentius Beyerlingius <note>A 17th-century theologian and encyclopedist.</note> included in its entirety in his *Theatrum*, Volume 6, Book 10, page 866. Thus the poets sing of wonders, but not things to be believed. Pliny <note>The Elder, in his *Natural History*.</note> records in Book 7, chapter 2, that after the battle is over, their huts are built from the spoils and remains of the enemy, shining with the feathers of cranes and the shells of eggs. But let us hear of another, more spirited deed, so that their high-mindedness might be known; after Antaeus was killed by Hercules, the Pygmies, to avenge his death, hatched a plan and rushed upon the sleeping Hercules. When he woke up, he wrapped all the <note>original Latin: homunculos humiles</note> "lowly little mannikins"—to use the words of Cicero in *Tusculan Disputations* Book 5—inside his lion skin. That *Battle of the Pygmies* <note>original Greek: Πυγμαιομαχία</note> is found in Philostratus in the book he titled *On Images*, and it is a story not unworthy of being laughed at, charming as it is. It is indeed a charming contest, from the description of which anyone would take some pleasure—but surely much more if it were given to be seen in person. Francesco Robortello <note>A 16th-century Italian Renaissance humanist.</note> had seen it expressed in a marble statue in Florence in the garden of Francesco Rucellai; he admired its craftsmanship so much that he did not know whether to admire more the pen of Philostratus in writing or the chisel of the sculptor in carving. Once, when someone saw the Emperor Caligula showing himself off in the dress of Jupiter, he dissolved into laughter, saying: <note>original Greek: μέγα παραλήρημα</note> "What a great madness!" Believe me, enemies would have said no different to the Tyrians here, if they had been present:

> O servile cattle of Pygmies, how often your tumults 
> Have moved me to laughter, and often to anger!

Since, therefore, historical faith does not admit them—indeed, Lucian added the Pygmies to his *True Stories* <note>A famous ancient work of science fiction and satire.</note>—we rightly wonder how this doctrine crept into the Commentaries? From this, I believe: that it is considered a sin to challenge the Vulgate version, because of the decree known to all <note>The Council of Trent's decree on the Latin Vulgate.</note>. But farewell to that decree; farewell, I say, to those empty terrors and masked fears, which would have produced laughter for the enemy and ignominy for themselves.

# Ezekiel 27:11

<margin>The Battle of the Pygmies.</margin>
You may see, therefore, that most interpreters are withdrawing from that stale explanation and those old wives' fables. However, for those who are not displeased by the explanation of the word *Gammadim* as mannikins of a cubit's length <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of a forearm.</note>, they reach the point of claiming that these soldiers appeared from a distance as if they were Pygmies in the very high towers where they kept watch. This is the opinion of Lavater <note>Ludwig Lavater (1527–1586), a Swiss Reformed theologian.</note> on folio 184b and Villalpandus <note>Juan Bautista Villalpando (1552–1608), a Spanish Jesuit known for his commentary on Ezekiel.</note> on page 14.

<margin>Dist. 5. On Christian Doctrine, § 273.</margin>
But Ivarus Stobaeus <note>A pseudonym for a scholar or a reference to a specific academic dissertation.</note> rightly says: *Who would believe that the Tyrians would want to entrust their safety to soldiers of this kind—whether the business was to be conducted at close quarters or from a distance—or that Pygmies themselves could serve as soldiers abroad, when they have such dismal wars with cranes at home? Ridiculous! These Gammadim, of whatever nation they may have been, were soldiers in no way secondary or inferior to the rest who are listed in the same place: Persians, Lydians, Libyans, Arvadians, and Sidonians. If you find men a cubit tall, they are not worthy of being counted as complete men. An aberration of nature does not make a whole race of Pygmies plausible to me; you will find them nowhere on earth, unless perhaps you station them in the cave of Trophonius.* <note>The Cave of Trophonius was a legendary Greek oracle site; here it implies a place of myths.</note> Hesiod <note>An ancient Greek poet, roughly a contemporary of Homer.</note> said in *Works and Days*, verse 160, that the race of heroes fell at Thebes and Troy:

<margin>Satire 13, v. 167.</margin>
> And some were destroyed by evil war and the dread battle-cry,
> Some at seven-gated Thebes, in the land of Cadmus,
> Fighting for the sake of the flocks of Oedipus.

Perhaps the Pygmies followed them in the next age (if it please the Gods!), born without doubt after the heroes in the cave of Trophonius—a versatile, crafty, sly, and prudent race, but not an eloquent one. Therefore, the idea that such a people of cubit-stature and an entire nation of <note>original Greek: σμιϰρῶν παντελῶς ἀνθρώπων</note> "utterly tiny men" ever existed is perhaps fabulous and empty; though such stories might suit Deimachus, Megasthenes, and other architects of lies and fables, they certainly do not befit lovers of truth and churchmen, much less the most holy Prophet and the divinely inspired Scriptures. These are the words of Nicholas Fuller <note>An English scholar (1557–1622) of sacred philology.</note> in book 6 of his *Miscellanies*, chapter 3. For what protection could have been expected from such <note>original Greek: ἀνθρωπίσκοις</note> "little mannikins"?

---

> Where the whole cohort is not taller than one foot. <note>A quote from the Roman satirist Juvenal, mocking the idea of Pygmy armies.</note>

<margin>Book 4, Elegy 9, v. 13.</margin>
There are, to be sure, mannikins of tiny stature among men, themselves <note>original Latin: "suos breviter concreti in artus"</note> "contracted into their own short limbs," to speak with Propertius. Indeed, under Theodosius the Great, a dwarf was seen, scarcely larger than a partridge, if faith is to be given to Nicephorus, who relates these things in his *History*, book 12, chapter 37, page 307: <note>original Greek: Δύο σώματα ὤφθη ἀνθρώπων... εἰς ἄπιστον βραχύτητα καταλήγον.</note> "Two bodies of men were seen, one of which in Syria exceeded human nature in size; the other in Egypt reached an unbelievable smallness. This Egyptian was so shortened that he was much like a partridge." The same accounts exist in almost the same words in Philostorgius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 10, page 142. Cardanus <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath.</note> notes in book 11 of *On Subtlety*, pages 370 and 372, that a man of full age, but only a cubit long, was carried around in a parrot's cage; there he also hands down the method for procreating and even artificially "making" Pygmies: *Pygmies,* he says, *can be made no differently than Maltese dogs. For they are born from a small father and mother, are bound tightly in bandages, and are not fed abundantly, but thinly.*

<margin>chapter 40, p. 298.</margin>
But in book 8 of *On the Variety of Things*, Cardanus teaches that the history of Pygmies is fabulous, and he states that not only did Strabo <note>An ancient Greek geographer.</note> among the ancients feel this way, but our own age confirms it, since almost all the wonders of the world have now become known. His full words are: *It appears that the history of Pygmies is fabulous, which Strabo sensed*

<column-break/>

<margin>The Battle of the Pygmies.</margin>
*and which our own age declares, since almost all the wonders of the world have now become known to me.* But what deceived such a great philosopher was the authority of Homer, which was not light among them, and a certain common rumor about a very clever type of monkey; or rather, and most significantly, Sinibaldus <note>Giovanni Benedetto Sinibaldi (1594–1658), a Roman physician.</note>, the Chief Physician and Roman Professor, who explained how the generation of Pygmies could happen. He himself acknowledges their existence, moved by ancient tradition accepted from Pliny and Aristotle. I will set down his words: *How such tiny natures are generated is not very difficult to teach, since a scarcity of seed is the cause for offspring being born with diminished bodies; just as an abundance of the same leads to the greatness of bodies, so scarcity leads to smallness. The race returns to its authors. The origin itself is tiny. From small things, only small things can be produced. From the puny, the puny arise. Therefore, when in that kingdom, either because of the rigor of the sky or some other unhappiness of the earth, men began to be born of such tiny stature—as nature always tends to fall away into the worse—in the progress of time they departed into the smallest figure, so much so that they are even said to enter into battle with partridges.* He denies that the little man receives strength from the scarcity of seed or the thinness of the generation, which cannot attain perfection; on the contrary, he says growth comes from its abundance. While we admit this, it does not lead us to believe that the Sower of all things willed such a scarcity of seed that ancestors would exist from whom an entire nation might rise. I do not, of course, deny that tiny men are sometimes given. Our own age saw in the court of John Sigismund, Elector of Brandenburg, a certain dwarf, the son of a certain peasant from the Duchy of Brunswick, named Just Bertram, two cubits long, as witnessed by Johannes Cernitius in the *History of the Ten Electors of Brandenburg*. Pictorius relates in book 7, chapter 2, that he saw in the court of Archduke Ferdinand of Austria a Pygmy who was only three palms long. Zeiler and Plater narrate that this man, wearing armor, was presented inside a meat pie <note>original Latin: "artocreante"</note> at the wedding feast of Duke Wilhelm of Bavaria and the daughter of Duke Renatus of Lorraine, celebrated at Munich in February 1568, and was set upon the table of the princes. Likewise, Georg Sabinus in his notes on Ovid's *Metamorphoses* says that Cardanus saw a man in Italy (if it is right to call him so) of mature age, no larger than a cubit, carried around in a parrot's cage.

<margin>Geneanthropeia, book 8, tract 2, ch. 4, p. 867.</margin>
<margin>The Orient, ch. 40, p. 143.</margin>
Andreas Thevet <note>A 16th-century French explorer and writer known for exaggerated tales.</note> writes that he saw five Pygmies in Egypt (I would believe they were <note>original Greek: Cercopithecos</note> "long-tailed monkeys") who come to Cairo every year for the sake of trade, and escorted by two Janissaries <note>Elite Ottoman soldiers.</note>, they exchange their goods, especially coral. But he is a writer lying in many things, so much so that what Homer says can be said of him:

<margin>Odyssey, Book 14, v. 125.</margin>
> Wandering men
> tell lies, and do not wish to tell the truth.

In the Dresden court, they show the skeleton of a Pygmy, which is undoubtedly that of an embryo; Heintzner reported that he saw a similar one a span long in the house of Felix Plater <note>A famous Swiss physician (1536–1614).</note>. The boots of a Pygmy are seemingly shown at Enkhuizen in North Holland in the "cabinet of wonders" of Dr. Paludanus. No one would deny the existence of dwarfs, but that a whole race of dwarfs hides somewhere...

<meta>This page continues the author's skeptical examination of the "Pygmies." # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Battle of the Pygmies.</margin>
Who would affirm that they grow and mingle in bloody wars with cranes? For as to where in the world the Pygmies might be, there has been such *ambiguity and disagreement* <note>original Greek: ἀμφιβολογία καὶ διχοψία</note> among writers that the line of Plautus might be applied:

->*By Pollux, I believe that unless a Sibyl reads these,*<-
->*I think no one else can untangle them.*<-
<note>The Sibyl was a legendary prophetess; Plautus is joking that the subject is so confusing only a divinely inspired person could make sense of it.</note>

The ancient patrons of the Pygmies know of no certain dwelling place to attribute to these most notable little men. If it pleases a painter to indicate a form for a sketch: <margin>Book 7, ch. 2.</margin> call upon Pliny*, who handed down the tradition that they fashion houses out of mud, feathers, and eggshells. But if that same painter is led to Aristotle, <margin>History of Animals, Book 8, num. 12.</margin> he* will point out caverns, from which dwelling they were called Troglodytes <note>Cavedwellers</note>. Hence a double palace exists for them: one which the Latin writer [Pliny] devised, and another which the Greek [Aristotle] devised. With the former, you would believe they live with swallows; with the latter, with mice and moles. They are truly unhappy both in their nests and their caverns, because, awakened by the clangor of cranes and terrified by the flapping of wings, they are forced to leave their "blessed seats" and betake themselves elsewhere. For what misery, I ask, is it to always change these healthy and spring-like dwellings and flee elsewhere from the farthest part of the mountains of India to Thrace—chilly, cruel, barbarian, horrid, stony, and snowy Thrace (which are the epithets of the poets)? Lest these things seem *absurd* <note>original Greek: ἄτοπος</note> to you, know that Pliny*, the inventor of many things, taught that the Pygmies (lest he serve up the same old "reheated cabbage" <note>The Latin "crambe maffufculam" refers to a stale, repetitive story.</note> to unworthy people) live in the farthest part of the mountains <margin>Book 4, ch. 11.</margin> of India; he also taught they were in Thrace*, and having been put to flight by cranes, they sought new homes for themselves. This opinion is by no means to be proscribed, since I would believe that <margin>Satire 13, v. 167.</margin> Juvenal* was looking toward that same idea:

> To the sudden birds of the Thracians and the noisy cloud
> The Pygmy warrior runs in his small arms.

But where are the Pygmies now? They were. Unless, with Paolo Giovio in his *On the Legation of Moscow*, p. 538, you place them beyond the Lapps. For he says: *Beyond the Lapps, in a region between the Northwest and North winds, oppressed by perpetual darkness, some witnesses of exceptional faith have reported that Pygmies are found. After they have grown to their peak, they hardly exceed the measure of a ten-year-old boy of our lands. They are a fearful race of men, expressing speech with a chirping sound, so that they seem as close to monkeys as they are remote in stature and senses from a man of proper character.* Or perhaps you might make a journey with a trio of brothers to Utopia for the sake of visiting the region of the Pygmies. In that stupendous pilgrimage of the three brothers Theophilus, Sergius, and Hyginus, which is read in the *Life of St. Macarius the Roman* in Rosweyde [Book 1 on the *Lives of the Fathers*, p. 225], the region of the Pygmies was encountered. *Having set out toward the East, when we had spent one hundred and ten days wandering on our journey, we entered the land of a nation called the Pichiti. This nation in its stature and height had no more than the measure of a single cubit <note>About 18 inches</note>, and seeing us, they fled, struck with fear. We, however, praising God, who delivered us from their hands, accelerated our pace daily.* Certainly, the fear must have been immense for a whole nation to flee at the visit of three men, perhaps thinking that the Commanders of the Cranes had arrived to scout the enemy. But listen, I pray, to *other terrible things following one after another in this wondrous journey* <note>original Greek: τῆς πορείας θαυμαστῆς ἀλλεπάλιλα δεινὰ ἄλλα</note>, so that the borders of the Pygmy habitation

<column-break/>

may become known: [Chapter 7, p. 226] *After this, we came into very high and terrible mountains, where the sun does not enter, and neither tree nor grass grows. There we saw innumerable serpents, and dragons, and asps, but also basilisks, and vipers, and unicorns, and many wild oxen; also many other deadly beasts and poisonous animals, whose names or nature we are utterly ignorant of. It is a wonder from where so many wild animals got their nourishment in a land that nourished no grass nor produced any tree; you might think they lived off the inhalation of air like chameleons.* It is truly more wondrous that the Pichiti live unhurt in the vicinity of serpents endowed with every kind of cruelty; meanwhile, not safe from the cranes who raid them with impunity, they hide in the innermost corners of the mountains. And since no less remarkable things about Pygmies follow under another sun, it will not be out of place to relate them. *But we (they continue), being greatly afflicted (by the surrounding darkness) and persisting in prayer, after seven days a Dove appeared to us. Approaching us and flying around us for a long time, and beating its little wings strongly, it comforted us as if to make us walk. Then we, giving thanks to God, made our way through the pathless places, and behold, we found a very large arch (a guide for the way) with writing around it. Seeing that writing, we rejoiced and praised the Lord.* Now this was the writing: *Alexander the Macedonian Emperor, son of Philip, made this arch when he pursued Darius, King of the Persians. Whoever wishes to enter this land, let him go to the left hand; for to the right the land is impassable, and full of rocks and narrow passes. We, therefore, entering to the left, walked for many days and beheld a great lake.* In that lake, they saw a man of a hundred cubits <note>approx. 150 feet tall</note> bound to others, crying out so strongly that the voice of his shouting was heard for nearly forty miles. They heard in another place speaking birds [Chapter 11, p. 227] crying out loudly: *Spare us, Lord, who fashioned us; Spare us, merciful one, because we have sinned before thy face.* Therefore, struck with great fear, the brothers left that place and encountered another even greater fear, seeing four men with fire and sword guarding the way. Then, exhausted by a forty-day fast, they saw a wonderful crystalline temple; and after they were thoroughly tested by a hundred days of fasting, behold suddenly [Chapter 14, p. 227] *as they were going, an innumerable multitude of people, men and women, came to meet them, gathered into a mass; but among them they saw no one taller than the stature of one cubit. Hear now the stratagem of the brothers, by which they repelled fear with fear. Seeing them, we were very afraid. Then I, a miserable sinner, Theophilus, said to my brothers Sergius and Hyginus: "Letting down our hair (which was horribly long and uncombed), let us go against them; perhaps they will flee from us, and the Lord will deliver us from their hands." When this seemed good to them, having loosened our headbands and hair, we rushed upon them suddenly. They, seeing this, immediately snatched up their children and, gnashing their teeth, they all fled away very quickly.* Who, having read these things, would not be dumbfounded and tremble—even more so having seen them, even in a dream! Who now would not believe with a firm faith that there are Pygmies? For it is not likely that something told so simply and without

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

It was said with deceit <note>original: "fuco," literally "with seaweed dye," a metaphor for a fake or disguised appearance</note>, to twist with artifice and to deprave through malicious interpretation; this is all the more unworthy when done to those men who were always friends of candor and simple truth, and who held that reputation above all others since their ancient beginnings. It is therefore to be deplored, <margin>The Battle of the Pygmies</margin> <margin>3. 9. p. 61.</margin> that they ever **WERE**. The same Pomponius Mela <note>A Roman geographer</note> finally admits and writes: *Inland were the Pygmies, a tiny race, which perished fighting against cranes to protect their crops.* If Mela had not handed down the tradition that they were all destroyed to a man in battle (which is a pity), the only task remaining for the world's navigators today would be to search for this lovely nation. Therefore, Mela says "they were," which the defenders of the Pygmies might think applies to them, unless they wish the same fate to befall them as that Ovidian Battus, who says in the *Metamorphoses, book 2, verse 703:*

->beneath those<-
->*Mountains, he said, they were, and they were beneath those mountains.*<-

Consequently, to hunt for Pygmies in Tyre would be no different than looking for hares in Ithaca, weasels in Boeotia, wolves in England, or foxes in Crete <note>Proverbial expressions for seeking things where they do not exist or are extinct; wolves were famously eradicated in England</note>. Thus, I marvel at a certain theologian who, in a small work written about Pygmies, tried to persuade us from this Prophetic text that Pygmies exist. I prefer to profess my ignorance of what the "Gammadim" <note>original: "Gammadæi"</note> are, rather than to show what they are not. I would rather admit that Pygmies do not exist than to engage in a "pygmy-fight" <note>original Greek: πυγμαχεῖν</note> with mediocre men. Those who wish to read more about Pygmies should consult *Spigel, On the Fabric of the Human Body, book 1, chapter 7; Caspar Bartholin on Pygmies; and Zeiler, Letters, Volume 2, p. 402.*

>

>
> *You were in Eden, the garden of God; every precious stone was your covering: the sardius, topaz, and jasper; the chrysolite, onyx, and beryl; the sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald; and gold. The workmanship of your timbrels and your pipes was in you; they were prepared on the day you were created.*

<margin>Sacred Lithology.</margin> **L**anguages lend and borrow words from one another; indeed, the trade in words is no less frequent than the trade in natural goods. The East sends rare things to the West, among which pearls stand out. In size, color, integrity, purity, value, beauty, and power, they surpass the Western ones by many parasangs <note>A Persian measure of distance, roughly 3.5 miles</note>. Meanwhile, the West receives them with a grateful mind, and to demonstrate its spirit more fully, it sometimes retains the names themselves, either entirely or slightly changed. Regarding the catalog of stones and gems—especially

<column-break/>

those mentioned frequently in the Holy Scriptures <note>original: "S. Pandectis," referring to the Bible as a complete body of law/knowledge</note>—and their interpretation <note>original Greek: ἐξηγήσει</note>, it is no wonder we find <margin>Sacred Lithology.</margin> that the Hebrews sometimes hesitate and sometimes are completely off the mark <note>original Greek: δὶς διὰ πασῶν, literally "two octaves away," a musical metaphor for being totally wrong</note>. For how could they, being so far removed from their native land, not have erred in the interpretation of gems, trees, and animals? Therefore, as Grotius well advises *on Exodus, p. 81*, we should not trust those later Rabbis too much in these matters. Those things pertaining to law have been preserved well enough through a certain succession of books (and Selden has most learnedly cleared away the ruins in several volumes). But the tradition regarding Physical things has perished over so many centuries, and therefore we must follow conjectures. Goropius Becanus also aims at this in *Hermathena 9, p. 226*: *The ignorance of Hebrew interpreters regarding the names of stones and plants is marvelous,* he says, *so that I am not surprised if they make now this, now that, from the same name.* Hence, Theodor Bibliander writes in *On the Best Way to Explain Hebrew*: <margin>p. 83.</margin> *On physical matters, one should listen to the Physicists <note>Natural scientists</note>, who contribute more erudition regarding the parts of the human body, diseases, plants, stones, metals, living creatures, the heavens, and the stars, than all the libraries of the Jews. In this part, the writers of Arabia, both the Astrologers and the Doctors, will be of great use, for it seems much of the Hebrew language has been mutilated in this area.* In such great obscurity, what wonder if anyone were said to be hallucinating, even if he were Theophrastus himself? Though we cannot accurately investigate the origins and native meanings of the gems, we do not act like those who behave sluggishly, appearing satisfied if they merely say "it is the name of a gem" or "a species of stone." Let us do what we can concerning the gems, and let us not, like Aesop’s Cock, cast away the pearl even if we do not know exactly its power or use.

The "precious covering" made of various stones in Ezekiel denotes nothing other than the royal crown, which shades the head of the ruler; these small stones signify royal virtues which, just as precious stones adorn a crown, so do they honor the royal majesty, which ought to display its virtues far and wide. *Indeed, I think so,* writes Paschasius: <margin>9. Coron. 10 / p. 598.</margin> *The Prophet’s precious covering of stones is the royal crown, which, specifically, shades the head of the ruler.* Therefore, *as the insignia of such great power make the King more eminent than all others, so those virtues, which correspond to such great dignity, ought to make him more holy and august than all others. Oh, how great is the deformity of that head which is found unequal to this great burden! Just as the celestial lights temper the entire world, so do royal virtues temper the administration.* Thus he comments on the present passage. Among those things which are beautiful in the bodies of the earth, St. Bernard, in his *Sermon on the Feast of St. Martin, col. 409*, mentions the following: *Gold, the Gem, and the Lily, which are mixed with things not beautiful: gold in the mud, a gem in the dunghill, a lily among thorns.* Regarding the gems, although we spoke earlier on Exodus 28 concerning those which adorned the breastplate of the High Priest among the Hebrews, it pleased me to say a few things here. These, as Jean d'Espagnet writes in *Physics Restored, Canon 173*, draw their forms from the clearest fountains of the Heaven and the Sun, and their...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Lithology <note>The study of stones in the Bible.</note></margin>
...that these bodies are the purest droplets of exuberant dew, pregnant with celestial influences, and like solidified tears of heaven <note>original: "concretas coeli lacrymas"</note>. In this opinion <note>original: "δόξα"</note> of the Ancients was also *Pliny* (Book 9, chapter 35), and *Marbodaeus* expressed it in verse in chapter 60. Truly, **Pearls** <note>original: "Uniones," referring to large, single pearls of great value</note> are conceived in shells as if in their own womb, a fetus marvelous for its brilliance and birth, shining with a snowy whiteness, but dangerous to obtain due to the difficulty of the catch. For as *Isidorus of Charax* testifies in his description of *Parthia* found in *Athenaeus*, if divers seize them recklessly and insert a hand into the gaping shell, it happens that the shell snaps shut and their fingers are cut off. *Ammianus* adds another danger, which accounts for their high price: because the shells are accustomed to the shoreline, they retreat from the snares of the fishermen and hide around remote cliffs and the hollow retreats of the sea. Hence *Arrian* says in his *Voyage of the Erythraean Sea* that in *Comarina* the custom is that the diving for these shells <note>original: "κολύμβησις τῷ πιννικῷ"</note> is done by condemned criminals <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς καταδίκης"</note>. Among other regions and islands of the East, *Hormuz* was once most famous, even in the time of *Lucian* (*Images, p. 283*), "in the most shining mixture of pearls." For thus *Varthema* <note>Ludovico di Varthema, a 15th-century traveler</note> says of it:
<margin>Travels, Book 2, p. 220.</margin>
*Hormuz is second to no city in its abundance of Pearls. After a journey of two days, shells are gathered which produce pearls more beautiful and larger than other gems.* Regarding their capture, he adds: *In the middle of the ship, the man who has the task of fishing, with a pouch hanging from his chest and back and a stone tied to his feet, flings himself into the sea; he swims underwater in the manner of divers and remains submerged in the depths at fifteen paces until he has gathered the shells in which the pearls and gems hide. Once collected, he puts them in the pouch, immediately casts off the stone that weighed down his feet, and holding onto a rope, he emerges to the surface.* Nearly the same things are read regarding the province of *Malabar* in *Marco Polo the Venetian* (Book 3, chapter 23, p. 403). For he writes, *many merchants gather there, bringing many ships, large and small, and hiring men to plunge into the depths of the sea to fish for sea-shells from which pearls are collected. Those fishermen, when they can no longer bear being underwater, swim up, and then throw themselves headlong into the sea again, which they repeat many times throughout the day.* Now, for the first stone in this royal ornament, the Greek and the Old Latin translator, as well as *Luther* and *Pagninus*, hold it to be the **Sardius**. The Hebrews commonly explain this gem as a ruby, an opinion which seems to be supported by the name *Adam* <note>original Hebrew: אדם</note>, which is derived from "redness." The second in order is the **Topaz**, which the Chaldean translator calls *Yarkan* <note>original: ירקן</note>, meaning "green."
<margin>On Psalm 118, column 936.</margin>
Hence some wish it to be the *Prassine* <note>a leek-green stone</note> from its green color. Regarding the **Topaz**, let us hear *Jerome*: *As gold excels other metals,* he says, *so the Topaz excels other stones. For it is itself the rarest and most beautiful of all, and the largest. It is usually found in a place in the Thebaid called Alabastra. They also say in the writings of secular historians that it was found on the island of Topazos by its inhabitants, the Troglodyte Arabs, and brought as a gift to the mother of King Ptolemy of Egypt, under whom the scriptures of the Law were translated from Hebrew into Greek. It contains within itself the appearance of the other finest and most precious gems, and in that one stone is a mixture of the most diverse colors.*

<column-break/>

The third stone, if we follow *Luther* and *Junius*, is the **Diamond** <note>original: "Adamas"</note>; but they commonly interpret the Hebrew word *Jahalom* <note>original: יהלם</note> as **Jasper**. Great is the hardness of the diamond, especially the Arabic variety, whose hardness is so unyielding that when placed on anvils and struck with a hammer, it rejects the blow so that the iron on both sides shatters, and the anvils themselves fly apart; hence *Scaliger*, a man of the sharpest intellect, when asked why only goat’s blood can break a diamond, used the word "I DON'T KNOW" <note>original: "NESCIO"</note> as his solution. For that reason, by excellence and as a kind of proverb, all hard things are called "adamantine." *Statius* (Book 7, on the *Palace of Mars*):

->And the doors, closed with eternal<-
->diamond, flew open.<-

In the same author (Book 3), the horses of *Mars* chew on diamonds. And *Mars* himself in *Horace* is depicted in an adamantine tunic, and in *Manilius* (Book 1), discord is conquered by adamantine chains. The same speech is very frequent among the Greeks: hence men of firm and stubborn spirit are said by *Hesiod* to have "a strong-hearted spirit of diamond" <note>original: "ἀδάμαντος κρατερόφρονα θυμὸν"</note> (v. 146). And *Aeschines*, speaking against *Ctesiphon* regarding *Demosthenes*, says purely proverbially: "with walls of bronze and diamond, as he himself says, he fortified our region" <note>original: "χαλκοῖς καὶ ἀδαμαντίνοις τείχεσιν..."</note>. While we write this, a passage occurs to us in *Amos* (chapter 7, verses 7-8) that is highly relevant to this matter: "standing upon a wall of *Anach*" <note>original Hebrew: נצב על חומת אנך</note>. For thus the interpreters commonly read it as "a wall of a plumb line." But in truth, the word *Anach* is so obscure that even the presence of the most learned Hebrews cannot dispel those shadows. The illustrious *Drusius* seemed in his time to be the sun of Hebrew literature above all others, yet no daylight shone upon our word from this sun. "I see that interpreters," he writes, "vary greatly over the explanation of the word *Anach*; therefore I have decided to report their opinions in this chapter with no judgment of my own interposed, nor do I hope it will be attributed to me as a fault, since the hidden meaning of that vocabulary does not permit us to decide recklessly upon it." But what light do the Hebrews shed? What do the Greeks? Among the Hebrews, one understands this as lead, another as a plummet made of lead. *Rabbi David* <note>David Kimchi</note> in his commentary on this place walks a very remote path and considers the word from Arabia, reporting that in the Arabic language *Anach* (with a *dagesh* in the letter *Caph*) means "tin." *Abenezra* had written this before him, so that *Rabbi Kimchi* in his *Book of Roots* seems to see nothing else than white lead—likewise, a plummet, which in the Israelite language is made of tin or lead. It would be the Arabs to whom we must go, for unless they were reached, *Anach* would perhaps have remained in eternal darkness. *Rabbi Jarchi* <note>Rashi</note>, along with some man named *Done* <note>likely Dunash ben Labrat</note>, also a Hebrew, builds a wall. Concerning the Greeks, where we have in the *Vulgate* translation, "the Lord standing over a plastered wall," the *Septuagint* <note>original: "LXX"</note> reads, "a man standing upon an adamantine wall." And where in our books it is: "And in his hand a mason's trowel," in the *Septuagint* we read, "and in his hand a diamond." *Symmachus* also translates it the same as the *Septuagint*, as noted by *Jerome*, whose words are: *Symmachus and the Septuagint, for that which is written in Hebrew as* Anach, *translated it as diamond.* *Aquila* translates it as "unwalled." *Theodotion* as "melting"; one of which signifies tinning, the other wasting away. Those who plaster a wall with lime... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence at the end of the page.</note>

<margin>Sacred Lithology <note>The study of stones in the Bible.</note></margin>
...they are said to **anoint** <note>original: "ἀλείφειν"</note>, and from this, the anointing itself is **smearing** or **unction** <note>original: "ἀλείφωσις" and "ἄλειψις"</note>. But what does "tinning" <note>original: "stagnatura," likely referring to the setting or casting of the stone</note> mean? Understand it as "tinning," yet I do not quite understand what the Holy Father <note>Likely referring to a specific Church Father or commentator like Jerome</note> intended, by whom it was not correctly translated; nor was that word **molded** <note>original: "τυπούμενον"</note>, which I believe is meant in the sense of melting rather than wasting away. Regarding the name of the diamond, I wish to add the words of **Franciscus Lambertus** <note>A 16th-century Protestant reformer</note> in his Commentary, folio 62b: *Through the diamond, at once the most precious and hardest stone, what is captured if not the strongest hand of divine protection and help, and at the same time his most precious and invincible truth? This is followed by **Shoham** <term>שׁהם</term>. To some, this is the **Sardonyx**. It takes its name from its place of birth and *onyx*, for they say it was first found in Sardinia. It is a stone of red brilliance, but of a whitish color. <gloss>A Sardinian gemstone that is red mixed with white.</gloss> A brilliant testimony of this fact, and of its excellence and <margin>Satire 13, v. 134.</margin> use in rings, was left to us by **Juvenal***:
->and the chief gem,<-
->the **Sardonyx**, which is guarded in ivory boxes.<-
It was engraved for use as a seal, to which the Poet referred when speaking of the signed documents <note>original: "chirographis"</note> given to creditors. **Calvin** grieved because of money denied to him by the person with whom it was deposited. Juvenal consoles him in his lack of goods, explaining to him the perfidy of the age, and says it must be attributed to common malice that men deny their own signatures, since all things are (v. 131):
->full of similar wild complaints.<-
Perjured men are found who, according to verse 113:
->Call the legal signatures of useless wood "vain."<-
Who call their obligations—read and sealed on wax tablets by even ten different witnesses—"vain lies," even though their own handwriting and the very seal of sardonyx, which is kept in a box made of ivory and was pressed into the cautionary document itself, convicts them. Regarding this gem, there is a passage

<margin>Sacred Lithology. Epigram 4. 61. v. 6.</margin> that is obscure in **Martial***, the cloud of which **Rutgerfius** has attempted to disperse. It is, however, from the common edition:

We return to our **Shoham** <term>שׁהם</term>. **Abraham Ibn Ezra** confesses that he is ignorant of this stone. **Aquila**, **Symmachus**, **Theodotion**, **Jerome**, and **Pagninus** translate it as **Onyx**. But if it is Onyx according to Jerome's version, by what reasoning can there truly be so many and such varied versions of this same word among the LXX, who render it sometimes as a **leek-green stone** <note>prasinum</note>, sometimes a **sard**, sometimes an **emerald**, and sometimes a **beryl**, following the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> who reads **Burla** <term>בורלא</term>? Yet **Hopkinson** (*On Paradise*, p. 14) not undeservedly rejects the opinion of Jerome and others regarding the Onyx, since the onyx is a common gem, not of such great price, and it grows abundantly in many places. He believes, along with **Josephus**, that it is the **Sardonyx**, that stone of red brilliance and sometimes white or black color, composed of Sarda and Onyx according to Pliny. Following this in order is **Yashpheh** <term>ישׁפה</term>. To some, this is the **beryl**. In other contexts, the study of gems is noted in **Maecenas** by Meibom (*In Maecenatem*, ch. 21, p. 125); and since he was a great lover of little stones, he held Beryls as his delights—and not undeservedly, for **Pedo Albinovanus**, in the poem where he honors the death of Maecenas (v. 19), sings thus:
> The Beryl surpasses common sands,
> which the wave moves at the edge of the shore.
Memory of Beryls is not so infrequent <margin>Ch. 3, *On the Soul*, p. 530.</margin> in **Tertullian**, for he says*: *The substance of Thunder-stones <note>original: "Cerauneis"</note> is not fiery because they gleam with a reddish glow, nor is the matter of Beryls watery because they fluctuate with an inherent brilliance.* To **Luther**, **Junius**, and others, it is **Jasper** <note>original: "Iaspis"</note>, a word that agrees with the Hebrew. However, it is not just one kind of stone, since among them the purple and green varieties excel. That which the Greeks name **aspis**, **Agricola** thinks is called in our language <gloss>a Turquoise</gloss>. The excellence of this gem is also verified by these lines:
> What is better than gold? Jasper. What is better than Jasper? Virtue.
> What is better than virtue? God. What is better than deity? Nothing.
Nor should we overlook that skillful carving in Jasper of seven oxen, which **Polemon** mentions in the *Anthology* (Book 4, ch. 18, p. 736):
> A tiny Jasper stone held a seal of seven oxen,
> all looking as if they were alive, as if they were one.
> And perhaps the little oxen might have escaped, but now
> the little herd is enclosed in a golden pen.
The seventh in this royal vestment <note>original: "ἱματισμῷ βασιλικῷ"</note> is **Sapphirus** <term>ספיר</term>, the **Sapphire**; the name itself suggests it, and the Chaldean and all other interpreters we have seen agree; see above at Exodus 28:17 and following. To this, attached by an inseparable bond, is **Nophekh** <term>נפך</term>. To **Onkelos** and **Vatablus**, this is the **Emerald**. To **Buxtorf**, it is the **chrysoprase**.
