# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Lithology <note>The study of stones in the Bible.</note></margin>
...others call it a pearl or a crystal. To the Greeks and in the Vulgate <note>The 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note> it is the carbuncle <note>original: "carbunculus"; usually a red gemstone like a garnet or ruby</note>. Among the treasures of the Church of Mainz, there once stood an image of the crucified Christ; in its head, in place of eyes, were two gems which they call carbuncles. These were of such great size—as large as two egg yolks, according to Bishop Christian II in the *Chronicles of Mainz, page 451* as cited by Reuler—that they glowed in the dark. Inscribed upon this cross was the following verse:

->**This golden cross holds six hundred pounds of gold.**<-

The final stone in this group is the *Bareketh* <note>original: "ברקת"; Hebrew for "lightning-flash," usually translated as emerald</note>, which is commonly translated as Emerald. The emerald refreshes the sight with its greenness by gently gathering the spirits in the eye; for greenness—which possesses a dominance of blackness mixed with a small amount of brightness—collects the visual spirits and prevents them from scattering, as taught by Licetus in *Annals, chapter 19, page 77*. Vartomannus <note>Ludovico di Varthema, a 15th-century traveler</note> testifies in *Travels, book 6, chapter 28, page 271* that the island of Guaya provides the most elegant emeralds in the entire world. In the ecclesiastical furnishings of the Great Cathedral of Mainz, Conrad also records in the *Old Chronicle* <margin>page 10.</margin> an emerald having the size and thickness of a melon. Because it was hollow, it was customary to pour water into it along with two or three small fish; when the lid was placed on top and the fish moved, simple people and old women would claim that the stone was alive.

*Varablo* is a carbuncle; some think it is the same as the pyrope or ruby, others think it different. On the <margin>Travels, book 3, page 253.</margin> island of Ceylon <note>Modern Sri Lanka</note>, Vartomannus writes* that there are Pyropes: "Not far off is seen a mountain of vast length, at the base of which Pyropes are found. These are precious little stones, commonly called Rubies. Not far from said mountain, countless precious stones are found where a great river flows in, especially hyacinths, sapphires, and topazes, and many stones of that kind." From these accounts, it is clear how much ignorance regarding precious stones led the ancients into various conjectures, and indeed, confusion. Indeed, the names of gems are so difficult to grasp that whatever has been said or written about them, by both Christians and Hebrews, is mostly of such a nature that nothing can be asserted with certainty. Most things are skeptical and **uncertain** <note>original: "ἀπορητικὰ"</note>, such that those words of the Sceptics—**"I withhold judgment, I believe, and it seems to me"** <note>original: "ἐπέχω, οἴομαι, καὶ δοκῶ"</note>—must often be repeated. Nevertheless, effort must be given as much as possible so that they do not remain **incomprehensible** <note>original: "ἀκατάληπτα"</note>, lest we also seem like unfair judges against the Hebrews, whose ignorance in this matter is manifest. For now, we have provided these collected notes until better information is brought to light. The choice is given to the reader to pick what pleases them. Let those more learned in gemology, who possess a bit more wit and skill, polish this little thicket of information more finely. But before we prepare for our complete departure from this topic, we must consider that vision of John, no less illustrious than it is supremely delightful, concerning the **foundation** <note>original: "θεμελιώσεως"</note> of the wall in the heavenly Jerusalem made of pure pearls, *Revelation 21:19-20*: **"The beautiful foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every precious stone."** <note>original: "καλοὶ θεμέλιοι τοῦ τείχους τῆς πόλεως παντὶ λίθῳ τιμίῳ κε코σμημένοι"</note> The structure of the wall surrounding the heavenly Jerusalem consisted of Jasper, and the first foundation of the city wall was of the same stone. Regarding jasper, those skilled in nature and gems report that it cleanses the filth of the eyes and sharpens the sight (Bartholomew the Englishman, *On the Properties of Things, book 16, chapter 53*), and that it frees from adverse accidents 

<column-break/>

the one who wears jasper on their finger, according to Franciscus Rueus, *book 2 on gems, chapter 1, page 206*. Rueus attributes to it in the same place the power to stop flowing blood and to recognize individual diseases. This is what they say of the ring of Galen <note>A famous 2nd-century Greek physician</note>, in which there was a jasper depicting a man wearing a bundle of herbs hanging from his neck. We speak rather of Christ our Lord and Physician*, whose

->*Medicine heals all human sorrows.*<-

He alone is the Chief Physician <note>original: "Archiater"</note>, while all other doctors are his disciples, as Origen says in *Volume 2, Homily 1 on Psalm 37, page 53*: "Just as he prepared medicines for the body from herbs composed by art and discipline: so also he prepared medicines for the soul in his words, which he sowed and scattered through the Divine Scriptures. Thus, those who are oppressed by some sickness, as soon as they feel the power of the disease or perceive the sting and pain of some wound—that is, when they see something acting against nature—they may seek out the rational discipline suitable and fitting for them, which can heal them through the commandments of God." John had seen, as he records at the beginning of *Revelation chapter 4:3*, God sitting, similar in appearance to a Jasper stone and a Sardis. Isidore enumerates seventeen kinds of Jaspers in *Etymologies, book 16, chapter 7*, among which is the *aerizusa*, similar to the air, as Pliny says*, or to the morning autumn sky; Pliny also suggests in *chapter 2 of the same book* that this stone is of a fiery color. Hence, when it is attributed to God, it marks the infinite excellence of his Deity, according to that poem, which it is pleasing to repeat here for its elegance:

> *What is better than gold? Jasper. What better than Jasper? Virtue.*
> *What better than virtue? God. What better than the deity? Nothing.*

For God, as one who can be seen by no mortal, says to his servant Moses in *Exodus 33:20*: "You cannot see my face; for man shall not see me and live." He dwells in **unapproachable light** <note>original: "φῶς ἀπρόσιτον"</note>, *1 Timothy 6:16*. Thus he appears to Moses for the first time in a bush burning with fire, *Exodus 3:2*, and so he presents himself to Israel in thunder, lightning, and fire, *Exodus 19:16, 18*. He does this so that he might indicate his invisible and incomprehensible essence and glory in this way; which cannot be seen except from "the back" <note>referencing Moses seeing God's back in Exodus</note>, according to that common saying: "God is darkness after all light, and is recognized only by the mind's ignorance." Concerning the jasper, Marbodeus the Briton, Poet and Bishop of Rennes, sang around the year 1150 (according to Bale):

> *Carried chastely, it puts fever to flight and wards off dropsy,*
> *When applied, it helps the woman in labor:*
> *And it is believed to be a protection for the wearer.*

For when consecrated, it makes one pleasing and powerful. The wall, I say, which fortified this heavenly city, consisted of jasper. A truly wonderful gem, says Blessed Cluverus*, from which an entire wall was made—and such a great wall, 375 miles high, and 144 cubits thick, and how many thousands of miles long? Furthermore, the first foundation was Jasper. For this wall consisted of twelve foundations, of which the first was Jasper, concerning which we have spoken so far. The second foundation was seen by John to be made of Sapphire stone, which is thought to have medicinal virtue, though otherwise useless for engraving. It is green with intervening crystalline centers, and occasionally translucent with certain gold-

### Ezekiel 28:13 — Page 679

<column-1>
<margin>Sacred Lithology <note>The study of stones in a religious or biblical context.</note></margin>
...shining with little points, from which Franciscus Rueus <term>chapter 2, in the place cited</term> declares this stone to be endowed and adorned with all the qualities suitable to the ecclesiastical order. **The third is of Chalcedony**; this stone shines like fire, similar to a pale lamp, and its color appears under the open air or sky, but not under a roof. If it grows hot, either by the rays of the sun or the touch of fingers, it attracts straws to itself <note>A description of static electricity, often noted in amber or tourmaline but here attributed to chalcedony.</note>. Bartholomaeus Anglicus <term>in the place cited, chapter 28</term> also attributes to it the power of conquering if it is worn perforated.

<margin>Exodus 25, 26.</margin>
The **fourth** foundation of the wall consists of the most noble and precious of green gems, namely the Emerald <note>original: "Smaragdus"</note>, which gives its own color to those things it is placed near, soaking them and rendering the surrounding air green. Furthermore, it is most loving of bodily purity and most impatient of sexual matters, whence it betrays those devoted to wicked Venus by its cracking, as Franciscus Rueus cites several examples of this matter <term>in the place cited, chapter 4, page 211</term>.

<margin>Book 37, chapter 8.</margin>
The **Sardonyx** moreover adorned this wall of the Heavenly Jerusalem, and the **fifth** foundation consisted of this stone. This gem is like a human fingernail, or certainly reflects the color of a human nail where it clings to the flesh, from which it also took its name; for *onyx* <note>original: "ὄνυξ"</note> among the Greeks signifies a nail. And since it participates in the nature of both the Sard and the Onyx—drawing redness from the Sard and whiteness from the Onyx—it is for this reason that the name **Sardonyx** was given to the composition of both gems. Those which vary in color—first, say, black, white in the middle, and red on top—are considered more precious. The **sixth** was the **Sardius**, a stone which is of a blood-red color; it sharpens the wit and endows men with sagacity of mind, as Rueus indicates <term>chapter 6, page 213</term>. The **seventh** foundation was formed of **Chrysolite**, reflecting the appearance of gold, from which it also has its name; for among the Greeks *chrysos* <note>original: "χρυσός"</note> is gold. It diffuses burning sparks and drives away terrors at night. Besides the color of gold, it has a certain similarity to a sea-color, which is why it is called *Tarshish* <note>original: "תַּרְשִׁישׁ"</note> by the Hebrews. Bartholomaeus Anglicus reports of it <term>chapter 29</term> that it diminishes melancholy, and Franciscus Rueus <term>chapter 7, page 214</term> says it contributes much to the respiratory parts as well as to asthmatics. Rueus further testifies that a "stamped" <note>original: "τετυπωμένον"; meaning engraved or naturally marked</note> Chrysolite was found, in which a woman was depicted by the skill of nature, holding a bird in one hand and a fish in the other. This is an image of Venus, that is, the innate desire in all to generate their own likeness; for this was planted in all by divine blessing, according to Lucretius:

<margin>At the beginning of Book 1.</margin>
> Finally, through seas and lands, and rushing rivers,
> and the leafy homes of birds, and green fields,
> striking alluring love through the breasts of all,
> you cause them to eagerly propagate their generations, kind by kind.

<margin>Commentary on this passage.</margin>
The **eighth** consisted of **Beryl**, regarding which Franciscus Rueus mentions <term>chapter 8</term> that it aids watery eyes. Those skilled in Nature report that two colors are in it: one green, the other pale, but it does not shine unless it is shaped into a hexagonal form by polishing. For by the reflection of the angles, its splendor is sharpened, and it is said to burn the hand of the one holding it. The **ninth is of Topaz**, which is more precious the rarer it is; it reflects two colors: one of the purest gold, the other shining with ethereal clarity, and it flames more intensely whenever it is struck by the rays of the Sun.
</column-1>

<column-break/>

<column-2>
<margin>Sacred Lithology.</margin>
The **tenth is of Chrysoprase**; this is a green gem, reflecting the color of leek juice, declining into gold with falling golden drops, according to Marbodeus:

> Glowing with fire by night, it vanishes in the light of day,
> lying without luster, buried in the paleness of gold.

The **eleventh** foundation of the wall which surrounded the Heavenly Jerusalem was the **Hyacinth** <note>Often identified as the Sapphire or Jacinth today.</note>, which by its violet color represents the hyacinth flower, and reflects a celestial color like the Sapphire, and changes its color with the face of the sky; for in a serene and bright sky it is clear, but in a troubled sky covered with clouds, this stone is dark. Among its innate virtues, Cardano <term>Book on Subtlety</term>, Bartholomaeus Anglicus <term>chapter 54</term>, and Franciscus Rueus <term>chapter 12</term> report that it renders those wearing it safe from lightning, procures sleep, increases riches, and delivers from the danger of plague.

<margin>page 339.</margin>
The **Amethyst** closed the line of gems on which the wall of the heavenly city represented in the vision to John rested. This gem is indeed of low price, as Cardano has it <term>page 364</term> because of its abundance and plenty (compare Ursinus, *Symbolic Theology, book 151, page 176*); yet being of a violet color, it flashes more brilliantly than the hyacinth and is easy to carve. Among purple gems, the Indian amethyst holds the primacy; it is purple mixed with a violet color, like the luster of a rose, and lightly pouring out little flames. They report that it radiates with a threefold color, namely rose, violet, and purple, concerning which Marbodeus says:

> ...opposed to drunkenness,
> it would rightly be held more dear if it were rarer,
> but now it is neglected, because it is considered common.

With these ornaments, the walls of the heavenly city luxuriated in the eyes of John; upon these foundations rested the wall, the structure of which was of Jasper stone, while the city itself was pure gold, like clear glass. To human estimation, nothing is more precious than gold and gems, which is why the most wise Architect of the heavenly city represented to the eyes of his servant the beauty and delights of the eternal city and **human standards** <note>original: "καὶ ἀν θρωπινὰ ὅσιαν"; likely meaning using human values to describe divine things</note> in the appearance of those things which are held most precious before the world. Nor did this cause any difficulty for this most wise and **Almighty** <note>original: "παντοδυνάτῳ"</note> Architect, as it was not impossible for Him in the first creation of things to assign to the Elements their place, to adorn the winds with wings, to calm the storms of the sea, to distinguish the dry land without help, to raise the hills, to cast down the valleys, to give roots to the trees, light to the Sun, metals to the mountains, and life to living things. But why this adornment of the heavenly city? Since it is established that the heavenly city into which Christ entered is not **made by hands** <note>original: "χειροποίητον"</note>, <term>Hebrews 9:24</term>, but is the holy city, **coming down out of heaven from God** <note>original: "καταβαίνουσαν ἐκ τῷ οὐρανοῦ ἀπὸ τῷ Θεῷ"</note>, <term>Revelation 21:10</term>, which the **all-wise and almighty** <note>original: "ὁ πάνσοφος & παντοδύνατος"</note> Architect adorned with such splendors so that He might demonstrate His glory, majesty, omnipotence, goodness, and all-wisdom. To what end a wall built of pure jasper, and gates and towers built of every kind of gem? Since this heavenly city does not need walls and gates, for it does not fear enemies, on account of whom it might have need of these as fortifications for its defense. By the wall is denoted quiet security, that no danger threatens it from enemies. To others, however, it represents Christ Himself, who is not only of the Church militant...
</column-2>

It can be called the wall not only of the Church, but also of the triumphant Church, because it is He himself who both protects the Church on this earth and surrounds it in the heavens with the greatest security for all eternity, according to that passage of Isaiah:
<margin>chapter 26, verse 1.</margin>
*Salvation will be set in her as a wall and a bulwark.* And Zechariah, chapter 2, verse 5: *I will be to her a wall of fire all around.* Next, it is the constant opinion of interpreters that the apostolic virtues are figured by the names of the gems upon which the wall rests as a foundation, which become especially known in the heavenly life.
<margin>on Psalm 86.</margin>
Hence Augustine <note>original: "Augustinus"</note> says: "In what way are the Prophets and Apostles the foundations, and in what way is Christ Jesus the foundation, beyond whom there is nothing further? How should we think of this, unless it is as it is plainly said: He is the Holy of Holies, so figuratively He is the Foundation of foundations."
And Juan de Torquemada <note>original: "Iohannes de Turrecremata"</note>:
<margin>book 2, *Summa* chapter 19.</margin>
"Foundation is spoken of in two ways. In one way, it is that to which the first part of the building adheres, which however is not included in the building itself, such as solid earth or a rock or a cliff. In another way, the first part of the building, upon which the rest of the building is founded, can be called the foundation. In the first sense, the foundation that sustains the entire building is Christ; but the foundation spoken of in the second sense well suits others, namely the Apostles." Thus he speaks. Hence, according to the division of Johannes Clüver <note>original: "B. Cluveri"</note>, the stones <note>The OCR reads "lapsis," likely a typo for "lapides."</note> are usually explained as follows: **Jasper** refers to the most invincible and excellent strength of Peter’s soul, which he demonstrated after the resurrection. **Sapphire** refers to the heavenly migration of Saint James, which he, the first of all the Apostles, obtained, as if sprinkled with the purple of his blood. **Chalcedony** refers to John the Evangelist. **Emerald** refers to the faith of Andrew, whose faith so flourished before all others that he immediately warned his brother Peter that the Messiah had been found, and he carried Christ's Gospel to the most remote and barbarian Scythians. **Sardonyx** refers to the patience of Philip. **Sardius** refers to Bartholomew, most truly made red <note>original: "rubricatum"</note> when he was cruelly killed by having his skin stripped off. **Chrysolite** refers to Matthew, shining with gold, while he was the first to weave the evangelical history. **Beryl** refers to Thomas, who was initially slower in faith, but who afterward did not yield to the other Apostles in the multitude of his labors. **Topaz** refers to James the son of Alphaeus on account of his innocence of life. **Chrysoprase** refers to Jude Lebbaeus <note>Thaddeus</note> because of his faith in Christ and his love of eternal glory. **Hyacinth** refers to Simon because of his zeal. **Amethyst** refers to Matthias because of his contempt for the world. Johannes Clüver treats this more extensively in his *Commentary on the Apocalypse*; compare also Viega in this place and others.

### Daniel 2, verse 4.

<note>Hebrew: "And the Chaldeans spoke to the king in Aramaic: O king, live forever!"</note>
וּדִבְּר֤וּ הַכַּשְׂדִּים֙ לְמַלְכָּ֔א אֲרָמִ֑ית מַלְכָּא לְעָלְמִין חֱיִ֕י

<note>Greek: "And the Chaldeans spoke to the king in Syriac: King, live into the ages!"</note>
Καὶ ἐλάλησαν οἱ Χαλδαῖοι τῷ βασιλεῖ συριστὶ. Βασιλεῦ, εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας ζῆθι.

And the Chaldeans answered the King in Syriac: *O King, live forever.*

<margin>The use of secular Chronology in sacred matters.</margin>
There are many things in this Prophet which pertain to the state of the nations. Indeed, in most of Daniel's prophecies—which embrace the series of many years and the history of various nations (the Babylonians, Medes, Persians, Greeks, Romans, etc.) as if in a summary <note>original Greek: "ὡς ἐν συνόψει"</note>—there are things that can scarcely, if at all, be understood without secular history. The redemption of the human race was indicated to Daniel by the Angel,

<column-break/>

to follow after
<margin>70 years.</margin>
the seventy weeks of years. We agree with Chytraeus that these weeks cannot be calculated without an accurate knowledge of histories and the times of the Monarchies, and of Persian and Greek chronology <note>The OCR "Chie" is likely a clipping of "Chronologiæ."</note>; this was demonstrated by those most learned men, Marianus Helvicus and Bartholomaeus Meyerus, who are now among the saints <note>original Greek: "οἱ νῦν ἐν ἁγίοις" — a formula indicating the authors are deceased.</note>, in their dissertations on the weeks, published at Gießen and Leipzig. It was announced to Daniel by the Angel what the condition of the Jewish people would be under the Persian, Egyptian, and Syrian Kings. Here, unless you consult the monuments of those peoples yourself, you will stumble. Hence, some praise is deserved by the Englishman Hugo Broughton (and others after him), who diligently collected testimonies from Appian, Strabo, and many others that bring much light to the Prophecy of Daniel in his *Commentary on this Prophet*. Andreas Franckenbergerus—once Rector of the Gymnasium of Danzig and later Professor of History at the University of Wittenberg—required the same study in almost all the Prophets in his book *On the Amplitude and Excellence of Prophetic History*, which is greatly commended by Joachim Zehner. Compare the treatise by the same man to which
<margin>Phill.</margin>
he gave the title *Instruction on Antiquity and Histories*. We mention these things so that the student <note>original Greek: "φιλομαθὴς" — a lover of learning.</note> may learn from them that we have truly spoken to the point in what we have said.

<margin>...by</margin>
Leaving aside those things by which Daniel—knowing all times and being a "Polyhistor" <note>An expert in many fields of history.</note> of the whole world—sets traps for the sons of Chronologists, we shall not pass over the *formula of salutation* which we find in this sacred history.

The Chaldeans, having been brought before the King of the Babylonians, addressed him in these words in "Syriac," that is, in the Babylonian language (for Strabo and Pliny testify that Babylonia was once encompassed by Syria). *O King, live forever: tell the dream to your servants, and we will show its interpretation.* The
<margin>Daniel 2:4, 3:9, 5:10, 6:6, 21.</margin>
**Chaldeans**, accusing the Jews, say to Nebuchadnezzar: *O King, live forever.* The Queen, speaking to King Belshazzar, says: *O King, live forever.* The Satraps, coming into the sight of Darius, greet him thus: *Darius the King, live forever.* Indeed, Daniel himself addresses the King with this personal <note>original Greek: "ἰωτικῶ," likely a typo for "ἰδιωτικῶς" — privately or familiarly.</note> greeting: *O King, live forever.*

Moreover, this was a solemn formula so that those who approached the Kings of the East would pray for eternal life and empire for them. Quintus Curtius, in the 6th book of his *Histories*,
<margin>* p. 235.</margin>
writes that Artabazus, the most faithful of Darius's men, met Alexander with his relatives and children, and having been kindly received, said: *May you indeed, O King, flourish in perpetual happiness. I, happy in all else, am tormented by this one thing: that in my headlong old age I cannot enjoy your goodness for long.* A completely sweet story is told by Aelian in book 1 of his *Various History*, chapter 32: A certain Persian named Sinates, happening upon Artaxerxes far from his cottage, and not having a gift to offer the King according to custom, ran immediately to the nearby flowing river named Cyrus. Drawing up the waves with both hands, he addressed Artaxerxes thus:
*O King, god, may you reign for an eternity* <note>original Greek: "Βασιλεῦ, θἐε, ἐξ ἧς ἂν αἰῶνος βασιλεύοις."</note>: *Now I indeed, as best I can, honor you with these waters of the Cyrus. But if you come to my station, I will honor you with those things in my house which are most precious to us.* To whom the King replied: "Your gift... [to me]"

### Chapter VII, verse 3 and following.

> <note>original Hebrew: "וָאַרְבַּע חֵיוָן רַבְרְבָן סָלְקָן מִן־יַמָּא..."</note>

<margin>
The State of the IV Monarchies.
</margin>
Who is not familiar with the praise given to Calchas in Homer, as a seer of this kind in *Iliad book 1, verse 70*:
> “Who knew the things that are, the things that will be, and the things that were before.” <note>original Greek: "Ὅς ᾔδη τά τ' ἐόντα..."</note>

<margin>
*in Antioch.*
</margin>
One who knew, as Virgil interprets it:
> *“What is, what has been, and what is soon to come.”*

This is indeed the greatest praise, which fits not that pagan seer, but our Prophet Daniel, who was <term>theodidaktos <gloss>taught by God</gloss></term>, delivering not only what belonged to the present age, but what was yet to come. This "Calchas" of our Jewish people predicts and foretells the fates of the Church and of Republics, such as have never been predicted or foretold by any other teacher. We cannot sufficiently admire the divine power which, among other benefits toward mortals, wished this proof of His goodness—concerning the beginnings, increases, and decreases of the Monarchies—to be recorded in writing by Daniel and woven into various patterns, so that from there we might grasp the course of kingdoms and the fates of the Church. The merciful and all-wise God is accustomed to express the marks of future events through certain signs, and to hand down the truth of things to come through certain obscure coverings of figures and images. Therefore, nothing is more common for God than to indicate prophecies about the future state of the Church and Republics under the cover of signs and symbols. This is proven by the prophecies of Daniel in the Old Testament and the Revelations of John in the New Testament. In these prophecies, you may see an abyss of profound wisdom and a sea of inexhaustible divine goodness, such that those who take it upon themselves to open the mysteries of these books have total need of God’s <term>cheiragogia <gloss>guidance by the hand</gloss></term>. There are, moreover, two wondrous visions in the prophecy of Daniel. The first is that of King Nebuchadnezzar, as he was pondering the future outcomes of his reign.

<column-break/>

<margin>
The State of the IV Monarchies.
</margin>
The other was offered to the Prophet Daniel himself, both regarding the Monarchies through a dream. Many things have been discovered here by pious commentators, many things explained, and the prophecy has been made much clearer today through the outcomes of events and history. For Daniel, the <term>polyhistor <gloss>man of great and varied learning</gloss></term> of all times, cannot be explained except by an interpreter equipped with a great variety of historical knowledge. Indeed, one who is ignorant of Syrian, Persian, and Greek affairs will never understand the prophetic chapters of Daniel concerning them, but will wander through them just as Strigelius says in his *Oration on History, page 167*: <margin>* so that it may be a Volume.</margin> as if a blind man were preaching to a deaf one. Therefore, to wish to probe Daniel’s writings without a knowledge of history—to say nothing of other things—would be like trying to cross the Hellespont in a fragile boat. We shall take up a small portion of it here, first seeing in the "Colossus" the periods and fates of the four World Monarchies. Before we examine the structure of this Colossus, we shall set forth the preceding events: what tortured the King Nebuchadnezzar, who was most observant of dreams, and what he decided to do with all the Magi and Dream-interpreters of his kingdom after the dream had slipped his mind. Nebuchadnezzar, that King of Babylon, had dreams more hidden and terrifying than any he had ever had. When these had escaped his mind, and only a certain confused appearance remained in his memory of what had occurred to him during the night in a dream, he immediately ordered the four types of men to be summoned who were then seen to excel in wisdom and learning in the kingdom: namely, the *Genethliaci* <note>astrologers who cast birth charts</note>, the *Magi*, and the *Chasdam* <note>Chaldeans</note>. He put the matter to them and demanded a narration of the dream and its explanation. When they hesitated and pleaded that this was an unheard-of request, he threatened them with slaughter unless they could reveal both the dream itself and its solution. However, when DANIEL, among the others, was also sought for the slaughter along with his companions, he asked the King for time to meditate and investigate this perplexed question. This being granted, and the matter being revealed by God, he returned to the King and offered to satisfy his demands. The text reads as follows in *Chapter 2, verse 1: In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar dreamed dreams.* As for the phrase *“in the second year,”* it must be understood as referring to the reign now pacified and confirmed, the Monarchy now established, when—all the Eastern nations having been brought under the yoke—no one remained who could cause him further trouble. Thus the Hebrews calculate from the total subjugation of the opposing nations, and Jerome followed them <margin>* column 1106.</margin> writing: *“This is called the second year of his reign over all the barbarian nations, not only Judea and the Chaldeans, but also the Assyrians, Egyptians, Moabites, and the rest of the nations which he had overcome by the Lord's granting.”* And Johann Wigand, page 44: *“In the second year, namely of the Monarchy, after the Egyptians and Moabites and other peoples were defeated; for it is solemn custom, even in our own age, that when a greater empire is received, a new computation of years is assigned, just as today the Emperors are accustomed to assign specifically and separately the year of their local kingdom and likewise the year of the Empire or the Imperial rule.”* Therefore, understand *“in the second year”* as being about the kingdom which he now held over all nations, not about the time when he brought Judea under his power; nor about the beginning of his reign as Theodoret thought (whom Pererius refutes), but, if we stand with Josephus,

...we stand, finally, in the twenty-fifth year of his own reign, and the seventh of the Babylonian captivity of the Jews. And so, in the second year of his Monarchical rule, with his kingdom firmly established on all sides, *he dreamed dreams* <note>original Hebrew: חלמות - "chalomot"</note>. Although it was only one dream presented to the King at one and the same time, it is not called "dream" <note>original Hebrew: חלום - "chalom"</note> in the singular, but *dreams* in the plural number. This is because many dreams were essentially contained within that one dream; specifically, many different metals were seen in a single statue, serving as images and symbols of the different Monarchies that would succeed one another. However, after this dream was divinely set before him, *his spirit was troubled, and his sleep was broken for him.* The loss of the dream is presented physically, with the cause assigned: a violent consternation had scattered his very intent to think and had muddled the visions of the dreams. As Thucydides also writes, "the memory of it will be struck away." He had felt such immense consternation due to the ferocity and majesty of the presented image that he woke up from it. *His spirit was confounded, and sleep was broken within him* <note>original German: "Sein Geist war verschlagen/ und der Schlaff ward in ihm gebrochen."</note>. Our version says: *He was so terrified by it that he woke up.* <note>original German: "Davon er erschrack/ daß er auffwacht."</note> The Swiss version: *From which his mind was struck, (his heart pounded) and it broke his sleep.* <note>original German/Swiss: "Ab dem ihm sein Gemüth erklopfft/ (sein Herz klopfft W.) und ihm den Schlaff brach."</note> Palpitation of the heart and distress of the chest occurred, and his limbs trembled at the shadow of the dream. Awakening, he lay with a trembling body; that "breaking" of the dream is not to be understood as if he had sunk into a deeper sleep during the dream itself, but rather "it was done" <note>original Hebrew: נהייתה נהיתה - "nehiyetah"; original Greek: ἐγένετο - "egeneto"</note>, meaning "it was finished" or "ended."

You place the highest and the lowest, the right hand changing to the left. The Old Version says: *His dream fled from him.* His sleep was interrupted so that he could in no way find rest. Anxious cares and worried thoughts about this dream distracted his soul, so that all sleep

Furthermore, the second cause was not natural, and it is more illustrious and certain: namely, that God Himself withdrew the image of the dream from the King's mind. This was done so that by his anxious searching, an opportunity would be provided to recognize Daniel's interpretation, and so that this very thing might serve as a testimony that the dream was by no means a physical occurrence or some deceptive phantom, but was entirely divine, foreshadowing real things necessary for the whole world to know. Among these, Jerome says: *Those we call Soothsayers, others have interpreted as 'epaoidei,' that is, Enchanters. Therefore they seem to be nothing but singers who perform their work with words.* Magicians are those who philosophize about signs. Evildoers <note>original Latin: "Malefici"</note> are those who use blood and victims, and often touch the bodies of the dead. Furthermore, among the Chaldeans, I think "genethliaci" <note>Casters of birth-charts or horoscopes.</note> are signified, whom the common people call Mathematicians. Our Interpreter: *He commanded all the star-gazers and wise men and sorcerers and Chaldeans to be called together.* <note>original German: "Er hieβ alle Sternseher und Weisen und Zauberer und Chaldeer zusammen fordern."</note> The Worms version, and with it the Swiss: *Then the King commanded that they should call together all the soothsayers and black-magicians, sorcerers and Chaldeans.* <note>original German: "Do befahl der König/ man solte alle Wahrsager und Schwarzkünstler/ Zauberer und Chaldeer zusammen beruffen."</note> The Belgian: *Then the King said that one should call the sorcerers and the star-peepers and the jugglers and the Chaldeans.* <note>original Dutch: "Do sagde der König/ daß man rufen solte die Zauberer und die Sterngucker und die Gauckeler und die Chaldäer."</note> Four kinds of wise men are summoned from all the provinces, and when they had come, they stood before the King. Since not one of all the Conjecturers and Diviners was found to be comparable with Daniel and his companions, who were ten times more excellent, how is it that they did not stand before the King in this illustrious assembly? Had the King forgotten that he once found such men, adorned with gifts by which they surpassed all the wise Magicians in the entire Babylonian kingdom, standing in service before him? We have here a testimony of the wondrous economy of God, who leads His own in a wondrous way. We also have a testimony of the craftiness of the Wise Men, by which they hid the Command so that Daniel would not be preferred over them in Wisdom. They seem to have been neglected, oppressed by the envy of others, and suppressed by the malevolence of the Courtiers. Courtly fame and favor is also faster than smoke, with the King no longer caring for Daniel's wisdom. To "sell smoke" <note>original Latin: "fumos vendere," an idiom for making empty promises or boasting of influence one does not have.</note> is considered the most courtly of acts. Jerome on verse 14, column 1108: *The Chaldeans, knowing that Daniel and the three boys were ten times wiser and more understanding than all the soothsayers and magicians sought in all of Chaldea, hid from them the King's questioning, lest they be preferred over themselves in the interpretation of the dream.* In order that Nebuchadnezzar might find out how vain was the boasting of his wise men, and how important it is for a court not to forget its Veterans, God allowed the King to forget the dream. ...of things: *I have dreamed a dream* <margin>verse 3</margin>, and my spirit was troubled <insert>and his spirit was troubled <note>original Hebrew: וַתִּפָּעֶם רוּחוֹ — "watipa'em rucho"</note></insert> to know the dream. The Old Version <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> says: *Being confused in mind, I do not know what I saw.* For the King did not have a total forgetfulness of the dream, but a confused memory of it remained with him; otherwise, it would have been easy for the Chaldeans to devise some dream and assign an interpretation to it. Hence, although the King did not know the dream specifically, the confused knowledge stuck in his mind, so that a lie could easily be detected. Thus <margin>column 1107</margin> Jerome <note>St. Jerome, a 4th-century scholar famous for translating the Bible into Latin</note> says: *A certain shadow, and, so to speak, an air and trace of the dream remained in the King's heart, so that when others reported it, he could remember what he had seen, and they could in no way deceive him with lies.* He reveals his anxiety about knowing the dream with a shortened manner of speaking, as those who are confused in mind are wont to speak. They boast and promise an explanation, trusting in their diabolical arts, which were of no use in matters offered by God. In dreams sent by the Devil, they might have prevailed by their art, for we believe that the evil Spirit can present foul dreams and reveal them to his false prophets. He was able to offer visions to false prophets, and those so plausible that they did not doubt they were true visions offered by God. Such were the dreams of the prophets of Baal, of whom Satan says: *I will go forth* <margin>2 Chronicles 18:21</margin> *and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.* They were persuaded by Satan with the most certain outcome that those things they were promising to King Ahab with such confidence would follow. But just as they could not perform the latter, so they could not do the former; for no certain and firm interpretation of dreams could be sought either from human conjectures or from the suggestions of devils. They do not add, *We will call upon our gods, by whose revelation we will explain this secret to you,* but trusting in their own deceptions, they immediately promise mountains of gold. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

It was brought about by God that the King should utterly forget the dream, clearly so that the glory of God might be manifested, and that through divine revelation, some protection might be provided for the people afflicted in captivity, while authority was secured for the Prophet himself. It was also done largely for the sake of the King himself: that, being abandoned by his own Magi, he might—through such a great revelation from a Jew, and a captive at that—turn toward the God known in Israel, and through the explanation of the dream, be able to correct his pride and haughtiness. For the Lord showed him, through this somber image, the ruin of the most splendid empires, so that he might know that nothing, either for himself or any mortal, will be lasting and stable in this world; and so that he might learn, having set aside his pride, to fear the Lord and show himself more just toward both the captive Jews and all those subject to his empire. Thus God, who brings about the changes of things, used this occasion of the dream to turn the boasting and glory of the Babylonian philosophers into confusion and shame, while changing the miseries of Daniel and his countrymen into the highest splendor of life. He did this in a wonderful way, which you shall now hear. *The King,* <margin>verse 12.</margin> *moved by great anger and fury, ordered that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed, and he entrusted this slaughter to Arioch, the Captain of the Guard.* <note>The Latin 'spiculatorum Præfecto' refers to the chief of the royal bodyguards or executioners.</note> <margin>Chapter 13, folio 105. b</margin> *He, in order to find and recover (these are the words of the Abbot of Deutz* <note>Rupert of Deutz, a 12th-century Benedictine theologian</note>*) the dream that had escaped the King, showed himself cruelly greedy and greedily cruel, while in great fury and anger he commanded that all the wise men of Babylon perish because they could not reveal the dream to him. But God and His word used that cruelty of his, without him knowing it, in a merciful way. The wisdom of God made good use of the excessive curiosity of the furious King. But how? While the Sophists* <note>Here used to mean the worldly-wise men or magicians</note> *were despised and condemned to death,* <margin>verse 13.</margin> *Daniel and his companions were sought at the same time to be killed.* Already all the wise men, down to the last one, were to be killed; Daniel himself was to be killed. *For the decree went out, and the wise men were being killed,* that is, they were meant to be killed. The Hebrew participle <gloss>matbahalin <note>original: מתבהלין</note></gloss>, although it is in the present tense, signifies here a time shortly in the future, just as in Jonah 1:3: *He found a ship going to Tarshish,* which means "soon to go." And Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a prominent 14th-century Franciscan commentator</note> rightly explains this phrase: *Arrangements were being made for their killing;* indeed, it had already been decided then; for it follows that the wise men were first hunted for, so that they might later be killed in a single troop. Holy Daniel, with his most pious company, remained hidden at home, exposed to the slanders of the impious diviners; for he had not been present at the assembly, the reason for which Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar</note> recorded from the Hebrews: <margin>column 1108.</margin> *The Hebrews ask why Daniel and the three boys did not enter to the King with the other wise men, and yet were ordered to perish with the rest when the sentence was pronounced. They explain it this way: at that time, when the King was promising rewards, gifts, and the greatest honor, they did not wish to go, lest they seem to shamelessly seek Chaldean riches and dignity. Or certainly the Chaldeans themselves, envying their glory and knowledge, entered alone as if they alone were to receive the rewards, and later, in the face of danger, they wanted to have as partners those whom they had rejected in the hope of glory.* The interpreter Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius, a 16th-century Jewish-Christian Hebraist</note> <margin>p. 245.</margin> gives two causes for their absence: first, because he was a youth and something of a newcomer compared to the others who had long held mastery in the Babylonian school and were considered the most practiced and skilled; and second, because the Chaldeans, as natives, envied 

<column-break/>

this honor of approaching the King to foreigners. Having heard the King's edict, Daniel asked the King's prefect, Arioch: <gloss>Why is the decree so urgent from before the king? <note>original Aramaic: על-מה דתא מהחצפה מן-קדם מלכא</note></gloss> He asks for what reason the decree had been published so hastily and precipitously. And when Arioch had explained the whole matter to him, Daniel, having obtained access, went to the King, *and requested that he would give him time to show the interpretation to the King.* The Abbot of Deutz <note>Rupert of Deutz</note> considers two things here (Chapter 10, folio 104b and Chapter 13, folio 106): first, that Daniel was not found to reveal the dream and open its interpretation until after the sentence had gone out that the wise men should be killed; and second, that the dream was not revealed to Daniel himself until he had first gone in and asked the King to give him time to show the solution. Having obtained permission, *he went to his house, and showed the matter to his companions Ananias, Misael, and Azarias, and they implored mercy from the face of the God of heaven concerning this secret, lest they should perish with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.* It should be considered carefully that the King, although completely driven by fury, nevertheless mercifully admitted Daniel’s prayers and granted the delay without grievance—a delay he had previously refused to the others, suspecting it as a trick. This was because God was turning and governing the King's mind, looking out for the safety of His people in this way. For the consolation of the Captives, God reserved the royal dream to be explained by no one but Daniel, and indeed only after the bloody edict, so that the expectation of all the wise men might rest on him alone; for they were hanging under the sword about to die, as the Abbot of Deutz says (Chapter 13, folio 106a), *unless Daniel, by relating the dream, became a protection against the common danger.* Because of this, everyone from the greatest to the least, along with the King himself, was attentive to hear, *ready to receive, most desiring and very teachable to understand, and well-disposed to praise.* The extraordinary piety of Daniel also shines forth: in such great dangers—for he himself was sought for death along with the other wise men—he did not despair of divine help. Instead, by an ardent imploring of the divine name, to which he earnestly exhorted his brothers, he obtained the revelation of the mystery and the interpretation of the dream. Jerome says: *Daniel asks for time, not so that he might search out hidden things by the exercise and shrewdness of his mind, but so that he might pray to the Lord of hidden things; and therefore he joins Ananias, Misael, and Azarias in prayer, lest he seem to presume alone on his own merit; so that since the danger was common to them, the prayer might also be common.* In his distress, he runs to the invocation of God, and through that invocation, the dream is opened to him. Through solemn prayers, he wrests the announcement of the dream and its interpretation from God as if by a certain force—a force pleasing to God. Through faith, he promises that he will find what was impossible for the other wise men to find. He cries out for the mercy of God over the secret; he is heard, he obtains it, and he celebrates the mercy of God with praises, according to the scripture: *Call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me.* Through faith, the secret was revealed to him in a vision of the night, <gloss>the mystery was revealed in a vision of the night <note>original Greek: ἐν ὁράματι νυκτὸς τὸ μυστήριον ἀπεκαλύφθη</note></gloss>. *He learns the King's dream by his own dream.* By the revelation of God, he knows the dream and its interpretation, which the demons did not know, and the wisdom of the world could not understand. It was revealed...

For this remarkable revelation <note>original: "Apocalypsi"</note>, he blessed the God of heaven and said: *Blessed be the name of God from age to age. His is the wisdom and the majesty. He changes the time and the hour. He rejects and appoints Kings. He bestows wisdom upon the wise and prudence upon the prudent. He reveals deep and hidden things. He knows that which is in the darkness, and light remains with Him.* Daniel attributed nothing to himself or his own sharp-wittedness—as the Chaldeans did—nor to human skill, but credited everything to divine mercy. He confessed to the God of his fathers, proclaiming that He had granted him wisdom and strength, and had indicated what he requested: namely, the revelation of the King's business. This brief song is one of thanksgiving <note>original: "Eucharisticum," from the Greek word for gratitude</note>, but it has a long concluding statement <note>original: "epiphonema"</note> which we leave to the theologians to explain in detail; for we are not writing "commonplaces" <note>general theological themes</note> here, as they are usually called. Furthermore, political thinkers may find here material to write concerning the genuine virtues of statesmen, in which **Wisdom** and **Fortitude** ought to stand out. Wisdom is for forming plans, and fortitude is for executing them. But it is not our purpose here to write political commonplaces either. After his thanksgiving to God was completed, Daniel wished to be led to the King *by Arioch, so that he might declare the interpretation to the King. At the same time, he interceded for the Wise Men of the Chaldeans, saying: <note>Hebrew: "אל-תּוֹבֵד לַחַכִּימֵי בָבֶל"</note> Do not destroy the wise men of Babylon.* He offered to show the King both the dream and the interpretation, which the entire school of wise men had been ignorant of. He favored the Babylonian wise men so much that he excused their ignorance and prayed that they might not be killed because of it. This is a rare example of charity toward enemies, whose great slaughter would have followed had Daniel not intervened. Jerome says: *He imitates the mercy of God, because he prays for his persecutors, and does not wish those to perish because of whom he himself was about to perish.* Meanwhile, he was brought to the King by Arioch, the Master of the Horse <note>original: "Magistrum Equitum"</note>, who, seeking to gain favor at court, said to the King: *I have found a man among the sons of the captivity of Judah who will announce the solution to the King.* See the character of the courtier, of whom Jerome says: *He credits God's grace to his own diligence, and says he "found" him, even though Daniel offered himself voluntarily to be introduced to the King. In this, the nature of messengers is shown: when they bring good news, they want it to seem like their own doing.* Daniel was summoned and addressed by the King: *Are you he who can make known to me <note>Aramaic: "חֶלְמָא דִי-חֲזַית וּפִשְׁרֵהּ"</note> the dream which I saw and its interpretation?* To this Daniel, with the mystery already opened to him by God, replied with a joyful face: *The mystery that the King asks, none of the Wise Men, Astrologers, Magicians, or Diviners will be able to show the King. But there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets. He makes known to King Nebuchadnezzar what is to come in the sequence of days.* This preface to the King is modest and pious; he denied that the secret of the dream could be reached through magical arts or any mode of human wisdom. He asserted it was not within the power of any man, even those most practiced in secular wisdom, to narrate or describe the dream through his own art and reason. By this, he struck down the arrogance of the Chaldean sages, who—making no mention of their gods—ascribed far too much to their own skillful **true knowledge** <term>ἐπίγνωσιν <gloss>epignōsin - precise or experiential knowledge</gloss></term>. Daniel, on the contrary, renounced the faculty of divination for himself and assigned it to God alone. By this, he affirmed that the dream was a matter of **revelatory knowledge** <term>ἐπίγνωσιν</term>, and at the same time removed the King’s *wicked suspicion* that human skill could find what is reserved for the knowledge of God alone. Fortifying himself with the name of the one God—by which *he secretly withdrew the King from the worship of many gods toward the knowledge of the one God—he revealed the dream.* First, however, he showed what the King’s predisposition was, and, so to speak, the prior thoughts through which he came into this dream. *Your thoughts, O King, rose up in your bed, as to what would happen hereafter.* The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> puts it best: <note>Greek: "Σὺ, Βασιλεῦ, οἱ διαλογισμοί σου ἐπὶ τῆς κοίτης σου ἀνέβησαν, τί δεῖ γενέσθαι μετὰ ταῦτα"</note> "You, O King, your thoughts rose up upon your bed, what must happen after these things." The thoughts are said to have "ascended," for the Chaldean word <term>סְלִק <gloss>seliq - to go up</gloss></term> implies this, just as we use the word "climb" <note>German: "Steigen"</note> regarding thoughts, and the Belgians express it here with the word "rise" <term>stömmen</term>. He provided the occasion for the dream: the King had been having thoughts about his Monarchy, anxious about his kingdom and whether it would remain successfully with his posterity. Hence Jerome (col. 1110): *When it is said, "You, O King, began to think," it indicates the causes of the dream; that God revealed the mysteries of the future to him because the King himself wished to know things to come. And so that Nebuchadnezzar might marvel at the grace of divine inspiration, Daniel explained not only what he saw in the dream, but what he had silently thought before the dream.* And Rupert of Deutz says: *Truly, a presumptuous and proud thought was the cause of that same dream, as Daniel himself testifies, saying: "You, O King, began to think upon your bed what would be hereafter." As if something had already been achieved in the fact that he was made King, and as if nothing greater or better than his kingdom could be made, he thought about what would be hereafter. God answered his thoughts as he deserved: namely, so that he could not even understand it nor bear it, yet, being astonished and confused, he remembered that something had happened to him.* Therefore, the dream responded in its own way to those things he had thought about during the day and those thoughts with which he had fallen asleep. This often happens in natural dreams, where images of daily actions occur at night. Indeed, the verses of Claudian are well-known, from the preface to Book 6 of *On the Consulship of Honorius*:

The "Colossal" dream of Nebuchadnezzar is as follows: He seemed to see a certain large and sublime statue, with a head of gold, chest and arms of silver, belly and thighs of bronze, legs of iron, and the feet partly of iron and partly of clay. After he had seen these, he finally saw a very large stone torn from a mountain by its own accord and hurled with great force against the statue. By that blow, first the iron and clay parts of the feet, and soon all the other parts, one by one, were crushed and ground like chaff, and scattered by the wind so that not even a trace of them remained. But the fragment from the mountain itself grew and expanded into such a great mountain that it filled the whole earth. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The State of the Four Monarchies.</margin>
...of his kingdom there shall be no end. King Nebuchadnezzar and his reign belonged to the first Monarchy, which was the Kingdom of the Assyrians and Chaldeans. It pleased God, the founder of Empires, to raise four kingdoms above all other kingdoms of the entire world, and to adorn them beyond all others with power, dignity, and glory, so that compared to these highest empires, the others—of which there is a vast number and variety—would seem like obscure shadows. Indeed, He chose **four Monarchies**, or four universal kingdoms, and preferred them over the rest, so that they might be superior and more celebrated than all the kingdoms of this world. These are the Monarchies of: 1. The Assyrians or Babylonians. 2. The Medes and Persians. 3. The Greeks. 4. The Romans. Dionysius of Halicarnassus lists these same four great empires of the world in the same sequence:

<margin>Roman Antiquities, Book 1, pages 2, 3.</margin>
<note>original Greek: "ἡ μὲν γὰρ Ἀσσυρίων ἀρχὴ..."</note> *For the rule of the Assyrians, being ancient and reaching back to the times of the Medes, held sway over only a small part of Asia. But the Median rule, having overthrown the Assyrians and encompassing a greater dynasty, held power for a short time, being destroyed in the fourth generation. The Persians, who conquered the Medes, eventually ruled almost all of Asia, but though they also attacked the nations of Europe, they did not bring many under their sway. They remained in power for a time not much longer than two hundred years. The Macedonian dynasty, having overthrown the power of the Persians, surpassed all those before it in the size of its empire, yet it did not flourish for long itself; after the death of Alexander, it began to decline. For having been torn apart into many leaders immediately by his successors, and having continued in strength after them until the second or third generation, it became weak of itself and was finally obliterated by the Romans.*

<margin>See History.</margin>
And from the Latin writers, Velleius Paterculus says: <note>original: "Assyrii Principes omnium gentium..."</note> *The Assyrian leaders were the first of all nations to hold power. Then the Medes, and afterwards the Persians. Then the Macedonians. Subsequently, after the two kings Philip and Antiochus (who were of Macedonian descent) were subdued not long after the defeat of Carthage, the supreme power of the Empire passed to the Roman people.* In considering these most celebrated kingdoms, we shall organize our study according to the vision of Nebuchadnezzar and Daniel, as presented in the second and seventh chapters, and then from *History*, which acts as a telescope <note>original: "perspicillum," an early term for a spyglass or telescope</note> for this Vision. History will show us the outcomes of the predictions and will instruct us from hindsight. History will place before our eyes and illuminate the indubitable certainty of the prophecies concerning these kingdoms. History will explain to us the fatal end of the first three Monarchies and the wonderful course of the fourth, showing what fortune each Monarch enjoyed and what ends they met. History will declare how God has cast down Kings and established Kings; these words of Daniel declare that kingdoms are divinely established and preserved, that boundaries and times of reigning are fixed for Governors by God, and that it is God's work to bestow kingdoms and to transfer them. That same Prophet says, He *changes the time and the hour*. God, the supreme arbiter of all empires, surrounds all empires with their boundaries and predefines and ends them by His will, according to that passage in Ecclesiastes: *To everything there is a season.* God alone is He in whose hand are kingdoms and Kings, either to preserve or to destroy, which Hezekiah confesses in these words: *Lord of Hosts, God of Israel, who sits above the Cherubim, You alone are the God of all the kingdoms of the earth.* Therefore, let us look at the vision of the Monarch concerning the change and succession of kingdoms, and concerning the transfers and
<margin>Ecclesiastes 3:1.</margin>

<column-break/>

overthrows of empires. Let us see how Kings succeeded Kings and Kingdoms succeeded Kingdoms; how the most flourishing kingdoms of the Babylonians, Persians, and Greeks fell, and how the Roman-Germanic kingdom rose, which by the benevolence and blessing of the Lord is still flourishing today. After the Chaldeans and Assyrians gained possession of the Monarchy, they extended the borders of their empires far and wide, especially under Nebuchadnezzar, of whom the Prophet splendidly says: *You, O King, are a King of Kings, to whom the God of heaven has given a kingdom, power, strength, and glory, and all things in which the children of men dwell.* And again: *You are the King who has become great and grown strong, and your greatness has grown and reached unto heaven, and your power to the ends of the entire earth.* That hyperbolic <note>exaggerated for effect</note> speech, following the accepted custom, denotes that his power reached even to the far-distant world, and that he commanded many great Kings, in respect to whom he was called "King of Kings." His kingdom is compared to a Tree reaching to heaven, to a Head of Gold, and to an Eagle with great wings.

No Monarchy was ever so great as to have tamed the entire world; therefore it is established that this is said hyperbolically <note>original Greek: "ὑπερβολικῶς"</note>, since many provinces remained untouched by the hand of the Babylonians. However, it is noted by this hyperbole <note>original Greek: "ὑπερβολῇ"</note> that the Babylonian kingdom was at that time the most extensive and powerful of all, and as secure as possible from the attacks of enemies! That Monarchy laid its first roots under Nimrod, which it drove deeper under **Nebuchadnezzar**, and was finally uprooted under **Belshazzar**, whom God pulled out by the roots through the hand of Darius, teaching us that no Monarchy is fixed with roots so deep that it cannot be torn out. We place the beginning of the Babylonian Monarchy in Nimrod. He was the great-grandson of Noah and grandson of Ham; about one hundred years after the flood, he took control of affairs as a Monarch formidable to this whole world and a predator of other kingdoms, whence he was customarily called a mighty *Hunter*. In any Monarchy, one must consider: 1. *The rise and beginning; progress and middle; departure and end.* The rise in any of them is seen to have been violent, the end turbulent (especially in the first three), and the same is to be expected of the last. Nimrod's beginnings were not good; they were the beginnings of a hunter; <note>German original: "Es ist Jägerisch angangen" — it started in a predatory/hunting fashion.</note> An illustrious power claimed the empire for itself by force and arms, and established the seat of his kingdom and empire in the land of **Shinar** or **Chaldea**, which is also called **Babylonia**. Four of his cities are listed, which he either founded or occupied after driving out the legitimate Lords. The first is **Babel**, the second **Erech**, the third **Accad**, and the last **Calneh**. This was a "Tetrapolis" <note>a group of four cities</note> situated in Chaldea and Mesopotamia. The stories that Annius comments on regarding a "four-city" or a city divided into four parts are trifles <note>referring to the forgeries of Annius of Viterbo</note>. He was the first after the flood who began to exercise power and empire insolently among men, which is what the words of Moses mean: *He began to be*
<margin>Genesis 10, v. 8 etc.</margin>
<note>Hebrew: גִּבּוֹר בָּאָרֶץ</note> **gibbor baarez**, a mighty one on the earth, through force and tyranny, despising religion and the fear of God, so that he surpassed all inhabitants of the earth in might, strength, and resources; relying on these, he invaded others with violence and brought them under his yoke. He began to be the first Monarch in the world, establishing the first kingdom. As Methodius writes in the *Revelations*: <note>original Greek: "Ὁ Νεβρὼδ πρῶτος ἐβασί..."</note> *Nimrod was the first to rule as king...*
<margin>p. 1. Genesis v. 8.</margin>

### Dan. II. v. 13. and following: 687

<margin>The State of the Four Monarchies.</margin>
<note>original Greek: "ἐβασίλευσεν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς"</note> *He reigned upon the earth.* He was also <note>original Hebrew: "גִּבּוֹר־צַיִד לִפְנֵי יְהוָה"</note> *a mighty hunter before the Lord, so that from him a proverb was born: "Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before Jehovah."*

<margin>verses 17, 4, 19.</margin>
His tyranny became a proverb even among the men whom he hunted, to such an extent that it was <note>original Greek: "πολυθρύλλητον"</note> *widely rumored* of any brutal man that he was "another Nimrod," following in the footsteps of Nimrod’s tyranny, *according to Musculus on this passage.* It is customary in the Scriptures for Princes who exercise tyranny to be called *hunters*. Nimrod was therefore the first King after the flood to oppress men with his power, and he did so so impiously and wickedly that he exercised his force openly, without any respect or fear of God, as a rebel and an impious man.

He began to be mighty; for before him, no one like him had emerged from the descendants of Ham, whether in the strength of his empire or the insolence of his spirit. Indeed, he was a man of immense spirit, driven so far that he began to build a tower of stupendous magnitude along with a city. The Divine Power opposed this proud endeavor and sent a confusion of tongues, from which the name *Babel*—that is, *confusion*—remained for the place and the people.

Josephus claims he was the author of the building of the tower, and his words are: He began to be powerful in the city of Babel, founded by him, which is also called Babylon, and which he made the seat of his kingdom and his metropolis. The first man who reigned at Babylon is called *Belus* by secular writers; they say he held the kingdom for sixty-five years and left it to his son *Ninus*. But the person whom historians call Belus, the founder of Babylon, we identify as Nimrod, the first King of the city of Babel.

Methodius makes him the author of the city, and by inventing a certain era, he writes:
<margin>Genesis 10:10.</margin>
> <note>original Greek: "Τῷ δὲ ὀκτακοσίῳ..."</note> *In the eight hundred and ninetieth year of the third millennium, Great Babylon was built, and Nimrod reigned in it.*

*Furthermore, as the Scripture testifies*,
<insert>the beginning of his kingdom was Babel, and Erech, and Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.</insert>
Therefore, since Nimrod was the first author of the Babylonian Monarchy, the first King, and the founder of the tower and city of Babel, it will not be out of place to say a few things about that city which gave its name to the most famous and first of all kingdoms—partly because it is called the *Babylonian Monarchy* after the metropolis of the established kingdom. The first seat of the kingdom was Babylon, though it was not inhabited for long, for the throne was soon transferred from there to Nineveh and Assyria; hence it is called sometimes the *Monarchy of the Babylonians* or *Chaldeans*, and sometimes that of the *Assyrians*.

<margin>Book 6, chapter 26.</margin>
*Babylon, the metropolis of Chaldea*, is described by Pliny in this way: *Babylon, the head of the Chaldean nations, long held the highest fame in the whole world, because of which the remaining part of Mesopotamia and Assyria was called Babylonia. It was enclosed by walls sixty miles in circumference, two hundred feet high, and fifty feet wide. Each foot was measured by three fingers' breadth more than our own measure. The Euphrates flowed through it, with wonderful engineering on both sides.*

<margin>Book 16 of his Geography, page 508.</margin>
Regarding the site of this city, its magnitude, its circuit, the height and thickness of its walls, its towers, and its hanging gardens, Strabo *has handed down many things. Aristotle reported such great vastness of the city in Book 3 of his Politics, chapter 2, page 430, that when the city was captured, a certain part of the city only realized it on the third day.*

<margin>Book 2, page 93.</margin>
It was not founded and completed by Nimrod alone, but was increased immensely little by little by many Kings, which Herodotus teaches, in whose work one can also read

a description of the temple of Belus with its tower. Wherefore
<margin>Book 23.</margin>
Martial said in Book 1, epigram 75:
> ->Ceaseless labor lies upon Babylon.<-

Ammianus Marcellinus recorded that the citadel was constructed by the most ancient King *Belus*, but the walls were built by Semiramis. If she built the walls, why do Strabo, Diodorus, Justinus, and Solinus write that the city was founded by her? Josephus makes Nimrod the first founder, and we agree with him.

<margin>The Antiquities of the Jews, Book 1, chapters 5 and 6.</margin>
The same Semiramis enlarged it and adorned it with walls so wide that one chariot could pass another coming from the opposite direction. She built a hanging garden supported by stone columns with such art and skill that it was counted among the seven wonders of the world, as witnessed by Herodotus in Book 1 and Curtius in Book 5, chapter 1.

Nebuchadnezzar also enlarged and magnificently repaired it, fortifying the channel of the river. He built three circuits of walls within the city and surrounded it with three more on the outside, according to Berosus in Josephus. And so, it was first founded by Nimrod, according to Josephus in Book 1 of the *Antiquities*, Zonaras in Volume 1, and Cedrenus in his *Compendium of History*; nor do the Holy Scriptures disagree in Genesis 10:10. It was increased by Ninus and Semiramis regarding the walls, but by Belus regarding the citadel, as witnessed by Ammianus Marcellinus (23.20) and Orosius (2.6); and finally, it was repaired and magnificently restored by Nebuchadnezzar.

The first of mortals were long content with a simple way of living and, being ignorant of burdensome rule, they lived together moderately. If any were in charge of others, they administered everything in a civil manner with modest dignity, and possessed more authority than power. Those who were lower were ruled peacefully, not by compulsion.

This moderate state first began to be changed by the grandson of the impious Ham, Nimrod, of whom you might rightly say that line from Seneca:
> — — — the race returns to its authors,
> and degenerate blood reflects the first stock.

The impious follows the impious, and a perverse offspring reflects its lineage and follows the footsteps of the grandfather. Affecting a new cheapness and a new kind of government, he took royal power for himself: he rejected moderate administration among men, and with open force and without fear of God, he invaded the men of his own blood, subdued his neighbors, ruled fiercely, exercised tyranny, and, as if forgetting he was a man, wished to be worshipped with a higher and more eminent reverence.

He was the first King after the flood to raise himself above the usual custom; he erected a monarchical empire with great power and chose the seat of his empire in the land of Babylonia, a region especially pleasant and fertile.

This is why the Holy writer Moses left it recorded concerning his power and tyranny: *He began to be mighty on the earth. To be mighty on the earth is not evil in itself, but he, not content with his own borders, began to exercise power and force beyond what was right, and to extend them beyond what was lawful, by preying, plundering, and acting ferociously, without any respect for Divinity or Justice.*

<margin>Genesis 10:9.</margin>
Hence Moses says again: *He was mighty in hunting before Jehovah; therefore it is said: Like Nimrod, mighty in hunting before Jehovah.* It is common in the scriptures for Princes who exercise tyranny to be called "Hunters," or for the likeness of "Hunting" to be attributed to this matter.

Justinus, following Trogus, attributed this most ancient state of the world—in its malice—to Ninus; but it ought to be traced back to Nimrod by us, who have been taught more certain truths from our sacred Annals, while the Assyrians...
