### ANTIQUITIES OF THE BIBLE

<margin>
The State of the Four Monarchies, Book 1.
</margin>
It is said that the Assyrians were the first to seek out foreign nations through war. *The Assyrians*, says Justin, *are reported to be the first of all mortals, under the leadership of King Ninus, to dare to carry arms against foreign nations, many of whom they brought under their subjection.* There are, however, those who wish Ninus to have been Nimrod, such as Mercator and others. Truly, what Justin wrote of Ninus applies to Nimrod: Ninus, King of the Assyrians, was the first of all to *change the ancient and almost ancestral custom of nations through a new desire for empire.* Although even if Ninus is said to be the second ruler, the same spirit could be attributed to the <note>original Greek: "τῷ Φιλοπράγμονι" — the meddler or busybody</note>, and in both cases, it can be called an example of the lust for dominating. Their axiom
<margin>
Euripides, *The Phoenician Women*.
</margin>
was: *If right is to be violated, it is to be violated for the sake of empire;* and their rule: <note>original Greek: "Εἴπερ γὰρ ἀδικεῖν τυραννίδος πέρι κάλλιστιόν τ’ ἄλλα δ’ εὐσεβεῖν χρή" — If one must do wrong, it is best to do it for the sake of sovereign power; in all other things, one ought to be pious.</note> Thus Seneca, in his description of the Theban war regarding Eteocles and Polynices (in *The Phoenician Women*), writes: *For the sake of the kingdom, I would be willing to give my country, parents, and wife to the flames; empires are well-bought at any price.*

The history of Assyrian and Chaldean affairs is quite remarkable, but the path to it is extremely intricate because complete histories of the Babylonian Monarchy do not exist today. The genuine books of Berosus <note>Berosus was a 3rd-century BC Babylonian priest and historian</note> regarding the affairs of the Chaldeans have perished except for a few fragments; the version of Berosus published by Annius <note>Annius of Viterbo, a 15th-century scholar known for producing forged historical texts</note> is filled with many fictions. Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, and Ctesias provide very conflicting accounts. Nevertheless, with a grateful and devoted mind, we take up and reflect upon those things which God has handed down to us through the hands of *Moses* and the Prophets, just as He revealed them through the *Histories of the Kings and the book of Judith*. There were very grave reasons for the Greatest God to want the sequence of the world's ages to be known, and why He wanted the beginning of the empire and the affected domination of Nimrod, the first leader of the Assyrians, to be understood.

That illustrious testimony regarding Nimrod, that he was *mighty on the earth and a Hunter before the Lord*, is to be valued not by the fewness of the words, but by their weight. The dominion of that tyrant lay wide, reaching both to other lands and to the most pleasant shores of the Euphrates and the widest mouths of the Tigris. This divine revelation—concerning what was the beginning of the Assyrian dominion, and when, where, and how it began—is to be highly valued, especially since we are not reliably taught about the start and first root of this lineage by any profane historian outside of this revelation. Regarding this matter,
<margin>
Henricus Mollerus, Vol. 2, *Introduction to Wittenberg*, fol. penniss.
</margin>
*Henricus Mollerus* says: *Indeed, it is a great honor for the Church that in the Prophetic history alone has an intact series of years been retained from the beginning of the world until the Persian Monarchy; for no complete ethnic histories exist in which the beginnings and deeds of the first Monarchy are contained in order. Herodotus, first among all, begins his history with the Persian Monarchy; he barely touches upon earlier times. Thucydides and Xenophon follow him, and others later who wrote of Macedonian and Roman affairs. Thus, by a singular benefit of God, the series of the greatest changes has been preserved.* Nor is it a wonder that in such an ancient and remote matter so few things are known, and so many are fabulous. Why indeed? After the confusion of tongues, there was a trade of goods, not of languages. In that first scattering, there was no writing of books among the barbarians, and no love for the sciences. How then could deeds be propagated without letters? Fame passing to others becomes either confused or lying. All things were

<column-break/>

scattered: people, minds, and events. Therefore, it is not surprising, even in the judgment of Xylander <note>Wilhelm Holtzman, known as Xylander, a 16th-century German humanist</note>, if the ancient histories are fabulous, or if there existed those who attempted to acquire a name for themselves with trifles and fables when they had nothing certain. Hence those fables regarding the *Egyptian* kingdom up to the time of Pharaoh. For this reason also, we have no certain description of the Babylonian kingdom.

Profane writers treat Ninus as the figure for the earliest antiquity. Macrobius says that nothing remarkable was committed to writing before Ninus. They write that the Chaldeans were the first of men to rule widely, yet when it comes to providing examples, you see them take their start from Ninus. *All histories*, says Orosius, *begin from Ninus*. So for Diodorus Siculus, *Ninus is the first of those <note>original Greek: "τῶν εἰς ἱστορίαν καὶ μνήμων παραδεδομένων" — handed down into history and memory</note>*. Eusebius took the beginning of his Chronicle from him.

Yet what discordance is encountered regarding the names and number of the Assyrian Kings from Nimrod all the way to Sardanapalus. According to Diodorus, the rule lasted through thirty kings; according to Eusebius, thirty-six kings; according to Africanus, forty-one kings. A similar, or even more difficult, <note>original Greek: "δυσαγωγία" — intractability or difficulty of management</note> is observed regarding the duration of the Assyrian kingdom from its first founder to Sardanapalus. According to Diodorus Siculus, it lasted 1360 years, and also according to the same author, more than 1400 years; according to Herodotus, 520 years; according to Justin, 1300; according to Velleius, 1700 or, as some correct it, 1070; according to Eusebius, 1240; according to Augustine, 1305; and according to Africanus, 1484. All of these are either invented, of doubtful trust, or <note>original Greek: "τερατώδη καὶ πίστιν οὐκ ἔχοντα" — monstrous and lacking credit</note>, to apply Plutarch's words about the early affairs of Greece here with equal merit. Indeed, Assyrian affairs were transmitted to posterity by historians who were not sufficiently suitable; for those who survive and are brought forward are mostly Greeks and Latins, who were accustomed to speak somewhat freely about things far removed from them, as the vice of rumor brought it to them then. He who sets out to investigate a consensus will exhaust himself in vain.

Nor will it be helpful to consult those spurious works of Berosus by Annius, which at first deceived many when they sought light there and believed them to be the work of Hermes. Scaliger, sensing this amid the immense studies with which he weighed historical matters, spent no small part of his labor in more correctly establishing the Assyrian and Babylonian affairs. He cleared greater paths here than anyone before him and excelled, for which he deserves praise. For we do not side with those who, in place of gratitude, repay with insults the one who showed the way for the labor he endured. He could not do everything, nor could he take away from others the license to remove or add. *Petavius* and recently *Conringius* used this freedom, examining those things brought forward by Scaliger regarding the Assyrians just as they did the rest; they made observations and applied a sponge to wipe away some stains. The antiquity of that nation deserves sharp eyes, not so much in seeking out the beginnings as in investigating the progress and the end. As much as we are allowed to see, we cannot fully discharge the duty we owe in such a thorny disagreement of authors—and few authors at that. If we did not have some things brought forth in the Sacred Scriptures, which show us the first roots, we would be in even greater darkness. Ninus, however, having extended the borders of his rule even to the borders of Libya, left the greatest kingdom to his underage son...

# Dan. II. v. 13. etc.

<margin>The State of the Four Monarchies.</margin>
...he left to the young Ninus or *Ninyas*, after he had fallen from an arrow wound during the siege of a certain city. Because of his age, the son was not permitted to take up the rods of empire; therefore, his mother *Semiramis* took his place. She was a woman of uncontrollable lust, golden-haired, ambitious, and greedy for power. When she sought to satisfy her lust through the incestuous embraces of her son, she was killed by her son’s sword. Having gained the kingdom, *Ninyas* entrusted the care of the realm to Governors, while he himself spent his time in luxury among women, <term>it is enough to eat and drink</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀρκεῖ ἐσϑίειν τε καὶ πίνειν"</note>, according to the testimony of Phoenix of Colophon in Athenaeus. <margin>§ 12. p. 219.</margin> He had thirty successors in the empire, and likewise in wickedness, each one more depraved than the last—Kings in name, but in truth the slaves of lust. Whoever desires their names should consult Scaliger. You may find the character of the grandsons closely related to that of their ancestors, the traits of the later ones being poured into the traits of the forebears, so that the saying of the Emperor Julian in his *Misopogon* holds true: <term>Just as in plants it is natural for qualities to be passed down for a long time, and perhaps even entirely in the same way for things to be like those from which they naturally sprouted, so too among men it is natural for the character of descendants to be similar to that of their ancestors.</term> <note>original Greek: "ὥσπερ ἐν τοῖς φυτοῖς εἰκὸς ἐστὶ διαδίδοσθαι μέχρι πολλοῦ τὰς ποιότητας ἴσως δὲ καὶ ἐπίπαν ὁμοίως τὰ μὴ ταῦτα τοῖς ἐξ ὧν ἐβλάστησε, φύσει. οὕτω καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων εἶναί εἰκὸς παραπλήσια τὰ ἤθη τῶν ἀπογόνων τοῖς προγόνοις."</note> *Sardanapalus* spread a bad harvest with no less malice; he was the thirty-fifth King of the Assyrians and the last of the undivided kingdom. He was by far the most effeminate of all, for among the common women he handled the distaff and wool in the feminine manner, so completely immersed in the women’s quarters that he hardly ever showed himself to anyone except Eunuchs and Concubines, thinking his infamous weakness could be hidden by walls and roofs. Meanwhile, to his own destruction, he entrusted the management of affairs to Governors, one of whom, *Arbaces*, persuaded the subjects no longer to endure such an androgynous rule. Therefore, hating the more-than-womanly weakness of their King, they formed a conspiracy under two Governors: Belochus of Babylon and Arbaces of the Medes. Sardanapalus himself, now defeated by his own luxury, advanced with difficulty into battle with his half-man entourage, and after the affair went badly, he fled back into the Palace. There, having built a funeral pyre, he threw himself, his concubines, and his treasure into the fire—a punishment well-suited to his lust—imitating men in this one deed alone. These two Governors afterwards divided the Monarchy between themselves: Belochus became the King of Babylon, and Arbaces the King of the Medes and Persians. Velleius Paterculus <margin>V' History p. 566.</margin> has recorded the number of Kings from Ninus down to Sardanapalus, and their destruction, more accurately than any other of the ancients: *He related that Sardanapalus, King of the Assyrians, flourishing in luxury and too much good fortune to his own misfortune, was born thirty-third in line from Ninus and Semiramis, who had founded Babylon, such that the son was always the successor to his father's kingdom, until Pharnaces (who is also Arbaces) the Mede deprived him of his empire and his life.* Thus, with this King, the succession through the family of Ninus began to collapse, and at the same time the Assyrian Monarchy faded somewhat. There followed the beginnings of a mixed and divided empire between the Assyrians and Medes in the second Dynasty, the head of which was Phul-Belochus (called *Belesis* by Diodorus), the tail was *Esarhaddon*, and those in between were *Tiglath-Pileser*, *Sargon*, *Shalmaneser*, and *Sennacherib*. No one is so ignorant of sacred history as to be unaware that their names are recounted in the books of Kings and Isaiah. Thus Phul-Belochus was the first to transfer the kingdom to the neighboring Medes, after it had stood for one thousand three hundred and sixty years from Nimrod through thirty-five Kings; for most

<column-break/>

of the Kings lived for a very long time. Of those before the Monarchy, Nimrod <margin>The State of the IV Monarchies.</margin> ruled for sixty-five years, and his son for fifty-two; if you add the forty-two years of his wife Semiramis's reign, the rule of these three totals 159 years. Sacred history calls *Belochus* by the name *Phul*, to whom Menahem, King of Israel, had made himself a tributary for a thousand talents of gold—not paid from the treasury, but <margin>2 Kings 15:19.</margin> by the nobles. The tyrant Menahem had lived against the will of Jehovah (verse 18), and when Phul, King of Assyria, came into that region, Menahem gave him <term>a thousand talents of silver</term> <note>original Hebrew: "אלף ככר-כסף"; original Greek: "χίλια τάλαντα ἀργυρίου"</note> (a sum which amounts to ten hundred thousand Thalers), so that he might bring him aid and confirm the kingdom he had won by blood. Following the Hebrew text, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> rendered it accurately: <term>that his hand might be with him</term> <note>original Greek: "τὸ εἶναι χεῖρα αὐτοῦ μετ’ αὐτοῦ"</note>, <term>to strengthen his kingdom in his hand</term> <note>original Greek: "κραταιῶσαι τὴν βασיλείαν ἀυτοῦ ἐν χειρὶ ἀυτοῦ"</note>. The Old Latin version says: *so that he might be a help to him, and strengthen his kingdom. So that the hands of Phul might be with Menahem to strengthen his kingdom in his hand, he redeemed peace and help with a great sum of money, and he assessed* <margin>v. 20.</margin> (<term>the silver upon Israel</term> <note>original Hebrew: "וַיּוֹצֵא"</note>), *exacting it from all who were men of wealth, namely fifty shekels of silver from each man. Having received this money, the King of Assyria turned back and did not stay there in the land.* Phul-Belochus was succeeded by Phul-Assur, whom the Book of Kings calls *Tiglath-Pileser*, <margin>2 Kings 15:29.</margin> who took several cities of Judea and led their inhabitants away as captives to Assyria. This servitude of the Israelites to the Assyrians occurred <term>in the days of Pekah, King of Israel, when Tiglath-Pileser, King of Assyria, came</term> <note>original Hebrew: "בימי פקח מלך ישראל בא תגלת פלאסר מלך אשור"</note>. *The King of Assyria, whom the Greeks call <term>Theglath Phalasar</term> <note>original Greek: "Θεγλάϑ Φαλασὰρ"</note>, took Ijon, Abel-beth-maachah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and carried them away to Assyria.* King Ahaz of Judah, under whom Isaiah lived, appealed to this same Tiglath for help <margin>2 Kings 16:7.</margin> against the King of Syria and sent him gifts. For he sent messengers to Tiglath-Pileser saying: *I am your servant and your son; come up and save me from the hand of the King of Aram and from the hand of the King of Israel, who have risen up against me (v. 7). And Ahaz took the silver and gold that was found in the house of Jehovah and in the treasures of the royal house, and sent a gift to the king of Assyria.* But he fared no better for it, for in Chronicles we read that he was burdened by the Assyrian, not assisted, having in vain bestowed upon him the resources of the Lord’s temple and of the king and nobles to bind him to himself. Instead of help, he found destruction, and instead of the treasure given, he received a Scorpion, according to that line from Phaedrus, fable 31:
> He who commits himself to the protection of a wicked man,
> While seeking aid, finds his own destruction.
King Tiglath seems to have been followed by <term>Sargon</term> <note>original Hebrew: "סרגון"</note>, who is mentioned in Isaiah, <margin>ch. 20 v. 1.</margin> indicating a slaughter of the Egyptians and Ethiopians carried out by Sargon, King of the Assyrians, because they had entered into a treaty with the Philistines against the Assyrians. Sargon had sent his commander <term>Tartan</term> <note>original Hebrew: "תִּרְתָּן"</note> to besiege Ashdod, one of the chief cities of the Philistines. Hebrew interpreters identify him as Sennacherib, and most follow them. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
The State of the Four Monarchies, Book 1.
</margin>

...held that they were the first to attack foreign nations in war. *The Assyrians, it is said, were the first of mortals who, led by King Ninus, dared to take up arms against foreign nations, many of whom they brought under their subjection.* <note>original Latin: "Assyrii, ait, primi mortalium Rege Nino duce ausi in exteras gentes arma ferre narrantur, quarum multas sibi subjecerunt"</note> There are those, however, who wish for *Ninus* to be identified as *Nimrod*, such as Mercator <note>Gerardus Mercator, the famous cartographer and chronologist</note> and others. Certainly, what that author wrote about Ninus is true of Nimrod: *Ninus, King of the Assyrians, was the first of all to change the old and, as it were, ancestral custom of nations through a new desire for empire.* <note>original Latin: "Primus omnium Ninus Rex Assyriorum veterem & quasi avitum gentium morem novâ imperii cupiditate mutavit"</note> Even if Ninus is said to be the second, it can be said that the same spirit belonged to <term>the one who loves being first</term> <note>original Greek: "τῷ Φιλοπρώτῳ"</note>, and in both there is an example of the lust for power. Their axiom was: *If justice must be violated, it must be violated for the sake of empire;* and their rule: *For if one must do wrong, it is best to do wrong for the sake of tyranny; in all other things, one should be pious.* <note>original Greek: "Εἴπερ γὰρ ἀδικεῖν χρὴ, τυραννίδος πέρι κάλλιστον ἀδικεῖν· τἄλλα δ᾽ εὐσεβεῖν ἂν ᾖ"</note> <margin>Euripides, *The Phoenician Women*.</margin> Similarly, Seneca, in his description of the Theban war regarding Eteocles and Polynices (in *Thebais*), says: "For the sake of the kingdom, I would be willing to give my country, parents, and wife to the flames; empires are well bought at any price." The history of Assyrian and Chaldean affairs is quite remarkable, but the path is extremely intricate because complete histories of the Babylonian Monarchy do not exist today. The genuine books of Berosus <note>a Babylonian priest who wrote a history of Chaldea in the 3rd century BCE</note> regarding the affairs of the Chaldeans have perished, except for a few fragments, and the version of Berosus published by Annius <note>Annius of Viterbo, a 15th-century scholar notorious for forging "ancient" texts</note> is filled with many fictions. Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, and Ctesias provide accounts that are quite dissonant. Yet, with a grateful and devoted mind, we look up to and contemplate those things which God has handed down to us through the hands of *Moses* and the Prophets, and likewise made manifest through the *Histories of the Kings and the book of Judith*. There were most serious reasons for God the Greatest why He wanted the sequence of the world's ages to be known, and why He wanted the beginning of Nimrod's empire and affected dominion—the first ruler of the Assyrians—to be recognized. That illustrious testimony concerning Nimrod, as a powerful man on earth and a hunter before the Lord, should be weighed not by the fewness of the words, but by their weight. The dominion of that tyrant stretched far and wide, reaching even to the most pleasant banks of the Euphrates and the broadest mouths of the Tigris. This divine revelation—concerning what was the origin of the Assyrian dominion, and when, where, and how it began—is to be valued greatly, all the more because we are taught nothing certain about the beginning and first root of this lineage by any secular historian outside of this revelation. On this matter, Heinrich Möller writes: <margin>Volume 2. On Genesis. Wittenberg. second to last leaf.</margin>

> *Indeed, it is a great glory of the Church that in prophetic history alone an entire series of years has been preserved from the beginning of the world until the Persian Monarchy; for no complete ethnic [secular] histories exist in which the beginnings and deeds of the first Monarchy are included in order. Herodotus, the first among all, begins his history with the Persian Monarchy, and barely touches upon earlier times lightly. He is followed by Thucydides and Xenophon, and others later who wrote of Macedonian and Roman affairs. Thus, by a singular benefit of God, the series of the greatest changes has been preserved.*

Nor is it a wonder that so little is known and so much is legendary regarding matters so ancient and remote. But why? After the confusion of languages, there was trade in goods, not in languages. In that first scattering, there was no writing of books among the barbarians, and no love for the sciences. How then could deeds be propagated without letters? Fame passing to others becomes either confused or a lie. Everything was

<column-break/>

scattered: the people, the mind, the affairs. Therefore, it is not surprising, even in the judgment of Xylander <note>Wilhelm Xylander, a 16th-century German humanist</note>, if ancient histories are legendary, and if people emerged who attempted to acquire a name for themselves with trifles and fables when they had nothing certain. Hence those fables regarding the Egyptian kingdom all the way to Pharaoh. For this reason also, we have no certain description of the Babylonian kingdom. Secular writers fix the first antiquity, as it were, in Ninus. Macrobius says that nothing remarkable was recorded in literature before Ninus. They write that he was the first of men to rule the Chaldeans widely, and when it comes to examples, you see them begin with Ninus. All histories, says Orosius, *begin from Ninus*. So Diodorus Siculus says: *Ninus was the first of those handed down to history and memory.* <note>original Greek: "Ninus primus τὸν εἰς ἱστορίαν & μνήμην παραδεδομένων"</note> Eusebius took the beginning of his *Chronicle* from the same man. But what dissonance is encountered regarding the names and number of the Assyrian Kings from Nimrod all the way to Sardanapalus. During this whole time, according to Diodorus, there was a rule of 30 kings; according to Eusebius, 36 kings; according to Africanus, 41 kings. No less different, but almost <gloss>more difficult to reconcile</gloss> <note>original Greek: "δυσάγωγος"</note>, is the path regarding the duration of the Assyrian kingdom from its first founder down to Sardanapalus. According to Diodorus Siculus, it lasted 1360 years, and likewise according to the same author, more than 1400 years; according to Herodotus, 520 years; according to Justin, 1300 years; Velleius, 1700 years—or as they correct it, 1070; Eusebius, 1240; Augustine, 1305; Africanus, 1484. All these accounts are either made up, of doubtful trust, or <term>monstrous and lacking credibility</term> <note>original Greek: "τερατώδη καὶ πίστιν οὐκ ἔχοντα"</note>, to apply Plutarch's words concerning the first affairs of Greece here with equal merit. Indeed, the affairs of the Assyrians were not transmitted to posterity by sufficiently suitable historians; for those who exist and are brought forward are mostly Greeks and Latins, who were accustomed to speak of things most remote from themselves somewhat too freely, and as the vice of rumor then brought it. He who decides to investigate a consensus will exhaust himself in vain. Nor will it be permitted to consult those spurious works of Berosus by Annius, which at first deceived many when they sought light there and believed they found a guide. Sensing this, Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, the 16th-century father of modern chronology</note>, among the immense studies with which he weighed historical matters, spent no small part of his labor on more correctly establishing Assyrian and Babylonian affairs. He cleared more ground here than anyone before him and excelled, for which he deserves praise. For we do not side with those who, in place of gratitude, repay the one who shows the way for his exhausted labor with insults. He could not do everything, nor could he take away from others the license to subtract and add. This liberty was used by *Petavius* and recently *Conringius* <note>Hermann Conring, a German polymath</note>, who examined those things brought forward by Scaliger regarding the Assyrians just like everything else, made observations, and applied a sponge to wipe away certain stains. The antiquity of that nation deserves keen eyes, not so much in searching out its beginnings as in investigating its progress and departure. As much as we are permitted to see, we cannot sufficiently fulfill the duty we owe in such a thorny disagreement of authors—and indeed few authors. If we did not have some things revealed in Sacred Scripture, which shows us the first roots, we would be in even greater darkness. Ninus, moreover, having extended the boundaries of his rule all the way to the borders of Libya, left a massive kingdom to his young son...

# Dan. II. v. 13. seqq.
### Daniel Chapter 2, Verse 13 and following

<margin>The State of the Four Monarchies. Notes on Sleidan, p. 16.</margin>
<margin>The State of the Four Monarchies.</margin>
...left the empire to the young *Ninus* or *Ninyas*, after he had fallen from an arrow wound during the siege of a certain city. Because the son was not yet of age to take up the rods of power, his mother *Semiramis* took his place. She was a woman of unrestrained lust, cruel, ambitious, and greedy for power. When she sought to satisfy her lust through the incestuous embraces of her son, she was killed by his sword. Having gained the kingdom, *Ninyas* committed the care of the realm to governors, while he himself spent his time in luxuries among women, <margin>§. 11. p. 219.</margin> <term>worthy of nothing except eating and drinking</term> <note>original Greek: "ἄξιος οὐδὲν ἢ ἐσθίειν τε καὶ πίνειν"</note>, according to the testimony of Phoenix of Colophon in Athenaeus. He had thirty successors to the empire, who were equally successors in wickedness, each one more depraved than the last. They were kings in name, but in truth they were slaves to lust; anyone desiring their names may consult Scaliger. You will find the character of the grandsons to be related to those of their ancestors, for the habits of the descendants were transformed into the habits of the forefathers. As the Emperor Julian says in his *Misopogon*: <margin>Book 1, Chapter 2, part 1.</margin> <note>original Greek: "ὥσπερ ἐν τοῖς φυτοῖς εἰκὸς ἐστὶ διαδίδωσθαι μεχρι πολλᾶ τὰς ποιότητας... ἔτω καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων εἰνὴ εἰκὸς παραπλήσια τἄνθη τῷ ἀπογόνων τοῖς προγόνοις"</note> *Just as in plants it is likely that qualities are passed down for a long time... so too among men it is likely that the "flowers" of the descendants are similar to their ancestors.* A bad harvest was spread with no less malice by *Sardanapalus*, the thirty-fifth King of the Assyrians and the last of the undivided kingdom. He was by far the most effeminate of all, for he handled the distaff and wool in the manner of a woman among his concubines. He was so totally immersed in the <term>gynaeceum</term> <note>the women's quarters of a house</note> that he was hardly ever seen except by eunuchs and concubines, thinking that his infamous softness could be hidden by walls and roofs. Meanwhile, to his own destruction, he committed the management of affairs to governors. One of these, *Arbaces*, persuaded the subjects no longer to endure such an <term>androgynous rule</term> <note>original Latin: "androgynicum imperium"; a government perceived as lacking masculine strength</note>. Therefore, hating the King’s more-than-womanly softness, they formed a conspiracy under two governors: *Belochus* of Babylon and *Arbaces* of the Medes. The King, already conquered by his own luxury, advanced with difficulty into battle with his half-manly retinue. When the battle went poorly, he fled to the palace. There he built a funeral pyre and threw himself, his concubines, and his treasure into the fire—a punishment well-suited to his lust. In this one act alone did he imitate a man. After this, these two governors partitioned the Monarchy between themselves: *Belochus* became the King of Babylon, and *Arbaces* became King of the Medes and Persians. Velleius Paterculus, <margin>History, p. 566.</margin> with an accuracy no other ancient writer matched, recorded both the number of kings from Ninus to Sardanapalus and the empire's destruction: *Sardanapalus, King of the Assyrians, flourishing in luxury and being overly fortunate to his own misfortune, was the thirty-third in line from Ninus and Semiramis, who had founded Babylon. Though the son was always the successor to the paternal kingdom, Pharnaces (who is also Arbaces) the Mede deprived him of both his empire and his life.* Thus, with this King, the succession through the family of Ninus began to collapse, and with it the Assyrian Monarchy. This was followed by the beginnings of a mixed and divided empire between the Assyrians and the Medes in a second dynasty. Its head was *Phul-Belochus* (called *Belesis* by Diodorus), its tail was *Esarhaddon*, and those in between were *Tiglath-Pileser*, *Sargon*, *Shalmaneser*, and *Sennacherib*. No one is so ignorant of sacred history as to be unaware that their names are recounted in the books of Kings and Isaiah. Thus, *Phul-Belochus* was the first to transfer the kingdom to the neighboring Medes, after it had stood from the time of Nimrod through thirty-five kings for one thousand three hundred and sixty years. For most of these kings lived very wealthily; of whom the first

<column-break/>

monarch Nimrod commanded for sixty-five years, and his son for fifty-two. <margin>The Four Monarchies.</margin> If you add to these the forty-two years of the reign of his wife Semiramis, the rule of these three totals 159 years. Sacred history calls *Belochus* by the name *Phul*, to whom *Menahem*, <margin>2 Kings 15:19.</margin> King of Israel, made himself a tributary for a thousand talents of gold—a sum paid not from the royal treasury, but by the aristocrats. The tyrant *Menahem* had lived contrary to the will of Jehovah (verse 18), and when *Phul*, King of Assyria, came into that region, *Menahem* gave him <note>original Hebrew: "אלף ככר־כסף" (eleph kikar-keseth)</note> <term>one thousand talents of silver</term> (a sum that amounts to over one million Thalers) so that Phul might bring him aid and confirm the kingdom he had gained through blood. According to the Hebrew text, the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> rendered it accurately: <note>original Greek: "τὸ εἶναι χεῖρα ἀυτῶ μετ᾽ ἀυτῶ, τοῦ κραταιῶσαι τὴν βασιλείαν ἀυτῶ ἐν χειρὶ ἀυτῶ"</note> *that his hand might be with him, to strengthen his kingdom in his hand.* The old Latin version says: *that he might be a help to him, and confirm his kingdom.* So that the hands of *Phul* might be with *Menahem* to strengthen his rule, he redeemed peace and assistance with a great sum of money, and <margin>v. 20.</margin> <term>exacted</term> <note>original Hebrew: "הוציא" (hotzi)</note> the silver from Israel, demanding it from all the men of wealth—namely, fifty shekels of silver from each man. Once he received the money, Phul turned back and did not stay there in the land of Assyria. Phul-Belochus was succeeded by *Phul-Assur*, whom the Book of Kings <margin>ibid, v. 29.</margin> calls *Tiglath-Pileser*. He captured several cities of Judea and led their inhabitants away as captives to Assyria. This enslavement of the Israelites to the Assyrians occurred <note>original Hebrew: "בימי פקח" (bi-yemei Pekach)</note> *in the days of Pekah*, King of Israel. For then came <note>original Hebrew: "תגלת פלאסר"</note> the King of Assyria, whom the Greeks call *Thagla-Phalasar*, and he took *Ijon*, *Abel-beth-maachah*, *Janoah*, *Kedesh*, *Hazor*, *Gilead*, and *Galilee*, all the land of *Naphtali*, and carried them away to Assyria. *Ahaz*, King of Judah, <margin>2 Kings 16:7.</margin> under whom Isaiah lived, appealed to this same Tiglath for help against the King of Syria and sent him gifts. *For Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-Pileser saying: "I am your servant and your son; come up and save me from the hand of the King of Aram and from the hand of the King of Israel, who have risen up against me" (verse 7).* And *Ahaz took the silver and gold that was found in the house of Jehovah and in the treasures of the king’s house, and sent a gift to the king of Assyria.* But he fared no better for it; for in the book of Chronicles, we read that he was distressed by the Assyrian, not helped, and it was in vain that the riches of the Temple of the Lord and the wealth of the king and the nobles were bestowed upon him to win his favor. Instead of help, he found destruction; and in return for the treasure given, he received a scorpion—just as in the 31st fable of Phaedrus:
> He who commits himself to the protection of a wicked man,
> While he seeks assistance, finds his own destruction.
Following King Tiglath, it seems, was *Sargon*, <margin>ch. 20 v. 1.</margin> who is mentioned in Isaiah as indicating the slaughter of the Egyptians and Ethiopians carried out by Sargon, King of the Assyrians, because they had entered into a treaty with the Philistines against the Assyrians. Sargon had sent his commander *Tartan* to besiege *Ashdod*, one of the chief cities of the Philistines. Hebrew interpreters identify him as Sennacherib, and many follow them. Sargon was followed by *Shalmaneser*, to whom Hoshea, King of Israel, <margin>2 Kings 17: 3, 4, 5.</margin> <term>became a servant and rendered him a gift</term> <note>original Hebrew: "עבד וישב לו מנחה"</note> or tribute.

...captured Samaria, the capital of the Israelite kingdom, after a three-year siege. Shalmaneser was succeeded by Sennacherib, whom the Greek calls <term>Sennacherib</term> <note>original Greek: "Σενναχηρίβ"</note> and from that the Latin calls *Sennacherib*. In the fourteenth year <margin>v. 13.</margin> of King Hezekiah, he went up <gloss>against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: "כל-ערי יהודה הבצורות ויתפשם"</note>, *against all the fortified cities of Judah, and took them.* He poured into Judea with a massive army, laying waste to all of Judea with fire and sword, threatening Jerusalem with destruction, urging the people to defect, and mocking the King who trusted in his God. He did not bear such insolence with impunity, for by the strike of the Angel of God, he lost in a single night <margin>v. 35.</margin> one hundred and eighty-five thousand men, just as God had confirmed to King Hezekiah shortly before. He himself, having departed, returned to Nineveh, where after he had settled, <margin>v. 37.</margin> Adrammelech and Sharezer, his own sons, struck him down with the sword while he was *worshipping in the temple of Nisroch his god*. In his place, as the two sons fled, reigned his son <margin>v. 38.</margin> <gloss>Esarhaddon his son</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: "אסר-חדון בנו"</note>, whom the Greeks call <term>Asardan</term> <note>original Greek: "Ἀσαρδὰν"</note> but the Latin translator names *Asarhaddon*. After he was attacked by his brothers' weapons and finally defeated by Merodach, a new metamorphosis of the kingdom took place with a change of families; the seat of empire was transferred back to Babylon, from which the "new-old" Third Dynasty of the Babylonians emerged. The division of the Monarchy is no obstacle here, for as far as its form is concerned, the empire remained one and the same, with only the persons changed. The kingdom, snatched from the Assyrians, migrated again to Babylon, and once more confirmed through Merodach (whose mention is in the Prophet Isaiah 39:1), the Empire took on new growth until it reached its <term>peak</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀκμὴν"</note> during the reign of Nebuchadnezzar. Under him, the supreme power was at its highest degree and was already laboring under its own weight. Empires have their stages, which generally fall when, having been carried to the highest summit, they can no longer sustain their own mass; for where, as Seneca says, there is no room for growth, the end is near. Nabonassar had laid the foundations for the fame of the kingdom in the third Dynasty, from whom begins the Nabonassarean era so often celebrated by chronologists. Several kings followed Nabonassar, but they were quite obscure, until they came to Nabopolassar, the father of Nebuchadnezzar, famous for his reputation and deeds throughout Egypt, Coelesyria, and Phoenicia, about whom Berosus can be read in Josephus. <margin>Antiquities Book 9, ch. 11 and Against Apion Book 1, p. 1044.</margin> The son was more famous than the father through great wars successfully waged, so much so that Megasthenes (in Josephus, *Antiquities* Book 10, ch. 11 and Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* Book 9, ch. 4) does not hesitate to write that he was stronger than Hercules himself, and that he subdued all of Libya and the rest of Asia as far as the Armenians. He amplified his kingdom with wonderful progress, for immediately from his first years he made war on the Egyptians and took from them the entire region that lies between the Euphrates and Pelusium. Not content with this fortune, he turned his arms toward the whole East, subjugating the Ammonites, Moabites, and whatever nations were surrounding Judea; finally, after a long siege, he took Jerusalem,

<column-break/>

plundered it, burned it, blinded the King of the Jews, <margin>iv. s</margin> and led the remnants of the people away in chains to Babylon along with their last kings. Thus, having raged far and wide for many years in perpetual war, he established and secured for himself a Monarchy by far the most flourishing in the entire East, which is signified by the head of gold. Elated by these successes, he thought no less anxiously about expanding the Monarchy as about preserving it; and in these fluctuating thoughts concerning the future growth and state of his kingdom, sleep crept over him. Simultaneously, from his preceding waking thoughts, a wondrous dream occurred, by which God—under the appearance of a great statue—wished to represent to him not so much the fate of his own kingdom as the future changes, turnovers, and successions of the more famous kingdoms of this world. This was so that he might learn that empires are established and preserved by divine power, not human industry, and that nothing in human affairs is firm and stable, but all things, especially kingdoms, are subject to perpetual changes. Therefore, God presented to the King, who was proud from his successes, *a single great statue, terrible in appearance;* He presented a variegated statue so that, under its type, He might not only outline the number and series of the Monarchies, but also show the change and succession of such things. These are the words of Daniel: *You, O KING, saw, and behold <gloss>one great statue</gloss> <note>original Aramaic: "צלם חד שגיא"</note>, a statue that was large, and its splendor was excellent; it stood before you, and its form was terrible.* By these epithets, the power, splendor, magnitude, majesty, and terror of empires are designated. To these general marks is added a specific designation of the material of which the statue appeared to consist, which is attributed as fourfold: *gold, silver, bronze, iron,* each of which excellently declares the condition of that kingdom of which it is a sign. Indeed, he understands four kingdoms according to the variety of the four materials: *the Chaldean, Persian, Greek, and finally the Roman,* which were the most powerful and flourishing of all the kingdoms this world has seen. This number of four is to be taken not from the diversity of materials, but from the division of the body parts; for the statue is divided into: <term>1.</term> a *head of gold.* <term>2.* *chest and arms of silver.* <term>3.</term> *Belly and thighs of bronze.* <term>4.</term> *legs of iron and feet partly of iron, partly of clay.* The golden head of the statue signifies the Babylonian Monarchy, from which the other three following are numbered: the Persian, Greek, and Roman, which held the world in a continuous succession and series. These supreme <term>empires</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀρχαὶ"</note> are aptly depicted, and indeed the Babylonian by *shining and solid Gold.* It is surely easy and obvious to anyone why the comparison is made with the head and with gold. In the entire race of living creatures, the *head* holds the leadership, and similarly in the entire class of metals, *Gold* does. As the head is the highest part of the body, so this is the highest and first of the Monarchies. It is called Golden because of its nobility; for it was more prominent than the others and more conspicuous with its radiating scepter. For although there were those who defiled the honor of the empire with the greatest foulness, it nevertheless did not lose its greatest strength and greatest splendor, even if it did not exercise them at all times. Indeed, it had great splendor under Nebuchadnezzar, who, by his bravery, success, and power, washed away the stains of certain predecessors and exalt-

### Daniel II. v. 13. and following

<margin>The State of the Four Monarchies.</margin>
And he exalted his throne with great speed, and while he did so, he *radiated with a golden peak* <note>original: "aureo vertice radiavit"</note>. In raising the monarchy to such heights, he spared no labor; in a short time, it acquired such sublimity that he stood out as one of the most exceptional monarchs.

<margin>verse 38.</margin>
*You are the golden head*, Daniel said to him. Nebuchadnezzar was the first "golden head," just as God demonstrated through him; he was the primary pillar of the flourishing Monarchy, in whose person the Monarchy showed its splendor. For of him it was said, as we heard before, *You are the King of Kings*. In him, the amplitude of the empire was predicted, and that he would have many nations and great kings in his service, as said through

<margin>Jeremiah 27:6.</margin>
Jeremiah: *I have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon, my servant. All nations shall serve him, and his son, and his son's son, until the time of his own land comes.* What are these lands and these nations? He announces captivity to the neighboring kings. Symbolically, Jeremiah is commanded to send bonds and yokes <note>Hebrew: *moserot u-motot*</note> to the *King of Edom, the King of Moab, the King of the children of Ammon, the King of Tyre, and the King of Sidon* (verses 2, 3), with this command added: that these very minor kings will serve the King of Babylon, no less than the King of Judah and the King of Egypt. Thus was fulfilled what Habakkuk (chapter 1:9, 10) says of the same king, who gathered innumerable captives like sand: *He shall gather the captivity like sand, and he shall triumph over kings, and tyrants shall be a laughingstock to him.* According to the Vulgate version. In the Hebrew: *He shall scoff at kings, and princes shall be a derision to him.* <note>Hebrew: *melakhim yitkallas ve-roznim mischaq*</note>. He will mock kings; <note>German: "er wird die überwundene König spöttisch halten/ verschimpffiren," meaning he will hold the conquered kings in mockery and put them to shame.</note> These kings are understood to be those of Egypt, Tyre, Sidon, Arabia, and especially King Zedekiah, as may be read in 2 Kings 25:10 and Jeremiah 25:29. He will deride every fortification and capture every walled mound. Relying on that power, he received the surrender of not only that most ancient and fortified city *Tyre*, but almost all the cities of the land of Canaan, as if by a tide or torrent of fortune; so much so that, as Daniel said, all peoples, tribes, and languages trembled and feared before his face. It is the work of the Lord, subduing the kingdoms of Canaan in this way through the iron rod of Nebuchadnezzar, who thought this work belonged to his own gods, attributing his strengths to his little deity Bel, saying <note>Hebrew: *ve-zakhu le-eloho*</note> which the Septuagint translates as: *this strength belongs to my god.* <note>Greek: αὕτη ἡ ἰσχὺς τῷ θεῷ μου</note>. He was an impious King, who did not give glory to God, but attributed his remarkable victories to his own gods—yet in such a way that he felt himself not inferior to the gods, in which name he ordered a golden statue to be erected for himself. For with so many kingdoms and cities conquered, and so many fortresses devastated, he assumed a spirit greater than a man’s. Regarding this impious arrogance of the King, the words of the Prophet are to be understood: *Then his spirit shall change, and he shall pass over and offend.* <note>Hebrew: *az chalaf ruach va-ya’avor va-ashem*</note>. Those three words exaggerate the matter, and suggest that with such great success he sinned by being excessively elated; for through the terms *change* <note>Hebrew: *chalaf*</note>, *pass over* <note>Hebrew: *avor*</note>, and *sin/offend* <note>Hebrew: *ashem*</note>, they show an insolent spirit and other crimes. Our version <note>German: "Alsdann werden sie ein neuen Muth nehmen/ werden fortfahren und sich versündigen"</note>: *Then they will take a new courage/spirit, will proceed and commit sin.* In the Hebrew: to change or exchange the spirit. The sense is that in favorable circumstances he would become most proud, which the Belgian notes express thus: *He shall become differently minded*

<column-break/>

<margin>The State of the Four Monarchies.</margin>
*than he was before, and through this lucky prosperity fall into terrible pride.* <note>German translation of the Dutch notes: "Er soll anderst gesinnt werden/ dann er zuvor gewesen ist/ und soll durch dieses sein glückliches Wohlergehen in schröcklichen Hochmuth fallen."</note> In my opinion, this explanation is better than the Herborn version of Piscator, which holds: *They will not continue to war against more peoples.* This was also the position of the Tremellius version, which the translator always kept before his eyes and from which he frequently "fishes" his interpretations. It is hardly convenient to interpret this as a cessation of expeditions. Rather, an insatiable desire for ruling contended to go *ever further* <note>Latin: "plus ultra"</note>, so that with a proud and typhonic spirit he might cross boundaries and limits, committing more than one crime, after the fashion of victors who become insolent and fierce from their victories. A sign of a proud victor is to *soar higher*, which in the phraseology of Habakkuk is called *changing the Spirit*. Explaining this are the words of Daniel (chapter 5:20): *His heart was lifted up, and his spirit* <note>Hebrew: *ruach*</note> *was hardened in pride*; <note>German: "Sein Herz erhub sich/ sein Geist war stolz und hochmüthig."</note> In this way, the mind of Alexander the Great was carried away after many victories, so that he wished to be regarded as Jupiter. No less hated in such great victors was their *pride* as much as their *cruelty*, two vices which usually accompany victories. Nebuchadnezzar *whom he would he slew, and whom he would he struck, and whom he would he exalted, and whom he would he humbled.* That great golden head became a great head of pride and mercilessness. Because of his mercilessness and tyranny, he is called in Isaiah 14:4, 22: *the oppressor, the exactor* <note>German: *Treiber*</note>; *the staff of the wicked* <note>Hebrew: *matteh resha’im*</note>, *the scepter of rulers* <note>Hebrew: *shevet moshlim*</note>. *An unjust and impious King over all the earth*, as the three youths sent by him into the furnace of burning fire testify in their prayer.

<margin>Isaiah 13:19.</margin>
And to the city of Babylon it is attributed here that it was *the beauty of the Chaldeans' pride* <note>Hebrew: *tif’eret ge’on Kasdim*</note>, because of which the Chaldean masters of the world grew proud. We shall join to the sacred testimonies the profane ones of Berosus, Megasthenes, and Alexander Polyhistor, which are no less significant regarding the dominion of this most powerful King. Berosus had written a history of the *Chaldeans*, from which illustrious fragments survive in Josephus and Eusebius; by preserving these, he did a service to posterity. I think I shall do no unwelcome thing if I bring forward certain well-regarded points from there. Berosus relates that Nabopolassar, ruling over Egypt, Coelesyria, and Phoenicia, had been preceded by a Satrap of that region; when the Satrap failed, his son Nebuchadnezzar was sent to restrain the deserter by war. While he was victorious, Nabopolassar passed away, and the Son hurriedly went to Babylon to take up the kingdom. We said a little earlier that the Babylonian Monarchy reached its peak <note>Greek: αἰχμὴν, likely meaning *akme* or highest point</note> under Nebuchadnezzar, whose height <note>Greek: ἀκμὴν</note> falls upon his son Evil-merodach, and its end <note>Greek: τελευτὴν</note> upon *Belshazzar*. For while these were reigning, the Kingdom fell far from the strength and virtue of its ancestors, and finally under Belshazzar, it failed by divine retribution. <meta>This page continues the historical analysis of the Babylonian monarchy, moving from the reign of Evil-merodach to the downfall of Belshazzar as recorded in the Book of Daniel and classical sources like Xenophon.</meta>

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>State of the Four Monarchies.</margin>
The Chaldean [Evil-merodach] rightly showed great generosity; for what greater act of *magnificence* <note>original Greek: megalodōrea</note> is there than to release someone from prison and raise them to the highest dignity? This is implied by the phrase *to lift the head*; for those committed to prison are accustomed to sit with heads bowed, while those set free walk joyfully with heads held high. <margin>verse 32.</margin> Moreover, he spoke *kind words* <note>Hebrew: tovot millim</note> to him, testifying to his most earnest goodwill with gracious speech, and granted him this further favor: that he should be preferred above all the captive kings in Babylon, as indicated by the words: *And he set his throne above the throne of the kings who were with him in Babylon.* He had received other kings into favor, *those who were with him from Babylon* <note>original Greek: tous met’ auto ek Babylōnos</note>, but he deemed the King of the Jews worthy of greater favor. As Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a first-century Jewish historian</note> records, he held him among his closest intimates and, by granting him many gifts, caused him to be esteemed among kings. Having secured the King’s favor, he changed his prison garments and ate with him all the days of his life. However, once Evil-merodach was killed, Belshazzar was declared King. In the fourth year of his reign, he started an unnecessary war against Astyages, King of the Medes, and his son Cyaxares, taking Croesus, King of the Lydians, into a war alliance. By this very act, he incited the Medes and Persians against himself, and it was fulfilled <margin>v. 5. 28.</margin> as Daniel said: *Your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians.* Nor do the words of Isaiah chapter 13 mean anything else when he addresses the Persians and the destroyers of Babylon: *Go up, O Elam; besiege, O Media!* Also in verse 17: *Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, who shall not regard silver, and as for gold, they shall not delight in it.* <note>original Hebrew: henni me’ir aleihem et-Madai</note> Hence, Daniel presents the ruin of the Babylonian Empire and the death of King Belshazzar as brought about by his own impious madness. He brings Belshazzar like a criminal to the Judge’s tribunal, where he is first accused according to the way of a judicial process, and soon a sentence is brought down from heaven upon him after he is convicted. This sentence is promulgated by Daniel as a kind of scribe and *Chief Secretary* <note>term: Archigrammateus - a high-ranking administrative official</note> of the Divine Judgment, and a horrific execution follows this proclamation. The accusation is contained in these words:

> King Belshazzar made a great feast for his nobles and princes, and having become drunk, he ordered the vessels taken from the Temple of Jerusalem by his father Nebuchadnezzar to be brought, so that they might drink from them. While drinking, he praised gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone.

It is not the merriment of the banquet that is condemned, but the impiety and sacrilege of the King and his fellow drinkers. They praise their own gods and inflict atrocious blasphemies upon the true God of Israel. The vessels of the Temple, which King Nebuchadnezzar had set aside as sacred items in the idol-temple after the destruction of the city and the Temple of Jerusalem, they abuse for profane uses. They did this at the peak of danger for him and his people, being surrounded by a hostile army. Where he ought to have called upon God, he and *all the Babylonians drink and revel the whole night* <note>original Greek: pantes Babylōnioi tēn holēn nykta pinōsi kai kōmazōsi</note>, as <margin>Book 7, Cyropaedia</margin> Xenophon <note>a Greek historian and soldier</note> testifies. He was being besieged by Darius the Mede and Cyrus the Persian, but relying on the strength of his fortifications, he despised his most vigilant enemies, keeping a festival day not for God, but for Bacchus <note>the Roman god of wine</note> or his own belly. Johannes Wigandus (page 163.b) notes: It seems he was observing a certain pagan festival; for Xenophon also mentions this banquet, noting that the Babylonians are accustomed to celebrate a festival with their usual food and drink, which happened at the very time Babylon was 

<column-break/>

surrounded by the siege of Darius, King of the Medes, and Cyrus, King of the Persians. In 그 banquet he praised his gods, while despising and cursing the God of Israel. The impious King imputed the calamity of the Empire to the Jewish teaching, which his father and grandfather had—if not embraced—at least tolerated. Jerome <note>an early Christian scholar and Bible translator</note> on this passage (column 1126) writes: What folly! Drinking in golden vessels, they praised gods of wood and stone. *As long as the vessels were in the idol-temples of Babylon, the Lord was not angry.* For they seemed to have consecrated the property of God to divine worship, albeit according to a mistaken opinion. But after they contaminate divine things for human uses, punishment follows immediately upon the sacrilege. Moreover, they praise their gods while insulting the God of the Jews, because they drank in His vessels while attributing victory to their own gods. While he was secure among his cups and joyful among his nobles, as if the kingdom would last forever, behold, in that same hour there appeared fingers like a human hand, and they wrote upon the plastered wall of the royal hall opposite the lampstand. This writing contained the most sorrowful sentence brought divinely against the blasphemous King. Just as in other cases—whether civil or criminal—the sentence is usually conceived and written before it is proclaimed, so it was inscribed upon the wall in the area of the lampstand so that it could be seen, as if upon a piece of parchment. At the sight of this hand, the King turned pale, and was so terrified by the thought that *the joints of his hips and his doors* <note>a biblical metaphor for the loins or legs</note> *clashed together*, and he cried out vehemently for the Magi, Chaldeans, and soothsayers to be summoned. Seized by unspeakable terror, the King seeks help from every side and orders interpreters of the fatal writing to be found. His whole body staggers, his whole face changes, *and the joints of his loins were loosed, and his knees smote one against another* <note>original Greek: kai ho syndesmos tēs osphyos autou dielyonto, kai ta gonata autou synekroteinto</note>, as the Greeks best express the words of the text. These are the thunderbolts of a wicked mind conscious of its own guilt, and those hidden lashes of the executioner of conscience, of which Juvenal <note>a Roman satirical poet</note> wrote:

> Do you think they have escaped, whom a mind

The disturbed King consults the Magi, just as his grandfather had done. But seeing that the Magi can offer no counsel at all, he is *more vehemently disturbed, so that the King's countenance changed entirely, and his grandees were astonished.* When neither the King himself nor any of the diviners can divine anything, he is struck in a wondrous way and, entirely beside himself, is overwhelmed with terrors, feeling that nothing but hardships are being denounced. His conscience strikes this terror into him; for this is the reason why, having only seen the joints of the fingers writing the sentence on the wall—when they could not yet read what was written nor hear it from another—he is so greatly lifeless and utterly consternated that all his limbs tremble with dismay and horror. Consider there, for me, how in a brief moment the noise of this insane banquet and its proud pomp, the sweetest symphony of musical instruments, and the magnificent preparation of all things were changed into the deepest grief and unspeakable distress. A little while before, dissolved in mere laughter, he turned up his nose in scorn at the religion of the Jews, and with hands clapping for joy, he extolled the majesty of his kingdom and his gods. The "Anointing of power" is a <note>original Greek: χρηστὸν (chrēston), meaning "good" or "useful"</note> title, and the name of the "Messiah" bestows the authority of Redemption; so that he might redeem or liberate the Church from the yoke of the Assyrians <note>The author uses "Assyrians" here to refer generally to the Mesopotamian power of Babylon</note>, for it is for the sake of this manumission <note>The formal act of freeing a slave</note> that he is called <term>Messiah</term> <note>original Hebrew: משיח (Mashiach)</note>. Jerome, on this passage, page 321: *That man was called Christ, that is, the anointed of the Lord, which was the sign of royal power among the Hebrews; just as among us the diadem and the purple were given only to Emperors, so among the Hebrews those who were to reign were drenched with ointment.* Therefore, having been made the Emperor of Babylon, he granted the power of leaving the Babylonian captivity by a public edict, in which these words were inscribed: <term>Who is among you of all his people? May Jehovah his God be with him, and let him go up.</term> <note>original Hebrew: מי-בכם מכל-עמו יהוה אלהיו עמו ויעל (Mi-vakhem mikol-ammo Yehovah elohav ammo ve-ya'al); see Ezra 1:3</note> Once this edict was promulgated, the people began their return and vowed the rebuilding of the temple, for which purpose Cyrus <margin>1 Esdras 1:8, 1:1</margin> *counted out* the sacred instruments belonging to the Temple—which Nebuchadnezzar had carried off to Babylon as spoils seventy years earlier—through the hand of Mithredates the Treasurer to Sheshbazzar, the Prince of Judah. This he did in the *first year* after the capture of Babylon, simultaneously commanding all the provinces through which the Jews were to travel to provide these beloved travelers with expenses and supplies for the journey. However, nothing more sorrowful could have happened to the Jews than the news of Cyrus being killed by the Scythians through an ambush; this miserable death cast the Jewish people into new miseries, for under Cyrus's son, Cambyses, and under Darius, the rebuilding of the temple and the city was hindered. Sad events always intervene upon happy news, and Tyrants often follow good Princes. Cyrus pursued the Jews with every kind of clemency, but Cambyses persecuted them. Cyrus was outstanding in war, and so was Cambyses, but by a long interval. He was indeed warlike, for he had conquered Egypt while his father was absent and occupied in the Scythian war, but otherwise he was vicious, in no way reflecting his father’s virtue. Concerning the expeditions of Cyrus, the kingdoms of Asia brought under his power, and likewise the capture of the city of Babylon, one should read Herodotus, who in his first book lucidly described the history of Cyrus’s birth, his exposure as an infant, his miraculous preservation, and his achievements. One should also read Xenophon, as Jerome <margin>on Isaiah p. 321.</margin> advises: *Let us read the eight books of Xenophon’s history of Cyrus the Elder, and we shall see the prophecy of Isaiah fulfilled.* Regarding how Cambyses left monuments of his impiety and madness in Egypt, Strabo teaches at length; and Herodotus, in his third book, records several examples of his foul cruelty and rages. Darius, the son of Hystaspes, succeeded Cambyses as the second King of the Persians, after the Magi who had seized the kingdom were slain. He recovered the peoples who had revolted because of Cyrus's death and the great calamity of his army, and he also added Babylon back to his empire after a long siege. Darius was succeeded by his son, *Xerxes*, who is called <term>Ahasuerus</term> <note>original Hebrew: אחשורוש (Achashverosh)</note> in the Holy Bible. He set out to pursue the war against the Greeks that had been started under bad omens by his father; an insolent and proud warrior, who, having been defeated by the Greeks in both naval and land battles, returned ingloriously to Asia in a shameful and unhappy flight with only a single ship, and was killed on account of his poor management of affairs by Artaba-

<column-break/>

nus, his uncle. Herodotus begins the account of that memorable expedition in book seven and concludes it in book nine, explaining the *three battles*, the first of which took place at *Thermopylae*, the second at *Salamis*, and the third at *Plataea*, in which the Persians were driven out of Greece. Daniel understands this Xerxes to be among the four kings mentioned when he writes of the wealth of the fourth: *Behold, three more kings shall stand up in Persia; and the fourth shall be far richer than them all: and by his strength through his riches he shall stir up all against the realm of Javan.* <note>Javan is the Hebrew name for Greece</note> The King of Javan is the kingdom of Greece, which Xerxes attempted to conquer with an army so vast that the number can hardly be believed. Saint Jerome says: *He says that four kings would rise in Persia after Cyrus: Cambyses son of Cyrus, and Smerdis the Magus who took Pantaptes the daughter of Cambyses as his wife; when he had been killed by the seven Magi and Darius had taken up the empire in his place, the same Pantaptes married Darius and bore him a son, Xerxes, who as a most powerful and wealthy king led an innumerable army against Greece and performed those deeds which the histories of the Greeks narrate.* Xerxes was succeeded by his son *Artaxerxes*, called *Longimanus* <note>Long-handed</note> because his right hand was longer than his left, according to Plutarch. By his concession and kindness, the Jews accomplished what had been begun in the time of Cyrus; in the twentieth year of his reign, the building of the temple of Jerusalem, which had been hindered for many years, was finally completed. Much mention is made of these five Persian kings, especially in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. After Artaxerxes, *Darius Nothus* gained power, born of a concubine (from which he received his surname); Scaliger maintains that the temple of Jerusalem was restored under him. Many chronologists are accustomed to take the beginning of the calculation of the 70 weeks of Daniel from him, though Pererius disagrees, beginning the count from Artaxerxes. There were two under the name of Darius: *Artaxerxes Mnemon and Cyrus* [the Younger], the former of whom succeeded his dead parent, while the latter held Ionia and Lydia; but not content with his lot, he made war on his brother and was defeated and killed, which Plutarch describes at length. From Mnemon reigned *Artaxerxes Ochus*, the youngest of three sons, successful in his affairs but unhappy in his death, for he was killed by the eunuch Bagoas and became food for cats—the worst of all kings. Ochus was succeeded by *Darius Codomannus*, raised to the throne by the efforts of Bagoas. Alexander, the son of Philip, King of the Macedonians, made war upon him. Having destroyed Thebes and pacified Greece, Alexander crossed into Asia with small forces, with which he did not hesitate to engage Darius, who is said to have had ten hundred thousand <note>one million</note> soldiers in his army and to have boasted that he had ten men for every one of Alexander's soldiers. But he succumbed, defeated in three battles, the last of which took place at Arbela. In flight, he was killed by his own prefect, Bessus; and with that disastrous event, the second Monarchy fell. *Alexander*, whom the supreme Will of God raised up to change the empire, used his victory with moderation and by the same effort took over the Persian empire, which had stood for approximately two hundred and thirty-two years. The kingdom which had its beginning in a *Darius* saw its end in a *Darius*, and the **bronze belly** succeeded the silver breast.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES #

<margin>The Status of the Four Monarchies.</margin> This second Monarchy <note>The Medo-Persian Empire</note> is compared to *silver*, and the first <note>The Babylonian Empire</note> to *gold*, because they were unequal in strength, virtue, forces, and power, and one surpassed the other in splendor. Just as gold is followed by silver lower on the statue, so the second kingdom was inferior in strength, virtue, and durability. <margin>6 of the Word of God, page 107. b.</margin> Rupertus <note>Rupert of Deutz, a 12th-century theologian</note> says: *The Kingdom of the Medes and Persians is therefore marked by silver because it stood as much cheaper than the Babylonian kingdom as silver is valued lower than gold, which is not difficult to prove from historical records.* Alexander, through many distinguished victories, subjected to himself almost all the lands toward the rising sun; he transported the height of imperial power from Asia into Europe and established the third Monarchy, which <margin>column 1111.</margin> was foreshadowed in that fateful statue by the *bronze belly*. It is compared to bronze, as Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century biblical translator</note> prefers, because just as bronze is the most resonant among all metals and rings more clearly, its sound being spread far and wide, so Alexander's Monarchy excels not so much in fame, power, and speed as it does in the eloquence of the Greek language. Rupertus says on this point: *They say the Kingdom of the Greeks is signified by the metal bronze because bronze is both hard and very resonant, and the Greeks were strong and, above all, eloquent.* He "ruled over the whole earth," says Daniel. Having become greater than the vast Persian kingdom, he occupied Babylon and Persepolis, and extended his shield as far as the Indians, conquering so many peoples and subjugating so many kingdoms that he obtained the title *The Great* for his glorious deeds. <margin>Pliny, book 3, chapter 5.</margin> Having returned to Babylonia, he heard embassies from almost the entire world seeking to enter into friendship with him; he was the most famous man in the whole world, and none was better known to writers. <margin>In the Life of Alexander.</margin> Our Alexander proclaimed Achilles fortunate indeed because he had found Homer as the herald of his deeds. But our Macedonian Achilles was far more fortunate than the original Achilles, for he found many writers for his victories: Ptolemy the king of Egypt, Hecataeus, Onesicritus, Aristobulus, Callisthenes, Diodorus Siculus, Curtius, Plutarch, Justin, Arrian, and others, who consecrated his name to eternity. But such is the instability of things and the weakness of men that he could not bear or manage such great kindness and indulgence of fortune for long. He acted so insolently and cruelly in many matters that he even wished to be held as a deity and worshipped as the son of Jupiter. He also obscured all his virtues with the single vice of intemperance—known as gluttony—being excessively devoted to luxury and feasting. It is a great shame that a man whom no hero could defeat was conquered by lust, and one whom iron could not conquer was conquered by wine. He was accustomed to feasting for entire nights, establishing drinking contests, and serving his belly and Venus <note>Refers here to sexual lust</note> strenuously; for that very reason the Monarchy could be <margin>on Daniel, books 10 and 11, page...</margin> likened to the *Belly and Thighs*, for not only Alexander but also his successors were most devoted to the vices of drunkenness and lewdness. When he had returned to Babylon, he contracted a fever from intemperance after drinking too deeply, by which he was extinguished—or, as some record, by poison—when he was thirty-three years old and had reigned for twelve years. He performed the greatest deeds throughout the entire world so exceptionally that he has no equal. Upon his death, his kingdom was divided into four parts, though the title of the Monarchy was retained. This distraction

<column-break/>

<margin>The Status of the Four Monarchies.</margin> of the Monarchy was predicted by Daniel, not only in the various spots <note>Refers to the leopard's spots in Daniel's other vision</note> but also in the four wings and four <margin>Oration 6, 7.</margin> heads which the beast was seen to have. After the death of Alexander, the mass of the empire was divided among the leaders, where Seleucus obtained the rule of Syria, Ptolemy of Egypt, Antigonus of Asia, and Antipater of Macedonia, while all of Alexander's relatives were oppressed. Furthermore, there were the most bitter wars between these successors and their sons and grandsons, especially between the Kings of Syria and Egypt, who persecuted each other with the heaviest wars. This is what usually happens when a mind infected by ambition cannot rest and strives to increase its own power through injury to others. This tearing apart of Alexander's empire was destined, for it was predicted by Daniel in the four-headed beast, which clearly indicates the four-part division of the kingdom after Alexander's death, as Theodoret <margin>Oration 7 on Daniel.</margin> agrees. Consuming themselves in these continuous wars, the remnants of the Alexandrian Monarchy and all its power eventually came into the power of the *Roman* people. Having gained control of affairs far and wide through Asia, Africa, and Europe, they created the *fourth* and final Monarchy, and the iron legs gradually absorbed the bronze belly. That Monarchy is compared to *feet partly of iron, partly of clay*. That mixture portends the diversity and mixture of the Empire that would exist in this Monarchy, as indicated by the division of the feet into *toes*. The *Roman* empire was to be divided among various governors, among whom there would be the greatest future difference. This Monarchy suffered many paroxysms <note>Sudden attacks or crises</note> and was often weakened; however, it could be destroyed by the power of no one, nor will it ever be destroyed, but it will remain the last Empire of this world. The name of the Emperors and the sublimity of the Caesars will remain until the end of the world. Thus it was disposed by God, who reserved to Himself alone the power to finally overturn it, along with all the kingdoms of the entire world, by His powerful voice on the last day of the world. It is compared to iron because *the kingdom shall be strong as iron*. *Iron excels in strength and hardness.* <margin>Chapter 2, verse 40.</margin> So the Roman empire has so far excelled in strength and majesty that it could be destroyed by no kingdom, however powerful. It can be weakened, but not destroyed. It persists stable and unconquered, and although it may be weakened, it will nevertheless restore itself from time to time. The clay notes the weakening, the iron the strength and perpetuity. The root and mother-mold of this kingdom is iron, firm and solid; unless it had strength from an iron root, it would have fallen long ago. In iron there is immense strength and remarkable hardness. The strength of iron signifies the power of the Roman Empire. All things yield to iron; by iron and steel instruments all other metals and materials are pounded, cut, engraved, and sculpted. The hardness of iron signifies cruelty; hence the expressions *iron hearts* and an *iron tongue*. The power of the Roman Empire is to be understood from this, so that it might be called the *iron hammer of the whole world*, for it carried its arms into every region of the world. Its savagery can also be noted from this, for it was at times like a scourge of God through devastation and plundering, and through horrendous punishments. Sometimes, saturated with foreign blood, it raged against its own vitals and drained civil blood without limit in so many domestic and internal wars.
