# 696 BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES #

<margin>Status of the Fourth Monarchy.</margin>
<margin>Ibid. chapter 20, folio 109.</margin>
We consider the Republic to have been consumed by the civil wars of Pompey, Caesar, Augustus, Brutus, Cassius, Lepidus, and Antony, so much so that Rupert of Deutz <note>original: "Rupertus Tuicensis," a 12th-century Benedictine theologian</note> believed those civil discords—specifically those of Pompey and Caesar, and Augustus and Antony, which were far more savage than the rest—were uniquely signified by the *iron and the clay* in the feet of the statue. He concludes the section on this point as follows: *“The sum of these things that have been said is this: through the discrepancy of the clay and the iron, the civil discords of the fourth kingdom, that is, the Roman, can be rightly understood.”* Furthermore, no other Monarchy raged against the Church of God more frequently or more atrociously than the Roman one. For besides the Jewish exile, which no tongue can sufficiently describe, the Church was attacked by ten persecutions under the Roman Tyrants and Princes. Under Diocletian, for ten continuous years, no day passed on which ten Christians were not slaughtered in Alexandria; and under Maximinus, the worship of Christ was forbidden, and it was commanded by edicts even engraved in bronze that Christians should not be seen anywhere, neither in villages nor towns, with impunity. This is to say nothing of the *Arian Persecution, when the whole world groaned to find itself Arian.* <note>The Arian controversy was a major theological dispute in the 4th century regarding the nature of Christ; St. Jerome famously noted that the world "awoke and groaned" to find it had leaned toward this heresy.</note>
<margin>Jerome against Luciferians, chapter 3.</margin>

This final kingdom of the Romans is described through the comparison to iron more copiously than the others, not only because it was to be harsher than the rest, but also because Christ was to be born under it, and it was to be destroyed only through Him. The author notes four points deserving consideration. 1. He calls it <term>ολοσχιδὲν</term> <note>Greek: *holoschidèn*, meaning "all-shattering" or "cleaving entirely"</note> saying: *“The fourth kingdom will be as hard as iron. For just as iron subdues, crushes, and draws out all things, so this shall subdue and break all things.”* He immediately added the reason why it is compared to iron: because the Roman Republic subjected kingdoms to itself in every direction, while acknowledging no superior Lord itself. This iron subdued the Germans and Gauls, broke the Spanish and Gauls, crushed the Jews, shattered the Carthaginians, and subjected the Asians. Thus, Roman power, like iron, truly crushed everything through the harshest wars waged here and there, against nations and Jews, and against Christ and His Church. The Roman Empire was truly iron when Augustus conducted the census of the whole world, and with his iron, he organized the provinces and powerfully guarded such a massive weight of empire. 2. He shadows this kingdom through *two feet*. A human body has two feet. The body of the Republic sometimes had two Augusti <note>Two co-emperors</note>. The two feet are the East and the West, that is, the Eastern and Western Empires, a division that occurred in the time of Constantine and later in the time of Charlemagne. Constantine the Great moved the seat of the Empire from Rome to Constantinople: thus he divided the head of the Roman Eagle so that one part looked toward the East and the other toward the West, and by that division, the Roman Empire stood as if on two feet. 3. He shadows this kingdom through the *toes of the feet, partly of iron and partly of clay and tile.* The Prophet gives the reason: *“the kingdom shall be partly strong and partly weak, partly solid and partly fragile.”* This can be shown by the examples of certain powerful and invincible Caesars, and others who were weak. The iron feet are the strenuous Princes who achieved great things through signal victories. The clay feet signify the unfortunate, weak, and unwarlike Princes of the Roman Empire, who, having been affected by disasters from the Goths, Lombards, Vandals, and others, possessed a faint

<column-break/>

and muddy Republic. Sometimes the feet of the Eastern Empire were iron, while the feet of the Western Empire were clay, and vice versa. Sometimes the West had "Augusti" <note>Great Emperors</note>, while the East had "Augustuli" <note>Lesser or "little" Emperors</note>. Jerome says: *“It is iron, which crushes and subdues all things, but its feet and toes are partly iron and partly clay, which is most clearly proven in this time (under the Goths and others). For just as in the beginning nothing was stronger or harder than the Roman Empire, so at the end of things nothing is weaker, when we require the help of other barbarian nations both in civil wars and against various nations.”* The Roman Republic, from the reign of Augustus, when its status was iron, up until the capture of Rome by the Goths, was administered with varying fate for about four hundred years, under Caesars who were partly iron and partly clay, and under Caesars who were largely shameful and wicked. Under Augustus, the Roman Empire was by far at its most flourishing and peaceful, so much so that many of the most robust nations, who had previously clashed with the Romans in almost perpetual wars, both sought alliance with the Roman Empire and voluntarily restored the military standards or signs formerly taken from the Romans, a thing we read was done by the Parthians. In the progress of time, the face of the empire often appeared muddy and mournful, especially under <term>Theodosius the Younger</term>, under whose reign the Western Empire was greatly weakened, with the Goths under the leader Alaric devastating Rome and Italy. The Goths were followed by the Vandals, who under the leader <term>Genseric</term> plundered Rome. At that time, there was certainly "mud" in the West, yet it was not pure mud, for in this very mud God left something of the strength of iron, especially in the East under <term>Justinian</term>, who through his General Belisarius expelled the Goths from Rome, snatched Carthage from the Vandals, and thus brought iron back to the West. Soon the Lombards invaded Italy, devastated it, and established their seat, from which the name of Lombardy remains to this day. And so again, the Western Empire was more like clay than iron, until, after the Lombards were shaken off, Charlemagne <note>Carolus M.</note> received the Empire and transferred it to the Germans. During his reign, the kingdom was led back from muddy fragility to iron firmness. Later, there were established throughout Germany the great-souled Fredericks, Conrads, Henrys, and Ottos, under whose shield the empire remained invincible like iron. Meanwhile, in the East, as the power of the Saracens grew, a decline occurred, and finally Constantinople, the Caesarean seat of the East, fell into Turkish power. At this time, the East degenerated into "muddy mud," to speak with Plautus in *The Little Carthaginian, Act 1, Scene 1, line 30.* In the West, the seat of the empire, Rome, and the greatest part of Italy yielded to the Pontiff, a type of administration that remains to this day; he who presides is known by the common word "Pope," and by the proper title <term>Greatest Pontiff</term> <note>Maximus Pontifex</note>, or rather <term>Monarch of God</term> in the whole world, as witnessed by Annius in *The Refinement of Berosus, folio 61. a.* But if anyone should compare the ancient purple of the Roman Empire with this our purple of the Germano-Roman Empire, he would easily see which excels the other. For whoever wishes to compare the state of the Roman Empire as it is now to its ancient flower and power, will be forced to confess that scarcely a toe of the foot of that most flourishing empire remains, whereas once, not unfairly, the whole thigh...

It argues that the Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation is the direct legal successor to ancient Rome, despite its territorial decline.</meta>

# Daniel II, v. 13. etc. 697 #

<margin>
The state of the Four Monarchies.
col. 1111. c.
</margin>
The Eagle of the Empire, which once marveled at its own outstretched wings—first under the Eastern world and soon after the Western—would now find its thighs and shins barely equal to those of a common bird, being almost entirely dismembered. That kingdom, which was once iron, has now for a great part begun to be clay, as Rupert of Deutz <note>original: "Rupertus," a 12th-century Benedictine theologian</note> writes in his 6th book on the *Victory of the Word of God* <note>original: "V. V. D." refers to *De Victoria Verbi Dei*</note> during the time of
<margin>* 11. f. 104.</margin>
Henry V, around the year 1124; he died under Lothair III. What would he say if he saw it today? He would, I believe, cry out: *O ancient kingdom, with what unequal glory you bloom!* Sleidanus <note>Johannes Sleidanus (1506–1556), a famous historian of the Reformation</note> calls it a *thin and bloodless little body of an empire* that barely clings to its bones—a dry and flaccid nursery of an Empire. Once, Spain, Gaul <note>modern France</note>, Italy, Greece, Asia, and other provinces constituted the single Roman Monarchy. A greater Monarchy could not have flourished. But how much it has lost! Only Germany barely remains, and how many adversaries it feels! In the East, the Ottoman camps are pitched opposite us, to say nothing of the West and the North. Germany now scarcely holds the glory of the Empire, whose "fingers" <note>referring to the toes of the statue in Daniel's vision</note> are clearly divided. Though they may be distinct and dissimilar, they nonetheless arose and propagated from the iron of the legs and shins. This must be noted from the prophetic interpretation: *Whereas you saw (he said) the feet and toes, partly of potter’s clay and partly of iron, the kingdom shall be divided; yet there shall be in it something of the strength of the iron, just as you saw the iron mixed with ceramic clay.* Just as in the human body the feet and toes arise from the shins, so the Roman kingdom, forged from iron and clay, arises from the strength of the iron. Though the Roman power may be weakened and split, and many kingdoms lost through that division, there remains in those remnants of the Roman Empire something of the "iron planting" or substance. Even today, the Empire rests upon this iron stock, and its Emperors preserve the nature of iron through the use of Roman Law. For our Empire still has its strength, its laws and customs, rites, rights and institutions, its official duties, and its inaugurations—all with ancient virtue, even if not with ancient might, such as when it flourished under the most powerful Roman Augusti. The Seven Electors <note>original: "Septemviri," the high-ranking princes who chose the Emperor</note>—indeed, now Eight—appointed throughout Germany, choose a man worthy of such a high peak as Caesar. You would not call that German Empire a new thing, or something severed from the Monarchy of the Romans; for it is the iron stock transferred from the Romans to the Germans by God’s design. Those who deny this glory of succession are "German-scourges" <note>original: "Germano-mastiges," those who disparage German history</note>. A change of location does not change the nature of the thing itself. *The transformation* <note>original Greek: "hē metastásis"</note> *will make it one thing and another, or similar, but not something entirely different.* If it ceased to be Roman because it was transferred to the Germans, then the Roman Empire would have expired long before Charlemagne—specifically at the time when it moved from Rome to the Greek Emperors in Byzantium. Therefore, regarding what almost everyone asserts about the Four Monarchies described to us by the Prophetic Spirit, the political writer Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and political philosopher</note> dares to call it an "ancient error." He especially mocks us Germans for claiming the dignity of the Fourth Monarchy for ourselves, arguing as follows: *The Germans hold scarcely a hundredth part of the world under their jurisdiction. Therefore, they do not justly usurp the Roman Monarchy.* On the contrary, we take this very point in our favor: the fact that this Empire, which once encompassed almost the entire 

<column-break/>

<margin>The state of the Four Monarchies.</margin>
world, has been reduced to such narrow straits, can be proof that it is now in the hands of the Germans. For Daniel explicitly prophesies that the feet of that statue would be partly of clay; what else does this teach us than what experience has shown us so far? Namely, that the strength of the fourth Monarchy, after it reached its *decline* <note>original Greek: "parakmē"</note>, was diminished, and that supreme power would be weakened. This serves as evidence of the imminent Final Judgment, in which a stone cut out from a high mountain shall reduce that statue to nothing. I will remain silent on other points which others bring against Bodin, among whom (besides Franckenberger in *Prophetic History, p. 174 etc.*) Master Heinrich Kipping today has argued against Aubry, an Assessor of the French Parliament. Nevertheless, the name of ancient glory and dignity remains among the Germans; the same dominion remains, even if the Monarchy migrated from the Romans to the Germans without the same wide-reaching extent of rule, so to speak. His *audacity* <note>original Greek: "Tolmēria"</note> in defining the Baltic Sea is perhaps too presumptuous, about which Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), French historian</note> says in book 2: *Even if the kingdoms of Greece and others are taken away by their location, the iron stock remains.* The original foundation is still iron, even though it is divided, and the most powerful Romans no longer possess it. The plant remains iron; that is, for the sake of its origin, the Roman Empire remains firm, whether it falls to the Greeks or the Germans. This is true even though the toes, which extend out from the iron sole of the foot, are made of clay—meaning they are weak and powerless compared to the previous power—as Georg Wicel writes in volume 3 of his *Works, folio 162b, in his Annotations on Luther’s version.* Even Luther <margin>* Preface on Daniel.</margin> clearly confirms what we have said so far; the reader who favors Luther will not be annoyed to have all his words cited here: *The dream and the image are clearly interpreted in the text by Daniel himself as the four kingdoms. The first is the Assyrian or Babylonian. The second, the Medes and Persians. The third, that of Alexander the Great and the Greeks. The fourth, the Romans. In this interpretation and opinion, all the world is in agreement, and the events and histories also powerfully prove it. But he speaks most and longest about the Roman Empire, therefore we must listen diligently. At the end, where the iron thighs begin to divide into the toes on the feet, he interprets three parts of the Roman Empire. The first is that the toes are divided, but they nonetheless keep their origin from the iron feet. Just as in the human body the toes also divide, yet they still grow out of the foot and belong to the foot. Thus the Roman Empire is divided, since Spain, France, England and other pieces have come from it. It has nonetheless grown out of it, and like a plant, was moved* (as they call it) *or transferred from the Greeks to the Germans, so that the nature of the iron remained there; for it still has its Estates, offices, rights and laws, just as it had in former times. Therefore he says here: Although it will be a divided kingdom, yet the root, plant, or stem of iron shall be within it. The second part is that such divided toes are unequal, partly iron and partly clay, which he himself interprets to mean that it shall be such a divided kingdom that is sometimes powerful, sometimes weak.* The

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES 698 #

<margin>The State of the Four Monarchies.</margin> It is found to be so; for the Empire has often had many a valiant Emperor, such as Charlemagne, the three Ottos, and the like, who were invincible. Conversely, it has also often had weak and unfortunate Emperors who were frequently defeated. But all this is said so that we may know how the Roman Empire is destined to be the last, and no one shall break it except Christ alone with His kingdom. Therefore, even if many kings have set themselves against the German Empire, and the Turk also rages against it, and they all perhaps win a battle now and then, they still shall not prevail over or utterly uproot such an iron root and plant. It must remain until the Last Day, however weak it may be. Luther reduced the Prophet's prophecy concerning the fourth kingdom to three main points. We have dealt with the first two so far. The third remains in these words: *Just as you saw the iron mixed with ceramic clay, so they shall be joined by the seed of men; but the one shall not cling to the other, just as iron does not mix with ceramic clay.* <note>Daniel 2:43</note> They explain that word, <term>mix</term> <note>original: "balal"</note> and <term>human seed</term> <note>original: "nabash"</note>, as referring to Marriages, by which the Eastern and Western Emperors repeatedly attempted to rejoin and consolidate the empire, but they were in vain. The great ones of the kingdoms strive to seek union through marriages, and they intended this also in the torn-apart Roman Empire, where it was customary to seek reunification with foreign kingdoms through confederations and family ties, so that it might recover its ancient glory. He warns that these affinities are made in vain—like iron combining with clay—and signifies that the Roman Princes, in this infirm old age of the empire and conscious of their own weakness, would seek some strength for themselves from foreign Kings through either family ties or treaties; but such couplings would be neither firm nor lasting, nor would this attempted society easily coalesce into a Monarchy, just as iron and clay cannot bond. *They shall not cohere*, he says. For although the mud, while it has moisture, seems to be glued to the iron, as soon as it dries, it falls off. Luther says on this passage: The third piece—that such divided and unequal parts are mixed together, or stand exchanged one for the other—he himself interprets to mean that it will be such a weak Empire that it will patch and strengthen itself here and there with other Kings through alliances and friendship. But it will not help, nor find any loyalty, and must therefore have its strength and victory through God's providence alone, when it is meant to be.

<margin>In Daniel, folio 17. b.</margin> Johannes Draconites <note>A 16th-century theologian and colleague of Luther</note> asks: What is it that he says, "They shall be joined indeed but shall not cohere"? It means the Roman Empire will seek help and protection from foreign kingdoms through confederations and family ties, but shall not find it. Indeed, the kingdoms will try to create a Monarchy among themselves, but will not complete it. Therefore, just as the division and diversity of the parts makes the army divided, one part will be more warlike than another. So, the fact that clay does not mix with iron signifies that the kingdom shall remain invincible only by the power of God until the final day. God said that this joining through marriages would by no means be stable, nor would those marriages be the stabilizers of the kingdom. Therefore, help is sought from this source in vain,

<column-break/>

for it does not please God to rescue collapsing affairs through such aids. In vain did they once hope that the discord between Julius Caesar and Pompey could be set aside by a marriage contract. In vain was Octavia, the sister of Augustus Octavian, given in marriage to Mark Antony, so that these two relatives might apply themselves to promoting the majesty of the Empire with a greater union of minds. On this matter, one should read Rupert of Deutz, *folio 110.* In vain was the consolidation of the Empire through marriage attempted in the House of Theodosius the Great, which Blessed Christopher Helvicus <note>A 17th-century chronologist and historian</note> detailed with several examples in his *Synopsis of Universal History, page 55.* Discussing this lack of mixing between clay and iron, Clutenius <note>Joachim Cluten, a legal scholar</note> adds other points: *Certainly, family ties by no means produce a constant and sincere friendship unless God Himself joins the hearts of men and associates them with the bond of charity. Why say more? Family ties have provided the occasion for great grudges and hatreds (the examples are manifest, though odious) rather than constant and sincere friendship. Indeed, it often happens that family ties cohere with difficulty; sometimes they end in hidden grudges, and sometimes they break out into open enmities.* In these most recent times, the Illustrious House of Habsburg is considered fortunate in the name of marriages; for through marriages they have received very many kingdoms. But, (as Leyser <note>Polycarp Leyser, a Lutheran theologian</note> adds in *The Babylonian Colossus, page 157*), those same kingdoms and territories cause them much trouble; for they are now kept in obedience with greater difficulty than they were initially acquired; some even openly rebel. To such an extent is it true what Daniel says: *They shall not cohere.* And these are the principal kingdoms of the world, which were shown to Nebuchadnezzar in the Colossus through *gold, silver, bronze, and iron* in a dream. God willed those four kingdoms we have outlined so far to stand out above all other kingdoms of the world in power, size, wealth, and magnificence, but with a cycle of change, at certain periods and with the difference of <term>power leading to a noose</term> <note>original: "archēn eis anchonēn," a Greek idiom suggesting that great power often leads to its own destruction</note>, where we hear that silver came from the golden, bronze from the silver, and iron from the bronze. The *Golden Kingdom* was that of Babylon, which was succeeded by the *Silver Kingdom* of the Medes and Persians; the *Bronze Kingdom*, which was that of the Macedonians; and the *Iron-and-Clay Kingdom* of the Romans. Hesiod seems to have taught these things, though ignorant of the source, in his fiction regarding the metamorphosis of the ages—the golden into silver, this into bronze, and bronze into iron—to show that age succeeds age for the worse. For the Poets do not depart from those things which Daniel set down concerning the golden, silver, bronze, and iron ages, so that they seem as if they were pupils in the School of Daniel. For those lines of Maro <note>The Roman poet Virgil</note> regarding the Golden Age come very close, which he has concerning Saturn:
> And the Golden Ages, as they say, were under that King;
> Thus he ruled the peoples in calm peace.
Regarding the Silver Age, over which they place that oath-taking Father Jupiter, Naso <note>The Roman poet Ovid</note> sings thus in the 1st book of the *Metamorphoses*:
> After Saturn was sent into dark Tartarus,
> The world was under Jupiter, and a silver offspring succeeded,
> Worse than gold, but more precious than yellow bronze.
But regarding the third age, which was bronze, the same poet says:
> After that one, the third succeeded, the bronze offspring,
> Fiercer in disposition, and readier for horrific arms,
> Yet not criminal.

Their arguments will stir up no dust before anyone's eyes, since they have often been worn down and winnowed.

I would like the same to be said regarding the <term>Vision of Daniel</term>, which remains for us to see. For we have undertaken to deal with both visions: that of Nebuchadnezzar and that of Daniel. A new Vision was offered to the Prophet Daniel in the form of prodigious <term>Beasts</term> regarding the number and sequence of the <term>Monarchies</term>; to this is added, for the consolation of those who were awaiting a deliverer, an illustrious sermon concerning the person of the <term>Messiah</term> and His eternal kingdom, and concerning the final judgment and the end of the world. We shall see concerning both, as much as is granted to see within <term>prophetic</term> <note>original: "προφητικοῖς"</note> coverings. God reveals the future to His prophet Daniel, as he sleeps at night, under the unusual appearance and form of animals. The first was like a <term>Lioness</term>, but lifted up by the rowing of eagle’s wings; the second like a <term>Bear</term>, but horrible with the deformity of three ribs or teeth; the third like a <term>Leopard</term>, but winged, and enormous with the mass of four heads; the fourth was a <term>Beast</term> most different from the previous ones, with iron teeth and ten horns, threatening destruction from afar and bringing it most presently at hand. Animals of unusual form usually portend something unusual. These most powerful and ferocious beasts show the tyrannical cruelty of the kingdoms of the age, and their Princes truly did not reign in God; indeed, the kingdoms which were mentioned were not so much kingdoms as certain great and public robberies, in the judgment of Rupert of Deutz;* who in the preface to these thirteen books had also premised this: <term>Kingdoms were rightly figured by the most ferocious and blood-thirsty beasts for this reason: because they were full of cruelty, and bestially filling the world with bloodshed, they also crushed the saints of the most high God.</term>

The rising Monarchy of Nimrod brought a great <term>surge</term> <note>original: "κλύδων"</note> to the world, like the storm of the winds.

<meta>This page transitions from the general history of the four world empires to the specific prophetic symbolism found in Daniel chapter 7. While the previous page discussed the "Colossus" statue from Daniel 2, here the author begins a detailed analysis of the "Four Beasts" vision, focusing on the first beast—the winged lion representing the Babylonian Empire.</meta>

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES ###

<margin>
The State of the Four Monarchies.
</margin>

They climbed to the summit, and those kingdoms ascended as if by stairs to a lofty height, just as the **Beasts** are read to have ascended from the sea in *Daniel chapter 7*. What was Nimrod? A grandson of Ham, whose portion was no larger than that of his brothers; not content with this, he began to rebel, to stir up sedition among families, to seek a kingdom for himself, and to turn his weapons against foreigners. What were the Persians? They were servants of the Medes. What was the race of the Macedonians? A race extremely obscure and despised. What were the Romans? They began their kingdom with banditry, spoils, and plunder. The first beast *was like a Lion*, <note>original Aramaic: "קדימתא כאריה וגפין די-נשר לה"; original Greek: "τὸ πρῶτον ὡσεὶ λέαινα, καὶ πτερὰ αὐτῆς ἀετοῦ"</note>.

The first was like a *Lioness*, and *had the wings of an eagle*. A Lion—or, as the ancient translator prefers, a *Lioness*—provided with eagle’s wings, presents the image of the First Monarchy. Jerome preferred to understand it as a lioness, writing in *column 1135*: *The Babylonian kingdom, on account of its ferocity and cruelty, or perhaps because of its luxury and life devoted to lust, is called not a Lion but a Lioness. For those who have written on the nature of beasts say that lionesses are more ferocious, especially if they are nursing cubs, and are always eager for mating.* However, the word <term>Aryeh</term> <note>original: "אריה" and "ארי"</note> is <term>common</term> <note>original: "ἐπικοινὸν" — a grammatical term meaning the word can be either masculine or feminine</note>, embracing both sexes within itself. The translator preferred to embrace the feminine <margin>Hosea 13:8.</margin> gender, just as with the name <term>Lavi</term> <note>original: "לביא"</note>, which he translated there as a *she-bear*, but here as a *bear*. The Lion is the prince of wild beasts, the highest in strength among all quadrupeds, just as the *Eagle* is among birds. The former excels chiefly in the strength of the body, the latter in speed. The author of Proverbs testifies to this in *chapter 30, verse 30*: <note>original Hebrew: "ליש גבר בבהמה"</note>, *The Lion, strongest among animals, does not turn away for any animal*, that is, as the ancient version correctly expressed it, *he fears the meeting of no one*. This is also seen in *2 Samuel 1:23*, where Saul and Jonathan are proclaimed by David to be *stronger than lions and swifter than eagles*. Therefore, by the fitting likeness of a Lion, immense strength is especially indicated, and by it the fiercer dispositions of the Babylonian Princes are expressed. Among them, Nebuchadnezzar, fierce in warfare, is expressly called a Lion by Jeremiah, writing of him in *chapter 4, verse 7*: *The Lion has ascended*, <note>original Hebrew: "עלה אריה"</note>, *from his lair*, <note>original: "ומשחית גוים"</note> *the destroyer of nations has set out, he has gone forth from his place, to make your land a wilderness, and your cities shall be destroyed, with no inhabitant*. He is called a Lion because of the ferocity he exercised in the persecution of the Jews and their abduction; concerning the magnitude of this coming calamity, the prophet says to the great men of the kingdom: *And it shall be, in that day, the heart of the King shall perish and the heart of the Princes*, <note>original Hebrew: "לב-המלך ולב השרים"</note>, *and the Priests shall be astonished, and the Prophets shall be dismayed*. No more ferocious creature than the Lion exists, a strong, noble, and predatory animal. The Kings of the Babylonians surpassed in cruelty and ferocity of mind all the nations that existed then; but the most cruel of all those Kings who lived then was Nebuchadnezzar, who in a <term>lion-like manner</term> <note>original Greek: "λεοντωδῶς"</note> put many Kings to death through fierce war and other arts. Vatablus <margin>Is. l. p. 544.</margin> says: *Nebuchadnezzar was a Lion, that is, warlike, who quickly conquered all neighboring nations, which is signified by the wings*. He is said *to have been like a Lion, that is, most excellent, just as he was previously compared to gold; for as gold surpasses other metals, so the Lion surpasses other animals*. Wings are attributed to the first Monarchy, and specifically eagle’s wings, so that the speed of their achievements may be indicated, or, as Hiero-

<column-break/>

-nymus <note>Jerome</note> holds, the pride of a most powerful kingdom. For Nebuchadnezzar flourished with marvelous speed in occupying kingdoms, as seen in *Jeremiah 4:13, 48:40, Ezekiel 17:3 and following*. To these Habakkuk harmonizes in *chapter 1, verse 8*, describing the admirable speed of his army: *His horses*, he says, *are SWIFTER than leopards, and sharper than evening wolves* <note>original Hebrew: "מזאבי ערב"</note>, words which Guevara understands as referring to hyenas in his commentary on this passage. *The horsemen shall abound, who shall come from afar and shall fly like an eagle hastening to eat*, <note>original: "ויעפו כנשר חש לאכול"; original Greek: "πετασθήσονται ὡς ἀετὸς πρόθυμος εἰς τὸ φαγεῖν"</note>. He compares the cavalry army to an eagle, which, having seen its prey from on high, flies in most swiftly and is carried headlong toward its food. Eagles have a very hooked beak, and no less <term>curved claws</term> <note>original Greek: "γαμψώνυχες"</note>, and are also gifted with lynx-like eyes, so that from their very appearance you may recognize a predatory and all-devouring bird, fit and born for plunder and predation. Hence the *eagle's claw*, meaning those who are predatory, is used in Plautus’s *Pseudolus*. And of this predatory bird, Ovid says:

> Not otherwise than when, with hooked feet, the bird of Jupiter
> Has deposited a hare in its nest.
<note>Ovid is referring to the eagle as the "bird of Jupiter."</note>

The eagle is <term>high-flying and swift-flying</term> <note>original Greek: "ὑψιπέτης καὶ ὠκυπέτης"</note>; it enters the clouds themselves and flies the highest of all birds. Whence it is known as the *Queen of Birds*, and the Poets salute it as *Jupiter's armor-bearer*, as Virgil does in the *Aeneid, Book 5*:

> ——— whom the swift one from Ida
> Snatched up on high with hooked feet, as Jupiter’s armor-bearer.

And to the same author it is *Jupiter’s bird* in *Aeneid, Book 1*, imitating this verse of Theocritus:
<note>original Greek: "Ες τρις ὑπαὶ νεφέων Διὸς ἄμβροτος ὄρνις" — "Thrice beneath the clouds, the immortal bird of Zeus."</note>
And from here the proverb originates: *an eagle in the clouds*, found in Suidas; and another: *you pursue an eagle with heat*. Holy Scripture takes expressions from the flight of the eagle—by which it is carried more directly than other animals—to indicate speed, as in *2 Samuel 1:23*: <note>original: "מנשרים קלו", Greek: "ὑπὲρ ἀυτὰ νέφεα"</note>, *swifter than eagles*, regarding Saul and Jonathan; and *Lamentations 4:19*: <note>original Hebrew: "קלים מנשרי שמים"</note>, *swifter than the eagles of heaven*. Homer celebrates the <term>eagle as the most perfect of winged things</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀιετὸν ὡς πετεηνῶν τελειότατον"</note>. The Poet delights in the likeness taken from Eagles, by which he compares the most spirited Hector to an Eagle, whom the right hand of Jupiter himself pushed from behind so that he rushed upon the stationed ships, not otherwise than the sharpest of winged eagles rushes upon a flock of either geese or cranes or long-necked swans, feeding in places near rivers:

> <note>original Greek: "Ὡς τ’ ὀρνίθων πετεηνῶν ἀιετὸς αἴθων / Ἔθνεος ἐφορμᾶται ποταμὸν πάρα βοσκομενάων / Χηνῶν, ἢ γεράνων, ἢ κύκνων δολיχοδείρων." — "As a tawny eagle rushes upon a flock of winged birds feeding by a river—geese, or cranes, or long-necked swans."</note>

Menelaus, looking around carefully through the ranks of his companions to see the son of Nestor, he compares to a high-flying eagle that then sees clearly (*Iliad, book 17*):

> <note>original Greek: "Πάντοσε παπταίνων, ὥστ’ ἀιετὸς, ὃν ῥά τεφασὶν / Ὀξύτατον δέρκεσθαι ὑπουρανίων πετεηνῶν." — "Peering every way, like an eagle, which they say has the keenest sight of all winged things under heaven."</note>

From the same bird he takes a comparison for Achilles, who rushed like the most excellent of eagles, outstanding in strength and speed (*Iliad, book 21*):

> <note>original Greek: "Αἰετὸς ὄμματ’ ἔχων μέλαν-, τῶ θεωρηטῆρι- / Ὅς θ’ ἅμα κάρτιστός τε καὶ ὤκιστος πετεηνῶν. / Τῷ ἔικὰς ἤϊξεν." — "Having the eyes of a black eagle... who is at once the strongest and swiftest of winged things. Like it, he sprang forth."</note>

<summary>This page analyzes the first of Daniel's four beasts—the lion with eagle's wings—identifying it as the Babylonian Empire under Nebuchadnezzar. The author draws on Biblical texts and Classical poets like Homer and Virgil to explain how the lion symbolizes fierce strength and the eagle represents rapid conquest.</summary>

Having previously discussed the Babylonian Empire as a winged lion, the author now transitions to the fall of the Babylonians under Belshazzar and the rise of the second monarchy, the Medes and Persians, symbolized by a bear.</meta>

### Daniel VII, verse 13 and following ###

<margin>
The State of the Four Monarchies.
3. u. 351.
</margin>
Likewise, Quintus of Smyrna, an "inspired" <note>original Greek: "ἐμπνεύσας"</note> poet, compares the Eagle of the Monarchies to one driving away enemies with strength and speed, just as the eagle—the most excellent of birds—drives vultures away from carcasses.
<margin>
Just as an eagle, most excellent of birds, will strike fear.
</margin>
From this apt symbolism, the eagle’s wings signify the sudden growth of the Babylonian kingdom, and no less the wonderful speed of Nebuchadnezzar in expanding his empire. He, like a "wingless eagle" <note>original Greek: "ὡς αἰετὸς ἀνύπτερος"</note>, extended his wings and flew like an eagle hastening to its prey. Like a "high-flying eagle" <note>original Greek: "ὡς αἰετὸς ὑψιπετης"</note> looking down from the heavens with mockery, he wished to exalt himself, saying in his proud heart: <margin>Isaiah 14:13.</margin> *I will ascend to heaven, above the stars of God I will exalt my throne.* <margin>verse 14.</margin> *I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High.* <note>original Hebrew: "אעלה השמים ממעל לכוכבי-אל ארים כסאי" and "אעלה על-במותי עב אדמה לעליון"</note> With the same type of boastful language, the "pride" <note>original Greek: "ὑπερηφανια"</note> of Antiochus is noted in *2 Maccabees 9:7, 10*: *He who thought he could command the waves of the sea because of his superhuman arrogance, and reach for the stars of heaven.* Indeed, such is the nature of pride: when it has attained power, it attempts to raise itself above the human lot, <margin>6. Metamorphoses.</margin> and "to strike the heavens with its head," <note>original Greek: "καὶ τῇ κεφαλῇ τὸν οὐρανὸν ἐξαγάσσων ἐπιχειρεῖ"</note> if I may use the words of Synesius. <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD) was a Greek bishop and philosopher; the author quotes his letters.</note> Nebuchadnezzar <margin>Letter 57, p. 164 & letter 76, p. 262.</margin> <margin>Psalm 73:8.</margin> spoke iniquity from on high, as the Psalmist says of the impious; but the lofty hand of God quickly cast down this braggart, as the Prophet <margin>Isaiah 14:15.</margin> continues to narrate: *To the underworld you shall be dragged down, into the deepest recesses of the pit.* <note>original Hebrew: "אך-שאול תורד אל-ירכתי בור"</note> He thought the crown of his head touched the clouds and wished to be worshipped as a god in a golden statue, but behold, God drags the "petty-god" <note>original Latin: "Deastrum"</note> <margin>Anthology 1. 80. 16. v. 4. p. 236.</margin> from the clouds down to Hades.

The Supreme Divinity plucked the wings from that winged Monarch, whose power he wished to tear away with the sharpest of tweezers. The majesty of a kingdom that seemed impossible to uproot, whose foundations appeared unshakable, was collapsed by a horrible fall, so that those looking on would say: <margin>verse 16.</margin> *Is this the man who troubled the earth, who shook kingdoms?* <note>original Hebrew: "הזה האיש מרגיז הארץ מרעיש ממלכות"</note> <margin>verse 17.</margin> *Who made the world like a desert, and destroyed its cities, and did not open the prison for his captives?* <note>original Hebrew: "שם תבל כמדבר ועריו הרס ואסיריו לא-פתח ביתה"</note> Behold, he who strove to place his throne among the clouds is quickly stripped of his kingdom and stripped of his human heart, so that he was changed into a beast, about which we must read in the fourth chapter. The wings are plucked from the winged King and the winged Kingdom; at last, the kingdom is plundered and overturned, as indicated by the words: *Its wings were plucked.* <note>original Aramaic: "מריטו גפיה"</note> Jerome says: <margin>ibid. 1. c. v. 695.</margin> *The fact that its wings were plucked—that is, the Lioness or Eagle—signifies the other kingdoms which it previously ruled and flew over in the world. And it was lifted up, he says, from the earth, namely by the subversion of the empire of the Chaldeans.* God establishes and removes kings at his will; he gives wings and plucks them. Through him, it stands to preserve kingdoms as well as to lay them waste, and to depose from the throne those Nebuchadnezzars inflated with the swelling of pride. The ruin of the Monarchy was the wicked pride of Nebuchadnezzar, exalting himself above what he was, whence it could be said to him: *Though you soar aloft like the eagle, from there I will bring you down* (Obadiah 1:4; compare Amos 9:2-3). The ruin would be the even more wicked foolishness of Belshazzar, who, not softened by the example of his father and grandfather, proceeded to be insolent toward God. The Monarchy that was wavering under Evil-merodach fell from its highest peak under Belshazzar,

<column-break/>

and was stripped of all the glory in which it boasted at the same time. Thus, a fall follows with a swift foot upon preceding pride, just as destruction follows blasphemy. <margin>The State of the Four Monarchies.</margin> Belshazzar did not allow himself to be moved by the example of his grandfather; rather, by his blasphemy of the true God, his adoration of false gods, and his profanation of sacred objects, he brought death and destruction upon himself and his kingdom. For on that very night in which he was occupied with impiety, he was taken away—struck down by the just hand of God in the midst of his strength, his triumphs, and his delights—the same hand which had carved these words on the wall:

<insert>
| M | N | A |
|---|---|---|
| T | K | L |
| P | R | S |
</insert>
<note>This grid represents the Aramaic "Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin." The author suggests a "cryptographic" reading where the wise men failed to read it because they looked at it horizontally while the secret was in an "oblong" or vertical reading.</note>

The wise men did not understand the Writing, because they read it in a straight line, whereas they should have read it vertically. If we read these words, they are a "mnemonic" <note>original Latin: "mnemonicon" — a memory aid.</note> for the epilogue of the kingdom, for on the same night that the Script was carved, Belshazzar was killed. We are made more certain of this night by Xenophon, who writes that Babylon was captured on the night they were celebrating a feast to their god with great security. Thus the glory of the Kingdom passed, once the city was captured, to the Medes and Persians, who, after the Chaldean empire was removed, caused the second Monarchy to arise, the depiction of which is in these words:

<margin>
*And behold another beast, a second, like a bear, and it was raised up on one side, and there were three ribs in its mouth between its teeth.* <note>The author provides the text in both Aramaic and Greek.</note>
</margin>

And behold, another beast like a bear stood on one side, and three ribs (the Old Version translates as "three rows") were in its mouth between its teeth.

The Persian kingdom is type-cast as a Bear, notably well-toothed and voracious. Indeed, in its gaping mouth, among other teeth, were seen three teeth representing the size of ribs, which said to it: *Arise, devour much flesh.* <note>original Aramaic: "קומי אכלי בשר שגיא"</note> The Bear is a wrathful and savage beast, though not indeed as quick to anger as the noble Lion, but somewhat slower; but if you once stir the bile in its nose, know that it is slowly put aside. If you irritate it, you will see its nose wrinkle; concerning which Martial elegantly writes: <margin>Epigrams, Book 6, 64, v. 270.</margin>
> Nor, possessing a rabid mouth,
> should you provoke the steaming nose of a living bear;
> Though he be peaceful and lick your fingers and hands,
> If pain and bile, if just anger compels him,
> He will be a Bear.

Masters of wild beasts are accustomed to throw effigies of men filled with hay or tow to bears to irritate them; they are also accustomed to throw fireballs into caves so that, being irritated, they might come out to fight in the spectacles. Seneca <margin>On Anger, 3.30.</margin> relates that they were irritated by a cloth. The slow-moving animal is dragged to the fight with difficulty, but once it has conceived anger, it comes forth from its den with a roar and performs its part strenuously. Those who see it admire its skill in fighting no less than its caution—though otherwise it is a stupid animal—and this can be understood from <margin>History of Animals, 5.8.</margin> what Aristotle relates: that a bear throws itself on its back in a conflict with a bull, [seizing] its horns with its feet...

It highlights the downfall of Belshazzar due to pride and provides a cryptographic explanation for the "writing on the wall."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the four great world monarchies described in the Book of Daniel. The previous page discussed the Babylonian Empire as a winged lion; here, the author transitions to the second monarchy, the Medo-Persian Empire, symbolized by the bear.</meta>

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES ###

<margin>The state of the four Monarchs.</margin>
...to embrace with its feet, and to attack the bull's shoulders with its teeth until it has been cast down. As the Greek naturalist observes: <note>The author likely refers to Aelian or a similar ancient naturalist describing animal behavior.</note> "The bear, as if charging at the bull face to face, settles itself underneath; while the bull tries to strike, the bear wraps its arms around the horns, and by biting the shoulders with its mouth, it brings the bull down." <note>original Greek: "Ἄρκτ. (ait) ὥσπερ κυρίσασα τῷ ταύρῳ κατὰ πρόσωπον ὑπτία καθίσταται, καὶ τῷ ταύρῳ τύπτειν ἐπιχειροῦντι, τοῖς μὲν βραχίοισι τὰ ἅυρα τὰ κέρατα περιλαμβάνει, τῷ δὲ στόματι τῶν ἀκρωμίων δάκνουσα, καταβάλλει τὸν ταῦρον."</note> Pliny "plucked" this passage <margin>Book VIII, 36. chapter 29.</margin> when he wrote: *Bears exhaust bulls by hanging from their mouths and horns with the full weight of all their feet.* And Solinus adds: *Whenever bears attack bulls, they choose the parts where they can best hang on, seeking nothing but the horns or the nostrils. They take the horns to exhaust the bull with their weight, and the nostrils so that the pain is sharper in such a tender place.* Aelian records the same in his sixth book *On Animals*, chapter 9. Just as that observation about the Rhinoceros’s slow but savage anger <margin>Martial, Epigram 22.</margin> can be applied here:

> While the masters skillfully provoke the Bear to fight,
> The beast’s great anger gathers slowly within.
> The promised battles of Mars were despaired of,
> Yet that well-known fury finally returned.

From this, I believe the nature of the Persians is represented—a people who remained quiet in their own lands for a long time. But once the Babylonian Lions had dragged the "neighboring nations" <note>original Greek: "τὰ γειτνιῶντα ἔθνη"</note> into their clutches as prey, and had even provoked the Persian people, the *Persian Bear* emerged irritated from its mountains and caves. With a steaming nose and gaping mouth, it made an assault upon the Babylonian "eagle wings." Once these wings were thoroughly plucked, one might say of the Babylonians what the poets say of Icarus "traveling through the air" <note>original Greek: "ἀεροπορεῖ"</note>, or what Martial said <margin>Epigram 8.</margin> of Daedalus:

> Daedalus, since you are thus torn by a Lucanian bear,
> How you wish you had your wings now.

Bears become most exasperated and put on their greatest savagery when they realize their cubs have been snatched away. The Sacred Writers themselves teach this. God, when provoked in His patience, says <margin>Hosea 13:8.</margin> of Himself: *I will meet* Israel *like a bear robbed* <note>original Hebrew: "דב שכול" (dob shakkul)</note> *of her cubs*, which the Ancient Interpreter <note>Referring to the Vulgate or a similar early translation.</note> well explains with a clarifying note. God compares Himself to a bear whose cubs have been stolen to show, as if before one’s eyes, His most hostile intent toward the disobedient. Just as a bear is rendered more ferocious when its cubs are taken, so God is more angered by the deplorable impiety of men, whom He otherwise wished to carry like an eagle carries its young or cherish like a hen with her chicks (*Exodus 19:4; Deuteronomy 32:10-11; Matthew 23:37*). A bear that has lost its cubs tears apart whatever it meets; so too God, if He sees the hearts of men snatched away from Him through extreme wickedness of life, <margin>v. same chapter.</margin> tears *the enclosure of their hearts, and consumes them like a lion.* <term>Hushai the Archite</term> <note>A friend and advisor to King David who acted as a double agent during Absalom's rebellion.</note> proposed this symbol of a raging bear to Absalom <margin>2 Samuel 17:8.</margin> to indicate the nature of his father and the soldiers with him, who were stirred up after suffering a heavy loss: *You know your father and his men, that they are mighty men, and they are bitter in spirit, like a bear robbed of her whelps in the field.* <gloss>“Like a bear bereaved of her children in the plain.”</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ὥσπερ ἄρκτος ἠτεκνωμένη ἐν τῷ πεδίῳ"</note> The Vulgate translates more closely: *Just as a female bear rages in the forest when her cubs have been snatched.* The author of the Proverbs <margin>chapter 17, v. 12.</margin> uses this same savagery of a mother searching for her cubs to describe the mind of a fool, saying it is better to meet "a bear robbed of her whelps" <note>original Hebrew: "דב שכול"</note> than a fool in his folly. Here the Ancient Interpreter says: *It is more profitable to meet a bear with her young snatched away than a fool trusting in himself in his folly.* That female bears are fiercer because of their cubs, let us hear from other authors. Jerome, commenting on Hosea, says: *Those who have written on the nature of beasts say that among all wild animals, nothing is fiercer than a bear when it*

<column-break/>

has lost its cubs. What Jerome says is confirmed everywhere by writers of natural history, such as Aristotle: <note>original Greek: "χαλεπαὶ καὶ αἱ θήλειαι ἄρκτοι μετὰ τῶν σκύμνων"</note> *Female bears are also dangerous when they are with their cubs.* Ovid, in the 13th book of the *Metamorphoses*, verse 54:

---

-> Harsher than a thistle, more truculent than a mother bear. <-

---

The word "FOETA" <note>Often meaning "pregnant" or "having recently given birth."</note> is ambiguous, as Columella (Book 6, chapter 24) and others use it to denote both a belly full of young and one recently emptied. I do not doubt that here it means a bear recently delivered of its birth, for there follows the description of those found by Polyphemus:

---

-> A shaggy bear with cubs on the highest mountains. <-

---

And that Cyclops, when he could not win Galatea by threats or gifts, declares his anger in a similar way:

---

> He rises and, like a bull maddened by the loss of his cow,
> He cannot stand still, but wanders through the woods and well-known glades.

---

Oppian writes of this bear-madness in his 4th book *On Hunting*, verse 413:

> For bears are greatly grieved in heart,
> Both in their jaws and their troublesome paws.

He describes their appearance in Book 3, verse 139:

> A murderous race, of shifting counsel,
> Of no good form, with bright faces on dark bodies,
> Jagged-toothed and howling.

The bear indulges its belly and satiates itself with the filth of being a "raw-flesh eater" <note>original Greek: "ὠμοβόρος"</note>. Jerome accommodates this bear-like gluttony to Ahasuerus, whom Haman persuaded to destroy the Jewish nation in a single slaughter. But why not apply it to Cyrus, the founder of this Monarchy? For according to Herodotus, Cyrus burned with an insatiable desire for ruling and subjecting all nations to himself. Regarding this lust for power, Justin and Orosius write that in the Scythian war, the head of this great King was cut off by <term>Tomyris, Queen</term> <note>The legendary ruler of the Massagetae who defeated Cyrus the Great.</note> of the Scythians, to avenge her son's blood. She cast his head into a bag full of blood with this reproach of his cruelty: *You thirsted for blood, now drink blood; be filled with blood, for which you were insatiable for thirty years.* Rupert of Deutz notes: *Cyrus did not submit his heart to the worship or religion of the living God, though he managed external affairs for Him; therefore it is no wonder that, as he went through the world driven by his greed, he met a miserable end to his life. For histories record that Queen Tomyris of the Scythians, having trapped his entire army by an ambush, slaughtered them along with the King—200,000 Persians—and cut off Cyrus's head and cast it into a sack filled with human blood.* The Prophet makes the bear carnivorous, assigning it three long teeth for the purpose of signifying the three principal kings: Cyrus, Darius Hystaspes, and Artaxerxes. These kings, with their vast gluttony and full jaws, devoured massive provinces in Africa, Asia, and Europe, and amassed a great force of gold through tributes from the nations subject to them. The Persian Bear, grim with its teeth, after satiating itself for many years with plunder and voracity, was eventually slaughtered and pierced through by Alexander the Great. The Persian kingdom was transferred to the Macedonians by the "Macedonian sword" <note>original Greek: "μαχαίρᾳ μακεδονικῇ"</note>, and another Monarchy was instituted. This is called the Third Monarchy, prefigured under the image of a *Winged Leopard with four heads.* For thus says Daniel: *After this I looked, and behold...*

# Daniel VII. v. 4. and following #

<column-break/>

<margin>
The state of the four Monarchies. 6. chapter 4. 11.

-> ...another beast like a leopard, and it had four wings of a bird upon its back, and the beast had four heads. <-

> *Another beast like a leopard, and it had four wings of a bird upon its back, and the beast had four heads.* <note>original Greek: ἕτερον θηρίον ὡσεὶ πάρδαλις, καὶ αὐτῇ πτερὰ τέσσαρα πετεινοῦ ὑπεράνω αὐτῆς, καὶ τέσσαρες κεφαλαὶ τῷ θηρίῳ.</note>

The Monarchy of the Greeks is most excellently compared to a leopard, for no other animal could have more aptly represented the nature of the Greek character. The leopard is a spotted animal, reflecting the cunning and versatile disposition of the Greek intellect through the variety of its spots. Alexander sensed just how mobile their minds were at the very beginning of his reign; for though they had elected him Commander against Darius by common vote, they defected from him while he was occupied with war in Thrace. Upon his return, he overthrew the city of Thebes but received the Athenians back into his favor. The leopard was seen with four wings and four notable heads, which seem to signify those four kingdoms that arose from the shattered Monarchy of Alexander: namely the Syrian, Egyptian, Asian <note>Referring to the Kingdom of Pergamon or the broader Asian territories.</note>, and Macedonian. Great is the speed of the leopard, as Martial says:

<margin>
v. 37.
</margin>

<margin>
Mat. 14.
</margin>

> And with a long wound, he stretched out the winged leopard.

Alexander is similar to the swift leopard because of the incredible speed of his deeds. As Jerome says (column 1136), he ran across the world from the Illyrian and Adriatic seas all the way to the Indian Ocean and the Ganges river, more by victories than by battles, and in six years he subjugated part of Europe and all of Asia to himself. The same author, writing on Jeremiah chapter 5, page 528, says that the leopard watching over their cities prefigures Alexander’s attack and his swift passage from the West all the way to India. He calls him a leopard, however, on account of his "variety" <note>This refers to the "spotted" nature of his empire, made of diverse conquered peoples, or his own changing character.</note>. Hence, Philip Melanchthon wrote:

<margin>
book 7. chapter 28. folio 130. b.
</margin>

> Behold the leopard of Pella <note>Alexander was born in Pella, Macedonia.</note>, than whom no other was more beautiful
> In the beautiful world which he had conquered; nor ever
> Did anyone perform such deeds in fewer years.
> Though they were old men, worn by age and the labor of war,
> He defeated them all with his counsel in the flower of youth.
> Therefore, neither weapons nor enemies harmed him,
> But foul drunkenness and lazy pleasure.
> You who are wise, and labor to preserve the glory
> Of unconquered virtue, always flee the leisure of a lazy life,
> But be mindful that God, since He is most chaste,
> Punishes the polluted and finally exalts the chaste.

Nothing was swifter than Alexander's victory; having <unclear>taken up</unclear> arms, he gained possession of all Egypt, Syria, Palestine, and all Asia as far as India in a short space of time. What can be thought of as more similar than the Leopard and Alexander? *There is such audacity*, as Milichius explains the image, *such speed and strength in leopards, that they cannot even be captured or killed by armed hunters; instead, they are captured when put to sleep by Wine and Venus.* <note>Venus here refers to lust or sexual indulgence.</note> You see Alexander himself, who was later extinguished in a sudden moment of leisure by wine and lusts. His four illustrious companions are also similar to the leopard, indicated by the four heads, just as they are by the four horns of the he-goat in Daniel 8:8. With their help, he subdued the whole world in such a short time, and after their Emperor's death, they divided the prize acquired in so many wars into four parts among themselves. Ptolemy received Egypt, Seleucus received

Syria, Antigonus took Asia, and Antipater took Greece. Jerome says in the same place: "Moreover, he says the four heads are his Generals, who later stood forth as successors to the kingdom: Ptolemy, Seleucus, Antigonus, and Philip." The Jews, above all others, felt the bloody cruelty of the leopards during the time of the Maccabees, as Josephus and the books of the Maccabees testify. Under the wings of the Macedonian leopard, that Monarchy achieved excellent glory, which the words hint at: "And dominion was given to it." <note>original Aramaic: ולשלטן יהיב לה; original Greek: ἐξουσία ἐδόθη αὐτῇ.</note> He says it was "given" to show that it happened not by Alexander's bravery, but by the will of the Lord. However, this power did not last much beyond two hundred years; as those years ran out, another more terrible Animal arrived, which trampled the Panther <note>The author uses "Panther" and "Leopard" interchangeably.</note> and established a new Monarchy, which was called the Roman. That Monarchy is expressed through the image of a terrible, fearsome, and robust animal, endowed with iron teeth. Let us hear the words of the Prophet, who in verse 7 prophesies about this beast thus:

> After this I saw in the visions of the night, *and behold a fourth Beast, terrible and wonderful and exceedingly strong, which had great iron teeth, devouring and crushing, and trampling the remainder with its feet; and it was different from all the beasts that were before it, and it had ten horns.*

The Prophet depicts this beast for us in a truly horrible form, far surpassing the other beasts in atrocity. He expresses neither its name nor its species, as he had done with the three prior beasts. He attributes to it iron teeth, which he had given to none of the preceding Beasts, *crushing all things*, and *feet trampling all things*, so that it left nothing remaining; ten horns are also attributed to it. Let us now look at these more specifically. That immense beast clearly and aptly displays that immense power and tyranny of the Roman Empire, which was fearsome to the whole world—things that can only be accurately understood from Latin and Greek history. Those epithets, trembling with their very sound, signify nothing other than that the Roman Empire would be the hardest of all, and the most terrible in the harshest wars at home and abroad. No species of beast could be found suitable to represent it, just as we read that the prior kingdoms were displayed under a certain specific beast. Jerome says: *I wonder enough that, while he placed a lioness, a bear, and a leopard for the three kingdoms above, he compared the Roman kingdom to no beast; unless perhaps, to make the beast fearsome, he kept silent on the name, so that whatever more ferocious thing we might imagine among beasts, we should understand the Romans to be that.* And in Hosea chapter 2, column 93: *The most savage beasts are mentioned, so that a greater fear might be increased in those who are to be devoured. ...of the beast, to which the Roman Republic is likened, was compared to various things because the comparison is uncertain and doubtful. *Romulus* is similar to a wolf, whom they say was nurtured by a she-wolf, and most of Romulus’s successors, because they sucked that wolf-milk, swallowed up the riches of almost the entire world, not unlike a wolf devouring sheep. For was not all of Africa, all of Spain, all of Gaul, all of Greece, all of Asia as far as the Euphrates, all of Syria, and all of Egypt stripped bare by the Romans? Germany also felt the wolf’s teeth, as did England and Belgium. The beast of this kingdom suggests a varied and changeable form. He who has even a basic taste of historical elements will not deny that it was not of one form, but of many. First, it was *Royal* for 264 years; then, with the Kings expelled, it became *Consular*, and they began to create two Consuls each year. Business was often conducted for the Consuls sometimes through Tribunes, sometimes through Dictators, so that at times you may not know whether the latter ruled more than the former—concerning which matter the Roman writers should be read. We shall consider somewhat more extensively the origin of the Roman Monarchy, its progress, <gloss>peak</gloss>, its flower, and its decline. The beginning of the city of Rome was at the time when Shalmaneser was ruling the Assyrians—specifically in the first year of the Seventh Olympiad, according to Plutarch. This was in the 3,225th year of the world's creation. *In the prologue of his Epitome, Florus* <note>Lucius Annaeus Florus, a 2nd-century Roman historian.</note> *assigns four ages to it, as if it were some man, when he writes thus of it:*

<margin>page 1.</margin>
> *If one considers the Roman people as if a man and surveys its entire age—how it began, how it grew up, how it reached a certain flower of youth, and how it afterwards grew old, as it were—he will find four stages and progressions.*

From the smallest beginnings it grew to the highest power, and that city, which is said to have been founded by shepherds, finally emerged as the Mistress of the world. In this way that eternal city—Mistress of things, citadel of nations, head and Queen of the world, and metropolis of the earth—shone forth. I think I must briefly explain how it gradually reached that highest pinnacle of affairs, and how it afterwards gradually declined toward its end. This is so that it can be understood how the iron legs and feet of that fatal statue <note>A reference to the statue in King Nebuchadnezzar's dream in Daniel 2, where the legs of iron represent the Roman Empire.</note> consisted of untamable iron; how Rome, growing slowly and little by little, drew the kingdoms of the world into itself and transferred that whole bronze belly of the Greek Empire into itself; and how finally the toes of the feet degenerated and fell away. From its first origin even until its fall, the Roman Republic was subject to various and great vices, which were followed by dangerous diseases and finally death itself. Regarding other Republics, some may see one cause and others another, and different people may judge differently, which we will not inquire into at present. It is my pleasure to set forth the history of the City and what happened in it—as if in the first and highest home of the world—and how the Republic grew and decreased amidst its vices. It is usually the case that the greatest cities are afflicted by the greatest vices; and just as the greatest geniuses are usually set over the largest cities, so they very often suffer something human <note>A polite way of saying "failings" or "weaknesses."</note> above others. There is no great genius without a mixture of vices, and vice always has some virtue with which to compete. Let us recall the beginning of the city in our memory, and let us represent in Romu-

<column-break/>

-lus the first miseries of the city, the first evils of the city. The origin and cradle of the City of Rome are ascribed to *Romulus*. It was first inhabited by many people brought in from Alba Longa and neighboring tribes; nor was entry prohibited to anyone, however much a fugitive or even a criminal. For this purpose, an Asylum was established near the citadel, where people might flee from the harms of other cities for the sake of protection. From such small beginnings such a great City emerged. The new people lacked women, and since Romulus could not obtain the right of marriage from neighboring peoples for his citizens, he lured the Sabine women into the city under the guise of games called the *Consualia*, whom he ordered to be seized. From this arose the first war with Tatius, the King of the Sabines. Tatius, though initially a Victor, was defeated shortly thereafter and returned to favor with the Roman Chieftain, and this through the prayers of the kidnapped women. These women, rushing across the battle lines, broke up the battle—which had been joined on their account—with their entreaties. *Tatius* was taken into a share of the kingdom, and with the kingdom united, the Sabines moved to Rome, so that they might be joined more closely to those they had lost. The King, having divided the citizens into *30 curiae* <note>Administrative groupings of citizens.</note>, gave them the names of the Sabine women, and lest wisdom be lacking to their strength, he chose one hundred Senators. This city, which was occupied elsewhere in adopting new sons, grew in such a short space of time that it transplanted Roman stocks into foreign parts of the world. This transplantation took its name from *Colonies*. Moreover, it served the increase and greatness of the empire that they easily and willingly granted the *right of citizenship*, which was the unique means by which they brought a Republic of moderate power to distinguished dominance. At the beginning, while it was still raw, Romulus—with a prudent though wicked plan—admitted the unrefined, the robust, the obscure, and the flawed without distinction. The Faliscan people were also admitted, whom Numa afterwards, with a more shrewd plan, forced into order by the bonds of laws. He restrained them by the dread of religion and led that looser way of living back into itself. Then the third *King, Ancus Martius*, ensured that they excelled in spirit and counsel in every way, and the republic, which had hitherto been hidden within the city, sought space outside of it. They exercised dominion within small limits, and gradually began to extend those limits and dominate somewhat more widely under the rule of the Consuls. For Romulus’s successors held the scepters of the kingdom until *Tarquinius the Proud*, by whose powerless rule, coupled with the unbridled lust of his sons, the royal power ceased, after it had been ruled by seven Kings for 264 years. With the Kings expelled, two Consuls began to be created each year. Sixteen years after the flight of the kings, a sedition arose among the common people against the Senate. To calm this, Menenius Agrippa was sent, a man of the Senatorial order, who reconciled the commoners to the Fathers <note>The Senators.</note> with a memorable fable about the conspiracy of the body's limbs against the Belly. There, the Fathers granted *Tribunes* to the common people, who would watch over the people against the injustices of the Magistrates. Thus, the consular right was first diminished, and with the power of the Tribunes growing, the empire seems to have taken on the form of a Democratic state. When the greatest dangers were imminent, a *Dictator* was created, whose authority was supreme, but which did not extend beyond a period of six months. The Dictatorship...

### Daniel II, verse 13 and following ###

<margin>The state of the IV Monarchies.</margin>
This dictatorship was established with great benefit, which often freed the Republic from many difficulties—indeed, it raised it to a peak—at a time when nearly forty peoples had once struck a treaty among themselves to destroy this new Republic. Frequent and great contentions arose between the Fathers <note>The Senate</note> on one side, and the tribunes of the people and the commoners on the other. The people, having become more insolent through wealth and fortune, turned their weapons against themselves more than once. For it is impossible, as Dio Cassius <note>original: "Dio Cassius * observat" — a 3rd-century Roman historian and senator.</note> observes, that in such a state of the Republic where the power is in the hands of the people, if it has been raised to the highest peak and to such great power as that of the Romans then was, the citizens could moderate their own minds. The Fathers, when they could not protect affairs otherwise, sometimes yielded to the commoners, allowing many things to be imposed upon them, now by the Decemvirs, now by the Tribunes. At last, after affairs abroad in *Asia, Africa, and Europe* were well conducted, the city, having become more insolent, was unable to rule itself. Hence, with the strength of Italy worn down by the Social War, and the Republic reduced to a confused order by the domination of *Cinna and Sulla*, the power of *Pompey and Crassus* grew strong. This power, however, quickly passed to *Gaius Julius Caesar*, who used the power of the tribunes and the dictatorship; then through the arms of *Lepidus and Antony*, it passed to *Augustus*, though much blood of the citizens was shed in various battles. The *Pompeian* civil war was the greatest of all civil wars, conducted in various places by various leaders in different ways, in which *Julius Caesar* finally emerged superior and seized a perpetual dictatorship. There followed the *Triumvirate of Mark Antony, Marcus Lepidus, and Octavian Caesar*, and the civil war waged against *Brutus and Cassius*; soon another war broke out between *Octavian and Lucius Antonius*, and yet another between *Octavian and Sextus Pompey*. Finally, with Pompey crushed and Antony defeated at *Actium*, peace was secured on land and sea. *Augustus* alone received the name of *Emperor* by a Decree of the People—not such as was customarily given for a victory in the ancient manner, but one by which the supreme command of the Empire was demonstrated. In this way, the *popular method of ruling was changed into a Monarchical state*, and that method of governing was first expressed by the mild name of the *Principate* <note>The early period of the Roman Empire, where the ruler styled himself as "First Citizen" (Princeps) rather than King.</note>. It should be considered not without the reason of divine providence that *Rome*, which was born enslaved under *Kings*, lost the liberty gained under *Consuls*; it was captured by the *Gauls* in the three hundred and sixtieth year after it was founded under the *Decemvirate* and defiled by widespread fires. Finally, after a miraculous restoration, when pride and vices grew along with power and surpassed wealth, it was torn apart by civil wars. Ultimately, around the 700th year, it submitted its neck to one Master, *Caesar*. For after the *Caesars* began to reign, their power broke the consular dignity and authority, which had remained free and intact for 447 years, from *Lucius Brutus and Publius Valerius*, the first Consuls, to *Pansa and Aulus Hirtius*, the last Consuls, who fell in the same battle at *Mutina* during the *Antonian* civil war. The name of *Consuls* did indeed remain with others without any power, but from the year 1164 from the founding of the city, which was the reign of *Honorius and Theodosius*—the year in which *Rome* was captured by the *Goths* under the Consuls *Flavius and Varro*, in the 410th year after the birth of Christ—the name vanished along with the reality. With the empire of *Augustus* established,

just as waves are accustomed to grow quiet after a heavy storm at sea when the winds subside, so all discords everywhere grew quiet. The Savior of the human race, CHRIST, illustrated this happiness of the times and simultaneously that new Monarchy by His own saving advent into this world. Augustus held the Empire successfully and moderately; when it was well-strengthened and expanded, *he turned toward peace, and he coerced the age—which was prone toward all evils and flowing into luxury—with many grave and severe laws*. On account of these many great deeds, he was called Perpetual Dictator and Father of the Fatherland. *It was even discussed in the Senate whether he should be called Romulus because he had established the empire, but the name of Augustus seemed more holy and reverent, so that even then, while he inhabited the earth, he might be consecrated by the very name and title.* Thus I seal these laudably performed deeds of *Augustus* with the same words with which *Lucius Annaeus Florus* <note>original: "Lucius Annæus Florus *" — a Roman historian of the 2nd century AD.</note> concludes his entire book on Roman affairs. <margin>Book 4, chapter 12, page 392.</margin> Most of the successors disgraced the most flourishing Republic handed to them through the hands of *Augustus* with every wickedness and laziness. For more than the first two hundred years, up until *Trajan*, the Republic grew old and wasted away, as it were, through the inertia of the Caesars, *except that under the Prince Trajan it moved its muscles, and beyond the hope of all, the old age of the empire revived as if youth had been restored*, as *Florus* observes. <margin>Book 1, number 8, page 20.</margin> Truly, under *Trajan*, that most fortunate Emperor, the Roman Republic flourished most greatly, with *Arabia, Armenia, and Mesopotamia* in the East and *Dacia* in the North being added to the Empire. The majestic <note>A pun on the name Augustus, meaning "majestic" or "venerable."</note> Empire of *Rome* began under *Augustus Caesar* and stood out at its majestic peak under *Trajan*, under whom the power became truly majestic. No power under heaven was then greater than that of the Romans, to which almost every empire under the Sun bowed itself; hence came that audacity in their minds, so that they called themselves *Lords of the World*. Before him, the degeneration of the empire began to be felt somewhat under the *Tiberiuses and Neros*, who advanced toward power through the detriment, accusations, and exile of citizens. For seven hundred whole years, Rome possessed an empire agitated by perpetual movements of arms, neither peaceful nor firmly quiet. For the Italians, there were battles, slaughters, dissensions, factions, pretenses, hatreds, envies, and killings, sometimes within the walls and sometimes outside them, so much so that among so many and such great difficulties, it scarcely had breath. Starting in some way from the first, it was restored from the Senonian Gauls by the bravery of one man, Camillus, who was then an exile. After the battles of Allia, Ticinus, Trebia, and Trasimene, it returned again to the battle line. After the ignominy of the Caudine peace, it revived itself by the work of Africanus. Fabius the Delayer made hesitating fortune compliant to himself. The invincible hope of one man, Fabius, excited the wavering minds of the old men. Hence, even if that majestic empire which it once held ceased to be under the last *Augustus*, who was thereafter surnamed *Augustulus* <note>Meaning "Little Augustus," a mocking diminutive for the final Western Roman Emperor.</note>, nevertheless the city itself has stood in this current year 1656 for 2371 years—a felicity that has happened to no other city under the Sun until now. For the history of the Romans is 750 years from the founding of the City to the birth of JESUS CHRIST, which was the twentieth year of the Empire of Augustus in which he reigned alone; so that if the Romans had nothing further, they could glory in this alone.
