# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES #

<margin>
The state of the Four Monarchies.
</margin>
The decline began with those remaining Emperors who succeeded Trajan. Under Constantine the Great, when the Imperial seat was moved to Greece <note>Specifically to Byzantium, renamed Constantinople</note>, a beginning was made which Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a German abbot and polymath, in his *Chronologia mystica*, section 16</note> identifies as the cause of the entire Monarchic decline. For the Emperors whom Rome then possessed while Constantine established his seat at Byzantium could scarcely sustain themselves, as their authority depended on the Eastern Empire at Constantinople. As Andreas Osiander says <margin>on the last times, 4.a.</margin>, *Rome was then not so much like a living body that could govern itself, but rather like a dead corpse whose funeral and burial were cared for by others*, until at last, after the devastation wrought by Alaric and Genseric <note>Leaders of the Goths and Vandals who sacked Rome in 410 and 455 CE</note>, the remnants of the wretched city of Rome fell into such misery and contempt that after the fall of *Augustulus* <note>Romulus Augustulus, the last Western Emperor</note>, she was no longer even worthy of having a Master—that is, a Western Emperor. She was so far from ruling over others in the ancient fashion. After the time of Theodosius, all Roman learning was shattered along with the remaining majesty of the Empire as various peoples and barbarian nations rushed into Italy. The body of the Empire seemed to mourn at the death of such a great Prince. When it began to slip under Honorius and Arcadius, to head toward a precipice under Valentinian, to collapse under their successors, and to fail in the West, the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnici"</note> attributed this decline of the Empire to the abandonment of the Ancient Rites and the practices of the new religion <note>Christianity</note>. Indeed, once Honorius was moved to the helm of government, the empire began to decline, and all that splendor of the Roman Empire began to be largely obscured, so much so that the once-flourishing empire of the world began to become a kind of fatal prey for all the nations of the earth. Nearly all peoples, having shaken off this Roman yoke, established their own kingdoms; hence, new kingdoms gradually arose: the English, the Spanish, the French, and the Italian. Then the face of the Roman Empire was greatly changed. Indeed, by the kindness of Honorius, the Goths held Aquitaine, having returned from Spain, and the entire region which ended at the Pyrenees mountains between the Rhone and Loire rivers. Honorius's successor, Valentinian III, an unhappy Emperor of the West, held a reign infamous for manifold slaughter and finally the downfall of the empire. Affairs in Gaul were then so deplorable that the Romans barely struggled to maintain a third part of it. Meroveus, King of the Franks, having crossed the Rhine, occupied a large part of Gaul. Also hanging over their necks was that devastator of Germany, the scourge of God, **Attila**, King of the Huns, who destroyed and laid waste to many great towns. Thus Rome was exposed more than once to prey and plundering under the leader Genseric; the Vandals carried off the imperial ornaments and insignia with them to Africa, as Justinian writes <note>original: "de offic. praef. praetor. Africae"</note>. Rome therefore experienced what the preceding Monarchies had lamented. Kingdoms fall, and kingdoms arise. Kingdoms are mixed, and kingdoms are divided. Kings are exalted, and kings are cast down. Kingdoms pass from nation to nation, from people to people, from region to region. As the Chaldean Monarchy <note>Babylon</note> falls, the Persian arises. As the Persian ends, the Greek comes forth. As the Greek goes to ruin, the Roman is born. Thus the corruption of one is the generation of another. With **Nimrod**, the beginning of the first Monarchy is placed in its infancy...

<column-break/>

...infancy, which in its adulthood had *Nebuchadnezzar*, the most perfect Monarch, and which in its old age was brought to an end in *Belshazzar*. The beginning of the second Monarchy is counted from *Cyrus*; its end in *Darius Codomannus*. It pleased God, the distributor of these kingdoms, that upon the fall of the Chaldean Monarchy and the rise of the Persian, His people should be freed. It pleased the King of Kings that, once the Persian dominion was extinguished, a Greek Monarch should rule, and the dominion should be transported from Asia into Europe. Finally, it pleased the Divine Power, having set aside the Assyrians, Persians, and Greeks, to choose the Romans as the head of nations. What ought to be attributed to divine arrangement, the historian Plutarch <note>A Greek-Roman biographer and philosopher</note> adjudged to the inconstancy of Fortune, whose words I will set down here: <quote>Fortune, having left the Persians and Assyrians, flew cheerfully through Macedonia, and quickly shook off Alexander; having traveled through Egypt and Syria, she passed through many kingdoms, and turning frequently, she supported the Carthaginians. But approaching the Palatine Hill and crossing the Tiber, she (as it seems) laid down her wings, stepped out of her sandals, and abandoned her unfaithful and shifting globe. Thus she entered Rome, as if intending to stay.</quote> Xylander <note>Wilhelm Holtzman (1532–1576), a scholar who translated Plutarch into Latin</note> translates this as: *Fortune, having deserted the Persians and Assyrians, when she had flown lightly through Macedonia and quickly cast aside Alexander, and then by wandering through Egypt and Syria had passed through kingdoms, and having often turned had carried the Carthaginians; after she approached the Palatine by crossing the Tiber, she put down her wings, took off her winged sandals, and having sent away that unfaithful and versatile globe, she entered ROME in such a way as to remain.* This man <note>Plutarch</note> was a prophet, but truly a foolish one. The Roman Empire, as if growing young, moved its muscles under Trajan (as Florus says, see Johann Friedrich Pöpping, *The Illustrated World on the Romano-German Empire, p. 53*). Under Hadrian, it began to decrease; under Valens and Valentinian, Gratian and Theodosius, it began to be violently shaken; after which it began to be foully torn apart, with many on all sides fighting for the Empire by force and guile, by price and by arms, and finally it was exposed, like prey, to the Goths, Vandals, Franks, Lombards, Huns, and finally the Saracens and Turks. Where then was that "eternity" of the Roman Empire, which the omens, oracles, and auguries of the Pagans so often babbled about? Where is that Empire which Jupiter is said to have given "without end"? Where then is the "unceasing" Royal Sceptre <note>original: "ἄπαυστον"</note> which the poetess Erinna predicted? Where did Fortune, a wanderer among the Assyrians, a guest among the Persians, a vagrant among the Greeks, then stick, having finally left her rolling globe to inhabit the City forever—to use Plutarch’s words? Thus the Roman Empire began to decline most especially when Italy was occupied by the Lombards, so that there has been no Monarchy like this one, exposed to such varied changes. For because of that mixture of clay <note>original: "ἐπίμιξ" — referring to the feet of the statue in Daniel 2</note>, it was now like clay, now like iron, and again like clay. Now the Goths, now the Vandals, now the Lombards, having left their own lands and seats, invaded Rome, destroyed her, and plucked her feathers. The Monarchy then suffered heavy calamities and was all but overturned. Indeed, it was in such a state that unless the Emperor Justinian had come to its rescue like a "god from a machine" <note>original: "ἀπὸ μηχανῆς" — a theatrical device where a god is lowered to resolve a plot</note> with a very strong remedy, it would have expired completely and totally. Whence Lentulus says in *On the Ark of Kingdoms*, chapter 6: *The outcome of all these wars was that the Germans not only warded off Roman arms but snatched the lands of the entire West with the eternal city itself from their enemies. For Italy...*

For Italy was occupied, possessed, and cultivated by the Lombards, Gaul by the Franks, Britain by the Saxons, and Africa by the Vandals. *If anyone refuses to believe the assertion that all these peoples poured out from the heart of Germany, I refer them to the ancient books of Geography and to Tacitus's Germania.* <note>Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56–120 CE) wrote a famous ethnographic work on the Germanic tribes.</note> Eventually, through the Franks, the very right and name of the *Empire* was brought down to the Germans, and the "eagles"—which had been fleeing in fear—finally fixed their seat there. <note>The "eagles" refer to the *aquila*, the standard of the Roman legions, symbolizing imperial power.</note> Thus, the Roman Empire, which had been torn apart under various Emperors, was restored by Charlemagne and, like a *new body*, to use the words of Sleidan <margin>Book 3, page 118.</margin>, *resumed its color and appearance, with so many great provinces brought back under the rule of a single Prince.* But hardly had it been restored and gathered together when, as Sleidan says on folio 121, *it perished again and was divided into various <margin>On the Fortune of Rome, page 317.</margin> provinces under the jurisdiction of many who possess them as their own private property. They do not even acknowledge the source from which they flowed; so much so that the august and once-celebrated height of the Roman Empire is today nothing more than a thin shadow of a great body, since it has been reduced from such an immense mass to a single small portion of Europe: Germany.* For by the ill-considered generosity of Charlemagne, Rome—which was once the home of the Roman Empire—was left to the Pope as his seat. Alongside the disgrace of the Empire, the Pope’s power gradually increased, and papal rule grew until things finally reached the point where anyone who denied or called his seat into question was condemned for heresy, according to *Distinctio 22, chapter 1, "Omnes."* <note>A reference to the *Decretum Gratiani*, a collection of Canon Law.</note> On this matter, one should see what Antonius de Roselli writes in his *Treatise on the Power of the Pope and the Emperor, folio 21, column 2, and following.* The throne of the Papacy became great through three "Greats." When *Constantine the Great* left Rome to the will of the Pontiff, he took poor counsel for the Roman Empire. By that withdrawal, the majesty and authority of the Empire were greatly weakened, providing the Pope with the opportunity to preside over and command the Western Churches. Next, the *Throne of the Roman Anti-Christ* <note>The author uses standard Protestant Reformation rhetoric, identifying the Papal office with the "Anti-Christ."</note> received the SPARKS of secular power through the generosity of *Charlemagne*, having previously been mostly content with ecclesiastical power (though with much abuse). Although all of this was done by Charles, it was nevertheless often lamented by later Emperors. For the *Cowl* <note>Latin: *Cucullus*. A metaphor for the clergy or monastic orders.</note>—brought forth by the generosity of the most pious Princes—eventually dared to devour its own mother, not once but many times, as Louis the Bavarian and others experienced to their great misfortune. Under Otto the Great, through various and notable donations, the Pontifical seat gathered further "rays" of power, especially in Germany. As for Italy, Otto removed John XII from the papacy on account of his treachery, foul lusts, and other crimes; after removing Benedict V, he ended the schism and put Leo VIII in their place. Leo then issued a decree restoring to the Roman Emperor the right and power of choosing and consecrating the Roman Pontiff, arranging matters pertaining to the Apostolic See, and confirming and appointing Bishops. This decree exists in *Distinctio 63*; shortly after it comes the formula for the oath by which they say Otto bound himself to Pope John: that he wished no danger to the Pope's life, nor to take away his honor or dignity. The last was Clement VII, who crowned Charles V as King of the Lombards and Emperor of the Romans. During that coronation, celebrated at Bologna, a massive bridge upon which they were walking collapsed. This fall of the bridge was taken as an omen that *no other Emperor would ever again be crowned by a Pope*, as reported by <margin>On the Coronation of Emperor Charles, p. 165, vol. 2 of his works.</margin> Cornelius Agrippa. And indeed, since the Popes and their "coronation oil" were bid farewell, our Germany has stood more splendid and more peaceful, after neither the two Maximilians, nor the three Ferdinands, nor Rudolf, nor Matthias—all of most glorious memory—accepted coronation from a Pope. This is the strength of the Empire: if the Caesar’s authority is preserved unharmed, so that the empire (which is one) does not become double; and if the business of the empire is handled by those to whom those affairs belong. On this subject, the two orations of Johannes Sleidan deserve to be read—one to Emperor Charles V, the other to all the Princes and Estates of the German Empire, which Conrad Rittershusius has recently published. Certainly, the Majesty, dignity, and breadth of the Empire were greatly undermined by the arts of the Popes, and the face of the Empire was much changed by their various schemes. In that state of <term>anarchy</term> <note>original Greek: *anarchia*</note>, there was no certain King, and everyone in that period of turmoil did what seemed right in his own eyes; seeing this opportunity, many withdrew themselves as the evil grew daily. Under Emperor Wenceslaus <note>Wenceslaus IV (1361–1419), King of Bohemia and King of the Romans, often criticized by historians of this era as ineffective.</note>, a man more inept for a kingdom and more curious about wine than the Empire, the Imperial Majesty fell into a lethargy. In the year 1399, when the dignity of the Empire seemed to be falling into ruin due to the laziness, drunkenness, cruelty, hatred of learning, and other vices of Emperor Wenceslaus (which Trithemius recites at length in the *Chronicle of Sponheim*, and Cuspinianus in *The Emperors, p. 388* and following), Frederick, Duke of Brunswick, was elected as the new Emperor. However, Frederick was murdered near Fritzlar shortly after his election, and Wenceslaus was deposed from the Empire. For the decree of this deposition, see the *German Historical Tome* by Christian Ursistitius. Aventinus writes: "he did not hold such things in high regard; rather, he said he was well satisfied if they would only bring him four wagons full of French wine to Prague every year, so that he might have it to drink." When he also heard that one of his castles had burned down, he said that as long as the cellar with the wine was unharmed, he would easily get over the loss, according to *Paul Matthias Wehner on the Transformation of Republics, page 143.* That Fourth Monarchy in Asia, Africa, and Europe once extended its scepter under the vast power of the Romans, but our ancestors were not only driven from the possession of Asia and Africa, they also lost the best part of Europe. Within what narrow straits is the kingdom now confined! It is hardly granted to us to carry our shields into the territories of others; we are even excluded from our own borders. For the Roman Empire emits only the faintest sparks of its ancient splendor, and that noble monarchical building is developing cracks, with its weak columns threatening ruin. Regarding what remains, we must speak of it not as a whole or intact entity, but as the fragments and relics of a scattered Principality, which the pillar of the Austrian House <note>The Habsburg dynasty.</note> has sustained until now—most powerfully because of the kingdoms of Hungary and Bohemia joined to it—so that it still stands unshaken. Thus, the Eagle of the German people, once two-headed but now "one-headed," so to speak, fluctuates in uncertainty. Like the last and very thin strength of a lamp about to die, its final vigor and its very extinction seem mixed and mingled together, not unlike the iron toes of the feet mixed with clay in Daniel's colossus <note>A reference to the statue in Daniel 2:33, representing the final, divided stage of the Roman Empire.</note>. What still remains to our Emperor today are like the ruins of a magnificent building and the shadow of a once-mighty Empire, which will remain until the end of the world. Hence, we can rightly say with Buchholcer (*Chronology, p. 377*), quoting Petrarch: "That once powerful Roman Empire, venerable to nations and Kings, prefigured in the iron shins, when once nothing was missing except a small part of the East, now, alas, possesses nothing except a small part of the West." Regarding that decrease of the narrowed empire, Petrus de Andlo <note>A 15th-century jurist who wrote on the constitution of the Holy Roman Empire.</note> addressed a complaint and an exhortation to Frederick the Great <note>Likely referring to Frederick III (r. 1452–1493).</note>. Accept it, O Nobles, and

hear: "The borders of the Empire have been reduced to such a narrow space that, while the nourishing crown once possessed the entire world except for small parts of the East, it is now seen to have lost all the shores of sea and land except for a few regions of the West; and hardly a shadow of the former Empire remains to us. But, illustrious Princes of Germany, I address you in my speech; for I cannot restrain myself, driven by an excessive affection for the Commonwealth of the Empire. Your ancestors deserved a great portion of the world with immense care and a noble heap of praise and the exercise of virtues, and they added that still-wide and most ample realm to your keeping; but by your negligence, your laziness, and, if I may say so, your discord, it has been reduced to the state we see today with mourning eyes. Lift up your eyes round about, and help the most beautiful and excellent empire, long since worn down by various ailments, with pious aid. Let the examples of your ancestors approach you. Let the ancient praise of Germany flourish again." Furthermore, the same de Andlo says: "Now all the parts of the empire have disappeared from around me; they are plucking the feathers from my Eagle, my power is diminished, my virtue exhausted, and my treasury is meager." Upon these words, the commentator Marquard Freher <note>A German jurist and historian (1565–1614).</note> measures the Earth's curve with an arithmetic stone and a geometric foot, and it is entirely as we should likewise consider: "When once almost all the cultivated worlds and provinces, except Germany, belonged to the Roman Empire, such a reversal of things has occurred that today it has nothing besides this, and not even all of that. The Turk, the French King, the Spaniard, the Pole, the Dane, the Princes of Italy, the Venetians, the Duke of Lorraine, the Swiss, the Belgians—who has not? They have plucked the Eagle's feathers. And see, I pray, the fate and diminution of the Roman Empire: while its size was greatest under the rule of Ulpius Trajan, or Diocletian and Constantine with their colleagues, from the furthest Spain and Africa to the borders of Parthia, its length was 90 degrees (of which 360 complete the circle of the whole world), and its width from the equator toward the north was at least 45 degrees. Geographers assign sixty miles, or fifteen medium German miles, to a degree. Now, if we calculate those lands which are counted today under the jurisdiction of the Roman Empire in both Germanies—this side and that side of the Rhine to the borders of France and Sarmatia <note>An ancient name for Eastern Europe/Poland.</note>, and the Ocean, as well as in Raetia, Noricum, Illyricum, and Italy—they will hardly fill a length and width of 10 degrees; that is, they will hardly equal a fortieth part of the old Roman Monarchy. Subtract further what the Frenchman recently took in Alsace; what a tiny portion of the empire is left now?" Why then do the political thinkers of our Empire exhaust themselves concerning the extending and expanding of this final Monarchy? The limits are set and closed under a narrow space, as Daniel, the <term>first</term> <note>original Greek: *protos*</note> of political thinkers, taught. Why then these anxieties? Indeed, we should be concerned with preserving those things which we possess by the grace of God, since any further expansion of the Empire is no longer to be hoped for. ...He lived such a life, and afterward ascended into the heavens. So also this same Lord Jesus Christ, having completed thirty-three years and nearly half a jubilee year, is set to return with the glory of His majesty to judge the living and the dead. A jubilee year is a span of fifty of our civil years from one jubilee to the next. And it is this year that fits the comparison with the history of Christ. For 33 jubilee years make 1650 of our years <note>The author is using a common 17th-century millenarian calculation: 33.5 jubilees (50 years each) equals 1675, or roughly 1650 as a significant milestone for the end of the world.</note>, to which a few are added in proportion to the days that Christ lived among us beyond thirty-three years; these converge toward the determined and imminent end of the world. So says the author.

<margin>
* Chronicles.
</margin>
Indeed, as Philipp <note>referring to Philipp Melanchthon, a key Protestant Reformer</note> says in the beginning, God willed the series of Monarchies to be known because He wants it to be known that these confusions of the human race will not be everlasting. Instead, there will eventually be an end and a secure, better life for the Church. To this better life, Christ, the *Archegus* <note>original: "Archegus," a Greek term for a leader, founder, or pioneer</note> of the eternal Kingdom—blessed forever and ever—leads us out of this instability and fleeting nature of the Monarchies. May that same thrice-blessed God add blessing upon blessing and grant a 京-devout successor to the pious, deceased Caesar <note>The Holy Roman Emperor</note>. For unless the Lord guards the kingdom, those who keep watch—and the Electors who gather—do so in vain. We worship God, the Monarch of Monarchs, with all our heart, so that He does not abandon us in this weak and exhausted old age of the Roman Empire, but that He might remain with us longer by His grace, **for it is toward evening, and the day has declined** <note>original Greek: "ὅτι πρὸς ἑσπέραν ἐστὶ, καὶ κέκλικεν ἡ ἡμέρα," a reference to Luke 24:29</note>, so that He may preserve His holy seed, scatter the nations that desire war, and finally, on the last day of all Empires, transfer us into His perpetual kingdom. Depart now, you monarchies of the world; perish! Let the heavenly Monarchy remain, which is better than the goodness of all things. In it is the power to fulfill every desire of everyone, and in it we shall enjoy every goodness which we have held until now only in our imagination. May it be well with us in this temporal Monarchy, so that it may be eternally well in the eternal Monarchy. 

The last Monarchy was recently "nailed to the beams" <note>An idiom suggesting the Empire was stabilized or fixed in place</note> with keys forged of the best iron, which also includes the "feet of clay" <note>A reference to the statue in Daniel 2:42, representing a kingdom that is partly strong and partly brittle</note> tinted and tempered by the material. This building was joined together by the peace made in recent times <note>Likely the Peace of Westphalia in 1648</note> from new planks—cedar planks, we hope—which are joined but never to be removed. Furthermore, keys made of Swedish iron, never seen before, have been added. The House of Austria <note>The Habsburg Dynasty</note> still stands, strong and firmly fixed and compact, which has given us Emperors in an unbroken series and succession for 220 years and more. It shall stand further by the grace of God, and we with it, unless the South Wind sends forth turbulent blasts. Whatever happens: the Word of the Lord will remain, and therefore we have less to fear, even if the prisons of hell are opened or the monsters of Hesiod are let loose. I shall speak **profitably** <note>original Greek: "συμφέρουσα"</note> and without offense. The Roman-German Monarchy cannot be torn apart by any force except at the consummation of the world, until that **Stone of Daniel**, pushed by no hand but rolling by its own weight, shall crush the towering Colossus of the Empire. For then the statue will collapse and be reduced to nothing, and what seemed to be gold and silver will be revealed as chaff and ashes. Thus far we have seen in the huge Colossus, and we have also seen in the four savage beasts, the four Kingdoms rising from the earth. The logic of our 

<column-break/>

undertaking requires us to add a Kingdom far different from those four in location, dignity, and durability—a Kingdom rising from heaven from eternity. A Kingdom compared to which no kingdom under heaven is anything. A Kingdom which has no beginning and no end. A Kingdom to which all kingdoms are subject, which all peoples and tribes serve, and in comparison to which all the greatest kingdoms of this world are more nothing than nothing itself, if I may put it that way. 

There were indeed (these are the words of Rupert <note>Rupert of Deutz, a 12th-century theologian</note>) those great beasts among men: the first like a Lioness, another like a Bear, another like a Leopard, and the fourth very terrible. Nevertheless, in consideration of the majesty of that Ancient of Days, they would scarcely deserve to be called mice; they would scarcely be compared to a caterpillar, a locust, a beetle, or rust, because they are of no consequence. In the fourth kingdom, which belonged to the Romans, during the reign of Augustus, the Messiah came—the King of Kings and Lord of Lords. His form of reigning was far different, such as no Nebuchadnezzar, no Cyrus, no Alexander, and no Augustus could either create or establish. 

"In the days of those kings," says Daniel in chapter 2, <insert>In the days of those kings</insert> <note>original Aramaic/Hebrew: "בימיהון די מלכייא אנון"</note>. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> correctly renders this: <insert>in the days of those kingdoms</insert> <note>original Greek: "ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις τῶν βασιλείων ἐκείνων"</note>. The Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note> does not translate it well as: "In the days of those kingdoms." It refers to the Kings of the Roman Empire. 

It is pleasing to bring in the words of Johannes Petrus Postellus <note>Guillaume Postel, a 16th-century French linguist and mystic</note> on this matter from part 1, page 118: "In the Hebrew it is held not 'in the days of the kingdoms,' but 'in the days of those Kings,' which I would more readily approve. For when Christ came, the previous three kingdoms had been completed; the fourth and iron kingdom still stood, which had its own Kings—not indeed by name, but by power." For they were not called Kings, but Caesars, Consuls, and Dictators; nevertheless, they possessed the entirety of royal power. Daniel’s word is to be understood regarding these: "In the days of those Kings," that is, as long as the iron Roman Kings reigned and disturbed the whole world, seeking wars not only against foreign peoples but even against one another. In that time, when no friendship or civil society was respected, but individuals wanted to reign, dominate, and usurp all power according to their own whim, then the eternal kingdom shall begin, and its King shall be born. 

While this Kingdom of the Romans endures, the God of heaven will raise up a kingdom which shall not be destroyed forever, and its kingdom shall not be handed over to another people. It shall break in pieces and consume all those kingdoms, and it itself shall stand forever (verse 45). Just as you saw that a stone was cut out of the mountain without hands, and it broke in pieces the iron, the bronze, the clay, the silver, and the gold. In this place, a very clear and sweet prophecy concerning the eternal kingdom of Christ is set forth, teaching when, how, to whom, and for how long King Christ is to rule. The Prophet sets forth this kingdom accurately and clearly; he mentions not only the time and both of His comings (the gracious and the glorious), but he also elegantly describes the majesty and eternity of that kingdom under the type of the stone cut from the mountain. 

Luke <note>referring to the Gospel of Luke</note> gives us the circumstance of time when he writes that Christ was born in Bethlehem under Augustus, according to the prophecy of Micah. According to the prophecy of Jacob, "Shiloh" <note>A messianic title from Genesis 49:10</note> is said to be coming when the scepter and power had been transferred from the Jews to the Gentiles. That happened under Augustus, with the Romans holding the Monarchy and Judea simultaneously, whose state was then miserable under the tyrant Herod.

*King Nebuchadnezzar made a golden statue, sixty cubits high and six cubits wide; and he set it up in the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon.*

**V**irtue is its own incentive; it is a retribution of glory given to others, which by a wonderful example incites one toward virtue. An excellent kind of reward among the ancients was the erection of columns and statues, with which those were adorned who exposed themselves to death for their fatherland, parents, and children, * or who earned a reputation of immortality for other deeds. For columns and statues were formerly erected for this purpose: not to serve as a support for anything, but to encompass the memory of great deeds through inscribed victories, or at least to testify by their very existence to what had been accomplished. Thus, who does not know of the columns erected at Gades <note>Modern Cádiz, Spain</note> as markers and goals of the labors of Hercules? So also Alexander the Great, after nine infantrymen and 120 cavalrymen fell in that first battle with Darius, the Monarch of the Persians, in the plains of Adrastia where the Granicus river flows—from which this battle is called "the Granicus" by * Strabo—he honored them greatly as an example and consolation for the rest with *equestrian statues*, which, as Arrian relates in book 1, the sculptor Lysippus fashioned, as Justin mentions in book 11, chapter 6. Thus also Augustus offered the honor of memory to **Leaders** second only to the immortal Gods, because they had rendered the Roman Empire the greatest from the smallest beginnings. Therefore, he both restored the works of each with their titles remaining, and dedicated statues of all in triumphal attire in both porticos of his Forum. He declared by edict: *that he devised this so that he himself while he lived, and the Princes of following ages, might be held by the citizens to their example*, as recorded by Suetonius, *in Octavian, ch. 31.* What, says Isidorus <note>Likely Isidore of Pelusium or of Seville</note> to Ausonius (whom the Emperor had honored with a golden statue), *is a more splendid prize for good labors than this?* <note>original Greek: "γδ τύτε λαμπρότερον τδ ἀγαθῶν πόνων ἔπαθλον"</note> because in this way the memory of outstanding men, who had fallen bravely in war or had otherwise deserved well of the Republic, was transmitted to posterity and inscribed in the temple of eternity. A statue, moreover, was a likeness made of stone, bronze, or another metal erected in memory of a certain person or deed; and in this it differed from an *image* <note><term>Imago</term>: often referring to a bust or portrait of only the upper body</note>, which at least represented that part of the human body between the crown of the head and the breasts, and thus showed the shoulders, neck, and head, just as the <term>Plastae</term> <note>Modelers or sculptors working in clay or wax</note> used to shape those members and still do. A statue, however, represented the whole man, set up, as we said, on account of merits toward the Republic—yet not for the sake of adoration. Hence Suetonius says *in Caesar, ch. 76: Caesar [placed] a statue among the Kings, and likenesses among the Gods, to indicate the distinction,*

# Daniel III. verse 1.

<margin>
The erection
of Columns
and
Statues.
</margin>

...the distinction, which once upon a time existed between a "statue" [statua] and an "image" [simulacrum], although it was not perpetual or observed everywhere; as Pliny testifies in Book 36, Chapter 5, sometimes the images of the Gods from the first captured cities were thrust into the class of statues. We read of an abuse of this word, where this distinction was not observed, in Gregory of Tours.

<margin>
1. History
of the Franks.
</margin>

The firstborn son of Ham was Cush. Ham, however, was the source of all magical art—with the Devil as his teacher—and the first discoverer of idolatry; he was the first to establish that a statue should be adored. They ascribe to him the magical arts by which stars and fire seem to fall from heaven, and he is the one who, when he had passed over to the Persians, was called Zoroaster, which they interpret as "living star." In the divine law, it was not the making of images <term>eikonopoieia</term> <note>original Greek: εἰκονοποιΐα, the craft of making likenesses</note> but the worship of images that was forbidden. Indeed, images and statues did not seem to exist in such great numbers among the Jews as they did among the Gentiles, who marveled that the Jews had no statue to worship, nor did they worship God in images. Hence Dio, in Book 37, page 41, writes: "Nor did it [the Temple] have any image among the hieroglyphics." <note>original Greek: Οὐδ' ἄγαλμα οὐδὲν ἐν τοῖς Ἱερογλυφικοῖς ἔχον.</note>

<margin>
History 5. 8.
</margin>

And Cornelius Tacitus writes: *The Jews understand the one Godhead with the mind alone. They consider profane those who fashion images of God from mortal materials into the likeness of men. That supreme Being is eternal, neither changeable nor perishable. Therefore, there are no statues in their cities, let alone in their temples. They do not grant this flattery to Kings, nor this honor to the Caesars.* Among the Latins, the name for a statue comes from "standing" [stando] or "establishing" [statuendo]. Among the Greeks it is <term>andrias</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνδριὰς</note>, that is, a "man-image," as if it were the likeness of a man, to which corresponds another Greek word <term>bretas</term> <note>original Greek: βρέτας, an archaic wooden idol</note>, of which Clement of Alexandria writes in his *Exhortation* in this manner: After statues began to be formed by men, they began to be named <term>bretas</term> from the word <term>brotôn</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῷ βροτῶν</note>, that is, of mortals. By the Hebrews it is called <term>matzevah</term> <note>original Hebrew: מצבת, a pillar or standing monument</note>, regarding which word see the entries for <term>pesili</term> <note>original Hebrew: פסילי, carved images</note> and <term>tselem</term> <note>original Hebrew: צלם, an image or shadow</note> in Genesis 16:26, Daniel 2:31, and Daniel 3:5; the proper meaning of which is "image," as seen in Genesis 1:27, 9:6, Numbers 33:52, and 2 Kings 11:18. From the actions of carving and casting, a statue is also called a "sculpted work" or "cast work" among the Jurists (Code, concerning statues and images). Hence, as Chyträus <note>David Chyträus (1530–1600), a Lutheran reformer and historian</note> well advises, the words <term>pesili and masekah</term> <note>original Hebrew: פסילי ומסכה</note>, "sculpted and cast," are often joined in the Holy Book; for images and statues were first carved from wood or stone, and then were usually covered and clothed with a cast plate of gold or gilded bronze. This comes from <term>pasal</term> <note>original Hebrew: פסל</note>, to hew or carve out, and <term>nasak</term> <note>original Hebrew: נסך</note>, to pour, cover, or overlay. It was also the custom that whatever was erected as a monument to a thing—whether it be a statue, a pyramid, a column, a tomb, an altar, or anything similar intended to last a long time—was erected either with an inscription <term>epigraphē</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπιγραφῇ</note> or without one, to serve to refresh the memory of a benefit, a victory, or some other matter. Hence Dio the Rhodian (column 338) teaches that statues were erected for some who were especially famous, such as Achilles, Sarpedon, Theseus, Memnon, and others, without an inscription; but for others, and more frequently, they were with an inscription. Compare Figrellus in his admirable work *On the Illustrious Statues of the Romans*, chapters 27 and 28, page 228 following. Regarding the Egyptian obelisks "with inscriptions" <term>epige-grammenois</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπιγεγραμμένοις</note>, Kircher reports in his *Hieroglyphic Obelisks*, book 2, chapter 5, page 117: *The Egyptians,* he says, *were accustomed to communicate sacred things among the Priests in certain fictional letters, so that they would be secrets from the common people, thereby remaining objects of wonder for longer and being more attentively grasped; hence those Colossi, statues, altars, and arches publicly inscribed with the sacred letters of the Egyptians stood out to be seen by everyone, but were understood by none except the initiates and*

<column-break/>

*those who had been started in the hieroglyphics.* Truly, the power to erect columns and statues was situated in the sole judgment of the one in whom the supreme authority rested among the Romans. The "Centurion of Shining Things" [Centurio rerum nitentium] was the name given to the official who held the care of images and statues made of bronze and marble in the city, as Valesius teaches in his notes on Marcellinus, book 16, page 107. Afterward, statues were erected and destroyed by the authority of the Emperor alone. For Tiberius, according to Suetonius, prohibited statues and images from being placed unless he gave permission, and he only permitted it under a certain condition.

<margin>
Tiberius 26.
</margin>

Caligula repeated the same edict: that no one should place a statue or image of any living person anywhere without consulting him, as the same Suetonius records in *Caligula*, chapter 34. Although sometimes, out of the indulgence and connivance of the Emperors, this was not so strictly observed. They were usually placed not in just one location, but especially in temples; hence in the Capitol at Rome, seven statues of as many Kings were seen consecrated, as Casaubon teaches regarding Suetonius (*Caesar* 76), citing Pliny book 34, chapter 5. Brutus stood in the middle of the Kings, and the statue of Caesar was placed next to that of Brutus—an act which Cicero counts among excessive honors in his *Speech for Deiotarus*, section 33, and Tacitus in *Annals* 1, 7, 4. They were also placed in the Palace among the Romans, but very rarely: Suetonius mentions in *Otho* 1 that a statue was erected there to the Emperor L. Otho by the authority of the Senate. The Forum was the common and accepted place for statues, as can be seen from Roman history. Rosinus <note>Johannes Rosinus (1551–1626), an antiquarian who wrote on Roman customs</note> recounts the more important forums of Rome, among which the Roman or "Old" Forum stood out, in which were the *Rostra* <note>The speaker's platform</note> and the *Comitium* <note>The assembly space</note>. In the Rostra were the statues of the Ambassadors who were slain at Fidenae, as Livy testifies (4.17). In the Comitium was the statue of Horatius Cocles, regarding whom and his heroic deed the same Livy writes (2.11).

<margin>
9. Roman
Antiquities 7.
</margin>

People would flee to the statues of the Princes as to the safest refuge (according to the single law in the Code concerning those who flee to statues, and the Institutes on those who are under their own or another's power). Not only slaves who were heavily oppressed by their masters fled there, but also those weighed down by debt, so that they might escape the hands of their creditors, as is clear from the law *Fulcinius*. There were many kinds of statues among the ancients, nor were they erected for the same reason; names were fashioned according to the diversity of the deed accomplished. Hence there were statues that were triumphal, pedestrian (on foot), equestrian (on horseback), likewise crowned and laureled, toga-clad, palm-bearing, suspended, armored, and those featuring two-horse chariots, three-horse chariots, or the massive Colossal statues, regarding which see Pliny (book 39, chapters 4, 5, 6) and Lazius (book 9, chapter 19). Tacitus calls statues "the decorations of the ancestors." For whoever the ancients wished to have their name consecrated to immortality, they solemnly decreed statues for them, so that by the sight of them, a perpetual memory of the deed accomplished would remain.

<margin>
History 3. 7. 3.
</margin>

This custom prevailed everywhere among nations; thus in the Pontic region, though it was considered barbarian, we read that statues were in use. There were seen the statue of Pharnaces, the first king in Pontus, and that of Mithridates Eupator, both of which were led in triumph to Rome by Pompey, as Pliny records (34.12). Regarding the statues of other nations, we shall speak later. Among the Romans, all writers of Roman history unanimously confess that statues were included among the insignia of honor which were conferred upon the well-deserving by public decree of the State. Compare...

<meta>This page continues a scholarly discussion of monuments, shifting from the legal right to erect statues to their historical use as marks of both extreme honor and lasting shame across Roman, Greek, Jewish, Egyptian, and Babylonian cultures.</meta>

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The erection of columns and statues.</margin> Cicero, *Philippics 9 §. 3. 15 and 5. §. 41*; Livy 2. 13; Velleius Paterculus 2. 61. 3; Pliny the Younger, *Epistles 2. 7*; Seneca, *Consolation to Marcia 16*; Valerius Maximus 8. 14. 5; Lipsius, *Politics 4. 11. 162. and following.* Yet the same Cicero records *Against Vatinius* that statues were also erected in prisons for those who were condemned, intended for the perpetual ignominy of their family. A contemporary example of this can be seen in Frankfurt am Main: a statue of Vincent Fettmilch <note>original: "Vincentii Fettmilchii"</note>, the leader of the rebellion against the City Council in this century; it stands not in a prison, but on the site of his house, which was razed to the ground. Just as it was honorable to be granted a statue, it was equally shameful to be stripped of one once it was given. Tiberius grew more despised and hated by the day, <margin>On Tiberius, 13.</margin> to the point that the people of Misenum overturned his images and statues, as Suetonius testifies. Similarly, Tacitus relates in *Histories 3. 85. 6* that soldiers forced Vitellius to watch his own statues being pulled down. However, those who violently attacked statues erected by public authority out of a spirit of riot were once severely punished; hence Ambrose, in his *Sermon 10 on Psalm 118, page 669*, says:

> He who crowns the image of the Emperor certainly honors the one whose image he crowned, and he who treats the statue of the Emperor with contempt is seen to have done an injury to the Emperor himself, whose statue he held of no account.

Why then were statues honored, but not the sculptors? Seneca answers this in Fabricius's *Christian Poets, page 52.* Pliny, in *Book 36*, names three distinguished sculptors whose works he praises: Phidias, Myron, and Praxiteles; Lucian also joins these names together in *The Dream*. Regarding Polyclitus, the sculptor from Sicyon, it is noted in the *Aphorisms of Hippocrates, page 643*, that he made a bronze statue so perfect that it was called the <term>kanon</term> <note>Greek: κανὼν; meaning "rule" or "standard"</note> by other artists, who sought the principles of their art from it as if from a certain rule or archetype. Discussing statues consecrated to men in Book 34, Pliny provides nothing certain regarding their origin. In the fourth chapter, he states: *Human likenesses were not usually portrayed except for some illustrious cause deserving of immortality.* And shortly after: *I know not whether the Athenians were the first of all to publicly set up statues to the tyrant-slayers Harmodius and Aristogiton. This was done in the same year that the Kings were expelled from Rome. Thereafter, this practice was adopted by the whole world out of a most civilized ambition. Soon, statues began to be an ornament in the forums of every municipal town, to prolong the memory of men, and to have honors read for ages, inscribed upon bases so they would not be read only on tombs. Soon they were in the forum, in private homes, and in courtyards. The respect of clients established the custom of honoring Patrons in this way.* In ancient times, statues depicted in the toga were common. Nude statues holding a spear also became popular, modeled after the gymnastic figures of youths; these are called <term>Achilleas</term> <note>Achilles-style statues</note>. If we believe Cedrenus, Serug and Terah, who are mentioned in the Holy Scriptures <note>Genesis 11:22, 26</note>, were the first makers of idols; see also Bulenger’s *On Painting, chapter 18, page 51.* It is well known from Holy Scripture <note>Exodus 31:2; 32:4</note> that sculpture, engraving, painting, and modeling, as well as other arts, were in use among the Israelites many years before other nations. To this add Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews, Book 3, chapter 10*, and Bulenger, *ibid., page 70 and following.* Regarding the columns of Seth, see Vossius, *The Art of Grammar, Book 1, pages 40 and 125.* One may also read in the aforementioned Bulenger, *page 54*, about the stones erected by the Patriarch Jacob in perpetual memory of such great favor, which were anointed with oil and called <term>Betuli</term> <note>Baetyls, or sacred stones</note> after Bethel, where Jacob erected the stone; these were famous among the Jews and survived even after the general destruction.

<column-break/>

Regarding Absalom's statue, Celada (page 122) and Nieremberg (page 65) discuss it at greater length; Josephus calls it a <term>stēle lithou marmarinou</term> <note>Greek: στήλην λίθου μαρμαρίνου; a pillar of marble stone</note>. The Septuagint uses the same word, which the Vulgate translates as *Statua*. Vatablus calls it a <term>titulum</term> <note>title or inscription</note> or a *pyramid*, or a triumphal arch; Pagninus calls it a *monument*. In the Hebrew text, the word <term>matzevah</term> <note>מצבה</note> appears, which Mercerus teaches in his *Thesaurus of the Sacred Language* can be understood broadly as anything set up and erected for the sake of memory or to signify something. This word is expressly distinguished from a "heap of stones" in *Genesis 31:51, 54, etc.*, although some conclude from *Genesis 28:11* that it refers to a structure of many stones. From the Israelites we hasten to the Egyptians, of whom Strabo mentions in *Geography, Book 17, page 658* that they had no idols, or at least none in human form, but rather in the form of some brute animal; this coincides with what is read in Tacitus, *Histories 5. 5. 4* <note>OCR error says 5. 8</note>, that the Egyptians worship many animals and composite images. From this one may gather that statues shaped in human form were not as common a custom as among other nations. Regarding the Pyramids of Egypt and obelisks carved with hieroglyphic letters, one may read Kircher (cited above), Ammianus Marcellinus (*Book 17, page 344 and following*), and Valerius's notes on him (*Book 22, page 240*), Pancirollus (*Book 1, section "On Pyramids"*), Salmuth on Pancirollus (*page 81 and following*), Pomponius Mela (*On the Situation of the World, Book 1, chapter 9, page 29*), and Solinus (*chapter 35, page 360, question 2*). Veslingius writes in *Observations on Plants, page 59*, that he saw three pyramids famous for their size near Memphis. Leo Allatius, in his notes on Philo (*pages 37, 38*), mentions pyramids built by Joseph. Others assert these were used as granaries, but it may rightly be said of such people that they have never seen them nor heard them described; Goropius Becanus rejects this opinion with just cause, showing how they are not capable of storing grain, especially in great abundance. One is inclined here to laugh with him at Stephanus, who relates that it is called a <term>Pyramid</term> because the King of Egypt, by amassing all the grain into pyramids, caused a shortage of grain throughout the rest of the region, so that "Pyramid" was called <term>pyron ainon</term> <note>Greek: πυρῶν αἶνον; literally "praise of wheat" or "heap of wheat"</note> as if it were a harvesting sickle taking all the grain—when in fact, there is not enough space found in the Pyramids to suffice for storing a large quantity of wheat; indeed, there are some in which no space is left at all, as they consist of a solid body. As for the Chaldeans, who should perhaps have been placed first, the use of statues among them was not infrequent. This can be gathered both from the idol of Bel, whom they worshipped in the form or statue of a man, and from the statue of Semiramis, who, according to Caelius Rhodiginus, ordered her likeness to be carved into the rock of a mountain in Media named <term>Bagistanus</term> <note>Behistun</note>, seventeen stadia high, which a hundred men honored with gifts. From Holy Scripture, the Statue of Nebuchadnezzar is well known; Josephus also mentions it in *Antiquities of the Jews, Book 10, chapter 12, page 348*, and Philostratus (*page 36*). As the Prophet Daniel suggests, he ordered an image of insane size to be sculpted, such as he imagined in his pride. The height of the statue was sixty cubits—that is, ninety Babylonian feet—and it stood six cubits wide. Oh, in this statue, the nose would be three feet long! Oh, the neck would be four cubits!

<summary>This page explores the dual role of statues in antiquity as symbols of supreme honor or eternal shame, detailing their use in Rome, Greece, and Israel. It also refutes the historical myth that the Egyptian pyramids were built as granaries and discusses the colossal proportions of Nebuchadnezzar's golden statue.</summary>

<meta>This page explores the motivations behind King Nebuchadnezzar's golden statue in Daniel 3, comparing theological, political, and personal explanations, while drawing parallels to other historical figures like Alexander the Great and King Saul.</meta>

### Daniel III. verse 1.

<column-break/>

**Column 1:**

<margin>
The erection of Columns and Statues. 2 Samuel 18:18.
</margin>

According to Herodotus in his first book, *Clio*, Babylonian cubits were three fingers larger than common cubits. I believe it is worth the effort to investigate more diligently and laboriously into the reasons for this statue erected by Nebuchadnezzar. Indeed, three primary opinions are found among commentators: There are those who believe it was erected in honor of God, who had revealed Daniel's hidden dream, and thus it was intended to preserve the memory of that noble and fateful dream discussed in chapter 2, as Blessed Luther notes in his margins. However, the sin in this was that he ordered divine honors to be paid to it without God's command, which is the height of blasphemy. Others oppose this view, saying: If the statue had been erected with this intention, it undoubtedly would have been distinct and variegated according to the pattern of the dream, so that it would correspond to the model in every way—namely, having a head of gold, a chest of silver, a belly of bronze, etc.—and thus it would not have been cast entirely of gold. Furthermore, this statue betrays a certain unusual pride. The dream described in chapter 2, which threatened the destruction and cutting off of the Babylonian empire, should have shaken all that pride out of the King and prevented this golden statue, had he not forgotten it. Finally, if it had been erected in memory of the dream, the King would undoubtedly have obeyed Daniel and other pious men advising against it; since we do not read that this happened, it is much less believable that this statue was erected to honor God and preserve the memory of a divinely inspired dream. A second opinion is that the image was placed there so that the King might unite the countless and diverse nations he had conquered by arms through this common worship, so that being joined in this way, they might obey more willingly and be more easily kept in their duty. There is no bond of society stronger or more powerful than unity and conformity in religion; conversely, nothing is more powerful for scattering and overturning kingdoms than a disparity of religion and a discrepancy in divine worship. This cause seems to have driven the greatest Princes—including the most praised among them—to propagate the true religion most sharply and to expel those of different opinions from their regions. Antiochus Epiphanes also seems to have followed this plan, though he was by no means a good man, when he attempted with such fervor for his own heterodoxy <note>original Greek: *ἑτεροδοξίαν*—literally "different opinion," referring to his imposition of Greek paganism</note> to extinguish and root out the true religion among the Jewish people before the birth of Christ.

<margin>
7. Hieroglyphics pages 98, 99.
</margin>

With these motivations, they finally conclude that this statue was placed by the King in honor of the true God, to be worshiped and adored by all the inhabitants of his kingdom; and for the judgment <note>original Greek: *ἐπίκρισιν*</note> of their opinion, they appeal

<margin>
verses 98, 99, 100.
</margin>

to the King's confession to be read at the end of the chapter:

> *King Nebuchadnezzar, to all peoples, nations, and languages that dwell in all the earth: Peace be multiplied to you. High God has performed signs and wonders toward me. It has therefore pleased me to proclaim His signs, for they are great, and His wonders, for they are mighty; and His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and His power is from generation to generation.*

Those who favor the third opinion claim the Babylonian King, in constructing this statue, looked to the Pyramids and Colossi of the Egyptian Kings, whom he seems to have wanted not only to imitate but to surpass, since he devised colossi not of stone, as

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

they did, but of gold. Just as those kings sought an immortality of name with their most expensive Pyramids and Colossi, so the Babylonian King seems to have wanted to acquire for himself an immortal and never-perishing memory of his own illustrious deeds. And in this, they continue, he seems to have sinned in two ways: *partly* because he ascribed the victories to himself, which he ought to have credited to God alone—which can be illustrated by the example of Saul, the first King of the Israelites,

<margin>
The erection of Columns and Statues.
</margin>

<margin>
1 Samuel 15:12.
</margin>

who made himself unworthy of the kingdom by erecting a triumphal arch or monument for himself after defeating the Amalekites; and *partly* because he wanted divine honors bestowed upon that image. The King was driven to this madness by flatterers and sycophants, though for a very different purpose: *the former*, to win favor with the Prince. We have an example of this in Alexander the Great, the conqueror of the entire Orient, who, ensnared by the arts of flatterers, fell into such madness that he was not ashamed to be worshiped and to openly boast that he was the son of Olympian Jupiter. The courts of Princes are as full of this sort of person as fields are of crows, such that it was most wisely said that it is better to fall "among the crows than among the flatterers" <note>original Greek: *ἐς κόρακας ἢ ἐς κόλακας*</note>, a most elegant wordplay <term>paronomasia: a play on words that sound similar</term> of Greek words, because crows only prey upon dead bodies, but flatterers, not content only with the corruption <note>original Greek: *διαφθοράν*</note> of the body, also corrupt the soul. *The latter* group, however, plotted against the safety of the pious through this plan. While they saw their piety toward God and their due devotion to the King, and fearing they would oppose their own pursuits, they saw no other way to overthrow them through calumny than if they became the authors of such plans to the King. For they were sufficiently persuaded that these pious men, on account of their faith, would in no way obey the King commanding such impious things, and by their constancy would bring certain destruction upon themselves. Therefore, the envy of the courtiers increased the pride of the King in erecting the golden statue, as they resented the power of Daniel and the three

<margin>
Nieremberg, 2. Miscellany, page 57.
</margin>

Jews who were Governors of the Babylonian province. For the virtue of these most upright men overcame all slander, so that the envious despaired of being able to undermine them with their tricks without the aid of their very innocence. Hence the Chaldeans, seized by spite to slander the Jewish governors—since their integrity shone above all slander—made a crime out of virtue. They persuaded the King to propose the royal statue for adoration by all the Satraps and Ranks, testing their constancy in the worship of the one Deity, so that by refusing to adore the idol, they might be proven criminals against the King—men who were most approved and faithful to God and whose virtue was tested by the danger to their lives. Just as the Satraps of Darius,

<margin>
chapter 6:4.
</margin>

driven by envy, were the authors to Darius of a foolish and impious edict, by the violation of which they hoped they would overthrow Daniel, since they could find no other handle for slandering the holy man who was faithful and diligent in his administration. Thus the nobles and high officials of Nebuchadnezzar, driven by depraved desires—namely greed <note>original Greek: *πλεονεξía*</note>, envy, ambition, and rivalry—prepared this trap for pious men, stretching these snares for them so that they might remove them under some honorable pretext, which the Magi had undoubtedly supplied to them. This is made clear by the observation and accusation of the nobles: "At that time," says the text—that is, immediately—"they approached and accused the Jews." Not only did they accuse them, but they also vehemently exaggerated the charge so they could more easily inflame the King's mind against these innocent men. The matter turned out as they wished; and it is a wonder that the King's advisors did not previously suggest that the vessels of the Temple of Jerusalem, which were of great value, should be melted down and spent on this most costly statue. But just as God, by a singular plan and governance, willed those vessels to be reserved until the time of liberation, so too, though these <term>Sycophants</term> <note>In this context, professional accusers or informers.</note> triumphed for a time, God knew how to stand by and assist His faithful even in the very flames, as history testifies, resulting in a manifest end for the most unhappy accusers. Regarding Daniel's enemies, history bears witness that they eventually paid a heavy price for their counsels when they themselves, by the most just judgment of God, were cast headlong into the pit they had dug for the pious Daniel, and were thrown to the lions with their entire families. Thus, there is no doubt and no light conjecture that those sycophants—who performed all their labor in destroying these three men and casting them into the furnace for the King, and who had previously so gravely accused the pious before the King—were finally consumed by the flame erupting from the furnace. Menochius, Junius, Cornelius à Lapide, Pererius, and others incline toward this opinion. We believe, however, that these causes or reasons can be joined together, since one thing may have several ends. The King could have intended one thing, and his courtiers another—whom the shaven cohort of the Magi joined, having noticed that the King was leaning toward the worship of the True God after Daniel’s interpretation. 

A doubt arises concerning Daniel: where was he at that time, since he is not mentioned even once in this whole action? Commentators usually answer in various ways; some think Daniel was in such high authority and favor with the King that those sycophants did not dare to accuse him. Others, again, think he was away on the King’s business, or was ill, or had known the outcome by divine revelation and therefore allowed his companions to be dragged into mortal danger so that the glory of the miraculous divine liberation might be more illustrious. Whatever the case may be (for nothing can be affirmed for certain), it is widely acknowledged that Daniel by no means worshipped the golden statue. 

Finally, crossing from Asia into Europe at the Hellespont, we encounter Greece, where we shall examine the inhabitants’ <term>statues and monuments</term> <note>original Greek: ἱδρύματα (foundations), ϛήγματα (supports), δείκηλα (images), ἀγάλματα (glory-statues), ἀνδριάντας (statues of men), βρέτας ἀπὸ τοῦ βροτοῦ (images from mortals), εἰκόνας (icons), εἴδωλα (idols) & ϛήλας (steles).</note>. Lest we stumble at the beginning, we wish to note from Philander’s annotations on **Vitruvius**, Book 2, **Architecture**, Chapter 8, that statues made for the Gods were called *idols* <note>Greek: εἴδωλα</note>; those for heroes, *wooden images* <note>Greek: ξόανα</note>; those for Kings, *statues of men* <note>Greek: ἀνδριάντας</note>; those for wise men, *likenesses* <note>Greek: εἴκελα</note>; those for well-deserving men, *mortal images* <note>Greek: βρέτα</note>. However, one easily notices by diligent reading of Greek authors that this distinction is not observed everywhere; compare **Caelius Rhodiginus**, **Ancient Readings**, Book 12, Chapter 11. The Athenians rewarded those who served the Republic well with various kinds of honors, whether by granting immunity, erecting a bronze statue, or providing food in the <term>Prytaneion</term> <note>The seat of government in ancient Greek cities where honored citizens were fed at public expense.</note>. **Ulpian, in his commentary on Demosthenes**, expressly mentions this custom: <note>original Greek: "Among the Athenians, the benefactors of the city receive various honors: either a bronze image, or maintenance in the Prytaneion, or immunity, though not from all public services."</note>. ...with inscriptions of their great achievements, they would publicly decree these honors so that a spur might be applied to others to perform similar deeds, and that the glory of those men might be perpetuated. Dionysius of Halicarnassus mentions the statue of Romulus, the Founder of the City (page 116), and Martianus mentions the statue of Faustulus the Shepherd, who raised Romulus (Book 3, chapter 17 of his *Topography*). Because of rare examples of Roman bravery, <term>they erected a bronze image in the temple of Hephaestus</term> <note>original Greek: εἰκόνα χαλκῆν ἔστησαν ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ τοῦ Ἡφαίστου</note>, as Plutarch testifies in his *Life of Poplicola* (page 106). Likewise, statues were placed for Mucius Scaevola and the virgin Cloelia, as Victor relates in *On Illustrious Men* (chapter 11, page 121; chapter 12, page 127; chapter 13, page 133). Thus, among the statues of the seven Kings, a statue was also erected to Julius Caesar, as noted by Dio (Book 43, page 267), who also restored the statues of Sulla and Pompey that had been cast down by the common people, as Suetonius records in his *Life of Julius* (chapter 75). Velleius (page 581) says Augustus was honored with a statue, and Barthius mentions Domitian (notes on Statius, pages 9, 12). A Colossus was erected in honor of Vespasian, reaching a height of 107 feet, according to Cassiodorus in his *Life of Vespasian* (page 690). Thus Titus, once he had become Emperor, placed a golden statue for Britannicus, and dedicated another equestrian statue made of ivory, which was carried at the head of the Circensian procession, being mindful of their <term>sharing of meals</term> <note>original Greek: συνοσιτίας</note> and <term>mutual fellowship</term> <note>original Greek: συμπαθείας</note>; for they had been <term>schoolfellows</term> <note>original Greek: συμφοιτηταὶ</note> and <term>educated together</term> <note>original Greek: συμπαιδευθέντες</note>, trained in the same disciplines and under the same masters, as we are taught by Suetonius in his *Life of Titus* (chapter 2). Alexander Severus followed the diligence of the ancients in setting up statues; he placed statues and colossi of the greatest men in many parts of the city, having searched out craftsmen from everywhere, according to Lampridius (chapter 25, page 348). In this, he showed greater honor to the monuments of his ancestors than Gaius Caligula, who ordered all such statues to be thrown down, as Suetonius notes in his *Life of Caligula* (page 251); compare also Bulenger, *On the Emperor* (chapter 13, page 125). Rome abounded not only in statues of Emperors and Consuls, but also of others. A young man is praised because, in a futile attempt to stop the concord of Lepidus with Antony and preserve it through his counsel, as Velleius says, he pierced himself with a sword. Because of this, the Senate decreed a eulogy, a statue, and a public funeral for him, according to Cicero’s letter to Plancus and Dio (Book 46, page 369). However, they removed the statue of Lepidus, judging him an enemy. Xiphilinus (pages 344, 345) lists statues placed by Trajan for Sosius, Celsus, and others. Cicero discusses a statue placed for himself <margin>In *Against Piso*, column 747.</margin>: "They presented me with a gilded statue; they adopted me as their sole Patron." Likewise, Vopiscus records in his *Life of Numerianus* that a statue was placed for Numerianus in praise of his eloquence, with these words: "His speech sent to the Senate is said to have possessed such eloquence that a statue was decreed for him in the Ulpian Library, not as a Caesar, but as a Rhetorician, inscribed as follows:"

->TO NUMERIANUS CAESAR<-
->THE ORATOR<-
->THE MOST POWERFUL OF HIS TIMES.<-

Plutarch, in his *Life of Cato the Younger* (page 794), mentions statues placed for Cato of Utica holding a sword; and Novarinus (Volume of *Inscriptions*, page 428) mentions Cornelius Tacitus. Thus the Romans consecrated a bronze statue to Proaeresius, whom Constantius had sent there, with this inscription:

->ROME, THE QUEEN OF THINGS<-
->TO THE KING OF ELOQUENCE.<-

Or as Eunapius records it in Greek, <term>Queen Rome to the reigning word</term> <note>original Greek: ἡ βασιλεύσα Ῥώμη τὸν βασιλεύοντα λόγον</note>. Among the statues erected in Rome, we shall finally place the marble statue of Claudian of Alexandria, a poet most practiced in both languages, erected and placed in the Forum of Trajan by the Emperors Arcadius and Honorius. While he was alive, they also honored him with the most ample gifts. Concerning the idols of the ancient Germans, consult Tacitus, *Germania* (9.1 and following). Hermion, King of the Germans, famous for his fourth-rank bravery and success in conducting wars, even had a name matching the reality: for <term>Heer</term> means <term>army</term>. His image was honored and placed everywhere in temples; it was a statue in the likeness of a man in armor, holding a spear in his right hand and a scale in his left, bearing a lion on his shield. From him, the idol called the <term>Irmen Seul</term> <note>The Irminsul, a sacred pillar-like object of the Saxons.</note> took its name; it stood at Merseburg and elsewhere, according to Munster (Cosmography 5, chapter 393) and Hoeping (On the Law of Insignia, section 6). After death, a place was given to him among the stars; and for the Germans, that faithful constellation, which is perpetually observed by us in the sky under the name of the <term>Great Bear</term>, was called the <term>Heerwagen</term> <note>The "Army Wagon" or "Charles's Wain".</note>, as if it were <term>Herrman’s Wagon</term>, as Henning testifies in his *Genealogy of the German Kings*. Likewise, Suetonius writes in his *Life of Titus* (chapter 4) that Titus was honored throughout Germany and Britain with a multitude of statues, images, and titles while he served as a military tribune in both provinces. Among the statues of ancient Germany, the <term>Statue of Roland</term> is deservedly counted; it is seen in many cities of Saxony—at Magdeburg, Zerbst, and elsewhere—as well as in Hamburg, where it is included on the bridge they call the <term>Rutland Bridge</term> from it. Thus, for the sake of honor, as Crusius records, a stone equestrian statue was placed for the Emperor Rudolf of Habsburg at Strasbourg <margin>Annales Suevici, Book 3, ch. 10, p. 169.</margin> above the last entrance of the great cathedral, with <term>an inscription</term>: *Rudolf, Count of Habsburg, King of the Romans*. Among more recent statues in Europe, one must include the bronze pedestrian statue at Neuss in Germany, consecrated in the forum to Emperor Frederick III, the liberator of the city from the siege of Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy. In France, they boast in Paris of the bronze equestrian statue of Henry IV on the New Bridge, and that of his son Louis XIII at the Place Royale; see *The Voyage of France* under the entry "Paris," pages 179 and following. In Antwerp in the last century, a proud statue of the Duke of Alba was seen, about which Ludovico Guicciardini writes in his *Additions*: In this courtyard, Alba placed a statue <margin>Part 1, *History of the Low Countries*, page 138.</margin> of his own form and stature—indeed, a monument of his glory to posterity—made from cannons captured long ago at Jemmingen, by the hand of Jacob Jungeling. It depicted him with a bare head and an unarmed right arm, while the rest of his body was clad in armor. Under his feet, a man was being trampled who had two heads and four hands; in the first hand was a lighted torch, in the second a broken mallet, in the third a knotty club, and in the fourth an axe. Regarding Andrea Doria, Carlo Sigonio records that, due to his merits toward the Republic of Genoa, he was not only proclaimed <term>Father of the Fatherland</term> and <term>Liberator</term> by decree of the Senate, but a bronze statue was also erected to him in the great hall of the Palace. ### Daniel IX. v. 24.

Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city. <note>original Hebrew: שבעים שבעים נחתך על-עמך ועל-עיר קדשך</note>

Seventy weeks have been cut short for your people and for the holy city. <note>original Greek: Ἑβδομήκοντα ἑβδομάδες συνετμήθησαν ἐπὶ τὸν λαόν σου καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν πόλιν τὴν ἁγίαν.</note>

->**THE SEVENTY WEEKS**<-
->*have been shortened (decreed) over your people, and over your holy city.*<-

In sacred History, not only are many decrees established regarding the future sequence of events—whether political or ecclesiastical—but also certain, clear, and definite oracles are sometimes issued. These warn openly and, as if pointing with a finger, demonstrate future events; sometimes they even indicate the very moment and turning point of time, with the years having been counted beforehand. We rightly marvel at God's Providence from the foundation of the world toward the Human Race, especially in shaping those things necessary for the state of the Church. To this end, He proposed not only *Miracles* as the works of an all-knowing Nature, but also *Prophecies* as <term>signs</term> <note>original Greek: σημει̃α (semeia)</note> of an almighty Nature regarding future things, such as the birth of the *Messiah* from a Virgin, the changes of Monarchs and Empires, and similar matters. He proposed everything so accurately and certainly that He even expressed the circumstances of time and persons. Most accurately, through the Prophecy of Daniel, He expresses the time of the Messiah's coming in a span of seventy weeks; through Isaiah, He teaches and expresses the person from whom the Messiah is to be born; through Jeremiah, He not only predicts the Babylonian Exile but also defined its limit and the time of liberation. The Prophecy of Daniel provides a most abundant collection of both prophecies and miracles. To Daniel, a very lovely name is added by the Angel, calling him a <term>man of desires</term> <note>original Hebrew: איש חמודות (Ish Chamudot), meaning "greatly beloved."</note>—one whom God clearly embraced with the highest love and fatherly benevolence, guarding him like a precious thing or a signet ring, as the Lord speaks of Zerubbabel in Haggai chapter 2:23. The Prophecy of Daniel, I say, provides us with excellent examples of divine Providence in preserving and protecting the Church, as appears from that wonderful story of the three Men...

Conversely, He is seen in the punishment of tyrants, as shown by the stupendous <term>transformation</term> <note>original Greek: μεταμόρφωσις (metamorphosis)</note> of Nebuchadnezzar, and the horrific omen of the hand appearing from the wall, followed immediately by the slaughter of King Belshazzar. Furthermore, He presents to us a brief body of all Chronology and History, as it were, in the conversation of Nebuchadnezzar and in the Four Beasts signifying the four greatest Empires of the world. These things are expressed <note>original Hebrew: בקצר ובחרות (bekatzer uvecharut)</note> "briefly and concisely," or as if wrapped in riddles, as Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a prominent medieval Jewish scholar</note> says.
