Among other prophecies of this Prophet, that of the 70 Weeks regarding the Restoration of Grace and Evangelical Justice stands out as truly golden; one might truly call it a compendium of all the graces to be sought in the Messiah, and a truly historical mirror of all things which Divine Wisdom directed toward the times of the Messiah. For the Prophet Daniel pours out a golden river of speech in his prophecies through all times, whether they be of *grace* or of *judgment*. He wisely explains God’s counsel to us, carefully divides the ages, and accurately defines the moments and turning points of time in a manner of predicting that is unique to him and not found in the rest of the choir of Prophets. In the ninth chapter, he presents us with a wonderful example of divine grace and judgment, in which he deals with the true and only Messiah, the Son of David. This is shown by the emphatic title "Messiah the Prince" in *verse 24*. This is a record of an anointing marked for a specific time. 3. The works to be performed by this Messiah: by consuming sin, bringing in eternal righteousness, and putting an end to vision and prophecy. For the sake of greater evidence and certainty, he prefixes a specific time-marker of 70 Weeks, corresponding to the 70 years of the Captivity. For when Daniel was held captive in the Babylonian exile along with the rest of the Jewish people, and reflected in his <margin>Jeremiah 29:10.</margin> mind on what the Prophet had said—that the captivity would not last beyond 70 years—and recognized that this number of years had now passed, he began to pray with a greater Spirit, crying out to God and imploring Him to be mindful of His promise and willing to liberate them from exile. *While he was still speaking in prayer, behold the man Gabriel, flying swiftly, touched him about the time of the evening sacrifice, and said:*
> Seventy weeks are decreed for your people and for your holy city. Then transgression shall be finished, sin shall be covered, guilt shall be expiated, eternal justice shall be brought forth, vision and prophecy shall be sealed, and the Holy of Holies shall be anointed.
Daniel turns the sacred books over and over; he reads and re-reads Jeremiah; he prays, mingles his prayers with groans, and inquires into the divine promises. While he is occupied in these meditations, and while he prays that, the 70 years predicted by the Prophet having elapsed, the restoration of the holy city and the merciful return of the people might occur, God—looking further ahead than Daniel—reveals a new matter of greater importance: namely, another 70 "weeks" established in divine judgment, which it is of the greatest interest for the Church of God to know. The Messiah was to be revealed after the aforementioned 70 weeks, and he adds at the same time a closing clause: that in the last of the 70 weeks, 

<column-break/>

the city and the sanctuary would be cut off. It can be seen throughout the works of authors of respected <margin>The 70 Weeks. In Ezekiel ch. 39 & Matthew 6:15.</margin> credit that the number seven, because of its unique excellence and the operations it seems to perform, has been allotted many honorable names. To St. Jerome, it is called *sacred and full of mysteries and sacraments* because it is a most holy <term>treasured possession</term> <note>original Greek: κειμήλιον (keimēlion)</note> of both physical and spiritual things. Philo <margin>In the book "On the Creation of the World."</margin> seeks mysteries in numbers above all else; he admires the number seven so much that he does not know if it can be praised enough, for he thinks it more excellent than can be expressed by any eloquence. He thinks the "name-givers" <note>the ancient creators of language</note> attributed veneration to it, calling <term>seven</term> <note>original Greek: ἑπτὰ (hepta)</note> the <term>venerable thing</term> <note>original Greek: τὰ σέβασμα (ta sebasma)</note>, so that "heptas" (seven) is almost "septas" (venerable). Nature also, as Plato testifies, directs almost all her works toward the number seven as if toward a <term>Helice</term> <note>The Great Bear or Ursa Major, used by sailors for navigation; a guiding principle.</note> or some guiding star. Hippocrates teaches that there is great power in the *septenary* (number seven) in the fetus, both from its formation within the womb—whether it be the rough form which occurs on the seventh day, or the exact form which is completed either in four sevens of days or six sevens—and from the perfection and maturity of the fetus, which it attains in the womb in the seventh month. On this subject, one may read Hippocrates' booklet <term>On Sevens</term> <note>original Greek: περὶ ἑβδομ (peri hebdomon)</note>, at the end of which he promised he would write a special commentary on the powers and efficacy of numbers. And to digress from the book of Nature to the observation of history, political thinkers have observed "fatal" periods, established by certain numbers, for Empires and Republics throughout the history of all times. These periods, as has been noticed through much experience, mostly lead to 70 weeks, which is 490 years. Thus, a common period of great changes, whether in the Church or in the State, usually happens around five hundred years, after which a change, a transfer, or a destruction usually occurs. The five-hundredth year mostly either converts or subverts. This limit is not perfectly exact, but is either exceeding or preceding it. As far as we can cast our eyes from earliest antiquity to these times, we find that the more powerful kingdoms and Republics have generally flourished for 500 years; many did not reach this limit, and none or very few exceeded it. Richter declares this with the words of Melanchthon, Strigelius, Peucer, and Bodin, as well as with outstanding examples in his *Political Axioms, book 1, page 1 and following*. If we took the 70 weeks as "weeks of days," they would make up only one year, four months, and fourteen days when collected. It is certain that in such a small time neither was the people returned nor the building of the city completed. Therefore, "weeks" here does not mean weeks of seven days, but weeks of seven years, which <term>well-named</term> <note>original Greek: εὐώνυμοι (euōnymoi); here meaning auspicious or specifically designated</note> weeks, collected together, make 490 years. He indicates that when these years have unfolded, the Messiah will surely be present and the true Jubilee will be instituted. Consequently, just as these are not weeks of days, so they are not weeks of Jubilees <note>periods of 50 years</note>, nor of Centuries, as Pererius teaches against the opinion of the Jews and Origen. Likewise, they are not decades or centuries because of their excessive length, and much less days, because during the 70 weeks of days [these things] did not happen...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES #

<margin>The 70 Weeks</margin> ...they have noted the things which Daniel predicts will come to pass. Therefore, it is necessary that there be 70 weeks of years, making together a time of four hundred and ninety years. If these years are understood to be solar, they consist of three hundred sixty-five days and nearly six hours; many understand them this way, such as Chrysostom in his *Second Oration against the Jews*, Jerome *on the ninth chapter of Daniel*, Driedo in *Book 3 on Dogmas, chapter 5*, Johannes Lucidus *on the Correction of Times*, and Galatinus in *Book 4, chapter 14*. This opinion is more likely, first, because Scripture ordinarily uses solar years in the commemoration of human age; and second, because those years were in use among the Romans, Greeks, and Egyptians, as Strabo teaches in *Book 17 of his Geography*. Furthermore, the Egyptians were taught the duration of years and astronomical observations by the Hebrews, according to the testimony of Josephus <margin>Antiquities 10.16</margin>; and the most ancient of the Hebrews divided the year into 365 days and nearly six hours, as Mirandula teaches in *Book 11, chapter 9 of Astrology*. However, if they are understood to be lunar years, consisting of only 354 days, they make up only 475 solar years; this is how Julius Africanus, Rupertus, and Bede understand them. They argue that the seventy weeks are called "abbreviated" <note>original Latin: *abbreviatas*</note> by Daniel because they are understood as lunar years, which are 11 days shorter than solar years. But a more likely explanation is that they are called "abbreviated" because they contain a short time if compared to the long past since the Messiah was first promised. Yet, from where that calculation of the weeks should begin, there are as many opinions as there are calculators.

"Different men take pleasure in different pursuits" <note>original Greek: Ἄλλως δ’ ἄλλοισιν ἀνὴρ ἐπίτερπεται δεσμοῖς</note>. The most learned Jerome <note>Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> in columns 1147 and following, remains undecided <note>original Greek: ἐπέχει (epechei)</note> here, content to have reviewed the words of Africanus, Eusebius, Hippolytus, Apollinaris, Clement of Alexandria, and Tertullian without any judgment <note>original Greek: ἐπικρίσει (epikrisei)</note>, leaving it to the reader’s choice as to whose exposition they wish to follow. Among the more recent writers, Conrad Pellican <note>a Protestant reformer and Hebrew scholar</note> writes: *Not without fear and hesitation do I approach the explanation of these four following verses, which many most learned and pious men have dreaded to handle according to their worth—indeed, some have despaired of it.* Oecolampadius also falls almost into that same opinion, writing:

<margin>Commentary on Daniel, folio 109. b.</margin>
> This is hardly one of the most difficult places in Scripture, which so fights against the Jews that they can by no means escape; yet it is handled by few according to its worth, and I know not if the Doctors vary so much in any other place, for there are almost as many meanings as there are heads. The chief dispute is about the calculation, for here a most certain reckoning of times is absolutely necessary, without which nothing certain can be affirmed, and by which those who do not hit the mark can easily be refuted. Oecolampadius himself presupposes this in this controversy, and says that *he has not yet been satisfied in all things by anyone.* He then places his own judgment on the calculation and which authors should be used for it. We shall review the principal opinions of the authors and then state our own. The Angel wished, by careful effort, to remove every doubt and stumbling block while so clearly placing the beginning at the "going out of the word" concerning the restoration of Jerusalem. But because this cannot be understood as only one "going out" of a word, the calculators "have a heart divided in two" <note>original Greek: διάνδιχα θυμὸν ἔχουσι (diandicha thymon echousi)</note> on the matter. Galatinus, along with Lyra and Vatablus, take the beginning quite early, from the fourth year of

<column-break/>

Zedekiah, when the word went out from the mouth of Jeremiah <note>Jeremiah 28:1 and 51:59</note>, specifically concerning the restoration of Jerusalem <note>Jeremiah 29:10 and 30:18</note>. However, even if we remain silent about Galatinus favoring this opinion based on a Jewish hypothesis, it enjoys no probability—not to say truth—since more than 650 years would have passed from then until the death of Christ. The Jews, whom we place in the second rank, relying on their false principle regarding the duration of the Second Temple, begin the weeks from the destruction of Jerusalem under Zedekiah and end them at the final destruction under Vespasian; they count 70 years of desolation and add to them the 420 years during which they say the rebuilt temple stood. Oecolampadius seems to have leaned toward this Jewish opinion in his commentary on this passage. But this opinion of the Jews regarding the beginning of the 70 weeks is rejected by Rabbi Abraham himself, who writes: *I marvel at the words of the [Jewish] expositors, how the desolation and the perfection of the Temple can be in one number.* This interpretation has neither taste nor smell. Thus speaks "their own prophet" <note>original Greek: ὁ ἴδιος περὶ προφήτης (ho idios peri prophetis)</note>! There are others who take the beginning of the weeks from the first year of either Darius the Mede or Cyrus. Jerome once favored the former; Clement of Alexandria, and after him Beroaldus, Broughton, and Wichmann, favored the latter. Both chronology and the fact that Cyrus's edict was hindered by his successor because of his expedition against the Scythians cry out against them. Others, among whom are Petavius, Langius, Vossius, and others, begin the weeks from the 20th year of Artaxerxes <note>Nehemiah 2:1</note>, since at that time the building of the city was brought to an end under Nehemiah the Governor. However, this opinion does not equal the full number of 70 weeks but is smaller than it should be. Funccius, however, leads the beginning of the 70 weeks from the 7th year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, whose opinion suffers from this difficulty: that the Artaxerxes who followed Ahasuerus and preceded Darius Longimanus persecuted the Jews and hindered the structure of the temple, as witnessed in Ezra <term>chapter 4</term>. Finally, those deserve a fifth place who refer the edict of restoring the city to Darius; they fix the seat of their arguments both in the words of Haggai <note>1:1</note>, Zechariah <note>1:1</note>, and Ezra <note>5:1</note>, and in the words of the King in Ezra <note>6:12</note>, whereby the outcome followed effectively—which was not done at the prior edicts <note>compare Ezra 4:last verse</note>. But they agree neither on which Darius nor on which year. Luther, Melanchthon, and Cunmann favor *Longimanus*; Cyril and Eusebius favor *Darius Hystaspes*; Scaliger, Calvisius, and those who follow them in great number favor *Darius Nothus*. We do not so much disapprove of the opinion of those who establish the beginning of the 70 weeks in the second year of Darius Longimanus, from which time power was given to the people by edict to restore Jerusalem. The same power had indeed been granted by Cyrus, but with him being removed in the Scythian expedition, his son Cambyses again prohibited the building. Thus, the father Cyrus was a friend to the exiled Jews, but the son was an enemy and foe; the father was a most gentle Prince, but the son Cambyses was most fierce. *It is a shame,* says Strigelius, *what sort of changes occur in courts. That which the Father builds, the Son destroys. What the Father planted, the son had uprooted.* Cyrus was the gentlest of all Kings, but he had a degenerate son.

# Daniel IX. v. 24. #

<margin>The 70 Weeks.</margin>
...the younger Cambyses <note>Cambyses II, son of Cyrus the Great, reigned 530–522 BCE.</note>, who surpassed almost all tyrants, except for Nero, in his cruelty and savagery; and as much as his father was a friend to the Church, he was an enemy and a hater. Basil, the Bishop of Seleucia, mentions this prohibition in his *38th Oration, page 330*: <note>original Greek: Βασιλεύοντος δὲ Καμβύσου κεκώλυται τὰ τῆς οἰκοδομῆς ἐξ ἀναφορᾶς τῶν ἐγχωρίων ἀρχόντων ἔτη ς.</note> "While Cambyses held the kingdom, the construction was interrupted for six years due to the delays caused by the local governors." Those who were "in the regions" included Rhathynus, Belthemus, Semelius, and others, who could not bear to see the structure of the City rising from the ashes. This calculation from the time of Darius Artaxerxes, who received the nickname "Long-hand" <note>Artaxerxes I Longimanus</note>, <margin>Preface to Daniel.</margin> was favored by Luther, who writes: <note>original German: "Unsere Meinung ist / daß man soll anfahen mit diesen 70. Wochen am andern Jahr des Königs Darii, der Langhand hies..."</note> "Our opinion is that one should begin these 70 weeks in the second year of King Darius, who was called Long-hand; for in that same year the Word of God came through the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, and told Zerubbabel to build the Temple, as one finds in the first chapter of both prophets. That same Darius also gave a command, and his decree went out; for from the first year of Cyrus, who set the captive Jews free, until the second year of Darius, there are 46 years, in which they could not and dared not build because of the prohibition of Cambyses, the son of Cyrus, so that they even despaired and said: 'The time has not yet come to build the Lord's house.'" The Angel divides these seventy weeks into three parts, saying: *“Know and observe: from the time the decree is issued to restore Jerusalem until Christ the Leader, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks; then the streets and walls shall be restored, though in a narrow time. After sixty-two weeks, however, Christ shall be slain and shall have nothing.”* Seven weeks make forty-nine years, which is the time attributed to the repair of the city and temple; it is called a <term>narrow time<gloss>original: tempus angustum; often translated as "troublous times"</gloss></term> because of the difficulty of building while being repeatedly hindered, so much so that they found it necessary to gird themselves with swords against the attacks they feared at every moment from the hand of the enemy. Regarding this time, Johannes <margin>page 35. b.</margin> Draconites writes: "I call 'narrow time' the difficulty of building and all the persecutions they endured from the Samaritans, the Persian governors, Ochus, the Assyrians and Egyptians, and others who wished Judea extinct." There are indeed others who interpret "narrowness of time" as a short duration, since according to Nehemiah chapter 6, the wall was completed by Nehemiah within 52 days. But in truth, the word <term>צוק<gloss>tsuq</gloss></term> does not signify a short span of time, but rather calamity, pressure, and affliction, a meaning which the state of the Jews <margin>Book 2 of Chronicles, p. 67.</margin> described in Nehemiah chapter 4 more than sufficiently indicates. Therefore, at the beginning of the weeks divided into three parts, the Angel assigns *seven weeks*, that is, 49 years, in which the Temple and City were to be repaired. To the middle period he gives 62 weeks; add the 7, and you have 69 weeks, which is 483 years. After so many years—namely 69 weeks—Christ was to be cut off and crucified, specifically in the fourth year after the 69 weeks, when Christ

<column-break/>

<margin>The 70 Weeks.</margin>
had already preached the Gospel of the grace of God to all Israel for three and a half years. Just as these things were predicted, so they were fulfilled while the Romans were already holding the monarchy of the world, and the scepter had been transferred from Judah to Herod the Idumean, a foreigner. From this, the Jewish Synagogue correctly conjectured that the time spoken of by the Prophets regarding the coming of the Messiah was now fulfilled; suspecting he was present in the world, they deliberated on seeking him. And when they saw the distinguished and wonderful holiness in John the Baptist, and observed his unprecedented way of life, they doubted whether he himself might be the Messiah. For although he had withdrawn into the desert and walked about dressed in humble clothing, they nevertheless sent messengers to him and asked: *“Who are you?”* John’s reputation among all people was extraordinary: <note>original Greek: προσδοκῶντος τοῦ λαοῦ, καὶ διαλογιζομένων πάντων ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις αὐτῶν περὶ τοῦ Ἰωάννου, μήποτε αὐτὸς εἴη ὁ ΧΡΙΣΤΟΣ.</note> "The people were in expectation, and everyone was reasoning in their hearts concerning John, whether he might be the Christ" (Luke 3:15). In Jerusalem, how many leaders were there, how many Pharisees, Scribes, and Priests! Yet no such honor was deferred to any of them, only to John, even though he was austere and kept away from human company. Nor was it given to Christ himself, even if John pointed him out with his finger, saying: <note>original Greek: Αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ ὁπίσω μου ἐρχόμενος, ὃς ἔμπροσθέν μου γέγονεν.</note> "This is he who comes after me, who has been before me." But there was a perpetual conflict with the Jews, who dreamed that the Messiah would have a *worldly kingdom*, and would be such a Governor who, more majestic than Augustus Caesar of the Romans, would deliver them from Roman servitude through great and mighty battles. They were in this majestic hope especially during those very times in which Christ was born and lived among them—he whom the people at one time demanded as their King. Hence that speech of the travelers going toward Emmaus: *“We were hoping he would deliver Israel.”* How lowly and complainingly did their "WE WERE HOPING" sound! This blind hope and opinion about a worldly kingdom of the Messiah had also settled so tightly within the rest of the disciples that, as Christ was just about to ascend into heaven, they questioned him, saying: <note>original Greek: Κύριε εἰ ἐν τῷ χρόνῳ τούτῳ ἀποκαθιστάνεις τὴν βασιλείαν τῷ Ἰσραήλ;</note> "Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" It is also well known what Suetonius records <margin>chapter 4.</margin> regarding Vespasian: *“An ancient and constant opinion had spread through the whole Orient that it was in the fates that at that time, those coming from Judea would become masters of affairs.”* It is altogether noteworthy <note>original Latin: ἀξιομνημόνευτον</note> that the rumor had spread through the whole Orient that at that time, those who would be Monarchs would come out of Judea. B. Frantzius cleverly relates <margin>Oration 12.</margin> in his *Treatise on the Interpretation of Holy Scripture, p. 210*, that the Jews held this from the calculation of Daniel's weeks and, joyful with hope, spread it abroad: "According to the calculation of Daniel's weeks, the end of those weeks was already approaching at that same time, and it was proclaimed in the whole Orient that the promised Monarch would now be present; this the Jews well knew, but in the time of Christ they interpreted it poorly, having grown weary of the humble appearance of the Messiah." Others, therefore, dragged this toward the then-growing Roman Republic, and many flatterers adapted it to Vespasian himself, although Cicero, speaking of the same business in the *second book of Divinations*, says: "Henceforth neither Gods nor men in Rome want there to be a King." Thus the world has always allowed itself to be led away by external things from the seeking and acquisition of heavenly goods. Nor is it a wonder that that rumor [spread] through the whole Orient...

<meta>This page continues the technical and theological analysis of the "Seventy Weeks" prophecy from Daniel 9:24. Having established the chronological starting point on the previous page, the author now addresses historical misinterpretations by Roman historians and Jewish scholars, before concluding with a Christological interpretation and moving to a new section on the Prophet Hosea.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES #

<margin>The 70 Weeks.</margin>
Indeed, the rumor was spread even in the West—where Suetonius <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, a Roman historian</note> heard the same report—because the Jews, who were prolific beyond all belief in every age, lived in all provinces under the whole sun. As for his claim that flatterers applied this prophecy to Vespasian <note>Roman Emperor, reigned 69–79 AD</note>, understand it thus from Tacitus: <margin>Tacitus, *Histories*, Book 5.</margin> *Many were persuaded that it was contained in the ancient writings that the East would grow strong, and those proceeding from Judea would gain mastery over affairs; these things had predicted Vespasian and Titus.* From this, Valerius Flaccus also <note>Roman poet, *Argonautica* 1.5</note> vows and promises that the future reign of Vespasian and Domitian would be favorable. Being aware that these things also existed in the Sibylline oracles, he makes himself privy to them and says he will sing of Vespasian’s deeds from the books of the Prophets: namely, that Vespasian is that prince who was predicted so long ago, while he himself is the one who can interpret those songs of the Sibyls. It is no wonder that the Pagans fell into this false opinion, as they neither possessed the Holy Scripture nor believed in it. But it is truly a wonder that the Jews themselves, the librarians of the Holy Scripture and guardians of the Sacred Codex, have erred so enormously—and still err—concerning the person of the <term>Messiah</term> <note>original Hebrew: משיח (Mashiach)</note>. For by the <term>Messiah</term>, certain shrewd men <note>original: "Verpulorum," perhaps a derogatory term for those twisting the text</note> wish to understand Cyrus, the first monarch of the Persians, and they call upon the passage in *Isaiah 45:1* to support their cause, where Cyrus is called the *anointed of the Lord*. Yet it is known to everyone that in the Sacred Scriptures, this name is common to kings and priests, who are called "Messiahs" or "anointed ones," meaning those divinely raised up; hence it is said in *Psalm 104:15* concerning all the faithful: *Touch not <term>my anointed ones</term>* <note>original Hebrew: משיחי (Meschichi)</note>. Furthermore, if they are men of reason, let them show the works performed by Cyrus that are commemorated here regarding the benefits of this Messiah—to say nothing of the fact that Cyrus lived long before the beginning of Daniel’s 70 weeks. Others distort the prophecy to refer either to Zerubbabel the leader, Joshua the High Priest, or Nehemiah the Governor. But to none of these can it be rightfully attributed; for if all lived at the beginning of the "Weeks," and none of them reached the end, much less can the benefits of the <term>expiation of iniquity</term> <note>original Hebrew: כפר עון (Kapper Avon)</note>, the abolition of sin, and the restoration of eternal righteousness be said of any of them. The assertion of Eusebius is also foul and should not be passed over here, <margin>Eusebius, *Proof of the Gospel*, Book 8.</margin> where he did not blush to explain this prophecy as referring to Hyrcanus, the last High Priest of the Jews from the Hasmonean family; yet chronology itself refutes this, not to mention more solid arguments. Therefore, since this does not fit any of those men—as the Angel Gabriel speaks here of the Messiah—and since the Evangelists testify that each and every thing was performed by Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Mary, we rightly acknowledge Him as the true Messiah promised in Paradise. For the "good" of the Messiah is the restoration of righteousness and grace, and the bringing back of the righteousness lost through our unrighteousness via His expiatory, sacrificial death, which is applicable to others. To the formal reasoning belongs: 1. The consideration of lost righteousness and the resulting unrighteousness. Our Prophet coordinates these so as to say <term>to restrain the transgression</term> <note>original Hebrew: לכלא הפשע (Lekalle ha-pesha)</note>; for the word <term>to restrain</term> <note>original Hebrew: כלא (Kala)</note> properly denotes that which was first of all done in the Adamic sin, to which the Prophet leads us back, saying it is to be consumed and ended. He then considers those sins by reason of the guilt accusing us, and asserts that it is "sealed up," which we take as the imputation of sins made to Christ, so firmly established in the

<column-break/>

judgment of God as if it had been corroborated with a seal. Finally, the penalty of the guilt is added, namely the expiatory removal of iniquity; in this way, since righteousness is said to be lost through apostasy, the loss and the following guilt and penalty were joined together in God's judgment. By this reasoning, no further righteousness can have a place in the whole human race. 2. There is required the intervening expiation of the Mediator through a sacrificial death; an elegant description of this mediatorial Lord is given here. For he is called absolutely <term>Messiah</term> <note>Mashiach</note>, the one Leader, and the "Holy of Holies" itself to be anointed, so that he is the most holy anointed one. Although this anointing also concerns his humanity, the end of the office of anointing was that his humanity, anointed in time with divine power without measure, might concur in the work of satisfaction. Furthermore, the means through which the anointed Messiah would benefit us is his sacrificial death, insinuated by the word *to be cut off*, to which is added *cut off, and not for himself*. If this is taken absolutely, it must be explained from *Jeremiah 31:15* as a description of real death, that he is truly cut off from the land of the living; but if it is explained reciprocally as *not for himself*, it indicates a vicarious death undertaken for others, and thus fruitful for others, not himself. This very death will also be sacrificial because it is ordained for the expiation of sacrifices, which can only be done through a sacrifice; hence, with the "cutting off" of the Leader is joined the *cessation of sacrifice*—not as was said in chapter 8 concerning the Anti-Christ by violent inhibition, but by the imposition of an end due to fulfillment through his true and real sacrifice. Thus, the strengthening of a new covenant is assigned to him, which cannot be done without blood; and so through this death *eternal righteousness* is brought in. This is not only asserted in explicit words but is also confirmed by the sealing of prophecies and visions, and most fully demonstrated by the true and real anointing of the Holy of Holies, so that nothing can be missing or excluded. We conclude this <term>study</term> <note>original Greek: μελέτησιν (meletēsin)</note> on Daniel's 70 Weeks with the words of John Prideaux <note>an English bishop and scholar, 1578–1650</note>, in his work *On Ecclesiastical Writers and Dogmas*: *"Where the weeks of Daniel begin and where they end still seems uncertain, although it is certain that they have already passed a long time ago."*

***

### Hosea II. 2. ###

-><term>And let her put away her adulteries from between her breasts.</term><-
<note>Hebrew: ונאף ופיה מבין שדיה</note>

->*And her adultery from the midst of her breasts.*<-
<note>Greek: Καὶ τὴν μοιχείαν αὐτῆς ἐκ μέσου τῶν μαστῶν.</note>
->*And her adulteries from the midst of her breasts.*<-
<note>Latin: Et adulteria sua de medio uberum suorum.</note>

**I**t was formerly a custom that things most dear to the heart, engraved or incised on gold and silver tablets or plates, were hung at the breast; Ferdinand de Salazar compares these rites with the words of the Wise Man in *Proverbs 3:3, 6:3, and 22:20*. To these they add Hosea, whom Ludovicus de la Cerda <note>a Jesuit scholar</note> in his *Sacred Adversaria, ch. 80*, thinks should be understood as referring to images of this kind, in which an idol was engraved, or to phylacteries of idols. He undoubtedly drew this opinion from the tradition of the Ancients, among whom was *Augustine*, who interpreted it thus: *Let her take away the idols, that is, the idols with which she commits spiritual fornication, from the midst of her breasts.*

### Hosea 2:2 ###

<margin>Idolatrous amulets.</margin>...because she wore a metal plate or a locket <note>original Latin: *bullam*</note> between her breasts and above her heart, in which an idol was hidden, so that she might display herself as a worshiper of such an idol. In this same way,

<margin>On Genesis.</margin>the Father <note>Likely referring to Saint Augustine</note> believes that Jacob buried the earrings of his people because they wore the images of their idols in them. *It is asked,* he says, why they also gave earrings; for if they were merely ornaments, they would not pertain to idolatry, unless it is understood that they were <term>phylacteries</term> <note>From the Greek *phylakterion*, meaning a protective amulet or charm, rather than the Jewish prayer boxes</note> of their Gods. For the Scripture testifies that Rebekah received earrings from the servant of Abraham, which would not have happened if it were not permitted to wear earrings for the sake of decoration.

<margin>Homily on Genesis 35.</margin>Therefore, those earrings, which were given up along with the idols, had been the amulets of the idols. John Chrysostom <note>An early Church Father and famed preacher, c. 347–407 AD</note> agrees with this explanation: *And they gave Jacob the foreign Gods—for they were not theirs—and the earrings that were in their ears. For perhaps these were signs of those idols, and so these things are brought to Jacob along with the Gods.* The Rabbis, who are clever in creating legends, spin a tale that Abraham wore such an image around his neck, as Buxtorf reports in the *Chaldean-Talmudic Lexicon* (p. 2106). There is also a tradition <note>original Greek: *παράδοσις* (paradosis)</note> among them that Haman wore a certain golden or silver image hanging from his neck, and for that reason Mordecai—lest he should seem to worship an idol—refused to bow before Haman or show him reverence by any external sign. However, the prayer of Mordecai found in the additions to the Book of Esther suggests this tradition is of shaky reliability.

<margin>Epistle 73.</margin>We have elegant testimony concerning earrings containing images of the Gods in Augustine, when he writes the following about the Africans: *The cursed superstition of "bindings" <note>original Latin: *ligaturarum*, referring to amulets tied to the body</note>, in which even the earrings of men suspended from the top of the ear on one side are employed, is used not to please men, but to serve Demons.* It is otherwise well-established from ancient coins and rings that people possessed various images of Gods and Goddesses, which superstitious men often used as amulets and to ward off the "evil eye" <note>original Latin: *fascinum*</note>. This is also proved from that maxim of Pythagoras which forbids a God to be engraved on a ring, as noted by Sanchez in his commentary on Isaiah 44:5; add to this other examples from Kirchmann’s *Commentary on Rings* (chapter 11), Crucius’s *Observations on Heliodorus* (p. 257), and Naudé’s *Work on Military Study* (p. 376). Indeed, Laurentius Pignorius (Epistle 1, *Symbols*) affirms that the faces of idols were very common on the rings of the Egyptians; and they were even used to cure diseases, as Alexander of Tralles (Book 10, ch. 1) suggests, where he says that the image of Hercules standing and suffocating a Lion, engraved on a stone and set in a gold ring, cures colic. Clement of Alexandria mentions an image of Venus on rings in his *Exhortation to the Heathen* (p. 40). Regarding the philosopher Asclepiades, Ammianus Marcellinus (Book 22) records that he used to carry with him a small silver figurine of the "Celestial Goddess" wherever he went, believing it would make the Goddess favorable to him—just as it is recorded that carrying an agate makes one pleasing to the Gods. When Sulla obtained a small image of Apollo at Delphi, he used to carry it with him in battle. The people of Byzantium had images of the Gods struck onto iron coins, according to the testimony of Hesychius: *Iron Gods, as in Byzantium; they are still found on the thin coinage, which the Byzantines used as iron and of very small value.* Salmasius (*On Climacteric Years*, p. 568) shows an amulet ring with a Lion’s head and a serpent’s tail, inscribed with the name *Chnebis* <note>A Gnostic solar deity</note>; see also pages 576 and 579. Whatever the truth may be regarding those images struck or sculpted in iron or gold,

concerning the words of Hosea, we feel no differently than what we have stated at length: that the Prophet rebuked every form of idolatry under the metaphors of adultery and prostitution. It was the custom of harlots to paint their faces with artificial color and to decorate or even expose their breasts to lure lovers. Juvenal, in *Satire 6* (v. 121), writes of Messalina <note>The wife of Emperor Claudius, infamous in Roman literature for her lust</note>:

> She entered the warm brothel with an old patchwork quilt, 
> Into a vacant cell, her own. Then she stood naked,
> Her nipples gilded, falsely assuming the name "Lycisca."

The nipples were "gilded"—that is, she opened her breasts and surrounded them with gold to entice lovers. She hung this "ivy" of her breasts for sale. The Greeks express that space between the breasts as the *mesaulyon* <note>original Greek: *μεσαύλιον*</note>. Regarding this space decorated with ornaments, the Jerusalem Targum <note>An Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible</note> on Numbers 31:50 says: *necklaces from the house of their breasts* <note>original Aramaic: והמוכניא מן בית תדיהון</note>. Instead of "house," the *Aruch* <note>A famous 11th-century dictionary of the Talmud</note> writes *biz*, which can also mean "between." This is explained as a woman’s chest ornament used to compress the breasts; as Elias <note>Elias Levita, a Renaissance Hebrew scholar</note> believes, for the root word means "to compress," often used in the context of lustful pressure, as seen in Ezekiel 23:2. Furthermore, for the Hebrew word *kumaz* (which Junius and Castalio translate as a "hanging belt" or "necklace"), Onkelos <note>Author of a famous Aramaic Targum</note> uses *mahunia*, and Jonathan uses *mahukania*, adding that it was a chest ornament hanging from the "house of the breasts." The Rabbis are rather crude <note>original Latin: *spurci*</note> in explaining that ornament. I follow the exposition of François Vatable <note>A renowned 16th-century French Hebraist</note> and add: *The Prophet alludes to the practice of harlots, who are accustomed to lure their lovers with excessive finery, as if to say: let her put away from herself the feminine finery and the alluring ornaments of harlots that invite fornicators to debauchery and adultery—namely, the decoration of the face, head, and chest.* This explanation is consistent with the text and genuine, and Dr. Rivet <note>André Rivet, a French Huguenot theologian</note> follows it learnedly in his commentary on Hosea, correctly stating that other interpretations have more cleverness than substance. Moreover, no one who is not entirely unlettered <note>original Greek: *ἀναλφάϐητος* (analphabetos)</note> in sacred matters is unaware that it is very common for the Prophets to rebuke idolatry and the worship of foreign Gods under the metaphors of adultery and prostitution, and to lash out at the ceremonies underlying an idolatrous conscience. In the Book of Wisdom (chapter 14), there is an illustrious and detailed description; and in verse 12: *The beginning of (spiritual) prostitution is the devising of idols.* Luther says: "To set up idols is the greatest harlotry." From this, we must also explain that passage in Jeremiah <margin>chapter 2:27</margin>: *I said to the wood, "You are my father," and to the stone, "You gave birth to me."* In the Book of Ezekiel, the city of Tyre is sketched with the very fitting comparison of a harlot (chapter 6); additionally, in chapter 16, the rebellion of the Jewish people is described under the figure <note>original Greek: *hypotyposis*</note> of an adulterous woman; having left the marriage of the Church, they committed adultery with foreign Gods. Likewise, in chapter 23, he declares the idolatry of Samaria and Jerusalem under the parable of two harlots. In chapter 8, verse 5, the "idol of Jealousy" is mentioned—according to Polychronius, this is a metaphor taken from women who, because they leave their husbands for strangers, provoke their husbands to jealousy. Hence, God calls himself "Jealous," a metaphor drawn from that jealousy of men, by which he shows that the covenant entered into with the Church as a bride is violated by those who commit idolatry. <meta>This page continues the theological and linguistic commentary on the Book of Hosea, specifically expanding on the metaphorical relationship between God and His people as a marriage, and the use of "harlotry" as a symbol for idolatry. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES #

<margin>Amulets of idols. Hosea 7 verse 14.</margin>
Just as a husband cannot endure harlotry in a wife, nor a rival in his bed; so God does not endure the worship of another among His people, nor <term>Samaritanism</term> <note>A term used here to describe religious syncretism or corrupted worship, named after the Samaritans who blended Israelite and foreign traditions</note> in the Church; nor *wailing in the chambers*—that is, in temples dedicated to idolatrous worship, according to the interpretation of some. By a similar allegory, Hosea in chapter 1, verse 2, represents the Jewish Synagogue through "a woman of harlotries" <note>Hebrew: *eshet zenunim*</note>; he contends with her as with a prostitute 
<margin>chapter 4 verse 17, chapter 5 verse 7.</margin>
who violated the faith given to her husband and associated *herself with idols*, being treacherous toward the Lord. For she bore "alien children" <note>Hebrew: *zerim*</note> from the Church through spiritual adultery, while she destined for foreign gods those whom she ought to have consecrated to God, who was her husband. Having abandoned the true God, she followed foreign rites and gods, which is declared in many ways in the first, second, and third chapters in the rebuke of the Israelites for their idolatry, which is expressly called harlotry. Indeed, the prophet indicates this *emphatically* <note>original Greek: *ἐμφατικῶς*</note> in Hosea chapter 1, verse 2, by using the *future tense*, which in a general sense signifies a certain staying and duration of the thing he describes in that same span of time, as Ribera <note>Francisco de Ribera, a 16th-century Jesuit commentator</note> observes there. For the Hebrews often use the future tense to signify what is in common use and perpetual custom; thus, their most intense devotion to idolatry is rebuked. In the same way, in Isaiah 57 verse 5, the same thing is indicated by the word "inflamed" <note>Hebrew: *vaham*</note>; for it was like the heat of lust with which an adulteress grows warm toward an adulterer. In the book of Hosea, the Holy Spirit uses the plural, *fornications and adulteries*, to signify the frequent and continuous act of spiritual impurity in every way. Jeremiah, attacking Jerusalem under the name of a prostitute, says in chapter 2: *How can you say, "I am not polluted? I have not walked after the Baals?" See your ways in the valley, know what you have done.* All these things serve the explanation of verse 2, chapter 2 of Hosea, where he says: *Plead with your mother, plead; for she is not my wife, and I am not her husband: let her put away her harlotries from her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts.* After he compared her to a prostitute, he also ascribes to her what is customary for prostitutes; for the prophet, not content to sketch the character of the Israelites by calling her a *prostitute* who would not keep the faith of spiritual marriage, added further—to better and more clearly depict their idolatrous ways—the loathsome habits of prostitutes *by the baring of the face and the breasts*; by which signs their impurity and the baseness of an impudent soul are marked. For he alludes to the shameful, painted arts of prostitutes, with which they stain their faces, and even show their youthful breasts and their whole body to provoke the lust for fornicating, so that they may bait the souls of lovers with "beautification" <note>original Greek: *καλλωπισμὸν*</note> and false colors on their cheeks and lips, and entice them into embraces by the foul and indecent uncovering of the breasts. These are called adulteries of the face and breasts because in those parts of the body the impurity of prostitutes betrays itself externally; and these are included under the *prostitute’s attire* in Proverbs chapter 7 verse 10 (Luther: *Hurrenschmuck*). Also, Solomon Jarchi <note>Rashi, the medieval Jewish commentator</note> noted on Hosea the same manner of adulteresses: how they adorn themselves between their breasts and adulterate their faces with various kinds of cosmetics, so that they might appear beautiful to the eyes of fornicators. By that metaphor taken from the breasts, in both sacred and 

<column-break/>

profane writings, it is customary to describe both chaste love and unchaste love. One may see both. The author of Proverbs, chapter 5, verses 18–19, symbolically designates the vehement and continuous love of spouses through the breasts, using these words: *Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice with the wife of your youth: a most dear hind, and a most graceful fawn; let her breasts intoxicate you.* Where the word "satiate" <note>Hebrew: *ravah*, meaning to be irrigated or drenched</note> refers to the fullness of the breasts, translated by the Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> throughout as "to be drunk" <note>original Greek: *μεθύειν*</note>, it signifies sufficient delight. Johannes Draconites <note>A 16th-century German theologian</note> wishes to teach that through the word *breasts*, he means conjugal affection, and through *let them intoxicate you*, he means the vehemence of love, signifying by repetition that conjugal affection ought to be vehement and constant. The author of the Song of Solomon repeatedly uses this in expressing the love of Christ toward the Church, according to the interpretation of the Vulgate, Luther, Osiander, and others. For what is in Hebrew "your loves" <note>Hebrew: *Dodecha*</note>, they elegantly explain as "your breasts" <note>Hebrew: *Dadecha*</note>, as if those two words exchanged their meanings with each other. *Better,* he says, *are your breasts than wine.* And again in chapter 4, verse 10: *How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my spouse, and your breasts are more beautiful than wine.* These spiritual breasts the Holy Spirit had praised for their richness, brightness, sweet scent, symmetry, and loveliness, so that He might commend the singular love and goodness with which He burned toward the Church as His bride. Thus, He established the sign of love in the breasts in chapter 4, verse 5: *Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, which feed among the lilies.* And He closes the final chapter with the same words: *Flee, and be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices.* He designates the burning affection in nourishing the offspring with the milk of the divine word no less excellently through the likeness of fawns than through the breasts. But why does He join fawns? This metaphor can be understood if those who have dwelled on Eastern matters provide help. They report that there is a most elegant kind of gazelle in the Eastern regions, consisting of the finest and most shining hair, with limbs aptly and gracefully arranged. Hence, whatever the Arabs wish to commend, they call it a gazelle, because it is customary for these to be among the delights; as Maltese dogs are to our maidens. Hence, by Catullus <note>Roman poet, c. 84–54 BC</note>, a girl is called *more delicate than a kid.* Hence also that Arab poet, the most learned Tograus <note>Al-Tughra'i, a 12th-century Persian physician and poet</note>, described his love (if one may compare small things to great). But harlotrous and impure love is described from the "vestibule," so to speak, of wandering eyes, by which the rest of the interior adornment may be judged. For this reason, Solomon repeatedly warned that we should not be captured by the nods of adulteresses, who cast up their eyes to seize itching flesh for themselves and invite it to luxury with signs, so that they may kindle the lust of those looking on with the impure movement of their eyes; just as Isaiah complains of the daughters of Israel, *with the nodding of their eyes*; although some believe the Spirit of God said this rather to indicate the pride and arrogance of the girls of Jerusalem. Ennius <note>Early Roman poet, c. 239–169 BC</note> gracefully expresses these flatteries of an impudent prostitute in these words: *As if playing ball in a dance, she gives herself from hand to hand and makes herself common. She holds one, nods to another, her hand is busy elsewhere; she pinches the foot of one, gives a ring to another to look at, and calls another with her lips, while singing with yet another.*

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Hosea’s prophetic metaphors, moving from the general concept of spiritual harlotry to specific anatomical and social imagery—eyes, breasts, and veils—used by both biblical and classical authors to describe seduction and the betrayal of religious devotion.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES #

### Hosea Chapter 2, Verse 2 ###

<margin>Amulets of idols.</margin>
Even in the works of <term>Petronius</term><note>A Roman courtier and writer known for his satirical and often bawdy depictions of Roman life</note> there are lascivious words, yet within those lascivious passages are maxims that even a virtuous author would not regret. The virtuous woman Judith <margin>Judith chapter 9, verse 10</margin> testifies that in love, the eyes are the leaders and the snares for lovers; she calls upon God to capture Holofernes by his sight alone with these words: *Let him be caught by the snare of his eyes upon me, and strike him by the grace of my lips.* Similarly, the divine author of Proverbs notes that the breasts, eyes, and hair of a beautiful girl are things that wound the hearts of onlookers and lovers. In the same way, a recently praised Arabic author looks for a sign of love—the very thing he sighed for day and night—described as *a single cast of open eyes*, by which he might refresh his eyes, weary and exhausted with sorrow. <margin>Numbers 25:1 & chapter 31:16</margin> It was by this plan and a remarkable stratagem that the concubines of the Moabites were sent by Balaam to the camp of the Israelites, to entice them from moral integrity and modesty toward lust and idolatry; *and they caused them to rebel against the Lord in the matter of Peor, and so the people were struck.* In the most proper sense of this word, among the ancients, "to sin" (*peccare*) was "to be enticed" (*pellicari*), which is to act as a harlot or adulterer. Hence, in Scripture, those who disregard divine precepts are called "transgressors" because, having spurned and abandoned the bed of Christ, they commit adultery with foreign gods; having prostituted the purity of the Church, they revel freely with the flesh, the world, and the Devil. Just as among the Hebrews a harlot is called <term>zonah</term> (זֹנָה) <margin>Proverbs 3:20, 22:14, & 23:27</margin>, either because she alienates herself from her husband by breaking the faith of conjugal love, or because she receives a stranger by wandering abroad. For a harlot is so called because she is always accustomed to wander; she is called <term>naphqat bara</term> (נָפְקַת בָּרָא) <note>Aramaic: "she who goes outside"</note>, *a woman going outdoors*. She was usually one who lived outside the city, near paths and side-roads, which is why Salazar, in his commentary on the first chapter of the Song of Solomon, taught that they were called *pathway-harlots*. They even waited for a customer at the doors of brothels; for this reason, Plautus in his play *The Little Carthaginian* calls harlots *Prosedae*, as if "sitting before the doors." As Solomon says in Proverbs chapter 7, verse 11, regarding the harlot wandering now in the streets, now in the squares, *her feet could not stay at home.* If one wished to make a comparison, these three things fit together elegantly: the harlot who bears a bastard outside of marriage, and the Gentile who is outside the Church, born through spiritual fornication—especially since Holy Scripture calls idolaters "adulterers." But lest I myself slide into being a mere philologist or grammarian while doing something else, I remind you that Solomon taught that a vicious habit of love breaks high and noble spirits, turns authority into luxury, and eventually bestows pestilential things with weariness. <margin>Proverbs 29:4</margin> *For the lips of a harlot drip like a honeycomb, and her throat is smoother than oil.* (Plautus says the same in *The Ferocious Man*: *Your tongues and speeches are in honey*) *but her end is bitter as wormwood*, (Plautus says in the same place: *Their hearts are located in gall and bitter vinegar*) and *her tongue is sharp as a two-edged sword*, says the King in his Exhortations <margin>Proverbs 5:3</margin>, having been taught by his own example. For he himself, through the improvident force of burning affection, rushed into the embraces of foreign women <margin>1 Kings 11:2</margin> whom he sought from the whole world; and at last, when insatiable desire and this "stolen sweetness" of Venus (Proverbs 9:17) burned out, he spent the remaining time of his life in tears and lamentations.

<column-break/>

<margin>Amulets of idols.</margin>
In the end, he became an object of loathing to himself, and in a sort of "swan song" in the various books which the holy codex has consecrated to immortality, he—the wisest of men—handed down true wisdom more correctly than Seneca, Plutarch, and the rest of the philosophers in their immense volumes. If you unroll all of those, you will find that the robbery and prey of harlot-love never turned out happily for any mortal. Just as fornication is now described from the "wantonness of the eyes," so also it is described from the "baring and enticement of the chest and breasts," which they allow to be handled and squeezed in the brothels. Thus, the harlot—talkative and wandering, impatient of quiet, unable to keep her feet in her own house, lying in wait now outside, now in the streets—says: <margin>Proverbs 7:18</margin> *Come, let us be intoxicated with breasts and enjoy the desired embraces until the day dawns.* The Hebrew word is <term>dodim</term> (דּוֹדִים), meaning *loves*, which is aptly expressed by the word *to be intoxicated*. For lust and luxury are a kind of drunkenness, which, once it seizes someone, robs them of their mind and judgment—a point Chrysostom elegantly draws out in his *Fifth Homily Against the Jews*. Hence, "handled breasts" in Ezekiel chapter 23, verse 3 (a passage which Rabbi Kimchi correctly relates to Hosea) are signs of harlots: *In their youth they played the harlot; there their breasts were handled, and the paps of their virginity were bruised.* Here, most elegantly, the "swelling breasts" are said by the Translator to be *bruised* by handling; you will see the force of this word explained by J. F. Gronovius in the 16th chapter of his *Diatribe on Statius*. So also for our Prophet, the "adulteries of the breasts" are nothing other than either the seductive *adornments* <note>Greek: kalōpismata</note> of the breasts, or, to use the words of Plautus <margin>Pseudolus 5.1.16</margin>, *the little squeezes of shivering little nipples* <note>original Hebrew: ma'asit ha-shadayim</note>. In the same sense, Horace <margin>Odes, Book 1, Ode 15, v. 19</margin> spoke of the *adulterous hair* of Paris, by whose grooming and beauty Helen's desire was incited to adultery and desertion above all else. In the work of Aristaenetus, Telesippe allowed Architeles to pluck kisses and touch her breasts. Apollonius says of Jason and Medea: *beautifully grasping the breasts of the maiden* <note>Original Greek from the Argonautica</note>. Allegorically, from that petulance of which we have spoken, Hosea rebukes the worship of foreign gods. For, as Jerome's words state elsewhere, Holy Scripture wants the people to be taught not only by the ears, but also by the eyes. These are the words of God to the Prophet <margin>Chapter 1, verse 2</margin>: *Go, take to yourself a wife of harlotries, and make for yourself children of harlotry.* Here the Scripture has something more manifest and deeper; it aims to shape minds not so much through things sent slowly into the ear, but through things *subjected to the faithful eyes*, as Horace says in his *Art of Poetry*. Now, consider how significant it is that modest Eastern virgins (from which the Hebrew <term>almah</term> <note>Meaning a young woman or maiden</note> is explained) and matrons kept themselves at home. When they did go out, whether for divine worship or other necessary duties, for the sake of honor they did not walk without a veil for the face and a cloak for the whole body, which covered the woman's head down to the hips, in which there were also two holes open for the eyes <margin>Antonio Giggei, Treasury of the Arabic Language, Vol 1, page 759</margin>. For they covered the head with a robe and the face with a mesh, which was woven from the finest thread or silk, marked with tiny spots and meshes. In Greek, the authors use the word <term>kekryphalon</term> <note>A hair-net or veil</note>, as Synesius <note>Epistle 3, p. 160</note> and Xiphilinus in *Avitus* (p. 370) use for a woman’s covering, and it is rendered by Translators as *a mesh, a transparent mesh*. Indeed, modest virgins...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES #

<margin>Amulets of idols.</margin>
That virgins did not bare their breasts, nor show prominent nipples, is shown not only by ancient customs but also by recent ones throughout the entire East. This was also attested by Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note>, who was a resident of Palestine, and who confessed that his knowledge of that land greatly profited him in understanding many things in the sacred writings. <margin>Volume 5, page 20</margin> In his commentary *On Isaiah*, he says: *We cannot call the "Theristra"* <note>A light, rectangular summer veil or shawl</note> *the little cloaks with which Rebecca was wrapped, just as today in Arabia and Mesopotamia women are covered by them; it is named from the Greek "en therei"* <note>original: "ἐν θέρεϊ"</note>, *that is, in summer and heat, because they protect the bodies of women.* Tertullian, in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 17, writes: *The pagan women of Arabia not only cover the head, but also the entire face, so that they are content with only one eye being free, preferring to enjoy half the light rather than prostitute the whole face.* For which reason I do not know if I can approve of the words of <term>Bessarion</term><note>A 15th-century cardinal and scholar who sought to reconcile Plato with Christian theology</note> in <margin>Venice edition, folio 70. b.</margin> his second book *Against the Calumniators of Plato*: *In our times, Italian women, who walk with face, neck, and breast open, do not move a continent man to lust any more than Turkish women, who go out from home with all their limbs covered. For there is no praise for a virgin to go about in public with neck and breast open, which even now many among us, oh the shame, do. That the eyes are the "proxenetae"* <note>original: "proxenetas" — agents, go-betweens, or pimps</note> *of luxury, especially where occasion flatters, is shown by David’s entrance to Bathsheba; and from the testimony of many we know that, just as flame is close to smoke, so even in the best of men that image has sometimes excited the flame of desire.* Plutarch says in *On Love*: *For sight is the handle of passion.* <note>original: "ἡ γὰρ ὄψις τοῦ πάθους ἐστὶ λαβή"</note> Therefore, Alexander the Great prudently did not wish even to look upon the wife and daughters of Darius; but having greeted them, he kept his eyes fixed on the ground. For as that man said in a festive performance in <term>Curtius</term><note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, a Roman historian who wrote a biography of Alexander the Great</note>, *the Persian girls were "eye-pains"* (Bessarion might add the Italian ones); *whom he passed by as if they were statues.* We are men, and not sufficiently taught to bridle these most vehement passions. I wish they would free the eyes of true Christians from such a foul spectacle (may no offense be taken at the word), and cast away "the offense of the eyes" (which are the words <margin>chapter 20, verse 7.</margin> of Ezekiel, though in another sense regarding idols)! Propertius speaks sincerely in *Elegy 2, 12*:
> *He who sees, sins; he who has not seen you, therefore*
> *will not desire. The eye holds the crimes of the deed.*
But what course of speech has snatched us away into this contention? Truly, it was done by a certain explanation coming from great men of the Church, by which the prophetic words concerning images of that kind—into which an idol was engraved and which were fit for <term>phylacteries</term><note>Here referring to amulets or charms rather than the Jewish prayer boxes</note>—are explained.

<margin>Money and Weights.</margin>
The system of coinage is very intricate, both because of the variety of times and because of the character of people, to whose either greed or liberality the currency was obliged to submit.

<column-break/>

Long ago among our ancestors, before the invention of the coin, all commerce consisted in exchange; according to Aristotle in *Ethics, Book 5, chapter 5*: *Exchange existed before money did.* <note>original: "ἡ ἀλλαγὴ ἦν, πρὶν τὸ νόμισμα ᾖ"</note> And Pomponius Mela <note>A Roman geographer</note> testifies concerning the Sarmatians <note>Ancient nomadic people of the Eurasian Steppe</note> (Book 2, 1, page 30): *Ignorant of gold and silver, those greatest of plagues, they carry out trade by the exchange of things.* Especially since the ancestors, particularly those before the Flood, to whom the use of gold and silver was unknown, measured their riches by the abundance and multitude of cattle; among them all trade consisted in the exchange of cattle. From this, "pecunia" <note>money</note> seems to be named, either because coins were first marked with a "pecu" <note>original: "pecu" — head of cattle</note>, or because it succeeded in the place of cattle, with which the purchase of necessary things once happened. Indeed, we call all those things "pecunias" whose value is measured in coins, which is substituted by agreement as a stand-in for need; whence it is also called "nomisma" <note>original: "νόμισμα"</note>, because it exists not by nature but by "nomos" <note>original: "νόμῳ"</note>, that is, by institution and law, and it is within our power to change it and render it useless, as Aristotle teaches in *Ethics, Book 5, chapter 8*. Hence almost nothing is so greatly exposed to changes as the matter of money, which is greater and wider as the men succeeding one another are more changeable. Moreover, every change is accustomed to happen either in quality or in quantity, sometimes in one of these, sometimes in both. Sometimes the currency increases, sometimes it decreases, and the greed of those to whom the rights of the currency are to be entrusted can do much, to say nothing of other causes of changes. We desire nothing so much as currency and coins, and we strain every nerve toward this: that we may possess them. There is nothing that is more greedily sought, nothing with greater anxiety, and there is no need for us to warn about this huge desire here. We have another vow of "having," and I wish it were from a true vow! The word "moneta" <note>money/coinage</note> "monet" <note>warns/reminds</note> us to deal with something of its matter and form and various types. Indeed, the matter of currencies is intricate, and the reasoning is not clear; it is a place where that phrase "It is not clear" <note>original: "Non liquet" — a legal term used when a judge finds the evidence insufficient</note> must be repeatedly muttered. Hence Blondus <note>Flavio Biondo, a Renaissance humanist</note>, dealing with the *Money and Weights of the Ancients*, says: *To show exactly what and of what kind these were through each age would be no more difficult than it is impossible, not only because they were handed down by the ancestors in obscure words unknown to our age, but because almost every age had its own variety of having and form.* We shall pursue it, however, so that we may attain it; and if we do not attain it, it will be a matter of praise to have investigated it. We will go where we can; where we cannot, there we shall stand. At the very threshold, however, Paulus the Jurist <note>Julius Paulus, a 3rd-century Roman lawyer</note> comes to our aid, defining money as *matter struck with a public form, providing use and ownership not so much from its substance as from its quantity.* He clearly opens the matter of coinage, for in every coin these two must be examined: Matter and Form. In the matter, first the *substance* must be looked at, then the *weight*. The matter seen as worthy for money was *gold, silver, and copper.* Unworthy were iron (though Aristotle admits this), *tin, and lead.* Gold is deservedly held as primary, which gave, as it were, "Spirit" and increased the affairs of men more and more; whence even under the first Monarchy, mention is made of currencies especially of gold and silver, both in Sacred and secular writings, which was also for that reason (as some think) called the "Golden Age," and it is better known than can be treated extensively here, although there are those who deny...

# Amos VIII #

<margin>
Money and Weights.
</margin>

<margin>
Money and Weights.
</margin>

Regarding money among the Hebrews—if one excludes those bronze coins, one side of which shows us Moses with horns reaching to his ears <note>original: "Mofen [Mosem] auribus tenus cornutum"; this refers to the traditional artistic depiction of Moses with rays of light, often mistranslated or depicted as horns</note>, wearing a collar with an added inscription; <note>original: "משה"</note> **Moses**; and the other side showing the words of the first commandment, <note>original: "לך אלהים אחרים על פני לא יהיה"</note> **"You shall have no other gods before me"** (Ezekiel 45:12)—the use of bronze money is discussed by Hottinger in his third dissertation on Oriental Coins. Concerning the Arabs, they also had coins made of copper and even leather, such as the Persian *Schehreva*, which means the "will of the King" <note>original: "voluntas Regis"</note> (Gentius, *Rosarium*, p. 602). Thus, Plato writes in *Eryxias* that skins <note>original: "τὰ δέρματα"</note> served the Carthaginians in place of money, and Aristides calls them leather coins <note>original: "σκότινα νομίσματα"</note>. Seneca also mentions leather struck with an official seal, as does Nicolaus of Damascus regarding the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, <note>original: "νομίσματα χωρίνα σκυτίνω"</note> **leather currency**, from whom Seneca took the idea. Among the Greeks, Phidon is said to have been the first to strike coins in Aegina. That the Greeks received the concept of money from the Eastern peoples is sufficiently shown by the very names by which they called its chief types. Among the Romans, who had "mint masters" <term>Triumviri monetales</term> <note>A board of three magistrates responsible for overseeing the minting of coins</note> who were put in charge of striking money, bronze <note>original: "as"</note> was first held in value; Servius Tullius was the first to mark it with the sign of cattle <note>original: "pecudum"</note>, which is why money is thought by some to be called <term>pecunia</term> <note>Derived from "pecus," meaning cattle, the earliest form of wealth</note>, whereas before they used raw bronze. Five years before the Punic War, under the consulship of Fabius, as Pliny testifies, silver was first marked with the sign of two-horse and four-horse chariots; and in the year 585 from the founding of the City [Rome], and sixty-two years later, the gold coin was struck. The oldest mention of money is inserted into the history of Abimelech by the author of *Sacred Origins* 

<margin>
Genesis 20:16.
</margin>

who explains that he gave <note>original: "אלף כסף"</note> **one thousand pieces of silver** to Abraham for his wife Sarah, that is, one thousand shekels of silver, or 500 <term>Joachimsthalers</term> <note>original: "Joachim-cos"; these were large silver coins from Bohemia, from which the word "dollar" is derived</note>. Likewise, in *Genesis 23:15-16*, mention is made of <note>original: "כסף עובר לסוחר"</note> **silver passing to the merchants**, that is, approved public money, <note>original: "geld/ das hin unnd wieder gang und gäbe war / gute gangbare Müntze"</note> **money that was common and current everywhere, good passable coin**, just as we Germans are accustomed to speak in exactly the same way. For the verb "to pass" <note>original: "עבר"</note> when applied to money, seems to signify precisely what the Italian phrase *moneta corrente* or the Spanish *de moneda que corre* <note>"current money" or "money that runs/circulates"</note> means, as Villalpandus says. In this matter, at least, a doubt remains as to whether the silver was stamped, or whether it was measured by weight, for Moses testifies that Abraham did not count but weighed out four hundred shekels. So also in *Genesis 43:21*, the sons of Jacob say they are bringing back money according to its weight, by which is mostly understood the quantity or public estimation—the power, dignity, price, and value that belongs to the coin, and is commonly indicated by its circulation and use. The form of a coin includes the image <note>original: "εἰκόνα"</note> and the inscription <note>original: "ἐπιγραφήν"</note>, as attested by the Master of Truth concerning Christ, when he asks the Jews: <note>original: "τίν@ ἡ εἰκὼν αὕτη καὶ ἡ ἐπιγραφή;"</note> **"Whose image and inscription is this?"** Suetonius calls these "icons" with which money is distinguished. In our language, it is called <note>original: "der Schlag"</note> **the strike**. There were various types of coins among the Hebrews, which I intend only to list. The <term>Gerah</term> <note>original: "גרה"</note> was a silver coin used in the Sacred Scriptures, weighing as much silver as 16 grains of barley, or two kreuzers, which make one of our "white coins" of 8 obols. Thus Rambam <note>Maimonides</note> says: <note>original: "מעה שהיה בימי Maab."</note> the *Maah* which in the time of Moses our teacher was called a **Gerah**

<column-break/>

consists of 16 barley grains. According to the judgment of Levi ben Gershon and Rabbi Jehaia, it is estimated at a weight of 17 barley grains. Frequent mention of it is made in the Sacred Scriptures (*Exodus 30:13, Leviticus 27:25, Numbers 3:47, chapter 18:16*). It is so named from the word <note>original: "גרה"</note> **to cut off** or to cut down, as if you were to say a "cut" or "clipped" piece, that is, a very small portion of silver from which this coin was struck. The <term>Agorah</term> <note>original: "אגורה"</note> was likewise a tiny silver coin, of the same value as the Gerah, namely 16 grains or two German kreuzers, of which express mention is made in *1 Samuel 2:36, 1 Kings 2:26, and 2 Kings 22:9*. It is so named from the word <note>original: "אגר"</note> **to collect** or heap up, because several characters were collected on this coin. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> attributes the same weight to it as the Gerah: <note>original: "אגורה משקולת עשרים גרה הוא"</note> **The Agorah is of the same weight as the Gerah, twenty of which constitute a Shekel**; and Rabbi David <note>Kimchi</note> says: <note>original: "הוא כמו גרה"</note> **The Agorah is the same as the Gerah.** Others, however, feel differently. The <term>Kesitah</term> <note>original: "קשיטה"</note>, properly meaning **lamb or ewe**, is so named from <note>original: "קשט"</note>. Mention of it is primarily made in *Genesis 33:19, Joshua 24:32, and Job 42:11*. In the first passage, the Septuagint <note>LXX</note> translates it as <note>original: "ἑκατὸν ἀμνῶν"</note> **one hundred lambs**. Both the Samaritan versions read *Kesitah*. Hence, interpreters are divided into two parties: some think that Jacob exchanged one hundred lambs or ewes for that portion of the field, since in those times, before the use of money was devised, it was common to conduct trade by the exchange of livestock. Others, however, understand them to be coins upon which the figure of lambs or sheep was engraved, just as certain Athenian and Roman money had the figure of an **ox or a sheep**. From this is taken the proverb: <note>original: "Bos in lingua"</note> **"An ox on the tongue"** <note>Meaning a person has been bribed to silence, as if the weight of the silver coin (the ox) were pressing down their tongue</note>. The coins of the Argives featured a wolf or a mouse; those of the Rhegians a hare; those of the Lacedaemonians a dragon; those of the Thessalians horses. And we see even today coins named after livestock; for example, in Switzerland, there are "Ravens," "Bears," and <term>Batzen</term> <note>original: "Batzen / Patzen"</note>; regarding which Zuichemus says in his *Commentary on the Institutes of Law*, p. 371: <note>original: "die wir Batzen (Patzen) nennen / kommen von den Schweitzern her / welche ein Beeren darrauff geſchlagen."</note> **"Those which we call Batzen come from the Swiss, who struck a bear upon them."** We agree with this latter opinion, since it seems more probable that in those passages, by a figure of speech, *Kesitoth* refers to coins marked with the image of a lamb or ewe, especially since Stephen in *Acts 7:16* is a witness that <note>original: "ἀβραὰμ ὠνήσασθαι τιμῆς ἀργυρίᾳ"</note> **Abraham bought it for a price of silver**. The fourth type of money among the Hebrews was the <term>Zuz</term> <note>original: "זוז"</note> or *Zura*, or as others prefer, *Zuz* or *Zuza*, mentioned in *Tobit 5:21*. This word generally denotes money, just as among our people it might refer to denarii, gold pieces, "batzen," or sometimes even thalers and ducats. Or it denotes a specific type, and in this sense, a fourth part of a silver shekel, as Elias and Rabbi David Kimchi explain: <note>original: "רבע שקל הכסף"</note> **A shekel is four Zuzim.** It is commonly said to be of the same value as the Greek drachma or the Roman denarius (compare Waser, *On Coins*, chapter 10). Among the coins of the Hebrews there was also the <term>Darcon</term> <note>original: "דרכמון"</note> or *Adarcon*. The word appears in *1 Chronicles 29:7, Ezra 2:69, and Nehemiah 7:70*. However, there is disagreement about its origin. Brerewood wishes the *Darcon* or *Darcemon* to be so named as if marked with the image of Darius (see *Apparatus of the Polyglot Bible*, p. 31, regarding weights, etc.); and thus the *Dracmon* would be the same...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES #

<margin>Phylacteries of idols.</margin>
That virgins did not bare their breasts, nor show protruding nipples, is shown not only by ancient customs but even by recent ones throughout the whole Orient; to which Jerome also testified, having been an inhabitant of Palestine, and having professed that his knowledge of that land was of great benefit to him for understanding many things in the sacred writings. <margin>Volume 5, page 20</margin> In his commentary *on Isaiah*, he says: *We cannot call the small cloaks in which Rebecca was wrapped "Theristra" <note>A Greek term for a light summer garment or veil</note>, as even today women in Arabia and Mesopotamia are covered, because they protect the bodies of women "in the summer" <note>original Greek: ἐν θέρει</note>, that is, in the heat.* Tertullian, in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 17, says: *The pagan women of Arabia do not only cover the head, but the whole face as well, so that they are content with one eye being free, preferring to enjoy half the light rather than prostitute the whole face.* For this reason, I do not know whether I can approve of these words of Bessarion <note>Johannes Bessarion (1403–1472), a Greek scholar and Cardinal who attempted to reconcile Plato with Christian thought</note> in <margin>Venice edition, folio lib. 2, *Against the Calumniators of Plato*, p. 70 b.</margin> Book 2 of *Against the Calumniators of Plato*: *Nor in our times do Italian women, who walk with face, neck, and chest open, move a continent man to lust more than Turkish women, who go out from home with all their limbs covered.* For there is no praise in a Virgin walking about in public with neck and chest open, which even now many among us do—alas, the shame! That the eyes are the "pimps" of luxury, especially where opportunity flatters, is shown by David’s entrance to Bathsheba; and we know from the testimony of many that, just as flame is close to smoke, so sometimes that image has excited the flame of desire even in the best of men. Plutarch says in *On Love*: *For sight is the voice of passion.* <note>original Greek: ἡ γὰρ ὄψις τῶ πάθους ἐστὶ λαλή</note> And therefore Alexander the Great prudently did not wish even to look upon the wife and daughters of Darius; but having greeted them, he fixed his eyes on the ground; for what he said in a festive performance in Curtius <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, a Roman historian of Alexander the Great</note> was: *the Persian girls were pains to the eyes* (Bessarion might add "Italian"); *whom he passed by as if they were statues.* We are human, and not sufficiently taught to bridle these most violent of affections. Would that they would free the eyes of true Christians from such a foul spectacle (may there be no ill-will in the saying), and cast away the "stumbling blocks of the eyes" (which are the words <margin>chapter 20, verse 7.</margin> of Ezekiel, but used in another sense regarding idols)! Sincerely, Propertius writes in Book 2, Elegy 12:

> He who sees, sins; he who is not seen, therefore, 
> will not desire. The light holds the crimes of the deed.

But what course of discourse has snatched us away into that contention? Surely it was a certain explanation coming from great Men of the Church, by which the prophetic words concerning images of that kind, in which an idol was engraved and suitable for phylacteries <note>In this context, protective amulets or charms rather than the Jewish prayer boxes</note>, are explained.
