<margin>Money and Weights.</margin>
The system of coinage is very intricate, both because of the variety of times and because of the character of the persons to whose greed or liberality the coin had to submit itself.

<column-break/>

In the past among our Ancestors, before the invention of the coin, all commerce consisted in exchange; according to Aristotle in Book 5 of the *Ethics*: *Exchange existed before coinage.* <note>original Greek: ἡ ἀλλαγὴ ἦ πρὶν τὸ νόμισμα ἦ</note> And regarding the Sarmatians, Pomponius Mela testifies (2.1. p. 30): *Ignorant of gold and silver, those greatest of plagues, they carry out commerce by the exchange of things.* Especially indeed, since the Ancestors, particularly those before the Flood, to whom the use of gold and silver was hidden, measured their wealth by the abundance and multitude of cattle, among them all trade consisted in the exchange of cattle, from which "money" <term>pecunia</term> <note>The Latin word for money, *pecunia*, is derived from *pecus*, meaning cattle</note> seems to have been named, either because coins were first marked with them, or because it succeeded in the place of cattle, with which the purchase of necessary things was once made. Indeed, we call all those things "money" whose value is measured in coins, which is substituted as if by agreement in the place of need, whence it is also called "currency" <term>nomisma</term> <note>From the Greek *nomisma*</note>, because it stands not by nature but "by law" <note>original Greek: νόμῳ</note>, that is, by institution and law, and it is in our power to change it and render it useless, as Aristotle teaches in *Ethics* 5.8. Hence almost nothing is so greatly exposed to changes as the matter of money, which is greater and wider insofar as the men succeeding one another are more changeable. Moreover, every change is accustomed to happen either in quality or in quantity, sometimes in one of these, sometimes in both. Now the money increases, now it decreases, and the greed of those who have the right of striking money can do much, to say nothing of other causes of changes. We desire nothing quite as much as money and coins, and we strain every nerve to possess them. There is nothing that is more greedily sought, nothing with greater anxiety. Concerning this huge desire, it is not for us to warn here. We have another wish for possession, and would that it were according to our wish! Money <term>moneta</term> warns <note>A wordplay on the Latin *moneta* (money/mint) and *monere* (to warn/advise)</note> us to treat something of its material, form, and various species. The material of coins is indeed intricate, nor is the reasoning clear, and there are places where that phrase: *It is not clear*, must be repeatedly doubled. Hence Blondus <note>Flavio Biondo (1392–1463), a Renaissance humanist historian</note>, treating *On the Money and Weights* of the Ancients, says: *What and of what sort they were through each age, it would be no more difficult than impossible to show exactly, not only because they were handed down by the Ancestors in obscure words unknown in our age, but because almost every age had its own variety and form of striking.* We shall follow them, however, so that we may attain it; and if we do not attain it, it will be to our credit to have investigated. We shall go where we can; where we cannot, there we shall stand. At the very threshold, however, the Jurist Paulus <note>Julius Paulus, a 3rd-century Roman jurist</note> comes to our aid, defining money as material struck with a public form, providing use and ownership not so much from its substance as from its quantity. He clearly opens the matter of coinage, since in every coin these two must be examined: Material and Form. In the material, first the substance must be looked at, then the weight; Gold, silver, and bronze were seen as material worthy for money. Unworthy were iron—although Aristotle also allows this—tin, and lead. Gold is deservedly held as primary, which gave, as it were, Spirit, and increased the affairs of men more and more, whence even under the first Monarchy, mention is made of coins primarily from gold and silver both in Sacred and secular writings, which for that reason, as some think, was called the "golden age," and is more noted than bronze, which need not be treated extensively here, although there are some who deny that among...

# AMOS 8:5 #

## Currency and Weights ##

<sig>Vuuuu 2</sig>

<margin>Money and Weights.</margin>
Among the Hebrews—if you except those bronze coins, one side of which shows us Moses "horned" up to his ears <note>original: "Mosen auribus tenus cornutum"; a common artistic depiction based on a mistranslation of "shining" in Exodus 34:29</note>, wearing a collar with an added inscription "Moses" [משה], and the other side featuring the words of the first commandment: "You shall have no other gods before me" [לא יהיה לך אלהים אחרים על פני]—bronze currency was indeed in use, as you may see in Hottinger’s *Third Dissertation on Oriental Coins*. As for the Arabs, they even had coins made of copper and leather, such as the Persian *Schehreva*, which means "the Will of the King" <note>original: "voluntas Regis"</note>. From this, Plato writes in his *Eryxias* that skins served as currency for the Carthaginians, and Aristides calls it "dark money" [σκότινον νόμισμα]. Seneca also mentions leather struck with an official seal, as does Nicolaus of Damascus concerning the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, saying "they use leather currency" [νομίσματι χρῶνται σκυτίνῳ], a detail he took from Seneca. Among the Greeks, Phido is said to have been the first to strike coins in Aegina. That the Greeks received their coinage from Eastern peoples is sufficiently shown by the very names they call the principal types. Among the Romans—who had "money masters" [Triumviri monetales] appointed for minting—bronze was first held in value; Servius Tullius first marked it with the image of cattle [pecus], from which some believe the word "money" [pecunia] is derived, whereas previously they used raw bronze. Five years before the Punic War, under the consul Fabius, silver was first marked—as Pliny testifies—with the image of two-horse [bigae] and four-horse [quadrigae] chariots, in the year 585 from the city's founding. Two and sixty years later, the gold coin was struck. The first and oldest mention of money inserted in the history of the writer of *Sacred Origins* concerns Abimelech

<margin>Gen. 20:16.</margin>
who explains that he gave "one thousand silver pieces" [אלף כסף] to Abraham for his wife Sarah—that is, a thousand silver shekels, or 500 Joachimstalers <note>A large silver coin from the 16th century, the origin of the word "dollar"</note>. Likewise in Genesis 23:15–16, mention is made of "silver passing to the merchant" [עובר לסוחר כסף], that is, approved public currency—"money that was passing to and fro, good current coinage" <note>German: "Geldt / das hin unnd wieder gang und gäbe war / gute gangbare Müntz"</note>, just as we Germans are accustomed to speak in exactly the same way. For the verb "to pass" [עבר] applied to money seems to signify exactly what the Italian phrase *moneta corrente* or the Spanish *de la moneda que corre* <note>meaning "current money"</note> means, as Villalpandus says

<margin>p. 387.</margin>
In this matter at least, a doubt remains whether the silver was stamped or actually weighed out by mass; for Moses testifies that Abraham did not count but weighed out four hundred shekels. So also in Genesis 43:21, the sons of Jacob tell Joseph they are returning the money "according to its weight," by which is mostly understood the quantity or public estimation—which is the power, dignity, price, and value of the coin, commonly called its "rate," "course," or "use." The form of the coin comprises the "image and inscription" [εἰκόνα & ἐπιγραφήν], as witnessed also by Christ, the Master of Truth, when he asks the Jews: "Whose image and inscription is this?" [τίν' ἡ εἰκὼν αὕτη & ἐπιγραφή;] <margin>cf. Roman Triumph, p. 111</margin>. Suetonius calls these "icons" [iconum], by which the money is distinguished. In our language, it is called the "strike" <note>German: "der Schlag"</note>. There were various types of coins among the Hebrews, which I intend only to review. The *Gerah* [גרה] was a silver coin used in the sacred scriptures, weighing as much silver as 16 grains of barley, or two *crucigeri* <note>Kreuzers, a small German coin</note>, which make our "white coin" of 8 obols <margin>cf. Politics 6</margin>. Thus Maimonides <note>referred to here as Rambam</note> says that in the time of Moses our Teacher, it was called a *Gerah* [מועה גרה]

<column-break/>

and consists of 16 barley grains. According to the judgment of Levi ben Gerson and Rabbi Isaiah, it is estimated at a weight of 17 barley grains. Frequent mention of it is made in Exodus 30:13, Leviticus 27:25, Numbers 3:47 and 18:16, and Ezekiel 45:12. It is so named from "to cut off" or "concede" [גרה], as if you were saying a "cut" or "clipped" piece of silver—that is, a small portion—from which this coin was struck. The *Agorah* [אגורה] was likewise a small silver coin of the same value as the Gerah, namely 16 grains or two German Kreuzers, of which explicit mention is made in 1 Samuel 2:36, 1 Kings 2:26, and 2 Kings 22:9. It is so named from "to collect" [אגר], because many characters <note>letters or symbols</note> were collected on this coin. Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] attributes the same weight to it as the Gerah: "The Agorah [אגורה] is of the same weight as the Gerah, twenty of which constitute a Shekel," and Rabbi David [Kimchi] says, "The Agorah is the same as the Gerah." Others, however, feel differently. The *Kesitah* [קשיטה], properly "a lamb," is named from *kashat* [קשט]. Mention of it is made especially in Genesis 33:19, Joshua 24:32, and Job 42:11. In the first passage, the Septuagint [LXX] translates it as "a hundred lambs" [ἑκατὸν ἀμνῶν]. Both Samaritan versions keep the term *Kesitah*. Hence interpreters are divided into two camps: some believe that Jacob exchanged a hundred lambs for that portion of a field, since in those times, before the use of money was devised, it was common to conduct trade by the exchange of livestock. Others, however, understand them as coins on which the figure of lambs or sheep was engraved, just as certain coinage of the Athenians and Romans bore the figure of an "ox or sheep." From this comes the proverb: "An ox on the tongue" <note>referring to someone being bribed into silence</note>. The Argives had a "wolf or mouse"; the Rhegians a "hare"; the Lacedaemonians a "dragon"; the Thessalians a "horse." And we still see coins named after animals today; for example, in Switzerland there are Ravens, Bears [ursati], and the *Batzen* <note>a Swiss coin</note>—about which Zuichemus says in his *Commentary on Civil Law*, p. 371: "Those we call Bazen (Passen) come from the Swiss, who struck a bear upon them." We favor this latter opinion, since it seems more probable that in these passages *Kesitoth* is understood metonymically as coins marked with the image of a lamb, especially since Stephen in Acts 7:16 testifies that Abraham bought it "for a price of silver" [τιμῆς ἀργυρίου]. A fourth type of Hebrew coin was the *Zuz* [זוז] or *Zura*, or as others prefer, *Zuz* [זוז] or *Zuza* [זוזא], mentioned in Tobit 5:21. This word commonly denotes "money," just as among our people it might come under the name of a coin, a denarius, a gold piece, a batzen, or sometimes even a thaler and a ducat. Or it denotes a specific type, and in this sense, a fourth part of a silver shekel, as Elias explains it as "a quadrant of a silver Shekel" [רבע שקל], and Rabbi David Kimchi says, "A Shekel is four Zuzim" [ארבעה זוזים שקל]. It is commonly said to be of the same value as the Greek drachma or the Roman denarius; compare Waser *On Coins*, chapter 20. Also among the coins of the Hebrews was the *Darcon* [דרכמון] or *Adarcon* [אדרכון]. The word appears in 1 Chronicles 29:7, Ezra 2:69, and Nehemiah 7:70. However, there is disagreement about its origin. Brerewood wishes the *Darcon* or *Darcemon* to be so called as if marked with the image of Darius; see the *Biblical Apparatus of the Polyglot*, p. 31, regarding weights, etc. Thus the *Dracmon* will be the same...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES #

<margin>
Money and Weights.
1. Final Paragraph.
</margin>
...it will be that which is called the *Daric* <note>original: "Daricus"; a gold coin of the Persian Empire</note>. The Jews recognize this as Persian currency; the Greeks are favored by the linguistic similarity to the word *dareikon* [δαρεικὸν] or *drachma* [δραχμὴ]. However, since this coin is mentioned under the name *Adarkon* [אדרכון] in the generous and munificent donation of the Leaders of Israel under David for the building of the temple, it should rightly be numbered among the coins of the Hebrews. (Compare Hottinger, *3rd Dissertation on Oriental Coins, p. 103*). Beyond these coins, there is a very ancient tradition received among the Jews that other coins were once in use: those of **Abraham** *featuring the figures of an old man and an old woman*; those of **Joshua** *with a bull and a monoceros* <note>a unicorn or one-horned rhinoceros</note>; those of **David** *with a traveler's pouch and a tower*; and those of **Mordecai** *with the image of a sack and a crown*. Since there is no express mention of these in the Holy Scriptures, nor among authors of proven reliability, we leave them to the Jews for examination. And so we descend to the consideration of the **Shekel**, which in the Holy Language was called *Schekel* [שקל], from the root *shakal* [שקל], *to weigh*, because among the Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Syrians, money was weighed out; that is, its total value was gathered by weight, and the weight of the Shekels was examined. Indeed, this was the principal and most common coin among the Hebrews, just as the Drachma, Mina, and Talent were among the Greeks, and the Denarius and Sestertius were the principal and most common types of money among the Latins. Furthermore, the Shekel served as both a **coin and a weight**. In this section, we consider the Shekel as a coin; a little later, we shall speak of it as a weight. It was two-fold in the Law and among the Hebrews: the **common** and the **sacred**. The former, which was also called the *vulgar, political, or civil* shekel [שקל של חול], the *provincial* shekel [שקל המדינה], and the *royal* shekel [שקל המלך], was already accepted in political affairs (such as among merchants) before the Law was given. Its weight was that of a quarter-thaler <note>The "thaler" was a large silver coin used in Europe during the author's time</note>, concerning which Waser says in his *Book on Hebrew Coins, chapter 5*: *Then, the Imperial German currency established this shekel as a quarter of an ounce of silver, or a thaler; thus, four such shekels make a whole thaler, that is, an ounce of silver.* These words of Waser agree with Hesychius, who says: "the shekel is worth two Attic drachmas" [δύναται δὲ ὁ σίκλος δύο δραχμὰς ἀττικάς]. For the **Sacred Shekel**, as we shall say next,
<margin>See the same work, dist. 4, ch. 28.</margin>
consisted of four drachmas. Villalpandus denies this distinction, claiming it was born only in the brains of the Rabbis and cannot be sufficiently proven from Holy Scripture. Concerning the inscription of the **common shekel**, let us hear the same Waser in the location cited: *In the time of David,* he says, *and his son Solomon, it is believed that the marking and inscription of this common silver shekel was in use such that on one side this was seen:* **Jerusalem the Holy City** [ירושלים עיר הקדש], *with even a citadel depicted; and on the other:* **The King’s Shekel, and his son Solomon the King, David the King** [שקל המלך, ובנו שלמה המלך דוד המלך]. Concerning the **Sacred Shekel**, as they call it (of which it is probable Christ was sold for thirty), order requires that we speak: This is called in the Holy Language the *Holy Shekel* [שקל הקדש]; in the Septuagint [LXX] the *holy* [ἅγιος], which was instituted by God in the Law for sacred matters—namely for the structure and decoration of the Tabernacle or Temple, for the equipment and perfection of the Holy Ministry, for the propitiation of the Divine Power, and for the redemption of each individual. It was twice as large as the common shekel. Thus, it is valued at twenty <term>Gerahs</term> [גרה] <note>the smallest Hebrew weight, similar to an obol</note>, which is half an imperial thaler, so that two ecclesiastical shekels make a whole thaler. Concerning this Sacred Shekel, Josephus writes in Book 3 of the *Antiquities*: "the shekel, being a coin of the Hebrews, contains four Attic drachmas" [ὁ σίκλος νόμισμα ἑβραίων ὢν, ἀττικάς δέχεται δραχμὰς τέσσαρας]. Agreeing with him, Hesychius writes, calling such a sacred shekel an "Attic four-drachma

<column-break/>

coin" [τετράδραχμον ἀττικόν νόμισμα], and Rabbi Jechaias, in the book he titled *The Chain of Tradition* [שלשלת הקבלה] in the *Treatise on Money*, writes thus: *We have learned from the Kabbalah that the sacred shekel weighs 320 grains of barley in pure silver.* Jerome states the same in his *Commentary on Ezekiel, ch. 4*, as do Pagninus in his Lexicon, Maldonado, Jansen, and today almost everyone. Furthermore, there were two principal markings or impressions on the Sacred Shekel: on one face it had the image of a small golden urn which, holding a full <term>Omer</term> [עמר] <note>a dry measure of about 2 liters</note> of manna, was first placed in the Tabernacle and later in the Temple before the Ark (*Exodus 16:33; Hebrews 9:4*). On the other side, however, was the greening rod of Aaron with this inscription: **Jerusalem the Holy** [ירושלים קדושה], while the first side had **Shekel of Israel** [שקל ישראל]. Some feel this Shekel was struck with **Samaritan letters** <note>an older form of the Hebrew script</note> until the defection <note>the schism between the Jews and Samaritans</note> when the Samaritans instituted a new worship and temple, abandoning the divine worship and the Temple at Jerusalem. For then the Jews, out of hatred for that secession, inscribed the Shekel with the letters still in use today. Nor is it a wonder that Samaritan letters were once so common, since Samaria was a city that, from the time of Moses to the time of Elisha, was a most studious cultivator of letters, from which the sons of the Prophets flourished there most greatly. On another sacred Shekel was seen on one side the likeness and name of our Savior **Jesus** [ישוע], and on the other these words: **The Messiah comes in peace; God was made man** [מלך יבא בשלום אלהים אדם עשוי], as the inscription of Theseus Ambrosius has it. Waser’s version, however, says: **Light from Jesus; God made man** [אור בן דוד, אור מאדם עשוי]. In place of these, on some coins, these words are read: **I was born God-Man, God was made man** [אלהים אדם נatus fui, Deus homo factus]. Or as a silver coin in Hottinger’s Table 6, No. 5 has it: **Light made from man** [אור מאדם עשוי]. Besides this common Shekel and the one they think was worth two drachmas, there was found a **half-shekel** with almost the same inscription as the whole shekel, as well as a **third-shekel** of the sacred kind, called by the Hebrews *Shelisith* [שלישית] (from "three"), which Nehemiah imposed upon those returning from Babylonia for the restoration and preservation of the Temple and sacred worship (*Nehemiah 10:32*). There was also a **quarter-shekel** called *Reba* [רבע], in Greek *tetarton* [τέταρτον], mention of which is made in 1 Samuel 9:8. For the rest, whether the sacred shekel was twice as large as the profane one is no small controversy among philologists, some going for the affirmative and some for the negative opinion; see these in Hottinger. <note>unclear section</note> ...whether the sacred shekel was consecrated only for sacred things or also for profane ones. The affirmative pleases Waser in the place cited. To us, however, the negative reasons seem stronger. For **Ezekiel 45:11** suggests the contrary, where justice itself warns that the Princes of the people should not entirely "skin" them, and should abstain from those robberies and most iniquitous usury, using just weights and just measures, namely the ephah, the bath, etc. And verse 12 continues: **The shekel shall be twenty gerahs** [השקל עשרים גרה]; it must be understood from the context that: *A shekel shall be worth twenty gerahs among you.* Indeed, matters had reached such a point (as Amos also complains in chapter 8:5) that they would set up deceitful scales, diminish the measure, and **enlarge the shekel**, which Cornelius à Lapide and Francisco Ribera thought happened whenever they used deceitful balances. Specifically, one scale-pan—in which the shekel was to be weighed to see if it was of the just weight...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Hebrew currency and weights, specifically analyzing the shekel as used in trade and biblical history, before moving to larger units like the Mina and the Talent.</meta>

<header>Amos VIII, 5.</header>

<margin>Money & Weights.</margin>...of the weight, *which those buying would pay for the goods purchased, was made heavier and more burdensome. Thus, a shekel of the correct weight, when placed on these deceitful scales, would appear lighter than it should; as a consequence, those buying were forced to add several extra silver drachmas.* The Prophet <note>referring to Amos 8:5, which critiques merchants who "make the ephah small and the shekel great" through fraud</note> is speaking of that shekel which was supposed to contain 20 gerahs, and which was then in use among all the common people, but which the wicked greed of the wealthy increased or diminished according to their own authority and whim. Now, truly, if the **Sacred Shekel** had been intended solely for sacred uses, the Jews could not have used it in buying and selling other things—a practice which the Prophet seems to imply here. As to how the value of Shekels can be equated to the money of our own century, Willebrord Snellius <margin>*On Matters of Coinage, p. 68, 69.*</margin> provides the following comparisons:

**Abraham** (Genesis 23:15) bought a field from Ephron the Hittite for a burial place for 400 *shekels of silver*, which equals 160 French crowns, or 234⅔ imperial thalers <note>The thaler was a standard large silver coin used throughout Europe in the author's time</note>.

In Exodus 21:32, a fine of 30 shekels of silver is written for the Master whose ox kills another’s servant; this would be 12 French crowns.

**Achan** confessed to stealing 200 silver shekels by sacrilege (Joshua 7:21), which are 80 French crowns.

**Menahem** levied fifty shekels per man from the people of Israel to be given as a gift to the King of Assyria (2 Kings 15:20), which is 20 French crowns per person.

When the Midianites were utterly destroyed (Numbers 31:32) and no soldier was missing from the Israelite camp, they consecrated to God all the gold they had gathered from the spoils. That entire gold offering which they presented to Jehovah was 16,750 Shekels. This is to be understood by the weight of the gold: 16,750 half-ounces of gold, or 8,375 ounces. The total sum of this votive gold is 33,500 crowns.

**David** (2 Samuel 24:24) bought a threshing floor and oxen for 50 shekels to build an altar, which equals 20 French crowns. For that same site, Ornan (1 Chronicles 21:25) weighed out 600 gold shekels of just weight; this is understood to be for the entirety of Mount Moriah, where Solomon later built the Temple to the Lord, and equals 300 ounces of gold.

The iron head of **Goliath’s** spear was 600 shekels in weight (1 Samuel 17:7), which is 300 ounces or 25 pounds, assigning 12 ounces to each pound. From this, the size and thickness of the rest of the spear—likened to a weaver’s beam—is not difficult to estimate. And so much for the Shekel insofar as it constituted a coin. Let us briefly discuss the Shekel as it functioned as a measure of weight for gold, silver, bronze, iron, and other metals—using the words of Alsted <margin>*Prolegomena of Theology, book 2, p. 554.*</margin>: The **Sacred Shekel** of gold weighed four Hungarian gold pieces; the **common** shekel weighed two. For the sacred, see Numbers 7:50 and 31:52. For the common, Genesis 24:22, Joshua 7:21, 2 Chronicles 3:9, Judges 8:26, 1 Kings 10:16, and 2 Chronicles 9:6. The **Sacred Shekel** of silver weighed half an imperial thaler; the **common** shekel, a quarter of an imperial thaler. Thus, for example, for the value of a sacred silver shekel, they weigh out as much silver as ten ounces should weigh, or ten imperial thalers; and conversely, twenty common shekels weigh as much as five ounces. The **Royal Shekel** weighed a *tetradrachm* <note>a Greek silver coin worth four drachmas</note>, or three drams <note>original: "drein quentlein"</note>, or what they call a fourth part of an imperial thaler and a half. For the sacred silver shekel, see Numbers 7 and 13. For the common, 2 Samuel 14:27. The **Sacred Shekel of bronze** and iron should be measured at the rate of half-ounces; the **common** at the rate of two drachmas, as was done above; see 2 Samuel 21:16 and 1 Samuel 17:5, 7. This concludes the discussion of the Shekel as a weight.

מנה, **Maneh** or **Minah**, which also functions as a *coin* (even if it was not a specific minted coin but a fixed sum) and as a *weight*, is called *mnea* [μνέα] or *mna* [μνᾶ] by the Greeks. Aeschines mentions it <margin>*In Ctesiphontem.*</margin>: *They pledged the public revenues to him for three talents, and did they bring the bribe to Demosthenes in a drachma, or a mina, or minas, until they paid back the principal?* <note>original Greek: "Υπέθεσαν αὐτῷ γ τάλαντα τὰς δημοσίας προσόδους..."</note> He is speaking of the pledging of public income under the name of a talent. Furthermore, one **Sanctuary Mina** was worth 60 lots <note>a unit of weight, roughly 1/2 ounce</note> or 30 imperial thalers. The other, the **vulgar** <note>common</note> mina, was worth 30 lots or 15 imperial thalers. Among the Greeks, it consisted of twenty-five *staters* <note>another Greek coin</note> of its kind, one hundred drachmas, or six hundred obols. This was established in Athens by Solon; previously, before the *seisachtheia* <note>Solon's "shaking off of debts" reform</note>, it was 73 drachmas, as Plutarch records in *Life of Solon*: *He made the mina consist of one hundred drachmas, whereas it had previously been seventy-three.* <note>original Greek: "ἑκατὸν ἐποίησε δραχμῶν τὴν μνᾶν..."</note> From that time, Snellius posits <margin>*On Matters of Coinage, p. 46.*</margin> that the decimal (hundred-count) was received among all nations, citing the testimony of Pliny, Hero, Pollux, Plutarch, and Livy. Taken as a weight, the **common Maneh** weighed 60 double-drachmas or 15 imperial thalers; the **royal** weighed 40 triple-drachmas; and that of the **Sanctuary** weighed 240 Attic drachmas, which is 60 lots or 30 imperial thalers. However, this Mina of the Hebrews was distinct from the Egyptian and Antiochian Minas, which weighed 133⅓ Attic drachmas.

The same principle applies to ככר **Cicar**, or **Kikar** as others write it <note>the Talent</note>. For it functions as both a coin and a weight, hence it is called both monetary and ponderous. It was either sacred or common. The **Sacred Talent** contained 3,000 sacred shekels; therefore, in gold, it was 12,000 ducats, and in silver, 1,500 thalers. The **Common Talent**, which they also called Royal, contained three thousand common shekels; therefore, in gold, it was 6,000 ducats, and in silver, 750 imperial thalers. This matched the former in terms of weight. Regarding the talent by which Moses weighed the silver, bronze, and gold in the construction of the Tabernacle, Snellius writes that it was 120 Attic minas. For if you subtract the double of 1,775 (which is 3,550 half-shekels) from 603,550, the remaining 600,000 half-shekels make one hundred talents, with 6,000 half-shekels in each. Moreover, Josephus <margin>3 *Antiquities* 39</margin> teaches that a Shekel is equal to an Attic tetradrachm; therefore, a half-shekel equals two drachmas, and 6,000 half-shekels equal 12,000 drachmas. Thus, 120 Attic minas will equal one Mosaic talent, because 100 drachmas make a mina. Shortly thereafter, he weighed the bronze by the same weight. And so, from the *name of a weight*, the meaning of the **talent** passed over to the *coinage*; for when a certain sum of money was struck from a certain number of pounds of silver, a heap of several such pounds was called a *talent*. Hence, every talent—whether it be placed for any weight whatever or for a sum of money—contains, according to Snellius's calculation <margin>*ibid. p. 40.*</margin>, 60 minas of its kind, 1,500 staters, 6,000 drachmas, or 48,000 obols.

<meta>This page continues the technical and moral discussion of biblical standards, shifting from the specific values of the shekel to the broader categories of weights and measures (linear and capacity), while maintaining the critique of commercial fraud found in the Prophet Amos.</meta>

### ANTIQUITIES OF THE BIBLE

<margin>Money & Weights.</margin> Things that consist of number, weight, and measure are used in three ways, according to the observation of Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a leading scholar of the Renaissance</note> in his work *On Coinage, p. 23*: either *according to an exact calculation*, or *according to more*, or *according to less*. The correct standard, which is called *exact calculation* <note>original Greek: ἀπαρτιλογία</note>, is termed *currency* <note>original Greek: νόμισμα (nomisma)</note>. Thus, in coinage it is *silver currency*; in weights, *weight currency*; and in measures, *measure currency*. In Athens, according to Suidas, those officials who took care and saw to it that all things were distributed and sold by *just measure* were called *Metronomoi* <note>original Greek: Μετρονόμοι, meaning "law-givers of measure"</note>; fifteen of them were in the Piraeus <note>the port of Athens</note>, while nine were in the city. We believe it is not unworthy of mention that various languages agree on the names for measuring; for both the Greeks, Latins, Germans, and Dutch have retained the root <term>מדה</term> <note>Middah: Hebrew for measure</note>. Indeed, the origin clearly relates back to the Greek *metreo*, the Latin *metior*, the German *Messen* / <term>מדה</term> Mas / and the Dutch *maet* / measure, *metron*. This is perhaps for the purpose of showing that God demands a just weight and an uncorrupted measure. Thus Moses, taught by God, promulgated the equity of *Weight and Measure*, lest any deceit or fraud should arise from that matter thereafter. Indeed, after many sound precepts, after a just scale and equal weights, he also makes mention of the *Ephah* and the *Hin*—or as the Hebrew has it, <term>Ephi</term> and <term>Hin</term>—intending for the former to safeguard dry goods and the latter for liquids. Among the measures of continuous length, the <term>אמה</term> <note>Amah</note> or **Cubit** deserves meditation. First, there is the *sacred cubit*, which was used for sacred structures: hence the *cubit of the Sanctuary*, and the *cubit of truth* or the *true cubit*; likewise the *cubit of the building* (that is, of the Temple). Then there is the <term>common cubit</term>, which architects used in measuring civil matters. Next is the <term>חבל</term> <note>Chevel</note>, the *measuring cord*, with which the Hebrews and other Eastern peoples were accustomed to divide ancestral land (Amos 7:17, 10:17, 2). However, the length of that instrument varied among different peoples, so it cannot be precisely defined by us. He who measured fields with a cord was called an *arvipendiator* <note>a Latin term for land-surveyor</note>, from which comes the French *arpenteur*. The term *arvipendium* is said to come from *weighing the fields* <note>Latin: ab arvis pendendis</note>, that is, *measuring* them, regarding which Salmasius writes in *Solen. p. 683*. Regarding this, Ambrose <margin>Commentary on Psalm 118, Sermon 8, p. 654.</margin> says: *There are cords which they use who measure the boundaries of fields, distinguish limits, and determine the spaces of possessions. Those cords are stretched out as far as each person's possession extends. Thus was Israel made the cord of His inheritance.* These, therefore, are "good cords." The term is also used metonymically for a "region" (Deuteronomy 3:4, Zephaniah 2:5). Regarding this usage, Jacobus de Valentia <margin>On Psalm 15, folio 108.</margin> notes: *Observe that 'cords,' 'cord,' and 'measuring line' are commonly used in Holy Scripture for a lot and an ancestral portion, because inheritances and portions of land were measured with cords or lines, and thus portions were distributed among brothers and kinsmen according to merit, as is clear in the book of Joshua, who measured and distributed the whole Promised Land with cords. Even so, God, according to the cord and purpose of His will, has from eternity predestined and prepared various mansions for His elect in the kingdom of heaven, which the Son afterwards distributed to those same elect called and justified through Him.* Similarly, the <term>Reed</term> <term>קנה</term> <note>Kaneh</note> is reckoned among the types of measure, which makes ten feet. Hero and others in Salmasius testify that the Egyptians were accustomed to measure their fields *with ropes and reeds* <note>original Greek: τοῖς σχοίνοις καὶ τοῖς καλάμοις</note>, for they had an abundance of these. Mention of this instrument is also made in Ezekiel 40:3, 6.

<column-break/>

In Ezekiel 42:16, he measured the East side with the measuring reed, <term>חמש אמות קנים</term> <note>five hundred reeds</note>. Capellus <note>Louis Cappel (1585–1658), a French Protestant scholar of the Hebrew Bible</note> suggests it should read <term>מאת</term> <note>hundred (cubits)</note>, because the following measurements require it, and that is how the Septuagint, Vulgate, Targum, and Masoretes read it. Yet the Septuagint seems to follow both readings; for although when they measure the East, West, and South sides they have only *five hundred* <note>Greek: πεντακοσίους</note>, yet when they measure the North side they have *five hundred cubits* <note>Greek: πήχεις πεντακοσίους</note>. From this, it seems they read it as *five hundred cubits* in that place, and in none of these four sides do they read *reeds* <note>Greek: calamos</note>, from which it is manifest that they understood this measure not as reeds but as cubits. The Vulgate counts five hundred reeds on each side, but in the final verse, where the same measure seems to be repeated, the Prophet speaks thus: *He measured its four sides; and it had a wall all around, the length of which was five hundred, and the breadth <term>חמש מאות</term> five hundred, namely, of reeds.* Jerome, however, implies *cubits*, taking the breadth of the wall to mean its thickness or depth, not the length of the courtyard. In that place, the Angel is not measuring the court of the people, which was five hundred cubits on each side, but is measuring the circuit of the mountain itself upon which the temple was set, which was five hundred reeds. These are the thoughts of Capellus. In our prophetic passage, among the names of measures, there occurs the <term>איפה</term>, <term>ephah</term>, which was a larger measure among the Hebrews, containing as much in dry goods as a *bath* did in liquids (Ezekiel 45:11, compare Isaiah 5:10). It contained three <term>Sata</term> or <term>Seah</term>, which are mentioned in Genesis 18:6, 1 Samuel 24:18, and elsewhere; these make ten *Omer* <note>Homer</note> or eighteen *Kabs*. The <term>Cor</term> <note>Corus</note> was the largest measure of the Hebrews for dry goods, which held ten Ephahs or 30 Seah. But exactly how much an Ephah or any other measure, whether dry or liquid, would be compared to modern standards is a matter for a laborious commentary and difficult experimentation. Many have attempted it, but not all with the same or equal success. Blessed Johannes Major, in his commentary on the book of Ruth—which, as far as I remember, is *unpublished* <note>Greek: ἀνεκδότῳ</note>—compared them and calculated them against the measures used in Jena <note>A university city in Germany</note>. In this context, all other measures are understood through "synecdoche" <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note>. For the Ephah was not only the most common and familiar measure, but also the most noble (Deuteronomy 25:14, Proverbs 20:10), where Martin Luther also generally translated it as *Measure* <note>German: Mas</note>. For those "scourgers" <note>greedy merchants</note> were diminishing the other measures as well, and for that reason they are scourged here by Amos. For it is not enough for these "Dardanians" and "Nabals" <note>classical and biblical archetypes of greedy or foolish men</note> to diminish measures, increase prices, and weigh things deceitfully; they have even reached such a point of wickedness that they would buy grain with a larger bushel and sell it with a smaller one, contrary to the most severe interdict of the Lord (Leviticus 19:35, 36; Deuteronomy 25:13, 16; Ezekiel 45:10, 11). There is a proverb about this in the Gemara <note>a component of the Talmud</note>: *A large Kab and a small Kab shall roll away and go down to hell*, as Drusius interprets it. The Prophet further exaggerates their lust and *greed* <note>Greek: πλεονεξίαν</note> for making profit by portraying them as wishing for the month to pass so they might decrease the measure. By <term>חדש</term> <note>Chodesh</note>, some understand any period of time; others, the first day of each month, which the Greeks call the Calends and the Septuagint calls the *New Moon* <note>Greek: νεομηνίαν</note> (1 Samuel).

It frames these standards as divinely ordained laws meant to prevent the commercial fraud and greed condemned by the Prophet Amos.</summary>

<header>Amos VIII, 5. <note>Amos 8:5: "When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell corn? and the sabbath, that we may set forth wheat, making the ephah small, and the shekel great, and falsifying the balances by deceit?"</note></header>

Regarding 1 Samuel 20:5 and 2 Kings 4:23, some interpret this as the sacred month—the seventh month, September—in which people rested almost entirely after the harvest was gathered (Leviticus 23:23). Others suggest it refers to an emblematic month, which was added to the twelve every three years so the lunar year would equal the solar year. You may see these interpretations expanded upon at length in the works of Cornelius à Lapide and others. However, without a doubt, the expression is general; it refers not to a specific month or day of the year, but to a "month" defined by the greedy themselves. Indeed, any time that delayed these <term>miserly ones</term> <note>original Greek: Φειδωλῶν (Pheidolōn), referring to those who are excessively stingy</note> and "scourgers of the grain supply" <note>profiteers who drove up prices</note> from their predatory and shameful trade was loathsome and burdensome to them. Among the evils of a Republic, there is none worse than the adulteration of measures and currency. Around the year 1327 AD, a terrible debasement of currency prevailed in Bohemia, leading to the complaints of the common people and craftsmen described by the author of the *Chronicle of the Royal Hall*, commonly known as the <term>Königs-Saal Chronicle</term>:

> For every shoemaker said of these coins: "I am abused."
> And the Tailor said: "By these coins I am too much constrained."
> The baker laments: "All my profit is numbed by these coins." 
> Even the smith becomes sad over these small pennies. 
> The peasant in the fields mocks this.
> Crowds of craftsmen in the city cry out over this.
> They wish the wicked money were quickly destroyed,
> For no one is exempt from suffering loss
> Through such fraud; if it ceases, then sing praise!

This was loathsome to every conscientious and pious Magistrate. Thus Boleslaus of Bohemia wrote to his son, Boleslaus III (as recorded by Cosmas of Prague):
<margin>book 1.</margin>
*No disaster, no plague, nor mortality, nor enemies devastating the whole land with plunder and fire would harm the people of God more than the frequent changing and fraudulent debasement of the coinage.* This can rightly be said of every such adulteration. Therefore, Solomon, the wisest of Kings, warns in four places in the book of Proverbs that those who vary weights, measures, and scales do an abominable thing. He speaks elegantly
<margin>
Prov. 11:1.
*Deceitful balances
</margin>
of these deceits, saying: <gloss>Deceitful scales are an abomination before the Lord.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: מאזני מרמה תועבת יהוה; original Greek: ζυγοὶ δόλιοι βδέλυγμα ἐνώπιον Κυρίου</note>. Conversely, a just weight will please God; hence he adds: <gloss>A perfect weight is His delight.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: ואבן שלמה רצונו; original Greek: στάθμιον δὲ δίκαιον δεκτὸν αὐτῷ</note>. In the Hebrew, the word <term>stone</term> <note>Hebrew: אבן (eben)</note> is used for "weight," because small stones were used as weights. With a singular passion, he censures this perfidy more than once; and as it is said, "beautiful things should be repeated seven times," so the Wise Man in chapter 20, verse 10, instills the same:
<gloss>A stone and a stone, a measure and a measure, both of these are an abomination to Jehovah.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: אבן ואבן איפה ואיפה תועבת יהוה גם שניהם</note> Literally: "A stone and a stone" means having two different weights (one for buying, one for selling). He repeats this Hebrew idiom in verse 23, explaining it as he writes: <gloss>A stone and a stone (diverse weights) are an abomination to Jehovah, and a deceitful balance is not good.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: תועבת יהוה אבן ואבן ומאזני מרמה לא־טוב</note> These people are most hateful to God—those who, in shops and markets, commit the crime of forgery. The laws rightly punish them, such as the *Lex Cornelia* regarding forgers, which punishes the crime of false weights. Among good men, business ought to be conducted in good faith. 

<column-break/>

Profit is not profit, but a loss, when it is sought through deceitful scales in contracts and other acts of buying and selling. While foul gain is sought, the soul suffers a loss of conscience and the ruin of fortunes.

## Jonah I. 2.

->Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city<-
<note>original Hebrew: קום לך אל־נינוה העיר הגדולה</note>
->Arise, and go to Nineveh the great city.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἀνάστηθι, καὶ πορεύθητι εἰς Νινευῒ τὴν πόλιν τὴν μεγάλην</note>
->Arise, and go into Nineveh the great city.<-
<note>original Latin: Surge, & vade in Niniven civitatem grandem</note>

<margin>The size of the City of Nineveh.</margin>
In topographical matters, the reader will not fail to notice how useful it is to read secular writers. We shall be content with a single example: the size of *Nineveh*. It is declared more than once in the history of Jonah that it was an exceedingly large city; for it is called by Jonah <margin>chapter 3:3.</margin> <gloss>a city great to God</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: עיר־גדola לאלהים (Ir-gedolah l'Elohim)</note>, that is, of the highest and most admirable magnitude. For when the Hebrews wish to signify something grand and extraordinary above all others, they add the genitive or dative of "God" to exaggerate the matter, because nothing but what is great is suitable for God. Thus Rabbi David Kimchi <margin>* Commentaries on 1 Sam 16 and Psalm 68.</margin> says: <gloss>A thing which the Scripture wishes to magnify, it joins to God or the name of God for the sake of greatness.</gloss> And elsewhere: <gloss>The word Elohim is a title for the greatest and most wonderful things.</gloss> This eulogy and addition is attributed to no city in the Holy Scriptures except this one. For that reason, it is not only an <term>emphasis</term> <note>original Greek: ἔμφασιν</note> or a distinction by which this city is expressly discerned from others, but also <term>explanatory</term> and <term>superlative</term> <note>original Greek: ἐξήγητικὸν καὶ πλεοναστικὸν</note>, illustrating its greatness because it was the metropolis of the kingdom and the royal seat of the Kings of Assyria. Abarbenel respects this when he says: <gloss>Because the thrones of the Assyrian Kings were placed there, it is the metropolis of their kingdom.</gloss> Nineveh was a most powerful city and the metropolis of the whole Assyrian empire, built by Nimrod (Genesis 10:11, 12). Others, however, make its first founder <term>Asshur</term>, the grandson of Noah through Shem. Thus commentators fall into conflicting opinions, though all appeal to the words of Moses in the place cited above. The disagreement is chiefly regarding verse 11: <gloss>From that land went forth Asshur, and built Nineveh, and the streets of the city, and Calah.</gloss> Verse 12: <gloss>Resen also between Nineveh and Calah: this is the great city.</gloss> Junius and Tremellius, however, interpret verses 11 and 12 thus: *And from this land he proceeded into Assyria, where he built Nineveh, and the city of Rechoboth, and Calah: and Resen between Nineveh and Calah: That is that great city.* Pagninus and Arias Montanus agree with the Vulgate (except that they seem to depart from Jerome and the Chaldean translation, who translate the name *Rechoboth* as "streets" and take it as a common noun). Those authors, however, correctly retain the Hebrew name of the city, which was a very large and beautiful city situated near the Euphrates, surrounded on all sides by walls, extremely well-fortified, and furnished with the most beautiful suburbs of gardens and paradises, as Benjamin [of Tudela] speaks in his *Itinerary*. <margin>concerning this</margin>

<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>
The magnitude of the city of Nineveh.
</margin>
<margin>
On this word, see B. Gerhard, *Commentary on Genesis*, p. 258. B. Fr. *Commentary on Genesis*, p. 47. B. Glass, *Sacred Rhetoric*, Book 4, Treatise 1, p. 780.
</margin>
**Asshur** is interpreted by some as the proper name of a man—specifically, the son of Shem. They claim that he departed from the land of Shinar or Chaldea either **voluntarily** <note>original Greek: ἑκουσίως (hekousiōs)</note>, of his own accord to avoid the reputation of colluding with Nimrod, or **unwillingly** <note>original Greek: ἄκοντι (akonti)</note>, driven out by Nimrod’s tyranny and cruelty. He is then said to have built Nineveh, the metropolis of all Assyria, in that region of Asia which was later named after him. Others, however, who follow in the footsteps of Junius and Tremellius, interpret the word as the region itself. They suggest a <term>prepositional ellipsis</term> <note>a grammatical omission where a word like "into" is implied but not written</note> of the letter **L** <note>the Hebrew prefix ל (le), meaning "to" or "into"</note>, which is very common in Holy Scripture. In this view, Nimrod, not content with his own domains, invaded the land and, as the text says, built four cities there, the primary one and capital being Nineveh.

Indeed, they argue that Moses—God’s Chancellor and the historiographer of the first birth of the world—is engaged from verse 6 through verse 20 in recounting the genealogy of the sons and descendants of Ham **continuously** <note>original Greek: ἀδιακόπως (adiakopōs)</note>. There appears to be no firm trace in the text as to why he would have felt the need to speak of Asshur (who is not mentioned until verse 22 among the other sons of Shem) by interrupting the order of the narrative. Rather, he continues the discourse begun concerning Ham and his sons, and mentions Nimrod as a tyrant subjugating neighboring regions and exercising his tyranny over them as he pleased. Using a common phrase in Scripture (compare Judges 2:15, 11:3, and 2 Samuel 11:1), he is said to have "gone out" to expand the borders of his kingdom into neighboring Assyria. Having conquered it, he added it to his previous kingdom, and to keep it in subjection, he founded four heavily fortified cities within it, chief among which was Nineveh. See the works of Blessed Gerhard and Friedlieb cited above, as well as
<margin>
*Sacred Geography*, Book 4, ch. 12, pages 259, 260.
</margin>
Samuel Bochart*, who defends this latter assertion with six arguments. To this we may add, as Bochart testifies, that Diodorus (citing Ctesias) and others teach that Ninus and Babylon had the same masters from the very beginning, and that the famous Belus, who was worshipped in Babylon, was the father of Ninus, from whom Nineveh took its name. Thus, it is most frequently called **Ninus** by secular writers (compare Strabo Book 16, Pliny 6:13, 26, Ptolemy’s *Geography* 16:1, Lucan Book 3, Ammianus Marcellinus Book 23, and Athenaeus Book 12). However, they were not ignorant of the other name, hence Ptolemy in Book 8 calls it "that which is both Ninus and Nineveh" <note>original Greek: ἡ καὶ Νινὸς ἡ καὶ Νινεῦΐ</note>.

The name is derived from King Ninus, from the Hebrew *Neveh* <note>נוה</note>, meaning "habitation," and *Nin* <note>נין</note>, meaning "Ninus." Thus, according to Hebrew **analogy** <note>original Greek: κατ' ἀναλογίαν</note> and the dropping of the second letter **N**, it is called *Neveh Nin* <note>נוה נין</note> instead of *Neveh Ninn*, meaning the "Habitation of Ninus." Although Junius prefers the Hebrew name Nineveh to be a compound word meaning "pleasant habitation," from *Ninus* and *Na'ah* <note>נוה</note>, "beautiful," as if to say *Ninus the pleasant* or *the beautiful*. Aben Ezra, in his commentary on Jonah, mentions that this city (according to the translation of Drusius and Mercerus) was also called **Aurtia**. The words of Aben Ezra in that place are: *Which is called Aurtia; and the wise men of Israel who are in the land of Greece say that this is Nineveh.* But Samuel Bochart*
<margin>
Cited place, p. 273.
</margin>
thinks that *Aurtia* can better be referred to Assyria. I will transcribe his words in full, since his book is in the hands of few: "It has escaped Mercerus, Drusius, and others," he says, "that **Aurtia** <note>אורטיא</note> in Aben Ezra is a corruption of **Aturia** or **Atyria** for Assyria (with the letter S changed to T in the Chaldean manner)."

<column-break/>

When Aben Ezra says in his notes on Jonah 1: *Nineveh was Assyria, which is today desolate,* and says that the wise men of Israel in Greece call that land **Aurtia**, we should read it as **Aturia** <note>אטוריא</note>. If the letter T is restored from the fourth position to the second, that reading is correct. Learned men intend this as the name of the *land*, not the city. For why give a city a name it does not have?

Regarding the location of the city, which is the theme of our discussion: It was situated in Assyria by the River Tigris, in the region called Adiabene, according to Ammianus Marcellinus (Book 18). Strabo calls it the "City of Ninus," while Josephus calls it the **Royal City of Ninus** <note>original Greek: Νῖνος Βασίλεια</note>. Therefore, it must be distinguished from the "Chaldean" or "Euphratensian" Nineveh located near the Euphrates in Syria Comagena, which is elsewhere hailed as Ninus and is very often confused with that most famous city of Assyria, as Bochart concludes (Book 4, ch. 20, p. 282) from Philostratus and Ammianus. There is also another small town of this name located in the corner of Arabia, mentioned by Eusebius in his book on Hebrew places, as reported by Drusius*: "There is also another city of the Jews," he says, "even to this day, named Nineveh, in a corner of Arabia, which they now corruptly call Nineveh."

We must proceed further and examine from both literary sources the width and magnitude of this city, once so celebrated in the Eastern region. It is called **Great** <note>Hebrew: גדולה (Gedolah)</note> in Jonah 3:3, with the epithet **of God** <note>Hebrew: לאלהים (l'Elohim)</note>. As we noted above, this was added by the Holy Spirit as an **intensifier** <note>original Greek: αὐξητικὸν (auxētikon)</note> to indicate the city's vast size. Some call it "great before God," as Blessed Glassius teaches (*Sacred Philology*, Book 3, Tr. 1, p. 62), where the divine epithet is used for something supreme, excellent, maximum, or most vehement.

However, these explanations do not please Rabbi Aben Ezra. He thinks the phrase indicates the piety of the Ninevites—handed down to them from their ancestors and predecessors—rather than the city's size. We cite his words from his commentary on Jonah 1:2, following our interpreter Johannes Leusden, Professor at Utrecht:

> "The city was great to God because they had feared the Lord of old. But as for him who explains that it was a city 'great and precious in the eyes of the Lord' to save it, this is not according to the custom of the language. For it is written, 'my way shall be great in the eyes of the Lord,' not 'to the Lord.' And behold, it is written: 'all nations are as nothing before Him,' and He does not care, even for the ends of the earth. And the exposition 'to God' is because they feared the Lord in ancient days; but now in the days of Jonah they began to act wickedly. And were it not for the fact that they had been men of God in the beginning, He would not have sent His Prophet to them. And so we see that they returned with a repentance that has no equal. And you will not find it written that there were altars of Baal, or that they cut down idols; behold, from this we learn that they were not worshippers of idols."

But these arguments are not of such weight for establishing a true worship of the true God among the Ninevites from ancient days that we should depart from the common interpretation. Indeed, this case <note>the dative case "to God"</note> is attached indifferently in the Holy Books to created things, both animate and inanimate, as Blessed Glassius shows with innumerable examples in the work cited above. <meta>Continuing the discussion from the previous page regarding the origins of Nineveh, the author now turns to the specific descriptions of the city's size as recorded in the Book of Jonah, debating whether its "greatness" is merely a figure of speech or a literal description of its physical vastness and divine importance.</meta>

# Jonah 1:2.

<margin>The magnitude of the city of Nineveh.</margin>
We oppose this small point. For Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a prominent Jewish statesman and theologian</note> refutes the reasoning of Ibn Ezra <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a renowned Spanish-Jewish scholar</note>, saying: He calls Nineveh a
<margin>(The Prophet)</margin>
<margin>Commentary on Jonah, chapter 3.</margin>
great city to accommodate the ears of the Prophet and to persuade him that, because of the city's greatness, God Himself is concerned with it. From this he further says, "Nineveh was a city great to God." This is not the sense of Ibn Ezra, for the land of Asshur and the people inhabiting it were impious and enormous sinners; rather, the title "of God" is attributed to it because of its magnitude, just as we say "mountains of God" for the highest peaks, or "the flame of God," and similar expressions. It was great primarily because the King resided there. We oppose him with the **universal worship** <note>original Greek: *πανσέβειαν* (pansebeian)</note> of divine service, contrasting it with the universal flood of idolatry throughout the world, so much so that not even Abraham and his fathers were said to be immune from idolatry, but served foreign gods (Joshua 24:3). What shall we say of others? Let us touch upon what is said in 2 Kings 17 regarding the Assyrian peoples placed by Shalmaneser in the location of the exiled Israelites: each worshipped their own petty gods. How, then, will the Rabbi free the predecessors of the Ninevites from the superstition of these petty gods? Furthermore, this fellow <note>original: *Verpulus*, a derogatory Latin term for a circumcised person</note> betrays his envy toward the nations—namely, the Christians—whom he knows as well as his own finger have succeeded as God's special property, the branches having been cast out through unbelief (that is, those who are sons of Abraham by nature but not by faith). For if it is not inconsistent for the title "of God" to be granted to an inanimate object in the Holy Scriptures, what prevents the same from being said of the nations, who were created in the image of God along with the Jews at the very origin of things? Our Great Hero <note>original: *Megalander*, a title of high honor</note> Luther answers perfectly
<margin>Commentary on Genesis chapter 30, folio 453b.</margin>
on our behalf, as his words are cited by the Blessed Glassius in Book 5, page 66: *Santes Pagninus and Munster,* he says, *translate: "With the wrestlings of God I have wrestled with my sister" [Genesis 30:8]. And they add this reason: that in the Hebrew language, all magnificent things are called divine. Hence the "City of God" Nineveh, that is, magnificent; the "Cedar of God," that is, lofty and great. However, although I do not claim for myself the final judgment on the Hebrew language, I nonetheless hate the audacity of distorting things that were spoken simply. As if Nineveh were not also a city of God in its uncircumcision, but only the circumcised were the people of God! All these things flow from the pride and arrogance of the Jews, who cannot bear to have anything called magnificent <note>Translator's note: for "called magnificent," it seems it ought to read "called divine," or "of God," for the preceding and following sections show this.</note> unless it pertains to themselves. And on chapter 13, folio 172, regarding the passage: "Sodom and Gomorrah were like the garden of the Lord" [Genesis 13:10]: This interpretation is invented by the Jews out of their excessive wisdom and innate pride, so that they alone might be called the people of God and not the nations. Nineveh, they say, cannot be called a city of God as if God dwelt there, as He did with us in Jerusalem; the reason for this title is simply that it is a great and august city. But this explanation is vain. For we know that God is also the God of the nations, even in a temporal sense. Nineveh is therefore called the city of God because God gave it its growth and blessing, and He cares for and governs it. So the "trees of God" are those which the Lord made and cares for, providing rain, sun, and winds, from which they take their growth, even if the impious possess them. And indeed, it is no small consolation that He establishes, preserves, and protects empires; they do not, as we mostly think,*

<column-break/>

<margin>The magnitude of the city of Nineveh.</margin>
*either grow or fall by chance. The nations do not see this governance, but dream that empires are established and governed by their own industry. In Hannibal there were greater gifts, with which a great mind and singular industry successfully manage affairs; by these, he thought he would conquer the Romans. In Alexander the Great we see the same. We do not see the divine governance by which empires are either stabilized or overturned. This is the true meaning of why Nineveh is called the city of God: for they are governed and nurtured so that they may increase. For although human industry and labor also help, these would be in vain without the blessing of God. And who, I ask, cares for the woods and groves, who cares for the trees in the vast wildernesses? Thus Christ says: "Your heavenly Father makes His sun to rise on the good and the bad." He calls the sun "God's sun," which He himself created to give life to nature. In this way, this garden [Genesis 13:10] is called the "garden of God," not as the foolish Jews claim because it is merely large, but because it is cultivated not only by the hands and zeal of men, but divinely, with the Lord making it fruitful and blessing it.* Thus far the Blessed Luther. But the Holy Spirit proceeds in describing the
<margin>chapter 3:3.</margin>
vastness of this city, calling it **great, a journey of three days** <note>original Hebrew: *מהלך שלשת ימים* (mahalakh sheloshet yamim)</note>. Regarding this "three days' journey," commentators disagree. In explaining this, we find Rabbi David Kimchi <note>c. 1160–1235, a major medieval Hebrew grammarian and commentator</note> occupied, who explains it as the length in a straight line, drawn through the diameter **from one end to the other** <note>original Hebrew: *מן קצה אל הקצה* (min katzeh el ha-katzeh)</note>; and Rabbi Abarbanel, who uses the same measure, namely **from one gate to another** <note>original Hebrew: *משער לשער* (mi-sha'ar le-sha'ar)</note>. But this opinion extends the city beyond belief and disagrees with secular history. More likely is the opinion of Luther, Vatablus, and others, who understand it as the time for surveying the individual streets in a three-day period; however, in this view, the city seems to be enclosed in limits shorter than is right. Therefore, we think the opinion of those who explain it as the circuit of the walls or the circumference of the city within a **three-day period** <note>original Greek: *τριήμερον* (triēmeron)</note> should be preferred. Thus Rabbi Ibn Ezra: **A journey of three days in the circuit of the city, which is a journey of one day from end to end** <note>original Hebrew: *מהלך שלשת ימים בסביב המדינה והיא מהלך יום אחד מן הקצה אל הקצה*</note>. Nor should this
<margin>Historical Library, Book 2.</margin>
seem strange to anyone, for it is established from Diodorus Siculus <note>a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> that the circuit of the city was 480 <term>stadia</term> <note>an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet or 185 meters</note>. It was extended in length, as witnessed by Pliny (Book 6, chapter 13) and Fuller (Sacred Miscellany 3, p. 6), toward the Tigris River facing the sunset, for 150 stadia; in width for 90 stadia. A city of truly stupendous circumference! For since its shape was **oblong** <note>original Greek: *ἐτερομήκης* (heteromēkēs), meaning having sides of unequal length</note>, so that of the two unequal sides, the larger comprised 150 stadia and the smaller 90, the entire circuit (the **perimeter** <note>original Greek: *περίβολος* (peribolos)</note>) when collected into its total sum made 480 stadia. Of these, seven and a half stadia make one mile, according to the calculations of Suidas <note>a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note>. From this it can be further gathered that the width of the city contained almost three German miles; the length almost five German miles; and the circuit 15 German miles, or 60 Italian miles. Nor can this be far from the truth, since Strabo reports of Babylon that it contained as many stadia in its circuit as there are days in a year, which by calculation...

<margin>The magnitude of the city of Nineveh. Politics book 2, chapter 3, page 191.</margin>
By calculation, they estimate it to be nearly 12 German miles. Likewise, at the beginning of *Book 16 of his Geography*, Strabo asserts that Nineveh was much larger than Babylon. Regarding Babylon, Aristotle reports that when it was captured by enemies, a certain part of the city only heard of and felt the event on the third day. <margin>Travels of the Holy Land, page 191.</margin> If any doubt such great magnitude, let them consult Heinrich Bünting *, who attributes a circumference of 15 German miles to Cairo, a city in Egypt, today. Or Diego de Pantoja, a Jesuit, who reports concerning *Nanjing*, once the capital of the kingdom of China, that it contained 11 or at least 12 German miles in its circuit, and that 200,000 citizen houses could be counted within it. See also Justus Lipsius on the city of Rome, and other geographers who describe the city of *Quinsai* <note>Modern-day Hangzhou</note>. <margin>verse 4, last part.</margin> Into that city, so large, in which there were *, <note>original Hebrew: שתים עשרה רבוא אדם אשר לא ידע בין ימינו לשמאלו</note> *one hundred and twenty thousand people who did not know how to discern between their right and their left:* This is commonly interpreted by commentators as referring to infants. Junius interprets it as clearly *boys*. Vatablus speaks of those *who have not yet reached the years of discretion, so as to be able to know the difference between the right and the left.* Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> and Kimchi explain it as <term>קטנים</term> <note>original Hebrew: *qetannim*</note>, *little ones*. Compare Tarnovius and Gerhard on this passage, as well as Hector Mithobius, Sermon 33 on Jonah, page 1315. Severus Sulpitius interprets this as referring to the inhabitants of Nineveh in general, having been deceived—in the judgment of Drusius—by the Greek edition, where the text reads *twelve myriads of men* <note>original Greek: *δώδεκα μυριάδες ἀνδρῶν* (dodeka myriades andron)</note> instead of *people* <note>original Greek: *ἀνθρώπων* (anthropon)</note>; Abarbenel also wishes it to be understood in this sense. However, such a small number of inhabitants is diametrically opposed to the vastness of this city, since it is established that in cities far smaller, many more inhabitants were counted. <margin>Book 7 of the Jewish War, chapter 17.</margin> For according to Josephus *, in Jerusalem, which in its circuit barely made up one German mile, 300,000 people were gathered at the time of the siege, of whom 110,000 perished and 97,000 were captured. Regarding the city of Rome, the Annals testify that under the rule of Augustus, 4,100,000 citizens were counted, and not long after, 9,000,000; or rather 4,164,000 people, and then 9,370,000. Under Claudius, there were 6,900,064. At the beginning of the Third Punic War, the Carthaginians had in their city *sixty myriads* <note>original Greek: *μυριάδας ἑξμήκοντα* (myriadas hexēkonta)</note>, that is 700,000, as witnessed by Diodorus Siculus in Book 12 and Strabo in Book 6. In Paris <note>Lutetia Parisiorum</note>, during the reign of Henry IV, King of France, even counting the suburbs, 140,000 people were numbered. What wonder is it, therefore, that in such an enormous city, 120,000 infants were counted? By calculating from this, Bochart probably concludes that the total number of inhabitants was 600,000. To convert such a great multitude, so many tens of thousands of people, the Prophet is ordered to go and cry out with a loud voice against its destruction. The inhabitants escaped this for a time through their repentance, but 200 years later it was captured by Cyaxares, King of the Medes and great-grandfather of Cyrus, according to Herodotus in Book 1. It was finally overturned by Nebuchadnezzar, the Monarch of the Babylonians, just as the author of the Book of Tobit writes in the last chapter: *And he heard before he died of the destruction of Nineveh, which Nebuchadnezzar and Ahasuerus had taken captive.* <note>original Greek: *καὶ ἤκουσε πρὶν ἢ ἀποθανεῖν αὐτὸν τὴν ἀπώλειαν Νινευῆ, ἣν ᾐχμαλώτευσε Ναβουχοδονόσορ καὶ Ἀσύηρος.*</note> These words are omitted in the Hebrew Tobit published by Munster, which only consists of 

<column-break/>

13 chapters, as well as in the Vulgate and Luther’s translation, but they are read in the Frankfurt Edition of the year 1597; see Rainoldus, *Volume 1, Lecture 67, page 753 and following.* Isaiah (chapter 31), Zephaniah (chapter 2), and Nahum (chapters 1, 2, 3) had predicted this destruction by Nebuchadnezzar. Nineveh was indeed restored afterward, but with far less glory, and it is uncertain if it was in the same location, until finally it was overturned and leveled to the ground by Tamerlane, the King of the Tartars. Today, however, it lies desolate, and thus the location of ancient Nineveh is sufficiently established (whatever recent writers think about the city of *Mosul* in the borders of Greater Armenia being built from the ruins of Nineveh in that place), according to the prophecy of Nahum, chapter 3, verse 17: *Its place is not recognized.* This is also the testimony of Lucian of Samosata in the Dialogue *The Observers*: *Nineveh has already perished, and no trace of it remains, nor could you say where it once was;* <note>original Greek: *ἡ Νῖνος μὲν ἀπόλωλεν ἤδη, καὶ οὐδὲν ἴχνος ἔτι λοιπὸν αὐτῆς, οὐδ᾽ ἂν εἴπῃς ὅπου ποτ᾽ ἦν*</note> as well as Haitho <note>Hayton of Corycus</note> in his book on the Tartars, chapter 11, page 425: *Nineveh is a very large and ancient city near the river Tigris. That city at present is totally devastated, but by those things which are still visible in the same, it can be firmly believed that it was one of the largest cities of this world.*

### Jonah 4:6.

<margin>And the Lord God prepared a kikayon, and it came up over Jonah.</margin>

> And the Lord God commanded a gourd, and it went up over the head of Jonah. <note>original Greek: Καὶ προσέταξε κύριος ὁ Θεὸς κολοκύνθῃ, καὶ ἀνέβη ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς Ἰωνᾶ.</note>
>
> *The Lord prepared an ivy, and it went up over the head of Jonah.*

Since the East has its own plants and trees, almost unknown to us inhabitants of the Western world, there is more labor in investigating the substance of an exotic land which cannot yet be brought to our knowledge by a direct path. However, those who, attempting the way through a foreign nation, handle human and divine things together, dare to seek out the *conception* <note>original Greek: *ἐπινοίωμα* (epinoioma)</note> and traces of plants by a winding course. From these, whatever we have perceived in remote soil, let us bring forth that stalk which Jehovah God prepared near Nineveh, that city great to God, as a shelter for the Prophet Jonah. Our translator <note>The Vulgate</note> identifies it as *ivy* <note>original Latin: *hedera*</note>, which is a shrub more broken and weaker than it can raise and sustain itself by its own strength; it entwines itself around taller shoots and elms, and once entwined, binds itself more tightly, and in this way creeps by an embrace from the lowest parts to the highest. Three species of it are handed down by botanists following Dioscorides, one of which is white, with white fruit; another is black with black growth, but with white small vines and leaves that are small, angular, and more elegant. Its qualities or powers—whether it warms or cools—were once controversial, as Plutarch sharply debates the question in *Table Talk*, book 3, chapter 2, page 647. To Galen, it is of a mixed nature (*On Simple Medicines*, book 7, chapter 29). Botanists pronounce all ivy to be hot, and nothing is established among doctors regarding its internal use, because it is adverse to the head and the nervous system. Meanwhile, the ancients mention that ivy vessels or any cups made of ivy are beneficial for those with spleen issues. Pliny teaches that drink is frequently taken from an ivy vessel *, saying: *Of this*...

# Jonah 4:6

<margin>Jonah’s bower. Chapter 22, folio 135.</margin>
I also find that those suffering from spleen ailments are healed by drinking from a vessel made of this wood <note>ivy wood</note>. We find that Quintus Serenus* recorded the same:

> When the spleen binds the loins with a swollen bond,
> And the limbs show the full stiffness of the spleen,
> Cups are turned from soft ivy wood;
> From these, the sick draw their accustomed liquids.

The wood communicates its power to the drink; that such cups were common is proven not only by the word *kissybion* <note>Greek: κισσύβιον, a cup made of ivy wood</note>, which is counted among table vessels, but by other testimonies. An ivy-wood bowl of vast capacity is mentioned by Euripides in the *Cyclops*, which was said to be three cubits wide and four deep:
<margin>Cyclops, verse 389.</margin>
*And an ivy cup. It appeared three cubits wide and four deep.* <note>original Greek: Σκύφος τε κισσίν. παρὰ θἐτ᾽ εὐς ἐυρὺ θ᾽ τριῶν Πήχεων, βάθΘ. δὲ τεσσάρων ἐφαίνετο.</note>
And also in the work of the same poet, Hercules takes up an ivy cup.
<margin>Alcestis, verse 756.</margin>
*And taking an ivy cup in his hands, he drinks the unmixed wine of the black mother.* <note>original Greek: Ποτῆρα δ᾽ ἐν χείρεσσι κίσσινον λαβὼν Πίνει μελαίνης μητρὸς εὐζωρον μέθυ.</note>
From this, others conclude that ivy is of a cold quality, because an ivy crown was granted to Bacchus, both for its cooling power and to soothe the *karēbareia* <note>Greek: καρηβαείαν</note> or headache resulting from a hangover. For this reason, the Bacchante women in the retinue of Bacchus wreathed their hair with ivy garlands, dancing in an unseemly leaping fashion; Lucian vividly paints these women when he describes them as *crowned with ivy* <note>original Greek: κιττῷ ἐστεμμένας</note>. Valerius Flaccus describes this same crowd of Bacchants in his second book:

> She takes the garlands and the youth's hair, puts on the robes of Lyaeus <note>Bacchus</note>, and—herself full of silent fear—binds the baskets to her breast and her limbs with the attending ivy.

Carolus Paschalius discusses the use of ivy in coronation in two chapters of his work *On Crowns*, 17 and 18, page 52, etc.
<margin>Jonah’s bower.</margin>
But let us return to our purpose, having completed our journey among the followers of Aesculapius <note>god of medicine</note> and Bacchus <note>god of wine</note>. There are very learned men, Johannes Mercerus and Benedictus Arias Montanus, who teach in their commentaries on this passage that this is the herb we commonly call *Ricinus* <note>the castor oil plant</note> or *Palma Christi* <note>the Palm of Christ</note>. Dioscorides (Book 4, chapter 158) and Pliny (Book 15, chapter 7) call the same plant *Kiki*, which is called by another name *croton*, and in Syria—according to Jerome—*Elkeroa*. This agrees in sound with the Hebrew *Kikajon* <note>original Hebrew: קיקיון</note>; and thus Junius, Drusius, Arias Montanus, Mercerus, and others—whom the obscurity of the matter forces to take refuge in the affinity of words—have interpreted it as the *Ricinus*. The Genevans and the Swiss retained the word *Kikajon* in their version; they are followed by the Reverend Dr. Resenius in the Danish translation of the Bible. The English, in their version, place "palmecrist" <note>Palma Christi</note> in the margin, so named from the shape of the *Ricinus*, which emulates the palm of the hand with fingers spread. The Arabs call it *Alkarva*, which also helps us; for Jerome says in his *Commentaries* (page 133) that the plant *Kikajon* in the language of the Syrians and Carthaginians is *Elkeroa*. Which "Syrians" he means is as obscure as the name itself; for Drusius says in his *First Question* (53) that the *Cicajon* of the Hebrews is *Cicejan* to the Syrians. I do not know if *Elkeroa* has migrated into the collection and society of Syriac words; it is more likely Arabic if you slightly change the shape of the letters. The Greek and Lat-

<column-break/>

in Fathers often devise many things about foreign speech quite loosely, and sometimes preposterously; I would wish this to be taken with a grain of salt. Jerome is the one most widely learned (*polymathēstatos*) among the Latins, as Augustine himself testifies in his book to Cyril (if it is genuine), writing that Jerome mastered not only Hebrew, Greek, and Chaldean, but also Latin, Persian, Arabic, and Median. Raphelengius* thinks the Arabic *Kikajon* is the same as the Hebrew *Kikajon*; however, that Arabic word in the *Arabic Lexicon* (folio 536) means a gourd <note>Latin: cucurbita</note>. Luther renders it in this sense (whom Piscator, the "Ape of Tremellius," follows, which I greatly marvel at), adapting it to our regions. We remember that this was done more than once by the "God-man" <note>Luther</note> himself, suiting it to popular understanding. Similarly, Jerome himself put "Ivy" (*Hedera*), because he thought it came closest to the sound of *Kikajon*, even though he confessed it was not ivy. The appearance and nature of the plant (if it is a plant) would easily persuade us that Jonah's bower was the *Ricinus*, if we had certain knowledge. Carolus Clusius is an eyewitness witness that in Spain, near the Strait of Gibraltar, there existed a *Ricinus* shrub the thickness of a human and the height of three men, and Matthias Lobelius records this from him in his *Observations of Plants*.
<margin>page 392.</margin>
Bellonius, who traveled through Palestine and Syria, saw *Ricinus* in Crete of tree-like magnitude. Furthermore, I myself have seen the American *Ricinus* in the very well-cultivated and exotic-rich garden at Leiden, consisting of a hollow, thin, and soft stem, with leaves nearly a foot and a half long. I add this as well: Dr. Adolf Vorstius, while showing that plant in public demonstrations, affirmed—though with doubt—that it was the same plant used for Jonah’s shelter. Moreover, Dr. Caspar Bauhin, a physician from Basel, when industriously inquiring into the various names of every herb in his *Pinax of the Botanical Theater*, referred the *Kikajon* of Saint Jonah to the *Ricinus*.
<margin>book 11, section 50.</margin>
See *Mattheius, Medical Questions 74*, page 221. Rembert Dodoens did the same in his *History of Plants* (book 2, page 367).
<margin>page 432.</margin>
The most recent note on the name was made by Marcus Marinus in *Noah's Ark*.
<margin>Volume 2, folio 135. a.</margin>
Regarding *Kikajon*, he says, there is doubt about what it signifies, although it is almost certain it is a species of shrub. Some interpret it as ivy, others a gourd, others a colocynth. Some guess it is what the Latins call *Ricinus*, commonly called *Palma Christi*. And indeed, according to the opinion of some, the Greeks call the *Ricinus* "Chichi" and "Croton," the Arabs "Cherva," and the Germans "Wonder-tree" (*Wunderbaum*) and "Cross-tree" (*Creutzbaum*). They repeatedly say it is characteristic of this seed that, when taken in a certain number of grains, it usually provokes vomiting besides its other powers; if this is true, perhaps it is called in Hebrew *Kikajon* as if it were "the vomitory," providing the power of vomiting, from the root *Ki* <note>original Hebrew: קיא</note> from which is also derived *Ki* <note>original Hebrew: קיא</note> "vomit." In this 6th verse, the root is doubled to increase the meaning, which I would wish you to note again and again. In the version and exposition of Jonah that first appeared in Wittenberg, the translation says:
> The Lord provided a wild turnip; it grew over Jonah so that it gave shade over his head, and delighted him in his evil; and Jonah rejoiced greatly over the wild turnip.

The exposition sounds like this:
> Concerning the wild turnip, which in Hebrew is *Kik*, and here is called *Kikajon*, that is, a "little Kik" or "small Kik," the teachers in former times...
