# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
Jonah’s
bower.
</margin>
...has certainly been explored. The Elders <note>The translators of the Septuagint</note> called it a **gourd**. Later, St. Jerome arrived and translated it as *Hedera*, which is **ivy**, and he claimed it does not grow in Latin lands, but rather in Syria. He describes it as a shrub that grows very rapidly and soon becomes so large that it provides a hut and thick shade, with leaves like grapevines. This is perhaps why the ancients wanted to make it a gourd. We consider it to be the shrub that naturalists call *Vitis alba* in Latin, which in German is called **wild vine** <note>original: "wilde Rüben," likely referring to White Bryony</note>. Our pastor, Mr. Johann Pommer <note>Johannes Bugenhagen, the Reformer of Pomerania</note>, believes it is called "holy root" among his fellow Pomeranians, and that it grows so large it covers a house, resembling the nightshade; for ivy, as Jerome identifies it, cannot be correct, as he himself admits. *In a single night this shrub grew and then withered, gnawed by a worm, like a solstitial herb; of which Ausonius says:*

> Like the solstitial herb is wont to be,
> Displayed and snatched away at once.

<margin>
Pseud. Att.
1. sc. 1.
</margin>
> And in the comedian Plautus:
> I was like a solstitial herb for a short while:
> Suddenly I sprouted, and suddenly I died.

Just as the sudden destruction of the *Ricinus* <note>The castor oil plant, often identified as Jonah’s plant</note> is elegantly expressed in the text: "It was a son of a night, and as a son of a night it perished" <note>original Hebrew: כִּבְנ־לַיְלָה הָיָה וּבִן־לַיְלָה אָבָד</note>; meaning that in one and the same night, so to speak, it was both born and unborn. There are those who, following the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint</note>, explain it as the **Colocynth**, which is a type of wild gourd; they want this to be understood as in 2 Kings 4:39, 44, where we read that Elisha used flour to remove and correct the harmful power of the colocynth. For it harbors something of a malignancy within itself and, as Mesue says, infects nearby plants like a poison; so much so that it is extremely harmful to the heart, liver, and stomach, causing nausea and griping of the intestines, and opening the mouths of the vessels; as 

<margin>
book 4 ch. 71
page 643.
</margin>
Matthioli teaches in his commentary on Dioscorides. Therefore, they said in verse 40 to designate its bitterness: "Death is in the pot, O man of God." To correct its toxicity, however, antidotes are added to perform that task; namely, mastic, cinnamon, ginger, and others that have the power to restrain it; from these, lozenges are formed and kept ready in pharmacies, called *Albandali*. Regarding that passage of scripture, Vallesius <note>Francisco Vallés, a 16th-century physician</note> 

<margin>
on Sacred Philos. ch. 36
p. 250.
</margin>
advises that it was indeed partly natural that the power and biting nature of the colocynth were mitigated by the sprinkling of flour; but he adds it was much more supernatural, so that he might persuade us that a natural cause was joined with that divine one. For we see that as often as God acts beyond the order of nature, He simultaneously approaches nature itself. Although this is not always the case, we will find that God has mostly worked in such a way that He exceeds the course of nature yet does not entirely depart from it. Just as when He wished to gather quails into a heap in the desert and give meat to His people, He stirred up an eastern wind. Thus in *John 5:4*, we read that by the touch of an angel and the movement of the waters, certain diseases were removed and the sick person was healed who first lowered himself into the pool. But let these matters be judged in the court of **Theologians**; it is their place to prescribe laws, while it is the place of **Philologists** to obey.

<column-break/>

-> Judith 11:5 <-

> "To announce to them to prepare for me earth and water."
> <note>original Greek: Ἀπαγγελεῖν αὐτοῖς ἑτοιμάζειν μοι γῆν καὶ ὕδωρ</note>

A custom prevailed in the Orient that when Kings of a Great Kingdom brought nations under their power and commanded the tokens of empire and dominion to be delivered to them, they would demand **Water and Earth** as symbols of surrender. They wanted them, as it were, "to bring or give earth and water," to prepare earth and water, which are the two most necessary things in a foreign land—the commerce of sea and land—by which they believed the dominion of both sea and earth was designated, as Drusius showed from Herodotus, and Aristotle says in his *Rhetoric*: "He commanded them to give earth and water." Whence Nebuchadnezzar, about to declare war on neighboring nations through Holofernes, orders that earth and water be prepared for him. Similarly, Darius demanded earth and water from Indathyrsus, King of the Scythians. Likewise, according to Herodotus in Book 7, page 424, the same Darius sent legates to the Greeks to demand water and earth as symbols and signs of surrender; the Greeks threw some of them into a pit and others into a well, telling them to carry Earth and Water to the King from there. Xerxes also demanded them from the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, and both demanded them from the people of Cos, as they themselves testify in a spiritedly written letter to Artaxerxes. See the words in John Selden’s *The Closed Sea* <note>Maris clausi</note> and add Nicolaus Serarius. This manner of speaking, taken from water and fire, is also common when treaties were being sanctioned: water and fire were used to finalize them. Hence "to interdict from water and fire" <note>Exile/Outlawry</note> is said of those we prohibit from our society; just as "to prepare or provide water and earth" is said of those whose dominion and possession we claim. However, for "the earth to be before someone" in the phrasing of Scripture (Genesis 12:9, 20:15, Jeremiah 40:4) is the same as everything the soil contains being subjected to someone's power and judgment. All things are made through the benefit of earth and water; hence, he who once sought earth and water was demanding power over all things. On account of the great utility that water and earth confer upon mortals, both were honored with divine worship. Among the worshipers of water were the Egyptians, who brought at least the water of the Nile (not the rest) as sacred to Osiris, of whom Plutarch testifies in his book *On Isis and Osiris*: "Nothing is so honored by the Egyptians as the Nile" <note>original Greek: Οὐδὲν οὕτω τιμὴ Αἰγυπτίοις, ὡς ὁ Νεῖλος</note>. Athanasius, "an Egyptian by race," writes something similar in his *Oration Against the Heathen*, page 20: "Others have preferred rivers and springs, but most of all the Egyptians have honored water and proclaim it as gods" <note>original Greek: Ἄλλοι ποταμὸς καὶ κρήνας καὶ πάντων μάλιστα Αἰγύπτιοι τὸ ὕδωρ προτετιμήκασι, καὶ θεοὺς ἀναγορεύουσι</note>. Thus also Julius Firmicus testifies: "The Egyptian inhabitants, perceiving the benefits of the waters, worship water, pray to the waters, and venerate the waters with superstitious continuity." Heliodorus left the same testimony in Book 9 concerning the Egyptians: "They worship the Nile as the greatest of the gods, boasting of it as a river rivaling heaven, because without clouds or eternal rains, it waters their land and provides rain regularly every year." The Nile was most religiously worshiped of all by the Gymnosophists <note>Indian "naked philosophers" encountered in Egypt</note>, who considered it to be both earth and water together, according to Philostratus in Book 6...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of ancient customs, moving from the botanical identity of Jonah’s plant on the previous page to the ritual symbols of surrender (earth and water) as referenced in the Book of Judith, Chapter 2. # Judith II. 5.

<margin>
Symbols of
Surrender.
</margin>
<margin>
Book 2 of 
Church History.
</margin>
Plutarch, in the place cited, says that for the Egyptians, the Nile is Osiris, who unites with Isis, who is the earth. The Egyptians asserted the <term>divinity</term> <note>original Greek: θειότητα</note> of their god, the Nile, quite cleverly against the Chaldeans, as Rufinus testifies. For when, in the time of Constantine the Great, the Chaldeans traveled throughout the whole world to prove that their God—whom they worshiped in the form of fire—was superior and more powerful than all other gods (because fire could dissolve and destroy the statues of other gods), they finally came to the Egyptians. There, they matched their god in a duel against the god of the Egyptians. The Egyptian priests brought out a massive statue of the Nile, which was hollow inside and contained a great volume of water. It was, however, full of holes on all sides, which had been sealed with wax by clever craftsmanship so that it would hold the water, but could by no means withstand the power of fire. Unaware of this stratagem, the Chaldeans entered the contest exultantly and surrounded the Nile statue with fire. Scarcely had the fire touched the statue when the holes suddenly opened as the wax melted; a great force of water burst out, extinguished the fire, and exposed the god of the Chaldeans to everyone's mockery. So says Rufinus. Suidas recounts this story slightly differently under the entry *Canopus*. Regarding the Persians who paid divine honor to water, one may read Laertius in the *Introduction* to his work, Clement of Alexandria in his *Exhortation to the Heathen*, Arnobius in *Book 6*, Sidonius Apollinaris in his *Panegyric to Leo*, and Agathias in *Book 2*. Indeed, Herodotus in *Book 7* reports that when the Magi came to the river Strymon, they sacrificed white horses to it. And Tacitus, in *Book 6 of the Annals*, reports regarding Tiridates that when he was about to cross the Euphrates with Vitellius and his troops, he sacrificed a horse to it to ensure the river remained appeased. This same Tiridates, when about to travel to Nero from Armenia, refused to sail upon the Euphrates <margin>Book 30, chapter 11.</margin> because, as Pliny records, *he did not think it lawful to spit into the seas or to violate that nature with other human necessities*. Regarding the Persians, Strabo in *Book 15* and Herodotus in *Book 1* report that they venerated rivers to such an extent that it was a religious taboo for them to urinate in them, or to empty their bowels, or to spit, or to throw in a corpse or anything filthy, or even to wash their hands in a flowing river; a custom which Hesiod seems to have respected in his *Works and Days*, verse 755:

> Never urinate at the mouths of rivers flowing to the sea,
> Nor upon springs, but strictly avoid doing so,
> Nor ease yourself there, for it is better for you 
> to act thus. <note>original Greek: Μηδέ ποτ' ἐν προχοῇ ποταμῶν... This reflects the ancient belief that water sources were sacred and inhabited by spirits.</note>

The Catti, according to Surius in *Chapter 8*, and the Bohemians, as Johannes Dubravius writes in *Book 1 of his Bohemian History*, sacrificed to springs. Joseph de Acosta reports in *Book 5, Chapters 2 and 4* that the Peruvians likewise worshiped the sea, rivers, and springs as gods. Similarly, the earth (or Tellus) was held in no less worship in ancient times because of the great benefits it bestowed upon the human race. The Syrians worshiped it under the name of the *Syrian Goddess*, and the Assyrians under the name of *Atargatis*, according to Lucian and Macrobius in *Book 1 of the Saturnalia, Chapter 23*. The Phrygians called it *Cybele* and *Rhea*. The Egyptians used the name *Isis*, as is clear from Plutarch. The Samothracians used the name of the <term>powerful gods</term> <note>original Greek: δυνατῶν θεῶν</note> and the Cabiri, as the interpreter of Apollonius records in *Book 1 of the Argonautics*. The Thracians used the names of *Ceres*, *Juno*, *Vesta*, *Rhea*, *Ops*, *Proserpina*, *Pluto*, and so on. The verse of Orpheus (or Onomacritus) is well known:

> Earth mother of all, Demeter giver of wealth. <note>original Greek: Γῆ μήτηρ πάντων, Δημήτηρ πλουτοδότειρα.</note>

<column-break/>

*Earth mother of all, Ceres giver of riches.* <margin>Symbols of Surrender.</margin> Thus the worship of the Earth became known to the Gauls and was practiced among them under the name of *Dis* <note>The Roman name for the god of the underworld, often associated with the riches of the earth</note>, to whom they traced the origin of their race, as Caesar records in *Book 6 of the Gallic War*. The Germans worshiped *Hertha*, whom Tacitus interprets as Earth, and the Scythians under the name *Apia*, as Herodotus mentions in *Melpomene*.

But to return to the symbols of surrender: this demand for earth and water did not prevail everywhere. It was no less common a custom to hold out the right hand as a sign of surrender, as Livy records—that some townspeople showed their bare right hands to signify friendship and submission. Thus the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, as Thucydides testifies when they were surrounded by the Athenians, <term>shook their hands</term> <note>original Greek: τὰς χεῖρας ἀνέσεισαν</note> as a sign of peace and surrender. Thus, to say nothing of other rites and signs of surrender, today the custom of offering the keys of the city has prevailed, by which the conquered subject themselves to the hand and will of the victor, imploring his mercy and testifying to their subjection and devotion. This was observed by the people of Frankfurt am Main during the Schmalkaldic War, who offered the keys to Maximilian van Egmond, Count of Büren and Imperial General, as a sign of surrender, as Sleidanus testifies. Although he had previously despaired of their surrender, he proceeded even more vigorously with his army to bring them under the Emperor's power. <margin>Book 18 of his Commentaries, page 339.</margin> And as he was of a frank disposition, when the Senate gave him a banquet, he is said to have joked with them about their so slight and timid surrender: *Surely the people of Darmstadt are the ones worthy to inhabit Frankfurt, while the Frankfurters themselves ought to be moved to Darmstadt.* <note>The Count was mocking the proud citizens of Frankfurt, suggesting they acted with the cowardice associated with a smaller, less defensible town.</note> Indeed, the circumstances of that time allowed no other means of settling matters and returning to the Emperor's favor, especially as Sleidanus himself records, because the people of Ulm and Württemberg, and indeed all of Upper Germany, had reconciled with the Emperor; they alone were not of such power and strength that they could have further resisted the Emperor’s victorious arms. Not to mention that in the German edition of Sleidanus, that joke of the Count is marked with an asterisk, as he could not have forgotten it.

### Judith IX. 9.

> They gloried in the arm of their infantry; they trusted in shield and spear and bow and sling. <note>original Greek: Ἐγαυρίασαν ἐν βραχίονι πεζῶν ἥλπισαν ἐν ἀσπίδι & γαισῷ καὶ τόξῳ καὶ σφενδόνῃ.</note>

<margin>Ancient warfare with bow and sword.</margin>
<margin>1 Sam. 18. 4.</margin>
Regarding the <term>weapons</term> <note>original Greek: ὅπλοις</note> of the ancients, since they do not exist today, one must rely on conjecture rather than certain knowledge. The primary weapons were the Bow and the Sword. Jonathan, to demonstrate his sincerity of heart, gave his bow and sword among his other armor to David, his faithful friend. For *Jonathan stripped himself* of the cloak he was wearing and gave it to David, along with his inner tunic, and even his sword and his bow and his belt. The bow here is called <term>Qeshet</term> <note>original Hebrew: קֶשֶׁת</note>, and no other name for it is found; the Septuagint calls it a <term>toxon</term> <note>original Greek: τόξον</note>. They translate it the same way in Genesis 47:22, where Jacob says he took the field of Shechem (which he gave to Joseph as an extra portion) from the hand of the Amorite with his sword and his bow—that is, by force of arms and with his troops.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<column-break/>

<margin>
Ancient warfare with bow and sword.
</margin>
...with his forces, by his own might, and by the right of war; how this was actually done is expressed nowhere else. Therefore, the interpretation of those who think this was said metaphorically or improperly is forced. *By sword and bow*, all kinds of arms are usually designated. <margin>Psalm 37:14.</margin> The same point is intended in Psalm 37:14: *The wicked have drawn out the sword and have bent their bow.* And verse 15: *Their sword shall enter into their own heart, and their bows shall be broken.* So too in Psalm 44, verse 6: *For I did not place my hope in my bow, nor could my sword have saved me.* And in Psalm 46, verse 8: *Come, I pray you, and behold the works of the Lord, to see what wonders He has designated upon the earth.* Verse 9: *He makes wars to cease throughout the whole world and all its corners; He has broken the bow, destroyed arrows and spears, and burned the war-chariots with fire.* This is from the paraphrastic interpretation of Johannes Campensis <note>Johannes Campensis (1490–1538) was a Hebrew teacher at Louvain known for his Latin versions of the Psalms</note>. Similarly, Psalm 76, verse 3 speaks of God: *There He broke the powers of the bows, the dart, the sword, and the battle.* Regarding this, Euthymius <note>Euthymius Zigabenus, a 12th-century Byzantine monk and commentator</note>, in the edition by Philippus Saulus, folio 213b, writes: *According to history, this pertains to the destruction of the Assyrians; for there in Zion, God crushed the strength of the bow—that is, He dissolved it and rendered it useless.* By the word "dart," for which we read <term>hoplon</term> <note>original Greek: ὅπλον - generally meaning "tool" or "weapon," but often implying a shield</note> in the Greek reading, we should not understand offensive weapons in this place, but rather defensive ones, such as a breastplate or something similar. For this reason, among the Greeks, they called a soldier armed with a breastplate a <term>hoplite</term> <note>original Greek: ὁπλίτην</note>, to distinguish them from those soldiers who lacked this kind of armor, whom they called <term>psiloi</term> <note>original Greek: ψιλοὺς - meaning "bare" or "lightly armed"</note>, that is, naked. Indeed, he spoke of the "powers" or "strength" of the bows because the Assyrians used the bow most extensively and placed their primary strength in that kind of weaponry. Therefore, by "dart," he signified all defensive weapons, and by "bow," all offensive weapons. Through that <term>synecdoche</term> <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole, such as "wheels" for a car</note>, the cessation of war is indicated by the "crushing of the bow"; conversely, the "stretching of the bow" indicates preparation for war. This military <term>hypotyposis</term> <note>a vivid, lifelike description</note> concerning God, as one equipped with buckler and shield, is spoken <margin>Psalm 35:2-3.</margin> *according to the language of the sons of men* <note>original Hebrew: כְּלוֹשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם - a Jewish hermeneutical principle that the Torah speaks in human language to be understood</note>, or <term>anthropopathically</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνθρωποπαθῶς - attributing human passions or physical members to God</note> by the Psalmist in these words: *Seize the buckler and shield, and bring help to me. Draw out the spear and sword* <note>original Hebrew: הַחֲזֵק מָגֵן וְצִנָּה... וְהַרֵק חֲנִית וּסְגֹר</note> *to meet my pursuers.* By this metaphor, the Sacred Book frequently indicates that protection which God—slow to anger—wonderfully provides to His own, as can be read in Genesis chapter 15, verse 1; 2 Samuel 22:31; Psalm 91, verse 4; and in very many other places. By the same form of speaking, God is described as angry in Psalm 7, verse 12: *God will whet His sword and bend His bow.* And in Psalm 38, verse 2: *Your arrows stick fast in me.* And in Isaiah chapter 34, verse 6: *The sword of the Lord is said to be drunk and full of blood;* in the same sense as Deuteronomy chapter 32, verse 42: *My arrows shall be drunk with the blood of the slain.* In Nahum 2, verse 3, the <note>original Hebrew: מָגֵן גִּבֹּרָיו מְאָדָם</note> *shield is made red*, and in Virgil, it is called a "bloody corselet" (*lorica sanguinea*). Moreover, the military apparatus consisting of quivers, chariots, horsemen, and shields, sent by God in the form of the Elamites or Persians to invade the city of Jerusalem, is elegantly recounted by Isaiah in chapter 22, verse 6, exactly as if the army with all its armor were already present before everyone's eyes. No less does God speak against Pharaoh Necho in Jeremiah <margin>Chapter 46, verse 3</margin>: *Prepare the shield and buckler.* For the Hebrew *magen* and *tsinnah* <note>original: מָגֵן וְצִנָּה</note>, the Chaldean <note>The Aramaic translation or Targum</note> has: *agila* and *tereisa* <note>original: עֲגִילָא וּתְרֵיסָא</note>. The word *tereis* is frequent for "shield." Or in verse 4: *Stand in your helmets, polish your spears.* To "stand" is a technical term

<column-break/>

in military service, taken from the sentry-duty of soldiers, or the function of standing and keeping watch. Compare Ezekiel chapter 33. Thus it is found in Virgil, in the 9th book of the *Aeneid*:
> The son of Arcentis stood in magnificent arms,
> His cloak embroidered by needle, and bright with Iberian rust.
And again:
> Aeneas stood fierce in arms.
The word *tsinnah* <note>original: צִנָּה</note>, just like the word *arma* among the Latins, is often taken specifically to mean shields, which were prepared for defending the body from imminent missiles; and because of their form and material, they received various names among the Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins. The *scuta* <note>Latin for shields</note> were more oblong than they were wide; therefore the Greeks call them <term>thyreous</term> <note>original Greek: θυρεοὺς</note>, because they bear a resemblance to doors <note>Greek "thyra"</note>, which are longer than they are wide. However, the *clypei* <note>round shields</note> were <term>round bucklers</term> <note>original Greek: ἀσπίδες εὐκυκλοι</note>, circular and fashioned into a perfect orb. Friedrich Taubmann demonstrated this distinction with figures in his commentary on Virgil’s *Culex*, verse 311. Among the Hebrews, scholars strive to find this distinction in the words *magen*, *socherah*, and *tsinnah*: of which, if you examine them accurately, the *magen* is a buckler, but the *tsinnah* is a shield much larger than the buckler, covering almost the entire man, as one may compare in the aforementioned Psalm 35. There, the Chaldean translator used a word that implies roundness, *agila* <note>original: עֲגִילָא</note>, and it is a very well-known word from the same language, *agal*, concerning a circle and various round things. In the same way, the French call a small shield a *Rondella*; for *rond* to them is "round" or "orb-shaped," hence *rondelle* or *rondache* and *tarque ronde*, and *rondelier*, a "shield-maker." As for the *socherah* <note>original: סוחרה</note> in Psalm 91, verse 4 (compare Becman page 29), some like it to be the *sagaris* because of the sound—which is a Persian sword, or another kind of sword with which they fought conveniently at close quarters, just as they used arrows from a distance. When Absalom was defeated in battle and caught by his hair in an oak tree during his flight, he was pierced while hanging by Joab with three weapons <note>original Hebrew: שְׁלֹשָׁה שְׁבָטִים - literally "three rods"</note>, which the Vulgate and Luther explain as three lances. The Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> has <term>three darts</term> <note>original Greek: τρία βέλη</note>. The Chaldean has *tlata nissin*, "three darts" or "points." The word *nissa* or *nissasa* is a javelin, from the Greek <term>gaisos</term> <note>original Greek: γαῖσος</note>. Furthermore, what a *gaisos* is can be found in the works of the ancients, as Alexander ab Alexandro (Book 6, chapter 22) and Tiraquellus in his notes (page 972), Lipsius in his *Poliorceticon* (Book 4, dialogue 4), and Xylander in his notes on Plutarch (Volume 1, page 679) explain. By this word, the Septuagint translates the Hebrew *kidon* <note>original: כידון</note> in Joshua chapter 8, verse 18: *Stretch out your hand with the javelin* <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ γαῖσῳ</note> *that is in your hand toward the city.* The Vulgate translates it: "Lift up the shield which is in your hand against the city." Symmachus translated it as <term>aspida</term> <note>shield</note>, as Theodoret testifies regarding Joshua: *the gaisos, with which Joshua aroused those in ambush, Josephus interpreted as a shield, as did Symmachus.* For Luther, it is a *Lantze*, which is said by us to come from *lancea*, whence comes *Landsknecht* <note>original: Landsknecht - a term for a mercenary infantryman, though the author suggests it should more correctly be "Lanzknecht" or "Lance-servant"</note>. The stretching out or lifting high of the signaling-spear or lance during the occupation of the city of Ai was given as a sign to those lying in wait to rush into the city, and for those fleeing to turn their faces toward the enemy; both those fleeing and those in ambush were warned by that signal—the former to turn against the enemy, the latter to come out of hiding to burn the city of Ai. Hesychius says the *gesum* (which others write as *gassum*) was <term>a type of javelin made entirely of iron</term>. Servius, in his commentary on Virgil’s *Aeneid* Book VIII, interprets it as a "manly spear." Festus (page 68) calls the *gesum* a "heavy javelin." Common copies...

...copies have: *thrown*. It had been written as *jaculum* <note>Latin: javelin</note>. Papias <note>An 11th-century lexicographer</note> says: *Gesum* is a spear or a javelin. Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century encyclopedist</note> says: *Gesum* is a spear, a javelin, or a *bolis* <note>Greek: βόλις, a missile</note>. Regarding the very ancient use and invention of the sling, the matter is not so obscure. A sling is an instrument by which stones are thrown, and, as it were, poured out against the enemy. The Latin interpreter used the word *Fundibula* in 1 Maccabees 6:51, from which comes *fundibularius* <note>slinger</note> in 2 Samuel 3:25, Judith 6:8, and 1 Maccabees 9:11. In Greek, it is *sphendonētēs* from *sphendonē* <note>σφενδόνη, a sling</note>.

Instead of this, Vegetius <note>A 4th-century military writer</note> calls him a *Fundibulator*, and a *funditor* <note>slinger</note>, whose words are these: *Fundibulatores are those who throw stones with staff-slings [fustibali] (some read "fustibulatores" here). A staff-sling [fustibalus] is a staff four feet long, to which a leather sling is tied in the middle, and when swung with both hands, it directs stones almost like an onager <note>a large Roman siege engine</note>. Slingers [funditores] are those who, using slings made of linen or hair (for they say these are better), direct stones by whirling their arm around their head.* Nonius <note>a 4th-century grammarian</note> in chapter 18 says: *Slingers are those who fight with large slings.* Plautus in *The Little Carthaginian*, act 2: *I poured quite large globes into the slings. I ordered those flying things to be slung.* Regarding this *lithologia* <note>Greek: λιθολογία, the science or study of stones/slinging</note> see Pineda on Job chapter 41, verse 19, and Martinius in his *Philological Lexicon*, page 965.

## JUDITH. XIV. 15.

<margin>The rending of clothes common in mourning. *Question 10, page 188.*</margin>
> But when the leaders of the Assyrian force heard these words, they immediately tore their tunics and their souls were greatly troubled. <note>original Greek: ὡς δὲ ἤκουσαν ταῦτα τὰ ῥήματα οἱ Ἄρχοντες τῆς δυνάμεως Ἀσσὺρ, διέρρηξαν εὐθὺς τὰς χιτῶνας αὐτῶν καὶ ἐταράχθη ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτῶν σφόδρα.</note>

> *When the leaders of the power of the Assyrians heard this, they all tore their garments, and an intolerable fear and trembling fell upon them.* <note>original Latin: Quod cum audissent Principes virtutis Assyriorum, sciderunt omnes vestimenta sua, & intolerabilis timor & tremor cecidit super illos.</note>

IN the history of Judith, the tragic end of Holofernes, who was beheaded by Judith, is well known. When Bagoas (others call him Vagao or Biguai) reported his death to the leaders of the Assyrian troops, they were so struck by the news that they immediately tore their tunics. This rite was frequent and ancient, common to almost all early peoples, by which they tore their clothes in grief and sorrow, whether public or private; by this, those ancients testified that their hearts were, as it were, torn with misery.
<margin>Gen. 37. 39.</margin>
Regarding the *Jews*, the matter is certain from the Sacred Book, if you look at the examples of *Reuben*, who hindered his brothers from killing their brother Joseph and persuaded them to cast him into a cistern. Reuben, the elder and firstborn, used this artifice and a certain pious deception to restrain the impulse of the brothers and to provide for his brother in some way, since he could not fully rescue him. *But he was striving to deliver him*, as the Vulgate well explained; for his plan tended toward restoring him alive to his father after he had been cast into a

<column-break/>

waterless <note>Greek: ἄνυδρον</note> pit. Thus, he discouraged his brothers from such a crime, saying: *Do not shed his blood*, etc. However, Joseph was sold during a time of mourning while Reuben was unaware and absent, not participating in that usual plan; therefore, when Joseph was not found in the waterless pit, he rent his clothes. We find the same examples elsewhere in the Sacred Book: Jacob (Genesis 37:34); the brothers of Joseph (chapter 44:13); Joshua and Caleb (Numbers 14:6); Jephthah (Judges 11:35); the man of Benjamin (1 Samuel 4:11-12); David (2 Samuel 1:11); the Israelites (chapter 3:31); Tamar (chapter 13:19); David and his servants (verse 31); Hushai (chapter 15:32); Ahab (1 Kings 21:27); the King of Israel (2 Kings 5:7 and 6:30); Athaliah (chapter 11:14 and 2 Chronicles 23:13); Eliakim with his colleagues (2 Kings 18:37); Hezekiah (chapter 19:1 and Isaiah 37:1); Josiah (2 Kings 22:11 and 2 Chronicles 34:19); Ezra (Ezra 9:3); Mordecai (Esther 4:1); Job (chapter 1:20); Mattathias and his sons (1 Maccabees 2:14); Judas and his army (chapter 4:39); Jonathan (chapter 11:71); and Caiaphas the High Priest (Matthew 26:65 and Mark 14:63). Cunaeus <note>Petrus Cunaeus, a 17th-century scholar of Hebrew law</note> notes in his work *On the Hebrew Commonwealth* (book 2, chapter 3) that Caiaphas’s act was singular and clearly against the law; on which matter one may read the opinion of Casaubon in his *Exercise 16, Discourse 68*. Also, Paul and Barnabas (Acts 14:14). Concerning this Jewish custom, see what Schindler collected from Holy Scripture under the root *Kara* <note>Hebrew: קרע, meaning to rend or tear</note>; and what Schickard gathered from the Rabbis in *The Law of the King* <note>Hebrew: משפט המלך, Mishpat HaMelekh</note>, page 150 onwards; and after them, most accurately and extensively, the famous Geier in his *Treatise on Hebrew Mourning*.
<margin>c. 2. 12.</margin>
Regarding the *Gentiles*, besides the example from the history of Job <note>The book of Job is often treated as reflecting ancient non-Jewish customs</note>, where we read that his friends, seeing the bitterness of his grief, rent their clothes, the matter is clear from secular writers—so clear that proving it seems like adding light to the midday sun. One might see Brissonius on Persian customs; P. Faber in *Semestria*, book 2, chapter 10; Serarius on Joshua; Dilherr’s *Philological Dialogues*; and Rumphius. Some tore the garment some way downward so that the ruptured part was left hanging for several days; others tore it lower down in a place where it wouldn't interfere much with the hands, and they did this for seven days, if Schindler is to be believed. Regarding the clothing that befits mourning and misery, there are different opinions. Having renounced more elegant dress during the days of mourning, and setting aside white garments, they walked about in dark and dirty clothes so that they might appear more pitiable. Livy, in book 45, tells of the Rhodian ambassadors: *When they were first seen in white clothing, which befitted those offering congratulations, had they worn squalid dress, they might have appeared to be mourning the downfall of Perseus.* They also sometimes testified to mourning by being clothed in haircloth and sackcloth as suppliants to the Deity, as we see in the history of the Ninevites in the prophet Jonah. For they, having heard the preaching of Jonah, *were clothed in sackcloth from the greatest to the least; and the word reached the King of Nineveh, who rose from his throne, cast off his robe, and was clothed in sackcloth, and sat in ashes.* There we read that even the beasts and cattle were subjected to a fast in the public mourning. This should not seem strange to anyone, especially one who has read Plutarch in *Aristides*, who writes: The Persians in mourning shave not only themselves, but also their horses and mules. Herodotus likewise reports in book 9 that the Persians, on account of the death of Masistius, who led the cavalry troops in battle, shaved themselves, their horses, and their beasts of burden out of grief. Thus also after the death of Hephaestion, as a sign of sorrow, Alexander shaved all the horses... <meta>catchword: ...of mourning [πένθες]</meta>

BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES.

<margin>
The tearing of garments was a common custom in mourning.
</margin>
...in mourning and on mules, he moreover ordered the battlements of the walls to be overturned, as Plutarch records in his *Life of Alexander* <note>original: "ut in ejus vita Plutarchus commemorat"</note>. They sprinkled themselves with dust in mourning and sat in ashes; we are taught that this was also the custom of penitents from *Matthew* 11:21 and *Luke* 10:13. Secular history <note>original: "historia... profana"</note> provides us with this same twin custom; and to omit other testimonies of antiquity, we read in Lucian, in his book *On Mourning* <note>original: "περὶ πένθους"</note>, where he describes all the gestures of mourners: dust thrown on the head and prostration on the ground. Similarly, P. Faber (2. *Semestr.* 10), Bernartius (*On Statius* p. 64), and Kirchmann (*On Roman Funerals*, book 2, ch. 11, p. 208ff.) note that the Greeks and Romans defiled their hair and faces by throwing dust or ashes and prostrating themselves entirely on the ground. The Syrians, dressed in sackcloth, falling to the ground <note>original: "ἐν σάκκῳ χαμαιπετέντες"</note> to testify to their humble spirit, would supplicate their Goddess; as P. Victorius (12. *Var.* 15), Selden (2. *On the Syrian Gods* 3, p. 270), and Benef. (2. *Var. Lect.* 11, p. 210) show from Menander. There is a testimony of Menander in <margin>In book 4 of *On Abstinence from Animal Food*.</margin> Porphyry which we shall include:
> — Then they took a small sack, then they
> sat by the road on dung, and they
> greatly appeased the goddess by humbling themselves.
<note>original Greek: — εἶτ’ ἔλαβον σάκκιον, εἶτ’ εἰς τὴν ὁδὸν ἐκάθισαν αὐτὶ ἐπὶ κόπρῳ, καὶ τὴν θεὸν ἐξίλασάν τε ταπεινῶσαι σφόδρα.</note>

Haircloth <note>term: Cilicium; a rough garment made of woven goat's hair, typically from Cilicia, used as a sign of penance or mourning</note> was truly a type of light, dense, and hard clothing with which they girded or covered themselves in mourning, in penance, in supplication (an example is Ben-hadad the Syrian in 1 *Kings* 20), or in servitude.

They also shaved their beards and hair in mourning, a custom of mourning which God forbade the Jews in *Deuteronomy* 14:1–2, where He commands them to mourn *without shaving the head or cutting the flesh*, adding the reason: *because they are the children of God, a holy people*. Some from every foreign nation <note>original Greek: Τινὲς δὲ πᾶν ἀλλόφυλον ἐθνῶν...</note> used to shave the hair of their heads and offer it to the dead; some the hair of their beards, others that of their eyebrows. Nevertheless, from the interaction between the Gentiles and the Israelites, even in the time of the Prophets, that practice began to be used, as is clearly gathered from *Jeremiah* 16:6. There, Jerome <margin>H. Junius *On Hair* ch. 6. Cunaeus *On the Hebrew Republic* 2. ch. 23.</margin> testifies that in his own century it was still the custom among the Jews to create bald spots and cut their arms in mourning. The pagan poet Choerilus (unless he invents this poetically) called the Jews "round-shorn" <note>original Greek: "τροχοκουρὰς"</note>, referring to those shorn in a circle, which was the custom of neighboring nations; yet this type of tonsure was forbidden to them in *Leviticus* 19:27, on which one should consult Bonfrerius (p. 613 and 673). Concerning this custom, one may observe many passages in various authors. Euripides described the habit of penitents and mourners as "shaved in the Scythian fashion" in *The Trojan Women*, line 1026, and "locks of hair shaved with a razor" in *Electra*, line 241. In these passages, "to shave in the Scythian style" is explained by Suidas as "to shear off," or by Hesychius as "to cut away." See also Antonius Hotman's treatise *On the Beard and Hair*, Kirchmann (book 2 *On Funerals*, chapters 13 and 14), and Bernartius (*On Statius*, p. 102). We have said more on this matter in our notes on *Jeremiah* 16:5.

### Judith. XVI, 8.

> Neither did the sons of the Titans strike him, nor did high Giants set upon him.

<margin>Giants and Titans.</margin> It was once the accepted practice that the death of godly men should be celebrated with a solemn panegyric, while the

<column-break/>

unhappy end of the wicked should be mocked with a song and a certain abusive chant instead of a funeral rite. This was customary among the Jews from praised tradition, as it was among the Greeks by law. Judith, the Hebrew heroine, bringing the head of Holofernes back to her fellow citizens, sings a song of victory <note>original Greek: ἐπ’ ἐπινυχίοις</note>. The Philistines, once Samson was defeated, sang a Paean <note>term: Paean; a song of triumph or thanksgiving, originally dedicated to Apollo</note>. The Greeks had two Paeans: one for Mars, which they used at the start of a battle; the other for Apollo, which they sang once the enemy was routed and slaughtered, as noted by Fr. Lursinus (2. *Parerg.* 12). Judith, a woman of no small womanly spirit, uttered the same triumphal Paean when she had finished her tragedies with a comedic face <note>i.e., she ended a tragic situation with a joyful result</note>. Regarding her heroic deed, Fabritius sings thus:

> O God of Israel, strengthen me, guide my right hand,
> Look upon the great deeds of my intrepid hand.
> The deed I approach in faith, bring to completion:
> That the holy glory of your name may become famous.
> Without delay, she cuts the neck with a hooked blade,
> The maid carries the enemy's swollen head in a bag.
> Both, through the friendly silences of the shimmering moon,
> Depart the Persian camp in swift flight.
> Him, who spoke other things against the Lord,
> The woman of Samaria removed while she remained unharmed.

In her song of triumph <note>original: "Pæane"</note>, one may also read the fable of the Titans and Giants. This clearly shows that this book was written by some more recent author who betrays himself as a "little Greek" <note>original: "Graeculum"; a term suggesting a later Hellenistic author mimicking Greek style</note> rather than a Hebrew. The Holy Spirit of God never speaks this way in the authentic books as to send us to the vain fictions of the poets; far be it from Him to introduce such profane and exotic things, mixing heaven and earth. Whatever others may say, there is a deliberate allusion to the fables and barbarian nonsense of the Gentiles in such sacred songs. The Titans are imagined—with whom Jupiter waged a ten-year war, as Apollodorus noted (book 1 of the *Library*)—to have piled mountains upon mountains to build a path to heaven for themselves: namely, Pelion upon Ossa, and Ossa upon Olympus, so they might ascend to the sky. Regarding their attempt, Homer says:

> They strove to set Ossa upon Olympus, and then upon Ossa
> Leafy Pelion, so that heaven might be scaled.
<note>original Greek: Ὄσσαν ἐπ’ Οὐλύμπῳ μέμασαν θέμεν· αὐτὰρ ἐπ’ Ὄσσῃ Πήλιον εἰνοσίφυλλον ἵν’ οὐρανὸς ἀμβατὸς εἴη.</note>

Natalis Comes expressed this in his *Mythology* (book 6, ch. 21) thus:
> Great mountains they rolled, so heaven could be reached,
> Upon Ossa the leafy, and then upon Olympus,
> Along with forests and stables, high Pelion above you.

But Jupiter cast thunderous mountains upon them and prostrated them in this manner, about which Euripides says in *Hecuba*, line 472:

> The race of Titans,
> whom Zeus the son of Cronos lulls to sleep
> with a flame of surrounding fire.

"And he lulled them to sleep," says Euripides—that is, he made them sleep and silenced them with fire-breathing lightning. When the Titans were partly slaughtered and partly put to flight, the Earth <note>original: Tellus</note> gave birth to Typhon, who surpassed all in strength and size; for he was taller than the peak of any mountain, even up to his thighs. His head touched the stars; one hand stretched to the East, the other to the West. From his shoulders, a hundred heads of dragons emerged. On his legs, great...

# Judith XVI. 8. 741

<margin>Giants and Titans in Mount Etna.</margin>
The Giants were said to have the coils of vipers for feet. Virgil describes *most extensively* how Jupiter finally crushed one of them by throwing Mount Etna upon him:

> *Jupiter overwhelmed the dying Enceladus*
> *with the weight of the massive mountain, Etna,*
> *which seethes and breathes fire from its wide-open jaws.*
<note>original Latin: "Morientem Iupiter Ætna / Obruit Eneladum..." from Virgil's Aeneid.</note>

Furthermore, the same poet from Mantua <note>Virgil</note> imagines that Mount Etna looms over the head of Typhoeus, while Lilybaeum presses his legs, Pachynum his left hand, and Pelorus his right:

> *He indeed struggles and often fights to rise again,*
> *but his right hand is held down by Ausonian Pelorus.*
> *Pachynum is upon your left, his legs are pressed by Lilybaeum,*
> *and Etna weighs down his head.*
<note>original Latin: "Nititur ille quidem pugnatque resurgere sæpe..." from Ovid's Metamorphoses, though the author attributes the sentiment to Virgil.</note>

<margin>Volume 3 of German Poets, page 42.</margin>
The myths also record that after the Giants were defeated, the three brothers—Jupiter, Pluto, and Neptune—divided the world among themselves by lot: heaven went to the first, the underworld to the second, and the sea to the third. Regarding these, consult Natalis Comes in the book cited above, for it is wearying to collect more fables from myths to explain our own "fabulous" <note>The author likely means "legendary" or "allegorical" here.</note> passage. There are those who interpret the *Gigantomachy* <term>The Battle of the Giants</term> as a depiction of those who take up arms against laws and the magistrate. For this reason—and so that people would detest such wicked men even more—they depicted them as "snake-footed" <note>original: "pedesanguinos"</note>, because nothing is more monstrous or savage than to plot against God, the Magistrate, the laws, or what is right and just. Thus, Camerarius explains the snake-feet of the Titans as a reference to "impious Counselors," upon whose foul support Tyrants rely as if on feet. Gerhard Vossius—drawing from *Book 1 of Apollodorus's Library*—relates this *Theomachia* <term>Battle of the Gods</term> of Typhoeus and the other Titans <margin>Book 1 of *On Idolatry*, section 26, page 288.</margin> to the history of Joshua. He believes that Hercules was taken as an ally in the war, and that he defeated the Titans; some were slaughtered, and the Phoenicians—among whom were many of the race of giants, as is clear from *Numbers 13:29, 34*—were put to flight, though not all were of giant stature. As evidence for this, he brings forward Og, the King of Bashan, who, according to Scripture, remained as a remnant of the Giants (*Deuteronomy 3:3-11*). He says the Greeks call him *Typhon*, from the word *typho*, meaning *I burn* or *I set on fire*. Hence, his mouth is said to breathe fire in Mount Etna. For "Og" and "Typhon" agree in meaning, <margin>Homer's Odyssey, book 11, line 314.</margin> because "Og" comes from the Hebrew *ug* <note>original Hebrew: עוג</note>, meaning *he burned* or *scorched*; and *typhein* <note>Greek: τύφειν</note> signifies the same. From this, he concludes that "Og" and "Typhon" refer to the same man. And since Scripture mentions his iron bed, he links it to Virgil's line:

> *...And the hard, lifeless bed*
> *placed upon Typhoeus by the commands of Jupiter.*
<note>original Latin: "Durumque cubile / Inanime, Iovis imperiis impoſta Typhæo."</note>

Similarly, when Joshua fought against the five kings on behalf of the Gibeonites, God helped him by raining down stones, by which a great part of the enemy was destroyed. As they fled from the children of Israel, the author of the *Book of Joshua* says in *Chapter 10, verse 11*, while they were on the descent of Beth-horon, the Lord cast down great stones from heaven upon them as far as Azekah; and many more died from the hailstones than the children of Israel struck down with the sword. This miraculous slaughter of the Canaanites also reached the ears of the Gentiles, who—instigated by the Devil—perverted this and countless other miracles and wondrous deeds of God, darkening them with their own fables and fictions. They attributed it to their own Hercules, and being uncertain about the location, they guessed it happened in a place where a great heap of stones could be seen, which could hardly,

<column-break/>

if at all, have been gathered into one place by human industry. Now, <margin>Giants and Titans.</margin> since such a place is visible in Narbonese Gaul between the Rhone and Marseille, they located the battle there, as can be read in Pomponius Mela <margin>Book 2, chapter 5.</margin>: *Between Marseille and the Rhone, the sea-marsh of the Avatici sits; the Marian Trench pours out part of that river in a navigable channel. Otherwise, the coast is unremarkable, known as "The Stony Plain," where they say Hercules, fighting against Albion and Bergion (the sons of Neptune), was aided by a rain of stones from Jupiter after his weapons failed. You would believe it had rained: so many stones lie scattered far and wide.* It is no wonder that this true history of Joshua, the conqueror of the Palestinians, was mixed with fables by the Gentiles, whose knowledge consisted only of bare tradition; for even the Jews, who had Moses and the Prophets, told stories about Og, the King of Bashan, that were much more "fabulous" <note>In the sense of being mythological or exaggerated.</note> than the myths, as we reviewed above on *page 24*. Why is it surprising then, if Hesiod—that "babbler of trifles"—fell into so many and such great fabrications in his *Theogony*, when in the Apocryphal books of Esdras one may read things not a bit better. Nor should this be held against Homer, Hesiod, and others, since they were permitted to paint and invent whatever they wished, according to the saying of Taubmann:

->A Poet is such a man / who can lie with elegance:<-

Regarding this license of poets, Virgil <margin>in Etna.</margin> sings aptly:

> *The Poets lied about the Stygian waves and the hounds [of hell].*
> *They know the wars of the Gods, they know marriages*
> *hidden from us, and how often they sin under a false image—*
> *as a Bull for Europa, as a white bird for Leda,*
> *and how Jupiter flowed as a precious shower for Danaë.*
> *This is the liberty owed to songs.*

We do not believe that mere falsehoods and fictions are found in the books of the Poets, but rather truth mixed with falsehood. Nor do we compare the origin of the Giants to the fiction of the Centaurs, whom the myth-makers say were born from the union of Ixion and a cloud-mare, which he had seized thinking it was Juno. For they say that Ixion, invited by Jupiter to a banquet of the Gods, made advances on Juno; hence Sophocles calls him "the visitor of Jupiter's bed" <note>original Greek: πελάτης λέκτρων τοῦ Διὸς</note>, who dared to approach the marriage bed of Jove, "as one who attempted to seduce Hera, the consort of Jupiter," as the Scholiast <term>ancient commentator</term> explains on page 408. When Ixion later boasted among men that he had slept with Juno, he was cast down to the underworld and punished by being bound to a winged wheel. Hence the Scholiast of Pindar <margin>in Pythian Ode 2, page 205.</margin> says: *Ixion, moved by love for Hera, attempted to unite with her. Zeus, learning of this, fashioned a cloud in the likeness of Hera. Ixion, seeing this, united with it and produced from it a savage and monstrous man, whom he named Centaurus, etc.* This history of the Giants carries little weight with many who have plainly doubted their origin and existence, even relegating them to the fictions of Chimeras. Among the ancients, Thucydides writes that he has found nothing certain about their race, where they came from, or where they went: "I can neither speak of their race, nor from where they entered, nor to where they departed." Philostratus is even harsher toward their history than Thucydides; he plainly ascribes their origin to the fables of poets. His words are: "Homer recounts these things..."

<meta>This page continues the exploration of giants in biblical and classical contexts, specifically addressing the etymology of terms like 'Rephaim' and 'Nephilim,' and debating whether giants were the offspring of fallen angels or simply the descendants of the line of Seth.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Giants and Titans.</margin>
...Homer passes over this, cutting short the Trojan narrative, dedicating it rather to *Ulysses*, for whose sake the race of the Cyclopes was devised by him—though they existed nowhere on earth; likewise the *Laestrygonians* were depicted, whom no one knows where they ever were. <note>The author is quoting a Greek commentary on Homer’s Odyssey, specifically regarding the mythical nature of the giants Ulysses encountered.</note> The Poets have told wonderful stories about their origin: for a Giant [Gigas] seems to be derived from *to be born* and *earth*, so that it is the same as *earth-born*, born from the earth, or son of the earth. In this way, the Chaldean translator rendered the Hebrew <term>Rephaim</term> <note>רְפָאִים - a biblical term often translated as 'giants' or 'shades'</note> in Proverbs 1:16, and you will find them called "earth-born" in Proverbs chapter 9 verse 18. Hence Jerome writes:
<margin>Isaiah 14. Ef. p. 44.</margin>
*Giants are named according to the custom of the Pagans, who consider them to be earth-born, whom the earth itself brought forth.* The same author says in his commentary on Amos, chapter 5, page 93: *In the Book of Kings, the Greeks translated the Hebrew <term>Rephaim</term> as Titans, which is a very famous myth among the Pagans, about which they write 'Giant-Battles' in praise of the Gods, and describe the weapons of Typhoeus, and Mount Etna placed upon Enceladus, at whose movement Sicily [Trinacria] trembles.* They handed down that the Giants were born from the earth and the blood of heaven at the time when Saturn cut off his father's genitals, as Hesiod—that talkative teller of trifles—reveals in his *Theogony*, along with Orpheus in book 8 of the *Sacred Discourse*:
<margin>W. 183.</margin>
> *As many bloody drops as fell and were spat out,*
> *the Earth received them all. And as the years rolled round,*
> *she gave birth to the fierce Furies and the great Giants.*
<note>original Greek: "Ὅσαι γὰρ ῥαθάμιγγες ἀπέπτυσεν αἱματόεσσαι..."</note>
However, Apollodorus in book 1 thinks they were only sons of the earth, brought forth by an angry Ops (or the Earth) in place of the slain Titans, about whom Ovid writes in book 5 of the *Fasti*:
> *The Earth brought forth the Giants, fierce offspring and huge monsters,*
> *who would dare to enter the home of Jove.*

Within the boundaries of the Church, another opinion arose concerning the origin of the Giants, where men of no small standing seem to assert that the antediluvian Giants were primarily procreated from the intercourse of angels and women. Among the Fathers favoring this opinion are Justin Martyr *in his Apology to the Roman Senate and in another Apology to Antoninus Pius*; Tertullian *in his book On the Apparel of Women*; Clement in book 3 of the *Stromata*; Irenaeus in book 4 chapter 7; Lactantius in book 2 *On the Origin of Error, chapter 15*; Eusebius *in book 5 of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 4*; and Ambrose *in book 1 On Noah and the Ark, chapter 4*. To these add Philo *in his book On the Giants*; Josephus *in book 1 of the Antiquities of the Jews, chapter 4*; and Sulpitius Severus *in book 1 of his History*. Among more recent authors, Francisco Georgio, Tostatus *on Genesis chapter 6*, Francisco Valles *in Sacred Philosophy chapter 8*, and others whom we omit for the sake of brevity. They place the foundation of their assertion in the Mosaic words:
<margin>Genesis 6:4.</margin>
*The <term>Nephilim</term> <note>נְפִלִים - typically translated as 'Giants' or 'fallen ones'</note> were on the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown.* But in this passage, it does not signify *Angels*, but rather *sons of men*, and specifically the pious ones, who are contrasted with the *daughters of men*, that is, the *impious*, namely the descendants of Cain. For the term "Sons of God" is only attributed to good angels, upon whom

<column-break/>

this wicked disgrace does not fall. This is the explanation given by Augustine: *They are called sons of God,* he says, *either because they had once been so, or because their ancestors had obtained this title.* And Theodoret in his 47th question on Genesis says: *They were named sons of God just as we are called Christians after Christ.* Likewise Thomas [Aquinas], part 1, question 51: *By the sons of God are understood the sons of Seth, who were good; but the Scripture names as daughters of men those who were born from the stock of Cain.* Consult also Dionysius the Carthusian on Genesis 6, Cassian in his 8th Conference, and William of Paris *in the last part of On the Universe*, chapter 23; but we do not wish to be too wordy in such a clear matter. There is great controversy over the word <term>Nephilim</term>, which the Septuagint rendered as "Giants." Aquila translated it as "those who fall upon" or "attackers." Symmachus as "the violent ones." Luther as "Tyrants," and Piscator as "Giants." For others understand Giants as men of the most ferocious stature and infidels, and those most robust, about whom Basil the Great says: *A Giant is one who makes use of natural power and bodily strength.* Chrysostom in *Homily 22 on Genesis* says: *Scripture here calls those who are strong in body Giants.* Diodorus Siculus writes: *The Giants are mythologized as being earth-born because of the exceptional size of their bodies.* Among more recent scholars, Drusius, Mercerus, Junius, and Tremellius agree with this sentiment. In the most ancient annals of the Hebrews, several trustworthy histories remain concerning Giants to whom a peculiar tallness was given. Those scouts sent into the land of Canaan at the command of Jehovah through Moses spoke thus when they returned: *The land through which we have gone to search it is a land that eats up its inhabitants; and all the people that we saw in it are men of a great stature. And there we saw the Giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the Giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.* They use hyperbole both to describe the immense bodies of the Giants and to strike greater fear into their own people. The Sacred Books [Pandectae] mention not one but several of immense height: *Deuteronomy 3:11*, Og, the only one remaining of the remnant of the Giants; *Joshua 14:15*, Kiriath Arba, who was the greatest man among the Anakim; and *1 Samuel 17:5*, Goliath the Philistine, a man of the height of six cubits and a span, which Luther renders as *six ells and a hand-breadth*. Understand these to be "work-cubits" [Werck-Ehlen], each of which encompasses a measure of 24 fingers, as noted by Gerhard in his *Commentary on Genesis chapter 6*. He calculates these six cubits of Goliath, and from there—if a cubit corresponds to nearly two feet, as it certainly should—they conclude that David, given the proportions of Goliath's body, could not have carried Goliath's head. This is because Goliath’s body would have been 54 feet long and his head 8 feet; yet even the tallest men are only four cubits in length, as Peter Martyr says in his *Commentary*. Therefore, it must be that the term "four cubits in length" exceeded David, which is hardly likely, or that Goliath's head was not of such great length and weight. Yet the proportion of the body to the head (and vice versa) requires this, as does the mass of his armor, which demanded a man of wonderful height and strength. But we leave it to others more learned than us to solve this knot...

### Judith. XVI. 8.

<margin>Giants & Titans.</margin> We wish to leave aside the matter of the Giants. Regarding others born of immense size among the Philistines, this is discussed in 2 Samuel 21:16, 18 and 1 Chronicles 20:5, 6, 20. The great height and the size of the weapons described there prove that they all exceeded the common stature of man. If you desire examples from secular history, consult the records of the Ancients and Moderns. They will inform you about Sigonotho, Godfrey of the Iron Tooth, Amadis and his brothers, as well as Orlando, Ruggiero, Rodomonte, Siegfried the Dragonslayer, Wolfhart, Ilsung the Monk, and many others. They also tell of female warriors like Bradamante and Marfisa—though these stories are for the most part very similar to Aesop’s fables. It is established from both the sacred texts we cited and secular history that men of greater height were found in the past; indeed, anyone who wishes to deny this entirely must be as blind as a bat in the midday sun. We find even clearer and more manifest evidence of this among more recent writers, evidence so significant that it excludes any room for doubt. For this, we refer the Benevolent Reader to Thomas Bartholin’s *Anatomical Observations*, Felix Plater, Philipp Cluverius, and others. <note>The author lists a long series of 16th and 17th-century scholars who collected "wonders" and anomalies of nature.</note> However, we do not deny that in the most recent writers one reads things that hardly deserve belief. Such is the report of Symphorien Champier in his *French Garden*, mentioning a certain Giant two hundred cubits long <note>roughly 300 feet</note> found in Sicily near Trapani; add to this what is read in Pliny, Plutarch’s *Life of Sertorius*, Josephus, and Augustine. <margin>Book 7, 16.</margin> *I myself saw,* says Augustine in the cited passage, *and not alone but with several others, a human molar tooth so enormous that, if it were cut into small pieces the size of our teeth, it seemed it could have made a hundred of them; but we believed it belonged to some Giant.* <margin>Commentary on Augustine.</margin> Ludovicus Vives adds: *When we went to greet the feast of St. Christopher, a molar tooth larger than a fist was shown to us at the great cathedral of our city, which they said was his.* Whether this is true, we not undeservedly leave undecided. Johann Jacob Hermann conjectures that this could have been the tooth of a large sea fish. <note>Early modern scholars often struggled to identify dinosaur or megafauna fossils, frequently misidentifying them as human giants or sea monsters.</note> Conringius rightly judges that nothing certain can be concluded from the bones, teeth, and limbs so frequently brought forth from the womb of the earth, because of the deception that could easily occur. This remains true even if they are cited with approval by writers like Pliny, Pausanias, or Acosta in his *History of the Indies*. Swenter feels the same about a rib five cubits long found in an old chapel in Mainz. In America, especially in the regions of Chile and Chica, geographers write that giants are still found, in comparison to whom the Dutch were like crows or little dogs.

<column-break/>

<margin>Giants & Titans.</margin> Magellan experienced for himself that giants live in the same province called Patagonia, of which Gotfridus reports in his *History of the Antipodes*: They sighted a giant there on the shore who was so tall that the Spaniards hardly reached up to his belt; later they captured another ten feet tall, who ate a whole basket full of hard-tack biscuits at one time and drank half a bucket of water in one breath. <note>Original German: "Daß Sie daselbst eines Riesen am Ufer ansichtig worden..."</note> The *West Indian Histories* records the same regarding Amerigo Vespucci, who on his second journey to America found the "Island of Giants" there. His words are these: Since they could get nothing on this island, they departed and came to another island; because they initially saw no people, they thought it must be entirely uninhabited. But when they went ashore, they noticed several large footprints in the sand, from which they could suspect that large people and giants must live on this island. This was later proven when nine of them went down a path to find fresh water and came upon five houses after a mile's walk, where they encountered two large women with three girls, at which they were greatly amazed. <note>Original German: "Wie Sie nun auff dieser Insul nichts bekommen mochten..."</note> And a little later: Then six naked men came in, who were a great deal larger than the women, and so well-formed in body that it was a sight to see. And again: The Spaniards later called this the Island of Giants, because they encountered these large people there.

The second opinion is held by those who understand the <term>Nephilim</term> <note>נפילים - often translated as giants</note> to be violent oppressors of others, who, abusing the robustness of their strength, fell violently upon others. For the root <term>naphal</term> means to fall upon, to rush, or to cause to fall; they made others fall before them and subjected them to their power. Hence they are also called <term>Gibborim</term> <note>גבורים - mighty ones</note>, those robust and most powerful men, and "Men of Name" [Anshei HaShem], that is, famous or celebrated men, who labored to acquire the glory of a name and proof of their power through the oppression of others. Thus Luther translated the word as "Tyrants," Aquila as "those falling upon," and Symmachus as "the violent"—that is, those rushing in violently, crushing others, and driving others to ruin. This is the view of Chrysostom, Cyril, Gerhard, and others. All these understand the "giants" in this Mosaic passage not by quantity or stature, but by quality. For the annals of almost every age testify that heroes were found at all times possessing marvelous strength and fortitude, to which was sometimes added a fitting but not excessive height. Maximinus, the successor and murderer of Alexander Severus, was endowed with such height and strength (according to Julius Capitolinus) that he seemed to exceed eight feet; his thumb was so vast that he used his wife's bracelet as a ring. He could pull wagons with his hands, and if he struck a horse with his fist, he would knock out its teeth; if he kicked it, he would break its legs. He could crumble pumice stones and break young trees. For this reason, he was called Milo of Croton by some, Hercules by others, and Antaeus by yet others. Of the Emperor Aurelian, Flavius Vopiscus left it written...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Giants and Titans.</margin>
...of his own <note>The text likely refers to the Roman Emperor Maximinus Thrax, known for his giant stature</note>, because his stature was taller than all others. He possessed the strongest muscles; as Theoclius, the Imperial Historian, records, he killed 42 men with his own hand in a single day during the Sarmatian war, and on various distinct days he killed 950. He was so renowned that even the boys who operated the catapults and the military dancers composed songs like these about Aurelian <note>Lucius Domitius Aurelianus, another Roman Emperor</note>, which they would dance to in a military fashion on feast days: *A thousand, a thousand, a thousand, a thousand, a thousand, a thousand we have beheaded: A thousand, a thousand, a thousand, may he live who killed a thousand, a thousand. No one has as much wine as the blood he has shed.*

Regarding George Castriot, Prince of part of Albania, whom the Turks called *Ischenderbeg* <note>Skanderbeg</note>—that is, "Lord Alexander"—because of the greatness of his deeds, Paolo Giovio reports that he killed over two thousand men. Or, as Marinus Barletius of Shkodër writes (who described his deeds in a specific book, which Johannes Panicianus later translated from the Latin language into our vernacular), he killed three thousand barbarians with his own hand, particularly in various battles. Indeed, he was accustomed to dispatching each opponent who met him with only a single blow, for he used a very large and heavy scimitar <note>original: *acinace*</note> with such strength and skill that he would cut enemies in half to the navel, or divide them crosswise, and often easily lop off entire limbs, including shoulders and arms, right through the neck.

Concerning Georg von Frundsberg, Baron in *Mindelheim*, writers of the previous century report that he was so strong in his limbs that by merely extending the middle finger of his right hand, he could easily move any strong man who was standing on firm footing. He could stop a running horse by grabbing its bridle. Alone, he could push a wall-gun <note>A heavy, early firearm</note> wherever he wished by leaning it on his shoulder. While traveling, he would gladly give up his horse and walk on foot ahead of the common soldiers and youths with steady strides. See Paolo Giovio, *Elogia, Book 6, page 284*, and Martin Crusius, *Part 3, Book 11, Chapter 1*. Wilhelm Dilich, in his *Topography of Hesse*, records the great strength of Henry the Iron, Landgrave of Hesse, and Count John of Ziegenhain.

It would take too long if we wished to run through the annals of all centuries; Joachim Camerarius recounts more in *Century 1, Chapter 82, page 376*, as does Martin Zeiller in *Rose-Garden of Wondrous and Sad Histories, History 6, page 196 and following*. While we agree with Blessed Gerhard and other patrons of the latter opinion, we intend at least this: that from the single and bare word *Nephilim* <note>original Hebrew: נפילים</note> in Genesis 6:4—the passage under controversy—it cannot be proved that these were "Giants," as the Vulgate and Piscator argue. However, in other places cited above, besides the word *Nephilim*, the circumstances—namely the tallness of stature, the size of weapons, etc.—clearly show that giants are meant. We approve of what the Lexicographers and Commentators write about the names by which Giants are distinguished among the Hebrews. In the Holy Code, the word *Rephaim* <note>original: רפאים and רפא</note> occurs quite often, which signifies not only "to care for" or "to heal," but also "to strengthen," whence *Rephaim* denotes "the powerful" or "the strong."

<margin>Davidic Lexicon, root 1043, page 818.</margin>
Schereus alludes to the first meaning: *From the root* Rapha, *he healed or cured, as if you were to say healthy, strong, or "healths."* The name of the Giant in *Job*, whose sons are written about in 2 Samuel 21:16, was of monstrous size, and therefore all Giants and Tyrants are called *Rephaim*. So he says. Others derive it 

<column-break/>

from the root *raphah* <note>original: רפה</note>, meaning "he let go," "he was slack," or "he failed." Thus a Giant is called *Rapha* because he would weaken the spirits of others with his horrendous stature and make them slack. Hence Rabbi Bechai writes on Deuteronomy 2:10: *They are called* Rephaim *because whoever looked at them, his hands became slack <note>original Hebrew: נקראים רפאים משום שכל הרואה אותם ידיו מתרפות</note>, surely out of fear.* From this they are also called *Emim*—"terrors"—as if they were called terrifying and formidable. For *Emim* occurs in Deuteronomy 2:10, from *eymah* <note>original: אימה</note>, "terror" or "dread," from an unused root *ayim*, from which comes *ayom*, "formidable." Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> writes here: *This is to say: They are so called because their terror is cast upon the creatures, that is, other men.* <note>original Hebrew: אמים על שאימתם מוטלת על הבריות</note>

Regarding the word *Nephilim*, we spoke above; however, Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra</note> thinks Giants were so called to mean "defectors," because they fell away from God through impiety, or perhaps "Dejectors," who caused men to fall by their immense height. Rabbi David Kimchi <note>Radak</note> thinks they were so called because other men fell down in dread of them due to their huge and vast bodies. Nahmanides <note>Gerundinensis</note> wishes them to be so called because they had "fallen" from common build, and exceeded their fathers in stature and power. Hence they are usually categorized among monsters by Conrad Gessner, as a punishment for such negligent immodesty and fornication, so that a monstrous coupling might be marked by a monstrous offspring. In support of his opinion, he cites Augustine, Gregory Nazianzen, Theodoret, Ambrose, and Cyril. Johannes Sperling and Posner defend the contrary view.

One might wonder, however, why such robust and tall men are not born in modern times, even in our lands, as modern historians report concerning the inhabitants of Chile and the Chicca provinces of America. There are those who seek the cause of this in a certain hidden property of the region. Others ascribe it to the luxury of modern times, whence Binsfeld <note>Peter Binsfeld, a theologian and witch-hunter</note> responds: *Because through the intemperance and ignorance of men, nature is greatly corrupted and infected with diseases; and natural things—especially since even the earth is failing from its original integrity—are not of such vigor and virtue as they were in the beginning of Creation.* Immediately after the creation of things, by divine disposition, all things were of greater perfection: the constitution <note>original: complexio</note> of men was stronger and more constant, and the influence of the heavens more healthful. He cites Francisco de Vitoria and Josephus Angles in support of his opinion. Juvenal points to this:

> For this race was already decreasing in the time of Homer,
> The earth now brings forth evil and puny men.

And Virgil in the *Aeneid*, Book 12:

> Scarcely twelve chosen men could lift it on their necks,
> Such bodies as the earth produces now.

Horace conforms to these in *Odes*, Book 1, 3:

> Daring to endure all things,
> The human race rushes through forbidden sin.
> The daring son of Iapetus [Prometheus]
> Brought fire to the nations through evil deceit.

# Judith. XVI. 8.
<page-num>745</page-num>

<margin>Giants & Titans.</margin>

> *After fire from the heavenly home*
> ->*Was stolen, a wasting sickness and a new troop*<-
> ->*Of fevers brooded over the lands,*<-
> ->*And the slow necessity of death, previously*<-
> ->*Far removed, quickened its pace.*<-
<note>original Latin: *Post ignem atheria domo / Subductum, macies & nova febrium / Terris incubuit cohors / Semotique prius tarda necessitas / Lethi corripuit gradum.* This is a quote from Horace’s Odes (1.3.29-33) regarding Prometheus stealing fire from the gods.</note>

We readily grant that immediately after the Creation all things were in a state of perfection, and consequently, men were also much longer-lived and of a grander stature. However, we do not agree with those who assert that the first humans, Adam and Eve, and nearly all the "Antediluvians" <note>those living before the Great Flood</note> were of giant stature. This opinion is supported by Esdras in Book 4, Chapter 5; Hieronymus Magius in *Miscellanea*; the Conimbricenses in their commentaries on Aristotle's *Physics*; Genebrardus in his *Chronography*; Scaliger regarding the Samoyed peoples; Moses Bar-Cephas in *On Paradise*; Johannes Lucidus in *On the Emendation of Time*; Pliny; Varro (quoted by Aulus Gellius); and among the Church Fathers, Cyprian, Jerome, and Augustine. Among more recent authors, Dr. David Christianus argues this (though we believe not entirely seriously) in his *System of Geography*, where he writes: *Geometers and Geographers are persuaded by the facts themselves; when they compare the "feet" <note>units of measurement</note> of different peoples, they notice the Toledan foot is shorter than the Heidelberg foot, the Heidelberg shorter than the Etruscan, the Etruscan shorter than the Old Roman, that shorter than the Attic, the Attic shorter than the Gallic, and the Gallic shorter than the Egyptian. There is no better reason for these manifest differences than that the older a measurement is, the longer it is. Thus, the Gauls were once taller than the Italians and Greeks, though the difference is now gone. Since we gather from Scripture that the Hebrews had three types of cubits, the largest being double the smallest, what prevents us from believing that men in the times of Adam and Noah were ten times longer-lived <note>original Greek: μακροβιωτέρους</note> and at least twice as tall as they began to be from the time of Moses?*

<margin>Note on Genesis chapter 6, question 7, pages 156, 157.</margin>
Truly, either our present stature is monstrous, or Adam’s must have been. And why is it that crows, despite their great longevity <note>original Greek: μακροβιότητα</note>, are not said to be larger than usual? Compare this with the works of Hermann, Jonston on the *Constancy of Nature*, and Conring. As a concluding note, it is pleasing to add the account of Hemo, the Egyptian Hermit, regarding many stupendous things as recounted by Francesco Patrizi—though it reeks more of the fabulous curiosity of the Egyptians than of true piety. Among other things, he says: "We preserve in memory that in the first cycle of years, men were of such a great body that, while standing on the earth, they hid their heads among the stars; they were called *Emephimos*. These were followed by others called *Phtaimos*, slightly smaller, yet whose heads still touched the clouds. Others followed them, called *Gygini* in Egypt, whom I think you call Giants, who lasted until the time of Noah; and as they were of great body, so they lived healthy and unharmed for many years."

<margin>Satire 15, verse 69.</margin>
But from the Deluge—

<column-break/>

—everything began to rush toward the worse, both in other matters and especially in those concerning the arts and virtue.

<margin>Giants & Titans.</margin>
### 1. Maccabees III, 48.

->They opened the book of the law, concerning which the nations searched for the likenesses of their idols.<-
<note>original Greek: ἐξεπέτασαν τὸ βιβλίον τοῦ νόμου, περὶ ὧν ἐξηρεύτων τὰ ἔθνη τὰ ὁμοιώματα τῶν εἰδώλων αὐτῶν.</note>

->They spread out the books of the Law, in which the Gentiles sought the likeness of their own images.<-

Religion is a matter of great importance, even to the point of <margin>A perversion of sacred rites:</margin> zealotry; even the Pagans commended it as a "unifying bond of every society" <note>original Greek: συνεκτικόν τι πάσης κοινωνίας</note>. The wise Stagirite <note>Aristotle</note> also prescribed the highest rule of affairs: "First is the care for divine things" <note>original Greek: πρῶτον ἡ περὶ τὸ θεῖον ἐπιμέλεια</note>. This was the <margin>Politics, Book 7, Ch. 8.</margin> only spur to virtue and some honesty of life in the minds of the Heathens, preventing most from being swept away into the sea and whirlpool of Epicureanism. No nation was so forsaken that it did not believe some God should be worshiped, even if it was ignorant of how to worship the true God rightly. However, the Devil's greatest care was to keep the Gentiles in his superstitious worship by mixing truth with obscurity, so that his worshipers understood nothing less than what they ought to understand. The overturning of divine truth was the raising up of fables, an open field for idle minds to create whatever fictions they pleased. What did the ancients not involve in the veil of ingeniously devised fables? Their work here was very extensive, as anyone who diligently studies the writings of the ancient poets will easily discover. Those who examine more deeply the fables, riddles, symbols, and other fictions passed down by the Pagans usually refer many of them to Nature and History. For we must not believe, as Arnobius says, <margin>Against the Nations.</margin> that these things exist in vain without their own origins, or that they lack causes joined to their first institutions. Clement of Alexandria confirms this in *Stromata*, Book 5, writing: "All who have treated of divine things, both Barbarians and Greeks, hid the beginnings of things; they handed down the truth in riddles, symbols, allegories, metaphors, and similar modes." And on page 575: "Being philosophers, they established mysteries and buried their own doctrines in myths so they would not be plain to everyone." Origen, in *Against Celsus*, Book 8, says: "Festivals are shown to be inventions of historical events or natural explanations concerning water, the earth, or its fruits." Eusebius <margin>Preparation for the Gospel, Book 1.</margin> reports this at length from ancient monuments, where Philo of Byblos complains that many clouds and fables were drawn over historical truth by the mystics—except for Sanchuniathon of Berytus <note>Beirut</note>, who, having been admitted to the ancient books of Ammun, rejected fables and brought forth everything as it actually happened. There is no philosophy or theology more obscure than that of the Egyptians. "For this reason, they place Sphinxes before their temples, as if to show that their doctrine about the Word is something enigmatic and obscure," as Clement testifies. Arnobius laughs at their riddles because they inserted the forms of dumb animals into divine causes. Nor can it be denied by these first and principal architects of fables and riddles, who took many things from the mysteries of the Hebrews...
