...[Maximinus?] <note>The OCR reads "piscus," but the context of the Sarmatian War and the verses following clearly refer to the Roman Emperor Maximinus Thrax, known for his giant stature.</note>, who was of such a towering height and possessed of the most powerful muscles that, as Theoclius the Imperial Historian records, he killed forty-eight men with his own hand in a single day during the Sarmatian War, and over various days a total of nine hundred and fifty. It is the name of a Giant in Nob, concerning whose sons it is written in 2 Samuel 21:16; since he was of monstrous size, all Giants and Tyrants were therefore called <term>Rephaim</term>. This is his view. Others derive it

<column-break/>

from the root <term>raphah</term> <note>original Hebrew: רָפָה</note>, "he let go, he was slack, he failed," whence a Giant is called <term>Repha</term> because he would weaken the hearts of others by his horrifying stature and make them go limp. Hence Rabbi Bechai writes on Deuteronomy 2:11: <note>original Hebrew: שמשכר רפו אותם ידי מן הצרות</note> *whence they are called Rephaim for the reason that whoever looked upon them, his hands became limp, namely, from fear.* For this reason, they are also called <term>Emim</term> ("Terrors"), being named as if they were terrifying and formidable. Indeed, in Deuteronomy 2:11, <term>Emim</term> <note>original Hebrew: אֵמִים</note> occurs, from <term>eymah</term> <note>original Hebrew: אֵימָה</note> ("terror, dread"), from an unusual root from which comes "the formidable." Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> writes here: <note>original Hebrew: מפני שאימתם מוטלת על הבריות</note> that is: *They are so called because their terror is cast upon the creatures, that is, other men.* Concerning the word <term>Nephilim</term>, we spoke above; however, Aben Ezra thinks Giants are so called as "defectors," because they fell away from God through impiety, or as "those who cause others to fall," because they made men fall by their immense height. Rabbi David Kimchi thinks they were so named because other men fell down in dread of them on account of their large and vast bodies. Nachmanides <note>Gerundinefis</note> wishes them to be so called because they had "fallen away" from the common bulk of body, and exceeded their fathers in stature and power. Hence they are usually classified among monsters by Gesner, as a punishment for such supine lewdness and whoredom, so that a monstrous coupling might be marked by a monstrous offspring. To prove this opinion, he cites Augustine (book 15 of *Questions on Genesis*), Gregory Nazianzen (*Oration 27 on the Love of the Poor*), Theodoret (*Question 48 on Genesis*), Ambrose (*On Noah and the Ark*), and Cyril (book 3 on *Genesis*). Johannes Sperling (book 1 of *Physics*) and Posner (*Disputation on Monsters*) defend the contrary. One might wonder why such robust and tall men are not born in modern times, even in our own lands, just as modern historians report concerning the inhabitants of the provinces of Chile and Chica in America. Some look for the cause of this in a certain hidden property of the region. Others ascribe it to the luxury of modern times, whence Binsfeldius (in *On the Confession of Witches*) responds: *Because through the intemperance and ignorance of men, nature is greatly corrupted and infected with diseases, and natural things—especially since the earth itself fails from its original integrity—are not of such vigor and virtue as they were at the beginning of Creation.* Immediately after the creation of things, by divine disposition, all things were of greater perfection: the constitution of men was stronger and more constant, and the influence of the heavens more healthful. Francisco de Vitoria (in *Relection on the Art of Magic*) and Josephus Angles support this opinion. Juvenal points to this:

> For this race was already decreasing in the time of Homer;
> The earth now brings forth bad and tiny men.

And Virgil in *Aeneid* book 12:

> Scarcely could twelve chosen men support it on their necks,
> Such bodies of men as the earth now produces.

Horace follows these (Book 1, Ode 3):

> Daring to suffer all things,
> The human race rushes through forbidden sin.
> The daring offspring of Iapetus
> Brought fire to the nations by an evil fraud.

# Judith. XVI. 8. 745

<margin>
On Giants and Titans.
</margin>

> After fire was stolen from its celestial home,
> a wasting sickness and a new army of fevers
> settled upon the earth;
> and the previously slow necessity of death, 
> once far off, quickened its pace.
<note>original: "Post ignem etheria domo / Subductum, macies & nova febrium / Terris incubuit cohors / Semotique prius tarda necessitas / Lethi corripuit gradum." These lines are from Horace’s Odes (Book 1, Ode 3), referencing the myth of Prometheus stealing fire and the subsequent decline of human health and longevity.</note>

We easily grant that immediately after Creation, all things were in a state of perfection, and consequently, men were much longer-lived and of a grander stature. However, we do not agree with those who assert that the first humans, *Adam* and *Eve*, and almost all the "Antediluvians" <note>Those living before the Great Flood of Noah.</note> were of giant-like stature. This opinion is supported by *Esdras (Book 4, ch. 5, v. 52 and following)*, *Hieronymus Magius (Miscellanea, book 1, ch. 4)*, the *Conimbricenses (Physics, book 8, ch. 2, q. 3)*, *Genebrard in his Chronography*, and *Scaliger* regarding the Samgethian people. Also *Moses Bar-Cephas (On Paradise, book 1, ch. 14)*, *Johannes Lucidus (On the Amendment of Time, book 1)*, *Pliny (book 7, ch. 16)*, and *Varro* as cited by *Aulus Gellius (book 3, ch. 10)*. Among the Church Fathers, *Cyprian (Against Demetrianus)*, *Jerome (on Matthew ch. 27)*, and *Augustine (City of God, book 15, ch. 9)* hold this view. Among more recent authors, *Dr. David Christianus* discusses it—though we suspect not entirely seriously—in his *System of Geography (book 1, ch. 10, p. 208)*. We cite his words in full: *“Geometers and Geographers are persuaded by the facts themselves; for when they compare the ‘feet’ <note>Standard units of measurement</note> of various peoples, they notice that the Toledan foot is shorter than the Heidelberg foot, the Heidelberg shorter than the Etruscan, the Etruscan shorter than the Ancient Roman, that shorter than the Attic, the Attic shorter than the French, and the French shorter than the Egyptian. Though the difference is not monstrous, it is manifest and not to be ignored. They find no better reason for this than that the more ancient a ‘foot’ is, the longer it is. Thus, the Gauls were once taller to the Italians and Greeks, but now that difference is gone because most Italians and Gauls descend from Germans and Cimbrians. Therefore, since we gather from Scripture that the Hebrews had three types of cubits, the largest being twice the size of the smallest, what stops us from believing that in the times of Adam and Noah, just as men lived ten times longer, they were at least twice as tall as they became starting from the time of Moses?”* But if this were true, either our present stature is "monstrous" <note>deformed or unnaturally small</note>, or Adam’s must have been. And why is it that crows, despite their great longevity, are not said to be larger than usual? Compare *Hermann Conring* and *Jonston (On the Constancy of Nature)*. To crown this discussion, I will add the story of Hemo, an Egyptian hermit, regarding many stupendous things as recorded by *Francesco Patrizi*—though it smacks more of the tall tales of the Egyptians than true piety. Among other things, he says: "We preserve in memory that in the first cycle of years, men were of such grand bodies that, standing with their feet on the ground, they hid their heads among the stars; they were called <term>Emephimos</term>. These were followed over time by others called <term>Phtaimos</term>, slightly smaller, but still whose heads touched the clouds. These were followed by other large ones called <term>Gygini</term> in Egypt—whom I think you call giants—who certainly lasted until the time of Noah. As they had grand bodies, they lived healthy and unharmed for many years. But from the Del-

<margin>
Notes on Genesis ch. 6, p. 136, 157.
</margin>

<margin>
Juvenal, Satire 15, v. 69.
</margin>

<column-break/>

-uge, all things began to fall into a worse state, both in other matters and especially in those concerning the arts and virtue."

### 1 Maccabees III, 48.

They unrolled the book of the law, about which the nations searched for the likenesses of their idols.
<note>original Greek: Ἐξεπετάζαν τὸ βιβλίον τοῦ νόμου, περὶ ὧν ἐξηρεύτων τὰ ἔθνη τὰ ὁμοιώματα τῶν εἰδώλων αὐτῶν.</note>

-> *They opened the books of the Law, in which the Gentiles sought the likeness of their own images.* <-

Religion is a matter of great importance; indeed, even the misguided and the Pagans have commended it as "something that holds together every society." <note>original: "συνεκτικὸν τι πάσης κοινωνίας" (a cohesive element of every community). The OCR text "κοι- λια rituvovius" appears to be a corruption of this phrase.</note> The wise Stagirite <note>Aristotle</note> also prescribed this rule: *“First, the care concerning things divine.”* <note>original: Πρῶτον ἡ περὶ τὸ θεῖον ἐπιμέλεια. From Aristotle's *Politics*, book 7, ch. 8.</note> For in the minds of the Heathen, this was the sole spur toward virtue and some honesty of life, preventing most from being swept away into the sea and whirlpool of Epicureanism <note>A philosophy often associated in this period with atheism or pure pursuit of pleasure</note>. No nation was so abandoned that it did not think some God ought to be worshipped, even if it was ignorant of how to worship the true God rightly. However, it was the Devil's greatest care to keep the Gentiles in superstitious worship of himself by mixing truth with obscurity, so that his worshippers understood nothing less than what they ought to have understood. The overturning of divine truth was the erection of fables, and the field was open for idle minds to create whatever fictions they pleased. What did the ancients not wrap in the veil of ingeniously devised fables? Their work here was most profuse, as anyone who diligently studies the writings of the ancient poets will easily discover. Those who examine the fables, riddles, symbols, and other fictions handed down by the Pagans more deeply and intimately usually refer many of them to *Nature* or *History*. For we should not believe, as *Arnobius* says, *“that these things were created in vain without origin, or that they became empty, having no causes joined to their first institutions.”* This is confirmed by *Clement of Alexandria (Stromata, book 5, p. 556)*, writing: "All who have spoken of divine things, both Barbarians and Greeks, have hidden the beginnings of things; they have delivered the truth in enigmas and symbols, and again in allegories and metaphorical ways." And on *page 575*: "Those who established the mysteries, being philosophers, buried their doctrines in myths so that they would not be clear to everyone." *Origen (Against Celsus, book 8, p. 403)*: "Festivals are proven to be inventions of those who, for whatever reason, based them on human histories or legislation, or on physical theories about water, the earth, or the fruits that seem to come from it." *Eusebius* recorded this extensively from ancient monuments; in his work, *Philo of Byblos* complains that many clouds and fables were drawn over historical truth by the mystics—with the sole exception of *Sanchuniathon* of Berytus, who, having been admitted to the ancient books of Ammunaeus, pruned away the fables and produced everything as it actually happened. No philosophy or theology is more obscure than that of the Egyptians. *“For this reason, they set up Sphinxes before their temples, as the speech concerning God is enigmatic and unclear,”* as witnessed by *Clement (p. 561)*; and *Arnobius* laughs at *“their enigmas, because they inserted the forms of mute animals into divine causes.”* Nor can it be denied that these first and principal architects of fables and enigmas took much from the mysteries of the Hebrews...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES #

<margin>Giants and Titans.</margin> ...to have been [giants], because his stature was taller than others and his muscles were most powerful. As Theoclius, the Imperial Historiographer, records, this man killed 48 enemies with his own hand in a single day during the Sarmatian war, and over many distinct days killed 950; so much so that even the young soldiers and those performing military dances composed such songs for Aurelian, which they would leap to in military fashion on feast days: *A thousand, a thousand, a thousand, a thousand, a thousand we have beheaded: A thousand, a thousand, a thousand, long live he who has killed a thousand, a thousand. No one has as much wine as he has shed blood.* <note>original Latin: "Mille, mille, mille... Tantum vini habet nemo, quantum fudit sanguinis." These are rhythmic chants or 'fescennine' verses sung by Roman soldiers to celebrate the prowess of their leaders.</note> Regarding George Castriot, Prince of part of Albania, whom the Turks—on account of the greatness of his deeds—called *Ischender begum*, that is, "Lord Alexander" <note>Better known as Skanderbeg (1405–1468), a national hero of Albania who led a rebellion against the Ottoman Empire.</note>, Paulus Jovius reports that he killed over two thousand men. Or, as Marinus Barletius of Shkodër writes (who described his deeds in a specific book, which Johannes Panicianus later translated from Latin into our vernacular), he killed three thousand barbarians with his own hand across various battles. For he was accustomed to finish off those he met in combat with only single blows; he used a massive and heavy scimitar <note>original: "acinace," a type of Persian or Turkish sword.</note> with such strength and skill that he would cleave enemies through the middle to the navel, or divide them crosswise, and often easily lopped off entire limbs, including shoulders and arms, through the neck. Regarding Georg von Frundsberg, Baron in Mindelheim, writers of the previous century report that he was so powerful in the strength of his limbs that, with only the middle finger of his right hand extended, he could easily move the strongest man who was standing on firm footing; he could stop a running horse by seizing its bridle; and, leaning his shoulder against it, he could alone propel a wall-gun <note>original: "tormentum murale," a heavy piece of early artillery or a large-caliber siege firearm.</note> wherever he wished. While traveling, he would gladly dismount his horse and, on foot, would outpace the regular soldiers and young men by many full strides. See Paulus Jovius, *Elogia, book 6, page 284*, and Martin Crusius, *part 3, book 11, ch. 1*. Wilhelm Dilich, in his *Topography of Hesse*, records the great strength of Henry the Iron, Landgrave of Hesse, and John, Count of Ziegenhain. It would take too long if we wished to run through the annals of every century; Camerarius lists more in *Century 1, ch. 82, p. 376*, as does Martin Zeiler in his *Wondrous and Sad Historical Tales, history 6, p. 196 and following*. While we agree with B. Gerhard and other patrons of the latter opinion, we intend at least this: that from the lone and bare word <term>נפילים</term> <note>Nephilim</note> in *Genesis 6:4* (the place where the controversy lies), "Giants" cannot be proven, which is what the Vulgate and Piscator defend. Indeed, in other passages cited above, besides the word <term>נפילים</term> <note>Nephilim</note>, the circumstances—namely, the height of stature, the size of armor, etc.—evince that giants are to be understood. The things that Lexicographers and Commentators write concerning the names by which Giants are designated among the Hebrews are pleasing. In the Sacred Code, there frequently occurs <term>רפא</term> <note>Rapha</note> and <term>רפאים</term> <note>Rephaim</note>, which signifies not only "to care for" or "to heal," but also "to strengthen," whence <term>רפאים</term> <note>Rephaim</note> denotes "the powerful" or "the strong." Schareus alludes to the former meaning; <margin>Lexicon of David, root 1043, p. 818.</margin> from the root <term>רפא</term> <note>Rapha</note>, "he healed, he medicated," as if you were to say "the healthy," "the strong," or "the healings." The name of a "Giant" in Nob, concerning whose sons it is written in *2 Samuel 21:16*, who, since he was of monstrous size, therefore all "Giants" and "Tyrants" were called <term>רפאים</term> <note>Rephaim</note>. Thus he says. Others derive it

<column-break/>

from the root <term>רפה</term> <note>Raphah</note>, "he let go," "he was slack," or "he failed." In the hithpael form <term>התירפה</term> <note>Hithraphah</note>, a Giant is called <term>רפא</term> <note>Rapha</note> because by his terrifying stature he would weaken the hearts of others and render them slack. Hence Rabbi Bechai writes on *Deuteronomy 2*: <term>רפאים רפאים שהיו רואה אותם ידיו מיתרפות</term> : "because whoever looked upon them, his hands became slack," namely, out of fear. From this they are also called <term>אמים</term> <note>Emim</note>, meaning "terrors," as if called terrifying and formidable. For <term>אימה</term> <note>Eimah</note> occurs from <term>אום</term> <note>Um</note> or <term>אמם</term> <note>Amam</note>, from <term>אימה</term> <note>Eimah</note>, "terror, dread," from the unusual root <term>אימי</term> <note>Eimi</note>, from which comes <term>אימנים</term> <note>Eimanim</note>, "formidable." Rabbi Solomon writes here: <term>היו מהלכים אימתם על הבריות</term>, that is: "They are so called because their terror was cast over the creatures," i.e., other men. Regarding the word <term>נפילים</term> <note>Nephilim</note>, we spoke above; but Aben Esra thinks Giants were so called as "defectors," because through impiety they fell away from God, or because they were "Dowers" [Dejectores], who by their immense stature made men fall. Rabbi David Kimchi thinks they were so named because, on account of their large and vast bodies, other men fell down in fear of them. Nachmanides <note>original: "Gerundinensis," referring to Moses ben Nahman of Gerona.</note> wants them to be called thus because they had "fallen" away from common corpulence and had exceeded "their fathers in stature and power." Hence they are usually classified among monsters by Gesner, as a punishment for such prostrate shamelessness and fornication, so that a monstrous cohabitation might be marked by a monstrous offspring. He brings forward as proof of his opinion Augustine (*Book 5, Questions on Genesis, q. 3*), Gregory Nazianzen (*Oration 27, On the Love of the Poor*), Theodoret (*Question 48 on Genesis*), Ambrose (*On Noah and the Ark, ch. 4*), and Cyril (*Book 3 on Genesis*). Johannes Sperling (*Physics, book 1, p. 261*) and Posner (*Disputation on Monsters*) defend the contrary. One might wonder, however, why such robust and tall men are not born in modern times, even in our own lands, just as modern historians report concerning the inhabitants of Chile and Chica, provinces of America. There are some who seek the cause of this matter in a certain hidden property of the region. Others ascribe it to the luxury of modern times; whence Binsfeld, in *On the Confession of Witches, Doubt: Since nothing is affected etc., conclusion 8 at the end*, answers thus: "Because through the intemperance and ignorance of men, nature is greatly corrupted and infected with diseases, and natural things—especially since the earth itself fails from its original integrity—are not of such vigor and virtue as they were in the beginning of Creation." Immediately after the creation of things, by divine disposition, all things were of greater perfection: the physical constitution of men was stronger and more constant, and the influence of the heavens more healthful. He cites in support of his opinion Francisco de Vitoria (*Relection on the Art of Magic*) and Josephus Angles. Juvenal aims at this same point:
> For this race was already decreasing in the time of Homer:
> The earth now nourishes bad and tiny men.
<note>original: "Nam genus hoc vivo jam decrescebat Homero / Terra malos homines nunc educat atque pusillos." (Satire 15, lines 167-168).</note>

And Virgil in the *Aeneid, Book 12*:
> Twelve chosen men could scarcely lift it on their necks,
> Such bodies of men as the earth now produces.
<note>original: "Vix illud lecti bis sex cervice subirent / Qualia nunc hominum producit corpora tellus." (Aeneid 12, lines 899-900).</note>

Horace conforms himself to these in *Odes, Book 1, Ode 3, v. 25*:
> Bold to endure all things,
> The human race rushes through forbidden sin.
> The bold offspring of Iapetus
> Brought fire to the nations by an evil fraud.
<note>original: "Audax omnia perpeti / Gens humana ruit per vetitum nefas..." Iapetus's offspring is Prometheus.</note>

# Judith. XVI. 8. #

<margin>Giants and Titans.</margin>
> After fire was stolen from the heavenly home,
> wasting disease and a new troop of fevers
> settled upon the earth,
> and the slow necessity of death, previously far off,
> quickened its pace.
<note>original Latin: "Post ignem aetheria domo / Subductum..." This is a famous passage from Horace's Odes (1.3), describing how Prometheus's theft of fire brought disease and shortened human life.</note>

We readily grant that immediately after the Creation, all things were in a more perfect state, and consequently, humans were much longer-lived and of a grander stature. However, we do not by that same token give our applause to those who assert that the first humans, Adam and Eve, and nearly all the Antediluvians <note>Those living before the Great Flood.</note> were of a gigantic stature. This opinion is favored by *Esdras in Book 4, Chapter 5; Hieronymus Magius in Miscellaneous Works, Book 1; the Conimbricenses in Physics, Book 8; Genebrard in his Chronography; Scaliger regarding the Samghithis people; Moses Barcepha in On Paradise, Book 1; Johannes Lucidus in On the Amendment of Time; Pliny, Book 7; Varro (cited by Aulus Gellius); and among the Church Fathers, Cyprian against Demetrianus, Jerome on Matthew 27, and Augustine in The City of God, Book 15.* Among more recent writers, *Dr. David Christiani*—though we believe not entirely seriously—discusses this in his *System of Geography*. We cite his words in full: *Thus, let the Geometricians and Geographers believe; they compare feet among themselves and notice that the Toledan foot is shorter than the Heidelberg foot, the Heidelberg shorter than the Etruscan, the Etruscan than the Ancient Roman, that than the Attic, the Attic than the Gallic, and the Gallic than the Egyptian. For this difference, which is not indeed monstrous but nonetheless manifest and not to be despised, no better reason occurs to them than that the older each "foot" is, the longer it is. Thus, the Gauls were once taller than the Italians and Greeks, but now that distinction is not apparent, because most of both Italians and Gauls are descended from Germans and Cimbrians, etc.* Since, therefore, we gather from several passages of Scripture that there were three types of cubits among the Hebrews—the largest of which was twice as big as the smallest—what prevents us from believing that in the times of *Adam and Noah*, men were at least twice as tall as they began to be from the time of *Moses*, just as they were tenfold in longevity? But either our present stature is monstrously small, or Adam’s must have been monstrously large. And what would be the reason why crows, despite their <term>μακροβιότητα</term> <note>original Greek: "makrobiotēta," meaning longevity or long life.</note>, are not said to be taller than usual compared to men? Compare *Hermann, Jonston on the Constancy of Nature, and Conring.* As a finishing touch, it is pleasing to add the narrative of *Hemo, the Egyptian Hermit*, concerning many stupendous things as recounted by *Francesco Patrizi*—if indeed it does not savor more of that fabulous Egyptian curiosity than of true piety. Among other things, he says: "We still preserve this in memory: that in the first circuit of years, men were of such a grand body that, standing with their feet on the ground, they hid their heads among the stars, and were called *Emephimos*. These were followed in the succession of years by others named *Phtaimos*, slightly smaller, but who nonetheless touched the clouds with their heads. These were followed by other greats, called *Gygini* in Egypt; I think you call them Giants. These certainly lasted until the time of *Noah*, and as they were of grand body, so also they lived for many <margin>Satire 15, verse 69.</margin> years healthy and unharmed. But after the Flo-

<column-break/>

-od, all things began to rush toward the worse, both in other <margin>Giants and Titans.</margin> matters and especially in those concerning the arts and virtue, etc."

### 1. Maccabees III, 48. ###

-> They opened the book of the law, concerning which the Gentiles searched for the likeness of their idols. <-
<note>original Greek: Ἐξεπέτασαν τὸ βιβλίον τοῦ νόμου...; original Latin: Expanderunt libros Legis...</note>

Religion is a matter of great importance; indeed, even the Heathens <margin>As the Pagans also commended it as "a binding element of every society."</margin> commended it as <note>original Greek: συνεκτικόν τι πάσης κοινωνίας; a unifying force for the community.</note>. The wise Stagirite <note>A common nickname for the philosopher Aristotle, who was born in Stagira.</note> also prescribed this rule: <term>First is the care concerning the divine</term> <note>original Greek: Πρῶτον ἡ περὶ τὸ θεῖον ἐπιμέλεια.</note>. For in the minds of the Pagans <margin>7 Politics 8.</margin> of old, this was the sole spur to virtue and some honesty of life, preventing most from being swept away into the sea and whirlpool of Epicureanism <note>The philosophy that pleasure is the highest good, often misinterpreted as mere hedonism.</note>. No nation was so forsaken that it did not think some God ought to be worshiped, even if it was ignorant of how to worship the true God rightly and correctly. However, this was the Devil's greatest care: to keep the Gentiles in the grip of his superstition and to mix truth with obscurity, so that his worshipers understood nothing less than what they ought to understand. The overturning of divine truth was the erection of fables, and the field was opened for idle minds to create whatever fictions they pleased. What did the Ancients not wrap in the veil of ingeniously devised fables? Their labor here was quite profuse, as anyone who diligently unrolls the writings of the Ancient Poets will easily discover. Those who examine more deeply and intimately the fables, enigmas, symbols, and other fictions handed down by the Pagans are accustomed to refer many things to *Nature* and *History*. For it is not to be believed, as *Arnobius* says, that these things are vain and without their own origins, <margin>in Against the Nations.</margin> nor that they lack causes joined to their first institutions. *Clement of Alexandria* confirms this in *Stromata*, Book 5, writing: <term>All who have treated of divine things, both Barbarians and Greeks, concealed the beginnings of things; they handed down the truth in riddles and symbols, and again in allegories and metaphorical modes.</term> <note>original Greek: Πάντες οἱ θεολόγησαντες... This reflects the idea that ancient wisdom was intentionally hidden from the "uninitiated" or common people.</note> And on page 575: <term>Those who established the mysteries, being philosophers, buried their own dogmas in myths so that they would not be clear to everyone.</term> *Origen* in Book 8 of *Against Celsus*: <term>These festivals are proven to be inventions of those who, however it happened, through certain human histories either made laws or natural theories about waters, or earth, or the fruits thought to participate in it.</term> *Eusebius* recorded this extensively from the monuments of the ancients; in his work, *Philo of Byblos* complains <margin>1. Preparation for the Gospel.</margin> that many clouds and fables were drawn over historical truth by the mystics, with the sole exception of *Sanchoniathon* of Berytus, who, having been admitted to the ancient books of *Ammunaeus*, rejected the fables and brought forth everything as it actually happened. There is no Philosophy or Theology more obscure than that of the Egyptians. <term>For this reason, they also set up sphinxes before the temples, as the discourse concerning God is enigmatic and obscure,</term> as *Clement* witnesses in the cited place; and *Arnobius* mocks their enigmas because they inserted the forms of dumb animals <margin>3. Against the Nations, p. 64.</margin> into divine causes. Nor can it be denied by these first and principal architects of fables and enigmas, who [drew] many things from the Hebrews...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES #

<margin>The <term>cacozelia</term><note>A technical term referring to a "perverse imitation" or a distorted rivalry, where one culture takes the rituals or stories of another and twists them for their own purposes.</note> of rites and sacred things.</margin>
...they adulterated with mysteries, and foul errors spread to the rest of the world. Not a few things are shrouded in a certain fragment of our sacred monuments, and have been darkened from ancient times by wickedness and fraud, so that the traditions of the sacred books might be rendered either suspect or utterly despised. It is worth mentioning what happened in Mizpah, where Judas Maccabaeus had called a solemn assembly after the unspeakable madness of Antiochus Epiphanes against the holy things of Jerusalem. While they were unfolding the Bible, they found it defiled with the images of foreign deities and the inscriptions of myths. The enemies of divine truth were occupied with great zeal in ensuring that Jews might believe those idols—which they refused to worship—and other mythical narrations were found to be in conformity with their own Sacred Books, so that they might follow and point them out from their own books. I will not examine here the various writings of that place, which are compared by the Interpreters, among whom <margin>p. 889.</margin> **Jacques Tirinus** says: *It is a more consistent explanation that the Gentiles were loose in transferring all the more notable Biblical histories and divine miracles to their own false gods; for example, the war of the giants, the flood, the Tower of Babel, Joseph, Moses, the Red Sea, the solstice of Joshua, Samson, the chariots of Elijah, and others. Indeed, Rupert notes that the Gentiles even translated the sacred rites and ceremonies, by which God wished to be worshiped, into the insane rituals of their own gods.* And this is properly *to search for the likeness of idols within the sacred books.* The Devil, the adulterer of healthy discipline, produced such <note>original: "σχεδιάσματα" (schediasmata), meaning sketches or hasty compositions.</note> wicked examples on the stage in emulation of divine truth and divine works; he attempted to involve primeval antiquity in myths when he could not entirely shroud it in oblivion and silence, so that it might not be clearly seen or understood. Hence, in the ritual books of the Heathens, mention of the true God known in Israel and of the true worship is either nonexistent, obscure, or certainly intended as an insult—a fact that no one even moderately skilled in ancient knowledge can ignore. **Tertullian**, in *The Prescription Against Heretics*, <margin>ch. 40.</margin> writes: *The Devil, whose part it is to invert the truth, even emulates the very circumstances of the divine sacraments in the mysteries of idols. He himself also baptizes certain people, namely his own believers and faithful; he promises the expiation of sins from a font; and if I still remember Mithra <note>An ancient Persian deity whose mystery cult was a major rival to early Christianity in the Roman Empire.</note>, he signs his soldiers there on their foreheads, celebrates an offering of bread, introduces an image of the resurrection, and redeems crowns under the sword. What of the fact that he establishes a Chief Priest limited to a single marriage? He also has Virgins, and he has those who practice continence.* Furthermore, if we revolve the superstitions of Numa Pompilius, if the priestly offices, insignias, and privileges, if the sacrificial ministries and their instruments, and the very vessels of their sacred rites. **Natalis Comes**, in the last book and chapter of his *Mythology*, p. 1074: *It is easy to judge from the entire body of myths itself that the divine laws, which were divinely handed down to those holy Fathers before the coming of Christ, were hidden by the ancient Greeks under the shrouds of fables.* **Richard Montagu** in *Diatribe*, p. 18: *The Pagans once usurped many things transcribed and taken from the divine <note>original: "πολιτείᾳ" (politeia), meaning commonwealth or way of life.</note>, which were afterwards darkened by the wickedness and frauds of the Devil.* **Friedrich Taubmann** on Virgil’s *Ciris*: *In the Sacred Scriptures, there are few histories which the Devil, whose part it is to invert the truth, did not strive to express through imitation, as Tertullian says,*

<column-break/>

Who would deny that many things, from the original tradition of true worship established by Adam, were carried to foreigners in a nefarious way, depraved by the wicked progeny of Cain and interpolated with deceptive lies? Many documents were also left as a tradition by the sons of Noah, even to those descendants who neglected the bosom of the Church. Everyone could have knowledge of the Law and ceremony from the founder of their nation; thus the Moabites and Ammonites drew their traditions from Lot. Thus the Ishmaelites from Hagar. But it happened in the course of time that, either through a zeal for novelty or the vice of superstition, those things which had been well-handed down were perverted by wicked rivals and pulled apart into forms more astonishing than Ovidian metamorphosis. We shall proceed to examples, teaching briefly how one must go beyond myths to historical truth, relying on the authority of writers both ancient and recent, so that fortified by their authority we may not listen <note>original Greek: "ἐκ μικρᾶς ἀφορμῆς" (ek mikras aphormēs), meaning "on slight grounds" or "from a small starting point."</note>. Saint Justin, in his second *Apology*, tries to teach that the myths of Bacchus, likewise of Bellerophon, and Hercules, and almost the entire theology of the nations, proceeded from a depraved sense of the scriptures; other Fathers make the same judgment, though they sometimes seem to have departed from this judgment, which we are not to discuss here. We shall speak briefly of this <term>Cacozelia</term>, referring ourselves to the authors, and the strokes of our brush will be outlines rather than solid figures. *But I think,* says **Clement** in the 5th book of *Stromata*, p. 561, *that what is now possessed is sufficient to demonstrate the point, setting forth a few inklings.* <note>original Greek: "Ἀπέχῃ δὲ οἶμαι τὰ γὲ νῦν κεκτημένα, εἰς ἔνδειξιν τὲ προκειμένω, ὀλίγα τινὰ ἐκτιθέντα ψελάφισματα."</note> I leave the matter to be handed down more explicitly by those who have the leisure and more diffuse erudition <note>original Greek: "τῆς δυσσεβειῶν φλυείας ὅλον δὶ ὅλυ διεξῃγεῖσθε..." (to relate in full the nonsense of the impieties... and to speak of the wordiness of that faithless person regarding the much-wandering superstition).</note>.

### ADAM. ###

The first of men was called Adam, whom God formed from the soil taken from the ground. Knowledge of this our primeval parent reached the nations who were ignorant of the true God; they involved this Founder of theirs in myths and did not preserve the name which God had given him, doing so in their own manner, as they often either deprave names or hand down another nomenclature to posterity. So that what Josephus says is true: *For the prophecies have either entirely vanished, or in some cases, by undergoing changes and re-arrangements to fit other opinions, they do not succeed [in being recognized].* <note>original Greek: "Αἳ μὲν προφητεῖαι, τῇ μὲν καὶ παντελῶς ἐξίτηλοι γεγόνασιν..."</note> Thus Adam was involved under another name, namely that of Saturn, and was worshiped under various names. Adam was a farmer and taught his people agriculture. The symbol of this: the reaping sickle. Adam’s mother was clay and the dust of the earth. Saturn’s mother was also the Earth (Tellus). The age of Saturn was the Golden Age. This aptly fits the first age of the first man. Had I not said in recent memory that I would propose these sacred-profane myths briefly, I would have spoken of these things more extensively; but, so that words may harmonize with the subject, I shall refer myself to the authors, and here to **Vossius**, book 1, chapters 18 and 38, in which last chapter he also derives the German god *Tuisto*, as being born from the earth, from the Adamic history. And thus the remnants of the ancient doctrine concerning Adam, born of the earth, would have flowed down even to our own very distant nation. Vossius thinks these things in that work...

...among the Poets (for there were many Jupiters and Prometheuses), is absent from Sacred Scripture. Cain and Abel are called brothers in Scripture. Jupiter and Prometheus, according to the Pagans, were kinsmen. The latter are said to have sacrificed to Heaven; the former to God. Abel sought a victim from his flocks; Prometheus is held to have been the first to kill—that is, to sacrifice—an ox. Abel’s sacrifice was more acceptable to God than Cain’s sacrifice. -> PARADISE <-
The ruins of Paradise are detected in the Elysian Fields, as well as in the Gardens of Adonis. With a very lovely description, the Pagan writers commend the field they call Elysium, in which a gentle breeze blows, fragrant with scent, and where there are the most pleasant valleys blooming in perpetual spring. Plato, in the *Phaedo*, calls it <note>original: "γῆν μακάρων"</note> "the land of the blessed." Suidas says <note>original: "πεδίον εἶναι, ἐν ᾧ παρ' Ἕλλησι δίκαιοι αὐλίζονται μετὰ θάνατον"</note> "it is a plain in which, according to the Greeks, the righteous dwell after death." Virgil <margin>6. Aeneid</margin> calls them "joyful places, the pleasant greenery of the fortunate groves, shaded woods, meadows fresh with streams, and verdant valleys." Gregory of Nazianzus thinks that not a few things were transferred by the Pagans from the Mosaic description of Paradise to the Elysian Field; and Johannes Rosa in his *Oration on Eternal Life* teaches that it contains some shadow and picture of it. See also Becmann on *The Origin of the Latin Language, p. 330*. Justin Martyr thinks that the Garden of Alcinous, described by Homer in <margin>Odyssey, book 7, v. 112</margin>, foreshadows the delights of Paradise, and that in its description there is a manifest imitation of Paradise. Lambert Daneau, in *Antiquities of the First World, section 1, ch. 3, p. 62*, judges that the Garden of Adonis and the Garden of the Hesperides, celebrated in foreign writings, were something similar and a certain vestige of that Garden of Eden. To place the happiness of the future age in bodily pleasure is the delirium of the Pagans, concerning which one may consult Neander in *Pindaric Aristology, ch. 41 and following*, as well as from Plato, Plutarch, and Lucian; likewise the Jews and Mohammadans, whose sweet dreams about the future blessedness of the good are recounted by Gerhard.

Eve, the first mother of the world, was deceived by a serpent. Regarding what they fable about Proserpina—that Jupiter, having turned into a serpent, offered her violence, and from that Dionysus was born—they transmit under that foul fiction the history of Eve being deceived by Satan under the image of a serpent. Satan wished this first stratagem of his, which he used to deceive the woman, to be known to the whole malignant world, while he impelled and excited unstable minds to worship and adore serpents, snakes, and dragons. They hand down that the same history was wrapped in the covering of another fable: that of Pandora’s Box, given to Epimetheus, through which they write that every kind of evil, misery, disease, and death was first brought into the world. In this sense, they refer to what Homer handed down concerning the destructive *Ate*, the first daughter of Jupiter, who ruined all. Lambert Daneau <margin>in the cited place, p. 182</margin> writes: *From a woman, not from a man, Homer and Hesiod handed down that the beginning of evil and sin arose; Homer indeed in Iliad 19, for what he sings there of Ate, a certain woman, to all of us...*

### THE FLOOD ###

The pagans, since they could not penetrate into the most ancient things with certain knowledge, and the notice of the beginning of things escaped them; nevertheless, something of the most ancient matters became known to them through those things which they increasingly wrapped in their myths. However, the most ancient report of the **Flood** had reached them, but its beginning had escaped them. *For*, says **Driedo** \*, *those things which the Sacred history teaches in the book of Genesis regarding the Universal Flood under **Noah**, and many other things recounted by him, were also known to the pagans in some way. Nor did God leave the nations entirely without knowledge of Himself. Hence, beyond the talents of nature and the things innate to nature—like certain seeds which, when cultivated by hearing and will, bear fruit—the testimony of the Creator and also many deeds and miracles designated in the Sacred Scriptures, which are known only by faith from hearing, were not entirely hidden from them. Hence, lest they should seem to have drawn from external sources, they changed the names; from this emerges the myth of the **Flood of Deucalion and Pyrrha** his wife, and of the throwing of stones after the flood, from which humans grew. Natalis Comes (Book 18, chapter 17, page 901) writes: *“By this myth of Deucalion, he exhorted men toward integrity and the worship of the Gods; a story which was excerpted, so it seems to me at least, from the Sacred Scriptures.”* Although the Poet describes a particular flood that invaded Thessaly, he follows his narration with such circumstances that it appears he was dealing with a universal one, albeit unknowingly. For he agrees with the history of Moses in describing the causes of the flood, where he mentions the Giants, their impiety toward God, and their violence toward men. It is established from Moses that men distinguished by strength, robbery, and tyranny (whom the Chaldean translator calls "sons of the magnates," <margin>1st book of *Miscellany*, page 47.</margin> or <term>the sons of the rulers</term> <note>Original Greek: *τοὺς υἱοὺς τῶν δυναστευόντων*.</note> in Symmachus’s version) were the greatest and primary cause of the flood by their crimes. In Genesis 6:2, it says the sons of God came unto the daughters of men and fathered Giants (<term>Nephilim</term> <note>Original Hebrew: *נפלים*, referring to "fallen ones" or "giants."</note>). These were the mighty (<term>Gibborim</term> <note>Original Hebrew: *גברים*, meaning "mighty ones."</note>) *from of old, men of renown*, or <term>men of the name</term> <note>Original Hebrew: *אנשי השם*.</note>. It is as if Moses had said they were the first to exercise tyranny *in the world through power, and from them began an excessively licentious and unbridled desire for dominion*, as Vatable explains. Regarding what is written there about their cohabitation, Dresser writes that it was pulled into the myth of *Ixion*: *“From the cohabitation of the sons of God with the daughters of men was born, without doubt, the myth of Ixion, who sought a blessed marriage with Juno, but instead coupled with a dark cloud. From this, the deformed and monstrous centaurs were procreated.”* Berosus (Book 1, page 6) wrote that the lust of the Giants before the flood extended even to mothers, daughters, sisters, males, and beasts. Lucian, in *On the Syrian Goddess* (page 694), reports that the cause of the Deucalionean flood was the *<term>outrageous deeds of men</term>* <note>Original Greek: *ὕβριστα ἔργα τῶν ἀνθρώπων*.</note>, which included perjury, inhospitality, and ruthlessness. Furthermore, Ovid celebrates Deucalion with a eulogy of piety, stating that no one was more just or a greater observer of equity than he, plainly as Moses celebrates the piety of Noah, because God saw him as *just* <margin>Gen. 7:1.</margin> (<term>Tzadik</term> <note>Original Hebrew: *צדיק*.</note>) *before Him in that generation*, that is, among the wickedest men of that age. The Poet also mentions the Rainbow, <margin>verses 9, 12.</margin> which God gave as a token of the covenant * regarding the not bringing of a flood hereafter: <term>a sign of the covenant</term> <note>Original Hebrew: *אות ברית*; Greek: *σημεῖον διαθήκης*.</note> that there would be no flood in the future. Furthermore, he records that from the entire human race, Deucalion and his wife escaped, whom a ship kept safe. Lucian (in the same place) records that he was saved in a <term>larnaka</term> <note>Original Greek: *λάρνακα*, a chest or coffer.</note> or ark. Indeed, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> call Noah’s ark <term>kibotos</term> <note>Original Greek: *κιβωτὸν*.</note>, which to the Hebrews is <term>Tevah</term> <note>Original Hebrew: *תהבה*.</note>, and it was a vessel covered in the manner of a chest. Finally, the Poet mentions the decree about the world no longer being destroyed by water. *“All of which things,”* says Aegidius Hunnius <margin>Questions on Genesis, folio 110a.</margin>, *“were obtained either from reading the writings of Moses or from the ancient accounts of the Fathers.”* Compare also Daneau (page 407) and John Annius in his commentary on Xenophon (pages 115, 116). Saint Augustine <margin>18th book of *City of God*, chapter 8.</margin> denies that this universal flood was known to the pagans, but says mention was only made of either the O-

<column-break/>

gygian or Deucalionean floods, both of which occurred long after that first one. Martial, Bishop of Limoges, in his Epistle, denies it along with Augustine, but in vain, as the interpreter of Augustine, Ludovicus Vives, has demonstrated. G. Sabinus also taught this clearly from Lucian in his commentary on Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* (Book 1, pages 19, 20, 21). To further strengthen this, we add that many foreign writers mentioned the flood, though not without some corruption of the truth. Eusebius cites them in the 9th book of *Preparation for the Gospel* (chapter 4). Cyril, in his first book against Julian the Apostate (who accused the history of the flood of being a frivolous myth), opposes him using Alexander Polyhistor and Abydenus, who relate that Saturn foretold to *Xisuthus* (that is, Noah) that there would be a flood, and that an ark should be built in which he himself, along with others, ought to sail for safety. Josephus, the Jewish historian, <margin>Antiquities 4, page 10.</margin> cites Berosus the Chaldean, Hieronymus the Egyptian, Mnaseas, and Nicolaus of Damascus; seek their testimonies in that same place. Compare also Plato in *Critias* (page 111b). A booklet circulates under the name of Berosus of Babylon, edited by Annius, which I would produce concerning that famous disaster of the waters if it were genuine. See Mornaeus, *On the Christian Religion* (chapter 26); Daneau (pages 405 ff.); Neander, *Greek-Latin Gnomology* (page 14); and Guillaume Postel, *On the Harmony of the World* (page 39). It is most worthy of note here that in Plutarch’s book *On whether land animals have more reason*, one reads that a dove sent out from the ark gave Deucalion a sign of the subsiding waters. This is obvious in the history of the flood in Genesis 8:8, where it is indicated that after the raven was sent out and did not return, a dove was sent out after it. See Zehner in *Adages* (page 710) and Frantze’s *History of Animals* (page 447).

->**NOAH**<-
He was the other parent of the second world. It is a very likely opinion that the pagans fashioned their **Janus** from him. Antiquity judged Janus to be "bifrons" (two-faced), who <term>looks forward and backward at once</term> <note>Original Greek: *ἅμα πρόσσω καὶ ὀπίσω λεύσειν*.</note>, seeing sharply and letting nothing pass unobserved. In that same way, Noah saw the prior world which perished in the flood, and simultaneously that world which was restored after the flood. Eilhard Lubinus <margin>on Persius, Satire 1, page 645.</margin> writes: *“Janus was the most ancient God of Italy and King of Latium, from whom the Janiculum was named. He was undoubtedly Noah, who was himself two-faced, looking back into the age before the flood and forward to the one after.”* Genebrard, in his *Chronology* (A. 2. b.), says: *“Noah, the restorer of the world—the pagans, being ignorant of the Genesis of the world, called him Heaven, Janus, and the Father of the Gods. He was the first to make the wild vine into a cultivated one and showed the use of the vine to men. From this invention, Janus was perhaps named, for 'Yayin' to the Hebrews is wine.”* Basilius Faber in his *Thesaurus* (page 307) says: *“Janus is in truth Noah himself, looking toward the world—both the one that had entirely perished in the flood, and the one that had begun to be propagated anew after the flood.”* See also Vossius (Book 1 on Idolatry, 18, page 137), who further affirms on page 141 that the things said about the flood occurring under Prometheus suit no one better than Noah. Among six surnames, Janus was invoked as *Consivius*, from "sowing" or "planting," which was said either regarding the propagation of the human race or of the vines which were planted by his authority. This very thing is attributed to Noah, who was the first planter of vineyards; for concerning him, Genesis 9:20 says: <term>And Noah began to be a man of the soil</term> <note>Original Hebrew: *וַיָּחֶל נֹחַ אִישׁ הָאֲדָמָה*.</note>, <term>and he planted a vineyard</term> <note>Original Greek: *ἐφύτευσεν ἀμπελῶנה*.</note>. <margin>On Genesis, page 163.</margin> * Jacques Bonfrère says: *“Not a few feel that Noah is the same as Janus, and that Janus is named from the Hebrew* <gloss>yayin</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: יין</note>, *which signifies wine. Compare Macrobius, Saturnalia Book 1, Chapter 7.* Janus, reigning in Latium, minted a farthing coin which had his two-faced head on one side and the likeness of a ship on the other. This man (says Schickard in his *On Hebrew Coins*, page 8), by most likely conjecture, is Noah, who saw both worlds—before and after—having crossed from the former to the latter through the flood in the ark; he propagated the symbol of that memorable event on his coins for all posterity. Likewise, Nannacus <note>A legendary king of Phrygia said to have lived before a great flood.</note> seems to designate Noah, as Zuinger conjectures in his *Theater* (Vol. 5, book 4, f. 1487). Indeed, Vossius (in *On Idolatry*, 19, p. 144) teaches that the history of Noah lies hidden in the fables of Bacchus—or Boachus. Before him, Danaeus felt the same, asserting that Bacchus was the same as Janus. To Bacchus is ascribed the invention of the vine, and he is called by Diodorus <margin>Book 5.</margin> <gloss>of noble birth from the vine and its cultivation</gloss> <note>Original Greek: εὐγενὴς τῆς ἀμπέλου καὶ τῆς ἐν ταύτῃ ἐργασίας.</note>. Hence Jacob Hermann says: *“Sacred Scripture records that Noah planted a vineyard after the flood. Therefore, Noah is the Dionysus, Father Liber, or Bacchus of the Poets. For the poets, through ignorance of true history, lapsed into fables.”* Noah had three sons: <margin>Genesis 6:10.</margin> 1. <gloss>Shem</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: שם</note>, 2. <gloss>Ham</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: חם</note>, 3. <gloss>Japheth</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: יפת</note>. Vossius is of the opinion that Noah was also foreshadowed in Saturn, whose three famous children were the dividers of the world. Ham, the degenerate son of Noah, degenerated among the gentiles into the well-known fable of Jupiter Ammon. There is little difference between "Cham" or "Ham" and "Ammon," from which the Egyptians in their language made *Amun*, and the Greeks *Ammon*. On this, see Philip Melanchthon, Boissard, and Vossius, from whom Bochart departs, thinking that Zoroaster was not Ham, as he was more recent; however, Annius fashioned Zoroaster from the same man. <margin>Antiquities, Book 3, p. 25.</margin> writing: *“Ham was the younger of the three first sons of Noah; he was always studying magic and poisoning and obtained the name Zoroaster. When his father Noah lay drunk, Ham grasped his genitals and—*

<column-break/>

muttering silently with a magical song—deluded the stone <note>The Latin "petri" here likely refers to a "pith" or "stone," implying a magical ritual involving a symbolic object to cause impotence.</note> and made him sterile, as if castrated; nor could Noah thereafter father any female. Truly a story worthy of the old wives' tales of Annius. Hugo of Saint Victor <note>A 12th-century mystical theologian.</note> agrees with this same naming, and it seems (he says) that Zoroaster, King of the Bactrians, was believed to be the first discoverer of Magic; some assert he is Ham, the son of Noah, but with a changed name. Some make him the discoverer of Chemistry. And Kircher <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit polymath who studied Egyptian hieroglyphs and "ancient" magic.</note> says: *“That true and first Zoroaster was Ham, the son of Noah, the inventor of all Magic and idolatry, who learned those illicit arts and sciences before the cataclysm from the impious lineage of the Cainites, and after the flood, he diligently taught them to his descendants. For when he had heard wonders from Methuselah (with whom he lived for many years before the flood) about his translated father Enoch, and had diligently sought the impious arts of the Cainites, he is said to have performed such works after the flood—affecting divinity and plunder in this world—that everyone worshipped him as a sort of deity. Therefore, when Egypt was filled with a numerous offspring, he left the kingdom to his son Mizraim and went to Chaldæa, Persia, and Media to seek other colonies among the peoples of Assyria. There he professed Astrology and magical arts and earned such a name among the natives that he was everywhere held in place of a Deity and called Zoroaster—that is, the "image of the secret fire." Among the Persians and Medes, he also taught the worship of Fire, which has remained to this very day. Then on page 17: The second Zoroaster was Cush, the son of Ham, a diligent investigator and indeed heir of his father's disciplines among the Chaldæans; he also affected the name of his father Ham and taught his son Nimrod the giant arts performed with the help of a Demon. Nimrod is said to have been the first to invade the Kingdom of Babylon by their help.”* From this, all those who performed wonders by magical art were later called "Zoroastres." They say the same Ham passed down magic and chemistry to his son Mizraim, whom the Egyptians named Osiris; Vossius conjectures that various honors were given to him. Japheth became known to the nations not among mortals but among the number of the celestials, and they called him "Iapetus." <note>Iapetus was a Titan in Greek mythology, the father of Prometheus and Atlas.</note> Tubal-Cain seems to be Vulcan, of whom Genesis 4:22 says he was a <gloss>hammer-worker and a smith in all works of brass and iron</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: לוטש כל-חרש נחשת וברזל</note>, where the Greek translator says: <gloss>a hammer-beater and worker in brass and iron</gloss> <note>Original Greek: σφυροκόπον καὶ χαλκεὺς χαλκοῦ καὶ σιδήρου.</note>. The word *lotush* <note>The Hebrew root L-T-SH (לוטש).</note> means to sharpen and to polish. Danaeus suspects that this Tubal-Cain, the discoverer of the art of copper and iron, is Vulcan (by changing a few letters), whom the fables make the blacksmith of the Gods, and whose sister and wife was Venus <note>In Genesis, Tubal-Cain's sister is named Naamah; the author links her name to the "pleasantness" associated with Venus.</note>. Ludovicus Vives <note>A 16th-century Spanish humanist and student of Erasmus.</note> agrees in his commentary on Augustine's *City of God*.

<header>1 Maccabees 3:48 <note>This verse mentions how the Gentiles "laid open the book of the law, wherein the heathen had sought to paint the likeness of their images," which the author uses as a biblical basis for his theory that pagan myths are distorted copies of scripture.</note></header>

...Book 15, chapter 20. Dressler, *Historical Introduction to the Millennium*, Book 1, page 41; Beckmann, *Origins of the Latin Language*, page 1107; Vossius, *On Idolatry*, Book 16, page 124. They say that from Vulcan comes <note>Original Greek: τὴν περὶ τὸν σίδηρον ἐργασίαν...</note> "the working of iron, and matters concerning bronze, gold, and silver, and all other things which allow for working by fire," as witnessed by Diodorus Siculus in *Library of History*, Book 5, page 235. He also writes from the traditions of the Egyptians that Vulcan first reigned in Egypt, and that divine honors were granted to him after his death because of his discovery of fire; a temple was also established for him in Memphis (page 37), and his worship is especially preferred by mechanical artisans, <note>Original Greek: τοῖς περὶ τὸν σίδηρον...</note> "those who work with iron, bronze, gold, and silver" (Book 5, page 235).

<margin>Genesis 4:21.</margin>
**JUBAL.** He is called <gloss>the father of all those who handle the lyre and pipe</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: אבי כל-תפש כנור ועוגב</note> because he invented the art of music. The Pagans, in order to more highly commend this invention, attribute it to Apollo. In this way, they preserved the benefit of Jubal—given for the common joy of mankind—under the name of Apollo through the immortal memory of consecration, so that it might be more illustrious. "There is no doubt that Jubal is that most ancient Apollo," says Vossius (in the cited work, page 127), and he adds on page 128 that, among different nations, this Jubal was marked by some with the name of Apollo and by others with the name of Mercury.

<margin>Genesis 10:8.</margin>
**NIMROD,** the founder of Babylon and the Babylonian empire, <gloss>began to be a mighty one on the earth</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: גבור בארץ</note> on account of his skill in arms and warfare. From this, it is a likely suspicion that the surname "Belus" (that is, "Lord") was attributed to him <term>kat' exochen</term> <note>A Greek phrase meaning "par excellence" or "preeminently."</note>. "Baal" <note>Original: בעל</note> is the Chaldean form for Lord or Ruler, which in Hebrew is "Ba'al" <note>Original: בעל</note>. Jacques Tirinus, in his commentary on *Genesis* (page 104), writes: "Nimrod was Jupiter or Belus, the son of Saturn and father of Ninus; for the details handed down by the ancients regarding time, place, tyranny, empire, and depraved character fit both figures." Belus (or Bel and Baal) were the surnames of Nimrod and Jupiter. This man, skilled in arms, was transformed by the myth-makers into Mars, <note>Original Greek: ὃν μυθολογοῦσι...</note> "whom they mythologize as having first prepared full armor, and armed soldiers, and introduced the active contest in battles," as Diodorus Siculus spoke of him in Book 5, page 235, according to the opinion of the Cretans. Vossius felt the same (cited work, page 124), writing: "That inventor of arms and warfare was Nimrod, who, as Scripture witnesses, began to be mighty on the earth and is compared to a hunter, because just as men hunt wild beasts, so he hunted men." The nations are ignorant of the name Nimrod, but he is called Belus by them. "That Belus is the same as Mars, we clearly learn from Histiaeus of Miletus." Belus, whom antiquity makes the founder of Babylon, is none other than Nimrod; from his name, Hyginus thinks the Latins doubled the 'L' to create the word *Bellum* (War), writing in *Fable 274*, page 145: "The Africans and Egyptians first fought with clubs; later Belus, son of Neptune, waged war with the sword, from which 'war' [*bellum*] was named." Cassiodorus agrees with him (Book 1, Epistle 30), a point I leave undecided. Thurras, the third Assyrian king after Belus, was likewise an outstanding warrior, from which he received the name of Mars; from this I take the conjecture that the epithet remained, so that <note>Original Greek: θεὸς Ἄρης</note> "God Ares" was said of Mars by the Greeks. See Suidas under "Thurras." The *Alexandrian Chronicle* calls him a "bitter warrior."

The history of the Tower of Babel, which Moses gave in Chapter 11, gave birth to that famous "War of the Giants" against the gods, whom they are fabulously said to have wished to drive from

<column-break/>

their heavenly seat. The author of the construction of that stupendous mass of the tower was that impious tyrant Nimrod; in order to betray his exalted spirit to all, he strove to build a tower whose peak would reach the clouds. He would have completed it, had he not been hindered in the work itself by a confusion of languages sent from God. Caspar Peucer, in *On Divination* (page 179), writes: "The fable of the Giants, who intended to build an approach to the heavens by piling up mountains and thereby drive down Jupiter, seems to have been birthed by the mention of Giants in Genesis and the history of the divinely hindered building of the Tower of Babel." For Josephus assigns this plan of building a tower <margin>verse 4.</margin> "whose top may reach unto heaven" to Nimrod, <margin>*Antiquities*, Book 5, page 12.</margin> who stood out as the leader of the others out of pride and contempt for God in that insane construction, so that his name might exist eternally and that it might be a place of refuge if a flood were again sent upon the earth. It is likely that the poets took the occasion from here to invent the <term>Theomachia</term> <note>Original Greek: "Battle against the Gods."</note> of the Giants, who are said to have placed mountains upon mountains to wage war on the gods, but were cast down by Jupiter’s lightning. "There is no doubt," says Bonfrère (*On Genesis*, page 163), "that the fable among the heathens about the Giants waging war on heaven, and attempting to thrust Jupiter from heaven by piling high mountains on top of others, took its origin from here." Compare also Danæus (pages 384, 385). It is worth adding that Vallesius, in *On Sacred Philosophy* (chapter 8, page 92), wrongly produces the race of Giants from a poor explanation of the words <margin>Genesis 6:4.</margin> "the sons of God cohabiting with the daughters of men," as if the "sons of God" were not pious men, but angels or <term>incubi</term> <note>Demons traditionally thought to have sexual relations with sleeping women.</note> who approached women. Rather, those were called "sons of God" who were of the seed of Enos; from their marriages with the "daughters of the world" (who were of the seed of Cain), there were brought forth fierce, grim, and bloodthirsty men.

**JOSEPH.** That Viceroy of the Egyptians had provided immense benefits to Egypt. When famine and want threatened the rest of the world, he ensured through his prudence and foresight that there was bread in all the land of <margin>Genesis 41, verses 54, 56.</margin> Egypt, and that granaries were seen everywhere full of grain. Moved by this remarkable benefit of the supply of food, the inhabitants decreed divine honors for him after his death and celebrated his memory under the name of Serapis. Firmicus wrongly derived this from the Greek words for "tomb" and "Hades," but Varro (cited in Augustine’s *City of God*, Book 18, chapter 15) says he was a prince and was worshiped along with Isis by the Egyptians; a capital penalty was even established for anyone who said they had been mere men. He had given a grain supply to the Alexandrians who were suffering from hunger, according to Suidas under the entry "Serapis." But those followers of darkness attributed the benefit that belonged to Joseph to Serapis, to whom a bull was consecrated as a proof of worship. The bull is well known from the history of Pharaoh, in the dream of the seven fat cows and seven <margin>Genesis 41, verses 2, 3.</margin> lean ones. A dream is fit for indicating fertility and sterility, for fertility is found especially in livestock. Moses, blessing Joseph, uses the word <gloss>shur</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: שור</note> denoting an ox or bull (Deuteronomy 33:17); hence, if you were to derive "Serapis" from this, perhaps you would not do so foolishly. Or even "Osiris," whose name Plutarch says was <margin>*On Isis and Osiris*, page 36.</margin> "Arsaph," which could easily have been made into the name Joseph. Jacques Bonfrère, in *On Genesis* (page 303), writes: "It is believed by many that Joseph was [worshiped] by the Egyptians under the names of Serapis and Osiris..."

Moses was well known to the Gentiles; for his wars and expeditions could not remain hidden. We will show elsewhere what Diodorus Siculus learned from the Egyptian priests; and if you desire testimonies, Mornay (*chapters 24 and 26*) has provided them. It might seem marvelous to some that several authors derive the mythology of Bacchus from the history of Moses; Martinius touches on this briefly in his Lexicon (*p. 105*): *There are those who think that he whom the Gentiles call Bacchus was Moses himself, whose birth, beauty, expeditions, and wars waged with giants, as well as his exile, flight, and unknown grave, coincide so well with the history of Moses. He is "bimater" <note>original: "bimater," meaning having two mothers</note> because he had a true mother and another by whom he was adopted. His "Nisa" is "Sina" <note>Mount Sinai</note> by <gloss>rearranging the letters</gloss> <note>original: ἀνασχέσθω (anaschestho)</note>; his "Moera" is Miriam, the sister of Moses; his "dog" is Caleb, which is the Hebrew word for dog; and the story that he was sewn into Jupiter's thigh refers to his delay on Mount Sinai for forty days. His "horned brow" refers to the shining rays of his face when he returned with the tablets of the Law.* But what of the fact that Bacchus is called the inventor of wine? They say this comes from the "Story of the Cluster" <note>The biblical story of the spies carrying a massive cluster of grapes from the Promised Land (Numbers 13:23)</note>. There is hardly a fable among the Gentiles as fertile and widespread as that of Bacchus, about whom:

> The Greeks breathe out lies with their massive bellows.

Yet some truth may lie beneath these lies, in the same way that histories are usually obscured by storytellers. It is even said that they attempted to extract that sacred history of Moses from under the stupid fables of Bacchus—something that Hugo Sanford (*Book on the Descent of Christ to Hades*) and most recently Vossius <margin>On Idolatry, book 1, ch. 36, p. 225</margin> and in the eight following pages, have attempted; we shall not plunder their desks here.

**JOSHUA.** It is also possible, and even likely, that the history of Joshua—or perhaps Samson—lies hidden under the fable of Hercules. Whatever has been handed down about the Egyptian, Arabian, and Tyrian Hercules seems naturally suited to this matter. Just as Joshua is said to have made war on the Giants, so too did Hercules; Hercules <term>defeated the giants</term> <note>original: τοὺς γίγαντας κατεπολέμησε (tous gigantas katepolemēse)</note> in the Phlegraean fields, as Eustathius records (*on Homer, p. 291*). Joshua, and after him Samson, performed great deeds against the inhabitants of Palestine, whose exploits the pagans confused. Joshua cut down the Enacim (*chapter 11:20*), who were giants (*Numbers 13*). He defeated Og, King of Bashan (*chapter 12:4*). This man was a giant of the remnant of the Rephaim (<term>among the giants</term> <note>original: ἐν τῷ γιγάντων (en tō gigantōn)</note> they translate here, but in *Deuteronomy 3:11* they use <term>from the Rephaim</term> <note>original: ἀπὸ τῶν ῥαφαὶν (apo tōn rhaphain)</note>) from the land of the Giants, which contained sixty fortified cities, as read in *Deuteronomy 3:4, 5, 11, 13*. Vossius conjectures (*On Idolatry, book 1, ch. 26, pp. 189–190*) that the Gentiles described this man as *Typhaeus*. Concerning King Og, the Rabbis report that he placed a huge mountain on his head so that he might crush the entire multitude of Israelites with a single throw. These extravagant fables <note>original: "sesquipedalia commenta," literally "foot-and-a-half long comments"</note> agree with Ovid, where he says:

I think it superfluous to pursue Joshua's deeds further through the labors and hardships of Hercules, since the industrious Vossius has relieved many of this work (*On Idolatry, book 1, ch. 26, pp. 188, 190, 191, 194; ch. 27, p. 204; and Addenda to book 1, p. 12*). The Samson of the Hebrews is no other than the Hercules of the Gentiles, whom chronologists observe to have lived at one and the same time; this is also taught by Cornelius à Lapide in his *Commentary on Judges, ch. 16, pp. 178–179*; Pererius *on Genesis ch. 49*; Bonfrerius and Tirinus *on Judges, pp. 376, 211*; and Casp. Sanchez *on the 12 Prophets, p. 805*. We read that Samson's hair was cut off by Delilah, from which Martin de Roa (*Singularities, book 5, ch. 7*) argues the fable arose concerning the purple lock of Nisus, which his daughter Scylla cut off. The history of Jonah held inside the sea monster was fabulously adapted to Hercules, whom a sea monster held in its belly for three nights. Jacob Tirinus <margin>on Jonah 8, 9</margin> writes: *taking the opportunity from Jonah, the Gentiles feigned that Hercules, when returning from Colchis with the Argonauts, fell into the sea during a storm and was devoured by a fish, but emerged safe from it after three days.* So say Lycophron and others. Vossius felt the same (*ch. 15, pp. 381–382*) as did Lilius Gyraldus (*In the Life of Hercules, p. 35*), whose words we cite in full: *Hercules is said to have been once devoured by a whale, from which he nevertheless emerged unharmed, except that he was stripped of all his hair, obviously because of the internal heat of the beast.* This is how the story is handed down by the Greeks, which Theophylact—an author of great authority among Christians—also applies to Jonah. Lycophron touched on the same, and Isaac Tzetzes the interpreter explains it. How cunning the Devil is, "God’s Ape" <note>original: "simiaster," a mocking term for an imitator</note>, in his works is more than clear from the aforementioned examples. Nor is his power unknown, which by the just judgment of God he usurps over unbelieving men devoted to foolish superstitions. Furthermore, it is generally admitted that the Pagans affected the worship of God in many things, and snatched up certain shadows of divine truth superficially—like a dog drinking from the Nile <note>A common ancient proverb for doing something in a hurry to avoid danger</note>—from the memory of the Holy Book, and afterwards celebrated them with the praise of singular antiquity. Whoever wishes to follow these shadows will often, like Aesop's dog, lose the substance itself. We see the traces of real events sticking within fabulous wrappings; when the Fathers and other Christian writers unroll these wrappings, it must certainly be admitted that they sometimes entangle them further, luxuriating in sterile material to be brought over and applied to the forum of theology. *Justin* <margin>Apology for the Christians.</margin> sweated most over unraveling these; in order to convince the Gentiles, he busied himself with a certain pious curiosity to deduce almost all the heads of theology from the writings of the profane, and he rebuked the Poets more than once for twisting prophetic predictions about Christ into their own fictions. Many other ancient Doctors pursue mythological matters to draw them toward our sacred rites and mysteries. Relying on the authority of these Ancients, writers of a later age have more obstinately investigated fables; with such rubbish, they neither give any honor to God nor satisfy our religion. Regarding this darkness in which we see origins shrouded among ancient writers, we hold this for certain: they heard great things about sacred history, but were ignorant—though not entirely—of what Moses or a later writer wrote concerning the beginning of the world, the first creation of man, his propagation, the institution of religion, and other matters.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
The <term>distorted imitation</term><note>Latin: *Cacozelia*. A rhetorical term here used to describe the perversion or poor imitation of sacred truths by pagan authors.</note> of rituals and sacred matters.

...they were not able to obtain any clearer knowledge, because they were deprived of that language in which the Annals of the first world were recorded. Lest they should seem entirely ignorant of those things which they received from the Hebrews through reliable reports, they defiled them with the foul spit of errors: they changed the Hebrew names above all else. In this matter, the Greeks were more anxious than other nations to boast of their own people; they attributed foreign names and foreign rituals to themselves, so that outsiders might seem to have taken from them, as students from teachers. Plutarch thinks that most of the sacred names of the Egyptians flowed from Greek sources, and from these he derives the nomenclature of Isis, Osiris, Anubis, and Horus. In the same way, he twists and turns the sacred matters of the Jews upside down, so that he might elicit from them a bit of glory for his own language. Others went even further. The impious Celsus thinks that those things written in Genesis concerning the tower and the confusion of tongues are corrupted versions of the fable of the Aloadae <note>In Greek myth, the Aloadae were giants who tried to storm heaven by piling mountains on top of each other; the author views this as a distorted memory of the Tower of Babel.</note>, as witnessed by Origen in his 4th book *Against Celsus*, page 179. With similar impudence, that glutton compares what Moses relates concerning Sodom and Gomorrah being destroyed by fire because of sin with the story of Phaëthon. And as for the foul things that Strabo, Justin, Cornelius Tacitus, and others devise about the Jews, this happened either because they were far removed from any commerce with the Jews, or because certain deceivers carried over what they heard to others through lying traditions. More distant things are usually wrapped in fables and lies. Strabo himself says of Pytheas: <note>original Greek: ὡς ἐπιψεύσασαι μᾶλλον περὶ τῶν ἐκτετοπισμένων</note> *that they lie more about things that are remote.* And likewise: <note>original Greek: εἰ δὲ τῆς θάλης ἔτι μᾶλλον ἀσαφὴς ἡ ἱστορία, διὰ τὸν ἐκτοπισμόν</note> *if the history of the sea is even more obscure, it is because of its remoteness.* Just as he also said in his third book: <note>original Greek: τὸν ἐκτετοπισμένον & διεσπασμένων ἐθνῶν οὐκ ἀσφαλῆ εἶναι ὑπομνήματα</note> *that the records of distant and scattered nations are not reliable.*

So too, the Gentiles could write nothing certain about the Jews, nor about their sacred rites; but whatever they either received from their ancestors or even learned from the Jews (for it is related by many testimonies by Selden <note>John Selden, a famous 17th-century legal scholar and Hebraist.</note> in book 1 *On Natural Law and the Law of Nations according to the Hebrews*, that the Gentile philosophers, especially Pythagoras, learned many things from the Jews) they either hid entirely, or set forth in an obscure and concise kind of speech, or veiled in the coverings of fables, so that they might escape the notice of the unlearned multitude. And although many wrote perversely and with little sincerity about sacred things, nevertheless, some things are occasionally reported that should not be rejected—some things that are sincere, though very few—so that one may notice sparks of the divine spirit shining forth even in the deepest darkness of superstitions. Regarding the fall of the Angels, the heathens received snippets of truth, which Caelius Rhodiginus noted long ago, saying: *In the monuments of the Ancients, it was handed down by Pherecydes that Demons fell from heaven, and that Ophioneus—that is, the Demonic serpent—was the leader of the host.* In the *Mysteries*, we have noted that Jupiter sometimes thrusts the lower demons down to the infernal regions. Nay, even the Pythagoreans imagine that broken souls fall from heaven, which they distribute into nine grades. Homer, under the name of Ate <note>The Greek goddess of mischief and ruin.</note>, which signifies guilt, seems to have pointed to the fall of Lucifer. Besides this, it is more than certain that the heathens drew many things from the Mosaic sanctuaries. For what is that fable of the Poets concerning *Nectar and Ambrosia*, if it is not a certain fiction about the tree of life? From where else did the Colchians, Egyptians, Ethiopians, and others have

Regarding this, Villalpandus <note>Juan Bautista Villalpando, a Jesuit scholar known for his massive commentary on Ezekiel.</note> says: *It is not new that the Romans received many things from the Greeks, the Greeks from the Egyptians, and the Egyptians from the Israelites—many of the Sacraments of our piety; for Epiphanius is the author who states that the Egyptians, mindful of that day on which the Israelites were liberated (who had smeared the doorposts of their houses with the blood of the Lamb), were accustomed at the beginning of the vernal equinox to take red earth and smear all the trees and entire houses, crying out that at this time fire once devastated all things, and they believe the blood-colored red earth is a remedy against that plague.* Compare Selden in his *Prolegomena*, p. 30; Causin *On Eloquence*, p. 90; Conring *On Hermetic Medicine*, ch. 12, p. 142. From these sayings, it is more than clear enough that sacred histories were wrapped in the coverings of such fables among the Gentiles. Hence Christopher Besoldus says: *Fables tell of the origin of the world, the golden age or state of innocence, the flood, the attempt of the Titans and Giants or the Babylonians, and similar true histories, with fictitious circumstances.
