The Garden of Eden is the Elysian Fields. Prometheus, who is imagined to have stolen fire by ascending to heaven, and is therefore wretchedly tortured, yet is called the founder of men, is Adam, who wanted to become like God; and the fact that he is said to have made man from clay, in the image of the Gods, denotes the creation of Adam. Pandora’s box, and the punishment of Prometheus himself, are the evils that followed after the fall. The Pythian serpent slain by Phoebus is the Dragon who deceived Adam and was removed by Christ. The fall of Phaëthon is the fall of Lucifer.* Under this scheme and covering of fables, the Philosophers and Poets encompassed the truth when certain knowledge of the truth had failed them. I would even dare to assert that more antiquarian knowledge lies beneath the ancient fables than has perhaps been explained by anyone until now. *The learning of the Poets,* says Rhodiginus, *is often manifold and hidden beneath the skin, not to be looked at by dim or nocturnal eyes.* Regarding Philosophy, so that you may see it clearly, go to Vossius’s book *On Idolatry*, who elicits the sense from the Philosophers of the Gentiles once the veil is removed. We see that the interpreters differ in opinion, so much so that nothing certain can be elicited from the fables themselves without the aid of the Authors themselves, through whose "ivory gate" they exited. By what path and by what key the truth may be revealed from the obscurity of fables is not as easy to say as many imagine. For in them, the naked bark of the words is not the only thing to be considered. They denote something other than what the simple sound of the words gives of itself. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>
The <term>distorted imitation</term><note>Latin: *Cacozelia*. A rhetorical term for a poorly executed or perverted imitation. Here it refers to how pagan myths are seen as "bad copies" of Hebrew truths.</note> of rituals and sacred matters. 4 *Gallica*, page 93.

...and they collected delusions so that they might lead the reader to other things. In trifles there are often more trifles, and sometimes not. "In vain," says **Goropius Becanus***, "did those ancient authors of fables fashion **Satyrs** and **Sileni** with pointed ears for us; in vain did they add masks to the **Muses**, if everything is heard nakedly, according to how it first sounds. What does the whole **Bacchic equipment** have except absurdities, if only the winnowing fan <note>Latin: *vannus*. A basket used to separate grain from chaff, often carried in the processions of Bacchus.</note>, by which chaff is winnowed on the threshing floor, is understood? What of the little basket, what of the crawling snake, what of the phalli, what of the rest? Are they not mere mockeries, and indeed colder than the cheapest children's rattles? But while you see the masks hanging, while you see the pointed ears of the satyrs raised toward heaven, you ought to think that these things are not to be looked at idly and only at first glance; rather, the masks must be pulled off and ears must be pricked up from earthly and bodily things toward heavenly ones, so that those things which are seen and heard in the body may be transferred to the mind." This is indeed the case, since nothing was more familiar to the Heathens than to deal with mysteries through fables. Whatever could have a mark of obscurity was counted among divine things, as clearly shown by the *Egyptian Hieroglyphs*, in which the Egyptians sharply fashioned and refashioned various fables and monsters. Yet one must think of them as they deserve: namely, that the wisdom of the Heathen is a foolish wisdom, in which they seem wise to themselves, but most foolish to the true worshippers of divine truth. What is more subtle than those webs, but what is more useless? A little spider sometimes catches a fly, but sits idle and bloodless in its own subtle threads. So it is with those who are too wasteful of irrecoverable time, spending their whole lives catching and explaining these subtleties. These people intend with every effort to grasp the foolish wisdom of the Heathen, whether of the Egyptians or the Greeks, and they presume to teach others "decorated trifles" with the allurements of words. But while they boast that they have captured "verisimilitudes" <note>Appearances of truth.</note> in those subtle webs, they cheat the truth with their subtlety. They are like merchants who strive more eagerly to gain a price for their wares, even if the merchandise is not precious. We desire the abuse to be removed, not the use. For it was also customary for the ancient doctors of the Church to accommodate ancient superstitions, which they could not entirely root out from men's minds, to Christian ritual. In these ancient fables, **Goropius Becanus** searches too much for the truth of a superstitious religion; for he feels that sacred history, both of the Old and New Testament, was mythologically enclosed by the Heathen. He everywhere directs his vigorous force to drag names either to the Triune God, or to God's ministers, or the ministry, whether Jewish or Christian. While we do not deny this entirely, we do not affirm it beyond measure, in the way he extends it to every part, so that he finds and reveals the oracles of God in a dark cave. It cannot be said how much he twists himself here, so that it is a marvel that, while he could have excelled in other praiseworthy things with his sagacious wit, he has grown old in this "dunghill." He insists on the agreement of fables and Holy Scripture with great fervor, so much so that he becomes billious <note>Angry or irritable.</note> if anyone denies that "the origins of fables are holy," to use his words*, where he refers **Minerva** and her robe to Christ with a profane mouth, claiming for himself alone the healthy and primary understanding of fables. With excessive curiosity...

6. *Hermathena*, p. 130.
</margin>

...he refers the three Emperors of Plato to the three persons in God (4. *Hermathena*, p. 72). He twists the fable of **Hercules** (*Hieroglyphics*, p. 22), of **Minerva**, **Orpheus**, etc. (6. *Hermathena*, p. 134), and of **Dioscorus**, **Castor**, and **Pollux** (10. *Hieroglyphics*, p. 259) to Christ and John the Baptist. In a new way and manner, he also explains the fable of **Prometheus** and refers everything to **Noah**, the builder of the ark, in his *Indo-Scythians*. He wants either **Adam** or **Noah** to be hidden under **Saturn** (*Hermathena*, p. 23), yet he asserts that he is truly called **Neptune** (8. *Hermathena*, p. 194). He slips into another opinion about Noah (although in 5. *Gallica*, p. 145 he agrees with others that Noah was the Greek **Deucalion**) while Noah seems to him to be **Apollo**, and **Japheth** to be **Branchus**, whom Apollo loved recklessly; for he writes thus*: "To no mortal after the flood could this nomenclature of Apollo be more conveniently given than to **Noah** himself, who revealed all science, all art, all history, and finally all things divine and human to his sons and grandsons—not only those things which had passed, but also those which would be many centuries in the future. Not without merit, therefore, was a certain distinguished and singular love of Apollo toward **Branchus** <note>In myth, a youth loved by Apollo who received the gift of prophecy; Becanus identifies him with Noah's son Japheth.</note> boasted of, because Noah is sufficiently proved by the blessing itself to have loved him more than the other sons, since he is known to have bestowed more grace and favor upon him. Therefore, those who transferred this history and this prerogative granted to Japheth by Noah into Mythology, handed down that Branchus was Apollo’s darling—which fable has no other veil of truth than the exchange of proper names in those words, which denoted unique gifts in those whom they wished to signify." Yet he makes the same **Japheth** the same as **Janus** (2. *Hispanica*, p. 24) and **Cadmus** (1. *Hieroglyphics*, p. 11), and calls **Noah** the father and father-in-law of Cadmus; in this he thinks correctly, while he asserts that the name of Cadmus had its birth not from Greece but from the East. Let us hear his own words: "The first founder," he says, "of this part of Syria, which most of the ancients called Phoenicia, is said to have been Noah, whom the Syrian tongue called **Agenor**. His son **Japheth**, therefore, handed down both the figures and names of letters to the Phoenicians, whom they called **Cadmus**; and because he had come from the east with his father, and so that posterity might perpetually remember it, both the names and figures of the letters had their origin from the Scythian Nysa. After Japheth had taught the Phoenicians for a long enough time, he was ordered by his father to sail into Europe, which he is said to have loved. Agenor ordered that Cadmus seek Europe. Therefore, **Japheth is Cadmus**, and he is that eastern Teacher of letters among the Phoenicians, who showed [their origin], and so soon thereafter carried the same to Europe as well. Hence the old rumor that the Phoenicians were the first inventors of letters, because doubtless after the Babylonian confusion, Japheth had first delivered them into Syro-Phoenicia." Those who seek harmony in the matters of pagan fictions with our sacred histories think that **Serapis** represented **Joseph**, but they seem to have done so quite liberally. This is what we will further demonstrate in Becanus (16. *Hieroglyphics*, p. 262): "We have in **Serapis**..."

<summary>This page critiques the theories of Johannes Goropius Becanus, who argued that Greco-Roman and Egyptian myths were encoded versions of Biblical history, identifying figures like Noah with Apollo and Saturn, and Japheth with Cadmus. The author cautions against such "subtle webs" of interpretation that risk obscuring divine truth with pagan "trifles."</summary>

<meta>Continuity note: This page continues the exploration of "Cacozelia"—the idea that pagan myths are distorted echoes of Biblical truths. The previous page introduced Johannes Goropius Becanus's theory that even the absurd elements of Bacchic rituals contain hidden theological meanings. This page applies that logic to Egyptian mythology and then transitions to ancient military technology mentioned in the Book of Maccabees.</meta>

# 1 Maccabees 3:48

<margin>
The <term>distorted imitation</term><note>Latin: *Cacozelia*. A term used here to describe how pagan cultures supposedly mimicked and corrupted sacred Hebrew history into myths.</note> of rituals and sacred matters.
</margin>
...rapidly, he says, that monument of antiquity—namely, the grain measure placed upon the crown of the head—which both *Rufinus* and *Maternus* mentioned. This gave some people the opportunity to think that **Serapis** was actually the biblical **Joseph**, because he measured out grain for the Egyptians by the bushel <note>Latin: *modius*. A dry measure of about 8.7 liters.</note>, and through his wisdom provided food for starving people during a period of extreme scarcity. But this interpretation departs far from the ancient custom of hieroglyphics; just as nothing in them pertains to the history of deeds done by any specific person, their very name declares that the entire discipline regards sacred matters. I wish that **Becanus** <note>Johannes Goropius Becanus (1519–1572), a physician and linguist known for his eccentric theories that all mythology points back to Adam and Noah.</note> had been as restrained elsewhere as he was here; but here, with equal ease, he would have excluded Christ. Since we are dealing with Egypt, we must further see how Becanus shows the Egyptian slavery of the Israelites to be wrapped in the fables of the Heathens. <margin>6 *Hispania*, page 87.</margin> They say that **Busiris** <note>A mythical king of Egypt who sacrificed all foreigners to the gods.</note> killed guests everywhere and was finally slain by Hercules. I conjecture that what is said about guests being mistreated pertains to the Israelites; through one of them (Joseph), the Egyptians were saved from a seven-year famine, yet they were later so ungrateful toward them that they ordered their male infants killed and condemned them to the most unjust labors. Among these labors, the building of the city of Busiris was counted, which gave rise to the fiction that guests were slaughtered by Busiris—specifically at altars, because among other works, the construction of temples was the most grueling and exacted with such cruel rigor that it was considered equal to death. The city of Busiris fits the role in the fable primarily because the Israelites were most tormented there, and because, descending from there, they eventually drew the King’s entire army into the Red Sea, where they were overwhelmed. They had built that city last, with intolerable labor and expense, and from there they began their departure into the land promised by God. In this way, the old fable is sifted by being compared to the Mosaic history, and how much truth is in it is revealed. One can easily guess that the report of the seven-year famine reached the nations, which the lying Heathens changed into a nine-year famine. <margin>Book 1 of *The Art of Love*</margin> **Ovid** writes:
> It is said that Egypt lacked the rains that aid the fields,
> and was dry for nine years.

In this way, **Goropius** traces all heathen rites—wherever he observes them—back to the point where he may ascend to the very first beginnings of superstition and from there derive the doctrine of true religion. He does this with such marvelous sharpness that I have often admired him for it, while grieving that he did not display the light of his genius in some other field. For even if what Becanus writes is not far from the truth <margin>page 163.</margin> (7 *Hermathena*), that nothing was celebrated in the rituals of the most ancient people that did not contain symbols of the true religion, nevertheless these things remain for the most part <term>disputed</term><note>Greek: *ἀμφίσβητα* (amphisbeta). Matters that are debated or uncertain.</note> and doubtful. For no one will deny that under a dark and dusky mask, the Devil hid the truth and made the mysteries of true religion into a sort of game, as if he were holding his own Bacchanalia. However, to proceed from there to demonstrate the truth of the Christian religion—as many ancient and modern writers do—is something I would neither easily praise nor believe is done with a happy outcome, as the history of the ancient Church bears witness. Meanwhile, a man is a worthless shell and a "fungus" <note>A common Latin insult for someone dull-witted or useless.</note> if he prattles that nothing but nonsense is to be found in the writings of the ancient poets

<column-break/>

<margin>
The distorted imitation of rituals and sacred matters.
</margin>
and other Heathens. For by that very act he betrays his own ignorance, not knowing that those fictions are full of wisdom and erudition, and have more in their depths than they show on the surface. Nor were they written and fashioned to make the lives of men worse or more shameful, but rather to encourage good morals and a more honorable life. As we prepare to conclude our remarks, we end with the words of **Theodor Zwinger** in the "Proscenium" of his *Theater*: <margin>page 14.</margin> *"Certainly there is no fable that does not contain either a trace of truth or some probable appearance of it. This can be understood from Diodorus Siculus, a most serious historian, who wove together a narrative of the deeds of the ancients and showed that history underlies the removed fables. For one must not think that the divine geniuses of the ancient poets reached such a point of stupidity and wickedness that they themselves embraced—or thrust upon others—shameful and ridiculous fables about the gods, often even impious and superstitious ones, as if they were true history. A mystical sense lies hidden, sometimes physical, sometimes ethical, sometimes theological, which can only be open to the initiated—that is, those imbued with solid philosophy."*

## 1 Maccabees 6:51.

> <term>He set there engines of war, and machines, and fire-throwers, stone-throwers, and scorpions for throwing bolts, and slings.</term><note>Original Greek: *Εστησεν εκει βελοστασεις, και μηχανας, και πυροβολα, λιθοβολα, σκορπιδια εις το βαλλεσθαι βελη και σφενδονας*.</note>
> He stationed there ballistae and machines, and fire-darts, and engines for hurling stones, and small bolts, and scorpions for sending forth arrows, and slings.

We shall now transition to military matters, though as civilians; and we shall produce something regarding the **Scorpio** (scorpio or scorpion) from the writers of war history. The Scorpio is an instrument of torture <note>The author uses "tormenti," which means both "engine of war/catapult" and "torture."</note> by which arrows are sent, just as stones are sent by ballistae, as **Vitruvius** records in Book 10, Chapters 15 and 16. **Ammianus** records that stones are sent by scorpions and arrows by ballistae, and he identifies the "onager" <note>Literally "wild ass."</note> and the scorpion as the same thing; <margin>Book 23.</margin> let others judge this disagreement. We will speak of its form from Ammianus himself, whose words are: *"The form of the Scorpion, which they now call the onager, is as follows: Two axles of oak or holm-oak are hewn and slightly curved so that they seem to bulge into humps; these are connected in the manner of a blacksmith's machine, perforated broadly on both sides. Between these holes, sturdy ropes are bound, holding the frame together so it does not fly apart. From the middle of these ropes, a wooden arm <note>Latin: *stylus*.</note> rises obliquely and is erected like the pole of a wagon, so entangled in the knots of the sinews that it can be raised higher or tilted down. To its top, iron hooks are joined, from which hangs a sling of tow or iron. In front of this wood, a huge cushion is laid out—a haircloth stuffed with fine chaff—bound with strong ties and placed over heaps of turf or brick mounds. For if such a mass were placed on a stone wall, it would shatter whatever was beneath it by the violent concussion, not by its weight. Therefore, when it comes to battle, a round stone is placed in the sling, and four young men on each side, turning the bars to which the ropes are attached, pull the arm back toward the hook. Finally, the Master standing above releases the pin that holds the bonds of the whole work, striking it with a strong hammer; from there, the arm, released with a flying blow..."*

<meta>This page continues the discussion of ancient artifacts and names, moving from the symbolic interpretation of pagan myths to the literal history of technology and resources mentioned in the Bible. The previous page explored the "distorted imitation" of Joseph in the myth of Serapis; this page examines the "Scorpion" (both as a machine and a whip) and provides a "Sacred Metallurgy"—a history of mining and metalworking from Adam to the Roman conquest of Spain.</meta>

# ANTIQUITIES OF THE BIBLE

<margin>Scorpion, a military engine of war.</margin>
...the bolt, and with the force of many strands of hair <note>original: "cilicii" - goatskin or hair rope used for torsion in ancient catapults</note>, it hurls stones, crushing whatever it hits. It is called an "Engine" <note>original: "Tormentum"</note> because all its power comes from the twisting <note>original: "torquetur" - the root of the word 'torment'</note> of its ropes. It is called a "Scorpion" because it has an upright sting on top. Later ages also gave it the name "Onager" <note>The wild ass</note> because wild asses, when hunted, kick stones behind them with such force that they pierce the chests of those following or shatter their skulls. This topic was discussed by Anton Valtrinus (Book 5 on military matters, chapter 6). Pliny (Book 7, chapter 56) identifies the Cretans as the first inventors. See also the more extensive notes of Lipsius (Book 3 on Siege Engines, Dialogue 4, page 164), where he explains the mechanics of this machine. Add also Turnebus (Book 18, *Adversaria*, chapter 1).

<margin>1 Kings 12, verse 11.</margin>
In another sense, we read in 1 Kings 12:11, in the history of Jeroboam, "with scorpions" <note>original Greek: "ἐν σκορπίοις"</note>, which in Hebrew <note>original: "בַּעֲקְרַבִּים" - *ba'akrabbim*</note> Tremellius and Junius translate as "thorny whips." It is a whip made of hooks and spikes, shaped like the stinger in a scorpion's tail, or perhaps named because it stings like a scorpion. Compare Zehner's *Sacred Proverbs* (Century 4, Adage 25, page 610). "The arrow, the bolt, and the gold are still there" <note>original Greek: "Βέλος τ’ ὀϊστὸς καὶ χρυσὸς ἔτ’ ἐκεῖ"</note>. What these things were to the ancients is taught by Drusius in his notes on this passage, Stewichius in his commentary on Vegetius (page 323), and Rosinus (chapter 1). Regarding the sling and slingers, consult Martinius’s *Philological Lexicon* (page 965). To pursue every tiny detail is not our intention here.

->### 1 MACCABEES 8:3<-

> "And what they [the Romans] did in the land of Spain, to take possession of the mines of silver and gold that were there." <note>original Greek: Καὶ ὅσα ἐποίησαν ἐν χώρᾳ Ἱσπανίας, τοῦ κατακρατῆσαι τῶν μετάλλων τοῦ ἀργυρίου καὶ τοῦ χρυσοῦ τῶν ἐκεῖ.</note>

Then, whatever they [the Romans] did in the province of Spain, so that they might obtain the mines of gold and silver that were there.

<margin>Sacred Metallurgy.</margin>
**B**y the blessing of Divine Providence, various benefits of nature are offered to men from the earth. Some are born on the surface, like plants and trees, while others are in the subterranean depths, like metals. Thus we find what Cicero said to be true (Book 2, *On the Nature of the Gods*, section 60): *"We extract iron from the caverns of the earth, a thing necessary for cultivating the fields; we find veins of copper, silver, and gold, hidden deep within, both useful for practical needs and beautiful for decoration."* Experience proves that utility lies hidden not only above ground, but also in the deepest shadows of the earth, for those who, driven by a laudable desire for inquiry and the laborious work of digging, lay open the inner parts of the world. The bowels of our sacred mother earth faithfully produce metals, gems, stones, and minerals <note>original: "succos" - literally 'juices' or 'extracts'</note>, things that serve to display wealth, defend society and the body, satisfy refined tastes, provide for the necessities of building, and prolong human life and health. We might say that "Metal" is better derived from the Hebrew word <term>Metil</term> <note>original: "מְטִיל" - meaning a forged bar or rod</note>—both in name and essence—than from the Greek *meta* and *hama* <note>together with</note>, although that derivation is closer to the truth than the one taken from the verb *metallan* <note>to search/inquire</note>. Metals and minerals are torn from the bowels of the earth by miners so that men may enjoy them. The "bowels of the earth" are said to be those hidden places containing metal; <margin>Preface to Book 34.</margin> hence Pliny says: *"We enter the bowels of the earth and seek riches in the seat of the Underworld."* Thus Ovid, the poet, sings of the Iron Age in Book 1 of his *Metamorphoses*:

<column-break/>

> *"...And the wealth she had hidden near the Stygian shadows. Riches are dug up—the provocations of evil."*

To an investigator, it is necessary to scrutinize the earth and the veins of metals to better judge their nature. For the inquirer, a workshop is brought forth where metals are cooked and smelted; for the word <term>Tsaraph</term> <note>original Hebrew: "צָרַף"</note> means to pour out or to smelt for purification; and <term>Tzoreph</term> <note>Hebrew: "צֹרֵף"</note> is the smelter. Also, <term>Mitzreph</term> <note>Hebrew: "מִצְרֵף"</note> is the vessel in which gold is smelted and purified. Considering the power of this word, it follows by probable reasoning that **Sarepta** <note>original: "Tzarpatham"</note>, or as it is commonly pronounced, **Sarfand**, was a place famous for metal mines; as Becman notes, no better place could then be found, situated in the region of the Sidonians, as Scripture testifies: *"Arise,"* says the Lord to Elijah, *"and go to Sarepta, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there."* <note>1 Kings 17:9</note>. Sidonian craftsmen were highly praised for their skill in many things, including metalworking, so that they were known to Solomon above all others when he sought laborers for his building project. He sent word to Hiram saying: *"Behold, I intend to build a house to the name of the Lord my God... Now therefore command that your servants cut down cedars from Lebanon for me... For you know that there is no one among us who knows how to cut wood like the Sidonians."* <note>1 Kings 5:5-6</note>. The digging of metals is ancient, being in use even before the Flood by the antediluvians. It is the constant opinion of all learned men that **Adam** was the first of the metallurgists; placing his tent at the roots of Lebanon, he discovered a mine through digging, which Cain's descendants later made more and more famous. And so men went into the bowels of the earth both before and during the time of **Tubal-cain**, where metals lay hidden as if in storehouses. Whether it was Tubal-cain—whom the Gentiles called **Vulcan** by dropping the first syllable (see Mathesius, *Sarepta*, Sermon 2, page 37, where he excellently compares the pagan Vulcan with Tubal-cain)—or someone else who labored in the mines. Before the Flood, the metal veins supplied nothing but iron material, and for a long time men had no knowledge of gold, silver, or other metals. After the Flood, the descendants of Japheth in the West and the descendants of Ham in the East sought the hidden metals through more subtle inquiry, especially gold. For we are taught by experience that the best gold and gems come from the South and East, while the best of other metals and veins of silver come from the West and North. From this arose the poets' fable of the voyage to Colchis to bring back the **Golden Fleece**, and of **Midas**, the wealthiest metallurgist of Phrygia, who is said to have lived in the time of Gideon and to have dug for metals there. To this we can refer the stories of the garden in Iberia <note>Ancient Spain</note> bearing golden apples, guarded by a dragon of immense size. For **Iberia**, which we today call **Spain**, is praised by Pliny for its metal veins fertile with gold and silver; he says that in no other part of the world has there been such fertility for so many centuries. For this reason, Petrus Redanus (Commentary on 1 Maccabees 8:3) praises it, while at the same time disagreeing with Serrarius, who thought that Spain’s mines had been exhausted or made barren...

It traces the origins of mining from Adam and Tubal-cain to the legendary wealth of Spain mentioned in the Book of Maccabees.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of natural resources mentioned in the Bible, transitioning from the historical context of Roman conquests mentioned in 1 Maccabees to a detailed technical study of mining, which the author calls "Sacred Metallurgy." It specifically links the biblical mention of Spanish silver and gold to contemporary 17th-century mining practices in Spain and Germany.</meta>

### 1 Maccabees 8:3

<margin>Sacred Metallurgy.</margin>

In response to this history, he answers in this manner: "The Spaniards certainly carry back immense treasures of gold and silver from the New World, not without great glory and benefit for Spain, nor small profit for other nations—though it provokes great envy in many. Yet the Spaniards cannot carry back from the New World those gold and silver mines of Spain itself, which could not be moved across the ocean. Furthermore, even if it were granted that the mines of Spain have already ceased to produce, no fair judge of affairs should wonder at this; for since the generation of metals is a slow and sluggish process, they do not reach maturity or become ready for smelting except after the span of many centuries. Once the first mines are exhausted, others are not immediately at hand, suddenly hardened and ready. There are no mines so fertile that they cannot eventually be drained." Human industry, the force of desire, and the thirst of avarice are greater than the speed of nature in supplying gold and silver. However, it is entirely false that the gold and silver mines in Spain have ceased, because the veins of both metals still swell, dispersed throughout the whole body of Spain. Indeed, more than five hundred very rich mines were recently opened, as Pineda proves at length. There is no need for us to demonstrate with many words how fertile our own Germany is in gold, silver, and other metals; <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555) was a German scholar known as the "Father of Mineralogy." His work *De Re Metallica* is the foundational text of mining science.</note> Georgius Agricola, that most learned "dweller of the mines," has shown this to us with his profound erudition and exquisite judgment. He diligently surveyed the deepest birthplaces of these metals and received the most excellent information from skilled craftsmen, as evidenced by that remarkable book he left us on the subject of metal mines. 

Furthermore, the discoverers of metals are distinguished by various excellent titles and praises. By Firmicus, they are called "those who pursue the hidden veins of gold, silver, and other species with subtle inquiry." Ammianus Marcellinus calls them "those skilled in following veins of gold." Claudian, in his work on the consulship of Theodoric, speaks of "following the veins." Even the Emperors speak this way in Law 7 of the *Code on Metals*, where everyone who contributes to the mining industry is called a <term>metallarius</term> <note>original Latin: a professional miner or mine manager</note>. All these are free men according to the law, and by this very name they are distinguished from <term>the condemned</term> <note>original Latin: "Metallicis," referring to those sentenced to "damnatio ad metalla," or forced labor in the mines</note>, who are slaves. However, this penal slavery was abolished by the *Novels of Justinian* (Novel 22, chapter 8). 

But before we descend into the very bowels of the earth to dig out gold, silver, and other metals, we will first set forth the formulas of speech used by miners, which occur in our common tongue <note>The author uses German technical terms, common in the mining heartlands of the Holy Roman Empire</note> and are not found everywhere. Miners are occupied either with establishing mines, where first occurs the word specific to them: <term>A Shaft</term> <note>original German: "Ein Schacht"</note>, which you might more accurately render as a pit or a cavern. From this are born the miners' phrases: <term>to prospect</term> <note>original German: "Schürffen," searching for veins</note>; <term>to break ground</term> <note>original German: "Einschlagen," to begin a pit</note>; and <term>to sink</term> <note>original German: "Sencken," to descend by digging</note>. You cannot better express <term>a discovery mine</term> <note>original German: "Eine Fundgruben"</note> in Roman words than as a pit detecting a new vein. <term>A flat shaft</term> <note>original German: "Ein flacher Schacht"</note> is a pit going off at an angle. <term>A water-shaft</term> <note>original German: "Ein Wasser-Schacht"</note> is a pit made for the sake of receiving water (compare Agricola's *On Mining*, Book 5). They call the wooden structures of the mines <term>the timbering</term> <note>original German: "das Gezimmer"</note>. The beams of these structures are called <term>support posts, yokes, cross-beams, wall-rods, and bolts</term> <note>original German: "Tragstempel, Jöcher, Donhölzer, Wandruthen, Riegel"</note>. Next...

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Metallurgy.</margin>

...those things which concern the veins also have their own peculiar names: <term>the internal site of the mountain</term> <note>original German: "das Geschicht"</note> is rendered in Latin as the internal layout. <term>A lode or strike</term> <note>original German: "ein Gang" or "Strich"</note> is a vein, which is a subterranean path or channel containing metals. From this comes <term>to dress a vein</term> <note>original German: "einen Gang austrichten"</note>, meaning to uncover it; <term>the strike of the vein</term> <note>original German: "das streichen deß Gangs"</note>, its forward progress; <term>the footwall</term> <note>original German: "das liegende"</note>, the underlying foundation; and <term>the hanging wall</term> <note>original German: "das hangende"</note>, the overhanging roof of the vein. <term>A vein falling into the depths</term> <note>original German: "Ein Gang der in die Tieffe fällt"</note> is called a vein tending toward the deep, which happens either 1. *perpendicularly*, <term>falling straight down</term> <note>original German: "Seigergericht"</note>, or 2. *obliquely*, <term>a flat vein falling into the deep</term>. Furthermore, <term>a floating vein or seam</term> <note>original German: "ein schwebender Gang" or "Flöze"</note> is called a vein stretching across the mountain. <term>A deposit</term> <note>original German: "Ein Geschütt" or "Geslöck"</note> is a vein that holds together in a continuous channel through the length, depth, and width of the mountain. <term>A main lode</term> <note>original German: "Ein Hauptgang"</note> is a principal vein, larger or fuller. <term>A cross-vein</term> <note>original German: "Ein Quergang"</note> is a less principal vein. If this disjoins and cuts across the principal vein, it is called in our language <term>a cross-lode</term> <note>original German: "Creutzgang"</note>. If they touch and run over it together, they are <term>veins that head over the main lode</term> or <term>cross the main lode</term>, or at least <term>veins that head toward the main lode</term>. Additionally, <term>a narrow seam</term> <note>original German: "eine schmale Fleß"</note> refers to very small veins going off across the mountain; <term>a wedge-mountain</term> <note>original German: "ein Keilberg"</note> is the earth lying between two veins; "Mountains" <note>original German: "Berg"</note> are the earth and stones of the mine. When these are cast out, they are called <term>the mine dumps</term> <note>original German: "Halden der Gruben"</note>. If the material for digging is hard, it is called <term>the fortress</term> <note>original German: "Festung"</note>; if soft, <term>brittle</term> <note>original German: "schnettig"</note>. We will deal with the names of the metals themselves below. 

Nor should we pass over 3. *the miners' instruments*, <term>the mine-gear</term> <note>original German: "Der Bergzeug"</note>, which they use either for *extracting metals*, <term>the hewer's tools</term> <note>original German: "der Häuerzeug"</note>, which include the <term>sledge, sorting-hammer, or crushing-hammer</term>. Likewise the <term>mallet, wedge, feathers, blocks, pickaxe, scratching iron, crowbar, breaking iron, pry bar, mining iron, sump iron, and irons</term> used to make breakthroughs, and <term>toggles</term>. Or for *collecting materials*: <term>scrapers, shovels, ore-troughs, ore-buckets, mine-buckets, baskets, leather sacks, wheelbarrows</term> (one-wheeled), and <term>the "dog"</term> <note>original German: "Hund," a small four-wheeled cart used in narrow tunnels</note>. Or 3. *in extracting*: <term>the windlass or hoist</term> <note>original German: "Sucula" or "der Haspel"</note>, which has parts such as the <term>crank-station, hanging-bench, hoist-support, the axle-tree, the hoist-handle, or winch</term>, and the rope or chain <term>cable and hook</term>. Or 4. *in measuring*: for the mines, the <term>Mining Compass</term>, which is a geometric instrument; <term>the fathom</term> <note>original German: "Das Lachter," a large cubit or arm-span</note>; and for the metals, <term>the tun</term> <note>original German: "die Donne"</note>. To this, add things serving for *water extraction*, such as <term>ring-buckets and cans</term>; or *drainage*, the <term>water-channel</term> <note>original German: "die Wasser-Seige"</note>; or for *ventilation*, the <term>wind-catchers</term>; or other things: <term>the ladders</term> <note>original German: "Die Fahrten"</note>, iron handles, <term>ladder-hooks, mine-lights, tallow-pouches, iron straps, and the miner's stool</term>. Or for the work itself, which being varied, also receives various names: <term>to timber</term> <note>original German: "verspfenden"</note> is to strengthen a structure with wedges. <term>Casting in the rope and bucket</term> is the first act of extraction. They call it <term>settling in</term> <note>original German: "angesessen"</note> if they begin the site of a mine by digging. <term>To tip ore or water</term> is the same as what is commonly called <term>pouring</term>. When they throw down a huge quantity of very hard material, they call this <term>thrown by the forest</term> or <term>driven off</term>. To pass a vein while digging is <term>to miss, over-drive, or over-run the lode</term>. *To seek and follow a passed vein* is called <term>tracking</term>. To break apart...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Metallurgy.</margin>

Regarding the processing of metals, <note>original: "re metalla"</note> crushing the ore is called *pounding* <note>original: "Est bochen / vulgo est zerkloppfen"</note>; the drawing and pouring of water they call *infusing* <note>original: "eingiessen"</note>. The time designated for mining labor is called a *shift* <note>original: "Schicht"</note>; when it is short, namely eight hours, it is the *short shift* <note>original: "die kurtze Schicht"</note>; when it is long, namely twelve hours, it is the *long or "Kühn" shift* <note>original: "die lange vel KühnSchicht"</note>. To measure or survey is named by them *boundary-marking* <note>original: "Marckscheiden / Marckscheiden / abziehen"</note>. The places in which the mines are located are called *pits, mines, hollows, huts, stamp-mills, or mountain-smithies* <note>original: "die Zechen / Gruben / Hollen / Hütten / Puchwercke / Bergschmiede"</note>. An adit <note>original: "Stollo / ein Stolln"</note> is a subterranean passage, stretching from the foot of the mountain all the way to the bottom of the mine, dug for the purpose of either leading water away, letting in fresh air, or carrying out the excavated material; it was invented for the benefit and convenience of the mines, whence they call digging an adit *driving an adit* <note>original: "einen Stollen treiben"</note>, the bottom of which is called the *adit-floor* <note>original: "deß Stollen Sohlen"</note> and the entrance the *adit-mouth* <note>original: "deß Stollen Mundloch"</note>. Furthermore, they are infested by a certain kind of phantom, which they call a *mining demon* <note>original: "Dæmonem metallicum"</note> or the *Mountain Devil* <note>original: "den Bergteuffel"</note>, as Agricola reports in his sixth book <note>Georgius Agricola, "De Re Metallica."</note> and at the end of his book *On Subterranean Creatures*. But that kind of demon which they call the *Mountain Monk, the Little Mountain Man, the Kobold, or the Güttel* <note>original: "den Bergmünch / das Bergmännlein / den Kobel / den Güttel"</note> they do not fear, but rather desire its presence. Agricola mentions this in his treatise *On Subterranean Creatures*. We have wished to set down these modes of speaking used by miners—though certainly not all of them—at some length because books published on the mining of metals are not in everyone's hands nor easily found. Having considered these things, let us now descend into the very bowels of the earth to investigate gold, silver, and other metals, which we shall apply to pious uses and secret matters, as well as others, with the "divining rod" <note>A tool used by miners to find ore veins; here used metaphorically.</note> pointing the way; for there are never any veins so good as those which lead to heavenly or super-heavenly things, or to moral truths. We shall immediately submit a study of such matters, beginning from the metal of metals: Gold, which is more precious the more rarely it reveals itself. Gold is the most perfect and most splendid metal, born from perfectly refined mercury, the most excellent red sulfur, and the finest salt <note>This reflects the "Mercury-Sulfur-Salt" theory of alchemy popular in the 17th century.</note>. Because of the most exquisite mixing of its principles, it is both very fine and very solid; its substance is corrupted neither by earth nor air. Nor is it consumed by fire, but is more and more purified by it. Furthermore, because of its fine solidity, it is the most soft and ductile of all metals. Therefore, that which is more reddish and splendid will be of the best value; likewise that which is softer, so that it can be most easily drawn out.
<margin>Physical Distinctions, book 6, chapter 15.</margin>
Experience has shown, as Dr. Graevius writes, that a third part of a single grain of gold can coat a wire 134 feet long, and if it is to be extended over silver plates with a hammer, a single ounce of gold can cover eight pounds of silver. Thus, a single ounce of gold is worth as much as twelve of silver, or a whole pound. Among the other metals it excels in *natural power* <note>original: "φυσικῇ δυνάμει"</note>, whence also in the Holy Tongue <note>Hebrew</note> it has its name from its innate power of strengthening the human heart. Regarding this, Melanchthon wittily said: "Gold is said to strengthen the heart, but we wretched scholars experience little of it" <note>Philip Melanchthon (1497–1560) was a German reformer; this is a joke about scholars being poor.</note>. The purest and most perfect gold is called *Zahav* <note>original: "זהב"</note>. In polishing it, to make it bright and splendid, they formerly used the Samian stone, 
<margin>Book 5, chapter 173.</margin>
about which Dioscorides says, "which goldsmiths use

<column-break/>

for smoothing and polishing," just as Pliny says in book 36, chapter 21, that it is useful for polishing gold. Mixed with the raw earth, it is first extracted from the mines in the form the Greeks call *unfired gold* <note>original: "χρυσὸν ἄπυρον"</note>; then, when it has been tested and explored by fire, it is called by the Greeks *blazing fire* <note>original: "αἰθόμενον πῦρ"</note>, because it shines and flashes remarkably like fire, as in Pindar's *Olympian Ode 1, verse 2*, a passage which Timon references in Lucian. In Latin it is called *obryzum* <note>refined gold</note>, which however seems to some to be a corrupted word derived from *Ophir*; compare Mathesius in *Sarepta, Sermon 3, page 175*. Most famous, however, is that expedition of Solomon from Ezion-Geber, a port of the Red Sea, into the maritime region of Ophir. *Ophir* is an Egyptian word, whence Athanasius Kircher in *Prodromus Coptus Aegyptiacus, chapter 4*, believes the Egyptians made expeditions into Persia, India, and even to the furthest borders of the Chinese, and this by the benefit of the Erythraean <note>Red</note> Sea, in which they had most convenient ports for sailing to Ethiopia, Persia, and the rest of India. Whether Ophir is truly that region which we today call Peru, as Arias Montanus, Postellus, and others wish to gather from the word *Parvaim* in 2 Chronicles 3:7, is unclear; indeed, sacred history mentions the gold of Parvaim and Ophir more than once. Paul Merula, in his *Dissertation on Customs*, tries to prove through a pleasant rearrangement of letters <note>original: "metathesei"</note> from Job 28:16 and Isaiah 13:2 that this is the same as "Peruvian." However, Pererius constantly denies this, because in the region of Peru, neither elephants, nor peacocks, nor monkeys, nor the most precious woods are found, which we read were brought from Ophir. "It is not likely," he says, "that Solomon—leaving aside a nearer region more fertile in many precious things—would have instituted a navigation from the Red Sea (on whose shore was Ezion-Geber, from which the fleet set sail) in an immense circuit to the region of Peru, when he could have reached that region more conveniently from Joppa or another port of the Mediterranean Sea through the Strait of Gibraltar <note>original: "fretum Gaditanum"</note> by a much shorter sailing time of about five months." Thus says he. Gold—to say nothing now of its virtue and powers in strengthening the heart, brain, liver, etc.—is the most precious metal, which rarity and the magnitude of its price commend, and which rarely appears in the money-chest of the poor. The anxiety of the rich in both seeking and guarding gold is immense and monstrous, such that they dread no danger, not even the gravest; whence it is called by Euripides in *Danae, verse 31*, "a possession desired by mortals." For the greed of having much caused Polydorus—fearing no such thing—to be slaughtered by the treacherous Polymnestor, King of the Thracians. Having been sent by his father Priam to the home of his Thracian host so that he might live there more safely, he was killed for the sake of possessing his gold. Thus Polydorus says of himself in Euripides:
> He kills me, the wretched one, for the sake of gold,
> My father's guest-friend, and having killed me, into the swell of the sea
> He cast me, so that he himself might have the gold in his halls.
Hence Virgil in *Aeneid, book 3, verse 166*:
> ->This Polydorus, formerly with a great weight of gold,<-
> ->Unhappy Priam had secretly entrusted to be raised<-
> *By the Thracian King, when he already distrusted the arms*
> *Of Troy, and saw the city surrounded by siege.*
> *That man, when the power of the Teucrians was broken and fortune receded,*
> *Following Agamemnon's cause and victorious arms,*

# 1. Maccabees VIII. 3.
<sig>Aaa aaa 2</sig>
<meta>Catchword: mind</meta>

<margin>1. Sacred Metallurgy.</margin>
He breaks every sacred bond, murders Polydorus, and seizes the gold by force. To what do you not drive mortal hearts, O cursed hunger for gold! <note>These famous lines are originally from Virgil's Aeneid (3.55-57), describing the betrayal of a Trojan prince for wealth.</note>
Thence Ovid writes in the 13th book of his *Metamorphoses*:
*There is a land, opposite Phrygia where Troy once stood, inhabited by the Bissonian men. There was the wealthy palace of Polymestor, to whom your father secretly committed you, Polydorus, to be raised, removing you from the Phrygian arms. A wise counsel, had he not added great riches, the rewards of crime—an incentive for a greedy mind. When the fortune of the Phrygians fell, the impious King of the Thracians took his sword and plunged it into the throat of his own ward.*
With this, Prudentius agrees in his *Life of Saint Lawrence*:
> Modesty is dissolved through gold,
> Integrity is violated by gold,
> Peace dies, faith perishes,
> And even the laws themselves fall away.
And again:
> If you seek truer gold,
> It is light and the human race.

<margin>2. On the Lament of the Church 7. page 27. b.</margin>
But that gold, which is called "truer" by the Poets, is not the gold that Jeremiah attributes to the Jews in *Lamentations 4:1*, where he compares treacherous and impious princes to "darkened gold." On these words, Alvarus Pelagius <note>A 14th-century Franciscan bishop known for his critiques of Church corruption.</note> writes: *Gold excels five other metals in five ways: namely in clarity, purity, preciousness, weight, and durability. In clarity, the splendor of divine wisdom, good reputation, and virtues are signified. Regarding the purity of gold, what shall I say of the Ministers of the Church? Where today is the purity of heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith? Let the preciousness of gold be referred to the work of martyrdom, for "precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints." The weight of gold is to be referred to the gravity of faith and morals, and constancy. The fear of God properly creates this weight. In durability, the virtue of the good is understood as perseverance. These virtues and others, signified by the properties of gold, have today failed in the Church.* Therefore it is rightly said: *How has the gold grown dim?* And Paschasius Ratbertus <note>A Carolingian theologian.</note> in book 4 on Jeremiah’s Lamentations, column 1478: Through the "darkened gold," the Prophet mourns the treachery of the Jews, because in them that ancient vigor of faith and the splendor of innocence grew dark in the night as treacherous malice rushed in. And they themselves were dispersed, not only through all the business of vanity, but were even led into captivity among foreign nations. They were "gold" because of their knowledge of God and the nature of the Patriarchs; but they were "darkened" by the filth of their sins and the stains of treachery. Through "darkened gold," he deplores the reprobate life of the chosen ones, the priests, or the ministers of God in various orders—a life once clear through the glory of virtues, but now darkened by the lowest actions and the business of the world. Thus far we have spoken of the abuse of gold—gold, I say, the most precious gift bestowed most abundantly by God upon men from the bowels of the earth. To this is compared whatever is best in its own kind. The Author of the Book of Wisdom, speaking in the persona of the Wisest of Kings <note>Solomon</note>, compares Wisdom to the best of metals, gold; indeed, he prefers it by many leagues.

<margin>Hecuba line 25.</margin>
<margin>Wisdom 7: 8.</margin>
\* <note>original Greek: "οὐδὲ ὡμοιώσα αὐτῇ λίθον τίμιον..."</note> *Neither did I liken to her any precious stone, because all gold, in her sight, is but a little sand, and silver shall be accounted as clay before her.* The righteous man possesses this heavenly Wisdom, and is thereby greater than any rich man, any ruler, or any King. <note>original Greek: "Κἂν γδ` τις ᾖ τέλειοϛ..."</note> *For though a man be never so perfect among the children of men, yet if your Wisdom be not with him, he shall be nothing regarded.* Whence, inviting all to acquire Wisdom in *Proverbs 16:16*, he says: *How much better is it to get wisdom than gold! and to get understanding rather to be chosen than silver!* By which very thing he teaches that wisdom is more powerful than all treasures; Melior Laubanus captures this sentiment in this four-line verse in his *Gleanings of Solomon*, number 8:

> Wisdom is not worth less than precious gold, though
> That gold be dug from the inner earth.
> Nor is prudence less dear than silver; happy
> And wealthy enough is whoever is famous for both.

To this may rightly be referred what is read in Augustine's *Commentary on Psalm 71, column 784*: *Wisdom so excels among all teachings as gold does among metals; whence it is written: To receive prudence like silver, and wisdom like tested gold.* Since gold is a thing more desirable than all others among these earthly things, other desirable and precious things are often compared to *Gold*. Above all greed, the treasure of the Divine Word is to be desired, which is not unmeritedly called the *desire for grace*.

<margin>On Psalm 118, p. 766.</margin>
Hence Prosper says: *The mandates of God are loved above gold and topaz, that is, above those things which are held precious on earth, when in the observance of the mandates no temporal reward is sought, but justice itself, because nothing is better than that good by which man himself becomes good.* When the Psalmist introduces the Church as the heavenly Bride of the heavenly Groom, clothed in a gilded garment, *Psalm 45:10*, Cassiodorus explains those words about the Queen in gilded and variegated clothing as the adornment of the soul, writing: *In gold, charity is understood; for that which is golden is entirely of gold; that which is gilded has gold, but is also something else. The Queen stands in a gilded garment of good works, not a golden one, lest charity be alone; rather, let there be other things present which charity adorns. She is clothed in a variety of merits; and thus there is unity in charity with gold—that is, with the doctrine of the Apostles—and with scarlet—that is, the confession of the Martyrs—and with gems—that is, the purity of virgins—and with purple—that is, the laments of the penitents. Thus is the Queen adorned.* Truly, just as gold and silver are usually rendered purer by fire and tested by the same, a comparison is often established between them and the force and efficacy of tribulation and calamities. Thus the Son of Sirach says in *chapter 2, verse 5*: <note>original Greek: "Ὅτι ἐν πυρὶ δοκιμάζεται χρυσὸϛ..."</note> *For gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of adversity.* On these words Chrysostom says in his *4th Homily*: *Just as gold becomes purer when tested by fire, so also the soul, conversing with tribulations in dangers, comes forth more bright and shakes off every stain of sin.* Let us hear God saying in *Zechariah 13:9*: *I will refine them as gold is refined, and will try them as silver is tried.* Compare this with *Malachi 3:2*, where <term>refiner's fire</term> <note>original Hebrew: "אש מצרף" (esh metzaref)</note> is the fire for *melting or testing in the fire*. For as the goldsmith tests gold through fire, so the pious *certainly*, says Tertullian in *Scorpio*, page 610, are tested through torments...

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Metallurgy.</margin>
The instruments of fire and punishment through the martyrdoms that examine faith. To this end, Augustine writes: *My tribulation comes, and my purging will come. Does gold not shine in the goldsmith's furnace? In me, nothing will shine; in the ornament, it will shine; yet let it endure the furnace, so that through purging from filth it may come to the light. That furnace: there is the chaff, there is the gold, there is the fire, and there stands the goldsmith. The world is the furnace, the wicked are the chaff, the righteous are the gold, tribulation is the fire; God is the goldsmith, and whatever else He holds there.* <note>original: "Venit tribulatio mea... Fornax mundus, palea iniqui, aurum justi, ignis tribulatio; aurifex Deus." From Augustine's commentary on the Psalms.</note>
<margin>On Psalm 61, column 624.</margin>
From gold, the most noble of metals, we proceed to the other, which is inferior to it by many degrees. Silver, which in the Sacred language is called <term>keseph (כסף)</term>, whether it be stamped or not, comes from the root <term>keseph (כסף)</term>, meaning "he desired" or "he longed for," because it is sought after by men with great desire. Hence the rhymes in our mother tongue:
> ->There is a word that has an S.<-
> ->Whoever sees it / desires it fast;<-
> ->When the S. is not within it /<-
> ->It is my highest treasure on earth.<-
<note>original: "Es ist ein Wort das hat ein S..." This German riddle likely plays on the word "Geld" (money) or "Gold." If the "S" is removed from a word like "Golds" or perhaps "Silbers," it leaves the "highest treasure."</note>
Regarding the Silver Age, one should read Hesiod, <term>line 126</term>, and Danaeus, <term>Antiquities part 2, 18. 4. 51.</term> Since this age was much worse, as Hesiod says, it brought even greater evils into human life, which Creon in Sophocles' work commemorates at length:
<margin>in *Antigone*.</margin>
> For no such evil institution as money <note>original: "argyros" (silver/money)</note>
> has ever cropped up among men. This even destroys cities,
> this drives men from their homes.
> This trains and perverts the good minds
> of mortals to set themselves to shameful deeds.
> It has shown men how to practice villainies,
> and to know the impiety of every work.

The metal nearest to silver is copper, whose name in the Sacred language is <term>nechoshet (נחשת)</term>, so called from rust and virulent filth; hence the "bronze serpent" <note>original: "nechash nechoshet"</note> erected by Moses at God's command was given its name in 2 Kings 18:4, because it was fashioned in the likeness of the fiery serpents. Indeed, in the East, especially toward Egypt and Ethiopia, serpents have red or bronze-colored bodies due to the excessive heat. Its use and nature were also known to those before the Flood, for the Sacred Book mentions copper—or rather bronze, by which name copper is understood—in <term>Genesis 4:22.</term> From this, Pliny in <term>Book 7, chapter 56</term> maintains that bronze was discovered before iron. This same opinion is confirmed by Pausanias in <term>Book 3</term>, and Homer writes that the arms of the heroes, the most ancient of men, were made of bronze, not iron. See Danaeus <term>on the first age of the world, part 2, page 233.</term> Bronze is distinguished by its ringing sound, which is why the voice of Cerberus <note>The three-headed hound of Hades.</note> is called "brazen" by Hesiod in <term>Theogony, line 311</term>:
> Cerberus, the flesh-eater, the brazen-voiced hound of Hades.
That is, "mighty," about which Virgil writes in <term>Aeneid 6</term>:
*This mighty Cerberus.*
Furthermore, since bronze can be worked in either direction, it is often called "ductile" by others; thus it happened that vessels and instruments of every kind were fashioned from it, even to the point that it was the material for weapons until iron was discovered. Homer joins iron with bronze and gold in *Iliad 6, line 48*:
> Bronze and gold and iron wrought with much toil.
For iron is more useful than all gold for cultivating the land and protecting life. Noah could not have done without iron, though he could have done without gold. The mechanical arts require iron for various effects

<column-break/>

necessary for human affairs. While the world could have existed comfortably without knowing gold, it cannot perform the work of agriculture without iron. Thus Goropius Becanus <note>A 16th-century physician and linguist.</note> says: *Vain is the commerce of those who cook gold chains in their broths, or boast that water receives more strength to invigorate the internal organs from glowing gold than from iron; for only filth is left behind by gold, and no faculty of the gold passes into the water or the broth. If that were to happen, it would be recognized by a difference in taste or some other way, none of which experiments have shown me so far.* Hence gold is most suitable for cauterizing when we want none of the metallic property to be left in the wound. But let the Chemists settle that. Before the use of iron, battles were fought in a "fist-fight" <note>original: "pugna"</note> or with hands folded into a "fist" <note>original: "pugnum"</note>; for <term>pygme</term> comes from <term>pygmos</term> <note>Greek terms for boxing/fist.</note>, because men first fought with their fists. Donatus in the <term>Prologue to Terence's Hecyra</term> says: *In ancient times, before the use of iron and weapons, they fought with fists, heels, bites, and by wrestling their bodies.* Cassiodorus in <term>Variae, Letter 30, page 59</term> states: *The name for "fight" (pugna) was taken from the "fist" (pugno).* Later, Belus was the first to bring forth the iron sword, from whom it was decided that "war" (bellum) should be named. Hence Titus Lucretius says:
> Ancient weapons were hands, nails, and teeth,
> as well as stones and branches broken from the woods.
First Cain—the Cacus <note>A fire-breathing giant from Roman myth, here used as a metaphor for Cain's brutality.</note> of all men—attacked Abel with a hard club and a fierce hand, so that Ovid's line in the <term>1st book of the Fasti</term> might be said of him:
> Cain <note>The text inserts "Cain" here into the Ovid quote about the giant Cacus.</note> moves the first battles in hand-to-hand combat,
> and fiercely wages the matter with stones and clubs.
Therefore, Cain, after his brother-murder <note>original: "adelphoktonian"</note>, studied the course of metallurgy, and improved this art from day to day; and Tubalcain, whom Holy Scripture calls <term>lotesh kol-choresh (לטש כל־חרש)</term>, "a sharpener and smith," the Septuagint calls <term>a hammer-beater and smith</term> <note>original: "σφυροκόπον καὶ χαλκέα"</note>. By "sharpeners," iron-smiths are understood in the craft of bronze and iron, whom we in our mother tongue call <term>the Smith</term> <note>original: "der Schmid"</note>. Matthesius <note>Johann Mathesius, a theologian who wrote about mining.</note> derives the origin of this word from the Hebrew <term>tsemidim (צמידים)</term>, the name given to the "bracelets" on the hands of Rebecca in <term>Genesis 24:30</term>. Those preparing weapons and instruments of every kind, the word <term>lotesh</term> means he sharpened, wiped clean the sword, or polished iron or bronze instruments so that they might shine. Iron becomes stronger if it is immersed in cold water, as Homer teaches, who says that <term>tempering</term> <note>original: "baphēn"</note> is <term>giving strength to iron by dipping it in cold water</term>. Hence iron is preferred over other metals for its constancy and hardness. Thus it is fitting for a seasoned, faithful, religious, and constant Theologian to have an "iron forehead" and to be entirely made of iron against the stubborn and perverse, like the Prophet Jeremiah, to whom the Lord said: *Behold, I have made you today <term>be-od amud barzel (בעוד עמוד ברזל)</term> into an iron pillar, <term>u-le-chomot nechoshet (ולחומות נחשת)</term> and into walls of bronze, against the Kings of Judah and its Princes: its Priests and the people of the land. And they shall indeed fight against you, but (v. 19) they shall not prevail against you, for I am with you.* Furthermore, against an "iron mind"—that is, one unmerciful and prone to cruelty—Homer opposes a soul inclined to compassion:
> ...and to me my heart
> in my breast is of iron, but it is merciful.
Necessity requires us to speak of minerals in a general way <note>original: "hōs typō eipein"</note>; among them, Sulphur, Nitre, and Salt stand out. Sulphur is the parent of all metals, since...

### 1. Maccabees VIII, 3.

<margin>Sacred Metallurgy.</margin>
By the benefit of sulfur, almost all metals are generated, even if sulfur itself is not usually counted among the metals; yet no metal is found without sulfur, for by it—just as the Spirit rules the human Body—the metals are preserved. <note>original: "Thurneißer in Pisone l. 3. c. 7. p. 68." Leonhard Thurneisser (1531–1596) was a famous miracle doctor and alchemist.</note> Nitre, or saltpeter, is a word of Hebrew origin <term>nether (נתר)</term>, in Greek <term>nitron (νίτρον)</term>, and from its abundance, the name was given to Nitria, a city in Egypt. Its name comes from "leaping," for <term>nether</term> signifies to leap or spring out, which is why the poets called salt the *Leaping grain* <note>original: "Salientem micam."</note>. What the nitre of the Ancients truly was is not yet certain, except that it was cooked from the water and sand of the Nile.

<margin>Proverbs 25:20.</margin>
Solomon, the most prudent of Kings, mentions its power: *Like one who sings songs to a heavy heart, so is vinegar poured upon nitre.* <note>The author is paraphrasing Proverbs 25:20. In ancient chemistry, vinegar reacts violently with nitre (natron), causing it to foam or "bite."</note> Here one must know the power of vinegar and the power of nitre. Both things are very biting. But when vinegar is dropped upon nitre, the "mordacity" <note>biting sharpness</note> of the nitre is increased. So it is when we sing a good song and deliver good doctrine to the depraved heart of a perverse and malignant man: such a person becomes far more biting and petulant. Salt <note>Latin: "Sal"</note> has its name from *salting* <note>original: "salsendo"</note>, because it preserves meat, fish, and other things from corruption; hence it is called by the Hebrews <term>melach (מלח)</term> from the root *malach*. And in *Numbers 18:19*, the covenant which God struck with Abraham and his seed forever is called a <term>berit melach (ברית מלח)</term>, a *covenant of salt*, that is, incorruptible and perpetual. No one is so dull <note>original: "insulsus," literally "unsalted" or "witless."</note> as not to know that the primary use of salt for mortals is to easily preserve things that are otherwise prone to decay. Thus, it has always been held in great price and esteem, especially if it could be obtained without too high a cost. From this it happened that, out of singular mercy, Demetrius granted the Jews immunity from the salt tax, which was dearly exacted, writing to them in *1 Maccabees 10:29*: <note>original: "Ἀφίημι πάντας τοὺς Ἰουδαίους ἀπὸ τῶν φόρων, καὶ τῆς τιμῆς τοῦ ἁλὸς καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν φάνων..."</note> *I release all Jews from taxes, and from the price of salt, and from the crown-gold, and instead of the third of the seed and instead of half of the fruit of the trees.*

<margin>Book 3.</margin>
However, that "price" refers to what is owed to the public treasury in the name of Salt. Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian.</note> writes that in the Troad, the Tragasaean salt was set out for the use of the common people without price, but he records that when Antigonus imposed a tax, the salt dried up. That the ancients used salt as a side-dish <note>original: "obsonio"</note> is indicated by Diogenes, when he replied to King Craterus, who had invited him as a guest, that he would rather *lick salt in Athens* than feast on sumptuous banquets elsewhere. <note>original: "Ἀλλὰ βούλομαι ἔφη, ἐν Ἀθήναις ἅλα λείχειν..." From Diogenes Laertius, Book 6.</note> Salt is the ornament of a frugal table and the seasoning of the poor; hence Horace writes to Grosphus:

<margin>Odes Book 2, 16, line 13.</margin>
> He lives well on little, for whom the paternal
> salt-cellar shines on a slender table.

The same author brings in Tigellius the singer, content with few things, speaking thus: <note>original: "1. Sat. 3. v. 13." Horace's Satires.</note>
> Let me have a three-legged table, and
> a shell of pure salt, and a toga that can
> ward off the cold, however coarse it may be.

The writer of Natural History <note>Likely referring to Pliny the Elder.</note>, while bringing an entire chapter on the types of salt, its preparations, and medicines into his thirty-first book, writes among other things: *By Hercules,* human life cannot be led more civilly without salt; and it is so necessary an element that the intellect transfers it even to the pleasures of the soul; for thus "salts" <note>original: "sales," meaning "wits" or "jokes."</note> are named, and all the charm of life and the highest

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Metallurgy.</margin>
merriment and rest from labors consists of no other word more than this. It is even interposed in military honors, from which "salaries" <note>original: "salariis," the origin of the English word salary.</note> are named, having great authority among the ancients, as appears from the name of the Salarian Way, because that was the route by which salt was accustomed to be carried to the Sabines. King Ancus Marcius gave six thousand measures of salt as a gift to the people and was the first to establish salt works. Varro also is the authority that the ancients used it in place of a side-dish; for salt existed with bread and cheese, as is apparent from the proverb. Regarding the proverb he mentions, it helps that it was once said *according to the proverb* <note>original: "κατὰ παροιμίαν"</note> that many bushels of salt must be eaten together so that men may know one another; *according to the proverb*, says Aristotle in his *Ethics to Nicomachus*, *it is not possible to know each other until the so-called salt is consumed together*; and it is from here that Cicero warns in *On Friendship* <note>original: "in Laelio"</note> that many bushels of salt must be eaten with one before the duty of friendship can be fulfilled or joined by the bond of friendship. We know from the Sacred Scriptures that the wife of Lot was changed into a pillar of salt, which some imagine happened because she refused to give salt to Lot when he asked for it to season food, as one who was averse to hospitality. In truth, not demonstrative but at least probable reasons are usually brought forward for this; for this woman had wisdom, of which Salt is the Symbol. Our sacred records <note>original: "Pandectae," a term for the Bible or legal codes, here used for Scripture.</note> teach us that this Wisdom consists mostly in believing and obeying; compare Nicolaus de Lyra's *Commentary on this place*. Nor is this reason so absurd, since from other parallel places, and likewise from many authorities and profane rites, it is sufficiently established that salt was held and used as a sign of Wisdom.

<margin>Matthew 5:13.</margin>
Christ, the very fountain of Wisdom, also seems to aim at this: <note>original: "ὑμεῖς ἐστὲ τὸ ἅλας τῆς γῆς"</note> *You are the salt of the earth*, so that the Disciples, whom He was addressing, might salt and season earthly men—who are referred to by the phrase *of the earth* by a metonymy of the container for the contents—as if with a certain salt, namely, the purity of heavenly doctrine and the praise of an innocent life. Furthermore, it is not our intention here to deal expressly with the transformation of Lot's wife into a statue of salt retaining a human figure, and that transformation being substantial; Josephus testifies that it still lasted and existed in his own time (*Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 1, Ch. 11), as does Justin (*History*, Book 36, Ch. 2). Nor is it contrary to the nature of salt to last for so many thousands of years. Posterity is rightly seized with admiration by what Petrus Petreius reports in the first part of his *History of Muscovy*: that two miles from Astrakhan, a city of Tartary, not far from the Volga River, at a place the inhabitants call *Basin*, they find such a great supply of snowy and marble-like salt that, although 3,000 men might cut masses of it daily, yet not even the smallest part of that immense mass would seem to be taken away; indeed, the more that is taken from the said salt, the greater the quantity that grows back, so that it suffices for the whole year for all the regions of the *Medes, Persians, Armenians, Tartars, and Russians*. Thus, even though salt is by nature liquid, this statue of Salt could be liquefied or disturbed by no rain nor any storm. Cyprian expressed this in a poem:

<margin>On Sodom, line 120.</margin>
> It still lasts indeed, standing bare under the air,
> neither dissolved by rains in its place, nor destroyed by winds.

Hence Borchardus <note>A 13th-century Dominican traveler.</note> testifies that this statue still existed in his own age, and Adrichomius <note>Christiaan van Adrichom (1533–1585), a Dutch priest and cartographer.</note> that it still 

<meta>The catchword "pereße" (remains) indicates the sentence continues on the next page: "remains today."</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Metallurgy.</margin> ...asserts that she remains. The Jerusalem Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> states that she will last until the day of the final judgment; *And so it happened,* it says, *that she became a pillar of salt lasting until the time of the resurrection, when the dead shall live again.* One might aptly apply to this pillar of salt the Epigram of Agathias concerning the legendary transformation of Niobe into stone, which Demetrius Triclinius also recorded in his *Scholarly Notes on Sophocles' Electra, p. 87.*

> This tomb within holds no corpse.
> This corpse without has no tomb.
> But it is itself both corpse and tomb for itself.
<note>original Greek: "Ο τύμβος οὗτος ἔνδον οὐκ ἔχει νέκυν. / Ο νεκρὸς οὗτος ἔκτος οὐκ ἔχει τάφον. / Ἀλλ’ αὐτὸς αὑτῷ νεκρός ἐστι καὶ τάφος."</note>

Regarding the more ignoble metals, such as *tin, lead*, etc., let it suffice to say a few things by way of a concluding flourish so that we do not skip over them. Tin, called <term>badil (בדיל)</term> in Hebrew from the word <term>badal (בדל)</term>, meaning *to separate*, because,

<margin>16 Orig. 22</margin> as I may explain the "separation" using Isidore's <note>Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century encyclopedist.</note> words, *it dissociates metals that have been mixed and adulterated with one another through fire.* Hence, as much as it favors lead, it is just as hostile to other metals, which it makes brittle; if bronze or silver is melted in a crucible where tin has been smelted, it suffers breakage, except for the purest gold, which rejects its power. Among the Greeks, it is called <term>kassiteron (κασσίτερον)</term>, as is clear from Homer's *Iliad* and elsewhere, from which miners get their term *Sitter* or *Zwitter*. It is mentioned twice in the Sacred Scriptures, in *Numbers 31:22* and *Ezekiel 27:12.* It is joined to lead by a singular friendship, even if it is surpassed by lead in weight; for its dryness almost prevents the same degree of condensation that occurs in the moisture of lead. Lead is called <term>molybdos (μόλυβδος)</term> by the Greeks and <term>opheret (עופרת)</term> by the Hebrews, from the word for "dust," because *whereas other metals*, as Gregorius Francus writes*

<margin>Ezekiel p. 338</margin> *are consumed and diminished by dust as long as they are in it, lead, on the contrary, gains something while it is in the dust;* a fact which experience abundantly confirms. Because of its density, it is adapted for various uses, wherefore a person is called "leaden" who pours out worthless and useless words, or who speaks without grace. Gillebertus says in *Sermon 15 on the Song of Songs: A leaden mouth is one that speaks nothing subtle, nothing sharp, nothing of heavenly things, but is entirely sluggish, entirely dull, perhaps entirely of the depths and of iniquity; for iniquity sits upon a talent of lead.* <note>A reference to the vision in Zechariah 5:7-8.</note> Meanwhile, it is marvelous that it wipes away the filth of gold, silver, and gems; it is also very easily joined with the rest, but while it cannot endure the power of the fire in the cupel <note>A small shallow vessel used in assaying or refining precious metals.</note> for long, it flies away, and at the same time carries off the filth of the others. The Greeks call this filth <term>skoria (σκωρίας)</term> <note>Dross or slag.</note>, from which the Latin *Scurra* <note>A buffoon or jester.</note> is derived, and both seem to descend from the Hebrew <term>sheqer (שקר)</term> <note>Meaning "lie" or "deception."</note>, which is somewhat evident from*

<margin>Psalm 119:119.</margin> clear. To the Hebrews, they are called <term>sig (סיג)</term>, whence the Lord’s complaint in *Ezekiel 22:18: The house of Israel has become <term>dross (לסיג)</term> to me; all of them are like bronze, tin, iron, and lead in the midst of the furnace.* Hence Alvarus Pelagius in *The Lament of the Church, book 2, fol. 27. b.* says these words: *Which literally today, alas, can be said of the Church; as if to say: I wished to purge them through the fire of tribulation and make them gold or silver; but they themselves have become bronze or tin, iron and lead, because they break out not into virtue but into vices during tribulation.* Therefore, one must buy gold, <term>gold refined by fire</term> <note>original Greek: "χρυσίον πεπυρωμένον ἐκ πυρὸς"</note>, that is, Spiritual Wisdom and piety perceived from the Word of God (*Psalm 12:7, 19:10, 119:127, 1 Peter 1:7, 1 Corinthians 1:5*) rather than lead, by which iniquity is prefigured in the woman sitting upon the lead (*Zechariah 5:7-8*) <note>The text incorrectly cites this as Ezekiel 5.</note>. It is better, therefore, as Augustine testifies *on Psalm 14, col. 1680, to have dirty gold than the most purified lead.* And so, as we began with gold, let us also end with gold, lest we conclude a noble beginning with an ignoble end, and it be said of us: *He begins in gold and ends in mud.*

### What are Helepolis engines?

**T**he **Helepolis** was an instrument most suitable for capturing and overturning town walls, named <term>from "taking the cities"</term> <note>original Greek: "ὡς τὸ ἑλεῖν τὰς πόλεις"</note>. Ammianus Marcellinus in *Book 23* describes it according to the usage of his age: *In place of battering rams, which were now viewed with suspicion because of their commonness, an engine known to historical writers was built, which the Greeks call the Helepolis: by the long-term use of which Demetrius, the son of Antigonus, was called "the Besieger" (Poliorcetes) after attacking Rhodes and other cities. It is built in this manner: A massive "tortoise" <note>A protective shed or cover.</note> is fastened together, strengthened with very long beams, and fitted with iron nails, and it is covered with ox hides and a fresh weaving of twigs, and its top is sprinkled with mud, so that it may deflect flaming and missile hits. On its front are attached three-pronged spikes, heavy with iron weights, such as painters show us for lightning bolts or sculptors for thunderbolts, so that whatever it strikes, it may break open with its protruding points. This powerful mass is steered with wheels and ropes by a numerous force of soldiers inside, and moved with swift strength against the weaker parts of the walls: and unless the strength of the defenders from above prevails, it opens huge breaches by smashing the walls.* Appianus in his *Mithridatic War* writes: <term>He raised many mounds, and fixed engines, towers, and ram-bearing tortoises, and a city-taker (helepolis) of a hundred cubits, from which another tower was raised, discharging catapults, stones, and various arrows.</term> Dionysius says of the year 293: <term>Neither tortoises (creepers), as men of that time did not know how to prepare them, nor those called "city-takers" (helepoles);</term> regarding which passage of Dionysius see <unclear>Zeium</unclear> in *Lipsius's Poliorcetica, Book 1, Dialogue 3, p. 13, 14.* By the Jews in the siege of Jerusalem, the largest Roman Helepolis was named <term>Nikon</term> <note>Conqueror</note>, <term>from "conquering everything,"</term> as Josephus relates in *Book 2*; where he also says, <term>it was called Nikon because the wall gave way to it.</term> Another passage concerning the engine from Athenaeus’s unpublished book on military engines is cited by Schott in *Observations, book 5, ch. 26, p. 238.*
