# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

### II. Maccabees III, 19.

<margin>The Women’s Quarters for Virgins.</margin> The Greeks were accustomed to call this the <term>parthenon</term> <note>original Greek: παρθενῶνα; a private chamber for unmarried women</note>, where they were kept under guard. From this practice, the Greeks called such women "enclosed" <note>original Greek: κατάκλειστοι; translit: katakleistoi</note>, and the Hebrews used a most elegant term in the same sense: <term>almot</term> <note>original Hebrew: עלמות</note>, meaning "the hidden ones," from the root <term>alam</term> <note>original Hebrew: עלם</note>, which means "to hide" or "to shut up." This was because they were essentially shut away in a "chamber" <note>original Greek: θαλάμῳ; translit: thalamō</note> before being joined to a husband. As the Poet of Ascra <note>Hesiod</note> said of such virgins:
> "She remains inside the halls with her dear mother,"
<note>original Greek: δόμων ἐντὸς ᾗ φίλῃ μητέρι μέμνει</note>

<margin>Hesiod, Works and Days, v. 518.</margin> so that they might not easily go out into public. Regarding this custom of hiding virgins, we consider the young woman in Isaiah 7:14 to be called in Hebrew <term>almah</term> <note>original Hebrew: עלמה</note>. Sebastian Verro, a Freiburg Papist, mocks us in his *Questions on the Word of God and Holy Scripture* (Question 18), saying that we interpret the Prophet Isaiah more like Jews than Christians. To him, we oppose the *Vocabulary for Preachers* published in Strasbourg in 1486, produced by the efforts of Master Jodocus Eychman of Calw, Professor of Sacred Literature at Heidelberg, and compiled and edited by Master Johannes Melber of <margin>B 2. b.</margin> Gerolzhofen. There it reads: *“Alma in Hebrew is said to mean ‘secret’ or ‘holy’ in Latin; an unknown virgin, a hidden virgin, who was never exposed to the sight of men, but covered herself everywhere with veils so that she would not be seen bare in the streets, and whom no man ever touched or truly saw.”* See also Casaubon, pp. 118–119; Barradius, *Harmony*, Vol. 1, Book 8, Ch. 6; Schindler’s *Lexicon*, p. 1329; Erasmus on Matthew 2, p. 10; and Drusius, *Parallels*, p. 79. Charming is the etymology provided by the *Etymologicum* <note>An ancient Greek dictionary</note> for the word "Mother" (<term>Mētēr</term>), which the author thinks is named <term>dia to mē tēreisthai</term> <note>original Greek: διὰ τὸ μὴ τηρεῖσθαι; because she is not guarded</note>. He says in column 584: *"For women, before they become mothers, are guarded so that their virginity is not defiled. But when they become mothers, they are no longer guarded."* The ancients took careful account of virgins—even the Latins, who did not wish them to be present at banquets where speech tends to be more unrestrained. Varro is a witness to this among the Latins, writing in his *Agatho* (p. 306): *"Let the virgin be led away from the banquet, because our ancestors did not want the ears of a ‘bitter’ virgin to be stained with the vocabulary of Venus"* <note>Venus here refers to love or sexual desire</note>. He elegantly uses the term "bitter virgin" <note>Latin: virgo acerba</note>, which the Greeks call <term>aōros</term> <note>original Greek: ἄωρος; unripened</note>—one who is "not yet of age for marriage" <note>original Greek: μὴ ὡραία γάμῳ</note>, or not yet ripe for a husband, a metaphor taken from unripe fruit. The same custom still holds in Italy, regarding which Erasmus says in *The Institution of Christian Marriage* (p. 575): *"Among the Italians, great care is taken to keep unmarried virgins at home; among the Venetians, if they happen to go out, they do not do so without a guardian, nor unless a veil covers the head down to the shoulders—you would say they were nuns."* Greek virgins and women were kept under even stricter guard than Roman ones; for the Romans were allowed to stay in the atrium of the house, but the Greeks were not. Aemilius Probus <note>Often identified with Cornelius Nepos</note> states this expressly in the Preface to his *Lives*: *"For which of the Romans is ashamed to lead his wife to a banquet? Or whose mistress of the house does not hold the first place in the home and move about in society? This is much different in Greece; for she is not invited to a banquet except those of relatives, nor does she sit anywhere but in the interior part of the house, which is called the Gynaeconitis."* The <term>gynaikōn</term> or <term>gynaikōnitis</term> was the part of the house where the women lived, just as the <term>andrōnitis</term> was where the men stayed separately. Hence, when Homer describes Penelope, the chaste wife of Ulysses, he never has her speak <margin>Odyssey, Book 1, v. 328.</margin> except from her chamber—which he calls the *upper room* <note>original Greek: ὑπερώϊον; translit: hyperōion</note>—with her face covered by a veil and leaning on her handmaidens:
> "From her upper chamber, the daughter of Icarius, 

<column-break/>

> wise Penelope, heard the divine song in her heart.
> She descended the high staircase of her home,
> not alone, for two handmaidens followed her.
> When this divine woman reached the suitors,
> she stood by the doorpost of the well-built hall,
> holding a glistening veil before her cheeks.
> A faithful handmaiden stood on either side of her."

<margin>The Women’s Quarters for Virgins.</margin> Diogenes discusses both chambers in the biography of the Cynic of the same name: *"He was returning from Lacedaemon [Sparta] to Athens. To one who asked, ‘Where to and from where?’ he replied, ‘From the men’s quarters to the women’s quarters.’"* And Xenophon in his *Oeconomicus*: *"They showed her the women’s quarters, separated from the men’s quarters by a bolted door."* The peoples of the East guarded their wives solicitously; for that reason, they added castrated servants to the women’s quarters, whom they called by the common name "Eunuchs," as Lucian testifies in *The Images* (p. 284). They rarely appeared in public, and if they did, it was with their faces covered. Thus, we read of Susanna in the Apocrypha that she went out covered with a veil, hiding her face out of modesty, veiling her beauty with a chaste countenance. Regarding this veil, Tertullian says: <margin>On the Soldier's Crown, ch. 4.</margin> *"If Susanna, having been unveiled at her trial, was more beautiful when veiled, then here the veil was a matter of choice. She had come as a defendant, blushing at her own infamy, rightly hiding her beauty, perhaps because she feared to please any longer."* Otherwise, I do not think she would have walked veiled in her husband's garden, where she was already pleasing. And Ambrose in Book 1 of *On Offices* (ch. 18): *"Susanna shunned the gaze of men. For there is modesty even in the eyes, such that she wished neither to see men nor be seen by them."* To these may be added Diego de Celada in his *Commentary on Susanna* (p. 672): *"Susanna is not veiled by the shame of a crime she did not know; but out of a devotion to modesty, which she always cultivated. The face of chaste Susanna is beautifully flooded with a blush, and being adorned with the color of virtue, she refutes the foul crime cast against her better than if she had used words. The innocent modesty of Susanna is much more to be praised."* Even today, the names of women in the East are known, but their faces are unknown because of the veiled face. They observe this custom of veiling the face so strictly that they would sooner allow themselves to be prostituted than permit their faces to be uncovered. For when Vartomanus <note>Lodovico de Varthema, a 16th-century traveler</note> tells of the lust of the Mamluks, <margin>Book 1, Voyage 7, p. 192.</margin> which they sometimes exercise upon the women of Damascus, using them licentiously, even when the Mamluks try to uncover their foreheads (*for they walk with veiled faces*), the women resist with all their might, not wishing to be recognized. *"The Mamluks insist more boldly, asserting with their usual petulance that they want to uncover them. But the women say: 'Is it not enough and more that you have disgraced our bodies and used them for your pleasure, unless you also uncover our foreheads?' Then the Mamluks let them go."* Regarding the women of the island of Yucatan, Peter Martyr records in his book *On the Recently Discovered Islands* (p. 550), describing their dress in these words: *"The women are clothed from the waist to the ankle, and they cover their heads and breasts with various veils, and modestly take care that neither foot nor leg is seen by them."* However, this veiling of virgins did not prevail everywhere on earth. Among the Spartans, married women indeed covered themselves so as not to please others, but the virgins still walked with open faces, so they might more easily find a husband. Thus, among the Lombards, it was a mark of maidenhood to walk with the head not veiled, which they themselves called being "in the hair" <note>Latin: in capillo</note>, and this was for the sake of speeding along a marriage. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>The Women’s Quarters for Virgins.</margin> For the Hebrews greatly cherished marriage and sought out virgins early for the sake of propagating their lineage. Likewise, the Pagans <note>literally "the Ethnicis"</note> also desired marriage rather than lifelong virginity. Thus, Hecuba's daughter in 
<margin>Euripides, *Hecuba*, line 417.</margin>
Euripides* laments that she must die without having known marriage:
> Unwedded, without a bridal song, deprived of what I should have had.
<note>original Greek: Ἄνυμφον, ἀνυμέναιον, ὧν ἐχρῆν τυχεῖν.</note>

In the same way, Electra laments in Sophocles, line 960:
> A painful old age is at hand, during which 
> time they grow old without a marriage bed or a wedding song.
<note>original Greek: Πάρεσι δ' ἀλγεινὸν τὸ γῆρας, ᾧ χρόνῳ ἄλεκτρα γηράσκουσιν, ἀνυμέναιά τε;</note>

For this reason, when a virgin emerged from her <term>Parthenon</term> <note>the private maiden's quarters</note> into the open for her nuptials, presenting herself to the eyes of her groom with a joyful and open face, she was said to "unveil herself" <note>original Greek: ἀνακαλύπτει</note>. From this comes the term <term>anakalypteria</term> <note>unveiling gifts</note>, mentioned by Philostratus and noted by Rhodiginus in his *Ancient Readings* (Book 11, chapter 59, p. 599). These were the gifts contributed by the husband, his household, and his friends when the bride first revealed herself to be seen. And since virginity is the best "unmarried treasure" <note>original Greek: ἀγὰμα</note> of a woman, careful guarding of a virgin ripe for a husband is not criticized. For having reached this age, she begins to "ripen" <note>original Greek: ὀργᾶν</note>, to use the common Greek term. If that "ripening" <note>original Greek: ὀργασμὸς</note> presses upon her, then celebrate the rites <note>a play on the word "Orgia"</note> of marriage with your daughter. "If you are a virgin," says Jerome*, 
<margin>Epistle 47, column 296.</margin>
"why do you fear careful guarding? If you are already corrupted, why do you not marry openly?" Jerome is a biting Patron of Virgins; even as he speaks of the "corrupted," he speaks bluntly, for though he was a monk and a priest, he was not ignorant of the minds of most young women. His remarks on the virgin who hides her love at home or feigns it are quite festive (*Epistle 47, column 298*): "A lustful mind pursues 'honorable' things more ardently, and suspects that what is forbidden is sweeter. The very garment—cheap and dark—is a sign of a silent mind, provided it has no wrinkles, and does not trail on the ground to make you seem taller, and if the tunic is ripped on purpose to both open and hide what is foul, while revealing what is beautiful. Even the black and shiny boot of the walking girl calls out to young men with its creaking. The breasts are squeezed by bandages, and the chest is narrowed by a rippling belt. Hair falls either over the forehead or the ears. The small shawl sometimes falls so as to bare white shoulders, and as if she wished to be seen, she hurriedly hides what she had intentionally uncovered. And when she covers her face in public as if out of shame, she uses the art of the brothel to show only that which, when shown, might please more." He likewise argues in his *Epistle to Demetrias* (column 76) that a virgin should avoid "dandyish" boys with curled hair and skins smelling of foreign customs—about whom Petronius Arbiter said: *He does not smell good, who always smells good*—as if they were certain plagues and poisons to modesty. For virginity is a tender thing, not unlike a milky rose, which loses something of its natural grace even with a light breeze. Thus, Bernard*:
<margin>Homily 3, in praise of Mary, p. 36. I.</margin>
"Virgins who are truly virgins are always fearful and never secure; to be careful through fear, they dread even what is safe, knowing that they carry a precious treasure in earthen vessels." Thus Jerome advises in his *Epistle to Gaudentius* (column 116) that the female sex should be joined only to its own sex; she should not know, or rather, should fear playing with boys. She should never see young men, never see those with curled hair. They advise the virgin to stay within her mother's house; she ought not to be seen outside it unless the occasion demands it, which is why she is often represented by the image of a tortoise carrying its little house <note>original Greek: οἰκίσκου</note>.

<column-break/>

This is the image of the modest virgin, a type about which Dionysius Fauchitus (p. 408) wrote:
> The tortoise bears the mark of virginal modesty,
> While the cause of her shame lies hidden in its hard shell.

Among the precepts of Phocylides is this: to guard a virgin diligently in the "inner chamber" <note>original Greek: θαλάμῳ</note> or, as Homer says, in the "recesses of the halls" <note>original Greek: μυχῷ δόμων</note>, lest she be seen outside until her wedding day (line 213):
> Guard the maidens in well-locked chambers.
> Nor let them be seen before the house until the wedding.
<note>original Greek: Παρθενικὰς δὲ φύλασσε πολυκλείστοις θαλάμοις. Μηδέ μιν ἄχρι γάμων πρὸ δόμων ὀφθῆναι ἐάσης.</note>

The Poet calls this the <term>thalamon</term>, following Homer, as the place where virgins hid before the time of marriage while waiting for a husband. For this reason, they were called "awaiting men" <note>original Greek: μενάνδρους</note> and "chambered ones" <note>original Greek: θαλαμευομένας</note>, as well as "low-voiced" or "enclosed" <note>original Greek: ὑποκωφους ἢ κατακλείστους</note> from their hiding places. Melanchthon—the author of our German version of the Maccabees and the Zurich Bible—translates this as *those who do not go among people / who are guarded within*. From this you will understand Theocritus, who in *Idyll 2*, line 136, calls an untouched and pure virgin "a virgin in the chamber" <note>original Greek: παρθένον ἐν θαλάμῳ</note>, one who was still hidden and guarded in her father's house. Danaë, the daughter of Acrisius, King of the Argives, was handed over by her father's command to be guarded in an "enclosed women's quarter" <note>original Greek: gynæceo ἐγκατακλείστῳ</note> so that she might not come into the sight of men; of her, Euripides* says:
> In the maiden-quarters which he had built,
> He gave her to the Argive girls to guard,
> Taking care lest she come into the sight of a man.
<note>original Greek: Ἐν παρθενῶσι δ' εὐθὺς, οἷσιν ἐδείματο, Δίδωσιν Ἀργείασιν ἐν φρουρᾷ κόραις, Εἰς ἀνδρὸς ὄψιν εὐλαβώμενον μολεῖν.</note>

And later in line 58:
> But the father, having locked her up,
> Guards her body with seals in the maiden-quarters.
<note>original Greek: Πατὴρ δέ μιν κλήας Ἐν παρθενῶσι σφραγῖσι δέμας φυλάσσει.</note>

Horace calls Danaë "the girl enclosed in a tower" and "the hidden virgin" (*Odes*, Book 3, 16, line 1 and following):
> The bronze tower, the sturdy doors,
> And the grim watch of wakeful dogs
> Had sufficiently fortified the enclosed Danaë
> Against nocturnal adulterers;
> Had not Jupiter and Venus laughed at Acrisius,
> The fearful guardian of the hidden virgin;
> For the way would be safe and open
> Once the God turned himself into a bribe.
> Gold loves to pass through the midst of guards,
> And to break through rocks, more powerful
> Than a thunderbolt's strike.

The Poet refers to the myth where it is recounted that Jupiter, poured into the Virgin’s lap as a golden shower, defiled her. This signifies that even the best-guarded modesty can be violated by gold. Hesiod describes a chaste virgin (*Works and Days*, Book 2, line 10):
> She who remains inside the house beside her dear mother,
> Not yet knowing the works of golden Aphrodite.
<note>original Greek: Ἥτε δόμων ἔντοσθε φíλη παρὰ μητέρι μίμνει, οὔπω ἔργ' εἰδυῖα πολυχρύσου Ἀφροδíτης.</note>

Thus in Euripides, the Tutor addresses Antigone in *The Phoenician Women* (line 187):
> O child, enter the house, and within the roof
> Remain in your maiden-quarters, since you have had
> Your fill of the pleasure of looking.
<note>original Greek: ὦ τέκνον εἴσβα δῶμα, καὶ κατὰ στέγας ἐν παρθενῶσι μεῖνε σοῖς, ἐπεὶ πόθου εἰς τέρψιν ἦλθες.</note>

Later Antigone herself, when her mother Jocasta says "Go!", responds (line 263): "Where? Leaving the maiden-quarters?" On account of this discipline of the Ancients, Clytemnestra sharply rebukes her daughter Electra in Seneca's *Agamemnon* (line 950): "By what custom do you, a virgin, seek public places? Who would believe you are a virgin?" She refers to her wandering outside, for it was considered a vice for girls to go out, which Euripides also teaches in *Orestes* (line 108).

<summary>This page explores the ancient practice of secluding virgins in private quarters (the Gynaeceum or Parthenon) to preserve their modesty and value for marriage. It draws upon a wide range of classical Greek poets and early Church Fathers to illustrate the cultural emphasis on female enclosure and the symbolic "unveiling" at the wedding.</summary>
<keywords>Gynaeceum, Parthenon, virginity, modesty, marriage customs, Danaë, St. Jerome, seclusion of women, classical antiquity, unveiling, bridal gifts</keywords>

## 2 Maccabees 3:19

<margin>The Virgins' Quarters.</margin>
"It is not honorable for virgins to creep into a crowd." 
<margin>in *Anthology*, p. 465.</margin>
<note>original Greek: εἰς ὄχλον ἔρπειν παρθένοισιν οὐ καλόν.</note>
Thus, among the ancients, the sight of women and virgins in public was rare, and if they were seen, it was with a covered face. Agathias introduces girls complaining about this severity: 
"It is not lawful for us even to look upon the light, but we are hidden in the halls, wasting away with gloomy anxieties." 
<note>original Greek: Ἡμῖν δ' οὐδὲ φάος λεύσσειν θέμις, ἀλλὰ μελάθροις Κρυπτόμεθα, ζοφεραῖς φροντίσι τηκόμεναι.</note>
->Which P. Melissus renders into Latin:<-
> "But for us, we may not enjoy the light; left behind
> hidden in enclosures, alas, a poor little crowd with black cares."

Phidias's statue of Venus at Elis alluded to this <term>oikouria</term> <note>home-keeping or domesticity</note> by placing a tortoise under her feet, so that by that sign they might be warned that women must live at home. Plutarch’s precept in *On the Precepts of Marriage* (p. 142) should also be applied to virgins: "Phidias made the Aphrodite of the Eleans treading on a tortoise, a symbol of domesticity and silence for women." <note>original Greek: τὴν ἡλείων ὁ Φειδίας Ἀφροδίτην ἐποίησε χελώνην πατέων, οἰκουρίας σύμβολον ταῖς γυναιξὶ καὶ σιωπῆς.</note> Thus it is rightly considered a vice if they run about from house to house and set up I-know-not-what gatherings, upon whom mothers should impress that line of Hesiod (Book I, v. 363): 
"It is better to be at home, since staying outdoors is harmful."
<note>original Greek: Οἴκοι βέλτερον εἶναι, ἐπεὶ βλαβερὸν τὸ θύρηφι.</note>
We know how poorly the wandering of Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, turned out, which example should be carefully noted by roaming virgins. There is also that common proverb of our people: *A hen and a woman, if they wander far from home, easily go astray.* This can be seen in the Sabine virgins, who went to the Roman spectacles and were changed from virgins into matrons <note>a reference to the legendary Rape of the Sabine Women</note>. A modest virgin has her eyes and feet at home, and when she goes out, she keeps her eyes cast down to the ground. An immodest one, however, knows no rest and turns now here, now there, like that harlot in the sacred Proverbs; as Plautus says in *The Merchant*, she can never rest well, "whose soul is outdoors when she is at home, and when she is outdoors, her soul is at home." For this reason, the Chaldeans call a harlot *napka* <note>original: נפקא</note>, from *napaka* meaning "to go out" or "to come forth," since her feet do not stay at home (as Solomon says), but she seeks her lust by wandering. You might call them "virgins who are not virgins" (to use Horace’s phrasing), like the one in Dionysius of Halicarnassus who was killed by her brother for having gone out of the house indecently and against custom. In most Eastern places, that <term>katakleismos</term> <note>seclusion or shutting-in</note> still holds today, as various travel journals report. In the previous century, Bernhard von Breydenbach, Dean of the Mainz Chapter, undertook a journey to Palestine and described the customs among the Syrians (as they were called) in these words (f. 129. b.): 

*Their housewives guard and shut them in with great diligence, and allow neither wives nor daughters to go into the streets except surrounded by sheets and their faces covered with a black cloth. The virgins among them observe this so strictly that even the men to whom they are betrothed may not see their faces until the first night after they have been laid together. The Saracen virgins do the same, following the example (as they say) of the Patriarch Jacob, who thought he had lain the first night with Rachel, his beloved.*

I remember reading about this severe custom of bringing a bride of unknown desire <note>i.e., whose face has not been seen</note> in the *Persian Journey* of Adam Olearius. The meaning of that passage from the books of the Maccabees, concerning virgins shut up in their parents' houses, is now easily understood. Those virgins, when Heliodorus had entered the city to plunder the temple treasures, forgot

<column-break/>

the virginal custom. Leaving the women's chambers, some ran together to the vestibules and gates, others to the walls, and some looked out through windows with necks craned, surely astonished by the novelty of the event. As the author of the *Ordinary Gloss* rightly wrote: "The virgins who were shut in—that is, they did not leave their parents' houses for the sake of virginal shame and modesty—nevertheless in that disturbance went out contrary to their usual custom." 

It is therefore all the more surprising that some learned men, "instead of pearls, offer trifles" <note>original Greek: ἀντὶ πηρῶν λεπτολογήματα</note>, trying to thrust upon us the idea of "vowed virgins" (whom they call nuns) and comparing them to the Athenian virgins consecrated to *Artemis Munichia* for service. These were called "bears" <note>original: ἄρκτοι</note> and "those acting as bears" <note>original: ἀρκτευόμεναι</note>, and hence the "bear-rite" <note>original: ἀρκτεία</note> or the ceremony of the virgins acting as bears (concerning which see Justin, *Parergon* 1. 25). Isaac Casaubon, in his work against Baronius (*Exercise* 1. n. 53. p. 87. 88.), rightly showed that these were <term>katakleistous</term> <note>shut-in</note> virgins bound by a vow in a certain sacred ministry. I add more regarding that maidenly domesticity from Montague (*Apparatus* 9, *Ecclesiastical Origins* n. 21, p. 322), Hugo Grotius (*Annotations on the Gospels* at Matt. 1:23, p. 26), Spanheim (*Evangelical Doubts*, p. 298), Dausquejus (*On Calaber* lib. 12, p. 242), Gebhard (*Crepundia* 3, 15), and Heinsius (*Readings in Theocritus* c. 6, p. 314).

Just as it befits virgins to "stay inside" <note>original Greek: ἔνδον μένειν</note>, so also it befits matrons hidden at home to protect their modest shelter, as Macrobius rightly advises. Euripides teaches this with a notable testimony in *Iphigenia* (v. 477):
"For a woman, silence and sobriety 
Are most beautiful, and to remain quietly within the house."
<note>original Greek: Γυναικὶ γὰρ σιγή τε καὶ τὸ σωφρονεῖν Κάλλιστον, εἴσω θ' ἥσυχον μένειν δόμων.</note>
Most duties of women are *within the roof* and *at the hearth*, for it befits men to care for those businesses that are *at the forum*. For this reason, they were called by the Latins *cesaria* <note>meaning unknown, likely "house-cut"</note> and *focaria* <note>hearth-keepers</note>, as noted by Rolbagius. 
<margin>* *On the Certainty of the Masculine Family*, c. 26 p. 248.</margin>
The Greeks call them "house-helpers" <note>original: οἰκωφελεῖς</note> and "domestic ones" <note>original: οἰκουρικοὶ</note>, for the virtues of Matrons are to guard the house, administer the family property, and to know nothing beyond the linen and the distaff. Homer calls this "to increase the household" (*Odyssey* 20.21), "to care for the home" (*Odyssey* 16.74), and "to guard all things steadfastly" (*Odyssey* 11.176). Hence <term>oikouros</term> <note>stay-at-home</note> is a special epithet given to a wife in Titus 2:5, and she is best described by Solomon in *Proverbs 31*: that she rises in the night (v. 15), considers a field (v. 16), seeks wool and flax (v. 13), applies her hands to the distaff (v. 19), and considers the state of her household (v. 27). This domesticity is also commended by Orestes in Libanius the Sophist’s *Declamation*, as he says farewell to his wife: "You are the house, and the faithful guardian of the home." 

The great praise of the Shunammite woman in 2 Kings 4:13 is that she is "resting in her house" <note>original Greek: οἴκῳ ἡσυχάζουσαν</note> (as it is in the Greek), keeping herself within the walls, and having no business with anyone outside, whether in the court or in the forum. Among the Greeks, there is the famous saying of that wrinkled creature <note>the tortoise</note>: "Home is dear, home is best," which Cercides recites in his iambics in Stobaeus (*Sermon* 56, n. 224) and Aesop in *Fable 105*. Therefore, a good mother of a family is likened to a vine, which "bears fruit on the sides of the house" (Psalm 128:3). Catullus also uses this simile, but for the man, when describing the nuptials of Julia and Manlius, saying (v. 106):
> "Just as the slow vine entwines
> the trees planted near it,
> so will she be entwined
> in your embrace."
On shut-in virgins, see Jerome, Vol. 2, Book 1.

<summary>This page explores the ancient and cultural mandate for virgins and matrons to remain secluded within the home (oikouria), using the tortoise as a symbol of domesticity. It contextualizes the panic of Jerusalem's virgins during Heliodorus' raid in 2 Maccabees as a rare and shocking breach of this social norm.</summary>

BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
<page-num>766</page-num>

<margin>The Quarters of the Virgins.</margin> Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, col. 54. Radbertus on *Matthew*, col. 108. Lavater on *Esther*, p. 696. Rivetus, *Apology for Mary*, p. 73. Salmasius on *Pollux*, p. 177. Heinsius, *Notes on Hesiod*, p. 292. Fusselius, *Sacred Adversaria*, book 2, p. 134. Barthius, *Adversaria*, p. 1866.

### 2 Maccabees 4:19

"The wicked Jason sent spectators from Jerusalem, as if they were citizens of Antioch, carrying three hundred silver drachmas for the sacrifice of Hercules."
<note>original Greek: Ἀπέστειλεν Ἰάσων ὁ μιαρὸς θεωρὸς ὡς ἀπὸ Ἱεροσολύμων Ἀντιοχεῖς ὄντας, παρακομίζοντας ἀργυρίου δραχμὰς τριακοσίας εἰς τὴν τοῦ Ἡρακλέους θυσίαν.</note>

*The wicked Jason sent spectators from Jerusalem, as if they were Antiochenes, three hundred silver drachmas for the sacrifice of Hercules.*

<margin>Hercules worshiped by the Tyrians.</margin> There was altogether a great confusion of religion during the time of the Maccabean leadership, such that it seems to have merged Judaism and Paganism, if we examine the books of the Maccabees. One may read in Chapter 4 of the second book how violently the <term>Pseudo-Pontiff</term> <note>Jason, a Hellenizing usurper who bought the High Priesthood</note> Jason raged against the Church. He bought the High Priesthood with gold, deposed his brother Onias from the office, defected to the pagan religion, observed Gentile rites, and introduced all the impiety of the pagans into the Jewish Commonwealth. He employed every fraud and crime to drag the people along with him into these impious sacred rites. For as soon as he was elevated to the throne of the High Priest with the consent of King Antiochus, he thought he could give no greater sign of his affection for the King than by accustoming his people to the rites of the Gentiles (v. 10). The piety and care he owed to his own most illustrious order he instead withdrew, and he introduced a new form of superstition toward which the common people, through the iniquity of the times, were already strongly inclined. He removed and abolished the pious institutions, sacred rites, and honorable exercises that had been established by the ancient Kings, and began to substitute perverse Gentile institutions against the laws of the fatherland (v. 11). A certain powerful man named John, the father of Eupolemus (who was later sent to Rome by Judas Maccabeus to make a treaty with the Romans), was a not unwilling spectator of this tragedy (v. 11 and 1 Maccabees 8:17); with his support and counsel, Jason managed his affairs more successfully, in which nothing was so necessary as craftiness and schemes. This Ecebolus <note>a nickname meaning "fickle" or "changeable," often applied to political turncoats</note> took up this part of the labor as eagerly as he administered it maliciously and swiftly. The princes and leaders, who by their example and authority ought to have deterred and pulled others away from illicit worship, were the first and foremost to fail in this kind of impiety; as it must be said here, what Ezra said regarding the sin of the Israelite people contracting marriages with pagan women: <margin>Ezra 9:2.</margin> *The hand of the princes and magistrates was first or chief in this transgression.* By this very fact, pagan impiety grew strong (v. 11), so much so that the priests themselves, despising the temple, eagerly joined themselves to foreign sacrifices and institutions (v. 14). How could such a sudden banishment of ancestral religion fall upon the heights of the faith? Those who should have been the supporters of a fleeing faith and the preservers of a sickening one, forgetting their order, hurried to the theaters to be 

<column-break/>

participants in the <term>palaestra</term> <note>a Greek wrestling school or gym</note>, whether to perform or to watch: and also to share in the distribution of the prizes which were usually given and paid out to the victors in those games and contests. Those whose duty it was to have a familiarity with God and divine matters instead spent their time on games and other worldly delights. They held ancestral honors as nothing, but considered Greek glories to be the best (v. 15). Because among the vain Gentiles these were considered among the "goods of glory"—such as the Isthmian, Pythian, and other types of contests—they numbered them among the splendors. And from this source, those contentions with which they pursued divine institutions flowed like channeled streams into the minds of the common people. From this came the institution of training with the discus (v. 14), the <term>ephebia</term> <note>youth military/athletic training</note> and other <term>gymnasmatas</term> <note>exercises</note> (v. 12). For that impious Priest, the iniquity was greatest: he did not hesitate, when the five-year games were celebrated at Tyre, to send three hundred silver drachmas for the sacrifice of Hercules, to buy victims to be offered to Hercules (v. 18, 19, 20). But those who went on the embassy to fulfill the vows to the Tyrian "god-ling," entreated the King that this money not be spent on sacrifice, because it would not be proper, but that it be assigned to other expenses (v. 19). The King granted this just petition and ordered it to be spent on the construction of <term>triremes</term> <note>ancient warships with three banks of oars</note> (v. 20). Those religious envoys are called <term>Theoroi</term> <note>original Greek: Θεωροὶ - official state observers of festivals or oracles</note>, whose selection was to be observed with singular sacred care to consult oracles. In the old Latin version, we mistakenly read "Sinners" [*Peccatores*] instead of "Spectators." There was a very ancient temple of Hercules at Tyre, of which Herodotus says he saw a shrine of Hercules at Tyre richly furnished; in it, he says, "were two pillars, one of refined gold, the other of emerald stone shining greatly at night." And Arrian in Book 2: "For there is in Tyre a temple of Hercules, the oldest of which human memory is preserved." Lucian, in *On the Syrian Goddess*: "Tyre had a temple of Hercules... not the Hercules whom the Greeks sing of, but as I say, one much older, the Tyrian Hercules." His surname was Desanaus, if the writing in Eusebius does not deceive, whose words in the *Chronicles* (no. 137) state: "Hercules, surnamed Desanaus, is held famous in Phoenicia." From which even to our memory he is still called Desanaus by the Cappadocians and Elians. Where this name is derived from is unknown. For the conjectures Vossius has about it, see volume 1, *On Idolatry*, 22, p. 168-169. Hercules was also worshiped to excess in Sidon, as Strabo witnesses in Book 16. He was also worshiped in Amathus, a city of Phoenicia. Hence Hesychius: "The Amathusians call Hercules *Malica*." That word *Malica* is to be explained from the Phoenician language, which differs from Hebrew only by dialect. <note>original Hebrew: מלך</note> *Melek* means King, from which the Amathusians said *Malica*. Sanchoniathon (who wrote the history of the Phoenicians in the Phoenician language, and whom Philo of Byblos translated into Greek and Eusebius preserved for us, decorating the first book of his *Preparation for the Gospel* from that treatise) reports among the gods the Phoenicians made, he includes Hercules, who was called *Melicarthus*. <note>original Greek: Μελιχάρϑος</note> Eudoxius of Cnidus reports that the whole world sacrificed to him. That word is composed of <note>original Hebrew: מלך</note> *Melek* (King) and <note>original Hebrew: קרת</note> *Qeret* (City); so that he is the "tutelary god of the city." Unless one derives it, with Selden, from *Artes* (as Mars was called by the Egyptians). Alexander the Great wished to honor this tutelary god of the Tyrians, whom he had begun...

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence with the catchword "fasti," indicating the next page likely continues the discussion of Alexander the Great's interaction with the Tyrian cult of Hercules/Melqart.</meta>

<summary>This page details the Hellenization of Judea under the usurping High Priest Jason, specifically his attempt to fund sacrifices to the Tyrian Hercules during the quinquennial games, and discusses the Phoenician origins of the deity Melqart.</summary>

--- Page 891 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Hellenization of Judea under the usurper High Priest Jason, specifically elaborating on the cult of the Tyrian Hercules mentioned in 2 Maccabees 4:19. It traces the spread of this deity's worship through Phoenician colonies like Gades (modern Cádiz) and analyzes the various historical and mythological identities attributed to Hercules.</meta>

<header>2 Maccabees 4:19</header>

<margin>
Hercules worshiped by the Tyrians.
</margin>
...they arrogantly refused to admit him <note>Alexander the Great, who wished to sacrifice to the Tyrian Hercules</note>, which resulted in great loss for them. Arrian reports this in the same place. The people of Gades—for the Strait of Gades <note>the Strait of Gibraltar</note> is named after the Phoenician Hercules because he was sent there, and it is said he led a colony to the island of Gades and neighboring Spain, according to Vossius in *On Idolatry*, book 2, chapter 69—were Phoenician colonists. For Gades was their colony, as found in Strabo book 3, Velleius book 1, Plutarch in *Scipio*, and others. The sacred rites of the Tyrian Hercules were also transferred to this colony. Justin says the same in <margin>book 44.</margin> *When the people of Gades, having come from Tyre (from where the Carthaginians also originate), were commanded in a vision during their rest to transfer the sacred rites of Hercules to Spain and had founded a city there, the neighboring peoples, being envious of the new city and harassing the Gaditanians with war, sent for help from their Carthaginian kinsmen.* To the Tyrians, therefore, Hercules was the most accepted divinity, because they lived upon the waters with a "Herculean" spirit, caring little for other, milder gods. Nor did they recommend any other worship to the Carthaginians, their colonists, as can be seen in Reinefius' *On the Punic Language*, chapter 2, number 9. These people also, as colonists of the Tyrians, worshiped this Tyrian divinity and sent him a tenth of their produce, as Diodorus reports in book 10. For this reason, they sent Cartalo to Tyre to bring the tithes to Hercules from the Sicilian booty captured by his father Malchus, according to Justin, book 18. As for the people of Gades, their naming is Phoenician. *Gadir* is a Punic word,

*For the Carthaginian calls a place Gadir which is "fenced" everywhere,*
according to the testimony of Avienus. Hesychius says: *Gadeira* <note>Greek: Γάδειρα</note>, the fences of the Phoenicians. Solinus in chapter 26 says: *The Carthaginians in their own language called it Gadir, that is, a hedge.* And Procopius in *The Vandal War* says: *It was called "the Enclosure" [Septum] by the Romans.* However, he errs in explaining it from the Greek word for "seven" <note>Greek: ἑπτὰ (hepta)</note>. So Pliny in book 4, chapter 22 says: *The Carthaginians call it Gadir, which in the Punic language signifies a hedge.* For it is the Hebrew word *Gader* <note>Hebrew: גדר</note>, the feminine form of which is *Gederah* <note>Hebrew: גדרה</note>, meaning an "enclosure" for the Hebrews; from this the Carthaginians named it, because it would be a fortification against the Spaniards. The worship of Hercules was introduced into Gades and the neighboring islands by the leader of that colony, whom Mela says is buried at Gades. Pliny reports in book 26, chapter 5, that he was worshiped with human sacrifices. Just as there was not only one Hercules, so there was not just one form of worship, but a variation of cults according to the variety of regions. The Greeks were quite ambitious in citing the antiquity of their own race. How many Hercules figures they chatter about! How many brave deeds at Troy they enumerate! What fables they tell about the voyages of the Argonauts! Greece here is trifling and wordy through its peddling poets, diligently seizing every opportunity to boast about these kinds of antiquities. There was a place sacred to Hercules among the Athenians which they called *Kynosarges* <note>Greek: Κυνόσαργας</note>, the reasoning for which name Meursius notes from Pausanias and other Greeks in *Athenian Attica*, book 2, chapter 2. Regarding "Musical Hercules" who dwells with the Muses, see Passeratius on Propertius' *Elegies*, book 4, poem 10, page 684; not to mention anything now of Hercules as the "Guardian of Boundaries," from whom people promised themselves the protection of their border-houses.
<margin>book 3.</margin> Diodorus discusses three Hercules figures: namely, the Egyptian, the Cretan, and the Theban. Cicero lists six in *On the Nature of the Gods*, and Arnobius in book 4. Varro, however, numbered forty-three Hercules figures. Many writers mix them up and confuse them into one, so that you can hardly tell them apart. The Theban Hercules is

<column-break/>

celebrated by everyone. The Egyptian Hercules make their own Hercules older than him, and Diodorus reports in book 5, page 236, that his most famous deeds and honors remain among the Tyrians as the *most ancient God in Egypt* <note>Greek: παλαιστέρῳ Θεῷ κατὰ τὴν Αἴγυπτον πράξεις τε καὶ τιμάς ἐπιφανεστάτας διαμένειν</note>, and that a city was founded by him. In Rome, the "Greatest Altar" <note>Ara Maxima</note> was built to Hercules, which Virgil mentions:
->He established this altar in the grove, which will always be called "Greatest"<-
->by us, and will always be the Greatest.<-
Lucian described the "Gallic Hercules" in a festive dialogue, which appears in Gyraldus, page 9. Plautus celebrates the fabulous birth of Hercules in his play *Amphitryon*. He is imagined as the son of Jupiter and Alcmene, who was married to Amphitryon, the son of Alcaeus—who was also called *Alkaius*—hence Hercules was called *Alcides* <note>Greek: Ἀλκείδης</note>. To others, however, he was born of Jupiter and Juno, whence he was also named *Heracles* <note>Greek: ἡρακλῆς</note> from *Hera* <note>Juno</note> and *kleos* <note>glory</note>, because his glory would proceed from Juno; or, as the mythologist Natalis Comes says in *Mythology*, book 7, chapter 1, because he was to become glorious due to the hatred of Juno. Macrobius provides the former etymology in <margin>Saturnalia, book 1, chapter 20</margin> and refers those things which the poets invent about Hercules to the Sun and the measurement of time. In Rome, Hercules was worshiped with various surnames and honors. Fabius dedicated his statue, brought from Tarentum, on the Capitol; compare Victor, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 43, page 332. A very elegant statue of him, crafted by the hand of the most skilled Glycon of Athens, exists in Rome; it was found in the ruins of the Baths of Caracalla <note>Latin: *thermarum Antoninianarum*</note> under Pope Paul III and placed in the inner portico of the Farnese House at the Campo de' Fiori. Antonio Lafreri of Sequanus produced bronze prints of it in the year 1562, and it appears in the *Mirror of Roman Magnificence*, number 26. On it, at the feet of Hercules, it is written:
->GLYCON THE ATHENIAN MADE THIS<- <note>Greek: ΓΛΥΚΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ ΕΠΟΙΕΙ</note>
Among the Sabines, Hercules was known by the name Sancus, and *Deus Fidius* <note>God of Faith/Oaths</note>, which Fulvius Ursinus discusses from Dionysius and an ancient inscription from Rieti in *On Roman Families*, page 290. But we return to the sacred rites of the Roman Hercules. Evander was the first to establish an altar—the one mentioned above—to Hercules near the Cattle Market <note>Latin: *forum boarium*</note>, according to Dionysius in *Antiquities*, book 1, where a temple was also dedicated to him under the name of "Hercules the Victor," as was another at the Triple Gate <note>Porta Trigemina</note>. The Tyrian Hercules seems to be none other than Joshua, for the things reported about him can be seen in the deeds of Joshua, as Vossius shows in *On Idolatry*, book 1, chapter 26, page 194; and thus, through the Devil’s work, the Tyrians transfer those things read in the Holy Scriptures <note>Latin: *S. Pandectis*</note> concerning Joshua to their own Hercules. Hugo Sanford proves this perversity <note>Greek: κακοζηλίαν, literally "malicious imitation"</note> with many examples in book 1 of *On the Descent of Christ into Hell*. To put a finishing touch <note>Greek: κολοφῶνα</note> to the sacred rites dedicated to Hercules, we conclude with the words of Hercules himself, who, when he saw a statue of Adonis in a temple, said indignantly: "You are nothing sacred."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Hellenization of Judea. Having previously discussed the influence of the Tyrian Hercules, the author now turns to the desecration of the Temple in Jerusalem and the sanctuary on Mount Gerizim by Antiochus IV Epiphanes, specifically focusing on the imposition of the cult of Jupiter Olympius.</meta>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

### 2 Maccabees 6:2

To also defile the temple in Jerusalem and to name it after Jupiter Olympius, and the one on Mount Gerizim—just as those who lived in that place were accustomed to do—after Jupiter the Hospitable. <note>original: "Μολύναι δὲ καὶ τὸ ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις νεὼν, καὶ προσονομάσαι Διὸς Ὀλυμπίου, καὶ τὸν ἐν Γαριζὶν, καθὼς ἐτύγχανον οἱ τὸν τόπον οἰκοῦντες, Διὸς ξενίου."</note>

*To defile also the temple which was in Jerusalem, and to call it the temple of JUPITER OLYMPIUS: and that in Gerizim, as were they who inhabited the place, the temple of JUPITER THE HOSPITABLE.*

<margin>
Jupiter the Olympian and the Hospitable.
</margin>
It is not necessary now to say how wretched the state of the Jewish Church was after the Babylonian captivity under the Greek Monarchy, from the end of the reign of Seleucus Philopator until the times of Demetrius Soter. The present history is sufficient for us. For the city of Jerusalem was shaken by storms all the more, not so much by treacherous inhabitants as by Antiochus Epiphanes <note>The Seleucid king (r. 175–164 BC) who attempted to suppress Jewish law</note>: the city felt his arms; the city was captured; citizens were slaughtered without distinction of sex or age; the temple was despoiled; the worship of the true God was abolished; and that Temple of the true *Divinity*, of immense wealth, was converted into a Temple of *Jupiter Olympius*. His idol was placed in the temple by Antiochus, so that it could truly be called by the writer of Maccabees <term>the abomination of desolation</term> <note>original: "τὸ βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως"</note>. By this very phrase, the writer refers to the wording of Daniel, where the Greeks translate <term>the abomination that makes desolate</term> <note>original Hebrew: "השקוץ משמם" (Ha-shikkutz meshomem)</note> as "the abomination of desolation" in chapter 11:31; likewise <term>the abomination of desolation</term> <note>original: "τὸ βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως"</note> for the Hebrew <term>detestable thing that causes desolation</term> <note>original Hebrew: "שקוץ שומם" (shikkutz shomem)</note> in chapter 12:11. This was done with the help of an old man from Antioch, to whom this task was entrusted by the King. Under a new name, he publicly celebrated a new dedication, and obeying the king's command, he compelled the Jews to *turn away from the laws of their fathers and of God* and follow the institutions of the Greeks. Sixtus Senensis, in *Library of the Bible, book 2, page 50*, gave seven principal points of these institutions collected from the books of Maccabees and Josephus.

<margin>
From where Jupiter was called "Olympian."
</margin>
Who *Jupiter Olympius* was to the Heathens, I do not see from where it might be more conveniently drawn than from their own traditions. Among the gods, the Greeks and Latins assign the first and highest place to *Jupiter*; hence it is that in the addressing of the gods or their descriptions, they separate <term>Zeus</term> <note>original: "Δῖα"</note> and *Jupiter* from the other gods. The author of the *Attic Nights* <note>Aulus Gellius</note> relates that the name *Jupiter* coalesced from the twin words *Jovis* and *Pater* (Father), just as *Marspiter* was said from *Mars and Pater*. Others derive it from *helping* <note>original Latin: "juvando"</note>. But whatever the case regarding the etymology and meaning of the word, Jupiter—the most celebrated of the pagan gods, the one and all-encompassing God—was honored with various noble surnames to increase his splendor. These could be listed here if anyone wished to endure the labor; but Xystus Betulejus performed it long ago in his notes on *Lactantius, book 1*, where you may read the various names of Jupiter <margin>On False Religion, ch. 22.</margin> collected <term>alphabetically</term> <note>original: "κατὰ στοιχεῖον"</note> and their origins. From this it also happened that the Pagans invented several Jupiters whom we find in the ancient literature of the Greeks and Latins, attributing to them various locations, various upbringings, and deeds; regarding these, see *Natalis Comes*. Truly, no surname is more celebrated or more ancient for him <margin>Mythology, book 2, ch. 1, p. 79 seq.</margin> than that which is derived from the heavens. Regarding this epithet <term>Olympian</term> <note>original: "ὀλυμπίῳ"</note>, we find two different reasons assigned: one in the *Olympian Odes of Pindar*, who wrote thus in *Ode 2*:

<column-break/>

> *But O son of Cronus and Rhea,*
> *Who dwells on the seat of Olympus.* <note>original: "Ἀλλ' ὦ Κρονίε παῖ ῥέας. / Ἕδ' Ὀλύμπῳ νέμων."</note>

This is because he once had his seat principally on Olympus (the highest mountain of Bithynia, looming over the city of Prusa, with a summit always snowy, sterile halfway up, but in the lower part most fertile with pomegranates, chestnuts, and other fruits, as the eyewitness Stephen Gerlach reported in his *Letter to Heiland* found in Crusius' *German-Greece, p. 229*). The second reason records that Jupiter was called <term>Olympian</term> because he was educated by Olympus the Egyptian. But we do not wish to linger on these trifles. Concerning Jupiter the Olympian, or the heavenly inhabitant, who surpasses all others in Olympus by age and honor, we shall rather provide witnesses. Sophocles in *Ajax*:

> *And the most ancient father of Olympus.* <note>original: "Ὀλύμπου τεδ' ὁ πρεσβύτων πατήρ."</note>
> *That is, he who holds the honors of the gods on Olympus.*

He is the most honored of the heavenly beings, and to him honor is usually deferred above the others; for this is what the term <term>most ancient</term> <note>original: "πρεσβύτατον"</note> implies. And Xenophon says: *Having come from there to Olympia, he sacrificed to Olympian Zeus.* <note>original: "Ἐκ τότε ἐλθὼν ἐς Ὀλυμπίαν, ἔθυε τῷ Δῖι τῷ ὀλυμπίῳ"</note>. The same mention is made everywhere of the Olympian Temple. For the Greeks, receiving their fame from the East, heard him called Bel-Hamon <note>A Phoenician/Carthaginian solar deity</note>, and from that they made him <term>Celestial Zeus</term> and <term>Olympian Zeus</term>. Afterwards, they erected temples to him from all over Greece. At Athens, King Perseus had begun a temple to Jupiter Olympius, but, prevented by death, he left it unfinished. Regarding its magnificence, Livy says: *The Temple of Jupiter Olympius at Athens is a work of true magnificence toward the Gods; the only one on earth started on a scale proportionate to the greatness of the God.* And Strabo: *The King, dying, left the Olympian temple half-finished.* <note>original: "τὸ Ὀλύμπιον ἡμιτελὲς κατέλιπε τελευτῶν ἀναθεὶς ὁ Βασιλεύς"</note> This work, fruitlessly attempted by others, was completed by the Emperor Hadrian, according to Pausanias. There was also a very famous contest in Elis, a region of the Peloponnese, notable for its gymnastic games, where the Greeks diligently applied themselves to gymnastic exercises so that they might be better prepared for the state of the Olympic Games to be performed for Olympian Jupiter; and they were accustomed to celebrate these festivals every year. We read that in these games, a performance was given before the eyes of all Greece with such applause that they drew the sequence of the years (Olympiads) from this very assembly. Furthermore, out of a belief in Jupiter’s singular piety, many gifts were offered by all of Greece, among which stands a statue of Jupiter made of solid gold, donated by Cypselus, the Tyrant of the Corinthians. From there, the Romans later transported many things; and Suetonius reports that Caligula took care to have the statue of Jupiter Olympius and others brought from Greece so that, their heads being removed, he might place his own upon them. Dio tells the same. From this it is clear that this statue of Jupiter was fashioned in the likeness of a man, which greatly pleased the Greeks, as is evident from many other passages of foreign authors. It is also clear in Pindar: *A bowl was offered in libation to Olympian Jupiter. At the games in the Isthmus*

*to those offering to Jupiter the Olympian Savior.* <note>original: "σωτῆρι πορσαίνοντας Ὀλυμπίῳ"</note>

Where the Interpreter testifies that it was an ancient rite to take the first cup at banquets in praise of Olympian Jupiter; the second in honor of the Heroes; the third in honor of Jupiter the Savior: and he proves this with verses from Sophocles and Aeschylus; regarding which practice of the cups—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the desecration of the Jewish holy sites. Having described the transformation of the Temple of Jerusalem into a shrine for Jupiter Olympius, the author now examines the renaming of the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim and provides an extensive cultural history of "Jupiter the Hospitable" and the ancient laws of hospitality.</meta>

# II. Maccabees 6:2

<margin>
Jupiter Olympius and the Hospitable. See Book 1 of the *Parerga*, chapter 7, and *On the World*, chapter 7.
</margin>
Regarding the dedication, see Francesco Luisini, where he incorrectly cites Pindar’s *Olympians*; the passage is actually in the *Isthmian Odes*, as we have already noted. You will also note this: Phidias fashioned the image of this Jupiter from ivory as a <term>statue-maker</term> <note>original: "ἀγαλματοποιὸν"</note> (as Aristotle calls him), which is numbered among the wonders of the world. Pliny mentions the same work in several places: Book 34, chapter 8; Book 7, chapter 38; and Book 36, chapter 5. Similarly, the colossus of Caesar Augustus built by Herod is relevant here, which, according to Josephus in Book 1 of *The Jewish War*, chapter 16, resembled Jupiter Olympius in form and magnitude.

Mount Gerizim is the highest mountain in Samaria. On it, Sanballat had built a temple with the permission of Alexander the Great, in which the Samaritans performed their sacred rites, having spurned the Temple in Jerusalem. For this reason, it is also called the *mountain of transgressors*, because fugitive Jews found a harbor and a place of safety there. That same temple was destroyed by Hyrcanus <note>John Hyrcanus, the Hasmonean leader (r. 134–104 BC)</note>, as 
<margin>Book 13 of the *Antiquities of the Jews*, chapter 17.</margin>
Josephus testifies. Nevertheless, sacred rites did not cease to be performed there, as seen in John 4:20. It was dedicated, however, to Jupiter *the Hospitable*, and given his name. Concerning this epithet of Jupiter, consider the following: there was once a great reverence for guests among nations that were not entirely barbarian, who holily cultivated the law and necessity of hospitality. Cornelius Tacitus, a Roman writer and not a local one, testifies to the <term>hospitality</term> <note>original: "πολυξενίᾳ," referring to an abundance of guests</note> of the Germans:
> No other nation, he says, indulges more profusely in feasts and hospitality. To turn away any mortal from one’s roof is considered a sin. According to his means, each man receives a guest with a prepared feast. When the food runs out, he who was just a guest becomes a guide to the next place of hospitality and a companion; they go to the nearest house uninvited. It makes no difference; they are received with equal humanity. No one distinguishes between known and unknown regarding the right of hospitality. Upon leaving, if the guest asks for anything, it is the custom to grant it, and there is the same freedom to ask in return. They delight in gifts, but they neither count what is given as a debt nor feel obligated by what they receive. Living among guests is courteous.

Thus, it was also not permitted among them to violate guests; rather, they were to be protected from every injury and held sacred, 
<margin>Book 6 of the *Gallic Wars*, page 23.</margin>
as Julius Caesar testifies. Likewise, it was forbidden by law among the Lucanians for anyone to expel a guest who turned to them at sunset; those who violated this law were accused of <term>inhospitality</term> <note>original: "κακοξενίας"</note> and heavily fined. Hence, among the other things for which the Athenians are commended is that they were <term>welcoming</term> <note>original: "δέξιοι"</note> toward strangers, meaning humane toward guests. Indeed, it is clear that ancient nations were so religious in receiving guests that even the daughters of kings considered it honorable to wash guests in the baths, as 
<margin>Book 4 of the *Miscellanies*, chapter 2.</margin>
Petrus Nannius observes from Homer. For this reason, antiquity believed Jupiter—whom they called *Xenius* (<term>the Guest-Friend</term> <note>original: "ξένιον"</note>)—to be the presiding officer and avenger of hospitality, 
<margin>Book 1 of the *Aeneid*.</margin>
and that he gave laws to guests, as Virgil speaks:
> Jupiter, for they say you give laws to guests.

Where Dido, when she had poured a libation to Jupiter the Hospitable, soon gave the cup to Bitias; thereafter other nobles were also invited to the cup. Plutarch, in his book *On Exile*: <term>Many and great are the honors of Jupiter</term> <note>original: "Ζεὺς Διὸς πολλὰ τιμαὶ καὶ μεγάλα"</note>. And in the 
<margin>In the *Erotikos*.</margin>
*Amatorius*: <term>Jupiter the Hospitable hears and punishes the wrongs done to guests and suppliants</term> <note>original: "ξένων καὶ ἱκετῶν ἀδικίας ὁ ξένιος ὑπακόει κολασὴς ζεύς"</note>. There is more than one parallel passage in Homer, the source of all pagan wisdom, in whose works much mention is made of hospitality, where Eustathius on Book 9 of the *Odyssey*, line 270, writes regarding the law of hospitality and suppliants: Jupiter

<column-break/>

<margin>Jupiter Olympius and the Hospitable.</margin>
-> Jupiter is the avenger of suppliants and strangers <-
-> The Hospitable One, who attends to venerable strangers. <-
-> that is: <-
Jupiter is the avenger of both suppliants and guests, the Hospitable one who assists guests who are at the same time respectful. He is said to <term>attend</term> <note>original: "Ὀπηδεῖν"</note> because he takes care of them and brings certain help; for this is what it means to accompany them here. Hence he was also called <term>the Suppliant-protector</term> <note>original: "ἱκετήσιος"</note> or by syncope <term>Hikesios</term>, because he was believed to take care of suppliants and to punish those who would not admit the prayers of suppliants, as is clear from the same *Odyssey*, Book 9, line 213:
-> Jupiter the Suppliant-protector has punished them, he who <-
-> watches over other men and takes vengeance on whoever sins. <-
They were so religious in receiving guests of old that they thought guests, strangers, and exiles were under the protection of the Gods, and especially Jupiter, whom they therefore named *Xenios*. Hence Eumaeus says in Homer:
-> Stranger, it is not right for me, not even if one baser than you should come, <-
<margin>*Odyssey* 14, line 55.</margin>
-> to dishonor a guest. For from Jupiter come all <-
-> strangers and the poor. <-
Nausicaa had also said these final words to 
<margin>*Odyssey* 6, line 207.</margin>
Ulysses; and Ulysses, when he was brought to the Phaeacians, said: 
<margin>*Odyssey* 4, line 447.</margin>
-> He is venerable even to the immortal gods, <-
-> whichever of men comes as a wanderer, as I do now. <-
Hence the <term>suppliant-branches</term> <note>original: "ἱκετηλάτας"</note> which the suppliants carried, which among some was an olive branch wrapped in wool. Jupiter was also called <term>Friendly to Guests</term> <note>original: "ξύξεινος"</note> by Apollonius in the *Argonautica*, Book 2, and by Aristotle in *On the World*, chapter 7, where he discusses the various names of Jupiter: <term>companionable, friendly, hospitable, and warlike</term> <note>original: "ἑταιρεῖός τε καὶ φίλιος, ξένιος, καὶ στράτιος"</note>. But let us not say too much.

Whenever hospitality was violated, guests invoked him as a guardian God, just as friends invoked the <term>Friendly</term> <note>original: "φίλιον"</note> Jupiter, and comrades the <term>Companionable</term> <note>original: "ἑταιρεῖον"</note>, and kinsmen (that is, relatives) the <term>Family-protector</term> <note>original: "ὁμόγνιον"</note>, and those of the same clan the <term>Brotherhood-protector</term> <note>original: "φράτριον"</note>, and those joined by a treaty the <term>Oath-protector</term> <note>original: "ἐνόρκιον"</note>, as the avenger of a sworn oath. This was learnedly observed by Budé <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), French humanist</note> in the section on the office of the proconsul regarding <term>guest-gifts</term> <note>original: "exenia," though he thinks it should be read "Xenia"</note>. Consequently, when at the start of the Trojan War, Priam had sent his son Polydorus to Polymestor, the Tyrant of Thrace, and entrusted him to his faith, but the Thracian slaughtered him against the laws of hospitality, 
<margin>Euripides, *Hecuba*, line 706.</margin>
Hecuba, the mother of Polydorus, in order to avenge her son's murder, not only complained of this injury to Jupiter but also, with the help of the captive Trojan women, blinded Polymestor and killed his sons, as Euripides teaches in the same place, lines 1017 and 1028. Furthermore, it was also a placed custom that <term>hospitality tokens</term> <note>tesserae; physical tokens broken in two and shared between host and guest as a permanent record of their bond</note> were given to guests, by which they identified themselves. Regarding these symbols of hospitality, see the interpreters on that line 
<margin>*Poenulus*, Act 5, Scene 1, line 25.</margin>
of Plautus: *I carry with me the god of hospitality and the token*. See also Isaac Casaubon’s *Commentaries on Athenaeus*, Book 3, chapter 31. Alluding to this, Tertullian in *Apoc. 20* calls the hospitality of the ancient Christians the *confederation of Catholic communion*; the token of which was <term>P. Y. A. P. that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</term> <note>original: "Π. Υ. Α. Π. i. e. Πατὴρ, Υἱὸς & Ἅγιον Πνεῦμα"</note>. On this subject, see Cornelius à Lapide in his commentary on the Epistles of Paul, page 975. Today, hospitality—a thing to be deplored—is in exile among Christians, about which Xystus Betulejus complains in this four-line poem: 
<margin>Scholia on Book 1 of *Offices*, page 121.</margin>
-> Jupiter the Hospitable has now been worshipped for many years, <-

<meta>catchword: Nec (Not)</meta>

<summary>This page explores the Hellenistic renaming of the temples in Jerusalem and Gerizim, focusing specifically on the attributes of "Jupiter the Hospitable." It provides a deep dive into ancient Greek, Roman, and Germanic traditions of hospitality, citing classical authors to illustrate the sacred status of guests and strangers.</summary>

<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>Jupiter Olympius and the Hospitable.</margin>

->Nor do the holy teachings suggest anything more.<-

->Public edicts of the powerful now command something else;<-
->Morals are overturned; now piety is considered a crime.<-

In the duty of performing the kindness of hospitality, the Tartars and other peoples alienated from the true faith are more religious than we Christians, who are <term>unobservant</term> <note>original: "ἀθεωρητοῖς"</note>; regarding these, see Haithon on the Tartars, chapter 48, page 467; Marco Polo the Venetian, book 1, chapter 46, page 350; and Peter Martyr’s book *On the Newly Discovered Islands*, page 14.

The pagans also had their own *Mystagogues* <note>original: "Mystagogas"; religious guides who explained sacred mysteries</note>, who were given this duty in their republics: to urbanely receive foreigners and lead them through the city, and to courteously open the temples, theaters, and porticos. These were the men *who used to lead guests to the things worth seeing and point out each one.*

<margin>Cicero, book 4, *Against Verres*.</margin>
For this reason, it seems Antiochus wished for the *temple on Mount Gerizim* to be named—just as those who inhabited the place were named—after *Jupiter the Hospitable*. This was clearly because those Samaritans professed that, as newcomers and arrivals from the Persians and Medes, and thus guests of those seats, they ought to worship a God of hospitality. The pagans held Jupiter in such high honor, even though it is well-established from history that he was the worst of all. Indeed, we know from reading the pagan writers how dishonorable, how deceptive, and how impure Jupiter was. In him, they describe every kind of foulness; they make him an adulterer and list his sons born from various adulteries.

<margin>Natale Conti, *Mythology*, book 2, chapter 1, page 96.</margin>
> *Into what form was he not changed so that he might obtain his desired loves? Or what husband of a more beautiful woman could depart from home in security? How many did he defile by trickery? How many did he ravish? How many did he carry away from their homelands? What then? Was he content with the embrace of nearly innumerable women? Is it not believed that he held Ganymede, the most beautiful youth of his age, among his delights? The life of Jupiter was said to have been contaminated by so many impure crimes, yet most were not ashamed to call him a God.*

But how could he be better than his own mother? From his mother Rhea, who cheated on Saturn, a son <term>matching her</term> <note>original: "ἐφάμιλλ@"</note> could not help but be produced. The son had his beloved Ganymede, and Rhea had *Attis*, a Phrygian youth. A truly honorable mother, who sought out *Attis* as a partner in her marriage! But was not the jealousy of Jupiter to be praised, who, bearing *Attis* with difficulty, removed him from the scene by sending a wild boar? He observes the marriage bonds of his mother, yet neglects those of his own Juno, the goddess of the <term>marriage-yoke</term> <note>original: "ζυγίᾳ" or "Iugæ"</note>. The Scholiast <note>an ancient commentator</note> on Nicander related the indignation of Jupiter and the sadness of Rhea in these words:

<margin>page 64.</margin>
*It is told that Attis was a Phrygian shepherd. While shepherding and singing hymns to the mother of the gods, namely Rhea, he was loved by her. Appearing to him frequently, she deemed him worthy of honor. But Jupiter, being distressed by this, did not kill him openly out of respect for his mother, but sent a wild boar. Rhea, mourning him, buried him.* <note>original Greek: "Ἱστορεῖται, ὅτι ποιμὴν ἦν Φρὺξ ὁ Ἄττις..."</note>

Therefore, "as the King is, so is the flock," and the entire pagan world was composed according to the King's example, beginning to misuse their Jupiter as an excuse for their own corrupt morals. If this "noble" reward for the marriage bed pleased the supreme Jupiter, then it should not seem surprising that men imitated the character of the God.

Bunting <note>Heinrich Bünting, author of "Itinerarium Sacrae Scripturae"</note> reports that the ruins of this temple on Mount Gerizim exist to this day; but whether <margin>Itinerary, part 2, page 21.</margin>

<column-break/>

the Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus—which Aelius Hadrian took care to have built in the restored Jerusalem (which he called *Aelia* after himself and *Capitolia* after the temple) following the destruction of the city by Titus—still stands, is not now clear to us.

### II. MACCABEES VI. v. 7.

*And they were led by bitter necessity on the day of the king's monthly birthday to the sacrificial feast. And when the feast of Dionysus occurred, they were compelled to go in procession for Dionysus, wearing ivy.* <note>original Greek: "Ἠγοντο δὲ μετὰ πικρᾶς ἀνάγκης..."</note>

They were led with bitter necessity on the day of the King’s birthday to the sacrifices, and when the sacred rites of Bacchus were celebrated, they were forced to go around for Bacchus crowned with ivy.

Antiochus, surnamed Epiphanes, is read to have forced the Jews—after their ancestral laws were condemned and cast aside, and divine institutions despised—to celebrate the <term>Orgia</term> <note>secret rites</note> in the manner of Bacchants, bound with ivy, and to lead a procession for Bacchus within Jerusalem; those who refused to do so were punished with death (verse 9). How great a grief do you think was in the hearts of the pious in Judea when they saw the Bacchanalia celebrated in the City where the temple of the true God stood? But God heard the people sitting in great sorrow and groaning, and in the month immediately following the Lupercalia, He destroyed the pagans and restored the Temple through the Maccabees.

We might truly say that in all antiquity there was no reception or worship more insane than the sacred rites of Bacchus, which the most foolish nations celebrated with senseless rituals and ceremonies, with the most monstrous banqueting and gluttony, and finally with foul and obscene games. For in the *Orgia* of Bacchus (for "Orgia" was properly and first said of the sacred rites of Father Bacchus and Ceres, and then distorted to signify any other things which the ancients wished to be kept secret; hence Synesius in epistle 143 speaks of "orgies of philosophy," compare Meibomius on the Hippocratic Oath, chapter 12, page 105), no crime or disgrace was omitted, according to Livy, who reported certain astounding things about the abominable crimes of the Bacchanalia. We might also truly affirm that among the ancient Gods, there is none whom they distinguished by so many different names. In our verse, this "little god" is given the surnames *Dionysus* and *Liber*. First, let us look at the name of Bacchus, previously brought forward by Ausonius in his poem to the "Bearded" Father Bacchus:

> *Ogygia calls me Bacchus,*
> *The Indians think me Dionysus,*
> *Egypt considers me Osiris,*
> *The Roman rites call me Liber,*
> *The Mysians name me Phanaces,*
> *The Arabian race calls me Adoneus, etc.*

The name of Bacchus (whom they make Theban, Egyptian, and Indian—Arrian discusses whether he is one and the same in book 8 of the *Anabasis of Alexander*; see also Philostratus book 2; Pausanias in his *Description of Boeotia*) is derived by Eustathius from <term>to shout</term> <note>original: "βαχεῖν"</note>, and he wants him to be so named from the disordered howling with which the raving Bacchantes resounded; as if the letter 'k' is inserted as a stimulus so that it might sound more monstrous. A better notation has seemed to be that which refers back to the Hebrew word *to weep* <note>original: "בכה"</note>, which means to cry, to shed tears, or to wail, according to Heinsius in *Aristarchus*, chapter 1, in which, for the most part...
