<header>II. Maccabees VI. 7.</header>
<meta>catchword: mines</meta>

<margin>
The Bacchanalia and the Hippodrome.
</margin>
Mayer follows the scholar who discusses the origins of names from Hebrew, especially those concerning this pagan "little god" <note>original: "Deastrum"; a diminutive, often pejorative term for a pagan deity</note> Bacchus. It is in vain that others attempt to give him a Greek origin; they do this with other deities as well, striving to summon gods and goddesses to their own language by their names and claiming for themselves things that belong solely to "barbarians" <note>In the classical sense, meaning non-Greeks</note>. From this arises that chaos of beautiful etymologies. If Bacchus is from the Orient, *one should not seek a Greek etymology for him* <note>original: "οὐ χρὴ ζητεῖν ἑλληνικὴν ἐτυμολογίαν αὐτῷ"</note>. Authors vary on why he was named Dionysus: either because he pricked the thigh of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> while horned, according to Stesimbrotus in Natalis Comes (page 478)—which is why he was often depicted with horns—though Athenaeus (Book 11) offers another reason: that the ancients used to drink from large horns to drench themselves more fully. Or perhaps because he was sewn into the thigh of Jove, according to Nonnus in his *Dionysiaca*, an etymology no less ridiculous than it is clever. Or because he was educated by Zeus <note>original: "ἀπὸ Διὸς"</note> and the Nymphs of Nysa, according to Diodorus in Rosinus. Artemidorus (Book 2, chapter 22, page 250) derives it *indiscriminately* <note>original: "ἀδιακρίτως"</note> because he facilitates and perfects all things. Various etymologies are proposed for why he was called *Liber* <note>The Roman name for Bacchus, meaning "Free"</note>, as is the custom among triflers.

<margin>
Book 2, chapter 11.
</margin>
The ancient commentator on Juvenal thinks the surname *Liber* was given to Bacchus because he was worshipped as the vindicator and champion of liberty for cities, with a statue erected in the forum.

<margin>
On Satire 14, verse 193.
</margin>
For he is said to have made the cities of Boeotia free and to have been the first to celebrate a triumph. Varro, informed I know not how, claimed that *Liber* and *Libera* preside over procreation, seeking the reason for the name in the "weighing" <note>original: "librandis"</note> of the testicles during the act of love. Varro must have been drunk on Liber <note>i.e., wine</note> when he wrote this. We rightly omit the rest.

<margin>
Philological Lexicon, page 1499.
</margin>
See Martinius on this; and we hasten to the Ivy, of which our paragraph speaks. Who does not know that ivy was received into the sacred rites of Bacchus? The rite is clear enough that there is no need to "hang the ivy" <note>A reference to the proverb "good wine needs no bush (ivy)"</note>. We read in 3 Maccabees 2:29 that the Egyptian King Ptolemy Philopator, in honor of Bacchus, ordered an *ivy leaf* to be branded into the bodies of the Jews as a mark of shame <note>original: "stigmata"</note>, as it was the insignia of Bacchus. The words of the text are: *those being registered were to be branded even by fire on their bodies with the sign of Dionysus, an ivy leaf* <note>original: "τούς τε ἀπογραφομένους χαράσσεσθαι καὶ διὰ πυρὸς εἰς τὸ σῶμα παρασήμῳ Διονύσου κισσοφύλλῳ"</note>. With this, Bacchus himself was crowned, as were his priests; but also the Poets, because *Bacchus is the God of Poets*. Just as Mount Parnassus had a twin peak, one sacred to Apollo and the other to Bacchus, so too are Poets crowned both with the Laurel of Apollo and the Ivy of Bacchus. Hence, because these things were proper to Bacchus, Hesychius says that *to act like a Bacchant* <note>original: "τὸ βακχᾶν"</note> means *to be crowned with ivy* <note>original: "ἐστεφανῶσθαι κισσῷ"</note>. Regarding the ivy of Bacchus, the Author sings in the *Hymn to Jove*, which they attribute to Orpheus:

<margin>
Epistle 29.
</margin>
> I begin to sing of Dionysus, the rouser, wreathed in ivy,
> The glorious son of Zeus and the renowned Semele.

In Latin meter it sounds roughly like this:
-> *We sing of Dionysus, stained with ivy, roaring with mead,* <-
-> *The bright offspring from the blood of Jove and Semele.* <-

From this, Bacchus himself was given the surname *ivy-bearer* <note>original: "κισσοφόρος"</note> for Bromius <note>A name for Bacchus meaning "the roarer"</note> in Euripides' *Cyclops* (verse 616) and *ivy-wearer* in Pindar's *Olympian Odes* (11, page 17). *The ivy-bearing child loves*, and they were called "ivy-bearers" who wore ivy in the rites of Bacchus. He is called "Of the Ivy" by Pausanias in his *Attica*, and *Berry-bearer* <note>original: "Corymbiferus"</note> by Ovid 

<margin>
Book 1 of the Fasti.
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
The Bacchanalia and the Hippodrome.
</margin>
Valerius Flaccus most elegantly describes the rites of Liber in the *Argonautica* (Book 2), as does Catullus in the *Galliambic* meter, which begins:

-> *With hair bound back by ivy, I sing of Father Bromius.* <-

And Dionysius in his *Description of the World* <note>original: "Cosmographia"</note>:
> They perform the sacred rites for Bacchus according to the law,
> Wreathed in clusters of dark-leaved ivy,
> By night; and the sharp-sounding noise of the clatter rises up.

That is: *They perform the sacred times for Bacchus, driven by law, with branches*
-> *Bound with black ivy, and with pale clusters* <-
-> *By night: and a great clamor rises to the heavens.* <-

There is also a most beautiful description of a very soft man devoted only to the service of the orgies in Statius Papinius, *Thebaid* (Book 7, verses 650 and following). This *superstition* <note>original: "δεισιδαιμονία"</note> occupied almost the entire world, the Devil acting so that, under the veil of religion, he might more conveniently propagate and transfer all crimes of impurity to Bacchus.

<margin>
2nd Geography, Book 1, page 477.
</margin>
Bochart, with singular industry alongside Vossius and Heinsius, further deduces and shows that the cult of Bacchus was born in Assyria, spread from there to the Syrians and Phoenicians, and through the Phoenicians flowed to the Greeks, to whom Cadmus commended the antiquity of this cult, saying it was strengthened by the tradition of his ancestors:

> The traditions of our fathers, which we have possessed
> As long as time itself, no argument shall cast them down.

However much the glory of the Athenians increases from their study of Wisdom, just as much it decreases because of their *ithyphallic* <note>Rituals involving the display of the phallus</note> rites. For if we wish to measure their *superstition* by a just standard, you will find scarcely viler rites anywhere. In their floral festivals, which they called *Anthesteria*, there was the greatest license and gorging. A proverb indicates they were accustomed to being crowned with ivy: *Ivy after the Anthesteria* <note>Meaning something that comes too late</note>. Here we note in passing that Erasmus was unaware that these *Anthesteria* rites of Bacchus were the subject of the proverb: *Out with the Carians, the Anthesteria are over*; regarding which, see the explanation of Zenobius, Diogenianus, and Suidas in Andreas Schott, who edited these (pages 89, 221, and 445).

<margin>
Rules, chapter 15.
</margin>
Furthermore, comic and tragic actors, along with their performers and flute-players, used to contend and exercise their art most greatly in these Bacchanalian games; for there were present *Wonder-workers, rhapsodes, lyre-lovers, singers to the lyre, singers to the flute, flute-players, and trumpeters*, who were called *Artists of Dionysus*, about which see Stephanus's *Lexicon*. The Bacchic chorus of dancers itself was called a *thiasos* <note>A ritual procession or troupe of worshippers</note>, regarding which a passage from Demosthenes is noteworthy: *In the daytime leading those fine thiasoi through the streets, those crowned with fennel and white poplar, squeezing the puff-adder snakes and waving them over his head, and shouting EVOI SABOI, and dancing to HYĒS ATTĒS, ATTĒS HYĒS. Being addressed by the old women as leader, guide, ivy-bearer, and basket-bearer.*

<margin>
Volume 3, column 1436.
</margin>
They also received Demetrius, King of the Macedonians, not only with incense, crowns, and wine-pouring, but also with processional songs and choruses, and *ithyphallics* <note>Songs or dances involving phallic symbols</note> with dancing and singing met him, as Athenaeus reported in Book 6 of the *Deipnosophistae*. It is a shame to say what *ithyphallics* mean; read about them with shame, if it is worth the effort, in the aforementioned Book 14 of Athenaeus and Lucian’s *On the Syrian Goddess* (page 761). For in his sacred rites, abandoned men—

<page-num>772</page-num>
<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES. II. Maccabees VI. v. 7.</header>

<margin>
The Bacchanalia and the Hippodrome. See pages 760 & 778.
</margin>
...men erected statues of Priapus <note>Priapus was a minor Greek fertility god, usually depicted with an oversized phallus, symbolizing protection and abundance</note> in the temples, and they carried small wooden figures of men in processions; the pen is ashamed to write the rest of the details. Statues of Priapus also stood in the vestibules of the hippodrome <note>The ancient stadium for horse and chariot racing</note>, and Lucian mentions two very large ones in the same place, which bore the inscription: <gloss>Dionysus's mother has already dedicated these phalli.</gloss> <note>original Greek: "τὰς δὲ φαλλὸς Διόνυσ᾽ ἤδη μητέρη ἀνέθηκε"</note>

->I, Bacchus, have placed these statues of Priapus here for you, at the command of Juno, my stepmother.<-

Because of this, the foul festival was called the *phallagogia* <term>phallagogia: a procession where phallic symbols were carried</term> according to Hesychius, and also *Phallanogia*. In this filth, the army of Alexander—or rather the royal cohort—marched for seven days <margin>Book 9.</margin> crowned with various flowers and garlands to imitate the triumph of Father Bacchus, as recorded by Curtius. Mark Antony, the fiercest enemy of Cicero, proceeded so far into madness through his love of pleasure that he ordered himself to be called the <margin>2. 82. p. 75.</margin> *New Bacchus*, according to Velleius Paterculus. Crowned with ivy and veiled with a golden wreath, holding a thyrsus <note>A staff tipped with a pine cone, carried by Bacchus and his followers</note>, he was carried in a triumphal chariot in the manner of Father Bacchus through Alexandria and Athens. This event is recorded by Seneca in his *Persuasions* (Book 1) and Dio in his *History* (Book 48). You may search for their words and meaning in Hadrian Junius (Book 5, chapter 1) and A. Schott (Observation 15). From Plutarch’s *Life of Antony*, Petrus Cassellanus also touched on this in his *Syntagma on Greek Festivals*, where he dealt more extensively with the Dionysia on pages 75 and following. We have a similar example in *Marius*, who, after his triumphs over Jugurtha, the Cimbri, and the Teutones, *wanted to be like Father Bacchus, who was said to be the first to enter India and triumph over the Indians; following Bacchus's example, he drank from a cantharus* <note>A deep, two-handled drinking cup associated with Bacchus</note> *so that he might compare his own victory to that of Bacchus*, as Valerius Maximus records. With the same pride, King Antigonus <margin>3. Example 6. 6. p. 122.</margin> imitated Father Bacchus in all things, placing ivy around his head and carrying a thyrsus as a scepter instead of the Macedonian diadem, as Herodian <margin>Life of Demetrius p. 894.</margin> relates in Book 1. Hence, Plutarch numbered it among the evils of the human race that the names, rites, and honors of God were bestowed upon men. By a public decree at Athens, Antigonus and *Demetrius* were woven into the *Peplos* <note>The sacred robe dedicated to Athena</note> along with Jupiter and Minerva; furthermore, the Bacchanalia were renamed the *Demetria*. At that time, it is said the gods showed their offense through portents, and the poet Philippides added verses against those who had decreed divine honors to Demetrius, the son of King Antigonus of Macedonia, so that he might be worshipped as a god:
> Because of him, the frost burned the vines;
> Because of him, for his impiety, the sacred robe was torn in the middle,
> He who turns the honors of the gods into those of men.
> Such things destroy a people, not comedy.

Regarding Ptolemy Philadelphus, who celebrated this festival in Alexandria *without much display* <note>original Greek: "μὴ πολλῆς φαντασίας"</note>, see Athenaeus, Book 5. From this, one can recognize how great the foulness was in these Orgia <note>Secret rites or revels</note>, and where blind superstition led those wretched nations. Truly, various authors devise various reasons why *ivy was attributed to Bacchus*. Tertullian, in *On the Soldier's Crown* (page 451), argues from Harpocratiim: *That Bacchus is the same as the Egyptian Osiris, and Harpocratiim purposefully crowned him with ivy because* the nature of ivy is to protect from heat <margin>Casellanus Book 1. Var. ch. 19.</margin>. But who can account for everything? From this, the plant was also called the *Bacchic herb*; for this reason, the custom seems to have been introduced where innkeepers would hang out an ivy sign when they were about to sell wine; hence the

<column-break/>

proverb: *Good wine needs no ivy hung out.* <note>The Latin "Vino vendibili non opus est suspensâ hederâ" is the origin of the English proverb "Good wine needs no bush."</note>
For it seems that even this custom was introduced into our regions along with the rites of Bacchus. The Romans received it from the Greeks—though according to Tertullian, the Romans, with the authority of their Senate, expelled Father Bacchus not only from the city but from all of Italy—and from the Romans, the Papists <note>The author is writing from a Protestant perspective, using "Papists" to refer to the Roman Catholic Church</note> accepted and introduced it into the whole of Christianity. Especially at that time when the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, was made a sacrifice for us on the cross, we ought to remind one another to compose our minds to the thought of the wondrous plan of redemption and the magnitude of our sins. Indeed, an illustrious testimony by the Catholic *Simon Heinsius* is to be observed in Melchior Adam's *Lives of the Theologians* (page 15). Furthermore, the author mentions that those initiated into Bacchus performed sacrifices with dances, for which reason Dionysus was called the *dancing god* <note>original Greek: "ἐνόρχης δαίμων"</note> or the God of the Tripudium <note>A rhythmic, three-step dance</note>, as Lycophron says:
> *The dancing god, Phigaleus, the Shiner.*
->*God of the dance, Phigaleus, Phausterius.*<-
We spoke a little above about the chorus of dancers from Demosthenes. The word *orcheisthai* <note>original Greek: "ὀρχεῖσθαι"</note> means to dance the tripudium. Herodotus, in the book he calls *Euterpe*, teaches that Melampus explained to the Greeks *the name of Dionysus, the sacrifice, and the procession of the phallus*; Melampus learned this from Cadmus (as I suppose), as he adds shortly after. We noted above that this Cadmus taught the Gentiles the festivals of Bacchus, and Heinsius agrees with us. Let us note on this matter the words of Aeschines, in *On the False Embassy*: *And who ever saw him behaving indecently, either by day in the procession of the Dionysia, as you claim, or by night?* Scaliger notes in *Poetics* (Book 1, chapter 10) that songs in honor of Bacchus were sung by the *phallus-bearers*, citing Artemidorus. Thus, the Devil, the maker of a thousand crafts, works everywhere *in the sons of disobedience*. <note>A biblical reference to Ephesians 2:2</note>
That I have lived and written thus far is the gift of God alone; and as I have from Him *my being and my writing* <note>original Greek: "τὸ εἶναι καὶ τὸ γράφειν"</note>, so I consecrate to the same God what has flowed from Him. I give to You what You have given, my God; I consecrate what You have shared. By Your grace, it is done that I have finished this labor, etc. And at this threshold, I conclude, and here shall be the END:
->**GOD BE WITH ME.**<-

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
### Psalm 139:15.

-> **רקמתי בתחתיות ארץ** <-
-> <note>original Hebrew: "Rikamti be-tachtiyot aretz"</note> <-
-> <term>I was embroidered in the lowest parts of the earth.</term> <-
-> <note>original Greek: "Ἐποικίλθην ἐν τοῖς κατωτάτοις τῆς γῆς."</note> <-
-> *My substance was in the lower parts of the earth.* <-

The Vulgate <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note> translates it this way, but poorly. The Psalmist introduces a most elegant metaphor from *embroiderers* to demonstrate the intricate <note>original Greek: "πολυποίκιλον" (polypoikilon), meaning many-colored or complex.</note> formation of the human body, consisting of various members—veins, arteries, bones, flesh, and skin—with elegant variety in the lower parts of the earth (that is, in the mother's womb). This metaphor penetrates the minds of readers as much as the sweetness and greatness of the Hebrew word itself, **רקמתי** <note>Rikamti: derived from a root meaning to weave or embroider with colored threads.</note>, so that one may scarcely find an equal expression in secular literature. Indeed, he uses a word more than significant, **רקם** <note>Rakam</note> 
<margin>David de Pomis in his Dictionary, folio 196.</margin>
(from which flowed the Italian word matching the Hebrew <note>The Italian "ricamare," meaning to embroider.</note>, which Arias Montanus transformed into the Latin *racamare*). He compares our "formation" <note>original Greek: "Διάπλασιν" (Diaplasin)</note> to those garments which the Phrygians of Mount Ida, clever artisans, invented, and from which they were called *Phrygiones* <note>Phrygiones: famous ancient embroiderers from Phrygia, known for gold-thread work.</note>. He calls that admirable texture of bones, nerves, arteries, vertebrae, and that spine—so musically and precisely fashioned—the "work of the Phrygians." It extends with marvelous craftsmanship from the neck to the sacred bone <note>The "os sacrum" or sacrum at the base of the spine.</note>, like a woven painting. The sons of physicians and anatomists abundantly declare how much the rest of the body's *adornment* is full of art and beauty; a benefit for which he does not allow us to be ungrateful to the immortal God, the giver of all praiseworthy things. Moreover, **רקם** <note>Rakam</note> signifies in Belgian <term>to write and to paint</term> <note>original Greek: "γράφειν καὶ ζώζειν"</note>, *to paint with a needle, to interweave garments with gold and various threads of different colors, or to paint with Phrygian art.* **רוקם** <note>Rokem</note> is the *embroiderer* who weaves garments with a needle, who knows how to fashion various forms and figures with many colors in a tapestry; the Egyptians were skilled in this craft above other nations. Hence in Proverbs chapter 7, verse 16, *tapestries and coverings brought from Egypt* are praised. The Tyrians also practiced this art, which the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek version of the Old Testament.</note> mentioned when explaining a passage in Job (chapter 38, verse 36) regarding women who, in the Babylonian or Phrygian manner, either weave with multicolored threads or paint little flowers and animal forms with a needle. But others explain this much differently. And to add these things in passing concerning our own nation, I remember admiring outstanding examples—which display all the most illustrious deeds of the Kings of Denmark in various colors— 
<margin>Aristarchus, Book 6, Chapter 6.</margin>
at the fortress of Kronborg, which overlooks the Danish strait at Elsinore, as well as in the most splendid castle of Frederiksborg among other *sights worth seeing* <note>original Greek: "ἀξιόθεα" (axiothea).</note>. Therefore, the paraphrast Johannes Campensis (whose work I read with some pleasure, printed in Roskilde, Denmark, in the year 1536 with notes by Resen) did not render this <term>without support</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀνερμάτως" (anermatōs).</note>: *I was woven like a tapestry from nerves and veins in the womb of my mother, in a place more hidden than any cave of the earth.* The Septuagint translates it as <term>I was variegated</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐποικίλθην" (epoikilthēn)</note>, that is, to 
<margin>Ephesians 2:21.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
make varied, to distinguish diversely. From this, a *Variegator* is called a <term>variegator</term> <note>original Greek: "ποικιλτὴς" (poikiltēs)</note>, a word used by Johann Forster to translate the Hebrew. Philoxenus rendered it "feather-worker" (*plumarius*), a word the *Vulgate* uses elsewhere, and from which comes the term <term>feather-work</term> <note>original Greek: "πλεμαείνον" (plemaeinon)</note> in the Lexicon, discussed by Johannes Meursius. 
<margin>In the Glossary, pages 430, 431.</margin>
Feather-workers are those who make garments from the feathers of birds, or who imitate feathers while painting with a needle, as Philander described in his notes on those words of Vitruvius: 
<margin>Book 6, chapter 6.</margin>
*The texture of the feather-workers and the workshop of the painters;* just as many peoples of America arrange garments for themselves most elegantly from bird feathers, since there is a multitude of various birds of every kind among them. Benedictus Balduinus notes this, and Drusius 
<margin>On the Footwear of the Ancients, chapter 3.</margin>
noted in his commentary on him that feather-work still persists among the Indians, as observed by Nicolaus Fullerus. However, I believe Salazar has spoken in his commentary on the Song of Solomon (chapter 3, verse 10) about how it was once customary for blankets and tapestries to be painted with a needle and elaborated with figures. Understand Corippus regarding that art:

> *Ascending the golden throne and his father's seat,*
> *Constructed with feathers and fit with beautiful tapestries.*

Which of men does not discover God, the Best and Greatest Artisan, in the human body? If he considers that most admirable formative power, so that organic parts are made from those things which serve the natural, vital, and animal faculty; if he looks at the rest of the framework of the limbs, aptly arranged among themselves, so that the first correspond to the middle, and the middle to the last by a most fitting connection. All these things are of such great and astounding wonder that the Royal Prophet deservedly exclaims: *I was wonderfully formed in the womb. Formed, he says, and wonderfully formed with various members in the manner of the Phrygian embroiderers, and in the mother's womb, which is like a most rich treasury and a certain divine storehouse; I was formed with embroidered images.* Nature itself, whose field is the womb, proclaims with a full voice that no fortuitous collision, no influence of heavenly minds, or any other chance could perfect a generation so pleasant, lovable, and admirable in every part. Job, who is more eloquent in his senses than in his words, acknowledging this in chapter 10, verse 10, says: *Your eyes saw my mass or my rolling together;* alluding to that varied wrapping of the embryo in membranes and the gathering of the body parts into a ball, which he compares to the curdling of cheese: *Did you not, he says, pour me out like milk, 
<margin>Verse 10.</margin>
and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh, and covered me with bones and nerves.* Galen (in *On Semen*, book 2), Gellius (book 3, chapter 16), and Pliny (book 7, chapter 15) follow this same comparison, so that they themselves, led only by the light of nature, admired this artisan of marvelous structure. Hippocrates, in his book <term>On the Nature of the Child</term> <note>original Greek: "περὶ φύσεως παιδίου"</note>, described this wondrous conformation thus: <term>The flesh, increasing by the spirit, is articulated, and each similar part comes into itself as like to like, the dense to the dense...</term> <note>original Greek: "Ἡ δὲ σὰρξ αὐξομένη ὑπὸ τοῦ πνεύματος ἀρθροῦται, καὶ ἔρχεται ἐν αὐτῇ ἕκαστον τὸ ὅμοιοv ὡς τὸ ὅμοιον, τὸ πυκνὸν ὡς τὸ πυκ-", text breaks off.</note>

<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
<note>The following Greek and Latin text is from Hippocrates, *On the Nature of the Child*.</note>
Furthermore, as the flesh grows, it is articulated by the spirit <note>original: *spiritu*, referring to the vital breath or "pneuma"</note>, and each part moves toward its like: the dense toward the dense, the rare toward the rare, the moist toward the moist. Each part moves into its own proper region according to its kinship, toward that for which it was created. Whatever was generated from dense materials is dense; whatever from moist is moist; and the rest follows the same logic in its growth. The bones harden, being solidified by heat. Indeed, they branch out like a tree, and both the internal and external parts of the body become even better articulated. The head itself gains its distance from the shoulders, and the arms and forearms from the sides; the legs are separated from one another. The nerves spring up around the nature of the joints and grow. The nose and ears stand out from the flesh and are perforated; the eyes are filled with pure fluid. The sexual organs become clear, showing which they are, and the internal organs are fully formed. After reciting these words, Valleriola <note>François Valleriola (1504–1580), a French physician</note> adds in *Commonplaces 18, page 372*: *What could be said or even imagined more fitting than this description of our structure brought forth by Hippocrates?* Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and alchemy</note> in the *Poimandres* marveled at the works of God in the single human body; for he wondered who wonderfully shaped the ears and nostrils, who stretched the lips of the mouth, who tightened and bound the nerves, who carved the shape of a pyramid into the heart, and other such things. From this, he commanded us to beware lest we ever separate the craftsmanship from the Craftsman. We must certainly listen to Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity</note> and gather something good even from a pagan author. Galen, a pagan man, so admired the structure of the human body that he called his books *On the Use of the Parts* a "sacred discourse," adding words worthy of being preserved in boxwood and cedar <note>A metaphor for enduring and precious writing</note>:

<margin>Book 3, chapter 10</margin>
<margin>See the notes of Caspar Hoffmann.</margin>
> *I am composing a true hymn to our Creator. I believe that true piety consists not in sacrificing hecatombs of bulls <note>A "hecatomb" was a grand public sacrifice of 100 oxen</note> or burning mountains of incense, cassia, and six hundred other perfumes and ointments. Rather, it consists in me first coming to know, and then explaining to others, the nature of His wisdom, His power, and His goodness. For the fact that He wished to adorn everything with fitting care, and that nothing should be deprived of His benefits, I consider to be the form of most perfect goodness; and for this reason, His goodness is to be celebrated by us with hymns. To have discovered the way in which all things might be most perfectly adorned is the height of wisdom. To have fully accomplished what He willed is the mark of invincible and unsurpassed power.*

Read his seventeen books, which he laboriously composed on the human body—or rather, as many hymns to divine perfection—

<column-break/>

and admire the <term>supreme genius</term> <note>original Greek: *ἄκρον ingenium*</note> of this ethnic man. Imitate this goodness of mind, and rise with him toward God as a worshiper and preacher of His power and majesty. With a grateful heart, proclaim God’s wonderful craftsmanship: in the shaping of the body, in the joining of the limbs, in their arrangement, admire, worship, and adore His providence, power, and wisdom.

A wide field of considerations opens here before us, leaving us uncertain what should be said first, second, or next. Here, let all theologians examine their papers; here, let the anatomists roll and unroll their anatomical scrolls. Here, let doctors learn the "footprints of God" in their healings.

Man is an animal skillfully composed, in whom all things are bound together in a wonderful series and woven with such artistic order that nothing can be taken away without the remainder becoming defective; and nothing can be added that would not seem out of place and unnecessary. In the human body, nothing is superfluous and nothing is lacking. Physicians and anatomists know this; nor are theologians ignorant of it, if they look upon the sacred use of the limbs.

It is a wonder, then, that Plautus, Pliny, Cicero, and those who follow them, lament the condition of man—complaining that nature has provided other animals with feathers, others with scales, and others with various things in abundance, while man alone was not so much created as neglected and cast aside, helpless and naked. *It is not enough,* says Pliny, *to judge whether nature has been a better parent to man or a more sorrowful stepmother. Above all, man is the only creature she covers with the resources of others; to the rest, she gives various coverings: shells, bark, hides, thorns, fur, bristles, hair, down, feathers, scales, and wool. She has even protected the trunks of trees with bark, sometimes double, against cold and heat. Man alone she cast aside on the day of his birth, naked on the naked ground, immediately to wailing and weeping; and no other of so many animals is prone to tears at the very beginning of life. The first hope of strength and the first gift of time makes him like a quadruped. When does man walk? When does he speak? When is his mouth firm for food? How long does the crown of his head throb—the sign of his supreme weakness among all animals?*

The most eloquent master of Roman eloquence, Cicero, complains no differently regarding human weakness: *Man,* he says, *was brought into life by nature not as if by a mother, but as if by a stepmother: with a naked, fragile, and weak body; with a mind anxious toward troubles, humble toward fears, soft toward labors, and prone to lust.*

Cicero and others dare to object these things and more against God and Nature. However, we are far from agreeing with them in all things; rather, we hold the opposite opinion, which is by far the truest and most consistent with Holy Scripture and sound reason. For although man is born into this light fragile and weak at the beginning (which no one denies), and this is common to him and other animals, he is nevertheless sufficiently equipped and adorned. The fact that he comes forth naked from his mother does not prove him to be inferior to the rest of the living creatures. Indeed, Nature left man thus naked—without the fur of dogs, without the hooves of horses, without the beaks

### Law of Psalm 139:15

<columns>
2

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> Nature brought forth the cranes, the hornless stags, and other such creatures into this light, not as a harsh stepmother, but as a gentle mother—compelled not by any hatred, but by love. Come then, what if a man were horned? What if he were shaggy? What if he were beaked? Would not such a man, by the consensus of everyone, rightly be counted among the number of monsters and portents? Let us place before our eyes King Nebuchadnezzar of the Babylonians, the most powerful ruler, who, after being cast out from human society and living among the beasts, grew hair like <margin>Daniel 4:30</margin> eagle feathers and claws like those of birds, as Scripture testifies. Let us bring forward from antiquity the Satyrs, with shaggy bodies and goats' feet, yet with human faces, about whom the writers of the greater nations have recorded many things in literature—though a great part, if not all, is mythical. *There are also apes,* says Solinus <margin>chapter 10</margin>, *which they call <margin>Book 2, chapter 2 on Roman Satyrs</margin> Satyrs; they have a very pleasing face and are restless in their gesturing habits.* And Isaac Casaubon <note>A famous French classical scholar (1559–1614)</note> reports that not so many years ago, a truly horned man, who had hidden for thirty years in the shadowy mountains, was found in France and brought to the King of the French to the wonder of all. If Pliny, or Cicero, or anyone else had seen him, would they not say that nature itself had wandered astray in forming this man? Would they not proclaim such a man to be <term>inhuman</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπάνθρωπον</note> and merely <term>human-shaped</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνθρωπόμορφον</note>? Would they not mutter to themselves that line of Virgil?
> A monster, horrific, shapeless, huge,
> <margin>Introduction to Book 7, page 41</margin> Turn away this unnatural pest from the earth.

Our people, when they see in someone—contrary to the common law of nature—either six fingers, or overly long ears, or a nose a bit too hooked, or a defect of the eye, or a goiter on the neck, or perhaps another tumor not commonly found in others, they immediately stand frozen in astonishment. They give thanks to nature—or rather to God, whose ordinary power is nature—that He did not instill such stains or blemishes in them. Thus, a man would be foolish to wish for horns, a beak, or hooves for himself; and he would be far more foolish, if not indeed wicked, who accuses nature, our procreatress, on the grounds that she willed the human race to lack those instruments which are not beautiful, but beastly. For if man is a kind of king over the other animals—as he is entirely a creature of foresight, sagacity, variety, sharpness, memory, and full of reason and counsel, as Cicero says elsewhere (even if he sometimes contradicts himself) <margin>Book 3, *On the Nature of the Gods*</margin>—certainly his physical structure could not and should not have been established otherwise than we see it established; indeed, <margin>Book 1, *On the Laws*</margin> we marvel at it. *Nature thought of us before she made us,* are the words of Seneca <note>Seneca, *On Benefits* 6.23</note>: *nor are we such a slight work that we could have fallen from her mind by accident.* See how much she has permitted us; see how the condition of human empire is not confined only to humans. See how far our bodies are allowed to wander; she did not restrict them to the boundaries of the lands but sent them into every part of herself. See how much our minds dare; how they alone either know the Gods or seek them, and with their thoughts directed on high, they follow the divine. Know that man is not a makeshift or unthought-out work.* So he said. Away then from man go the limbs given to brute animals: the horns of oxen, the beaks of pigs, the hooves of horses, the multicolored feathers of birds, or the

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> variegated scales of fish, and other such things. For a distorted figure of the body sometimes betrays a distorted character, as the second Epigram in the <term>Anthology</term> <note>The Greek Anthology, a collection of poems and epigrams</note> <term>On the Lame</term> <note>original Greek: εἰς χώλους</note> reads regarding a lame man:
> <term>Your mind is as lame as your foot; for truly</term>
> <term>your nature displays your inner image on the outside.</term>
<note>original Greek: Χωλὸν ἔχεις τὸν νῶν, ὡς τὸν πόδα, καὶ γὰρ ἀληθῶς εἰκόνα τῆς ἐντὸς σὴ Φύσις ἐκτὸς ἔχει.</note>

These things can be seen as nothing other than superfluous wastes that taste of the earth, not of heaven; they suit those cast down toward the ground, not those raised up toward heavenly goods. For man was so created by God that, just as he is upright in body and face, so he should not cling to earthly things but should carry his soul upward to the celestial, as the Poet sang:
> While every other living creature looks down at the earth,
> Man alone turns his face toward the stars of heaven.
<note>Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 1.84-86</note>

Among all animals, man alone is created with an upright face and eyes that can turn toward heaven, so that he may know the purpose of his creation and his way of life. Basil of Seleucia <note>A 5th-century bishop and writer</note> says in Oration 1, pages 7-8: <term>For other animals either drag their whole body along the ground, or walk bent over according to the law of nature—not walking but creeping—or they bow toward the earth because their shape gives them no inheritance in heaven. Man alone, through his physical formation, displays his nobility. He stretches upright toward heaven. While his feet touch the earth, as he is nourished upon it, his face is lifted toward heaven as a friend.</term> Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux, 12th-century mystic</note> says in his Sermon on the Feast of St. Martin, column 409: *Therefore He made man upright even in his very body, and gave man a sublime countenance—while other living creatures look down at the earth—so that lifting his face to the stars he might immediately look up to where he perceives his blessed and everlasting mansion. For does not the vision of such a luminous region provide a powerful incentive for love and a provocation of the most fragrant desire to us who gaze piously and faithfully? The stars of heaven are not like the clods of the earth. There is no small distance between the splendor of the Sun and the darkness of this soil.* Later, in column 410: *God wants us to forget the things that are behind, to look down upon the inferior things, to desert earthly habits and innate vices, to seek the heavenly things above, and to gape at the things that lie before us.* Man alone possesses a rational soul, which the most wise Creator first breathed into Adam. For God created man as an intelligent nature—not a log or a stump, not a camel or a mule. He imparted the gift of mind to man, and also speech for the interpretation of divine workings; He gave them counsel, and a tongue, and ears, and eyes, and a heart for thinking, and filled them with the knowledge of doctrine, as the son of Sirach <note>Referring to the Book of Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 17:1-6</note> most excellently writes in chapter 17. Regarding this excellence of man, let us hear Cicero again <margin>*On the Nature of the Gods*</margin>: *The soul,* he says, *is composed of and a partaker in reason, than which nothing better has been procreated by the best and wisest parent.* The same says elsewhere: *God, or nature the mother of all things, gave us a soul; than which nothing is more excellent or more divine.* To this Tyrius Maximus <note>A Greek rhetorician and philosopher</note> in Dissertation 38 harmonizes: <term>The human soul is closest and most similar to God.</term> Plato in the *Epinomis*: *When the soul, which is the best thing, conducts itself with counsel according to the best intellect, then that which is truly perfected according to the intellect necessarily results without persuasion, nor...*

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>

Book 4, near the end.
</margin>

...would be more solid or immovable than adamant <note>The hardest legendary stone, often identified with diamond.</note>. Hence the poet Manilius <note>Marcus Manilius, a 1st-century Roman poet known for his work on astronomy.</note> says:

> Can one believe it right for men to be born from anywhere but heaven? 
> All other animals lie cast down upon the earth, 
> or submerged in the waves, or hanging in the air.

And why should I collect more arguments on this subject, which are encountered everywhere else? Therefore, Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) often called the "Christian Cicero."</note> rightly followed the admirable structure of the human body and its parts in order in his short book *On the Workmanship of God* written to his pupil Demetrianus, where he says among other things: *If man is endowed with reason, what need will there be for the body's defenses? Since reason, once granted, can fulfill the duty of nature—which indeed is so powerful for adorning and protecting man that nothing greater or better could have been given by God. There is nothing that man does not attempt and perfect with both mind and hand. Nothing is positioned so high that man does not strive for it. Nothing is so remote that man does not pursue it. Nothing is hidden so deeply in the lowest hiding places of the earth that man, by his industry, does not dig it out, according to that saying of Virgil:*

-> ——— Relentless labor conquers all, <-
-> and poverty pressing in harsh circumstances. <-
<note>original: *Labor omnia vincit Improbus, & duris urgens in rebus egestas*</note>

Man plows, harrows, digs, sows, and reaps; and then, alongside him, the other animals enjoy the fruits. Man alone speaks, counts, paints, writes, sculpts, and prints books; no other animal does this. Man weaves, sews, mends, bakes, builds, and produces other works which seem most necessary in times of both peace and war. Thus, though man may be deprived of those other feathers, he measures the air—indeed, even the blue temples of heaven—by the wing of his own genius. By that noble and new spyglass, which they call by the Greek name <term>telescope</term> <note>original Greek: τηλεσκοπεῖον</note>, he is carried aloft like an eagle; and having been carried through immense intervals of space, he detects new spots on the Sun and Moon, new moons around Jupiter and Saturn, and numerous stars in the firmament, even those that are <term>ever-moving</term> <note>original Greek: ἀεισύρτους, referring here to stars that are always visible or in constant motion</note>, about which the Mathematicians may see more. Manilius contributes his own symbol to us in the place cited above, when he says:

> ——— He alone stood with the height of his head
> Erect, and as a victor sends his starry eyes
> Toward the stars, and views Olympus more closely,
> He seeks out Jove, and not content with the mere
> Appearance of the Gods, he scrutinizes heaven on high.

Not to mention certain people found who, with wondrous agility and audacity, in the manner of birds (to use the words of Claudian), *launch themselves into the breezes*; because of this flying—which in Greek is <term>to fly</term> <note>original Greek: πέταμαι (*petamai*)</note>—they called them <term>petaminarios</term> <note>An ancient term for acrobats or "flyers" who performed aerial leaps.</note>. Though man may be without scales and fins, let it suffice to mention the *divers*, who endure unharmed under the waves for several hours, to say nothing of the stupendous ships by which man has measured each and every sea far and wide. To the brutes belong their dens, caves, and nests, by which they are covered against the inclemency of the sky and air; but for man there are houses, citadels, and towers, constructed not only for necessity but also for elegance and refinement.

<margin>2 Samuel 2:18</margin>

The deer and the hare run swiftly; but in the *Pandects* <note>Here referring to the historical records of the Bible</note> Asahel is celebrated—the brother of Joab, pierced through by Abner—who (to speak with Catullus):

> ——— Outran the footsteps of the swift, fiery deer.

Nor, because of their wondrous <term>sharpness</term> <note>original Greek: ὀξύτητα (*oxytēta*), here meaning speed or keenness</note>, should we pass over

<column-break/>

chariots—especially those sail-bearing ones recently invented in the Netherlands—by which we are carried along most swiftly, even to the point of a miracle. Natural philosophers report of the porcupine that it shoots out quills, but for man, on the other hand, arrows from bows and stones from most powerfully whistling slings come to his aid. The boar rages with a lightning-fast tusk; the ox and the deer fight most rigidly with horns; the lion and the bear prevail with immense strength. But for man, on the other hand, swords, broadswords, spears, javelins, cannons <note>original: *bombardæ*</note>, and muskets <note>original: *sclopeta*</note> are at hand, by which the force of animals is inhibited, their speed is repressed, their ferocity is restrained, and their onset is brought low. Even if deprived of these aids, some have killed the most raging beasts by the native firmness and strength of their limbs, just as Scripture records of Samson tearing apart a roaring young lion like a young goat in *Judges 14:6*, and of David, while still a youth, killing a lion and a bear.

<margin>1 Samuel 17:35</margin>

Not to mention what secular writers record concerning Milo of Croton <note>A famous 6th-century BC Greek wrestler of legendary strength.</note> or Polydamas, the son of Nicias. For there is no need to illustrate the matter with more such ancient examples, since we ourselves daily see a horse ruled with a goad, an ox with a rod, and even a dog with a stick—even by a child. No animal is found, whether it prevails by the bulk of its body, the speed of its feet, or its strength, that escapes the fortitude of man, aided by mind and hand. Therefore, it is a wonder that Pliny, Cicero, and others—so ignorant of their own faculty—accused God, the Parent of Nature, with such a title as if He produced men weaker and more feeble than is right. It is indeed true that the entrance of our life is tearful, its progress weak, and its exit lamentable; but this is not to be ascribed to nature, but to the flaw added to it through the Fall. Since Pliny was ignorant of this, he thundered against Nature and its Parent; yet, having returned to himself, he sometimes wrote and felt better concerning man and his excellence over the beasts—which will be clear to anyone unrolling the seventh book of Pliny a little more diligently. For in that book, he will observe many things that serve to commend the nobility of the limbs, strength, speed, the excellence of the senses, the promptness of memory, authority, manifold science, and other things. One may observe the same in Cicero in the second book of *On Ends*, the second book of *On Duties*, and the second book of *On the Nature of the Gods*. "The whole Psalm informs us of the perfection of man," says Ambrose concerning Psalm 119 in *Sermon 13*. Hence the Greeks, considering this, rightly called man a <term>microcosm</term> <note>original Greek: μικρόκοσμον (*mikrokosmon*), or "little world"</note> because of the supreme harmony among the members of the human body. For in man, some members are formed for <term>living</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ ζῆν (*to zēn*)</note>, others for <term>living well</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ εὖ ζῆν (*to eu zēn*)</note>. In man, a certain supreme harmony and a single, as it were, concert is seen, while each member performs its duty. The heart produces the Spirit, so that life may be provided to the living being. The brain ensures that the animal feels; the lung that it breathes. Concerning nutrition, the stomach performs some tasks, but the liver performs more. Man, the microcosm, consisting of the most becoming <term>good proportion</term> <note>original Greek: ἐυρυθμία (*eurythmia*)</note> of parts, was most skillfully formed in his connection and position. In him are many spheres. Stephanus Rodericus à Castro <note>A Jewish-Portuguese physician (1559–1627) who lived in Florence.</note> shows the "Meteors" <note>In the Aristotelian sense, meaning natural phenomena or bodily "weather."</note> in man in a specific treatise in his book *Meteors of the Microcosm*, in folio, which was published in Florence...

<summary>This page argues for human superiority over animals by highlighting how human reason, technology (like telescopes and firearms), and architecture compensate for a lack of natural defenses. It refutes classical thinkers who viewed man as naturally weak, attributing human frailty instead to the Biblical Fall while celebrating the body as a "microcosm" of divine harmony.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the general philosophical defense of human physical structure to a specific "Sacred Anatomy," beginning a systematic exploration of the body's regions and organs as divinely ordered masterpieces. It references both classical philosophers like Plato and early medical authorities like Galen and Herophilus.</meta>

### FROM PSALM 139:15.
<note>original: "ex Psalm. CXXXIX. 15." This verse refers to being "intricately woven in the depths of the earth," a common theme in early modern anatomical theology.</note>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
...has come forth. *Vegetation* in the same way was treated by *Johann Vesling* <note>A 17th-century German anatomist and botanist.</note> in his *Exhortation on Botany*, showing the affinity between plants and human nature. The divine Plato, weighing within himself the human body—so skillfully constructed, so well tempered, so elegantly shaped, and adorned on all sides with such various members—called it a *wonder of wonders* <note>original: "θαῦμα θαυμάτων"</note>. And when Abdalas <note>Likely referring to a medieval Arabic source, possibly Abdullah ibn al-Muqaffa.</note> was asked what he thought was most admirable in the nature of things, he replied that man alone is the one who surpasses all admiration. And this is not without merit: for both our outer and inner man have their own members—ears, feet, mouth, and others—by which they complete and carry out what must be done. For whatever the sense perceives outwardly, the imagination represents inwardly, thought forms, genius investigates, reason judges, memory stores away, the intellect separates, and understanding grasps and invites to contemplation. This miraculous structure of the body’s parts, and the singular excellence and nobility of man above all other living creatures, will be more rightly understood and more accurately grasped if the entire fabric of the human body, and all its figure, site, magnitude, order, process, color, heat, and other things of that kind, are perceived. For since in the body of man things are disposed more wonderfully and stupendously than in others, Plato, Galen, and other Ancients had reason to marvel at the human fabric, which they called the *body* <note>original: "σῶμα"</note> *preeminently* <note>original: "κατ' ἐξοχὴν"</note> because of the admirable structure of its members. Bartholomew Fontius so admired the elegance of Plato in describing the human body that he proved in a famous oration that neither Lactantius, nor Celsus, nor Cicero himself could approach the wonderful eloquence of Plato in describing this matter, as Marsilio Ficino commends <margin>on Plato's Timaeus, p. 728.</margin>. This miraculous divine workmanship cannot be understood unless the parts are explained. Therefore, led by a certain honorable curiosity on the occasion of the Royal Prophet’s <note>Referring to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> words, we shall institute a sacred *Anatomy of the human body, with God's help* <note>original: "Anatomen ξὺν Θεῷ"</note>. Anatomy, which is the alphabet of Medicine, is performed on dissected and opened human bodies; it was cruder among the Ancients than in the modern subdivision into 36 parts, over which they used to place as many Genii <note>Guardian spirits or astrological influences.</note> as curators of the individual parts. Among the Egyptians, *Kings* used to cut into the bodies of the dead to investigate diseases, according to Pliny <margin>Natural History, book 19, chapter 5.</margin>; hence, among the lost books, Eusebius <margin>Greek Chronicle, p. 141.</margin> lists the *Anatomical Books of Atholthis*, a King of Egypt, and a book by Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and medicine.</note> on the Anatomical argument of the body's construction, as mentioned by Clement of Alexandria in the sixth book of the *Stromata*. Galen, the leader of the ancient anatomists, especially cultivated *Anatomy*, in which Hippocrates had been less skilled. That man of Pergamum <note>Galen.</note> was so highly esteemed for this knowledge that all Physicians subsequently followed him. A *certain man named Herophilus* <margin>Tertullian, On the Soul, ch. 4, p. 531.</margin> is spoken of badly by Tertullian because of anatomy; of him he says: *That physician, or rather butcher, Herophilus, who cut up seven hundred people to investigate nature, who hated man in order to know him—I do not know if he clearly explored all his internal parts, since death itself changes the things that were alive.* These words of Tertullian are perhaps too severe against Anatomy, the use of which, when skillfully observed, is great for

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
healing both external and internal ailments, so much so that without a clear knowledge of it, a Physician must very often be effectively blind. Indeed, three regions or "Bellies" of the entire body are established. The highest is the *head*, which ends at the neck. The middle is the *chest* or thorax, which is enclosed by the ribs. The last contains the *Abdomen*, or what is properly called the *Belly*. And finally, the *Limbs*—that is, the arms, hands, legs, and feet—complete this division accepted by Anatomists. In each region there is a *metropolis* <note>A "mother city" or primary governing organ.</note>, which strengthens and adorns its province. There are three *metropolises*, one in each region. In the head is the *brain*, in the chest the *Heart*, and in the belly the *Liver* <note>original: "Epar"</note>; it is for the sake of these that the other parts were created. For the lung, and indeed the entire thorax, was made for the sake of the heart, so that it might have respiration. The stomach, however, and the intestines, the spleen, the two bladders <note>The gall bladder and the urinary bladder.</note>, the kidneys, and finally the whole Belly seem to have been made chiefly for the sake of the liver, in which, according to the Ancients, the blood is crafted; for the stomach prepares food for the liver. The intestines distribute it into the mesenteric veins to be carried to the liver and purge it of thick dregs. The spleen is thought to purge the blood of earthy dregs. One bladder secretes bile, the other (with the kidneys) secretes and stores the serum or watery excrement. The brain through the *nerves*, the heart through the *arteries*, and the liver through the *veins* are connected to the whole body and govern it, bestowing nourishment, heat, sense, and motion to each and every part. From the liver, *blood* is flowed out through the veins into all the rest of the body. From the heart, *arteries* are led to all parts, through which heat flows into the parts. From the brain, *nerves* are derived to all parts, through which all the rest of the body receives the power of sensing and moving. The heart holds the sovereignty by reason of the inflowing heat, without which neither the brain nor the liver can do its duty. The heart needs both for the protection of its heat. This distribution of the Ancients is disapproved by some more recent writers and partly approved; we shall leave the discussion of its goodness or falsity to the Physicians. We, meanwhile, shall follow this *arrangement* <note>original: "διανομὴν"</note> of the Ancients, beginning from the *belly*—not the lower one, which usually feels the anatomist's finger first because of the organs residing there which are easily prone to rot—but from the *supreme* one, namely from the *head*. Let us observe the order of dignity, and begin from the first belly, which is the most noble of all and most pleasant to those who look upon it.

The *Head*, the highest part in the human body, is spherical, and is called so from its use, because it *takes in* <note>A pun on the Latin "caput" (head) and "capere" (to take/contain).</note> the brain within itself. Varro relates that it is called the head because senses and motion take their beginning from it; for the head is the source of the senses and of voluntary motion, indeed the primary seat of both internal and external senses. To the Greeks it is *kephale*, *karanon*, or *kara*. To the Germans it is *Haupt* from "having" and *Kopff* from the Latin *Caput*. To the Hebrews it is *Rosh* <note>original: "ראש"</note>, from which others derive the Latin *Caput*. One part of the head is hairy, the other *bare*. Its front part is the *Synciput* <note>The forehead/crown.</note>, or *bregma*, from the word *to moisten* <note>original: "βρέχειν"</note>, for in infants this part is very soft and moist. The back and reverse part is the *Occiput*, *inion*, or *opisthion*, named from the fibers and nerves which they once thought originated there. From the head, without which a man is a mere trunk, all beauty and ornament come to man. *The head*, says Isidore <margin>Letter 24, p. 634.</margin>, *is as it were the citadel of the body.* <note>original: "ἡ καθάπερ ἀκρόπολις τοῦ σώματος"</note>

<page-num>778</page-num>
<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
...for from the most necessary and most precious of human parts <note>original: "ἐκ γὰρ τῶν ἀναγκαιοτάτων καὶ τιμιωτάτων ἀνθρωπίνων"</note> to those things which must be understood through the arrangements of the mind. And Augustine says in his commentary on Psalm 29, column 148: *In your members, there is a great distance between the head and the other members. In the other members, you feel nothing except by touch. By touching, you feel in the other members; but in the head, you see, you smell, you taste, and you touch.* Such is the excellence of the head compared to the other members. Therefore, the head of our body holds the leadership over all members; it is the citadel of the body, and in the kingdom of the **Microcosm** <note>The "small world"—a common Renaissance idea that the human body mirrors the entire universe.</note> it occupies the highest place, claiming for itself the supreme command of all affairs and offering itself through its various paths for the contemplation of all things. Indeed, it is like a temple and a small chapel for the soul, in which all the senses and powers of the mind reside. <margin>Among the powers of the soul, says Anton Mocker—Professor of Ethics and Poetry in a small work containing the Orations and Programs proposed under his Rectorship at Erfurt\*—that which is rational is like a Priest, dwelling in the head as if in a temple or chapel. Its brain is the altar, upon which the functions appropriate to this Priest's office take place, such as cognition and reasoning; and the brain is stirred, both by the Spirits already converted from a fiery nature into a celestial one, and by the nerves—the carriers of sense and motion—which grasp sensible things.</margin> <margin>p. 207, 1591 edition.</margin> The human head is spherical or globe-shaped because of the supreme perfection and excellence of the whole man, whereas the heads of other living creatures lack this perfect form. It was fashioned by the **all-wise Creator** <note>original: "πανσοφωτάτῳ"</note> so that more brain could be contained within it, and so that, by its roundness, it might more easily avoid all blows and be able to turn itself here and there. From the proportion of the head with the rest of the human body's members, **Hippocrates**, the Father of Physicians, judges the good temperament and constitution of a man. <margin>Physical Anthropology, m. 620.</margin> If the body is large, says Sperling\*, and the head is large, it is a good sign. If the body is average, and the head is average, it is likewise a good sign. But if either exceeds the proper proportion—so that the head is small and the body large, or the body small and the head large—it is a sign of a bad condition: in the former, because the Spirits are not sufficient for such a large body, and those that are present either grow too hot or are suffocated; in the latter, because the vital Spirits (which are the material of animal life) are not supplied in sufficient quantity, nor are they properly refined in an oversized head. Thus, commonly, those who are **large-headed** <note>original: "μεγαλοκέφαλοι"</note> but endowed with a small body are numbered among the unteachable and dull, while those who are **small-headed** <note>original: "μικροκέφαλοι"</note> and **large-bodied** <note>original: "μεγαλόσωμοι"</note>—that is, burdened with a large body—are numbered among the reckless, who act hastily and without consideration. In <margin>Iliad, book 2, line 212.</margin> **Homer**, **Thersites** <note>A soldier of the Greek army during the Trojan War, often depicted as ugly and impudent.</note> is ill-reputed for his pointed head, being the foulest of all the Greeks, so much so that it became a proverb for a truly deformed and monstrous man: "a Thersitean look" <note>original: "Θερσίτειον βλέμμα"</note>.
> *Thersites alone still chattered on, boundless in speech,*
> *who knew in his mind many disordered words,*
> *to idly and unseemly strive against the kings,*
> *but whatever he thought would be laughable to the Greeks,*
> *that he would say. He was the ugliest man who came to Troy.*
> *He was bandy-legged and lame in one foot; his two shoulders*
> *were rounded, hunched over his chest; and above them*
> *his head was warped, and a thin stubble sprouted upon it.*
Since man is therefore a divine animal, in him also

<column-break/>

**Nature**, the Parent, had such regard for man that in fashioning him, she granted him something singular and divine above all other created things; we see this also observed, among other things, in the adorning of the human head. *To man alone among animals,* says **Laurentius**\*, *was a head turned in an orbicular shape, both for capacity and for the **protection of the brain** <note>original: "φυλακὴν ἐγκεφάλου"</note>, so that it might easily receive blows, for easier motion, and finally because it was to be the domicile of reason, the soul having been infused into us from the round heaven; yet it is not perfectly spherical, but somewhat oblong, bulging with twin crowns, and compressed on both sides at the temples.* And since the excellence of the human head is so great, for this reason in the **Bible** the name *head* is assigned to whatever is considered best and most outstanding in its kind. Sometimes the name **Rosh** <note>Hebrew: ראש</note> is placed before it in common usage, as in *Ezekiel 27:22*: *with the head of all spices* <note>original: "בְּרֹאשׁ כָּל בֹּשֶׂם"</note>, that is, with every most excellent spice—"all kinds of precious spices," as our version and the Herborn version have it: *with the foremost seasonings* <note>original: "μετὰ πρώτων ἡδυσμάτων"</note>. Such are similar phrases like *heads of spices* <note>original: "רֹאשׁ בְּשָׂמִים"</note>, which the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> reads as *full myrrh*, Aquila as *select*, Symmachus as *the first fruits*, in *Song of Solomon 5:14*; and likewise in *Exodus 30:23*: *head of myrrh* <note>original: "רֹאשׁ מֹר"</note>, which the Septuagint renders as *the flower of myrrh*. Sometimes the name is placed after, as in *Psalm 141:5*: *oil of the head* <note>original: "שֶׁמֶן רֹאשׁ"</note>, that is, the most excellent oil; compare *Exodus 30:12, Isaiah 15:2, Zechariah 4:7*. Thus the **Bride**, in her praise of her **Groom**, begins from the head and descends. But the Groom, praising the Bride, begins his praises from the feet, *Song of Solomon 5:10 and 7:1*. Why is this? Concerning this, **Cornelius à Lapide** <note>A 17th-century Jesuit exegete.</note> says: *The Bride praising the Groom starts from the head and finishes at the feet. Here, conversely, the Groom praising the Bride begins from the feet and finishes at the head. The reason for the disparity is that the Groom descended from heaven to earth to join the Bride to himself. But the Bride, called out from the earth to heaven by the Groom, ascends upward. Therefore, the praise of the Groom is in the descent, and the praise of the Bride is in the ascent.* It is no less frequent in Holy Scripture that **Christ** is called our head; hence **Prosper of Aquitaine**\* says: *The blessing flowing from the head, that is, from Christ, descends not only onto the beard, but even to the hem of his garment, that is, down to the lowest members. In the beard, however, which first received the oil flowing from the head, the Apostles and Martyrs are signified, in whom the virtue of the head stands out both by Sacrament and by example.* The Groom mentions this divine blessing, flowing most abundantly from the head into its members, in the Sacred Song of Solomon. For that reason, **Ambrose**\* says: *The Church of God in the Canticles says: The voice of my brother knocks at the door. Hear him knocking, hear him desiring to enter. Open to me, my Sister, my Bride (Cant. 5:2), because my head is filled with dew. Then one must be vigilant, lest when the groom comes, he departs excluded. For if you sleep, and your heart is not awake, he departs before he knocks. If your heart is awake, he knocks and asks for the door to be opened for him. It is the soul that has a door and has gates. To this door Christ comes and knocks; he knocks at the gates. Open therefore to him; he wishes to enter, he wishes to find his Bride vigilant. Do not, therefore, cause delays for a good lover; otherwise he departs, and you, by the sleep of your sluggishness, will seem to have shut out the one knocking.* And again in the same Psalm, *Sermon 17*.

ex Psalm. CXXXIX. 15. 779
Q 442.

On page 726, he writes: The Church, like a well-deserving Queen, is crowned by Christ’s blood, just as it is written: **The ornament of your head is like purple (Song of Songs 7:5). Christ’s blood is the purple dye that colors the souls of the Saints, resplendent not only in its hue but also in its power, because it makes them kings—and better kinds of kings—to whom He grants an eternal kingdom.** And rightly, regarding such great beauty of the Church, upon which the blood of Christ shines, the Holy Spirit cries out: **How beautiful and sweet you have become, O love, in your delights.** She is beautiful in the glory of her virtue, and sweet in the joy of grace and the forgiveness of vices; she is a love no longer troubled by the bitterness of sin. From the head, as the principal and primary part of man, many and various expressions have been drawn in the Sacred Scriptures. In the list of rewards and punishments in Deuteronomy 28:13, God promises that He will place the Jewish people as the head and not the tail (that is, in servitude), if they stand firm in His covenants. For that promise of dominion included obedience; otherwise, if it were not so, He threatens God's wrath. Thus, it is stated among the curses: *If you turn away from me, the stranger in your midst will be raised to the highest power, and you will not be the head, but the tail.* This happened to them when they were led into the Ba-
<margin>Lamentations 1:5</margin>
bylonian captivity, concerning which Jeremiah says of the enemy's success: <note>original Hebrew: "היו צריה לראש"; original Greek: "ἐγένοντο οἱ θλίβοντες εἰς κεφαλήν"</note> Her enemies have become the head. Vatablus 
<margin>page 383.</margin>
says there:
> To be the head is to be superior and to dominate someone; that is, their enemies began to rule over them. 

For those who refused God as their head, what else could they expect but to have the Babylonian Tyrant as their head and prince, who would vex and afflict them in every way. Therefore, the "head" is often used to signify what a man carries in his mind. The proud man walks with a raised head, the melancholy with a bowed head, the sad with a lowered head, and the needy with a drooping head. Likewise, "raising the head with a finger" <note>original Greek: "ἀνάγειν τὴν κεφαλὴν δακτύλῳ"</note> is a sign of a doubtful mind; shaking the head is for those who are indignant; and veiling the head is for those condemned to death, specifically to the gallows (see Forster’s Lexicon, p. 271), as is clear from Livy. This was the same as covering the face, just as it is read that it was done to Haman, with whom Ahasuerus was angry, according to the custom of the Persians in Esther 7:8. But it is 
<margin>Genesis 40:13, 19.</margin>
often asked: what does it mean in the story of Pharaoh's court to "lift the head"? Jarchi and Aben-Ezra <note>Two famous medieval Jewish commentators.</note> explain it as "to reckon" or "to review," and they argue it signifies a restoration of status and dignity; just as the Cupbearer was to be lifted from the lowly place into which he had been cast. Thus, "lifting the head" is the opposite of the "diminution of the head" <note>A legal term for loss of status or civil rights.</note> (to speak with the legal scholars) and denotes adding ancient honor or restoring a former office. Castalio explains it in the same way: 
> Within three days, he says, Pharaoh will order you to be brought forth and restored to your former state, so that you may stand at his cup just as you used to do before. 
<margin>Observations 2.7 & 3.5.6.</margin>
Drusius argues that Joseph, in using this phrase, was referring to a custom of the ancients. 
> Long ago, he says, the names of offices were inscribed on a white board or counting board. Holes were made in the board according to these names, and "head-pins" or pegs were placed into these holes. These were used to keep a ready account of days, months, years, offices, actions, services, money allocated or counted, and similar things. 

According to this custom, Joseph's words can be explained thus: Pharaoh will lift your head—that is, he will review his servants to know whom

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
he wishes to leave in their offices and whom he wishes to deprive of them. He does this by removing the pins from the board. He will "lift and remove" your head—that is, your pin, on which your name is inscribed—from its base so that he may read your name written there. And when he has read it, he will restore you—that is, he will put that pin with your name back into your base (the hole intended for your pin). By this restoration, he will testify that he wishes to leave you in the office entrusted to you. However, when the same phrase <note>original Hebrew: "נשא ראש" (lift the head)</note> recurs in verse 19—which the interpreters commonly explain in verse 13 as a restoration of honor to a former rank of dignity—what will happen to the Baker? For he was not restored, but is read to have been hanged after three days. Others respond that Joseph used <term>antanaclasis</term> <note>A rhetorical device where a phrase is repeated but with a different meaning each time.</note>, turning a phrase that signified elevation to a rank of honor into one signifying the physical lifting of the head onto a gallows. Others explain the prefix "from" in the word "from-upon-you" <note>original Hebrew: "מעליך"</note> in a "privative" sense <note>Meaning "to take away" or "deprive."</note>, in this way: Within three days Pharaoh will review you, but the review will be "away from you," meaning it is the last time you will be counted. Thus say Junius, Tremellius, Friedlieb, Glassius, and others.
<margin>Sacred Grammar, Book 4, Observation 4, pages 650, 657.</margin>
The words of the Blessed Glassius are as follows: 
> The meaning is: he will order your name to be deleted from the catalog of his servants. "To lift the head" is a common phrase in Scripture for "to take a census" or "to reckon," and it is said of many others in Exodus 30:12, Numbers 1:2, 49, chapter 4:2, 22, and chapter 31:26. Here, however, and in 2 Kings 25:27 and Jeremiah 52:31, it refers to individuals, yet with respect to others. (Rabbi Solomon says: It is a term for numbering and accounting.) 

That the meaning of the phrase is the same (namely, to reckon) when it is used of the cupbearer in verse 13 and the baker in verse 19 is clearly evident from verse 20. Therefore, the Chaldean <note>The Aramaic Targum (translation).</note> translates it inconsistently: in verse 13 regarding the cupbearer, he translates it as "he will remember you," but in verse 19 regarding the Baker, "he will remove or take away your head from you." The Latin Vulgate also expresses both of these. But the Baker was by no means decapitated, but hanged, etc. Compare Blessed Gerhard’s *Commentary on Genesis 40, p. 708* and Blessed Walther’s *Biblical Harmony on Genesis, p. 162.*

<margin>Book 5, p. 168.</margin>
The hairs—some of which hang forward over the temples and cheeks, while others hang back—are called by Apuleius "the covering of the head," as Salmasius notes in his work on Tertullian, page 299. Like trees on the ridges of mountains, they wall in the forehead. Although some count them among the excrements and impurities of the human body along with fingernails and toenails, we nevertheless owe them greater honor. We know that the beauty of the head consists in the hair, as we might say with Hilary in his commentary on *Psalm 68*, and that hair is the "honor of the head."
<margin>Sermon 11 on Psalm 118, p. 683.</margin>
Serenus (ch. 8, v. 4) calls it "beauty"; the Salerno School (ch. 62, v. 7) calls it "the glory of the head"; and Erhard in his notes on Petronius (p. 685) agrees. Ambrose speaks aptly about hair in this regard in his book *On the Ark and Noah*, chapter 7: 
> The hairs of the head, he says, clothe the head with such a pleasing garment, like attendants in a royal court, so that the brain does not get cold, nor the rain strike it, nor the sun burn it. 

Compare the same author in his *Hexaemeron*, book 6, chapter 9. We shall say more about the use of hair at the end of our meditation. All the adornment of a human being, whether woman or man, is from the head; if it is bared and stripped of hair, beauty perishes...
