<meta>This page continues the "Sacred Anatomy" series. Having previously discussed the head as the "citadel" of the body and a symbol of leadership or servitude, the author now focuses on the hair, exploring its aesthetic value in classical antiquity and its profound allegorical significance in Biblical texts like the Song of Songs and the book of Ezekiel.</meta>

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> When the hair is lost, all human beauty perishes. Indeed, the Latin word for "to adorn" (*comere*) is derived from the care of the hair or tresses (*coma*). This is described excellently by Apuleius in his second book: *If you were to strip the hair from the head of even the most excellent and most beautiful woman, and bare her face of its native beauty—even if she were fallen from heaven, born of the sea, or raised from the waves—even, I say, if she were Venus herself, surrounded by the entire Choir of the Graces, accompanied by the whole host of Cupids, girt with her famous belt, and fragrant with cinnamon and balsam; if she walked forth bald, she could not please anyone, not even her own Vulcan.* <note>Apuleius is a 2nd-century Roman novelist. Here he emphasizes that hair is the essential crowning glory of beauty.</note> And shortly after: *Such is the dignity of the hair that no matter how much a woman walks adorned in gold, fine clothes, gems, and every other luxury, she cannot be seen as "adorned" unless she has arranged her hair.* Among the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note>, who wore their hair long and nourished it, they believed that committing anything unseemly or illiberal was beneath them. <term>Aristotle</term> says in his first book on *Rhetoric*: <note>original Greek: "Ἐν Λακεδαίμονι κομᾶν, καλόν. ἐλευθερίας γὰρ σημεῖον· ᾧ γὰρ κοσμῆται ῥᾴδιον οὐδὲν ποιεῖν ἔργον θητικόν"</note> "In Lacedaemon, it is a beautiful thing to wear long hair, for it is a sign of freedom; it is not easy for someone so adorned to perform any menial labor." Hence a Laconian in the fifth Idyll of <term>Theocritus</term> took the sign of his praise from his hair, which he grew in the Laconian fashion; he preferred himself over two others in dignity and rank because he was a shepherd, and in status because he was free and noble-born, as <term>Heinsius</term> notes in his *Readings on Theocritus*. For in ancient times, slaves were forbidden from growing their hair long, as <term>Aristophanes</term> witnesses when he says: <note>original Greek: "δέχ’ ὢν, κόμην ἔχεις"</note> "Though you are a slave, do you wear your hair long?" The Israelites grew their hair according to divine precept in <margin>Leviticus 19:27</margin>, <note>original Hebrew: "לא תקפו פאת ראשכם"</note> which the Septuagint translates as: "You shall not make a rounded fringe from the hair of your head." The Vulgate says: "Neither shall you shave your hair into a circle," and <term>Arias Montanus</term> translates word-for-word from the Hebrew: "You shall not surround the corner of your heads." <term>Pagninus</term> renders it: "You shall not cut the hair of your head in a circuit." Regarding these words, <term>B. Friedliebius</term> notes: "This was an ancient custom of the Egyptians and other gentiles; even now, other nations shave the whole head, leaving only a certain part uncut, either on the crown or the forehead, from which a tuft of hair arises." The Septuagint's "do not make a circle" refers to this rounding of the hair. "These unusual and barbaric tonsures of the hair were considered an insult to God the Creator, as if He had not created the human head with sufficient beauty." Monks today emulate these pagan customs. Likewise, Priests in the Old Testament were prohibited from shaving the hair around their chins in Leviticus 21:5. On the other hand, the proper use of hair is celebrated in more than one place in Scripture. The heavenly Bride is very often commended for her hair; in Song of Songs 5:11: <note>original Hebrew: "קוצותיו תלתלים שחורות כעורב"</note> "His locks are bushy," that is, "curly," as <term>Pagninus</term> and <term>Arias</term> translate. The Vulgate renders it: "His hair is like the branches of palm trees," following the Septuagint's "His locks are like fir trees." Others, looking to the Hebrew, translate it as "densities," because the hair is dense like a forest; and "black as a raven," meaning they are very black, which is to say, most beautiful and elegant. The divine writer accommodates himself to the custom of his nation, for whom blackness of hair was counted as beauty—a fact which writers of the New World also testify regarding the Americans, who take great delight in black hair. Likewise, in two places—namely chapter 4:1 and chapter 6:4—the heavenly Bridegroom compares the hair of his Bride to a flock of goats that have ascended

<column-break/>

and appeared from Mount Gilead. He takes this metaphor from the tenderness of the wool of sheep that graze on the mountains of Gilead, which abounded in good pastures; hence, this mountain received no small praise from its fat sheep and their tender wool. Nor should we overlook that steadfastness of the Bridegroom in <term>chapter 7:5</term>: <note>original Hebrew: "וראשך עליך ככרמל ודלת ראשך כארגמן"</note> which the Septuagint translates: "and the braid of your head is like purple; a king bound in the galleries." That is, "the hair of your head is like royal purple bound in channels." <term>Beda</term> <note>Venerable Bede, an 8th-century English monk and scholar</note> explains that the hair of the head can be understood as the holy meditations of Christ, in which he very often thought of death and the shedding of blood. <term>Beda</term> also explains it as the pious thoughts of the faithful soul: "The hair of the Bride's head are the thoughts of the faithful soul. The purple of the King signifies the imitation of the Lord's passion, to which the hair of the Bride's head is rightly compared, because every thought of the elect is fortified by faith in the holy cross; the entire intention of their heart stands ready to suffer for the Lord, so that they may deserve to be resurrected with Him." Conforming to this is what is read in <term>Theodoret</term> on this passage: "He calls the hair a weave and fold compared to purple, beautifully and decorously composed and pronounced, which is dyed and sprinkled with Christ’s blood." <term>Martin Luther</term> praises this interpretation of the words when he says: "One must ascend with the Bride into the mountain of myrrh, etc. This is Christ crucified with all the saints, etc." From this, the Bride is commended because her hair is like royal purple—that is, her meditation is reddened by the memory of the Passion. This meditation pleases the heavenly Bridegroom, and from it he gathers the love of the Bride toward him; for that reason, earlier in chapter 4:9, he commends the hair of the Bride: <note>original Hebrew: "באחד ענק מצורוניך"</note> "with one [hair]," saying: "You have wounded my heart with one hair of your neck," as the Old Interpreter translates it. The Septuagint has: "with one ornament of your neck." Aquila says: "with one braid of your neck." Symmachus: "with the likeness of your neck." Pagninus: "with one chain of your neck." Arias: "with one necklace from your necks." One hair of the neck is joined to one of the eyes; namely, when the mind of the Bride is one, when her thought is one, and there is one pleasure in the one Bridegroom; when the eye of the soul tends toward nothing but the Bridegroom, when she looks back at Him alone, she is rendered His alone. For what is more pleasing to the Bridegroom than when the soul of the Bride always has her Bridegroom present, prays with the Bridegroom, always desires the Bridegroom, and neither wishes nor is able to think of anything except the Bridegroom, or about the Bridegroom, or for the Bridegroom. Indeed, this unity of thoughts pleases the Bridegroom so much that he praises the Bride for it again and again. Ezekiel is said to have been snatched up by his hair in chapter 8:3 by an angel, which <term>Gregory the Great</term> explains morally as the renovation and reformation of the intellect, writing: "What is a lock of hair, if not the collected thoughts of the mind, so that they do not flow away scattered, but remain constrained by discipline? Therefore, the hand is sent from above, and the Prophet is lifted by the locks of his head, because, when our mind collects itself through watchfulness, a power from above draws us away from the lowest things." The mind is truly elevated between earth and the high heaven, toward God and the divine vision and holy tranquility, if it cuts away worldly cares and thoughts. But we must return from this digression; the word <note>original Hebrew: "רהטים"</note> is explained in various ways by interpreters: some translate it "in the galleries" or "walkways"... <note>The text ends mid-sentence as it reaches the catchword for the next page.</note>

It builds on the idea of hair as a "crown" by exploring how biblical commentators have linked the structure of hair to water channels, royal purple, and the suffering of Christ.</meta>

<page-num>781</page-num>
<header>From Psalm 139:15</header>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
...the sense would be that if the King saw you passing by, he would stop in his walkways to gaze upon your beauty. Pagninus <note>Sante Pagnini, a 16th-century Hebraist</note> translates the Hebrew word as "beams," <note>original: *tignos*</note> so that the meaning is: the King would wish to be bound as if to the very rafters—that is, to remain in her house because of his great love for her. Arias <note>Arias Montanus</note>, along with the Ancient Interpreter <note>The Vulgate</note>, translates it as "channels," <note>original: *canales*</note> in this sense: like a King surrounded by channels—that is, living near watercourses where there is water, which was a most commendable thing in the Holy Land. For well-watered land was of the highest value. 

Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, an 8th-century monk and scholar</note> explains these "channels" mystically as a symbol of humility: *The channels,* he says, *which look up to the King’s purple, are the hearts of Christ’s faithful. The wool, however, which is sent bound into the channels to receive that purple color so that after dyeing it may be used for the King’s ornament, is that very mild humility and most gentle conscience of the believer, which through suffering and works of justice advances into the garment of the Eternal King. This wool, bound in the channels, is stained with the purple color because the virtue of humility, fixed and as if tied in the hearts of the elect by the continuous memory of the Lord's cross, is animated to endure temporal tribulations, through which it may reach the fellowship of the Lord's kingdom.* He illustrates this with the example of Ly-
<margin>Acts 16:14</margin>
dia, the seller of purple in *Acts 16:14*, who, despising the shame of Christ’s cross, received Paul after being converted to Christ. Bede continues: *Lydia the purple-seller designated, by her craft, her belief, and her service, the Church of the Gentiles, which, imbued with the confession of the Lord’s passion and itself ready to shed its blood, would receive the doctrine of the Apostles into its innermost heart after it was expelled by unbelievers.* 

Following the Blessed Gerhard <note>Johann Gerhard, a prominent Lutheran theologian</note>, we follow the Blessed Luther, who translates it: **the hair is like the King's purple enclosed in folds**; <note>original German: *die Haar ist wie die Purpur des Königes in Falten geschloßen*</note> for those folds of hair resemble channels, or they run down through the garment. For hair gathered into distinct braids and hanging from the shoulders presents the shape of channels through which water flows distinctly or is sent out into dry places. Nor does the Hebrew text oppose this exposition, which literally sounds like this: *The hair of your head is like purple: the King is bound in the channels,* since the *Athnach* accent <note>A Hebrew grammatical mark indicating a pause</note> is not always a divider, as is clear from this very Song of Solomon, chapters 2:16 and 4:5. 

Careful and exquisite meditation on the passion and death of the Lord is required in a godly person to further incite love toward the Bridegroom, Christ; hence every day the Bridegroom,
<margin>Song of Sol. 5:2</margin>
as night falls, stands in the open air, crying out:
> Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled; for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night.
Consider the discomfort of the Beloved from the inclemency of the night, while the Bride lingers in her peaceful and soft bed, though the Bridegroom surrounds her so he might be refreshed by the Bride's hospitality. The Beloved was suffering, while the Bride was luxuriating. He stood; she lay down. He was awake; she slept. The Bride did not hear the Bridegroom calling; later, she called him herself, but the Bridegroom, who had called before, did not answer. The Bride did not admit the Bridegroom when he sought her; later, she herself did not find the very one by whom she had been sought a moment before. 

The hair on the head is called <term>kome</term> <note>original Greek: *κόμη*</note> from "ornament" and "careful cultivation," for just as baldness is a sign of deformity, so hair is a sign of majesty and beauty. Hair is to be revered in the elderly, venerable in Priests,

<column-break/>

decorous in youths, adorned in women, and sweet
<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
in young girls. *The hair of the Saints is light,* says St. Paulinus in his 4th Epistle, *but that of the impious is heavy; the former is of virtue, as in Samson, or of Sanctification, as in Samuel. The latter is either of weight, as in Absalom, or of squalor, as in Nebuchadnezzar.* 

God usually chooses to use things that seem irrelevant to the matter at hand and makes them effective, so that the splendor of the deed may be greater, and so it may strike the eyes as being not of man, should miraculous works occur. What strength, I ask, is there in hair? And yet God willed his Power to be within it, so that in the eyes of men—who usually look for strength in the loins and sinews—the deeds of Samson might be more illustrious, and so it might be perceived that the strength came from someone other than the man Samson himself. Hence, with his hair preserved, he slew a thousand Philistines, carried away the gates of the City of Gaza with the greatest ease, and performed other heroic deeds surpassing the usual strength of man. There was a marvelous fortitude from unshorn hair; but when it was cut off, Samson was weak, he was bound, his eyes were gouged out, and he was dragged into the mill to turn the grindstone. 

The hair of Absalom was beautiful, and he was proud of it, but it led to his destruction when he hung from an oak tree by it, as if by a rope. While writing this, we happened upon these words by Gretser regarding the "hair-hanging" of Absalom, which are read where he writes: *Let no one wonder that I have called the oak in which Absalom hung by his hair
<margin>Book 1 on the Cross, ch. 6</margin>
a cross: for it was truly a cross and a manifest figure of the cross, in which Absalom, hanging, prefigured Christ.* Truly, one might not undeservedly exclaim with Aristophanes in *The Clouds* upon reading this: <note>original Greek: *πότε μοι λεκάνην* - "Someone bring me a basin!" (an expression of nausea at a bad argument)</note>. 

The hairs of the head are not only for ornament but also for a covering, a point we make not with our own words but with those of Ambrose cited
<margin>Book on Noah's Ark, ch. 7</margin>
above: *How gracefully the hairs of the head clothe the head, like certain attendants of a royal palace, lest the breeze harm the brain, or the rain strike it, or the Sun burn it.* This is why nature gave man the most hair on the back part of the head (these are the words of Spigelius <note>Adriaan van den Spiegel, a 17th-century anatomist</note>) and around the crown; because since he walks with an upright body, he has these parts more exposed to external injuries, especially those falling from above, such as rain and hail. Furthermore, the male sex in humans abounds in hair on the [top] part of the head compared to the [lower] part, because in walking and running with an upright body, he exposes this part to many evils. For if anyone walks through rain, snow, and winds, he will see that the front part suffers greater injuries from rain than the back. From this it follows that those who inhabit Northern regions, like the Germans, protect the front part more than the back with thicker or more numerous clothes. 

Just as it is proper to maintain a decent head of hair according to the custom of the place and time, so it is improper to exceed in nourishing it in the manner of women. This is a practice accepted today, where we see many walking about with great disgrace, adorning themselves—like an "ass in a lion's skin"—with adulterated or artificial hair and wigs, which the Greeks call <term>phnase</term> and <term>pinase</term> <note>original Greek: *φνάση* & *πινάση*</note>. Regarding this indecent use of hair and men who (to speak with Eustathius) "act like women and are fond of their hair," <note>original Greek: *γυναικιζομένους, οἳ τριχῶν φίλωνται*</note> we shall say more below regarding *Isaiah 3:16, 17, etc.* It suffices to note sharply here that Jacob Wimpheling of Sélestat <note>A 15th-century German humanist and reformer</note> rails against curled and counterfeit hair.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "Sacred Anatomy," specifically focusing on the moral and symbolic implications of hair. While the previous page dealt with the beauty of hair as a "crown" and its connection to the purple of royalty and Christ’s suffering, this page shifts to warnings against vanity (curling and dyeing), the physical causes of baldness, its role as a divine punishment, and the honor associated with gray hair as a sign of wisdom.</meta>

<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>
Sacred Anatomy, Book on Youth, chapter 37, folio 17b.
</margin>
writing: *“If long hair, which brings disgrace to a man or a youth, is forbidden by the Holy Scriptures, how much more serious a crime is it not only to twist the hair—which nature gave flat and straight and tinted with a natural color—making it fierce and curly, but also to stain and paint it with deceptive colors. A modest and chaste youth should abstain from such vanity and feminine grooming; for among the Ancients, nothing made one more suspicious of great vice than this most vile curling and shameful wickedness. What greater folly is there than to love one's locks more than one's head, and to cherish the color of the hair more than the liveliness of the senses?”* This is similar to what Dietericus of **Handschuhsheim** <note>literally "Glove-home"</note>, a strong and honorable Knight, wittily said to the illustrious Count in Löwenstein. *“Curling the hair excludes one from the kingdom of heaven; for how will God, the Greatest and Best, deem him worthy of the kingdom of the blessed who, not at all content with his own image, his own face, and his own hair which God handed to him, did not blush to fashion for himself deceptive features, being a despiser and hater of the divine gift and a craver of someone else's? Surely on the last day, the Just Judge will be able to reproach the one with curled hair, saying: ‘We did not create this man; we did not give him this face; these are not the hairs that we bestowed upon him at birth.’”* Thus he wrote. In ancient times, people were exceedingly proud of their hair, and women still persist in that same degree of vanity; they used to use hairpins or "comatory" needles to keep their hair coiled in a circle so it would not flow loosely, about which Isidore <margin>19. Origins 31. column 1307.</margin> says: *“Pins are those things by which the structure of the hair is held together in women for the sake of adornment, lest it flow too loosely and the scattered hair be dissipated.”* Jerome also described them in his commentary on the third chapter of Isaiah, from which the final words could be corrected, for here it is written: *“and being scattered, they are dissipated.”* On this same subject, Martial wrote in a poem titled "The Golden Pin":

> Lest the wet hair violate the thin silk,
> Let the pin pierce it and hold the scattered locks.

Another couplet by the same author refers to this:

> One single ringlet from the whole world of hair had strayed,
> Not well fastened by the inserted pin.

Baldness is the successor to curling and, in general, to all—to use Suetonius’s word—artificial hairpieces. Just as trees lose their leaves, birds lose their feathers, and fish lose their scales, so too do humans lose their hair. If this occurs on the front part of the head, it is called <term>alopecia</term> <note>hair loss starting from the forehead</note>; if on the back, it is called <term>ophiasis</term> <note>hair loss that snakes around the back or sides of the head</note>. It commonly arises from a lack of matter, and its location is the skin of the head, specifically insofar as it is dry; the drier it becomes, the more a man is disposed to "become bald again" <note>original: *recalvescere*</note>. Hence, it follows old age, where coldness and dryness lead the chorus and accelerate the onset of pale death. Sometimes, however, baldness stems from other causes, namely from excessive sexual indulgence, as Aristotle records in Book 3 of the *History of Animals*, and after him Mendoza in *On Generation and Corruption*, page 370; though Mendoza later adds that many lose their hair who have never engaged in such acts. For the moisture of the brain can fail due to excessive study or other deep causes, resulting in the loss of hair. Indeed, I have seen with these very eyes a three-year-old boy, almost bald, who had very thin and elongated hairs on his forehead, which barely lasted two years in that meager state. Very often, baldness occurs as a just punishment from God,

<column-break/>

which God threatens the Jews here and there in the Holy Scriptures because of their former pride, as in *Isaiah 3:16 and elsewhere*. Let us hear what Gaspar Grajat, a Professor at the Academy of Salamanca, has to say on this matter. <margin>Sacred Anatomy on Micah, section 4. A.</margin> *“He turns his speech to the Synagogue of the Hebrews and says: ‘Make yourself bald and shave.’ Show signs of the greatest mourning and sadness over your children, whom you nurtured so indulgently and raised in such luxury. When you see them as captives, and placed in such want and poverty, you shall be made bald; you will be reduced to the greatest shame. It was a disgrace to be bald, which appears evident from what we read: the boys taunted Elisha with this reproach, saying, ‘Go up, you baldhead! Go up, you baldhead!’ And so in Isaiah 3, God threatens the daughters of Zion with it as a maximum evil: ‘The Lord will make bald the crown of the head of the daughters of Zion.’ And further: ‘There shall be baldness instead of curled hair.’ And so he says, you shall be made bald—that is, you shall be reduced to the greatest shame—when your most delicate children are to be led into captivity. And he adds ‘shave,’ which was also said to be shameful, as is clear from Demosthenes, who, when he did not wish to leave his house for the sake of his studies, shaved his head so he would not be forced out by his friends. And so we read in Ovid: ‘A mutilated flock is a shameful thing, and so is a head without hair.’”*

From the Ancients, we add Alvarus Pelagius, Bishop of Silves, who flourished around 1320 AD during the time of Pope John XXII, of whom he was a most fierce defender. He writes, among other things: <margin>2. On the State of the Church 76. folio 204.</margin> *“Pride in hair is found especially in women. Isaiah 3 says: ‘The Lord will make them bald,’ etc. It happened in Paris during a general procession that a monkey snatched the head-veil from a certain lady in front of everyone, along with the false hair she was wearing, and she remained shamed and bald. Hair was given to women for a covering, not for vainglory.”* To this, relate what Strigenitius records in his *14th Sermon on the Deluge, page 65*, about a certain maiden in Saxony who was going to a wedding and adorned herself with someone else's hair. While she was still grooming herself, a skeleton approached her, demanding the foreign hair back and adding a warning that she should take it off to avoid a great evil.

In the Holy Scriptures, "gray hair" <note>original: *canities*</note> receives a greater encomium, being commended for its association with prudence. For prudence grows with age and flourishes in seniority. Comparing the old and the young in the pursuit of wisdom, Jerome writes in *Letter 2 to Nepotian*:

> Almost all the virtues of the body change in the elderly; while Wisdom alone increases, all else decreases. Old age becomes more learned by time, more practiced by use, wiser by the passing of years, and it reaps the sweetest fruits of ancient studies.

He then lists Plato, Isocrates, Pythagoras, Democritus, Xenocrates, Zeno, and Cleanthes, who flourished in the study of wisdom at a great age. However, youth cannot be entirely excluded from all prudence, for sometimes—though rarely—a singular and utterly divine prudence is found in them, as experience and Holy Scripture attest regarding Solomon, Daniel, and others. Hence, Ambrose discusses a similar understanding of youth: <margin>Sermon 2 on Psalm 118, page 604.</margin> *“Gray hair is the understanding of men who possess maturity of counsel and gravity.”* Thus in Jeremiah chapter 1, verse 7, it is said: *“Do not say, ‘I am a youth.’”* And though he was indeed young in age, God forbids him from calling himself a youth, as he possessed a more mature prudence. Daniel, when he was but a boy, received the Spirit...

<meta>This page continues the discussion within the "Sacred Anatomy," moving from the symbolic nature of hair to the physical and spiritual significance of old age and the skin. It focuses particularly on the biblical figures Daniel and Jeremiah as models of youthful wisdom, before transitioning into a dense philological and anatomical study of the skin, centered on the famous "Resurrection" passage in Job 19:26.</meta>

<page-num>783</page-num>
<header>from Psalm 139:15</header>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> ...a rite by which he might be considered worthy of the first fruits of old age, so that he might refute the Elders—himself being older not in years, but in grace. For in him, the age of seniority was an immaculate life. To him, that saying of David applies well: *I have understood more than the ancients.* <note>Psalm 119:100</note> Therefore, the divine Oracle pronounced him a Man of knowledge, as if possessing the counsel and feelings of a veteran: *Who is more prudent than Daniel?* The same Prelate <note>Referring to an ecclesiastical writer, likely Ambrose or Jerome</note> repeats nearly the same things about Jeremiah in Sermon 13 on the same Psalm, page 693. *To Jeremiah making excuses,* he says, *that he was a youth, the response was: Do not say, "I am a youth," because he was not judged a youth by the divine definition, as he possessed a hoary prudence which the grace of heavenly sanctification brought forth.* The cause of gray hair is commonly established by Physicians as an abundance of phlegm <note>original: "pituita"</note>; hence the elderly are said to grow gray because they abound most in phlegm. Truly, phlegm alone does not make gray hair, as experience testifies; compare Scaliger, *Exercise 312*, and Johannes Sperling, *Physical Anthropology, book 1, chapter 16, question 4, page 594.* The corruption of any blood, whether it be melancholic, choleric, or phlegmatic, generates and causes gray hair. For in the elderly, *the flesh is shriveled* <note>original: "vieta"</note>, that is, languid, without force and deprived of natural strengths, to explain it as Festus does. And an old man is shriveled, withered, and flaccid; hence

<margin>The Eunuch, 4.4.</margin> Terence says:
> This man is old, shriveled, lethargic, an elder.

And Prudentius in his second book against Symmachus:
> Whitening with snowy hair and a shriveled brow.

And it is true what the Presbyter of Stridon <note>St. Jerome</note> says in *Epistle 10 to Furia concerning her father, now an old man at death's door <note>original: "capulari," literally "near the funeral bier"</note>, column 95*: *Now the head has grown gray, the knees tremble, the teeth fall out, and with a brow plowed with wrinkles due to old age, death is near at the doors, the funeral pyre is marked out close by. Whether we wish it or not, we grow old.*

Among the common coverings of the head—indeed, of the entire body—the *skin* touches the head and the rest of the body in the most immediate way. Of this, Job says in *chapter 10:11*: <term>skin and flesh</term> <note>Hebrew: "‘or u-basar"</note> *you have clothed me with.* And in *chapter 19:26*: <term>and after my skin they have destroyed this</term> <note>Hebrew: "ve-achar ‘ori niqpu-zot"</note>. The Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note> renders it: *And again I shall be surrounded by my skin,* whom Luther follows: *I shall be surrounded with this my skin.* Pagninus puts it slightly differently: *And after they have worn away this skin of mine.* And Arias <note>Arias Montanus</note>: *And after they shall have worn away this skin.* The Greek versions vary somewhat: In the Royal edition, it is read as <term>the skin</term> <note>Greek: "to derma me"</note>, <term>exhausting these things</term> <note>Greek: "to antlen tauta"</note>. In the Basel edition of 1545 and the Frankfurt edition of 1597, both in folio, it is read as <term>the skin</term>, <term>enduring these things</term> <note>Greek: "to anatlen tauta"</note>, not to mention the different punctuation. The Basel edition along with the Frankfurt has <term>anatlen</term>, a participle from <term>anatleo</term>, *I draw out, I consume*, from which the Latin *antlare* and *exantlare* <note>to draw out or endure to the end</note> is derived; in this way, Job's misery and his tolerance or "exhausting" of evils is indicated at once. Job uses the word <term>skin</term> <note>Hebrew: "‘or"</note> in this confession of his concerning the Resurrection of all the dead, which signifies a pelt or skin, so called from "nakedness." For the root is <term>‘ur</term>, *he made naked, he poured out, he tore out*. Some derive it from <term>‘ir</term>, *he was excited, he was awakened*, because in the skin there occurs an excitation or awakening to various things due to the power of sensing, or as Avenarius prefers, because it is "excited" by hairs. Schindler

<margin>Lexicon, column 1199.</margin> understands * putrefaction, and renders the words of Job thus: *After (the putrefaction) of my skin.* All the interpreters I have seen depart from the Vulgate or the old Interpreter, except for Luther, whose words

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> we just cited, and Sebastian Castalio, who translates it in this way: *And afterward this very self shall be surrounded by my skin.* Piscator of Herborn, following Tremellius, reads it thus: *And although after my skin they have pierced through this.* However, how this is founded, and what sense might finally emerge from Luther's version with it, I cannot guess. They intend to find fault with the Vulgate and Blessed Luther, because, they say, he gathered the sense from the context of the speech; and because mention is made of the restoring of the flesh, he wished to judge that the man would also be surrounded by this skin and pelt. This was for the sake of greater certainty of faith, and because this exposition is founded in the rest of the Scriptures. But because in Hebrew it says <term>niqpu</term>, which is the 3rd person past in the Piel conjugation from the root <term>naqaph</term>, it signifies not *surrounding*, but the *cutting off* and *erosion of the skin*, which is done by worms. Truly, for that meaning of *surrounding* to be left a place, the root should not be established as <term>naqaph</term>, but <term>qaph</term>, which indeed signifies *to surround* or *to move in a circle*, but it is only used in the Hiphil, of which no traces appear here; for it would be read as <term>heqiphu</term>, not <term>niqpu</term>, which would then be translated as *I shall be surrounded*. But whatever the case may be, Dr. Hannekenius—formerly our colleague in the Academy of Marburg, afterward the most deserving Superintendent of Lübeck, now triumphing among the Saints—determined that Blessed Luther’s version could be defended even from Grammar. Namely, if <term>niqpu</term> is derived from <term>naqaph</term>, just as from <term>yatsaq</term> is derived <term>yatsaqnu</term>, so that Job speaks literally: *And after my skin, these*—namely bones and flesh—*shall be surrounded* (Hebrew past for the future). Thus, <term>niqpu</term> is not active but passive, the Niphal past. And although the Munach accent alone seems to oppose this explanation, he nevertheless thinks it is not of such great importance, because the force of those accents in establishing the sense of scripture is still doubted. Meanwhile, according to the nature of that accent, the words of Job could be rendered thus: *And after my skin, namely the lost one, these shall be surrounded by my skin*; so that the Holy Spirit notes two things: 1. that the skin will be worn away, and 2. that the flesh will be surrounded with skin. These are his thoughts. Blessed Meisner explains in almost the same way in a certain disputation *whose title is "The Faith of Job"*, except that he also recognized a change in number <note>enallage</note> in the verb <term>niqpu</term>, specifically plural for singular, and thus translated: *I know that my Redeemer lives, and that I shall be raised in the last days. And after my resurrection, all this which you see, which is in the world, shall be cut off and perish. But I shall remain a survivor and shall see my God in my flesh.* Job observes in chapter 10 the order of generation in the formation of man: where first the thin skin <note>pellicula</note> is made, then the flesh in it, and only gradually do the harder parts follow. Anatomists are accustomed to divide the parts of the body into the *containing* and the *contained*. Among the common containing parts, the *skin and cuticle* also occur. The skin is described by some as being a very thick membrane, generated from the mixture of seed and blood, possessing a most moderate temperament, the organ of touch, and the covering and defense of the underlying parts. As Galen writes, the skin is the true medium of all extremes—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—and especially that which is in the hand.
<margin>Held at Wittenberg in the year 1616.</margin>

### SACRED ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> This [the skin] is the standard for all things sensible; it is, of course, the instrument of touch, unique to the most prudent of animals. For this reason, it was necessary for the skin itself to be at an equal distance from all extremes. The **cuticle** <note>the outermost layer of the skin, the epidermis</note> is truly a very thin flowering of the skin, insensible and almost bloodless, produced from a thicker residue of the skin—just as a small crust forms immediately on porridge from the cold, or a membrane forms on clotted blood. It is denser than the skin, which is why watery humors being expelled from the inside to the surface of the body easily permeate the skin but stick to the cuticle, and from this, pimples arise. The skin is therefore like a garment for the whole body, with which the entire body is dressed, covered, and surrounded; hence Job uses the word <term>beged</term> <note>Hebrew: בגד</note>, which properly signifies *to clothe, or to put on a garment*. For just as clothing or a dress not only covers nakedness but also wards off all injuries of the air, cold, and heat from the body, so the skin provides the same use. Lest the immoderate approach of air bring harm to the internal members of the body, Nature clothed the whole body and fortified it with this thicker covering to ward off all kinds of injuries. Even though this skin is endowed with remarkable hardness, density, and thickness and is a continuous thing, it nevertheless has very many openings which Nature has preserved for the health of man, from which the rule of Physicians arose: *The more breathable the body is, the healthier it is.* The openings are either manifest or obscure. The former are defined, prepared for the sake of letting something into the body or sending something out. Such are in the eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth, navel, private parts, and anus. The latter are infinite, made for insensible transpiration and the exclusion of sweats and "sooty" vapors. They are called pores, and they differ from the former in size. They are called "insensible," although they do not entirely escape the sharp gaze of the eyes. For they are seen during sweating, when we perceive droplets flowing abundantly from the skin. They are also seen in winter time, when the skin becomes like a goose's <note>"goosebumps"</note>. On summer days, in those of a warmer nature, they are quite open. They are seen, moreover, even in the dead, if the skin is scorched with boiling water or a <gloss>candle</gloss>. Because of these openings, Plato compared the skin to a creel <note>original: "nassa"; a wicker fish trap</note>; for just as entry into a creel is easy but exit is difficult, so the entry of things into the body is ready, but the return is not so easy. The skin is provided with a roof, namely the cuticle, although the skin is six times thicker than the cuticle in all parts of the body, and thus frequently also on the head. Closely following this is the <term>fat</term> <note>original: "pinguedo"</note>, produced for the protection, moistening, and movement of the underlying parts; it is thin on the head, lest vapors be hindered from exhaling by too much softness, but thicker in other parts of the body. *For it covers the whole body*, says Spigelius\*, <margin>book 4, chapter 1</margin> *and protects it against external injuries, and preserves natural heat. It protects, indeed, both against cold and heat, and thus in both summer and winter time, etc.* Consult him in the cited place for more discussion on this matter. Beneath it, in our head, is contained the <term>fleshy layer</term> <note>original: "panniculus carnosus"</note> or *fleshy membrane*, as they call it, sometimes also called <term>flesh</term> <note>original: "caro"</note> by Hippocrates and Aristotle, although in the head a human has little flesh and fat, lest the pores be hindered and closed by it, and the senses of the head might be purer and more perfect. Beneath these integuments

<column-break/>

hitherto reviewed are contained the bones which constitute the skull-cap and contain the substance of the Brain within themselves; in a single word, they are called the <term>Cranium</term>. They are covered by a membrane which in other parts is called the <term>periosteum</term>, that is, the *covering of the bones*; in the head, however, it takes its name from the cranium and is called the <term>pericranium</term>, as if <term>around the skull</term> <note>original Greek: περὶ τὸ κρανίον</note>, because it is around the cranium or skull-cap. This membrane adheres chiefly to the Cranium and its sutures, through which it exits: for it flows in origin from the **dura mater**, exiting through the sutures within the Cranium to form the pericranium. Thus, it is no wonder if, when the pericranium is injured, inflammation can be communicated to the dura mater. As for what concerns the Cranium, it is so called because like a <term>helmet</term> <note>original Greek: κάρα, "head," linked here to the Latin "galea" or helmet</note> it defends the brain from external injuries; it is harder in males than in females. The upper part of the head is what properly constitutes the <term>calvaria</term> <note>the skull-cap</note>, and it is composed of eight bones in adults, and nine in a child, for in the latter there are two *frontal bones*, but in adults only one; two *sincipital* or *bregmatic* bones <note>the parietal bones</note>; two *temporal* bones; one *occipital*; the *Sphenoid* or *wedge-shaped* bone, and the *Ethmoid* or *sieve-like* bone, from which bones the round head is constructed. It is not, however, entirely spherical, for it produces prominences in the posterior and superior parts, and a depression in the lateral parts, all of which are joined and bound by their own sutures, which Anatomists treat by profession. All the sutures come together into a triangle in the middle of the head, placed here by Mother Nature for the purpose that, among other uses it provides the head, they may serve for the easier emission of the head’s irritating vapors; whence it is established by experience that men lacking the proper number of these sutures suffer especially and most frequently from <term>headache</term> <note>original: "cephalalgia"</note> compared to those in whom Nature produced the sutures in the proper number.

Concerning the brain, which according to the Philosophers is the *instrument of the heart*, whence Aristotle\* says: *The brain moderates the heat and fervor of the heart, and brings about a balance.* According to the Physicians, however, it is the principle of the animal faculty, the principle of sense and motion, as Galen describes it in *book 8 on the use of the parts, chapters 2 and 5*. Regarding its two membranes, which are called <term>meninx</term> <note>original Greek: μῆνιγξ</note> by the Greeks, and by Aristophanes <term>thrion</term> <note>original Greek: θρῖον</note> because they are similar to the leaves of figs, but are called <term>mothers</term> <note>original: "matres"</note> by the Arabs, it remains for us to touch upon them briefly for you. There are two meninges: one external, the other internal. The former is closer to the skull, the latter to the brain. The former is hard and thick, the latter thin and soft. They are called "mothers," either because like mothers they watch over and protect the safety of the brain, or because it was believed by the ancients that the rest of the membranes originated from them as if from mothers and fountains. The <term>Dura Mater</term>, as they call it, has four sinuses, two of which are positioned at the sides between the cerebrum and cerebellum; these indeed, originating from the Sphenoid bone and tending toward the back, are terminated in the region of the Occiput. The third, which is larger than the aforementioned, is located in the upper part above the falcate process <note>the falx cerebri</note>; this arises from the anterior part of the head, near the ethmoid bone, and extending upward and tending toward the occiput, reaches its goal along with the lateral ones. The fourth, more slender than the others, descends into the cerebrum and cerebellum, which after it has sent out the vein from which the <term>choroid plexus</term> arises, [continues] almost to the middle...

### FROM PSALM 139, VERSE 15.

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
...the sickle-shaped process <note>the *falx cerebri*, a fold of the brain's outer membrane</note>, toward the front, reaches the internal side and there finds its end. The use of these parts is to receive the veins; for when the internal jugular veins reach the hard membrane <note>the *dura mater*</note>, they enter the sinuses, through which they carry blood to the brain. Many branches of veins exit from these ends, and especially from the third—indeed, an infinite number—which surround the brain, wrapped in the thin membrane <note>the *pia mater*</note> both in the lower part and the upper part; then, spreading through the hard membrane, they tend toward the skull, which they even perforate. The thin membrane, or the "pious mother" (*pia mater*) as they call it, is delicate and transparent; it is three times larger and more expansive than the hard membrane, which surrounds the brain at least in one part like a sickle, but the "pious mother" covers the entire brain, both on the outer upper and lateral parts, as well as the internal. Indeed, it seems to have been made by the Parent of Nature for this purpose: to cover the whole brain, for it wraps all the windings or coils, and to hold the vessels which are scattered through the brain by its mediation, lest they be torn from their positions. The brain is fortified by these coverings, which according to Plato is "most divine" because of the wonder of its creation and arrangement. The brain is the most excellent among the internal organs and is closest to heaven, which is why Homer even calls it "heaven." For just as these lower things are governed by God and the influences of the heavens, so the rest of the organs of the human body are governed by the brain. Hence Strigelius writes in his third book of *Elegies* (i. v. 45):

> The brain is the citadel of the whole; with its rotating healthy vapor,
> ->It is the path for movements and tender senses.<-
> The heart holds the kingdoms of vital heat in the middle,
> ->And performs its sweet duty with the brain assisting.<-

And Pliny in Book 2 of his *Natural History*, chapter 37, says: *The brain, the most exalted of all organs and closest to the heaven of the head, is without flesh and without impurities. This is the citadel held by the senses.*
<margin>4. Medical locations 9 p. 91.</margin>
*All the force of the veins from the heart tends here; here it ends. Here is the highest peak, here is the governance of the mind.* For the brain diffuses sensation and motion to the body through the nerves. The heart bestows the vital spirit through the arteries. The liver provides nourishment to the body through the veins. The senses occupy this citadel, as does the intellect itself. For that reason, Constantinus Africanus <note>a 11th-century physician and translator</note> states: *It is established that the brain is the dwelling and foundation of the animal virtue* <note>original: *virtutis animalis*, meaning the powers of the soul or "anima" that govern movement and sense</note>. *The ordering which is effected by the brain alone is divided into three: fantasy, reason, and memory. These three virtues—fantasy, reason, and memory—are called the Mind, by which we differ from irrational animals, and especially by the intellect, because the other two proceed from the intellect.* The ancient Sages located the three operations of the mind in the brain such that "common sense" or apprehension is found in the front part; fantasy and judgment in the middle; and the seat of memory in the back part of the brain. This is why, when we are led by a desire for forgotten things, we are accustomed to rub the back of the head to remember that which has fallen out of memory—hence, "to rub the memory" means to bring it back to mind. Indeed, according to the description of the Interpreters of Nature, the brain is a soft and white part—soft, so that it might more easily receive the things to be known. For that reason, the front part of the brain is softest, the middle somewhat harder, but the back part, where the storehouse and seat of memory is, is the hardest, so that things to be known may be most easily apprehended, judged once grasped, and preserved in perpetual me-

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy v. 791.</margin>
-mory. It is white because the color white is more perfect than the rest and easily admits others. Hence Sophocles calls it *leukos muelos*, or "white marrow." There is a passage in *The Women of Trachis* regarding Hercules, who, having seized Lichas, dashed him against a rock protruding from the sea:
> ...and from the middle of the shattered head
> the white marrow flows out together with the blood.
> <note>original Greek: κόμης δ' λευκὸν μυελὸν ἐκφαίνει μέσῳ / Κρατὸς διασφαγέντος, αἵματός θ' ὁμοῦ.</note>

The brain is larger in man than in other animals; larger in the male than in the female. By its nature, it is moist and cold, so that the whole body may be moistened by it and the heat of the blood may be cooled. From the brain come the nerves, which in our language we call <term>the sinews and span-veins</term> <note>original German: *die Senn- und Span- Adern*</note>, to say nothing of the ligaments by which the joints of the head, trunk, and our limbs are bound and united, and the tendons, <term>the flaxen sinews</term> <note>original German: *die Flachs- Sennen*</note>, which take their name from "stretching" because, like a string, they stretch the limb to be moved and pull it toward themselves. From the brain, I say—understanding at the same time the spinal marrow, which is also called the "oblong marrow" <note>*medulla oblongata*</note>—the nerves arise, dedicated and consecrated to containing and conducting the animal spirit. Therefore, Bonifacius Simoneta says in Book 5, *Epistle 33*: *The brain is the beginning of the nerves; through the mediation of the nerves, it gives motion and sensation to all members. The flesh is also strengthened through the nerves; indeed, the body becomes stronger. Members that lack nerves, such as the liver, spleen, and lung, have a nervous binding.* And Nicolaus Selneccerus says: <margin>Physiology, page 402.</margin> *Since the brain is like a roof built over a smoky house, it receives the breaths or sooty vapors collected and ascending from the whole body; it was necessary that nature grant it more passages than other members, through which it could emit the filth it received. While it confers motion and sensation to the rest of the members, it is not deprived of its own motion, but has its own movement. Daily experience shows this in newborn children, as long as the skull has not yet grown together.* It is also seen in deep wounds of the skull, and I saw it once, not without wonder, when an intimate friend received a wound that lay open all the way to the brain. This nervous genus fosters almost invisible pores; we see indeed nerves pierced by a visible cavity, but the tiny points of the pores are scarcely seen, almost escaping the senses; through these narrow passages, the nerves run out into the entire periphery of the body and exert their power. For through the mediation of the nerves, the eyes see—whence there is a pair of *optic* and *motor* nerves; the ears hear—whence there is a pair of nerves called *auditory*; the nostrils smell—whence a pair of *olfactory* nerves; the tongue tastes—whence there is a pair of *gustatory* nerves. I shall pass over the remaining pairs of nerves, of which physicists count eight from the brain, and another thirty which are said to descend from the spinal marrow alone (though still by mediation of the brain), referring the Benevolent Reader to the books of the Anatomists. Job also mentions the nerves when he says: <margin>chapter 10, verse 11.</margin> **"You have woven me together with bones and nerves."** <note>original Hebrew: וּבַעֲצָמוֹת וְגִידִים תְּשׂוֹכְכֵנִי</note> Just as the natural faculty is diffused with the blood and thicker spirit through the veins, and the vital faculty with the spirit and thinner blood through the arteries, as if through channels, into all parts of the body: so the *animal, sensory, and motor faculty* is carried with the thinnest spirit alone through the nerves, as if through cords, into the parts destined for motion and sense...
<column-break/>
...is carried.

<meta>This page continues the "Sacred Anatomy" series, moving from the physical structure of the brain's membranes to the complex network of nerves that connect the mind to the rest of the body. It transitions into a theological and anatomical study of the eyes, which the author views as the most noble sensory organs.</meta>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
...is carried down. Every nerve at its origin has multiple fibers composed of medullary substance and a thin membrane; as these descend, they are gradually separated from the medulla, and as they approach the openings of the vertebrae, they are clothed in a thick membrane. Joining together, they constitute a single nerve. After this nerve has exited the opening, it is divided again into small cords. As we say, all nerves spring from the brain as if from a common source, and they are all considered to be paired, so much so that no "odd" or single nerve is found.

> You see, says Montanus on pages 233 and 234: In Anatomy, there is a **multitude of arteries wrapped around the brain and spreading throughout it**, because the brain required many **Spirits** <note>original: "Spiritibus"; in historical medicine, these were "vital spirits" or "animal spirits," believed to be the subtle fluids that allowed the soul to move the body</note>, which are transmitted through the arteries, as their proper instruments, throughout the whole body. Where many spirits were necessary, wise and provident Nature fashioned many vessels and receptacles. Thus, since spirits are transmitted to the head, there is a very great consensus through the arteries and veins between the brain and the heart; the heart is the principle of life, while the brain is the principle of the soul. **When the heart suffers, the spirits sent to the brain are raw and "uncooked," and thus unfit for performing mental operations.** <note>original: "animales operationes"; "animal" here refers to the *anima* or soul/mind</note>

So says Montanus in the cited place.

## THE EYES

<margin>2. On Free Will, 18 column 662.</margin>
The eyes, like scouts, occupy the highest place in the human head; they are located *at a certain peak of dignity, as Augustine says*, for the protection of health and many other comforts of life. The Wise Architect of things willed that we behold objects with two eyes, not just one, and these twin receptacles of light were skillfully and cleverly perforated with two sockets. The eyes were established as the dwellings of light, the windows of the mind and intellect, and as Ecclesiastes says in <term>chapter 12:3</term> "those that look through the windows" <gloss>original Hebrew: *be-arubot*; Vatablus understands this as the faculties exercising their office through the windows of the eyes, like stars in the microcosm <note>the "microcosm" is the human body viewed as a small-scale model of the entire universe</note>, which is why the Creator of the Eyes Himself calls them</gloss> <margin>Matt. 6:22</margin> *the light of the body* <note>original Greek: "φῶς σώματὸς"</note>.

Blessed Martin Luther, in his *Commentary on Genesis 29*, compares the eyes, which excel in beauty, to the sun and moon: for just as those two luminaries in heaven are more beautiful and lovely than the other planets, so the eyes surpass the other organs of the face and countenance in their beauty. *The eye is the strongest sensory organ of the head*, says Theophanes in *Homily 42, p. 301*, who had discussed the structure of the eye on <term>page 297.</term> When the heavenly Groom described the beauty of the Bride part by part, he began with the grace of the eyes, for the sake of which the whole body is usually beautified; hence it is said with admiration: <margin>Song of Solomon 1:15</margin>

> How beautiful you are, my love, how beautiful you are; your eyes are like doves.

The Bride also, in <term>chapter 5:12</term>, commends her Groom for the beauty of his eyes and likens them to the eyes of a dove. Those skilled in nature say of the dove's eyes that they are pure because they drink pure water, and they are bright, perceptive, and lovely. On this passage, Ambrose writes in *Sermon 15 on Psalm 118, page 509*: "His eyes are like doves." These are living eyes, clearly adorned with spiritual senses, which are sharp for seeing mysteries and ready for penetrating the divine secrets of Scripture, in which there is no spotted confusion of deceit, but rather the pure and immaculate sincerity of simple affection.

Christ continues with this same similarity in <term>Song of Solomon chapter 4, verse 1 and following</term>, and pathetically outlines the sacred ministry under the name of the "Friend" of singular beauty through an enumeration of her parts.

<column-break/>

Hence, according to some, the simplicity of the Ministers is designated by the "dove-like eyes," the harmony of the ministers by the "curls of the Levites" <note>referring to trimmed hair</note>, the integrity of the Teachers in their actions by the "falling teeth," the parts of doctrine (the Law and the Gospel) by the "ruddy lips," external conduct by the "ruddy cheeks," and the office of correction by the "neck like a tower." Man possesses nothing more precious than his eyes: for mortals begin their life with sight. What is living without sight, if not acting like one deceased in the darkness? Hence, antiquity imagined Death to be the daughter of Night, and an animal without sight is thought of as being without life. The pupil of the eye is, as it were, the eye of the eye itself, says Spigelius in *Physical Anthropology, book 3, chapter 4, page 642.* The eye is the most precious part of our body, and the pupil is the most precious part of the eye. When God Himself expresses His love, He compares each of the faithful to this part: *He who touches you, touches the apple [pupil] of my eye (Zechariah 2:8).* From this arose the proverbial expression calling that which is of the highest value to a person their "eye," which is guarded strictly lest it suffer any harm. Thus Jerome calls *Innocentius, one of his friends, his "eye":*

> Of the two, he says, I have lost one eye; for the heat of a fever has completely snatched away Innocentius, a part of my soul. Now I enjoy only one light with my friend Evagrius.

Ratbertus also aims at this in his *Commentary on Matthew, chapter 5, column 280*: It is common for someone who wishes to show that they love another vehemently to say: *I love him as my own eyes.* And so, to emphasize the greatness of divine love, one reads everywhere that God loves and guards His own like an eye. In Deuteronomy <term>chapter 32:10</term>, the Greek Septuagint has: *He guarded him as the pupil of the eye* <note>original Greek: "ὡς κόρην ὀφθαλμοῦ"</note>. In the Psalm of David <term>chapter 17:8</term>: *Keep me, O Lord, as the pupil of the eye*. In Lamentations, the Greek has, <term>chapter 2:18</term>: *Let not the pupil of your eyes be silent*. And in Ecclesiasticus <term>chapter 17:22</term>: *The favor of a man He will keep as a pupil*. The pupil contains within it an image, which the Greeks call *kore* and *parthenos* <note>meaning "maiden" or "girl," referring to the tiny reflection of oneself seen in another's pupil</note>; those who wish to know the wordplay of the Ancients on this should consult Paulus Leopardus, *Miscellany 24*. In the order of the senses, nothing is more pleasing or useful than the pupil of the eye. *Sight*, says Fulgentius, *inspects the other four senses, because it sees the one who perceives, notes by touching, affects by tasting, and intends by smelling.* The eyes are our "crowned ones" of the body, placed in the highest spot of the head; they lead us into the knowledge of all things and teach us accurately and learnedly to speak of the heavens, air, water, earth, and of both animate and inanimate things contained within them. Eyes are commended for their blackness; hence in Hiscl. *Characters, page 316*, Cassandra is praised for her black pupils and is called *melankoros* <note>black-pupiled</note>, and Polyxena is called *melanophthalmos* <note>black-eyed</note>. Horace, in his *Art of Poetry, line 37*, praises black eyes and black hair together as something pertaining to beauty:

> To be looked at for his black eyes and black hair.

Likewise in his *Odes, book 1, Ode 32, lines 11–12*:

> And Lycus with his black eyes.

So David asks of God *to be guarded* <term>original Hebrew: *ishon bat-ayin*</term>, *as the blackness of the pupil of the eyes*. Arias and Vatablus translate it literally as *the pupil, the daughter of the eye*. However, the word *ishon* <term>Hebrew: אישון</term> in this place does not mean "daughter," but is a contraction, and thus properly signifies "blackness," as is clear from <term>Proverbs 7:9</term>, where it says...

<meta>This page continues the "Sacred Anatomy" series. Following the previous discussion on the nerves of the brain, the author now focuses on the intricate anatomy and spiritual symbolism of the eyes, specifically the protective structures of the eyelids and eyebrows, and the moral implications of "haughty eyes" in scripture.</meta>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
...is called the blackness of night. Regarding the blackness of the eyes, consult Rigaltius’s notes on *Artemidorus*, page 12, and Lambert Alard’s notes on *Valerius*, page 424. The pupils are small, adorned with an iris or "crown," and surrounded by the white of the eye; they are covered by the eyelids, which serve to close and open the eyes. To protect the pupils, the eyelids are fortified with eyelashes <note>original: "ciliis vallatæ"</note> to repel all harm from the eyes. We observe two of these on each side—that is, two *lower* and two *upper* eyelids—which differ in size, as the upper ones exceed the lower. 

<margin>Philippus Presbyter on Job chapter 16, page 66.</margin> Philippus the Presbyter says that *they are called "palpebrae" (eyelids) because they move and throb <note>original: "palpitent"</note>.* They are moved primarily by two muscles: one is external and forms the eyebrow, called the "closer of the eyelids," while the other is internal and called the "elevator of the eyelids." Nature has further gifted the eyes with hairs <note>eyelashes</note> so that nothing, especially flying insects, may enter the eyelid and harm the eye. These hairs extend both toward the forehead and toward the lower parts; hence they are called the "upper" and "lower" lashes. If one of these should ever turn toward the eye and touch it, tears are constantly provoked and vision is impaired until the hair is removed. 

Furthermore, two eminences are seen outside the eye, produced by the processes of the frontal bone. These are sprinkled with hair and possess a lunar shape; they are called *supercilia* (eyebrows) from their location <note>literally "above the lashes"</note>. These were formed by nature so that sweat descending from the forehead would not reach the eye, and so that vision might be sharpened by their shade. Regarding these, Caelius Rhodiginus writes in *Ancient Lessons*, book 26, page 70: *The eyebrows,* he says, *were placed over the eyes with skillful ingenuity so that moisture flowing down might be diverted elsewhere, like a decorative tiling or a gutter—or as the Greeks say, a "geisoma" <note>Greek: γείσωμα, meaning an overhanging eave or cornice</note>.* Although *geison* <note>γείσον</note> properly refers to that which projects over the eyebrows. Hence the term "tent-mates" <note>Greek: Συγεισῶται</note> used in Xenophon. Pollux also mentions this place: 

<margin>Pollux, book 2, chapter 4, page 80.</margin> *The parts of the face are the eyebrow, the eyebrows; and the "cornices" of the eyebrows are the projections. Xenophon says to "overhang" with the eyebrows.* 

It is common to use the word "eyebrow" <note>Greek: ὀφρύς (ophrus)</note> for any eminence of a thing; Strabo uses the same for the "eyebrow of hills" <note>a ridge</note> in book 5, page 165. Similarly, Hesychius testifies concerning the word *ambon* that Aeschylus calls the ascents of mountains *ambones*; compare Eustathius, page 1616. Similarly, the word *ambonis* is read for the edges of the hip-sockets in Galen's *On the Causes of Disease*, book 2. 

David, recounting God’s various favors in delivering him from the hand of his enemies and Saul in *Psalm* 18:27, sets before us the nature of God in His favor toward the humble and His hatred toward the proud: for He is accustomed to be present with the humble and to give them grace. On the contrary, He humbles "haughty eyes" <note>Greek: ὀφθαλμοὺς ὑπερηφάνων ταπεινώσεις; "you will humble the eyes of the proud"</note>, where we read in the Hebrew text: *einayim ramot tashpil* <note>Hebrew: עינים רמות תשפיל</note>. 

Eyes, if they are lifted up, are indicators of pride, which the Psalmist discusses in *Psalm 101:5*. Hence, among the things "hateful to God," Solomon numbers in *Proverbs 6:17* "haughty eyes" <note>Hebrew: עינים רמות</note>, or an "insolent eye" <note>Greek: ὀφθαλμὸν ὑβριςήν</note>. Aquila and Symmachus read this as "lofty" <note>Greek: ὑψηλόν</note> or sublime eyes, from which the Psalmist says he is estranged in chapter 131. In secular literature, the expression "to raise the eyebrow" occurs very frequently, used for an arrogant man. This originates from the fact that just as the ancients established the forehead as the seat of shame, the spleen for laughter, and the nose for anger, so too they determined the eyebrows to be the seat of haughtiness and pride. For by these, disdain and arrogance are declared. Therefore, when they signify that someone is of a lofty mind, the proverb is tossed about: *to raise the eyebrow*...

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> ...when they indicate this vice of the soul; the opposite is *to lower the eyebrow*. For those who despise others and hold them in contempt are accustomed to raise their eyebrows, stiffen their necks, and turn their eyes in various directions by a most wicked habit. Petronius says in his *Satyricon*: "That proud man lifted up his face after he felt himself loved; he raised his eyebrow higher." Pliny writes in book 11, chapter 37: *The eyebrows of man are movable both together and alternately, and in them is a part of the mind: with these we deny, with these we grant: these most especially indicate haughtiness. Pride has a receptacle elsewhere, but here it has its seat; it is born in the heart, but here it climbs, and here it hangs.* Arnobius writes in book 1, page 5 of the Hamburg edition: *It is an exceedingly lofty thing,* and on page 13, *necks lifted with a raised eyebrow,* and in book 5, page 97, *supercilious <note>eyebrow-raising/arrogant</note> cities.* Lansius uses this figure of speech on page 3, concerning the *haughty speech of the Chinese*: *To look down with a high and arrogant eyebrow.* See also Taubman on Plautus’s *The Braggart Soldier*, page 703; Elmenhorst on *Arnobius*, page 22; Pontanus in his *Exercises*, volume 2, dialogue 7, pages 36 and 41; Lange’s *Adages*, page 342; Erasmus’s *Adages*, chiliad 1, century 8, number 49, page 277; and Schott’s *Adages*, page 508.

But so that the eyes might be moved conveniently toward all differences of place—upward and downward, to the right side and the left—Nature granted them seven muscles, as Galen is the authority in *On the Use of Parts*, book 10, chapter 8. Although elsewhere he said that only six were destined for the eyes of humans, which latter number Dominicus de Marchetti also approves in his *Anatomy*, chapter 15, page 207; he recognizes the *seventh* only in animals, which, originating near the optic nerve and involving it, is inserted into the base of the eye, specifically at the place where the optic nerve is. We move no dispute with anyone on this matter, as its debate properly touches the Anatomists; let them see how they settle this dispute among themselves.

The same must be said *concerning the number of tunics <note>coatings</note> or,* as others call them, membranes, regarding which there is also a great dispute among Anatomists: 

<margin>book 10, chapter 9.</margin> *the leaders,* says Spigelius. For the eye is constructed from various parts, but the most principal are the tunics and the humors. Of the former, some count seven, while others count *five*, concerning which see Jacobus Turmannus’s *Dissertation on Vision*, book 1. Of the humors, there are only three: the *Aqueous, Vitreous, and Crystalline*. 

In the eye, the *corneal tunic* is encountered first; it is devoid of color, lest images be infected by a false color from it. It is denser than air, so that visual rays reaching from a thinner medium into a thicker one might be refracted. There follows the *aqueous humor*, which is made thinner than the *cornea*, so that a new refraction may occur. Following this is the *uveal tunic*, so called from its resemblance to grapes <note>Latin: "uva"</note>; in this, one must consider its blackness, the likes of which is seen in no other part of the body. By this, visible things become clearer in the eye, and it prevents them from being so easily scattered by light. This tunic is soft, smooth, and thin, protecting the crystalline humor lest it be harmed by the hardness of the cornea, which is very hard and thick. 

The third is called the *crystalline <note>the lens</note>*, which is likewise smooth and thin, immediately girding the crystalline humor. It also acquired its name from its thinness, so that it is even called the "aranea" <note>spider-like</note>, because by its thinness it resembles the webs of spiders. As for what pertains to the humors, let us note from the encyclopedias of the Physicists: the *Aqueous* is fluid like water, situated in the anterior part, thin and pure; the *Vitreous* is of the thickness and consistency...

...the consistency is similar to molten glass, thickened in color and transparency, situated behind the crystalline humor, most abundant, and filling almost the entire eye. The **Crystalline** humor <note>The lens of the eye</note> is transparent in the manner of crystal, located almost in the middle of the eye, pure, thin, and not prone to flowing away. In praise of this part, we cannot help but record the words of Laurentius *:
<margin>Book 2, chapter 7</margin>
> *To the **Crystalline**, he says, the highest honor is owed. For it is more precious than any diamond, more illustrious than any gem. Therefore, it is often called the soul of the eye, the inner mirror, and the center of the eye. This part alone is altered by colors and receives the "species" <note>The visual images or forms of objects</note> of visible things. When this is present, the faculty of sight is established; all other parts either preserve vision or make it more excellent. Finally, every single part in the eye serves this one as if it were a prince. For the **crystalline** uses the **cornea** like glass for the perfection of human emission. It delights in the **uvea** <note>The vascular layer of the eye</note> as if it were a most pleasant garden, smiling with a variety of colors. The **pupil** acts as a window. The **Aranea** <note>The lens capsule, literally "spider-web"</note> retains the images so they do not flow away, like the lead backing in a mirror. The **Aqueous** humor, like a bulwark, breaks the glare of external light and serves as a medium for carrying images. The **Vitreous** humor, like a cook, prepares nourishment. The **optic nerve** carries the visual spirits to the crystalline, and transmits the images from it to the brain as if to a censor and judge. The muscles and the nerve of the second conjugation <note>A classification of cranial nerves used at the time</note> turn the crystalline and the whole eye in every direction, like a horse. Thus, all things are subservient to the crystalline.*

So he says. Thus far we have spoken of the eye, both external and internal, and its parts, as much as is necessary for our purpose from the school of the Natural Philosophers. There is a noble and intricate controversy among Philosophers and Anatomists—which it suffices to touch upon here with a word—concerning the **mode of vision**. Nor do the Philosophers blow into a single horn <note>meaning they do not agree</note>. For the **Platonists** teach that light goes *out* from the eye, and is joined with the meeting light emitted from objects; that which is formed from the internal and external light is imbued with the form of the objects, and thus vision finally occurs. The **Aristotelians**, however, defend the view that vision happens only by the *reception* of visible forms within the eye. Anatomists admit this question of the mode of vision is intricate and most difficult to solve; among them Realdus Columbus <note>An Italian anatomist, 1516–1559</note> mentions this in *Book 7, chapter 14, On the Fabric of the Human Body*. Vesalius, however, chooses <term>τὸ ἐπέχειν</term> <note>original: "to epechein," meaning "to suspend judgment"</note>. The eye is the instrument of sight, and vision cannot happen except by means of the eye; however, how it happens—whether by emitting or by receiving—we wish to leave to others to dispute. Vision is hindered by various symptoms, and its instrument, namely the eye, is rendered unfit for seeing. From the *Introduction* or the *Physician* of Galen, Renatus 
<margin>in Tertullian, page 148.</margin>
Laurentius de la Barre says that he has numbered more than one hundred and twenty-one afflictions that affect the whole eye. I have not been able to unroll that full count now. However, those things that afflict the eyes can be placed into three categories: namely, from **inflammation** <note>original: "phlegmone"</note>, **discharge**, and **ulcerations**, which Physicians treat more at length. Those who sail toward **Amboyna, Banda, and the Moluccas** <note>The Spice Islands in modern-day Indonesia</note> are often infested with weakness of sight, and even total blindness, caused by thick and slow vapors filling the head, brain, and optic nerves; yet this blindness does not always remain, but often recedes with a change to a different climate or a better diet. The inhabitants of these 

<column-break/>

Islands believe this condition originates (which experience has also proven) from the frequent use of **hot rice**. For rice is usually planted in wet and marshy places, from which it contracts something dreg-like and damp, which penetrates more deeply in heat than in cold; for even the smell of dry and raw rice weighs down the head and induces a certain sleepiness, according to Bontius in *On Indian Diseases*. The light of the eyes fails during a fainting spell. For that reason, in his most mournful complaint of calamities, **David** amplifies the inner sorrows of his soul—which he perceived from the sense of sin and divine wrath—by the joined pains of the body, which stirred the heart of the most afflicted King more toward repentance and prayers. For he seems to have been afflicted in the face of some heavier transgression when, in the devout meditation of the Penitential Psalm (which is held as the third in common numbering), he says: *My heart* סחרחר <note>original Hebrew: "sechar-char"</note> *trembles* or *palpitates; my strength has forsaken me, and the light of my eyes, even they are not with me.* <note>Psalm 38:10</note> It is probable that David at that time also endured external afflictions of the body, by which the inner sorrows of the soul are usually sharpened and incited, and these in turn are increased by the former; since there is a certain <term>συμπάθεια</term> <note>original: "sympatheia," or mutual suffering</note> between the soul and the body, the sorrows of the soul overflow into the body, and those of the body into the soul. It is customary for the Prophets to describe sad and calamitous things by the darkening of the eyes and the failure of sight, as is evident throughout the Sacred Books. Concerning the eyes of the elderly, **Chrysostom** uses the word <term>ὀφθαλμιᾷν</term> <note>original: "ophthalmian," meaning to suffer in the eyes</note> in *Volume 7, question 735*, and thus calls the eyes of the old <term>ὀφθαλμιῶντας</term> <note>original: "ophthalmiontas"</note>, sunken eyes or failing eyes. Such were the eyes of **Isaac**, who was so devoid of the light of the eyes that, even when he did not wish to, he blessed by mistake, being deceived by error (*Genesis 27*). So too **Eli** the High Priest (*1 Samuel 4:15*), and **Jacob** the Patriarch (*Genesis 48:10*). Concerning Jacob's eyes, dim because of extreme old age, **Jerome** says in *Letter 3 to Castrutius, column 265, Volume 1*: *Jacob's sight had grown dull; and while with his inner eyes and a Prophetic Spirit he looked forward to things far in the future, and saw that Christ was to come from the royal line, he could not see Ephraim and Manasseh.* For just as there is a double eye—namely, of the mind and of the body—so also is there a double blindness. *My eyes failed for your word, saying, "When will you comfort me?"* <note>Psalm 119:82</note> Regarding this "failing," Ratbertus writes aptly in *Lamentations of Jeremiah, Book 2, column 1388*: *Praiseworthy and happy is the failure,* he says, *not coming from the weakness of the flesh, but from the strength of desire; because entirely the mind of the Saints, when it intends more ardently and intently upon those things which are not seen and are eternal, fails in its external gaze upon those things which are of the present life and are vain. "For your word," he added. Happy failure, which receives not loss but increase, while the eye grows toward those things which it intends.* Regarding physical blindness, Jerome consoles **Abigaus** and congratulates his soul's eye in a letter given to him: *Do not grieve if you do not have that which ants, flies, and serpents have—that is, eyes of the flesh—but rejoice that you have that eye of which it is said in the Song of Songs: "You have wounded me, my sister, my Spouse, with one of your eyes," by which God is seen,* and of which it is said by **Moses**: *Passing by, I will see this great vision.* And in *Letter 33 to Castrutius, column 265...*
