Joseph, a most chaste youth, is solicited by his Mistress because he was "seen." Dinah, being "seen" by Shechem, led to the destruction of an entire people. The Sons of God, "seeing" the daughters of men, brought about the drowning of the world. David "saw" Bathsheba and solicited her; she, by consenting to her husband's death, prepared a wounded conscience for David. Evil Elders gaze with lustful eyes upon the chaste Susanna, and the dishonest gaze of a woman harms old age. Having "seen" the honorable Susanna, the spirit boils, the eye sparkles, and the body foams with lust. The eyes
<margin>Daniel 13:12.</margin>
of the wicked Elders did not cease, but they observed every day more solicitously to see Susanna. *The Elders saw her,* says the Scripture, *entering and walking about, and they burned with lust for her.* The fire of lust gained strength from constant affection; the location and the eye fed the passion. First there was the danger of the *sight*, then *observation*, soon *conspiracy*, and finally the *seizing* of her in solitude, which Nierembergius elegantly derives in his 8th *Stromata*, chapter 8. The mind, excited by the sting of beauty, immediately conceives malignant desires, and first presents the entire scene of lust within itself and describes the gestures. Old age does not blush to become youthful for lust and luxury, and wandering eyes stir up fires from bones that are as if dead. Is no sight safe at any age! The Old Men burn within, though colder than snow, and feed on a hidden fire, as I might say
<margin>Aeneid, Book 4, v. 2.</margin>
with Virgil, *until it has broken out into a great flame.* For a lustful person, as Jerome says in Book 3 on Ezekiel, ch. 8, col. 776, *who cleverly hides his vices, sometimes demonstrates them through his speech; and a small desire for a thing signifies a greed lurking within; for greater things are shown by smaller ones, and the conscience cannot be disguised by the face and eyes, while a luxurious and lascivious mind shines in the face; and the secrets of the heart are indicated by the movement of the body and by gestures.*

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES ###

<columns>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
...are called. To Solomon, the eye of perversity is mentioned in *Proverbs 21:10*: *he who winks with the eye*, <note>original Hebrew: *yikats ayin*</note> he says, *brings grief*. *He who shuts his eyes to devise perversities, moves his lips, and brings evil to pass.* And in *chapter 21:10*, he continues: *The soul of the wicked desires evil; his friend is not pleasing or favored in his eyes.* <note>original Hebrew: *lo-yechun be-einav re’ehu*</note> The meaning, as explained by <margin>Spicilegium, p. 257.</margin> Rhemius, is: *The envious are to be distinguished by their eyes; they wish well to no one but themselves, and if it goes badly for others, they do not care a bit, because they desire evil to happen.* Just as the mark <note>Greek: *charakter*</note> of envy is a distorted eye, so the mark of a slippery soul is an eye that is inconsistent with itself. A strange man indeed, who does not nod with his head but with his eyes; who speaks not with his tongue but with his feet; who teaches not with his mind but with his fingers. The wicked man, says Solomon in *Proverbs 6:12–13*: *A worthless man, a wicked man, walks with a perverse mouth; he winks with his eyes* <note>original Hebrew: *koretz be-einav*; Greek: *en-neuei ophthalmo*</note>, *he speaks with his feet, he teaches with his fingers.* He composes his whole self so that he might not be recognized; he fakes his expression, blinks his eyes, and uses gestures so that he might seem courteous and refined. "But he is a man of nothing, against whom one must be on guard," as Sirach teaches: <note>Ecclesiasticus/Sirach 27:22</note> *He who winks with the eye contrives evil things, and he who knows him will depart from him.* From the motion or agitation of the eyes, those skilled in physiognomy <note>the art of judging character from physical features</note> judge perversity, a judgment which Aristotle discusses in *Problems, section 31*. Yet, judgment concerning the nature and morals of men taken from the movement <note>Greek: *kinesei*</note> of the eyes is difficult, and it is highly doubtful and uncertain. For we cannot be certain by the testimony of the eyes or the judgment of the mind, as the malice of men often hides itself through various tricks. This is shown by the examples of Absalom, Tiberius, Nero, and many other Princes; at first, out of hope for the purple <note>the imperial robes/power</note>, they walk in the guise of virtue, but once they have obtained the scepter, they cast off the mask. Brunnerus writes elegantly on this matter: <margin>7. Annals of Bavaria, p. 372.</margin> *Among all human honors, the most difficult is the judgment of virtues, whose seat is in the soul, and therefore removed from the eyes; and the signs that come forth are not always sincere, because wickedness long ago simulated the face of virtue with the worst artifice under a mask; and although it has no color of Truth, it has a dye with which even work full of lies is polished; its only reward is the applause of the common people and the whisper of a kinder reputation,* etc. Otherwise, a man’s character is known by what the Hebrew Sages say with an elegant wordplay <note>Greek: *paronomasia*</note>: *in the purse, in the cup, and in anger.* <note>original Hebrew: *be-kis, be-kos, u-be-ka'as* — a famous rabbinic saying from the Talmud, Erubin 65b, noting that a person's true nature is revealed by how they handle money, wine, and temper.</note> In angry people, one can see the wrathful emotion, the bristling and fierce, sparkling eyes; hence Persius says: <margin>Satire 3</margin>
> Now, with the torch applied, the blood boils, and with anger
> the eyes sparkle.
And Lucretius in *Book 3, v. 289*:
> There is also that heat in the soul, which it takes on in anger,
> when it boils, and a fiercer fire flashes from the eyes.
"Terrible eyes" <note>Greek: *Deino osse*</note> are attributed to Pallas Athena in Homer’s *Iliad, Book 1, v. 200*:
> [He recognized] Pallas Athena, and her eyes shone terribly.
Thus in Hesiod, those who show anger in their faces are said "to have eyes that storm"; compare Barth on *Claudian p. 311*, Alard on *Valerius p. 267*, Plautus in *The Captives 3.4.62*, *The Menaechmi 5.2.26*, and Statius in *Thebaid Book 11, v. 532*. In terrible eyes, the soul of one raging is described in *Job 16:9*. Regarding this place, Philip the Presbyter writes on *Job, p. 64*: *In terrible eyes, he describes the soul of the invisible enemy raging against him.*

<column-break/>

The passage can also be understood this way: that when Job closed his eyes, composing himself for desired sleep, then a certain dark and horrid shadow of images was threatened against him by the Devil and his associates. Augustine reckons five "doors of corruption": *To many,* he says, *corruption comes through the eyes, to many through a wicked taste, to many through the embrace of adultery.* The same Bishop of Hippo repeats the same sentiment, though in different words, in his commentary on *Psalm 147, column 1712*: *Through five doors something enters through the body to the soul: either it enters through the eyes, which may desire wrongly; or through the ears, or through smell, or through taste, or through touch. Whoever does not admit corruption through these five doors is counted among the five Virgins.* <note>A reference to the Parable of the Ten Virgins in Matthew 25.</note> Radulphus Ardens writes similarly for the *2nd Sunday after Trinity, f. 199*: *Through the five senses, exterior things are tested. The eye tests what is most beautiful, the ears what is most melodic, the nose what is most fragrant, the taste what is most savory, and the touch what is most soft.* This is indeed the duty of the senses enjoined upon them by the Parent of Nature; if they leap across these limits and exceed them, they are warned of their duty by God the Creator. It is indeed difficult to persist on the "royal road" among so many and such great incitements of the flesh, wherefore Ambrose discourses aptly on the danger of the five senses: *Who,* he says, *among so many passions of this body, among such great allurements of this age, can keep his path safe and untainted? The eye looked, and overturned the sense of the mind; the ear heard, and bent the intention; a scent was inhaled, and hindered thought; the mouth tasted, and brought back a crime; the touch felt, and kindled a fire.* The Bishop of Milan was looking back to the fall of our First Parents. For what kind of eyes Eve had in Paradise, we have learned with great loss and indeed inexpressibly <note>Greek: *anekphrastos*</note>; and that she abused them, we deplore not without unceasing groans. Eve saw that the tree was good for eating, and beautiful to the eyes, and delightful to the feeling; she took of its fruit and ate, and gave to her husband, who ate, and their eyes were opened. She saw and she loved; she saw and she ate; she ate and the eyes are opened. She saw and loved vanity; she saw and forgot the commands of God. The apple was beautiful, but the precept of God—which was far more beautiful and delightful—should have occurred to her eyes first. *Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death.* Eve heard this, and since she had the eyes in her own power, she ought to have turned her eyes away from the beauty of the tree. She turned her ears away from the precept; she trusted her eyes more than her ears; she loved the wood, and at the same time plucked the apple, offering her ears as empty to a lie, and her eyes open to the vanity which the Serpent had suggested, saying: *You shall not die, for you shall be like Gods.* This, this was the origin of all evils: to have seen vanity and to have loved it. They are read to have seen, but as if through a dream; having awakened from this dream, they find themselves deceived by the empty phantoms of things. They discover vain images of things in place of true goods. They discover the false pleasure they had loved. If Eve had turned her eyes away from vanity, and turned them to the way of the Lord, she would not have gone astray, and she would not have been the author of death for us.

Crefollius, in his *Sacred Anthology, chapter 11, section 8, page 389 and following*, writes with great elegance regarding the necessary moderation and care of the eyes, as well as their abuse. Our senses must be corrected daily and turned away from the enticements of evil, lest they run headlong into sensuality and vanish into mere physical sensations. Use your eyes not to look upon worldly things with lust, but rather with contempt. Let the ears not listen to illicit or scurrilous talk, but to things that are honorable. Let the nostrils not smell the perfumes of harlots—as <margin>Homily 1 for the 19th Sunday, folio 272.</margin> Radulphus Ardens <note>Radulphus Ardens (c. 1100) was a famous French preacher known for his homilies.</note> says—but rather *spiritual things, the sweetness of virtues. Let the taste not be ensnared by seductive flavors, but by fasting. Let the touch not delight in illicit contact, but in chastity.* Above all, avoid any corruption of the eyes; let the pupils of the eyes be *Virgins*, as Amphilochius elegantly puts it in *verse 113*. Restrain your eyes, and do not let them be cast here and there, for that instability and restlessness signifies a frivolous and inconstant mind. *Let us turn away*, says Ambrose in *Sermon 5 on Psalm 118, page 628, our eyes from vanities, lest the soul lust after what the eye sees. Close the window when you see the beauty of another's wife, lest death be able to enter; let your eyes not see foreign things, nor your tongue speak perversity. Therefore, close your window, so that death does not lie open to the one entering.* But also beware of another's window. *One gazes from her window when the lust of a wanton eye tempts someone.* <margin>On Fleeing the World, chapter 1. page 309.</margin> *Therefore, close this window with the door of the Word, lest you be captured by the eyes of the harlot and snatched away by her eyelids.* Compare this to the same author in *Sermon 6, page 635.* Ratbertus, writing on *Matthew chapter 5, column 278*, says: In the business of piety, one must never retreat, but having loathed the cares of the world, one must strive toward heaven with an un-turned eye and a repentant heart. *The voice of repentance*, says Hilary in his commentary *on Psalm 118, page 512, is to pray with tears, to groan with tears, and through this confidence to say:* **I will wash** my bed every night. *This is the table of the sinner: to weep at the fountain of weeping, and to be moistened by a wide shower of tears.* A tear is defined by Theophanes in this way: <term>A tear is a painful condition, a moisture of the muscles contracted by grief, which, like a squeezed-out drop, is delivered to the veins of the brain, and from there the excess is sent through the entirety of the eyes as nature thrusts it out.</term> <note>Original Greek: Τὸ δάκρυον λυπηρὰ πάθος ἐστὶ νοτὶς συστελλομένων ὑπὸ λύπης τῇ μυῶν, ὡς πὺ ἀποθλεβομένην λιβάδα πρὸς τὰς τὸ ἐγκεφάλου φλέβας ἀποδίδονσαι, κἀκεῖθεν διὰ τῶν ὅλων τῇ ὀφθαλμῶν παραπέμπεσθαι τὸ περιττὸν ἀποκροομένης τῆς φύσεως.</note> According to the teachings of the Masters of Nature, those who are particularly prone to tears and weep at the slightest occasion are those endowed with a colder and moister constitution of body—delicate, soft, and feminine—with a wet, moist, and sluggish brain. Therefore, children and women weep more than men, and any men who possess womanly souls pour out tears more easily and abundantly. Tears also flow more copiously and frequently for those who have larger and looser caruncles <note>The small pink nodule at the inner corner of the eye.</note> and channels in the corners of the eyes. It is known from both sacred and secular literature that tears are not always indicators of a grieving mind, but very often of a rejoicing one. When Joseph and his brothers received one another, their faces dissolved into tears, as seen in *Genesis 45:2, 14.* Likewise, Jacob wept for joy regarding Joseph, who was still alive and had been raised to the highest dignity under the King of the Egyptians, in *Genesis 46:29.* In Cicero, near the beginning of *Scipio’s Dream*, we read: *When he saw Paulus coming, he poured forth a force of tears.* Regarding tears arising from joy, one may consult Weitzius on *Terence’s The Self-Tormentor, 2.3.*

<column-break/>

and in *Prudentius, page 533.* See also Lælius Bisciola, *volume 2, Horae Subcesivae, book 15, chapter 6*; Barth on *Rutilius, page 187*; Camerarius’s <margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> *Historical Meditations, Century 1, chapter 29, and Century 2, chapter 26*; Lotichius on *Petronius, page 414*; and Rittershusius on *Gunther, page 115.* Mary Magdalene, that great sinner mentioned in *Luke chapter 7:38* <note>The text says chapter 9, but the reference is likely 7:38.</note>, washed the feet of Christ with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head as a sign of a heart and soul seriously grieving and truly repentant; concerning her, Christ pronounced in that same place, saying: *Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much.* Regarding tears that sometimes testify to serious repentance, Ambrose speaks thus: <margin>on Psalm 118, Sermon 17, page 727.</margin> *He expressed the repentance of the one performing it greatly, saying that streams of water descended from his eyes; either because through them, as if through the channels of surging floods, a certain flow of such overflowing tears poured itself out, and he was irrigated by weeping through a certain continuous and perpetual flow, or because the eyes themselves descended. For the force of the highest grief has this effect: that with the tears, the eyes themselves seem in a way to descend, because the force of the tears is so great that the eyes are sought to be dissolved into weeping and poured out into tears. Thus the eyes themselves descend as if into streams of water, by which word the vehement impulse of those mourning is declared.* But to finally make an end of speaking about this most noble part of the head, we must use our eyes well while we live in this valley of miseries—namely, to behold the goodness of God in His creatures. Basil of Seleucia elegantly advises this in his *First Oration, page 1*, that we should cast our eyes upon the beauty of the creature, and from there recognize and venerate the Creator of the creature. <term>The whole life of men is set forth to strive for virtue, and the intervals of life look toward the doctrines of the knowledge of God. For what use is it for a man to be formed by God, and to have hoped for that wide hand, and to flourish the eyes with the beauty of creation, but to be blind toward the Author of the world?</term> <note>Original Greek: Ἅπας ὁ τῶν ἀνθρώπων βίος... τυφλώττειν δὲ πρὸς τὸν τῶ κόσμο παραίτιον;</note>

**THE EAR;** The eye is the <term>organ of sight</term>; the ear is the <term>organ of hearing</term>; the nostrils are the <term>organ of smell</term>; the tongue and palate are the <term>organ of taste</term>; the nerves are the <term>organ of touch</term>. <note>The Greek terms used here are *Aisthētērion tēs horaseōs* (sight), *tēs akoēs* (hearing), *tēs osphrēseōs* (smell), *tēs geuseōs* (taste), and *tēs aphēs* (touch).</note> Ears differ little from the eyes in position, but much in judgment. Hence, in Hebrew, Ears are called <term>moznayim</term>, <note>Hebrew: מֺאזְנַיִם</note> a name which signifies a scale or a balance. For they are like two pans, in the middle of which is the pointer, which the Italians call the *linguetta* (little tongue); this is because the tongue, before it leans to one side or the other, must examine and diligently weigh through the ears what needs to be done. However, it cannot do this unless it has first received into the scale-pans everything that is to be received, so that it may then pass judgment through the tongue as to which side weighs more. Therefore, one must first hear, then respond and pass judgment. Octavianus de Teso on *Ecclesiastes chapter 10, verse 8, page 440.* Julius Mazzarinus also observes the same: <margin>on Psalm 50, page 516.</margin> *The Hebrews,* he says, *use the word <term>ozen</term> <note>Hebrew: אֺזֶן</note> in the plural number, which signifies both ears and a balance or scale. For the ears are attached to the head on this side and that in the manner of a balance, in the middle of which sits the little tongue, decreeing the weight for each thing—that is, Reason or Judgment, which works and rests in a peculiar way in the head because of the senses, the ministers of reason, dwelling there; and thus two ears were attributed to man, not so much for hearing as for diligent weighing...*

<meta>This page continues the "Sacred Anatomy" series. Having previously discussed the eyes and the discipline of the senses, the author now transitions into a detailed anatomical and spiritual examination of the ears and the nose.</meta>

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES ###

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
*By the examination of reason, one may judge the things heard, so that afterward he may cast them aside, preserve them, or excuse them, and congratulate himself by saying: "but you have perfected my ears."* <note>The author quotes a variation of Psalm 40:6, often cited in early modern theology to discuss the "prepared" or "opened" ear of the believer.</note> Indeed, the ears are to be esteemed with no less dignity and value in the human head than the eyes; in fact, some consider them superior to the eyes. For although we see all things by means of the eyes, if hearing fails, we cannot investigate the knowledge of things or their virtues. When the ears fail, we are unable to bring forth words or hear their sound. Hence, Galen and Hippocrates <note>Galen and Hippocrates were the foundational authorities of ancient Greek medicine; their works remained the standard for anatomical knowledge well into the 17th century.</note> testify that those who are deaf from birth are simultaneously mute. Therefore, the ears are of such nobility that the <note>original Greek: $\pi\alpha\nu\sigma o\phi\omega\tau\alpha\tau o\varsigma$ ("all-wise")</note> most wise Architect willed them to be placed in a higher part of the body, so that sound and air might be better received by them. He fashioned them as a pair so that we might have perfection in hearing, and if one should fail, the other might serve. The dignity of their arrangement itself reveals the reason for the order among the members of the head, concerning which

<margin>
Sermon on Sight, column 487.
I.
</margin>
> Bernard* <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and influential mystic.</note> says: *Among the senses of the body, Sight is indeed worthier than all the others; Hearing is worthier than the remaining three. Although perhaps not in utility, Hearing seems to surpass smell, taste, and touch in dignity. Likewise, Taste excels touch, as is manifested by the very arrangement of the members. For who does not know that the Eyes are placed at the summit and the Ears are below them? So too the Nostrils are below the Ears, and the Throat below the Nostrils. It is manifest that the Hands and the rest of the body parts pertaining to Touch are subject even to the Throat.*

So he says. The structure of the ears is no less miraculous than that of the eyes, both in their placement at the temples and whether you look at their internal or external parts. The external part is called the <term>auricula</term> <note>The auricle or pinna; the visible part of the outer ear.</note>; it is immobile in humans but movable in most beasts, and fleshier than in humans. It was formed by the Parent of Nature in an oval shape, not merely for ornament, but primarily to receive sound, so that it might more easily catch and retain it; for the harder a thing is, the more it resonates. The internal part is embedded in the head and bears the name of the whole. In this resides the true instrument of hearing, where one first encounters the <term>narrow and round passage</term> <note>The external auditory meatus or ear canal.</note>, designed so that the exterior air, rushing in suddenly and in a heap, might not damage the membrane that terminates this passage. For they also have their own cavities, membranes, small bones, and a muscle. The cavities are: the <term>tympanum</term> <note>The eardrum or middle ear.</note>, so called because with its membrane it represents the shape of a military instrument, namely a drum; the <term>Labyrinth</term>, which is provided with one opening called the "oval window" because of its shape, where the stirrup bone ends. It is composed of four round cavities shaped like a labyrinth in which air is received and, having been made purer, descends to the <term>cochlea</term>; for the <term>Cochlea</term> <note>Latin for "snail shell."</note> is the third among the cavities, having the shape of a snail shell. There are several <term>Membranes</term>, among which the most notable is the membrane of the tympanum; if it is harder or thicker than it should be, it produces deafness. The *Ossicles* <note>The "little bones" of the middle ear.</note> are three: the <term>Malleus</term> (Hammer), located toward the front, so named because of the rough shape it shares with a blacksmith’s hammer; the <term>Incus</term> (Anvil), so called for its likeness to a smith's anvil—it has two legs and a cavity or sinus in which the head of the hammer rests; and the <term>Stapes</term> (Stirrup), named for the shape of a stirrup it displays, which has a singular sinus in which one 

<column-break/>

foot of the anvil is stationed. It has fifteen tiny <term>Muscles</term> and nerves which contribute much to the winding fabric of the ears, and from the lack of which hearing is rendered imperfect. Hence, those whose external ear has been cut off hear less distinctly and perceive voices like fluctuating water or the sound of a chirping cicada. For just as the flavors of food are perceived and judged by taste—which is sweet, which is bitter, harsh, or endowed with any other quality—so too speech is to be discerned and judged by the ear: whether it be true or false, whether it is to be approved or indeed rejected. To this Job* looked: *Does not the ear test words, and the palate taste food for itself?* <note>Job 12:11</note> Since knowledge and arts are increased through hearing, and the truth of things is judged, there are those who prefer hearing to sight. This is due to the greater utility of hearing over sight, because hearing serves as an aid even to those who are sleeping, so that, awakened by a sound, they may protect themselves. Furthermore, faith comes from hearing, according to the saying of Saint Paul in Romans 10:17. For the ears were given to us for this purpose: that we might hear God speaking to us in and through the Scriptures. We must not be deaf to His voice, nor should a callus be allowed to grow over the ears; rather, we should imitate David, who says: *I will hear what God speaks in me, for he will speak peace to his people.* <note>Psalm 85:8</note> Happy and obedient are the ears that perform this spiritual duty; hence Ratbertus* <note>Paschasius Radbertus (785–865), a Carolingian theologian.</note> says: *Those are the blessed ears of which Isaiah speaks: "The Lord has given me an ear."* So too Job says, *"By the hearing of the ear I have heard you."* <note>Job 42:5</note> For one does not hear except with the ear. But he rightly says he "hears himself" because that which he heard was within, He who spoke was within, and that through which he heard was within. Whence David says, *I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me.* Otherwise, there is no blessedness in hearing and seeing what everyone else hears and sees. But so that this sentence of David may strike our ears and minds more forcefully and cling more deeply to our soul, let us see how the ears are compelled to hear God calling. Through Jeremiah He says in chapter 7:23: *Hear my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people; and walk in all the ways that I have commanded you.* Behold the invitation of God! *And they did not hear,* He says in verse 24, *and they did not incline their ear.* Behold the refusal of the people! On account of this <note>original Greek: $\pi\alpha\rho\alpha\kappa o\eta\nu$ ("disobedience")</note> failure to listen, Ambrose* says God calls the elements to witness to rebuke those who will not keep the divine precepts, so that He may block off every refuge of excuse. Let us accommodate our ears to God, not to the world, nor to Satan, nor to our flesh and its evil affections. For one must be most cautious not only in speaking but also in hearing. *Not only,* says Ambrose in *The Offices, book 1, chapter 18, is it necessary to speak nothing unbecoming, but we ought not even to lend an ear to such words. Just as Joseph fled, leaving his garment behind, lest he should hear things unsuited to his modesty, so also he who delights to listen provokes another to speak.* Therefore, guard your ears, and another's tongue will not harm you.

### THE NOSE ###

is the space between the eyes; it begins from the eyebrows and, extended like an equal ridge, both separates and protects each line of sight. Regarding it, Xenophon says in the *Symposium, page 520*: <note>original Greek: $\dot{\eta} \delta\hat{\epsilon} \dot{\upsilon}\psi\eta\lambda\dot{\eta} \dot{\rho}ì\varsigma, \ddot{\omega}\sigma\pi\epsilon\rho \dot{\epsilon}\pi\iota\rho\epsilon\pi\epsilon\hat{\iota}\varsigma \gamma\epsilon, \delta\iota\alpha\tau\epsilon\tau\epsilon\iota\chi\iota\kappa\epsilon \tau\dot{\alpha} \hat{o}\mu\mu\alpha\tau\alpha$. ("But the high nose, like a handsome wall, has divided the eyes.")</note> Regarding its elegance, Theophylactus says: <note>original Greek: $\dot{\eta} \delta\hat{\epsilon} \dot{\rho}\grave{\iota}\nu \lambda\acute{\iota}\alpha\nu \sigma\epsilon\mu\nu\hat{\omega}\varsigma \dot{\epsilon}\tau\epsilon\tau\acute{o}\rho\nu\epsilon\upsilon\tau o$. ("The nose was most honorably/gracefully fashioned.")</note>

### SACRED ANATOMY ###

#### From Psalm 139:15 ####

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
*...fashioned it, and as the creator of nature on earth, he displayed his skill.* <note>original Greek: τόρνευσε, καὶ πολλῶν γῆς δημιουργὸς φύσεως τὴν ἐπισήμην ἀπήλεγχε. This refers to the divine craftsmanship of the human face.</note> Within the nose, though it is a simple member, three duties are established: the first is *for drawing in spirit and breath*, the second is *for catching scent*. For by this we perceive the sweetness of scents breathed out from flowers, the burning of frankincense and spices, the fragrance of apples, and the delights of perfumes. We perceive not only sweet and pleasant odors, but also the foulest smells of the mouth, the body, corpses, and other things which even beasts cannot bear due to the intolerable filth of the odor. It is natural for the brutes themselves to flee from such things, not only for men, who are refreshed and wonderfully captivated by a sweet scent. Indeed, some possess such a sharp sense of smell that they can scent from a great distance what smells good or bad. Thus men have handkerchiefs to cover their nostrils, because they cannot endure the heavy stench of any mud or other filth of a foul odor, and for this reason, they are accustomed to blow their noses frequently. The instrument for receiving scent is the *internal nose*, which consists of the *sieve-like bone* <note>term: osse cribroso. Known today as the ethmoid bone, it has small holes like a sieve to allow nerves to pass through.</note> and the *nipple-like processes* <note>term: processus mamillares. An early anatomical term for the olfactory bulbs at the base of the brain.</note>. Through the sieve-like bone, the types of scents are carried with the air to the brain to strengthen it. The principal organ of smell, however, is the *nipple-like processes*, about which Laurentius <note>André du Laurens (1558–1609), a prominent French physician and anatomist.</note> says: *The air, altered in those windings, is carried with the scent-type into the nipple-like processes; these are the softest nerves proceeding from the membranes of the brain, both the hard and the thin, though they are not veiled like other nerves. These processes, because they have a peculiar nature, shape, and composition—whereas the bones, cartilages, and membranes are similar everywhere—are believed to be the principal organs of smell.* The third duty is that through its openings and caverns, the waste and mucus of the brain may drip and 
<margin>Chapter 12, 11.</margin>
<margin>On Matthew 3, column 579.</margin>
<margin>Question 74, page 220.</margin>
be filtered out as if through a channel and tube; whence Caesarius* says: *The nose, mediating between the cheeks, draws in and gives back air, channeling it out, along with the fluid from the cranium.* <note>original Greek: Ἡ ῥὶς ταῖς παρειαῖς μεσιτεύουσα ἐφέλκεταί τε καὶ ἀντιδίδωσι τὸν ἀέρα ἐξωχητεύουσα καὶ τὴν ἐκ τῶν κρανίων ἰχῶρα.</note> You will see that the shape of the nostrils is not the same among all men; for some have aquiline <note>term: aquilinis. Eagle-like or hooked.</note> noses, who are generally thought to be endowed with great genius and judgment. Others, however, have snub noses, that is, flattened into the likeness of apes. In the Old Testament, no one dared to approach the priesthood who had a nose that was too small, too large, or crooked (*Leviticus 21:18*). In the Sacred Language <note>the "Sacred Language" refers to Hebrew.</note> the word *charum* <note>original Hebrew: חרום</note> appears. The Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> in their version read *koloborrhin*, meaning "mutilated in the nose" <note>original Greek: κολοβόρριν</note>, as some explain it. In Suidas, *koloborrhin* is "small-nosed" <note>original Greek: μικρόῤῥιν</note>, while *kolos* is "snub-nosed" <note>original Greek: σιμὸς</note>. Whence Rabbi Salomon and others explain it as one who has a nose that is too depressed. The Chaldean Jonathan <note>Refers to the Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> says: *one who is struck in his nostrils* <note>original Aramaic: דלק בחוטמיה</note>, meaning one whose nostrils are flattened as if by a blow; compare Blessed Luther *in his marginal Gloss*. Aben Ezra explains the word *charum* as *superfluous in limbs*, or having one limb larger than the other, but a person with superfluous limbs is actually denoted by the word *sarua*, as is well known. A well-composed nose, corresponding equally to the face, is a singular ornament in a man's countenance; hence the nose of the Bride is praised by the heavenly Bridegroom because it excels in smelling: *Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus.* <note>Song of Solomon 7:4.</note> On Mount Lebanon, there was a tower used as a watchtower, looking toward Damascus, which was the land of enemies; from it, they watched for approaching enemies so they might prepare for war and avoid their snares. Thus the nose of the Church smells from afar 

<column-break/>

the enemies, and just as hunting dogs sagaciously scent everything and most sharply track the footprints of wild beasts, so the Church investigates its enemies most diligently, girds and prepares itself for war, keeps watch, and bears itself strenuously. Regarding this same vigilance of the Bride, Willeramus sings in his Paraphrase on Canticles 7, verse 97:
<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>

> Bride, your nose is skilled to foreknow what smells,
> Like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward the face of Damascus.
> The duty of the nose is to discern with sweetness
> That which reeks badly, that which soothes, or that which
> causes horror.
> So also a fragrant power of soul belongs to your Teachers,
> A sagacious, provident, and truthful discerner of spirits,
> Which is delighted enough by the scent of pure faith,
> And equally abhors the stenches of heretical sects.

No less skillfully than appropriately does the Bishop of Milan, *Ambrose*, discourse upon this likeness of the Bride's nose to the tower of Lebanon: <margin>* Nostrils, Sermon 5 on Psalm 118, page 629.</margin> *Let the nostrils of your soul be turned away from the stench of various crimes; for in these, there is, as it were, a certain mark of judgment. Whence it is said to the Bride: Your nostrils are like the tower of Lebanon, looking out upon the face of Damascus; because the ointment of the True Priest, which descends from the head onto the beard—that is, that divine odor, the odor of Spiritual grace, which was from the Father in Christ and, by the Sacrament of the incarnation, descended to the lands so that all things might be filled with the poured-out ointment—may stand out by the power of high judgment, and fill the nostrils of the soul, so that it may discern between the well-smelling and the foul; the sweet scents of the saints, who can say, "We are the good odor of Christ," from the foul stenches of sinners. These are the nostrils, like the tower of Lebanon raised high above the world, and therefore it looks upon the face of Damascus—namely, the Gentile people—scenting its faith, by whose grace he wiped away the stench of their sins. The face of Damascus, therefore, is the faith of the nations, shadowed by no surrounding, covered by no clothing, naked and free, intent more upon heaven than upon the earth.* These the nostrils of the Church watch and look upon, gathering what is sweet and fragrant in her by the breathing of grace. And her nostrils are rightly like the tower of Lebanon, because in sacrifices there is the odor of the Church's peace, in which there is the victim of good odor: the remission of sins. Physiognomists <note>Scholars who studied a person's character or future from their facial features.</note> attribute much to the nose: to them, a *long* nose signifies an upright and bold person; a *thick* one, the impudent; a *very large* one, a person who reproaches the things of others and extols his own; a *small* one, a shifty person; a *straight* one, a person intemperate in tongue; an *inwardly curved* one, the impudent; and a *hooked* one, the magnanimous. In general, the nose is believed to be the symbol of an angry mind, and its breath usually shows rage. An unfaithful friend is called a *master of the nose* <note>original Hebrew: את־בעל אף ואת איש חמות</note>. The Septuagint reads: *Be not a companion to a hot-tempered man, and do not dwell with a friend prone to anger.* <note>original Greek: Μὴ ἴσθι ἑταῖρος ἀνδρὶ θυμώδει, φίλῳ δὲ ὀργίλῳ μὴ συναυλίζου</note>. Symmachus reads: *do not befriend.* Arias: *Do not associate with the author of the nose, and do not go with a man of heat.* Santes Pagninus: *Do not become a friend to the angry, and do not go with a furious man.* The Vulgate Translator: *Do not be a friend to the angry, nor walk with a furious man.* Luther: *Do not keep company with an angry man, and do not hold yourself to a fierce man.* <note>original German: Gesell dich nicht zum zornigen Mann / und halte dich nicht zu einem grimmigen Mann.</note> Upon these words, Celada* <note>Diego de Celada (1586–1661), a Spanish Jesuit commentator.</note> writes: The Hebrew words translate as: *Do not associate with the Master of the nose; it is the same as one powerful in anger, who abounds in wrath; for this shows itself most especially in a wrinkled and burning nose. Unless you prefer to refer the nose to sneers, mockery, and jests.* Rabbi David Kimchi investigates why the nose is called *aph* <note>original Hebrew: אף</note>, whom I have cited <margin>on Ruth, number 60, page 121.</margin>

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES ###

<margin>Sacred Anatomy page 101.</margin>
See also the work of Kyler in his *Meditations on Lamentations*, chapter 3. In the dual form, the Hebrew word is <term>אפים</term> <note>Appayim; literally "two nostrils"</note>, and it signifies the nostrils; the dual form properly denotes the twin nostrils, and from there it is also applied to the Face, because the face appears as if doubled due to the space between the nostrils. From this comes <term>פנים</term> <note>Panim</note>, which also signifies the Face and is a plural-only noun. Hence, the word <term>אף</term> <note>Aph; "nose" or "anger"</note> appears in the same grammatical form, as in: <term>קצר אפים עשה אולת</term> <note>Qetsar appayim asah ivvelet</note> *Short of nostrils* (that is, quickly becoming angry, or headstrong in wrath) *acts foolishly*, Proverbs 14:17. *Long of nostrils* <note>original: ארך אפים (Erech appayim)</note>, that is, slow to anger, is said of God in Exodus 34:6. The Talmudic scholars ask: Why is God described here as <term>אפים</term> in the dual form, rather than the singular <term>אף</term>? They respond that he is *Long of nostrils* <note>Long-suffering</note> toward both the righteous and the wicked, so that both types of sinners may be invited to repentance through his slowness to anger, *Sanhedrin folio 111* and *Bava Kama folio 50.* This passage is quite controversial due to the <term>interpretations</term> <note>original Greek: ἐξηγήσεις (exegeseis)</note> of the translators regarding Isaiah 2:22: <term>חדלו לכם מן-האדם אשר נשמה באפו כי-במה נחשב הוא</term>. Arias translates it: *Cease you from man, whose breath is in his nose, for in what is he to be accounted?* The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> omitted this verse, but it was restored from Aquila and other translators in the Frankfurt Edition in this way: <term>Cease you from the man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for in what was he accounted?</term> <note>original Greek: Παύσασθε ὑμῖν ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, ὃς ἀναπνοὴ ἐν μυκτῆρι αὐτοῦ, ὅτι ἐν τίνι ἐλογίσθη</note>. Pagninus translates: *Cease fearing for yourselves from man, whose soul is in his nostrils? For what is his reputation?* The Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note> has: *Rest then from man, whose spirit is in his nostrils: because he is accounted as lofty.* Commentators also argue over the meaning. There are those who explain it as referring to common man, a view shared by Piscator of Herborn, whose words follow. *Cease you from man.* The pronoun "you" <term>is redundant</term> <note>original Greek: παρέλκει (parelkei)</note>. The sense is: Cease to trust in man: as is understood from the following words, *in whose nose is breath.* These words contain the reason for the preceding warning against placing trust in man. The sense seems to be: An angry man may indeed huff and puff, but that anger is nothing but a thin and ineffective breath, which is very easily taken away from a man, so that once it is gone, the man perishes. *How much is he to be valued?* In Hebrew: *In what* (that is, with what thing) *shall he be accounted* (that is, compared)? Namely, man. It is as if to say: There is nothing with which he can rightly be compared; he is of no value at all. This is also the opinion of Vatablus, who believes this verse belongs to what follows, and that the next chapter should have begun with it. Assuming this meaning, the Prophet's final words would be the same as saying: *What is he worth? What is there to be done with him?* <note>original German: Was ist doch wol an ihm zu thun?</note> Junius asks: *How much should he be valued?* (he says in his Notes) *What is man? What belongs to man? Or what can be in him that is so great that it does not perish of itself, or is not lost by the will of God in a single moment?* Piscator translates: *Then rather, how highly is he to be esteemed?* <note>original German: Dann lieber wie hoch ist er zu achten?</note> Hetzerus: *Then for what is he regarded?* <note>original German: Dann wofür acht man ihn.</note> Others, however, interpret this as referring to Christ the man, but they adapt it in various ways. Jerome wants the Prophet to mean that the impious ought to restrain themselves regarding Christ, and not oppose him. For even if Christ the man has breath in his nostrils—that is, he is subject to infirmities like other men—he is nevertheless "lofty" because of his divine nature and majesty, and therefore 

<column-break/>

formidable to all. Luther, indeed, attributes it thus: *It is a concluding exclamation: you ought therefore to fear Christ, who is to come here that he himself may reign.* Johann Forster maintains that those words, *to whom Spirit is in the nose*, signify nothing other than a vivid description of the vehement anger or burning indignation of Christ against his enemies, which is discussed in Psalm 2:5 and 13. But the words: *in how much he is accounted*, he takes to refer to the majesty of Christ the man, which he possesses from the grace of personal union with the <term>Word</term> <note>original Greek: λόγῳ (Logō)</note>, and his subsequent <term>exaltation</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπερυψώσεως (hyperypsōseōs)</note> to the right hand of divine majesty. Thus the mind of the Prophet is none other than this: You impious enemies of Christ have heard so far what fate is destined for you, and how great the King's majesty and power are; therefore I seriously exhort and warn you to cease from your impiety and from the desire to oppose yourselves to the King Messiah. If you do not, he will scatter and destroy you with the breath of his wrath. For he is not merely a "pure and simple" man as you suppose, but is one individual person with the eternal and omnipotent Son of God, exalted to the throne of Divine Majesty at the right hand of the eternal Father. The Old Translator seems to look toward this sense: *Because he himself is accounted lofty.* And Blessed Luther says: *You do not know how highly he is esteemed.* <note>original German: Ihr wisset nicht/ wie hoch er geachtet ist.</note> Both read <term>Bammah</term> for <term>Bammeh</term> <note>A subtle change in Hebrew vowels that alters "In what?" to "How great!"</note>.

->THE FACE, which begins where the forehead and hair<-
end, and runs down to the chin, consists of the forehead, nose, eyes, cheeks, lips, mouth, and chin. Among so many thousands of thousands of us humans—who alone are endowed with a face, for the brutes <note>animals</note> do not have a face, nor do they have a variety of faces—Sperling says 
<margin>Compare Argument 41.</margin>
that not even two are found who are alike in every part of their countenance. This itself ought to be counted among the wonders and miracles of nature. Hence, the divine <term>shaping</term> <note>original Greek: πλαστική (plastikē)</note> power is celebrated, as is the wonderful carving of divine craftsmanship. Most Wise Nature has made so many varied things, even making identical things different, so that the countenances of men do not match; so many thousands of faces each have a different form, which is certainly a great prelude to divine majesty and power. Regarding this <term>manifold</term> <note>original Greek: πολυποικίλῳ (polypoikilō)</note> distribution, Julius Firmicus discusses it in *Mathesis, Book 3, page 6*: *Our citizens,* he says, *are all formed with a dissimilar variety of countenance, nor is the form of everyone the same or even similar. If anyone doubts this, which I do not expect, let him look when a multitude of the whole people has gathered in one place, as usually happens in theaters or assemblies. Let him turn the sharp gaze and judgment of his eyes to the form of the whole crowd, and show me, if he can, at least any two among so many thousands of men who seem to be formed with the same and similar lines of limbs. Let fathers, children, and brothers come forth together; though they are joined by the necessity of a single bloodline, they are yet seen with a different designation of forms. Nor is anyone found so similar that his face does not disagree in some part from the face of another.* Felix Platerus also marvels at this same variety of nature in the faces of men in *Book 1.* 
<margin>Question from 10.</margin>
And this is wonderful, he says, especially in man: that from one single human form, the face is so skillfully constructed that so many different forms arise. Scarcely any other diversities of a thing are found in the whole world like this; nor is there one face which, in such a great multitude of men, exists as identical to another in all respects, but for the most part they differ greatly.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the human form as a divine masterpiece, shifting from the anatomical function of the nose to the physiognomy of the entire face. It discusses the theological and philosophical implications of facial diversity and the historical belief that outward appearance reflects inner character.</meta>

### From Psalm 139:15 ###

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
Even among those born of the same parents, the features differ. And although some similarity of faces may be found not only among relatives but even among those of different blood—sometimes so great that we have seen and read of cases, especially among those born in the same birth <note>i.e., identical twins</note>, where they could scarcely be distinguished from one another—this is never so exact that they cannot be distinguished by certain different marks if they are properly observed. This happens in a contrary way in other animals, where many of the same genus are found with forms so similar as to be indistinguishable by hair or feathers. For a perfect analogy is rare, and if any is found in the faces of two men, there is nonetheless no total equality in every line. Pasquier, in *Researches on France*, and after him Martin Zeiler in *Historical Sad Stories*, page 272, testify that Nicolas and Claude de Rouffy were twins endowed with such equality of face, manners, speech, and other qualities that they could not be distinguished. Zeiler cites more examples of this from Fulgosus (Book 9, 15) and Pietro Messia in *The Forest of Varied Lessons* (Part 1, Chapter 38); compare also his *Miscellanea*, page 212. Isidore treats this variety more extensively in *Epistle 114*, page 474. Nothing adorns a man more than his face, and those things which are loved usually depend chiefly on the countenance. I would believe, with Sturm in *Academic Epistles*, page 202, that an obscurity of countenance hindered Pallas <note>Athena</note> in the Judgment of Paris, and that Juno was rejected in the same judgment because of the sorrow in her eyes, which jealousy had brought on. Deformity of the limbs of the body often indicates a deformed soul, as the Ancient Poet says in Stobaeus, *Sermon 88*:

<margin>Anthropology Book 2, Chapter 6, page 639.</margin>
> Having a form unpleasant to the sight,
> Do you also have ways similar to it?
<note>original Greek: Μορφὰς, ἀτερπεῖς ὄψεσιν κεκτημένος, Παρεμφερεῖς ταύταισι τοὺς τρόπους ἔχεις;</note>

In Vatinius, the deformity of the body competed with the baseness of the soul, so that his soul seemed enclosed in a most worthy dwelling, as Vellejus Paterculus says. So too Zeno, whom the Emperor Leo the Great removed from the hope of succession because of a spirit that was not at all noble and a form unworthy of the Empire; he had both a most hateful face and a far worse soul, according to Zonaras in *Leo the Great*. Hence Aristotle also warns elsewhere that one must carefully beware of those whom nature has marked with an indecent appearance, as if they were worse people. This also points to that French saying: *he is marked by the B.B.* <note>The "B.B." stands for Bastard, Borgne (one-eyed), Bègue (stammerer), Boiteux (lame), and Bossu (hunchback). Historically, physical disabilities were often cruelly associated with moral failings.</note> And Martial agrees in his epigram about Zoilus:

<margin>Book 2, epigram 69.</margin>
> Red-haired, black-mouthed, short-footed, one-eyed,
> You perform a great feat, Zoilus, if you are good.

Also:

> Your mind is as lame as your foot; nature
> holds certain external marks of the internal self.

And Palladas on a lame man:

<margin>Book 2, Epigrams.</margin>
> You have a lame mind just as you have a lame foot; for truly
> your nature possesses an external image of what is within.
<note>original Greek: Χωλὸν ἔχεις τὸν νοῦν, ὡς τὸν πόδα. καὶ γὰρ ἀληθῶς Εἰκόνα τῆς ἐντὸς σὴ φύσις ἐκτὸς ἔχει.</note>

Which Jean Brodeau translates thus:

<margin>See Aristotle’s Physics Book 1, Chapter 2, page 26.</margin>
> As in foot, so in soul you are lame; for the outer limbs
> are the simultaneous images of your internal mind.

And although it sometimes happens that even those of ugly...

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
...form—no less than others, if not by nature then at least by the habit of doing good—carry a mind cultivated by virtues, and they carry that saying of the Poet everywhere:

> If difficult nature denied me beauty,
> I repay the losses of beauty with my talent.

and that one:
*Ulysses was not handsome, but he was eloquent.*
However, this usually happens more rarely, and it moves much suspicion among men, as if the person were of a far worse soul and condition, whom nature itself wished to mark with the deformity of his body and demonstrate him as such to public judgment. Far more is contributed to authority if a soul worthy of a Prince also inhabits a worthy dwelling. For:

->virtue is more pleasing coming from a beautiful body.<-

And every most majestic appearance is believed to have much of heaven in it, whether that divine soul about to enter a body first measures out a worthy lodging, or when it has come, it fashions a dwelling according to its own character, or whether one thing grows from the other, and when equals are joined together, both are greater. (Latinus Pacatus in *Panegyric to Theodosius*, Chapter 6). Concerning the elegance and loveliness of form, the term <term>יפי</term> <note>Yofi; beauty or grace</note> occurs in the Sacred Language, whose proper meaning is grace, because loveliness of form usually procures grace; Moses uses this regarding Joseph in Genesis 39:4, 21. Helen is commended for the loveliness of her form among profane writers; to recover her, a deadly war arose between the Greeks and Trojans, which did not end except with the total destruction of Troy. But what Manasses writes in the *Troics* concerning the commendation of Helen, we apply to the beauty of Sarah, the wife of Abraham—for to compare their morals would be a sin:

<margin>verse 38.</margin>
> The woman was exceedingly beautiful, with fine brows and a lovely complexion,
> with beautiful cheeks and a beautiful face, with large eyes and skin like snow,
> with curling lashes, a tender grove full of graces,
> white-armed, delicate, her beauty literally breathing,
> her face charming, her eyes seasonable,
> a beauty unstudied, self-dyed, of its own color,
> where a rosy fire tinged her whiteness.
<note>The author is using a highly stylized Greek poetic description of feminine beauty to describe the biblical Sarah.</note>

The principle of modesty consists most of all in the face and the look of the whole body, which must be so composed that it shoots a certain ray of internal virtue through all the limbs, and the mind shines in the external face, just as Solomon thoughtfully advises: *Wisdom shines in the face of the wise, but the eyes of fools are in the ends of the earth.* <margin>Proverbs 17:24</margin> Virtue is a great light and consecrates the body, says Seneca skillfully in *Epistle 66*. Correctly, poets are accustomed to paint and sculpt modesty veiled by the face, because even the eyes ought to be chaste and continent. For such is the dignity of the face that from it manifest signs of temperaments and certain diseases can be taken and tracked down. Indeed, we can judge internal things from external ones, as if from their marks and signs. Since the soul uses the ministry of the body, the character, <term>πάθη</term> <note>pathe; passions or emotions</note>, and affections of the soul mostly shine through in it as in a mirror. Thus the face is the mirror of a sad, or stupid, or loving, or joyful soul. A man is known chiefly from his face—who and of what sort he is, both according to the body and according to the soul. As for the body, physicians look for <term>εὐχρωσία</term> <note>euchrosia; a healthy or good complexion</note>, from which the wise old Hippocrates began his discipline of foreknowledge...

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES ###

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
The ability to know and predict character from the face is discussed by Aristotle in the first problem of his 36th section. Those who claimed to thoroughly understand the manners and natures of men from their bodies, eyes, and countenances were called <term>physiognomists</term> <note>From the Greek *physiognomones*, meaning "judges of nature."</note>. Origen mentions three such experts from antiquity: Zopyrus, Loxus, and Polemon <note>Original Greek: $\zeta\acute{\omega}\pi\upsilon\rho\omicron\nu$, $\lambda\acute{\omicron}\xi\omicron\nu$, $\pi\omicron\lambda\acute{\epsilon}\mu\omega\nu\alpha$</note>. Zopyrus is also mentioned by Maximus Tyrius and by Cicero in the fourth book of his *Tusculan Disputations* and in his book *On Fate*. Gregory, in his second *Invective*, writes that he detected a hidden wickedness in the face of the Emperor Julian. For the face, as we have said, is the image of the soul, and the eyes are the soul’s indicators: if the soul is sad, the eyes are sad; if joyful, joyful; if angry, angry. 

Politicians, however—at least those who "do not have a liver made of pumpkin" <note>A Latin idiom meaning those who are sharp-witted rather than soft-headed or foolish.</note>—strive to ensure that nothing is betrayed through the eyes. When their facial expression is deliberate, their mind may hold no such feeling. There is great control of the eyes even in the worst of men, so that no firm conclusion can be drawn from them. Those who wish to outwit politicians use a political stratagem: they suddenly ask a question without preparation, yet after more refined preliminary inquiries, to catch the true expression of the face. In such a moment, the face often betrays the mind. Therefore, once someone has ensured that nothing foolish or overly expressive
<margin>3. On the Orator</margin>
is visible, they must exercise great prudence with their eyes. For as a rule, as Cicero* observed, there are as many signs and changes in expression as there are movements of the soul. Hence Seneca says in his sixth book *On Benefits* (chapter 12): *"I already understand what you want to ask. There is no need for you to speak. Your face speaks."* A cheerful face is the indicator of a joyful mind. Athanasius, in the *Life of St. Anthony*, writes: *"A cheerful countenance follows the joy of the soul, and the disposition of the mind is felt and known from the movement of the body."* <note>Original Greek: $\alpha\pi\grave{\omicron}$ $\tau\tilde{\eta}\varsigma$ $\psi\upsilon\chi\tilde{\eta}\varsigma$, $\iota\lambda\alpha\rho\grave{\omicron}\nu$ $\epsilon\chi\epsilon\iota\nu$ $\kappa\alpha\grave{\iota}$ $\tau\grave{\omicron}$ $\pi\rho\acute{\omicron}\sigma\omega\pi\omicron\nu$, $\kappa\alpha\grave{\iota}$ $\alpha\pi\grave{\omicron}$ $\tau\tilde{\omega}\nu$ $\tau\omicron\tilde{\upsilon}$ $\sigma\acute{\omega}\mu\alpha\tau\omicron\varsigma$ $\kappa\iota\nu\eta\mu\acute{\alpha}\tau\omega\nu$ $\alpha\iota\sigma\theta\acute{\alpha}\nu\epsilon\sigma\theta\alpha\iota$ $\kappa\alpha\grave{\iota}$ $\gamma\iota\nu\acute{\omega}\sigma\kappa\epsilon\iota\nu$ $\tau\grave{\eta}\nu$ $\tau\tilde{\eta}\varsigma$ $\psi\upsilon\chi\tilde{\eta}\varsigma$ $\kappa\alpha\tau\acute{\alpha}\sigma\tau\alpha\sigma\iota\nu$</note> This is proven there by examples from Holy Scripture: Proverbs 15:13; Laban in Genesis 31:15; and David in 1 Samuel 16:12. Laban, the father-in-law of Jacob, is noted for his facial hypocrisy, yet he did not have his face so well under control that it did not betray his deceiving mind to his son-in-law Jacob. Regarding facial hypocrisy, Apuleius* says: *"Testifying to deeply hidden fraud with a broad face."* And elsewhere: *"To hide joy with the face and suppress the expression."* Virgil also touches on this in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*:

> She hides her plan with her face, and clears hope on her brow.

And again:

> He feigns hope with his face, while pressing deep grief in his heart.

But for the most part, the face reveals the secrets of the heart. Sallust elegantly writes in the *Jugurthine War*: *"The Moor, having summoned his friends and then immediately changed his mind, is said to have wrestled much with himself after the others were removed, his face and body varying along with his mind; these movements, though he was silent, revealed the secrets of his heart through the appearance of his face."* The change of expression and face in Nebuchadnezzar was a companion to his fierce pride, as Nierenberg writes: *He is filled with a fury that glory could never satisfy. Fury is the solemn miscarriage of pride. Whoever does not flatter him, he considers an enemy, and he turns his frustrated lust into a madness which, though the mind does not taste it, it belches out through the face, showing a deformed vice with a deformed look.* There is no constant face for one who is full of desires. His face changes as often as his desires; it is painted by whatever circumstances occur and colored by his emotions. He is never consistent, as he is driven by the inconstancy of

<column-break/>

desire and not led by reason. The internal changes of an indignant soul shine forth in the face through changes of color, as Horace says in his first book of *Odes*:

> My burning liver swells with difficult bile;
> Then neither my mind nor my color
> Remain in a fixed seat.

The faces of the angry are seen to catch fire, which is said of Cassius: *"Anger is a sudden rush of the spirit, which overflows with fire."* <note>Original Greek: $\dot{\eta}$ $\mu\grave{\epsilon}\nu$ $\grave{\omicron}\rho\gamma\grave{\in}$ $\alpha\theta\rho\acute{\omicron}\alpha$ $\tau\tilde{\omega}$ $\pi\nu\epsilon\acute{\upsilon}\mu\alpha\tau\iota$ $\epsilon\sigma\tau\iota\nu$ $\epsilon\nu\delta\rho\omicron\mu\grave{\eta}$, $\acute{\omicron}\pi\epsilon\rho$ $\pi\epsilon\rho\iota\alpha\sigma\epsilon\acute{\upsilon}\epsilon\iota$ $\pi\upsilon\rho\omicron\acute{\iota}$.</note> Thus, Claudian, in his *Panegyric* for Mallius, commends a tranquil mind:

> The eyes maintain their temperance, nor does fervor
> Sharpen the light, or spread rabid blood through the veins,
> And no storm of a changed face is betrayed.

**THE FOREHEAD** is the most excellent part of the face, which is not covered by hair as in brute animals, but is open; for it does not belong to the hairy part, but the smooth. The human forehead is hairless <note>Greek: $\alpha\tau\rho\iota\chi\acute{\omicron}\varsigma$</note>, a unique ornament of the human race. It is the index of sadness, joy, mercy, severity, magnanimity, modesty, and even immodesty. For when we are angry it becomes clouded, and when we rejoice it is smoothed out. This smoothing is called *chalada* by Aristophanes*: *"Listen now, my little horseman, relaxing your forehead a little"* <note>Greek: $\chi\alpha\lambda\acute{\alpha}\sigma\alpha\varsigma$ $\acute{\omicron}\lambda\acute{\iota}\gamma\omicron\nu$ $\tau\grave{\omicron}$ $\mu\acute{\epsilon}\tau\omega\pi\omicron\nu$</note>. To "relax the forehead" means to loosen a drawn and wrinkled brow and let those wrinkles flow away, which Horace said in his 13th *Epode*:

> Remove the cloud from your brow; for the most part the modest man
> Takes on the appearance of the gloomy, and the silent man the appearance of the bitter.

Conversely, we are said to "contract" and "draw" the forehead when we are either angry or sad, about which Horace says in the same *Epode*:

> It is fitting that old age be released from its drawn forehead.

And Juvenal in his 9th *Satire*:

> I should like to know why, Naevolus, you so often meet me
> Sad, with a drawn forehead, like the defeated Marsyas.

The forehead is the index of the mind, which is why we say we "perceive from the forehead" that which becomes known to us at first glance. Hence Cicero to Antony: *"For not only from your speech, but even from your face, your eyes, and your forehead, as they say, you could have perceived my love for you."* Yet the nature of each person is often covered by many layers of wrinkles and as if by certain veils; the forehead, eyes, and face very often lie, and speech most often of all—so much so that in this time of ours, the forehead says one thing and the mind another. Aristophanes alluded to this in *The Knights*:

> It is evident to us by our faces, 
> Whether they rejoice in words and in deeds.
> <note>Original Greek: $\epsilon\pi\iota\delta\acute{\eta}\lambda\omicron\nu$ $\dot{\eta}\mu\tilde{\iota}\nu$ $\tau\omicron\tilde{\iota}\varsigma$ $\pi\rho\omicron\sigma\acute{\omega}\pi\omicron\iota\sigma\iota\nu$ $\pi\omicron\iota\epsilon\tilde{\iota}\nu$, $\tilde{\eta}\nu$ $\tau\omicron\tilde{\iota}\varsigma$ $\epsilon\pi\epsilon\sigma\iota$ $\chi\alpha\iota\rho\omega\sigma\iota$ $\kappa\alpha\grave{\iota}$ $\tau\omicron\tilde{\iota}\varsigma$ $\pi\rho\acute{\alpha}\gamma\mu\alpha\sigma\iota.$</note>

The forehead was sacred to modesty in antiquity (compare Rigolt on Artemidorus), which was also said of the face, hence Artemidorus*: *"The face is the image of shame and of honor."* <note>Original Greek: $\epsilon\sigma\tau\iota$ $\tau\grave{\omicron}$ $\pi\rho\acute{\omicron}\sigma\omega\pi\omicron\nu$ $\tau\tilde{\eta}\varsigma$ $\alpha\iota\delta\omicron\tilde{\upsilon}\varsigma$ $\kappa\alpha\grave{\iota}$ $\tau\tilde{\eta}\varsigma$ $\epsilon\pi\iota\tau\iota\mu\acute{\iota}\alpha\varsigma$ $\epsilon\iota\kappa\acute{\omega}\nu.$</note> Conversely, a person is said to have "rubbed their forehead" <note>An idiom for losing all sense of shame.</note> who has renounced and forgotten all modesty. Hence Seneca says in his 40th *Epistle*: *"You ought to rub your forehead, so that you do not even hear yourself."* Concerning a sinner in Holy Scripture who offends God and is not flooded with a blush of shame, Jeremiah 3:3 says: *"The forehead of a harlot woman is made for you; you refused to blush."* And Augustine on Psalm 141: *"What does it mean, 'he has no forehead'? He is impudent."* One might refer here to the secular Horace, who sings in his second book of *Epistles*:

> Nearly all the Fathers cry out
> that modesty has perished.

**THE CHEEKS** lie beneath the ears, nose, and eyes on both sides...

They are located below [the eyes] and extend to the chin; because of the roundness with which they are mostly endowed, they are called the "apples" <note>Original Latin: *mala*, referring to the cheekbones or the fleshy part of the cheeks.</note>. Their color is commonly white and red, and they are witnesses of one's temperament or <term>good health</term> <note>Original Greek: *euexia* (εὐεξίας), meaning a sound constitution.</note>. Thus, in Homer, a man whose cheeks bloom with their native color is called **beautiful-cheeked** <note>Original Greek: *kalliparēos* (καλλιπάρῃος), Iliad book 1, line 143</note>. Purple cheeks are also a part of graceful beauty in Ovid’s *Amores* (Book 1, Elegy 4). The bride’s cheeks are likewise praised for their loveliness by the groom in the <margin>Song of Solomon 1:10</margin> **Song of Solomon 1:10**: *Your cheeks are beautiful between the rows* <note>Original Hebrew: *torim* (תּוֹרִים)</note>, *amidst the strings of jewels.* Rabbi David Kimchi says that these "rows" (*torim*) are gems or pearls bound together in a certain order or arrangement, as is customary in the headbands of noblewomen; he argues the word *tor* means the same as <term>form or disposition</term> <note>Original Hebrew: *tecunath* (תְכוּנָה)</note>. Others translate it as "lines of small stones." Others see "figures depicted" in the likeness of a turtledove (which is also called *tor* in Hebrew), and therefore some translate it as "with the beauty of turtledoves." Similarly, in chapter 5:10, the bride praises the groom's cheeks, saying: *His cheeks are like beds of spices*, pleasant in both sight and scent. Redness in the cheeks is the heat of virtue. Regarding the face of Christ the Savior, Nicephorus (Church History, Book 1, Ch. 40) testifies that his face was **wheat-colored** <note>Original Greek: *sitochroos* (σιτόχροος)</note> and that his face had a moderate reddish tint.

### THE CHIN

The chin is the lowest part of the inferior jaw, for the upper part pertains to the cheeks. In the human face, it is shorter and rounder as a singular ornament, and for that reason, it is immobile, to avoid the deformity of wrinkles during eating and speaking. In animals, the chin is a place of great strength, which is why they do not easily allow themselves to be grabbed by it; yet we read that David did this <margin>1 Samuel 17:35</margin> (1 Samuel 17:35). In ancient times, it was a sign of affection when someone took a friend by the chin to offer a kiss, a gesture Joab used when meeting Amasa <margin>2 Samuel 20:9</margin> (2 Samuel 20:9). The chin ends in a circular shape. Those who have a very round chin are categorized by **physiognomists** as "womanly"; those with a **small** chin as "harsh" and "treacherous"; those with a **long** chin as having "good morals"; and those with a **cleft** chin as "deceitful" and "fickle." A youth begins to **grow a beard** <note>Original Greek: *geneian* (γενειᾶν)</note> from the fifteenth year and brings blood to the chin, according to Solon's <margin>Solon, Elegy of the Weeks</margin> *Elegy of the Weeks*:
> In the third [seven-year period], the chin grows hairy
> on the growing limbs, as the bloom of the skin changes.

<margin>Oneirocritica 6. 41 p. 32</margin>
Achmet says: *The hairs of the beard are the ornament of the body.* And Hilary (on Psalm 132) says: *The beard is the ornament of the male age.* Hence Diogenes said he wore a beard so that he might remember he was a man. For the beard shows the man, and it is not the way of a man to love smooth cheeks. Thus Clement of Alexandria (Book 3, Ch. 3) asks: *Is it not womanish to shave, pluck, and smooth the jaws?* And shortly after: *God adorned the man with beards like lions, and with hairy chests... this is a sign of strength and authority.* And a little later: *This beard is the token of a man, by which the man is revealed.* For the beauty of a man is one thing, and that of a woman another. Nature gave man a beard to recognize the maturity of the body, to differentiate the sexes, and to cover the parts, says Sperling (*Anthropology*, Book 2). But sometimes among the ancients, the custom of shaving the chin <margin>Oneirocritica p. 219</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
and the head prevailed, and sometimes the custom of growing the hair and beard long <margin>Hist. tr. P. 802</margin>. Regarding this custom, William of Tyre <note>A 12th-century chronicler and archbishop.</note> says: *It is the custom for Orientals, both Greeks and other nations, to nourish their beards with all care and anxiety, and to consider it the greatest reproach and the worst ignominy that could ever be inflicted if even one hair is injuriously pulled from the beard.* How shameful the shaving of the beard was in the time of David is clear from 2 Samuel 10:4, a crime David punished severely among the Ammonites. Regarding Mephiboseth, the author of 2 Samuel (19:24) records that he went down to meet the returning David, *and he had not dressed his feet nor trimmed his beard* <note>Original Hebrew: *v’lo-asah raglav v’lo-asah sephamo*</note>. The Septuagint reads "mustache" <note>Original Greek: *ton mystaka* (τὸν μύστακα)</note>, a term Arias retains. But Pagninus and Vatablus translated it as "lip," and Junius as "beard." The old translator says, "with unwashed feet and an unshaven beard," meaning he had not cared for the shaving of the hair on his upper lip. Jerome (Questions on the Book of Kings) writes on this passage based on the opinion of Hebrews and Jews: *It should be noted that in the Hebrew it reads 'uninfected feet': for Mephiboseth had made for himself wooden feet, which he used as if they were natural, as the lame are accustomed to do.* But this is ridiculous and conflicts with the context, unless one wishes to imagine something similar about his beard.

### THE TOOTH

The tooth (*dens*) is said by some to come from "eating" (*edendo*), as if it were "the eater." To others, it comes from the Greek *odous*, though that also comes from "to eat." Finally, others derive it from the Hebrew *shen*, from which, by rearranging the letters, comes *ens*, and by adding the letter 'd', *dens*. Teeth are counted among the bones, and not without reason. For their material is bone, which is animated by nature so that it may feel; hence they are described as very cold, very dry, and very hard—the hardest of all bones, hollow inside, provided with nerves, veins, and arteries, and dedicated to chewing and preparing food. In their hardness, they surpass stones, and thus they cannot be consumed by fire <margin>Gatack on Mark, p. 124</margin>. Although they are not surrounded by skin like other bones, they still feel, especially cold and vinegar, which "sets the teeth on edge," as Solomon testifies <margin>Proverbs 10:26</margin> (Proverbs 10:26). The cause of this sensitivity is commonly attributed by researchers of nature to a membrane hidden in the deeper ends of the teeth and a nerve with which the inner part of the tooth is provided. In the <term>sockets</term> <note>Original Greek: *bothria* (βόθρια)</note> or cavities of each jaw, the teeth are fixed; in an adult human, there are **thirty-two** of them, sixteen in each jaw. They lie hidden for a time in the jaws, even though they begin to form from seed in the womb, so that they do not harm the mother's breasts. They erupt in the seventh month or later; when these fall out around the seventh and fourteenth years, new teeth emerge in both jaws, much harder, more solid, and thicker than the first. The teeth are held in two rows, one upper and one lower. However, history records that Direptina, daughter of Mithridates, had double rows of teeth, and Hercules had triple rows in each jaw. The teeth in our mouth do not all have the same name, but some are for cutting food...
