<meta>This page continues the anatomical and physiognomic study of the human body, moving from the cheeks discussed on the previous page to a detailed examination of the teeth and lips, blending biological function with moral and biblical symbolism.</meta>

<page-num>798</page-num>
<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
They take their name from this, and are thus called *Incisors* or "front teeth"; among the Greeks they are known as **splitters** <note>original Greek: *dichastēres* (διχαστῆρες)</note>, because they split the food, and for that reason they are also called **cutters**, **combs**, and **the laughers** <note>original Greek: *tomeis* (τομεῖς), *ktenes* (κτένες), and *gelasinoi* (γελασινοὶ), so called because they are visible when one smiles.</note>. Following these in both the upper and lower rows are the *canines* <note>original Greek: *kunodontes* (κυνόδοντες)</note>, so named because they can crush even the hardest things, or perhaps called **eye-teeth** because of the nerve that extends toward the eyes. Closing the ranks of all the teeth are the molars, the **cheek-teeth** <note>original German: *die Backen-Zähne*</note>. A tooth is called a "key" <note>original Hebrew: *maphteach* (מַפְתֵּחַ)</note> in the Talmud <note>Tractate Shabbat, folios 49 and 89</note>, where the word **lock-key** <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: *kalkelida* (קַלְקְלִידָא)</note> appears, which seems to me to be taken from the Greek **key** <note>original Greek: *kleis kleidos* (κλείς κλειδός)</note>. The initial letter *Q* <note>original Hebrew: *koph* (ק)</note> is a linguistic addition, and so that word is undoubtedly distorted from the Greek, just as many such terms were brought by the Rabbis into their own language. Among the Greeks, they are called **completers** <note>original Greek: *krantēres* (κραντῆρες)</note> because they appear last, and **soberers** <note>original Greek: *sōphronistēres* (σωφρονιστῆρες)</note>, the **wisdom teeth** <note>original German: *die Zähne der Weißheit*</note>, which usually grow only in the twentieth year of life, or sometimes even in the sixtieth year in old women. Cæsarius <note>A 4th-century physician and brother of Gregory of Nazianzus</note> mentions this division of the teeth in his <margin>Question 74, page 220.</margin> writings: *Teeth,* he says, *are by nature the servants of food. Some are for cutting, others for grinding; the cutters are in the front, the grinders are further in, appropriately named for thinning and smoothing the things brought to them.* Teeth were created for chewing. As Jerome says <note>In his first book against Jovinian</note>, *it is the office of the teeth to chew, and to transmit those things which are chewed into the belly.* And Ratbertus <note>Paschasius Radbertus, a Carolingian theologian</note> says: *There are different chewing duties for the teeth. Some indeed divide; others crush and ruminate; others form voices and, with the tongue, distinguish sounds.* We also consider the teeth ethically, believing they were given to men so that the tongue might be restrained by them; hence in Homer the phrase **the fence of the teeth** <note>original Greek: *herkos odontōn* (ἕρκος ὀδόντων)</note> is frequent:
<margin>Book 1 on the Lamentations of Jeremiah, column 1355.</margin>
-> What word has escaped the fence of your teeth? <-
The ancients used to place great care in cleaning and polishing their teeth, which they also washed and rubbed. To make them brighter, they polished them daily with urine or other most foul substances, as Apuleius testifies in his *Apology*. But it is also clear from the same source that such care for the teeth was once considered a cause for reproach. Hence Jerome says: *You may see them rage with a rabid mouth, and tear at Christians with pumice-polished teeth.* And to the Deacon Sabinianus: *You clothe yourself in linens, load your fingers with rings, and rub your teeth with powder.* This was not a powder composed of "Arabian fruits," such as the one Apuleius had sent to Calpurnianus, as his verses testify:
> Greetings Calpurnianus, in these my verses,
> I have sent, as you asked, cleansers for the teeth,
> Polishes for the mouth from Arabian fruits.
But instead, our mother Eve, by the instinct and persuasion of the Infernal Physician, used a truly poisonous substance, by which her teeth were so infected and fouled that the **indelible** <note>original Greek: *anexaleiptos* (ἀνεξάλειπτος)</note> impurity was transplanted into all her posterity. The tooth was poisoned when Eve pressed it into the apple, from which poison came into the entire human race. A single bite of the apple threw the soul into a thousand disturbances and exposed the body to a thousand diseases. That bite was a sign of disobedience; thus, whatever internal or external miseries have arrived, they came from that bite. If there had been no bite, no death would have come. Life would have remained tranquil and free from all disturbance

<column-break/>

if Man had remained obedient. Thus, that one tooth branches out beyond measure into many poisonous teeth, such as anger, greed, lust, hatred, gluttony, avarice, and so on. *These are evil and tenacious teeth.* For through these, says Hilary <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers</note>, they rule over us once we are captured and torn apart, making us either servants or companions of their vices; by these, they would chew not our flesh, but our souls, if God were not within us. It is clear from the Holy Scriptures regarding the impious that they gnash and grind their teeth to overthrow the godly (Psalm 35:16). Ambrose, commenting on Psalm 36, says: *It is the custom of one who is indignant and boiling with anger to gnash his teeth. But the wicked also have their own teeth, with which they are accustomed not to make noise, but to tear. Traps, plots, and wickedness are the teeth of the sinner.* Hence David, snatched from the predatory gaping of their teeth and freed from the deadly snares of their traps, walks full of joy, proclaims the divine benefit with a free voice, and praises his most powerful deliverer with a similar formula of thanks, saying: *Blessed be the Lord (Psalm 124:6), who has not given us as a prey to their teeth. Our soul, like a bird, has been snatched from the snare of the hunters.* From the body to the soul, therefore, expressions are frequent, such as that concerning the gnashing of teeth, to which Hilary refers: *The divine word signifies the vices and movements of souls under the guise of bodily offices; as in the Song of Deuteronomy: "The beloved grew fat and kicked," rebuking the luxury of impiety under the sign of a bodily habit; or that phrase: "Who devour my people as the food of bread." Or also: "You have broken the teeth of the sinners." And also that of the Apostle: "But if you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another," so that the duty and action commanded for each individual limb is referred to the effectiveness of minds and souls.* When about to commemorate the effects of either persecutors or detractors, he says: *The sons of men, their teeth are a shield and an arrow, and their tongue a sharp sword; since they both consumed by the cruelty of power and wounded with the darts of detractions.* Thus he spoke.
**LIPS** are the covers of the teeth and mouth, and are divided into upper and lower. They serve the teeth, which they guard; they also contribute to the breaking of the air and lead to the formation of the voice, which is why certain letters that cannot be pronounced without their help are called **labials**. From the variety of lips, Physiognomists are overly generous in their judgment. For red lips denote a good temperament to them, while lead-colored ones denote a bad one. Thick lips signify foolishness, thin ones a high-spirited person, tiny ones a fearful person, hanging lower lips a lazy person, and protruding upper lips an injurious person and a liar. Appropriately, the lips are called a **door** <note>original Hebrew: *delet* (דלת)</note>, according to Rabbi Mordechai Nathan, because they are opened and closed in the manner of a door. During prayer, the lips move themselves, which is called **the lips moving** <note>original Greek: *ta cheilē dialelein* (τὰ χείλη διαλελεῖν)</note> by Lucian. Regarding Hannah, the mother of Samuel, the Holy Scripture testifies that she spoke only in her heart, with only her lips moving and her voice not heard at all. Lips are named after wisdom (Proverbs 14:7): **lips of knowledge** <note>original Hebrew: *shiphte-da'at* (שפתי-דעת), Greek: *cheilē sopha* (χείλη σοφὰ)</note>, which adorn a man and are accepted by all. However, the words and deeds of a fool are unpleasant, whose company is to be avoided, as Solomon says: *Go from the presence of a foolish man, when you do not perceive in him the lips of knowledge.*

It contrasts the physical function of chewing with the "poisonous bite" of sin and the "lips of knowledge" praised in scripture.</summary>

He was not a **Man of words** <note>original Hebrew: ish devarim (אִישׁ דְּבָרִים)</note>, as an eloquent man is called in the idiom of the Holy Tongue in Exodus 4:10. The lips are open for kisses, and the seat of love lies in the little lips of the bride. Hence, the love of the Church, described as a bride for her groom, is expressed with delightful words at the very beginning of Solomon’s Hymn <note>The Song of Solomon or Song of Songs</note>: *Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.* Kisses are impressed upon the mouth, and from this the name is derived, because kisses are fixed upon the little lips of the mouth. "Affix, I pray," says the bride to the groom, "kisses; give a thousand and then another thousand kisses. Grant that I may enjoy the lips of your sacrosanct mouth; press your lips to mine. Let this be the first sign of our love. Let there be a bond of kisses by which I am tied to you." The bride begins her discourse from a custom common among Eastern peoples, so that she might all the more manifest her desire for her groom. Ambrose valued these words of the bride so highly that he mentioned them several times, such as in Sermon 1 on Psalm 118, page 597. In the Song of Songs, he says, the mystical shines forth alongside the moral, expressing the sweetness of flatteries and the affection of lovers: *Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine.* Imagine a virgin betrothed for a long time, burning with a righteous love, who has learned of the many noble works of her Beloved through the testimony of reliable witnesses; she is frequently delayed with suspended desires and, no longer tolerating delays, she has done everything to see her groom. Finally obtaining her wishes, she is overwhelmed with joy at the groom's unexpected arrival; she does not offer the usual beginnings of a greeting or an exchange of words, but immediately demands what she had desired. So it is also with the Holy Church, which was betrothed in Paradise at the beginning of the world, prefigured in the flood, announced through the law, and called by the Prophets; she waited for the coming of the Beloved for the redemption of men and the beauty of the Gospel. Impatient with delay, she rushes into kisses, saying: *Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth*, and delighted by the kisses, she adds: *For your breasts are better than wine.* He continues: the Church or the soul of the righteous man had seen the groom looking through the windows, standing out above the lattices; she exults and rejoices because she is also loved by the groom, who, as if himself wounded by the beauty of love, was present for kisses when asked by his beloved who was previously absent. For he is asked when it is said: *Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.* Then he did not despise the prayers and flatteries of the bride, who offered her breasts to her beloved, and he kindly led her into the inner parts of the house. Then, as if playing with a frolicsome love because he wished to test the senses of the lover, he often went out to be sought by the bride, and often returned to be invited to kisses. He stood behind the wall, looked through the windows, and leaned over the lattices so that he was not entirely absent, nor did he enter as one who was fully sought, so that he might call the bride to himself, and that the interactions of coming to one another might become more serious, and the force of love might grow through these playful delays. Ratbertus <note>Paschasius Radbertus, a 9th-century theologian</note> imitates this in his Exposition on Psalm 44, column 1263. The Bride says: *Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.* For she knew that the Almighty had diffused this grace upon the lips of

It is not that the fullness of grace was diffused only on the lips and not on the whole person; rather, it is said to be on the lips because the part represents the whole, and because the grace of the divine word flowed from the fountain of Christ's mouth and filled the entire world. The kiss that is made on the lips is most sweet, which is why Proverbs 24:26 says: <term>He shall kiss the lips <note>original Hebrew: sefatayim yishaq (שְׂפָתַיִם יִשָּׁק)</note></term> who answers right words. Of the lips of the Church, His Bride, the Groom says: *Your lips, my sister, my bride, are like a dropping honeycomb*; her lips are compared in the preceding third verse to *scarlet ribbons*. Gregory the Great, in *Moralia* book 2, chapter 38, interprets these words thus: *A ribbon binds the hair of the head. Therefore, the lips of the bride are like a ribbon because, by the exhortation of the Holy Church, all the scattered thoughts in the minds of the listeners are bound together, lest they flow away in relaxation, or spread themselves through illicit things, or, once scattered, weigh down the eyes of the heart; rather, they collect themselves as if into a single intention while the ribbon of holy preaching binds them.* Theodoret, Philo of Carpasia, Cassiodorus, Gregory, Bede, Anselm, Bernard, and others understand "lips" to mean the Doctors <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to the great Teachers or theologians of the Church.</note> of the Church. Among them, Theodoret says: *The lips signify the Doctors of the Church, who carry, as it were, honeycombs of bees on their lips and flow with drops of honey; yet they have not only honey, but also milk, bringing forth salvific food for everyone—fitting for infants as well as for the perfect. The honeycomb of honey carried on the lips of the Doctors is the Divine Scriptures, which contain both the wax and the makers of honey: namely, the holy Prophets and Apostles, who, flying through the meadows of the Holy Spirit and establishing the cells of the divine scriptures, distending them with the honey and nectar of doctrine, transmitted them to us for our benefit. Indeed, the letter appears similar to the wax, but the sense hidden within it is like the honey; drops of this honey flow from the lips of pious Doctors.* And Gregory says: *In the honeycomb, the honey is hidden and the wax is seen. Rightly, therefore, are the lips of the Bride called a honeycomb, because while great wisdom is held within the fragility of the flesh, it is hidden like honey in wax; but when any chosen one preaches, when he reveals heavenly joys to those who do not know them, then the honeycomb drops, because he manifests to the listeners through the fragility of the mouth how much sweetness of wisdom lies hidden in the heart.* Thus he says. Bede, comparing both verses of this fourth chapter, says: *It is not contradictory that the lips of the Bride were compared above to ribbons and now to a honeycomb, since the latter delights the throat with satiation, while the former binds the hair by tying it: the latter refreshes within, the former binds without. For the same Doctors are both ribbons in their salvific precepts and a honeycomb in their heavenly promises: ribbons while they call us back from the flow of carnal pleasures; a honeycomb when they promise us the gifts of supernal joys.* Our lips, considered according to the **inner man** <note>original Greek: kat’ esō ton anthrōpon (κατ' ἔσω τὸν ἄνθρωπον)</note>, are like a honeycomb in the mouth of Christ, insofar as we draw the honeycomb from the apiary of Holy Scripture: otherwise, in themselves, they are void of all good, indeed, full of uncleanness, which is why Isaiah cries out: *Wretched am I, for I have unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips.* Immediately, one of the Seraphim descends and approaches him, touching his lips with a coal to cleanse his unclean lips.

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
For this reason, the mouth is concave, so that it can both receive and contain food, and also admit and release the air itself. Based on the structure of the mouth, those who practice divination <note>This refers to physiognomy, the ancient practice of judging character from physical features.</note> claim that a *large* mouth indicates a bold, warlike, and gluttonous person; a *small* one indicates an effeminate nature; one that is *overly widened* indicates a person who is voracious, impious, and cruel; and one that is *protruding* suggests a person is senseless and a boaster. The mouth is closed and opened by the lips. The lips are like a door to the mouth, whose slips are various and through which we can easily fall. Regarding this "door of the mouth," the Psalmist speaks in Psalm 141:3: *Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips.* Some take the word <term>shomrah <note>original Hebrew: שמרה, meaning "a guard" or "watch"</note></term> as a verb, which Junius and Tremellius translate as: *Arrange, O Jehovah, a watch over my mouth.* Most others translate it as a noun, following the form of <term>chochmah <note>original Hebrew: חכמה, meaning "wisdom"</note></term>. He asks God to be guarded, lest he compete with his enemies in curses, or, considering the prosperity of the wicked, break out into murmuring against God from impatience. Similarly, some translate <term>nitzrah <note>original Hebrew: נצרה, meaning "keep" or "watch"</note></term> as a verb, "observing" or "guarding." Others translate it as a noun, "observation," following the form of <term>shifchah <note>original Hebrew: שפחה, meaning "maidservant"</note></term>. They say the letter *Tsade* has a *Dagesh* <note>A dot used in Hebrew grammar to indicate emphasis or doubling of a letter.</note> for the sake of euphony, and that this word is governed by the verb "set." Let us note what Hilary <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century theologian.</note> writes on these words of the Psalmist:

<margin>on Psalm 140 page 618.</margin>
> *He prays for no light guard to be placed over his mouth—specifically, a door around the bones—so that this guard is not just a simple observation, but a barrier. For the slip of the tongue is dangerous and very easy; from it, curses, lies, perjury, and slander are brought forth with a quick movement and an open path. Let us therefore pray for a "door of restraint" for ourselves. In that book which is inscribed as Solomon's among us, but is held as the Wisdom of Sirach <note>Also known as Ecclesiasticus.</note> among the Greeks and Hebrews, we are thus warned: "Make a door and a bar for your mouth, and a yoke and a measure for your words." He ordered a door and a bar to be placed on the mouth, lest there be an easy exit for words. By these same words, he established a yoke and a measure, so that, subjected to the yoke of reason, they might hang balanced by the measure of moderation.*

In both sacred and secular literature, the word "mouth" is understood in various ways and attributed to various things, not all of which are our purpose to list here. A "mouth" is attributed to the earth in Genesis 4:11, receiving the blood of Abel killed by Cain, the first fratricide.

<margin>on Job 9 page 34.</margin>
*Just as there is an excess in some things,* says Philippus the Presbyter, *insensible things are sometimes said in the Scriptures to feel, as in: "Cursed is the earth, which opened its mouth to receive the blood of your brother."* He notes on these words: *My garments shall abhor me; for clothes cannot abhor anyone, being inanimate and insensible things, but he said this to exaggerate the filth of wounds and rot.* Because of the Devil’s tricks, which are difficult to scout out, Job attributes a mouth to him when he says in chapter 41:4: *Who shall enter into the middle of his mouth?* Regarding this, Gregory the Great in his *Morals* (Book 33, 22) says: *Understand this as: "unless I, through the discerning minds of the chosen, discuss the words of his suggestions, and show that they are not as they sounded." For they seem to promise good, but they pull toward a lost end. To enter into the middle of his heart, therefore, is to penetrate the words of his cunning, so that it is not weighed by what they sound like, but by where they intend to go.* Adam did not want to enter the middle of his mouth when he neglected to cautiously weigh the intention of that persuasion; for he believed he would receive divinity through it, and yet he lost immortality. Thus says Gregory. Through the taste and instinct of the Devil through the woman, Adam, the first man, lost

<column-break/>

these gifts granted to him by God, the giver of all good. In the matter of taste, therefore, be sober; and you will think you have progressed in it only if, through an exquisite flavor, you know the "taste" by which the Lord is sweet, according to that word of the Psalmist:

<margin>* Psalm</margin>
> *Taste and see how sweet the Lord is. Taste, how great is the multitude of sweetness for those who fear Him, and for those who love Him in truth.*

If you apply yourself to this "devout taste" with a devoted heart, you will learn through happy experience that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. Then the speech of the Lord will become sweet in your mouth and in your throat, more than honey and the honeycomb; and your soul, fattened by these feasts, will easily be able to despise the delights of food and meat, through the abundance of which the flesh rises against the Spirit. The Psalmist does not speak of physical taste, nor of the mouth of the body, nor of the spirit and desire for material things, but of the taste and sweetness of divine speech. Whence also in Psalm 119:131, he says: *I opened my mouth and drew in the Spirit, because I longed for your commandments.* With such sharp desire and greedy mind did he long for the celestial glory of God, that having set aside all the riches and pleasures of the world, he rested in the word of God and His glory alone. Hence in Psalm 51:15, he breaks out into these words, and we with him: *O Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth shall declare your praise.* Appropriately, therefore, Hilary writes: *Just as we take in food for the nourishment of the body through the mouth, so through the heart we receive the food of heavenly doctrine for the vivification of the soul; which, unless they are drawn in by an enlarged and open heart, will not help. It is written in the Law: "Write these things on the width of your heart." For the preaching of God is received by the heart, not the mouth. When the heart is open through faith, and gaping with desire to drink it in, the understanding of heavenly doctrine is received.*

THE TONGUE <note>Latin: *Lingua*</note>, according to Varro, seems to be named from "binding" <note>Latin: *ligando*</note>, because it is surrounded and bound by the fence of the teeth as if by a wall. To others, it comes from "licking" <note>Latin: *lingendo*</note>, because it licks by flattering, bites by detracting, and attracts by lying. To Scaliger, it comes either from the Greek <term>leicho <note>original Greek: λείχω, meaning "to lick"</note></term>, or from the Hebrew <term>lashon <note>original Hebrew: לשן, meaning "tongue"</note></term>, whence <term>al-shon <note>original Hebrew: אל-שון, perhaps referencing the definite article and tongue</note></term>, speech. Nature hid the tongue as if in a cave and bound it with many fetters: above, under the furthest parts of the palate; then at each side of the furthest throat; then with restraints stretching to the chest; and below, in the lower jaw even to the rampart of the teeth. This part is called the <term>hypoglottis <note>original Greek: ὑπογλῶττις, meaning "under the tongue"</note></term> by the Greeks; it is so restricted that for some, an incision is necessary so that they may speak clearly. It is moved by muscles upward, downward, forward, backward, and to the sides (right and left), in which fibers are interwoven—see Bartholin, Book 3, *Anatomical Institutions*, chapter 13. For this little body is joined together from various parts. It consists of nerves, arteries, a ligament, a frenulum, muscles, a membrane, and its own flesh, which in the human mouth is very soft and wide, so that it can contract, dilate, extend, etc. It is primarily the organ of taste, to which speech is added. So that it might perform both duties, it received salivary moisture. Hence the great dignity of the tongue, since the nobility of speech is so great. For everyone has their own speech, just as they have their own face; and there are as many speeches as there are mortals. The tongue is the organ of speech—not the eyes, nor the ears, nor the fingers, nor the feet. Whence the tongue is called by Dresser <term>the mother of speech and messenger of the soul <note>original Greek: λαλιῆς μήτηρ καὶ ψυχῆς ἄγγελος</note></term>, and similarly by Nonnus in Book 26, line 262.

Sacred Anatomy: The heart is a storehouse. For this reason, Philip the Priest <note>A 5th-century commentator and student of Jerome</note> says in Book 2 on Job 19, page 79: *The teeth, the tongue, and the lips are the vessels of words; for through these, the storehouse of the heart is displayed from the outside, while they bring forth for us the inner senses through the service of their own distinct parts.* He says the same in chapter 31, page 138: *Articulate voice is produced by the teeth and the plectrum <note>The 'plectrum' of the tongue refers to its role in striking against the teeth or palate to produce sound, much like a pick strikes a lyre.</note> of the tongue.* The tongue is the character of the mind, through which we explain and set forth the thoughts of our mind. How much evil there is in a perverse tongue, and how much good in a modest tongue, Solomon teaches in Proverbs chapter 18:21: *Death and life are in the power of the tongue.* The best treasure of the tongue, according to Hesiod, is found if that rule is observed: *Nothing in excess.* <note>original Greek: μηδὲν ἄγαν</note> Speech serves wisdom if it is established with self-censorship; for this is the beginning of speaking well, as David teaches in summary. He wisely saw this and said from experience: *I said, I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue.* For, as Ambrose says in *On Duties* (Book 1, chapter 2): *Because he knew no one could keep themselves pure from the uncleanness of speech, he imposed upon himself a law of silence for the sake of innocence, so that by staying silent he might avoid the fault he could hardly escape by speaking.* A wise man guards his ways so he does not sin, observing the path of the kingdom of silence. Thus Ambrose exclaims in his commentary on Psalm 38, page 521: *O silence, the strong shield of circumspect defense! O most faithful foundation of stability, in which if anyone can stand, he cannot easily slip into a reckless word. For many, even those firm in heart, yet incautious, have often fallen through the error of wavering speech.* The same Father, recently praised, continues on the same Psalm (page 522): *Silence is both safe and decorous, which preserves caution with gravity.* For what are our lips if not a kind of bond for us? *Everyone is bound by the chains of their own lips.* Therefore, a wise man remains silent at the right time and considers within himself when he ought to speak, about which Solomon himself brilliantly says: *The lips of the Wise are bound by understanding.* Therefore, when you see a wise man remain silent before mocking and arrogant people, say: *This man has bound his lips with understanding—that is, he is wisely silent.* For the same reason, "thought" is attributed to the tongue in *Psalm 50:4* <note>In some numbering systems, Psalm 52:2</note>, since one must not speak unless the thought is premeditated. Whence,

<margin>on Psalm 51, p. 362.</margin>
Here Saint Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century theologian</note> says: *The duty of the human tongue is, by natural impulse and reason, through various and changing movements, to distinguish the voice into words, so that through it, speech should emerge from the confused sound of the breaking Spirit as something distinct for the understanding of things; and although its rational movement is for this purpose, it is understood to be subject to reason rather than possessing the sense of reason itself. But that which lacks the sense of intelligence also lacks the instinct of reason and the meditation of counsel: and how is it correctly understood as being said by the Prophet, that the tongue "thinks" on justice, since thought is entered upon from the rational sense of a living soul, but the tongue is established for the service of a rational nature? But another Prophet demonstrates the authority of this perfect and prophetic saying, saying: "In the mouth of fools is their heart," because they treat nothing with the counsel of reason or weigh it with the meditation of the heart, but only with the reckless movement of an unguided tongue do they speak of chance and disordered things. And therefore, the heart of fools is in their mouth, because they do not speak what they have thought, but they think what they have spoken.* *And this is certainly true of the tongue of a fool.*

Job slipped in his speaking, even though his lips were barely clinging to his teeth, as he felt corruption everywhere in his body. He slipped with his lips when the opportunity arose as his friends were brought in to engage in long conversations with him. For that is the time when an untimely word most easily slips out, or the emotions are stirred—when we are in some pain or sadness, or the mind grows sick with indignation, or is hindered by various anxieties, or occupied with disputes, <margin>Epistle 113. p. 853.</margin> according to that saying of Seneca: *The speech of an angry man is angry;* the speech of one who is too moved is incited; the speech of a delicate man is tender and flowing. The tongue can be both beneficial and harmful. Erasmus of Rotterdam shows what the tongue can do in *The Preacher* <note>Ecclesiastes</note> by citing Isaiah. <margin>Volume 5. page 686.</margin> An educated tongue has raised many to the throne, but a bad tongue has also cast many down from their rank, as the son of Sirach testifies, which Medea confirms by her own example in Euripides, speaking thus to Creon:

Remarkable is the sentiment of Caesarius <note>Likely Caesarius of Arles</note> on this matter: *The evil of a vice returns to its own author. As the divine word says: "Son, if you are evil, you alone shall drink your evils." The malicious man stains his own tongue; the slanderer wounds his own heart; the angry man blinds the light of his own mind; the envious man corrupts his own soul like a moth; and just as vipers are born from ulcerated parents, so human hearts are first torn apart by the passions they have conceived. Those hearts, I say, from which the serpentine generation of vices is brought forth, are themselves first violated by the monstrous fertility of the birth. Of such a birth the divine word says: "Behold, he has been in labor with injustice, he has conceived sorrow, and brought forth iniquity. His sorrow shall be turned back upon his own head."* The tongue is capable in every direction. It knows how to diminish great things, it knows how to amplify small things, it knows how to color black things as if they were white, and white things as if they were red. It can foster an evil cause as a patron of malice. It can procure envy, hatred, favor, rivalries, and dissensions through various bold acts, according as it is hired. Protected by royal power, it is proud; it speaks proudly and despises the inferior. Having obtained the power of superiors, it can engineer frauds, by the craftsmanship of which it can suppress the sincerity of virtue. A tongue eager to slander builds up an unjust opinion and spreads false rumors.

But the bow of the homicidal tongue is always bent, and the sharpness of its sword is ready in its speech. Its lethal arrows fly, and there is no doubt what they achieve, *namely, that they might shoot the innocent from the shadows.* <note>original Latin: "scilicet, ut sagittent in obscuro immaculatum," a reference to Psalm 11:2</note> The tongue often deceives under the guise of good and destroys more often and sooner than you would have thought; and since it is a hidden evil, we must ask God that we be taught to beware of that deceitful tongue. This is why David implores God to be illuminated with the wisdom to distinguish it, 
<margin>Psalm 120:2</margin>
saying: *O Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue.* Augustine asks in his commentary on this passage: What is a deceitful tongue? And he answers: *It is treacherous, having the appearance of giving counsel but the destruction of doing harm.* Jerome, in his commentary on Isaiah chapter 5, noted that David asked for a remedy against wicked conversations and the crafts of the Devil, and received a divine-like response: *What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you against a deceitful tongue?* In much speaking there is vain speaking; for this reason Stobaeus, in Sermon 130, brings forward the verses of Philonides:
-> One will not be admired for saying many things, <-

-> But do not consider him who speaks well to be "long," <-
-> even if he speaks a great deal and for a long time. <-
<note>original Greek: Τὸν μὴ λέγοντα τ’ῶ δεόντων μηδὲ ἕν, Μακρὸν νόμιζε, κἄν δύ’ εἴπῃ συλλαβάς. Τὸν δ’ εὖ λέγοντα, μὴ νόμιζ’ εἶναι μακρὸν, Μήδ’ ἂν σφόδρ’ εἴπῃ πολλὰ, καὶ πολὺν χρόνον.</note>
These verses are quite well-rounded. Apollonius, in his *Letters to Friends*, hands down a sign for recognizing noble men: "The best of men," he says, "are the most brief in speech." <note>original Greek: οἱ κράτιστοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων, βραχυλογώτατοι.</note> So much does the "incontinence of speech or of the tongue" <note>original Greek: ἡ ἀκρασία τῶ λόγου, ἤγε τῆς γλώσσης</note>—*a flood or deluge of the tongue*—displease the wise. The exhortation of Bernard deserves notice: *Bind your speech, I warn you,* he says, *lest it grow wanton or lewd, and gather sin to itself in much speaking. Let it be more restricted and confined within its own banks; an overflowing river quickly gathers mud.* If you lack the ability to speak of divine things and other useful matters, if the weight and difficulty of the subject deter you, let heavenly power encourage you. Seek help so that He, who is the author and craftsman of the mind, the voice, and the tongue, may give you the matter and the daring to speak—He who says: *Open your mouth, and I will fill it.* For we must not think that His help will fail us; what our own industry cannot achieve, His grace will supply when a discourse is undertaken concerning things that pertain to His worship and glory. Outstanding, therefore, is the saying of Gregory Nazianzen in his *Sermon on the Nativity of Christ from the Virgin*, page 230: that man is an *intelligent and speaking herald of God*, while other creatures are *silent praisers of the magnificent works of God.* <note>original Greek: σιγῶντες ἐπαινεταὶ τῆς μεγαλοργίας Θεοῦ</note> Indeed, among all the traces of God’s wisdom and goodness, none is more evident than man himself. The mind of man, by its own excellence, 

<column-break/>

depicts God outside of itself in ineffable ways that make Him more illustrious. The heavens indeed declare the glory of God, but man does so far more illustriously.

In addition to the teeth and the tongue, God created the <term>Gingivae</term> <note>The gums; the author notes they are named from the Latin 'gignendis dentibus', or 'producing teeth'</note> in our mouth, which take their name from the production of teeth, so that their flesh may include and surround the teeth. He also created the **Palate**, which is the interior and superior part of the mouth, walled in by the teeth; for this reason, some think it is named from *palando*, which means *to fence or fortify*. Being made of hard bone, it contains the openings of the passages that purge the brain and aids and perfects the sense of taste during eating and drinking; hence Plutarch praises a person "whose palate is perceptive." <note>original Greek: ᾧ ὑπερῷα ἐναίσθητα</note> From the palate, near the passages of the nostrils, there hangs down into the mouth a fleshy and spongy substance called the *uvula*, the *gurgulio* <note>throat/windpipe</note>, the *plectrum* <note>a pick or striker</note>, and the *columella* <note>little column</note>. It was formed for this purpose by the Parent of Nature: partly to temper the colder air so it does not harm the lungs (hence those to whom air colder than usual is sent to the lungs, or those whose uvula is damaged, tend toward consumption and are said to waste away); partly to aid pronunciation (which is why it is called a *plectrum*); and those whose uvula is damaged are found to speak poorly. It also serves to block liquids so they do not flow back through the passages to the nose. The **Throat** <note>original Latin: Fauces</note>—for the word rarely occurs in the singular—denotes the entire capacity seen when the mouth is open. Because of the narrowness that occurs between the rough artery <note>the trachea</note> and the esophagus, Galen calls it the "Isthmus." Pliny calls the top of the gullet the *fauces*, and the furthest part the stomach. From this narrowness of the throat, an impediment to the voice very often arises, especially in terror, where the voice is accustomed to stick within the throat or be suppressed; hence Virgil in the second book of the *Aeneid*:
-> *...The voice stuck in the throat.* <-
And Phaedrus in *Fable 2, verse 15*:
-> *The cowardly flee, and fear shuts off the voice.* <-
To which Gunther adds in *Book 3*:
-> *Scarcely can the throat, loosened into words,* <-
-> *provide a path for the voice.* <-
Near these are the **Tonsils**, called *paristhmia* or *antiades* by the Greeks, and *Mandeln* by the Germans. These are glandular and spongy bodies, positioned near the tongue, which catch the moisture from the brain and convert it into saliva, so that the mouth, tongue, and throat are soaked in moisture. Here also many muscles of the head are seen, some of which move the entire head, while others are dedicated to specific parts. Hence we have the muscles of the forehead, eyelids, eyes, nose, cheeks, lips, ears, the lower jaw, the tongue, the hyoid bone, the throat, and the larynx—all destined for their specific uses by the Author of Nature.

Having examined the first "belly" <note>An archaic anatomical term referring to the cavities of the body; here, the head</note>, and the upper one at that, between the head and the chest lies the **Neck**. The Doctors of Nature <note>Natural philosophers or scientists</note> dispute whether it should be referred to the head or the chest. The head is supported by the neck as if by a round column. The **Neck** <note>original Latin: Collum</note> takes its name from "cultivating" <note>from 'colendo'</note> because it is accustomed to be adorned with necklaces, a custom introduced among almost all nations. A man's neck differs from a beast's neck due to its roundness and length <note>original Greek: μακρότητα</note>. For in oxen, bears, and wolves, it is curved. It consists of two parts: the throat <note>guttur</note> and the nape <note>cervix</note>. The throat and the palate contribute to the formation of Latin letters, a subject discussed by Johannes Goropius Becanus <note>A 16th-century physician and linguist</note> following Martianus Capella and Terentianus Maurus.

It combines classical wisdom and theological warnings with a scientific description of how the vocal apparatus and neck are structured.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Sacred Anatomy" series, moving from the tongue and palate to the structures of the throat, larynx, and neck. It explores both the biological function of these parts and their metaphorical significance in Scripture, particularly regarding the themes of divine praise and human pride.</meta>

# From Psalm 139, verse 15

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
On pages 48 and 49, the Bride commends the throat of her Bridegroom, saying: <margin>Song of Solomon 5:16</margin> *The throat of the Bridegroom is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable.* The phrase "most sweet" shows that this sweetness overflows. Having tasted this sweetness, she calls him desirable—not just in one part or some parts, but totally, everywhere, and in every way. In the throat is the "trumpet" and the *head of the rough artery* <note>the trachea</note> which stands out like a shield. For there are two channels whose openings are joined in the throat. One is for drawing breath, the other for taking food. The former leads to the lungs, the latter to the stomach. The first is called the *rough artery* <note>trachea</note>, and the second is called the *gullet* or *esophagus*. It is called an "artery" because of the air, and "rough" to distinguish it from other smooth arteries; it leads into the lungs by a very straight and short path and is divided within them. The esophagus, however, passes by the lungs, pierces the diaphragm, and ends in the stomach immediately below the diaphragm. The trachea is located in front of the gullet, and the opening of the trachea is in front of the opening of the gullet. Attached to the opening of the trachea is a *cartilaginous lid* which closes during swallowing and opens and lifts during breathing. This lid is called the *epiglottis* <note>Greek: ἐπιγλωττὶς, literally "over the tongue"</note>. For the *glottis* is the slit in the larynx where high and low voices are formed. This epiglottis is pressed down when food and drink arrive and closes the opening of the larynx while the food and drink pass over it as if over a small bridge. The *Larynx* was created in a wonderful manner by God the Creator to form voices; thus Aristophanes calls it the vehicle or passage of the voice. According to Galen <margin>Commentary on the Aphorisms</margin> it is the head and door of the trachea, consisting of thirteen muscles and five cartilages. The first of these is shaped like a shield—though it is more prominent in males—and is called the *Adam's apple* <note>Latin: pomum Adami</note>, which people jokingly say is a remnant from the most unfortunate eating of the forbidden fruit. Anatomists speak more extensively of the rest. The *Neck* <note>Latin: Cervix</note> is so named because some say it is the "way of the brain" <note>a Latin folk etymology: "cerebri via"</note>. For the Hebrews, it is named for "division" (*miphreketh* from the root *pāraq* <note>Hebrew: מפרקת, "neck-joint" or "vertebra"</note>); it is bony so that it may support the head more strongly and guard and defend the brain better. It consists of seven vertebrae, called *spondulois* by the Greeks <note>Greek: σπονδύλοις</note>, because the neck turns and moves around those bones. Thus Pollux says: *The vertebrae are also called "turners" because the neck turns through them, and "pivots" because they revolve.* The neck <note>Latin: collum</note> takes its name from "cultivating" <note>Latin: colendo</note>, because precious things are placed on the neck and used to adorn it. Solomon seems to have looked to this custom when commending the exercise of the law and the accurate meditation on divine things in Proverbs. He takes a metaphor from that part of the body which is observed more than others, and where precious treasures are usually hung, namely from the neck or throat, saying: <margin>Proverbs 6:20-22</margin> *My son, keep the commandment of your father, and do not leave the law of your mother. Bind them always upon your heart,* and <note>Hebrew: ענדם על-גרגרתיך, ‘andem ‘al-gargrotêka</note> *fasten them around your throat.* The Septuagint translates this elegantly: *Collar them here upon your neck.* When Moses urges this constant consideration of the divine law and its mysteries, he takes a metaphor from the fingers, upon which rings are usually fastened, saying: *These words, which I command you today, shall be in your heart, and you shall tell them to your children, and meditate on them sitting in your house and walking on a journey, sleeping and rising; and you shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be moved between your eyes.* Deuteronomy 6:6-8.

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
The Bride, who is entirely beautiful, is commended for her neck in Song of Solomon 1:10 and 4:4, 9, where gold shines in collars and precious necklaces hang, set with various gems. The Church Fathers—Gregory, Eucherius, Justus of Urgell, and Philo of Carpasia—interpret this mystically as the Word of God, the rule of faith, life, and morals. Among them, Gregory says: *The throat is in the neck, and the voice is in the throat; what therefore is signified by the neck of the Church, if not its sacred utterances?* From the "eyebrow" mentioned above and the "neck," pride is noted, because the neck is an indicator of arrogance. <margin>Homily 15</margin> Thus Theophanes joins together *lofty eyebrows* and *high necks*. And Jerome, in his commentary on Habakkuk chapter 2, says: *Pride is properly shown in the stretching out of the neck and the erection of the spine.* Moses foretold <margin>Deuteronomy 33:29</margin> that the Israelites would trample upon the *high places* <note>Hebrew: במות, bamoth</note>, namely the necks of their enemies, a fate we read about in Joshua 10:24. The neck and nape are called "high places" because they are in the highest part of the body and are the seat of pride. Hence the Greek term *trachēliān* <note>Greek: τραχηλιᾷν</note> means to lift the neck. In Isidore, the proud are said to "stiffen the neck," lifting the neck or nape like proud horses. They also call this *gauriān* <note>Greek: γαυριᾷν, to prance or be haughty</note>. From this, it metaphorically signifies not so much "to be proud" as "to carry oneself petulantly and fiercely against another," as Hesychius explains it as *raising the neck to oppose and disobey*. Gregory the Theologian uses it of those who exalt themselves against the Lord: *to lift the neck against the Almighty Lord and to fall from that loftiness*. There, the translator renders it "to take up horns against the Lord," which is more properly *keratiān* <note>Greek: κερατιᾷν</note>, a metaphor taken from petulant bulls, as noted in Henri Estienne’s Treasury of the Greek Language. Hence also "to walk with an outstretched neck," which the Septuagint rendered *to walk with a high neck*, is read in Isaiah 3:16. Regarding this pride of the daughters of Zion, Burmeister, imitating Martial <margin>6 Parody 55, p. 417</margin>, writes:

> Because you lift your neck, putting on buskins <note>theatrical boots</note>,
> And proud, you smear your face with rouge,
> And you burn with the scent of musk in golden vessels,
> God will punish you, O Zion, for your smelling;
> You would prefer to smell of nothing than to smell so "well."

Eliphaz uses almost the same phrase in Job 15:26 while describing the rebellion and insults of the impious against God, saying: *He ran against Him with a stiff neck, and was armed with a fat neck.* Kimchi writes in his *Book of Roots* that the Hebrew word *gab* <note>Hebrew: גב</note> signifies in general the face or more prominent surface of any thing; hence it is transferred to various meanings. Since the phrase "of his shields" follows here, as Pagninus and Arias correctly translate, we shall well interpret *gabbim* as *bosses* <note>the central protruding part of a shield</note>, as in *the thickness of the bosses of his shields*. The strength of an animal—ox, horse, lion, etc.—consists mostly in the neck; therefore Eliphaz describes the force with which the impious are carried against God with two metaphors: one taken from a fierce ox, which is carried against an adversary with a stiff neck and nape; the other from a reckless man making an assault against the central bosses of the enemy's shields. Junius, Tremellius, Vatablus, and others depart from this interpretation, explaining these words of Eliphaz as referring to God and His vengeance. However, the context itself sufficiently proves that the discourse here continues concerning the deeds of the impious man and his insurrection against God.

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Anatomy Book 1, on Job ch. 15, p. 61.</margin>
Hence, offering support to the former exposition, Philippus the Priest <note>Philippus Presbyter, a 5th-century commentator and disciple of Jerome</note> writes: **"The fatness named upon the neck demonstrated an over-abundant and almost excessive pride, just as the Prophet says when speaking of the pride of such men: Their iniquity has come forth as if from fat."** <note>original: "Prodiit quasi ex adipe iniquitas eorum"; see Psalm 73:7</note> A new edition of the Psalms seemed to me to say clearly: **"Their eyes have stood out because of fatness,"** that is, the senses or thoughts of the excessively proud have broken out into blasphemy. The same author, regarding the words: **"He has run against him with a stiff neck,"** <note>Job 15:26</note> says: **"Which antiquity holds in this way: 'I have been the shield of a thickened neck.' For this reason, he called the aforementioned pride by the name of a 'shield,' in which every elated and puffed-up person glories, and thinks himself protected; by which also, as if fortified by a shield, he stubbornly tries to resist God. Wherefore, this very verse seems to me to have the same sense through the recently published translation: 'and he is armed with a fat neck.'"** In the following chapter 16, verse 12, Job complains of God's hostility toward him, that He has delivered him into the hands of enemies. Regarding this verse, Philippus the Priest says again in the same place, page 65: **"In the neck, the strength of wrestlers is most especially signified. Job says this part of himself was seized by the Devil, as if by one more powerful, whom he [the Devil] crushed like a defeated man, and playing with him, set him up as a target for himself, as those who are in arms are accustomed to do when they set up certain signs made of any kind of wood at a distance and hurl weapons as if at fixed spots; because of which it follows, saying: 'He has surrounded me with his lances'; just as we sometimes see happen in those kinds of targets, when the same marks are either struck by men with javelins or even shattered, so that the lances or arrows sometimes hang fixed in the targets themselves. Hence, in this place, the names of pains are significantly understood as the piercings which Job suffered, by which he testifies he was surrounded."** Saint Jeremiah says with the same sense in the Lamentations: **"He bent his bow, and set me as a mark for the arrow; he sent into my reins the daughters of his quiver."** <note>Lamentations 3:12-13</note> The "daughters," that is, the arrows, are the weapons which the saints testify are fixed in their loins or kidneys. The <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> departs from the sacred text in *Psalm 129:4*, where the <term>Septuagint</term> reads <term>necks</term> <note>original Greek: "αὐχένας"</note> for the Hebrew <term>The Lord is righteous; he has cut the cords of the wicked</term> <note>original Hebrew: "יהוה צדיק קצץ עבות רשעים"</note>, which Capellus <note>Louis Cappel, a 17th-century French Protestant scholar</note> conjectures in *Crit. fol. 248* they read as <term>throats</term> <note>original: "גרונ"</note> or <term>backs</term> <note>original: "doras"</note>, evidently because of the double sound of the letter <term>Ayin</term> <note>ע</note>. The Vulgate follows these: **"The just Lord will cut the necks of sinners."** And the Mainz edition: **"Has cut off the neck of the sinner."** <note>original German: "Hat den Nacken der Sünder abgeschnitten"</note> Aquila and Symmachus read <term>snares</term> <note>original Greek: "βρόχους"</note>, that is, the nooses or ropes by which horses or oxen are tied to the plow. However, through "ropes," some understand the tightly twisted and coherent plans and machinations, according to *Isaiah 5:8*. Luther, Pagninus, and Arias Montanus likewise translate it as "ropes." Theodotio reads <term>collars</term> <note>original Greek: "κλοίους"</note> or <term>shackles</term> <note>original: "cabaftas"</note>, from which others want to refer to the chains by which captives are held within prisons and imposed labors; when these are cut, all obedience simultaneously is removed and ceases; see Dr. Geier, *Commentary on Psalm 129, p. 1076*. Hilary, following the Old Translator <margin>on Psalm 118, p. 558.</margin> explains this as the proud and insolent neck that must be cut by the decree of just judgment: **"The Lord is just,"** he says, **"that is, patient in vengeance, ignoring for a time of repentance, not more prompt to punishment at the beginnings of human iniquity, but waiting for the wild will of sinners to cease from crimes,"**

<column-break/>

<margin>Anato-
my</margin>
**"then he will cut the necks, when sins are stretched out at length, when now all the time of suffering mercy has been excluded."** We remember it is always cast as a reproach against the stubborn that they are of a "hard neck," as when Moses argued to God that they were a stiff-necked people; when the Prophet reproaches the daughters of Zion because they walk with a high neck: the neck, of course, designating a yoke, and being insolent to the works of faith, with the patience of God refusing to extend the length of their sins. The same Bishop of Poitiers <note>St. Hilary</note> exhorts us toward the sweet yoke of Christ, to which he commands the neck be submitted—namely, the yoke of humility and gentleness, with which must be joined the study of solemn and true repentance. To undertake this, Ambrose warns: <margin>on Psalm 118, sermon 12, p. 673.</margin> **"He is bowed down who acts in repentance, because he bows his neck while he is humbled to the Lord, and especially the interior neck, that is, the neck of the mind and heart; for of this neck it is said: 'Do not bend your neck like a circle.' For he who does not bend his heart has bent his neck in vain. It is good to be bowed, so that we may be humbled to the Lord, and the Lord may have mercy. Let him be bowed by humility who seeks refreshment for his soul, so that he may more quickly reach the mercy of the Lord."**
We have come to the middle belly <note>the chest/thorax</note>, which is adorned by nature with no less singular gifts than the highest part. For here, as we might say in the words of Sperlingius: <margin>Has Anatomy page 67</margin> **"It has the heart, and the remaining parts destined for the vital faculty. As great as is the dignity of the highest part, so great is the necessity of the middle: To feel presupposes living; we live, however, by the work of this 'belly.' Animal spirits presuppose vital spirits; this middle belly itself supplies them."** Here the Heart dwells in its palace, which the lungs, diaphragm, and other parts serve. We shall deal with these in the order and method prescribed to us, and in a summary way. Under the name of "Thorax" commonly comes that other part of the body which lies between the head and the abdomen, girded almost everywhere by ribs and distinct from the lower belly. It is called Thorax <term>θώραξ</term>, not <term>from "watching over the divine"</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τοῦ θεῖον ὠρεῖν"</note> because it contains within us that which is divine, namely <term>the thinking faculty</term> <note>original Greek: "τὸ διανοητικὸν"</note>, for Galen exploded this etymology long ago in *Book 3, chapter 5 on the opinions of Hippocrates and Plato*. For the ancients placed in the heart not only the affections but also the principal faculties, and consequently also the <term>thinking faculty</term>, whose seat is nevertheless the head. For in the brain, says Laurembergius, *in diseases:* in the thorax is <term>life</term> <note>original Greek: "ζωή"</note>; <margin>Anatomy p. 11</margin> in the belly is <term>nourishment</term> <note>original Greek: "θρέψις"</note>. Therefore, it is rather called <term>thorax</term> <term>from "leaping"</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τοῦ θορεῖν"</note>, because of the continuous motion of the heart, for the heart leaps in the thorax. Otherwise, this word denotes something artificial, namely a breastplate <note>a cuirass or armor</note>, but it was drawn from there to natural things to indicate the part of the body which the ribs circumscribe. And thus the thorax is called <term>as if an acropolis, in which the vital spark of nature lies</term> <note>original Greek: "οἷον ἀκρόπολις, ἐν ᾗ τὸ τῆς φύσεως ζωπυρῶν κεῖται"</note>, as if it were a certain citadel of the body in which the hearth of Nature is hidden—which are the words of the Philosopher [Aristotle]—and because it is <term>a well-fenced wall</term> <note>original Greek: "εὐερκὲς τεῖχος"</note>, a very strong wall indeed, prepared by Nature for the heart and lungs, as per Galen and Hoffmann. Of the parts from which the thorax consists, some are external and some are internal. Among the external parts, the first to be considered is the *chest* [pectus], the middle of which is called the *sternum*, hairy in some people, at the sides of which...

# From Psalm 139:15

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
On the sides in men are the nipples, but in women the breasts, in the center of which the nipples stand out. In young girls not yet ready for the <term>acts of Venus<note>A common euphemism for sexual maturity or marriage</note></term>, these only just appear. However, in those reaching puberty and <term>approaching menstruation<note>original Greek: πρὸς τὰ ἔμμηνα</term></note>, the breasts grow to nearly two finger-breadths. In mature women, they equal the size and shape of apples and can almost be held in the hand. For then girls are recognized as marriageable and are given away by their parents. Let us hear Ambrose on this matter in his 21st sermon on Psalm 118, page 764.

<margin>Psalm 118, p. 11.</margin>
> The daughters of Jerusalem heard that the Lord Jesus was now joining the Church to himself; and because, considering the greatness of the man, they judged themselves unequal to such a great marriage—fearing perhaps they could not sustain the weight of such a union—they excused themselves saying: "Our sister is small, and she has no breasts." <note>A reference to Song of Solomon 8:8</note> For so those who wish to defer marriage are accustomed to make excuses, pretending the weakness of immature age, and asserting they have no breasts, which signify the time of marriageable age. This is the common sign for all virgins about to marry: when the breasts begin to stand out, they are then indicated as fit for union. Disturbed, therefore, because the bridegroom urges the marriage with the zeal of love, they say: "What shall we do for our sister in the day when she shall be spoken for?" or, as Symmachus <note>An ancient translator of the Old Testament</note> has it, "when he shall speak to her," that is, in the celebration of betrothals, which usually happens through conversation and the confirmation of the marriage.

In pregnant women, as the womb and fetus grow and they approach birth, the breasts become quite swollen. In old women, however, they become flaccid and hang down unseemly; we will discuss their use in what follows. Thus, the chest constitutes the front part of the <term>thorax<note>The upper trunk of the body</note></term>, the back constitutes the rear, and these are joined by the sides, both right and left, each of which consists of ribs and flesh. Regarding the "side," Zanardus <note>Paolo Zanardi, a 17th-century philosopher/physician</note> notes this:

<margin>Anthropology Book 2, Chapter Article 2, p. 1. On the parts of the body 7, question page 25.</margin>
> It is called the "side" (*latus*) because it lies wide (*latet*) in those reclining, and there are two sides: the right, which is more agile for movement, and the left, which is more suited for carrying; hence the left part is called *leva*, from *levando* <note>meaning "lifting"</note>, because it is found more fit for lifting and carrying. For it carries the shield, the sword, and the quiver. The <term>sternum<note>The breastbone</note></term> is called "ensiform" from its <term>sword-like shape<note>original Greek: ξιφοειδές</note></term>. In the first stage of development, it is entirely cartilaginous, later it changes into bones—sometimes more, sometimes fewer—the last of which ends in a pointed cartilage. It is joined with the true ribs, to which the two <term>scapulae<note>Shoulder blades</note></term> are attached. These are called <term>omoplatai<note>original Greek: ὠμοπλάται</note></term>, which the two <term>clavicles<note>Collarbones</note></term> join to the sternum. Regarding these, Spigelius <note>Adriaan van den Spiegel, a famous Flemish anatomist</note> says:

<margin>Book 2 on the Fabric of the Human Body, ch. 15. Human Anatomy p. 305.</margin>
> The collarbones, he says, called <term>kleides<note>original Greek: κλείδες, meaning "keys"</note></term> by the Greeks, are named not because they "close" the chest, as some anatomists have claimed, but because they resemble the shape of ancient keys. For they express the form of the elongated Latin letter 'f', in the likeness of which keys for houses were made in ancient times. I remember, while I was a youth in Padua <note>A leading center for medical study in Italy</note> devoted to literature and medicine, seeing keys of this shape still used in the oldest houses.

From the front part, God the <term>all-wise Creator<note>original Greek: ὁ πάνσοφος</note></term> fortified the royal seat—the dwelling place of the heart—with the sternum. At the sides, He joined the ribs to it, of which we count twelve on each side. From the back part is the spine, whose parts include the shoulder blades (quite visible in thin people) and the Spine, called <term>rhachis<note>original Greek: ῥάχις</note></term> by the Greeks, which runs through the length of the back and divides the rear into right and left parts. At the sides of the spine in the back is the sacrolumbar region, which he also

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
calls the <term>sacrum bone<note>os sacrum</note></term>. It is the <term>unbending part<note>original Greek: Ἀκλιντον</note></term> of the body, upon which the entire upper mass rests, situated between the hip bones near the sacrum. If a straight line is drawn from the center of the body between the hip bones near the sacrum, it comes out through the top of the head. Thus, the crown of the head is placed directly above the center and rests upon it, and a burden placed on the crown is further removed from this center. Because a burden that rests on the center and is further from it is carried more easily, burdens are carried more easily on the crown of the head than on other parts of the body. For carrying such things, the Author of Nature destined the shoulders and the robust ligaments which the shoulders enjoy. Hence, the positioning of the shoulders for describing the burden of tribute is placed by Jacob regarding the tribe of Issachar, which "bowed his shoulder to bear, and became a servant to tribute."

<margin>Genesis 49:15.</margin>
<note>Hebrew original: "And he bowed his shoulder to bear, and became a servant to tribute."</note> The Greeks translate this as: <term>"and he bowed his shoulder to labor, and became a husbandman."<note>original Greek: καὶ ἔκλινε τὸν ὦμον αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸ πονεῖν, καὶ ἐγενήθη ἀνὴρ γεωργός</note></term> The Latin rendered the words better: "He was made a servant to tribute." The Issacharites were <term>productive in a fertile land<note>original Greek: Ἐν χώρᾳ εὐφόρῳ ἐπιφόρως ἐγενήθη</note></term>, not only for Judges and Kings, but perhaps even for foreigners, so that they might buy peace and quiet with gold and silver, or by whatever means. Great men are accustomed to lean on the shoulders of their close associates, as Homer relates of Penelope, Justin (Book 14, ch. 6) of Olympias the mother of Alexander the Great, and Suetonius (ch. 43, p. 361) of Nero. The Princes and Great Ones of the earth are accustomed to place burdens on the shoulders of their subjects. But the kingdom of the Messiah is very different from political kingdoms, for Christ takes His Church onto His own shoulders along with its burdens, sins, and infirmities; He carries it, and indeed gave His back to the whips, as Isaiah witnesses in chapter 50, verse 6. Regarding these words, let us hear Tertullian:

<margin>Against Marcion, page 167.</margin>
> I assign two causes to be recognized in prophetic utterances. One, by which future things are sometimes announced as if already passed; for it is fitting for divinity to regard whatever He has decreed as already perfected, because there is no difference of time with Him, with whom eternity itself directs a uniform state of time. And it is more familiar to prophetic divination that what it foresees, while it foresees it, is shown as already seen and thus already finished—that is, it will happen in every way—just as through Isaiah: "I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair; I hid not my face from shame and spitting." For whether Christ was then pronouncing this about Himself according to our view, or the Prophet about himself according to the Jews' view, it nevertheless sounded like a past event though it was not yet done. There is another type, by which many things are portended figuratively through enigmas, allegories, and parables, to be understood differently than they were written.

Examples of this are to be read there. From the external parts of the middle belly, our pen now turns itself to the <term>study<note>original Greek: μελέτησιν</note></term> of its internal parts, among which the breasts first present themselves, whose external shape we have examined thus far. In men, the nipples consist of skin, a fleshy membrane, the small points in the center, and a tiny amount of fat. In women, however, besides the skin, membrane, and nipples, they are provided with remarkable glands and abundant fat, created in this sex not just for the ornament of the body and the protection of the heart...

...not only for that purpose, but also for the nourishment of the infant. Indeed, the most excellent and primary action of the breasts is the generation of milk, which nature ordained for the nursing of offspring recently brought forth into this light. While still hidden within the enclosures of the mother’s womb, blood serves as food and drink; but once brought outside the womb, that blood, which used to flow to the uterus, seeks the breasts. There, by a wondrous play of nature, it is turned white and becomes food and drink. For this purpose, two breasts were bestowed upon females by divine providence, so that they might suffice not just for one child, but so that if they should happen to give birth to twins, twin fountains of nourishment would be present. Hence Plutarch, in his book *On the Education of Children*, says: <note>original Greek: Σοφῶς ἄρα ἡ πρόνοια διττὰς ἐνέθηκε ταῖς γυναιξὶ τὰς μαζὰς, ἵνα κἂν εἰ δίδυμα τέκοιεν, διπλᾶς ἔχοιεν τὰς τῆς τροφῆς πηγάς.</note> “Wisely, therefore, providence placed two breasts in women, so that even if they should bear twins, they might have double fountains of nourishment.” The Bridegroom in Solomon’s Song uses a charming and pleasant simile drawn from the abundance of the breasts to lift up the afflicted and tempted in *Chapters 4:5 and 7:3*. What sweeter figure could be imagined or spoken than when the Church—the most kind mother of us all—puts on the affection of a mother coaxing her little infant son with breasts full of the sweetest milk? She promises to raise up and console the terrified godly in the same way a mother refreshes her infant son with her own milk. *“Your two breasts,”* says Christ of his Bride, *“are like two twin fawns of a gazelle.”* Interpreters apply these to the two Sacraments; others also to the diverse doctrines of the Law and the Gospel, which, having proceeded from the one author, God, ought never to be confused in the Church, yet always joined together. Regarding these breasts, Willeram writes *thus:*

A double membrane is found in the middle of the belly <note>The chest or thoracic cavity</note>, namely the *pleura* and the *mediastinum*, to which others join the *Pericardium* <note>The sac surrounding the heart</note>; compare Spigelius, *Anatomy* 9. 3, 4, 5.

<column-break/>

chapters. Concerning the **Pleura**, it is a hard and thick membrane, girding the ribs by means of the <term>periosteum<note>The membrane covering the outer surface of bones</note></term>, but immediately girding the heart, the lungs, and also the vessels existing in the thorax. It is *thick* in that part which adheres to the vertebrae from which it arises; *moderate* where it is bound to the ribs; *thin* where it girds the vessels; and *thinnest* where it clothes the lungs. From this description, its use is also evident: namely, to cover the middle belly and to bind the viscera and vessels. Hence it is called by Galen <note>original Greek: ὑμὴν ὁ ὑπεζωκὼς</note> the *succingens* or "girding membrane." The other membrane of the thorax is called the **mediastinum**, because it stands in the middle of the thorax, just as a <term>mediastinus<note>A lower-level household slave or bath-servant who was 'in the middle' of all chores</note></term> waits in the middle of a house or bath-house at the commands and nods of all; see Hofmann, *Book on the Thorax, 5, p. 6*. Galen calls these <note>original Greek: ὑμένας διαφράττοντας</note> "distinguishing" or "partitioning" tunics, from which it is clear that there are not one but two membranes—one on the right, the other on the left—the use of which consists in dividing the lungs and keeping the heart in its proper place. But the anatomists treat both membranes and their use more extensively. From this second membrane, namely the pleura, that affliction <note>original Greek: πλευρῖτις</note> **Pleurisy** takes its name, by which the parts surrounding the middle belly are attacked. It is called *Pleuritis* by Valerianus and Pliny (*Book 5, ch. 14*); and *Pleuresis* by the barbarians. <note>original Greek: Ὀδύνη πλευρᾶς</note> "Pain of the side" is used everywhere by the <term>Coan<note>Referring to the medical school of Hippocrates on the island of Cos</note></term> and his interpreters for pain of the upper side. Hippocrates, in his writings on internal affections, interprets <note>original Greek: πλευρᾶς</note> "of the side" as being through the side of the lungs; this is followed by those who locate the pleuritic passion in the lungs, clearly following the Coan example, who in the *Coan Prognostics* numbered lung pain among the side affections in the manner of the <term>Peripneumonics<note>Those suffering from pneumonia</note></term>. For Duretus's reasoning is of no value—that it is not pleuritic pain if it is relieved by a flow of the bowels—since Avicenna, Aetius, Trallianus, Valleriola, Salius, Panarolus, and others testify that Pleuritics are also purged and relieved through the belly. This happens through <note>original Greek: μετάπτωσιν</note> a "shift," the matter being transferred from the lungs to the common passage, as Castrensis rightly explains; compare Thomas Bartholin, *Dissertation on the Side of Christ, ch. 12, p. 8, 9.*

There is another membrane which, like an intermediate wall, distinguishes the middle belly from the lower, called by the Greek name **diaphragma**, for this reason: because it <note>original Greek: διαφράττει</note> "partitions off" the instruments of the Spirit and separates them from the alimentary ones. That is, it divides the natural parts, which serve nutrition, from the spiritual parts, which serve life. Hence it is also called the *septum transversum* by Celsus and the *disseptum* by Macrobius. Furthermore, it is the nearest instrument of breathing and aids in forming and emitting the voice. Anatomists do not agree on its origin; see, if you like, the *Anatomy* of Domenico de Marchetti, *ch. 9, p. 108*. Laurentius describes its composition thus: "The entire body of the diaphragm consists of two circles, one membranous, the other fleshy; two veins, as many arteries, and two nerves on each side; it is also pierced by two tunics and two openings, so that this entire muscle is <note>original Greek: διχότομος</note> *dichotomous* [divided in two] in its structure, and produces a double action: namely, inspiration and expiration." The first of the circles is nervous, situated in the middle like a center, from which very many fibers run out to the circumference. Everyone else establishes this muscle as the beginning and the head; I, on the contrary, maintain it is the end and the tail. The other cir-

### FROM PSALM 139, VERSE 15.
### PAGE 807

<margin>

...a fleshy circle altogether, surrounding the leathery parts on all sides, attached at its front part to the sternum and the false ribs; at its back, it is joined to the highest vertebrae of the loins by the intervention of two tendons.

<margin>
To Glaucon
