In the middle of the chest, a membrane is found called the pericardium, because it is "around the heart" <note>original Greek: <term>περὶ τὴν καρδίαν</term></note>, and it embraces the heart just as a purse encloses a gold coin. Hence it is also called the capsule of the heart, its covering, or its garment. By Galen, it is called a <term>χιτὼν</term> <note>a tunic or cloak</note>, or the "overcoat of the heart" <note>original Greek: <term>ἐπιθυμὴν τῆς καρδίας</term></note>. It is of such great size that the heart resides in its center as if in its own citadel, yet it stands as far away from the heart as the heart’s expansion requires. Furthermore, it contains water within itself, which differs in quantity according to age, sex, temperament, and disease. A small amount of watery fluid is always found in it, though it is usually very slight. Sometimes, however, a great deal of water collects there, so that the heart almost floats in it. Charles Piso, in his book *On Diseases Arising from Serous Overflows* (Observation 51), recounts a remarkable history of abundant water contained in the pericardium. In healthy people, this water is clear, but in disease, it is sometimes like turbulent urine, or sometimes like water diluted with blood. At this point, some writers draw a connection to the water that came out with blood from the most holy side of our Savior when a soldier opened his side with a spear. Whether this outflow was natural or "supernatural" <note>original Greek: <term>ὑπέρφυσιν</term></note> is a very grave debate among the learned, which Isaac Casaubon treated most extensively in his *Exercises* (page 467 and following). The heart remains within this sac as if in its own home; it is defended by it so that it is not inconvenienced by neighboring parts, and the fluid contained within it moistens and refreshes the heart. 

Regarding the origin of this fluid, the "sons of the physicians" <note>a poetic way of referring to medical scholars</note> follow different judgments. Some believe that vapors exhaling from the heart, as soon as they reach this bloodless, nervous, and cold capsule, are turned into water, just as we see little droplets generated on the lids of pots placed over a fire with food inside. Others believe that this water comes from the drink we take, which trickles down through the windpipe <note>original Latin: *asperam arteriam*</note> into the lungs while drinking, and further into this capsule; they believe this happens so that not only are the lungs (which are occupied in perpetual motion) moistened, but also the heat of the heart itself is tempered. The patrons of this latter assertion appeal to "Experience, the Teacher of all things." They say that when singers’ lungs and windpipes (the organs of the voice) are so dried out by singing that the voice often sticks, they immediately regain a voice sufficient for singing by taking a drink, which they argue descends by no other means than through the lungs and windpipe. Furthermore, they usually verify this by the excretion of phlegm; for it is well known that phlegm is expelled through the windpipe, and after a draft of red wine, phlegm is ejected tinted with a red color—a clear sign that red wine descends through the windpipe. Likewise, those suffering from "syncope" <note>a fainting spell</note>, an affection of the heart, immediately return to themselves if wine is given to them, which reaches this capsule of the heart through the lungs and windpipe. But these matters are "outside our little field." Having examined the home of the heart, let us instead turn ourselves more closely to the "study" <note>original Greek: <term>μελέτησιν</term></note> of the heart itself, to which both its dignity and its necessity invite us. For what is the **Heart**, which holds the middle seat of the body, from which the term "middle" <note>original Latin: *medium*</note> and "heart" <note>original Latin: *cor*</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred Anatomy
</margin>
are used interchangeably? As in that passage: "Sarah laughed in her midst" <note>original Hebrew: <term>תצחק שרה בקרבה</term></note>, which Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum correctly translate as "in her heart"; but Onkelos translates as "in her viscera." For the heart is said to be in the middle of man, and although it inclines more to the left, it is nevertheless believed to be in the center or the "hub" of man because it is *within* man; for whatever is inside a thing is said to be in its "middle." Compare B. Gerhard’s *Commentary on Genesis 18*, page 377. What, I say, is the Heart? What the root is to a tree, the Heart is to an animal. What the *Sun* is in the macrocosm <note>the great world or universe</note>, the Heart is in the microcosm <note>the "little world" of the human body</note>, where the "vital spark of nature" <note>original Greek: <term>τὸ τῆς φύσεως ζωπυρὸν</term></note> continually shines. Clementinus wrote elegantly on this:

<margin>
Reflections on Temperaments, p. 6.
</margin>
> *Just as the Sun stands among the stars, so the Heart excels among the other members. The Heart, therefore, and the spirit (which is the most subtle part of the blood), is hot and dry, like the Sun and its rays. The brain, the marrow, and the nerves are likened to the Moon, which is cold and moist—though the nerves lean toward dryness. The liver and the blood are hot and moist, like Jupiter. The genital members and the seed are likened to Venus. The stomach and phlegm are cold and moist, like Saturn. The gallbladder and yellow bile are hot and dry like Mars, as are other things there. For the principal and governing members of the body, according to Avicenna in his Songs (num. 224), are the Liver, Brain, and Heart—often abbreviated by the word CIC (Cor, Iecur, Cerebrum)—because here the spirits are lodged like Princes in a citadel. The Vital spirit flourishes in the heart, the Natural spirit in the liver, and the Animal spirit in the brain. But of these, only the Heart acts by its own authority; the Brain is like a Chancellor, and the Liver acts like a Governor. The Heart alone acts by its own strength, insofar as it is the master of heat; the brain, liver, stomach, and all other parts act only by the strength and benefit of the heat transmitted from the Heart. For this reason, the Peripatetic philosophers call them organs of "molding" <note>original Greek: <term>ἀναπλασέως</term></note>, which do not produce the action themselves, but only manifest it, just as a Chancellor does those things which the King commands. See Hofmann, On the Chest, book 1, page 20.*

The Heart, whose position is at the head of the *vena cava* <note>the "hollow vein" that brings blood to the heart</note>, is hence the fountain of human nature and the river of the microcosm, the "root and source of the arteries" <note>original Greek: <term>ἀρτηριῶν ῥίζωμα & ικατυριγο</term></note>, the fountain of the veins, the path of the Spirits, the head of life, and the wellspring of heat. Regarding this, Caesarius says in Question 78: "The heart exists as a storehouse or watchtower of the vital cause and strength within us; it is a certain beginning of our life, from which the blood-like passages, growing through one another in various forms, diffuse the warm and fiery spirit through the whole body." <note>original Greek: <term>ἡ καρδία οἰονεὶ ταμιεῖον ἢ φρύκεον ὑπάρχει τῆς ζωτικῆς ἐν ἡμῖν αἰτίας καὶ ῥώμης, κεάν τις καὶ ἀρχὴ τῆς ἡμετέρας ζωῆς, ἀφ' ἧς αἱματοειδεῖς πόροι πολυειδῶς ἑτεροῖ δι' ἑτέρων διαφυόμενοι ὅλῳ τῷ σώματι τὸ θερμὸν καὶ πυρῶδες διαχέουσι πνεῦμα.</term></note> Thus the Heart is the fountain of heat. The Liver is the fountain of blood-making and blood. The Brain is the principle of motion and sense. From these three principal organs, the lesser organs obtain their own powers of acting: heat from the heart; nourishment from the liver (for both the limbs and the spirits are nourished by blood); and motion and sense from the brain. Whatever specific privilege or faculty the remaining parts have, they have it all granted by these three; nor can they use or enjoy those immunities without the concurrence, consent, and influence of the primary organs. They depend on them just as vassals depend on their Lords. See David Crusius’s *Hermetic-Hippocratic Theater*, book 1, chapter 1. The Heart, like a prince and Monarch of the microcosmic empire, sits upon its royal

# ANTIQUITIES OF THE BIBLE

...on his throne, surrounded on all sides by a crowd of purple-clad attendants; when he is cheerful, the entire court is cheerful; when he is moved to anger, it shudders, turns pale, and trembles. From him, the office of the Chancellery is handed over to the **brain**, where the assistant deliberates on the weightiest matters, consulting for the kingdom according to law and equity so that a firm peace may grow between the states. Beside him sits the Liver, like the Secretary of the kingdom, writing down and executing decrees. These assist in the manner of faithful vassals; when necessity demands, they are ready with counsel and aid. See Crusius, chapter 2, and the authors cited there. The supreme providers of the kingdom are the stomach and the lungs, of which the former is the steward of bodily food, and the latter the steward of spiritual food <note>referring to the breath or "spiritus"</note>. These are surrounded by their own doorkeepers, one of whom, named the Pylorus, preserves the royal court from impurity; to the other is given the task of freeing the chamber of the court from all sooty impurity through exhalation, keeping the air pure. The Chief of the Kitchen is called the Esophagus, who has his assistants: the *Hands, teeth, and feet*.

Therefore, the most excellent part of man is the Heart, the foundation and fountain of vital action. By its benefit, every action of life is administered; for from the heart, heat is diffused through every part of the body, nourishing all members and providing them with their own strength. It is the primary dwelling place of the soul. If you consider the sacred duty it owes to God its Creator, you will exclaim with

<margin>
Sacred Anthology, ch. 3, sect. 2, p. 85.

Louis Cresol*: **The heart is the courtroom of the Holy Spirit, built for every delight, the palace of the Divine, the august Royal Hall of God, fortified by the protection of Angels, in which He is accustomed to take His pleasure with the children of men.** But if you ponder its gifts with Masius (on Joshua 5:1, page 79), you will say: **The heart is called that part of the mind in which fortitude and constancy are placed. The Spirit, however—that is, the** *Ruach* <note>Hebrew: רוח</note>—**is that power of the soul by which we are wise; by which we discern and deliberate what should be done and what should be omitted. This is** the intellectual faculty, and the productive power of discernment <note>original Greek: <term>τὸ νοητικὸν, καὶ ἡ ποιητικὴ διαγνώσις καὶ δύναμις</term></note>, **which the Septuagint** <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> **calls** prudence <note>original Greek: <term>φρόνησιν</term></note>. **For when the heart "melts"—namely, when fortitude fails through fear—the faculty of wisdom must necessarily be disturbed at the same time.** The heart is therefore the symbol of mind and wisdom, just as prudent men are called "Wise-hearted" [*Cordati*], while the imprudent are called "Senseless" [*Vecordes*] or "Heartless" [*Excordes*]. Jeremiah touched upon the senselessness of the Jewish people with these words in chapter 5:21: *Hear now this, O foolish people, and without heart* <note>original Hebrew: <term>שמעו-נא זאת עם-סכל ואין לב</term>; the author notes this means one who has no heart, as the Old Interpreter reads</note>.

<margin>
Against Marcion, book 4, ch. 10.

Attacking the insane imprudence of Marcion, Tertullian* says that he has neither a heart nor a brain. Ausonius played cleverly on this sense in his 47th Epigram, stinging a petty rhetorician for using the word *Reminisco* <note>an incorrect, non-Latin form of the verb "to remember"</note>:

> Rufus said "Reminisco" in his verse,
> Thus the verse has a heart <note>meaning: "sense"</note>, but Rufus has no heart <note>meaning: "wit" or "memory"</note>.

From this, thought, intelligence, wisdom, and folly are attributed to the Heart in Holy Scripture (Genesis 6:5; 8:21; Isaiah 6:10). Two peculiar gifts were granted to Man by God above all other animals: Reason and Speech. Reason or Intellect was given to man so that he might recognize God his maker; Will, so that he might love the One recognized above all things; Memory, so that by recollecting Him and by pious remembrance, he might continually have His benefits before the eyes of his mind and seek rest in Him alone. For the Mind is the ruler of the body, but God is the ruler of the mind, as Leo cleverly says (Sermon 14 on Lent, f. 71. a). Nor is there a more excellent word among monosyllables

<column-break/>

than that by which the more excellent part of man is called, among both the Latins and the Greeks—namely, *Nous* <note>Greek: <term>Νους</term></note> to the latter, and MIND [*MENS*] to the former. For what the incorporeal "portion of God" <note>original Greek: <term>μοῖρα Θεοῦ</term></note> is, that is *Mind and Reason* in the soul. The mind is a divine particle, and man has nothing of his own if this particle is not perfected within him. But why do we call it a "particle"? Everything that a man is, is from this part and flows from it. Hence, a temperate man is cleverly called *sophron* <note>Greek: <term>σώφρων</term></note> by the Greeks, as if he were *sos ten phrena*—one whose mind is safe, or who is endowed with a sound mind. The name is most fitting to the thing, for "madness" [*paraphrosyne*] takes its name from intemperance in drink; with which Hosea 4:11 agrees: *Harlotry, wine, and new wine—that is, in a word, intemperance—take away the heart*, that is, the sanity of the mind.

For the mind or reason dwells in the heart as if in its own proper seat. Physicians and Philosophers contend: the former fight for the primacy and leadership of the brain, the latter for the heart. For in whichever part the soul dwells as its proper seat, that part is absolutely the prince or the principal part. Since not only the generation of vital spirits occurs in the heart—so that the whole body is refreshed by the heart as if from a fountain of native heat and life-giving nectar—but also because the heart is the foundation of preservation, and indeed the instrument through which life reaches all members in general, and specifically the brain; so that thereafter, by the benefit of life which arrives from the heart to the brain, sense and motion are imparted by the brain to all members (compare Joseph Albo, book 1, ch. 12, p. 12. b). Thus, Philosophers rightly grant the prerogative to the heart over the brain.

Great indeed is the analogy of the heart with the brain, and great also is the "sympathy" <note>original Greek: <term>σύμπάθεια</term></note> between them, because of the fibers branching from the sixth pair of cranial nerves as they pass to the principal parts: the heart, lungs, windpipe, and esophagus. Yet the heart rules over all the rest, conferring and preserving life for them, whence Galen* says: *The heart, because it is the native heat that governs the living creature, is like a hearth and a fountain* <note>original Greek: <term>ἡ καρδία, διότι τῆς θ’ ἐμφύτου θερμασίας, ἢ διοικεῖ τὰ τὸ ζῶον, ὅιόν ἰς ἰατίς καὶ πηγὴ</term></note>. For whoever is without a heart has ceased to be and to be numbered among the living. While the heart flourishes, all things flourish; when it languishes, all things languish; and when it perishes, every single thing perishes.

No animal in the nature of things is "heartless" [*Excors*]; none, I say, is deprived of this divine particle by the Parent of Nature. Indeed, according to that accurate investigator of Nature, Laurenbergius*: *The heart truly exists in bloodless creatures (for the liver is not the true workshop or laboratory of blood, as has been believed until now, but the heart), such as Shellfish, Prawns, Crabs, Snails, and Shrimps; even in wasps, hornets, bees, and flies (where it clings to the upper part of the tail). In these, I say, anyone may not only discover a heart, but will clearly see it pulsing with the aid of an optical tube* <note>a microscope</note>, *by which the most minute things grow large to the eyes, although that pulse is slow enough, especially in winter and in cold places.*

This most noble part of the middle cavity has its name among the Latins from *cura* [care/worry], because in sadness and solitude the heart is constricted, and as if compressed by a noose...

<meta>This page continues the "Sacred Anatomy" series, moving from the physical description of the heart as the center of the body's "royal court" to a discussion of how the emotions—specifically grief, fear, and joy—physically impact the heart and the vital spirits.</meta>

# SACRED ANATOMY
### FROM PSALM 139:15

<margin>
Sacred Anatomy
</margin>
...is weighed down; we read concerning Sara, the daughter of Raguel, in the third chapter of Tobit, verse 12, that she wasted away in the greatest sorrow even to the "compression of her spirit" <note>original Greek: *ἐλυπήθη σφόδρα, ὥστ' ἀπάγξασθαι*, meaning "she was so deeply grieved that she considered hanging herself"</note>. These words are not found in the Latin version; however, the term for "hanging" is used in such a way that it also implies immense grief. For many people are extinguished by sorrow of the mind alone, and for no other cause. The learned among the Hebrews apply the example of Ahitophel <note>A counselor to King David who betrayed him for Absalom</note> to this, believing that he perished not by a noose, but by sheer sadness. Many have exhaled their spirit due to sudden fear or unforeseen consternation, the cause of which Aristotle explains in these words: <margin>On Respiration, chapter 19</margin> "Those who are afraid," he says, "grow cold in their upper parts. The heat, fleeing and contracting, causes a movement pushed into a small space, so that the life-force is most easily extinguished and they die because of fear." <note>original Greek: *οἱ φοβούμενοι... ἀποθνήσκειν διὰ φόβον*</note> 

He who struggles against sorrowful thoughts fights with thorns and briers; the thistles of sadness prick the roots of the heart, suck the blood from the **portal vein**, and drain the marrow. One who is thinned by cares is called by the Greeks "wasted away by anxieties" <note>original: *ἐκτετηκὼς ὑπὸ φροντίδων*</note>, as Lucian says in *The Cock*, page 634: "entirely withered, evidently wasted by cares, for otherwise he was not said to be sick." Therefore, the term "wasted" is used of one who is driven by many cares, as if he were so emaciated and thinned that the fat of his body had melted and dripped away like oil. Tears are also said to "melt" <note>original: *ἐκτακῆναι*</note> and to cause the body to liquefy, as this is what "melting" <note>original: *τήκειν*</note> means. Hence Homer in *Odyssey* book 19, line 204, says "she melted into tears" concerning a weeping woman; and in line 200 of the same book, he warns that the mind must not be wasted away because of an absent husband (compare Stephanus, volume 3, page 1455). 

For it is so arranged with the passions of the mind that they impress various movements and effects upon the body. When the mind suffers—according to the quality of the thing perceived, whether arising from hate or love, hope or fear, joy or sadness—it first sends the **vital spirits** <term>spiritus: in early medicine, these were subtle fluids that carried life and thought through the nerves</term> rushing back through various nerves. This moves different muscles, arteries, and veins according to the situation, and even moves the heart itself—that is, it either contracts and closes the heart, as in sadness and fear, or it opens and dilates it, as in joy. These effects of the mind's passions are so clearly perceived by everyone that it is commonly said the heart "closes" in sadness and "opens wide" in joy. 

Secondly, by reason of the constriction or relaxation of the muscles, arteries, and veins, there follows a smaller or larger flow of blood through the body and toward the brain. The spirits generated there are similarly distributed through the body. Thus, the effects of the passions already arisen in the rational mind are multiplied—that is, doubled or tripled—by the movement of these tiny particles (the spirits). Augustine refers to this when he says: <margin>City of God, Book 14, Chapter 8</margin> <margin>Anatomy of the Human Body, page 355</margin> "The Virginian verse has encompassed the four perturbations with the greatest brevity":

> Hence they fear and desire, they grieve and rejoice, nor do they see the breezes. <note>From Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book 6, line 733</note>

He says the poet captured the four principal emotions. Horace also encompasses them with equal brevity, saying: <margin>Epistles, Book 1, Epistle 6, line 12</margin>

> Whether he rejoices or grieves, desires or fears, what does it matter?

Jerome also mentions this verse of Virgil in his *Commentary on Ezekiel*, chapter 1. Sadness contracts the mind, while joy diffuses or expands it.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred Anatomy
</margin>
The Psalmist says in Psalm 119, verse 32: *I have run the way of your commandments, when you dilated my heart.* This uses a metaphor from a race in a stadium; for a successful course cannot be undertaken by those who are sluggish with sorrow. Likewise, the saints, who are perpetually tortured by internal fears, cannot correctly or skillfully perform the duties of their calling. On the contrary, when the Lord makes the heart joyful, they can act with human alacrity, joy, zeal, and that dexterity which the nature of their duty requires. 

Sadness suppresses the ardor of the Spirit; this is why God so often incites His people to joy, repeatedly redoubling that sweetest voice: *Rejoice in the Lord; shout for joy, you righteous.* The Psalmist speaks here of a tempered joy. It is well known elsewhere that things which happen suddenly and abruptly—whether joyful or sad—move, strike, and shock human minds more vehemently and sharply than expected, almost producing an **ecstasy** <note>original: *ἔκςασιν*, here meaning a sudden displacement of the mind or shock</note>. For if joy invades a person like a sudden flash of lightning, it is a truly fatal **passion** <note>original: *πάθημα*</note>. 

As Goropius Becanus says: <margin>Jerome, volume 8, page 177</margin> "Extreme and sudden joy more often brings death, because it suddenly and abundantly dissolves the vital spirits." Examples of this are cited from history; among the most famous is the disaster at Cannae <note>After this battle, Roman mothers reportedly died of joy upon seeing sons they thought were dead</note>. I remember a similar thing happening at Rome to a certain noble matron upon the sudden appearance of her son, whom she had believed to be dead. 

Likewise, the example of Diagoras of Rhodes exists in Aulus Gellius (Book 3, *Attic Nights*, 15), who, in the sight and arms of his three sons—whom he saw conquer and be crowned on the same day at Olympia—suddenly breathed his last breath because of unexpected joy. Fabricius records a nearly identical example <margin>Annals of Meissen, volume 3, page 88</margin> regarding Nicolaus Graupa, who, when he was declared Vicar of the Bishop of Meissen in the year 1536, expired from joy. He was in Annaberg, and the Bishop had long ago promised him a greater priesthood; when it was offered to him by letter while he was not expecting it, he died before fully reading it. 

Hence Constantinus Africanus says in *On Medical Locations*: "Joy sometimes kills, if it be sudden, because of the outpouring of natural heat out of the body and its dispersion into the exterior parts." He says someone once died from excessive and sudden joy coming upon them. A few lines later, he adds a remedy: "When a man has an intolerable exaltation, he ought to recall some calamity that might possibly happen in the future, lest the natural heat, exiting, should chill the interior by scattering itself through the exterior." 

But if God had also granted this to Physicians—that they could provide medicine for the vices and perversions of the human mind—they would carry away a great reward. Meanwhile, the good Physician advises those things which benefit health, even regarding the mind, so that it may be well with both mind and body. For to care for health and recover wellness, one needs not only diet and bodily treatment, but also a mind free of cares and devoid of angers. Galen says: "Grief appears to all to be an evil, just as pain is in the body" <note>original Greek: *Ἡ λύπη... ὥσπερ ὁ πόνος ἐν τῷ σώματι*</note>, to which Julius Alexandrinus adds: <margin>On the Diagnosis and Cure of Affections, chapter 7</margin> "For just as pain afflicts and tortures the body more vehemently than labor, so that it can more rightly be called an evil; so sadness and grief afflict the mind more than the other passions—especially if by the name of sadness, envy is also understood."

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
### SACRED ANATOMY

<margin>
Sacred Anatomy
</margin>
...should be understood: *A sorrowful spirit (they say) dries up the bones:* how much more so does **envy**. Hence Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father known for his preaching.</note> in *Volume 3, Homily 27, page 691*, where he had said that envy is worse than any snake, adds: <note>original Greek: Ὁ φθόνος ἐν εὐσπλάγχνοις καλινδεῖται... "Envy rolls about in the inward parts, but it turns in the depths of the soul and is a passion difficult to erase... even if you set a table of ten thousand things before it, it consumes the soul itself, biting from every side, mangling and dragging it."</note> Therefore, a Physician does not only care for the disturbances of bodies, but also of minds, by advising those who wish to prolong their life or return from illness to health to beware of *anger, fear, sadness, anxiety, heavy cares and arduous meditations, and even from unrestrained joy.* For these are the causes of many diseases, either because the spirit and heat are called away to the brain, hindering the digestion of food and other natural functions necessary for life, or because they affect and alter the heart and other parts in various ways through the turbulent movement of fluids and spirits inward and outward. One ought to learn the explanation of these things in detail, and what else is required here, from Physicians, as taught by Matthias Flacio, a Physician of Rostock, in *Book 4 on Life and Death, chapter 14, page 195.* Among the Greeks, the heart is noted by various names. It is called *Kardia* as if it were *kaudia*, taking its name from strength or redness, because it stands out above the other members; it is the fount and origin of **vital heat** <note>In ancient medicine, "vital heat" was the innate fire believed to be produced by the heart to sustain life.</note> and blood, the first to live and the last to die. From this, the Latin **Goddess Carna** seems to be named, as if *Cardiana*, whom they believed presided over the vital parts of man, especially the heart. Her sacred rites were celebrated in the month of June with bean porridge and lard, because strength is bolstered by these foods; hence the Kalends of June were called *Fabaria* <note>The "Bean Kalends."</note>. Macrobius mentions this in *Saturnalia, Book 1, chapter 12*, and Ovid in the *Fasti, Book 6, verse 101*:

->*The first day is given to you, Carna: she is the Goddess of the hinge.*<-
<note>Ovid connects Carna with "cardo" (hinge), though the author here connects her to "cor" (heart).</note>

Junius Brutus dedicated a temple to this Goddess on the Caelian Hill after the expulsion of Tarquin, because by the benefit of the heart he had restored the public state. Next, it is called *splanchnon* <note>Greek for internal organ/bowel.</note>, because the heart is the most noble of all the viscera. Certain viscera are placed as the seats of affections, such as the *heart of mercy, the spleen of laughter, the liver of love*, according to the verse:

->*The spleen makes one laugh, the liver compels one to love.*<-

Certain viscera are also in the service of the emotions. By metonymy <note>A figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it.</note>, the Greeks use the word *splanchna* to denote emotions, whether of anger (hence Aristotle speaks of "warming the viscera toward anger," for the heart is the seat of anger, which is defined as the boiling of the blood around the heart) or of *mercy*, but most especially the feeling of *mercy*. From this comes that word of Christ the Savior, *splanchnizomai* <note>A Greek verb meaning "to be moved with compassion," literally "to feel it in the bowels."</note>, in *Matthew 9:36, Mark 6:34*, and elsewhere. I will set down the remaining names used by the Greeks in the words of Homer, from *Iliad Book 1, verse 188*, where the Poet deals with the mind of Achilles being stirred and turning into various thoughts:

->- - - Grief came upon the son of Peleus, and his heart<-
->within his shaggy breast was divided in counsel.<-

He later explained that impulse in *verse 193* thus:

->While he was revolving these things in his mind and in his spirit.<-

In these verses, *etor* (heart), *phren* (mind), and *thymos* (spirit) are joined, whereby the "revolving in counsel" is emphasized; his *thymos* <note>Spirit or passion.</note>, by the impulse it possessed, urged slaughter, while his *phren* <note>Rational mind or midriff.</note> and reason

<column-break/>

dissuaded him from it. To these Homeric lines, one can add the words of Virgil, if you attend to the sense:

> And now he divides his swift mind hither, now thither,
> And hurries it into various parts, and turns it through all things.

In the Hebrew language, it receives a most sweet name, being called *Lev* <note>לֵב</note>, from which comes the German custom of declaring the affection of love by calling that which we estimate as most precious and dear to us "the heart," as our people say: *I love you as my own heart*. Hence, under the name of the heart, a dear and pleasing thing very often appears in the Holy Scriptures. The Bride calls the Bridegroom *her heart*, saying: *I sleep, but my heart wakes.* <note>Song of Solomon 5:2</note> The heart wakes from a most burning love, which passes the night in vigils, does not allow one to sleep, and compels one to watch so that it may provide, even while the Bride, having forgotten the Bridegroom, is seized by sleep. Concerning his own most burning love toward the Bride, the Bridegroom himself testifies, saying in *chapter 4, verse 9*: *Libbabtini* <note>לִבַּבְתִּנִי</note>, *You have ravished my heart*, according to Aben Ezra. Rabbi Solomon says: *You have drawn my soul to you*, as if you have "hearted" me. The ancient Talmudists say: *You have coupled my heart with yours*. The ancient translator looks to the emotion, rendering it: *You have wounded my heart*. Ambrose, in *Sermon 16 on Psalm 118, page 718*, expresses it thus: *In the Song of Songs, it is said to the Church: You have taken my heart, my sister, my spouse; you have taken my heart with one of your eyes*, so that this "eye" may be the grace of one who has acquired the fuller charity of Christ for themselves. Most, however, take the "two eyes" of the Church in this place to mean: one which sees *mystical* things, and the other which sees *moral* things, because the Holy Church not only holds the discipline of *morals*, but also teaches the secrets of the heavenly mystery. Similarly, in Theocritus, in the eleventh Idyll, concerning the single eye, than which nothing is sweeter:

->And burning, I would endure for her my soul<-
->And my one eye, than which nothing is sweeter to me.<-

In the *Epithalamium* <note>A wedding song.</note>, the same author, when speaking of the Bride, says:

->In her eyes are all desires.<-

Regarding a heart wounded by the arrows of Love, the same says: *That god has struck my heart.*

Sweet and tender is the request of the Bridegroom, greeting the Bride thus: *Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm.* <note>Song of Solomon 8:6</note> The excellence of love is requested in this way; for this is what it means to *set as a seal*, not only *upon the heart* through the strong love of God, but also *upon the arm* through love of neighbor; in the *heart* are thoughts, and in the *arm* are actions, says Gregory on this passage. *He is placed upon the heart, because in the holy soul, it is designated how much he is loved both in will and in action.* Cassiodorus agrees when he writes: *Set me so that I may be in your memory; and set me as a seal upon your arm, that is, have me always present through constant meditation in your actions.* The words of Ambrose on this place are **memorable**: *Christ is a seal on the forehead, a seal on the heart, a seal on the arm. On the forehead, that we may always confess; in the heart, that we may always love; on the arm, that we may always work. Therefore, let his image shine in our confession, shine in our love, and shine in our works.*

...in works and deeds, so that, if possible, His entire likeness may be expressed in us. For Honorius says on this passage: *He places Christ upon his heart as a seal*, <note>Honorius Augustodunensis (1080–1154), a popular theologian and geographer. The quote refers to Song of Songs 8:6.</note> who keeps His doctrine and life in his heart in such a way that he seems to see Him always present. He places Him upon his arm *as a seal* when he constantly looks upon the examples of Christ’s works and desires to imitate them. So he says. There is nothing in Holy Scripture that is required more often or demanded more lovingly than the HEART; nor is there any member in which more is situated. In the very "head" <note>Referring to the primary or most important commandment.</note> of the Law, God requires the Heart, and that it be whole and solid, saying: *You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.* <margin>8th Aeneid, verse 20.</margin> <margin>Letter on life's vows 6. 48.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἀγαπήσεις Κύριον τὸν Θεόν σε ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ καρδίᾳ σε</note> *You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,* Matthew 22:37. **Umbertus** <note>Likely Humbert of Romans (c. 1190–1277), a Dominican master general.</note> says: *Let us strive most diligently to withdraw from sin with all our heart by detesting guilt; let us be converted to the Lord with all our heart by increasing our penance; let us seek the Lord with all our heart by praying for pardon; let us cling to the Lord with all our heart by loving Him above all things; let us serve the Lord with all our heart by praising Him; let us follow the Lord with all our heart by imitating His footsteps. We rightly owe these things to the Lord, because He bestows innumerable benefits upon our heart; for God Himself aids our hearts by His power and governs them by His wisdom: He enriches them with goodness, feeds them with sweetness, invites them with beauty, unites them with charity, allures them with promises, instructs them with lashes, shakes them with threats, and softens them with benefits. God Himself, most sweet, looks upon our hearts with approval, touches them by examining them, visits them by consoling them; He brings them to life by justifying them, and opens them by bedewing them—for all of which things it is fitting that we return thanks unweariedly.* <margin>Song of Songs 5:2.</margin> <margin>v. 32.</margin> To this One alone let your heart be consecrated; by loving the One, let it remain one. If the heart begins to flow away through earthly desires, it is divided into as many parts as there are things it lusts after. Greed and disordered lust split the heart, scatter it, break it into pieces, and crush it. He "has no heart" who does not fear the Lord from his heart, or who does not love God at all; and those who have no heart, how shall they have the joy of the heart? They live without life, because they do not have a heart dedicated to God. Such were the "heartless ones" to whom the Lord speaks through Jeremiah: *Hear, O foolish people, who have no heart.* <margin>Song of Songs 8:6.</margin> And again through Hosea: *Ephraim has become like a seduced dove, having no heart.* The Heart is the innermost chamber of our body, which may indeed be hidden from men, but not at all from God; and he who loves God acts from the heart without hypocrisy. For God looks upon the heart, 1 Samuel 15:7. He tests the hearts and the reins <note>term: reins</note> <note>From the Latin *renes* (kidneys). In biblical thought, the kidneys were considered the seat of emotions and hidden desires.</note>, Psalm 7:10, and in every work of divine worship He says to us: *My son, give me your heart.* <margin>Proverbs 23:23</margin> While David attributes the scrutiny of the heart and reins to God, the name "heart" signifies thoughts, and "reins" signify pleasures. The meaning is that God sees what each person thinks; He sees what delights each person; He sees where we are heading; He sees what we hope for; He sees our cares, and the goals of those cares. The former is to *search the heart*; the latter is to *search the reins*, by which lust and every pleasure are signified, as explained by Cornelio Musso at the Synod of Bitonto, page 26. <note>Cornelio Musso (1511–1574) was a famous Italian bishop and orator at the Council of Trent.</note> Along the same lines, **Bugenhagius** <note>Johannes Bugenhagen (1485–1558), a major figure in the Protestant Reformation and associate of Martin Luther.</note> writes <margin>Book on Isaac and the Soul, chapter 8.</margin> <margin>among c. 11. folio 1. a.</margin>: *God is a just judge; He cannot err in judgment, because He tests and knows the hearts and the reins. The hearts are our thoughts, counsels, purposes, efforts, and our hidden things. The reins are our desires, our lusts, our inclinations*

<column-break/>

<margin>
Sacred Anatomy
</margin>
*and affections. For just as thoughts and intelligence are in the heart, so the delight of the flesh is in the reins. Therefore, these two words, Hearts and Reins, are understood this way in the Scriptures.* The enticements of the Heart are stirred up by external objects—by sight, or hearing, or touch. Poison is swallowed readily through the eyes. Hence the Wise Man did not say in vain: *What was created more wicked than the eye?* Therefore, those who are held by the desire to preserve purity restrain their eyes, lest they wander too licentiously. Concerning this zeal for preserving himself, **Job** said: *I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin.* <margin>chapter 31:1.</margin> That David profited much in the purity of heart and Spirit from the examination of conscience is shown by those words in Psalm 77:7: *I meditated in the night with my heart, and I exercised myself, and I swept my Spirit.* The ancient translator says "I swept" (*scopebam*); for just as houses are cleaned with brooms (*scopis*), so by that examination and scrutiny, the heart of a religious man—the dwelling place and sanctuary of the Holy Spirit—is cleaned. The man of God searched his soul to find what might be hiding in it, just as a house is swept and stirred up with brooms so that a lost coin may be found, as Augustine explains. Indeed, that examination of the heart, to which the Prophet Jeremiah exhorts in chapter 31:21—*Direct,* he says, *your heart toward the right way*—is exceedingly necessary and useful because of the innumerable enticements of pleasures; it is a task of great work and labor to restrain the fickleness of the heart from individual sins, as **Leo** <note>Pope Leo I (c. 400–461 AD).</note> says in Sermon 11 on Lent 2, folio 93. a. Hence the words of **Ambrose** <note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), Bishop of Milan.</note> have a place here: <margin>On Fleeing the World, chapter 1. p. 308.</margin> *Frequently the enticement of earthly desires creeps in, and a flood of vanities occupies the mind, so that what you strive to avoid, you think about and turn over in your soul; it is difficult for a man to beware of this, and impossible to strip it away.* The Prophet testifies that this is more a matter of a wish than an accomplishment when he says: *Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to greed.* For our Heart and our thoughts are not in our own power; they pour out unexpectedly and confuse the mind and soul, dragging them elsewhere than you had proposed. They call us back to secular things, bring in worldly matters, thrust in pleasures, weave in enticements, and in the very time when we prepare to elevate the mind, we are mostly cast down to earthly things by the insertion of empty thoughts. But who is so blessed as to always ascend in his heart? Yet how can this be done without divine help? In no way at all. This scrutiny of the heart is also useful because it pleases God, and in it consists the true worship of God. Moreover, the strength to institute and continue such an examination is not situated in us, as **Ambrose** rightly warns in the preceding sentence, but proceeds from God alone. For God must be served with a great mind, just as the Jews of Jerusalem exhorted their brothers to worship God with a generous mind and to carry out the divine will with a great heart, saying in 2 Maccabees 1:3: *May He give you all a Heart to worship Him and to do His will with a great heart and a willing mind.* Concerning this heart and the works with which we ought to serve God, Nierembergius <note>Juan Eusebio Nieremberg (1595–1658), a Spanish Jesuit mystic and author.</note> discusses it thus in *4. Ascetic Doctrine 40, page 318*: *Divine service and our perfection do not [depend...]*

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
#### Page 812

<margin>

</margin>
This is not such an unworthy or trivial occupation that one should approach it except with nobility and greatness of soul; for both the excellence and the difficulty of virtue demand a large heart, and require a noble and upright mind. Its honor is so great that it ought to be sought with all our strength and the fullest heart: its labor is so great that it cannot be acquired except by those same strengths and a massive heart. To this is added the infinite greatness of God, whom we serve; and our infinite obligation, which, since we are unable to fulfill it in fact and effect, we should at least strive toward with the spirit and nobility of the heart. For just as God, with clearly upright and profuse liberality, bestows benefits upon us constantly without measure or number, so it is necessary for us to be liberal and magnanimous, so that we may at least be shown to be grateful, and not serve our most liberal and magnanimous Lord and Benefactor with a small and base heart. God must be served courageously, fervently, and with a great heart. 

In that most elaborate fabric of the heart, one may observe the "similar parts" <note>A term from Galenic anatomy referring to uniform tissues like membrane or fiber, as opposed to "dissimilar" organs composed of multiple tissues.</note> from which its complex structure is woven. For at the base of the heart, the **auricles** <note>Now commonly called atria.</note> hang on both sides; they are so named from a slight resemblance they have to the ears of dogs, and from their connection, since they are attached to both sides of the heart as ears are to a head. The auricle of the heart on the right exceeds the one on the left in size, because the right one acts as a kind of doorkeeper to the *vena cava*, through which blood travels to the right ventricle of the heart, which we shall now discuss. 

For the heart also has cavities or **two ventricles**, a left and a right. This right one is larger than the left, and reaches from the base or "head" of the heart all the way to the point. The left one, however, is carved exactly into the middle of the heart; if the right side were removed, it would seem to represent the entire heart on its own, so that the right side is placed there like an appendix. Aristotle testifies in various places in his *History of Animals* that in large and massive beasts, such as the elephant, rhinoceros, and camel, three ventricles are found. In smaller and aquatic creatures lacking lungs, at least one is found. In mid-sized animals—for example, in man, the dog, the ox, etc.—there are two, which differ in size, position, and shape. 

According to the common opinion of anatomists, they are also distinguished by their actions, such that the **right** ventricle prepares and refines the nourishment suitable for the lungs from the blood it receives from the vein; once it is sufficiently "cooked," <note>The author uses the traditional Galenic concept of "coction" or heat-based digestion of bodily fluids.</note> it sends it to them through the *arterial vein* <note>original: "venam arteriosam." This is what we now call the pulmonary artery.</note> passing from the right chamber into the lungs. The **left** ventricle, however, receives the air coming from the lungs and draws blood from the right ventricle, along with its other duties taught in the School of Anatomists. *These two chambers are separated from one another by an intervening partition or septum, lest what is in one be carried by a direct path into the other.* Furthermore, four vessels are observed around the base of the heart: **two veins** and **two arteries**. The veins are the *vena cava* and the *arterial vein*, both of which are located on the right side of the heart at the right auricle. The *vena cava* is the largest of all in the entire body; according to the opinion of recent authors, it ascends from the heart, but according to the opinion of the ancients, it ascends from the liver through the diaphragm to the right auricle, opening into the right chamber of the heart with a wide mouth or gap. Its function is to carry blood to the heart. The *arterial vein* is believed, by common anatomical opinion, to carry

<column-break/>

nutritional blood for the nourishment of the lungs. The arteries are the *venous artery* <note>original: "arteria venosa." This is what we now call the pulmonary vein.</note> and the *great artery*, which is also called the **Aorta**, as if <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ τὸν αἶρα τηρεῖν (*apo to ton aira terein*)</note> "from the keeping of the air." <note>This reflects the ancient belief that arteries primarily carried "vital spirit" or air rather than blood.</note> The former received its name because it supplies the lungs with "spirituous" blood (which is characteristic of arteries). The latter [the Aorta] spreads two branches from the head of the heart near the left auricle: one ascending and the other descending, and it derives the spirituous, vital blood—already perfected in the heart—through the entire body. 

This doctrine regarding the parts of the heart is entangled in various subtleties, which we shall leave to the anatomists to discuss. When the critic Momus <note>A figure from Greek mythology representing mockery and unfair criticism.</note> had caught sight of so many corners and recesses in the construction of the heart, he criticized it because it lacked a window through which one might look into those dark and twisting windings. Anyone may acquire such a "window" for themselves if they consult some most skillful craftsman, such as **Vesling**, **Riolan**, **Bartholin**, or another. <note>Refers to Johann Vesling, Jean Riolan the Younger, and Thomas Bartholin, famous 17th-century anatomists.</note> The veins and arteries are vessels, channels, and organs fashioned by God for conveying the animal spirits, so that they may flow into various parts of the body for sensation and movement. Through the veins, as if through channels, the whole body is irrigated and receives blood as nourishment. For the vital spirit, mixed with the blood and enclosed in the arteries, flows to all parts and returns in a circle, <note>A reference to William Harvey’s discovery of the circulation of the blood, which was becoming standard medical knowledge when this was written.</note> subject to the powerful dominion of the heart. Hence, one can somehow draw a connection to the verse of the Orient:

> *Faces, color, blood, vein, skin, bones, hair,*
> *As they now glide away, so they shall come again.* <note>A Latin couplet reflecting on the cycle of life and the eventual resurrection of the body.</note>

It is a **wondrous work** and exceeds the measure of our reason when we see the blood, by nature, driven as if in a circle through the heart, lungs, arteries, and veins, flowing and ebbing in the bodies of "perfect" animals. For venous blood flows through the heart into the arteries, and arterial blood flows through openings into the veins, so that in a healthy adult human, no less than twenty pounds [of blood] falls from the systole of the heart into the arteries every hour; see **Thomas Bartholin**'s *book on the veins and arteries*.

Around the base of the heart, also like a kind of glue to moisten and refresh it, there adheres **fat** (soft fat) or rather **suet** (hard fat). For *soft fat* <note>original: "pinguedo"</note> differs from *suet* <note>original: "adeps"</note> in that soft fat is under the skin, while suet is around the heart and kidneys. Soft fat is softer and more humid; it is quickly melted by heat, and when melted it retains the appearance of oil, and hardens again more slowly. Suet, however, is of greater hardness; it liquefies with more difficulty, and once liquefied, it easily condenses again. Thus Aristotle himself in book 3, *History of Animals*, chapter 17, and Galen, the Prince of Physicians, distinguish soft fat from suet; compare Pliny 11. 27 and Peter Lauremberg’s *Anatomy of the Human Body*, page 63. Suet is found more abundantly in man than in beasts, and sometimes in such great quantity that the heart is entirely hidden and obscured, so that it is not even believed to be present—a thing which is well known from the writers of secular literature to have very often happened to the ancient soothsayers. <note>Referring to the *haruspices* who examined animal entrails for omens; a missing or obscured heart was considered a dire sign.</note> 

The Holy Spirit very often argues from natural things to signify those things which transcend the laws of nature. From the fat by which the heart is sometimes hidden, the Spirit of God establishes a comparison to the natural heart to hint at the spiritual dullness and hardness of the heart. It stands in Psalm 119, verse 70: <note>original Hebrew: טָפַשׁ כַּחֵלֶב לִבָּם (*Tafash kachelev libbam*)</note> *Their heart is curdled like*

### from Psalm 139, verse 15.

...their heart is like fat. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translates this somewhat incongruously as "their heart was curdled like milk" <note>original Greek: ἐτυρώθη ὡς γάλα ἡ καρδία αὐτῶν</note>, referring to the coagulation of milk. In Hebrew, the word is *taphash* <note>original: טפש</note>, meaning to be thickened or made fat; metaphorically, it means to be dull or sluggish, referring to human wisdom that becomes foolish and lacks judgment. This word occurs only once, specifically in this passage. Fat—which in its Hebrew letters closely relates to the word for "flesh"—clings to the meat, and just as a body is called "thick" from having much flesh and fodder, so it is called "fat" from having much suet. In Greek, it is *pimele* <note>original: πιμελὴ</note>; indeed, "fatness" and "suet" <note>original: πιμελὴ</note> entirely correspond in sound and sense to the word *pademah* <note>original: פדמה</note>, which denotes internal fat. But what is this "oiliness and richness of the heart" <note>original Greek: λιπαρότης καὶ πιότης τῆς καρδίας</note>? It is surely "callousness" <note>original: Πώρωσις</note> and stupidity. An explanation for this can be provided by physicists: for if the "spirits" of the heart are thin and subtle, the effects produced in the mind are subtle; but if they are thick, the operations are more sluggish. Hence, "hardening of the mind" remains to be understood as occurring when the judgment of the mind is depraved, "and the intellect is diseased" <note>original Greek: καὶ γνώμην νοσέει</note>, as Hippocrates says in his *Aphorisms*. Unless you prefer to refer those words of the Psalmist to the pleasures and delights of the heart which are found in the Law, for there follows immediately: "I delighted in your law" <note>original Hebrew: אני תורתך שעשעתי</note>. Thus, "fat" <note>original Hebrew: חלב, chelev</note> is used for the abundance and excellence of the subject being discussed. Furthermore, that word "delighted" <note>original: שעשע</note> comes from the root *sha’ah*, which denotes looking most attentively, as happens when an object charms us; hence it means to delight oneself. Fat is characterized by hardness, especially that found around the base of the heart. Those who, like the "cows of Bashan" <note>A biblical reference to the wealthy and indifferent, from Amos 4:1</note>—to use the Prophet’s words—have fattened themselves and put on a hardness of heart against obeying God, are said in Holy Scripture to be "hard of heart," "stiff-necked," and "uncircumcised in hearts and ears." Concerning this manner of speaking, Bernard of Clairvaux, in his *On Consideration* to Pope Eugenius, says:

<margin>Commentary part 1, verse 261</margin>
> * A hard heart is that which is neither torn by compunction, nor softened by piety, nor moved by prayers; it does not yield to threats, is hardened by lashes, is ungrateful for benefits, treacherous in counsel, savage in judgment, shameless in disgrace, fearless in danger, inhuman toward human affairs, reckless toward divine ones, forgetting the past, neglecting the present, and not providing for the future.

Finally, after many other points, he concludes:

<margin>Book 2, sheet 237</margin>
> No one with a hard heart has ever obtained salvation.

It is certainly a great benefit from God to soften a hard heart like wax; God promised this as a supreme gift through Ezekiel, chapter 36, verse 26: "I will give you a new heart" <note>original Hebrew: לב חדש, lev chadash</note> and "a new spirit" <note>original Hebrew: ורוח חדשה, ve-ruach chadashah</note> I will put within you; "and I will take away the stony heart" <note>original Hebrew: את-לב האבן, et-lev ha-even</note> from your flesh, "and I will give you a heart of flesh" <note>original Hebrew: ונתתי לכם לב בשר</note>. Upon these words, Jerome says:

> When a new heart and a new spirit are given, then all hardness, which is compared to stone, shall be taken away from the Jewish heart, so that in place of a stony heart there may be a heart of flesh—soft and tender—which can receive the Spirit of God within itself.

Eucherius of Lyon says the same:

<margin>Book 3, face 11</margin>

When God says he removes the stony heart and puts in a fleshy one in Ezekiel, he is removing the impediment that was in the malice of the heart. "The removal," <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐξαιρεθῆναι</note> says Origen in *Philocalia*, chapter 20, page

289, "of stony hearts" <note>original Greek: τὰς λιθίνας καρδίας</note> is nothing other than the removal of the vice by which one is hardened, which God wills to be taken away. And "for a fleshy heart to be engendered" so that one may walk in the precepts of God and keep His commandments—what else is this but to become yielding and not resistant to the truth, and active toward virtue? The consciences of those who are secure and impenitent are harder than iron, and their hearts thicker than any fat; hence they feel neither the weight of sin nor the wrath of God against the magnitude of their sins. But the consciences of the pious are softer than any oil; they are daily concerned with a "clean and new heart" to be created in them by God, whence they repeat with David in Psalm 51:12: "Create in me a clean heart, O God." Create such a heart in me, O God; produce it from nothing; and that which cannot exist by nature, let it become such through grace.

THE LUNGS <note>original Latin: PVLMO</note>, among the Greeks, take their name from breathing; called *pneumon* <note>original: πνεύμων</note> from *pneein* <note>original: πνέειν</note>, "to breathe." They are situated in the middle of the chest, concerning which seat Theocritus <note>A Greek poet.</note> says:

<margin>Idyll 25, verse 237</margin>
> And I struck the middle of the chest, where the lungs sit. <note>original Greek: Μεσσηγὺς δ᾽ ἔβαλον στήθεων, ὅθι πνεύμονες ἕδρα.</note>

Surrounding the heart, they fill almost the entire cavity of the thorax; when the thorax expands, the lungs also expand, swell, and fill; when it contracts, they sink back into themselves. They are the bellows or fan of the heart; indeed, they are its cushion and a kind of support. For that reason, Plato in the *Timaeus* says not inelegantly that "the lungs are the steward of the breaths for the body" <note>original: τὸν πνεύμονα esse τὸ πνευμάτων τῷ σώματι ταμίαν</note>. That is, they dispense the spirit in the body just as some treasurer in a King's court dispenses money for various uses. To the Greeks, *tamias* <note>original: ταμίας</note> refers to a "steward" of things to be stored or brought forth, like one in charge of a pantry, a wine cellar, or a granary; likewise, one who is in charge of the treasury is called a *quaestor* or a treasurer. Its flesh is like curdled foam; when it is liquefied, the blood proceeding from the substance of the lungs is soon turned into foam, reflecting the likeness of the internal organ, as noted by Fischer in his *Aphorisms of Hippocrates*, page 246. Moreover, it consists of vessels of three kinds: 1. the "rough artery" or trachea, extended forward and backward from the middle of its substance. 2. the "venous artery" <note>Now called the pulmonary vein.</note>, led from its anterior region into the left ventricle of the heart, in such a way that both are joined throughout the entire substance of the lung to the small branches and forks of the trachea by "anastomosis" <note>The connection between two vessels.</note>. 3. the "arterial vein" <note>Now called the pulmonary artery.</note> led from the posterior part of the lungs into the right ventricle of the heart. In shape, it resembles an ox's hoof, convex on the outside and hollow on the inside, so that with its lobes, as if with two hands, it can embrace the heart. Some deny that the lung has its own motion, thinking that it is moved by the motion of the entire sternum and by the power of the pectoral muscles. But all motion from an outside source is "violent" <note>In the Aristotelian sense of being forced rather than natural.</note>, and everything violent is contrary to nature; hence, with Sennert <note>Daniel Sennert, a famous 17th-century physician.</note>, we assert that the lung has its own motion, whose complete words I am pleased to record here:

<margin>Book 1 of the Institutes, chapter 11</margin>
> The lung has a peculiar power of movement, like the heart. For although by itself alone...

...does not finish the work, but rather the movement of the chest is also necessary. Nevertheless, because this entire movement is directed toward the end of drawing in air, and this drawing in is performed by the lungs, the lung is rightly established as the primary organ of respiration for all. A specific power has been placed within it—just as in the heart—which is distinct from the animal faculty; compare Felix Plater <note>A Swiss physician (1536–1614) known for his work on pathology.</note> in *Pathological Questions, 29*. Its use is to serve respiration, which encompasses both inhalation and exhalation; the former happens while the lungs are compressed, the latter while they are dilated. The lung draws in air, without which a man cannot live as a respiratory organ, and communicates it to the heart so that man may breathe and live. In the lungs, says Ratbertus <note>Likely Paschasius Radbertus, a Carolingian theologian.</note>: *the vital breaths flourish, and the health of life is tempered.* How much the lung contributes of benefit is evident from the book of nature, and indeed from experience itself. The Psalmist points this out to us, as if with a finger, in *chapter 104, verse 29*: *You take away their breath,* he says, *and they fail.* Join to this Isaiah *chapter 2, verse 22*: *Cease then from man, whose breath is in his nostrils: for of what account is he?* Those who breathe with difficulty are said by physicians to suffer from asthma; others trace the words of Job to this: *He does not grant my breath to rest*, that is, he does not let me breathe. Wherefore Philippus the Presbyter in *Job 9, page 32* says: he called himself "asthmatic" <note>original Greek: ἀσθματικὸν</note> in effect. For it is a weakness generated in the lungs; for certain passages <note>original: Itopiros</note> of the lungs are blocked, which the Greeks call "openings"; and thus constricted and shut up in the lungs, as physicians say, they make it so the squeezed lungs are not sufficient to receive or return the Breath. Because of excessive pain and hurried sighing, he was emitting repeated and, as it were, cut-off breaths. Furthermore, the lungs are the organs of the voice, which is why they touch the heart at a closer degree and intimately surround it. Just as a Chancellor is second to a King or Prince, so the lung, as the organ for forming the voice, immediately touches the heart, says Melanchthon <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560), a German reformer and educator.</note> *on the Spirit of the Soul*. All air in the chest comes from the lung, and man needs more air than other living creatures, both for speech, for song, and for submersion in water. Whence Augustine says: *The lung of our breast is like a kind of bellows of the reciprocating breath, which breath, once conceived, is expressed into voice and sound when we arrange words. Nor can any voice sound from our mouth unless the squeezed lung has sent it forth.*

Thus far we have seen, according to the reason and measure of our undertaking, the upper and middle cavities. Anatomists are accustomed to dedicate their first efforts to the lowest cavity because of the putrefaction and stench to which it is subject compared to the middle and upper ones. In this "sacred anatomy," since that concern does not touch us, we have given the lowest place to the lowest cavity, inasmuch as that which yields in honor to the rest should also yield in its place—though it exceeds the others if one considers the types, number, and multitude of its parts. For it contains the liver, the stomach, the spleen, the intestines, the kidneys, the uterus, the penis, the bladder, and others; the "insatiable abdomen," as we might say with Sperling <note>Paul Sperling (1605–1679), a German physician and physicist.</note>. There are members here that always seek and are never filled; for what is more insatiable than the belly, or what more than the uterus? On account of this great "voracity" <note>original Greek: ἀδηφαγίαν</note>, they almost make this divine animal—man, I mean, full of reason and counsel—

worse than the beasts. The lowest belly, called by the poets the *Aqualiculus* <note>A poetic Latin term for the lower abdomen or "the little water-pot."</note> and by anatomists the *Abdomen*, is divided into three regions: the *epigastric, umbilical, and hypogastric*. In the first, we show the liver on the right side, the spleen on the left, and at the same time the stomach and intestines. In the second, the navel, by which a man must necessarily perish [if severed at birth], and beneath it the intestine, which is called by the Greek name *colon* <note>original: κῶλον</note>, either from *kōlyō* (to delay or hinder) or from *kōlazesthai* (to be tormented), on account of the griping pains and tortures that occur there. Its length, says Adrianus Spigelius <note>Adriaan van den Spiegel (1578–1625), a Flemish anatomist.</note>, *is seven palms and as many fingers, while its width equals a fist. For it is very spacious, so that whatever of the more useless chyle remains, it may receive into itself and hold for a while, lest man—an animal devoted to the study of the Muses—be continually interrupted by the need to expel feces.* In the third region are the Kidneys, the Vessels, the Bladder, and the parts serving generation. The Parent of Nature surrounded the Abdomen with various fortifications. Those who move their hand to cut the abdomen first encounter the *cuticula* <note>epidermis</note>, which together with the abdomen surrounds the entire external surface of the body and is, as it were, the covering and blossoming of the true skin, called by the Greeks the *epidermis* <note>original: ἐπιδερμὶς</note> or *epidermatis*, meaning "over-skin." Directly beneath this lies the *skin* (*cutis*), which is itself six times thicker than the cuticle—thin and subtle in children, but thicker and denser in adults. After this follows the *fat* (*pinguedo*), produced by the soul from oily blood for the protection, moistening, and movement of the underlying parts. Beneath this lies the *fleshy membrane*, which others call the *panniculum*, which surrounds and embraces almost the entire body; for it adheres not only to the fat, but simultaneously to the skin through the intervention of veins, arteries, nerves, and fibers, which is why, even if the fat is consumed, the skin remains connected to the rest of the body. Consecrated to the lower belly alone is a certain membrane of no small importance, whose name comes from "stretching around" <note>original Greek: περιτείνεσθαι</note>: the *peritoneum* <note>original Greek: περιτόναιον</note>; for the Latins, when they could not find a suitable word in their own tongue, granted this one citizenship in their own. This membrane veils the entire lower belly and its internal parts, which it clothes, surrounds, and covers, lest they be harmed by injuries or depart from their proper place; it also covers the ends of the vessels and fosters heat, lest it be easily dissipated. If you look at its position, in the upper part it adheres most firmly to the diaphragm and the first and third vertebrae, and cannot be separated from them without rupture; in the posterior part, it adheres to the pubic bone and the ilium. Following this is another membrane, and a doubled one at that, which is called the *epiploon* <note>original Greek: ἐπίπλοον</note> among the Greeks, the *Omentum* by the Latins, and the *Reticello* by the Italians, from the similarity it has to a fisherman's net—hence it is also called the "Net" <note>original German: Netze</note> by the Germans. It embraces most parts of the abdomen, winding itself into the intestines and their coils; it adheres to the lobe of the liver, the bottom of the stomach, the colon, the pancreas, and with its largest portion to the spleen. However, it is not of as great a size as the peritoneum, since it does not pass the navel; when it exceeds its natural size and extends down to the groin, it causes an *Epiplocele* <note>An omental hernia.</note>, and in women, if it is bound to the uterus, it produces sterility. In man, it is larger in proportion than in beasts. ## Page 815

From Psalm 139, verse 15.

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> In the holy language <note>original: "lingua sancta," referring to Hebrew</note> it is called <term>fat</term> <note>original: חלב (*chelev*)</note>, as seen in Exodus 29:13, 22 and Leviticus 3:9. All suet was sacred to God as a burnt sacrifice before the altar. This signified that Christ was the most pleasing victim for our sins, offered on the altar of the cross to appease the wrath of God the Father. Origen <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) known for allegorical interpretations.</note> understands the term "fat" to mean all carnal thoughts and the "gluttony of the heart" <note>original: ἀδηφαγίαν (*adephagia*)</note>, which he writes must be removed and burned away if one wishes to hear and perceive the word of God fruitfully.

<margin>Homily 5 on Leviticus</margin> <note>The asterisk in the text refers to Hesychius, book 1 on Leviticus.</note> *Hesychius says: "Therefore, he commands that the 'intelligible fat'—that is, all our desire or appetite—be devoted to the Spirit."*

<margin>Isaiah 41, chapter 2.</margin> Hesychius later praises Origen’s opinion: *"So that there might be a teaching,"* he says, *"by which a simple people might be warned not to pursue the delights and pleasures of the flesh, but to mortify them by the fire of the Holy Spirit. Hence Solomon says: 'He who loves wine and fat things shall not be enriched' <note>Proverbs 21:17</note>."* He continues: *"The burning of the fat in sacrifice signifies the passion and death of Christ, who, being by far the best and most beloved of all the human race, is foreshadowed by the fat. For only the passion of Christ possesses this holiness and majesty, being the expiation for our sins and our reconciliation with God. Those who transfer this majesty to the merits of human righteousness profane and insult the passion of Christ, etc. Thus, hypocrites who trust in the merits of their own righteousness are said to 'eat the fat' against the law, and they become subject to the gravest punishment of the law, which says: 'If anyone eats the fat that ought to be offered as incense to the Lord, he shall perish from his people.'"*

Approaching the inner parts of the lower belly, the <term>Stomach</term> <note>Latin: Ventriculus</note> presents itself in the epigastric region. This is the storehouse of the entire body, from which the juice of life proceeds through the mixing of the four humors. It is that most industrious "grinding-mill" of the body, whose "millstones" are the teeth, the sound of which the author of Ecclesiastes <note>referring to Ecclesiastes 12:3-4</note> seems to compare to the noise of a mill. It is the larder and the steward, of which Philippus the Presbyter says:

<margin>On Job, book 1, chapter 15, page 57.</margin> <insert>It is a certain receptacle of the body in which the vitals of the organs are contained, and we call this by the name of the Belly.</insert> Ratbertus attributes the same epithet to it in his commentary on the Lamentations of Jeremiah: *"The Belly,"* he says, *"is the receptacle of all foods, where the sustenance and substance of the whole body is gathered and cooked down."* This is the kitchen common to all the limbs, granting each its own share and preserving the peace of all; for this reason, the Stomach is adorned with a royal crown by Quintus Serenus <note>A Roman physician and poet.</note> when he says:

> Those who contend the stomach is the King of the whole body
> Seem to rely on true and solid reason.

Theodorus Abucara <note>A 9th-century theologian.</note> compares it to a pot: *"Because the throat is for eating and drinking, it descends into the stomach as into a cooking pot. With the liver lying around the stomach, being hot, the food is cooked and turned into chyle <note>The milky fluid of digested food.</note>. The thick part goes downward, while the thin and chyle-filled part floats on top."* Among the Greeks, the name for the stomach is <term>koilia</term> <note>belly/cavity</note>, and sometimes also <term>stomachos</term> <note>gullet/mouth of the stomach</note>, using the name of the part for the whole. In the holy language <note>Hebrew</note> it is called <term>kivah</term> <note>קבה, the stomach or maw</note> because of its shape. Its size is not fixed, but varies according to the individual. It is endowed with a rounded, oblong shape, similar to a leather bottle or the bag of a bagpipe <note>original: "tibiæ utricularis"</note> used by ancient musicians, where the esophagus and the attached intestine represent the pipes.

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> It has two openings and one base. The <term>upper</term> or left opening, which sits on the left side of the stomach, is called the <term>stomachos</term> by the Greeks because food descends through it; it is also called the <term>cardia</term> <note>heart-opening</note> because its sensations have a certain similarity to those of the true heart. The <term>lower</term> or right opening, because it touches the stomach on the right, is named the <term>pylorus</term>, or the <term>Gatekeeper</term>, because through it the nourishment is sent from the stomach into the intestine. When the lowest part of the stomach turns slightly toward the right and narrows into the top of the intestine, the Greeks call this junction the <term>pylorus</term>, since like a gate it sends out into the lower parts those things we are about to excrete. This is written by Celsus, who also calls it the "gate of the stomach" when discussing the celiac disease. Galen calls it the *"bottom of the belly"* <note>Greek: Πυθμένα τῆς κοιλίας</note>.

<margin>Book 4, chapter 8, page 42b.</margin> But <term>pylorus</term> means a gate-guardian or janitor, from a word meaning to watch over; it has this name because it guards the things sent into the stomach until they are digested, and once digestion is complete, it passes them through. The base, however, receives, contains, and digests the food and drink. For the action of the stomach consists of this: receiving food and drink sent down from the mouth and converting it into chyle by its own innate power.

Continuous with the stomach are the <term>Intestines</term> or <term>Bowel</term>. The ancients used the masculine form <note>Latin: "Intestinus"</note>, as is clear from Pliny, whose words are: *"The intestine in man is attached to the bottom of the stomach, similar to that of a dog."*

<margin>Book 21, chapter 37.</margin> They are called <term>intestines</term> because they "stand within" <note>Latin: "intus stant"</note>, and are called <term>interanea</term> for the same origin and reason. To the Greeks they are <term>entera</term>, especially in the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> at Exodus 12:9, 29:7, and Leviticus 4:8. To ensure that the impure breath of filth was far removed from the most pure palace of the mind, and so that filth could be more conveniently ejected, provident Nature assigned the intestines a place in the lowest belly. She adorned them with fat, membranes, fibers, veins, arteries, and nerves. Certain fat or suet was forbidden to the Hebrews—not all of it, for God sometimes commends animals for their fatness. They were permitted one type of <term>fat</term> <note>Hebrew: חלב (*chelev*)</note>, but not the <term>interior fat</term> that covers the intestines and tends to thicken and cool. However, the fat that adheres immediately to the meat and is sometimes mixed with the meat was permitted for them to eat. Based on their consistency, the intestines are divided into <term>thin</term> <note>small</note> and <term>thick</term> <note>large</note>. The thin ones are three: the <term>duodenum</term>, the <term>jejunum</term>, and the <term>ileum</term>. The "thin" ones got their name because their substance is very thin. The ancients called them <term>Lactes</term> <note>milky vessels</note> and <term>Pantices</term> <note>paunch</note>. From this they read "weary in the guts" <note>Latin: "lassas lactibus"</note>.

<margin>Book 6.</margin> Priscian <note>A 6th-century Latin grammarian.</note> says they are called <term>galaktides</term> <note>Greek for "milky"</note>, and his words are: *"The word for salt-fish [halec] and milk [lac] has no plural. For these 'lactes' are parts of the intestines, named from the Greek 'galaktides,' and they preserved the same gender among us, the singular of which is 'this Milk' [haec Lactis]."* Pomponius says in *The Household God*: *"I pray you, Base, by your guts [lactes]."* Among the thin intestines, the first is the <term>Duodenum</term>, named <term>dodekadactylon</term> because it is "twelve fingers" long. However, it is scarcely eight or nine fingers in length, so it more rightly deserves to be called the "eight-finger" or "nine-finger" organ. It lies on the right side, descending straight toward the spine without any twists. It is denser than the other thin intestines, though narrower, so that digested food does not fall from the stomach into the intestines too quickly.
