# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
## Page 816

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> The second in the order of the small intestines is called by the Latins the *Jejunum*, because it is for the most part empty and void; the Greeks call it the *nēstis* <note>original: νήστις, meaning 'fasting'</note>. It is also known by another name, particularly among the comic playwrights and poets, who call it the *Hilla* <note>A term often used for a small sausage or a delicate part of the entrails</note>. By Festus and also by Plautus in his play *Curculio*, it is called the *Hira*. From this, Varro says that a pork sausage is derived from "hilo," that is, something very small; and Plautus writes: *And smoked sausages [Hillas] and sow’s udder.* Horace likewise says <margin>a. Satire 4, line 60.</margin>
> —rather than ham, or rather than *sausages [Hillis]*,
> *He demands to be restored to his appetite.*

It begins at the duodenum and ends in the Ileum, measuring twelve palms and three fingers in length. The third of the small intestines is called the *Ileum* <term>twisted gut</term> <note>original: εἰλεός (*eileos*)</note>, from the word <term>to be rolled up</term> <note>original: τὸ εἰλεῖσθαι (*to eileisthai*)</note>, because of its various windings; it is the longest of all the intestines, reaching twenty-one palms, beginning at the jejunum and ending at the cecum. In addition to the small intestines we have just seen, anatomists also count three Large ones: the *Cecum*, the *Colon*, and the *Rectum*. The first is called the *Cecum* <note>meaning 'blind'</note> and "one-eyed," because it lacks a second opening, and thus the chyle <note>The milky fluid of digested food</note> enters and exits through the same opening; although there are some among the more recent scholars who claim to have found two openings in it (compare Knoblauch, *Anatomical Institutions, Dissertation 4, v. 118*). It arises from the end of the ileum and the beginning of the colon, having a length of four transverse fingers and a width of a thumb. However, where the ileum intestine ends and that appendage called the cecum is attached—namely, at the beginning of the colon—a remarkable valve presents itself, which Caspar Bauhin <note>A famous 16th-century Swiss botanist and anatomist</note> boasts of having discovered (see his *Treatise on the Parts of the Human Body*). The second of the large intestines, situated between the cecum and the rectum, is roomier and wider than the others; it is called by the Greeks the *kolon* <note>original: κόλον and κῶλον—it occurs with both spellings</note>. It possesses a valve that acts as a barrier against backed-up waste and gases, and being composed of many small cells, it creates a delay for the descending waste. Adrian Spigelius <margin>b. Anatomy, p. 296.</margin> recommends this valve to the reader as *a great and outstanding specimen of divine providence*. When this intestine is even slightly afflicted, *it is a cause of great pain*, as Pliny also testifies (Book 2, Chapter 37), for it shakes the intestines with the most violent agonies. The last of the large intestines is called the *Rectum* for this reason: because it is extended in a straight path all the way to the anus. Thus, Aristotle calls it the <term>straight gut</term> <note>original: εὐθύεντερον (*euthyenteron*)</note> and the <term>archos</term> <note>original: ἀρχός, meaning 'the beginning'</note>, because it is the first part encountered when starting from the anus, but it actually begins where the twists of the intestines end. In males, it is located beneath the bladder; in females, however, it is beneath the uterus. From this, a <term>sympathy</term> <note>original: συμπάθειά (*sympatheia*), here meaning a physical or physiological connection</note> of these parts arises with it. It has a length of one and a half palms and a width of three fingers. It is richer in fat than the others to help promote excretion. Job makes mention of the fat <term>of the intestines</term> <note>original: τῶν ἐντέρων (*tōn enterōn*)</note> <margin>chapter 21, verse 24</margin>: *His intestines are full of fat, and his bones are moistened with marrow; but another dies in the bitterness of his soul without any wealth.* The condition of living in this world is varied: one person abounds while another lacks; one rich man shines in purple and fine linen while another walks in rags. Regarding this diversity, Saint Job, in the passage just cited, is commented upon by the Priest Philosopher <margin>page 86</margin> as follows: *It is this which we see happening now: that some are fat with delights and abundance, and rich with excessive wealth; while others waste away in the greatest poverty, and yet*

<column-break/>

*the condition of being born and dying is the same for both the rich and the poor.* Thus he writes. But while we consider the end of what is to be said about the intestines, Macrobius comes to mind (*Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*), discussing the intestines in this way: *There are three principal intestines,* he says, *one of which is called the Disliptum, which separates the stomach and the other intestines. The second is the middle one, which the Greeks call the <term>mesenterion</term> <note>original: μεσεντέριον</note>. The third, which the Ancients called the Hira, is considered the chief of all the intestines and carries away the refuse of food.*

Among the intestines, Cicero likewise lists the <term>mesentery</term> <note>original: μεσεντέριον</note> (*On the Nature of the Gods*, Book 3), which takes its name from its position, as if it were the <term>middle of the intestines</term> <note>original: μέσον ἐντέρων (*meson enterōn*)</note>. Although it is not technically one of the intestines, it is at least their bond and is situated in the middle of them. Its function is to bind the intestines together and keep them in their proper place so they do not become tangled; it also warms them and connects them to the vertebrae of the loins so that they are not shaken by immoderate movement of the body or disturbed from their seats. It is also called the <term>mesaraion</term> <note>original: μεσάραιον</note>, not because it is <term>araion</term> <note>thin or rare</note> (as Asellius taught from Sylvius, since there is no thinness in the membranous substance of the Mesentery), but from <term>araiēs</term> <note>original: ἀπ’ ἀραιῆς</note>, which word, as Hesychius notes, refers to the small intestines. Similarly, it is called the <term>mesocolon</term> <note>original: μεσόκωλον</note> from the word <term>kōla</term> <note>original: ἀπὸ κώλων</note>, which are the large intestines. The more curious, says Laurenbergius, distinguish between these two: for when the Peritoneum adheres to some part of the small intestines (<term>araias</term>), it is called the *Mesareum*; but because it is bound in another part to the large intestines (<term>kōla</term>), it is called the *Mesocolon*. Although its circumference does not extend beyond three cubits, from it arise the *Mesaraic* veins, through which, as if through channels, a path lies open from the intestines into the liver and the other veins of the body. You might compare the mesaraic veins to *Roots*, because through them, like roots, the liver seizes nourishment from the belly. Furthermore, there are very many mesaraic veins which, when they approach the liver, unite into one single trunk, which then branches out again with much "offspring" through the flesh of the liver. This trunk is called the *Portal vein* [Vena porta], because through it, as if through gates [portas], nourishment is carried into the liver. This trunk is located in the hollow part of the liver that faces the stomach. On the opposite side of the liver, which is called the "hunch" [gibba], the small veins scattered through the liver unite again into another trunk, which is called the *vena cava*, about which we speak elsewhere. Following the Mesentery is the *Pancreas*, a glandular part of the lower belly, not very wide; it does not exceed the width of two fingers, though it is somewhat long. It took its name from the flesh [kreas] which it resembles, because of its softness and redness <note>The name Pancreas comes from the Greek "pan" (all) and "kreas" (flesh)</note>. It has thin membranes, veins, arteries, and nerves. It is the beginning of the <term>secretion</term> <note>original: ῥιτωσέως (*rhitōseōs*), likely a Greek anatomical term for flow</note> of the lacteals, if we follow Agellius, the discoverer of the lacteal ducts. Its use consists in this: namely, that it provides safe passage for the vessels, serves as a sort of underlayer and soft cushion for the stomach, and fills the empty spaces between the stomach, spleen, and liver.

Intending to survey the Umbilical region of the Abdomen, we encounter in it the *Umbilicus* [Navel], called the *omphalos* <note>original: ὀμφαλὸν</note> by the Greeks. Among the Latins, it receives its name from "umbo" <note>The central boss of a shield</note>, because the navel is very nearly the center or midpoint of a human, such that it stands at an equal distance from the upper and lower parts,

# SACRED ANATOMY

—it stands as that which is called the **Root** <note>original: *Radix*</note> by Aristotle; just as a root sitting in the earth provides sap and life to the entire tree, so does the navel to the fetus in the mother’s womb. It is seen at the summit of the Abdomen, which the Hebrews call *tabbur* <note>original: טבור</note>, a word that metaphorically denotes an elevated place, as in *Judges 9:37*. Avicenna states it is the first thing generated in the womb. Its purpose is so that the fetus, while still contained in the womb, may be nourished and grow. As soon as a person reaches a more mature age, these vessels grow together into a tendon, their primary actions having already ceased. The navel of a human deserves to be compared to the stem or pedicel of a fruit. For through the stem, the fruit receives nourishment from the tree, just as the fetus does from the mother through the navel. This is how we should understand Galen <margin>Aphorism 1.</margin> when he says: *The connections to the wombs of fetuses have the same proportion as the connections of fruits to plants.* By the name "connections," he signifies the *acetabula* <term>vessel openings</term> and the *cotyledon* <term>maternal-fetal junctions</term> in that same passage. Protagoras calls the *acetabula* the mouths of the veins which are carried to the womb; Galen agrees with this in his *Aphorism 45*, and also in *Book 1 on the Seed, chapter 7*. Very often in the Holy Scripture, mention is made of the navel under the name *sharir* <note>original: שריר</note>, which, as Aben Esra advises, takes its name from "firmness"; for among the Rabbis, *sharar* denotes something *firm*.

<margin>Chapter 16:4.</margin>
<margin>Anatomical Exegesis 4, page 113.</margin>
*And on the day of your birth, says God in Ezekiel, your navel was not cut.* Just as the cutting of the navel can cast a person into the most immediate danger of life, as experience testifies, so it is not only shameful but even lethal for a fetus born into this world unless it is liberated from that internal "hose" through which the infant received its nourishment in the womb—and which, once born, still attaches it to the mother—by cutting the cord, compressing the blood, and keeping out the air. The navel <note>original: ὁ ὀμφαλὸς (*ho omphalos*)</note> also stands as a sign of lust, as Fulgentius says:

For the womb is also bound there as if by a chain; which is why the structures near the kidneys [epinephridia] are placed in that same spot to steady the fetuses.*

And Eucherius of Lyons in his *Formulas, page 11*: *The Navel represents the appetite of concupiscence [lustful desire], as in Job:* "His strength is in the navel of his belly." Thus, through the navel, he signifies the female genitals, just as through the "loins" he signifies the male. The Bride is also praised by the Groom in *Song of Solomon 7:3* for her well-placed navel: *Your navel is a rounded crater <note>or cup</note>, that is, like a round bowl, or, it is similar to a round bowl, by which it is signified that the Church always cherishes her spiritual children and nourishes them.* Whence Ambrose says:

Furthermore, keeping to our order, in the first region of the Abdomen we encounter the **Liver** <note>original: *Hepar*</note>. The Hebrews signify the *heart, liver, lung, and spleen* with a single name, *kaved* <note>original: כבד</note>, if we follow Avenarius; but in *Exodus 29:13* and *Ezekiel 21:21*, the liver specifically is called *kaved*, so named from "gravity" or "weight," which is why Galen says the Liver is the heaviest and densest of all the internal organs.

<margin>Book 6, On the Use of Parts, chapter 17.</margin>

In the usual order of nature, it occupies the right side, but in unusual cases, the left. In the size of the liver and the brain, man alone surpasses the lower animals, because in him there is a greater variety of actions and a more frequent expenditure of "Spirits" <term>vital forces believed to power the body</term>. *The size of the liver*, says 

<margin>Book 8, chapter 12.</margin>
Adrian Spigelius, *is so great that it fills the entire right hypochondrium <note>the area below the ribs</note>, and sometimes extends itself all the way to the umbilical region. Furthermore, it varies greatly according to the diversity of the subjects: and I have mostly observed this proportion, that those who have a large liver also have a large stomach, and vice versa. However, man possesses the largest liver of all animals, considering the proportion of his body. For I have frequently seen such a vast mass of it that it was connected to the diaphragm by strong ligaments even near the region of the spleen.* The size itself also varies greatly according to age: *for it is largest in children, so that more blood may be produced for the growth of the body; it is smaller in adults, and smaller still in the elderly, so that the liver gradually decreases according to age.* The body of the liver is made of different materials, composed of a thin membrane, small nerves, flesh, arteries, and veins. Regarding the fibers <note>lobes</note> of the liver, John Lygaeus writes:

<margin>Book 2, Harmony of the Human Body, page 20.</margin>

The liver does not, however, have the same number of fibers in all men. Names were assigned to these fibers by the Ancients. The **First** was called the *focus* <note>hearth</note>, for it contributes most to the "cooking" <term>digestion/coction</term> of the juices, just as a hearth is for cooking food. The **Second** received the name *mensa* <note>table</note>, because it acts as a table, since the nourishment for the limbs is placed upon it. The **Third** is named *culter* <note>knife</note>, for it divides and separates the humors from one another, or if there is something thicker to be distributed, it cuts and transforms it. The **Fourth** has the name *auriga* <note>charioteer</note>, for the refined humors govern the natural powers well and lead them straight toward improvement. This is the most noble part in the lower belly, to which—besides the natural use it provides to the whole body—the ancients attributed and placed within it the seat of lust and love, which is why Horace says:

<margin>Book 1, Ode 25, line 13.</margin>
> When burning love and lust,
> Which are wont to madden the mothers of horses,
> Shall rage around your ulcerated liver.

And in *Book 4, Ode 1, lines 8 and 12*, addressing Venus:

> Whither the charming prayers of youths recall you...
> If you seek to scorch a suitable liver.

Hence, insane antiquity put the friendly star of Venus in charge of this part, just as they assigned Saturn to the Spleen, Mars to the Gallbladder, the Sun to the Heart, and the Moon to the Brain; compare *Caelius Rhodiginus, Book 4, Chapter 7*. Regarding the use of the liver by the Ancients in sacrifices, we have spoken elsewhere—those who, out of excessive superstition, devised various uses for the liver concerning sacred rites, from which came **Hepatoscopy** <term>divination by inspecting the liver</term>. From its inspection, they predicted signs of health or destruction. For a victim in which the liver was well-constituted was a sign of a happy outcome; if it were bad, it was unhappy; see Cicero, *Book 2, On Divination*. It is the workshop of blood for us: *For blood, the final nourishment which is common to the whole body, is finished in the liver for the public use of the whole body. to all the members: In this same way, the liver, by its own natural power, sends nourishment through the veins to all the members. Indeed, from these three—namely, the liver, the heart, and the brain—as if from perennial springs, common virtues flow into all parts: from the liver comes the <term>natural virtue</term> <note>The "natural faculty" responsible for nutrition and growth.</note>, carrying nourishment to the limbs through the veins; from the heart comes the <term>vital virtue</term>, imparting life to them through the arteries; and from the brain comes the <term>animal virtue</term> <note>The "animal faculty" (from *anima*, soul) governing sensation and movement.</note>, distributing sense and motion through the nerves. The liver is a noble organ, and the chief among the organs of nutritive power, because it is the workshop of the blood. The veins are the pathways of the blood, which, like certain aqueducts originating from the liver, are led into the whole body. From the blood it receives from the liver, the heart generates another kind that is purer, thinner, and hotter, and with it many "Spirits," which the arteries carry together with the said blood into the entire body. Thus the liver is the workshop of <term>hematosis</term> <note>original: αἱματώσεως; the process of blood formation.</note> and <term>chylification</term> <note>original: χυμώσεως; the turning of food into chyle.</note>. After the stomach has altered, cooked, and turned the food into <term>chyle</term> <note>A milky fluid produced during digestion.</note>, and the cooked chyle has been expelled to the intestines so that a separation of useful juice from excrement might occur there, the mesenteric veins carry into the liver that which they suck out of the chyle—which has been pushed into the intestines as if into a basin—so that it may be cooked a second time, altered, and converted into the substance of blood. While the chyle boils in the vessels of the liver, as if ignited by the liver's heat, something thick and something thin breaks out from the separation of the different parts. The liver separates both from the nutritional mass and expels them to their own receptacles: the thick part to the spleen, but the thin, foamy, and hotter part, which they call <term>yellow bile</term>, to the <term>gallbladder</term> <note>original: cystim felleam</note>, and the colder part to the kidneys. The gallbladder holds its seat in the hollow part of the liver, where it embraces the side of the stomach. Its neck, at the place of the liver where the portal vein exits, ends in a narrow canal that stretches its processes upward and downward. The former, which is carried upward around the front region of the portal vein, is cut into various small shoots through the body of the liver between the branches of the portal vein and the offshoots of the vena cava, carrying the bile into its vessel. The latter, however, which stretches obliquely downward to the end of the duodenum and the beginning of the jejunum, carries the bile pushed out from its vessel into the intestines. These tubes, as they agree with reason, so they match perfectly the purging of bilious excrement; while the expulsion begins in the "upper court," where the portal vein enters the liver, it continues descending to the bladder, which stands out in the "lower court" outside the substance of the liver, like a secret <note>A reference to the "Augean stable" from the myths of Hercules—a place of great filth that required purging.</note> Augean stable, which a hurrying nature desires to be evacuated, and has therefore banished to a lower and more despised place. Black bile is a sluggish humor, which, when it has become <term>savage</term> <note>original: efferus</note>, is accustomed to induce various passions in the mind, sometimes sad, and sometimes (though very rarely) joyful, which we have deduced with various examples in the *Physician* when we treated Melancholy. Certainly, that humor is placed by Aristotle in his *Problems* as the cause of more vehement commotions of the minds, and indeed in great variety, according to its measure and mixture: from which some become wrathful, others fearful, others exultant, others sad or furious, so that there are different effects of that bile—fear, pain, wrath, and insanity. And since insanity may flow from this, the Greeks used the term <note>original: τὸ χολᾷν; meaning to be full of bile or to be mad.</note> "to be bilious." Thus an abundance of bile and hotter blood pro-

<column-break/>

-duces wrath, for the character of the mind naturally tends to follow the dominance of the humors. Horace, *to Lydia*, his mistress at whom he was angry because she had admitted his rival Telephus, moved by jealousy, says that his liver was steeped in bile:

> ->When you, Lydia, praise<-
> ->The rosy neck of Telephus, the waxen<-
> ->Arms of Telephus, alas, my<-
> ->Burning liver swells with difficult bile.<-

These are not words of levity, says Ratbertus, *which come from the commotion of the gall, but the severity of a judge, and a sentence long suspended, full of fairness.* In the Holy Scriptures, "gall" denotes the supreme bitterness of evils because of its own bitterness. Concerning this, the Jewish people in Jeremiah chapter 8:14 say: <term>The Lord our God has made us silent, and given us water of gall to drink; for we have sinned against the Lord.</term> God Himself repeats this in chapter 9:15 through the mouth of the prophet, saying: *Behold, I will feed this people with wormwood, and give them water of gall to drink: I will scatter them among the nations.* And again: *I make them eat wormwood, and I will make them drink water of gall, for from the prophets in Jerusalem ungodliness has gone out into all the land.* Join to these the passage from Lamentations chapter 3:5: <term>He has built against me, and surrounded me with gall and weariness.</term> This passage, clear in itself, the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> surrounded with darkness when they constructed this version: <term>He built up against me and surrounded my head, and he labored in dark places.</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀνοικοδόμησε κατ᾿ ἐμοῦ καὶ ἐκύκλωσε τὴν κεφαλήν με, καὶ ἐμόχθησεν ἐν σκοτεινοῖς.</note> They took the Hebrew word *rosh* <note>original: ראשׁ</note> for "head," which here means "gall," and for "weariness," "labor," they read <note>original: תלאה</note> in the future hiphil, and joined it with <note>original: במחשׁכים</note> "in dark places," from which word it is nevertheless separated by a *Soph Pasuq* <note>A Hebrew punctuation mark indicating the end of a verse.</note>.

With a provident nature most studious of its own preservation, it constructed the <term>Spleen</term> opposite the Liver—called <term>splen</term> <note>original: σπλῆνα</note> by the Greeks—with marvelous sagacity. Positioned under the left hypochondrium opposite the liver, it sometimes—though rarely as a spectacle of nature—occupies the right side; in its upper part it adheres to the diaphragm, in its lower part both to the left kidney and the adrenal gland, and in its inner part to the pancreas. It has the shape of a rough, oblong-round ox tongue, or square, and is sometimes seen in other forms according to the constitution of the human body. In a human, it is smaller than the liver, though sometimes its size varies, and it errs more in greatness than in smallness. Usually there is only one spleen in a human naturally, but Aristotle noted two in *Book 4 on the Generation of Animals*, and Master de Marchetti in his *Anatomy, chapter 4, page 45*; very rarely three, such as Fallopius saw. Regarding the use of the Spleen as well as other parts of the human body, let us note the verses of the ancients:

<margin>The spleen makes one laugh; the liver compels one to love.</margin>
->The heart burns, the lung speaks, the gall provokes anger,<-
->The spleen makes one laugh, the liver compels one to love.<-

The ancients attributed laughter to the spleen, as is well known, hence also Persius in *Satire 1*:
> ->What shall I do? But I have a petulant spleen; I burst with laughter.<-
Among the ancients there were, and still are, those who write that the Spleen was created by God not only in vain, and thus of absolutely no use to the animal, but even that it is more a hindrance than a benefit. But Aristotle feels otherwise: <term>the reason is that in those which of necessity have a spleen, the spleen might seem to be like a "bastard liver."</term> <note>original Greek: τότε δ' αἴτιον, ὅτι ἐν μὲν τοῖς ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἔχουσι σπλῆνα, δόξειεν ἂν οἷον νόθον ἧπαρ εἶναι ὁ σπλήν.</note> However, as to what the action of the spleen properly consists of, it is not yet agreed upon among Anatomists. With Galen, many say the spleen is a receptacle of the humor...

### From Psalm 139, verse 15

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> Regarding the **melancholic humor** <note>Also known as "black bile," one of the four humors in ancient medicine, thought to cause sadness or "melancholy."</note>, others—and not without merit—deny its presence here, since the organ has neither a cavity nor a proportion in substance or quantity consistent with melancholic humor. For this reason, a more noble office is assigned to it by others: namely, the **elaboration of blood**, a task it shares with the liver. Indeed, the structure of both is similar: both have **parenchyma** <note>The functional tissue of an organ.</note> suitable for the making of blood; both have an appropriate size, shape, and location; and both possess innumerable veins and arteries. From both, veins go to the intestines to draw away the **chyle** <note>The milky fluid of digested food.</note>. For this reason, the spleen was called the "bastard liver" by Aristotle <note>original: ἧπαρ νόθον</note>, the "left liver" by Hippocrates <note>original: ἧπαρ ἀριστερὸν</note>, and by Plato, the "liver-wiper" <note>original: ἧπαρ ἐπίμαγεῖον; referring to the idea that the spleen cleanses the liver.</note>.

<margin>on Matthew, column 873.</margin> In the lowest region of the Abdomen, which is usually called the **hypogastric** region <note>The area below the stomach, or the lower belly.</note>, besides the Kidneys, we see the Ureters, the Bladder, the Uterus, and the remaining parts necessary for generation. We shall survey these in order, but **briefly** <note>original: ὡς ἐν συνόψει</note>. For modesty sometimes forbids us to speak openly; things that are shameful, foul, or obscene can be indicated privately, leaving the interpretation to the reader or listener. Just as Jerome, writing <margin>on Fabiola</margin> about a *disgrace that could not be named honorably*, leaves it to the reader's knowledge, saying: *A noble girl was forced to suffer what no maidservant would endure.* The neighborhood spoke of it; she herself remained silent. At the spine of the back, we encounter the **Kidneys**, which some claim are named from the word "to flow" <note>original: ῥέειν; the author links the Latin *renes* to the Greek *rheein*.</note>, because urine flows through them as if through a sieve. The Greeks call them **nephroi** <note>original: νεφροὶ</note>, because like clouds, they transmit impure humors to the bladder. Their natural seat is at the spine, where they rest directly beneath the liver and spleen against the inner loins, whose duty it is to provide motion for the legs. The **Loin** is called **osphys** <note>original: ὀσφὺς</note> by the Greeks. Properly, the *osphys* signifies that entire part of the back where we are girded; it is composed of the thickest and largest vertebrae of the entire spine, five in number, located between the back and the "sacred bone" <note>The *os sacrum*.</note>. Hesychius teaches that it indicates that part which is empty near the sides. It should be known, says Serrarius <margin>on Judges chapter 8, question 5, page 203.</margin>, that in the Latin language there is no single word that properly expresses the force of the Greek *osphys*, but it uses sometimes "loins" (*lumbi*) and sometimes "flanks" (*ilia*) for that term. <margin>in the Notes, folio 197.</margin> That part of the human body is said to be where the **fifth rib** is located, just as that word has its use in 2 Samuel 2:23 in the story of Abner, where it reads: *When Asahel refused to turn aside, Abner struck him with the butt of his spear* <note>original Hebrew: אל־החמש; *el-ha-homesh*</note> *in the fifth rib.* The Old Translator says: *In the groin.* The Septuagint: *Upon the loin* <note>original: ἐπὶ τὴν ὀσφὺν</note>. <margin>page 31.</margin> In the fifth rib—that is, in that part of the body where the fifth rib is, namely where the seat of the gall and liver is located. Down to that part, the body is usually covered by breastplates or other protection, and from this, it is thought the "armed men" <note>original Hebrew: חמשים; *hamushim*</note> are named, of whom mention is made in Joshua 10:1, 14. There, Masius comments: *What "Hamushim" (which I have translated as "girded") means, not all Hebrews hold the same opinion. Most, along with the Chaldean, think they are called "armed" from "homesh" (five), which is that part of the human body where the fifth rib is located, as in the story of Abner. The Septuagint there interpreted it as "loin" (osphys); for they say arms cover the body down to almost that part. And indeed, it is quite credible that from "homesh" (loins) comes "Hamushim," since we see that "Haluzim"* <note>original Hebrew: חלוצים; another term for "girded" or "equipped" men.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> is entirely a twin to it, if you look at both form and meaning; for it is most certain that the name is formed from *Halazaim*, that is, the loins. But whether these terms—I mean *Hamushim* and *Haluzim*—signify those covered with armor down to the fifth rib or the loins, or rather those "girded" with a military belt, I cannot sufficiently determine. The former pleases Aquila; the latter the Seventy Interpreters; for he translates it as "well-girded" <note>original: εὔζωνοι</note>, and they as "well-girded." But truly, **well-girded**—that is, tucked up and ready—pleases me more; for it is very common in sacred history for "girded loins" to signify ready strength, active and prepared zeal, and strenuous courage. There are also those who interpret *Hamushim* as if the ranks of the army were thickened by **five men** each. But I reject this opinion entirely because of the similarity to the name *Haluzim*, since this would be foreign to the meaning of the latter. It is customary in the Holy Language for the "girding of the loins" to signify ready strength, eager study of affairs, as well as strenuous courage and **chastity**; compare Flacius, *Key to the Scriptures*, page 599. Whence Robert Holkot, in lecture 24 on the Wisdom of Solomon, page 86, says: *Girding has four zones (belts). One for the breast, one for the belly, one for the kidneys, and one for the loins. The Golden Zone is for the breast; the Linen Zone for the belly; the Rope Zone for the kidneys; and the Skin Zone for the loins. The **Golden Zone** is of mental cleanliness and purity, and this ought to be placed at the breast against foul thoughts. The **Linen Zone** is temperance against excessive superfluity, and this ought to be placed at the belly against gluttony. The **Rope Zone** is of rigid and austere penitence, and this ought to be placed at the kidneys against the itchings of lust. And the **Skin Zone** is the remembrance of our mortality, and this ought to be placed at the loins against the delights of pleasure.* Regarding this same girding, Theophanes <margin>Homily 14, page 86.</margin> treats it thus: *The belt, when it binds the loin and pulls up the tunic that flows downward, signifies **sober reasoning**, by which the slackness of life's enjoyments is drawn in, and the burning heat of the kidneys is bound.* Philippus the Presbyter writes in the same sense on Job chapter 38, page 167: *Everyone who is about to speak with God is first commanded to gird his loins with chastity.* Even the people about to receive the Law and celebrate the Passover in the desert are commanded to "gird the loins of their minds," lest the flowing folds of carnal thoughts hinder the step of holy conversation—just as when we gird our clothes over our physical loins, we do so to avoid being entangled and falling. Hence, the "girding of the loins" is so frequently commanded in Holy Scripture, because the strength of a man consists in his loins. *Therefore, gird up your loins and arise*, God commands Jeremiah in chapter 1:17. That is: prepare yourself for the duty enjoined upon you. *Let your loins be girded*, the Savior warns his Disciples <margin>Luke 12:35.</margin>, so that they might be unencumbered, prepared, and robust for the work of propagating the truth and the kingdom of Christ. Upon these words, Fulgentius says in his *Sermon on the Confessors*: *In the loins, carnal concupiscence is shown. By commanding our loins to be girded, God undoubtedly commanded carnal desires to be restrained.* In the same place: *The loins of the faithful are girded while evil desire is compressed, while wicked thought is restrained, while the soul resists lust, while wantonness is denied its effect, while luxury is trampled upon, etc.* Regarding the pain of the loins—

David complains of his loins in Psalm 38:8 <note>Psalm 37 in the Vulgate numbering.</note>: *My loins are filled with illusions*. Thus the Vulgate translates the word *biklah* <note>original: בקלה</note>, imitating the Greeks, who read it as *empaigmata* <note>original: ἐμπαίγματα; meaning "mockeries" or "delusions."</note>. Arias translates it as "foulness." Junius as "vileness." The root is *biklah*, meaning to parch or roast. In the *Niphal* <note>A Hebrew verb form usually denoting the passive or reflexive voice.</note> it means to become vile. But in the *Niphal* sense, the word *biklo* is an adjective and means "vile." Here, however, that word is a noun. Therefore, we should better translate it as "parching," "burning," or "heat," just as the Poets otherwise say of fevers, that the limbs are parched by fevers and the internal organs by hidden fires. At this point, let us note what Nicholas de Jauov <note>A 14th-century theologian from Prague known for his works on church reform and superstitions.</note> wrote in an unpublished *Treatise on Superstitions*, using these words as an introduction and explaining them thus: It is established that true faith, formed by charity, exists as the light of human souls, and is the life of the same and of the "girded loins" of the spirits—namely, the intellect and the affection. The intellect, I say, by reason of the light of truth, which purges it from the illusion of phantasms of error; and the affection by reason of vital operation, which purges it from the illusion of the suggestions of vice. Truly, knowing this, that most sharp deceiver, our adversary the Devil, goes about day and night seeking how he may fill these loins, by darkening the intellect with phantasms of error (and consequently obscuring the light of truth or faith) and perverting the affection with suggestions of malice (and consequently excluding charity, which is the order and life of the soul). Just as he is known to have done to our first parents, whom God created perfect. But why the girding of the loins is so seriously commanded in Holy Scripture, Origen indicates in his *First Homily on Psalm 38*, saying: *The receptacle of human seeds is said to be in the kidneys or the loins, by which that kind of sin is indicated which is carried out through lust.*

<margin>on Psalm 37, p. 513.</margin>
And Ambrose: *In the loins are the stirrings of lust. In the loins of a man are the seeds; in the womb of a woman. Therefore, the loins are the common symbol of venereal pleasure, and are, as it were, the nursery of lust.* In the loins, says Philip the Presbyter <note>A 5th-century commentator on the Book of Job.</note> in *On Job*, Book 3, Chapter 40, page 196, *and in the navels of the belly, the will of the flesh or luxury is understood, which was inserted into the members after the fall of the first man, so that those members—beyond the limit of natural law and even when a man does not wish it—are tickled by the incentives of lust.* Because, therefore, one sates the loins with Venus <note>A common metaphor for sexual activity.</note> and wine, he becomes "loined-less" <note>original: "elumbis"; meaning weakened, spineless, or impotent.</note>; he who gives himself to luxury, dislocates his limbs; he who devotes himself to gluttony, defiles his body with filth. What is more excellent than talent, what more than memory? But if you judge either by excess, it blunts the edge of talent and obscures the light of the intellect. Much could be said here about the manifold detriment and various ruin caused by Venus, but it is pleasing to refer the reader to Sinibaldus <note>Giovanni Benedetto Sinibaldi (1594–1658), author of the "Geneanthropeia," a massive work on human generation and its hazards.</note>, who is quite prolix in teaching that venereal pleasure primarily depraves the soul, undermines natural power, brings weakness to the body, and accelerates gray hair. But we hasten to the meditation on the Kidneys, from which we have departed longer than is right on the occasion of the "vein of life" <note>original: φλεψ ζωῆς</note>. Nature gave the living creature not one, but twins—one on the right and the other on the left part of the loin—so that the serum ejected from the vessels of both sides might be received more promptly and fully, which would not happen as conveniently if a single one stood in the middle. The body of the kidneys is dissimilar <note>meaning heterogeneous or composed of different parts.</note>, yet in it one can observe the liberality of Nature, which endowed them with

<column-break/>

fat, glands, membranes, flesh, cavities, and vessels—that is, veins, arteries, and nerves. Sometimes it happens by accident that **calculi** <note>Kidney stones.</note> or stones are generated in them, which bring about the sharpest pains. If you look at their use, it is twofold. For the principal action and native duty of the Kidneys is established by some as the separation of serum and blood, though this is denied by other Physicians; see Laurenberg <note>Peter Laurenberg, a 17th-century polymath and anatomist.</note>, page 205 and following; and Sennert <note>Daniel Sennert, a famous early modern physician who bridged Galenic and chemical medicine.</note>, Book 3, part 7, section 1, page 790. The other use consists in this: they are said to contribute no small labor to generation, whence both in sacred and profane literature the kidneys are held to be the seat of lusts. *In the kidneys*, says Jerome, *the fatty incentives of lust are to be thinned out. For unless we restrain the flowing things of the kidneys of the loins, we cannot have lamps in our hands.* <note>A reference to the Parable of the Ten Virgins, linking physical restraint to spiritual readiness.</note> Through the kidneys in the Sacred Pandects <note>A term for the complete body of Scripture.</note>, wicked concupiscence is indicated, and the desire for venereal matters is understood. Whence Pagninus notes that they are called *kilyot* <note>original: כליות</note> by the Hebrews from the root *kalah* <note>original: כלה</note>, which is "to desire," because the desire for coitus happens there: Jeremiah 11:20, Psalm 51:8, Proverbs 23:16. To this, some refer the words of Job 19:27: *My kidneys are consumed by desire in my bosom*, where the word *kalu* <note>original: כלו</note> hints at a vehement desire, as when one is almost consumed by desire while waiting, as in Psalm 119:81–82: *My eyes are consumed* (*kalu*) *for your word. My soul is consumed* (*kalah napshi*) *for your salvation.* The desire of the soul is expressed as being so vehement that she almost faints. Thus Job says his kidneys are held by such a great desire for the vision [of God] that they almost fail and are consumed in his bosom. Gregory the Great looks toward this desire of the kidneys: *What is understood by the kidneys,* he says, *except the delight of the flesh? Whence also the Psalmist asks, saying: "Burn my kidneys." For if he did not know that pleasure was in the kidneys, he would by no means have asked for them to be burned.* And Radulphus Ardens <note>A 12th-century preacher.</note> in his 18th Homily for Trinity, folio 270: *We command chastity more deeply, and we indulge ourselves in our kidneys.* From this also it happened that the kidneys and the groin were held sacred among the Gentiles, just as the head was to Jupiter, the eyes to Minerva, and the feet to Mercury, as reported by Fulgentius in Book 3 of his *Mythologies*, page 897. Hence these verses among the Ancients:
> The kidneys are the seat and nourishment of luxury.
And again:
> I pray you, O youths, restrain your kidneys.
From the kidneys to the **bladder**, the Ancients proceed; it is so called from its office, because they "keep the urine" <note>original: τηρῶσι τὸν οὗρον; an etymological play on the Greek word.</note>. Positioned with a long duct between the kidneys and the bladder, the **Ureters** carry water from the kidneys into the bladder; thus they begin from the kidneys and end in the bladder, to which they adhere so firmly that they cannot be separated from the bladder without being ruptured. Asclepiades, Paracelsus, and others thought that urine "sweated" from the kidneys into the bladder, being ignorant of the ureters, by whose assistance the urine is carried from the kidneys into the bladder. If you look at their number, there are as many as there are kidneys, namely two. They are endowed with a rounded shape, long and perforated; in those with stones they are larger than in those who do not labor under the stone. They have their beginning from the kidneys, as we have said, which beginning is called the **infundibulum** <note>Latin for "funnel."</note>, from which arise small membranes or valves which close the openings of the Ureters that gape into the capacity of the bladder, and shut off the reflux of serum back toward the kidneys. The Bladder follows the Ureters, an organic part of the lowest belly, placed in the cavity of the hypogastrium. In men, it adheres to the rectum, the prostate glands, the capsules, and the seminal vesicles; in women, to the vagina.

The bladder is attached at its upper part to the uterus and the pubic bones. It is endowed with three coats <note>The word "tunicis" refers to the layers of the bladder wall.</note>, the first of which clothes the bladder as an offshoot of the peritoneum; it not only makes the bladder stronger but also causes it to adhere to adjacent parts. The second, which is the middle layer, is called "fleshy" because of its resemblance to meat, and many fibers are seen within it; it is also called a muscle by others rather than a membrane, by which means the urine is expelled and the bladder is kept warm. Finally, the third layer, which is the innermost, lines the cavity of the bladder, covered with a very thin crust against the sharpness of the urine, so that it does not corrode the bladder. Furthermore, it consists of a neck and a base. The base is the upper part, wider toward the abdomen, to which the Urachus <note>A fibrous cord connecting the bladder to the navel.</note> is attached by means of a doubled membrane of the Peritoneum that covers it, which indeed adheres to the Navel with a strong connection. The Urachus was made to support the bladder so that it does not slip lower. The neck, however, is the more sloping part, narrower and fleshier, where the *Sphincter* muscle, or constrictor of the bladder, is located. It is not lacking in veins, arteries, or nerves, by whose benefit it is nourished, warmed, and preserved. Its duty is to receive urine from the ureters, collect it, preserve it, and eject it in its own time. Just as in the kidneys, stones are generated in the bladder, causing pain greater than the pain of those giving birth; some small growths <term>caruncles</term> are generated in the neck of the bladder from Gonorrhea, and sometimes ulcers, which are cured with the greatest difficulty and eventually bring death to men after they have endured the most severe pains.

<margin>Homily 20 on the Gospels</margin>
It remains for us to consider the genital members in both sexes. "Obscene things are not to be spoken of openly," says Isidore in Epistle 5, page 692. The Hebrews are modest in describing venereal matters, not knowing here the impudent words which the Greeks use in excess, such as *binein* <note>original: βινείειν; to have sexual intercourse.</note>, *baukalizein* <note>original: βαυκαλίζειν; to lull or caress.</note>, and others unpleasant in sound. How deceptive the language of the Greeks and Latins is in noting the genital parts is reported by Antonius Ludovicus in his *Short Work on Shame*, folio 55. b.

<margin>Anthropology of Physics p. 618.</margin>
Sperlingius says: "These members were made for the purest people by the Purest One, where there was neither shame nor baseness. They are called 'shameful parts' <term>pudenda</term> by accident, because when uncovered at an inconvenient time and place, they produce shame." *This fact that you blush*, are the words of Ambrose in Psalm 61, page 595, *that you must be covered, was taught by guilt, not nature. There would be no shame of the genitals if there were no guilt.* Amerigo Vespucci discusses the naked Indians in his *First Navigation*, page 159: *Although they walk naked among the women, nevertheless their shameful parts are so honorably placed that they can in no way be seen, except for that anterior region which we call by the more modest name "lower chest," which nature itself left to be seen in them in no other way than honorably. But they do not even care about this, since they are no more moved by the sight of their own genitals than we are in the display of our mouth or face.* Therefore, sin uncovered the shameful parts previously unknown, and as Tertullian says*, *when they tasted of the tree of knowledge, they felt nothing before that which was to be blushed at.* Thus, each marked the understanding of their own sex with a covering.

<margin>on the Veiling of Virgins p. 392.</margin>
The Jews were forbidden from building an altar with steps, lest the Priests, while descending, should betray their nakedness. Concerning the genitals of both sexes, we must speak and think *moderately and reverently* <note>original: μερείως καὶ εὐλαβῶς</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
This material is not impure if you do not bring an impure mind. Regarding the foolish man, the Psalmist says <margin>Psalm 53:1</margin> that he says in his heart, "There is no God," where Hilary, page 368, notes: *It is a human vice to speak of shameful things, because he would not commit to hearing them with the words of the mouth, but by the urging instinct of interior wickedness, he speaks them within his heart; while the iniquity of the will struggles against the necessity of public shame, he is not ashamed to think what he is ashamed to say. And therefore the fool says in his heart: "There is no God," because if he wished to speak this with the words of his mouth, he would be proven a fool as he is by the judgment of public consensus. For who, looking upon the world, does not sense that there is a God? But it happens frequently that while the necessity of truth compels us to the confession of God, the delight of vices nevertheless persuades us that there is no God for us, and what we believe against faith, we nevertheless speak from the counsel of an impious heart.* So that we may say a few small things about the genitals of the Man, that divine command given to Abraham provides us an occasion, concerning the circumcising of every male offspring in his house, Genesis 17:10 and following. This circumcision, which it should be noted God had instituted as a covenant with Abraham and his descendants, was a sign of distinction by which the Israelite was distinguished from the other nations. *Circumcision,* says Damascenus <margin>Book 4, chapter 26</margin>, *was given to Abraham as a sign that would discern him, his children, and his servants from the nations among whom he lived. The proof is that when the Israelites lived by themselves for forty years in the desert and had no commerce with any other nation, of those who were born in the desert, none at all were circumcised.* Chrysostom, in Homily 40 on Genesis, is of the same opinion. From this circumcision came a "gentility" <note>Here meaning a tribal identity.</note>, so that by this sign the Jews were recognizable and sequestered from other nations. The Philistines were discerned from the Jews by their foreskins, wherefore Saul wanted foreskins to be brought to him, not ears, not heads or noses, so that he might know that those killed were no others than Philistines; *the King*, says Basil of Seleucia in Sermon 3 on David, page 143, *does not want a dowry, but a hundred foreskins of the foreigners. This scripture is proven if it should show the manner. For he reasoned, it says, to cast David into the hands of the foreigners. Not so that he might move the bridegroom to behold the marriage, but so that before the bridal chamber the bridegroom might become a waste, and death might anticipate the marriage, making the foreigners a weapon for his envy.* Circumcision was also a sign of faith and profession, of regeneration, justice, and sanctification. *Through circumcision,* says Abulensis <margin>from Deuteronomy 22, question 2</margin>, *the Jews protested that the Messiah would arise from his own blood.* And Jerome in Book 1 of his Epistle to the Galatians says: *Because Christ was to arise from the seed of Abraham, and many ages were to pass from Abraham until Christ, God, providing lest the offspring of beloved Abraham be mixed with other nations and his family gradually become uncertain, marked the Israelite flock with a certain brand of circumcision.* The blood of the foreskin, therefore, was a type of the blood of Christ, who himself took circumcision upon himself in our place, concerning which Bernard <margin>Sermon 3 on the Circumcision</margin> says: *What is circumcision,* he asks, *except a sign of superfluity and sin? In you, Lord Jesus, what is superfluous that should be circumcised? Are you not the true Lord God from God the Father: true man without any sin from a virgin mother? But what wonder is it if the Head accepted the cure for the members, which*

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
## Page 822

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
...however, He did not have this necessity in Himself! Is it not true that in our own limbs, a cure is often applied to one part for the sake of another’s infirmity? If the head aches, a vein is cut in the arm; if the kidneys ache, the treatment is applied to the leg. Thus, today, for the decay of the whole body, a certain cautery <note>A medical treatment involving burning or cutting to remove infection.</note> has been fixed in the head. Finally, what wonder is it if He deigned to be circumcised for us, for whom He deigned to die? And so, circumcision was performed on the male genitals, which has now vanished with the coming of Christ, having been repealed and long ago abolished. Let these remarks on the male genitals suffice, since a more specific description of them belongs to the anatomists. We shall observe the same method in reviewing the female genitals. Both sets of genitals are usually called the *pudenda* <note>Latin: "things to be ashamed of," a common historical term for private parts.</note>. If you look at the origin of the word used by the Germans for the female genitals, it will give you the Hebrew word *patah* <note>original: פָּתָה</note>, which Isaiah uses in chapter 3, verse 17: *the Lord will lay bare their secret parts* <note>original: פִּתְהֵן יְעָרֶה (*pithen ye'areh*)</note>, predicting the baring of that part which they had used for lust. The Israelite people were stiff-necked, and to them God, for the sake of social order <note>original Greek: οἰκονομικῶς (*oikonomikōs*), meaning "dispensationally" or for the sake of management.</note>, not only permitted polygamy and divorce, but even gave this law: that a groom might divorce a bride whom he did not find to be a virgin. Regarding this law, these words exist:
<margin>Deuteronomy 22:17</margin>
*“Look, these are the tokens of my daughter’s virginity”; and they shall spread the cloth before the elders of the city.* It was a custom among the Hebrews that virgins betrothed to men, at the first cohabitation, would not admit the man unless a clean cloth was spread beneath them. This was because at the first union, the small membrane—which the Greeks calls the *hymen* <note>original: ὑμήν</note>, from which that most famous Latin word for marriage songs, "Hymen," is derived—acts as a barrier across the passage and is usually broken, and that breaking typically occurs with blood. The Hebrews call the signs of virginity *betulim* <note>original: בְּתוּלִים</note>, which by a figure of speech means "virginities." The word for virgin is *betulah* <note>original: בְּתוּלָה</note>, which the scholar Tremellius elegantly explained by dividing the word into *bat* (in), *tel* (sign), and the feminine pronoun *lah*, as if to say a "sealed virgin" who carries the mark of her integrity with her. The parents would then take the blood-stained cloth and keep it as a perpetual testimony of virginity, preserved until the day of a marriage remained unblemished. Gerundensis <note>Likely referring to the scholar Nachmanides, also known as Rabbi Moses ben Nachman of Gerona.</note> describes this ancient Jewish custom thus: *“They would lead the Groom and Bride into the chamber (which they call a* Chuppah <note>original: הופה</note>*) and test them. Witnesses, however, watched them from outside, specifically those whom the Sages call* Shoshbinim <note>original: שושבינין</note>—*friends of the groom, companions, and attendants. And when they had separated, the witnesses entered and took the garment upon which she lay, and they saw the blood: which is known from the Talmud and Siphre Aggada, and they call that garment a* Sudar <note>A cloth or handkerchief.</note>. *Therefore the Scripture says: The father and mother unfold the cloth, which they received from the hand of the witnesses, and say: ‘This is the virginity of my daughter,’ etc.”* Paul Fagius notes the same in this passage. Nachmanides says: *“Before the bridal chamber stood two companions called* Shoshbinim, *who, going in first, explored the bedroom lest anyone set a trap for the other regarding the judgment of virginity; standing by all night with great joy and cheerfulness of soul, they kept watch like guards for a King and Queen. It was their duty, when the Groom and Bride came out, to rush in immediately, explore everything again, and having identified the previous cloths in which they had slept, they took them and delivered them to the mother.”*

<column-break/>

Thus, they report and announce that the girl’s virginity was taken away on that night by means of these cloths. Matthew de Afflictis, in his *Neapolitan Decisions* (236), claims that this Israelite sign is also observed by the people of Nola. John Leo <note>Leo Africanus, a famous traveler and geographer.</note> testifies that a nearly identical custom is still observed among the people of Fez in Africa: *“As soon as the Groom and Bride have returned home from the solemn wedding preparations, with the chamber locked, while the wedding feast is being prepared, they must come together for the celebration of the marriage. The now-married woman hands a bloodied cloth to the groom, who gives it to an old woman waiting outside the doors. She carries the bloodied cloth triumphantly into the middle of the crowd of guests, as the best spoil and symbol of taken virginity; and in this way, they were permitted to sit down and feast.”* See also Hottinger, *Augen. Epist.* and *Consult. Medic.* Vol. 2, book 1.

It is often doubted and discussed by many whether that evidence should be taken from a transverse membrane with a small opening that is broken at the first union, called the *hymen* by the ancients. There are those who maintain that it is not a membrane positioned across the passage, but rather "caruncles" <note>Small fleshy growths.</note> folded within the neck of the womb that are torn at the first union, and that the blood of virginity flows from the rubbing of these caruncles. Pinceus, a Parisian surgeon who wrote an entire book on the signs of virginity, considers the hymen to be four myrtle-shaped caruncles, bound by a single membrane, placed within the "fold of modesty." These opinions can be joined if we understand that it is not so much the hymen or transverse membrane of the uterine neck, but rather the associated caruncles, from which blood is first released at that entrance. Others, departing from this common opinion of Doctors and Theologians, deny that a membrane is broken during the loss of virginity, nor is there anything in the "guard of virginity" that the first man destroys. If a small membrane exists in some, they claim it is a sign of a certain disease, not of virginity. For virginity, as they would have it, exists without any membrane, consisting only in the compression of the labia and the narrowness or "coalescence" of the parts; since these cannot admit a man without dilation, the pain and blood result from the rupture of these joined veins. But "hands off the tablet" <note>A Latin idiom meaning "enough said" or "stop here."</note>. It is better to have remained silent here than to have said too much. These things should be kept at home, and knowledge of nature's secrets should be enclosed like a modest virgin. B. Gerhard deals extensively with the method of proving virginity used formerly among the Israelites in his *Commentary on Deuteronomy 22*, page 1342 and following.

The embrace of the thing contained is so full of care that it is even called a "mother" <note>original Greek: μήτηρ (*meter*)</note>, the womb. We do not side with the filthy Marcion <note>An early Christian heretic who rejected the material world as evil.</note>, who, as Tertullian witnesses in his third book *Against Marcion*, page 174, calls the womb a "sewer." Marcion perhaps followed Hippocrates in his book *On the Places in Man*, section 6, and Aristotle in *On the Generation of Animals*, book 4, chapter 7—all of whom were insulting toward the venerable works of nature. Instead, following Scripture and reason, we grant the greatest honor to our first home before birth. By a most beautiful personification <note>original Greek: προσωποποιία (*prosopopoia*)</note>, the Church is represented as having a womb, conceiving and giving birth to children, of which it is said in the Song of Songs, chapter 7, verse 2: *Your belly is like a heap of wheat set about with lilies.* These words of Solomon <margin>Book on the Institution of Virgins, chapter 14.</margin> are explained by Ambrose* regarding the Virgin Mary, the mother of the Savior, saying: *In Mary’s womb, the grace of the heap of wheat and the lily-flower sprouted together, because she gave birth to Christ, the grain of wheat and the lily.* Others, however, explain this as the fruitfulness of the Church, and by "lilies" they understand the spiritual children whom the Church bears for her Groom; compare this with the same Ambrose in his *Commentary on Galatians 4* and Philo of Carpathia, who comments on this passage: *The multitude of the faithful in the Church is aptly compared to a heap of wheat. For just as one mound is gathered from many grains, so from many Christian peoples the one Church of all the faithful is joined together.* Isaiah refers to this in chapter 60, verse 4, when he represents the Church as a mother situated in the middle of the earth, to whom sons and daughters are gathered from every side from all peoples and nations: *Your sons shall come from afar, and your daughters were born at your side.* <note>The author provides the Greek Septuagint version here: "your daughters shall be carried on shoulders."</note> The Old Latin version says: *your daughters shall suckle at your side.* A similar passage exists in the same author, chapter 49, verse 18, where in almost the same words the Church is commanded to lift her eyes and look around at the huge multitude of men flowing toward her. The word *gaster* <note>Greek for "belly" or "stomach."</note> is used for the belly in Proverbs 22:18: *Which will be beautiful for you,* says Solomon, *when you have kept it in your belly, and it shall overflow upon your lips.* The Greek explains this best by translating it as "heart" <note>original Greek: καρδίαν (*kardian*)</note>, namely regarding the law which is to be kept and stored in the innermost chambers of the heart. When he exhorted this study in chapter 3, verses 1 and 3, he said: *Write them on the tablets of your heart.* For it is not uncommon for the Holy Spirit to compare the mind with <margin>In Psalm 39, page 535.</margin> the womb, whence Ambrose* says: *There is a belly and a womb of the mind, which conceives the seeds of the senses, of which Isaiah says in chapter 26, verse 18: In the womb we have received, and we have brought forth the Spirit of salvation.* The same author says in Psalm 43, page 547: *Wisdom always gives birth like a fertile mother; discipline, like a more severe schoolmistress, draws us tight; understanding, like a diligent seeker, finds and searches out true justice and judgment.* Ratbertus also takes "belly" in this sense in *Lamentations of Jeremiah*, column 1354: *In sacred speech,* he says, *the Mind is usually designated by the name of 'Belly' or 'Womb'.* And this is why it is said through Solomon in Proverbs 20:27: *The lamp of the Lord is the spirit of man, which searches all the secrets of the belly.* Therefore, the light of God is said to search the secrets of the belly because it penetrates the hidden things of the mind, and brings back before the eyes for weeping those deeds which were hidden from the soul itself. *Moreover, the Mind is rightly understood by the name of the 'Belly', because just as offspring are generated in the womb, so thoughts are generated in the mind; and just as food is contained in the belly,* <margin>See Institutes of Medicine, page 105.</margin> *so also it is contained in the mind.* Regarding the food of the mind, he had said before that it is received through faith, then digested by the fire of charity, through a good way of life and meditation—a comparison taken from the ventricle or

Truly, while our meditation is occupied with the description of the womb, it is worthwhile to briefly <note>original Greek: ὡς ἐν βραχεῖ (*ōs en brachei*)</note> outline our conception, formation, and generation in the womb. For to be a human being and to be ignorant of one’s own beginnings is a mark of gross ignorance, which is in no way unpardonable <note>original Greek: ἀνεπιπολογήτῳ (*anepipologēto*), meaning inexcusable.</note>. Small indeed are the principles and beginnings of human offspring: tiny and few droplets of seed and blood, which provide the first origins for all humans without exception. If anything after God is necessary for a man to know, it is to "know thyself" <note>original Greek: γνῶναι σεαυτόν (*gnōnai seauton*)</note>, that is, his own principles and his own causes. What is man before generation but a thin and lowly drop of blood, which nevertheless in the mother’s womb gradually raises itself, until at last a living man comes forth into the light, endowed with body and soul. From the seed of both parents, the first sketch of all parts is made, and the "threads" <note>term: stamina</note> of this texture are drawn from the female principle, so much so that all the seed is consumed in the generation of the "spermatic parts" <note>Parts of the body believed to be formed directly from the reproductive seed, such as bones and nerves.</note>. Once the parts of our body have been sketched out, the flowing blood adds the "weaving" <note>term: subtegmina</note> to the threads originating from the woman, and being poured into the fibrous and membranous parts of the organs and muscles, it brings the required perfection to all things, and thus completes the wonderful structure of the parts, as Doctor Schelhamer* teaches. <margin>On the Diversity of the Human Body, chapter 7, page 19.</margin> Job, dealing with the composition of the human body in the womb, uses a comparison from the curdling of milk into cheese in chapter 10, verse 10: *Have you not poured me out like milk, and curdled me like cheese?* This is approved by the Wittenberg physician Salomon Alberti in the Dedicatory Epistle of his *History of the Parts of the Human Body*, in these words: *Job,* he says, *seems to pursue the matter of generation* <note>original Greek: ὕλη γενέσεως (*hyle geneseos*)</note>—*that is, the material for generating a man—somewhat roughly, but he by no means leaves it without a clear appearance. Which is truly milked from the males, and is gathered into itself in the womb like a curd, from which time industrious Nature herself separates the whey as being too fluid and negligent of the kitchen-work; the rest, which is thicker and more pliable, she keeps for herself, and is occupied in skillfully and craftily shaping it, giving it a body, and finally animating it with the immortal breath of life.* Homer uses the same comparison of milk in the *Iliad*, book 5, line 903, to describe the very swift closing and healing of a wound: *As when the fig-juice quickly curdles the white milk, though it is liquid, and it is very quickly turned as one stirs it.* <note>The original Greek text is quoted here.</note> But how the generation of man and the fabric or shaping of all the parts in the womb actually happens, we rightly refer to "the unsearchable and inscrutable things" <note>original Greek: τὰ ἀνεξερεύνητα καὶ ἀνεξιχνίαστα (*ta anexereunēta kai anexichniasta*)</note>, which are known to God alone, whatever others may write and think to the contrary. For although the anatomists say something, they do not say everything, and—what is the heart of the matter—they do not explain how, without a sculptor's hand and tools and brushes, the infant is formed with distinct little bones, veins, and a framework decorated with an appropriate fitting-together of skins and membranes; how, from the four humors, the body is so aptly arranged—so small, tender, and soft—painted with various colors, nourished, moved, and hastens to be brought forth mature into the light.* I say nothing—

### BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> It is the highest mystery how the body is animated; for physicians know and declare that it happens on the fortieth day, but from where the soul comes, they do not know; and not even theologians, varying in their opinions, are able to establish anything certain. The Blessed Luther holds the same view regarding the wonderful formation of man in the womb, saying: *Even if the maternal womb were open to view, an exact knowledge of this would still escape us, just as we see trees, leaves, and fruits grow, yet we do not know from where they take their increase.* <note>Martin Luther often used the mystery of biological growth as a metaphor for the hidden workings of God.</note> In the meantime, however, in such an obscure matter, we rightly commend the diligence of those who, taught by experience, have given us a description of the formation of the human fetus in the womb as best they can. Regarding the order and manner of the fetus's formation in the womb, the Doctors of the church and science philosophize in various ways.

William Harvey <note>William Harvey (1578–1657) was the English physician who first described the systemic circulation of blood.</note> describes four processes. He says: *Having become more certain from those things which I observed in a hen’s egg and the live dissection of animals, I establish that the blood is the first reproductive part, and the heart is its organ, destined for its circulation.* Indeed, the function of the heart is the propulsion of blood, as is clearly evident in all red-blooded animals. The same is the duty (in the generation of a chick) of the "pulsing vesicle," which I have frequently shown in the first conceptions of animals (no less than in a hen’s egg) to be visible, smaller than a spark, shimmering, and in its action contracting itself, squeezing out the blood contained in it, and receiving it again by its relaxation. Therefore, the first process is of the first-born part, namely the reproductive blood with its receptacles, or if you prefer, the heart with its veins. Concerning the second process, the head; the third, the outlining of the internal organs; and the fourth, the formation of parts of the lowest condition and order, consult Harvey himself.

Others prescribe a different mode of formation in the womb, sketching it thus: In the first six or seven days, the seeds are not idle, but they boil, as it were, and are heated by the generative spirit and the heat of the womb. By this, they become thick and dense, and from the heat, a windy spirit is generated, by which the mixed seeds swell and puff up. Soon, tiny bubbles filled with spirit arise, from which, when joined together, one cavity is made, containing a rich supply of the Spirit. This spirit, being enclosed and becoming hotter, seeks cooling for its own preservation and prepares a path for itself, so that through breathing, tempered spirit may enter by the same way to cool the fervor. By the same force of the Spirit, three bubbles are generated: one for the heart, a second for the brain, and a third for the liver. For the purer part of the seed passes into the material of the heart, the thicker and fattier part into the liver, and the colder and rawer part into the brain. These parts, like all the rest afterward, are perfected, nourished, and increased by the inflowing blood. Furthermore, the entire mass of seed, dried and hardened on the outside, is covered with a thin membrane, just as in bread while it is baking, a thin skin-like layer separates on the surface. This membrane prevents the seed from flowing away, the Spirit from exhaling, or the three bubbles of the first principles—still soft and thin—from being given over to the hardness of the womb. This was indeed done according to the example of the Great Architect, who first prepares a roof under which, protected from injuries, He can afterward build a magnificent edifice.

<column-break/>

All these things, along with the umbilical vessels, are believed to happen within the space of seven days, and they call this term "foaming" or "milking," <term>spumification or lactation</term> <note>Terms from medieval embryology describing the initial white, frothy appearance of the embryo before blood vessels appear.</note> according to the verses of Aegidius:

> *Six days in milk, three times three in blood,*
> *Twice six shape the flesh, thrice six the limbs.*
> <note>original: "Sex in lacte dies, ter sunt in sanguine trini, / Bis seni carnem, ter seni membra figurant." A traditional mnemonic for the stages of fetal development.</note>

From such a tiny drop of blood or animated seed, the fetus formed within seven days finally reaches perfection as a male on the thirtieth day after conception, but as a female on the forty-second day. It consists of so many bones, cartilages, veins, arteries, nerves, ligaments, and membranes. Among these, the bones are like columns supporting the whole mass. The joints are encrusted with cartilage; the limbs are bound and tied together with ligaments. The body is irrigated by veins as if by small streams. The parts are drenched with life-giving nectar by the arteries as if by tubes. The muscles and attached limbs are moved by nerves as if by reins.

In a wonderful manner and reason, the fetus thus formed is nourished in the mother's womb, with maternal blood being drawn and assimilated through the umbilical vein—specifically in the first months—and then by milk, when the fetus begins to move, as some would have it. Likewise, it lives in the womb in a wonderful way, receiving vital spirits from the mother; although it lives essentially and formally in the maternal womb through its own proper soul, it happens accidentally through the mother's work, since it not only has her blood for nutrition but also draws vital spirits for life through the umbilical vessels; compare Laurentius*. <note>Refers to André du Laurens (1558–1609), a French physician who wrote on anatomy and fetal development.</note> The fetus is moved by the work of the soul and animal spirits in the maternal womb at a time defined for it by nature. For in the first months, due to the weakness of the brain and the softness of the nerves, the tender fetus cannot toss its limbs; but when the bones, nerves, membranes, and ligaments—full of slow humor and mucus—begin to dry and firm up, then the fetus begins to kick and move. Indeed, the male does so on the ninetieth day of conception, which completes the third month, but the female on the hundred and twentieth day, which completes the fourth month.

Nor does the womb allow the fetus to slip from its embrace before it has reached completion; and the usual natural term is the ninth month of conception. For those born in the ninth month are considered most legitimate and viable, with experience approving and witnessing this, while on the contrary, an eight-month-old is commonly said to be barely viable. Yet, even a ten-month term is not rejected, although that time seems very long. *In ten months,* says Hippocrates, *which is the longest time, the infant is born.* Jerome mentions such a birth in his writing *On Avoiding Suspect Living Arrangements*: *Your mother carried you long in her womb (he had said before, you were enclosed in the womb for ten months), nourished you long, and with gentle piety endured the difficult ways of infancy; she washed the filth of your swaddling clothes and was often defiled by unclean dung; she sat by you when you were sick, and the hardships she endured for her own sake, she also suffered for yours to bring you to this age.* <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420) often used the physical labor of motherhood as a moral argument for filial piety.</note> Eleven-month and twelve-month births are very rare; yet the Praetor L. Papyrius did not hesitate to establish one born in the 14th month as the legitimate heir to his father’s honors, according to Pliny. The time of giving birth is certain for man, but not as certain as for other animals. A dog gives birth in the fourth month, a doe in the eighth, a mare...

### From Psalm 139:15

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> ...the horse in the ninth month, the elephant in the second year. Likewise, the sheep broods for three weeks, the goose and duck for four. Only for man are the days of gestation and birth neither fixed nor certain; for sometimes the time is extended, and sometimes it is brought forward. The limit of conception is indeed Birth, when after the ordinary gestation of seven or nine months, the fetus breaks forth from the mother's womb into the light through certain paths of nature then opened, in an exceedingly painful delivery. The work of the one giving birth is most difficult. 
<margin>Genesis 3:16</margin>
God imposed the first penalty upon Eve for being the first to transgress God's law: *I will surely multiply your pains and your conceptions, and in pain you shall bring forth children.* <note>original Latin: "Multiplicando multiplicabo dolores tuos..."</note> From this it can be known and easily concluded that Eve, from her first conception, suffered the greatest pains of Cain both in birth and before birth, and felt many <note>original Greek: πάθη (pathē) - sufferings or affections</note> of the womb, so that she might feel her state and know in herself that God had not spoken in vain. All women are subject to this sentence and feel the heaviest pains in childbirth.

<margin>In Jeremiah's Lamentations, book 3, page 1466.</margin>
Ratbertus <note>Paschasius Radbertus (c. 785–865) was a Carolingian theologian.</note> says: *A woman, when she gives birth, has sadness, and with the <note>original Greek: ἐκδοχῇ (ekdochē) - reception or opening</note> of the womb, by which the principal part of her breast is pressed, she suffers immense and innumerable distresses.* It is concluded, therefore, that the distresses of the mind are no less than those of the body. For the agitations and fevers of the soul are greater than those of the body. The pains of birth are proven by examples and noted in Scripture: Rebecca, complaining in Genesis 25:22, *If it was to be thus for me, why was it necessary to conceive?*; Rachel in Genesis 35:16; and the daughter-in-law of Eli in 1 Samuel 4:19, for whom the birth was <note>original Greek: θανατοφόρος (thanatophoros) - death-bringing or fatal</note>.

That pagan Medea confessed that she would rather stand three times in the line of battle than give birth once. <margin>Proverbs 31:1.</margin>
The Mother in the presence of Solomon recalls to memory <note>original Greek: τὰς ὠδῖνας (tas odinas) - the birth pangs</note> which she endured in labor, as well as in his gestation, saying: *Son of my womb:* and through the words: *Son of my vows*, she reminds him of maternal love, which ensures that he holds nothing dearer in life than her. Let the woman, however, revere the Man as her head and Lord. # BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
<margin>Book 2 on the Nature of the Gods</margin>
...as Goropius Becanus says in *Hispania*, page 77. The sentiment of Cicero* is notable: *What shall I say,* he asks, *of the bones? These, placed beneath the body, have marvelous joints, suited for stability, accommodated for strengthening the limbs, and adapted for motion and every action of the body.* While this bodily support is not yet hardened, we are neither able to steady our steps nor to walk, as we see in infants, whose bones have not yet solidified to support the mass of the body like pillars. When these fail or change, the entire framework is shaken and weakened, as the elderly teach us by their example, as well as those struck by fear, of whom Virgil says: *a cold tremor runs through the depths of the bones*, and Ovid:
