->*--- fear shakes the bones,*<-

Let us consider here also the terror of Habakkuk, which filled his very bones so that they trembled. In chapter 3:2, he says: *Lord, I have heard your report, and I was afraid*; I considered your works and I was terrified. And then he says: *Tremor entered into my bones, and my strength moved beneath me.* <note>Habakkuk 3:16</note> This is how it sounds from the Greek, for there it is written: <note>original Greek: Εἰσῆλθε τρόμος εἰς τὰ ὀστέα μου, καὶ ὑποκάτω-μέ συνεταράχθη ἡ ἰσχύς μου</note>. The Vulgate version has: *Let rottenness enter into my bones, and let it swarm beneath me.* The Hebrew text has: <note>original Hebrew: יבוא רקב בעצמי ותחתי ארגז (Yavo rakev b'atzmai v'tachtai ergaz)</note> *Rottenness entered my bones, and I trembled in my place.* Behold, says Ratbertus in his commentary on Psalm 44, column 1257: *Such a great Prophet, though elevated by the power of God, felt his own strength collapse beneath him.* Indeed, there is a most fitting <term>harmony<gloss>Greek: ἁρμονία (harmonia) - a fitting together or joining</gloss></term> and conformity of the bones throughout the whole body, about which Aristotle* says: <note>History of Animals, book 3, chapter 7</note> <note>original Greek: Τὰ δὲ ὀστᾶ τοῖς ζώοις ἀφ’ ἑνὸς πάντα συνήρτηται... (The bones of animals are all connected to one another...)</note> that is: *Bones are bound to one another, and all are fitted together, continuing in a single series like veins, and there is no bone that stands alone by itself.* They are arranged throughout the entire body, and there is no part of the body that is not provided with its own bones. Hence, so many bones are prominent: large, small, medium; flat, round, three-sided, four-sided; solid, hollow, movable, immovable; those with feeling, and those lacking sensation; upper, lower; front, and back. If you look at the number, it is so great that some count 249, others 304, and others as many as there are days in a year. Some hold their place in the head; others in the chest; others in the back; others in the limbs, where in the upper limbs they count sixty: two of the shoulders, four of the elbows, sixteen of the <term>carpus<gloss>the wrist</gloss></term>, eight of the <term>metacarpus<gloss>the palm</gloss></term>, and thirty of the fingers. In the lower limbs, there are sixty-two: two of the hips, two of the thighs, two of the knees, four of the shins, fourteen of the <term>tarsus<gloss>the ankle</gloss></term>, eight of the <term>metatarsus<gloss>the midfoot</gloss></term>, and thirty of the toes. The limbs, with which our meditation is now occupied, are usually divided into hands and feet. In the hand, one sees the arm, the elbow, and the small hand. In the foot, the thigh, the shin, and the small foot. The hand is that organ with which Nature alone blessed man, distinguishing him by it from the beasts, although the monkey and the squirrel use their front feet, and the elephant uses its trunk in place of a hand. Only man has hands because of his soul, and feet because of his hands. With the hand we build, mold, paint, sculpt, and in a word, perform manual labors; indeed, we sometimes even signify the feelings of our mind with it. Aristotle calls the hand the

<column-break/>

"tool of tools" <note>original Greek: ὄργανον πρὸ ὀργάνων (organon pro organōn)</note>, and it seemed good to God to give hands to man above all other living creatures. As Borrhaus says in his commentary on Judges, chapter 1, column 101: *they provide the instrument for the many arts that man practices, as can be seen in the arts of weaving, sewing, building, painting, sculpting, writing, and cultivating the fields, and handling weapons; for which use divine providence, when it formed man from the dust of the earth, joined a fitting shape to the hands: for they are divided and multi-fingered, and they have the bends of the fingers most convenient for grasping and pressing, which ability to catch and hold is especially aided by the strength of the thumbs, without which nothing can be grasped or retained.* Therefore, Nature—the ingenious creator of men and things—gave us two instruments, or rather doubled the instruments, so that works might be carried out more perfectly and accurately. To man, says Cassiodorus*, *the divine powers granted double hands, partner ears, and twin eyes, so that the duty might be performed more robustly, which was a shorthand provided by the partnership of two.* There were various symbols of the hands, and various are their actions and works. With the hand we confirm pacts, which is why Abraham, demanding an oath from his steward Eliezer, commands that he swear with his hand placed under his thigh (Genesis 24:2). Regarding this, Augustine says in his work against the second Manichaean, chapter 23: *Abraham, demanding the loyalty of an oath from his servant, said, "Place your hand under my thigh, and swear by the God of heaven." The servant indeed swore by obeying him, but Abraham also prophesied by commanding him—namely, that the God of heaven would come into that flesh which was descended from him.* In the story of Susanna, the two Elders placed their hands upon her head in the midst of the people to confirm their assertion against her. Regarding this, Diego de Celada says on page 10: *By this ceremony, both of them devote a most innocent person to capital punishment. O priest, remove your hand, for you are not a executioner, but a sacrificer.* Salianus notes: *The accusers lay hands on Susanna's head as if it were a cursed thing, pretending a conflict with as much stability as they could through slander, mixing truth with lies so they might gain credit for the latter.* And Sanchez in his commentary, note 32: *The witnesses placed their hands upon the head of the accused, by which they testified that the head was wicked and worthy of death.* So too Johannes Eusebius Nieremberg in his *Sacred Miscellany* (8.14): *This ceremony of accusation devoted the guilty to punishment, upon whose head it fed.* We are also accustomed to show our devotion both toward God and toward superiors with the hand. In the first clash of the Israelites with the Amalekites*, those two leaders of the Jewish people, Aaron and Hur, supported from either side the extended and uplifted hands of Moses as he prayed and supplicated to God, so that they might be faithful and stand firm, and not fall, either pressed down by weight or failing from weariness. Tertullian mentions this action in *Against Marcion*, book 3, page 178: *Moses, who surely only then, when Joshua was fighting against Amalek, ceased to pray with expanded hands; whereas in such astonishing circumstances, he ought rather to have commended his prayer with knees dropped, hands falling on his chest, and face rolling on the ground.* And Hilary, in his commentary on Psalm 140, page 617: *In the raising of the hands, the duty of a high work is shown, so that, when Moses elevated*...

# From Psalm 139:15. 827

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> ...the prophet was commanded to stand with his hands raised, while the people were either victorious or defeated depending on the lifting or lowering of his hands. <note>A reference to Moses during the battle against the Amalekites in Exodus 17.</note> The Psalmist provides an elegant testimony to the lifting of hands in chapter 141:2. <margin>Septuagint</margin> <note>original Hebrew: כְּבֹר מִנְחַת־עֶרֶב (ke-vor minchat-erev)</note> <note>original Greek: ἔπαρσις τῶν χειρῶν μου θυσία ἑσπερινή</note>: *May the lifting up of my hands be as an evening sacrifice.* This sacrifice is legitimate and acceptable to God if the mind is focused on high things, if the hands are not arrogantly raised, if the hands are washed with the tears of repentance, and if the mind, purged of vices, is free for heavenly matters. Otherwise, the stretching out of hands does not please God but rather displeases Him, as seen in *Isaiah 1:15*: *And when you stretch out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you.* Regarding this, Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century theologian.</note> in the place cited says: *The Lord, rejecting the prayers of the impious through the Prophet Isaiah, spoke thus: "If you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes from you." Certainly not if you "lift them up," but if you "stretch them out," which is the physical posture of prayer in stretching the hands; however, the effectiveness of a perfected work is in "lifting them up."* A mind purged from the dross of vice can say with a humble gesture: *The lifting of my hands is an evening sacrifice.* <margin>Letters of John p. 628</margin> <margin>Book 3 against Celsus p. 152</margin> Origen* says: <note>original Greek: Ὅστις χεῖρας καθαρὰς, καὶ διὰ τοῦτ᾽ ἐπαίρων... (Hóstis cheíras katharás...)</note> *Who is he that has clean hands, and because of this lifts them up, and because of this lifts up holy hands to God, and because of the distinction of visions is able to perform them, can say: "The lifting of my hands is an evening sacrifice"?* Relying on this, David, singing of the goodness and justice of his cause against his enemies, places his hope in the purity of his hands; in his recounting, he twice mentions the "purity" <note>original Greek: καθαρότητος (katharotētos)</note> of his hands, saying first in <margin>Psalm 18:21</margin> *Psalm 18:21: The Lord will reward me <note>original Hebrew: כְּצִדְקִי (ke-tzidki)</note> according to my righteousness; <note>original Hebrew: כְּבֹר יָדַי יָשִׁיב לִי (ke-vor yadai yashiv li)</note> according to the purity of my hands he will repay me.* The Greek version expresses this excellently: <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἀποδώσει μοι Κύριος κατὰ τὴν δικαιοσύνην μου... (Kai apodōsei moi Kyrios...)</note> *And the Lord will reward me according to my righteousness, and according to the purity of my hands he will repay me.* For while he offers a sacrifice of praise to God the Deliverer and graphically depicts the manner of his liberation, attributing everything to God, in his remembrance of evils and dangers he also wished to add the justice of his cause—namely, that he did not thirst for <margin>at the Year of the World 438, number 28</margin> the blood of his enemies or of Saul, but in the recognition and fear of the true God, he kept and retained unspotted hands through God's grace, saying: *According to the purity of my hands he will reward me.* He repeats this <term>exegetically</term> <note>meaning to explain or interpret further</note> and indeed a second time in verse 25: *The Lord repaid me according to my righteousness, <note>original Hebrew: כְּבֹר יָדַי לְנֶגֶד עֵינָיו (ke-vor yadai le-neged einav)</note> <note>original Greek: πλὴν τὴν καθαρότητα τῶν χειρῶν μου ἐνώπιον τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῷ (plēn tēn katharotēta tōn cheirōn mou enōpion tōn ophthalmōn autō)</note> according to the purity of my hands before his eyes.* "Purity of hands" means "clean hands," as the Greeks explain <margin>Exodus 17:12</margin> in Job chapter 9:30 <margin>in Job chapter 9:30</margin> <note>original Hebrew: כְּבֹר יָדַי (ke-vor yadai)</note> as <note>original Greek: χερσὶ καθαραῖς (chersi katharais)</note> "with clean hands." But how could David claim such justice and purity of hands? He could certainly do so because of the righteousness of faith, which produces purity of hands and makes David entirely pure and unspotted. The rite of blessing is also usually performed with the hand. <margin>on 1 Kings 2, page 421, Volume 1</margin> *There was not*, says Francisco Mendoza*, *among the Hebrews a single vocal or verbal form of blessing, but various forms were used according to the piety of those blessing and the needs of those being blessed. It seems to me that the gesture of those blessing was usually expressed by no other part of the body than the hands; for while the body remained still, the hands alone were moved to bless.* There were four ways of positioning the hands to impart a blessing. *First, the lifting of hands to heaven; second, the ex-*

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> *tension of hands toward the people; third, the imposition of hands upon the heads of those being blessed; fourth, the transposition of hands, or changing them into the form of a cross.* <note>A reference to Jacob blessing Ephraim and Manasseh with crossed arms.</note> And who will be able to recount all the actions of the hands? Conversely, a *slack* hand is a symbol of a negligent person, just as a laborious and diligent hand represents the industrious, <margin>Proverbs 12:24</margin> *Proverbs 12:24: The slack hand will be tributary <note>original Hebrew: יַד־רְמִיָּה תִּהְיֶה לָמַס (yad-remiyah tihyeh lamas)</note>; that is, it will be overwhelmed by debt.* Ruling and serving are contrasted there: the former comes from a diligent and careful hand, the latter from a slack and negligent one. <margin>Lamentations 1:1</margin> A parallel passage is *Lamentations 1:1*, where the same words appear regarding *having dominion and serving under tribute.* Those things that are "in hand" for anyone, the Greeks call <note>original Greek: πρόχειρα ἔχειν (procheira echein)</note> "having at hand." All tools that are ready and useful to have at hand are called <note>original Greek: πρόχειρα (procheira)</note>; in Latin, they are called *amanuensia* <note>meaning "at hand" or "hand-servant"</note>, a name taken from the hand, because the most important works are usually carried out by the benefit of the hands. Hence, a *work without hands* is considered imperfect and poorly executed. <margin>Sacred Tropology, column 1183</margin> Westhemerus* refers to this: *Your work was done without hands, that is, you acted poorly, as if hands were missing to complete the work, or they erred, or your work is without hands.* It seems to be a proverbial saying, meaning: *Your work has no hands. Your work has no use.* We have a similar one in the German language: *It has neither hand nor foot.* <note>original German: Es hat weder Hand noch Fuß</note> That is, it is frivolous, empty, and useless—even a monstrosity. The hand begins at the shoulders and ends at the fingers. The first part is the *arm* <term>brachium</term>, everything that hangs from the shoulder blades and extends to the nearest joint. The arm consists of bones, muscles, and ligaments, by which it is bound and strengthened. In both sacred and secular literature, the arm is taken <term>analogically</term> for the strength with which it is endowed and signifies various things; primarily it denotes power, which is why Horace* <margin>2 Epistles 2, verse 48</margin> *uses "arm" for the power of Augustus, where he says that the troops of Brutus were by no means equal to the muscles (or forces) of Augustus Caesar.*

> The tide of civil war carried the man unskilled in weapons into arms
> That would not answer to the muscles of Augustus Caesar.

In Sacred Scripture, to say nothing of other places that can be seen in Matthias Flacius in the *Key* under the word *Arm* <margin>Flacius in the Key under the word Arm.</margin>, Mary, the <term>Theotokos</term> <note>God-bearer or Mother of God</note>, praises the strength of God's omnipotence in Luke 1:51, saying: *He has shown strength with his arm.* Nor is it unusual for Kings and other great men to show their power by the name of "the arm," just as, conversely, the weakening of the arm is a sign of diminished and broken power. The voice of the Prophet Isaiah is sad and complaining regarding the distraction of the Jewish Republic and the miseries and calamities of his people when he says: *Manasseh eats the shoulders and his own arms.* <note>Isaiah 9:20</note> This is a pathetic and mournful picture or image of a horrible and abominable thing, taken from the fury of wretched men who rage against their own vitals; or even the extreme necessity of those who are killed by hunger; for these, to preserve life, incited by the madness of starvation, tear their own flesh with their teeth and disfigure parts of their body with cruel butchery. So, says the Prophet, our King slaughters the members of his own Republic, his own citizens, with cruel savagery; he cuts off his own helping hands and weakens his own kingdom, which is soon after to be overwhelmed by a foreign enemy. The second part is called the *elbow* <term>cubitus</term>, namely everything that begins from the arm and extends to the end...

# SACRED ANTIQUITIES. 828

<margin>Anatomy of the sacred body</margin>
...extending as far as the hand. The forearm is composed of two bones, the lower and the upper; the former is called the *ulna* <note>original: *ulna*</note>, which is quite distinct, long, and not round, but rather triangular, flat, and without rounded joints. The other is called the *radius* <note>original: *radius*</note>, which is equipped with two processes that the anatomists describe as being <note>original Greek: ὡς ἂν καμπῇ (hōs an kampē)</note> "as if for bending." Finally, the third part is called the *hand proper* <note>original: *manus parva*</note>, and it comprises everything extending from the forearm to the tips of the fingers. Divided into three parts, it first shows us the *carpus* (wrist), consisting of eight bones, followed by the *metacarpus* (mid-hand), which consists of four bones—for the thumb lacks a metacarpal bone, and in its place, the first joint extends further. The *fingers* <note>original: *digiti*</note> complete the hand; they are the most powerful instruments for grasping. When they are spread out, they form the *palm* <note>original: *palma*</note>; when they are drawn together, they form the *fist* <note>original: *pugnus*</note>. Thus, the extended hand is called the palm, and the contracted hand the fist. The hand consists of the back and the *hollow* <note>original: *vola*</note>, where there are "mounts" and lines from which those who practice chiromancy <note>Palm reading</note> divine various things, though we discuss their divination elsewhere. At this point, it is pleasant to note the verses which the palm-reader Caspar Barlaeus <note>A Dutch polymath and poet, 1584–1648</note> wrote in an elegant and delightful poem:

<margin>4 Heroic. p. 680.</margin>
> *The little mounts carry so much weight. This is called*
> *The line of life; this, of the liver; and the triangle of Mars*
> *Is enclosed by them. This is the table of the hand. If the line of life*
> *Traces its path in a long, colored furrow,*
> *A long-lived day goes with us. But Atropos* <note>One of the Three Fates in mythology who cuts the thread of life.</note> *cuts the years*
> *More swiftly, and after a life led through a thousand dangers,*
> *They blame the gods, if the thread flows in short circles,*
> *Cut off here and there. If the line wanders narrow*
> *And retreats into the middle curves, the mind is provident of what is right.*
> *If it is pale, if it is wide, diligent effort grieves*
> *To lie idle, and a spiritless inertia breaks the whole body,*
> *And the mind is unconsulted within a dull brain.*

Regarding Jacob, it is recorded in Genesis 32:25 that the Son of God, wrestling with him until dawn, touched the <note>original Hebrew: כף-ירך (Kaph-yerekh)</note> "hollow of the thigh." The Septuagint <note>The Greek Old Testament</note> translates this as <note>original Greek: τὸ πλατὺς τῷ μηρῷ (to platys tō mērō)</note> "the broad part of the thigh." The Old Interpreter <note>The Vulgate</note> calls it the "sinew of the thigh." Pagninus <note>Santes Pagnino, a Hebraist</note> calls it the "palm of the thigh." Arias Montanus <note>A 16th-century Spanish orientalist</note> calls it the "curvature of the thigh." The Hebrew word is *nashah*, from the root *nashash*, meaning to bend; it properly signifies the inner surface and the sole of the foot. Here,
<margin>Commentary on this passage, p. 615.</margin>
says Blessed Gerhard <note>Johann Gerhard, a Lutheran theologian</note>, it is taken for the part of the thigh having the shape of a curved hand, as Kimchi <note>A medieval Jewish exegete</note> explains. Others take the word *Kaph* for the curvature found in the thigh, meaning that the man squeezed the hip of Jacob, and from that contact, the thigh nerve was displaced. Luther, in his commentary on Genesis chapter 32, folio 167a, says: *"Caph signifies the hollow, that is, the hand curved in the manner of a spoon, whence Moses calls the spoons 'Caphos' (in German: Roten); and because of the similarity, he calls the vertebra or the concave bone, which the Greeks call the* <note>original Greek: ἴσχιον (ischion)</note> *'hip-joint,' into which the bone of the upper leg is inserted and turns. The nerves are wrapped around so that a junction of two bones is made, and the leg is moved by that vertebra. He means to say, therefore, that the Man moved Jacob's thigh bone out of its place. When a dislocation occurs, the nerves are moved and contracted, and because of the meeting of many nerves there, the sharpest pains are stirred up, and numbness of the limb follows."* There are various names for the fingers. According to Pollux <note>Julius Pollux, a 2nd-century grammarian</note>, the "small" finger of the hands <note>original Greek: μικρὸς (mikros)</note> is called the *auricularis* <note>the "ear-finger," used to scratch the ear</note> or *minimus* (the least) by the Latins. Next to this is the <note>original Greek: παραμέσσος (paramessos)</note> "next to the middle," called the *annularius* (ring-finger) by the Latins because gold rings are worn on it; it is

<column-break/>

otherwise next to the smallest and fourth in order. After this is the <note>original Greek: μέσσος (messos)</note> *medius* (middle finger), and then the <note>original Greek: λιχανὸς (lichanos)</note> from *aleicho* (to lick), which the Latins call the *Index*, because people are accustomed to use it for pointing. The fifth is called the <note>original Greek: ἀντίχειρ (anticheir)</note> "opposite the hand" by the Greeks, because it stands in place of the hand and is more powerful (hence the Latin name *pollex* from *pollere*, to be powerful) than all the other fingers; this one alone, although shorter, equals them in strength and power. It is also called <note>original Greek: δικόνδυλω (dikondylō)</note> "two-knuckled," while the others are <note>original Greek: τρικόνδυλω (trikondylō)</note> "three-knuckled," because of its two joints or curves. For although Nature was more sparing in granting it knuckles, she made up for that defect by giving it two extensor muscles by which it is moved powerfully, and two muscles—the abductor and adductor—which are found as <note>original Greek: καταμύας (katamyas)</note> "under-muscles" in the other fingers.

Having seen the hand, the *Foot* <note>original: *Pes*</note> remains, which is divided into three parts: the first is called the *femur* (thigh), the second the *crus* (leg) or *tibia* (shin-bone), and the third is called the *Foot*. The feet enable a human to be upright, to sit, stand, walk, and run. They make it possible to gaze at the stars, to climb towers, and to approach those things that cannot be grasped by the hands. The feet carry the human, as Homer says in the Iliad, book 15, verse 405:
-> *And so, having spoken thus, his feet bore him.* <-

In the Sacred Scriptures, there is a frequent naming taken from the position, posture, and members of the body to designate the occupations and status of men. Thus "to walk," which pertains to the foot, sometimes signifies to organize one's life in a certain way so as to reach a fixed goal (Genesis 17:1). Thus "to stand" is often taken for remaining in one's state (Psalm 102:27). Thus "to sit" is sometimes said in Holy Scripture of that which always remains in the same way and is not easily changed (Psalm 125:1). Hence Philippus the Priest says: *"By the word 'feet' in the Scriptures, we should usually understand a certain manner of human conduct and the course of life. 'I washed,' he says, 'my actions from every stain of sin, and I lived with innocence and simplicity.' For we should know that this is signified here by the name of 'milk,' because of the simple food of innocent cattle. Therefore, he washed the steps of his soul with the fruits of good works, simplicity, and innocence."* By the name of the foot, the Scripture marks the affections that must be maintained in the path of piety and virtue. Innocent III <note>Pope from 1198–1216</note> says in his commentary on the 3rd Penitential Psalm: *"The foot of a man is his affection, his work, and his support. Each is double, namely right and left. Of the feet of affection it is said:* 'I have washed my feet, how shall I defile them?' <note>Song of Solomon 5:3</note> *Of the right: 'My foot has stood in the straight way.' Of the left: 'Let not the foot of pride come against me.' Of the feet of operation it is said: 'He made my feet like the feet of hinds,' and 'He will keep the feet of His saints.' Of the right ones: 'Their feet are straight.' Of the left ones: 'Their feet run to evil.' Of the right foot of support, Blessed Job says: 'I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame.' Of the left foot of support, the Truth <note>Christ</note> says: 'If your foot causes you to sin, cut it off.'"* The Prophet uses an excellent comparison in the first Psalm, using a non-inelegant collection of "walking," "standing," and "sitting." "Walking" marks the beginning, "standing" the middle, and "sitting" the end. Happy is he, and happy again, who does not look back at the deceits of the wicked; much less does he organize his life according to them; and least of all would he depart into their family and filth, professing the same crimes. If you see someone running in the way of sinners—a drunkard, or a lecher, or a profligate, or a robber...

# SACRED ANTIQUITIES. 829

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
...turn away from his way, depart, withdraw, run back. Do not stand or linger in the way of sinners, for it is a way of pestilence. The order of Blessedness, however, requires one not to stand in the way of sinners, and not to sit in the seat of pestilence <note>original: *Ps. 1. 1.*</note>. Hilary asks what it means to "restrain one's feet from every evil way," and he even explains it*: <margin>On Psalm 118, p. 495.</margin> *This is the perfect voice of a man of the Gospel: to abstain from every way of malice, and, among so many paths of error encountered everywhere, to walk in none of them through which wickedness is approached.* The nature of our body carries us into every course of crime, and the impulse of human desires forces us onto this path. We must resist and struggle, first to keep ourselves from every evil way, and then, if any instinct begins to carry us there, to pull ourselves back. To "sit" denotes a <term>pre-eminence of honor</term> <note>original Greek: τιμῆς ὑπεροχὴν</note>, about which Theophanes says in Sermon 24, p. 153: Scripture tells us of two who went out and sat: the King of the Ninevites, sitting humbly on his throne, and Job, sitting patiently on a dung heap. In ancient times, Judges did not pronounce judgment while walking, as the Philosophers did, but while sitting. Hence that line from Propertius, book 3:

— The judge of the age sits less. —

And in book 4:

— The judge Aeacus sits, once the urn has been placed. —

That act of sitting symbolically notes that a judge ought to be of a constant soul, a settled heart, and a well-composed mind. The **thigh** <note>original: *Femur*</note> is the upper part extending from the buttocks to the knees; it is joined to the sacred bone <note>The sacrum</note> and slopes toward the knees. In ancient times, a hand was placed under the thigh during an oath. When Abraham was about to send his steward Eliezer to Mesopotamia to bring back a wife for his son, he first ordered the servant to place his hand under his thigh, both to honor the circumcision and for the mystical sense regarding the Messiah who was to arise from the loins of Abraham, according to Photius*: <margin>On Job, ch. 29, p. 122.</margin> <margin>Letter 74, p. 122.</margin> <term>The Two Meanings of the Thigh-Oath</term> <note>original Greek: Δυὸ ταῦτα παραδηλοῖ τὴν νυμφαγωγίαν προστάττει θεράποντι, ἕν γε καὶ πρόχειρον, τὸν ὅρκον εἰς τὸ τῆς περιτομῆς σεβάσμιον εἰσπραττόμενον. δεύτερον δὲ, καὶ νοούμενον, ἕν τῷ ἐξ αὐτοῦ τεχθησόμενον χριστὸν καὶ θεὸν ἡμῶν. / Translation: He shows two things here in commanding the servant regarding the leading of the bride: one, quite obvious, is the oath taken in reverence for circumcision; the second, and more spiritual, is that from him would be born Christ and our God.</note> On this ritual, see Drusius on the Scriptures, p. 54. It is established that the thigh consists of very robust muscles, varied in shape, and diverse in name and use. From the wrestling match he had with the Angel of God, Jacob walked with a limp because, after his thigh was touched, the sinew had become numb. The Fathers aptly explain this struggle as the mystery of the Incarnation of the Son of God. Ambrose says*: <margin>On Psalm 43, p. 590.</margin> *Christ is that man who wrestled with Jacob and touched his thigh; by this touch, the Patriarch’s sinew went numb, signifying that Christ would come from his line according to the flesh, and that He would be "hamstrung" <note>rendered weak or crippled</note> by the Jewish people in the passion of His body. Not understanding this, they established a mystery so that the sons of Israel would not eat the sinew.* And Theodotus in the *Selection*, verse 117:

> Jacob, meeting the Lord in a long struggle,
> Lost the sinews of his thigh while refusing to yield;
> The entire line of his descendants does not eat the sinew,
> Groaning at this wound as if it had happened to their Parent.

The Groom commends his Bride for the elegance of her thighs in Song of Songs 7:1: *The joints of your thighs,* he says, *are like jewels, which were crafted by the hand of an artist.* Regarding these, Willeram sings in verse 21:

> It is clear that the joints of your thighs are such,
> As if they were jewels made by the skilled right hand of a craftsman.

<column-break/>

-> How the joints of the thighs are the places of generation. <-

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
Thus for me, you now bring forth spiritual offspring
Through the word of faith and the washing of the holy stream.
It joins together the like-minded faithful from a twin people <note>Likely referring to Jews and Gentiles</note>,
Just as two thighs are bound together into one joint.

> Since they mix the zeal of doing with faith,
> Doing what my words command, they shine like beautiful jewels.

In these words, Willeram joins both interpretations, which others treat separately. For Cassiodorus explains this as the joining of peoples in one faith; this explanation fits best with what the Groom said in the preceding verse, which was the last of the previous chapter. Let us also hear Ambrose*: <margin>On Psalm 118, p. 725.</margin> *The Church, the daughter of Aminadab (that is, of the willing or well-pleasing), because a willing and well-pleasing person gathered her, is beautiful even in her sandals. Fittingly, it was added in the Song of Songs: The movements of your thighs are like necklaces, the work of a craftsman's hands, so that the ornaments of the Church's future generations might be praised. For through the thigh, we recognize distinguished generation. These "moduli" <note>ornaments or rhythmic measures</note> are called precious decorations that are usually hung around the necks of matrons. Therefore, such a great progress of the Church is signified that it is compared to the most precious ornaments and to the necklaces of those in triumph.* For these ornaments belong to warriors. Hence Symmachus used the term <term>neck-ornaments</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπιταρχήλια (epitarchēlia)</note>, that is, those things which are around the neck. Whether it be the generation of Christ from the flesh, or the propagation of the Church—in appearance like necklaces adorned by a craftsman’s hand—it has truly crowned the necks of the faithful with spiritual signs of virtue.

The **leg** or **shin** <note>original: *Crus* or *tibia*</note> is the lower part situated between the thigh and the small foot, and the joint by which the shin is joined to the thigh is called the **knee** <note>original: *genu*</note>. Its anterior part is called the **cap** or **patella** <note>original: *mola* or *patella*</note>, while the posterior part is called the **ham** <note>original: *poples*</note>. Strength is attributed to the knees, about which Caesarius speaks quite elegantly*: <margin>Question 78, p. 228.</margin> <note>original Greek: ἐνέλη ὑμῖν διηθρωμένα στροφαῖς καὶ τόρνοις συμβεβλημένα, οἱανεὶ στύλοι ἀχθοφόροι, τὸ ὅλον ἐπερείμενοι σῶμα, ἐπὶ κεφαλίδας μὲν τὰ γόνυ ἔχοντες, βάσιν δὲ τὸν ἀστράγαλον. / Translation: [The legs] are articulated for you with hinges and joints, fitted as if by a lathe, like weight-bearing columns supporting the entire body, having the knees as their capitals and the ankle as their base.</note> He says that the shins are the columns of the body for bearing weights, and that the knee is at the head of these columns, while the ankle is the base, etc. Hence, investigators of natural things have examined this part of the body with great care, using it to designate the strength of a man or the stages of a man's life. We must first quote Theocritus, who* describes a man in the flower of his age by this part, attributing "manly knees" to him in these words: <margin>Idyll 14, v. 10.</margin>

> — — — From the temples we all
> Become old, and time creeps onto the cheek,
> Whitening it. One must act while the knee is still green <note>symbolizing youth and vigor</note>.

Then Horace, *Epode* 12, verse 4:

> — while the knees are green <note>vigorous</note>

And it is fitting that old age be loosened from the clouded brow. In old age, not only are the knees weakened and deprived of their strength, but God also sometimes takes away their vigor. The voice of God is severe toward the Israelites if they do not keep His commandments; while He announces various kinds of curses to them through Moses, among them is this one from *Deuteronomy 28:35: Jehovah will strike you with a grievous ulcer on the knees and on the hips, so that you cannot be healed*, <note>original Greek: ὥςε μὴ δύνασθαι ἰαθῆναι</note>, which from the root of the language is correctly <note>original Hebrew: אשר לא-תוכל להרפא (asher lo-tukhal le-herape)</note> "which you cannot be healed from."

# SACRED ANTIQUITIES. 830

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>...are turned. But if plagues of this sort come from God and others like them, God himself provides the most proven remedy for healing in Jeremiah 3:22. <margin>Jer. 3:22.</margin> *Return, you rebellious children*, <note>original Hebrew: ארפה משובתיכם, *Arpah meshuboteikhem*</note> *that is, I will heal your turnings-back.* Ambrose looks toward the same antidote in *On Fleeing the World*, chapter 7, page 317: *Isaiah cries out: "Strengthen the weak hands and the feeble knees," <note>original: *Esaias clamat: Convalescite manus remissæ & genua dissoluta*</note> that is, let the knees—not of the body, but of the soul—grow strong, so that the step of the mind may be lifted up, directed toward the highest reaches of heaven, so that your doctrine may be more solid, your life more mature, your grace more full, and your prudence more circumspect.* While strength is still whole and in the flower of age, Sirach <note>The author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus</note> exhorts youth to labor in chapter 25:5: *If you have not gathered in your youth, how will you find anything in your old age?* <note>original Greek: Ἐν νεότητι οὐ συνήγοχας, καὶ πῶς ἂν ἐύρης ἐν τῷ γήρᾳ σου.</note> In the flowering age, he says, you did not gather; how will you be able to find it in your old age? This is a most useful lesson for life, both for sustaining oneself and for finding joy in old age. Everyone must labor from youth so that they may have comfort in old age. Labor is the provider of happiness and wealth, and the greater the labor, the greater the benefit. He who flees labor in youth must necessarily lack in old age. Youth is useful for gathering things, and "the works of the young" <note>original Greek: ἔργα νέων</note> ensure that old age is more restful and comfortable for itself, for old age does not know how to bear labor. One ought to conduct business while the knee is green—while the hamstrings are vigorous—to speak with Theocritus, for his precept is similar:

->One must do something while the knee is green.<-
<note>original Greek: ποιεῖν τι δεῖ, οἷς γόνυ χλωρόν. "Green" here signifies youth and vitality, like a young plant.</note>

<margin>Eclogue 6. 6.</margin> that is, as Eobanus Hessus translates it:
>Therefore some work must be done while age sustains us,
>and while I am able to be sufficient for labor with a green knee.<

In old age, the bent hamstrings can scarcely sustain the weight of the body, let alone be sufficient for labor. Thus, "green knees" <note>virentia genua</note> perform labors opportunely, <margin>7th book of the Republic, f. 706.</margin> "knees at their peak," <note>original Greek: γόνατα ἀκμάζοντα</note> for, as Plato says, "all the great and many labors belong to the young." Though these labors are great, they compensate with the joy of manifold fruit; indeed, "the more the toil, the greater the gain," <note>original Greek: ὅπερ γδ πλείων κόπΘ, πολὺ κέρδΘ</note> according to Ignatius, Letter 8 to Polycarp; and according to Pindar: <margin>Nemean Ode 7, antistrophe 5.</margin>

->if there was toil, the pleasure following is greater.<-
<note>original Greek: ἐι πόνΘ ἦν, τὸ τερπνὸν πλέον παρἔρχεται.</note>

<margin>7. Education, p. 199.</margin> Xenophon writes in agreement with these: "Good things delight us more, the more someone has previously labored for them." But it is better that we look at the small foot, divided into the *Pedium* <note>Tarsus</note>, *Metapedium* <note>Metatarsus</note>, and *Digits* <note>Toes</note>. The extremities of these, as in the hands, are protected by nails, one for each. Those are in vain who think any of these parts were made in vain. Momus <note>The Greek god of mockery</note> used to praise slender shins and said the calf should be removed. But his foolish judgment is to be laughed at. That fleshy part of the shin, together with the rest, is a singular defense and ornament for a human being; every little part, even the smallest in us, shows the care, providence, and wisdom of God. Hence Nemesius says concerning the soul: "In every part of the body, the foresight of Providence is manifest." <note>original Greek: παντὶ μορίῳ τῶ σώματΘ ἐμφαίνεται τῆς προνοίας ἡ προμήθεια.</note> The *Pedium*, which is also called the *tarsus* <note>original Greek: ταρσὸς</note> by the Greeks, is the forward part of the footprint after the heel, where the first joint of the bones begins that constitute the sole; it is between the shin and the metapedium, and is called the *calcaneus* <note>heel bone</note>. Truly, the bone that is in the heel is called the *talus* <note>ankle bone</note>, from which the name of the *talaris* garment <note>ankle-length robe</note> is derived, which descends all the way to the heels. For they wore ankle-length garments to cover the heels, which it was considered a disgrace to uncover.

<column-break/>

From this, the words of Psalm 40:16 <margin>Ps 40. 16.</margin> and 70:4 are to be understood: *upon their heel while they are in shame*, <note>original Hebrew: עקב בשתם, *Eqev boshtam*</note> as Ludovicus de Dieu agrees with Cloppenburg in *Brielish Biblical Delights, pages 244-245.* <margin>244. 245.</margin> Since that bone is quadrangular in shape, for this reason the Architects <note>likely referring to "master builders" or creators of terms</note> called it "the Die" <note>original German: *die Würffel*</note> in games of chance; compare Andreas Senftleb on the *Dice of the Ancients*, chapter 4, section 3, page 35. The *Metapedium* or metatarsus is that part of the foot that comes between the heel and the toes. Among the Greeks, *pedion* <note>original Greek: πεδίον</note> signifies a field or a plain. Metaphorically, however, it is also <margin>116</margin> used for the upper part of the foot, adjacent to the toes. Hence Pollux: *Parts of the foot: the upper part before the toes is the "pedion" [plain], either because it was flat or broad, being composed of bones and sinews.* <note>original Greek: Μέρη ποδὸς, τὰ μὲ ἄνω πρὸ ἦ δακτύλων πεδίον, ἢ ὅγε ἦν ἢ πολύς ων, ἐξ ὧν κἂνεύρων συγκέιμενον.</note> The toes conclude the foot. The *Peltza* <note>πέλζα</note> is the ankle-bone <note>malleolus</note> of the foot, which word is often used in a broader sense for the sole of the foot and the whole foot. Zenodotus, in his book *On National Phrases*, recorded that the Arcadians and Dorians called the foot *peltza*, as Galen testifies. Feet are commended for their speed, just as they are usually disparaged for limping. In the Sacred Scriptures, Asahel is called "a runner," and in Homer, Achilles is "swift-footed" <margin>Iliad book 13, line 348; book 17, line 709; book 18, lines 354, 358.</margin> <note>original Greek: πόδας ταχὺς</note>, as also in *Iliad* book 18, line 69:

->around the swift Achilles.<-
<note>original Greek: ταχὺν ἀμφ' Ἀχιλλῆα.</note>

Concerning the speed of feet, Aristotle says in *Rhetoric, book 1*: "The swift man is also strong. For he who is able to throw his legs and move them quickly and far is a runner." <note>original Greek: καὶ ὁταχὺς, ἰσχυρός ἐσιν. ὁ γδ δυνάμενΘ ῥίπτειν πῶς καὶ κινεῖν ταχὺ καὶ πόῤῥω, δρομικός.</note> In the Sacred Volumes, Mephibosheth is read as limping, so that he seems to have been similar to Aristophanes' Plutus, who walked in a squalid and filthy manner:
<margin>Plutus, scene 2, line 28.</margin>
*who, being lame, suddenly became [so]* <note>original Greek: ὃς χωλὸς ὢν ἐξαπίνης ἐγένετο</note>
In Homer, Tydides and Ulysses walk limping—the former wounded in the sole of the foot, the latter in the side—wherefore they also leaned on spears as they walked, *Iliad* book 19, line 47:

->and those two, the servants of Mars, went limping along.<-
<note>original Greek: τὼ δὲ δύω σκάζοντε βάτην ἌρεΘ θεράποντε.</note>

No one is supported by such firmness that they should trust in their own stability; for various are the slippery ways of this world, as even the Prophet says in the Psalms: *But my feet were almost moved; my steps had well-nigh slipped.* It is a haughty presumption to believe oneself secure among the temptations of this life, when everything is full of dangers. Man is swift toward evil, but slow toward good. Hence, among those six things which the Wise Man lists as *hateful to God, one is: Feet that are swift in running to evil. Prov. 6:18.* Therefore, one must walk cautiously on the slippery paths of this life, where innumerable falls and slips present themselves. St. Ambrose thus taught and <margin>On Duties</margin> commended modesty of gait: *Modesty must be maintained even in movement, gesture, and gait; for the habit of the mind is seen in the state of the body. From this, the hidden man of our heart is judged to be either lighter, or more boastful, or more turbulent—or, on the contrary, more grave, constant, and mature. Thus, the movement of the body is a kind of voice of the soul. There are those who, by walking slowly, imitate the gestures of actors, and [move] like the floats in processions or the nodding of statues, so that every time they take a step, they seem to observe a certain rhythm. Nor do I think it honorable to walk at a run, except when the cause of some danger or just necessity demands it. A commendable gait is one in which there is an appearance of authority and the weight of gravity, the trace of tranquility—provided that study and affectation are absent, and the movement is pure and simple.*

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> ...is simple, for nothing faked is pleasing. Beautiful are the steps of the Bride, which the heavenly Groom <margin>Song of Solomon 7:1.</margin> praises along with her shoes. Those who describe a beloved person curiously seek out and hand down praises for every limb. What does Ambrose mean, he asks <margin>In Psalm 118, Sermon 17, page 725; on Song of Solomon chapter 7.</margin> in his 17th sermon on Psalm 118 (page 725) regarding chapter 7 of the Song of Solomon, when he says the steps of the Church are beautiful in her shoes? He signifies the beautiful beauty of the soul, which uses the flesh as a shoe; it suffers no hindrance from it, but excels in the grace of its gait. Therefore, the grace of the ecclesiastical soul clothes itself in flesh so that it may pass through the course and transition of this life with grace. This happens if the shoe is not defiled by bodily mud, nor submerged in the abyss of vices—if one disciplines the flesh so that it is not shaken from its course or weighed down by the heavy weight of fat like an ox. Paschasius Ratbertus <note>A 9th-century Carolingian theologian</note> intends something else in his commentary on Matthew, column 489. The Bride, he says, is praised in the Song of Solomon as beautiful in her shoes, because she is also remembered as flowering like a lily among thorns. Therefore, walking through the desert of this world, she must be shod so that she is not harmed by the bites of serpents or the stings of sin. With a verse no less elegant than it is polished, Barlæus <note>Caspar Barlaeus, a Dutch polymath and poet</note> graphically sketches the loveliness of the most radiant Bride and the harmony of all her limbs <margin>4. Heroic Poems, page 601.</margin> from the Song of Solomon: *

We have provided an anatomy that is not bloody, but bloodless—not consisting of cutting, but of contemplation. We have seen man, we have contemplated his body, and in it the head; in the head the eyes, those twin Suns, which Mother Nature has adorned with many parts: coatings, fluids, nerves, veins, arteries, and muscles; the ears, the brain, and the rest of the limbs. The chest, and in it the heart, the principle of vital actions. The abdomen, and in it the liver, the workshop of the blood. And the limbs, although <term>ἐκ μήκυς μίσυς</term> <note>original Greek: *ek mēkous misos*, meaning "out of a loathing for excessive length"</note> we refrain from reviewing the remaining parts, there are as many miracles meeting our eyes daily as there are limbs, arranged and crafted with such industry and order that there is nothing to add or take away. As Sophocles truly said: *Mother Nature never produced anything as astounding as man.* The members of the human body are held in such high esteem by God

<column-break/>

that He attributes many of them to Himself, so that He might more closely conform Himself to our Sacred Anatomy. God is accustomed <margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> to deal with humans in such a way that He speaks according to human nature, and declares spiritual things through human things accessible to the human intellect, by a merciful dispensation for our salvation. Listen, says Ambrose, <margin>In Psalm 45, page 370.</margin> to certain *members of God, and recognize His virtues.* For His hands are the fullness of His goodness; His face is the illumination of the mind. And Hilary <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers</note> in <margin>In Psalm 129, page 561.</margin> his commentary on Psalm 129, page 561: *It must be understood that God is incorporeal, and does not consist of certain parts or the functions of limbs from which a single body is made. For God is Spirit, an invisible, immense nature, eternal and remaining within Himself. It is also written: "A spirit does not have flesh and bones." For the members of the body consist of these things, which the substance of God does not need. But God, who is both everywhere and in all things, hears entirely, sees entirely, acts entirely, and moves entirely. Therefore, the power of God, which is equal and indivisible, takes the names of functions and limbs: so that the power by which He sees is called "eyes"; the power by which He hears is "ears"; the power by which He acts is "hands"; the power by which He is present is "feet"—the power of this virtue performing the diversity of functions. God is everywhere, and everywhere He is present, hears, sees, and acts.* Nothing is further from all sensible matter than God. Samuel Bohlius <note>A 17th-century theologian known for his controversial literalism</note> indeed published a treatise entitled *On those things which properly belong to God*, where he put forward this new paradox: that the arm, ears, eyes, etc., belong to God properly—indeed, most properly. Several professors from Rostock opposed this opinion at the time, as did Johannes Musæus from among the students at Jena (now the primary Professor of Theology at Jena), and this opinion soon expired with its author. Scripture speaks of God in a human manner, not because He is like that, but because we, who are slower and denser in wit and judgment, understand nothing of God except through the things we are used to, which we see, hear, and touch daily. For He who bore the weakness of all also spoke by tempering Himself to our weakness; so that through <margin>In Psalm 55, page 385.</margin> our sins, in the words of Hilary*, He frequently used both voice and tears. Because the Egyptians used to paint God in hieroglyphics with long nostrils, so God speaks with us in these hieroglyphics, saying in Psalm 145:8: *The Lord is gracious and full of compassion*, <note>original Hebrew: ארך אפים, *erekh appayim*</note> which they translate as "long of nostrils" <note>This is a literal translation of the Hebrew idiom for being "slow to anger" or "patient."</note>. Bartholomæus Westhemerus published a work on the Tropes and Figures of the Old and New Testament, dedicated to King Edward of England, where in that part of the book containing 153 rules, he forms the first rule in this way: <term>Anthropopathôs</term> <note>Greek: "with human feeling/passion"</note>, <margin>page 98.</margin> that is, with human affection, or <term>anthropicos</term> <note>Greek: "in a human way"</note>; God speaks everywhere in Holy Scripture in this way, doing so in many ways, whether from a limb, a sense, or a physical movement, etc. For Divine Scripture is accustomed to form "infantile delights" <note>Simple metaphors suitable for children</note> from things found in creation, by which the affections of the weak might be moved—according to their small capacity—to seek higher things and leave behind lower things; however, those things which are said properly of God, and which are found in no creature, Scripture sets down very rarely.* There is nothing bodily in God, but because of our weakness, certain things are said according to the passible nature of man.

It further discusses the theological concept of anthropomorphism, explaining that while God is a spirit without physical limbs, Scripture uses human terms like "eyes" or "hands" to describe His divine powers in a way humans can understand.</summary>

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES 832

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> Certain things are said about God in Holy Scripture so that our infancy <note>A common theological metaphor for the limited nature of human understanding compared to divine truth.</note> might be able to grasp something of Him. <margin>on Psalm 85, page 428.</margin> *As Erasmus says \*, regarding God, who is the purest and simplest mind, nothing is corporeal, nor of those things that happen to bodies, nor any of those human affections such as anger, mercy, grief, joy, repentance, or hatred; but Scripture, "stammering" <note>original: "balbuciens"</note> in the words of men so that it may be more familiarly understood, accommodates itself to human weakness, just as a nurse or a mother speaking "baby talk" <note>original: "blasè loquitans"</note> with her little infant so that she might even thus be understood. Therefore, God is neither raised up nor lowered in place, but according to the manner of human speech, He "turns away His ear" when He does not grant what we ask, and "inclines His ear" when He favorably hears our prayers; just as He is "angry" when He punishes, and "shows mercy" when He saves and forgives. Just as it is commonly said that those who favor a petitioner listen with "bent ears," while those who do not favor them listen with "upturned and averted ears."* Therefore, human affections, as well as corporeal members attributed to God, always signify things incorporeally—as Abdias Prætorius <note>A 16th-century German theologian and Hebraist</note> says in his little book on Hebrew phrases—and for the most part must be understood according to the nature of their kind. Tertullian also aims at this in his book *On the Trinity*, page 497: *Divine efficacy is shown through limbs; no habit of God, nor corporeal features are set down; for when "eyes" are described, it is expressed that He sees all things; and when an "ear," it is proposed that He hears all; and when a "finger," a certain significance of His will is opened; and when "nostrils," the perception of prayers as if they were odors is shown; and when a "hand," it is proved that He is the author of every creature; and when an "arm," it is declared that no nature can resist His strength; and when "feet," it is explained that He fills all things, nor is there anywhere where God is not. For neither limbs nor the functions of limbs are necessary to Him, at whose sole silent decree all things both serve and are present. For why should He require eyes, who is Light? Or why should He seek feet, who is everywhere? Or why should He desire hands, whose silent will is the craftsman for the establishment of all things? Nor does He need ears, who knows even silent wishes. Or for what reason should He seek a tongue, to whom to have thought is to have commanded?* For these limbs were necessary for men, not for God. And after a few words: *He is all eye, because He sees all; and all ear, because He hears all; and all hand, because He works all; and all foot, because He is all everywhere.* But, to come to particulars: a "face" is attributed to God, and this only through <term>anthropopathia <note>The attribution of human emotions or physical traits to God; from the Greek for "human feeling."</note></term>, to signify His power by which He manifests and is recognized, as Augustine teaches in book 83 and on Psalm 67, column 694: *The "face of God" is the name given to His presence through His Church.* For He is present to His faithful through grace—that is, graciously—which presupposes His substantial presence. Hilary <note>St. Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century bishop and theologian.</note> deals with the gracious face of God: <margin>on Psalm 66, page 425.</margin> *There is a need, he says, for the blessing of God, so that His face may shine upon us, so that the light of His knowledge may radiate upon our dark hearts, so that the Spirit of His majesty may grant light to the senses of our obscure understanding, and we may henceforth be permitted to glory, saying: "The light of your countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us." Moreover, His mercy, which began in us through the remission of sins, bestows this illumination of His face upon us.*

<column-break/>

Every creature yields to the mere sight of the majesty of God and falls down trembling, as Job says in chapter 41:1: *Who can resist my face?*—that is, my power. God has neither countenance nor face; that God is read to have spoken to Moses "face to face" cannot be understood literally, as the absurdity of the sense itself declares. *For God,* says Erasmus \*, *has no face, but it must be taken as a comparison: Moses knew God more clearly than the others.* Indeed, Moses, who had seen God and spoken with Him, asks, saying: *Show me your face*, Exodus 33:18. He received this response from God: *You will not be able to see my face, for no man shall see me and live.* A doubt arises here: what kind of vision is being discussed? Yet it seems to deal only with the vision of the face of that figure in which God then appeared to Moses; for God asserts that when He has passed by in His glory, He will place Moses in a cleft of the rock and place His hand over him until He has passed; but afterward He will remove His hand, and then Moses will see His "back parts," <note>original Hebrew: וראית את-אחרי, transliterated as 'v'raita et achorai'</note> *and you shall see my back.* Therefore, God denies Moses the vision of that figure in which He appeared to him at that time, because surely the brightness of that face of His was so great that a mortal eye could not see or bear it without loss of life. God, however, grants Moses the vision of His "back parts" or the back of that figure in which He appeared, because in that part the splendor was more tempered, so that it could be seen in some way by mortal eyes. Therefore, in Moses' request to see the face and countenance of God, God calls to mind the weakness or feebleness of human sight, which is so great that it cannot see the essence of God without coverings. Whence he received this response: *No one shall see my face and live.* Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose of Milan, a 4th-century Doctor of the Church.</note> explains these words both "morally" and "mystically," as he calls them. *Morally* in these words: *The holy Prophet of the Lord certainly notes that he cannot see the invisible God face to face, but holy devotion exceeds the measure, and he thought even this was possible for God: to make that which is incorporeal capable of being grasped by corporeal eyes. This is not a blameworthy error, but even a grateful and insatiable desire, because he desired to hold his Lord as if by the hand and to see Him with the gaze of his eyes. For he knew that man was made in the image and likeness of God. For when he was chosen by the Lord God to liberate the people, he was filled with the Spirit of wisdom. He had seen that Angel and his face in glory. Finally, he was terrified by his shining light, and he saw the Bush burning and not being consumed. With his sight he caught the glow, which he approached in wonder, provoked by desire and grace, so that he might more diligently consider that glow in the Bush. Therefore, if he received such heat, and underwent such desire when he had seen the Angel in a flame of fire from the bush, so that although seized with fear he did not dare to look, yet he wished to look; how much more did he desire to see the face of the Lord corporally? The effect of the petition was indeed void, but the affection was commendable in a servant who, having progressed in devotion beyond his nature, estimated from the Angels of the Lord how much more he might desire in the face of the Lord, with which he longed to satisfy his desire. Mystically* indeed: *Moses, as a figure of the Law...*

<summary>This page explores the theological concept of "Sacred Anatomy," explaining that physical descriptions of God in the Bible are metaphors (anthropopathia) adapted to human limitations. It specifically analyzes Moses' request to see God's face, concluding that God's true essence is too brilliant for mortal sight and is only revealed through tempered manifestations.</summary>

...took its form: the Law announced Christ through hidden mysteries, yet it did not show him face to face as the Gospel has shown. A voice is attributed to God in the Sacred Scriptures <term>Pandects; a term for the complete body of the Bible</term>, as Isaiah testifies in chapter 1, verse 20, and elsewhere. And a mouth. For "the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things." These words from the "mouth of the Lord" are better suited for our level of understanding. Thus, the Priest speaks from the mouth of God when he speaks against those who live and teach wickedly, from which both the dignity of the teacher and the authority of the speaker are evident. God says to Ezekiel in chapter 33:7:
<margin>4. on the method of preaching, page 911.</margin>
"You shall hear the word from my mouth." <note>original Hebrew: "שמעת מפי דבר"; original Greek: "Ἀκύσῃ ἐκ τῆ στόματός με λόγον"</note> Prosper <note>Prosper of Aquitaine, a 5th-century Christian writer</note> carefully weighed this divine word, instructing Priests—the watchmen <term>speculatores; literally 'scouts' or 'lookouts'</term> of the Most High God—under a faithful exhortation: *He to whom the distribution of the word is committed, even if he lives a holy life, yet either blushes or fears to rebuke those living ruinously, perishes along with all those who died while he remained silent. I would be lying unless the Lord spoke this through Ezekiel the Prophet under the denunciation of a certain terror, saying to him: 'You, son of man, I have given you as a watchman for the house of Israel.' We ought not to hear this in passing, that he calls the Priest a watchman; so that just as it is the watchman's job to look out from a higher place and observe more than everyone else, so the Priest ought to be higher than all in his established sublimity, and possess a grace of greater knowledge, by which he can instruct those living under him. Let us now see what the divine word contains: 'Hearing,' He says, 'the word FROM MY MOUTH, you shall announce it to them.' FROM ME. So that the Priest may say this: what he has learned from me through divine reading; what God has inspired in him, not what he has discovered by the presumption of human sense. 'You shall announce it to them,' He says, 'from me.' FROM ME, you shall speak my words, not from yourself. There is nothing that you should insert into them as if it were your own. 'From me,' He says, 'announce it to them.'* Laughter is performed by the benefit of the mouth. Against those who despise and mock His wisdom, God says in Proverbs chapter 1, verse 26:
<margin>Book on the Contemplative Life, 20, p. 235.</margin>
"I also will laugh at your destruction." <note>original Hebrew: "אגי באדכם אשחק ובתעלעג"; original Greek: "Κἀγὼ τῇ ὑμετέρᾳ ἀπωλείᾳ ἐπιγελάσομαι"</note> He adds: "I will mock when your fear comes." <note>original Hebrew: "בלעג נבא פחדכם"</note> In the third chapter, verse 34: "Surely He mocks the mockers." <note>original Hebrew: "אם ללצים ילץ"</note> Likewise,
<margin>Sermon 8 on Psalm 118, page 649.</margin>
in Psalm 2:4: "He who dwells in the heavens (shall laugh) <note>original Hebrew: "ישחק"</note>, the Lord shall mock them." <note>original Hebrew: "לעג לאדני"; original Greek: "Κύριος ἐκμυκτηριεῖ αὐτοὺς"</note> Mockery and derision are attributed to God metaphorically, like other things regarding the body, so that the severity of divine justice and punishment might be expressed. For though He is so merciful that He is said to be "touched with inward grief of heart" when about to destroy man, He is nevertheless provoked by the crimes of some, so that, His patience being violated, He intends to laugh at and mock those impious people. God does not laugh through "malicious joy" <term>epichairekakia; taking pleasure in the misfortune of others</term>—far be it from anyone to think so—but just as in the human way someone is judged worthy of derision who rushes into evil by his own fault after not following sound advice, so God speaks in a human manner about those who, through malicious disobedience, treat God with contempt and thus bring temporal and eternal punishment upon themselves. Regarding this way of speaking, let us hear Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers, 4th-century theologian</note> on Psalm 2, page 348: *There is no difference between mocking and laughing, for both are performed by the service of the mouth according to the affection of the will. For according to our understanding, the sense of divine

<column-break/>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
things is explained through bodily forms, so that mocking and laughter would be named in the eluding of those who had gathered against the Lord and against His Christ—not because a contraction or drawing back of the mouth would happen to the incorporeal God, but so that we might know, from the custom of our own nature, what the judgment of the divine will is toward the impious.* Hearing and smell are attributed to God; the latter when Abel offers a burnt offering to God from the firstfruits of his crops (Genesis 4:4), and when Noah, after the universal flood, offered burnt offerings to God from all clean cattle and birds, "God smelled a sweet odor" (Genesis 8:20, 21). On both passages, Tertullian writes:
<margin>2 Against Marcion, p. 100.</margin>
*Even if He took notice of Abel's offerings and freely smelled Noah’s burnt offerings, what pleasure is there in the entrails of rams or the smoke of burning victims? Rather, it was the simple and God-fearing mind of those offering the things they had received from God that was credited as a "sweet savor" in God’s grace—not the things being done for the sake of one who needed them, but the reason why they were done: namely, for the honor of God.* There is almost nothing found more frequently in sacred writings than that which is read about God. Hilary says on Psalm 54, page 380: *The ears of God are always ready for the prayers of men, because He who imparted the nature of hearing to the human race cannot Himself be outside the nature of hearing. And He who everywhere works this sense of hearing in us cannot fail to have in Himself that which He provides. Thus God always hears everywhere; but it is not everyone's merit that He should grant what He hears. His hearing is indeed penetrated by the voice of the one praying, but the worthiness of those things being heard is earned only by the innocence of the prayer.* By the benefit of the eye, a man knows what is happening in his presence. But God’s eye is "all-seeing" <note>original Greek: "παντέφορος"</note> and "unsleeping" <note>original Greek: "ἀκοίμητος"</note>, as Isidore <note>Isidore of Pelusium, 5th-century monk</note> says in Epistle 5, 491, page 704. His words placed a little earlier, in Epistle 5, 368, page 670, are worthy of memory: "Great is the sharp-sighted and unsleeping eye of Divine Justice, which not only looks upon things done in the open but also tracks down things dared in secret and grasps the movements of the heart." <note>original Greek: "Μέγα εἰ, ὁ ἐξυδερκὴς, καὶ ἀκοίμητος ὁ τῆς θείας Δίκης ἐστὶν ὀφθαλμὸς, καὶ ὁ μόνον τὰ ἐν φανερῷ δρώμεנה ἐφορᾷ, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ ἐν παραβύστῳ τοלμώμενα ἀνιχνεύει, καὶ τὰ τῆς καρδίας κινήματα καταλαμβάνει"</note> David made a vow to God that he would build a Temple for God, and gathered innumerable riches for its structure, with which Solomon later built a most magnificent temple. He poured out a prayer to God that the eyes of God might be open over that house and that He might hear those praying in that house; and God answered that his prayer had been heard, and He said, "My eyes and my heart shall be there for all days." 
<margin>1 Kings 9:3.</margin>
This is to be understood regarding the eyes of Jehovah's kindness and His gracious gaze, concerning which the Psalmist says in chapter 34:16: "The eyes of Jehovah are upon the righteous." <note>original Hebrew: "עיתי יהוה אל-צדיקים"; original Greek: "ὀφθαλμοὶ Κυρίου ἐπὶ δικαίους"</note> And in chapter 80:4: "Make your face shine and we shall be saved." <note>original Hebrew: "הָאֵר פָּנֶיךָ וְנִוָּשֵׁעָה"</note> Where there is no gracious gaze, there is instead the gaze of His horrible wrath, just as it is said in Psalm 34:17: "The face of Jehovah is against those who do evil, to cut off the memory of them from the earth." <note>original Hebrew: "פְּנֵי יְהוָה בְּעֹשֵׂי רָע"</note> Hence, God's "looking" is twofold: gracious and angry. He is said to have looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 18:21) and upon the camp of the Egyptians (Exodus 14:24). In the same sense, He is said to turn away His eyes. The turning away of the eyes is a mark of contempt; whence also that expression in Latin custom, where "to look away" means not to attend to, or to care for, to reject, to despise...

# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
...to despise. *God turns His eyes away* when help is denied, and prayer is rejected on account of the vices of those praying.

Such was the discourse conceived by the Prophet Isaiah, speaking in the name of God: *I will turn my eyes away from you*, when He threatens that He will not be favorable because of their most wicked deeds. Regarding this "looking away" or turning away of the divine face, Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century bishop and theologian</note> <margin>on Psalm 54, page 580.</margin> writes: *Prayers that are light, conflicting, useless, anxious with the cares of the world, entangled in the desires of bodily things, and barren of the fruits of good works are looked down upon. These prayers, then, are despicable, unworthy of God’s esteem, concerning which He says through the Prophet Isaiah: "When you stretch out your hands to me, I will turn my eyes away from you." And He immediately added the cause for despising the prayer, saying: "Your hands are full of blood." Where the work of iniquity stands forth, there the prayer of the one pleading is despised. But indeed, it is extended to the one who hopes, when the silent faith of the Spirit is restrained by the reverence of conscience.* In contrast, He looked with favor upon Abel *Genesis 4:4*, Noah *Genesis 7:2*, Hagar *Genesis 16:13*, the calamity of His people *Exodus 3:6*, David *1 Samuel 16:18*, David’s humility *Psalm 9:14, chapter 69:17*, and the poor *Psalm 10:8*. Thus, we read throughout the Old Testament that a "heart" with its affections is attributed to God. But let us accept the "knowledge," "repentance," "anger," "indignation," and all the "affections" of God—not as a fault of human speech, but as a sense of the divine majesty—as Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the primary translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> excellently advises in *on Zechariah chapter 8, column 565.* Regarding Abraham’s obedience, which was beyond human strength, it is said that *God knew* <note>Genesis 22:12</note> the fear Abraham had toward Him. Likewise, God is said to *know the way of the righteous* <margin>on Psalm 1, page 345.</margin> *Psalm 1:6.* On these words, Hilary writes: *God "knows," not by the science of ignorance <note>meaning, He doesn't learn something He didn't know before</note>, but by the favor of recognizing; for there is no such change of human passions in God that He either knows or does not know something. Abraham, previously "unknown" for a long time—that is, the seventy-year-old to whom God’s word had already come—when he proved himself faithful to the Lord through the offering of Isaac, was received into divine familiarity by such favor: "Now I know that you fear the Lord your God, and have not spared your beloved son for my sake." He certainly was not ignorant of Abraham’s faith, which He had already credited to him as righteousness when he believed concerning the birth of Isaac; but he who had given a great proof of his devotion by offering his son is now "known," now "proven," and now "worthy" of not being ignored. Thus, God "acknowledges" when Abraham is recognized as faithful and worthy: to be known by a God who, in truth, is ignorant of nothing.* Regarding God in the Sacred Scriptures, it is frequently said that He "remembers" and even "forgets." At that time, says Augustine <margin>on Psalm 87, column 965.</margin>, God is said to "remember" when He acts; and to "forget" when He does not act. For neither does forgetfulness fall upon God, because He is changed in no way; nor does recollection, because He does not forget. When the malice and perversity of the men of the first world had grown beyond measure *Genesis 6:6*, it is read that God "repented," as—to remain silent on other examples—God says of Himself regarding the election of Saul as King, *1 Samuel 15:11: "It repents me that I have established Saul as King."* Hence Isidore <note>Isidore of Pelusium, a 5th-century monk and prolific letter writer</note> writes in *Epistle book 1, 439, page 112* that this indicates <term>οἴκτω καὶ φιλανθρωπίας τοῦ θεοῦ ὑπερβολὴν</term> <note>original Greek: "the excess of God's pity and love for humanity"</note>, a certain singular and incredible mercy and humility of God, since the people drew this upon themselves by obtaining the King they had demanded—a man cruel and bitter, and what was the head of the matter, disobedient to God—from which they were

<column-break/>

affected by heavy inconveniences. Regarding this manner of speaking, Celada <note>Didacus de Celada, a 17th-century Jesuit commentator</note> says: *God is said to "repent" and "grieve"* <term>anthropopathōs</term> <note>original Greek: "after the manner of human feelings"</note>; *otherwise, repentance and grief are far from God. Repentance pertains to the form of a man about to be destroyed, as if by a reversal; but "grief of the heart" clearly looks toward compassion for human destruction, as the whirlpools of the impending flood drew near. Oh, the love of God toward men, expressed by the compassion of a divine heart grieving to its very marrow!* God, through compassion, anticipates the sorrow; He is said to be touched inwardly by grief of heart over the future slaughter of men; *for there was grief where there was love. He loves with the heart, He sympathizes with the heart.* So says he. There are no "affections" in God truly and properly so called, nor divine commotions; but if any such thing is attributed to Him, it is to be understood metaphorically and explained in a manner suitable to God. Hope, desire, joy, love, etc., do not properly fall upon God, much less despair, fear, anger, fury, or hatred; all these in God are not "feelings" or "agitations," but designate either the nature or the effects of God. God, says Ambrose <note>Ambrose, the 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note>, *is not subject to passion so as to be angry, since He is impassible <note>incapable of suffering or being moved by emotion</note>; but because He punishes, He "seems" to be angry. This appears so to us, because we ourselves are accustomed to punish with agitation. Yet, for the most part, even men are found who, when they punish, are not moved, but carry out the punishment and exercise torments with the greatest patience. Why, then, should you wonder at this in God, if you occasionally recognize it in a man?* However, you do not say that love, hatred, anger, fury, etc., are attributed to God only for the sake of grace, nor to note some "accidental agitation" in God—as Conrad Vorstius <note>A controversial Dutch-German remorse theologian accused of Socinianism</note> *Treatise on God, page 489* quite impiously felt—but to demonstrate divine justice. From Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the famous Renaissance humanist</note>, let us note what he aptly writes in *on Psalm 2, page 179, Volume 5:* *Frequently in divine literature, human affections are attributed to God—fury, anger, repentance, joy, grief, mercy—though none of these fall upon the divine nature, which is altogether immutable. But from the change of things that happens to us, the names of affections are attributed to God according to the custom of our scripture; so that He is said to be "angry" as often as we, afflicted by evils, pay the penalties for our crimes; to be "furious" as often as we are more harshly afflicted; to "pity" as often as we enjoy happier circumstances beyond our merit, or as often as we are warned by milder evils to repent; to "repent" when we live in such a way that we seem altogether unworthy of His benefit, and as often as He takes away from us His gifts which we abuse. In us, therefore, are either the causes or the effects of such affections, while God is always tranquil and unmoved.* The same Erasmus writes in *book 3, on the method of preaching, pages 848, 849:* *Why should I mention the Discourses with which the sacred books abound everywhere, especially of the Old Instrument <note>The Old Testament</note>, through which things present in us either according to the body or according to the soul are attributed to God? Such as when He is said to be angry, to rage, to repent, to hate, to forget, to remember, to look upon, to turn away His face, to stretch out His arm, to sit, to rise, to incline His ear, and innumerable others of this kind, which, if you take them simply <note>literally</note>, have a false and impious sense.* A trope <note>a figurative use of a word</note> is not to be summoned if the direct speech has a pious and sound sense and is congruent with other places in Scripture, unless the trope employed serves the simple meaning. For example, when we hear God...

<summary>This page explores "anthropopathisms"—the attribution of human emotions like anger, regret, and memory to God. It argues that these are metaphors for divine justice and action, emphasizing that God remains tranquil and immutable despite the human-like language used in the Bible.</summary>
