<meta>This page continues the exploration of "Sacred Anatomy," moving from the discussion of God’s eyes and heart to other physical metaphors used in the Bible. It focuses on the theological necessity of interpreting these human-like descriptions (anthropomorphisms) as metaphors for divine power and action, specifically focusing on the womb, arms, and hands.</meta>

### from Psalm 139:15

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
When we find God saying, *It repents me that I have made man*, or when we read of *God’s arm, face, ears, and feet*, a literal sense is clearly absurd. Therefore, we must necessarily turn to figurative language, as Scripture plainly declares that God is a Spirit and is not subject to any human emotion, being an unchangeable essence. *I am*, He says, *who I am.* However, that "absurd" literal sense is not truly the meaning of Scripture, if we wish to speak properly, but rather an understanding based on the simple sound of the words. Meanwhile, I am scrupulous about attributing "fury" to God, and I agree with Masius <note>Andreas Masius (1514–1573), a Flemish Catholic Hebraist and diplomat</note>
<margin>on Joshua, chapter 8, page 139.</margin>
who writes that those who translate the Hebrew <note>original: חרון (*charon*), meaning burning anger</note> as "indignation" use the word better; for like many others, I have a religious hesitation to say "fury." To attribute such a disease of the mind to God, even in words, seems like an impious habit. Furthermore, "fury" is not truly implied by that word, which properly signifies a "glowing heat," and is often used not for a stir of bile <note>In ancient medicine, "bile" was thought to cause anger</note>, but for the distress and weariness of the mind. Not only is a heart attributed to God, but also a womb, in which God carries us, about which Ratbertus <note>Paschasius Radbertus, a 9th-century Carolingian theologian</note> writes in his commentary on *Matthew, columns 1250 and 1251*, as does Eucherius, Archbishop of Lyon, in his preface to the *Formulas of Spiritual Intelligence*:
<margin>Psalm 37, verse 509 <note>likely a reference to a specific edition or commentary</note></margin>
> Since in the holy books the eye of the Lord, the womb of the Lord, feet, and even the weapons of the Lord are found written, and since it is far from the Catholic faith of the Churches that God—who is invisible, incomprehensible, and infinite—should be defined by a body, it must be asked how these things are to be explained as figures of speech through the Holy Spirit.

To sketch out for us the immense and supreme power of God, Holy Scripture attributes <term>limbs</term> <note>original: *artus*</note> to God—namely, an arm, hands, and feet. This is what Eucherius of Lyon teaches in these words:
<margin>Questions on the Old Testament, page 23.</margin>
> It is the custom of Scripture to show divine movements and effects through human terms, so that it might be clearly understood by men. Just as when it speaks of God’s "arm," it designates His power and strength; when it speaks of "ears," it is because He hears all things without doubt; with "eyes," because He sees all things without distinction; with a "soul," because He lives eternally; or because all things are given life by Him as their author.

Therefore, God’s great efficacy is indicated by a "finger," a greater efficacy by a "hand," and the greatest by an "arm." Three times the Psalms use the word <term>Arm</term> <note>original: *Brachium*</note> concerning God. First in Psalm 89:10, saying: <note>original Hebrew: זרוע עזך פזרת אויביך</note> *With the arm of your strength you have scattered your enemies.* Then in verse 13: *Yours is an arm with power* <note>original Hebrew: זרוע עם גבורה</note>: *Your hand is robust; your right hand is exalted.* Thirdly:
<margin>verses 20, 21.</margin>
*I have found David my servant. With my holy oil I have anointed him. With him my hand shall be firm; and indeed my arm shall strengthen him.* Isaiah (chapter 52:10) foretells that the arm of the Lord is to be made manifest among all nations, and that all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of God, seeing in the Spirit the future preaching of the Apostles throughout the whole world. In the Hebrew it is <note>original: חשף (*chashaf*)</note>, "He has bared," which the Greek translator correctly renders as <term>ἀποκαλύπτειν</term> <note>apokalyptein: to reveal or uncover</note> to capture the sense, because that <term>γύμνωσις</term> <note>gymnosis: a stripping or baring</note> is nothing other than a "revelation." Tertullian also writes of this in *Against Marcion*, book 3, page 182: *The Lord had revealed His holy one with His arm*, that is, Christ by His power before the nations, so that all nations and the ends of the earth might see the salvation which was from God. So too, Bertharius of Monte Cassino <note>9th-century Abbot of Monte Cassino</note> understands Christ by the name "arm of God" in his *Antivequio*, book 1: *The hands,* he says, *are the power*

<column-break/>

*of God, as are the fingers. Christ is called the Arm of the Lord.* Just as the arm of God denotes power, so does His hand. The "Hand of God," says Augustine,
<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
<margin>on Psalm 75, column 823.</margin>
is the commended power of God. For even of men it is commonly said: "He has this in his hand," meaning he has it in his power to do it when he wishes. Otherwise, the Holy Spirit—that power of the Most High God—is also called the *Hand of God*, because of the power He exerts in men through the Holy Spirit, just as a man completes his works with the help of his hands. For thus it speaks of Elijah in 1 Kings 18:46: *The Hand of Jehovah* <note>original Hebrew: יהוה</note> *was present with Elijah to strengthen his loins; thus he ran before Ahab until he came to Jezreel.* And of Ezekiel in chapter 8:1: *It happened that the hand of the Lord Jehovah fell upon me there.* Nor is it infrequent in Holy Scripture for a "blow" or "plague" to be noted by the name "hand of God." Thus David in 2 Samuel 24:14 calls the pestilence the "hand of the Lord." Whence Ludwig Lavater <note>16th-century Swiss Reformed theologian</note> in his commentary on *Chronicles, folio 77, verso*: *He calls the plague the 'hand,' that is, the work of God, because in a plague God acts by Himself and does not use the labor of men.* Indeed, famine and war are also the "hand of God," but in those, God uses the hands of evil men—usurers, monopolists, and greedy soldiers who raise the prices of things, who trample, plunder, and burn everything. David did not choose the plague in which he would have had less to suffer, but the one that was equal for everyone. If a famine arose, many could have hoped to enrich themselves; in war, many would have placed hope in arms, in their own strength, or in the fortifications of places. But in a plague, help can be hoped for from nowhere else but God. When God brings temporal evils, He is said to "extend His hand" or "touch with His hand." These expressions should be weighed in the book of Job. Satan speaks to the Lord in chapter 1: *Extend your hand a little over him, and touch all that Job possesses.* To "touch" is to afflict. Job himself hints at this in chapter 19:21: *Have pity on me, have pity on me, for the hand of the Lord has touched me.* God extended His hand a little and touched Job; He did not strike or crush him. Thus Job, though afflicted but not conquered, felt this hand of God—heavy indeed on the body, but healthy for the soul. Once his spirit was healed so that his body might be well again, he said: *Take your hand far from me, and let not the dread of you terrify me.* If a man patiently endures the iron of a doctor cutting or cauterizing so that a bodily defect may be removed, why does he refuse to bear the hand of God, who cuts so that the health of the soul may be secured? For the soul is His work or "handiwork," according to that passage in Job: *Your hands have made me and fashioned me all around.* And He does not let His work perish, but places His hand beneath it (*Psalm 39:24*), because He has "engraved them on His hands" (*Isaiah 49:16*). On these words of Isaiah, Theodor Snepf <note>16th-century Lutheran theologian</note> writes:
<margin>page 724.</margin>
> The Holy Spirit did not wish to set forth the Lord's care for His Church in bare words, but used a proverb, saying that He has the outlines of the walls in His hands, either engraved or sketched; for architects are accustomed to make a prototype and sketch of a future building, which they may afterwards imitate. Thus the Lord says that He has the form of His city expressed on His fingers: for what we have in our hands is always before our eyes, and we can never forget it. Thus the Latins, when speaking of something extremely well-known and familiar to us, say they know it as well as their own fingers.

<summary>This page discusses the biblical use of physical metaphors like the "arm" and "hand" of God, explaining that these terms represent divine power and direct action rather than literal body parts. It emphasizes that God’s "touch" can be a form of spiritual healing through physical affliction, much like a surgeon’s tool.</summary>

<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>
<language>Latin</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
Regarding the words of Job and David: *Thy hands have made me*; Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), a Bishop of Milan and one of the four original Doctors of the Church</note> writes: "He used a great opening of commendation by saying he was the work of God, so that the favor of the Author might more easily incline toward the grace of His own work. It is also a great prerogative in human affairs that someone should favor his own works and benefits, and not look for another's merit, but intend the gift of his own grace, lest he should seem to take away what he himself has given. Therefore, even if our substance is from the mud of the body, we are clothed in flesh, and the body is woven with bones and nerves, yet no one would doubt that we are the most precious work of God; for if anyone considers the fabric of the human body itself, he can judge nothing on earth more precious. For man is lofty in stature, handsome in face, and graceful in hair; not bent over toward the belly in the manner of other animals, but sublime by the very law of nature, who looks into heaven with a free gaze, not pressed down to the earth by any slavery of a captive neck, but as if conscious of his own liberty, and a rich witness of his own Author." And Philippus Presbyter <note>Philip the Presbyter (died 455 AD), a student of Jerome known for his commentary on Job</note> on Job chapter 10, page 36: "In the 'hands,' divine operation must be understood, just as the 'fashioning of the hands' can refer to the clay from which man was made; whence also man <note>original: *homo*</note> received his name from the ground <note>original: *humo*</note>, which is clay. The 'making' can truly be referred to the condition of the soul." David says to the Lord in the same words in Psalm 119:73: *Thy hands have made me and fashioned me.* Therefore, Saint Job speaks of the condition of the first man under his own person; and the speech has this meaning: *Since man is a precious and great thing, whom You Yourself deigned to fashion, why then have You broken me—a work ennobled by Your sacred hands—like a most worthless little vessel, in the ruin of this calamity?* Furthermore, "fingers" are attributed to God. For it is read that He made two stone tablets and inscribed the ten commandments on them with His finger. A "finger" is attributed to God <term>ἀνθρωποπαθῶς</term> <note>original: anthropopathōs; meaning "in a human-like way," attributing human emotions or body parts to God</note>, and nothing else is signaled by this formula than that God, through His omnipotence, caused the characters of the letters to appear on the stone tablets, no differently than if God specifically had fingers and had carved those letters on the stone tablets through the intervention of fingers, just as men write through the intervention of fingers. Elsewhere, the Holy Spirit is also accustomed to be called the "finger of God," hence Ambrose:

<margin>on Psalm 43, page 564.</margin>
"The finger of God is the Spirit of God. For God is Spirit, and has nothing corporeal in His substance, but is entirely Spirit." Saint David says in Psalm 8: *Since I will see Your heavens, the works of Your fingers.* That is, the heavens are the works of Your Spirit, just as it is written: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the breath of His mouth.* When the priests of Memphis <note>The Egyptian magicians in the book of Exodus</note> saw that the works of Moses transcended all human and created power, they were forced to confess that *the finger of God was there.* By the "finger of God" in Exodus 8:19, Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian (c. 210–258 AD), Bishop of Carthage</note> understands the Holy Spirit in his *Sermon on the Holy Spirit*, page 436. And regarding those stupendous works of God in Egypt, Hilary <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), a theologian sometimes called the "Hammer of the Arians"</note> thinks thus in his commentary on Psalm 135, page 588: "Moses did many wonders in Egypt, but the magicians and enchanters bear witness because 'the finger of God is in those works,' from which it is shown that the power of God operated through Moses, by whose ministry those things were then being carried out." Those things which are typically performed by the feet and through their ministry are also attributed to God in Holy Scripture. God, wishing to take punishment upon Adam, did so having taken

<column-break/>

the form of a man. Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most significant Latin Church Fathers</note> draws this from the word *walking* <note>original: *adeambulabat*, used in Genesis 3:8</note>, namely in human form and with human steps, as if He were ashamed or it were repugnant to Him to punish in the form of God. By the name of "feet," if they are attributed to God, the Holy Codex understands His presence. Eucherius <note>Eucherius of Lyon (c. 380–449 AD), a bishop and writer on scriptural interpretation</note> says in his *Formulas for Spiritual Understanding*, page 1: "The Feet of the Lord are the stability of eternity; the darkness under His feet and the footsteps of the Lord are the signs of His secret works." And the "steps of the Lord" are the coming or visitation of the Lord. He is said to "come" and "go" throughout Holy Scripture. Out of infinite places, let us cite that of Job, chapter 9:11: *If He comes to me, I will not see Him; if He goes away, I will not understand.* Where Philippus Presbyter says on page 30: "It must not be understood as if an immense substance were enclosed in corporeal places, so that He would be smaller than the things by which He is enclosed, but rather it is said because there is the presence of God 'coming' when He becomes known to man and has mercy; and when He is hidden and leaves for a little while, the absence of Him 'going away' is indicated. Therefore, whether He comes, manifesting Himself, I will not see Him with these corporeal eyes because He is Spirit; or whether He goes away, hiding Himself from me, I will not understand Him with my mind, for He does not offer Himself to my understanding." So too is "transition" or "passing" attributed to God, which—as a <term>διάστασις καὶ πάροδος</term> <note>original: diastasis kai parodos; a Greek term for an "interval and passing by"</note>—indicates a visitation of punishment. Indeed, the Hebrew word *abar* <note>original: עָבַר, meaning to pass over or through</note>, from which by a transposition of letters comes the Greek *perao* <note>original: περάω, to pass through</note> and *peiro* <note>original: πείρω, to pierce or run through</note>, is used with the preposition *be* in Amos 5:17: *I will pass through the midst of you* <note>original: אֶעֱבֹר בְּקִרְבֶּךָ; Greek: ἐλεύσομαι διὰ μέσου σου</note>. This is a phrase taken from a military passage, where the enemy passes through the land with great force, sparing no one who wishes to hinder him. Likewise in Exodus 12:12: *And I will pass through the land of Egypt* <note>original: וְעָבַרְתִּי בְאֶרֶץ־מִצְרַיִם; Greek: καὶ διελεύσομαι ἐν γῇ Αἰγύπτῳ</note>. He also attributes "arising" to the Church in peril, saying in Psalm 7:7: *You, arising, will have mercy on Zion.* In the word "arising" there is an <term>ἀνθρωποπάθεια</term> <note>original: anthropopatheia; "human feeling," a metaphor where God is described as having human reactions</note>, by which God is said to "arise" in a human manner when He puts forth some illustrious testimony of His presence and help, He who for a long time seemed as if to sleep. For just as God is said to "rest" and as if "sleep" when He winks at the injuries of the Church and hides them for a time, so He "arises," as if awakened from sleep, when He asserts His faithful ones with a powerful hand and vindicates them from the tyranny of enemies. Hence Ambrose: "What does it mean," he says, "that God is sometimes said to proceed, or go out, or arise, or descend? For God is not moved corporally, nor does He exit from any place, or pass to another, who is above all things; nor does He truly 'arise' as if He lay in some bed or sat corporally in some seat; but these things are said so that you may understand when and to whom He is said to go out, and whom He is said to arise for." "To descend," therefore, used of God, notes the manifestation of His presence and justice, whether gracious or judicial (Genesis 11:5, 7; 18:21; 48:4; Exodus 3:8). When He wishes to be present as a helper in tribulation and ultimate necessity, then He is said to "descend," so that He may snatch away and be present more promptly with divine help. God, "seeing by seeing" the affliction of the Israelite people, is said to have "descended" in Exodus 3:8 to free them. As if it were too little to "see by seeing" the troubled ones, or to send help from heaven and His seat, the Lord rejoices to descend Himself to bring aid and to enter into the situation Himself. Thus also to exercise His justice, He is very often read to have "descended." To the <term>συγχέοιν</term> <note>original: syncheoin; to confuse or pour together</note>, or the confounding of language, God "descended" (Genesis 11:5, 7). So also to...

<summary>This page explores the metaphorical use of "hands," "fingers," and "feet" in the Bible to describe God’s creative power, the Holy Spirit, and His interventions in human history. It explains that these physical descriptions are "anthropopathies"—human-like language used to help mortals understand the actions of an infinite, formless Spirit.</summary>

While the previous page focused on the "hands" of God in creation, this page discusses God's "descent" to earth and the metaphorical nature of His "eyes, ears, and feet" as seen in the Church Fathers' writings against early heresies.</meta>

<header>from Psalm 139, verse 15.</header>

Genesis 18:21.

To certify and investigate the outcry concerning the perversions of the Sodomites, which had reached even to heaven, God says: *I will go down and see* <note>original: "Descendam & videbo"</note> whether they have fully committed the deeds according to the outcry that has come to me; and if not, I will know. In the history of Sodom, God presents an example to judges of what ought to be done; for although He knows all things before they happen, He is said to "descend" out of His kindness to perceive the outcry of the Sodomites. <margin>on Psalm 143, page 630.</margin> As Isidore <note>Saint Isidore of Pelusium (died c. 449 AD), an abbot and prolific letter writer</note> says in *Epistle 310, page 83*, God is "teaching us the principle of patient inquiry" <note>original Greek: "ἡμᾶς ἀνεξικῶς ἐρεύνης διδάσκων ὑπόθεσιν"</note>. Concerning the descent of God in general, Hilary <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), a Bishop and Doctor of the Church</note> says: *The Lord descends by inclining His heavens, not by a physical movement—as if the heaven itself bends down as He descends—but the spiritual sense is instructed through physical imagery. Thus, when sleep, wakefulness, memory, forgetfulness, departure, and arrival are attributed to God, it is because, according to the difference of our merits, He appears to each of us as either sleeping or waking, forgetting or remembering, absent or present.* In this way, God conforms Himself to our understanding, attributing to Himself a body, limbs, and human actions. This is not because He actually possesses a human body or limbs, or performs His divine works in a human manner, but so that He may accommodate Himself more to us. Under these forms and "wrappings" of the human body's structure, He reveals to us His all-wisdom, all-knowing, all-presence, and all-power. Justin Martyr <note>An early Christian apologist (c. 100–165 AD)</note> reproaches Trypho in his *Dialogue, page 4*, for the fact that the ancient Jews devised a corporeal God, saying: *Just as your teachers wish, imagining that the Father of all things and the unbegotten God has hands, feet, fingers, and a soul like a created and composite living being; for this reason, they even teach that the Father Himself appeared in His own form to Abraham and Jacob.* The Muslims <note>original: "Mahumetani"</note> cover up this same error, likewise attributing a physical essence and soul to God, as Gregory Abul-Faraj <margin>on the origin and customs of the Arabs</margin> of Melitene <note>A 13th-century Syrian scholar and bishop</note> relates and testifies: certain people named the Sifatiyah went so far in asserting God's hearing, sight, and speech that they claimed He possessed a physical body. In the early Church, the Audians arose around 372 AD, following Audius the Syrian; out of monastic stupidity, they taught that God was <margin>Psalm 43, verse 23.</margin> physical and similar to the human form. There were also the Anthropomorphites, according to Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) and advisor to Constantine</note> in *Book 4, chapter 30*. Against these, Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> urges the <margin>Commentary on Psalm 94.</margin> words of Scripture: *He who planted the ear, shall He not hear?* Regarding these words, he notes: "This passage," he says, "works most strongly against those who are Anthropomorphites, who say that God has the same limbs that we have. For example, it is said that God has eyes: 'The eyes of the Lord look upon all things.' 'The hand of God made all things.' And it says, 'Adam heard the sound of the feet of the Lord walking in Paradise.' They hear these things literally and attribute human weaknesses to the magnificence of God. But I say that God is *all eye*: He is *all hand*: He is *all foot*. He is all eye because He sees all; all hand because He works all; all foot because He is everywhere. Therefore, see what he says: 'He who planted the ear, shall He not hear?' He did not say: 'He who planted the ear, therefore He Himself has an ear.' He did not say: 'Therefore He Himself has eyes.' But what did he say? 'He who planted the ear, shall He not hear? and He who

<column-break/>

fashioned the eyes, does He not consider?' He removed the physical members, but granted the functions <note>original: "efficientias," meaning the power to act or the capacity for the sense</note>." Compare Novatian <note>A 3rd-century scholar and priest in Rome</note> in *On the Trinity, chapter 6*; Damascene <note>Saint John of Damascus (c. 675–749 AD)</note> in *Book 1 of The Orthodox Faith, chapter 13 and following*; and Anselm <note>Saint Anselm of Canterbury (c. 1033–1109 AD)</note> in his *book on the explanation of the acts and members of God*. Therefore, to declare His majesty, to help the weakness of our intellect, and to call to our memory the creation of the first man (formed in the image of God), God uses this manner of speaking. He deals with us and speaks to us in a human way to instill His love and mercy toward us, so that, mindful of our daily infirmity and misery, we might long for that original glory from which we fell. The Creator had clothed us in an incorruptible garment; He had dressed us in a skin that does not wither, and surrounded us with a polished hide worthy of all praise. That ancient and infernal serpent stripped this from us, and thus man—that most excellent animal, once immortal and subject to no kind of corruption—suffers punishment for this one fault. Think of it as "unavoidable and indestructible" <note>original Greek: "ἀνεπίδετον & ἀνώλεθρον"</note>; man suffers not because he was born, but because he is brought onto the stage of this world having been conceived and born *IN SIN*. Hence those tears! <note>A classic idiom, "Hinc illae lacrymae," from the playwright Terence, meaning "so that's the reason for all this fuss."</note> Hence that mournful origin! Hence ignorance in the intellect, malice in the will, and perverse longing in the appetite! Hence the pains of the body, diseases, and death—most certain, though its timing is uncertain! Man holds nothing dearer than himself, that is, his own life. Of all the things he possesses, even those he uses of necessity at home, he would easily bear the loss of any one of them, provided he might keep his life. Job understood this when he said in *chapter 2, verse 4*: *Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his soul.* Nothing is usually dearer to us than life; and although there is nothing stable in it—so that it ought rather to be considered as nothing—yet we all shrink from dying. Regarding the most miserable outcome of life, there are sayings of writers everywhere you turn, so many that great volumes could be forged from them. We ourselves feel it daily through various experiences, yet we prefer, if it were possible, to be counted among the perpetual survivors rather than among the shades and the dead. For Job, there was not even a moment of rest from the various blows of fortune, which even stunned his friends; yet, as one may marvel, amidst the bitterest pains, he did not wish to turn away from the light of life. In theory, you may find men professing with a full mouth—with Plato—that philosophy is the "meditation on death"; but when it comes to practice, philosophy is rather the "shunning of death." Just as his own health and life are most commended to each man, so for the sake of preserving it, he spares no expense, even if the costs of thirty years must be spent on a single medicine. From this, the Medical art was rendered most profitable, which the sick look up to with stupendous veneration—indeed, even with contempt for all other things. How they would surrender their life and pour out their soul! They would sooner give the world itself to a Physician, if they were the owners of the whole thing. *What,* says Ludovicus Vives <note>Juan Luis Vives (1493–1540), a Spanish scholar and humanist</note> in *On the Corruption of the Arts, page 187*, *would a man not lavish upon his liberator? Is anyone truly so insane that he would spare his money in a life-threatening danger? For what time does he reserve the use of his coins if he is about to perish immediately? Skin for skin, as Job says, and all that a man possesses, he will give for his soul.* Witty was Philip, the father of Alexander...

<page-num>838</page-num>
<header>BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES</header>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> A father, while suffering from a dislocated collarbone <note>The Latin word for collarbone is *clavicula*, which is a diminutive of *clavis*, meaning "key."</note>, was repeatedly asked for money by his doctor. He finally said, "Take everything you want now, since you already have the KEY." It is clear from the sacred writings that David—to say nothing of other saints—very often used to describe the heavy sorrows of his soul resulting from his sins by exaggerating the pains of those passions which are usually endured in the body due to disease. An example of this is found in Psalm 38, where, recognizing his sins—for which he deserved both the wrath of God and punishment—he speaks at one moment like a man who is cachectic <note>term: cachectic - suffering from "cachexia," a physical wasting away and loss of weight often associated with chronic illness</note> or hectic <note>term: hectic - a reference to "hectic fever," a recurring fever common in consumption or tuberculosis</note> in verse 3: *There is no health in my flesh because of your wrath; there is no peace in my bones because of my sin.* And in verse 5: *My scars have rotted and become corrupt; my loins (v. 7) are wasted, and there is no health in my flesh.* At another moment, he cries out like one who is lipothymic <note>term: lipothymic - prone to fainting or sudden loss of strength</note> in verse 8: *My heart throbs, my strength has failed me, and the light of my eyes has also left me.* This is nearly the same as what Tertullian <note>Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155–220 AD), an early Christian author from Carthage</note> writes concerning the functions of the members of the body <margin>on the Resurrection of the Flesh, p. 63.</margin> which no longer perform their duties:

> Why this cavern of the mouth, and the station of the teeth,
> And the slide of the throat, and the crossroads of the stomach,
> And the abyss of the belly, and the tangled length 
> Of the intestines, where there will be no place for food and drink?
> Why do such members admit, subdue,
> Roll down, divide, digest, and expel?
<note>original: "Quo spelunca hæc oris, & dentium statio... Quid hujusmodi membra admittunt, subigunt, Devolvunt, dividunt, digerunt, egerunt?"</note>

In the life after this life, there is no use for these things, as Scripture testifies; but in this life, when each member does not perform its duty, the state of that man is most miserable. He attributes *expelling* to the intestines (where a door is given), *digesting* to the principal organs of the belly, *dividing* to the stomach; and he calls the stomach a *crossroads* <note>original: "compitum"</note> because everything that is sent through the mouth (to which he attributes the *admitting* of things) meets there as if at a fork in the road or a well-trodden path. Josephus Albo <note>A Jewish philosopher (c. 1380–1444) known for his work *Sefer ha-Ikkarim* (Book of Principles)</note> in *Ikkarim* book 3, chapter 35, folio 194, divides human life into three "fathers"—namely, the years of ascension, station, and descent. While a man is in the "ascension," he acts as an infant who can only express his desires through tears, nourished mostly by his mother's milk and other foods suitable for that age. From the step of infancy, he ascends to boyhood, then to be instructed in piety, manners, and letters, which befit this age and do not exceed his strength. ☙ Having been made ready, he is either consecrated to the study of the Muses or ordained to another way of life; and thus, the years of ascension having ended, he enters the years of "station." In these years, his cares do not decrease, but grow and are increased daily. For in this state of life, there is no rest for the soul, no tranquility for the whole; indeed, even the time that nature otherwise granted for rest is not permitted to be qui-

<column-break/>

-et, inasmuch as dreams terrify, visions disturb, or business hinders him. Concerning the diverse pursuits of men who have progressed before the years of station, and their various anxieties, Innocent <note>Likely Pope Innocent III (1161–1216), who wrote "On the Misery of the Human Condition"</note> discourses thus: *Mortals run and wander through hedges and paths, they climb mountains, cross hills, fly over rocks, speed across the Alps, step over pits, enter caves; they probe the bowels of the earth, the depths of the sea, the uncertainties of the river, the shadows of the grove, the pathless places of the wilderness. They expose themselves to winds and rains, to thunder and lightning, to floods and storms, to ruins and precipices. They mine and smelt metals, carve and polish stones, cut down and hew timber, set up looms and weave, cut and sew garments; they build houses, plant gardens, cultivate fields, dig vineyards, light ovens, construct mills, fish, hunt, and bird-watch. They meditate and think, consult and arrange, complain and litigate, snatch and steal, deceive and trade, contend and battle, and do innumerable such things to amass wealth, to multiply gain, to seek profit, to acquire honors, to exalt their dignities, to extend their power—and this* too is labor and affliction of the mind. But when the years of station are led to their end, the mind begins to grow dull, the hands to tremble, the eyes to grow dim, the tongue to stammer, the foot to falter, and a great terror occupies all the joints. Then the lips tremble, the forehead is plowed with wrinkles, and the cold blood stands around the heart; and then it happens to the body, as it tires after sixty years, what usually happens to old buildings: while they are being repaired in one part, another part threatens a fall and ruin. It happens to us then what Valerius Cato <note>A Roman poet and grammarian of the 1st century BC</note> says in *Dirae*, verse 125:

> Alas for me, my dying limbs waste away with pain,
> And heat departs as the chill of death is poured in.
<note>original: "Heu mihi tabescunt morientia membra dolore, Et calor infuso decedit frigore mortis."</note>

And Columbanus <note>Saint Columbanus (543–615 AD), an Irish missionary and poet</note> in his poem to Hunald against avarice:

> Many troubles of the fragile flesh vex the old man,
> For his languid limbs waste away with foul thinness;
> Then the joint of the knees stiffens, and through all his veins
> The blood grows cold in his whole body.
> Thus, leaning on a staff, he supports his lifeless limbs.
> Why should I mention the sad groans, which the weariness of the mind [produces]!
> Sleep is absent from his eyes; every sound rouses him.

But how many are there, who do not even once [reach] the years...

<page-num>839</page-num>
<header>From Psalm 139, verse 15</header>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
...they [most people] barely surpass the first step of the ascent [of life]; indeed, I might say that not even a hundredth part of humanity has tasted the "delights"—or rather, the burdens—of the stable and declining years, and this is due to the brevity of life. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 342–420 AD), a Church Father known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> says: <margin>Epistle 21, column 167, Volume 1</margin> <margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin> *At the very beginning of human life, death follows the one being born, testifying that the passing ages daily fall into decay.* <note>original: "Humana vitæ exordio, mors fecuta nafcentem, labentia quotidie in vitium fecula profitetur."</note> David discourses on the brevity of his own life in *Psalm 101, verse 24*, and among other things says: *Tell me the fewness of my days; do not call me away in the midst of my days.* So too Job speaks on the brevity of years in *chapter 16, verse 22: Behold, short years have passed, and I walk the path from which I shall not return.* And in *chapter 9, verses 25 and 26* of the same book: *My days have passed swifter than a runner; they have passed away like ships carrying fruit, and like an eagle flying to its prey.* Likewise, in verse 6 of the same chapter: *My days have passed swifter than a weaver’s web is cut, and they are consumed without any hope.* Whence Peter <note>Likely Petrus Riga (c. 1140–1209), author of the *Aurora*, a versified Bible.</note> writes in the *Aurora*:

> My life is cut faster than a weaver’s thread,
> Remember that your life is like the wind;
> Which flees without delay, and passes in a single hour.

See how short and small, how unstable and fleeting this present life of ours is; for as it is written in *Sirach 18, verse 8: The number of a man’s days is at most a hundred years.* But that number has become smaller as time has progressed, for it is said in *Psalm 90, verse 10: The days of our years are seventy years; and if through strength they be eighty years, yet is their pride but labor and sorrow.* But what is this span of eighty or even a hundred years to be considered? It should be called a moment of eternity rather than a length of time, since even *a thousand years before the eyes of the Lord are as yesterday when it is past, and pass quickly like a shadow.* Truly, truly, this life of ours is like a shadow because of its slipperiness and brevity. But what does it profit to reach many years and then finally die? On this, Sedulius <note>Coelius Sedulius (5th century AD), a Christian poet.</note> writes in book 2 of his *Paschal Works*, verse 9:

> Alas, there were once two who were eternal; but after they began 
> To increase, their origin perished, and took its ruin from the seed.
> What did many days profit, or what did it help in that time
> To happily see more than nine hundred years,
> And to wait for the tenth generation of grandsons, 
> Already not knowing one's own kin? Since, conquered by the final

<column-break/>

> Course, the irreparable fate of the ultimate hour—
> though it might come late—and life through a long age
> <margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
> being brief, would teach that nothing is long that has an end;
> Nor would hope bring returning aid, and the grave 
> of the first earth-born man would swallow his grandsons with its blind maw.

The present time, as Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC–65 AD), a Stoic philosopher.</note> writes in <margin>On the Brevity of Life, 10</margin> is extremely short, so much so that to some it seems to be nothing: for it is always in motion. It flows and rushes headlong: it ceases to be before it arrives; nor does it suffer delay any more than the world or the stars, whose restless agitation never remains in the same footprint. Life’s very vitality is confined within such narrow limits—as Pliny <note>Pliny the Younger (c. 61–113 AD), a Roman lawyer and author.</note> testifies in <margin>Book 3, Epistle 7</margin>—that those royal tears seem worthy not only of forgiveness, but even of praise. For they say that Xerxes <note>King Xerxes I of Persia (ruled 486–465 BC).</note>, when he had looked upon his immense army, wept because so brief a setting threatened so many thousands, and within a hundred years not one of such a great youth would be left alive. But, as Seneca well puts it again, *he who was weeping was himself about to bring fate upon them, and was destined to lose some on land, others at sea, others in battle, and others in flight,* <margin>On the Brevity of Life, 16</margin> and within a short time he would consume those for whom he feared their hundredth year. Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher.</note> also looked to this when he sang: <margin>Book 3</margin> <note>The OCR says "lib 4", but this quote is from Book 3 of *De Rerum Natura*.</note>

> Even he himself, who once paved a way through the great sea,
> and gave a path for his legions to go through the deep,
> and taught them to overcome the salt pools on foot,
> and, tramping upon them with horses, despised the murmurs of the sea:
> his light being taken away, he poured out his soul from his dying body.

How truly Seneca <margin>Epistle 70</margin> says: *We sail past life;* and just as Virgil <note>Publius Vergilius Maro (70–19 BC), the Roman epic poet.</note> says in <margin>Book 3 of the Aeneid</margin>:

> —lands and cities recede,

so also: *—life hastens with a swift course.* <margin>Seneca, Hercules Furens</margin> <margin>Cited Epistle</margin> And, as Seneca writes again, in this course of most rapid time, first we unlearn childhood, then adolescence, then whatever that middle stage is between youth and old age, placed on the border of both, then the first years of old age itself; finally, the public end of the human race begins to be shown. For as Juvenal <note>Decimus Iunius Iuvenalis (1st/2nd century AD), a Roman satirist.</note> sings in <margin>Satire 9</margin> <note>The OCR says "Satyr. 3", but this is likely from Satire 9.</note>:

> The swift little flower of our narrow and wretched
> life hastens to run its course;
> while we drink, while we call for garlands, perfumes, and girls...

<page-num>840</page-num>
# BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES from Psalm 139:15.
<language>Latin</language>

<margin>Sacred Anatomy</margin>
*We feed ourselves, while unperceived old age creeps up.*

If you were to carefully examine all our joys, all our pleasures, and whatever from this entire world either entices our sight or charms us in its use, the whole life of man is but a single day. Hence Simonides <note>Simonides of Ceos (c. 556–468 BC) was a Greek lyric poet famous for his epitaphs and reflections on the human condition.</note> says:

> For us, the time of being dead is long;
> but we live for a numbered few,
> and all our years are ill.
> <note>original Greek: "Πολλὸς γ’ ἡμῖν τὸ τεθνάναι χρόνῳ / ζῶμῳ δ’ ἀριθμῷ / Πάντα κακῶς ἔτεα."</note>

Therefore, the greater part of humanity complains about the "malice of nature"—that we are born for such a meager span of life, and that these spaces of time granted to us run their course so swiftly and rapidly. Even the greatest of physicians, <margin>1 Aphorism 1.</margin> Hippocrates, made this exclamation: *Life is short, but art is long.* Considering these things, <margin>Tusculan Disputations, Book 3, Chapter 2.</margin> Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle.</note>—as Cicero writes of him—complained against nature even as he was dying, because she had given a long life to stags and crows (for whom it was of no importance), but had given such a brief life to humans (for whom it mattered most). Pedo Albinovanus <note>A Roman poet and friend of Ovid.</note> lamented this same point, singing thus:

> *Crows are said to live for many a year:*
> *Why are we held in such narrow conditions?*

But Death is not so much a condition of nature as it is a punishment for sin, as <margin>On Predestination and Grace, 3.</margin> Augustine warns. The poets ascribe this to the act of Prometheus <note>In Greek mythology, Prometheus stole fire from the gods, leading to various punishments for humanity.</note> under the <margin>Odes, Book 1, Ode 3.</margin> veil of fables; to which that passage of Horace pertains:

> *After fire was stolen from the heavenly home,*
> *wasting sickness and a new troop of fevers*
> *settled upon the earth;*
> *and the slow necessity of death, previously far off,*
> *quickened its pace.*

Death was given to the sinner as a punishment, and derived its name (*mors*), as <margin>Book 11, chapter 1, page 357.</margin> Caesarius of Heisterbach <note>A 13th-century Cistercian monk and author.</note> says, from the "bite" (*morsu*). For when the First-Created ones [Adam and Eve] were not obedient to the decisive voice and law of the Supreme Commander regarding the forbidden fruit of a single tree, it happened that they were cast down from a state most happy in soul and body into a secondary and utterly miserable state. In this state, they are not only subject and bound to many calamities and infirmities, but also to the necessity of undergoing death. Because of their disobedience, we have received shackles, so that the whole course of human actions is hindered by the bonds of mortality, as Prosper <note>Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, a 5th-century Christian writer.</note> says. Whoever, therefore, is born in the common manner and through natural propagation from Adam the law-breaker, is bound by the law of nature and destined to pay the tribute of mortals. No man dares to hope for immunity from this, nor ask for a privilege; nature herself grants no favor to anyone from her necessity, but when the years and days of their sojourn are completed, she follows her own

<column-break/>

law, and demands what is owed simultaneously from the highest and the lowest. For they enjoy the same right, and are not distinguished by titles, lineage, or royal purple, though their lifespan may differ. *For some it leaves at the very entrance of life, others it deserts when they are already exhausted by the course of life in extreme old age,* in the words of Seneca. Pale Death seizes some in their homeland, and there it knocks at the towers of kings as well as the huts of the poor with an equal foot; but others it calls in a foreign land, so that they may "go to the many" <note>A classical euphemism for joining the much larger population of the dead.</note>. Then in vain did the sick Tibullus <note>Albius Tibullus, a Roman elegiac poet.</note>, or whoever it was, burst into these words:

> *Phæacia holds me sick in unknown lands,*
> *I pray, black death, hold back your greedy hands.*
> *Hold back, black death, I pray; no mother's here*
> *To gather my burned bones with many a tear*
> *To her sad breast; no sister to bestow*
> *Assyrian scents, and let her loose hair flow*
> *Before my tomb, etc.*

And this happens according to the inscrutable providence of the Eternal Divinity, whose counsels it is proper not to scrutinize or curiously investigate, but rather to venerate silently. Since things are so, let us meditate on death daily, and prepare ourselves for departure at any hour, at any moment. Let us follow God without murmuring when He commands us to change our station, following the example of Cleanthes <note>A Stoic philosopher whose prayer was famously translated by Seneca.</note> in Seneca, who said: <margin>Epistle 1.</margin>

> *Lead me, Father, ruler of the high heavens,*
> *Wherever you please, there is no delay in obeying.*

Thus one ought always to live, says Innocent III <note>Pope Innocent III (1160–1216); this quote is from his influential ascetic work on the misery of human life.</note> in his book *On the Contempt of the World*, chapter 24, page 429, *as if one must always be dying; for it is written: Remember, for death does not delay. Time passes, and death approaches. Future things are always being born, present things are always dying, and whatever is past is entirely dead. We die while we live, always, and then only do we cease dying when we cease living.*

# TO THE BIBLICAL ANTIQUITIES
# OF JOHANNES CONRADUS DIETERICUS,
# A MOST ACCURATE INDEX
### OF SUBJECTS AND WORDS.

<column-break/>

**A.**
*Aaron is joined to Moses in the embassy to Pharaoh, page 169. The high priesthood is conferred by God upon him and his descendants, 192. His rod blossoms, 532. The story of the Rabbis concerning it, 534. It was not the same as the rod of Moses, 534.*
*Abarim, the mountains of, 302.*
*Obadiah, his name derived from service <note>The Hebrew name Obadiah (Ovadyah) means "Servant of Yahweh."</note>, 244.*
*Abel, a type <note>A biblical "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic precursor to something in the New Testament.</note> of the pious, 220.*
*Absalom, his reason for rebelling against his parent, 192. He hunts for the favor of the people, 353. He is compared with Saul, 354. His court and courtiers, 357. His physical stature, 358 and following. He perishes miserably, 359.*
*Abraham, according to a Jewish legend, was cast into fire for refusing to worship the Sun, 24. He possessed two names <note>Abram and Abraham.</note>, 233. He gave an unheard-of example of obedience, 334.*
*The Hawk, a predatory and unclean bird, 476. In different respects, an image of both the pious and the impious, 477. Fit for catching other birds, 477. A symbol of the wind and worshipped with divine honor among the Egyptians, 477. They are of three kinds, 490.*
*Acclamations of vows, also used in ancient times, 134.*
*Agate and Amethyst, in the breastplate of the High Priest, 197.*
*Ahithophel conspires with Absalom, 356. Hushai subverts his counsel, 357. Various opinions on his death, 358.*
*Adam, the first man created from the earth, 65. The inhabitants of the island of Ceylon <note>modern-day Sri Lanka</note> boast of his origin there, 66. He was not <term>androgynous</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνδρόγυνος; meaning having both male and female characteristics</note>, nor was he <term>fish-shaped</term> <note>original Greek: ἰχθύτυπος; a reference to obscure theories about Adam's original form</note>, 67. He could have easily obeyed the first command of God, 82. For the sake of his wife, he transgressed the command of God, 83. He shifts the cause of the transgression onto his wife, 91. His punishment, 92. He was the first to offer a sacrifice to God, at God's command, 206, 207. The origin of the word "Adam," 227. He gave names to all the beasts, 416. He was the master of all animals, 417. He fell from this dominion because of his lapse, ibid. His tomb is shown on the island of Ceylon, 469. He was not a giant, 745. His history reached the Gentiles but was corrupted, 746. We have lost the accurate <term>knowledge</term> <note>original Greek: γνῶσιν</note> of living creatures that Adam possessed.*
*The Diamond, a stone of great hardness, 676.*
*Adarcon, a type of currency among the Hebrews <note>likely the gold Daric</note>, 727.*
*Adonis, who he was, 651. His sacred rites, 650. The same as Tammuz, 651.*
*The object of true adoration is God alone, 256.*
*Adramelech, the same as Moloch, 552. Explained as a "lesser god" or false deity, 261.*

<column-break/>

*The vessels of the Egyptians, not explained literally by the Fathers of the Church, prolegomena 7, 32. They were the first inventors of idolatry among all nations, 22, 584. They detested the Hebrews as shepherds of flocks, 23. They preserved the bodies of the dead, 23. They abstained from eating animals, 23. Those living near the Red Sea learned mathematical arts from Joseph, 57. They were most devoted to magic, 127, from which superstition spread into all other parts of the earth, 127. Their language was distinct from Hebrew, 134. They loathed the Hebrews excessively; the cause of this loathing, 136. They worshipped living creatures as gods with abominable rites, 137, 138. The most superstitious of all people, 138. They were greatly occupied with the funerals of the dead, 144. They preserved corpses with spices, 145 and following. The bodies of the deceased were given as collateral for loans, 151. They mourn Jacob for 70 days, 155. Who the "New King" was, 160. He felt the ten plagues, 167. They are suffocated in the Red Sea, 179. The history of this drowning reached the Gentiles, ibid. The first authors of idolatry, 274. They abounded in horses, 325. Their founder was Mizraim, 581. Devoted to superstitious astronomy, 585. They were heard to be the wisest of all, 590. Rain is very rare in Egypt, 596. The granary of the Romans, 597. They abounded in cavalry, 667.*
*Bronze <note>or Copper</note>, known to those before the Flood, 760.*
*The Golden Age, described by the Heathen poets, 78.*
*The region of Ethiopia, an overseas land in respect to Judea, 579.*
*Agesilaus, refused to have a statue erected to himself, 718.*
*The Lamb or Ewe, a species of currency among the Hebrews <note>referring to the 'Kesitah,' often associated with the value of a lamb</note>, 727.*
*In Cairo <note>original: Alcairi</note> in Egypt, a great shortage of water, 319.*
*The Elk, an animal known among the northern peoples, 420. It is not the same as the Reindeer, ibid. It can survive in Germany, ibid. Aristotle and Pliny were ignorant of it, 421. It does not correspond with the Hebrew word 'Zemer' <note>referring to an unidentified animal in Deuteronomy 14:5</note>, 421.*
*The Quran, published in Venice, 25.*
*<term>Anointers</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀλείπται; those who anointed athletes with oil</note> among the ancients, 341.*
*The corpse of Alexander the Great, preserved from corruption for a long time, 153. The founder of the Greek Monarchy, 695. He perished from drunkenness, 695.*
*An excessive zeal for allegories in the Church Fathers is rebuked, 76. However, allegories are not to be entirely discarded, 76.*
*The use of Altars in the true and false Church, 208, 209.*
*Amethyst, in the breastplate of the High Priest, 197.*
*The use of Amomum <note>a fragrant spice plant</note> in preparing funerals, 149.*
*Conjugal love, the most excellent of all, 512. It is natural, 513.*

**Palmistry** relies on false and doubtful principles. 413.
**Rock Badger** <note>original: "Charogryllus"</note> is said to nest among the rocks. 442.
